## Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library

... of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have appeared during the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared carefully with one another and with certain manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continually illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume and each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and also by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any theme may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which the reader may readily discover which Fathers have commented on the several books of Scripture, and in what places of their works they have done so.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others if the following features are properly weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the corrections, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the highly convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and above all this collection—unified, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time gathered in our library from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In this series appear the Fathers, Doctors, and writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the Complete Courses in the several branches of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions: one Latin, the other Greek-Latin.

The Latin edition is sold in 1,200 volumes for 1,000 francs; the Greek-Latin edition in 1,300 volumes for 1,800 francs.

The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; but the Eastern authors are presented in it only in Latin translation.

## Walafrid Strabo, Monk of Fulda

### First Part of the Works—Theological

#### Ordinary Gloss

In the year of the Lord 849. Walafrid Strabo, monk of Fulda.

[Col. 0009]

# Historical Notice Concerning Walafrid Strabo

*(Fabricius, Bibliotheca medii et infimi Latini.)*

[Col. 0009A] Walafrid Strabo, or Strabo, so called from a defect of the eyes. Scholars dispute about his homeland. Balaeus, *Century* XIII, 9, and Pitseus, chapter 112, make him an Anglo-Saxon, either a brother or a kinsman of the Venerable Bede, and consequently the full brother of Haymo. They add that he was first a monk at London and afterward at Fulda, and that he also had Alcuin as his teacher. But neither the facts themselves nor the chronology agree. For if Walafrid died in the year 750, he could not have been educated in the monastery of Fulda. Sigebert of Gembloux therefore makes him German, together with Trithemius and others; for he was Swabian [Note: [Col. 0009C] Thus Walafrid himself says in the preface to Book I of *The Life of Saint Gall*: “I found that the land in which we Alamanni, or Swabians, dwell is very often called Altimania.”], although his native place still cannot be identified.

He was first educated in the monastery of Saint Gall, as Ermenric, a monk of Reichenau, teaches in his book *On Grammar*, which is presented in Mabillon’s *Analecta*, p. 421. There the author addresses Grimold as follows, after previously speaking of other distinguished men educated in that monastery:

“Lord Walhafred, well known to you, whom you yourself, as a skilled teacher, nurtured as a skilled sophist.”

Indeed, he himself, as Goldast testifies, [Note: [Col. 0009C] See the *Prolegomena on the Authors* in volume I, part II, of the *Alemannic Writers*. Jodocus Metzler discusses this more fully [Col. 0010C] in *On the Illustrious Men of Saint Gall*, II, 68, although Johann Egon attacks the same view with no less effort in *On the Illustrious Men of Reichenau*, II, 13.] writes somewhere that he attended school in the monastery of Saint Gall, although I have not yet been able to investigate the passage.

From there he came to the monastery of Fulda and had Rabanus Maurus as his teacher. He was first dean of the monastery of Saint Gall and afterward, in 842, abbot of Reichenau in the diocese of Constance. He died in 849, and indeed in Gaul, where he had been sent to settle some affair. Trithemius reports that he was head of the schools in the monastery of Hersfeld. Add Bulaeus, *History of the University of Paris*, vol. I, pp. 446–447.

The following works survive from his writings:

1. *On Divine Offices*, or *On the Origins and Developments of Ecclesiastical Institutions*. Pitseus wrongly makes two books out of this work. It exists in the collection of Johann Cochlaeus entitled *Mirror of Ancient Devotion Concerning the Mass*, no. 2; in Melchior Hittorp’s collection *On the Divine Offices and Ministries of the Catholic Church*, no. 7; and also in the Libraries of the Fathers.

2. *Two Books on the Life of Saint Gall the Confessor*. They are found in Surius under October 16; in Goldast’s *Writers on Alemannic Affairs*, vol. I, part II, p. 142; and in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century II*, p. 227.

3. *On the Life of Saint Othmar, Abbot*: in Surius under November 16; in Goldast, p. 177; and in Mabillon, *Benedictine Century III*, part II, p. 153.

4. *Life of Saint Blaitmaic, Abbot of Iona and Martyr*: in Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. VI, new edition, vol. II, part II, p. 201; in the *Acts of the Saints*, vol. II for January, p. 236; in the *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, vol. XV, p. 210; [Col. 0010A] in the *Acts of the Saints of the Benedictine Order*, at the cited place, p. 439; and in John Colgan’s *Acts of the Saints of Ireland*, vol. I, p. 128.

5. *Life of Saint Mamma, or Mammas, the Monk*: Canisius, p. 184; *Library of the Fathers*, p. 205.

6. *Life of Saint Leodegarius*: Canisius, p. 210.

7. *On the Visions of Saint Wettin*: Canisius, p. 204; *Greatest Library of the Fathers*, p. 212; Mabillon, *Benedictine Century IV*, part I, p. 272.

8. *The Little Garden*, which Johann Atrocianus published under the name of Strabo of Saint Gall. It may perhaps have been written as *The Little Garden of Strabo, Dean of Saint Gall*, which they did not understand correctly. It was first published at Nuremberg by Johann Weyssenburger in 1512, in quarto. Johann Atrocianus afterward issued it at the end of Aemilius Macer’s *On the Powers of Herbs*, Freiburg im Breisgau, 1530, in octavo. It was also published with Helius Eobanus Hessus’s *On Preserving Health*, Frankfurt, 1564–1571, in octavo; at Venice by Aldus in 1547, with the ancient medical writers, p. 247; and at Basel in 1627, in octavo. It was subsequently included in the Cologne and Lyons *Libraries of the Fathers*, and by Canisius, vol. VI, p. 672. It exists in Andreas Rivinus’s *Collection of the Ancients on Herbal Matters*, Leipzig, 1655, in octavo. Canisius was the first to publish the dedication to Abbot Grimold. Barthius corrected and elucidated some passages of it in *Adversaria* IV, 24, and he also pointed out that the dedication ought to be restored to its proper place. Bartholinus laments that he lost a manuscript written in Walafrid’s own hand in the burning of his library, pp. 89–90. To add this incidentally, this Strabo is cited by Macer *On the Powers of Herbs*, chapters 25, 19, and 25; from this one may perhaps form a conjecture about his date. Bulaeus notes that our Walafrid wrote a poem, which he called *The Little Garden of Children*, to Grimold, abbot of Saint Gall.

9. *Sermon, or Treatise, on the Destruction of Jerusalem*: Canisius, vol. VI, p. 331; new edition, p. 275.

10. *Various Poems*: in Canisius, p. 537; in the *Libraries of the Fathers*; Baluze, *Miscellanies* IV, p. 551.

11. They also say that he was the author of the so-called Ordinary Gloss on Sacred Scripture, or rather that he took it down from the mouth of Rabanus Maurus. Its editions are listed in the *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 62.

12. *Commentary on the New Testament*, published by Marcianus in volume V of Jerome’s works, p. 847.

13. He prefixed a preface to Theganus’s *Deeds of Louis the Pious* and divided that work into chapters.

14. *Latin-Barbarian Glosses on the Parts of the Human Body*, again copied by Walafrid from the teaching of Rabanus Maurus: they exist in Goldast’s *Alemannic Writings*, vol. II, part I, p. 64.

15. *Pictures of the Histories of the New Testament*: found in Goldast’s *Biblical Manual*, Frankfurt, 1620, p. 85.

16. *Homily on the Beginning of Matthew’s Gospel, on the Genealogy [Col. 0011A] of Christ*: published by Bernard Pez in *Newest Treasury of Anecdotes*, vol. II, part I, p. 39.

17. *Exposition of the First Twenty Psalms*: found in the same work, vol. IV, part I, p. 471.

18. *Epitome of Rabanus Maurus’s Commentaries on Leviticus*: found in volume II of Rabanus’s works, p. 296.

19. French authors attribute to our Walafrid the beginning of the *Fulda Annals*, in the *Literary History of France*. See also the *Mémoires de Trévoux*, January 1742, p. 97.

His unpublished works are: a *Book on the Life of Saint Gall* in verse (*sermone ligato*), which is said still to survive in the monastery of Saint Gall; a *Book of Homilies*; letters to various persons; a heroic poem on the miracles of the Blessed Virgin; and other works reported by Metzler. A chronicle of the abbots of his monastery is in the Vatican Library, as Bernard de Montfaucon testifies in *Library of Manuscript Libraries*, p. 74.

See Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 246; Balaeus, *Century* XIII, 9; Pitseus, chapter 112; Johann Metzler, *On the Illustrious Men of Saint Gall*, II, 69; Johann Egon, *On the Illustrious Men of Reichenau*, I, 12; II, 13; Lyser, *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, p. 235; *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 59 ff.

[Col. 0011]

# Editor’s Notice to the Following New Reprinting of the Ordinary Gloss

When we gather together the works of Walafrid Strabo or Strabo, the Ordinary Gloss, whose principal author is considered to be Walafrid, meets us first.

There were many editions of this Gloss in various regions, from 1472 to 1634; their enumeration may be seen, if desired, in the *Literary History of France*, vol. V, p. 62. For six centuries the authority of the Ordinary Gloss was great. Gradually, however, as the years passed, many additions accumulated, and it was enlarged to such an extent that it has reached us in six enormous volumes, as they say, in the largest folio format, in which one can scarcely recognize Walafrid’s work.

Moreover, it is foreign to our purpose to reprint additions by writers of the twelfth, thirteenth, or even fifteenth century. We have therefore judged that only Walafrid’s work, in the form offered by the more ancient and authentic manuscripts, ought to be preserved.

Nevertheless, lest readers should miss an outline of a work that had enjoyed such authority for so many centuries, we have reproduced, insofar as it concerns us, its general structure, and have reprinted the *Prolegomena* prefixed to the Douai edition of the theologians of 1617. From these the nature of the Ordinary Gloss discussed here may be learned.

Many things, however, that we have printed in these *Prolegomena* have already appeared in various volumes of this *Patrology*. It will therefore be sufficient to indicate the places, so that we may not repeat the same material twice.

Likewise, only the opening words of each verse of Sacred Scripture need be included, in order to make intelligible the commentaries of the Fathers to which they are prefixed. For our readers would rightly be wearied if, on the occasion of Walafrid’s work, we were to reproduce the entire Sacred Bible.

# Prolegomena of the Douai Theologians to the Ordinary Gloss

*(From the Douai edition of 1617.)*

[Col. 0011]

## Greetings and Happiness to the Catholic Reader

[Col. 0011B] There are some people excessively inflamed by a passion for novelty who wholly reject and detest all the labor that learned men devote to preserving the monuments of an educated antiquity, as though it were superstitious and diverted or frightened excellent minds away from devising new and outstanding discoveries. They observe, of course, that good men, especially in literature and the liberal arts, esteem scarcely anything highly unless it has acquired authority for itself through age.

Such people will undoubtedly mock us, who are striving to reprint this Ordinary Gloss and the Postilla of Nicholas of Lyra, and to press them into the hands of students—names which, by their very sound and the inflection of the voice, strike their refined ears as something horrifying and barbarous.

They would have preferred some new work, previously unheard of, or at least commentaries by modern authors adapted to this subject. The supply of such authors in this age of polygraphers and universal scholars is so abundant that they are almost innumerable.

For our part, we have not sought to please readers of this kind. We have no doubt that our undertaking will be approved by modest and Catholic readers who know and recognize that, in the other arts, even the most recent discoveries may possess their own grace and dignity, sometimes surpassing that of many ancient discoveries; but that, in opening up the hidden meanings of the divine word, the best things are those that are most ancient, and those closest to the best are those nearest to the most ancient. They are more closely joined to the purest fountain of truth and therefore farther removed from the stagnant pools and mire of perverse spirits, from which the salutary and limpid waters of Scripture are often polluted and disturbed.

“For in the ancients there is wisdom,” says the Wise Man; and in the ancient interpreters of the Church the traces of our diligent labor are set down securely, without the danger—at least the harmful and destructive danger—of falsehood. With these recent writers, however, who show little reverence for the ancients, our study can proceed only at the greatest peril to souls and with the surest waste of precious time.

Those earlier writers, distinguished for the praises of piety and modesty, judged that nothing should be written or maintained by them unless it had been approved by the judgment of the pontiff of the Catholic Church and of the other teachers who persevered in communion with him. They recognized that, just as there is an ordered hierarchy of souls, so there is one of minds within the Church; that “the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets”; and they always kept before their eyes Solomon’s oracle:

“The words of the wise are like goads”—

which prick with the sharpness of truth and do not flatter with the little flowers of adulation—

“and like nails driven deep”—

with the solid foundation of Catholic faith laid beneath them, not the shifting sand of human wisdom—

“which are given through the counsel of masters”—

since no one is permitted to indulge as he pleases in divine matters, but all are compelled to speak according to a definite rule. No one, however great or even greatest, dares to prefer his own judgment to the agreement of other devout men. For this reason they submit themselves to the vicar of Christ, through whom the Holy Spirit governs the tongues and pens of teachers, so that they may be worthy to receive the deifying light of truth—

“from one Shepherd,” who is our Redeemer.

But these admirers of novelty, “not enduring” the “sound doctrine” of the ancients, testing and killing the doctrine of truth according to their own desires, “heap up teachers for themselves,” paying no attention to the profit of souls but, “having itching ears,” turning away from the simple and solid truth and giving themselves wholly “to fables” and to the seductive ornaments of destructive opinions. It is therefore no wonder if they “turn away their hearing from the truth” and are converted to such things.

For you, therefore, Catholic reader, worshiper and admirer of the ancient and ancestral faith, this labor of ours has been undertaken. While other outstanding teachers of the Church now flourishing display to you the riches and weapons of their intellect, with which you can be armed to declare a powerful and tireless war against the enemies of the Catholic faith and the plunderers of souls, we also wished to provide you with the best commanders of the Middle Ages. In their own time they stood as a wall and rampart for the Church. Among them, the authors of these commentaries fight in no inferior place. We bring them into the battle line again, after wiping away some of the rust that they had acquired.

From this it will become especially clear by what spirit our predecessors were guided when they approached the interpretation of Sacred Scripture: by the divine, not human, counsel of teachers, which we heard above from Solomon, each teacher humbly deferring to the others, and all governed under one Shepherd and by one Shepherd. Their purpose was to open the salutary recesses of the heavenly oracles.

The author of the Ordinary Gloss was the first to attempt to place before our eyes, as though on a mathematical abacus or diagram, the harmony and agreement of these teachers in the exposition of the divine word, as a council and “counsel of masters.” It was called the Ordinary Gloss because later generations habitually consulted it as a workshop of ecclesiastical meanings whenever it was necessary to return to the sense of Scripture. They did not think that they ought to understand anything other than what they had found transmitted by that “counsel of masters.” Thus they accepted the wise man’s warning, which he added after the words:

“Do not seek anything beyond these, my son,”

and supplied the evident reason:

“Of making many books there is no end.”

It is as though those who do not submit the words of the wise to examination through the counsel of masters, and do not rest in the judgment of the one Shepherd, never cease wandering through all the twisting paths of errors and lies, but are tormented by endless questions.

This work of the Gloss, in the scarcity and poverty of books under which that age labored—an age exceedingly poor in this respect when compared with our own—required not only immense vigils but also considerable expense. Doctors of the sacred sciences had to be sought and copied from everywhere, since printing had not yet been invented, that miraculous art multiplying books which, as someone said of the Nile watering Egypt, carries with it infinite “good things and harmful things” (*ἔσθλα καὶ ὕργα*), worthy and harmful writers alike.

Through the benefit of this art, that highly praiseworthy labor of compilation could be made more illustrious and complete by adding and suitably attaching other expositions of the holy Fathers that would serve to clarify the sacred pages. The divine genius of Thomas Aquinas accomplished this in the Gospel history, and the more recent Greeks did so in many books of Scripture; most abundantly in Genesis and Exodus, the learned bishop of Verona, Lippomanus. Perhaps we too shall attempt this someday, if God grants us life and strength.

In the meantime, however, the fact that something can be made more perfect—for it is very easy to add to discoveries, but extremely difficult to make the first discovery—does not mean that this work of the Gloss ought to have been neglected or rejected. It was the first to introduce the holy Fathers, as though gathered in council, interpreting Scripture by comparing their testimonies. It therefore had to be restored by us to its original brightness, so that later generations might always read it with praise and blessing for its authors, as our predecessors have held it in the highest honor for eight centuries.

At the same time we judged it useful that there should exist so lucid a testimony not only to the Catholic method that our Fathers always followed in interpreting Scripture, but also to their most diligent industry in sacred letters. We wished also to close the mouths of the most shameless heretics who have dared to boast that among us the word of God lay buried and neglected until the torch of the Gospel—the Gospel, that is, of the fifth age—was lit by them.

The numerous theories, meditations, and writings of our people on the Sacred Scriptures, published before those heretics arose, testify that this is utterly false. Above all, the commentaries of the Gloss and of Lyra demonstrate it. From them these foreigners compiled whatever they say correctly about Scripture, adding nothing of their own except a certain brilliance of expression and excursuses loaded with curses and blasphemies, in which they attempt either to establish their own ravings or to attack the foundations of our faith.

The occasion for this edition was provided, among other things, by what had been noted by the Reverend Father Antonio Possevino in his *Sacred Library*. When printers wished to reprint the Gloss in the form in which it had been published at Paris in 1588 after the revision of three doctors—Francis Feuardent, James de Cuelly, and John Dadraeus—they were shown Possevino’s judgment, which that most diligent investigator of the ecclesiastical library had expressed in these words:

“Indeed,” he says under the entry *Ordinary Gloss*, “the distinguished theologians could not fully carry out the careful work they had begun in it, because the printers were pressing the edition forward and the civil disturbances in Gaul were disrupting literary affairs.”

Since these words appeared to have been written by that man for sound reasons, the printers asked us gradually to compare the copies. When the comparison had been made, we found many gaps in the words, sentences, and testimonies; many passages repeated at length twice on the same pages; certain statements by authors that were sufficiently dangerous; and a very large number of passages scarcely relevant to the subject, suited more to filling the spaces of the pages—which were quite large—than to illuminating the meaning.

Thus Possevino seems to have indicated with great moderation what he found lacking in that edition and to have assigned as the sole or principal cause of so many defects the bitter calamity of the civil wars.

We were therefore compelled, dividing the watches of labor among ourselves, to examine the entire work against manuscript copies and earlier impressions, and to consult the original works of the Fathers. We restored to each author his own words, from whom the passages had been taken, exactly as those authors had written them, that is, in corrected form. For each surviving testimony we indicated the books and places of the authors. In place of material repeated merely to fill the empty spaces of the pages, or inserted superfluously, or selected without sufficiently sound judgment, we supplied other statements of the classical Fathers.

Moreover, we removed the testimonies of the rabbis—with one or two exceptions—as well as those of profane writers such as Pliny, Justin the historian, Josephus the Jew, and Philo. In the Paris edition these had been added beneath little stars. In their place we substituted sayings of the holy Fathers. The glossator himself wished only these to have a place in that chain or harmony of authorities, not authors alien to faith and to Christ.

Anyone can see that we have not said these things here without reason or merely boastfully, provided he wishes to compare our edition with the Paris edition or with other editions made from it. If, at the end of each volume, we had listed the passages restored, corrected, deleted for good reasons, or supplied, quite a few additional gatherings would have been necessary.

Nor should this observation of ours injure the reputation of the very wise men whom we named above and who established the form of the Paris edition. For not only could the military and civil disturbances of that period have snatched pens and books from the hands of all devout men, but we cannot persuade ourselves that the order prescribed by those great men was actually observed by the workers. The press was hurried forward for the reasons suggested by Possevino, and the prescribed order was for the most part disregarded.

Otherwise, the industry of those men, joined with their great learning, and their zeal in defending the cause of God and the Church, are amply demonstrated by their other labors published in the light of day and by their learned sermons delivered against the heretics.

[Col. 0016B] Nor do we ourselves claim so much that we suppose we made no error at all in revising this work. We too encountered difficulties that were equally troublesome. One of our colleagues was prevented from working for nearly an entire year by a long and serious illness. Two others, by the authority of their superiors, were assigned to the care of souls and were drawn away from the shaded retreats of the academy into the heat of pastoral care. They too caused no small delay to the edition and made us wait three years—as the Parisians said of their own edition—for the birth of this offspring.

Nevertheless, we dare to say that the reader will not find errors of great importance, or even many errors of lesser significance. We observed that other editions contained an almost infinite number of them.

[Col. 0016C] Know, most courteous reader, that we have altered absolutely nothing in the ancient Gloss—not its order, nor its actual words—except where we discovered from ancient manuscripts, old copies, and the original works themselves of the saints that something was false or corrupt. We likewise altered nothing in Lyra’s literal and moral Postilla. Thus we left entirely untouched certain slight etymologies and certain grammatical blunders, because they appeared to have been written in that form by the author himself; for postillators often make mistakes in such derivations.

The additions that the Parisians made to the ancient Gloss are marked with a single asterisk or star. Those that we have added have a double asterisk before them, and are distinguished by these signs from the authorities of the ancient Gloss. The same judgment applies to certain notes that we inserted here and there into Lyra’s Postilla. They too are preceded by stars, so that it may be recognized that they are not Lyra’s words but our own.

In the replies of Matthias Tornigi, however, we assumed somewhat more authority. We frequently removed certain insults that he heaped with excessive and excessive repetition upon the venerable Burgensis. For it was not fitting that an edition of so necessary a work, destined to be in everyone’s hands, including those of the Church’s enemies, should contain such indecorous and unworthy petulance from a learned man.

The author defends his Lyra in such a way that he openly shows that he has not entered into dispute with the Burgensis for the sake of discovering the truth, but only so that Lyra might not appear to have been justly criticized. Although the Burgensis reproaches Lyra with complete justice in many matters, and although Lyra himself claims the right of a doctor to attack others, Tornigi nevertheless resents the fact that Lyra is criticized in passages where he deservedly ought to be criticized, and there he drags the matter into a contentious dispute.

Since it matters little to the glory of the Postillator whether he is rightly or wrongly criticized in matters indifferent, which concern neither faith nor morals, Tornigi heaps insults there upon a venerable bishop, a holy man who had served the Spanish Church extremely well, and lightly casts upon a faithful confessor the reproach of Judaism—as though salvation had not come from the Jews, and as though his own Lyra had not himself once been a Jew.

We therefore removed almost all those insults because they occurred too frequently. Beyond that, however, we wished to alter nothing, not even in the author himself.

These, then, are the matters concerning our plan and concerning what, with God’s guidance, we have accomplished in this edition.

Perhaps it will not be unwelcome if we append some information about the authors of the Glosses and Postillae themselves, gathered especially from Sixtus of Siena and other learned men.

The principal author of the Ordinary Gloss—which is placed around the sacred text—is universally celebrated as WALAFRID STRABO, a Benedictine monk of the monastery of Fulda in Germany, distinct from the English monk Strabo, the brother of the Venerable Bede. He acquired the surname Strabo from a defect of the eyes. He was a pupil and amanuensis of Rabanus Maurus, a Benedictine and abbot of the same monastery, later archbishop of Mainz.

He was a man thoroughly polished in secular learning, highly skilled in Sacred Scripture, delighted by varied and constant reading of ancient authors, and, for his age, by no means an unsuccessful poet.

This collection of expositions of Scripture is therefore his. Later generations valued it so highly that they called it the Ordinary Gloss, or even the language of Scripture itself, because through it we understand Scripture as speaking to us; without it, when reading the sacred words, we might think we were hearing a language we did not know.

The Master of the Sentences calls this Gloss, *κατ’ ἐξοχήν*—“preeminently”—an authority in Book IV, distinction 4. For when introducing the Epistle to the Hebrews, chapter 6, he says:

“Hence the authority says that the Apostle spoke in the plural of the foundation of baptisms because there is baptism in water, in blood, and in repentance,” and so forth.

You will find all these things in the Ordinary Gloss on that chapter.

It appears, however, that later writers enriched it, as Trithemius judges in his *Catalogue*, and as is often apparent from the attached name of Remigius, who lived later than Strabo. Unless, perhaps, we should say that the name of Remigius was written down in place of Augustine’s, from whom Remigius took most of his material in his customary manner.

For the names of the authors are not written everywhere in the manuscript copies of the Gloss; identifying them was the work of later diligence.

Strabo flourished under Louis the Pious, in the year of the Lord 840.

The author of the Interlinear Gloss, however, is Anselm of Laon, also a Benedictine monk, surnamed “the Scholastic.” A Frenchman by nationality, he was learned through constant study in the divine Scriptures and the books of the sacred doctors, and was moderately trained in every discipline. He was sharp in intellect, concise in expression, and fond of a certain Laconian brevity.

Accordingly, in a new and unusual mode of exposition, he explained the books of both Testaments by means of very brief summaries of notes taken from the Fathers. He fitted these notes together with an industry no less curious than useful, writing them in the smallest characters between the very lines of Scripture, which were written in larger letters. He called this work the Interlinear Gloss to distinguish it from Strabo’s Gloss, which is written in the margins of the sacred text.

He flourished under the emperor Henry IV, in the year of the Lord 1110.

When already an old man, he once engaged in controversy with Peter Abelard, a monk of the same order, who at that time, swelling with philosophical pride, spoke about matters of faith with insufficient sobriety. Abelard was afterward corrected and, living a holy life in the monastery of Cluny under Peter the Venerable, died a praiseworthy death.

Both Glosses—the Ordinary and the Interlinear—have always enjoyed the greatest authority among all theologians. This is evident to anyone from the way Alexander of Hales, Thomas Aquinas, and the other principal masters of the schools make frequent use of their authority.

Sixtus of Siena has the following to say about Nicholas of Lyra:

> “Nicholas of Lyra, an Englishman by nationality—or, as some write, from the town of Lyra in Brabant—by descent a Jew, and from earliest childhood instructed in Hebrew letters; after his conversion, however, devoted to the Franciscan order; a professor of scholastic theology and a not undistinguished expositor of the Sentences; endowed also with such true, pure, and genuine understanding of the divine Scriptures that, in expounding them, he had no equal among the most learned theologians of his age.  
>   
> He published, on each of the books of both the Old and the New Testament, eighty-five books of scholastic Postils, not merely useful but very necessary for students of the sacred Scriptures, and especially for beginners hastening toward more advanced study. In the first fifty of these books he expounded the entire body of sacred Scripture, without rhetorical embellishment or verbal concealment, in plain and open language. With the greatest diligence in each case, he disclosed and elucidated the literal sense—the more excellent, but also more difficult, of the senses of divine Scripture—bringing to bear not only the expositions of the ancient Fathers of the Church but also the opinions of the Rabbis, who possess the highest authority among the Jews.  
>   
> When this work was completed, he undertook the labor anew and, in the thirty-five later books, illuminated both Testaments with a moral exposition. He flourished under Pope John XXII and the emperor Louis of Bavaria.”

This is what Sixtus says. Lyra also produced a third work on the whole of the Old Testament, which he entitled *The Work of Differences*. In it he most diligently noted all the expressions in which the Vulgate translator appeared to differ from the Hebrew source. It exists separately in print, although it is found only very rarely.

As for Sixtus’s statement that some consider Nicholas an Englishman, I do not know on what foundation they rely. Those who consider him a Brabander have his epitaph in their favor, which formerly stood in the town of Lyra between Antwerp and Mechelen. Among other things, it contains this couplet:

> To whom humane Brabant’s Lyra gave the name,  
> For Lyra was the town in which he first saw the light.

The epitaph concludes with this couplet:

> Here the hierophant sits, radiant with a diadem from God,  
> A glory worthy of Brabantic soil.

Likewise, in the edition of the Gloss made at Basel in 1520, the following appears at the end of the sixth part:

> “The sacred Bible with the ordinary gloss, etc.; and the Postil of Nicholas of Lyra the Brabander ends here.”

Nicholas of Lyra died in the great Parisian college of the Friars Minor in the year 1349, on 14 October. His epitaph is also found there, from which others infer that this same Nicholas was a Norman from the Norman town of Lyra. It is also a plausible conjecture, since he frequently uses examples from the French language, but nowhere examples from Brabantine or English. Let the reader choose whichever account he prefers.

Paul of Burgos follows. He was a Spaniard by nationality, surnamed “of Saint Mary,” a Hebrew by descent, and formerly, among his fellow Hebrews, a rabbi of the highest distinction. After his conversion to the Christian faith, he was first bishop of New Carthage and then of Burgos in Spain, as well as arch-chancellor of Castile and León. For the benefit of his son Alfonso, dean of the church of Compostela—whom, while still a layman, he had fathered by his wife—he discussed numerous passages from each of the books of sacred Scripture. In them he attempted to correct and supplement Lyra’s explanations, and he entitled the work *Additions*. He flourished under the emperor Sigismund, in the year of the Lord 1430.

He also wrote a notable work against Jewish unbelief, which he called *Scrutiny of the Scriptures*. He was a man of the greatest authority in Spain, appointed tutor to the orphan king because of his loyalty and prudence, and a man of acknowledged piety. He was especially devoted to the teaching of St. Thomas and to the Dominican order, for which he built and endowed a splendid monastery in his own city. By the power of the divine word and by his zeal he so strengthened that city and the region of Burgos in the faith of Christ the Lord that afterward no one from among them, or from their descendants, is known to have withdrawn from that faith, as Navarrus testifies in his counsels.

For this reason his family, called “of Saint Mary,” is still renowned and of distinguished nobility. It alone in Spain is a civic family and is admitted to all public honors, while all other families of Hebrew blood are excluded.

Against this Paul of Burgos, Matthew Dornick, or Tornigus, a Saxon by nationality and a Minorite of the Saxon province, formerly its minister and an outstanding professor of scholastic theology, writes in these commentaries. Having entered the contest in defense of his teacher Nicholas of Lyra, he sought to overthrow the additions of Burgos by publishing new disputations, which he appended to Lyra’s commentaries immediately after the additions of Burgos. He entitled them *Replies*, or *Corrective Against the Corruptor of Burgos*. In them he made many sufficiently learned observations, but, as we have said, he could not refrain from insults, with which he attacked Burgos quite unjustly. He flourished under the emperor Frederick III, in the year of the Lord 1440.

You should also be advised, kind reader, that we have left the sacred text itself exactly as we found it in the ancient editions of the Gloss and of Lyra, because this seemed to correspond better with Lyra’s expositions. He does not read everywhere in the same way as our present Vulgate, which has now been corrected by the pontiffs. At the end of each volume, however, we have added the Roman corrections collected by Dr. Francisco Luca of Burgos, and have attached to them our own conjectures. By these we wished to indicate what the Roman Fathers may have followed in those corrections, and why they approved these readings rather than those.

We have also supplied each volume with an index, a brief one containing only the principal matters and those explained at greater length. To include in the index everything explained in any way would have amounted to copying the commentaries a second time. Moreover, the smaller and briefer matters generally serve the verbal explanation of the text and will therefore be found more easily by locating the sacred text to which they refer than through an index. We have placed in the index only those matters that are treated more carefully and at greater length both in the Gloss and by Lyra.

[Col. 0019]

# ON THE CANONICAL AND NON-CANONICAL BOOKS

[Col. 0019D] Since many people, because they do not devote much attention to sacred Scripture, think that all the books contained in the Bible should be revered and honored equally, not knowing how to distinguish between canonical and non-canonical books—which the Hebrews separate from the canon and the Greeks count among the apocrypha—they often appear ridiculous before learned people and become confused and scandalized when they hear someone treating something found in the Bible with less reverence than all the other books. For this reason we have distinguished them here and listed first the canonical books and afterward the non-canonical books, between which there is as much difference as between certainty and doubt.

For the canonical books were composed under the dictation of the Holy Spirit; but the non-canonical, or apocryphal, books were published at an unknown time and by unknown authors. Nevertheless, because they are very good and useful and contain nothing opposed to the canonical books, the Church reads them and permits the faithful to read them for devotion and moral instruction. Their authority, however, is not considered sufficient for proving matters that are disputed or controversial, or for confirming the authority of ecclesiastical doctrines, as blessed Jerome says in his prologues to Judith and to the books of Solomon.

The canonical books, on the other hand, possess such authority that whatever they contain must be held firmly and without dispute to be true; consequently, whatever is manifestly concluded from them must likewise be held true. For just as in philosophy truth is known by reduction to self-evident first principles, so in the Scriptures handed down by the holy doctors, truth—so far as concerns those things that must be held by faith—is known by reduction to the canonical Scriptures, which have been received through divine revelation, in which there can be no falsehood whatsoever.

Thus Augustine says to Jerome:

> “I have learned to show this fear and honor only to those writers who are called canonical, so that I firmly believe that none of them erred in writing. If I encounter in them anything that appears contrary to the truth, I will not hesitate to think that either the manuscript is corrupt, or that the interpreter did not grasp what was said, or that I myself have understood it very inadequately. But I read other writers in such a way that, however great their holiness or learning may be, I do not consider something true merely because they themselves thought so; rather, I do so because through those canonical authors, or through probable arguments, they have been able to persuade me that what they say does not depart from the truth.”

[Col. 0021B] There are therefore twenty-two canonical books of the Old Testament, corresponding to the number of the twenty-two letters of the Hebrews, as Eusebius reports Origen to have written concerning the first Psalm in the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*. Blessed Jerome says more fully and distinctly in his *Prologue with the Helmet* to the book of Kings that the Hebrews divide all of them into three parts: the Law, that is, the five books of Moses; the Prophets, eight books; and the Hagiographa, nine books. This will immediately become clearer, although some separate the book of Ruth from the book of Judges, and the Lamentations of Jeremiah from Jeremiah, and count them among the Hagiographa, so that there are twenty-four books.

[Note: [Col. 0021D] The Hebrews who approve this division call their Bible [the Hebrew term is absent from the supplied text], that is, “twenty-four,” for this reason: according to the number of the twenty-four elders whom Revelation portrays worshiping the Lamb (Rev. 5).]

These are the books that are in the canon, as blessed Jerome writes at greater length in the *Prologue with the Helmet* prefixed to the books of Kings.

First are the five books of Moses, which are called the Law: the first is Genesis, the second Exodus, the third Leviticus, the fourth Numbers, and the fifth Deuteronomy.

Second follow the eight prophetic books. The first is Joshua; the second, the book of Judges together with Ruth; the third, Samuel, that is, the First and Second Books of Kings; the fourth, Malachim, that is, the Third and Fourth Books of Kings; the fifth, Isaiah; the sixth, Jeremiah together with the Lamentations; the seventh, Ezekiel; and the eighth, the book of the Twelve Prophets. The first of these is Hosea, the second Joel, the third Amos, the fourth Obadiah, the fifth Jonah, the sixth Micah, the seventh Nahum, the eighth Habakkuk, the ninth Zephaniah, the tenth Haggai, the eleventh Zechariah, and the twelfth Malachi.

Third follow the nine Hagiographa. The first is Job; the second, the Psalter; the third, Solomon’s Proverbs; the fourth, his Ecclesiastes; the fifth, his Song of Songs; the sixth, Daniel; the seventh, Chronicles, which among the Hebrews is one book, not two; the eighth, Ezra together with Nehemiah—for they constitute one complete book; and the ninth, Esther.

Whatever lies outside these books—I am speaking of the Old Testament—is, as Jerome says, to be placed among the apocrypha.

These are the books that are not in the canon, although the Church admits them as good and useful books, not as canonical books. Some of them have greater authority and some less.

Tobit, Judith, and the books of Maccabees, as well as the book of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus, are highly approved by everyone. Thus Augustine, in Book II, chapter 3, of *On Christian Doctrine*, counts the first three among the canonical books and says of Wisdom and Ecclesiasticus that they deserved to be received as authoritative and ought to be counted among the prophetic books. Speaking of the books of Maccabees in Book XVIII, chapter 31, of *The City of God*, and of the books of Ezra, he says that although the Hebrews do not regard them as canonical, the Church regards them as canonical because of the intense and marvelous sufferings of certain martyrs.

Of lesser authority, however, are Baruch and the Third and Fourth Books of Ezra. For Augustine, in the passage mentioned above, makes no mention of them, although, as I have said, he numbers other apocryphal books among the canonical. Rufinus likewise, in his *Exposition of the Creed*, and Isidore, in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, where they report Jerome’s division, remember none of these books.

If one counts them in the order in which they occur in the Bible, although they were composed in another order, the first are the Third and Fourth Books of Ezra, which are called the Third and Fourth because before Jerome the Greeks and Latins divided the canonical book of Ezra into two books, calling Nehemiah’s account the second book. These Third and Fourth Books, among all the non-canonical books, are of lesser authority, as I have said. Hence Jerome, in the prologue to Ezra, calls them “dreams.” They are found in very few manuscript Bibles, and in many printed Bibles only the Third Book is found.

The second is Tobit, a very devout and useful book.

The third is Judith, which Jerome says in his prologue was counted by the Council of Nicaea among the sacred Scriptures.

The fourth is the book of Wisdom, which almost everyone holds to have been written by Philo of Alexandria, the highly learned Jew.

The fifth is the book of Jesus son of Sirach, which is called Ecclesiasticus.

The sixth is Baruch, as Jerome says in his prologue to Jeremiah.

The seventh is the book of Maccabees, divided into First and Second Maccabees.

No one should be troubled by the statement in the prologues to Judith and Tobit that these books are read among the Hagiographa by the Hebrews, for this is clearly an error, and “apocrypha,” not “Hagiographa,” must be read. The error is found in every manuscript I have seen, and, I think, became established through the piety and devotion of the scribes, who were horrified to number such devout histories among the apocrypha.

That this error had occupied manuscripts for many years is shown by the Master in his history of Judith, where he says:

> “This book is counted among the histories by the Chaldaeans, and among the apocrypha by the Hebrews.”

Jerome says this in the prologue that begins, “The twenty-two letters.” If, therefore, the prologue to Judith is found anywhere to read “among the Hagiographa,” it is a scribal fault, which can be detected in the title itself.

For this reason I am surprised that the aforementioned Master did not notice the same error in the prologue to Tobit, where he himself says:

> “The Hebrews place this history among the apocrypha.”

Nevertheless, Jerome in his prologue says “among the Hagiographa.” The Gloss on that prologue to Tobit says that he should rather, and more correctly, have said “among the apocrypha.” Alternatively, he may be using “Hagiographa” in a broad sense, as though it meant “the writings of holy men”; in that case Tobit is not among the nine books properly called Hagiographa, which belong to the catalogue—that is, to the number of the twenty-two biblical books.

For when Jerome, in the *Prologue with the Helmet*, after enumerating the canonical books, says:

> “This prologue to the Scriptures, as a helmeted beginning, can be applied to all the books that we have translated from Hebrew into Latin, so that we may know that whatever lies outside these is to be placed among the apocrypha. Therefore Wisdom, commonly inscribed with the name of Solomon, the book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the Shepherd are not in the canon,”

how can we believe that he later wrote in those prologues that these books were among the Hagiographa and thus contradicted himself?

Moreover, if anyone examines Jerome’s words in those prologues with a more open-minded scrutiny, he will notice that Jerome wrote “apocrypha,” not “Hagiographa.” For in the prologue to Tobit he says:

> “You demand that I bring a book written in the Chaldaean language into Latin style—the book, namely, of Tobit, which the Hebrews, cutting it away from the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, assigned to those writings that they call apocrypha.”

In Judith he says:

> “Among the Hebrews the book of Judith is read among the apocrypha, and its authority is judged less suitable for strengthening matters that come into dispute.”

Since he says that the Hebrews cut Tobit away from the catalogue of the divine Scriptures, and that the authority of Judith is judged less suitable, if he counted it among the Hagiographa rather than among the apocrypha, he would appear to have written contradictory things in the same place.

But, as I have said, scribes, horrified by the name “apocrypha,” wrote “Hagiographa” out of a certain devotion and piety, having rejected the term “apocrypha.”

Rufinus, in the passage mentioned above, after enumerating the canonical books—in which he agrees with Jerome—adds:

> “These are the books that the Fathers enclosed within the canon, from which they wished the affirmations of our faith to be established. Yet it must be known that there are also other books which our predecessors called not canonical but ecclesiastical, such as the Wisdom called Solomon’s, and the other Wisdom called that of the son of Sirach.”

And farther on:

> “Of the same order are the little book of Tobit, Judith, and the books of Maccabees. All these they wished to be read in the churches, but not to be brought forward as authority for confirming matters by their testimony. The remaining writings they called apocryphal, and they did not wish them to be read in the churches.”

It must also be known that in the book of Esther only those passages are in the canon that are written up to the place where we have inserted:

> “The book of Esther ends here, as it is in the Hebrew; what follows is not in the canon.”

Likewise, in Daniel only those passages are in the canon that extend to the place where we have inserted:

> “The prophet Daniel ends here; what follows is not in the canon.”

Although David—that is, the Psalter—is not placed among the Prophets by the Hebrews but among the Hagiographa, nearly all the Latins nevertheless call him not only a prophet but the greatest of the prophets, or the second prophet. They also count Daniel among the Prophets.

Some Latins have divided the Old and New Testaments in another way, namely into legal, historical, wisdom, and prophetic books.

They call the five books of Moses in the Old Testament “legal”; in the New Testament they make the four Gospels correspond to them.

They call Joshua, Judges, the books of Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Esther, and Job “historical”; in the New Testament the Acts of the Apostles correspond to these.

They call the three books of Solomon—Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs—“wisdom books”; in the New Testament the Epistles of Paul and the books called Catholic correspond to these.

They call David—that is, the Psalter—Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, the Twelve Prophets, and Daniel “prophetic”; in the New Testament the book of Revelation corresponds to these.

All the books of the New Testament that appear in the Bible are canonical, according to Jerome, Augustine, and Isidore in the passages cited above.

These are the four most holy Gospels: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.

There are fourteen Epistles of the apostle Paul: one to the Romans; two to the Corinthians; one to the Galatians; one to the Ephesians; one to the Philippians; two to the Thessalonians; one to the Colossians; two to Timothy; one to Titus; one to Philemon; and one to the Hebrews.

There are also the Acts of the Apostles.

There are seven Epistles called Catholic: one by James; two by Peter, the chief of the apostles; three by John, the apostle and evangelist; and one by Jude, who is elsewhere called Thaddeus.

Finally there is the book of Revelation.

All these books are regarded as canonical, although before Jerome many people doubted the Epistle to the Hebrews, a doubt that he removed by many arguments. Likewise, in the primitive Church there was considerable doubt about the Epistle of Jude and about the Second and Third Epistles of John—whether they ought to be received into the canon.

Of the first of these, Jerome says in his book *On Illustrious Men*:

> “Judas, the brother of James, left a short Epistle, which is one of the seven canonical Epistles. Because he draws testimony in it from the book of Enoch, which is apocryphal, it is rejected by many; nevertheless, through its antiquity and use it has already earned authority and is counted among the holy Scriptures.”

Of the other two Epistles, which begin with the word “The Elder,” Jerome says in the same book, in the chapters on John and Papias, that they were claimed to belong to John the presbyter, a disciple of John the Evangelist, who was called John the Elder. Nevertheless, by the common approval of all they have now been received and, without anyone’s opposition, are regarded as canonical.

[Col. 0023]

# TRANSLATORS OF THE BIBLES

[Col. 0023C] It should be noted that there were many translators and interpreters of the Bible. For, as the Master says in the histories, 341 years before the Lord’s incarnation, in the time of Ptolemy Philadelphus, king of Egypt, the Seventy Interpreters flourished, who translated the Law and the Prophets in the following manner.

[Col. 0023D] Ptolemy, a studious man and lover of books, learning that the Jews possessed a law issued from the mouth of God and written by his finger, sent letters and gifts and asked Eleazar, the Jewish high priest, to send him elderly men skilled in the Hebrew and Greek languages who would be able to interpret and translate it. For he desired to have it translated into Greek and inserted into the royal archives.

Eleazar, assenting to his request, sent six experts in the Law from each tribe. These were the seventy-two interpreters. Although they were seventy-two, they are commonly called the Seventy in accordance with the usage of sacred Scripture, because, even if two are left over, this is a small matter in relation to seventy.

When they came to the king, translating the Pentateuch and the Prophets, they disputed before the king about the worship of one God and about the fact that no creature was God. Hence, whenever they encountered something in their translation concerning the Trinity, they either passed over it in silence or translated it obscurely, lest they appear to have taught that three gods should be worshiped. They did the same with the incarnation of the Word.

Thus the translation of the seventy-two is sometimes excessive and sometimes defective.

After the Lord’s incarnation and Passion, 124 years later, a certain Jew named Aquila, who had converted to the faith but afterward fell into heresy, produced the first alternative translation from Hebrew into Greek, in the time of the emperor Hadrian.

Then, fifty-four years later, Theodotion produced a third translation under Commodus.

Thirty years afterward, the translator Symmachus became famous under Severus.

Eight years later, a certain translation was discovered at Jerusalem, whose author is unknown and which was called the Fifth Edition.

Twenty-eight years later, in the time of Alexander, Origen appeared. Seeing that these translations were imperfect, he began to correct the translation of the seventy-two by means of the later translations already mentioned—or, according to some, he incorporated only the translation of Theodotion—supplying what was lacking and cutting away what was excessive.

Wherever he added something to the translation of the seventy-two from the subsequent translations, he placed an asterisk, that is, a star or star-shaped sign. By this he indicated that through the addition those things which had previously been lacking were made to shine.

Ἀστερίσκος (*asteriskos*) means “asterisk,” and is a diminutive, as it were “little star.”

Wherever there was something excessive, he placed an obelus. For ὀβελός (*obelos*) is called *sagitta* (“arrow”) or *veru* (“spit” or “skewer”) in Latin, thereby indicating that the letter there was superfluous.

Afterward Origen himself, as Jerome says, discovered the sixth and seventh translations through extraordinary labor. Although their authors are unknown, as Jerome likewise says, these translations nevertheless preserve their differences so credibly that they retained authority without names.

Later, certain people wishing to possess all these translations together wrote books arranging them so that in the middle of each page they placed six columns descending from top to bottom. In the first they placed the words of the first translation, in the second those of the second, and so forth. These books were called ἑξαπλά (*hexapla*), from the Greek ἕξ, meaning “six” in Latin, as though “sixfold.” Alternatively, *hexapla* may mean a book containing six straightened or corrected translations.

In those times many half-learned men in both languages produced other translations into Latin from the Greek translations mentioned above.

Finally blessed Jerome, who was skilled in three languages—Hebrew, Greek, and Latin—first corrected the translation of the seventy-two into Latin with asterisks and obeli. Later he translated the Bible directly from Hebrew into Latin without asterisks and obeli. The whole Roman Church now uses this translation everywhere, although not in every book.

His translation rightly takes precedence over the others because it adheres more closely to the words and is clearer in the precision of its meaning.

The first translation, that of the seventy-two, was made in the city of Alexandria, which is the metropolis of Egypt. The other translations were made in various parts of the world where teachers were then flourishing.

Note that wherever an error is found in the books of the Old Testament, one must have recourse to the volumes of the Hebrews, because the Old Testament was first written in the Hebrew language. If, however, the error is in the books of the New Testament, one must return to the volumes of the Greeks, because the New Testament was first written in the Greek language, except for the Gospel of Matthew and Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews.

[Col. 0025]

# IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY TRINITY, HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF THE VENERABLE FATHER, BROTHER NICHOLAS OF LYRA OF THE SERAPHIC ORDER OF SAINT FRANCIS, ON THE COMMENDATION OF SACRED SCRIPTURE IN GENERAL

[Col. 0025B] “All these things are the book of life,” etc. (Ecclesiasticus 23).

As blessed Gregory says in Homily 35 on the Gospels:

> “Temporal life, compared with eternal life, should rather be called death than life.”

The sciences handed down by philosophers are ordered toward attaining an end in the present life. For the practical sciences transmitted by them are ordered toward political happiness, speaking of the politics of the present life. Likewise, the speculative sciences are ordered toward contemplative happiness, speaking of the contemplation that can be possessed in the present life by the way of nature, which depends upon the phantasm.

Hence it is said in Book III of *On the Soul* that “when we understand, we must contemplate phantasms together with the act of understanding.” Of this kind of speculation it is said in the same place that “understanding is corrupted in us when something within is corrupted.”

Sacred Scripture, however, is ordered toward the happiness of the future life, which the philosophers did not know, as blessed Jerome says in his letter to Paulinus concerning all the books of sacred Scripture:

> “The learned Plato did not know this; the eloquent Demosthenes was ignorant of it.”

From this it follows that the books written by the philosophers, containing sciences naturally ordered toward an end attainable only in this temporal life, should, when compared with the books of sacred Scripture—which are ordered toward the end of eternal life—be called books of death rather than of life.

But the book containing sacred Scripture—which, although divided among many partial books, is nevertheless contained within a single book and is generally called the Bible—is properly called the book of life, according to the words cited above: “All these things,” and so forth.

In this passage sacred Scripture is described in four ways, according to four excellences by which it surpasses every other writing.

First, it is described as possessing singular eminence, indicated by the singular pronoun when it says “this.”

Second, it is described as possessing universal comprehensiveness, indicated by the universal term when it says “all.”

Third, it is described as possessing contemplative understanding, indicated by the condition of the book when it says “book.”

Fourth, it is described as possessing saving efficacy, indicated by the attainment of the intended end when it says “life.”

Concerning the first point, it should be known that one science is more eminent, or more honorable, than another for two reasons, as is established in Book I of *On the Soul*.

One reason is that it concerns a nobler subject; the other is that it proceeds in a more certain manner.

For both reasons sacred Scripture—which is properly called theology, since it alone is the text of this science—surpasses all the sciences.

First, it has God as its subject, and God is at the summit of all nobility. For this reason it is called theology, as though it were “discourse about God.”

Second, it proceeds in a more certain manner. Other sciences discovered by human beings proceed through an investigation of human reason. Although there is no error in this process concerning the first principles, which are self-evident—as is said in Book II of the *Metaphysics*, “Who can go wrong at the threshold?”—there can nevertheless be error in the deduction of conclusions from principles, especially with regard to conclusions that are far removed from the first principles.

Thus all philosophers who relied solely upon human investigation are found to have fallen into error. For this reason, concerning the singular eminence of this science, Deuteronomy 4 says:

> “This is your wisdom and your understanding before the peoples.”

Wisdom, properly speaking, is the science that considers the highest causes, as is established in Book I of the *Metaphysics*. Sacred Scripture, however, has God as its subject, as has been said; and God is simply the first cause of all things. Therefore sacred Scripture is properly called Wisdom.

The word “your” is appropriately added in order to distinguish the wisdom of the saints, or of Catholics—which is sacred Scripture—from the wisdom of the philosophers. This distinction is made especially in two respects: the properties known concerning God and the end of knowledge.

Although the philosophers possessed knowledge of God, it extended only to those properties that can be concluded concerning him through an investigation of reason proceeding from creatures. Thus the Philosopher proves his unity in Book XII of the *Metaphysics*, the infinity of his power in Book VIII of the *Physics*, and similar points elsewhere.

But the holy prophets and apostles who handed this Scripture down to us through the revelation of the Holy Spirit possessed knowledge of divine properties that transcend rational investigation: for example, the plurality of persons, their distinction within the unity of essence, and similar matters.

Furthermore, the philosophers did not order their knowledge of God toward any other end. They sought it merely in order to contemplate God insofar as he is the perfection of the one who knows.

The knowledge of God handed down in sacred Scripture, however, is sought principally so that through it the one who studies or contemplates may be carried into love of the object known—namely, God—loving him above himself and above all things.

For this reason the Savior says in Matthew 22 that:

> “On these two commandments of charity depend the whole Law and the Prophets.”

And the Apostle says in 1 Timothy 1:

> “The end of the commandment is charity from a pure heart, and a good conscience, and unfeigned faith.”

Because the philosophers, relying upon their own judgment, did not attend to this end, they fell into error. Consequently their wisdom is called foolishness, in Romans 1:

> “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks; but they became futile in their thoughts, and their foolish heart was darkened. For while claiming to be wise, they became fools.”

But since sacred Scripture surpasses other sciences not only because it concerns a nobler subject, but also because it proceeds in a more certain way—namely, through divine revelation, in which no falsehood can exist—the cited authority adds:

> “And your understanding before the peoples.”

Understanding properly denotes the habit of principles, concerning which there is no error, as has already been said. Therefore whatever is directly concluded from those principles is judged simply true, and whatever is found to conflict with them is judged simply false.

In the same way, whatever is manifestly concluded from sacred Scripture is judged true, while whatever conflicts with it is regarded as simply false. For this reason sacred Scripture is called not only wisdom but also understanding.

Thus Ecclesiasticus 15 says:

> “He will fill him with the spirit of wisdom and understanding.”

And Colossians 1 says:

> “Be filled with the knowledge of his will in all wisdom and understanding,”

and so forth.

Thus the first point is clear.

Concerning the second point, it should be considered that under the subject of any science there falls not only its subject itself, but also those things that have an attribution to it, as is stated in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*. Thus, under the physician’s consideration there falls not only health, or the body capable of being healed, but also urine, insofar as it indicates health; a potion, insofar as it produces health; a diet, insofar as it preserves health; and so with other things.

Now all created things have an attribution to God himself, who is the subject of this science. For this reason, this science in a certain way considers all things. Here its general comprehensiveness becomes apparent, as is indicated by the word previously introduced, [Col. 0027D] “all.” In this sense the statement in Wisdom 1 may be explained: “That which contains all things has knowledge of speech.” The meaning is: This—that is, the volume of sacred Scripture—which, although divided into several partial books, is nevertheless brought together into one volume called the Bible—contains all things, because this science in a certain way considers all things.

“It has knowledge of speech.” It is characteristic of speech that it signifies a word, and it is proper to sacred Scripture that it expresses the divine Word, as is clearly stated in John 1: “In the beginning was the Word,” and so forth. And because all things were made through the Word, as is added there, all things therefore fall under the consideration of this science—not, however, under the proper definitions of each individual thing, for that belongs to particular sciences devised by human beings, but insofar as through all created things we are led to the knowledge and love of God by true faith formed by charity, toward which the consideration of this science is ordered, as was said above.

This is what Augustine says in *On the Trinity*, book 14, chapter 1: “Certainly, he does not attribute to this science everything that can be known by human beings concerning human affairs, where there is a great deal of useless vanity and harmful curiosity, but only that by which the most health-giving faith, which leads to true blessedness, is generated, nourished, defended, and strengthened.” Hence, in John 16, the Savior, speaking of the Holy Spirit, by whose revelation this Scripture was delivered, says: “He will teach you all truth”; the Gloss adds: “necessary for salvation.” Thus the second point is clear.

Concerning the third point, which is speculative understanding and is indicated by the word “book,” it should be considered that a book resembles a mirror. For just as perceptible forms appear in a mirror, so intelligible truths shine forth in a book. Hence divine foreknowledge, in which all truths shine forth, is also called a book. In that book are read the holy apostles and prophets who transmitted this science.

This is what the Gloss says on Isaiah 38: “Set your house in order,” and so forth: “The prophets can read in that book of God’s foreknowledge, in which all things are written.” This must not, however, be understood to mean that the prophets saw God’s very essence, which is identical with his foreknowledge; for prophetic knowledge, since it possesses an enigma, is abolished in such a vision, according to what the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 13. Rather, the prophets are said to have read in the book of God’s foreknowledge because, through forms divinely impressed upon the minds of the prophets and through the prophetic light proportioned to them, they saw in their own manner the truth derived from God’s knowledge to them through revelation. This is like the possible intellect, by the power of the light of the agent intellect, beholding in forms received from phantasms truths proportioned to itself.

But we, who do not possess such knowledge and have not been illumined by prophetic light, cannot read in that book; rather, we read in the book of sacred Scripture delivered to us by the prophets.

This book, however, has the special feature that one letter contains several senses. The reason is that the principal author of this book is God himself. It is in his power not only to use words to signify something—which human beings also can and do do—but also to use the things signified by words to signify other things. Thus it is common to all books that words signify something, but it is special to this book that the things signified by words signify something else.

Accordingly, according to the first signification, which is through words, the literal or historical sense is understood. According to the other signification, which is through the things themselves, the mystical or spiritual sense is understood. This is generally threefold. If the things signified by words are referred to signify what is to be believed under the New Law, the allegorical sense is understood. If they are referred to signify what we are to do, it is the moral or tropological sense. If they are referred to signify what is to be hoped for in future blessedness, it is the anagogical sense. The term is derived from ἀνάγω, meaning “I lead upward.” Hence the verse:

The letter teaches what was done; allegory, what you should believe;  
The moral sense, what you should do; anagogy, where you should strive.

An example of these four senses may be given in the word “Jerusalem.” According to the literal sense, it signifies a certain city that was once the metropolis of the kingdom of Judah, first founded by Melchizedek and later enlarged and fortified by Solomon.

According to the moral sense, it signifies the faithful soul; in this sense Isaiah 52 says: “Rise up, sit down, Jerusalem,” and so forth.

According to the allegorical sense, it signifies the Church militant; in this sense Revelation 21 says: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband.”

According to the anagogical sense, [Col. 0029A] it signifies the Church triumphant, as Galatians 4 says: “The Jerusalem above is free, which is our mother.”

And just as the example has been given in one word, so it could be given in one sentence, and just as in one sentence, so also in others. Accordingly, of this book, which under one letter contains several senses, Ezekiel 2 says: “Behold, a hand was sent to me, in which a book was rolled up; and he spread it out before me, and it was written within and without.” And Revelation 5 says: “I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without.”

The writing on the outside is the literal sense, which is more evident because it is signified immediately through words. The writing on the inside is the mystical or spiritual sense, which is more hidden because it is designated through the things signified by words, as was said above. Thus the third point is clear.

Concerning the fourth point, in which saving efficacy is indicated by the word “life,” it should be considered that, as was said at the beginning, no other writing than this one leads immediately to blessed life, which alone is life simply speaking, because it knows no death. Therefore the Savior, in John 5, speaking of the efficacy of this sacred Scripture, said to the Jews learned in the Law: “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life.”

Regarding this, it should be understood that the word “think,” which conveys a false opinion or at least doubt concerning the truth, does not refer to sacred Scripture itself, which contains no falsehood, as is clear from what was said above. Nor is there any doubt that it leads to blessed life, since it is an instrument for attaining eternal happiness, as is clear from the words of blessed Augustine cited above. Rather, “think” refers to the learned interpreters of the Law who explained sacred Scripture badly and lived badly. Because of this, they deserved to be deprived of attaining eternal blessedness, which is the end of this science. Those who understand it soundly and live devoutly according to its sound meaning undoubtedly attain that end, as Ecclesiasticus 24 says: “Those who make me clear will have eternal life.”

Sacred Scripture is made clear through its true interpretation and through holy action, because this Scripture, as being superior to all others, contains the perfections of practical and speculative science. Thus, through knowledge of the truth and the practice of the good, it leads to blessed life—which may he grant us who lives and reigns without end.

[Col. 0029]

## SECOND PROLOGUE: ON THE AUTHOR’S INTENTION AND METHOD OF PROCEEDING

[Col. 0029B] “I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without.” (Revelation 5.)

As was said in the preceding prologue, this book is sacred Scripture. It is said to be written on the outside with respect to the literal sense, and on the inside with respect to the mystical and spiritual sense. Although, as was said above, the latter is generally divided into three parts, and although under each member there can be a multiplication of mystical interpretations in particular, all of them nevertheless presuppose the literal sense as their foundation.

Therefore, just as a building that departs from its foundation is disposed to collapse, so a mystical interpretation that disagrees with the literal sense is to be judged unfitting and inept—or at least, other things being equal, less fitting and less appropriate. For this reason, those who wish to make progress in the study of sacred Scripture must begin with an understanding of the literal sense, especially since an argument for the proof or clarification of a difficulty can be drawn from the literal sense alone, and not from the mystical sense, according to what Augustine says in his letter against Vincentius the Donatist.

Furthermore, it should be considered that the literal sense, from which one must begin, as was said, appears to have been greatly obscured in modern times. This is partly through the fault of scribes, who, because of the similarity of letters, wrote differently in many places from what the truth of the text has; partly through the ignorance of certain correctors, who in many places inserted punctuation where it ought not to be inserted, and began or ended verses where they ought not to begin or end. Through this the meaning of the letter is altered, as will become clear in the appropriate places below, with the Lord’s permission.

It is partly also because of the manner of our translation, which in many places differs from the Hebrew books, as Jerome explains in his book *On Hebrew Questions* and in many other places. Other interpreters of sacred Scripture say the same when reading or writing. Yet, according to Jerome in his second prologue to Genesis and in many other places, when the truth of the letter is sought in the writing of the Old Testament, one must have recourse to the Hebrew codices.

Nevertheless, great caution is required concerning those passages of the Old Testament that speak of Christ’s divinity and of matters consequent upon it. The Jews corrupted some of these passages in defense of their error, as I partly explained in a certain question concerning Christ’s divinity, and will explain more fully when such passages occur, with the Lord’s permission.

In passages where it is not likely that they changed anything, since they had no reason to do so, there seems to be no danger. Rather, according to the statement of blessed Jerome, it is safer in doubtful matters to have recourse to the Hebrew text as to the original, in order to clarify the truth of the text.

It should also be understood that the literal sense has been greatly overshadowed because of the method of interpretation commonly handed down by others. Although they have said many good things, they have touched the literal sense only slightly and have multiplied mystical senses to such an extent that the literal sense, intercepted among so many mystical interpretations, is partly suffocated.

They have also divided the text into so many particles and introduced so many cross-references to suit their purpose that they partly confuse understanding and memory, drawing the mind away from grasping the literal sense.

Therefore, intending to avoid these and similar things, with God’s help I intend to concentrate on the literal sense and occasionally to insert only a very few and brief mystical interpretations, though rarely. Likewise, I intend to cite not only the statements of Catholic doctors but also those of the Hebrews, especially Rabbi Solomon, who among Hebrew doctors spoke more reasonably when introducing an explanation of the literal sense.
