I will occasionally, though very rarely, insert certain statements of the Hebrews that are extremely absurd—not in order to maintain or follow them, but so that through them it may appear how great a blindness has occurred in Israel, according to the statement of the Apostle Paul in Romans 11. For this reason, one must not adhere to the statements of the Hebrews except insofar as they agree with reason and the truth of the letter.

Moreover, omitting the prologues, I will begin at the beginning of Genesis. This is partly because I do not believe that the remainder of my life will suffice for an exposition of all sacred Scripture, and therefore I did not wish to linger over the exposition of the statements of blessed Jerome or of any other doctor; and partly because, as it seems to me, those prologues contribute little to understanding the books that follow.

I have nevertheless expounded the prologues of certain books on which I wrote before beginning with the book of Genesis.

Finally, because I am not so skilled in the Hebrew or Latin language that I could not fail in many matters, I therefore declare that I intend to state nothing assertively or determinatively except insofar as it has been plainly determined by sacred Scripture or by the authority of the Church. Let everything else be accepted as stated scholastically and by way of exercise.

Accordingly, I submit all that has been said and all that is to be said to the correction of holy Mother Church and of every wise person, asking for a devout reader and a charitable corrector.

Before descending to the exposition of the letter, however, I first set forth seven rules for interpreting sacred Scripture, which Isidore touches upon in the first book of *On the Highest Good*, chapter 20. Some call these rules “keys,” because through them the understanding of Scripture is opened in many places.

The first concerns the Lord Jesus Christ and his mystical body, which is the Church. Because of the connection between head and body, sacred Scripture sometimes speaks of both under one context, as though under one person, passing from one to the other. For example, Isaiah 61 says: “He clothed me with garments of salvation, and covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom adorned with a crown and as a bride adorned with her jewels.”

What is said here—“as a bridegroom,” and so forth—is understood of Christ; what follows—“as a bride,” and so forth—is understood of the Church itself.

Likewise, Song of Songs 1 says: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth, for your breasts are better than wine.” When it says, “Let him kiss me,” and so forth, this is the voice of the bride desiring to enjoy the bridegroom; what follows, “for your breasts are better,” and so forth, is the voice of the bridegroom commending the bride. Therefore, in such passages, which are connected for the reason given above, the prudent reader should attend to what pertains to the head and what to the body.

[Col. 0031C] The second rule concerns the true and simulated body of the Lord. The Church, which is the mystical body of the Lord, as was said above, is like a net not yet drawn onto the shore. Therefore it contains the wicked mixed with the good until the judgment, when the former will be separated from the latter.

For this reason, in sacred Scripture the wicked are sometimes commended together with the good among whom they are mixed, as in Hosea 11: “Israel was a child, and I loved him.” Conversely, the good are sometimes reproved together with the wicked, as in Isaiah 1: “The ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood.”

Sometimes, even within the same text, what pertains to the good and what pertains to the wicked is expressed, as in Song of Songs 1: “I am black, but beautiful, daughter of Jerusalem, like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon.”

These are the words of the bride. On account of the wicked contained in the Church she says, “I am black”; but on account of the good she adds, “but beautiful.”

What follows—“like the tents of Kedar”—is referred to the wicked. Kedar was a son of Ishmael, as Genesis 25 states, and from him the Saracens descended. What follows—“like the skins of Solomon”—is referred to us. For by Solomon here God himself is understood, according to Catholic and Hebrew interpreters; therefore his skins are those with which the tabernacle was covered, in which the good worshiped God.

The third rule concerns spirit and letter, insofar as historical and mystical senses are received under the same letter. The truth of the history is to be maintained, yet it is to be referred to spiritual understanding. This is the way in which this rule is commonly explained.

It may also be explained otherwise, so that it refers only to the literal sense, as do the other rules. Concerning this, it should be considered that the same letter sometimes has two literal senses. For example, 1 Chronicles 17 says that the Lord spoke of Solomon: “I will be his father, and he shall be my son.” Literally, this is understood of Solomon, insofar as in his youth he was God’s son by adoption. For this reason the prophet Nathan called him beloved of the Lord, as stated in 2 Samuel 12.

The same authority—“I will be his father,” and so forth—is brought forward by the Apostle in Hebrews 1 as literally spoken of Christ. This is clear from the fact that the Apostle introduces it to prove that Christ was greater than the angels. Such a proof cannot be made through the mystical sense, as Augustine says against Vincentius the Donatist, as cited above.

The foregoing authority was fulfilled literally in Solomon, though less perfectly, because he was God’s son only by grace; in Christ it was fulfilled more perfectly, because he is God’s Son by nature.

Although both interpretations are simply literal, the second, concerning Christ, is nevertheless spiritual and mystical in a qualified sense, insofar as Solomon was a figure of Christ.

The fourth rule concerns species and genus, or part and whole, when the text passes from one to the other and conversely. Thus Isaiah 13 first speaks specifically against Babylon, when it says: “The burden of Babylon,” and so forth; then it passes to understanding the statement generally of the whole world, when it adds: “From the summit of heaven the Lord, and the vessels of his wrath, to destroy the whole earth.”

Afterward it returns to speaking specifically against Babylon, when it says: “Behold, I will raise up the Medes against you, who will not seek silver,” and so forth, because Darius the Mede, together with Cyrus his grandson, captured Babylon and killed Belshazzar, king of Babylon, as stated in Daniel 5.

The fifth rule concerns times, and occurs in four ways.

First, through synecdoche, when part of a period of time is put for the whole, as when the Gospel says that Christ lay in the tomb for three days, although the first and third days were not complete.

Second, because of fractions of time, which are sometimes counted in Scripture and sometimes omitted. Accordingly, when sacred Scripture speaks in several places of a certain number of years, it sometimes gives more years in one place by counting the aforementioned fractions, while in another place it gives fewer by omitting them.

Third, because the reckoning of years begins in one place from an earlier point and in another from a later point. Thus in Genesis 15 it was said to Abraham: “Your offspring will be strangers for four hundred years.” In Exodus 12 it is said concerning this sojourn that the dwelling of the children of Israel in the land of Egypt lasted four hundred and thirty years.

The reckoning of the larger number begins from the time when it was said to Abraham in Genesis 12: “Go out from your land,” and so forth. The reckoning of the smaller number begins from Isaac’s birth, which occurred thirty years after Abraham’s departure from Aram, as will be seen more fully below in Exodus 12.

Fourth, this occurs because sacred Scripture speaks of the future in the manner of the past, as in Isaiah 9: “A child is born to us,” and so forth. This is to indicate the certainty of the prophecy, whose future event is as certain as if it had already taken place.

This is because of the certainty of divine foreknowledge, from which revelation is made to the prophet. It should nevertheless be observed that this manner of speaking applies only to predestination prophecy. This occurs when some contingent future event is revealed to the prophet in the manner in which it exists in God’s foreknowledge, which infallibly beholds future things as present and past things.

It does not apply to threatening prophecy, which occurs when some punishment is revealed to the prophet as about to be inflicted upon a people or an individual, not according to the manner in which it exists in God’s foreknowledge, but according to the order of secondary causes—for example, according to human demerits. Such is the prophecy in Jonah 3: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” The sins of that city deserved this overthrow.

Nevertheless, because such a cause is changeable, the effect sometimes does not follow. This is what happened in the case at hand: the Ninevites did penance, and thus the Lord did not inflict the threatened punishment.

The sixth rule concerns recapitulation and anticipation. In sacred Scripture, events and deeds are not always written in the same order in which they occur. Therefore, when later events are placed first, this is called anticipation; when the reverse occurs, it is called recapitulation.

Thus Genesis 10 says concerning the sons of Noah: “From these the islands of the nations were divided in their lands, each according to his language,” and so forth. Later in the same chapter it says: “These are the sons of Ham according to their families and languages and generations,” and so forth. Then in chapter 11 it says: “Now the earth had one language and the same words.”

It is therefore clear that the statement made beforehand concerning the division of languages is made by anticipation.

Likewise, in Genesis 2, after Moses had described in chapter 1 the creation of heaven and earth, and the distinction and adornment of the parts of the world, it is said: [Col. 0034A] “These are the generations of heaven and earth on the day when they were created.” It is therefore clear that this is said by recapitulation.

The seventh rule concerns the devil and his body. According to what blessed Gregory says in Homily 10, the devil is certainly the head of all the wicked, and all the wicked are members of this head. Therefore, because of the connection between head and members, Scripture, when speaking of one, passes in the same context to speak of the other.

Thus Isaiah 14, while speaking of the king of Babylon, who was a member of the devil, passes to speak of the prince of demons when it adds there: “How you have fallen from heaven, Lucifer, who used to rise in the morning!”

Likewise, Ezekiel 28, while speaking of the prince of Tyre, passes to speak of the devil when it adds: “You were the seal of likeness, full of wisdom and perfect in beauty; you were in the delights of the paradise of God.”

With these rules, or keys, for interpreting sacred Scripture set forth, let us now, with confidence in divine assistance, descend to the exposition of the letter.

[Col. 0033]

## PROLOGUE OF THE SAME NICHOLAS OF LYRA ON THE MORAL INTERPRETATIONS OF THE BIBLE

[Col. 0033B] “I saw in the right hand of him who sat upon the throne a book written within and without.” (Revelation 5.)

He who sits upon the throne of glory is the glorious and exalted God, ruling the universe. In his right hand is sacred Scripture, divinely given, according to what is said in Deuteronomy 33: “At his right hand was a fiery law.”

The Law of the Old and New Testaments is rightly called fiery because it was inspired through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, who is divine fire.

This Scripture is also rightly called a book written within and without: outside, with respect to the literal sense; inside, with respect to the mystical sense hidden beneath the letter.

For God, who is the author of this Scripture, uses not only words to signify something, but also the things signified through words. Thus the events of the Old Testament signified those that take place in the New Testament, as the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 10: “All these things happened to them as figures.”

The sense signified through words is properly called literal; the sense signified through things is called mystical. The latter is threefold: if something pertaining to the articles of faith is signified in this way, it is called allegorical; if it pertains to matters to be done, it is called moral; and if it pertains to things to be hoped for in future blessedness, it is called anagogical—ἀναγωγικός, that is, mystical, leading us upward. Hence the verse:

The letter teaches what was done; allegory, what you should believe;  
The moral sense, what you should do; anagogy, where you should strive.

An example is found in the name “Jerusalem.” According to the literal sense, it signifies a certain city situated in the land of Judea. Since this city was chosen by God for divine worship, as stated in 1 Kings 14, and since God is worshiped in the soul of the just man, in the Church militant, and also in the Church triumphant, Jerusalem in sacred Scripture therefore signifies, according to the moral sense, the faithful soul; according to the allegorical sense, the Church militant; and according to the anagogical sense, the Church triumphant.

It should be understood, however, that although sacred Scripture has the four senses mentioned above, this is not so in every part of it, according to what is said in the *Collations of the Fathers*, Collation 8.

In some passages it has only the literal sense, as in Deuteronomy 6: “Hear, O Israel: the Lord your God is one Lord. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and so forth. In these and similar passages, a mystical sense is not to be sought.

In some places, properly speaking, it does not have a literal sense. For example, Judges 9 says: “The trees went to anoint a king over themselves,” and so forth. Likewise Matthew 5 says: “If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you.”

The literal sense is properly that which is signified, as was said above, and such a sense is not present here or in similar passages. Otherwise it would follow that the sense of sacred Scripture was false, since trees never did this and could not do it. Likewise, the Savior did not literally command a person to cut off his hand.

In these passages, therefore, there is only the mystical sense, which is understood through the things signified. The trees signify the inhabitants of the city of Shechem, who made Abimelech king over themselves, as the text itself explains. The hand that is to be cut off signifies a friend, however close, who provides an occasion of ruin; a person ought to cut off such familiarity from himself.

When certain doctors say that the parabolic sense is literal, this is to be understood broadly. Where there is no sense signified through words, the parabolic sense is primary; therefore, speaking broadly, it is called literal, since it is first when no other sense is present. To signify this, they say that the parabolic sense is contained under the literal sense. In this manner of speaking, I have called the parabolic sense literal in several places when writing on the books of sacred Scripture.

In some places, however, sacred Scripture has both a literal and a mystical sense. Thus in Genesis it is said that Abraham had two sons, Isaac and Ishmael. This is true according to the literal sense and likewise according to the mystical sense. For allegorically those two sons signified the two Testaments, as the Apostle says in Galatians 4.

In the same way, morally they can signify two spiritual sons of one prelate, one of whom would advance and the other decline; and anagogically, angels standing and falling.

Moreover, as was said, the mystical sense is that which is signified through things. A single thing, considered in itself, has several real properties, sometimes very different from one another. Therefore one thing, considered in itself, sometimes signifies several and different things mystically.

Thus, by its property of steadfastness, a lion signifies Christ in Revelation 5: “Behold, the lion of the tribe of Judah has conquered”; but by its voracity it signifies the devil, in 1 Peter 5: “Your adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, prowls around seeking someone to devour.”

After expounding sacred Scripture with God’s help according to the literal sense, and after God granted me an extension of life, I intend, trusting in God’s assistance, to expound it again according to the mystical sense wherever it is to be expounded mystically, insofar as the Lord grants me this.

I do not, however, intend to write down every mystical sense or to proceed through every single word. Rather, I will arrange certain matters briefly, to which readers of the Bible and preachers of the word of God may have recourse as and when they deem it useful.

Let no one wonder if I omit many things in the mystical exposition. I will do so for the sake of brevity, and because earlier interpreters did the same. Christ also did so: when explaining the parable of the sower in Matthew 13 and Mark 4, he left unexplained what is said at the end—“Some produced fruit, a hundredfold, some sixtyfold, and some thirtyfold.” He did the same in his explanations of other parables.

Accordingly, in the name of Jesus Christ I will begin with the book of Genesis and proceed successively through the others for as long as the Lord, by his grace, grants me life.

[Col. 0035]

## ADDITIONS TO THE POSTILLA OF MASTER NICHOLAS OF LYRA ON THE BIBLE, PUBLISHED BY THE REVEREND FATHER LORD PAUL OF BURGOS, MASTER OF THEOLOGY, BISHOP OF BURGOS AND ARCHCHANCELLOR OF THE MOST SERENE PRINCE LORD JOHN, KING OF CASTILE AND LEÓN, BEGIN HERE

He dedicated them to the venerable Alphonso, doctor of laws and dean of Compostela, his son born in lawful marriage, prefacing them with a prologue in the following form.

He completed them in the year of the Lord 1429. They also contain the Replies of Master Matthias Döring, a friar of the same Order of Friars Minor and an excellent theologian, as will become clearer in the course of the work.

[Col. 0035B] What do you wish me to give you while I am alive, dearest son—or to leave you by way of inheritance after my death—except something that may contribute to knowledge of the sacred Scriptures and confirm your steps in the firmest zeal for Catholic truth? For this is the truth that I carry in my heart and profess with my lips, and concerning which I think it was written: “The father will make his truth known to his children.” Since I had not received it from my earliest years, but had been born under the perfidy of Jewish blindness, and had not learned the sacred writings from sacred teachers, I was drawing erroneous interpretations from erroneous masters, striving rashly, like the other leaders of that perfidy, to twist the straightforward text by crooked sophistries.

But when it pleased him whose mercy has no measure to call me back from darkness to light, from the murky whirlwind to the clear air, the scales somehow fell from the eyes of my mind. I began to reread Holy Scripture with somewhat greater diligence, and now to seek the truth not perfidiously but humbly. Not trusting in the powers of my own intellect, I asked the Lord with all my heart to deign to impress upon my heart whatever would be more salutary for my soul; and night and day I awaited his help. Thus it came about that the desire for the Catholic faith burned more strongly in my mind from day to day, until I publicly professed the faith that I carried in my heart. At nearly the age you are now, I received the sacrament of baptism in the holy font of this church, taking the name Paul. You, then rejoicing in the innocence of infancy, were cleansed after me at that tender age by the sacred washing from original sin, before you could have been stained by actual sin, receiving the name Alfonso before you had learned to utter the names of letters.

As time went on, devoting myself to the study of the sacred writings, I applied myself to reading both Testaments. Sometimes I listened to living teachers; often, by the divine gift of mercy, I reread the works of the holy doctors and other distinguished men who had passed from this life. Thus I, who had previously been a teacher of error, became a disciple of truth, until I reached the old age that you see.

And, to tell you the truth, amid the pressures of the world and the cares of our court, by which I have at times been buffeted, this was my chief delight and my singular consolation: to contemplate the eternal and immutable God, and his wondrous works, in reading his holy and immaculate law.

Nor were the successes that the common people call prosperity lacking. For although wholly unworthy, by divine grace I was raised to no insignificant rank in the Church. First promoted to the see of Cartagena, and then to this see of Burgos, I was nourished by the Church of God with the greatest favors. Ecclesiastical honors were also joined to secular ones, since I was engaged in sufficiently close association both in the household of the glorious-memory just and most righteous King Henry and in that of his illustrious offspring, our renowned king, after undertaking a very high office.

How mercifully and piously the clemency of the Almighty has treated your elder brother and you, I shall not recount; you yourselves know it. There is one matter that I cannot consign to silence: that we, descended from Levitical blood, have been shown to some small degree the truth written so many centuries ago: “The tribe of Levi was not given a possession, because the Lord is its possession.” For God is our possession, and Christ is our inheritance. He, who was anciently proclaimed by the prophetic voice as the one who would purify the sons of Levi so that they might offer sacrifices to the Lord in justice, now permits the true sacrifice to be handled by our hands—may he accept it even as he endures it.

Nor do I want you to think that I have inserted these matters needlessly or boastfully, or that I have announced my life to you for no purpose. I consider it not superfluous but necessary to recognize the benefits of the Almighty; and an open and unfeigned confession of one’s own weakness should not be attributed to arrogance. This is especially so when I am speaking to you, from whose memory I would never wish these matters to fall away. Nor do I think that I would prove a sufficiently grateful recipient of such great benefits if, with my life, their acknowledgment also came to an end.

To you, then, I gladly recount these things among others, so that what you did not see by virtue of your age you may at least commit to memory by hearing it from your father, and so that you may often recount them, when occasion arises, to younger people who perhaps have not heard them; that they may recount them to their sons, lest they forget the works of the Lord but seek his law. Since study and discipline contribute greatly to a clearer pursuit of that law—and I see you, although occupied from childhood with the study of law, sometimes striving toward these things, and amid the studies of law and the business of forensic disputes attempting, as it were furtively, to chew over the ears of grain of both Testaments—I often resolved to stimulate you with some small gift and to assist your desire with paternal favor.

[Col. 0036D]

[Col. 0037A] And since, among the almost countless works by whose variety divine Scripture shines forth surrounded and adorned, the Postilla of Nicholas of Lyra is distinguished both by its relative recency and by the renown it deserves—for, diligently traversing both Testaments, he presented the literal sense, which is chief among the other senses, with abundant clarity—I resolved to give it to you.

Although detained by the peril of human frailty and ignorant of the end of my days, I nevertheless rightly suspect that, because of my age, it is approaching more quickly. I remember that I had already selected it for you from my library twice before. But since the mercy of the supreme Father has mercifully prolonged my life, it seemed to me that what I had intended to bequeath I should now give openly while still alive, and that I should enlarge a paternal gift with paternal additions, adding something—however little—to the treasury of him who has added days to my life. For just because we cannot give much, we are not permitted to withdraw our hand altogether.

Each person is a debtor to the extent that the powers of his intellect are able to pay; and no one is unable to pay before God when he is not asked for more than he can afford. Nor is a debtor richer when he possesses nothing that he has not received; rather, God’s mercy is content with what we are able to give, while his justice surpasses everything we can do.

When, therefore, I had gone through this Postilla and saw that it had been written with the greatest solemnity and astonishing abundance, I nevertheless considered it useful to add certain things in some places, since no human work is so perfect that something cannot be added to it, and since it is written only of divine Scripture: “Do not add anything to his words” (Prov. 30). I added especially in those places where I saw that the teachings of the saints had been passed over to some extent.

It was not my intention to investigate laboriously what I should supply. Rather, I gladly passed over the work without additions except where the additions themselves called me. Accordingly, I did not set out to write a volume, nor to boast of the title of a book, but to give you the Postilla itself with only a very few additions copied in the margin. Novice students themselves often do the same: when they read a book attentively, they fill the margins with little glosses written in their own hand, so that what they have read may be committed more firmly to memory.

I have not yet been able to go through the whole Postilla as I had intended, both because of the weight of age and the severity of the illnesses attached to it, because of the slowness of my intellect, because of the multitude of my occupations, and because of the variety of human circumstances that stand in the way and are sometimes abundant in these regions. But although I have not yet completed it in every respect, I immediately give you what has been traversed; the remainder I shall give you if God permits it to be completed. I did not wish to retain what had been written on the pretext of its incompleteness; rather, I wished at once to hand it over as a kind of earnest of our exchange.

This, then, is my testament, my son; these are my codicils. Recognize this bequest from them: “Let your will be in the law of the Lord, and meditate on his law day and night.” By rereading these and similar things, you will surely make your meditation purer and sweeter.

Receive this gift, therefore, with gratitude and with the filial affection with which it has been given by your father, and with a joyful hand. But let us leave these matters aside. Having invoked in the most humble prayers the aid of Almighty God, whose work we are undertaking, and from whom and with whom all wisdom has always existed and exists before the ages, let us now put our hand to the plow, expressing whatever we have added to this Postilla in plain style, with every flourish of language laid aside.

[Col. 0037D]

Above the first prologue of the Postilla, which begins, “All these things are the book of life.” Likewise above the second prologue of the same Postilla, which begins, “I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne,” and so forth.

## THE ADDITION ABOVE BOTH PROLOGUES FOLLOWS

Since the Postillator’s intention is concerned chiefly with the literal sense, it therefore seems necessary to ask first whether the literal sense is more worthy than the other senses of sacred Scripture. It appears that it is not.

For according to the Apostle, 2 Corinthians 3: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” But the literal sense is properly founded upon the letter, whereas the spiritual sense is properly founded upon the spiritual signification by which the things signified through the letter signify other things in turn. Therefore the literal sense of sacred Scripture does not give life but kills, and consequently is not more worthy than the other senses.

Furthermore, the teaching obtained through the spiritual senses is more worthy than that obtained through the literal sense; therefore the spiritual senses are more worthy. The consequence is valid because “whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15). The assumption is proved as follows: through the allegorical sense we obtain what must be believed, which pertains to faith; through the anagogical sense, what must be hoped for, which pertains to hope; and through the tropological sense, what must be done, which pertains to charity. It is chiefly through these three virtues that God is worshiped, according to Augustine. Through the literal sense, however, we obtain history alone.

That the four senses mentioned above signify the four things just described is clear from the verse cited in the prologue of the Postilla, where it says:

> The letter teaches events, allegory what you should believe,  
> Tropology what you should do, anagogy what you should hope for.

Furthermore, according to the Philosopher, *Posterior Analytics* I: “Everything is for the sake of something else, and that thing is more important.” But the literal sense exists for the sake of the spiritual sense; therefore the spiritual sense is more worthy. The consequence is valid, and the antecedent is proved as to its second part: the literal sense stands in relation to the spiritual senses as a foundation stands to a building, as the Postillator states in his second prologue. It is clear, however, that the foundation exists for the sake of the building, and not conversely.

Furthermore, the literal sense is understood according to the first signification of the letter, by which words signify things, as is commonly held and as the Postillator states in his first prologue. But according to this first signification, by which words signify things, many false statements are found in sacred Scripture, especially when something is attributed to God that in no way belongs to God, such as local movement, as in Genesis 11: “God descended to see the city and the tower,” and so forth. The same is true of many other passages, whereas such things are not found in the spiritual sense. Therefore the literal sense is not more worthy.

Furthermore, what is more inward is more worthy than what is outward, both in bodily and in spiritual matters. In bodily things, those parts in which animal life principally consists are inward, such as the heart. The same is evident in spiritual matters: what is inward is stronger and more excellent in dignity, as is shown by the tabernacle of the covenant, in which the ark of the covenant was placed in the innermost place called the Holy of Holies, while other things were placed in more outward areas according to their degree of holiness, as is clear from Exodus 40 and likewise from 1 Kings 8.

The same is evident in the sacraments of the Church, in which invisible grace, given inwardly, is more worthy than the visible form that appears outwardly. Since the literal sense is said to be “written in the book outside,” while the mystical sense is “inside,” as is clear from Revelation 5 in the passage cited by the Postilla, where it says, “I saw in the right hand of the one seated upon the throne a book written within and without,” it follows that the literal sense is of lesser dignity in comparison with the spiritual sense.

Furthermore, human knowledge generally proceeds from less perfect things to more perfect ones. This is evident not only in the human sciences, which proceed from the senses and particulars and terminate in the highest causes of things, but also in matters pertaining to knowledge of divine things. Hence Romans 1: “The invisible things of God are clearly seen and understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made.” But in the study of sacred Scripture one must begin with an understanding of the literal sense, as the Postillator says in summary. Therefore the literal sense is not more worthy.

Furthermore, that sense of Scripture should be called more worthy which supplies the deficiency of another. But the spiritual sense sometimes supplies the deficiency of the literal sense. For Gregory says in the *Moralia*: “When the order of the history fails, the mystical understanding shows itself to us as though the doors had already been opened, as if it were plainly crying out: Since you recognize that the reason of the letter has failed, it remains for you to return without hesitation to the spiritual sense.” Therefore the literal sense is not more worthy than the spiritual.

### On the contrary

That sense to which alone the honor properly due to sacred Scripture belongs is more virtuous, or more worthy, than the other senses, since honor is the principal sign of virtue, as is stated in *Nicomachean Ethics* I. But the literal sense of sacred Scripture is such a sense. Therefore the literal sense is more worthy among the others.

The minor premise is clear from Augustine’s letter to Jerome: “For I have learned to show this honor only to the books of Scripture that are called canonical: to believe most firmly that none of their authors made an error in writing.” It is clear, however, that sacred Scripture does not possess this honor according to the spiritual sense. For if it did, an entirely effective argument could be drawn from such a spiritual sense, which would be contrary to Augustine in his letter to Vincent the Donatist, where he says that an effective argument is taken from the literal sense alone.

In this question six matters appear to require consideration:

1. What should be called the literal sense of sacred Scripture, and what the spiritual sense.
2. Whether every passage or text of sacred Scripture is expounded according to the four senses mentioned above.
3. Whether every passage or text of sacred Scripture has only one literal sense, or sometimes several.
4. If one text or one authority of sacred Scripture sometimes has several senses, which of them is to be preferred to the others.
5. Whether an effective argument can be drawn from every literal sense.
6. The answer to the question, and so forth.

[Col. 0039C] Concerning the first matter—namely, what should be called the literal sense of sacred Scripture and what the spiritual sense—it should be said that the literal sense is sometimes called that according to which a historical event is narrated literally. This seems to be what Gregory’s words mean in the third book of the *Moralia*, where, speaking of the literal sense, he says: “While it narrates the deed, it discloses the mystery.” Likewise, in the verse cited above it is said: “The letter teaches events.”

According to this account, however, only the historical portions of sacred Scripture would be said to have a historical or literal sense, and not the doctrinal or prophetic portions or similar passages, since in such passages no history seems to be narrated. But this conflicts with the common opinion of interpreters, who commonly attribute a literal sense to the authorities of sacred Scripture.

Accordingly, the literal sense is otherwise and more properly defined as the sense obtained through the signification of the letter, by which words signify things. The spiritual sense, on the other hand, is the sense obtained through the signification of the things signified by the words, as in the First Part, Question 1, last article. This is the common opinion followed by the Postillator in his prologue.

It must be noted, however, that the foregoing does not provide an adequate definition or description of the literal sense under discussion. For certain things are handed down in sacred Scripture which, if understood according to the signification by which words commonly signify things, would be false, as is evident in parabolic expressions and similar passages, as will become clear below.

Therefore the foregoing must be supplemented as follows: for a sense of sacred Scripture to be called literal, it is required that it be intended by the author of sacred Scripture, who is God. The reason is that the literal sense of any writing is the sense intended by its author, since words are signs of the passions that exist in the soul, as is stated in the First Book of *On Interpretation*. But it is established that the author of sacred Scripture is God. Thus it is clear that the literal sense under discussion is the sense intended by God and signified through the words contained in the letter.

It follows that the literal sense of sacred Scripture should not be called a sense that in any way conflicts with the authority or determination of the Church, however much such a sense may conform to the signification of the letter. Such a sense is not only not intended by the author but is heretical. Hence Jerome says: “Whoever understands Scripture otherwise than the sense of the Holy Spirit, by whom it was written, demands, may be called a heretic.” This is understood of one who twists his exposition of sacred Scripture so that it contradicts what has been revealed by the Holy Spirit, as in the Second Part of the Second Part, Question 11.

It also follows that a sense that conflicts with right reason must not be regarded as the literal sense. Such a sense is not intended by the author—namely, God, who is the first truth and from whom all truth derives. For this reason Augustine, in his commentary on Genesis according to the letter, says:

> Since divine Scripture can be expounded in many ways, no one should cling so rigidly to one exposition that, if it is established by certain reasoning that this is false, he would presume to assert that this is the sense of Scripture. For Scripture would thereby be ridiculed by unbelievers, and the way to belief would be closed to them.

So far Augustine.

The same must also be said of the spiritual sense of sacred Scripture, which is obtained through the signification of the things signified by the words contained in the letter: namely, that such a sense must not conflict with the authority of the Church or with right reason. For if it did, that spiritual sense could not be attributed to sacred Scripture, which was revealed by God, the highest truth.

Concerning the second matter—whether every passage or text of sacred Scripture is expounded according to the four senses mentioned above—it should be said that it is not. For Augustine says in Book II of his commentary on Genesis that in certain passages only the literal sense is to be sought.

This is plainly evident. There are many passages in the canonical books, both of the Old and of the New Testament, that possess nothing but a literal sense. This is clear in many passages, and especially in the two commandments of charity on which the whole law and the prophets depend, as stated in Matthew 22.

Although these commandments—“You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself”—contain many matters requiring or admitting exposition, pertaining both to the object of charity and to its interior and exterior acts, as well as to its order and other related matters, all of these nevertheless belong only to the literal sense. For in this passage the things signified by the word “God,” or by the word “neighbor,” or by the word “you shall love,” do not again signify other things from which a further spiritual sense might be obtained. Therefore everything handed down in the exposition of these commandments belongs only to their literal sense.

The same is generally true of the other moral commandments of the Old Testament and of many other passages, which I omit for the sake of brevity.

Many things are also handed down in the Gospels to which a mystical sense should not be assigned, but only a literal sense—for example, passages given as commandments, such as John 14: “You believe in God; believe also in me,” and similar passages. The same applies to passages given as counsels, such as Matthew 19: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give to the poor.” In these and similar passages, one should not seek a spiritual sense obtained from the things signified by the words, but only the literal sense obtained from the signification of the words, as is evident.

Likewise, when in Luke 8 Christ interprets his parable, saying, “The seed is the word of God,” and so forth, it is evident that those interpretive words need not have other spiritual senses, since the interpretation itself explains the preceding parable.

Similarly, the letters of Paul, which must be considered one of the principal parts of the New Testament, possess almost throughout only a literal sense. For there he speaks as the universal teacher of the Church, explaining and reconciling both Testaments.

Although the letters themselves contain profound and difficult matters pertaining to faith, as well as explanations of both Testaments, these are not handed down allegorically or anagogically but only literally. For Paul himself, speaking historically—that is, literally—shows how certain passages of Scripture are to be understood in a spiritual sense, as when in Galatians 4 he says of Abraham’s two sons, “These things are spoken allegorically.”

The Apostle’s words, therefore, are not to be allegorized or moralized, or treated in similar fashion; rather, they are to be unfolded so that their true literal senses may be drawn out. From these, many great and profound conclusions can be inferred discursively, just as in the other human sciences many conclusions are inferred discursively from certain and true principles, as stated in the First Part, Question 1, Article 7. All of these belong to the literal sense, from which they are rightly deduced.

Thus it is clear that not every passage of sacred Scripture is to be expounded according to four senses. Rather, as Saint Thomas notably teaches in the seventh *Quodlibet*, Question 24, sacred Scripture is sometimes to be expounded according to these four senses, sometimes according to three, sometimes according to two, and sometimes according to only one.

Thus things that, according to the literal sense, concern the events of the Old Testament may be expounded according to all four senses. Likewise, things literally said about Christ the head may be expounded literally concerning Christ’s deeds; allegorically, by referring them to his mystical body; morally, by referring the same things to our acts, which ought to be regulated according to Christ; and anagogically, insofar as in Christ the way of glory has been shown to us.

Things that are said literally about the Church may be expounded morally and anagogically. Things that are said morally according to the literal sense are customarily expounded only anagogically. Things that according to the literal sense pertain to the state of glory are not customarily expounded according to any other sense, because that state is not a figure of other things but is itself figured by all the others. All these matters, and others pertaining to them, are explained more fully in the question mentioned.

[Col. 0041C] Concerning the third matter—whether every passage or text of sacred Scripture has only one literal sense—it appears that it does not.

For according to Augustine, in his book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, three things belong to the literal sense. The first is when the letter is expounded simply; this he calls the historical sense. The second is when the cause of what is contained in the letter is assigned or explained; this sense he calls etymological. The third is when the truth of that letter is shown not to conflict with the truth of another Scripture; this he calls anagogical.

For example, when Genesis 2 is read: “The Lord God built the rib that he had taken from Adam into a woman,” and so forth, the historical sense of this statement is obtained when what is contained in the letter is simply expounded.

The etymological sense is obtained when the reason is given why the woman was formed from the man’s side rather than from another part of his body, and likewise why the rib was taken from him while he was sleeping and not while he was awake, as is discussed in Book II, Distinction 18.

The anagogical sense is obtained when it is shown that the truth of this statement does not conflict with the truth of another Scripture, where Genesis 1 says of the creation of humanity: “Male and female he created them,” and so forth. From this passage it appears that the male and the female of the human species were created simultaneously and at the same time, not successively, as though the woman had been taken from the man’s side after the creation of the man.

But careful consideration shows that Augustine’s analysis does not establish that three kinds of exposition are contained under the literal sense, so that each of them is properly a literal sense. Rather, the first exposition alone is the literal sense; the second gives the cause of the literal sense itself; and the third resolves a seeming contradiction in it.

Thus, although the second and third expositions pertain to the literal sense because they perfect or elucidate it, they are not properly to be called literal senses.

These three kinds of exposition pertaining to the literal sense may be understood in 2 Esdras 8, where it says: “They read in the book of the Law of God distinctly and clearly, and they added understanding.”

In the statement “they read in the book clearly,” one may understand the exposition of the letter itself. This is like the gateway to all the expositions that follow, without the opening of which no one can enter correctly into the other expositions.

When it says “and distinctly,” one may understand the anagogical sense named by Augustine, because contradictions that sometimes appear in the sacred Scriptures are resolved through proper and true distinctions.

When it then says, “and they added understanding,” one may understand knowledge of the cause of the law, or of the history, or of some statement of sacred Scripture. Since “to understand” means “to read inwardly,” the person who arrives at knowledge of the cause through knowledge of the effect is properly said to understand. This sense Augustine calls etymological.

But it must further be noted that under each of the three kinds of exposition mentioned above, which pertain to the literal sense as stated, there may be many species. For not only one cause but several causes may be assigned for a single statement; likewise, contradictions may be resolved not in only one way but in several, as is evident.

Furthermore, as regards the simple exposition of Scripture, which arises from the primary signification of a word, it is evident that several literal senses are handed down—not only by interpreters or writers generally, but also by holy doctors. This is clear in Genesis 1, where, as the Master says in Book II, Distinction 13, certain holy Fathers who examined the words and mysteries of God seem to have written almost as though they were offering different accounts.

Thus it is clear that not every text of sacred Scripture has only one literal sense.

If it is objected that, although different people attribute different senses to a sacred passage, it does not follow that there are several literal senses of that passage, but only that the literal sense is the one intended by the author, the answer is as follows.

According to Saint Thomas in the First Part, Question 1, because the author of sacred Scripture is God, who comprehends all things simultaneously in his simple intellect, it is not impossible, as Augustine says in Book III of the *Confessions*, that even according to the literal sense of sacred Scripture there should be several senses.

This must be understood provided that such senses conform to the letter and do not conflict with the determination of the Church or with right reason, as stated above; and likewise provided that they are mutually compatible.

When, however, two literal senses that are incompatible with one another are attributed to a sacred authority, it is necessary to say that only one of them is literal. Thus, for example, in Daniel 10, concerning the prince of the kingdom of Persia, Blessed Gregory states in the *Moralia* that he was a good angel presiding over the kingdom of Persia, while others say the opposite. The same situation arises in many other passages.

It should also be noted that the literal sense of sacred Scripture has such capacity or power that it contains virtually everything pertaining to faith, good morals, and the virtues. Hence the Master, who compiled the opinions of the Fathers in a brief volume, and in the exposition of whose volume later doctors or writers introduced, as it were, all theological matters, founded his entire work on testimonies of this literal sense.

For in his prologue he says:

> By God’s assistance we have assembled a volume from testimonies of truth founded for eternity.

It is clear that testimonies of truth founded for eternity are testimonies of sacred Scripture taken according to the literal sense. According to Augustine in the passage cited above, testimony or argument can be drawn from this sense alone.

But it must be considered in this connection that not everything obtained from sacred Scripture according to the literal sense is immediate, in the sense that it is understood from the primary signification of the letters. Sometimes the addition of another truth is required, from which, when joined to the literal sense, another truth may be deduced.

For example, in Luke 20, from the testimony of the words “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob,” Christ concludes against the Sadducees, who denied that human beings have another life after the present one. He argues as follows: “He is God either of the dead or of the living.” That is to say: From the literal sense we have learned that God is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and reason dictates that God is called the God of one who exists in reality. Therefore it follows that Abraham and Isaac existed in reality, which the Sadducees denied.

It is clear, however, that this conclusion is not deduced from the sense of the words “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac,” and so forth, unless the additional true proposition stated above is added. Thus the point is established.

It can also happen that such a conclusion is drawn from sacred Scripture through one deduction or through several successive deductions. The same occurs in the sciences or liberal arts: some conclusions are immediately deduced from first principles that are naturally known, while others are deduced through many mutually ordered intermediate steps, as is evident.

The true literal sense that arises from the primary signification of the letter should therefore be called the first literal sense. The subsequent senses are secondary senses, whose certainty depends upon the certainty of the first sense; the first sense is more certain than the secondary senses, just as first principles that are naturally known are more certain than the conclusions deduced from them.

This consideration should be kept in mind in many passages of sacred Scripture.

Concerning the fourth question—namely, when several literal senses are given for one passage of Sacred Scripture, which of them should be preferred to the others?—it should be said that no single general rule seems capable of being given here. Rather, certain considerations must be kept in view, presupposing what was said above in the first article concerning the literal sense.

First, that sense seems preferable whose conclusion rests more firmly upon reason. Hence, in the Decretals, Distinction 20, chapter *Decretales*: “For the more a person’s words rely upon reason, the greater their authority seems to be.” Likewise, that sense seems preferable to the others which agrees more closely with the text. Thus, according to Augustine in Book III of *On Christian Doctrine*, doubtful matters are to be determined according to the interpretation drawn from the clearer passages of Scripture. It is evident, however, that the clearer passages are those which conform more plainly to the wording of the text.

Likewise, all other things being equal, the literal sense handed down by the holy doctors is to be preferred to the other senses handed down by other interpreters. Hence, in the Decretals, in the chapter cited, the holy doctors are preferred to the supreme pontiffs in expositions of Sacred Scripture, and therefore, with still greater reason, to other writers. [Col. 0043C]

Again, when there are two senses of the text, neither of which conflicts with the authority of the Church or with right reason, but one is handed down by Catholics and the other by unbelievers, the Catholic sense should then be preferred. This is so, first, because it is more reasonable to presume that those who are within the bosom of the Church—to which Christ promised the Spirit of truth—possess the true understanding of Sacred Scripture than unbelievers, who commonly oppose the truth of faith; and, second, so that unbelievers may not be given occasion to believe that they interpret Sacred Scripture better than Catholics. Hence Pope Leo, in a certain letter to the bishop of Alexandria, says that the enemies of the cross of Christ lie in wait for us in our deeds and words; therefore, we should give them no occasion, however slight. [Col. 0043D]

For this reason it seems that when a passage of Sacred Scripture is interpreted in the same way by Catholics and unbelievers, the authority of that interpretation should be attributed to the Catholics, not to the unbelievers, for the reason given above—especially if that interpretation first arose among Catholics. The contrary, however, is found to some extent in the *Postilla*, as will be evident below, at Genesis 1, where the question is asked why on the second day it is not said, “And God saw that it was good,” as it is on the other days.

Nevertheless, when a plurality of literal senses occurs, it rarely happens that one of the aforesaid senses surpasses the others in every respect. Rather, one sense excels in one way and another in another way. Therefore, in such cases, the statement in Romans 14 seems applicable: “Let each person abound in his own sense,” always preserving the reverence and authority due to the saints. [Col. 0044A]

Concerning the fifth question—namely, whether an effective argument can be drawn from every literal sense of Sacred Scripture—it should be said that, although an effective argument can be drawn from the literal sense of Sacred Scripture alone, as Augustine makes clear in the passage cited above, an effective argument is not drawn from every literal sense of Sacred Scripture.

For since there are many passages in Sacred Scripture that are interpreted in different ways even by the holy doctors, as was said above in the third article, it follows that no effective argument can be drawn from any one of those conflicting senses; otherwise one would be arguing from a disjunction to one of its alternatives. If, however, such diverse senses agree in some respect, an effective argument may indeed be drawn from them—at least concerning the point on which they agree. Thus, in Daniel 9, concerning the calculation of the seventy weeks, although interpreters—both Hebrews and Latins—differ not only regarding the point from which the weeks begin but also regarding the course of the calculation, nevertheless, since according to all of them the final term of the weeks has long since passed into the past, an effective argument is drawn from that authority to conclude that Christ has already come, as will be clear in that passage. [Col. 0044B]

It follows from this that, when the literal sense of Sacred Scripture is not the same for everyone in certain passages, it may happen that a valid argument can be drawn from one literal sense against some people—for example, against those who hold that same literal sense—while no valid argument can be drawn from that sense against others, namely, those who maintain another interpretation or literal sense. This difference occurs especially often between us and unbelievers.

There are indeed passages of Sacred Scripture whose sense, which is literal and true among Catholics, is insufficient to furnish an effective argument against unbelievers or heretics. This does not, however, prevent that Catholic sense from being considered true and literal among Catholics. [Col. 0044C]

For example, when the Psalmist says, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Psalm 32), and so forth, the true and literal sense among Catholics is that by the Word of the Lord—that is, by the Son of the Father—the heavens were established. Among Catholics this interpretation is virtually necessary, and it also agrees with what is said in John 1: “And the Word was with God, and all things were made through him,” that is, through the Word.

Yet no effective argument is drawn from this sense against unbelievers who do not accept the Gospel. For they do not admit any real distinction in the divine nature, such that there is a divine person eternally proceeding from another by way of a mental word. Thus, when it is said, “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established,” they say that the Psalmist is speaking in a human manner—just as, when things are done at the command of some lord, they are said to have been done by his word. [Col. 0044D]

Nevertheless, from this authority a valid argument can be drawn among the faithful concerning the distinction of persons in the Godhead, as in the First Book of the *Sentences*, Distinction 2.

It follows that a Catholic explaining this authority of the Psalmist ought to explain it in a Catholic manner, without worrying whether an effective argument can be drawn from it against unbelievers who deny the Trinity. For it is not necessary that an argument be drawn from every literal sense for everyone, as has just been said.

The Postillator, however, seems to observe the opposite in this passage and in several others, as will be clear in their respective places. For he seems to believe that a sense is not literal unless a valid argument can be drawn from it even against opponents. This, however, must not be understood in that way, as has been said.

Concerning the sixth question—namely, in response to the principal question—it seems that the literal sense may be compared with the other senses in two ways: in one way universally, with respect to Sacred Scripture as a whole; and in another way particularly, with respect to certain particular passages of Sacred Scripture. [Col. 0045A]

If it is compared in the first way, and Sacred Scripture is considered insofar as it is principally speculative, then the literal sense is, in one respect, of the same dignity as the other senses, while in another respect it is more dignified than the others.

To understand this, one must know that one speculative science is said to be more dignified than another for two reasons. First, because of the dignity of its subject. For, as the Philosopher says in Book XI of *On Animals*: “The least knowledge that can be had of the highest things is more desirable than the most certain knowledge possessed concerning the least things.” [Col. 0045B]

According to this consideration, the literal sense and the spiritual sense of Sacred Scripture, taken generally, are of the same dignity. For under both senses the subject is the same, namely, God and creatures insofar as they are referred to God, as stated in the First Part, Question 1.

In another way, one science is said to be more dignified than another because of certainty. In this respect, that science is more dignified which is more certain. According to this consideration, it is clear that the literal sense is more dignified, since it is more certain than the others. The entire certainty of the other senses of Sacred Scripture depends upon the certainty of the literal sense. Hence Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine*: “There is nothing that is taught obscurely in one place of Sacred Scripture which is not explained clearly elsewhere.”

The reason is that a spiritual exposition must always have support from some literal exposition of Sacred Scripture, as is fully set forth in the *Quodlibet* and in the question cited above.

If, however, the literal sense is compared with the other senses with respect to particular passages of Sacred Scripture, it is evident that in many passages the spiritual sense is more dignified, because it treats of a higher subject. Thus, when we read in Genesis 21 that Abraham “had two sons,” and so forth, the Apostle interprets this allegorically in Galatians 4 as referring to the two Testaments. There it is clear that the allegorical sense is more dignified than the historical sense of that passage. The same is evident in many other cases. [Col. 0045C]

If Sacred Doctrine is considered insofar as it includes practical knowledge, then the literal and spiritual senses may likewise be compared in two ways, universally and particularly, as has been said.

If they are compared universally, then the literal and spiritual senses are of the same dignity. For that practical science or art is more dignified which is ordered to a further end, as civil science is more dignified than military science, according to Book I of the *Ethics*. It is evident, however, that the ultimate end of all Sacred Doctrine insofar as it is practical—whether according to the literal sense or according to the spiritual sense—is one and the same, namely, eternal beatitude.

If they are compared in the second way, according to particular passages, then it is evident that in some passages the spiritual sense is more dignified, as being closer to the ultimate end. This is clear in many ceremonial precepts, as when Deuteronomy 25 says: “You shall not muzzle the ox when it is treading out your grain.” The Apostle interprets this spiritually in 1 Corinthians 9, showing that the literal sense of that precept has little usefulness. He says: “Is it for oxen that God is concerned? Or does he not certainly speak for our sake?” And the same may be said of many other passages. [Col. 0045D]

There are also other considerations according to which the literal sense surpasses the spiritual senses. One concerns extension. The literal sense extends to every part of Sacred Scripture, for every passage of Sacred Scripture has some literal sense. The spiritual senses, however, do not extend to all of Sacred Scripture, as is clear from what was said in the second article.

Another consideration concerns universality. The literal sense is more common, or more universal, because even the uneducated, who are not capable of grasping intelligible things, apprehend spiritual realities through the literal sense—at least under corporeal likenesses—as stated in the First Part, Question 1, Article 9. It is evident, according to Book I of the *Ethics*, that the more universal a good is, the more divine it is. [Col. 0046A]

From these three considerations, then—by which the literal sense, considered simply in comparison with the other senses, is more dignified—three grounds may in some manner be taken for commending this *Postilla*, namely, that of Master Nicholas.

The first concerns the literal sense, which is more dignified than the others in the manner stated above. For among the *Postillae* that have come into common use, this *Postilla* attends more closely to the literal sense, leaving aside the other senses or touching upon them only briefly, as he himself says in the prologue.

The second concerns its extension. There have been certain solemn *Postillae* on particular or individual books of Sacred Scripture that did not extend to all the books. This one, however, extends to both Testaments, omitting nothing from them. [Col. 0046B]

The third concerns its universality, or common use. For this *Postilla*, at least in these regions of Spain and, as I believe, of France, is more widely used than the others, alongside the *Glossa ordinaria*. Not only theologians, but also jurists and others who desire to possess a clear understanding of Sacred Scripture have recourse to it.

Although, therefore, this *Postilla* is simply commendable on the basis of the three points mentioned above, there are nevertheless three other respects in which it seems, at least in certain passages, to be less adequate.

First, because it seems irrationally to place the expositions of the holy doctors below its own exposition in many passages, and sometimes even below the expositions of the Hebrews. This is inappropriate, as was said above in the fourth article. Among these holy doctors, it seems repeatedly and irrationally to attack Saint Thomas, sometimes expressly and sometimes tacitly. I firmly believe that the words of this holy doctor have been tested by the fire of charity and purified in many ways by the dictate of natural reason. The Postillator himself also frequently takes much from this holy doctor, although he cites him only in order to criticize him. [Col. 0046C]

Second, because he does not seem to have been sufficiently instructed in the Hebrew language, to which he often has recourse—as though he had learned it in childhood—but rather seems to have acquired his knowledge of it in adulthood through the borrowed assistance of others. This makes a great difference in many passages of Sacred Scripture, as will be clear in their respective places.

Third, because, as he himself says in the second prologue, among Hebrew doctors he relies chiefly upon Rabbi Solomon, who, he asserts, spoke more reasonably than the others for clarifying the literal sense. The contrary, however, is evident among the Hebrews. Although they regard Rabbi Solomon as a distinguished doctor in Talmudic matters, they do not do so in matters concerning faith and the exposition of Sacred Scripture. Rather, among them certain others are regarded as greater or more distinguished in such expositions, such as Rabbi Moses the Egyptian, Rabbi Moses of Gerona, Rabbi Aben Ezra, and others, as will now be seen. [Col. 0046D]

In order that the matters mentioned above, together with certain others, may become clearer—which is thought to be highly useful—I have considered the universal circulation of this *Postilla*, to which even unbelievers sometimes have recourse, and often not in order to learn but rather in order to criticize.

For, as the Master says in the prologue: “When dispositions and ways of life differ, the understanding of minds also differs.” Therefore, moved by zeal for divine truth, I resolved to pass through it and, wherever something seemed to require addition according to the measure of my weakness, to add it in the margins, and to give the *Postilla* itself to you together with the additions, as I said in the preface.

Do not, however, think of me as correcting or asserting anything rashly—God forbid!—but simply as proposing these matters to you and to others, if they should read them. I humbly and devoutly leave the definition of what I say, and its approval or rejection, to the judgment of the holy mother Church and of anyone who judges more rightly. [Col. 0047A]

When you wish to read one of these additions, you must first examine the complete statement of the *Postilla* in the same passage. For every addition presupposes that the Postillator’s statement in that place is already understood.

I am not unaware that this little work will not please everyone who may happen to read it. Rather, to speak with Bernard, I fear that on this account I may incur the indignation of many and that I may sometimes be judged superfluous and sometimes presumptuous.

But since I have not dared to lay hands upon the work as a new expositor, and since I have written nothing after the Fathers that is against the Fathers—but, as I believe, for the Fathers—and have instead presented this small work that you will see in a plain manner, leaving the mysteries of profound matters to those more experienced, I think that the charge of presumption is removed.

Nor do I believe that I incur the fault of superfluity, since I did not intend so much to expound Sacred Scripture—which many of our elders have already done—as to take an occasion from speaking about it: first, to stir up the devotion of my advancing age; second, to assist you in some measure by exhorting you to our studies; and third, because I took pleasure in speaking with you and thought it worthwhile to discuss this subject at greater length, since it was both honorable and useful. [Col. 0047B]

If, nevertheless, you find some superfluity or presumption—although I do not perceive it—you may perhaps discover it. For certain faults, especially spiritual ones, are sometimes unknown to their possessors. May the Savior, in his infinite clemency, deign to forgive them. As for you, bear with them patiently, considering the zeal rather than the result.

Let us now turn to the question proposed by responding to the arguments.

To the first, it should be said that when the Apostle says, “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3), he does not intend to distinguish between the literal and spiritual senses under discussion here. Rather, he distinguishes between the old law, which had been given in written letters—that is, on the tablets of the Decalogue and in the books of the Mosaic Law—and the new law, which was given in the spirit, namely, in hearts, as had been prophesied in Jeremiah 31. Hence the old law is called the law of the letter, and the new law the law of the spirit. [Col. 0047C]

Because the Old Testament gave knowledge of sin, by which concupiscence was increased incidentally through human wickedness, which always strives toward what is forbidden, but did not give grace by which a person might be assisted in fulfilling the divine commandments, the Apostle therefore says, “The letter kills”—that is, the law of the letter kills incidentally in the manner described above. But the new law, which is called the law of the spirit, gives life insofar as it is the law of grace, by which a person is assisted in fulfilling the divine commandments.

To the second, it should be said that the literal sense does not contain only history, namely, accounts of things done. It also contains what is to be done, as is clear from the commandments of charity, upon which, according to Christ’s teaching, the whole law depends.

Likewise, the literal sense contains what is to be believed, such as the unity of God in Deuteronomy 6: “Hear, Israel: your God is one”; and the Trinity of persons in Matthew 28: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”; and likewise other matters belonging to faith and hope. [Col. 0047D]

Hence, according to Thomas, in the First Part, Question 1, final article, in the response to the first argument, nothing necessary to faith is contained under the spiritual sense that Scripture does not somewhere clearly present under the literal sense. This is Augustine’s position in *On Christian Doctrine*. So much for him.

Therefore, from the fact that in certain passages of Sacred Scripture the literal sense teaches only events that occurred, it does not follow simply that through the literal sense one does not possess what must be believed, done, and hoped for as necessary to salvation.

To the third, it should be said that in spiritual matters the foundation is often said to be nobler or more dignified than the building. For Christ, who is incomparably more dignified than all the other elements presumed in the Church, is called the foundation. Hence 1 Corinthians 3 says: “No one can lay any foundation other than the one that has been laid, which is Christ Jesus.” [Col. 0048A]

This is said by way of likeness. For just as, in corporeal things, the foundation supports the building and precedes it, and when the foundation fails the building tends toward ruin, so in the spiritual building Christ supports the entire body of the Church and precedes it in dignity and causality, without him the ecclesiastical building would be emptied of meaning.

The same should be said, in its own way, of the literal sense: it is a foundation with respect to the other senses, by a certain likeness. For just as, when the foundation of a corporeal building is removed, the building tends toward ruin, so the entire spiritual sense of Sacred Scripture would collapse if the literal sense were wholly removed, since the spiritual sense concerning matters pertaining to salvation must be founded upon the literal sense, as has been said.

To the fourth, it should be said that many things in Sacred Scripture are presented parabolically or metaphorically, that is, under the likeness of corporeal things. This occurs for two reasons: first, from necessity; second, for usefulness. [Col. 0048B]

Because the weakness of our knowledge, which begins from the senses, cannot understand divine things unless they are veiled beneath a variety of sacred coverings, according to Dionysius in Book I of *The Celestial Hierarchy*, it is therefore necessary that divine things be communicated to us under such likenesses.

There is also a certain usefulness in this: spiritual realities are thereby presented, at least under corporeal likenesses, to the uneducated, who are not capable of grasping intelligible things. Hence, after the Savior had proposed the likeness, saying, “A sower went out to sow,” and so forth, he later said to the disciples: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom,” but to the others in parables, and so forth.

Thus, according to Thomas, in the First Part, Question 1, final article, in the response to the third argument: in such parabolic or metaphorical expressions, the parabolic sense is contained under the literal sense.

The reason is that words signify something properly and something figuratively. In such passages, the literal sense is not the figure itself but what is represented by the figure. Therefore, when Scripture speaks of God’s arm, the literal sense is not that God possesses such a corporeal limb, but what is signified by the limb, namely, operative power. [Col. 0048C]

The same should be said when God is said to descend, and in similar cases: the literal sense is not that God moves in some way, but that he acts in the manner of one who descends, applying his providence to lower things. Thus it is clear that from such expressions the literal sense of Sacred Scripture can never have something false underlying it.

To the fifth, it should be known that although the book of Sacred Scripture—of which Ezekiel 2 and Revelation 5 speak—is said to be “written on the outside” because of the literal sense, which is said to be more powerful insofar as it is immediately signified by the words, and is said to be “written within” because of the mystical or spiritual sense, which is more hidden, it does not follow that the literal sense is universally of lesser dignity. [Col. 0048D]

It is so only particularly, namely, in those passages of Sacred Scripture in which two senses occur together: one, the spiritual sense, which treats of a higher or more useful subject; and the other, the literal sense, which treats of events that occurred and are of lesser dignity, as was said above.

From this consideration, however, it follows that, speaking simply, the literal sense is more dignified, because knowledge of it extends not only to the wise, who understand mystical things, but also to the uneducated, in accordance with Romans 1: “I am under obligation both to the wise and to the foolish.”

It is therefore plainly said that the sense of Sacred Scripture is written within and without even according to the literal sense alone. For, as was established in the third article of this question, among the matters pertaining to the literal sense some are more inward than others.

To the sixth, it should be said that just as the study of human sciences begins from principles naturally known, so the properly ordered study of Sacred Scripture begins from the articles of faith divinely revealed in Sacred Scripture, which are founded upon the literal sense of Sacred Scripture. [Col. 0049A]

From these articles, together with other matters handed down in Sacred Scripture or discovered through true and correct reasoning, one proceeds to prove certain conclusions. Thus the Apostle, in 1 Corinthians 15, argues from Christ’s resurrection to the general resurrection.

Through this process one arrives at everything that is truthfully taught in sacred theology. All of it is reduced to the literal sense of Sacred Scripture itself, as has been said.

It is therefore clear that the study of Sacred Scripture begins with an understanding of its literal sense taken primarily, and ends with the matters handed down in that same Sacred Scripture or deduced from them in the manner described above. The other matters belonging to the spiritual sense must be founded upon these, as has been said. [Col. 0049B]

From this the excellence of the literal sense is clear, insofar as it includes, concerning divine knowledge through faith, both what functions in other sciences as understanding—namely, first principles—and what functions as science—namely, conclusions deduced from principles—as well as what concerns the highest causes of things, which belongs to wisdom, as in Book III of the *Ethics*.

But what the Apostle says in Romans 1—“The invisible things of God are perceived with the understanding through the things that have been made, from the creation of the world”—is properly understood of what is known about God through creatures, as the philosophers knew. Hence he says there: “What can be known about God is manifest to them,” and so forth.

To the seventh, it should be said that Gregory’s authority must not be understood to mean that the literal sense of Sacred Scripture—namely, the sense intended by the author—fails in any passage in such a way that it contains either something false or something entirely useless. [Col. 0049C]

The first would undermine the whole authority of Sacred Scripture, as Augustine says; the second would contradict the Apostle, who says: “Whatever was written was written for our instruction.”

Rather, because the literal sense understood from the signification by which words signify things sometimes fails, Gregory says that in such a case one must return to the signification by which the things signified through the words signify something further, which belongs to mystical exposition.

In such cases, the literal sense principally intended by the author is not the sense first understood through the signification of the words, but rather the sense obtained further through the signification of the things signified by the words.
