This occurs in Sacred Scripture in many ways. First, in parabolic expressions, as was said in the response to the fourth argument.

It also occurs when Scripture, speaking literally about one thing, passes to another of which the first is a figure, as is clear in the first and final rule of blessed Isidore, which are included in the second prologue of this *Postilla*. [Col. 0049D]

It also occurs when some history, understood solely according to the signification of the words, provides no instruction in faith or useful moral teaching, nor does it lead to any form of uprightness in human conduct, but rather seems to introduce or approve some appearance of evil. In such a history, a sense adapted according to mystical signification and useful for one of the purposes just mentioned must therefore necessarily be sought, in accordance with Isaiah 48: “I am the Lord, teaching you what is useful.”

Gregory’s words in the authority cited above also suggest this, when he says, “When the order of the history fails.” For sacred history is ordered toward our instruction. When, however, it fails in this respect according to the signification of the words, it is evident that the order of the history fails. Thus, without doubt, one must return to the spiritual sense in the manner described above, which in such cases is to be regarded as the literal sense.

An example is found in 1 Kings 1, in the story of Abishag, who was brought to David in his old age, as Jerome notably explains there. (See the second Addition in that passage.) [Col. 0050A]

This failure in the sense understood solely according to the signification of the words frequently occurs in Sacred Scripture in the manner described above. Therefore, in such passages one must have recourse to the authority of blessed Gregory just mentioned, which deserves very close attention.

## Copy of a Certain Letter Sent to the Author of the Additions by a Certain Master in Sacred Scripture of the Order of Friars Minor, Against the Determination of the Question Above

Most honored prelate,

As another aged Simeon, renowned for your study of divine law, you have offered your venerable old age as an evening sacrifice. In this you may perhaps have received from the Holy Spirit the answer that you would not see death before you had first illuminated, through explanatory additions, the literal explanations of both Testaments—as though a vein of life were present and its light were visible in your light.

For this reason, praise and honor are due to you in the Church of the saints, just as they have been granted to others who elucidate Sacred Scripture.

And because, most honored prelate, summit and shepherd, mirror and luminous image, the prologue introducing your work, entitled *Additions*, reached the hands of me, a poor and sighing Friar Minor—first by reputation, then in writing—I perceived in it your mind’s uprightness, planted together with a branch of the good natural law, [Col. 0050B]

[Note: [Col. 0049] That is, growing on the same tree as the branch.]

which Paul inserts so that the fathers may treasure it for their children.

No less did I perceive the conclusion of the question in which your ingenious diligence asks whether the dignity of literal understanding surpasses the other senses of Sacred Scripture. In support of the contrary side, you brought forward eight Achillean arguments concerning the firm foundation of the truth in question, thereby greatly reinforcing its solidity. In all this, assigning the decision due to the virtue of honor, you placed it under the sixth heading.

Although great usefulness abounds in all these matters, ingenious subtlety does not refresh the elevated mind; nor does the affirmative determination of your question satisfy me, since its own supporting argument rather concludes the opposite. [Col. 0050C]

For just as an image is worshiped not on account of the image itself but on account of what is represented, so reverence and honor are given to the letter on account of the spirit. And that on account of which each thing exists is itself the more important; for honor and reverence pass over to the prototype.

It was not the golden vessel full of manna, the rod, and the tablets that were reverenced on account of the ark of the covenant; rather, the ark was reverenced on account of such things.

What are the interior things, unless they are spiritual understanding? What is the ark, unless it is the letter?

The vision of Ezekiel makes this still clearer, when it depicts these things more beautifully under the metaphor of a wheel within a wheel: a wheel within a wheel, the letter of grace within the letter of the law. It grants life not to these, but to spiritual understanding, when it adds: “And the spirit of life was in the wheels.” [Col. 0050D]

For this is the true life that the Word of life preached to Jewish blindness when he said: “Search the Scriptures,” and so forth.

Nor does the first determination satisfy me, nor the second, nor the third, nor the fourth, nor the fifth, and not even the sixth, where the literal sense is compared with the mystical sense. Between these senses comparison is impossible, because they belong to different species; comparison by degrees occurs only through the gradual intensification of a single specific nature.

For this reason, the argument based on the threefold consideration by which the literal sense, simply compared with the other senses, is said to be more dignified also fails.

It fails first with respect to extension, since all the sacred utterances are full of the Lord’s mysteries. Paul recognized this greater extension of the spirit beyond the letter when he said: “All these things happened to them in figure”—not only what was written, but also whatever was transmitted in any other way. [Col. 0051A]

For this reason the second argument also fails, namely, the argument from universality, since the more universal something is, the more communicable it is. But because of its limitation, the literal sense, according to famous doctors—and especially according to the Irrefutable Doctor—is incommunicable. It is not divided, but the mystical sense is multiplied almost without limit.

I will set out the doctor’s multiplication of senses. For, he says, a passage either concerns morals or faith. In the first way it is tropological; in the second way there are two possibilities, since it concerns either faith in the deity or faith in the humanity. If it concerns the deity, it is anagogical; if the humanity, allegorical.

The third argument also fails. For the dignity of these senses is considered according to the greater usefulness that follows from greater certainty, insofar as this depends upon the nature of the matter itself. The certainty of spiritual understanding is not the certainty of speculation, as is the certainty of literal understanding. Rather, it is the certainty of experience, according to affection and by way of taste, through the inspiration and testimony of the Holy Spirit.

From these considerations no basis arises for commending the *Postilla* of Doctor Nicholas. But, trusting in your benevolent disposition, to which I devoutly commend myself, I judge that the basis for commending it arises from the contrary qualities by which you strive, so undeservedly, to criticize Nicholas. [Col. 0051B]

A person is commended on the basis of his own work. Thus he placed the opinions of the doctors below his own as though they were irrelevant, in order to authorize his work through the doctors of the Church, from whom he did not depart.

Nor do you prove what you say, namely, that the words of Saint Thomas have been tested by the fire of charity, since in many of his determinations they have been attacked by many ingenious theologians—men of remarkable ability, whether they wrote as though they were in the body or outside the body, God knows.

Second, he is commended not for possessing the proper character of the Hebrew language, which he did not suck in with milk, but for the truth of his judgment, in which he did not err, mingling it with the theological formation by which he was nourished.

Third, he is commended for having chosen Rabbi Solomon from among all the Hebrew doctors, because he found him the better theologian among them all.

I write these matters—undigested as they are—to your well-digested prudence, most honored prelate, with a very short pen, commending to your ingenious knowledge the shortcomings of an ignorant pen. [Col. 0051C]

Nevertheless, with God as my witness, I am now more devoted to you than to one living in this world, since you are now more virtuous than other mortals. Out of reverence for you, I would have applied myself assiduously to your work had its presence come before me.

Farewell in grace, that you may live forever in glory.

## Copy of the Response to the Letter Above
Man of venerable religion, most dear brother and friend,

I acknowledge that I have received your letter. At its beginning you call me another Simeon, with whom I believe myself to resemble in nothing, except perhaps in old age—would that it were fruitful! But after surveying the course of your letter somewhat, I could rather call you another Samaritan: for you have brought, with considerable artistry, the oil of praise together with the wine of criticism. I believe, however, that you have brought more of each than the occasion required. For I do not feel myself to be such and so great as you have described me; nor, insofar as the measure of my intellect enables me to understand them, do I find my statements, which are under discussion, deserving of your criticism. If they are, however, I shall gladly accept correction: for it is not my purpose to acquire a vain reputation, but to seek the truth. [Col. 0051D]

But to pursue this matter at greater length: first, as regards your benevolent affection toward my person, from which I perceive that this oil has flowed, I give you thanks, and I judge it worthy of repayment with gratitude. As for the second, I willingly embrace its effect: iron is sharpened by iron, and truth shines forth more clearly through the resolution of opposites. I have therefore decided to proceed through your arguments one by one and, setting aside every rhetorical embellishment, to respond to each in plain words, such as we customarily use in investigations of the sciences, repeating your objections in their proper places so that, once all confusion has been removed, the truth of each matter may become more evident.

You say first, concerning my question in general:

> “Although great usefulness overflows in all these matters, nevertheless ingenious subtlety does not refresh an elevated mind.”

[Col. 0052A] On this point I am greatly astonished at your discretion. For if the words that overflow with great usefulness in the exposition of sacred Scripture do not refresh an elevated mind, what then? One of the prophets wrote: “I am the Lord, teaching you what is useful” (Isaiah 48). He did not say “what is subtle” or “ingenious.” For such things as, in your words, refresh an elevated mind, if they are distinguished from what is useful, seem rather to belong to thinking lofty thoughts than to sobriety.

Next you say that an affirmative determination of the question does not satisfy you, and so forth. From this it appears that you did not see, or perhaps did not carefully consider, my determination—especially in the sixth responsive article, where it is clearly stated that my decision or determination was not simply affirmative but discriminating. For there are three distinctions there: according to one, the natural sense is superior; according to another, it is of equal dignity; and according to another, it is even of lesser dignity than the spiritual sense.

Next you say that the reverence and honor due to the letter are on account of the spirit, “because of each thing, and of that thing more so”; from which you attempt to conclude that the literal sense is honored on account of the spiritual sense. To this you bring the example of the Ark of the Covenant, which was owed honor because of what it contained, and not conversely.

[Col. 0052B] My dearest brother, it seems to me that here you have confused the propositions. For if by “letter” you mean the characters expressed on tablets, and by “spirit” you mean the sense signified through them, your point is certainly granted—but your argument does nothing against me. For the literal sense is that which is first understood through the letter, and honor is due to it rather than to the material letter.

If, however, by “letter” you mean the literal sense, and by “spirit” the mystical or spiritual sense, then a distinction must be made. In certain passages of sacred Scripture—for example, in the historical books of the Old Testament, or in ceremonial matters and the like—the mystical sense is more worthy than the literal, as was shown in the sixth responsive article of the aforementioned question; [Col. 0052C] and in such cases the foregoing example of the Ark of the Covenant may have a place.

In other passages, however, where, according to Augustine, only the literal sense is sought, the example appears to have no place, as is evident in the very subject about which you are speaking. For in the tablets of the Testament enclosed in the Ark of the Covenant nothing other than the precepts of the Decalogue was contained. These precepts, moreover, are not expounded principally or commonly except according to the literal sense, to which all their expositions, however numerous, are reduced.

Next you introduce Ezekiel’s vision of the wheel within the wheel in order to demonstrate your position; but this plainly seems invalid. If you invoke this vision according to the literal sense, ask Master Nicholas, who follows the literal sense above all, and he will tell you that by the fourfold number of the animals and wheels in Ezekiel’s vision is understood the four successive kingdoms—[Col. 0052D] namely, those of the Chaldeans, Persians, Greeks, and Romans. Thus your authority, according to the literal sense, does nothing against me.

If, however, you invoke it according to the mystical or spiritual sense, consult Gregory, who elegantly expounded this vision in his Homilies on Ezekiel and explained the wheel within the wheel as the New Testament within the Old. It is evident, however, that in both Testaments, and consequently in both wheels, the literal sense is found.

But you say that although the literal sense and spiritual life are found in both Testaments, life is granted only to spiritual understanding, since it is added: “And the spirit of life was in the wheels.” Listen, I ask you: if by spiritual understanding you meant only the spiritual or mystical sense, excluding the literal sense, you would plainly depart from the truth of sacred doctrine. For it is evident that everything taught in sacred Scripture as necessarily to be believed or done for salvation is found under the literal sense.

[Col. 0053A] The mystery of the supreme Trinity and Unity, which holds the highest place among the things to be believed, is founded upon the authorities of sacred Scripture understood according to the literal sense. Hence Augustine, discussing the order to be observed when treating of the Trinity, says in Book IV of *On the Trinity*:

> “First, it must be demonstrated against the authorities of the sacred Scriptures whether the faith is so constituted; then against the chatterers,”

and so forth.

It is evident that the authorities of sacred Scripture which oblige us to believe in the mystery of the Holy Trinity are those which say this according to the literal sense. For, according to the same Augustine in *On Christian Doctrine*, an effective argument is taken only from such authorities. Hence all the testimonies which the Master adduces in Distinction 2 of Book I in order to establish this mystery are understood according to the literal sense, as is clear there.

As for the mystery of the Incarnation of the Word, in knowledge of which eternal life consists—for it is said, [Col. 0053B] “This is eternal life, that they may know you God, and your Son whom you sent” (John 17), and so forth—it is evident that everything concerning this which must be believed for salvation is principally taught in the literal sense.

Thus, when the Incarnation is spoken of—“The Word became flesh” (John 1)—this signifies the true Incarnation according to the literal sense. Likewise, when his death is spoken of—“Crying out with a loud voice, he expired” (Mark 15)—and similarly in the other matters concerning Christ’s humanity that must be believed, all these are found in the literal sense.

The same holds for the creation of the world and for the other articles of faith proposed to us for belief: all are found under the literal sense and therefore possess binding force, as has been said.

As for the things that must be done for salvation, I take only those two manifest commandments on which the whole law and the prophets depend, according to the Savior’s testimony: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart” (Matthew 12), and so forth; and “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (ibid.).

These commandments have [Col. 0053C] only a literal sense. For in this passage the things signified by the word “God,” or by the word “neighbor,” or by the word “you shall love,” do not in turn signify other things from which another sense is derived, as is evident.

And observe that not only the foregoing matters, which must be done for salvation, but also those belonging to the state of perfection and given as counsels are conveyed through the literal sense. Thus, when it is said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, and give to the poor” (Mark 19), all those things belonging to the state of perfection are included in these words understood according to the literal sense, as is evident.

Likewise, what sense conveys the doctrine of the Church’s sacraments, through which justifying grace is given or increased? Is it the literal or the mystical? There can be no doubt that it is the literal.

For when it is said, “Whoever believes and is baptized” (Mark 16), and so forth, [Col. 0053D] the institution of the sacrament of baptism is understood according to the literal sense. Similarly, when it is said, “My flesh is truly food, and whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood,” and so forth (John 6), the power or efficacy of the sacrament of the Eucharist is understood according to the literal sense of such sayings (*dictorum*; the printed text has the apparent OCR reading *doctorum*).

Likewise, through the literal sense of the statement, “Confess your sins to one another” (James 3), we understand the sacrament of penance.

Who, then, being of sound mind, would dare say that the spirit of life is not in the literal sense, when through it everything to be believed and done that pertains to spiritual life is taught?

But perhaps you would say that all the foregoing matters are also found in the mystical sense: for through the allegorical sense we have what is to be believed, and through the tropological sense what is to be done.

To this it must be replied that nothing necessary to faith or morals is contained under the spiritual sense that Scripture does not manifestly teach somewhere through the literal sense. [Col. 0054A] Hence Augustine says to Vincentius the Donatist:

> “Who would not be acting most imprudently in attempting to bring forward something placed in an allegory on his own behalf, unless he also had clear testimonies by whose light obscure things might be illuminated?”

But further, concerning the mystical sense, you seem to say the following: this is the true life which the Word of life preached to Jewish blindness when he said, “Search the Scriptures, in which you think you have eternal life” (John 5).

From these words of yours I gather that you judge Christ’s command to the Jews to search the Scriptures to mean that he commanded them to draw or extract from the sacred writings a spiritual or mystical sense. With due respect, I say that this contains no truth.

I dare tell you, brother: search through all the sacred Gospels of God, and you will never find Christ invoking any authority of sacred Scripture—whether to instruct his disciples, to answer disputing Jews, or even to respond to the devil’s temptation—except as [Col. 0054B] understood according to the literal sense.

Therefore Master Nicholas, rightly considering this, throughout his entire *Postilla* on the Old Testament, whenever a text is cited in the New Testament by Christ or by the disciples, always expounds it according to the literal sense. Indeed, he even explains the Psalmist’s statement, “The stone which the builders rejected has become the cornerstone” (Psalm 117), as referring to Christ according to the literal sense, because Christ applied that text to himself when citing it to the Jews.

Similarly, he attempts to reduce to the literal sense all the authorities of the Old Testament which the Apostle cites in Hebrews 1 to prove Christ’s divinity and his other mysteries, however much they may at first sight appear to have another meaning. This is necessary if they are to be effective in establishing the intended conclusion. The same is true in all the other passages of the entire *Postilla*.

From this it is concluded against you that Christ commanded them to search precisely these senses—the senses about which he himself taught, preached, and disputed daily. These are only [Col. 0054C] the literal senses, as has been said. Therefore Christ’s statement, “Search the Scriptures,” which you cite in support of your position, is explained by the aforementioned master as referring to the mysteries of Christ found in the sacred Scriptures understood according to the literal sense.

For, commenting on the words “Search the Scriptures,” he says:

> “Thus the Scripture of the Old Testament designates the time of his coming: Genesis 49, ‘The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah,’ and so forth; and Daniel 9, where the coming of the Holy of Holies is determined by a fixed number of weeks. It also determines the place of his birth, Micah 5: ‘And you, Bethlehem?’ It determines the manner of his birth, Isaiah 7: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive.’ It also determines the manner of his conduct, Zechariah 9: ‘Behold, your king comes to you.’ It determines the manner of his death, Isaiah 54: ‘Like a sheep he shall be led to the slaughter,’ and so forth. [Isaiah 54.] In brief, all the mysteries of Christ are found expressed in the Old Testament and fulfilled in Christ.”

Thus far he.

[Col. 0054D] It is evident, however, that all the foregoing authorities, cited by the Postillator, signify these mysteries according to the literal sense. It is therefore clear that when it is said, “Search the Scriptures,” this refers to the literal sense, which is the point at issue.

But perhaps you will say that the literal sense does not require searching, since it is received from the things signified by the word and thus immediately presents itself to the intellect with little examination or investigation of reason. It therefore seems superfluous for Christ to have preached “Search the Scriptures” to Jewish blindness, since they had been sufficiently instructed in this sense.

Not so, my brother, not so. For although the literal sense of sacred Scripture is received from the things signified by the word, many have nevertheless gone astray in discovering or acquiring it, both in the Old Testament and in the New. The reason is this:

Just as it is written through the prophet concerning the ways of the Lord—which are his commandments or counsels—“The ways of the Lord are straight, and the just shall walk in them; [Col. 0055A] but transgressors shall fall in them” (Hosea 14), so it occurs with the literal sense. Although it is straight—that is, plain—and the just—that is, those possessing the light of faith—shall walk in it, adhering to the intentions and things signified by the literal sense through faith, transgressors nevertheless—that is, those lacking this light, namely faith—shall fall in it.

In the Old Testament, the Jews contemporary with Christ went astray in many ways concerning this literal sense, as do their modern successors, who follow the errors of their predecessors, as is evident in many passages of the Gospel.

Thus, in the precepts of the Decalogue, which are principal among the commandments of the law, they erred so greatly that by the commandment concerning observance of the Sabbath they understood that it was literally forbidden for anyone to heal his neighbor on the Sabbath—something inhuman. Christ refuted them on this matter, showing that it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, saying:

> “Which of you, if he has one sheep and it falls on the Sabbath” (Matthew 12),

and so forth.

[Col. 0055B] Similarly, concerning homicide, they understood that only the killing of a human body was forbidden. The Lord opened their understanding, asserting that every wrongful impulse to harm one’s brother must be counted as homicide.

Augustine explains the same point against Faustus concerning all those matters of which it is said in the Gospel, “You have heard that it was said to the ancients.”

They also erred concerning the commandment to honor parents, nullifying God’s commandment on account of their tradition, as Matthew 15 and Mark 7 testify. For this reason Isaiah was said to speak concerning them: “This people honors me with their lips,” and so forth.

Regarding this and the other errors to which they adhered because they failed in the literal sense of sacred Scripture, the Gospel concludes concerning them: “They are blind, and leaders of the blind.”

Thus the Jewish blindness condemned by Christ consists in a false understanding of the literal sense.

This is also evident from the foregoing authorities of the Old Testament cited by the Postillator in connection with the words “Search the Scriptures.” These authorities signify the mysteries of Christ according to their true literal sense, as was said above. [Col. 0055C] Yet the Jews, perverting this literal sense in many ways, did not hesitate to deny the truth of the faith expressed through them. Hence Christ rightly says to them, “Search the Scriptures”—that is, attend carefully to the true literal sense contained in them.

It must also be observed that, since among the foregoing errors the more dangerous concerned knowledge of Christ, about which they were most obstinate—for Luke testifies that when Christ once explained to them in the synagogue the passage from Isaiah 61, “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me; therefore he has anointed me to preach to the poor,” and so forth, as referring to himself, they ultimately drove him outside the city in order to throw him down—it was deservedly to such people that Christ said, “Search the Scriptures.” For if they had possessed the true literal sense of those Scriptures, they would have found true testimony concerning Christ. Therefore he adds: “These are they which bear witness of me.”

[Col. 0055D] Testimony from sacred Scripture is certain only through the literal sense, as Augustine testifies in many places.

The same is evident in the New Testament. For if Arius had possessed the true literal sense of the statement, “I and the Father are one,” understanding this unity in the divine nature, and likewise had possessed the true understanding of the statement, “The Father is greater than I,” understanding the greatness with respect to the assumed nature, he would not have fallen into his condemned heresy.

But because he understood these statements literally in a manner different from that in which Catholics enlightened by the Holy Spirit understood them, he fell into the snare. Thus it is clear that the error in question consists in a false understanding of the literal sense of the Gospel; and the same must be understood of the other cases. From this the point at issue is evident.

Further, you say that the first, second, third, fourth, and fifth determinations of my decision do not satisfy you. [Col. 0056A] If you had shown the reason for your dissatisfaction, perhaps you would have been satisfied. But since you omitted to assign a reason, I offer you no response, except that one must beware of the insatiability of the heart, which is condemned in sacred Scripture.

With regard to the sixth point, since there you explained your mind, it is right to answer you.

You say first that comparison between the literal and mystical senses is impossible. I consider this very irrationally stated: first, because you yourself compare the aforementioned senses with one another—for you asserted that the mystical sense is more worthy, and consequently, according to you, they are comparable; second, because no rational person could deny that the Creator is more worthy than the creature, while the distance between Creator and creature exceeds every distance between created things, as is evident; and third, because these two senses of which we are speaking are species contained under the genus of exposition of sacred Scripture, as is clear from all the doctors who discuss the matter, such as Bede, Augustine, and others.

[Col. 0056B] For nothing prevents us from saying that, just as the human species is more worthy than the brute or irrational species, so one sense of expounding sacred Scripture may be more worthy than another.

Next, since I said in my conclusion that the literal sense was more worthy in respect of extension, because every proposition of sacred Scripture has a true literal sense, whereas the mystical senses do not extend throughout the whole of sacred Scripture, you object as follows:

> “This is mistaken, since all sacred utterances are full of the Lord’s mysteries.”

Here you seem to confuse the propositions by your use of the word “mystery” (*sacramentum*).

If you take “mystery” properly, as signifying the sacraments of the New Law and also of the Old, then your assumption is false. There are many utterances in which no mention of sacraments is made, regardless of the sense in which such utterances are taken.

If, however, by “mystery” you mean a sacred secret, so that it signifies the mystical sense, your assumption is likewise false. For it was shown in the second article of the question under discussion that there are many passages in sacred Scripture in which only the literal sense is to be sought; [Col. 0056C] this is also Augustine’s position in his treatment of Genesis according to the letter.

If, finally, by “mystery” you mean any sacred doctrine, then you speak truly—but this does nothing against me. For in those passages in which only the literal sense is to be sought there are many sacred teachings concerning faith or morals, as was established above. Thus it is clear that the extension of the literal sense remains fully effective.

But to prove your assumption—that the mystical senses extend throughout the whole of sacred Scripture—you cite the following:

> “Paul recognized this extension of the spirit beyond the letter when he said, ‘All these things happened to them in figure’ (1 Corinthians 10), not only things written, but also things handed down in any other way.”

If you attend carefully, this authority of Paul does nothing against me. He is speaking there only about the deeds of the people who lived under the Old Testament, whose life was prophetic. [Col. 0056D] Thus, after recounting in the same chapter certain of their deeds—both in the crossing of the sea and under the cloud, and the like—he concludes: “All these things happened to them in figure.”

He did not merely say “all things happened,” but added “all these things,” thereby showing that he was speaking only of those matters and similar ones.

Likewise, it is not said that all things were said to them in figure, but that they “happened” to them. This plainly shows that he is speaking of events that occurred, not of things revealed or commanded to them.

Did what is said in the Old Law—“Hear, Israel: your God is one” (Deuteronomy 6)—happen to them in figure? Or what is said, “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart,” and the like? Far from it. In such passages only the literal sense is to be sought, according to Augustine’s position.

[Col. 0057A] From this consideration the preeminence of the literal sense in respect of extension becomes even clearer. For it extends to the more notable and excellent authorities of sacred Scripture mentioned above, in which the mystical sense has no place.

Next you say that the literal sense is not more universal, because the more universal something is, the more communicable it is; but the literal sense, because of its limitation—and especially according to the Irrefragable Doctor—is incommunicable, since it is not divided, whereas the mystical sense is multiplied.

Attend, brother, I ask you: if you compare the senses of sacred Scripture with one another according to their limitation to the subjects they treat, it is evident that each mystical sense is limited to a particular subject. The tropological sense treats only of what must be done according to morals; the allegorical sense of what must be believed; the anagogical sense of what must be hoped for. The literal sense, however, treats of each of these and also plainly of things already accomplished.

Nor do I believe that the Irrefragable Doctor asserts the opposite. Thus your comparison rather supports my position.

Furthermore, if you have considered the universality that I attribute to the literal sense, it is sufficiently clear that it consists in this: not only the literate or wise, but also the uneducated, who are not suited to grasp intelligible things, nevertheless apprehend spiritual realities through the literal sense, at least under bodily likenesses, in accordance with the Apostle’s statement: “I am a debtor both to the wise and to the foolish” (Romans 1). In this respect the literal sense plainly possesses preeminence.

[Col. 0057B] You object here concerning incommunicability. If this is your opinion, you plainly depart from the truth. For the literal sense is communicated to every proposition of sacred Scripture, as has been said. Moreover, in many cases one passage has multiple literal expositions, as was shown in the third article of the question.

The literal sense is also an abyss containing many things, because of the great difficulties found within it concerning matters of faith and morals. This should not be surprising. [Col. 0057C] For in the books of the human sciences, in which only the literal sense is to be sought, there are very many commentaries and numerous expositions or writings. There are likewise multiple questions for understanding or clarifying the minds of the authors, as is evident in works on physics, metaphysics, and ethics.

The same holds in the faculties of both laws and in similar disciplines, in which neither the text nor the gloss contains any sense other than the literal.

If, therefore, in those works where only matters that can be known by the light of natural reason are treated, so many diverse commentaries, questions, expositions, and the like are found concerning the literal sense, how much more may multiple literal senses—or expositions, questions, and the like—be found in divine Scripture, where matters are treated that can be known only by supernatural light?

[Col. 0057D] Nor do I believe that you are unaware that, according to Augustine in his book *On the Usefulness of Believing*, the literal sense is divided into three species: historical, etymological, and anagogical, as I explained in the third article.

Similarly, the seven keys of its rule which Isidore gives in his book *On the Supreme Good*, and which the Postillator places in his prologue, are nothing other than certain species of the literal sense, as anyone who understands the matter can see.

From these points it is plainly evident that the literal sense is communicable and capable of multiplication.

You also say next that the dignity of these senses is assessed according to the greater usefulness that follows upon greater certainty. I grant this to you, insofar as it was more fully developed in the aforementioned question.

But when you add that the certainty of spiritual understanding is not speculative, as literal understanding is, but is the rectitude of experience, according to affect and by way of taste, through inspiration and the testimony of the Holy Spirit, you plainly confuse the propositions.

For you attribute to the spiritual or mystical sense what has a place in a spiritual person. [Col. 0058A] But it does not belong to the essence of the spiritual or mystical sense that it should give grace to the person who understands or discovers it. Nor is it necessary that one who possesses the true mystical or spiritual sense of sacred Scripture be in sanctifying grace.

For the correct discovery or possession of the spiritual or mystical sense, it is sufficient to possess or participate in the gift of prophecy or the gift of interpretation of utterances. Although these are graces, they are merely freely bestowed graces. Thus the certainty you describe as belonging to the manner of taste pertains to the gift of wisdom, according to which the spiritual person judges all things, even the deep things of God, according to the Apostle (1 Corinthians 2). But that is not the matter at issue.

From your statement it would also follow that no one could have certainty concerning any mystical or spiritual sense of sacred Scripture unless he were in grace. Since, under the common law, no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, it would follow that no one could know himself to possess such certainty concerning the aforementioned mystical sense under the common law. This would be entirely contrary to reason.

Next you say that I do not prove the words of Saint Thomas to have been tested by the fire of charity. [Col. 0058B] If you paid careful attention to my words, I said:

> “I believe the words of Saint Thomas to have been tested by the fire of charity.”

Therefore no further testimony is required concerning my belief than that in my sayings and writings I always follow this holy doctor—would that I did so worthily and sufficiently!

Nor am I unaware that his statements have been attacked in many matters by numerous ingenious theologians, admirable men, as you say. This does not hinder my belief or my continued adherence to him.

First, because true doctrines are often attacked, both in theological matters—whose principle is set in the sign that is contradicted—and among the Peripatetics. Second, because, as I firmly believe, those matters in which he is contradicted do not concern the exposition of any passage of sacred Scripture, whether it should be held in one way or another. For this reason, to me, who am concerned solely with the true understanding of sacred Scripture and divine matters, such questions are more curious than [Col. 0058C] fruitful.

Hence the Apostle says of similar matters that they produce questions rather than edification, and so forth.

Finally, you commend Master Nicholas because he placed the opinions of the holy doctors after his own opinion, in order, you say, to authorize his work. If you were simply commending him, you would certainly be acting rightly. He deserves commendation for expounding sacred Scripture with such great study and labor, in a plain and agreeable style.

But I am astonished that you commend him for placing his own opinions before the statements of the saints, as you say, in order to authorize his work, since sacred Scripture itself not only opposes such commendation. For it is written: “It is not the one who commends himself who is approved” (2 Corinthians 10); and Proverbs 27 says: “Let another’s mouth praise you, and not your own.”

Natural philosophy also teaches this. The Philosopher says: “We praise those who criticize themselves.” Conversely, to praise oneself or place oneself above others is not commendable—especially [Col. 0058D] since the Postillator of whom we are speaking, as a worthy professor of the Order of Friars Minor, should be thought to follow humility rather than presumption.

Those who wear soft clothing and live in kings’ houses are accustomed to think highly of themselves. Nor can I be persuaded to believe that you consider it worthy of commendation to place the opinion of Jerome, or of any holy doctor, after the statement of Rabbi Solomon—especially where reason does not support doing so.

Praise him, then, in those things in which he ought to be praised: namely, in the upright intention which I believe he possessed, and for the great labor that there is no doubt he endured in order to expound sacred Scripture, for the most part correctly. Do not praise him, however, because he sometimes departed improperly from the expositions of the holy doctors.

Second, you commend the Postillator because, through his theological habitus, he possessed the truth of the matter, although he had not imbibed the proper character of the Hebrew language with his milk. With due respect, this seems less [Col. 0059A] reasonably stated.

For it is well known that the theological habitus does not extend to possessing the gift of languages. Therefore, when a theologian says, “This is how it stands in the Hebrew truth,” while it is not found there, he is not thereby to be commended.

Third, you commend him because among the Hebrew doctors he found no better theologian than Rabbi Solomon.

On this point it is evident that if, in truth, Rabbi Solomon was less learned than others, he should not be commended because he followed him—especially in matters that depart from, and are inconsistent with, the authorities of the saints.

Commend him, then, as I have said, in those things and for those things in which he ought to be commended, and I shall gladly embrace your commendations.

In conclusion, therefore, dearest brother, do not think that I wished to criticize the Postillator, as you say. Far be that from me. Rather, I explicitly asserted in the aforementioned question that his *Postilla* should simply be [Col. 0060A] commended, although I feel that in certain passages it is less than sufficient. This is not considered a fault in an absolute sense, for no mortal can examine everything perfectly; Homer himself often nods.

In all the sciences, and especially in divine Scripture, one must always place truth first.

Would that you, dearest brother, were in my company, at least for a little while, so that together we might examine these little additions and you might learn by experience that, in those passages where I seem to depart from his statements, I proceeded out of zeal for the truth, not from a desire to criticize him. Nor did I depart from them by my own judgment, but by following the opinion of my predecessors.

Farewell, brother, in the Lord; and always strive after the better gifts, and so forth.

[Col. 0059]

# HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE TO THE REPLIES IN DEFENSE OF THE *POSTILLA* OF THE VENERABLE AND DEVOUT FATHER, BROTHER NICHOLAS OF LYRA

Issued from the additions of Lord Burgensis, edited by the venerable and religious Father, Brother Matthias Thoring, minister of the sacred Order of Friars Minor of the province of Saxony, at the request of very many who embrace the aforesaid *Postilla* as shining with truth.

## [Col. 0059B]

It was fitting that just and holy men should preserve ancient modesty and not burden others with regularly ordered but vexatious injuries. For just as things less well done require the file of correction, so things done excellently require praise and glory. But since complete perfection belongs only to divine matters, in all human works something deserving reproof may be found—yet with modesty, as blessed Augustine says at the beginning of the *Retractations*, a modesty that has a place not only in matters to be done but also in matters to be known. For, according to the true understanding of sacred Scripture, error does not occur concerning divine knowledge. Therefore Scripture alone claims for itself this honor: rightly understood, it stands without reproof, as blessed Dionysius maintains in chapter two of *On the Divine Names*; and nothing is contrary to it unless it is altogether false. Nor is anything absurd found in it, according to Augustine, *On Genesis*, book XI, chapter 1.

Diversity and contradiction, therefore, do not originate in that irrefragable doctrine itself, but in the fact that its interpreters have not attained its complete meaning, as blessed Hilary maintains in book II of *On the Trinity*. Yet this diversity among interpreters is not wholly useless; indeed, through it the sluggishness of students is shaken off, so that the truth may be sought. Thus heresies arising in the Church prove beneficial, as blessed Augustine says in book I of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*. All the ancient holy and Catholic interpreters of sacred Scripture, therefore, earned immortal thanks—not only by agreeing, but also by disagreeing with their successors while preserving the faith.

After them and through their venerable and holy labors, sons were born as teachers in place of their fathers; these moderns, in comparison with them, arose deserving no small praise. Laboring over the exposition of sacred Scripture so that they might possess the eternal life promised to such people, they elucidated it by seeking its literal sense as the more authoritative one. Among them Master Nicholas of Lyra, skilled alike in the Hebrew and Latin languages, is found to be the more universal and distinguished. God mercifully raised him up, illuminating his spirit as a younger child from the Order of Friars Minor. Once raised up in this way, he shared without envy what he had learned without deceit. Becoming a debtor to the wise and the foolish, to the great and the small, and wishing to satisfy them, he composed an outstanding work. In his poverty, like the poor widow, he offered it to the treasury of the holy Church for the benefit of those wishing to study; and he resolved to call this very work his *Postilla*.

This work of the *Postilla*, even if it possessed such adequacy that not only the small but also the great, and not only the faithful but also unbelievers, might seek in it the literal understanding of sacred Scripture concerning doubtful matters, nevertheless led Master Nicholas, as a truly humble man, to acknowledge himself imperfect. And as a pious man, acknowledging blame where perhaps there was none, he submitted himself and the writings composed through him to the determination of holy mother Church in the preface to his work, and begged the benevolent reader for charitable correction, knowing that no one is blessed in every respect.

Therefore Paulus, venerable archbishop of Burgos, judging that some matters had been explained by the Postillator less appropriately and others less fully, composed additions to Master Nicholas’s *Postilla*. In them he tried to correct what seemed to him less suitable and to supply what he judged to be lacking. But lest these corrections of Burgos diminish the authority of the Postillator among the uninstructed, I resolved to examine them. Whatever does not conflict with Nicholas’s statements I shall leave untouched; nor shall I force the matter where he explains a passage differently from the Postillator. For we know that even among holy teachers the same passage has various explanations. In those matters in which Nicholas corrects [Burgos], I shall show what and how much force those corrections have against the *Postilla*.

In this work, and in any other work composed by me or to be composed hereafter, I submit myself entirely to worthy and legitimate correctors. I presuppose concerning the literal sense—which both the Postillator and Burgos principally seek—what the adequate account of the literal sense is: namely, that the literal sense is that which is true, reasonable, intended by the Holy Spirit, and signified without absurdity through words or things. This adequate account of the literal sense is found in blessed Augustine’s *On Genesis Literally* and in blessed Gregory’s *Morals*, as Burgos cites him for this purpose in the discussion of the preliminary question.

### Reply against certain statements of Burgos in the preliminary question

## [Col. 0060D]

In article four of this question Burgos observes two things concerning the Postillator. First, that he gives greater weight to the exposition of unbelievers; second, that he concealed the reverence and authority due to the holy doctors. What is true in the first point will be stated at the place cited by Burgos, namely Genesis, chapter 1.

Concerning the second, it should be noted that the authority and reverence of the saints, when they spoke as saints, must always be venerated by the faithful, as is clear in distinction 15 of the *Decretum*, throughout. But when they spoke as human beings and from opinion, the saints themselves do not wish such honor to be accorded them, as is clear in book IV of *On Genesis Literally*, chapter 22. For the saints knew that one may contradict a wise person’s opinion of wisdom without fault; indeed, it seems beneficial for doubts to be raised in matters open to opinion.

For, as blessed Augustine says in book I of *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, heresies arising in the Church serve to shake off sluggishness. For the same reason, it is beneficial for contrary opinions to exist in the Church. That holy doctors hold contrary opinions in many passages of sacred Scripture is known only to one who is not ignorant of the sayings of the saints.

Nor do I think it objectionable that the statements of unbelievers should be used in the exposition of sacred Scripture and in the confirmation of difficulties that arise. Blessed Augustine does this in book III of the *Confessions* at the beginning, and in many other places, where he adopts and praises the statements of Cicero, Plato, and others. Everything that is not contrary to the faith may be adopted as assistance. For every truth is consonant with truth, according to the first book of the *Ethics*.

Perhaps, moreover, a truth of the faith stated by an unbeliever confirms matters belonging to the faith, as is said in book XI of *The City of God*, chapter 21. And in book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, blessed Augustine says for the present purpose:

> If they should happen to say something suitable to our faith, these things are not only not to be feared, but are to be reclaimed for our use from them as unjust possessors.

After giving the example of the Jews despoiling the Egyptians, he adds:

> Thus had Cyprian, that most gracious teacher and most blessed martyr, Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary acted.

Burgos therefore reproves the Postillator to no purpose on this point, since he himself also brings forward Aristotle’s statements several times.

In the article of his question, after truly praising the Postillator, Burgos himself censures him in three respects.

First, he says that in the *Postilla* the statements of the saints, especially those of Saint Thomas, are irrationally given secondary place. He says that Thomas’s statements have been examined by the fire of charity and purified in many ways by the dictate of natural reason.

To this I reply that Burgos should not have been displeased with the Postillator for doing what he himself often does. For in very many places—as will become clear in the course of this work—he gives secondary place, without justification, to blessed Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, Isidore, and Saint Thomas. This is not found in the Postillator, who rejects no statement of any saint unless he shows that it must be set aside on the basis of greater reason and authority.

In particular, a charge of lèse-majesté seems especially to apply to this Burgensian, since he appears to prefer the statements of Saint Thomas to those of Augustine, Gregory, Jerome, and others, as though the latter had not, like the former, been examined by the fire of charity and as though, unlike the former, they did not require retraction. Blessed Augustine says at the beginning of his *Retractations*:

> In much speaking sin will not be absent. Whoever does not hold the first place of wisdom, namely, teaching rightly, should at least hold the second, namely, retracting errors.

And he concludes:

> Those who will know these things should not imitate me in error, but in progress toward what is better.

It would have been modest for Burgos not to prefer Saint Thomas to blessed Augustine, as though all Saint Thomas’s statements were first truths, since many statements of blessed Augustine are matters of opinion today. He himself also considers his books *On Genesis Literally* to be more investigative than definitive. Moreover, some of his statements, even though not retracted, are not commonly accepted by the modern school, such as his account of the meaning of the works of the six days, and so forth. Burgos therefore should not be displeased if the statements of blessed Thomas are not accepted in every respect.

Second, Burgos observes against the Postillator that he was not perfect in the Hebrew language because he had not learned it from childhood. But this argument is invalid, since an old man may learn any language perfectly. Nor should Burgos have criticized the Postillator on this account; rather, he should have thanked him, because he devoted so much study to the exaltation of the Catholic faith and the love of sacred Scripture that, even as an adult, he merited to attain an understanding of the Hebrew language. If this is blameworthy, then blessed Jerome must likewise be blamed—which God forbid.

Third, Burgos faults the Postillator because he followed Rabbi Solomon rather than other Hebrews whom Burgos considers superior. I reply that the Postillator follows neither him nor the others except insofar as reason and faith permit. Indeed, those whom Burgos prefers to Rabbi Solomon are not found to have favored faith and reason more, or to have explained Scripture more clearly, than Rabbi Solomon, as will become clear in their proper places.

## [Col. 0061]

### Preliminary Materials of the Ordinary Gloss

(Augustine, *On Genesis Literally*, volume III, book I, chapter 21, [Note: [Col. 0061D] The reader is referred back to the volumes of our *Patrologia*. EDITOR.) “When we read all the divine books,” etc., up to “it is not useless to have drawn out a suitable meaning.”

[Col. 0062] (The same work, chapter 18.) “In obscure matters and matters most remote from our eyes,” etc., up to “since rather we ought to wish that what belongs to the Scriptures should be ours.”

[Col. 0063A] It should be noted that this Scripture is woven with allegorical words in such a way that it contains an allegorical sense without losing the historical truth of the events that occurred. It is called *Genesis* from its beginning, according to the custom of the Hebrews, who chiefly give books their names from their beginnings. Thus Matthew calls his Gospel history the “Book of Generation,” although both Scriptures contain much else in what follows in which no mention of generation is made.

This history introduces the first man as a figure of the future: formed from virgin earth, through whom earthly beings were to be generated for transitory life. The Gospel, correspondingly, introduces the new man, born from a virgin mother, who was to generate sons for eternal life. In this Scripture, therefore, there are figures of future things; in the Gospel, the manifestation of things accomplished.

According to Hebrew custom, this book is called *Genesis* from its beginning because it treats of the generation of heaven and earth, although many other matters follow, just as Matthew’s Gospel is called the “Book of the Generation of Jesus Christ.” Moses introduces the first man, formed from virgin earth, as a figure of the future, one who would generate earthly beings for transitory life; likewise, the Gospel introduces the second man, namely Christ, born from a virgin mother, who would generate heavenly beings for eternal life. Here, therefore, there is the figure; in the Gospel, the truth.

[Col. 0063B] (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, volume III, col. 937.) “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” “Most people suppose,” etc., up to “who give books their names from the beginnings of the books.”

There are four rules of sacred Scripture: history, which speaks of events that happened; allegory, in which one thing is understood from another; tropology, that is, moral discourse, in which the ordering of conduct is treated; and anagoge, that is, spiritual understanding, through which, when we are about to treat of lofty and heavenly matters, we are led upward. As though by four wheels, all divine Scripture is carried along by these four modes.

For example, according to history Jerusalem is a city; according to allegory it signifies the Church; according to tropology, that is, morality, it signifies the soul of every believer who longs for eternal peace; according to anagoge, it signifies the life of all heavenly beings who behold God with unveiled face.

At times divine Scripture makes eternal things known, as in: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). At times it narrates things that happened, as in: “When the Son of Man comes in his majesty,” and so forth. At times it commands what is to be done, as in: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Divine Scripture is divided in two, because some things are said according to figure, as in: “Adam heard the voice of the Lord walking in paradise”; others according to the truth of events, as in the fact that the people leaving Egypt walked on foot through the sea; and others are said in both ways, such as the crossing of the Red Sea and the miracles that the Lord performed in the Gospel.

This Scripture signifies in three ways that the generation of the world was brought about. Something is said to have been made by will alone, as in: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Or by will together with either a commanding utterance, as in: “Let there be light,” or a deliberative utterance, as in: “Let us make man in our image and likeness.” Or by will, utterance, and definition, as in: “Increase and multiply and fill the earth,” and: “Let the earth bring forth green vegetation producing seed,” and so forth.

Those things said to have been made by will alone and by utterance were made as new things. But those made through definition are similar to things newly made; these are the things that God works from the seventh day until the end, and they proceed from that definition.

Some posited three principles: God, exemplar, and matter, all uncreated and without beginning. They held that God did not create matter but, like a craftsman, made the world according to an exemplar from pre-existing matter. Others posited two principles, matter and form, together with a third called the operative principle; they held that the world always had existed and always would exist.

Opposing these and similar errors, Moses narrates, in one Spirit and at one beginning of time, that the world was made by God the Creator, with such speed that the effect preceded the perception of time. Knowing God as the beginning of all things, he teaches us to understand him as eternal and omnipotent: so great was the speed of the work that the first moment of the newly born world had not yet elapsed when the world is said to have been created, in these words: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

(STRABO.) “In the beginning,” and so forth. Moses relates that the world was made by God the Creator at one beginning of time, so that the effect of the will might precede the perception of time. Thus we know that God existed before the beginning of time and that he himself is the beginning of all things.

Plato considered there to be three beginnings or principles: God, exemplar, and matter—each uncreated and without beginning—and regarded God as an artisan, not a creator. Aristotle held there to be two: matter and form, with a third called the operative principle; he held that the world had always existed and always would. Against these and similar views, therefore, it is said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

(AUGUSTINE.) Just as Paul learned the Gospel through revelation, so Moses, taught by the Holy Spirit, learned the beginning of the created world.

In this book Moses treats of the lower world for the instruction of man. Since man was to be set above the visible world, he first describes the kingdom prepared for him, and afterward introduces the ruler whom the fullness of the kingdom was to serve. Thus he says: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.”

By the name of heaven and earth, whatever God made may be understood to have been made materially at the same time, but without form, whether it was spiritual or bodily. He then explains how God gave forms to individual things and established the distinctions among his works. Since the forms were not yet distinct, he adds concerning the earth: “The earth, however, was empty and void”—namely, with respect to those things that were to proceed from it. “And darkness was over the face of the abyss.” By the abyss the remaining elements may be understood, which were still confused and uncertain as to the forms they would possess.

God works in four ways. First, in the Word; second, in formless matter. Hence Ecclesiasticus 18: “He who lives forever created all things together.” Third, through the works of the six days he distinguished the various creatures. Fourth, from primordial seeds arise not unknown but known natures, which are repeatedly renewed so that they may not perish.

(AUGUSTINE, ISIDORE, BEDA.) Mystically. The beginnings of the human race, when it first began to enjoy the light itself, are rightly compared with the first day, on which God made light. This age should be regarded as the infancy of the whole universe, which we ought to conceive as one man in proportion to its magnitude. For when each human being is first born and comes forth into the light, he passes through his first age in infancy.

This age extends from Adam to Noah through ten generations. Its evening occurs in the Flood, because our infancy too is wiped away as though by a flood of forgetfulness. The morning of the second day begins with the time of Noah, like childhood, and this age extends to Abraham through another ten generations. It is rightly compared with the second day, on which the firmament was made between water and water, because the ark in which Noah and his family were was a firmament between the lower waters on which it floated and the upper waters by which it was drenched.

This age was not erased by the Flood, because neither is our childhood removed from memory through forgetfulness. We remember that we were children; we do not remember being infants. The evening of this age is the confusion of languages among those who were building the tower, and its morning comes from Abraham.

But this second age did not yet generate the people of the Lord, because childhood is not suited to generation. The morning of the third day begins with Abraham, and the third age follows, resembling adolescence. It is rightly compared with the third day, on which the earth was separated from the waters. For the faithful people are separated from all the nations whose error is unstable and movable in every direction, like all the winds, through the vain teachings of idols—which is well signified by the name “sea.”

The people of God were separated from this vanity of the nations and from the waves of this age through Abraham, like the earth when it appeared dry, that is, thirsting for the heavenly rain of divine commandments. By worshiping the one God, like watered earth able to bear useful fruits, this people received the sacred Scriptures and prophecies.

This age could already generate the people of God, because the third age, that is, adolescence, can already have children. Therefore it was said to Abraham in Genesis 17: “I have appointed you the father of many nations; I will increase you exceedingly, and I will make nations of you, and kings shall come from you. And I will establish my covenant,” and so forth.

This age extends from Abraham to David through fourteen generations. Its evening lies in the sins of the people, by which they transgressed the divine commandments, continuing until the wickedness of the worst of men, Saul. Then, mystically, the morning of the fourth day occurs: namely, the kingdom of David.

This age resembles youth. Indeed, among all the ages, youth reigns, and it is itself the firmament of all the ages. Therefore it is rightly compared with the fourth day, on which the stars of heaven were made in the firmament.

What signifies the eminence of a king more clearly than the splendor of the sun? The splendor of the moon displays the obedience of the people, as though it were the Synagogue itself; and the stars signify its leaders and everything founded in the stability of the kingdom, as in a firmament.

Its evening, so to speak, lies in the sins of the kings, through which that nation deserved to be taken captive. Then comes the morning of the fifth day: the migration to Babylon, when the people in captivity were gently placed in foreign leisure.

This age extends to the coming of Christ. It is the fifth age, corresponding to the decline from youth into old age—not yet old age, but no longer youth. It is the age of the elder, whom the Greeks call *presbytēs* (πρεσβύτης); for an old man they say not *presbytēs* but *gērōn* (γέρων).

Indeed, this age in the Jewish people was bent and broken away from the strength of the kingdom, just as a person passes from youth into the age of an elder. It is rightly compared with the fifth day, on which the animals in the waters and the birds of heaven were made. For then those people began to live among the nations as in the waters, possessing an uncertain and unstable dwelling like flying birds.

But clearly there were great sea creatures there—that is, great men—who ruled the waves of the world more than they served in that captivity. They were not corrupted by any terror into the worship of idols.

Here it should be observed that God blessed those animals, saying: “Increase and multiply and fill the waters of the sea, and let the birds multiply upon the earth.” For in truth the Jewish nation, since it was dispersed among the nations, has multiplied greatly.

The evening of this day, that is, of this age, is the multiplication of sins among the Jewish people, for they were so blinded that they could not recognize God and our Lord Jesus Christ.

Mystically, the morning of the sixth day is the preaching of the Gospel through Jesus. When the fifth day, that is, the fifth age, was completed, the sixth began: namely, the old age of the old man, in which man is less powerful and is tending toward the end of life.

This too is evident because that carnal kingdom has already been greatly worn down: the temple of God has been thrown down and the sacrifices have ceased. Now, as far as the strength of the kingdom is concerned, that nation is dragging out something like its final life.

Yet in this age, as in the old age of the old man, the new man is born, who now lives spiritually. For on the sixth day it was said: “Let the earth bring forth a living soul.” On the fifth day it had not been said, “Let the waters bring forth a living soul,” but rather, “reptiles of living souls.” For just as bodies are reptiles, so at that time the people of the nations still served the law in bodily circumcision and sacrifices, as in the sea.

But he calls this a living soul because they are now beginning to desire eternal life. The serpents and cattle that the earth produces signify the nations that are now to believe the Gospel with stability. Concerning them it is also said what was shown to Peter in the Acts of the Apostles, chapter 10: “Kill and eat.” When he said that they were unclean, the response was given to him: “What God has cleansed, you must not call common.”

Then man is made in the image and likeness of God, just as in this sixth age our Lord is born in the flesh, concerning whom it was said through the prophet: “And he is a man, and who will know him?” And just as male and female were joined on that day, so in this age Christ and the Church are joined.

On that day man is placed above cattle, serpents, and the birds of heaven. So also in this age Christ rules the souls obeying him, which came to his Church partly from the Jewish people and partly from the nations, so that they might be subdued by him and become tame: human beings devoted either to carnal desire, like cattle; or darkened by obscure curiosity, like serpents; or lifted up by pride, like birds.

And just as on that day man and the animals with him are fed by seed-bearing plants, fruit-bearing trees, and green herbs, so in this age every good man who is a minister of Christ and imitates him well, as far as he can, is spiritually nourished with the people by the food of the holy Scriptures and the law of God.

He is nourished partly for conceiving the fruitfulness of arguments and words, like seed-bearing plants; partly for the usefulness of morals and human conduct, like fruit-bearing trees; and partly for the vigor of faith, hope, and charity unto eternal life, like green herbs that cannot wither under the heat of any tribulations.

The spiritual person is nourished by these foods so that he understands many things; the carnal person, that is, the child in Christ, like God’s cattle, is nourished so that he believes many things he is not yet able to understand. Nevertheless, they all have the same foods.

The evening of this age is that of which the Lord says in Luke 18: “When the Son of Man comes, do you think he will find faith upon the earth?” After that evening the morning will come, when the Lord himself will come in glory.

Then those will rest with Christ from all their works to whom it was said in Matthew 5: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your heavenly Father is perfect.” Such people perform very good works; after such works rest is to be hoped for on the seventh day, which has no evening.

Therefore it cannot in any way be stated exactly how God made heaven and earth and every creature that he created. Yet this exposition, by arranging matters according to the days, indicates something like a history of events that happened, while chiefly observing the preaching of future things.

If anyone is troubled by the fact that, in these ages of the world, we observe the first two ages unfolded through ten generations each, while the three following ages are woven through fourteen generations each, and this sixth age is defined by no number of generations, it is easy to see that in each human being the first two ages—infancy and childhood—are attached to the bodily senses.

There are five bodily senses: sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch. The number five, doubled because the human sex is twofold, from which such generations arise—male and female—makes the number ten.

From adolescence onward, however, when reason begins to prevail in man, knowledge and reason are added to the five senses, and life is governed and administered by them. Thus the number seven begins to appear, which, similarly doubled, stands out and becomes manifest in fourteen generations. These belong to the three following ages: adolescence, youth, and the age of the elder.

The age of old age, however, just as among us is not defined by any fixed number of years but is assigned to old age after the preceding five ages for as long as each person lives, so in this age of the world no defined generations appear, so that the last day may remain hidden. The Lord usefully shows that it ought to remain hidden.

(AUGUSTINE, in the work cited above.) Morally. Each of us has in upright works and an upright life these six days, distinct as it were, etc., up to “I serve the law of sin.”

(ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, chapters 1 and 2, and the beginning of book III.) On the fourth day, when in that firmament he already works and distinguishes spiritual understandings of discipline, etc., up to “and may enjoy pleasant leisure.”

(ISIDORE, in the same work, chapter 1.) Mystically. “In the beginning God created heaven.” Namely, those who bore the image of heavenly things, etc., up to “it is a great thing if we reap your carnal things.”

(AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis Literally*, book VIII, chapter 1, volume III.) [Col. 0068A] In the narration of events that happened, etc., up to “in which alone it is formed and illuminated, lest it be darkness or abyss.”

(GREGORY, *Morals*, book XXXII, chapter 12, volume II.) The question arises how God created all things together, while Moses himself describes them as created distinctly through the changing succession of days. But the matter of things was created together, etc., up to “which do not come forth together through the increase of time.”

# The First Part of the Complete Works of Walafrid Strabo of Fulda, or Theological Works

## The Ordinary Gloss

## [Col. 0067]

### The Book of Genesis

Called *Beresit* in Hebrew, that is, “In the Beginning”; in Greek, *Genesis* (ΓΕΝΕΣΙΣ), that is, “Generation.” (G)*

### Chapter One

## [Col. 0067B]

### Verse 1

> “In the beginning he created,” etc.

He does not say: “In the beginning God said, ‘Let heaven and earth be made.’” But he said: “Let there be light, and there was light,” because whatever God made had to be comprehended universally under the name of heaven and earth, and afterward the manner in which he made it had to be explained in detail.

Hence what follows: “God said, ‘Let there be,’” that is, he made it through his Word. Or, because when the formless spiritual or bodily matter was first being made, it was not appropriate to say, “God said, ‘Let there be.’” For it was incongruous for God to say “Let there be,” since imperfection does not imitate the form of the Word unless, through the conversion of its kind toward the Creator, the creature becomes perfect. Thus, when it is said, “God said, ‘Let there be,’” we should understand that he is recalling the creature’s imperfection to himself.

Therefore, when it is said, “In the beginning God made heaven and earth,” the Son is commemorated, because he is the Beginning. But when it is said, “God said, ‘Let there be,’” he is commemorated as the Word.

Through “the Beginning,” the origin of the creature’s existence from him is indicated; through the Word, the perfection of the creature recalled from him to himself, so that it may be formed by imitating the unchangeable form of the Word.

The Word of God does not possess formless life, for in it being is the same as living, indeed living is the same as living blessedly. The spiritual creature, however, possesses formless life: for it does not have being identical with living, nor living identical with living blessedly, because, turned away from the wisdom of God, it lives foolishly and miserably.

### “In the beginning,” etc.

(BEDA, *Hexaemeron*, book I, volume II, col. 13a.) In indicating the creation of the world, Scripture first shows, in its opening word, the eternity and omnipotence of God. For the one whom it declares to have created the world at the beginning of time, it thereby signifies to have existed eternally before time. And the one whom it narrates to have created heaven and earth at the beginning of creation, it declares omnipotent by the speed of his operation: for him, to will is to do.

It is rightly said, therefore, “In the beginning he created,” and so forth. Both things were made together, although human speech does not say that both were made together. Hence the prophet shows that the earth was made at the beginning when he says, in Psalm 101: “At the beginning you founded the earth, O Lord,” and so forth.

### “In the beginning,” etc.

Heaven means not the visible firmament but the empyrean—that is, fiery or intellectual heaven—which is called fiery not because of heat but because of splendor, and which was immediately filled with angels. Hence Job 38: “Where were you when the morning stars praised me?” and so forth.

Note that three elements are mentioned here. By the name “heaven” we understand the air. By the name “earth,” the earth itself and the fire hidden within it. The fourth element, water, is mentioned in what follows.

## [Col. 0069A]

(ALCUIN, *On Genesis*, volume I.) “In the beginning”: through the Son, by whose incarnation it became evident who were heavenly and who were earthly.

“Heaven”: the spiritual creature, perfect and blessed from the beginning.

“Earth”: bodily matter, still imperfect.

“Heaven”: the formless matter of spiritual life, insofar as it can exist in itself without being converted to the Creator in whom it is formed.

“Earth”: bodily matter, without any of the qualities that appear in formed matter.

(BEDA, *On Genesis*, volume II, col. 191.) Scripture says: “You who made the world from formless matter” (Wisdom 11). Matter was made from nothing; the form of the world was made from formless matter. Therefore God made two things before all time: the angelic creature and formless matter.

Although Solomon says, “He who lives forever created all things together” (Ecclesiasticus 18), nevertheless, in origin, formless matter precedes formed appearance. Thus God made the world, the angels, and the soul from nothing; but man and the other creatures from something.

(Ibid., col. 192.) There are seven heavens, whose names are these: air, ether, Olympus, space or the fiery heaven, the firmament, the heaven of the angels, and the heaven of the Trinity. Jerome, however, says that the heaven of the Trinity is first, the heaven of the angels second, and the firmament third.

Mystically:

> “In the beginning God created heaven”—

namely, those who bore the image of heavenly things.

> “And earth”—

that is, those who afterward, through pride, carrying earth—that is, the image of the earthly man—made themselves deformed.

> “The earth, however, was empty”—

because it had laid aside its good form.

> “And void”—

of the fruit of good works.

> “And darkness was”—

namely, the deprivation of the true light—

> “over the face of the abyss”—

that is, over the hearts of the proud.

### Verse 2

> “The earth, however, was empty,” etc.

(BEDA, *Hexaemeron*, volume II.) It shows what kind of heaven was made in the beginning together with the earth. For concerning the earth it adds something that it did not wish to be understood concerning heaven.

That higher heaven, which is separated from the world’s revolution, was filled with holy angels as soon as it was created. The Lord testifies that they were created in the beginning together with heaven and earth when he says in Job 38:

> “Where were you when the morning stars praised me, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?”

He calls the same angels “morning stars” and “sons of God.” Concerning the heaven in which the luminaries were placed, he later says how and when it was made.

(STRABO.)

> “Empty and void”—

that is, useless, unfruitful, and unformed. For all the elements were mixed and confused, and the entire space of the air was full of waters—not waters such as they are now, but thin as mists, like those that are still above the heavens.
