(BEDA, as above.) “There was darkness,” etc. We must not heed those who, by way of criticism, say that God created darkness before light; for he did not make darkness in the water or air, but, in the ordered sequence of providence, first created the waters together with heaven and earth, and, when he willed, adorned them with the grace of light. It should also be noted that two elements of the world were created together with heaven, into which the other two were inserted—namely, water and earth, which contain fire and air. The waters covered the whole surface of the earth at such a height that they reached even those regions where some of them still remain above the firmament. Earth and water themselves are called formless matter, because everything we see either took its beginning from them or came from nothing; and before things came into the light, there was nothing from which they could receive form.

“And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters.” (AUGUSTINE, Book I of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 5, vol. III.) Either he called the whole bodily matter “water,” to indicate from what source all things were made and formed which we see taking shape on earth from moist nature in various forms; or he meant spiritual life before the form of conversion, as though it were drifting. The Spirit of God was borne over it because what he had begun to form and perfect lay subject to the Creator’s good will. It is also said, “The Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” so that God would not be thought to love the making of things through the necessity of need rather than through the abundance of his benevolence. For it is fitting that something already begun should first be indicated, something over which the Spirit might be borne—not locally, but by a power surpassing all things.

“And the Spirit of the Lord was borne,” etc. (JEROME, on Genesis, vol. III, col. 939.) In Hebrew the text has *merahephet*, that is, “was brooding” or “was warming,” like a bird over eggs, animating them with heat. We therefore understand that this is not said of the spirit of the world, as many suppose, but of the Holy Spirit, who is himself the giver of life to all things. But if he is the giver of life, he is also the Creator; and if he is the Creator, he is God. Psalm 103: “Send forth,” he says, “your Spirit, and they will be created.”

“And the Spirit,” etc. In him we would rest, subsisting through his breath made alive and washed in the water of baptism. “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” etc. That is, God the Creator presided over the drifting and confused matter, so that he might distinguish it whenever he willed. Thus the whole Trinity is understood to have worked here: God, namely the Father; “the beginning,” the Son; and the Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit.

“And the Spirit,” etc. (ISIDORE, on Genesis?) That is, over wavering hearts which had lost the mind’s tranquillity, because the Spirit did not rest upon them but was borne over them, as one powerful enough to recall nature from confusion to a better state. Thereafter, throughout the whole text of this Scripture, we see six laborious ages, distinguished, as it were, by neighboring boundaries, so that rest may be hoped for in the seventh; and these ages bear a likeness to the six days in which the things that Scripture records God made were created. The beginning of the human race, when it began to enjoy this light, is compared with the first day, on which God made light. This age is like the infancy of the whole world, which we conceive as one human being in proportion to its magnitude. For when a human being is first born into the light, he passes through infancy, the first age, which extends from Adam to Noah through ten generations. The flood is like the evening of this day, because our infancy is wiped out by a flood of forgetfulness.

**VERSE 3.—** “And God said: Let there be light.” (AUGUSTINE, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book I, chapter 17, vol. III.) The light made on the first day is understood as spiritual or bodily, etc., up to “the beginning of the morning of the future.” (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) If bodily light was made on the first day, the adornment of the world appropriately begins with light, by which the other things that were to be created could be seen. If it is asked where it was made, since the abyss covered the whole height of the earth, it is clear that it was made in those regions which the sun’s daylight now illuminates. Nor is it strange that light could shine in the waters, since even now they are often illuminated by the work of sailors, who, when immersed in the deep, pour oil from their mouths and thereby light the waters around them. At that time the waters were much thinner than they are now, because they had not yet been gathered into one place.

“And God said: Let there be light.” (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 2.) Not temporally: for if temporally, then mutably; and if mutably, then through a subject creature. Therefore it is not the first creature that is meant by light. But perhaps, etc., up to “so that it might exist and remain.”

“Let there be light.” (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapters 4, 5, and 9.) That is, under the condition by which all things subsist timelessly in God’s wisdom before they subsist in themselves. “And light was made,” that is, the angelic and heavenly substance came to be temporally in itself, just as it existed eternally in wisdom insofar as wisdom is immutable. Alternatively, the formlessness and imperfection of this creature is indicated before it was formed in the love of the Creator; for it is formed when it turns toward the immutable light of the Word.

“Let there be light.” (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapters 10, 11, and 16.) If light was made bodily, etc., up to “for there were not yet animals to which this alternation could be displayed.”

**VERSE 4.—** “And God saw the light,” etc. (STRABO.) God made light and darkness; hence Daniel 3: “Bless the Lord, light and darkness,” when every creature is invited to bless him.

(ISIDORE, on Genesis, chapter 2.) Each person has six distinct days in his works and upright life, after which he hopes for rest. On the first day, there is the light of faith, since at first he believes in invisible things, on account of which faith the Lord deigned to appear.

“And evening was made.” (AUGUSTINE, *Against the Manichaeans on Genesis*, Book I, chapter 4; BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) As the light gradually set and, after the passage of a divine length of time, entered the lower regions, evening came to be, as now happens through the customary circuit of the sun. Morning came to be when it returned over the earth and began another day, and one day of twenty-four hours was completed. It should be noted, however, that during those three days the night was wholly dark; after the stars had been created, it became bright with some light. It was also fitting that the days should begin with light and extend into the morning of the following day, so that it might be signified that God’s works were begun from light and completed in light.

**VERSE 5.—** […] “And evening was made,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, Book VIII, chapter 6, vol. I.) In this life, sin is not abandoned through the practice of righteousness in such a way that one remains steadfastly free from it. For even if uprightness drives guilt away, guilt sits at the doors of our thoughts, knocking so that it may be admitted. Hence Moses says, “Light was made,” and shortly afterward, “Evening was made.” The Creator, who knew human guilt beforehand, then expressed in time what now takes place in the mind. For the shadow of temptation follows the light of uprightness. But because the light of the elect is not extinguished by temptation, it is not night but evening that is said to have come to be: temptation hides the light of righteousness but does not destroy it.

(AUGUSTINE, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book IV, chapters 22–23, vol. III, col. 311–312.) It should be noted that the other creatures, etc., up to “so that the one belongs to the day and the other to the evening.”

**VERSE 6.—** […] “Let there be a firmament,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, Book XXVII, chapter 24.) The angelic powers that remained steadfast in the love of God received this in their recompense: that they should remain in the contemplation of the Creator in perpetual happiness and eternally subsist in the state in which they were created. Hence Moses says that heaven was made and later calls it the firmament, because the angelic nature was first created subtle in the higher regions and afterward wonderfully strengthened so that it could never fall.

“Let there be a firmament,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 2, col. 264.) It is asked whether the heaven that now exceeds the regions of the air is being made, etc., up to “because its interval divides certain vapors of water from the waters that are on the earth.”

“Let there be a firmament,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 4.) It should be noted that the firmament is not called so because of standing still, etc., up to “but however they may be there, we do not doubt that they are there.”

“Let there be a firmament in the midst.” (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*, vol. II.) The heaven in which the fixed stars are placed, etc., up to “What they are like and what use they serve is known by the one who created them.”

**VERSE 7.—** “And God made the firmament,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 8, col. 269.) It is asked why, after saying, “Let there be a firmament, and it was so,” he later adds, “And God made the firmament,” etc., up to the words, “And God said, Let there be,” etc.

(Ibid., chapters 1, 3, and 5.) Above the air there is pure fire, etc., up to “The neighboring presence of the supercelestial waters therefore makes it cold.”

(Ibid.) It should be noted that on the first day, when light was made, it was said only, “Let there be light”—this in the word—and “light was made”—this in the work. Immediately created light adhered to uncreated light, so that it was nearer to and more receptive of every creature. On the second day there is some delay and an increase of words: “Let there be,” “God made,” and “It was so.” We are thus to understand that these natures are prone to fail and less ready to obey.

(JEROME, Book I *Against Jovinian*, vol. II, col. 211.) It should also be noted that, according to the Hebrews, the works of this second day are not called good, although they are good like the others. This is because of the number two, the first principle of alternation, which is the first number to depart from unity; it is associated figuratively with bigamy and with many reprehensible things. Hence those creatures that enter the ark in pairs are unclean, while an odd number is clean. Alternatively, they are not called good because in this work the separation of the waters is not completed perfectly; that occurs in the next work, where he says, “Let the waters be gathered,” as will be said there.

(AUGUSTINE, as above, chapter 9.) It is customary to ask what shape the heaven has. But although our authors may have known this, the Holy Spirit did not wish to teach it through them except insofar as it benefits salvation. It is also asked whether heaven stands still or moves. If it moves, they say, how is it a firmament? If it stands still, how do the stars fixed in it revolve? But the firmament can be called so not because of standing still, but because of its firmness or because it is an impassable boundary for the waters. If it stands still, nothing prevents the stars from moving and revolving. On the second day, something like the firmament of discipline was made, distinguishing between carnal and spiritual things, as between the lower and higher waters.

(ISIDORE, on Genesis, chapter 2, vol. V, col. 213.) On the second day he established the firmament, namely, the Holy Scriptures in the Church. Of these Isaiah 34 says: “Heaven shall be folded up like a book.” By this firmament he distinguishes the higher waters—that is, the people of the angels, who do not need to hear the word of God in reading—from the lower peoples. He placed that firmament above the weakness of the lower peoples, so that, by looking up to it, they might learn how it distinguishes between carnal and spiritual things, as between the higher and lower waters.

“And he divided the waters that were,” etc. (AMBROSE, Book II of the *Hexaemeron*, chapter 3, vol. I, col. 148.) When you hear this, why are you surprised that a wave could be suspended above the firmament? etc., up to “The Jordan too, when its stream is turned back, returns to its source.”

**VERSE 8.—** […] “And evening was made,” etc. (ISIDORE, as above.) The morning of the second day begins with Noah, etc., up to “because childhood too is not suited to procreation.”

**VERSE 9.—** “And God said,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 11, vol. III.) On this day it appears to have been made, etc., up to “Thus the water is gathered and the earth appears: water is unstable and flowing, while earth is stable and fixed.”

“Let the waters be gathered?” (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) All the waters that had filled everything between heaven and earth are gathered into one place, so that the light which during the preceding two days had illuminated the waters with bright radiance might shine more brightly in the clear air; so that the earth, which had been hidden, might appear; and so that what had been muddy with waters might become dry and suitable for producing shoots. If it is asked where the waters were gathered, since they had covered every part of the earth up to heaven, it could have happened that the sinking earth provided hollow regions into which the flowing waters might be received. It may also be believed that the primordial waters were thinner, covering the lands like a mist, but that through their gathering they became denser.

**VERSE 10.—** “And God called the dry land earth.” (BEDA, ibid.) First, to distinguish the waters, he called the entire more solid part of the world “earth,” saying, “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” After the world began to take shape and the surface of the earth appeared as the waters receded, the portion that could be dry received the name “earth,” to distinguish it from the part that was still pressed down by the waters, because it is trodden by feet.

“And he called the gatherings of waters seas.” Among the Hebrews, all gatherings of waters are called this, whether salt or fresh. Because he had said that all the waters on earth were gathered into one place through their continuity, he now calls them “gatherings” in the plural on account of their many branching inlets. Although there are many seas, he says that the waters were gathered into one place because they are all joined to the great sea. If some lakes appear enclosed within themselves, they nevertheless flow back into the sea through hidden channels. Well-diggers also prove this, because the whole earth is filled with water through invisible veins whose origin is in the sea.

**VERSE 11.—** “And he said: Let the earth bring forth vegetation,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 12.) The restraint of the one who orders things should be observed. Although the created kinds of herbs and trees are distinct from the forms of earth and water, so that they cannot be numbered among the elements, nevertheless, because they are attached to the earth by their roots, he willed them to belong to the same day.

(BEDA, as above.) These words make clear that the world was completed and adorned in springtime, when green herbs normally appear and trees are laden with fruit. It should also be noted that the first shoots of herbs and the kinds of trees did not come forth from seed, but from the earth. At the single command of the Creator, dry land appeared adorned with herbs and clothed with groves, producing from itself the fruits and seeds proper to its kinds. For it was fitting that the form of things should first emerge perfect at God’s command, just as the human being—on whose account all things exist—was fashioned in the prime of life.

(AUGUSTINE, ibid., Book III, chapter 18.) A question also arises concerning thorns, thistles, and certain fruitless trees: why or when were they created, since God said, “Let the earth bring forth vegetation,” etc.? But the word “fruit” signifies a certain usefulness, and the usefulness of all that the earth nourishes from its roots may be manifest or hidden. We can answer plainly that, after the sin, the earth brought forth thorns and thistles for human labor—not that they were previously born elsewhere and afterward in the fields cultivated by human beings, but that they existed both before and afterward in the same places, though before they did not grow for human beings and afterward they did. Hence, “It shall bring forth for you” means that they began to arise for your labor, although previously they grew only as food for other animals.

“Producing seed.” (BEDA, ibid.) Everything was created perfect; the human being was perfect in age, and the trees had leaves and fruit. Hence it says, “a fruit-bearing tree.”

**VERSE 12.—** “And the earth brought forth vegetation,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, Book XIX, chapter 12; Book VI, chapter 16, vol. I.) What history attests was truly accomplished in this way so that it might signify something else that was to be done. For the earth is the Church, which refreshes us with the nourishment of the word and protects us with the shade of its advocacy: it feeds by speaking and shelters by helping, so that it may bring forth not only the grass of refreshment but also the tree of protection.

“And the tree.” The tree produced seed according to its kind when our mind, by considering itself, gathers what it should do for another and brings forth the shoot of a righteous deed. Hence a certain wise man says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4). And elsewhere: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them” (Matthew 7). As it were, look upon your own kind in one another and learn from yourselves what you ought to provide for others.

“Seed.” (STRABO, RABANUS.) *Sementis* is used of crops and trees; *semen* of human beings and animals. *Seminium* or *sementum* means the beginning of any thing. On the third day, when a human being prepares his mind to sow the fruits of good works, having separated himself from the pollution and waves of carnal temptations, he has the earth dry and separated from temptations, so that he can say: “With my mind I serve the law of God,” etc. (Romans 7).

**VERSE 13.—** “And evening and morning were made.” (ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. V, col. 207.) The morning of the third day begins with Abraham, etc., up to “The evening consists in the sins of the people by which they transgressed the divine commandments, up to the wickedness of Saul.”

(ISIDORE, ibid.) On the third day he gathered the lower and salt waters, namely, unbelievers who were being shaken by the waves of desires and temptations; and he separated from them the dry land, that is, the faithful who thirst for the fountain of faith. He restrained the unbelievers, so that they might not disturb the dry land—that is, the soul thirsting for God—with the waves of their iniquity, but so that it might be permitted to produce the fruits of good works and love its neighbor. Thus it may have within itself seed according to its own likeness: namely, that from its own weakness it may have compassion on another in need and produce a strong, fruit-bearing tree—that is, one that does good—by rescuing the oppressed and providing him with the shade of protection.

**VERSE 14.—** “And God said: Let there be lights,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book II, chapters 13–14.) Since two days were assigned to the establishment of the visible world, namely, to the world’s highest and lowest regions, the remaining three were assigned to the visible and moving parts of the world that are created within it, etc., up to “at the beginning, or at the rule, of night, which occurs when it is full.”

“And let them divide the day.” (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) This division is such that the sun illuminates the day and the moon the night. When the stars were made, this was added to increase the original light, so that the night too might become luminous, radiated by the brightness of the moon or stars, whereas until then it had known only darkness. Although the night appears dark because the air nearest the earth is obscured, the higher regions of the air are always bright with the radiance of the stars.

(AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 18.) It is customary to ask whether these lights are bodies alone or whether they have directing spirits and are given vital inspiration by them, just as animal flesh is animated through animal souls. But nothing should be rashly believed about so obscure a matter.

“And let them be for signs,” etc. (BEDA, ibid.) Before the stars were made, the order of times was marked by no indications—not by midday or by any other hour. Thus the lights are “for signs,” etc., not because times, days, or years began with their creation, but because the order of times, days, and years is marked by their risings and settings.

**VERSE 15.—** “So that they may give light,” etc. (BEDA, ibid.) The lights always shine in the firmament, but at appropriate times they illuminate the earth. Sometimes a cloudy atmosphere obstructs them; the rising of the sun, with its greater light, also prevents the moon and stars from illuminating the earth. Hence the sun is so called because during the day it alone shines upon the earth, outshining the dim moon and the other stars.

**VERSE 16.—** “God made two great lights.” (BEDA, ibid.) We may understand “great lights” not so much in comparison with others as in themselves, just as heaven is called great and the sea great. The sun is called great because it fills the globe of the earth with its heat, just as the moon does with its light. Wherever in the heaven they may be, they illuminate the whole earth and are seen by everyone. Their great size is demonstrated by the fact that the same disk appears to all human beings. For if it appeared smaller to those far away and larger to those near, that would indicate smallness.

“The greater light,” etc. The sun, not only because of the form of its body but also because of the magnitude of its light, since it illuminates the lesser light and the stars. It is also greater in heat, because it warms the world, whereas during the preceding days, before its creation, there had been no heat. As for the fact that the moon appears equal in size to the sun, they say that this is because the sun travels much farther and higher from the earth than the moon; consequently, its magnitude cannot be discerned by us. Everything farther away appears smaller.

“And the lesser light,” etc. Even if the moon and stars sometimes happen to appear larger during the day, it is nevertheless clear that they bring the comfort of light not to the day but to the night.

(AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 15, vol. III.) The moon is seen at the beginning of the night when it is full, but not otherwise; and during the day it begins to be seen before the full moon, and as the night progresses.

**VERSES 17–18.—** […] “So that they might give light,” etc. These words may be understood of the great lights and the stars: “so that they might rule the day” applies specifically to the sun; “and the night,” which follows, applies to the moon and stars; and “that they might divide the light from the darkness” applies equally to all of them. Wherever they travel, they carry light with them; and when they are absent, they leave everything dark. If it is asked what the daylight could have been like before the creation of the stars, we answer that it was like what we see when sunrise is approaching but has not yet appeared: the day is then lit by the dim rays of the stars, but the risen sun has not yet shone forth.

(ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. V, col. 207.) On the fourth day the lights shone in the firmament of heaven, etc., up to “because illumination comes after good works, by which the form of the heavenly truth is seen.”

(AUGUSTINE, *Against the Manichaeans on Genesis*, Book I, chapter 24, vol. III, col. 194.) On the fourth day, when the mind works upon and distinguishes spiritual intelligences in that firmament of discipline, it sees the immutable truth, which shines like the sun in the soul; it sees how the soul becomes a participant in it and bestows order and beauty upon the body, like the moon illuminating the night. It also sees how all the stars—that is, spiritual intelligences—shine in the obscurity of this life as in the night.

**VERSE 19.—** “And evening and morning were made,” etc. (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*, vol. II, col. 13.) In this evening the people of God offered a lamb in Egypt, etc., up to “would grant hope and faith.”

“And evening was made,” etc. (ISIDORE, as above.) The morning of the fourth day is the kingdom of David. This age resembles youth, which rules among all the ages and is the firm foundation of every age. Hence it is compared with the fourth day, on which the stars were made in the firmament of heaven. The splendor of the sun represents the excellence of the kingdom; the people obeying the king is shown by the splendor of the moon, as though by the Synagogue. Its princes are the stars, and everything is established in the stability of the kingdom as in the firmament.

**VERSE 20.—** “And God said,” etc. (BEDA, as above.) After the face of heaven had been adorned with lights on the fourth day, the lower regions of the world—namely, water and air—are adorned with their animals on the fifth day.

“And God said: Let the waters bring forth creeping things,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book II of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 1–6, vol. III.) It was fitting, in creating the inhabitants of the lower region, etc., up to “This must be understood only as their having been changed into the nature of the waters through the quality of denser air.”

“Living soul.” (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 8.) That is, those things that are in living souls, just as one says, “the ignoble things of human beings,” meaning those who are ignoble among human beings. Some, because of their dullness of understanding, suppose that this was said because fish have no memory; but it is absolutely certain that they do have memory.

(AUGUSTINE, as above, chapters 3–4.) There is a question concerning the transformation of the elements. Some say that everything can be transformed into everything else, etc., up to “For it is from this that we perceive waters and winds by touch; hence solid earth is mixed with all the elements, though it is felt more strongly among the denser ones.”

“Under the firmament,” etc. Although an immense space lies between them, birds fly beneath the starry heaven, and they fly above the earth, just as human beings who are on the earth are said to be beneath heaven. Another translation has: “Beside the firmament of heaven,” because these regions of the air that carry the birds are near the ether.

(AUGUSTINE, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, Book III, chapters 9–10, vol. III, col. 284.) It should be noted that certain philosophers distributed animals among the elements in such a way that each element had its own animals, etc., up to “Nevertheless, they were permitted to occupy only the dark regions of the air, which are like a prison for them until the time of judgment.”

**VERSE 21.—** “And God created the great sea creatures,” etc. (THEODORET, Question 18 on Genesis.) Children need both frightening devices and straps or rods: by the former we frighten them, and by the latter we educate them. Since God observed that we too are inclined toward laziness, he created beasts as certain straps and frightening devices, so that by frightening us through them he might draw us to himself and make us implore his help. But just as those who are mature despise such frightening devices and straps, so those who have been trained in virtue do not fear the attacks of beasts. Indeed, before Adam sinned, beasts stood beside him, professing obedience. Again, when Noah entered the ark, the lion, the leopard, and all the most savage beasts followed him like sheep. Lions were present with Daniel; although otherwise hungry, they did not dare approach him because they saw in him characters bearing the divine image. Likewise, when the viper struck the Apostle’s hand with its teeth, finding nothing sinful, tender, or soft in him, it immediately recoiled and threw itself into the fire, in a sense punishing itself because it had attacked a body wholly unsuitable to it. We fear beasts because we neglect virtue. Moreover, beasts are not useless to us in other respects: physicians prepare many medicines from them to drive away illnesses. Therefore, no one should look at beasts and complain about the Creator, but should investigate their usefulness.

“And every living soul,” etc. This distinguishes them from the human being, who was to be made in the image of God and, if he kept the commandments, would remain in perpetual immutability. The other animals, however, were made so that some might serve as food for others or perish from old age.

**VERSE 22.—** “And he blessed them,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *The Unfinished Literal Commentary on Genesis*, chapter 15, vol. III.) He intended the blessing to serve fecundity, which appears in the succession of offspring, so that, through the blessing by which weak and mortal creatures were created, they might preserve their kind by procreation.

(CHRYSOSTOM, Homily 7 on Genesis, vol. IV, col. 66.) That blessing consists in increasing in great number and multitude and in multiplying. Since these creatures were living animals and desired to exist perpetually, he therefore added, “Increase.” That word preserves them even to the present day. “Increase and multiply,” etc. (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) This pertains to both kinds of living creatures made from the waters, namely fish and birds. For just as all fish can live only in the waters, so can very many birds. Although they sometimes rest on the earth and produce offspring there, they do not live from the earth but from the sea, and use the sea more readily than the earth.

**Mystical interpretation.** (ISIDORE and AUGUSTINE, as above.) On the fifth day creeping things of living souls were made in the waters—that is, human beings renewed into life through the sacrament of baptism. Flying creatures were made—that is, souls flying toward heavenly things. The mind, having advanced to the fifth day, begins to work amid the turbulent activities of the world, as in the waters of the sea, for the benefit of fraternal society. From bodily forms of knowledge belonging to the sea—that is, to this life—it brings forth creeping things of living souls, namely, works that benefit living souls; and great sea creatures, namely, the strongest forms of knowledge by which the waves of the world are broken and despised; and the birds of heaven, namely, voices proclaiming heavenly things.

**VERSE 23.—** “And evening and morning were made,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Against the Manichaeans on Genesis*, Book II, chapter 23, vol. III.) Mystically, the morning is the migration into Babylon, when, through that captivity, the people were lightly placed in foreign leisure, etc., up to “because they were so blinded that they could not recognize Christ.”

**VERSE 24.—** “And God said: Let the earth bring forth,” etc. (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*, vol. III, col. 13.) After heaven had been filled with stars and the air with flying creatures—which, because of its proximity, is called heaven—etc., up to “the name ‘quadrupeds’ includes everything except beasts and creeping things, whether tame or wild and untamed.”

“Let the earth bring forth,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book III on Genesis, chapter 11, vol. III.) It followed that the earth should now be adorned with its animals. By saying three times “according to its kind,” etc., up to “the name ‘cattle’ and ‘beasts’ generally includes every irrational animal.”

“According to its kind.” (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 12.) Perhaps these things are said to be according to their kind because they arose in such a way that others might be born from them and preserve the form of their origin through succession. This was not said of the human being, because one was made, from whom the woman was also made. For many kinds of human beings were not made, as many kinds of herbs and trees were, so that it might be said “according to its kind,” as though it meant “by kinds,” in order that those belonging to similar things and to one origin of seed might be distinguished from the rest.

(AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 14.) There is a question concerning certain small animals, etc., up to “except that they were potentially and materially pre-seeded within them.”

(AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapters 15–16.) A question is asked concerning poisonous and harmful creatures, etc., up to “all of which, when rightly considered, are praised.”

(AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 17.) Another matter also causes concern, etc., up to “but they do not hesitate to prepare the numbers of holy courage for all things.”

(THEODORET, Question 18 on Genesis.) We must not despise beasts as though we were wholly unharmed by them, as if they had no power. Sometimes God permits two or three people out of many thousands to be stung by scorpions or bitten by serpents, so that, fearing that we may suffer something similar, we may call upon God the Creator for help.

(AUGUSTINE, on Genesis, Book III, chapter 13.) It is asked why here there was not added what was said of the animals of the waters: “And God blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply,” etc. Perhaps because what had been said about the first living creature was left to be understood of the second, especially since he was going to say several other things in the works of this day. Perhaps he judged herbs and trees unworthy of this blessing because they do not possess the desire to reproduce. It was necessarily repeated in the case of the human being, so that no one might think that the begetting of children was sinful, as fornication without marriage is.

**VERSE 25.—** “And God made the beasts of the earth,” etc. (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) The order has been changed. In our manner of speaking, there is no need to worry about which creatures we name first, since God created everything at once.

(ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. V, col. 207.) On the sixth day the earth brings forth a living soul, when our flesh, abstaining from dead works, produces the living shoots of virtues according to its kind—that is, by imitating the life of the saints. Hence 1 Corinthians 4: “Be imitators of me,” etc. We live according to our kind when we imitate the saints as those near to us. The earth brings forth beasts—that is, people who are savage in their pride; cattle—that is, those who live simply; and serpents—that is, the crafty, who distinguish good from evil and, as though crawling, scrutinize earthly things through which they may understand heavenly things.

**VERSE 26.—** “Let us make the human being.” (AUGUSTINE, ibid., chapter 19.) The plurality of the persons of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit is intimated, and immediately afterward the unity of the Godhead, when it says, “And God made the human being in the image of God,” not “the Father made him only in the image of the Son.” It would not truly be said, “in our image”; rather, it is said, “God made the human being in the image of God,” as if it had said, “in his own image.” When it says “in the image of God,” although above it had said “in our image,” it signifies that the plurality of persons does not mean that we should believe in several gods, but that we should understand the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit to be one God.

“Let us make the human being.” (BEDA, *Hexaemeron*.) It is clear why it was said in this way, whereas the other things were made, etc., up to “but to show that after death he had truly recovered flesh.”

“And let him rule,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Book III on Genesis, chapter 20.) It should also be noted that, after saying “in our image,” he immediately added, “And let him rule over the fish of the sea and the birds of heaven.” We are thus to understand that the human being was made in the image of God in this respect: that he excels irrational creatures. This is reason, or mind, or intelligence—or whatever more suitable name it may be given—the faculty by which he adheres to the contemplation of truth.

**VERSE 27.—** “And God created the human being in his image,” etc. (BEDA, on Genesis, chapter 1.) Whoever practices righteousness not by imitating some one of the saints but by contemplating truth itself, so that he may understand and follow that truth, receives power over all things. For once made spiritual and like God, he judges all things and is judged by no one.

“And God created,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, as above, chapters 20–22.) It should be noted that just as, in the creation of light, it says, “Let there be light,” and immediately adds, “And light was made,” so, when it says, “Let us make the human being,” it adds, “And God made the human being in the image of God.” This is because the intellectual nature is like that light, and for it to be made is to recognize the Word through which it is made, etc., up to “but were pre-seeded materially.”

“Male and female he created them,” etc. (BEDA, on Genesis, chapter 1.) Later it is explained more fully both from what and how human beings were made, etc., up to “although virginity is preferred.”

(Bede, Isidore, as above.) After this, “God made man in his image and likeness,” namely, the perfect man, etc., up to “Thus Paul says: ‘We have sown spiritual things among you; is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?’ (1 Cor. 9).”

**VERSE 28.**—[lacuna] “And have dominion over the fish,” etc. What he had previously spoken of them as though by way of consultation, he now states as a command, so that man has dominion over all creatures in the lower part of the world. He explains this point individually.

“And have dominion over the fish of the sea.” (Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*.) It is asked for what benefit man received dominion among the other living creatures, etc., up to “and that the jaws of beasts and the venom of serpents ceased.”

**VERSE 29.**—“And God said: Behold, I have given,” etc. (Bede, same work.) It is clear that before man’s sin the earth produced nothing harmful: neither poisonous grass nor barren trees. For every herb and tree was given as food to human beings, to birds, and to the creatures of the earth. Hence it is clear that at that time animals did not live by eating animals, but fed harmoniously on herbs and fruits.

**VERSE 30.**—[lacuna] “And it was so.” (Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 3, chapter 13.) It should be noted that where man is given power to eat herbs and fruits, it is added, “and it was so.” This signifies that, when God said this, man understood that these things had been granted to him for food, not that he immediately ate them. For if we refer the statement “and it was so” to everything mentioned above, it will follow that we must say that they had already multiplied on the sixth day, although this occurred many years later.

**VERSE 31.**—“And God saw,” etc. (Augustine, same work.) It is asked, since the other things are each called good individually, why is the man made in God’s image called good together with the others? Perhaps God foresaw that he would sin and would not remain in the perfection of the image. One who is individually good is more so together with all, but the statement is not reversible. It was therefore arranged that this should be said in a way that would be true in the present and signify foreknowledge of the future. God, however, ordered all things so that, even if some things individually became disfigured through sin, the whole would nevertheless always be beautiful together with them.

“And evening was made and morning,” etc. (Isidore, *On Genesis*, book 5, column 207.) The morning of the sixth day is the preaching of the Gospel through Christ, etc., up to “who has no evening.”

**Morally.** (Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 1, at the end.) On the sixth day the earth brings forth a living soul, that is, man from the stability of his mind, where he has spiritual fruits, namely good thoughts. He governs all the movements of his soul, so that there may be in him a living soul—that is, one serving reason and righteousness, not earthliness and sin. Thus man is made in the image and likeness of God, male and female; that is, intellect and action. Through their union, a spiritual offspring may fill the earth, that is, subject the flesh, together with the other matters already discussed in connection with human perfection. In these days, evening is the perfection of each individual work, and morning is the beginning of the works that follow.

## CHAPTER II

**VERSE 1.**—“Thus the heavens and the earth were completed,” etc. (Alcuin, *On Genesis*, book 1, column 517.) It cannot in any way be stated how God made heaven and earth. This exposition, however, presents an account of created things in the order of the days, as though it were history, but chiefly attends to the proclamation of future things, etc., up to “which the Lord has shown it useful to conceal.”

[Col. 0082B] “Thus the heavens and the earth were completed, and all their adornment.” (Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 1, at the end.) Allegorically: After those works, as it were, of six days, let man hope for everlasting rest and understand what is meant by “God rested on the seventh day from all his works,” because he himself works these good things in us, commanding us to work. He is rightly said to rest, because after all these works he will grant us rest—just as the head of a household builds a house while commanding his servants to work, and afterward rests from his works when, the building having been completed, he orders them to rest.

(Augustine, same work.) Each of us possesses in his works and upright life what are, as it were, these six distinct days, after which he ought to hope for rest. On the first day there is the light of faith, when he first believes in visible things, on account of which faith the Lord deigned to appear visibly. On the second day there is, as it were, the firmament of discipline, which distinguishes between carnal and spiritual works, just as the firmament distinguishes between the lower and upper waters. On the third day, when he prepares and raises his mind to bring forth the fruits of good works, separated from the defilement and waves of carnal temptations, he has his mind, as it were, dry land, freed from the disturbances of the sea, so that he can already say: “With my mind I serve the law of God” (Rom. 7), etc.

**VERSES 2–3.**—“And God completed,” etc. (Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*.) Another translation has: “God completed on the sixth day the works that he had made.” This raises no question, because what was made on it is clear, etc., [Col. 0082D] up to “for Solomon did some work when he dedicated the temple.”

(Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, book 3, column 935.) In Hebrew it reads “on the seventh day.” We shall therefore press the Jews, who boast of the Sabbath’s rest, because already at the beginning the Sabbath was dissolved, since God works on the Sabbath, completing his works on it.

“And God completed,” etc. (Augustine, book 4 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 4.) It is asked whether, etc., up to “according to him they would not have been made perfect.”

“And God rested,” etc. (Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*.) Not as though he were tired from working, but he rested from the whole work because he ceased to make a new creation. To rest is said to mean to cease, as in Revelation 4: “They had no rest, saying: Holy, holy, holy,” that is, they did not cease saying it.

(Bede, same work.) It may also be understood more profoundly that he rested from all his work, etc., up to “but gave rest in himself to rational creatures.”

“And God rested,” etc. (Augustine, as above, chapter 8.) God did not labor in creating, since he made everything by a single word, saying, “Let it be.” Nor does a human being labor by saying, “Let it be.” But perhaps one might say that he labored by thinking about what would come to be. To have rested from such concern once things were completed is what is meant. But to think this is foolish. God’s resting, then, means that he granted rest in himself to the rational creature, so that we may be carried there by desire and rest there—that is, seek nothing further. Just as God is said to make when we make through his working in us, and to know when we know, so he is said to rest when we rest through his gift.

(Same work, chapter 11.) It is not surprising if, prophetically announcing that day on which Christ would rest in the tomb, he said in this manner, “He rested on the seventh day,” intending afterward to work out the ages of the world.

(Same work, chapter 12.) It may also be understood that God rested from making the kinds of creatures, etc., up to “and does not cease to govern.”

(Same work, chapter 14.) God was neither wearied by creating nor refreshed by ceasing; rather, through his Scripture he urges us toward the desire for rest, saying that he sanctified the day on which he rested. For the other days of his work are not said to have been sanctified, as though rest were worth more to him than activity.

[Col. 0083C] (Same work, chapter 15.) It is also a fault of the soul to take such pleasure in its own works, etc., up to “that rest from which he never departed.”

(Same work.) If it were said that he rested from making, etc., up to “but by him we were blessed.”

(Same work.) God always rested in himself. But on the days in which the completion of things is narrated, he rested only on the seventh day, which follows the perfection of things; for he rests from things that have been perfected, since he does not need perfected things in order to be more blessed.

(Same work, chapter 17.) We see his works, which are good; but we shall see his rest after our good works. To signify this, he commanded that one Sabbath day be observed. This was abolished in the time of grace, in which the one who, in hope of the future, works all good things observes an everlasting Sabbath and does not boast in his good works as though he had not received them.

(Same work, chapter 18.) With him there is neither morning nor evening in his rest, because it is neither opened at a beginning nor closed at an end. In perfected works, however, there is morning but no evening, because the perfected creature begins to turn toward the rest of its Creator, but its perfection has no end. Thus God’s rest is begun not for God himself but for the perfection of things, and it has in him a morning because it is perfected by him; but in its own kind it is brought to an end as evening. In God there is no evening, because nothing will be more perfect than perfection itself.

(Same work.) In those days, etc., up to “which are mentioned as having been created before the luminaries.”

(Same work, chapter 20.) It is asked how it can be said on the seventh day, etc., up to “unless those things which had previously been created and called days.”

(Same work, chapter 21.) But how could the light move around, etc., up to “and the rest.”

(Same work.) But it is easier for us to confess that we do not know, etc., up to “and it will be false to say that he completed all his works on the sixth day.”

(Same work, chapter 22.) But since bodily light, etc., up to “and that by which the creature is known in itself is rightly called evening.”

(Same work, chapter 25.) Since the angels know the creature in itself in this way, etc., up to “therefore no evening followed on the seventh day.”

(Same work, chapter 28.) Let no one suppose, etc., up to “and a truer morning?”

(Same work, chapter 35.) That first day, then, etc., up to “and for this reason deserved to be sanctified.”

(Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*, book 2, column 13.) Allegorically: Hence it is said in Exodus 20, “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” This blessing and sanctification signifies a greater blessing and sanctification, etc., up to “therefore this day is not written as having an evening.”

**VERSE 4.**—“These are the generations.” (Rabanus.) It addresses those who say that the world has always existed without a beginning, or who think that it was made by God but from matter that he did not make and that was coeternal with him.

[Col. 0084C] “On the day when he made,” etc. He uses “day” for the whole period during which the primordial creation was formed, etc., up to “without rain and human labor.”

“These are the generations of heaven,” etc. (Isidore, *On Genesis*, book 5.) The six days are counted in which the whole universe proceeds from beginning to end, etc., up to “if he had not sinned.”

“Before it arose on the earth.” That is, before he sinned—that is, before he subjected himself to earthly desires. Hence it follows: “For God had not rained upon the earth.” This means that he had not yet caused the soul to live by sending down the rain of the word through prophetic or evangelical clouds. And “there was no man to work the earth,” because after the sin man began to labor upon the earth. He needed those clouds, through which the plant—that is, the soul—might grow green. The fountain of life, that is, the inundation of truth speaking in his understanding, watered it, so that before he sinned he had no need of rain from the clouds. Such was the condition of man before sin.

(Augustine, book 5 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 1.) Another translation has: “This is the book of the creation of heaven and earth,” etc., up to “great ones with truth and little ones with gentleness.”

(Augustine, same work, book 6, chapter 10.) In the first creation of the world, etc., up to “seed from the grass.”

**VERSE 5.**—“And every plant,” etc. (Augustine, same work, book 5, chapter 4.) The earth is understood to have produced grass and trees causally, that is, to have received the power of producing them. For in it, as in roots, those things had been made which were destined to exist in future times. Thus he made them before they existed upon the earth, according to the potential form of matter of the things that were to be formed by his word; their formation was preceded not in time but in origin.

“For the Lord had not rained,” etc. (Augustine, same work, chapter 5.) As though God had not then made things in the same way as now, etc., up to “nor could the creature move.”

**VERSE 6.**—“But a fountain,” etc. (Rabanus.) By the irrigation of this fountain, whatever its character, the earth, already clothed with herbs and trees, came forth. One fountain is said to have risen because of some unity at the boundaries of the earth; or the singular is used for the plural.

“But a fountain,” etc. (Bede, *On Genesis*, chapter 2.) Here he seems to indicate what occurs according to intervals of time, etc., up to “to be known in some fashion through these things that are familiar.”

**VERSE 7.**—“He formed,” etc. (Augustine.) Mystically: The more extensive account is figuratively explained concerning man, etc., up to “so that he neither despises what he is nor claims to be what he is not.”

“So the Lord God formed man,” etc. (Augustine, *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 3, chapters 20 and 25.) First the animal body was formed from the mud of the earth, etc., up to “for it has the necessity of dying.”

(Same work, chapter 27.) The first garment is either the righteousness from which he fell, or, if it signifies bodily immortality, he lost it because through sin he could not attain it. Thus Adam had an animal body not only before paradise but also in paradise—although in the inner man he was spiritual—which he lost through sin, and he deserved bodily death, whereas without sin he would have deserved transformation into a spiritual body.

“He formed,” etc. (Augustine, book 6 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 1.) It must be considered whether this is a recapitulation, so that the account now tells how man was made, although we read that he was made on the sixth day; or whether, when God made everything simultaneously, he also made man among them, so that with the passage of time man might come to exist in this visible form in which he now lives—just as the grass, made before it sprang up, emerged with the passage of time and through the irrigation of the fountain, so that it might appear upon the earth.

(Augustine, same work, chapters 2–3.) According to the recapitulation, let us first see, etc., up to “but then invisibly, potentially, and causally, how future things come to be, though they have not yet been made.”

“He formed,” etc. (Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*.) The creation of man, etc., up to “he created the place in which he would live.”

(Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 6, chapters 13 and 17.) It is asked whether God suddenly made man at mature age, etc., up to “and therefore it necessarily had to happen.”

“And he breathed into his face the breath of life, and man became a living soul.” (Augustine, same work, book 7, chapters 3, 5, and 7.) Without doubt, one must say “he breathed, or blew,” etc., up to “punishment if he should despise it?”

(Same work, chapter 26.) It must be said, etc., up to “there is no license to doubt.”

(Same work, chapter 27.) It is usually asked whether, if it does not wish to be incorporated, it is compelled, etc., up to “he made them.”

[Col. 0086A] (Same work, book 6, chapter 7.) But perhaps the souls made on the sixth day, in which the image of God shines forth, etc., up to “which ought to be preferred in such matters.”

(Irenaeus.) One thing is the condition of life that makes man an animal being; another is the life-giving Spirit who makes a spiritual man. Hence Isaiah says: “He who gave breath to the peoples upon the earth, and spirit to those who tread upon it.” God gave breath to every people that is upon the earth, but spirit only to those who tread upon earthly desires. Thus breath is temporary, whereas the Spirit is eternal, since it is properly God’s gift.

**VERSE 8.**—“Now he had planted,” etc. (Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*, book 3.) From that beginning he planted paradise, etc., up to “and because he was about to speak specifically of the tree of life and of the knowledge of good and evil.”

“The Lord God planted a paradise in Eden toward the east,” etc. (Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 8, chapter 1.) There are three general opinions about paradise. One belongs to those who wish it to be understood only bodily; another to those who understand it only spiritually; and the third to those who take paradise in both ways. I confess that I favor the third view: that the man formed from mud, which is the human body, should be understood to have been placed in a bodily paradise. Although Adam signifies something else, because he is a form of the future, he is understood in his proper nature as a human being.

(Same work.) “The Lord planted a paradise in Eden,” that is, in delights. He then recapitulates this to show how God planted paradise: “And God brought forth from the earth every tree,” etc. For the earth had already produced every tree, namely on the third day. But since trees of these kinds were established in paradise, it brought forth openly and in their proper time what it had already produced causally on the third day.

(Strabo.) Some manuscripts have: “Eden toward the East.” From this we may infer that paradise was situated in the East. Wherever it may be, we know that it was terrestrial and, separated from us by the Ocean and obstructing mountains, extremely remote from our world, situated high up and reaching as far as the lunar sphere. Hence the waters of the Flood did not reach it at all.

“In which he placed him.” (Augustine, as above, chapter 5.) If anyone thinks that souls separated from their bodies are contained in bodily places, etc., up to “one measure of bread by which God freed man from hunger for forty days.”

**VERSE 9.**—“And the Lord brought forth also the tree of life.” (Augustine, same work, chapter 4.) Wisdom is spoken of in these words: “She is a tree of life to those who grasp her.” But there is also the eternal Jerusalem in heaven, etc., up to “which recounted events accomplished in their proper times.”

“The tree of life,” etc. (Bede, *On the Hexaemeron*, book 3, column 13.) In one tree there was a sign of the obedience that man owed; in the other, a sacrament of eternal life, which he would merit through obedience. It was called the tree of life because it received from God the power that whoever ate from it would have his body strengthened with enduring health and would not decline or perish through any illness or old age.

(Strabo.) Historically: The tree of life naturally possessed this power: whoever ate of its fruit was clothed in perpetual firmness and was wearied by no illness, anxiety, burden of old age, or weakness.

“And the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” (Augustine, as above, chapter 6.) It was bodily, like the other trees, and not harmful as food, etc., up to “which followed upon the transgression.”

“The tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” (Augustine, book 2 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis against the Manichaeans*, chapter 10.) The soul’s middle position and ordered integrity are signified by the fact that it was planted in the middle of paradise and called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For the soul, which ought to extend itself toward God, if it abandons God and turns toward itself and wishes to enjoy its own power without God, learns through the punishment that follows, by experience, what lies between the good it abandoned and the evil into which it fell. This will be its having tasted from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

**VERSES 10–14.**—“And a river went out.” (Bede, as above.) To water paradise, etc., up to “and soon afterward emerging to follow its accustomed course.”

(Augustine, as above, chapter 7.) Another translation has: “A fountain went out from Eden, which waters paradise,” etc. These rivers signify the nations, etc., up to “namely, trees beautiful and fruitful.”

(Isidore, Augustine.) Mystically: The river flowing out from paradise is the abundance of eternal joy, etc., up to “by enduring adversity.”

(Gregory.) Morally: The earth is watered by four rivers flowing out from paradise. The solid structure of our reason contains prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice, because the entire structure of good works arises from these four virtues. Four rivers water paradise because, when the heart is infused with these four virtues, it is tempered against every fever of carnal desires.

“Havilah.” A region of India that after the Flood was possessed by Havilah, son of Joktan, son of Heber, the patriarch of the Hebrews. *Havilah* is interpreted as “giving birth,” because one who speaks the truth labors in birth more than he gives birth. Pliny says that the regions of India abound in veins of gold more than other regions.

“Bdellium.” According to Pliny, this is an aromatic tree as large as an olive tree. Its tear-like resin is clear, bitter in taste, of good odor, and more fragrant when infused in wine.

“Onyx.” This is a precious stone so called because it contains a whiteness mixed in the likeness of a human fingernail, since “fingernail” is called *onyx* (ὄνυξ) in Greek. The ancient translation has “carbuncle and prasius.” A carbuncle is fiery in color and is said to illuminate the darkness of night. Prasius is green; hence it received its Greek name from the leek, which is called *prason* (πράσον).

**VERSE 15.**—“Therefore the Lord God took,” etc. (Augustine, as above, chapter 8.) He has already said that man was placed in paradise. He now recapitulates to explain why he was placed there: “to work it,” etc. For it is not believable that before sin God condemned him to labor, [Col. 0088A] etc., up to “hence Ecclesiasticus 10 says: ‘The beginning of man’s pride is to depart from God.’”

“Therefore the Lord God took the man,” etc. (Gregory, *Morals*, book 19, chapter 17, volume 1.) It must be considered that good things cannot help if the evils that creep in are not avoided, etc., up to “but through pride they fall beneath the very things over which they preside.”

“And the Lord God took,” etc. (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) In Hebrew, instead of “pleasure,” there is *Eden*. Thus the Septuagint sometimes translated it as *Eden*, sometimes as “pleasure.” Symmachus, who had earlier translated it as “a flourishing paradise,” here used “pleasantness” or “delights.”

“And he placed him,” etc. (Isidore.) Mystically: From the addition, “and to guard it,” it is indicated what kind of work it was. In the tranquility of blessed life, where death is absent, every work consists in guarding what one possesses. The command was given that they should take from every tree of paradise, but not from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. That is, they were not to enjoy it in such a way that, by usurping what was forbidden, they violated the integrity of their nature.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he commanded him,” etc. (Augustine, as above, chapter 13.) He was prohibited from one tree, etc., up to “what lies between the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.”

(Augustine, as above, chapter 17.) It is asked whether the command was given to the man alone or also to the woman, etc., up to “let them ask their husbands at home.”

(Procopius, *On Genesis*.) Some say: If God wished to clothe us with immortality, what need was there of a command because of which we were destined to sin and afterward to feel the sharp stings of his judgment? I answer: Since he is kind and gentle, and wished to establish the human race in an incorruptible and immortal condition, he acted in this way so that they would not attribute the benefit to their own power or virtue, but would give thanks to him. He also appointed the present life for them as a training ground and, as it were, an instruction in the future life. Then, by inflicting death on account of sin, he wished us to recognize our weakness and afterward to desire the future gift more eagerly.

“And he commanded him, saying: From every tree,” etc. (Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, book 8, chapter 28.) If it is asked how he spoke these words, we cannot properly comprehend it. It is certain either that he spoke through his own substance, etc., up to “but through a creature subject to him.”

It is asked how they could speak, or understand one who spoke, when they had not learned by growing up among speakers or through instruction. But God had made them such that they could speak and could learn from others if there were others.

(Augustine, as above, chapter 14.) Christ is spoken of in Isaiah 7: “Before the child knows good or evil, he will reject evil in order to choose good.” How can he reject or choose what he does not know? etc., up to “which he ought not to lose.”

**VERSE 17.**—“But from the tree,” etc. (Augustine, as above, chapter 15.) The tree derived its name from this, etc., up to “that is, what they loved, which they would not lose.”

(Severianus.) There were three kinds of trees in paradise. One was given to him so that he might live, another so that he might live well, and a third so that he might live forever.

“For on whatever day,” etc. He does not say, “If you eat, you will become mortal,” but “you shall surely die.” Man died in soul when he sinned, because God, who is the soul’s life, departed from him. Bodily death followed when the soul, which is the body’s life, departed from it; this happened to Adam when he ended his present life. It can also be understood that when they sinned they were immediately punished by that death of which Romans 7 says: “Wretched man that I am! Who will free me from this body of death?” And in Romans 8: “The body is dead because of sin.” He does not say “mortal,” but “dead,” although it was mortal because it was destined to die. We must not believe that before sin those bodies were already in this condition. They were animal, not yet spiritual, but they were not dead—although they necessarily had to die—which occurred on the day of the transgression.

“You shall surely die.” A double death is signified: the death of the soul, when the Lord, who is its life, departed; or the death of the body, which he received at the end of life. But he immediately incurred the necessity of dying.

**VERSE 18.**—“And the Lord God also said,” etc. (Augustine, book 9 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 8.) Those who think that intercourse was not permitted in paradise for the begetting of children, etc., up to “soul from soul, or however the soul may come to be.”

**VERSE 19.**—“He brought them,” etc. (Augustine, book 9 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 14.) Not as hunters or bird-catchers do, nor was a voice of command made from a cloud, which rational souls customarily understand. Beasts and birds do not naturally understand such a voice, etc., up to “are understood to have been created from the earth.”

(Jerome.) It appears that the first language of the human race was Hebrew, because the names that we read in Genesis up to the division of languages are evidently Hebrew.

**VERSE 20.**—“And he called,” etc. (Augustine.) Mystically: This signifies the nations that would be saved in the Church through Christ and would receive the name of Christ, which they previously did not possess. Hence Isaiah 65: “I will call my servants by another name.”

“But for Adam no helper was found,” etc. (Augustine, book 9 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 15 and following.) It must be considered how the woman’s formation took place, which is mystically called a building, etc., up to “so that we may understand that Adam spoke these things through divinely given ecstasy.”

[Col. 0089D] “But for Adam no helper was found.” No faithful righteous person can be compared with Christ. Psalm 44 says: “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men.” No one could free the human race except him. Hence Revelation 5 says: “No one was found worthy to open the book and break its seals,” etc.

“But for Adam no helper was found,” etc. (Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 2, chapter 13.) The woman was made as a helper for the man, etc., up to “and, with the dominion of reason cooperating with grace, subject it.”

**VERSE 21.**—“Therefore the Lord caused,” etc. (Isidore, from Augustine, as above, chapters 13–14.) Mystically: These things cannot be seen with bodily eyes. But the more a person withdraws from visible things into the secrets of understanding, as though by falling asleep, the better and more sincerely he sees, etc., up to “and must be referred to the Church.”

(Augustine, book 10 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 1.) Those who think that the soul comes from the soul, etc., up to “which had been said concerning the man.”

(Augustine, same work, chapters 19–20.) If it is asked from where Christ received his soul, I would rather hear the better and more learned, etc., up to “I have not yet found what answer could be given to these matters.”

“Therefore the Lord caused a deep sleep,” etc. (Gregory, *Morals*, book 30, volume 2.) We do not attain the summit of contemplation unless we cease from the oppression of outward concerns. Nor do we perceive ourselves, so as to know that in us there is one thing that is rational and rules, and another that is animal and is ruled, unless, returning to the secret of silence, we are lulled to sleep away from outward disturbance. Adam sleeping aptly represented this, for a woman soon came forth from his side. Whoever is carried away toward understanding inward things closes his eyes to visible matters, and then understands that within himself there is one thing that ought to rule, like a man, and another that ought to be ruled, like a woman.

**VERSES 22–24.**—“And he built … Therefore he will leave,” etc. (Isidore, *On Genesis*, book 5.) What was completed historically in Adam, etc., up to “for the serpent prefigures the poisons of heretics.”

**VERSE 25.**—“Now both were naked.” (Augustine.) If something is said in the words of God or of any prophet that seems absurd literally and is therefore spoken figuratively, we must nevertheless not doubt that it was said for the sake of its meaning. The bodies of the two human beings in paradise were naked, and they were not ashamed, because they had not felt in their members any law opposed to the law of the mind, which followed disobedience. They thought that nothing needed to be covered, because they had felt nothing that needed to be restrained.

(Augustine, *City of God*, book 14, chapter 17, volume 7, column 425.) It is rightly the case that lust causes the greatest shame, etc., up to “and made them confused.”

(Rupert.) Their nakedness was not a disgrace but an honor; their lack of shame at their nakedness was not foolishness but security. For what? Did they receive from their Maker something that is shameful and disgraceful, a work of God that ought to be hidden? Or does nature produce such shame, rather than conscience? This torment of shame has indeed become almost part of our nature; nevertheless, its origin arose not from the first condition of humanity but from a later fault. We are ashamed of our nakedness because we are conscious of how much weakness—indeed, how much rebellion against us—we carry in our flesh.

But then the conscience of the heart was sound, since no desire of the eyes disturbed it. For the desire of the flesh is the punishment of sin, by which the earlier pride of the mind is punished. Scripture says, “God made man upright.” Human uprightness consists in this: that the spirit should rule and command the flesh, which is inferior to it. For the rational spirit of man was placed between God and his flesh so that it might obey God and command the flesh. Because the first man disturbed and broke this order by rejecting God’s command, the one who had been superior—the spirit—was subjected to the lowest flesh, so that the one who had refused to be rightly subject to what was superior might justly be subjected to what was inferior.

Hence that confusion of the face, breaking forth from the hidden places of conscience into public view, compelled the punishment of disgrace to proceed under the wretched solace of coverings. This weakness, or rebellion, of the flesh did not yet exist. Thus both were rightly naked and were not ashamed, because they had nothing of which to be ashamed.

Having lost that security of nakedness, we groan because we have been stripped of glory and honor and wrapped in little garments. For, dressed in this way, we truly walk naked, even if—and this is impossible—we were clothed as the lilies of the field are clothed. “Not even Solomon in all his glory was clothed like one of these.” Even if, I say, we could be clothed as these are, we would still be stripped and naked. Therefore we await our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ, who will reform the body of our lowliness, conforming it to the body of his glory. For when the righteous shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father, will they be covered with tunics and cloaks? Certainly not. Rather, whatever vessels of mercy they will be, they will be open to one another’s glorious vision, radiant outwardly and joyful inwardly, sound in body and happy in spirit—blessed in body and soul alike.

“Now both were naked,” etc. (Isidore, in Genesis, from Augustine, *The Literal Meaning of Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book 2, chapter 15.) That they were naked and were ashamed, etc., up to “because conscience is held guilty in the consent.”

## CHAPTER III

**VERSES 1–4.**—“But the serpent was more cunning than all the animals,” etc. (Augustine, book 2 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapters 2–3.) Some have “most prudent,” used figuratively. Some manuscripts have “wisest,” not in the proper sense in which wisdom is ordinarily understood of God, angels, or the rational soul, etc., up to “but the power came from God.”

“But the serpent,” etc. (Strabo.) Thus the devil spoke through the ignorant serpent, just as he speaks through the possessed or the frenzied: whoever he seizes, he deprives of understanding and reason. The good Spirit, however, makes those whom he fills with grace seeing and understanding; hence the spirit of the prophets is subject to the prophets.

“Who said to the woman.” (Augustine, book 2 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 30, and drawn from chapters 7, 8, 6, and 10 in various places.) The woman’s transgression is inexcusable, because she remembered God’s command. Yet forgetfulness, etc., up to chapter 10: “He foresees the good and the evil who will come to be, and creates them, offering himself for enjoyment to the good and also granting many things to the evil.”

“Why did he command,” etc. (Strabo.) The cunning enemy asks this and recalls God’s command so that, once she has sinned, she will not have an excuse on the grounds that she had forgotten.

“Why did he command,” etc. (Gregory, *Morals*, book 23, volume 2.) The enemy of the human race does the same thing every day: he tries to tear God’s words from the hearts of human beings, weaken his threats, and invite them to believe what he falsely promises. He urges them toward temporal things so as to diminish what God threatens—eternal punishments. Promising the glory of the present life, he says: “Taste, and you will be like gods”; touch temporal desire and appear exalted in this world. And when he tries to remove fear of the divine judgment, he says in a certain sense: “Why did God command you?”

(Augustine, book 2 of *The Literal Meaning of Genesis*, chapter 4.) It is asked why God permitted man to be tempted, etc., up to “whether earthly, as the human soul.”

(Same work, chapter 5.) Nor should we think that man would have been cast down unless a certain pride had first arisen in him that needed to be restrained, so that through the humility of sin he might learn what he had falsely presumed about himself, and that a created nature is not rightly ordered if it withdraws from its Creator. For how good God is is demonstrated when no one fares well by departing from him.

(Same work, chapter 18.) This question concerns the blessed life, etc., up to “less than in the life of the holy angels.”

(Same work, chapter 16.) It may not without reason be thought that the devil fell at the beginning of time, etc., up to “to whom God did not give foreknowledge concerning themselves.”

(Same work, chapter 14.) But how can those whose blessedness is uncertain be blessed? etc., up to “I do not see from where they derive their assertion.”

(Same work, chapter 21.) But it must not be thought without reason that from the very beginning of creation, etc., up to “foreseeing how much he would accomplish from him by his goodness.”

(Ibid., ch. 22.) “The beginning of the forming” is said, etc., up to “so that they might be wicked men.”

(Ibid., ch. 23.) That the devil is therefore thought never to have stood in the truth, etc., up to “many more things apply to his body.”

(GREGORY, Homily 16 on the Gospels, vol. II.) The devil tempted our first parent in three ways, etc., up to “we are overcome by delight and bound by consent.”

**VERSE 5.** — [lacuna] “You will be like gods,” etc. (STRABO.) Mystically. He skillfully composes his words so that, if he cannot overthrow them through contempt of disobedience, he may at least boast of having conquered by corrupting their faith and persuading them to idolatry; but if he seduces them through contempt of disobedience, he is victorious in both respects.

(AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, ch. 15, vol. III.) The woman, when questioned, replied, etc., up to “for God alone is blessed, since no one rules him and he is blessed by his own power.”

**VERSES 6–7.** — “Then she saw,” etc. (ISIDORE, drawing on Augustine above.) How could they see if their eyes were closed? It is said so that we may understand that their eyes were opened after they had eaten from the fruit: with these eyes they saw that they were naked and found themselves displeasing—that is, with the eyes of cunning, by which simplicity is displeasing. For when someone has fallen away from the innermost light of truth, there is nothing in which pride wishes to take pleasure except deceitful pretenses. From this hypocrisy arises: hypocrites appear very discerning because they have been able to deceive whomever they wished.

“Then she saw,” etc. (GREGORY, *Morals*, book XXI, ch. 2.) So that we do not dwell upon slippery thoughts, we must not look upon what we are not permitted to desire, etc., up to “the discipline of the outward senses must also be maintained.”

“And she gave it to her husband, who ate. And the eyes of both were opened,” etc. (ISIDORE, drawing on Augustine above, chs. 16–17.) Of these it is said: “Then they saw that they were naked”—namely, with perverse eyes, by which nakedness, that is, simplicity, seemed shameful, etc., up to “My soul is deeply troubled within me” (Psalm 41).

“He ate,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis*, book XI, ch. 3, vol. III, col. 429.) Namely, so that they might desire one another, etc., up to “which would convict the sinner by deed and instruct the reader by writing.”

“They sewed fig leaves together.” (ALCUIN, on Genesis, vol. I.) Because they had lost the glory of simple chastity, they fled to the twofold itch of lust; hence John 1: “When you were under the fig tree, I saw you, and I came down”—understand, “to free you.”

**VERSE 8.** — “And when they heard,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, book II of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 33.) They were appropriately visited at that hour, because they had fallen away from the light of truth, etc., up to “he may be believed to have appeared to bodily senses through local and temporal motion.”

“He hid himself,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, ibid.) When God turns his face away inwardly and the human being is troubled, things resembling madness arise, through excessive fear and shame, while a hidden impulse also remains active, so that they unknowingly did things that would signify something to later generations, for whose sake these events were written.

“At the breeze after midday.” Hence Christ gave up his spirit at the ninth hour (Matthew 27). He was crucified at the sixth hour, so that at the same hour in which the human being had been expelled from paradise, he might be restored.

“In the midst of the tree of paradise.” He hides who, turned away from the Creator’s commandment, lives according to the error and self-will of his judgment.

**VERSE 9.** — “And the Lord God called Adam.” (AUGUSTINE, as above, ch. 34.) He called him by reproving him, not because he was ignorant, etc., up to “now, however, we are not presenting things symbolized but defending things that happened.”
