**VERSES 10–11.** — “He said: I heard your voice,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, as above, ch. 34.) Historically. It is plausible that, through an appropriate creature, a human form customarily appeared to the first human beings, etc., up to “and what caused shame followed.”

“Your voice,” etc. (ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. V.) Mystically. He replies that, having heard his voice, he hid himself, etc., up to “and not obey God’s commandment.”

“And God called Adam,” etc. (GREGORY.) Because he saw him fallen into guilt and already under sin, as though hidden from the eyes of truth—for he does not approve the darkness of his error, and, as though unaware where the sinner is, he calls and seeks him, saying: “Adam, where are you?” When he calls, he signifies that he is recalling him to repentance; when he seeks him, he indicates that he does not recognize sinners who have been justly condemned.

**VERSE 12.** — “And Adam said: The woman whom you gave me,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) He does not say, “I have sinned”: pride possesses the ugliness of shame, not the humility of confession. This was written, and these questions were asked, so that they might be recorded truthfully and profitably, so that we may know how grievously afflicted by the disease of pride are those today who attempt to attribute evil to the Creator and to credit themselves with whatever good they do.

“The woman whom you gave me,” etc. As though she had been given for this purpose: that she herself might not obey her husband, and that both might not obey God.

“The woman whom you gave me,” etc. (GREGORY, *Morals*, book IV, ch. 27, vol. I, col. 661.) Sin is perpetrated in the heart in four ways, etc., up to “finally, it is nourished either by the seduction of false hope or by the wretched obstinacy of despair.”

**VERSE 13.** — “And the Lord God said to the woman,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) She too does not confess her sin, but shifts it onto another—within a different sex, yet with equal arrogance. From these two, however, David was born, who says to the end of the world: “I said: Lord, have mercy on me; heal my soul, for I have sinned against you” (Psalm 40). This should have been said by them; but God did not yet regard the necks of sinners: there remained the labors and pains of death, the crushing burdens of the world, and the grace of God, which comes to the aid of the afflicted in due time, teaching them not to presume upon themselves.

“The serpent deceived me,” etc. As though the persuasion of anyone could prevail against God’s commandment.

“The serpent deceived me,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, ibid., book II, ch. 30.) How, in these words, etc., up to “since she did not see that she had died by eating that food with him.”

(AUGUSTINE, ibid., ch. 28.) It should be noted that the devil was not permitted to tempt the woman, etc., up to “but reason shows that he had envied the human being because of this.”

(ALCUIN.) The angel’s sin was concealed, but the human being’s was exposed, because the former was incurable whereas the latter was healed.

“Then she saw,” etc. (STRABO.) He is openly shown to be without excuse, since he was allowed, with such deliberation, to perceive the enemy’s deceits.

**VERSE 14.** — “And the Lord God said,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, as above, ch. 36.) This entire sentence is figurative. Nevertheless, we must believe that everything was said. The serpent is not asked why he did it, because it was not by his own will and nature that he acted, but the devil acted from him, through him, and in him—the devil who had already been destined to eternal fire because of his impiety and pride. What is said to the serpent therefore refers to him, and it shows what he would become for the human race.

Mystically. “And the Lord God said to the serpent,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, ch. 17.) The serpent, without being questioned, first receives punishment, etc., up to “so that it may exclude the very beginning of evil suggestion.”

“Upon your breast,” etc. (JEROME.) The Septuagint added “belly,” but in Hebrew there is only “breast,” so that it might disclose the cunning and deceitfulness of his thoughts—that is, that every step of his is wickedness and fraud.

“Upon breast and belly you will crawl.” (GREGORY, *Morals*, book XXI, ch. 2.) The evil of lust is perpetrated either in thought or in deed. For when the enemy is driven away from the accomplishment of the deed, he attempts to pollute the secret places of thought. He crawls upon his belly when, slippery and using the human members subject to him, he exercises lust in action. He crawls upon his breast when he pollutes the mind in thought. But because one proceeds from thought to action, he is described as crawling first upon his breast and afterward upon his belly.

**VERSE 15.** — “I will put enmity between you and the woman . . . She will crush your head,” etc. (GREGORY, *Morals*, book I, ch. 38.) To crush the serpent’s head is to uproot the beginnings of suggestion from the entrance of the heart by careful reflection. When he is detected at the beginning, he attempts to strike at the heel, because one whom he does not strike in the first temptation he strives to deceive at the end. But if the heart is corrupted in temptation, the middle and end of the subsequent action are possessed by the enemy, because he sees the entire tree bearing fruit for himself after he has damaged it at the root with his poisonous tooth.

(JEROME.) “She will watch over your heel, and you will crush his heel.” The Hebrew is better: “She will crush your head, and you will crush her heel,” because the serpent impedes our steps, while the Lord will crush Satan beneath his feet.

**VERSE 16.** — “And to the woman,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, as above, ch. 37.) These things are better understood figuratively and prophetically, etc., up to “nature will be corrupted and guilt increased.”

“I will multiply your afflictions,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, ch. 19.) It is clear that the woman’s pains were multiplied, etc., up to “but first there was resistance, with pain, to the evil habit.”

**VERSES 17–18.** — [lacuna] “Cursed is the earth,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, ibid., ch. 38.) No one is unaware that these are the labors of the human race upon the earth, and it is unquestionably clear that they would not exist if the happiness that was in paradise had been retained.

(STRABO.) The earth is cursed, not Adam, so that all those for whose sake these things were written might be frightened and, by doing similar things, might not be punished with a similar penalty. Cain himself, however, because he added fratricide to the first transgression, is cursed when it is said: “You will be cursed upon the earth,” etc.

(AUGUSTINE.) He cursed the earth, not the waters, because the human being ate against the prohibition from the fruit of the earth, not because he drank from the waters; and in the waters the sin contracted from the fruit of the earth was to be washed away. Terrestrial animals also bear more of the curse than aquatic animals, because they live more from the cursed earth. For this reason, after his resurrection Christ ate fish, not a terrestrial animal.

“Cursed is the earth in your work.” (GREGORY, *Morals*, book IV, chs. 5–6.) God curses the sinful human being, etc., up to “and he burned two groups of fifty with flame.”

“In labors,” etc. (RABANUS.) Thorns existed before, but not so as to impose labor upon the human being; after sin they became instruments of labor and affliction, just as serpents and everything harmful had previously been harmless. It should also be noted that an external punishment is imposed upon Adam: “Cursed is the earth in your work”; but upon the woman an internal one, when it is said: “I will multiply your afflictions,” etc., because she was seduced and then seduced her husband.

**VERSE 19.** — “You are dust,” etc. (GREGORY, as above.) The human being was formed in this way, etc., up to “old age passes into death.”

**VERSE 20.** — “And Adam called his wife’s name Eve,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, as above.) These were the words of the first human being, since “she is the mother of all living,” as though he were giving the reason for the name he himself imposed—namely, why he called her Eve.

Mystically. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, ch. 21.) After the sin and the judge’s sentence, Adam called his wife Eve, etc., up to “it is expressed in the skins stripped from dead bodies.”

**VERSE 21.** — “And he made,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis*, book XI, ch. 39.) This too was done for the sake of signification; in deeds we ask both what was done and what it signifies, and in words both what was said and what it signifies.

(STRABO.) They made loincloths for themselves in order to hide their sin; but God made leather tunics, with which he clothed their entire bodies, because he justly condemned them both in body and in soul. It is foolish to ask how or by whose agency the skins were removed from animals: he who created everything from nothing made these things in whatever manner and by whatever means he wished.

**VERSE 22.** — “And he said: Behold, Adam has become like one of us,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, ibid., ch. 41.) The plural number is used on account of the Trinity, etc., up to “just as in the Church people are accustomed to be removed from the Church’s visible sacraments by ecclesiastical discipline.”

(AUGUSTINE, as above, ch. 42.) It is remarkable if Adam was spiritual in mind, etc., up to “which he thought to be true when it was false.”

“Like one of us.” (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, ch. 21.) “Like one of us” can be understood in two ways: “like one of us,” that is, God, etc., up to “until the one who had died is brought back to life by God’s mercy.”

(RUPERT.) “Lest he eat from the tree of life,” and, having done this, Adam—made such and so wretched—live forever. For what if, having become such, he were to live forever? Surely nothing but eternal evil. Since he had already become wretched, if he were also eternal, what would he have except eternal misery? Let us spare him, lest in this way it be evil for him to be “like one of us”; lest, just as each of us is eternal—for the Father is eternal, the Son eternal, and the Holy Spirit eternal—so he too should be eternal, and for this reason the evil eye of the devil, who promised him the likeness of God, should laugh at its own truthfulness. Indeed, it is evil for him to be temporal, but it would be the worst thing for him to be eternal. This likeness to God is exceedingly evil and false. It is much better for him to be entirely unlike God. How? Clearly, since he is wretched, let him also be temporal—that is, let him be entirely unlike God. For God is eternal and blessed, and his blessedness is eternal: a blessed eternity. The devil lost one of these, blessedness, but did not lose eternity; and he possesses eternal unhappiness, an unhappy eternity. Let us spare the human being, I say; and because he lost blessedness, let us also decree temporality for the unhappy man, so that in neither respect may he be “like one of us.” For us there is eternal blessedness, a blessed eternity; for him let there be temporal misery, or miserable temporality, so that eternity may then be beneficially restored to him when blessedness has been recovered. Thus, in great anger, the Lord remembered great mercy precisely in this: that he did not grant the tree of life to the miserable human being. For he wished him to be so unlike himself that he would not be like the devil in both respects—that is, so that the human being would not live like the devil until the final judgment and, like him, pass without temporal death into eternal fire.

**VERSE 23.** — “And he sent him out,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis against the Manichaeans*, book II, ch. 22.) Into a place suitable for him; just as often an evil person, when he has begun to live among good people, is expelled from the gathering of the good by the weight of his evil habit if he refuses to change for the better.

**VERSE 24.** — “And he cast Adam out.” (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*, vol. III.) The Septuagint has: “And he cast him out, and made him dwell opposite the paradise of delight, and stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword, which turns to guard the way of the tree of life.” The Hebrew has another sense; for it says: “And the Lord cast out”—namely, Adam—“and made the cherubim dwell before the paradise of delight, and the flaming sword.” It does not mean that he made Adam dwell opposite the paradise of delight; rather, after casting him out, he placed the cherubim and the flaming sword before the gates of paradise, so that no one could enter.

“And he placed,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, as above.) We must believe that this was also done through heavenly powers in the visible paradise, so that through angelic ministry there might be a certain fiery guard—not without purpose, but because it signifies something concerning the spiritual paradise.

“He placed,” etc. (STRABO.) This means that he established a fiery guard through the ministry of angels. The flaming sword signifies the tribulations, pains, and labors of this life by which we are tested; or the sentence of just condemnation given to the human being, who was condemned in such a way that he could be redeemed by Christ’s passion. Hence it is called a turning sword, because it can be removed. It was removed for Enoch and Elijah, and every day it is removed for the faithful who pass from this life to heavenly blessedness. It does not say “flame and sword,” but “flaming sword”: those who return to paradise must necessarily burn away all the desires of this life with the fire of the Holy Spirit and cut off everything harmful with the sword of God’s word.

“He placed,” etc. (ISIDORE, on Genesis, vol. V.) The cherubim is the fullness of knowledge; this is charity, which is the fullness of the divine law. The flaming sword signifies temporal punishments, which are turning because times are changeable. Therefore one does not return to the tree of life except through the cherubim—that is, the fullness of knowledge, namely charity—and through the turning sword—that is, endurance of temporal things.

# CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 1.** — “Now Adam,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, book IX of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, ch. 4.) In paradise there was virginity, outside it marriage, etc., up to “but afterward she was born in exile.”

“She conceived and gave birth,” etc. Cain and Abel, born of one mother, are figures of all human beings who are propagated in this life from the root of sin. Some will love the earthly city and its deadly pleasures and, as far as they can, possess them through ambition; Cain signifies these, for his name is interpreted as “possession.” Others will seek the city to come and, mourning over the miseries of this dwelling, will pass with total desire toward future glory; Abel signifies these, for his name is interpreted as “mourning,” and he is the later one, because what is spiritual does not come first, but what is natural. Hence Cain is called a “cultivator,” that is, one occupied with earthly works; Abel, however, is called a “shepherd of sheep,” loving simplicity and innocence.

Allegorically. (ISIDORE, on Genesis.) Adam’s two sons represent two peoples: the Jewish people, the elder by birth, etc., up to “as though reason does not permit a perverse movement to come into effect but strives to subjugate it.”

**VERSE 2.** — “Now Abel was,” etc. In him are signified those who mourn over their earthly dwelling. Abel is interpreted as “mourning,” or “vapor,” because he was a grief to his parents or vanished quickly like vapor.

**VERSES 3–4.** — “And it came to pass,” etc. “Abel also offered,” etc. Because the righteous person strives to please God in everything he does through faith and charity—from which the other virtues arise and without which they are of no benefit—this is signified by the fat portions that were offered. Hence Psalm 62: “Let my soul be filled as with fat and richness.” Without charity the soul is emaciated and languid and pleasing to God in nothing.

“And the Lord looked upon Abel,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*, vol. III.) How could Cain have known this unless Theodotion’s translation were true: “And the Lord kindled a fire over Abel and over his sacrifice, but over Cain and his sacrifice he did not kindle it”? We read that fire customarily came from heaven to consume sacrifices, as at the dedication of the temple under Solomon and when Elijah built an altar on Mount Carmel.

(ISIDORE, as above.) “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned”: for although the Jews formerly offered those things correctly, they are guilty because they did not distinguish the New Testament from the Old.

**VERSES 5–7.** — [lacuna] “At the doors.” (ALCUIN.) That is, whether you enter or leave, sin will accompany you, and the Lord will not guard your coming in and going out.

**VERSE 8.** — “And Cain said,” etc. (ISIDORE, *Questions on Genesis*, vol. V.) He does not heed the Lord’s command, “Rest,” etc., up to “therefore Christ, the head of the younger people, is killed by the elder.”

**VERSE 9.** — “And the Lord said to Cain.” (ISIDORE, as above.) The Lord questions Cain not as one ignorant who wishes to learn, but as a judge who wishes to punish. To this day, when we question the Jews through the Scriptures about Christ, they reply that they do not know what we are saying. Cain’s lying ignorance is the Jews’ false denial. They would truly be guardians of Christ if they believed in their hearts and confessed with their mouths.

**VERSE 10.** — “The voice of blood,” etc. Great is the power of justice, which demands vengeance for innocent blood.

**VERSE 11.** — “Now therefore you will be cursed,” etc. (RABANUS.) It should be noted that in Adam’s sin the earth is cursed. Cain, however, is cursed because, knowing the condemnation of the first transgression, he added fratricide.

**VERSE 11.** — “Now therefore you will be cursed,” etc. By place, things located in that place are signified. It is as though he says: You will be cursed by those who are upon the earth, who opened their mouths in confession of sins to receive the blood poured out for their forgiveness from the hand of the persecutor—one who refused to be under grace but wished to be under the law, so that he might be cursed by the Church, which understands and shows him to be accursed. For those who are of the works of the law are under a curse.

**VERSE 12.** — “When you work,” etc. The reference is made according to the wording, not according to the sense, because “earth” is understood differently here and above: there it signifies the Church; here it signifies the earthly work that the Jew still practices—that is, carnal circumcision, Passover, Sabbath, and similar observances, which possess a hidden power pointing toward the understanding of God’s grace but do not give fruit to Jews unwilling to pass over to Christ. “Earth” may be understood as Christ’s flesh, in which the Jews worked our salvation by crucifying him. “For he died because of our offenses, and rose again because of our justification”; but because they denied him, they were not justified.

“A wanderer and a fugitive,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Dispersed among the nations, a fugitive from Jerusalem. The Septuagint: “Groaning and trembling.” Groaning because of the loss of the kingdom; trembling because of the multitude of the Christian people, lest you be killed. “My iniquity is greater,” etc. He magnifies his guilt but confesses it arrogantly and does not ask forgiveness.

**VERSE 13.** — “My iniquity is greater.” (ISIDORE.) Adding sins to sins, he despairs and does not believe that he can obtain forgiveness. This is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, which is not forgiven in this age or in the age to come, because he thinks either that God does not wish to forgive or that he cannot—as though God were unable to do everything or envied salvation. He does not consider it serious that God is angry with him, but fears that he will be found and killed.

**VERSE 14.** — “Therefore everyone who finds me,” etc. (STRABO.) Because, from the trembling of his body and the agitation of his frenzied mind, whoever finds me will recognize that I am guilty of death.

**VERSE 15.** — “By no means will this happen.” That is, you will not die quickly, as you wish, to relieve your torment; rather, punishment will be imposed upon you sevenfold. You will live in torment until the seventh generation, in which you will be killed by Lamech. Therefore everyone who kills you—understand, will free you from that torment of a bad conscience. This sense is clearer. According to the Septuagint: “Everyone who kills Cain will pay seven punishments,” that is, whoever kills you in the seventh generation will free you through death from the torment in which you are to be preserved alive until that time, solely for punishment—a punishment that would quickly end if you were killed quickly. Thus, whoever would punish the Jews with visible death would take away from them seven punishments to which they are bound because of the guilt of Christ’s murder, since he would lighten the miseries and dispersions that they suffer.

“Everyone who kills Cain,” etc. The Septuagint: “He will pay seven punishments.” Aquila translates “sevenfold”; Symmachus, “sevenfold”; Theodotion, “through a week.” This signifies that he will be punished for a long time and completely, so that no one dares to repeat murder.

“Whoever kills Cain,” etc. (JEROME, letter to Damasus.) If anyone kills you, “he will be punished sevenfold,” that is, he will be punished with the gravest vengeance. A human being should not kill one whom God has preserved alive, either for his own punishment or for the correction of others.

“But everyone who kills Cain.” (ISIDORE, as above.) This should be read by aposiopesis, etc., up to “and that saying is fulfilled: ‘Scatter them by your power’” (Psalm 53).

(JEROME, as above.) What Aquila rendered “sevenfold,” etc., up to “and might deserve to be released.”

“And the Lord placed a sign upon Cain,” etc. (ISIDORE, *Questions on Genesis*, vol. V.) Although all the nations subjugated by the Romans passed over into their customs, the Jewish people, whether under the nations or under Christian kings, did not abandon the sign of circumcision and carnal observance, etc., up to “where paradise was planted.”

“He dwelt in the land toward the eastern region of Eden.” (JEROME, as above.) The Septuagint: “He dwelt in the land of Naid” (Ναΐδ). In Hebrew it is called *nod*, that is, unstable, fluctuating, and of uncertain habitation. It is not the land of Naid, as our common people think; rather, the Lord’s sentence is fulfilled when he wanders as a fugitive here and there.

**VERSE 17.** — “And Cain knew his wife.” (ISIDORE, ibid.) Figuratively, the offspring of the ungodly, seeking a foundation at the very beginning of the world, built in this life a city that he called Enoch, which means “dedication,” because the wicked dedicate themselves at the beginning by planting the root of their heart in this present life, which comes first, so that here they may flourish according to their desire and wither away from future glory. Of them it is said in John 5: “I saw the fool firmly rooted, and he immediately cursed his beauty.” Abraham, however, lived in tents, because the saints recognize themselves as guests and pilgrims, awaiting a city with foundations whose architect is God.

“And he built a city,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *City of God*, book XV, ch. 8, vol. VII.) It is asked with what helpers he built it, if there were no more human beings than Scripture says. But we must understand that there were many more at that time, since by living long they could beget many. Nor is it surprising, since the children of Israel are read to have multiplied during four hundred years to such an extent that the army could not be numbered.

**VERSE 18.** — “Moreover, Enoch,” etc. (JEROME.) No certain mysteries are carved out of all these things, nor would they be found unless certain roots of history had first been laid down. Nor would you gather fruit from the branches of trees unless you had first planted the trunks.

**VERSE 19.** — “Who took two wives,” etc. (ISIDORE, as above.) It should be noted that the generations from Adam through Cain end with eleven, in which transgression is signified. Lamech is the seventh, and three sons and one daughter are added to him so that the eleven may be completed, through which sin is signified. The generation is also closed by a woman, who was the beginning of sin, through which carnal pleasure resists the spirit. Hence she is called Naamah, that is, “pleasure.” In this lineage Lamech was the first to commit adultery contrary to custom and nature, through bigamy.

**VERSE 20.** — “And Ada gave birth to Jabal,” etc. (JEROME, in *Hebrew Questions*.) From bigamy Jabal is born, dwelling in tents; these movable dwellings represent the instability of those who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Tubal is also born, who invented music, etc., up to “like Jabal, Tubal, and Tubal-cain.”

**VERSE 21.** — “And the name of his brother was Jubal.” (RABANUS.) Josephus writes that he inscribed music on two columns, one of stone and the other of brick. One of these would not be dissolved by the Flood, while the other would not be destroyed by fire. Adam had foretold these two judgments.

**VERSE 22.** — [lacuna] “Tubal-cain.” (RABANUS.) According to Josephus, he practiced the arts of war and taught the craft of ironworking skillfully; he also invented certain things pertaining to the desire of the eyes.

**VERSE 23.** — “And Lamech said,” etc. (RABANUS.) The Hebrews say that Lamech, because he lived a long time, suffered blindness of the eyes and had a young man as his guide and director on journeys. While hunting, therefore, he shot an arrow in the direction indicated by the young man and by chance killed Cain, who was hiding among the bushes. This is what he says: “I have killed a man to my wound,” that is, by the wound I inflicted I killed not a beast but a man. Thereupon, inflamed with rage, he killed the young man as well.

**VERSE 23.** — [lacuna] “I have killed a man,” etc. (STRABO.) That is, Cain: “to my wound,” because I will be wounded on his account, that is, killed; “and a young man to my bruise,” because on his account also I will be condemned.

**VERSE 24.** — “Sevenfold vengeance will be exacted,” etc. (ALCUIN.) Allegorically. The sin of Lamech—whose name means “humbled”—signifies the downfall of the human race, which fell when Adam transgressed and could not rise again through the law, circumcision, or its own righteousness, until, after seventy-seven generations according to Luke, Christ came into the world and erased sin by the shedding of his blood. Hence Matthew 18:

“I do not say to you seven times, but up to seventy times seven”—that is, the Jew is to be received after seventy-seven punishments if he repents and seeks Christ’s forgiveness. The number seven signifies totality; multiplied by eleven it produces seventy-seven, in which complete transgression is signified. Yet the Gospel commands that this be forgiven to the penitent.

(JEROME, letter to Damasus.) They say that from Adam to Christ there are seventy-seven generations according to Luke. Therefore, just as Cain’s sin was dissolved in the seventh generation—“For God will not judge the same thing twice,” and one who received punishment once in life will not suffer in death the same torments that he suffered in life—so too Lamech, that is, the sin of the whole world, will be dissolved by Christ’s coming. A certain Hebrew told me that seventy-seven persons came forth from Lamech, all of whom perished in the Flood.

**VERSE 25.** — “And he knew again,” etc. Through Seth, whose name means “resurrection,” Christ’s life from the dead is signified. This is expressed in his mother’s words: “God has appointed for me another seed,” as though the Church were saying: “I who suffered mourning over the dead now rejoice over the one who has been raised.”

**VERSE 26.** — “Whom he called Enos,” etc. Enos means “human being.” He “began to call upon the name of the Lord,” because through Christ’s death, which Abel signified, and through the resurrection, which Seth signifies, a human being comes to confess the Lord as creator and restorer of lost life.

(JEROME.) “Whom he called Enos.” Enos means “human being,” and he “began to call upon the name of the Lord.” Just as Adam means “human being,” so Enos, according to the Hebrew truth, means “human being” or “man.” And appropriately, because he bore this name, it is said that at that time the calling upon the Lord’s name began, although many of the Hebrews think that at that time idols were first fashioned in the name of the Lord and in his likeness.

# CHAPTER V

**VERSES 1–2.** — “This is the book of the generation of Adam.” He was made in the likeness of God. Others read, “in the likeness of Adam.” This is like a conclusion to what precedes, with a recapitulation. “On the day when God created the human being.” He was indeed created on a day because he was established in the brightness of divine contemplation. “In the likeness of God.” Because God gave him reason, by which he could distinguish good and evil through understanding, love what he understood, and not consign what he loved to oblivion, thereby retaining the likeness of God. But after he destroyed this likeness through disobedience, having become earthly, he begot earthly beings. Hence, as the earthly one was, so are the earthly.

(CHRYSOSTOM, Homily 21 on Genesis, vol. IV.) Consider how he used the same words as at the beginning, so that he might teach us that, after those generations had become reprobate, Scripture no longer considers them worthy of remembrance; rather, it begins the genealogy from Seth, who has now been born to them. From this you may learn how greatly God takes account of the human race and how he turns away from those whose minds are bloodthirsty.

**VERSES 3–23.** — “Now Adam lived,” etc. (JEROME, in *Hebrew Questions*.) It should be known that up to the Flood, wherever our books say that someone begot children after “two hundred” and more years, the Hebrew has “one hundred years” and the remaining years that follow.

“And he begot,” etc. It is as though this one too bore the image of the earthly man who was appointed in place of righteous Abel, and by the interpretation of his name signifies Christ. But all first bear the image of the earthly human being before that of the heavenly one, although many, through faith, possessed the same grace by which Christians are saved even before Christ’s coming.

(STRABO.) They say that after Abel’s death Adam vowed that he would no longer know his wife or beget a son. But at God’s command he broke his vow, so that the Son of God might be born from him and the human race redeemed; for he ought not to be born from Cain’s line. Hence Adam is not read to have begotten anyone before Seth, whereas afterward it is said that he “begot sons and daughters.” This reckoning of genealogies spreads out like the branches of histories, from which the fruits of the mysteries are gathered in their proper places. It should also be noted that in Seth’s genealogy no woman is named individually, as in Cain’s genealogy: it belongs to the righteous to do everything manfully, to appropriate nothing feminine or weak. This genealogy also proceeds by tens up to Noah, in whom the fulfillment of the commandments is signified, just as transgression is signified by eleven in Cain’s genealogy. In the genealogy of the unrighteous, Enoch appears first; his name means “dedication,” because the reprobate fix the root of their hope in the present life and wither away from love of the imperishable inheritance. Of them it is said in John 5: “I saw the fool firmly rooted, and he immediately cursed his beauty.” In the genealogy of the righteous, Enoch is placed seventh from Adam, because they do not seek a city that remains here, but extend their expectation to the end of time, which is completed by the cycle of seven when the eighth, eternity, succeeds it. Hence this Enoch, who is placed seventh and was translated because he pleased God, signifies the seventh rest, to which, after this life, the one who steadfastly clings to God is transferred without delay. The interpretation of the names in this genealogy signifies the same thing: Adam means “human being” or “red earth”; Seth, “appointed” or “resurrection”; Enos, “human being”; Cainan, “lamentation”; Mahalalel, “praising God”; Jared, “strengthened”; Enoch, “dedication”; Methuselah, “sending forth of death”; Lamech, “humbled”; Noah, “rest.” Thus the human being proceeding from earth, rising from sins, will be a human being who calls upon God and mourns his former sins. In this way, praising God, strengthened by God’s Spirit, he is dedicated to eternal life. And as a conqueror, subject to God, he possesses everlasting rest, which is signified by Noah, whose name means “rest,” and who is counted in the tenth place, because the kingdom of heaven is possessed through the fulfillment of the commandments.

**VERSE 24.** — “And he walked with God,” etc. (ISIDORE, on Genesis.) Enoch, the seventh from Adam, pleasing God, etc., up to “for three times four make him.”

(Alcuin.) Enoch is preserved from death for so long a time, thereby showing that human beings would always live if they had not sinned.

**VERSE 25–30.**—“Methuselah also lived,” etc. (Augustine.) It is asked how Methuselah could have lived beyond the Flood according to the calculation of the years, since everyone except those who entered the ark perished. But this question arose from the corruption of the manuscripts: for not only is the matter found differently in the Hebrew texts, but even in the Septuagint interpretation, in a few manuscripts Methuselah is found to have died seven years before the Flood. The reason why, according to the Septuagint, his years are counted beyond the Flood is that he signifies Christ, whose life experiences no age, so that he might appear not to have experienced the Flood even in the greater matters.

**VERSE 31.**—“And all the days,” etc. (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*, vol. III.) “And all the days of Methuselah, which he lived, were nine hundred and sixty-nine years, and he died.” According to careful calculation, he is reported to have lived fourteen years after the Flood, etc., up to the year, that is, in which the Flood began.

“And Noah, when he was five hundred years old,” etc. (The same work.)

Noah is interpreted as “rest,” because under him all former works rested through the Flood.

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 1.**—“And when human beings had begun to multiply upon the earth.” (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*.) The Hebrew word *Elohim* is of both numbers: for it signifies both “God” and “gods.” Therefore Aquila ventured to say “sons of gods,” understanding holy gods or angels; following him, Symmachus says: “The sons of the mighty saw the daughters of human beings.”

**VERSE 2.**—“The sons of God saw,” etc. (Strabo.) The sons of Seth are understood by “sons of God”: overcome by desire, they took wives from the daughters of human beings—that is, from the stock of Cain—and begot powerful men: immense in bodily size, proud in strength, and uncivilized in conduct; these are called giants. It is not incredible that such men were begotten by human beings, not by angels or by certain demons who are wanton toward women, since after the Flood too the bodies not only of men but also of women existed in incredible size.

**VERSES 3–4.**—“And God said: My Spirit shall not remain,” etc. (Jerome, the same work.) Hebrew: *loiadon*, “My Spirit shall not judge human beings forever, because they are flesh.” That is, because the condition of human beings is fragile, etc., up to “but those whom he was going to destroy by the Flood.”

“And their days shall be,” etc. (Strabo.) Before the Flood, namely, for the performance of repentance. But because they persisted in wickedness before the appointed limit, they were destroyed in the hundredth year.

**VERSE 5.**—“But when the Lord saw,” etc. Repentance or grief of heart does not befall God, whose judgment concerning all things is as fixed as his foreknowledge is certain. Scripture nevertheless uses familiar expressions, accommodating itself to our smallness, so that from what is known we may come to know what is unknown. For the anger of God is not a disturbance of mind but a judgment inflicted upon the sinner; and the thought of his heart is the unchanging order by which things are changed.

**VERSES 6–8.**—“It repented him that,” etc. (Gregory, *Morals*, book V.) Often in sacred discourse the wise men of God derive an illustration from the wise men of the world. Thus now, for the benefit of humanity, the Creator himself assumes within himself the language of human passion, although it is clear that he who sees all things before they come to be did nothing of which he could repent. Therefore, just as it is not surprising that spiritual beings often use the words of the carnal, so it is not surprising that the Creator of all things, in order to draw the flesh toward understanding him, preserves or assumes within himself the speech of the flesh.

**VERSES 9–12.**—“Noah was a righteous man.” By his deeds he signifies Christ, who says in Matthew 11: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble in heart.” He alone is found righteous, and on account of his righteousness seven persons are granted deliverance. Christ likewise is righteous and perfect; to him the seven churches, illuminated by the sevenfold Spirit, are granted as one Church. Noah and his household are delivered through water and wood; so the household of Christ is delivered through baptism and the cross.

“In his generations.” As though he were not of perfected righteousness, but righteous in accordance with his generation.

**VERSE 13.**—“I will destroy them with,” etc. The teachers report that after the Flood the earth’s greenness and fertility were far inferior; and therefore the eating of meat was granted to human beings, whereas previously they had lived only on the produce of the earth.

**VERSE 14.**—“Make yourself an ark of wood.” Namely, of strong and indestructible wood, tightly joined; another translation says “squared,” so that it would be dissolved neither by the force of the winds nor by the inundation.

“Small chambers,” etc. (Strabo.) The Septuagint says: “You shall make the ark two-chambered and three-chambered: two-chambered in the lower parts, three-chambered in the upper parts.” Thus it was divided into five compartments. The first, the lower one, was for refuse, where the dung flowed away, so that those in the ark would not be harmed by the stench; the second was the storeroom; the third was for untamed animals and serpents; the fourth for tame animals; and the fifth, the uppermost, for human beings and birds. The door was where the two-chambered and three-chambered sections joined, that is, between the storeroom and the dwelling of the animals. (Augustine.) In the first dwelling, in the lower part, the ark was single-chambered; in the second, above the lower dwelling, it was two-chambered; and in the third, above the second, it was three-chambered. Others say that there were two small chambers in the lower part, and thus the ark was two-chambered. The lower of these received the refuse; the second held the food and was called the storeroom. In the upper part it was three-chambered, where human beings and animals were contained in suitable divisions.

(Isidore, on Genesis, vol. V.) Noah built the ark of incorruptible wood, etc., up to “he was prophetically represented in the five, and evangelically represented in the sixth.”

**VERSE 15.**—“Three hundred cubits,” etc. (Isidore, the same work.) The wood of the cross can be represented by the three hundred cubits, etc., up to “because there is one God from whom all things come, and one faith, and one baptism.”

(Gregory, *Homily XVI on Ezekiel*.) The ark, which was commanded to be made three hundred cubits in length, fifty in breadth, and thirty in height, etc., up to “through whom all advance who acknowledge themselves to be sinners.”

**VERSES 16–18.**—“You shall finish it at the top with a cubit.” Thus the Church, gathered into unity, is raised up and perfected. Hence Matthew 12: “Whoever does not gather with me scatters.”

“But you shall make a door for the ark,” etc. No one enters the Church except through the sacrament of the remission of sins, which flowed from the opened side.

“Upper rooms and a third story,” etc. The Septuagint says: “Two-chambered and three-chambered.” For from all the nations the Church gathers either a twofold multitude, from circumcision and uncircumcision, or a threefold one, from the three sons of Noah, whose descendants fill the world. The lower parts of the ark are divided because in this earthly life there is a diversity of nations; but at the top all are perfected into one, because Christ is all things and in all.

(Alcuin.) Properly, the ark was made pointed at the top, like a narrow roof, so that it might shed the threats of the rains; while at the bottom it stood square and stable in the waters and could not be tilted or sunk by the force of the winds, the violence of the waves, or the restlessness of the animals inside.

(Gregory, in the *Morals*.) The ark is broad below and narrow above, etc., up to “great heaps of straw, which are burned by fires.”

(Gregory.) In the moral sense, whoever turns away from the love of the world builds the ark of salvation in his heart. He has in himself length—that is, faith in the Trinity, and length of life and immortality; breadth in charity, by which he can do good even to his enemies; and height in hope, by which he raises himself toward heavenly things and refers the summit of his actions to one end.

**VERSES 19–20.**—“And from every living creature,” etc. (Augustine, *City of God*, book XV, final chapter, vol. VII.) A question is raised concerning the smallest creatures; thus good and evil are present together in the sacraments of the Church.

**VERSES 21–22.**—“Therefore you shall take,” etc. It is usually asked about animals thought to eat only flesh: whether, beyond the stated number, they were present without violating the command, because the necessity of feeding the others compelled their inclusion; or, as is more credible, whether there could have been food besides meat suitable for all. For many animals whose food is flesh also eat fruits and nuts, especially figs and chestnuts. Thus the righteous and wise man, instructed by God, could find and store food suitable for each creature apart from meat. Hunger compels all creatures to eat, and there is nothing that God cannot make sweet and wholesome; he could even have granted them, by divine power, to live without food.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSES 1–3.**—“And the Lord said,” etc. “From all clean animals you shall take seven and seven,” etc. (Rabbanus.) We should not understand a doubled seven, that is, fourteen, but only seven. Similarly, “two and two” means not four but only two, male and female. It should be noted that clean animals are brought in an odd number, namely seven, while unclean animals are brought in an even number, because the odd number signifies virtue, whereas the even number signifies weakness. There are more clean animals so that, when Noah left the ark, he would have something to sacrifice and eat.

(Isidore, on Genesis.) “From all living creatures,” etc. This does not mean that there are more good people than evil, etc., up to “the third day after the Passion, which is third in the number of days revolving through all time, and is both the first and the eighth.”

(Augustine, on Genesis.) It is asked whether such a large ark could have been built in a hundred years by four men, namely Noah and his three sons. But if they could not have done it, there was no great difficulty in employing other builders, although, having received payment for their labor, they did not care whether Noah acted wisely or foolishly and did not enter it because they did not believe what he believed.

**VERSE 4.**—“I will bring rain,” etc. (Isidore, *Questions on Genesis*, chapter 7.) Because every offense against the Decalogue is committed throughout the whole world, which is divided into four parts—and four times ten makes forty—whether guilt is contracted through prosperity, which pertains to the days, or through adversity, which pertains to the nights, it is washed away in baptism.

**VERSES 5–6.**—“So Noah did everything,” etc. “And he was six hundred years old,” etc. (Isidore, the same work.) Noah was five hundred years old when the Lord commanded him to make the ark, etc., up to “which is the square of three.”

**VERSES 7–9.**—“Noah entered, and his sons, his wife,” etc. (Rabbanus.) It should be noted that Noah enters the ark separately with his sons, and their wives separately. Therefore it says distinctly, “Noah entered, and his sons,” and adds distinctly, “his wife and the wives of his sons.” But men and women left together, for it is written: “Noah went out, and his wife. There is a time for embracing and a time for abstaining” (Ecclesiastes 3).

**VERSE 10.**—“And when they had passed,” etc. Because we are baptized in hope of the future rest signified by the seventh day, all flesh outside the ark was consumed by the Flood. For outside the Church the water of baptism, although it is the same water, does not avail for salvation but for destruction.

**VERSES 11–14.**—“In the six hundredth year,” etc. Allegorically, it should be noted that the waters of the Flood covered the earth in Noah’s six hundredth year, because in the sixth age of the world the sacrament of baptism was first commended. This occurred on the seventeenth day of the second month, because the number ten signifies the Decalogue. The number seven, on account of the Sabbath, signifies the seventh rest; and because renunciation of vices is seen in the Decalogue, whoever is initiated in baptism professes, for the sake of eternal rest, to renounce all vices.

“Floodgates.” Windows—namely, clouds—which were opened so that unusual and greater rains might be poured out from them. Properly, however, “floodgates” are the mouths of the Nile, but the word is used improperly for all windows.

(Rabbanus.) It is commonly asked whether the ark, with the capacity described, could have carried all the animals said to have entered it, together with their food. Origen solves this by the geometric cubit, asserting that Moses was not said without reason to have been educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, who loved geometry, and that the geometric cubit contained as much as six of our cubits.

**VERSES 15–16.**—“Two and two,” etc. (Augustine, in the work cited above.) Earlier he commanded seven and seven of the clean animals and two and two of the unclean. How then does he now say that two and two entered, whether clean or unclean? This does not refer to the number of clean and unclean animals but to male and female. In all cases there are two, male and female.

It should also be noted that it says, “in which was the spirit of life,” not only of human beings but also of cattle. Some want the words “he breathed into his face the spirit of life” to be understood of the Holy Spirit; but some manuscripts have the better reading, “the breath of life.”

**VERSES 17–19.**—“For forty days,” etc. (Alcuin.) The rain flooded the earth for forty days, a number that signifies the tribulation of repentance. After forty days Noah opened the window, signifying that heaven is opened to those who fast. Hence Moses, Elijah, and the Savior himself consecrated fasts by the number forty, as though they were necessary in three periods: before the Law, under the Law, and under grace.

**VERSES 20–22.**—“Fifteen cubits higher,” etc. (Augustine, on Genesis.) If the soil of Mount Olympus, as history relates, could invade the region of tranquil air, etc., up to “for preserving rest and faith in the resurrection.”

“Fifteen.” Some think that neither the quality of the earth nor the height of the mountains was before the Flood as great as it is today.

**VERSES 23–24.**—“They were destroyed from the earth.” (Alcuin.) Therefore the land animals perished more than the aquatic animals, because they live from the accursed earth.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSES 1–3.**—“But God remembered Noah,” etc. “He brought a spirit over the earth,” etc. (Alcuin, *Questions on Genesis*.) This may be understood of the Spirit of whom it was said, “The Spirit of God was moving over the waters.” Then he was moving so that, when the waters were gathered into their own [or, in some manuscripts, “one”] place, the earth might appear; now he is brought forth so that, when the waters of the Flood had been removed, he might reveal the face of the earth. The spirit may also be understood as wind, in accordance with Psalm 106: “And the spirit of the storm stood still,” by whose blasts the water would recede.

**VERSE 4.**—“And the ark rested in the seventh month,” etc. (Isidore.) It signifies the rest of the seventh number; and because the perfected rest there, the number of the previously mentioned square is also repeated. For the sacrament is commended on the twenty-seventh day of the second month and confirmed again on the twenty-seventh day of the seventh month, when the ark rested. What is promised in hope is displayed in reality.

(Augustine.) It is asked whether these things happened after one hundred and fifty days, or whether everything was recalled by recapitulation—things that began to happen after the forty days of rain—so that only this statement, “one hundred and fifty days,” refers to the period during which the water rose as far as the mountains, either after the rain had ceased but the fountains of the abyss were still flowing, or because the water remained at that height, no wind having dried it. The other things that are stated did not all happen after one hundred and fifty days, but were recalled; they began to happen at the end of the forty days.

**VERSES 5–6.**—“For in the tenth month.” It should be noted that in the tenth month the peaks of the mountains appeared, which the waters of the Flood had exceeded by fifteen cubits. This is because the mysteries of eternal rest and the glory of the resurrection—which the wisdom of the proud did not know—were understood through the excellence of the saints by the fulfillment of the commandments. Hence Psalm 118: “From your commandments I have gained understanding.” And elsewhere, Luke 10: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Which was going out,” etc. (Isidore.) The fact that the raven did not return after forty days—either seized by the waters or attracted by a floating corpse—figures the foulest impurity of desire. It signifies those who are excessively intent upon the things outside, in the world: either that they are rebaptized, or that they are seduced and held fast by those whom baptism killed outside the ark, that is, outside the Church.

(Augustine.) It is asked whether the raven died or could somehow have survived. For if there was land on which it could rest, the dove likewise would have found rest. Hence it is inferred that the raven could perch upon a corpse, from which the dove naturally recoils.

**VERSE 8.**—“He also sent out,” etc. (Isidore.) The dove was sent out but, finding no place of rest, returned. This signifies that through the New Testament rest was not promised to the saints in this world. For it was sent out after forty days, a number by which the life lived in this world is signified.

(Strabo.) The ark contains both a raven and a dove, and the Church contains both good and evil. The raven, once sent out, does not return because the reprobate, clinging to the enticements of the world, perish. The dove returned, carrying in its mouth an olive branch with green leaves, because the saints, rejoicing in simplicity, carry the gift of peace in their mouths, saying: “With those who hated peace I was peaceful; when I spoke to them,” etc. (Psalm 119).

**VERSE 9.**—“It returned.” (Augustine.) The question is how the dove did not find a place on which to rest, since, according to the order of the narrative, the peaks of the mountains had already been uncovered. This can be resolved by recapitulation, so that what happened earlier may be understood to have been narrated later; or, rather, the ground had not yet dried.

**VERSE 10.**—“Having waited,” etc. After another seven days, the dove was sent out on account of the spiritual work signified by the number seven. It brought back a fruitful olive shoot, signifying that many baptized outside the Church, provided they do not lack the richness of charity, will at a later time be brought back into the fellowship of unity in the mouth of the dove, as though in a kiss of peace.

**VERSE 11.**—“Carrying a branch.” (Alcuin.) After the Flood, the dove brings an olive branch to Noah, the foulest bird having been driven away. This is because the dove of the Holy Spirit, coming to Christ after baptism, announces peace through a branch of refreshment and light.

**VERSE 12.**—“Nevertheless he waited another seven days,” etc. (Isidore, on Genesis.) After another seven days the dove was sent out and did not return. This signifies the end of the world, when the rest of the saints will exist—not in the sacrament of hope by which the Church is now joined together, as long as it drinks what flowed from the side of Christ, but in the perfection of salvation, when the kingdom will be handed over to God the Father, so that in that visible contemplation of truth we will need no mysteries.

**VERSE 13.**—“In the six hundred and first year,” etc. (The same work.) In the life of Noah, that is, after six hundred years had been completed, the roof of the ark was opened, etc., up to “with one added, on account of the bond of unity.”

**VERSE 14.**—“In the second month.” (Strabo.) Historically, that is, in May: Noah spent a year in the ark, and on the very day on which he entered, he left. He entered on the seventeenth day of the second month; the text now says that he left on the twenty-seventh day of the same month. But it should be understood that if eleven days are added to the present day, the moon will be in the same phase on that day a year later. Thus, when Noah entered, it was the seventeenth moon, or the seventeenth day of the second month. Therefore, after eleven days had been added to the year, it was the twenty-seventh day and the seventeenth moon.

“In the second month,” etc. Mystically. As stated above, on the seventeenth day of the six hundredth year the earth was moistened by the waters of the Flood; but on the twenty-seventh day of the second month it dried out, when Noah was commanded to leave the ark and received the covenant that he would never again perish by the waters of a flood. This may be understood as follows: through seventeen, as stated above, the condition of beginners may be signified, when they renounce vices; through twenty-seven, the advancement of the perfected in the completion of virtues. For if you add ten and seventeen, they make twenty-seven. If to the ten commandments by which one renounces sins you add evangelical perfection, through which one is commanded not only not to become angry but also to love one’s enemies, and similar commandments, you have reached that age of perfection in which you no longer need the previously mentioned sacraments. Leaving the ark—that is, passing from hope to sight—you will find the rest promised in the sacraments.

**VERSES 15–19.**—“Go out from the ark,” etc. (Isidore.) Those who entered separately leave together, because now “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh.” But in the resurrection of the righteous, in perfect peace, the body will cling to the spirit, with no need or desire for change resisting it.

**VERSE 20.**—“And taking,” etc. (Augustine.) Clean and unclean animals entered the ark, but after leaving, only the clean are offered to God. The statement, “I will not strike down every living creature as I have done,” followed by the benefits that goodness generously grants to the undeserving, may perhaps signify the indulgence of the New Testament: the former vengeance belongs to the severity of the Law, while this belongs to the goodness of grace.

**VERSES 21–22.**—“For the inclination,” etc. (Gregory, *Morals*, book XXXVIII.) Let no one attribute to himself the victory if he has overcome his thoughts. The evil of corruption, which each person takes from the origin of carnal desires, exercises itself as age advances. Unless the hand of divine strength restrains it quickly, the fault of nature devours every good thing into the depths: “Neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth” (1 Corinthians 3).

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 1.**—“And God blessed Noah and his sons,” etc. “Increase and multiply.” Humanity is placed over the other animals as a terror to them, as a consolation after the vengeance that had occurred, so that a few human beings would not be overwhelmed by many beasts, and so that they might know that they rule irrational creatures, but not rational beings.

**VERSES 2–3.**—“And your terror,” etc. (Gregory, *Morals*, book II, chapter 11.) The virtue of humility is great in powerful men, etc., up to “who seek not their own glory but the usefulness of their subjects.”

**VERSES 4–8.**—“Flesh with blood.” (Isidore.) All animals are given to them as food, because in the calling of the nations to faith there is no distinction, as is represented in Peter’s sheet. They are forbidden to eat blood so that their former life may not be retained in the conscience as though suffocated, but may be poured out through confession. The eating of meat appears to have been permitted after the Flood because of the barrenness of the earth and the frailty of humanity.

**VERSES 9–12.**—“Behold, I establish a covenant,” etc. God established a testament between himself and human beings and every living creature, so that he would not destroy it by a flood: namely, the bow that appears in the clouds and never shines except from the sun. Those who are separated from the Church do not perish in the Flood if, in the prophets and all the Holy Scriptures—as in the clouds of God—they recognize the glory of Christ and do not seek their own glory. But so that worshipers of this sun may not swell with pride, they should know that Christ is signified by the sun just as he is signified by the lion, the lamb, and the stone: by likeness, not by the substance of identity.

**VERSES 13–17.**—“I will set my bow,” etc. (Alcuin, on Genesis.) God gave the bow as a sign of security, so that fearful people would not be afraid of being destroyed by another flood whenever they saw the inundations of rain. It was placed in the sky so that it could be seen by everyone, and so that in every tribulation we might raise the eyes of our hearts toward him who dwells in heaven. Since the bow exists only from the rays of the sun and a moist cloud, it appears that there had been no rains before the Flood. The earth could, however, have been made fertile by dew and the overflowing of springs.

(Strabo.) The bow has two colors, blue and fiery, which express two judgments: one of water, which has passed; the other of fire, which is believed to come at the end of the world. Hence the blue color is on the outside, while the fiery color is on the inside.

**VERSES 18–20.**—“Now the sons of Noah were,” etc. (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*.) Often the Septuagint, unable to render the letter *heth*, which produces a doubled aspiration, added the Greek letter chi, χ, when translating into Greek, thereby indicating aspiration in such words. Thus they translated *Cham* for what is *Ham*, from whom Egypt is called *Ham* in the language of the Egyptians even to this day.

**VERSE 21.**—“And drinking wine,” etc. Christ too was made drunk when he suffered and was stripped when he was crucified. “In his tent,” that is, among the members of his own bloodline: then the mortality of the flesh was exposed. He was “a stumbling block to the Jews and foolishness to the Gentiles, but to those who are called, Jews and Gentiles”—like Shem and Japheth—“the power of God and the wisdom of God; for what is foolish of God is wiser than human beings.”

(Alcuin.) After the Flood Noah became drunk, perhaps because he did not know that wine could cause drunkenness. Indeed, human beings are not read to have used wine before the Flood. Therefore it is specifically said of Noah that he planted a vineyard. The uncovering of the thigh follows drunkenness just as lust follows satiety.

**VERSE 22.**—“When he had seen this,” etc. (Procopius, on Genesis.) These circumstances magnify Ham’s sin. He despises his father, blurts out how shamefully his father had lain, and reports it not to one brother but to both. If more had been present, he would have exposed the deed to everyone. What ought to have been least amusing to him seemed ridiculous; the deed deserved modesty and caution, lest his father’s disgrace spread to others. Nor does he announce it to those who were members of the household, but to outsiders.

(Isidore.) The Jews, seeing Christ’s death, mocked him. But Shem and Japheth, the two peoples who believe from uncircumcision and circumcision, turned away and covered him, etc., up to “as though running together into the peace of the corner.”

**VERSE 23.**—“But Shem and Japheth,” etc. (Gregory, in the *Morals*.) We are said to turn away from something that we reject. What then does it mean that the sons, turning away as they came, covered their father’s nakedness by throwing cloaks over their backs, except that good subjects are displeased by the faults of their superiors in such a way that they conceal them from others? They carry the covering while turned away because, judging the deed and honoring the master, they do not wish to see what they cover.

**VERSES 24–25.**—“Cursed be Canaan, the boy,” etc. (The same work.) God does not leave sins unpunished, but begins judgment in our correction and brings it to rest in the condemnation of the reprobate. For judgment begins from the household of God. What then will be the end of those who do not believe and do not experience temporal scourges? They will perish forever; their wickedness was prefigured in the sin of Ham. To him it is said: “Cursed be Canaan, the boy,” etc. The son received the sentence when the father sinned, because the wickedness of the reprobate prospers for a time here but perishes in the future.

**VERSE 26.**—“Blessed be the Lord, the God of Shem.” Although he is the God of all nations, he is called, as though by a proper name, the God of Israel even among those nations. This results from the blessing of Japheth, because the Church has occupied the world among the people of the nations; this was foretold when it was said: “May God enlarge Japheth.”

“Canaan.” (Strabo.) From him come the Canaanites, who are prophetically destined by this curse to be expelled from their dwelling place.

**VERSES 27–29.**—“May God enlarge Japheth,” etc. (Jerome.) The Jews are from Shem, the Gentiles from Japheth. Since the multitude of believers is broad, breadth is named from the breadth called *Japheth*. When he says, “And let him dwell in the tents of Shem,” this is prophesied of us, who, after Israel has been expelled, occupy ourselves with the instruction and knowledge of the Scriptures.

“May God enlarge Japheth,” etc. (Isidore.) Shem, the elder by birth, is the Jewish people, from whom came the patriarchs, prophets, and apostles, etc., up to “that is, their work.”

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.**—“These are the generations,” etc. The generations of the two sons of Noah who were blessed, and of the middle one who was cursed, are now traced. From them arose seventy-two generations: fifteen from Japheth, thirty from Ham, and twenty-seven from Shem. To these the Lord sent seventy-two disciples.

“Shem.” (Alcuin.) Shem, as they think, received Asia; Ham, Africa; and Japheth, Europe.

“Japheth.” He was the younger son, from whom seven sons were born. They occupied the northern region from Taurus and Amanus, the mountains of Cilicia and Syria, as far as the river Tanais; in Europe, as far as Gades. We leave their names to the places and peoples, many of which have been changed while the rest remain.

**VERSES 2–6.**—“Gomer.” According to Josephus, these are the Galatians, who in Latin are called *Gallograeci*, “Greek Gauls.”

“Tubal.” The Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom Celtiberia derives its name, although some suspect that they were Italians.

“Canaan.” He obtained the land that the Jews later possessed after expelling the Canaanites.

**VERSE 8.**—“Regma and Sheba,” etc. (Jerome.) They gradually lost their ancient names, and it is not known which names they now bear.

“Sheba.” This is different from the preceding one, and they differ in writing. The former is written with *samekh*, the latter with *shin*. Thus, where we say, “The kings of the Arabs and Sheba shall bring gifts,” the Hebrew has both *sheba* and *seba*.

**VERSE 8.**—“Nimrod.” He wished to penetrate heaven contrary to nature. He signifies the devil, who says: “I will ascend above the stars of heaven.” According to Josephus, Nimrod seized tyranny through a new desire for kingship and was the originator of the tower’s construction, so that it would touch heaven. “He began to be powerful,” or “a giant,” according to others. But Scripture records that giants were born earlier. Perhaps, however, the novelty of the human race being restored after the Flood is being recalled: “because he began to be a giant upon the earth.”

**VERSE 9.**—“A mighty hunter.” (Alcuin.) That is, an oppressor and destroyer of human beings, whom he enticed to build a tower against God.

**VERSES 10, 12.**—“Babylon.” It means “confusion,” because there the division of languages took place.

**VERSE 11.**—“Asshur.” The empire of the Assyrians, which first existed under Ninus. He built Nineveh, which is called beautiful because of its repentance.

**VERSES 13–20.**—“But Mesraim,” etc. (Jerome.) Except for the Lehabim, from whom the Libyans were later named, although they were previously called Putites, and the Casluhim, who were later called Philistines, whom we incorrectly call Palestinians, the other six nations are unknown to us because they were overthrown in the Ethiopian war. They possessed the land from Gaza to the furthest boundaries of Egypt.

“Ludim and Anamim, Lehabim, Naphtuhim,” etc. All these are unknown, either because the nations were destroyed in the Ethiopian war or because it is not known what names they now bear.

**VERSE 21.**—“From Shem.” He speaks of him last because he proceeds through his generation and the line of his descendants.

“Heber.” He is nevertheless the fifth from Shem, the son of Noah. It is rightly asked whether the Hebrews were so called from him, or whether the genealogy passed through him to Abraham. Which is more probable: that the Hebrews are called *Heberaioi*, as though “Heberites,” or *Abraaioi*, as though “Abrahamites”?

**VERSES 22–24.**—“Asshur.” He built Nineveh.

**VERSES 25–30.**—“And sons were born to Heber,” etc. Heber means “one who crosses over,” from whom come the Hebrews, that is, “those who cross over.” The true Hebrews are those who pass from present things to future things and from things that perish to things that endure. These nations possessed the whole region called Geria, from the river Conus onward.

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 1.**—“Now the earth had one language,” etc. (Augustine, on Genesis.) It was stated earlier that the sons of Noah, or of his sons, were distributed throughout the lands according to their languages. Here, by recapitulation, he recalls afterward what had occurred earlier. But the obscurity arises because he arranges the account in such a form of expression that it seems as though the narrative of what happened later follows from it.

**VERSE 2.**—“And when they set out.” (Chrysostom, on Genesis.) See how the human race cannot remain within its own limits but, desiring more, always seeks greater things. This is what destroys the human race: it does not wish to recognize the measure of its nature but always desires greater things. “For,” he says, “they saw a plain in the land of Shinar”; migrating, they abandoned their former place and dwelt there.

**VERSE 3.**—“Come.” They feared another Flood; therefore, at Nimrod’s instigation, they wished to establish a tower for themselves in which they would not fear a flood. It was a foolish and impious boldness, from which punishment and the division of languages followed.

(Isidore, on Genesis.) The tower signifies the pride of the world or the doctrines of heretics, etc., up to “the unity of confession and faith.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Come, therefore,” etc. He is understood to have spoken to the angels; or according to the statement, “Let us make the human being in our image and likeness.” For the singular number follows: “and he divided them,” etc., just as there it says: “God made the human being in his own image and likeness.”

(Gregory, *Morals*, book II, chapter 5.) “Come,” etc. Those who cling to God are told, “Come,” because never to decline from divine contemplation but always to increase, and never to withdraw in heart, is always to be coming through a stable movement. The angels ascend by contemplating the Creator; they descend by pressing down, through the scrutiny of strict judgment, the creature that illicitly raises itself up. Therefore, to say, “Let us descend and confuse their language,” is to show within himself what is rightly done and, through the force of inward vision, to breathe judgments into their minds by hidden movements.

**VERSES 8–9.**—“He divided them.” (Alcuin.) In this division of languages God did nothing new; rather, he divided modes of speaking and forms of language among the various nations. Hence in different languages we find the same syllables and letters of the same power joined differently, and often the same names or words signifying something else. Thus, where Psalm 2 says, “with a rod of iron,” the Greek has ἐν ῥάβδῳ σιδηρᾷ (*en rhabdō sidēra*). Therefore, in Latin *sidera* does not mean “iron,” as it does in Greek, but “stars.”

(AUG. *City of God*, book XVI, chapter 4.) The evil intention is rightly punished, even when the intended result does not follow. But what kind of punishment was it? Since the ruler’s authority lies in speech, pride was condemned precisely there, so that the one who had refused to understand in order to obey God’s command would not be understood when commanding human beings.

**VERSES 10–25.**—“Shem was one hundred years old.” [Col. 0115C] (BEDE, *Hexaemeron*, book III, tome II, col. 131.) A major difficulty arises for us according to the literal sense: how can Shem be said to have been one hundred years old two years after the Flood, when it was stated above that he was born in Noah’s five-hundredth year, and that the Flood came in Noah’s six-hundredth year, etc., up to “because God took him.”

**VERSES 26–30.**—“Terah fathered Abram and Nahor.” (AUG. *Questions on Genesis*, question 25.) Not at the same time, but at the appropriate periods of his life, after he began to father children. In these matters the order of birth is not to be considered, but rather the indication of the future dignity in which Abram excels.

**VERSES 31–32.**—“In Ur of the Chaldeans.” (JEROME.) In Hebrew, *in Ur Chesdim* (), that is, “in the fire of the Chaldeans.” The Hebrews tell here the story that Abram was cast into the fire because he refused to worship the fire honored by the Chaldeans, and that, being delivered by God’s aid, he escaped from the fire of idolatry. Hence God says to him: “I am the one who brought you out of Ur of the Chaldeans.”

“Aram, the father of Milcah.” (The same.) He was the father of both women. Aram, son of Terah and brother of Abram and Nahor, fathered two daughters, Milcah and Sarai, also called Jeschah. Nahor married Milcah, and Abram married Sarai. For marriages between uncles and nieces had not yet been forbidden; at the beginning, marriages even between brothers and sisters had been practiced.

“Then Terah took Abram,” etc., up to “the days of Terah were two hundred and five years, and he died in Haran.” (AUG.) It is first said that, “when Terah was seventy years old, he fathered Abram,” and afterward that he remained in Haran with all his household and died there. And Abram was told to leave Haran, and he left when he was seventy-five years old. But by recapitulation it is shown that the Lord commanded him while his father was still alive, etc., up to the one from whom the Jews received their name, because of the royal tribe.

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 1.**—“Go out from your land,” etc. (AUG., in the work cited above.) Stephen’s account of this matter must be considered, etc., up to: thus Abram was settled in that land when he lived there until the birth of Jacob.

(STRABO.) It should be noted that he had already gone out from his land, but at that time he had departed bodily, not in mind and will; for perhaps he still intended to return when he was told: “Go out,” etc.

(ISIDORE.) Christ left the land and kindred of the Jews and was magnified among the nations. We too must leave our land—that is, earthly possessions and riches—and our kindred—that is, the practice of vices, which have clung to us from birth and are joined to us like blood relationships—and “our father’s house,” that is, the memory of the world. Thus, renouncing it, we may be enlarged with the people of God and, when the time comes, be brought into the land of the heavenly promise.

**VERSES 2–3.**—“I will make you into a great nation,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Two things are promised to Abram. One is that his descendants will possess the land of Canaan, as is said: “And come into the land that I will show you.” The other is far more excellent: not concerning a carnal but a spiritual offspring, by which he would become the father not only of the Jewish nation but of all nations that follow his faith. This is promised in the words: “In you all the nations of the earth shall be blessed.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Seventy-five years old.” (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) If Terah, Abram’s father, was in the region of Chaldea, etc., up to the statement that he stayed there for a longer time.

**VERSES 8–12.**—“Bethel.” (RABANUS.) It is interpreted as “house of God”; afterward it was called Bethaven, that is, “house of the idol.”

“Hai.” Mystically, *Hai* is interpreted as “eye” or “spring.” Thus the patriarch, journeying toward the land of promise, pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai, because the saints, regenerated by the fountain of baptism and watchful during the course of this life, hasten toward God’s tabernacle, that is, the heavenly city.

**VERSES 13–14.**—“Say, I beg you,” etc. (AUG., *City of God*, book XVI, chapter 19.) It is asked why the patriarch wished to lie, etc., up to the point of preserving both his own life and his wife’s chastity.

**VERSES 15–20.**—“The woman was taken away.” (RABANUS.) Sarai is excused, since she was taken against her will into Pharaoh’s house—not only because the body is not defiled, nor the soul except by the consent of the mind, but also because the act occurred with her husband’s agreement and permission.

(AUG., *Questions on Genesis*.) She was able to remain untouched in Pharaoh’s household for so long because in Esther it is recorded that girls were not immediately brought to the kings, but were kept in custody for a year: for six months they were anointed with oil of myrrh, and for the other six months they were treated with various perfumes. Thus she could remain untouched during this interval. Meanwhile the Egyptians treated Abram and his household well, until Pharaoh, struck by God and learning that she was his wife, returned her untouched.

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSES 1–2.**—“So Abram went up,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) He is rightly said to have gone up after being delivered from Egypt; but how could he have been “very rich”? In the Hebrew truth it reads *gravis vehementer*, “very burdened”: for he was weighed down by Egypt. And although these possessions may appear to be gold and silver, if they are Egyptian they are burdensome to a holy man. Nor, as the Septuagint reads, did he “go from where he had come into the desert as far as Bethel”; rather, according to the Hebrew, he “went on his journey through the Negeb as far as Bethel.” He departed from Egypt not to seek the desert that he had left in Egypt, but to come through the south, which is opposite the north, to the house of God, where his tabernacle stood between Bethel and Hai.

**VERSES 3–5.**—“In Bethel,” etc. Bethel is a small town twelve miles from Aelia, on the right for those traveling toward Neapolis. It was formerly called Luz, that is, “almond tree,” and lay in the tribe of Benjamin. Hai, however, lay in the tribe of Judah and was assigned to the priests. Bethel means “house of God”; Hai, “eye” or “spring.” Thus he rightly pitched his tent between Bethel and Hai and built an altar to the Lord, because the saints, withdrawing from the prince of the world and from the pleasures of the age, washed in the holy spring of baptism, proceeding thoughtfully through the course of the present life and offering God a sacrifice of praise and good works upon the altar of faith, happily hasten toward the house of God, that is, the heavenly Jerusalem.

**VERSES 6–9.**—“For their possessions were many,” etc. “Let there be no strife,” etc. Let us likewise put nothing before harmony and charity, but whether through the right hand of prosperity or the left hand of adversity, let us persevere in peace and love. The quarrel between the shepherds of Lot and the shepherds of Abram signifies the conflict between Catholic shepherds and heretical subverters. Thus Lot signifies the founders of heresies, for his name is interpreted as “one who turns aside,” and he chose for himself the region around the Jordan, that is, around “the descent.” His shepherds signify heretics and schismatics, who seek what is beautiful and downward-sloping, but do not ascend the mountain with Moses to the Lord, preserving peace and unity. They accept the freedom to go wherever they wish and, fleeing grace, entrust themselves to free will. Abram’s shepherds, however, signify Catholic teachers, who even avoid heretics geographically, in accordance with the words addressed to Titus III: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second correction.” This takes place among the nations of the Canaanites and Perizzites, in the land of promise, because there is commonly contention between Catholics and heretics over which of them will possess the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0118A] “For we are brothers.” In holy Scripture people are called brothers in three ways: by nature, as Jacob and Esau; by kinship, as Abram and Lot; and by nation, as all Jews. Hence: “If your brother is weakened and sells himself to you,” etc.

**VERSES 10–12.**—“Like paradise,” etc. From this we learn that there is an earthly paradise, to which earthly irrigation is compared. This region was level and open country, watered by the flowing Jordan, just as Egypt is watered by the Nile.
