**VERSE 13.**—“Before the Lord.” The crime is entrusted to him for punishment; for a crime may also be manifest to human beings without being punishable by them.

**VERSE 14.**—“Lift up your eyes,” etc. As though he were to look toward the four quarters of the world, possession of Palestine is promised to him and to his seed. In some manuscripts, “the sea” is placed for the west, because Palestine has the sea on its western side.

**VERSES 15–17.**—“All the land,” etc. This alone was not promised. For it was not said, “I will give you as much land as you see,” but, “I will give you the land that you see.” Since land farther away was also being given on every side, that which was seen was especially given. Hence he also added: “Rise and walk through the land,” etc., so that by walking through it he might reach the land that he could not see while standing in one place. This signifies the land that Israel, Abram’s seed according to the flesh and not according to faith, received—Israel that would become like the sand of the sea, because it could not be numbered.

[Col. 0118C] “To you I will give it.” The inheritance of all nations is promised to Christ, who spread his Church throughout the whole world, to whom the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm II). And in Psalm LXXI: “And he shall rule from sea to sea.”

**VERSE 18.**—“In Hebron.” This is a city in the tribe of Judah, also called Cariatharbe, that is, “city of four”: *cariat* is “city” in Hebrew, and *arbe* means “four.” Adam the great, Abram, Isaac, and Jacob are buried there.

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 1.**—“Amraphel.” His name is interpreted as “he said, ‘Let him fall,’” and he is king of Shinar, which is interpreted as “shaking of the teeth” or “their stench.” He signifies heretics, who tend toward ruin and vomit forth a foul meaning in deceitful words.

“Arioch.” This is interpreted as “drunk” or “drunkenness.” He signifies the folly of the gentiles, who, drunk with iniquity, worship the creature instead of the Creator and are swept along by the allurements of the world.

“Chedorlaomer.” This is interpreted as “beautiful sheaf.” He is king of Elam, that is, of this world. He signifies hypocrisy, which, although vain and destructive, appears beautiful on the surface; but what it has been will be revealed in the future.

“Tidal.” This means “knowing the yoke” or “explorer.” He is king of the nations and signifies greed, which is shrewd and cunning and subjugates many to itself.

[Col. 0119A] “Amraphel,” etc. These four kings represent the four principal vices, opposed to the four principal virtues. They strive to subjugate the five senses through the five kings represented, through the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and worldly ambition.

**VERSES 2–13.**—“Bela.” (JEROME.) In Hebrew it means “devouring.” The Hebrews relate that this place was elsewhere called Salissah, and “the staggering heifer,” because it was swallowed up by a third earthquake. From the time when Sodom and Gomorrah, Admah and Zeboiim were overthrown by divine fire, it was called “the little one.” *Segor* is translated as “little,” and in the Syrian language is called Zoara. The Valley of Salt, where the bitumen wells were, was turned into the Dead Sea after God’s anger and the rain of sulfur. Among the Greeks it is called the Asphalt Lake, that is, the lake of bitumen.

Mystically, the four kings overcome the five when hostile powers, abusing the five bodily senses, entangle and enslave them through vices.

Allegorically, such kings first overcome Bera, whose name is interpreted as “malice” or “creature,” king of Sodom, that is, of blindness or of the silent beast, when they persuade those who persist in ancient wickedness to follow the blindness of lust like animals. They also defeat Birsha, that is, “one established in distress,” king of Gomorrah, that is, of a swelling and rebellious people, when they overwhelm and overthrow those who are harassed by worldly cares and do not fear to commit the crime of plunder. They likewise overcome Shinab, king of Admah, that is, of “the earthly,” when they urge those who think only of earthly things to remain in luxury, so that they say: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (1 Cor. XV). They overcome Shemeber, whose name is interpreted as “destruction there,” king of Zeboiim, that is, of “the belt of sorrow,” when they deceive the unwary through anger and envy. Hence Job V: “Anger kills the fool, and envy slays the little one.” They also overcome the king of Bela when they cast the fainthearted into despair; for Bela is interpreted as “precipitation” or “swallowing.” Above all, the devil strives to cast a person into despair after the fall into sin.

**VERSES 4–6.**—“Twelve,” etc. The number twelve is excessive. In this excess our five senses serve vain superstition, which is signified by Chedorlaomer, and the four vices associated with it. Those who wish to withdraw suffer severe persecution and are often overcome.

**VERSES 7–12.**—“And they struck.” (JEROME.) Another edition has … up to “because there God judged the people.”

“Rephaim at Ashtaroth,” etc. The names of the places and nations signify those who live carnally, whom vices easily overcome.

**VERSE 13.**—“To the Hebrew.” The Septuagint has “to the one from beyond the river,” since he came from Mesopotamia, crossed the Euphrates, and settled in the land of Canaan. Hence Joshua son of Nun: “Why do you wish to serve the gods of your fathers who are beyond the river?”

[Col. 0120A] **VERSES 14–17.**—“When Abram heard this,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Mystically, when our faith has been strengthened by the principal Spirit, it subjects the five bodily senses, as five kings, triumphing through the word of God over the outer person. He defeated his enemies with three hundred and eighteen men because, through the mystery of the cross—which the letter *tau* signifies, and which represents three hundred—we overcome the five carnal senses that had previously taken us captive through various vices. Eighteen, formed by multiplying three and six, signifies faith in the Trinity and the perfection of works, by which complete victory over vices is achieved through the virtues.

(STRABO.) Allegorically, Abram’s war with the four kings signifies the war between virtues and vices. Therefore the father of faith, and the first path of belief, fought and conquered for his brother Lot, not with a large army but with three hundred and eighteen trained household servants. In the same way, each person should wage war for his own soul against spiritual wickedness with three hundred and eighteen household servants, that is, with the help of the holy cross; for the letter *tau*, which has the shape of a cross, expresses three hundred.

Dan is one of the sources of the Jordan; the other is called Jor, which is interpreted as “stream.” When the two sources, which are not far from one another, are joined into one stream, it is called the Jordan.

**VERSES 18–19.**—“But Melchizedek,” etc. (JEROME.) The Hebrews now say that he was Shem, Noah’s son, and by calculating the years demonstrate that he lived as far as the time of Isaac. They also say that all the firstborn from Noah to Aaron were high priests. Salem was later called Jerusalem. When the Apostle speaks of Melchizedek as “without father and mother,” he refers this to Christ and through him to the Church of the nations, because the glory of the head is referred to the members. For Melchizedek blessed Abram, who was circumcised, and in him Levi, and thus Aaron, from whom the priesthood afterward descended. From this he wishes to infer that the priesthood of the Church, which possesses the foreskin, blessed the circumcised priesthood of the Synagogue. Since he says, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” our ministry is signified as belonging to the true order: it is not consecrated by sacrificing irrational victims, as under Aaron, but by offering bread and wine, that is, by consecrating the body and blood of the Lord.

(STRABO.) Melchizedek, whose name is interpreted as “king of righteousness,” and who is called “king of peace,” signifies Christ, through whom we have been reconciled and who will judge justly at the end of the age.

**VERSES 20–23.**—“He gave him tithes.” (ISIDORE.) Thus the patriarch, knowing … up to the point of not refusing the wages lawfully owed to those who fight.

**VERSE 24.**—“Those who came,” etc. Faith sometimes makes use of the testimony of unbelievers. Hence the Apostle says to Titus I: “Evil beasts, lazy bellies”—but for the benefit of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 1.**—“After these things had taken place,” etc. “Do not be afraid.” After the multitude of vices has been conquered, the hope of every believer is strengthened by the Lord, so that he does not waver but awaits his reward.

**VERSE 2.**—“And Abram said.” (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) “I am going without children,” etc., up to the statement that they say Damascus was both named and founded by him.

**VERSES 5–8.**—“Look up at the sky,” etc. Above he said: “Your seed will be like the sand of the sea,” because among that people there were some who were carnal and earthly, compared with sand because they were dry and unfruitful in good works; while others were like shining stars.

(RABANUS.) A twofold meaning of the promised seed is given. After the stars have been shown to him, he is told: “So will I make your seed,” that is, the Christian people, whose father you will become, will shine with the light of faith, namely, faith in the resurrection. But after the sand has been shown to him, he is told: “So will your seed be,” etc.; that is, the Jewish nation will be numerous, but dry and unfruitful.

**VERSES 9–10.**—“Take for me,” he said, etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, tome V.) The three-year-old cow is the Jewish people placed under the yoke of the Law, etc., up to the time when the good will be separated from the evil by fire.

“A three-year-old cow and a three-year-old she-goat,” etc. For from Adam to Noah, and from then to Abram, and thereafter to David, the people grew to maturity.

**VERSE 11.**—“And the birds descended,” etc. (GREGORY, book XVI of the *Moralia*, chapter 20.) Tropologically, intrusive thoughts thrust themselves into the very sacrifice of prayer, wishing to seize or violate it. But we must guard with the hand of holy discernment what we offer outwardly, lest evil spirits and perverse thoughts carry it away.

**VERSE 12.**—“Terror fell upon him,” etc. (AUG., *Hebrew Questions*.) This question must be treated because of those who maintain that such disturbances cannot fall upon the mind of a wise person, etc., up to the point where it should not be called a disturbance.

**VERSES 13–15.**—“Know with foreknowledge,” etc. (ISIDORE.) It is prophesied that the people of Israel would serve in Egypt—not that they would serve the Egyptians for four hundred years, but because this number was completed during that affliction, since the reckoning begins from the time when these things were promised to Abraham.

“Know with foreknowledge,” etc. (AUG., *City of God*, book XVI, chapter 24.) This should not be understood as though the people of God had been in that exceedingly harsh servitude for four hundred years, etc., up to the statement that the people of God suffered under harsh servitude in Egypt.

**VERSES 16–21.**—“But in the fourth generation,” etc. (JEROME, letter to Damasus.) Moses says elsewhere, etc., up to the point where they reach Solomon.

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 1.**—“Now Sarai, Abram’s wife,” etc. (RABANUS.) Abram is not an adulterer because he joined himself to a servant woman while his wife was alive, since the Gospel law of one wife had not yet been promulgated. He had heard that his offspring was to be multiplied, but he did not know through which woman, since he knew Sarai to be barren. His intercourse was not driven by lustful pleasure but by dutiful love for the sake of obtaining offspring. His wife also desired and urged this, since she could not have children; therefore she wished him to receive from another woman a child whom she could adopt in place of her own.

**VERSES 2–11.**—“Go in to my servant,” etc. (JEROME.) Note carefully that the begetting of children is called “building” in Hebrew, etc., up to the point where, as though the sentence had been delivered through an angel, she returns to grace and submits herself.

(RABANUS.) These two women are the two Testaments. Hagar is the Old Testament, which in the Synagogue nurtured the Jewish people in bondage. Sarah is the New Testament, which brought forth the Christian people into the freedom of faith. The children of the servant woman multiplied so that they could not be counted because of their multitude; above, they are compared with sand. Thus that people, fierce in its rivalry, opposed to every good thing, and especially persecuting the Christian people throughout the world as envy spurs it on, is scattered far and wide and, wandering and conducting business, burdens everyone.

**VERSE 12.**—“He will be a wild man.” Others have “a rustic.” (JEROME.) In Hebrew it reads *phara*, which is interpreted as “wild ass.” It signifies that his descendants will dwell in the desert, that is, the wandering Saracens, with uncertain settlements. They attack all the nations adjoining the desert on its side and are themselves attacked by everyone.

**VERSE 13.**—“And Hagar called.” She rightly gave him that name, because he freely gives counsel to the wretched and consoles the humble. Hence: “You consider trouble and sorrow, and the poor man has been left to you,” etc. “Surely here I have seen the back of the one who sees me.” This resembles the saying: “You will see my back, but my face shall not be seen by you.” “For no human being shall see my face and live” (Exod. XXXIII). No one can see that manifestation of God’s wisdom and live. This is the vision for which the one who loves God with all his heart, soul, and mind longs; in order to contemplate it, he builds himself up as far as he can by loving his neighbor as himself. We now contemplate his back—that is, his incarnation, which he assumed in the last times—by desiring it through faith and love; and in the future we shall enjoy it in eternal contemplation.

**VERSES 14–16.**—“Therefore he called that well,” etc. (JEROME.) To this day Hagar’s well is shown in the desert of Arabia, between Kadesh and Barad. It signifies the Scripture of the Old and New Law, which our Creator, the life of the living and hope of the dying, gave to mortals out of his loving compassion, so that, instructed and corrected from their vices, they might deserve to be worthy forever of the vision of God.

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSES 1–4.**—[lacuna] “And I will establish my covenant,” etc. In Hebrew, *berith* (), which signifies not a testament but a covenant or pact.

**VERSES 5–7.**—“Your name shall no longer be called Abram.” (JEROME.) The Hebrews say that God added to Abraham’s name the letter *h* from his own name, which among them is the tetragrammaton, and likewise added it to Sarah’s. Abram was called *Abram*, which means “exalted father”; afterward he was called *Abraham*, which means “father of many,” for “of nations” is not expressed in the name but understood. Nor is it surprising that among the Greeks and among us an *a* appears to have been added, while they say that the letter *h* was added. For it is characteristic of the Hebrew language to write *h* and read *a*, and conversely to pronounce *h* and write *a*.

**VERSES 8–9.**—“I will give to you and to your seed … all the land of Canaan.” Canaan is interpreted as “their movement.” Its land is received into possession by the faithful when the mind, previously driven about by various movements and changed for the better, afterward stretches forward with unwavering eyes toward what lies ahead.

“Into an everlasting possession.” (AUG.) Scripture calls something “everlasting” when no end is assigned to it, or when it is not done in such a way that thereafter it need not be done, insofar as this concerns the care or authority of the one who performs it. Hence:

“He will serve forever who does not know how to use what is small.”

**VERSE 10.**—“Every male among you shall be circumcised,” etc. (STRABO.) This was commanded to Abraham for three reasons. First, so that by obedience to the command he might please God, whereas Adam had displeased him through transgression. Second, so that by this sign he might be distinguished from the other nations. Third, so that, being circumcised in the member where lust commonly rules, he might understand that he must preserve chastity and cut away impurity.

**VERSES 11–13.**—“The flesh of the foreskin.” (RABANUS, STRABO.) Circumcision performed on one member signifies spiritual circumcision, which must be displayed in the heart and in all the senses. The heart must be circumcised so that we do not conceive harmful thoughts; the eyes, so that we do not look upon vanity; the ears must be circumcised, that is, stopped, so that they do not hear bloodshed. Thus circumcision must be performed in all the senses.

(ALCUIN, *On Genesis*, tome I.) Circumcision was commended to Abraham for this reason, etc., up to the point where formerly transgressors generated children for death.

Allegorically, even then, in anticipation of the future pilgrimage, the covenant of circumcision was given as a sign, so that his seed would not be mixed with the nations. It signifies nature renewed through baptism, after the old person has been stripped away through Christ, who rose after baptism. He commanded native servants and purchased slaves alike to be circumcised, in order to teach that the grace of redemption belongs to everyone. There too the names of the parents are changed, so that everything might resound with newness. Abram means “exalted father”; Abraham, “father of many nations.”

**VERSE 14.**—“The male whose flesh of the foreskin,” etc. (ISIDORE.) It is asked how boys who were not circumcised could perish—boys who had not broken God’s covenant, but whose guardians had neglected to circumcise them. The covenant of God was broken not according to the deed but according to origin, in the first human being, in whom all sinned. Everyone is born sinful, not personally but originally. Therefore all who are not freed through regeneration perish.

**VERSES 15–16.**—“Sarai your wife,” etc. [Col. 0124A] (ISIDORE.) The promise concerning the calling of the nations is declared in Isaac, the son of promise—that is, of grace and not of nature—for he was born of an aged father and a barren mother. Since this was to occur not through generation, as with Ishmael, but through regeneration, circumcision was commanded when Sarah’s son was promised as a type of the Church, not when Ishmael, who is a type of the Jews, was promised.

(JEROME–ISIDORE.) Those are mistaken who think that Sarah was first written with one *r* and that another *r* was later added. Because *r* signifies one hundred among the Greeks, they imagine various absurdities concerning this name. Yet however they wish to alter the word, it must be explained according to Hebrew, not Greek, usage. It is Hebrew. No one calling someone by name in another language derives the etymology of the name from a different language. Thus Sarai was first called () with *shin*, *resh*, and *yod*. After the *yod* was removed, the letter *he* was added, which is read as *a*, and she was called Sara (). Formerly she was called “my princess,” because she was like the mother of one household; afterward simply “princess,” since she was destined to be the princess of all nations. Some very foolishly suppose that she was formerly called “leprous” and afterward “princess,” since *sarai* is the Hebrew word for leprosy (), which appears somewhat similar in our language but is entirely different in Hebrew. It is written with *tsade*, *ayin*, *resh*, and *tav*, and thus plainly differs from the three letters above—*shin*, *resh*, and *he*—with which Sara is written.

**VERSES 17–18.**—“Abraham fell on his face and laughed in his heart.” (JEROME.) A little later it says: “And you shall call his name Isaac,” which is interpreted as “laughter,” from Abraham’s laughter, not from Sarah’s. For after his son was called Isaac because of Abraham’s laughter, Sarah is then read to have laughed.

“His name is Isaac.” It should be known that four persons in the Old Testament were openly called by their names before they were born: Ishmael, Isaac, Samson, and Josiah. Read the Scriptures.

**VERSE 19.**—“I will establish my covenant,” etc. The Lord’s covenant with Isaac signifies the faithful people whom Mother Church brought forth through faith and baptism. “And an everlasting covenant,” because possession of eternal life is promised only to the one who, with Christ his head, will always possess the kingdom of heaven.

**VERSE 20.**—“Concerning Ishmael,” etc. Historically, Ishmael signifies the Jewish people, which became exceedingly numerous. He fathered twelve leaders, just as the multitude of carnal Jews, descended from the twelve patriarchs, was divided into twelve tribes.

**VERSE 21.**—“In the following year.” The following year, in which Sarah bore Isaac, signifies the times of regeneration, when Christ’s blood was poured out and the human race was restored to life.

**VERSE 22.**—“God went up from Abraham,” etc. (Greek Gloss.) Therefore, so to speak, he had descended and had made himself humble by establishing the law of circumcision.

**VERSES 23–27.**—“Then Abraham took,” etc. God did not intend that only Abraham’s flesh and that of his offspring should be circumcised; rather, he was conferring the gifts of the eternal covenant upon the one whom he had chosen from among all. Hence Paul says in Philippians III: “For we are the circumcision, who serve God in the Spirit.” And elsewhere, in Romans II: “For he is not a Jew who is one outwardly, nor is circumcision outwardly, in the flesh.”

Let us therefore circumcise our ears, lips, heart, foreskin, and all the members of the flesh by the word of God. Circumcision of the ears is spoken of in Luke VIII: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” With uncircumcised ears we cannot hear words of wisdom and truth. Let us circumcise our lips, so that we may speak nothing shameful, evil, or idle. The one who uses the flesh of the foreskin only for the sake of offspring, at proper and lawful times, in marriage, circumcises it; whoever acts otherwise does not circumcise it. The Church, strengthened by the grace of Christ crucified for her, not only abstains from illicit acts but also from permitted ones. Like a virgin bride of Christ, she flourishes with chaste virgins, in whom true circumcision of the foreskin is preserved in the flesh.

The one who does not commit adultery through obscene desires, heretical thoughts, or blasphemous assertions, but preserves the purity of faith in conscience, is circumcised in heart. Of such a person it may be said: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (Matt. V), etc. Let the hands be circumcised, so that they do no evil; the feet, so that they do not run toward evil; the sight, so that it does not desire what is unlawful; the taste, so that it eats and drinks for the glory of God; the sense of smell, so that it receives the fragrance of Christ and spreads the fragrance of sweetness through works of mercy. Each member, if it serves God in its duties, is circumcised. If it indulges beyond the prescribed law, it is uncircumcised.

(JEROME–STRABO.) It is often asked how women were saved, since they were not circumcised. They were saved through faith and the offering of sacrifices, just as holy men were cleansed before circumcision. Hence: “Cleansing their hearts by faith.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“The Lord appeared to him in the valley of Mamre.” (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*.) Abraham bears three figures. First, he represents the Savior, who left his kindred and came into the world. Second, the Father, because he sacrificed his only Son. Third—and this is the figure appearing in this passage—the saints who received Christ’s coming with joy. Abraham’s tabernacle signifies Jerusalem, where the prophets and apostles dwelt for a time, and where Christ, on coming, was received by believers and hung upon the wood by unbelievers.

**VERSES 2–3.**—“Three men.” The three men announce Christ’s coming, accompanied by two angels: according to some, Moses and Elijah. One is the lawgiver, who indicated the Lord’s coming in the Law; the other is the one who will come at the end, announcing Christ’s second coming and preaching his Gospel. Hence they are seen with him when the Lord is transfigured on the mountain. “He saw three and worshiped one,” thereby showing the Savior, whose coming he awaited. Hence: “Abraham saw my day and rejoiced” (John VIII). He foresaw the mystery of the future sacrament. Hence he washed their feet, to show the future purification of the washing at the end of the world; for feet signify the final things.

“When he had seen them.” (GREGORY, book IX of the *Moralia*, chapter 51.) Morally, Abraham met three angels because a man and master of the household—that is, spiritual understanding—must, in knowledge of the Trinity, go beyond the barriers of the flesh and go out as though through the door of his lowly dwelling. Care for the flesh, which Sarah signifies, should not appear outwardly for display, but should remain behind the man, that is, under the discretion of the spirit, occupied only with necessities. It should not expose itself presumptuously but be modestly restrained.

(The same, book XXVIII, chapter 4.) Abraham could not have seen the angels, received them as guests, and served them food unless they had assumed bodies from the air. They would not have appeared or eaten food unless they had solid bodies composed of a heavenly element. Nor is it surprising that they are sometimes called angels and sometimes the Lord, since they are called angels when they minister outwardly, while the Lord is revealed as the one who inwardly commands them.

**VERSES 4–5.**—“But I will bring.” He returns to the duties of hospitality, which can also be offered to angels when they assume bodily form from the elements. Understanding this, Abraham worshiped the divinity in unity and ministered to the angelic dispensation in visible form.

**VERSE 6.**—“Three measures.” These words are spoken as a type of the Church, which has been gathered from the three parts of the world into the unity of faith and, like unleavened bread, has been baked by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

(STRABO.) A *sat* is a kind of measure. The three measures signify the three sons of Noah, from whom the whole human race was spread abroad. Thus the Church, or evangelical doctrine, is signified as destined to be spread throughout the world and multiplied in the three parts of the world: Asia, Africa, and Europe.

“Three measures,” from which Sarah makes cakes baked under the ashes, signify Noah’s three sons, from whom the whole human race was born. Believing in the divine Trinity, they were sprinkled with the water of baptism through Sarah—that is, through the Church—and formed into one loaf, the body of Christ. These are the three measures of flour that the woman in the Gospel leavened. The loaves are unleavened because the unity of believers must be free from the leaven of malice, the bitterness [or: rancor] of wickedness, and the fervor of perverse doctrine.

“Cakes baked under the ashes.” Cakes baked under the ashes are those who, cooked by the vapor of the Holy Spirit through repentance for their sins, become acceptable food to God.

**VERSE 7.**—“A very tender calf.” The tender and fattened calf is Christ’s body, which was sacrificed for the salvation of the world on the tree of the cross. This is the calf that is slaughtered for the prodigal son.

### Verse 8

“Butter and milk” he served with the meat of the calf, because milk signifies the Old Law; hence 1 Corinthians 3: “I gave you milk to drink, not food,” and so forth. For he had handed on to them the commandment of the Law, as though it were milk expressed from the breasts of the two tablets—that is, the testament of faith—because they were not yet able to receive the solid food of evangelical teaching. The richest and fattest butter is the evangelical testimony, which is given to the faithful like oil as a sign. He served the calf with milk and butter, because neither the Lord’s body can exist without the milk of the Law, nor the latter without the Gospel. They sat beneath the tree as a sign of the Lord’s Passion, whose preachers they are.

### Verse 9

“Behold, he is in the tent,” and so forth. (STRABO.) Abraham is outside with the angels, while Sarah is in the tent: for it belongs to the strong and learned to preach openly and instruct by examples, but to the weak and unlearned to learn and remain subject.

### Verse 10

“And he will have a son,” and so forth. God promises a son to barren Sarah, saying: “At this time I will come.” He signifies not the time but the character of his coming, since through the promised son a faithful people was to be born. Hence Isaiah 54 and Galatians 4: “Rejoice, you barren woman who do not give birth,” and so forth.

“When she heard this,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) Sarah is rebuked because she laughed, but Abraham is not, although he likewise laughed; for Abraham’s laughter was one of amazement, whereas Sarah’s was one of doubt—a distinction that could be made by the one who knows hearts. Sarah denies that she laughed, although nothing can be hidden from God; but perhaps she thought they were human beings. Abraham, however, understood that he was dealing with God, while nevertheless offering the services of hospitality that are necessary only for weak human flesh. This is astonishing—unless he first thought them human beings, yet recognized in them that God was speaking through certain signs of divine majesty, just as Scripture often testifies that God appeared in human form, though afterward they learned that they had been angels.

### Verse 11

“But they were old,” and so forth. The age of the *seniores* is less advanced than that of the *senes*, even though the old may be called *seniores*. Thus, according to physicians, an older man cannot beget children by an older woman, even if she still experiences menstrual flow. In this respect Abraham marvels at God’s power concerning the promise of a son, and we may understand this to be the miracle to which the Apostle refers. His body was not altogether dead to generation—for if the woman had been of youthful age, he could have generated offspring—but he could not beget a child from an advanced age. For afterward he begot children by Keturah because she was a young woman. Physicians indeed report that an old man cannot beget a child by a woman of advanced age, even if she still menstruates, though he can by a young woman. Conversely, a woman of advanced age, even if she still menstruates, cannot bear a child by an older man, though she can by a young man. It was therefore a miracle because both were old and advanced in age, and Sarah’s menstruation had ceased.

### Verses 12–14

“Shall I give myself to pleasure?” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book 9, chapter 51.) “The care of the flesh,” and so forth, up to “what else does our mind give birth to but joy?”

### Verse 15

“I did not laugh,” and so forth. (AMBROSE.) She denied that she had laughed because she did not understand; she laughed because she prophesied.

### Verses 17–19

“Can I hide from Abraham what I am about to do?” The Lord rightly entrusts his secrets to Abraham, whom he knew to be a faithful executor of his will and secrets—from whom he himself was to be born according to the flesh—he “in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (II Corinthians 2). He also promises Abraham not only rewards but the righteousness of his children’s obedience, and that the promises would be fulfilled concerning them. Isaac is again promised as one who would become “a great nation,” and that “in him all the nations of the earth would be blessed.” By these words two things are promised to him: the Jewish nation according to the flesh, and all nations through faith.

### Verse 20

“The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) If we understand these words not as those of one who doubts but of one who is angry and threatening, there is no difficulty. For God speaks to human beings in human fashion, and his anger is without disturbance, because he is immutable. We often speak in this threatening way: “Let us see whether I will not do this to you,” or “whether I shall not be able to do it to you”; or, “I will know”—that is, “I will test whether I am unable to do it.” But disturbance does not befall God. This is the custom of human speech, to which God accommodates himself so as to correspond to human weakness.

(GREGORY, *Moralia*, book 5, chapter 7.) Sin accompanied by voice is guilt in action; sin accompanied by a cry is guilt accompanied by license.

### Verses 21–23

“I will go down and see,” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, chapter 33.) Let us not believe the evils of human beings before we have tested them. And behold, through angels he descends to ascertain their evils; and when he finds them entangled in such a great crime, he appears to have set aside patience and anticipates the day of judgment with the fire of judgment. He judges calmly, so that greater crimes may be believed slowly but, once truly recognized, punished swiftly.

(GREGORY, *First Book of Kings*, chapter 178, volume 1.) Where would God descend, so as to learn what had been done? Or could he, who is everywhere, fail to know? Rather, to give an example of discernment for our ignorance, so that we might understand that we ought not to believe grave evils merely because we have heard of them, he says that he descends to ascertain them—although it is clear to all that, even without descending, he would know everything.

(HILARY, *On the Trinity*, book 9.) We have here God not knowing something, although he is not ignorant of it. For although he knows that the sins are exceedingly great, he again descends to see whether they have reached completion; and, if they have not yet reached completion, to know. We understand that he does not then know them because he was previously ignorant of them, but that he knows them then because the time for action has arrived. God’s “not knowing,” therefore, is not a diminution of ignorance but the fullness of time.

### Verses 24–26

“If fifty righteous are found,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) The number fifty, from which he descends as far as ten, signifies repentance. Hence the fiftieth psalm is also penitential. If they had turned back, they would have been saved. But when God sees sinners unwilling to turn to repentance, he immediately restrains the burning of immoderate lust with the fire of Gehenna. He said that Sodom would not perish if ten righteous were found there, because if Christ’s name is found in anyone through the keeping of the ten commandments, that person will not perish. The figure of the number ten also signifies the cross of Christ.

### Verse 27

“I will speak to the Lord,” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book 18, chapter 33.) Mystically: the more the saints contemplate the inner things of divinity, the more they perceive themselves to be nothing. Abraham is nowhere recorded as having professed himself to be dust and ashes except when he merited to have speech with God. And he says: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust,” and so forth. For perhaps he would have thought himself to be something if he had not perceived the true essence that is above him. Hence David also exclaims: “Remember, Lord, that I am dust” (Psalm 10), and so forth.

Morally: in some people, the swelling of their disposition does not elevate them, but works of mercy do; others, while they see themselves abounding in earthly goods, do not seek true riches and do not love the eternal kingdom, because they think temporal things sufficient. It is therefore not the material itself that is criminal, but the disposition. Everything that God created is good. But the one who uses good things badly acts so that, through the gluttony of overeating, he dies from the bread by which he ought to have lived. The poor Lazarus came to rest, while torments afflicted the proud rich man (Luke 16); yet Abraham had been rich, he who held Lazarus in his bosom. Nevertheless he says: “I will speak to my Lord, although I am dust and ashes,” and so forth. How could he esteem his riches, who regarded himself as dust and ashes? We clearly see the position in which he placed himself, since he considered himself dust and ashes even when speaking with God. By what punishment, then, should those be struck who do not advance toward the highest things but exalt themselves over the smallest?

### Verses 28–33

“If five are found.” Five cities were burned by fiery rains. For all who have indulged the five bodily senses lustfully are destined to be consumed by the future fire.

“What if they are found?” and so forth. (ALCUIN.) This need not be understood concerning every place. It could be said concerning Sodom because God knew that not even ten were there; thus he answered Abraham in order to magnify the iniquity of the Sodomites.

“Ten.” The number ten signifies the cross of Christ, because the letter X, by which ten is expressed, is formed in the shape of a cross.

“He said.” For he knew that there was not even one there apart from Lot. This is said to magnify the iniquity, as in Jeremiah: “See whether you can find a man doing justice” (Jeremiah 5); as if to say: “Find even one, and I will spare them.”

## Chapter 19

### Verse 1

“And two angels came,” and so forth. It should be noted that three angels appeared to Abraham, an odd number, because God delights in an odd number. They came to Sodom in an even number, namely two; this number departs from unity and is the first principle of duality, as though representing feminine softness. They came “in the evening,” because the sun of justice had already set for the Sodomites. “When he had seen them,” and so forth. When Lot runs to meet them and worships, he appears to understand that they are angels; when he invites them to refresh their bodies, he appears to think that they are human beings. The same should be understood of those who appeared to Abraham. From this passage of Scripture, as from many others, the virtue of hospitality is commended. Hence Paul says in Hebrews 13: “Do not neglect hospitality, for through it some, without knowing it, welcomed angels as guests.”

(Gloss in Greek.) It should be noted that where God’s benefits are explained, God himself is present; but where punishments are carried out, angels are sent. Thus we may know that doing good is especially pleasing and agreeable to God, whereas vengeance is displeasing to God.

### Verse 2

“Wash.” This is what is customarily done for guests, so that those whose affections have been soiled by earthly dust, by sloth, and by faintheartedness may be cleansed as though from dusty filth. Hence in monasteries a prayer is celebrated for those arriving from a journey.

### Verses 3–7

“He compelled them.” (ALCUIN.) The angels enter Lot’s house as though compelled, so that his charity, having been tested and proved, might be rewarded, and so that the greatness of hospitality might be shown. They entered the house of a hospitable man and rescued their host; fire entered the houses closed to guests and destroyed the sinners.

### Verses 8–9

“I have two daughters.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) It is rightly asked whether compensation for crimes, or for sins of any kind, is to be admitted—whether we should do evil so that worse evils may not occur—or whether this should be attributed to Lot’s disturbance rather than to deliberate counsel. Such compensation is certainly admitted only with extreme danger. But if it arose from mental disturbance, it is in no way to be imitated.

### Verse 10

“And they brought Lot inside to themselves.” (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book 6, chapter 16.) While evil adversaries attack, Lot is brought back inside the house and protected, because every righteous person, when enduring the plots of the wicked, returns to his inner self and remains undaunted. The Sodomites cannot find the door of Lot’s house, because corrupters of minds find no opening for accusation against the life of the righteous. Struck with blindness, they go around the house, because in envy they scrutinize the deeds and words of the righteous. But because a strong and praiseworthy action everywhere confronts them in the life of the righteous, they wander about and grope along the wall.

### Verses 11–13

“And they struck them with blindness.” (AUGUSTINE, as above.) In Greek, ἀορασία (*aorasia*), that is, “invisibility,” if such a word may be used: it makes invisible not everything, but what is not needed. For how would they have become exhausted by seeking the door if they had been struck with blindness so as to see nothing? Overcome by their own calamity, they would have sought nothing further. They had been struck with this ἀορασία—the men who were seeking Elisha, and those who, after the resurrection, walked with Christ but did not recognize him.

### Verse 14

“He went out,” and so forth. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) In what follows, Lot’s daughters are said to have been virgins; and he himself said to the Sodomites: “Behold, I have two daughters who have not known a man,” and so forth. Yet now he is said to have had sons-in-law. Some think that those who had husbands perished in Sodom, while those who were virgins went out with their father. But the Hebrew truth has it: “Lot went out and spoke to his sons-in-law who were going to take his daughters.” Thus his virgin daughters had not yet been joined in marriage.

### Verses 15–16

“When it was morning,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) Mystically: Lot, Abraham’s brother, righteous and hospitable in Sodom, signifies the body of Christ, which among all the saints groans amid the impious, does not consent to their deeds, and will be freed from their mixture at the end of the age, while they are condemned to the punishment of eternal fire.

### Verses 17–19

“Into the mountain.” (STRABO.) Morally: the mountain signifies the height of virtues, to which the angel urges him, according to the saying in Mark 19: “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you possess,” and so forth. But whoever sees that he cannot climb higher should remain in Zoar—that is, in the small place—content with a lay and common life, rather than seize the mountain of virtue and return to worldly things. Virginity is a high mountain to which the angel urges him. If anyone sees that he cannot climb it, let him remain in Zoar—that is, in lawful marriage—for it is better to use a moderate good than to be hurled down the cliffs of lust. Hence 1 Corinthians 7: “Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife.” “I cannot reach the mountain”: that is, in his disturbance he did not believe the Lord, whom he recognized in the angels; and, being disturbed, he prostituted his daughters.

### Verse 20

“There is a city,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) Allegorically: Sodom is interpreted as “blindness” and expresses worldly desires; the height of the mountains signifies the contemplation of the perfect. But because many flee worldly allurements and yet, being engaged in action, cannot attain the summit of contemplation, Lot went out from Sodom but did not reach the mountains. Hence Lot says: “There is this city nearby,” and so forth. It is called “nearby,” yet it is safe for salvation, because the active life is neither wholly separated from the cares of the world nor alienated from the joy of eternal salvation.

“To which I can flee,” and so forth. Those who are not strong enough to ascend to the contemplative life take refuge in the active life, in which they are saved.

(GREGORY, *Pastoral Rule*, book 3, chapter 28.) Morally: “To flee burning Sodom,” and so forth, up to “therefore it is said to Lot.”

### Verses 21–23

“Behold, I have also accepted your request in this matter,” because when prayer is poured out before God, such a married life is not condemned. Hence 1 Corinthians 7: “Do not deprive one another,” and so forth.

### Verse 24

“Then the Lord rained upon Sodom,” and so forth. (GREGORY.) Sulfur signifies the stench of the flesh; fire, the burning of carnal desire. When the Lord determined to punish the crimes of the flesh, he made the stain of the crime known through the character of the punishment. Sulfur stinks and fire burns; therefore those who had burned with the stench of the flesh toward perverse desires rightly perished through sulfur and fire, so that by a just punishment they might learn what they had done through unjust desire.

(STRABO.) It should be noted that the first sinners were destroyed by the water of the Flood, since they had likewise offended God through carnal desire. But the Sodomites perished through a more severe punishment, namely a flood of fire and sulfur. Although the former exceeded the proper measure, they sinned as though naturally; the latter sinned against nature. Therefore they were condemned as an example of the gravest punishment.

### Verse 25

“All the inhabitants.” (ALCUIN.) The infants were burned with their parents in Sodom, so that the most impious crime of the Sodomites might not be shown to have left any trace in their descendants. Provision was also made for them so that, if they lived long, they would not follow their parents’ examples and be punished more severely. The parents are guilty both on their own account and on theirs. For the death of children is the crime of their parents. Therefore the children will become their accusers. It is also some kind of benefit not to be guilty, even if one is not glorious; for it benefits the one who cannot be a king not to be poor.

### Verses 26–28

“And his wife looked back.” (ISIDORE.) Mystically: the wife represents the class of those who, having been called by grace, look back and strive to return to the things they had left behind. Of them it is said in Luke 9: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” They are therefore forbidden to look back. This shows that those who have been regenerated by grace must not return to their former life if they wish to escape the final fire. The wife who looked back was turned into salt, becoming both an example and seasoning by which others might be salted. Hence Christ says in Luke 17: “Remember Lot’s wife,” so that she might season us like salt, lest we become negligent but might prudently take care.

### Verse 29

“When he overthrew,” and so forth. Scripture indicates that God rescued Lot especially because of Abraham’s merits, so that we may understand that he was called righteous, in a certain sense, chiefly because he worshiped the one true God and, by comparison with the Sodomites, among whom he lived, could not be bent toward a similar crime. “He remembered Abraham.” It is clear that Lot was freed because of Abraham’s merits; Scripture calls him righteous. It should be understood, however, that he was righteous not as Abraham was, but in comparison with the Sodomites.

### Verse 30

“And he went up,” and so forth. Thus married people sometimes ascend from the lowliness of the active life to the height of the contemplative life.

“And Lot went up from Zoar,” and so forth. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*, volume 3.) It is asked why, although at first he preferred Zoar to the mountain as a place of refuge, and so forth, up to “he ought not to have doubted.”

### Verse 31

“And the elder said to the younger,” and so forth. This is said as an excuse for the daughters, because they thought that the human race had perished and therefore lay with their father. But it does not excuse the father when what follows says, “and he did not know that they had lain with him.” For the Hebrews place an obelus above the words, as though they were superfluous, as though it were incredible because nature does not permit anyone to have intercourse unknowingly.

(STRABO.) Lot is inexcusable, first because he did not believe the angel; then because he became drunk, and sin became the cause of sin.

(JEROME.) Thus evil suggestion and pleasure lie in wait for the continent, like incestuous women, so that, having seized an opportunity, they may steep the sluggish in the wine of deception and, as though unknowingly, cast them down from the position of uprightness.

### Verse 32

“Come, let us make our father drunk,” and so forth. (ALCUIN.) The two daughters of Lot had learned that the consummation of the world would come through fire. But, like immature girls, they did not know that, after the Sodomites had been destroyed by fire, a great extent of land would remain intact. They suspected that something like what they had heard had happened in the time of Noah, and that they and their father were the survivors for the restoration of the human race. Although intercourse with their father was a great crime, it seemed a worse impiety to destroy the hope of posterity after their chastity had been preserved. Therefore they formed a plan, softened their father’s grief or resistance with wine, and on successive nights each received conception from him while he was unaware, without repeating the act.

### Verses 33–35

“They gave,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) In this passage Lot signifies the Law, because some who were begotten from it and placed under it, by misunderstanding, become drunk in a certain sense; and by using it unlawfully, they produce works of unbelief. For the Law is good if one uses it lawfully.

### Verse 36

“Thus both daughters of Lot conceived,” and so forth. (JEROME.) Moab is interpreted as “from the father,” and the whole name has an etymology. Ammon, for whom the explanation of the name is given as “son of my people,” or, as is better in Hebrew, *ben-ammi*, that is, “son of my people,” is derived in such a way that part of the name is its meaning and part is itself the word. For Ammon, from whom the Ammonites derive their name, means “my people.”

### Verses 37–38

“She called his name Moab,” and so forth. (THEODORET.) The first woman appears more shameless, since she wished to transmit her incest even to posterity. Moab signifies “from the father”; the other was more modest, since she gave her son the name Ben-ammi, that is, “son of my people.”

## Chapter 20

### Verse 1

“He departed from there,” and so forth. Kadesh means “fountain of judgment”; Shur means “narrowness.” These signify patience.

### Verses 2–6

“He said concerning Sarah,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) It is customary to ask how, at that age, Abraham feared for his life because of Sarah’s beauty. But the power of her beauty is astonishing, since she could still be loved.

“He said concerning Sarah,” and so forth. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, volume 6.) He concealed that she was his wife and said that she was his sister, lest he himself be killed and she be seized and possessed by foreigners, confident that God would preserve her inviolate, just as he had done with Pharaoh, and so forth, up to “Do not call anyone your father on earth, for one is your Father, who is in heaven.”

“He said,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) When Abimelech says concerning Sarah, “I spared you so that you would not sin against me,” it should be understood that God acted when he warned him that she was Abraham’s wife, although he thought she was his sister. It should also be noted that one sins against God when people commit acts that they think are either not sins or are regarded as minor sins, as though they were merely sins of the flesh.

### Verses 7–11

“He will pray for you,” and so forth. (CHRYSOSTOM, *Homily 45 on Genesis*.) Know that his prayers will give you life.

### Verse 12

“Yet she is truly my sister,” and so forth. (JEROME.) In Hebrew there is *vegam*, that is, “also”: “She is truly my sister, the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother.” This sounds more clearly as though she were Abraham’s sister. We offer as an excuse that such marriages had not yet been prohibited by law.

“Daughter of my father.” Another translation says more plainly, “from my father, and not from my mother”; for she was the daughter of Haran, Abraham’s brother, and Lot’s sister.

### Verse 13

“After God brought me out from my father’s house, I said to her,” and so forth. After the word of God was rejected by Judea, all the faithful are brothers and sisters of Christ. Hence Matthew 12: “Whoever does the will of my Father, who is in heaven, is my brother, sister, and mother.”

### Verse 14

“Therefore he took,” and so forth. Allegorically, Abraham signifies Christ and Sarah the Church. Abraham is honored because of Sarah’s beauty, and Christ because of the Church. Hence Psalm 67: “God is wonderful in his saints.” Sarah had a husband, but he was hidden; the Church has Christ, who is not seen in the world, having been received into heaven.

### Verse 15

“Wherever you wish,” and so forth. Those who had once delayed believing through fear of rulers, when commanded by those same rulers, betook themselves to the Church, which is Christ’s sister and wife, and spread the glory of Christ and the Church through all the parts of the world.

### Verse 16

“A thousand pieces of silver,” and so forth. He speaks as though joking, because she had said that the man who was her husband was her brother; he urges her to remember this in the future, lest she again incur a similar reproach when the matter is discovered. A thousand pieces of silver are given to Christ when eloquent teachers of the world are taken from pagan conduct to hold and proclaim the faith of Christ. For the number one thousand, being the square of ten, signifies the stable and solid teaching of evangelical preaching.

### Verse 17

“When he prayed.” When the Son prays to the Father, the barrenness of worldly peoples, rulers, and subjects is healed.

## Chapter 21

### Verses 1–3

“God visited Sarah,” and so forth. Circumcision has a manifold significance. According to the Apostle, it is the sign of the righteousness of faith belonging to Abraham and his seed, and a judgment by which those who belong to this seed and faith are chastised. It is also a prophecy concerning the seed of the Savior, who in the present cleanses us from every sin through baptism and in the future, after the resurrection, frees us from every corruption of death. The number eight corresponds to the glory of the resurrection: the Lord rose on the eighth day, that is, after the seventh day of the week. We too, after the six ages of this world and the seventh day of the week—that is, the rest of souls that meanwhile takes place in the other life—will rise as though in the eighth age, stripped of all the corruptions and vices of carnal desire, in which lust reigns especially.

### Verse 4

“He circumcised him,” and so forth. (STRABO.) Although circumcision was commanded for many reasons, it especially foreshadowed Christ, who through baptism strips us of the old man and in the future, after the resurrection, will circumcise away all mortality and corruption. The fact that Isaac was circumcised on the eighth day signifies the eighth age of the world, when the general resurrection of the saints will take place.

### Verse 8

“Then the child grew,” and so forth. He grows who, arranging ascents in his heart, reaches the solid food of teaching. Hence: “Grow, and you will eat me.”

“He grew,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Abraham made a feast neither on the day of his son’s birth nor on the day of his circumcision, but on the day of his weaning, because the joy of spiritual maturity ought to be great when a person has become one who is nourished by solid food. This is similar to what is said in 1 Corinthians 3: “I gave you milk to drink, not food.”

### Verse 9

“When Sarah saw,” and so forth. (JEROME.) This is explained in two ways: either that Ishmael played idolatrous games, according to the saying in Exodus 32: “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play”; or that, as though he were of greater age, he claimed the privileges of the firstborn against Isaac. When Sarah heard this, she could not endure it.

### Verse 10

“Cast out this slave woman,” and so forth. (BEDE, chapter 21; ISIDORE, chapter 17 on Genesis.) It is asked why Sarah previously wished to receive a son from the slave woman, or why she now orders him to be expelled with his mother. She did not do this because she was inflamed by jealousy, but because she was compelled by the mystery of prophecy. For, according to the Apostle, Hagar bore a carnal people into slavery, whereas Sarah bore a spiritual and free people, by the freedom with which Christ has freed us. This mystery therefore signified that the former people, generated in slavery, would not remain forever in Sarah’s house—that is, the Church—nor be heirs or companions of Christians, nor possess the kingdom of glory with the noble son, that is, the faithful people.

### Verses 11–12

“He took it hard,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) It is asked why Abraham was grieved, since this was a prophecy that he ought to have understood even better than Sarah. But Sarah spoke this by revelation of what had first been revealed to her. Abraham, however, was moved by paternal affection, and the Lord afterward revealed it to him. Or perhaps neither of them initially knew what it meant, and it was prophesied through Sarah in her ignorance when she was stirred by a woman’s feelings because of the slave woman’s arrogance.

### Verse 13

“Because he is your seed.” (AUGUSTINE.) It should be noted that Ishmael too is called by God Abraham’s seed, as the Apostle says in Romans 9: “It is not the children of the flesh, but the children of the promise, who are counted as seed.” Yet this properly pertains to Isaac, who is not a son of the flesh but of the promise, and is spiritual seed from the promise, not from the flesh.

### Verse 14

“Taking bread,” and so forth. (ALCUIN, from BEDE, chapter 21.) When Abraham expelled Hagar, taking bread, he therefore placed it on her shoulders, and so forth, up to “because some from the people will seek refuge under the shadow of the wood of the cross.”

“He took bread and a skin of water.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, volume 3.) It is asked how he placed such a large boy on her shoulders. For Ishmael, who had been born before Isaac, was circumcised at thirteen, when Abraham was ninety-nine, and Isaac was born when his father was one hundred. Ishmael was playing with Isaac when Sarah was angered—plainly with a boy considerably older, who had already been weaned. He was therefore more than sixteen years old when he was expelled with his mother. But if we understand the statement that he played with the child as having been spoken by recapitulation, before Isaac was weaned, even so a boy more than thirteen years old could not have been placed on his mother’s shoulders. We must therefore supply: “He gave her her son,” and so forth.

“He placed it on her shoulder.” (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) When Isaac was born, Ishmael was thirteen years old, and after Isaac’s weaning he was expelled with his mother. Among the Hebrews there is disagreement: some assert that the time of weaning was fixed at five years, others at twelve. We therefore choose the shorter age and calculate that Ishmael was expelled with his mother after eighteen years. It is not plausible that a young man then sat upon his mother’s neck. But the idiom of the Hebrew language is genuine: every son is called an infant and little one in comparison with his parents. At Rome also, to this day, all sons are called infants.

### Verses 15–21

“She cast the boy away,” and so forth. (JEROME.) The passage that follows reads: “And she cast the boy under one of the fir trees, and, going away, sat opposite him at a distance about the flight of an arrow.” For she said: “I will not see the death of my child,” and she sat opposite him; and immediately it follows: “The boy cried out and wept.” The Lord heard the boy’s voice from heaven, where he was, and the angel said to Hagar: “Let nothing disturb you.” For in Hebrew the following is written first: “I will not see the death of my child.” Accordingly it is read that Hagar sat opposite the boy, raised her voice, and wept, and that God heard the voice of the child. While the mother wept and awaited her son’s death, God heard the child whom he had promised would become a great nation. The mother laments not her own death but that of her son.

(AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, volume 3.) It is asked how the mother, and so forth, up to “as walkers of any age often do.”

### Verse 17

“But he heard.” (BEDE AND ISIDORE, as above.) The boy cries out weeping, and God hears. When the angel points it out, she sees a spring. This is said concerning those who turn to Christ: when they lament their sins, they are heard, and, with the eyes of their hearts opened, they see the spring of water—that is, Christ, who says in John 7: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink.” The angel signifies Elijah, through whom the people will come to believe. Hence Malachi 4: “Behold, I will send you Elijah, who will turn the hearts of fathers to their children.”

“The angel of the Lord.” (ISIDORE.) Scripture first calls the one who speaks to Hagar an angel and afterward calls him Lord. He should be believed to have been the Son of God, who spoke through the Law and the Prophets, who is called an angel because of his obedience to the Father’s will, but is God according to his nature.

### Verse 22

“At that same time.” (AUGUSTINE, as above.) It may be asked when Abraham made a covenant with Abimelech, and so forth, up to “which she did not know.”

### Verses 23–30

“Therefore swear to me,” and so forth. Often those who are outside, prompted by the conduct of the faithful, desire to join themselves to them and to be shaped for the better by their examples, so that they may care both for themselves and for the salvation of their neighbors.

### Verses 31–32

“Therefore it was called,” and so forth. There are two reasons why it was called Beersheba in Hebrew. Either because Abimelech received seven ewe lambs from Abraham’s hand—for seven are called *sheba*—or because they swore there, since *sheba* means an oath. If we read above that this was the reason for the name, it was said by prolepsis, just as Bethel and Gilgal were called by names different from those they bore before receiving these names. It should be noted from the earlier and present passages that Isaac was not born beside the oak of Mamre—*alon* in Hebrew, “oak” in Latin, as the Hebrew has it—but in Gerar, where Beersheba is a town to this day. This province was called Palestina Salutaris not long ago after the division of the governing districts of Palestine. Hence Abraham lived in the land of the Philistines for many days.

### Verses 33–34

“But Abraham,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Abraham, as Stephen says, had received no inheritance there, not even the space of a foot. But the inheritance should be understood as that which God was going to give freely, not that which was purchased at a price. The space around the well is understood as corresponding to the area purchased with the seven ewe lambs that had been given when Abimelech and Abraham swore to one another.

## Chapter 22

### Verse 1

“After these things,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, volume 3.) James says that God tempts no one; but in ordinary usage we say “to tempt” for “to test.” James is speaking of the temptation by which someone becomes entangled in sin. Hence 1 Thessalonians 3: “Lest the tempter should have tempted you.” Elsewhere it is written in Deuteronomy 13: “The Lord your God is testing you, to know whether you love him”—that is, to make you know. For a person does not know the strength of his own love unless he learns it through experience.

### Verse 2

“Take your son,” and so forth. (ALCUIN, *On Genesis*, volume 1.) Abraham was not immediately ordered to kill his son, but to lead him for sacrifice over three days, so that the temptation might be increased by the length of time. During those three days, as his anxieties grew, the father’s innermost feelings were tortured. Over that prolonged interval the father looked upon his son, ate with him, and through so many nights the boy hung in his father’s embrace and lay in his lap; at every moment the pain of killing his son accumulated in his paternal affection.

“Whom you love,” and so forth. (BEDE, *On Genesis*, chapter 22.) The temptation is intensified by the reminder of love and by the recollection of the name, and paternal affection is stirred by the memory of the promise, since it had been said: “In Isaac shall your seed be called.” It would be as though, if he were killed, the entire hope of the promise would be destroyed.

“Go into the land.” (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*, volume 3.) The Hebrews say that this is the mountain on which the Temple was afterward built, on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. Hence 2 Chronicles 3: “They began to build the Temple in the second month, on the second day of the month, on Mount Moriah.” It is interpreted as “illuminating” and “shining” because the *debir* is there—that is, the oracle of God—and the spirit that teaches human beings the truth and inspires prophecies.

### Verse 3

“Leading his donkey,” and so forth. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, chapter 18.) The donkey signifies the senseless stupidity of the Jews, which carried all the mysteries and did not understand them.

### Verse 4

“On the third day.” (JEROME, as above.) It should be noted that the journey from Gerar to Mount Moriah, that is, the site of the Temple, takes three days, and Abraham is said to have reached it on the third day. They are therefore wrong to think that Abraham at that time lived beside the oak of Mamre, since from there the journey to Mount Moriah would scarcely have taken one full day. The three days by which they came to the place of sacrifice signify three ages: before the Law, from Abraham to Moses; under the Law, from Moses to John; and from then until the Lord. Whatever remains is the third day of grace, in which the sacrifice of Christ was completed during the third age.

### Verses 5–8

“Wait here,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, cited above.) Hear the Apostle: “A partial blindness has come upon Israel” [Col. 0138C], that is, “with the donkey,” so that “the fullness of the Gentiles might enter,” that is, “after we have worshiped.” When the sacrifice of the cross has been proclaimed among the Gentiles, that is, “when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, we shall return to you,” that is, “and thus all Israel will be saved.” The two servants who were dismissed and not brought to the place of sacrifice are the Jews who, living as slaves and reasoning carnally, did not understand the humility and passion of Christ. They are two because they were to be divided into two parts, which happened when Solomon sinned, when the people were divided with respect to the kingdom—not through an error of impiety, as it is said in Jeremiah 3: “Israel the apostate and Judah the transgressor.”

“I and the boy,” etc. (ALC.) He wished to slaughter his son with an unwavering mind. He is to be praised for his steadfastness in offering and for his faith in resurrection. For he knew with absolute certainty that God could not deceive, and that even if the boy were killed, God’s promise would nevertheless remain secure. Hence the Apostle says in Hebrews 11: “By faith Abraham did not hesitate when he offered his only son, in whom he had received the promise, believing that God was also able to raise him from the dead.”

“Abraham said.” (ISIDORE, cited above.) Abraham, leading his only son to be sacrificed, signifies God the Father. Abraham received his son in old age, whereas God does not grow old; but the promise concerning Christ had, in a certain sense, grown old when he was born. It began with Adam, when it was said, “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2), and it was completed in the sixth age of the world. [Col. 0139A] Sarah’s old age, in the people of God—that is, in the multitude of the prophets—signifies the same thing, because at the end of time Christ was born from the people of holy souls. Her barrenness signifies that in this world we have been saved in hope, and that in Christ, as in Isaac, we have all been born; him the Church [variant: “the Church’s offspring”] brought forth at the end of time, not by nature but by grace. Abraham therefore signifies God the Father, and Isaac Christ. For just as Abraham offered his only and beloved son as a victim to God, so God the Father handed over his only-begotten Son for us. And just as Isaac carried the wood upon which he was to be laid, so Christ carried the cross upon which he was to be fastened.

### Verses 9–11

“When he had bound him,” etc. (ISIDORE, cited above.) Isaac is placed upon the altar with his feet bound, [Col. 0139B] and Christ is fastened to the cross. But what was prefigured through Isaac was transferred to the ram, because Christ is a sheep. He is the son because he was born; the ram because he was sacrificed. The ram is caught in the thicket; the cross has horns. For if two pieces of wood are joined together, the form of a cross is produced. Hence Habakkuk 3: “Horns are in his hands.” The ram caught by the horns is therefore Christ crucified. The thickets are thorns; the thorns are the wicked, who suspended the Lord. He was suspended among the thorns of sinners. Hence Jeremiah says: “This people has surrounded me with the thorns of its sins” (Jeremiah 38). Others understand this ram, bound in the thicket, as Christ crowned with thorns before his sacrifice.

### Verse 12

“You did not spare,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, cited above.) Did Abraham not spare his son because of the angel? But the Lord is represented in the angel, for he is God and the angel of the great counsel. God was in the angel, and he spoke in God’s person. This will become clearer in what follows, where it is said: “And the angel of the Lord called Abraham a second time from heaven, saying: By myself I have sworn, says the Lord.” For it is not readily found that Christ calls the Father “Lord,” especially before the incarnation. In accordance with the flesh, however, this is appropriately said; thus in Psalm 2 it is said: “The Lord said to me,” etc. But what is said in the same place, chapter 9, “The Lord said to my Lord,” etc., refers to the prophet who is speaking, just as does the statement: “The Lord rained from the Lord,” that is, our Lord, namely the Son, from our Lord, namely the Father.

### Verse 13

“A ram.” (ALC.) Historically: We do not think that the ram sacrificed in place of Isaac was merely figurative; it was real. It is therefore more plausible that the angel brought it from elsewhere than that the Lord produced it there from the earth after six days of work.

“A ram among the thickets,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) Aquila rendered the word by “thicket” or “thorn-brake,” etc., up to the point where it is said thus in Hebrew.

### Verses 14–19

“And he called the name,” etc. (JEROME, cited above.) Instead of what is found here, etc., up to the point concerning the incarnation.

### Verses 20–24

“Milcah.” (JEROME, cited above.) From Milcah, the wife of Nahor, etc., up to the point where the same is read in Isaiah.

## Chapter XXIII

[Col. 0140A]

### Verses 1–6

“Now Sarah lived,” etc. “And she died in the city of Arbee,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) “Which is in the valley”: this is not found in the authentic books, etc., up to the point where it is clearly demonstrated in the book of Joshua.

### Verses 7–15

“Abraham rose,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) It is asked how Abraham worshiped the people of the land, etc., up to the point where it is therefore said that the worshiper ought to be corrected.

### Verse 16

“When he had heard this,” etc. (JEROME, *On Hebrew Places*.) In Hebrew, as we have rendered it, etc., up to the point where even the one who accepts unwillingly is reproved.

### Verses 17–20

“And the field was confirmed,” etc. [Col. 0140B] (GREGORY, *Moral Expositions*, book 6, chapter 25.) He indicates a twofold tomb, etc., up to the point where he postpones contemplation because of the urgency of action.

“Cave.” Together with the surrounding field, planted with trees, it is purchased by the patriarch from the lords of the land for four hundred shekels of silver, in order to bury Sarah. For a quiet place is acquired by preachers for devoting themselves to wisdom and applying themselves to action beneath the leaves of mystical words, as beneath fruitful trees, only when eternal blessedness is commended to earthly powers through evangelical teaching, shining with the brilliance of silver. This is suitably represented by four times one hundred, because it is transferred from the left to the right.

## Chapter XXIV

[Col. 0140C]

### Verses 1–2

“Now Abraham was old . . . . . And he said to the oldest servant: Put your hand,” etc. (GREGORY.) He orders him to put his hand beneath the thigh and to swear by the God of heaven, because through that limb the flesh of the one who would be Abraham’s son according to humanity and divine according to divinity was to descend; as though he said: “Touch my Son and swear by my God.” Nevertheless, he orders him to put his hand not upon the thigh but beneath the thigh, because from there the one who was human but would be above human beings was to descend. Hence it was not fitting for him to put his hand upon the thigh, because no flesh is above it.

### Verses 3–8

“So that you may not take,” etc. (GREGORY.) Allegorically. Isaac is forbidden to take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites because no soul of the reprobate is joined to Christ. He is ordered to take a wife from his own kindred because only the Church of the elect was to be joined to Christ; the Only-begotten himself, through predestination and foreknowledge, did not regard her as a stranger. The servant sent to bring the wife is the order of the prophets, apostles, and all teachers; when they proclaim the word, they become, as it were, the agents appointed to unite each soul to the Only-begotten Son.

### Verse 9

“Therefore he placed,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) The Hebrews report that at his consecration, etc., up to the point where they bravely endure the weight of tribulation, which the camels signify.

### Verse 10

“From all his goods,” etc. (GREGORY.) Those who speak about the Lord display within themselves the riches of virtues, so that they invite others to follow God all the more quickly because they show their hearers in themselves the things they proclaim.

### Verses 11–13

“By the well.” (GREGORY.) He stood beside the spring and, from the judgment already determined, set forth what should be chosen, because holy preachers consider words that flow forth. From these they gather to whom, or before which hearers, they should assume the confidence of certainty.

### Verses 14–16

“Then the girl,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) It must be asked how unlawful divinations differ from this petition, etc., up to the point where God is forbidden to be put to the test.

“Bend your water jar.” Humble worldly eloquence in order to draw up prophetic speech, so that I may incline your will to my persuasion. [Col. 0141B]

### Verses 17–21

“The servant ran to meet her and said: Let me have a little,” etc. (GREGORY.) Allegorically. Every preacher thirsts for the soul of his hearer; therefore the servant asks, and Rebecca supplies drink, because the Church of the elect satisfies the desire of preachers through the power of her faith. For when she confesses the God whom she hears, she offers the preacher water of refreshment and relief. It should be noted that she inclined the water jar from her shoulder and set it down, because that confession is pleasing which proceeds from good works. Or she supplied water because, in what she believed, she did not remain empty. Immediately she proclaimed what she had heard, and by speaking she produced many preachers from herself. The water in the jar is knowledge of preaching in due measure. For she takes care not to think more highly than one ought to think. [Col. 0141C] The jar measured by a cubit is the measure of preaching in action. She supplies drink not only to all his companions but also to the camels, because the word of life is preached not only to the wise but also to the foolish. Romans 1: “I am a debtor to the wise and to the foolish.” Or water is also given to the beasts of burden when provision is made for how the care of the flesh is to be maintained, so that it is neither expended through pleasure nor denied through necessity. Hence Romans 13: “Do not make provision for the flesh in its desires”; and Ephesians 5: “No one has ever hated his own flesh.”

### Verses 22–24

“The man brought forth,” etc. (JEROME.) A *beka* (), which is rendered here as a didrachm, is half an ounce; but a *shekel* (), which in Latin is called, though corruptly, a *siclus*, is an ounce. (GREGORY.) Because the preached word adorns the hearing of the Church through obedience and the hands through action. The earrings weigh two shekels and the bracelets ten, because the first virtue of obedience is charity, which is love of God and neighbor; and good work is completed through the perfection of the Decalogue, so that once good deeds have begun, no evil deeds are done.

### Verses 25–28

“And there was also straw.” Because the Church, receiving spiritual things, gives earthly support in return to preachers. Hence 1 Corinthians 9: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great matter if we reap your carnal things?”

“A spacious place.” The Church showed that it knew the law of nature from the former people and received preaching in the broad bosom of charity. For to a teacher a spacious dwelling is the breadth of charity in the heart of the hearer. Hence 2 Corinthians 6: “You are not restricted by us, but you are restricted in your own hearts”; as though he said: Enlarge the place of your mind for receiving teaching, and narrow it for thinking about carnal things.

### Verses 29–32

“He had,” etc. Because carnal people joined to the faithful, when they see spiritual gifts, are suspended in admiration and admit preaching at least as far as accepting the faith, even if not as far as good works. For when they see the good shining through miracles, they do not reject what they hear about eternity, although they do not follow the Church in their way of life and remain in carnal activity.

“And he had.” Because there are carnal people joined to the faithful who, through their familiarity, sometimes come out to hear the word. Seeing the gifts bestowed upon the faithful, they marvel and receive the word in their hearts, though they do not strive to fulfill it through good conduct. [Col. 0142B]

### Verses 33–36

“I will not eat.” Because there are people prepared to retain teachers through temporal support, but those teachers refuse to accept it unless they first obtain eternal things.
