For if they find no fruit in souls, they disdain to receive sustenance for their bodies; they do not wash their feet because the aspirations of their labor are relieved by no consolation.

### Verses 37–41

“And he made him swear,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, cited above.) The judgment is the same, though not all the words are identical, whether these words or others were spoken in precisely this way. This must be said because of those who slander the evangelists on the ground that they do not agree completely in some words, although the event and the judgment are the same. [Col. 0142C] For one author wrote this book and, when Abraham gave his command, could have set down the things he said above, or the rest, if he had judged them relevant. The truth of a narrative requires only that the truth of its events and judgments be preserved, so that the will—for the communication of which words are used—may sufficiently appear.

### Verses 42–52

“So come today,” etc. (JEROME.) It is written in Hebrew, etc., up to the point where the Jews should therefore show that *alma* is used somewhere to mean a young woman and not a virgin.

### Verses 53–58

“And when they had brought forth,” etc. (GREGORY, cited above.) After the servant had obtained the matter of the marriage, etc., up to “He gave them to Rebecca.” Rebecca is not adorned with the gold of Bethuel, because the ornaments of a barbarian and an uneducated man are not worthy. She receives ornaments from the house of Abraham, [Col. 0142D] because patience is adorned from the house of wisdom. From Abraham’s servant she receives earrings, that is, golden words in her ears; and bracelets, that is, golden works in her hands; and other ornaments, by which various kinds of virtues are represented.

### Verses 59–60

“And her nurse.” It was proper that a virgin departing for marriage without her parents should be comforted by the companionship of her nurse.

### Verse 61

“Therefore Rebecca,” etc. (GREGORY.) The Church has with her souls of lesser merit, which follow her in conduct but are not raised to the bedchamber of contemplation. She also had certain boys in her company, because there were people with the prophets who lived well though they did not possess the spirit of prophecy, and people with the apostles and teachers who preserved their way of life but did not preach. [Col. 0143A]

“Who hurried,” etc. The servant hurries back to his master because, when preachers have obtained the life of their hearers, they attribute it to God, from whose gift they have received it, and not to themselves.

### Verse 62

“At that time Isaac,” etc. (GREGORY, cited above.) The Lord is the one who lives and sees, etc., up to the point where he at one time endured a crown of thorns and at another the cross.

“He lived,” etc. (PATERIUS, *On Genesis*, from the sayings of GREGORY.) When Rebecca came, Isaac lived in the southern land because, when the Church came to him, Christ dwelt in the minds of those whom not bodily cold but the warmth of charity held fast. Such were Anna, Simeon, and certain people from the Jewish nation.

[Col. 0143B]

### Verse 63

“And he had gone out,” etc. (JEROME.) By the southern land he means Gerar, from which Isaac had been brought to be sacrificed. He went out to exercise himself in the field. In Hebrew it reads: “Isaac went out to speak in the field, with evening already falling.” This signifies that the Lord prayed alone on the mountain, and that Isaac, who was a type of the Lord, went out from the house for prayer like a righteous man at the ninth hour or before sunset, offering spiritual sacrifices to God.

(GREGORY, cited above.) The field is the world into which Christ went forth, because he graciously deigned to appear visibly.

Hence Habakkuk 3: “You went forth for the salvation of your people.” Isaac went out into the field to meditate because Christ, offering an example of humility and exercising long-suffering, displayed examples of passion and patience, just as young men trained in the use of arms are accustomed to practice. The practice of arms is the repeated experience of passion. For he who endured blows, spittle, the lance, and the cross permitted passion to be repeatedly inflicted upon him even unto death. We call sufferings weapons because through them we are freed from our adversaries. Hence Luke 21: “By your patience you will possess your souls.”

“With evening falling,” etc. Because he accepted the exercises of suffering near the end of the world. Hence Psalm 140: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice.”

### Verse 64

“She descended from the camel,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moral Expositions*, book 1, chapter 14.) Rebecca is brought to Isaac on a camel, etc., up to the point where they carry riches upon the crooked backs of camels.

[Col. 0143D]

### Verses 65–66

“Who is that man,” etc. (GREGORY, in Paterius.) After seeing Isaac and asking the servant who he was, Rebecca learns his identity, because the Church understands from the words of the prophets and apostles what it ought to believe about Christ. She immediately covered herself with a cloak, because the more deeply she penetrates the mysteries of Christ, the more she is ashamed of her former life. Thus she tries to cover her weakness with a cloak. She who had previously been carried freely upon the camel is covered as she descends in modesty; to her it is said, as though with greater shame: “What fruit did you have then in those things of which you are now ashamed?”

“But she,” etc. (JEROME.) Another edition reads “*teristrum*,” which is still a kind of Arabian garment with which the women of that province cover themselves.

[Col. 0144A]

### Verse 67

“And he brought her in,” etc. (GREGORY, as above.) Isaac brought her into his mother’s tent and took her as his wife because, in the place of the Synagogue from which Christ was born, he loves the Church, so that she who had been close by kinship—that is, by predestination—might become his wife, joined to him in love.

“And he loved her so greatly,” etc. (GREGORY, as above.) Through the gain of the Church Christ wiped away the sadness caused by the destruction of the Synagogue, because, while the Church coming from the Gentiles is led to the bedchamber of contemplation, Judea is regarded as nothing. Isaac is also called “laughter,” while Rebecca is called “patience”: laughter comes from joy, and patience from tribulation. Although the Church is already suspended in contemplation of heavenly joy, it nevertheless has within itself that which grieves over the burden of the flesh. Isaac and Rebecca are therefore joined—that is, laughter and patience—in accordance with Romans 12: “Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation,” so that prosperity may gladden through contemplation and adversity may disturb through tribulation.

## Chapter XXV

### Verses 1–2

“Abraham took another wife,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Allegorically. After Sarah’s death Abraham took Keturah. Not because of incontinence, since he was already advanced in age; nor for the sake of obtaining children, since offspring as numerous as the stars of heaven had been promised to him through Isaac. But just as Hagar and Ishmael represented the carnal people of the Old Testament, so Keturah and her sons represent heretics, who consider themselves to belong to the New Testament. Yet each was a concubine, while Sarah alone was a wife. Hence Song of Songs 6: “My dove, my perfect one, is one,” etc.

Allegorically. After the Church had been taken up, many souls deceived by heretical depravity adhered to Christ. They produced not Catholics but schismatics, who divided the unity of the Church. These are signified by the sons of Keturah, who are enumerated below.

(JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) Keturah, in Hebrew, means “joined,” etc., up to the point that the more exhausted someone is in the flesh, the stronger he is in spirit and the more suited to the embraces of wisdom.

### Verses 3–4

“The sons of Dedan were Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim. From Midian came Ephah, Opher, Enoch, and Abida.” (JEROME.) They think that *Asshurim* should be translated as “merchants,” etc., up to [Col. 0144D] the regions of India occupied by many of the sons of Abraham through Keturah.

### Verses 5–7

“And Abraham gave,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Gifts are given to the sons of the concubines, that is, to carnal people; but heretics and Jews do not reach the promised kingdom because they pursue carnal gains. Isaac alone is heir, because those who are regarded as offspring in the seed are not the children of the flesh but of the promise.

### Verses 8–11

“And failing, he died in a good old age, advanced in years and full of days, and he was gathered to his people. And they buried him,” etc. (JEROME.) The addition in the Septuagint, “Abraham died failing,” is incorrect, because it is not fitting for Abraham to fail or diminish. [Col. 0145A] The expression that we have rendered “an old man in a good old age” is also given more fully in the Greek manuscripts as “full of days.” Although this appears to explain the meaning—because he had set at evening, full of light and the works of the day—it is even more suitable to the allegorical interpretation if it is simply rendered “full.”

(Greek Gloss.) Behold, Moses knew the life of the age to come, for no one can be added to those who do not exist.

### Verse 12

“These are the generations,” etc. These peoples are counted before the sons of Isaac. Although they are descended from Abraham, they are not counted among the seed, because what belongs to the soul comes first, and afterward what is spiritual. Therefore, after the counting of the carnal descendants, the genealogy of Isaac is set down, from whom the promise was made and the succession of the elect was to be propagated.

[Col. 0145B]

### Verses 13–15

“And these are the names of his sons according to their names and their generations: Ishmael’s firstborn was Nabaioth, then Kedar and Abel,” etc. (JEROME.) Twelve sons were born to Ishmael. His firstborn was Nabaioth, from whom the entire region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabataea; it is part of Arabia. For their settlements, villages, and tribes are known by the names of these men. From one of them, Kedar in the desert is named; another region is called Duma; Thema lies to the south; and Chedma, or alternatively Chethma, lies toward the east. What we read at the end of the chapter according to the Septuagint, “He lived opposite all his brothers,” is more accurately rendered as we have given it: “He died in the presence of all his brothers,” that is, he died in the hands of his sons, while his children were still alive. For sons are called brothers; hence Jacob says: “Let it be placed before my brothers and your brothers, and let them judge between us.” For it is not to be believed that Jacob had any brothers with him apart from his children.

### Verses 16–17

“Twelve princes of their tribes. And these were the years of Ishmael’s life,” etc. The number twelve, just as it is sacred in the apostles and apostolic men, is accursed in the reprobate, who are spread against the faith of the Trinity and the Gospel through the four quarters of the world.

### Verses 18–19

“He lived from Havilah to Shur, which faces Egypt,” etc. The region around which the Pishon flowed was named after Havilah, the grandson of Noah, and is a desert opposite Egypt. Shur too [Col. 0145D] is a desert between Kadesh and Bered, extending the wilderness as far as the Red Sea and the borders of Egypt.

### Verse 20

“From Mesopotamia, the sister of Laban.” A barren region, which is so called in Greek because it lies between the two rivers, the Tigris and the Euphrates. For *mesos* (μέσος) means “middle,” and *potamos* (ποταμός) means “river”; hence *hippopotamus*, that is, “river horse.”

### Verses 21–22

“And he entreated,” etc., “but the children struggled in her womb.” (JEROME.) The Septuagint rendered it “played” or “kicked” instead of “struggled”; Aquila, “the children were fighting in her womb”; Symmachus, “they were carried along like a ship upon the surface.” (GREGORY, *Dialogues* 1.8.) The things that the saints accomplish by praying, etc., up to the point where this man—through whom God had predestined that Abraham’s seed should be multiplied—obtained through prayer that he might have children. [Col. 0146A]

“He heard her.” (CHRYSOSTOM.) Do not think that she immediately and at once obtained what she desired. For she remained praying and entreating God for twenty years. Just as he taught us how old Isaac was when he took Rebecca—namely, forty—so he showed us how old Isaac was when his sons were born. “He was sixty,” he says, “when the children were born to him.”

“And she went,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) It is asked where she went, since there were not yet prophets or priests of the tabernacle or temple of the Lord. Perhaps she went to the place where Abraham had erected an altar. [Col. 0146B] But Scripture is silent about how answers were given there—whether through some priest. It would be strange if there had been one and he had not been named, and if no mention at all had been made of priests. Perhaps, after they had expressed their desires in prayer there, they slept so that they might be instructed through a dream. Or perhaps Melchizedek was still alive, whose excellence was so great that there was uncertainty whether he was a man or an angel. Or perhaps even at that time there were men of God through whom God could be consulted. Whatever the case—whether this or something else—Rebecca nevertheless, according to Scripture, consulted the Lord and was worthy to receive his answer.

### Verse 23

“And he answered and said: Two nations,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) In its historical meaning, the answer is found to have been fulfilled when, on behalf of Israel—that is, Jacob—the younger son overcame the Idumeans, that is, the nation descended from Esau, and made them tributaries through David. This continued for a long time, until the reign of Joram (2 Kings 8). Then the Idumeans rebelled and threw off the yoke from their neck, as Isaac prophesied when he blessed the younger in place of the elder and said the same thing to the elder when he later blessed him.

### Verses 24–26

“The time had come,” etc. (JEROME.) Where we have rendered “hairy,” the Hebrew has *seyr* (), from which Esau, as we read elsewhere, was called *seyr*, that is, “hairy.”

“Immediately the other,” etc. (ISIDORE.) This event, in its figurative meaning, is known even to unbelieving Jews: how the people of the Church overcame the people of the Synagogue, and how the Jewish people, older in time, became servants of the younger Christian people. [Col. 0146D]

(BEDE, on this chapter, book 2.) This can also be said of individuals. “Two nations and two peoples” are within us: the people of vices and the people of virtues. The former is greater, the latter smaller; for the wicked are more numerous than the good, and there are more vices than virtues. Yet one people overcomes the other, and “the greater shall serve the lesser”: the flesh serves the spirit, and vices serve virtues. Esau comes out first, red and entirely rough like a hairy skin; afterward Jacob comes out holding his brother’s heel. The former people, stained with the blood of the prophets and Christ, is surrounded by the squalor of sin and wickedness. The younger holds the heel of the elder because the smaller people overcame the greater.

### Verses 27–28

“Esau became,” etc. (GREGORY.) He signifies the life of those who, spread out in external pleasures, follow the flesh. He is also called a farmer because lovers of the world cultivate external things all the more while leaving their interior uncultivated.

“Simple.” (GREGORY.) The simple refuse to be scattered among external cares; they remain established in thought and in the dwelling-place of conscience. He lives in tents who confines himself within the hidden places of the mind, lest, while he gapes outwardly at many things, he should depart from himself, alienated in thought.

### Verses 29–30

“Jacob cooked,” etc. (JEROME.) “Red” or “ruddy”: in Hebrew it is called *Edom*. Because Esau sold his birthright for red food, he received the name “Ruddy,” that is, Edom.

### Verses 31–32

“Jacob said to him,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The fact that Esau sold his birthright to his younger brother for food and afterward was deprived of the paternal blessing promised to him signifies the Jewish people. In Exodus this people is called God’s firstborn son, but for the sake of the world’s gains it not only lost the honor of its primacy but also failed to obtain the prepared reward of the heavenly kingdom. Hence it is reproachfully said in Matthew 12: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to the Gentiles,” etc. The birthright was a priestly garment, in which the elder sons, clothed with their father’s blessing, offered victims to God like high priests. The Jews lost this gift through their desire for earthly love, together with the glory of the kingdom to come.

### Verses 33–34

“Esau swore,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moral Expositions*, book 30, chapter 13.) It must be understood that the vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways, etc., up to the point where he says that one should seek not what the desire for eating suggests.

## Chapter XXVI

### Verses 1–7

“Now a famine arose over the land,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) It is asked when this happened, when Isaac went to Gerar, etc., up to the point where we understand that temporal things can neither be given nor prosper except from the one God.

### Verses 8–11

“When they had stayed there,” etc. (ISIDORE.) From the time of Christ until the time of Constantine, the faith was preached not in public gatherings of peoples but as though in hiding; Christians assembled secretly. At last, when Christian rulers saw through Christ’s miracles that his majesty had been adapted to human weakness so that they could be joined together and become “two in one flesh,” they permitted the mystery of Christ and the Church to be preached openly, and they lamented that it had been hidden for so long.

“He saw him playing,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) What this signifies, in the mystery of Christ and the Church, etc., up to the point where it says, “so that he might dwell among us.”

### Verses 12–13

“Isaac sowed in that land,” etc. (JEROME.) Although Isaac sowed in a foreign land, I do not think that he had such a great abundance of barley. Therefore I consider the Hebrew reading, which Aquila translated, better: “He found in that year a hundredfold, according to the estimate.” Since Scripture does not state what kind of grain produced the hundredfold increase, it seems to display in him the multiplication of every virtue. [Col. 0148A]

### Verses 14–16

“Because of this they envied,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Isaac, Christ, who first wishes to dig wells, etc., up to “we shall go.”

“And they stopped up the wells,” etc. (GREGORY.) Morally. Often, when we devote ourselves to divine words, we endure the ambushes of demons more severely. They scatter the dust of earthly thoughts over our minds so that they obscure the eyes of our attention from the light of inner vision. We dig wells when we penetrate the depths of Scripture, but secretly the Foreigners fill them, because they inject earthly thoughts and remove the water of divine knowledge. Hence Psalm 118: “Depart from me, evildoers, and I will search out the commandments of my God.”

[Col. 0148B]

### Verse 17

“And he departed from there,” etc. (JEROME.) “Isaac departed from there, came to the valley of Gerar, and lived there.” Instead of “valley,” the Hebrew has “torrent.” For after Isaac had become great, he could never have lived in a valley, but in a torrent. Concerning it, Psalm 109 says: “He shall drink from the torrent on the way.” Elijah drank from it in the time of famine; but because he was not perfect like Christ, the torrent dried up for him. Christ, however, was also handed over in the torrent, dedicating our regeneration and the sacrament of baptism.

### Verses 18–19

“He dug other wells,” etc. (ISIDORE, from Gregory.) Isaac dug wells among a foreign people. Through this we are admonished, during this pilgrimage, to penetrate the depths of our thoughts, and, until the water of true understanding returns, not to let the hand of inquiry grow sluggish in drawing out the earthly things of the heart. The Foreigners fill the wells while lying in wait, because unclean spirits, when they see us digging diligently, inject the troubles of temptations into our thoughts.

### Verses 20–21

“Against the shepherds,” etc. (JEROME.) Aquila and Symmachus translated it “adversarial” and “contrary,” but in Hebrew it has “Satan”; hence it is clear that “Satan” is interpreted as “adversary.”

### Verses 22–25

“Broad space.” In Hebrew, *Rehoboth* (), “broad places.” Hence what was said above in chapter 10 is proved: “He himself built Nineveh and Rehoboth,” that is, its broad streets.

“Now the Lord has enlarged,” etc. Isaac was enlarged and filled the whole earth with knowledge of the Trinity; and he established the breadth of the Church throughout the world, though he was first known in Judea and named in Israel. Later “their sound went out into all the earth” (Psalm 18), that is, the sound of the apostles, who dug wells throughout the whole world and showed water to everyone, baptizing all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28). He gave the wells which Abraham had opened the same names that his father had given them. For Moses and the prophets are called among us by their own names, and the names of these wells are not changed.

### Verses 26–31

“To that place,” etc. (JEROME.) Abimelech does not always have peace with Isaac, etc., up to the point where there are many other matters in which philosophers disagree or agree with us.

[Col. 0149A]

Instead of “Ochozath, the bridal attendant,” the Hebrew has “the company of his friends,” so that the word signifies both a man and the crowd of friends who had come with the king. Phicol, the commander of his army, was among them.

“Abimelech and Ochozath,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, book 5.) Two men came with Abimelech: Ochozath, his son-in-law, etc., up to the point where he is a debtor to the wise and the foolish.

### Verses 32–35

“Behold, they came.” (JEROME.) I do not know how, in the Septuagint, the following appears: “And Isaac’s servants came and reported to him about the well which they had dug, and they said to him: We have found no water. And he called its name ‘Oath.’” For what etymology would explain its being called “Oath” for that reason, etc., up to the point where it does not agree [Col. 0149B] that Isaac found no water?

## Chapter XXVII

### Verses 1–2

“Isaac grew old,” etc. (HIPPOLYTUS OF ROME, from Jerome’s letter to Damasus, book 1.) Mystically. Isaac bears the image of God the Father; Rebecca, of the Holy Spirit; Esau, of the former people and the devil; Jacob, of the Church and Christ. Isaac’s old age signifies the consummation of the world. His dimming eyes signify that faith has perished from the world and that the light of religion has been neglected. Because the elder son is called, this signifies the acceptance of the law by the Jews. Because the father loved his food and his catch, these are human beings saved from error, whom every righteous person hunts through teaching. The Word of God; the blessing of the promise; and the hope of the future kingdom, in which they will reign with Christ and celebrate the true Sabbath. Rebecca, filled with the Holy Spirit and knowing what she had heard before she gave birth—that “the elder shall serve the younger”—represents the Holy Spirit, who, knowing what was to happen in Christ, contemplated it beforehand in Jacob and speaks to the younger son.

“Go to the flock and bring me two excellent young goats”: this prefigures the Savior’s coming in the flesh, in which he would free those held captive by sins. Young goats everywhere signify sinners. Two are ordered to be brought so that the taking up of two peoples may be signified. They are tender and humane—namely, teachable and innocent souls. Esau’s garment is faith, namely the Scriptures of the Hebrews, which were first given to them and with which the people of the Gentiles were afterward clothed. The skins wrapped around his arms are the sins of both peoples, which Christ fastened with himself to the cross when he stretched out his hands. For in his body he bore not his own sins but those of others.

## VERSE 2

“Esau called.” (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, book V.) Esau was a hunter and a farmer; Jacob, however, who was simple, lived in tents. Esau signifies the Hebrew people, while Jacob signifies the Gentile people. Isaac, however, signifies God, who made both peoples his sons, the one through the Law and the other through faith.

Esau was a farmer because the Jew served God for earthly things. He was not told to be poor in spirit, meek, peaceful, merciful, or patient under persecution, so that he might have abundant reward in heaven; rather: “If you keep my commandments, I will give you rains in their seasons,” and so forth—things that pertain to the pleasures of the flesh. He was also a hunter, because through the shedding of the blood of rams, calves, and goats he sought to appease God.

“Jacob, who was simple, lived in tents,” because the elect from the Gentiles strove to please God by faith and good will. By the tents we understand either the various Churches throughout the world or their various orders.

## VERSES 3–5

“Take your weapons,” and so forth. Isaac loved Esau because he ate from his hunting. Rebecca loved Jacob. Isaac signifies God, while Rebecca represents God’s foreknowledge, because God loved the Jewish people, since he was continually appeased by their offerings. But, foreknowing that the Gentile people would become much better, through the grace of his foreknowledge he loved them more.

While Esau delayed in hunting, so that he might provide his father with food from wild animals and receive the blessing, his mother brought Jacob to his father to obtain the blessing. This signifies that, while the Jews still linger in the observances of the Law and come late to faith in Christ, the mother—grace—offered the Gentiles, who eagerly received the faith, to obtain the blessing owed to the Jews. How they merited the gift of blessing is shown by Jacob’s deeds, which he performed in order to receive the blessing.

## VERSES 6–13

“She said to her son Jacob: ‘I heard your father speaking,’” and so forth.

Allegorically, by the two goats we may understand the confession of the sins of the Gentile people and their repentance. They are excellent goats because the confession of sins and repentance are highly acceptable to God. Hence Luke 15: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents,” and so forth.

Historically, by the one sinner he understands the Gentile people, and by the ninety-nine righteous ones the Jews, who seemed righteous to themselves in their observance of the Law. Hence Luke 16: “Why do you justify yourselves before men?” and so forth. They are placed in an imperfect number because the Law brought no one to perfection.

## VERSE 14

“She prepared the food,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) Mystically, by the pleasing foods prepared from the goats we understand the works of repentance, and so forth, up to: “often brings past sins before the eyes of the mind.”

## VERSES 15–19

“And with Esau’s garments,” and so forth. (JEROME.) At this point the Hebrews relate that the firstborn exercised the priestly office and possessed priestly clothing, wearing which they offered sacrifices before Aaron was chosen for the priesthood.

## VERSES 20–24

“How,” he said, “could you find it so quickly, my son?” (HIPPOLYTUS.) Isaac asks Jacob why he has come so quickly, marveling, of course, at the swift faith of believers. Pleasing foods are offered because the sacrifice acceptable to God is the salvation of sinners. Since the blessing follows after the eating, and he enjoys its fragrance, he plainly proclaims the power of the resurrection and the kingdom.

“Behold, the fragrance of my son is like the fragrance of a full field.” This is the blessing. The world is filled with the fragrance of Christ’s name, like a field. The blessing is from the dew of heaven—that is, the rain of the divine word—and from the richness of the earth—that is, the gathering of the peoples. “With an abundance of grain and wine”: this is the multitude whom he gathers from the sacrament of his body and blood.

The peoples serve him—that is, the converted Gentiles. The tribes of the peoples, converted and believing through circumcision, adore him. He is the Lord of his brothers—that is, of the Jews. The sons of his mother adore him, because according to the flesh he was born from her. Whoever curses him will be cursed, and whoever blesses him will be blessed.

Christ is blessed—that is, truly proclaimed—from the mouth of a people that does not know the Father, but the Jews think that another is being blessed: the one whom those in error await.

## VERSES 25–26

“When he had eaten the food brought to him,” and so forth.

Mystically, after Isaac had taken the food, Jacob offered him wine. Thus the food signifies the works of the active life; wine, which makes minds lose their ordinary state, signifies contemplation, which alienates the minds of the elect from the love of the world. After food and drink Jacob is blessed, because those receive heavenly blessing from God who strive to please him to the end by good works.

## VERSE 27

“While blessing him, he said,” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Homily 6 on Ezekiel*.) One is sent out to hunt, and so forth, up to: “which the elder, going outside, left within.”

(GREGORY, same work.) Isaac, his eyes dim, blessed Jacob without recognizing his son; he foresaw what was to come, but did not recognize the one standing before him. For it is clear that the Jews, who had fully learned the Law, knew of Christ’s coming. Thus in Matthew 2 Herod asks the chief priests where Christ was to be born, and they immediately answer him: “In Bethlehem.”

Therefore they previously knew the one whom, when they despised him at the time of his Passion, they did not recognize. Their earlier knowledge and later ignorance are signified by Isaac’s dimness of sight. While he blessed Jacob, he foresaw what would happen to him in the future, but did not recognize that he was standing before him. In the same way, the Jewish people received the mysteries of prophecy but retained blinded eyes in contemplation, because they did not see the one who was present, although they foresaw much about him in the future. They could not recognize before them the one whose coming they had announced long beforehand.

(GREGORY, *Homily 10 on Ezekiel*, book II.) Isaac does not recognize the son whom he blesses, and so forth, up to: “and because through some he rises into contemplation, while through others he grows rich in the works of the active life.” It continues:

## VERSES 28–29

“May God give you of the dew of heaven,” and so forth.

Dew falls from above gently and subtly, and we receive something from the dew of heaven whenever, through the infusion of inward contemplation, we perceive something of heavenly things faintly. But when we perform good works through the body, we are enriched by the richness of the earth.

“An abundance of grain,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) This is the multitude whom he gathers from the sacrament of his body and blood.

## VERSES 30–32

“Esau came,” and so forth.

Esau returns late to his father because the earlier people will be converted at the end. Hence Psalm 58: “They will return toward evening and suffer hunger like dogs, and they will go around the city.” And elsewhere: “They opened their mouths like one eating in secret.”

## VERSES 33–35

“Isaac was terrified.”

When the elder son repeated the promised blessing, Isaac was terrified and realized that he had blessed one person instead of another. Yet, once he understood the mystery, he did not become indignant; rather, he confirmed the blessing, saying: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”

This is the first blessing given by Isaac to the lesser people, the Christians. But the elder son was not wholly rejected, because, when “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved.” This is the prophecy of the second blessing:

“In the richness of the earth, and in the dew of heaven from above, shall your blessing be.” “In the richness of the earth”—that is, in the fertility of possessions and the power of the kingdom that existed among that people—“and in the dew of heaven”—that is, in the utterances of God. For to them the utterances of God and the covenants of the Law were entrusted.

“You shall live by the sword,” because that people, devoted to bloodshed, inflicted death on Christ and the prophets. “And you shall serve your younger brother”—that is, the Christian people. “The time will come when you will shake off and loose his yoke from your necks,” namely, when, converted through knowledge of the faith and the grace of Christ, you lay down the burden of the Law. Then you will no longer serve the younger, but through faith you will be called his brother.

“Isaac was terrified,” and so forth.

This indicates a certain alienation of the mind, called ecstasy, which commonly occurs in revelations of great things. Thus Isaac should be understood to have been spiritually admonished to confirm the blessing in Jacob, although he ought rather to have been angry with him because he had deceived his father. Ecstasy also came upon Adam before he said: “The two shall be one flesh” (Genesis 2), which is “a great mystery in Christ and in the Church.”

“And I have blessed him,” and so forth. (ALCUIN.) If the will of a righteous man is good, why did Isaac bless not Esau, whom he wished to bless, but Jacob, whom he did not wish to bless? The will of a righteous man is good insofar as his conscience is concerned; but God alone judges future things. Isaac, in the human manner, thought that the elder son should be blessed. But God, who knows hidden things, showed that the younger was worthy of blessing, so that he might show that the blessing belonged not to man but to God. Therefore in Numbers it is said to Moses and Aaron, the priests: “Put my name upon the children of Israel. I, the Lord, will bless them” (Numbers 6). It is the priest’s office to bless, but to God belongs the granting of the effect. When Isaac understood through the spirit of prophecy that the blessing had been assigned to the younger, he said: “I have blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”

## VERSES 36–39

“His name has rightly been called Jacob, for he has supplanted me,” and so forth. (JEROME.) Jacob is interpreted as “supplanter.” Therefore, referring to the fact that he had previously deceived his brother, he alluded to the name: he was called Jacob beforehand because at birth he grasped his brother’s heel.

## VERSE 40

“And you shall serve your brother,” and so forth.

Because the Idumeans were tributary to Israel, who is called Jacob.

“The time will come when you will shake off and loose his yoke,” and so forth. This was fulfilled when the Idumeans rebelled so as not to remain under Judah.

“The time will come,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: The Jewish people will be freed from slavery to sin at the end, so that, when “the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

## VERSE 41

“He said in his heart.”

Since Scripture says that Esau planned his brother’s death in his heart, how, or through whom, was this reported to Rebecca? It is to be understood that all things were divinely revealed to her. Because of the Jews’ incurable hatred, the apostles were commanded through the spirit of counsel to leave Judea and go over to the Gentiles.

“The days of mourning will come,” and so forth.

For he did not wish to do this while his father was alive, lest he incur his hatred and be cursed by him.

(DIODORUS.) What is written—“Esau said in his heart”—signifies that Esau desired his brother’s death not in sudden anger but with the full consent of his mind.

## VERSE 42

“These things were reported to Rebecca,” and so forth.

Here the mother’s intervention is appropriately introduced when it says, “These things were reported.” From this it is clear that Esau did not conceal the plot in his heart so completely that it failed to appear outwardly in signs and words.

“She sent and called Jacob,” and so forth.

She intended to persuade him to give way to anger and withdraw for a time. It continues:

“Why should I be deprived of both sons?” and so forth.

As though she were saying: If he attacks you, it may happen that both of you will be killed; or, if one remains, he will have to be a fugitive from me.

“Rebecca also said,” and so forth.

Since Jacob could not suitably leave without his father’s knowledge, Rebecca turned to persuading Isaac to send his son Jacob to Laban, so that he might take a wife there. She said:

“I am weary,” and so forth.

That is, because of Esau’s wives. She did not tell Isaac the other reason—namely, Esau’s plot to kill Jacob—lest she distress him excessively in his old age.

“If Jacob takes a wife,” and so forth.

It is as though she were saying: If you love my life, send him to the house of my brother, so that he may take a wife there.

# CHAPTER 28

## VERSES 1–9

“Isaac therefore called,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) The Latin manuscripts have: “Go to Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel,” and so forth; the Greek manuscripts have: “Flee to Mesopotamia,” and so forth, so that it may be understood that Isaac too had realized that Esau was plotting his brother’s death.

“But he departed.” (ISIDORE.) Jacob, fleeing from his brother’s treachery, leaves his homeland and his parents and goes to a distant region in order to take a wife. Likewise Christ, leaving his parents according to the flesh—that is, the Jews—and his homeland—that is, Jerusalem—and all the regions of Judea, went to the Gentiles to take the Church as his own, in accordance with Hosea 2: “I will call the one who was not my people,” and so forth.

## VERSE 10

“Jacob therefore went out,” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Moral Exposition*, book V, chapter 11, book I.) To sleep on a journey, and so forth, up to: “because the Lord is sweet.”

## VERSE 11

“He took one of the stones,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) Jacob’s sleep on the journey signifies Christ’s death on the cross. The stone placed beneath his head is Christ according to his humanity, whom Jacob anointed so that Christ might be signified. For *christos* (χριστός) is Greek, while *unctus*—“anointed”—is Latin. The head, however, is Christ as God. Thus the stone placed beneath Jacob’s head signifies Christ’s humanity joined to God, who assumes it. “The head of the man is Christ, and the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11).

## VERSE 12

“He saw in a dream,” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Register*, book I, letter 24.) Jacob signifies preachers who not only desire to contemplate the Head of the Church, Christ, but also descend in compassion to his members. This is shown by the angels ascending and descending.

Hence Moses frequently enters and leaves the tabernacle. The one who is caught up within to contemplation is pressed outside by the affairs of the weak; within, he considers hidden things, while outside he bears the burdens of the carnal. Whenever he is uncertain, he returns to the tabernacle, consults the Lord before the ark of the covenant, and provides an example for rulers: when they are uncertain outside about what they should decide, they should return to the mind as to a tabernacle and, as before the ark of the covenant, consult the Lord about their doubts, searching inwardly within themselves for the pages of sacred speech.

Morally, to sleep on a journey is to rest, on the road of this age, from the impediments of worldly activities. Jacob saw angels while sleeping because those behold divine things who close their eyes to the desire for temporal possessions. The devil rightly opened these eyes when he said: “On whatever day you eat, your eyes will be opened” (Genesis 3).

“He saw in a dream,” and so forth. (ISIDORE.) The angels ascending and descending by the ladder are the evangelists and preachers of Christ. They ascend in order to understand his divinity, surpassing every creature, so that they may find “the Word in the beginning with God,” through whom all things were made. They descend in order to find him “made of a woman, made under the Law,” and so forth.

That ladder also extends from earth to heaven, from flesh to spirit, because through progress the carnal become spiritual, as though ascending. The spiritual descend to nourish them with milk, because they cannot speak to them as to spiritual people but as to carnal people.

He himself is above in the Head and below in his body, that is, the Church. He himself is the ladder, who says in John 14: “I am the way,” and so forth. One ascends to him in order to understand him in the heights, and descends in order to nourish him in his little members. Through him they raise themselves up so that they may await the exalted one, and they humble themselves so that they may proclaim him loftily and with restraint.

## VERSES 13–15

“I am the Lord, the God of Abraham,” and so forth.

Mystically, this signifies the command of divinity directed toward Christ’s humanity. The earth—that is, the Church—is promised to him, and also to his seed—that is, to the Christian people. Hence Psalm 2: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession.”

## VERSES 16–17

“When he awoke,” and so forth.

Whoever, after the torpor of inertia, awakens and truly rises through the exercise of good works will understand in the Church the transcendent grace of God and the entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

## VERSE 18

“Therefore, rising,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book III.) When Jacob “raised up” the stone “that he had placed beneath his head” as a pillar and poured oil over it, he did nothing resembling idolatry. He did not then or afterward regularly worship the stone or sacrifice to it. Rather, it was a sign and prophecy relating to anointing, from which Christ receives his name.

## VERSES 19–21

“He called the name of the city Bethel,” and so forth. (JEROME, *On Hebrew Places*.) From the statement, “How terrible is this place,” and so forth, he gives the place the name Bethel—that is, “house of God.” Previously it was called Luza, that is, “nut” or “almond.” Hence some absurdly think that the Hebrew word *ulam* is the name of the city, whereas *ulam* means “formerly” or “before.”

The order of the reading is therefore: “He called the name of that place Bethel, whereas Luza had previously been the name of the city.” Ancient writings, however, are full of the word *ulam* or *olam*, which signifies nothing except “formerly” or “before,” and also vestibule, threshold, or doorposts, and so forth.

## VERSE 22

“And this stone shall be called the house of God,” and so forth.

This is a prophecy that the house of God would be there. On his return there, he also sacrificed to God.

# CHAPTER 29

## VERSES 1–10

“Jacob therefore departed,” and so forth. “He saw a well in the field,” and so forth.

The water of the well is the knowledge of the Old Testament. A stone closed it because the letter of the Law concealed its spiritual meaning. But when Christ came, the stone was removed: through the preaching of the New Testament, the shadow of the Law was excluded and the truth of the Gospel was revealed.

Allegorically, the well signifies baptism and the field signifies the world. The three flocks lying beside the well signify those who belong to the reception of faith in the Trinity and seek the grace of baptism in humility.

“The stone”: the hardness of unbelief. When this is cast away, the baptism of life is received. The shepherds are the leaders of the Church, who, after removing the stone, desire through Jacob to water the flocks. When Christ removes unbelief from the hearts of those whom he has predestined for the sacrament of baptism, they are washed with the water of purification.

## VERSES 11–16

“He kissed her.” (AUGUSTINE.) It was especially customary in the simplicity of the ancients for relatives to kiss one another, and this is still done in many places. But one may ask how she accepted a kiss from a stranger if she later revealed Jacob’s kinship. It must therefore be understood either that he, who knew the relationship, confidently rushed to kiss her, or that Scripture later narrated the matter by recapitulation, after Jacob had first disclosed who he was.

## VERSES 16–19

“The name of the elder was Leah,” and so forth.

Victorinus the martyr interpreted Rachel and Leah as representing the Church and the Synagogue. He considers Leah, the elder by birth, to signify the Synagogue because she first bore the people of God. She is said to be weak-eyed because the Law given through Moses was veiled and signified.

Rachel, younger and beautiful, first barren and afterward fruitful, signifies the Church, later in time but holy in body and spirit. Her eyes are beautiful because she deserved to see the Gospel. Yet she remained barren for a long time while the Synagogue bore the people.

Jacob served for Rachel, and Leah was substituted for her, because, in order to take the Church as his own, Christ first joined the Synagogue to himself.

## VERSES 20–35

“Jacob therefore served seven years for Rachel.”

Jacob’s seven years of service for his two wives signify the time of the present life, which revolves through seven days. In it the Lord took the form of a servant, obedient to the Father even unto death.

Jacob served because “the Son of Man did not come to be served but to serve” (Matthew 20). Jacob fed sheep, and Christ said: “I am the good shepherd” (John 10). Jacob took for his wages livestock of various colors; Christ gathered for himself the diversity of the nations.

Jacob placed three rods, with their bark cut away, in the watering troughs so that the sheep would multiply at the sight of them. Likewise our Lord, in the water of baptism, set before the faithful people the names of the three persons—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—so that whoever gazes upon this with a full heart may become a sheep of God.

“And they seemed to him like a few days,” and so forth.

One must ask how this was said, since even a short period seems long to lovers. It was said on account of the labor of service, which love made easy.

(AUGUSTINE, *Against Faustus*, book XXII.) Jacob is charged with four wives as a grave crime. But since it was customary then, it was not a crime; now, however, it is a crime because it is not customary, and so forth, up to: “unless by the burning of carnal desire.”

(ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, book V.) Thus Jacob has two free wives, for both are daughters of the remission of sins, and so forth, up to: “and he saw the Word in the beginning with God, and wishes to give birth but cannot, because ‘who will declare his generation?’” (Acts 8).

(ISIDORE.) Jacob’s two free wives signify the two lives preached to us in the body of Jesus Christ, and so forth, up to: “But this cannot occur in the land of the dying, which is signified by these words.”

## VERSE 26

“It is not customary in our place,” and so forth. (ISIDORE, same work.) The elder is called elder because she is earlier in time, and so forth, up to: “therefore one must strive toward one thing, but for this reason many things must be endured.”

(ISIDORE, same work.) Accordingly, the life appropriate to the pursuit of contemplation, and so forth, up to: “hence below, chapter 30: ‘Rachel envied her sister.’”

(ISIDORE, same work.) Accordingly, because the pure intellect concerning that divine substance, and so forth, up to: “not because it is a deity.”

# CHAPTER 30

## VERSES 14–31

“Reuben went out,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Against Faustus*, book XXII.) Why Scripture did not pass over the deed in silence, and so forth, up to: “and whatever is said about this piously and wisely may profitably be understood, at least in part, without the phantasm of carnal thought.”

“Reuben went out,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Historically, I know that some people suppose of this kind of plant that, when taken as food by barren women, it produces fertility, and that Rachel therefore insisted on obtaining it. I do not think so, nor would she have conceived in this way at that time.

But since, after Leah had borne two other children from that night, the Lord granted Rachel offspring, there is no reason for us to suspect anything of the mandrake such as we have experienced in no woman. Since I myself had seen these fruits and was glad that, because of this passage of sacred reading, I had encountered them—for the plant is rare—I investigated their nature as far as I could, not through some more recondite science removed from common experience, which teaches the properties of roots and powers of herbs, but as far as sight, smell, and taste disclose. I found the object beautiful and sweet-smelling, but tasteless. Why, then, the woman desired it so greatly, I do not know, unless perhaps because of the rarity of the fruit and the pleasantness of its fragrance.

## VERSES 32–43

“Go around all your flocks,” and so forth. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) The meaning is very confused in the Septuagint, and so forth, up to: “the end is near.”

(ALCUIN.) Why Jacob is not accused of fraud at this point is undoubtedly because he acted as a prophet; nor should we believe that he did it without spiritual revelation.

# CHAPTER 31

## VERSES 1–11

“After he heard,” and so forth … “He changed my wages,” and so forth. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.)

Where we have translated, “He changed my wages ten times,” the Septuagint has “ten years,” although the Hebrew word *monim* signifies a number more than years. The following context confirms this meaning: Laban changed the agreement at each birth.

If he saw livestock of varied coloring being born, he would say: “I want animals of varied coloring to be born to me in the future.” Then Jacob would not place the rods in the channels, so that the offspring would be of one color. When this happened, Laban would say that those animals ought to belong to his share. Thus the agreement was changed up to ten times; and whatever Laban had arranged should be born for him was turned into the opposite color.

Now, however, ten birthing periods within six years would seem incredible. But read Virgil, where it is said: “Twice-pregnant sheep.” The nature of Italian sheep and those of Mesopotamia is said to be the same.

## VERSE 12

“For I have seen everything,” and so forth.

From this we learn that Jacob did nothing through evil deceit but by divine dispensation, or because everything was being enacted symbolically. Hence he deserved to be strengthened by an angelic vision.

## VERSES 13–31

“Now therefore arise.” (GREGORY, *Moral Exposition*, book XXX, chapter 16.)

After a long period of service the Lord commanded Jacob to return to his homeland. Then, without his father-in-law’s knowledge, he hastened away with his wives and retinue. Laban, however, caught up with him on Mount Gilead in anger, searching for the idols, but did not find them.

In this passage Laban represents the devil. For his name is interpreted as “whitening.” Although the devil is dark, he “transforms himself into an angel of light.” Jacob served him—that is, the Jewish people, in part belonging to the rejected, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh.

## VERSES 32–39

“…He did not know that Rachel had stolen the idols.” (JEROME.) Where we read “idols,” the Hebrew has *teraphim*, which Aquila translates as “figures” or “images.” I mention this so that we may know what *teraphim* means in the Book of Judges.

“Toward Mount Gilead,” and so forth. This does not mean that the mountain was called Gilead at that time; rather, it is called by anticipation by the name it received later.

“He took his brothers and pursued him,” and so forth. (GREGORY.) Historically, the world can be represented by Laban. He follows Jacob in anger because he tries to oppress the elect, who are members of Christ.

Jacob took the daughter of the world—or of the devil—when Christ joined the Church from the Gentiles to himself. To her it is said through the prophet in Psalm 44: “Forget your people,” and so forth.

Avarice is signified by the idols, for it is the service of idols. When Laban came to Jacob, he did not find the idol, because, after displaying the riches of the world to our Redeemer, the devil found no trace of desire for them.

But what Jacob did not have, Rachel concealed by sitting upon it. Rachel is interpreted as “sheep” and signifies the Church. To sit is to seek the humility of repentance. Hence Psalm 126: “Rise after you have sat.”

Rachel covers the idols by sitting because the Church, following Christ, has covered the vice of earthly desire through the humility of repentance. Hence Psalm 32: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven and whose sins are covered.”

Thus Rachel signifies us when, by sitting upon the idols, we suppress them, if by repenting we condemn the sins of avarice. The uncleanness of avarice does not impede those who run manfully, but those who walk effeminately are dissolved by the allurements of the world. This is signified by the words: “It has happened to me according to the custom of women.” For she made it known, as it were, that she was undergoing a woman’s condition.

“That I might kiss my sons and daughters.”

In accordance with Scripture’s usage, Jacob calls his sons and daughters his own, just as it calls sons or brothers relatives. Hence later: “Jacob said to his brothers: ‘Bring stones.’” In the Gospel also, the sons of Mary, the Lord’s maternal aunt, are called his brothers in Matthew 12.

“I was afraid that you might forcibly take away your daughters; but as for your accusation of theft against me,” and so forth.

It is as though he were saying: I did not reveal this to you lest, through the harshness of persecution, you overcome the weak souls newly taken from you.

## VERSES 40–45

“By day I was scorched by heat, and by night by frost. Sleep fled from my eyes.”

The effect of heat and cold is one and the same.

## VERSES 46–52

“Bring stones,” and so forth. (JEROME, *On Hebrew Places*.) “Heap” in the Hebrew language, and so forth, up to: “in which he lived, he had altered the wording.”

(ISIDORE.) Mystically, among the faithful, both Jews and Gentiles, the prominent stone is a witness in the likeness of Christ; the heap of stones is the multitude of believers.

## VERSES 53–54

“Jacob swore,” and so forth.

He swore by the fear with which he feared God, whom he had mentioned above when he said: “And the fear,” and so forth.

## VERSE 55

“Laban, however, rose early in the morning,” and so forth.

Because Laban and Jacob went beyond the river, this may signify the two peoples coming through baptism to the Church. But when Jacob proceeded farther, Laban returned, because, while the sons of light advance in virtues after baptism, the rejected, after the dignity they received, return after Satan into apostasy.

# CHAPTER 32

## VERSES 2–6

“These are the camps of God.”

Where the camps were established, the Hebrew has *Mahanaim*, so that, whenever this word is translated elsewhere, we may know what place it signifies. And fittingly, as he goes to meet his hostile brother, he is received by choirs of accompanying angels.

## VERSES 7–9

“Jacob was afraid,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.)

One may ask how he trusted God’s promises when he said this. But it could have happened that Esau destroyed his camp, and that afterward, following this affliction, God would be present and fulfill what he had promised. We are also admonished by this example that, although we believe in God, we should nevertheless do what must be done for the protection of salvation.

Jacob’s words must also be considered when he says: “God of my father Abraham,” and so forth, because in these words both human weakness and faithful devotion appear.

## VERSE 10

“I crossed the Jordan,” and so forth.

Through baptism the wall from the Gentiles has been joined to the one from the Jews. Yet the primitive Church does not lack fear of the Jews, which is signified by Esau.

## VERSES 11–19

“Deliver me from the hand,” and so forth.

He prays in such a way that he moderates hope with fear and consoles fear with hope. He signifies that we should take care for our own life and that of our household, while nevertheless calling upon God’s aid.

## VERSES 20–27

“I will appease him,” and so forth.

These words have been inserted by the writer. For it is not prudent to disclose one’s own strategy and thus make oneself suspect to those with whom one is dealing.

(GREGORY, *Homily 14 on the Gospels*, book II.) Mystically, when Jacob returns to his own parents, and so forth, up to: “so that we may grasp God with inward sweetness.”

“And behold, a man,” and so forth. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, book V.) In this passage the image of the Lord’s principal mystery is represented, and so forth, up to: “so that she could no longer bear children.”

## VERSES 28–29

“He said: ‘Your name shall no longer be called Jacob, but …,’” and so forth. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.)

Josephus, in the first book of his *Antiquities*, and so forth, up to: “we are guided more by the authority of Scripture and of the angel—or of God, who himself called him Israel—than by that of any secular eloquence.”

## VERSES 30–32

“Jacob called,” and so forth.

The passage that follows also says: “He blessed him, and Jacob called the name of that place Phanuel, saying,” and so forth. In Hebrew it says “Phanuel,” so that we may know that this is the same place which, according to the Hebrews, is read as Phanuel in the other books of Scripture.

(GREGORY, *Moral Exposition*, book IV, chapter 6.) It is asked: Since the Truth says, “No one will see my face,” and “No one has ever seen God,” how does Jacob testify: “I saw the Lord face to face”? For when human minds have been cleansed in their inner eye, and so forth, up to: “Hence 1 Corinthians 13: ‘Then I shall know fully, even as I have been fully known.’”

# CHAPTER 33

## VERSES 1–9

“Jacob lifted up his eyes … and divided Leah’s and Rachel’s sons,” and so forth.

Aquila has “divided in half,” so that he made one wedge of the maidservants with their children and another of the free women with their children. He sent the maidservants first and the free women second; he himself went before them all to adore his brother.

## VERSES 10–13

“For thus I have seen,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book III.) Whether these are the words of a fearful and troubled mind, and so forth, up to: “who are accustomed to hear and understand Greek.”

## VERSE 14

“And I will follow,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) It is asked whether he promised his brother a lie. For, as Scripture relates, he did not do this; rather, he proceeded along the road that led to his own people. Or did he promise with a truthful intention but afterward choose something else in his thoughts?

“Succoth.” (JEROME.) Where we have “tents,” the Hebrew reads *Succoth*. To this day there is a city beyond the Jordan with this name, in the region of Scythopolis, about which we have written in the book *On Places*.

## VERSES 18–20

“He crossed over to Salem,” and so forth. (JEROME.)

A question arises: How can Salem be called the city of Shechem, since Jerusalem, in which Melchizedek reigned, was previously called Salem? Either both cities bear one name—which we find in the case of several places in Judea, where the same name belongs to a city or place in different tribes—or we may say that this Salem, now called Shechem, should be translated as “completed” or “perfect,” while the one later called Jerusalem means “peaceful.”

With a slight difference of accent, the word has both meanings. The Hebrews relate that Jacob’s limping thigh was healed there, and therefore the city received the name meaning “healed” and “perfect.”

# CHAPTER 34

## VERSE 1

“Dinah went out,” and so forth. (GREGORY, *Pastoral Rule*, chapter 30.)

Dinah goes out to see the foreign women of the region when the mind, neglecting its own studies, takes care of the affairs of others and wanders outside its proper order. Shechem, the prince of the land, oppresses her because the devil corrupts the mind when he finds it occupied with external concerns.

“His soul was joined to her,” because he regards as united to himself the one he has bound through iniquity. And because a mind recovering from guilt is afflicted and tries to mourn what it has done, the corruptor places empty hope and security before its eyes, so as to remove the usefulness of sorrow.

Hence it is added: “He soothed her sadness with flattering words.” At one moment he speaks of the more serious deeds of others; at another, of the insignificance of what has been done; at another, of God’s mercy and the time granted for repentance. Thus, while the deceived mind is led along by these things, repentance is postponed, so that it may then receive none of the good things, though it is now grieved by evils, and may then be more fully overwhelmed by punishments, having now rejoiced in pleasures.

## VERSES 2–32

“When Shechem saw her … and slept with her,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book III.)

“He directed his attention to the soul of Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, and loved the virgin, and spoke according to the sense of the virgin.” How can she be called a virgin if he had already slept with her? Perhaps “virgin” is a designation of age according to Hebrew usage. Or rather, perhaps what had happened earlier is mentioned afterward by recapitulation. For he could first have directed his attention to her soul, loved the virgin, and spoken according to the sense of the virgin, and then slept with her.

“Peaceable ones.” Where the Septuagint translated it as “peaceable,” Aquila rendered it “completed” or “perfected,” for which the Hebrew reads *Selemim*. From this it is clear that what we said above about Salem is correct.

[Col. 0161C] “I have assented,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Shortly before, when Jacob speaks with Esau, he indicates that his sons are infants, etc., up to the point where his sons are named in this deed as though they were leaders and authors of it.

“Having seized,” etc. (STRABO.) Thus the shepherds of the Church ought to avenge sin of the flesh or of the soul with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God, being “ready to punish every disobedience.”

“We are few,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) He says this because very great wars could arise, not because he had far fewer men than would be sufficient to conquer the city.

“Is it to be treated like a prostitute?” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) The zeal of Jacob’s sons in avenging their sister morally admonishes the shepherds of the faithful to care for the souls entrusted to them, [Col. 0161D] lest they succumb either to bodily violation through sin or to spiritual fornication. “Let them be ready to punish every disobedience,” and let them strike the adulterer with the sword of excommunication, so that he may not escape unpunished.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### VERSES 4–5

“So they gave him,” etc. (JEROME, *Questions on Genesis*, vol. III.) Clearly, one must ascend to Bethel—that is, to the house of God, which is the Church of Christ—in this order and through these stages. First, one must renounce former errors and profess faith in the one true God, which means removing foreign gods; then one must be baptized, which means being cleansed; and afterward one must walk in newness [Col. 0162A] of life, which means changing one’s garments. The false earrings signify the trappings of false doctrine, glittering in speech but empty of the meaning of truth.

“And the earrings,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) The question is what sort of earrings these were, since they were ornaments not necessarily connected with idolatry. But it should be understood that they were phylacteries of foreign gods.

### VERSES 6–9

“So Jacob came to Luz,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) It should be noted that three names for this city are mentioned, etc., up to the point that names are added or changed for many reasons.

(JEROME.) Here it is most clearly demonstrated that Bethel was not formerly called Ulam, as was said above, but Luz—that is, “almond.”

### VERSE 10

“You shall no longer be called,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Since it was once said, “You shall no longer be called Jacob,” etc., why is Jacob later said to have been called by that name? But this name belongs to that promise in which God is seen as he was not previously seen by the fathers, when the old name will no longer exist: for nothing belonging to the old condition will remain in the body itself, and the vision of God will be the supreme reward.

(JEROME.) “You shall no longer be called Jacob,” etc. For the angel does not yet impose the name on him, but foretells that it will be imposed by God. What, therefore, is promised as future there is here shown to have been fulfilled.

### VERSES 11–13

“Grow and multiply.” Morally, this promise concerns Jacob’s spiritual offspring, just as was already said concerning Abraham. [Col. 0162C] For all who supplant vices, put off the old person with his deeds, and direct the eyes of their mind toward God properly belong to Jacob, whose faith and actions they imitate. “And kings shall come forth from his loins”—that is, saints who truly rule themselves and their subjects according to God’s will. From his spiritual offspring, that is, from the imitation of his faith, they are made fruitful in good works.

### VERSES 14–15

“But he erected a stone monument in the place where he had spoken,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) What had previously happened was done again in this place; or what had happened earlier is here recalled. But whichever of these is the case, Jacob poured a libation over the stone, not to the stone. Therefore he did not act as idolaters commonly do, setting up altars before a stone and pouring a libation to the stone as though it were a god. [Col. 0162D]

### VERSES 16–17

“Ephrath.” (JEROME.) Ephrath and Bethlehem are names for the same city, with corresponding interpretations. Ephrath means “fruitful,” and Bethlehem means “house of bread,” because of the bread that descended from heaven.

### VERSES 18–20

“When she was departing,” etc. (ISIDORE.) What does it mean that Rachel, while giving birth, called him Bennoni, “son of my sorrow”? Does it not signify that Paul would arise from this tribe, one who would afflict the children of the Church during his persecution? Alternatively, Benjamin signifies earthly Jerusalem, which lies in the tribe of Benjamin. Its people afflict their mother with great sorrow by shedding the blood of the prophets and crying out for Christ’s [Col. 0163A] death: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27).

“And it happened, when she was giving up her soul.” (JEROME.) As she was dying, “she called his name Son of my sorrow; but his father called his name Benjamin.” In Hebrew the similarity of the names is audible. “Son of my sorrow,” the name imposed by the dying mother, is called *Bennoni*. But “Son of the right hand,” that is, of strength—the name Jacob changed it to—is called *Benjamin*. Hence those who think that Benjamin means “son of days” are mistaken: “right hand” is *iamin*, ending in *n*, whereas “days” is *iamim*, ending in *m*.

### VERSE 21

“He departed from there,” etc. (JEROME.) The Hebrews wish this place to be understood as such, etc., up to the point where—or, more truly, by a certain prophecy—the mystery that was to come was already being revealed. [Col. 0163B]

### VERSES 22–26

“Reuben went,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Allegorically, this crime would not have been recorded unless it had foretold the future perversity of the people. Although it was a disgraceful act in that individual, Scripture contains a prophecy of what was to come, because Reuben, the firstborn, signifies the people of Israel. He polluted his concubine’s bed—that is, he defiled the law of the Old Testament by transgressing it. Paul shows that the concubine signified the Old Testament when he says in Galatians 4: “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave woman and the other by a free woman,” etc.

“And there were,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) The question is how this can be true, etc., up to the point where it is to be understood by synecdoche. [Col. 0163C]

### VERSES 27–29

“The city of Arbee.” (JEROME.) In place of *Arbee*, the Septuagint has “the plain,” although Hebron lies in the hill country. In ancient times the same city was called Mamre, after Abraham’s friend.

“The city of Arbee,” etc. It signifies angels or holy souls, to whom he was joined, with no anxiety from temptations or danger from sins remaining.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### VERSES 6–19

“He departed into another region.” (STRABO.) One may ask why Esau is said to have gone to Seir and withdrawn from his brother after their father’s death, when, by the time Jacob arrived, Esau is already said to have lived in Seir. [Col. 0163D] But it could have happened that, while Jacob was fleeing to Mesopotamia, Esau, distressed over the blessing he had lost, withdrew from his parent and lived in Seir during the twenty years Jacob was absent. After Jacob’s return, Esau was reconciled with him and came back from Seir; he lived with his brother while their father was alive. After their father died, he withdrew from his brother because they were wealthy and could not live together.

### VERSES 20–21

“These are the sons of Seir,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*, vol. III.) After enumerating Esau’s sons, Scripture goes back further and names those who had previously been chiefs in the land of Edom, from the race of the Horites, whose name means “free.” Deuteronomy states more clearly how the sons of Esau came and, after killing the Horites, inherited their land.

[Col. 0164A] “The sons of Seir,” etc. (STRABO.) That is, free men, who, as we read in Chronicles, first lived on Mount Seir; after they were expelled, the Idumeans lived in their place.

### VERSES 22–23

“She was the sister,” etc. (JEROME.) This is Thamna, of whom it was said above: “And Thamna was the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn,” etc. The Horites are mentioned because Esau’s firstborn took a concubine from among their daughters. Since Theman, Cenez, Amalec, and the others are mentioned, we should understand that names were later assigned from these figures to regions and nations of the Idumeans.

### VERSES 24–28

“This is Ana,” etc. (STRABO.) Some say simply that he discovered warm waters in the desert, which we call hot springs.

[Col. 0164B] “This is Ana,” etc. (JEROME.) Various matters are debated among the Hebrews concerning this chapter, etc., up to the point where mules were born contrary to nature.

### VERSES 29–30

“These are the chiefs.” He is speaking of those mentioned earlier, who came from Seir, not of those whom he now begins to enumerate, who came from Esau.

### VERSES 31–43

“But the kings.” It should be understood that he does not mention all the kings who existed before the sons of Israel had kings—the first of whom was Saul—but only all those who reigned before Moses died.

“But the kings.” He lists them according to the time in which the writer lived. When Seir, who fathered these men, lived there, before Esau came into that land, it was called the land of Edom after him.

(AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, vol. III.) It is not surprising that, when the lineage is reckoned from Abraham through Esau, the father of the Edomite nation, etc., up to the point that in the line where more people are counted they died sooner than in this one, where fewer are counted. [Col. 0164C]

“Husan.” (JEROME.) Some suspect that this was Job, as was added at the end of his book; but the Hebrews assert that he was descended from the line of Nahor, as was already said above.

## CHAPTER XXXVII

### VERSE 2

“Joseph, when he was sixteen years old,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) Historically, how could Isaac’s death have occurred, etc., up to the point that Joseph nevertheless began to be seventeen years old while Isaac was still alive?

“And he was with the sons of Bilhah,” etc. Joseph, one [Col. 0164D] of Jacob’s twelve sons, was loved by his father more than the others and signified Christ, whom God the Father, born according to the flesh, preferred to the other brothers descended from Abraham’s stock. Hence Jacob loved him “because he had begotten him in his old age.” For as the world grew old, the Son of God was born from a Virgin, like a son of old age.

“And he was with,” etc. In the primitive Church he did not reject those who adhered to him through the preaching of the pseudo-apostles, whom Jacob’s slave women signify; nor did he wish to prohibit them when they performed miracles in his name.

### VERSE 3

“And he made him a many-colored tunic.” (JEROME.) In place of “varied tunic,” Aquila translated *ἀστραγάλον* (*astragalon*), that is, “reaching to the ankles”; Symmachus translated it “with sleeves.” The expression may refer either to a garment descending to the ankles and distinguished by the extraordinary variety of its workmanship, or to one that had sleeves. For the ancients more commonly wore *colobia*, that is, garments without sleeves. [Col. 0165A]

(GREGORY, *Homily 25 on the Gospels*.) Because Joseph is described as having remained righteous among his brothers to the end of his life, he alone is said to have possessed a garment reaching to the ankles. What is a long garment but a completed action? Just as a garment extended downward covered the body’s ankle, so a good action governs us before God to the limits of life. Hence Moses commanded the tail of the victim to be offered, so that we might complete the good work we begin with a persevering end.

### VERSES 4–9

“But when his brothers saw,” [Col. 0165B] etc. Joseph’s brothers according to the flesh were the Jews, from whose kinship he took flesh. But because they saw that the grace of virtues was being manifested in him, which testified to the Father’s special love, they were envious and could not speak peacefully to him. They repeatedly plotted against him and blasphemously claimed that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, the prince of demons.

(ISIDORE.) This was spiritually fulfilled in Christ, etc., up to the point concerning the figure of the stars.

### VERSES 10–11

“Am I to,” etc. One may ask, in the literal sense, when he was worshiped by his father, represented by the sun, and by his mother, represented by the moon. For Jacob is not recorded as having worshiped him when he descended into Egypt, and his mother was already dead. [Col. 0165C] But let us turn to the allegory, which is fulfilled in Christ.

### VERSES 12–22

“When his brothers were,” etc., “in tending the flocks,” up to “Tell me,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Jacob sends his son to care for his brothers; God the Father sent his only-begotten Son to visit the human race, weakened by sins. Hence Galatians 4: “God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh.” Joseph was sent to see whether all was well with the sheep, and Christ says in Matthew 15: “I was sent only to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel.”

“In Dothaim.” “Defection.” For those who were plotting fratricide were in a great state of defection. “Reuben.” The prophetic word, foreseeing this and signified by Reuben—whose name means “vision of a son”—deterred them with prophetic threats, so that they might keep themselves innocent from the blood of Christ, their brother according to the flesh. [Col. 0165D]

### VERSES 23–24

“They stripped him,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Mystically, the Jews stripped Christ through death of his bodily, many-colored tunic—that is, of the garment adorned with the diversity of all virtues. They sprinkled the tunic with the blood of a kid, because, accusing him with false testimonies, they brought him under the charge of sin through envy. Joseph was cast into a cistern, that is, a pit; and Christ, stripped of human flesh, descended into hell.

### VERSES 25–27

“They saw Ishmaelite travelers.” (AUGUSTINE.) The question is why Scripture calls them Ishmaelites, etc., up to the point where some say that Hagar and Keturah were one and the same woman. [Col. 0166A]

### VERSES 28–33

“Drawing him out.” (ISIDORE.) Allegorically, Joseph, lifted from the cistern, is sold to the Ishmaelites; and Christ, returning from hell, is purchased by all nations through the commerce of faith. Joseph is sold for thirty pieces of silver through Judah’s counsel, and Christ is sold for the same number through the counsel of Judas Iscariot.

“They sold.” (JEROME.) The Hebrew truth has “for pieces of silver.” For the Lord ought not to have been sold for a baser metal than Joseph.

### VERSE 34

“And having torn his garments,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Jacob, mourning the loss of his descendants, lamented his son as a father would mourn a lost child, and as a prophet foretold the destruction of the Jews (Matthew 26). He tore his garment, as the high priest did during the Lord’s Passion (Luke 23). The veil of the temple was also torn, prophesying that the people had been stripped bare and showing that the kingdom had been divided. [Col. 0166B]

### VERSES 35–36

“I shall go down to my son,” etc. The question is how this should be understood: do only the wicked descend into hell, or do the good also descend there? If only the wicked do, how can this man say that he wishes to go down mourning to his son? It is not believable that he is in the punishments of hell. Or are these the words of a troubled and grieving man, exaggerating his misfortunes even here? Or is it credible that before the Lord’s Passion there were certain hidden places in hell, less subject to punishment, to which even the saints descended? For no one could enter paradise until Christ removed the [Col. 0166C] fiery sword.

(JEROME.) The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar the eunuch, Pharaoh’s chief cook. Scripture often uses *ἀρχιμαγείρους* (*archimageirous*), that is, “chiefs of cooks,” for commanders of armies. For *μάγειρος* (*mageiros*) means “cook” in Greek, and *mageireuein* means “to kill,” because cooks kill the animals that are to be cooked. Joseph was therefore sold to the chief of the butchers—not to Petefre, as it is written in Latin, but to Potiphar the eunuch. Here the question arises how he is later said to have had a wife. The Hebrews report that this man bought Joseph, because of his extraordinary beauty, for a shameful service; and that, after his master’s male organs had withered, Joseph was later chosen according to the custom of the *hierophants*, that is, those who speak sacred things, for the priesthood at Heliopolis. They say that Aseneth was his daughter and that Joseph later took her as his wife. [Col. 0166D]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

### VERSES 1–2

“At that time,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) The question is how these events could have happened. If, after Joseph came into Egypt, etc., up to the point that he fell in love with the woman whom he married, before Joseph had been sold.

“Judah,” etc. Here, like the other patriarchs, he signifies Christ, who descended from the baptism of John.
