Hiras means “seeing God”; the Odollamite means “testimony in water,” because John, seeing Christ coming to baptism, said: “Behold [Col. 0167A] the Lamb of God,” etc. (John 1). The Synagogue, signified by Shua, the daughter of the Canaanite, adhered to Christ on the strength of this testimony, because the lowly land of profession was to be given to her, which is what Canaan means. Thus the Synagogue first adhered to Christ when Peter, Andrew, and the other disciples of John became Christ’s disciples. The following narrative signifies the order in which these things were fulfilled, recounting how Judah went in to Tamar, who signifies the same thing as Shua.

### VERSES 3–4

“She conceived,” etc. The Synagogue gave birth to rulers who presided over it as husbands. Some were harmful, signified by Er, whose name means “leathery”—for skin signifies death, since the first parents were clothed in skins and subjected to death. Others were useless, signified by Onan, [Col. 0167B] whose name means “their sorrow,” because such rulers benefit no one.

### VERSES 5–12

“She also bore a third,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, vol. V.) The third son, who is not joined to Tamar, etc., up to the point that for this reason he bore witness in water like the Odollamite.

“Judah,” etc. From Judah proceeded the royal tribe, which long ruled the Jewish people, signified by Tamar. Her name means “bitterness,” because she showed herself bitter toward Christ in his Passion.

(ISIDORE.) The Jewish people, from whose tribe of Judah came kings, etc., up to the point that God nevertheless killed both, because he removes the kingdom from such men.

### VERSE 13

“To shear the sheep.” (STRABO.) Allegorically, the Lord came to shear the sheep—that is [Col. 0167C], to relieve them of their sins—of whom it is said: “Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep.” Tamar changes her appearance, for her name is also interpreted as “one who changes.” She changes her appearance and name so that the Synagogue may become the Church. Yet the name of bitterness remains—not the bitterness with which she served gall to the Lord, but that in which Peter wept bitterly. Judah is also called “Confession.” Therefore bitterness must be joined to confession, so that true repentance may be signified. This repentance becomes fruitful when the Church is established among all nations. For it was necessary that Christ suffer and rise again, and that repentance and forgiveness of sins be preached in his name among all nations.

The garment of a prostitute also signifies confession of sins. Tamar signifies the Church called from the nations. She sits in this garment at the gate of Enaim, [Col. 0167D] which means “spring,” because she ran like a deer to the springs of water in order to reach the seed of Abraham. Without his recognizing her, she is made fruitful, according to Psalm 17: “A people whom I did not know served me.” In secret she received a ring, a necklace, and a staff: by calling she is marked, by justification adorned, and by glorification exalted. “Those whom he predestined, he also called; and those whom he called, he also justified” (Romans 8)—but in secret, where the conception of holy abundance takes place.

### VERSES 14–19

“After she had removed the garments of her widowhood,” etc. It should also be noted that in the time of the patriarchs widows had distinctive clothing, different from that of married women.

[Col. 0168A] “She sat at the crossroads.” (JEROME.) “And she sat at the gate of Enaim, which is on the road to Thamna.” The Hebrew word *Enaim* is translated as “eyes.” It is therefore not the name of a place, and the meaning is: “She sat at the crossroads,” or at the junction, where the traveler must look carefully at the path he is taking.

### VERSES 20–24

“Judah sent,” etc. The promised kid is sent to the prostitute—that is, the reproach of sin is sent—through the Odollamite, as though through one crying out, “Brood of vipers,” etc. But the reproach of sin does not find her, for the bitterness of confession has changed her. In this act Judah’s sincerity in righteousness is not apparent, but his faithfulness to his promise. If he had preserved righteousness by preserving chastity, he would not have gone in, as he supposed, to a prostitute; but he faithfully sent through the shepherd what he had promised. [Col. 0168B]

### VERSE 25

“When she was being led out,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Later, by the public proofs of the ring, necklace, and staff, she overcame the Jews who judged rashly—those whom Judah already signified. Even today they say that this is not Christ’s people and not Abraham’s seed; but when the documents of our calling, justification, and glorification are produced, they are confounded and will confess that we have been justified more than they have.

The Church reports that she possesses pledges, although the Jews accuse her as an adulteress against the law. But she shows that the staff is the sign of the Passion, the necklace the lawful bond of the law, and the ring the pledge of immortality.

### VERSE 26

“Who, having recognized,” etc. (JEROME.) “Judah recognized,” etc. In Hebrew it reads: “She has been justified from me”—not that she was righteous, but that by comparison with him she had done less evil, not through indiscriminate immorality but by seeking children. [Col. 0168C]

### VERSES 27–28

“When the time came,” etc. The fact that the first child, called Zerah, put out his hand, and the midwife tied a scarlet thread around it, but when he withdrew his hand the other child, called Perez, thrust out his hand and was born first, signified that Israel would extend its hand in the work of the law, then withdraw it, stained with the blood of the prophets and of Christ. The people of the nations, however, would afterward burst forth, so that “the first would be last, and the last first.”

### VERSES 29–30

“Why has the partition been made?” etc. (JEROME.) In place of “wall,” Aquila and Symmachus translated “division,” which in Hebrew is called *Phares*. From the fact that he divided the membrane of the afterbirth, he received the name of division. Hence the Pharisees, who separated themselves from the people as though they were righteous, were called Pharisees—that is, “the divided.”

Zerah means “rising” or “east.” He was the first to appear, or because many righteous people were born from him, as is said in Chronicles.

## CHAPTER XXXIX

### VERSES 1, 6

“Joseph was therefore brought down into Egypt,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis*.) Scripture returns to the sequence from which it had departed, so that it may recount what happened above.

“And he was,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book VI, chapters 11ff.) Many people, puffed up with human wisdom, while they regard divine judgments as contrary to their desires, etc., up to the point that it lightens the burdens he willingly bears. [Col. 0169A]

### VERSES 7–11

“After many days, his mistress cast,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book XXX, chapter 19.) Whoever is lifted up by worldly success, etc., up to the point that, because pleasure arises from prosperity, he is struck down by considering it.

“His mistress cast herself upon him,” etc. (ISIDORE.) This is a figure of the Synagogue, etc., up to the point that from the place to which he had descended as though to be punished, he liberated others.

### VERSES 12–23

“He left his cloak in her hand,” etc. Thus the allurements of the flesh tempt us and pull away our garment of flesh; but the chaste man prefers to break every bond rather than subject himself to shame.

“He left,” etc. (GREGORY.) Allegorically, because the Synagogue wished to bind Christ in an adulterous embrace, believing him to be merely human, he placed the covering of the letter before its eyes and made himself visible to the nations so that they might recognize the power of his divinity. Hence to this day, whenever Moses is read, a veil lies over the eyes of their hearts: the adulteress retained the cloak and lost naked the one whom she had wrongly held. [Col. 0169B]

## CHAPTER XL

### VERSES 1–8

“After these things, it happened that two eunuchs sinned,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, vol. V.) Joseph found two eunuchs in prison, etc., up to the point where he is hanged on the wood of transgression.

“The cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the baker, against his master,” etc. (JEROME.) Where we have “chief of the wine servers,” the Hebrew has *masqeh*, the word that we earlier read in the name of Abraham’s servant. In ordinary speech we may call him a cupbearer, and even today among the barbarians it is a position of the highest dignity to offer the cup to a king.

### VERSES 9–15

“I saw a vine before me,” etc. (JEROME.) “And behold, a vine was before me, and on the vine were three branches, and it itself was producing three branches.” The Hebrew expression signifies three shoots, branches, or runners, which they call *sarigim*.

### VERSES 16–19

“Three baskets.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) Where the Latin manuscripts read “three baskets of fine flour,” etc., up to the point that every kind of baked product was in the same upper basket.

### VERSES 20–23

“Pharaoh’s [Col. 0169D] birthday.” Pharaoh and Herod celebrated their birthdays because from the hour of their birth they thought themselves to have been kings.

## CHAPTER XLI

### VERSE 1

“After two years Pharaoh saw a dream. He thought that he was standing,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, vol. III.) As Abraham’s servant said, etc., up to the place where earthly animals dwell.

### VERSES 2–8

“From it seven cows were coming up,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) “Behold, from the river seven beautiful cows were coming up to be seen,” etc., up to the point that they joined the Greek letter χ.

### VERSES 9–16

“Then at last the chief cupbearer remembered,” etc. At last the gentile people, through the presentation of past events, introduced themselves into hope for the future. [Col. 0170A]

### VERSES 17–32

“I thought that I was standing,” etc. The seven years represented by the seven full ears of grain or the seven fat cows signify spiritual gifts, through which the abundance of faith overflows in generous devotion. The seven sterile and hungry years signify, in the final age, a hunger for truth and righteousness.

### VERSE 33

“Now therefore,” etc. We see this fulfilled in the present age of grace: when apostolic teaching abounded, ministered through the sevenfold Spirit, bishops and teachers were appointed by divine providence in the individual cities. They wrote holy books from the abundance of teaching divinely bestowed upon them, so that when the hunger for the word increased and teachers failed, we might refresh our need. [Col. 0170B]

### VERSES 34–37

“And let him collect a fifth part of the harvest,” etc. It should be noted that the Egyptians gathered a fifth part of their crops into the king’s storehouses, because the children of darkness, devoted to the five senses, do not care for heavenly things. True Israelites, however, give tenths, because they labor to restore the heavenly homeland, a tenth part of which has fallen.

(ISIDORE.) Joseph gathered all the abundance of grain during seven years: that is, he stored the grain of the saints’ faith in the storehouses through the seven gifts, as though through seven years. When the seven years of scarcity began—that is, when the iniquity of the seven capital crimes arose under Antichrist, when there was a famine of faith and salvation—they would then possess an abundant harvest of righteousness, so that their faith would not fail for lack of the word. [Col. 0170C]

### VERSES 38–40

“Who is full of the Spirit of God,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) This is, if I am not mistaken, the third time in this book that the Holy Spirit is intimated to us. First, where it was said above, in chapter 1: “The Spirit was borne over the waters”; second, where God says above, in chapter 6: “My Spirit shall not remain in these men,” etc.; third, when Pharaoh says that the Spirit of God is in Joseph. Yet we have not read the words “Holy Spirit.”

### VERSE 41

“Then Pharaoh said again,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Allegorically, Joseph, who bore the figure of Christ, was given a chariot, and a herald proclaimed before him. Pharaoh appointed him over the whole land of Egypt. Likewise, after our Lord was sold by Judas, as Joseph was sold by his brothers, and after he rose from the [Col. 0170D] prison of hell, he mounted the chariot of the heavenly kingdom, concerning which Psalm 67 says: “The chariots of God are innumerable thousands.” He received from the Father the power to preach and to judge. Hence Philippians 2: “He gave him the name that is above every name,” etc.

He also received a ring, that is, the priesthood of faith, by which the souls of believers are marked with the sign of salvation, and the figure of the eternal King is impressed upon our foreheads and hearts through the sign of the cross. He is clothed in a linen robe—that is, in holy flesh more radiant than linen, and in the robe of immortality. He also received a golden chain, that is, sound understanding. A herald goes before him, namely John the Baptist, who says in Matthew 3: “Prepare the way [Col. 0171A] of the Lord.” He will also have another herald, because he will come with the trumpet of an angel.

### VERSES 41–42

“Behold, I have appointed you over the whole land of Egypt,” etc. Joseph is brought out of prison and appointed over Egypt; and Christ, rising again, received “the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Philippians 2).

### VERSES 43–44

“When the herald cried out,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) “And he cried out before him, and appointed him over the whole land of Egypt.” In its place Aquila translated: “And he cried out in his presence for genuflection.” Symmachus, etc., up to the point that he was a father in prudence to everyone, but in age a very tender youth and boy. [Col. 0171B]

### VERSES 45–49

“And he called,” etc. (JEROME, in the same work.) “And Pharaoh called Joseph’s name,” etc., up to the point that the Hebrews’ suspicion concerning him, mentioned above, is confirmed.

“And he gave him a wife,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, in the work cited above.) It is often asked whose Potiphar this was—elsewhere called Petefre, as many have it, though corruptly, as was said above, etc., up to the point that this is neither dangerous to faith nor contrary to the truth of Scripture.

### VERSES 50–58

“Two sons were born to Joseph,” etc. (JEROME.) Observe, in view of the question that will later be raised concerning Joseph’s sons, that before the time of famine, before Jacob entered Egypt, Joseph had only two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim. [Col. 0171C]

### VERSES 56–57

“And Joseph opened all the storehouses,” etc. Allegorically, Joseph saves Egypt from the scarcity of grain, and Christ frees the world from famine of the word. Christ opened his storehouses throughout the world and subjected all things through the distribution of his grain. If Joseph’s brothers had not sold him, Egypt would have perished; if the Jews had not crucified Christ, the world would have perished. Joseph means “increase” or “enlargement,” but in that Joseph only Egypt received enlargement; in our Joseph, the whole world did. The former distributed wheat; our Joseph distributes the word of God: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Psalm 18).

## CHAPTER XLII

[Col. 0171D]

### VERSES 1–15

“When Jacob heard that food was being sold in Egypt,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, vol. V.) There is grain in Egypt; and God the Father says in Hosea 11: “Out of Egypt I called my Son.” Ten older brothers descend, that is, the Jews, placed under the Decalogue. He recognizes them, but is not recognized by them. The Hebrews are recognized by Christ, but they themselves do not recognize him. They gave him money; but Joseph, that is, Christ, gave them grain and returned their silver, because Christ is not bought with money but with grace.

### VERSES 16–22

“Send one of you,” etc., “otherwise, by the life of Pharaoh, you are spies.” [Col. 0172A] (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*.) What does it mean that Joseph, a wise man, etc., up to the point that it will be God—not that he will be, but that he will be regarded as such.

### VERSES 22–26

“But they did not know,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, in the same work.) What does it mean that, while they were repenting among themselves concerning Joseph, etc., up to the point that they had sold him into foreign provinces.

### VERSES 27–34

“When one of them opened,” etc. Joseph’s brothers give silver because converted Jews abandon the letter that kills and receive the Spirit that gives life. Yet the silver is found in the mouths of their sacks, because, for the sake of the fruit of spiritual understanding, the splendor of eloquence is not abandoned.

### VERSES 35–36

“Each one found,” etc. Joseph’s brothers gave money for the purchase of grain, but after receiving the grain [Col. 0172B] they received the money back, because our Joseph does not seek what belongs to us, but seeks us. He gives his gifts freely and makes us richer through our purchase.

### VERSE 37

“Reuben answered him,” etc. (STRABO.) Reuben said: “Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you,” etc., but he did not obtain his request. Judah, however, said: “I shall be guilty of sin against my father forever,” and prevailed, because Benjamin was entrusted to him. It is therefore greater to be guilty of sin than to be killed bodily.

### VERSE 38

“You will bring down my gray hairs,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) The question is whether he says this because he will descend into hell in sorrow, or whether, even if sorrow were absent, he would speak of descending there by dying. For there is a great question concerning hell, [Col. 0172C] and wherever Scripture mentions it, we must observe what Scripture thinks about it.

## CHAPTER XLIII

### VERSES 11–22

“A little resin, honey, and storax,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*, vol. III.) Some resin, honey, etc., up to the point that various spices are preserved in it.

### VERSES 23–28

“Your God and the God of your father has given you treasures,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) This appears to be a lie, but it should be believed to signify something. The silver that is given and is not diminished, and that is called “tested,” may be the silver of which Psalm 11 says: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold”—that is, perfectly tested. [Col. 0172D]

### VERSES 29–31

“Joseph lifted up his eyes and saw Benjamin,” etc. (ISIDORE.) In Acts 9, Paul was surrounded as if by light. He was little because he had not yet reached maturity of faith. Hence he is also read of as a young man while he guarded the garments of those stoning Stephen. Joseph wept; Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping. Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom Christ was to be seen by many.

(AUGUSTINE.) The disposition of a good soul is always inclined toward compassion. Thus in Joseph we can consider an abundance of virtues. He was chaste when he rejected his mistress’s immodesty; wise when, through careful investigation, he tested his brothers’ attitude [Col. 0173A] toward their uterine brother; just in applying discipline to wrongdoers; and compassionate in the conversion of penitents.

### VERSES 32–33

“When the food had been set before them,” etc. Joseph’s food was set apart, as though he were a foreigner, and the brothers’ food was set apart, as though they belonged to another nation. The Egyptians also ate separately, as natives who considered it profane to dine with foreigners.

“...and it was called tested.” This perhaps refers to what is said in Psalm 11: “The sayings of the Lord are pure sayings, silver tested by fire, tested by the earth, purified sevenfold” [Col. 0172D]—that is, perfectly tested.

**VERSES 29–31.**—“But Joseph, lifting up his eyes, saw Benjamin,” etc. (ISIDORE.) In Acts 9, Paul was surrounded as though by light; he was little, since he had not yet attained mature faith. Hence he is also called a young man when he guarded the garments of those stoning Stephen. Joseph wept: Paul’s blindness is Christ’s weeping. Christ washed his face when Paul was baptized, through whom Christ was to be seen by many.

(AUGUSTINE.) The disposition of a good heart is always inclined toward compassion. Thus in Joseph we can observe an abundance of virtues. He was chaste when he rejected his mistress’s immorality; wise when, through careful inquiry, he examined his brothers’ minds to discover how they felt about their brother by the same mother [Col. 0173A]; just in applying discipline to offenders; compassionate in the conversion of penitents.

**VERSES 32–33.**—“When these had been served,” etc. Joseph’s food was set apart, as for a foreigner, and separately for his brothers, as foreigners by nation; it was also set apart for the Egyptians, as natives, who thought it profane to dine with foreigners.

**VERSE 34.**—“And they drank and became drunk,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Drunkards commonly cite this testimony in their own defense, on account of Joseph, who is praised as exceedingly wise. But in Scripture this word is used of being satisfied. Thus Psalm 64 says: “You visited the earth and intoxicated it,” because the expression is used in a context of blessing and God’s gift is being commemorated. It is therefore evident [Col. 0173B] that this drunkenness signifies satiety; for to become drunk as drunkards do is not useful even to the earth, since it is corrupted by more moisture than it can bear—just as the life of a drunkard is not filled with satisfaction but drowned in a flood.

## CHAPTER 44

**VERSES 5–14.**—“The cup that you stole,” etc. (ISIDORE.) What does it mean that Joseph’s cup was found in Benjamin’s sack, except that the utterance of heavenly doctrine was already shining in Paul’s heart while he was learned in the law? But because he was not subject to God, the cup was inside the sack: doctrine was inside the law, and the lamp inside the bushel. Yet Ananias was sent and laid his hand upon him; he opened the purse, and the silver shone forth. When the scales fell away like bonds and the sack was opened—that is, when the veil of the law had been laid aside—he obtained the freedom of grace and, with the face of the word unveiled, preached the Gospel.

**VERSE 15.**—“Do you not know that there is no one like me in the knowledge of divination?” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) The meaning of this is often asked. Was it because the statement was made not seriously but jokingly, etc., up to the point where he recognized the brother whom they thought had been lost to them?

**VERSES 16–34.**—“To whom Judah said,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *ibid.*) Many things in Judah’s speech are stated differently from the way Joseph had dealt with them, etc., up to the point that he inserted them into his speech in order to move him to compassion, knowing that Joseph knew this.

## CHAPTER 45

**[Col. 0173D]**

**VERSES 7–9.**—“God sent me,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) What is the meaning of the reading found in certain other copies: “For God sent me before you, to leave survivors for you upon the earth and to nourish a great remnant of your descendants”? For this does not entirely agree, etc., up to: “and thus all Israel might be saved.”

**VERSES 10–15.**—“You shall dwell in the land of Goshen,” etc. (JEROME.) In Hebrew it is written *Gosen* (). Hence the error arose that the land of Gessen is in Arabia. Moreover, as it appears in our manuscripts, it is written with a final *m*, *Gessem*, which I by no means approve as signifying “a land drenched with rain.” For *Gessem* is translated as “rain,” and in many copies it is also found as *Gessem* [Col. 0174A].

**VERSES 16–21.**—“And Pharaoh rejoiced,” etc. These words that Pharaoh spoke to Joseph about Jacob and his sons signify the joy of the Gentile people over the conversion of the Jews. Great indeed is the devotion of the Church of the Gentiles when the Israelite people come to faith. If they convert and become participants in faith, she promises them the spiritual riches of the virtues and the grace of the Holy Spirit. Whoever receives this will not suffer from a lack of goodness.

**VERSES 22–28.**—“But to Benjamin he gave,” etc. Three hundred pieces of silver are given to Benjamin. These are received from Christ by the one who preaches the Trinity or the cross of Christ. Hence Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2: “I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified.” He received five garments, that is, the wisdom of all the senses. Paul therefore excels in the abundance of his merits. But the brothers—that is, the other preachers—also have their own grace, namely two garments each, so that they may confess Christ as God and man. Hence Proverbs 31 says: “All her household are clothed in double garments,” that is, with mystical and moral understanding.

Gifts are also sent to the father, and Christ invites his people with promised gifts. The asses carry the gifts—that is, the Gentiles, once useless and laborious; but now, in the figure of Christ, they carry useful gifts in the Gospel of the giver of gifts.

(ISIDORE.) Jacob was terrified, that is, the unbelieving people. But after learning of Christ’s deeds, his spirit revived; the one who seemed dead was brought to life by faith in Christ’s resurrection. He is therefore called by his sons—that is, by Peter, Paul, and John—the Jewish people to grace. Judah, whose name means “confession,” meets him, because confession precedes those whom unbelief formerly possessed. Thus Joseph—that is, Christ—meets him, receiving the Jewish people, already aged with time, at the end of the age, not according to merits but according to the election of grace. He places his hand upon his eyes and removes his blindness—something he delayed so that the one who formerly thought belief impossible might be the last to believe. Hence Romans 11 says: “Blindness in part has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter, and thus all Israel might be saved.”

## CHAPTER 46

**[Col. 0174D]**

**VERSE 26.**—“All the persons who entered Egypt with Jacob,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) We must consider what answer should be given to those who use this testimony to establish that souls are propagated from parents together with bodies. No one doubts that “souls” is used for human beings, with the whole signified by a part in a figurative expression. But how can we detach the part itself—that is, the soul, by whose name the whole human being is signified—from the statement “they came out of his thighs,” so that we understand only flesh to have been born from him, although only souls are named? The various modes of expression in Scripture must be investigated.

**VERSE 27.**—“But the sons of Joseph,” etc. (JEROME, [Col. 0175A] *Hebrew Questions*, book 3.) “All the persons of the house of Jacob,” etc., up to the point where many maintain that Luke, as a proselyte, did not know Hebrew letters.

**VERSES 28–31.**—“And he sent Judah,” etc. (JEROME, *ibid.*) “He sent Judah before him to Joseph,” etc., up to the point where they believe that the village was once called Arsenoyte.

**VERSES 32–34.**—“And the men are shepherds,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) The patriarchs are commended because they had been keepers of livestock from their youth, etc., up to the point where they will possess perfectly ordered and everlasting happiness at the end.

## CHAPTER 47

**VERSES 9–10.**—“The days of my pilgrimage,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) What does Jacob say to Pharaoh, [Col. 0175B] etc., up to the point that they do not remain in the house forever?

**VERSE 11.**—“And Joseph gave his father and his brothers ... Rameses.” It must be asked whether the land of Rameses itself is Goshen, for they had requested this land and Pharaoh had ordered it to be given.

(ISIDORE.) Allegorically, Joseph gave his father and brothers the best land, Goshen, providing them with food because famine had oppressed the land. So too the Lord gives the best land to the fathers—that is, the patriarchs and prophets, from whom he is descended according to the flesh—or to all the saints, of whom he says in the Gospel through Matthew 12: “These are my brothers, who do the will of my Father.” Of this land Psalm 26 says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord in the land of the living.”

**[Col. 0175C] VERSES 12–15.**—“Providing food for each,” etc. Joseph measured out grain for his father, yet his father did not worship him either when he saw him or when he received the grain. How, then, do we suppose that the dream was fulfilled, unless it contains a prophecy of something greater?

**VERSES 16–19.**—“Bring your livestock, and I will give you [food],” etc. It is asked: while Joseph was gathering grain by which people would live, what did the livestock live on, when such a severe famine had prevailed and Joseph’s brothers said to Pharaoh, “There is no pasture for the livestock of your servants,” etc.? If pasture had failed in the land of Canaan because of the famine, why had it not failed in Egypt, since the same famine existed everywhere? Or, as those familiar with the regions report, could pasture have remained available in many Egyptian marshes even when there was a famine of grain, which normally grows through the inundation of the Nile? They say that those marshes produce pasture more abundantly when the water of the Nile rises less high [Col. 0175D].

**VERSES 20–21.**—“So he bought,” etc. Joseph is not accused of injustice or wrongdoing. Indeed, his faithfulness is commended by this: he showed favor to no person but repaid each according to the purchaser’s price with an even measure.

Mystically, however, this signifies that all who are in spiritual Egypt and seek its riches are slaves. No Egyptian who is carnal and sold under sin is free, for Pharaoh subjected them. Hence perhaps Exodus 20 says: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of Egypt, from the house of slavery” [Col. 0176A]. Hence Romans 6 says: “Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body,” etc. And in the same place: “You are slaves of the one whom you obey, whether of sin leading to death or of obedience leading to righteousness.”

The Egyptians were forcibly reduced to slavery, whereas the Hebrews were forcibly reduced to servitude. But the Egyptians sold themselves, and the steward is not at fault where deserved recompense is given for merits. Paul did the same when he handed over to Satan the one who was unworthy of the number or fellowship of the saints (1 Corinthians 5). Let no one therefore say that Paul acted too harshly when he expelled a man from the Church, so that, once expelled, he might learn not to blaspheme. The human will is wicked when, loving earthly things, it despises heavenly ones and subjects itself to the devil because of greed. God’s permission, however, is just when he abandons to his own will the person who, scorning better things and choosing worse, falls [Col. 0176B].

“So he bought,” etc. Allegorically, Joseph’s purchase—by which he bought the land of Egypt with grain—signifies Christ’s redemption of the world through doctrine and the price of his blood. When he says, “Take seed and sow the fields so that you may have crops,” etc., the seed is the word of God. The fields are human bodies, plowed by the Gospel’s plowshare and sown with spiritual seed, which bring forth the fruit of virtues. The fifth part given to the king is the tribute of the five senses, which must be paid to Christ the king. The remaining four parts are left to the possessors for seed and food, because the use of the active life is granted to each person, so that he may sow works of virtue and reap the fruit of righteousness unto eternal life, which is bestowed upon us by Christ. Hence Joseph is told: “Our salvation is in your hand,” because the salvation of the world is in Christ’s power [Col. 0176C].

**VERSES 22–28.**—“Except the land of the priests,” etc. This signifies that the land of the Church, in which the true priests dwell, is free from worldly tribute. It is continually nourished by the divine word and will suffer no loss of spiritual bread.

**VERSES 29–30.**—“When he saw that the day of his death was approaching,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Genesis*, book 3.) He binds his son by an oath, etc., up to the one who appeared in baptism at nearly thirty years of age.

**VERSE 31.**—“When he had sworn.” (AUGUSTINE, *ibid.*) What the Latin manuscripts have—“He worshiped upon the head of his staff”—some more accurately read as: “He worshiped upon the head of his staff,” or “at the head of his staff,” or “at the top, or above the top, of his staff.” Therefore it is rightly asked what is meant by the statement, etc., up to the point where the figure of a future event was foreshadowed.

(JEROME.) “And Israel worshiped toward the top of his staff.” Here too some falsely pretend that Jacob worshiped the top of Joseph’s scepter, namely, that by honoring his son he worshiped his power. But in Hebrew it is read quite differently: “And Israel worshiped at the head of the bed,” because, after his son had sworn to him, secure in the fulfillment of his request, he turned toward the head of the bed and worshiped God. For the holy man, devoted to God and weighed down by old age, had his bed arranged so that his posture while lying down was ready for prayer without any difficulty [Col. 0177A].

## CHAPTER 48

**VERSE 1.**—“After these things had happened ... taking his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim.” (JEROME.) “And he took his two sons with him, Manasseh and Ephraim.” From this it is clear that what we said above is correct: at that time Joseph had only two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh. If, after many years, when Jacob was dying, he brought only these two for the blessing, then at that earlier time, when his sons were not yet able to beget children but were little and still nursing, he could not have had grandsons by them when his father and brothers entered Egypt.

**VERSES 2–4.**—“When Israel had gathered strength,” etc. (JEROME.) “And Israel, having gathered strength, sat upon the bed.” I do not know why the Septuagint rendered the same word in different ways, but I boldly assert that the same word, *mittha*, which here they translated as “bed,” they earlier called “staff” when they said that Jacob worshiped upon it [Col. 0177B].

**VERSES 5–6.**—“The two sons who were born,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.) It is clear that seventy persons entered Egypt, etc., up to the point that Ephraim and Manasseh were included as appendages among the three tribes.

**VERSES 7–11.**—“For when I was coming from Mesopotamia, Rachel died, and I buried her,” etc. Joseph, as though speaking to someone who did not know, indicates where and when he buried his mother, perhaps prophetically recalling that his mother was buried in the place where Christ was to be born.

**[Col. 0177C] VERSES 12–15.**—“When Joseph had taken them from his father’s lap,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, book 5.) As happened with Esau and Jacob, when the Lord said, “The elder shall serve the younger,” so too with Joseph’s sons, etc., up to the point where he placed the younger on the right rather than the left.

**VERSES 16–21.**—“Let my name be invoked over them.” (AUGUSTINE.) It should be noted from this passage that not only being heard but also invocation is spoken of—things that belong not to God but to human beings.

**VERSE 22.**—“I give you one portion,” etc. (JEROME, *On Genesis*, book 3.) “I have given you Shechem as a special portion above your brothers, which I took from the hands of the Amorites with my sword and my bow.” [Col. 0177D] *Shechem* is declined according to Greek and Latin usage, etc., up to the point where his mausoleum can still be seen there today.

(AUGUSTINE.) Jacob says that he gives Shechem as a special portion to his son Joseph and adds that he possessed it by sword and bow. It is asked how this agrees literally with Genesis 34. He bought that possession for a hundred lambs; he did not seize it by right of war. Or was it because his sons had conquered the city of Shechem, so that it could become his by right of war, since their war against those who had first inflicted injury by violating his daughter may be considered just? Why, then, did he not give it to his elder sons, who had done this? Moreover, if he now gives it to Joseph while boasting of the victory, why did he then disapprove of the sons who committed it? Finally, when he blessed them, why did he mention it as a reproach? [Col. 0178A]

A prophetic mystery therefore lies hidden here, because Joseph, by a special signification, represented Christ. That land is given to him where Jacob buried the foreign gods (Genesis 35), so that Christ may be understood as possessing the nations that renounce the gods of their fathers and believe in Christ.

## CHAPTER 49

(ALBINUS.) In Jacob’s blessings, the historical meaning must be maintained and the allegory investigated: the history concerns the division of the Promised Land; the allegory concerns Christ and the Church, which is to be revealed in the last times. First, however, the foundations of the history must be laid.

**VERSES 3–4.**—“Reuben, my firstborn,” etc. (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions on Genesis*.) “Reuben, my firstborn [Col. 0178B], you are my strength” and the beginning of my sons, etc., up to the point where you lost the rank of the firstborn.

**VERSE 5.**—“Simeon and Levi,” etc. (JEROME, *ibid.*) The Septuagint reads: “Simeon and Levi, brothers, completed the wickedness of their invention,” etc., up to: “Let my soul not enter into their counsel.”

**VERSE 8.**—“Judah, your brothers shall praise you,” etc. (JEROME, *ibid.*) Because Judah is interpreted as “confession” or “praise,” etc., up to the point where, in other words but with the same meaning, the Church is shown, of which Matthew 5 says: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Judah is a lion’s cub; you have gone up to the prey, [Col. 0178C] my son; resting, you have lain down like a lion,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The lion’s cub rested in sleep because of power, not necessity. Hence: “I have power to lay down my life, and no one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself” (John 10). But when he adds, “and like a lion’s cub,” he means that he died from the place from which he was born. Physiologists say that when a lion’s cub is born, it sleeps for three days and three nights. Then the roar of its father shakes the place of its den and awakens the sleeper. Christ likewise, lying for three nights in the chamber of the tomb, fulfilled the sleep of death. Christ therefore rested fittingly like a lion: he conquered not only the bitterness of death but also its dominion, and he was like a lion’s cub because he rose on the third day. Hence it is added:

**[Col. 0178D]** “Who shall raise him up?” etc. No one, that is understood, except the one who said in John 2: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.”

**VERSE 10.**—“The scepter shall not be taken away from Judah,” etc. Kings from the seed of Judah continued among the Jews until Christ was born of the Virgin. The first foreign king among the Jewish people was Herod, when Christ had already been born. Therefore, whoever denies that Christ came should show a king from the tribe of Judah among the Jewish people.

**VERSE 11.**—“Binding his colt to the vine,” etc. These are the Gentiles whom he subjected to himself. Hence Ezekiel 18 says: “As I live, says the Lord, I will surely clothe these men as a garment.” Christ cleansed us in the blood of the grape when he hung like a cluster upon the wood of the cross, and water came from his side for washing, while blood came forth for redemption [Col. 0179A].

**VERSE 12.**—“His eyes are more beautiful,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Because their teaching surpasses the austerity of the old law, and the evangelical commandments are clearer than the commandments of the law.

“By milk,” that is, the teaching of the law, which fed the carnal or immature people with milk; but “whiter” are the teachers of the Church, who eat and distribute the strong and solid food of the word. Hence Hebrews 5 says: “Solid food belongs to the mature.” They are rightly called “whiter than milk,” because they are bright, pure, and free from every stain.

**VERSE 13.**—“Zebulun shall dwell on the shore,” etc. So that it may display [Col. 0179B] a refuge for believers and a harbor of faith for those in danger. Firmly established against all the boundaries of the world, it awaits the shipwreck of the Jews and the storms of heretics, who are carried about by every wind of doctrine. Some of the apostles were also taken from there; the Lord often taught there. It reaches as far as Sidon, that is, it extends to the Gentiles. Hence Isaiah 9 says: “The land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali, the way of the sea beyond the Jordan,” etc. Sidon means “hunting,” and from those places hunters were taken, concerning whom Jeremiah 16 says: “I will send many hunters, and they shall hunt you on every mountain.”

**VERSES 14–15.**—“Issachar.” (JEROME, *Hebrew Questions*.) He desired [Col. 0179C] the good, resting among the middle boundary-lines, etc., up to the point where all the tribes serve him, bringing gifts as to a teacher.

“Lying between the boundaries,” etc. To lie down means to rest while awaiting the end of the world and to seek nothing worldly but to desire the final things. The strong ass saw rest and an excellent land, when the simple Gentile people rose to the strength of action because they were striving toward the homeland of life.

**VERSES 16–18.**—“Dan shall judge his people,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Genesis*, book 5.) Some think that these words predict that the Antichrist will come from the tribe of Dan, etc., up to the point where, after the benefits of feigned sweetness, he exercises the horns of his power.

“Dan shall judge his people as one of the scepters of Israel. Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a basilisk in [Col. 0179D] the path, biting the horse’s hooves, and let its rider fall backward. I shall await your salvation, Lord.” (JEROME, *ibid.*) Samson, judge of Israel, was from the tribe of Dan, etc., up to the point where he himself will be the expectation of the nations.

**VERSES 19–20.**—“Gad.” (JEROME.) A marauder will maraud before him, etc., up to the point where he fought bravely after defeating his enemies.

“Gad, girded, will fight before him.” (ISIDORE.) Christ will fight against the Antichrist both before and behind: before, by the hidden coming of humility; afterward, when the glory of majesty has been revealed. Hence Moses says in Deuteronomy 33: “Blessed is he who enlarges Gad; he rested like a lion and seized the arm and the crown of the head, and he saw his principality.” Christ rested in the tomb, humbled the crown and pride of the exalted, and principality, honor, and kingship were given to him [Col. 0180A].

**VERSE 21.**—“Naphtali.” (JEROME.) Allegorically: a spreading branch, giving beauty to the nation, etc., up to the point where he taught there especially, as is also written in the Gospel.

“Naphtali is a swift deer,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The apostles and preachers, leaping swiftly like deer, transcend the obstacles of the world. Meditating on exalted things, they give utterances of beauty, that is, they preach the teaching of the Savior.

**VERSES 22–26.**—“Joseph is a growing son,” etc. (JEROME, *ibid.*) “A growing son beside a spring,” etc., up to the point where he also rules the ten tribes of Israel.

**[Col. 0180B] VERSE 27.**—“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf,” etc. (JEROME, *ibid.*) “In the morning he will eat the prey, and in the evening he will divide the food.” Although the prophecy most clearly concerns Paul, who in his youth persecuted the Church and in his old age became a preacher of the Gospel, etc., up to the priests who, serving the altar, live from the altar (1 Corinthians 9).

“Benjamin is a ravenous wolf,” etc. (ISIDORE.) Some of the teachers applied this to Jerusalem, etc., up to the point that he will then divide the food, understanding that the letter must be divided by the spirit, because “the letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3).

**VERSES 28–31.**—“All these are in the tribes,” etc. It is asked [Col. 0180C] why Jacob established as sons and heirs with equal honor all those whom he had begotten by free women and maidservants. It is because Christ likewise grants heavenly rewards with equal honor and glory to all who are joined to his body through faith. “For there is no distinction there whether one is Jew or Greek, barbarian or Scythian, slave or free, because Christ is all and in all.” He assumed the form of a slave and served both the free person and the slave, so that he might grant an equal gift to all. Whoever wins the Lord’s approval by faith is not darkened by any stain of carnal birth. Hence Joel 2 says: “I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.”

**VERSE 32.**—“And being gathered to his people,” etc. (STRABO.) It must be asked of what people this is said. There is no question concerning the fathers, for it is known that he was gathered to Abraham and Isaac; but a people is a multitude [Col. 0180D]. Those men, however, were too few to be called a people. We must therefore understand this also as referring to the angels, to whose fellowship the saints are added when they pass from the world. Hence Hebrews 12 says: “You have approached Mount Zion and the heavenly Jerusalem and the gathering of angels,” etc.

## CHAPTER 50

**VERSES 1–3.**—“When Joseph saw this, he fell ... forty days passed.” (STRABO.) This number is appropriate to penitence and humility. Hence it was observed in the law and in the Gospel by the prophets and by the Lord himself.

(AUGUSTINE.) [Col. 0181A] The forty days of burial mentioned by Scripture perhaps signify penitence, by which sins are buried. For the forty days of fasting were not established without reason: Moses, Elijah, and the Lord himself fasted for that number of days, and the Church calls its principal observance of fasting the Forty-Day Fast. Hence Jonah says concerning the Ninevites: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah 3). Through those days, which are especially suited to the humiliation of penitents, they are understood to have mourned their sins in fasting and obtained mercy.

Nor is this number suited only to the grief of penitents. For the Lord was with his disciples for forty days after the resurrection, coming and going, eating and drinking; those were days of joy. Nor should we think that the Seventy Translators were in error when they said: “Three days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown.” For, [Col. 0181B] endowed with greater authority than belongs to the office of translators, they set down “three days” through the prophetic Spirit. They are said to have agreed with one voice in their translations—a great miracle—even though they knew that “forty days” was read in Hebrew. They understood that sins were dissolved and abolished in Christ’s glorification, “who was delivered up for our offenses and rose for our justification.”

The Lord’s glorification is recognized in his resurrection and ascension. Hence here, although he gave one and the same Spirit, he gave it first after he rose and second after he ascended. Because he rose after three days but ascended after forty days, the Hebrews signify by the number forty the one event [Col. 0181C] that happened later; the Seventy mention the other event, the three days, which pertains to the same matter—not through the servitude of translation but through the authority of prophecy. Let us not therefore say that one of these is false or quarrel over one translator against another. Those who translate from Hebrew prove that what they translate is written, while the authority of the Seventy, commended by so great a divinely wrought miracle, is confirmed by such ancient standing in the Churches.

“Seventy days.” (STRABO.) The pagans mourned their dead for nine days. Hence the ninth day was called the *novendial*, when they were buried. Worshipers of God held funeral rites for seven days. Thus Sirach 22 says: “The mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but the mourning of a fool lasts all the days of his life.” The number seven signifies rest. Hence the seventh day is called the Sabbath, that is, rest [Col. 0181D]. They therefore observe the seventh day for the dead, wishing them to rest with the Lord from the labors of the present life.

Hence it is said: “Egypt mourned him for seventy days,” which is seven multiplied by ten. Seven times ten is seventy. It may also be said that, just as the third day is observed by the faithful for the dead so that the soul, which has a threefold nature, may rest, so the seventh day is observed so that the soul may be reconciled to the body, since it sinned through the body’s enticement. Within the number seven there are also three and four: three pertains to the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible, and rational; four pertains to the body, which consists of four elements [Col. 0182A].

**VERSES 4–21.**—“When the time of mourning was completed,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Joseph commanded the powerful men of Egypt to say to Pharaoh in his name: “My father made me swear, saying: In the tomb that I made for myself in the land of Canaan, there you shall bury me.” It is asked how this can be true, since these words of his father do not appear in the account of his burial. The words must be referred to the meaning, just as other words above were similarly repeated. Words ought to serve the expression and communication of the will. Jacob is nowhere previously said to have dug a tomb for himself; but certainly, unless he had dug one, it would not have been said in this manner.

**[Col. 0182B] VERSE 10.**—“And they came to the threshing floor of Atad,” etc. This place is beyond the Jordan and is seventy thousand paces from Hebron. They therefore passed beyond the place where they were supposed to bury him and, after crossing the Jordan, returned to the place of the double cave. It may therefore be asked why they did this. Someone might say that they feared wars, just as the children of Israel were led around through the desert for forty years until, after crossing the Jordan, they came to the Promised Land. But this was done for a more significant reason. In the place called the threshing floor of Atad, a multitude of the children of Israel was later consumed by divine fire after murmuring against the Lord. Thus it was not Jacob’s death so much as the future ruin of the people that was mourned with such grief.

**VERSES 22–23.**—“And he lived one hundred and ten years.” [Col. 0182C] (AUGUSTINE, *On Genesis*, book 3.) Since Scripture says that Joseph saw these sons of sons, or grandsons, during his lifetime, how does it include them among the sixty-five persons with whom Jacob is said to have entered Egypt, etc., up to the point concerning what was propagated during his lifetime through the one by whom it came about that he entered?

**VERSE 24.**—“Carry away my bones,” etc. (STRABO.) Joseph, like his father, desired the Promised Land with all his heart and detested residence in Egypt. He also instructs us morally that, as long as we are in this world, we should always desire the Promised Land—that is, the land of the living—and wish to rest there. This is rightly accomplished if we imitate Joseph’s number of years in our conduct. He died after completing one hundred and ten years of life. Let us likewise strive, through observance of the Decalogue, to reach eternal blessedness, which the number one hundred signifies [Col. 0182D].

**VERSE 25.**—“Embalmed with spices.” (STRABO.) Blessed is the soul which, seasoned with the spices of virtues and dwelling in the little chamber of the body, is reserved for eternal life by daily progress. If it has been guarded in faith, hope, and charity, it will deserve through Christ’s grace to reach the vision of divine contemplation, whose perfect adoption is joy. Hence Psalm 15 says: “You will fill me with joy in your presence.”

**[Col. 0183]**

# THE BOOK OF EXODUS

In Hebrew, *Veelle Semoth* (), that is, “These are the names”; in Greek, *Exodos* (ΕΞΟΔΟΣ), that is, “Exit.” (G)*

## PREFATORY MATERIAL ON EXODUS

**[Col. 0183A]**

(RABANUS.) Among the books of the Pentateuch, Exodus is outstanding, for in it nearly all the mysteries by which the Church is instructed are expressed figuratively. The bodily departure of the children of Israel from Egypt signifies our bodily departure from spiritual Egypt. The Red Sea, the drowning of Pharaoh and the Egyptians, signify the mystery of baptism and the destruction of spiritual enemies. The sacrifice of the typological lamb and the liberation of the Hebrews signify the passion of the true Lamb and our redemption. Manna is given from heaven, and water from the rock. This is the bread that descended from heaven (John 6), and the teaching of Christ.

On the mountain, commandments and judgments are given to the people of God, so that we may be subjected to heavenly disciplines [Col. 0183B]. The tabernacle and its vessels are constructed, and worship and sacrifices are commanded; these signify the adornment of the Church and spiritual sacrifices. Mystical anointing and incense are prepared, by which the sanctification of the spirit and the perfumes of prayer are commended. Hence Paul says: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink,” etc.

(1 Corinthians 10.) Hence also John says: “These things happened,” he says, “so that Scripture might be fulfilled: You shall not break a bone of it” (John 19).

(BEDE.) *Veelle Semoth* () in Hebrew; *exodos* (ἔξοδος) in Greek; in Latin, “exodus,” “departure,” or “going out.”

## CHAPTER ONE

**VERSE 5.**—“So all the persons who [Col. 0183C] came forth from Jacob’s thigh were seventy,” etc. The seventy persons—that is, the seventy disciples—enter Egypt with Jacob, that is, with Christ, sent to preach. Alternatively, the seventy persons who entered Egypt are mystically understood according to the number of remission, so that forgiveness of sins may be granted to this age, which is represented by Egypt, after so many sins.

**VERSES 6–7.**—“When he had died,” etc. (ISIDORE, *On Exodus*.) Thus, after the true Joseph tasted death for all and destroyed the one who held the power of death, the people of the faithful multiplied. For unless the grain of wheat had died in the earth, it would have remained alone.

(ORIGEN, *Homily 1 on Exodus*.) If Joseph dies in you [Col. 0183D]—that is, if you receive Christ’s mortification in yourself and put your members to death with respect to sin—the children of Israel are multiplied in you, namely, good and spiritual thoughts. For if the thoughts of the flesh are put to death, the thoughts of the soul increase; when vices die in you, virtues grow; and the earth multiplies in good works, which are performed through the service of the body.

The earth had multiplied Paul, who said: “To remain in the flesh is more necessary for your sake.” While he remains on earth—that is, in his flesh—the Church is multiplied by believing, acquiring a people for God, and preaching the Gospel from Jerusalem as far as Illyricum [Col. 0184A].

**VERSES 8–10.**—“Meanwhile a new king arose over Egypt,” etc. (ORIGEN.) Allegorically, this is the devil, who said in his heart, “There is no God.” To his own people—that is, to the apostate angels—he says: “Behold, the people of the children of Israel,” namely, those who can see God with the mind, “are more powerful than we are. Come, let us wisely oppress them.”

The devil perceives that the people of Israel are great and stronger than he is, because he has often engaged them and has often been defeated. He knows that Jacob wrestled and, with the angel’s help, prevailed against his adversary and prevailed with God. He has also experienced the struggles of other saints and endured spiritual conflicts. He fears that war may someday arise, that they may join his adversaries, defeat them [or, after he has been defeated], and depart from his land [Col. 0184B].

It seems to me that, from the things indicated to the patriarchs and prophets concerning Christ’s coming, he senses that the one who will strip him of his principalities and powers is coming, triumph over them confidently, and afflict them upon the wood of the cross.

(RABANUS, *On Exodus*, book 2.) In the *Chronicles* of Eusebius and Jerome we read, etc., up to the statement that many Pharaohs existed and that one perished in the Red Sea.

## (ORIG. Homily 1)

**Moral interpretation.** First I wish to ask who the king in Egypt is who knows Joseph, and who does not know him. While the one who knew Joseph was reigning, the children of Israel are not said to have been afflicted, nor consumed in mud and brick; neither are their males killed and their females kept alive. But this began when the one who did not know Joseph began to reign.

If the Lord governs us, and the understanding of our mind or soul is illuminated by God, remembering that Christ rose from the dead, then in Egypt—that is, in our flesh—our spirit holds sovereignty with justice, and does not consume the children of Israel, that is, rational understandings or virtues, in mud and brick, nor wear them down with earthly cares. But if our understanding loses the memory of these things and no longer knows Christ, then the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God, succeeds to the kingdom. It addresses its own people—that is, bodily pleasures—and, having summoned the leaders of the vices for consultation, deliberates against the children of Israel: how they may be surrounded and oppressed, [Col. 0184D] crushed with mud and afflicted with brick; how they may expose the males and nourish the females; how the Egyptians may build cities and fortified cities.

Nor should we think that the divine books recount the deeds of the Egyptians without reason. Rather, “whatever was written was written for our instruction” (Rom. 15), so that if you hear these things—if perhaps you have been baptized and numbered among the children of Israel, and have received the Lord as king within you, and afterward wish to turn aside and perform the works [Col. 0185A] of the world, carrying out the tasks of the earth and fulfilling services of mud—you may know that another king has risen up within you, one who does not know Joseph, the king of Egypt. He compels you to his works, to work brick and mud. He places overseers and taskmasters over you, drives you with whips to earthly labors, and makes you build cities for him. He makes you roam through the world, disturbing the elements of sea and land according to desire; he makes you beat upon the marketplace with lawsuits and weary relatives with quarrels over a small patch of earth; he makes you plot against chastity, deceive innocence, commit disgraceful acts at home, cruel acts abroad, and shameful acts within your conscience. Know that in such things you serve the king of Egypt: that is, you are driven by the spirit of this world.

## Verses 11–13

“Therefore he set over them,” etc.

**(ORIG.)** The devil, having summoned his people, wishes to oppress the rational understanding, which is now figuratively called Israel. He appoints overseers of works who compel them to learn the works of the flesh, according to the Psalm: “They mingled with the nations and learned their works” (Ps. 105).

He teaches them to build cities for Pharaoh: Pithom, which means “mouth of defection,” or “of the abyss”; and Rameses, which is “the movement of the moth”; and On, that is, Heliopolis, which is called “the city of the sun.” The mouth fails when it speaks falsehood rather than truth and proofs. He was a liar from the beginning, and therefore wishes such cities to be built for him: the mouth of the abyss, because the abyss is the place of his destruction; another of his cities is the movement of the moth, for whoever follows him stores up treasure where “moth destroys and thieves break in and steal” (Matt. 6). He also builds the City of the Sun, falsely transforming himself into an angel of light. In these things he occupies minds that were made to see God.

Yet he perceives that wars are threatening him and that the destruction of his people is approaching. Therefore he says, “The people of Israel are stronger than we are”—as if to say, “Would that we too might find ourselves stronger than they”: namely, that I should not receive the thoughts and evil desires he casts into me, but repel his burning arrows with the shield of faith; and in everything he suggests, say: “Get behind me, Satan; for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matt. 4).

But also in what he says—“Lest war should befall us, and they join themselves to our adversaries”—he foresees from the prophetic utterances that war will come upon him, that he will be abandoned by the children of Israel, that they will consent to his adversary and be added [Col. 0185D] to the Lord. This is what Jeremiah says (chap. 17): “The partridge cried out; it gathered what it did not hatch; it made riches, and not by judgment. In the middle of its days they will abandon it, and at its end it will be a fool.”

Thus he understands that he is the partridge that gathered what it did not hatch, and that those whom he gathered without judgment will abandon him and follow Christ, who gave them birth. He himself will remain a fool when every creature flees to its maker and parent. Therefore he is indignant, saying: “Lest they overcome us and depart from our land.”

He does not want us to leave his land, so that we may always bear the image of the earthly, lest, abandoning him, we flee to the one who prepared the kingdom of heaven, leaving behind the image of the earthly and receiving the image of the heavenly. Therefore he appoints overseers of works to teach their arts [Col. 0186A] and make us craftsmen of wickedness.

And because there are many teachers of wickedness whom Pharaoh has appointed—men who command, demand, and extort earthly works—therefore, when Christ came, he raised up other teachers to fight against them. These teachers subdue all their principalities, powers, and virtues; defend the children of Israel from violence; teach Israelite works and how to see God with the mind; teach them to abandon Pharaoh’s works, leave the land of Egypt, strip off Egyptian ways and the entire old man with his deeds, and put on the new man, who was created according to God.

**(ISID.)** Israel signifies the Christian people; Pharaoh signifies the devil, who imposes the heaviest yoke of mud and brick—that is, slavery to earthly and muddy work—mixed with straw, that is, light and irrational deeds, so that, with all oppressed under the burden of sins, no one may be found who destroys or conquers his kingdom.

## Verse 15

“Then the king of Egypt said to the midwives,” etc.

**(ORIG., Homily 2.)** We find these things not only in the world, which is spiritually called Egypt, but also in each one of us. The prince of this world does not want the males to be kept alive, but the females. In the female, flesh and the affection of the flesh are signified; the male, however, is the rational understanding, and the intellectual spirit, which can grasp heavenly things, understand God, and seek the things that are above.

The prince of Egypt hates this and wishes it killed. But he wants the things of the flesh to live, and those that pertain to bodily matter not merely to live but also to increase and be cultivated. He wants all to think according to the flesh, to seek temporal things and what is upon the earth; no one should raise his eyes to heaven, no one should ask from where he has come, and no one should remember his homeland, paradise.

When, therefore, you see people leading their lives in pleasures, floating in luxury, devoting themselves to banquets and shamelessness, know that in them the king of Egypt kills the males and keeps the females alive. But if one out of a thousand turns to God, raises his eyes upward, seeks eternal things, hates pleasures and luxury, and loves self-restraint, Pharaoh wants that person killed as a male. He persecutes him and attacks him with a thousand devices; he hates such people and does not allow them to live in Egypt. Hence it is that in this world the servants of God are held in contempt and exposed to insults; hence hatreds and persecutions are stirred up against them.

### “To the midwives”

**(ORIG., ibid.)** He also tries to corrupt these midwives. One of them was called Shiphrah, that is, “sparrow”; the other Puah, meaning “reddish” or “modest.” Through them he seeks to kill the males and keep the females alive. But the midwives feared God and did not do as he had commanded them.

The midwives taught us beforehand to maintain a certain form of rational instruction. For midwives are physicians, and they care for and nourish both male and female infants at birth. Common education, therefore, is rational knowledge, and reaches almost every understanding; it instructs and nourishes all. If someone possesses a manly spirit within it and wishes to seek heavenly things and pursue divine things, then, as one healed and strengthened, he will come through these forms of instruction more prepared for understanding divine matters.

One of them, like a sparrow, teaches higher things and, on the wings of rational doctrine, summons us upward. [Col. 0187A] The other, “reddish” or “modest,” is moral instruction: it orders one’s conduct, teaches modesty, and teaches honor.

Yet for my part—since Scripture says of them that they feared God and did not act according to the command of the king of Egypt—I think that they preserve a figure of both Testaments. Shiphrah, whose name is interpreted “sparrow,” is suited to the Law, which is spiritual; Puah, “reddish” or “modest,” indicates the Gospels, which are red with the blood of Christ and shine throughout the world with the radiance of his passion.

By these midwives, therefore, souls that are born in the Church are, as it were, healed and assisted, because every medicine of instruction is supplied from the Scriptures. Yet Pharaoh attempts through them to kill the males when he suggests heresies and perverse doctrines to those who study the divine Scriptures.

But the foundation of God stands immovable. [Col. 0187B] The midwives fear God—that is, they teach the fear of God, which is the beginning of wisdom. Thus what follows is fitted together more appropriately: “Because the midwives feared God, they made houses for themselves.” Taken literally, this has no connection; a house is not made simply because God is feared. But if you see how the Scriptures of the New and Old Testaments, by teaching the fear of God, build houses for the Church and fill the entire world with houses of prayer, the statement will appear rationally written.

Thus these midwives, because they fear God—that is, because they teach the fear of God—do not obey the command of the king of Egypt, but keep the males alive. Yet it is not said that they obeyed by keeping the females alive. I say confidently that they do not keep the females alive. For neither are vices or luxury taught in the Church, nor are sins nourished. This is what Pharaoh desires when he orders the females to be kept alive; only virtue is cultivated and nourished.

Let us apply these things to each individual. If you fear God, do not obey the command of the king of Egypt. He commands you to live in pleasures and desire present things. But you, if you fear God and perform the office of a midwife, if you wish to contribute something to your soul, keep the males alive—that is, heal and nourish the inner person who is within you—and through good actions and understandings acquire eternal life.

## Verses 16–21

“If it is a male,” etc.

**(ISID.) Allegorical interpretation.** Pharaoh commands that the males be killed and the females kept alive. So too the devil, lest the strength of faith prevail, wants the vices to live after the virtues have been killed. He strives to kill the strong and manly understandings of the soul by which we taste divine things—that is, reason, prudence, steadfastness, innocence, and faith. Whatever is feminine, weak, fragile, and prone to vices, he wants to survive: ambition, violence, lust, anger, and similar things, which are represented by the female.

## Verse 19

“They answered,” etc.

**(AUG., On Genesis, vol. III.)** The question is whether such lies were approved by divine authority, etc., up to the point where he says that those whose conduct is already in heaven should not, in his judgment, take from the example of the midwives a rule concerning the manner in which they ought to speak about truth and falsehood.

**(GREG., Morals, book XXXVIII, chapters 2–3.)** Lies must be avoided with the greatest care, etc., up to the point where he says that, by sparing them, they tried to preserve the infants’ lives, and by lying, their own.

**(AUG., On the Book of Expressions in Exodus, vol. III.)** “And because the midwives feared God,” etc., up to the point where he says that this seems to refer to the building of that very house, concerning which Laban subsequently proposes that wages be established.

## Verse 22

“Therefore Pharaoh commanded,” etc.

**(ORIG., Homily 2.)** The Egyptians, whom Pharaoh here commanded to keep only the females alive, hated the males. For they hated virtues and nourished vices. Even now the Egyptians lie in wait, in case a male should be born to the Hebrews, so that they may kill him immediately—unless they take care, watch, and conceal him.

Scripture relates that a man from the tribe of Levi fathered a male child, saw that the infant was beautiful, and concealed him. Therefore let us not perform our righteousness before human beings, but, with the door closed, let us pray to our Father in secret; and let the left hand not know what the right hand is doing, lest the Egyptians seize it, attack it, and drown it in the waves.

If I give alms because it is a work of God, I beget a male. But if I seek praise from human beings and do not conceal it, it is seized by the Egyptians and plunged into the river. With such labor and such effort I have begotten a male for the Egyptians.

### “Whatever is feminine”

**(HIERON., On Ecclesiastes, chapter 3.)** Wherever a female is mentioned in Scripture, and the weaker sex, let us transfer the meaning to matter. Hence Pharaoh does not want males to be born, but females, which are close to matter. Conversely, hardly any saint is said to have fathered females, except very rarely. Only Zelophehad, who died in his sins, fathered only daughters. Jacob was the father of one daughter, and because of her he was put in danger.

# Chapter II

## Verses 1–5

“He went out,” etc.

**(RAB.)** Josephus says here: “But Amram, fearing that he might succumb if seized by the king’s anger,” etc., up to the words “whether to bring out,” as Moses was brought out from the river.

**Allegorical interpretation.** The parents of Moses, whose faith and works were adorned by the natural law **(ID., ibid.)**, etc., up to the point where it is also taught to blush at worshiping idols.

**“A man from the house,” etc. (DIOD.)** The father of Moses is not mentioned without a providential reason: Christ too, whose type Moses bore, is without a father.

## Verse 2

“And seeing,” etc.

**(CHRYSOST., Homily 54 on the Acts of the Apostles.)** It is remarkable that everything is done for us not through what appears to promise security, but plainly through its opposite. Pharaoh commanded that the boys be thrown into the river. If the boys had not been thrown in, Moses would not have been saved. When he was being saved, he was not honored; when he was exposed, then he was honored. A Jew threatened him, saying, “Do you intend to kill me?” And this benefited him, so that he might practice philosophy in solitude and live in safety.

**(ORIG., Homily 2.) Allegorical interpretation.** Pharaoh’s daughter is the Church gathered from the nations, to whom the prophet says: “Forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty” (Ps. 44). [Col. 0189A] She, therefore, is the one who went out from her father’s house and came to the waters to be washed from the sins she had contracted in her father’s house. Immediately she received a compassionate heart and had pity on the infant.

When she came to the marsh, she found Moses lying there, exposed by his own people, and had him nourished. He is nourished among his own people and spends his infancy there. When he has grown stronger, he is brought to her and adopted as a son.

Moses signifies the Law. When the Church comes to the waters of baptism, therefore, she receives the Law enclosed within a basket and coated with bitumen. The basket is a kind of covering woven from papyrus and formed with reeds or from the bark of trees. The Law lay enclosed in such a covering, coated with pitch and bitumen—that is, with the cheap and sordid interpretations of the Jews. It remained obscure and neglected until the Church came from the nations and took it from muddy and marshy places into the halls of wisdom and royal dwellings.

Yet it spends its infancy among its own people. Among those who do not understand it spiritually, it is small and infantile, possessing the food of nursing infants. When it comes to the Church, Moses is stronger and more powerful; for when the veil of the letter has been removed, perfect nourishment is found in its reading.

He receives payment for his nourishment from Pharaoh’s daughter, with whom the Law is born and nourished. But what payment does the Synagogue receive from the Church? I think it is what Moses says: “I will provoke you to jealousy by those who are not a nation; by an ignorant nation I will anger you.” The Synagogue therefore receives this payment from the Church: that it no longer worship idols. For when it sees the nations turned to God so that they no longer know idols, it is ashamed to continue [Col. 0189C] worshiping idols.

We too, if we had Pharaoh as our father, if he begot us in evil works, when we come to the waters should take up the Law of God. Let the letters not seem sordid to us, like a dark covering. Let us eat what is small and infantile in it; let us take what is perfect and gather it within the royal chambers of the heart.

We have a great and powerful Moses. Let us think nothing small or worthless concerning him, but everything magnificent, everything excellent, everything beautiful. For everything spiritual, and everything belonging to sublime understanding, is great.

## Verses 6–8

“And seeing the child in it,” etc.

**(THEOD.) Mystical interpretation.** Circumcision could chiefly have revealed this to her, for the Egyptians had not yet admitted such a mystery, although in time to come they would observe the law of circumcision in imitation of the Hebrews. Hence Jeremiah says: “I will consider all who circumcise the foreskin: Egyptians and the sons of Edom” (Jer. 9).

**(ISID.)** Moses—that is, Christ—is found by the faithful at the river of the washing and the water of baptism, etc., up to the point where they receive and protect him with religious observance.

## Verses 9–11

“And she handed over the grown child,” etc.

**(RAB.)** Josephus relates that Pharaoh’s daughter brought the grown Moses to her father, who placed his crown upon him. Moses immediately threw it down because he saw an image carved upon it. Therefore the priest who was present there wanted to kill him, saying that Egypt would be overthrown through him, as he had learned from the oracle of demons. [Col. 0190A] But Pharaoh’s daughter rescued him.

When he had reached maturity, Pharaoh sent him against the Ethiopians. Since he knew that he would travel through deserts full of serpents, he took ibises—that is, Egyptian storks—and, having marked out the camp, brought them forward so that they would devour and drive away the serpents. Thus the army spent the night safely.

When he came to the city he was about to besiege, the Ethiopian queen fell in love with him and, according to their agreement, handed the city over to him and married him. This is why Aaron and Miriam quarreled against Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman as his wife.

## Verse 12

“And when he had looked this way and that,” etc.

**(AUG., Questions on Exodus.)** We discussed this deed of Moses at sufficient length in the work we wrote against Faustus on the life of the patriarchs: whether the disposition in him by which he committed this sin was praiseworthy, just as rich soil, before it bears useful seed, is praised for a certain luxuriance of useless vegetation; or whether the deed itself should be justified.

The latter does not seem possible, because he did not yet possess any legitimate authority, either divinely received or ordered by human society. Yet, as Stephen says in the Acts of the Apostles, he thought that his brothers understood that God was giving them salvation through him. By this testimony Moses appears to have been divinely warned already—although Scripture is silent about it at that point—and thus able to dare this act.

**(ISID.) Allegorical interpretation.** Moses, that is, Christ, kills the Egyptian—that is, the devil, who wrongs us in this pilgrimage—by defending us, and buries the slain man in the sand. For he lies hidden among those who do not possess a stable foundation.

But he builds the Church upon a rock and compares those who hear and do his word to a wise man who built his house upon solid rock. Others he compares to a foolish man who builds upon sand.

## Verse 13

“And going out the next day,” etc.

In this Moses bore the figure of Christ, who sought to reconcile the discord of two peoples in himself as the cornerstone. The one who committed the wrong and despised the reconciler is the Jew, who rejected the preaching of Christ the reconciler and remained an enemy of the believing people. Hence John 9: “You are his disciple; we are disciples of Moses.”

## Verses 14–21

“Moses was afraid,” etc.

**(AUG.)** “If this word has been spread abroad”—there are two things to attend to in this expression: first, that the sentence is suspended and then completed with “so”; and second, that the word is used in place of the deed.

## Verse 22

“She gave birth,” etc.

**Allegorical interpretation.** Christ joined to himself the Church from the nations, which, through the gift of the sevenfold Spirit, is one in the Catholic faith. Hence: “My dove is one.” She gives birth to a son who is called “sojourner,” and another who is called “the help of God.” For the saints are sojourners upon the earth, but they never lack the help of God.

## Verses 23–25

“After a long time,” etc.

After Moses had taken a wife in the land of Midian, the king of Egypt died. This means that when Christ converted the nations to the faith throughout the world, the principality of the devil was destroyed.

### “Groaning”

Unless the king of Egypt dies within you, you will not recognize that you are oppressed by the slavery of Egypt and by works of mud and brick. You will neither groan in your heart nor cry out to the Lord to free you.

# Chapter III

## Verses 2–3

“And he appeared to him,” etc.

**(ISID.) Allegorical interpretation.** There was a flame in the bush, and it was not consumed.
