The bush signifies the thorns of the sins of the Jews; the flame in the bush is the word of God, that is, the Law given to that people. Yet the flame does not consume the bush because the Law given to them does not consume their sins.

Others understand the burning bush as the Church, which is inflamed by persecutions but is not consumed when the Lord speaks to it. The fact that the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush shows that he appears to the faithful in the Church, and nowhere else.

The Hebrews say that God appeared to Moses in the bush so that the Jews would not be able to carve an idol for themselves from it. God always cuts off the occasion of idolatry.

**(GREG., Morals, book XXII, chapter 20.)** Moses, mingling with the Egyptians, was as though awake to the world and therefore did not hear the voice of the Lord. But after he killed the Egyptian and fled into the desert, where he spent forty years, he fell asleep to earthly tumult and therefore perceived the divine voice.

For when the mind is lulled to sleep concerning external things, the word of God penetrates more truly. The tumult of earthly thoughts resounding within closes the ear of the heart. A person divided between the two cannot adequately attend to both: when he opens his hearing outwardly, he becomes deaf inwardly.

## Verse 4

“And when the Lord saw,” etc.

**(GREG., Preface to the Morals, chapter 2.)** The angel who is described as having appeared to Moses is sometimes called “Lord” and sometimes “angel”: angel because he serves by speaking outwardly; Lord because, presiding inwardly, he grants effectiveness to the speech. When the speaker is governed from within, he is called both angel by reason of his service and Lord by reason of his inspiration.

### “He called him from the midst,” etc.

**(GREG., Morals, book XXVIII, chapter 5.)** God often speaks through angels simultaneously to earthly and heavenly substances, as here when he joined fire and the bush, connecting one above with the other below. This occurs only when something great is signified by the conjunction.

For, speaking to Moses through the burning bush, he showed that Moses would become a teacher of the people who would receive the flame of the Law but would not avoid the thorn of sin. Thus one would come forth from that people who, through the fire of divinity, would receive the sins of our flesh as the thorn of the bush and preserve the unconsumed substance of humanity within that same flame of divinity.

## Verses 5–7

“Remove your sandal,” etc.

**(THEOD.)** He orders him to remove his sandals for two reasons. First, to make him more and more religious and reverent, so that he might receive his commands with trembling. Then he also teaches him the manner in which priests minister in the tabernacle of God, for they performed their priestly service barefoot.

**(ISID.)** No one can stand worthily or see God unless he lays aside all earthly and mortal things. Alternatively, it was the custom of the ancients that if a bridegroom repudiated his bride, he removed his sandal as a sign of repudiation. Therefore Moses is ordered to remove his sandals, and not to approach the Church, which is signified by the bush, as a bridegroom wearing sandals. This is to be reserved for Christ, who is the true bridegroom. Concerning him John says: “I am not worthy to loosen the strap of his sandal” (John 1).

## Verse 6

“I am the God,” etc.

**(HILAR., book IV, On the Trinity.)** We must speak about God only in the manner in which he himself has spoken about himself for our understanding. It is the angel of God who appeared in the fire from the bush, and God speaks from the bush in the fire. You have a divine dispensation in the angel, because in the angel there is an office, not a nature. You have God in the name of nature, because the angel of God is God.

## Verse 7

“I have seen the affliction,” etc.

**(GREG., Morals.)** When minds are scattered outwardly, it is difficult for each person to return to himself, because once captured, crooked paths hold them with all the greater pleasure precisely because what one desires is not permitted. When the duty of discipline does not intervene, no punishment of retribution is foreseen to inspire fear.

With the eyes of the heart closed, the soul is hurled downward, and it penetrates temporal evils all the more securely because it despairs more harshly of eternal goods.

Yet this wickedness of the reprobate separates the life of the elect from them like grain from chaff, and while it afflicts, it sets free. For while it inflicts violence, it compels them to hasten toward heavenly things. This is signified in the people of Israel, with Moses calling and Pharaoh raging.

Moses was sent to call them, while Pharaoh pressed them with harsh works, so that one might draw them by calling and another drive them by rage, and the people, shamefully fixed in slavery, might be moved either by being called or by being driven. The same thing happens daily when the reprobate are permitted to rage against the elect while heavenly rewards are preached, so that Egypt—that is, the present life—which oppressed them by flattering them, may help them by pressing them; so that while God summons them, suffering may drive them onward.

## Verses 8–13

“And I will lead them out of the land,” etc.

**(GREG., Homily 32.)** Something had to be promised to an inexperienced people from the present life, so that they might be strengthened more firmly in the future. For if they did not receive small things, they would not believe great things. Thus God, by granting earthly things, persuades them of heavenly things, so that, receiving what they saw, they might hope for what they did not see.

### “Into a good and spacious land, into a land flowing with milk,” etc.

**(Ibid.)** Present prosperity is sometimes given to summon people to a better life, and sometimes to condemn them more fully forever. Hence the land of Canaan is promised to the Israelites, so that they might at some point be summoned to hope for eternal things. An inexperienced people would not believe promises unless it received something nearby from the one who promised.

Therefore we are drawn not only to things by hope, but sometimes to hope by things. Hence Psalm 104: “He gave them the lands of the nations, and they possessed the labor of the peoples, that they might keep his ordinances and seek his law.”

## Verses 14–16

“He who is has sent me to you,” etc.

Moses is sent to punish Pharaoh and ultimately to kill him; the Law was sent to destroy the devil.

Jerome, writing to Marcella about the ten names of God, places in sixth position the name *ehieh* (), which is read in Exodus: “He who is has sent me to you.” God alone, who has no beginning, possesses the name of true essence. This name was spoken through the angel to Moses when he asked for God’s name, because in comparison with the one who truly is, since he is immutable, mutable things are as though they are not. For what is said to have been is not; and what is said to be will be is not yet. God alone is he who does not know having been or being destined to be. The Father, together with the Son and the Holy Spirit, alone truly is. Compared with his essence, our being is not. Hence we say, “God lives,” because divine essence lives as life, which death does not possess.

## Verses 17–20

“To a land flowing with milk and honey,” etc.

**(AUG., Questions 4 on Exodus.)** Should we understand this spiritually, since according to the literal meaning this was not the land that was given to the Hebrews? Or is it a manner of speaking by which the fertility and sweetness of the land are praised?

## Verse 21

“You shall not go out,” etc.

**(AUG., ibid.)** The Lord commanded the Hebrews to receive from the Egyptians vessels of silver and gold and clothing, and added, “You shall plunder them.” No unjust judgment can be made concerning this command. It is God’s command, and it was not to be judged but obeyed. He himself knows how justly he commanded; it is the servant’s responsibility obediently to do what he commanded.

## Verse 22

“Silver vessels”

We ask silver and gold from the Egyptians, from which we may construct a tabernacle for God, when we read poets and philosophers so that we may expound divine Scripture more wisely and eloquently.

# Chapter IV

## Verses 2–5

“What is it that,” etc.

**(GREG.)** Moses signifies the Jewish people; the staff, the power of divinity; the serpent, the mortality of Christ, because death is signified through the serpent and mortality through the serpent.

Or because it is written in Matthew 10, “Be wise as serpents,” and because supreme wisdom—that is, the wisdom of God—was incarnate, his mortality is rightly represented by the serpent. Hence John 4: “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up.”

Moses held the staff because the Jewish people, before the coming of the Redeemer, trusted in the power of God. He threw it upon the ground because, through the patriarchs and prophets, he announced that God would become incarnate. The staff is changed into a serpent because Christ, remaining God in himself, became mortal in man.

Moses was terrified when he saw the serpent and fled, because the Jewish people, when it saw Christ as mortal, was afraid to believe him God. He is commanded to grasp its tail because the people that now refuses to believe will gather itself to faith in the final part of the Lord’s body—that is, at the later time of the Church, at the end of the world. It grasps the serpent’s tail because, at the final stage of the Church, it will confess as its Redeemer the one whom it had previously despised as mortal.

Immediately the serpent returns to a staff, because when the Jewish people believes in Christ, he will immediately appear for judgment in the power of his divinity. Thus the serpent becomes a staff, because the one who was despised on earth as a man will be seen coming from heaven as God above the angels.

**(ISID.)** The serpent persuaded the human being to die. Death, therefore, comes from the serpent; the staff in the serpent signifies Christ in death. Moses was terrified and fled, because when Christ died the disciples were terrified and withdrew from the hope in which they had stood.

He grasped the tail, that is, the later part, and it became a staff, because after first being killed, and after all things had been accomplished, Christ returned through resurrection to what he had been. Once death had been consumed through life, nothing of the serpent appeared in him.

Alternatively, the serpent’s tail is the end of the world, because the mortality of the Church rolls through slippery times. Some depart and others come through death, as through the serpent through which death was sown. But at the end of the world, like the tail, we return to the hand of God; once grasped, we shall be restored, and when the final enemy, death, has been destroyed, we shall rise and be the staff of the kingdom in the right hand of God.

## Verses 6, 8

“Put your hand,” etc.

**(PROCOP.)** Some assert that this portent occurred to show that the Law was not imposed upon the righteous. Although afterward he establishes laws specifying how the disease of leprosy is to be examined and how someone is to be declared unclean, nevertheless most laws are enacted as though they were given to fools and infants. So greatly does God accommodate himself to our weakness!

**(ISID.)** The white hand signifies uncleanness, for whiteness of the skin is leprosy, not brightness. The inheritance of God itself—that is, the people—was sent out from him and became unclean. Hence Psalm 73: “Why do you turn away your hand and your right hand,” etc.

But the hand was called back into the bosom and returned to its own color. So the Jewish people, alienated from the bosom of God, remained unclean outside; but when called back, it will return to its former color when it recognizes the Savior. For “a hardening in part has happened to Israel” (Rom. 11).

## Verses 9–10

“Take water,” etc.

**(ISID.)** Water signifies the people. Hence Revelation 17: “The waters that you saw are peoples and nations.” The people, therefore, is changed into blood—that is, into faith in the blood of Christ.

## Verse 10

“Please, Lord,” etc.

**(AUG., Questions on Exodus.)** When Moses says to the Lord, “I beg you, Lord, I am not eloquent, neither from yesterday nor from the day before, nor since you began to speak to your servant,” this can be understood as believing that, by God’s will, he could suddenly become eloquent. When he says, “nor since you began to speak to your servant,” he seems to show that it could have happened that one who had not been eloquent before yesterday or the day before suddenly became eloquent from the moment the Lord began to speak with him.

(ORIGEN, Homily 3 on Exodus.) While Moses was in Egypt and was being educated in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, he was neither weak-voiced nor slow of tongue, nor did he profess himself ineloquent. For, in the judgment of the Egyptians, he had a sonorous voice and incomparable eloquence. But when he heard the voice of God and received the utterances of the Lord, he perceived his voice to be weak, thin, slow, and impeded, and he declared himself mute when he began to know the true Word who was in the beginning with God (John 1). For an uneducated human being will appear eloquent when compared with mute animals; but when compared with the educated and eloquent, he will seem foolish and mute. If, however, someone looks upon the word of God and divine wisdom as far more weighty than it is regarded among us, he will confess himself a mute animal before God. Hence Psalm 72: “I became like a beast before you.” Since, therefore, he advanced in understanding to the point of recognizing what he was—which is a great part of wisdom—divine condescension rewarded him, saying: “I will open your mouth,” etc. Blessed are those whose mouth God opens so that they may speak. Hence Psalm 80: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” Likewise Paul says to the Ephesians 6: “That speech may be given to me in the opening of my mouth.”

Therefore God opens the mouth of those who speak the truth; but of those who speak lies, give false testimony, utter buffooneries and obscenities, and of whisperers, slanderers, and those who speak idle words, the devil opens the mouth. It is reported of Judas in John 13 that Satan entered into him and put it into his heart to betray Jesus. He opened his mouth, therefore, so that he might speak with the Pharisees about how he would betray him after receiving the money. It is no small grace to distinguish the mouth that God opens from the mouth that the devil opens.

God also opens the ears of the saints to hear divine words; hence: “The Lord will open my ear.” He opens the eyes, as he opened Hagar’s eyes, and she saw a well of living water; hence Elisha: “Open, Lord, the eyes of your servant, that he may see, because there are more with us” (4 Kings 6). The ear, however, which is opened through the Lord’s instruction, is sometimes open and sometimes closed; hence: “Do not receive a vain report” (Ecclesiasticus 45). If vain, profane, or shameful things are being said, the person who knows the Lord’s instruction closes his ear and says: “But I, like a mute man, did not open my mouth, and like a deaf man I did not hear” (Psalm 37). If, however, what is said concerns the soul’s benefit—if the subject is God, if it teaches morals, invites to virtues, and cuts away vices—then let the ears and the whole gateway of the soul be opened.

It should be noted that the Law used the greatest moderation when it said: “You shall not receive a vain report.” It did not say, “You shall not hear,” but “You shall not receive.” For we often hear vain things: Marcion, Valentinus, and all those who argue against the Creator speak vainly. We often hear them, nevertheless, so that we may contradict them; but we do not receive what they say, because the devil opens their mouth. May the Lord deign to open our mouth, so that we may refute the one who contradicts and close the mouth that the devil opens.

**VERSE 11.**—“Who made the mouth of man?” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 8.) There are people who slander God—or rather, the Scripture of the Old Testament—because it says that God made a person mute. What, then, do they say about Christ, who plainly says in John 10: “I came so that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind”? Who, unless ignorant, would believe that something could happen to a person, in accordance with bodily defects, which God did not will? Yet no one doubts that he justly wills the whole of it.

**VERSES 12–13.**—“Go, therefore,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Allegorically. When the Lord says to Moses: “But now go, and I will open your mouth and instruct you in what you shall speak,” it is evident that not only the instruction of the mouth but also the very opening of it belongs to God’s grace. For he does not say, “Open your mouth, and I will instruct you”; rather, he promises both: “I will open it, and I will instruct it.” In Psalm 80, however: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it.” There he signifies in a human being the will to receive what God gives to the willing, so that “Open your mouth” belongs to the beginning of the will, while “I will fill it” belongs to God’s grace.

**VERSE 14.**—“The Lord was angry with Moses and said,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 10.) He seems, as though Moses were distrustful, not to have given him the fullest capacity, etc., up to the point where Moses represents the figure of a mediator between God and Aaron, and Aaron between Moses and the people.

**VERSES 15–18.**—“And I will be in your mouth and in his mouth,” etc. (ORIGEN.) It is promised not only that Moses’ mouth will be opened by the Lord, but also Aaron’s. For it is said: “I will open your mouth and his mouth, and I will instruct you in what you are to do.”

**VERSE 19.**—“Then the Lord said,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Expositions on Genesis, volume 3.) “After many days the king of Egypt died. The Lord said to Moses in Midian: ‘Go, return to Egypt,’” etc. Several kinds of expression must be noted in these words. First he says: “Go, return to Egypt,” as though one of the two expressions were not sufficient. Then he says: “All those who sought your life have died,” although Scripture said only that the king of Egypt had died; and earlier it had been said only of him that he sought to kill Moses. Or did he die last, after the other enemies? If this is so, then the matter concerns not the wording but the sense.

**VERSE 20.**—“Therefore Moses took,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 12.) It is said that Moses placed his wife and children upon a vehicle so that he might go to Egypt; but afterward his father-in-law Jethro met him there with them, after he had brought the people out of Egypt. It must therefore be understood that, after the killing which was to be carried out by the angel, Moses’ wife or the wife of the child returned with the little ones. For some thought that the angel terrified Moses for this reason: so that the female sex would not accompany him as an impediment to the divinely imposed ministry.

**VERSES 21–23.**—“I will harden his heart.” (AUGUSTINE, Sermon 88.) What does “I will harden his heart” mean except that, when my grace is absent, his own wickedness hardens him? Just as water, whenever it is congealed by excessive cold, is dissolved when the sun’s heat comes upon it, and, when the sun withdraws, is hardened again: so, through the cold of sins, the charity of many grows cold, and they are hardened like ice; but when the heat of divine mercy comes upon them, they are dissolved.

We recognize this in Pharaoh: whenever the scourges were removed, he rose up hardened against God; whenever he was afflicted, he begged for mercy. Therefore there is no injustice in God. Hence it was not so much God’s power as his patience that caused Pharaoh to become hardened. We customarily exercise the same treatment toward our servants, whom we pardon even when they sin frequently, saying: “I made you such a person; by sparing you, I nourished your arrogance and negligence.”

**VERSE 24.**—“The Lord met him,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 11.) Another version reads: “And it happened on the way, at the lodging-place, that an angel met him and sought to kill him. Then Sephora took a flint, circumcised the foreskin of her son, fell at his feet, and said: ‘The blood of the circumcision of my child has stopped,’ and he withdrew from him because she said: ‘The blood of the circumcision has stopped.’” First it is asked whom the angel wished to kill, etc., up to “unless I am mistaken, in a great sacrament.”

**VERSES 25–26.**—“You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” etc. According to the historical sense, the gentile mother, astonished at the novelty of the event, could say to Moses: “You are a bridegroom of blood to me,” as if to say: “The rite of your people compels me to shed the blood of my son, something that is not customary among other nations.”

Mystically, however, Sephora signifies the Church from the nations. She strips the foreskin of her son—that is, of the gentile people—with the sharpest stone, meaning the teaching of the Holy Spirit, or that rock of which it is said in 1 Corinthians 10: “The rock was Christ.” She strips him so that he may be cleansed from every pollution of flesh and spirit: “And put off the old man with his deeds” (Colossians 3). The blood of circumcision indeed stops when “this corruptible shall have put on incorruption.”

**VERSES 27–31.**—“And the Lord said,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 32.) Aaron met Moses and came out from Egypt. But it matters where he meets Moses, whose mouth is to be opened by the Lord: he meets him at the mountain of God. Rightly is his mouth opened who meets him at the mountain of God.

Peter, James, and John also deserved to see the Lord Jesus transfigured on the mountain, and Moses and Elijah with him in glory. You too, unless you climb the mountain of God and there meet Moses—that is, unless you climb the lofty ascent of the Law, unless you seize the summit of spiritual understanding—do not have the door opened by the Lord.

If you remain in the low place of the letter, you have not met Moses on the mountain of God; God has not opened your mouth, nor instructed you in what you ought to say. If Aaron had not met Moses on the mountain, if he had not seen his lofty understanding, he would not have spoken God’s words to him, nor handed on the power of the signs, nor made him a participant in so great a mystery.

# CHAPTER 5

**VERSE 1.**—“[Lacuna] Let my people go.” (ORIGEN, Homily 3 on Exodus.) Moses does not want the people, while remaining in Egypt, to serve God; rather, he wants them to go out into the wilderness and serve him there. For while someone remains in the dark deeds of the world and is entangled in the obscurity of business, he cannot serve God. “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6). We must therefore leave Egypt: the world must be abandoned, not in place but in disposition, if we wish to serve the Lord. Hence John says: “Little children, do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world” (1 John 2).

**VERSE 2.**—“Who is the Lord?” He expresses the devil’s pride. Disdaining submission to God, he says: “I shall be like the Most High” (Isaiah 14); and, as though doubting the Lord’s sonship, he says: “If you are the Son of God, command that these stones become loaves” (Matthew 4). Later, as though compelled, the demons cried out: “Why have you come before the time to torment us? We know that you are the Son of God” (Matthew 8). After the torments they know what earlier they had refused to know.

Pharaoh too, after being scourged, asks that intercession be made for him to the Lord. “Who is the Lord, that I should hear his voice?” etc. You see what savage pride does; shortly afterward you will see how much he advances through the scourges, how much better he becomes when beaten. The one who now says, “I do not know the Lord,” when beaten will say: “Pray to the Lord for me.”

Let no one, therefore, be so untrained in divine discipline as to think that divine scourges are destruction and a punitive death. Behold, even the hardest Pharaoh advances when beaten: before the scourges he does not know the Lord, but once beaten he asks that intercession be made for him; and, advancing through punishments, he learns to recognize why he is being punished.

“I do not know the Lord,” he says. In the Gospel, once beaten, he corrects this statement, because the demons cried out: “We know who you are: you are the Son of the living God.” After the scourges he will also release Israel, and will even urge them to leave. “There is no fellowship between light and darkness, no share between the faithful and the unbeliever” (2 Corinthians 6).

**VERSE 3.**—“The God of the Hebrews has called us,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, On Exodus.) The question is how it can be said to the people, etc., up to “so that he may receive a just judgment.”

(ORIGEN.) Morally. We make the three days’ journey from Egypt if we preserve ourselves from every defilement of soul, body, and spirit in such a way that our spirit, soul, and body may remain whole for the day of Christ.

(ORIGEN.) We make the three days’ journey from Egypt if, taking rational, moral, and natural wisdom from worldly matters, we turn it toward divine institutions. We make the three days’ journey from Egypt if, purifying within ourselves our words, deeds, and thoughts—for these are the three ways in which human beings can sin—we become pure in heart, so that we may see God.

But when the prince of Egypt sees that he is being pressed more forcefully to release the people of God, he wants, as a second measure, to obtain that they not go very far, so that they do not complete the entire three-day journey, saying: “Do not go far away.” He does not want the people of God to become far removed from him. He wants them, if not in deed, then in speech, or if not in speech, then at least in thought, to sin. He does not want them to make the entire three-day journey away from him. He wants to possess one day in some of us, two days in others, and the entire three days in still others. Blessed are those who withdraw from him for the whole three days.

**“A three days’ journey into the wilderness, and let us sacrifice to God,” etc.** (ISIDORE.) We walk a three days’ journey as we leave Egypt, so that we may reach the place where we ought to sacrifice to the Lord. This way is Christ, who says in John 14: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.” Whoever confesses Christ with his mouth and believes in his heart that God raised him on the third day will be saved, reaching the place where a sacrifice of praise is offered.

(STRABO.) “A three days’ journey,” etc. At the third encampment, after crossing the Red Sea, they reached Etham, which place is also called Marah because of its bitter waters. Or “three days” means three months, because in the third month after they left Egypt they reached Sinai, where they sacrificed and received the Law, and where the tabernacle was also erected.

(ORIGEN, Homily 3 on Exodus.) Even now Moses, whom we have with us—for we have Moses and the prophets—that is, the Law of God, wants to lead you out of Egypt if you listen to it. He wants to take you far from Pharaoh and rescue you from the work of clay and straw, provided that you listen and understand spiritually. He does not want you to remain in deeds of flesh and darkness, but to go out into the wilderness, that is, to a place free from the disturbances and waves of the world, and to the repose of silence. For the words of wisdom are learned in silence and quiet.

In this place you will be able to sacrifice the Law of God to the Lord and recognize the power of the divine voice. Therefore Moses wants to cast you out from the waves of business and the tumult of peoples, and from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of ignorance—so that you may hear the Law of God and grasp the light of knowledge.

**VERSES 4–8.**—“Why do you, Moses and Aaron, trouble [the people],” etc. (ORIGEN, in the same work.) While the people are with him, working clay or brick, while they are occupied with straw, he does not think that he is acting perversely but that he is proceeding rightly. But if someone says, “I want to go a three days’ journey and serve the Lord,” he says that the people have been perverted through Moses and Aaron.

Even today, if Moses and Aaron—that is, prophetic and priestly speech—trouble a soul toward service of God, toward leaving the world, renouncing all that it possesses, and attending to the Law and word of God, you will immediately hear the like-minded friends of Pharaoh saying: “See how people are being led astray and young men perverted, so that they do not work, serve, or do anything useful. Having abandoned necessary things, they pursue follies and idleness. What does it mean to serve God? They do not want to work and are looking for opportunities for idleness.”

These were Pharaoh’s words then, and his friends speak them now—not only with words but also with blows. He orders the Hebrew scribes to be beaten; straw is not supplied, yet the work is demanded. The fathers suffered these things, and now the people of God suffer them.

Those who have given themselves wholly to the prince of this world prosper; everything, as they think, turns out successfully. But even a small and humble livelihood does not succeed for the servants of God. These are the straws that were supplied by Pharaoh. Hence certain exhausted people say to Pharaoh: “Why do you afflict your people?” Overcome by blows, they fall away from the faith and confess that they are Pharaoh’s people; for “not all who are from Israel are Israelites.”

**VERSES 9–13.**—“Let them be oppressed with their labors and let them complete them,” etc. Mystically. From the moment Moses began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God are afflicted more severely. From the moment the word of God reaches the soul, the devil rises up more fiercely and introduces greater vices. Before the word of God came to rebuke vices, they remained in peace; but when it came, great turmoil arose.

**VERSES 14–20.**—“And those who were beaten,” etc. The children of Israel were more harshly oppressed after they decided to leave Egypt, because those who wish to renounce the world and evil works are attacked by the devil with more savage temptations.

**VERSE 21.**—“May the Lord look upon you,” etc. (GREGORY, Moralia, book 29, chapter 14.) When divine light illumines the human heart, he grieves as though he were becoming foul in Pharaoh’s eyes.

**“Because you have made us foul,” etc.** (ORIGEN, Homily 3.) Allegorically. They speak the truth, although they do not know it, like Caiaphas, who said: “It is expedient that one man should die for the people” (John 18); he did not know what he was saying. For, as the Apostle says: “We are the good odor of Christ, to some unto life, to others unto death.” So prophetic speech is a sweet odor to believers; but to the doubtful and unbelieving, and to those who confess themselves to be Pharaoh’s people, it becomes an execrable odor.

Moses himself also says to the Lord: “From the time I spoke with Pharaoh, you have afflicted your people,” because before the word of God is heard there is neither tribulation nor temptation. But when the trumpet of preaching displays the sign of war, the battle of tribulations arises.

From the moment Moses and Aaron began to speak to Pharaoh, the people of God are afflicted. From the moment the word of God is uttered into your soul, a struggle is stirred up within you between virtues and vices, which previously remained at peace within you. But when the word of God begins to distinguish between them, great turmoil arises and war is born without treaty, because injustice does not accord with justice, nor drunkenness with sobriety, nor falsehood with truth.

Therefore let us not be troubled if we seem to Pharaoh to be an execrable odor. Virtue is called the execration of vice. But just as Moses stood before Pharaoh, let us also stand: let us not bend, having our loins girded in truth and our feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace (Ephesians 6).

Let us stand confidently and beseech the Lord to set our feet upon a firm rock, so that our feet may not be moved. Let us stand—that is, resist—according to 1 Peter 5: “Whom resist, strong in faith,” so that Satan may quickly be crushed beneath our feet. For the more steadfastly and firmly we stand, the weaker Pharaoh becomes. But if we begin to be weak or doubtful, he will grow stronger.

When Moses lifted his hands, Amalek was defeated; when he lowered them as though weary, Amalek grew strong. Let us therefore raise our arms in the power of Christ’s cross and lift holy hands in prayer, so that we may merit God’s help. Hence James says: “Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 3). Let us act, therefore, so that he not only flees but is crushed beneath our feet, destroyed in the depths of the abyss.

But when we depart from Egypt, from our vices, we escape the waves of the world as though by a solid path, through Jesus Christ.

**VERSES 22–23.**—“Lord, why have you afflicted this people?” (AUGUSTINE.) These are not words of defiance or indignation, but of inquiry and prayer, as is evident from what the Lord answered. For he did not rebuke Moses’ unbelief but revealed what he was going to do.

# CHAPTER 6

**VERSES 3–6.**—“[Lacuna] And my name Adonai I did not reveal to them.” As with you. Through the succession of generations, the increase of divine knowledge grew. The Lord appeared to Abraham; he spoke face to face with Moses; David, however, says in Psalm 118: “I have understood more than the elders,” etc. The apostles saw the Son of God present and asked him whatever they wished; to them also it is said in Luke 2: “Many kings and prophets,” etc.

**VERSES 7–8.**—“From the prison of the Egyptians.” *Ergastulum* and *ergasterium* mean “workshop,” namely, the place where condemned persons were bound for the performance of labor.

**VERSES 9–11.**—“They did not listen to him,” etc. Note God’s clemency: he is not believed by the children of Israel, yet he does not cease to admonish them. He is despised by Pharaoh, yet he waits with great patience.

**VERSES 12–13.**—“Behold, the children,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 16.) The Septuagint reads: “Behold, I am weak-voiced, and how will Pharaoh hear me?” Nevertheless, he does not seem to excuse himself on account of the weakness of his voice because of the multitude of the people, but even because of one man. It would be remarkable if his voice were so weak that he could not be heard even by one person. Or perhaps royal arrogance did not permit them to speak with him at close range.

**VERSES 14–19.**—“These are the leaders,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions 15.) Scripture, wishing to demonstrate Moses’ origin, began with the firstborn of Jacob, namely Reuben, as the course of Moses’ activity required; then it proceeded to Simeon, and from Simeon to Levi. It did not proceed farther, because Moses was from Levi.

These are the men who had already been mentioned among the seventy-five with whom Israel entered Egypt. God did not want the first or second tribe, but the third tribe, that is, the Levitical tribe, to be priestly.

**VERSE 20.**—“Amram took Jochebed as his wife,” etc. (STRABO.) Amram is interpreted as “exalted father,” signifying Christ; Jochebed, “the grace of God,” signifies the Church. From Christ and the Church are born Moses—that is, the spiritual Law—and Aaron, namely, the true priesthood.

“He took her,” etc. She was from the tribe of Judah, the sister of Nahshon, who was the leader of the tribe of Judah in the wilderness. For it had not yet been commanded that each person take a wife from his own tribe. These two tribes—the Levitical and the royal—were joined already then so that it might be understood that Christ, king and priest, would arise from them.

**VERSES 21–26.**—“The sons also of Izhar,” etc. (STRABO.) It is asked why Korah, whom the earth swallowed alive on account of his wickedness, is written in the genealogy of the righteous. But he signifies that heretics will be present in the Church together with Catholics.

**VERSES 27–30.**—“This is Moses.” (STRABO.) Ezra adds this from his own material; after the Babylonian captivity, he restored the entire library, after all the books had been burned by Nebuchadnezzar. Or Moses himself speaks about himself as though about another person.

# CHAPTER 7

**VERSES 1–6.**—“And the Lord said to Moses: Behold, I have appointed you as lord,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 17, volume 3.) It should be noted that when Moses was sent to the people, he was not told: “Behold, I have made you God to the people, and your brother will be your prophet.” Rather, he was told: “Your brother will speak to you to the people.” It was also said: “He will be your mouth, and you will be to him in matters pertaining to God.” It was not said: “You will be God to him.”

To Pharaoh, however, Moses is said to have been given as a god, and, by analogy, Aaron was given as a prophet to Moses—but in relation to Pharaoh. This teaches us that God’s prophets speak those things which they hear from him; and that a prophet of God is nothing other than a spokesman of God’s words to human beings, who either cannot or do not deserve to hear God directly.

(GREGORY, Homily 8 on Ezekiel.) Sometimes God is called so by designation, and sometimes essentially. By designation, as here: “I have appointed you god of Pharaoh.” And elsewhere: “Bring him near to the gods.” And elsewhere: “God stood in the assembly of the gods,” etc.

Essentially, as here: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Wishing to distinguish this, Paul says: “From whom Christ was born according to the flesh, who is God blessed forever.” He is called God by designation among all things, but essentially above all things. Thus, to show that Christ is God by nature, Paul remembered that he is not merely God but God above all things. Every righteous person is a god, but only among all things, because this is by designation; Christ, however, is above all things, because he is God by nature.

(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 18.) God repeatedly says, etc., up to “I will harden,” that is, “I will demonstrate how hard it is.”

**VERSES 7–8.**—“Now Moses was eighty years old,” etc. (STRABO.) This refers to circumcision, which was commanded to be performed on the eighth day. The number eighty has the same significance as the lesser number eight contained within it. Moses was eighty years old. When Moses and Aaron spoke to Pharaoh, Moses was eighty, while Aaron was eighty-three, because the Law, offered to the nations through preachers, taught spiritual circumcision; and they themselves strove to be perfectly cleansed, and thus preached faith in the Holy Trinity.

**VERSE 9.**—“When Pharaoh says to you,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions 19 and 20.) Here there was no need for the voice, on account of whose weakness Aaron seemed to have been given to Moses; rather, the rod was to be thrown down so that it might become a dragon. Why, then, did Moses himself not do this? It was because Aaron’s mediation between Moses and Pharaoh represents a figure of great faith.

This too should be noted: it is written, “Aaron threw down his rod.” Perhaps, if it had said simply “he threw down the rod,” there would have been no question. But since it adds “his,” although Moses had given it to him, perhaps this was not said without reason. Or was that rod common to both of them, so that whichever of them it was called “his,” it would truthfully be called so?

(STRABO.) Moses’ rod signifies Christ, who took flesh from the royal stock. Hence the same rod, when changed into a serpent, devoured all the rods of the magicians, because Christ’s death consumed our death.

(ORIGEN, Homily 4 on Exodus.) The Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 14: “Strive after spiritual gifts, but especially that you may prophesy.” Let us also attempt to take up zeal for good things, while awaiting from the Lord the fullness of the gift. For the former it is said in Psalm 80: “Open your mouth, and I will fill it”; for the latter: “Prick the eye, and it produces a tear; prick the heart, and it produces understanding.”

I therefore think that Moses, coming to Egypt and carrying the rod with which he chastises and scourges Egypt with ten plagues, signifies the Law of God, by which he reproves and corrects the world with ten plagues—that is, with the ten commandments of the Decalogue. The rod by which these things are done, Egypt is subdued, and Pharaoh overcome, is the cross of Christ, through which the world and the prince of the world—that is, the devil, together with principalities and powers—are overcome.

When the rod is thrown down, it becomes a dragon or serpent and devours the serpents of the Egyptian magicians. The serpent is customarily taken to represent wisdom or prudence; hence Matthew 10: “Be wise as serpents,” etc. And Genesis 3: “The serpent was more prudent than all the animals,” etc.

Therefore the cross of Christ, whose preaching seemed foolish, and which Moses—that is, the Law—contains, according to the saying in John 5: “He wrote about me,” after it was thrown upon the ground—that is, after it came to human faith—was changed into wisdom, and into such wisdom as would devour all the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, of this world.

Consider how God made the wisdom of this world foolish after he revealed Christ crucified to be the power and wisdom of God. The whole world has now been seized by him who said in 1 Corinthians 3: “I will seize the wise in their craftiness.”

**VERSE 10.**—“And Aaron took,” etc. (ISIDORE, On Genesis, volume 5.) “And he took the rod before Pharaoh,” etc., up to: “I shall be your death, O death,” etc.

**“Which was changed into a serpent.”** The Law of Moses was like a tasteless rod; but when changed into a serpent—that is, into spiritual understanding—it became drinkable and pleasing.

**VERSE 11.**—“But Pharaoh called the wise men,” etc. It should be understood either that, through demonic illusions, they deceived the eyes of spectators, so that things remaining in their own nature appeared to be something else; or, according to Augustine, that although demons are evil, they have not lost their nature. Therefore, when through incantation their magicians attempt to accomplish something, the demons run throughout the world and suddenly bring the seeds of the things through which the deed is performed. From these, with God’s permission, they produce new forms of things.

Likewise, in the first plague, when the water is changed into blood; in the second, when frogs swarm; in the third, when gnats descend; in the fourth, when the dog-fly is produced; and in the fifth, when the hand of the Lord is upon the livestock of the Egyptians, they are said to do similar things.

**VERSE 12.**—“Dragons.” They are called *drakontes* from the Greek δέρκειν (*derkein*), meaning “to see,” because they see more sharply than other animals.

**“But it devoured,” etc.** (AUGUSTINE, Questions 21.) If it had been said, “Aaron’s dragon swallowed their rods,” it would have been understood that Aaron’s real dragon did not swallow imaginary fabrications but rods, etc., up to “but God alone is the true Creator, who implanted the causes themselves and the seminal principles in things.”

**VERSES 13–14.**—“And his heart was hardened,” etc. God hardened Pharaoh’s heart because, after sin, he hardened the devil in such a way that he is never softened by the compunction of repentance, as it is said in Job 41: “His heart will be hardened like a stone.”

**VERSES 15–16.**—“Go to him in the morning; behold, he will go out,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 4.) At first Moses does not enter to Pharaoh but meets him as he goes out to the waters; afterward he enters; after that he neither enters nor goes of his own accord but approaches when summoned.

For whether our struggle with Pharaoh is in the word of God and the assertion of religion, or whether we are trying to rescue souls possessed by him and there is a contest within us in disputation, we must not at the first assault enter into the deepest places of the questions. Rather, we must meet the adversary at his waters—that is, at the authorities of the gentiles and philosophers—so that we may first refute them and show that they have erred; then we must enter into the interior of the contest.

For the Lord says: “Unless someone first binds the strong man, he cannot enter his house and plunder his goods” (Mark 3). First, therefore, the strong man must be bound and constrained by the bonds of questions; then one must enter to plunder his goods and free the souls whom he had possessed through deception and fraud.

When we have done this repeatedly and stood against him, with our loins girded in truth, standing in the Lord and acting manfully, the ancient and crafty artificer will pretend that he has been defeated and is yielding, so that he may make us more negligent in the contest. He will also pretend repentance and beg us to depart, but not far away: he wants us to remain near him in some respect.

But unless we withdraw farther from him, cross the sea, and say in thought, word, and deed, “As far as the east is from the west, so far has he removed our iniquities from us,” we cannot be saved. Let us therefore pray for God’s mercy, that he may rescue us from the land of Egypt, from the power of darkness, and plunge Pharaoh with his army into the fiercest water like lead. Once freed, let us sing a hymn to the Lord with joy and exultation. “For he has been gloriously honored,” etc.

(ISIDORE.) The plagues were bodily events in Egypt, but they take place spiritually in us. For Egypt is a figure of the world.

**VERSES 17–19.**—“The water of the river,” etc. (STRABO.) The water changed into blood signifies worldly wisdom, in which everyone who remains is killed, as a fish is killed in blood. For worldly wisdom considers it foolish that God should die for human beings; therefore whoever clings to it will not be able to live.

(ORIGEN.) The water of the river is changed into blood. To that river the Hebrews had handed over their children to be killed, so that it might return to the authors of the crime a drink of blood; and by drinking they might feel the gore of the polluted stream which they had stained with the slaughter of children.

Allegorically also, the waters of Egypt are the wandering and slippery doctrines of philosophers, by which they deceived the little ones in sense and understanding. But when the cross of Christ displays the light of truth, they are made to pay the penalty for the death of their own people and the guilt of their blood. Hence: “Every blood that has been shed upon the earth shall be required of this generation” (Matthew 23).

**VERSES 20–21.**—“Which was changed into blood,” etc. (RABANUS.) The first commandment concerns the worship of the one God: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” The first plague was the water changed into blood. Compare the first commandment with the first plague: water, from which all things are generated, signifies the one God, from whom all things come; blood signifies mortal flesh.

The water, therefore, was changed into blood because they exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of the image of corruptible man. This exchange takes place in the heart of the impious.

**“Into blood,” etc.** Because those who think carnally about the causes of things are reproved by punishments of this kind, so that from the character of the penalties they may recognize their error.

**VERSES 22–23.**—“And Pharaoh’s heart was hardened.” (AUGUSTINE, Questions 22.) Pharaoh’s heart seems to have been hardened for this reason: the Egyptian magicians did similar things. But what follows shows how great that hardness was, even after the magicians failed.

**VERSES 24–25.**—“But they dug,” etc. Because the gentile world, confounded by its meditation on secular philosophy, sees that there is nothing vital or wholesome in it and strives by investigation to seek everywhere a draught of wisdom, but does not find one until it reaches him who says: “Let the one who thirsts come to me and drink” (John 7).

# CHAPTER 8

**VERSES 2–6.**—“Behold, I will strike all your borders with frogs,” etc. (STRABO.) There are three kinds of frogs: one is river-dwelling and vocal; another is the kind called *calamita*, of which it is said that if it is thrown into the mouth of a barking dog, the dog immediately becomes mute; the third is the kind called *rubeta*, because it lives among brambles.

(ORIGEN.) Frogs signify the songs of poets, which, with empty and inflated modulation, like the sounds and songs of frogs, have brought stories of deception into the world. For that animal is useful for nothing except that it produces the sound of its voice through shameless and importunate cries.

(RABANUS.) The second commandment is: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” The name of God is truth, for he himself says: “I am the truth.” Whoever speaks the truth speaks of God; whoever speaks a lie speaks from himself. To speak truth is to speak rationally; to speak vanity is to make a noise.

The second commandment, therefore, concerns love of truth, opposed to which is love of iniquity. Truth speaks; vanity clamors. The second plague, the abundance of frogs, is opposed to truth, because their loquacity signifies vanity.

Those who love truth do not take the name of God in vain, because they do not depart from truth into vanity. But those who contradict the truth, and, deceived by vanity, deceive others, are frogs: they bring weariness to the ears, not nourishment to the minds.

Hear people speaking rationally, as in Psalm 18: “There are neither speeches nor words whose voices are not heard.” Hear the frogs: “They have spoken vain things, each one to his neighbor,” etc.

### Verses 7–9

“But the magicians did so,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 23.) It is asked how this could happen, if it had already been done everywhere. But a similar question arises concerning how they turned water into blood, if all the water of Egypt had already been turned into blood. It must therefore be understood that the region where the children of Israel lived had not been struck by such plagues; from there the enchanters could draw water which they would turn into blood, or bring forth frogs as a display of magical power. They may also have done this after those things had been restrained, but Scripture, in its narration, joined together what could have happened later.

### Verses 10–14

“Who answered: Tomorrow.” (THEODORET.) When Pharaoh wanted to know whether the prayers of Moses and Aaron had any power with God—for he supposed that they would rest during the night—he said, “Tomorrow,” so that he himself might go to the river and see whether the frogs had ceased. Therefore, so that Moses might be believed, God not only caused the frogs to cease at the very time Moses had appointed, but also commanded those that were on the land to die, lest anyone suppose that the same frogs had returned.

### Verse 15

“But when Pharaoh saw,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 24.) Here it becomes clear that Pharaoh was hardened not merely because the enchanters had done similar things, etc., up to the point where he did not say “gifts” or “rewards,” but “your judgments.”

### Verses 16–17

“Stretch out your rod,” etc. Mystically. Moses, with his rod chastising Egypt, signifies the Law, which chastises the world with the ten plagues of the commandments. The rod by which Egypt is corrected and Pharaoh overcome is also the cross of Christ, through which the world is conquered and the devil overcome, or triumphed over. When the rod is thrown down, it becomes a serpent, which signifies wisdom, according to the saying in Matthew 10: “Be wise as serpents,” etc. The rod devoured the serpents of the magicians, and the cross of Christ, whose preaching appears to be foolishness, surpasses all the wisdom of the world. Hence: “For he wrote of me” (John 5). The rod thrown upon the ground became a serpent because, when the mystery of the cross came to human faith, it made the wisdom of the world foolish.

“And let there be gnats,” etc. (ORIGEN.) This creature is suspended by wings and flies through the air, but it is so subtle and minute that it escapes the sight of the eyes unless one sees very sharply. Yet when it settles upon the body, it pierces it with an exceedingly painful sting, so that one who cannot see it flying nevertheless feels it stinging. This creature is therefore compared with the dialectical art, which pierces souls with the minute and subtle stings of words and surrounds them with such cunning that the deceived person neither sees nor understands from what source he is being deceived.

(RABANUS.) Morally. The third commandment is: “Remember to sanctify the Sabbath day.” By this is signified the repose and tranquillity of mind produced by a good conscience. There is sanctification there, because the Spirit of God is there. Hence: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, unless upon the humble and quiet?” etc. (Isaiah 66). Those who are restless therefore recoil from the Holy Spirit: they provoke quarrels, love accusations, and do not admit the rest of the spiritual Sabbath. Be gentle, then; let there be no tumult in your heart from fantasies flying about in corruption and pricking you. Hear God saying in Psalm 45: “Be still and see that I am God.” Through restlessness you do not wish to be still, yet, blinded, you demand to see what you cannot see. Consider the opposite plague: gnats were born in the land of Egypt from the mud, namely exceedingly small and restless flies, flying disorderly, rushing into the eyes, and denying human beings rest. When driven away, they return; so too do the fantasies of restless people. Keep the commandment; beware of the plague.

### Verse 18

“And there were gnats.” Blood is the teaching of the philosophers; frogs are the inventions of the poets; gnats are the sophisms of the dialecticians. All these deceived the world.

### Verse 19

“This is the finger of God,” etc. (ISIDORE, from Augustine, Letter 119.) At the third sign the magicians fail, saying, “This is the finger of God.” They possessed the character and arrogance of heretics. Hence: “As Jannes and Jambres resisted Moses, so these also resist the truth, men corrupted in mind, rejected with regard to the faith,” etc. (2 Timothy 3). Those who were restless through corruption of mind failed at the third sign, confessing that the Holy Spirit who was in Moses was against them. For the Spirit, who is the finger of God, is placed third. Just as, when appeased, he grants rest to the meek and humble in heart, so, when angered, he drives the harsh and proud into agitation through restlessness. This was signified by the most grievous flies, beneath which the magicians failed, saying, “This is the finger of God,” though they did not understand the source of their deception.

(STRABO.) It should be noted that the magicians were defeated at the third sign because every unbelief and worldly wisdom, or philosophy, is overcome by faith in the Trinity. Although they discovered philosophy and debated the machinery of the whole world, they could not arrive at knowledge of the Trinity. By the finger, the Holy Spirit is understood—not because he is less than the Father and the Son, but because there are many divisions in a finger, and through the Holy Spirit the distribution of graces is given.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 25 on Exodus, volume 3.) What the magicians said to Pharaoh, etc., up to the point where, although they did not keep silent about the Son.

### Verse 20

“Thus says the Lord,” etc. (RABANUS.) The fourth commandment is: “Honor your father and your mother.” The fourth plague, namely the dog-fly, is contrary to this. It is characteristic of a dog not to recognize its parents; hence their puppies are born blind.

### Verse 21

“Every kind of fly.” (ISIDORE.) Mystically. Egypt is struck by flies in the fourth place. The fly is an insolent and restless creature, in which the insolent cares of carnal desires are represented. Egypt is struck by flies because the hearts of those who love the world are afflicted by the restlessness of their desires. The Septuagint used *cynomyia*, that is, “dog-fly,” by which doglike behavior is signified, in which the pleasure of the human mind and the lust of the flesh are reproved. The forensic eloquence of human beings may also be signified by the dog-fly, since they tear one another apart like dogs.

(PROCOPIUS.) In attacking Egypt, God does not use great beasts, but summons the service of the most contemptible little animals and insects, lest the result be attributed to their power. He gives those despised and feeble creatures unconquerable strength, so that Egypt despairs of being able to resist them and cries out, “This is the finger of God.” For the whole world, gathered together, cannot bear the hand of God.

(ORIGEN.) The *cynomyia* is the sect of the heretics [or, alternatively, “Cynics”], who, in addition to the other wickednesses of their deception, proclaim pleasure and lust to be the highest good. Since the world was previously deceived by each of these things, the coming Word and Law of God rightly reproves it with such chastisements, so that from the character of the punishments people may recognize the character of their own error.

### Verses 22–23

“And I shall make a distinction,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 26.) This must be understood to have occurred in the earlier signs as well: the land in which God’s people lived was not afflicted by any such plagues. It was fitting, however, that this should be stated openly here; from this point the signs begin which the magicians did not attempt to imitate. For it is certain that gnats were everywhere in Pharaoh’s kingdom, but were not in the land of Gessen, or Goshen. There the magicians attempted to do something similar and could not. Until they failed, nothing was said about the separation of that land; but once the events began which they did not even dare to attempt, it was stated.

### Verses 24–25

“And the most grievous fly came,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, in the same place.) “Fly” is used in the singular for a multitude of flies. I do not know how it is that, through customary speech ingrained in the minds of human beings, what is said in the singular often seems greater than what is said in the plural. For example: “There is a soldier there” signifies more than “There are soldiers there”; “There is a fish there” signifies more than “There are fish there.”

### Verses 26–31

“Abominations.” The perverse abominate good things. The Egyptians—that is, citizens of this world—abominate sheep, that is, the simplicity of the good. For just as the good abominate evil, so the wicked abominate good. Hence the good abominate an impious man, and the impious abominate those who are on the right path.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 28.) Moses said that he wished to go into the wilderness, where the Egyptians would not see their abominations. This must be understood mystically as signifying what we said about the shepherds, who were abominable to the Egyptians; and for this reason the Israelites received a separate land in Egypt. The sacrifices of the Israelites are therefore abominations to the Egyptians, just as the life of the righteous is an abomination to the wicked.

(STRABO.) Historically. The Egyptians abominate sheep and worship them because of Jupiter Ammon, who is depicted with the head of a ram. Likewise, the Egyptians worship a bull consecrated to Apis, just as they worship a cow consecrated to Isis. Apis was the greatest deity of the Egyptians, appearing to their priests once a year at a fixed time. They followed him with hymns and praises and, as though possessed, prophesied.

(GREGORY, Book 18 of the Moralia, chapter 28, volume 2.) Egypt is struck by flies, etc., up to “Be still and see that I am God.”

### Verse 32

“And it was made heavy,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 29.) When the locust had been removed, it was said of Pharaoh: “Pharaoh hardened his heart even at this time, and he was unwilling to let the people go.” Certainly it is not now said, “The heart of Pharaoh was hardened,” but, “Pharaoh hardened his heart.” The same is true in all the plagues. The origin of vices comes from the human will. Human hearts are moved by causes—some in one way, others in another—even when the causes are not different, often acting differently according to their own qualities, which arise from the will.

## Chapter 9

### Verses 1–6

“And the Lord said to Moses,” etc. (PROCOPIUS.) Horses are counted first among beasts of burden; they are deceptive, or false, with regard to salvation. Next come unclean animals, which neither divide the hoof nor chew the cud, though they are harnessed to a chariot. Then come camels, which, although they are regarded as clean because of their chewing the cud, are nevertheless considered unclean because their hoof is not divided. Yet camels are said to be partly of clean and partly of unclean condition. Since this plague was thought to be relatively harmless because unclean animals were held in little esteem, it passes to cattle and then to the gentlest of animals, the sheep.

(ORIGEN, Homily 4.) In the fifth place Egypt is scourged by the death of animals and cattle. In this the senselessness or folly of mortals is reproved: as though irrational beasts, they imposed the worship and name of God upon images—not only of human beings but also of animals—impressed in wood and stone. They revered Jupiter Ammon in a ram, Anubis in a dog, Apis in a bull, and the other monstrous forms of the gods that Egypt admires, so that in those things which they believed to receive divine worship they might see a pitiable punishment.

(RABANUS, on Exodus, volume 2.) The fifth commandment is: “You shall not commit adultery,” etc., up to “Observe the plague: if you are a beast, at least fear death.”

### Verse 7

“And it became heavy,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 30.) If the Israelites’ animals had died, there would have seemed to be a reasonable cause for his heart to be hardened in contempt of God, as though his magicians had killed the Israelites’ animals. But he should have been moved to fear or believe by the fact that this did not happen; instead, his heart was hardened, and that hardening continued even to this point.

### Verse 8

“Take full handfuls,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 31.) Another text reads: “Take full handfuls of ash for yourselves from the furnace, and let Moses scatter it,” etc. The earlier signs were performed by means of the rod, which Moses did not extend, but Aaron extended over the water or used to strike the earth. Now, after two signs have intervened—namely, the dog-fly and the deaths of the cattle, in which neither Aaron nor Moses performs anything with his hand—it is said that Moses should scatter ash toward heaven. Both are commanded to take it, but he alone is commanded to scatter it—not upon the earth but toward heaven. It is as though Aaron, who had been given for the people, ought to strike the earth or extend his hand over the water or earth, whereas Moses, who was concerned with matters belonging to the Lord, is commanded to scatter the ash. What do those two earlier signs mean, in which neither Moses nor Aaron performs anything with his hand? What does this difference itself signify? It cannot be nothing.

(RABANUS.) The sixth commandment is: “You shall not kill.” The sixth plague is boils on the body: blisters swelling and bursting, the burning of wounds, and furnace ash. Murderers burn with anger and madness. If you could see the souls of murderers, you would mourn them more than the decaying bodies of those covered with sores.

### Verses 9–12

(ORIGEN, in the same place.) Wounds and blisters appear with burning heat in the sixth scourging. In the sores, deceitful and festering wickedness is reproved; in the blisters, swelling and inflated pride; in the burning heat, anger and the madness of fury.

### Verses 13–15

“And the Lord hardened the heart,” etc. (ORIGEN, in the same place.) Observe that in the sixth plague it is not said, “The heart of Pharaoh was hardened,” but something more terrible is added. For it is written that “the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” etc. Again, in the seventh plague, when hail and fire devastate Egypt, Pharaoh’s heart is indeed hardened, but not by the Lord. In the eighth, when the locust is produced, it is said that the Lord hardens Pharaoh’s heart. In the ninth, when palpable darkness comes, and finally, when the firstborn have been destroyed and the Israelites have departed, it is said: “And the Lord hardened the heart of Pharaoh king of Egypt and his servants, and he pursued them.” Again, when Moses is sent from the land of Midian to Egypt and is commanded to perform signs, it is added: “You shall perform them in the sight of Pharaoh; but I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart,” etc. This was first said by the Lord: “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart,” etc. A second time, after the rulers had been enumerated, Israel is told: “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart,” etc.

This variation was not made without reason: sometimes the Lord is said to have hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and sometimes it is said to have been hardened of its own accord. I see Paul, as though understanding the difference between “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened” and “the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart,” saying in Romans 2: “Do you despise the riches of his goodness, patience, and long-suffering? Do you not know that the kindness of God leads you to repentance?” etc. Here he undoubtedly condemns the one who was hardened of his own accord. Elsewhere, as though proposing a question about this, he says: “Therefore he has mercy on whom he wishes, and whom he wishes he hardens,” etc. He also adds: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?” (Romans 9). By this, concerning the one who is said to have been hardened by the Lord, he answered not so much by resolving the question as by apostolic authority, in view of the incapacity of his hearers, just as he says elsewhere: “And he heard secret words which it is not permitted a man to speak” (2 Corinthians 12). Hence, in what follows, he warns the person who, not so much from the merit of study as from a desire for knowledge, plunges too inquisitively into more secret questions, saying in Romans 9: “O man, who are you to answer back to God?”

(RABANUS.) The seventh commandment is: “You shall not steal.” The seventh plague is hail upon the fruits. No one has unjust profit without just loss. When you steal, you acquire clothing but lose faith; visible profit, invisible loss; profit from your blindness, loss from the Lord’s cloud. Those who steal outwardly through evil desire are inwardly pelted with hail from judgment, and the field of their heart is devastated.

### Verses 16–17

“But for this very reason I have appointed you,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 32.) The Apostle used these words, etc., up to the point where Pharaoh was therefore preserved for their benefit.

### Verse 18

“Behold, tomorrow I shall rain,” etc. (ORIGEN.) Up to this point punishments are measured out to the world through figures of its errors; after this, scourges come from above.

### Verses 19–21

“Therefore send now,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 35 on Exodus, volume 3.) God appears to give this warning not so much indignantly as mercifully, etc., up to the point where God threatened the death of the animals, although Scripture did not state this.

(PROCOPIUS.) It happened through divine providence that all the beasts did not perish. For animals were needed to draw the chariots with which Pharaoh would later pursue the fugitives in order to slaughter them in the wilderness. Divine providence, however, governed the whole matter otherwise.

### Verse 22

“Stretch out your hand,” etc. (PROCOPIUS.) The reader should be warned here that Moses was not commanded to perform all the wonders with the rod, but only some of them. Some he merely foretold, such as the gnats and the death of the animals; others he performed through the ministry of his hands, as when he took soot from the furnace and stirred up the hail. But what is the reason for this? It was so that the populace would not suppose that the rod had been made through magical superstition and attribute those wondrous effects to it.

### Verses 23–29

“And Moses stretched out the rod,” etc. (ORIGEN, in the place cited above.) It should also be noted that some scourges are said to be inflicted upon Pharaoh or Egypt by Aaron, some by Moses, and some by the Lord himself. In the first plague, when the waters are turned into blood, Aaron raises the rod and strikes the water. In the second, he strikes the waters and brings forth frogs. In the third, he extends his hand and strikes the dust of the earth with the rod, and gnats come forth. In the fourth, the Lord is said to have caused the dog-fly to come. In the fifth, when the animals are destroyed, it is said that he performed this deed. In the sixth, Moses scatters the soot, and sores and blisters appear. In the seventh, he raises his hand toward heaven, and thunderous voices and hail come forth, etc. In the eighth, he likewise extends his hands toward heaven, and the Lord brings up the wind and brings in the locusts. In the ninth, he extends his hand toward heaven, and darkness and gloom come forth. In the tenth, the Lord himself brings about the conclusion and perfection of the whole work. For it is said: “And the Lord struck every firstborn in the land of Egypt.”

(The Same.) Another difference should be observed. In the first plague, when the water is turned into blood, Moses is not yet told to enter Pharaoh’s presence, but “Go to meet him,” etc. In the second, after the first plague has been consistently and faithfully administered, he is told: “Enter to Pharaoh,” etc. In the third, gnats are inflicted, and the magicians yield, confessing: “This is the finger of God.” In the fourth, Moses is commanded to rise early and stand before Pharaoh as he goes out toward the waters, when the houses of the Egyptians are filled with the dog-fly. In the fifth, when the animals are destroyed, he is commanded to enter Pharaoh’s presence. In the sixth, Pharaoh is disregarded, and it is not said that Moses and Aaron entered him, because sores and blisters appeared with burning heat even upon the magicians, and they could not resist Moses. In the seventh, Moses is commanded to rise very early and stand before Pharaoh when he brings forth hail, fire, and thunderous voices. In the eighth, he is commanded to enter him when the locust is produced. In the ninth, Pharaoh is again disregarded, and Moses is commanded to stretch out his hands toward heaven so that palpable darkness may come; he does not enter, but is summoned to Pharaoh. Likewise in the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed, Pharaoh summons them at night and says: “Rise, go out from among my people, you and the children of Israel,” etc.

“And the Lord gave thunder,” etc. (THE SAME, Homily 4.) Observe the moderation of divine correction. He does not scourge in silence, but gives thunderous voices and sends teaching from heaven, by which the chastised world may recognize its fault. He gives hail, by which the tender things still emerging—namely, the beginnings of vices—are devastated. He also gives fire, knowing that there are thorns and thistles which it must consume. Concerning this the Lord says in Luke 12: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth.” By this fire the incitements of pleasure and lust are consumed.

(The Same.) Many other things should be observed, in which divine wisdom is indicated. First, Pharaoh is not moved when the water is turned into blood. In the second, he appears to soften somewhat, for he summoned Moses and Aaron, saying: “Pray to the Lord for me,” etc. In the third, the magicians yield, saying: “This is the finger of God,” etc. In the fourth, after being scourged by the dog-fly, he says: “Go and sacrifice to the Lord your God,” etc. In the fifth, when the deaths of the animals are announced, he does not yield, but becomes still more hardened. The same occurs in the sixth, concerning the plague of sores. In the seventh, when he is devastated by hail and fire, he summons Moses and Aaron, saying: “I have sinned even now; the Lord is righteous, but I and my people are wicked,” etc. In the eighth, when he is pressed by the locusts, he hastily summons Moses and Aaron, saying: “I have sinned against the Lord your God and against you. Accept my sin; even now pray to the Lord your God.” In the ninth, when he is overwhelmed by darkness, he summons Moses and Aaron, saying: “Go and serve the Lord your God.” In the tenth, when the firstborn are destroyed, he summons them at night and says: “Rise, go out from among my people, you and the children of Israel,” etc. He adds: “But bless me also.”

These things cannot be explained except by the same Spirit by whom they were accomplished, because, according to the Apostle, “the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets” (1 Corinthians 14). Thus the words of the prophets are not said to be subject to just anyone for explanation, but to the prophets.

### Verses 30–35

“But I know that,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 35 on Exodus.) Pharaoh was terrified by the crash of heaven and the hail. Hence he asked Moses to pray for him, confessing the wickedness of himself and his people. But Moses was seeking another kind of fear. It is easy to fear punishment, but this is not fearing God with that fear of piety of which Jacob says: “Unless the God of my father Abraham, and the fear of Isaac, had been with me, now you would have sent me away empty” (Genesis 31).

## Chapter 10

### Verses 1–3

“... For I have hardened his heart,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 36 on Exodus.) He did not say this as though God needed anyone’s wickedness, but it must be understood as though he had said: “I was patient toward him and his servants, so that I would not remove them, in order that my signs might come upon them in due order.” Because God’s patience made the evil mind more obstinate, he is said to have burdened his heart, on account of the patience he exercised toward him. The chastisement of the Egyptians is instruction for the children of Israel, lest they likewise become hardened and suffer similar things. When the pestilent man is punished, the child will become wiser.

(ORIGEN.) The ten plagues by which Egypt is scourged through the Israelites can be compared with the periods of the Roman Empire, because these things were done as a figure of our own. The Christian and Israelite peoples belong to one God; the same cause was imposed upon both: the synagogue upon the Egyptians, the Church upon the Romans. The Egyptians persecuted; the Romans also persecuted. There Moses is opposed ten times; here ten edicts are issued against Christ. There are different plagues of the Egyptians; here different calamities of the Romans.

There the first plague is that blood flows from wells and rivers; here the first plague under Nero was that blood was everywhere shed—either corrupted by diseases in the City or poured out in wars throughout the world. There the second plague is frogs in the inner chambers, and famine almost destroys the inhabitants; here under Domitian, frenzied satellites, at the command of a bloodthirsty prince, and scarcity almost scattered all Roman citizens.

There the third plague is gnats, most savage little flies which, in midsummer, fly in swarms through desolate places and inflict a burning bite upon human hair and the bristles of animals; here the third plague under Trajan stirred up the Jews. Previously scattered and quiet, as though they scarcely existed, they were moved by a sudden heat and began to ravage. Moreover, many cities collapsed in earthquakes during those same times.

There the fourth plague is dog-flies, fosterers of decay and mothers of worms; here under Marcus Antoninus a pestilence spread through many provinces and delivered Italy, the city of Rome, and the Roman army, dispersed among various winter quarters, over to death, decay, and worms.

There the fifth plague is that of cattle and beasts of burden; here under Severus the persecutor, through civil wars, the very entrails and supports of the state—that is, the populations of the provinces and the legions of soldiers—were crushed.

There the sixth plague is swelling blisters and flowing sores; here was the plague that followed the persecution of Maximinus. He had ordered the leading bishops and clergy of the churches to be tortured, leaving aside the common people. Swelling repeatedly with anger and treachery, this persecution was exalted not through the slaughter of the populace but through the wounds of dying princes and powerful men.

There the seventh plague is hail gathered in the air, destructive to human beings and animals; here under Gallus and Volusian, who succeeded the persecutor Decius, pestilence spread throughout the entire extent of the Roman Empire and delivered almost the whole human race to death.

There the eighth correction is the locusts stirred up everywhere; here nations stirred up everywhere devastated the Roman world with slaughter and fires.

There the ninth plague is darkness that can be handled, threatening more danger than it causes; here, when the persecutor Aurelian issued his decree, a terrible bolt of lightning fell amid dreadful storms at his very feet, showing what such a great avenger would do if he were not patient. Nevertheless, within six months three emperors were killed: Aurelian, Tacitus, and Florianus.

There the tenth and final plague is the slaughter of the firstborn; here it is the destruction of all the idols, which they had first made and loved above all. There the king tested and experienced the power of God, feared it, and released God’s people; here too he did all these things, and even believed.

(The Same.) There God’s people were not brought back into slavery, nor were they later compelled to idolatry. There the precious vessels of the Egyptians were handed over to the Hebrews; here the precious pagan temples passed to the Christian churches.

(The Same.) When the Egyptians pursued the Hebrews after the ten plagues had released them, destruction from the sea overwhelmed them. We too, as pilgrims, remain subject to the persecution of the Gentiles until, with Christ as leader and judge, we cross the Red Sea—that is, the fire of judgment. Those who persecute Christians, together with their king, Antichrist, will be submerged in the lake of eternal fire.

### Verses 4–12

“Behold, tomorrow I shall bring locusts,” etc. (RABANUS.) The eighth commandment is: “You shall not bear false witness.” The eighth plague is the locust, an animal harmful through its teeth. For a false witness harms by biting and consumes by lying. Hence: “If you bite and devour one another, see that you are not consumed by one another” (Galatians 5).

(ORIGEN, Homily 4 on Exodus.) I think that through this kind of plague the inconstancy of the human race—always divided and discordant within itself—is reproved.
