For although the locust has no king, according to Scripture it leads an ordered army; human beings, although made rational, could neither govern themselves in an orderly way nor patiently endure the governance and discipline of God who rules them.

(STRABO.) Through the locust, which has no king, the recklessness of those who, although punished with various penalties, always remain in their hardness is signified, as though they had no ruler.

“Locust.” (ISIDORE.) Locusts are understood in reference to the mobility of lightness, like souls wandering and leaping about for the sake of worldly pleasure.

### Verses 13–18

“And Moses stretched out the rod.” (RABANUS.) Some wonders are performed through Moses, some through Aaron, and some through the Lord himself, so that we may understand that in some matters we must be cleansed through the sacrifices of priests and the intercessions of bishops, which Aaron’s person represents; in some matters we must be corrected through knowledge of the Law, which Moses’ office represents. In more difficult matters, however, we need the power of the Lord himself.

(GREGORY, Book 31 of the Moralia, chapter 20.) The plagues inflicted upon Egypt from heaven, etc., up to the point where they weaken the works of certain people already regarded as strong through empty praises.

### Verses 19–20

“Not even one remained,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Scripture certainly commemorated God’s benefaction when it removed the locusts, and then went on to say that the Lord hardened Pharaoh’s heart—by his benefaction, namely, and by his patience, through which Pharaoh became more obstinate while being spared. In this way all evil human hearts grow hard when they misuse God’s patience.

### Verse 21

“Stretch out your hand,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) This is the third time Moses is told: “Stretch out your hand toward heaven,” so that the plague of darkness might also occur. Aaron, however, is never told to stretch out his hands toward heaven. Since Moses was told, “Stretch out your hand over the land of Egypt, and let the locust ascend over the land,” I believe this signifies that the one who can do more can also do less; but the one to whom lesser things are entrusted cannot thereby immediately do greater things.

(ORIGEN.) The ninth plague is darkness, so that their blindness of mind may be reproved, or so that they may understand how obscure are the ways of divine administration and providence. For God made darkness his hiding place (Psalm 17). They searched it out boldly and rashly, asserting one thing after another, and thus fell into the thick and palpable darkness of errors.

(STRABO.) Through the darkness the ignorance of those Jews is shown, who were afflicted and did not know toward what end their punishments were proceeding. Darkness may also signify the mystery of divine judgment, by which he mercifully saves the righteous and justly condemns the wicked.

### Verses 24–29

“Sheep only,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Expressions in Exodus, book 52.) The Greek has: “Apart from the sheep and cattle, leave [them],” and this is an unusual expression unless, after the distinction, “leave” is supplied and “these things” is understood, so that the sense is: “Go, apart from the sheep and cattle, and leave these things behind.” Such ellipsis frequently occurs in the expressions of Scripture.

(RABANUS.) The ninth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” The ninth plague is dense darkness. There is also a kind of adultery in desiring another man’s wife, when one is not satisfied with his own and attempts another’s as well. Truly the darkness is dense: nothing is so painful to the one who suffers, and nothing is so unwillingly endured by the one who causes it. Whoever does this is truly blinded by horrifying madness.

## Chapter 11

### Verse 2

“Therefore you shall say to all the people,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 94 on Exodus, volume 3.) No one should take an example from this, etc., up to the point where even those who had not been struck by the other plagues would not be afflicted by this loss.

“That a man should ask,” etc. (GREGORY, Book 28 of the Moralia, chapter 17.) Minds clinging to the use of carnal life, etc., up to the point where greater strength of spirit is announced.

### Verses 3–4

“But the Lord will give grace to his people before the Egyptians,” etc. These were the people who lived with the Hebrews in the land of Gessen and had not been harmed by the previous nine plagues, and therefore loved them. They were afflicted by the tenth plague after the Hebrews had departed from them.

### Verses 5–6

“And every firstborn shall die,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 4.) Finally, destruction is inflicted upon the firstborn. Perhaps there is in this something beyond our understanding: what the Egyptians committed against the Church of the firstborn, which is enrolled in heaven. Hence the destroying angel is also sent for this service, and he spares only those who have both doorposts marked with the blood of the lamb.

Again, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed—whether we call them principalities and powers and the rulers of the darkness of this world, whom Christ, at his coming, led away captive, that is, carried off and took captive, when he triumphed upon the wood of the cross; or whether we call them the authors and inventors of false religions, which the truth of Christ extinguished together with their authors.

The principalities, powers, and rulers of this darkness are the firstborn of the Egyptians. In the final plague, when the end of the world has come, when he separates the sheep from the goats and the grain from the chaff, they will be condemned, having lost the freedom to wander and tempt.

(ORIG.) Morally. While the soul lives in this world amid errors, in ignorance of the truth, it is situated in Egypt. If the law of God begins to draw near, it turns waters into blood—that is, it turns the fluid and slippery life of youth toward the blood of the Old or New Testament. Then the law draws out from it empty and vain talk against divine providence, resembling the croaking of frogs. It also cleanses its evil thoughts and drives away the stings of cunning, like the bites of gnats. It repels the bites of lust, resembling the darts of dog-flies; and it rebukes folly and an understanding like that of beasts, through which a human being, when honored, did not understand but was compared with senseless animals, etc. (Ps. XLVIII). It reproves the sores of sins, the swelling of arrogance, and extinguishes the heat of anger. After this it brings forward the voices of the sons of thunder—that is, evangelical and apostolic teachings—and the chastisement of hail, so as to restrain luxury and pleasures; and at the same time the fire of repentance, so that one may say: “Was not our heart burning within us?” (Luke XXIV). It also removes from the soul examples of locusts, by which all its restless and turbulent movements may be consumed, so that it may learn to do everything in due order.

When it has been sufficiently chastised according to its conduct, when it has recognized the author of its blows and, confessing that “it is the finger of God,” has received a small measure of knowledge, then especially it sees the darkness of its deeds and the gloom of its errors, and then it will deserve that the firstborn of Egypt be extinguished in it. For every soul, when it reaches the fullness of age and, as though the natural law had begun to defend its rights within it, brings forth its first impulses according to the desire of the flesh, produces those impulses which the inciting force of the fuel of desire or anger has stirred up. Hence the prophet speaks of Christ as possessing a singular privilege: “He shall eat butter and honey; before he does or utters evil, he shall choose the good” (Isa. VII); for before the child knows good or evil, he will resist wickedness so as to choose what is good.

David, however, says of himself: “Remember not the sins of my youth and my ignorances” (Ps. XXIV). Since, therefore, these first movements of the soul, brought forth according to the flesh, rush into sin, the firstborn of the Egyptians are rightly placed, in a moral interpretation, among the first things: they are extinguished if the conduct of the remaining life directs its course toward greater amendment. Thus, in the soul which the divine law has taken up from error and chastises, the firstborn of the Egyptians are destroyed—unless, after all this, it persists in unbelief and refuses to be joined to the Israelite people, so as to come out from the depths and escape unharmed, but remains in wickedness and descends like lead into exceedingly deep water. For according to Zechariah (Zech. V), wickedness sits upon a talent of lead; and therefore whoever remains in wickedness is submerged like lead into the depths.

[Col. 0217C] VERSE 7.—“Among all,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, in the Book of Expressions.) This is a most elegant expression: by “dog” he signified the lowest or least, whether among human beings or among cattle. In this way he emphasized how great the peace would be among the Hebrews, while the Egyptians cried out amid bitter bereavement.

VERSE 9, 10.—“Pharaoh will not listen to you,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 40 on Exodus.) It might seem that Pharaoh’s disobedience was necessary so that those signs might be multiplied, since they were usefully performed to terrify the people of God and, through that very distinction, to instruct them in piety. But this was God’s work, making good use of the wickedness of Pharaoh’s heart—not Pharaoh’s work, who abused God’s patience.

## CHAPTER XII

[Col. 0217D] VERSES 2–4.—“This month,” etc. (RABANUS.) This is April, called Nisan among the Hebrews and Ξανθικός (*Xanthikos*) among the Macedonians. April is so called as though from *aperilis*, because at that time the earth is opened to bring forth shoots, herbs, and flowers; or April derives its name from Venus, as though from *Aphroditis*, for Venus is called Aphrodite in Greek. The Hebrews regard this as the first month because its first day was the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April: the fourteenth day was the second, the thirteenth the third, and the twelfth the fourth—the days on which the sun and moon were created and when the first equinox occurred. For the sun in the east and the moon in the west divided the sphere of the world equally.

(STRABO.) This is Nisan according to the Hebrews, in which the world was made. Its full moon, after the spring equinox, must always be observed. In this month the people of Israel are freed from Egyptian servitude, and the human race is rescued from the power of the devil by the blood of Christ. On the tenth day of the month the lamb is taken; on the fourteenth it is sacrificed, because in the law the passion of Christ is prefigured and fulfilled when the grace of the Gospel shines forth. The number ten signifies the law because of the Decalogue; the number four signifies the four Gospels.

VERSES 5, 6.—“It shall be,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 42 on Exodus, vol. III.) That expression may cause difficulty, etc., down to the question of what was signified by that command.

“According to that rite,” etc. Allegorically. Because Christ assumed flesh from both the righteous and sinners, so that no one would despair of pardon. Or because Christ was a kid to the Jews, who said, “This man is a sinner” (John IX), but to us he is a lamb without blemish. Or because he appeared in the likeness of sinful flesh and died for sin, although he had no sin (1 Pet. II).

(STRABO.) On the tenth day of April he came to Jerusalem; on the following day he was received by the crowds with palm branches and divine praises. For the remaining three days he was kept under guard by the Jews until the fourteenth day, that is, until Thursday, when he dined with the apostles and was afterward betrayed.

VERSE 7.—“And they shall take of its blood,” etc. (GREGORY, Homily 22 on the Gospels, vol. II.) The blood is applied when it is imbibed not only by the mouth of the body but also by the mouth of the heart, etc., down to “because we carry the cross of his passion upon our forehead.”

VERSE 8.—“And they shall eat the flesh,” etc. (GREGORY, ibid.) We eat the lamb at night, etc., down to “for he sacrifices praise from leaven who prepares a sacrifice for God from plunder.”

“With bitter herbs,” etc. (GREGORY, ibid.) Wild lettuce is exceedingly bitter, etc., down to “so that he may know that everything is administered through the power of the Holy Spirit.”

VERSES 9–11.—“Its head with its feet,” etc. (GREGORY, ibid.) “The head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. XI). To devour the head of the lamb, etc., down to “no one should grow sluggish on the journey of this life, lest he lose his place in the homeland.”

(GREGORY OF NYSSA, *On the Life of Moses*.) By those coverings of things he admonishes us that through these riddles we should consider and understand that this life of ours is a kind of passage. Once we have entered it, we are continually compelled by a certain necessity toward its exit, and he wishes us to be prepared for that exit with our hands, feet, and all the other equipment required for a journey.

Therefore, lest our feet be injured by thorns on this difficult road of life, we ought to travel not barefoot but protected by sturdy shoes. The thorns which, fixed in the feet, not only hold and delay them but also kill, are sins. The hardness of the shoes protects against them—namely, a restrained, spare, and rigorous life, which weakens and breaks the points of the thorns by which sins proceed from a small and slight beginning into what lies ahead, until they utterly destroy us.

For undertaking this life, a trailing and flowing garment—that is, a luxurious and vicious manner of living, which spreads very widely—is an impediment. Therefore it must be drawn in and constrained by a kind of belt, lest it flow out in every direction. The belt is moderation and a careful manner of living, which teaches us to use things for necessity, not pleasure. The staff with which we drive away wild beasts and are sometimes supported is hope. The food set before us is cooked only by fire, because the faith signified by that food ought to be most ardent, possessing nothing moist or unstable.

**Passover.** In Hebrew it is *Pesach*, in Greek Πάσχα (*Pascha*), that is, “Passage,” because it was first celebrated when the children of Israel migrated from Egypt. We too must migrate from transient things to eternal things, from earthly things to heavenly things.

VERSES 12, 13.—“Against all the gods,” etc. The Hebrews relate that all the idols of Egypt were shattered on that night, as were the temples, either by an earthquake or by an inundation of the Nile. Allegorically, when we depart from the Egypt of error, the idols of error collapse for us, and the worship of every perverse doctrine is shaken.

VERSES 14–17.—“You shall have this day,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus* 43, vol. III.) “And you shall make this day lawful for your generations,” eternal or everlasting—the Greek word is αἰώνιον (*aionion*)—must not be understood in this way, etc., down to “simplicity must be preserved and wickedness avoided throughout the whole time of the present life.”

VERSES 18–20.—“In the first month, on the fourteenth,” etc. (RABANUS.) Mystically. The evening of the fourteenth day of the first month, on which Passover is celebrated and the sacrifice of the lamb is completed, signifies the laying aside of the old person and the beginning of the new, which begins in baptism, prefiguring Christ’s death. Hence: “As many of us as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death,” etc. (Gal. III). From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month until the evening of the twenty-first we are commanded [*they are commanded*] to eat unleavened bread for a complete week, because from receiving baptism until the end of life we ought to live simply and without deceit. Hence Peter: “Having put away all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy, as newborn infants,” etc. (1 Pet. II).

VERSE 21.—“The elders.” Note that God first communicates his commands not to children or young men but to elders, because wisdom belongs to the aged and prudence to length of days.

VERSE 22.—“And a bundle of hyssop,” etc. (STRABO.) Hyssop is a low-growing herb born among rocks, cleansing the chest and lungs; it signifies true humility, whose example Christ gave us in himself. We dip a bundle of hyssop in blood when, mindful of Christ’s humility, we strive to imitate him.

“Dip it in the blood,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 46 on Exodus.) It is asked what blood he means when he says “beside the door,” since the blood of that lamb is to be understood, by whose sacrifice Passover is celebrated. Does he command that it consequently be done in such a way that, although he has not said so, the same lamb should be killed beside the door? Or, what is more credible, did he say “from the blood which is beside the door” because the person who is to smear it will place beside the door the vessel itself in which he received the blood, [Col. 0220A] so that he may have it at hand while he dips?

VERSES 23–29.—“And he will not permit the destroyer,” etc. (STRABO.) Whether the destroyer was a good or an evil angel need not be investigated: whoever he was, he obeyed the Lord’s command. It should nevertheless be understood that evil angels are accustomed to inflict such plagues by God’s permission.

The tenth commandment is: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property,” etc. The tenth plague, the death of the firstborn, is opposed to this. Theft is prohibited by another commandment, and robbery is also condemned by it; for it is worse to seize something violently than secretly. Whoever wishes to take something openly or secretly has his commandment. But it is not permitted to covet one’s neighbor’s property, even if one seeks it by lawful succession.

Those who wish to possess another’s property as though justly, and seek to become heirs when its owner dies—when you praise the property left behind as though possessing it by right, God condemns you for desiring it unjustly. For when you seek to become someone’s heir, you do not wish him to have heirs, among whom nothing is dearer than the firstborn. Rightly, therefore, you are punished in your own firstborn: while coveting another’s property and seeking, as it were, the shadow of a legal claim, you lose the firstborn of your heart, which are the better things.

The firstborn is indeed faith. No one does good works in whom faith has not gone before. All good works are spiritual children, but among these the firstborn is faith. Therefore whoever secretly covets another’s property inwardly loses faith. You serve him not with charity but with deceit, as though loving someone whose death you desire so that you may succeed him.

[Col. 0220C] VERSES 30–33.—“For there was not a house,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 44 on Exodus.) Since only the firstborn died, how was there no house in which someone had not died? Or had this also been divinely arranged, so that in every house there would be firstborn upon whom the Egyptians—even those living in the land of Gessen—could be struck? For the firstborn here were human beings or animals, not the land: that is, human and animal firstborn died by a hidden angelic blow. Nothing had happened to earth or sky, as with the frogs, locusts, or darkness.

When the land of Gessen had been spared such plagues, the benefit extended to the Egyptians who lived there with the Hebrews; by this plague, however, all were struck.

VERSE 34.—“The flour that had been sprinkled,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) [Col. 0220D] Mystically. The children of Israel depart from Egypt without leaven, so that, as we leave this world, we may cast away the leaven of malice and wickedness and feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

VERSES 35, 36.—“And they asked,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 45.) This had already occurred before the deaths of the firstborn. But it is now repeated by recapitulation, for it was narrated when it happened. How could it now have been done amid such great mourning, unless someone should perhaps say that the Egyptians who lived with the Hebrews had also not been struck by this plague?

“Gold vessels,” etc. These signify teachings learned through the customs of the nations by a useful application of study; or precious souls from the nations, like vessels of gold and silver, together with garments—that is, bodies—which join themselves to the people of God so that they may once and for all be freed from this world as from Egypt.

VERSES 37–45.—“And they set out,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Exodus.) Whoever is preparing to depart from Egypt, whoever desires to leave behind the obscure deeds of the world and the darkness of errors, must first set out from Rameses, which is interpreted as “the shaking of the moth.” If you wish to come to the point at which God is your guide and the rock follows you, providing spiritual food and drink, depart from Rameses, lest you store up treasure where moth destroys and thieves break in, etc.

“If you wish to be perfect, go, sell everything you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven; then come, follow me” (Matt. VI). This means: depart from Rameses and follow Christ.

[Col. 0221B] “From Rameses to Succoth,” etc. (ORIGEN, ibid.) Let us see what the place of the camp is to which they come. From Rameses they came to Succoth, which is interpreted as “tents.” When, therefore, having left Egypt, you have shaken off the moths of every corruption and rejected the impulses of vices, you will dwell in tents—tents from which we do not wish to be stripped but to be clothed upon. Dwelling in tents indicates that the person who hastens toward God is unencumbered.

But we must not stop even there. The camp must also be moved from Succoth, and we must hurry to Othon, which is interpreted as “signs for them,” because there you will hear that God goes before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. This did not occur in Rameses or in Succoth, which are the second camp. The third camp is where divine signs take place. This was the three-day journey toward which Moses and Aaron hastened, while Pharaoh opposed them, saying, “Do not go farther.” He did not want the children of Israel to reach the place of signs, so that they could enjoy the mysteries of the third day. Hence Hosea VI: “God will revive us after two days; on the third day we shall rise and live in his sight.”

The first day for us is Christ’s passion; the second, when he descended into hell; the third, when he rose again. Therefore on the third day he went before them by day in a pillar of cloud and by night in a pillar of fire. It is necessary, then, that those who are baptized into Christ be baptized into his death, be buried with him, and rise on the third day—those whom he raised with himself and made to sit with him in the heavenly places (Rom. VI).

“About six hundred thousand,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 47.) It is asked whether the Hebrews reached such a number during those years in Egypt, etc., down to “that is, after Joseph’s death they were oppressed by harsh servitude.”

VERSES 46–51.—“Nor shall any of it,” etc. The bone of Christ was not broken on the cross, because when those who saw that he was already dead came, they did not break his legs. Or the strength of divinity in the flesh is not corrupted by blasphemy, because he is not merely a human being but true God.

## CHAPTER XIII

VERSES 2–8.—“Sanctify to me every firstborn,” etc. Because I killed all the firstborn of the Egyptians in your deliverance.

VERSES 9–12.—“And it shall be as a sign,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 48 on Exodus.) What does he mean when, giving the command concerning Passover, he says, etc., down to “otherwise grace would no longer be grace”?

VERSES 13–15.—“But every firstborn of human beings,” etc. (CYRIL.) He commands that human firstborn be redeemed, so as to prohibit murder—he who created all things to be incorruptible.

(GREGORY, *Moral Commentary*, Book XXVII, chapter 1.) The ass signifies uncleanness; the sheep, innocence. Therefore to exchange the firstborn of an ass for a sheep is to transform the beginnings of an unclean life through the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now bring forth by his actions things that can be placed upon God’s altar.

For we were all born in sin and conceived through the pleasure of the flesh, and we contracted original guilt. Hence we are also entangled in sins by our own will. But the person who turns from the wickedness of the flesh to innocence of heart exchanges the firstborn of the ass for a sheep, that is, the wickedness of his former life. Whoever ceases to be what he previously was and, having embraced purity of the flesh, guards innocence, has exchanged the firstborn of the ass for a sheep as an offering to God.

VERSE 16.—“And as something hung or attached.” The Jews, understanding this badly, used to bind *pictatia* or phylacteries around their heads, in which they kept the Ten Words written before their eyes.

VERSE 17.—“And when he had let them go,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moral Commentary*, Book XXIV, chapter 13.) Often those who are converted receive, at the very entrance of their conversion, tranquility of the flesh, the gifts of prophecy, the proclamations of doctrine, miracles of signs, or the grace of healings. Later they are wearied by severe trials of temptation, from which they had believed themselves free. For if the bitterness of temptation assailed them at the beginning, they would easily return to the vices from which they had only recently withdrawn.

Therefore, when those departing from Egypt are nearby, wars are held back from them: when people leave the world, a certain tranquility is first shown to them, lest, disturbed in their very tenderness and beginning, they return to what they had abandoned. First they experience the sweetness of security; first they are nourished by the quiet of peace. But after they have come to know that sweetness, they endure the struggles of temptation all the more tolerably, the more deeply they have learned in God what they should love.

VERSES 18–20.—“God did not lead them,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 49.) Here it is shown that everything ought to be done which can rightly be done through prudent counsel, in order to avoid what is adverse, even when God is most openly helping (Letter to Damasus, vol. I).

“And the children of Israel went up armed,” etc. (JEROME.) Aquila, who interprets word for word—not contentiously, as some think, but diligently—where the Septuagint put, “And the children of Israel went up from the land of Egypt in the fifth generation,” translated, “And the children of Israel went up armed from the land of Egypt,” although, instead of what we call “armed,” the ambiguity of the Greek expression may permit “equipped” or “provided,” on account of the goods with which they despoiled the Egyptians.

But where the Septuagint wrote “in the fifth generation,” those who carefully examined the books of the Hebrews report that it is written not “fifth” but “five,” so that the meaning is: “Five went up from the land of Egypt.” Since this seemed difficult to understand, the word “generation” was added. Aquila, however, is said to have translated this passage, as well as the others, and especially this one, literally, as all the benches of the synagogues unanimously attest.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 53.) “In the fifth generation,” etc. Whether he wishes to reckon a generation as one hundred years, etc., down to “Naasson begot Salmon.”

VERSES 21, 22.—“The Lord went before them,” etc. (ORIGEN.) When the mystery of the third day has been received by you, God will begin to lead you and show you the way of salvation.

(GREGORY.) In the fire there is terror; in the cloud, the gentle consolation of vision. Day signifies the life of the righteous; night, that of the sinner. Hence Ephesians V: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord,” etc.

By day the pillar was shown through the cloud, and by night through fire, because almighty God appears gentle to the righteous and terrible to the impious. Coming to judgment, he soothes the former through the gentleness of kindness, but terrifies the latter through the severity of justice.

Alternatively, the pillar of cloud went before the people in the wilderness, and the brightness of fire shone not by day but by night. For Christ, by offering the example of his conduct as a guide to those who follow him, shone with no light for those who were confident in their own righteousness; but for those who acknowledged the darkness of their sins, he shed the fire of his love.

Christ is cloud and pillar because he is upright, firm, and supports our weakness; because he shines by night but does not shine by day, so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind (John IX). The mystery of Christ is also manifest as though by day, in the flesh as in a cloud; but at the judgment it will be as terror in the night. For then there will be great tribulation: he will shine like fire for the righteous and burn like fire for the unjust.

## CHAPTER XIV

VERSE 2.—“Pi-hahiroth, which is between Migdol,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Exodus.) Let us see which road is commanded to be chosen. “Turning from Othon,” he says, “make your journey between Epauleum and Migdol, which is opposite Baal-zephon,” etc. *Epauleum* is interpreted as “twisted ascent”; *Migdol* as “tower”; *Baal-zephon* as “ascent of a lookout” or “having a lookout.”

Perhaps God seemed to promise that he would show a level and easy road, but it is an ascent, and a twisted one. For the road by which one advances toward virtues is not easy; one ascends narrowly and with difficulty. Hence Matthew VII: “Narrow and constricted is the way that leads to life.”

The road, then, along which one proceeds is a twisted ascent and an ascent of a lookout, or one having a lookout. The ascent pertains to deeds; the lookout to faith. It is therefore shown that there is much difficulty and labor both in deeds and in faith. Many temptations confront those who wish to do the things of God, and many obstacles.

In faith also you will find many crooked things: very many questions, objections from heretics, and contradictions from unbelievers. This, then, is the road to be traveled by those who follow the Lord.

There is also a tower on this road, of which Luke XIV says: “Who among you, wishing to build a tower, does not first sit down and calculate the cost, whether he has enough to complete it?” This is the tower, lofty and exalted through these virtues. When Pharaoh saw it, he said: “They are wandering.”

In Pharaoh’s eyes, whoever follows God is said to wander, because the road of wisdom is twisted and has many difficulties and winding turns. If you confess one invisible Father, and his one only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, and one Holy Spirit, this seems twisted, difficult, and incredible to unbelievers. If you say that the God of majesty is the crucified Son of Man who descended from heaven, these things seem twisted and difficult. Whoever hears this—unless he hears it with faith—says, “They are wandering.”

But remain fixed in this faith, knowing that God has shown you this road of faith, the one who says: “Taking up the camp from Othon, place it between Epauleum and Migdol.”

[Col. 0224B] “He would have been,” etc. (ORIGEN.) Fleeing Egypt, you come to the ascent of works and faith and to the building of a tower. You come to the sea, and waves of temptations meet you. Hence 2 Timothy III: “All who wish to live piously in Christ will suffer persecution,” because our life upon earth is a time of temptation.

But if you follow Moses, that is, the law of God, Egypt pursues you. See, however, what will happen: “The angel of the Lord,” it says, “who went before the camp of Israel, rose up and went behind them.” He also raised the pillar of cloud from before them and stood behind them, and it entered between the camp of the Egyptians and that of Israel.

This pillar of cloud became a wall for the people of God. It imposed darkness upon the Egyptians; the pillar of fire was not transferred to the Egyptians so that they might see the light, but the pillar of cloud, so that they might remain in darkness, because they loved darkness rather than light.

And you, therefore, if you withdraw from the Egyptians, if you flee from the power of demons, see how much assistance is prepared for you, provided that you remain strong in faith. Let neither the cavalry and chariots of the Egyptians terrify you, nor let you complain against the law of God—that is, against Moses—saying: “Were there no graves in Egypt, that you have brought us out?”

VERSES 11, 12.—“Perhaps there were no graves,” etc.? (ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Exodus.) These are the words of a spirit failing under temptation. Blessed is the person who receives temptations in such a way that no thought of doubt steals upon him. Peter is also told in Matthew XIII: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” These are words of temptation and weakness.

Otherwise the statement is false: it is better to die in the wilderness than to serve the Egyptians. For whoever dies in the wilderness, by the very fact that he has been separated from the Egyptians—that is, from the rulers of darkness and from the power of Satan—has made some progress, even if he could not reach completion. It is better for one seeking a perfect life to die on the road than never to set out.

Hence the opinion of those who, while describing the road of virtue as difficult and dangerous, judge that it should not even be begun appears to be mistaken. It is better to die on the road than to be killed among the Egyptians and overwhelmed by false and bitter waves.

VERSES 13, 14.—“For the Egyptians whom you now see,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 5 on Exodus.) “As you have seen the Egyptians today, you shall never again see them for all eternity.” But how should these words be understood, since the Israelites later saw the Egyptians? Or is it because those who were seeing them then did not see them afterward, since both those who pursued them died and all these others died, each on the day of his death? Their descendants, however, saw the descendants of the others.

Or should “you shall not see them as you see them today” be understood to mean: not as persecutors and enemies, so that there is no difficulty either concerning the eternal time mentioned here? For even if they will see one another at the time of the resurrection, they will not see one another in the way they do today.

VERSES 15–17.—“Why do you cry to me?” etc. (GREGORY.) Our words do not make voices in the ears of God, but our desires. If we ask for eternal life with our mouths but do not desire it in our hearts, while crying out we remain silent. But if we desire it in our hearts, while silent with our mouths we cry out. Thus, in the wilderness, when the people resounded with shouting and Moses was silent amid the noise of their words, he was heard in silence, and it was said to him: “Why do you cry to me?” For the hidden cry of desire does not reach human ears but fills the divine ones.

(ORIGEN, as above.) No voice of Moses is heard, and the Lord says: “Why do you cry to me?” I would like to know how the saints cry out to God without a voice. The Apostle says in Galatians IV: “God will give the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, ‘Abba, Father.’” And he adds: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.” Again, in Romans VIII: “He who searches the hearts knows what the Spirit desires.” Thus, when the Holy Spirit asks in silence, the cry of the saints is heard.

Moses is commanded to strike the sea with his staff, so that it may yield to the people of God as they enter, and so that the waters which were feared, becoming a wall on the right and left, may not only know no destruction but also provide protection. The fluid receives solidity, and the floor of the sea dries into dust. Understand the goodness of the Creator: if you obey his will and follow his law, he compels the elements to serve you contrary to their nature.

I have heard from our elders that separate divisions of water were made for each tribe, with a road belonging to each one. This is shown by what is said in Psalm CXXXV: “He divided the Red Sea into divisions,” etc. And elsewhere, in Psalm LXVII: “There was Benjamin, the younger, in astonishment; the princes of Judah, their rulers; the princes of Zebulun and the princes of Naphtali.” The entrance of each tribe seems to be enumerated separately.

The Apostle says that baptism was completed in Moses, in the cloud and in the sea, so that you who are baptized into Christ in water and in the Spirit may know that the Egyptians are pursuing you and trying to call you back into servitude—namely, the rulers of the world and the spiritual powers of wickedness whom you previously served.

But you descend into the water and emerge unharmed and new, washed clean of the filth of sins and prepared to sing a new song. The pursuing Egyptians are drowned in the abyss, even if they seem to ask Jesus not to drown them again in the abyss.

(ID.) Alternatively, if you flee Egypt—that is, the darkness of ignorance—and follow Moses, that is, the law of God, and the sea meets you—that is, the waves of those who contradict—then you too must strike the opposing waves with the staff, that is, with the word of the law and vigilance toward the Scriptures. Open a road for yourself through your disputation against your opponents, and the waves will yield to the victor.

While those who previously contradicted look on in wonder and astonishment, cut a straight road of faith through the lawful lines of argument. Advance so far through the word of doctrine that your hearers, whom you have instructed in the words of the law, now rise up against the Egyptians like waves of the sea and not only attack but overcome and extinguish them.

For the person who does not perform the works of darkness extinguishes Egypt; so does the person who lives not carnally but spiritually, who either drives filthy thoughts from his heart or does not admit them at all, according to Ephesians VI: “Taking up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one.”

In this way we can also see the Egyptians dead today, and Pharaoh himself, if we live with such faith that God may soon crush Satan beneath our feet through Jesus Christ.

VERSES 19, 20.—“And the angel of God, who was rising up,” etc. (STRABO.) The angel, whose name means “messenger,” signifies teachers who announce to us the commands of life. Together with the cloud—that is, knowledge of the Scriptures—they go before the camp of Israel, that is, the Church, because they preside with knowledge of the Scriptures.

When the Egyptians come upon them, he moves to the rear, because in a time of persecution they place themselves in the way on behalf of those subject to them. The cloud was dark to the Egyptians but bright to the Hebrews.

VERSES 21–31.—“All night,” etc. Because throughout the entire period of this life, which is signified by night, the grace of the Holy Spirit makes the waters of baptism passable for the faithful, so that they may cross from spiritual Egypt into the land of promise; but it drowns the army of their enemies.

(ISIDORE.) The Red Sea signifies baptism, consecrated by the blood of Christ. The enemies pursuing from behind die with their king, because past sins are wiped away in baptism and the devil is suffocated. The Egyptians press on as far as the sea, and sins as far as baptism.

After crossing the Red Sea, the people sing while the unbelieving enemies are submerged, and the faithful, rising from the washing with their sins extinguished, sing a hymn, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously,” etc.

## CHAPTER XV

VERSE 1.—“Then Moses sang,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 6 on Exodus.) We read many songs in the Scriptures, but this is the first of all to be sung after the Egyptians and Pharaoh have been submerged and victory has been won.

It is the custom of the saints, whenever the adversary is conquered—for they know that the victory was achieved not by their own strength but by God’s grace—to offer God a hymn of glorification. Yet the singers also take tambourines in their hands, as is reported concerning Mary and Aaron.

You too, therefore, if you cross the Red Sea, if you see the Egyptians submerged and Pharaoh hurled into the abyss, can gratefully sing a hymn to God and say: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously,” etc. You will say this more worthily if you have a tambourine in your hand—that is, if you have crucified your flesh with its vices and desires.

“For he has triumphed gloriously,” etc. (ORIGEN.) It is not enough to say, “He has been glorified”; for being glorified is one thing, and being glorified gloriously is another. When Christ assumed flesh for our sake, he was glorified: he came to seek what had been lost. Yet he was not glorified gloriously, because he had neither appearance nor beauty.

He was glorified when he came to the cross and endured death. Hence John XVII: “Father, the hour has come; glorify your Son,” etc. His crucifixion was therefore also a glory, in which he was glorified—not gloriously, but humbly. Hence Philippians II: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.” And Wisdom II: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.”

In these things, then, he was glorified concerning himself humbly, not gloriously. Hence Luke XXIV: “Was it not necessary that Christ should suffer and so enter into his glory?” When he comes in the glory of the Father and of the angels to judge the earth, and destroys the true Pharaoh—that is, the devil—with the breath of his mouth, when he shines forth in the majesty of the Father, then he will be glorified gloriously, when all honor the Son as they honor the Father.

“He has been magnified; he has cast horse and rider into the sea,” etc. This is shown in the signs performed in Egypt. But he was magnified gloriously because he submerged Pharaoh and his army. Or he was magnified by performing miracles before his passion, by preaching, and by dying on the cross; but he was magnified gloriously when he rose victorious, with the devil conquered and hell despoiled.

**Horse, etc.** (ORIG.) The people who persecute us are horses; and all who are born in the flesh are, figuratively, horses, and they have their own riders. There are some whom the Lord rides, and they go throughout the whole earth; concerning them it is said in Habakkuk III: “Your cavalry is salvation.” Others are ridden by the devil and his angels. Judas was a horse, and when he had the Lord as his rider, he belonged to the cavalry of salvation: for, sent with the other apostles, he bestowed salvation on the sick and healing on the afflicted. But when he submitted himself to the devil, who entered into him after the morsel, he became Satan’s horse; led by that one’s reins, he rode against the Lord. All persecutors, therefore, are neighing horses, but they have evil angels as riders, by whom they are driven, and for that reason they are fierce. If you see your persecutor raging excessively, know that he is being spurred on by his rider, and that is why he is savage and brutish.

**VERSE 2.**—“This is my God,” etc. (ORIG.) He will therefore be both my God and the God of my father. Our Father, who made and begot us, is Christ, who said in John XVI: “I am going to my Father,” etc. If, then, I recognize that he is my God, I will glorify him; and if I also recognize that he is my Father’s God, I will exalt him. For the higher understanding is how Christ, in order to bind together and unite the truth of the one God, calls his God the one whom by nature he knows as Father.

**VERSE 3.**—“The Lord is like a warrior,” etc. (ORIG.) Another text reads: “The Lord will crush wars.” Amos IX: “The Lord is his name.” He crushes not only visible battles, but also those which we wage against principalities, powers, and the rulers of this darkness. “The Lord is his name,” and there is no creature whose Lord he is not. “Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he cast into the sea; his chosen riders, his three-riders, he drowned in the Red Sea.” Pharaoh, as more powerful in wickedness and holding the kingdom of evil, drives chariots. It is not enough for him to ride one horse; he drives several at once and compels them with a twisted whip. When you see people who are more shameful in lust, more savage in cruelty, and more hideous in greed, know that they belong to Pharaoh’s chariots, which he subjugates to his own car. In them he is borne and flies across the open fields of crimes, with the reins let loose. There are other chosen riders, namely, for wickedness.

(ORIG.) They are called *ternistratores*—“three-riders”—because there are three ways by which human beings sin. They sin in deed, in speech, and in thought. They are therefore called three-riders individually because they possess these three ways of sinning in us, and they are always watching and acting by stealth, so that one may draw an evil word from the wretched human being, another may extort an unrighteous deed, and another may seize a most wicked thought. Finally, the place where the seed of God’s word falls and perishes is described in three ways: beside the road, among thorns, and on rocky ground. Conversely, the good earth produces a threefold harvest: sixtyfold, a hundredfold, and thirtyfold (Matthew XIII). For there is also a threefold way of doing good, since something good is done either by deed, by thought, or by word. Hence the Apostle says in I Corinthians III: “Who builds upon the foundation with silver, gold, and precious stones,” indicating a threefold way of good things; while he calls the way of evil “wood, hay, and straw.” These three-riders, then, are wicked angels, who watch along these ways in order to lead anyone into sin. The Lord will plunge them into the Red Sea, hand them over to the fiery waves on the day of judgment, and cover them with the sea of punishments.

**VERSES 5–6.**—“They went down into the depths like a stone.” (ORIG.) Such people were not stones from which children of Abraham could be raised, but stones that loved the deep and liquid element—that is, the bitter and fleeting pleasure of present things. Hence it is said of them: “They sank like lead in the mighty waters.” Sinners are heavy, and iniquity is said to sit upon a talent of lead. Therefore the wicked sink into the depths like lead, while the saints walk upon the waters because they are light and are not weighed down by the burden of sin. Christ walked upon the waters, for he truly committed no sin. Peter also walked, but he hesitated briefly; he had some lead in him, and therefore it was said to him in Matthew XIV: “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”

All, therefore, are saved through fire, so that if something of the appearance of lead has perhaps been admitted, the fire may boil it down and dissolve it, so that all may become the finest gold—for the gold of that land which the saints will possess is excellent—and just as a furnace tests gold, so tribulation tests righteous people. Everyone must therefore come to the smelting furnace. For God sits and melts and purifies the children of Judah. If someone has brought many good works and little iniquity, that little is dissolved and purified as by fire, and all that remains is pure gold. If someone has brought more lead, more of him is burned, so that he may be boiled down more thoroughly, and so that, even if little, at least some purified gold may remain. But whoever comes entirely of lead sinks like lead in the mighty waters.

**VERSES 7–10.**—“You sent forth your anger,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus* 55.) Another text reads: “You sent your spirit, and the sea covered them,” etc., up to: “Scripture merely commands without the assistance of grace.”

**VERSE 11.**—“Who is like you?” etc. (ORIG., as above.) He does not compare God with the idols of the nations, nor with the demons who falsely appropriate for themselves the name of gods. Rather, he calls those gods who are named so through grace and participation in God, according to the saying of Psalm LXXXI: “I said, You are gods.” And in the same place: “God stood in the assembly of gods.”

But although these beings are capable of God and appear to be granted this name through grace, no one is like him in power or nature. As for the statement, “We shall be like him,” this likeness is referred not to nature but to grace. Thus a painting is like the one whose image is expressed in it, insofar as grace is concerned, but is far unlike him in substance. The former is the appearance of flesh and the beauty of a living body; the latter is a coloring of pigments and wax laid upon senseless panels.

No one, therefore, among the gods is like the Lord: he is invisible, incorporeal, unchangeable, without beginning and without end. There is no creator of all things except the Father, who creates all things through the Son and sanctifies all things in the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0229C] **VERSES 12–13.**—“You stretched out,” etc. (ORIG.) The statement troubles me: “You stretched out your right hand, and the earth devoured them,” as though the reason they were devoured by the earth were that he stretched out his right hand. If you consider how the Lord, exalted upon the cross, stretched out his hand all day toward the unbelieving but contradicting people, and how death by iniquity overwhelmed the unbelieving people who cried, “Crucify him, crucify him” (John XIX), you will understand how he stretched out his right hand and the earth devoured them.

Yet there is no reason for complete despair. If the one who has been devoured repents, he can be vomited out like Jonah. At some time the earth was devouring all of us and holding us in the innermost places of hell. Therefore Christ descended not only to the earth but also to the lower regions of the earth. There he found us devoured and sitting in the shadow of death. From there he brought us out—not merely from the earth, so that we might not be devoured again, but he also prepared the kingdom of heaven.

(ORIG.) Even today the earth devours the wicked: those who are always thinking about earthly things, doing earthly things, speaking about the earth, quarrelling over it, desiring the earth, placing their hope in it, not looking toward heaven, not thinking about the future, not fearing God’s judgment, and not desiring his promises. When you see such a person, say that the earth has devoured him. And if you see someone given over to lust and bodily pleasures, in whom the mind has no power but desire possesses everything, say that the earth has devoured him.

**VERSES 14–15.**—“The nations heard and were angry; pains seized the inhabitants of Philistia,” etc. (ORIG.) As far as the historical account is concerned, it is clear that none of these nations was present at the wonders. How, then, were the Philistines, Moabites, Edomites, and the other nations whom he lists terrified with fear or anger?

Spiritually, however, you will find that the Philistines—that is, “those falling by the cup”—and Edom, namely “the earthly,” tremble. Their princes run about and are afraid, constrained by pains, when they see their kingdoms, which are in hell, penetrated by the one who descended into the lower regions of the earth in order to rescue those who were possessed by death. They fear and tremble because they have perceived the greatness of his arm. The inhabitants of Canaan—that is, “the changeable and unstable”—also melted away when they saw their kingdoms shaken and the strong one bound.

Let fear and trembling therefore come upon them. The demons tremble and fear the cross of Christ, by which they were triumphed over and their principalities and power were stripped from them. Fear and trembling will therefore fall upon them when they see the sign of the cross firmly fixed in us, and the greatness of the arm which the Lord extended upon the cross, as Isaiah LXV says: “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a people who did not believe,” etc. They will fear you in no other way, nor will your trembling fall upon them, unless they see the cross of Christ in you, so that you may say: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians VI).

**VERSES 15–16.**—“Let them become immovable like a stone,” etc. (ORIG.) To become like a stone is not to be stone by nature. For something would not become what it already was. We have said this on account of those who claim that Pharaoh and the Egyptians were of an evil nature and were brought to this condition not through freedom of choice, and who accuse God the Creator as cruel, as though he turned human beings into stones.

He did not say merely, “Let them become like stones,” and stop, but established a time and measure of domination: namely, “until your people pass through.” The earlier people who existed before us became like a hard and unbelieving stone—not so that the nature of stone might remain in them, but until the people whom the Lord acquired should pass through. Hence Romans XI: “A partial blindness has happened to Israel, until the fullness of the nations should enter, and then Israel would be saved.” Through unbelief Israel became like a stone. Hence Matthew III: “For God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham.”

But since he is the creator of all things, how is he said to have acquired what is unquestionably his? For it is said in the song of Deuteronomy: “Is he not himself the Lord your God, who made and created you and acquired you?” (Deuteronomy XXXII.) It seems that each person acquires what was not his.

Hence heretics say concerning the Savior that those whom he acquired were not his. They say that, having paid a price, he bought the human beings whom the Creator had made, and they maintain that each person certainly buys what is not his own. For the Apostle says in I Corinthians VII: “You were bought with a price.”

But hear the Prophet: “You were sold because of your sins, and because of your iniquities I dismissed your mother” (Isaiah L). We are all therefore God’s creatures, but each person is sold by his own sins and departs from the Creator. We are God’s, insofar as we were created by him; but we have become servants of the devil insofar as we were sold by our sins.

When Christ came, he redeemed us, servants of the devil, to whom we sold ourselves by sinning. Thus he appears to have received back as his own those whom he created, and to have acquired as outsiders those who, by sinning, had acquired an alien master. Yet he is rightly said to have redeemed us, since he gave his blood as the price for us.

But what did the devil give as such a price by which he might buy us? Homicide is the devil’s money, for he was a murderer from the beginning. You committed homicide: you received the devil’s money. The same must be said of adultery, sacrilege, theft, false witness, and similar acts. With this money he buys and makes his servants all who receive however much from this kind of revenue belonging to him.

**VERSE 17.**—“You will bring them in and plant them,” etc. (ORIG.) The Lord does not wish to plant us in Egypt, nor in fallen and lowly places, but on the mountain of his inheritance. Concerning this planting the Prophet says in Psalm LXXIX: “You brought a vine out of Egypt; you drove out the nations and planted it. You were the guide of its journey before it; you planted its roots, and it filled the earth. Its shadow covered the mountains, and its branches the cedars of God.”

Do you see how and where God plants? He does not plant in valleys, but on mountains, in high and exalted places. Those whom he brings out of Egypt—that is, from the world—to the faith, he does not wish to place again in lowly places. Rather, he wishes their way of life to be exalted, and for them to dwell on mountains and in high places, not to crawl along the earth.

He no longer wishes his vine to have its fruit cast down in a low place, but wants its shoots to be led upward, placed on high, and made into layers—not upon lowly trees, but upon the lofty and highest cedars of God, namely the prophets and apostles. If we are joined to them, and if the vine which God transferred from Egypt spreads our shoots through their branches, and if, joined to them, we become layers bound together by the bonds of mutual love, we will bear abundant fruit. For every tree that does not produce good fruit will be cut down and thrown into the fire (Matthew III).

**“In your most firmly established dwelling,” etc.** (ORIG.) “In the habitation which you have prepared, O Lord.” See the Lord’s merciful goodness: he does not wish to lead you into labor, nor does he wish you yourself to make a dwelling for yourself. He will bring you into a dwelling already prepared. Hence John IV: “Others have labored, and you have entered into their labors.”

**“Your sanctuary,” etc.** (ORIG.) “Your sanctimonium, O Lord,” etc. *Sanctimonium* is called the tabernacle of God, or the temple, because it sanctifies those who approach. Hebrews IX says that this was not made by human hands but by the hand of God. For your sake, therefore, God both plants and builds; he becomes farmer and builder, so that you may lack nothing. Hence the Apostle says in I Corinthians III: “You are God’s cultivation, God’s building.”

What, then, is this *sanctimonium* prepared not by human hands but by God? Proverbs IX: “Wisdom built herself a house”—that is, the flesh of Christ—not by human hands, that is, not by human work. The temple of the flesh is built in the Virgin; but the stone cut without hands grew and became a great mountain (Daniel II). This is the sanctuary of the assumed flesh, cut without hands and without human work from the mountain of human nature and the substance of flesh.

**VERSE 18.**—“The Lord will reign,” etc. (ORIG.) “O Lord, who reigns unto the age, and unto the age, and beyond.” Whenever “forever” is said, a length of time is indicated, but some end is also implied. If it is said “into another age,” something longer is indicated, but an end is nevertheless posited. And whenever “ages of ages” are mentioned, perhaps some limit is indicated—unknown to us, certainly, but established by God.

But when he adds here “and still further,” he leaves no sense of any limit or end. Whatever you may conceive, in which you think the end consists, the prophetic word always says to you, “and still further.” It is as though it said to you: “Do you think the Lord will reign into the age of the age? And still further, do you think he will reign into the ages of ages?” “And still further.” Whatever you may say about the duration of his reign, the prophet always says to you, “and still further.”

**VERSE 19.**—“But the children of Israel,” etc. (ORIG.) And you, if you are a son of Israel, can walk on dry ground in the midst of the sea. If you are in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, walking like the sunlight in the midst of sinners, the moisture of sin will not soak into you. As you pass through this world, no wave of lust will sprinkle you, and no heat of desire will beat against you.

The one who is Egypt and follows Pharaoh is overwhelmed by the waves of vices. But the one who follows Christ and walks as he walked has water become a wall for him on the right and on the left. He himself proceeds along the middle way; on dry ground he turns neither to the right nor to the left, until he comes out into freedom and sings a hymn of victory to the Lord, saying: “Let us sing to the Lord,” etc.

**VERSES 20–21.**—“The timbrel.” (STRABO.) According to Jerome, this is a kind of trumpet having at its top a reed or pipe through which it produces a sonorous voice. According to the same author, the chorus is a simple skin with two pipes: through one it is inflated, and through the other it produces sound. By both, therefore, the narrow understanding of the Old Law is signified. Its brevity and smallness are shown by the fact that it is carried in a woman’s hand.

According to Cassiodorus, the timbrel is a skin stretched between two pieces of wood, by which the mortification of the flesh is signified. The chorus is a multitude singing together, and it is called *chorus* as the singing of people of the same age. Since all the voices in a chorus resound equally, charity is signified by it, through which we are all one in Christ.

Whoever, therefore, renders praises to God in jubilation should do so in the chorus—that is, in charity—and in the timbrel—that is, in the mortification of the flesh. Hence Psalm CL: “Praise him with timbrel and chorus,” etc.

**VERSE 22.**—“Moses brought Israel,” etc. Those who have been baptized are led through the world as through a desert after the crossing of the Red Sea. They do not yet possess the promised homeland, but hope and wait with perseverance while they are wearied by laborious and dangerous temptation. But, lest they turn back in their hearts toward Egypt, Christ does not abandon them there either; for that pillar also does not depart.

**VERSES 23–24.**—“And they came,” etc. (ORIG., *Homily 6 on Exodus*.) After the crossing of the Red Sea, after the choruses and timbrels, after the triumphant hymns, they come to Marah—to bitter water, which the people could not drink. They come to the danger of thirst. But Moses cried out to the Lord, and God showed him a piece of wood, by which the water was made sweet. There God established ordinances and judgment for him, precisely where there was bitterness and thirst and, what is more serious, in the abundance of waters there was no other place more suitable or appropriate.

Moreover, when it says that God showed him a piece of wood, and that he put it into the water and it became sweet, it seems almost as though God could not make the water sweet without wood, or Moses did not know the wood. But if the Law is understood according to the letter, it too is bitter Marah. For what is as bitter as for a child to receive the wound of circumcision on the eighth day, and for tender infancy to endure the severity of iron?

The people of God have a bitter cup in the Law—not the people who were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, but those who cannot drink and taste in spirit and water, nor endure the bitterness of sacrifices, nor the observance of the Sabbath. But if God shows the wood to be cast into this bitterness, the water of the Law becomes sweet and drinkable.

Proverbs III: “Wisdom is a tree of life to all who embrace it.” If, therefore, the wood of Christ’s wisdom is cast into the Law, showing how circumcision, the Sabbath, the law of leprosy, and similar matters should be understood, the bitterness of the Law is changed into the sweetness of spiritual understanding, so that the people who have abandoned idols and fled to God can drink.

If someone hears the Law teaching about sacrifices, he immediately recoils and cannot drink. Into this bitterness, therefore—that is, the letter of the Law—God placed ordinances and testimonies, as though he enclosed [or stored] the treasures of his wisdom and knowledge in some vessel. Hence: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels” (II Corinthians III).

Therefore, so that this water may be drinkable, God shows the wood to be cast into it, so that whoever drinks may not die or feel its bitterness. If someone drinks without the tree of life—that is, without the mystery of the cross, without faith in Christ, and without spiritual understanding—he will die of bitterness. Hence: “The letter kills”—that is, the water of Marah, if it is drunk without being changed and turned into sweetness.

**VERSES 25–27.**—“He showed it to him,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus* 57.) Was it a kind of wood possessing this power? Or could God, who performed such great wonders, have done it with any piece of wood? Yet the wording seems to signify what was said: “He showed it to him,” as though the wood already possessed this property. Unless perhaps it was a place where no wood could be found at all, so that the very fact that the Lord showed Moses a piece of wood where none existed was a divine act of assistance, and by means of the wood made the waters sweet, prefiguring the glory and grace of the cross. But even in such a piece of wood, whom should anyone praise except the Creator and the one who showed it?

**“There he established ordinances for him.”** (ORIG., *Homily 7 on Exodus*.) Why did he add: “After God had established ordinances and judgments for him, there he tested him, saying: If you will hear the voice of the Lord your God”? It seems to explain why he gave them ordinances and judgments: namely, to test whether they would hear the voice of the Lord their God and keep his commandments.

For, as regards the earlier people, what good or perfect thing could be commanded to those who murmured and contradicted, who shortly afterward, having forgotten God’s wonders, turned to idols? Ordinances are therefore given by which they may be tested. Hence: “I gave you commandments and ordinances that were not good, by which they shall not live” (Ezekiel XX).

When tested by the commandments, they are not found faithful. Therefore it was discovered that what had been for life became for them a commandment leading to death. The same commandment, if kept, produces life; if not kept, death. Thus the commandments are called “not good” for those who do not keep them, and commandments “by which they shall not live.”

But when the wood of the cross is added, when they are turned into sweetness, understood spiritually, and kept, the commandments become commandments of life.

**“All the sickness which I brought upon Egypt I will not bring upon you.”** It seems to say that if someone keeps the commandments, he will suffer no illness—that is, neither fevers nor other bodily pains. Yet the entirely righteous Job, full of every form of piety, is covered from head to foot with a most grievous ulcer.

But the righteous do not have those illnesses which the Egyptians have. Egypt is the world. To love the world and the things that are in the world is an Egyptian sickness. To observe months, to follow the courses of the stars, to serve the flesh, to devote oneself to lust, and to occupy oneself with pleasures is an Egyptian sickness.

[Col. 0234C] **“And they came,” etc.** (ORIG., same work.) The people are not led first to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water containing no bitterness, but much pleasantness because of the density of the palms. Rather, they are first led to salt and bitter waters, which, after being sweetened by the wood shown by the Lord, bring them to the springs.

If we follow history alone, it does not greatly edify us to know which place they reached first and which second. First, however, the people are led to the letter of the Law, from which, while it remains in its bitterness, they cannot withdraw. When it has been sweetened by the tree of life and understood spiritually, they pass from the Old Testament to the New, and to the twelve apostolic springs, where seventy palm trees are found.

For the twelve apostles alone did not preach the faith of Christ, but also the other seventy, through whom the world recognized the palms of Christ’s victory. It is therefore not enough for the people of God to drink the water of Marah, even though it has been sweetened through the tree of life. The Old Testament alone is not sufficient to drink; one must come to the New, from which one drinks without hesitation or difficulty.

Even now the Jews are at Marah—that is, at the bitter waters. God has not yet shown them the wood by which they are sweetened, because unless they believe, they will not understand (Isaiah VII).

**CHAPTER XVI**

**VERSE 2.**—“And the whole congregation of Israel murmured,” etc. (ORIG., *Homily 7 on Exodus*.) O ungrateful people! They desire Egypt, although they saw the Egyptians destroyed; and they desire the flesh of Egypt, although they see the flesh of the Egyptians given to fish and birds!

They murmur against Moses—indeed, against God. But at first they are forgiven, and a second time, and perhaps a third. But if they do not cease, and persist, hear what follows. It is related in the Book of Numbers (Numbers XXI), and the Apostle repeats the same thing, saying (I Corinthians X): “Neither murmur, as some of them murmured, and perished by serpents.” These things were written for us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.

But if we do not cease murmuring and complaining against God, we will incur a similar danger of offense or receive a similar example. For when we complain about unseasonable weather, the infertility of crops, the scarcity of rain, the prosperity of some and the misfortune of others, we murmur against God. These things are forgiven at first, but those who persist are severely punished, because serpents will be sent among them—that is, they will be handed over to unclean and poisonous spirits, who will consume the innermost parts of the heart with hidden bites.

(ORIG.) For the correction of readers, the people’s sin is indicated: they murmured and were ungrateful for divine benefits, although they had received the heavenly manna. “In the second month, on the fifteenth day of the month”—something that was not written without reason. Recall the laws of Passover that were given (Numbers IX), and you will find that this was the time appointed for celebrating a second Passover for those who were unclean in soul or occupied with foreign business.

Those who were not unclean in soul or traveling far away celebrated Passover on the fourteenth day of the first month. Those who were far away and unclean celebrated the second Passover at this time, when the manna descended from heaven. On the day when the first Passover is celebrated, manna does not descend, but on the day when the second is celebrated. The first Passover is that of the Jewish people; the second is ours.

For we were unclean in soul, since we worshiped idols; we were strangers and far away, guests and foreigners to the covenants of God, etc. (Ephesians II). But manna is given from heaven not on the day when the first Passover is celebrated, but on the day when the second is celebrated. For “the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI) did not come to those who were celebrating the first solemnity, but to us, who received the second. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed,” and he, the true human being, the bread from heaven, descended (I Corinthians V).

For the moment, let us see what is shown to have taken place on this day: “On the fourteenth day of the second month the people murmured,” etc.

**VERSE 3.**—“We sat by the pots,” etc. They had flocks of sheep and herds of cattle from which they could eat; but they burned with desire for the fish and birds in which Egypt abounded.

**VERSE 4.**—“Behold, I will rain,” etc. (ORIG., *Homily 8 on Exodus*.) I would first like to discuss this passage with the Jews, to whom the words of God were entrusted: what do they think of the statement, “For six continuous days you shall gather, but on the sixth day twice as much”?

It is clear that the sixth day is the day placed before the Sabbath, while the Sabbath is the seventh day. I therefore ask on what day manna began to be given, and I wish to compare our Sunday with the Sabbath of the Jews. For it is clear from Scripture that manna was first given on Sunday, gathered for six continuous days, and ceased on the seventh, which is the Sabbath.

Since, therefore, God rained manna on Sunday and not on the Sabbath, let the Jews understand that even then our Sunday was set above their Sabbath. It was indicated that God’s grace did not descend to them on that day, and that the heavenly bread, which is the word of God, did not reach them. Hence Hosea III: “For many days the children of Israel shall sit without a king, without a prince, without a sacrifice, without an offering, and without a priest.”

But on our Sunday the Lord always rains manna—that is, heavenly words, which are joyful for us. Those unfortunate people sigh even now for manna, like their fathers, and do not deserve to receive it. For they cannot eat what is small like coriander seed and white like frost. They perceive nothing small, subtle, and spiritual in the word of God, but everything as fat and coarse. “The heart of this people has grown fat.”

The interpretation of this name also conveys the same meaning. *Manna* is interpreted as “What is this?” The very force of the name invites one to learn, so that when you hear the Law of God being read, you may always inquire and say to your teachers, “What is this?”

If you wish, therefore, to eat manna and receive the word of God, know that it is small and extremely subtle, like coriander seed. It has something of a vegetable with which it can nourish and refresh the weak. “The weak person eats vegetables” (Romans XIV). It also has a certain severity, and therefore it is like frost; but it has great whiteness and sweetness. What is whiter or more radiant than divine instruction? What is sweeter or more pleasing than the words of God, which are above honey and the honeycomb?

**“Breads.”** That is, manna. It is a usage by which “bread” is placed for nourishment; Scripture, however, more readily uses the plural “breads” than the singular “bread.”

**“That I may test them.”** This testing is a trial, not a seduction into sin; nor are they tested because God does not know. Rather, he shows them to themselves, so that they may become more humble in seeking assistance and in recognizing God’s grace.

**VERSE 5.**—“But on the sixth day,” etc. (ORIG., *Homily 7*.) On the sixth day, let them gather twice as much for storage, enough also for the Sabbath. The sixth day is this present life in which we now are; for God made this world in six days. In this day, therefore, we must store up as much as will be sufficient in the future.

For whatever good work you acquire here, whatever justice, mercy, or piety you commend here, this will be food for you in the future. Whoever acquires ten talents here will receive ten cities there (Luke XIX), and whatever a person sows, that he will also reap (Galatians VI).

The rich of this age store up things which decay in this age—or rather, together with this age. But the good things stored up remain until the next day.

It is written that those who were unfaithful kept some of the manna, and worms boiled out of it and it rotted; but what was stored up for the Sabbath remained intact. And you, if you hoard wealth for the sake of the present life and love of the world, worms immediately boil out of it, concerning which Isaiah LXVI says: “Their worm will not die.” Avarice and the blind desire for riches generate these worms in those who possess money and, while seeing their brothers in need, close their hearts to them.

Hence the Apostle commands the rich (I Timothy VI) not to be high-minded and not to hope in the uncertainty of riches, etc. Nor do worms arise in us from anywhere except from manna—that is, from the word of God. Hence John XV: “If I had not come and spoken to them,” etc.

After receiving the word of God, therefore, if someone sins, the word itself becomes a worm which continually digs into his conscience and gnaws at the secrets of his heart.

**VERSE 6.**—(ORIG.) “In the evening you shall know,” etc. “In the evening you shall know that I am the Lord; but in the morning you shall see the glory of the Lord.”

Let the Jews answer me: how is the Lord known in the evening and his glory seen in the morning? Where was he recognized in the evening, and where was his glory seen in the morning?

This is understood only in the Gospel (Matthew XXVIII), in which, “in the evening of the Sabbath, as the first day of the Sabbath was dawning,” Mary Magdalene and the other Mary came to the tomb. They found the stone rolled away from the tomb, an earthquake had occurred, and the tombs had been opened. The centurion and the guards of the tomb were saying: “Truly this was the Son of God.”

The Lord was recognized in that evening, because he was himself the Lord; he was recognized in the power of his resurrection, and in the morning his glory was seen. When the other women came very early on the first day of the Sabbath, they found angels sitting at the tomb in great brightness and saying: “He is not here, but he has risen from the dead. Come and see the place,” etc. (Luke XXIV.) His glory was therefore seen in the morning, because his resurrection was also announced through the angels.

**VERSES 7–11.**—“But what are we?” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus* 59, vol. III.) They wished to be no less powerful than God, etc., up to: “He showed that the Holy Spirit is God by adding, in Acts V: ‘You have not lied to human beings, but to God.’”

## Verses 12–13

“You shall eat meat in the evening” (ORIGEN, as above). Morally, we can understand that each of us has a morning and the beginning of a day: the time when we are first enlightened and kindled toward the light of faith. At this time we cannot eat the meat of the Word—that is, we are not yet capable of perfect doctrine. But after long exercises, after considerable progress, when we are already approaching evening—that is, the perfection of faith—we become capable of more solid food.

Let us therefore hasten to receive the manna, which produces in each person’s mouth whatever taste he desires. Hence Matthew 9: “Let it be done for you according to your faith.” You too, therefore, if you receive with complete faith and devotion the Word of God preached in the Church, let whatever you desire be done for you. If you are afflicted, it comforts you, saying: “A contrite and humbled heart God will not despise” (Psalm 50). If you rejoice in hope of what is to come, it increases your joys for you, saying: “Rejoice in the Lord and exult, you righteous” (Psalm 31). If you are angry, it says: “Cease from anger and abandon indignation” [Col. 0238A] (Psalm 36). If you are in pain, it heals you, saying: “The Lord heals all your illnesses” (Matthew 4). If you are consumed by poverty, it consoles you, saying: “The Lord raises the needy from the earth and lifts the poor from the dungheap” (Psalm 112).

If, however, someone receives it faithlessly, he does not eat it but hides it; worms boil out of it. Do not be troubled if the Word of God is brought to the point where it is thought to become a worm; for he himself says: “I am a worm and not a man” (Psalm 21). For just as he is the one who becomes for some a downfall, but for others a resurrection (Luke 2), so he himself is the one who becomes, in the manna, the sweetness of honey for the faithful, but a worm for the faithless.

For he is the Word of God who reproves the minds of the wicked and pierces their conscience with the arrows of correction. He is also the one who becomes for those to whom he opens the Scriptures [Col. 0238B] a fire, so that they say: “Was not our heart burning within us?” etc. (Luke 24). To others he is fire, burning the thorns of the bad soil—that is, consuming evil thoughts in the heart. Therefore, for sinners neither the reproving worm ever dies nor the consuming fire is extinguished; but for the righteous and faithful he remains sweet and pleasant.
