Hence Psalm 33 says: “Taste and see,” etc.

(ORIGEN, as above.) Another version reads: “In the evening you shall eat meat, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.” Let the Jews say what coherence there is in eating meat in the evening without bread, or bread in the morning without relish. What divine gift, what moderation of heavenly grace, is revealed in this? Can they recognize God in this—those who eat meat in the evening without bread and say that the majesty of God appears if, in turn, bread is eaten without meat? Let them keep such things for those who, agreeing with them, think that God is recognized in quail. But we, for whom at the end of the world, toward evening, “the Word became flesh,” say that God is recognized solely in that flesh which he assumed from the Virgin. For no one ate this flesh of the Word of God in the morning or at midday, but in the evening: for the Lord’s coming in the flesh occurred toward evening, just as John also says: “Children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2).

“In the morning,” he says, “you shall be filled with bread.” For us, therefore, the bread is the Word of God: “He is the living bread that came down from heaven and gives life to the world” (John 6). But what he says about this bread being given in the morning, although he became incarnate in the evening, must be understood in this way: the Lord came toward the evening of the world and near its end; but by his coming, since he is the sun of righteousness, he restored a new morning for believers—a new light of knowledge, in which those who received his commandments are filled with bread.

Nor should you wonder that the Word is called both the flesh of God and bread, and is also called milk and vegetables, for it is named differently according to the measure of believers and the capacity of those who receive it. Or else, after the resurrection that took place in the morning, he filled believers with bread, because he granted for the instruction of the Church the books of the Law and the Prophets, previously unknown; and he himself becomes the bread in the Gospel, while the other books of the Law, the Prophets, and the histories are called many loaves, with which believers from the nations are filled. Hence: “They shall ascend the mountain, drink wine, and be anointed with ointment.”

Thus, appropriately, we receive meat in the evening and are filled with bread in the morning: for we could neither eat meat in the morning, since the time had not yet come, nor at midday, since even angels scarcely eat meat at midday, and perhaps that time is granted to that order.

“And in the morning.” On the ninth day, when Christ, the sun of righteousness, restored what had been lost to believers by his coming.

(ISIDORE.) The food of birds signifies preaching sent by God, which passes through resounding words, flying through the air like winged creatures; by these those who journey toward the heavenly homeland are nourished through faith. Or it signifies the utterances of the Old Law, which fed the carnal people like flesh through words sent by God, as though through flying creatures. Hence it is given in the evening, because everything granted to them in a carnal manner was destined to come to an end. But by the manifest light of faith the manna is given, which is Christ, namely, the living bread that came down from heaven (John 6), rained upon the whole world through the evangelical clouds—not upon the murmuring and tempted Synagogue, but upon the believing and hoping Church.

## Verse 14

“In the likeness of frost upon the earth.” Frost signifies Christ: for manna was first given on the Lord’s Day, and Christ rose on the Lord’s Day.

“Tusum.” That is, most pure. For just as grain, millet, or anything similar is pounded in a mortar with a pestle and stripped of its husks, so the body of Christ, through the tribulation of the Passion and the pestle of the cross, was stripped of mortality. Or the manna being made fine signifies the subtlety of heavenly doctrine, which is pounded so that the literal sense may be stripped away.

## Verse 15

“Man hu.” (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book 27, chapter 7.) What is signified by the manna given from above to the children of Israel, if not wonder at heavenly sweetness? For the sweet food received from above is called *man hu*, which is interpreted, “What is this?”—what we say when we behold something we admire because we do not know it.

The soul therefore perceives the manna from above when, raised up by the voice of compunction, it is astonished at a new form of eternal refreshment, so that, filled with divine sweetness, it rightly answers, “What is this?” For while it is lifted away from lowly thought, it beholds what is above and marvels at it as something unfamiliar. And when, through this voice, the deafness of our torpor is broken, the practice of the old life is changed, so that the soul, breathed upon by the Spirit from above, desires in the heights what it had despised and despises in the depths what it had desired.

## Verses 16–17

“According to the number of your souls,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Locutions*, 78.) Scripture often calls human beings “souls,” naming the whole from a part. It does not readily use “fleshes” for human beings, but “flesh”; thus Psalm 56 says: “I shall not fear what flesh can do,” while the same psalm states more clearly, “what man can do to me.” It would not say, “according to the number of your fleshes,” as it says, “according to the number of your souls.”

## Verses 18–19

“According to what they were able to eat,” etc. For in the present life each person ought to learn as much as he can, so that he leaves nothing unexplored and does not begin to learn only when he is unable.

## Verse 20

“But some of them left some of it until morning,” etc. This signifies the beginning of the other life, in which there will be no opportunity to devote oneself to doctrine; rather, the manna will decay and swarm with worms—that is, it will produce eternal punishment for them.

## Verse 21

“When the sun grew hot, it melted.” For then every meaning of Scripture will be opened, since now “we see through a mirror in an enigma,” but then “we shall see face to face” (1 Corinthians 13).

## Verse 22

“Double portions.” Namely, what is necessary for soul and body. For on the seventh day, which is understood as the age of the dead, there will be no place for working.

## Verses 23–32

“The Sabbath rest,” etc. This means hearing the Word of God and doing it, or living well and showing mercy to others. What was stored up for the Sabbath did not decay, because good deeds performed for future rest remain intact in the future life. Otherwise, worms boiled out and what had been stored decayed; for those who store up treasures for the sake of the present life and love of the world, the worm that will not die boils out for them.

## Verses 33–34

“And place it before the Lord,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus*, 61.) It may be asked where Aaron was to place it before the Lord, since there was not yet any tabernacle and the ark of the covenant had not yet been established. Or perhaps, because it concerned the future, he said “place it,” so that it might be understood that it was then capable of being placed before the Lord, when the future ark would exist. Or is “before the Lord” rather said of what is done through the very devotion of offering, wherever it might be placed? For where is God not present?

But what follows—“And Aaron placed it before the tabernacle for safekeeping”—supports the former interpretation more strongly. In this way Scripture spoke by anticipation of what later happened, when the tabernacle of the testimony began to exist.

## Verses 35–36

“The children of Israel ate manna for forty years,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *ibid.*, question 62. Another version reads: “The children of Israel ate manna for forty years,” etc., up to “for God knew what they desired and by what kind of flesh he would satisfy them.”)

“They ate manna for forty years.” Namely, the body of Christ, the Word of God, which we now perceive in an enigma, but then face to face (1 Corinthians 13).

“Until they came into an inhabited land,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus*, 63, volume 3.) Another version reads: “Until they came into the region of Phoenicia.” By repetition he explains what land he called inhabited, etc., up to “for antiquity changed the names of many lands, places, rivers, and cities for definite reasons.”

# Chapter 17

## Verses 1–2

“Then the whole multitude of the children of Israel set out,” etc. (ORIGEN, *Homily 11 on Exodus*.) All who wish to live piously in Christ suffer persecution and are attacked by enemies. As he travels the journey of this life, he must always be prepared and remain in the camp. Thus the entire synagogue of the children of Israel set out from the desert of Sin according to its camps, through the Word of God.

There is indeed one Synagogue of the Lord, but it is divided into four camps, which are described in Numbers [Col. 0241A] around the tabernacle of the Lord. Therefore, armed and serving as a soldier in the Lord’s camp, do not entangle yourself in worldly affairs, but keep watch continually in the Lord’s camp, so that it may be said of you that you set out through the Word of the Lord from the desert of Sin and came to Rephidim.

Now *Sin* is interpreted as “temptation,” while *Rephidim* means “health of judgment.” Whoever comes safely out of temptation reaches the health of judgment. On the day of judgment he will be sound. Hence Revelation 2: “To the one who conquers I will give from the tree of life, which is in the paradise of my God.” Whoever orders his words well in judgment reaches the health of judgment.

“Sin.” Here *Sin* specifically denotes one encampment among the five that lay between the Red Sea and Mount Sinai, which Josephus describes by name. In general, that entire desert is called Sin [Col. 0241B], just as it is also called Rephidim.

“They encamped at Rephidim.” (JEROME, *On Hebrew Places*, volume 3.) It is a place in the desert near Mount Horeb. It should be known, however, that the entire wilderness as far as Mount Sinai is called Sin, and that one encampment in the whole region also received the name, just as Moab is the name both of a city and of a province.

In this wilderness there are five encampments: Zuph, the desert of Sin, Alush, Dophkah, and Rephidim. Hence it is rightly said that the whole multitude of the children of Israel set out from the desert of Sin by their encampments, according to the command of the Lord, and came to Rephidim. From this it is clear that several encampments are designated by the name of a single region.

## Verses 3–4

“Therefore the people thirsted there,” etc. (ORIGEN, as above.) Another version reads: “The people thirsted for water,” he says, “and murmured against Moses.” It would have been sufficient to say that they thirsted; why was it necessary to add “for water”? The addition is not superfluous. There are therefore different kinds of thirst, and each person has his own.

Those who are good “hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 5). Others also say: “My soul has thirsted for you, O God” (Psalm 41). But sinners suffer not thirst for water or hunger for bread, but hunger and thirst to hear the Word of God. The people therefore thirsted for water, when they ought to have thirsted for righteousness.

But God, the instructor of children and teacher of the foolish, corrects faults and amends errors, telling Moses to take the staff, strike the rock, and bring forth water. For he wishes them already to drink from the rock, to advance, and to come to the inner mysteries.

They murmured against Moses; therefore the Lord commands him to show them the rock from which they should drink. For if there is someone who, while reading Moses, murmurs against him and dislikes the Law according to the letter because in many matters it does not seem to have coherence, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, so that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst.

But this rock gives no water unless it is struck; when struck, it produces springs. For Christ was struck and slain on the cross, and produced the springs of the New Testament. Hence Zechariah 8: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered.” For unless he had been struck and blood and water had come forth from his side, we would all suffer thirst for the Word of God. Hence: “They were drinking from the spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

(ISIDORE.) The thirsty people murmured against Moses because of the water [Col. 0242A]; therefore God commands him to show them the rock from which they should drink. If someone, while reading Moses, murmurs against him and dislikes the letter of the Law, Moses shows him the rock, which is Christ, and leads him to it, so that he may drink from it and refresh his thirst.

## Verse 5

“Go before the people,” etc. Moses alone does not lead the people to the waters; the elders of the people do so as well. For it is not the Law alone that announces Christ, but also the prophets, the patriarchs, and all the elders.

“And the staff,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus*, 64.) Aaron, not Moses, is recorded as having struck the river with the staff. Moses divided the sea with that same staff, not the river. What, then, does “Take the staff with which you struck the river” mean? Or perhaps he called the sea a river; and an example of this expression must be sought. Or what Aaron did is attributed instead to Moses because God commanded through Moses what Aaron was to do: authority belonged to the one, service to the other. Hence: “It shall be for you before the people, while you shall be for him in matters concerning God.”

## Verses 6–7

“You shall strike the rock.” Christ, who was struck by the Jews on the cross; the staff, that is, the wood of the Passion, was applied to him so that water might remain for the faithful.

## Verse 8

“Then Amalek came,” etc. (STRABO.) Amalek was a son of Ishmael, from whom came the Amalekites, who are also Ishmaelites; they are the Saracens. The name is interpreted as “drinking” or “licking blood,” and signifies the devil, who always attacks the saints as they leave Egypt and journey toward the promised land, desiring to drink the blood of souls.

(ORIGEN, *Homily 2 on Exodus*.) The battle fought with the Amalekites is described. Before the people ate bread from heaven and drank water from the rock, it is not said to have fought; rather, it was told: “The Lord will fight for you, and you shall be silent.” There is therefore a time when the Lord fights for us: he does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear, nor does he allow those unequal in strength to engage in combat with a strong opponent.

Job, too, completed the contest of his temptation when he was already perfect. You, therefore, when you begin to eat manna, the heavenly bread of the Word of God, and to drink water from the rock, and when you approach the inner matters of spiritual doctrine, should expect battle and prepare yourself for war.

## Verses 9–10

“Moses said to Joshua,” etc. (ORIGEN, *ibid.*) Another version reads: “Moses said to Jesus: Choose men for yourself.” Until this point, no mention had ever been made of the blessed name of Jesus. Here Moses first called him Jesus and said to him: “Choose men for yourself.”

Moses calls Jesus; the Law calls upon Christ to choose for himself powerful men from the people. Moses could not choose them, but only Jesus, who says in John 15: “You did not choose me, but I chose you” (Matthew 12). He is the leader of the chosen and the prince of the powerful. He himself fights with Amalek. For he enters the house of the strong man, binds the strong man, and plunders his goods.

“I shall stand on the top of the hill.” (ORIGEN, as above.) Moses, he says, ascended not to the top of a mountain but to the top of a hill. The ascent to the top of the mountain was being reserved for him for the time when Jesus would ascend, and Moses and Elijah with him, and when he would be transformed in glory. Now, therefore, as one not yet glorified through the transformation of Jesus, he does not ascend to the top of the mountain but to the top of the hill.

“And when Moses raised his hands, Israel prevailed.” Moses raises his hands; he does not extend them. Jesus, who, exalted on the cross, embraced the whole world, says: “I stretched out my hands to a disobedient people” (Isaiah 65).

To raise one’s hands means to lift one’s deeds toward God, so that one’s deeds are not cast down and lying on the ground, but pleasing to God and raised toward heaven. He raises his hands who stores up treasure in heaven. For where the treasure is, there are the eye and the hands. He raises his hands who says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm 140).

If, then, our deeds are raised up, Amalek is defeated. Hence Isaiah 35: “Strengthen the slack hands and the feeble knees.” If the people keep the Law, Moses raises his hands and the adversary is defeated. If they do not keep the Law, Amalek grows strong.

Since our struggle is against the rulers and authorities, the cosmic powers of this darkness, if you wish to conquer, raise your hands—that is, your deeds. Let your conduct not be on earth but in heaven. You too, raise your hands toward heaven, to God; fulfill the Apostle’s command: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5). Then what is written will come to pass: “As a calf licks up the green grass in the fields, so this people shall lick up the people who are upon the earth.” Here it is indicated that the people of God fought not so much with hand and weapons as with voice and tongue, and overthrew their enemies by prayer.

Raise your deeds, therefore, and persist in prayer. This is the Christian battle, which overcomes the enemy. I think, moreover, that through this figure two peoples are signified. One, from the nations, raises Moses’ hands and lifts to a higher level what he wrote and its meaning, and thus conquers. The other, namely the Jewish people, does not raise Moses’ hands from the earth, understands nothing high or sublime in him, and is therefore defeated by its adversaries.

“Having the staff of God,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 65.) The staff of God is now mentioned, although earlier it was called Aaron’s and afterward is called Moses’. The same is true when the spirit of Elijah is called the Spirit of God, of whom Elijah is said to be a participant, and when the righteousness of God is called ours. Hence: “They did not know the righteousness of God, and sought to establish their own” (Romans 10), that is, as though prepared by themselves for themselves.

## Verse 11

“And when Moses raised his hands,” etc. (STRABO.) When the Law is understood mystically and the Passion of Christ is considered spiritually, the devil is defeated and driven away. But when the hands are lowered—that is, when the commandments of the Law are practiced with less zeal—the enemy prevails and pursues.

## Verses 12–13

“Then they took a stone,” etc. (GREGORY, *Homily 33 on the Gospels*.) “Moses sat upon the stone,” etc., up to “whom those things justly condemn, he mercifully liberates.”

## Verse 14

“For I will blot out,” etc. (RABANUS.) This signifies that almighty God, through the Law—which Moses signifies and which speaks concerning Christ—blots out the memory of spiritual enemies. Hence Psalm 19: “Their memory has perished with a crash.”

## Verses 15–16

“Moses built an altar,” etc. All those who conquer the devil ought to build in their hearts altars of faith, upon which they may offer spiritual sacrifices.

# Chapter 18

## Verses 1–4

“When Jethro heard,” etc. The fact that Moses, when he was going to free the children of Israel, sent away his wife and sons, whom he later received in the desert, signifies that preachers, when they are sent to the work of preaching, ought to relieve themselves of temporal concerns. But when they are afterward appointed to the episcopate or another dignity, they ought then to care for those subject to them in both spiritual and temporal matters.

## Verses 5–11

“Then Jethro came,” etc. (ORIGEN, *Homily 11 on Exodus*.) Another version reads: “After these things Moses came to the mountain of God, and Jethro, who was coming to meet him, went out from the camp to meet him.” He did not lead him to the mountain of God but to his own tent.

For the priest of Midian could not ascend the mountain of God, nor could Moses’ wife descend into Egypt; but now she came to him with her sons. She could not descend into Egypt and undergo the contests of the Egyptians unless she were a proven athlete, one who, striving in the contest, abstains from everything.

Moses, because he was a great and powerful athlete, descended into Egypt for contests and exercises of virtue. Abraham and Jacob also—Jacob himself being an athlete by his very name—when he descended into Egypt, became like the stars of heaven in multitude.

For others, descending into Egypt has an opposite significance. I know that Jeroboam, fleeing from Solomon, descended into Egypt and tore apart and corrupted the people of God; for when he descended into Egypt, he received from King Shishak as a wife Tethimene, his wife’s sister.

## Verses 12–25

“Then Jethro offered,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Locutions*, 85.) “And Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, took burnt offerings,” etc. “Took” is used for “offered,” “placed.” Or perhaps this is a matter of meaning rather than expression, so that he is understood to have taken them in order to offer them. Yet Moses is not read to have sacrificed, nor Aaron, nor any of the Hebrews who were led out of the land of Egypt; nevertheless, it was said above that Moses established an altar.

We read that Jethro was a priest of Midian, that is, of the people of Midian. It is surprising if Moses began to sacrifice at his arrival, rather than Jethro himself, who was the priest.

“And they came,” etc. (ORIGEN, as above.) Another version reads: “The elders of Aaron and all Israel came to eat bread with Moses’ father-in-law in the sight of God.” Not everyone eats bread in the sight of God, but those who are elders—those who are mature, proven in their merits—who, whether they eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God.

Everything the saints do, therefore, they do in the sight of God; the sinner flees from the sight of God. After Adam sinned, he fled from the sight of the Lord, and when questioned he answered: “I heard your voice, Lord, and I hid myself because I was naked” (Genesis 3). Cain went out from the face of the Lord because he was unworthy of the Lord’s presence.

Therefore, those who receive fuller knowledge of God, if they do evil, do so before God. Hence Psalm 50: “Against you alone have I sinned,” etc. Whoever does evil before God immediately repents and says, “I have sinned.” Whoever departs from the sight of God does not know how to turn back and cleanse his sin through repentance. This, then, is the difference between doing evil before God and departing from the sight of God.

(ORIGEN.) Jethro did not come to Moses without reason, nor did he without reason eat bread with the elders of the people in the sight of God. He gave Moses sound and useful advice: to choose men and appoint as rulers of the people men who worship God, are powerful, and hate pride.

Those who are appointed in this way ought not to be proud but to hate pride; that is, they should not merely be free from vice themselves, but should hate vices in evil people. I mean not the people, but the vices.

“In the sight of God,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 66.) It may be asked where this occurred, since there was neither a tabernacle nor an ark of the covenant, both of which were established later. Nor can we understand this as referring to the future, as with the manna that was placed in a vessel, namely a golden one. We must therefore understand that something is done “before God” when it is done in the Lord’s honor.

## Verses 16–18

“I shall show them the commandments,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 67.) It may be asked how Moses said this here, etc., up to “he could not judge justly.”

## Verses 19–20

“But now hear my words,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, [Col. 0245C] *Questions*, 68.) The first question is why God’s servant, etc., up to “by which he becomes fuller in proportion as he extends himself more freely toward what is heavenly and eternal.”

“Be you for the people,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 69.) As for what he adds, etc., up to “but I do not know from where this can be proved.”

## Verses 21–23

“But choose,” etc. He is instructed by a foreigner as a safeguard of humility, so that he who learned so many divine mysteries from God himself would not become elated and think that he had no need of human counsel.

It was also prefigured that the doctrine of the nations would surpass the knowledge and pride of the Jews, and that believers from the nations would suggest the completion of what was lacking in the Law and bring spiritual understanding to the Law of God.

Moses also knew that the Law would listen to this people and do whatever it said, and that the diminution of the Law would take place at the prompting of the Gospel.

“And appoint,” etc. (ORIGEN, *Homily 11.) “You shall appoint them,” he says, “tribunes and centurions, and they shall judge the people at all times; whatever is more serious, however, they shall refer to you.”

The rulers of the people and the elders of the congregation, who ought at all times to judge the people, should always and without interruption sit in judgment, settle disputes, reconcile those who disagree, and restore the divided to harmony.

Let each person learn his office from the Holy Scriptures. Moses, he says, should remain in matters concerning God and explain the Word of God to the peoples. The other rulers, whom he called tribunes because they preside over tribes, or centurions, or commanders of fifty, preside over lesser judgments, settling matters that concern individuals.

I think this order is also to be preserved in the future age. Hence Matthew 19: “When the Son of Man sits upon the throne of his majesty, you also shall sit upon twelve thrones,” etc. You see, therefore, that it is not only the Lord who judges—to whom the Father has given all judgment (John 5)—but that he also appoints rulers to judge lesser cases; whatever is more serious they refer to him.

Therefore the Lord says of one person (Matthew 5): “He will be liable to the council”; but of another (Matthew 12): “He will be liable to the fire of Gehenna.” They are also said to give an account of every idle word. For this reason it is not said that we shall give an account to God, as it is said concerning perjury: “You shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.”

Matthew 12: “The queen of the South will rise in judgment with the men of this generation and will condemn it.” Here is another kind of judgment. Matthew 13: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear.” For all these things are a shadow of heavenly realities and an image of things to come.

(IDEM.) As it is written in Ecclesiastes 1: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing,” neither can we be satisfied by considering what has been written, by which he builds us up and instructs us in so many ways.

When I observe that Moses was a prophet full of God, with whom God spoke face to face (Exodus 33), yet received counsel from Jethro, his father-in-law and the priest of Midian, I am struck with immense amazement. Moses heard the voice of his father-in-law and did everything he told him.

He did not say: “Since God speaks to me about what I ought to do, how shall I receive counsel from a human being—and from a foreigner, a gentile, a stranger to the people of God?” Rather, he listened not to who was speaking but to what was said.

Therefore, if we find something wisely said by gentiles, let us not reject the sayings because of the speaker’s name. Nor, because we possess the Law of God, is it fitting for us to swell with pride and despise the words of the wise. Instead, testing everything, let us hold fast to what is good.

Those who preside over peoples today—I do not mean only if something has already been revealed to them by God, but even if they possess some merit in knowledge of the Law—despise the counsel of an inferior, even of a priest, let alone a layman or a gentile.

But Moses, who was meek above all human beings (Numbers 12), accepted the counsel of an inferior, in order to give rulers a model of humility and to signify an image of the future sacrament.

He knew that the time would come when gentiles would offer good counsel, bringing to Moses a good and spiritual understanding of the Law; and that the Law would listen to them and do everything they said.

For the Law cannot do as the Jews say, because the Law is weakened in the flesh—that is, in the letter—and according to the letter it can accomplish nothing. “The Law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews 7).

According to the counsel that we bring to the Law, however, everything can be done spiritually, and sacrifices can be offered, which cannot now be offered in a carnal manner; the law concerning leprosy can be observed spiritually.

Thus, according as we understand, perceive, and give counsel, the Law does everything. According to the letter, however, it does not do everything, but only a few things.

## Verse 24

“Moses did everything that he had suggested,” [Col. 0247A] etc. A man familiar with God, most wise, and unashamed to be taught by an inferior and a gentile, provided teachers with a model, so that they would not be ashamed to learn from anyone.

## Verses 26–27

“Whatever was more serious,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Locutions*, 88.) Others have: “But they referred the serious matter to Moses.” For so the Greek expression reads, which the Latins translated as “to Moses.” In that expression, the care itself is also signified: when it says that the matter was placed “upon Moses,” it is as though a burden imposed upon him were indicated. “Serious word” is used for “serious question.”

# Chapter 19

## Verses 1–2

“In the third month,” etc. (ORIGEN.) Another version reads: “In the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from the land of Egypt, on this day they came into the desert of Sinai. They set out from Rephidim and came into the desert of Sinai, and Israel encamped there opposite the mountain. And Moses went up to the mountain of God, and the Lord called him from the mountain, saying: ‘Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob and announce to the children of Israel,’” etc.

And a little later: “‘Go down and testify to the people, and purify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day. For on the third day the Lord will descend upon Mount Sinai in the sight of all the people.’”

On this day the Law is found to have been given, written on stone tablets by the finger of God, as what follows teaches. This third day appears to be the third day of the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

From the day on which they celebrated Passover—that is, sacrificed and ate the lamb—which was the fourteenth day of the first month, until this day on which the Law is given, fifty days are counted: seventeen days of the first month, namely the days remaining after the fourteenth; then all thirty days of the second month, making forty-seven; and the third day of the third month, which is the fiftieth day from the solemnity of the slaughtered lamb.

Thus, in this shadow of the future, according to the day of the sacrificed lamb, there is a festival: because the Law was given on the fiftieth day, written by the finger of God. Likewise, in the very truth of the New Testament, fifty days are counted from the feast of the sacrificed Lamb, Jesus Christ, on which the Holy Spirit was given from the heights, and he is the finger of God.

“On this day,” etc. Namely, on the forty-seventh day after they had gone out from Egypt—on the first day, that is, of June—they reached Mount Sinai. After completing the two days during which they were sanctified, on the third day, that is, the fiftieth, they received the Law. This is Pentecost.

(RABANUS.) There was one encampment at Sinai, but it was the greatest of all. For there the Law was received and the tabernacle erected. There Exodus, most of Leviticus, and nearly all the books of the Law were written.

## Verse 3

“Moses, however,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book 6, chapter 27.) Another version reads: “Moses went up to the mountain, and the Lord descended to him.”

The mountain is the height of contemplation. We ascend it so that, by looking, we may be raised toward those things that lie beyond our weakness. But the Lord descends because, when the saints make great progress, he reveals a small part of himself.

## Verses 4–5

“On the wings of eagles.” He calls the doctrines of the two Testaments wings, because they carry us from the lowest things to the heavenly.

## Verse 6

“You shall be for me a priestly kingdom,” etc. Namely, members of the high priest who are destined to enter the kingdom of heaven.

## Verses 7–9

“He set forth all the words,” etc. (GREGORY.) It should be noted that the Law is not imposed upon the unwary or ignorant. Rather, once the rewards owed to those who keep it, the past benefits they have already experienced, and the miracles have been set forth, and once they willingly devote themselves to observing the Law, the Law is given to those who ask for it. Thus, according to their promise, those who violate it are judged as persons bound by a vow, and they cannot claim that violence was inflicted upon them.

## Verse 10

“Go to the people,” etc. (ORIGEN.) “Go down and testify to the people; purify them today and tomorrow; let them wash their garments and be ready for the third day,” etc.

Whoever wishes to come to the Word of God should hear what the Lord commands: he must come sanctified and with washed garments. For if you bring dirty garments, it will be said to you, as in Matthew 22: “Friend, how did you enter here without a wedding garment?”

No one, therefore, can hear the Word of God unless he has first been sanctified—that is, holy in body and spirit and with washed garments. For shortly afterward he is to enter the wedding feast, eat of the flesh of the Lamb, and drink the cup of salvation.

No one enters this feast in dirty garments. Hence Ecclesiastes 9: “At all times let your garments be clean.” Your garments have been washed once by the grace of baptism. “You have been purified in body and cleansed from every defilement of flesh and spirit” (2 Corinthians 7). “What God has cleansed, do not make unclean” (Acts 11).

Hear the form of sanctification: “Do not approach a woman today and tomorrow,” so that on the third day you may hear the Word of God. This is what the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians 7: “It is good for a man not to touch a woman,” though a marital remedy is nevertheless permitted to the weak. And in 1 Corinthians 7: “Because the time is short, let those who have wives live as though they had none.”

Sanctify them, etc. (RAB.) Whoever desires to come into the presence of God must sanctify himself by faith and conduct, and wash his garments—that is, his works—today and tomorrow, namely, in the present and in the future, so that he may attain the glory of the resurrection, which the third day signifies.

**VERSE 11.**—For on the third day, etc. On this day the law was given, [Col. 0248D] written on stone tablets by the finger of God. This is the third day of the third month from the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt. From the day on which they celebrated the Passover—that is, the fourteenth day of the first month—until the law was given, fifty days are counted: namely, seventeen days of the first month, counting from the fourteenth; all thirty days of the second month, making forty-seven; and the third day of the third month, which is the fiftieth from the slaughter of the lamb. So, from the passion of Christ until the Holy Spirit was given, fifty days are counted. For the finger of God signifies the Holy Spirit.

(ISID., *Questions on Exodus*, chapter 28, volume V.) On the fiftieth day after the Passover the law of Moses was given, etc., up to: “or because [Col. 0249A] he spoke the truth of the law to unbelievers through obscurity, so that seeing they may not see, and hearing they may not understand” (Isa. VI).

**VERSE 12.**—Beware, etc. (RAB.) Previously he forbids the people to ascend the mountain and threatens death; now he orders them to ascend the mountain when the trumpet sounds, restraining human presumption and inviting obedience. For at the sound of preaching we ought to lift ourselves toward heavenly things, neither presuming on our own initiative to investigate the mysteries, but following God’s call.

**VERSE 13.**—Trumpet. As though from *vocina*, “little voice”: from *vox*, “voice,” or from *vocare*, “to call,” or from *bucca*, “mouth.”

**VERSES 14–17.**—And when they had washed their garments, etc. It is not enough, for the virtue of contemplation, to cleanse one’s works with the tears of repentance, unless [Col. 0249B] purity of mind and body follows. Hence Matthew V: “Blessed are the pure in heart,” etc. And Wisdom I: “Wisdom will not enter into a malicious soul.”

**VERSES 18, 19.**—Now the whole mountain of Sinai was smoking, etc. (GREG., *Morals*, book VI, chapter 27.) In order to give the law, the Lord descended in fire and smoke, etc., up to: “they conquer what they are.”

(ID., *Morals*, book II, chapter 2.) Sacred utterances, at the beginning of their narratives, express qualities and sometimes define the limits of events by the position of a place, sometimes by the position of a body, sometimes by the quality of the air, etc., up to: “but they are said to have come in the evening to punish Sodom.”

**VERSES 20–25.**—And the Lord descended, etc. (ID., *Morals*, book V, chapter 26.) Moses ascended, etc., up to: “[Col. 0249C] we render an indistinct echo to him by stammering to some degree.”

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 2.**—I am the Lord your God. (ORIG., homily 8 on Exodus.) Whoever despises the present age—that is, Egypt—and, having been transferred through the word of God, is not found hastening toward the future age, is addressed by God in these words: “I am the Lord your God,” etc. This is said not only to those who went out from Egypt, but to those who no longer serve the Egyptians, having been led out of Egypt, out of the house of bondage (Ps. LXXX).

The affairs of the world and the activities of the flesh are the house of bondage; abandoning worldly things and living according to God is the house of freedom. Hence John VIII: “If you remain in my word, you will know the truth, and [Col. 0249D] the truth will set you free.” Therefore Egypt is the house of bondage; Judea and Jerusalem are the house of freedom. Hence Galatians IV: “The Jerusalem above is free.”

Just as earthly Egypt is called the house of bondage for the children of Israel in comparison with Judea and Jerusalem, which is their house of freedom, so, in comparison with the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of freedom, the whole world and everything in it is called the house of bondage. And because, through sin, humanity came from the paradise of freedom into the bondage of the world, the first statement of the Decalogue concerns freedom: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt,” etc. You cannot hear this voice in Egypt.

Even if you are commanded to celebrate the Passover, gird your loins, take sandals [Col. 0250A] on your feet, hold a staff in your hand, and eat unleavened bread with bitterness, still you are not judged fit—neither in the first station, nor in the second, nor in the third, nor after you have crossed the Red Sea, even if you have reached the sea and your bitterness has been turned into sweetness; nor at Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees; even if you have passed through Rephidim and climbed onward through the remaining stages, you are not yet judged suitable. Only when you have come to Mount Sinai do you scarcely deserve at last to receive the commandments of freedom and to hear: “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage.”

Yet this is not the commandment itself, but it shows who it is that gives the commandment. Therefore the first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods besides me.”

[Col. 0250B] (AUG., *Questions on Exodus*.) The question is how the ten commandments of the law should be divided, etc., up to: “unless with reference to what was said: You shall have no other gods besides me.”

(ISID.) God gives Moses the law of our innocence and of the knowledge of himself, which consists in ten words written on stone tablets by the finger of God. Three concern love and knowledge of the Trinity, and seven concern love of neighbor, through which human society is not harmed.

The first pertains to God the Father: “The Lord your God is one God,” so that, hearing this, you may worship one God, the Father, and may not pour out your fornication upon many fabricated gods. The second pertains to the Son: “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain”; that is, you must not think that Christ, the Son of God, is a creature, since every creature is subject to vanity, but [Col. 0250C] must confess him equal to the Father, God from God, light from light.

**VERSE 3.**—You shall have no foreign gods, etc. (ORIG.) The first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods besides me”; and it follows: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness,” etc. Some consider all of these together to be one commandment. But if they are counted in this way, the number of ten commandments will not be completed.

Therefore the first commandment is: “You shall have no other gods besides me,” etc. The second is: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness,” etc.

Let us begin, then, with the first commandment: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” If he had said, “There are no other gods,” the statement would seem more absolute. But because he says, “There shall be no other gods,” he did not deny that they exist; rather, he forbade them to be gods for the one to whom these commandments are given.

I think Paul took this from here when he says in 1 Corinthians VIII: “Although [Col. 0250D] there are those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth.” In other places as well you will find gods being named, as where it says: “A great king above all gods,” and “God has spoken to God,” etc.

The Apostle says the same concerning lords: “Whether thrones or dominions,” etc. (Col. I). Dominions are nothing other than a certain order and multitude of lords. Here the Apostle seems to disclose the meaning of the law, as though he were saying: Although there are many lords who rule over other nations, and many gods who are worshiped by others, nevertheless there is one God for us, and one Lord.

Hence Deuteronomy XXXII: “When the Most High divided the nations and separated the sons of Adam, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God.” Scripture therefore calls the angels to whom the Most High entrusted the nations “lords” [Col. 0251A] or “gods”: gods, as having been given by God, and lords, as having received authority from the Lord.

Hence it is said to them in Psalm LXXXI: “I said: You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High. But you shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes,” namely, imitating the devil, who became the prince of all for their ruin. It is therefore clear that transgression made them accursed, not their nature.

To you, therefore, O Israel, who are God’s portion and his cord of inheritance, he says: “You shall have no other gods besides me.” For truly there is one God, and truly there is one Lord. To the others, however, created by him, he granted this name not by nature but by grace.

These things are not said only to Israel according to the flesh, but also to you who have become Israel in mind by seeing God, and who have been circumcised in heart, not [Col. 0251B] in flesh—provided that you conduct yourself in such a way that you are worthy to be God’s portion and to be measured within the cord of his inheritance. Otherwise, let those be an example to you who had been called for this purpose, to be God’s portion, but because their sins demanded it were scattered among all nations and, having been led out of the house of bondage, now serve not only the Egyptians but all nations. For whoever sins is the slave of sin (John VIII).

**VERSE 4.**—You shall not make, etc. (ORIG.) You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness, etc. Idols are one thing, gods another. Concerning gods the Apostle says in 1 Corinthians VIII: “Although there are many gods and many lords,” etc. Concerning idols he says that “an idol is nothing in the world.” Concerning likenesses, however, he did not add that they are nothing. Here, however, it is said: “You shall not make for yourself an idol, nor any likeness.”

To make an idol is therefore one thing, [Col. 0251C] and to make a likeness another. For example, if someone in gold, silver, wood, or stone makes the form of a quadruped, serpent, or bird and sets it up to be worshiped, he makes not an idol but a likeness. But whoever makes what does not exist—namely, a form that the eye has not seen but the mind has imagined—such as forming a dog’s or ram’s head with human limbs, or two faces on a single human body, or the hindquarters of a horse or fish joined to a human breast, makes not a likeness but an idol. For he makes what does not exist and has nothing resembling itself.

Therefore the Apostle says that an idol is nothing in the world (1 Cor. VIII). Its form is not taken from anything that exists, but from what an idle and curious mind has devised.

A likeness, however, exists when something is formed from things that are in heaven, on [Col. 0251D] earth, or in the waters. But just as it is easy to pronounce this concerning likenesses of things on earth or in the sea, so it is also concerning heavenly things—unless one says that this may be understood of the sun, moon, and stars, whose forms paganism represents.

But Moses, instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, wished to prohibit even those things that were hidden among them, such as Hecate and other forms of demons, which the Apostle calls “spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Eph. VI). Perhaps it is of these that it is said: “My sword has drunk its fill in heaven” (Isa. XXXIV). By these forms and likenesses they invoked demons in order to repel or avoid evils.

It must nevertheless be understood that, when you resolve to keep this commandment and to have only one God and Lord, you [Col. 0252A] thereby declare war on all the others whom you renounced at baptism, confessing only God the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

But if, while confessing this, we do not love the Lord our God with our whole heart, with our whole soul and our whole strength, clinging to him, we have not become God’s portion. Rather, we stand on the boundary and suffer the hostility of those from whom we fled, while failing to make the one to whom we fled favorable toward us.

To such people the prophet says: “Woe to the double-minded” (Eccli. II). And again: “How long will you limp on both feet?” (3 Kings XVIII). We are therefore struck by those whom we flee like fugitives, while our Lord does not defend us because we are unstable. Hence Jeremiah IV: “Your lovers have become your enemies.”

There are many lovers of the soul, captivated by its beauty, with whom it has played the harlot, saying: “I will go after my lovers, who give [Col. 0252B] me my wine,” etc. (Hos. II). She offended these when she returned to her former husband.

Unless, therefore, you remain with your husband in complete faith, you are suspect because of the crimes you have committed. He observes all your movements, looks, and steps; he can no longer bear to see anything wanton, dissolute, or extravagant in you.

If, then, you neglect the grace you have received and entangle yourself in worldly affairs, the unclean spirit immediately returns with seven spirits more wicked than himself (Matt. XII), so that it may not be expelled again, and the last condition becomes worse than the first.

There is therefore no fellowship between the temple of God and idols. If we belong to God, we must be such as those in whom God dwells and walks. Hence Isaiah LII: “You who carry the vessels of the Lord, go out and do not touch what is unclean, and I will receive you,” etc.

He therefore says: “You shall have no other gods besides me.”

[Col. 0252C] **VERSES 5–11.**—You shall not worship, etc. To serve is one thing, to worship another. Someone may worship unwillingly, either by flattering idolatrous kings or because he has been overcome by torments, while knowing that an idol is nothing. But to serve is to devote oneself wholly to them in affection and zeal. He therefore cuts off both: neither are you to serve them in affection nor worship them in outward form.

“I am the Lord,” etc. Observe God’s goodness: in order to teach us and make us perfect, he does not refuse to accommodate himself to the weakness of human affections. He does and suffers everything for our sake, speaking to us in ways familiar and customary to us.

(ORIG., in the work cited above.) Every woman is either under a husband and subject to her husband’s laws (Eph. V), or she is a prostitute and uses the freedom to sin. Whoever goes in to a prostitute knows that he has entered one who is prostituted and open to everyone; therefore he cannot [Col. 0252D] be indignant about others.

Whoever makes use of a lawful marriage does not tolerate his wife’s sinning, but is inflamed with zeal to preserve the chastity of the marriage, so that he may become a legitimate father.

Thus every soul is either prostituted to demons and has many lovers who enter her—now the spirit of fornication, now avarice, after that the spirit of pride and many others. Yet one does not envy another or become jealous; instead, they invite one another. Hence [the spirit] “brings with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself,” etc. (Luke XI).

Thus the soul prostituted to demons suffers no jealousy from its lovers. But if it is joined to a lawful husband, that is, to Christ, even if it has once been sinful, he does not allow it to sin thereafter, nor [Col. 0253A] can he endure its playing with adulterers. His jealousy is aroused against it, and he defends the chastity of the marriage.

But if he sees it violating the rights of the marriage and seeking an opportunity to sin, he gives it a bill of divorce. Hence Isaiah L: “Because of your iniquities he sent away your mother.” The one who speaks here is both jealous and moved by jealousy.

There is also this new kind of his goodness: that even after adultery he receives the woman who returns and repents with her whole heart. Hence: “If a woman leaves her husband and sleeps with another man, will she return again to her husband?” etc. And elsewhere: “After you committed fornication in all these things, I said: Return,” etc. (Jer. III).

When this jealous God seeks and desires your soul to cling to him, when he preserves, rebukes, and becomes indignant with it, as though exercising a kind of jealousy [Col. 0253B] toward you, recognize that you have hope of salvation.

But if you despise his rebuke, his jealousy departs from you, according to the saying: “Therefore my jealousy will depart from you,” etc. (Ezek. XVI).

Observe God’s mercy and compassion. When he wishes to show mercy, he says that he is indignant and angry, as he says through Jeremiah: “You shall be chastised with pain and scourging, Jerusalem, so that my soul may not depart from you” (Jer. VI). For he scourges every son whom he receives (Heb. XII).

This, however, is dreadful and final: that we are not rebuked for our sins. For when we exceed the measure of sinning, God’s jealousy is also taken away from us, and he is angry no longer.

“Visiting iniquity,” etc. (ORIG.) “Returning the sins of the fathers upon the children,” etc. Heretics say that this is not the speech of a good God, who says that one person is [Col. 0253C] punished for another’s sins. Yet they call the God of the law just, and they cannot show how he is unjust if he punishes one when another sins.

Our inner person is said either to have God as father, if it lives according to God, or the devil, if it does his will. Hence John VIII: “You are from your father the devil, and you wish to do your father’s desires.”

Therefore, just as the seed of God is in us when, keeping the word of God, we do not sin—according to 1 John III: “Whoever is from God does not sin, because God’s seed remains in him”—so, when we are persuaded by the devil to sin, we receive his seed. When we do what he persuades us to do, he has already begotten us; through sin we are born as his children.

But because we generally do not sin without assistance—just as no one commits adultery alone—it is necessary for an adulterous partner to be involved; and if not several, at least one man or woman must be joined [Col. 0253D] to the criminal act. All of them, as though one were generated from another according to the order of persuasion, derive their lineage from the devil.

Thus, in the betrayal of the Lord, the devil entered Judas’s heart and first begot the son of sin, who could not do this alone. Judas therefore went to the scribes, Pharisees, and chief priests; and from Judas a third and fourth generation of sin was born.

Let us therefore see how God returns the sins of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation, and not upon the father himself. For nothing is said about the fathers.

Because the devil has already exceeded the measure of sinning, like a garment congealed in blood he will not be cleansed in this age; he is not scourged [Col. 0254A] for sin, for everything is reserved for him in the future. Hence Matthew VIII: “Why have you come before the time to torment us?”

The sins are returned upon the children whom he has begotten through sin, who, while they are in the flesh, are scourged. God does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he turn and live (Ezek. XXXIII).

Therefore, in his mercy, God returns the sins of the fathers upon the children, because the devil and his angels, who also become fathers of sin, are unworthy to be corrected in the present. Their children, and those who through them have been recruited into the fellowship of sin, receive in the present what they have done, so that, having been purified, they may not become the devil’s companions in punishment.

Hence Psalm LXXXVIII: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod,” etc., “but I will not remove my mercy from them.” For God is jealous, and he does not wish the soul he has [Col. 0254B] betrothed to himself in faith to remain in the pollution of sin, but wishes it to be purified quickly.

If it refuses to be purified, he will laugh at their destruction, saying to them in Matthew XXV: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire,” etc.

Let us therefore understand that we are corrected in the present so that we may rest in the future. Hence: “When we are chastised, we are corrected by the Lord, so that we may not be condemned with the world.”

(ID.) Heretics commonly reproach us on this point, saying that this is not the speech of a good God, who judges one person for another’s sins. But those who call the God of the law who commands these things not good nevertheless call him just; nor can they themselves show how it seems compatible with justice for one person to be punished when another sins.

[Col. 0254C] (ISID.) The first commandment forbids stealthy deception; the second, error; the third destroys love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth, cruelty; the sixth, fornication; the seventh, robbery; the eighth destroys falsehood; the ninth, desire for the world; the tenth, the thought of adultery.

It should be noted that, just as the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues, so the tablets were written with ten commandments, by which God’s people are governed and demons are killed.

The law was written on two tablets to signify the two Testaments; or because there are two commandments of love—of God and of neighbor—on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matt. XXII).

On one tablet are three commandments pertaining to love of God; on the other are seven pertaining to fellowship with one’s neighbor.

The tablets were [Col. 0254D] of stone because the heart of the Jews was stony and insensitive, hard and foolish. Hence Ezekiel XXXVI: “I will take away the heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh.” And the Apostle says (2 Cor. III): “Not on stone tablets, but on tablets of fleshy hearts”—that is, hearts capable of feeling and understanding.

**VERSE 12.**—Honor your father, etc. This is the first of the seven commandments that pertain to one’s neighbor. It is fitting that there are seven. For the number seven consists of three and four. Three corresponds to the soul, which is irascible, concupiscible, and rational; four corresponds to the body.

**VERSE 13.**—You shall not kill, etc. (AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 61.) When it is said, “You shall not kill,” it should not be thought [Col. 0255A] that the law acts contrary to this commandment when it kills or when God commands someone to be killed. The one who does this is the one who commands; and it is not lawful to deny service to the one who commands.

**VERSE 14.**—You shall not commit adultery. (ISID.) The question also arises how “You shall not commit adultery” differs from what is said shortly afterward: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.”

For in the statement “You shall not commit adultery,” that other matter could also have been understood, unless perhaps in those two commandments—the prohibition of adultery and the prohibition of theft—the acts themselves are marked, while in these final commandments the coveting itself is prohibited.

The difference is such that someone may sometimes commit adultery without coveting another’s wife, when he joins himself to her for some other reason. At another time he may covet her but not join himself to her, fearing punishment. Perhaps the law [Col. 0255B] wished to show that both are sins.

(ID.) It is also commonly asked whether fornication is included under the term adultery, etc., up to: “and the illegitimate use of those members must be understood to be prohibited.”

**VERSE 15.**—You shall not steal, etc. (AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 71.) The question arises again how “You shall not steal” differs from what is said shortly afterward concerning not coveting one’s neighbor’s possessions.

It is not that everyone who covets another’s possession steals; rather, everyone who steals covets another’s possession. The general statement prohibiting the coveting of one’s neighbor’s possession could have included what pertains to theft as well.

**VERSES 16, 17.**—You shall not speak against your neighbor, etc. (AUG., in the work cited above.) Likewise, concerning what is said, etc., [Col. 0255C] up to: “and things of this kind.”

**VERSE 18.**—Now all the people saw the voices, etc. (AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 72.) It is usually asked how the people saw the voice, since a voice seems to belong not to sight but to hearing, etc., up to: “we do not usually say, ‘Hear what shines.’”

**VERSE 19.**—Speak to us yourself, etc. (AUG., question 73.) This signifies that fear pertains more properly to the Old Testament, just as love pertains to the New, although the New lies hidden in the Old and the Old is disclosed in the New.

But how can it be attributed to such a people that they saw the voice of God—if [Col. 0256A] “seeing” is to be understood as “understanding”—when they fear that God may speak with them lest they die? This is not sufficiently clear.

**VERSE 20.**—Do not be afraid, etc. (AUG., question 74.) They had to be restrained from sins by fear—namely, fear of suffering perceptible punishments—because they were not yet able to love righteousness. They were being tested by the Lord so that their character might be revealed, not so that they might become known to God, from whom nothing about them was hidden, but so that they might become known to one another and to themselves.

**VERSES 21, 22.**—And the people stood, etc. (GREG., homily 6.) In certain passages of Scripture the historical meaning must be preserved, etc., up to: “Moses approached the darkness in which God was.”

You shall not make gods, etc. (AUG., question 76.) What was said in the first commandment is repeated. By silver [Col. 0256B] and gold all images are understood, as in Psalm CXIII: “The images of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.”

**VERSE 24.**—An altar of earth, etc. He shows that, once images have been forbidden, an altar made of earthly material is permitted so that offerings and sacrifices may be made upon it to the one God.

(GREG., *Morals*, book III, chapter 20.) To make an altar of earth for God is to hope in the incarnation of Christ. Our gift is then accepted by God when, upon this altar, our humility lays whatever it does upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation. We therefore place a gift upon an altar of earth when we establish our actions firmly upon faith in the Lord’s incarnation.

**VERSES 25, 26.**—Of hewn stones. (ISID.) Hewn [Col. 0256C] stones are those who divide unity and separate themselves from the fellowship of the brethren. Christ does not receive such people into his body, whose figure is signified by the construction of the altar.

The unhewn stones from which the altar is commanded to be built are those who are made firm in unity through faith. Of them it is said in 1 Peter II: “You are living stones, built together into spiritual houses.”

No iron was applied to these stones because they are incorrupt, and they have not received the flaming darts of the wicked one. All together they form one altar in the unity of faith and the harmony of charity.

> **Note:** [Col. 0255C] In enumerating the commandments of the Decalogue, Origen and Augustine, in the testimonies of the Gloss included at the beginning of the chapter, appear to follow opposed positions. Origen [Col. 0255D] thinks that the number of ten commandments cannot be counted unless the second is: “You shall not make for yourself an idol nor any likeness,” etc.

> Augustine, although he does not reject Origen’s enumeration, nevertheless judges another, different arrangement to be more suitable. He considers the prohibition against making idols and images for the purpose of worship to be an explanation of the first commandment. He then establishes two commandments to restrain forbidden desires: one by which the coveting of another’s wife is restrained, and another by which the coveting of all other possessions belonging to one’s neighbor is restrained.

> Origen is followed by Athanasius in the *Synopsis of Scripture*; Gregory Nazianzen in the poem in which he enumerates the ten commandments; Chrysostom in his second exposition of Matthew, homily 49; Jerome; and Ambrose in chapter VI of the Epistle to the Ephesians.

> The scholastic teachers follow Augustine’s enumeration in the same sense as Augustine himself: they prefer it to the former arrangement, yet do not consider the former incongruous.

> In truth, the opposition that a depraved inclination finds [Col. 0256C] in subduing these two forms of coveting seems rather to have required two distinct commandments. Some people covet another’s wife while nevertheless disdaining to covet another’s [Col. 0256D] wealth or slaves, and conversely. But no true worshiper of God finds difficulty in rejecting idols.

> In any case, this difference of enumeration produces no difference in the matter itself. Augustine does not posit a commandment that Origen denies, nor Origen one that Augustine denies. Rather, one joins commandments on the basis of a certain subordination, while the other separates them on the basis of their verbal connection, and conversely.

> Augustine joins the commandment against making idols to the commandment against worshiping any god but the one God, because the former is subordinate to the latter and is a more explicit extension of it, also reaching to the prohibition of pagan ceremonies.

> Origen, however, divides them into two commandments because the very sequence of the wording seems to distinguish them, without any indication of connection, just as in the other commandments that follow: “You shall have no foreign gods”; “You shall not make for yourself a graven image”; “You shall not take,” etc.

> Again, Origen gathers the two prohibitions concerning the two forms of coveting into one commandment because the continuity of the wording makes them seem to belong to one statement: [Col. 0257D] “You shall not covet your neighbor’s house, nor desire his wife, nor,” etc.

> Augustine, however, divided them into two commandments because, as I have said, the commandment against coveting a wife is not subordinate to the prohibition against coveting wealth. Nor is the forbidden desire for pleasure ordered toward the desire for possessions; rather, they produce vices of different kinds and are [Col. 0258D] therefore prohibited by different laws.

> Thus the whole difference is in agreement concerning the matter itself. Whether something is prohibited by one law or by two distinct laws, the result is the same, provided that one acknowledges that the same things are prohibited by the same words, even if one is uncertain whether those words constitute one law or two.

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0257A]

**VERSES 1, 6.**—These are the judgments, etc. (AUG., *Expositions on Exodus*, section 91.) From this point onward the matters pertaining to one’s neighbor are explained more distinctly. The wording should be noted: Moses is told, “These are the judgments that you shall set before them”; what follows is addressed to the people.

If you buy a Hebrew slave, etc. (AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 77.) So that Christians would not demand this here from their masters, the Apostle commands slaves to be subject to their masters (1 Pet. II), lest the name of the Lord and the teaching be blasphemed. It is clear that this command has a mystical meaning, because God commanded the slave’s ear to be pierced with an awl against the door, since he had refused freedom.

(GREG., homily 3 on Ezekiel, volume II.) It must be understood that, since [Col. 0257B] the active and contemplative life come from God’s grace, etc., up to: “because that profound rest is seen in a mystery.”

“Six years.” (ISID.) After serving through the six ages of this world, we shall be freed on the seventh day—that is, in the eternal Sabbath—provided that, while serving sin in this world, we have wished to be free.

But if we have not wished this, the ear will be pierced as a testimony of disobedience, and with our wife and children, whom we preferred to freedom—that is, with the flesh and its works—we shall serve sin forever.

**VERSES 7–12.**—If anyone sells his daughter, etc. (AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 78.) She shall not depart in the same way as female slaves depart, etc., up to: “it is understood that she will go out freely with him, not separated from her husband.”

**VERSES 13–17.**—But whoever did not lie in wait, etc. (RAB., on Exodus, volume II.) Concerning involuntary homicides, etc., up to: “he will be saved if he has placed himself in Christ.”

(AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 79.) But if he did not will it, and God delivered the person into his hands, etc. This is said in such a way, etc., up to: “and therefore Judas delivered him justly.”

**VERSE 18.**—If they quarrel, etc. (RAB.) The same applies if someone, contending with his neighbor, provokes him through hardness of heart or stinginess—that is, by despising him or failing to care for him—and the other, weakened by sorrow, languishes in the fervor of love.

Let the guilty person, through confession, the work of repentance, and the expense of promised amendment, provide for physicians—that is, teachers—who may raise up the sick person with the staff of consolation and restore him to his former state of love through the remedies of preaching.

[Col. 0257D] In correction, discretion is necessary, lest the person who ought to correct kill the other or drive him into despair or hatred.

**VERSES 22–28.**—If they quarrel, etc. (ID.) If someone, after a word has been conceived, harms another’s soul through negligence or deceit, so that it cannot bring forth the living germ of a good work in soundness—even if that soul, still living in the faith, has persisted, so that through repentance [Col. 0258A] it may restore the harm inflicted—it will necessarily require the ministry of the Gospel.

But if that soul, killed through error after producing a miscarriage—that is, a deadly work—has persisted in unbelief, without doubt its seducer, as a true murderer, will be liable to eternal death.

(AUG., *Questions on Exodus*, question 80.) That the law did not want an unformed miscarriage to be regarded as homicide, etc., up to: “and therefore it had not yet been endowed with sensation.”

(ORIGEN, Homily 10 on Exodus.) “But if two men quarrel and strike a pregnant woman, and her child comes out still unformed, he shall suffer a penalty in whatever amount the woman’s husband imposes, and he shall pay for his life. But if it is formed, he shall give life for life, eye for eye,” and so forth. Let us first examine the case of the child who comes out not yet formed: why is one of the quarrelers—when two are mentioned—commanded to be punished by a monetary penalty? What is meant, moreover, by the fact that the woman’s husband imposes this on him, not on them, and that he shall pay, rather than that they shall pay? If the child comes out already formed, we readily understand “life for life”: namely, that the sin is avenged by death. But what follows deserves explanation. For it does not seem that even a formed child, struck by the heel of one of the quarrelers, could have lost an eye in the womb, while he certainly had no teeth at all. If we refer this to the mother, how does a woman who miscarries lose an eye or suffer pain in her teeth? But suppose that, struck either in the eye or in the tooth, she miscarried and received a bruise or wound: what, then, are we to say about “burn for burn”? Could the woman standing beside the quarrelling men have been burned, so that burn should be paid for burn? Nor can these matters easily be explained in Deuteronomy.

Nevertheless, in Scripture the members of the soul are named by the same terms and functions by which the members of the body are used or designated. Thus, Matthew 7 says: “You see the speck in your brother’s eye, but you do not see the beam that is in your own eye.” And Matthew 13 says: “He who has ears to hear, let him hear.” And Romans 10 says: “How beautiful are the feet of those who proclaim peace!” Therefore, let us not be confused by the similarity of the terms.

There are consequently two quarrelers: two who argue and dispute over doctrines or questions of the Law, fighting over controversies of words. Hence the Apostle says, 2 Timothy 2: “Do not contend in words,” and in the same place: “Avoid questions of the Law, knowing that they produce quarrels.” Those, therefore, who quarrel in such questions to the subversion of their hearers strike the pregnant woman and cast out the child, whether formed or still unformed.

The pregnant woman signifies the soul that has recently conceived the word of God. Hence: “Because of your fear, O Lord, we conceived and gave birth” (Isaiah 26). Those who conceive and immediately give birth are not to be regarded as women but as men and as perfect persons. Hence elsewhere: “If the earth gave birth in one day, and a nation was born all at once” (Isaiah 66). This, then, is the generation of the perfect, which is conceived and born on the same day.

Men give birth according to the saying in Galatians 4: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” The perfect, therefore, and men give birth immediately—that is, they bring the word of faith that they have conceived into action. But the soul that conceives, retains the child in the womb, and does not give birth is called a woman. Hence Isaiah 37: “The pains of childbirth have come upon her, yet she has no strength to give birth.”

This woman, then, when two men quarrel among themselves and produce scandals, is struck and scandalized, so that she casts out the word of faith that she had conceived faintly, before it was formed. In some there is a formed word, in others an unformed one. Hence: “Until Christ is formed in you” (Galatians 4), for Christ is the Word of God.

[Col. 0259B] Therefore the one who caused the miscarriage shall suffer loss. Concerning losses the Apostle says, 1 Corinthians 3: “If anyone’s work is burned, he will suffer loss,” and so forth. The Lord himself says in the Gospel, Matthew 16: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses his soul?” Hence it appears that certain sins lead to loss but not to destruction, because one who has suffered loss is said to be saved, though as through fire. Thus John says that some sins are unto death and some are not (1 John 5). What sins are unto death, however, cannot easily be discerned: “For who understands his offenses?” (Psalm 18).

But when, over the five minas acquired, another five are gained, and over the two, another two (Luke 19), the one who loses the profit of this acquisition is said to be struck with loss, just as the one who has given occasion for scandal to a weaker and womanly soul.

He shall pay according to what her husband imposes, and he shall pay with honor to the soul that is learning. The husband is Christ the teacher, or the teacher of souls who acts in Christ’s place. The one who quarrels to the subversion of his hearers shall therefore suffer loss on behalf of the soul that has not yet had a formed child; this may be understood of the scandal of a catechumen.

It may also happen that the one who caused the injury instructs and restores the soul that suffered loss, and does so with honor—that is, with moderation and gentleness, not with quarrelling, as when he caused the scandal.

But when the child has been formed, he shall give life for life. The formed child may be understood as the word of God in the heart of the soul that has received the grace of baptism, or as the word of God received more clearly and distinctly. Therefore the one who struck will return life for life on the day of judgment, before the Judge who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna.

Alternatively, the one who is conscious of having caused so great a scandal may put his own life in place of the life of the scandalized person and labor unto death to restore that person to the faith.

“Eye for eye”: if he injured the eye of the soul—that is, disturbed its understanding—his own eye shall be taken away by the one who presides over the Church, namely, his understanding.

If he injured a tooth—the faculty that used to receive the food of the word of God and grind it with its molars, so as to transmit a refined meaning into the soul’s stomach—if he troubled and pulled out this tooth, so that through its crushing the soul could no longer receive the word of God in a subtle and spiritual manner, his tooth shall be taken away, because he did not properly crush and divide the food of the word.

For this reason it is perhaps said of the Lord: “You have broken the teeth of sinners” (Psalm 3). And elsewhere: “The Lord will break the molars of lions” (Psalm 57). Thus the soul is said to be injured and struck through its members.

He also demands hand for hand and foot for foot. The hand of the soul is its power to hold something and to strengthen the heart, that is, its actions and strength; the foot is that with which it walks toward good or evil. Since the scandalized soul is cast down not only in faith but also in its actions, which are signified by the hands, its hands are taken away, because it does not act well; and its feet are taken away, because it does not walk well.

It shall also receive burn for burn, because it burned the soul and handed it over to Gehenna. Through each of these penalties it is shown that the one who struck, after all his members have been cut off, is expelled from the body of the Church, so that the others may fear when they see it and may not act similarly.

For this reason, when the Apostle describes the teacher of the Church, among other things he commands that he must not be a striker (1 Timothy 3): lest, by striking pregnant women—that is, foolish souls—he be required to give life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and so forth.

Concerning such persons it is said in Matthew 24: “Woe to those who are pregnant and to those who nurse in those days,” when they will be scandalized, if possible, even the elect. Yet it must be understood that it is not the perfect who are scandalized, but women or little ones. Hence Matthew 18: “If anyone causes one of these little ones to stumble,” and so forth.

VERS. 29–36.—“But if an ox that has horns,” and so forth. (RAB.) This means: if the lord—that is, the spirit—does not restrain the proud movement of the mind, and it brings destruction upon souls or injury upon bodies, guilt falls back upon the keeper. Hence Proverbs, chapter 16: “The heart of a man instructs his mouth, and adds grace to his lips.”

“Thirty shekels.” That is, according to the commands of the Law, he shall make amends through faith, hope, and charity.

“Of silver.” He shall make compensation with the brightness of the divine word, by which they were instructed in faith in the Trinity and in knowledge of the Decalogue.

“If anyone opens,” and so forth. (GREGORY, Moral Works, book 17, chapter 13.) To open a cistern is to penetrate the secrets of Holy Scripture with a vigorous understanding, and so forth, up to the point where the weakness of the hearers may fall down to the depths.

“If someone’s ox,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) This is not to be observed only in the case of an ox, but in the case of every animal; for the whole is understood from a part. But this cannot be done with the flesh of slaughtered animals, since they do not eat it.

CHAPTER XXII

VERS. 1.—“If anyone steals,” and so forth. (STRABO.) According to the literal sense, five oxen are returned for one ox, and four sheep for one sheep, because the ox has five uses and the sheep four. The ox is sacrificed, plows, feeds, gives milk, and supplies leather for various uses; the sheep is sacrificed and feeds, and provides milk and wool.

Allegorically, every Jew is understood by the ox. If a Jew sells him, he will be subject to the penalty of the Law, which is contained in the five books of Moses. By the sheep is understood the Christian who imitates Christ, concerning whom it is said: “He was led like a sheep to the slaughter” (Isaiah 53). If anyone sells this sheep, let him return four sheep—that is, let him perform penance according to the institution of the four Gospels.
