VERS. 2–5.—“If a thief breaks into a house, or digs through,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 84.) If a thief is found breaking through and is struck and killed, and so forth, up to the point that he is already more than a thief.

VERS. 6–13.—“If fire goes out,” and so forth. (RAB.) We kindle fire when we prepare correction for those subject to us, so that we may consume the thorns of vices. But we must see to it that, while we pursue vices, we do not injure virtues, and that we do not harm before maturity those who have begun to produce the fruit of good works. Whoever has committed this offense should therefore perform fitting penance and diligently restore what he damaged through negligence.

“Ears of grain.” Tender hearers who have not yet reached the maturity of fruit. Whoever reproves their vices harshly and without discernment is like one who sends fire into ears of grain and does not allow them to reach maturity.

VERS. 14–16.—“If anyone borrows from his neighbor,” and so forth. We ask a loan from our neighbor when, in expectation of eternal reward, we undertake the care of the Lord’s flock. But if we always set the fear of God, as of one who demands payment, before the eyes of our heart, we are always as though in his presence. Hence 2 Corinthians 5: “Knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade people.” And elsewhere, 2 Corinthians 12: “As in the presence of God, we speak in Christ.”

Therefore the death or weakness of livestock is not imputed to the shepherd if he has diligently cared for it, as though God were present; otherwise he is compelled to repay the loss. Hence Matthew 5: “He will not go out from there until he has paid the last quadrans.”

VERS. 17.—“If the father of the virgin,” and so forth. (RAB.) The historical sense is the sense of the statement from which the discourse arises. If, therefore, the historical sense builds up the kingdom of charity and destroys covetousness, it is not necessary to explain it allegorically. Nevertheless, the reader ought to honor the statement with the dowry of sound faith and leave it untouched by his exposition.

VERS. 18–20.—“You shall not allow sorcerers to live.” Understand as heretics those who act through magical tricks and diabolical fabrications. They must be excommunicated from the fellowship of the faithful, who truly live, until the sorcery of their error dies within them.

VERS. 21.—“You shall not afflict a stranger.” (RAB.) He commends love of neighbor through compassionate mercy, lest, moved by the spur of anger or greed, we neglect the law of nature. Rather, let us do to them what we want people to do to us, and let us not do what we do not want done to us.

VERS. 22–24.—“You shall not harm a widow or an orphan.” (RAB.) The widow may be understood as the holy Church, which awaits Christ on the day of judgment and does not now possess him visibly; the orphan as the Christian people, whose father is the dead world and whose mother is Babylon. He forbids that this people be afflicted through persecution or worldly arrogance, lest such harassment bring spiritual destruction upon those who needlessly trouble them with hatred and insults.

VERS. 25.—“If you lend money,” and so forth. (RAB.) He warns the preachers of the Gospel not to seek excess, but, having food and clothing, to be content with these, according to Matthew 10: “You received freely; give freely.”

VERS. 26, 27.—“If you take a pledge,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, Passage 99.) He has put the genus for the species. For the statement is made as though he had given a pledge consisting of every garment, whereas the subsequent words of Scripture show that he is speaking specifically of one who has no garment except that with which he covers himself at night.

(GREGORY, Moral Works, book 16, chapter 2.) The pledge is confession of sin. For our neighbor becomes our debtor, and so forth, up to the point where he immediately feels from us that what he has done wrong has been released.

VERS. 28.—“You shall not speak evil of the gods,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 86.) The question is whom he called gods, and so forth, up to the point where they are honored with the services of worship.

VERS. 29–31.—“Your tithes,” and so forth. (ISIDORE, On Genesis, volume 5.) By the first fruits of crops or of the firstborn are signified the beginnings of good works, and so forth, up to the point where the result of perfection is granted.

CHAPTER XXIII

VERS. 3.—“You shall not pity the poor in judgment.” (AUGUSTINE.) This means that you should not favor the poor against justice under the pretext of mercy. Mercy is good, but it must not be contrary to judgment. Scripture calls judgment that which is just. But lest anyone suppose from this statement that God forbids mercy, the following appropriately comes next:

[Col. 0262C] VERS. 4–6.—“If you meet your enemy’s ox,” and so forth. It is as though he were saying: show mercy even toward your enemies when you have the power to act without judging. For when you lead back your enemy’s wandering ox and return it, you are not sitting as a judge among litigants.

VERS. 7–9.—“You shall flee from falsehood.” (RAB.) The Lord loves truth and judgment, and he urges his people to carry them out, because he is not a respecter of persons.

VERS. 10–12.—“For six years you shall sow your land.” (AUGUSTINE.) The question is what the poor will gather if the land is spared in the seventh year in this way, and so forth, up to the point where what has been sown is gathered during six years.

(RAB.) In the number six is the perfection of works, and so forth, up to the point where “he who sows in blessings will also reap in blessings.”

VERS. 13.—“And by the name of foreign gods,” and so forth. He permits one to swear by his own name, not because it is good to swear, but because he knew that human beings are inclined to swear. He does not want them to swear by the names of foreign gods, lest frequent swearing lead them into their worship. Thus God does not approve sacrifices either, yet he prefers that they be sacrificed to him rather than to idols.

VERS. 14–18.—“Three times each year,” and so forth. Here God requires faith in the holy Trinity: at Passover the Son is sacrificed; at Pentecost the Holy Spirit is given; at the Feast of Booths the power of the Father’s majesty is revealed.

“Three times each year,” and so forth. (RAB.) This means: throughout the whole time of the present life, in confession of the holy Trinity, through faith, hope, and charity, you shall offer to God your Creator the service of good works.

We celebrate Passover in the month of new things when, through the blood of the spotless Lamb, we are freed from Egyptian slavery and pass through spiritual waters from the old man into the new—not in the oldness of the letter but in the newness of the Spirit—by which, through the grace of Christ, we arrive in the promised land.

We celebrate the feast of the month of first fruits when we consecrate to the Lord the first fruits of our works, intentions, and words. We also celebrate the feast at the end of the year, when, after the fruits have been gathered—that is, the fruits of virtues—we strive to arrive at the end of life and the entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

For seven days we remain in booths, remembering that throughout the whole time of the present life we are strangers and pilgrims, and that we seek rest not here but in the future, taking diligent care not to appear empty in the sight of God.

“The feast also,” and so forth. (RAB.) That is, when the crops are ripe and the fruits of the whole year have been gathered, in September, which the Hebrews call *Tishri* by a Chaldean name, while the Macedonians call it ὑπερβεραῖον (*hyperberetaios*). At its beginning the Jews, keeping holiday, blow the trumpet more than in the other months and offer more sacrifices. In this month occur the Day of Atonement and, on the fifteenth day, the Feast of Booths.

VERS. 19.—“You shall not boil a kid,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 90.) How this is to be understood according to the literal meaning of the words, I do not know whether it can be discovered, and so forth, up to the point where afterward they suffered—not lambs in milk, but rams in the flock.

(STRABO.) Morally, the kid—that is, the sinner—must not be boiled in its mother’s milk, that is, dissolved by flattering words, but must be harshly rebuked and reproved.

VERS. 20, 21.—“Behold, I shall send an angel,” and so forth. (RAB.) Joshua signifies the leader of the people. He is called an angel because he is sent to announce the Lord’s will; for ἄγγελος (*angelos*) in Greek means “messenger.”

VERS. 22.—“I shall be an enemy,” and so forth. (GREGORY.) The root of every evil is pride, concerning which Ecclesiasticus 10 says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin.” Its offspring are seven principal vices: vainglory, envy, anger, sadness, avarice, gluttony, and lust. Because our Redeemer grieved that we were held captive by these seven vices of pride, he came full of the sevenfold Spirit of grace for the spiritual battle of liberation.

VERS. 23, 24.—“And the angel shall go before you.” (RAB.) Joshua led the Israelite people into the promised land, expelling seven nations and destroying their idols and altars. Mystically, the true Jesus exterminates these nations together with their idols when he expels from our hearts the seven principal vices and every idol of the enemy, so that we may securely possess the land of our nature.

“Whom I shall crush.” (CHRYSOSTOM.) Each vice has its own dwelling in our heart. Claiming it for itself, it expels Israel—that is, the contemplation of higher things—from the recess of our soul, and does not cease to resist. For virtues cannot dwell together with vices.

But when the vices have been overcome by the Israelites—that is, by the virtues—the place possessed by the spirit of lust or fornication will be occupied by chastity; the place seized by fury will be reclaimed by patience; the place occupied by sadness that produces death will be possessed by salutary and joy-filled gladness; the place laid waste by sloth will be cultivated by fortitude; the place trampled down by pride will be adorned by humility.

Thus, once each vice has been expelled, its place—that is, its affection—will be possessed by the opposing virtue. These virtues are called “sons of Israel,” that is, of the soul that sees God. When they have expelled all the passions of the heart, they should be considered not so much to have seized another’s possessions as to have recovered their own.

For according to the ancient tradition, the sons of Shem received the land of the Canaanites by lot in the division of the world, but the Canaanites violently occupied it; hence they were expelled by the just judgment of God. The will of the Lord likewise assigned possession of our heart not to vices but to virtues. After Adam’s transgression, however, the virtues were driven from their own region by the insolent vices, like Canaanites. When, through God’s grace, they are restored by our diligence and labor, they do not so much occupy another’s land as recover their own.

VERS. 25–27.—“I shall bless your bread,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Another text reads: “I shall bless your bread and your wine,” and so forth. Although these promises can also be understood spiritually, and so forth, up to the point concerning what the impious will not receive.

[Col. 0264C] VERS. 28.—“Sending hornets.” (AUGUSTINE, Questions 93.) “I shall send wasps,” and so forth. God promises this, and so forth, up to the point where something is said by Christ.

Another text reads: “I shall send wasps before you, and he shall drive out the Amorites,” and so forth. He changes from the plural to the singular. The meaning is “he shall drive out the Amorites,” with “wasp” understood in the singular, just as “locust” and “frog” are used—not because there is only one, but because the plural is understood through the singular.

VERS. 29–33.—“I shall not drive them out from your face,” and so forth. (STRABO.) These nations signify the vices that are not extinguished in the saints all at once or at the same time, lest the monsters of the earth multiply—that is, lest they rise up in pride, vainglory, and similar vices.

For when the saints fight against and conquer the greater vices, they leave the lesser ones, and these are permitted to rule, lest they fall more grievously through elation. Hence a thorn in the flesh was given to Paul for the preservation of humility (1 Corinthians 22).

CHAPTER XXIV

VERS. 1.—“And he said to Moses: Come up to the Lord, you and Aaron,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 85, volume 3.) Up to this point the Scripture’s “ordinances” are understood, and so forth, up to the point where the Latins say that the ordinances are those which the Greeks call δικαιώματα (*dikaiōmata*, “ordinances” or “judgments”).

“You and Aaron,” and so forth. (STRABO.) Moses and Aaron, Nadab and Abihu: through these four men the evangelists are signified, namely, those who follow the evangelical commandments.

Through the seventy—whose number is formed either by seven multiplied by ten or by ten multiplied by seven—are signified those who, assisted by the grace of the Holy Spirit and fulfilling the tenfold Law, strive toward contemplation of the Creator. Or, literally, these are the men of whom Numbers 11 says: “Take for yourself seventy men,” and among whom Eldad and Medad were included.

VERS. 2.—“Moses alone shall go up to the Lord.” (RAB.) First it is commanded that Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and the seventy elders go up to the Lord. Immediately afterward it is added that Moses alone should go up to the Lord, while the others should not approach but should worship from afar.

Here we are morally instructed to weigh our strength and not attempt to reach the summit of contemplation beyond our ability, but only as far as divine mercy calls and the rule of Scripture urges us.

(GREGORY.) Moses ascended to high places in order to receive the sublime commandments of God; and, in order to penetrate inward things, he was hidden from external tumult. For holy men who are compelled by necessity to serve in external duties always diligently flee to the secrets of the heart. There they climb the summit of their innermost thought and receive the Law, as it were, upon a mountain, when, setting aside the tumult of temporal actions, they examine the judgment of the heavenly will at the peak of their contemplation.

VERS. 3–5.—“We shall do.” (AUGUSTINE, Questions 95.) It should be noted that the people again, and so forth, up to the point where they “obtained righteousness.”

VERS. 6–9.—“And so he took,” and so forth. (ID., Questions 98.) It should now be noted that Moses sacrificed for the first time, and so forth, up to the point where it is later evident that the Decalogue was written on stone tablets.

“Bowls.” A *cratera*, or *crater*, is so called ἀπὸ τοῦ κρατεῖν (*apo tou kratein*), “from holding,” because it is capable of holding a large quantity of wine.

VERS. 10, 11.—“Under his feet.” God is not contained by a place, nor does he possess bodily members according to bodily positions such as sitting, lying, standing, and similar things, which belong only to bodies. God, however, is spirit. Therefore, when he shows himself in bodily form or through signs expressed bodily, it is not his substance that appears—that which he himself is—but the assumption of visible forms, which is subject to his entire power.

VERS. 12.—“Come up to me,” and so forth. (BEDE, On the Tabernacle, book 1, chapter 11, volume 2.) We shall speak about the figure of the tabernacle, and so forth, up to the point where it was signified that the Church would speak throughout the world in the languages of all nations.

“And I shall give you.” (ID.) Similar is the saying: “Teaching them to observe everything that I have commanded you” (Matthew 28). Therefore Moses, the apostles, or anyone else ought not to teach anything other than what the Lord taught and prescribed by the decree of his counsel to be observed. In these things he wished us to possess eternal life. Nothing of these matters ought to be passed over; rather, it is necessary to entrust to the hearers everything that he commanded.

VERS. 13.—“Moses and Joshua arose.” (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Exodus 103.) Joshua, who was not mentioned among those four, suddenly appears with Moses, and so forth, up to the point where it is stated that at that time he was not yet called Jesus, but was so called when it was written.

(BEDE.) Joshua signifies Christ by name and by action. He is called the minister of Moses because Christ did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matthew 5). He follows in Moses’ footsteps in all things, because he is typologically represented in everything Moses wrote; if one searches carefully, he is found as an inseparable companion. Hence John 5: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also.”

(BEDE, On the Tabernacle, book 1, chapter 1, volume 2.) Aaron () is interpreted as “mountain of strength”; Hur () is interpreted as “fire” or “light,” and so forth, up to the point where the mind burns with love for the Creator.

VERS. 15.—“And when Moses had gone up,” (BEDE, same work.) Just as a mountain signifies the height of perfection, and so forth, up to the point where it protects with heavenly blessing.

VERS. 16.—“And the glory of the Lord dwelt.” (ID., same work.) Not only the height but also the name of the mountain, and so forth, up to the point where we are commanded to rest on the seventh day.

“Covering it with a cloud.” (ID., same work.) For six days it is covered by the cloud and glory of the Lord, and so forth, up to the point where he might reach the higher gifts of divine vision and conversation.

VERS. 17.—“And the appearance was.” (ID., same work.) The appearance of the glory of the Lord appeared like a burning fire, and so forth, up to the point that, although they cannot follow him fully.

VERS. 18.—“And Moses entered,” and so forth. (ID., same work.) Moses entered the midst of the cloud and climbed the mountain, and so forth, up to the point where they may attain eternal salvation through observing them.

CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0266C]

VERS. 2.—“Speak to the children of Israel, that they may take first fruits for me,” and so forth. (BEDE, On the Tabernacle, book 1, chapter 3, volume 2.) We offer the first fruits of good things to God when, attributing everything good that we do to divine grace and confessing with our whole heart that we can have neither the beginning of a good action nor of a good thought except from the Lord, we recognize that evils are always begun and completed by us at the instigation of the devil, and can be released only when the Lord grants it.

VERS. 3–6.—“These are the things that you shall receive,” and so forth. (ID., same work.) Everything that the Lord commanded to be offered materially for the construction of the sanctuary, we too, who desire to be spiritual children of Israel—that is, imitators of the people who see God—ought to offer spiritually. Through these voluntary offerings we should make the sanctuary itself within us, so that he may deign to dwell in our heart and consecrate a dwelling for himself.

VERS. 7.—“Onyx stones,” and so forth. (ID., same work.) These are what we offer, and so forth, up to the point where the merits of martyrdom added to good works are signified.

VERS. 8.—“And they shall make me a sanctuary.” (ID., same work.) The Lord showed Moses the tabernacle on the mountain, and so forth, up to the point where it received the splendid multitude of holy souls.

VERS. 9–11.—“According to every likeness,” and so forth. (ID., same work.) We ought to imitate the angels by loving God and neighbor, and so forth, up to the point where after this life he may introduce you into that tabernacle which you imitate.

“Of all the vessels.” (BEDE.) The vessels of the tabernacle are the individual persons of the angels, from whom Jerusalem, the mother of us all, consists in true peace and unity.

“And thus you shall make it.” The ark, and so forth. (ID., same work, chapter 4.) The ark is commanded to be made, and so forth, up to the point where he came in the likeness of sinful flesh.

“Whose length.” (ID.) The question is what size this cubit is, and so forth, up to the point where it is clear that it signifies the cubit made by two spans.

“Breadth.” (ID., same work.) The breadth of one cubit signifies, according to the dispensation of the Lord’s charity, and so forth, up to the point where we enter by loving him with our whole heart.

[Col. 0267B] (ID.) Mystically, the length of the ark signifies Christ’s long-suffering, and so forth, up to the point where he patiently endured the slowness of the disciples.

“Height, one cubit,” and so forth. (ID., same work.) The ark has a height of one cubit, and so forth, and up to the point where we possess this very little thing only from him.

VERS. 12–15.—“And four rings,” and so forth. (GREGORY, Pastoral Rule, chapter 11, volume 3.) The ark is the Church, and so forth, up to the point concerning what is in you.

“Two rings.” (BEDE, as above.) Because, in the figure of the four living creatures, and so forth, up to the point where they expressed the things that pertain to the glory of the future life.

VERS. 16.—“The testimony that I shall give.” (ID., same work.) Concerning this the Apostle says, and so forth, up to the point where he taught the Judge of all ages.

[Col. 0267C] VERS. 17.—“The mercy seat.” (ID.) The mercy seat was a golden slab of the same dimensions as the ark. It was so called because there God appeared to Moses and spoke with him, and was reconciled to the people; and it signifies mercy. It was therefore rightly placed above the ark, because his mercy is over all his works.

VERS. 18–21.—“You shall also make two cherubim,” and so forth. (ID.) This is because of the fellowship of angelic peace, which cannot exist with fewer than two. The cherubim signify the angelic army. The angels contemplate Christ in the highest harmony and tranquility. Hence, with their faces turned toward one another, they look toward the mercy seat, because they understand that they possess that blessedness by God’s grace.

(GREGORY, Homily 6 on Ezekiel.) The two cherubim, who are called the fullness of knowledge, and so forth, up to the point where he would promise one thing while denying another.

(BEDE, same work.) In the singular it is *cherub*, but in the plural *cherubim*, and so forth, up to the point where they are represented with wings spread out and prepared for flight.

VERS. 22.—“From there I shall give commands,” and so forth, “above the mercy seat.” (ID., same work.) Above the mercy seat, and so forth, up to the point where Habakkuk says: “In the midst of the two living creatures you will become known” (Habakkuk 3).

(BEDE, same work.) The ark may signify the Church, and so forth, up to the point where they stand established upon the foundation of supreme truth.

(BEDE, same work.) The table is made of acacia wood, and so forth, up to the point where Song of Songs 2 says: “The king brought me into the wine cellar and ordered love in me.”

VERS. 23.—“Its height shall be one cubit,” and so forth. (BEDE, same work.) Since its height is one and a half cubits, and so forth, up to the point where it is not represented by a full cubit.

VERS. 23.—“You shall make a rim for it,” and so forth. (BEDE, same work.) A golden rim is made around the table, and so forth, up to the point concerning the glory of each according to the diversity of merits.

VERS. 24.—“A crown,” and “above it another crown.” (BEDE, same work.) A golden crown is added when, through the Gospel, those who keep the commandments, and so forth, up to the point where a more exalted glory is reserved for him in the resurrection of bodies.

VERS. 26.—“For each,” and so forth. (BEDE, same work.) The table of the tabernacle has four feet, and so forth, up to the point where they enter the kingdom of heaven.

VERS. 27.—“So that poles may be put through them.” (ID., same work.) Poles are inserted through the rings to carry the table, and so forth, up to the point where they carry the Lord’s table with its loaves and vessels in the four rings.

VERS. 29.—“You shall also prepare dishes and bowls.” (ID., same work.) The various vessels made for offering libations, and so forth, up to the point where he says: “Who, then, do you think is the faithful and wise steward?” (Luke 12).

VERS. 29.—“You shall prepare bowls,” and so forth. (GREGORY, Homily 6 on the Gospels, volume 2.) What is signified by bowls and cups except the measure of preaching? And so forth, up to the point where even small and subtle teachings provide knowledge as though by taste.

(ID.) One person, full of the doctrine of truth, intoxicates his hearers and offers, as it were, a bowl. Another cannot express fully what he perceives, but because he announces it in some fashion, he provides a taste through a cup. Therefore those who cannot serve bowls through the doctrine of wisdom should, insofar as divine generosity enables them, offer their neighbors cups of the word.

[Col. 0268C] VERS. 30.—“And you shall place upon the table the bread of the Presence before me always.” Josephus says that twelve loaves were made from fine flour, each from two-tenths of a measure; on the Sabbath they were placed upon the table, six on one side and six on the other. Above each loaf was placed a golden dish with a handful of frankincense. They were kept in this way until the following Sabbath, when the frankincense was burned; the priests ate the loaves hot, replacing them with frankincense.

[Col. 0268D] “And you shall place upon the table,” and so forth. (BEDE, cited above.) They are rightly called the bread of the Presence, because the word of salvation ought always to be open to all the faithful, and the word of consolation ought never to be absent from the Church. The Lord wished this word, presented to the world through heralds of truth, to appear in his presence and to abound incessantly, until the end, for those who hunger and thirst for righteousness.

VERS. 31.—“You shall also make a lampstand,” and so forth. (GREGORY, Homily 6 on Ezekiel.) The lampstand is Christ, in whom the nature of humanity shone with the light of divinity, and so forth, up to the point where the cups and spheres pertain to labor, while the lilies pertain to recompense.

“You shall make a lampstand of hammered work, of purest gold.” [Col. 0269A] (BEDE, same work.) The lampstand of the tabernacle, and so forth, up to the point where it displays the brightness of the word to all by preaching and by doing.

“And its branches, cups, and spheres.” (ID., same work.) Namely, the preachers proceeding from the shaft, and so forth, up to the point where it blooms eternally for holy souls, that is, for flowers.

VERS. 32.—“Six branches,” and so forth. (ID., same work.) The number six, in which the world was made, and so forth, up to the point where Paul says: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the charity of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be always with you all.”

“Three from one.” (ID., same work.) Three branches from one side, and so forth, up to the point where he will enjoy its vision.

(ID., cited above.) Cups are made on the lampstand in the form of a nut, and so forth, because the three orders of saints of that age had the same distinction of times.

VERS. 33.—“In the form of a nut.” (ID.) The nut signifies the Church. Hence: “He went down into the garden of nuts.” A nut has sweet fruit within, which is not revealed outwardly unless the shell is broken. So the life of the saints preserves the sweetness of grace in the heart; it is not known outwardly unless, when the dwelling of the flesh has been dissolved, they behold themselves in the heavenly light.

(ID.) Likewise, the third branch has three cups, spheres, and three lilies, because there were many married people before the Law, under the Law, and under the prophets who rejoiced to hear the word of the Lord, to run along his way, and to await the rewards of good works.

[The same author] Likewise, on the other side, the first, second, and third branches had three cups and globes; they also had three blossoms, because in both Testaments there were, among teachers, the continent, and the married devoted to God, three orders separated by periods of time. Namely, in the primitive church from Israel, in our election from the nations, and in the final gathering of the remnant of Israel. All of them, each in its own time, having been filled with the word of life, desire to hasten along the way of peace and to see the brightness of perpetual light.

**VERSE 34.**—“On the lampstand itself,” etc. ([The same author], cited above.) We have said that the lampstand itself, etc., up to “but receive hearts renewed by the Spirit.”

**VERSE 35.**—“And globes and blossoms for each.” The globes are beneath two branches, etc.

([The same author], same work.) There are globes together with blossoms beneath each of the cups, etc., up to: “Therefore, his left hand is beneath my head, and his right hand will embrace me.”

([The same author], same work.) The cups, globes, and blossoms are beneath the two branches, etc., up to “all the fullness of divinity bodily.”

**VERSE 36.**—“And therefore the globes and the branches.” ([The same author], same work.) The entire work of the lampstand, etc., up to: “You enlarged me in tribulation,” etc.

**VERSE 37.**—“You shall make.” ([The same author].) The seven lamps are the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, who always remained in Christ and were distributed to the faithful according to his will. These are placed upon the lampstand, because the Spirit of wisdom and understanding rested upon him (Isaiah 11).

[Col. 0270A] “That they may give light,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The lamps of the lampstand illuminated the tabernacle opposite them, when Christ, full of grace and truth, gave to all from his fullness: entrusting the word of the Gospel to the meek and the poor, and granting the penitent the healing of forgiveness. He affirmed that now was the time for mercy, but that the future would be the time of universal judgment.

**VERSE 38.**—“The snuffers also, and the receptacles for them.” ([The same author], same work.) Divine words by which it is clearly indicated in many places that not the letter of the law but its spiritual meaning must be preserved; hence: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

([The same author], same work.) The snuffer, and the vessels in which the things snuffed out are extinguished, etc., up to his saying: “Whether prophecies will be abolished, or tongues will cease,” etc.

[Col. 0270B] “The snuffers also,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) There are certain precepts in Scripture, etc., up to: “And elsewhere: Behold, I make all things new.”

**VERSE 39.**—“The whole.” ([The same author], same work.) This is the body of Christ together with its head, namely, all the elect, etc., up to “because by the punishment of their crimes they fall into the abyss that weighs them down.”

**VERSE 40.**—“Look.” ([The same author], same work.) The model of the lampstand that he was to make was shown to Moses on the mountain, etc., up to “he displays the model to his hearers through the execution of the work and the word of instruction.”

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 1.**—“The tabernacle, moreover, shall be made in this way,” etc. (Bede, *On the Tabernacle*, book II, chapter 3, vol. II.) The tabernacle that Moses made in the wilderness, and the temple that Solomon made in Jerusalem, etc., up to “and may they be joined by divine and mutual love.”

([The same author], cited above.) The figure of both sanctuaries can be distinguished in this way, etc., up to “he depicts it with an astonishing variety of figures.”

“Variegated with twisted linen, violet, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet.” ([The same author], cited above, chapter 2.) In these four colors of the curtains, etc., up to “purple signifies hearts devoted to God and prepared to die for God, being of the color of blood and dyed with the blood of shellfish.”

**VERSE 2.**—“The length of one curtain shall be twenty-eight cubits, and its width four,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) If you count all the numbers in order from one through seven in their complete sequence, etc., up to “so that by faith and good works he may press on toward rest.”

“Of one measure,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) Although the curtains differed in their varied decoration, they were nevertheless all of one measure in length and width, because although the elect possess different gifts, there is nevertheless one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all.

([The same author], cited above.) Josephus relates, etc., up to “as though the tabernacle were adorned by the single joining of ten curtains.”

**VERSE 4.**—“You shall make violet loops on the sides,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The curtains are joined to one another by violet loops, etc., up to “and trust that they will remain in it forever.”

(Bede, same work.) It was also commanded that fringes be made at the corners of garments, etc., up to “we shall be gathered from the four winds and joined in indivisible fellowship.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Fifty,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) In the fiftieth year, etc., up to “it is rightly represented as that in which one truly rests and rejoices.”

([The same author], same work.) The curtains have fifty loops because, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, the elect are joined to one another in the fellowship of peace, which is the bond of perfection. The hope and memory of the future fellowship and peace possessed in this life also make those separated by times or places harmonious through one devotion.

[Col. 0271B] ([The same author], same work.) The curtains have loops on both sides, etc., up to “when the righteous are bound together by a harmonious quality of virtues.”

“You shall make fifty clasps.” ([The same author], same work.) This is explained more fully when it is said, etc., up to “indeed, Christ’s Church is perfected from all the elect.”

**VERSE 7.**—“You shall also make tent-cloths,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) This is found in the following passage: “He also made eleven tent-cloths of goats’ hair,” etc. The tent-cloths with which the tabernacle is covered, etc., up to “while, like tent-cloths, they endure storms outside.”

Tent-cloths of hair signify the coarse minds of human beings, which, although they are advanced harshly by the hidden judgment of God, do not fear serving temporal concerns, so that they may endure the winds and rains of temptations.

“You shall also make tent-cloths,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) Haircloth belongs to penitents, etc., up to “whose perfection of heart, however, is revealed when it is said: The length of one tent-cloth,” etc.

([The same author], same work.) Tent-cloths of hair, or of goats’ hair, etc., up to “nor receive apostolic grace.”

(Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 108.) There are eleven curtains of hair, etc., up to “and whose sins are covered.”

They are for covering the tabernacle, namely, so that its tender interior parts may not be disturbed by any adversity; otherwise neither does the linen shine, nor does the scarlet sparkle, nor is the violet adorned with its blue color. Those, therefore, who advance within the bosom of the Church ought not to despise their superiors if they see them occupied with external matters.

**VERSE 8.**—“The length of one tent-cloth.” (Bede, *On the Tabernacle*, book II, chapter 3, vol. II.) Its length has the number ten, etc., up to “who nevertheless are raised among human beings according to the measure of human perfection.”

“It shall have an equal measure.” ([The same author], same work.) Because there is one faith in which the whole Church is saved, etc., up to “where the solid strength of the wall was lacking.”

([The same author], same work.) Consider also the measure of the curtains, etc., up to “This concerns the curtains.”

([The same author], same work.) The tent-cloths have thirty cubits in length, etc., up to “in that they are leaders of the Lord’s flocks that follow.”

[Col. 0272A] **VERSE 9.**—“The sixth tent-cloth at the front.” Mystically, the sixth tent-cloth is doubled at the front of the covering when all who enter the holy Church are initiated by faith and by the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion in such a way that they understand that they must always live in imitation of it. For, as it were, at the entrance the sixth tent-cloth is doubled, so that we may receive the sacrament of the Lord’s Passion and be instructed by his examples. Concerning the sacraments Peter says: “He regenerated us into a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead.” And concerning imitation of the Passion he says: “Since Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought.”

**VERSE 10.**—“You shall make fifty loops at the edge of the one tent-cloth.” (Bede, same work.) As we explained these matters above concerning the curtains, etc., up to “he seeks such help from his neighbor as may strengthen him.”

**VERSE 11.**—“Bronze clasps by which the loops are joined, so that one covering may be made from the whole,” etc. ([The same author].) The clasps are rightly bronze, made, that is, from a resonant metal, because the humble conscience of the righteous has a great voice before God. Hence the poor man David, when he was distressed and was pouring out his prayer not in the ears of human beings but in the sight of God, said: “Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come to you.”

**VERSE 12.**—“But whatever remains,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) So that these matters may be understood more fully, etc., up to “ten again descending beside the boards of the eastern wall.”

**VERSE 13.**—“And a cubit.” Because the tent-cloths extended beyond the curtains by one cubit on the southern side of the dwelling and by another on the northern side, they therefore reached the ground, because the former were thirty cubits long, while the latter had two fewer.

**VERSE 14.**—“You shall also make a covering.” (Strabo.) The first covering was of curtains of linen, purple, and scarlet; the second consisted of the eleven tent-cloths; the third was of reddened rams’ skins; the last was of violet skins. The curtains covered the structure in such a way that they descended along the sides but did not reach the ground. The tent-cloths, however, covered the roof and sides and reached the ground. The reddened or violet skins covered only the roof and did not slope down toward the other parts.

“Of skins,” etc. (Bede, same work, chapter 4.) Rams are teachers, the leaders of the Lord’s flock. Hence: “Bring to the Lord, sons of God, bring,” etc. It is as though he were saying: O angels devoted to this office, bring to the Lord in heaven those who imitate the apostles. For this reason also the sixth station of the people who went out from Egypt is called Elim, that is, “rams”; it had twelve springs and seventy palm trees, so that in name and appearance it might preserve the figure of the apostles.

“Reddened.” ([The same author], same work.) The rams’ skins are reddened to cover the roof of the tabernacle, etc., up to “they fortify them so that they may not fail amid pressures.”

“Of violet skins.” ([The same author], same work.) Violet is the color of heaven, etc., up to “that is, imitating the life of heaven.”

**VERSE 15.**—“Of acacia wood.” ([The same author], same work.) These boards signify the apostles and their successors, through whose preaching the Church was enlarged, etc., up to “nor was the Hebrew name translated, because this wood is scarcely found among other peoples.”

**VERSE 16.**—“Each shall have ten cubits in length and a cubit and a half in width.” (Bede, same work.) The length of the boards is their height, which was ten cubits, etc., up to: “And I will show him my salvation” (Psalm 90).

**VERSE 17.**—“On the sides.” ([The same author], same work.) It is fitted into the sides of the boards, etc., up to “we receive them into the bosom of love, and believe that we are received by them.”

**VERSE 18.**—“Of which twenty shall be on the southern side.” ([The same author], cited above, chapter 6.) How great the length of the tabernacle was, etc., up to “so that no one may think that virtues without works are sufficient for him.”

**VERSE 19.**—“For them forty silver bases,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The bases supporting the boards are the words and books of the law and the prophets, by which the apostles and evangelists proved that what they wished to write and preach was true and divine. Hence: “Then what was spoken through the prophets was fulfilled.” And elsewhere: “But all this happened so that the Scriptures of the prophets might be fulfilled” (Matthew 21). Peter also says: “We have the prophetic word made more certain” (2 Peter 1).

(Bede, Gregory.) Through the bases of silver beneath the boards, the order of the prophets is signified. Since they were the first to speak of the Lord’s incarnation, they rose like bases from the foundation, supported the weight of the structure placed upon them, and sustained the boards—that is, the apostolic preaching spread throughout the world—like firm and cast supports. For the life of the apostles is instructed by their preaching and strengthened by their authority. Hence two bases are placed beneath each board: because, when the prophets agree in their words concerning Christ’s incarnation, they build up the preachers who follow, so that, since they do not differ from one another, they may fix them more securely. They are commanded to be cast from silver. The brightness of silver is preserved through use; without use it turns black. Before Christ’s coming, the sayings of the prophets were not used in spiritual understanding, since they could not be perceived because of their obscurity, and therefore remained, as it were, black. But after Christ came and wiped them clean before our eyes with the hand of his incarnation, whatever light lay hidden in them shone forth, and he gave the meaning of the earlier fathers for use, because he explained the words through realities.

(Bede.) Two bases are rightly placed beneath each board, so that the agreement of prophetic testimony in all that the apostles said may be demonstrated. Or two are placed beneath the two corners, so that, with the corners well supported, the whole board may stand properly, because the beginning of every apostolic and evangelical word is foreshadowed in the prophetic books, and the entire life of the apostles and their successors, from the beginning of faith to the end of the present life, is inserted in the mystical boards of the Old Testament.

**VERSE 20.**—“On the second side also.” The southern side, which slopes toward the south, signifies the ancient people of God, who, having once received the light of knowledge of the law, burned with love of God. The second side, which slopes toward the north, signifies the nations, which until the time of the incarnation languished in the darkness and cold of unbelief. Concerning their calling it is said: “I will say to the North, Give; and to the South, Do not withhold” (Isaiah 43). It is as though he were saying: I will say to the people of the nations, long cold without faith: “Let your sons come to the faith of my confession and love.” And also to the Israelite people, which already enjoys the light of my knowledge: “Do not prevent the nations from being received into the lot of election.”

“Twenty boards.” (Bede.) The board on either side had one and the same number, measurements, and construction, because one and the same faith, hope, and charity are preached to both peoples through the apostles, and both are called to the promised land of the heavenly kingdom. They receive the general command concerning both: “Go into all the world and preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16), that is, to the uncircumcised and the circumcised. And without any distinction it follows: “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved.”

**VERSE 21.**—“Two bases.” A basis is a foundation, from the Greek *baseia* [βασεία], that is, “I lay a foundation” or “foundation.” The prophets are signified by the bases, upon whose authority the apostles and all teachers rely. They are called “two” because of the agreement of the prophets, who all held one meaning.

**VERSE 22.**—“On the western side,” etc. (Bede, same work.) The western region, etc., up to “they will remain in the Church until the end of the world.”

[Col. 0274C] “On the western side,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The tabernacle is rightly completed in the western region, etc., up to “but also for the evils from which he delivered them.”

([The same author].) The western region, which is said to face the sea, rightly consists of six boards, because the number six signifies the completion of good work: in six days the Lord completed the adornment of the world; on the sixth day he created the human being in the beginning; and in the sixth age he restored the human race through his Passion. Or because there are six ages of the world, in which we must be perfected through good works so that we may reach the eternal glory of the resurrection.

**VERSE 23.**—“And again two others.” ([The same author].) Because two further boards, in addition to the first six, are commanded to be erected at the corner behind the tabernacle, receiving the wall coming from the eastern side and joining it to the wall of the western side, this pertains to the reward of the future life, which, after the labors and periods of one life, is secure—or made secure. It is divided into the Sabbath-rest, that is, the rest of souls after the dissolution of bodies, and the glory of the resurrection, common to both peoples and destined to have no end.

**VERSE 24.**—“And they shall be joined to one another.” ([The same author], same work.) Because the entire life of the elect tends toward heavenly things through one faith and charity, reaches one end in the vision of God, and the speech of all holy preachers converges in one voice of sound doctrine. The framework of the boards would withdraw from one another if one prophet or apostle denied what another had said.

[Col. 0275A] “And for the two boards,” etc. (Bede, same work.) The corner boards are joined in every respect to the boards of the walls, etc., up to “the prophets foretold with harmonious voice that these things would come to pass.”

([The same author], same work.) Here the measure of the bases is not given, etc., up to “but would be preserved immovable in secure rest.”

“You shall make bars of wood,” etc. ([The same author], same work, chapter 7.) The five bars that hold together the boards of the tabernacle, etc., up to “and imposed nothing other than the commandments of the law.”

**VERSE 29.**—“You shall also overlay the boards with gold.” ([The same author], same work.) The gilded boards of the tabernacle shine brilliantly, etc., up to “but also read the light of the heavenly reward.”

“Which you shall cover with plates.” ([The same author], same work.) The bars are covered with golden plates, etc., up to “when spiritual understanding is displayed as full of mysteries.”

**VERSE 30.**—“You shall erect the tabernacle.” ([The same author], same work.) The model of the tabernacle, etc., up to “they order both the work and the mind.”

**VERSE 31.**—“You shall also make a veil.” ([The same author], same work, chapter 8.) Even according to the literal sense, this corresponds to the beauty of the heavenly vision. For if you consider the beauty and flames of the stars, the manifold appearance of the clouds, and the rainbow itself, drawing out a thousand and various colors when the sun is turned away, you will observe in heaven paintings far more numerous and beautiful than those on the veil of the tabernacle.

“You shall also make a veil,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) This veil, etc., up to “so that he may appear before the face of God on our behalf.”

“You shall also make a veil of violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen.” ([The same author], same work.) Up to this point concerning the southern wall, etc., up to “colors when the sun is turned away.”

**VERSE 32.**—“Which you shall hang before four,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The four columns, etc., up to “there will be no such place where nothing at all is evil.”

“Which themselves are gilded.” ([The same author], same work.) The columns before which the veil is hung are gilded because the angelic powers placed within the veil of heaven are clothed with the grace of supreme brightness. They have golden capitals because the mind by which they are governed is illuminated by the presence of divine knowledge and vision.

([The same author], same work.) The columns have silver bases, etc., up to “the brilliance of words is shown by silver.”

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVIII, chapter 6.) He commands the bases of the four columns to be silver, etc., up to “they carry the words of the evangelists by mouth and by deed.”

[Col. 0275D] **VERSE 33.**—“The veil shall also be inserted,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) Because it was in the eternal counsel of the Divinity, etc., up to “on the day of judgment.”

“Within it you shall place the ark of the testimony,” etc. Within this veil the ark of the covenant was placed because Christ, acquainted with the secrets of the Father, ascended after his Passion and resurrection to the heaven of heavens and sits at the right hand of the Father.

“They shall be divided.” Because the Church, which consists of angels and human beings, partly journeys in the lower regions and partly reigns in the heights, it still has its citizens separated from one another by the veil of heaven.

**VERSE 35.**—“And the table outside the veil,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The table and lampstand of the tabernacle signify the temporal benefits of God, etc., up to “bearing witness to him.”

**VERSE 36.**—“You shall also make a screen,” etc. ([The same author], same work, chapter 9.) After the account of the veil has been explained, etc., up to “because he rejoiced in the restraint of flesh and spirit.”

([The same author].) Literally, the tabernacle was a house consecrated to God, etc., up to “of fifty cubits in width.”

**VERSE 37.**—“And five columns.” ([The same author], same work.) The columns from which the screen is suspended, etc., up to “the evangelical Scripture not yet having been disclosed.”

“Of acacia wood.” ([The same author], same work.) The columns of wood, etc., up to “but Jesus Christ.”

“Whose capitals shall be golden,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The golden capitals signify Christ, etc., up to “it is built upon the souls of the elect, which are free from corruption.”

## CHAPTER XXVII

**VERSE 1.**—“You shall also make an altar of wood.” (Bede, *On the Tabernacle*, book II, chapter 11, vol. II.) Namely, because the hearts in which the Holy Spirit dwells ought to be pure and incorrupt.

“And three cubits.” ([The same author], same work.) Such is approximately the stature of a human being, etc., up to “does not pertain to the altar.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Its horns, moreover,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The altar of holocausts has four corners, etc., up to “it remains inviolable, indeed stronger.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And you shall make for its use cauldrons.” ([The same author], same work.) The various vessels of the altar, etc., up to “charity, which can never be extinguished, will burn.”

[Col. 0276C] “Tongs also.” ([The same author], same work.) The tongs are preachers, etc., up to “and command them to shine.”

“And forks, and fire-pans,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The forks, which in Greek are called *kreágrai* [κρεάγραι], etc., up to “surpass the measure of our capacity.”

“Fire receptacles.” These were assigned for the purpose that by means of them the holy fire might be carried from the altar of holocausts to the altar of incense in the evening and morning, in order to place the incense there. For teachers carry fire from the altar of holocausts to the altar of incense when, by teaching, they lead their hearers from virtue to virtue and, as their merits increase, to higher things and to the inner secrets of the divine vision. They also imitate the fervent hearts of their neighbors in piety and become receptacles of fire, because they strive to kindle in themselves the flame of the heavenly sacrifice that they see in the minds of their brothers.

[Col. 0276D] **VERSE 4.**—“And a grating in the form,” etc. (Bede, cited above, chapter 18.) The altar was commanded to be made entirely hollow, etc., up to “we think that he learned this from the Jewish teachers.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Beneath the hearth,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The altar has a hearth, etc., up to “and be brought to the perfection of the end.”

([The same author].) If anyone is troubled by the literal sense, etc., up to “the cleaner it is found to be.”

**VERSE 6.**—“You shall make bars.” Namely, teachers, who call Judaea and the Gentiles with harmonious voice and deed into the one grace of faith. Or the bars will be for carrying the altar on both sides when preachers teach the minds of the faithful to maintain steadfastness in virtue in prosperity and adversity.

**VERSE 8.**—“As it was shown to you on the mountain.” (Bede, same work.) All the things that are mystically given to us, etc., up to “we are commanded always to do.”

**VERSE 9.**—“You shall also make the court.” ([The same author], cited above, chapter 13.) Just as the Holy of Holies, etc., up to “but its memory is uprooted from the innermost heart.”

“One hundred cubits.” ([The same author], same work.) It is established that the number one hundred, etc., up to “and assume temporal continence.”

**VERSE 10.**—“And twenty columns.” ([The same author], same work.) The columns from which the screens are suspended, etc., up to “because they sound nothing other than the word of God.”

[Col. 0277B] “With their bases,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The bases of the columns, etc., up to “they will never lack the fruit of their reward.”

“Silver.” ([The same author].) Their capitals are not silver-plated but wholly silver, because teachers subject themselves entirely to divine Scripture and devote soul and body to meditating and preaching the divine words. For just as limbs cannot live without a head, so they, considering the divine utterances their life, never cease to carry them through obedience and to exalt themselves by humbling themselves.

**VERSE 11.**—“Likewise on the side.” ([The same author], same work.) The same things are repeated concerning the northern side, etc., up to “are commanded to be made on one side of the tabernacle.”

**VERSE 12.**—“But in width,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The width of the court facing the setting of the sun, up to [Col. 0277C] “ten columns raise and lift up.”

**VERSE 13.**—“Also in that part of the court.” The width of the court facing the east, etc., up to “and the life of the age to come.”

“There shall be fifty cubits.” ([The same author].) By the fifty cubits of the eastern side, the beginnings of believers in general are signified, because they are celebrated in the remission of sins and in the hope of future blessedness. Their particular distinction is then added, which, when carefully considered, is referred to the same end. For it follows:

**VERSE 14.**—“In which fifteen cubits of screens shall be assigned to one side, and three columns,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) Fifteen, then, etc., up to “and preserve the body without reproach until the day of the Lord.”

**VERSE 16.**—“And it shall have columns,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) At the entrance of the court there are four columns, etc., up to “they expend all the senses of the body in the obedience of charity.”

“Of violet,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) It is right that at this entrance of the court the screens, etc., up to “adorn a screen woven with a beautiful variety of colors.”

**VERSE 17.**—“All the columns,” etc. ([The same author].) He repeats more carefully what he had said, in order to admonish the reader diligently that no one among the teachers of truth—namely, the columns of the heavenly court—can be counted among them unless he has learned to possess invincible patience amid adversities, like bronze; unless he has adorned and fortified himself on every side, like silver plates, through observance of heavenly things and proclamation of words; unless he has subjected himself in complete obedience to the divine commandments, as to a silver capital; and unless he has established himself in the fear of God, as upon a bronze base.

**VERSE 18.**—“In length,” etc. ([The same author].) One hundred cubits in length, etc., up to “and it shall be made of twisted linen,” etc.

**VERSE 19.**—“All the vessels,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) These vessels are the human beings in the Church, etc., up to “the courts of the Lord.”

**VERSE 20.**—“Command the children of Israel.” ([The same author], book III of *On the Tabernacle*, chapter 1, vol. II.) After all the adornment of the tabernacle had been arranged, etc., up to “may display the light of good action.”

“Of olive trees.” ([The same author], same work.) It should be noted that the children of Israel are commanded to offer oil, etc., up to “to kindle the incense of prayers.”

**VERSE 21.**—“And they shall place it.” ([The same author], same work.) For it is not the task of everyone to preach the mysteries of faith to the people, etc., up to “as James says to such people: ‘Do not become many teachers, my brothers,’” etc. (James 3).

“It shall be perpetual,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) This conclusion, like the one concerning the tabernacle, etc., up to “when God is all in all.”

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Bring also to yourself,” etc. (Bede, book III of *On the Tabernacle*, chapter 1, vol. II.) Just as the tabernacle, etc., up to “and all the teachers of the Church.”

([The same author].) “Bring also,” etc. After the construction of the tabernacle had been described, [Col. 0278C] etc., up to “they are consumed by the fire of heavenly vengeance.”

**VERSE 2.**—“And you shall make holy vestments.” ([The same author], same work.) The holy vestments of Aaron, etc., up to “and dispenser of the word of God.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Now these,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) How each of these things was made, etc., up to “ought to be splendid and glorious before the sight of the inner judge.”

(Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, book II, chapter 3, vol. III.) The priest is commanded to bear on each shoulder, etc., up to “as twisted linen shines forth in the various appearance of the ephod.”

**VERSE 6.**—“They shall make the ephod.” (Bede, book III of *On the Tabernacle*, chapter 4.) Because we carry burdens on our shoulders, etc., up to “when the flesh is wearied through abstinence.”

“And twice-dyed scarlet, twisted linen, and embroidered work.” ([The same author], same work.) Scarlet gleams in the likeness of fire, etc., up to “displaying scarlet in his attire.”

**VERSE 7.**—“It shall have two edges joined together on each side of the upper parts, so that they may come together as one.” ([The same author], same work.) Concerning this it is said below, etc., up to “for which we seek the rewards of invisible life.”

**VERSE 8.**—“The texture itself and all the variety of the work shall be of gold, violet, purple, twice-dyed scarlet, and twisted linen. And you shall take.” ([The same author], same work.) Gold is not to be in one part, etc., up to “the priest ought to be resplendent.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Two stones,” etc. So that the priest may imitate the faith and life of the patriarchs, remember the twelve tribes in sacrifices and prayers, and, with the people looking on, may not stray from the merits of the patriarchs.

**VERSE 11.**—“Enclosed in gold,” etc. (Bede, same work.) It is fitting that the stones be commanded to be enclosed and surrounded with gold, etc., up to “may be able to slip away from the custody of the mind.”

**VERSE 12.**—“And Aaron shall bear their names before the Lord upon both shoulders as a memorial.” Because the priest, carefully considering at every hour the life of the saints who preceded him, ought to be fortified in prosperity and adversity with the adornment of virtues, so that, advancing with the weapons of righteousness on his right and on his left, he may not be bent toward any side of lowly pleasure.

(Bede, same work.) For three reasons Aaron bears the names, etc., [Col. 0279B] up to “or may set before them the examples of the fathers to follow.”

**VERSES 13–14.**—“You shall also make hooks of gold, and two chains of pure gold joined to one another, which you shall insert into the hooks.” ([The same author], same work.) These hooks were at the upper corners, etc., up to “must be joined by charity and good intention.”

(Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part II, chapter 2, vol. III.) It is commanded that the breastpiece of judgment be marked upon Aaron’s breast by the binding ribbons, etc., up to “those subject to them must be governed not without great fear.”

**VERSE 15.**—“You shall also make the breastpiece of judgment by skilled work,” etc. (Bede, cited above, chapter 5.) Just as the perfection of works is represented in the ephod, etc., up to “carefully to consider what agrees with the pursuit of virtue.”

[Col. 0279C] **VERSE 16.**—“Double.” ([The same author], same work.) The breastpiece was made, etc., up to “so that he may grasp the prize of God’s heavenly calling.”

**VERSE 17.**—“And you shall place in it.” ([The same author], same work.) This placement of the various gems in the breastpiece, etc., up to “so that they too may deserve to become members of the High Priest.”

([The same author].) We can understand in the varied beauty of the stones, etc., up to “it profits him nothing.”

**VERSE 19.**—“Onyx.” ([The same author].) It is right that there be two onyx stones, etc., up to “he himself may progress toward better things.”

**VERSE 22.**—“You shall make on the breastpiece,” etc. ([The same author].) The order of the work, etc., up to “and move away from one another.”

([The same author], same work.) The ephod signifies the completion of good works, [Col. 0279D] etc., up to “unless, hastening him toward good action, it holds him by its hooks.”

([The same author].) The ephod was fastened tightly with a belt, etc., up to “through the practice of virtues.”

**VERSE 28.**—“A violet ribbon,” etc. ([The same author], same work.) The violet ribbons by which the two priestly garments are joined are bonds of heavenly desire. Fastened into golden rings, they tighten the ephod to the breastpiece when, having recognized the light of the eternal homeland, we sigh for that glory and strive to serve in the tabernacle of the present Church so that we may deserve to enter it through harmonious faith, life, work, and profession.

**VERSE 29.**—“And Aaron shall bear the names of the children of Israel on the breastpiece of judgment,” etc. Aaron bears the names of the children of Israel on his breast as a memorial before the Lord forever when the prelate never ceases to care for his subjects, but strengthens their life by consoling, rebuking, exhorting, and encouraging them, and strives to commend it for protection to the Lord through frequent prayers.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVIII, chapter 9.) When the priest enters the tabernacle, he is commanded to carry on his breast twelve stones engraved with the names of the children of Israel. This is our Redeemer, who, offering himself as a sacrifice for us, carried twelve stones beneath his head at the first part of his body, since at the beginning he had strong preachers.

The priest ought to carry the memory of the fathers on his breast, especially when he ministers at the altar, so that, in the more sacred ministry, he may adorn himself with greater diligence and with the full devotion and industry of his mind, and, looking to the examples of the saints with his body, may present himself as their diligent imitator before the divine sight.

**VERSE 30.**—“And you shall place on the breastpiece of judgment,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) So that the priest may remember, etc., up to “in that which he administers in God’s place.”

“You shall place on the breastpiece,” etc. (Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 117.) The demonstration and truth are placed upon the breastpiece in what kind of material or metal, etc., up to “placed upon the *logion* [λογίον].”

**VERSE 31.**—“You shall make the robe,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) The priest is clothed in an entirely violet, ankle-length robe, etc., up to “rightly it is added.”

**VERSE 32.**—“In its middle above there shall be an opening, and a woven edge around it, as is made,” etc. The violet robe has a very strong opening and an edge woven from the same material, so that it may not easily be torn. This occurs when the beginning of a good work, supported by the firm root of the fear of the Lord, is proven to be fortified against all the snares of the ancient enemy. Such an edge clothes and adorns the priest’s neck all around when it gives the ruler confidence to preach heavenly things: namely, when he has not only lived rightly in the course of his life but has also begun from the beginning with uprightness, like Samuel, Jeremiah, and John, who were filled with spiritual grace from infancy and set apart in the order of teachers. Since the voice is in the neck, the proper use of speaking is expressed through the neck. As is customary with the lower parts of garments, just as works are signified by garments, so the completion of works is signified by the lower parts of garments.

Or the lower parts of garments are our final concerns, by which the faithful, when compelled to finish life, strive more earnestly to cleanse themselves from every stain of evil. They take care with fear and trembling lest, brought before the strict judge, they be expelled into the outer darkness on account of the filthy garment of vices, but instead appear clothed, as God’s elect, with compassion, kindness, modesty, patience, and charity, which is the bond of perfection (Colossians 3).

The violet robe therefore has a woven edge at its opening, as is customary with the lower parts of garments, when an outstanding teacher begins the work of virtues at a level of perfection that another scarcely reaches after prolonged labor; and when he walks with his God every hour in such fear of service as another scarcely possesses at death and on entering the final judgment. But because the entire perfection of the priest consists in works and the teaching of truth, according to the saying, “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts 1), it is rightly added: “At the bottom, toward the feet of the same robe” (Exodus 28).

“You shall make the robe,” etc. (Bede, as above.) It is called the ephod-robe, etc., up to “it ought to be covered with the grace of virtues from head to foot.”

### Verse 33

“Below, toward the feet,” and so forth. Gregory, *Book I of the Registers*, chapter 29. When a ruler prepares to speak, and so forth, up to: “hold fast to the unity of faith with careful observance.”

Bede, as above. “At the bottom, toward the feet of the tunic,” and so forth, up to: “they reveal it by the distinct sound of their speech.”

The same. We may understand in the twelvefold number of the jewels of the breastpiece, and so forth, up to: “Of the same year David also says: ‘You will bless the crown of the year with your kindness’” (Psalm 64).

The same. Or, as was said above, and so forth, up to: “in the splendor of varied virtues.”

### Verse 35

“So that it may be heard,” and so forth. Gregory, in the work cited above. When the priest enters or returns, and so forth, up to: “the very works of the priest may cry out.”

Bede, in the work cited above. If we wish to attend to Josephus’s words, and so forth, up to: “it would be preached to the four quarters of the square world.”

### Verse 36

“You shall also make a plate,” and so forth. The same, in the same work, chapter 7. The golden plate on the forehead of the high priest, and so forth, up to: “so that we may acknowledge that she rose again.”

“Holy to the Lord,” and so forth. The same. That which is commanded to be engraved on the plate, and so forth, up to: “which he restored by his passion.”

The same. We carry “Holy to the Lord,” engraved in gold, on our forehead, and so forth, up to: “who ought to offer an example of virtue to all.”

### Verse 37

“You shall bind it.” The plate containing “Holy to the Lord” is fastened with a hyacinth-colored ribbon to the high priest’s tiara. Strengthened in faith by the hope of heavenly rewards, which the hyacinth signifies, we preserve all the more firmly the mysteries of our redemption, or the undefiled image and likeness of our Creator and Redeemer, the more clearly we have recognized that there is no other path of salvation. The tiara will be discussed in its proper place.

### Verse 38

“And Aaron shall bear it.” The priest bears, that is, the iniquities connected with the offerings and gifts which they presented to the Lord and which the sons of Israel consecrated, when he absolves from the guilt of crimes on account of the fruits of worthy repentance—that is, almsgiving and the other works of justice performed by penitents. Divine instruction represented these things as needing to be carried out in the high priest’s clothing and taught them plainly in words.

Alas, however, some receive—or rather demand—gifts, yet neither carry away nor rebuke the iniquities of the people, although they ought to take material things for this reason alone: because they minister spiritual things. But because the one whose mind is always endowed with the remembrance of the divine name can labor, preach, and entreat the Lord effectively on behalf of his subjects, it is aptly added: “The plate shall always be on his forehead,” and so forth.

“The plate shall be,” and so forth. Bede, in the work cited above, chapter 8. If the plate bearing the name of God was always on Aaron’s forehead, and so forth, up to: “they hasten to obtain it.”

### Verse 39

“You shall gird the tunic.” The same, in the same work. Why it is called “tight,” and so forth, up to: “And you shall make a linen tiara,” and so forth.

Bede, in the same work. How this was made, and so forth, up to: “make it harsh and hard for the hearers.”

“And the tiara,” and so forth. The tiara, which is called a *cidaris* and a *mitre*, and so forth, up to: “he would perfect it through the fear of God.”

The same. Concerning the making of the belt, and so forth, up to: “and the other garments,” when it is said:

### Verse 40

“Moreover, for Aaron’s sons you shall prepare linen tunics,” and so forth. In the same work. We must speak of the high priest’s belt, and so forth, up to: “and faith is the girdle of his loins.”

“You shall prepare tunics,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. The priests have linen tunics, and so forth, up to: “and their sense of smell may be kept worthy of God.”

### Verse 41

“You shall clothe them with these,” and so forth. The same, in the same work, chapter 9. Aaron and his sons were to be clothed with all these garments, but distinctly: he himself was to use all of them, while his sons were to use the final three, which are specifically assigned to them, when it is said: “Moreover, for Aaron’s sons you shall prepare linen tunics,” and so forth.

The same. The undergarments made to cover the shame of the body or flesh, and so forth, up to: “with the undergarments,” namely, the tight linen garment, the belt, and the tiara.

## Chapter 29

### Verse 1

“But you shall also do this,” and so forth. Bede, in the work cited above. Thus far the nature of the clothing that Aaron and his sons ought to have, and so forth, up to: “they figuratively demonstrate.”

“Take a calf.” Strabo. Whoever is a high priest or priest ought to offer a bull—that is, firmly believe in and imitate Christ’s passion—and two rams, so that he may believe that the same Christ consists of body and soul; and unleavened bread, that is, purity of life; and unleavened bread sprinkled with oil, so that among all the virtues he may not neglect works of mercy, or may believe that he possesses them not from himself but as a gift of grace.

### Verse 2

“And a cake.” Bede, in the work cited above. We offer to the Lord a cake mixed with oil for our consecration when everything we do grows rich through the inward grace of the Spirit in the devotion of the heart. We offer flat cakes smeared with oil when we unmistakably show by our outward example of life that the spiritual things we do are genuine. By these offerings our consecration is completed, while, through good works and pure thoughts, and by God’s gift, we acquire for ourselves the merit of holiness.

“And when you have washed the father,” and so forth. The same. They are first commanded to be washed and afterward to be adorned with garments, because whoever assumes the office of priesthood ought to cleanse himself with a flood of tears, so that he may approach the divine ministry worthily.

Bede. In this washing one might understand the baptism of the sacred font, if it followed that someone elected to the priesthood was then first washed with baptismal water for the remission of sins, and if the Apostle did not contradict this when he says: “Not a recent convert, lest, being puffed up, he fall into the judgment of the devil” (1 Timothy 3).

### Verse 5

“You shall clothe Aaron,” and so forth. The same. It should be noted that although in Exodus Aaron is affirmed to be clothed in eight garments, and so forth, up to: “because he came in the name of the Father, saying: ‘I am in the Father and the Father is in me’; and whoever sees me sees the Father” (John 4).

### Verse 9

“Afterward,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 25. Another version reads, and so forth, up to: “to be sanctified by Moses.”

### Verse 10

“You shall bring,” and so forth. Augustine, question 126. Another version reads, and so forth, up to: “upon the calf to be sacrificed.”

### Verse 18

“It is an offering to the Lord.” Augustine. “An odor of sweetness to the Lord,” and so forth, up to: “leads it to the smell of bodily nostrils.”

### Verse 22

“And the right shoulder.” Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part 2, chapter 3. The priest, by divine law, and so forth, up to: “invite him to higher things by the shoulder of his work.”

### Verse 30

“And he who shall enter.” Augustine, question 129. How, then, does he say that it belongs specifically to this one alone, and so forth, up to: “and that on both sides what is written might be preserved: ‘Mercy triumphs over judgment’” (James 2).

## Chapter 30

### Verse 1

“You shall also make an altar,” and so forth. Bede, in the work cited above, chapter 11. When the commands of consecration have been completed, and so forth, up to: “they also draw near in the body.”

“An altar.” The same, in the same work. Appropriately, the altar of incense was as much superior in the brilliance of its metal as it was smaller in size: for the holier they are, the fewer they are.

“Of acacia wood.” The same, in the same work. Appropriately, it was made of acacia wood, resembling white thorn and incorruptible, and so forth, up to: “he gives life through the varied grace of gifts.”

### Verse 2

“Having one cubit.” The same, in the same work. The length and breadth of the altar are one cubit, and so forth, up to: “let him perform the duty of piety.”

“Four-square.” The same, in the same work. Rightly, the altar of incense, and so forth, up to: “it will be everlasting joy for them.”

“Horns.” The same, in the same work. The horns signify the eminence of faith and virtue, and so forth, up to: “having the appearance of piety, but denying its power.”

### Verse 3

“You shall overlay it,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. It was appropriately overlaid with gold, and so forth, up to: “with what sweetness of God they are refreshed in the hiding place of his countenance.”

“Also the grating,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. The grating of the altar is rightly, and so forth, up to: “it is correctly added.”

“You shall also make a crown for it,” and so forth. The altar of incense has a crown all around it. This signifies those who are lesser in merits and do not dare openly to declare that the reward of good struggle, service, and faith has been stored up for them. Nevertheless, they do everything with the intention of pleasing God, but in the hope of receiving a reward.

### Verse 4

“And two rings,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. These rings may be understood as the four books of the Gospel, and so forth, up to what follows: “You shall place the altar,” and so forth.

### Verse 7

“And he shall burn incense,” and so forth. The same, in the same work, chapter 12. Incense, or aromatic offering, and so forth, up to: “let us give thanks.”

The same. “And he shall burn incense,” and so forth. When the sun has risen in the morning, all things are clear, and so forth, up to: “in a place of darkness.”

“In the morning, when he arranges it.” The same, in the same work. In the morning Aaron offers incense, and so forth, up to: “they delight in devoting themselves to prayers.”

### Verse 9

“You shall not offer,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. In what follows, and so forth, up to: “they water their bed each night.”

The same. We can interpret these altars, and so forth, up to: “it may be understood.”

### Verse 10

“And he shall make atonement,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. Since Christ is our priest, and so forth, up to: “he rightly adds”:

“And he shall make atonement,” and so forth. Aaron makes atonement upon the altar of incense, and so forth, up to: “Isaac and Israel,” and so forth.

### Verse 11

“And the Lord spoke,” and so forth. After the altar of incense has been described, there remains the description of the bronze basin in which the priests entering the tabernacle were to wash their hands and feet; but one command is placed first.

### Verse 12

“When you take,” and so forth. Bede, in the work cited above, chapter 13. David forgot this command, and so forth, up to: “his own wealth.”

### Verse 13

“Half a shekel.” The same, in the same work. That is, ten obols, and so forth, up to: “it cannot be corrupted by any disturbance of unbelievers.”

### Verse 14

“Who is enrolled in the census,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. The number twenty, and so forth, up to: “he awaits in heaven.”

### Verse 15

“The rich shall not add,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. Whether someone is great in merits and perfect, or small and advancing in virtue, the law of the Decalogue—which commands love of God and neighbor—is imposed equally upon all.

### Verse 16

“And you shall receive the money,” and so forth. The same, in the same work. This occurs when whatever good we do, and so forth, up to: “will be struck by the blow of strict vengeance.”

### Verse 17

“And the Lord spoke,” and so forth. The same, in the same work, chapter 14. In this basin or laver one may understand, and so forth, up to: “which kept watch at the entrance of the tabernacle.”

### Verse 18
