“With its base.” The same, in the same work. The base on which the basin was placed, and so forth, up to: “that you may present your bodies,” and so forth (Romans 12).

“For washing,” and so forth. Christ also was washed with the water of this laver before entering to be offered upon the altar and kindling the incense of his sacred body for our salvation on the altar of the cross; for love of us he shed tears, as at the resurrection of Lazarus.

### Verse 21

“Lest they die.” Bede, in the same work. The death to be feared is eternal, and so forth, up to: “if he eats and drinks,” and so forth (1 Corinthians 11).

### Verse 23

“Take for yourself.” Strabo. Greek *smyrna* (σμύρνα), in Latin *myrrha*, is a tree in Arabia five cubits high. The Arabs burn its branches so that they may sprout and bear fruit more abundantly. Without the counteracting smoke of storax, people would contract incurable diseases from its odor. The gum of this tree is properly called *stacte*; improperly, it too is called myrrh.

“Cinnamon.” The cinnamon is a shrub that grows in India or Ethiopia and is only two cubits high. It is called *cinnamon* because it has thin, folded reeds like a cane, gray or black in color. When broken, they emit a visible vapor; the fine kind is valuable, but the coarse is cheap and despised. The aromatic reed is a species found near Lebanon. Myrrh, cinnamon, reed, and cassia: these four species signify the four principal virtues by which the Church of God is to be dedicated and sanctified with the oil of anointing, that is, with the grace of mercy.

### Verse 29

“And they shall be,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 135. Namely, when they have been anointed. What, then, will now distinguish those inner things that are covered by the veil?

“Whoever touches.” The same was said above concerning the altar of sacrifice. It is to be understood in this way: the people were permitted to touch the tabernacle when they brought sacrifices or any gifts, and by touching they were sanctified, because of the oil with which everything had been anointed—not as the priests, who were anointed from it so that they might perform an eternal priesthood.

### Verse 34

“Onycha.” Onycha is said to be a small, sweet-smelling shellfish, the size of a human fingernail. Hence it is called *onycha* in Greek, because Greek ὄνυξ (*onyx*) means “fingernail.”

“Galbanum.” Galbanum is said to be the sap of a fennel-like plant, of which the finest grows in Syria. It is cartilaginous and not very woody; its odor drives away snakes.

“And frankincense.” Greek *thus*, Latin *libanum*, takes its name from Mount Lebanon in Arabia. There is another Lebanon in Phoenicia, where cedars grow.

The finest frankincense is what is called “male,” because it is round like a human testicle. Its tree grows in Arabia, twisted according to the quality of the air and in a contorted, crooked branch.

Mystically, these four species signify kinds of holy virtues.

### Verse 35

“You shall make incense,” and so forth. Gregory, *Moralia*, book 1, chapter 39, volume 1. We make incense compounded from aromatics, and so forth, up to: “does not spread a subtler fragrance from itself.”

Isidore. Incense, which is composed of four very fragrant substances ground to the finest powder—namely, stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense—signifies the prayers of the faithful. Some also see these four substances as signifying the four elements: frankincense, being bright, corresponds to air; stacte to water; galbanum and onycha to earth and fire. Thus, through these, a pleasing incense to God is offered of all things that are in heaven and below heaven, on earth, and in the waters.

“By workmanship,” and so forth. Augustine, question 136. We should not suppose that an ointment is being made, but rather incense or aromatic offering, which is placed on the altar of incense, where sacrifice was not permitted and which stood within the Holy of Holies.

### Verse 37

“Such a one,” and so forth. Rabanus. We ought not to use these divine prayers and praises in human flattery. For one must serve God alone in this way; hence it was forbidden above that human flesh be anointed with it.

## Chapter 31

### Verse 2

“Bezalel,” and so forth, whose name is interpreted as “in the shadow of God,” as though the name said: “The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 62). David is said to have descended from him, and the name *polymitarius* is attributed to him because Bezalel constructed the tabernacle with embroidered work.

### Verse 3

“And I have filled him.” Augustine, question 128. Are these works, which seem to belong to craftsmanship, to be attributed to the gift of the Holy Spirit? Or was this also said figuratively, so that they might pertain to the divine Spirit of wisdom, understanding, and knowledge, which are signified by these things? Moreover, although he is said here to be filled with the Spirit, the Holy Spirit is not yet explicitly mentioned as the Spirit of divine wisdom and knowledge.

### Verse 6

“Oholiab,” whose name is interpreted as “my protection,” as though it said: “The Lord is the protector of my life; whom shall I fear?” (Psalm 26). Those who trust so steadfastly in the Lord fittingly build the tabernacle.

Strabo. It should be noted that the mystery of the Trinity is displayed in the construction of the tabernacle, just as in baptism and the Transfiguration. In baptism, the Father sounded in a voice, the Son was baptized, and the Spirit appeared in the form of a dove. Oholiab, whose name is interpreted as “my father is protection,” represents the person of the Father. Bezalel, whose name signifies “in the shadow of God,” represents the person of the Holy Spirit, of whom it is said: “The power of the Most High will overshadow you.” For the power of the Most High is understood to be the Holy Spirit. Hence the Lord says: “I knew that power had gone out from me” (Luke 8). The command—that is, the Word—by which the tabernacle was ordered to be made is the Son, through whom the Father accomplishes all things in the power of the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 13

“See,” and so forth. The Jews boast in vain about legal observance. It is plainly said that this is a sign of what is to come, namely, rest and blessedness; or of the rest of the saints in the present, since they rest from the tumult of worldly works and vices.

### Verse 18

“Two tablets.” Augustine, question 140. Although God spoke many things, only two stone tablets are given to Moses, and they are called tablets of testimony, because all the other things God commanded are understood to depend upon the ten commandments written on those two tablets, if they are carefully sought out and rightly understood. The ten commandments themselves depend upon two commandments—namely, love of God and love of neighbor—on which the whole law and the prophets depend (Matthew 22).

## Chapter 32

### Verse 1

“Make gods for us,” using the plural, although only one calf was made, evidently in the likeness of the bull Apis, whom the Egyptians worshiped. But whoever practices idolatry subjects himself to every vice and serves as many gods and demons as he has vices.

### Verse 2

“And he said to them,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 141. Aaron is understood to have commanded something difficult in order, by this means, to turn them back from their intention. Nevertheless, that very difficult thing came to pass: there was gold for making the idol. I have thought this worth noting for those who are distressed if something of this kind is divinely done or commanded to be endured with equanimity for the sake of eternal life.

### Verse 6

“And the people sat down to eat,” and so forth. Eating and drinking impelled them to play; play led to idolatry. If the fault of vanity is not carefully restrained, the unwary mind is gradually swallowed up by iniquity. Hence: “Whoever despises small things will gradually fall.” For if we neglect to attend to small matters, we are imperceptibly led astray and eventually commit even greater offenses boldly.

### Verse 8

“These are your gods.” Augustine, question 142. The Lord, showing Moses what the people had done with the calf and the idol they had made from their gold, says that they declared: “These are your gods, Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” Scripture does not record them saying this; but God reveals that such was their intention. They carried in their hearts the meaning of these words, which could not be hidden from God.

### Verse 10

“Let me go,” and so forth. Gregory, *Moralia*, book 9, chapter 11. What does it mean for him to say to his servant, and so forth, up to: “he was unable to restrain God’s anger on his own behalf.”

The same, *Moralia*, book 20, chapter 6. To build up the reader according to the historical sense is possible, and so forth, up to: “nor mercy without discipline.”

### Verse 13

“Remember Abraham, Isaac,” and so forth. He invokes the fathers, who are loved, on behalf of their sons who offend and do not deserve to be heard, because the good deeds of holy fathers often come to the aid of their sons.

### Verse 14

“And the Lord was appeased, so that he would not do the evil.” Augustine. Here he intended “evil” to mean punishment, as in: “Their end was reckoned as evil.” In this sense good and evil are said to come from God, not according to the wickedness by which evil people are evil. God is not evil; rather, because he is just, he inflicts evil things upon the wicked.

### Verse 19

“And he became exceedingly angry.” The same, question 144. Moses, being angry, appears to have broken the tablets of testimony written by the finger of God. Yet the repetition of the New Testament was symbolically represented by a great mystery, because the old covenant had to be abolished and the New established. It should certainly be noted with what great supplication to God he labored on behalf of the people, since he was so severe in punishing them.

### Verse 20

“And taking the calf which they had made.” Isidore, *On Exodus*, volume 5. The body of the devil is signified by the calf, and so forth, up to: “was swallowed up.”

“And he gave some of it to the sons of Israel to drink.” The Hebrews report that, when the sons of Israel drank the water infected with the powder of the calf, those who had committed idolatry carried the gold dust in their beards. By this sign the guilty or the innocent were made apparent: the guilty were killed.

### Verse 24

“And they gave it to me,” and so forth. Augustine, question 145. He spoke briefly, and so forth, up to: “he did not rebuke him.”

### Verse 25

“For Aaron had stripped him for the disgrace of filth and among his enemies,” and so forth. It should be noted that what the people did is attributed to Aaron because he consented to do what they had wrongly requested. It is more properly said that Aaron stripped them, because he yielded to them, than that they stripped themselves, since they had demanded so great an evil. They were stripped of the ornaments from which the idol had been fashioned, either because he had revealed an evil intention that had previously been hidden, or because he had lost God’s help and protection.

### Verse 27

“Let each man put his sword,” and so forth. Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part 3, chapter 26. “Sword,” and so forth, up to: “Hence it is added:”

“Let each man kill his brother,” and so forth. He killed those whom he found deserving of punishment by the sword of rebuke, and he did not spare even those whom he loved according to the kinship of the flesh. Therefore, if the one who is stirred to strike at vices by zeal for divine love is called God’s man, surely the one who refuses, as far as he is able, to rebuke the life of carnal people denies that he is God’s man.

### Verse 28

“And they did,” and so forth. Augustine, *On Expressions*, expression 124. He used the plural for the singular, and so forth, up to: “these expressions are inserted according to definite rules.”

### Verse 31

“Either forgive them,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 147. He says this confidently, and so forth, up to: “so that he might pour out those words to God on their behalf.”

### Verse 35

“Which Aaron made.” Augustine, question 148. Since Aaron was earlier said to have stripped the people, and so forth, up to what the Apostle says, crying out: “How inscrutable are his judgments,” and so forth (Romans 11).

## Chapter 33

### Verse 1

“And the Lord spoke,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 149. God, being angry, and so forth, up to: “he terrified them by his voice.”

“Go,” and so forth. The same, question 150. Immediately, as though he were speaking to Moses himself, and so forth, up to: “from the presence of the Lord.”

### Verse 2

“I will send an angel before you.” Augustine, question 150. God is with the righteous by visiting, showing mercy, and strengthening them; but with the wicked by avenging and punishing them. The meaning is: “I cannot be with these people on your account, to avenge and punish; nor on their account, to visit and strengthen. At least I will send my angel.”

### Verse 4

“When the people heard.” Rabanus. He says that the people heard an exceedingly bad message, that is, one that was most cruel and sorrowful. For what greater benefit can be granted to anyone than to have God’s grace present and to know that his Creator is favorable to him? Or what greater danger is there than to suffer the anger of one’s Maker? Whoever is deprived of the grace and presence of his Creator has nothing good.

### Verse 7

“Taking the tabernacle,” and so forth. This should be understood as a prolepsis if it refers to that tabernacle which had been shown to Moses on the mountain and constructed, at the Lord’s command, by Bezalel and Oholiab. Or it may have been another tabernacle, to which they were already gathering for judgment.

### Verse 8

“And when he went out,” and so forth. Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homily 13. The Hebrew people, having been freed from Egyptian slavery, and so forth, up to: “they try to advance.”

“And they looked,” and so forth. Strabo. Moses represents the Law. The Jewish people therefore looked upon Moses’ back because they did not wish to understand anything mystical or spiritual in the Law, but only the surface of the letter. For this reason his face was hidden, that is, true and pure knowledge.

When he entered the tabernacle, the pillar of cloud descended and stood at the entrance. Another translation says that, when Moses wished to enter the tabernacle, the cloud stood before him and prevented him. Here, however, it says that after he had entered, the cloud spoke with him before the entrance. We must therefore understand that he entered only some part of it, namely the court; and then, before he entered the tabernacle, the cloud stood in his way. This passage therefore signifies those who are less perfect in knowledge and works and are unable to penetrate the innermost parts of Scripture. Elsewhere, when he entered into the midst of the cloud, he represented the perfect—namely, those who investigate the secrets of mystical meanings.

“And the Lord spoke.” Scripture speaks according to the opinion of the people, who thought that Moses spoke with God mouth to mouth, although God spoke and appeared to him through a subordinate creature, that is, through an angel and a cloud. No one, whether human or angelic, could see his substance as it is. Hence: “To the King of ages, immortal, invisible,” and elsewhere: “He dwells in inaccessible light,” and so forth (1 Timothy 1 and 6).

Gregory, *Homilies on 1 Kings*, chapter 10. The face of God is his knowledge. God is known through a mirror; he is known through himself. Here he is known through a mirror, but in heaven through himself. The mirror is that light in which God dwells; indeed, God himself is that light.

“If, therefore, I have found favor,” and so forth. Augustine, question 151. By these words Moses showed, and so forth, up to: “so that they may keep themselves pure and undefiled and make progress.”

### Verse 17

“And I know you also,” and so forth. Augustine, question 153. “Since I know you above all,” and so forth. Does God, then, know some things more and other things less? And so forth, up to: “but it must be sought more carefully in the earlier parts of Scripture whether this is truly so.”

### Verse 19

“I will show,” and so forth. Augustine, question 154. When Moses had said to the Lord, and so forth, up to: “the Lord Christ is called among all nations.”

“And I will call.” Augustine, question 154. He said “I will call,” not “I will be called,” using an active verb for a passive one, an unusual form of expression by which he perhaps wished to signify that he himself would bring this about—that is, that by his grace the Lord would be called among all nations.

“And I will have mercy,” and so forth. Augustine, in the work cited above. What he added, and so forth, up to: “thus God declared that he would show mercy.”

Augustine, *On Predestination and Grace*, chapter 10. People are called by God without any preceding merits, and so forth, up to: “if the one who called should abandon him.”

“You cannot,” and so forth. Augustine, question 154. After commending his mercy, and so forth, up to: “this life must be died.”

### Verse 20

“For not,” and so forth. Gregory, *Moralia*, book 18, chapter 37, volume 1. John also says, and so forth, up to: “because satisfaction is always kindled by desire.”

### Verse 21

“Behold,” he said, “there is a place beside me, and you shall stand upon,” and so forth. Augustine, question 154. Again, with the article inserted, Scripture says, and so forth, up to: “the faithful people stood upon the rock.”

Gregory, *Moralia*, book 25, chapter 16. “There is a place beside me,” and so forth. The place is the Church. The rock is the Lord. Moses is the Jewish people, who did not believe in the Lord when he preached on earth. Thus it stood upon the rock, looking at the back of the passing Lord, because, after the Lord’s passion and ascension, it was brought into the Church and deserved to perceive Christ through faith; and although it did not see his presence, it came to know his “back,” that is, what followed afterward.

Gregory, in the same work. “There is a place beside me,” and so forth. It is the Church, and so forth, up to: “Of this firmness it is said: ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church.’”

### Verse 22

“And when my glory passes by,” and so forth. Eucherius, *On the Form of the Spirit*. God is also said to pass by when, from the hearts of certain people in whom he had previously been believed through faith, he afterward departs when unbelief or some sin secretly enters, and passes over to others: from the Jews to the Gentiles, from heretics to Catholics, and from the irreligious to the religious.

“And I will protect,” and so forth. Augustine, in the work cited above. “And I will cover you with my hand,” and so forth, up to what the Lord says afterward: “Cut for yourself two stone tablets,” and so forth.

## Chapter 34

### Verse 7

“Who repay the iniquity of the fathers to their sons and grandsons, to the third and fourth generation,” and so forth. Gregory, *Moralia*, book 15, chapter 22. Although it is written, and so forth, up to: “who saw what they would follow to their harm.”

### Verse 14

“The Lord is jealous.” Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 158. For the Lord God is jealous, and so forth, up to: “and destroys everyone who commits fornication away from him.”

### Verse 20

“The firstborn of a donkey,” and so forth. Isidore. By the donkey impurity is signified; by the sheep, innocence. Therefore, to exchange the firstborn of a donkey for a sheep is to convert the beginnings of an unclean life to the simplicity of innocence, so that after the sinner has done those things which the Lord rejects as unclean, he may now produce, by doing them, those things which are clean to place upon God’s altar.

### Verse 21

“On the seventh day.” Augustine, question 160. When he gave the command concerning the Sabbath, and so forth, up to: “that one ought to cease from work on the Sabbath at all times.”

### Verse 24

“No one shall lie in wait.” Augustine, question 161. What he said, and so forth, up to: “where God was to have the tabernacle or temple.”

### Verse 25

“You shall not sacrifice,” and so forth. Augustine, questions 162 and 163. What does he mean by saying: “You shall not kill the blood of my sacrifices upon leaven”? Does he here call “his sacrifices” those victims that are killed at Passover, and command that there be no leaven in the house when the days of unleavened bread are being observed?

### Verse 26

“You shall not boil a kid in milk.” Augustine, in the work cited above. “You shall not boil a lamb in its mother’s milk,” and so forth, up to: “but it is a historical narrative.”

Isidore. Moses fasted for forty days, as did Elijah and the Lord himself. We are given this command from the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel. This testimony is found in all three. Hence, on the mountain, the Savior shone between the two figures, so that we might restrain our appetite from all the attractions of the world as though by the fast of temperance, while the perfection of the Decalogue is preached throughout the four regions of the world, that is, throughout the whole earth: ten multiplied by four signifies the number forty.

### Verse 28

“And he wrote on the tablets,” and so forth. Augustine, question 166. It is said of Moses that he himself wrote, and so forth, up to: “but through the grace of God.”

### Verse 29

“And when he descended.” Isidore, *On Exodus*, volume 5. Moses went up the mountain again, and so forth, up to: “whose image was on the tablets.”

Isidore, in the same work. When Moses descended with the tablets, and so forth, up to: “Hence: ‘Open my eyes, and I shall contemplate the wonders of your law’” (Psalm 118).

### Verse 30

“But when Aaron saw,” and so forth. Origen, *Homilies on Exodus*, homily 12. It is written that Aaron and all the sons of Israel saw Moses, and so forth, up to: “for the things he speaks possess glory, but it is covered and concealed, and all its glory is inward.”

Origen, in the same work. Consider also that in the Law Moses’ face is glorified, although it is covered by a veil, and so forth, up to: “freed from the slavery of the world, let us seek the liberty of knowledge.”

### Verse 34

“And then he spoke to the sons of Israel all that had been commanded to him,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 172. After Moses descended from the mountain, and so forth, up to: “so that they might receive this name.”

## Chapter 35

### Verse 5

“Set apart.” Origen, *Homilies on Exodus*, homily 13. Another version reads: “Take from yourselves a redemption for the Lord,” and so forth, up to: “and your silver, that is, your word, tested.”

The same. You who are accustomed to attend the divine mysteries know, and so forth, up to: “all these things that are in us bring about.”

“Everyone.” The same. Another version reads: “Each one of you,” he says, and so forth, up to: “so, if the Lord comes and finds something of yours in his tabernacle, he defends you as his own and calls it his.”

“Bronze.” The same. It appears to be used for strength, and so forth, up to: “Let everything be offered to God—sense, speech, and voice.”

### Verse 6

“Hyacinth.” The same. Let us consider the remaining materials: hyacinth, and so forth, up to: “and you shall offer firstfruits to the Lord.”

“And scarlet twice-dyed.” The same, *Homily 13 on Exodus*. Let us see why scarlet is doubled, and so forth, up to: “so that he may mingle a spark of severity with the light of knowledge.”

The same. If someone rightly understands the departure of the Hebrews from Egypt, and so forth, up to: “and signifies the nobler garments: ‘Put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and do not make provision for the flesh in its desires’” (Romans 13).

Gregory, in the work cited above. In the construction of the tabernacle, and so forth, up to: “as though they produced a sound without light.”

Origen, in the work cited above. After this, the men received things from their wives, and so forth, up to: “Not everyone can receive this word, but those to whom it has been given” (Matthew 19).

### Verse 6

“And goat hair.” Origen, homily 19. Goat hair is offered, and so forth, up to: “who offers rams’ skins to the Lord.”

### Verse 21

“Whatever is for the service,” and so forth. Gregory, in the work cited above. In the adornment of the tabernacle men offer gifts together with women, and so forth, up to: “they bring forth according as he himself has given.”

### Verse 27

“But the princes offered stones,” and so forth. Origen, in the work cited above. The princes offered their gifts, and so forth, up to: “so that they might be worthy to preside over peoples.”

Origen, *Homily 9 on Exodus*. The princes also offer oil useful for the lamps and for anointing, and so forth, up to: “when the Lord has placed you in a green pasture beside the water of refreshment.”

### Verse 30

“Bezalel.” Rabanus, *On Exodus*, volume 2. He is called “shadow,” and so forth, up to: “they strengthen their brothers by exhorting them in justice and judgment.”

## Chapter 36

### Verse 1

“So Bezalel made,” and so forth. Rabanus, *On Exodus*. It should be noted that not only those of the royal tribe, and so forth, up to: “he wished to make them belong to the unity of his body.”

### Verse 2

“And when he had called them,” and so forth. Origen, in the work cited above. “And after the people had offered,” Moses says, “he called,” and so forth, up to: “and fit and bring it forth in its proper place.”

“And all who willingly,” and so forth. Augustine, *Questions on Exodus*, question 170. “And all who were willing to go freely to the work, so that they might complete it,” and so forth. Moses mentioned certain people, and so forth, up to: “but devoted freely and willingly.”

### Verse 4

“Therefore the craftsmen,” and so forth. Augustine, question 171. Note that the skilled workers were also holy in character. If they had wished, they could have taken many things away; but modesty restrained them, or religious fear deterred them.

## Chapter 37

### Verse 1

“Now Bezalel made the ark.” Isidore, *On Exodus*, volume 5. In the ark of the covenant there was a golden urn, and so forth, up to: “ever flourishing with the evergreen vitality of immortal memory.”

### Verse 2

“A golden crown,” and so forth. Because, in that the Church is extended throughout the four regions of the world, it is proclaimed as girded with the four holy books of the Gospel; yet it is enclosed within the circumference of a single crown—that is, within the firmness of the same faith, namely, unity.

### Verse 4

“And the poles.” Isidore, in the same work. Strong and persevering teachers are to be sought as though they were incorruptible wood. Always clinging to the instruction of the sacred volumes, they proclaim the unity of the Church and, as though inserted through the rings, carry the ark. They are also commanded to be overlaid with gold, so that when their speech resounds in the ears of others, they themselves may also shine with the splendor of their life.

**Verse 6.**—“He also made the mercy seat,” etc. (ISIDORE, same work.) The mercy seat over the ark of the covenant, etc., up to “because Christ is the head of the Church.”

**Verse 17.**—“And he made the lampstand,” etc. This signifies the Holy Spirit, who by his sevenfold grace illumines the Church abiding in the unity of faith; or Christ, bearing the seven churches, in which the splendor of the sevenfold Spirit shines forth.

**Verse 23.**—“With the snuffers.” These are called *forceps* in Isaiah: the two Testaments, namely, by which sins are cleansed, and which are joined together within themselves by the [Col. 0293B] unity of the Holy Spirit.

## Chapter XXXVIII

**Verse 8.**—“He also made the bronze basin,” etc. (GREGORY, *Homily 17 on the Gospels.) Moses places the bronze basin,” etc., up to “so that by these things we may strive to advance, through which we recognize that those whom we venerate advanced.”

**Verse 20.**—“And the tent pegs also.” (STRABO.) Literally, the pegs were fixed at the tops of the columns, to which the ropes were tied. These ropes raised the curtains from the ground; fastened above by certain loops and tied below to the aforesaid pegs, they stretched out the curtains so that they would not form a wrinkle.

Mystically, the ropes signify Sacred Scripture, of which Solomon says: “A threefold cord is not easily broken” [Col. 0293C] (Ecclesiastes 4), because Sacred Scripture, consisting of history, morality, and allegory, cannot be torn apart by any doctrines of heretics. The pegs, made in the form of a tongue, signify the tongues of teachers who expound Scripture. They also raise and stretch the curtains from the ground, because they teach those subject to them to follow and imitate heavenly things and to contract no wrinkle of evil work or deceit (Ephesians 5).

## Chapter XXXIX

[lacuna]

## Chapter XL

**Verse 1.**—“And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: In the first month,” etc. (STRABO.) The first month of the year is Nisan, also called April, in which the Jews [Col. 0293D] celebrated Passover and the tabernacle was erected. Allegorically, the first month signifies the beginning of grace, when the tabernacle of God—that is, the Church—was erected, when Christ, crucified, brought forth from his side the mysteries of blood and water, by which the Church is dedicated and consecrated.

It should be noted that this was the first month of the second year. The first year was before the law; the second was under the grace of the Gospel, which the Lord blessed. Hence: “You will bless the crown of the year of your kindness” (Psalm 64). It was the year of kindness in which the salvation of the human race appeared through Christ’s humanity. Therefore, in that year the tabernacle of God was erected—that is, the Church was founded and exalted.

[Col. 0294A] (RABANUS, *On Exodus*, book 2.) The first year signifies the whole period of the law, etc., up to “so that the teachers of the Gospel may use these things in confirmation of the faith.”

**Verse 9.**—“You shall anoint the tabernacle,” etc. (STRABO.) The tabernacle with its vessels is consecrated by the oil of anointing, because the holy Church ought to dedicate and consecrate everything it does, with its virtues, to the grace of the Holy Spirit. The oil of anointing is compared with spiritual grace, by which the works of all the virtues are consecrated to the Lord.

**Verse 12.**—“And you shall bring Aaron near,” etc. (STRABO.) The doors of the tabernacle—that is, of the holy Church—are the apostles, through whom one must enter the heavenly court. Aaron and his sons—that is, the entire assembly of the saints, and especially those set over others—must be [Col. 0294B] brought to them, so that they may imitate them and follow in their footsteps.

**Verse 16.**—“And the bars.” A bar not only joins the walls but also strengthens the columns of the entrance, lest they fall or deviate from their upright position. Thus the Lord joined both peoples in the one faith of love, and strengthens their teachers so that they may persevere in faith, conduct, and preaching.

Nor is it surprising if Christ is understood both through the capitals themselves and through the bar that holds the capitals together, because he is the governing head of every elect person. Hence: “The head of the man is Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). He not only raises individuals toward the pursuit of heavenly things but also holds them all together; he confirms them by the bond of peace, so that they may neither deviate from uprightness nor be separated from one another by discord.

Something similar occurs when the Lord is called both lamb, shepherd, and door, although the shepherd feeds the lamb and both enter through the [Col. 0294C] door. Properly, he is the Word in the beginning (John 1, 10); none of these other names is proper to him, but each is figurative. He is shepherd because he leads to the pastures of life; door because no one reaches the Father except through him; lamb because he saves from Egypt. So here also he is figured through the capitals because of the governance by which he presides over individuals, and through the bar because of his universal providence, since he strengthens everyone (Numbers 9; 1 Kings 8).

(BEDE.) Thus the soul receives different names according to its various actions. When it gives life to the body, it is called soul; when it wills, it is called mind; when it knows, understanding; when it recollects, memory; when it judges, reason; when it breathes, spirit; when it perceives, sense.

**Verse 33.**—“And Moses could not,” etc. (STRABO.) [Col. 0294D] Moses therefore, here as in many other places, represents the Jewish people. Moses could not enter the tabernacle because the cloud prevented him; likewise, the Jewish people were never able to penetrate the mysteries of Scripture.

For the cloud of the Lord rested over the tabernacle by day, and fire by night. In this passage the fire signifies knowledge of divine mysteries. Holy Scripture is light to the holy and to those who confess their ignorance; but to the wicked and to those who boast of their knowledge it is a cloud, because it blinds them.

(AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Exodus*, question 176.) A very remarkable matter must be noted, etc., up to “a cloud by day and a flame by night.”

In the tabernacle of the Lord there were tablets, whose [Col. 0295A] rings had bars inserted into them, made of acacia wood, by which they could be lifted and carried from one resting place to another. All these things are full of mysteries.

By the tabernacle we understand the present Church, in which there are tablets—that is, saints filled with humility—to which five bars are attached. These signify the spiritual knowledge of the five books of Moses, by which they raise themselves and others to the splendor of eternal blessedness.

By the bars, therefore, as we have said, we understand the five books of Moses: Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, the Book of Numbers, and Deuteronomy. In them are contained the beginning, middle, and completion of the world. Genesis describes the creation of the world; Exodus, its re-creation; Leviticus, the administration of the Church’s mysteries; the Book of Numbers, Evangelical [Col. 0295B] preaching; and Deuteronomy, the final blessing. Hence it also ends with blessings.

Thus Genesis contains the order of creation; Exodus, the mystery of re-creation; Leviticus, the holiness of ecclesiastical administration; Numbers, the consolation of evangelical preaching; and Deuteronomy, the completion of eternal blessing.

Among these five books of Moses, Exodus is preeminent—the book we now have in hand. For it contains both the things that happened figuratively to the children of Israel and, in full, the mysteries of Christ and the Church.

Here, however, the subject first is the actual departure of the carnal children of Israel from historical Egypt. This signifies the spiritual departure of spiritual Israelites from the true Egypt, namely, from the darkness of vices.

The passage of the Red Sea [Col. 0295C] and the drowning of Pharaoh and his army, and the deliverance of God’s people are also treated. In this is figured baptism, consecrated by the blood of Christ, in which the vices of the devil are submerged and the souls of the faithful are delivered.

The battle of the Israelites with Amalek is also described, in which the victory of Christ and his people, and the confusion of the devil, are figured.

Finally, after the list of the resting places has been set out, the law given on Mount Sinai is discussed. This suggests to us that, having been raised above earthly things, we should learn to submit ourselves to heavenly disciplines.

The construction of the tabernacle and its vessels, the garments of the priests, and the anointing are then discussed. By these are understood the present Church and the various persons of the faithful assigned to different offices, just as the vessels were assigned to different uses or offices, together with the sweetest fragrances of sacred mysteries and prayers.

So much for these matters. It must now be said that, according to the order of history [Col. 0296A] and according to allegory, this book is appropriately the second in the Pentateuch. After Genesis dealt with the creation of heaven and earth and with the entry of the children of Israel into Egypt, it was fitting that the next subject should be their departure.

This is appropriate according to the order of history. According to allegory also, it was not unfitting. After Genesis had spoken of the carnal generation by which, through the sin of the first man, we are born as children of the devil, it was fitting that it should immediately add the account of spiritual regeneration, by which, through the justification of the second man—that is, Christ—we are reborn as children of God.

This book is called *Exodus* in Greek, ἔξοδος (*exodos*), and *Veelle Semoth* in Hebrew, meaning “the departures” or “the going out” in Latin, because it deals with the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt.

It may be asked why this book is called Exodus [Col. 0296B] because it deals with their departure, when at the beginning it treats not of their departure but of their entry. The answer may be that although it intends to deal specifically with their departure, a considerable period elapsed between the departure discussed here and the entry with which the first book ends, or had ended. Therefore, in order to join its narrative more suitably, it briefly repeats the account of the entry and then proceeds more effectively to the departure.

We likewise, in our sermons, when a long interval has intervened and we are about to discuss other matters, repeat what came before, so that we may continue our discourse more coherently.

Having considered these matters, we must examine the subject: the bodily departure of the children of Israel from Egypt and the holy [reading uncertain] spiritual departure of the saints from the world.

The purpose is to urge us spiritually to depart from conformity [Col. 0296C] to the world, just as they physically departed from Egypt, so that, just as we were conformed to the world, we may likewise be conformed to God.

The method is as follows. Briefly touching upon the entry of the children of Israel into Egypt, the book discusses their multiplication; then the new king who did not know Joseph and began to oppress the people; then the plagues of Egypt; and finally their departure, the passage of the Red Sea, and the drowning of the Egyptians.

At last it reaches Mount Sinai, where the law was given, and treats of the tabernacle, its vessels, the garments of the priests, and the anointing; and so it ends.

Note that although the history Moses undertook to write is one and indivisible, it is divided by chapters and sections, or by books, in order to relieve readers’ weariness, just as a traveler divides a road—which is itself undivided—into daily stages, so that the labor may be reduced and weariness avoided.

[Col. 0295]

# THE BOOK OF LEVITICUS

In Hebrew, *VAIICRA* (G)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0295D]

(ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) This book is called Leviticus because the subject of the entire book is revealed in its name. The tribe of Levi received the ministry of the tabernacle, in which sacrifices, first fruits, and offerings of the firstborn [Col. 0296D] were commanded to be presented, because all sacrifices pertain to the Levites (Numbers 18). From them this book appropriately received its name, since it arranges all these matters in order.

In Latin it is called *Offertorius* or *Sacrificativus*, because [Col. 0297A] it deals with sacrifices and ceremonies. It is rightly placed after Exodus. In Exodus the tabernacle is arranged; in this book are contained the things that the Lord spoke to Moses concerning the tabernacle, together with the ceremonies of the tabernacle.

If someone asks why the books of the law were divided, since the history is continuous in time, the answer is that the division of the books removes the reader’s weariness, just as a traveler divides the distances of a road so that, as though divided, the labor may be reduced.

Rabanus collected much from Isichius, bishop of Jerusalem, who expounded Leviticus quite fully. He also added certain material to his work from other Fathers who had expounded some of Isichius’s statements. Alternating the opinions of many teachers, he arranged in a certain order of exposition the confused order of their statements [Col. 0297B].

(ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) Above all, it is necessary to draw the interpretation of the law toward anagogical meaning and to seek spiritual understanding within the letter. This does not contradict the law but defends it.

Christ himself showed that spiritual understanding must be diligently sought. In his parables (Matthew 13), he called the field the world; the farmer who sows good seed, the righteous; the weeds, the wicked; the reapers, angels; and the enemy who sows over the seed, the devil.

Who, then, forbids us to call the ox one who works righteousness, the sheep one who is simple, and the dove one who is innocent; and the turtledove those who act on a higher level and devote themselves to contemplation?

Did not Ezekiel call Jerusalem a lioness, and her cub [Col. 0297C] Eliakim, who was led into Egypt, and another cub, Joachim, who was led into Babylon? (Ezekiel 19.)

Paul shows that not only things spoken in parables, but also things related according to history, must be led toward a higher understanding, saying: “It is written that Abraham had two sons,” etc. After this he added: “These things are spoken allegorically: for these are the two Testaments,” etc. (Galatians 4).

Perhaps the letter, stripped of spiritual understanding, will be harmful and liable to various criticisms. Hence, through Ezekiel, the Lord calls the law both good and not good, saying: “I gave them my statutes and showed them my judgments, which a person shall do and live in them.” And elsewhere: “I gave them statutes that were not good, and judgments [Col. 0297D] in which they would not live.”

It is therefore clear that some are good and some are not good, and that there are statutes in which people live and others in which they do not live. Whoever guards the Holy Spirit lives in them; whoever acts according to the flesh dies, because he does not recognize the life contained in them.

Furthermore, the lawgiver did not always, but only at a particular time, wish the surface observance of the law to be maintained, in order to restrain the hard neck of the Jews. Hence: “I know that this people is stiff-necked” (Exodus 32). Hosea calls the Jews a restive heifer, one that cannot be tamed in any way. And elsewhere: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing; I passed over the beauty of her neck” (Hosea 10), by which obedience is signified.

For he imposed the yoke of the law so that, once humbled, they might willingly receive the light and easy yoke of the Gospel (Matthew 12).

[Col. 0298A] (ORIGEN, *Homily 1 on Leviticus*.) If, following certain people—even some of our own—we accept a literal understanding and receive the lawgiver’s voice without any, as they themselves jokingly call it, verbal twist or cloud of allegory, then I, a churchman living under the faith of Christ and placed in the midst of the Church, am compelled by the authority of the divine command to sacrifice calves or lambs and to offer fine flour with incense and oil.

Therefore, the Lord himself and the Holy Spirit must be entreated to remove every cloud of sin that darkens the sight of our heart, so that we may behold spiritual understanding, according to the words: “Open my eyes, and I will consider wondrous things,” etc. (Psalm 118).

(ISIDORE.) Every variety of sacrifices prefigured Christ’s sacrifice. Therefore, when the reality was offered, the shadow [Col. 0298B] ceased (1 Corinthians 15), prefiguring the true sacrifice of the true and eternal priest.

Animal sacrifices were offered for cleansing, but one true sacrifice, Christ’s, was promised, in which remission would be made for sins contracted from flesh and blood, which will not possess the kingdom of God, because bodily substance will be changed into a heavenly quality.

Christ was offered in the calf because of the power of the cross; in the lamb, because of innocence; in the ram, because of sovereignty; in the goat, because of the likeness of sinful flesh; in the turtledove and dove, because he is God and man.

The Mediator between God and humanity was shown in the union of two substances. In the sprinkling of fine flour, it was shown that the Church—that is, the body of Christ—was gathered together through the water of baptism.

Morally, [Col. 0298C] we offer the calf when we overcome the pride of the flesh; the lamb when we correct irrational impulses; the kid when we overcome lust; the dove when we are simple; the turtledove when we are chaste or preserve chastity; unleavened bread when we feast not in the leaven of malice but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

(RABANUS.) He says that each sacrifice—indeed, nearly every syllable—and Aaron’s garments, as well as the entire order of Leviticus, breathe heavenly mysteries.

Origen also says: Just as in the last days the Word of God came into the world clothed in flesh from the Virgin Mary—his flesh was seen by everyone, while his divinity was hidden and known by only a few elect—so the Word of God is brought forth to human beings [Col. 0298D] through the prophets, covered there by a veil of flesh and here by a veil of the letter.

The letter is looked upon as flesh; the spiritual sense is perceived as divinity.

## CHAPTER ONE

**Verse 1.**—“He called,” etc. (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) By the conjunction, he joins what follows to what came before, namely, the beginning of this book to the end of the preceding one. For the work of one and the same day is contained in both.

The Book of Numbers, since nothing lies between it and Leviticus, likewise has a similar beginning: “And the Lord spoke to Moses in the wilderness of Sinai,” etc. (Numbers 1).

After the history of Leviticus, therefore, the people did nothing before the history of Numbers; nor had they changed their location, because they had not yet dedicated the tabernacle [Col. 0299A], and not much time had passed. They began in the first month of the second year, at the beginning of that same month.

In Exodus and Genesis, however, because a long period had intervened between Joseph’s death and the departure of the children of Israel, the conjunction does not stand at the beginning. Instead, an opening appropriate to the divine arrangement is supplied: “These are the names of the children of Israel who entered Egypt.”

(ISICHIUS.) According to the Septuagint: “He recalled.” Just as, according to them, God recalled Bezalel by name when he commanded the tabernacle to be made according to the pattern shown on the mountain, so now he commanded the description of a certain image of intelligible sacrifices. This recalling suggests a certain arrangement of matters or words that look back to what came before [Col. 0299B].

(ORIGEN, *Homily 1 on Leviticus*.) “And he called,” etc. “In the beginning,” etc., up to “those who bring purified inner ears to hear these things.”

(ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) That God does not love the sacrifices of the Jews, etc., up to “and this calling plainly suggests an arrangement of words or matters looking back to what came before.”

(ORIGEN, *Homily 1 on Exodus*.) The human being whom he first appointed to offer to the Lord, etc., up to “the sacrifice also is twofold, saving both earthly and heavenly things.”

(IDEM, same work.) A human being who lives rationally, having been made in the image and likeness of God, etc., up to “and his neck like that of a turtledove.”

[Col. 0299C] (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) He designates a simple person, etc., up to “salvation is granted even to animals.”

(IDEM.) God requires sacrifice so that it may benefit us, not himself, etc., up to “which at last testify either for us or against us.”

**Verse 3.**—“From the herd,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The first sacrifice is the calf, that is, Christ, from the herd, that is, born from the stock of the patriarchs. By the plow of his cross he subdued the soil of our flesh and enriched it with the seed of the Holy Spirit and the fruit of virtues.

(ORIGEN, as above.) The proud calf is our flesh, etc., up to “but they did not have the oil of love, peace, and the other virtues.”

“To make atonement,” etc. According to the Septuagint, this says that it is acceptable to the one offering. For if it is truly acceptable to us, and our heart, judging rightly and clinging to no passion, has judged the gift worthy to be received, then we can pray in the presence of the Lord—that is, obtain remission.

Hence we shall persuade our hearts before him, because if our heart condemns us, we know that God is greater than our heart and knows all things, etc.

**Verse 4.**—“And he shall place,” etc. What we call a sacrifice is called in Greek καρπώμα (*karpōma*), in which an intelligible whole burnt offering is signified.

One bears spiritual fruit who becomes a whole burnt offering through a spiritual way of life. Therefore the one who offers places his hand on the head of the victim. This signifies the beginning of the aforesaid way of life, for the one who offers it makes himself responsible through the [Col. 0300A] promise.

He offers willingly, because it is a gift, and every [Col. 0299D] gift is voluntary. If he violates his promise, he accuses himself when he suffers punishment. Thus the offering will be acceptable and beneficial for his expiation when, by placing his hand upon it, he shows that he offered willingly and not under compulsion.

**Verse 5.**—“And he shall slaughter,” etc. (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) For we ought to offer God not only our own conscience and way of life, etc., up to “just as Christ is called the door, so also is the apostolic teaching that he grants.”

“The sons of Aaron.” (ORIGEN, in the work cited above.) Annas and Caiaphas, and the others who declared Christ guilty of death and poured out his blood [Col. 0300B] at the base of the altar, were of Aaron’s family. For he was killed where the altar and its base were, hence: “It is not fitting for a prophet to perish outside Jerusalem.”

**Verse 6.**—“And having drawn off,” etc. (ORIGEN, same work.) The priest removes the skin, etc., up to “he joined earthly things to heavenly and human things to divine.”

(IDEM.) He commands that the entrails and feet be washed with water, as a sign of baptism. He washes the entrails who cleanses his conscience; he washes the feet who receives the completion of the sacrament.

For the one who is clean needs only to wash his feet, since he is entirely clean (John 15). No one can have a share with Jesus unless he has washed his feet.

(ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) The skin is removed when we are stripped of riches and of whatever is worldly, etc., [Col. 0300C] up to “imitating Christ as far as we can.”

(GREGORY, *Moral Exposition*, book 1, chapter 40.) We remove the skin of the victim, etc., up to “let him place nothing slippery upon the altar of his prayer.”

**Verse 10.**—“But if,” etc. (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) With a few changes he says the same thing, etc., up to “hence: ‘A son shall not bear the iniquity of his father,’” etc.

“A year-old,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The lamb offered is Christ, crucified in innocence. Hence: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world.”

The kid is rightly offered, because through Christ’s death the devil, the author of sin, is slaughtered.

(ISICHIUS.) He did not command this concerning cattle, etc., up to “therefore it is also called a whole burnt offering without the work of [Col. 0300D] righteousness.”

**Verse 11.**—“At the side,” that is, the altar faces toward the Gentiles, because Christ’s passion was celebrated for the Gentiles. We offer our sacrifice toward the northern side of the altar when we remember and believe that Christ’s passion was accomplished for the Gentiles.

**Verse 13.**—“He shall burn all of it.” He commands that the one offering place all these things upon the altar, so that we may adapt our whole person to the spiritual Scriptures spoken concerning the intelligible altar of the Lord’s body and strive to live in imitation of him.

“And the odor.” When our sacrifice becomes a whole burnt offering, and we offer everything upon the intelligible altar, conforming the conduct of our [Col. 0301A] life to Christ as his imitators, then a most pleasing odor is offered to the Lord.

**Verse 14.**—“But if,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The turtledove signifies the flesh of Christ, according to Solomon’s words: “Your cheeks are beautiful like those of a turtledove.” The dove signifies the Holy Spirit. Hence: “Upon whom you see the Spirit descending like a dove, this is my Son.”

The turtledove and the dove therefore signify the flesh of Christ joined to the Spirit. A human being—that is, Christ—offers these three sacrifices, namely, from cattle, sheep, and birds.

(ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) The subtlety of the words is marvelous, etc., up to “they contemplate and taste heavenly things, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God.”

## CHAPTER TWO

[Col. 0301B] **Verse 2.**—“A soul,” etc. The whole human being is signified by the better part. For the passage requires a spiritual and perfect hearer, because the soul is capable of wisdom, not the flesh.

(ISIDORE.) “A soul,” etc. The soul offers the fourth sacrifice. Fine flour signifies the Church, which is gathered from many persons as from grains; separated between letter and spirit by the millstone of the Law and the Gospel; united through the water of baptism; anointed and strengthened by chrism; and made an acceptable offering through spiritual fire and humility.

(ORIGEN, *Homily 2 on Leviticus*.) “A soul”—one that has no calf, etc., up to “with the oil of divine mercy or grace.”

Mystically, this signifies the same as in the passage: “All the souls that [Col. 0301C] entered Egypt with Jacob,” etc. (Genesis 46). Luke likewise says: “We were all two hundred and seventy-six souls in the ship” (Acts 27).

Perhaps by “soul” he signifies a Gentile. Above, he commanded the children of Israel to offer sacrifices with blood. Here, however, when he commands one who is without the law to offer, he does not say “a man,” as above, but “a soul.”

The Gentile was animal-like, not understanding the things of God, but he is called to offer by God’s mercy, so that he may receive salvation. When he arranges sacrifices for sins, since he has neither sheep nor goat, he is commanded to offer a turtledove or dove; if he does not have that, fine flour.

For he is no longer saved by works, being poor in virtues, but by the knowledge of God alone. Although this is the beginning of salvation, incense and [Col. 0301D] oil must nevertheless be added, so that grace may be mingled with almsgiving and prayers.

Hence the angel says to Cornelius: “Your prayers and your almsgiving have ascended to the Lord” (Acts 10).

In incense, inward passions are healed, and by its smoke eyes made tearful by illness are healed. Prayer heals the soul’s passions, cures the inner eyes of ignorance, and drives away the tears kindled by the sickness of sin.

**Verse 2.**—“The sons,” that is, the ministers of the Church, because whatever we offer we must share with the holy teachers of the Church. Hence Paul shared the Gospel with the apostles, lest he should have run in vain (Galatians 2).

“Of which.” The unity of the Church takes a handful of fine flour, because each believer ought to seek knowledge of Scripture according to the capacity of his understanding. Hence: “Not to think more highly than one ought to think, but to think soberly.” “Of which one,” etc. (Romans 12).

It should be noted that he commands a handful of the fine flour and oil to be offered, but all the incense. The wisdom signified by the fine flour and the love or mercy signified by the oil cannot be complete in this life. Hence: “Now we see through a mirror in an enigma,” and, “Now I know in part,” etc. (1 Corinthians 13).

Part of the oil is offered because mercy is never completed. Even if you show as much mercy as you can, you ought still to desire more. Love, too, which is signified by oil, begins in the present life and will be perfected in the future. But all the incense is burned because one must always persevere in prayer.

[Col. 0302B] “Of the fine flour.” Of the knowledge or understanding of God. Knowledge is received from God, which faith can comprehend. Just as one who wishes to grasp more than a handful grasps nothing, since everything slips away, so faith is the measure of the knowledge of God.

One who approaches God must believe, and whatever is not from faith is sin (Hebrews 11).

“The memorial,” etc., signifies perfect knowledge of God, of which we shall be mindful and which is never destroyed. It does not destroy present knowledge as something contrary, but shows that what now exists is only a small part in comparison with its fullness: “When the perfect comes, what is partial will be abolished” (1 Corinthians 13).

**Verse 3.**—“Of the sacrifice,” etc. (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) Of that perfect knowledge hidden in the heavens and stored up in Christ [Col. 0302C], in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden (Colossians 2).

“Aaron” is interpreted as “mountainous,” that is, understanding higher things concerning God; or as “hidden,” as though possessing within himself the law and utterances of God. He can offer sacrifice.

The holy of holies is from the offerings to the Lord. What remains is partial, yet it surpasses all knowledge and raises it to perfection.

**Verse 4.**—“When you offer a sacrifice,” etc. (ISICHIUS, same work.) The sacrifice is Christ, slaughtered for us.

“Cooked in an oven” means in the Virgin’s womb. The oven receives both bread and fire; so the Virgin’s womb received the bread of life—that is, the Word of God—and the fire of the Holy Spirit from heaven. Hence: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” etc. (Luke 1).

If, therefore, you offer the gift [Col. 0302D] of Christ’s incarnation, which took place in the Virgin’s womb, it is not acceptable to God unless it is made from fine flour—that is, from knowledge or understanding of God.

Regarding this matter, we receive a saying from the apostles and prophets: the apostles’ words are loaves, while the prophets’ are *lagana*—flat cakes. Just as loaves are more suitable for nourishment than *lagana*, so the apostles’ words surpass the words of the prophets.

Both, however, are unleavened, without the leaven of secular knowledge. Yet both are made with oil, for they wrote harmoniously about Christ’s compassion. The apostles and prophets wrote alike, but the apostles wrote more fully, because they showed as completed what the prophets announced as future.

“Lagana.” Broad, thin bread, signifying prophecy and [Col. 0303A] the law. The distance between the solidity of bread and the thinness of a *laganum* corresponds to the distance between the Gospel and the words of the law and the prophets.

Yet these are coated with oil, because the law and prophecy foretold the love of Christ, through which he came for the salvation of the human race.

**Verse 5.**—“If your offering is,” etc. (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) The offering from the frying pan, etc., up to “and therefore he departed from its knowledge.”

“Fine flour mingled,” etc., because he died and had mercy on us.

“Without leaven,” that is, without blemish.

**Verse 6.**—“You shall divide it into small pieces.” We should carefully distinguish the account of his sufferings, which came in parts: the slaps, blows, spitting, and wounds [Col. 0303B].

“And you shall pour oil over it,” etc., so that, just as he mercifully died for us, we too may have mercy on our brothers unto death.

“From the frying pan.” Just as the frying pan lies between fire and food, so in a certain way the cross lies between the impassible divinity and the humanity that was roasted by the fire of suffering.

And just as soft things become hard and hard things become soft in a frying pan, so in the passion of the cross stony hearts were softened, while soft and unstable hearts were strengthened.

Therefore, to offer a sacrifice from the frying pan is to speak with reverence about the mystery of the cross.

**Verse 7.**—“But if it is from,” etc. (ISICHIUS, *On Leviticus*.) Just as the cross is signified in the frying pan, etc., up to “for out of mercy he endured death and administered the [Col. 0303C] resurrection.”

“But if,” etc. Morally, one offers fine flour who strives to conduct himself well in certain ordinary practices of life. It must be mixed with oil, because every soul needs the oil of mercy and cannot escape the present life unless heavenly mercy is present.

The oven expresses the weight of temptation; the frying pan, constancy and strength of spirit; the griddle, manifold opposition.

**Verse 11.**—“Every offering.” (ORIGEN, *Homily 2 on Leviticus*.) Someone may say, etc., up to “in this way you offer sacrifices more truly and perfectly according to the Gospel, which Israel can no longer offer according to the law.”

“Of leaven and honey.” Nothing pleasurable, nothing sweet, is pleasing to God, but only what contains some bitterness and [Col. 0303D] severity. Hence the Passover is eaten with bitter herbs.

“And honey.” This signifies the eloquence of the Gentiles, sweet in sound but not in substance. Hence: “The lips of a harlot drip honey” (Proverbs 5).

What is said in the Song of Songs—“Honey and milk are under your tongue” (Song of Songs 4)—does not contradict the present passage. It says “under the tongue,” not “on the tongue,” to show that the wisdom of the pagans and the letter of the Jews are subject to the tongue of the Church, that is, to her teaching.

He does not wish their entire doctrine to be offered. Hence he says: “It shall not be burned as a sacrifice,” that is, as a whole burnt offering; “you shall offer only their first fruits.”

We offer the first fruits of that wisdom, not the whole of it. Thus Paul said to the Athenians: “As your own poet said: ‘For we are [Col. 0304A] also his offspring.’” Whatever he found compatible with the knowledge of God he did not reject, but he did not multiply testimonies beyond that, because it pleased God through the foolishness of preaching to save those who believe.

Hence Moses says: “They shall not be placed upon the altar.” Although it could have been said simply, “They shall not be placed,” he says, “They shall not be placed as a pleasing odor,” signifying that if we attempt to attain knowledge of divinity from external things, such a sacrifice does not ascend to the altar but is pressed down into earthly things, because it is from the earth.

(BEDE, *On Leviticus*, book 2.) That honey was not to be offered in God’s sacrifice, etc., up to “we omit whatever is imperfect.”

**Verse 13.**—“You shall season every offering with salt, and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant.” This is apostolic wisdom. Hence: “You are the salt of the earth,” etc. [Col. 0304B] (Matthew 5).

Just as every food is seasoned with salt, so the word of preaching is seasoned with apostolic doctrine. Therefore salt is commanded to be offered with every sacrifice, so that we may live according to apostolic doctrine, instruction, and imitation of conduct.

Hence Paul says: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Corinthians 4). And elsewhere: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Ephesians 2).

Therefore the lawgiver did not simply say “salt,” but “the salt of the covenant of your God.” Just as the covenant is rational, so also is the salt rational. He wished to remind us, therefore, of the salt of the evangelical Testament and of the apostles.

Oil is offered in sacrifice if we offer with gladness, not from sorrow or compulsion. For God loves a cheerful giver (2 Corinthians 9).

Salt, which has an astringent power and is opposed [Col. 0304C] to honey, is commanded to be added to sacrifices. Salt is a symbol of prudence, which restrains and dries up pleasure.

In every offering, etc. For nothing that has not been corrected according to the standard of his will can please God. For if, in human affairs, one of the wise men of this world admonished that such great caution must be exercised that he said, “Every action ought to be free from rashness and negligence,” what must be thought concerning the things of God?

But if you offer, etc. (ORIGEN, Book I on Leviticus.) In the second place, concerning firstfruits, etc., up to “because the letter was separated from the spirit.”

(ISICHIUS.) You shall break it into pieces, etc. He did not merely command them to have knowledge of God, etc., up to “for divine knowledge is perfected in us through almsgiving and prayer.”

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0304D]

**VERSE 1.**—But if the offering, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 3 on Leviticus.) Passing over the other matters, he speaks of sacrifices of salvation, which are offered from animals—that is, oxen, goats, and sheep—and nothing else is substituted for sacrifice; not even birds, which were substituted above for the offerings of gifts. Whoever offers sacrifices of salvation is conscious of his salvation; therefore he must offer what is great and perfect. Hence the Apostle says: “The solid food is for the mature” (Heb. V).

(ISICHIUS.) But if the offering, etc. According to the laws, there are diverse ways of human conduct, etc., up to “for they must conduct themselves worthily, so that they may attain salvation.”

[Col. 0305A] A male or a female, etc. (ISICHIUS.) Above, only males are offered as holocausts, etc., up to “that is, weak works together with stronger ones.”

**VERSE 3.**—The fat that, etc. (IDEM.) An intelligible fat ought to be offered, etc., up to “and by deliberation let us sanctify the mass.”

The vital parts. The Septuagint: “the belly,” that is, the heart, which it mentions a second time according to the Septuagint, because, according to physicians, it has a double function: through one part it draws in food, and this they call the upper belly; through the other it separates excrement, and this they call the lower belly. The kidneys are the ministers of generative seed, sharing their function with the belly and thighs. First, therefore, he commands the fat that is above the belly, the two kidneys, and the fat that is above them—that is, above the thighs, which are near the kidneys—to be offered; for they are situated between the thigh and the belly.

**VERSE 4.**—The lobe of the liver: that is, of the liver, in which pleasure or desire resides. Hence, according to the Septuagint, the lobe of the liver shall be removed together with the kidneys; for the liver supplies the kidneys with the power of activity.

**VERSE 6.**—But if it is from sheep, etc. (ISICHIUS.) Whom he commands to offer an ox, etc., up to “also in the loins there is the function of generation.”

**VERSE 9.**—And the tail. The Septuagint: “the unblemished, entire loin,” so that one thing is not offered to God and another to the adversary. For it is enough for this person, for the sake of forgiveness, not to do the things that belong to virtue; but if he does evil, he does not obtain forgiveness. Hence: “Be innocent as doves.” [Col. 0305C] For doves possess great innocence and no malice. Whoever offers sacrifice from oxen does not need to offer the loin to God, since he binds and exercises it in good works. Whoever sacrifices from goats does not have an unblemished loin to offer, because he formerly stained it with sin. Therefore, whoever has not been in sins can offer an unblemished loin; not one who has been a sinner. For this reason, in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he distinguished goats from lambs.

**VERSE 17.**—Nor the fat. We must not possess our own desire, that is, carnal desire: “For each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire.” He forbids blood to be eaten, lest we kill anyone; for to eat the blood of beasts—that is, of cruel creatures—is itself cruel. Therefore it is added without qualification, so that we may spare both our neighbors and ourselves. But the soul must be sacrificed to God; hence he commanded the blood to be poured around the base of the altar.

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSES 1–2.**—And the Lord spoke, etc. The soul that has sinned, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 2 on Leviticus.) He rightly says “soul,” etc., up to “and the spirit is a guide to virtue, if it wishes to follow him.”

(ISICHIUS.) When the soul has sinned, etc. The legislator omitted nothing necessary, etc., up to “hence, ‘He who knew no sin was made sin for us.’”

**VERSE 3.**—If the priest, etc. (ORIGEN.) It must be observed that, in the sin of the high priest, the legislator does not add [Col. 0306A] that he sinned unknowingly or unwillingly; for ignorance cannot befall one who has advanced in order to teach others.

(IDEM.) If the priest, etc. Terror and mercy together, etc., up to “who is tormented by the awareness of his weakness.”

(IDEM.) If the priest, etc. The high priest, the faculty of piety and religion, etc., up to “he is restored through the death of Christ.”

**VERSE 3.**—An unblemished calf for the Lord, etc. (IDEM.) Secondly, we find that the high priest offers a calf as a holocaust, etc., up to “in which Christ suffered.”

**VERSE 5.**—He shall also take some of the blood, etc. He brought the blood of the calf into the tabernacle, that is, into heaven: when, after the resurrection, he ascended into heaven, he stood before the face of the Father, as though offering the blood of his passion and interceding for us.

**VERSE 6.**—Seven times: namely, for the remission of sins and under the administration of spiritual gifts. Blood signifies passion, according to the saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man.” And elsewhere: “His blood be upon us,” etc. Concerning this sprinkling Peter says: “For obedience and sprinkling with the blood of Christ,” etc.

The veil signifies the humanity of Christ. For just as the veil stood between the Holy of Holies and the outer tabernacle, so the flesh of Christ stands between us, who are the outer tabernacle, and the divinity, which is signified by the Holy of Holies. Therefore the priest sprinkled the blood of the calf against the veil of the testimony, because Christ [Col. 0306C] stained his flesh with the blood of his passion.

Against the veil, etc. He calls the Lord’s flesh by many names, because its operation is manifold. Hence the Lord himself called himself, by transferred names, now a sacrifice (Luke XXI), now a shepherd, again a vine, then the bread of life and a grain of wheat (John X, XV, VI, XII). Thus Moses also called his flesh a veil. Hence Paul says: “He inaugurated for us a way through the veil, that is, his flesh” (Heb. X). The veil is also thereafter called the veil of the sanctuary, because in it the flesh is figured as the Holy of Holies.

**VERSE 7.**—Upon the horns. This altar signifies the seat of God, that is, the Seraphim. Hence Isaiah says: “One of the Seraphim flew to me, and in his hand was a live coal, which he had taken with tongs from the altar” (Isa. VI). Incense, according to the Septuagint, signifies the composition of all virtues. For where should virtues be harmoniously composed if not in the seat of God? For they descend to us from heaven. Hence James says: “But the wisdom from above” (James III). The four virtues—wisdom, justice, fortitude, and temperance—are called horns because they contain the kinds of all the other virtues. God anoints these with his own blood, strengthening them with the greater and more perfect virtue, so that they may prevail against hostile powers and forces.

The altar, etc. The angelic virtues. For if human beings offer God the pleasing fragrance of good works, how much more do the holy angels, who remain in the purity of their nature? Although they did not admit the sin that was to be cleansed by Christ’s blood, nevertheless they were reconciled to us through his blood, and their number was restored.

At the base. The base, the lower part of the altar, signifies weak human beings. For through Christ’s blood not only was the number of angels restored, but humanity was also redeemed; therefore Christ is called the redemption of the angels as well (Col. I).

Of the altar of holocausts. The body of Christ. For he himself is priest, sacrifice, and altar. Just as he performs many works, so he is suitably called by many names. Hence Paul says: “We have an altar from which those who serve the tabernacle have no authority to eat” (Heb. XIII): that is, the body of Christ, from which the Jews are not permitted to eat. This altar is at the entrance of the tabernacle, that is, of heaven, because through it we have entrance into heaven.

And the fat. Mystically, the pleasures and desires of the flesh; yet these are not all to be received into Christ, such as the desire for gluttony and sexual intercourse. Whatever he had, he had from us: thirst, hunger, and things of this kind. These he offered to the Father, to whose glory he transferred them, and he set them before us as an example, so that we might refer our desires to God.

**VERSE 9.**—The two kidneys and the lobe that is above them, near the loins. (ISICHIUS.) These things are done also in the sacrifice of peace offerings, or of salvation. And he divides the sacrifice into two, so that all may imitate the sacrifice of Christ: both those whose conduct is lower, for whom the sacrifice of peace offerings is appropriate, and those who pursue higher things, for whom it is enough if they imitate what follows.

**VERSE 11.**—But the hide and all the flesh, with the head and feet and the rest. He commands this so that you do not divide Christ, as certain people divide him by saying: “The one who suffered is from Mary; the one who did not suffer is from God.” But for us there is one God, Jesus Christ, through whom all things are (I Cor. VIII). For flesh in the Lord means the whole of his humanity, according to what is said: “The Word became flesh” (John I). Hence he says: “His flesh with the head and feet,” or “extremities,” according to others, so that through these words we may believe that the one who suffered for us is the first and the last; for he is before all things, and all things hold together in him.

With the intestines and dung. The Septuagint: “with the belly and dung.” The belly signifies the mind; therefore let us have no doubt that the one who suffered for us possessed a human mind, which certain heretics deny. Dung signifies the sin of the human race, which the crucified one took upon himself. Although dung is unclean, it does not defile the one who carries it; nor is it part of our nature, although it is within us. Thus our sins, which the Lord bore, were foreign to him and did not defile him.

With the intestines and dung, etc. (ORIGEN.) Perhaps by way of comparison, etc., up to “the legislator more fully figures its mystery in what follows.”

**VERSE 13.**—But if the whole congregation, etc. (ISICHIUS.) He gives the same command for the sacrifice of the congregation and of the priest, etc., up to [Col. 0308A] “for he prayed even for those who crucified him: ‘Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.’”

**VERSE 21.**—He shall bring the calf outside the camp. (IDEM.) The conclusion of the law is sufficient for us to make present matters clear, for nothing is commanded here to be changed in the case of the sin of the multitude. It is evident that he understands the sin of the people and of the priest to be the same; therefore he ordained the same sacrifice in both cases.

**VERSE 22.**—If a ruler has sinned and has done, etc. (IDEM.) As in voluntary sacrifices, etc., up to “for the Sabbath was given for the cessation of evils.”

(ORIGEN.) This ruler can be understood as the power of reason that is within us. If it sins, so that we do something foolish, let us fear that saying: “You are the salt of the earth.” But if the salt becomes tasteless, it is useful for nothing except to be thrown outside and trampled by people (Matt. V).

**VERSE 23.**—A male goat from the goats. Not a she-goat, that is, something easy or moderate, but a difficult and harsh penance. For the more someone excels in understanding, the greater punishment he endures for a greater fault if he sins.

**VERSE 24.**—He shall place his hand, etc., thereby making his sin known through himself and offering his confession. But according to the Septuagint he does not kill it himself, but others do; for he needs the help of others so that his penance may be accepted, and the priest is not commanded to kill it. For he says:

And when he has sacrificed, etc. He did not add who ought to sacrifice it, although in the sacrifice of penance it is permitted to use the assistance of another. Hence James says: “Pray for one another, so that you may be saved.”

Where it is customarily slaughtered, etc. For worthy penance for sinners and the strong works of the righteous are likewise pleasing to God.

**VERSE 25.**—The horns of the altar, etc. Upon the cross are offered the firstfruits of the blood that is offered for sin, because the work of the cross and its effect is the perfect remission of our sins.

And pouring out the remainder. That is, attributing all penance to evangelical preaching, whose purpose is that the repentant person correct himself and be saved. Hence, at the beginning of the Gospel, the Lord wisely says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is near” (Matt. III).

**VERSE 27.**—But if he has sinned, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 2 on Leviticus.) Committing one of all the commandments of the Lord, etc., up to “when he recognizes that he must sacrifice a sacrifice of praise.”

From the people, etc. (ORIGEN.) To distinguish him, etc., up to “he considers it necessary for us.”

But if it is from the flock. (ISICHIUS.) Concerning the offering of the goat that those from the people offer, etc., up to “he gives similar commands concerning a goat and a sheep.”

## CHAPTER V

**VERSE 1.**—If a soul has sinned, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 1 on Leviticus.) He appears to say that a person sins, etc., [Col. 0309A] up to “but immediately he added: ‘The soul that has touched anything unclean,’ etc.”

(ISICHIUS.) If he has sinned, etc. He does not repeat what he said above, etc., up to “because we must not consent to another’s sins or error, but rebuke them.”

**VERSE 2.**—The soul that has touched. (ISICHIUS.) Not the body, etc., up to “but he can say with David: ‘Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters’” (Ps. CXXIII).

(GREGORY, Book XXXII of the Moralia, chapter 4, volume II.) To utter an oath is to bind ourselves by a vow to divine service, etc., up to “we burn with the fire of sorrow.”

**VERSE 4.**—The soul that has sworn, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 2 on Leviticus.) Why is no sacrifice prescribed for a silent perjury, or for touching a corpse, or for some unclean thing?
