But for what someone swears falsely without knowing it, he commands a lamb or goat to be offered. Or should this sacrifice be understood as applying to all the matters mentioned above? For after enumerating all these things, he added a sacrifice of expiation.

He has recognized the offense. (ISICHIUS.) It must be noted that the offense, etc., up to “as the following passages show.”

**VERSE 7.**—But if he cannot, etc. (IDEM.) Let us add this: if a ruler should commit any of these sins, he shall offer a male goat from the goats—namely, a penance worthy of himself, since he ought neither to sin, nor to share in the sins of others, nor to provoke his subjects to sin. What therefore ought not to have happened he left unexamined.

But if, etc. (IDEM.) Whoever cannot continually afflict himself, etc., up to “because he sacrifices himself completely to God.”

**VERSE 8.**—He shall twist back its head. (GREGORY, Homily on Ezekiel.) The death of Christ in relation to the joining of his body, etc., up to “he united all of us more truly to himself in his very death.”

(GREGORY.) He shall twist it back, etc. In God’s sacrifice we ought to be a turtledove, so that our head may be turned back toward the feathers, that is, so that the mind may be turned toward the virtues. By the head we understand the mind, because just as the head governs the body, so the mind governs actions. But the head is attached to the neck and is not completely severed, because our mind must be separated from the pleasure of the flesh, not from the necessary care of the flesh; nor should we make provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. XIII). Therefore the head of the turtledove should be partly severed and partly remain attached to the neck.

[Col. 0309D] Let it be broken off, etc. He wishes us not to serve the body, but to break away or turn back, so that the law of sin may not reign in our members. Yet because we must not hate our body or, with the heretics, regard it as the devil’s creation, but must subject it to the mind, he does not command the body to be separated from the neck; for both belong to one and the same creation.

**VERSE 9.**—The foundation, etc. The Septuagint: “the base,” which is the Gospel, because, according to the intention of Christ’s sacrifice and of the Gospel, a sacrifice must be offered for sins. Hence he adds: “Because it is for sin”; for nothing rescues from sin in such a way as imitation of Christ and obedience to evangelical preaching.

[Col. 0310A] But if he cannot. Because not every time is readily suitable for penance—namely, when we abuse penance itself and destroy its fruit by returning to sin—the legislator indicates this by saying: “But if his hand cannot,” etc.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 8 on Leviticus, volume III.) It is asked whether what has been said must be understood everywhere, etc., up to “so that all the other matters from these people would belong to that general category.”

**VERSE 11.**—An ephah. (ISICHIUS.) It is a measure of three measures, etc., up to “so that those who are under his hand may not perish.”

He shall not put oil upon it, etc. As if to say: This is not perfect penance; therefore it has no oil, that is, no spiritual joy of gladness, nor frankincense, because one must not trust him in prayers. Rather, let the one who offers the offering hand it over to the priest—that is, let him entrust the hope of salvation to divine mercy.

Which is for sin. Because he does not know whether the prayer of one who frequently transgresses is of good fragrance. Hence: “Who knows whether he will turn and God will forgive, and leave a blessing behind him?” (Joel III). Therefore he neither permits despair nor permits presumption, lest they again become negligent.

**VERSE 12.**—A handful. In the handful Scripture is signified, by which one writes. It is written: “I do not say to you seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. XVIII). By the handful, therefore, he indicates that God must be entreated to remember his written mercy and grant it to us, just as he commands it to be granted to our brothers. For this the great priest will cleanse the one who prays.

**VERSE 13.**—If a soul, having transgressed, etc. (ISICHIUS.) One must abstain from every sin, but especially from the sin committed against holy things. How dreadful it is, the offering itself testifies. For nowhere from the beginning of the narrative, except here, is a ram commanded to be offered; by this the necessity and usefulness of the sacrifice are proclaimed. Here no male goat, no she-goat, no sheep, no pair of turtledoves, and no two young pigeons is offered.

Through the ceremonies, etc. (ORIGEN.) There are many kinds of sanctification. There is oil with which the tabernacle alone is anointed; and incense, concerning which it is said: “Whoever makes such a composition shall perish from his people.” There are also the bread of the Presence, which only males of the line of Aaron eat. Mystically, however, he sins against these sanctified things who irreverently uses something in a sacred place or handles divine things unworthily.

**VERSE 15.**—With two shekels. The two shekels are the two commandments of charity, by which the sinner purchases confidence in remission. For penance is worth nothing without the grace of remission. Hence, according to the Septuagint, the ram is purchased for fifty shekels, because through penance and observance of the twofold charity perfect rest is acquired when remission of sins is given. The Septuagint: “fifty shekels of silver, by the holy shekel.” No one acquires the Lord’s sacrifice except through the Holy Spirit, because no one can say “Lord Jesus” except in the Holy Spirit (I Cor. XII). Fifty signifies the coming of the Holy Spirit, because he came to the apostles on Pentecost, that is, on the fiftieth day. The Septuagint: “by the holy shekel.” In the holy shekel he signified the power and operation of the Holy Spirit. A shekel is worth twenty obols; the age of twenty is not subject to sin. Hence those who went out from Egypt, when they were twenty years old, did not bear the punishment of the people’s sin (Num. XIV); for the spiritual person is clean from every sin.

**VERSE 16.**—And a fifth part, etc. (ISICHIUS.) Whoever has sinned through a sacred vessel or food, etc., up to “for thus he will plead for our sin.”

**VERSE 17.**—If a soul has sinned, etc. (IDEM.) He appears to have forgotten what he had commanded. For concerning the sins for which he commanded a she-goat or sheep to be offered, he now appears to command a ram to be offered. But he has neither forgotten the earlier matters [Col. 0311B] nor commanded anything contrary. There, by “soul,” he signified a Gentile; here, the one who transgresses the commandments of the law through ignorance.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 7 on Leviticus.) It is asked how this offense is distinguished from those which he has generally included, etc., up to “or some matter in sacred services.”

**VERSE 18.**—He shall offer a ram, etc. Above he commanded the penitent to offer a she-goat; here he commands a ram to be sacrificed, because it is useless to sacrifice the harshness of penance unless you resolve to place full confidence in Christ’s sacrifice.

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSES 1–2.**—And he spoke, etc. The soul that has sinned, [Col. 0311C] etc. (ISICHIUS.) The same sin is committed against holy things, etc., up to “it is like robbery.”

(ORIGEN, Homily 4 on Leviticus.) The soul that has sinned, etc. I think that our soul, etc., up to “For no one puts new wine into old wineskins.”

A lost thing, etc. (ORIGEN.) The Septuagint: “destruction.” Heretics labor to find “destruction” in the Scriptures, from which they can construct their error. But perhaps, when they hear ecclesiastical words, they come to their senses, understand that what they had found was destruction, and return it—that is, surrender it to its author.

**VERSE 5.**—And in addition a fifth part, etc. The tongue, in which one of the five senses resides; it is offered so that he may not sin thereafter, because through it each of the aforementioned offenses was committed.

[Col. 0311D] (ORIGEN.) The Septuagint: not “a fifth part,” but “fifths,” that is, twice five, etc., up to “let us refer everything to the one God.”

**VERSE 8.**—And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying. (ISICHIUS.) Here he speaks of the continual sacrifice, etc., up to “and order his entire life toward perfection.”

**VERSE 10.**—Of linen, not wool: he wants the tunic and undergarments to be linen, not wool (Exod. XXVIII). Linen clothing is supple and soft and clings to the body; wool is rough. For justice and chastity are supple and closely joined to the soul. Linen clothing can also easily be obtained, and so can virtues, if someone wishes to attain them.

[Col. 0312A] And he shall remove the ashes, etc. Ashes signify the completion of a good work. Aaron shall carry the ashes outside the camp; after this life, good works present themselves through the great high priest, Christ, to God the Father. There they are reduced to ashes while he stands before the face of God for us. For the camp is the present life, in which we are always fighting against spiritual wickedness (Heb. IX). They are placed beside the altar when the completion of good works is stored in the ark of the heart. For the altar in this passage signifies the heart. “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience,” etc. (II Cor. I).

**VERSE 11.**—And having put on other garments. (ORIGEN.) It must be observed that the priest uses one set of garments in the mystery of the sacrifices and another when he goes out to the people. Hence: “We speak wisdom among the mature” [Col. 0312B] (I Cor. II). And elsewhere: “Wearing a much lower robe, I judged that I knew nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II).

**VERSE 12.**—The fire on. (AUGUSTINE, Question 12 on Leviticus.) He does not wish the fire to be completely extinguished; rather, after the holocaust has burned until morning, once the remains have been removed, it is renewed so that the other things placed upon it may burn.

Which the priest shall tend. Allegorically: Christ was judged in the morning and crucified in the evening. Therefore fire is applied morning and evening, because the love of God is nourished in us when we remember Christ judged in the morning and crucified in the evening.

(GREGORY, Book XXV of the Moralia, chapter 7.) The altar of God is our heart, etc., up to “so that the more God is seen, the more he may be loved.”

[Col. 0312C] And after placing the holocaust upon it, he shall burn it, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 13 on Leviticus.) It must be considered whether no day was omitted, etc., up to “it is surprising if he remained silent and did not advise that such things be offered in the evening.”

**VERSE 14.**—This is. The legislator appears to repeat what he has said, renewing memory by repeating the command and showing the usefulness and necessity of the law. Yet he inserts something new, by which he indicates that the command is necessary and inescapable. Thus, just as he repeated the sacrifices of the holocausts, mixing in the requirement of continual observance—as in the statement, “Let the fire on the altar always burn and never fail”—so, in the sacrifice of fine flour, that is, of theology, he adds that it must be eaten only in a holy place and by a male.

And before the Lord. According to what Christ has revealed, [Col. 0312D] for he is the true altar. Therefore let us establish theology in the things Christ incarnate handed down to us, so that in him we may contemplate the Father, and the Son in the Father, and that the Spirit is the Son’s and proceeds from the Father.

**VERSE 16.**—The remainder, etc., so that we may not cease entirely from theology, because the summit of knowledge is directed toward the future.

In the place. The Church, which is the entrance and vestibule of heaven: in it one ought to speak about divinity. Hence Psalm LXVII says: “Bless God in the churches.” Each person is a church for himself when he ceases from earthly affairs; here he can speak to himself about God and practice theology. Such are those to whom a portion of the sacrifice is given: namely, to meditate upon and speak about God.

[Col. 0313A] **VERSE 17.**—As for sin. This sacrifice indicates something similar to that which is both for sin and for offense. For speech about God serves especially for the expiation and cleansing of the soul when the sacrifice of the word of God—that is, theology—is joined to oil and frankincense, that is, to almsgiving and prayer.

**VERSE 18.**—Males only. Not everyone is fit to dispute about God, but those who have nothing feminine and nothing unstable in their thoughts or works. It is a lawful and eternal ordinance. For we must not presume to dispute about God while, through worldly fantasies, we decline from the dignity of males.

Everyone who touches. (ISICHIUS.) This cannot stand according to the literal sense: surely, if a murderer or profane person touches it, will he be sanctified? No one is excepted. But Christ, in whose type these things preceded, is sacrificed; whoever touches his flesh—that is, whoever, with faithful heart, places the whole hope of salvation in his passion and resurrection—will immediately be sanctified.

(IDEM.) Everyone who, etc. Every remembrance of God grants sanctification. Hence: “It is sanctified through the word of God and prayer.” But when he says that the one who touches is sanctified, he clearly shows that, in disputing about God—that is, in theologizing—it is enough for us merely to touch upon the subject. For whoever wishes to be warmed, if he puts his hand into the fire, will suffer burning instead of warmth.

This is the offering. (AUGUSTINE, Question 14 on Leviticus.) There are other sacrifices that he mentioned in Exodus, by which the priests are sanctified for seven days so that they may perform the priesthood. Another is the one he mentions as being offered by the high priest when he is appointed, that is, when he is anointed. Hence he adds: “On the day when he anoints him,” not “them,” although he also commands the subordinate priests to be anointed. This sacrifice is perpetual through the succession of priests—or because what it signifies is eternal.

This is, etc. Aaron means “mountain of strength,” that is, Christ; his sons are all the faithful; the day of anointing is the time of the incarnation, when he was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.

An ephah. The humanity of Christ. The ephah, which holds three measures, signifies the Trinity—provided that the Lord’s flesh is the ephah—so that the eminence of divinity and the inseparability of the Lord’s flesh from it may be shown. Nevertheless, it is a perpetual sacrifice. For by one offering he perfected forever those who are sanctified; hence he is also able to save forever.

In the sacrifice. (ORIGEN.) The law of Moses is the priest’s sacrifice, etc., up to “in which nothing is diminished and nothing luxurious” (Matt. XVI).

Morning. The Lord’s passion began in the morning, from the time when he was struck with blows in the courtyard of Caiaphas, and it continued until evening. Since darkness interrupted it, it is divided from the sixth hour until the ninth hour between morning and evening.

**VERSE 21.**—Which is made in a pan. (GREGORY, Homily 12 on Ezekiel.) No sacrifice of this kind belongs to God, etc., up to “it is assigned to God as a holocaust.”

**VERSE 22.**—The priest. The Septuagint: “The anointed priest from among his sons shall perform these things for him.” For Christ is for Aaron, not in his place, because he transferred the priesthood to himself and removed Aaron. “From among his sons,” because he descended from Jacob through Mary and from the same tribe.

Who belongs to the Father. One is the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom all things are (Rom. XI). For the Lord of glory was crucified, and the passion of the incarnate Word took place in the flesh of Christ: “He emptied himself completely, taking the form of a servant and becoming obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross.”

**VERSE 23.**—For every, etc. Whatever he commands to be done in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he commands to be done in this sacrifice as well.

And no one. What is eaten is broken down; he breaks down the sacrifice of Christ who says that he died for sins, although he committed no sin.

[Col. 0314B] (ORIGEN.) And no one shall eat it. The sacrifice in this passage must be understood as the Word itself and its teaching, which no one eats—that is, discusses or retracts—but it is a holocaust. Whatever he said and whatever he established endures through eternal consecration.

The priest who, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 18 on Leviticus.) Not what he imposes, etc., up to “this he also briefly recalls now.”

(ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Leviticus.) Some offerings belong to God alone, etc., up to “we reserve these matters better for the fire.”

**VERSE 27.**—Whatever it touches. Although it is the offering of another, that is, of the penitent, the one who touches it will be sanctified even if he does not repent. Likewise, if a little child has been baptized, although he has not yet sinned on his own, he is cleansed from original sin.

If it is from the blood, that is, if the substance of the flesh has been stained by sins. Hence: “The garment mixed with blood shall be for burning, and food for the fire” (Isa. IX). It shall be washed in a holy place, that is, it will have hope in baptism, which not only washes away past sins but also instructs a person so that he may be able to repent of future ones.

**VERSE 28.**—But an earthen vessel, etc. The weak person—that is, the feeble one—who, after completing penance, falls back into sins must be broken by fear of judgment.

**VERSE 29.**—Every male, etc. The priest who offers and eats the whole sacrifice is Christ, who offers our penance and consumes the salvation of sinners. Since the flesh of the sacrifice pertains to penance, every male among the priests eats it—namely, the strong and vigorous person, to whom it is said: “Act manfully, let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Ps. XXVI).

**VERSE 30.**—It shall not be eaten, etc. Because it pertains to Christ, who by his own authority and by the power of his divinity grants remission. For his passion, through which remission is procured for us, was not the passion of a mere human being, but of God incarnate. Therefore it is not eaten by human beings but consumed by fire, because granting remission belongs to God alone, who is signified by fire: “For our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV).

## CHAPTER VII

[Col. 0315A]

**VERSE 1.**—For an offense. (ISICHIUS.) “Offense” sometimes means, etc., up to “but the offering of the kidneys, the lobe of the liver, and the thighs is holiness.”

(ORIGEN, Question 5 on Leviticus.) Some say that an offense occurs when we do not do what we ought, whereas sin occurs when we do what we ought not; but this distinction is not observed everywhere.

**VERSE 2.**—Its blood, etc. (ISICHIUS.) Whatever is done in the sacrifice of peace offerings, he commands to be done in this one as well.

**VERSE 7.**—As for sin, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 20 on Leviticus.) Sin is the perpetration of evil; offense is the abandonment of good. For just as turning away from evil is one thing and doing good another, so abstaining from good is one thing and doing evil another; the former is an offense, the latter a sin. Or an offense is committed unknowingly, while sin is committed knowingly.

(ORIGEN, in the same place.) As for sin, etc. Likewise, he commands the fats of the ram, etc., up to “that is, the things that turn the sinner from the way of sin.”

To the priest, etc. Christ, who was made propitiation for us. Therefore every sacrifice is ministered and performed in him, and whatever follows from penance is referred to him. For he came to save us, saying: “I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners” (Matt. IX).

The victim of the holocaust. (ISICHIUS.) Not, namely, the good of oxen or sheep, etc., up to “in view of whom we have patience in sufferings.”

**VERSE 9.**—He shall have the hide. The circumstance of wealth that they ought to offer to the true priest, who wish to become a holocaust. Satan called the circumstance of wealth a hide, saying: “Skin for skin, and all that a person has he will give for his life” (Job II). Job gave this as a hide, that is, so that he might retain patience, which is called a hide because many useful things are made from it.

And whatever is prepared on the griddle, etc. Because these things are close to the theology of the incarnation, they necessarily belong to the priest who offers them, that is, to Christ who was born, suffered, and rose again.

**VERSE 10.**—Whether sprinkled with oil, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Leviticus.) The sacrifice is commanded to be made in oil, etc., up to “one in a pan, a third on a griddle.”

[Col. 0315D] (ISICHIUS.) He speaks of a sacrifice of fine flour sprinkled with oil, etc., up to “he assigned it to the sons of Aaron.”

**VERSE 12.**—If the offering is for thanksgiving. Literally, the offering is made for thanksgiving when someone gives thanks after being delivered from great tribulation, as Moses did after crossing the Red Sea (Exod. XV). Mystically also, whoever has not committed greater crimes gives praise to God’s mercy, since God has kept him free from dreadful sins.

And unleavened cakes anointed with oil. Bread, namely, thin and broad, which signifies the knowledge of the prophets. As much as the solidity of bread differs from the thinness of a cake, so much does the knowledge of the Old Testament differ from that of the New. Therefore the loaves are sprinkled with oil, while the cakes are anointed, because the light and grace of the New Testament are greater than those of the Old.

And baked fine flour and cakes of oil, etc. The divine wisdom, namely, which is baked in the fire of love. For Christ, the Wisdom of God, because of his exceeding love, handed himself over to death.

**VERSE 14.**—It shall be offered to the Lord, and it shall belong to the priest, etc. The Septuagint: “And from all his gifts he shall offer a praise of God to the priest who pours out the blood; it shall belong to him.” For it depends “not on the one who wills or on the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX). But the firstfruits must be offered to Christ, who ministers and completes the sacrifice.

VERSE 15.—“Its flesh shall be eaten on the same day,” etc. (ORIGEN, in the passage cited above.) Another food of the soul is milk, [Col. 0316B] etc., up to: “Let them be,” he says, “new and old.”

“Until morning.” The future age, where there will be a true day succeeding the night of this age, does not wish our life—through which we must be saved—to remain incomplete; for in the future it will not be possible to work.

VERSE 16.—“Whether by vow or freely,” etc. Every sacrifice of peace offerings, or salutary sacrifice, is voluntary; hence it was placed above among the gifts. But the sacrifice of thanksgiving or praise, although it belongs to that category, is not called voluntary, because it is rational: since, inasmuch as we are rational beings, we owe our Creator, in a certain special way, a due and rational sacrifice.

“Likewise.” Because some, after the end of this life, have described another such age, introducing a period of a thousand years in which Jerusalem would be rebuilt, its temple and the Holy of Holies restored, and sacrifices offered. But if anyone believes this and, in a certain sense, eats it in his mind, hoping to eat during that period—which is impossible—his offering is not accepted, because it is polluted; he also incurs sin. Hence he says: “Whatever soul has defiled itself with such food,” etc.

“But if anything,” etc. (ORIGEN, in the passage cited above.) The two days on which it is permitted to eat the flesh of the sacrifice, etc., up to: “Therefore I will not claim for ourselves the knowledge of all things.”

VERSE 17.—“On the third day it shall be found.” The future age in which there will be the general resurrection, which Christ’s resurrection signified. When the third day has dawned, whatever remains will then be consumed by fire. For whatever salutary thing we leave incomplete, or whatever evil we have done, will be consumed by fire like wood, hay, or straw; “but we shall suffer loss” (1 Cor. III).

VERSE 19.—“The flesh which,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Leviticus.) The holy flesh is understood as the divine words, up to: “and is polluted by foreign uncleanness.”

VERSE 21.—“Or of a beast.” Unclean beasts signify those who are devoted to unclean and earthly actions; hence fornicators are called “horses in heat.”

VERSE 23.—“The fat of a sheep,” etc. That is, neither the good intention nor desire of the strong, the innocent, or the penitent is to be corrupted by a sinister interpretation, as though it had been done through hypocrisy, lest anyone seek to destroy another’s merit and, as it were, diminish it by eating it.

(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 21, vol. III.) He said above, etc., up to: “they chose for themselves the death of sin.”

VERSE 24.—“For various uses.” Not only by imitating the works of the good, but also by drawing the works of the wicked into our own experience as examples. For we read that Herod celebrated his birthday and stained the feast with blood (Matt. XIV). We put such a desire to use so that we may beware; but conversely we remember with mourning and affliction the day of our birth, when we were in paradise. The Pharisee, exalting himself, says: “I give you thanks, because I am not like the rest of men,” etc. (Luke XVIII). Let us say the opposite: “God, have mercy on me, because I am not like your servants who lead an angelic life on earth.”

VERSE 25.—“If anyone eats the fat,” etc. (ORIGEN.) As though he said: “Let no one cause one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” etc. Blood is forbidden to be eaten, as though he said: “Do not boast over the broken branches, lest you be cut off, and they, if they do not remain in unbelief, be grafted in” (Rom. XI). The blood is rightly understood as the Jewish people: for they descended not from the faith or spirit of Abraham, but only from his blood.

VERSE 29.—“He who offers the victim.” (ORIGEN, Homily 5 on Leviticus.) Another text reads, etc., up to: “and, conscious of his salvation, gives thanks to the Lord.”

(IDEM, in the same place.) The sacrifice called salutary, etc., up to: “who carry the vessels of the Lord.”

VERSE 30.—“He shall hold it in his hands,” etc. (JEROME, Letter to Fabiola, vol. I.) In the salutary victims the priests offer the fat, etc., up to: “so that he may learn to despise what he sees himself cast into the sewer.”

The Septuagint: “He who offers the salutary sacrifice to the Lord shall offer his gift to the Lord from his salutary sacrifice.” Explaining this, it adds: “He shall hold the fat of the victim in his hands.” Or, according to the Septuagint: “His hands shall offer it from the victim to the Lord.” For he himself must perform the things that pertain to his salvation, because “the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII).

“But the breast shall be,” etc. (ISIDORE.) The breast is given to the priest so that he may possess a pure thought and knowledge of doctrine. The right arm is given so that he may have good works, proceed with an armed hand to battle against the devil, and accomplish by the example of his works what he has conceived in his heart. A jaw is also given from the private portions, so that he may excel in eloquence; the belly is given so that he may extinguish lust and despise gluttony.

VERSE 32.—“Of the priest.” (AUGUSTINE.) Of Christ, represented in the priest. Hence only the priest can perform this sacrifice. To begin our good is ours; to perfect it and bring it to completion belongs to divine grace. It is not of one who wills or runs, but of God who has mercy, to direct our actions; hence it is also called the arm of God. Therefore he rightly received the shoulder, or, according to the Septuagint, the arm.

VERSE 33.—“He who has offered the blood,” etc. Christ is the one who offers the true blood of the peace offerings and the fat—that is, the souls and desires of those who are being saved. He is one of the sons of Aaron, namely the unique and pre-eminent priest, to whom the right arm falls as his portion—that is, every good and perfect action.

VERSE 35.—“This is the anointing.” (ISICHIUS.) These things therefore appear to pertain to the anointing of the priests, etc., up to: “But what he understood by the aforesaid anointing he shows in what follows.”

VERSE 37.—“This is the law of the burnt offering,” etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 5.) When the legislator had proposed, etc., up to: “in which the truth of the figures is preserved.”

“This is the law,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) You see the differing ways of life that unite a person to God: honor, namely, and perfect wisdom, signified by the burnt offering; or moderate righteousness, which performs the things pertaining to salvation. The law rightly understood the sacrifices of peace offerings, whether through the burnt offering [Col. 0318B] or through the offering, as useful for priestly dignity. Hence, on the day when he commanded the law of anointing, he added the matters concerning the sacrifices and briefly recalled them all.

VERSE 28.—“On Mount Sinai.” This is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” Temptation is like a bush: it is a rough shrub and difficult to grasp. Thus the crown of a good life is scarcely attained amid temptations and tribulations. Hence: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, for when he has been tested, he will receive the crown of life” (James II).

CHAPTER VIII

VERSE 2.—“Two rams.” The passion of Christ is signified, for he is the leader of the people. Two rams are rightly sacrificed, because Christ entrusted to us the mysteries of his passion twice: first, when he ate the mystical lamb at the supper; second, when he established the same mysteries in the consecration of bread and wine.

VERSE 3.—“And you shall gather.” Moses summoned the entire synagogue. Although the Lord had chosen and commanded it, the synagogue is nevertheless summoned: the presence of the people is required when a priest is ordained, so that all may know and be certain that the one who is superior to the whole people—more learned, holier, and more eminent in virtue—is the one chosen for the priesthood.

“So he washed him and clothed him.” In what garment? In a tunic, and he girded him with a belt. Again: “He clothed him in a long tunic” (Sirach XLV), or, as we read elsewhere, “an inner garment” (2 Sam. XV). I see the high priest clothed in two tunics. Jesus, however, forbids the apostles to wear two tunics, although Moses and Jesus—that is, the Law and the Gospel—ought to agree (Matt. X). Others say that Jesus’ command not to have two tunics is not contrary to the Law but more perfect than the Law: just as the Law forbids murder (Exod. XX), whereas Jesus cuts away anger (Matt. V); and whereas the Law forbids adultery, Jesus cuts away lust.

I do not confine the priestly mysteries within the narrow limits of this interpretation. I think something greater is shown by this form. That priest whom Moses was then ordaining knew that circumcision was spiritual; nevertheless, he observed circumcision of the flesh, because he could not be uncircumcised. He therefore had two tunics: one of the mystery of the flesh, the other of spiritual understanding. For he could not be the priest of those who then existed unless he offered fleshly sacrifices, even though he knew that they ought to be spiritual. Thus he appropriately had two tunics.

But the apostles, who were going to say, “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V), and who would entirely reject literal observance, are rightly forbidden to have two tunics. One is sufficient for them, and that one is the inner tunic. They do not want the tunic of the Law that is outside, because Jesus permits them to have one tunic, and that one the inner tunic.

VERSE 6.—“And when he had washed him.” (JEROME, in the passage cited above.) Even then he signified the purification of the world, etc., up to: “so that we may accomplish in deed what we conceive in our mind.”

(ORIGEN, Homily 6 on Leviticus.) Let Moses wash you, etc., [Col. 0319B] up to: “in what order the high priest is constituted.”

VERSE 7.—“He clothed him.” (JEROME, in the same place.) Let us first learn the common garments of the priests, etc., up to: “because such work cannot be done in a woven fabric.”

(IDEM.) The second is the linen poderis, that is, a long garment of double linen, which Josephus calls byssine. It clings closely to the body, with tight sleeves, so that there is no wrinkle anywhere in the garment, and it descends to the legs. Soldiers commonly wear such linen garments, which they call shirts, fitted and tight to their limbs so that they may be ready for every task. The priests use this tunic, possessing the beauty of clothing and the speed of nakedness; it is called the linen garment.

The third is a belt resembling the skin of a serpent, which it sheds in summer, woven into a long, rounded pouch beneath a covering of scarlet, purple, hyacinth, and fine linen. For beauty and strength, it is decorated with such varied workmanship that one might think that different flowers and gems had been woven into it by the craftsman’s hand, rather than added to it. With this belt the linen tunic is tightened between the navel and the chest. It is four fingers wide and descends for the most part to the legs; when freedom of movement is needed for the sacrifices, it is turned back over the left shoulder.

(JEROME.) The fourth is round, etc., up to: “about to die immediately.”

(IDEM.) The sixth, in Hebrew, etc., up to: “let him carry it on his shoulders.”

(IDEM.) The seventh is small, etc., up to: “and to the eyes of those who saw it, it might seem to be one piece of weaving.”

[Col. 0319D] (IDEM.) The eighth is a golden plate, etc., up to: “and may the name of God crown and protect the entire beauty of the high priest.”

But the pomegranates and bells placed below signify lightning and thunder, or earth and water and all the elements harmonizing with one another and so intertwined that all things are present in each of them.

(JEROME.) The Hebrews say that there are four colors, etc., up to: “his providence penetrates all things.”

(ORIGEN, Homily 6 on Leviticus.) In Exodus, where instructions are given concerning the priestly garments, etc., up to: “so that what is holy may not be given to dogs and pearls placed before swine” (Mark VII).

“And clothing him,” etc. The Septuagint: “He clothed him with a tunic, girded him with a belt, and clothed him with the ephod.” He expounds the incarnation of Christ. For he assumed the whole human being, body and soul. He called the tunic earthly, because it is from the earth; the shoulder-garment heavenly, because ὑπωμίς is the poderis. He assumed both and saved both.

(JEROME.) On the hyacinth-colored tunic are pomegranates and bells, because the knowledge of the high priest ought to be so great that his steps, movements, and everything vocal about him should speak, and that the truth he has conceived in his mind should resound through his conduct; whatever he does and whatever he says should be doctrine. Without bells, varied colors, gems, and flowers of virtues, he neither enters the Church nor is he a high priest.

[Col. 0320B] “The shoulder garment,” etc. (ORIGEN.) Moses placed upon the high priest the shoulder garment, which is an ornament of the shoulders formed by the encircling of the garment. The shoulders signify labor and work. He therefore wishes the high priest to be adorned in his works; knowledge alone is not sufficient, but “the one who does and teaches will be called great” (1 Tim. III; Matt. V).

“The shoulder garment.” (JEROME.) The shoulder garment and the two emerald or onyx stones that cover the shoulders above are interpreted as the two hemispheres, one above the earth and the other beneath the earth; or as the sun and moon that shine above.

(IDEM.) The two stones on the shoulder garment signify Christ and the Church, containing the names of the twelve apostles who were sent to preach; or the letter and the spirit, in which all the mysteries of the Law are contained—the spirit on the right, the letter on the left (2 Cor. III). Through the letters we come to the words; through the words we come to the meaning. The order is beautiful, the garments themselves signifying the mysteries: works are on the shoulders, reason on the breast; hence the priests eat the breast.

VERSE 8.—“Which he fastened.” (ORIGEN, in the passage cited above.) He girded him according to the workmanship of the shoulder garment, etc., up to: “because he uses the belt of virtue according to his works.”

“He fitted the breastpiece,” etc. (JEROME.) The breastpiece placed in the middle indicates the earth, which, like a point, although it contains all things within itself, is surrounded on every side by all the elements.

(ORIGEN, in the passage cited above.) He placed the logion upon him, λογίον, etc., up to: “for after this nothing more is added to the head of the high priest.”

(JEROME, in the passage cited above.) The breastpiece is twofold, open and hidden, etc., up to: “and doctrine and truth should follow these preceding things.”

(IDEM.) The twelve stones, etc., up to: “demonstrating knowledge to us.”

“He placed the plate.” (IDEM.) All learning is useless unless it is crowned by the knowledge of God, which is always with him and with the Father. Hence he placed the plate upon the turban.

(IDEM.) Everything is imperfect unless a driver is sought for the chariot, and unless the Creator, standing above creatures, himself governs what he created. What was formerly shown in the plate is now shown in the sign of the cross: the blood of the Gospel is more precious than the gold of the Law. Formerly, according to Ezekiel, the sign was placed on the foreheads of those who groaned in the form of the letter tau (Ezek. VIII); now, carrying the cross, we say: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us,” etc. (Ps. IV).

The golden plate on the forehead of the high priest, with the name of God inscribed upon it, signifies that everything on earth is governed by God’s will. It was just that the priest of God, bearing in his garments the type of all creatures, should indicate that all things need God’s mercy; and when he sacrificed, the condition of the universe should be expiated. He prayed, by voice and appearance, not for children, parents, and relatives alone, but for every creature.

VERSE 10.—“He took,” etc. He is the Son of God, who anoints and is anointed: he anoints with the word of divinity, according to which he shares everything with the Father and the Holy Spirit. He is anointed by the Father according to: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness,” etc. (Ps. XLIV). The Holy Spirit anointed him according to Isaiah: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me” (Isa. LXI). Whatever the Father and the Holy Spirit do, the Son also does. He therefore anoints according to his divinity and is anointed according to his humanity. Hence Daniel sees him offered, but does not see him offering, because he offers himself. Moses therefore anointed and offers, bearing the figure of Christ.

VERSE 11.—“They sanctify.” (ORIGEN.) This signifies the heavenly creature enriched by our sanctification—that is, through the Lord’s flesh taken from us. Hence: “so that the principalities and powers might be made known through the Church,” etc.

VERSE 12.—“Pouring,” etc. The head of Christ is divinity. For just as the head is not separated from the feet, so Christ’s divinity is not separated from his humanity after the anointing (1 Cor. XI). Hence he says: “God, your God, has anointed you,” etc. (Ps. LIV). Thus God is anointed and sanctified.

VERSE 13.—“The sons,” etc. (ORIGEN, in the passage cited above.) Observe the difference between the lesser priests and the greater, etc., up to: “even if he has received the title of first.”

“And he clothed them,” etc. Tunics and belts or girdles, turbans or miters, like those of Aaron, are placed upon Aaron’s sons. They put him on, are girded with him, and carry him on their heads. For their loins are girded with truth, which is Christ, and they are clothed with the breastplate of righteousness. Christ is righteousness, just as he is also the helmet of salvation; for he himself is the salvation of God.

VERSE 14.—“He offered,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) What the force of this law is, etc., up to: “the sons of Aaron necessarily lay their hands upon it as sharing in the sacrifice.”

(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 23.) When he recalled the sacrifices for sins, etc., up to: “and the blood poured out at the base of the altar of sacrifices.”

“He offered,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) The Law, in many respects portraying Christ in the priest, etc., up to: “he commanded concerning sheep.”

“He offered,” etc. The ram signifies the handing down of the mysteries and the mystical Passover that Christ celebrated with his disciples (Matt. XXVI). It is called the second ram because, after the lamb had been sacrificed at the supper, he offered himself. Hence Aaron laid his hands upon the head of the ram with his sons, because Christ celebrated a common supper with his disciples. But Moses offered this sacrifice specially, because more than the others he expressed the figure of Christ, who above all made his own sacrifice.

VERSE 24.—“He touched the tip of the ear,” etc. If we understand Christ through Aaron, the tip of his ear was touched with blood because he obeyed the Father unto death. If we understand the priests of the Church, their ears and the thumbs of their hands and feet must be touched, so that they may consecrate the excellence of their actions and steps to the Lord.

“He touched the tip,” etc. The effect of this sacrifice is shown by the anointing of the ears, hands, and feet: it is celebrated on account of our obedience, good actions, and conduct, so that, freed from Adam’s disobedience, we may attain the obedience of the Only-Begotten.

“His hands,” etc. So that we may be strengthened in good action. For the things that are anointed are strengthened; those that are not anointed are destroyed. Where there was no anointing with the blood of the sacrificed victim, Egypt was struck. But first the priest, and afterward his sons, were anointed with blood, because Christ first received the blood at the supper and then gave it to his disciples.

“He poured it upon the altar.” When he drank and gave the apostles to drink, he poured intelligible blood upon the altar—that is, his body. The Church, however, is the body of Christ. Hence Mark: “And taking it, giving thanks, he gave it to them, and they all drank from it, and he said to them: This is my blood of the new covenant, which will be poured out for many” (Mark XIV).

“But the fat.” What these things signify in the salutary sacrifice or the peace offerings has been stated. The Septuagint, however, renders “tail” as “loin”; “intestines” as “stomach”; and “the fatty lobe of the liver” as “the lobe of the liver.” It is not without reason that these are also mentioned now in connection with the ram.

VERSE 26.—“From the basket.” The Septuagint has “basket of completion,” which is the tongue of the Lord, who introduced the chief and perfect doctrine. For he did not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it (Matt. XIII). It is rightly called a basket on account of the woven structure of his teaching, since he had spoken many things in parables. It was also a dish and a table of the whole doctrine. Rightly, therefore, he sets forth the mystical bread from the basket of completion.

“Bread.” The apostolic, legal, and prophetic doctrine. The Law, the prophets, and the apostles all make mention of him. The Law says: “This is the bread which the Lord has given you” (Exod. XXVI). The prophet says: “His bread will be given,” etc. (Isa. XXXIII). Prophetic and legal doctrine nourish less than apostolic doctrine. Hence Paul: “God placed in the Church first apostles, then prophets” (1 Cor. XII). The apostles draw their testimonies from the Law and the prophets, and through these the cakes (collyrida) and thin cakes (lagana) are subjected to them.

[Col. 0323A] “And the shoulder.” (GREGORY, Book I of the Register, Letter 24.) By command of the Law the priest offers the right shoulder, etc., up to: “and Moses says in what follows.”

VERSE 39.—“He took the breast.” (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 23.) Above, because he was giving a general command, etc., up to: “for from the beginning it is said: He will give you what concerns the people, and you will give him what concerns God.”

VERSE 30.—“And you shall take the anointing oil.” (IDEM, Questions 24.) The question is raised: after Moses’ death, who anointed the priest, etc., up to: “by serving, not by surpassing.”

“He sprinkled,” etc. Whatever good things are in us must be referred to him as our head. Hence: “For them I sanctify myself, so that they too may be sanctified in truth.” He plainly called his passion his sanctification, and this sanctification is given to us.

“And upon the sons.” (AUGUSTINE.) It was not apparent which of the sons would succeed the high priest. Scripture does not establish that it was the firstborn or the elder, unless this occurred through some divine judgment. Nevertheless, it appears to have arisen from rivalry that afterward several high priests were appointed, because, when the more eminent contended, the honor itself was granted to several as a means of ending the dispute.

VERSE 31.—“The loaves also.” He commanded the flesh to be eaten with the loaves, so that we might understand the body of Christ, which is flesh, and the bread that came down from heaven (John VI); and this ought to be celebrated only in the Church.

VERSE 32.—“But whatever.” We see this being done in the Church: whatever remains uneaten is handed over to the fires. He does not say how many days the uneaten portions may remain, so that whenever they remain they are handed over to the fire. He indicates that if we refrain from eating the sacrifice and cannot determine whether what we see is the Lord’s body, we should nevertheless not leave it behind but hand it over to the fire, so that the Holy Spirit may eat what we cannot. He eats it when we consider that the things we cannot do are possible for him.

VERSE 33.—“From the entrance.” This signifies that throughout the whole time of the present life one must not depart from the tabernacle but must persist in God’s service.

(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 24.) At the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony, etc., up to: “for this name means habitation.”

“For seven,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) The fiftieth, with the sevenfold number multiplied within itself, etc., up to: “observing the Lord’s commands,” etc.

VERSE 36.—“And they did,” etc. Aaron is joined to his sons and does not leave the door of the tabernacle. He himself was to be proclaimed, and was to preach in them, just as he himself consecrates and is consecrated in his members.

CHAPTER IX

VERSE 1.—“On the eighth day,” etc. The eighth day after the dedication signifies the day of Pentecost, when the Holy Spirit came (Acts II). The seven days from the dedication indicate seven times seven days, which were from the resurrection until Pentecost—namely, forty-nine—with Pentecost itself added as an eighth day.

Pentecost, which occurred on the day of the resurrection, bears the figure of the future and of the consummation of the present age, because the age unfolds through seven days. For it was fitting that the Spirit should come on the same day on which Christ rose. Then he commands Aaron, his sons, and the elders to be called. For then the spectacle of the Church was summoned, in which there is Aaron—that is, Christ—and his sons, who are of lofty conduct and therefore ministers of the priesthood, and the elders, that is, the presbyters. For the body of the Church consists of these.

VERSE 2.—“Take from,” etc. Aaron takes a calf for a burnt offering and a ram and offers them to the Lord. Christ then made his sacrifice known when, at the coming of the Spirit, he gathered Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and the firstfruits of all nations into the apostles’ upper room (Acts II).

[Col. 0324B] Aaron offers the calf and the ram when the teachers of the Church announce the mysteries of the passion and declare that they have been celebrated for the salvation of the human race.

“Take.” The apostles offered a goat on the day of Pentecost when Peter, announcing repentance, said: “Turn and do penance.”

(AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 26.) “Take one goat from the goats,” etc., up to: “but where all are, there are also individuals, though it is not changed.”

VERSE 6.—“This is the word,” etc. The word means the commanded action: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke XXII). He calls it a word because the dispensation of this mystery is considered or established more fully in the word, and especially because the Lord’s word transfers the visible things into something greater and intelligible. Hence he also says concerning the manna: “This is the bread which the Lord has given you to eat; this is the word which the Lord established” (Exod. XVI).

In these words he signifies that, while they were performing the holy mystery and celebrating the Lord’s supper, the Holy Spirit came upon them. It was the Lord’s Day, on which it was fitting for the apostles to celebrate the sacred mysteries; following their traditions, we assign the Lord’s Day to divine assemblies. Likewise, we find that Christ was made manifest after the resurrection through the mystical supper and the breaking of bread.

VERSE 7.—“And offer for sin,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 27.) Another text reads, etc., up to: “it is not necessary to place it upon the burnt offering.”

[Col. 0324D] “Offer the burnt offering,” etc. He does not say “the burnt offering of completion,” as above, when it was offered so that he might be perfected through sanctification and exercise the priesthood to which he had been appointed. It should certainly be noted that, when sacrifices were offered for the people, sacrifices for sin, a burnt offering, and a salutary sacrifice were commanded. But for the priest, a sacrifice for sin and a burnt offering of completion were offered, not a salutary sacrifice. The offering of completion was made when the priests were sanctified. Moses offered these things for Aaron and his sons. Later, Aaron, already exercising the priesthood, was commanded to offer a calf for sin and a ram as a burnt offering, not as a burnt offering of completion. At that time it was offered so that he might be perfected through sanctification and be able to exercise the priesthood; once he was exercising it, there was no need to perfect it again.

VERSE 8.—“And immediately,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) For what reason these sacrifices are also performed here, we explained above, etc., up to: “hence we clearly see both offered in the person of the priest.”

(AUGUSTINE, in the passage cited above.) It also raises a question that, when Aaron was making the gifts of the people mentioned above, etc., up to: “whether he meant two breast portions from each of the two animals.”

VERSE 15.—“And for sin,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) What figure these things bear, etc., up to: “and did not cease to teach the Church what it should meditate upon.”

“Extending his hand,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 28.) Standing at the altar, he ministered, etc., up to: “who prohibited steps from being there.”

VERSE 22.—“And when all this had been completed,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) He evidently wishes to explain the whole figure of the Church, etc., up to: “the things that follow demonstrate this.”

VERSE 23.—“But Moses and Aaron entered the tabernacle of testimony,” etc. (IDEM.) Because he is speaking of the intelligible tabernacle, etc., up to: “he is fit to bestow a blessing.”

“But they entered.” He first says “entered” and then adds “went out,” because the priest enters the tabernacle when he prays for himself or for the people, or devotes himself to divine contemplation. He goes out when he teaches or blesses the people, or when he returns to his conscience by examining himself, lest he offend in preaching.

“And the glory of the Lord appeared.” In the form of fire, as on the day of Pentecost. Hence he adds: “And fire went out from the Lord.” Thus Luke also says: “There appeared to them divided tongues, as it were of fire.”

“To all the multitude,” etc. Luke says something similar: “When this voice occurred, the multitude gathered and was confused in mind” (Acts II). It not only gathered but was also terrified. Hence it follows here: “They were astonished and wondered,” etc.

“Which were upon the altar.” He finds it necessary to place the aforesaid sacrifices and their interpretations upon the intelligible altar of Christ’s body, so that our intention may sigh toward that altar, and then the nourishment of the intelligible fire—that is, of the Holy Spirit—will be present. Of this it is said: “The Lord our God is a consuming fire” (Deut. IV).

CHAPTER X

[Col. 0325D]

VERSE 1.—“And Nadab took,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 31, vol. III.) When fire went out from the Lord, Aaron’s sons died, etc., up to: “they will suffer torments.”

“And having taken,” etc. (ISIDORE, Questions on Leviticus, vol. V.) They offer foreign fire, etc., up to: “lest we burn with vices.”

(ISICHIUS.) Here he treats those who teach foreign doctrines, etc., up to: “from which they could have merited life.”

(AUGUSTINE, in the passage cited above.) Another text reads, etc., up to: “through whom he gave us Scripture.”

VERSE 4.—“But Moses called Mishael and Elzaphan.” Mishael means “touching of God.” Elisaphan, or Elzaphan, means “illumination of God” or “mirror of God.” These men are rightly commanded to carry Nadab and Abihu outside the camp. For they signify the saints, who, illuminated by God, touch him with the hands of faith and contemplate God with perfect faith.

Hence they are rightly called sons of Uzziel, which signifies the Gospel. It is said that he was Aaron’s cousin, because there is a close kinship between the Gospel and the Law. For the Gospel is an exposition of the Law. The sons of the Gospel therefore drive heretics, truly dead, out of the camp of the Church.

Alternatively, Misadai and Elisaphan: the former means “touching of God,” that is, Misadai; Elisaphan is interpreted as “the mirror of my God.” Whoever knows how to touch God and contemplate—namely—the flesh and divinity of Christ, like Thomas, who, touching the flesh with his hand, said, “My God and my Lord” (John XX), can remove the fire of foreign doctrine from before the holy ones, that is, the priests.

The tunics of the priests signify the conduct and life with which they are clothed in the priestly habit. They are therefore cast out, together with their priesthood, from the company of the priests and also from that of the people. Hence he adds “outside the tabernacle,” that is, outside the assembly of the people; the sons of Aaron’s uncle do these things.

Aaron—that is, David, through whom the prophecies are understood—[signifies] prophecies which make Christ manifest and, in a certain sense, give birth to him for those who are ignorant. The brother of prophecy is the Gospel: for the things done in the Gospels were foretold by the prophets. Therefore the sons of the brother of Aaron’s father—that is, of the Gospel—cast out such men. Hence: “If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house” (2 John).

VERSE 6.—“Your heads,” etc. Literally: because they had recently been consecrated to God, he commands them not to remove their holy garments but to stand ready to serve God.

Allegorically, however, it means that they must not create a division of persons in Christ. The head of Christ is God; Christ consists of divinity and humanity. The tiara of the head—that is, of the divinity—is the humanity by which the divinity was covered, as by a cap. This must not be removed, nor may a division of persons in Christ be preached; rather, there is one person of two substances.

“Your heads,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions on Leviticus 32.) So that they may not remove their turbans, etc., up to: “hence he adds:”

“Let your brothers and the whole house of Israel mourn the burning.” (ISICHIUS.) We are not ignorant of what the turbans signify, etc., up to: “of which he says: His anointing teaches you about all things.”

VERSE 9.—“Wine and anything that intoxicates.” (IDEM.) The Church observes this law even now, etc., up to: “that is, to have inspired spiritually.”

“Wine and anything that,” etc. They are commanded to abstain from those things that lower or overturn the state of the mind when they enter the tabernacle. We, however, must never become intoxicated, but must always be sober in mind and body.

“When you enter.” (AUGUSTINE, Questions 33.) When, then, were they permitted to drink, etc., up to: “so that this may be the legitimate and perpetual office of the priests throughout their generations.”

[Col. 0327A] VERSE 10.—“So that you may have the knowledge to distinguish.” (AUGUSTINE.) This too is placed ambiguously, etc., up to: “or should it rather be referred to both?”

VERSE 12.—“Take the sacrifice,” etc. (ISICHIUS.) The breast signifies confidence, etc., up to: “but whatever pertains to the peace offerings and salutary offerings belongs to the whole people.”

“Take,” etc. The secret and profound mysteries of Scripture, which the common people do not grasp, are to be retained and eaten by the perfect, beside the altar—that is, beside the faith in and authority of the Lord’s passion.

VERSE 14.—“The breast,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions 34.) “The breast.” Although individual parts have been given individual names, etc., up to: “it was placed upon the altar from the breast.”

[Col. 0327B] VERSE 16.—“Meanwhile.” (ISICHIUS.) Since every sin is erased through repentance, and those who committed the aforementioned sin of foreign doctrine and blasphemy were not saved, the legislator explains the cause of their death.

“Meanwhile, the goat,” namely, because Aaron’s sons did not eat what was for sin in the holy place—that is, they did not allow repentance for the sin committed to be performed in the Church. This command is addressed to those whom Christ appointed as his vicars in the Church. For he offered the blood of his oblation, which was offered for our blood, in the holy place—that is, in heaven—in the presence of the Father.

This sacrifice ought to be eaten in the holy place—that is, the Church—for the propitiation of sins. Hence he adds: “As it was commanded to me,” that is, as I commanded. Moses bears the person of Christ.

He found it burned up because they had sinned against the Holy Spirit; the offering for repentance had been removed by the intelligible fire of the Holy Spirit. For “no sacrifice for sin is left for those who sin willingly” (Heb. X). Just as true repentance obtains pardon, so feigned repentance provokes God, because “the Holy Spirit of discipline will flee deceit” (Wis. I).

The holy Fathers called this the unforgivable sin and blasphemy against the Holy Spirit: to persevere in crimes until the end of life, to despair of one’s salvation, and to distrust the power and mercy of the Redeemer.

(ADAMANTIUS.) Not to sin belongs to God alone, etc., up to: “unless it is true and sincere.”

[Col. 0327D] (AUGUSTINE, *Question 36 on Leviticus*) Indeed, since six animals are commanded to be offered for the people, etc., up to “all of which had been for sin.”

**VERSE 19.—Aaron answered, etc.** In the person of the Church, whose figure he bears, just as he also bears that of Christ, Aaron appears to say this. It is as though he said: Since, after the Savior’s coming, ministers were appointed to serve, to offer for repentance, and to expound the prophetic life. Alternatively: The teachers perished, and these things happened among them in the Church, so that the death of priests and teachers was mourned; hence he could neither eat what was for sin today nor pray, and this displeased the Lord.

(AUGUSTINE) “Aaron answered, etc.” If today they offered what was for their sin, etc., up to “This [Col. 0328A] is why Aaron answered, and it pleased Moses.”

**Today.** As though he said: If they had committed this sin before the Savior’s remission, perhaps they would have been forgiven, since knowledge had not yet been manifested to the world: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin; but now they have no excuse for their sin” (John 15).

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 1.—The Lord spoke.** (ISICHIUS) Whatever has been made by God is clean by the authority of its institution itself. In animals, therefore, human dispositions, actions, and intentions are depicted, and from these people become clean or unclean.

[Col. 0328B] (ID.) “God said to Noah: Everything that moves and lives shall be food for you” (Genesis 9), etc. It is also said in Genesis: “God saw all that he had made, and it was very good” (Genesis 1). Here, however, certain things are forbidden as though evil and are declared unclean. Yet these statements are not contradictory. For the Lord both restrains the Jews’ gluttony to a moderate degree, and the spiritual exposition of the commandments instructs what sort of people they ought to be. For the Law, when rationally understood, is nourishment for the rational soul. Just as above he represented those who offer through the offerings, so now through the things eaten he depicts those who eat.

**VERSE 3.—Everything that has, etc.** (ISIDORE) Among fish, whatever has neither fins nor scales is abominable; rough things are regarded as clean. For harsh, bristly, firm, and weighty human dispositions are approved. Those without these qualities are called unclean, and light, slippery, weak, and effeminate dispositions are added to them. He joins fins and scales together also: all fish that have fins have scales as well. If some are ignorant in a way that can be remedied, they possess elevated knowledge and a heavenly life; but those who are not such should not eat food with them.

**Morally.** (GREGORY) Fish that have fins customarily leap over the waters. In finned fish, therefore, chosen souls are represented, and they alone pass into the body of the heavenly Church. Supported by the fins of the virtues, they leap through heavenly desire toward contemplation, although they slip back within themselves through the frailty of the flesh. Thus only those pass into the body of the elect as chosen food who, while serving earthly things, ascend to what is above by leaps of the mind, so that they do not always lie hidden in the depths of cares, where they have no concern for the highest love, like the care of free air. Those who are occupied with temporal affairs therefore order external things well when they diligently withdraw into inward things; they do not love the clamor of disturbance, but rest within themselves in the bosom of tranquility.

**VERSE 10.—Whatever has fins, etc.** There are also fish that have a shell instead of skin, whose scales cannot be removed, because they neither lay aside the scales of ignorance through the word of God nor receive the knife of the Spirit. Although they may be found in the sea of baptism or [Col. 0329A] in the rivers of repentance, they are nevertheless abominable among those things that move and live in the waters, because by living badly they corrupt the rebirth and life that they received in baptism.

**VERSE 11.—Flesh.** (RABBI, on Leviticus) When he forbids the pig, etc., up to “those seeking the darkness of night.”

**VERSE 13.—These are the things concerning birds, etc.** (ISICHIUS) He adds those things that pertain to the life of contemplatives, etc., up to “little women weighed down with sins.”

**VERSE 14.—The vulture according to its kind.** (ID.) The one who delights in wars. Hence it follows: “following an army,” awaiting the corpses of the dead. For one who devotes himself to contemplation ought not to feed on another’s grief.

**VERSE 16.—The ostrich.** The ostrich is a bird, but it cannot fly and is always near the ground, like some who serve God while entangling themselves in secular affairs (Job 39; 2 Timothy 2).

**The owl.** They say that it sees sharply at night and poorly during the day. Such are those who glory in contemplating the Law but cannot receive the light of the Gospel.

**The night-raven.** It hunts only at night. Such are the nations intent on the works of night, which are fornication, uncleanness, and licentiousness (Galatians 5).

**The gull.** The gull is an animal that lives both in water and on land: it flies and swims. Those who venerate both circumcision and baptism are compared to it.

**The hawk.** The hawk is among the birds of prey, but it becomes tame and carries out plunder with human beings. Those who appear gentle but, together with the powerful, greedy, and rapacious, strive to seize things by force imitate it.

[Col. 0329C] **The cormorant and the ibis.** These have long necks and, as is said, draw their food from the depths of the earth or water; they are not to be imitated. For one who devotes himself to contemplation ought to strive toward what is above and not be concerned with things below.

**VERSE 19.—The hoopoe.** This bird is mournful and loves mourning. But worldly grief produces death. One who loves God ought to rejoice, pray without ceasing, and give thanks in everything (1 Thessalonians 5).

**The bat.** It flies near the earth and uses wings instead of feet; this is foreign to those who contemplate, lest their contemplation become occupied with earthly things.

**VERSE 20.—Every creature among the winged things that walks on [Col. 0329D] four feet, etc.** Those who appear similar to contemplatives but, like creeping things, cling to earthly desires—even if they walk on four feet, that is, if they pretend to proclaim the Gospel, which calls to repentance—are abominable, because they do not truly embrace a communal life but serve pleasures.

**VERSE 21.—Whatever walks, etc.** Although they are in the flesh, they do not walk according to the flesh (2 Corinthians 10); rather, they leap away from sordid actions and mix with earthly people in order to instruct and teach, as the Lord did with sinners and tax collectors (Matthew 9). We ought to have legs higher than our feet, lest we limp on both feet, like the Jews in the Law and the Prophets; but we should have straight legs, like the cherubim, of whom it is said: “Their legs were straight, and their feet were winged” (Ezekiel 1).

**VERSE 22.—The young locust.** It leaps, but less than the *attacus* or the locust, which leap more vigorously. Such are those who associate with sinners for the sake of association, not for agreement or imitation.

**The serpent-fighter.** It fights with serpents; our struggle, however, is with the ancient serpent and his angels (Revelation 12).

**VERSE 25.—So that he may carry it.** As one who calls evil good and bitter sweet (Isaiah 5): by praising the evil from which he ought to have restrained someone, he makes it his own and carries it.

**VERSE 26.—Every animal that, etc.** (ISICHIUS) The Law leaves no sin unaddressed; whatever is forbidden in the Gospel is expressed through the enigmas of the Law, so that “every word may be established by the mouth of two witnesses” (Matthew 18), and so that in both Laws you may praise God and, as it forbids, flee evil.

**VERSE 27.—Whatever walks on its hands, etc.** One who abandons evangelical conduct but walks on his hands—that is, lays hands upon things for the sake of shameful profit (1 Timothy 4)—is rightly compared with every beast, whether you call him an adulterer, a miser, a murderer, or something similar. For through his perverse laying on of hands he shares in everything.

**VERSE 28.—Whoever carries such carcasses.** By giving false testimony, calling the unworthy worthy, and the clean unclean.

**VERSE 29.—The weasel.** “Gluttony.” For the mouse avoids no danger on account of the belly’s gluttony.

**The crocodile.** One of hard skin and malicious character, feeding on mud.

**VERSE 30.—The chameleon.** It takes pity and, out of weakness, pretends to be gentle, although it is cruel.

**The mole.** A blind animal born from the earth. For, as they say, it is created from earth that has been soaked and turned to mud, but first corrupted.

**VERSE 31.—Whoever touches, etc.** If such things were naturally unclean, the living person who touched them would also be unclean. The carcasses of such things are actions—that is, deceit, theft, duplicity, and the like—in which there is death for the soul.

**VERSE 32.—And upon whatever, etc.** (ISICHIUS) The legislator employs an admirable division, etc., up to “both a wooden vessel and a garment.”

**VERSE 34.—Every food, etc.** He understands food and drink as good works; therefore he said: “The food that you shall eat, and whatever liquid is drunk,” etc. For the food and drink of evil actions are forbidden, so that no one may participate in them. If, therefore, any carcass falls upon good actions, which are in every vessel—that is, in every human being—the action will necessarily become unclean. If pride, deceit, hypocrisy, or any carcass—that is, anything that brings death to the participant—falls upon a good action, that person too will be unclean. For an evil intention falling upon a good action pollutes it.

**VERSE 34.—If water is poured over it.** (AUGUSTINE, *Question 37 on Leviticus*) This concerns a vessel that had been made unclean by unclean carcasses, if it happened to contain water.

**Water.** Baptismal water. For the discussion concerns the baptized; he makes no mention of unbelievers. Hence Paul says: “I wrote to you not to associate with fornicators” (1 Corinthians 3), certainly not with the fornicators of this world, etc.

**VERSE 35.—Whether ovens.** Through these the teachers are signified, in whom the food of sacred doctrine is cooked by labor and the fire of the Holy Spirit. Nor is this surprising: Moab is called a pot: “Moab is the pot of my hope” (Romans 2).

**Pottery vessels, etc.** For those who teach not to steal do steal, and those who preach not to commit adultery do commit adultery; nevertheless the doctrine is clean. Hence the passages concerning springs and the rest.

[Col. 0331B] **VERSE 37.—If it falls.** (ISICHIUS) He leaves nothing unexamined, etc., up to “if any carcass falls upon them, they become unclean.”

**VERSE 39.—Whoever touches its carcass shall be unclean.** (ISICHIUS) We ought to abhor the life of the wicked and imitate that of the righteous. Whoever touches the life of the wicked will be unclean until he repents.

**VERSE 40.—Whoever eats it.** That is, whoever defends it as an advocate and takes it upon himself by giving assistance to it must wash his garments—that is, his evil actions—until he repents.

**VERSE 41.—Everything that creeps upon the earth.** The legislator explained this above, but repeats it in order to admonish the hearer to frequent meditation on the Law.

**VERSE 47.—And so that you may know what to eat.** It is not these foods that cleanse or pollute us, but we ourselves. For we give life to the things that are eaten, and just as “every food is good” (1 Peter 2), and nothing is to be rejected when received with thanksgiving, so the things that are eaten—that is, the things that nourish the soul, namely good actions—we give life to if we use them well, but kill if we use them badly. For one who gives alms from plunder kills the alms and deprives it of its power; and those who abstain from food but slander their brothers kill their abstinence.

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 2.—If a woman, having received seed.** (ISIDORE, *Questions on Leviticus*, vol. 5) The week is the present life, etc., up to “nor will she be cleansed in the future.”

[Col. 0331D] **She shall be unclean.** (ISICHIUS) Because the sower is unclean, as Adam’s heir, who became unclean through transgression and thus was joined to his wife. For after he left paradise he knew his wife, and thus the human race is propagated.

**For seven days.** (ID.) Because Adam, etc., up to “when Adam, separated from paradise, fell into this misery.”

**On the eighth day, etc.** (ID.) The eighth day, etc., up to “But disobedience brought upon us uncleanness and filth.”

**VERSE 4.—For thirty-three days, etc.** (ID.) With seven days added, etc., up to “for it is uncertain whether they give birth to a female or a male.”

[Col. 0332A] (AUGUSTINE, *Question 40 on Leviticus*) What difference is there between seven days, etc., up to “in the case of the female, eighty.”

**She shall touch no holy thing.** What sanctuary is meant, since only priests ought to enter the tabernacle, and only as far as the second veil? Beyond the veil, however, where the ark was, only the high priest entered. Perhaps the area before the tabernacle, where the altar of sacrifices is, could be called the sanctuary. For the courtyard too is often called a holy place, as when it is said: “In the holy place they shall eat them.” Perhaps women entered there to offer their gifts, which were to be placed upon the altar.

**VERSE 6.—When the days have been completed.** He makes the intention clear: natural impulses do not produce pollution, but sin, concerning which David says: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities” (Psalm 50), etc. He calls nature “mother” and signifies that the uncleanness of Adam and Eve’s sin descended upon the whole human race. Therefore Moses commanded that, when the days of purification were completed, a burnt offering and a sacrifice for sin be slaughtered, clearly showing that the image of God grants perfection to our race. For the days of purification indicate formation, while the burnt offering indicates perfection.

(AUGUSTINE, in the same place) Is giving birth a sin? etc., up to “not so that they should say ‘for the son’ or ‘for the daughter,’ but ‘on behalf of the son’ or ‘on behalf of the daughter.’”

It should also be noted how poor the Lord wished to be born: an offering was not made for him of a lamb and a young pigeon or turtledove, but of a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons, in accordance with the Gospel and with what the text of Leviticus then commanded to be offered if the hand of the one making the offering did not possess a lamb. This is a very significant point.

(BEDE, *On Leviticus*, vol. 2) Our Lord was not only a human being, etc., up to “and afterward, in the heavenly Jerusalem, will arrive commended to the Lord by the sacrifices of good works.”

**VERSE 7.—From the flow, etc.** As though someone were to ask from what she who has given birth lawfully will be cleansed, he says: “from the flow of her blood,” that is, from the disobedience from which uncleanness and punishment flowed, through meditation and contemplation of the Law, whose neglect brought uncleanness upon humanity.

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 1.—And the Lord spoke.** (ISIDORE) God speaks once, and two things are heard: Moses, as the higher, hears the Spirit; Aaron, as the lower, hears the letter and announces the letter to the people. Hence God himself says: “He shall speak to the people for you, and you shall be to him in matters that concern God” (Exodus 4).

**VERSE 2.—A man.** (ID.) Sometimes “man” is understood in an excellent sense, as one who preserves the image of God and the dignity of nature. Sometimes it means a sinner, in whom that dignity is disfigured, as here.

**In whose flesh, etc.** One who strives to persuade people toward carnal or external things bears leprosy in flesh and skin, like the Corinthians, who thought that the resurrection would take place in the pleasure of the flesh; and sins are not reckoned against those who remain in the faith, even if they live carnally.

**Or as something shining.** One leprosy is excessively or moderately dark, when passion has not yet boiled over and requires much deliberation. Another is excessively bright and conspicuous, with knowledge that is manifest.

**The plague of leprosy.** (ISIDORE) Leprosy is false doctrine; lepers are heretics who, lacking the unity of true faith, profess various errors of doctrine, mixing truths with falsehoods and staining the Church by spreading them, just as leprosy stains bodies.

One bears leprosy in his body who attacks the Church, like the Carpocratians, who deny the resurrection of the flesh, and the Novatians, who condemn marriage and take repentance away from sinners.

**Or to one of any of his sons, etc.** To relatives according to the spirit, from whom he has the priesthood, and in whom there is perfect and complete prophecy, so that they may discern subtle things and the hidden movements of the soul.

**VERSE 3.—The hairs.** Thoughts by which the soul is adorned and the mind covered, and from which they are generated, just as the head generates hairs by which it is adorned and covered. Hence: “The hairs of your head are all numbered” (Matthew 10). For this reason the Nazirite does not cut his head (Numbers 6), because he does not have superfluous thoughts; but to cast away holy thoughts is a holy loss.

**Lower than the flesh, etc.** Lower than himself; hence he rightly does not deserve pardon. To be conquered by another who is greater is bearable; but not to do the good commanded by God—for the Lord divides it as he wills—and thereby to become worse than oneself is intolerable.

**VERSE 4.—He shall shut him up.** He is shut up a second time so that he may be carefully examined and, after a double investigation, strict judgment may be rendered. The sin was evident to the priest, but he did not know whether the mind consented to the passion; he only inferred it. Therefore he examined him again. For this reason, after Peter’s denial, the Lord asks him three times what his mind is like (John 11), so that we may not judge quickly but investigate repeatedly. He is shut up for seven days. The number seven signifies the fullness of the present life, which is carried out in seven days; when it is completed, sin and service will cease. Hence the seventh day is called rest in the divine Scriptures.

**VERSE 6.—He shall cleanse him, because it is a scab.** Thus Paul removed from the tabernacle of the saints the man who had committed fornication in Corinth, because his passion was manifest, and handed him over to Satan; when he examined him a second time and saw that he had repented, he ordered him to be received (1 Corinthians 5).

[Col. 0333D] **VERSE 10.—When there is a white color in the skin.** The manifest transgression of the letter of the Law, which is proper to the Jews, as in sacrifices, purifications, and similar matters. There is also a form common to the nations, concerning adultery, plunder, greed, and the like.

**VERSE 12.—But if it has blossomed.** (ISICHIUS) He shows that the Jewish people are leprous in part, as transgressors of the Law in part; hence the priest expels them as unclean. But he does not expel the Gentile who is leprous over his whole body and transgresses the whole Law; rather, he judges him clean, because he was not subject to the yoke of the Law.
