(JEROME) “But if it has blossomed,” etc. In this leprosy, as though blossoming and white, various crimes are signified. For when the pleasure of worldly life is regarded as something white and flourishing, then a serious contagion of vices spreads through the body. The stains of either greed or lust become visible. But the crime of greed can easily be cut away; hence: “Give alms, and behold, everything will be clean for you.” Lust too is cleansed by fasts and abstinence. Yet a remedy is applied to all things through the priest. One kind is cleansed by offerings of sacrifices; another more easily; another is cleansed when placed outside the camp; another is not cleansed at all.

**VERSE 14.—Living flesh, etc.** (ISICHIUS) The Jewish commandment, which is called living insofar as it is a commandment, or because when correctly understood it brings life.

**VERSE 18.—For the flesh, etc.** (ISIDORE) One bears leprosy in living flesh who holds something false concerning the soul, which is the life of the flesh. Such are the Luciferians, who say that the soul is propagated from the substance of the flesh, and the Arabs, who think that the soul dies together with the body.

**VERSE 19.—A scar, etc.** (ID.) Those bear leprosy in the scar of a healed wound who, after recognizing the faith and receiving God’s medicine in Christ, again display some sign of the error or unbelief of their former doctrine.

**White.** Because it comes from the wound of transgressing the Law; for the Law is white and has not been warmed by the sun of justice (Acts 15).

**Reddish.** Because it comes from transgression of the Gospel, such as eating food sacrificed to idols or blood, or what has been strangled; both are done against Christ, whose are the Law and the Gospel.

[Col. 0334C] **VERSE 20.—It shall contaminate.** Because sin is in the condition of the body, and an evil feeding of the soul has settled upon the ulcer. Hence he called it leprosy blossoming from a wound.

**The flesh and skin that fire had burned, etc.** (ISICHIUS) He appears to repeat what was said above, but partly says the same thing and partly adds something. He presents another passion but gives the same indication. For he dealt with an ulcer that is generated and grows from some illness of neglected flesh. The ulcer of our flesh is therefore pleasure, drunkenness, gluttony, and the like, which arise when the body luxuriates and itches within itself. Now, however, he speaks of a greater wound, namely a burning by fire. Concerning this it is said: “Fire shall consume the adversaries” (Isaiah 74).

**VERSE 25.—Because it is a plague, etc.** The Manichaeans have leprosy in the scar of a burn, because they burn their bodies in the torment of abstinence and, through unbelief, produce leprosy from it rather than purity.

**VERSE 29.—A man or a woman.** One who errs concerning the divinity, like the heretics who not only deny that the Father is the creator of the world but also assert that he is the author of evils, as does Manichaeus.

**Or the beard, etc.** (ISIDORE) Those bear leprosy in the beard who think perversely about Christ’s apostles and disciples and fabricate false preaching. For the beard is a man’s adornment, and the apostles are the teachers of Christ’s body.

(ISICHIUS) We find that the legislator established six kinds of leprosy, etc., up to “because they openly defend the unbelief of their error.”

(ID.) He sets forth different colors of leprosy, etc., up to [Col. 0335A] “signifies a lying tongue and weakness.”

**VERSE 31.—He shall shut him up for seven days, and on the day, etc.** Not so much for punishment as for strict examination; for time must be observed in all matters, and more strictly in those whose tongue runs wild concerning divinity.

**VERSE 34.—If on the seventh day.** If the one who sinned denies the word in which he transgressed once, he ought not to be judged. For who judges him guilty on the basis of the very word by which he denies that he voluntarily declared himself?

**After washing his clothes he shall be clean, etc.** (JEROME) Other things committed before baptism, etc., up to “concerning which it is said: Whoever sins against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven.”

**VERSE 37.—Black hair.** That is, if he has mourned his impiety and truly practiced repentance. For mourners and penitents are disfigured by black clothing.

**VERSE 38.—A man or a woman, etc.** (ISICHIUS) In transgression of divine doctrine, etc., up to “by which they do not live.”

**VERSE 40.—He is bald and clean.** Simple, not foolish; for there is no one who does not retain at least a few hairs.

**VERSE 44.—Therefore whoever is stained, etc.** (ISIDORE) Heretics are expelled from the Church until they are cleansed. With their garments torn—that is, their secrets revealed—they are ordered to sit. With their heads uncovered, so that their nakedness may be seen by everyone. With their mouths closed, so that they may no longer speak impiously.

**VERSE 46.—He shall dwell outside the camp.** Thus John excludes the intelligible leper from the intelligible dwelling: “Do not receive him into your house or say greetings to him if he does not bring this doctrine” (2 John 10).

(ISICHIUS) These things are ridiculous when interpreted according to the letter, etc., up to “lest it be said to him: You who preach against stealing, do you steal? But God said to the sinner: Why do you recite my righteous acts?” (Romans 2).

**VERSE 47.—A woolen garment, etc.** (ID.) Woolen, precious and warming the soul, etc., up to “namely, good works.”

**VERSE 48.—In the warp, etc.** (JEROME) The warp is the soul. When it is twisted by the spindle of temptation into the slenderness of threads, it is bound together by the solidity of stronger virtue. The soul therefore stands upright, while the senses of the body lie beneath it like the weft. The sins of the body are one thing, those of the soul another.

(ISICHIUS) Those who attend only to the letter, etc., up to “but also what is accustomed to occur concerning the virtues.”

(ID.) Leprosy in a linen garment, etc., up to “in the conduct of this life.”

**The skin or whatever, etc.** (ID.) The temptation of tribulation, etc., up to “nor receive it rashly as clean.”

**VERSE 49.—If it is white, etc.** (ID.) The Septuagint: “Greenish and yellowish,” that is, pride, which flourishes for a short time; hence: “Like the herbs of the field, they quickly wither” (Psalm 36), or vainglory. For Christ wishes the virtues to exist without empty glory.

**VERSE 56.—He shall tear it away.** Through repentance he will cut off the passion: pride is torn away by applying humility; vainglory by removing flattery and empty praise.

**VERSE 57.—The flying leprosy.** (GREGORY, *Homily 10 on Ezekiel*) Sometimes we recognize that we have done evil and avoid it, etc., up to “through immoderate continence he passes over into the vice of anger.”

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 1.—And he spoke.** (ISICHIUS) Because he healed the stains, etc., up to “for he himself healed every sin.”

**VERSE 4.—Two sparrows.** (ID.) The divinity and humanity of Christ. They are clean because he had no sin, and living because he was not subject to death on account of sin.

[Col. 0336B] **Which he commands to be eaten, etc.** Because “the Word became flesh,” and unless we eat the flesh of the Son of Man, we shall not have life in ourselves.

**Cedar wood.** (ISICHIUS) The cross, which is strong against all things, just as cedar is strong and imperishable.

**Scarlet.** The Septuagint: “twisted scarlet,” namely passion, because scarlet is red, twisted through suffering and woven together with impassibility.

**Hyssop.** The grace of the Holy Spirit, which cooperates in our cleansing. Hence: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed,” etc. (Psalm 50).

**VERSE 5.—Over the waters, etc.** Of baptism. “As many of us as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized into his death” (Romans 6).

**VERSE 6.—He shall dip it in the blood, etc.** Because everything is comprehended in the power of baptism. The living sparrow is dipped in the blood of the slaughtered sparrow, because we are baptized not only into the passion of a human being but into that of God and man.

**VERSE 7.—Seven times, so that he may rightly be cleansed.** On account of the sevenfold Spirit, in whom there is all cleansing and remission; or so that the soul may be cleansed from seven demons.

**And he shall release the sparrow.** Because it is held, in a certain way, under the contemplation of the human intellect.

**VERSE 8.—His garments.** His works and whatever virtues he may have possessed, because sin also pollutes these.

**And when he has been purified, truly.** Yet above it was said that the leprosy was cleansed; this should be understood as meaning that it was made capable of being cleansed.

**Outside the tabernacle.** The fellowship of the saints, from which sinners are excluded. Hence: “Do not even eat with such a one” (1 Corinthians 5).

**VERSE 9.—The hairs.** Thoughts that provide adornment to a human being as a rational creature and one who engages in much debate, just as the hairs of the head do.

**And his eyebrows.** These establish the contemplative person in lofty and more divine things, which is signified by the eyebrows’ position in the upper regions.

**Of his whole body.** Even of the private parts, so that none of the former thoughts may remain, and so that, wholly renewed and as though newly born, he may put off the old person and put on the new. For how do new hairs arise after the old have been shaved, unless new thoughts toward better things spring up after the old have been cut away?

[Col. 0337A] **VERSE 10.—On the eighth day.** On which the Lord rose, and on which the leper enters the camp that the patriarch Jacob saw, when angels came to meet him; hence he called the place “the camp of God” (Genesis 32).

**Afterward.** On the first day, when the priest goes out, he commanded that the leper be cleansed by a sacrifice slaughtered outside the camp; on the eighth day he substituted other sacrifices. For these have the same force as the first, because all time is completed in weeks. The eighth is therefore also the first that follows. It should be noted that he shows leprosy—that is, sin—to be avoided with the utmost care, since he commanded it to be cleansed so diligently.

**Unblemished lambs, etc.** All these things signify the sacrifice of the Savior, who was offered as a victim for us. The sacrifice is made from both sexes because he saved both sexes.

(JEROME) In the two lambs are represented the two advents of Christ, by believing in which one is to be cleansed from the leprosy of sins. For he came and suffered first; he will come a second time in glory.

**A year-old female lamb.** He commands the sacrifice to be a year old, as something perfect; for among the animals mentioned above, those a year old are perfect. Hence they are then also suitable for generation.

**And three-tenths.** One who is cleansed by the sacrifice of the Only-Begotten ought to be marked by faith in the Holy Trinity: three-tenths of fine flour, that is, the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—having perfection in each person. For ten is a perfect number.

**Fine flour.** The Only-Begotten. Although the passion of the Only-Begotten took place, it is nevertheless the work of the whole Trinity. Hence we are baptized in the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, while we are baptized into the death of Christ.

(ISIDORE) There is the leprosy of sin, etc., up to “and obtain forgiveness.”

**A sextarius of oil.** For each of the things mentioned above is understood and carried out through faith. A sextarius is a measure that holds neither more nor less. Whatever is more spills out; if there is less, it is not a sextarius. So faith is given according to the measure of our mind, and it receives neither more nor less than what is distributed by God. Whatever is more or less lies outside faith.

**A sextarius of oil.** The abundant mercy and grace of God; and if he has not been able to display the most radiant face of holiness, let him not extinguish the lamp of faith.

[Col. 0337D] **VERSE 14.—Upon the tip.** So that he may fortify the hearing and make it cautious, lest he hear the serpent’s voice again.

**And of the foot.** So that our movement and way may be directed in God’s sight. When these things mentioned above are guarded through the lamb’s blood and his faith—which is given to us through his mercy and compassion—the intelligible leprosy is driven away.

**VERSE 16.—And he shall sprinkle, etc.** For such a priest presumes before God that he can cleanse and forgive sins. Hence he sprinkles seven times, because this number signifies remission and grace.

**VERSE 17.—But whatever, etc.** So that the priest’s faith may be shown through works. For it does not otherwise exert its power unless it is taken up by the hand, that is, confirmed and sealed by action. He puts the oil into his left hand and dips his right finger in the oil, so that through the weapons of righteousness he may conduct himself on the right and on the left, through glory and dishonor, through ill repute and good repute.

**VERSE 19.—And he shall make the sacrifice, etc.** From what has been said about offenses, what is for sin may be inferred; for the two are close and common, as belonging to the same general matter.

**The burnt offering, etc.** The sacrifice of Christ first cleanses us from offenses and sins, and then our burnt offering is completed. When, through intelligible cleansing, we have become spiritual by sanctifying our body and soul, then we are made worthy to ascend the altar. For then we receive complete cleansing and need nothing else. There are indeed stages of cleansing: one frees from the pollution of leprosy; another brings one into the camp; another presents those who have been completely cleansed before the altar.

**VERSE 21.—But if he is poor and his hand cannot, etc.** (JEROME) That is, if he does not possess the riches of heavenly gifts—for example, if he was unable to preserve virginity, let him keep his marriage bed undefiled; if he could not win the trophy of martyrdom, let him at least preserve himself unconquered.

**But if he is poor, etc.** He wonderfully condescends and, granting pardon to poverty, commands sacrifices suitable for the poor, lest anyone be dismayed if sacrifices beyond his strength are demanded. Yet what if he has neither bread nor money with which to buy a lamb, pigeon, or turtledove? Through these things we are therefore called to spiritual realities, so that we may understand leprosy as wickedness and the sacrifices as repentance and cleansing. The works of repentance are necessary and able to erase sins. Hence: “Bear fruits worthy of repentance” (Luke 3). There are many, however, who cannot pay what the strictness of repentance demands. It demands constant prayer, almsgiving, vigils, sacred fasting, and the ability to say: “My tears have become my bread day and night”; and: “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears,” etc. (Psalm 14). And: “For I ate ashes like bread,” etc. (Psalm 101). For those who wish but cannot, he seeks another way of repentance, that is, other kinds of sacrifices.

**VERSE 20.—He shall place it upon the tip of his right ear, of the one who, etc.** (ORIGEN, *Homily 8 on Leviticus*) Do you see how, through the final and highest purification, etc., up to “and through all things the Son of the Father is restored.”

**VERSE 34.—Canaan.** (ISICHIUS) The land of the Canaanites was promised to Abraham, etc., up to what is evident there in: “Greet Nympha and the church in her house” (Colossians 4).

**VERSE 40.—Outside the city.** Not merely outside the house, because they are to be expelled from the universal Church, which is the city of the living God.

**VERSE 42.—And other stones.** The doctrines of truth, concerning which it is said: “Living stones roll upon the earth” (Zechariah 9); and elsewhere: “Whoever builds upon the foundation with gold and silver,” etc. (1 Corinthians 3).

**VERSE 44.—The returning leprosy and the walls, etc.** That is, if, after false doctrines have been expelled, the doctrine of impiety is again found to have been spread through subtle exposition.

**VERSE 48.—But if, upon entering, etc.** Remember what you have read concerning the cleansing of the leper. For it clearly represents the church of the heretics, who act against the dispensation of Christ’s incarnation. Therefore, in order to cleanse the house, he adds such sacrifices as can express the mysteries of Christ’s flesh and passion and heal the sins committed within it.

**VERSE 54.—This is the law.** Because he has expounded the laws of leprosy at length, he necessarily recapitulates: first he explains the general kind, then its parts.

**Of leprosy.** Of impious doctrine, which can also affect laypeople; therefore it is added: “A man or woman in whom there is the plague of leprosy, and let him go.” If he had meant priests alone, he would not have added “woman.” After this he set forth leprosy as it exists in the virtues, for these are the soul’s garments. Then he dealt with the leprosy found in the teachers of the Church, who are the walls of the house. Finally he recalls scars and erupting pustules, describing true leprosy—namely, that which exists in sins, whether doubtful or manifest.

## CHAPTER XV

(ISICHIUS) The Septuagint has it thus, etc., up to “into a perfect man,” etc.

[Col. 0339C] **VERSE 2.—** (GREGORY, *Moral Exposition*, book 33, chapter 15, vol. 2) “A man who suffers,” etc. What is speech except seed? etc., up to “the fruit of everlasting reward.”

(ISICH.) Since there are many forms of false doctrine, etc., up to “if he has become a participant in his doctrine, following his disciples.”

**VERSE 9.**—The pack-saddle on which, etc. (ISICH.) The Septuagint has έπισαγμα ὅνον, that is, “the covering of an ass.” By this is understood a more negligent disciple, who must be changed because he is soft-hearted. For pack-saddles are soft.

**VERSE 13.**—He shall number seven days. (ID.) Since remission of sins is granted through the sevenfold Spirit, those who must be perfectly cleansed require his seven gifts.

**VERSE 14.**—Two turtledoves. (ID.) A sacrifice appropriate to teachers. For the turtledove signifies meditation, while the dove, frequently producing offspring and being simple, signifies the Holy Spirit. A teacher must indeed generate spiritually; therefore he dedicated this sacrifice fittingly to priests and masters.

**VERSE 15.**—Before the Lord, that he may be cleansed. According to the will and law of God, he is cleansed by repenting of the matters in which he sinned, offering sacrifices of prayers, and thereafter living rightly and thinking perfectly.

**VERSE 16.**—The man from whom it proceeds, etc. (ISICH.) “Unless someone,” etc., up to “he cleansed the human race.”

(ID.) Since many, etc., up to “the traditions of their teachers.”

**VERSE 17.**—The garment and the skin. He expresses the misery of original sin, by which the human race, having been polluted, also pollutes insensible things. He represents women who, for the sake of lust, unite with men for the temporal use they provide; and the garment and skins that have become old are likewise cast away, while a woman’s customary relationship is rejected as the friendship grows old.

**VERSE 19.**—A woman, etc. Menstruation signifies evil thoughts. For she who suffers menstruation does not touch another’s flesh, yet pollutes herself with her own. Thus evil thoughts and desires, although they are not carried out in deeds, are regarded by God as deeds and are punished.

The woman whose condition returns. (ISICH.) He intends both women, etc., up to “which is the corruption of the human race.”

For seven days, etc. This signifies the totality of times, up to its completion, when the Gospel was revealed. For human beings were separated from God until evangelical preaching joined them together.

Whoever touches her garment shall wash, etc. Thus one must abstain from idolatry: we must touch neither idolaters nor their disciples or supporters, whom they use, as it were, for beds or vessels, nor may we have fellowship with them.

**VERSE 25.**—The woman who, etc. Since we have said that the person suffering from a discharge of semen represents one who teaches obscene and corrupting things, and that the person following Jewish doctrine is represented by the one from whom the semen of intercourse proceeds, there remain those who spread the doctrine of the Gentiles, which is appropriately called a discharge of blood, as though it were the seduction of idolatry. For demons rejoice in blood.

**VERSE 29.**—He shall offer. Above, he commanded that the person suffering from a discharge of blood should take two turtledoves or pigeons as a sacrifice, because he had assumed the position of a teacher; here too, therefore, the one who suffers a discharge of blood is represented as one who was also a teacher of idolatry.

**VERSE 31.**—You shall teach. He did not establish this concerning lepers or those who touch corpses.

Uncleanliness. Every sin is uncleanness of the soul, but idolatry above all.

The tabernacle. The inner person, in whom is the image of God. The Word also became flesh and dwelt among us.

**VERSE 32.**—This. He customarily links together things that belong together and have a common meaning, so as to show how they ought to be understood and which things are joined to which by kinship of meaning.

And whoever, etc. Whoever teaches Jewish precepts, and teaches good things wrongly, is unclean when he brings forward matters belonging to the letter outside their proper time, just as he treats clean things as unclean. Hence: “All things are clean to the clean,” etc.

**VERSE 32.**—And whatever, etc. These are those who teach impiety, while the human race is held in the error of idolatry during its menstruation, that is, in separation from wickedness.

# CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 1.**—And the Lord spoke, etc. (ISICH.) He makes one body of the law, etc., up to “therefore, after their death, the Lord speaks these things to Moses.”

**VERSE 2.**—Speak to Aaron, etc. (ID.) How greatly God spares us, etc., up to “which is guarded against by the present words.”

Before the propitiatory. (ISICH.) The Septuagint: “Before the face of the propitiatory,” etc., up to “or which we receive from the Lord’s flesh.”

**VERSE 3.**—He shall offer a calf for sin. (ISICH.) The order is remarkable. Having said that one must not always enter the holy places, lest we presume to approach rashly and without circumspection, he shows when and how we should enter.

He shall offer a calf for sin. Christ is the beginning of divine preaching, and so is his Passion. If this had not occurred, and if he had not freed people from both Gentile and Jewish error, he could not have spoken of the Father’s divinity. For “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. 11).

**VERSE 4.**—He shall put on the linen tunic, etc. Whoever is going to speak about God and behold him according to his capacity must be armed with every virtue, of which there are four general kinds: justice, chastity, fortitude, and wisdom.

Underwear. (HIERON. Letter to Fabiola, vol. I.) Where he relates how Moses clothed his brother Aaron, etc., up to “let us die by death.”

(ID.) According to the Hebrews, etc., up to “therefore the loins or thighs are covered with linen underwear.”

When he has been washed. (ISICH.) The water of baptism, etc., up to “but desiring to understand the dispensation of Christ.”

**VERSE 5.**—And he shall receive from the whole assembly, etc. (ID.) Christ was sacrificed for us, etc., up to “hence Paul says: ‘You have been put to death through the body of Christ’” (Rom. 8).

**VERSE 7.**—Two male goats, etc. (ISICH.) Since both for sinners and for the righteous, etc., up to “saying: ‘You shall have no others’” (Exod. 20).

(AUG., Questions on Leviticus, question 55, vol. III.) Two male goats. The goat that is to be sacrificed, etc., up to “an allegorical meaning.”

(ISICH.) He shall make the two male goats stand. Since Christ is God and man, etc., up to “and the other to Christ as the scapegoat.”

**VERSE 10.**—Into the wilderness. That is, into the bosom of the Father, to which no one approaches except he himself and the Holy Spirit. Thus “he went away,” that is, he restrained the power of acting, and bore our iniquities—not in order to possess them, but to consume them. For God is a consuming fire.

Into the wilderness, of which it is said: “In a deserted, impassable, and waterless land,” etc. (Ps. 62). There the enemy has no place, where God dwells. For the divinity is said to have gone into heaven at the time of the Passion—not changing its location, but in a certain manner restraining its power, so that the impious might be able to complete the Passion.

**VERSE 11.**—The calf. When Christ is offered for the liberation of the Jewish people, he is called a calf because he observed the justification of the law. Hence he says: “I have not come to destroy the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5); he “was made of a woman, so that he might redeem those who were under the law” (Gal. 4). He is therefore rightly called a calf, as though subjected to the commandments of the law.

(ISICH.) The legislator reveals that Christ’s sacrifice is accomplished as flesh through the power of divinity, in the good pleasure of the Father, and as a propitiation for our sins, and that it is carried out for the provision of the Spirit.

**VERSE 12.**—From the coals of the altar, etc. With spiritual words, which John wrote at the supper after Judas had gone out, he explains how Christ, being in the Father and the Father in him, sends the Spirit; how the Father is the farmer, he himself the vine, the apostles the branches; and many other things that kindle devotion like fiery coals (John 18).

Taking in his hand. The Septuagint: “He shall fill his hands with incense,” a finely composed substance—that is, praying for refined spiritual things, not earthly ones.

Incense is prayer. Hence: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight.” For Christ prayed for his disciples.

**VERSE 13.**—So that when they have been placed, etc. Aaron, by virtue of his priesthood, signifies Christ and the other priests. Christ places spices upon the fire—that is, doctrine—which means prayer; and the vapor of the cloud, that is, the power of prayer, covers the oracle, that is, the flesh, from which we receive the propitiation of sins in Christ, who is also the testimony. Every priest who speaks about Christ likewise places, upon the fire of spiritual doctrine, the spices of prayer, whose power covers the oracle that is above the testimony and does not permit him to inquire into those things concerning Christ’s Passion that are beyond the power of the inquirer; thus he will not die through immoderate questions.

And he shall not die. His flesh did not see corruption, because it was covered by the power of prayer, like vapor from spices. Of this it is said: “You will not give your holy one to see corruption” (Ps. 15).

**VERSE 14.**—Against the propitiatory. Because Christ suffered for our propitiation and illumination; he is called the propitiatory and the rising one. Hence: “Behold, a man, the rising one,” etc. (Ps. 15). And elsewhere: “The rising one has visited us,” etc. (Zech. 6). Or, “against the propitiatory,” that is, in the sight of the Father, seven times, because he granted us the remission of sins and the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 15.**—And when they have slaughtered, etc. Since Christ was made from the common mass of humanity, he is rightly called a goat, because this animal is rough and hairy, and because the human race is subject to sin. Hence he appropriately says: “When he has slaughtered the goat for the sin of the people” (Hos. 1), that is, of the human race—which once was not a people but is now a people, from the time Christ assumed its firstfruits. To show, therefore, that Christ bore the firstfruits principally of the Jews, but also of the whole nature that is under sin, he took both the calf and the goat; and because there is one sacrifice and one effect, the same things are necessarily done with the goat and the calf. For you see that the goat is killed before God, that is, the Father, and that its blood is brought inside the veil, that is, to the same Father. The sanctuary is expiated, namely, the mass of the human race, which was holy from the beginning, and the tabernacle of the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 16.**—The tabernacle of testimony, etc. What he called the sanctuary above, here he calls the tabernacle of testimony. For the mass of the human race is called both the holy place and the tabernacle of testimony for the same reason. Thus the tabernacle of testimony is heaven and is rightly called the holy place. Our heavenly man is of it, concerning whom Paul says: “As we have borne the image of the earthly,” etc. (1 Cor. 15). He is rightly called holy here, because he is in the midst of uncleanness, since Christ is assailed by the passions of the flesh.

The sanctuary. The human race, through the assumption of flesh, so that he might plead on the cross in the sanctuary of his own flesh.

**VERSE 17.**—Until he goes out. That is, sending forth his spirit in human fashion and leaving his flesh in the tomb.

**VERSE 18.**—And having taken the blood. Through his Passion he sanctified the horns of the altar, that is, the four principal virtues.

**VERSE 19.**—He shall expiate. They are expiated by Christ’s sacrifice. Hence: “The heavenly things themselves are expiated by greater sacrifices” (Heb. 2), greater than these.

From the uncleannesses. As far as the heavenly powers are concerned, they do not need to be expiated, since they exist in perpetual sanctification. But because the smoke of our sins frequently rises—of which it is said, “Smoke rose in his anger” (Ps. 17), and concerning Nineveh, “Its wickedness has risen before me” (Jonah 1)—he rightly expiates the heavenly choirs from our uncleannesses, so that he may remove the offensive odor. Therefore he does not sprinkle them simply once, but seven times, because the heavenly things are cleansed by the forgiveness of our sins.

**VERSE 20.**—Afterward. (AMBR., Letter to Simplicianus.)

“As there are two in the field,” etc., up to “which produces tranquility of mind.”

**VERSE 21.**—And having placed both hands, etc. The laying on of hands administers in sacrifice either blessing, remission of sins, or the Holy Spirit. These cannot exist in the one upon whom the lot of the devil falls. There are also many circumstances that contradict that interpretation.

And having placed them. To show that the Word of God, impassible and immortal, assumed in the flesh for us a sufficient sacrifice, all sins are rightly placed upon him, because he bore our sins in his body. The Septuagint: “He shall place them upon the head of the living kid.” This signifies the crown of thorns impressed upon his head, for sins are signified by thorns.

Through a man, etc. Christ, who is all things: the priest of his own sacrifice, the sacrifice, the worship, and the altar. He was prepared according to the saying: “But I do not resist; I did not turn back. I gave my body to those who struck me,” etc. (Isa. 50). Christ, therefore, sacrificing himself through the living kid, himself sends the living goat into the wilderness through the prepared man—that is, through his own power—namely, his immortal and impassible divinity, into places inaccessible to us and deserted by every evil. Hence: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands, and that he had come forth from God and was going to God” (John 13).

ORIGEN, in his homilies on Leviticus, says that the goat sacrificed to the Lord signifies those who are destined for the Lord’s stronghold, such as that Lazarus who was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16). But the goat that is sent into the wilderness signifies the reprobate, or the Jewish people, who are cast away from the Lord’s presence on account of their sins, like the rich man clothed in purple who was buried in hell. The prepared man signifies Christ or his angels; hence each person receives what he deserves.

**VERSE 26.**—But the one who let it go, etc. (ORIG., Homily 9 on Leviticus.) “Has desire risen into your heart?” etc., up to “and here the same figure can be maintained in the washing of garments.”

**VERSE 29.**—In the seventh month, however. (ORIG., in the same place.) “In which the solemnity of reconciliation,” etc., up to “that is, rejected and repudiated.”

# CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—And he spoke, etc. The present law demonstrates that the Lord speaks not only to Moses but to everyone collectively. He wants all to know what is advantageous for all: namely, that the law is temporal and that, once its time has been completed, it is observed to no purpose. The completion of its time is made clear by the destruction of the place in which he commanded sacrifices to be offered, when he intimates that whoever sacrifices outside the camp, or outside the tabernacle of testimony, shall perish from among his people. Thus, once the tabernacle and its place have been destroyed, sacrifices will come to an end. But he did not confine holy actions and those that build up the human mind—such as honoring father and mother, loving one’s neighbors, and similar duties—to a place, because they are always beneficial and agree with the Gospel. Whoever, therefore, now performs the figures belonging to the destroyed place sheds blood and stains the common life, and sins publicly, like those who shed the blood of those whom they lead into error by their example.

**VERSE 3.**—Any man, etc. As though the figures of the law were temporal and belonged to a fixed place; once that place is destroyed, they cannot remain.

If he has killed a sheep. (AUG., Questions on Leviticus, question 56.) “He does not speak about these,” etc., up to “whatever he did in this matter could not be contrary to the law, because he is the giver of the law.”

**VERSE 7.**—And they shall no longer sacrifice their offerings to demons, etc. Although the Lord had said, “You shall not make for yourself an idol or any likeness of those things that are in heaven above, or on earth below, or beneath the earth” (Exod. 20), they made a cast calf and offered it a sacrifice, wishing to consume the sacrifice greedily. Therefore the Law, like their pedagogue, commanded them to sacrifice to God (Exod. 32), so that, being occupied with this, they might abstain from sacrificing to idols. Yet he established such sacrifices as signify future mysteries.

With whom they committed fornication. He calls idolatry fornication because God betrothed our souls to himself. Departure from him is therefore called fornication. He also terrifies those who fornicate in the flesh when he compares the sin of fornication with the worship of idols and the offering made to demons.

**VERSE 8.**—Any man of the house of Israel, etc. (AUG., in the same place.) “If the same commandment is repeated,” etc., up to “they boast in vain that they are Israelites or Jews.”

**VERSE 10.**—Among the sojourners. Among the Gentiles, who are not joined to the Jews but live among us. For we were among them, possessing their law, prophets, and promised inheritance, yet adhering not to them but to God. Therefore, according to the Septuagint, he says “every man, every man,” to show that both those who adhere to God in circumcision and those who do so in uncircumcision must keep this commandment.

If he eats blood, etc. We understand blood as homicide; hatred of a brother is homicide: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3). We must therefore abstain from all hatred of our brothers, because over such a soul—one that eats such blood, according to the saying, “They devour my people as though eating bread” (Ps. 13)—God sets his face against it—namely Christ, who is the image of the Father. For “whoever sees the Son sees the Father also” (John 14). He is the judge of whom it is said: “The face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth” (Ps. 33). He destroys the one who eats blood from his people, that is, from the common human race, because, as one without mercy and impious, he sends him with the evil spirits into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels (Matt. 25). To show how merciful and loving we ought to be toward one another, he showed that he poured out his own blood for our expiation, saying: “I have given it to you”—namely, the blood of Christ.

**VERSE 11.**—The life of the flesh. (AUG., Questions on Leviticus, question 57.) “There is something vital in the blood,” etc., up to “to whom he was acquiring such merit.”

**VERSE 13.**—Any person, whoever he may be. (ISICH.) God is greatly concerned for us, lest we harm another. Therefore he commands the one who strikes the cheek to offer the other, and the one who takes away the cloak to give up the tunic, and not to contend in judgment, lest through contention we wish also to harm him (Matt. 5), but rather correct him by suffering. For this reason the legislator recapitulates the commandment concerning blood, so as to remove the various frauds and schemes of harming others, saying: “Whether by hunting or by bird-catching,” etc.

By hunting. By fraud that concerns blood and life. Hence: “They lay in wait for the soul of the righteous and condemned innocent blood” (Ps. 43). And again: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Ps. 123). This means that, if he sees someone sinning who has been exposed to hunting and deceit through weakness or simplicity—

Or a sheep, etc. Namely, one who removes himself from earthly things, which it is permitted to eat. For the violent and greedy devour such people. Hence: “If you bite and devour one another, take care that you are not consumed by one another” (Gal. 5). Or because they were previously righteous, they are rightly counted among the clean animals.

The earth shall cover him, etc. The earth covers the sins of those who confess, as things that remain below and have been put to death through repentance. Their cry is prevented from ascending to heaven, unlike the cry of Sodom, whose inhabitants were unwilling to repent (Gen. 18).

**VERSE 15.**—The person who has eaten, etc. Above it was said: “Whoever touches a carcass taken by beasts,” that is, whoever shares in such things. Here, however, it says: “The person who has eaten,” namely, one who has made the whole sin his own and fulfilled his desire through it.

# CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 2.**—I am the Lord. As though he were saying: Know your creator; carefully keep his commandments.

**VERSE 3.**—According to the custom, etc. He reveals the intention of the whole law: that we abstain from evil and hold fast to good.

Nor according to their statutes, etc. For he commands them to abstain not only from fornication, greed, and pride, but also from divinations, auguries, and the superstitions of all peoples.

**VERSE 5.**—He shall live in them. I am the Lord. For true life is found in these for those who believe in Christ, because “whoever sees the Son and believes in him has eternal life” (John 6). He did not add this in the earlier judgments and commandments, for the law does not give life unless the Gospel follows.

**VERSE 6.**—No man shall approach his near relative, etc. He forbids us craftily to approach those who sin under the law on the pretext of kinship, so that, having finally learned their shameful deeds, we may expose them. Hence he adds: “I am the Lord.”

Every man. The Septuagint: “No man shall approach any of his near kin according to the flesh,” etc. Just as a human being is twofold, so there are twofold commandments, teaching the inner and outer person. The external law forbids intercourse with blood relatives, as did the Gentiles whose inheritance Israel was about to receive. Israel had become so dissolute and devoted to the pleasures of the flesh that one man took many wives; at least in this way they were to abstain from foreigners. The legislator therefore lists the generations in order, from whom they must abstain, lest generations be confused and inheritances perish. He calls such unions shameful, to show that they are detestable and horrifying. It should also be noted that, although at the beginning of this law he had said, “I am the Lord your God,” he repeats here, “I am the Lord,” signifying that he has been joined to us in the flesh and has become a participant in our kinship. To offend such kinship is therefore damnable.

I am the Lord. Not exposing human sins, but erasing and covering what has been erased or disclosed through confession.

The shame, etc. (AUG., Questions on Leviticus, question 58.) He forbids lying with one’s mother, etc., up to “for he sins in charity, which is the fullness of the law” (Rom. 13).

**VERSE 9.**—She was born outside. (ID., Questions, question 59.) “From the mother, if she was born of a former husband,” etc., up to “which he had previously stated obscurely.”

**VERSE 11.**—The daughter of your wife, etc. (AUG., in the same place.) He does not appear to forbid intercourse with the daughter of a stepmother by a former husband, since she is not a sister to the man who is forbidden the union, either by father or by mother. He added that she was from the same father.

**VERSE 14.**—The shame of your father’s brother, etc. (AUG., Questions, question 61.) It is asked whether this, etc., up to “for someone might think that he was permitted to marry such a woman without fearing adultery.”

And you shall not approach, etc. The Septuagint: “And you shall not enter upon his wife.” Accordingly, they say that this is the shame of his father’s brother, that is, the uncle’s private parts—namely, his wife.

**VERSE 16.**—The shame of your brother’s wife, etc. In the mother, desire is understood; in the daughter, action; in the granddaughter, death. For desire gives birth to sin, and sin to death (Jas. 1), or to another sin—as David, from desire, committed adultery and, on account of adultery, killed.

**VERSE 17.**—So that you may uncover her disgrace. Sin is, as it were, something familiar and kin to us. Therefore we ought to suffer with one another and bear one another’s burdens, so that we may fulfill the law of Christ, who bore our sins.

**VERSE 18.**—Your wife’s sister, etc. (AUG., Questions on Leviticus.) He does not forbid, etc., up to “lest he make her commit adultery.”

You shall not take her in rivalry, nor uncover, etc. The Septuagint: “You shall not take her for jealousy,” as though jealousy existed only between sisters, and not also between women who are not sisters. Or perhaps the meaning is that this should not be done with the intention that one sister be brought in as a rival to another. God has called us to peace; let us have peace with everyone (Rom. 12), especially with those near to us. In the Jewish way of life, too, it is not fitting to take up ecclesiastical observance, to celebrate the typological Passover together with the true Passover, or circumcision together with baptism. Hence Paul says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you” (Gal. 5). Once the Jewish way of life has been put to death, therefore, it ought to be joined to the Church, which is the sister of the law and has the same teachers and the same prophets. But the Jewish way of life is jealous because its riches have passed over to the Church. Hence Paul says: “They are jealous of you, not rightly, but in order to exclude you,” etc. (Gal. 4). The first wife is jealous because the second enters in. Hence Leah says: “Is it a small matter to you that you have taken my husband from me?” (Gen. 30).

**VERSE 19.**—To a woman, etc. (AUG., Questions on Leviticus, question 64.) Although he had sufficiently forbidden this above, etc., up to “but it is forbidden as harmful to conceiving offspring.”

**VERSE 20.**—With another man’s wife, etc. (ISICH.) Adultery is again forbidden here, although it is also forbidden in the Decalogue. From this it is apparent that the prohibition was expressed in such a way that even after their husbands’ deaths they were not to marry the wives whose shame he forbids to be uncovered.

**VERSE 21.**—From your offspring, etc. (ID.) These matters are appropriately joined together, etc., up to “nor are we mixed with the error of the Gentiles.”

Nor shall you pollute, etc. Not only by indulging in lust or sacrificing to idols, but also by introducing the philosophy of the Gentiles into the Church. For what agreement is there between the temple of God and idols?

**VERSE 23.**—A woman shall not, etc. The law was established not only for men but also for women (2 Cor. 9). Hence: “Who will find a strong woman?” (Prov. 13). Just as the male signifies a strong and steadfast soul in virtues, so the woman signifies one who guards her dignity. For she was made as a help for the man (Gen. 2); and such a woman ought not to be polluted by intercourse with animals.

**VERSE 24.**—Nor shall you pollute yourselves by all these things, etc. (ISICH.) How great the pollution in the foregoing matters is, the punishment of the polluted shows. Nor should it be passed over carelessly that he gathers into one the things joined together, to show that whoever is polluted in one matter offends in all (Jas. 2).

All the nations have been contaminated, etc. Demons are called all the nations because of their multitude. Although they rejoice in every sin, they rejoice especially in fornication and idolatry, because in these both body and soul are polluted, as is the whole person, who is called “earth.” But God has visited the earth, that is, the human race.

**VERSE 29.**—Every person, etc. Those who commit such acts after evangelical preaching have no other remedy for their evil; they will belong not to the lot of human beings but to that of demons.

**VERSE 30.**—Keep my commandments. As though he were saying: These commandments are mine, not man’s. You were made in his image, and you must not pollute it, because you are the temple of God and the Spirit of God dwells in you (1 Cor. 3).

# CHAPTER XIX

**VERSES 1–2.**—The Lord spoke … You shall be holy. (ORIG., Homily 12 on Leviticus.) What this word “holy” signifies, etc., up to “so that you may conduct yourselves in the world.”

**VERSE 3.**—Each person. He builds upon the foundation, as though saying: Be holy, so that the Holy One may dwell in you; and show the goodness of your nature by honoring father and mother.

Keep my Sabbaths. (ISICH.) Wishing to recapitulate the commandments of the law—“You shall not kill,” “You shall not steal,” and so forth—he says: “Keep my Sabbaths.” The true Sabbath is to cease from every evil. Hence Moses says: “You shall do no servile work on it” (Exod. 31).

Keep my Sabbaths. Wishing to teach us about intelligible rest and about the consummation of the world, when it is impossible to prepare food or work or occupy oneself with anything bodily, he says through Moses: “Today is a Sabbath to the Lord; you will not find it in the field” (Exod. 16), etc. Note that he does not say “the Sabbath” but “Sabbaths,” because intelligible rest is not free and detached from one bodily matter alone but from all bodily matters. Therefore, in this passage, the name “Sabbaths” is first placed in divine Scripture, so that you may know that the Sabbath is complete and perfect rest.

**VERSE 5.**—If you offer, etc. He repeats nearly every chapter of the law in order to impress its memory upon his hearers, but especially those things that are necessary, such as this commandment, which he had previously set forth when discussing sacrifices. He accepted a sacrifice of salvation, in which it is necessary to perform those things that pertain to salvation; but for it to be acceptable, piety and chastity must be sacrificed. According to the Apostle, this is good and acceptable before God our Savior, who wishes all people to be saved (1 Tim. 2). To eat on the day of sacrifice and on the following day means to perform in the present life whatever pertains to salvation. “Today” and “tomorrow” are taken to mean the present age; hence James says: “You who say, ‘Today or tomorrow we shall go into such and such a city,’” etc. (Jas. 4). The third day, because on it the Lord rose from the dead, bears the figure of the future age and the resurrection, in which it will not be permitted to work but to receive the reward of works. Whoever therefore lives here as though he were going to work there, as though he were going to eat the sacrifice on the third day, is forbidden by the legislator to do this, because he leaves his virtue incomplete, as though he could perfect it there.

**VERSE 9.**—When you reap, etc. This chapter commands us to have love for one another and to be lovers of and merciful toward the poor. We ought to give to those in need, not violently demand what is owed, and grant the remains of our goods, imitating God, the giver of all things. Therefore he wishes those who reap or gather grapes to leave something for the poor and the proselyte, lest they appear ungrateful to the giver of all things, who gave riches to some and wished others to live from the remnants of others, thereby testing the stewardship of the rich and the patience of the poor. For he does not reject the poor and proselytes, since he has provided them with sustenance even in this way. Hence he adds: “I am the Lord your God”—namely, the one who makes the rich, who becomes poor for your sake, who on account of the misery of the needy and the groaning of the poor will sometimes rise up.

When you reap, etc. He plainly shows that the teachers of the Jews do not grasp the interpretation of the whole law, but leave certain things for the poor and the proselyte—that is, for the Gentiles, to whom it is said: “Blessed are the poor,” etc. (Matt. 5). They are also proselytes because they insert themselves into the kinship of Abraham. Therefore, let the teachers of the Jews reap what is said, “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery”; but let those things that have a spiritual interpretation—such as purifications, sacrifices, and similar matters—be assigned to the teachers of the Church, along with what falls away during their reaping, that is, what they themselves do not understand.

**VERSE 10.**—Nor in the vineyard. (ISICH.) “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts,” etc., up to “so that the divine utterance may be confirmed by experience.”

**VERSE 11.**—You shall not commit theft, etc. (AUG., Questions on Leviticus, question 86.) “This is placed in the Decalogue,” etc., up to “and those who follow such an error detest it.”

You shall not lie. He shows the kinship of sins. We consider many things small that are very serious, such as lying and perjury. These are joined to theft, and rightly so, because they cooperate with theft.

**VERSE 12.**—You shall not swear falsely, etc. The Septuagint: “You shall not lift up,” etc., up to “such oaths ought not to be made, or, if they are made, ought not to be kept.”

Nor shall you pollute, etc. By cursing, because you cannot transgress an oath. God, by whom you swear, desires good to such an extent that, even if he threatens evil, he does not inflict it when he sees those who repent, so that he may show mercy.

**VERSE 13.**—You shall not act deceitfully. (AUG., in the same place.) Everything that is forbidden as an offense against one’s neighbor must be referred to this one statement: “You shall not harm your neighbor.” For what follows—“You shall not steal”—unless it is referred to the prohibition against harming by stealing, it could happen that someone harms another by not stealing, as when a sword must be taken away from a madman.

**VERSE 13.**—Nor shall you oppress by force, etc. He gradually instructs his hearer and joins things that appear small to great things, so that those who are terrified by the defined punishment of grave evils may abstain from lesser ones. For things joined in the commandment are also joined in the punishment. Whoever offends in one matter is guilty of all (Jas. 2). Therefore he joins force to deceit. It makes no difference how someone loses his possessions—whether through fraud, power, or any other means.

The wage shall not remain, etc. The wage by which he perhaps lives with his wife, children, and parents. If it is delayed, his livelihood fails; and even if he receives it on the following day, he has suffered force and deceit because in the meantime he had nothing by which to live.

The work of the hired laborer, etc. The preacher’s wage comes from the word of preaching. It must not remain with us, that is, be idle, until morning—until the future age, which succeeds this night and in which there is unquenchable light. For the teacher’s wage grows from the disciple’s progress.

**VERSE 14.**—You shall not curse the deaf. To curse the deaf is to disparage someone who is absent and does not hear. To place a stumbling-block before the blind is to perform an act that is indeed discerning, but to provide an occasion of scandal for one who lacks the light of discernment.

**VERSE 15.**—You shall not act, etc. (ISICH.) The sum and perfection of justice, etc., up to “and mocking the deaf and the blind belongs to the rich and powerful.”

**VERSE 16.**—You shall not be a slanderer. (ISICH.) The Septuagint: “You shall not walk about in the house,” etc., up to “who is closely joined to such a great crime.”

You shall not stand against. As though he were saying: You shall not join yourself to those who lie in wait for their neighbors, as many do when, associating with others, they accomplish what they cannot do alone.

**VERSE 18.**—You shall not seek revenge. That is, do not let yourself be carried away by the desire for vengeance while reproving someone, so that you wish to rejoice or take comfort in another’s evil; rather, seek his welfare, whom you reprove. Hence, according to the Septuagint, the following is added: “You shall not be angry with the children of your people,” etc. Anger has rightly been defined as the desire for vengeance.

**VERSE 19.**—Your animals, etc. These things appear ridiculous according to the letter, and they were not observed by prophets and spiritual men. Hence David says: “Put my son Solomon upon my mule” (Eccli. 19). According to the letter, however, one ought to abhor what was born from such a mixture. Hence: “The strong woman will find wool and linen, and she has worked with her hands at what is useful” (Prov. 31).

**VERSE 20.**—If a man has slept, etc. (ISICH.) Since he had forbidden animals to be mixed with animals of another kind—that is, those who are under Christ’s yoke to take up the yoke of the law—he appropriately added this, showing that, even before Christ’s coming, whoever outwardly mixed with the Jews needed the sacrifice of the true ram.

It is worth noting how great the difference is between freedom and servitude. For a free betrothed woman, death is the penalty for adultery; but in the case of a slave girl who is betrothed—or, according to the Septuagint, “kept for a man,” that is, betrothed—a sacrifice is ordered to be offered, not death inflicted. Nevertheless, these things are to be understood spiritually.

**Betrothed.** The Septuagint has “kept for a man,” that is, the Synagogue kept for the Law, which could not be betrothed to Christ before the letter of the Law had died. Hence: “You have died to the Law through the body of Christ, so that you may belong to another” (Rom. 7). The Synagogue is a slave girl, according to the statement: “Abraham had two sons, one by a slave girl and one by a free woman” (Gal. 4).

**Both shall be scourged.** The Septuagint has: “There shall be visitation for them,” that is, they shall be freed from slavery to the Law, in accordance with what is said to the Israelites about their deliverance from Egypt: “Visiting, I have visited you.”

**And they shall not die.** Although they acted according to the letter and not according to the spirit, because they did not understand the legislator’s intention, they nevertheless more easily obtained pardon.

**VERSE 23. — When you have entered, etc.** He remains with the same subject, showing that the Jews did not possess good fruit before Christ’s coming, when he says that the fruit was not to be eaten for three years, nor was it clean, but that it was to be made clean in the fourth year; yet he does not say what this cleansing was. Therefore, what is said must be understood spiritually.

**When you have entered the land.** He calls the divine Scripture “the land,” which the Jews first received. Hence they were commanded to plant fruit-bearing trees. The planting of trees is meditation on the Law and preaching, according to what is said: “I planted, Apollo watered,” etc. (1 Cor. 3). The commandments were indeed good, like fruit-bearing trees, but they did not do what they ought to have done, following only the letter. The fruit, therefore—that is, the working of the Law—was unclean for three years: from Abraham to David, from David to the Babylonian captivity, and from then until Christ, as Matthew divided the periods (Matt. 1). In the fourth year he commends the fruit of the Law as holy and praiseworthy, but not yet edible for the Jews. For the fruit of the Law in the fourth year—that is, at Christ’s coming—was holy and praiseworthy; he made it the Holy of Holies, whose works were praiseworthy and glorious. Hence, in the case of the paralytic carrying his pallet, they glorified God (Matt. 8), who had given such authority to human beings; but the Jew was not yet eating it, because he had not been converted. In the fifth year, however—that is, when the apostles were preaching—all who believed ate its fruit.

**And when you plant, etc.** (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 8, chapter 35.) “Fruit-bearing trees,” etc., up to “to rejoice in the night of the present life.”

**VERSE 26. — You shall not eat, etc.** He uproots the entire leaven of Jews and Gentiles. Hence at one point he forbids slavery to the Law, and at another the error of the Gentiles.

(Augustine.) Not eating upon the mountains means not feeding upon proud thoughts, concerning which Isaiah says: “Every mountain and hill shall be humbled” (Isa. 40). Not practicing divination by birds means not attending to things that snatch away the seed of devotion. Cutting the hair round in a circle means consecrating one’s thoughts to demons. Shaving the beard means corrupting the perfection of virtue by acting hypocritically. Not making cuts in the flesh means not admitting pleasures that harm the soul and corrupt the body. The marks are perverse doctrine, which is impressed upon the soul and is difficult to erase.

**You shall not practice divination, etc.** He signifies the whole by a part, condemning all superstitions of this kind. For whoever is concerned to observe such things seems to defame God, as though he had granted more knowledge to birds than to human beings.

**VERSE 27. — Nor shall you cut the hair round in a circle, etc.** As barbarians do. Everyone ought to be content with natural adornments, lest he seem to accuse the Creator of being unable to complete his work; nor should he nourish and foster locks in honor of demons, as pagans make a practice of offering boys’ heads to demons. This is what he especially seems to prohibit here.

**VERSE 28. — The marks.** The legislator also cares for our bodily appearance, so that we do not misuse the flesh even in things that disfigure the body.

**VERSE 29. — Do not prostitute your daughter.** Either the daughter in the flesh or the soul. Hence Psalm 21: “Deliver my soul from the sword, O God, and my only one from the hand of the dog.” These, by withdrawing from God, prostitute themselves with demons.

**VERSE 30. — Keep my Sabbaths.** From one Sabbath, every legitimate rest is called a Sabbath. Thus, by means of one general abstinence, the legislator aims to cover each particular case, commanding us to abstain from every evil. Hence he adds: “And reverence my sanctuary.” For just as those who approach worthily sanctify it, so those who presume to approach wickedly and uncleanly pollute it, insofar as they are able, like Nadab and Abihu. Hence the Apostle says: “Among you many are weak and sickly,” etc. (1 Cor. 11). Then he adds: “I am the Lord”—holy, that is, and also dwelling among the holy and avenging injuries done to the holy.

**VERSE 31. — To magicians.** The Septuagint has “ventriloquists,” that is, pythonic spirits or false prophets who bring forth from the belly of their heart certain fables and foul doctrines.

**Nor shall you consult diviners, etc.** The Septuagint has “sorcerers,” who invoke the names of demons and sometimes heal the body in order to destroy the soul.

**VERSE 32. — In the presence of a gray head, etc.** “In the aged is wisdom, and in length of days understanding” (Job 12). Hence Paul says: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in word and doctrine” (1 Tim. 5).

**VERSE 33. — If an immigrant dwells with you, etc.** The land given to us by God is the cultivation of virtues and sound doctrine. If someone therefore wishes to convert to our faith and to be enrolled as a citizen of our land, let us not afflict him or impose a heavy yoke upon him, as the Pharisees did, of whom it is said: “They bind heavy and unbearable burdens, but they themselves are unwilling to move them with their finger” (Matt. 23). Let him be to us like a native, one who has been nourished in the faith and has grown in devotion. Hence Peter says to those who wished to circumcise believers from the Gentiles: “Why do you test God by placing a yoke upon the necks of the disciples?” (Acts 15).

**VERSE 35. — You shall not act, etc.** In the preceding passages he commands justice to be maintained in judgment; here he commands it in weights and measures, and forbids us to misuse the limits of justice for injustice. These are the boundaries for sellers and buyers, just as laws are for judges, so that every injustice against one’s neighbor may be avoided. What fields, possessions, and treasures of money are to the rich, measures of wine and grain and similar things are to the poor.

[Col. 0353C] (Isichius.) **You shall not act, etc.** In the judgment of the mind we must not act unjustly or corrupt the measures of natural justice, judging our own sins one way and our neighbor’s another. “With the judgment with which we judge, we shall be judged, and with the measure with which we measure, it shall be measured to us” (Matt. 7).

**VERSE 36. — Just scales, etc.** (The same.) Let us also have divine scales and divine measures, that is, let us observe the laws of divine Scripture holily and justly, introducing nothing of our own and taking away nothing of what belongs to it, lest this be said to us: “Why do you transgress the commandment of God for the sake of your tradition?” (Matt. 15).

## CHAPTER 20

**VERSE 1. — The Lord spoke, etc.** The Law frequently repeats the same things in order to impress them upon the memory of the reader; nevertheless, it inserts certain new matters so that it may not seem superfluous. But by seeking out the new, let what has already been said be investigated more diligently. Hence above, when prohibiting certain things, it kept silent about the penalty, so that when we ask what sort of penalty it is, we may investigate it carefully in what follows. For when above he prohibited sacrifices to Moloch, he repeats the same matter by adding the penalty: the people of the land shall stone him, not merely the rulers. Nor, content with this, does he add: “I will set my face against him,” etc.

**VERSE 4. — But if, being negligent, etc.** He summons others against him and terrifies them if they neglect the penalty so carefully prescribed, with God himself growing angry and pronouncing judgment.

[Col. 0354A] **And he is unwilling, etc.** (Isichius.) It is evil to permit even those who are outside to fornicate from God and cling to the devil; but it is much worse to permit this from the midst of the people. For this is to hand over the entire flock to the wolf. Those who consent—those who are able to accuse, rebuke, or admonish, but do not do so—will not escape judgment. God sets his face against the one of whom it is said: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil,” etc. (Ps. 38).

**VERSE 6. — The person who turns to magicians, etc.** It is a great sin to turn to magicians and diviners; for this is to depart from God. There are, however, intelligible magicians, who prophesy falsely in the Lord’s name; and there are diviners who are deceivers and flatterers, who corrupt the hearing of many with poisonous words and turn them away from the truth.

**VERSE 9. — Whoever curses his father, etc.** (Origen, Homily 11 on Leviticus.) Concerning these matters he gave commandments above, etc., up to “lest he punish the contemptuous servant.”

(The same.) The name of father or mother, etc., up to “turn them, through their depraved interpretations, toward some earthly city?”

**His blood is upon him, etc.** Because he himself is the cause of his death. If the one who curses his earthly father is punished in this way, how will the one who blasphemes Christ and does not obey him when he says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” etc. (John 3), be punished? He will certainly die by death, alienated from the kingdom of heaven and guilty; for no grave, difficult, or burdensome command has been given to him.

[Col. 0354C] **VERSE 10. — If someone commits adultery, etc.** (Augustine, *Questions on Leviticus*, question 73.) Here he intended something to differ, etc., up to “as a human being does to a human being.”

**If someone commits adultery, etc.** (Isichius.) Adultery is a bodily evil, etc., up to “the one to whom he entrusted this care.”

**VERSE 11. — Whoever lies with, etc.** These matters were stated and explained above, where it was said: “You shall not uncover the nakedness of your father,” etc. But here he openly touches upon the person who does the same thing as his neighbor and, not ashamed of sharing in the sin, exposes him; against such a person the legislator enacted the penalty of death. He joined the stepmother to the husband because what is committed against the father by the son is committed against the son by the father; in both cases the impiety is similar.

(Origen, cited above.) It was said above, etc., up to “not only according to its quality but also according to its quantity.”

**VERSE 13. — Whoever lies with a male, etc.** This sin is an injury against nature; hence it was decreed that it should also be punished by death. Spiritually, however, let us beware of making one who is strong in spirit and masculine—for in divine Scripture a man is called one perfect in virtues—effeminate through corrupt words or actions, lest we be dissolved and die together with him.

**VERSE 14. — Whoever [takes someone] in addition to a wife, etc.** He decrees a savage penalty for this crime. For those born of the mother and those whom the daughter has borne have one father, and it is uncertain whether they are brothers or uncles. Such an uncertain union must therefore be avoided. But because desire is the mother of every sin, if we have any desire, let us not join an action to it. Whoever does this is burned by fire, both his desire and his action. “If we put to death the deeds of the flesh by the Spirit, we shall live” (Rom. 8).

**VERSE 15. — Whoever lies with an animal, etc.** Excessive severity is exercised against those who are so wicked and devoted to lust that they desire unheard-of crimes; hence he imposed the penalty of death upon men or women who unite with quadrupeds. This law will not be superfluous for believers if we understand quadrupeds as perverse desires bent toward the earth. They do not have hands like human beings, because they lack every human action; hence they have no kinship with us. A man or woman who has clung or united to them, not through weakness of nature but by deliberate choice, is guilty of death. They too are said to die with those who are put to death; for they do not subsist by themselves, nor is there any substance of sin, but sin operates in sinners.

(Augustine.) **Whoever lies with an animal, etc.** The question is how the animal can be guilty, since it is neither rational nor capable of the Law. Is this perhaps like the transfer of metaphorical words from one animal to another, as when one speaks of a “wicked wind” or an “angry sea,” and so here the expression is transferred from the rational to the irrational? For animals are ordered to be killed because, having been polluted by such a crime, they revive the disgraceful memory of the deed.

**VERSE 17. — Whoever takes his sister, etc.** (Isichius.) This seemed tolerable because Abraham says of Sarah: “She is my sister by my father, but not by my mother.” Yet when Moses lists those born from Terah, Abraham’s father, he nowhere mentions Sarah. If Abraham married his sister, he did so before he knew God. The Law therefore rightly prohibited such a union.

**Whoever takes her, etc.** Tropologically, the one who sees and accepts the nakedness of a sister by the same father but not by the same mother is the person who admires and imitates a shameful action of a father or mother—that is, an action in which they sinned. He not only scrutinizes what he ought not to scrutinize but joins himself to the perversity of his parents, which is called his sister, as though it had been born from the same parents. Since children make their parents’ sins public by doing similar things, punishment is rightly inflicted in the presence of the people; or, according to the Septuagint, “in the presence of the children of his people,” that is, of those who are considering imitating such things, so that the affliction of one may be the correction of many.

**He has seen her nakedness, etc.** (Augustine, question 75.) That is, he has known her by lying with her, as in the statement: “Adam knew his wife” (Gen. 4), that is, he was joined to her. What he says, “They shall bear their iniquity,” means that the sin itself was the punishment.

**VERSE 20. — Whoever lies with, etc.** The legislator intends to encourage continence, so that we do not continually mingle with women like animals, but gradually approach the practice of restraint as though compelled to do so. It is surprising, however, that he now commands such people to be destroyed from among their people, although above he imposed upon them a law of purification.

Let us therefore contemplate the menstruating wisdom of the Gentiles, removed from God, disputing about the flight of birds, the courses of the stars, and the measurements of heaven. To lie with this wisdom—that is, to take pleasure in it—or to uncover and openly proclaim its shame, and to listen to it as it explains the source of every error, is impious. Therefore such a woman shall be killed from the midst of her people, so that he may not be called a human being who, through ignorance of the image of God and of himself, has alienated the Creator from himself. She too shall be killed, so that it may not be called wisdom, because “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3).

**Nakedness, etc.** He forbids the sons of parents’ sisters to unite, so that generations may not be confused and reverence may be shown to parents. Spiritually, however, we ought both to cover our parents’ sins and to cover the sins of those who are associated with them, as with brothers and sisters; when these are exposed, the parents cannot remain hidden. Hence he adds: “He shall uncover the shame of his flesh.” The Septuagint has: “He shall die childless,” that is, without virtues, which is the worst kind of barrenness.

**Whoever lies with, etc.** (Isichius.) He shows that the cause concerns children, etc., up to “it is similar to the preceding matters.”

(Augustine, question 76 on Leviticus.) **Whoever lies with his father’s wife, etc. Whoever lies with his near relative, etc.,** up to “that is, they shall succeed their parents by no right.”

**VERSE 22. — Keep the laws, etc.** It is not enough to keep part of the Law; we must observe all the commandments and judgments.

**VERSE 23. — Do not walk, etc.** These things must be observed not only by the Jews but by all nations, if they wish to serve God.

**VERSE 24. — Milk.** The delights of blessedness, than which nothing is more pleasant or sweeter, and which will exist without any labor or pain, like honey and milk, which are prepared without our labor.

**VERSE 26. — I am the Lord.** Do not think and say: “What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed?” For the Gentiles seek all these things (Matt. 6). Those who pursue a more sublime manner of life and a higher reward must be separated from the other nations.

**Separate, etc.** By animals or cattle he calls the common people; by birds, he calls contemplatives. Every common person is judged by many to be clean because of his simplicity. The contemplative is similar, but it is not so. The common person ought to be prudent in good and simple in evil; only such a person is clean. The contemplative too ought to have a clean conscience and sincere faith. Those who do not have these qualities turn to empty talk, understanding neither what they say nor what they confidently affirm (1 Tim. 1). The clean must therefore be carefully separated from the unclean, so that we may follow the clean and flee the unclean.

It should also be noted how distinctly the legislator here distinguishes quadrupeds and birds, but not the reptiles of the earth. For everything that moves upon the earth is unclean; they savor earthly things, and “their god is their belly” (Phil. 3).

**And which, etc.** (Augustine, question 76 on Leviticus.) He seems to say that these things are not unclean by nature but because of some sacramental sign, since he says that he showed them to be unclean, as though they would not have been unclean to them unless they had been shown to be so.

[Col. 0357A] **By stones.** Because they lead the simple people astray through empty errors; hence they nourish their belly and wish to please their hearers. There are many such people in the Church today, of whom Paul says: “For such people do not serve Christ but their own belly, and by smooth words and blessings they deceive the hearts of the innocent” (Rom. 16).

## CHAPTER 21

**VERSE 1. — The Lord also said to Moses … He shall not be defiled, etc.** (Isichius.) That is, he must omit nothing among the things that it is appropriate to teach the priest, etc., up to “for he will not be able to be ignorant of the sin of those living with him.”

**VERSE 2. — Except only among his relatives.** (Jerome, Letter to Fabiola, vol. 1.) “Over every soul that has died,” etc., up to “but some indulgence is granted in lesser matters.”

**VERSE 5. — They shall not shave their heads.** (The same, in the same work.) “But the high priest,” etc., up to “to whom Christ granted that they should be light.”

**They shall not shave their heads, etc.** (Isichius.) The Law forbids priests to grieve excessively over the dead, etc., up to “so that he may be able to exhort, rebuke, and reprove.”

**They shall not profane the name, etc.** (The same.) “Which is great among the nations.” But you, says Malachi, have profaned it by saying: “The table of the Lord is despised” (Mal. 1). For in the sin of the sacrifice the priests profane the name of God.

**VERSE 7. — A prostitute, etc.** Any priest, for later he will say of the high priest that he must marry only a virgin.

**Or one who has been divorced, etc.** Because she is found blameworthy, the priest ought not to take her as his wife, nor to proclaim her observance of the letter of the Law.

**VERSE 8. — Let them therefore be holy, etc.** If priests preserve the sanctification already given to them by God, they sanctify God himself. Although he is holy by nature, he wished to be sanctified by those who share in his glory.

**VERSE 9. — The daughter of a priest, etc.** It is a serious matter for anyone’s daughter to commit fornication, but especially for the daughter of a priest, who ought to have children subject to him in complete chastity.

**The daughter of a priest.** The Synagogue is called not only God’s wife but also God’s daughter; but by corrupting both relationships, she became alienated. Hence: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard,” etc. (Isa. 1). And elsewhere: “Their mother committed fornication” (Hos. 2). The traces of the fire show that she was burned up.

**VERSE 10. — The high priest, etc.** Christ is our great Lord, and great is his power; for our sake he became both priest and victim.

**They have been consecrated.** The other priests were consecrated or perfected in the blood of a calf and a ram, namely, their hands; but he was consecrated by his own blood, with his hands crucified.

**He shall not tear his garments, etc.** (Isichius.) Since the Word became flesh, etc., up to “these are truly holy garments.”

**VERSE 11. — To any dead person, etc.** (Isichius.) The Septuagint has: “A dead soul.” “The soul that sins shall itself die” (Ezek. 18; Isa. 53). The Gentiles especially perished by this death, since they had neither the Law nor instruction; but Christ bore the sins of all and nevertheless remained undefiled.

(Augustine, question 81 on Leviticus.) **To any dead person, etc.** The Septuagint has: “He shall not enter over any dead soul.” How does he speak of a dead soul, etc., up to “which he did not prohibit in the second case.”

**VERSE 12. — He shall not go out from the holy places.** (The same, question 82.) While their funerals are being celebrated, he is forbidden to leave the holy places, etc., up to “when incense was not imposed for certain days.”

**For his father.** (Origen, Homily 14 on Leviticus.) Every human being is defiled in his father and mother, etc., up to “or those who stain the freedom of their heavenly mother with the unworthy slavery of sin.”

(Augustine, question 85 on Leviticus.) It may be asked, etc., up to “as Scripture testifies concerning Aaron himself.”

**I am the Lord.** (Augustine, question 84.) It was also said concerning Moses, etc., up to “nor was visible sanctification judged superfluous, since invisible sanctification had preceded it.”

**VERSE 13. — He shall take a virgin as his wife.** (Jerome, Letter to Fabiola.) A widow is a woman whose husband, etc., up to “hence: ‘I betrothed you to one husband, as a pure virgin,’” etc.

I do not want the disciple and wife of the high priest to possess anything of the old person. If we have risen with Christ, let us seek the things that are above, forgetting what has passed and longing eagerly for what is to come. Unfortunate Simon: after baptism he thought about his former marriage and had not attained virginal purity; he was unworthy of fellowship with Peter.

**VERSE 14. — But he shall not take a widow or a divorced woman, etc.** (Origen, Homily 12 on Leviticus.) Whoever sins is rejected. Even if a bishop remains silent, whether through ignorance or negligence, such grace does not help; Christ does not take as his wife a rejected soul, nor one that is polluted—that is, one that has desired and chosen such great sin—for the high priest requires an altogether pure soul to join to himself and make one spirit with it.
