“From the sons, not from the daughters.” For it is not without reason that elsewhere he names daughters together with sons, while elsewhere he does not mention daughters. These matters, however, are to be referred specifically not to sex but to the discernment of souls.

(ID.) You will scarcely find saints to whom God gives outstanding testimony for having begotten daughters. Abraham and Isaac did not beget daughters. Jacob alone begot one daughter, and she herself became a reproach to her brothers and parents and stirred her brothers to furious vengeance.

**VERSE 9.**—“And this shall belong to you from the holy things that are sanctified, from the sacrifices,” etc. (ID.) The Holy Spirit is so holy, etc., up to the point that, in the third place, from this fruit I ought also to love my enemies.

(ID., *Homily 11*.) The Law commands the firstfruits of all crops to be offered to the priests, [Col. 0407C] etc., up to the point that you will find them marked under the title of the Law by Moses.

(ID.) But where it says: “You shall not kill,” “You shall not commit adultery,” and similar commands, it did not preface them with the title of the Law. For these are commandments, and therefore among the disciples of the Gospel they are not emptied but fulfilled. It is not the commandment, but the Law, that is said to have the shadow of future goods.

(ID.) It should be noted, however, that the Law is spoken of in two ways. In general, all these things—commandments, ordinances, precepts, testimonies, and judgments—are called law. In a particular sense, some portion of what is written in the Law is called law, as in the passages mentioned above. Law is understood generally when it is said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew V). And elsewhere: “Love is the fullness of the Law” [Col. 0407D] (Romans XIII). For he called everything written in the Law “law.”

(ID.) Elsewhere also: “Pursue,” he says, “what is just, and only what is just” (Deuteronomy XVI). And what need is there to seek an allegory even in these matters, when the letter itself edifies?

(ID.) I also ask whether there are some things, etc., up to the point that the Apostle nevertheless added: “Now these things are allegorical” (Galatians IV).

“Every offering,” etc. (ID.) It is the task of a wise and learned scribe concerning the kingdom of God to know how to bring forth new and old things from these treasures, and how either wholly to cast away the killing letter and seek the life-giving Spirit (Matthew XIII; I Corinthians III), or to affirm the useful and necessary teaching of the letter, or, while retaining the historical sense, to introduce the mystical sense as in the present passage.

(ID.) It is useful for the priests of the Gospel to offer firstfruits, etc., up to the point where it is said to the disciples: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew V).

(ID.) Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, not from the curse of the commandment, testimony, or judgments, lest we should be subject to circumcision of the flesh, observance of Sabbaths, and similar things contained in the Law but not in the commandments (Galatians III). Therefore our righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees (Matthew V). They do not dare taste the fruits of the earth before offering firstfruits to the priests and separating tithes for the Levites; but I, doing none of these things, use the fruits of the earth in such a way [Col. 0408B] that neither priest, Levite, nor altar of God perceives it.

(ID.) Peter and Paul also, etc., up to the point that he chooses and offers the firstfruits of the individual Churches.

(ID.) Every teacher, because he teaches, preaches, and instructs his hearers, seems to cultivate the field of his Church—that is, the hearts of believers. He also has the fruit of his cultivation, and among that fruit someone chosen and outstanding whom he may offer as firstfruits, another as firstborn, and another as tithes.

(ID.) Perhaps someone has firstborn and inferior members whom he can offer neither as firstfruits nor as firstborn, but as tithes.

**VERSE 11.**—“By perpetual right.” How can what is visible be eternal? For things that are seen are temporal (I Corinthians V); the firstfruits offered to Aaron are visible. Circumcision, unleavened bread, and the visible Passover likewise necessarily are not eternal but temporal. Therefore invisible circumcision, which is hidden, is eternal, as are the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (Romans II). So too these things are called eternal ordinances for the one who is a Jew not outwardly but inwardly, who keeps the Law in spirit and not in letter, according to the inner person (II Corinthians IV).

**VERSE 12.**—“All the fat,” etc. (ORIGEN.) We have shown the command concerning the firstfruits of crops, etc., up to the point that through an angel he appears to have been offered to God as a kind of firstfruit.

Christ is the firstfruit of firstfruits. Cornelius is the firstfruit of the Gentiles. Others are firstfruits of Churches: some, for example, of Asia, others of Achaia.

[Col. 0408D]

(ORIGEN.) Each of the angels will be present, etc., up to the point that it is the portion not of angels or of a ruler, but of God.

(ID.) Therefore the angels offer firstfruits from us, etc., up to the point that they seek the things above, not the things on earth.

(ID.) The angels offer firstfruits, etc., up to the point that one is appointed prince over many, while another is placed under a principality.

(ID.) The fields of the angels are our hearts; each of them offers the firstfruits to the Lord from the field he cultivates.

(ID.) Just as Christ is King of kings, etc., up to the point that this grace would suffice for us.

**VERSE 13.**—“All the produce.” (AUGUSTINE, *Question 32 on [Col. 0409A] Numbers*.) All the firstborn, etc., up to the point that they were taken first.

**VERSE 15.**—“Whatever is first.” (ORIGEN.) Perhaps those are called firstborn who have not been defiled with women, or perhaps the martyrs. Virgins may also be called the firstfruits of the Church (Revelation XIV); the tithes may be those who live in continence after marriage.

“Every one.” (RABANUS.) In both Testaments, offerings and tithes are given to the ministers of the altar for their necessities, lest they dare long for earthly possessions or seek profit from their ministry. Hence: “Freely you have received; freely give. Do not possess gold or silver or money” (Matthew X).

Mystically, tithes signify observance of the Law, or the sincerity of the integrity of faith, or the perfection [Col. 0409B] of good works—qualities that those who present themselves for divine ministry ought especially to possess. In the number ten, knowledge of the creature and of the Creator is comprehended, because the number seven refers to human nature, with three parts signifying the power of the soul. Hence: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength” (Deuteronomy VI). The body, however, consists of four elements. If you add seven to the number three, which expresses faith and confession of the Trinity, you complete ten.

**VERSE 19.**—“A covenant of salt.” (RABANUS.) He calls the covenant of salt the totality of offerings that belongs to the ministry or right of the priests. Hence in Leviticus: “Whatever you offer as a sacrifice, you shall season with salt,” etc. [Col. 0409C] (Leviticus II).

Mystically, it is shown that wisdom belongs to priests and preachers of divine Law—not worldly wisdom but apostolic wisdom, of which Paul says: “We speak wisdom among the mature, but not the wisdom of this age” (I Corinthians II). Of this the apostles are told: “You are the salt of the earth” (Matthew V). Just as every food is seasoned with salt, so every discourse is seasoned with apostolic wisdom. Therefore the covenant of salt is everlasting for Aaron and his sons, because wisdom is necessary not only for bishops but also for priests, deacons, and all the orders. It is to be before God—that is, it must please God as pure and simple, without cunning or malice. For the wisdom of this world is hostile to God (Romans VIII).

## CHAPTER XIX

[Col. 0409D]

**VERSE 1.**—“And the Lord spoke.” (AUGUSTINE, *Question 33 on Numbers*.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that it profaned the observances of the Law.

(RABANUS.) Strength is signified by the male and weakness by the female. Therefore, through the cow, the weakness of the Lord’s incarnation assumed for sacrifice is represented. For Christ died through weakness but lives through the power of God (II Corinthians, last chapter).

“A red cow”—that is, red with the blood of the Passion. Hence: “My beloved is white and ruddy” (Song of Songs V): white through divinity, ruddy through blood, and white also through the justice of his life.

(GREGORY, *Moral Commentary*, book VI, vol. I.) We slaughter the red cow when we extinguish the flesh’s lustfulness. We offer it with hyssop, cedar wood, and scarlet when, through bodily mortification, we burn the sacrifice of faith, hope, and charity.

## Verse 2

**“Let there be no blemish.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 33.) “Without defect.” For this flesh was signified by the other sacrifices, etc., up to “which did not possess a defect in itself?”

**“Nor has it borne a yoke.”** Everyone who sins is a slave of sin. Since Christ therefore never sinned, he did not bear the yoke.

**(Augustine.)** Another translation reads: “And no yoke has been placed upon it,” etc. For it was not subjected to iniquity; finding those who had been subjected to it, he freed them and broke their bonds. Hence: “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise,” etc. For no yoke was placed upon that flesh of his who had the power to lay down his life and to take it up again.

## Verse 3

**“And you shall hand it over.”** The cow is handed over to the priest for sacrifice, because the incarnate Lord offered himself as a sacrifice for our redemption, delivered into the hands of the Jewish people.

**(Augustine.)** Another translation reads: “And you shall give it to Eleazar the priest,” etc. Why not to Aaron? Perhaps this was prefigured not for the time then present, but for the successors of that priesthood, to whom the Lord’s Passion would come.

**“Who has led it outside the camp.”** (The same.) Because Christ suffered outside the gate, so that he might lead us away from the conduct of the present life, as from a city (Hebrews 13).

**[Col. 0410C] (The same.)** “And he has led it outside the camp.” Thus the Lord, about to suffer, was led outside the city (John 19).

**(The same.)** “In a clean place,” because he had no evil cause. “And they shall kill it in his sight”: thus Christ’s flesh was killed in the sight of those who were to become priests of the Lord’s New Testament.

**“He shall sacrifice it.”** (Isidore.) No one can sacrifice the red cow, whose ashes are the purification of the people, except one who has not performed earthly works, has not drawn the yoke of sin, and has not been bound by the chains of sins.

**“In the sight of all.”** (Rabanus.) Because Christ was extinguished, as it were, in the sight of all: he was sacrificed in the sight of the Father, because what was punishment before human eyes was sacrifice before the eyes of the Father.

## Verse 4

**“And dipping his finger in its blood.”** [Col. 0410D] (Augustine.) Another translation reads: “And Eleazar the priest shall take some of its blood and sprinkle it seven times toward the front of the testimony, from its blood.” Because Christ shed his blood for the remission of sins according to the Scriptures, it was sprinkled toward the front of the tabernacle of the testimony, because this was not declared otherwise than it had been foretold by the divine testimony. And it was done seven times because that number pertains to spiritual cleansing.

**(Rabanus.)** Discrimination in action is signified by the finger. To dip the finger in the cow’s blood is to consecrate our works in the Lord’s Passion, so that we may imitate the Passion which we acknowledge: “For he suffered for us, leaving us an example, that we should follow in his footsteps” (1 Peter 2).

**[Col. 0411A] (The same.)** Eleazar the priest sacrifices and dips his finger in the blood because the Jewish people, from the party of the rejected, persecuted the Lord’s humility even to the Passion. In the elect, however, it imitated the operation of his humility—

**“He shall sprinkle toward the doors of the tabernacle.”** The tabernacle signifies the synagogue. Therefore whoever has dipped his finger shall sprinkle toward the doors of the tabernacle: that is, whoever imitates the ways of his Passion should offer the unbelieving and resisting synagogue a sign of right living through good examples and sound preaching.

**(The same.)** “He shall sprinkle”: that is, he will show the resisting people examples of Christ’s Passion through sound preaching and works.

**“Seven times.”** Because there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 0411B] which are distributed among the peoples of the Church through Christ’s blood, by which they are cleansed from every sin.

**(Gregory, *Moralia*, book 6, chapter 27.)** “Seven times,” etc. Perfection is signified or understood in the number seven; hence the whole of time is completed in seven days, and the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold. To dip the finger seven times in the blood therefore means to imitate the mystery of the Passion through perfect action. To sprinkle seven times toward the synagogue means to announce the Passion to unbelievers through perfect preaching.

## Verse 5

**“And he shall burn it while all look on.”** (The same.) By the hide, flesh, blood, and dung are signified the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which announced the Lord’s weakness. Because these things were afterward understood spiritually by the fathers, they were called dung with respect to the outward mystery. Hence Paul says: “He regards all things as dung” (Philippians 3). These things are handed over to the flame. Although they were first presented in a carnal manner, afterward they were consumed by the fire of understanding through the Holy Spirit.

**(Augustine.)** “And they shall burn it in his sight.” I think that the burning pertains to the sign of the resurrection. For it is the nature of fire to move upward and to transform into itself whatever is burned. Indeed, the word *cremare* itself was brought from Greek into Latin and derives from suspension. What is added—“in his sight,” that is, in the sight of the priest—seems to signify that Christ’s resurrection appeared to those who were to become a royal priesthood.

**[Col. 0411D] “Both its hide and its flesh,” etc.** (The same.) What follows—“Its hide and its flesh and its blood, together with its dung, shall be burned”—explains how it is to be burned. It signifies that not only the mortal substance of Christ’s body, indicated by the mention of hide, flesh, and blood, but also the disgrace and rejection of the people, signified by the dung, would be transformed into the glory indicated by the flame of the burning.

**(Rabanus.)** The exterior activity of Christ is signified by the hide and flesh; by the blood, his subtle and inward power, giving life to outward things; by the dung, weariness, thirst, hunger, fear of death, and everything he wished to suffer in his humanity. Whatever he possessed through the defect of mortality had to be cast away from him like dung. All these things must be burned by fire—that is, understood according to the truth of the Holy Spirit—so that what he accomplished bodily may be understood as arranged through the incorporeal Spirit of his divinity.

## Verse 6

**“And also cedar wood, hyssop, and scarlet twice-dyed.”**

**(Apollinaris.)** Concerning the death of sacred things, therefore, the prophet sang: “You shall sprinkle me, Lord, with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed; you shall wash me,” etc. (Psalm 50). And to the one to whom such a mystery of purification had been revealed, which was to come through Christ’s blood, he declared: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.”

**(Rabanus.)** Cedar is a tall and incorruptible wood. Hyssop is a very low-growing herb, which nevertheless removes inflation of the lungs. By the lofty cedar, therefore, persevering contemplation is signified; by hyssop, the humility of a gentle heart. Whoever is lifted through contemplation to heavenly things must descend through the compassion of humility to those below; he should not exalt himself because of what he possesses, but should willingly offer it through preaching to those who do not possess it.

**(Augustine.)** Another translation reads, etc., up to “so that our life might be hidden with him.”

**(Rabanus.)** Cedar may be understood as hope, etc., up to “until charity alone is multiplied in us at the end.”

**(Gregory, *Moralia*, book 6, chapter 17.)** “Let it be cast into the flame,” up to “so that in it he may learn the right works which he should perform.”

**[Col. 0412C] “Hyssop.”** (Isidore.) Baptism, because hyssop dipped in the blood of the lamb was used for sprinkling (Exodus 12).

**“And scarlet twice-dyed.”** (The same.) Scarlet twice-dyed is Christ’s blood, by which we are washed in mind and body. These three cleanse sins: cedar, that is, faith in the cross; hyssop, baptism or martyrdom; scarlet, the sacrament of the Lord’s blood.

**(Rabanus.)** The power of charity is expressed in the twice-dyed scarlet. Kindled by the flame of holy love, it is commanded to be displayed through two precepts, namely love of God and of one’s neighbor. Twice-dyed scarlet, therefore, is charity formed by a double commandment: God is to be loved in such a way that one’s neighbor is not abandoned, and one’s neighbor in such a way that God is not despised.

**“The priest.”** (The same.) All of us who believe in Christ are priests. Hence: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” etc. (1 Peter 2). Therefore whatever we perceive as lofty through contemplation, whatever we do through the gentleness of humility, and whatever we offer through the fire of charity, we must dip in the blood of Christ’s Passion, so that everything within us may imitate him from whom it comes; for apart from imitation of the Passion, it is not so much virtue as vice.

**(The same.)** This priest, who burns the cow’s flesh, hide, blood, and dung, may signify the order of the Jewish priesthood together with the subjected people consenting to the Lord’s death. Hence it follows: “And then, after washing his clothes and his body.”

## Verse 7

**“And then, after washing his clothes.”** (The same.) It may be understood, etc., up to “But a clean man shall gather the ashes of the cow,” etc.

**(Augustine.)** “The priest shall wash his clothes,” etc., up to “committing it, as it were, to resurrection through burning.”

## Verse 8

**“Until evening.”** (The same.) The priest enters at evening because the unbelieving people, who remained until evening—that is, until the end of the world—outside the commandments of life, as though placed outside the camp, and stained by evil works, are washed with the water of baptism and repentance and return, at the end of the world, to the camp, as it were.

## Verse 9

**“But he shall gather.”** (Augustine.) “And a man shall gather,” etc., up to “because, outside the observance of Jewish custom, evangelical honor shone forth.”

**[Col. 0413B] (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 6, chapter 17.)** The priest burns the cow, and a clean man gathers the ashes, because the Jew slaughtered the Lord’s weakness, while the Gentile understands his subtle mysteries. Those who preach Christ’s Passion to the nations are clean.

**“He shall pour them out.”** Because the Gentile does not cease to preach the mysteries he has recognized, but makes them manifest to those who do not know them.

**(Rabanus.)** The clean man pours the cow’s ashes in a most pure place when any learned person taken from the Gentiles seeks hearts among the Gentiles cleansed through humility and does not cease to hand over to them the mysteries of the Redeemer. When this is done, the faith of the Gentiles is multiplied, divine power is acknowledged, and observance of the commandments is maintained. Hence he adds: “So that they may be for the multitude of the children of Israel [Col. 0413C] a safeguard.” For Israel is interpreted as “a man seeing God”; and rightly the converted Gentile people are called Israel, since they now contemplate God through faith.

**“Outside the camp.”** Because all Gentiles were outside the law, outside the sacrifice, and outside the synagogue.

**“In a most pure place.”** Because the secrets of the Lord’s incarnation are not to be entrusted to minds that are perverse and polluted, but to those who have come to faith and cleansed their hearts.

**“For the multitude of the children.”** (Augustine, cited above.) Another translation reads, etc., up to “so that, having been washed outwardly as well, he might in some manner wash his clothes.”

**“As a safeguard.”** Because the more subtle mysteries, entrusted to the clean hearts of the Gentiles, are turned into a defense of the mind. For when we attend through imitation to the hidden and subtle operations of that one, by this means we take precautions against uncleanness. Thus the ashes become a safeguard for us because of their operation, but because of baptism they become water for sprinkling. We carefully keep the ashes as our protection when we diligently consider our Redeemer suffering for our sins. For we weigh what he will repay to the good, since he wished to die for the wicked; what we, brought to the righteousness of faith, owe to his grace, since, while placed in iniquity, we received the intercession of his death.

## Verse 10

**“They shall have this.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 33.) Another translation reads, etc., up to “which evening signifies.”

## Verse 11

**“Whoever touches it.”** (Augustine.) “Whoever touches a corpse,” etc. He begins to explain how people become unclean, etc., up to “according to this saying, I think, through the prophet: ‘For three transgressions and for four I will not turn away.’”

## Verse 12

**“If on the third day,” etc.** (The same.) “But if he has not been purified on the third day,” etc., up to “still—that is, even after death.”

## Verse 13

**“He shall pollute the tabernacle,”** as far as it lies within him, according to the saying: “Do not extinguish the Spirit” (1 Thessalonians 5), although he cannot extinguish it. For if Scripture wished this to be understood as making the tabernacle unclean, it would command that it be cleansed.

## Verse 15

**“The vessel which,” etc.** (Rabanus.) The covering of the lid or the binding is the regulation of discipline. Whoever is not restrained by it is rejected as an unclean and polluted vessel. For a vessel without a cover or binding is polluted; so too is one polluted who, through eagerness for display, lies open and is covered by no veil of silence.

## Verse 16

**(Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 34.)** “If anyone is in the field.” Another translation reads, etc., up to “that is, killed by a wound or dead without a wound.”

## Verse 19

**“He shall also wash himself,”** etc. (The same.) Another translation reads, etc., up to “he shall be unclean until evening.”

# Chapter XX

## Verse 20

**“And the children came,” etc.** (Isidore, *On Numbers*, volume 5.) The thirty-third station is in the desert of Zin; this is Kadesh. Zin, however, is interpreted as “holy,” by antiphrasis, just as a grove is called *lucus* when it gives very little light, or as a war is called dreadful. At this station Miriam dies and is buried. She signifies dead prophecy, just as Moses and Aaron signify the end of the law and priesthood, which cannot reach the promised land or lead the people out of the wilderness of this world. Only Jesus, that is, the Son of God, the Savior, does this.

**“Striking with the rod.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 35.) Because water was brought forth from the rock, etc., up to “for the two pieces of wood are the cross.”

## Verse 12

**“Because you did not believe.”** (Isidore, *On Numbers*.) Here Moses offended the Lord, etc., up to “Christ is the power of God and the wisdom of God.”

## Verse 13

**“This is the water of contradiction, where the children quarreled,” etc.** (Augustine.) What is said concerning that water, etc., up to “for it is said of him: ‘For a sign that shall be contradicted,’” etc. (Luke 2).

## Verse 22

**“To Mount Hor, which is on the borders.”** [Col. 0414D] (Rabanus.) This is the thirty-fourth station, etc., up to “an ascent to paradise.”

## Verse 30

**“But the whole multitude.”** (Bede.) Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned, because in the law there is a descent into the underworld, whereas in the Gospel there is a passage to paradise. The people wept for thirty days because, before the law, under the law, and under grace, the synagogue does not receive spiritual joy, but, sorrowful, rests upon the letter that kills.

# Chapter XXI

## Verse 1

**“When he had heard this.”** The Canaanite heard that Israel had come to the place of the spies, where the people had once offended; he entered into battle and led Israel captive. Once again battle is waged in the same place: the victor is conquered by a vow, and the conquered overcome. From this we understand that when enemies attack us and take us captive because we have been deprived of God’s help, we must not despair; it can happen that we conquer where we were conquered.

## Verse 3

**“Anathema.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 40.) Another translation reads, etc., up to “it is the same as ‘I devote’ and ‘I detest.’”

## Verse 4

**“They set out,” etc.** (Jerome, Letter to Fabiola.) The thirty-fifth station, etc., up to “with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

## Verse 8

**“Make a serpent.”** (Isidore, *On Numbers*, volume 5.) The bites of the serpents were healed by the bronze serpent when it had been raised up and looked upon, etc., up to “he lives through divinity, like bronze.”

## Verse 10

**[Col. 0415B] “The children of Israel set out and encamped,” etc.** This is the thirty-seventh station, at Oboth, which is interpreted as “magicians” or “python spirits.” For after the image of God, which is shown in the reasoning of the heart, and after the confession of faith expressed by the mouth, serpents and magical arts arise. But since we guard our heart with every vigilance, let us close our ears, lest we hear the voices of enchanters and the songs of sirens.

## Verse 11

**“From there they set out.”** (Jerome, cited above.) “At Iye-abarim,” etc., up to “but this properly belongs to those who contemplate the rising of the sun of justice.”

## Verse 12

**“They came to the torrent Zared,” etc.** (Rabanus.) The thirty-ninth station was at Dibon-gad, etc., up to “but let us fear the wilderness set before us.”

## Verse 14

**“In the book of the wars.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 42.) He did not say in which book it was written, etc., up to “the war of the Lord might be written in one of their books.”

## Verse 16

**“From that place,” etc.** (Origen, *Homily 12 on Numbers*.) What is the reason that the Lord commands with such insistence, etc., up to “because the Trinity has one substance and nature”?

**(The same, in the same work.)** Those wells too may be understood, etc., up to “and removed the earth which the Philistines had thrown into them.”

It should be noted that while Abraham was alive, the Philistines did not dare to fill his wells or throw earth into them. But after his death they grew powerful and lay in wait for his wells; they were restored, however, by Isaac. Abraham’s servant also found Rebecca at the wells; her name is interpreted as “Patience.” She became Isaac’s wife, but at the wells (Genesis 24, 29). Likewise Jacob, when he came to Mesopotamia bearing his father’s command not to take a foreign woman as wife, found Rachel at the wells; and Moses found Zipporah (Exodus 2).

Therefore, if you have understood what the wives of the saints are and what they are like, and if you wish to take patience, wisdom, or other virtues of the soul in marriage, and to say what is said concerning wisdom—“I sought to take her for myself as a wife” (Wisdom 8)—remain constantly beside these wells, and there you will find such a spouse, because it is certain that virtues dwell beside the streams of the living Word.

There are therefore many wells within the soul, and many others in the individual words and meanings of Scripture. Yet there is one more eminent well, which was dug not by just any men, but by princes, and by those superior to them, whom he called kings. Therefore God is hymned at this well, and it is written that this is the well over which the Lord spoke to Moses: “Gather the people, and I will give them water from the well.”

**“Gather the people, and I will give them.”** The Law summons you to the well, namely Christ, the Son of God, subsisting in his own substance but named, together with the Father and the Spirit, as one fountain of divinity. To this well, therefore—that is, to faith in Christ—the Law summons you. Hence he himself says: “Moses wrote about me” (John 4). It calls us to drink the waters and sing a song to him, that is, to believe with the heart unto righteousness and confess with the mouth unto salvation (Romans 10).

## Verse 17

**“Let the well rise up.”** (Origen.) “Initiate the well for him,” [Col. 0416B] that is, establish the well as the beginning of all things, because he is the beginning and firstborn of every creature (Revelation 3).

Or it may be understood this way, with the words addressed by Moses to the people: Give your heart a beginning, so that it may begin to understand what the well is, from which spiritual waters are to be drawn and the believing people refreshed. “Initiate it for him,” that is, for Israel, this well, so that if anyone sees the mystical meaning from the heart, he may draw God from the depths.

Moses, that is, the Law, gathers people to this well. Someone appears to reach it, but unless he is gathered through Moses, he is not acceptable to God. Marcion seems to himself to have come, and Basilides and Valentinus; but because they did not come through Moses and did not receive the Law and the Prophets, they cannot praise [Col. 0416C] God from the fountains of Israel.

Such people therefore do not come to the well which the princes dug (Genesis 14) and the kings excavated. There is a valley of salt in which there are bitumen wells. Every heresy and every sin is in a valley, and in a valley of salt. For sin does not rise upward but always descends to the depths and to lower things. Thus every heretical opinion and every sinful act is situated in a valley, salty and bitter. For what sweetness or pleasantness can sin possess?

But if you come to a heretical judgment and the bitterness of sin, you have come to the wells of bitumen, which is food and nourishment for fire. If you taste water from these wells—if you receive heretical thinking and the bitterness of sin—you will prepare within yourself fuel for fire and the flames of Gehenna. To such people it is said: “Walk in the light of your fire,” etc. (Isaiah 50).

## Verse 16

**“The princes dug it, and the kings excavated it.”** The princes dug, and the kings excavated. This is said from *excudere*, not from *excidere*. Something is said to be *excuded* when it is cut or shaped in stone.

The princes, as the lesser, dug: that is, they sank a certain depth into the softness of the earth. But those whom he calls kings, as the stronger, penetrate not only the depth of the earth but also the hardness of the rock, so that they may reach deeper waters and search out the very veins of the abyss, knowing that God’s judgments are a great abyss.

These are the apostles, one of whom says: “But God has revealed them to us through his Spirit; for the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God” [Col. 0417A] (1 Corinthians 2). Those who through the Holy Spirit can search and penetrate the deep things are called kings; they excavated the well in the rock because they penetrated the hard and difficult secrets of knowledge.

The princes therefore dug this well, and the kings of the nations excavated it—that is, the apostles, who gathered the nations to obedience to the faith and made the knowledge of Christ manifest to all, in whom all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden. For they fulfilled God’s commandment by teaching all nations and baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit (Matthew 28). By this they excavated it, that is, made the knowledge of the well manifest.

What we have in our hands is also a well for us, as is the whole Scripture of the Law and the Prophets. The Gospel and apostolic writings together are likewise one well. None can dig or excavate it except kings and princes—those, namely, who can remove the earth and take away the surface of the letter, bringing forth from the lower rock, where Christ is, spiritual meanings like living water.

They are called kings because they expelled the kingdom of sin and established the kingdom of righteousness in their members. For it is fitting that the one who teaches others should first do what he teaches. Hence: “Whoever does and teaches them shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5). To be great in the kingdom is to be a king.

## Verse 18

**“The princes.”** The same people may be called both princes and kings. Or let us understand the princes as the prophets. They placed the meaning and prophecy concerning Christ, dug out from the depth of the letter, in a hidden place. Hence it is said of them: “Unless you hear secretly, your soul shall weep.” And elsewhere: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you” (Psalm 30).

The apostles are kings: they search out the deep things of God and govern the churches. Hence Christ too is called the King of kings.

**“And they prepared it, the leaders.”** (Origen.) “They excavated it,” he says, etc., up to “searching out the secrets of the Word of God.”

**“They set out.”** (Origen.) “They set out from the well,” etc., up to “so that our affection and faith may be tested.”

Whoever drinks from this well advances toward possessing gifts to offer to God. Concerning these it is said in the Law: “My gifts are my gifts” (Leviticus 2). From what God has given, therefore, an offering is made to God. He has given knowledge of himself, and the human being offers him faith and affection.

**[Col. 0417D]** When we offer what comes from us, we obtain what comes from God. For when we have offered our faith and affection, then he himself bestows various gifts of the Holy Spirit, concerning whom it is said: “All things are from God” (Romans 11).

## Verse 20

**“In Bamoth.”** Bamoth signifies the coming of death, by which we die together with him in order to live together with him, and mortify our members upon the earth. For we have been buried with him through baptism into death (Romans 6). Whoever keeps the order of the way of salvation must carry these things out individually and, after much, come to this place.

**(Origen.)** “And from Bamoth,” he says, etc., up to “rather, through progress the soul’s journey is prepared for heaven.”

## Verse 21

**“But he sent.”** (The same.) Israel sends messengers to the king of the Amorites, etc., up to “he gathers for himself broken or shattered cisterns.”

**“To Sihon the king.”** Sihon, interpreted as “a fruitless tree” or “the exalted one,” is the king of the Amorites, who are interpreted as “those bringing into bitterness” or “those speaking.” He is the exalted and fruitless devil, concerning whom it is said: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14). And elsewhere: “Behold, the prince of this world shall be cast out” (John 12)—not because he created the world, but because there are sinners in the world and he is the prince of sin, according to the saying: “The whole world is placed in the evil one” (John 5). That is, he is the prince of the world.

## Verse 22

**“The royal road.”** The road that says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Concerning it, it is said: “Give your judgment to the king, O God” (Psalm 71). We must walk along this road and turn aside nowhere—not into a field or into a vineyard, that is, neither toward works nor toward diabolical meanings—if we wish to pass peacefully through the world.

But what we say—that we do not wish to remain with the prince of this world, linger with him, or touch anything belonging to him—provokes him all the more. Therefore he becomes angry, stirs up persecutions and dangers, and threatens torments. Hence it says: “Sihon gathered his people,” etc.

## Verse 23

**“With his army.”** That is, with the princes, judges, and all the ministers of wickedness of the world, who continually attack the people of God.

**“At Jahaz.”** Jahaz, in Hebrew *yahtsah*, is interpreted as “the fulfillment of the commandment.” For if we come to the fulfillment of the commandments, we overcome the proud and exalted one. To fulfill the commandment is to overcome the devil and his army. Nothing will be able to harm us if we come to Jahaz—that is, if we keep the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ.

## Verse 24

**“By the edge of the sword.”** “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every sword,” etc. (Hebrews 4). The Apostle says of it: “And the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 5). Sihon—that is, the devil—falls by its edge.

**“His land.”** Every earthly region is called the land of Sihon; but Christ and his Church rule throughout the whole land of Sihon.

**(Rabanus.)** Jazer, the city and boundary of Sihon’s kingdom, etc., up to “his name was called Israel.”

## Verse 25

**“Therefore Israel took.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 44.) Here Israel possessed the cities of the Amorites, etc., up to “but they turned away from them.”

**“Israel.”** (Origen, *Homily 13 on Numbers*.) The one who is Israel in Christ, etc., up to “and he wishes it to be kindled.”

**(Isidore.)** In the thirty-ninth station, etc., up to “and, once understood, is bravely overcome.”

## Verse 26

**“Of Sihon the king.”** Sihon means “speaking.” Those who act under the devil know only how to speak, but they speak empty things, as do certain astrologers and philosophers. The kingdom of the faithful, however, which comes from God, is not in speech but in the power of God (1 Corinthians 4).

**“Moab.”** (Rabanus.) Moab, which is interpreted as “,” etc., up to “they fall and are consumed.”

## Verse 27

**“Therefore it is said.”** (Origen, cited above.) Another translation reads, etc., up to “not of the Amorites, but of the children of Israel.”

## Verse 29

**“Woe to you, Moab.”** (Rabanus.) Chemosh is interpreted as “,” etc., up to “against which it is said: ‘Do not hand over to beasts the souls confessing you’” (Psalm 73).

## Verse 32

**“Jazer, that is, their strength.”** These are the very strong doctrines of heretics, constructed through dialectical skill. **“And they possessed it.”** By converting them from error and teaching the Lord’s commandments, so that from their correction and progress they might acquire a heavenly homeland for themselves.

## Verse 33

**“Og, king of Bashan.”** (Origen.) “To Og, king of Bashan,” etc., up to “for nothing that is shameful can be honorable.”

# Chapter XXII

## Verse 2

**“When he saw.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 46.) What Scripture says, etc.; there were not one people but two neighboring peoples.

## Verse 5

**“Therefore he sent messengers to Balaam son of Beor.”** (Origen, *Homily 13.) War threatens you, King Balak, etc., up to “therefore the king sends to him, saying: ‘Come now, curse this people for me,’” etc.

## Verse 6

**“If somehow I may be able.”** He seems not to trust Balaam completely, having been terrified by the reputation of the wonders performed among God’s people.

**“For I know that whoever you bless is blessed.”** (Origen.) I do not believe that he knew that whoever Balaam blessed would be blessed. Rather, he said this to flatter him, praising his art so as to make him more willing to help. Magical art does not know how to bless, nor do demons know how to bless Isaac, Jacob, and all the saints. None of the impious knows how to bless.

## Verse 7

**“The price of divination.”** Others: “Divining instruments in the arts which human curiosity has devised.” There are certain things which Scripture has called divining instruments. Gentile custom calls them tripods, curtains, or by similar names; these are treated and moved as though consecrated for this purpose.

But divine Scripture, in the prophets, calls the *ephod* by the vernacular term; they say that it is the garment of prophets (1 Kings 30). Yet in divine Scripture prophecy is one thing and divination another. It says: “There shall be no augury in Jacob, nor divination in Israel.”

**[Col. 0419D]** Divination is therefore utterly rejected, for it is accomplished through the work and service of demons. Accordingly, when Balaam received the divining instruments, with which demons were accustomed to come to him, he saw that they had been driven away and that God was present. He says that he is consulting God because he does not see those accustomed to appear to him.

God therefore came to Balaam, not because Balaam was worthy, but so that those who had been accustomed to be present for cursing and doing harm might be driven away. For God was thereby providing for his people.

## Verse 8

**“God came,” etc.** It is not said whether this happened in a dream, although it is clear that it happened during the night. For afterward Scripture says: “Balaam rose in the morning,” etc.

Let no one boast if God speaks to him. For he knows how to speak with such people, since he also speaks with the reprobate. Even when he speaks through angels, it is he himself who speaks.

**(Origen, *Homily 13*.)** “God came and said to him,” etc. It may be objected: Although Balaam invokes demons, etc., up to “and they revered a little boy as though he were a great king, as an argument for great faith.”

## Verse 16

**“Thus says Balak son of Zippor,” etc.** Balak means “exclusion” or “devouring.” By him is signified some hostile power of this world, which wishes to exclude and devour spiritual Israel and uses no ministers except the chief priests, scribes, and Pharisees.

It invites them and promises them a reward. They, however, like Balaam, pretend in every way that they refer everything to the Lord and act out of zeal for God. For they say: “Search the Scriptures and see that no prophet rises from Galilee.” And: “We have a law, and according to the law he ought to die, because he has made himself the Son of God” (John 7, 19).

## Verse 18

**“If Balak were to give me,” etc.** (Augustine, *Questions on Numbers* 48.) What Balaam said when more honored messengers were sent to him again, etc., up to “Therefore they followed the way of Balaam son of Beor, who loved the reward of iniquity.”

## Verse 20

**“Therefore God came.”** Balaam is troublesome to God and almost extorts permission to go and curse the children of Israel, and to invoke demons, though God had already come to him.

**(Origen, *Homily 13*.)** It is difficult in the explanation of the history, etc., up to “because with God the works neither of the wicked nor of the good are idle.”

**“If he calls.”** (Rabanus.) Balaam was a diviner, etc., up to [Col. 0420C] “not so much in heart and understanding as with mouth and speech.”

**(Origen.)** “If you see a hostile power,” etc., up to “namely, believers from the Gentiles.”

## Verse 22

**“And the angel of the Lord stood.”** He was present, namely, for the children of Israel, concerning whom it is written: “My angel shall go with you” (Exodus 32).

## Verse 23

**“The she-ass saw the angel standing.”** The magician sees demons; the she-ass sees the angel—not because she was worthy to see him, any more than she was worthy to speak, but so that Balaam might be confuted. Thus the mute animal rebukes the prophet’s madness.

**(Gregory, *Pastoral Rule*, part 3, admonition 13.)** Balaam strives to reach his objective, etc., up to “because, proceeding to curse, he changed his voice, not his mind.”

## Verse 25

**“Against the wall.”** That is, against the wall of that vineyard in which the angel was not, because according to the Septuagint he was on the other side, among the furrows of the vineyards.

## Verse 26

**“To the place.”** He was no longer among the furrows of the vineyards but between the walls themselves, that is, in the road. He blocked the way so that the she-ass could go neither to the right nor to the left.

## Verse 27

**“It fell down beneath,” etc.** Because, though beaten, it did not go backward and did not turn aside. For the angel was not frightening it from either side; he was in the middle of the narrow road.

## Verse 28

**“And he opened.”** He opened her mouth so that Balaam might be reproved through her and confuted by the voice of a mute beast—he who appeared to be a diviner and wise.

**“And she spoke.”** (Isidore.) The she-ass on which Balaam sits sees the angel and speaks. This means that the brutish Gentile people, which Balaam—that is, the seducer into idolatry—once subdued to whatever error he wished, like a brutish animal incapable of resistance or reason, saw the angel whom the human being could not see. It saw him, reported him, and spoke, so that we might recognize that, at the coming of the great angel, that Gentile people, its harshness and stupidity changed, would speak with tongues released for God.

**(Origen, *Homily 14*.)** “The she-ass on which Balaam sat,” etc., up to “but greater than these is charity, which alone never falls.”

## Verse 29

**“He answered.”** He was driven on by such great desire that he was not terrified even by so great a miracle, but answered as though speaking to a human being. God had not transformed the she-ass’s soul into a rational nature; rather, he caused to sound from her whatever pleased him, in order to restrain Balaam’s madness. Perhaps this prefigured the saying: “God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise,” for the sake of the spiritual and true Israel.

## Verse 38

**“Behold, I have come. Can I speak anything other than what God,” etc.** (Origen, *Homily 15*.) Balaam is presented in Scripture now as blameworthy, now as praiseworthy, etc., up to “Balaam, illuminated by that Lucifer of whom it is said: ‘How has Lucifer fallen, who rose in the morning?’” (Isaiah 14).

# Chapter XXIII

## Verse 7

**“Come,” he said, “and curse Jacob for me.”** (Origen, *Homily 15*.) In Latin expressions, etc., up to “and therefore he says that the word of God was placed in his mouth.”

## Verse 8

**“How shall I curse?”** [Col. 0421C] (The same.) Another translation reads, etc., up to “and the authority of pronouncing is destroyed.”

He whom God has not cursed. This indicates the great merit of the one who is being cursed, and declares the judgment of one whom neither the nature of the sin nor the disposition of the sinner deceives. A human being, however, knows neither of these things and often curses when provoked by insults or injuries. Therefore the Apostle says: “Bless, and do not curse” (Rom. 12), so that the vice of reviling may be cut away.

**VERSE 9.—**From the heights, etc. That is: he ought not to be cursed because his life is lofty and heavenly. No one understands it unless he has risen to eminent knowledge.

(ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to those who, rising with Christ, will have exercised authority over the earth [Col. 0421D].

See, etc. The acts of Jacob, that is, of those engaged in active works, are seen; Israel, that is, those engaged in contemplation, is understood alone. Or, in the future resurrection, Jacob will be seen—that is, Israel’s body will be understood, namely, the soul and spirit of those who rise.

**The people alone.** Because it is not mixed with the rest of humanity, nor reckoned among the other nations, but is ennobled by its particular privileges, observances, and laws, just as the tribe of Levi is not mixed with the others.

**The people shall dwell alone, etc.** (ORIG.) Spiritual Jacob and Israel, etc., up to the point that it will no longer be reckoned among the nations.

**Who can count them?** (ID.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that he suffers those things which are written in the Second Book of Kings [Col. 0422A].

**VERSE 10.—**May my soul die. (ID.) He seems to prophesy concerning himself. Yet, according to the literal sense, this happened neither in Balaam nor in that Israel, nor could it have happened; for he did not die among them, but apart from them.

(ID.) “May my soul die the death of the righteous,” etc., up to “but faith working through love” (Gal. 5).

(GREG., *Moral.*, book 33, chapter 27.) “May my soul die the death of the righteous, and may my end be like theirs,” etc. Many within the Church, etc., up to “therefore his countenance was no longer changed in different ways” (1 Kings 1).

**And may my end be like theirs, etc.** (ORIG.) This can be understood of the Magi who came first from the East to worship Christ (Matt. 2). They belonged to Balaam’s lineage through their succession of descent and through the transmission of his teaching. For it is established that they recognized the star which Balaam had foretold would rise in Israel [Col. 0422B].

**VERSE 11.—**What is this? Balak, hearing blessings instead of curses contrary to his expectation, and unable to endure it any longer, interrupted the prophet’s words.

(ID.) The bitter king does not want blessing but seeks curses; for he belongs to the kin of the one to whom it is said: “Cursed are you by all the beasts of the earth” (Gen. 3).

**Then Balak said.** He supposes that Balaam was terrified by the multitude of Israel and therefore had not dared to curse, and that a change of place would benefit him.

[Col. 0422C] **VERSE 13.—**You cannot see it. The madman thought that Israel’s grace could be concealed by a change of place, not knowing that a city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.

**VERSE 14.—**He built. The matter was conducted through profane sacrifices, and divination was sought by magical art. Yet God, wishing grace to abound where sin had abounded (Rom. 5), deigned to be present—not because of the sacrifices, but to meet the one who was coming. There he gives his word and mysteries and proclaims the future, where the faith and astonishment of the Gentiles are especially at stake, so that those who do not wish to believe our prophets may believe their own divinely inspired ones.

**VERSE 15.—**Stand here beside your burnt offering. He stood at his sacrifice, stationed in his idolatry, and therefore fell all the more. The one who had fallen more deeply therefore seems to rise when he appeared to stand in idolatry [Col. 0422D].

“God is not like a human being, that he should lie.” (ORIG., homily 16.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that the punishment of his evils may not reach him.

**VERSE 19.—**Then he said, etc. (ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to the question: “But are these things to be perceived more secretly by the more perfect?”

**VERSE 21.—**There is no idol in Jacob. Another translation: “There will be no labor in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel,” namely, in the age to come.

(ORIG.) “There will be no labor in Jacob, nor will pain be seen in Israel,” etc. (2 Cor. 11.) The condition of the future life is announced, etc., up to the point that they may also hear the prophets.

[Col. 0423A] **The Lord God, etc.** (ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that he will receive the one “who wrestled and prevailed.”

**And the shout of the king’s victory is in him.** This is an admonition of preaching, through which the king—that is, Christ—triumphs over the devil in us.

**VERSE 22.—**God brought him out. (ID.) Another reading, up to the point that he will transform the body of our humiliation, making it like his glorious body.

**Whose strength.** Whose? Christ’s. Whatever belongs to him is one horn, that is, one kingdom, whose glory is spiritual Israel. For he himself says: “Father, grant them that, just as you and I are one, so they too may be one in us” (John 17).

**VERSE 23.—**There is no augury in Jacob. (ORIG., homily 16 on Numbers.) Another reading, etc., up to “nor divination in Israel.” It continues:

“In due time it will be said to Jacob, and to Israel, what God will accomplish”—that is, when it is necessary, when it is advantageous, etc., up to the point concerning those whom Moses, I believe for these reasons, called unclean.

**In Israel.** The one who sees God through purity of faith and cleanness of mind would not even receive Balaam, but he does not dare reject the word that God placed in Balaam’s mouth. For unless the word had come from God, he would not have revealed it to his servant Moses, who was far away, while Balaam was saying these things.

**VERSE 24.—**Behold, the people, etc. Others have: “Behold, like a lion’s cub he will rise up, and like a lion he will exult.” He is a cub when newly born rational infants receive the milk of the word without deceit [Col. 0423C]; but he is an exulting lion when the perfect man lays aside the things that belonged to childhood.

(ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that he gave those who believe in him the name of lion and lion’s cub.

**He will be raised up.** He says that the future people will be raised up; for, having spoken what he saw concerning it, he himself rose up.

**He will not lie down.** (ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to “and like an exulting lion.”

**And when he had led them.** (ORIG.) “And Balak took him,” etc., up to the point that worldly affairs were abandoned to God.

**Build me here.** (ID.) The things that the nations sacrifice, etc., up to those who do not receive the faith of Christ.

## CHAPTER XXIV

**VERSE 1.—**And when, etc. (ORIG.) When no demon, etc., up to the point that each one will obtain the glory of resurrection in his own order.

**He did not go away.** That is, he would consider God’s will not with foolish senses, as he had been accustomed to do among many animals and cattle, but would recognize that God is not concerned with oxen, sheep, birds, or other animals (1 Cor. 9; Rom. 15). He would understand that what has been written about them was written for human beings.

**VERSE 2.—**When the spirit rushed upon him. (AUG., question 51 on Numbers.) “And the spirit of God came upon him,” that is, upon Balaam, etc., up to many similar matters.

**VERSE 3.—**Balaam said. (ORIG., homily 17.) “Balaam the son of Beor said,” etc., up to the point that his eyes are said to have been opened because he was able to see what he saw.

**Whose eye was closed, etc.** (RAB.) Because in sleep, with his bodily eyes closed, he saw these things through the ministry of an angel. The eyes of his mind, however, are partly open and partly closed: he recognizes future mysteries but does not correct his error. So the wicked act one way in knowledge and another in conduct; they show one thing with their mouth and another by their deeds.

**VERSE 5.—**How beautiful. (ORIG., homily 17.) Another reading, etc., up to “like shady groves, like gardens beside rivers,” etc.

**VERSE 6.—**Like wooded valleys. (ORIG.) Others, etc., up to the point that they take delight in walking through their teaching as through the shadowed places of a forest.

**Like gardens irrigated beside rivers.** (ID.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that he is rightly said to dwell in the tabernacle [Col. 0424B].

**Cedars.** The cedars of God, that is, which receive the branches of the vine transplanted from Egypt; in them rests that fruit whose shadow covered the mountains.

(ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that he destroys death, the last enemy.

[Col. 0424C] **VERSE 8.—**God brought him out of. God brought him out of Egypt after the death of Herod, and therefore it says: “Out of Egypt I called my Son” (Hos. 11). This seems to have been taken from this passage and inserted into the Gospel, or else from the prophet Hosea.

After Herod’s death—or from the world—the Father brought him out to himself, so that he might make a way for those who were to ascend from this world to God.

**Whose strength is like, etc.** For, casting down all the kingdoms of the demons, he founded his one kingdom in glory, as a true unicorn; for the horn signifies a kingdom.

**They will devour the nations, etc.** (ORIG., in the place cited above.) “He will devour the nations of his enemies and consume their rich parts,” etc. The nations, that is, etc., up to the point that he is called intelligible and holy, both one and many, and subtle.

**And they will pierce with arrows.** The Septuagint: “With their darts they will shoot the enemy.” Christ conquered the devil by his words (Matt. 4), and overcomes and breaks all who oppose him. For everyone who sins is his enemy while he sins; but if, pierced by the words of God, he recognizes his sins and is stricken with remorse and turns to repentance, he is said to have been pierced by his darts [Col. 0424D].

**VERSE 9.—**Lying down, he slept like a lion, etc. If you have understood how much rest the way of wisdom possesses, how much grace and sweetness, do not dissemble and do not neglect it. Begin the journey, and do not dread the solitude of the wilderness; for heavenly manna meets the one who dwells in such tabernacles, and you will eat the bread of angels (Exod. 16). Only begin quickly, and angels will come into your company—the angels signified by the cedars.

**No one will dare to rouse him.** The Septuagint: “Who will rouse him?” At one time he is said to have been raised by the Father; at another, he himself says that he will raise the temple of his body (John 2). Therefore the disposition of one asking a question is indicated.

**Whoever blesses.** Those who bless bless Christ, having been taken into fellowship with the Father’s blessing. But those who curse are cursed. The Jews who cursed Christ are lamentably cursed. For what could happen to those who curse wisdom, truth, and life, except that they should lie exiled from all these things? Christ is all of them (John 9).

“Whoever curses you will be counted accursed.” And Balak, angry against … (ORIG.) I think that the one who speaks a curse against Christ is not the only one who curses him; so does the person who acts wickedly under the name of Christian, lives shamefully, and causes his name to be blasphemed by disgraceful words or deeds. Likewise, the one who blesses God is not merely the person who does so with words, but also the one whose actions, life, and conduct cause God’s name to be blessed [Col. 0425A].

[Col. 0425B] **VERSE 11.—**The Lord has deprived you of the honor he had appointed. The Lord shows that Balak too understood that Balaam was no longer being deceived through the ministry of demons, but was being transferred to better things by God’s power.

**VERSE 13.—**I cannot pass beyond the word of the Lord my God, whether for good. Balaam knew that responses were not being delivered to him through the customary ministers, but by the one who possesses authority over all. He therefore rightly declared that he could not pass beyond the Lord’s word or utter anything good or evil from his own mouth. For the one who speaks cannot be changed by sacrifices or gifts—before him there is no alteration—and therefore a priest cannot be changed by payment where God is not moved by gifts. Nevertheless, as Balaam is about to depart, he begins to prophesy again. And he says: “I give you counsel,” etc. [Col. 0425C]

**VERSE 14.—**I will give you counsel. (ORIG., homily 18.) “Come, I give you counsel,” etc., up to the point that he is like one who truly sees and truly hears.

**VERSE 15.—**Balaam said. (ID.) “Balaam the son of Beor,” etc., up to those things that were granted for the sake of usefulness.

(GREG., *Moral.*, book 15, chapter 22.) “The man whose eye was closed.” The wicked person does not know the evils he commits until he begins to be punished for them. Balaam offered counsel against the Israelites, but afterward, in punishment, he saw what he had previously committed through guilt. The elect, however, foresee things so that they may not sin; their eyes are open before the fall [Col. 0425D]. The wicked person opens his eyes after the fall, because after his guilt he sees in punishment that he ought to have avoided the evil he committed.

**VERSE 16.—**Who, falling, has his eyes opened. The wicked person often admires eternal judgments; when he hears preaching about the heavenly homeland, he loves it and is astonished at the works of God’s ordering. Thus, while lying prostrate, he considers miracles: he weighs God’s power by knowing it, but does not love it by living accordingly.

**VERSE 17.—**I shall see him, but not now. Another reading: “I shall show him, and not now. I shall make him blessed, and he does not draw near.” These statements refer to those whose person he represents. For the teachers of the law and the scribes show Christ promised in the Law and the Prophets, but not now—that is, not when he came. Rather, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered [Col. 0426A], then they will show him and then they will bless him; at present they blaspheme. But the time when these things will occur is far off, at the end of the age. Therefore he says: “I shall show him,” that is, the people who will then be saved, “but not now.”

“Not now, while I am saying these things,” because “when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4).

**A star shall rise out of Jacob.** (ORIG.) Concerning this star, etc., up to the point that both matters clearly appear to have been prophesied.

**And he will strike the leaders, principalities, and powers, fastening them to the cross** (Col. 2). He cannot otherwise save the Moabites unless he first destroys the leaders of ungodliness.

**And he will lay waste to all.** (ORIG.) “And he will plunder all the sons of Seth.” This is Seth, the son of Adam, etc., up to the point that he recalled them from death to life [Col. 0426B].

**And Edom shall be his possession.** (ID.) “And Edom shall be his inheritance, Esau his enemy,” etc. Edom is the same as Esau, etc., up to the point that through obedience of spirit he will become a participant in the future inheritance.

**VERSE 18.—**But Israel will act valiantly. (ID.) “And Israel acted in strength.” For at that time Edom, etc., up to the one who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna.

**And he will destroy the survivors of the city.** (ID.) “He will destroy the one delivered from the city,” etc., up to “if we die with him, we shall also live with him” (2 Tim. 2).

**VERSE 20.—**The beginning. This cannot refer to the historical Amalek, for he was not first in antiquity; rather, it refers to the spiritual Amalek, who turns peoples away from God and makes Gentiles out of worshipers of God. He is called Amalek and is said to be the beginning of the nations because he gave the beginning by causing human beings to become Gentiles, changing the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of the image of corruptible humanity. For just as Christ is the beginning among the people of God, so Amalek is the beginning among the people who turn away from God and become Gentile.

(ORIG.) “Amalek is the beginning of the nations,” etc., up to the point that every sect that turns the people away from God is to be interpreted in this way [Col. 0426C].

**VERSE 21.—**He also saw, etc. (ID.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that they may learn not to blaspheme.

He does not seem to name the Kenite with great blame, to whom Saul said: “Depart from the midst of Amalek, and I will not strike you, because you showed mercy to Israel,” etc. (1 Kings 15). His dwelling is secure if he places his nest in the rock, which is Christ [Col. 0426D].

(RAB.) The Kenite, etc., up to the point that they transcend everything passing away by the flight of the heart.

**VERSE 22.—**Chosen. The chosen, from the number of the wise and the seekers of truth, live an everlasting life; hence: “Those who enlighten me will have eternal life” (Ecclus. 24).

**Assur.** The devil, to whom heretics are handed over to be directed and corrected.

**VERSE 23.—**A parable. He is often said to speak parabolically, so that we may not take anything in these passages not as a parable but according to the literal sense.

**Who?** How blessed is the one who sees, feels, understands, and believes that God has done these things in this way.

**When will these things occur?** When the star rises from Jacob, a man arises from Israel, Amalek is destroyed, and his offspring perishes [Col. 0427A]. That is, when Christ comes, destroys the worship of idols, and subjects the power of demons.

**VERSE 24.—**They will come. This seems to signify that, in connection with the Lord’s incarnation, the Romans will come, overcoming the Assyrians, Hebrews, and all the peoples of the East, and will eventually lose their kingdom, according to Daniel’s statue (Dan. 2). Alternatively, at Christ’s coming at the end of time—represented by the western region—all the kingdoms of the world will be overcome by the sword of the Spirit, that is, by the word of God, and in the time of Antichrist the preaching of the Gospel will cease.

(ORIG.) Another reading, etc., up to the point that he will be given authority over every power of the enemy.

**Hebrews.** A Hebrew is one who passes from Egypt into the promised land, from darkness into light, from death into life. But he cannot obtain this without great struggle: he both afflicts and is afflicted, strikes the adversary and is struck. Thus the Assyrians afflict the Hebrews, that is, the people of God, just as they themselves are afflicted by them [Col. 0427B].

**They too will perish.** (ID.) “They likewise will perish.” Not together with the Hebrews, that is, but likewise, etc., up to those whom the devil’s deception led into death.

**VERSE 25.—**And he arose. (ID., homily 20.) Because Balaam, constrained by God’s power, etc., up to the point that King Balak immediately obeyed the counsel.

## CHAPTER XXV

**VERSE 1.—**Israel was dwelling, etc., at Shittim. In the interpretation of Hebrew names, we find that *Sittim* means in our language “response” or “refutation.” Israel therefore came to a response or refutation, but it did not come rightly.

(ORIG., homily 20 on Numbers.) The history itself edifies us, etc., up to the point that he is united into one body with falsehood and all evils.

**VERSE 2.—**They ate. That is: they even ate from things sacrificed to idols, which are abominable before God. For what agreement is there between God’s temple and idols?

(ORIG.) The Apostle says, etc., up to the point that the one who receives him eats things sacrificed to idols.

**And they worshiped their gods.** Note the order: evil servants are first deceived by desire, then by gluttony, and finally impiety takes them captive; its payment is fornication [Col. 0427D].

(ORIG.) When Solomon was the wisest of men, etc., up to “There is no number of maidens, yet she is my one dove.”

**VERSE 3.—**Israel was initiated, etc. He was consecrated, namely, to the mysteries of the idol that is especially worshiped among the Midianites by women. It is a form of shamefulness, but Scripture scarcely records what it is, what kind it is, or what its form may be—perhaps so as not to pollute the hearer. Since there are many forms of shamefulness, one is called Beelphegor. Therefore everyone who commits something shameful is consecrated to Beelphegor in some form of shamefulness.

(ORIG.) “And he was initiated into Beelphegor,” etc. Through all the sins that we commit, etc., up to the point that he foretells that bonds and prisons await him there [Col. 0428A].

(ORIG.) Perhaps these things refer to the angels, etc., up to the point that they will have to give an account for your souls.

(ID.) The people sin, etc., up to the point before whom nothing can be hidden and nothing obscured.

(AUG., question 52 on Numbers.) “And the Lord said,” etc., up to the point that he shows this sufficiently clearly to those who are prudent in faith.

**VERSE 7.—**When this happened, etc. (ORIG.) These things edified the earlier people, etc., up to the point that God may be made propitious to us through the true Phinehas, our Lord Jesus Christ.

**Taking a dagger.** This signifies that through the cross of Christ not only idolatry but every affection or desire of the flesh is put to death, and thus God is appeased.

[Col. 0428B] **VERSE 9.—**Twenty-four thousand were killed. Because they abandoned the light of truth and righteousness and loved the blindness of idolatry and fornication, they were deprived of the light of the eternal sun and fell into the darkness of death. The visible sun illuminates the world in twenty-four hours and drives away the darkness of night through its circuit; so Christ, through the apostles and prophets, illuminates the world to drive away the darkness of sin.

**VERSE 13.—**A covenant. Whoever, pierced by zeal for God, despises and restrains the impulses of the flesh, or corrects those subject to him so that they do not become wanton, acquires an everlasting priesthood belonging to the same one of whom it is said: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Ps. 109), and with him he will possess an eternal kingdom.

Phinehas is interpreted as “sparing with the mouth,” or “he rested with the mouth,” or “an oracle of the mouth”; Eleazar as “my God is helper,” or “the help of God”; Aaron as “mountain of strength,” or “strong mountain.” These names fittingly express the meaning stated above: whoever restrains his mouth so as not to speak wickedly and explains heavenly mysteries to his hearers, fulfilling a pious labor through God’s help, ascends happily to the mountain of strength, that is, to Christ [Col. 0428C].

**And there was, etc.** (RAB. on Numbers.) The Israelite who fornicated with the Midianite woman, etc., up to the place where he is tormented day and night until the final quarter-hour.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 1.—**After the guilty, etc. (ORIG., homily 21 on Numbers.) Because those who had first been enrolled fell through sin, etc., up to the point that all the promises were fulfilled for these people [Col. 0428D].

**VERSE 2.—**Count them all. The people and the Levites are counted again, so that, after the first carnal people have been killed, a new people of God may be numbered—one that will pass through the baptism of the Jordan and receive the promise of a heavenly inheritance.

**VERSE 53.—**To these the land shall be divided. (ORIG., in the place cited above.) The earlier people, who are in circumcision, are rejected, etc., up to those who, through purity, have become capable of pure divinity.

(ID.) The division of this land, etc., up to the part that is adjacent to the cities [Col. 0429A].

**VERSE 54.—**To the greater number, the greater portion. That is, the more numerous tribe should receive larger areas of land by lot, while the smaller tribe should receive a smaller area corresponding to its number.

One righteous person, insofar as he is accepted by God, is counted for many. Hence: “A city will be inhabited by one wise person, but a tribe of the wicked will be laid waste; and one righteous person is counted for the whole world.” The wicked, even if they are many, are insignificant and counted as nothing before God (Ecclus. 16). There is therefore a praiseworthy multitude. Thus to Abraham, whom he led outside, he says: “Look at the sky, if you can count the stars; so shall your offspring be,” etc. (Gen. 15). In this we should note that the righteous person always dwells in the inner realm, because he prays to the Father in secret, and all the glory of the king’s daughter—that is, of the royal soul—is within. Yet God brings him outside when circumstances require it and the nature of visible things demands it [Col. 0429B].

**VERSE 55.—**That the land should be assigned by lot. The inheritance is commanded to be divided by lot, but I observe that Moses himself, to whom these things were entrusted, did not divide by lot the inheritance of Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh (Josh. 15). Jesus son of Nave also assigned, apart from the lot, an inheritance to the tribe of Judah, to Caleb, to the tribe of Ephraim, and to half the tribe of Manasseh. In the other cases the lot was cast. Therefore I think that in the heavenly inheritance some will not come by lot, nor be numbered with the others—although they are holy—but their inheritance will be distinguished, as was the case with Caleb, the tribe of Judah, and Jesus son of Nave.

For just as, when spoils are divided after victory has been won, distinguished warriors are not brought to the lot with the others but receive the best portions according to the merit of their valor, while the rest use the lot by right of victory, so I think my Lord Christ will act. He will decree special and exalted honors for those whose magnificent deeds and lofty virtues he recognizes. Hence he says: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17). And elsewhere: “You too shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes,” etc. (Matt. 19). And elsewhere: “Just as you, Father, are in me and I am in you, so may they also be one in us” (John 17). None of these things come down by lot, but by the privilege of love [Col. 0429C].

**VERSE 65.—**Except Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun. (ISID.) Six hundred thousand armed men are said to have come out of Egypt, and only two entered the promised land. Many pass through baptism to the faith, but very few reach the heavenly homeland, according to the saying: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 20). Only two enter because of those who attain the heavenly kingdom from both peoples, or of those who are predestined to eternal blessedness through action and contemplation [Col. 0429D].

## CHAPTER XXVII

**VERSE 6.—**Give them. (ORIG., homily 22 on Numbers.) “You shall give him a possession,” etc. These things, according to the historical sense, etc., up to the point that the daughters of Zelophehad spoke rightly.

**VERSE 8.—**When a man dies without a son, etc. (ID.) A law concerning succession is inserted, etc., up to the point that he will not lose his reward [Col. 0430A].

**VERSE 12.—**Go up into the mountain, etc. (ID., homily 22.) See how the one who is perfect and blessed, etc., up to “Therefore only the one who did not commit sin ought to be sought.”

(ID.) The death of Moses is the end of the Law, etc., up to the point that our soul will rest beneath the veil of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 14.—**Because you offended. (AUG., question 53 on Numbers.) The Lord gives the same cause for Moses’ death as for that of his brother: namely, that they did not sanctify him before the people at the water of contradiction, that is, because they doubted that water could flow from the rock by his gift.

Mystically, however, this signifies that neither the former priesthood, represented by Aaron, nor the Law itself, represented by Moses, leads [Col. 0430B] the people of God into the land of eternal inheritance; rather, Jesus does so, in whom Christ is signified, that is, grace through faith. Aaron died before Israel entered any part of the promised land; but while Moses was still alive, the land of the Amorites was captured and possessed, although he did not cross the Jordan with them. For the Law is observed in part within the Christian faith. It contains commandments that Christians are ordered to observe even to this day. That priesthood and sacrifice, however, have no part in the Christian faith today, except insofar as they were performed and completed as shadows of future things.

When both brothers are told to be gathered to their people, it is clear that God’s anger—which separates from the peace of eternal fellowship—was not directed against them [Col. 0430C]. Thus it is evident that not only their offices but also their deaths were signs of future things, not punishments arising from God’s indignation.

**Let him provide.** Note that he did not choose sons or grandsons, nor ask that leaders be appointed; he entrusted the election to God’s judgment.

**VERSE 16.—**May the Lord God provide. (ORIG.) As he is about to depart from the world, etc., up to the point that the children of Israel may be able to hear him.

**Spirit.** The Holy Spirit, of course. He would not say this about the human spirit, since there was no one who did not possess that. Yet he is commanded to lay hands upon him, lest anyone, however richly endowed with grace, dare to refuse the sacraments of consecration.

**VERSE 20.—**And you shall give. (ISID. on Numbers.) Jesus succeeds Moses, etc., up to “and the remission of sins,” etc. [Col. 0430D]

**And a share of your glory.** That is, you will make him a sharer in your glory. Such things are not diminished as though divided into portions; rather, they are wholly possessed by all and wholly possessed by each who shares in them.

**That he may hear, etc.** (ORIG., homily 22.) If the sacrifices and legal institutions had remained to the present day, they would have excluded faith in the Gospel. For in them there was grandeur and a religion full of reverence, which would astonish anyone who saw it at first sight. Who, seeing the sanctuary, the altar, the priests completing the sacrifice, and the entire order of that observance, would not think that this was the fullest rite by which God, the creator of all things, was worshiped? [Col. 0431A] But thanks be to Christ’s coming, which destroys the things that seemed great on earth and transfers the worship of God from visible things to invisible, and from temporal things to eternal. Yet Christ himself requires ears that hear these things and eyes that see them.

**VERSE 21.—**For this purpose, etc. We are instructed morally that whoever receives authority over the people according to the teaching of divine law—which is especially commended in the office of the priest—must order and govern both his own life and that of his subjects.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 1.—**And the Lord spoke. (ORIG., homily 23 on Numbers.) Another reading, etc., up to the point concerning one who thinks he is offering something to God as though God were in need.

[Col. 0431B] (ID.) “On my feast days.” God has his feast days, etc., up to the point that, where there are still no sins, he calls them his feast days.

**VERSE 3.—**These are the sacrifices. Let us therefore inquire carefully, etc., up to the point that there are other feast days for those who cannot continually offer the sacrifice of chastity.

**VERSE 9.—**But on the Sabbath day. (RAB. on Numbers.) The second festival, therefore, is, etc., up to the one “who is a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 5).

**And two-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil.** (RAB.)
