This is offered by the person who, filled with spiritual grace and taught by the Holy Spirit, teaches his hearers the knowledge of the two Testaments through words and examples—not for temporal gain, but for the reward of eternal life [Col. 0431C].

**VERSE 11.—**At the beginnings of the months. That is, at the new moons, when the Church—or any soul—draws so near to the sun of righteousness that it becomes one spirit with him and, renewed through him, casts off the old person.

(ID.) The third festival is the day of the new moon, etc., up to the point that the renewed soul slaughters him.

**Young bulls from the herd.** In the two bulls the joy of good work can be signified, whether in the soul or in the body; this is offered to the Lord according to the two Testaments in the two commandments of love.

**One ram.** In the ram is represented the strong and immovable governance of discipline according to the unity of the Catholic faith.

**Seven yearling lambs.** The simplicity and gentleness of conduct for heavenly rest, through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit [Col. 0431D].

**VERSE 12.—**And three-tenths of fine flour. This is offered by the one who, illuminated by the oil of joy, presents spiritual knowledge in faith in the Holy Trinity together with good works.

**And two-tenths.** This is done by the one who strives to turn the law’s Decalogue toward his own benefit and that of his neighbors through the two commandments of love, and thus dedicates his entire life to the Lord as a sweet fragrance.

**VERSE 13.—**And one-tenth of a tenth, etc., for each lamb. This occurs when simplicity of conduct is established and adorned according to the rule of Scripture, with the grace of the Holy Spirit cooperating. All these things are rightly commanded to be offered as a burnt offering to the Lord, because we must do them not to seek human praise or present reward [Col. 0432A], but to please God, the giver of all good things, in everything and to merit the reward of eternal life.

**VERSE 16.—**In the month. (ORIG., homily 23 on Numbers.) The fourth place among the festivals is assigned, etc., up to the point that he keeps a feast with God and his angels.

**VERSE 17.—**On the fifteenth day. (ID.) A continuous festival follows this one, etc., up to the point that he becomes more wicked and worse.

(ID.) All who are to be instructed in higher disciplines, etc., up to the point of spiritual sacrifices offered in the purification of the mind.

**VERSE 26.—**The day of firstfruits also, when you offer new produce, etc. (ORIG.) This is called the sixth festival, that of new things, etc., up to goodness, gentleness, and similar virtues [Col. 0432B].

## CHAPTER XXIX

**VERSE 1.—**And the seventh month. (ORIG., homily 23 on Numbers.) The festival of the sevens follows, etc., up to the one whom God appointed as a propitiation through faith in his blood.

(ORIG.) The final feast day, etc., up to: “When perfection comes, what is partial will pass away” (1 Cor. 13).

## CHAPTER XXX

**VERSE 3.—**If anyone. No one rules over the vows of a soul that has attained the perfect man; it possesses freedom in them.

(ORIG., homily 24 on Numbers.) The law of vows is set forth, etc., up to the point that you do only what pertains to divine worship [Col. 0432C].

(ID.) Of the souls that are in the Church of God, etc., up to the point that we need no longer be left by the Father under guardians and stewards.

**If he binds himself by an oath, etc.** (AUG., question 56 on Numbers.) This does not apply to everyone, etc., up to the point that through a vow he himself makes something impermissible for himself.

**VERSE 4.—**If a woman, etc. That is, if she is a female and her soul is still tender, and a husband or father has authority over her vows: the fault is not always hers, but sometimes it returns to her husband or parents.

**And a vow;** the Septuagint: “And the determinations by which she determined against her own soul.” This does not mean that such vows harm her soul; rather, “against the soul” means against the animal pleasure, as in the saying: “You shall afflict your souls.”

(AUG., question 57.) It is rightly asked in this passage also about the vow of virginity. Women, including virgins, are customarily called this in Scripture, and the Apostle seems to speak about a father when he says: “Let him keep his virgin, and let him give his virgin,” etc. (1 Cor. 7). In this way some have understood “marry his virgin” to mean “marry his virginity.” Yet they demonstrate this by no comparable usage of Scripture, since such an expression is exceedingly uncommon [Col. 0432D].

**VERSE 6.—**Nor shall she be held liable. The Septuagint: “The Lord will cleanse her, because her father rejected her.” That is, he will regard her as clean and judge her accordingly, just as it is said: “The priest will cleanse him, and by cleansing you shall not cleanse the guilty” (Lev. 13) [Col. 0433A]. That is: you shall not call someone clean who is unclean.

**VERSE 7.—**If she has a husband. That is, if she is mature and of marriageable age for conceiving the seed of God’s word and receiving the secrets of spiritual teaching. Hence: “I wish to present all of you as a pure virgin to one husband, Christ” (2 Cor. 11).

(AUG., question 59.) Since the Lord commanded, etc., up to the point that God himself had commanded and willed this.

**VERSE 11.—**A wife in the house. (AUG.) He had previously spoken about the woman who made a vow in her father’s house, etc., up to the point that, nevertheless, she consents only insofar as that motion agrees with reason.

## CHAPTER XXXI

[Col. 0433B] **VERSE 2.—**Take vengeance first. (ORIG.) The Israelites had been led into stumbling through the Midianites’ deception, etc., up to the point where deception is rightly placed before one walking so as to lead him into sin.

**And thus you will be gathered.** Finally he says: “You shall be added to your people,” etc. This is directed against the Samaritans, who deny the resurrection of the dead and do not accept faith in the age to come. No one is added to those who do not exist; therefore it is clear that there is a people to whom Moses is said to be added.

### Chapter XXXI

**Verse 4.—A thousand men from each, etc.** (Rabanus, *On Numbers*, vol. II.) Observe the magnificence of divine power, etc., up to: for with such weapons equipped we shall put the camps of the devil to flight.

**Verse 8.—And their kings, etc.** (Origen, Homily 25 [Col. 0433C] on Numbers.) The kings of the Midianites are killed, etc., up to: he has been made for us by God “righteousness, and peace, and redemption.”

Balaam also. It is clear that, at Balaam’s instigation, the women of Midian who had deceived Israel had been suborned; hence he is killed here as though he were the author of the crime.

(Origen.) It was said above that Balaam returned to his own place. But perhaps he returned, although Scripture did not say so; or perhaps he returned to his own place from the place where he had been offering sacrifices—namely, to the place where, as a stranger, he had lodging. For it does not say that he returned to his own house or to his homeland. Of Balak, however, it says that he returned “to himself,” that is, to the place where he lived as a lord.

**Why the women?** (Rabanus.) Mystically, the man returning from battle keeps a woman as booty, etc., up to: so that we may desire what pleases God and strive to accomplish it.

**Verse 16.—At the suggestion.** Here it is shown more clearly that the women were suborned at Balaam’s suggestion.

(Isidore.) Balaam did not doubt that, when the opportunity of women was presented, the Israelites would fall into the ruin of fornication, because he knew that the appetitive parts of their souls were corrupted. Thus demons test each person, laying snares for those affections of the soul in which they perceive us to be sick.

**Verse 21.—Eleazar.** Note that Eleazar does not speak to the whole people, but to the men of valor [Col. 0434A] who were returning from battle. Men of valor are those who go forth to war, who contend in the arena, and abstain from everything else; the others, however, are not men of valor.

**Verse 22.—Gold.** The time of war in this world is against spiritual wickedness and carnal desires. The choir of angels watches us, and the holy expectation of the heavenly powers toward us awaits the time when and the manner in which we shall return from battle: who will bring more gold or silver, who will carefully inspect the precious stones. They also inquire who brings bronze, iron, lead, or a wooden or earthen vessel, or anything of this kind necessary for the uses of a great household. Therefore, according to what each person has brought, the merit of his dwelling-place will be assigned to him. Yet all these things are tested: some by fire, others by water; the fire will prove what sort of work each person’s is. [Col. 0434B]

**And you shall wash, etc.** (Origen, in the work cited above.) You see how everyone who emerges from the battle of this life needs purification, etc., up to: so that he may enter the city of God clean.

**Verse 27.—Those who fought.** (Origen, Homily 26 on Numbers.) There are certain people among the people of God, etc., up to: therefore the number of five hundred is much greater than that of fifty.

(Origen.) There are differences of progress and merits among the people of the faithful, etc., up to: the chains signify the connections of word and teaching.

**Verse 50.—You shall entreat.** (Origen.) To propitiate God on our behalf, etc., up to: for whom alone it is fitting that he should be propitiated. [Col. 0434C]

**Verse 51.—And they received.** Another reading: “And Moses and Eleazar the priest received the gold from all the tribal leaders and centurions, and brought it into the tent of testimony as a memorial for the children of Israel before the Lord.” Note that what is said refers not to visible sight but to the memory of the mind. Blessed is the person who remembers that he has done some good work before the Lord and offered gifts pleasing to God—namely, virtues of soul and ornaments of piety.

### Chapter XXXII

**Verse 1.—Now the sons of Reuben, etc.** (Origen, Homily 26 on Numbers.) Everything that is said must be weighed not only from the speech that is spoken, [Col. 0434D] but also from the person who speaks, etc., up to: but through Moses they receive an inheritance beyond the Jordan.

**Verse 4.—The land that the Lord struck.** (Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVII, chapter 10.) There are many in the Church who disdain to be little ones, etc., up to: while they are blinded by transitory things.

**Very numerous cattle.** (Origen.) There are many beasts of burden and flocks, etc. The former people, etc., up to: to enter the land that is the land of promise.

**Verse 29.—If the sons of Gad and the sons of Reuben cross over, etc.** (Origen, Homily 26.) Another reading, etc., up to: but the one that is above, free, and the mother of us all.

### Chapter XXXIII

[Col. 0435A]

**Verse 1.—These are the stations, etc.** (Origen, Homily 27 on Numbers.) God created various distinctions of foods, etc., up to: but another—the one that, after the resurrection, will ascend to heaven—does not descend suddenly or inopportunely, but through many stations, in each of which it is illumined by the light of wisdom until it reaches the Father of lights himself.

**With their companies.** The Septuagint has: “With his power,” namely Christ, who is the power and strength of God. Therefore one ascends with him who descended to us so that we might ascend. For the one who descended is himself the one who ascended, etc. (Ephesians IV). Hence: “With you I shall descend into Egypt,” etc. (Genesis XLVI). Therefore, there was not a weak person among their tribes. [Col. 0435B]

**By the hand of Moses and Aaron, whom he recorded, etc.** (Origen, same work.) For it is not only the knowledge of the law and of faith, etc., up to: for the work of both hands is one work, and the completion of perfection is one.

**Verse 2.—Moses, according to the places of the camps, which, by the Lord’s command, etc.** And Moses recorded their departures and their stations by the word of the Lord, so that readers, seeing how many departures and stations lie before us, might prepare themselves for this journey and not spend their time sluggishly. Otherwise, while we linger over vanities and take pleasure in all the things that come before sight, hearing, touch, smell, and taste, time will pass and we will not complete the distance of the road, but will fail in the middle of it, as though in the desert. [Col. 0435C] For this reason we have come into this world: to pass from virtue to virtue, and not, for the sake of earthly things, to remain on earth, like the one who said: “Soul, you have many good things; eat, drink, and be merry” (Luke XII). The Lord said to him: “Fool, this night your soul will be taken from you” (ibid.). He did not say “in this night” or “on this day,” but “this night”; for he is destroyed by night, like the firstborn of the Egyptians, because he loved the world and its darkness, being a companion of “the rulers of this world, of these darknesses.” This world is called darkness and night on account of those who live in ignorance and do not receive the light of truth; and therefore they do not pass from Rameses to Succoth.

**Verse 3.—Therefore they set out, etc.** The children of Israel, while still in Egypt, celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day [Col. 0435D] and made a kind of beginning of the feast. On the following day, which is the first day of Unleavened Bread—namely, the fifteenth day of the first month—they set out from Rameses and came to Succoth, so that there they might celebrate the feast of Unleavened Bread, or the day. Who can understand these things? Who can know them even in part? As the Apostle says: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part” (1 Corinthians XIII). For who understands how we celebrate feast-days in part, so that no one may judge us in respect of a feast-day, a new moon, or a sabbath? (Colossians II.) Every feast-day celebrated here is observed in part, not in its entirety; but when you have come out of Egypt, then the feast will be perfect for you. Know, however, that after that Passover which was once celebrated in Egypt, another is found celebrated in the desert, when the law was given; and after this it is nowhere celebrated except in the land of promise. [Col. 0436A]

(Origen.) This order and distinction of the stations is highly necessary, etc., up to: he sets out from Succoth and encamps at Etham.

**With an uplifted hand.** Where there is no human or earthly work but a divine one, the hand is called “uplifted”; for by “hand” a work is understood.

**Verse 4.—And against their gods.** All the gods of the nations are demons. Against them the Lord will execute vengeance on the day of judgment. He does so even now, when someone who had been deceived by them into worshiping idols is converted by the word of the Lord and worships God; or when a fornicator is converted to chastity and laments that he has gone astray, and the demon is burned by the tears of his repentance; or when someone turns from pride to humility and from luxury to frugality. With what torments do you think they are afflicted when they see someone sell all his possessions, give them to the poor, take up his cross, and follow Christ—or when they see the mists of their fraud opened up through knowledge of divine law? For sin is not completed without them. We must therefore act with the greatest care lest we raise up within ourselves the firstborn of the Egyptians or their gods, whom the Lord destroyed, by giving them room to perform in us what the Lord hates. Thus the Lord will punish the gods of the Egyptians through our correction and conversion. [Col. 0436B]

**Verse 5.—In Succoth.** In tents. While we are pilgrims in the body, we dwell in tents. When we have come out of Egypt—that is, out of the world—we first pitch tents, knowing that we are hastening onward to what lies beyond, to the holy land, that is, the heavenly land. [Col. 0436C]

**Verse 6.—From Succoth.** (Origen, Homily 27.) They set out from Succoth, etc., up to: so that he may not remain there, but may gain the victory.

**At Etham.** Etham means “sound strength,” or “profession,” in which we assume strength and vigor so that we do not fail on the way.

(Jerome, *Letter to Fabiola.) The fourth station is Pi-hahiroth, etc., up to: falsely taking for himself the name of virtue and the right hand, although he is wholly on the left.

**Verse 8.—At Marah, etc.** (Jerome, same work.) The fifth station is Marah, etc., up to: therefore do not shrink from arriving at bitterness. [Col. 0436D]

**Verse 9.—At Elim, where there were.** After setting out from bitterness, they came to Elim, where there were twelve springs of water and seventy palm trees. You see how pleasant are the places that receive you after bitterness and the harshness of temptations! You would not have come to the palms unless you had endured the bitterness of temptations, nor to the sweetness of the springs unless you had overcome sad and difficult things. This is not because the journey ends here or because all things are perfected here; rather, God, the steward of souls, inserts certain refreshments amid labors, by which the soul, restored, may become more ready for further labors. Elim is interpreted as “rams.” Rams are leaders of the flock; these are the apostles, leaders of Christ’s flock, and they are also the twelve [Col. 0437A] springs. But because Christ chose not only them but also another seventy, seventy palm trees are therefore said to exist; for they too are called apostles. Hence Paul says: “Then to all the apostles.” May this pleasantness receive you after bitterness, this rest after labor, this grace after temptation.

**Verse 10.—But having also departed from there, etc., beside the Red Sea.** For after apostolic teaching and the sweet fruits of victories, former dangers sometimes appear again.

They set out from Elim and encamped beside the Red Sea. Note that they no longer enter the sea; it is enough to have entered once. Rather, they encamp beside it. They see the sea and its waves, but they do not fear its movements and surges. [Col. 0437B]

**The Red Sea, etc.** (Jerome, work cited above.) In Hebrew, etc., up to: after they had departed from Rameses.

**Verse 11.—In the desert of Sin.** (Jerome, same work.) Having set out from the Red Sea, they encamped in the desert of Sin, etc., up to: because there are more children of the desolate woman than of her who has a husband.

Having set out from the Red Sea, they encamped in the desert of Sin. Sin is interpreted as “bush” or “temptation.” There the hope of good things first begins to smile, where the Lord appeared from the bush, gave answers to Moses, and initiated his visitation of the children of Israel. Temptation is usually present in visions; the angel of iniquity often transforms himself into an angel of light. Therefore one must act diligently in order to discern visions. Hence Joshua, when he saw visions, asked the one who appeared: “Are you for us or for our adversaries?” Thus, when the soul setting out has acquired discernment of visions, it will be proved to be spiritual. For discernment of spirits is among the gifts of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0437C]

**Verse 12.—At Dophkah.** In Hebrew, *Dophqah*, that is, “a knocking.” After the Lord’s answers, after the eighth number, that of Christ’s resurrection, we begin to knock upon the mysteries.

(Origen.) Having set out from the desert of Sin, they came to Dophkah, which is interpreted as “health.” Note the order of the departures. When the soul becomes spiritual and has discernment of visions, it reaches health, so that it may rightly say: “Bless the Lord, O my soul, who heals all your diseases.” There are many diseases of the soul—avarice, pride, boastfulness, fear, instability, and the like. [Col. 0437D]

**They encamped.** (Jerome, same work.) The tenth station is not found in Exodus, etc., up to: and the Scripture is fulfilled: “Man shall eat the bread of angels” (Psalm LXXVII).

Having set out from Dophkah, they came to Alush, that is, “labors.” Do not be surprised that labors follow health, because the soul is healed so that it may labor with delight, and it may be said to it: “You shall eat the labors of your hands; blessed are you, and it shall be well with you” (Psalm CXXVII).

**Verse 14.—Raphidim.** (Jerome, same work.) They encamped at Raphidim, etc., up to: the temptations of demons often arise. [Col. 0438A]

(Origen.) After this they came to Raphidim, which is interpreted as “the praise of judgment.” Praise rightly follows labors, but it is the praise of judgment: the soul becomes worthy of praise when it judges and distinguishes rightly—when, that is, it judges all things spiritually and is judged by no one.

**Verse 15.—In the desert of Sinai.** (Jerome.) Sinai is the twelfth station. Immediately let the number of the apostles come to mind. One among many, but greater than all, is not separated in rank but excels in merit. They reach this place on the forty-seventh day, as Scripture says: “In the third month after the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, on this day they entered the wilderness of Sinai” (Exodus XIX); afterward they come to the desert of Sina.

Sina is indeed a place in the desert, which he named above as Sin; [Col. 0438B] but here the place of the mountain that is in that desert is more particularly meant, and it is called Sina from the name of the desert. Therefore, after the soul has become praiseworthy in judgment and begun to possess right judgment, the law is given to it by God, because it is capable of divine mysteries and heavenly visions.

**Verse 16.—At the graves of desire, etc.** (Jerome.) The thirteenth station is the graves of desire. The meaning is that found in the Gospel: after the Lord Jesus had been baptized, he was immediately led by the Spirit into the desert and tempted by the devil (Matthew IV). Thus Israel, after familiar conversation with God, after dwelling beside Mount Sinai for one year and four days, by a wondrous arrangement of the camps went out into the wilderness of Paran, which is interpreted as “wild ass” or “wildness”; and there it succumbed to the evil beast, disdaining heavenly bread. [Col. 0438C]

(Origen.) Having set out from Sina, they came to the graves of desire, where desires are buried and covered over and every craving is extinguished, so that the flesh may no longer desire against the spirit, having been put to death by the death of Christ.

**Verse 17.—At Hazeroth.** (Jerome.) The fourteenth station is Hazeroth, which is interpreted as “courts.” There Aaron and Miriam murmur against Moses on account of the Ethiopian woman; and the Jewish people, as a type of one murmuring against the Church gathered from the nations, is covered with leprosy and does not return to the tabernacle with its former health until the appointed time of the fullness of the nations has been completed.

[Col. 0438D]

(Origen.) After this they come to Hazeroth, which is interpreted as “perfect courts” or “blessedness.” Consider more carefully, traveler, what the order of the departures is. After you have buried and mortified the desires of the flesh, you will come to the broad expanses of the courts, and you will come to blessedness. Blessed is the soul that is no longer oppressed by any vices of the flesh.

**Verse 18.—At Rithmah.** (Jerome, work cited above.) They encamped at Rithmah, etc., up to: and let us proclaim the Gospel with a clear sound. [Col. 0438D]

(Origen.) From there they come to Rithmah or Paran. Rithmah is interpreted as “completed vision”; Paran, however, as “visible mouth.” What else does this mean but that the soul should grow so that, when it has ceased to be oppressed by the troubles of the flesh, it may possess completed visions [Col. 0439A] and grasp a perfect understanding of realities—knowing more deeply the causes of the incarnation of the Word of God and the reasons for his dispensations?

**Verse 19.—At Rimmon-perez.** (Jerome.) “The division of the pomegranate,” by which the Church is signified as being enclosed like many grains under one rind, since it gathers the whole multitude of believers into the unity of faith. Or it signifies the variety and harmony of virtues, whence: “The multitude of believers was of one heart and one soul” (Acts IV); thus the individual ranks are divided in such a way that all are held together by the same structure.

(Origen.) From there they come to Rimmon-perez, where a separation is made between riches and heavenly things on the one hand and earthly and lowly things on the other. As the understanding of the soul grows, knowledge of exalted things is given to it, together with [Col. 0439B] judgment by which it knows how to distinguish eternal things from temporal and perishing things from everlasting.

**Verse 20.—At Libnah, etc.** That is, “brick.” In this passage we sometimes grow and sometimes decline, and after many advances we often return to brick—that is, to carnal works. After this they come to Libnah, which is interpreted as “whitening.” I know that in other places whitening is used culpably, as when it says “a whitened wall” and “whitened tombs.” Here, however, it is the whitening of which it is said: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Psalm L); and, “Though your sins be like scarlet, I will make them white as snow.” And elsewhere: “They shall be whitened with snow in Salmon.” The hair of the Ancient of Days is also said to be white, that is, white like wool. This whitening, therefore, is understood to come from the splendor of true light [Col. 0439C] and to descend from the brightness of heavenly visions.

**Verse 21.—At Rissah.** That is, “bridles.” For if we descend to muddy works, we must be bridled; and, wandering and rushing headlong, we must be directed by the restraints of Scripture.

(Origen.) After this there is a station at Rissah, etc., up to: therefore it is a visible or praiseworthy temptation.

**Verse 23.—At Mount Shepher.** (Jerome.) “Of beauty.” The mountain of beauty is Christ. The twentieth station is established at the mountain of beauty, concerning which it is said: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?” etc. (Psalm XIV). You see what the bridles accomplish: they draw us back from vices, lead us into the choirs of virtues, [Col. 0439D] and make us dwell in Christ, the most beautiful mountain.

(Origen.) Another reading. From there they come to Mount Shepher, which is called “trumpet-blowing.” The trumpet is a sign of war. When the soul feels itself armed with such and so great virtues, it necessarily goes forth to war, which is against principalities and powers and the rulers of this world. Or the trumpet sounds in the word of God—that is, in teaching and preaching—so that whoever hears the trumpet may prepare himself for battle.

**Verse 24.—At Haradah.** (Jerome.) “A miracle.” Note the order: after the bridles we are brought into the Church; from there we ascend to the mountain of Christ, where, established, we marvel at things that “neither eye has seen nor ear has heard.”

[Col. 0440A]

(Origen.) From Mount Shepher they came to Haradah, which is interpreted as “having been made fit,” so that one may say: “He made us fit ministers of the New Testament” (1 Corinthians II).

**Verse 25.—Makahaloth.** “Assembly.” This is the Church, of which it is said: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together” (1 Corinthians III). Or it is the harmony of all virtues.

(Origen.) From there they come to Makheloth, which is interpreted as “from the beginning.” For the person who strives toward perfection contemplates the beginning of things—or rather, he refers all things to the one who was in the beginning with God and never departs from that beginning.

(Jerome.) From there they come to Makheloth, which means “principality” or “rods.” In either case power is indicated, and that the soul has progressed so far that it rules the body, as though holding the rod of power—or rather, the whole world, when it says: “The world is crucified to me,” etc. (Galatians VI). [Col. 0440B]

**Verse 26.—Tahath.** “Fear,” which is the guardian of blessedness, so that the person who has climbed so high does not become proud. It is as though one were saying: You have come to the Church, you have climbed the most beautiful mountain, and in amazement and wonder you confess the greatness of Christ. You see there many companions in virtue: “Do not be high-minded, but think with sober judgment” (Romans XII). Fear is the guardian of virtues; security is unstable. Hence: “Your rod and your staff, they have comforted me” (Psalm XII). This means that while I fear punishments, I preserve the grace I have received.

(Origen.) After this there is a station at Tahath, which means “confirmation” or “patience.” For it is necessary that the person who wishes to benefit others suffer many things and bear all things patiently; hence: “For I will show him how much he must suffer for my name” (Acts IX). [Col. 0440C]

**Verse 27.—They encamped at Terah.** (Jerome.) That is, “malice,” etc., up to: and Elijah is fed by ravens.

(Origen.) From there they come to Terah, which means “contemplation of amazement,” that is, ecstasy, when the mind is astonished by admiration of some great thing.

(Jerome.) Terah means “malice” or “pasture,” which refers either to the leaders of the Church or to the guardianship of the soul, so that the one who feeds may be watchful lest the devil intrude into the sheepfolds—that is, the churches—through some opening made by vices.

**Verse 28.—Mithkah.** (The same author.) “Sweetness.” As though to say: You have climbed the lofty [Col. 0440D] mountain of the Father and marveled at the choirs of virtues; you feared falling and cast down the ambushers. Therefore the sweet fruit of labor follows you, so that the Psalmist may say: “How sweet are your words to my palate” (Psalm CXVIII)! Samson, who had driven the birds away from his fruits and had bound the foxes that destroy the vineyards, and had also killed the roaring lion, found a honeycomb in the mouth of the dead.

After this they came to Mithkah, which is interpreted as “a new death.” A new death occurs when we die and are buried with Christ, so that we may live with him.

**Verse 29.—Hashmonah.** It is interpreted as “haste,” because after the sweet fruits of labor we must not [Col. 0441A] be idle, but, forgetting what lies behind, we should stretch ourselves toward what lies ahead.

(Origen.) From there they come to Seman, which is said to signify “mouth” or “bones”; in it the strength and vigor of patience are declared.

**Verse 30.—Moseroth.** (Jerome.) “Bonds” or “discipline.” So that we may wear down the thresholds of our teachers and regard the precepts of virtues and the mysteries of Scripture as eternal bonds against the power and chains of the devil, by breaking which Samson conquered his enemies. Of these it is said: “You have broken my bonds” (Psalm CXV). The one who has been bound by the bond of Christ will say: “His left hand is under my head, and his right hand embraces me” (Song of Songs II).

(Origen.) From there they come to Moseroth, which means “excluding,” so that he may now exclude the suggestions of the hostile spirit from his thoughts. Hence: “If the spirit of the ruler rises against you, do not leave your place” (Ecclesiastes X). Therefore one must hold one’s place and exclude the adversary, lest he find a place in our heart. Hence: “Do not give the devil a place” (Ephesians IV). [Col. 0441B]

**Verse 32.—They came to Bene-jaakan, etc.** (Jerome.) “Sons of necessity” or “of gnashing of teeth,” the twenty-eighth station. Note the number: if you begin with one and gradually add until you reach seven, the result is twenty-eight.

(The same author.) Bene-jaakan is interpreted as “sons of necessity” or “of gnashing.” Of these sons it is said: “Bring to the Lord the sons of rams” (Psalm XXVIII). When you have been instructed in the divine Scriptures and have learned that their laws and testimonies are bonds of charity, then, contending with adversaries, you will bind them and lead them captive; and from enemies and captives you will make free children of God. The sons of gnashing, through fear of punishment, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth, will abandon the bonds of the devil and submit their necks to Christ. [Col. 0441C]

(Origen.) After this they come to Bene-jaakan, which signifies “springs” or “refinings,” where the soul draws up the springs of divine words until it refines them by drinking, so that not even the smallest commandment, indeed not one iota or one stroke of the word of God, is considered useless in its understanding.

**Mount.** (Jerome.) Gadgad or Galgad is interpreted as “messenger,” “action,” or “cutting.” For we cannot make sons of necessity unless we have killed their [Col. 0441D] teachers, and unless our hand spares neither the shoulder nor the tip of the ear when extracting it from the lion’s mouth, and unless we have announced future rewards and taught those who are girded how to rebel. Hence: “Cursed is he who does the work of God negligently and withholds his sword from blood” (Jeremiah XLVIII). And David: “In the morning I killed all the sinners of the land” (Psalm C).

(Origen.) After this he comes to Gadgad, which is interpreted as “temptation” or “constriction.” A certain strength in God and a fortress is the soul’s temptation. For it is so mingled with virtues that they seem thereby neither beautiful nor complete; and therefore, for those proceeding toward virtue, various and frequent stations occur in temptations. When you have passed through them, you will arrive at Jotbathah. Jotbathah is interpreted as “good”; therefore one reaches the good only after experience of temptations. [Col. 0442A]

**Of Jotbathah.** (Jerome.) Goodness, which is Christ. When we have come to the perfect man, to priestly maturity, and to the age of the fullness of Christ, in which Ezekiel was beside the river Chebar (Ezekiel I), may we be able to sing with David in the psalm: “Lord, in you I have hoped; let me never be confounded” (Psalm XXX). For the good shepherd lays down his life for his sheep (John X).

**Verse 34.—Hebronah.** (The same author.) “Passage,” that is, “the world.” For the form of this world passes away; the saints, coming into it, desire to pass on to better things. To this station comes the true Hebrew, that is, the one who passes over, who can say: “Passing by, I shall see this great vision” (Exodus III). Hence: “Those who passed by did not say, ‘The blessing of the Lord be upon you’” (Psalm CXXVIII). [Col. 0442B]

(Origen.) From there they encamped at Hebronah, which means “passage”; for everything must be passed through. Even if you come to good things, you must pass on to better things, until you come to that good in which you ought always to remain.

**Verse 35.—At Ezion-geber.** (Jerome.) “Wood of a man.” For the kinds of groves and of all trees can signify the multitude of the nations. Up to this point the wilderness of Paran contains eighteen stations, which, though listed here, are not included in the account of the earlier journey.

(Origen.) After this they come to Ezion-geber, which is interpreted as [Col. 0442C] “the counsels of a man.” If someone has ceased to be a child in understanding, he reaches the counsels of a man, like the one who said: “When I became a man, I put away childish things” (1 Corinthians XIII). Thus there are great counsels of a man; hence: “Deep water is counsel in a man’s heart” (Proverbs XX).

**Verse 36.—Into the desert, etc.** (Jerome.) The question is raised, etc., up to: concerning this station it is said: “The Lord will shake the desert of Kadesh.”

(Origen.) From here they come again to Sin, that is, “temptation,” because there is no other way by which this journey can properly be made. For when a goldsmith wishes to make a vessel useful, he repeatedly brings it to the fire and subjects it to hammers and scrapers, so that it may become purer and reach the form that the craftsman envisions.

(The same author.) After this they came to Paran of Kadesh, etc., [Col. 0442D] up to: one dies in the valley, another in the plains, another on a mountain, and another on the mountain of a mountain.

(The same author.) From there they came to Mount Hor, which is interpreted as “mountainous.” For he comes to the mountain of God so that he may become a fruitful mountain, a mountain made firm. Or he is called “mountainous” because he always dwells on the mountain of God.

**Verse 38.—Aaron the priest died in, etc.** (Isidore.) Aaron died in the same year in which the new people was about to enter the land of promise. Although on the mountain he left the priesthood to Eleazar, and although the law leads those who fulfill it to the summit, that very height is not beyond the waters of the Jordan but at the furthest limits of earthly works. The people mourned him for thirty days. Aaron is mourned; Jesus is not mourned. Under the law there is descent to the underworld; in the Gospel there is ascent to paradise. [Col. 0443A]

**Verse 40.—And the Canaanite heard.** (Isidore.) The Canaanite also heard that Israel had come, and at the place of the spies, where he knew that the people had once offended, he entered into battle and took Israel captive. Again he is defeated at the same place; the victor, overcome by his vow, is conquered, and the conquered prevail. By this we understand that, when enemies have taken us captive because we were deprived of God’s help, we should not despair of salvation but fight again. It can happen that we conquer where we were conquered. The name of that place was called Hormah, that is, “anathema.”

**Verse 41.—At Zalmonah.** (Jerome.) They encamped at Zalmonah, etc., up to: they grow weary of manna and are wounded by serpents. [Col. 0443B]

(Origen.) It follows, etc., up to: it is Christ and the Holy Spirit.

(Jerome.) Zalmonah means “a little image,” because there the image of the Savior was represented through the bronze serpent that hung upon the wood.

**Verse 42.—Punon.** “Mouth,” because when we recognize the passion of the Son of God, what we believe with the heart we proclaim with the mouth, according to the saying: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness,” etc. (Romans X).

(Origen.) From there they come to Punon, which we think means “restraint of the mouth.” For whoever has been able to contemplate the mystery of Christ and of the Holy Spirit, and has seen or heard things that it is not lawful for a human being to speak, will necessarily exercise restraint of mouth, knowing to whom, when, and how one ought to speak about divine mysteries.

[Col. 0443C]

**Verse 43.—Oboth.** (Jerome.) “Magicians” or “python-spirits,” because after the image of God displayed in the heart through reason and the confession of faith spoken by the mouth, serpents and magical arts rise up to provoke us to battle. But, guarding our heart with every care, let us close our ears so that we do not hear the voices of enchanters and the songs of sirens.

(Origen.) After this they come to Oboth. Although we have not found an interpretation of this name, we do not doubt that, as with the other names, the sequence of progressions is preserved here also.

**Verse 44.—At the borders.** According to the literal sense, this signifies that up to this point they had been in the territory of the Edomites, and now they come to the borders of Moab.

(Origen.) After this the station Gai follows, that is, [Col. 0443D] “chaos.” For through this progression he approaches the bosom of Abraham, who says: “A great chaos has been fixed between us and you” (Luke XVI), so that he may rest with Lazarus.

**At Dibon-gad.** (Jerome.) Dibon-gad, etc., up to: but, on the contrary, let us recognize that the wilderness has been set before us.

(Origen.) From there they come again to Dibon-gad, etc., up to: so that it may be known how perfectly and devoutly he thinks about God.

**Verse 46.—Almon-diblathaim.** (Jerome.) Which is interpreted as, etc., up to: scarcely freed by the prayers of the people. [Col. 0444A]

(Origen.) After this they come to Almon-diblathaim, which is interpreted as “contempt of figs,” that is, a place where earthly things are utterly despised. For unless the things that seem attractive on earth have been despised, we cannot pass over to heavenly things.

**Verse 47.—They came to Mount Abarim, opposite Nebo, etc.** (Jerome.) The forty-first station is translated as “the mountains of those who pass over,” and it is opposite Mount Nebo.

(Origen.) The station Abarim follows, which means “passage,” opposite Naban, which means “departure.” When the soul has passed through all these virtues and ascended to the summit of perfection, it now passes out of the world and departs like Enoch, who was not found because God translated him. Even if he still seems to be in the world and to dwell in the flesh, he is nevertheless not found in any worldly activity, because God has translated him [Col. 0444B] into the region of virtues.

(Jerome.) Here Moses dies, having already seen the land of promise. Nebo is interpreted as “conclusion,” in which the law comes to an end and its memory is no longer found, while the grace of the Gospel endures without end. It should also be noted that the station of those who pass over is situated in the mountains and still requires progress. For after the mountains we descend to the plains of Moab and the waters of the Jordan, whose name is interpreted as “descent.” Nothing is more dangerous than the desire for glory and boastfulness, and a mind swollen with the consciousness of its virtues.

**Verse 48.—To the plains of Moab.** (The same author.) In the forty-second station, etc., up to: and the thorns that choked the seed of the word of God, concerning which it is said: “I was afflicted while [Col. 0444C] a thorn was fixed in me” (Psalm XXXI).

(Origen.) The last station is, etc., up to: they indicate the progress of the mind and the increase of virtues.

**Verse 51.—When you have crossed the Jordan,** that is, when you have been baptized—as though to say: when, having put off the old person with his deeds, you have put on the new (Colossians III), who is renewed in the knowledge of God.

**Verse 52.—Destroy them all.** When we enter the holy land of promise through faith, let us extinguish all vices together with idolatry.

**The inhabitants.** Wicked spirits, phantoms of vices, together with their suggestions. Hence: “Blessed is the one who will seize and dash his little ones against the rock” (Psalm CXXXVII).

**Verse 54.—To the greater number you shall give the wider portion.** For those who possess an abundance of virtues hope for a breadth of rewards; but those who are content with a small number of virtues receive a recompense according to their merit. Hence: “Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows with blessings will reap from blessings,” etc. (2 Corinthians IX).

[Col. 0444D]

### Chapter XXXIV

And the Lord spoke, etc. (Origen, Homily 1 on Numbers.) Not everyone is worthy of divine numbers, etc., up to: as though they proceeded from the head of the apostles.

Therefore the Lord spoke to Moses in the desert of Sinai those things that we briefly summarized above, [Col. 0445A] where it is commanded that everyone who goes forth in the strength of Israel, from twenty years old and upward, be counted, etc. Thus, if someone goes forth in strength, he is counted—not in just any strength, whether of Egyptians, Assyrians, or Greeks, but in the strength of Israel, which is taught by God through the Scriptures and handed down through apostolic and evangelical faith.

(ORIG.) The distinction of the tribes and the differentiation of their orders, etc., up to “so that he may be able to belong to the Israelite number.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Toward the northern region,” etc. The Hebrews say that the northern region begins at the Great Sea, which stretches along the shores of Palestine, Phoenicia, Syria (which is called Coele), and Cilicia, and extends through Egypt toward Libya. But when it is said that they reached as far as the highest mountain, they believe that Mount Amanus, or Taurus, is meant; the latter seems more likely.

**VERSE 9.**—“And the boundaries shall proceed,” etc. From the end of the northern region, that is, from the court of Hena, the boundaries extend as far as Sephama, which the Hebrews call Apamea; from Apamea they descend to Reblatha, which is Antioch of Syria. Hence he adds, “opposite the spring,” which plainly is Dan, from which Antioch enjoys an abundance of water.

**VERSE 13.**—“This shall be the land,” etc. (ORIG.) In the earlier division, the land beyond the Jordan was divided through Moses among the two tribes, Reuben and Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, etc., up to “and they are separated, joined even to those walls.”

[Col. 0445C] (ID.) It also seems to some, etc., up to “These are truly numbered by God with sacred numbers—or rather, all their hairs have been numbered” (Matt. X).

## CHAPTER XXXV

**VERSE 11.**—“Appoint the cities.” (AUG., *Question 64 on Numbers*) What does he mean when he says, etc., up to “if it should be made manifest in the judgment that he killed unwillingly.”

(RAB. on Numbers) If perhaps, because of the consciousness of their sins, the cities of the Promised Land, etc., up to “because Shechem was purchased from foreigners for one hundred lambs.”

**VERSE 16.**—“Guilty,” that is, liable to eternal death. Hence: “Whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” etc. (Matt. XVIII). And elsewhere: “Everyone who hates his brother is a murderer, and he does not have eternal life” (I John III). According to Exodus, such a person is commanded to be dragged away from the altar (Exod. XXI), because one unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments is removed from participation in the sacred altar [Col. 0445D] and is not restored to pardon except through worthy repentance.

**VERSE 28.**—“But after he has died.” (GREG., *Homily 6 on Ezekiel*) After the death of the high priest, the murderer is commanded to return to his own land, because, after the death of the true priest, Christ, the human race, having brought death upon itself through sin, received absolution from its guilt.

**VERSE 26.**—“You shall not pollute the land of your habitation.” He pollutes the land of his habitation who commits bloody and wicked deeds, scandalizing his neighbors and killing them spiritually. Unless the desires of the flesh are put to death through confession of sins and worthy repentance, the land of his body will in no way be cleansed, nor will the Creator of all dwell in his soul [Col. 0446B], where He sees the squalor of a filthy way of life reigning.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**VERSE 1.**—“The leaders also approached,” etc. (RAB. on Numbers, vol. II) Pious thoughts ought to take care, etc., up to “lest, if they are carried out with a perverse intention, they be invaded by unclean spirits”; hence: “Take heed that you do not perform your righteousness before men” (Matt. VI).

**VERSE 6.**—“Let them marry.” The Apostle says something similar: “Let her marry whom she wishes, only in the Lord” (I Cor. VII), that is, a Catholic man, lest the possession of good works and right faith be lost if she marries a gentile or a Jew.

In the tropological sense, however, the woman—that is, a pious intention—may through good action join herself to whatever labor she wishes, provided that she preserves piety and religious devotion in everything, lest she suffer loss in the work for which she hopes to possess an eternal inheritance, if she joins herself to what is alien, that is, to what is earthly.

(RAB.) This happens when someone from the number of Jewish believers joins himself to a believing teacher from the nations, so that through his instruction he may beget children, that is, works of piety. Those chosen from the nations may also be called “uncles,” because they are brothers of the holy preachers who were established in Judaea. There should be no schism in spiritual kinship, where there is one faith in its confession. And just as there is one shepherd, there ought to be one sheepfold: “For we are all brothers” (John X; Matt. XXIII; II Cor. XI).

[Col. 0446D] Whoever strives to possess humility and takes pleasure in his infirmities celebrates a solemnity for himself, offers pleasing gifts to God, and becomes king of his own conduct; he is moved forward by the progress of the virtues, walking from virtue to virtue.

[Col. 0445]

# THE BOOK OF DEUTERONOMY

In Hebrew, **ELLEH HADDEBARIM**, that is, **THESE ARE THE WORDS**. (G)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0445D]

“A choice cluster of myrrh is for me.” Myrrh is an aromatic tree that grows only five cubits high; its bark, root, leaves, and everything else are bitter. Myrrh is bitter and is applied to corpses to ward off the rotting of worms. This is the Old Law, contained in five books: bitter—that is, sparing no one; hence it was also designated by *Marah*; applied to corpses—that is, given for sinners, so that it might keep the corruption of their crimes away from them.

This cluster is Deuteronomy, that is, a collection of many little branches gathered into one. For once the law had been completed in four volumes, this fifth was added, briefly collecting together what had been stated at length and also supplying certain omissions. It was added to them in order to satisfy the legal number. For the number five belongs to the Law, while the number four belongs to the Gospel. Hence the feeding of the five thousand in the Gospel refers to the fathers of the Old Testament, while the feeding of the four thousand refers to the fathers of the New Testament. To the former earthly things were promised and given, things subject to the five senses; to the latter, things squared [Col. 0447B], that is, the solidity of the land of the living.

This book also serves the Gospel in its name, in the sequence of its explanation, and in its dignity. For in Hebrew it is called *Elleh Haddebarim*, that is, “These are the words”; in Greek, **δευτερονόμιον** (*deuteronomion*), which in Latin is “the second law.” This does not mean, as some have said, another law after the preceding one—so that in the preceding books it was said, “The Lord spoke,” whereas here it is said, “Moses spoke”—but a second law in the sense of one repeated a second time. By this name it prefigures the Gospel, which succeeded the Law and will itself have no successor.

Since it briefly gathers many things together and supplies certain omissions, it prefigures the form of the Gospel. For this is the abbreviated word that the Lord made upon the earth, and it supplies what was incomplete in the Law; hence: “I have not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it” (Matt. V).

When this work is said to be so worthy that it is commanded to be carried in the hands of a king, it reveals the dignity of the Gospel, which was ordained in the hand of the Mediator. Since it thus serves the Gospel, it is rightly a beloved cluster to Christ—not so much on its own account as because it displays “a wheel within a wheel.”

Its purpose is to recapitulate what was previously said for three reasons: so that it may be more firmly entrusted to memory, so that the usefulness of what was previously said may be impressed upon us, and so that the hardness of the Jews may be condemned, since they did not understand what had been said so many times. For what is useful should be said often, and this ought neither to be burdensome, as the Apostle says (Phil. III), nor tedious to hear.

The method of the work is as follows. First, it places a kind of prologue, in which it shows who wrote and what he wrote, etc. Then it recalls the serious offense for which they perished in the wilderness, so that it may rouse them to listen through fear of this example. Next, it distinguishes the cities of refuge. Then it recapitulates the good and evil things that were said and done, and supplies what was lacking. Afterward it commands that this book be placed in the ark and read to all Israel in the year of the Feast of Booths. Then it adds the song beginning, “Give ear,” as a memorial of their murmuring and punishment, their obedience and reward. After that come the blessings of the tribes. Finally, it treats of the death of Moses.

## CHAPTER I

**VERSE 1.**—“These are the words,” etc. The lawgiver places at the beginning the title, as a kind of prologue, in which he indicates the author’s name, what he did, and where and when he did it. As will be distinguished shortly in the gloss, it ends, as some think, at the words “in the fortieth year,” or farther below, at “the Lord our God.”

To clarify what is contained in the prologue and what follows, a little of the historical truth must be touched upon. From the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt until they reached the plains of Moab above the Jordan, forty-two years elapsed; during these they made forty-two encampments at various times. Whenever the cloud was lifted, the camps were moved, and when it stood still, they were fixed and remained in the same place until the cloud was lifted again.

The first encampment was at Rameses, the last in the plains of Moab. From Rameses to Mount Sinai, over a period of forty-seven days, they made twelve encampments in the first year, and there they remained for almost the entire year. There the law was given; there Genesis was written, as well as Exodus and Numbers, and [Col. 0448B] a large part of this book. From there, setting out in the second year, they reached Cadesbarne, and within that interval made twenty encampments. From Cadesbarne they sent out spies, who returned reporting that the land was good but that they had found strong and gigantic men there. Terrified, they wished to return to the land of Egypt, and the Lord became angry with them.

They turned back and traversed Mount Seir for thirty-eight years; there the murmurers died and fell. In the fortieth year they came to Cadesbarne, from which they again went back through the wilderness, making nine more encampments during that interval. Over eleven days, before coming to Cadesbarne, Moses recapitulated the Law orally; from Cadesbarne to the plains of Moab, during that interval of eleven days, he wished to commit it to writing [Col. 0448C].

Thus there were twelve encampments in the first year, twenty-one in the second, and nine in the remaining years—forty-two encampments altogether.

This was the reason for the composition of this book: that what had happened might be collected briefly and held more firmly in memory, for things said briefly are easily retained.

(RAB. on Deuteronomy) “These are the words,” etc. The beginning of Deuteronomy appears to be the title of the entire work, because it indicates the author’s person, what he did, the place, and the time. The name of the book also reveals the grace of the New Testament. For *Deuteronomy* is interpreted as “the second law,” and it signifies the Gospel, which explains spiritually the mysteries of the Old Testament [Col. 0448D]. Just as the book of Deuteronomy is a repetition of the four books of the Law—for those contain their own particular subjects, while this repeats everything and also has its own mysteries.

(ID.) “These are the words.” He speaks about himself as though about another, etc., up to “so that no one can doubt that Moses wrote these things.”

“He spoke.” Moses is the Old Law, which taught the Israelite people beyond the Jordan, that is, before baptism. For the Jordan signifies baptism, in which Christ was baptized; the plain wilderness signifies the barrenness of the carnal people, which bore no fruit of virtue.

“In the wilderness”: in the barrenness of the people, to whom it is said, “Your house shall be left to you desolate” (Matt. XXXI; Luke XIII).

“Opposite the sea.” Because the perverse and crooked generation refused to believe in the washing away of sins through the blood of Christ.

“Between Pharan.” *Pharan* means “increased”; *Tophel*, “insipidity”; *Laban*, “whitening”; *Haseroth*, “courts.” The people increased in number, in the teaching of the Law and the prophets; but they were insipid because they did not possess the salt of wisdom. They were whitened by the ceremonies of the Law and by various purifications, which they believed they possessed from the letter of the Law. They are appropriately signified by “courts,” as though prepared through the divine Scriptures for entrance into faith. Hence many more readily received Christ at His coming, because they recognized Him whom they had previously learned was foretold. Thus Philip says: “We have found Jesus, the son of Joseph, from Nazareth, of whom Moses wrote in the law, and the prophets” (John I). These four mountains signify the four Gospels, by which the Church is surrounded.

**VERSE 2.**—“Eleven days.” The Law, explained through Moses over eleven days, signifies the transgression of the Jewish people against the commandments of the Decalogue.

The eleven days are the eleven apostles through whom, after Judas had been rejected, the Gospel of Christ was preached throughout the world.

“From Horeb.” In Hebrew, *Choreb* [the supplied text leaves the following Hebrew form blank]; beginning at Seir—that is, passing through the people hairy and filthy with vices—it came to Cadesbarne, which is interpreted as “changed,” “chosen,” or “noble,” signifying the literal meaning of the Law changed into the spiritual meaning through the Gospel [Col. 0449C]. For “all these things happened to them in figure, and they were written for our correction, upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (I Cor. X). The Law has not been abolished but fulfilled, and not one iota or one stroke will pass away until all things come to pass (Matt. V).

**VERSE 3.**—“In the fortieth year, in the eleventh month, on the first day,” etc. (ISID., on Deuteronomy, vol. V) Forty years, etc., up to “will remain without corruption.”

The number forty consists of ten and four, and signifies the fulfillment of the Law and the Gospel, which takes place in the Church. For ten belongs to the Law, while four belongs to the Gospel.

“In the eleventh month,” etc. Just as the eleventh signifies the transgression of the Law, so on the first day the lawgiver’s intention is fully awake for teaching. From the moment the disobedient people did not fear transgressing the Law, he immediately strove, by preaching and correcting, to make the Lord’s will known and did not cease to draw or summon them to better things by words and examples.

**VERSE 4.**—“After he had struck down Sihon,” etc. It should be noted that, after the two kings of the Amorites had been killed, the Law is recapitulated and the people instructed. Once scandals have been removed and the hosts of vices overcome, one may properly devote oneself to teaching, and the light of faith is worthily opened to those who desire it.

We must first kill the vices within ourselves and then hand on the divine commandments to the people.

“Sihon, king of the Amorites, who lived in Heshbon,” etc. (ISID.) In these kings, etc., up to “but, remaining outside, they always persist in wicked works.”

**VERSE 5.**—“In the land of Moab.” The people were indeed outside the law, since they did not possess the spiritual Law.

**VERSE 6.**—“The Lord our God.” In the Book of Numbers, the departure of the children of Israel from the wilderness of Sinai is narrated, but the Lord’s command to Moses concerning this journey is not mentioned. Instead, it speaks of the cloud that covered the tabernacle, which withdrew whenever they were to depart and went ahead to the place where the camps were to be set up. For it is written: “In the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, the cloud was lifted from the tabernacle of the covenant and rested in the wilderness of Pharan” (Num. X).

It is nevertheless clear that this journey was arranged by God’s command, although it is not mentioned there [Col. 0450B]. Hence elsewhere in the Book of Numbers it says that they pitched their tents at the Lord’s command and took them down at His command (Num. IX).

“You have stayed long enough,” etc. Moses is commanded to depart from the mountain on which he had received the Law, because a teacher ought not always remain intent upon contemplation but should sometimes descend in order to care for himself and for his neighbors. Hence: “Whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you.”

**VERSE 9.**—“And I said to you at that time,” etc. Concerning this division of authority, Exodus records that, before they came to Mount Sinai, Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ kinsman, suggested it to Moses himself (Exod. XVIII). Therefore it is rightly asked how the two accounts can agree. But when Moses is said here to have spoken at that time—“I cannot bear you alone,” etc.—the reference is not to the time when they departed from Horeb, but to the whole period during which, after departing from Egypt, they remained in the wilderness. Moses persuaded his people of this not on his own initiative but on the advice of his kinsman.

“At that time.” The saints do everything at the appropriate time; so God too, “when the fullness of time had come, sent his Son” (Gal. IV).

**VERSE 11.**—“May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add,” etc. He teaches teachers to rejoice in the progress of their subjects, to give thanks, and always to hope for better things.

“To this number,” etc. It is determined by God. He knows those who are His, He who numbers the multitude of the stars (II Tim. II).

(RAB.) See how carefully one must observe what Scripture says elsewhere: “My son, do not let your actions be many” (Eccli. XI). Consider also the words of Jethro giving counsel, for he says: “Listen to me, and I will give you counsel, and God will be with you” (Exod. XVIII). This appears to signify that a mind excessively occupied with human actions is in some way emptied of God; it becomes fuller in proportion as it extends itself more freely toward heavenly and eternal things.

**VERSE 13.**—“Give from among yourselves.” “Give yourselves,” not “I will”; as though he were saying: I do not wish to command you, but to obey you.

“I will appoint them.” Observe that he grants the subjects the choice but reserves the appointment to himself, lest the people despise or hate someone if they were not permitted to have the person they wished.

“Tribunes.” Leaders of thousands, in Greek **χιλιάρχους** (*chiliarchous*), who teach their subjects to hope for the eternal reward.

[Col. 0451A] “And centurions.” Centurions, in Greek **ἑκατοντάρχους** (*hekatontarchous*), who hand on heavenly commandments to the perfect. Those who are endowed with the number one hundred—that is, with perfection—are rightly placed in authority. They rule a hundred, as it were, while bringing them to perfection.

“And leaders of fifties.” In Greek **πεντηκοντάρχους** (*pentēkontarchous*), who proclaim works of repentance.

“Leaders of tens,” **δεκάρχους** (*dekarchous*): those who, possessing the perfection of the number ten and expecting the denarius of the vineyard, prepare many to share in that same denarius.

**VERSE 17.**—“For the judgment belongs to God,” not to men, because in judging you are God’s representatives, and He shows no partiality.

“But if something is difficult.” The greater and more difficult matters must be distinguished and judged by the greater; the small and easy matters by the lesser [Col. 0451B].

**VERSE 19.**—“And when we had come to Cadesbarne,” etc. That the people came in the second year after their departure into the wilderness of Pharan, which is Cades, where, after the spies returned with the fruits of the land and reported what they had seen, they murmured against Moses and Aaron and therefore perished, worn out by the fatigue of the long journey and by mortality—this passage provides clear evidence.

It should be noted here that the forty-two encampments they had from Egypt to the Jordan appear to correspond to only three periods of years: the first, the second, and the fortieth year after their departure from Egypt.

The first year clearly contains twelve encampments: the first, Rameses, entered on the fifteenth day of the first month; and the last, the wilderness of Sinai, reached on the first day of the third month. They did not leave it for eleven continuous months, because they were constructing the tabernacle and receiving instruction in the Law. Of these twelve encampments, only nine are expressly named in Exodus; three are indicated indistinctly under the name “the wilderness of Sin,” which is said to lie between Elim and Sinai.

The second year comprises twenty-one encampments. In the sequence of the narrative, all of these are included indiscriminately under the name “the wilderness of Pharan”; only the first, the second, and the last—namely, the Graves of Lust, Haseroth, and Cades—are distinguished by name. But in the catalogue of the encampments, all are shown, both in their number and by the names by which they were called.

The first encampment, namely, the Graves of Lust, was entered in the second month of that second year, on the twentieth day of the month [Col. 0451D]. For, as Scripture says, in the second year, in the second month, on the twentieth day of the month, they moved their camps from the wilderness of Sinai, and the cloud rested in the wilderness of Pharan. They departed from the mountain of the Lord on a journey of three days, until they came to the place of encampment, which rightly received the name Graves of Lust because of the people’s craving for meat.

It is not said on what day or in what month of that same year they entered the last of these, namely, Cades. Nevertheless, it is not concealed that it lies in the wilderness of Pharan and was visited in that same year. For it is written: “The people did not move from that place until Mary was recalled. And they departed from Haseroth and pitched their tents in the wilderness of Pharan, where the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: Send men to inspect the land of Canaan” (Num. XII–XIII) [Col. 0452A].

To prevent anyone from thinking that this command was given and carried out at the encampment immediately following Haseroth, but rather that it was fulfilled at the last of those included under the name Pharan, it is written below: “The spies returned from the land after forty days, having traversed the whole region, and came to Moses in Pharan, which is Cades.”

In Deuteronomy also Moses says to the people: “When you came to Cadesbarne, I said to you: You have come to the mountain of the Amorites,” etc.; and you said: “Send men to inspect the land,” etc. (Deut. I).

That they visited this same encampment in the second year after their departure, but because of the sin of their murmuring deserved to turn back, wander for a long time through the wilderness, and fall everywhere, Moses testifies in what follows, saying: “You remained in Cadesbarne for a long time. Then we departed and came into the wilderness that leads to the Red Sea, as the Lord had said to me; and we went around Mount Seir for a long time. And during the time in which we traveled from Cadesbarne to the torrent of Zared, thirty-eight years passed, until the whole generation of warriors was consumed.”

Zared is not the name of one of the forty-two encampments, but of a torrent to which they came—as is read in the Book of Numbers—after passing the eighteenth encampment, named Jeabarim. Leaving it, he says, they encamped opposite the Arnon, which is in the wilderness and projects into the borders of the Amorites. This took place in the fortieth year, as is clear; that final year contains ten encampments through the wilderness along the longest route [Col. 0452C].

The first of these was reached with great labor: Cades itself in the wilderness of Sin, which thirty-eight years earlier they had left behind when, because of their guilt, they turned back. Concerning it, it is written: “The children of Israel came into the wilderness of Sin in the first month, and the people remained in Cades. There Mary died and was buried in that same place. And when the people lacked water, they gathered against Moses and Aaron,” etc., up to: “This is the water of contradiction,” etc. (Num. XX).

It should be noted that this same Cades is said to have been both in the wilderness of Pharan and in the wilderness of Sin. Hence we infer that the part of the wilderness of Pharan where Cades is located was specifically called Sin. Alternatively, Sin is not the same Cades through which they passed shortly after crossing the Red Sea, between Elim and Sinai, but an entirely different place, written with different letters in Hebrew.

The second encampment of that fortieth year was Mount Hor, where Aaron died on the first day of the fifth month. The last was the plains of Moab above the Jordan, opposite Jericho, where they remained while meditating upon Deuteronomy until, after Moses’ death, they crossed the Jordan under Joshua’s leadership on the first day of the tenth month.

Thus the encampments of the first year total twelve; those of the second, twenty-one; and those of the final year, including Cades itself, twenty-one more—forty-two encampments altogether.

**VERSE 22.**—“And you approached me.” In the Book of Numbers it is written that the Lord told Moses to send men to inspect the land. Here, however, the people are said to have spoken: “Let us send men to inspect the land.” But the people first suggested this to Moses; Moses reported it to the Lord, and afterward, according to His command, sent out the spies.

**VERSE 23.**—“I sent from among you.” (ISID.) Twelve spies were sent to inspect the fertile land, etc., up to “because neither is Christ without the Law, nor the Law without Christ.”

“Twelve.” These signify the teachers of the Church, some of whom corrupt the people by teaching perverse things, while others advance them by preaching what is right.

**VERSE 33.**—“Showing the way by night.” The night signifies the sinner, the day the life of the righteous. In the pillar of fire is the condemnation of the wicked, to whom the Lord will appear terrifying in the judgment; in the pillar of cloud is the gentle and kindly vision by which the elect will be comforted.

“By day, through the pillar.” Shading and sustaining them amid the heat of this age through the strength and mercy of His flesh [Col. 0453B].

**VERSE 34.**—“He swore.” God is not subject to suffering or to the fault of anger. Rather, through these expressions Moses’ love for the people and God’s goodness, which surpasses all understanding, are made manifest.

**VERSE 35.**—“No one shall see it.” Something similar is said of those who excused themselves after being invited to the supper: “None of those men who were invited shall taste my supper” (Luke XIV).

The most wicked generation does not possess the good land, because it does not believe in the incarnation of Christ.

**VERSE 37.**—“Nor is this surprising.” Here Moses says, on account of the people, that the Lord was angry with him and said that he would not enter the Promised Land, whereas in the Book of Numbers we read: “The Lord said to Moses and Aaron: Because you did not believe me, so as to sanctify me before the children of Israel, you shall not bring these people into the land that I will give them.” But the sentence that follows appears to resolve the question: “This is,” he says, “the water of contradiction, where the children of Israel quarreled against the Lord,” etc. (Num. XX). The quarrel and rebellion of the people were the cause of anger and vengeance, both against the people and against Moses and Aaron.

“Neither shall you enter.” (ISID.) In Mary it appears, etc., up to “when Christ is recognized as exalted like the height of a mountain.”

**VERSE 41.**—“When you had armed yourselves.” This sentence strikes at human pride, which presumes upon its own strength and does not trust in God’s power. The Amorites, that is, “those who make bitter,” are spiritual enemies who dwell in the mountains of pride and kill the presumptuous, from Seir to Horma—that is, from the squalor of vices to the condemnation of punishments. For *Seir* means “hairy,” and *Horma* is interpreted as “anathema.” Whoever does not fear being polluted by the filth of vices must, according to his merits, be handed over to the fires of Gehenna.

The demons wish to entangle us in earthly desires; and if we persist in sins and do not cease to climb the mountain of pride, they strike us down with fiery arrows and lead us to perpetual anathema. Therefore, unlike the Pelagians, let us not presume upon our own power; rather, considering our weakness, let us obey the Lord in everything, so that, after overcoming our enemies, we may attain the promised joys of the heavenly homeland [Col. 0454A].

We must beware lest, while murmuring against the Lord, we ascend the mountain of pride, thinking that we can be saved by our own strength, and thus immediately be handed over to the Amorites, that is, to demons.

## CHAPTER II

**VERSE 1.**—“And we went around Mount Seir,” etc. Seir is a mountain in the land of Edom, in the region of Gebal, where Esau lived. The Horrite had lived there previously, but Chedorlaomer killed him. Seir received its name from Esau, who was hairy and shaggy—*Seir*, that is, “hairy ones.”

The Horrites, like the other nations whom the descendants of the patriarchs overcame, signify malignant spirits or vices. These can be overcome by those who follow the footsteps and teachings of the holy Fathers and carry on spiritual warfare under King Christ. Concerning this warfare it is said: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers,” etc. (Eph. VI).

**VERSE 9.**—“I gave it to the children of Lot.” Ar is the metropolis of the Moabites, on the bank of the torrent Arnon. It was formerly possessed by the very ancient people called the Emim and later held by the children of Lot, that is, by the Moabites, after its inhabitants had been overthrown. It can still be seen today on the summit of a mountain; the torrent descends through precipitous places and flows into the Dead Sea.

*Ar* is interpreted as “he raised up”; *Emim*, “terrible ones.” These are demons, who stir up quarrels and disputes and prepare weapons of wickedness against the faithful. The Enacim, too, descended from the stock of Enac and equaled the giants in stature. According to their name they signify demons, for they are interpreted as “a necklace upon a lofty neck.” Raised up by the arrogance of pride, they attribute all the equipment of their warfare to their own strength. Therefore they easily yield to those who trust in God’s power and say with the Psalmist: “The Lord is my strength and my praise, and he has become my salvation” (Ps. CXVII).

**VERSE 14.**—“From Cadesbarne.” (HIERON., *Letter to Fabiola*) Cabesbarne is a place in the wilderness adjoining the city of Petra in Arabia. There Mary died, and Moses, after striking the rock, gave water to the thirsty people. Even today Mary’s tomb is shown there; the princes of Amalek were also killed there by Chedorlaomer.

[Col. 0454D] **VERSE 26.**—“Therefore I sent messengers,” etc. Sihon signifies the devil, whose name means “useless shoot,” “fruitless tree,” or “the exalted one.” Israel signifies the Christian people, who desire to pass through the way of this world and reach the heavenly kingdoms.

Israel sends messengers to Sihon with peaceful words, promising that it will not dwell in his land but will merely pass through it and proceed along the royal road. Each person made this promise when he first came to the water of baptism and received the first seals of faith. For he renounced the devil and his pomp, his works, every form of his service, and his pleasures.

This is what is meant by the statement: “Israel shall not turn aside into his field or into his vineyard, nor drink water from his cistern” (Num. XXI), that is, it will no longer accept the discipline of astrology, magic, or any teaching opposed to piety [Col. 0455A]. Rather, it will drink from the springs of the Savior. It will not abandon the spring of living water in order to drink from Sihon’s spring, but will proceed along the royal road, which is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), and the king, according to the words: “O God, give your judgment to the king” (Ps. LXXI).

It will not turn aside into his field or his vineyard, that is, to his works or his perverse ideas. The Amorites are interpreted as “speakers” or “those who make bitter,” because they provoke God to bitterness and trust in words alone, like poets, astrologers, and philosophers, who speak empty things; but the kingdom of God is not in speech but in power.

The faithful wish to pass through in peace and to be peaceful even with the enemies of peace. But by saying that they do not wish to remain with him or touch anything belonging to him, they offend the ruler of the world all the more. Therefore, becoming more enraged, he persecutes them more fiercely, raises dangers, threatens torments, gathers his people, and goes out to fight against Israel.

His people are the rulers and judges of the world and all the ministers of wickedness who persecute the people of God. He himself also comes to Jahaz, which is interpreted as “fulfillment of the command.” Whoever comes to the fulfillment of God’s commandments will not fear Sihon or his raging army. For to fulfill God’s commandments is to overcome the devil and his army.

Thus God crushes Satan beneath our feet and gives us power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and upon all the strength of the enemy.

[Col. 0455C] **VERSE 30.**—“Because he had hardened.” He hardened him through long patience, by not correcting him; hence in Exodus: “I hardened Pharaoh’s heart” (Exod. X); and the Psalmist: “He turned their heart so that they hated his people” (Ps. CIV). The reason for the hardening is then added: “that he might deliver him into your hands,” that is, so that he might be crushed by you. This would not have happened unless he resisted, and he would not have resisted unless he had been hardened. If we seek the justice of this matter, his judgments are inscrutable, but there is no iniquity with God.

**VERSE 33.**—“And we struck him down.” Those who are true Israelites—not Jews according to the flesh but according to the spirit—dwell in all the cities of the Amorites, as the Churches of Christ are spread throughout the whole world. Each one of us was a city of King Sihon, because folly, pride, impiety, and everything suggested by the devil reigned in us [Col. 0455D].

But when the strong man was defeated and his vessels plundered, we became cities of Israel, the inheritance of the saints: the fruitless tree was first cut down, the exalted king cast out, and the gentle king began to reign in us, who says: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart,” etc. (Matt. XI).

The names of the places also fit the interpretation.
