For *Aroer* means “lifting up”; *Arnon*, “heap of sorrow”; *Gilead*, “heap of testimony.” From Aroer, therefore, which is on the bank of the torrent Arnon, etc., every person who trusts in the arrogance of pride or in worldly pomp, together with the persecutors who afflict Christians with various tribulations, even to the assemblies of heretics who fight against the Church with corrupted testimonies of Scripture, is handed over, defeated, into the hands of the saints, along with his habitations [Col. 0456A].

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 1.**—“Then we turned.” Against Og, who is king of Bashan, they do not deign to send messengers or ask permission to pass through his land. They immediately engage him in battle and overcome him and his people.

*Bashan* is interpreted as “turpitude.” Therefore no messengers are sent to this nation, nor is passage requested; we must have no passage or ascent toward turpitude, which must be attacked immediately and avoided altogether.

*Og* is interpreted as “confinement.” It signifies carnal things, by whose desire the soul is shut out and separated from God. Against these we must fight in such a way that no vice is left behind. Nothing ought to be left in the kingdom of turpitude; shameful things must be cut away so that honorable and religious things can be built up.

This is not commanded concerning the kingdom of Sihon or Moab. Perhaps we need something from those kingdoms, since the varied use of the present life requires it; otherwise we would have to leave this world. But from Bashan, that is, from turpitude, we leave nothing, because we need nothing from it. What is shameful cannot be honorable.

**Verse 4.—“Sixty.”** This confirms the preceding sense. For the number sixty, like six, signifies perfection. He appropriately mentions sixty cities destroyed in the region of Og, king of Bashan—that is, of the devil, who is the king of shame—for this signifies that the pleasure of all vices must be completely destroyed. **Argob**, that is, “cursed sublimity,” signifies earthly pride, which reigns in the sons of wrath. After the cities have been destroyed, he says that the men, women, and children were killed, and the animals and spoils seized, because, once the devil’s stronghold has been overcome, whatever we perceive in our flesh to be rebellious or wanton, together with its childish thoughts, must be crushed by zeal for God; but whatever we find suitable for God’s service in the simplicity of a pure understanding or in the adornment of our members, we ought to preserve.

**Verse 12.—“And the land.”** (Gregory, *Moralia*, book XXVII, chapter 10.) “There are many in the Church,” etc., up to “namely, empty desires and irrational movements of the soul.”

**Reuben and Gad.** (Rabanus.) Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, etc., up to “but with their women and children they strive to cross over and reach their homeland.”

**Verse 28.—“Command Joshua,” etc.** By God’s great dispensation it happened that Moses, who is a type of the Law, should not lead the people into the promised land, because the Law brought no one to perfection; but Joshua, a type of Christ, whose name is interpreted “savior” (for Christ saved his people), appropriately led them as guide and prince into the promised land.

### Chapter IV

**Verse 1.—“And now, Israel, hear the ordinances and judgments. You shall not add.”** He teaches the rule of equity and strikes down every heresy. For he forbids adding any perverse intention to sound doctrine or taking away anything from the truth: one must walk on the royal road, neither to the right nor to the left. Hence: “For the ways of the Lord are right, and the just shall walk in them” (Hosea XIV). John likewise says: “If anyone adds to these things, God will add upon him the plagues written in this book; and if anyone takes away, God will take away his portion from the book of life” (Revelation XXII).

**Verse 7.—“Nor is there another,” etc.** There is no other nation so great in dignity—that is, in the dignity of its gifts—not in the multitude of its people. For the Jewish nation did not surpass other nations in number or power, but by the prerogative of its fathers and by divine favor.

**Verse 9.—“Which they saw.”** Sight holds primacy among all the senses; therefore it is used for every sense.

**Verse 16.—“A sculpted likeness.”** (Augustine, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, question 4.) “Perhaps by these two words he signified one thing,” etc., up to “which is customary concerning human beings.”

**Verse 18.—“Which is beneath.”** (Augustine, question 5.) “Did he intend water and earth to be understood,” etc., up to “and could not possess earthly animals.”

**Verse 19.—“Which he created.”** (Augustine, question 6.) “It was not said in this way,” etc., up to “but not the worship that other nations have.”

**Verse 23.—“A sculpted likeness.”** (Augustine, question 7.) Here, speaking generally, he used “likeness” and omitted “image,” because if there is no likeness, there is no image either.

**Verse 26.—“I call heaven and earth to witness today,” etc.** Μετωνυμικῶς (*metonymically*): by the container he signifies what is contained.

**Verse 30.—“But at the latter time.”** He foretells Israel’s conversion to faith in Christ, so that, after the fullness of the nations has entered, all Israel may be saved.

**Verse 32.—“From the highest heaven.”** (Augustine, question 8.) “Why did he not similarly say ‘from the highest part of the earth,’” etc., up to “since this is said of the final gathering of the elect.”

### Chapter V

**Verse 1.—“Hear, Israel,” etc.** (Augustine, question 9 on Deuteronomy.) “Was it said for this reason,” etc., up to “and to see, and hear, and retain in memory?”

**Verse 4.—“Face to face,” etc.** (Augustine.) “A little earlier he took care to admonish,” etc., up to “although some have hoped for this.”

**Verse 5.—“Between you and God.”** (Idem, question 10.) “As though the Lord were in that place,” etc., up to “hearing from the midst of the fire the voice of God proclaiming the Decalogue of the Law.”

**Verse 9.—“Returning iniquity,” etc.** (Isidore.) “There are some who explain it in this way,” etc., up to “but delays the sentence for a long time.”

“To those who hate me, and showing mercy to many thousands of those who love me,” etc. This means those who hate the Lord through inherited impiety. For it is perverse to charge the sins of fathers to sons who have not sinned, since it is said through Ezekiel: “The son shall not bear the iniquity,” etc. (Ezekiel XVIII).

**Verse 11.—“You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain,” etc.** The first commandment pertains to the Father, concerning whom it is said later: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one” (Deuteronomy VI), so that, hearing this, you may worship one God the Father and not accept many gods.

The second pertains to the Son, concerning whom it is said here: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain”—that is, you shall not suppose the Son of God to be a creature. For every creature is subject to vanity; but believe him equal to the Father, God of gods, God with God, through whom all things were made.

The third pertains to the Spirit, whose gift promises eternal rest. Because the Holy Spirit is called sevenfold, God therefore sanctified the seventh day. On the other days the sanctification of works is not mentioned, except on the Sabbath, on which God rested. Rightly, then, this commandment pertains to the Spirit: both because of the name “sanctification” and because of the eternal rest belonging to the gift of the Holy Spirit.

It is said thus: “Remember that you sanctify the Sabbath day: six days you shall labor,” etc. In the work of the six days, the labor of six thousand years appears to be signified; in the seventh, the time of eternal rest, in which eternal rest is promised after good works. Therefore, whatever we do, if we do it for the sake of future rest, we observe the Sabbath.

**Verse 16.—“Honor your father and your mother, as he commanded you.”** After the three commandments come the seven that concern one’s neighbor. Among these seven, the first—but fourth in the total order—is: “Honor your father,” etc. For from his parents a human being opens his eyes, and this life begins with love for them. Hence this commandment is called the greatest and first, namely, on the second tablet.

We are therefore commanded to honor our parents and to show them the duty and reverence of filial devotion; for whoever does not do this for his parents, how will he do it for others?

Fifth: “You shall not commit adultery”—that is, you shall join yourself to no one besides your lawful wife.

Sixth: “You shall not kill.” One also kills who sees his neighbor dying of hunger or nakedness and does not help as far as he can.

Seventh: “You shall not steal.” In this he forbids every kind of robbery.

Eighth: “You shall not bear false witness.” He abhors the crime of lying and falsehood.

Ninth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s wife.” In this he also forbids adulterous thought.

Tenth: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.” In this he strikes at ambition and covetousness.

The first therefore forbids secret seizure; the second, error; the third, love of the world; the fourth, impiety; the fifth, fornication; the sixth, cruelty; the seventh, rapacity; the eighth, falsehood; the ninth, adulterous thought; the tenth, desire for the world.

It should also be noted that just as the Egyptians were struck by ten plagues, so the people of God are governed by ten commandments, and demons are put to death by them.

**Verse 22.—“On two tablets of stone that he gave me.”** (Isidore.) “The two Testaments,” etc., up to “namely, the sensible and the intelligible.”

**Verse 29.—“Who would grant that they had such a mind?”** God wishes it to be understood that this benefit is granted by his grace, so that in all things the righteousness of God may be by faith, not as though it were one’s own righteousness from the Law. Hence: “I will take away from them their heart of stone and give them a heart of flesh” (Ezekiel XXXVI)—that is, a sensitive heart, for flesh has sensation, whereas stone does not. And elsewhere: “He made us fit ministers of the New Testament, not of the letter but of the Spirit.”

### Chapter VI

**Verse 5.—“You shall love the Lord.”** (Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, book I, chapters 26–28.) “Charity will not be taken away,” etc., up to “who are more closely joined to us because of the suitability of places, times, or any circumstances.”

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book VII, chapter 10.) “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. “From love of God is born love of neighbor,” etc., up to “for in good circumstances the friend is not recognized, and in evil circumstances the enemy is not concealed.”

The soul is of a threefold nature; therefore it is commanded to love in a threefold way. God does not wish his love to be divided, so that we love both God and gold, or wife, or children. “No one can serve two masters” (Matthew VI). He alone must be loved above all, and love of him must be placed first.

**Verse 8.—“And you shall bind them as a sign.”** The Pharisees, interpreting this wrongly, wrote the Decalogue—that is, the ten words—on little parchment strips and carried them bound on their foreheads. The Babylonians do this to the present day, so that they may be thought religious. Hence: “They enlarge their phylacteries and lengthen their tassels” (Matthew XXIII).

**Verse 13.—“You shall swear by his name.”** (Augustine, question 12.) “They are permitted to swear by the name of God,” etc., up to “but whoever does not swear at all is far from perjury.”

**Verse 16.—“You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”** He tempts God who, although he has something he can do, irrationally exposes himself to danger, testing whether he can be delivered by God.

### Chapter VII

**Verse 1.—“Many nations.”** The seven nations are the seven principal vices, which the spiritual soldier is commanded to overcome and exterminate by God’s grace. They are said to be greater in number because there are more vices than virtues. In the catalogue seven nations are named; in the account of the conquest they are mentioned without number: “When he has destroyed many nations before you.” For the people of carnal passions, multiplied from the sevenfold source of vices, are more numerous than Israel.

From gluttony come feasting and drunkenness; from fornication, shameful speech, buffoonery, frivolity, and foolish talk; from avarice, lying, fraud, thefts, perjuries, the desire for shameful gain, false testimony, violence, inhumanity, and rapacity; from anger, murder, shouting, and indignation; from sadness, resentment, faintheartedness, bitterness, despair, and laziness; from acedia, idleness, drowsiness, intrusiveness, mental and bodily restlessness, instability, talkativeness, and curiosity; from vainglory, quarrels, heresies, boasting, and presumption concerning novelties; from pride, contempt, envy, disobedience, blasphemy, murmuring, detraction, and many other things.

Although these are greater in number than the virtues, when the principal vices have been conquered, all the rest are brought to rest and destroyed by perpetual death. We experience the greater strength of these pestilences in temptation: the pleasure of carnal passions fights more powerfully in our members than the pursuits of virtue, which are acquired through the utmost contrition of heart and body.

We possess the territories of these nations when, with the army of Israel—that is, with the virtues—we overcome the vices. Thus chastity may occupy the place of fornication in our heart; patience, the place of fury; saving joy, the place of sadness; fortitude, the place of acedia; humility, the place of pride. When each vice has been expelled, let the sons of Israel—that is, souls who see God—reign in its place.

When God spoke to Abraham about future events, however, he is read to have counted not seven but ten nations whose land was promised to his offspring: namely, after the idolatries of the nations, the blasphemy of the Jews, and the error of the heretics had been cast out, those among whom people dwell in spiritual Egypt before the knowledge of God and the grace of baptism. But whoever leaves that place and reaches the spiritual wilderness by God’s grace is freed from the attack of three nations and fights against seven.

**“The Hittite and the Girgashite,” etc.** (Jerome, *On Hebrew Names*, volume III.) “The Hittite,” etc., up to “that is, trampled upon or their manger.””

**“Seven nations.”** Abraham was told that ten would be destroyed. At that time there were ten, but when the children of Israel crossed over to the Jordan, three had already been destroyed. The sons of Lot destroyed the giants; the sons of Esau destroyed the Horites; and the Cappadocians destroyed part of the Hivites.

**“And stronger.”** Spiritual wickednesses are subtler and more effective at deceiving than human weakness is at resisting.

**Verse 14.—“Barren.”** There were some barren women among the Jews, but so few that, in comparison with the fertile, they seemed to be none.

**Verse 20.—“Moreover, hornets,” etc.** It is not recorded anywhere in history that God sent hornets or wasps ahead of them against their enemies. Rather, by the stinging creatures he signifies the piercing fears by which he drove the terrified enemies into flight.

**Verse 22.—“You will not be able,” etc.** He shows that one must beware lest, after sins have been expelled from our flesh, a spiritual beast—namely, vainglory, pride, or empty glory—rise up, since these are more difficult to uproot than carnal vices. For Lot, who remained continent in Sodom, was polluted by fornication in the mountain (Genesis XIX). Once a vice has been expelled, virtue must immediately be planted, lest the unclean spirit return and find the house empty (Matthew XII).

(Rabanus, Gregory.) God gives some people greater goods and does not grant them lesser ones, so that their minds may always have something for which to reproach themselves; and while they desire to be perfect but cannot be, they may not exalt themselves over what they possess, since they are unable by themselves to lack even small faults.

This is why he destroyed the strong and powerful adversaries, the Philistines, but preserved the Canaanites for a long time, so that Israel might be trained by having enemies against whom to fight and might not exalt itself over the greater enemies it had conquered. The same mind therefore grows strong through virtue and grows weary through weakness, so that, while it seeks what it cannot possess, it may humbly preserve what it does possess.

The heavenly realm likewise suffered losses in part among its citizens and stood firm in part, so that the elect angels, seeing others fall through pride, might stand all the more firmly because they stood more humbly. Thus the same thing occurs in every soul: sometimes the greatest gains are granted, sometimes the smallest are condemned.

**Verse 26.—“Anathema.”** Ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀναθήναι (*from setting above*), or from hanging up, as votive offerings were hung in temples and separated from those who gave them.

### Chapter VIII

**Verse 2.—“Forty years.”** He therefore permitted them to be afflicted for forty years so that they might recognize how great their frailty was.

**“To afflict you.”** (Augustine, question 13.) “Here it is said more openly,” etc., up to “which, if he had said it, would have to be understood as ‘he would make known.’”

**Verse 3.—“Manna.”** The flesh of Christ, by which, refreshed, we may come to the true promised land. For forty years we ate manna—that is, throughout the whole of our time, which revolves through four seasons, we are nourished by the sacrament of the Lord’s body.

“Man does not live by bread alone, but by every…” Spiritual food is commended here, by which souls destined to live forever are satisfied. The manna given from heaven signifies the flesh of Christ, who says: “I am the bread of life; this is the bread that came down from heaven” (John VI), because “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” Whoever eats this flesh has eternal life.

“Man does not live by bread alone,” etc. This signifies the twofold substance of our nature. For a human being consists of soul and body: the body, which is from the earth, is nourished by earthly food; but the soul lives by the word of God. The spirit of a human being is made alive by the Spirit of God, provided that the human being is in the body of the Church, that is, of Christ, and in faith in the Son of God.

Therefore he adds: “His garment did not wear out with age,” because the conduct of the new human being ought to remain in newness of life, and his foot was not worn down, because the path of his works is preserved unharmed: “For the Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the wicked will perish” (Psalm I).

**Verse 11.—“Judgments.”** These are the commands given to the people through Moses at various times after the Law had been given; in Exodus they are called “justifications.”

**“And ceremonies.”** Circumcision and the rites of sacrifices. Hence Ambrose, commenting on the Epistle to the Romans: “The Law is threefold: the first part concerns the sacrament of divinity; the second agrees with the natural law, which forbids sin; the third concerns the festivals of the Law, namely Sabbaths, new moons, and circumcision.”

**Verse 15.—“And the dipsas.”** A kind of asp called in Latin *situla*. Whoever it bites dies of thirst; it is so small that it cannot be seen when stepped on. Its venom kills before it is perceived, and the dying person feels no distress.

Mystically, the various serpents are heresies: different from one another, indeed, but all deadly.

### Chapter IX

**Verse 5.—“For neither,” etc.** (Augustine, question 14.) “These are the ones who did not deserve to perish in the wilderness,” etc., up to “where those who were not deservedly brought into the promised land provoked the Lord.”

**Verse 10.—“And he gave,” etc.** (Augustine, question 15.) “In Exodus it is read that the Lord gave the tablets to Moses,” etc., up to “endures forever.”

### Chapter X

**Verse 4.—“And he wrote on.”** (Augustine, question 14 on Deuteronomy.) “In Exodus Moses,” etc., up to “but he himself assists the freedom of the good will.”

**Verse 6.—“In Mosera,” etc.** In the Book of Numbers he is said to have died on Mount Hor, but perhaps the place has two names. Beroth, the place of the sons of Jaakan, is in the wilderness, as is Mosera, where Aaron died, as is recorded in books of places. It is shown even today on the summit of a mountain at the tenth milestone from the city of Petra.

**Verse 8.—“The tribe of Levi.”** Unless by this the entire royal priesthood belonging to the New Testament were signified, no one who was not of that tribe would dare say, “The Lord is my portion” (Psalm LXXII), or elsewhere, “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,” etc. (ibid., XV).

**Verse 14.—“The heaven of heavens,” etc.** Some say that there are three heavens: the airy, the ethereal, and the starry. Others say there are seven: the first airy, the second ethereal, the third Olympian, the fourth fiery, the fifth the firmament, the sixth watery, and the seventh that of the angels.

**Verse 16.—“Circumcise,” etc.** This signifies spiritual circumcision, that is, guarding the mind and true abstinence. It is as though he said: When you have extinguished the lust of the flesh, cut away also the superfluities of the mind. All the senses must be circumcised.

Hence Moses complains that he is uncircumcised in lips; and Stephen says to the Jews: “Uncircumcised in heart and ears,” etc. (Acts VII). Truly circumcised, therefore, is the one who stops his ears so as not to hear bloodshed, and closes his eyes so as not to see evil; who does not sin with his tongue; whose heart is not weighed down by gluttony and drunkenness; who washes his hands among the innocent and restrains his feet from every evil way; who chastises his body and subjects it to servitude, and guards his heart with all vigilance.

We also need a twofold circumcision: lest we seek empty glory from these things; lest we be clean outwardly but unclean within; and lest we suffer the penalties of counterfeit holiness, like the Shechemites, who imitated the circumcision of the patriarchs not out of love for God but for the sake of lust. Therefore they gained no reward, but on the third day they perished amid the ruins of their city. Such people, when the virtues in which they trusted have been emptied at the time of the resurrection, die forever.

**Verse 22.—“Your fathers went down into Egypt.”** One goes down into Egypt: “Easy is the descent to Avernus.” One ascends into Jerusalem, because narrow is the way that leads to life, and virtue stretches toward difficult heights.

### Chapter XI

**Verse 10.—“From which you came out.”** In the mind, with Moses as guide—that is, with the Law teaching—to despise earthly pleasures, and with Jesus as guide to enter the promised land.

**“In gardens.”** Because all carnal people seek to multiply for themselves present happiness and an abundance of temporal goods.

**Verse 12.—“From the beginning of the year.”** From the beginning of good will to the perfection of good work, he directs the course of life. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish according to his good pleasure (Philippians II).

**Verse 14.—“The early rain,” etc.** Because at the earlier time of the Law he granted his elect understanding; he gives the latter rain because, in the final age of his incarnation, he revealed to us the mystery of his incarnation.

**“And the latter rain,” etc.** Because it is the final hour when his preaching reached us, he who says: “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Psalm CXL).

**Verse 20.—“You shall write them on the doorposts.”** (Augustine, question 17.) “Is this meant literally, or is it a hyperbolical commendation, as many things are said?”

**Verse 29.—“Mount Garizim.”** Garizim is interpreted “Division” or “Stranger”; Hebal is interpreted “Ancient Abyss.” Those who separate themselves from vices and judge themselves strangers and sojourners in this world also deserve eternal blessing. But those who plunge themselves into the abyss of their former life, serving carnal desires, will be subject to eternal curse.

### Chapter XII

**Verse 6.—“Tithes and firstfruits,” etc.** (Augustine, question 18.) It must be asked how he commands that tithes of all fruits and the firstborn of all cattle not be eaten except in the city where the temple was, when in the Law he commanded that they be given to the Levites.

**Verse 13.—“Take care that you do not offer.”** He removes the opportunity for sacrificing to idols. For this reason he commands that offerings be made in the temple and at the Lord’s altar: so that where religion is whole and undivided, fitting worship may be offered. Mystically, he indicates that no gift is acceptable to God outside the Catholic Church. For this is the place that God chose, so that he might place his name there and dwell in it.

**Verse 16.—“Without eating it.”** He forbids murder. Blood is put for the soul, because the seat of the soul—that is, of human life—is in the blood.

**Verse 17.—“In your towns.”** That is, you shall not attribute to your own merits what you have received by divine generosity, nor to your own strength, but to God, by whose gift you have obtained it (Galatians VI).

**Verse 23.—“Take care of this alone.”** Literally, the apostles commanded this: “And in the blood” murder is forbidden, as is hatred of the brethren. “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer” (1 John III).

**“For their blood.”** Because there is something vital in blood, and through it life is sustained above all in this flesh, since it is diffused through all the veins. He calls it the soul—that is, the life of the body—which ends in death.

Mystically, it is indicated that carnal people, leaving behind their former way of life and joining themselves in the unity of faith and good works, must not turn their errors to our use; rather, we must pour them out—that is, assign them, once brought forth by confession, to earthly frailty—and cast them away as unworthy of spiritual men.

### Chapter XIII

**Verse 1.—“If there arises.”** He wishes it to be understood that things spoken by diviners, not according to God, even if they come to pass, must not be accepted in such a way that what they predict is done. Nor does he show that events occurring in this way are outside his power. But he supplies the reason why he permits them: namely, so that those who serve them may know how much they love God—not so that he who knows all things may know.

### Chapter XIV

**Verse 1.—“You shall not cut yourselves.”** Even to the present day many nations cut themselves at the funerals of the dead. Hence: “You shall not grieve as the others do who have no hope.” Those who do these things despair of the resurrection.

**“Nor shall you do.”** “The hairs of your head are numbered” (Matthew X), that is, your thoughts, which ought not to be removed from the dignity of the head and offered to the devil, as some offer their bodily hair to the devil.

**Verse 3.—“You shall not eat.”** The animals are unclean, but through their symbolism they express the ways, actions, and wills of human beings.

**Verse 5.—“The camelopard.”** It is covered with white spots, has a head resembling a camel’s, a horse-like neck, the feet of a buffalo, and in the remaining parts resembles a leopard. It is born in Ethiopia.

**“Every animal that divides.”** The Church receives and incorporates into its members those who split the hoof, who know how to distinguish good from evil, and who chew the cud—that is, meditate on the Law day and night.

**Verse 6.—“Which divides into two parts.”** This means one who accepts the two Testaments and establishes himself with firm steps in righteousness and innocence.

**Verse 7.—“The camel.”** The Jew, who strains out a gnat and swallows a camel, who chews the letter but does not have a divided hoof, because he does not divide the letter from the spirit. These are the scribes and Pharisees.

**“The hare.”** Through the rock-badger and the hare he signifies the multitude of the Jews, since both animals are weak and infirm.

**“Because they chew the cud.”** The Jews chew the words of the Law, but they do not divide the hoof, because they do not believe in the Father and the Son, nor accept the two Testaments. Some heretics, however, divide the hoof but do not chew the doctrine of truth in their mouths (Leviticus XI).

**Verse 9.—“These you shall eat from all that move in the waters.”** By these the Gentiles are understood, who are reborn in the waters of baptism.

**“Which have fins.”** They meditate on the Law of sublime and heavenly life. Because ignorance of divine law had long existed among the Gentiles, he adds fins and scales: for just as fish have scales and fins, so those who have temporal ignorance quickly receive knowledge of what is sublime and heavenly life.

**Verse 12.—“And the griffin.”** It is a quadruped with a head and wings like an eagle and the remaining body like a lion. It is abundant in the Hyperborean mountains and is especially hostile to horses and human beings.

**Verse 15.—“The ostrich.”** It does not rise from the earth but is entangled in worldly affairs.

**“The owl.”** It sees sharply at night but not by day, like those who boast of knowledge of the Law but do not grasp the light of the Gospel.

**“The gull.”** It flies like a bird and swims like a water animal; that is, it venerates circumcision and baptism. To such people Paul says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians V).

**“The hawk,” etc.** Those who appear gentle but associate with the powerful and the avaricious.

**Verse 16.—“The swan and the ibis.”** These are said to have long necks and to draw their food from the depths of the earth. We, however, ought to seek the bread that came down from heaven and not be anxious about what we shall eat (John VI; Matthew VI).

**Verse 17.—“The night-heron.”** It creeps and works at night, signifying those who devote themselves to the works of darkness, namely fornication, uncleanness, the worship of idols, and similar things.

**Verse 18.—“The hoopoe.”** It loves mourning. But worldly sadness produces death; we ought instead to rejoice in the Lord and give thanks in all things (2 Corinthians VII; 1 Thessalonians V).

**“The bat,” etc.** It flies around the earth and walks on wings. Our way of life, however, ought to be in heaven (Philippians III).

**Verse 21.—“But whatever,” etc.** Mystically, the ecclesiastical man is commanded to preserve himself in holiness and avoid every uncleanness of sin, while allowing the foreigner—that is, the Gentile—to remain in his own filth.

**“The foreigner who is within your gates.”** Leave unclean things to pagans and heretics. Hence in the Gospel demons are permitted to enter the herd of swine (Matthew VIII), and it is said: “Let the dead bury their own dead” (Luke IX).

**“In milk.”** This means moderate disciplines, but stricter ones, so that they might restore the bitter things they had lost—the sweet things.

**Verse 22.—“The tithe.”** As though he said: Perform the good things you do according to the precepts of the divine Law, and set them apart for the Lord, so that you may do everything for his praise.

**Verse 23.—“The firstborn.”** That is, the beginnings of good works, which must be tithed—that is, consecrated to the Lord.

**Verse 24.—“To carry.”** This means those who are far from the perfection of the saints and cannot climb the summit of the virtues or devote themselves to contemplation. Let them do what they can humbly and devoutly, make friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity, and lay up treasures in heaven, so that they may be received into eternal dwellings, where they may feast and rejoice with their friends—that is, with the saints and elect of God.

**Verse 26.—“And you shall buy with the same money,” etc.** Spiritually, it is commanded that we always devote ourselves to good works, so that after this life we may return to our home—that is, to our heavenly homeland.

**Verse 28.—“Another tithe.”** In addition to the one that you eat with your household and the Levites, in the place that the Lord will choose.

**Verse 29.—“And the Levite shall come.”** He clearly shows that this tithe is not to be shared with the one who offers it, but only distributed to those whom he commanded it to be given, among whom he placed the Levite first.

### Chapter XV

**Verse 1.—“In the seventh year.”** In this chapter compassion and love are commended, so that we may show mercy to our neighbors and await a reward from the Lord. For “in due season we shall reap, if we do not grow weary”; while we have time, let us do good to all, especially to those who belong to the household of faith (1 Timothy V). Hence: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven; give, and it will be given to you” (Luke VI).

**“In the seventh year.”** Because forgiveness is in the sevenfold Spirit. Almost all the solemnities of the Law are arranged around the number seven: the Sabbath is on the seventh day; Pentecost comes after seven completed weeks; the seventh year is also celebrated; and the jubilee follows after seven times seven years.

**Verse 3.—“From the foreigner.”** Although all are our neighbors, mercy must especially be shown to those who are members with us of Christ. For whoever has the substance of the world and does not give it to a needy brother—how does the love of God remain in him? (1 John III.)

**Verse 6.—“You shall lend at interest.”** As though he said: You will be richer than all nations. The Church also abounds in spiritual riches: she teaches and has no need to be taught.

**Verse 9.—“Beware.”** (Augustine, question 21.) The Septuagint has: “Pay attention to yourself, lest there be a hidden word,” etc., up to “if he cruelly thinks that it must not be given at the time when it ought to be given.”

**Verse 12.—“When he has been sold to you,” etc.** (Isidore.) “If a Hebrew boy has fallen into slavery,” etc., up to “namely, we shall serve sins forever.”

**“When he has been sold to you,” etc.** The Hebrew is a passerby who is journeying toward the eternal homeland, passing from vices to virtues and from earthly things to heavenly things. If such a person has sold himself to you—that is, has committed himself to your teaching—you shall teach him to strive to work in the present life so that he may reach rest.

He shall serve you for six years; in the seventh you shall release him free, and you shall not allow him to depart empty-handed. This is as though to say: You shall promise him eternal rewards and true freedom in the other life.

But if he says, “I do not wish to go out,” because he loves you and your house—that is, if he has done good things not for eternal reward but for human praise, as though loving the present life—you shall pierce his ear with an awl, that is, his mind with fear of judgment. You shall pierce it at the door of the house, because judgment will occur at the departure from this life and the entrance into the other. He shall serve you forever—that is, if he has loved the world more than God, you shall teach him that he is to be handed over to eternal punishments.

(Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, homily 3.) “Since the active and contemplative life are ours by God’s grace,” etc., up to “where the ear of the one refusing freedom is commanded to be pierced with an awl.”

**Verse 19.—“Of the firstborn.”** (Augustine, question 23.) “He calls them firstborn,” etc., up to “because he alone is of the substance of the Father, and equal and coeternal.”

**“You shall sanctify it to the Lord your God.”** Not for yourself, but for the giver of all things: “Every good gift is from above” (James I). Whatever is light in our thinking, blemished in our conduct, lame in the progress of our works, blind through ignorance of mind, or in any respect deformed or weak, we ought not to offer to God—that is, attribute it to him—but to ourselves.

**“You shall not work.”** (Gregory, *Moralia*, book VIII, chapter 34.) “To plow with the firstborn of an ox,” etc., up to “lest the deceived mind fail to detect the evils within them.”

**Verse 16.—“But if it has.”** There are certain works that, although they please God less, nevertheless benefit one’s neighbor; and if they cannot be offered to God, they may be eaten. For although they please God less because of the obscured intention that God sees, they nevertheless help one’s neighbors by their example.

It is like the doe and the stag. The doe moves by leaps; the stag is hostile to the serpent, leaps over rough and thorny places, and crosses the mountains. Therefore these animals are understood in a good sense.

### Chapter XVI

**Verse 1.—“Observe the month of new grain.”** In that month sheaves of ears of grain—that is, firstfruits—were offered to the Lord by the priest.

**“The first month,”** namely, of the Hebrews, called by them Nisan, by the Greeks also ξάνθικος (*Xanthikos*), and by the Latins April, in which the paschal lamb was killed.

**“He brought you out.”** Mystically, we too, liberated from the Egypt of this world and clothed with the new human being, should walk in newness of life, consecrating the firstfruits of good works and celebrating the Passover—that is, the good passage—so that, after leaving Egypt, we may come to the promised land.

**Verse 2.—“And from cattle in the place.”** (Augustine, question 24.) He adds cattle, although he had commanded only a sheep, which he ordered to be taken from sheep and kids or goats. Is this because of Christ, who according to the flesh was descended from both the righteous and sinners? For he does not say “from sheep or goats,” but “from sheep and goats,” although strictly speaking a sheep is not understood to come from goats, lest the Jews say that “goat” must be supplied. Why, then, were cattle added? Was it because of the other sacrifices that were to be offered during the days of unleavened bread?

**Verse 3.—“Leavened bread.”** Corrupt doctrine or an old way of life. Hence: “Let us feast not with the old leaven,” etc. (1 Corinthians V).

**“Seven.”** Throughout the whole time of the present life. Just as they ate unleavened bread for seven days, so let us conduct ourselves purely and simply during the seven days of this life, during which the Lamb is killed daily and the Passover is celebrated, if, having been renewed, we retain nothing of the old corruption. For what else is leaven than corruption of nature? Leavened dough departs from natural sweetness and is corrupted by adulterous rancor.

**Verse 4.—“It shall not appear.”** “Let us feast not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness,” etc. (1 Corinthians V), as though he said: Leave the old human being and put on the new.

[Col. 0468B] **It shall not remain.** In this life all the mysteries of the Lord’s Incarnation are to be examined and all his commandments fulfilled (Eph. IV), before morning—that is, the end of the age—arrives.

**VERSE 5.—You shall not be able.** The paschal lamb is eaten in one house, and the Passover is sacrificed in one place—that is, in the Catholic Church; outside it, the Passover is not rightly celebrated. He forbids the celebration of Christ’s mysteries in the conventicles of heretics.

**VERSE 6.—In the evening, at sunset.** In the final age of the world, when the true Sun set in his Passion and released the Egyptian captivity, when Christ our Passover was sacrificed.

**VERSE 7.—You shall go to your tents.** When the Lord’s service has been completed, at the morning of the Resurrection we shall pass into eternal [Col. 0468C] dwellings, so that we may rest from every labor and rejoice in the reward we have received.

**VERSE 8.—On the seventh day.** In eternal rest, which the number seven signifies: on account of the Sabbath, when there is no labor and no activity of working.

**VERSE 9.—Seven weeks.** This is explained more fully in Leviticus. “You shall therefore count from the second day of the Sabbath seven complete weeks, up to the second day of the investigation of the seventh week.”

**(AUGUSTINE, Questions, 25.)** “Seven weeks,” etc. If this Pentecost was commanded to be observed by the whole people, are we to believe that all were commanded to put the sickle into the harvest on the same day? But if each person observes this fiftieth day for himself, counting from the day on which he puts in the sickle, it is not one day for the whole people. That one day, however, is the day reckoned from the sacrifice of Passover to the day on which the Law was given on Sinai.

We too celebrate Pentecost—that is, the coming of the Holy Spirit, who is the finger of God, by whom the Law was written on the tablets.

**VERSE 13.—The feast.** Whoever uses the present world as a tabernacle can celebrate a festival and rejoice in it because of his expectation of the future: “For if our earthly house of this habitation is dissolved, he will have a house not made with hands in the heavens” (II Cor. V).

**When.** He signifies that, when the perfection of all good things has been completed and many virtues have been gathered, one should rejoice and exult with friends. When someone who has been generous in his gift here rejoices over the reward he has received, then the feast of tabernacles will truly be celebrated—not of things that pass away, but of eternal things. Hence: “That they may receive you into eternal dwellings” (Luke XVI).

**VERSE 16.—Male.** Not female; for nothing soft, fragile, or weak ought to exist in our manner of life. God demands from us all that is strong (Exod. XXIII, XXXIV; Ecclus. XXXV). If, with regard to the eternal reward and in faith in the Trinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, we labor in good works during the present life, we set up a male before the Lord.

**In all.** So that those arriving from every direction may find them prepared immediately at the entrance, and may receive just judgments from them.

[Col. 0469B] **VERSE 19.—The eyes of the wise.** Wise in human eyes, not in God’s eyes; to them it is said: “Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes” (Isa. V).

**VERSE 20.—Justly.** **(GREGORY, Moralia, Book X, chapter 19.)** He executes what is just unjustly who is stirred to defend justice not by zeal for virtue but by love of temporal reward, and is not ashamed to sell the justice he displays. To execute what is just justly, therefore, is to seek justice itself in the assertion of justice: “There are ways that seem just to men,” etc. (Prov. XIV). And: “Woe to you who justify yourselves before men” (Luke XVI).

**VERSE 21.—You shall not plant.** He cuts off an occasion for idolatry. The nations used to sacrifice and worship statues in shrines.

[Col. 0469C] **Sacred grove.** **(ISIDORE.)** “A wood: leafy, fruitless trees,” etc., up to “nor does he permit the invention of falsehood or error to be joined to Catholic truth.”

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 2.—And when they are found.** The Law especially detests error and idolatry, for it is the greatest crime to render the honor of the Creator to a creature. This is done by pagans and by wicked Catholics, who, although they do not depart from the Church, are nevertheless found to serve the devil more through various vices than to serve God through good works. He commands that those whom he foresees will be condemned by an irrevocable sentence be crushed with stones.

**VERSE 6.—By the testimony of two or three witnesses.** Namely, by the testimony of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel, according to this: “The word that I have spoken will judge him on the last day” (John XII). On the title of the cross also, three languages testify that Christ is the King of the Jews: Hebrew, Greek, and Latin (John XIX).

**No one shall be put to death.** Such is the harmony of the Old and New Testaments that neither exists without the other.

In human judgment, the authority of divine Scripture must first be sought.

**VERSE 8.—If it is difficult.** He instructs the priests of God to conduct ecclesiastical judgments reverently, according to the authority given them by God, and to decide justly—not according to their own will, but according to the decree of the Law—lest, by showing partiality, they alter the sentence.

[Col. 0470A] **VERSE 11.—According to.** Notice that it is not said to you that you must obey unless they have taught according to the Law. Hence: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat upon Moses’ seat” (Matt. XXIII).

**VERSE 12.—By the command of the priest.** Of Christ, who is priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek, and who appointed vicars in his place, saying to them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me,” etc. (Luke X). Therefore by the justice of condemnation he bears the sentence who despises the power of the divinity.

**VERSE 14.—When you have entered the land, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 26.)** It may be asked why the people displeased God when they desired a king, since here the king appears to be permitted. It must be understood that this was not according to God’s will in the proper sense, because he did not command it to happen but permitted it to those who desired it. Nevertheless, he commanded that the king should not be a foreigner, but a brother, a native of the same people, not an alien. When he says, “You shall not be able,” this must be understood as “you shall not be permitted.”

**I shall set over.** The inhabitants of the land appoint a king for themselves contrary to God’s sentence.

**VERSE 17.—He shall not have, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 27.)** It is clear that Solomon transgressed this commandment, etc., up to “reach the foreigners.”

**Nor silver.** “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matt. VI).

**VERSE 19.—And he shall read.** Observe with what assiduity priests ought to read, since kings are to read constantly. Reading itself is light and life; hence: “The words that I speak to you are spirit and life” (John VI).

**VERSE 20.—Pride.** As though to say: let him know that he is a brother. We all have one Father, God, to whom we say: “Our Father, who are in heaven,” etc. (Luke XI).

**Pride.** It is a blessing to reign over Israel—that is, by reigning, to make Israel consist of those who see God.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 1.—They shall not have.** In both the Old and the New Testament, the ministers of the altar are commanded to live from offerings and tithes, and they are not permitted to long for the acquisition of earthly possessions. Hence: “Do not possess gold or silver,” etc. (Matt. X); and shortly afterward: “The laborer is worthy of his food” (I Cor. IX). Elsewhere: “Those who serve at the altar share with the altar” (Num. XVIII). For it is not right that one who ought always to stand at divine service should long for earthly profit, since God is his inheritance. What, then, can be lacking to one who possesses him who possesses all things?

**VERSE 2.—Inheritance.** For good works: what one conceives in the mind, one must prove by action. Hence: “Jesus began to do and to teach” (Acts I).

**VERSE 3.—They shall give.** Because we ought devoutly to share with our teachers in bodily support and spiritual benefits. Hence: “Let the one who is catechized in the word share with the one who catechizes him in every good work” (Gal. VI).

**The stomach.** The belly is a receptacle for foods; all human labors and the momentary delights of the appetite are condemned in their end. He shows consecrated minds that everything we devour is cast out in due course. Hence: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for food; but God will destroy both it and them.”

[Col. 0471A] **VERSE 4.—Firstfruits.** The farmer who labors ought first to receive the firstfruits of his crops.

**VERSE 6.—If he goes out.** As though he leaves a city and a house, the one who serves God without payment and proclaims the Gospel without expense.

**VERSE 8.—Excepting. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 38.)** What the Septuagint says, etc., up to “what was provided for parents ought to be preserved.”

**VERSE 9.—When you enter. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 29.)** Since observers of portents are forbidden, etc., up to “thus those inspections of prodigies must be distinguished from the signs of miracles.”

[Col. 0471B] **VERSE 10.—Augurs.** Those who go around altars with unspeakable prayers and seek divination in the entrails of animals.

**Auguries.** As though from *avigeria*, things performed through the voices of birds; or *avigaria*, from the chattering of birds.

**VERSE 11.—Pythons.** Ventriloquists, from whose bellies demons speak; they are called *pythons* after Python—that is, Apollo, whom they believed to be the god of divination.

**VERSE 15.—A prophet from.** Although this can be understood historically of the prophets who, after Moses, were filled with the Spirit of God among the people of Israel, it is better understood of the Lord of the prophets. Of him the crowds, after being fed by him, said: “This is truly the prophet who is to come into the world” (John VI). Elsewhere: “A great prophet has arisen among us” (Luke VII).

[Col. 0471C] ## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 2.—Three.** Faith, hope, and charity, to which all penitents ought to flee.

Moses appointed three cities of refuge beyond the Jordan for homicides who had committed murder unintentionally, and commanded three others to be set apart around the Jordan (Num. XXXV; Josh. XX). Mystically, this indicates that before receiving baptism, whoever wishes to be saved from sin and liberated from spiritual enemies ought sincerely to confess the faith of the Holy Trinity, and after baptism to work manfully in faith, hope, and charity. Thus, living devoutly in the world—which was created according to the number six—he awaits eternal rest in the Sabbath-rest after the perfection of good works.

**VERSE 3.—Into three.** So that the one who is to be saved may escape more easily. Preachers too ought, by word and example, to counsel sinners and equally to commend the faith of the Trinity to all throughout the whole earth, so that they may recognize that the way of truth and the gate of faith are open to them, and that they will rightly be condemned if they refuse to enter.

**But has gone away.** For by an example he shows what sort of homicide is to be saved.

**(GREGORY, Pastoral Care, Part II, chapter X, Book III.)** “We go into the forest with a friend,” etc., up to “which is not perpetrated maliciously.”

**(AMBROSE, On Flight from the World, chapter 2.)** “It is clear that provision has fittingly been made,” etc., up to “let the sense of the flesh die, struck by the Levitical sword, so that your soul may live.”

[Col. 0472A] **VERSE 9.—You shall add to yourself.** In the Book of Joshua, six cities of refuge are assigned to such homicides (Josh. XX): Kedesh in Galilee, in Mount Naphtali; Shechem in Mount Ephraim; and Kiriath-arba, which is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah. Beyond the Jordan: Bezer, from the tribe of Reuben; Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad; and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh.

**(AMBROSE, in the work cited above.)** “The refuges of the six cities are,” etc., up to “or let us venerate him by avoiding what is forbidden.”

**VERSE 11.—But if anyone, hating his neighbor.** Whoever strikes someone with malice and leads him to the death of the soul is guilty of eternal death. Hence: “If anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in me to stumble,” etc. [Col. 0472B] Elsewhere: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and he will not have eternal life” (Matt. XVIII; I John III). Such a person is torn away from the altar as unworthy of the Lord’s sacraments, and earns forgiveness only through worthy repentance. But whoever kills unintentionally has cities of refuge—namely, the Catholic Church—where, restraining himself through the hardship of repentance, he should devote himself to good works throughout the whole present life. If he places his hope in the death of the supreme pontiff, that is, his Redeemer, he will at last deserve to be saved.

Whoever retains hatred of his brother in his heart cannot perform fruitful repentance or appease God.

**VERSE 14.—You shall not take and move boundary stones, etc.** Hence: “Do not cross the boundaries that your fathers established” (Prov. XXII)—that is, the rules and definitions for living handed down by preceding fathers.

**VERSE 15.—One witness shall not stand.** We must also observe this historically. Against the impious or heretics, when we need testimonies from Scripture, we bring forward two witnesses—that is, the Old and New Testaments—or three: the Gospel, the Prophets, and the Apostle; and thus the word stands.

**VERSE 21.—Soul for soul.** For whoever has caused a soul to go astray is not worthy of pardon.

**Tooth for tooth** (Exod. XXI; Lev. XXIV; Matt. V). The force of the words: teeth signify words, according to this: “The sons of men, whose teeth are weapons” (Ps. LVI). Elsewhere: “His teeth are whiter than milk,” that is, than the Law (Gen. XXIX).

[Col. 0472D] **Hand, etc.** Action: namely, those things are useful or harmful to him which he has perverted in another.

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 1.—Because the Lord.** Mystically. **(AUGUSTINE, Questions, 30.)** “For the Lord,” etc., up to “so that he might show that they themselves would also act.”

**VERSE 5.—Who is there. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 31.)** “He is not better in war who has already dedicated buildings,” etc., up to “but these provisions were established to test the courage of the men.”

**Who is there. (ISIDORE.)** He teaches that no one can undertake a profession of contemplation or spiritual [Col. 0473A] warfare, etc., up to “so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II).

It is better to avoid undertaking a profession or persecution than to succumb in it. One should not enter into disputation against heretics unless learned and mature, lest, being defeated, he scandalize others.

**VERSE 16.—You shall permit nothing at all.** No vice is to be spared in our manner of life, lest, corrupted by pleasures and appearing abominable before the eyes of the Lord, we hear our enemies exulting over our ruin: “Aha, aha, our soul! We shall devour him” (Ps. XXXIV).

## CHAPTER XXI

[Col. 0473B] **VERSE 1.—When it is found, etc.** A corpse is a body without a soul; and a soul without God, who is its life. “In the land that the Lord your God will give you”: that is, in the Church. “Guilty of the slaughter”: the author of sedition. “The elders”: those greater in life and wisdom. “The judges”: that is, the priests, whose office is to judge each matter—that is, to discern. “They shall measure from the place of the corpse”: they will investigate the author of the sedition with the greatest discernment. “They shall take a heifer from the herd”: that is, the flesh of Christ, which he took from the fathers. “Which has not drawn the yoke”: because he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth. “Nor has broken the earth with the plow” (I Pet. II): that is, he admitted no stain of sedition.

**And the guilty party in the slaughter shall remain unknown.** The devil, who is invisible and therefore said to be unknown; yet it is known that he “put it into Judas’s heart to betray him” (John XIII).

[Col. 0473C] **The elders, etc.** The apostles and teachers who learned through the testimony of Scripture that no nation was so ready for slaughter as the Jewish people, who shed both the blood of the prophets and of the Lord.

**VERSE 4.—And they shall lead her to a rough valley, etc.** Namely, a despised and most shameful death. Hence: “Let us condemn him to a most shameful death.” “Which was never plowed” (Wis. II), because Christ’s death was without guilt. “Nor received seed” (Matt. XIII): that is, the tares of sin which the enemy sowed over it. We may understand the rough valley as the Gentile world, which was rough; rocky, because it worshiped rocks. There the heifer’s neck was cut, because Christ’s death was celebrated for the salvation of the Gentiles. The neck signifies the strength of the flesh which he laid down in death. “They shall wash their hands over the heifer”: that is, they will purify their works through confidence in Christ’s Passion.

[Col. 0473D] **VERSE 6.—And they shall wash their hands, etc.** That is, they will show their works to be clean through Christ’s Passion. Although the mysteries of that Passion are repeated daily, their hearts and works nevertheless remain completely clean from every deceit of the Jews.

**VERSE 8.—Be favorable.** In fulfillment of their office they bless the people, so that vengeance for the crime may not be rendered, but salvation for redemption.

**VERSE 10.—If you go out to battle. (ISIDORE.)** Let the Jews say how they observe these things. What is the reason that the woman should be shaved and her nails cut? What if she should be found without hair and nails?

[Col. 0474A] **VERSE 11.—A beautiful woman.** Like Paul, who drew from Menander: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (I Cor. XV); and from Aratus: “In him we live and move and exist, for we are indeed his offspring” (Acts XVII).

Others think that this woman, beautiful in appearance, signifies the rational discipline discovered among the Gentiles. From it all the impurity of superstition must be cut away, so that it may be taken up for the pursuit of truth. For the disciplines of the Gentiles possess nothing wholly pure, since among them there is no discipline without some impurity or superstition mixed into it.

**VERSE 13.—One month**, that is, thirty days, so that after the faith of the Trinity and the work of the Law she may deserve to be joined to the Church; for three times ten makes thirty.

[Col. 0474B] **And afterward.** When there is nothing superfluous or unclean either on the head—that is, in the senses—or on the hands—that is, in works.

**VERSE 15.—If a man has two wives, etc.** Christ joined two wives to himself in the name of marriage: the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles. The synagogue is hated, always contentious, stiff-necked, uncircumcised in heart; the Gentile Church is beloved. But he cannot prefer the son of the beloved over the son of the hated—that is, he cannot prefer the Church from the Gentiles and her children to the apostles and the other primitive believers, who are sons of the synagogue. He acknowledges the firstborn of the hated wife and gives him double, because to the primitive sons of the synagogue he gave the Law and the Prophets and knowledge of his name, and preached the Gospel to them first. For this is her firstborn son.

[Col. 0474C] **One beloved.** The animal nature, which seems sweet and pleasing: it desires everything pleasurable and causes no sorrow.

**Another hated.** The rational nature, which does not indulge the body or serve pleasure, but rejects the hidden things of shame.

**VERSE 16.—The firstborn.** The apostles and apostolic men, who hold the place of the firstborn, whose authority the Church follows.

**VERSE 17.—But the son.** This must be done literally, so that no one follows the inclination, love, or hatred of his own mind, but nature.

**All things double.** The apostles received everything double, being endowed with doctrine and action.

**To another he shall give enough to live, not to abound**,  just as Abraham set the son of the slave woman over the nations, while to the son of Sarah he accumulated not only temporal but also spiritual things (Gen. XII).

**VERSE 18.—If he has begotten.** “Obedience is better than sacrifices, and to listen better than to offer the fat of rams, because resistance is like the sin of divination,” etc. (I Sam. XV). Moses therefore commands that a disobedient and vicious son be crushed with stones. The Gospel too rebukes such people with harsh reproaches, as with stones: “Brood of vipers, who taught you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke III).

**VERSE 22.—Hanged.** With his torment visible to the people. Hence: “Rebuke sinners before everyone, so that the others may have fear” (I Tim. V).

[Col. 0475A] **VERSE 23.—He shall not remain.** That is, he ought not to be left under the same condemnation, but should be recalled through the exhortation of teachers, so that reconciliation may be denied to no one while he lives.

**He shall not remain.** Repentance is not to be postponed from day to day, but undertaken immediately, so that through unfruitful repentance sins may be hidden from the eyes of God. Hence: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI).

**Cursed by God. (AUGUSTINE, Against Faustus, Book XIV.)** Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us (Gal. III). Adam fell through the wood of transgression; therefore he earned a curse for himself and for his descendants, concerning which it is said: “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” He accepted a cursed—that is, execrable and most shameful—death.

[Col. 0475B] **(THE SAME, in the work cited above, chapters 3–4.)** “Cursed by God is the one who hangs,” etc. Certain heretics transfer this sentence to slander Christ’s Passion, etc., up to “therefore that which God hates is rightly called accursed; this was what hung on the tree.”

**You shall defile.** We must wash away the stench of sins with the tears of repentance, lest it produce scandal for others and torment for ourselves.

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 1.—You shall not see.** Morally: your brother is a teacher of the Church. If you see his disciple or a learned person, signified by the ox, or an unlearned person, signified by the sheep, going astray, do not neglect him, but exhort him, [Col. 0475C] so that you may reconcile him to his brother—that is, to his teacher. “Bring him into your house” (I Cor. XI), that is, take care of him. And if he is not your neighbor—that is, of your Church—but belongs to another teacher, do likewise.

**VERSE 3.—Likewise.** To the Gentile, whose usefulness and uncleanness we must not despise.

**Clothing.** The people by whom the teacher is adorned. Literally too, all these things and similar ones must be observed.

**VERSE 5.—A woman shall not wear, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 32.)** Another edition, etc., up to “she ought not to have anything feminine or soft in her teaching.”

**Woman.** Her complexion, unchaste movement, and strength are naturally different; she is not permitted to teach or to exercise authority over a man, nor should she usurp the office of preaching (I Cor. XIII).

[Col. 0475D] It is contrary to nature for a man to act effeminately, curl his hair, or twist his locks. Hence the Apostle: “If a man grows his hair long, it is a disgrace to him.” Hair, however, has been given to a woman as a covering. Therefore a man shall not wear a woman’s garment—that is, conduct marked by excessive looseness and dissolution.

**(RABANUS.)** “We go along the road,” etc., up to “but we retain its allegorical meaning in the mind.”

**VERSE 8.—A new house**, that is, the Church.

**A wall around the roof**, that is, the guardianship of virtues.

**So that blood may not be shed in your house:** that is, so that you may not be held guilty when another sins.

**(GREGORY, Moralia, Book VIII, chapter 39.)** “So that blood may not be shed”: through carelessness and negligence. Hence whoever gathers virtues without humility carries them away like dust in the wind.

[Col. 0476A] **VERSE 9.—A vineyard:** doctrine, or the people entrusted to teachers, where the wine of spiritual grace ought to abound.

**With another seed:** that is, with heresy. The good seed is the word of God; the wicked seed is what the enemy sowed (Matt. XIII). One must therefore beware lest any error be mixed in and the seed of God be corrupted.

**VERSE 10.—You shall not plow. (ISIDORE.)** He plows with an ox and a donkey who receives the Gospels together with the observance of the Jews, which preceded in shadow. The ox also signifies the life of those who work well, and the donkey the dullness of fools. It is as though he were saying: do not join the foolish to the wise in preaching, lest, through the one who is unable to fulfill the task, you obstruct the one who is capable. [Col. 0476B] The foolish and the wise are rightly joined so that one may command and the other obey, not so that they may proclaim the word of God with equal authority.

Allegorically, he mixes wool or purple into linen garments who lives disorderly and combines different kinds of way of life—for example, if a nun wears the adornments of a wife, or a wife adopts the appearance of a virgin. What was then represented in garments is now expressed in morals.

**VERSE 12.—Tassels.** For distinction, just as the sign of circumcision separates the Israelites from others. Superstitious teachers, however, seeking popular applause and profit from little women, enlarged their phylacteries and fastened thorns to them, so that they would be pricked while walking or sitting and thus be admonished to serve God. Hence: “They enlarge their phylacteries and magnify their tassels.”

[Col. 0476C] **VERSE 13.—If he takes her. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 33.)** It is apparent how women subject to men, etc., up to “for which the other was to be punished.”

**VERSE 15.—Her father and mother.** The teachers of the Church, who cherish the people like father and mother: fathers in authority, mothers in compassion.

**VERSE 18.—And they shall beat him.** It is not surprising that the man who falsely accuses is ordered to be beaten and to pay a fine, while the girl, if guilty, is to be stoned. Through the woman came the beginning of sin: she seduced the man and sinned twice—first against God, then against the man—whereas the man sinned only against God.

**VERSE 19.—A hundred shekels, etc.** The perfection of doctrine [Col. 0476D] and solicitude that he should devote to the people subject to him, or of repentance. For one hundred signifies perfection, while fifty is consecrated to repentance.

**VERSE 23.—If a virgin girl is betrothed.** In this chapter, as in the two preceding and the two following chapters, bodily fornication is condemned.

**VERSE 26.—She shall suffer nothing.** Rather, she will be recalled to the faith she had begun through the grace of baptism, having been liberated from her enemies.

**VERSE 29.—He shall not be able. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 34.)** It is rightly asked whether this punishment means that he cannot dismiss her for the whole of his life, since he violated her disorderly and unlawfully. If we understand that he cannot—that is, must not—dismiss her for the whole of his life because she has become his wife, we encounter the fact that Moses permitted a man to give a bill of divorce and dismiss her. But in the case of those whom men violate unlawfully, he did not wish this to be permitted, lest the man seem to have acted in jest and merely pretended that he had married her. He ordered the same concerning the woman against whom her husband had brought an accusation that her virginity had not been found.

[Col. 0477A] **VERSE 30.—Not.** Our Father is Christ, whose wife is the Church. A man may not transfer the dignity of this bridegroom to himself, nor violate his bride by turning her love toward himself, seeking his own praise rather than God’s from the gift of virtues or from preaching. It is fitting for him to say: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Ps. CIII).

## CHAPTER XXIII

**VERSE 1.—He shall not enter.** All who live softly and do not accomplish a manly work [Col. 0477B] cannot remain in the congregation of the saints and are not worthy to enter the kingdom of heaven, which suffers violence, and the violent seize it.

**Mamzer.** Degenerate in understanding or morals; or one whom the depravity of heretics has made degenerate in receiving the sacraments; or whom the rite of paganism or Judaism has defiled. He will be received into the Church when he has preserved the Decalogue of the Law with an integral faith according to the teaching of the Gospel, and, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, has rejected carnal conduct. Hence: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (Matt. XIX). Elsewhere: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John X).

**VERSE 3.—Ammonites and Moabites. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 33.)** Another edition, etc., up to “they attributed it to the women, whom they preferred to preserve.”

**Moabites.** This signifies that heretics must always be expelled from the Church: “A heretical person, after one or two admonitions, avoid.”

**VERSE 4.—Because they would not meet us with, etc.** The Hebrews relate that these nations, which were related to them, came out to meet them as they were leaving Egypt with bread alone, although they knew that we were suffering especially from thirst in the desert; and for this reason they were subjected to this curse.

Mystically, they signify heretics, who, when those fleeing from the Egypt of this world toward the true promised land, offer polluted bread, not sweetened with the water of wisdom; and for this reason they have been alienated from the Church.

**VERSE 5.—And he turned.** Because persecution is often the cause of greater prosperity: “All things work together for good for those who love God” (Rom. VIII).

**VERSE 7.—You shall not abhor the Edomite.** “Edomite,” meaning bloody or earthly, signifies the flesh, whose matter is earthly. “Egyptian,” meaning dark, signifies the diseased body. We must not abhor our flesh, but nourish it and provide what is necessary for it; nevertheless, we must not make its care our desire. “He is your brother,” it says, because we consist of flesh and soul. We must not abhor the Egyptian—that is, the body—in whose land we were sojourners. The soul, which has a heavenly origin, dwells in the body as a sojourner. Hence the Apostle: “While we are in the body, we are away from the Lord” (II Cor. V). “Those who are born from them,” etc.: that is, they will gradually become spiritual.

[Col. 0478A] Through the Edomite and the Egyptian, the present life is signified. Although we renounce the Egyptian land—that is, our former way of life—and turn away from worldly desire, nevertheless, while we remain subject to the necessities of this world, we do not completely extinguish the Egyptian nation. Rather, separated from it in a certain way, we are content with daily food and clothing. In the third generation they will enter the Church, because a worldly person can be joined to God’s saints when he has come to believe perfectly in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, or when he has been adorned with hope, faith, and charity.

**VERSE 9.—When.** He instructs the spiritual soldiers of Christ, to whom it is said elsewhere: “Everyone who contends in the contest abstains from everything” (I Cor. IX).

[Col. 0478B] **If. (AUGUSTINE, On the Good of Marriage, chapter 20.)** The Law sets forth many things in the form of mysteries and shadows of future realities, etc., up to “not because a dead body is sin, but because it signifies the sin of a soul abandoned by righteousness.”

Mystically. **(GREGORY, Moralia, Book IX, chapter 40.)** “If there is among you a man who has been defiled by a nocturnal emission,” etc. A nocturnal dream signifies a hidden temptation, etc., up to “and be restored to the merits of the faithful, which are to be hoped for.”

**VERSE 12.—You shall have.** God loves bodily cleanliness; therefore he commanded that nothing foul remain in the camp.

Mystically. **(GREGORY, Moralia, Book XXXI, chapter 32.)** “You shall have a place,” etc. From the weight of corruptible nature, which burdens it, certain superfluous thoughts burst from the womb of our mind like the burden of the belly. But we must carry a stake beneath the belt, so that, always girded for reproving ourselves, we may have around us the sharp [Col. 0478C] goad of compunction, which pierces the soil of our mind with the pain of repentance and conceals what foulness bursts forth from us.

[Col. 0478D] **VERSE 13.—On your belt.** The loins are girded with a belt; therefore the belt signifies the restraint of evil will. Hence Job: “He loosens the belt of kings and girds their loins with a cord” (Job II).

**You shall cover with earth.** Considering our earthly frailty, we must cover our filth.

**VERSE 15.—You shall not hand over a slave. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 36.)** The Septuagint says: “You shall not hand over a servant to his master who has been assigned to you by his master.” Not that the master assigned him, etc., up to “he explains this by saying: ‘He shall dwell among you in any place where it pleases him’” (I Sam. XXVII).

[Col. 0478D] **VERSE 17.—There shall be no prostitute. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 37.)** The Septuagint says: “There shall be no prostitute,” etc., up to “there we discussed what seemed to us appropriate.”

**You shall not offer the fee of a prostitute. (AUGUSTINE, Questions, 38.)** The Septuagint says: “You shall not offer,” etc., up to “it had to be said that this is an abomination to the Lord.”

**The price of a dog, of a rapacious one.** The Most High does not approve the gifts of the wicked. Whoever offers a sacrifice from the substance of the poor is like one who sacrifices a son in the presence of his father (Ecclus. XXXIV).

**VERSE 19.—You shall not lend at interest to your brother.** He removes usury and greed and commands that charity be expended.

And there is money that is forbidden to be lent at interest, because it is a vice of covetousness to wish to demand what you know you did not lend. The Lord possessed this money [Col. 0479A] and entrusted it to be distributed to the poor, inviting us to generous liberality. There is another kind that we ought to lend at interest. Hence: “Should you not have entrusted my money to the money-changers, so that when I came I might have collected what was mine with interest?” (Matt. XXV).

**VERSE 20.—But to a foreigner.** To an unbeliever or wicked person to whom we lend money at interest, when in return for the word of preaching we demand faith, repentance, and good works.

**VERSE 21.—You shall not delay repaying.** Hence Solomon: “After vows, it is ruin for a man to reconsider or delay” (Prov. X).

[Col. 0479B] **VERSE 24.—When you enter your neighbor’s vineyard.** In another bishop’s church, one bishop may correct or strengthen some individuals, but he is not permitted to govern the entire people or handle major affairs.

**Outside.** It is not permitted to carry this grace outside the Church, because the flesh of the lamb is commanded to be eaten in one house.

**VERSE 25.—If you enter.** There are certain passages of Scripture that instill faith historically; some instruct in holy conduct morally; and some, not according to history but according to allegory, display venerable mysteries. One must therefore enter the field of one’s neighbor cautiously, so that by discerning one may gather food, rather than incurring the judgment of a prematurely cut harvest.

## CHAPTER XXIV

[Col. 0479C] **VERSE 1.—If he takes. (RABANUS, On Deuteronomy, Book II.)** “A man took a wife,” etc., up to “she remained abominable, as unworthy and polluted by error.” Hence: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken first to you, but since,” etc. (Acts XIII).

**(AUGUSTINE, Book I of On the Sermon on the Mount.)** There were many reasons in the Law for dismissing wives, etc., up to “so that those who have wives may be as though they had none” (I Cor. VII).

**He shall write.** “Because of the hardness of your hearts Moses wrote this commandment for you,” preferring to allow separation rather than permit murder.

[Col. 0479D] **VERSE 4.—Lest he sin.** He pollutes his land who defiles his body with carnal desires. Therefore the ambition of the present life must be subdued quickly, lest it become dominant. And once an earthly action has been rejected, it must not be taken up again, lest the one who has put his hand to the plow look back.

**VERSE 5.—When he has taken.** It is as though he were saying: whoever binds himself to carnal desires for the governance of the Church should recognize that he is unfit for spiritual warfare: “No one serving God entangles himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself” (II Tim. II). Hence: “Lay hands on no one hastily.”

**(ISIDORE.)** He removes the upper millstone who says to a weeping sinner, “You will not receive pardon for what you have committed.” He removes the lower one who, by caressing sin, says: “Do as much evil as you wish; God is merciful and ready to forgive.” Both millstones are usefully retained if hope exists together with fear in the one who is correcting himself, and fear together with hope.

[Col. 0480A] (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 16.) “You shall not take the lower [one] as a pledge,” etc. Sometimes, however, we use “to take” to mean “to offer,” etc., up to “and he fears in vain who does not trust.”

**VERSE 7.**—“You shall remove.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 39.) Scripture says this repeatedly, etc., up to the passage which he explains by saying: “Let the one who was stealing steal no longer” (Eph. IV).

**VERSE 8.**—“The plague of leprosy.” Note that this disease comes upon human beings because of sin, as in the case of Uzziah, who usurped the priesthood.

**VERSE 10.**—“When you reclaim.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 41.) It belongs to the work of mercy that the creditor should not enter the debtor’s house, etc., up to “having nowhere to sleep.”

“Is not ...?” The one who proclaims the Gospel should live from the Gospel (I Cor. IX). “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X).

[Col. 0480B] **VERSE 16.**—“They shall not be put to death.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 42.) The Law also says, etc., up to the point where he wished not three or four to be understood.

**VERSE 17.**—“You shall not pervert.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 43.) The Septuagint reads: “You shall not distort the judgment of the resident alien, the orphan, and the widow. You shall not take a widow’s garment in pledge.” Why does he not say, etc., up to “their continence is praised, not their desolation commended.”

“Of the widow.” The widow is the soul previously joined to the devil; once converted to faith, her garment must not be taken away.

**VERSE 19.**—“You shall not return.” Through envy of the nations, who are resident aliens with respect to God’s covenants.

**VERSE 20.**—“When you have gathered the fruits.” Even if the proud and the wicked gather, the person who leaves something behind with the intention that the needy may have it performs an act of mercy. Moreover, when these commands are given to the people, those who are not in need are warned not to seek such things. If they do seek them, they are to be judged as plunderers of the poor.

“Your vineyard.” The vineyard from which wine is gathered, “which gladdens the heart of man” (Ps. CIII).

## CHAPTER XXV

**VERSE 1.**—“If there is a dispute.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 45.) The Septuagint reads: “But if there is a quarrel between men,” etc., up to the point that sins which appear to be committed not against God but against a human being are nevertheless some worthy of death and others of beating.

**VERSE 3.**—“Forty.” The number forty is completed by four multiplied by ten. We, however, consist bodily of the four elements; the commandments of the Decalogue are understood through the number ten.
