He therefore commands that judgment or punishment, by which the sin of the flesh is chastised, be ordered according to the commandments, and he wishes all the commandments to be understood in the Decalogue.

(ISIDORE.) In the number forty this period is represented, etc., up to the point where “there we are found without sin.”

**VERSE 4.**—“The mouth of the ox that threshes.” (ISIDORE.) In the ox is represented the life of those who labor, concerning whom it is said: “The laborer is worthy of his wages” (Luke X). Scripture therefore wishes material support to be provided to those from whom we receive spiritual things, since those occupied with teaching cannot provide for their own necessities.

**VERSE 5.**—“When.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 46.) The Septuagint reads: “If brothers have lived together before,” etc., up to the point where either adoption made the other a father whom Joseph could have.

**VERSE 5.**—“If he has died.” He suffered and ascended into heaven while the barren synagogue still remained.

“But he shall receive,” etc. The one capable of governing, whom the unwilling woman spits upon in the face. For when someone does not care to benefit others through spiritual gifts, the Church, reproaching him for this, as it were spits in his face.

**VERSE 9.**—“The sandal.” Concerning which it is said: “With your feet shod in the preparation of the Gospel of peace” (Ezek. VI). If we care for our neighbor as we care for ourselves, we protect both feet with the sandal. But the person who, thinking of his own advantage, neglects his neighbors loses, as it were, the sandal of one foot in disgrace.

[Col. 0481B] He will show that he has been deprived of the foot—that is, of the reward of preaching. The feet of teachers are shod because, fortified by the examples of earlier fathers, they have imitated the steps of their preaching. He is shod on both feet who benefits both himself and others.

**VERSE 11.**—“And one against the other.” The Catholic and the heretic, whose contention is perpetual because their intention differs: one defends falsehood, the other truth. One must resist error, lest the fool appear wise to himself.

“And she has sent.” When, through false disgrace or some detestable action, she wishes to stain the Catholic’s way of life or defame his teaching.

“Private parts.” The weaker members of the Church, whom they wish to deceive by flattering them or mock by insulting them.

[Col. 0481C] **VERSE 13.**—“You shall not have in your bag.” The same is forbidden in Leviticus. Solomon also says: “A large weight and a small one, and double measures, are unclean before God” (Prov. XX).

(ISIDORE.) “You shall not have in your bag.” Spiritually, too, one must take care not to have different weights in one’s heart—that is, not to soften the rule of strictness for oneself while burdening those to whom we preach the word of God with stricter commandments, as though with heavier weights. When we do this, we weigh out the reward and fruit of the Lord’s commandments with different weights. Hence: “A double weight is an abomination to the Lord” (Prov. XX).

**VERSE 17.**—“Remember what.” The Hebrews relate that Amalek killed lepers, those suffering from seminal discharges, and others stationed outside the camp; they say that these were the rearmost of the Lord’s army. Amalek, “licking blood,” signifies the demons who oppose us as we come out through baptism from spiritual Egypt. By suggesting sins, they strive to kill those who are last in virtue and wearied on the journey of this life. Whenever the Lord grants us the power, we must utterly overthrow them and drive out and destroy their suggestions by every means, lest, if we preserve any remnants—as Saul did—we too may be overthrown with them as disobedient people.

## CHAPTER XXVI

**VERSE 1.**—“When you have entered,” etc. Just as the Israelites were commanded to offer their first fruits in the promised land as thanksgiving because they had been rescued from Egypt, so we, entering the land of the Church through the spiritual Jordan—that is, baptism—should place the first fruits of good works in the basket of our way of life and offer them to God upon the altar of catholic faith. Then our priest, Christ, will receive them, and there we shall confess to the Lord, saying that the Syrian—whose name is interpreted as “exalted” or “moistening,” that is, the devil—was persecuting our father, the first-formed man, in order to deprive him, once deceived through pride, gluttony, and avarice, of possession of paradise. Therefore, as an exile, he wandered in Egypt, this world, with a small number, because many followed idolatry and few remained faithful.

But after the Law was given, more arose, receiving knowledge and faith in the one God. The Egyptians—that is, the demons—afflicted them by imposing the heaviest burdens of sins. But God regarded the affliction and labor of the human race and sent his Son, who is called his hand and arm, to rescue them from the power of darkness and transfer them into the kingdom of light. Thus he gave us a land flowing with milk and honey—that is, the powerful Church—where there is the milk of innocence and the honeycomb of teaching with which the little ones may be nourished, and the sweet honey of manifold wisdom with which the mature may be satisfied.

[Col. 0482B] **VERSE 10.**—“Which the Lord your God has given,” etc. It is as though he were saying: “I offer nothing except what he has given,” for every good thing is from God.

“Of the Lord your God.” He will preserve it, as it were, before his eyes, and return it on that day as a righteous judge.

**VERSE 11.**—“You shall feast”—at a spiritual banquet, concerning which it is said: “Eat, friends, and drink deeply, beloved” (Song V).

“And the Levite”—the true minister of God, taken from among human beings and appointed on behalf of human beings in matters pertaining to God.

**VERSE 12.**—“When you have completed.” Tobit fulfilled this command of the Law; those who lived far from the Temple, however, in the third year gave the tithes collected over three years to the poor and to the Levites who lived with them.

## CHAPTER XXVII

**VERSE 2.**—“Stones.” Teachers ought to put away every harshness and therefore appear radiant, having the Law written in their hearts.

**VERSE 4.**—“When, therefore.” (ISIDORE.) How this was done, etc., up to the point where they are worthy of the construction of the altar.

Those who proceed beside Mount Gerizim, chosen for blessing, represent those who come to salvation, inflamed not by fear of punishment but by love of the heavenly promise. Those who proceed beside Mount Ebal, on which the curses were pronounced, are those who keep the commandments of the Law not out of love for blessings or promises but from fear of punishment. All proceed around the ark because they do not withdraw from the bosom of the Church. Yet the nobler are those who serve out of charity rather than those who serve from fear of punishment.

Jesus alone can know such minds and appoint some on Mount Gerizim for blessing and others on Mount Ebal for cursing—not so that they may receive the curse, but so that they may beware of the curses written and appointed for sinners and repent through fear of punishment.

[Col. 0483A] **VERSE 13.**—“And they shall pronounce.” Because the priest ought to preach the word earnestly and forcefully to the peoples, so that they may know what dangers await them if they transgress God’s commands and what benefits follow if they obey—namely, consolation in the present life and eternal reward in the future.

Historically, the curses and blessings pertain to those who love earthly happiness or fear earthly unhappiness. Christians, however, must above all beware lest through disobedience they suffer deprivation of spiritual things. For the perfect often experience want of earthly goods, while an abundance of virtues is always present in them. Hence: “To this very hour we hunger and thirst and are naked,” etc. (I Cor. IV).

“Cursed.” Not only is idolatry involving images forbidden, but every error of heretics as well. These are craftsmen of vanity and of superstitious doctrine who fashion for themselves from their own hearts whatever gods they wish.

**VERSE 16.**—“All the people.” All ought to praise what is good and detest what is evil, both rulers and subjects.

**VERSE 17.**—“Cursed is the one who moves the boundary markers.” This is the person who, not content with catholic faith and doctrine, introduces superstitions and sects.

**VERSE 20.**—“Cursed is the one who lies with.” Every incestuous act is an abomination, but this especially strikes heretics and schismatics, who corrupt the bride of Christ—who is the Father and Creator of all—through error. Tropologically, however, it forbids anyone to disgrace his father by imitating his wicked conduct and to expose his shame.

**VERSE 21.**—“Cursed.” Cursed is the person who follows the folly of the gentiles. A man or woman who clings to such intercourse not through weakness but perseveringly is guilty of death.

**VERSE 22.**—“Lies with”—that is, defiles another’s soul by teaching wickedly or displaying wicked examples. For our one Father is God, and the Church is our mother; we are all brothers or sisters.

[Col. 0483D] **VERSE 23.**—“With his mother-in-law.” The mother-in-law signifies the desire for wicked action, since desire is the mother of every sin. Let us therefore attend carefully, so that we resist desire and do not fulfill what we desire.

**VERSE 24.**—“Cursed.” To kill a human being in any manner is a sin. It therefore seems surprising that he spoke only of a curse against the one who strikes secretly. But perhaps to strike secretly means to hate in one’s heart. Hence: “The one who hates his brother is a murderer” (John III). And elsewhere: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Lev. XIX).

**VERSE 26.**—“Cursed is the one who does not remain.” This sentence embraces generally all the commandments of the Law, past, present, and future, and is all the more severe because it is general. For who can remain without transgression in all the words of the Law, since Paul also says: “All who rely on works of the Law are under a curse”? (Gal. III.) No one could escape this curse—not even the Lawgiver—except Christ. Hence: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law, having become a curse for us,” etc.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“But if you listen.” Just as he foretells curses and punishments for the disobedient, so he promises blessings and rewards to the obedient.

**VERSE 4.**—“The fruit of your womb.” He indicates various orders among subjects. Some provide teachers with bodily assistance; others are able to perform what has been commanded them; others, content with simplicity, strive to please God through an innocent life. Each person has his own gift from God.

**VERSE 5.**—“Blessed shall be your remnants.” The reward of good intention, even when the will does not achieve its effect, because “peace to people of good will,” etc. (Luke II).

**VERSE 6.**—“Entering.” The one who enters through the door is the person who, through catholic faith, meditates upon and handles within himself what accords with God’s will. He goes out when he manifests the same thing before human beings for the praise of God.

**VERSE 7.**—“Before your eyes.” So that you may rejoice: “The righteous shall rejoice when he sees the vengeance” (Ps. LVII).

**VERSE 8.**—“And he shall bless.” By granting increase and happy success to good works.

“Heaven.” The prophets and apostles, concerning whom it is said: “The heavens declare the glory of God.” The Lord opens them when, through them, he grants an abundance of teaching, so that hearts of flesh, watered by this rain, may bring forth the shoots of good works.

“You shall lend.” That is, such abundance will be yours that you will be able to lend money to the nations, while they will not have as much. Alternatively, this may be understood of ecclesiastical teaching.

“You shall lend to many nations.” The Church lends to many nations when she expends divine gifts upon peoples. She receives no interest, because she seeks not present repayment but future reward. For she excels all and is the head of the world, not its tail. She is always above and not beneath; although she suffers the pressures and persecutions of the wicked in the world, she is nevertheless stronger than her adversaries and surpasses all in faith and virtue. Hence: “The Lord will set you at the head,” etc.

[Col. 0484D] **VERSE 14.**—“You shall not turn aside.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 48.) The Septuagint reads: “You shall not depart from all the words,” etc., up to the point that “they are not to be worshiped on account of these things.”

**VERSE 15.**—“But if you will not listen.” Just as he promised blessing to those who keep the commandments, so he declares a curse against those who neglect them.

**VERSE 22.**—“The Lord shall strike you.” (AUGUSTINE, *Enchiridion*, chapter 98.) Who could be so impiously foolish as to say that God cannot turn to good the evil wills of human beings—whomever he wishes, whenever he wishes, wherever he wishes? But when he does so, he does it through mercy; when he does not, he does so through judgment—he who has mercy on whom he wishes and hardens whom he wishes.

“And with corrupted air.” A life polluted by carnal uncleanness. [Col. 0485A] A carnal life polluted by carnal uncleanness. A carnal life is expressed by air, because the human body is made alive by the breath of air.

**VERSE 23.**—“Let the sky be.” He compares the elements by which fruits are nourished to the hardest metals, because human sins change the order of things; and what was created for the consolation of the human race becomes its opposite. Hence: “The whole world fought on his behalf against the senseless” (Wis. V).

The sky is bronze for transgressors of the Law when they deserve no mercy from holy teachers but the harshest discipline, because they themselves possess not a heart of flesh and a tender spirit but a heart of stone and iron. Thus the Law was given on stone to a hard-hearted people, so that the recipient might be represented by the gift.

**VERSE 24.**—“May the Lord give the rain of your land dust.” It is as though he were saying: Just as dust and ashes produce no fruit, so the doctrine poured into you will not arouse shoots of virtue but will foretell eternal destruction. Dust signifies the barrenness of good works, and ashes signify burning, because the chaff of sins will be burned with unquenchable fire.

**VERSE 25.**—“And you shall be scattered.” Just as the Jews were taken captive and scattered across the breadth of the world because they gathered themselves against God, so the generation of the wicked, scattered by unclean spirits, is thrown into confusion through various punishments. Hence: “Your enemies shall perish, and all who work iniquity shall be scattered” (Ps. XCI).

**VERSE 27.**—“The Lord shall strike you with the ulcer of Egypt.” Painful, pus-filled ulcers signify malice. Swellings signify inflated pride. Scabies and itching signify burning anger and the madness of fury. In the present life, a punishment corresponding to sins is inflicted through these things; after this life—as is indicated later—they will endure the stench of their crimes in eternal torments.

“The Lord shall strike you.” Heretics and schismatics, while the Gospel shines throughout the whole world, are enveloped in the blindness of error and, exercising their madness, oppose the catholic faith. Therefore they endure the Church’s calumny and are overcome by the truth.

They were mad and blind when, seeing Christ’s miracles, they said that they were performed by Beelzebub and denied that Christ was God (Matt. VII); nor did they see the truth—that is, they did not understand it.

**VERSE 29.**—“And you shall grope.” Darkness came to be when Jesus was crucified, until the ninth hour, just as darkness existed in the hearts of the Jews.

“You shall not prosper.” They neither believed while Christ was preaching nor wished to be set right through repentance.

**VERSE 30.**—“You shall take a wife, and another,” etc. In the wife is understood the people joined to the heretics, with whom the devil commits fornication while they are led into error. The animals are seized from the heretics when their subjects are freed from them, and when the heretics themselves are deprived of life and teaching. The wealth that the Jews prepared for themselves in a special way through teaching and writing the Church converts to her own use.

**VERSE 33.**—“The fruit of your land.” The entire usefulness of the ceremonies has been transferred to the Church. She enjoys this abundance, while the Jews perish in poverty. Hence it is said through Isaiah: “My servants shall eat, and you shall hunger” (Isa. LXV).

**VERSE 35.**—“On the knees and on the shins.” May he take away strength and stability. Or, let the one whose final works are condemned be struck on the knees.

“From the sole of the foot.” Just as you practiced wickedness from the beginning of an evil will to the completion of the deed, so that “from the sole of the foot to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. I). This was fulfilled in the final captivity.

**VERSE 36.**—“And he shall lead you.” Heretics and wicked Catholics who despise God’s commandments are taken captive by demons and various vices. As the servant, so the master; as the king, so the people; as the teacher, so the disciple.

[Col. 0486B] “And the king.” Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, led Hoshea, king of Samaria, into captivity with the ten tribes. Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin and Zedekiah, king of Judah, captive with the people.

**VERSE 38.**—“Seed,” etc. We too must beware lest we lose the bread that strengthens the human heart, the wine that gladdens it, and the oil that makes the face shine.

**VERSE 43.**—“The resident alien.” The rejection of the Jews and the election of the nations are clearly signified. Hence: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits”; and elsewhere: “So the last shall be first, and the first last.”

(RABANUS, *On Deuteronomy*, book II.) “The resident alien who dwells among you,” etc. The Creator of all, through the mystery of his incarnation, etc., up to the point where he has regarded the blood of the covenant as polluted.

**VERSE 66.**—“And your life shall hang.” Nothing is worse among the curses that befell the Jews on account of their pride than to see their life—that is, the Son of God—hanging and not believe in him. When curses are spoken prophetically, they do not express an evil wish but foretell what will occur. The words could, however, have sounded to the Jews as follows: “You shall see your life hanging, and you shall not believe your life”—that is, amid the threats and treacheries of enemies, you shall see your life hanging in uncertainty.

## CHAPTER XXIX

**VERSE 1.**—“These are the words,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions on Deuteronomy*, 49.) The Septuagint reads: “These are the words of the covenant,” etc., up to the point concerning Abraham and circumcision or Noah.

[Col. 0486D] **VERSE 3.**—“Great temptations,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 50.) “And the Lord God did not give you a heart to know,” etc., up to the point that “although God’s judgments are hidden, they are nevertheless just.”

**VERSE 6.**—“You did not eat bread,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) From this it is clear that the Israelites, etc., up to “the beginning of war,” but “the beginning of wine.”

**VERSE 18.**—“Lest perhaps there be.” (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 52.) The Septuagint reads: “Is there perhaps anyone among you,” etc., up to the point that “he had not desired another man’s wife.”

**VERSES 19–20.**—“The drunkard with the thirsty, and the Lord,” etc. That is: lest anyone full of malice and idolatry seduce one who thirsts to learn and know the truth, as heretics do.

## CHAPTER XXX

[Col. 0487A] **VERSE 11.**—“This commandment, which I command you,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 54.) The Septuagint reads: “For this commandment,” etc., up to the point that, without it, even if things are done outwardly by the hands and not inwardly in the heart, God’s commandments are not fulfilled.

**VERSE 14.**—“The word is near you,” etc. That is, God’s commandments are proportioned and adapted to human capacities. This may be understood of Christ’s incarnation, since, having assumed humanity, he was seen upon earth and lived among human beings.

## CHAPTER XXXI

**VERSE 7.**—“And he called.” The words of Moses to Joshua signify that Christ distributes the land of the living to each according to his own merits and fulfills all God’s promises. He himself introduces the people into the promised land. Under his leadership we enter the heavenly homeland, for he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John XIV). And: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man who is in heaven” (John III); for whoever is united to him ascends through him.

**VERSE 10.**—“After seven years.” These signify the present life, which revolves according to the number seven; or the time of the Old Law, on account of the Sabbath. Therefore, after seven years, in the year of remission, the Law is commanded to be read in the assembly, because when observance of the Law has been completed, the spiritual Law succeeds it. Hence: “When the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son, born of a woman,” etc. (Eph. IV).

[Col. 0487C] **VERSE 24.**—“After Moses had finished writing.” Deuteronomy is entrusted to the Levites because the Gospel of Christ is deposited in the memory of the Church through the ministry of true priests. The Church is the ark of the Lord, in which heavenly treasures are stored. There are the two tablets of the covenant, namely, the books of the Law and the Gospel. There is the urn containing manna—that is, the flesh of Christ, in which is the food of eternal life. There is Aaron’s rod, which had blossomed, because there is the priesthood of Christ, which remains forever. It is to remain there as a testimony against you.

The words of the Law are for salvation to those who keep them, but for testimony to the stubbornness and disobedience of those who despise them. Hence: “There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope. For if you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, since he wrote about me” (John V). And elsewhere: “The word that I have spoken will judge him” (John XII).

**VERSE 30.**—“So Moses spoke.” Moses’ words are not to be understood simply, because historically he reproaches the Israelites for their faithlessness toward God, their benefactor; allegorically he instructs the holy Church; and tropologically he urges moral integrity. Therefore truth must be preserved in the historical sense, mysteries in the allegorical sense, and the practical usefulness of discipline in the tropological sense, so that in this way we may be raised to heavenly contemplation.

It should also be noted that it says: “Moses spoke the words of this song,” etc., so that the person who praises God with his mouth may not contradict him by his deeds. “Praise is not beautiful in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. XIII).

## CHAPTER XXXII

[Col. 0488A] “Hear, O heavens.” At the beginning he calls the greatest elements as witnesses, so that, if they neglect the commandments, he may punish them after convicting them by their testimony.

In Hebrew, *samaiim*, that is, “heavens,” is plural and masculine in gender; yet he wished it to be understood in the singular, just as we speak of individual cities by the names Thebes and Athens.

“Hear, O heavens.” (RABANUS.) Let the heavens hear the allegory and the earth the history.

## CHAPTER XXXII

**VERSE 1.**—“Hear, O heavens,” etc. Some think that heaven and earth, as though endowed with life, are summoned to hear, in accordance with the saying: “He looks upon the earth and makes it tremble” (Ps. CIII), whereas this belongs to God’s power, not to their understanding.

**VERSE 2.**—“Let it condense.” He compares the teaching of the Law to rain and dew, because it demands shoots of spiritual fruit from the hearts of the faithful. These are God’s field and vineyard. The same is expressed in Isaiah: “As the rain and snow descend from heaven and do not return there, but water the earth, moisten its surface, and make it germinate” (Isa. LV).

**VERSE 3.**—“The name.” He shows what the rain is. To invoke the name of the Lord is to preach the Gospel; whoever hears it and acts upon it will possess the fruit of life.

“Of God.” Hence: “The heavens and the earth and all their adornment were completed, and God finished his work on the seventh day” (Gen. II). This signifies the redemption of the human race, which he showed us when, completing the spiritual Sabbath, he rested in the tomb.

[Col. 0488D] **VERSE 5.**—“They have sinned against him,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Questions*, 55.) The Septuagint reads: “They have sinned—not against him—blameworthy children.” For whoever sins, etc., up to the point that they did not harm him by their sin but themselves.

“And not.” Because they were not from faith. “He gave them power to become children of God, to those who believe in his name.” But of unbelievers it is said: “You are of your father the devil.”

“A crooked generation.” Concerning which the Gospel says: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign” (Matt. XII). And elsewhere: “Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?” (Luke III).

**VERSE 6.**—“Is he not,” etc. The one God is the Creator and Maker of all, from whom, through whom, and in whom all things exist. The order is reversed: first God created by arranging things so that they should exist; second, he made by giving them form; third, by ruling he possessed them.

“He created.” He created when he established the matter from which things could be formed. He is therefore foolish and senseless who does not worship his Creator and Maker with fitting reverence. Forgetful of the benefit by which God rescued him from the hand of his enemies and claimed him as his own, led him through the Red Sea, and gave him manna from heaven, he ungratefully worshiped idols, saying: “These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (Exod. XXXII).

**VERSE 7.**—“The Father.” The teacher of the Law and preacher of the Gospel, whose teaching and example instruct you.

[Col. 0489A] **VERSE 8.**—“When he divided,” etc. It is as though he were saying: Although the multitude of human beings is innumerable, the Lord chose only the children of Israel as his inheritance, making known to them his power and secrets through the signs of the Law and the prophets.

“He established.” (GREGORY, *Homily 4 on the Gospels*.) Another edition reads, etc., up to the point that they ascend into their lot through similarity of conduct.

**VERSE 9.**—“But the Lord’s portion is his people.” Although God created all the nations, he chose the Israelites alone, glorifying them through knowledge of himself, signs, and miracles.

**VERSE 10.**—“He found.” Because he entered into a covenant with them at Sinai, gave them manna, brought water from the rock, supplied quail, and led them about in the wilderness for forty years, teaching them his commandments.

“He led them about.” By extending the Church throughout the world and directing her along the way of his commandments.

“He guarded.” Many were struck down in the wilderness after they had transgressed God’s commandments.

**VERSE 11.**—“As an eagle.” According to the natural philosophers, the eagle is so called because of the sharpness of its eyes. It sees so keenly that, when it is borne motionless over the sea on an unmoving wing and is invisible to human sight, it can see little fish swimming in the sea; then, descending like a projectile, it drags its captured prey to the shore with its wings.

It also beats its fledglings with its wings and urges them to fly. Thus Christ, exhorting us by words and examples, raises us to lofty things so that we may follow where he has gone before. Hence: “Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered” (Matt. XXIV). Exalted above the heavens and withdrawn from human sight, he sees with the eyes of mercy those swimming in the sea of this world and draws them with the wings of love to the shore of eternal security. Hence: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John XII).

“As an eagle,” etc. They say that when the eagle sees its young beginning to grow feathers, it turns them toward the sun and nourishes the one that looks at the sun’s rays with an unblinking gaze. If one turns its eyes away, it neglects it as degenerate. It urges the young to fly and supports the weary with its wings. So God invites us to the true Sun, sympathizes with our weaknesses, and supports us with the wings of grace.

“Urging.” The Lord urged his people to possess the land of Canaan, helped them, and protected them from enemies.

**VERSE 12.**—“The Lord.” The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. He does not say “the Father alone,” lest he exclude the Son or the Holy Spirit, but “the Lord alone,” that is, God.

“The Lord.” The heretics have as many lords as the errors they cultivate.

**VERSE 13.**—“The high place.” Palestine, which is mountainous; Egypt is flat and low-lying.

The Church is exalted in virtue and knowledge. In her the fruit of the fields is eaten, because there the good seed—that is, the word of God—germinates. There are the thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and hundredfold fruits, so that each person may eat sufficiently according to his capacity.

[Col. 0490A] “And he would suck.” (GREGORY, *Homily 26 on the Gospels*.) “That he might suck honey from the rock and oil from the flinty rock.” This is nowhere recorded as having happened according to the historical sense, etc., up to the gift of the devil through the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

Literally, honey signifies an abundance of all things.

**VERSE 14.**—“Of the sons.” Bashan is a region abundant in livestock because of its pastures. Therefore it was given to the Reubenites, Gadites, and half-tribe of Manasseh, because they possessed many animals.

“And goats.” These signify penitents, since goats were offered for sin. It is not enough for the faithful to receive gifts of virtue unless they strive to repent of their offenses. Hence: “Wash me yet more from my iniquity” (Ps. L).

[Col. 0490B] He calls them goats who, by their example, offer others works of repentance, although they themselves have committed no grave offenses; for they mourn the sins of their thoughts as though they had been deeds.

“With the marrow of wheat.” The body of Christ; hence: “Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground,” etc. (John XII).

**VERSE 15.**—“The beloved grew fat,” etc. Just as the Jews, grown fat through benefits, became idolaters, so some Christians turn the mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, which they have received, into their own destruction.

**VERSE 16.**—“They provoked.” Some become heretics, others idolaters, fashioning idols and abominations for themselves out of their own hearts.

**VERSE 17.**—“New and recent.” Departing from the worship of God, they found for themselves gods whom their fathers had worshiped.

**VERSE 20.**—“And he said: I will hide,” etc. Nothing is more serious than to be deprived of the vision of God. Hence: “Do not cast me away from your face” (Ps. L). Likewise: “Do not turn your face away,” etc. (Ps. LXXXVIII).

“They provoked me,” etc. It is as though he were saying: Just as they provoked me by worshiping a multitude of false gods and rejecting me, so I will provoke them by adopting and rejecting a multitude of nations.

“And I will provoke them,” etc. By handing them over to the nations—those who once were not a people but are now God’s people. Likewise, Christians who abandon the truth and turn aside to errors are handed over to wicked spirits, who have lost their angelic dignity. They are rightly called a foolish nation, hating righteousness and loving iniquity.

[Col. 0490D] **VERSE 22.**—“A fire has been kindled,” etc. (GREGORY, *Moralia*, book XVIII, chapter 12.) Concerning those whom scourges condemn but do not free, it is written: “You struck them, and they did not grieve,” etc. Their scourges begin in this life and will continue eternally. Hence Moses: “A fire has been kindled by his anger, and it shall burn down to the underworld and below.” The present striking is expressed by: “A fire has been kindled by my anger” (Jer. XV); the eternal follows: “And it shall burn down to the underworld and below” (Ps. LXXXVIII). Yet God does not judge twice for the same matter, for the scourge is one: it begins temporally and is completed in eternal punishments.

“And it shall devour the earth.” Others read: “They shall eat the earth and its produce,” that is, the flesh; an eternal flame will burn them because of the works of lust. The produce of the flesh signifies the works of carnal desire, which are fornication, uncleanness, and similar things.

**VERSE 24.**—“Birds with their bite.” Those that eat the seed beside the road.

“The teeth of beasts,” etc. Beasts and serpents drag the reprobate across the earth with furious teeth when, after first persuading them through flattery to follow carnal things and thereby seducing them, they furiously demand them from sinners in order to torment them.

**VERSE 25.**—“Outside.” The burning of eternal fire will torment the body, and the magnitude of anguish will torment the mind. Hence: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI).

“Young man.” No age will be spared, because idolatry has stained everyone.

**VERSE 26.**—“I will make them cease from among human beings.” Driven out of their land, they were scattered throughout the whole world. Generally, however, sinners will be removed from the land of the saints and from their memory. Hence: “Therefore your God will destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from the land of the living,” etc. (Ps. LI).

**VERSE 27.**—“I delayed.” So that they would not blaspheme my name, although I did not take away vengeance.

**VERSE 30.**—“How.” He shows how great was the fear of the Jewish nation after they sinned against the Lord: one of their enemies would put a thousand to flight, and two would put ten thousand to flight—that is, a few would put many to flight.

**VERSE 31.**—“Judges.” Approvers. Even those who worship idols understand that there is one God who made heaven and earth.

**VERSE 32.**—“From the vine,” etc. This signifies the wickedness of heretics, who received pure spiritual teaching from holy teachers but corrupted it with their own poison and changed it into the bitterness of gall and wormwood. Jerusalem is often compared with Sodom and Gomorrah. Hence: “Hear the word of the Lord, rulers of Sodom and Gomorrah” (Isa. I).

“Bitter clusters.” Their fruits—that is, their works—are exceedingly bitter, for they offered him wine mixed with gall.

**VERSE 33.**—“The gall of dragons.” It is as though they retained within themselves the poison of malice, lest they receive the medicine of salvation and correction. Heretics, like serpents, conceal bitterness and poison in order to injure the unwary.

[Col. 0491D] **VERSE 35.**—“Vengeance is mine,” etc. Paul took this from the present passage: “Vengeance belongs to me, and I will repay” (Rom. XII), according to merits.

“In due time.” It is as though he were saying: “When I have received the time, I will judge justly” (Ps. LXXIV). Hence he said to Moses, who was praying for the people: “On the day of vengeance I will visit this sin of theirs also” (Exod. XXXII).

Near is the day of destruction. For each one. For whatever comes to an end is very brief when compared with eternity. According to the historical sense, vengeance hastens upon the Jews, because in a short time they lost their place, their nation, and all prosperity, since they killed the prophets and the Savior.

[Col. 0492A] **VERSE 36.—“He will judge.”** By distinguishing them from the wicked, according to the saying: “Judge me, O God, and distinguish my cause” (Ps. XLII).

**“He will see that the hand has been weakened.”** Whatever your hand can do, perform earnestly, because in the underworld there is neither work, nor reason, nor wisdom (Eccles. IX).

**VERSE 37.—“Where are their gods?”** That is: the idols in which they trusted are of no use, nor are riches, honors, or the pleasures of the world; for they take nothing with them from all their labor.

**VERSE 39.—“See that I alone am,” etc.** A general admonition: abandon idolatry or heresy, reject all impurities, and turn to the true God.

**“I kill.”** (Gregory, *Moral Books*, VII, ch. 18.) “He kills in order to give life, strikes in order to heal,” and so forth, up to: “and through the ardor of charity makes them perceptive.”

**VERSE 40.—“I will raise.”** Another edition reads: “I will lift my hand to heaven, and I will swear by my right hand, and I will say: I live forever.” To lift or raise God’s hand to heaven is to show that the power of his eternity is exalted above all things. To swear by the right hand—that is, by the Son, who is the Father’s right hand—is to confirm his promises in the sight of human beings and to reveal his eternity to those who believe in him through the Gospel, because “his power is an eternal power” (Dan. VII).

**VERSE 42.—“Arrows.”** Demons, of whom Job says: “The arrows of the Lord are in me” (Job VI); that is, I will exercise such vengeance as could even suffice for demons.

**“And from captivity.”** The heads of captives were shaved; those who were led away were said to be sold under a crown. “From captivity”: the head of the enemies is uncovered when the plan of an evil mind is proved vain—the plan by which he thought he could sin with impunity. The heads of the enemies are also the teachers, upon whom the final vengeance will rebound. Hence: “Blood flowed from the winepress as far as the horses’ bridles” (Rev. XIV), that is, the vengeance of torments reaching as far as the rulers of the peoples.

**VERSE 43.—“For the blood.”** In the judgment the people of God will be praised, when they appear glorious, and the enemies will be punished with just retribution.

**VERSE 49.—“Go up into the mountain.”** *Abarim* is interpreted as “crossing over”; *Nebo*, “in conclusion.” Nebo is said to be a mountain in the land of Moab opposite Jericho, beyond the Jordan, on the brow of Pisgah, near Mount Peor; the region surrounding it is still called Pisgah. Moses therefore dies in Abarim and on Mount Nebo opposite Jericho, beyond the Jordan, because the law and circumcision proceeded as far as Christ and the sacrament of baptism, and there came to their conclusion, because Christ is the end of the law. Moses saw the promised land but did not enter it, because in the Spirit he foresaw and in the law foretold the future grace of Christ, but did not see him present. Hence: “Many righteous people and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it” (Matt. XIII).

# CHAPTER XXXIII

[Col. 0493A]

**VERSE 1.—“This is the blessing.”** It was fitting that he placed the blessing at the end of Deuteronomy, because Christ, after completing the Gospel and about to ascend into heaven, blessed his disciples with raised hands. The blessing with which he blessed the children of Israel in Deuteronomy—“the second law”—belongs to the grace of the New Testament, in which the mysteries of the ancient law are disclosed, and true Israelites receive the blessing foretold through Moses, the man of God, through Christ, the man. It is also fitting that the blessing is given as Moses’ death approaches, because, when the shadow of the law dies, the truth of heavenly gifts is revealed. Thus Moses, foreseeing the coming of the Savior and explaining the grace of the New Testament as though it were already past, joyfully exults in the voice of the primitive Church, saying: “The Lord came from Sinai,” etc.

(Augustine, *Questions*, 36.) Another wording, and so forth, up to: “Rejoice, nations, with his people.” “For a partial hardening has come upon Israel, until the fullness,” etc. (Rom. XI.)

**“Moses the man.”** Moses signifies the law, which before his death—that is, before it came to an end in him—foretold that the Church would be blessed in Christ.

**VERSE 2.—“The Lord came from Sinai.”** *Sinai* (the original interpretation is not supplied) is interpreted as “my amphora,” or “my measure,” or “commandment.” *Seir* (the original interpretation is not supplied) means “hairy” or “bristling.” *Pharan* (the original interpretation is not supplied) means “their ferocity” or “fruitful.” Sinai therefore represents the Old Testament, because, holding a fixed measure of commandments according to the decree of the Decalogue, it knows how to prohibit but not to help; nor does it liberate by the spirit of love, but binds its subjects through fear of punishment. Hence: “One, indeed, on Mount Sinai, giving birth to slavery,” etc. (Gal. IV). The Lord therefore came from Sinai—that is, he was made known from the law and the prophets to those who believed. For he came from there when he becomes known to the person who reads and understands there. Hence: “Beginning from Moses and all the prophets” (Luke XXIV), he explained the Scriptures to the disciples, to whose hearts he desired to come. Born from Seir according to the flesh—that is, from the Jews, a people most harshly bristling with the thorns of wickedness and faithlessness—he illuminated the faithful by the rising of a new light, like the true sun of righteousness. Hence: “The sun of righteousness will rise for us” (Mal. IV). And elsewhere: “A star will rise from Jacob, and a man will arise from Israel” (Num. XXIV).

**“The Lord,” etc.** Sinai is interpreted as “temptation.” The Lord therefore came from Sinai because he assumed our flesh, in which he would be tempted.

**“And from Seir,” etc.** That is, Edom or Esau. This is the Jewish people, which, through its desire for gluttony, lost the glory of primogeniture as though for a meal of lentils, and, supplanted by the faith of the younger people, lost the grace of blessing.

**“He arose for us from Seir,” etc.** They traversed this mountain for a long time and received certain commandments there. Seir, that is, “bristling” or “hairy,” signifies the Gentiles, who were terrifying because of their sins. From them the Lord arose—he who at the end will be preached to the Jews by the Church of the Gentiles, because “the remnant will be saved.”

**“He appeared from Mount Pharan,” etc.** Pharan is interpreted as “fruitful,” because from the Church of the Gentiles, fruitful in virtues, the faith of Christ was preached to the Jews. Christ therefore appeared from Pharan, because the more fiercely the unbelievers’ ferocity burned against him, the more deeply knowledge of his divinity grew. The more he was hidden amid the insults of his passion, the more brilliantly he shone through the power of his resurrection; and those who had first persecuted him in the ferocity of unbelief afterward clung to him in the ardor of love. Of them it is added: “And with him were thousands of holy ones.”

**“In his right hand was a fiery law.”** Namely, the tablets on which was the law that purifies and burns away sins. The Father’s right hand is also the Son, who brought the law of love, saying: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth,” etc. (Luke XII).

**“In his right hand was a fiery law.”** The right hand is the Gospel, through which eternal blessedness is promised; it is called the right hand, not the temporal one, as in the law, which is called the left. Hence: “His right hand will embrace me.” In this right hand is the fiery law—that is, charity, kindled by the Holy Spirit in the hearts of the elect. Hence he says: “The fullness of the law is love” (Rom. XIII). And elsewhere: “I give you a new commandment, that you love one another” (John XIII). Infused into the apostles through tongues of fire, this love of the Holy Spirit inscribed the whole fullness of the law as though by the finger of God, and made them fervent in spirit and radiant in their works. But because it was given not to one people, as Moses’ law was, but to all, he adds: “He loved the peoples.”

**VERSE 3.—“He loved.”** Hence: “No one has greater love than this, that he lay down his life,” etc. (John XV).

[Col. 0494C]

**“All.”** Without partiality; hence: “Whoever fears God and practices righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts X).

**“All the holy ones.”** Namely, those who heard: “Be holy, for I am holy,” etc. (Lev. XIX), and were sanctified in his name.

**“In his hand.”** That is, in the power by which they are protected. Hence: “No one will snatch them from my hand,” etc. (John X). Through love they are one kingdom in the Lord’s hand. Hence Isaiah: “You will be a crown of glory in the hand of the Lord, and a diadem of royalty in the hand of your God” (Isa. LXII).

**“And those who draw near,” etc.** That is: Let those who did not hear Christ teaching in the flesh not be saddened, as though they had been deceived by human beings. Christ speaks through the mouths of the holy ones; through their feet the teaching of the Head is heard. Hence: “Whoever hears you hears me,” etc. (Luke X). Or those draw near to his feet to receive instruction who, burning with spiritual desire, devote themselves day and night to the evangelical and apostolic Scriptures. But because these things have been said of the New Testament, what follows speaks through Moses’ voice about the old law: “He commanded us a law,” etc.

**VERSE 4.—“An inheritance.”** For this is the benefit of the law, the inheritance promised to Abraham: “If you are willing and listen, you shall eat the good things of the land.”

**“It will be with the most upright,” etc.** Jacob, blessed by the angel, was called Israel, that is, “upright with God”; and the Jew converted to faith, blessed by him after the resurrection—the one over whom he prevailed in the Passion—is called most upright because of his profession of righteousness. Hence: “Listen, Jacob my servant, and most upright one, whom I chose,” etc. (Isa. XLIV).

**VERSE 5.—“King.”** Christ. “But I have been established as king by him,” so that he who is the first king and power may establish a kingdom and power.

**“With the tribes of Israel.”** Those from whom the primitive Church arose. It is fitting that first the leaders, and then the tribes to be gathered, are mentioned, because the first were the apostles, and through them the others believed.

**VERSE 6.—“Let Reuben live.”** Having foretold the salvation of the primitive Church, he assigns particular blessings to each tribe. He foretells true Israelites from both peoples, prophesying now about Christ, now about the apostles, now about the primitive Church, and now about the whole Church.

[Col. 0495B]

**“Let Reuben live.”** That is: Although Reuben violated his father’s bed and lost the dignity of the firstborn, nevertheless let him live, and let him not die while doing penance. The sons of Reuben—that is, the Jews signified by Reuben—violated the Father’s bed, namely, they polluted Christ, his Son, with unclean spittle. Yet they are reserved for repentance, though few in number in comparison with the Church of the Gentiles.

**“Reuben.”** “Son of vision,” because his mother said (Gen. XXIX): “God has seen my humiliation.” He is the firstborn, signifying the elect from the Jews who, by denying and crucifying Christ, died but, converted through the preaching of the apostles, were given life through faith in Christ. These are sons of vision because they were saved through the regard of divine mercy.

**VERSE 7.—“This belongs to Judah.”** Judah, interpreted as “confession,” signifies the universal Church, in which there is confession of divine praise and thanksgiving. Of him his mother said: “Now I will confess to the Lord” (Gen. XXIX). This is the true bride of Christ, adorned with the jewels of virtues. She does not boast but gives thanks, and she prays for this: to be heard.

**“Hear, O Lord, the voice of Judah.”** Namely, of the kings who came from Judah and desired Christ, and of Christ himself, who said: “I confess to you, Father, king of heaven and earth,” etc. (Luke X).

**“His hands.”** He prayed to the Lord on behalf of Judah, to whom he now promises the Lord’s assistance, as though saying: Let Judah not presume upon his own strength, but trust in him who says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI). His hands fought against spiritual wickedness on the cross, so that through death he might destroy him who held the dominion of death.

**“The helper.”** So that he may conquer and say: “He will lead me upon my high places as victor” (Hab. III). For he conquers in us and, for his victory, crowns us in mercy and compassion.

**VERSE 8.—“Your perfection.”** That is: How perfect you are, and how holy is the teaching you declared through Moses. Or, your perfection and your teaching come from your holy man, that is, from the Levites. They ought to guard, perform, and teach the law.

**“Your perfection.”** These words are spoken of the choir of angels, martyrs, and all the perfected, who fulfilled the perfection of love by dying for the Lord and, renouncing the world, attained the summit of ecclesiastical teaching, like true Levites who have no share on earth, but say with the Prophet: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,” etc. (Ps. XV), according to the saying: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” etc. (Luke IX); “Whoever loses his life for my sake,” etc. (Matt. X). Christ, however, is the true Levi, who did and taught all these things. The Levites cling to him, imitating him even unto bloodshed. Concerning his passion it is added: “Whom you tested in temptation,” etc.

**“At the waters.”** This is the place where Moses and Aaron were prevented from entering the promised land.

**“At the waters.”** It signifies the law, which denied entrance into the kingdom of heaven to those living wickedly. The waters are the peoples who cried out in opposition: “Crucify him. His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). To complete Levi’s perfection he adds:

**VERSE 9.—“Who said to his father.”** When they made the golden calf, at Moses’ command the Levites, girded with swords, killed the idolaters from gate to gate. In avenging idolatry they did not recognize their own, because they killed without distinction. Hence: “Unless someone leaves father and mother and wife and children for my sake, he is not my disciple” (Luke XVIII).

**“Who said to his father and mother,” etc.** We ought also, in temporal matters, to benefit more those with whom we are more closely joined. We ought to acknowledge the bond of earthly kinship; but if it impedes the course of the mind, we ought to disregard it, so that affection may fill the depths of the heart without turning it away from its spiritual purpose. This is well signified by the cows which, proceeding toward the mountains beneath the ark of the Lord, moved forward with affection and stern resolve: they lowed as they went for their calves, but, once the journey had begun, they did not turn their steps aside.

**VERSE 10.—“They will place incense.”** As Aaron, standing between the dead and the living, interceded for the people. “They will place incense”: the prayer of the holy is a most fragrant incense to the Lord. When the people sin, it appeases the Lord’s fury, because, cleansed of every earthly stain and kindled by heavenly desire, it burns like incense in God’s presence and, like a burnt offering from the altar of a devout heart, rises to heaven in the flame of devotion. This applies especially to the apostles and martyrs, of whom it is said: “He tested them like gold in a furnace and received them as a sacrifice of a burnt offering” (Wis. III).

[Col. 0496D]

**VERSE 11.—“Receive.”** That is, receive them as pleasing, so that you may reward them. Now white robes are given individually, namely, the joy of souls; and at the judgment, having received immortality according to the body, they will shine like the sun and run like sparks through a reed-bed, consuming, that is, empty and fruitless adversaries. Their punishment follows:

**“Strike their backs.”** That is: They seemed to themselves to be shedding the martyrs’ blood with impunity, but punishment was being prepared behind them, as it were—eternal damnation, into which they will fall and from which they will not be able to rise. Hence: “A rod is for the back of the senseless” (Prov. XXVI).

**VERSE 12.—“And Benjamin.”** He appears to allude to the historical account, because Jacob, patriarch and prophet, filled with the Spirit, loved Benjamin uniquely; and by God’s dispensation a place dedicated to divine worship was assigned to his tribe for safekeeping. Hence he adds: “As in a chamber he will dwell all day,” etc.

**“Most beloved.”** Christ is the most beloved of God the Father, who said of him: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. XVII). He dwells confidently at the Father’s right hand, to whom it is said: “Sit at my right hand” (Ps. CIX).

**Alternatively:** Benjamin, called “son of sorrow” and “son of the right hand,” expresses Paul, who was made an apostle and vessel of election from a persecutor; for he was from this tribe. It was fitting that, just as the Lord’s precursor was foretold by a prophetic oracle, so the teacher of the Gentiles, destined to benefit the whole world, should be proclaimed amid the great mysteries of the Church. Christ dwelt confidently in his mind when he steadfastly preached him before Gentiles and kings amid countless dangers. Of his soul it is said:

**“He will remain all day as in a chamber.”** Either he enjoys marvelous delight in a marital union and is made fruitful by the offspring of virtues, abandoning the secret recesses of his peaceful heart to no disturbance of vice; or, residing in it as in a chamber like a handsome bridegroom, he joins the virginal minds of believers to his embraces through Paul’s preaching. Hence: “After her, virgins will be brought to the king” (Ps. XLIII). Paul himself also says: “I betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (II Cor. XI).

The divinity also dwells confidently in Christ’s humanity. “He will remain in a chamber” signifies that in the Virgin’s womb the Church was joined to the heavenly Bridegroom, and that it rests confidently in Christ’s power and works.

**“And between his shoulders he will rest.”** Burdens are carried on the shoulders; therefore steadfast endurance is signified in them. Christ rested in him all the more willingly because he endured the harshest labors for his sake; he embraced him all the more closely because no terror tore him away from Christ’s embrace. Hence he says: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Rom. VIII).

**VERSE 13.—“And he said of Joseph also.”** Joseph is interpreted as “increased.” He is Christ, who, rejected by his Jewish brothers, became ruler in the Egypt of this world and freed the human race from the famine of want through the distribution of the Gospel’s grain. He is truly the Savior of the world.

**“His land is from the blessing of the Lord.”** Literally, this signifies the fertility enjoyed by the two tribes descended from Joseph, Ephraim and Manasseh, in abundant crops, fruits, and pasture for flocks. This is Bashan, a most fertile region, whence its name is interpreted as “fatness.”

They delight in the temperate sky, the dew that produces fruit, and the abundance of springs and rivers, which are signified by the abyss.

**“You have blessed your land, O Lord.”** Namely, the Church, which is filled not by its own power but by the blessing of virtues from God. Hence: “Blessed be God, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (Eph. I).

**“The heavens.”** The apostles and evangelists are called heavens because of the unity of their faith and teaching. Elsewhere they are mentioned in the plural: “The heavens declare the glory,” etc. (Ps. XVIII). In these people, radiant in life and contemplation as in heaven, God dwells, thundering terror, raining consolation, and flashing miracles.

**“Dew.”** The heavenly preaching, of marvelous subtlety and grace, by which hearts are watered against the heat of temptation so that they may always flourish in virtues. Hence: “May God give you of the dew of heaven,” etc. (Gen. XXVII).

**“By the abyss,”** so that it may become richer, watered by the ascending spring like the paradise of God. Hence: “A spring rose from the earth, watering the whole surface of the ground” (Gen. II). His understanding abounded from the sea, and his thoughts from the great abyss. For the teacher’s word waters outwardly in vain unless the grace of the Creator moistens inwardly. Hence he adds: “From the fruits of the hills,” etc.

**VERSE 14.—“Of the sun.”** Of Christ, who is the sun of righteousness and who said: “The righteous will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. XIII), because we shall be like him.

**“And of the moon.”** Of the Church, which receives these fruits from the sun, that is, from Christ. Therefore let it always look upon the sun with complete devotion, lest, turning away, it lose the light.

**VERSE 15.—“From the fruits of the everlasting hills.”** The everlasting hills are the faithful of the Old Testament, humble children founded with immovable firmness on the faith of the prophets and patriarchs. Hence: “The mountain of the house of the Lord will be raised above the hills” (Isa. II). Their fruits bless Joseph’s land when the Church bears fruit in faith through the teaching of Christ, the example of virtue, and prophetic faith. It should be noted that above, in the fruits and dew of heaven, evangelical teaching is signified; here, in the summit of the ancient mountains and the fruits of the everlasting hills, the legal and prophetic teaching is signified. Joseph’s land is enriched by both, because the holy Church is instructed by the pages of both Testaments and by the examples of the new and ancient Fathers. Hence: “I have kept all fruits, my beloved, for you,” that is, new and old (Song VII); and: “Every learned scribe brings forth from his treasury new things and old” (Matt. XIII). Therefore the Manichaeans and the Jews—because the former do not accept the Old Testament and the latter do not accept the New—cannot inherit in this rich land.

[Col. 0498D]

**VERSE 16.—“And from the fruits.”** The Church, fruitful throughout the world in the fruit of righteousness and in the abundance of spiritual gifts, received from the fullness of its Joseph. Hence follows:

**“The blessing of him who appeared.”** The whole Joseph—that is, the head and the body—is full of blessing, but the fullness of blessing is especially in the head. Hence: “Like the oil on the head, running down upon the beard, the beard of Aaron,” etc. (Ps. XXXII). By the privilege of grace, he surpasses his brothers, that is, the faithful; as a true Samson, a Nazirite from the virgin’s womb—that is, consecrated to God—he shone with a sevenfold Spirit, as though with seven untouched locks.

**“Upon the head of Joseph,”** namely, of Christ, who is the head of the Church, in whom all nations are blessed. Concerning his passion and resurrection it follows: “As the firstborn of a bull,” etc.

**“As.”** (Augustine, *Questions*, 56.) “The firstborn of a bull is his beauty.” It should not be read as though it said “the firstborn of a bull.” Rather, since he is the firstborn, his beauty is the beauty of a bull, because of the horns of the cross.

Christ is the fattened calf, whom the Father sacrificed as the firstborn from the herd of the patriarchs when the Son returned. He was raised gloriously on the third day; he is the firstborn of the dead and the ruler of the kings of the earth. After the glory of the resurrection, he adds horns from the strength of his passion.

**VERSE 17.—“Horns.”** Joseph compares them to the horns of a rhinoceros, signifying that Ephraim would hold the chief place among the ten tribes, among whom Jeroboam of the tribe of Ephraim reigned during the time of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son.

**“The horns of the rhinoceros.”** He signifies the horns of the cross, concerning which Habakkuk says: “There his strength was hidden” (Hab. III). Through the weakness of the flesh, like a ram, he was crowned with the thorns of his mockers; he was fastened to these horns, yet in the incomparable strength of his passion he became a unicorn, victor over death and over him who held the dominion of death. Hence: “What is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I).

**“He will scatter.”** By the preaching of the cross he separates the chaff from the grain; for the word of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing.

**“The nations.”** “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations,” etc. (Ps. II). All these things are said of the inheritance of the true Joseph, which is the glorious land. Concerning its inhabitants, gathered from both peoples, it follows:

**“These are the multitudes of Ephraim.”** These two tribes from Joseph are blessed not in themselves but in their ancestor. They signify the children of both peoples who are blessed in Christ, according to the saying: “In your seed all nations will be blessed” (Gen. XXII). The patriarch Jacob, blessing Ephraim and Manasseh with crossed hands in the form of a cross and preferring the younger to the firstborn, signified that they would be blessed in the faith of Christ’s cross: in the younger, the faithful people from the Gentiles, lesser in time within Christ’s grace but greater in faith; to whom the grace of the Israelite people passed. Concerning their immeasurable multitude it is said: “These are the multitudes,” etc. Hence: “The children of the desolate woman are more numerous than those of the woman who has a husband” (Isa. LIV).

Manasseh, deprived of the honor of the firstborn and nevertheless blessed, is the Jewish people, rejected for unbelief in the greater part of its members but attaining blessing in the remainder. Hence: “A partial hardening has come upon Israel,” etc. (Rom. II).

**VERSE 18.—“And to Zebulun.”** Zebulun and Issachar received the passion in Galilee, where Christ taught most extensively and from which he chose the apostles. Through them, therefore, the apostles are signified, and joy is promised to them at their departure, because, going out from their own borders, they subjected the people of the Gentiles to Christ; and joy is promised in the tents on account of the conversion of the Jews, from whom they themselves had also been chosen. Therefore joy is promised to them on behalf of both peoples, both present and future, because in the present they rejoiced at their conversion and in heaven they were rewarded with eternal joy.

**“In the tents,”** namely, of the Jews. Hence: “May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell in the tents of Shem” (Gen. IX), because in the churches derived from the Jews the multitude of the younger people dwells through the unity of faith.

**VERSE 19.—“To the mountain.”** Namely, Zion or Jerusalem, or the contemplation and height of virtues.

**“They will call.”** They teach that righteousness exists only in faith in Christ. For “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Rom. X). They sacrifice victims of righteousness on the mountain when they teach all who come to Christ—in whom the Church is built—to be justified not by works of the law but by faith in Christ, according to the saying: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. I). True Christians are therefore victims of righteousness, sacrificed by the apostles when they are taught to mortify earthly desires so that they may be made alive in spiritual things. Hence: “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Rom. VIII).

**“There they will sacrifice.”** There is no place for the true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church, which has been established upon this mountain.

**“Those who draw upon the abundance.”** These tribes devoted themselves to commerce, bringing merchandise from overseas regions and drawing out hidden treasures—silver, gold, or gems—as though they were milk, that is, receiving them easily.

**“Those who draw upon the abundance of the sea.”** This signifies the calling of the Gentiles. The sea signifies the entire human race. Hence: “The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind” (Matt. XIII). The sea means the world; the net, teaching; every kind of fish, every sex, age, and condition. The apostles therefore sucked the abundance of the sea as though it were milk, because they drew the crowds of peoples flowing to the teaching of the Gospel into the growth of Christ’s body.

**“Hidden.”** “The Lord knows those who are his” (II Tim. II). For “many are called, but few,” etc. (Matt. XX).

**“The sands.”** The multitude of unbelievers; the treasures, the precious souls of the elect. Thus they sucked them in, so that among the hearers of the Gospel some might be transferred as vessels of honor into the king’s treasures, while others, like barren and useless sand, might remain empty.

**VERSE 20.—“And to Gad he said.”** In Gad’s blessing he seems to foretell the power of strong men or judgment, since Jephthah and many others of this kind came from that tribe.

**“In breadth.”** Because the fullness of every blessing rested upon Christ, and therefore he blessed his own.

**“Gad.”** That is, “girded”; he signifies Christ, who, about to fight against spiritual wickedness, appeared girded with the power of divinity in the weakness of the flesh, according to the saying: “The Lord has clothed himself with strength and girded himself” (Ps. CXII). And elsewhere: “The Lord is strong and mighty in battle,” etc. He is blessed in breadth because he received an immense kingdom not among the Jews alone but among all nations. Hence the prophecy says:

“From the rising of the sun to its setting, the name of the Lord is praiseworthy.” But because he attained this glory through the humility of his passion, it adds concerning his death:

**“Like a lion he rested.”** “I have power to lay down my life” (John X). The power, not the necessity, of death is expressed. Hence: “No one takes it from me, but I lay it down myself” (ibid.).

**“Like a lion he roared.”** Whatever he said, he fulfilled with power.

**“And he seized the arm and the crown of the head.”** When, rising from the dead, he subjected the strength of his enemies to himself. He also seized the crown of the head, that is, he inclined the eminence of worldly rule to receive the faith. Hence: “All kings will worship him; all nations will serve him” (Ps. LXXI). What follows concerns the new state of his kingdom.

**VERSE 21.—“And he saw his principality, that it was in his portion.”** When kingdoms and nations had been subjected to him, his power appeared—not through the terror of weapons but through the strength of teaching.

**“Set apart.”** Hidden, while he writes his laws in the hearts of the faithful. Hence he says: “You have an anointing from the Holy One, and you do not need anyone to teach you; his anointing teaches you about everything” (John II). Or, “set apart,” because he lay hidden in figures in the law and the prophets, teaching secretly what he openly declared in the Gospel. Hence: “Beginning from Moses and all the prophets, he interpreted to them” (Luke XXIV).

[Col. 0501C]

**“Who was with the leaders of the people.”** He is the helper. Hence: “The Lord working with them and confirming the word through the signs that followed” (Mark XVI), because he said: “Without me you can do nothing” (John XV).

**“He performed righteousnesses.”** That is, justifying those who believe in him, and at the end judging according to their merits with Israel—that is, with his people chosen for the vision of God.

**“Righteousnesses.”** The justifications of believers. For he himself justifies the ungodly by faith. “For no flesh will be justified by works of the law.”

**VERSE 22.—“And to Dan also.”** Some think that Antichrist is signified by Dan, whom they suppose will be born from this tribe. He is the lion’s cub, that is, the devil’s, who will flow abundantly from Bashan, because he will be full of confusion; for Bashan is interpreted as “confusion,” or “fatness,” or “cankerworm.”

Dan also means “judgment,” and Bashan means “shame.” Dan, however, signifies Christ, who says: “For judgment I have come into this world” (John IX). He is a lion’s cub because of his strength and because he deigned to become small; but, taking on our weakness, he did not lose his own power. For “what is weak in God is stronger than human beings” (I Cor. I). Of him it is said: “The lion from the tribe of Judah has conquered,” etc. (Rev. V). He endured the shame of the cross from the Jews, who thought that his name would be erased through death. But he who was a cub in the weakness of his flesh during the passion appeared as the unconquered lion in the resurrection through the power of his divinity. Hence the Apostle: “Although he was crucified in weakness, yet he lives by the power of God” (II Cor. XIII).

Thus he flowed abundantly from Bashan when, passing through the shame of death to the glory of immortality, he watered the whole world with the streams of the Gospel. Hence Isaiah: “The earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters cover the sea” (Isa. II).

**“Dan is a lion’s cub.”** He says this because of Samson, who was from the tribe of Dan and was strong like a lion, whose possession extended as far as Bashan. Antichrist, however, will flow abundantly from Bashan because he will be sated with the fatness of lust and every vice.

**“He will possess the sea and the south.”** Because his possession extends from the southern region westward as far as the Tyrrhenian Sea.

**“He will possess the sea and the south.”** Through the apostles, the Church is acquired for Christ from Jews and Gentiles. By the western sea—which is understood here—the Jews are signified, because they serve the shadow and the model and do not possess the light of knowledge and truth; and because the sun of righteousness has set for them, they have remained forever in darkness. The apostles possessed this west when they subjected many of them to Christ, illuminated by the grace of faith, so that those who had once been darkness might be light in the Lord. By the south is understood the Church gathered from the Gentiles, which, once the veil of the law has been removed, enjoys the light of the Gospel and, reclining with the Bridegroom at noon, contemplates the glory of the Lord with unveiled face.

**VERSE 24.—“And to Asher he said: Blessed among the sons is Asher; let him be pleasing to his brothers.”** Asher means “blessed”—namely, Christ, the hope of our blessedness, who showed us its first fruits by rising from the dead. He is blessed among his sons because believers, reborn through his grace, have filled the whole world in his likeness. To them it is said: “Believe in the light, that you may be sons of light” (John XII). They bear the fruit of light in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. This happened because he was pleasing in true love to his brothers—that is, to the apostles whom he chose from the Jews—so that, rejecting figures, they might rejoice in the truth of the Gospel and be worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus. And to explain the source of such abundance of love, he adds: “Let him dip his foot in oil,” etc.

**“Let him dip his foot in oil.”** Christ, our head, ascending into heaven, abundantly anointed the apostles—his feet, as it were—who would still remain on earth, traversing the world by preaching. He anointed them with the oil of the Holy Spirit so abundantly that they would not fail under any labor but would shine with the brightness of unfading joy. He also supplied the protection of an incorruptible sandal, concerning which it follows:

**“Iron and bronze [shall be] his …”** (Gregory, *Moral Books*, XXXIV, ch. 5.) This concerns the Church, and so forth, up to: “with these sandals the true Passover is to be celebrated.” [The final Latin word is materially uncertain in the supplied text.]

**VERSE 25.—“As the days of his youth.”** It signifies that this tribe abounded in prosperity and delights until the old age of captivity.

**“As.”** The Church is promised a vigorous and flourishing old age: just as she bravely overcame every assault at the beginning, so at the end she will overcome the fury of Antichrist. Hence: “Behold, I am with you all days, until the consummation of the age” (Matt. XXVIII). And elsewhere: “My old age is in abundant mercy” (Ps. XCI).

**VERSE 26.—“There is no God.”** Astonished at the things mentioned above, he joyfully breaks forth in praise of Christ, who accomplished all these things.

**“The rider of heaven.”** He ascended by his own power, and every day draws the Church to himself: “Draw me after you; let us run after the fragrance of your perfumes” (Song I).

**“The clouds.”** The apostles, who rain down words and flash with miracles. When he ascended into heaven, he sent them to preach. Hence: “The clouds gave forth a voice” (Ps. LXXVI). They move swiftly, delayed by no one, performing signs and wonders not by their own power but by Christ’s, and, as though by flashes of lightning, terrifying the hearts of mortals. Hence: “I have fought the good fight; I have finished the course” (II Tim. IV).

**VERSE 27.—“His dwelling place is above,” etc.** The body raised from the dead and placed at the Father’s right hand, concerning which it is said: “Destroy this temple” (John II).

Arms. That is, the power of the Passion, which protects everyone and which he received on the cross with his arms extended.

Under the arms. These arms, fighting against the true Amalek, defend them; nor, as in the case of Moses, are they weighed down by weariness, but they support them with tireless strength until they attain the true victory. Let us therefore venerate above the first fruits of our resurrection, and below the sacrament of our redemption, so that we too, when the adversary has been defeated, may attain the glory of immortality. Concerning this true Israel it is promised: “He will drive out the enemy from before you” [Col. 0503C].

And alone. That is, living according to his own custom and laws; hence Balaam: “The people shall dwell alone and shall not be reckoned among the nations” (Numbers 23).

**VERSE 28.**—The eye of Jacob. Here he labored to overthrow vices; there he will contemplate without interruption, with the lightest glance of the mind, the glory of Christ, who for our sake assumed the earth of true flesh. Here he was nourished sacramentally by his body and blood under the forms of bread and wine; there he will be filled by the perpetual vision of his divinity. Hence: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Psalm 16). And elsewhere: “I will manifest myself to him” (John 14).

Then Jacob, transformed into perfect Israel, will see God face to face, filled as though with the lightest dew by so abundant, subtle, and delightful a knowledge of God that the knowledge of the preachers by which we are instructed in the present life will seem to grow dim. Hence: “Whether knowledge, it will be destroyed” (1 Corinthians 13). And elsewhere: “Dark water in the clouds of the air, because of the brightness before his presence” (Psalm 17). When this has been attained, all this instruction will cease, and “all shall be taught by God” (John 6). Hence he rightly adds: “Blessed are you, Israel,” etc.

And the heavens will grow dim. That is, such abundant dew will be poured out to fertilize the earth that the sight of human beings will be darkened. This signifies that, because the Jews loved earthly wealth beyond measure, they became blind and could not recognize Christ. Hence: “If we let him continue thus, everyone will believe in him,” etc.

[Col. 0504A] **VERSE 29.**—Who is like you, people? As if to say: You are blessed, and no one is like you, because you hope for salvation not from your own strength but from the grace of Christ, who saves his people from their sins.

And the sword of glory. In the future he will strike the adversaries with unalterable severity, when he avenges the blood of his servants. Now the sword is hidden in the humility of those who suffer; it will be revealed in the glory of those who rise. Therefore Israel is called the sword of glory. Christ, therefore, protects the one who fights like a shield, and as the sword of glory he will avenge the triumphant one. To him, as to the head, the glory of the body is referred at the end of the prophecy, when it says:

They will deny. They will abominate and hate, as Balak did, who asked Balaam to drive the Israelites away by cursing them.

[Col. 0504B] You will trample. By subjecting them to the Church, which they abominate and persecute.

It should be noted that there are only eleven blessings. Simeon is not found among these blessings; in this Judas is excluded from the apostles, with only eleven remaining. For this reason too, the children of Israel reached the place where they received Deuteronomy from Horeb by eleven encampments.

# CHAPTER 34

**VERSE 1.**—And so he went up. Both Moses and the other fathers of the Old Testament, lifted up by the Spirit to the heights of contemplation, were able to foresee the grace of the New Testament, which was given in Christ, both through the bestowal of virtues and through the attainment of the heavenly kingdom. But they could not await it in the flesh; they died in faith and hope and were brought down to the underworld, where they awaited the coming of the Redeemer, who would free them from there by the blood of his redemption.

And he showed him. Moses saw the promised land but did not enter it, because the Law foreshadowed the coming of Christ and the teaching of the Gospel in words and figures, but brought no one to perfection.

**VERSE 2.**—All the land. A part of the whole land, as much as he could see from the highest mountain. Or, he showed him the whole land in the spirit.

**VERSE 5.**—And he died there, etc. God spares none of the elect and punishes even the smallest sins in his friends; hence: “Moses and Aaron among his priests,” and he added: “You were favorable to them, yet avenging all their inventions.” With the Law thus ended, the Law that served the Lord in its own time, the city and the altar destroyed, there are nowhere sacrifices, nowhere offerings, nowhere a priest or high priest.

**VERSE 6.**—In the valley. He died on the mountain and was buried in the valley, because the Law was glorious in its own time; but compared with the Gospel it appears hidden and humble. Hence: “I gave them statutes that were not good.”

And no one has known. The Jews suppose that this happened so that the Jews, always inclined toward idolatry, would not worship him after his death as a god. But allegorically it signifies that the time and manner of ending the Law have been hidden in God’s foreknowledge alone, and that the depth of God’s wisdom or the secret of his counsel is open to no one, because his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable.

[Col. 0505A] **VERSE 7.**—Moses was one hundred and twenty years old.
