If you add together the sums of the individual numbers from one through fifteen in their natural order—that is, one and two and three, and so on—they total one hundred and twenty. Fifteen, however, is formed from seven and eight: seven refers to the Sabbath, and eight to circumcision, because the boy was circumcised on the eighth day. If you look to the New Testament, you have the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, and in the eighth, the resurrection of Christ. Therefore one hundred and twenty signifies those who strive to fulfill the precepts of the Law and the Gospel in the Old Testament.

Moses was one hundred and twenty years old. This signifies that both he and the other fathers of the Old Testament, after the perfection of God’s commandments—which consists in the two commandments of love—are made fit through the grace of Christ and the redemption of his blood for eternal rest and the life to come. Their eye was not dimmed, that is, the sight of their devout intention was not obscured by cloud; nor were the teeth of malice stirred, because they were not disturbed by the storm of vices. Their order of discernment is represented by the lawgiver’s one hundred and twenty years, a number in which the height of Solomon’s temple was confirmed.

The primitive Church also, after the Passion and resurrection and the Lord’s ascension, received the grace of the Holy Spirit through this number of men. The fifteen, composed of seven and eight, signifies the future life, which is now enacted in the Sabbath of souls and will be completed in the resurrection of bodies. When fifteen is multiplied into a triangle, that is, when its parts are added to it, it produces one hundred and twenty. Appropriately, therefore, the blessedness of the elect in the future life is signified by one hundred and twenty, and the third story of the house of God is brought to completion, because after the labors of the faithful and after the rest of souls, the full happiness of the Church will be completed in the glory of the resurrection.

[Col. 0506A] **VERSE 8.**—And they wept. Because death reigned even over those who had not sinned, from Adam to Moses, tears accompany the one descending to the underworld.

(JEROME, Letter to Paula.) It is no wonder if Moses and Aaron, etc., up to “but to be inwardly present,” that is, to minister to the Lord’s will.

And when they had completed. From this the custom seems to have arisen that, for thirty days, acts of piety are performed for the faithful dead.

**VERSE 9.**—He laid his hands upon him. In his Scriptures he bore witness to him, saying: “God will raise up a prophet,” etc. (Deuteronomy 18); hence: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also” (John 5).

**VERSE 10.**—And there did not arise, etc. This, as it is said, Ezra added of his own. He restored by divine understanding the library burned by the Chaldeans and devised the letters that the Jews now use; hence he was also called a swift scribe.

And there did not arise a prophet. Because Moses was superior to all the prophets of the Old Testament; hence the Jews arrogantly say: “We are disciples of Moses” (John 9). But after the Lord of the prophets came incarnate into the world, all that former dignity and shadow of future things ceased, because “the law and the figure were given through Moses; grace and truth through Jesus Christ,” who is “the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Hebrews 10; John 1; Romans 10).

And he buried him in the valley. That is, the Lord did so. This signifies that, once the impediment of nature has been removed through Christ, the purified soul, separated from it, ascends to God, while the body that is buried remains in the earth until the judgment. Ecclesiastes 12: “Until the dust returns to the earth from which it came, and the spirit returns to God who gave it.” May he grant us this fortunate return, he who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

[Col. 0505]

# THE BOOK OF JOSHUA SON OF NUN

In Hebrew, *Yehoshua*. Preliminary materials for the Book of Joshua. (G)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 0505D]

(JEROME, *Divine Library*, vol. 8, col. 461.) At last, having completed the Pentateuch of Moses, as though freed from a great burden of interest, we extend our hand to Jesus son of Nave, etc.

(ADAMANTIUS, Homily 1 on Joshua.) God gave to Jesus Christ the name that is above every name; this is Jesus. Therefore, at the name of Jesus every knee bends, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth. And because this is the name above every name, it was not mentioned in any earlier generations. In Genesis we read of many righteous men, and none of them was named Jesus. [Col. 0506D] In Exodus I first find this name (Exodus 17), etc., up to: while we sin and the vices of our passions reign in us, although we may seem to have left the idols behind and come out of Egypt, nevertheless the reproach of Egypt has not been removed from us. But if you are circumcised a second time, if you cut away from yourself every vice—anger, pride, envy, lust, and the like—the reproaches of Egypt will be wiped away, and, transferred into the promised land, you will receive the heavenly inheritance through Jesus Christ our Lord.

# CHAPTER 1

**VERSE 2.**—Moses my servant. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 2 on Joshua.) “Moses my servant is dead.” Observe how Jesus reigns, etc., up to: the spiritual Moses is the one who lives in the spirit.

Rise and cross over, etc. Now therefore rise and cross this Jordan, etc. See how Jesus, the Son of God, was Moses’ minister. When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born of a woman, born under the Law (Galatians 4), because, being made under the Law of Moses, he became Moses’ minister. And Christ became a minister of circumcision, to confirm the promises made to the fathers.

**VERSE 3.**—Every place, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 2 on Joshua.) The letter of the Law is set upon the ground and lies below, etc., up to: so that you may become not only God’s heir but also Christ’s co-heir.

**VERSE 4.**—From the desert and Lebanon, etc. (ORIGEN, ibid.) The wilderness and Antilebanon. He did not say Lebanon but Antilebanon, etc., up to: the Church gathered from the nations through Jesus Christ.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 1 on Joshua, vol. 3.) From this testimony and others it is proved that Moses died as God’s servant and as one pleasing to God, although that punishment was completed in him, namely, that he should not enter the promised land. From this it may be understood that God also punishes certain things physically or temporally even in his good servants, while nevertheless counting them among honorable and useful vessels.

And Joshua commanded. (AUGUSTINE, Question 2.) It is asked how he gave this command after the Lord had exhorted him, etc., up to: his arrangement was changed at Jethro’s divinely inspired suggestion.

The Reubenites also. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 3 on Joshua.) Let us consider what form the two and a half tribes represent, etc., up to: those who hold the land flowing with milk and honey amid the bitterness of wickedness.

# CHAPTER 2

**VERSE 1.**—And so he sent, etc. (BEDE on Joshua.) Jericho is the world, to which the Lord Christ sent the two Testaments to examine human behavior. For, in order to test more fully the faith of believers or the obstinacy of rebels, before his judgment should come he sent, as two spies, the Law and the Gospel.

(ADAMANTIUS, Homily 3.) Spies are sent by Jesus into Jericho, etc., up to: if he has understood the goodness of his Lord in his mercy.

**VERSE 16.**—Go up into the hill country, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 3.) The wise prostitute gives mystical and heavenly counsel, etc., up to: she who was once a prostitute was cleansed by water and the Holy Spirit and by the blood of Christ.

# CHAPTER 3

**VERSE 3.**—When you see the ark of the testimony of our God, and the priests and Levites carrying it, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 3 on Joshua.) It was commanded that the ark go far ahead, etc., up to: when the cloud had been withdrawn, as though the veil had been removed.

Go before the people. (ORIGEN, Homily 4.) The people are led by the priests and journey to the promised land under the priests’ instruction. And below: They are the ones who teach the people to depart from Egypt—that is, from the errors of the world—and to cross the vast wilderness, that is, to pass through various kinds of temptations.

**VERSE 7.**—Today I will begin to exalt you, etc. (ID., cited above.) Many wonders were performed in the wilderness, and nowhere is Jesus said to have been exalted. But when the Jordan is crossed, it is said to him: “Today I will begin to exalt you,” etc. Jesus’ exaltation before the people takes its beginning from baptism. For those who are baptized are baptized into his death, and his death is completed in the exaltation of the cross. Therefore it is rightly then that Jesus is first exalted for each believer, when the person reaches the mystery of baptism. Hence: “God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name,” etc.

[Col. 0508B] **VERSE 9.**—Of the Lord your God, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 4 on Joshua.) To the sinner every creature is an enemy, etc., up to: “who turns the rock into pools of water and the cliff into springs,” etc.

**VERSE 10.**—Canaanite: possessing, or possession, or merchants, or changeable. Hittite: fearing or being astonished. Hivite: gathering stones. Perizzite: separating, or scattering. Girgashite: apply a settler, or cast out a settler, or an approaching foreigner. Amorite: bitter, or speaking. Jebusite: trampling, or their manger.

**VERSE 15.**—The harvest had become full. The Septuagint: “As in the days of the wheat harvest.” This seems unbelievable in our regions, but there—as those who know testify—the wheat harvest is at the beginning of spring. At that time, however, the river overflows and is filled more than in winter.

**VERSE 16.**—The waters descending stood still, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 4.) I do not think that this was written without a reason connected with the mystery, etc., up to: and one Spirit by whom all are purified in baptism, and one God, the Father of all.

# CHAPTER 4

**VERSE 7.**—Forever. (AUGUSTINE.) How can it be “forever,” when heaven and earth pass away? Or is it because it signifies something eternal, although they themselves cannot be eternal? Although what is in Greek can be rendered in Latin as “unto the age.”

**VERSE 10.**—And the people hastened and crossed over, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 2.) Those who crossed the Red Sea were baptized into Moses, etc., up to: when there is no longer anyone to terrify the children of Israel.

**VERSE 14.**—On that day, etc. Jesus was always exalted before the Father; but it is necessary that God exalt him in our sight, that is, that we recognize the height of his divinity. This happens if we cross the Jordan and arm ourselves for the wars to come with the various defenses of the sacraments.

**VERSE 16.**—Command the priests. (AUGUSTINE, On Joshua.) Command the priests carrying the ark of the covenant, etc., up to: because the Old Testament was given as testimony to a future event.

But the people. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 2.) It is not without reason that the time when they came to the Jordan is marked, etc., [Col. 0509A] up to: so that they signify that many perfections depend upon one day.

The twelve also—that is, the mystery of the lamb commanded in Egypt—was prescribed because on the same day on which we flee from the errors of the world, we enter the promised land. For the whole of the present life is one day. Therefore today—that is, while we live—let us hasten toward perfection and not defer it until tomorrow.

The twelve also. (ISIDORE.) When the children of Israel crossed the Jordan, they took twelve stones from the middle of the river and set them up as a testimony at the place of the second circumcision. This was done to signify to us that, when we rise from the bath, we ought to carry with us the firmest examples of apostolic life and always look to their testimony for models of virtue.

# CHAPTER 5

[Col. 0509B]

**VERSE 2.**—Circumcise Israel a second time. (AUGUSTINE, Question 6 on Job.) It is asked why he said “again,” etc., up to: or by certain heretics separated from the community of the Israelites?

Make for yourself stone knives, etc. (ISIDORE on Job.) Let the Jews say how anyone can be circumcised a second time with bodily circumcision, etc., up to: because through one member the stain is spread throughout the whole body.

**VERSE 5.**—But the people. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 6.) Those who had not obeyed the Lord’s commands are called uncircumcised. From this it is understood that those who do not obey God’s commands are called uncircumcised. But because God loves every soul, he sent Jesus, the Son of God, to circumcise both the worthy and the unworthy—not Joshua son of Nun, who did not circumcise the people truly and perfectly, but Jesus, the Son of God, who truly cleansed body and soul from every defilement of sin.

**VERSE 8.**—And after they had, etc. After the children of Israel had been circumcised, they rested in the same place, sitting in the camp until they were healed. It is not enough to be circumcised; after circumcision it is necessary to be healed and for a scar to form over the wound. To be circumcised by Jesus, therefore, is to lay aside vices and evil habits and to cut away whatever conflicts with the rule of honesty. But when we do this, we are constrained by a certain difficulty: with a kind of pain of soul, we avoid the fault of habit through a new way of life. At this time, therefore, we are said to remain, as it were, in the pain of our circumcision until, once the scar has formed, we are healed—that is, until we fulfill the new practices without difficulty and what previously seemed unfamiliar and difficult has become habitual. Then it is rightly said to us: “Today I have removed the reproach of Egypt from you.”

And they celebrated. After the reproach of Egypt had been removed, the children of Israel celebrated the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month. They could eat the flesh of the lamb neither before circumcision nor afterward, before they had been healed. You see, therefore, that no unclean person celebrates the Passover and no uncircumcised person does so. Hence: “Our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed.” Therefore let us celebrate the feast day, not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5).

[Col. 0510A] And they celebrated. (ISIDORE on Joshua.) After the circumcision of the Gospel, the Passover is immediately celebrated at the place of revelation, and the Lamb is sacrificed, who takes away the sins of the world. When the manna of the figurative Law ceased, the people first ate the bread of Christ’s body, which the incorruptible land of promise—that is, the Virgin Mary—brought forth, whose grain, falling into the earth, produced abundant fruit. Note the order: after we have crossed the streams of the bath under the leadership of Jesus Christ and have been marked by spiritual circumcision through faith, then at last we celebrate the Passover—that is, we believe that Christ was sacrificed for the salvation of the world—and, as believers, we are immediately nourished by the bread of the Lord’s body.

**VERSE 11.**—And they ate, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 6.) When the people went out from the land of Egypt, etc., [Col. 0510B] up to: For how could it be thought that, when the better food ceased, something worse succeeded it?

(JUSTIN, *Dialogue*.) In the beginning, before all creatures, God generated from himself a certain rational power, which is also called the Glory of the Lord, and at times the Son, Wisdom, Angel, Word, God, and Lord. At one time he also says that he is the Commander of the army, when he appeared in human form to Jesus son of Nave.

And he saw a man. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 6 on Joshua.) It happened when Jesus was in Jericho, etc., up to: who returned after receiving the kingdom.

**VERSE 15.**—Joshua fell forward, etc. It may be asked whether he prostrated himself before an angel and called him Lord, or rather, because he understood that he was God, recognizing by whom he had been sent, called that very one Lord and prostrated himself before him.

(ORIGEN, Homily 6 on Joshua.) Jesus is in Jericho, etc., up to: God immediately and willingly clings to us and stands by us.

# CHAPTER 6

**VERSE 1.**—Now Jericho, etc. (ISIDORE, on Joshua, chapter 7.) Jericho is interpreted as “moon,” etc., up to: that is, outside the Church no one is saved.

**VERSE 8.**—And when Joshua, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 5 on Joshua.) Jericho is overthrown by the priests’ trumpets, etc., up to: and the doctrines of the philosophers.

**VERSE 17.**—And let the city be, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 7.) Guard yourselves from the anathema, etc., up to: and they cause the people of God to be defeated.

**VERSE 20.**—Therefore. (ID.) The whole people is said to have shouted with a great shout, etc., up to: the people of the world were striving.

And when they sounded the trumpets. Each one of us ought to fulfill these things within himself. You have Jesus as your leader through faith. Make for yourself trumpets of beaten metal from the holy Scriptures; draw your meanings from them, your words from them. For this reason they are called beaten trumpets. Sing upon them—that is, in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs. If you sing on such trumpets and carry the ark of the covenant around seven times—that is, if you do not separate the mystical commandments of the Law from the trumpets of the Gospel—then likewise demand from yourself a harmony of jubilation. That is, let the people of your thoughts and senses always utter a concordant and harmonious voice. If you do not sometimes speak the truth and at other times lie through flattery; if you are not at one moment gentle and forgiving and at another savage with anger; if the flesh within you does not desire against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh, then send forth a voice of jubilation, because the world has been conquered for you. Hence Paul said: “But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (Galatians 6).

The walls immediately. At Jesus’ coming the walls of Jericho were overthrown; at Christ’s coming the world is conquered. Hence Paul: “He removed from the midst what was contrary to us, fastening it to the cross, and stripping off principalities and powers, he led them openly in triumph on the wood of the cross” (Colossians 2). [Col. 0511B] From these words I understand that, when the heavenly powers, principalities, and authorities saw Jesus’ battle, the strong one bound and his vessels plundered, they sounded with heavenly trumpets, because, when the prince of this world was bound, the world was conquered, and the heavenly army gave a voice of jubilation in Christ’s triumph (Matthew 12). Truly, therefore, the people of the nations have been set free—the people who know this jubilation, recognize the mysteries, and believe.

**VERSE 23.**—And the young men who entered led out, etc. (ADAMANTIUS.) Jesus brought out Rahab the prostitute and gave life to her father’s entire household, etc., up to: and those who were first became last.

# CHAPTER 7

**VERSE 1.**—And the Lord was angry, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 7.) We must not pass over this carelessly, etc., up to: who would go with me into Gehenna.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 8 on Joshua.) It is often asked how it is just for punishment to be inflicted on some for another’s sins, etc., up to: which he himself carries out in his judgment, a judgment to which human power does not aspire.

**VERSE 21.**—And the bar. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 7.) He stole the golden tongue, etc., up to: which became the cause of sin for the thief.

And the bar. The Septuagint: “The tongue”—that is, the doctrines of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular literature. For this is the golden tongue, fitted with polished speech. The heretics stole it from Jericho, as a golden bar, when they tried to introduce the sect of the philosophers into the Church. Many are destroyed by their anathema and, as though by a heap of stones, are extinguished by the multitude of their sins. Their leader is the devil, who, through their impiety, had conquered certain believers; he is again conquered and defeated, and, suspended by the people of God, is slain by the power of the cross.

(ISIDORE, on Joshua.) Jericho signifies the world. He hides some part of its anathema in his own tabernacle who inserts secular customs into the Church’s secrets; who, while remaining under the worship of God, loves the world’s festivals or spectacles; who consults diviners, haruspices, and augurs, or does the other things that were practiced in Jericho, that is, in the world.

And he stoned him. (AUGUSTINE, Question on Joshua.) It is asked concerning the one who had committed the theft, etc., up to: dying with his sin consumed along with him.

# CHAPTER 8

[Col. 0512A]

**VERSE 1.**—But the Lord said, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 8.) We were defeated first because of sins, etc., up to: those who follow Jesus, away from the burden of the Law.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 10 on Joshua.) When someone undertakes a just war, etc., up to: he should be judged not so much the author of the war as its minister.

(ID., Question 11.) It must be asked whether every intention to deceive should be considered a lie, and, if so, whether there can be a just lie by which someone who deserves to be deceived is deceived. And if this too is not found to be just, it remains that, according to some signification, what was done by ambush may be referred to the truth.

**VERSE 15.**—And while they were fleeing. (ADAMANTIUS, cited above.) What, do you think, does Jesus’ fleeing signify? etc., up to: those who flee fornication, deceit, lying, and the like.

**VERSE 24.**—Therefore, after all had been killed. (ADAMANTIUS, cited above.) They struck them with the edge of the sword, etc., up to: to be crowned with the palm of victory and with the reward of virtue?

**VERSE 29.**—The king. (ID., Homily 8.) The king of Ai is hanged on a double tree, etc., up to: but concerning the devil he says: “The last enemy to be destroyed is death,” etc. (1 Corinthians 15.)

(ID.) The Septuagint: “On a double tree,” that is, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, etc., up to: He is the last Adam in a life-giving spirit.

**VERSE 30.**—Then he built, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 9.) Jesus built an altar to the Lord, the God of Israel, etc., [Col. 0512C] up to: those who are worthy to construct the altar.

**VERSE 33.**—And all, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 9.) “And all Israel, and the elders,” etc., up to: namely, by fulfilling in deed what is written in the Law.

As the foreigner. (ID., cited above.) But both the proselyte and the native-born together, etc., up to: and let them beware of incurring the punishments appointed for sinners.

After this he read. (ADAMANTIUS, cited above.) It is reported, etc., up to: “so that we may know the things given to us by God” (2 Corinthians 2).

**VERSE 35.**—Nothing of these things. (ID.) There was no word apart from the things Moses commanded, etc., up to: or those who are already striving to be joined to the faithful.

# CHAPTER 9

[Col. 0512D] Gathered together, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 9 on Joshua.) From the things that occurred, etc., up to: “Satan will be crushed under the feet of his servants” (Romans 16).

**VERSE 3.**—But those who, etc. (ID., Homily 10.) “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14), etc., up to: do not listen to the words of the one calling you back to your former freedom, and become forever a servant of sin.

**VERSE 19.**—We swore. (AUGUSTINE, Question 13 on Joshua.) It is asked how the Hebrews believed that this oath should be kept with the Gibeonites, etc., up to: than if he had carried out what he had sworn in anger.

(ISIDORE on Joshua.) The Gibeonites signify those who believe and who appear devoted to the servants of God or to the worship of the Church, yet possess no amendment, devotion, or renewal in their conduct. Such people merely carry a certain sign of salvation within the Church for a time. But among spiritual people—that is, among the saints of God—they do not attain the eternal kingdom or freedom.

# CHAPTER 10

**VERSE 4.**—Go up to, etc. (ORIGEN, Homily 11 on Joshua.) When the soul joins itself to the word of God, etc., up to: and dispels the coming of night.

Therefore they gathered together, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 15 on Joshua.) It is asked how the king of Jerusalem, etc., up to: and yet that whole land is originally called the land of Canaan.

**VERSE 7.**—And Joshua went up, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 14.) When the besieged Gibeonites had sent to Jesus against the kings of the Amorites, etc., up to: and in a certain way rewarded their faith.

For five kings had fled, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 11 on Joshua.) What does he mean when he says, etc., up to: for this is why Jerusalem was once under King Adonizedek, and other cities under other kings.

(ADAMANTIUS, cited above.) Jesus kills the enemies, not teaching unbelief, etc., up to: let Jesus Christ alone reign in you.

(ADAMANTIUS, Homily 13.) “All these things happened to them as a figure. They were written for us,” etc., [Col. 0513C] up to: into the inheritance of the holy land, in the Israelite portion, after our enemies have been destroyed (Ephesians 2).

# CHAPTER 11

**VERSE 1.**—When Jabin heard this, etc. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 24 on Joshua.) When Israel according to the flesh read these Scriptures before Christ’s coming, etc., up to: so that they may attack us, who follow Jesus our Savior. But the Lord says: “Do not be afraid of them,” etc.

**VERSE 11.**—Tomorrow at this same hour. (ADAMANTIUS, Homily 14 on Joshua.) I see that today we cannot overwhelm all of them or kill them all; tomorrow they will be destroyed—that is, after the consummation of the world, when it will be said to them: “Go into the eternal fire which God prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matthew 25). Then, if we have conquered while following Jesus as our leader, we shall receive the kingdom that God prepared for his saints through Jesus Christ.

(ID., Homily 15.) Unless these wars represented spiritual things, etc., up to: therefore Jesus did as the Lord had commanded him.

(ORIGEN.) Jesus therefore fulfilled this according to God’s command, etc., up to: which is Christ, and which, at his command, must be slaughtered, so that nothing in us remains that can breathe.

**VERSE 12.**—And all, etc. (ADAMANTIUS.) Sin reigned in all of us and was present in all, etc., [Col. 0514A] up to: nor do you fulfill the command that the Lord Jesus gave.

As Moses had commanded him, etc. This is the word of the Law, in accordance with: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke 16). The Law therefore commanded us to kill all the kings of sin who provoke us to sin. Thus Jesus acted, and he transgressed nothing. For he is the one who destroys vices in us and the kingdoms of sin. Christ himself also did everything that Moses commanded in the Law; hence: “God sent his Son, born of a woman” (Galatians 4), etc. He fulfilled everything that the Law commanded, so that he might redeem us from the curse of the Law; he said: “I have not come to abolish the Law but to fulfill it” (Matthew 5).

**VERSE 15.**—As the Lord had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded. (AUGUSTINE, Question 16 on Joshua.) It should not be considered cruelty that Jesus left no living person in the cities handed over to him, because God had commanded these things. Those who think that God himself was cruel in this matter, and therefore refuse to believe that the true God was the author of the Old Testament, judge both God’s works and human sins perversely, not knowing what each person deserves and considering it a great evil when those who are destined to fall are thrown down and mortals die.

**VERSE 19.**—There was not, etc. (AUGUSTINE, Question 17.) It is asked how this can be true, since afterward, from the time of the judges and kings, the Hebrews were not able to capture all the cities of those seven nations altogether. But it must either be understood in this way: that Joshua approached no city in battle which he did not capture; or certainly that none of them was captured except those in the regions mentioned above. The regions in which the cities concerned were located were enumerated, and he captured all of them in war.

(ADAMANTIUS, Homily 15.) And Jesus received in battle all who had gone out to battle, etc., up to: when we do not perform their works.

(AUGUSTINE, Question 18 on Joshua.) Because the Lord caused their hearts to be strengthened, etc., up to: they captured them partly by fighting.

**VERSE 23.**—And it rested. (ORIGEN, Homily 15.) Not under Joshua son of Nave, under whom it scarcely ever ceased from wars, but under Jesus Christ. For you have come to Jesus and in baptism have obtained the remission of sins; now the flesh does not fight against the spirit in you, nor the spirit against the flesh (Galatians 5). Your land has therefore ceased from wars if you carry the death of Jesus in your body in such a way that, when all battles within you have ceased, you become truly a peacemaker and are called a son of God. But this will happen when you have completed the wars and subdued the adversaries. Then you will rest under your vine, which is Christ, and under your fig tree, which is the Holy Spirit.

# CHAPTER 12

**VERSE 1.**—(JEROME, *On Hebrew Places*.) Astaroth-karnaim, land of giants, formerly on the heights of the Sodomites whom Chedorlaomer killed. Even today there are two forts in Batanea bearing this name, nine miles apart. Edrei, where Og, king of Bashan, a giant, was killed. It is now Adara, a notable city of Arabia, twenty-four miles from Osdra. Heshbon, the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, in the land of Gilead; although it had previously belonged to the Moabites, it was possessed by the Amorites by right of war. Salecah, the city of King Og, in the region of Bashan. Maacah, a city of the Amorites on the Jordan, near Mount Hermon. Jarmuth, the city that Joshua overthrew, in the tribe of Judah, four miles distant from Eleutheropolis, near the village of Eshcol. Lachish, in the tribe of Judah. Isaiah and Jeremiah mention it; it is now a village seven miles from Eleutheropolis. Hormah belonged by lot to Simeon or Judah, etc.

# CHAPTER 13

[Col. 0515B]

(ADAMANTIUS, Homily 16 on Joshua.) Priests and elders are not called so on account of length of life, etc., up to: just as he is first in all things, because he is the head of all.

### Chapter XIII

**Verse 1.—“And the land.”** (The same.) Another reading: “And a very great amount of land was left.” It was said above, etc., up to: “But whoever is subjected by necessity, when the last enemy, death, is destroyed, will not be in grace.”

**Verse 6.—“And all.”** (Adaman., Homily 16.) After Jesus had listed very many nations, he said concerning the Sidonians alone: “And I will exterminate all the Sidonians from before the children of Israel.” The Sidonians are interpreted as “hunters.” These are the demons of whom the Prophet says: “They prepared snares for my feet” (Psalm 56). The Lord exterminates them, so that there may be no one to stretch out snares and nets for deceiving souls; and so that each person may rest beneath his vine and beneath his fig tree.

**Verse 7.—“And now.”** After this we read that Moses gave an inheritance to certain people, and afterward Jesus distributed the inheritance according to the Lord’s command. By Moses understand the Law: those who lived according to the Law received the inheritance first, but outside the promised land. Although they received it, they do not possess it, nor do they divide it among themselves; rather, they await the time when it will be distributed to them by Jesus as an allotted portion. Hence the Apostle says: “All these, though they received commendation through faith, did not obtain the promises, since God had provided something better for us, so that they should not be perfected without us” (Hebrews 11). They therefore already have their promise and have rested, judged worthy through Moses to receive their inheritance; yet they still fight on behalf of those who serve under Jesus. For all the Fathers who fell asleep before us fight together with us and assist us by their prayers. Hence: “That synagogue will lick this synagogue, as a calf licks green grass from the field.” For the Lord’s synagogue, which preceded us, will consume every opposing synagogue with mouth and tongue—that is, it will consume our adversaries through prayers. Therefore we must fight by prayers, meditation on the word of God, action, and right understanding.

(Adaman., Homily 17.) Just as shadows serve as a likeness of heavenly things, etc., up to: “They receive the inheritance through Jesus.”

**“To the tribes.”** Moses gave no inheritance to the Levites, nor did Jesus, because God himself is their inheritance. Perhaps these are those who surpass others in the Church through strength of spirit and the grace of their merits. Perhaps they are those who devote themselves to wisdom and knowledge among the people destined for salvation, keep their minds pure, cultivate them with every distinguished virtue, and teach the simpler how to attain salvation. Their inheritance is the Lord himself, who is Wisdom, whom they loved above all others.

**Verse 15.—“To the tribe of the sons of Reuben,” etc.** (The same.) Yet I find some difference in what Moses distributed, etc., up to: “The blind leading the blind will fall into the pit with him.”

**Verse 32.—“This.”** (Adaman., Homily 18 on Joshua.) Let us learn from the Law, etc., up to: “Jesus and Eleazar together for dividing the land.”

### Chapter XIV

**Verse 2.—“Dividing everything by lot,” etc.** (Isidore.) After the nations had been destroyed, Joshua divided the promised land among the peoples by lot. Christ likewise expelled from before his faithful the nations—that is, the spirits of pagan errors—and divided the land by lot, granting each person his own gifts.

**Verse 3.—“Two.”** (The same.) Moses gave only two tribes land beyond the Jordan, etc., up to: “Therefore perfection and the sum of all good things are in the Holy Spirit.”

**“Except.”** (The same.) The Levites do not receive an inheritance of land, etc., up to: “So that they may say: ‘The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,’” etc. (Psalm 15).

**Verse 4.—“Nor did they receive.”** (The same.) The dwellings of the Levites, etc., up to: “who live by the administration of all things.”

**Verse 6.—“He spoke.”** (Adaman., Homily 18.) Caleb first received his inheritance from Jesus, up to: “For he himself taught and disclosed everything; he himself revealed to Paul that the Law was spiritual.”

**“You know.”** (The same.) This is what the Lord said, etc., up to: “because he wrote everything wisely.”

**Verse 11.—“Thus strong.”** For the holy man is likewise strong in present and past things, in new and old things, in the Gospels and in the Law. This, therefore, is what he says: that he is as strong under Jesus as he was then under Moses, because the vigilant heart is strong in the mysteries of both Testaments.

**Verse 12.—“Give, therefore.”** The holy man seeks nothing lowly or cast down, but a lofty mountain, in which there are great and fortified cities, because the wise person occupies fortified cities and destroys the strongholds in which the ungodly trust.

**“In which.”** (Adaman., Homily 18.) The cities and walls are the doctrines of the ungodly, etc., up to: “just as God became the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob in Christ Jesus.”

**Verse 15.—“And the land ceased,” etc.** (Adaman., Homily 19 on Joshua.) This is not written in Moses’ distribution, but in Jesus’ distribution. If, therefore, you wish to become worthy to receive an inheritance from Jesus, you must first bring all wars to an end and establish yourself in peace, so that it may be said of the land of your flesh: “The land ceased from wars.”

### Chapter XV

**Verse 1.—“Therefore the lot of the sons of Judah,” etc.** Since it is customary for Holy Scripture to call the four quarters of the world axes or regions, in describing the boundaries of the tribe of Judah only two are named. It says: “And the boundaries of the sons of the tribe of Judah according to their clans were from the boundaries of Edom, from the wilderness of Zin westward.” After describing the boundaries from the west, it says: “And from the east, the Salt Sea”; but it leaves the north and south unmentioned.

The boundaries of Judea are therefore close to the boundaries of Edom, which is interpreted as “earthly.” Immediately after earthly things come the boundaries of Judea, but, it says, from the wilderness of Zin—that is, of temptations. After temptations, therefore, come the boundaries of Judah’s inheritance.

East and west are named as neighboring places, that is, the adjoining regions mentioned above. The Valley of Egypt is likewise designated as near the western parts, since it lies west of the wilderness. From the east the boundaries are enclosed by the Salt Sea.

After this, it says, by the hills that extend westward; and from there one ascends westward as far as Kadesh-barnea, and thus extends westward to Kadesh. These are their boundaries on the side of Africa, and from there it proceeded as far as the Valley of Egypt.

Observe how, in the western regions, it names Africa, Egypt, and the setting sun, so that each person may know that these things must be traversed, and that only then may one reach the royal tribe from which our Lord arose. From the boundaries of Edom there is the wilderness of Zin. Therefore we must cross the desert of temptations in order to reach the inheritance of the sons of Judah.

We must also ascend the ascent of the hills of Akrabbim, which is interpreted as “scorpions,” because we must pass over and trample the scorpions of whom it is written: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions,” etc. (Luke 10). Whoever, therefore, wishes to enter the inheritance of the tribe of Judah must ascend these heights, trample, and escape these scorpions.

Perhaps the Lord said this to Ezekiel as he made this journey: “Son of man, you dwell in the midst of scorpions” (Ezekiel 2). And, it says, the boundaries extend as far as Kadesh-barnea. Kadesh is interpreted as “holy” or “sanctification.” The boundaries of Judah therefore reach as far as sanctification.

It is also said that on the eastern side of Judah there is the Salt Sea; afterward, within its territory, the fountain of the sun and the city of the sun are named, and in the same tribe there is also the city of letters.

Therefore everyone who wishes to enter the portion of the sons of Judah must first cross the Salt Sea—that is, overcome the waves and storms of this world—and escape everything in this world which, because of its uncertainty and slipperiness, is compared with the waves of the sea. Thus he may reach the land of Judea and the fountain of the sun of righteousness, which is the fountain of water springing up into eternal life, and afterward find the city of the sun of righteousness.

There is also a city of the sun in Egypt, but that city received its name from the sun which the heavenly Father commands to rise upon the good and the evil (Matthew 5). The city that is in Judea, however, belongs only to the saints, because it is the city of God; and that fountain mentioned above, having become a river, makes glad the city of God (Psalm 45).

You too, if you are fortified on every side, surrounded by the wall of self-restraint, and strengthened by towers of patience and greatness of spirit, will become the city of God. But if you add to this the light of the knowledge of God, and the sun of righteousness shines upon you, you will become the city of the sun, or you will inherit the city of the sun by lot. If you devote yourself day and night to the Law of God, and the book of the Law does not depart from your hand, your inheritance will become the city of letters.

(Adaman., Homily 20 on Joshua.) No small benefit is conferred upon the soul, etc., up to: “But when one or two or three days have passed, in due time the power of the food or drink, conveyed to the sight through hidden channels, gradually cleanses the vision.”

**Verse 13.—“But Caleb.”** (Adaman., Homily 20.) The beginning of Jesus’ distribution, etc., up to: “Note that Caleb is called the son of Jephunneh, and Othniel the son of Kenaz, who is Caleb the younger—that is, his kinsman.”

**Verse 18.—“Sitting on the donkey. To whom.”** (Gregory, Book 3 of the Dialogues, chapter 34.) Achsah sits upon the donkey, etc., up to: “so that first the upper pool and afterward the lower one might be placed.”

**Verse 63.—“But the Jebusite, the inhabitant of Jerusalem, the sons of Judah could not destroy.”** (Adaman., Homily 11 on Joshua.) We understand spiritually that the Jebusite dwelt with the Jews in Jerusalem to the present day, according to the parable of the Gospel, etc., up to: “the sons of Judah could not expel them from Jerusalem to the present day.”

The Jebusite—that is, “trampling”—means those who create scandal in the Church and who, having received knowledge of the mysteries, trample upon the pearls of the word of God by attacking them.

(Origen, in the same place.) Jerusalem is interpreted as “Vision of Peace,” etc., up to: “but they cannot all be expelled at once.”

“To the present day,” that is, according to the manner of Scripture, for the eternity of the age. But this cannot stand literally: how can the Jebusite dwell with the sons of Judah in Jerusalem for as long as this age lasts, when the sons of Judah themselves do not dwell there forever?

### Chapter XVI

**Verse 1.—“It fell,” etc.** (Augustine, Question 19 on Joshua.) It follows.

**“We shall not be able to go up into the hill country.”** (Adaman., in the same place.) The mountain is not enough for us, etc., up to: “they make the Canaanites out of the Israelites.”

### Chapter XVIII

**Verse 6.—“I will send for you.”** (Adaman., Homily 23 on Joshua.) In human custom, etc., up to: “so that the earthly inheritance, which is a figure of the heavenly one, might not be given to another.”

(The same, Homily 23.) Bethlehem too is not without a definite reason distinguished as the fountain of Judah, etc., up to: “Hence he says to Timothy: ‘Remember the words which I commend to faithful people, and to those who are able to teach others’” (2 Timothy 2).

### Chapter XIX

**Verse 1.—“Of the sons.”** (Augustine, Question 20 on Joshua.) “And the Amorite remained to dwell in Elon,” etc., up to: “which he would not do.”

(Adaman., Homily 24 on Joshua.) According to the Septuagint, the Amorite remained to dwell in Elon and in Sannanim, etc., up to: “And the sons of Ephraim went to traverse the land according to their boundaries.”

**Verse 49.—“And when.”** (Adaman., Homily 24.) Observe the gentleness and humility of Jesus, etc., up to: “so that the Lord Jesus may willingly enter the lodging of our heart.”

### Chapter XX

**Verse 2.—“Separate cities of refuge,” etc.** (Origen, Homily 34 on Numbers.) Not all murderers flee to the cities of refuge, but those who committed murder unknowingly. For there are some sins which, if we commit them deliberately and willingly, make us murderers; and there are others which, if we commit them unknowingly, establish for us—and, I believe, by God’s command prepare for us—a certain place where we ought to dwell for a fixed time, if we have committed sins unwillingly, provided that we are found cleansed from those sins committed voluntarily. For this reason certain cities of refuge are set apart.

### Chapter XXI

**Verse 1.—“They approached.”** (Adaman., Homily 25 on Joshua.) All the sons of Israel received their portions in the land, etc., up to: “and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven.”

(Adamantius, Homily 26.) It was said above, etc., up to: “he filled the world and granted spiritual gifts to believers.”

**Verse 39.—“Therefore.”** (Isidore.) The fact that the Levites received forty-two cities signifies the preaching of the saints. They possess the teaching which consists of the Law’s Decalogue and the fourfold number of the Gospel, as though they possessed forty cities; two are added because everything they proclaim they announce in a moral and mystical sense.

**Verse 41.—“And the Lord gave.”** (Augustine, Question 21.) It is asked how, when Israel did not continue only until the day of Joshua’s death, etc., up to: “had already been given for a certain exercise.”

**Verse 42.—“And none of them.”** (The same, Question 22.) What he says, etc., up to: “before the places which each tribe had to defend were divided among them.”

### Chapter XXII

**Verse 1.—“At that same time.”** (Adaman., Homily 26 on Job.) Jesus gathered the sons of Reuben and Gad, etc., up to: “with every attack having ceased.”

**Verse 10.—“And when.”** (Adamantius, Homily 26.) The sons of Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, etc., up to: “Thus there is one flock and one shepherd: those righteous ones, and these righteous Christians.”

**Verse 17.—“Was it too little?”** (Adam.) Thus the people once fell in the wilderness and died, etc., up to: “and where is the true Israel in Christ Jesus our Lord?”

**Verse 29.—“Having been built.”** (Augustine, Question 32 on Joshua.) “And in the sacrifices of our salvations.” Since the sacrifices are expressed in the plural, etc., up to: “For he alone is the Savior himself.”

### Chapter XXIII

**Verse 14.—“Behold, today I am entering.”** (Augustine, Question 24.) But when Jesus says, etc., up to: “therefore this word too has been interpreted in this way.”

### Chapter XXIV

**Verse 3.—“Therefore I took your father.”** (Augustine.) What the Septuagint has, etc., up to: “which is the true seed of Abraham.”

**Verse 11.—“They fought.”** (Augustine, Question 26 on Joshua.) They protected themselves by closing the gates and surrounding the walls, etc., up to: “armed defense.”

**Verse 12.—“Hornets.”** (Augustine, Question 27.) Septuagint: “Wasps.” That is, perhaps figuratively, the sharpest stings of fear, by which they were somehow punished through their fears and fled; or hidden spirits of the air, of which it is said in the Psalms that they acted through evil angels—unless someone says that not everything that happened was written down and wishes real wasps to be understood.

**Verse 19.—“You will not be able.”** (Augustine, Question 28 on Joshua.) “You will not be able to serve the Lord,” etc., up to: “and afterward grace would abound through Jesus Christ, who is the end of the Law.”

**Verse 23.—“Take away.”** (Augustine, Question 29 on Joshua.) What does he mean when he says, etc., up to: “we shall know him face to face” (1 Corinthians 13).

(Augustine, Question 30 on Joshua.) “And Jesus established a covenant,” etc. Those who examine these words more deeply, etc., up to: “but all abandoned me; may it not be counted against them” (2 Timothy 4).

### Book of Judges

Hebrew: **SOPHETIM** (*Judges*). (G)*

### Preface

(Athanasius, in the *Synopsis*.) This book is called Judges because, after the death of Joshua son of Nun, God saved his people, oppressed by the nations left behind by the Canaanites, through judges. Their individual deeds and the length of their lives are contained in this volume, etc. There were thirteen of them in number, and their years amounted to four hundred and eleven.

(Isidore, in Book 1 of the *Judges*.) The history of the Book of Judges indicates no small number of mysteries. After Joshua come the Judges, just as after Christ come the apostles and rulers of the churches to govern the faithful, whom he himself leads to the hope of eternal promise.

Throughout this volume the sins of the Jewish people, their servitude and cry, and God’s compassion are contained. For many years they served because of their sins, and when they turned back they were delivered, because our sins provide strength to our enemies. When we do evil in the sight of the Lord, our adversaries—that is, the demons—are strengthened. But when we turn back, God raises up judges and saviors, that is, leaders and teachers whom he sends to assist those who cry to God with their whole heart.

(Augustine, Question 1 on the Book of Judges.) At the end of the Book of Joshua the narrator briefly extended the history until the sons of Israel turned aside to worship foreign gods. In this book the sequence is resumed: how the events that followed the death of Joshua took place. The book therefore does not begin from the time when the people fell away to worship idols, but from earlier events, with the intervening periods during which those things happened after they had reached that point.

### Chapter I

**Verse 2.—“And the Lord said: Judah shall go up,” etc.** (The same, Question 2.) It is asked whether a man named Judah was intended, or whether he customarily called the tribe itself by this name, etc., up to: “then the tribe of Simeon also was taken up for battle.”

**Verse 12.—“And he said,” etc.** (Augustine, Question 3.) “Whoever strikes the city of letters and captures it, I will give him my daughter in marriage.” This is mentioned in the Book of Joshua, etc., up to: “yet I do not think that Scripture recalled twice without reason that Caleb’s daughter was given as the victor’s reward.”

**Verse 19.—“Nor could he.”** (The same, Question 5 on Judges.) The Lord was in this very matter, etc., up to: “when the Apostle says: ‘So that he might not exalt himself because of the greatness of the revelations,’ etc.” (2 Corinthians 12).

**Verse 21.—“The Jebusite.”** (Augustine, Question 7 on Judges.) Above the same city is read about, etc., up to: “they did not hold the land they possessed without him.”

**Verse 27.—“Manasseh.”** (Augustine, Question 8.) “And Manasseh did not inherit Beth-shean,” etc., up to: “that at one time the Scythians held almost all Asia.”

**Verse 34.—“And it constrained.”** (Augustine, Question 11 on Judges.) “And it afflicted the Amorites, the sons of Dan, in the mountain, because it did not permit them to descend,” etc. This was anticipated and mentioned in the Book of Joshua; here it is recalled retrospectively.

### Chapter II

**Verse 1.—“And the angel went up.”** (Augustine, Question 12 on Judges.) “And the angel of the Lord went up,” etc., up to: “which he mentioned there by anticipation.”

**Verse 3.—“Therefore I did not wish to destroy.”** (Augustine, Question 13 on Judges.) From this we understand that certain sins proceed from God’s anger. Since the gods of the nations among whom the Israelites wished to dwell, without exterminating them, were to become a stumbling block to them—that is, were to cause them to stumble in their God and live while he was offended—God, in his indignation, threatened them. This plainly shows that it is a great sin.

**“Therefore Joshua dismissed.”** (Augustine.) This is repeated by way of recapitulation. For Joshua’s death is also mentioned in this book, so that, as though from the beginning, everything might briefly be indicated: from the time when the Lord gave them the land, how they lived under the judges, and what they suffered. Then the narrative returns again to the order of the judges, beginning with the one who was first appointed.

**Verse 7.—“And they grew old.”** (Adaman., Homily 1 on Judges.) The elders who were with Joshua or after Joshua, etc., up to: “but the days of the holy elders are long-lived and extended.”

**Verse 8.—“He died.”** (The same, Homily 2.) Jesus lives in Paul, etc., up to: “and another generation arose which did not know Jesus, etc.”

(Adaman., Homily 2.) “And they served the Baals,” etc., up to: “we love with our whole soul and all our strength; we worship idols.”

**Verse 13.—** (Augustine, Question 16 on the Book of Judges.) “And they served Baal and the Ashtaroth.” Baal is said to be the name of Jupiter among those peoples, etc., up to: “he wished Juno to be mentioned in the plural.”

(Augustine, Question 17.) But also in the Psalm, etc., up to: “they were not to be redeemed with monetary payment.”

**Verse 14.—“And the Lord was angry.”** (Origen, Homily 2 on Judges.) When someone serves God, etc., up to: “lest we be handed over to the devil.”

### Chapter III

**Verse 5.—“In the midst.”** (Augustine, Question 17 on Judges.) In Exodus God says, etc., up to: “their multitude would not allow the lands from which the adversaries were to be exterminated to remain deserted. But when he says, ‘lest the wild beasts multiply against you,’ it is remarkable if he did not wish bestial desires and lusts to be understood . . . for God could not exterminate human beings but could exterminate beasts.”

**Verse 8.—** (Adaman., Homily 3.) “And the Lord handed them over,” etc., up to: “the most foul odor of pride reeks.”

(Origen, Homily 3 on Judges.) See the gracious Lord, etc., up to: “who are designated through Othniel or Ehud.”

**Verse 10.—“The Spirit of the Lord was upon him.”** It is a great praise of the first judge that the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and that through the Spirit of God he judged the people. I do not much remember this being said of another. Today there are judges of the churches who have also been given judgment over souls; but I do not know whether anyone is worthy to be filled with the Spirit of God.

**“And it was in him.”** (Adaman.) After they had cried out to the Lord, that is. Who among us sends forth such a strong and righteous cry to the Lord that the people may deserve to receive a judge whom the Spirit of God fills, so that he may be able to maintain right judgment?

Hence this book is called the Book of Judges: they judged the people of Israel, men remarkable indeed, as Joshua was. Likewise the Book of Kings tells how each of the kings ruled and what he did, including what was evil, so that the leaders or judges of the Church may imitate their good deeds and avoid their evil ones.

**“And Israel served.”** (Adaman., in the same place.) After eighteen years, etc., up to: “to whom it will be said: ‘Depart from me, workers of iniquity; I do not know you. Go into the eternal fire,’ etc.” (Luke 13).

(The same.) Divine Scripture also indicates different measures of punishment: above it says eight years; here it says eighteen. It is certain that the periods of correction are determined according to the measure of sin and the delay of conversion. These eighteen years of servitude also passed, and it is not said that they cried to the Lord or turned from their wickedness, but afterward.

**Verse 15.—“A savior.”** (The same, Homily 3.) Saviors or judges, etc., up to: “which he says: ‘I am the way, the truth, and the life’” (John 14).

**“Who used both hands for the right hand.”** According to spiritual understanding, all the saints are called ambidextrous; the devil and his rulers are ambisinister. Everything they do is left-handed and perverse, assigned to eternal fire with those who are on the left.

**Verse 20.—“Ehud entered,” etc.** (Adaman., Homily 4.) Ehud is interpreted as “praise.” For he used a crafty and praiseworthy deception, etc., up to: “to whom the Lord says: ‘Well done, good servant,’ etc.”

**Verse 22.—“Very fat.”** (Augustine, Question 21.) The question is rightly raised, etc., up to: “Thus we find it. Eglon was exceedingly fat.”

**Verse 25.—“They took.”** (The same, Question 23.) How did the servants of King Eglon open the doors with a key which Ehud had not locked? Or, if he had locked them with a key, how had he not taken the key with him, so that they could not open them with a key either? Therefore either another key was brought, or it was a kind of fastening that could be closed without a key but could not be opened without one. For there are certain things of this sort, such as those called *verudata* [manuscripts: *veruclata*].

**Verse 31.—“After him.”** (Adaman., Homily 4.) Septuagint: Samgar, that is, “a stranger there.” For all the people of God are strangers in this world, as the one who said: “I am a stranger upon the earth with you, and a sojourner, as all my fathers were.” The Holy Spirit therefore calls this Samgar “a stranger there,” that is, “here”; for what is “there” to the Holy Spirit, who is in heaven, is “here” to us.

**“After him.”** (Augustine, Question 25.) It is asked how Samgar fought for Israel after Ehud and is said to have saved him. For Israel had not been captured or bound under the yoke of servitude. But he saved him not because the enemy had inflicted harm, but so that the enemy would not be permitted to inflict harm. We should believe that the enemy began to test him in battle and was driven back by this victory.

**“Who struck.”** (Adaman., Homily 4.) Samgar struck the Philistines with six hundred men, etc., up to: “so that you may say confidently: ‘But far be it from me to boast,’ etc.”

### Chapter IV

**Verse 1.—“And the sons added.”** (Origen, Homily 4 on Judges.) As though the good leader had died because of the people’s sins, etc., up to: “and to Jabin, the ruler of the Canaanites.”

**Verse 2.—“Into the hands of Jabin, king of Canaan.”** (Adaman., Homily 4 on Judges.) Jabin’s military commander, etc., up to: “whether the people of the Church is governed, or the understanding of each soul.”

**Verse 4.—“There was.”** (Adaman., Homily 5.) According to the Apostle, etc., up to: “because purity of mind, not difference of sex, confers this grace.”

**Deborah.** “Bee” or “speech,” signifying the prophetess, who prepares the sweet honeycombs of heavenly teaching and the sweet honey of divine utterance. Hence: “How sweet are your words to my throat, more than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Psalm 118). And elsewhere: “The judgments of the Lord,” says the Prophet, “are more precious than gold and exceedingly precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb” (the same, Psalm 18).

**Verse 5.—“And she sat beneath the palm,” etc.** (Adaman.) Observe in what places prophecy sits: among lofty things, namely, and the house of God. Nothing lowly, nothing vile, can be found concerning the seat of prophecy. As Solomon says, it stands in high places—namely, at the gates of cities—or dwells upon the battlements of walls, or acts freely in lofty towers. It is therefore said to dwell between the house of God and lofty places. For it does not teach us to seek the things that are on earth, but those that are in heaven, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God. To that place it urges us to ascend; there prophecy strives to move its disciples.

**Verse 8.—“If you will come.”** (Augustine, Question 29 on Judges.) What is the meaning of Barak’s reply to Deborah, etc., up to: “that is, he makes things prosper for me through an angel?”

(Adaman., Homily 5.) “I will not go up unless you go up with me.” You see how, to those earlier ones, prophecy first brought the utterances of God, etc., up to: “Sisera was handed over to Jael.”

**Verse 18.—“Then Jael went out.”** (Adaman., Homily 5.) Jael, a foreign woman, signifies the Church, etc., up to: “he handed him over to eternal sleep.”

**Verse 19.—“She opened.”** (Adaman., Homily 5.) Let every soul lull and extinguish Sisera within itself with this evangelical and apostolic milk, etc., up to: “but one prize of victory will be given to the first and the last.”

**Verse 22.—“And she went out,” etc.** (Adaman., Homily 5 on Judges.) Jael meets him, etc., up to: “by a faithful touch she first obtains healing.”

### Chapter V

**Verse 1.—“And Deborah and Barak sang,” etc.** (Adaman., Homily 6 on Judges.) If we remember what was said above, etc., up to: “or the fault that comes through our sloth.”

**“Listen,” etc. “The mountains flowed from before the Lord.”** (Adaman.) Hear with your ears, all satraps. Just as satraps are inferior to kings, etc., up to: “you will rightly be summoned as a king to hear divine words.”

**Verse 6.—“In.”** The paths are said to have rested which, in the days of Samgar, the leader of Israel, had been occupied by the enemies; and people did not dare to ascend to the house of the Lord for prayer. It is not written that Samgar fully delivered them from these enemies.

**Verse 9.—“My heart loves.”** (Adaman., Homily 6.) “My heart is directed toward the things appointed for this Israel.” As though he were saying: my heart, my mind, my understanding, and my whole intellect tend toward and look upon that which has been appointed and prepared for Israel. Hence: “I count everything in the world as dung, that I may gain Christ,” etc. (Philippians 3).

**Verse 10.—“Those who by their own will.”** Of these it is said: “You who willingly offered your souls to danger,” etc., because they subjected themselves to the Law of God and to his service, meditating on his Law day and night.

**“You who ride upon shining donkeys.”** (Adaman.) Powerful peoples, bless the Lord, because you ride upon beasts, etc. Our body is a beast: it has been given for the assistance and service of the soul. To the inner person it is said: “He who rides upon a beast”—that is, his own body—and has risen above bodily desires, controlling the body’s movements with the bridle of reason, so that he may bless the Lord.

**Verse 11.—“They were dashed together.”** It is as though he says: although God must always and everywhere be praised, ought he not rather to be praised and blessed here, he who overthrew our enemies just as he overthrew the Egyptians in the Red Sea?

**“There they shall recount.”** (Adaman.) Septuagint: “The righteous were strengthened in Israel.” Among other nations those who are stronger in bodily power are called mighty in battle; in Israel, those who are more righteous, because righteousness, even when weak in strength, conquers. But unrighteousness, even if it has many strong warriors, is overcome. Therefore in our people we either conquer through righteousness or are conquered through unrighteousness.

**Verse 12.—“Arise, arise.”** The Hebrew does not have this; rather, “Awake in spirit,” namely, in the spirit of prophecy. For the perfect teachers urge Deborah to awaken in the spirit of prophecy and praise.

**Verse 15.—“Having divided.”** This is the voice of Deborah rebuking Reuben, who did not obey the Lord’s command with his brothers to defeat the enemies, but, frightened and unbelieving toward the Lord’s words, separated himself from them. Therefore he was found magnanimous and proud. Hence he is rebuked in the spirit of prophecy in this way: “Why do you dwell between two boundaries?” etc. The Hebrew, however, does not have “two.”

**Verse 21.—“He dragged their corpses,” etc.** Into the Red Sea, which is *Cadumim*, interpreted as “of the ancients,” because ancient miracles occurred there when the sons of Israel crossed and the Egyptians perished. Thus, in place of the corpses of the Egyptians, the fish and beasts of the Red Sea have the corpses of the Canaanites.

(Adaman., Homily 7 on Judges.) They are not said to have prevailed against the people of God while they keep the commandments, etc., up to: “when we are abandoned by the grace of God.”

### Chapter VI

**Verse 3.—“And when he had sown.”** (The same, Homily 7.) This is what Israel suffered, etc., up to: “glorified by his death and washed in blood.”

**Verse 8.—“Who sent a prophet to them and spoke: Thus says.”** (Augustine, Question 31 on Judges.) Why is this prophet’s name not given, etc., up to: “why could an angel not be called a prophet?”

(Isidore, in Judges, volume 5.) Gideon signifies Christ, who, established beneath the shadow of the sacred cross and within the foreordained mystery of the future Incarnation, separated the election of the saints from the chaff of vices by the uprightness of judgment, as though with a rod.

**Verse 17.—“Give me a sign.”** (Adaman., Homily 8.) As an educated man who possessed the example of Jesus his predecessor, he acted more cautiously. For he knew that angels of darkness could transform themselves into angels of light; therefore he tests the spirit to see whether it is from God. The spiritual person examines everything. Thus his predecessor, Joshua son of Nun, when he saw the prince of the heavenly army, asked whether he was “for us or for our adversaries.” Therefore Gideon examines the angelic vision through the diversity and alteration of the signs.

**Verse 18.—“Carrying.”** (Augustine, Question 35 on Judges.) It must be observed, etc., up to: “as though he needed the assistance of his holiness being present.”

**Verse 19.—“He entered.”** (Gregory, Book 3 of the *Moralia*, chapter 17.) When Gideon was threshing wheat from the chaff, etc., up to: “but also cleanse everything that is shamefully bound within him through his thoughts.”

(Isidore.) The one whom his father assigned to deceit Gideon killed, and he offered another seven-year-old bull to God. In this he showed that, after Christ’s coming, all sacrifices of paganism were to be abolished, and that only the sacrifice of Christ’s Passion was thereafter to be offered to God for the redemption of the people. For he himself is the seven-year-old bull, that is, full of the sevenfold Spirit.

**Verse 33.—“Therefore.”** (Adaman.) The Midianites gathered against Israel, etc., up to: “they attack the people of God together with pagans and Jews.”

**“In the valley of Jezreel.”** (The same.) This is interpreted as “seed of God.” For the adversaries do not dare to go there, etc., up to: “because he has been established at the summit of spiritual understanding.”

**Verse 36.—“If you save.”** (Adaman., Homily 8 on Judges.) Since there are many and innumerable signs, etc., up to: “into which no moisture of the divine word was poured.”

**Verse 37.—“On the threshing floor.”** (Origen, Homily 8.) Not anywhere, not in a field, nor in a forest, but on the threshing floor where the harvest is, etc., up to: “let us recline in the banquet of the Bridegroom Jesus Christ with pure hearts.”

**“If there is dew on the fleece alone,” etc.** (Augustine.) In Gideon’s trial, what the Lord wished to foretell he showed by the fleece being drenched while the whole threshing floor all around remained dry. This represented the first people of Israel, among whom the saints were present with heavenly grace like spiritual rain. Then, when the threshing floor was drenched and the fleece dried, it represented the Church of God spread throughout the whole world, possessing heavenly grace not in the fleece as though under a veil, but openly, while the earlier people had become alienated from and dried up by that same dew of grace.

**Verse 39.—“I ask,” etc.** (Adaman., Homily 8.) In the meaning of the second sign also, etc., up to: “the grace of divine dew is poured into the whole earth.”

### Chapter VII

**Verse 3.—“Whoever is fearful,” etc.** (Adaman., Homily 9.) Jesus cries out the same thing today, etc., up to: “thus, among enormous and abominable crimes, the crime of fear and terror is included.”

The LXX: “He is fearful who, as the vice grows [Col. 0527C], is terrified by thought alone before seeing evils, rolling a chill of fear through his limbs, so that he is overcome less by the sight of evils than by hearing of them and expecting them. Therefore, according to the LXX, he is called fearful in heart, for this vice remains fixed in the heart and in the inner parts of the soul. But the timid man is one who trembles at the first sight when facing an encounter; yet he is not terrified with his whole heart, but can recover and be encouraged again.

**VERSE 4.** — “The people are still.” (Adamantius, Homily 9.) “As I see it, those who were rejected first,” etc., up to “nor is he cast down prostrate because of thirst for sin.”

**VERSE 5.** — “Those who with hand and tongue.” (Adamantius, Homily 9.) “He says that they lap water with hand and tongue,” etc., up to “and they bear the number of the perfect Trinity.”

[Col. 0527D]

**VERSE 6.** — “The number of them was therefore,” etc. (Augustine, Question 47 on Judges.) “The number of those who lapped with their own hand and tongue was three hundred men.” Most Latin manuscripts do not have “with their hand,” but only “with their tongue,” etc., up to “David too calls himself a contemptible dog.”

**VERSE 13.** — “He struck it and overturned it.” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXX, chapter 25.) “Concerning this battle, through the prophet,” etc., up to “that the sword of the enemy might be overcome by the wood of the cross.”

**VERSE 16.** — “And he divided them.” (The same, ibid.) “They were led to the river,” etc., up to “in his left hand he holds a trumpet, in his right a jar.”

**VERSE 20.** — “And when they had broken the jars.” (Adamantius, [Col. 0528A] Homily 9.) “They carry jars,” etc., up to “so that we may deserve to obtain victory from him.”

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 27.** — “And Gideon made an ephod from it,” etc. (Augustine, Question 41 on Judges.) “It is asked what the Ephod or Ephot was,” etc., up to “so that the numerous offspring of his sons might perish, as Scripture later testifies.”

(Augustine.) It must be understood that the statement that Gideon made an ephod contrary to the law of God from the gold taken from the defeated enemies is made by anticipation, so that both the source of the gold and what was done with it might be stated together. This sin was committed at the end of Gideon’s life, when the evils that Scripture connects with it followed, after it had said how many years the land rested in the days of Gideon.

[Col. 0528B]

“Afterward.” (The same, Question 43.) “And it happened, when Gideon had died, that the children of Israel turned away, prostituted themselves after the Baals, and made Baalberith their god,” etc. Baalim and Baalberith are to be understood as idols. Therefore the transgression and prostitution of the people after Gideon’s death was greater than that committed during his lifetime because of the ephod. Although the ephod had been made unlawfully, it nevertheless derived from the sacred objects of the tabernacle. But this idolatry has no false defense based on the religion of the fathers. Thus, even if Gideon’s ephod was not made at the end of his life but earlier, God bore with it patiently so that peace might continue in the land, because although something forbidden had been done, they had not departed far from the one who had commanded something of that kind to be made in his tabernacle in his honor. But when graver offenses were committed, and the people openly prostituted themselves after idols, he did not wish this to remain unpunished.

[Col. 0528C]

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 5.** — “And Jotham remained.” (Isidore.) The younger son, who escapes the enemy’s sword by fleeing, signifies the remnant of Israel who will believe at the end of time and escape the sword of Antichrist. He ascends to the summit of Mount Gerizim because no one can escape either prophesying or the persecution of Antichrist unless he has first ascended the mountain of blessing—that is, the sublimity of faith and virtues. For this is Mount Gerizim, which Moses appointed for blessing.

(Isidore, *On Judges*, volume V.) “If this event were not mystical,” etc., up to “he will bring persecution so that he may kill all the saints.”

**VERSE 10.** — “And they said.” (The same, ibid.) The trees of the forest are unfruitful people, etc., up to “and brought the most pleasing richness of Christ to glory and honor.”

(The same, ibid.) The vine is Christ, who said: “I am the true vine” (John 15). Therefore, because the people who serve Antichrist are given over to a depraved mind so that they may believe the lie—that is, Antichrist—because they refused to believe the truth, that is, Christ, they are rejected from the kingdom of the vine, that is, Christ; from the olive, that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit; and from the fig tree, that is, the sweetness of the divine law.

“And they said.” (The same.) The bramble is a kind of thornbush, commonly called the bear-thorn. It is exceedingly rough and thorny, and through it Antichrist is signified, as one who will devastate the human race with every kind of harshness and savagery. “Fire will go out from the bramble”—that is, iniquity from Antichrist—and it will devour together with him all who trust in him.

**VERSE 23.** — “And God sent.” (Augustine, Question 45 on Judges.) “And God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem.” Some have interpreted this word as “he also sent,” etc., up to the end.

**VERSE 32.** — “Rise.” (The same, Question 46.) “And now rise by night, you and the people with you, and lie in ambush.” Some Latin manuscripts have “you shall hasten,” etc., up to “God created the sun on the fourth day.”

[Col. 0529A]

## CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.** — “After Abimelech.” (Augustine, Question 47 on Judges.) “How was he, a man of the tribe of Issachar, the uncle of Abimelech?” etc., up to “so that the flesh of the Lord might be propagated not only from royal but also from priestly stock.”

## CHAPTER XI

(Augustine, Question 49 on Judges.) Jephthah is interpreted as “opening,” etc., up to “because they do not keep the commandments of the law and do not show faithfulness to him as to a husband.”

**VERSE 3.** — “He lived in the land of Tob.” (The same, ibid.) That is, in a good land, or rather a very good one. For what is *agathon* (ἀγαθόν) in Greek is called *optimum* (“best”) in Latin. This is interpreted as Tob, where the resurrection seems to be understood. For what land is more excellent than an earthly body clothed with the excellence of immortality and incorruption?

[Col. 0529C]

(The same, ibid.) “Before the Passion he ate with tax collectors and sinners,” etc., up to “so that they may be justified and learn his ways.”

“In those days.” (The same, ibid.) Those who had rejected Christ, etc., up to “so that the final times might be signified through old age.”

**VERSE 8.** — “And the rulers said.” (Augustine, ibid.) Something similar was represented in Joseph, etc., up to “in which his kingdom will have no end.”

“And fight.” (Augustine.) Jephthah is asked to lead the battle against the children of Ammon, by whose defeat those who wished to fight under his leadership would be delivered. For Ammon is interpreted as “the son of my people” or “the people of sorrow.” Either the enemies who remained in unbelief from that very nation are signified, or all those predestined to Gehenna, where there will be “weeping and gnashing of teeth,” as among a people of sorrow. Yet the devil and his angels may suitably be understood as the people of sorrow, either because they acquire eternal misery for those whom they deceive, or because they themselves have been appointed to eternal misery.

**VERSE 9.** — “I will be your leader.” (The same, ibid.) That is, a king whom that nation did not yet have in the period of the judges, etc., up to “but Jephthah signified the one who is the true king.”

(The same.) A king, as it is written in the title of the cross, etc., up to “as those contained in the books of Kings.”

“Is it not whatever he possesses,” etc. “Is not everything that Chemosh has inherited yours?”

[Col. 0530A]

**VERSE 29.** — “And he passed through Gilead.” (Augustine, Question 49 on Judges.) Gilead is interpreted as “casting away,” etc., up to “which signifies, by saying that he passed from the watchtower of Gilead and crossed over to the children of Ammon.”

**VERSE 30.** — “If you deliver the children of Ammon.” (Augustine, ibid.) Whatever Jephthah may have intended, he does not seem to have intended his daughter. For he would not have said, “Alas, my daughter! You have hindered me,” etc. [The text] indicates that he had been hindered from fulfilling what he had intended. But whom could he have intended if he had no sons? Did he intend his wife, and did God prevent this from happening while ensuring that it did not remain unpunished, lest anyone later dare to do such a thing, and so that, by great providence, a great mystery of the Church might be represented through what happened? Thus prophecy was adapted to both: what he intended when he made the vow, [Col. 0530B] and what happened against his will. For if he intended his wife, the wife of Christ is the Church. But because the wife of this Jephthah could not be a virgin, in that his daughter appeared instead, the rashness of the vow did not remain unpunished, and the virginity of the Church was represented, to which it is said: “Daughter, your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7).

(Augustine, Question 49.) There is commonly a great question concerning Jephthah’s daughter, etc., up to “so that everything that happened afterward may seem to be understood as the work of the Spirit of the Lord who had come upon him.”

(The same.) “But among praiseworthy men,” etc., up to “so that it may be entirely avoided, but only postponed.”

(Isidore, *On Judges*, volume V.) Jephthah signifies Christ, because, departing from the presence of his brothers—that is, the Jews—he received leadership among the nations, since, as though bound by an oath, he fulfilled all the mysteries of human salvation and offered his own flesh, as a daughter, for the salvation of Israel. He swore to the Father and made a vow according to the words: “As he swore to the Lord, he vowed to the God of Jacob”—namely, that he would fulfill the mystery of religion in the Passion of his flesh for the salvation of the human race. Thus these things were accomplished through Christ so that they might appear to have been completed in fulfillment of the oath.

**VERSES 37–39.** — “And I will mourn,” etc. “And he did to her,” etc. (Augustine.) The chaste virgin, that is, the Church, etc., up to “for whose sake the two Testaments are also called such.”

“From then on the custom arose.” (Augustine, Question 49.) As for what was done by command in Israel—namely, that they came together from year to year to lament Jephthah’s daughter for four days—it does not seem to me to signify anything after the completed burnt offering, which will be in eternal life, but rather the past periods of the Church, in which those who mourned were blessed. The four days represent her universality, because of the four regions of the world through which she has been spread far and wide. As a matter of historical fact, however, I do not think the Israelites established this practice except because they understood that in this event God’s judgment had been shown more against the father, in order that no one thereafter might vow such a sacrifice. Why was mourning established if that vow was a cause for rejoicing?

[Col. 0530D]

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 7.** — “And Jephthah judged,” etc. (Augustine.) Just as those two months, on account of the seventy days, signify the number six, representing the six ages of the world, so here the number seven multiplied by six signifies the same thing insofar as it pertains to the six ages of the world. For six times seven is forty-two, and it was not without reason that Jephthah himself judged the people for six years.

[Col. 0531A]

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 2.** — “But you shall conceive,” etc. (Isidore, *On Judges*.) Samson has certain features typifying Christ, etc., up to “and what was said of Christ through the prophet: ‘The sun of righteousness shall rise for you, and healing shall be in his wings.’”

**VERSE 3.** — “Nor anything unclean.” (Augustine, Question 50.)
