The unclean thing is the dissolution of discipline that had begun in Israel and had already caused them to incline toward eating the things that God had forbidden among animals; for they were already turning also to the worship of idols.

(Augustine, Question 52 on Judges.) When the woman said that an angel had spoken to her, etc., up to “the Nazirites observed this on appointed days, making vows and fulfilling their vows.”

**VERSE 19.** — “Then he took.” (Augustine, Question 53.) When Scripture says that Manoah did not know that it was the angel of the Lord, etc., up to “so that he might be delivered to the enemies for forty years.”

**VERSE 20.** — “When.” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book V, chapter 23.) What does it mean that, at the vision of the angel, the man is fearful but the woman bold, except that when heavenly things are shown to us, the spirit is shaken by fear, yet hope presumes? For hope rises to dare greater things precisely where the spirit is disturbed when it first sees what is above. When the mind, thus lifted up, beholds the higher mysteries of heaven, the entire solidity of human strength trembles.

[Col. 0531C]

(Augustine, Question 54 on Judges.) What does it mean that, after the angel had manifested himself to Manoah and his wife, etc., up to “not receiving the sacrifice but becoming the sacrifice himself”?

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 5.** — “Samson therefore went down,” etc. (Isidore, *On Judges*, volume V, chapter 8.) When Samson was going toward the foreigners in order to seek a wife, he killed a lion. Thus Christ, when he was about to call the Church from the nations, conquered the devil, who said: “Rejoice, because I have conquered the world” (John 16). A honeycomb is taken from the mouth of the slain lion because, as we observe, earthly kings who formerly roared against Christ now, their ferocity destroyed, preach the sweetness of the Gospel and provide protection.

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 8.** — “And he struck them,” etc. (Augustine, Question 55 on Judges.) The LXX: “Samson struck the foreigners in the leg above the thigh”—that is, so extraordinarily that, in astonishment, they placed the leg of one foot above the thigh of the other.

**VERSE 12.** — “Swear.” (Augustine, Question 56 on Judges.) What does Samson’s statement to the men of Judah mean, etc., up to “unless the modes of expression are learned by hearing or reading, so too with the forms of speech.”

**VERSE 16.** — “With the jawbone.” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XIII, chapter 6.) The jawbone of the donkey signifies preachers. For our Redeemer, holding the simplicity and patience of preachers in the hand of his power, killed carnal vices; and when the jawbone had been thrown upon the ground, it afterward poured forth water. Thus the bodies of preachers, handed over to death, displayed great miracles to the peoples.

## CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0532B]

**VERSE 1.** — “He also went,” etc. (Gregory, Homily 21 on the Gospels.) Whom Samson signifies in this deed, etc., up to “and by ascending penetrated the kingdoms of heaven.”

**VERSE 19.** — “And she called the barber.” (Isidore, *On Judges*, volume V, chapter 6.) Because the deceitful woman shaved Samson’s head, etc., up to “and, having prepared the battle, he will triumph over the demons most powerfully at the end.”

(Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXVII, chapter 13.) Samson, after losing his eyes, is assigned by the Philistines to the mill, etc., up to “they send him outside to labor in circles.”

**VERSE 30.** — “And much.” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXIX, chapter 7.) In this passage Christ is signified by Samson, etc., up to “by dying he struck them all down together.”

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 5.** — “And he made an ephod and teraphim,” etc. [Col. 0532C] (Jerome, Letter 130, volume I.) In the Book of Judges, etc., up to “is shown to have made them through the teraphim.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 7.** — “They came to Laish,” etc. (Jerome, *On Hebrew Place-Names*.) Laishan, the sons of Dan, etc., up to “near Eshtaol.”

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 25.** — “He brought his concubine out to them,” etc. (Augustine, *On the City of God*, chapter 34.) “Concubine” is sometimes used for “wife.” For Hagar and Keturah are called both wives and concubines of Abraham.

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 18.** — “They consulted.” (Gregory, *Moralia*, Book XXIV, chapter 13.) Whoever does not judge himself, etc., up to “but toward himself he should be strict, while toward all good people he should be submissive.”

## CHAPTER XXI

“And the children of Israel swore at Mizpah,” etc.

[Col. 0531]

# THE BOOK OF RUTH (G)*

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0531D]

**VERSE 1.** — “It came to pass.” Because of the scarcity of spiritual teachers who were given authority to judge, there came to be a famine of the word of God, when even the law had been corrupted by Jewish traditions.

“And a man went away.” (Rabanus.) Namely, Christ, born in Bethlehem of Judah, visited the pilgrimage of this world with his wife—that is, the Church—and with two children, namely the two orders of prophets and apostles, who were freed from the slavery of sin by Christ’s blood.

“A man went away.” (Rabanus.) Some understand this as the Decalogue of the law, his wife as the synagogue, and his two sons as royal and priestly honor. These acquired for themselves a union not only among the Jewish people but also among proselytes, as happened in the time of David, Solomon, and others.

[Col. 0533A]

**VERSE 2.** — Mahlon: “from the window” or “from the beginning.” This is the chorus of the prophets, through whom the first light of faith proceeded into the world from the window; they were also the first preachers of the true light, that is, Christ.

Chilion: “completion.” These are the apostles, who brought the enigmas of the prophets to the completion of full understanding. They are rightly called Ephrathites and are from Bethlehem of Judah: nourished by heavenly bread, they gathered the fruit of preaching through their proclamation of the Gospel. For Ephrathite means “fruitful,” Bethlehem means “house of bread,” and Judah means “confession.” Hence: “Give them something yourselves.” Likewise: “Go and preach the Gospel of the kingdom of God.” And elsewhere: “I chose you from the world so that you might go and bear fruit” (Mark 6; John 16).

[Col. 0533B]

**VERSE 4.** — Ruth is interpreted as “seeing,” “hastening,” or “failing.” In her the obedience and faith of the nations is signified, concerning which it is said: “The people whom I did not know served me,” etc. And elsewhere: “Ethiopia will hasten to stretch out her hands to God” (Psalm 66). Thus the two peoples were called by holy preachers into fellowship of faith and of God’s elect, so that one fold might be made from different flocks.

**VERSE 5.** — “They died.” After the perfection of their righteous labor, namely, they migrated from the exile of this world to the heavenly kingdoms, so that, having fulfilled the commandment of the Decalogue, they might receive the denarius of blessedness.

[Col. 0533C]

**VERSE 7.** — “She went out,” etc., both of them. The Church labors earnestly to lead to the unity of faith and fellowship of the Christian religion the peoples whom the apostles and prophets instructed in their own time. For she learned, according to the testimony of Scripture, that “the righteous man will not be forsaken, nor his offspring seek bread”—the bread that descended from heaven (Psalm 36).

**VERSE 8.** — “Go into your house.” The Church does not act indiscriminately, nor does she receive everyone indiscriminately. Hence: “Do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits to see whether they are from God” (1 John 4). These words can also apply to the synagogue, which draws back those coming to the faith of Christ, especially the statement that, overcome by the truth, it recognizes itself as too weak to bear fruit: “Return, my daughters.”

[Col. 0533D]

**VERSE 11.** — “Do I still have?” (Rabanus.) The voice of the synagogue confessing the truth and not concealing the guilt that has come upon it. Abandoned by the husband—that is, David—and deprived of sons—that is, kings and princes—it confesses after Christ’s coming that it is barren and weak for conceiving children for God.

**VERSE 14.** — “She lifted herself up.” Through these women—one grieving and mourning as she departs from her mother-in-law, the other clinging with a stubborn will—believers are signified. Some, having received the grace of baptism and the fellowship of faith, fall back into their former errors; Orpah signifies them, for she returned to her gods. Others, however, by deliberate decision, attain the grace they have received; Ruth signifies them.

[Col. 0534A]

**VERSE 16.** — “Wherever.” Thus the Church called from the nations, having left her homeland—that is, having abandoned idolatry, carnal conduct, and desires—professes that her God is the one in whom the saints believed; that she will go where Christ’s flesh ascended; that for his name she will suffer in this world even unto death; and that she will remain with the people of the saints, prophets, and patriarchs. Hence: “Rejoice, nations, with his people” (Romans 15).

**VERSE 18.** — “When she saw.” The Gentile people, with a steadfast mind, follows the preachers into the holy land and into the city of God, Bethlehem, where it is prepared to receive the bridegroom born from the stock of Abraham, in whom all the nations, or tribes, of the earth will be blessed.

[Col. 0534B]

**VERSE 20.** — “Do not call me.” The synagogue recognizes its own calamity, which it deservedly suffers after Christ’s coming, and refuses to be called beautiful because it sees the times of its prosperity coming to an end.

“When first.” That is, when the law turns the order of its incarnation toward the mystery of Christ’s Passion. The barley harvest expresses the time of the Lord’s Passion, which occurred in the month of new grain, that is, the first month. Therefore they rightly come to Bethlehem at that time, when the law, which teaches that Christ was born in Bethlehem, proclaims that he was killed at Passover, that is, in the month of new grain. The holy Church also labors with all her strength to imbue those whom she calls to faith with the merit of the incarnation, Passion, and resurrection.

[Col. 0534C]

The barley harvest expresses the faith of the Jews, who, after the mystery of the Passion had been accomplished, first came to the faith through the preaching of the apostles. Elsewhere they are said to have been fed by the Lord with five barley loaves.

## CHAPTER II

**VERSE 3.** — “It happened.” Because the holy Church belongs to Christ, whose bride and body she is. Concerning him it is said: “The Lord is my strength and my praise” (Psalm 117). And elsewhere: “The Lord is strong and mighty; the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23). He is the kinsman of Elimelech, born in Bethlehem and from the stock of David, bearing testimony from the law and the prophets. He brought words of salvation and peace to his household. At his birth the angels sang: “Glory to God in the highest, and on earth…” (Luke 2). When he came to Jerusalem, the crowd went out to meet him, crying: “Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord” (Matthew 21).

[Col. 0534D]

**VERSE 7.** — “And she asked.” Because the holy Church perseveres in the field of divine reading, following the reapers and preachers, gathering the mysteries of Scripture, so that she may recall in the bosom of her mind testimonies and examples of virtues. Or that field is the discipline of heavenly study; the harvest is spiritual understanding; the reapers are preachers; and the remaining ears are the sayings of Scripture, which, hidden to a great extent through mystery, remain, as it were, fuller for the exercise of the one who meditates. Thus the Gentile people eagerly desire ecclesiastical discipline, so that they may be admitted to meditation on the divine law and to fellowship with the saints, and may be refreshed by the teachings and examples of the saints.

[Col. 0535A]

**VERSE 8.** — “Do not go.” As though he said: Do not depart from the state of faith; do not follow the errors of heretics or schismatics. Rather, join yourself to holy souls, so that you may reap the holy Scriptures by meditating on them and fulfilling them in your works; and drink the draught of divine wisdom from the books of the two Testaments, from which the children—that is, the saints—drink.

**VERSE 10.** — “Who, falling upon her face.” The Church of the nations gives thanks to the Savior, who deigned to look upon her. He replied that he was pleased because, after her husband—that is, the devil—had died, she had abandoned her idolatrous parents, as well as the land of her birth—that is, carnal desires—and had joined herself to the people of the saints, who had previously been unknown to her when she followed the desire of the old man.

[Col. 0535B]

**VERSE 13.** — “May I find,” etc. Note the humility of the Gentile Church, which recognizes itself unworthy of so great a grace and does not dare to make itself equal to the primitive Church. Hence she says: “For even the little dogs eat from the crumbs,” etc. And elsewhere: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof, but only say the word and my child will be healed” (Matthew 8).

**VERSE 14.** — “When it was the hour.” The hour for eating was when it was said to the apostles: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 16). For the Lord had said: “Do not go into the way of the nations” (Matthew 10).

[Col. 0535C]

“Dip the morsel.” Read, that is, the reading which, having been meditated upon for a long time, remained among the former people and, corrupted by the conditions or traditions of the Pharisees, lost its native flavor. In this the Church dips the morsel: she says that the mystery of Christ’s incarnation is present in the Old Testament, and therefore believes more firmly because she recognizes that it had long before been prefigured.

**VERSE 16.** — “From your own.” Note the humility of the master of the household, who not only permits the remaining ears of the testimonies to be gathered, but also, through voluntary generosity, distributes sheaves of knowledge.

“Throw down from your bundles,” etc. Because he does not despise the weakness of the Gentile people or reproach them for their former errors, but by the diligence of study leads them to edification.

[Col. 0535D]

**VERSE 17.** — “As an ephah.” When, in reading, she learns the Catholic faith through confession of the Holy Trinity. In the measure of an ephah, which contains three measures, the one substance of divinity and the distinct property of the three persons are signified.

**VERSE 18.** — “Carrying them.” Because she displays her faith to her mother, the Church. Or the Church displays to the synagogue the grace that she received as a gift from her bridegroom, in order to provoke it to faith.

“She gave it to her.” “My heart has poured forth a good word”—namely, food of preaching from the fullness of the heart.

“Blessed.” As the Church from the nations preaches, the synagogue recognizes the Lord’s goodness and power and the strength of its protector. At last, compelled by the truth, it blesses the name of the Lord, who preserved grace for the dead that he had granted to the living.

[Col. 0536A]

**VERSE 20.** — “A kinsman.” The mother Church recognizes the kinsman through the gratuitous benefits bestowed upon the people of the nations, and, hearing his name, remembers ancient benefits. Hence: “I remembered the days of old; I meditated on all your works” (Psalm 142).

**VERSE 21.** — “He commanded me.” Because Christ commands all who come to him to join themselves more closely to his faithful for the harvest of the spiritual grain than to strangers. His mother-in-law agrees with this persuasion, saying: “It is better, my daughter.” The synagogue cannot deny that this is good and useful.

**VERSE 23.** — “Until the wheat.” That is, she clings to the teachers in meditation on the Scriptures until she stores knowledge of the Old and New Testaments in the chamber of her heart, from which she may have sufficient nourishment for the soul.

## CHAPTER III

**VERSE 2.** — “The threshing floor.” The synagogue of the Jews, where the barley of the law has been stored. Christ winnows it when, preaching the Gospel on the threshing floor, he threshes the intentions and wills of individuals toward himself. Hence: “Jesus did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people, and he had no need for anyone to testify about a person” (John 2).

[Col. 0536B]

**VERSE 3.** — “Do not.” For the faith of the Gentile Church did not appear before Christ fulfilled the mystery of his incarnation, when he lived bodily among human beings, using food and drink, and at last, dining with his disciples, shared with them the sacraments of his body and blood. Once the mystery of his dispensation had been completed, Christ’s Church from the nations approached the faith with confidence.

[Col. 0536C]

**VERSE 4.** — “You shall uncover,” etc. What he says means: Recognize that Christ suffered for you, and come with a devoted mind. Examine the covering of the letter of the Old Testament, under which the mystery of Christ’s incarnation is concealed. When you have recognized that salvation was promised there for you, flee humbly to his help, so that you may remain there always.

**VERSE 7.** — “The heap.” The testimonies of Scripture; hence: “The Son of Man goes as it is written of him” (Matthew 26). Or, according to the companies of faithful souls whom he recalled from the underworld by his death. The Church hurried to this bed, and, after uncovering the cloak, etc.

[Col. 0536D]

**VERSE 12.** — “But there is another kinsman closer than I.” John the Baptist, who was thought to be the Christ but did not claim the name of bridegroom, reserving it for Christ, saying: “He who has the bride is the bridegroom,” etc. He is closer because he was born earlier in the world. Or this kinsman is the Decalogue of the law, which seemed closer to the synagogue than the Gospel because it was given especially to that people and is earlier in time.

**VERSE 14.** — “She rose before.” Because, before the Jews instructed in the doctrine of the law came to know the rights of their nature, the Church of the nations, shaking off the sleep of her inertia, rose at dawn with the birth of faith and hurried to the grace of Christ.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0537A]

**VERSE 1.** — “Turn aside.” Because Christ saw that the law had been established for the Jews temporarily, and commanded it to turn aside to him, since he inclined it toward the mystery of his dispensation. Alternatively: he saw the kinsman passing by when he observed the advent of his forerunner hastening in the manner of human life, and mercifully turned him toward the office of forerunner.

“He spoke.” It was fitting that he offered the lawyers the portion of Naomi’s field for purchase, when he showed the teachers of the synagogue the portion of the people that remained after grace had already appeared, so that they might recognize their weakness and entrust to the true physician what they themselves could not do. Hence it is said to the lepers: “Go, show yourselves to the priests” (Luke 17), and as they went they were cleansed.

[Col. 0537B]

**VERSE 5.** — “That you may raise up.” It signifies that the people possess no other inheritance than union with the Church in marriage to Christ, who raised up the ancient name of the Son of God that the saints had at the beginning. Hence: “When the sons of God saw,” etc.; and Luke says: “Adam, the son of God,” whom he also raised up in the Church of the nations through God’s grace. Hence: “He gave them power to become children of God,” etc. The Decalogue of the law could not raise up this name among the nations.

But if you refer this to John the Baptist, you will find him yielding his right of kinship and saying: “I baptize with water; but among you stands one whom you do not know, whose sandal strap I am not worthy to untie.” [Col. 0537C] And elsewhere: “I am not the Christ, but I have been sent before him. He who has the bride is the bridegroom.” The law also yields to the Gospel: “The law entered so that transgression might abound. But where transgression abounded, grace abounded even more.” The rejection of the preceding commandment takes place because of its weakness, while the introduction of a better hope, through which we draw near to God, takes place through Jesus Christ.

**VERSE 8.** — “To loosen.” The sandal is the covering of the mysteries. The law, however, loosens the sandal from its own foot and gives it to Christ, because it could not disclose the mysteries through the teachers of the people, but reserved this for Christ to do. Therefore John did not claim the sandal for himself but for Christ, because he understood that the bride belonged to Christ alone. Hence he said: “I am not worthy to untie his sandal strap.”

[Col. 0537D]

**VERSE 9.** — “Witnesses.” Thus Christ has sufficient witnesses from both Testaments: the Decalogue, already completed, could not spiritually make fruitful the people of the nations, but Christ made all things fruitful with the seed of God’s word, possessing everything that the saints of earlier and later times had.

**VERSE 11.** — “And the elders.” (Isidore.) The blessing of the ten elders shows that all nations would be blessed in the name of Jesus. For iota among the Greeks signifies ten, and it is the first letter in the name Jesus.

“May the Lord make this.” He invokes prosperity upon the Church of the nations, so that it may receive the grace of fruitfulness that the first parents of the Israelites possessed.

“Rachel.” Possessing inner understanding of the truth through the hope of inward contemplation. Hence Rachel is good in face and beautiful in appearance, loved by every devout student, and for her sake he serves Laban, whose name means “whitening,” which he compares to the grace of God, who says: “Though your sins were like scarlet, they shall be made white as snow” (Isaiah 1).

“Leah.” The activity of this life in which we live is laborious through faith, and uncertain as to the outcome by which it may arrive at the benefit of those for whom we wish to care. She is Leah, Jacob’s first wife, who is said to have had weak eyes.

[Col. 0538B]

**VERSE 12.** — “Perez,” etc. He held the grace of the Gentile people and, at birth, preceded the brother who had first put out his hand. For Israel first put out its hand in the work of the law, then withdrew it stained by the blood of the prophets and of Christ. Afterward the people of the nations burst forth, “so that the first would be last and the last first” (Matthew 20). Tamar is also interpreted as “changing” or “bitterness.” For the Church of the nations, formerly foul and bitter in idolatry in both name and conduct, becomes sweet and beautiful in repentance.

**VERSE 13.** — “That she might conceive and give birth.” The Church is always made fruitful by the gift of the Holy Spirit. As some depart for perpetual light, others succeed them, so that the Christian name may remain forever and the most holy mother may have consolation in her old age from a new offspring. As the patriarchs and prophets departed, evangelists and apostles succeeded them. Hence: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.”

[Col. 0538C]

**VERSE 15.** — “For from the daughter-in-law.” The daughter-in-law of the synagogue is the Gentile Church, which married Christ, who was born from the synagogue. She could not produce him through the law, but she secretly carried, hidden beneath a veil and represented through the mystery of prophecy, the one whom she had conceived; and she performed the office of a nurse because she lacked the privilege of a mother.

“Better for you than seven sons,” etc. The multitude of those who in the Old Testament nourished the teaching of the law—those who did not believe the word of the Lord, sacrificed their sons and daughters to demons, and at last killed Christ and persecuted the apostles.

**VERSE 16.** — “And a nurse.” The spiritual lineage of the generation is demonstrated. Obed is interpreted as “serving.” [Col. 0538D] Jesse as “sacrifice in the sun” or “incense”; David as “strong of hand” or “desirable.” For whoever serves God earnestly offers him a pleasing sacrifice and the sweetest incense of fragrance through works of virtue and devotion to prayer. Thus, strengthened by faith and devotion, he is desirable and pleasing to God.

**VERSE 17.** — “The neighboring women.” The heavenly powers, who rejoice in the Church’s fruitfulness and call his name Obed—that is, “serving”—whom they desire to serve with him, the heavenly king.

**VERSE 18.** — “These are.” There are ten generations from the son of Judah to David. From this you recognize that the entire intention of the divine law tends toward Christ, who was born from the seed of David, so that it might proclaim his coming [Col. 0539A] and manifest the perfection of the law in him: “Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10). Before the law, therefore, Jacob spoke of Christ’s incarnation: “The scepter shall not be taken from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent.” To David, because Christ is from the seed of Judah, it was said: “I will set the fruit of your womb upon your throne.” It is therefore evident that the oracle of the prophets and patriarchs also pertains to the dispensation of our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0540A]

# JEROME’S PREFACE TO THE BOOKS OF KINGS

(See among the works of Blessed Jerome, volume VIII, column 547.)

[Col. 0539]

# THE FIRST BOOK OF SAMUEL, WHICH IS THE FIRST OF KINGS (G)*

## CHAPTER ONE
### Verse 1

**Ramathaim Sophim, from the hill, etc.** (Origen, *Homily on Elkanah*.) Or Armathaim, as it is found in other manuscripts, etc., up to “in which the nobility of all virtues is recognized as flourishing.”

**(Same author.)** Here he had two wives, etc., up to “let us also pray for this offspring in imitation of Hannah.”

**(Rabanus, in the Book of Kings.)** First, the generation of historical prophecy must be discussed, etc., up to “while her sister rejoiced in the number of her children.”

**(Jerome, *On the Names of the Hebrews*.)** Elkanah allegorically means “possession of God,” who is the Son of God, saying: “The Lord possessed me.” He is rightly called one man—not in number, but because God never changes and is never made otherwise than God.

Armathaim Sophim means “the heights” or “watchtowers”; this is the heavenly Jerusalem. Coming from there, he taught contemplation and by his death made it possessable.

Jeroham: “merciful.”

Eliu: “my God.”

Thohu: “marked” or “sealed.”

Suph: “pouring out,” because, coming to us through mercy and marked in his Passion, he said: “My God, my God” (Matthew 27). There, emptying himself, he poured himself out; hence: “Your name is an ointment poured out” (Song of Songs 1), poured out from his invisible realities into our visible ones.

Ephrathite: “fruitful,” because he abounds in the gifts of the Holy Spirit. He is called Ephrathite either from Ephrata, Caleb’s wife, or from the city Ephrata, afterward called Bethlehem, or from Ephraim, as some say, because he was from Ramatha, a city of Ephraim situated on Mount Sophim, which is a mountain in the tribe of Ephraim.

**(Gregory, in the Book of Kings.)** Peninnah is the synagogue, which, as the second, formerly bore children to God through the Law, but now remains barren because of unbelief. Hannah is the sterile Church of the Gentiles, formerly barren of spiritual offspring but now redeemed by Christ’s grace. For Hannah, whose name means “grace,” bears children to God through baptism and the Holy Spirit.

**Shiloh.** It is at the ninetieth milestone from Neapolis, in the region of Athabita.

### Verse 3

**The priests of the Lord** (Gregory, same work). How are they “the priests of the Lord,” when below they are called “sons of Belial”? At that time they were called “priests of the Lord” in order to distinguish them by this title from the priests of idols, who were designated by the names of false gods. These words praise their faith, not their life: they practiced wickedness, but they did not err concerning faith in the Creator.

Ophni: “barefoot,” or “the madness of conversion.”

Phinehas. (Origen, *Homily on Elkanah*.) “Mute mouth”; he signifies the scribes and Pharisees, etc., up to “therefore they were rightly dismissed and abandoned by God.”

### Verse 4

**Then the day came, and Elkanah sacrificed and gave portions to Peninnah, etc.** (Jerome, *On Hebrew Traditions*.) These portions are understood as garments, which, according to the custom of that people, were given at the three festivals—Passover, Pentecost, and Tabernacles—to wives, children, and servants.

But he gave Hannah one portion, sorrowfully, because she had no children to whom he might give more. He gave portions to Peninnah, that is, to the synagogue, and to her children—that is, temporal goods—according to: “He gave them the lands of the nations” (Psalm 104). And because the oracles of God had first been entrusted to them, he gave Hannah, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, one portion, namely, understanding. He says well:

**Sorrowful,** because the Lord had closed her womb; for the time had not yet come to show her mercy, so that she might become fruitful through spiritual grace. Just as Peninnah despised Hannah, so the synagogue despised the Gentiles. Many among the Gentiles awaited the coming of the Redeemer, as we find in Job; and because they persevered in prayer, at last the Redeemer brought consolation to the weeping Hannah, who could not receive food, saying:

### Verse 8

**Hannah, why are you weeping?** The husband of the Church, that is, Christ, is better than the ten sons whom she had from the synagogue. Sometimes she loves Christ—that is, his grace—more than those whom she bore carnally.

### Verse 14

**And he said to her.** The Septuagint reads: καὶ εἶπεν αὐτῇ παιδάριον Ἡλί — “And the boy Eli said to her.”

**How long will you be drunk?** A human being looks at the face, but God looks at the heart. Eli judged her drunk because he looked only at her mouth; the Lord, however, regarded her prayer, because he saw her heart. Here an example of prayer is handed down to us: we should pray not with many words, but with contrition of heart and an outpouring of tears, because “the sacrifice acceptable to God is a troubled spirit, a contrite heart,” etc.

### Verse 17

**Eli said, “Go in peace,” etc. And the woman went away, etc.** Do you see the woman’s faith? Before she received what she had asked for, she trusted as though she had already received it. The reason was that she had prayed with great fervor and without any hesitation. She went away with a tranquil spirit, as though she had obtained everything. Moreover, God had already driven all anxiety from her mind, intending to grant what she asked. Let us imitate this woman and flee to God in all our afflictions. If children have not been given to us, let us ask him for them; and if we receive them, let us raise them with great care, etc.

### Verse 18

**Her face was no longer changed in various ways.** (Rabanus, in the Book of Kings.) Another translation reads: “Her face no longer fell,” because she was absolutely certain that she had been heard.

**(Same author.)** For the Church did not change by turning aside from faith in and love of the Redeemer.

### Verse 19

**And the Lord remembered her.** (Same author.) Because Hannah devoutly asked the Lord, she conceived and bore a child. Thus the Church, praying through natural understanding, conceived the mystery of the Incarnation in her heart and gave birth to it through confession with her mouth.

### Verse 20

**And she called his name Samuel.** That is, “God.” Hannah’s firstborn was a prophet. Who is this except the Lord’s human nature?

**(Rabanus.)** Samuel means “petition of God” or “his name”; God was the agent of his birth, because he granted to the barren woman, while she prayed, a son who would serve him in the temple all his days.

**(Same author.)** The Church from the nations, etc., up to “when, with perfect faith, she joined herself to the primitive Church from the Jews.”

### Verse 23

**And I pray that the Lord may fulfill it.** Either what you vowed, or what he promised through Eli when he said: “May God grant you your petition,” etc.

The woman therefore remained and nursed her son until she weaned him. And she brought him. Hannah does not wish to bring the child to the house of God before he is weaned, because the Church advances no one to the priesthood while he remains a participant in infant milk and is not capable of solid food and spiritual understanding.

**(Jerome, *On Hebrew Traditions in the Book of Kings*.)** In Hebrew it reads: “A measure of flour,” but this has been corrupted through scribal error. For if he offered three measures of flour with three calves, he acted contrary to the Law, in which it is said: “One bull from the herd, one ram, seven unblemished male lambs”; and for their sacrifices, three-tenths of fine flour mixed with oil for each bull, two-tenths for each ram, and one-tenth for each lamb. This tenth was a tenth part of an ephah. Therefore it is understood that Elkanah did not offer three measures of flour with three calves, but nine-tenths.

### Verse 19

**And they worshiped.** (Origen, in the work cited above.) Prayer is not found in this song, etc., up to “but if he lets him go, he conquers Amalek, the enemy of God.”

## Chapter 2

### Verse 1

**My mouth has been enlarged.** (Rabanus.) Because the word of God is not bound by afflictions, nor is it bound in heralds.

**(Same author.)** This refers to Christ, whom the aged Simeon embraced and recognized as great, saying: “Now you dismiss your servant, Lord, according to your word, in peace. For my eyes have seen your salvation” (Luke 2). “If I rejoice in God’s salvation, then my mouth will be enlarged.” Through meditation on the word of God one comes to elevation of heart; hence: “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians; our heart is enlarged” (2 Corinthians 5). From the breadth of the heart wisdom is supplied to the mouth.

### Verse 2

**There is none holy.** (Rabanus.) “Besides you, Lord,” because no one becomes anything except through you. Even if there are those who are called “many gods” and “many lords,” none of them is naturally what God is, because he alone is the one who says: “I am who I am” (Exodus 3). A shadow does not exist in comparison with a body, nor smoke in comparison with fire.

**As the Lord is.** (Same author.) He does not say merely, “There is no one except the Lord,” but: “There is none like the Lord”—holy and sanctifying, just and justifying.

### Verse 3

**Do not multiply words.** He rebukes the Jews and the wise of this world, who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God. Solomon says: “Do not seek what is too high for you”; and elsewhere: “God is in heaven, and you are on earth; therefore let your words be few.”

**The old things, etc.** Seek knowledge concerning what belongs to the old man—that is, carnal conduct—which comes only from God, because he is the Lord of knowledge, in whom are all the treasures of wisdom.

**For thoughts are prepared for him.** Either because he withdraws from thoughts that lack understanding, or because thoughts are prepared for him—that is, revealed. Hence: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings.”

**God of knowledge.** (Rabanus, in the work cited above.) He knows you, etc., up to “and they do not come from the one from whom human beings come.”

### Verse 4

**(Rabanus.)** That is, the intention of those who seem powerful to themselves, as though they could fulfill the divine commandments without God’s help.

**And the weak.** (Rabanus.) Those who trust in God’s compassion say: “Have mercy on me, God, for I am weak” (Psalm 6). The Gentile people were weak when they were alienated from God’s covenant; but now, girded with strength, clothed with the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation and carrying the sword of the Spirit, they can extinguish the devil’s fiery darts.

### Verse 5

**Those who were formerly full hired themselves out for bread.** The Jews, formerly filled with the mysteries of the divine utterances, hired themselves out for bread—that is, separated themselves from God—or tore themselves away from their own places so as not to receive the Gospel, which speaks of the bread that came down from heaven. Those who were filled, and were also powerful—that is, the Israelites, to whom the divine utterances were entrusted—became diminished: they withdrew and did not believe in the Savior, and in those very loaves—that is, the divine utterances—they perceived only earthly things. But the Gentiles, to whom the Law had not been given, after they came through the New Testament to those utterances, passed through the land in great hunger, because they tasted in them not earthly but heavenly things. In Greek it reads: “Those who were full of bread became deficient, and those who were hungry passed over the land.”

**And the hungry.** That is, the Gentiles, formerly needy, now taste the bread of God’s word, because it is sweet. They have long been nourished by the knowledge of God.

**The barren woman has borne seven.** The universality of the Church is signified by the number seven. John likewise writes to seven churches, showing that he is writing to the fullness of one Church; hence: “Wisdom built herself a house and set up seven columns” (Proverbs 9). The Church among the Gentiles was barren before this offspring whom we see arose. We also see the earthly Jerusalem, once fruitful, now weakened, because whoever in it was a free child of its strength—now, because there is the letter but not the spirit, it has lost its strength and become weak.

**(Rabanus.)** In Hebrew and in the Septuagint, “seven” is found in many copies. The Jews say that when Samuel was born, Peninnah’s firstborn son died, and that as each of Hannah’s sons was born, one of Peninnah’s sons died. But Peninnah had seven, while Hannah had five. The Hebrews, however, count two sons of Samuel among Hannah’s children.

**(Same author.)** The barren woman, etc., up to “by her poverty we have been enriched.”

### Verse 7

**He makes poor, etc.** Jesus, who became poor for our sake, and enriches the same person with the glory of the resurrection.

### Verse 8

**From the dust.** From corruption he raises Christ; hence: “You will not allow your holy one to see corruption” (Psalm 15).

**From the dungheap.** (Rabanus, in the work cited above.) The Jewish people: after the Apostle had said that he persecuted the Church, he declares, “Whatever gains I had, I counted as dung [loss] because of Christ” (Philippians 3).

**To set them with princes.** (Same author.) To whom it is said: “You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 25).

**The throne of glory.** By sitting in the equity of the Father; and because the Father has given all judgment to the Son; and because his kingdom will have no end (John 5).

**The foundations of the earth.** Namely, the four regions of the world, in which he enlarged the Church’s sphere, and from sunrise to sunset they praise the name of the Lord (Psalm 112).

Mystically, these are the preachers, upon whom the world—that is, the Church—is established through their faith. Of them it is said: “Under him are bent those who bear up the world” (Job 9).

### Verse 10

**They will fear the Lord.** Because he will weaken his adversary. The ambiguous Greek may also be understood as “his own adversary.” For when the Lord begins to possess us, our adversary becomes his; and he is conquered by us, not by our own strength, since a man is not powerful through his own power.

**They will fear the Lord.** The adversaries are the Jews, over whom the Lord thundered in the heavens—that is, in the apostles—when he terrified them by threatening Gehenna and confirming the threats with signs; hence many were converted. Or they will fear him in judgment, whom they despised while opposing him here, and over whom he will thunder, saying: “Go into the eternal fire” (Matthew 25). So that this may not happen to everyone, the Lord thunders daily from the heavens—that is, from the Scriptures and teachers.

**In the heavens.** (Rabanus.) Just retribution will come on the day of judgment; meanwhile he thunders from his clouds, which he filled with the Holy Spirit after he ascended into heaven.

**The ends.** The extremes of a person, because those things are not judged which change for better or worse during the intervening time, but the final condition in which the person is found.

**And he will give.** That is, to Christ.

**Power.** That is, the Church; hence: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” Or “power” means the authority to judge, because the Father has given all judgment to the Son.

**To the king.** (Rabanus.) To the Christian people, to whom he gives the power to rule the flesh, so that he may conquer the world in him who shed his blood for him.

**His anointed one.** (Rabanus, in the Book of Kings.) The Christian people, anointed with chrism; nevertheless the whole body together with its head is one Christ. Hannah, Samuel’s mother, prophesied this: in Samuel the change from the old priesthood was then represented, and it is now fulfilled, when the fruitful woman has become weak so that the barren woman might have a new priesthood in Christ.

### Verse 12

**Eli.** (Same author.) The name is interpreted as “outsider,” for one who does not correct his subjects is alienated from God. Ophni means “disgrace of conversion”; he is rightly so called who delays being converted to better things. Phinehas means “hardness of mouth,” or “sparing the mouth.” We read of two priests named Phinehas: one just, the son of Eleazar; the other wicked, the son of Eli. Priests who guard their mouths so that no evil may come forth from them are represented by Eleazar’s son. Those whose mouths are stopped, either through ignorance or through consciousness of sins, are represented by Eli’s son.

**(Rabanus.)** Josephus reports, etc., up to “and the fault of their subjects will be imputed to them.”

### Verse 19

**A tunic.** The tunic that Hannah—that is, grace—made and gave to the boy signifies introductory teaching, by which the faithful receive their first instruction; hence: “I gave you milk to drink, not solid food” (1 Corinthians 3). The linen ephod, however, signifies chastity and continence together with good works. Whoever desires to serve the Lord must live chastely and continently and exercise himself in good works.

### Verse 25

**If a person sins.** (Jerome, in the work cited above.) One does not sin against a human being in the same way as one sins against God, because to sin against a human being—that is, against one’s neighbor—is lighter and more pardonable. To sin against God—that is, to withdraw from his worship—is the sin of impiety; it is punished more severely and forgiven more slowly. When someone sins against a human being, by appeasing that person he makes God favorable toward him. But when someone sins against God, who will pray for him? That is, through whom will he make God propitious to himself? This does not mean that forgiveness should never be hoped for by those who sin in divine service; rather, the punishment is greater and forgiveness slower for those who offend in matters consecrated to God than for those who injure their neighbor by word or deed, because the greater the glory, the graver the offense.

### Verse 27

**Your father, etc.** Aaron, certainly. For who else was in Egyptian slavery and, after liberation, was chosen as priest? Anyone descended from his line, when he sees the priesthood of Christians flourishing throughout the world while it has been taken away from him, wastes away with pain and grief.

### Verse 32

**A rival.** (Rabanus.) The rival of Eli’s house was Zadok the priest, who assumed the priesthood after Solomon rejected Abiathar. Hence: “Solomon expelled Abiathar, so that he would not be a priest of the Lord, fulfilling the word of the Lord that he had spoken against the house of Eli” (1 Kings 2).

### Verse 33

**So that they may fail.** (Rabanus.) So that someone from the house of Eli may always remain in the house of the Lord who, seeing another substituted in the dignity of the priesthood and himself deprived of it, may lose heart and waste away. This change of priesthood was fully completed in Christ, having been foreshadowed by Samuel. After Samuel, priests from the line of Aaron continued—Zadok, Abiathar, and others—until the time of Christ.

### Verse 35

**And my soul.** (Same author.) God does not possess a soul, but figuratively is said to have one, etc., up to “hence: ‘And the house of Israel rested after the Lord’” (1 Samuel 7).

### Verse 36

**It shall come to pass.** (Same author.) This is not said specifically of the house of Eli, but of the house of Aaron, from whose line people still come and are converted to this day.

**A morsel.** (Rabanus.) “The bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John 6). Since he had said that he had given the house of Aaron food from the sacrifices of the Old Testament, which were Jewish sacrifices, he says that a morsel of bread is to be requested for eating. This is the sacrifice of Christians and nourishment for souls.

## Chapter 3

**(Rabanus, in the Book of Kings.)** “In those days there was no manifest vision.” Because of the sins of the people and their leaders, the Lord did not appear through visions or angelic responses as he had appeared to the fathers.

### Verse 3

**The lamp.** (Same author.) It burned in the tabernacle before daylight. At daybreak it was extinguished; it burned until morning. Alternatively, this signifies that Eli remained in blindness until he was utterly extinguished with his offspring—that is, until he died.

Mystically, Eli’s blindness signifies the blindness of the Jews, who did not recognize the present Savior, nor the radiance of his miracles nor his teaching, until the priesthood, people, and temple were overthrown.

### Verse 11

**Will tingle.** (Rabanus.) God’s threat is against Eli and his house: because of the sin of Eli’s sons, the priesthood of the Lord’s house was being taken away from them. Thus the ears of those who hear will tingle with overwhelming astonishment.

### Verse 17

**These things.** This was a proverb among the Hebrews. Its meaning is: “If you hide from me the evil that the Lord has spoken to you concerning me, may it come upon your head.”

### Verse 18

**And he did not.** (Rabanus, in the Book of Kings.) Because he concealed nothing of what the Lord had spoken, etc., up to “he did this for a definite and useful reason.”

### Verse 20

**From Dan.** (Same author.) By the boundaries of Judea he comprehends the whole people. Dan is a village four miles from Paneas, still called by that name today. It is the northern boundary of the province of Judea; from it the Jordan bursts forth and takes its name from the place. For the Hebrews call a river or stream *Jor*. Dan is interpreted as “judgment” or “judging.”

**Beersheba.** It is a large village in the tribe of Judah or Simeon, twenty miles from Hebron, extending toward the south. A Roman garrison is stationed there. From it the boundaries of Judea extend northward to Dan. No one should be surprised to find cities of Judah in the tribe of Simeon or Benjamin. For the tribe of Judah, strong and warlike and often overcoming its adversaries, held primacy among all the tribes; therefore the allotments of the other tribes are counted within its cord. Otherwise Scripture makes clear that Simeon dwelt in the midst of the tribe of Judah.

## Chapter 4

### Verse 1

**And it came to pass.** Israel means “one who sees God” or “strong with God”; these are the believers. The Philistines mean “those falling by the cup,” namely demons, who, intoxicated by the cup of pride, themselves fell and hasten to corrupt human beings. Against them Israel—that is, the faithful—encamps so that they may not yield but overcome, beside the Stone of Help, that is, the law of Christ, where the stone—that is, Christ—is found. Concerning him it is said: “The stone that the builders rejected.”

But while the faithful meditate on the Lord’s law in order to find God as their helper, the Philistines came to Aphek, that is, “new fury.” When the faithful are seen to devote themselves more earnestly to the divine laws against unclean spirits, the latter construct fiercer and newer conflicts. Thus, trusting in their own strength and glorying in human wisdom, and consequently despising the grace of the Gospel, the unclean spirits easily overthrow, as it were, four thousand people.

**Beside the stone.** The Stone of Help that Samuel later set up as a sign when the Lord first helped him.

**Aphek.** (Rabanus.) It is a place near the village of Esron in the territory of Israel, where Saul fought in the allotment of Asher. It is interpreted as “new fury” or “one who apprehends”; those who deserved the Lord’s anger were seized by their enemies.

### Verse 4

**And they took it.** The sons of Israel took the ark where it had been captured. The faithful from the Jews transferred the two Testaments to the Gentiles.

**Who sits upon.** There was a slab over the ark, protected by the wings of the cherubim; there the Lord appeared through an angel and spoke. The cherubim signify the fullness of knowledge found in Christ and in the two Testaments.

### Verse 5

**With a shout.** The great shout is the voice of the preachers, strengthened by miracles and issuing from the two Testaments.

**And it resounded.** At the voice of preaching, the wise of this world and the demons also groaned, believing that they were being overcome.

### Verse 8

**From the hand.** The Jews worship one God, but the Gentiles speak according to their own custom.

### Verse 11

**And the ark.** The ark being captured by foreigners signifies the Testament’s transfer to the Gentiles.

### Verse 13

**And when.** (Rabanus.) Josephus reports these events in this way, etc., up to “and they received them again from the house of Eleazar.”

### Verse 18

**He fell.** When Eli fell from the priestly chair, the seat remained empty and the glory of the priests was extinguished.

**He died.** Eli dies, and his sons die as well, because the high priesthood together with the old priesthood comes to an end.

### Verse 19

**The wife.** The priest’s wife did not die before she had given birth to a son; nor did the synagogue perish completely before the primitive Church, which came from it, believed.

### Verse 20

**At that very moment.** This is represented by a clear sign: when the carnal priesthood of the Jews was extinguished, the carnal synagogue that clung to it carnally was extinguished as well.

**Do not fear.** Believers console the synagogue, but she, despairing, pays no attention and does not regard the new offspring as glory but as disgrace. Hence what follows:

### Verse 21

**And she called.** *Cabod* means “glory”; *Icabhod*, “the glory has departed.” Glory was transferred when the ark was captured; hence: “The kingdom of God will be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits.”

## Chapter 5

### Verse 1

**(Rabanus, in the work cited above.)** It is also called Asdod, one of the five cities of the Philistines. It had indeed been assigned to the tribe of Judah, but was not retained, because the tribe could not expel the native inhabitants. Its name is interpreted as “fire of the father” or “conflagration.” The place where the idol Dagon stood is rightly so called, because the ark’s arrival at Azotus was a conflagration for the devil, the father of all enemies and wicked people. Dagon, interpreted as “fish of sorrow,” signifies the devil, who devours sinners in the sea of this world and is also called Leviathan and Behemoth in Job (Job 40).

**Azotus.** It is the place where Samuel set up the stone (1 Samuel 7), as is shown below.

### Verse 4

**The head.** The pride of the devil, who is the beginning of every sin (Ecclesiasticus 10).

**Above.** (Rabanus.) This signifies the appointed limit at which idolatry would cease. For a threshold is the end of a journey.

### Verse 5

**The trunk.** They found only the back, after all the limbs had been broken off; this expresses the flight of idolatry. For one who flees gives his back to the pursuer; hence: “You will make them turn their backs” (Psalm 20).

### Verse 7

**And by.** Those who receive God’s Testament and love the hind parts of this life will justly be tormented in those very hind parts, which they ought to regard as dung. For those who receive God’s Testament but, looking backward, do not strip themselves of their former vanity are like those who placed the ark of the covenant beside their idols. The old things fall away from them even against their will, because “all flesh is grass.” But the ark remains forever: it is the secure Testament of the kingdom of heaven, where the word of God remains forever.

### Verse 8

**Let it be carried around.** So that wherever it goes, the blow may accompany it. We should know that what happened was a plague from God, carried out by his will and purpose, so that the plague might be common because the guilt was common.

## Chapter 6

### Verse 5

**Five golden anuses, etc.** (Rabanus.) Five golden anuses, etc., up to “there is true sorrow and perpetual barrenness.”

### Verse 7

**A cart.** The cross of Christ; the ark is Sacred Scripture.

**Two cows.** (Isidore.) The cows carrying the ark signify the saints who renounce the world and have not taken upon themselves the yoke of any sin. Just as cows, because of their affection for their calves, do not turn aside from the straight road, so holy fathers, through such affection, do not deviate from their good purpose.

### Verse 12

**Which leads, etc.** (Rabanus.) They go by the royal road to Beth-shemesh, that is, “the house of the sun,” namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, where the sun of righteousness always shines.

**Beth-shemesh.** (Same author.) It is a priestly city in the tribe of Benjamin, still visible today to those traveling from Eleutheropolis to Nicopolis, ten miles eastward. Another Beth-shemesh is in the tribe of Naphtali, where the ancient worshipers remained.

### Verse 13

**And they did not.** (Same author.) That is, they were not lifted up by prosperity, etc., up to “let her be softened in weeping.”

**Beth-shemesh.** “House of the sun.” This is the Church illuminated by the sun of righteousness. The men of Beth-shemesh reaping grain in the valley signifies the teachers of the Church handling the harvest of God’s word in humility. The stone in Joshua’s field is Christ in his Church. The wood of the cart is Christ’s cross. Sacrificing the cows upon the stone signifies putting to death, in imitation of Christ, those who have been converted from the world.

### Verse 17

**One for Azotus.** (Jerome, in the work cited above.) The five cities gave five golden tumors and five golden mice. The remaining cities of the provinces and the unwalled villages gave only mice; hence: “From the walled city to the village that had no wall,” etc.

### Verse 18

**Abel.** It is a city on the boundary of Israel, formerly called Beth-shemesh and now called Abel, either because of the mourning that occurred there over the men of Beth-shemesh, or to distinguish it from Beth-maacah, concerning which the wise woman cried out to Joab: “Let them ask in Abel” (2 Samuel 20).

### Verse 19

**He struck, etc.** Since they were not Levites, they dared to look at the ark. To prevent this, in Exodus the people stood far away, while Moses alone went up to the Lord.

**He struck, etc.** (Jerome.) In Hebrew it reads: “And he struck seventy men of the people and fifty thousand men”; “seventy men” means judges.

**(The Septuagint.)** The Hebrews say that no one was permitted to look upon the uncovered ark except the high priest. They were therefore struck because they were unworthy, or because they approached unworthily, or because they had not guarded the ark.

### Verse 21

**And they sent.** (Rabanus.) This signifies the transfer of the Lord’s Testament from the Jews to the Gentiles. Since the Jews had defiled the Law through carnal observance and Pharisaic superstitions and rejected the teaching of Christ and his disciples, it was said: “It was necessary that the word of God be spoken to you first; but since you judged yourselves unworthy, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

**Kiriath-jearim.** (Same author.) It is interpreted as “village of forests,” concerning which it is said: “Until I find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob. Behold, we heard of it in Ephratha; we found it in the fields of the forest” (Psalm 131). The Lord’s place is the tabernacle of the Christian people’s heart. The city of forests—that is, the gathering of the Gentiles—is a suitable place to receive the ark. It was in the house of Amminadab, whose name is interpreted as “my spontaneous father”; one may also say: “spontaneously, to you.”

**(Same author.)** Kiriath-jearim is a city of wooded country, one of the cities of the Gibeonites belonging to the tribe of Judah, nine miles from Elia on the road to Diospolis. The prophet Uriah, whom Jehoiakim killed in Jerusalem, came from this place, as Jeremiah writes.

## Chapter 7

### Verse 1

**Gibeah.** (Rabanus.) It is the hill of the souls of the humble; hence: “Let the mountains receive peace for the people,” etc.—that is, let the greater mountains be the hills of the lesser souls. Alternatively, Gibeah is interpreted as “sublimity,” where Eleazar was appointed priest.

**Eleazar.** (Same author.) “The help of God.” It is fitting that the one bearing this name was chosen to guard the Lord’s ark, because holy men attribute whatever good they have to God, not to themselves. Hence: “Our sufficiency is from God, who made us competent ministers of the New Testament” (2 Corinthians 3).

### Verse 2

It was the twentieth year when, in the seventh year of Saul’s reign, the ark was brought from Kiriath-jearim to the camp.

**The twentieth year.** (Rabanus.) This should not be understood in that way, etc., up to “because light has no fellowship with darkness.”

### Verse 6

**Mizpah.** It is a city in the tribe of Judah near Kiriath-jearim.

**(Rabanus.) Mizpah.** “Contemplation” or “watchtower,” etc., up to “and he will see them intent upon the love of the heavenly homeland.”

**And they drew water, etc.** So that, just as poured-out water does not return, they too would not return to idolatry.

### Verse 9

**A suckling lamb.** The lamb offered for God’s people grants victory; and when the demons were overcome through Christ’s Passion, peace was given to the faithful.

**(Rabanus.)** An innocent life kindled by the fire of charity.

**(Rabanus.)** When the Lord thunders through the preachers of the Gospel, spiritual enemies are put to flight before Israel—that is, before the people of God—and Israel pursues them as far as the house of knowledge, until every error is cleansed and God is truly known.

### Verse 11

**Beth-car.** (Same author.) “House of knowledge,” or “house of the lamb.”

### Verse 12

**And he set it up.** Another edition reads: “between the new Mizpah and the old,” and he called its name Eben-ezer, or Abenezer—that is, “stone of help.” This is the Savior’s midpoint, by which one must pass from the old Mizpah to the new: from the expectation that false blessedness will be found in a carnal kingdom to the expectation that true blessedness will be found, through the New Testament, in the kingdom of heaven. Since nothing is better than this, God helps us thus far.

Mizpah means “the intention of those who sit.” The stone placed between them is Christ, placed between the intention of the Old Testament and the preaching of the Gospel. He is called the stone because of the firmness of his help, since he assists his own as they fight against demons.

**Thus far the Lord has helped us.** Because those who cross beyond these boundaries, such as heretics, do not deserve God’s help.

### Verse 14

**And it was.** Christ is our peace, who made both one; through him those who were far off have been brought near.

### Verse 16

**Gilgal.** It is the city where Joshua circumcised the people a second time and celebrated Passover. When the manna ceased, Israel ate wheat bread there. The stones were also carried there from the bed of the Jordan, and the tabernacle of the testimony remained there for a long time. It fell within the allotment of Judah, and the place, revered by the people of that region, is still shown today, two miles from Jericho. Some, however, suspect another Gilgal near Bethel.

Gilgal is interpreted as “rolling” or “revelation.” Therefore the prophet rightly judged Israel at Bethel, Gilgal, and Mizpah; returning to Ramah, to his house, he judged Israel there and built an altar to the Lord. He thus provided an example that judgment must be carried out in the house of God—not indiscriminately or with a malicious mind, but according to what Scripture reveals, with good intention and fraternal love. In this way one must return to Ramah, to our house—that is, to the inner chambers of the heart—so that we may devote ourselves to contemplation and offer acceptable sacrifices of work and truth upon the altar of faith.

### Verse 17

**He also built there, etc.** The Law commanded that an altar be built only where the Lord had chosen; but he constructed this altar so that they would not sacrifice to gods, and he is not reproved for it.

## Chapter 8

### Verse 1

**And it came to pass, etc.; he appointed his sons.** (Rabanus, in the Book of Kings, volume 2.) According to Josephus, he appointed one in Bethlehem and the other in Beersheba.

### Verse 2

**Abijah.** (Same author.) “The father is lord,” or “the father was.” They are rightly so called because they did not remain in the righteousness they had begun and neglected the Lord’s fatherhood. They were named “God was” or “the father was” to signify that they were unworthy of God’s fatherhood.

### Verse 3

**And they did not walk.** Because they oppressed justice for the sake of gifts, turning aside to expensive food and luxurious banquets.

## Chapter 9

### Verse 2

**Named Saul.** (Rabanus, in the Book of Kings, volume 2.) Saul, who, after God was offended, was made king over Israel, etc., up to “and from being agreeable he became troubled.”

**(Same author.)** Because Saul, seeking his father’s donkeys, came to the prophet by whom he was anointed, this signifies that the Jews, pursuing the foolishness of carnal understanding, seek the world’s luxury through wandering errors. For the donkey is a brutish and lustful animal. Coming to the prophet—that is, Moses—they hear that the donkeys have been found, meaning that the good things of the land are owed to them. From him also the oil of anointing and the governance of the kingdom are promised, through which, for a time, they would rescue their brothers from the hand of their enemies.

**(Same author.)** According to the righteousness of the present life.

**(Same author.)** This applies more fully to Christ, of whom it is said: “Behold my chosen servant, whom I have chosen” (Isaiah 44). And elsewhere: “Who is like God among the sons of God?” (Psalm 86).

**A stater.** A stater is a shekel containing twenty obols, that is, ten denarii.

### Verse 7

**Let us give something to the man.** Although they decided to give something, we do not read that Samuel accepted it. Even if he had accepted it, it would not have been regarded as a reward for divination, but as the prophet’s support.

## Chapter IX

### Verse 9

**“Formerly in Israel.”** As Bede says, these are not the words of the historiographer but of Ezra.

**“Seer.”** He is called a prophet because, through the Spirit, he foreknows future events.

### Verse 11

**“The slope,” etc., “going out to draw water.”** A slope is a winding ascent of a mountain.

### Verse 16

**“And you shall anoint him as leader.”** Saul, anointed, signifies Christ, who himself was also called “Christ”; hence: “Why were you not afraid to lay your hand upon the Lord’s Christ?” (2 Samuel 1).

### Verse 19

**“All that.”** (Rabanus.) The Hebrews relate that Saul had in his heart the expectation that he would become king, since he had seen in a vision that he was placed at the top of a palm tree, which is a sign of one destined to reign.

### Verse 22

**“Taking him thus.”** The fact that Samuel led Saul up to the high place and provided him with refreshment signifies that the prophets, by their teaching, summoned the Hebrew people to higher things, so that, refreshed by spiritual knowledge, it might stand at the summit of the virtues and not fall back into vices.

**“Dining room.”** An upper room, so called from the three couches on which those reclining at table sat.

### Verse 24

**“Intentionally,”** that is, by Providence. It is understood that he had already eaten, though not fully, because, when the Lord revealed that Saul was coming, the banquet had been postponed.

### Verse 27

**“And when they were going down.”** They descended from the high place so that he might speak with him in a more private location about the kingdom and anoint him.

## Chapter X

### Verse 1

**“Then he took.”** A *lenticula* is a square earthen vessel with an opening in its side, through which the fragility of the kingdom is signified.

[Col. 0552A]

### Verse 6

**“And you shall prophesy with them.”** The Jews say that he prophesied about the future age, Gog and Magog, the rewards of the righteous, and the punishments of the wicked.

### Verse 7

**“Therefore, when.”** As though he were saying: By these signs you will be able to know that God has willed you to become king. Therefore act royally in everything, because the Lord is with you.

### Verse 8

**“For seven days,”** with “in the consecration of your kingdom” understood, just as during the consecration of priests victims were offered for seven days.

### Verse 10

**“And they came.”** This signifies that everything Moses and the prophets had foretold happened to the Jews. Yet they themselves, holding the books of the Law and the prophets, seem to practice divination when they are known to proclaim the future mysteries concerning Christ and the Church written in them.

[Col. 0552B]

### Verse 12

**“And who?”** As though he were saying: Who is greater than he in dignity and wisdom? Therefore he can move among the prophets as their father and teacher. And who is their father—that is, the father of the prophets—unless it is God?

Mystically, the elders of Israel, having rejected Samuel, asked for a king for themselves; and the scribes with the Pharisees, having rejected Christ the true priest, cried out: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19). Hence Samuel is interpreted as “his name is God”; Saul, “asked for” or “request,” because he was demanded by the people, is understood as Barabbas. Kish means “hard” or “vomiting”; Abiel, “my father is God.” For the Jews, being hard and vomiting, confess God the Father while denying the Son; but whoever denies the Son also denies the Father who sent him (1 John 2).

Saul, seeking his father’s she-asses, was taken up into the kingdom. The Savior, sent by the Father to the sheep that had perished, the house of Israel, was appointed king over the whole people. There are as many she-asses as sheep. Saul received a shoulder, and Christ received principality (Matthew 15). Saul was anointed by Samuel, and the Only-Begotten was drenched with spiritual anointing by the Father. Saul surpassed the others in height, because Christ, our head, is above us (1 Corinthians 11).

## Chapter XI

### Verse 1

**(Rabanus.)** Jabesh means “sense”; Gilead, “heap of testimony.” Nahash, that is, “serpent”—namely, the devil—rises against the sense instructed by the testimony of Scripture.

### Verse 2

**“And he answered.”** The war of Nahash signifies the war of heretics against the Church. Nahash is interpreted as “serpent”; Ammon as “pressing” or “constricting,” or “people of sorrow.” Jabesh means “dried up”; Gilead, “heap of testimony.” Nahash therefore signifies the ancient serpent, who is the prince of the Ammonites, that is, of heretics.

For this is the people of sorrow, which does not possess the joy of the Holy Spirit. It makes a covenant with the people of the Church in order to remove their right eyes—that is, the sight of sound orthodox faith. It leaves the left eye so that they may perceive only what is perverse. But the mind of the faithful, dried up from the filth of vices, gathers together a heap of testimony—that is, the knowledge of Holy Scripture—with which it may resist the enemy courageously.

### Verse 8

**“In Bezek.”** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. II.) In the city—namely, Adoni-bezek—[lacuna] up to the point where the Church spreads throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0553A]

### Verse 11

**“They were scattered.”** Because the assembly of the wicked is not joined by the unity of charity and faith but is separated from itself by disagreement; hence: “Your enemies, O Lord, shall perish and be scattered” (Psalm 91).

## Chapter XII

### Verse 17

**“Wheat harvest.”** (Rabanus.) That is, the gathering of the Gentile people into the faith.

**“Voices.”** That is, thunder and rain. It is not customary for it to rain in Judea during the summer.

## Chapter XIII

### Verse 1

**“A son of one year,” etc.** (Rabanus.) He speaks by anticipation of Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, [lacuna] up to the point that he had not judged the people for the whole period of his life, as others had.

[Col. 0553B]

### Verse 2

**“Gibeah.”** (Rabanus.) It is the city of Phinehas, son of Eleazar, [lacuna] up to the men who remained with Saul, Catholics firmly adhering to Christ.

### Verse 6

**“They hid themselves in caves.”** (Rabanus.) Having hidden themselves, that is, [lacuna] up to the point where they joined their companions in battle.

### Verse 13

**“You have acted foolishly, and have not.”** (Rabanus.) Some think that Saul sacrificed without guilt, [lacuna] up to the point where he is therefore rightly blamed and accused of folly.

**“If you had not done this.”** (Eucherius, *On the Book of Kings*, from Augustine.) This must not be understood as though the Lord had prepared Saul to reign forever and had refused to preserve this arrangement because Saul sinned; for he knew that Saul would sin. Rather, he had prepared his kingdom so that it would be a figure of the eternal kingdom. Hence he added: “And now your kingdom shall not endure for you.” What was signified in him has endured and will endure; but it will not endure for him, because he was not destined to reign forever, nor will his offspring. Thus, at least through descendants succeeding one another, it might seem that what had been said “forever” was fulfilled.

### Verse 14

**“But now your kingdom shall certainly not.”** Saul’s rejection signifies the removal of the kingdom from the Jews. David, surviving him, signifies Christ, who was to succeed the Jewish people.

**“He sought for himself.”** This is not as though he did not know where it was; rather, he speaks through a human being in a human manner, because by speaking in this way he also seeks us. For we were not only in God the Father but also in the Only-Begotten, who came to seek what had perished; thus we already existed as those chosen in him before the foundation of the world.

Therefore he said, “He shall seek for himself”: he will have what belongs to him. In Latin this verb takes a preposition and is called *acquire*; this is sufficiently clear. Even without the preposition, *quaerere*—“to seek”—is understood as “to acquire,” from which profits are called *quaestus*.

**“A man according to his heart.”** This signifies David, or the mediator of the New Testament himself, who was represented in the chrism with which David and his descendants were anointed. (Rabanus.) The devil also, through the pagans, [lacuna] up to the point where we seek the future.

## Chapter XIV

### Verse 1

**“Jonathan.”** “Gift of a dove.” These are those who are filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom the Lord disperses the gatherings of heretics and puts them to flight.

His armor-bearer signifies the spiritual disciples, who undertake a path not across level ground but over steep places. For priests cannot oppose their enemies unless they walk along the narrow way, proceeding between the two Testaments and between prosperity and adversity, as though between two cliffs on the right and left, and ascending to the heights of contemplation with the full effort of the mind.

Jonathan does not cross over to the enemy except when challenged, because Catholics do not stir up contention against heretics unless they are first challenged to combat. Jonathan therefore strikes down the enemies in the field of cultivation, and teachers overcome heretics in meditation on Scripture.

### Verse 27

**“But Jonathan.”** “Gift of a dove.” He signifies those who, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, prepare themselves to despise the allurements of the world. For no one can fight courageously against spiritual foreigners—that is, demons—if he does not know how to avoid the sweetness of the world.

**“Their eyes were enlightened.”** (Rabanus, from Eucherius.) Not for seeing, [lacuna] up to the point where they need the prayers of their brothers.

### Verse 33

**“The people sinned against the Lord by eating.”** (Rabanus.) To have sinned against the Lord, [lacuna] up to the point where they had eaten with the blood.

### Verse 34

**“Kill them upon this,” etc.** So that the blood might flow onto the ground. Or they ate with the blood because they ate before the evening sacrifice, which, after the slaughter, customarily took place before the meal. Or, as some think, they sinned in this: they did not bring their victims to the entrance of the tabernacle.

**“And they killed.”** The slaughter of animals is baptism, in which the old man dies. The great stone upon which the slaughter took place is faith, without which the old man does not die. Slaughtering on the ground signifies the baptism of heretics. They eat its blood when, without purification from sins, they gather to themselves those who have been washed.

These animals captured from the Philistines signify either those brought back from heretics or those converted from paganism. The ignorant rebaptize the former; they baptize the latter in a manner different from the tradition of the Church. Christ, like Saul, commanded that these—oxen and sheep, that is, human beings without distinction—be baptized and slain, as it were, upon the great stone of his faith.

### Verse 35

**“Then he first began to build an altar to the Lord,” etc.** Because he did so obediently and rightly. Earlier, when he was rebuked by Samuel, he is not said to have built an altar to the Lord, because he built it disobediently.

[Col. 0554D]

### Verse 38

**“Bring here all the corners of the people.”** He calls the leaders the “corners of the people,” because the people adhered to them on every side like walls joined to the corners of a building.

### Verse 44

**“Let this be done.”** This is a Hebrew oath understood by contraries, as though he were saying: “Let the evil that is due to you be charged to me if I do not kill you.”

### Verse 45

**“He who did.”** Past good deeds are of great benefit. For if Jonathan’s former good deeds had not helped him, he would not have escaped the evils that threatened him. God is not unjust so as to forget good deeds.

## Chapter XV

[Col. 0555A]

### Verse 1

**“And he said,” etc. “The ox,” etc.** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. II.) Therefore the Lord commands that the animals of Amalek be destroyed, [lacuna] up to the point where they cast God’s mockery into heaven.

### Verse 6

**“Saul said to the Kenite.”** (Rabanus.) The Kenite himself was Jethro, Moses’ kinsman, [lacuna] up to the multitude of the people.

### Verse 11

**“I repent.”** (Gregory, *On the Book of Kings*.) By this rebuke the king’s pride is cast down, [lacuna] up to the point where we ascend to greater things always through humility.

### Verse 17

**“Were you not, when.”** (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 34, and in Eucherius.) He is little in his own eyes, [lacuna] up to the saying: “They appointed you ruler; do not exalt yourself, but be like one of them.”

[Col. 0555B]

### Verse 22

**“Better is,” etc.** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*.) Because through sacrifices another’s flesh, [lacuna] up to the point where Paul boldly says: “I am ready not only to be bound in Jerusalem but even to die” (Acts 21).

### Verse 26

**“I will not return.”** (Rabanus.) Another edition, [lacuna] up to the point where he threatens here but does not persist.

### Verse 27

**“But he.”** Just as the high priest tore his garment during the Lord’s passion, so Saul tore the prophet’s garment. For the tearing shown through both powers—royal and priestly—indicates that the kingdom and priesthood of the Jews could not stand, because they had refused to receive the true king and priest, Christ.

(Rabanus, from Augustine.) He to whom he said, [lacuna] up to the point where it is not according to the one and identical nature of the human race.

### Verse 28

**“He tore.”** Although he afterward reigned for forty years, he then deserved that the kingdom be torn away from his lineage and handed over to a better man, David. Thus the kingdom is taken away from Saul—that is, from the Jews—and given to Christ.

He corrects the king for his disobedience, because he did not fulfill the Lord’s command, and he foretells the loss of the kingdom. Rightly does he lose the kingdom who does not know how to retain it. But the one rules well who obeys his superior and places his authority before his inferiors.

### Verse 33

**“And into pieces.”** When some read in Scripture that the saints spare none of their enemies, they call them cruel and do not understand the mysteries hidden beneath these words: namely, that when fighting against vices we should leave nothing wholly undefeated.

For if we spare them, it will be counted against us as guilt, as it was against Saul, who preserved the king of Amalek alive. The saints, however, like Samuel, leave no sin unpunished.

## Chapter XVI

### Verse 7

**“Do not look.”** After the elder sons of Jesse have been rejected, the youngest is chosen for the kingdom, because, with the Jewish priesthood and the kingdom of the former people rejected, Christ became the head, king, and priest of the lesser people.

### Verse 11

**“The youngest.”** David was transferred from the duty of tending sheep to kingship over men; Christ, however, was transferred from the sheepfold of the Jewish people to the kingdom of the Gentiles.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book 1, chapter 6; book 18, chapter 6.) Although the devil always desires the affliction of the righteous, [lacuna] up to the point where authority does not exist except from God.

[Col. 0556A]

### Verse 16

**“One who knows how to play,” etc.** (Rabanus, from Eucherius.) David was trained in musical songs, [lacuna] up to the point where he may be recalled, as though by the sweetness of the lyre, to the tranquillity of our speech.

### Verse 23
