**“Saul was refreshed.”** Previously he had been tormented by a demon even to the point of suffocation. Boethius relates that a certain philosopher drove a demon from a possessed body by touching a lyre.

## Chapter XVII

### Verse 1

**“Gathering together.”** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*.) Azekah is a city of the Canaanites in the tribe of Judah, to which Joshua pursued five kings. Today it is called the village of Azekah between Eleutheropolis and Jerusalem; its name is interpreted as “fortitude” and “snare.”

**Dammim.** It is a village in the tribe of Judah, on the borders of Eleutheropolis, twenty-seven miles from it. Dammim is interpreted as “silence” or “joy.”

### Verse 2

**“The terebinths.”** The terebinth is at Shechem, beneath which Jacob hid the idols near Neapolis.

### Verse 4

**“Illegitimate.”** Because he was born of an ignoble father but a noble mother.

### Verse 12

**“Eight sons.”** (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions*, vol. III.) In Chronicles only seven are mentioned, [lacuna] up to the statement that Isidore also says the prophet Nathan was from the Gibeonites.

### Verse 14

**“David.”** And the eighth, who is chosen for the kingdom, is Christ, who “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2), because through the glory of the resurrection he also obtained the kingdom among the Gentiles.

### Verse 21

**“For Israel had drawn up its battle line, but the Philistines.”** The battle of the Philistines against Israel can be understood as the battle of demons against the Church. Goliath signifies the pride of the devil, whom David—that is, Christ—struck down in single combat and delivered the people of God.

David, who killed the lion and the bear, signifies Christ who killed the devil and the Antichrist: the one now secretly lying in wait, the other later raging openly. Pride challenged humility; the devil challenged Christ.

David took the weapons of war, which he could not carry because of his age and small stature, and cast them aside. He took five stones from the stream and put them in a shepherd’s bag; armed with these, he conquered.

Thus Christ, at the time when the revelation of the New Testament was being announced and grace commended, laid aside the bodily sacraments of the Law, which were not imposed upon the Gentiles. We read them in the Old Law but do not observe them; rather, we understand that they were set forth and established for the sake of a certain signification. He laid these aside as burdens of the Law and took up the Law itself.

The five stones signify the five books of Moses. He took five stones from the stream—that is, from this age. For the mortal age flows away. The stones were as though in the stream among the first people: there they lay idle and profited nothing, while the river passed over them.

But David received grace, so that the Law might become useful, since it cannot be fulfilled without grace. “The fullness of the Law is love” (Romans 13). Because grace causes the Law to be fulfilled, grace is signified by milk. For this is something freely given in the flesh: where the mother does not seek to receive but to give, she gives freely and is saddened if there is no one to receive.

David showed that the Law cannot operate without grace. Wishing to join the five stones, by which the Law in its five books is signified, to grace, he placed them in the shepherd’s bag in which milk was customarily drawn.

Armed with these, he went out against the proud man. He took one stone and brought down one man; he struck him in the forehead, and he fell from that part of the body where he did not bear the sign of Christ.

He took five and used one. The five books were chosen, but unity conquers. Therefore the fullness of the Law is love, as the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in love, eager to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Ephesians 4).

After he had brought him down, he took his sword and cut off his head. Christ kills the devil from among his own members when the magi whom the devil held in his power—and through whom he slaughtered others—believed, turning their tongues against the devil. Thus Goliath’s head is cut off by his own sword.

[Col. 0557B]

### Verse 28

**“I know your pride and the wickedness of your heart, because.”** (Rabanus.) He thought that David was swollen with pride because of Samuel’s anointing, as though he had gained boldness from it, and he feared that, if David engaged the Philistine, he would be killed.

Hence he adds: “You have come down to see the battle,” that is, you appear proud in this respect: although you have no experience of fighting, you inquire about the conduct of battle as though you were a soldier.

### Verse 29

**“Is this not a word?”** (Rabanus.) As though he were saying: It is so, because I have no desire to fight; I only wanted to know what I did not know.

Nevertheless, he had drawn courage from having received the Holy Spirit. He had experienced God’s help against the lion and the bear, and therefore boldly offered himself for single combat—not so much desiring victory as seeking vengeance for the blasphemies against God and the injuries done to the people.

### Verse 41

**“And he went.”** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*.) Allegorically, the Philistines are demons, [lacuna] up to the point where they cut down the exalted Goliath with his own sword.

### Verse 51

**“And he took.”** (Rabanus, from Gregory.) The Catholic man also gathers the testimony of Scripture, [lacuna] up to the point where we overcome heretics by their own statements.

**“The head.”** David carried the head of the Philistine to Jerusalem in order to terrify those who trusted in the strength and height of their walls, believing themselves unconquerable, so that they would not fail to believe that they could be defeated by him.

### Verse 55

**“Whose son?”** (Augustine.) The fact that Saul and Abner did not know David, although he had remained among them for some time, was caused by his beard, which had grown on the young man while he had been absent.

**“He lives.”** (Rabanus.) This resembles the saying: “Naboth blessed God and the king.” Also: “May your soul not live, O king, if I know,” or “may I see your death, if I know.” The conjunction *si* (“if”) is also sometimes used in place of “not,” according to the saying: “If they shall enter into my rest” (Psalm 95), that is, “they shall not enter.” Hence it is clear that this should be explained: “If I know,” that is, “I do not know.”

## Chapter XVIII

### Verse 1

**“And it happened,” etc., “and he loved,” etc.** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*.) Jonathan loved David: a warrior, namely, loving a young man suited to battle.

Jonathan signifies those who among the Jews believed in Christ and, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, left everything for Christ and followed him. Hence Peter says: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you” (Matthew 19).

Thus Jonathan gave David his garments, from tunic to belt, when believers transferred everything they possessed into the service of Christ.

### Verse 7

**“Saul has struck,” etc.** This was the seed of hatred against David. So the Jews, hearing Christ—whom they had crucified—preached in the churches, and seeing believers rejoice in praise of him because of the victory by which he conquered the ancient enemy, endured it with great distress.

**“Saul his thousands.”** Namely, those who were killed while fleeing.

[Col. 0558B]

**“David his ten thousands.”** Namely, the Philistine who, after one man had been struck down, put them all to flight.

### Verse 10

**“He held.”** Thus, while Christ preached the Gospel, the Jews attempted to bring about his death. But while he withdrew for the salvation of the Gentiles, they harmed only themselves.

### Verse 17

**“And he said.”** (Isidore, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. V, chapter 11.) Saul, a crafty pretender, sought to bind David to Michal, his daughter, [lacuna] up to the point where he may be recalled by the tranquillity of speech.

### Verse 27

**“He struck,” etc., “and brought,” etc.** (Rabanus.) Thus Christ was first glorified among the Gentiles, when he joined the Synagogue to himself and first cut away uncleanness among the Gentiles. “When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved” (Romans 11).

## Chapter XIX

[Col. 0558C]

### Verse 3

**“In the field,” etc.** He used to come there for the purpose of giving consolation, although it had been agreed that David would be killed there.

### Verse 11

**“Therefore he sent.”** (Rabanus.) This does not refer to Christ’s cross but to his passion, [lacuna] up to the point where they pursue him as though he were a sinner.

### Verse 13

**“A skin.”** From it a small cushion was sewn which, with its uncut hair, could make the head of a wrapped man lying in the bed appear to be there.

### Verse 18

**“In Ramah.”** It is Saul’s city, in the tribe of Benjamin, six miles from Jerusalem, northward, opposite Bethel. Another Ramah is in the tribe of Asher.

These names fittingly correspond to the events themselves, because the words of the prophets possess both loftiness of knowledge and beauty of eloquence.

### Verses 21–22

**“He sent a third group,” etc. “He went,” etc.** (Rabanus.) Saul and his messengers signify the Jews. While they desire to oppose Christ, they have on their lips the mysteries of the Law and the prophets as testimony to Christ; and with the Church, as with the prophets, they debate from the Scriptures, just as those men prophesied with the prophets.

### Verse 24

**“He prophesied.”** These prophets were religious men called Nazarenes. They did not drink wine and were always occupied in singing hymns and psalms.

**“Naked.”** The Jews, stripped of faith, priesthood, and kingdom, still have the Law and the prophets on their lips.

**“Is Saul also?”** This is called a proverb because it often occurs in the mouths of speakers. It seemed a remarkable thing for such a profane man to prophesy. When we see ignorant people teaching, we rightly say: “Is Saul also among the prophets?”

(Rabanus.) A great question arises here, [lacuna] up to the point where it must be understood only of royal matters.

(Idem.) The question is also raised, [lacuna] up to the point where they did not use those gifts well.

## Chapter XX

### Verse 3

**“Only one.”** (Rabanus.) He calls the wall a “step,” by which he escaped through the window of the house, with the enemies who were besieging it between himself and them.

### Verse 16

**“And he asked.”** (Rabanus.) This is a prolepsis, that is, an anticipation, [lacuna] up to the point where the Lord avenges him.

### Verse 17

**“And he added.”** (Rabanus.) So that David might be shown to be immune from the destruction of his enemies, because he loved him according to God’s Law. Although death prevented him from possessing the earthly kingdom with David as he had hoped, without any doubt he received a share in the heavenly kingdom with the one whom he loved for his virtues, since he himself was also a man of virtue.

**“Why?”** As though he were saying: You love my enemy while opposing me, thereby showing that you were conceived in an adulterous union. For those born legitimately love their fathers more closely.

(Rabanus.) What is the meaning of Jonathan’s wishing to preserve David, [lacuna] up to the point where he did not know what Moses and the prophets had foretold.

## Chapter XXI

[Col. 0559C]

### Verse 1

**“Ahimelech.”** (Rabanus.) That is, “my brother is king,” [lacuna] up to the point where the apostles were sanctified by faith from the contamination of the Jews.

### Verse 5

**“The way.”** In the Hebrew, [lacuna] up to the point where, with the danger to life pressing, he would not eat them.

### Verse 6

**“Therefore he gave.”** As far as prophecy is concerned, [lacuna] up to the saying: “If they persecuted me, they will also persecute you” (John 15).

### Verse 7

**“In the tabernacle of the Lord.”** (Rabanus.) In the Hebrew: “bound before the Lord.” Perhaps he had made a vow, because he was to remain for several days in the tabernacle of the Lord and devote himself to prayers.

**Doeg the Edomite.** (Rabanus.) He was the keeper of camels—that is, of an unfruitful and crooked flock—[lacuna] up to the point where no one can harm Christ, the prince of priests, who ascended victoriously into heaven.

(Rabanus, from Isidore.) Achish is interpreted, [lacuna] up to the point where divine power lay hidden within, like a beard.

## Chapter XXII

### Verse 1

**“When this happened.”** (Rabanus.) It signified that our Redeemer, after completing the passion and redemption of the human race, first established the Church in Judea from the Israelite people, from whom he also took flesh.

There his brothers—that is, the apostles—and his father’s household—that is, those who believed from among the Jews—came to him. All who were afflicted gathered to him, [lacuna] up to the words: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matthew 11).

### Verse 2

**“In debt.”** (Rabanus.) That is, under the assessment of sins which they pay to the devil while they present their members for service to iniquity, resulting in further iniquity.

Such people must do penance in bitterness of spirit and come to David—that is, to Christ, desired by all the nations—so that he may become their prince. For he is the judge of the living and the dead and the prince of peace, whose kingdom shall have no end.

### Verse 5

**“And Gad said.”** (Rabanus.) Gad is introduced unexpectedly. No mention of him occurs earlier, just as with Elijah, where it is said: “And Elijah the Tishbite, from the inhabitants of Gilead, said” (1 Kings 17).

Therefore the prophet Gad spoke from the mouth of the Lord to David, so that he would not remain among the nations in a polluted land but would return to the land of Judah, where, according to the Lord’s will, he would endure persecution.

## Chapter XXIII

### Verse 11

**“He will come down.”** (Rabanus.) “If you remain here, Saul will come down, and the men of Keilah will hand you over to him”: therefore he revealed their intention.

The men of Keilah, ungrateful for the benefits David had bestowed on them when he delivered them from the hands of the Philistines, signify the faithlessness and instability of the Jews, who, ungrateful to their Redeemer, plot against him before the powers of the world.

Keilah is interpreted as “cast upon a sling” or “exalting itself.” “The wicked walk about on every side” (Psalm 12). And: “A fool changes like the moon” (Sirach 27).

[Col. 0560C]

### Verse 14

**“Ziph.”** (Rabanus.) They betrayed David, who was hiding among them, to Saul and plotted his death with him.

The Ziphites are interpreted as “flourishing” or “sprouting.” They signify those Jews who, desiring the flower of an earthly kingdom, plotted with their leaders how to seize Christ, betrayed through his disciple, and hand him over to the governor for execution. And those flourishing in the world betray Christ in his members, namely, the powers of this world.

## Chapter XXIV

### Verse 4

**“And he was there,” etc.** (Rabanus, from Eucherius.) The king, unexpectedly caught in ambush, [lacuna] up to the words of Samuel: “The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from your hand.”

(Gregory, *Moralia*, vol. II.) What does Saul signify except wicked rulers? [lacuna] up to the point where Moses, having learned that the people were complaining against him and Aaron, said: “For what are we?” (Exodus 16).

**“He lives,” etc.** Josephus supplies the defective text: “Those who were with him rebuked him.” For he spared the enemy whom he wished to destroy and quieted them, saying: “As the Lord lives,” etc.

## Chapter XXV

### Verse 1

**“Paran.”** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. II.) It is a town in Arabia near the Saracens who were in the desert. The children of Israel passed through it when they moved their camp from Mount Sinai.

It lies toward the south and is three days’ journey east of Ailah. Scripture records that Ishmael lived in the desert of Paran; from him come the Ishmaelites, now called Saracens. We also read that Chedorlaomer struck those who were in the desert of Paran.

### Verse 3

**“Nabal,” etc.** (Rabanus, in the same place.) A hard and very wicked man, [lacuna] up to the words: “There will be joy in heaven over one sinner who repents” (Luke 15).

### Verse 18

**“Sata.”** A *satum* is a type of measure containing a modius and a half. *Polenta* is extremely fine flour. Raisins are grapes that are dried in the sun for a long time before they ripen and are then preserved. “Cakes of figs” means bundles made from figs.

### Verse 29

**“The soul,” etc.** (Rabanus, from Eucherius.) By a most beautiful comparison, [lacuna] up to the point where they have been removed from human affairs.

### Verse 37

**“When he had sobered.”** (Gregory.) We correct angry people better if we withdraw during the very outburst of anger. For when they are disturbed, they do not know what they are hearing. But when they return to themselves, they receive words of exhortation more willingly, the more ashamed they are that they were borne with patiently.

To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears perverse. Thus Abigail commendably concealed Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, and commendably told him of it when the wine had passed. The evil he had done could harm him because, while drunk, he did not hear of it.

### Verse 44

**“To Phalti, son of.”** (Rabanus.) As the Hebrews relate, Phalti did not have intercourse with her. For if he had, David would not afterward have taken her back, since this is forbidden by the Law.

Phalti was from Gallim, that is, from “cleansing,” meaning from the Law. He was a teacher of the Law from Baurim, that is, “from the chosen,” when Michal was given to him.

Phalti means “going” when she was taken away; Phaltiel, that is, “escaping from God,” because God guarded him so that he would not touch her and become a transgressor of the Law. Nevertheless, he followed her weeping as far as Baurim, rejoicing because he had not touched her.

## Chapter XXVI

### Verses 1–5

**“And the Ziphites came,” etc. “Sleeping,” etc.** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. II.) The Jews persecute Christ, [lacuna] up to the point where he ascended to the height of heaven.

## Chapter XXVII

### Verse 8

**“They made raids upon Geshur and upon Gerzi,” etc.** (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Kings*.) These villages were not under Achish’s authority. They are said to have been inhabited from ancient times because they had been settled peacefully and securely and had suffered the attacks of no enemy.

## Chapter XXVIII

### Verse 3

**“Now Samuel.”** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. II.) Samuel is read above as having died; but the account of his resurrection is repeated because of Saul’s condemnation, since, having abandoned God, he consulted a pythoness contrary to the Law.

### Verse 6

**“And he consulted the Lord.”** (Rabanus.) As the Hebrews relate, an oracle was sought from God by fasting and praying; and God revealed the future to them through dreams. Saul is not read to have done this.

**“Nor through the priests.”** (Idem.) In the Hebrew: “Nor through the Urim,” that is, “instruction,” “nor through the ephod,” namely, the garment that the priest wore on his breast, on which was written: “Instruction and truth.”

### Verse 9

**“Magicians.”** Magicians use human blood and contact with the dead in their sorceries, while diviners foretell by words alone, that is, by incantations.

Apollo is called *Pythius*, a practitioner of these arts; from him come the Pythonesses, that is, diviners. Saul destroyed these people, supposedly out of zeal for the Law, because, as they say, compelled by demons, they proclaimed that David would become king.

### Verse 11

**“Whom shall I raise up?”** (Augustine, *Letter to Simplicianus*, vol. II.) You ask whether an evil spirit could raise the soul of a righteous person, [lacuna] up to the point where it may be referred to the equal condition of death: both had been human beings and could die, and the dead man foretold death to the living.

## Chapter XXIX

### Verse 5

**“Saul has struck.”** Envious of David’s glory, they say that David fought only among ten thousand, as though he possessed lesser power, while Saul fought among thousands, as though they were innumerable. They do not add how many he struck down, either because they envied David’s praise or lest they frighten their own men.

In the oldest books the reading is not “among thousands” but “as a thousand,” with only “ten thousand” added.

## Chapter XXX

### Verse 1

**“When the Amalekites.”** (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 29.) We must consider what it means that the Amalekites invade Ziklag and carry off the booty, [lacuna] up to the point where the world has despised possessing them in common.

### Verse 21

**“They had remained.”** The two hundred exhausted men who were left behind with the baggage signify the weak members of the Church, who cannot run along the road with spiritual men. Yet because they possess faith and preserve good works, they receive from Christ the reward of blessedness together with the perfect.

## Chapter XXXI

### Verse 2

**“They struck Jonathan,” etc.** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*, vol. II.) Jonathan, Abinadab, [lacuna] up to the point where he perished with his sons.

### Verse 4

**“Therefore he seized.”** With the sword by which he had spared the Amalekites contrary to God’s command, he deservedly killed himself. Thus whoever does not use, or misuses, the authority received for the common good plainly stabs himself with his own sword; the very weapon by which he ought to have been defended against the enemy instead helps the enemy.

### Verse 11

**“The inhabitants.”** Those whom Saul had defended from their adversaries repay what they can. Let us too, as far as we are able, rescue our benefactors, slain by the sword of sin, from the reproach of the Philistines.

[Col. 0563]

# The Second Book of Samuel, which for us is the Second Book of Kings (G)*

## Chapter I

[Col. 0563A]

### Verse 2

**“A man appeared, coming from the camp of Saul,” etc.** (Rabanus.) The Hebrews say that this man was the son of Doeg. For Amalekite and Edomite are the same, since Esau’s firstborn son was Eliphaz, and his son was Amalek. He possessed the diadem and the armlet entrusted to him by his father.

### Verse 15

**“Approaching,” etc.** Everyone who plots evil against his neighbor or rejoices in his destruction deserves the punishment of just retribution from the heavenly Judge. “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (Proverbs 26). And: “The lying mouth kills the soul” (Wisdom 1). This man, however, had lied that he had killed Saul.

### Verse 18

**“The sons.”** The sons of Judah are the sons of confession, whom the true David wishes to be armed with the bow of Scripture, lest through ignorance they fall before demons.

**“The bow.”** (Rabanus, *On the Book of Kings*.) Since the Philistines are archers, and Saul had been killed by that art of war, he wants them to learn the same art, or he commands that the kings of Judah be taught courage, so that they may be strong and attentive in the fear of the Lord and not perish as Saul did.

**“In the book.”** (Rabanus, in the same place.) It is read, or it is written. They assert that this book is found nowhere, like the Book of the Wars of the Lord, [lacuna] up to the point where Saul, departing from the fear of the Lord through disobedience, perished.

**“Consider, Israel.”** (Idem.) You who remain, consider on account of what guilt they were killed, and take care lest you too perish in their crime.

### Verse 20

**Geth.** The winepress—namely, Jerusalem, which killed the prophets (Matt. 23), and for which the Lord’s death and that of the apostles were a subject of mockery; for this reason the true David commanded that his Passion not be announced to them.

### Verse 21

**Mountains of Gilboa, etc.** (ID.) Others render it “high places,” because, O Saul, your disobedience was regarded as equivalent to idolatry in the high places, since refusal to obey is the crime of idolatry. The mountains of Gilboa were exceedingly fertile before the curse; they are said to have remained subject to the curse to this day, and it is reported that it never rains there.

King and prophet David, who did not repay his persecutors with evil, curses the mountains of Gilboa in his lament when Saul and Jonathan had fallen in battle: “Mountains of Gilboa, may neither dew,” etc., up to “and the divine power fulfilled the sentence of the one who cursed.” Thus, in response to the spectacle of the king’s death, the elements discharged their punishment.

(RAB.) “What did the mountains do wrong?” etc., up to “who, because of the demands of iniquity, deserved to receive the king’s death among them.”

### Verse 22

**From the blood of the slain.** Blood and fat give strength to the body; thus those subject to Saul and Jonathan supplied them with strength, as though they had been killed not by peasants. Or it may be understood this way: Saul was rejected by God and disgracefully killed by the uncircumcised, as though he had not been anointed with oil, because of the blood of the slain—namely, the seventy-five priests who offered fat to the Lord and whom Saul ordered to be killed though they were innocent.

**Bow.** This signifies that Jonathan and Saul were warlike and exceedingly brave, and praises in them the beauty of their appearance and the steadfastness of their spirit.

(RAB.) **Allegorically.** The devout prophet David figuratively mourns Saul and Jonathan, etc., up to “lest, defeated again in disgrace, they bring joy to their enemies.”

## CHAPTER II

### Verse 1

**So, after this, etc.** (RAB.) David’s ascent with his two wives to Hebron signifies the gathering of the two peoples into the catholic Church. For Hebron is interpreted as “marriage.” The Church alone is the bride of the heavenly King. David brought each man there with his household, because individual believers are summoned into that fellowship through the preaching of the Gospel, where there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

### Verse 4

**And they came.** (ID.) Because the elect, through the fame of preaching and the zeal for virtue, confess Christ to be king among his people to the proud and contemptuous who reject the grace of God.

### Verse 5

**And he said.** (ID.) Our Redeemer is greatly pleased with the one who consigns to oblivion, by condemning them, the deeds of the wicked who are dead in sins, and who does not imitate what displeases the Lord but remembers to do what he commanded.

### Verse 8

**Ishbosheth.** (ID.) He is interpreted as “son of confusion.” With Abner’s help—Abner being interpreted as “lamp of the father”—he reigned over all Israel, while only the house of Judah followed David. This signifies that, while only believers and those who truly confess followed Christ, the error of confusion reigned among the others, instigated by the devil, who transforms himself into an angel of light (2 Cor. 11).

**He brought him across.** In the Hebrew it says: “He brought him across to Mahanaim,” which is interpreted as “camps.” That is, he brought him across the Jordan and established him as king in the camps.

### Verse 11

**And it was.** (RAB., *On the Books of Kings*, vol. II.) He rightly said that David reigned seven years and six months in Hebron, etc., up to “the Egyptian city Tanis was founded seven years earlier.”

### Verse 12

**He went out.** (RAB.) Josephus explains this passage in this way, etc., up to “here he was pursuing Abner, inclining to neither side.”

### Verse 18

**Now Asahel was an exceedingly swift runner, like one of the gazelles.** (ID., from Gregory.) Asahel signifies those whom violent fury seizes and drives headlong, etc., up to “as though they die without the sword.”

### Verse 26

**Do you not know that despair is dangerous?** In the Hebrew it reads: “Do you not know that the end will be bitter if you seek to destroy the people?”

## CHAPTER III

### Verse 1

**There was therefore.** (RAB., *On the Books of Kings.) The house of David is the heavenly Jerusalem, etc., up to “and at last, according to its merits, it will be plunged into the depths of the abyss.”

### Verse 2

**And sons were born.** The six sons born to David in Hebron signify the perfection of the saints, who are born daily from the spiritual marriage of Christ and the Church through the grace of the Holy Spirit.

### Verse 5

**Of Eglah.** (RAB.) This is Michal, who alone is called a wife because David first took her as his wife in his youth. She is said to have died in childbirth; hence it is written later: “Therefore Michal, the daughter of Saul, had no child up to the day of her death,” because she died in that very childbirth.

### Verse 17

**The word.** (ID.) Abner urges all Israel, etc., up to “and everywhere they persecuted the faith of Christ.”

### Verse 29

**Discharge of semen.** Literally, he appears to be invoking an issue of lust, the affliction of leprosy, effeminacy, subjection to the sword of the enemy, and begging.

**Holding a spindle.** (AUG.) Through the circuitousness of the words, those who strive to defend their deceit are indicated.

**Falling.** “Whoever strikes with the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. 26). Heretics pierce others with the sword of their mouth, though they themselves were first wounded by the sword of impiety.

### Verse 39

**Delicate.** The ancients called things consecrated to the gods *delicata*; today we call them “dedicated.”

## CHAPTER IV

### Verse 2

**Now there were two men.** (RAB., *On the Books of Kings*, vol. II.) These two men were commanders in Ishbosheth’s army. After Abner’s death, as the Hebrews relate, they conspired with Mephibosheth to kill Ishbosheth and make Mephibosheth king. But Mephibosheth exposed the plot. Therefore the text introduces him in this way: “Now Jonathan’s son was disabled in his feet.” The two men, terrified by fear, fled to Gittaim and remained there until that time—namely, until they returned from there and entered Ishbosheth’s house.

**And the doorkeeper.** (ID.) A female doorkeeper cleans grain, etc., up to “so that enemies may not penetrate it through the opening of neglected thought.”

## CHAPTER V

### Verse 1

**And they came.** (RAB.) Thus all the nations come together to Christ and, as though flattering him, say: “We are your bone and your flesh,” since they love and venerate in him the incarnation that he assumed from our nature in the Virgin’s womb.

### Verse 3

**The elders.** (ID.) The prophets and apostles, with equal faith and devotion, hasten to Christ.

**And they anointed him.** (ID.) David is said to have been anointed twice, and Christ first assumed supremacy among the Jews and afterward among the Gentiles.

### Verse 4

**And forty.** (ID.) It is asked why, in the total, forty years and six months are not counted, etc., up to “which consists of four times ten and signifies the perfection of times and events.”

### Verse 5

**In Jerusalem.** The Hebrews relate that Shem, the son of Noah, whom they say was Melchizedek, founded Salem. The Jebusites later held it, and from them it received the name Jebus. Hence Jerusalem, as though “Jebus-Salem”; afterward, from Solomon, Jerosolyma, as though Jerosalomonia; later it was called Aelia by Aelius Hadrian.

### Verse 6

**The blind and the lame.** “Who are sufficient against you.” They said this, trusting in the walls. Or it may be understood thus: “You will not enter unless you remove us, whom you regard as unarmed like the blind and the lame and whom you think you can conquer.”

### Verse 7

**But he captured it.** (RAB.) As Josephus says, etc., up to “which is rightly called the fortress of Zion, that is, of observation, so that it may rightly be said of it: ‘His place has become peace,’ etc.” (Ps. 75).

David captured the fortress of Zion, after first removing the blind and the lame who hated David’s life. Thus the Lord acquired primacy in the Church of the Gentiles, rejecting its scribes and Pharisees, who, blind and lame, hated Christ’s life—that is, attempted to take it away.

### Verse 8

**Roofs.** That is, of rulers.

**Channels.** He calls channels conduits made of lead or a measuring rod, through which water flowed over the wall throughout the entire city.

**Channels.** They represent false knowledge or the doctrines of heretics, which the Lord destroys through Joab, that is, through preachers. “Jebusite,” meaning “one who tramples,” represents the Gentile world, which before the faith trampled upon God’s commandments. Likewise, “Jebusite” means “one trampled,” because the devil is trampled by the Lord and is subjected to be trampled under Joab.

### Verse 9

**And he built.** From the place so called, supply “a wall”; and within it, supply “another wall.” That is, he fortified the city with a double wall.

### Verse 11

**Hiram also sent.** Hiram, “living exaltedly,” represents the Gentile world exalted in Christ. He sends messengers to David—that is, teachers to Christ—and through them cedar wood, meaning incorruptible and strong people, and craftsmen, meaning those whose skill keeps minds incorruptible and makes them square, like stones, by the four virtues. Thus the house of David, that is, the Church of Christ, is built, and it is recognized that God established our David as king over Israel—that is, over those who see God.

(RAB.) The churches of heretics, which boast that they remain under the title of the Christian name. But because they follow Christ for carnal profits, they are called not wives but concubines. Now, however, if kings have several wives or concubines, it is a sin, because the figures for which this was once permissible have passed away.

### Verse 13

**And sons were born.** If Christ is signified by David, his sons are not improperly understood as Christians, who come from Jews and nations. The interpretations of their names correspond to them: Shammua, “boldness”; Shobab, “turning back”; Jabahar, “he chose”; Elishua, “the salvation of my God”; Nepheg, “applying to the mouth”; Japhia, “he illuminates” or “he shows”; Elishama, “my God hearing”; Eliada, “my God knows”; Eliphelet, “my God saving.”

### Verse 20

**Baal-perazim.** It is interpreted as “division of enemies.” The place may have been called this because the Philistines left their idols in the place where they were divided.

### Verse 23

**Pear trees.** In the Hebrew, “of those who weep,” that is, of idols, where the idols in which they trusted were situated. They are called “of those who weep” because they are worthy of tears and bring their worshipers to weeping and misery.

**At the summit.** (RAB.) The pear tree is called *pyrus* from the Greek πῦρ, which means “fire.” The holy ones are the pear trees; their summit is the loftiness of their life, in which, as the Holy Spirit breathed, the sound of preaching thundered. “That of one who walks”—that is, the gift of the one coming in the flesh—[is heard] at the summit of the pear trees, that is, above the height of the saints. While this sound is heard by our David, the intelligible Philistines are overcome.

## CHAPTER VI

### Verse 1

**He gathered together.** (RAB., from Eucherius.) David represents Christ, etc., up to “who, coming down from Judea, were teaching the brethren: ‘Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved’” (Acts 15).

### Verse 2

**Of the one sitting.** Above the ark there was a tablet, which two cherubim covered with their wings; between them the Lord appeared and spoke.

(RAB., from Gregory.) In the history of King and prophet David, when he is said to have brought the ark of God, approved humility, condemned pride, and punished presumption are displayed. David, who was not ashamed to dance humbly before the ark, immediately deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God who would be born from his line; but his wife, who despised humility, paid the penalty of perpetual sterility. The priest, too, who presumptuously touched the ark purged the guilt of his daring by a premature death. Here we must consider how great is the offense of one who approaches the Lord’s body while guilty, if the man who seized the ark, a figure of the Lord’s body, with less reverence than he ought, was punished by death.

(GREG., *Moralia*, book V, chapter 10.) Often, because they cannot understand, etc., up to “they would judge the deeds or words of better people as though they were defective.”

### Verse 7

**Who died.** (RAB., from Eucherius.) When the priest had died, he did not dare to turn the ark aside, etc., up to “‘Water,’ the Gittite people, may be called a people who says: ‘But far be it from me to glory except in the cross of the Lord’” (Gal. 6).

### Verse 11

**For three months.** (ID.) These signify faith, hope, and charity, etc., up to “and they undertake the leadership of the sheep, crowning themselves in the blood of martyrdom.”

**With instruments.** That is, instruments tied to the shoulder, while they are touched by the hands of the bearer. There is another kind of instrument that is made with water.

### Verse 14

**With a linen ephod, and David, etc.** (RAB.) Not in priestly attire but in a linen garment, as an expression of humility, etc., up to “he triumphed amid the scourges.”

### Verse 16

**When he had brought in the ark.** (ID.) While all were rejoicing and sounding hymns at the entrance of the heavenly ark, etc., up to “because those who receive the word of God only as far as the ear, without the offspring of good works, await the day of perpetual death.”

### Verse 20

**Michal, the daughter of Saul, went out to meet David, etc.** (GREG., *Moralia*, book XXVII, chapter 27.) It is pleasing to contemplate how many gifts of virtue David had received, etc., up to “yet he pressed down the neck of his heart within himself with the firm heel of discernment, saying: ‘I will be humble in my own eyes.’”

**Glorious.** When David was transferring the ark to Jerusalem, Michal mocked him. Likewise, when Christ was transferring the New Testament into his Church, he was an object of ridicule to the Jews on the cross. He appeared naked, concealing his power from them and displaying the weakness of his flesh like a linen ephod. The maidservants represent the saints, among whom he became more glorious through the triumph of the cross. While Michal mocks him, he appears more glorious than the maidservants, whereas she, representing the Synagogue, remained barren.

**And stripped.** He was not stripped completely, but of his royal garments. And because he was not ashamed to humble himself before the Lord, he immediately deserved to receive the promise of the Son of God who would be born from his line.

## CHAPTER VII

### Verse 3

**All that is in your heart, go and do.** (RAB., *On the Books of Kings*, vol. III.) It is evident that the spirit of prophecy does not always enlighten the minds of prophets. For “the Spirit blows where he wills” (John 3). Hence Elisha says: “The Lord has hidden it from me and has not told me” (2 Kings 4). God arranges this according to the dispensation of his mercy, because when he gives and withdraws the spirit of prophecy, he raises the minds of prophets to exaltation and preserves them in humility. Thus, when they receive the spirit, they discover what comes from God; and, when they do not have the spirit of prophecy again, they recognize what comes from themselves.

(GREG., *Moralia*, book VII, chapter 17.) One must be clean from vices within himself, etc., up to “he must be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbors.”

### Verse 5

**Perhaps.** Another translation, etc., up to “he himself will build a house for me.”

### Verse 10

**And I will appoint a place.** He describes the time of Solomon, when the children of Israel had peace on every side and were not afflicted as they had been in the time of the Judges.

### Verse 16

**And faithful.** (RAB., from Augustine, *City of God*, book XVII, chapter 8.) This is truly said of Christ, etc., up to “therefore the place of such peaceful and secure habitation is eternal, where the true Israel will be—that is, the one who sees God.”

**And he sat before.** To sit before the Lord is to confess his benefits in humility.

**The law of Adam.** (RAB.) That is, of man, so that he may serve you in simplicity of heart and purity, and so that you may deal with him according to your mercy, as you have dealt with me.

### Verse 23

**What is there.** Is there another nation on earth besides the chosen one, for whose sake the Son of God came into the world as into Egypt, in order to redeem for himself, through the commerce of blood, an acceptable people zealous for good works? We understand the God of that same people as the Lord’s man, whom he assumed from Egypt—that is, from the world—through the Virgin’s womb.

**From Egypt.** “The nation and its god,” or “the nation and its God”: the nation of Israel and its god, Moses, concerning whom it is said: “I have appointed you as god of Pharaoh” (Exod. 7).

### Verse 27

**Your servant has found.** Nothing is more fugitive than the heart; it is found when it is restrained through discernment.

## CHAPTER VIII

### Verse 1

**Bridle.** There were five cities of the Philistines that made Israel tributary. David took these for himself and made them tributary, as it is written: “David struck the Philistines and humbled them, and took Gath and its villages from their hand,” etc. (1 Chron. 18).

**Bridle.** Christ, triumphing over the powers of the air, broke the bridle of error that they had imposed upon the human race.

### Verse 2

**Making equal.** They were not so humiliated—these men living on earth—that they appeared equal to the earth by means of a cord stretched over it. Rather, they were so worthless and despised that they were no more valuable than earth that has no human beings upon it. He used a cord for the lot, because land is customarily measured with a cord, according to the passage: “He divided the land among them by lot, by the cord of distribution” (Ps. 77). This signifies that he divided the regions of the Moabites as freely as a possessor divides his own fields.

(RAB.) It signifies that he could kill whom he wished and spare whom he wished. The fact that he made Moab—which is interpreted as “from the father”—and Syria of Damascus and the other regions tributary signifies that Christ holds all nations under his rule, oppresses them, and exacts the tribute of good works. Damascus is a noble city of Phoenicia; it is called by the same name as the son of Abraham’s maidservant, Maseth, and is interpreted as “cup of blood.” Syria means “exalted” or “moistened.” For she who previously, moistened by lust, thirsted insatiably for human blood now, cleansed by the baptism of Christ and exalted through progress in virtues, desires the cup of his blood.

### Verse 11

**The king consecrated.** Thus Christ sanctifies all whom he summons from the nations: some as gold, that is, spiritually perceptive; others as silver, shining with the splendor of eloquence; and others as bronze, resounding in preaching, consecrating them to the Lord so that they may faithfully serve his tabernacle.

### Verse 13

**Having struck down.** (HIERON.) The statement found in certain manuscripts that twelve thousand were slain arose from a scribal error. David truly struck down eighteen thousand in the Valley of Salt, while Joab struck down twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm 58. This signifies that Christ, through the rigor of his judgment, extinguishes the folly of immoderate labor in those who hold perverse opinions about him.

### Verse 16

**From the records.** He acted in the king’s place, and laws were written according to his judgment. The scribe recorded the king’s words from his mouth.

### Verse 17

**Priests.** “Priest” is as though “sacred leader.” David’s sons, however, held leadership in the tribe of Judah.

(RAB.) They sat beside the king, guarding his body. Their names are interpreted as “killing” and “giving life,” because according to their judgment some who were worthy were reserved for life, while others were led to death.

## CHAPTER IX

### Verse 1

**And David said, etc.** (RAB., *On the Books of Kings*, vol. III.) Behold, David did not forget the oath and covenant that he had made with Jonathan, etc., up to “because those who were recently despised in the world appear glorious in the Church and become objects of the people’s wonder.”

## CHAPTER X

### Verses 1–2

**Now it happened after this that the king of the Ammonites died, etc.; I will do, etc.** (HIERON.) When David fled from the presence of Achish, king of Gath, he came to Nahash, king of the Ammonites, who showed him mercy. From Nahash he therefore came to the cave of Adullam, where his father, mother, and entire household came to him; from there he proceeded to Moab and left his father, mother, and entire household with him. When Achish, king of Gath, said, “Shall this man enter my house?” David departed from there and fled to the cave of Adullam (1 Sam. 21)—supply: from the house of Nahash. If it is asked why he returned to Achish, from whom he had previously fled, it must be understood that the one to whom he returned was the son of the man from whom he had fled. Hence later, concerning Achish, with whom David went down to battle, he is said to have been the son of Maoch. He did not take this patronymic from his father but from his mother, who was called Maacah.

### Verse 4

**So Hanun took David’s servants and shaved off half their beards, etc.** (RAB., from Eucherius.) These things signify the devil’s war against the Church. Hanun, that is, “their pain,” signifies the devil, who is the king of the Ammonites—that is, of the evil spirits, or the ruler of the people of sorrow, who is always established in anguish and desires to oppress or distress human beings. Hanun therefore shaves half the beard of David’s messengers when the devil, by corrupting them, stains the speech or conduct of certain preachers. He cuts their garments off at the hips when he reveals to human eyes the shameful deeds that he persuades them to commit. They must remain seated at Jericho until their beard grows, lest they become a reproach to others and a curse to all—that is, until virtues increase in them and they are deemed worthy to be presented to their king. Our David does not permit his soldiers to remain unavenged. Rather, having gathered his army, he avenges the injury done to his own; he not only confounds his adversaries through the victory of his saints but also hands them over to everlasting fires at the final judgment.

## CHAPTER XI

### Verse 1

**Now it happened at the return of the year, at the time when, etc.** (RAB., from Jerome.) That is, in spring, when, after the severity of the cold has been driven away, fodder is found for the animals, etc., up to “but they were conquered.”

### Verse 2

**While these things were happening.** (RAB.) David sinned grievously, etc., up to “who healed so grave a wound of sin through the confession of humility.”

**Bathsheba.** (ISID.) “Well of satiety,” or “seventh well.” The Church is called the well of living water, and the name of the number seven is joined to this well as a sign of the Holy Spirit, because of Pentecost, on which day the Holy Spirit was sent from heaven. To forty-nine—that is, seven times seven—one is added, because unity is commended. Hence: “Being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. 4). Thus, made by the spiritual gift, that is, by the sevenfold gift, the Church became the well of satiety, because in it there was made a fountain of water springing up into eternal life; whoever drinks of it will never thirst (John 4).

(GREG.) Still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh, we are unable to live in such a way that no pleasure of sin can assail us. But it is one thing to be unwilling to be touched, and another to consent. Holy men guard themselves with more watchful vigilance precisely because they disdain even to be touched momentarily by evil impulses. Thus, if the heart should perhaps desire something illicit, the eye, restrained by the discipline of instruction, refuses to look. For just as temptation is often drawn in through the eyes, so sometimes what has been conceived within compels the external eye to serve it. Often something is looked upon with an innocent mind, but in the very act of looking the soul is struck down by the sword of desire. David did not deliberately look upon Uriah’s wife because he had desired her; rather, he desired her because he looked incautiously. By a just examination of retribution, whoever negligently uses the external eye is blinded in the inner eye. Often desire already dominates within, and the enticed mind, by a tyrant’s authority, demands that the bodily senses serve its purposes and compels the eyes to serve its pleasures, opening the windows of light onto the darkness of blindness. Therefore, when holy men feel themselves assailed by an evil pleasure, they restrict the very lights through which the appearance of physical beauty enters the mind, by the discipline of instruction, lest vision, acting as a seductress, serve an evil thought. If this is ever neglected and not carefully guarded, the uncleanness of thought passes into action.

(GREG.) Often something is a virtue in the historical account but a fault in its meaning, just as at times a fault in the deed is a virtue in the prophetic writing. Who would not detest the fact that David, walking on the roof terrace, desired Bathsheba, Uriah’s wife, while nevertheless, when Uriah returned from battle, he urged him to go home and wash his feet? Uriah immediately replied: “The ark of God is under tents, and I shall rest in my own house?” David then received him at his own table and gave him the food by which he was to die.

David therefore represents the one of whom it is written: “He set his tabernacle in the sun” (Ps. 18). He orders Bathsheba to be brought to him—that is, he joins the law of the letter, united to the carnal people, to himself through a spiritual understanding. Bathsheba is called “the seventh well,” because through the kinship of the law, by the infusion of special grace, perfect wisdom is supplied to us. Uriah, however, signifies the Jewish people; his name is interpreted as “my light is God.” The Jewish people, exalted by the knowledge of the law it has received, glories as though in the light of God. But David took his wife away from him and joined her to himself, because the strong-handed Redeemer appeared and made it known that the law speaks spiritually of him. By the fact that the law was held according to the letter, he showed it to be estranged from the Jewish people and joined it to himself, because he declared that he was preached through it.

Yet David urges Uriah to go home and wash his feet, because, having become incarnate, he commands the Jews to return to their conscience and wipe away the filth of their deeds with tears, so that they may understand the commandments of the law in a special way and, after such hardness toward its precepts, find the fountain of baptism and hasten to the water after their labor. But Uriah, who remembers that the ark of the Lord is under tents, replies that he cannot enter his house. He says, as it were: “I see God’s commandments in carnal sacrifices, and I do not seek to return to my conscience through spiritual understanding.” He says that the ark of God is under tents because he understands God’s precepts only through the performance of carnal sacrifice.

David nevertheless calls Uriah, who refuses to return home, to his table, because, although the Jews disdain returning to their conscience, Christ still preaches spiritual things, saying: “If you believed Moses, you would perhaps believe me also, for he wrote about me” (John 5). The Jew holds the law, which speaks of Christ’s divinity, yet disdains to believe in him. Hence Uriah is sent to Joab with the letter by which he is to be killed, because the Jew carries the law by which he is convicted and condemned to death. For when he retains the commandments of the law and strives to fulfill them, he himself carries the judgment by which he will be condemned.

What, then, is more wicked than David in the deed? What is purer than Uriah? But in the mystery, what is holier than David? What is more faithless than Uriah? The one, through the fault of his life, signifies innocence in prophecy; the other, through innocence in his life, expresses guilt in prophecy. The virtue of sacred eloquence narrates past events in such a way as to express things to come; it approves a matter in the deed in such a way as to contradict it in the mystery. It condemns events as they occurred in such a way as to urge that they be enacted mystically.

### Verse 15

**“Set Uriah,” etc.** (GREG., *Moralia*, book XXXIII, chapter 10.) David’s and Peter’s sins were inserted into Scripture for this purpose: that the fall of the great might serve as a warning to the lesser, etc., up to “therefore, by the hidden order of providence, from the point at which the devil’s iniquity is permitted to rage, the goodness of God is perfected, because from the point at which he exercises the anger of his will, he obeys the commands of heavenly grace.”

## CHAPTER XII

### Verse 13

**And Nathan said to David, etc.** (RAB., from Eucherius.) Nevertheless, he afterward endured all the things that had been foretold to him because of his sin. God removes guilt but does not leave it unpunished. Either a person punishes himself through repentance, or God strikes while taking vengeance together with the person. Sin is therefore not spared, because it is not released without punishment. Thus David deserved to hear, after his confession: “The Lord has transferred your sin,” and yet, after many later torments, he escaped while expiating the guilt he had committed. Thus, by the water of salvation, we are absolved from the guilt of our first parent, but even after being absolved we still die bodily, because God cuts away our sins either through us or through himself, even when he forgives them. For he strives to wipe away, through temporal affliction, the stains of iniquity from his elect—stains that he does not wish to see in them forever.

### Verse 27

**And Joab sent messengers, etc.** (RAB.) This victory of David, which Joab began, etc., up to “and in the Gospel it is said: ‘Many will come from the east and the west and will recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven’” (Matt. 8).

**City of waters, etc.** Because of the abundance of water that was there; or, as some say, because of its abundance of peoples.

### Verse 30

**And he took, etc.** (RAB.) In Chronicles it is read this way: “David took the crown of Milcom from his head, and found in it a talent by weight of gold and very precious gems. And he made a crown for himself from it” (1 Chron. 20). For Milcom is not a proper name but is interpreted as “their king.” Milcom, according to the Hebrews, was the idol of the Ammonites. David is said to have melted down and purified the gold and gems of its crown according to the law and made a crown for himself.

## CHAPTER XIII

### Verse 6

**Little bowls.** Something suitable for sipping.

### Verse 14

**He overpowered her.** (RAB.) The incest of Amnon, David’s eldest son, with his sister Tamar, and Absalom’s murder of his brother Amnon warn us always to act cautiously, lest vices dominate us and the prince of sin—who promises a false peace to those in danger—find us unprepared and slaughter us unexpectedly. For Absalom is interpreted as “father of peace” or “the peace of the father”; Amnon as “giving”; and Tamar as “bitterness.” Whoever gives his members to lust and serves iniquity for iniquity’s sake falls into the bitterness of sin, even though the enemy presents himself as a father of peace and promises prosperity for such deeds. We must return quickly to repentance, lest the devil, through evil spirits, conspire for our destruction and hand us over to perpetual death.

### Verse 15

**And he hated her, etc.** We too should hate the crime committed more than we loved it before its perpetration. For this reason we shall obtain forgiveness more quickly, provided that we do not again offend through another vice, as Amnon did. Because he did not avoid drunkenness after the incest, he therefore did not escape death.

### Verse 37

**Talmai.** He was the father of Maacah, Absalom’s mother. The Hebrews say that David captured her in battle and, after cutting her hair and nails according to the law, took her as his wife and fathered Tamar and Absalom by her.

### Verse 39

**And he ceased.** In the Hebrew: “The king ceased going out after Absalom.” David is said to have wanted to go out after Absalom in order to call him back; but, thinking that whenever he saw him the death of Amnon would be brought back to memory, he ceased going out.

## CHAPTER XIV

### Verse 6

**And the maidservant, etc.** (HIERON.) The Hebrews say that this woman truly had two sons who contended over the inheritance, and that one was killed by the other. The woman, however, placed herself in David’s role, and the sons in the roles of Amnon and Absalom; the kindred who rise up against the son represented David’s other sons.

### Verse 9

**Upon me, my lord.** (ID.) As though she were saying: “Because one rose up against the other, let the iniquity be upon me, if there must be any; but let there be none upon you, because you are without guilt. Just as I am without guilt if one of my sons was killed by the other, so are you if Absalom killed Amnon, who deserved death.”

## CHAPTER XV

### Verse 1

**So, after this.** He remained in Jerusalem for two years and did not see the king; in the third year he was brought before the king; in the fourth year he made chariots and horsemen for himself. After that period he drove his father from the kingdom. He was not expelled from the kingdom for the seduction and killing of the priests, but for adultery and murder, as Nathan had foretold everything.

### Verse 7

**After forty years.** (HIERON., *Questions on the Books of Kings*, vol. III.) The fortieth year was being completed from the time when Saul overthrew the city of Nob, etc., up to “Isaac and Jacob.”

### Verse 24

**And they set down the ark, etc.** So that God might be consulted through Abiathar the priest concerning where David should go.

### Verse 25

**Zadok.** “Righteous” represents the saints, who at the time of the Lord’s Passion departed bodily but were not separated in love.

### Verse 32

**Hushai.** David’s friend. Hushai is interpreted as “hastening.” Returning to Jerusalem, he disrupted Ahithophel’s counsel; he signifies the Lord’s hidden disciples from among the Jews—Nicodemus, Joseph, and others like them.

## CHAPTER XVI

### Verses 9–10

**What is it to me?** Only Abishai had said: “I will go and cut him off.” David replied to Abishai and Joab: “What is it to me? Do you perhaps wish to kill this man as you killed Abner?”

**Let him alone.** (GREG., *Moralia*, book XXX, chapter 9.) Whoever, oppressed by verbal insults, cannot or does not have the strength to preserve the virtue of patience, etc., up to “through whose intervention, with God as judge, a harsher punishment is averted.”

### Verse 13

**But Shimei.** (RAB.) According to the Hebrews, this is Nabath, the father of Jeroboam. He is called the son of Jemini and curses David out of zeal for the house of Saul. His grandfather’s name, however, was Jemini. Shimei himself belonged to the tribe of Ephraim, the son of Joseph; hence he says to David: “Today I am the first to come from the entire tribe of Joseph.” But, as is read above, Shimei was related to Saul. Saul, however, was from Benjamin. In Ezra, Shimei is read as the son of Kish, because his father was called both Kish and Gera; he is read here as the son of Jemini, that is, Benjamin. Yet he is said to have come first from the tribe of Joseph because he lived in the territory of the tribe of Joseph.

### Verse 15

**Ahithophel.** (RAB.) He is interpreted as “ruin of a brother.” Judas, working toward Christ’s ruin, gave counsel to the Jews against Christ; both died by hanging.

## CHAPTER XVII

### Verse 10

**And the strongest.** (HIERON.) In the Hebrew: “The strongest man, whose heart is like a lion’s, will utterly melt with fear.” Supply: “This does not refer to David as the strongest man.” Hence: “For he knows.”

(ISID., *On the First Book of Kings*.) Allegorically, one must consider, etc., up to “from whose face Christ fled when he abandoned it and passed over to the Gentiles.”

### Verse 14

**Absalom.** Others understand Absalom as Judas the betrayer, whom Christ endured as though he did not know his thoughts, and with whom he shared a meal, in which he commended to the disciples the figure of his body and blood. In the very act of betrayal he received a kiss from him. Therefore Absalom is called “peace of peace,” because the father had the peace that Judas did not have.

Achitophel. (RAB.) He who, departing from David, etc., up to [the point] that, like Achitophel, he perished by hanging in his own house, although he had plotted against David’s life in another’s [house]. For “he who digs a pit will fall into it,” and “the wicked will be caught by their own schemes” (Prov. XI; XXV).

Hushai. (ID.) The ancient friend of David, the Archite, etc., up to [the point] that they might be converted through the occasion of receiving benefits.

(ID.) But as for Jonathan, whose name is interpreted as “house of the dove,” and his brother Ahimaaz, who, fleeing from Absalom, resolved to investigate Absalom’s deed and report it to David, etc., up to [the point] that men protected from the enemy’s persecution are delivered.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 9.**—It happened that Absalom encountered David’s servants while riding a mule. (RAB.) Absalom, fleeing on a mule, was hanged in an oak by the hair of his head, etc., up to [the point] that they pass into the dispersion of the nations; they lost both their leadership and their people together.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 22.**—“What is it to me?” David feared that, if Shimei were killed, the others who had likewise offended the king would refuse to make him their king.

**VERSE 24.**—“Unwashed.” In the Hebrew, “stained” (*infectis*; the reading is uncertain). For he had made himself wooden feet, according to the Hebrew, which he used instead of natural ones; for he was lame.

**VERSE 29.**—“You and Ziba.” (HIERON., *Hebrew Questions on Samuel*.) In the Hebrew: “I said, ‘You and Ziba divide the field.’” David, forgetful of the covenant and oath, etc., up to [the point] that he uttered words obliquely against the Most High.

**VERSE 37.**—“But he is.” In the Hebrew it reads: “Behold, your servant”—in Hebrew, *Chimehan the Canaanite*. “Canaan” is interpreted as “one sighing.” As long as he was with his father, he was called “one sighing”; but after he passed over to David’s instruction, he was called not *Canaan* but *Chimehan*, that is, “faithful,” etc., up to: “Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine like Reuben and Simeon.” Thus the great Moses and Joshua his successor allotted them a double portion.

## CHAPTER XX

**VERSE 9.**—“And he held,” etc. To hold the chin with the right hand is, as it were, to flatter someone out of kindness. But he sends his left hand to the sword who secretly strikes out of malice.

**VERSE 19.**—“Is she not?” (RAB.) This is the command of the Law, in which it is ordered that the Israelites, after entering the land of Canaan, first offer peace and make tributaries of those who accept peace, but destroy those who do not accept it. Therefore the wise woman is said to have cried out, “Is she not?”—as though she were saying: “Why are you destroying this city before offering peace according to the Law? Why do you not observe for the Israelites the Law that was once observed for foreigners?”

**VERSE 22.**—“Who was cut off.” (ID.) The return of the people to David after Absalom’s death, etc., up to [the point] that he returned, that is, Christ the Son of God.

## CHAPTER XXI

**VERSE 1.**—“There was.” (RAB.) A famine occurred in Israel because of the Gibeonites, etc., up to [the point] that they might no longer corrupt their lives by giving wicked advice.

**VERSE 8.**—“Therefore the king took two.” These, while still boys, killed the priests and the Gibeonites together with Doeg the Edomite—namely, Armoni and Mephibosheth.

“Her sons by Michal the daughter,” etc. Michal, David’s wife, who is also called Eglah, adopted them as her own sons among the children whom her sister Merab had received from the son of Barzillai.

**VERSE 18.**—“Gob.” This is interpreted as “pool,” because, just as someone is thrown into a pool of lions, so David sent himself against Goliath.

**VERSES 19, 20.**—“The third.” Josephus speaks in this way about the third battle, etc., up to [the point] that it is uncertain whether he called him Adeodatus or someone else.

“The fourth”: Goliath is mentioned again, referring to the battle David fought at the beginning, in Saul’s time. For in Chronicles he is recorded as having fought against the Philistines principally only for the third time.

(RAB.) The four battles of David and his servants, etc., up to [the point] where it says: “The salvation of man is vain. In God we shall act valiantly, and he himself will bring to nothing those who afflict us” (Ps. CVII).

“Bethlehemites,” etc. Because Naomi and Ruth, from whom he was descended, returned to Bethlehem during a time of abundance, and because Ruth’s association with bread is well known, that place was called “House of Bread.” Or because Naomi, together with her daughter-in-law, returned there and obtained an abundance of bread in the house of Boaz.

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 1.**—“He spoke,” etc. (RAB.) Only the seventeenth psalm is found in the Books of Kings, etc., up to [the point] that the gifts granted by the divinity are praised with great rejoicing.

## CHAPTER XXIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Now these are.” (HIERON.) They are the last [words], because he is said to have composed this poem after the Psalter and the other poetic meters. In it he says: “David son of Jesse speaks; the man speaks for whom it was established concerning the Christ of the God of Jacob.”

(RAB.) Because they signify the final praise of confession, which the saints will sing forever after conquering the enemy and completing the victory over death.

“Eminent.” Because he prophesied most brilliantly about Christ God, his incarnation, and the redemption of the human race.

**VERSE 3.**—“In the fear.” He who exercises authority over his subjects in the fear of God brings forth works of light illumined by the Sun of Justice. Nothing obscure remains in them; rather, watered by the rain of heavenly grace, while living in the flesh he produces the shoots of virtue as fruit.

**VERSE 5.**—“Nor is there.” (RAB.) He who meditates on the Law of the Lord day and night becomes like a tree planted beside streams, which yields its fruit in its season, and everything he does prospers.

**VERSE 7.**—“And if anyone.” Namely, the one who, because of the hardness of his heart, shares in the sins of others, is weighed down by the burden of iniquities and pierced by the arrows of sinners; his works, deserving of eternal fires, will be reduced to nothing.

**VERSE 8.**—“These are the names.” (ISID.) A catalogue of strong men is woven as a figure of the saints. Although they advance in the sublimity of virtues, they nevertheless do not attain to the excellence of the divine Trinity. For this is what is written: “He did not reach the first three.” For “who among the sons of God will be equal to the Lord in the clouds?”

“Strong men.” Concerning these strong men Josephus says: “The first of all was Eusebius son of Achimaea, who, frequently breaking through the enemy’s battle line, did not cease until he had killed nine hundred. After him was Eleazar son of Dodo, who had been with the king at Sarpha. When the Israelites feared the army of the Philistines and were fleeing, he alone stood his ground and killed many, so that the sword clung to his right hand because of the blood of those he had killed. But when the Israelites saw the Philistines turned to flight, they came down from the mountains in pursuit of them, and a famous victory came to the Israelites. The third was Semeias son of Heli, who, at the place of the jawbone, when the Hebrews were fleeing, alone bore the army of the Philistines, striking some down and putting others to flight.”

“He himself.” (RAB.) The rod from the root of Jesse produced a flower without marital intercourse. From one man who prefigured the nations, by a single assault—that is, by the command of his word—he expelled a legion of demons.

“Most tender of wood.” (ID.) The military and disciplined virtue of the man is signified, etc., up to [the point] that his strength is shown in the killing of eight hundred.

**VERSE 11.**—“Shammah son.” “Hearing.”

“Age,” etc. “Meditating” or “speaking.”

“Harari.” A highlander, who bears the role of Christ or of his preachers.

**VERSE 12.**—“He stood.” (RAB.) Christ, standing with the Holy Spirit in the field of the Church, protects the weak as barley; or, certainly, he defends the shame of chastity in the incontinent, as though reaping, with the sword of his mouth against lust.

**VERSE 13.**—“The three descended.” The three strong men named above: Jeshboam son of Hachamoni, whom Josephus calls Eusebius son of Achimaea; Eleazar son of Ahohi, whom he says was the son of Dodo; and Shammah son of Age, whom he calls Semeias son of Heli. But the Hebrews think that these three were Abishai son of Zeruiah, Sibbecai the Hushathite, and Jonathan son of Shammah, David’s brother, who were mentioned above in the battles against the Philistines. The following seems to agree with this opinion: “Abishai also, the brother of Joab, son of Zeruiah,” etc. For from this it is evident that Abishai was a leader and was named among the three who follow.

(GREG.) We must consider that one who has committed unlawful acts should abstain even from certain lawful things, so that by this he may satisfy his Creator: one who has committed what was forbidden should cut himself off even from what was permitted, and should rebuke himself in small matters, remembering that he sinned in great ones. The Law of the Old Testament forbids coveting another man’s wife; but it does not prohibit the king, under penalty, from ordering brave deeds of his soldiers or desiring water. David, however, coveted and took another man’s wife. Worthy blows followed that fault, and he corrected the evil he had committed through the lamentations of repentance. Later, when he had taken his position opposite the enemy’s ranks, he desired water from their cistern. His chosen soldiers broke through the enemy’s companies and brought him the water he had desired without injury. But the man trained by scourging immediately rebuked himself for desiring water at the risk of his soldiers, and poured it out before the Lord as a libation. For the water poured out was transformed into a sacrifice to the Lord, because through the repentance of his self-rebuke he slaughtered the guilt of his desire. Thus the one who had not feared to covet another man’s wife afterward became afraid because he had coveted water.

**VERSE 16.**—“But he poured it out.” He gave the soldiers an example of courage and steadfastness, conquering nature so that, though thirsty, he would not drink, in order that the army might learn to endure thirst.

In the mystical sense, however, he did not thirst for water but foresaw Christ, who would be born in Bethlehem from a virgin; he thirsted for his washing and blood. Therefore he did not drink the water but poured it out. For he thirsted for the eternal fountain, which is not sought through the dangers of others but washes away the dangers of others.

**VERSE 19.**—“The first three.” They wish wisdom, humility, and courage to be understood. David sat as the wisest; he himself, the little worm of wood—that is, the humble man—killed eight hundred as a strong man. None of David’s strong men reached these three virtues.

**VERSE 20.**—“And Benaiah.” He was a master from Kabzeel, that is, from the assembly of God, among the Cherethites and Pelethites, names interpreted as “those who kill” and “those who give life.” He struck down the men whom Chronicles calls the two Ariels of Moab. These men, therefore, had been very powerful in the kingdom of Moab, and for that reason they are also called lions. For *Ariel* is interpreted as “lion of God.”

“In the middle.” Josephus explains more clearly what this was: a very deep cistern, leveled with a heap of snow during winter. A lion unknowingly fell into it, and, trapped there, cried out with a great roar. Benaiah, who had come with the others to watch, leapt into the cistern and killed the lion. Benaiah, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord is builder,” signifies Christ, who builds the Church. Hence Paul says: “You are God’s building.” During the time of snow and cold—that is, when the grace of Christ shone upon the world and the coldness of charity refreshed human beings—he killed the lion, that is, the devil. But the Hebrew understands this lion as Moab, who was killed in the middle of the cistern, that is, in the house of the Lord, where he held the horns of the altar. The altar is called a cistern because, just as the water of a cistern washes and cleanses, so the sanctuary of the Lord purifies sins. “In the days of snow,” because he expiated sin through death. Hence: “You will wash me,” which was fulfilled in the middle of the cistern; and “I shall be whiter than snow,” which was fulfilled in the statement “in the days of snow.”

**[Col. 0579C] VERSE 21.**—“An Egyptian man.” Namely, an imitator of the Egyptian who blasphemed God and whom Moses killed at the Lord’s command. That man blasphemed God; this one, the prophet and king.

“Worthy.” For he was watched so that, if he came out from Jerusalem, he would be killed.

“Spear.” The Law of God: if he had meditated on it by remaining in Jerusalem, he would not have perished. But because he despised the king’s command, Benaiah came down against him with a staff, that is, with the uprightness of justice, and wrested away the spear that he was not holding properly.

**VERSE 23.**—“Those who were.” No one was troubled by the fact that, in the total, not thirty but thirty-seven are read. Thirty-seven are counted in this way: seven, namely, these strong men—David, who is called Adeodatus; Abishai; Sibbecai; Jonathan; Eleazar; Shammah son of Age the Hararite; and Benaiah—there are seven. The thirty are Asahel, Elhanan, and the others.

**VERSE 39.**—“Uriah.” He is placed last because of what follows: “And the anger of the Lord was kindled,” etc. For vengeance had already been carried out against David and his house, but not against the people, who either did not resist David or consented to him.

## CHAPTER XXIV

(GREG., *Moral Works*, book XXV, chapter 14.) According to the qualities of the subjects, etc., up to [the point] that, just as the deeds of teachers are displeasing, so the mind of the subjects should not withdraw from reverence for their teacher.

(HIERON.) It should be noted that in Chronicles it is written: “A thousand thousand and one hundred thousand from Israel, and from Judah four hundred seventy thousand,” which must be understood as numbers Joab counted but did not wish to disclose, except for the number written in the Book of Samuel.

**VERSE 10.**—“But he struck,” etc. (AMBR., *On Repentance*, chapter 9.) He submitted himself to the greater punishment so that he might arouse clemency. For the severity of justice is softened, etc., up to [the point] that the devastation poured down from heaven against the people would cease.

**VERSE 11.**—“The word of the Lord.” (RAB.) In Exodus it is written, etc., up to [the point] that seventy thousand were consumed.

**VERSE 13.**—“Or.” And it appears that those who are not fed with the bread of God’s word through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit suffer famine for seven years; those who have not been reborn in the name of the Trinity are unable to resist enemies, that is, demons; and, unbelieving, they die from the pestilence of impiety.

**VERSE 16.**—“Now there was.” (RAB.) It is also written in Chronicles: “Moreover, the angel of the Lord stood beside the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite. And David lifted his eyes and saw the angel of the Lord standing between heaven and earth, with a drawn sword in his hand, turned against Jerusalem. And both he and the elders, clothed in sackcloth, fell prostrate on the ground beside the threshing floor.” The threshing floor is the Church of the nations, in which, after the true David erected the altar of faith, the death of impiety immediately ceased. David bought this threshing floor for fifty shekels, because through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit Christ sanctified the gentile people, with all sins abandoned, as an everlasting house for himself.

**VERSE 18.**—“Araunah.” (ID.) It is interpreted as “threshing floor”; Ornan, however, means “light for us.” Therefore David, wishing to appease the Lord, is rightly commanded to establish an altar on the threshing floor of Araunah, or Ornan, because God cannot otherwise be pleased by a human being unless, on the threshing floor of the heart, through the light of right faith and true love, he establishes an altar of humility on which he may offer a sacrifice of offering and praise. Hence: “The sacrifice of praise will honor me,” etc. (Ps. XLIX). “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit,” etc. (ibid. L). The threshing floor of Araunah or Ornan is Jerusalem itself.

**[Col. 0580D] VERSE 25.**—“And he offered burnt offerings.” From this it appears in Chronicles that the tabernacle Moses had made in the desert and the altar of burnt offerings were at that time on the high place at Gibeon, and David was unable to go to the altar to entreat the Lord. For he had been terrified by excessive fear when he saw the sword of the Lord’s angel. And David said: “This is the house of God,” etc. According to the Hebrews, Abraham wished to offer his son at this place when a ram suddenly appeared; taking it, he offered it in place of his son.

**[Col. 0581]**

# THE THIRD BOOK OF KINGS

According to the Hebrews, **THE FIRST BOOK OF KINGS (*Malachim*)**. (G)*

## CHAPTER I

**[Col. 0581A] VERSE 1.**—“And King David had grown old.” (HIERON., *Letter to Nepotianus*, vol. I.) Does it not seem to you, if you follow the letter literally, to be a fable or the jest of an Atellan farce? An old man, cold, is wrapped in clothing and does not grow warm unless embraced by a young girl. Bathsheba was still alive, etc., up to [the point] where Rahab the prostitute, as a type of the Church, hung out a scarlet cord containing the mystery of blood, so that her house might be saved when Jericho perished. Hence it is said concerning the saints: “These are the ones who came from the heat of the house of Rechab” (I Chron. II). And elsewhere: “I came to cast fire upon the earth” (Luke XII), etc., namely, the fire that, kindled in the hearts of the disciples, compelled them to say: “Was not our heart burning?” (ibid., XXIV).
