“And when he was covered,” etc. David suffered extreme cold either because he had been born of elderly parents, or because he had shed much blood in battle, or, rather, because from the time when he saw the angel striking down the people he wasted away in great fear. Therefore he remained in the discomfort of cold even until death.

**VERSE 5.**—“But Adonijah.” He signifies the Jewish people, who seem to be the elder son because they received the Law first. Despising the gentile people, who were called later through the grace of God, he thought that he alone would reign with the Lord. For Adonijah is interpreted as “lordly ruler.” But the people of the Church, together with the true Solomon—that is, our Peaceful One, whose body it is—is installed in the kingdom by divine ordinance. Accordingly, the elder son, that is, the earlier people, is deservedly cast down because of his unbelief.

## CHAPTER II

**[Col. 0581C] VERSE 5.**—“You also.” David instructed Solomon concerning the just recompense of those who had been a support to him or had unjustly harmed him, whom he himself had patiently endured. Prophecy indicates what evil or good must occur in the future, which the true Solomon will fulfill. Meanwhile, God’s patience often permits the good to be afflicted and the wicked to enjoy pleasures.

**VERSE 19.**—“Therefore Bathsheba went to the king.” (RAB.) Adonijah, through Bathsheba’s intervention, etc., up to [the point] that neither does the Law exist, which the Jews think is their helper before God.

**VERSE 36.**—“And you shall not go out,” etc. The true Solomon commands us who dwell in Jerusalem never to go out. If those who were previously subject to us flee from us, we should not therefore go out to follow the tracks of fugitives, lest, while wishing to save those who flee, we ourselves perish. Rather, let the dead bury their dead, and, while it is permitted, let us tear out and cut away from ourselves the eye, hand, or foot that causes scandal.

## CHAPTER III

**[Col. 0582A] VERSE 4.**—“Therefore Solomon went.” At Gibeon there was a very great high place, where the tabernacle Moses had made stood, together with the bronze altar. Upon this altar Solomon offered a thousand victims and deserved a divine oracle.

**VERSE 14.**—“But if you walk in my ways,” etc. Without observing God’s commandments, no one can attain long days, that is, blessedness.

(GREG., *Moral Works*, book VIII, chapter 17.) After the Lord illumines the darkness of our error with the light of his knowledge, etc., up to [the point] that we may be restored to the substance of the promised incorruption.

(HIER., letter 131, vol. I.) Some think that this should be understood concerning the Synagogue and the Church, etc., up to [the point] where it must also be noted what the Church says against the Synagogue.

**VERSE 17.**—“I and the woman.” For after the Savior’s resurrection one people was gathered from both peoples. Elegantly he added: “I gave birth beside her in the chamber.” The Church from the gentiles, which did not possess the Law and the Prophets, gave birth in the house of the Synagogue; she did not leave the chamber but entered it. Hence: “The king brought me into his chamber” (Song II). And: “I will bring you into the house of my mother and into her chamber who conceived me” (ibid., III).

(RAB.) If you consider Pilate washing his hands and saying: “I am innocent of the blood of this righteous man” (Matt. XXVII); the centurion confessing: “Truly this was the Son of God” (Mark XV); and those who, before the Passion, wished to see the Lord through Philip, you will not doubt that the Church gave birth first. Afterwards she gave birth to the Jewish people, for whom the Lord prayed: “Father, forgive them,” etc.; and three thousand believed in one day, and another five thousand.

(GREG.) Through the nursing mothers the order of teachers, etc., up to [the point] that they receive their sons whole and alive when, at the final judgment, they obtain a perfect recompense from their way of life.

**VERSE 19.**—“He died.” (RAB.) While she follows the observance of the Law and joins the grace of the Gospel to the Law, she is covered by the error of darkness.

**VERSE 20.**—“She took the son.” Alive, namely—not in order to possess him but to kill him. For she did this not out of love for the son but out of hatred for her rival.

**VERSE 21.**—“When she looked more carefully,” etc. (RAB.) It would take too long to show how, through Paul and the other ecclesiastical writers, the Church understood that he who was feared under the Law was not her son, and recognized in the light the one whom she had not seen in the darkness. The two women, one of whom burned with love while dissimulation had crept into the other, represent the Church and the Synagogue, or heretical perversity. Each wickedly kills her own children by nourishing them, and persuades others by drawing them in until she destroys them. Between the two women, the Lord, while deciding what is just by the spirit of his mouth, restores to each what is due.

**VERSE 24.**—“Then he said.” (RAB.) Pretending ignorance, he measures human affections according to the dispensation of the flesh, as also where he says: “Where have you laid him?” (John XX); and elsewhere: “Who touched me?” (Luke VIII).

**VERSE 25.**—“Divide.” (ID.) The Lord tests nature through nature and wishes, according to the will of both women, to divide the living son between the Law and grace—not because he approves this, but he says that he wishes it in order to expose the Synagogue’s accusation.

**VERSE 26.**—“But she said.” (ID.) The Church, knowing that he is hers, willingly concedes him to her rival, so that he may at least live with her, lest, divided between the Law and grace, he be struck by Christ’s sword. Hence: “Behold, I, Paul, say to you that if you observe the Law, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. V).

## CHAPTER IV

**VERSE 22.**—“Solomon’s food.” (RAB.) The nourishment of Christ, who is fed by right faith and good works, which the Catholic Church offers to him daily.

**VERSE 23.**—“Twenty oxen.” (ID.) The preachers of the New Testament, who bear within themselves, as it were, a doubled Decalogue, since they preach the New and Old Testaments equally, filled with love of God and neighbor.

“Excepting the game.” There are various animals that are caught daily in the nets of the Gospel by spiritual hunters from different nations and are brought into the Savior’s pasture.

**VERSE 26.**—“Forty,” etc. The forty periods signify the ancient Law: Moses fasted forty days in order to receive it, and the people instructed by it remained forty years in the desert.

“And twelve.” This number signifies the present time, in which apostolic teaching nourishes the people of the New Testament.

**VERSE 28.**—“Barley,” etc. So that nothing may be lacking in the king’s house, the order of preachers labors by writing and speaking, so that the Lord’s table may abound with what will nourish the faithful.

**[Col. 0583D] VERSE 32.**—“And his songs numbered.” It is certain that neither Solomon’s songs nor his discussions exist today.

“Five thousand.” Because of the five senses: whoever governs them well through various virtues is blessed, and through them sings five thousand songs to the Lord, as it were.

**VERSE 33.**—“Hyssop.” (RAB.) Hyssop, a humble herb clinging to rock, etc., up to [the point] that it then bent the cedar—that is, the arrogance of the world—down to the humility of hyssop, that is, to the foolishness of the cross.

“And he discoursed.” (ID.) For everything is naked and open to Christ (Hebr. IV). He discourses when he sets before us in his Scriptures the rationale of each thing and reveals the mysteries that had been hidden from ages and generations, so that we may consider the blessedness of angels, the usefulness of human beings, and the cunning of demons; and, rejecting what is evil, pursue what is good.

## CHAPTER V

**VERSE 3.**—“And because he could not build the house,” etc. (BEDA, *Questions on the Book of Kings*.) The house Solomon built was a figure of the Church, etc., up to [the point] where it shows, in certain cases, human struggles rewarded together with the angels.

(ID., *On Solomon’s Temple*, chapter 1.) This spiritual house is also signified by the tabernacle made in the wilderness, etc., up to [the point] where it displays and prefigures the salvation of all nations in Christ in many ways.

**[Col. 0584B] VERSE 6.**—“Therefore command that they cut down for me,” etc. (RAB.) Hiram’s servants cut down cedars for Solomon from Lebanon, etc., up to [the point] that they knew the errors of the gentiles better and therefore overcame them with greater skill.

“For you know that there is no man among my people who knows how to cut timber,” etc. (BEDA, as above.) We must speak first about the workers of the temple, both where they came from and what sort of people they were, and about the material itself, etc., up to [the point] concerning wheat, namely, the word of God, and oil, namely, charity, anointing, and the illumination of the Holy Spirit.

**VERSE 10.**—“And Hiram gave Solomon cedar timber and fir timber, according to all,” etc. Tyre, from which King Hiram came, is an island devoted to commerce. There were excellent craftsmen of wood there, who supplied precious timber in exchange for food. For they live not by cultivating fields but by trading. There is Mount Lebanon, from whose trees the house of the Lord was made. Hence it is said of it: “Open your gates, O Lebanon” (Zech. XI).

**VERSE 13.**—“And King Solomon chose.” (BEDA, as above, chapter 3.) He did not choose workers from all Israel without reason, etc., up to [the point] where the mind of the faithful is regarded by the Lord in daily illumination like the moon by the sun.

“Workers from all Israel, and the levy was thirty thousand men.” These workers were proselytes. Their overseers were Jews, because he did not make anyone from Israel serve.

**VERSE 14.**—“Adoniram was over this levy.” (BEDA, ibid.) “My exalted lord.” This is Christ, who is placed over the workers of the temple, etc., up to [the point] that through prayers and fasts she may be worthy before the heavenly inspector and visitor.

**VERSE 15.**—“Solomon had seventy thousand of those who carried burdens and eighty thousand stonecutters in the mountain.” (BEDA, ibid.) It should not be passed over that the seventy thousand burden-bearers and eighty thousand stonecutters, together with their overseers, were not Israelites, etc., up to [the point] where it says: “Admonish the idle, encourage the fainthearted,” etc. (I Thess. V).

“Stonecutters.” (BEDA, ibid.) Stonecutters are those who cut stones, etc., up to [the point] that, rescued from the power of darkness, we reach the citadel of virtues, which is found in the unity of the Church.

**[Col. 0585A] VERSE 16.**—“Apart from the overseers.” The overseers are the authors of Sacred Scripture, whose instruction trains us to teach the ignorant, rebuke the contemptuous, and bear one another’s burdens.

“Three thousand.” Because of faith in the Trinity, which the sacred utterances proclaim. The fact that Chronicles records three thousand six hundred refers to their perfection. For the number six, in which the adornment of the world was completed, signifies the perfect works of the good; and because Sacred Scripture teaches that works of justice are to be practiced together with faith in the truth, it is rightly said that the overseers of the temple works numbered three thousand six hundred.

**VERSE 17.**—“And the king commanded them to quarry.” (BEDA, ibid.) In building the house of the Lord, timber and stones are first cut from the mountain, etc., up to [the point] where it says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. II).

“Great stones.” (BEDA, ibid., chapter 4.) Or, “precious, great, squared stones”: these are the first teachers, who heard the word of salvation from the Lord himself. The courses of stones or timbers laid above them are the priests and teachers who follow, through whose preaching the Church grows and is adorned with virtues.

(RAB. from Beda.) What color the stones were, etc., up to [the point] that white marble, from which the house of the elect was constructed, signifies clean action and a conscience chastened from every blemish of corruption. Hence: “Let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement,” etc. (II Cor. VII).

“For the foundation of the temple.” (BEDA, ibid.) The foundation is Christ, etc., up to [the point] that, once useless words, deeds, and thoughts have been rejected, they may become worthy to bear the burden of the Church.

**VERSE 18.**—“The Giblites prepared the timber and the stones.” (RAB. from Beda, ibid.) Gebal is a city of Phoenicia, etc., up to [the point] that the one who presumes to teach what he himself has not learned builds not a sanctuary for the Lord but a ruin for himself.

“For building the house.” (ID., ibid.) After the foundation has been composed from such materials, the house must be built from prepared timber and stones placed in order. They have been drawn away from their former position because, after the first rudiments of faith and after the foundations of humility have been laid in us according to the example of sublime men, a wall of good works must be added upward; and, as though by courses of stones laid one upon another, we must advance from virtue to virtue.

## CHAPTER VI

**VERSE 1.**—“And it came to pass.” (RAB. from Beda, *On Solomon’s Temple*, chapter 5.) The exodus from Egypt is recalled, etc., up to [the point] that Scripture which would disclose the grace of the New Testament was not absent from the Old.

“In the fourth year.” The house began to be built in the fourth year of King Solomon, because, after the dispensation of Christ’s incarnation had been completed and written in the four Gospels, the structure of the Church began when the Holy Spirit was sent.

“In the month of Ziv”—that is, the second month. (BEDA, ibid.) Since it was in the second month, etc., up to [the point] where it is clear that, immediately after the Passover had been completed, he began to build the house of the Lord, and the people, consecrated by a mystical solemnity, set their hands to the mystical work.

“He began to build.” (ID., ibid.) Where the temple was built is made clear in Chronicles, etc., up to [the point] that she was established not merely in external but in inward peace, which she possessed with her Creator.

“What David had prepared,” etc. David had prepared the place for the Lord by singing psalms, while the other prophets prepared it by prophesying—for the true Solomon, who would build the house there—because they established the hearts of their hearers in faith, urging them to receive the incarnate Son of God with faithful devotion. Hence: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, for they are already white for harvest; and he who reaps receives a reward and gathers fruit for eternal life, so that the one who sows may rejoice together with the one who reaps” (John IV). This means: “Lift up your eyes and see the place prepared for building the house.” The one who builds by teaching receives a reward and gathers precious stones for eternal life, so that both the one who prepares the place for the building and the one who builds may rejoice together: that is, the prophet who foretells the one to come and the apostle who preaches the Lord who has come may share one reward.

“In length,” etc. The length of the house signifies the Church’s long-suffering, by which it patiently endures adversity until it reaches its homeland. It is sixty cubits long because the number six signifies the perfection of good works: through long-suffering we must endure adversity in such a way that through good works we may deserve to enter the promised homeland.

“Twenty cubits.” Because of the twofold extension of charity, by which we love God and our neighbor.

“In breadth.” Breadth signifies charity, which, with the bosom of the mind expanded, loves friends in God and enemies for God’s sake, until, when they have been converted to peace or utterly destroyed, she rejoices in the Lord with friends alone.

(BEDA, ibid.) It should be noted that the thirty cubits of height did not reach to the roof of the temple but only to the lower upper chamber. It is clearly written in Chronicles that the height was one hundred twenty cubits. The mysteries of this matter will be treated more suitably below, when the order of the reading reaches the middle and third upper chambers.

**[Col. 0586D] “Thirty cubits.”** Because of faith in the Trinity, in whose vision all the desires of our hope are suspended. The individual numbers are multiplied by ten because through faith and observance of the Law patience is beneficially exercised, charity burns manfully, and hope is raised sublimely toward eternal things.

“In height.” Height signifies hope of future reward, for whose sake he despises prosperity and adversity until he sees the goodness of the Lord in the land of the living.

**VERSE 3.**—“There was a portico,” etc. Concerning this it is written in Chronicles: “The portico before the front, which extended lengthwise according to the measure of the breadth, twenty cubits” (II Chron. III). It is therefore clear that this portico was built on the eastern side of the temple. The temple faced east, as did the tabernacle, and according to Josephus it had a door on the east opposite the door of the temple, so that the rising equinoctial sun, with its rays directed in straight lines through the three doors—namely, those of the portico, the temple, and the oracle—might illuminate the ark of the covenant. The temple signifies the Church; the portico, which stood before the temple and first received the sunlight, signifies that part of the Church that preceded the Lord’s incarnation. In it the patriarchs and prophets first received the rising Sun of Justice, and by living, preaching, being born, and dying bore witness to the Lord who was born in the flesh.

“Twenty cubits in length, according to the measure of the temple’s breadth.” (BEDA, *On Solomon’s Temple*, chapter 6.) Because the ancient righteous waited in patience and long-suffering, etc., up to [the point] that nevertheless they were unable to hear his teaching and receive his mysteries.

**VERSE 4.**—“Slanting windows.” (ID., ibid., chapter 7.) The holy teachers are signified, those who, being lifted beyond themselves toward God, are granted a more intimate vision of the secrets of heaven. While they disclose publicly what they see in secret, they fill all the inner chambers of the temple, as it were, by admitting the sun’s light through windows. Hence they are said to be slanting, that is, wider inside, because whoever perceives the splendor of heavenly contemplation even for a moment immediately enlarges the bosom of the heart by greater discipline and prepares himself through diligent exercise to undertake greater things.

**VERSE 5.**—“And he built,” etc. (ID., ibid.) These upper chambers are called the pinnacles of the temple in the Gospel, where the Lord is tempted by the devil, etc., up to [the point] that the history of blessed Stephen more fully testifies that the greater part of them had left their wives, where it calls women who shared the same religious commitment not their spouses but their widows.

Sides. (ID., same work.) That is, little railings, so that no one might easily fall from them to the lower levels, etc., up to: “Sides,” that is, walls, barriers, or little railings: doctors sitting on the galleries, who preached to the people standing below around them.

## VERSE 6

“But he placed beams around the house on the outside.” (BEDE, same work.) The house that bears the galleries, etc., up to: “and yet from those things which they display outside by speaking, acting, or suffering, we find assistance for salvation.”

“Beams … on the outside.” They were of such length that their ends projected outward. In the lowest tier they were seven cubits, in the middle six, and in the highest five, so that the galleries might be arranged upon their ends—not fixed into the walls of the temple, but placed alongside the walls upon beams that extended from them.

## VERSE 7

“But when the house was being built…” This properly concerns that part of the Church which, after the labors and struggles of the world, has deserved to be brought into eternal rewards. For nothing defiled will enter that city.

“And neither hammer nor axe…” Here we are beaten by adversities and exercised by the discipline of truth, so that there we may be assigned to fitting places according to our merit; and, when correction has ceased, may be joined to one another by the sole bond of love and filled with one Spirit. Yet although it is said, “Noah was a perfect man in his generations,” and, “Blessed are the undefiled in the way,” and things of this kind, no one can truly walk the road of this life perfectly and without stain. For “there is no one who does good and does not sin.” But according to the measure of the present age, those are called perfect and undefiled who will then truly be perfected when, released from the bonds of the body, they have reached the immortal beauty of the house of the Lord.

## VERSE 8

“The door of the side.” (BEDE, same work, chapter 8.) Some who misunderstand this passage, etc., up to: “and rightly one door, because of the faith and love of truth that are harmonious in all the saints.”

“They went up to the middle chamber, and from the middle chamber to the third. And he built…” (BEDE, same work.) It should be noted that the thirty cubits of height mentioned above, etc., up to: “because with harmonious mind and voice all will praise together the glory of the divine majesty.”

## VERSE 9

“With ceilings.” (BEDE, same work, chapter 9.) The ceilings are galleries, composed and adorned with great beauty and fastened from below to the beams; and because the house of the Lord was made of three levels, it had three ceilings. These signify the more exalted saints, whose work and teaching are set before everyone in the temple and stand out, as though higher in the heights; all who, by interceding and exhorting, protect the souls of the weak lest they fail.

“Of cedar.” (ID., same work.) The cedar is an imperishable tree, etc., up to: “unless one loves God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength, and one’s neighbor as oneself.”

## VERSE 10

“A gallery above the entire house, five cubits in height.” (BEDE, same work.) Here the highest roof of the house itself is meant, etc., up to: “in the spirit and power of Elijah.”

## VERSE 15

“And he built the walls.” (BEDE, same work.) Inside, the house was clothed with cedar, etc., up to: “but they have none whom they may carry.”

“The walls of the house.” They are covered when the hearts of the faithful overflow with love of the virtues. For just as the cedar signifies the perfect, so, in their appropriate places, it signifies the height of the virtues by which perfection itself is reached.

“From the floor.” Everything is covered with wood, from the floor of the house to the top of the walls and to the ceilings, when the elect labor in good works from the first beginnings of faith to the perfection of good action and to entry into the heavenly homeland; and when, from the first righteous people to the last at the consummation of the age, all devote themselves to the virtues, by whose merit they may dare to say: “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God” (II Corinthians 2).

“And he covered the floor.” (BEDE, same work.) This is written more fully in Chronicles, etc., up to: “Above all these things, having charity,” etc. (I Timothy 1; Colossians 3).

## VERSE 16

“He built twenty…” (BEDE, same work, chapter 10.) The galleries, etc., up to: “and this spread throughout the whole breadth of the Church across the world.”

## VERSE 17

“Moreover…” (ID., same work.) Ten multiplied by four makes forty, etc., up to: “but the square signifies the world in which we struggle to acquire the same [perfection].” Hence: “He gathered them from the lands, from the rising and setting of the sun, from the north and from the sea” (Psalm 106).

## VERSE 18

“And all of cedar.” The cedar signifies the unsurpassable beauty of the virtues. The entire house is clothed with this wood inside when the hearts of the righteous shine only through love of good works.

“Having carved work.” (BEDE, same work, chapter 11.) The house has its carved work and skilfully made joinings in the cedar boards, when the elect are bound to one another by the most beautiful bond of charity, so that they have one heart and one soul. The carvings placed against the joints of the boards, so that one gallery may be made from all of them, are the works of charity by which the holy brotherhood is joined together and composed throughout the whole world into one house of Christ.

“Engravings.” They bring the works of the saints before others as an example, clearly showing what they are like. Hence Paul presents himself as an example both by his deeds and by his words.

“All of cedar…” (ID., same work.) The stones of the wall, or the floor, and the boards, and the gold, etc., up to: “and those who have perfectly received the grace of the Gospel enjoy eternal life together.”

## VERSE 19

“The inner sanctuary.” (BEDE, same work.) The inner sanctuary where the ark was, etc., up to: “who, after rising, ascended into heaven and placed the flesh assumed from the Virgin at the right hand of the Father.”

## VERSE 20

“Moreover, the inner sanctuary…” It is appropriate that the inner house is twenty cubits long, as a mystery of the twofold love already mentioned. In this life that love illuminates the minds of the elect for the most part; but in the homeland, when the works of the other virtues have ceased, it alone reigns.

“And also the altar.” (ID., same work, chapter 12.) The altar of incense, that is, etc., up to: “but what the stone, cedar, and gold signify has been explained above.”

## VERSE 21

“And also the house before the inner sanctuary.” (BEDE, same work.) The house before the inner sanctuary is covered with gold, etc., up to: “Therefore: ‘I will love him and manifest myself to him.’ And again: ‘The hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you in proverbs,’ etc.” (John 14; 16).

“With golden nails.” (ID., same work.) The nails are the commandments of charity, etc., up to: “who, coming again to perfection, says of the nails of love: ‘But it is good for me to cling to God,’ etc.” (Psalm 118:72).

## VERSE 22

“And there was nothing in the temple…” (ID., same work.) These matters are explained more fully in Chronicles (II Chronicles 3), etc., up to: “Set your minds on the things above, not on the things that are on earth” (Colossians 3).

## VERSE 23

“Cherubim of olive wood.” (BEDE, same work, chapter 13.) This is the name of an angelic dignity. In the singular it is *cherub*, and in the plural *cherubim*. By the cherubim, therefore, the angelic ministries that always stand before their Creator in heaven may be understood.

“Of olive wood.” Because the angels are anointed with spiritual grace, lest they ever wither away from the love of God. He himself, who created them, immediately filled them with the light of heavenly wisdom. Hence they are called cherubim—that is, “multiplication of knowledge” or “multitude of knowledge.” They were made of olive wood because they give us the light of knowledge, with the flame of God’s charity assisting, which is poured out in our hearts.

“Ten cubits.” (BEDE, same work.) They are ten cubits high because they enjoy eternal life through the number ten, possessing the unviolated image of their Creator and preserving the holiness, justice, and truth in which they were created. For a denarius consists of ten obols and customarily contains the name and image of the king. Therefore it corresponds to the figure of the heavenly kingdom, where the angels always remain in the image of their Creator, for whose likeness they were made; and where the elect receive again the image that they lost through sin. Hence: “When he appears, we shall be like him and shall see him as he is” (John 3).

## VERSE 24

“Five cubits.” (ID., same work.) When wings are placed in the figure of holy human beings, etc., up to: “they come to the denarius promised to those who cultivate life.”

“One wing of the cherub was five cubits.” They have two wings because the two Testaments declare that, through prosperity and adversity alike, they have always stretched and attained toward heavenly things with tireless purpose; and because they demonstrate that their hearers must do the same.

## VERSE 25

“Likewise, ten cubits.” (BEDE, same work.) They are ten cubits high because they preach that God must be served through observance of the Decalogue, and because they show that those who faithfully serve God will be rewarded with the denarius of the eternal kingdom.

(ID., same work.) “And the work…” Two cherubim were made to signify the fellowship of charity, etc., up to: “to whom, after the cold and darkness of idolatry, it was granted to know the light of truth.”

(ID., same work.) The two cherubim may signify the two Testaments, etc., up to: “but because the festival of inward blessedness is greater through the fellowship of united brotherhood.”

“In the middle of the inner temple.” (ID., same work.) It is clear from what was said above, etc., up to: “it expresses that grace of love by which they embrace one another.”

## VERSE 27

“And they stretched out their wings…” (ID., same work.) The cherubim stretch their wings toward both walls of the inner sanctuary, etc., up to: “their writers, now reigning with the Lord and praising him, take care of salvation and intercede for us.”

## VERSE 28

“He also covered the cherubim.” They are surrounded with gold because the authority of the Testaments has been confirmed by the illustrious works of their writers, and because knowledge of the divine Scriptures has been revealed throughout the world; or because this signifies the inner glory of the heavenly hosts. For the cherubim signify both angels and the Testaments.

## VERSE 29

“He carved them with various engravings.” (BEDE, same work, chapter 14.) The walls are carved with a lathe, etc., up to: “through long practice he learned by exercising the virtues.”

“And palm trees.” (ID., same work.) He makes palm trees when he impresses the memory of the saints’ eternal reward upon their minds, so that they fall less easily from the justice of the ark because they always have the reward of justice before their eyes.

“And various pictures.” He makes various pictures, as though projecting from and emerging out of the wall, when he grants the faithful the manifold operations of the virtues: the bowels of mercy, kindness, humility, patience, modesty, and so forth, but above all charity, which is “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3). When these virtues have become so habitual in the elect that they seem naturally implanted, what else do they resemble but the pictures of the house of the Lord projecting from the wall? For they no longer learn from others externally the words and works of truth; rather, these are rooted within them and are always ready to be brought forth from the depths of the heart as things to be done or taught.

We have also said that the evenness of the floor signifies the humble harmony of brotherhood. There, whether Jews or Gentiles, barbarians or Scythians, free or slaves, noble or low-born, all glory in being brothers in Christ and having the same Father in heaven. The profoundly harmonious humility of the heavenly citizens is beyond doubt. Thus Solomon covered the floor of the house with gold: inside the inner sanctuary, and outside in the temple; because Christ filled the angels and the souls of the righteous in heaven with the complete gift of perfection, and separated those who, as citizens of the heavenly homeland, are still pilgrims in the world from the baseness of mortals by the eternal seal of love. Hence: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13).

## VERSE 31

“And at the entrance of the inner sanctuary…” (BEDE, same work, chapter 15.) There was one entrance, but it was closed by two doors, etc., up to: “indeed, all the elect open for themselves access to the heavenly homeland through the weapons of light and piety.”

“Two little doors of olive wood.” (ID., same work.) There are two little doors because the angels and holy human beings love God and neighbor, and no one can enter the gate of life except through this twofold love. Or because the same gate of life is opened to the faithful of both peoples, namely Jews and Gentiles.

“And the doorposts of the corners.” The doorposts have five sides because the heavenly hall receives not only the souls of the elect but also opens its doors at the judgment to bodies endowed with immortal glory; for the body has five senses. Or each doorpost of the inner sanctuary is five cubits high because entry into the heavenly homeland is opened only to those who serve the Lord with all the senses of body and heart: with the body, when through those senses they do something for him; with the heart, when they soberly, justly, and devoutly determine in their thoughts what they ought to do through those bodily senses.

## VERSE 32

“Anaglypha.” It could be said to mean carving made at the joining of the boards, but the term is taken in a broad sense. (BEDE, same work.) In Greek, ἀνάγλυφα (*anaglypha*) are called *caelaturae*—“engravings”—in Latin, etc., up to: “by continually looking upon these things we direct our footsteps.”

## VERSE 33

“And he made at the entrance…” Just as the entrance to the inner sanctuary, by which one reaches the ark of the Lord and the cherubim, signifies the entrance into heaven, where we desire to be brought to the vision of God and the heavenly citizens, so the entrance into the temple signifies the beginnings of our conversion to God, when we enter the present Church. The former represents our entrance into hope; the latter our entrance into faith. Hence the doorposts of this entrance are four-sided because of the four books of the Gospel, whose teaching instructs us in the faith of truth.

“Doorposts of wood.” (BEDE, same work.) They are four-sided because of the four principal virtues, etc., up to: “after prudence, fortitude, and temperance comes justice.”

## VERSE 34

“On both sides.” Because they face one another, so that neither can exist without the other. The outer door signifies fraternal love, the inner door divine love: the former is earlier in time, the latter higher in dignity; and through the former one enters into the latter, because through love of neighbor one learns how the Creator ought to be loved.

“And both doors…” (BEDE, same work.) Because in both kinds of love two things must principally be observed, etc., up to: “because, once all sins have been extinguished, we pass to the shore and solidity of the virtues.”

(BEDE, as above.) It should be noted that at the exit of the inner sanctuary there are said to have been two doors, etc., up to: “the other prefiguring the dispensation of the mystery.”

“And they opened one another.” Or the door that held the other is opened when, through the ministry of the preacher, it is discerned what properly pertains to knowledge of the faith and what pertains to purity of life. These two cannot be separated. It is also insufficient merely to tolerate the evils of one’s neighbors without providing them with good, since both practices most certainly remain inseparably in the heart of the perfect.

## VERSE 35

“And he carved cherubim.” These matters have been explained above, because the same pictures or engravings were made on the walls of the house and on the inner doors. The same mysteries of faith, hope, and charity, which the exalted and perfect grasp in an exalted manner and which all the elect fully perceive in the eternal vision, are also handed on to beginners being catechized, to be learned and confessed according to each one’s capacity, so that those initiated into the sacred mysteries may eventually advance to grasp what they have piously believed.

## VERSE 36

“And he built the courtyard.” (BEDE, as above, chapter 16.) He speaks briefly about the inner courtyard, etc., up to: “Hence it follows: ‘He built the inner courtyard with three rows’” (I Corinthians 2).

“And one row.” One row of cedar wood signifies good action displayed without the corruption of pretense. Without this addition, faith, hope, and charity cannot be genuine. The wood of cedar, because of its fragrant quality and the imperishable power of its nature, signifies perseverance and the reputation of pious action. All the elect ascend to this courtyard who desire to please God through faith, hope, charity, and works. The perfect rise above it through the lofty grace of merits when they progress to such a height of virtue that they can say to their hearers: “Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ” (I Corinthians 4); and: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels, how much more matters of this life?” (Ibid. 6).

## VERSE 38

“This is the month.” (BEDE, as above.) It is asked how the house of the Lord is said to have been completed in the eighth month, in all its work, etc., up to: “Therefore David entitled a psalm ‘For the eighth,’ which he sang out of fear of judgment, saying: ‘Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath’” (Psalm 6).

“And he built it.” The Church is constructed from elect souls throughout the whole period of this age, which proceeds in a cycle of seven days; and at the end of the age it brings its growth to completion. Or this is because of the significance of spiritual grace, through which the Church receives what makes it truly the Church: without the gifts of the Spirit, no one can become faithful, preserve faith, or arrive at the crown of justice by the merit of faith.

# CHAPTER VII

## VERSE 1

“But Solomon built his own house for thirteen years…” (BEDE, *On the Temple of Solomon*, book 17.) Namely, the present Church, for which Christ, her husband, tasted death and rose again, etc., up to: “For bronze is exceedingly durable and resonant.”

## VERSE 14

“He completed all the work.” When the holy doctors faithfully devote themselves to the ministry of the word, they perform the work of God, because by speaking outwardly they open the way of truth to those whom he has inwardly enlightened and predestined to eternal life. Hence: “I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth” (I Corinthians 3).

## VERSE 15

“And he cast…” (BEDE, as above, chapter 18.) The column before the doors of the temple is eighteen cubits high, etc., up to: “so that we do not deviate at any point from the straight road by which we journey toward the promised homeland.”

“Ten, etc.” For three times six makes eighteen: three pertains to faith because of the Trinity; six to action, because the world was made in six days. Three is multiplied by six when the righteous person lives by faith and increases knowledge of pious faith through the execution of good action.

“And a line.” (BEDE, same work.) The apostolic rule surrounds both columns when a doctor sent to preach to Jews or Gentiles takes care to do and teach only what the Church received and learned through the apostles. Whoever wishes to teach, live, or preach otherwise, rejecting apostolic decrees or establishing new ones according to his own will, is not a column in the temple of God. By refusing to follow apostolic institutions, whether through the thinness of inertia or the heaviness of arrogance, he does not fit the twelve-cubit line.

## VERSE 16

“Two, etc.” (ID., same work.) The capitals of the columns, etc., up to: “the grace of evangelical perfection is implanted.”

## VERSE 17

“Sevenfold, etc.” (ID., same work.) This is written thus in Chronicles, etc., up to: “because the fathers of both Testaments received, through the grace of the one sevenfold Spirit, what made them elect.”

## VERSE 18

“And two…” (ID.) Pomegranates seem to have been made around the capitals, on the lower side, and from these pomegranates the latticework seems to arise, by which the capitals were partly covered. This signifies that virtues arise from virtues and that the saints walk “from virtue to virtue” (Psalm 83).

(ID., same work.) There were two rows of latticework around the capital, etc., up to: “and it is broadly evident in the things we understand.”

“So that they might cover.” (ID., same work.) Since he has spoken of the latticework, etc., up to: “the capitals that were above the heads of the columns are appropriately added.”

“Of pomegranates.” These enclose many seeds within a single outer rind, etc., up to: “but the grace of faith, hope, love, and the other goods of the soul that is within cannot be seen.”

## VERSE 19

“Like, etc.” (ID., same work.) Through the lilies is signified the brightness of the heavenly homeland and the pleasantness of paradise, fragrant with the flowers of immortality, etc., up to: “because that desired voice did not resound in the world except through the Gospel: ‘Repent,’ etc.” (Matthew 3).

“In the portico.” It should be noted in this passage of Chronicles that the same portico of the temple is also called the vestibule of the temple. Hence: “They were weeping between the vestibule and the altar,” that is, between the portico and the altar.

## VERSE 20

“And again…” (BEDE, as above.) Their form signifies the sublimity of the everlasting kingdom, etc., up to: “but because that fellowship is granted to the faithful of both peoples, it is rightly added: ‘Of pomegranates.’”

(ID., same work.) In the pomegranate he signifies the whole Church, etc., up to: “and they gather the elect of both peoples into one citadel of blessedness.”

“Column.” (ID., same work.) The right-hand column signifies the doctors of the primitive Church, etc., up to: “at least no diligence in understanding the errors of those over whom they have been set.”

“And he also made…” (ID., same work.) This sea was made as a figure of baptism, etc., up to: “when he foretold that it should be given to those laboring in the vineyard.”

## VERSE 23

“From rim to rim.” From the first person baptized in the name of Jesus Christ to the last person who will believe and be baptized at the end of the age, the entire chorus of the faithful must enter upon the same way of truth and hope from the Lord for the common crown of justice.

“Five cubits.” Whatever we commit by sight, hearing, taste, smell, or touch, the grace of God releases for us through the washing of the life-giving font. But forgiveness of past sins is not enough unless one thereafter devotes oneself to good works. Otherwise, if the devil who had gone out of a person sees that person idle and devoid of good works, he returns in greater numbers and makes that person’s last state worse than the first. Hence it follows:

“And a cord thirty cubits long encircled it.” This is the discipline of the heavenly commandments by which we are restrained from pleasures. Hence: “A threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4), because observance of the commandments, which is strengthened in the hearts of the elect by faith, love, and hope of heavenly reward, cannot be dissolved by any obstacle. The cord encircles the sea when we strive to strengthen the sacrament of baptism that we have received with pious works.

This cord is thirty cubits long, for five times six makes thirty. The number six, in which the Lord made the human being when he did not exist and remade him when he had perished, signifies our good action. Six is multiplied by five to reach thirty when all the senses of the body are subjected to the divine commands.

Alternatively: three times ten makes thirty, and after the flood the human race, descended from the three sons of Noah, filled the breadth of the whole world. Shem possessed Asia, Ham Africa, and Japheth’s offspring Europe and the islands of the sea. Since the mystery of baptism, together with the execution of works and hope of heavenly things, was to be administered to all nations, a cord thirty cubits long encircled the sea in which baptism was prefigured.

It should also be said here that, when the Lord was thirty years old, he came to baptism. Because by his baptism, which he received at the age of thirty, he consecrated our baptism, it was fitting that the cord of thirty cubits should encircle the sea that prefigured our baptism, signifying that, by the gift of him who underwent baptism without sin, baptism is dedicated for the remission of sins to us who believe in him.

“And engraving.” Since it was stated above that the cord thirty cubits long went around the sea, and it is now added that this engraving, placed beneath the rim, surrounded it for ten cubits, it is clear that the vessel was spread out and widened in the form of a bowl, narrowing from the circumference of thirty cubits at its rim to ten cubits. The engraving was historiated, imitating certain histories. Thus, through the historiated engravings surrounding the sea, examples of earlier times are signified for us to contemplate, so that we may see by what works the saints pleased God from the beginning, with what obstinacy the wicked persisted in crimes, and with what misery the reprobate perished.

Thus, at the beginning of the world, Cain was condemned for the wickedness of envy, Abel was crowned for the merit of justice, Lamech was cursed for adultery and murder, Enoch was taken back to paradise for the grace of piety, Ham was detested after the flood for impiety, Shem and Japheth were granted perpetual blessing for their dutiful reverence, Abraham became heir of the divine promise through the merit of faith, and the rest of the nations were abandoned because of unbelief. When the Lord likewise came in the flesh, Judea was rejected for its faithlessness, while the Gentiles were brought back to salvation by grace, and so forth. These examples, carefully considered in both Testaments, benefit the diligent.

Perhaps, therefore, there were two rows of historiated engravings on the bronze sea, so that those who have been steeped in the baptismal font might listen to the histories of both Testaments. They were ten cubits around so that, whenever they saw people devoted to these histories obeying the heavenly commands and intent with their whole purpose upon heavenly rewards, they might strive to imitate them.

## VERSE 25

“Twelve.” (BEDE, as above.) The twelve oxen signify the apostles, the evangelists—indeed, all ministers of the word. Hence: “You shall not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain,” etc. (I Corinthians 9). These carry the sea placed upon them when the apostles and their successors fulfill with ready devotion the ministry of the Gospel entrusted to them.

“Three of each.” Because they preach faith in the Trinity in all four regions of the square world. Hence also twelve apostles—that is, four groups of three—were chosen so that, proclaiming the faith and confession of the Trinity throughout the four quarters of the world, they might baptize all nations in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. We can easily see and know in the present, by reading, the words, deeds, and sufferings of these apostles and of their successors. But what glory of reward awaits them in the future, we cannot yet see.

## VERSE 26

“Thickness.” (BEDE, as above.) Whoever receives the bath of baptism for salvation and life must have faith, hope, and charity, without which no one can act rightly. Hence it follows: “Thickness.” The reception of baptism is fortified by the strength of faith, hope, and charity, and is shown to be beneficial to those who receive it only when the firm certainty of these virtues strengthens both their minds and their bodies.

“Lilies.” (ID., same work.) The lily, accompanied by the grace of fragrance, displays whiteness outwardly, etc., up to: “Hence it follows:”

“It held two thousand baths and three thousand, etc.” (ID., same work.) The bath is a Hebrew measure, etc., up to: “he makes them participants in the same kingdom.”

## VERSE 27

(ID., same work.) A thousand signifies perfection because it makes the denary solid and square. Ten times ten makes one hundred, which is already a square figure but still flat. But so that it may rise in height and become solid, multiply one hundred by ten, and the result is one thousand. By this number the stable and, as it were, square conscience of the righteous is signified. For wherever you place a square, it stands; so the spirit of the elect is not bent from its upright state by any temptation.

“And he made…” (ID., same work, chapter 20.) The same mysteries of our salvation are represented in many ways and by many means, etc., up to: “he made [them] burn with divine love.”

(ID., same work.) The ten bases were made for carrying the basins, etc., up to: “but invoking God the Father under one and the same name because of the gift of the one Spirit.”

## VERSE 27

“Four cubits in length.” (ID., same work.) The length and breadth of the bases were four cubits because the preachers, whether they endure outwardly the adversities of the world, the length of exile, and present labors, or expand their hearts inwardly in joyful love of God and neighbor, always devote themselves to the virtues: discerning wisely between good and evil, enduring adversity courageously, restraining the heart from the desire for pleasures, and maintaining justice in action.

## VERSE 28

“And this was the work of the bases.” The panels from which the bases were made were square, and on them were round designs called little crowns or wreaths, in the middle of which were engravings of lions, etc.

## VERSE 29

“Between the little crowns and wreaths were lions, oxen, and cherubim.” (ID., same work.) No surface of the bases was flat on any side, etc., up to: “hence here too, after the engravings of the cherubim, it is rightly added:”

“And beneath the lions.” Because the doctors, both in the severity of strictness with which they judge sinners and in the gentleness of leniency with which they forgive the repentant, fear the judgment of God, lest by binding and loosing unjustly they themselves be justly bound by him whose judgment cannot err.

## VERSE 30

“And four wheels.” (BEDE, same work.) The books of the four Gospels, etc., up to: “they lift them from below and, as though by wheels set in place, raise the axles of the bases higher from the ground.”

“Shoulders.” (ID., same work.) These were placed before the wheels to prevent them from slipping away from the axle. They signify the proclamations of the prophets, by which the evangelical and apostolic Scripture is confirmed, so that nothing may come into doubt for any reader. Hence: “We possess the prophetic word made more certain, and you do well to attend to it,” etc. (II Peter 1). Hence Mark also says: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet”; and Matthew: “All this took place so that the Scripture of the prophets might be fulfilled” (Mark 1; Matthew 26).

“Opposite.” (ID., same work.) Because all prophetic Scripture agrees with itself, as it was composed by one Spirit. There were four shoulders for each base, corresponding to the number of the wheels—not because there are only four prophetic books, but because everything spoken by the prophets bore witness to the four Gospels, so that from the agreement of both Testaments one faith and love of Christ might strengthen the hearts of us all.

## VERSE 31

“One cubit.” (ID., same work.) Because of perfection, etc., up to: “Hence: ‘We know in part and we prophesy in part,’ etc.” (I Corinthians 13).

“Middle.” He means the upper panel, which, like the others, was square and similarly engraved, and at its top had a round section of one and a half cubits, upon which the basin was placed.

## VERSE 37

“In this manner he made ten bases, with one casting, one measure, and one engraving, etc.” (BEDE, same work.) Why ten bases were made and an equal number of basins placed upon them has been stated above. But the fact that all the bases or basins had one measure and similar engraving does not signify that the merits of all doctors can be equal. Rather, it signifies that they have one faith of the Gospel, by which they are instructed; one sacrament of baptism, by which they are washed; and one and the same Spirit, by which they are all consecrated, although they have different gifts within that Spirit, who distributes to each as he wills.

## VERSE 38

“One basin held forty baths, etc.” (ID., same work.) Forty signifies great perfection, because four times ten makes forty. Ten are the commandments by which all our action is prescribed in the law of God. The four books of the Gospels reveal to us, through the dispensation of the Lord’s incarnation, the entrance into the heavenly homeland. Since all who belong to the mystery of baptism must, with faith and the sacraments of the Gospel, display the fruit of right action, each basin in which the holocausts were washed held forty baths.

“And it was…” (ID., same work.) It was stated above that it had one and a half cubits, but the text did not add whether this indicated breadth or height. It seems that he intended the bottom of the basin itself to be understood as having this breadth, which can easily be inferred from the measure of the base upon which each basin was placed. It is described in this way: “At the top of the base there was a round section of one and a half cubits, so fashioned that the basin could be placed upon it.” Therefore, the breadth of the bottom of the basins was one and a half cubits. The basins themselves had a capacity of four cubits—but whether in height, breadth, or both, let whoever knows say.

(ID., same work.) This was because of the four Gospels, in which the form of baptism is given; or because of the cardinal virtues by which the baptized must be instructed; or because of the four quarters of the world in which baptism is administered.

## VERSE 39

“And he placed ten bases, five on the right side of the temple and five on the left.” (ID., same work.) But he did not mean the right and left sides inside the temple itself, etc., up to: “and I consider them to be alien to the flame of divine charity.”

“And he placed the sea on the right side of the temple, etc.” (ID., same work.) And in this same courtyard, etc., up to: “through which that same love is poured into our hearts.”

## VERSE 46

“The king cast them in the clay ground of the Jordan.” (ID., same work.) In which our Lord was baptized, etc., up to: “he filled the whole breadth of the world.”

“Clay soil.” (ID., same work, chapter 21.) From this the molds were made for casting the vessels of Scripture, etc., up to: “so that by running well we may reach their rewards.”

## VERSE 48

“And Solomon made all the vessels in the house, etc.” (ID., same work.) Above he said that Hiram had made all the vessels for Solomon; now Scripture adds that Solomon made the same things. Solomon made them by dictating, Hiram by working.

“Golden altar.” (ID., same work.) The hearts of the perfect sparkle with the light of inward charity and purity, etc., up to: “but they offer him only the vows of tears and prayer, out of desire for the heavenly kingdom.”

(ID., same work, chapter 22.) Moses made the altar of incense, etc., up to: “hence those who labor in the vineyard of the great householder are counted by the denarius.”

“Table.” (ID., same work.) Scripture, bright with spiritual understanding, etc., up to: “which was once thought to be understood according to the letter.”

(Same author, same work.) Just as tables are set up as a figure of Scripture, etc., up to: so the elect are contained in Scripture, seeking and receiving heavenly good things from the Lord with their minds raised toward higher things.

**VERSE 49.**—“Like lilies.” (Same author, same work.) This appears to mean that the upper part of the lampstands was fashioned in the shape of an open lily.

“Golden lamps above.” By the container that which contains it is designated: that is, the golden vessels in which the oil burned brightly.

“Snuffers.” (Bede, same work.) That is, instruments with which the wicks were trimmed, so that, renewed, they might shine more brightly.

**VERSE 50.**—“Basins.” The basins signify the innermost hearts of the saints, filled with the water of wisdom and the wine of compunction.

“Forks.” The little forks with which the meats are prepared signify preachers, who administer the food of understanding to their hearers. Their office is to distribute Christ’s body and blood to believers and to withhold it from unbelievers.

“Of the inner house.” (Same author, same work, chapter 22.) The doors of the inner house signify the angelic powers, etc., up to: or the charity that they possess toward God.

**VERSE 51.**—“He completed all the work.” (Same author, same work.) While the present condition of the world continues, he indeed performs the work of the house of the Lord, but he does not yet complete it, because the Lord inspires and assists the hearts of the elect so that they may do good; yet he does not grant that anyone dwelling in this life should be without sin. For he reserves this for future blessedness. He truly completes all the work of Solomon’s temple and makes it fit for dedication when our Peaceful One, on the last day, glorifies the elect with the immortality of the resurrection and brings them into the eternal kingdom. Hence the temple was built over seven years but completed and dedicated in the eighth. The following statement corresponds to this:

“And he brought in the things that he had sanctified.” (Same author, same work.) David, Solomon’s father, sanctified the silver when God the Father strengthens eloquent people by the grace of his Spirit to speak the word of God. He sanctifies gold when he illumines those endowed with natural intelligence so that they may understand the law. He also sanctifies vessels when he bestows the grace of the Holy Spirit upon all the children of the Church. Solomon brings these sanctified things into the temple when the Lord, after judgment has been completed, introduces the company of teachers and the rest of the faithful into the joy of the heavenly kingdom.

“And he placed them in the treasuries of the house of the Lord.” (Same author, same work.) Because he hides his gods in the secret place of his face, away from the disturbance of men. There are many treasuries in the one house of the Lord, because within the one Church the saints differ in merit. And there is one heavenly homeland, although one star differs from another in glory (II Cor. XV). The dispenser of rewards demonstrated both facts when he said: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John XV).

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 6.**—“Into the holy place.” (Bede, *On Solomon’s Temple*.) The outer house of the temple signifies the pilgrim Church; the Holy of Holies signifies the blessedness of the heavenly homeland above. The ark brought into the Holy of Holies signifies Christ’s assumed humanity, introduced within the veil of the heavenly kingdom.

“Beneath the wings.” (Same author.) Moses made two golden cherubim, which he placed upon the mercy seat that was above the ark. Solomon added two larger ones, beneath whose wings he is now said to have placed the ark together with the mercy seat and the two earlier cherubim.

**VERSE 8.**—“And when.” (Same author.) This is made clearer, etc., up to: if the projecting poles extended beyond the doorway, they would leave no room for the doors to be shut.

“And they remained there.” In Chronicles it is stated: “Thus the ark remained there until the present day.” This was added by the historian to indicate that it had remained there until the time of his own generation. This cannot be understood as referring to Ezra, because by then the temple had already been burned; rather, it refers to Nathan or one of the prophets, by whom all the deeds of their own times are believed to have been written down.

**VERSE 9.**—“In the ark.” (Rabanus.) In the ark there was a golden urn containing manna, etc., up to: because only the citizens of the heavenly homeland fully contemplate the glory of the Redeemer there.

**VERSE 10.**—“The cloud filled the house of the Lord, and they could not.” (Same author.) That is, it filled the synagogue, because the darkness of unbelief had filled their minds. The priests could not minister because, while they disdained to investigate the mystical meanings covered by the veil of the letter and the mysteries of Christ’s birth, they lost the ministry due to their faith amid the cloud of error. Thus, as their merits demanded, they did not recognize the worship of faith, although in the cloud of their teaching the Lord had also related openly what concerned himself. But because the minds of the hearers had been filled with the darkness of unbelief, the intervening cloud concealed him like a cloud concealing a ray of sunlight.

**VERSE 55.**—“He stood.” In Chronicles it is reported [Col. 0600C] that Solomon had made a bronze platform, and had placed it in the middle of the basilica; standing upon it, he blessed all the assembly of Israel.

“And he blessed.” (Rabanus.) The temple of the Lord, etc., up to: and they benefit their neighbors by works of virtue.

**VERSE 64.**—“On the day.” (Rabanus, *On the Books of Kings*, volume III.) What does it mean that Solomon built the middle of the court, offering there, etc., up to: acceptable sacrifices are offered spiritually to God every day.

“Altar.” The altar that Moses made had been placed before the temple, opposite its doors. Since it was narrow and could not contain the offerings, Solomon sanctified the middle of the court beneath the open sky, where he placed the great altar that he had made, twenty cubits in size.

**VERSE 65.**—“The festival.” (Rabanus, as above.) In the Books of Days, etc., up to: Josephus also bears witness to this.

(Same author, same work.) The solemn celebration held by Solomon and all Israel, etc., up to: the things that the Father bestowed upon Christians in Christ.

“From the entrance.” (Rabanus, same work.) By the entrance of Hamath he designates the northern region of Judea; by the brook or torrent of Egypt, the southern region. This brook is not the Nile but another river that flows into the sea near Rivocorula. Hamath, however, is a city of Syria. It is now called Epiphany, after Antiochus Epiphanes.

**VERSE 66.**—“Rejoicing.” They sang hymns with delight, so that in that gladness they returned home without weariness.

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 11.**—“The king providing.” (Rabanus, as above.) Much gold and silver, etc., up to: because they did not bear a shoot together with the fullness of its fruits.

**VERSE 17.**—“He built.” (Rabanus.) The cities that he is said to have built, etc., up to: so that they might remain unconquerable by spiritual enemies.

(Rabanus.) The cities that Solomon built were from the remnants of the Amorites, whom the children of Israel had been unable to destroy, as is read in Joshua (Josh. IX). Later the king of Egypt overthrew them and gave them as a dowry to his daughter, Solomon’s wife; therefore Solomon rebuilt them.

**VERSE 18.**—“And Palmyra.” This was an uninhabitable region because water could nowhere be found. But at the place where the city was built, springs abound; and the palm, which in Greek is called *Palmira*, is itself Hamath, or Epiphany, or Antioch.

**VERSE 20.**—“All.” (Rabanus, as above.) Our Peaceful One made those who were not of the children of Israel tributary, together with those who are not numbered among the sons but are used in a servile condition for personal service. Although such people oppose the Church in many ways, they nevertheless often serve its needs when, in the present age, they provide assistance from their possessions.

“Of the children.” (Same author, same work.) Those who are not sons of a slave woman but of a free woman, etc., up to: and lead them along the paths of righteousness.

**VERSE 23.**—“Fifty.” (Same author.) On the fiftieth day after Passover the law was also given on Mount Sinai, and the Paraclete Spirit came upon the disciples. What, then, does this number of overseers signify except that those who, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, deserve to possess knowledge of the Lord’s law are able to govern both themselves and others well?

**VERSE 25.**—“He also offered.” (Same author.) Our Peaceful One offers, etc., up to: and asks for the things that are pleasing to God.

**VERSE 26.**—“A fleet.” (Same author.) The fleet is the Church, etc., up to: history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy in the two Testaments.

**VERSE 28.**—“In Ophir.” (Same author.) Ophir is the name of a province in India. It is named after Ophir, one of the descendants of Eber; it is also called the golden land because it has golden mountains inhabited by lions and the fiercest wild beasts. No one dares approach them in any other way than by standing in a ship near the shore and taking aboard whatever earth they find dug out by the lions’ claws, so that, if the beasts notice them, they may easily retreat into the sea.

## CHAPTER X

“Allegorically.” (Isidore, *On the Books of Kings*, volume V.) This queen signifies the future Church from the Gentiles, etc., desiring to become a fellow citizen in the hidden place of the saints.

**VERSE 4.**—“When she saw.” (Rabanus, as above.) The queen, having seen Solomon and his glory and being astonished at his wisdom, said: “True is the report,” etc. So the holy Church, having heard Christ’s miracles, was moved to seek him. When she found him through faith and, considering the testimonies of Holy Scripture, recognized the power of his divinity, she judged everything previously reported to her about him to have been little.

**VERSE 8.**—“Blessed are your men.” (Rabanus.) The queen, expressing admiration, burst into praise of Solomon, saying: “Blessed are the men.” Truly blessed are those whose king is Christ, who deserve to enjoy his eternal vision, who rejoice to behold the glory that he possesses with the Father and the Holy Spirit, and who continually receive the wisdom that reveals itself to the pure in heart.

**VERSE 11.**—“Wood.” (Same author.) Our Creator signifies precious wood, that is, etc., up to: and all the musical instruments.

**VERSE 12.**—“For the singers.” (Same author.) Whatever these people do in word or deed, they do entirely for the praise of God. Amid adversity and prosperity, they do not cease to proclaim praise with heart, mouth, and deed. Hence: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen; all day and all night they shall never cease to praise the name of the Lord” (Isa. LXII).

**VERSE 13.**—“And King Solomon.” (Same author.) Our Peaceful One will also give his Church everything she asks for. Hence: “Whatever you ask the Father in my name, he will give you.” He bestows by gratuitous generosity not only what we ask but also what human weakness either does not know or does not presume to ask.

**VERSE 16.**—“Two hundred.” (Same author.) In Chronicles golden spears are added to the shields, because the commanders who kept watch before the door of the king’s house used spears and shields. Hence: “Sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s couch.”

(Same author.) Keeping watch at the doors of the royal house, etc., up to: and, with the shield of faith, they extinguish the flaming arrows of the Evil One.

**VERSE 17.**—“The forest of Lebanon.” The forest of Lebanon signifies the Church of the Gentiles, which, cut away from the arrogance of pride, is fitted into the construction of the house of God. Hence: “We found it in the fields of the forest.”

**VERSE 18.**—“A throne of ivory.” (Rabanus.) A throne or seat is an imperial chair, called in the Song a *ferculum*—a carrying chair—because it carries those seated upon it or transports them from place to place. It was reached by six ascending steps. Beneath the seat was a golden footstool, and the top of the throne was rounded, supported externally by two hands or arms. Nearby stood two lions, helping to support the seat.

**VERSE 20.**—“And twelve.” The six ascending steps were set on either side as supports for the person ascending.

(Same author.) Solomon’s throne is understood to be the Church, etc., up to: they strive to fortify it.

“It was not made, etc.” This aptly applies to the Church, to whom it is said: “Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all” (Prov. XXXI).

**VERSE 21.**—“And all the vessels, etc.” All the vessels that serve our Peaceful One are golden, because all the souls of the saints, which are God’s vessels, shine with the splendor of wisdom and love as they serve the divine will; they contain the drink of life, and in them there becomes “a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John IV).

“And there was none, etc.” (Rabanus.) For, according to the Apostle, “The word of God is not in speech but in power and in the preaching of the Gospel” (I Cor. I). It does not consist in persuasive words of human wisdom but in the manifestation of the Spirit and of power, so that our faith might rest not on human wisdom but on the power of God.

**VERSE 22.**—“Bringing gold from there, etc.” (Same author.) What gold or silver signifies, etc., he goes on to discuss weapons of war.

**VERSE 26.**—“Solomon gathered together, etc.” (Same author.) Josephus gives the following account of these men. Their riders were adorned: young men in the flower of their beauty, of great stature, letting their hair fall over their horses as they rode, clothed in purple. Armed and carrying bows, they rode before the king whenever he was about to go somewhere.

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 1.**—“But King Solomon.” (Rabanus.) Scripture severely reproves Solomon, etc., up to: his evils signify the evils of the Church.

**VERSE 27.**—“A ravine.” The city wall had fallen because on one side it overlooked a precipice. When the king wished to level this ravine with the walls, he ordered the commanders to complete the work. But Jeroboam, who was chief of the tribe of Joseph, refused to obey the king. The king had previously placed him over the construction of the fortifications that he was building in Jerusalem, where he labored so diligently that the king appointed him commander of the army over the tribe of Joseph. But he became rebellious and left Jerusalem. A prophet met him and led him aside into a field so that no one would hear what he said to him. Elated by the prophet’s words, he urged the people to make him king. When Solomon heard this, he sought to kill him.

“And it was.” He refused this order to restore the walls. But where did he get such boldness? Because the king had appointed him governor.

“Take for yourself.” (Rabanus.) The ten tribes were separated from the house of David, etc., up to: because there is one God, one faith, one baptism.

**VERSE 42.**—“And the days.” Josephus said that he reigned for eighty years and lived for ninety-four. But divine Scripture records only those years in which he reigned before he transgressed.

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSES 1–4.**—“Then he came.” “Very harsh.” How is this true, when it was said above that Solomon did not appoint anyone from the children of Israel to serve? Certainly he did not make them labor in agriculture or in any other servile work. Rather, he appointed leaders from among them for each tribe, who supplied the king each month with provisions, etc.—the expenses of the king’s household described above—which they now call a very harsh yoke.

**VERSE 8.**—“Young men.” Aduram was one of these men, and he was later stoned. Scripture does not always call men young according to age but according to instability of character. For Rehoboam began to reign in the fortieth year of his life.

**VERSE 11.**—“Scorpions.” This is a kind of whip, like the knotted rods made from thorns or orchard branches. Or it may be the Saracen whip with two or three rods, which has leaden pellets at its tip—what others call hailstones.

**VERSE 23.**—“To Rehoboam.” (Rabanus.) Rehoboam belonged to the house of David, etc., up to: and whose rulers feast at their appointed time.

**VERSE 28.**—“He made two.” Why Jeroboam made the calf, or how he did so, Josephus explains sufficiently.

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Behold, a man.” His name is omitted here; in Chronicles he is called or named Gad. He is the same Gad who advised David to go into the land of Judah. (Rabanus.) A prophet sent by God, etc., up to: forgiveness might be granted to the penitent.

**VERSE 11.**—“The prophet.” This false prophet was chief among the priests and was held in great honor by the king as though he were divine. Fearing that, through the word of the man of God, the king might abandon the worship of idols and kill him as a sorcerer, he devised a way to deceive the man of God. He acted with considerable cunning, so that, when the man of God transgressed God’s command, he would incur God’s anger, as indeed happened when he believed a human being rather than God. In this way the things he had foretold would be shown to be false, and they could persuade the king accordingly. When the king heard what had happened, he considered the man of God’s words invalid and did not turn away from his evil way.

“All his works, etc.” (Gregory.) In the deeds of the prophet, marvelous things come first and miserable things follow. What do we learn from this except that, having gloried inwardly in his great deeds, he was soon shaken from his inner stability, and that sin crept into his conduct from the same place where glory had crept into his heart? Thus, deceived by a false prophet, he learned that what had previously happened was not due to his own strength at all.

**VERSE 21.**—“Thus says the Lord.” (Same author.) He rightly received the sentence of death from the mouth of the one whose return had led him away from the precepts of life, so that he might truly receive punishment from the same source through which he had negligently incurred guilt.

**VERSE 24.**—“And the lion was standing, etc.” (Rabanus.) This shows that the sin of disobedience was released in death itself, because the same lion that had dared to kill the living man did not dare touch the dead man. Although it had possessed the power to kill him, it was not granted permission to eat from the corpse, because the one whose guilt had been punished during life was already made righteous through death.

**VERSE 31.**—“Bury me, etc.” Knowing that what the man of God had foretold was coming to pass, the wicked prophet ordered that he be buried beside the man of God, so that, when his bones were later exhumed for burning, they would not be burned but preserved through the holy prophet, as this same book later testifies was fulfilled.

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 25.**—“Shishak went up, etc.” The king of Egypt was followed by twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand cavalrymen, and forty thousand infantrymen, many of whom were Libyans and Ethiopians. Thus invading the land of the Hebrews, he took the most strongly fortified cities without a battle, etc.

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 6.**—“Nevertheless there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam throughout, etc.” Jeroboam assembled a large army and encamped against Abijah, the son of Rehoboam, who had succeeded his father over the two tribes. When Abijah heard this, he was astonished; but, taking courage, he chose an army and met Jeroboam at a place called the Mountain of the Amorites. After addressing Jeroboam’s army, he finally said: “In what are you confident of victory? In the golden calves and altars that are signs of your impiety rather than of religion? Or has the multitude given you hope? But there is no strength where, even with many thousands, a single unjust man fights. Hope of victory rests only upon justice and piety, and this is found among us, who from the beginning have kept the laws and worshiped the true God,” etc. God, however, shattered Jeroboam’s boldness and made Abijah’s army prevail. For no battle is reported to have produced such a slaughter—not among Greeks nor among barbarians—as the remarkable victory God granted. Five hundred thousand of the enemy were struck down in battle, etc.

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 1.**—“And the word came.” This prophet is mentioned nowhere else; he is introduced suddenly, like others. Thus Obadiah is said to have fed one hundred prophets in caves, and Elijah says: “They have killed your prophets.” The sons of the prophets are also said to have gone out to meet Elisha, although no other mention or particular naming of them occurs.

**VERSE 3.**—“Behold.” (Rabanus, *On the Books of Kings*, volume III.) The Lord cuts off the posterity of this or any wicked person when he avenges sins after the end of life. He also cuts off the posterity of his house when he condemns an imitator to eternal torments. Therefore, whoever perseveres in evil works until the end of life will have his posterity cut off.

**VERSE 4.**—“Whoever dies.” (Same author.) Concerning Baasha—that is, concerning the body of the devil, full of confusion, etc.—up to: they drag them with themselves into eternal destruction.

**VERSE 6.**—“He reigned in Tirzah.” (Rabanus.) He spent six years in Tirzah and the remaining years in the city called Semeron, or Samaria by the Greeks. He named it Semeron after Semer, its former owner. It is the capital of the kingdom; afterward the entire region was called Samaria after it. It is now called Sebaste, where the bones of blessed John the Baptist rest.

**VERSE 34.**—“Hiel built.” (Rabanus.) Hiel means “living for God”; Bethel means “house of God.” Hiel rebuilt the walls of Jericho, which had been destroyed and placed under the ban by Joshua. When one of those who in the Church have assumed the religious habit returns to the sins from which the Lord Jesus had freed him on the day of baptism, and, by living luxuriously, seeks again the pomp of the devil that he himself had condemned; when he prefers the doctrines of error or the tales of the pagans to the ecclesiastical truth in which he was instructed, then, as though leaving Bethel, he raises up the ruins of Jericho. He also destroys the foundations of faith on which he had begun to build good works and the barriers of good conduct by which he ought to have been perfected.

“In Abiram.” (Same author.) When the builder of Jericho laid its foundations, his firstborn son, named Abiram, died. When he fortified its gates, he lost his youngest son, Segub, in accordance with Joshua’s curse.

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—“And he said.” (Rabanus.) Elijah is interpreted as “The Lord is my God,” or “My God,” or “God is strong,” and signifies Christ. Thesbite is interpreted as “captivating” or “converting.” Concerning the Lord it is written: “Turn back our captivity, O Lord.” As with Melchizedek, Elijah’s origin is left unspoken when his name is suddenly introduced, and this occurs as a foreshadowing of the Savior.

“In whose sight.” (Same author.) The righteous person stands in the sight of the Lord now and will stand there in the future: now, so that he may bring the Creator’s power to mind and live faithfully; in the future, so that he may truly receive the crown of life.

**VERSE 3.**—“Hide yourself.” (Rabanus.) Our Elijah was hidden, etc., up to: and the service rendered to the Lord by the faithful from among the Jews.
