“In the brook Cherith.” The brook Kishon, which is also called Cherith, is interpreted as “knowledge,” “cutting,” or “division”; this is fitting for the Jewish people.

**VERSE 10.**—“A woman.” (Isidore.) The widow whom the Lord feeds not with the bread of grain but with the bread of the word is she who, after her husband’s death, marries whomever she wishes—that is, after shaking off the yoke of slavery, she submits to Christ’s easy yoke and light burden.

(Rabanus.) This widow signifies the Church of the Gentiles, etc., up to: she is said not to have failed.

(Same author.) The widow with whom Elijah stayed, whose flour and oil he blessed, is the synagogue of the Jews. Widowed by the death of Moses, it was nourishing a little son—that is, the carnal Jewish people. At Elijah’s entrance, that is, at the entrance of our Savior, this son was weakened by the fever of unbelief, because he did not believe in him but rejected him. Hence the mother Synagogue complains about the Savior’s coming as though he were the cause of the people’s death, saying: “What have I to do with you?” and so forth. This is why Caiaphas said: “It is better for you that one man should die for the people, and not that the whole nation should perish” (John XI).

(Same author.) Just as the prophet was not angered by the widow’s words but rather took pity on her, so our Redeemer is not angered by the Jews’ wickedness but, having compassion on his people, took the child from his mother’s lap when he took him away from the carnal observance of the law and placed him upon his bed—that is, he showed him that he had life through the Savior’s death—and stretched himself out three times while making known the faith of the Trinity.

**VERSE 19.**—“And Elijah took.” (Rabanus.) Elijah took the boy and returned him to his mother when our Lord, saving the believing people, displayed signs and miracles to unbelievers, so that they might truly recognize that the one who believes in his name is alive. Thus it will happen that the Jewish people, overcome by the truth, will proclaim to Christ: “Now by this I know that you are a man of God.”

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 3.**—“Now Obadiah.” Obadiah, chief of the army of Israel, whose name is interpreted as “servant of the Lord,” prefigured those among the rulers of the Jews who believed and were secret disciples, such as Nicodemus and Joseph.

**VERSE 30.**—“He repaired the altar.” (Rabanus.) Our Redeemer, fighting against and overcoming the prince of the world and his satellites, repairs the altar of the Lord that had been destroyed—that is, cleansing the hearts of the faithful from the stain of iniquity, he dedicates an altar to God. It is remembered as having been constructed from twelve stones because from those who follow the prophetic and apostolic faith or teaching a most pleasing altar is built for God, upon which a sacrifice of praise is offered as a sweet fragrance.

**VERSE 32.**—“And he made.” (Same author.) From a contrite and humbled heart, etc., up to: let us sing in eternal thanksgiving, “The Lord himself is God.”

**VERSE 40.**—“Seize them.” (Rabanus.) So our Redeemer, when the day of judgment arrives, will send his angels, and they will gather all scandals out of his kingdom and throw them into the lake of fire, where they will be tormented according to the hardness and impenitence of their hearts.

**VERSE 41.**—“A great rain.” (Isidore.) When Christ, the Son of God, was born among human beings and assumed the tenderness of our flesh, after he had tasted death and ascended victorious from the world into heaven, he sent from above to earth the rain of divine grace through the sevenfold Spirit. This rain cleanses us from sin and enables us to produce spiritual fruits.

(Rabanus.) In Elijah’s virtues, through which he was powerful by God’s strength, he recognized what he himself was in his weaknesses. There he showed what he had received; here he guarded what he had received. In miracles he was displayed; in weaknesses he was preserved.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 3.**—“Then Elijah was afraid and arose and went away, etc.” (Rabanus.) Holy men are lifted by the Spirit and carried to the heights; but as long as they remain in this life, they are restrained by temptations lest they become proud. Thus Elijah, after performing so many mighty deeds, later fled from Jezebel, although she was a queen, yet a mere little woman. He who raised the dead, foresaw the future, and performed other notable deeds, struck by fear, fled from death at the hand of a woman but asked death from the hand of God—and did not receive it.

**VERSE 5.**—“And behold, an angel of the Lord touched him.” (Rabanus.) The angel who fed Elijah signifies the angel of great counsel, through whose work we subsist both in bodily and spiritual nature.

**VERSE 6.**—“And behold, at his head, etc.” (Same author.) Elijah’s being fed twice expresses the weakness of our nature, for whom a single meal is insufficient but a double one is necessary if we are to be able to ascend to higher things. For just as the body cannot subsist without bodily nourishment, so the soul cannot live without the word of God.

(Same author.) So too, when we shake off the sleep of idleness, we must, strengthened by divine consolation, hasten with all zeal throughout the whole time of the present life to ascend the mountain of God and his holy place, so that there we may find eternal rest.

**VERSE 11.**—“And the spirit.” (Same author.) The spirit before the Lord overturned mountains and shattered rocks, etc., up to: to begin to come forth into knowledge of the truth.

“Not in the spirit.” That is, do not suppose that the Lord will come with the wind. After the spirit of disturbance—that is, after the whirlwind and force of the wind—the fire will pass by; then the sound of a gentle breeze; after this the Lord will pass by, in order to speak with you.

**VERSE 14.**—“I alone, etc.” (Rabanus.) Was it so difficult for the prophet to recognize that servants of God remained in this world? Yet the humble man knew even God’s hidden things, while the proud man did not know even what was open and evident. Hence it is certain that the one who carefully weighs the good qualities of others is illumined by the ray of humility: when he sees outwardly, and in others, the things he himself has done, he suppresses the swelling of pride that tries to burst forth inwardly from a sense of uniqueness. Thus, by God’s voice, Elijah, who thought himself alone, is told: “I have left seven thousand men for myself,” so that, when he recognized that he alone had not remained, the glory of elation arising from his sense of uniqueness might bow down.

(Rabanus.) It was not in any other way except that he foretold that he would become king. He did not anoint Elisha in any other way than by casting his cloak over him. Nor did he himself anoint those two kings, nor did Elisha do so at his command; rather, a certain prophet was sent to anoint Jehu.

**VERSE 17.**—“Whoever.” (Same author.) Divine justice causes some guilty people to be punished by kings with the sword, and others to be pierced through by prophets and priests with the sword of the tongue.

**VERSE 19.**—“He departed.” When our Redeemer, descending from heaven, acquired by divine judgment a people still intent upon earthly works, he brought salvation to them when he converted them to faith. Elijah is interpreted as “The Lord God”; Shaphat as “judging”; Elisha as “the salvation of my God.” The prophet cast his cloak over Elisha when the Lord clothed the people with Catholic faith. Hence the Apostle: “You who were baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. III). He left the oxen and ran after Elijah because, when the chorus of the elect heard, “Unless someone renounces everything, he cannot be my disciple” (Luke XIV), it immediately ceased longing for earthly profits and serving worldly desires, and thus preached the word of life to others. This is what it means to kiss father and mother: to desire, by speech, to correct as many as one can, whether from the Jews or from the Gentiles.

(Rabanus.) The Christian people likewise slaughter the desires of the flesh and turn their entire force toward the work of evangelization, so that they may provide sufficient nourishment for their helpers.

**VERSE 21.**—“He followed.” (Same author.) He follows and ministers to our Elijah: following in his footsteps—that is, observing his commands—he earnestly strives to offer him service and honor fittingly.

## CHAPTER XX

(Rabanus.) Ben-hadad signifies the devil, who gathers various armies of evil spirits to overthrow the people of God. But he is defeated by the young men of the rulers of Israel—that is, by good hearers of teachers—because they fulfill in deeds what they hear with their ears. The ancient enemy is put to flight, and his entire army is thrown into confusion by the soldiers of Christ. These are said to number two hundred thousand and thirty-two, because those who perfectly possess the knowledge of both Testaments and preserve faith in the Trinity together with twofold charity are proved fit for the service of the supreme King.

**VERSE 10.**—“May the gods do this to me.” Samaria had ground inside the city almost level with the walls, so that, by this support, it could resist blows from a battering ram; outside, the height of the walls rose far above the surface of the ground. Therefore the proud king, terrifying the besieged, said that he possessed such a multitude that, if each soldier brought one stone, piece of wood, or clod of earth to construct a ramp against the city, a ramp would rise that would appear level with the ground inside the walls, so that from equal height they could fight against the city and hurl weapons and firebrands.

“Let the one who is girded not boast.” (Rabanus.) One who is surrounded by a belt is girded; one who has put aside his belt is ungirded. Thus the king of Israel said to the king of Syria, who was boasting as though he had already captured Samaria, which he had begun to besiege: “Let the one who is girded not boast as the one who is ungirded.” As though he were saying: Do not boast as a victor when you are still stationed in battle and do not know whom victory will follow. The one who thought he would conquer has been conquered.

**VERSE 20.**—“And he fled.” (Rabanus.) That is, the devil, the prince of the wicked, whose eyes are lifted high. Syria, meaning “lofty,” trusting in the horse of its pride, together with all the proud horsemen—for he is the head over all the sons of pride—is defeated by Christ’s army and put to flight. The king of Israel strikes the horses and chariots, etc., because the King of kings crushes spiritual wickedness by wiping away the sins of the human race.

(Same author.) Although the devil is often defeated by the saints, he nevertheless renews the battle against them and, when defeated in one way, immediately tries to conquer in another.

(Same author.) When evil spirits are defeated in spiritual matters, they prepare war in bodily matters, striving to hurl souls from higher things to lower ones, where they can conquer more easily. If they see that people desire heavenly things, they introduce earthly things to be loved. If they see people giving thanks to God when prosperity is granted, they work to break them through adversity. But just as the Syrians were overcome where they were confident of conquering, so were the demons.

**VERSE 38.**—“Therefore he went.” Micaiah used a parable because of the words he was about to speak to the king, in order to show that the matter concerned the king more than himself.

**VERSE 39.**—“The soul.” The servants of God must take care not to flatter themselves with the destructive security of Ahab’s example while the enemy lives, lest, considering themselves victors because the devil deceitfully promises peace, they be swiftly struck down. For just as the prophet then announced to the king that vengeance would come because of his ill-considered clemency, so the prophetic word now declares that, if we make a pact with the devil, eternal punishment threatens us on that account.

**VERSE 43.**—“And enraged.” Angry, Ahab ordered that the prophet be kept imprisoned; then, confounded by Micaiah’s words, he returned home.

## CHAPTER XXI

“After the words, etc.” (Rabanus.) Naboth is interpreted as “conspicuous,” etc., up to: but he was flowing away through empty desires.

## CHAPTER XXII

**VERSE 17.**—“I saw all Israel scattered, etc.” Through these words he showed that the king’s wickedness was the cause of the slaughter. For if he had had a good and pious shepherd, he would have overcome the enemies by force. Then he also showed the way by which salvation could be attained. “If the Lord is God,” he said to them, “let each person return to his own place in peace.” If you believe in God and wish to learn from him what must be done, dismiss the army.

### Verse 19

“I saw the Lord,” etc. (RAB.) The throne of the Lord is the angelic powers, over whose minds God presides, arranging all things below. The army of heaven is the multitude of ministering angels: the right side is the portion of the chosen angels, the left side the portion of the reprobate. For God is confined neither by the right nor by the left; he is within all things in such a way that he is also outside them. But how are the wicked part of the army of heaven? Although they have been driven from the ethereal heaven, they nevertheless still dwell in the aerial heaven; hence Paul says: “Against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). The whole army stands before God, because the will of the elect spirits serves the divine power, while the mind of the reprobate, serving its own wickedness, obeys the judgment of the Almighty.

[Col. 0611]

## THE FOURTH BOOK OF KINGS

According to the Hebrews, *MALAKHIM SECOND*. (G)*

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0611A]

### Verse 2

“And Ochozias fell.” (RAB.) The house of Ochozias is the Synagogue, which was enclosed on every side by the precepts of the Law, as though by the latticework of an upper chamber. But just as Ochozias, falling through the latticework by which he ought to have been protected, suffered a grievous illness, so also the Jew, overstepping the guardianship of the Law, fell into the incurable sickness of sins. Because he abandoned the protection of God, he found no remedy for his salvation. For, like an impious king, he fled to false gods; therefore he is rebuked by the prophetic voice, and his impending death is foretold. Ochozias signifies especially the leaders of the Jews, who, devoted to vices, persecute the truth. Hence: “The leaders and the Pharisees sent ministers to seize Jesus,” etc. (John 7).

[Col. 0611B]

### Verse 9

“And he sent to him a commander of fifty, and fifty men.” (RAB.) The fifty-man company signifies the confession of repentance, by which the remission of sins is declared. Therefore the Jews, unwilling to acknowledge Christ as God or as the prince of repentance, say to him: “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?”; and in the future they are burned in fire. The third company of fifty, because it was converted to faith in the Trinity and recognized the sacrament of repentance, obtained pardon.

## CHAPTER TWO

### Verse 2

“And it came to pass.” (RAB., in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) A whirlwind—that is, a very powerful wind—etc., up to: “The Lord was assumed through union, neither begetting nor begotten.”

[Col. 0611C]

### Verse 9

“Let there be in”—. Elijah excelled in prophetic spirit and in the performance of miracles; therefore he asked that the double grace which Elisha recognized to be active in his master should be granted to him. From this it is clear that he did not ask to be above his master as a disciple. (RAB.) With confidence received from the Lord, the Church asks for the Spirit of Christ. Since it needs the remission of sins, which Christ did not need, and the gift of virtues that Christ, from his fullness, bestows through the Holy Spirit—he who, ascending on high, “led captivity captive and gave gifts to men” (Ephesians 4)—it asks for these gifts for those, namely, who place their hope in him. Hence he says:

### Verse 10

“If you see.” That is, if you open the eyes of faith and faithfully believe my ascension together with my passion and resurrection, you will obtain the fulfillment of your request.

[Col. 0611D]

### Verse 13

“The mantle.” (RAB.) It is the Incarnation, through which he broke apart the river of Lethe and prepared for us a passage to life. Elisha retained it after Elijah’s passage, because the Church preserved faith in the Incarnation after Christ’s ascension; through this faith it strives to cross the waves of the present life. But just as Elisha divided the waters only after invoking Elijah’s name, so the Church can perform no virtues except through invocation of Christ’s name. For it is God who works in us both to will and to accomplish.

[Col. 0612A]

### Verse 17

“Send.” (ISID.) Salt—that is, wisdom—placed in an earthen vessel, that is, the human body, heals the waters; that is, through Christ’s Incarnation it makes peoples fruitful with the sweetness of love and good works.

### Verse 23

“But he went up.” (ISID.) Elisha means “salvation of God.” He is the one called Savior, and the Jews mock him because he was to ascend at the place of Calvary onto the cross. But after Christ ascended into heaven, just as Elisha went up to Bethel—that is, to the house of God—in the forty-second year, he sent two bears from the forests of the nations, namely Vespasian and Titus, who struck them down in a cruel slaughter; and their blood was poured out there where they had hanged the Lord.

## CHAPTER THREE

(RAB.) The three kings warring against Moab are the rulers of the faithful, who through faith in the Trinity fight with spiritual weapons against the prince and people of this world—that is, against philosophers, heretics, schismatics, and all the wicked. Moab is interpreted as “from the father”; this applies to those to whom the Lord said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). These oppose the Church with threats, persecutions, and deceit; but through Christ, who is the head of Christians, they are driven away.

### Verse 16

“Make.” (RAB.) The prophet provided, through a miracle, for the people exhausted by thirst; and the words of prophecy provide the faithful with instruction concerning how they may refresh the soul with spiritual teaching.

(ID.) He makes a ditch in the bed of the torrent who seeks profound mysteries in the Scriptures. These ditches are filled with water without rain or wind, because divine power often grants wisdom to those who investigate it without human assistance. Hence John says: “You have no need for anyone to teach you, but, as his anointing teaches you about everything,” etc. (1 John 2). Hence: “People and animals will drink” (John 3), that is, the intelligent and the simple will receive instruction.

### Verse 18

“And this is a small thing.” (ID.) It is not enough for the servants of God to know hidden mysteries; they must also preach them to others and refute those who contradict them. To these a certain victory over the enemy has been promised, so that they may strike every city.

[Col. 0612D]

### Verse 19

“City.” (RAB.) The city is secular wisdom, in which philosophers and heretics place their confidence; this is overthrown by preachers.

“Wood.” (ID.) Not wood that produces fruit, but deadly wood, which, cut down at the coming judgment, will become fuel for the eternal fire. The springs of water are stopped when heresiarchs, together with their followers, are condemned by Catholics. Excellent fields are covered with stones when the elegance of heretical and philosophical speech is buried beneath the weight of anathema. Only earthen walls remain—that is, false arguments—which are reduced to nothing by slingers, that is, by holy preachers.

(RAB.) Thus philosophers, considering the Word foolishness, mock the passion of Christ and regard the martyrdom of the Church as madness.

## CHAPTER FOUR

### Verse 1

“A woman,” etc. (RAB.) The holy Church is the mother of two peoples, namely the Jewish and the Gentile peoples, etc., up to: “For Abraham and Sarah received and fed three men.”

[Col. 0613B]

### Verse 18

“But the child grew.” (RAB.) Thus the Israelite people, after it had grown numerous in Egypt and, having been led into the desert through Moses, had heard the voice of the Lord, died as soon as it ought to have been enlightened by the light of understanding, immediately returning in spirit to idolatry.

### Verse 29

“And he.” (ID.) While the Lord, etc., up to: “Through the spirit of love the boy returned to life.”

### Verse 38

“The sons of the prophets.” That is, of the preachers who walk in the Law of the Lord and search his testimonies; they always live in the presence of the Savior.

### Verse 39

“He cut.” (RAB.) The person intent on the letter of the Law or devoted to philosophy, taking from the Law bitterness or from philosophers something deadly, mixes it with evangelical truth and, cooking such a stew in the pot of his heart, prepares this teaching for his hearers. For the Apostle says: “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life” (2 Corinthians 3). And: “The wisdom of the flesh is death, but the wisdom of the spirit is life” (Romans 8). The faithful, perceiving this, cry out that there is death in the pot. But flour is put into the pot when spiritual knowledge is introduced into such a seasoning, so that, once the bitterness has been removed, the food becomes wholesome.

[Col. 0613C]

### Verse 42

“But a man.” (RAB.) The man is the assembly of the fathers; he is from Baalalisa because he preserves the number three in the confession of the Trinity. Baalalisa is interpreted as “having the third.” This man offers the man of God loaves of firstfruits when, inspired by his grace, he offers the Redeemer books composed concerning the origin of creatures. He offers new grain in a sack when he presents the New Testament in the writings of the Gospel and the Apostles. Our Elisha commands the ministers—that is, the preachers—to distribute these things to the faithful and to bring forth from their treasure things new and old. We read this mystery in the Gospel in the breaking of the five and seven loaves, where, after the crowds had been satisfied, they collected twelve baskets or seven baskets of fragments, because no one comprehends all the mysteries of Scripture; when he has been satisfied, something remains for him, according to the word of the Lord.

## CHAPTER FIVE

### Verse 1

“Naaman,” etc. (RAB.) He signifies the Gentiles, who exercise leadership through the strength of war and enjoy the splendor of possessions. Hence Naaman is interpreted as “their beauty” or “their commotion”: a strong and wealthy man, but a leper, because although he appeared to rule through the power of his kingdom and abundance of possessions, he nevertheless showed himself disfigured by the leprosy of the error of idolatry.

[Col. 0614A]

### Verse 2

“Now from Syria.” (ID.) The raiders from Syria, etc., up to: “Just as the chief priests acted in the Gospel.”

(ID.) “And those whom he foreknew, he also called,” etc. The Gentile people come to the house of Elisha, etc., up to: “Because those who have been baptized ought to be strengthened by participation in the Lord’s body.”

### Verse 17

“I will take a burden.” (ID.) Naaman took with him a portion of the holy land, intending to place it in the temple of the idols and, standing upon it, worship the Lord to whom the land belonged, lest he offend his own lord if he did not worship him as well.

[Col. 0614B]

### Verse 20

“Gehazi.” (ID.) “A steep place,” etc., up to: “This is the dog returned to its vomit.”

## CHAPTER SIX

### Verse 5

“And it happened.” (RAB.) When, through the body in which Christ’s presence operated, he was cutting down the impious Jews as fruitless trees—hence: “Behold, the axe is laid at the root of the tree”—through the intervening passion that very body was made subject. It descended into the depths, and, once deposited in the tomb, it rose again when the spirit returned, as though to its handle.

(ID.) Great care must be taken lest understanding grow sluggish through idleness, or, in the exercise of work, vanish through the fault of pride.

[Col. 0614C]

(GREG.) The iron in the handle is understanding in the heart. Wood is cut when those acting wrongly are rebuked. But when this is done carelessly, when the fall of vainglory is not avoided, the iron is lost in the water, because through lax conduct the understanding becomes foolish. It was given for this purpose: that, through good action, it might be restored before the eyes of the one who gave it. Hence it follows: “This very thing.”

But when the elect offend, they quickly return to the heart and pursue their fault with tears. Hence: “Alas, alas,” etc. Weeping, they carefully examine not only the evils they have committed but also the good things they ought to have returned from the gift they received. This is expressed by: “Alas, alas, alas—and I had borrowed this”; as though he said: “Through the laxity of negligence I lost what I had received from the grace of the Redeemer in order to return it through good works.” Yet God never abandons the mind that truly recognizes itself in sins.

[Col. 0614D]

Hence Elisha sent the wood downward and brought the iron to the surface, because the Redeemer humbles the sinner’s heart and reforms the understanding that it had lost. Hence another translation says: “He cut the wood and threw it in, and thus lifted up the iron.” To break the wood is to crush the heart’s pride; to throw it downward is to humble it through reflection on its own weakness. Immediately the iron returned, because understanding returned to the use of its former exercise.

### Verse 14

“And when they had come.” (ID.) The one who trusts in the weapons of wickedness and prepares ambushes for Christ’s servants, blinded by the night of treachery, wages war against the Church.

[Col. 0615A]

### Verse 15

“Alas, alas,” etc. (GREG.) Here he indicates those who, through faintheartedness, fear bodily punishments.

### Verse 16

“Do not fear.” Do not fear those who kill the body and afterward have nothing more that they can do to you.

“More.” (ID.) “I can ask my Father, and he will present me with more than twelve legions of angels.”

“Lord, open.” (ID.) It is very necessary that our Elisha open the eyes of the heart for consideration, because all who trust in him will not be put to shame.

### Verse 18

“Strike.” (ID.) It is good for the eye that causes scandal to be torn out, so that the gaze of pride and wickedness may be closed and the eye of sound faith and simplicity opened.

(RAB.) After Elisha had brought the enemies into Samaria, he did not permit them to be killed; instead, he prepared food for them and sent them away in peace. Likewise, after Saul had long kicked against the goad, the Lord first blinded him and then enriched him with spiritual knowledge. He also commanded us: “Love your enemies and do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6).

### Verse 24

“He gathered.” (RAB.) Ben-hadad and his army signify the devil and the wicked—namely, pagans, Jews, and heretics—whom he incites to wage war against the Church. Through such people the people of God are afflicted; they are situated in Samaria, that is, in the guardianship of the Law. Famine arises when teachers are not permitted to preach the word of God.

[Col. 0615C]

But when Elisha reveals it—that is, when the Redeemer makes it known through the Gospel—salvation, which is far from sinners, is understood to be near to those who fear God. For the Lord says: “Tomorrow a measure,” etc. The measure of fine flour is the perfect measure of divine wisdom that is in the New Testament. The two measures of barley are knowledge of the Law and the Prophets; they are valued at one shekel, that is, at catholic faith, at the gate of Samaria, namely in apostolic preaching, through which one enters the Church. When the storm of persecution that is occurring today ceases, the Lord will give tomorrow—that is, in the future—a time of tranquility, so that preaching may be brought to complete fulfillment.

### Verse 25

“And famine occurred,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, Sermon 211, on the season.) When an evil people withdraws from the worship of God, it is oppressed by dreadful famine and distressed by a just necessity. Why do you suffer famine, most wretched one? Why are you torn apart by such great scarcity? The punishment of famine increases daily because guilt also increases daily. The scourges continue because sins also continue among the people. Henceforth amend your life; restrain your sins and curb your transgressions; turn back to God; abandon the idol. Then you will be able to conquer your enemies with divine help. No one will be able to harm you any further if, once wickedness has been condemned, the worship of God has taken root in you.

What a crime! The sinful people eat horrible corpses and the dung of doves, yet do not seek the worship of God. Hunger and necessity demand polluted flesh and dreadful foods, while they still stubbornly worship an idol. Piety is turned into food, and children who have been received are changed into nourishment. Parricide is committed before they approach the fatal banquet. Innocent blood is poured out so that the parents’ ravenous hunger may be fed.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

### Verse 3

“Four,” etc. (RAB., in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) They are lepers, etc., up to: “They may preach the truth of faith in the four parts of the world.”

### Verse 17

“Moreover.” The commander represents the scribes and Pharisees, to whom the Truth says: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who shut the kingdom of heaven before human beings; for you neither enter yourselves nor allow those entering to enter” (Matthew 23). The crowd trampled him at the gate because he impeded the step of those entering into faith. Therefore, deservedly trampled—that is, condemned by the judgment of the just Judge—he will be sent into everlasting darkness.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

### Verse 7

“Ben-hadad, king of Syria,” etc. When the king of the Syrians had come to Damascus and recognized that the Divinity had inspired fear and flight in him and his army, and that this had not been caused by an enemy invasion, he was exceedingly distressed because he understood that he had so angered God, and he fell into illness.

## CHAPTER NINE

### Verse 1

“Go.” (RAB., in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) He signifies the rule of the nations, which the Lord appointed to destroy with appropriate vengeance the sacrilegious city that had killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets and had persecuted his apostles; to destroy the priesthood that it had pointlessly retained after Christ; to overthrow the temple; and likewise to cast down from the height of the kingdom the impious Synagogue, which had always thirsted for the blood of the saints, and to kill its rulers.

[Col. 0616C]

### Verse 29

“And he reigned.” (RAB.) It is said of Ochozias, etc., up to: “And he reigned for one year.”

## CHAPTER TEN

### Verse 15

“Is your heart,” etc. From this it is therefore clear that even among the tribes there were certain men endowed with piety, on account of whom the Lord also cared for the others.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

### Verse 1

“But Athaliah.” (RAB.) Athaliah, who sought to extinguish the seed of David, expresses the impiety of the Synagogue, which lay in ambush against the seed of David, that is, Christ. At one time she appeared to reign, when she observed the ceremonies of the Law for a limited time. For Athaliah is interpreted as “the Lord’s temporality.”

But through the steadfastness of Jehosheba—whose name is interpreted as “the Lord’s fullness,” that is, the Church in which true delights are found—Joash, that is, “the memory of the Lord,” is preserved. He is Christ, in whom the memory of the Lord’s name exists, so that he may not be killed in the hearts of the elect by the cruelty of the raging enemy.

He is nourished especially in the house of Jehoiada, whose name means “beloved of the Lord,” concerning whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3). His house is the holy Church, where, dwelling in the holy faith of the elect, he daily brings about the growth of his body, until at the time of judgment he raises the scepter and power of the kingdom against those who were plotting to suppress him, and consigns the murderess of the saints to eternal punishments.

[Col. 0617A]

### Verse 4

“But in the seventh year Jehoiada the high priest sent,” etc. There were twenty-four divisions of priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, and they had an equal number of chief priests. Each in turn succeeded the others in order for an equal number of weeks, each having under him twenty-four priests, an equal number of Levites, and gatekeepers of the same number.

When the new high priest entered on the Sabbath for service with a new group of priests, Levites, and gatekeepers, the high priest with his group who had served during the preceding week returned after the Sabbath to his house and wife. For as long as they served, they abstained from conjugal relations and remained in the porticoes around the house of the Lord until the Sabbath.

But at that time the high priest, because it was necessary to increase the forces, retained those who had completed their week and received those who were to complete theirs. He also gathered other Levites from the cities and the heads of families. He arranged them in the following manner as he was about to bring out the king’s son: those who had completed their Sabbath duty were to stand armed around the king in the inner places of the court; those who had come for the Sabbath were to guard the king’s house, that is, the palace, and the gate of the shield-bearers, through which one descended from the temple to the palace.

[Col. 0617B]

The rest of the multitude were to guard the outer doors of the courts against the queen’s fury, in case she attempted anything. Afterwards he brought the king out of the house of the Lord where he had been hidden. They came through the way of the gate of the shield-bearers into the palace, and he sat upon the throne of the kings.

[Col. 0617C]

### Verse 6

“To the gate.” (RAB.) In the palace, the gate of Sur and the house of Messa—which are mentioned together with the gate of the shield-bearers—appear to have existed.

“Of the shield-bearers, and you shall guard the watches of the house.” (ID.) The shield-bearers were the king’s protectors, guarding the entrance hall of the palace.

### Verse 12

“And he placed the diadem and the testimony upon him.” (ID.) In the Book of Chronicles this is stated more clearly: “And they placed the diadem upon him and gave him the Law to hold in his hand.” This was certainly a salutary arrangement: after the tyrannical queen had been killed, the king’s son succeeded to the kingdom, and together with the royal insignia he was entrusted with the observance of the Law of God. He who saw himself placed over the people in order to govern them was to remember that he himself ought to be subject to divine laws in order to be governed.

[Col. 0617D]

### Verse 17

“Then Jehoiada made a covenant between the Lord,” etc. In Chronicles, “between themselves,” because he had placed himself in the position of the king and of God, whose minister he was. Hence Jehoiada is interpreted as “recognizing the Lord” or “loving him,” because he taught people to know and love the Lord.

He made a covenant between the Lord, the king, and the people, so that the king and the people would serve the Lord. He made a covenant between the king and the people, so that the people would act faithfully toward the king and the king would rule the people with justice.

## CHAPTER TWELVE

(RAB.) Our king commands that teachers receive all the money which passersby contribute to the treasury of the Lord from spiritual knowledge or good examples, or that it be applied to the work of preachers for the restoration of the spiritual temple, so that whatever they find there torn apart by error or vices they may restore, lest through the negligence of teachers the multitude of hearers perish.

[Col. 0618A]

### Verse 5

“Repairs.” (ID.) He speaks of the ruins of the house of the Lord, so that what had begun to fall might be propped up. For it is written in Paralipomenon that Athaliah and her sons—that is, the priests of the idols, since she is said not to have had a son—destroyed the house of the Lord and made Baal out of the consecrated objects.

### Verse 6

“Therefore until.” (ID.) Before the coming of Christ, although the teaching of the Law existed among the Jewish people, it was nevertheless corrupted in many respects through the negligence of teachers, until the one who gave the Law himself came and taught them, through faith in the holy Trinity, to observe the Decalogue spiritually in the writings of Moses and the Prophets.

### Verse 7

“Return it for the restoration of the temple,” etc. (ID.) The Lord says to the evangelical teachers: “Preach the Gospel to every creature; heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers. You have received freely; give freely” (Mark 16).

### Verse 9

“And he took.” (ID.) Our high priest, who offered himself as a sacrifice to God, set up one treasury—that is, he established one catholic Church—and opened an aperture above it, because he prepared from there a passage to the heavens.

“And he placed.” (ID.) The altar is the body of the Lord. Beside it, the treasury, together with the Church joined to Christ, is on the right of those entering the house. For those who enter the Church through faith aim to reach eternal blessedness, which the right side signifies.

[Col. 0618C]

Therefore the priests who guard the doors of the temple put into it all the money brought to the temple, when preachers who preserve the entrance of faith offer the vows of the faithful in words and deeds, and rightly commend them to God in the Church through prayers.

### Verse 10

“The king’s scribe,” etc. (ID.) They are the supreme teachers, who distributed the money collected according to number and measure to those in charge of the carpenters and masons—that is, to the dispensers of the word of God—who distributed to their fellow servants the measure of evangelical grain, to those who work in the house of the Lord and arrange works of virtue in the divine building.

(ID.) The Apostles, whom divine election established as leaders in the Church, scattered the seeds of the word throughout the whole world through their disciples, so that they might appoint capable workers of God’s will over their hearers.

[Col. 0618D]

Some worked the wood, when they strove to prepare themselves and those obedient to them as fruitful wood in the house of the Lord. Others repaired the damaged parts of the temple, when they rebuilt what had been torn apart by heresy and schisms. Others cut stones, when they strongly rebuked those hard of heart and unbelieving. Thus the restoration was completed in everything requiring expenditure for fortifying the house of the Lord, according to the saying: “To each one of you grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4).

### Verse 13

“Nevertheless, vessels were not made,” etc. (ID.) There ought to be one method for forming vessels for the service of the Lord and another for preparing wood and stones for the building of the house, because one kind of teaching is required to instruct the unlearned in faith and another to instruct those already mature toward the fullness of knowledge. The vessels of the Lord are those who are already fit to receive divine gifts and capable of God’s service.

“They were not made.” In Paralipomenon: “When they had completed all the work, they brought before the king and Jehoiada the remaining money, from which vessels for the temple were made.” There is no contradiction, because the vessels for the temple service were not made from the same money that the people offered for the restoration of the house of the Lord, but from the remaining money, which had also been collected through other donations.

“And little forks,” etc. (RAB.) The teachers, whose duty is to distribute the body and blood of the Lord to believers and refuse them to unbelievers, and also to distribute spiritual nourishment from the word to each person as appropriate. For among the words of God that he has deigned to reveal to our lowliness, there are others that surpass the measure of our capacity.

[Col. 0619B]

“Censers.” (ID.) They are those who offer God pure prayer from a clean conscience and sincere faith and say: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight” (Psalm 140).

“Trumpets, every vessel,” etc. (ID.) The teachers who send forth the voice of evangelical preaching throughout the whole world. Hence: “Raise your voice like a trumpet” (Isaiah 58).

### Verse 15

“And no accounting was required of them for all this,” etc. (ID.) They were so trustworthy that no one doubted that they handled God’s money without fraud. Hence it is clear how much discernment is required of those who distribute the money of the word of God to their fellow servants, since they must give an account of it, so that they may be found no less faithful in spiritual matters than those others were in bodily matters.

[Col. 0619C]

### Verse 16

“But the money for sin,” etc. (ID.) Here it is shown that confession of sins and repentance must be undertaken not according to each person’s private judgment but according to the judgment of priests. Their responsibility is to distinguish between clean and unclean and to judge the stain of leprosy.

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN

### Verse 14

“But Elisha.” (RAB.) Our Redeemer commands the rulers of the Church to be clothed in spiritual arms and to fight against the ancient enemy. The bow is sacred eloquence, which consists of both Testaments, as though of horn and string. Through the Old Testament it is represented by the horn because of its hardness; through the New, which came into being with the Lord’s Incarnation, it is represented by the string. When the string is drawn, the horn is bent, because when the New Testament is examined, the Old is bent from its rigidity toward spiritual understanding. The arrows are the words that teachers bring forth. Therefore, when we weigh the sayings of Sacred Scripture, we draw the bow; when we give words of teaching, we release the arrows.

[Col. 0619D]

### Verse 16

“He placed his hand upon him.” (ID.) Through his examples the Lord directs and strengthens the actions of teachers.

### Verse 17

“Open the window.” (ID.) He first urges his own people to be illuminated by the light of knowledge and thus to send forth the darts of words.

[Col. 0620A]

“Arrow.” (ID.) Holy preaching is the most certain destruction of spiritual enemies when it is carried out perseveringly. Therefore a teacher ought not, on account of avarice, neglect the care of souls, but should rather, through piety, extend himself toward eternal rest. This is signified by Aphek, for it is interpreted as “he will contain” or “he will grasp.” Hence, after listing vices, the Apostle adds: “But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness and piety, and seize eternal life” (1 Timothy 6).

### Verse 18

“Take.” “Who, when.” (ID.) Teachers are commanded, by the arrow of preaching, to strike the earth, etc., up to: “Faith without works is dead.”

(RAB.) The resurrection of the corpse, etc., up to: “And rather have a place there than here.”

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN

### Verse 1

“In the second year.” “And he did.” (RAB., in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) Amaziah did what was good in the sight of the Lord, but not with a perfect heart. He performed good works that pleased God, but not with a perfect heart, because he displayed them before human beings under a simulated appearance, and therefore they were not acceptable before God.

### Verse 7

“In the valley.” (ID.) The Valley of Salt was the place where salt was made—either from salty mud that was cut out, dried, and burned; or from salty well water that was heated and boiled until it reached the hardness of salt; or by whatever other method is customarily used to make salt.

“Petra.” (ID.) Petra is a famous city of Arabia in the land of Edom, called Rekem in the Book of Numbers and so named by the Syrians. But Josephus does not call it a city; rather, he says that it was a great rock situated in Arabia.

“Jectehel.” (RAB.) This is the name that Amaziah, the victor, gave it. It is interpreted as “assembly of God” or “help of God,” because he acted faithfully so that it might be remembered that he had taken it either through the assembly of God’s people or with God’s help.

### Verse 25

“He restored the boundaries of Israel,” etc. He speaks of Jeroboam: “He restored the boundaries of Israel, from the entrance of Hamath to the Sea of the Wilderness.” Hamath, now called Epiphaneia, was the northern boundary of Israel. The Sea of the Wilderness is the Dead Sea, which extends in width for five hundred and eighty stadia as far as Zoara of Arabia, and in length for one hundred and fifty stadia as far as the vicinity of Sodom.

[Col. 0620D]

Therefore Jeroboam, having encamped against the Syrians, devastated their entire province, as Jonah had prophesied.

“Which is in,” etc. Hepher was a tower not far from the temple, of enormous size and height. Hence Hepher is interpreted as “of darkness” or “cloudy,” because it raised its head as far as the clouds; in Zechariah it is called the cloudy tower.

## CHAPTER FIFTEEN

### Verse 1

“In the twentieth year of Azariah.” (RAB., in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) He is the same as Uzziah, etc., up to: “It is called the upper gate of Ephraim.”

### Verse 35

“He built.” (RAB.) Jotham built the high gate of the house of the Lord, which is called Beautiful in the Acts of the Apostles and is called the Gate of Jotham by the Hebrews.

## CHAPTER SIXTEEN

### Verse 3

“He consecrated.” (RAB.) Ge-Ben-Hinnom: “the valley of the son of Hinnom.” Topheth, or Tophat, is in the valley of Ben-Hinnom near Acheldemach, a once exceedingly pleasant place where they used to sacrifice to demons. In Hebrew it is *Gehennon*, that is, “the valley of Hinnom”; hence in the Gospel it is called Gehenna, because just as those who worshiped idols there perished in body and soul, so sinners who pass into hell will be punished by eternal condemnation.

### Verse 18

“Also the covered way.” (RAB.) It is a building placed in the vestibule of the temple, where the kings, whenever they went to the temple on the Sabbath, deposited alms. Thus the covered way of the Sabbath is the treasury of the kings, just as the *corban* is that of the priests.

“Also the covered way,” etc. (RAB.) He did not convert it into the temple of the Lord because it would serve the worship of God there, but so that the temple might be profaned with it. He was eager to please the king of the Assyrians more than God, so that when the king came there, seeing it, he might desire it and take it away, as well as many other things, with Ahaz granting them to him, in order that Ahaz might find favor with him.

## CHAPTER SEVENTEEN

### Verse 27

“You have brought.” (RAB.) The king of Assyria—that is, the devil with his army—afflicts the ecclesiastical people daily by besieging and devastating them, when, because of their committed sins, he uproots them from their own dwellings and carries them into a foreign land. Hence: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered Zion.”

[Col. 0621C]

### Verse 29

“And each one.” (ID.) In the Book of Places it is written that Benoth and Nergel were cities built in Judea by those who had crossed over from Babylonia. They also built Asima, a town, those who came to it from Hamath. Nebahan and Tharthac are cities that the Hivites established in Judea.

(ID.) According to the sequence of the passage and of the idols to which these peoples had previously been devoted, it seems possible to understand the names here as names of idols. For after it had been said, “Each nation made its own god,” the following words were added as a completion of the statement: “The men of Babylon made Succoth-benoth”—that is, tabernacles; Benoth being the name of an idol. In what follows it is shown that Adrammelech and Anammelech were the idols of the city of Sepharvaim. It therefore seems to follow that Nergel was the idol of the Cuthaeans, Asima of the Hamathites, and Nebahaz and Tharthak the idols of the Hivites.

### Verse 33

“And when.” (RAB., from Eucherius.) Heretics possess certain sacraments in common with the holy Church, etc., up to: “And we understand descendants.”

## CHAPTER EIGHTEEN

“ In the third year.” “Hezekiah.” (RAB.) “Grasping the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord.” For our Redeemer is the strong Lord, the Lord mighty in battle. He not only crushed the idols of the nations and destroyed the worship of idolatry so that they might possess knowledge of the one God and be rightly devoted to his worship; he also crushed the very letter of the Mosaic Law, which the legal people recited continually in reading and held in high regard, and taught them to understand its spiritual meaning.

[Col. 0622A]

### Verse 4

“And he broke.” Hezekiah broke the serpent because he trusted in the Lord God, not in the bronze serpent.

“He called it Nehushtan,” etc. This is interpreted as “their bronze,” so that they might recognize that the object they worshiped as a divinity was, in his words, metal and not God.

### Verse 17

“Rabshakeh.” (RAB.) Because he spoke Hebrew, some think he was the son of Isaiah, who had been a traitor together with Shebna; others think he was a Samaritan and therefore knew the Hebrew language. By his arrogance he imitated the prophets in a kind of opposing manner. The prophets say: “Thus says the Lord.” He said: “Thus says the great king, the king of the Assyrians.”

[Col. 0622B]

### Verse 18

“Eliakim.” (RAB.) Concerning this Eliakim Isaiah said: “I will call my servant Eliakim” (Isaiah 22). He was high priest after Shebna. The Hebrews relate that, terrified by Rabshakeh’s threats, he betrayed Jerusalem, and that, except for the citadel and the temple, the Assyrians captured the whole city. Some also maintain that Shebna went out with Eliakim to Rabshakeh.

### Verse 21

“Do you hope?” No history relates that Hezekiah sought the help of Pharaoh.

### Verse 22

“In the Lord.” (RAB.) It is true that they placed their confidence in God, but it is false that Hezekiah removed the high places of God and the altars. He did this not against God but for God, so that, after destroying the old error, he might command that God be worshiped in the temple at Jerusalem.

## Verse 23

“‘I will give you.’ (ID.) Rabsaces, in order to show the small number of the besieged, promises two thousand horses, for which Hezekiah would have no riders. This did not arise from the weakness of the people, as though they were ignorant of riding, but because God commanded that the king of Israel should not multiply horses and wives for himself.”

## Verse 25

“‘The Lord said.’ (ID.) To his statement, ‘If you say, “We trust in God,”’ he craftily replies that he had come not by his own will but at the command of God, who said, ‘Ascend.’ The argument is this: since I have captured many cities and part of Jerusalem remains untouched, it is evident that I have come by God’s will.”

[Col. 0622D] ## Verse 26

“‘We beg.’ (ID.) The sense is … up to the point where it had a likeness to the land of Judah, both in situation and in produce.”

## Verse 29

“‘Do not let Hezekiah deceive you,’ etc. Rabsaces’ accusation is testimony that Hezekiah had trusted in the Lord when the cities had been captured, and had encouraged the people to hope in the Lord. Therefore Rabsaces wishes to destroy what Hezekiah had built, and says to the people: ‘Let not Hezekiah deceive you, and let him not give you confidence in the Lord your God.’”

“(RAB.) He shows that the Samaritans had served the gods of these cities or nations, etc., up to the point where our translator rendered it.”

# Chapter XIX

[Col. 0623A]

“(RAB., in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) The king’s remarkable humility and prudence, etc., up to the point that the enemy would die in his own land.”

## Verse 9

“‘And when he heard.’ (ID.) By God’s will Rabsaces abandoned the siege of Jerusalem and found his lord attacking Lobnah, Lachish having either been captured or abandoned. Sennacherib, going to meet the king of the Ethiopians, sent letters to Hezekiah so that he might terrify by words those whom he had not captured by force. Herodotus relates that Sennacherib fought against the Egyptians and besieged Pelusium, and that, when the city was already about to be captured after embankments had been constructed, Tarachus, king of the Ethiopians, came to its aid.

“(RAB.) Formerly Hezekiah, terrified by the Lord’s dread, did not dare to worship in the temple or pour out free prayers there; now, when Isaiah says, ‘Do not fear the face of the words that you have heard’ (Isa. XLI), he boldly entreats the Lord.”

## Verse 21

“‘Virgin daughter.’ (RAB.) Because, while all the nations worship idols, she alone preserves the purity of the worship of the one God. And lest she provoke him to still greater blasphemy, she did not answer him immediately; after he had departed, she moved her head either to ask God for help or, certainly, to mock his arrogance, confident of vengeance. Nor did he blaspheme the Lord in person, but through his servants, so that his arrogance might be greater.”

## Verse 23

“‘The heights.’ (ID.) The height of the mountains and the ridges of Lebanon, the lofty cedars and fir trees. Or it should be understood metaphorically of all the nations and their rulers. Or of Jerusalem, which is Lebanon: its cedars and fir trees are the powerful and the nobles.”

## Verse 24

“‘And I dried up.’ (ID.) Either he dried up all the streams because of the multitude of his army, so that he was compelled to dig wells for himself; or the whole people, whom the waters signify, is ravaged by his army.”

## Verse 25

“‘Have you not?’ (ID.) These words are spoken in the person of the Lord, etc., up to the point where he subdues your ferocity and leads you back to Assyria.”

## Verse 29

“‘This shall be the sign.’ (ID.) Of the things that I foretell, etc., up to the point that he did it, indeed, out of the zeal with which he had been zealous for his people against the ungodly.

“‘Eat.’ Isaiah says: ‘Eat this year what grows of its own accord, and in the second year feed on fruits. In the third year sow, plant vineyards, and eat their fruits; and what has been preserved in the house of Judah shall send forth what remains as a root below, and shall produce fruit, because a remnant shall go forth from Jerusalem, and salvation from Mount Zion. The zeal of the Lord of hosts shall do this’ (Isa. XXXVII). After everything had been devastated by the army, eat what was able to sprout again, or what was able to escape beneath the horses’ hooves. In the second year, eat what grows of its own accord, without labor. Or this was said figuratively, because they thought that they would perish from hunger.”

## Verse 34

“‘And for the sake of David my servant.’ (RAB.) Through hope in future things, he removes present fear. He says that they are preserved not by their own merit but by God’s mercy, indeed also because of the memory of their father David. In this they are warned both of their own negligence and of his faith and justice, because God loves justice so greatly that he protects descendants through the virtue of their ancestors.”

## Verse 35

“‘And so it happened.’ (RAB.) So many are slain by one angel in a single night, and savage death runs through them without wounds. Concerning this it is written in Chronicles: ‘And the Lord sent an angel who struck every strong and fighting man, and the leader of the Assyrian army. And he returned with disgrace to his own land.’ He was spared so that he might become a witness to the majesty of the one whom shortly before he had despised.”

## Verse 37

“‘And while he was worshiping in the temple.’ (RAB.) As though he were carrying victory away from his enemies, the despiser of the true God is slaughtered in the shrine of a false deity. He does not perish by an angel’s sword, which would have been common, but by the murder committed by his sons.

“(ID.) Pharaoh too was preserved through the ten plagues of Egypt, so that he might perish last.

“‘Into the land of the Armenians.’ Ararath is a region in flat Armenia, through which the Araxes flows, of extraordinary fertility, at the foot of Mount Taurus. Therefore Noah’s ark was not brought merely to the mountains of Armenia in general, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlooks the plains of Ararath.”

# Chapter XX

## Verse 1

“‘In those days.’ (RAB. in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) So that Hezekiah’s heart would not be lifted up after his unbelievable triumphs, he is visited with bodily illness and hears [Col. 0624C] that he is going to die, so that, turning to the Lord, he might change the sentence.

“God, foreknowing all future things before the ages, decreed how they would be ordered throughout the ages. Thus it was determined how long one would live temporally within mortal life. For although God added fifteen years to Hezekiah’s life, when he allowed him to die he nevertheless already knew that he would die. When the sentence of death was pronounced upon him, life was immediately added in response to his tears. At that time he deserved to die because, being elated, he had not given thanks to the Lord for his unexpected victory, since he attributed it to his own righteousness and merits. The period of life established in God’s foreknowledge was not prolonged; rather, what he had lost by sinning was restored by God’s generosity. When God foretold that he would die, he had foreseen this before his repentance. He turned his face toward the wall of the temple because he could not go to the temple. He says ‘the wall of the temple’ because the palace was adjacent to it; or simply ‘the wall,’ so that he would not display his tears to those standing nearby and might entreat God with his whole mind.”

## Verse 2

“‘Who turned.’ (RAB.) A blessed conscience, etc., up to the point that God weighs the words of each person according to their heart.”

## Verse 3

“‘And so he wept.’ (ID.) He wept because of the Lord’s promise, etc., up to the point that we read that many were raised from the dead.”

## Verse 7

“‘Bring a lump.’ (RAB.) The word *sehim* or *schim* (as the Hebrews say) denotes an ulcer, not a wound: the former is inflicted, whereas the latter arises spontaneously. For Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion translated it as *aroc*, which they understand as the royal disease; foods taken internally or things applied to the body that are sweet are thought to be contrary to it. Thus God’s power is shown, when health is restored through harmful substances. Others suspect that *schim* means an abscess, when a swollen body becomes filled with cooked and putrefying pus. According to medical practice, every discharge is drawn to the surface of the skin by means of dried and crushed figs.

“(RAB.) A sign is given so that the sun may turn back ten degrees, etc., up to the point that the spans of life of those living through Christ’s resurrection may be extended in place of the span of life.

“(ID.) Some transfer the ten degrees of the lines to the mystery of Christ, etc., up to the point that he illuminated the whole shadow of the Law with the rays of truth.”

## Verse 12

“‘In that.’ (ID.) It is read above, etc., up to the point that they believed him worthy of greater worship than a human being.

“(RAB.) The Hebrews relate, etc., up to the point that he might be brought to the knowledge of men through the deed of his wicked action.

“(ID.) Hypocrites also decline after great accomplishments because they do not wish to remain hidden within those accomplishments. When, at the urging of evil spirits, they give in to vainglory, they open, as it were, a door to the enemies through which they lose what they had gathered over a long period. Hence: ‘He delivered their strength into captivity.’ Paul recalls his glory as the testimony of his conscience, because he does not seek the favor of another’s mouth. Therefore the things we do must be concealed, lest, carelessly carrying them along the road of this life, we lose them through the assault of the plundering spirit.

“(ID.) He is silent about what he feared would cause offense: that he had shown them everything he possessed, among which the furnishings of the temple were especially important.”

## Verse 13

“‘Hezekiah rejoiced at their arrival.’ (ID.) The Book of Chronicles says concerning Hezekiah, etc., up to the point where ‘he showed them the house of spices,’ etc.

“‘The house of spices, and the gold and silver.’ (ID.) Some think that these were the tombs of kings, which were full of spices, because in ancient times the bodies of kings were embalmed with ointments. Others understand it rather as the chamber of spices in the Lord’s temple, where fragrant substances were stored, from which the incense offered in the Lord’s temple was made.

“‘There was nothing that Hezekiah did not show them in,’ etc. (*In* is frequently used among the Hebrews for ‘in the matter of’): he showed them everything in his house and in all his power. Hence God’s anger was entirely just, since he showed them not only his treasures and palace but also the temple, which certainly lay within his authority, for he had already removed the plates from its vestibule doors.”

[Col. 0625D] ## Verse 14

“‘They came from a distant land.’ (RAB.) As if he were saying: The farther away the land from which they came, the more glorious I am, since they came on my account.

“‘To me from Babylon.’ He ought to have said this in order to glorify God for the greatness of the sign.”

## Verse 21

“‘And Hezekiah slept with his fathers,’ etc. In Chronicles it is said that Hezekiah was buried above the tombs of the kings, because his tomb was built higher on account of the piety with which he had worshiped God.”

# Chapter XXI

“(RAB.) In whose time Isaiah, as the Hebrews relate, was sawn in half with a wooden saw, because he called them princes of Sodom; they turned against him as a crime what he had said: ‘I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne’ (Isa. VI), while God says: ‘No man shall see me and live’ (Exod. XXXIII).

“(ID.) Manasseh turned to idols and abominations. When God, or the Lord, spoke to him, he refused to pay attention; therefore, once defeated, he was led to Babylon. In his distress he earnestly prayed to the Lord and practiced very great repentance, and his prayer was heard. He was brought back into his kingdom, and Manasseh recognized that the Lord himself is God. Therefore, after committing sins, let no one despair of God’s mercy; rather, through repentance let him maintain hope of forgiveness.”

## Verse 24

“‘Josiah.’ (RAB.) Josiah corrected every impurity of the idols and devoted himself vigorously to the worship of God, as had long before been foretold concerning him through the prophet.”

# Chapter XXII

## Verse 14

“‘In the Second.’ (RAB.) In Chronicles it is written concerning Hezekiah that he built the entire wall that had been destroyed, and another wall on the outside. Hence Zephaniah says: ‘A wailing from the Second.’ The prophetess therefore lived in the Second, that is, in the part of the second wall.”

# Chapter XXIII

[Col. 0626C]

## Verse 10

“‘He defiled.’ (RAB. in the Book of Kings, vol. III.) Josiah, by scattering there either the bones of the dead, as he is said to have done in the following places, or any other unclean things, made the place appear to all who saw it suited more to abhorrence than to delight.

“‘In the valley.’ (ID.) The Valley of Hinnom is beside the wall of Jerusalem toward the east, etc., up to the point that *Topheth* means ‘breadth.’”

## Verse 11

“‘He removed.’ (RAB.) The Jews had enslaved themselves to the superstitions of the nations. Among other things, they customarily painted or fashioned an image of the sun as a beardless boy, because no old age ever overtakes it through the ages, and it is born each day in a new rising. They assign to it a chariot and horses, because Elijah was carried up to heaven in a fiery chariot and with fiery horses. They see this painted on the wall among other things and are deceived by the similarity of the name: for *Elios* in Greek means ‘sun.’”

## Verse 13

“‘The high places.’ (RAB.) Scripture calls them places situated on leafy hills, where they either sacrificed to demons or, attracted by the beauty of the places, came together to offer sacrifice to the Lord contrary to the prohibition, abandoning the altar that was in the temple. Hence this book frequently says of less perfect kings: ‘Nevertheless, he did not remove the high places.’

“‘Which he had built.’ (ID.) Here it is shown that Solomon never fully repented of the crime of idolatry that he had committed. For if he had truly repented, he would have taken care above all that the idols he had built should be removed from the city; and he would not have left, as a stumbling block to fools, the erroneous things he had made while being the wisest of men, as though they had been wisely made.

“‘And Chemosh.’ (RAB.) Elsewhere it is read that Solomon built a shrine to Chemosh on the mountain that is opposite Jerusalem. But this is not contradictory, because that mountain was so near the city that it seemed to belong to it and to defile it with the filth collected there.

“‘As an offense to Moab.’ (ID.) Idols are called an offense because either God is offended by them or they bring offense and ruin upon their worshipers.”

## Verse 16

“‘He took the bones,’ etc. Josiah ordered the bones of the dead to be burned upon the altar because their sacrifices had been profane. Through the error of idolatry they offered not only animals to demons but also handed themselves over to the power of demons, because by God’s just judgment they were to be destroyed together with the altar they had built for the idols. Mystically, those who are enslaved to the service of the devil and temporally bring a sacrilegious life to an end will be consumed by eternal torments, with God repaying them according to their merits.”

## Verse 21

“‘Keep the Passover.’ (RAB.) Josiah bears the type of the Savior, etc., up to the point: ‘and the sun of righteousness shall rise for you who fear.’

“For such a Passover did not take place, etc. Because, when the figures have been removed on the day of judgment, the saints will pass from death to life, and thus will rejoice in the sight of their Creator, because ‘the God of gods will be seen in Zion.’

“(RAB.) The fact that Josiah is read to have celebrated the Lord’s Passover after expelling idols, diviners, soothsayers, and all impurities from the land teaches morally that we must first cleanse the land of the heart from vices, so that we may be able to serve God, and thus celebrate a Passover pleasing to the Lord: ‘not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth’ (I Cor. V).

“(ID.) Josiah was wounded in the field of Megiddo, and therefore died immediately. The people mourned him greatly, especially Jeremiah. At that time he is said to have lamented in this way: ‘How does the city sit solitary!’ Concerning this mourning it is said: ‘And there shall be a lamentation in Jerusalem, like the lamentation of Adremmon,’ which is the name of the king who was then reigning at Carchemish, to whose aid Josiah had come against Necho, king of Egypt.

“(ID.) The killing of Josiah by Pharaoh Necho at Megiddo signifies the persecution of the ancient enemy against preachers, whom he endeavors through envy to hand over to death and to remove from the land of the Church, so that he may more easily scatter the entire people. Pharaoh means ‘the one who scatters’; Necho, ‘striking’; Megiddo, ‘from temptation.’ For when the devil is permitted to rise up against the saints, he fights here with all his strength, so that by tempting he may strike and scatter the Lord’s flock, and first remove those whose assistance should have enabled the others to fight against the enemy.”

## Verse 30

“‘Jehoahaz, the son of Josiah.’ (ID.) He is called Shallum by another name. But because he was exceedingly wicked, he reigned for a short time. For Necho bound him, because the people had appointed him king against Necho’s will, and led him into Egypt.

“(ID.) The detained Jehoahaz signifies wicked teachers, whom the people of the land—that is, those devoted to earthly desire—choose as their rulers because they agree with their vices. Pharaoh bound them at Riblah, when the devil, weakening the hearts of rulers through a multitude of flatterers, deceives them, and thus plunges them, bound by chains of sins, into the dark abyss of spiritual Egypt.”

## Verse 35

“‘And he gave the silver and the gold,’ etc. (ID.) The evil one demands from the carnal people the tribute of his service, so that they may be ready to obey him in everything, both in understanding and in speech. Jehoiakim exacts the tribute by command of the king, because the devil, through teachers devoted to him, demands from each person, according to his strength, payment of the tribute of sin, and thus daily prepares perdition for those subject to wicked rulers.”

# Chapter XXIV

“(RAB.) When anyone has once enslaved himself to vice, etc., up to the point that he implores help from God.

“(RAB.) Josephus reports that this man was killed by Nebuchadnezzar and thrown down unburied before the walls of Jerusalem. Concerning him it had been foretold: ‘He shall be buried with the burial of a donkey’ (Jer. XXII).

“‘And Jehoiakim reigned,’ etc. (ID.) The name Jehoiakim is written differently when it designates the father, who is also called Eliakim, and differently when it signifies the son, who is also called Jeconiah. When it denotes the father, it is written with *k* and *m*; when it denotes the son, with *ch* and *n*.”

## Verse 8

“‘Jerusalem.’ (BEDA in the Book of Kings, question 30, vol. II.) Jerusalem and the land of Israel, etc., up to the point that spiritual knowledge is turned toward the works of sinners.”

## Verse 14

“(ID., ibid.) ‘The craftsman and the engraver, and nothing was left except the poor of the people of the land.’ (RAB. from Beda, ibid.) What is related above to have been done by the Philistines when they ruled the people of Israel, when it is said, ‘No blacksmith was found throughout all the land of Israel, for the Philistines had taken care that the Hebrews might not make a sword or spear for resistance’ (I Reg. XIII), the Chaldeans now endeavor to do likewise, so that no craftsman or engraver may remain in it who could repair or restore the demolished walls of the city.”

[Col. 0628D] “(RAB.) Evil are the rulers who misuse an office and divine gift and falsely claim for themselves the name of justice. For Mattathias, or Mattaniah, is interpreted as ‘gift’ or ‘present’; Zedekiah, ‘the Lord is just.’ He reigned eleven years because he was a transgressor of the Law, which is signified by the number ten. The number nine, which falls short of ten, signifies the imperfection of the Law, just as eleven signifies transgression. Therefore Nebuchadnezzar rightly besieged the city in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, in the tenth month and on the tenth day of the month. For when wicked shepherds neglect to fulfill in conduct and teaching the commands of the Decalogue, which they possess as knowledge, it is necessary that the ancient enemy, with his army, surround the people entrusted to them in a siege and enclose them with a fortification constructed from error and vices, by building a rampart around the city. Thus hunger prevails in the city—namely, hunger for the word of God, when the bread of teaching is not distributed to the people of the land.”

# Chapter XXV

## Verse 4

“‘And it was breached,’ etc. (RAB.) The people’s protection was breached through various temptations of demons, etc., up to the point that he is weighed down by evil practice and the multitude of his iniquity.”

## Verse 8

“‘In the fifth month.’ (RAB.) The order of the time corresponds to the logic of vengeance. In the fifth month the city was devastated because it had disdained to observe the Pentateuch of the Law; and on the seventh day of the month because it had not kept the Sabbath rest and had acted contrary to God’s commandments, vainly flattering itself about its security because of its habitation in holy places.

“(ID.) Nabuzardan came, whose name is interpreted as ‘winnowing fan,’ or ‘prophecy of another’s judgment,’ etc., up to the point that rather thorns and thistles of vices might grow up.”

## Verse 13

“‘And the bronze pillars,’ etc. (ID.) We understand the bases as teachers, who ought to have supported others through the resonance of their preaching and the firmness of faith. The bronze sea signifies the laver of baptism or the contrition of tears. The spiritual Chaldeans strive to remove and break all these things from the house of the Lord through the negligence of teachers.”

## Verse 14

“‘The pots also.’ (ID.) Because, taking away the various offices in the ecclesiastical orders from the service of God, they turned them to their own most wicked use.”

[Col. 0629C] ## Verse 15

“‘The censers and bowls.’ When they obstruct and overturn the prayer by which the divinity could be appeased, and the cup of the word by which the weary ought to have been refreshed.

“(ID.) Because the wicked enemy strives to remove both precious understanding and the beauty of eloquence from the house of the Lord, and to lead them with himself into confusion.”

## Verse 18

“‘He also took.’ (ID.) The devil strives to deceive and take captive as sinners not only ordinary people but also the strong and the rulers in the Church. Hence it is said of him in Job: ‘His chosen foods are’ (Job XXXIII).

“He took Seraiah, whose name is interpreted as ‘bound,’ the chief priest, when he binds with the chain of vices, through love of earthly pleasure, the first order of the Church, which is found in bishops. Similarly, he took Zephaniah, whose name is interpreted as ‘hidden,’ the second priest, when he subjugates to his dominion men of the second order, that is, presbyters, who had hidden the talent of the word by burying it in the earth. And three eunuchs, who ought to have opened the door of faith, but, holding the key of knowledge, neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter. The eunuch signifies the foolish virgins, who held vessels empty of oil in their hands: they abstained from bodily intercourse, yet were unwilling to have the oil of grace and mercy in their breasts. They are appointed over warriors in vain when they do not guard against arrogance. He took five men from among those who stood before the king [Col. 0630B] (Matt. V), that is, those who, serving pleasure through the five bodily senses, always attended upon the king of vices.

“‘Sopher the prince.’ (ID.) The name is interpreted as ‘scattering’ or ‘dividing,’ signifying those who, by wicked examples, scatter within the Church the inexperienced people whom they ought to have nourished for the service of Christ, and separate them from the assembly of the faithful through error. And sixty men from the people, that is, foolish workers, who rightly came from the people because they had neglected to learn the divine counsels and fulfill them in deeds.

“‘And sixty men.’ (ID.) Nabuzardan led all these to the king of Babylon, and they were killed, because the devil strives to bring the prey that he tears away from the Church to the destruction of perpetual death. The king of confusion strikes them at Riblah, that is, amid the multitude of crimes [Col. 0630C] and love of pleasures.

“(ID.) When those who appeared to possess the confession of God’s name in the Church are transferred from the land of the living through manifold crimes and led into the kingdom of confusion and error, etc., up to the point that he wishes to contemplate the face of our Creator throughout the ages.”

## Verse 23

“‘And Seraiah.’ The son of Seraiah the priest was spared, while the father was killed. From him Jesus the high priest was later born in captivity, and he brought back the people with Zerubbabel.”

[Col. 0629]

# Blessed Jerome’s Prologue to the Books of Chronicles

“See among the works of Blessed Jerome.”

[Col. 0629]

# Another Prologue of Saint Jerome

“See above.”

[Col. 0629]

# The First Book of Chronicles

“Hebrew: *Dibre ha-yamim*, that is, ‘Words of the Days.’ (G.)”

# Chapter I

[Col. 0629D]

## Verse 4

“‘Noah.’ (RAB. in Chronicles, vol. III.) Noah is shown to be tenth from Adam both in Genesis and in Chronicles, and appropriately tenth because ten is perfect. Hence: ‘Noah was a just and perfect man in his generations,’ etc. (Gen. VI.) He fathered Shem, Ham, and Japheth, through whom, after the flood, the renewed race of human beings was spread abroad.”

## Verse 5

“‘The sons of Japheth.’ (HIER.) These possessed the land in Asia, from the Amanus and Taurus mountains of Syria, Cilicia, and Chalcis, as far as the river Tanais. In Europe they extended as far as Gadara, leaving their names to places and peoples; many of these names were later altered, while the rest remain.

“‘Tubal.’ (RAB.) The Iberians, who are also the Spaniards, from whom Celtiberia derives its name, although some suspect that they were Italians.

“‘Meshech.’ (ID.) The Cappadocians, from whom their city is still called Masacha. The translators of the Septuagint, however, consider the Caphtorim to be Cappadocians.”

[Col. 0631B] ## Verse 7

“‘And the sons.’ (GREG.) From these the islands of the nations, their languages, kinships, and peoples were divided. From the Ionians, that is, the Greeks, came the Elisaeans, who are also called Aeolids. Hence this language is called Aeolic in Greek.

“‘Tarshish.’ (RAB.) Josephus considers these to be the Cilicians; hence their metropolis is also called Tarsus, famous because of the apostle Paul (Acts XXII).

“‘Kittim.’ (ID.) From them came the Cittaeans, also called Cittians, from whom the city of Cyprus is still called Cittia, or Cittium.

“‘Dodanim.’ (ID.) The Rhodians; thus the Septuagint translated it. Let us read the books of Varro on antiquities, and those of Sinnius Capito, and the Greek Phlegon and the others, and we shall see that almost all the islands, the shores of the whole world, and the maritime lands were occupied by Greek settlers, who possessed everything from the Amanus and Taurus as far as the British Ocean.”

## Verse 8

“‘Put.’ (ID.) The Libyans, from whom the river of Mauretania is also called Put, as is the region of Put. Many writers, both Greek and Latin, bear witness to this matter. Why, however, in one part of the climate-zone the ancient name of Libya remains while the rest of the land is called Africa is not a matter to discuss at this time.”

## Verse 9

“‘Sheba.’ (ID.) From him came the Sabaeans. Sheba is now interpreted as Arabia, whence in Psalm LXXI, where we have ‘the kings of the Arabs and Sheba,’ the Hebrew has ‘the kings of Sheba and Sheba’: the first with *shin*, the second with *samekh*.”

[Col. 0631D] ## Verse 10
