“‘He was the first to become mighty on the earth.’ Because he was the first to seize an unheard-of tyranny. He was a mighty hunter before the Lord because he turned people away from the worship of God. Hence Josephus says: ‘He made them arrogant for injury and contempt of God.’ Nimrod, the son of Ham, the son of Noah, was bolder than others and exceedingly strong in his hand. He persuaded people to attribute their prosperity not to God but to their own strength. Thus he recalled people from the fear of God and caused them to place their hope in their own power. Therefore they thought that God was threatening a flood. Hence they advised building a tower that the water could not reach. The multitude was ready to obey Nimrod, considering it a burdensome service to obey God. Nimrod reigned in Babylon and in Areth. This is Edessa, and Macha, which is Nisibis, and Chalamne, which was called Seleucia after King Seleucus, or which is now called Ctesiphon.”

## Verse 11

“‘And Mesraim fathered.’ (RAB.) Except for the Laabim, from whom the Libyans were named, who were formerly called Phutaeans, and the Casluhim, who were later called Philistines, whom we corruptly call Palestinians. The other nations are unknown to us because, having been overthrown in the Ethiopian war, they passed into oblivion together with their former names. They possessed the land from Gaza to the farthest boundaries of Egypt.”

## Verse 14

“‘The Girgashite, the Hivite.’ He founded the town of Arcas opposite Tripoli, at the foot of Lebanon. Not far from it there was another city called Sim, which, destroyed by wars through various reversals of fortune, preserved only its former name for the place.”

## Verse 16

“‘And the Arvadite.’ From him came the Arvadites, who possessed the island of Arad, separated from the Phoenician coast by a narrow strait.

“‘And the Samaraean.’ From him came the city of Samaria in Chalcis of Syria, which even now is called by both Syrians and Hebrews what it was called among the ancients.

“‘The Hamathite.’ (RAB.) From him came the city of Hamath. The Macedonians who ruled in the East after Alexander called it Epiphanea. Others think that Antioch was so named. Others, not supporting their opinion with a plausible name, think that the first stopping-place from Antioch for those traveling to Edessa was called Emmaus, and that it was the same place called Hamath in former times.”

[Col. 0632C] ## Verse 17

“‘The sons of Shem,’ etc. These occupy the regions of Asia from the Euphrates as far as the Indian Ocean. There is also Elam, from whom the rulers of Persia descend.

“‘Uz and Hul.’ Or Uz, the founder of Trachonitis and Damascus, held the principate between Palestine and Coele-Syria. From him came the land of Uz, from which Job was; hence, according to the Septuagint, he was ‘a man in the land of Ausitis,’ named Job as though from Usitis.”

## Verse 19

“‘Peleg.’ (RAB.) By a kind of prophecy. For *Peleg* means ‘division,’ because in his days the languages were divided in Babylon. Philo relates in his book of Questions on Genesis that, while Noah himself was still alive, thirteen thousand one hundred men were born from the three sons of Noah, apart from women and children, and that they had leaders over them. The sons of Shem had Jectan as their leader; the sons of Ham, Nimrod; the sons of Japheth, Suphene. After Noah’s death, the leaders gathered with their armies in the plain of Shinar to build a tower there. While they were building, God divided their languages and changed their appearances, and each person no longer recognized his brother or heard the language of his neighbor. When the master builders sought stones, the servants brought water; and when the former sought water, the latter brought straw. Thus, frustrated in their purpose, they stopped building and were scattered over the face of the earth.”

## Verse 20

“‘And Jectan.’ (HIERON.) I have not been able to discover the later names of these nations. But because they are far from us, either they are still called what they were called at first, or their changed names are unknown. They possessed the whole region of India from the river Cophene, which is called Hieria.”

## Verse 24

“‘Shem, Ar.’ (RAB.) Just as at the beginning he placed ten generations from Adam to Noah, so likewise he placed ten from Shem to Abram, not without the mystery of a sacred significance.”

## Verse 29

“‘The firstborn.’ (HIERON., Questions on Chronicles, vol. III.) Twelve sons were born to Ishmael. The firstborn was Nabaioth, from whom the entire region from the Euphrates to the Red Sea is called Nabaiothena; it is a part of Arabia. For their families, towns, villages, small fortresses, and tribes are designated by their name. Among them are Kedar in the desert, Duma, another region, Thebaram to the south, and Cedema toward the east.”

[Col. 0633B] ## Verse 32

“‘Of Keturah.’ (RAB.) As though ‘joined’ or ‘attached’; hence the Hebrews suspect that she was Hagar, who, after Sarah’s death, passed from being a concubine into the status of wife, so that the old man would not be accused of indulging in a new marriage.

“(ID.) The sons of Keturah, according to the historians of the Hebrews, occupied Trachonitis—others say Traconitis—and Arabia, which is now called Eidormo, as far as the boundaries of the Red Sea.

“‘Asshurim.’ Some contend that the Syrians were called from Asshurim, and that the regions of India were occupied by many of Abraham’s sons by Keturah.”

## Verse 33

“‘Epher.’ (RAB.) He is said to have led an army against Libya, to have settled there in victory, and to have given Africa its present name through his descendants.”

## Verse 36

“‘Timna.’ Since Timna is read in Genesis to have been the concubine of Eliphaz, from the race of the Horites who lived among the Idumeans in the land of Seir, and she bore Amalek to him, how is she counted among the sons when later Timna herself is read to have been the sister of Lotan, the son of Seir, who is also Edom? But *Seir* in Hebrew means ‘hairy’; he was rough like a hide. *Edom* in Hebrew means ‘red’ or ‘ruddy.’ He was therefore called Edom because he sold his birthright for red food. The Hebrews resolve the matter in this way: they say that Timna was Eliphaz’s concubine and bore Amalek to him, but that she was raised by him as a daughter among his sons.”

## Verse 40

“‘Alian, who was of the race of the Horites.’ In Genesis it is written *Aluah*, that is, ‘exalted.’ In Chronicles, however, *Alian*, that is, ‘cast out,’ signifying [Col. 0633D] that the Horites were exalted before Edom took their land, but afterward were cast out.

“‘Sephi.’ (HIERON.) That is, ‘one-footed.’ In Genesis, *Sepho*, that is, ‘two-footed’; nevertheless, both are written with the letter *shin*. He is called ‘two-footed’ because, as time passed, through the multitude of his offspring he possessed greater power than at first.”

## Verse 41

“‘Hamran.’ In Chronicles, *Hamram*, that is, ‘reddened,’ ‘filthy,’ or ‘swollen.’ In Genesis, *Amdan*, that is, ‘desirable’; but both are names of one man.”

## Verse 42

“‘Jaakan.’ (RAB.) Jaakan, the son of Aser and of the race of the Horites, is called Acan in Genesis, that is, ‘the troubler.’ In Chronicles, *Jaakan*, that is, ‘troubled.’ Names are changed according to various circumstances so that various mysteries may be signified.”

[Col. 0634A] ## Verse 43

“‘Denaba.’ The city of Hala, the son of Beor, king of Edom, after whom Jobab reigned. Even today there is a village called Denaba, eight miles from Areopolis on the road to Armon, and another Denaba beyond Mount Peor, at the seventh milestone from Jebus. Jerome, concerning Jesbii.”

## Verse 44

“‘Jobab, the son of Zerah,’ whom some suspect to have been Job. But the Hebrews assert that he was descended from the line of Nahor. Philo, however, in his book of Questions on Genesis, relates that he lived in those times and took Dinah, the daughter of Jacob, as his wife. He says that, before the contest of his temptation, she bore him seven sons and three daughters, who perished in the temptation. After Job was healed, however, the Lord restored everything to him twofold, and his wife again bore seven sons and three daughters, whose names were the same as those of the first children: Eliphaz, Armoe, Diasath, Philasia, Dipharceluth, and Thelon; and the daughters’ names were Meru, Lizath, and Zeli.

“‘Bozrah,’ etc. This is Bosor, a city in the desert beyond the Jordan, in the tribe of Reuben. There is also another city called Bosor, the city of Esau in the mountains of Idumea, concerning which it is said: ‘His garments are ruddy from Bosor.’”

## Verse 45

“‘Of the Temanites.’ The region of Teman received its name from Teman, the son of Eliphaz. Even today there is a village called Teman, five miles from the city of Petra, where a garrison of Roman soldiers was stationed. Eliphaz, king of the Temanites, came from this place. One of Ishmael’s sons was also called Teman. It should be known, however, that every southern region is called *Teman* in Hebrew.”

## Verse 46

“‘Madian.’ A city so called from the youngest of the sons of Abraham and Keturah. It lies beyond Arabia, in the desert of the Saracens, east of the Red Sea. Hence the Midianites and the region of Midian receive their names. The daughters of Moses’ father-in-law are also called daughters of Midian. But this is another city, bearing the same name, near Armon and Areopolis, whose ruins are still visible.”

**Verse 48.—Rohoboth.** A city beside the river where the king of Edom was situated; to this day there is a fort in the region of Gabalene, as well as a large village called by this name.

**[Col. 0634D] Verse 50.—“Matred’s daughter,” etc.** Two mothers are listed here to signify a mystery: that the goldsmith should have begotten the steward, and the steward the Lord’s benevolence. For from the depth of understanding eloquent speech is born, which begets in the hearts of its hearers a pure faith that merits the grace of God.

**Verse 51.—“Leaders,” etc.** It should be noted that he first called them kings of Edom, and afterward leaders, although they had previously been leaders. He names some of their mothers, such as Oholibamah and Timna.

**“The leader Aliha.”** In Genesis the name is read as *Alva*, whose interpretation is “elevation”; in Chronicles, *Aliha*, that is, “above her.”

## Chapter II

**[Col. 0635A] “Achar, who …”** (Jerome, *Questions on Chronicles*, vol. III.) Achar, who is also called Achan in Joshua, means “a serpent lying in wait”; Achar means “troubled,” etc., up to “they were extinguished by the multitude of sins.”

**Verse 9.—“Calubi,”** that is, “my dog,” who is also Caleb, that is, “dog,” one of the spies. Hesron and Jephunneh are likewise the same person; hence Caleb is read both as the son of Hesron and, at times, as the son of Jephunneh.

**Verse 13.—“Now Jesse begot …”** In the Book of Kings Jesse is said to have had eight sons, but in Chronicles no more than seven. The Hebrews, however, say that the prophet Nathan was the son of Sama—or Sammaa, or Simmaa—the son of Jesse. Jesse raised and nurtured him as a son, counting him among his sons. Nathan was brought with Jesse’s sons to Samuel; he was also Jonathan, who struck down the lion. It should be understood that where he is called a prophet, he is written as Nathan, not Jonathan.

**Verse 17.—“Jether.”** In Kings, “Jethra the Israelite”; but the quality of their merits produces the difference in names. For *Jethra* is interpreted “remainder,” whereas *Jether* means “a small remainder.” “Remainder” is joined with the Israelites, and “small remainder” with the Ishmaelites.

**Verse 19.—“Ephrata.”** (Jerome.) She is Mary, the sister of Moses, mother of Hur, father of Uri, father of Bezalel. Hur is the one who, together with Aaron, supported Moses’ hands while Joshua was fighting.

**Verse 22.—“Jair.”** He was a judge after Tola and judged Israel for twenty-two years. He had thirty sons, leaders of thirty cities, which were named after him, as is read in the Book of Judges.

**Verse 25.—“They were born.”** Up to this point the historian has woven together the genealogy of Hesron’s two sons, the two later ones—namely Aram and Calubi—about whom he previously narrated, because he wished in some manner to make known both royal and priestly dignity. Now he returns to the genealogy of the firstborn, Jerameel.

**Verse 26.—“Onam.”** He received this name from Onam, the son of Judah; but they are different persons. For the son of Judah is written through *Nun*, whereas the son of Jerameel is written through *Mem*.

**Verse 34.—“Sesan.”** The Hebrews say that this was Elimelech, Naomi’s husband, the father of Mahlon and Chilion. Therefore the writer implies in what follows that Sesan had no sons, but daughters, since his two sons died childless.

**Verse 43.—“Hebron.”** The city in which David reigned for seven years before he reigned in Jerusalem. These names indicate that the places received their names from Caleb’s descendants, since he received Hebron and its surrounding territory as his allotted inheritance.

**Verse 50.—“These were the sons.”** He recapitulates Caleb’s genealogy from Ephrata, which he had previously left aside when he related that Hur was born from Ephrata, that is, from Mary, the sister of Moses.

**Verse 52.—“Cariathiarim,”** also called Cariathabal, that is, “city of forests,” one of the cities of the Gibeonites, nine miles from Elia toward Diospolis, in the tribe of Judah.

**[Col. 0636A] Verse 54.—“Bethlehem.”** The city of David, in the tribe of Judah, in which the Lord was born, seven miles from Elia toward the southern region, beside the road leading to Hebron. The tomb of Jesse and David is shown there, and about a thousand paces away stands the tower of Ader, that is, “tower of the flock,” which in a certain prophecy foreshadowed the shepherds who would know of the Lord’s birth.

**“Who divided half the resting-places.”** (Jerome, in the same work.) That is, he received the allotments of Midian near the tombs of the patriarchs which are in Cariatharbe; and his sons were the Jetherites, etc. The Seraithites and Estaolites took their names from places, namely Sarai and Estaol, where Samson was buried. For a burial place is called a “resting-place.” Others understand “half the resting-places” as half the period during which the children of Israel began to possess the promised land: from the time when Moses gave the land of Gilead beyond the Jordan to Reuben and Gad and half the tribe of Manasseh, until the other tribes received their allotments. They say that Sobal died in the middle of this period, and thus “saw half the resting-places,” that is, reached the midpoint of that period.

Mystically, however, Sobal—meaning “empty antiquity” or “a bar for carrying”—signifies the Jews, who were formerly called the people of God and first received the law according to the letter. They carried the books of the Law and the Prophets, but did not understand the mystery of Christ’s incarnation. Hence they saw “half the resting-places,” that is, the historical account. But he possesses the fullness of the resting-places who, after good works, rejoices in eternal rest. Or he sees half the rest who, after the labor of the present life, possesses rest of soul. He will see the perfection of the resting-places when he enjoys the perfection of rest in both soul and body.

**Verse 55.—“Those dwelling there.”** (The same author.) The Hebrews relate that Jabes was a most learned teacher of the Law, in whose presence sat the sons of the Kenite, that is, of Jobab, Moses’ relative. Thus the scribes are called “those who sing and resound,” because they were constantly occupied with speaking of God’s Law. History also relates that they dwelt in the tents of kings.

Jabes signifies Christ, the true teacher of the saints who sing God’s praises. For Jabes is interpreted as “drying up,” whereas Christ dried up the flow of carnal desires in his faithful. **[Col. 0636D]** The Kenites—meaning “possession” or “those possessing”—are all the elect, of whom it is said, “Israel is my inheritance,” and whose possession is the Lord. Rechab is interpreted as “charioteer” or “one ascending.” These came from the heat of Rechab’s father’s house because, inflamed by the grace of the Spirit from the Father of lights, they ascend into heaven by the chariot of the virtues. Of them it is said: “All who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Rom. 8).

## Chapter III

**Verse 1.—“Now David …”** He returns to explain David’s lineage, which he had previously left aside when, while enumerating the offspring of Amram, the son of Hesron, he reached Jesse and his sons, David being the last of them.

**[Col. 0637A] “The Jezreelite woman.”** (Rabanus.) Jezreel is the city in which Naboth lived, whom Jezebel killed.

**“Daniel.”** (The same author.) Daniel is the one called Chileab in the Book of Kings, that is, “avenging the father.” According to the Hebrews, when he disputed with Mephibosheth about questions of the Law, he appeared victorious and seemed to avenge his father, lest a warlike man should be mocked in debate by a feeble man.

**Verse 3.—“By Eglah his wife.”** (Jerome.) It is asked why Eglah alone is called David’s wife. She is Michal, who, among the many, is called his only wife because he first took her as his wife in his youth; she is said to have died in childbirth. Eglah is interpreted as “heifer,” signifying the Synagogue, which accepted the yoke of the Law but corrupted it through wantonness. Hence: “Ephraim is a heifer trained to love threshing.” Our David took her when he joined her to himself by giving her the covenant. She died in childbirth because, when the Word of God appeared in the flesh and the Gospel was preached, she ought to have borne offspring through faith and good works; but, scandalized by his Passion, she brought eternal death upon herself.

**Verse 4.—“In Hebron, where he reigned,” etc.** We briefly discussed what is understood by David’s reign in Hebron and in Jerusalem when expounding the Book of Kings. It is written below: “The whole time that David reigned was forty years.” He reigned in Hebron seven years and in Jerusalem thirty-three. Hence it is asked why the total is not counted as forty years and six months. The Hebrews say that David fled from his son Absalom for six months, and that these months were rightly excluded from the total of his reign. They also say that he suffered bodily illness for six months in Hebron, and that therefore they should not properly be counted as part of his reign. They say that he began to reign in Hebron from the time when, after defeating the Amalekites, he sent spoils to the elders of Judah—namely, to those who were in Hebron and to the others.

**[Col. 0637D] Verse 9.—“All these were David’s sons,” etc.** All the sons of Christ await the eternal palm, but the sons of the concubines are excluded, since they did not deserve to be counted by name among the others. For Jews, heretics, and schismatics cannot share in this fellowship. The glory of the heavenly kingdom awaits the sons of David only from a noble marriage. “The son of the slave-woman shall not be heir with the son of the free woman” (Gen. 21).

**Verse 15.—“The sons of Josiah.”** (Rabanus.) Four sons of Josiah are read here, etc., up to “who was likewise transferred to the Chaldeans.”

**Verse 17.—“Asir, Salathiel, Melchiram, Phadaia, Senneser,” etc.** According to the Hebrews, these are the names of one man: he is Phadaia, the father of Zerubbabel and Shimei. Hence in Ezra and in Matthew Zerubbabel is written as Salathiel. Phadaia is interpreted as “redeemed by the Lord”; Asir as “imprisoned”; Salathiel as “the Lord’s shoot.” All these descriptions suit holy teachers, through whose ministry the ecclesiastical people are begotten. Chastened by various afflictions, they are redeemed by the Lord’s grace and bring forth shoots of virtue both in themselves and in those subject to them.

**[Col. 0638A] Verse 18.—“Senneser.”** He is Sheshbazzar, to whom Cyrus entrusted the vessels of the Lord’s house, as is said in Ezra. Senneser means “fashioned,” and Sheshbazzar “afflicted.” These names suit the guardians of God’s vessels, that is, of holy souls. Cyrus signifies Christ by name and by release; to him it is said, “Ask of me and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). Having released the captivity of the human race, he entrusted holy souls to be guarded. They are the numbered vessels of the Lord, because “the Lord knows those who are his” (2 Tim. 2).

## Chapter IV

**Verse 1.—“The sons of Judah.”** How are Perez, Hesron, and the three who follow said to be sons of Judah, when elsewhere we read that Perez and Zerah were sons of Judah and Hesron the son of Perez? The Hebrews assert that, with the names changed, the same sons of Judah whom Scripture names elsewhere by other names are expressed here. They say that Perez, whose interpretation is “division,” bears his proper name here. Hesron, however, is Zerah; but Hesron is interpreted as “court,” while Zerah means “rising.” Charmi likewise is Heber: Charmi means “my vineyard,” while Heber means “watchful.” Ur, they say, is Onam; Ur means “left hand,” while Onam means “murmuring.” Sobal, however, is Shelah, the youngest of Judah’s sons, whom Shua bore to him. Sobal is interpreted as “ear of grain” or “empty antiquity”; Shelah as “sent” or “his shadow.”

**Verse 3.—“Asalelphuni.”** (Rabanus.) They suspect that she was Samson’s mother, born from the tribe of Judah. Her husband was Manoah from the tribe of Dan, who is also said in the Book of Judges to have descended from Sara.

**[Col. 0638C] Verse 4.—“Gedor and Ezer.”** (The same author.) These are places possessed by the sons of Ur. But it is surprising that Ur is here called the father of Bethlehem, when above Salma was called its father, unless perhaps “father” here means ancestor, since Hur was the father of Salma, who was the father of Bethlehem.

**Verse 9.—“Now Jabes was …”** (The same author.) The order appears confused: after listing the sons of Helaah and Naarah, he suddenly introduces the relationship of Aharehel, the son of Aram, and then proceeds to speak of Jabes. The Hebrews, however, say that Asshur by Helaah begot Etam, and he begot Cos. Cos begot Soboba, and Soboba begot Jabes, who was a teacher of the scribes. Between Cos and Jabes the relationships of Aharehel—or Aharahel, elsewhere Aral—are inserted, because he is Obab, the son of Aram, that is, Jethro, the relative of Moses. Since Jabes taught them, they were inserted into his genealogy as though begotten by his ancestors.

And the mother is the Synagogue from whom Christ was born, who bore him in sorrow because, on account of unbelief, she grieved at his coming. Hence the Jews, out of envy, said: “If we let him go on this way, everyone will believe in him” (John 11).

**Verse 10.—“He invoked.”** This applies to Christ, whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, of whom it is said: “Behold the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world,” etc. (John 1). God blessed him by multiplying his children, whom the most holy Church bears through the water of baptism **[Col. 0639A]** (1 Cor. 1). He enlarged his boundaries because the Father gave him all nations as an inheritance and extended his possession to the ends of the earth. The Lord’s hand was with him, because the power of his divinity worked signs and miracles through him. He himself is also the power and wisdom of God, through whom the Father established all things in heaven and on earth. The malice of the Jews could not harm him, for he said of himself: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me.” Through him his members, that is, the Church, are also blessed. Through Isaiah it is said to her: “Enlarge the place of your tent,” etc. (Isa. 54). The Lord’s hand is with him because the Son of God, who is the arm and right hand of the Father, works in him. “The gates of hell shall not prevail against him,” nor shall the devil rule him, because authority over every power of the enemy has been given to him.

**Verse 11.—“Caleb, however, the brother …”** (Rabanus.) Above we read that Caleb was the son of Hesron, whose brothers were Ram and Jerameel. The Hebrews therefore say that Ram is here called Caleb’s brother, Sua. Ram is interpreted as “exalted,” and Sua as “humble,” which suits the Jewish people: they were exalted in the worship of the one God and in royal power, but because they refused to receive the Son of God, they became humble and contemptible, so that “the first may become last.”

**Verse 12.—** (The same author.) **“Recha.”** Some think that David is designated by the name Recha. Recha means “tender.” Hence David says of himself: “I am tender and an anointed king” (2 Sam. 3). He is also said to be tender, like a worm of wood. The men of Recha are mentioned because they were recorded here to express David’s genealogy.

**Verse 13.—“Now Saraia begot …”** Joab is said to have descended from Saraia. According to the interpretation of his name, he is called “father of the valley of craftsmen,” because among his sons were architects who built the Lord’s house. The craftsmen who dwell in the valley may signify teachers of the Law, whom knowledge does not inflate but charity builds up (1 Cor. 8). Modesty and humility exalt them, as with Gamaliel and his disciple Paul (Acts 5, 22).

**Verse 17.—“Ezra.”** (Rabanus–Jerome.) The Hebrews say that Ezra, whose name means “helper,” is Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron; that Jether, meaning “help,” is Aaron; and that Mered, meaning “rebelling,” is Moses. They also say that Epher, or Opher, meaning “dust,” is Heldad. Jalon and Meldath, who were among the seventy elders whom Moses received from God to assist in governing the people, are also identified. For they relate that after Moses received the Law in the wilderness, he persuaded his father to divorce his mother because she was his relative; she was a daughter of Levi. Afterward Amram took another wife, by whom he had Heldad and Meldath.

**“And he begot Miriam.”** (The same author.) They wish Sammai to be understood as Moses, etc., up to “because he governed the people in the wilderness and daily governs them by his teaching.”

**[Col. 0639D] Verse 18.—“Pharaoh’s daughter.”** (The same author.) He calls Pharaoh’s daughter Moses’ mother, who, according to the proper meaning of the name, is also called “daughter of the Lord,” because she had a good intention in raising the child. She is called Amared, that is, “received by Moses,” because, abandoning idols, she turned to the worship of God.

**Verse 21.—“Her, the father.”** (The same author.) He returns to the genealogy of Perez, from whom David arose, in order to bring to David the genealogy of Judah, from whom the royal tribe arose. They relate that this was Elimelech, Naomi’s husband. In his time, because of transgressors against the Law, the sun stood still so that, seeing the miracle, they might be converted to the Lord. Because they despised it, famine grew severe, and the man who had seemed foremost in the tribe of Judah was driven from his homeland by want, together with his wife and sons, and died with his sons in a foreign land.

**Verse 22.—“Securus and Incendens.”** (The same author.) Mahlon and Chilion, who are called here Securus and Incendens, were in Moab because they took Moabite wives. Hence in Hebrew they are called not “leaders” but “husbands,” as the teachers of that language relate.

**“Who returned to …,” etc.** Naomi and Ruth, who returned to Bethlehem after hearing of the abundance of bread.

**Verse 23.—“Potters dwelling there.”** We understand the potters who work in plantations and hedges as teachers, who form and fashion the vessels of the Lord. For we call *fingere* “to fashion,” and therefore we call those who fashion clay “potters.” They plant and cultivate the Lord’s vineyard through teaching, and protect it by exhortation and prayer. They remain with the king in their works because, abiding in the faith of Christ, whatever they say and whatever they do, they do for the glory of God.

**[Col. 0640C] Verse 28.—“They dwelt in,” etc.** The lineage of Ruth is said to have dwelt among these hedges and plantations when this plantation reached royal dignity and became a protection for the people.

**“And they dwelt there.”** Six are written in Genesis, but Sober is omitted here because no descendants came from him. Some names, however, are changed for specific reasons. In Genesis there is Gemuel, that is, “mother of God”; here, Hamuel, “reading with God.” One is called Echa in Genesis, but here Jarib, “quarrelling,” because from him came Zambri, who committed fornication with a Midianite woman and was killed by Phinehas the priest. Jacim in Genesis means “preparation”; here he is called Zara, “rising.”

**“And the whole relationship did not …,” etc.** Simeon did not have as many descendants as Judah. Hence it is said in Joshua: “Simeon received his inheritance according to his clans in the midst of the sons of Judah.”

**“These cities,” etc.** Ziklag and Beersheba belonged to Judah and were invaded by Simeon; David restored them to Judah’s former inheritance.

**Verse 38.—“These were named.”** After describing Simeon’s lineage and their deeds, the text mystically signifies that holy teachers—that is, the leaders of the Church who provide pasture for Christ’s flocks—proceed to Gedor, or Gader, which is interpreted as “his hedge.” This is the Church, the defense of the faithful. There are pastures there “as far as the east of the valley,” that is, to the incarnation of the Word, who emptied himself, taking the form of a servant **[Col. 0641A]** (Phil. 2). Pastures are found in him. For he himself says: “If anyone enters through me, he will enter and go out and find pasture” (John 10)—namely, virtues. In him there is a very broad and peaceful land, that is, an abundance of the grace of the Holy Spirit. The fact that descendants of Ham had previously dwelt there signifies that the multitude of the nations abandoned idols and gathered for the worship of the one God. Thus those whom we have named above came in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah—that is, at the coming of Christ. For Christ is the power of God, whom Hezekiah, namely “the strength of the Lord,” signifies.

**“They struck the tents.”** By faith he strikes the tents of the impious and their inhabitants when, renouncing all ungodliness and worldly desires, a sinner is cleansed from the filth of sins through Christ’s baptism. Thereafter he strives to live soberly, justly, and devoutly in this world, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “In the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of God” (Hos. 1).

**Verse 42.—“Five hundred men.”** The fathers of the New Testament went to Mount Seir and struck down the remnants of the Amalekites because, trampling underfoot the pride of this world, they suppress the deformity of vices. They are called four because, truly instructed in evangelical teaching, they fittingly wage spiritual war against demons. After striking the remnants of the Amalekites, they dwelt there because, once the demons have been expelled, they replace vices with virtues. Possession of these makes a person blessed “to this day”—a phrase that can always be applied until the end of the world, because the Church remains until the end of the world, in which the ancient enemy is daily defeated.

## Chapter V

**Verse 1.—“But when you violate,” etc.** (Rabanus.) Reuben’s birthright was taken away because he slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine, and was given to Joseph, the younger son, whose descendants multiplied and surpassed the royal power among the ten tribes.

Mystically, this signifies the ruin of the former people, who, as the firstborn, ought to have received the priesthood and kingdom. But because they defiled their father’s bed—that is, the body of Christ, in which the fullness of divinity dwelt—and suspended and killed him on the cross, the dignity of the firstborn was transferred to the spiritual Joseph, that is, to Christ and the people of the Church. To him the Father says: “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” etc. (Ps. 110).

**Verse 10.—“Against the Hagrites.”** (Jerome, on Chronicles.) It is plausible that Hagar was Keturah, since the following passage says that the Reubenites, Gadites, and half the tribe of Manasseh fought with the Hagrites and helped Israel against the Ituraeans, Naphish, and Nodab, the sons of Ishmael. Nodab appears to be the one called Kedemah in Genesis, meaning “of the ancients” or “preceding.”

**Verse 26.—“And he stirred up.”** It should be noted that in Kings it is said that Pul, king of the Assyrians, received a thousand talents of silver from Menahem, son of Gaddi, king of Israel **[Col. 0642A]** (2 Kings 15), so that he might assist him and strengthen his kingdom—not that Pul transferred him to Assyria, but that Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, in the days of Pekah, king of Israel, captured Ahion, Abel-beth-Maacah, Janoah, Kedesh, Hazor, Gilead, Galilee, and the whole land of Naphtali, and transferred them to Assyria.

Finally, the text relates that Shalmaneser, king of the Assyrians, besieged Samaria for three years, captured Hoshea, son of Elah, king of Israel, and transferred Israel to Assyria, settling them in Halah and Habor, beside the river Gozan, in the cities of the Medes. Hence the question arises: how can we say in Chronicles that Pul and Tiglath-pileser, kings of the Assyrians, transferred Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh to Halah, Habor, Aram, and the river Gozan, when Kings says that Shalmaneser did this, transferring Israel to Assyria and settling them in the places mentioned above?

The earlier kings of the Assyrians are said to have done this because they began, together with the Assyrian people, what that same people completed under later kings. Chronicles mentions Aram, which Kings omits. The Hebrews suppose that it was the city of Rhages in Media.

## Chapter VI

**Verse 6.—“The sons of Levi, Gershon,” etc.** **Johanan.** Passing over the other sons of Levi who were likewise priests in the Lord’s house, Johanan is especially praised because he bravely resisted King Uzziah when he wished to offer sacrifice himself. By steadfastness of mind and zeal for the Law he fulfilled the priestly office.

**[Col. 0642C] Verse 15.—“Moreover, Josedec.”** (Jerome, *Hebrew Questions on Chronicles*.) They say that Josedec is Ezra the priest, etc., up to “but Ezra was a priest, a just and glorious man.”

**Verse 28.—“Abiah.”** As the Hebrews relate, he was appointed judge and accepted gifts, while Joel, also called Vasni, his elder son, knew of it and did not correct him. Hence both are said to have sinned according to the Hebrew account. Thus: “When Samuel grew old, he appointed his sons judges over Israel,” and so forth.

**Verse 31.—“These are those whom he appointed.”** By anticipating the account of the duties of David’s singers, who sang praises to the Lord with musical instruments, he previewed their genealogy; in its proper order he will show how they performed this service.

**[Col. 0642D] Verse 44.—“Ethan, the son.”** Ethan was one of the three singers who clashed cymbals before David in praise of God. It should be noted that, just as there were three sons of Levi—Kohath, Gershon, and Merari—so there were three singers: Heman from Kohath, Asaph from Gershon, and Ethan from Merari. Mystically, they signify the holy teachers who, imbued with faith in the Holy Trinity, announce the Gospel to the whole world according to the dispensation of the true David.

**Verse 48.—“The Levites who …”** Every ecclesiastical order, according to the tradition of the apostles, including those who hold primacy, performs the whole ministry in the Church of God. Hence: “So that you may know how one ought to conduct oneself in the house of God, which is the Church of the living God,” etc. (1 Tim. 3).

**Verse 49.—“Aaron.”** He signifies Christ; his sons signify the people of the Church, to whom it is said: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” etc. (1 Pet. 2). The supreme priest taught them to offer upon the altar of faith the holocaust of good works and the incense of prayer, and to pray for Israel—that is, for the state of the Church—according to the precepts of the Law given through Moses. He repeats Aaron’s genealogy down to Ahimaaz, apparently as a tribute to him, because he was more faithful to David in all things.

## Chapter VII

**Verse 8.—“All these, the sons of Bechor.”** Whenever the Law says, “All these are the sons of this one or that one,” it is either because of excellence in their merits or because of deterioration in their merits: they are called the sons of the one whose imitators they became.

**Verse 14.—“And his concubine.”** She is said to have been the daughter of Balam’s son. Driven by famine, her father took her to Egypt to sell her. Manasseh, who was in charge of the storehouses of food supplied to her father, compassionately received her in marriage.

**Verse 15.—“Happhim,” etc.** These two names are said to belong to the first son of Machir. The second is said to be Zelophehad, and their sister Maacah, whom Hesron, when he was sixty years old, took as his wife; she bore him Segub, as was stated above.

**Verse 18.—“His sister was the Queen.”** The sister of Ulam, son of Perez, son of Machir, as was stated above. Some relate that she was the mother of Joshua, son of Nun, who is called “a beautiful man” on account of his distinguished virtue and leadership. Others say that she was Deborah, the wife of Lapidoth, the prophetess.

**Verse 20.—“The sons of Ephraim.”** The Hebrews tell the story that the sons of Ephraim, gathering together while their father was still alive, attempted to return to the promised land and were killed at Gath of the Philistines. Therefore the other tribes were led through the wilderness so that they would not see the bones of their brothers. Hence it is said in the Psalm: “The sons of Ephraim turned back on the day of battle” (Ps. 77).

## Chapter VIII

**[Col. 0643D] Verse 6.—“Those who were transferred to Manahath.”** This occurred when they fell by the sword because of the crime committed against the Levite’s wife, and only six hundred remained.

**Verse 7.—“Naaman and Ahiah.”** They were leaders, but they subjected themselves to Gera. Hence it is said in the singular: “He himself transferred them.” From him came the descendants of Gera, who was the father of Shimei.

## Chapter IX

**Verse 2.—“The Nathinaeans.”** (Jerome, *Questions on Chronicles*, vol. III.) “Gift,” or “serving in humility.” These are the Gibeonites whom Joshua spared and assigned to the service of the Temple, so that they might carry water and wood (Josh. 9).

**Verse 11.—“The sons of Hilkiah: Meshullam,” etc.** He was the high priest who found Deuteronomy in the Temple of the Lord in the time of Josiah, and he is said to have been the father of the prophet Jeremiah.

**Verse 16.—“Jeduthun.”** (Jerome.) David’s singer, that is. The Levite singers kept watch at the king’s eastern gate in their appointed divisions and came in turn to sing psalms with David. Before the Temple was built, the Ark of the Covenant was in the palace, and they served there as temple attendants.

**Verse 19.—“But Shallum, the son of Kore.”** The earlier one is written *Cora* with an aleph and sounds like *Cora*; the second is written with a he and sounds like *Core*. Cora is interpreted as “calling out,” Core as “bald.” This is the man who caused the rebellion against Moses in Numbers 16.

**“Keepers of the vestibules.”** (Jerome.) They guarded the outer door of the Tabernacle. Their fathers, who are listed below and whose names appear in the Psalm titles, guarded the inner door and were singers.

**Verse 20.—“Now Phinehas.”** He was Aaron’s grandson, who, as the Hebrews relate, was still alive and organized the divisions of the ministers. There were twenty-four divisions, which David arranged for the service of the Tabernacle. Hence in the Gospel: “Zechariah, of the division of Abijah” (Luke 1).

**Verse 26.—“These four Levites,” etc.** (Rabanus.) Who these four Levites were, to whom the whole number of gatekeepers was entrusted, is demonstrated when it says: “Of Hosah, that is, of the sons of Merari, Shimri the chief,” etc., as is found in chapter 26. The four leaders of the gatekeepers are the holy teachers, who, guarding the door of faith through the four Gospels, open it to believers and close it to blasphemers. The keys were entrusted to them together with Peter (Matt. 16). They guard the gates through the four winds because they call the nations to faith from the four regions of the world and vigilantly protect the Church.

**[Col. 0644C] Verse 28.—“Some of their kind were also over the vessels of the ministry.”** (The same author.) Mystically, they are ordained from the assembly of holy preachers, who keep vigilant watch over the vessels of the Lord—that is, the souls of the faithful, in whom God’s will is served daily. Under their guardianship are fine flour, wine, and oil, through which the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood are prepared and the grace of the Holy Spirit is bestowed through spiritual anointing. They arrange the incense of prayers and the spices of virtues in the Church **[Col. 0644D]** and make an acceptable wine before the Lord.

**Verse 31.—“Mattithiah the Levite, the firstborn of Shallum the Korahite, was in charge of what was fried in the pan.”** Christ is the author of the heavenly sacraments, in which bread and wine are offered daily in memory of his Passion. He is also the head of all who, following his example, crucify their flesh and surrender themselves to suffering for his name.

**Verse 32.—“There were the bread of the Presence.”** According to Josephus, the loaves were baked two by two separately before the Sabbath and placed upon the table on the Sabbath morning. We discussed them more fully in Leviticus.

**Verse 34.—“The heads of the Levites according to their families.”** It is fitting that the more someone is placed over others, the more devoted he should be to divine duties. He properly preserves the primacy of ministry who strives to remain in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of peace—so that he may flee the world’s tumult and the pleasures of the flesh and possess tranquility of mind in contemplation of God, saying with the Psalmist: “I rejoiced at the things that were said to me.”

**Verse 35.—“Jahiel.”** In Kings he is called Ahiel, the father of Kish, the father of Saul, and his name is interpreted as “my father is God.” Jahiel means “eloquent of God,” perhaps according to the difference in their merits. It should be noted that among Jahiel’s sons, Kish and Ner are called brothers and are brothers, as is stated in Kings. But below it says that Ner begot Kish—not that he fathered him, but that he raised him.

**Verse 39.—“Abinadab.”** As in Kings, he is related to have been killed together with his father. Abinadab is interpreted as “my father is a vow”; Abinadab as “my people is a vow.”

**“Eshbaal.”** “Husband of fire.” This is Ishbosheth, that is, “man of confusion.”

**Verse 40.—“Meribbaal.”** “Quarrelling against a husband.” This is Mephibosheth, whose name is interpreted as “from the mouth, shame.”

## Chapter X

**Verse 1.—“The Philistines,” etc.** (Rabanus.) Omitting many things that the history in the Book of Samuel relates about Samuel and Saul, he recalls the fall of Saul and his family. Mystically, he indicates that it is unnecessary to describe the life of one whose impious conduct deserved a swift end; and figuratively he demonstrates the end of the Jewish kingdom and the ancient priesthood. He then turns to David **[Col. 0645C]**, whose deeds and administration of the kingdom he weaves together. David bears the figure of the true David, who possesses the kingdom of heaven and earth.

As he approaches, the Philistines, according to their custom, fight against Israel and conquer, because, as grace drew near, the Gentiles, as before, attacked the purity of Israelite faith—now by displaying evil works, now by the worship of idols—just as Balaam taught Balak to place a stumbling block before the children of Israel, so that they might eat and commit fornication.

**“And the men fled.”** Those who appeared strong in the contemplation of God, while heedlessly following the works and teaching of the Gentiles, greatly aided the destruction of the heretics through secular learning. Hence someone said: “Philosophers, the patriarchs of heretics, stained the purity of the Church with perverse teaching.”

**[Col. 0645D] Verse 2.—“When they had drawn near.”** The Gentiles attacked the kingdom of Judah and his sons from every side, and corrupted the priests, scribes, and Pharisees—that is, the sons and seducers of that kingdom. They also corrupted the heretics, so that they would not preach or worship the grace of the Holy Spirit in simplicity.

**“Abinadab.”** So that we would not praise the Father who adopted us by a spiritual gift with a confession worthy of him, which the killing signifies: Abinadab, that is, “my spontaneous father.”

**“Melchishua.”** So that we would not believe in the salvation to come in Christ’s kingdom. Melchishua is interpreted as “my king is salvation.” The philosopher who seduced Arius killed him, as it were, as Melchishua; the one who seduced Macedonius killed Jonathan; the one who seduced Mani killed Abinadab. For the teacher of corruption taught the first to deny the omnipotence of the true King Christ, the second to diminish the gifts of the Holy Spirit, and the third to blaspheme the goodness of the supreme Father.

**Verse 4.—“And Saul said to,” etc.** The Hebrews say that this was Doeg the Edomite, who, seeing Saul dead and fearing David, killed himself. They say that the “young man”—because he brought Saul’s diadem and bracelet to David—was Doeg’s son, and that Doeg himself was the young man who had been with Saul when Saul was seeking his father’s donkeys.

**“To his armor-bearer.”** (Bede, on chapter 28 of Book I of Kings.) The teachers of the Law. For just as the weapons and arrows of the Philistines, etc., up to “not so that they might be defiled, but so that they might eat the Passover.”

### “But the armor-bearer was unwilling”

There can be no doubt that among the reprobate teachers of the Law there were some who did not wish to pervert the sharpness of the word for killing their hearers; nevertheless, the hearers themselves, who had received sound teaching from their masters, by despising or blaspheming it turned it to their own destruction. When these hearers had been seen to die—that is, through their obstinacy in sinning—the ministers of the word themselves also deteriorated over time, and the testimonies of the Law, which they had feared to interpret wrongly, became for them an occasion of ruin. Heretics likewise, wounded and bloodied by the arrows of their sins, turn the divine words into an argument for their error; as they are about to die, they turn their own weapons against their own breast. Any Catholic, too, when he pollutes by pride, vainglory, avarice, or the contagion of any other vice the skill he learned for the common benefit, stabs himself with his own sword, because the weapon by which he ought to have been defended against the enemy rushes upon him.

### VERSE 5

**When the armor-bearer saw this.** The unlearned, seeing the remedies of true humility and the bath of baptism, but unaware that their teachers in Judaea had been defeated in spiritual combat, and that a considerable part of the populace, closely attached to their teaching, had been driven from its former seat of steadfastness by the pursuing adversary, were thrown into confusion by the ruin of their elders and lost the works of virtue and the defenses of spiritual knowledge that they had possessed. Then the sins of the Gentiles came and corrupted all the Jews’ former pursuits of virtue through their perverse dwelling among them. Unclean spirits came and occupied hearts abandoned by the steadfastness of faith. The nations came and, by believing, made their own the Jews’ once-excellent pursuits. Hence: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matthew XXI).

### VERSE 10

**And the head.** (RABANUS, on Paralipomenon.) They fastened Saul’s head in the temple of the Philistine Dagon, etc., up to the point where it is shown that there is another Beth-shean in Judges and Joshua, which is interpreted as “house of security.”

### VERSE 11

**When the men of Jabesh heard this.** (The same author, ibid.) The men, that is, of the Church, etc., up to the point where this is identified as the city that Saul liberated from the enemy’s siege at the beginning of his reign.

### VERSE 12

**The oak in Jabesh [the printed reading is uncertain], and they fasted for seven days, etc.** So that they might reach rest. For after the six ages of this world, during which we labor in the flesh, comes the seventh age, the rest of souls.

Mystically, with regard to the blindness of the Jews who observe the Sabbath carnally, their fellow members—that is, the faithful—continually grieve and fast, as it were, for seven days. Once the mystery of the eighth day, the resurrection, has been received, both groups will rejoice in perpetual festivity.

Morally, however, holy men detest the death of the wicked and consign their examples to the burial of oblivion. They fast for seven days—that is, throughout the whole period of this life, which revolves according to the number seven—and they live in self-restraint, abstaining from every evil so that they may not die in the same way.

## CHAPTER XI

### VERSE 3

**The elders.** (RABANUS.) The prophets and apostles hasten together to Christ with equal devotion, hence: “The princes of the people gathered together with the God of Abraham” (Psalm II).

### VERSE 5

**And they said.** They placed the blind, the lame, and the lepers upon the walls as an insult to the king, saying that the blind and the lame had forbidden him.

Mystically, David’s expulsion of the Jebusite from Jerusalem signifies Christ’s expulsion of demons from the hearts of the faithful and his establishing his dwelling there. For “Jebusite” is interpreted as “trampled,” and Jerusalem as “vision of peace.” Hence he also says to his disciples: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents,” etc. (Luke X). Thus it is rightly written in Kings that, after the blind and the lame who hated his soul had been expelled, David captured the stronghold of Zion and called it his city. For when Christ expels evil spirits and the crowd of vices from the soul, illuminating it with wisdom, the stronghold of Zion is rightly called “watchtower” and “vision of peace.” Of it Psalm LXXV rightly says: “God is known in Judaea, and his name is great in Israel. And his place has been established in peace.”

### VERSE 8

**But Joab fortified the rest of the city.** By the soldier’s industry he fortified the city. Josephus, however, says that David fortified the upper city, joined it to the stronghold so as to make a single structure, and surrounded the whole with a wall. He says that he set Jacob over the work of the walls, expelled the Jebusites, and called it Jerusalem. For *Jero* in Hebrew means “fortification.” Christ likewise first preached the Gospel in Judaea and strengthened the Church with the fortification of his faith. Joab, who fortified the rest of the city, signifies the apostles and apostolic men who, after the Lord’s ascension, converted very many from the Gentiles. Hence: “We are God’s fellow workers; you are God’s field.”

### VERSE 11

**Jashobeam.** (JEROME.) Josephus calls him Eusebius and says that he was the son of Achimaas. Frequently breaking into the enemy’s battle line, he did not stop until he had killed eight hundred. Others understand this man to be David, because *Jashobeam* is interpreted as “sitting among the people.” *Ahamoni*, however, means “most wise”; hence it is written in Kings: “Sitting in the chair, most wise” (II Kings XXIII). There he is compared with a woodworm, because his wisdom was diminished on account of the sin he had committed against Uriah. Hence there he is said to have killed eight hundred in a single assault, whereas here he killed three hundred: for on account of his sin his fame was diminished.

### VERSE 12

**The Ahohite.** According to the Hebrews, Ahohi was the brother of Jesse, David’s father. His son was Eleazar, who was the most powerful of the three. Josephus says that these were Eusebius son of Achimaas, Eleazar son of Addi, and Semeiah son of Heli.

(GREGORY, *Homily 34 on the Gospels*.) One must consider most carefully, etc., up to the point where he was strict toward himself and abstained even from lawful things.

### VERSE 21

**Nevertheless, he did not attain to the first three.** Here it appears that Abishai was chief among the three who followed. But he did not reach the first three, Jashobeam, Eleazar, and Shammah.

Mystically, this signifies that none of the saints, however outstanding in virtues, reaches equality with the power of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. For “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord?” etc. (Psalm LXXXVIII).

### VERSE 22

**Ariel of Moab**, that is, “lions,” as it is said in Kings—namely, exceedingly brave men in the kingdom of Moab, like lions.

**He killed the lion.** A Hebrew understands this lion to be Joab, who was killed while holding the horns of the altar in the Lord’s house. For “altar” is said to mean “cistern,” because just as the water of a cistern cleanses, so the sanctuary of God expiates human sins.

(RABANUS.) The Book of Kings, etc., up to the point where he seized the spear that the other man was not holding properly.

**In snowy weather.** This may signify the grace of Christ, which shone upon the world, and the cooling of charity by which men grow cold. Benaiah, however, whose name is interpreted as “the Lord is builder,” signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “The Lord builds Jerusalem,” etc. (Psalm CXLVI). He performed many works, of whom it is said: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V). He is from Kabzeel, that is, “from the assembly of the Lord,” because every gathering of the saints belongs to him. Descending from heaven and becoming man, he killed and cast into hell the lion—that is, the devil—who possessed the world, numbed by the cold of its unbelief. He overcame the Egyptian—that is, the Antichrist, blackest with sins, abusing the five bodily senses for crimes—and, through the rod of the cross, condemned the guilty one to perpetual punishment by his own wickedness. He did this “in days of snow,” because through his death he expiated sin. Hence: “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (Psalm L).

### VERSE 24

**Among the three.** Abishai, Sobochai, and Jonathan were those with whom he was equal in strength; he was over the thirty, as the Hebrew asserts.

## CHAPTER XII

### VERSE 12

**These also came.** Up to this point he has listed David’s warriors who helped him reign over Israel.

**Who were exceedingly strong, etc.** Literally, this signifies that they were agile and vigorous in every kind of warfare. Mystically, however, it describes Christ’s soldiers as not sluggish but zealous in prosperity and adversity, on the right and on the left.

### VERSE 8

**Swift.** (RABANUS.) He says this on account of acuteness of understanding or agility of body. Mystically, those who profess Christ’s warfare must not be childish in understanding, but must provide what is good, not only before God but also before all human beings.

### VERSE 14

**The last, etc.** Here the teachers of the Jews and Gentiles are signified. Concerning them Paul says, from the tribe of Benjamin: “Peter, James, and John, who seemed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship,” etc. (Galatians II; the printed reference reads “Gal. XI”). These men, coming to Christ, were tested in every respect. Hence, in Matthew XVI: “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered for all: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.” The Lord said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.” And elsewhere: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them” (John XX).

### VERSE 15

**They crossed the Jordan.** The Jordan, in which Christ was baptized, signifies baptism. The teachers cross it in the first month, when it customarily overflows its banks, because, after the Lord appeared in the flesh and consecrated the acceptable year, and after he consecrated baptism through his own baptism, they spread it throughout the whole world by preaching and baptizing.

**And they put to flight all who dwelt there.** (RABANUS.) They put to flight the Jews, whom the eastern region signifies because of the rising of the knowledge of the Law, or the Gentiles, in whom natural prudence perished while they attributed the worship of God to idols, through the preaching of the Gospel. Hence: “You have given me my enemies beneath me, and you have destroyed those who hate me” (Psalm XVII).

### VERSE 19

**Moreover, from Manasseh.** These seven leaders who came from Manasseh signify the first teachers of the Church coming from Judaea. Enlightened by the sevenfold Spirit, they assist our David against marauders—that is, heretics or evil spirits—which never cease to rob and enslave those whom they can take from the Church. Hence: “But thanks be to God, who always triumphs us in Christ Jesus” (II Corinthians II; the printed reference reads “II Cor. I”).

### VERSE 22

**An army of God.** The Hebrews explain this as the army that came out of Egypt, namely six hundred thousand. Mystically, however, the number of the faithful in the army of our David grows daily, until those predestined to eternal life are complete.

### VERSE 23

**To transfer them.** For the holy teachers especially desire that the worship of the old Law be transferred into the spiritual understanding of the Gospel, and that all things become new.

### VERSE 27

**Joiada also, chief of the line of Aaron, etc.** The Hebrews relate that he was Phinehas, son of Eleazar; in comparison with him Zadok is called a boy, as lesser in age and merit.

### VERSE 32

**And also from the sons of Issachar, men, etc.** They relate that the teachers of the Law were from the tribe of Issachar. These teachers taught the observance required for each individual time of the ceremonies and prescribed what Israel ought to do. They signify the teachers of the Church, whose subjects obey their commands.

### VERSE 35

**Twenty, etc.** (RABANUS.) The apostles and apostolic men come together to our David and are spiritually joined to him. Others, both Jews and Gentiles, contend with one heart and one purpose so that David may become king and they themselves may be the kingdom of Christ.

### VERSE 39

**For three days.** That is, throughout the whole period they hold the faith of the Trinity. They receive the nourishment that the first teachers—the apostles—had prepared from divine Scripture, and they give thanks for the generosity of all good things.

## CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 1

**David entered into an agreement.** This refers to the apostles and evangelists, who transferred the faith of the Incarnation from the Jews for the salvation of the Gentiles. For this is what it means to transfer the ark of the Lord to oneself from the hill of Kiriath-jearim—which is in Judah and is interpreted as “city of forests”: to lead the faith of the Lord from the eminence of the Scriptures placed among the Jews, where the shadowy forest of figures abounds, to the understanding of the Gentile people, where the Church is founded.

### VERSE 3

**For it was not.** (RABANUS.) The people of the Old Testament could not open up the spiritual meaning that lay hidden, as it has now been revealed to the apostles and prophets: namely, that the Gentiles are fellow heirs and fellow participants in the Lord’s promise.

### VERSE 5

**From Shihor.** Shihor is a river of Egypt, said to flow from the Nile. Its name is interpreted as “new and turbid firmament”; hence: “Why do you now wish to go to Egypt, to drink the water of the Nile?” (Jeremiah II; the printed reference reads “Jerem. VII”).

**Kiriath-jearim.** This is the city of Damascus, which in Amos is called Emathabal, that is, “great Hamath,” now called Epiphany. Through Shihor and Hamath he comprehends the whole land of promise. Through Shihor, a stream or torrent, he signifies the southern part of Egypt; through Hamath, the northern part.

Kiriath-jearim, elsewhere called Kiriath-baal, “city of forests,” was one of the cities of the Gibeonites in the tribe of Judah, at the ninth milestone for those traveling from Aelia to Diospolis, Uriah the prophet came from there; according to Jeremiah, Jehoiakim killed him in Jerusalem. The son of Shobal is also called Kiriath-jearim, as is shown above.

### VERSE 6

**Every man.** The more noble of the chosen men. The number of these men is included in Kings, where we read: “David gathered all the chosen men of Israel, thirty thousand” (II Kings VI).

### VERSE 9

**When they had reached it, etc.** (RABANUS, from Jerome.) They came to the threshing floor of Chidon, etc., up to the point where it is as though he says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians VI).

### VERSE 11

**Because the Lord had struck Uzzah.** (JEROME.) The Hebrews relate that Abinadab the priest ordered his sons Uzzah and Ahio to carry the ark on their shoulders, according to the commandment of the Law. But because they did not carry it, nor give it to the Kohathites to carry, the Lord struck Uzzah and made a breach.

**The breach of Uzzah.** It is related that his arm and shoulder, where the ark of the Lord was to be carried, had withered, and that a certain separation occurred in that place.

### VERSE 17

**In the house of Obed-edom.** (JEROME.) He too was a Levite. Once the reason for which Uzzah had been struck was known, David ordered the ark to be carried on the shoulders of the Levites themselves, as is clear in what follows. One should note how great is the offense of anyone who receives the Lord’s body unworthily, if a devoted priest perished because he had seized the ark, which prefigured the Lord’s body, with less reverence than was due.

Allegorically, David signifies Christ and the ark the Church. Christ wishes to bring the Church into his city, hence: “I was sent only to the sheep that have perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew XV). And elsewhere: “A partial blindness has happened in Israel,” etc. (Romans XI).

## CHAPTER XIV

### VERSE 3

**David also took, etc.** (RABANUS.) David’s many wives signify the many nations that are joined to Christ through faith. The concubines signify the churches of heretics, which glory in the title of the Christian name. But because they follow Christ for carnal gains, they are called not wives but concubines. If kings now have several wives, it is a crime, because the figures have passed away.

### VERSE 8

**When they heard.** When the grace of the Gospel had been spread abroad and the kingdom of Christ proclaimed everywhere, the nations rose up from all sides in opposition to the Gospel of peace.

### VERSE 15

**At the summit of the pear trees.** (RABANUS.) In Hebrew, however, he commands them to come to the “weeping ones,” that is, the idols, etc., up to the point where the Holy Spirit directs them by forewarning.

### VERSE 16

**From Gibeon to Gezer.** Christ strikes those who stand upon the hill of pride and breaks the hedge of their hardness, dividing their obstinacy so that he alone may rule throughout the world. Hence it follows: “And David’s name became renowned in all the regions, and the Lord,” etc.

## CHAPTER XV

### VERSE 2

**Then David said: It is unlawful, etc.** (RABANUS.) Christ does not wish the unworthy to exercise ecclesiastical office. Rather, those learned in knowledge and distinguished for honorable conduct carry the ark of God—that is, the Church—upon the shoulders of devoted labor and rejoice. Hence: “Do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry” (II Timothy IV).

### VERSE 3

**And he gathered all Israel.** Not David alone, but also all the prophets, by their words and deeds, made room in the Church of Christ for the Incarnation, so that Christ might be received more quickly when he came, since he had previously been prophesied.

### VERSE 12

**Sanctify yourselves with your brothers.** The ministers of the New Testament must be pure in life and doctrine. To them it is said: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Leviticus XIX). By words of right faith and by the example of their works they must commend to the faithful the Incarnation of Christ and the redemption of the human race, etc.

### VERSE 16

**Namely, with nablia, etc.** *Nablum* in Hebrew, *psalterium* in Greek, and *laudatorium* in Latin. The psaltery has a broad belly in its upper part, so that the strings tied together and struck in an orderly manner produce a very sweet melody. The cithara appears to be its opposite, since it contains at the bottom what the psaltery contains at the top.

The psaltery with ten strings is the Church with the Decalogue of the Law. Opposed to it is the cithara, which is formed with twenty-four strings in the shape of the letter delta—as the most learned relate—and is driven by the fingers into various modes. This signifies the Church, which, with the doctrines of the twenty-four elders, has a threefold form in the shape of the letter delta and signifies faith in the Holy Trinity. Through the hands of the apostles and evangelists it is figuratively stirred into various melodies from the Old and New Testaments, differently in the letter and differently in the meaning.

**Lyres.** The lyre is called *lyra*, from the Greek expression ἀπὸ τοῦ λύριν, “from variety of voices,” because it produces different sounds. It signifies the Church, which, through the variety of different disciplines—historical, allegorical, tropological, and anagogical—expresses a sweet sound, yet does not depart from the simplicity of harmony.

Cymbals, when struck against one another, produce a sound, hence: “Praise him with well-sounding cymbals,” etc. (Psalm CL). The well-sounding cymbals are our lips, which, struck against one another, produce the sweet harmony of the human voice.

### VERSE 21

**They played for the octave, etc.** (JEROME.) They signified the Lord’s coming on the day of judgment, when, after the week of the world has ended, he will come to judgment. Hence Psalm VI, which is sung with trembling at the judgment, is marked with such a title. This number contains great mysteries. Eight souls entered Noah’s ark and were saved while the world perished. David was the eighth son of Jesse, whom the Lord chose. Circumcision purifies on the eighth day. On the eighth day—that is, Sunday—Christ rose.

### VERSE 24

**Moreover, Shebaniah and Jehoshaphat, etc.** These seven priests, singing with trumpets before the ark, are holy preachers filled with the sevenfold Spirit of grace. They preach the Gospel in the Church of Christ and proclaim the mystery of the Incarnation to their hearers.

**They sounded.** A trumpet is used in one way for gathering the people, in another for setting out, in another for victory, in another for pursuing enemies, in another for besieging cities, etc. The customary trumpet, according to those skilled in such matters, is formed in this way: air is blown into three bronze tubes through a narrow opening at the top, so that, like four bronze voice-conduits producing fourfold sounds through a bronze foundation, they emit a most powerful roar. These signify the Gospel, inspired divinely through the threefold confession of the three Persons, through a narrow opening—that is, in Christ’s birth—through the four bronze voice-conduits, that is, through the four evangelists. With a bronze foundation, that is, a firm foundation of faith and works, it emits throughout the world a most powerful voice, like the sound of a trumpet gathering the people.

### VERSE 27

**David, however.** Christ makes manifest the example of his Incarnation and Passion, previously hidden from the Jews. Wood, having arisen from the earth and reaching the brightness of a garment through manifold labor, displays the truth of the human flesh triumphing amid scourges. This is what is meant by: “David was in an ephod.”

(GREGORY, *Moralia*, Book XXVII, chapter 27.) It is pleasing to contemplate how great are the gifts of virtues, etc., up to the point where he says: “What sort of person I present myself outwardly while despising myself, such a person I attend to inwardly.”

### VERSE 29

**Michal, daughter of Saul.** (RABANUS.) While everyone else rejoiced and hymns resounded at the entrance of the ark, etc., up to the point where David despises her in her humiliation. For at the end, some Jews, believing in Christ by profession, follow the Antichrist in their deeds. What is said of Michal suits them: she is interpreted as “all water,” signifying the instability of the carnal, and she is called not David’s wife but Saul’s daughter. Those who serve Christ only outwardly are not crowned with him; rather, they are condemned with the persecutors whom they imitated.

## CHAPTER XVI

### VERSE 1

**Therefore they brought it in.** (RABANUS, on Paralipomenon, volume III.) The ark is placed in the middle of the tabernacle that David had spread for it. This signifies that the faith of the Church is preached, advances, and is implanted in the hearts of the faithful whom God has predestined to eternal life.

### VERSE 2

**He blessed the people.** Christ commends the devotion of the Church to the Father, to whom he also intercedes for us at the Father’s right hand; and, like the true David, he blesses and feeds the people with the nourishment of the saving mystery.

### VERSE 3

**And he distributed.** The faithful receive these gifts when, though many, they are one bread and one body in Christ. They chastise the wantonness of their flesh and subject it to service; they cook it in the fire of the Holy Spirit; and, through compassion for their neighbor, they make the fruits of good works exceedingly rich with the oil of mercy. In contrast, Saul’s daughter enters the king’s chamber in vain and bears no fruit, because those who receive the word of God only through the ear, without the offspring of good works, die.

**Fried in oil.** Flesh made completely clean from the salt of sin, roasted for the sake of human salvation in the frying pan of the cross and full of the oil of charity. For God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son, who suffered out of charity.

### VERSE 7

**On that day.** Because Christ established the order of teachers at the summit of ecclesiastical dignity. *Asaph* is interpreted as “gathering.” Asaph and his brothers, therefore, are the apostles and apostolic men appointed to gather the faithful. Of them it is said: “You will appoint them as princes over all the earth.” The historian inserted the form of praise that David himself composed, saying: “Give thanks to the Lord,” etc.

### VERSE 8

**Give thanks, etc.** “Alleluia” is placed as the title of this psalm, and according to Jerome it is of the neuter gender. *Allelu* means “praise [you]”; *ia* signifies the invisible God. It is one of the ten names of God, as Jerome explains in his letter to Marcella.

### VERSE 36

**And let everyone say.** (RABANUS.) This refers especially to the Gentile who was still an unbeliever when this was sung, but who, moved by the power of prophecy, was led to say, out of love for the whole community, “Amen, amen,” that is, “Let it be; let it be.” This is how the people respond today when prayers are offered, so that the devout intention of the priests and the sound devotion of the people may agree in prayer, according to: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about anything they ask, it will be done for them,” etc. (Matthew XVIII).

### VERSE 39

**In the high place.** Some say that, after the children of Israel entered the land of Canaan, the tabernacle of God was first at Shiloh, then at Nob, afterward at Gibeon, and finally at Zion. Others say that there was a place in Jerusalem called Gibeon, and that David placed the tabernacle and the ark there. For Gibeon is interpreted as “hill.” They think that the place was called “high” because of the dignity of divine worship.

But in the Book of Places we read that Gibeon was a metropolitan city of the Hivites in the tribe of Benjamin, and that a village of the same name is now shown at the fourth milestone west of Bethlehem, near Ramah and Ramon. There Solomon, after offering sacrifices, deserved to receive a divine oracle. It was separated for the Levites.

**To bless.** (JEROME.) He would devote himself to the generation of sons. Others understand “blessing” by antiphrasis; they take “house” to mean Michal, Saul’s daughter, whom David rebuked because she despised him dancing before the ark of the Lord.

## CHAPTER XVII

### VERSE 2

**And Nathan said.** (RABANUS, as above.) It is clear that the spirit of prophecy does not always illumine the minds of the prophets. Thus Elisha says: “Leave her, because her soul is bitter, and the Lord has hidden it from me,” etc. This occurs by divine dispensation, so that when they receive the Spirit they may discover what comes from God, and when they lose it, what comes from themselves.

### VERSE 4

**You shall not build.** Because you are a man of blood. Anyone who wishes to correct others must be clean in himself, fleeing earthly desires, and he will see what must be fled all the more perceptively the more truly he avoids these things in knowledge and life. A hand holding mud cannot wipe away dirt that has been thrown upon it.

According to the sequence of the ancient translation, this is rightly said symbolically and by a divine voice to David, who was laboring in external wars: “You shall not build a temple for me, because you are a man of blood.” He builds the temple of the Lord who devotes himself to correcting the minds of his neighbors. We are the temple of God, established for true life through his indwelling; hence: “The temple of God is holy, and you are that temple” (I Corinthians III). A man of blood builds the temple of God. For anyone who still clings to carnal things must necessarily be ashamed to instruct the minds of his neighbors.

### VERSE 9

**Nor shall the sons.** (RABANUS.) The foreign enemies returned at intervals of time, so that at one time there was peace and at another war. Yet longer periods of peace are found there than Solomon had. Under Ehud there were eighty years of peace. Therefore, far be it from us to understand these words as referring to Solomon.

### VERSE 11

**And when you have completed.** Solomon began to reign while his father was still reigning, something that happened to none of those kings. Thus it is evident that he is not the one whom this prophecy foreshadows. Christ, however, the true peacemaker, truly reigned after David’s death.

### VERSE 12

**He will build a house**, that is, the Church: the house of David, because it is the temple of God made from human beings, not stones, where the people may dwell eternally with God and in God, and God with the people. Therefore, although according to the Septuagint Nathan is said to have spoken: “And the Lord will announce to you that you will build a house for him,” David later says: “For you, God of Israel, have revealed to your servant’s ear, saying: I will build you a house” (II Kings VII). We also build this house by living well, and God builds it by helping; hence: “Unless the Lord builds the house,” etc. (Psalm CXXVI).

**And the throne.** Hyperbolically, this may be understood of the son of Jesse. But Christ, born from David’s seed, was exalted above every principality, power, and virtue. The Father gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, etc. (Philippians II).

## CHAPTER XVIII

### VERSE 1

**And the daughters.** (RABANUS.) The smaller cities belonging to a metropolitan city, etc., up to the point where the flesh is compelled to serve the spirit.

### VERSE 3

**Hadadezer.** His name is interpreted as “beautiful help.” He was king of Zobah, which is interpreted as “burning” or “turning.” He signifies the vices of paganism, kindled by natural fervor, against which Christ fights and conquers with the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Ephesians VI).

### VERSE 4

**He hamstrung them.** Christ hamstrings the proud height of the world’s wisdom when it resists him; yet whatever he finds useful and suitable for preaching, he reserves for himself.

### VERSE 6

**In Damascus.** Damascus, a noble city of Phoenicia, is interpreted as “cup of blood.” Syria means “lofty” or “moist.” Paganism, formerly fluid with lust and proud in spirit, thirsted for human blood; now, cleansed by Christ’s baptism and exalted through progress in virtue, it desires the cup of his blood.

### VERSE 7

**Quivers.** These signify the doctrines of the Gentiles, in which the liberal disciplines are contained. Christ took them away from paganism and converted them to the service of the Church; for they are useful for overthrowing error and confirming truth.

### VERSE 8

**Solomon.** Since our king is the peacemaker, he turned the antiquity of expression, arising from the humiliation of overthrown paganism, toward the purification of baptismal grace and the strengthening of faith through the preaching of sound doctrine, for the use of the Church. For *Tebah* is interpreted as “the little one has come,” and *Chun* as “beauty.” Whoever recognizes himself as little becomes beautiful and splendid in the adornment of virtues.

### VERSE 12

**In the Valley of Salt.** In Kings it is written as follows: “David made a name for himself when he returned from striking down Syria in the Valley of Salt, killing eighteen thousand” (II Kings VIII). This means that he erected a triumphal arch for himself. He also made a name for himself because, after Syria of Damascus and Syria of Zobah had been defeated, he is said to have erected another one.

**Ten.** In some manuscripts, however, it is found that David did not kill twenty-eight thousand in the Valley of Salt; this arose from a scribal error. Joab struck down twelve thousand, as is written in the title of Psalm LVII. Here, however, Abishai is said to have killed eighteen thousand, but the victory was attributed to David in accordance with the dignity of kingship. Since Christ, by the strictness of his judgment, extinguishes the folly of excessive taste in those who think perversely about him, hence: “He who twists his tongue falls into evil” (Proverbs XVII).

### VERSE 16

**Ahimelech.** That is, “my brother is king.” In Kings he is called Abimelech, that is, “my father is king.” He instructs the priests of the Church that those who, by the order of their dignity, hold the place of a father should, by humility, be regarded as brothers and should not lord it over the clergy.

### VERSE 17

**Pelethites.** (JEROME.) “Admirable ones” or “life-givers.” Some say that these were the seventy judges, after the model of those whom Moses chose in the wilderness at the Lord’s command.
