Philistines. “Of a twofold fall.” For *Philitshiim* is interpreted as “double ruin.” This happens when, through the forgiveness of sins, grace and power flow from the beginning of its course in baptism in the Jordan all the way to the conversion of all nations to faith in Christ, so that where there had been an outpouring of carnal desires, there the seed of virtues may be established; and where the twofold ruin of idolatry and the shameful conduct of peoples had been, there, through confession of the true faith and the worship of piety, the life of the faithful may rise to the heavenly kingdom. For his power reaches to the borders of Egypt—that is, to the dark minds of unbelievers—which he fills with the light of faith. Hence: “Before him the Ethiopians shall fall,” etc.

### VERSE 27

“And so great a quantity.” The true Solomon provides in the Church an abundance of silver, as though of stones, when he converts the insensible hearts of the Gentiles to understanding the true God. They had worshiped stones as gods; he turns them to meditation on the Law and the preaching of the Gospel. Of them it is said: “Those who make them become like them,” etc. (Psalm 113). And elsewhere: “God is able from these stones to raise up children for Abraham” (Matthew 3). He also provides a multitude of cedars, as though of sycamores, because he has lifted the barrenness of the Gentiles—who were unwilling to raise themselves upward—to the fruitfulness of good works and virtues.

### VERSE 27

“And of cedars.” The cedar is naturally imperishable, pleasant in scent, and bright in appearance; when kindled, its brilliance drives away and destroys serpents.

“The rest.” This refers to what he did after he transgressed God’s Law, when foreign women dragged him even into idolatry. Many indeed begin well like Solomon and end badly; no one should be called blessed before his death and final funeral rites.

## CHAPTER X

### VERSE 8

“He abandoned the counsel of the elders,” etc. (Jerome.) The Hebrews say that these were Benaiah son of Jehoiada and Jahiel son of Achamoni, who is also called Chilla. After abandoning their counsel, Rehoboam began to consult the young men, namely Aduram—who is said later to have been stoned—and others like him. We often call someone “young” not in age but in disposition. Rehoboam was not young in age but in understanding: he began to reign in the forty-first year of his life.

### VERSE 13

“And the king answered,” etc. This signifies wicked rulers in the Church who, devoted to earthly desires, neglect the care of their subjects and take pleasure in the multitude of those who obey them. Rehoboam is interpreted as “breadth of the people.” These are those who enter the broad way that leads to death, not the narrow way that leads to life. Having abandoned the counsel of the fathers—whose words and deeds tend toward the height of perfection—they choose to obey the counsel of young men who burden them with praise and flattery, men who are blind and guides of the blind. Hence: “Woe to you, land whose king is a child,” etc. (Ecclesiastes 10).

## CHAPTER XI

### VERSE 21

“He loved,” etc. He had eighteen wives joined to him by the law, and thirty concubines. He had eighteen sons and sixty daughters.

## CHAPTER XII

### VERSE 2

“But in the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign he went up.” (Rabanus.) By their negligence, wicked rulers provoke the prince of darkness against the Church. He carries away the treasures of the house of the Lord and the treasures of the king when he removes knowledge of the Scriptures and works of virtue from the unwary and sluggish.

### VERSE 9

“Shishak the king.” *Byssus cilicii* means “the fine linen of sackcloth” or “the joy of sackcloth.” Fine linen signifies subtlety; sackcloth, made from goat hair, signifies sins. Thus, in the fine linen of sackcloth, there is the cunning of the devil’s deceit in the persuasion to sin. Shishak takes away the wealth of Jerusalem when the devil, who craftily deceives and rejoices in the multitude of sinners, strips ecclesiastical men of spiritual knowledge and virtuous works; and those who seemed beautiful in the Church, once stripped, he plunges with himself into the abyss of destruction.

“Shields.” Solomon made golden shields and entrusted them to the guardians of his house when Christ committed spiritual knowledge, through the two Testaments, to the teachers of the Church for the protection of the people. The ancient enemy draws this away through negligence. For when they attend to earthly matters and care less for heavenly things, he leaves them stripped of their former office and knowledge, as though robbed of their possessions in their own house. But when such men see that they have been deprived of spiritual understanding, they seek an abundance of words through eloquence, and set the sound of their speech against enemies on behalf of their subjects like the strength of bronze shields. But just as bronze is inferior to gold, so eloquence is inferior to the fruit of true wisdom. Hence: “Where there are many words, there is often poverty” (Proverbs 14).

### VERSE 15

“Of Shemaiah.” He was the man who earlier rebuked Rehoboam and the sons of Judah for their sins.

“I add.” He is also called Abdo. He was sent by the Lord to rebuke Jeroboam concerning the altar he had made in Samaria, and was killed on the way because, having been deceived by a false prophet, he ate there contrary to the Lord’s command.

## CHAPTER XIII

### VERSE 4

“Semeron.” (Rabanus, from Jerome.) It is the city that Jesus captured after killing its king. They say that it is now called Sebaste, a town in Palestine, where the relics of John the Baptist were buried. We read in the Book of Kings that Omri, king of Israel, bought Mount Semeron from a certain Semer and built a city on its summit, which he called Semeron after the name of its owner, Semer.

### VERSE 19

“Bethel.” (Rabanus.) A city near the stone from which, when traveling from Aelia toward Neapolis, one turns to the right. It was formerly called Luza, that is, Amigdalon, and fell by lot to Benjamin, near Bethan and Hai, which Jesus conquered after killing its king.

“Ephron.” It is a city in the tribe of Judah. Hence, twenty miles north of Aelia, there is still called by this name a very large village, Ephrea.

### VERSE 20

“In the days.” Not of Jeroboam, in whose twentieth year, according to the Book of Kings, Asa son of Abijah ruled over Judah and Jerusalem, but of Abijah, who, after taking Bethel, preserved the idols for Israel as a stumbling block, as the Hebrews assert.

## CHAPTER XIV

### VERSE 2

“He went out,” etc. After Azariah had reigned for ten years, Zerah, king of Ethiopia, moved against him with a very large army: ninety thousand infantry, ten thousand cavalry, and three hundred chariots. When he had set up camp against him and Asa saw the multitude of the Ethiopians, he asked God with a great cry for victory, so that he himself might destroy so many thousands of men. For he said that one must trust no one except him who could make a few prevail over many and cause the weak to overcome the strongest.

## CHAPTER XV

### VERSE 15

“But Azariah,” etc. The prophet Azariah met them and ordered them to pause for a little while along their route. Then he began to tell them that this victory had been granted to them by God because they had preserved themselves as just and holy and had done everything according to God’s will. He said that, if they remained in his commandments, they would prevail over their enemies and enjoy happiness and prosperity through divine power. But if they abandoned their religion, they would fall into the opposite condition. A time would come when no truthful prophet or priest would be found among that people. For this reason their cities would be overthrown, their nation scattered throughout the whole land, and they would have a miserable and needy life.

## CHAPTER XVI

### VERSE 14

“With spices,” etc. This is the vain ostentation of fame that philosophers or poets offer after the death of their kings, and that false Christians likewise offer when their teachers die; they cast these things into the fire, because everything that they have produced here without usefulness or the edification of their brothers is shown to be subject to the fires of Gehenna.

“They burned over him,” etc. Note that, as the Hebrews report, out of reverence for kings, the burning of costly garments took place together with spices. Hence elsewhere: “They will make a burning for you like the burning of the great.” It was customary among the ancients for the costly ornaments of kings to be burned on the funeral pyre after their death, but without the bodies.

## CHAPTER XVII

### VERSE 3

“He walked in the ways of David,” etc. (Rabanus.) This shows that he was an executor of the divine commandments like David before David sinned with Uriah’s wife. The satisfaction made for that sin secured for David an everlasting memory.

### VERSE 5

“All Judah gave gifts to Jehoshaphat.” This signifies the faithful from the Gentiles who, having abandoned the error of their fathers, come together to Christ, washed in baptism and anointed with chrism, receiving from Christ the Christian name and royal dignity. Hence: “You are a chosen race, a royal priesthood,” etc. (1 Peter 2). For Jehoshaphat means “the Lord’s dowry,” or “he who is a dowry,” or “he who has been endowed.” Since the Church of the Gentiles, purchased by Christ’s blood and given the pledge of the Holy Spirit, has merited fellowship with the heavenly Bridegroom and participation in the kingdom, infinite riches have been made hers when diverse nations believe and acquire diverse virtues.

### VERSE 10

“And so great fear came upon them,” etc. Because of the virtues practiced in the Church, the boldness of the Gentiles is removed, and they are stirred to offer Christ the gifts of faith, the tribute of good works, pious confession, and the sheep of simplicity.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### VERSE 2

“And he went down,” etc. These are the founders of heresies who lead a crowd of the lost along the byways of error and plunge them into the precipice of death. Jehoshaphat was related to Ahab and went down to him in Samaria to assist him against his enemies. He signifies those who incline from the Catholics toward friendship with heretics. Although they do not depart from the path of the true faith, they nevertheless do not avoid the society and communion of those who err. Against such people it is said: “Avoid a heretical person after the first and second admonition” (Titus 3). Hence Jehoshaphat is rebuked by Jehu son of Hanani the seer—that is, by the son of that prophet who had rebuked Asa—because he had given assistance to an impious man and joined himself in friendship to those who hated the Lord.

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book 2, chapter 15, volume 1.) “The throne of the Lord is the angelic powers,” etc., up to “and he will be found all the harsher in punishment, the more securely he lived in guilt.”

## CHAPTER XIX

### VERSE 10

“Every case that comes before you,” etc. (Augustine, *The City of God*, book 4, chapter 3.) “When justice is removed, what are kingdoms but great robberies? For what are robberies themselves but little kingdoms?”

## CHAPTER XX

### VERSE 1

“Of the Ammonites.” He signifies the Idumaeans, but the historical writer preferred to designate what was happening by the name of the allied peoples rather than publicly disclose the impiety of the shameless.

### VERSE 2

“From these places,” etc. He signifies those places beyond the Salt Sea, which is otherwise called the Asphaltite Lake or the Dead Sea.

“Engaddi.” To this day it is called a very large Jewish village beside the Dead Sea, from which opobalsamum comes. Solomon calls its vineyards the vineyards of Engaddi.

### VERSE 16

“For they will go up by the ascent named Sis,” etc. (Rabanus, on Chronicles, from Jerome.) It is also called Jeruel according to the Hebrews. They say that Sis, etc., up to “fear was struck into the foreigners on every side.”

Mystically, the Moabites, Ammonites, and Idumaeans signify pagans, Jews, and heretics. They gratuitously stir up war against the faithful and strive to take away the Christian religion. But Jehoshaphat—that is, the people of Christ—attacks them not with bodily weapons but with spiritual ones, seeking heavenly help through the innermost devotion of the heart.

### VERSE 25

“So Jehoshaphat came,” etc. The holy teachers, together with the multitude of the faithful, gather from the spoils of the enemy whatever they have profitably learned through reading, writing, and teaching in physics, ethics, and logic. Through faith in the Holy Trinity they convert it to the use of the whole Church, so that what those men possessed unjustly and uselessly, the faithful may possess usefully and employ for the salvation of souls.

### VERSE 26

“Valley of Blessing.” The humility of the Church, where praises are worthily rendered to God. Whoever, instructed in the teaching of the four Gospels, reaches the unity of the Church through faith in baptism, will there rightly offer praise and live worthily before God. With praise and everlasting joy he will enter the vision of perpetual peace.

## CHAPTER XXI

### VERSE 2

“All these were the sons of Jehoshaphat,” etc. (Rabanus.) They were imitators of his works, while their brother Joram was always declining into worse things. Thus Joram himself is read to have killed them together with the princes of Israel.

### VERSE 14

“Behold, the Lord will strike you,” etc. This occurred through the Philistines and Arabs, who devastated his land and carried off the possessions, sons, and wives of Joram, whose name is interpreted as “Who is exalted?” He declined from a religious father into infidelity and caused the sons of Judah to commit fornication. He signifies those who, imbued with faith and regenerated through baptism, abandon the truth of the faith, follow the error of heretics, and pervert others along with themselves. Hence Elijah—that is, the prophetic word—rebukes them, because the entire authority of the divine books censures such people and, with the gravest denunciations, reproves them for the perversity they deserve.

### VERSE 20

“He reigned eight years,” etc. Concerning Joram, it is said that he reigned for eight years and lived for forty; but his son Ahaziah, when he began to reign, is said to have been forty-two years old. If this is so, he fathered a son two years before he himself was born. But the Hebrews say that Joram, who is described as having lived forty years and reigned eight, lived forty years and reigned twenty-eight. The eight years assigned to him in the kingdom are those during which he reigned before killing his brothers, while he was still living innocently. The remaining twenty years during which he reigned afterward are not counted because he lived in sickness and tribulation. Therefore they are assigned to his son, who, according to the Book of Kings, is said to have been no more than twenty-two years old, lest the remaining years in the total of the numbers produce an error in the calculation of the periods.

## CHAPTER XXII

### VERSE 6

“Azariah son of Joram,” etc. (Rabanus, from Jerome.) Above he is called Ahaziah, that is, “grasping the Lord”; Azariah means “the help of the Lord.” Therefore, according to the Hebrews, his name is changed for the better, because in accordance with the Lord’s command he visited the sick.

### VERSE 7

“Against Jehu,” etc. Jehu signifies the rule of the Gentiles, which Christ appointed against the sacrilegious city that killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets and persecuted the apostles. He appointed it to punish that city with a fitting vengeance and, after Christ’s coming, to destroy the priests’ shrine and overthrow the temple; and to hurl the impious synagogue, thirsting for their blood, from the height of the kingdom like Jezebel, killing its rulers.

### VERSE 10

“For Athaliah,” etc. Athaliah, who tried to extinguish the seed of David and destroy the royal line, signifies the impiety of the Synagogue, which, through the wickedness of its mind, lies in wait for Christ’s seed, raging with inexorable hatred. She once seemed to reign when she observed the ceremonies of the Law for a limited time. Athaliah is interpreted as “the temporal one of the Lord.” But through the courage of Jehoshabeath—which is interpreted as “the Lord’s fullness,” that is, the Church in which there are true delights—Joash, whose name means “the memory of the Lord,” is preserved. He signifies Christ, in whom the memory of the Lord’s name is found, so that through the cruelty of the raging persecutor he might not be killed in the saints but nourished in the house of Jehoiada the high priest. Jehoiada is interpreted as “beloved of the Lord,” that is, Christ, of whom the Father says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matthew 17). His house is the Church, where, abiding in the faith of the elect, he daily brings about the increase of his body, so that at the time of judgment he may raise the scepter and power of his kingdom against those who were suppressing him.

## CHAPTER XXIII

### VERSE 13

“Upon the platform.” (Rabanus.) That is, the column and its base, which Solomon had prepared and placed in the middle of the basilica, having a length of five cubits, a width of five cubits, and a height of three.

### VERSE 16

“Jehoiada made a covenant.” Jehoiada is interpreted as “knowing the Lord” or “loving.” For he taught the children of Israel to know the Lord. He therefore made a covenant between the Lord, the people, and the king, namely, that they should obey the Lord and his Law. He also made one between the king and the people, so that the people would act faithfully toward the king and the king would rule the people justly according to the teaching of the priests and Levites, whose duty it was to make the Lord’s commandments known.

## CHAPTER XXIV

### VERSE 4

“After this it pleased Joash,” etc. (Rabanus.) King Joash rebuked the priests, etc., up to “lest the multitude of the hearers should perish through the negligence of the teachers.”

### VERSE 7

“And his sons,” etc. This does not mean that he had sons at that time, since, after Ahaziah’s death, Athaliah—because he had no son—attempted to kill the entire royal seed. Rather, he calls the priests of the idols “his sons,” for they had despoiled the temple and adorned their idols with its ornaments. Often imitators are called sons.

### VERSE 12

“But they hired,” etc. The apostles do this when, through disciples subject to them, they scatter the seeds of the divine word throughout the world and appoint suitable workers over their hearers for the will of God. Some make wooden structures when they prepare themselves and those obedient to them as fruitful trees in God’s house. Others repair roofs when they rebuild what had been broken through heresy or schisms. Others cut stones when they strongly rebuke the hard-hearted and unbelieving. Others work iron and bronze when they seek from each person the strength of faith and confession of Catholic truth, so that the house of God may be fulfilled, according to the saying: “To each of us grace was given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” (Ephesians 4).

### VERSE 14

“The remaining part of the money,” etc. This appears contrary to what is read in the Book of Kings: “Nevertheless, basins for the temple and forks were not made from the same money” (2 Kings 12). But the present passage does not say that the sacred vessels used in the temple and for burnt offerings were made from the same money that the people offered in the temple of the Lord for the restoration of God’s house. Rather, they were made from the remaining money—that is, from money supplied by other donations. It could have happened that money offered at different times provided the material for different works, just as one kind of teaching is used to instruct beginners in the faith, and another to instruct the mature toward fullness.

### VERSE 18

“And wrath arose.” (Rabanus, from Jerome.) The Hebrews report that the princes of Judah worshiped the king as God and that he willingly accepted this. Therefore he gravely offended the Lord and suddenly experienced the wrath he deserved. For this same offense, Herod is also read in the Acts of the Apostles to have been struck by an angel.

### VERSE 25

“Of Zechariah son of Jehoiada,” etc. (Rabanus.) In the Gospel, when the Lord recalls Zechariah who was killed between the temple and the altar, etc., up to “which they call Siloam, pointing out red stones that they think were stained by Zechariah’s blood.”

### VERSE 26

“But they plotted against him,” etc. The Hebrews assert that the Ammonites and Moabites plotted against King Joash because of the unjust murder of Zechariah, in order to heighten the wickedness of the Israelites, who refused to avenge the priest of God, though the sons of foreigners avenged him.

## CHAPTER XXV

### VERSE 11

“To the Valley of Salt,” etc. (Rabanus.) It was where salt was made, either from salty hay cut, dried, and burned in many places, or from salty well water heated and boiled until it was brought to the firmness of salt. Alternatively, it was the place where Joab is also read to have struck twelve thousand Idumaeans. In place of “Valley of Salt,” the old edition added *Gemel*, as the name of a region.

### VERSE 16

“I know,” he said, “that God has determined,” etc. He does not wish anyone to perish, but by a just judgment he condemns the one who persists in sin. Amasiah therefore perished because, although warned by the prophet to repent, he did not obey but persisted to the end.

### VERSE 18

“The thistle that,” etc. The comparison implies that Amasiah, born of the noblest lineage and descended from the stock of David, became degraded and contemptible because of the shame of idolatry. Yet he did not consider his proper measure but raised himself beyond measure through the arrogance of pride.

### VERSE 21

“Beth-shemesh.” (Rabanus.) In the Book of Kings it is called a town of Judah because it belongs to the kingdom of Judah, that is, to the two tribes ruled by the house of David. But according to the location of the territory, it belongs to the tribe of Benjamin.

### VERSE 24

“And at Obed-edom,” etc. He carried away not only the vessels that he found in the house of God but also those guarded by the gatekeepers and custodians of the temple. In the Book of Kings, however, we read that David chose seventy-two from the sons of Obed-edom to minister in the house of God and to guard the temple.

### VERSE 27

“After he withdrew.” From the time he refused to listen to the prophet’s counsel and was unwilling to turn to the Lord, a conspiracy was prepared and delayed until it reached completion.

## CHAPTER XXVI

### VERSE 3

“Uzziah, when he began to reign.” He is also called Azariah. Uzziah is interpreted as “the strength of the Lord”; Azariah as “the help of the Lord.” As long as he acted rightly, he was assisted by divine aid, waged many wars successfully, and triumphed over his enemies. But after he had attempted unlawful things through pride, he was struck with leprosy, which obscured the dignity of his name and honor, and he was excluded from the people until the day of his death.

### VERSE 9

“Above the Valley Gate.” (Rabanus.) This is the Gate of Ephraim, etc., up to “concerning this gate and the other gates of Jerusalem we have spoken sufficiently in Ezra, following Bede.”

### VERSE 16

“But when he had become strong,” etc. Uzziah was at first just and did what was right in the sight of the Lord. Thus he defeated enemies and had many prophets in his kingdom. For as long as the priest Zechariah, whose name means “understanding,” lived, Uzziah pleased God by serving in the temple with complete reverence. But after Zechariah died, Uzziah wished to offer gifts himself. He seized the dignity of the priesthood not with piety but with presumption, and he did not obey when the Levites and priests protested. Therefore he was struck with leprosy on the forehead, which the priest covered with the golden plate that, in Ezekiel, the Lord commands to be marked with the impression of the letter *Thau*.

“He entered the temple of the Lord.” He entered the temple wearing the priestly robe during the solemn festival, intending to offer incense at the golden altar, according to Josephus. Hence, outside the city, at the place called Eroge, the middle part of a mountain was split toward the west; moving by its own rolling force for four stadia, it came to rest against the eastern mountain, so that it blocked the roads and overwhelmed the royal cities. The Hebrews wish this to have happened in the twenty-fifth year of Uzziah, of whose reign twenty-seven years remained.

Uzziah reigned for fifty-two years. At that time Amulcus ruled among the Latins and Agamestor among the Athenians. After Uzziah’s death, Isaiah saw the vision, as he himself testifies, at the very time when Romulus, founder of the Roman empire, was born.

### VERSE 23

“In the field of the royal tombs.” Not in the royal burial places, not in the city of David. For heretics and schismatics are unworthy of association and communion with the holy Church, and their memory is not preserved among Catholics. Stained by errors and fouled by vices, they are separated from the fellowship of the faithful.

## CHAPTER XXVII

### VERSE 1

“Jotham was twenty-five years old,” etc. At the beginning and at the end, he enumerates Jotham’s years because, just as he began in righteousness, he persevered in it to the end. Hence the periods of his life are proclaimed worthy of praise.

### VERSE 3

“He built the upper gate,” etc. In the Acts of the Apostles it is called the Beautiful Gate. According to the Hebrews, it is still called the Gate of Jotham because he built it.

“Ophel.” It was a tower not far from the temple, of remarkable height. Hence it received the name Ophel, that is, “of darkness” or “of cloud.” Where it is written in Micah, “And the cloudy tower of the daughter of Zion” (Micah 4:8), the Hebrew has “the tower of Ophel.” The tower of Ophel signifies the height of Scripture, which, founded on history, hides the summit of spiritual meaning among the clouds while concealing the greatness of knowledge from human eyes. Hence: “He made darkness his hiding place” (Psalm 17).

Jotham, whose life is praised, signifies Christ, of whom it is said: “Great is the Lord and greatly to be praised” (Psalm 47), etc. For Jotham is interpreted as “consummated” or “perfect,” and of Christ the Apostle says: “And being made perfect, he became the cause of eternal salvation to all who obey him,” etc. (Hebrews 5). He himself constructed the lofty gate of the house of the Lord and accomplished the mystery of his incarnation with wondrous power. Of himself he says: “I am the door. If anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). This was called the lofty gate, concerning which the Psalmist says: “The Lord is exalted above all nations” (Psalm 112), etc.

## CHAPTER XXVIII

### VERSE 3

“In the Valley of Ben-Hinnom.” (Rabanus.) This is the Valley of Ben-Hinnom, etc., up to “for all adulterers make their hearts like a furnace.”

## CHAPTER XXIX

### VERSE 3

“In that same year,” etc. (Rabanus.) Otherwise he would not have imitated David his father, who, devoted to God from childhood, magnified the worship of God at the beginning of his reign.

Morally, this admonishes the rulers of the Church not to be sluggish in the office entrusted to them, but to do everything diligently.

Mystically, Hezekiah, who not only energetically carried out God’s work himself and through his own people but also stirred others to similar zeal through messengers, signifies Christ; the interpretation of his name also testifies to this. For Hezekiah means “grasping the Lord” or “the strength of the Lord.” Christ, however, is the power of God and the wisdom of God. With his blood he washed away all the transgressions of the fathers that had occurred under the Law, and he plainly restored the worship of piety in the Church. He sent messengers to summon the nations to faith: first the prophets, then the apostles and their successors. He instituted the celebration of Passover in the second month, because, after the shadow of the Law had ceased, he taught the observance of the true Passover, concerning which Paul says: “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5).

### VERSE 6

“Our fathers have sinned,” etc. (Jerome, *Questions on Chronicles*, volume 3.) This is written out fully, etc., up to “and they worshiped toward the rising of the sun.”

## CHAPTER XXX

### VERSE 1

“He also sent,” etc. (Jerome.) After sending messengers publicly to all Israel, he secretly sent letters to Manasseh and Ephraim, whom he knew could be converted. They were more arrogant because of the royal dignity that existed in the house of Ephraim.

## CHAPTER XXXI

### VERSE 1

“They broke the images,” etc. After the coming of the Savior, idolatry was destroyed not only in Jerusalem and Judah but among all the nations of the world, and the devil’s pride collapsed. As the number of the faithful increases, the worship of demons decreases, until at the end of the world the last enemy, death, is overwhelmed and the Lord alone reigns on that day.

## CHAPTER XXXII

### VERSE 4

“They stopped up all the springs.” In fighting against pagans and heretics, diligent caution must be exercised and the mysteries concealed. Hence: “Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor throw your pearls before swine.”

### VERSE 5

“He built.” (Rabanus, on Chronicles.) Christ built the Church, which is the city of God, etc., up to “and appointed teachers as leaders of spiritual warfare.”

## CHAPTER XXXIII

### VERSE 12

“And he practiced profound repentance before the God of his fathers.” (Rabanus.) After hearing of Manasseh’s repentance, no one should despair of God’s mercy. Rather, through repentance, one should hope confidently for forgiveness.

## CHAPTER XXXIV

### VERSE 5

“Moreover, the bones,” etc. (Rabanus.) He burned the priests on the altars of the idols to show that the sacrifices of those men were deadly. They not only offered animal victims to demons but also handed themselves over to idolatry. This signifies that all who were enslaved to the devil’s service and ended their sacrilegious lives in time will be consumed by eternal torments according to each person’s deserts.

### VERSE 22

“To Huldah the prophetess,” etc. (Jerome.) Huldah was the wife of Shallum, the uncle of Jeremiah’s father and the father of Hananel. She lived in the Second Quarter. This was a place in Jerusalem outside the city wall and the outer rampart, called the Second; it is mentioned by the prophet Zephaniah.

## CHAPTER XXXV

### VERSE 1

“Josiah held the Passover in Jerusalem,” etc. (Rabanus.) We are admonished first to cleanse the land of our heart from every vice and then to celebrate the Lord’s Passover—not in the old leaven, nor in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Corinthians 5).

Mystically, Josiah, that is, “the strength of the Lord,” signifies Christ, of whom it is written: “The Lord strong and mighty, the Lord mighty in battle” (Psalm 23). Josiah is also interpreted as “the salvation of the Lord,” and Christ saves his people from their sins (Matthew 1). In his zeal for God, he cleanses the land of Judah and Jerusalem from every impurity. Through the prophet he said: “The zeal of your house has consumed me” (Psalm 68). Of him it is said elsewhere: “His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly cleanse his threshing floor” (Matthew 3). He celebrates the true Passover in the eighteenth year of his reign because, in the eighth age, after the general resurrection has been granted, he brings his saints, perfected in good works, to the denarius of eternal blessedness, after first removing every scandal from his kingdom.

### VERSE 3

“Put the ark in the sanctuary of the temple that Solomon son of David, king of Israel, built.” The Hebrews report that, in the time of Ahaz, the ark was removed from the temple when he introduced images into it and was transferred to the house of Shallum, the husband of Huldah and the uncle of Jeremiah. For it could not remain together with the images.

### VERSE 18

“There was no Passover like this,” etc. When the figures have been removed on the day of judgment, the saints will pass from death to life and from corruption to glory. In the presence of their Creator, in the heavenly Jerusalem, they will rejoice forever, because the God of gods will be seen in Zion and because he has glorified his mercy in the fortified city.

### VERSE 21

“Against whom God,” etc. From the words of Jeremiah and the other prophets, he could have learned the Lord’s will, according to which judgment was to be carried out against the sinful people. Hence Rabshakeh also said concerning Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians: “The Lord commanded me to go up against this land” (Psalm 83), because the prophets had foretold that he would go up, and this had not escaped his notice.

### VERSE 22

“In the plain of Megiddo.” The killing of Josiah by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo signifies the persecution of the ancient enemy against preachers, whom he tries to deliver to death and remove from the Church so that he may more easily invade and scatter the entire people. Pharaoh is interpreted as “the one who scatters,” Neco as “the one who strikes,” and Megiddo as “from temptation.” The devil is permitted to rise against the saints, and he strives with all his strength, so that, by striking the flock of God through temptation, he may first take them away by scattering them—their support being removed, those who remain fight against the enemy.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

### VERSE 4

“And he appointed.” Neco appointed Jehoiakim king and imposed a fine of one hundred talents of silver upon the land, because the devil demanded from the people of the lost the payment of servitude, so that they might be prepared to obey him both in understanding and in speech.

“And he turned.” It should be noted that the Book of Kings speaks of this same Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, as follows: “Jehoiakim slept with his fathers, and Jehoiachin his son reigned in his place” (2 Kings 24). Josephus, however, says: “When the king of Babylon entered the city, he did not keep faith at all. He killed the strongest and most handsome young men together with King Jehoiakim, whom he ordered to be thrown unburied before the wall. He appointed his son Jehoiachin king over the entire province. Those who held positions of authority, three thousand in number, he led away to Babylon; among them was Ezekiel, still a boy.”

Such, then, was the end of King Jehoiakim. He lived thirty years and reigned eleven years. His successor in the kingdom, a king named Ononimus, reigned three months and ten days.

It should be understood that when someone once enslaves himself to any vice, he becomes subject to many masters. Hence Jehoiakim, whom Pharaoh first compelled to pay tribute to him, was afterward forced by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, to serve for three years. Nebuchadnezzar signifies the same person as Pharaoh: namely, the prince of confusion and ruler of the darkness of this age. When the devil has compelled someone to pay him the tribute of sin, he brings the whole person under his dominion and demands complete service—through persuasion, pleasure, consent, thought, speech, and action.

(Jerome, *Questions on Chronicles*, volume 3.) It should be understood that the name of this Jehoiachin, etc., up to “they yield, together with their superiors, as prey to the devil, corrupted by their examples.”

## Verse 10

**“The king, moreover.”** Zedekiah signifies those who undertake governance among the people of God; for *Zedekiah* is interpreted as “the righteous one of the Lord.” They receive the seat of righteousness in order to perform works of righteousness; they receive the dignity of honor and office, especially because, through the grace of baptism and the anointing of chrism, they deserve to be called sons of Josiah—that is, of “the salvation of the Lord.” But when they degenerate, they relapse into the foulness of vices, turn their subjects to impiety, neither keep the faith they promised to God nor maintain covenants of peace with human beings.

Every day the divine law, the prophets, and the miracles of the apostles urge such people to withdraw from their sins and return to the Lord through repentance. But once hardened, they despise words of salvation. Therefore, in anger, God sends against them the king of the Chaldeans—that is, the devil with his attendants, namely spiritual wickednesses. Sparing no age and showing deference to no dignity, they carry whomever they capture into Babylon—that is, into confusion—and burn the house of the Lord, because they compel the faithful, who are the temple of God, to blaspheme. They destroy the walls of Jerusalem when they cast down the guardianship of shepherds; they burn the towers when they consume prelates through unlawful desires; they demolish every precious thing when they reduce to nothing those who applaud themselves for the privilege of virtue and knowledge.

The end of the Book of Chronicles is similar to the beginning of the Book of the Priest Ezra; therefore, there is no need to repeat here what we explained there. Concerning Cyrus also—how he signifies Christ, what is said about him, and what is referred to him—we have explained in Isaiah.

**(Rabanus, from Bede.)** Solomon built the temple of the Lord in Jerusalem over seven years, etc., up to the point where they receive the city of God from which they had been expelled.

[Col. 0691]

# THE FIRST BOOK OF EZRA

*(G)*

## Prologue of Blessed Jerome on Ezra and Nehemiah

*(See volume VIII of the works.)*

# Chapter I

[Col. 0691D]

**(Bede on Ezra, volume II.)** Just as Cyrus, after destroying the empire of the Chaldeans, liberated the people of God, etc., up to the point at which he proclaims the faith in his name and the hope of salvation to all who belong to his kingdom, that is, to the elect.

### Verse 2

**“And he himself commanded me to build him a house,” etc.**

**(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** The house or temple of God in the Holy Scriptures, etc., up to the point at which they likewise await the solemnities of its future dedication.

### Verse 3

**“Who is there among you?”**

**(Idem, in the same place.)** Great is the king’s faith in these words, etc., up to the point at which he would direct their minds and hands toward works that bring salvation.

**“Let him go up to Jerusalem.”**  
**(Idem, in the same place.)** Those who sin or concern themselves with worldly affairs are in the depths; those who desire to please God should sigh for heavenly things, rise above all the pomp and allurements of the world through love of eternal things, and build a house for God in Judea—that is, in confession of their own iniquity and of divine mercy. Let them prepare their hearts, in which God may deign to dwell and shine forth, and let them strive to invite their neighbors to the same by word and example.

[Col. 0693A]

### Verse 4

**“And all the others.”**

**(Bede, in the same place.)** The distinction of the words is to be noted, etc., up to the point where John says: “Therefore we ought to welcome such people, so that we may be fellow workers for the truth,” etc. *(3 John 8.)*

**“Let them assist.”** Those who abound in temporal goods ought not merely to provide what is necessary for Christ’s poor, but should also willingly perform whatever good works they can on their own behalf, so that through both benefits they may deserve to have a share in the temple of God, which is the Church.

### Verse 5

**“And they arose.”**

**(Bede, in the same place.)** Cyrus commanded—or rather permitted—everyone to go up to Jerusalem and build the house of the Lord, etc., up to the point where he therefore deserved to share in the mercy that had been bestowed.

**“The leaders.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** It belongs to the leaders of the fathers, that is, to teachers, to build by work and doctrine the minds of those who err, [Col. 0693B] in devotion to good work. They are the learned scribes of the kingdom of heaven, who, carefully examining the merits and understanding of their hearers, know how to judge whom they should advance to which degree of ecclesiastical ministry.

**“So that they might go up.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** By daily advances, as though by certain steps, one ascends to the summit of the virtues that exist in the vision of eternal peace. The first steps are to correct one’s own life; the second, to labor over the errors of one’s neighbors; the highest, after good works and teaching, to await the joys of perpetual reward.

### Verse 6

**“Their hands assisted with the vessels.”**** The companions of the builders’ hands are those who cannot build but assist by giving money, when laypeople entrust their children or household to preachers to be educated for the Lord, so that what they cannot do themselves they may offer to the Lord through those who can, as a gift of their devotion.

**“And with beasts of burden.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** That is, with those who are slower, etc., up to the point where, like varied furnishings, they are assigned to the leaders of the fathers for building the house of the Lord.

**“But he brought forth.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The various kinds of vessels, etc., up to the point where he preserves written in the book of eternal memory the number of those in whose figure it is aptly added: “And he counted,” etc.

### Verse 9

**“And this is.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Because the Lord knows the number of the elect, etc., up to the point where they are snatched away to everlasting punishment before they repent.

# Chapter II

[Col. 0693D]

### Verse 1

**“These are,” etc.**** That is, of Judea, not of Babylonia. For those born in Babylonia from the stock of the captives also belonged to this people. With their whole heart they longed for Judea and Jerusalem. Their figure is represented by their leader Zerubbabel, who by his very name shows that he was born in Babylon, but by his purpose and work was a citizen of Jerusalem.

In a higher sense, the children of the Church are children of the heavenly homeland—not only those who have already been imbued with the Church’s sacraments, but also those who, outside it, that is, wandering for a time among the impious, were predestined before the ages by divine election for life and are to be consecrated through the ministries of divine grace.

**“And they returned to Jerusalem.”** **(Bede on Ezra, volume II.)** When they have been liberated from the power of Satan, etc., [Col. 0694A] up to the point where the vision of peace and confession begin in the present and are perfected in the future.

**“Each one to his city.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Scripture therefore carefully distinguished from which generation of captives those who were released had returned to their homeland, etc., up to the point where he rewards them with a sure recompense.

### Verse 2

**“The number,” etc.** **(Bede, in the same place.)** He calls the people Israel the tribe of Judah and Benjamin, etc., up to the point where they are to be understood together with the priests and Levites who had received their allotment among them.

### Verse 58

**“The sons of the temple servants,” etc.** **(Bede, in the same place.)** The temple servants, who are listed after the priests, Levites, singers, and gatekeepers, were at that time those who are now called subdeacons in the Church. They obeyed the duties of the Levites and received the offerings from the people in the temple.

**“All the temple servants.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Here, even according to the literal sense, the grace of God is shown, by which gentiles were also received into salvation in the Old Testament. After the catalogue had been set out of those who were known truly to belong to the people of God, others were added whose origin—whether from Israel or from proselytes—was unknown. Their number is presented together among the children of Israel. Although, because of the long separation of their fathers from the temple or people of God, they were unable to show how they belonged to him, nevertheless, since they had gone up from captivity when general permission was granted, they were received as companions. For the rest of the Israelites rejoiced to have them as brothers and acquaintances through love of the common faith and religion, even though they knew them less well according to the origin of their flesh.

Allegorically, among penitents who, liberated from captivity to vices, go up to build the house of the Lord either in themselves or in others, there are some who are bound by many and grievous sins and appear so alienated from God by every act of piety and chastity that it seems no trace whatever remains in them of the goodness and religion they had received from their teachers. They cannot show whether they were born from Israel—that is, from the holy Church—for by sinning they have become as though they had never belonged to the Holy Spirit. Yet through repentance they are corrected and converted, so that their number may be written in heaven among the true Israelites, in whom there is no deceit.

### Verse 61

**“And from the sons of the priests.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** The children of the transmigration acted with the same caution toward the priests as toward the people. They took care that it should be clearly evident who truly belonged to the people of Israel or to the priestly stock, and who had been born either from a suspected line or certainly from proselytes—that is, from immigrants. They therefore removed the suspected priests from the service of the altar until their origin became more certain; nevertheless, they kept them in peaceful fellowship with the community of the transmigrants.

Mystically, the sons of the priests who go up from Babylonian captivity seek the record of their genealogy; when they do not find it, they are expelled from the priesthood. This occurs when ministers of the altar fall into such great crimes or abominable doctrines that, even if through repentance they return to the salvation of their souls, [Col. 0695A] they are nevertheless not worthy to be restored to the sacred rank. Although they may await eternal life among the faithful, they do not find among the perfect priests the record of their rank, which they are unable to reclaim.

**“The whole assembly as one man,” etc.** **(Bede, in the same place.)** These signify those who strive to overcome vices through progress in a more corrected life and to ascend to the summit of the virtues, yet are not still sufficient by themselves to provide a way of orderly life, but are restrained and directed by the diligence of those who preceded them in Christ.

**“And among them.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** Mystically, in the temple or people of God there are singers, etc., up to the point where, as though by the sweetness of their voice, they assist those who build the temple.

### Verse 66

**“Their mules.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** A mule is born from a male donkey and a mare, and a hinny from a stallion and a female donkey. Among the people who had gone up from captivity, the animals by which they were assisted are also described. Their number is specified as it is for human beings, because there are many in the Church who are slower in understanding or even carnal, yet obediently obey spiritual teachers, incline the back of their minds to bear the burdens of fraternal need, and, rescued with the other elect from the confusion of diabolical captivity, press on toward the walls of the heavenly city. Their number, too, is preserved whole in God’s memory. Hence: “Your eyes saw my unformed substance” *(Psalm 138)*. And elsewhere: “You will save humans and beasts, O Lord” *(the same, Psalm 35)*.

### Verse 68

**“They freely offered for the house of God,” etc.** **(Idem, in the same place.)** It is a sign of great devotion, etc., up to the point where they observe that they do not use even lawful things.

### Verse 69

**“According to their strength.”** This is the measure of perfection: for each person to labor for the Lord according to his ability, and to strengthen the condition of the Church first in himself and then in his neighbors. Those who conduct themselves in this way are rightly called leaders of the fathers, because by the height of their life and teaching they lead those who in the Church are called fathers through their diligent concern.

**“Gold coins.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** Gold and silver and priestly garments, etc., up to the point where the more seriously they remember having erred, the more ardently they devote themselves to good works.

### Verse 70

**“So the priests and Levites dwelt.”**** A Levite receives his city from the Chaldeans who held him captive when a deacon, by the Lord’s gift, regains the virtue of perfection that he had lost after being deceived by the devil. One born in Babylon enters the city when he comes to Judea, when someone regenerated in Christ and well instructed in the Church regularly preserves the diaconate once received. Just as the former is liberated by Christ’s grace from Chaldean servitude, so the latter, through the performance of good works in which the predecessors of that rank lived, ascend as though to the walls of their own virtue or city.

**“And all Israel.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** By “all Israel” he does not mean only the ten tribes, which were once called Israel in distinction from the two that were called Judah, etc., [Col. 0696A] up to the point where the Jews promise themselves that, when their Christ reigns, they will return to Judea with the other people of their race and reign throughout the whole world.

Allegorically, the priests, Levites, singers, gatekeepers, temple servants, and all Israel dwell in their cities when the ministers of the altar, teachers, and Christian people faithfully serve God in their respective ranks—whether those who had once stained or lost that rank through vices and have been corrected through repentance, or those who, recently coming from the kingdom of the devil to the Church, have acquired a good rank for themselves.

The Levites and children of Israel entered their own cities—not only those who had been taken captive and lost them, but also those born from captives who learned through paternal succession that they belonged to them. [Col. 0696B] But all those who were so taken captive that they never returned and left their estates for others to possess signify those who, by sinning, depart from the Church in such a way that they never come to their senses and leave to others the rewards promised to them. Hence: “Remember, therefore, from where you have fallen, repent, and do the first works; otherwise I am coming to you and will move your lampstand,” etc. *(Revelation 2).* And elsewhere: “Hold fast what you have, so that no one may take your crown” *(the same, chapter 3).*

# Chapter III

**“And the seventh month had already come.”** **(Bede on Ezra, volume II.)** For us this is October, more solemn than the other months in legal observance; in it the dedication of the temple was also celebrated. Accordingly, once they had first entered their cities and provided dwellings for themselves, they soon gathered in Jerusalem, built the altar, and did so at the time when the temple, together with the altar and all its vessels, had once been consecrated, and when they used to come annually for the day of its dedication.

Mystically, the seventh month signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. In this month, after captivity, we gather from our cities in Jerusalem when, after beginning good works, we are illumined by a greater grace of that same Spirit, once the filth of vices has been removed, and are kindled with love of heavenly peace, which exists in true unity. Jerusalem is interpreted as “vision of peace.”

### Verse 2

**“And Jeshua arose.”** From the priestly tribe, which signifies Christ the true priest, who washed us from sins in his own blood and now stands before the face of God for us.

**“And his brother priests.”** Of whom it is said: “Go and announce to my brothers” *(Matthew 28).* These are those in the Church who are higher and adhere more familiarly to Christ; they build up the Church. The following is also said to the whole Church: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood” *(1 Peter 2).* For they are chosen members of the high priest, offering their bodies as a living sacrifice.

**“And they built.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** With great foresight they first built the altar, etc., up to the point where they did not have Christ as an advocate with the Father.

### Verse 3

**“Its foundations.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Namely, the hearts of the elect, prepared to receive the sacraments of faith by the commands of teachers, as by the tools of craftsmen, etc., up to the point where the faithful humbly submit their hearts and bodies to put into practice through works what they believe.

**“And they offered.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** Morning and evening we offer a holocaust to the Lord upon his altar, etc., up to the words: “Let my prayer be directed like incense in your sight, the lifting up of my hands an evening sacrifice” *(Psalm 140).*

### Verse 4

**“And they celebrated.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Those who had gone up from Babylon to Jerusalem, etc., up to the words: “Here we have no lasting city, but we seek the one that is to come” *(Hebrews 13).*

**“The feast of Tabernacles.”** In Greek this is called *skēnopēgia*—that is, “the fixing up of tents.” It begins on the fifteenth day of the seventh month and lasts seven days. During these days the Lord commanded the people to live in tents and, searching the law daily, to offer holocausts to the Lord. For formerly they dwelt in tents in the wilderness while Moses preached the law and God frequently appeared to them, and they long awaited the promised rest, so that the grace of so great a benefit might never fall into oblivion.

**“In due order.”** Whatever is done disorderly loses the merit of perfection, because “the king loves judgment.” Whatever we certainly do in honor of the supreme King must necessarily be distinguished by the discernment of judgment, as to when and how much it should be done.

[Col. 0697C]

### Verse 5

**“At the new moons and at all [solemnities],” etc.**** That is, at the beginnings of the months, at the rising of the moon, from which the Hebrews always began their months, having no months except lunar ones. Hence, instead of “calends,” the Greeks more properly call them *neomeniai*—that is, “new moons.”

Now, if the months, because they are completed by thirty days, signify the fullness of works of light, when in faith in the Holy Trinity we fulfill the precepts of the Decalogue, what do the beginnings of the months signify—when the moon, so that it may shine again, is said recently to be kindled by the sun—unless the beginnings of good action, which, through the gift of the Creator’s grace, we perceive as though through the presence of the sun of righteousness?

Because of this sign of divine illumination, without which we can neither begin nor complete anything good, God commanded all the calends—that is, the beginnings of the months—to be celebrated. Hence: “Blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, on the notable day of your solemnity” *(Psalm 80).* It is rightly said that, after the feast of Tabernacles had been completed, the children of the transmigration offered the continual holocaust, etc., because once the soul has perfectly renounced this world, it ought to devote its entire self to obedience to the divine will.

### Verse 6

**“From the first day.”**** From the beginning, namely, of divine inspiration, by which the human conscience is changed and, after neglecting pleasures, burns only for the things that belong to the Lord. So it was with the apostles, who, inflamed by the Holy Spirit and made, as it were, a holocaust, proclaimed the mighty works of God in every language.

For this reason the seventh month is called the new year among the Hebrews: because through the Holy Spirit the faithful are granted the ability to fulfill the new commandment of charity and to offer a new song in the building of the house of God.

It should be noted that in the seventh month the people gathered in Jerusalem, and that, after everyone had assembled, Jeshua and Zerubbabel with their brothers are said to have built the altar and offered a holocaust from the first day of the seventh month. From this it is gathered that this altar was very quickly assembled from unhewn stones, not fashioned from wood and covered with bronze plates as formerly. For it could not otherwise have been begun and completed in one day, and prepared for offering the holocaust, even with a great crowd of builders at hand. In the Book of Maccabees it is said to have been made of stones: “And they took whole stones according to the law and built a new altar according to the pattern of the former” *(1 Maccabees 4).*

It should be noted that the beginning of the fifth age, like the four preceding ages, is consecrated by holocausts offered to the Lord. In the first age, Abel, the first martyr and the first of all the elect, offered a holocaust to God from the firstborn of the sheep; and he dedicated the entrance of the newborn world first with animal sacrifices and finally with his own blood.

Noah consecrated the beginning of the second age by offering to God holocausts from those animals that had been in the ark. Melchizedek and Abraham consecrated the third age: the former with bread and wine, the latter by offering his own son. David consecrated the fourth age to the Lord by building an altar on the threshing floor of Ornan the Jebusite and offering holocausts to God, by which he might appease the one whom he had offended by numbering the people. There Abraham is said to have offered his son, and after Solomon built the temple, the altar of holocausts is known to have been placed there.

Now Jeshua and Zerubbabel, having built an altar in the same place and offered holocausts to God, offered at the beginning of the fifth age, once the yoke of captivity had been shaken off; afterward, through a continual holocaust, they appeased the Lord on their behalf. All these things went before as a figure of the one who, in the sixth age, redeemed the whole world by the sacrifice of his flesh.

### Verse 7

**“And they gave.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** Those who had been freed from captivity and had come to Jerusalem, etc., up to the point where the foundation of the temple signifies those who, recently converted, prepare a place for the Lord in themselves. Hence: “Your members are the temple of the Holy Spirit,” etc. *(1 Corinthians 6).*

**“To the stonecutters.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Stonecutters in the construction of the house of God are those who instruct the hearts of their neighbors by teaching or rebuking, etc., up to the point of the tabernacle composed of curtains and boards.

**“To the masons.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Masons are preachers who, while binding together by the bond of charity those whom they instruct in good works, join them like squared and polished stones by pouring in mortar, lest they loosen the order of the structure. They say: “Above all, maintain constant mutual charity among yourselves,” etc. *(1 Peter 4).* Hence Paul: “Above all, have charity, which is the bond of perfection” *(Colossians 3).*

**“To the Sidonians and Tyrians.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The Sidonians and Tyrians likewise represent preachers who cast down from their former way of life people once elevated and radiant in worldly glory by the sure word of God, so that, after being salutarily laid low and, as it were, baked free from the corrupt moisture of inborn understanding, they may correct them from every stronghold of vices and demand them for the adornment or defense of the Church. Hence, in the psalm entitled “At the completion of the tabernacle”: “The voice of the Lord breaking the cedars” *(Psalm 2).*

**“To the Sidonians and Tyrians.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** The leaders of the fathers give, etc., up to the point where, although they are confident, they have affliction in the world because the Lord has conquered the world.

**“To bring timber.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** They bring cut timber down to the sea, etc., up to the point where, through reconciliation with the priests, we are joined to the Church.

**“Joppa.”** From there, clearly, the timber was to be brought overland for the work of the temple, as was done in the construction of the first temple. Solomon, however, through royal power, easily obtained from King Hiram whatever he wanted; these men, returning from captivity and lacking royal power, purchased everything.

**“And in the year.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** Although it is said above that they came to Jerusalem in the seventh month, etc., up to the point where he announces either the resurrection of bodies, which we hope for as those who do good works.

### Verse 8

**“In Jerusalem.”**** That is, at the site of the temple, where they desired to build the temple. For the Jews are mistaken when they say that the walls of the temple were never overturned by the Chaldeans, but only its roof, since it is clear that Ezra, the son of the transmigration, built the temple from its foundations.

[Col. 0699C]

**“And everyone who.”**** This shows the great devotion of the entire people. They rejoiced that they had returned from captivity; and to the extent that they detested the crimes of the proud city, they desired to see the beauty of Jerusalem; to the extent that they abhorred the shrines, they strove to restore the temple of God.

Thus not only bishops and presbyters ought to build the people of the faithful—that is, the house of God—but the people too, called from captivity to vices toward the vision of true peace, ought to choose the ministry of the word from those who know how to teach. These ministers of the word, that is, Levites, are appointed from twenty years of age and above, because those should be appointed and preferred to preach who not only display the Decalogue to their hearers by doing it, but also preserve purity and integrity of heart undefiled in the sight of God.

[Col. 0699D]

**“From twenty years of age.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** There is no doubt that the state of the Church is there prefigured by the Spirit, etc., up to the point where Zerubbabel was born from the royal tribe.

### Verse 9

**“And Jeshua stood.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Not the son of Josedec, etc., up to the point where they also praise through the hand of King David when they carefully attend to and imitate, as far as they can, the works of Christ that he performed in the flesh.

### Verse 10

**“The priests stood in their vestments.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The devotion of all the persons is displayed when, after the temple has been founded, all according to their rank praise the Lord’s mercy. The priests, indeed, clothed in holy garments as they had been accustomed to do while the temple still stood, sounding the trumpets and kindling the people’s heart toward the sweetness of heavenly praise; the Levites singing hymns to the Lord on well-sounding cymbals; and the people showing the affection of their hearts by praising God with a common shout.

### Verse 11

**“And they sang together in hymns.”** With the instruments that he himself made, or with the psalms that he instituted; or because, as the Books of Chronicles testify, David appointed Asaph and his brothers as leaders in giving thanks to the Lord when the ark was placed. It is said again of them: “His sons were under his direction, prophesying beside the king” *(1 Chronicles 15–16).* Accordingly, when the sons of Asaph praised and gave thanks to the Lord through the hand of David, they are to be understood to have done so according to his arrangement.

### Verse 12

**“They wept.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** They saw how far the poverty of that time stood from the magnificent power of Solomon, by which the former temple had first been founded, etc., up to the point where, in the second age, Christ and the apostles announce the grace of the New Testament and entrance into the heavenly kingdom.

**(Idem, in the same place.)** They wept during the building of the spiritual temple, etc., up to the point where, even amid the growth of the devout, the temptations of the wicked are not absent—those who strive to harm the saints either by deceptively displaying what is good or by openly inflicting evil.

# Chapter IV

### Verse 1

**“The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard,” etc.** **(Bede on Ezra.)** By the enemies of Judah and Benjamin he means the Samaritans, etc., up to the point where they are to receive blessing and the eternal kingdom at the right hand of the Judge. They therefore say:

### Verse 2

**“Let us build with you.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** When heretics seek to have authority granted them to preach among Catholics, etc., up to the point where he attacked him most fiercely in the person of an open enemy.

**“It is not for us.”**** It does not belong to heretics to build the Church from which they are alienated, but only to those who, adhering to Christ the true king and priest, have deserved to be called leaders of the fathers, because of the devoted care they have for those who desire to see Christ.

### Verse 3

**“But it came to pass.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Whenever heretics hindered the doctrine of the true confession by teaching perversely or even by raging, not only in cities but also in provinces, etc., up to the point where wise architects would have the means to rebuild that same house after its captivity.

### Verse 4

**“The people of Judah.”**** By the people of Judah—that is, of one who trusts and glorifies—he means the one who seeks to turn toward building for the Lord, that is, toward doing his will and seeking his glory, the minds and mouths of all whom he can.

### Verse 5

**“They hired.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The distinction of the words is to be noted, etc., up to the point where they acquire the support of earthly rulers against the Church—a fact whose harm to the faith became clearer than daylight during the time of the Arian perfidy.

**“In the reign of Ahasuerus.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** He identifies this man with Artaxerxes, etc., up to the point where he permitted him to handle and decide these matters as though he possessed lesser power.

[Col. 0701A]

**(Bede, in the same place.)** Artaxerxes, whom they persuade, and who, once persuaded, commanded that Jerusalem should not be built, etc., up to the point where, after again overcoming the enemies who held the neighboring regions, they took possession of them.

### Verse 14

**“Injuries.”**** Those who strive to attack the kingdom of the devil cannot endure them. They fear that wars will be stirred up in the Church, lest their heresies and deceptions be fought together with the doctrine of the gentiles, under the leadership of the one who said: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” *(Matthew 16).* And again: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth” *(Luke 12)*, etc.—the sword, namely, of the word of God, by which he may overthrow adversaries; and the fire of charity, by which, kindling the hearts of his own, he may burn all the weapons and shields of the opposing sect.

**“Because the city.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** The enemies themselves again confess that the city belongs to the Lord, etc., up to the point where, by living well and giving thanks, they return to God the beginning and perfection of the honors they had received from him.

### Verse 16

**“Beyond the river.”**** The Euphrates, namely, within which Syria lies. It signifies baptism, because it is one of the four rivers of paradise that water the whole world, just as the four evangelists, inspired by one fountain of life—that is, Christ—with harmonious voice preach the bath of salvation to all nations.

Or it signifies this because *Euphrates* is interpreted as “fruitful,” which suits the sacrament by which the world, washed and sanctified, produces for God the fruit of souls—thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold.

### Verse 17

**“The king sent a message to Rehum Beelteem.”** **(Bede, in the passage cited above.)** The king of the Persians asks, etc., up to the point where they persecute the Church and prevent it from being built.

[Col. 0701C]

**“The inhabitants of Samaria.”**** The enemies of Jerusalem dwell in Samaria, which is interpreted as “watch.” This does not mean that they keep the precepts of faith and truth, since they stubbornly resist the vision of true peace, but that they boast that the guardianship of the virtues remains with them while they fight against the walls of peace through heresy.

### Verse 23

**“And so the copy.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** The order of the history is clear, etc., up to the point where the king had merely prohibited the construction of the city.

# Chapter V

**“They prophesied.”** **(Bede, Book II on Ezra, volume II.)** It is written more fully in their books, etc., up to the point where Zerubbabel and Jeshua, and the people who were with them, are also proved to have possessed no less faith, since they obeyed the prophets who commanded rather than the authority of the one who prohibited.

### Verse 2

**“Zerubbabel.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Born in Babylon, etc., up to the point where anyone who, while invoking God, seeks nothing other than God himself may also call him Salathiel.

**“And Jeshua.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Jeshua or Jesus is interpreted as “Savior”; Josedec, “the Lord is righteous.” This man, like the son of Nun, signifies Christ. Both led the people into the promised land: the former from a long sojourn in the wilderness, the latter from a still longer service of captivity.

Thus the true Jesus, rescuing his elect from every evil, leads them into the promised joys of the heavenly kingdom. He is the son of Josedec—that is, of the righteous Lord—of whom it is said: “The righteous Lord will cut off the necks of sinners,” etc. *(Psalm 12).*

### Verse 3

**“In it.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The literal wording of the text is clear: strengthened by the words of the prophets, the leaders of the Jews could not be hindered from the holy work by the attacks of their enemies. While the prophets were still silent, they had ceased through fear of the enemies; so it now happens in the Church when those who, delayed by the snares of wicked spirits or human beings, had once been slower to undertake a good work are suddenly corrected by the words of teachers or of the divine Scriptures and cannot be overcome by any machinery of temptation or recalled from their intended purpose.

### Verse 4

**“To this we replied.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The person who wrote this appears to have been present, although Ezra is said to have written it, and is found to have come to Jerusalem much later, during the reign of Artaxerxes. Either, then, he was truly there at that time and returned to Babylonia after the temple was built in order to bring more of the children of Israel back to Jerusalem, or he joins himself to the builders, as though what is being done among the brothers were his own, or as though what they themselves do were his own, just as the Apostle says: “We who are alive, who remain until the coming of the Lord, shall not precede,” etc. *(1 Thessalonians 4).*

### Verse 6

**“A copy of the letter.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** This letter is very different from that one, etc., up to the point where, at last recognizing that this originated from the God of heaven and earth, who alone truly is God, they share in his sacrifices and rejoice to assist the building.

[Col. 0702C]

### Verse 8

**“Of unhewn stone.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Namely, a new stone, which they found unhewn but adapted to the building by shaping it, etc., up to the point whereas the other, enslaved to idolatry, had not cast off the deformity of a rustic and earthly mind through any skill of spiritual architects or practice of piety.

**“And timber is placed in the walls, and the work,” etc.** **(Idem, in the same place.)** The timber placed for the adornment or defense of the temple signifies the same life of the saints in the adornment of the Church as do the stones. Of these it is said: “All the trees of the forest will rejoice,” etc.

# Chapter VI

### Verse 1

**“Then Darius.”** **(Bede on Ezra, Book II, volume II.)** Josephus gives the name of the place where these letters of Cyrus were found in this form: “And the document was found at Ecbatana, a city built in the region of Media.” Another translation reads: “At Ecbatana, in the most secure building of the region of the Medes.” Hence it appears that the name *Medena* signifies nothing other than Media.

### Verse 3

**“So that they may lay the foundations.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** We need not explain this, etc., up to the point where it may refer to the portico of the house of the Lord that stood before the temple. Concerning this, when Solomon’s palace was being built, Scripture records: “He made a court,” etc. *(1 Kings 7).*

### Verse 5

**“Let them be returned.”** **(Idem, in the same place.)** Darius confirms the completed letters by his authority, restraining all the adversaries of the Jews and ordering the temple to be built in its place, etc.

[Col. 0703A]

### Verse 6

**“Now therefore.”**** Artaxerxes signifies those who oppose the building of the holy Church by stirring up persecutions and forbid the house of God and the city to be built. Among these the Church flourished especially through the victory of the martyrs.

Darius, however, signifies the pious devotion of those kings who, after recognizing the piety of the Christian faith, took care not to resist it but to assist it by their decrees. Many of them, after prohibiting the persecutions of their predecessors, wished to consecrate themselves, together with the peoples subject to them, through the sacraments of that same faith. To them Darius’ addition applies well: “But my command is that,” etc. For who could explain how much the Church has been assisted and enriched by the generosity of kings?

### Verse 8

**“From the royal treasury.”** **(Bede, in the same place.)** Funds are assigned from the king’s treasury for the work of God, etc., up to the point where he demonstrated that he had been taught by the elders of the Jews—that is, those who confess and praise God—what Cyril, John, and the other saints had said.

Calves and lambs. (ID., ibid.) These animals, which are clean, etc., up to the point that whatever he has learned from the men of the Church to be salutary, he expends entirely in divine worship.

**VERSE 9.**—According to the rite. For the vows of those offering will then be accepted only when they are offered according to the rite of catholic peace; but those mixed with pagan superstition or heresy are not good.

**VERSE 10.**—And let them pray. In accordance with the Apostle’s words: “Therefore I urge first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings, and for all who are in high positions” (1 Tim. 2).

**VERSE 11.**—Therefore from me. He wished to punish with the gravest penalty anyone who altered the decree—namely, with the loss of everything he possessed and of his own life, which, even fastened to wood, he would lose through prolonged torment.

Mystically, however, our works are compared with wood: good works with fruitful trees, but evil works with willows and things deserving the fire. The wood is removed from the house of the one who opposes the Lord’s burnt offerings, and it is set up, and he himself is impaled upon it, when the works of those who resist the peace of the Church are openly shown to everyone to be useless and perverse; and they themselves are proved to have acquired in them not the joy of life but the snare of death. The house of such people is also confiscated—that is, it is proscribed in the public register—when their bodies, with which they remained in this life, are handed over at the resurrection to savage exactors, unclean spirits, to be punished with everlasting torment.

**VERSE 12.**—But God. He desires his decree to be confirmed by divine power, and he himself, as a man endowed with a temporal kingdom, does everything he can by public law for the peace of God’s house. The same thing now takes place in the Church when earthly powers, converted to the faith, issue public edicts for the welfare of the Church and, with the Lord’s help and his defeat of its enemies, begin to enjoy lasting peace.

**VERSE 14.**—According to the prophecy. For they had foretold that, if they persisted in building the temple, then, with the Lord’s gift, they would soon complete the work itself and abound in every good thing.

(BEDA, as above.) No one should be disturbed by what Haggai says—that the foundations of the temple were laid under King Darius, etc., up to the point that at times they were separately designated by the names treasuries, chambers, porticoes, or courts; hence: “You who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God” (Ps. 133).

And under Artaxerxes. It is asked how the house is said to have been built at Artaxerxes’ command, when it is immediately added that it was completed and dedicated while Darius was still reigning—unless perhaps we should believe that Artaxerxes too, having sent gold and silver, gave orders that anything still incomplete in the construction or adornment of the temple or its vessels should be finished. For when Ezra hastened there, it is written that the same king sent very large quantities of gold, silver, and vessels to the temple with his princes or counselors.

**VERSE 15.**—The month Adar. (BEDA, ibid.) On its third day the house was completed, up to the point that all the more prominent parts were finished.

(ID., ibid.) The temple, although it signifies the chosen soul because the Spirit of Christ dwells within it, etc., up to the point that from the upper level also we enter the third, when we crown the blessedness of souls with the reception of immortal bodies.

**VERSE 16.**—And the children of the captivity celebrated. The children of the transmigration rightly rejoice, etc., up to the point that all the orders of the Church rejoice when sinners have been reconciled through repentance.

**[Col. 0704C] VERSE 17.**—And they offered. They offer sacrifices at the dedication when they give thanks to God for the conversion of those who have gone astray, and when many, seeing their devotion, gird themselves for greater works of virtue, so that they may not be less diligent in working than those who were more innocent through having sinned less. Many also who preceded them in the faith imitate the more fervent zeal of beginners.

Male goats.
