Male goats are offered in this life for sin when the elect beseech God to free them from sins; they are offered in the future when those who have been freed give thanks, and therefore “will sing of the mercies of the Lord forever” (Ps. 88), because they will always remember that they were wretched and were freed by his gift.

For sin. They also offer for the sin of all Israel, because those who are with us ought to favor good in this way: by imitating their good works, making them our own, so that we may also entreat the Lord for the state of the whole Church. Hence, in the Lord’s Prayer no one asks anything specifically for himself, but for all who have the same Father in heaven. Likewise, once the temple has been built, dedication follows, when, at the end of the age, the full number of the elect reaches the grace of heavenly rewards, in which sacrifices are offered. Concerning these the same house—that is, the Church—rebuilt after the captivity of mortal misery through the glory of immortality, says: “You have broken my bonds, Lord; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise” (Ps. 115). And because offerings are made not only for the gifts of virtues but also for cleansing from the worldly filth of vices, male goats are rightly offered after calves, rams, and lambs, for the sin of all Israel: for the grace that bestows the benefits of virtues also removes crimes. Nor does Pelagius have a place in the house of God, since he persuaded himself and his followers that by freedom of the will they could either be freed from evils or established in good works.

**VERSE 18.**—And they appointed. Order required that, once the house of God had been built, priests and Levites who would minister in it should immediately be appointed. This should be observed by those who magnificently build monasteries: they should establish teachers in them who exhort the people to the works of God, rather than serve their own pleasures there.

Priests. (BEDA, as above.) What he says—“the priests according to their orders,” etc., up to the point that we take care to reach the Lord’s rewards together with them.

**[Col. 0705B] VERSE 19.**—And the children celebrated. The celebration of Passover is specifically mentioned after the house of the Lord had been built and dedicated, although no one could doubt that religious people would celebrate Passover at its proper time. This was done to signify mystically that the highest perfection consists in meditating continually, with the whole intention of the mind, on entering the other life after all the allurements of the world have been left behind. Passover is interpreted as “transit,” because through the sacrifice of the lamb the children of Israel passed from Egyptian slavery to freedom; or the lamb itself—that is, Christ—sacrificed for us, passed from this world to the Father. We imitate this when we pass from the lowest pleasures to the pursuit of heavenly things, and we truly complete the passage when, released from the prison of the flesh, we enter the heavenly kingdom.

**[Col. 0705C]** (BEDA, ibid.) Why Passover is discussed after the house had been built, etc., up to the point that the longer it possessed a land empty of the virtue of the heart.

**VERSE 22.**—And they celebrated the solemnity. (ID., ibid.) In this passage the celebration of Passover can typologically be referred to the time of our resurrection, etc., up to the point where the Prophet commends to us its sevenfold grace.

Seven days. For throughout the entire period of the world life must be lived in sincerity and truth, indeed in all the sacrifices and burnt offerings of good works, because Christ tasted death temporarily at the time of Passover but conquered it by the eternal power of the resurrection.

With joy. For this is the greatest joy of the righteous, both now and in the future: that the work of righteousness, or of the Church, has been perfected, with the Gentiles also converted—those who once resisted—and that they now help to maintain its condition and confirm the peace of the Christian religion throughout the world.

# CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.**—After these things. (Beda, on Ezra, book II.) Up to this point the return of the people from Babylon to Jerusalem, etc., up to the point that they might have from which, once admonished, they could learn inwardly to be restored; and what follows is:

After these things. (BEDA, ibid.) Josephus thinks that this Artaxerxes, under whom Ezra ascended from Babylonia to Jerusalem, was Xerxes, the son of Darius, who reigned after him. But the books of chronicles make him the successor of that same Xerxes. Darius, under whom the temple was built, reigned thirty-six years; after him Xerxes reigned twenty years; after him Archabanus reigned seven months, which the chroniclers counted as a year; after him Artaxerxes reigned forty years.

(ID., ibid.) Ezra is called a swift scribe in the law of Moses, etc., up to the point that the earlier letters remained among the Samaritans, with which they used to write those five books of Moses—the only books of sacred Scripture that they accepted.

**VERSE 7.**—And they went up. (ID., ibid.) It should be noted that at the beginning of this book it is written that, by Cyrus’s permission, Zerubbabel and Jeshua went up from Babylon, etc., up to the point that I give to those who reach the heavenly homeland everlasting life.

**VERSE 9.**—For on the first day. (ID., ibid.) He began to go up from Babylon on the first day of the month, etc., up to the point that, as after four months of shining action during which we proceed on the way, we spend the fifth month of everlasting recompense in the light of the heavenly homeland.

(ID., ibid.) Ezra began to go up from Babylon in the first month, etc., up to the point that we may come to the promises above.

According to the hand of God. That is, strengthened by divine grace and protection, by which he would successfully complete what he had begun. So also Christ, because God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself, had the hand of God upon his humanity: by it he was exalted in his passion, ascended to the walls of the heavenly city, and opened the way for his faithful.

**VERSE 10.**—For Ezra had prepared. It is a great virtue in a person to prepare his heart for obedience to the divine will and to be able to say: “My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready” (Ps. 56).

(BEDA, ibid.) Christ also prepared his heart to investigate the law of the Lord, because in divine foreknowledge he saw that he would assume such a man—one who would be not only without sin but also full of grace and truth—who, with no law of sin resisting him, would keep the law of God without any contradiction of mind or flesh. Hence: “In the beginning of the book it is written of me,” etc. (Ps. 39). Likewise, the Lord investigated the law of God because, having rejected the traditions of the Pharisees, he taught the mystical understanding of sacred Scripture and showed that the decrees of the Gospel which he brought were more perfect and more acceptable to God than those which he had previously given through Moses. Hence: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: You shall love your friend, and you hate your enemy. But I say to you: Love your enemies,” etc.

**VERSE 12.**—Artaxerxes the king. Artaxerxes, who revered the temple and the priests of the Lord with devoted mind and served him, signifies Christian rulers, just as Darius does. Nor is it surprising that the successors of Cyrus—who had the temple and city built, who loved and assisted his servants and his law—should symbolize Christian kings, since the Lord himself said through the prophet that Cyrus signified his Son and honored him by his name, saying: “Thus says the Lord to my anointed, to Cyrus” (Isa. 45).

**VERSE 13.**—A decree from me. Because the report of divine power had reached the king, through which he had renewed the law that had been burned by the Chaldeans, using the same words as before, although in a different script.

**VERSE 14.**—To whomever. He grants everyone permission to go; he compels no one to go. Christian rulers, compelling no one—for the will of faith must not be uncertain—permit all who wish to worship Christ in their kingdom.

And of the seven counselors. In the book of Esther it is read that it was customary for the kings of Persia to use seven counselors in all matters that they undertook or judged. The faithful use seven counselors when in everything they do they follow the commands of divine Scripture. Concerning this it is said: “The words of the Lord are pure words, silver tested by fire, proved on the earth, purified sevenfold” (Ps. 11)—that is, perfected by the holy illumination of the sevenfold Spirit.

You have been sent. Ezra is sent from the presence of the king and his seven counselors to visit India and Jerusalem. Likewise, rulers of the world who have been converted to the faith and strengthened by the persuasion of the Scriptures desire Christ to come, through daily assistance—which the name Ezra signifies—to save the Church and gather it from the nations, saying: “Lord God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven,” etc. (Ps. 79).

Which is in the hand. It is remarkable that a word usually used by the prophets is found in Artaxerxes’ letter, when he says that the law of God is in the hand of his servant. For it is written: “The word of the Lord came by the hand of Haggai the prophet.” And: “The Lord did what he spoke by the hand of his servant Elijah.” And: “The Lord testified in Israel and Judah by the hands of all the prophets”—because the prophets proclaimed the things of God no less by doing than by speaking.

**[Col. 0707C]** Christ had the law in his hand because once he established it through Moses as he willed, and now, changing that same law through himself, he has transferred it to more perfect things.

**VERSE 15.**—And that you may bring. The faith and wisdom of the king and his counselors should be noted: they understood that their gifts ought to be offered through the one who had the law of God in his hand—that is, who fulfilled it in his works.

Whose dwelling is in Jerusalem. (BEDA, as above.) Faithfully and learnedly he says that he has his tabernacle in Jerusalem, etc., up to the point where John says of him: “He is the propitiation for our sins” (1 John 2).

**VERSE 16.**—And all the silver. By means of this money the faithful desire their good works to shine in the Church, so that through it they may have the Father together with the saints and others may advance through their examples. For sacrifices, offerings, and victims are acquired, as it were, from our silver and gold for offering to the Lord when, seeing the brightness of our works, our neighbors are converted to the practice of piety; through living well they too are consecrated to the Lord. There are also certain exceptionally illustrious virtues of the saints which cannot be displayed to everyone as examples of conduct but can only be recounted to glorify God’s grace: for example, that Daniel and Jeremiah prophesied while still boys; that John did so while not yet born; that Cornelius and his household received the Holy Spirit before being baptized; and countless miracles, like silver in the house of the Lord. Nor can offerings placed upon the altar be purchased only from this silver or gold, because when we hear such things, we ought indeed to marvel at them as divine, but we cannot imitate them as though they were within our capacity.

**VERSE 19.**—And the vessels also. The true Ezra delivered the vessels of mercy entrusted to him by human beings in the sight of the Father into the heavenly Jerusalem. Concerning these it is said: “How can anyone enter the house of the strong man and plunder his vessels, unless he first binds the strong man?” (Mark 3). For the king of Babylon—that is, the devil—was strong; but once bound and fettered by the Lord, he lost the vessels he unjustly possessed, namely, the hearts of the elect. Nor could he resist the one who took them away and restored them to the heavenly city, to which they properly belonged.

**VERSE 21.**—And from me. Christian rulers command their subjects to give without delay whatever Christ our high priest requests. Let them hold nothing back at all: let them give gold in confession of the true faith, grain in the display of good works, wine in the fervor of love, and oil in the cheerfulness of mercy. All these are commanded to be given under the number one hundred to the great priest and scribe of the law of the God of heaven—that is, to Christ, who, bringing us heavenly commandments from the Father, promised heavenly rewards in the Father’s house to those who obey. For the number one hundred, which in counting on the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, signifies the joys that are on the right—that is, eternal life. A talent is delivered in three measures: the smallest, fifty pounds; the middle, sixty-two pounds; the largest, one hundred and twenty pounds. A corus is thirty measures; a bath, which is also a tenth of a corus, is three measures.

**VERSE 22.**—Salt also. (BEDA, as above.) Salt signifies wisdom, etc., up to the point that they conquer through their adversaries.

**VERSE 24.**—You also. This privilege shows that the rest of the people of Israel, on reaching their homeland, paid the king’s taxes. The king is understood to have done this by deliberate provision, so that those who were occupied with divine service might be free from his service, and so that no one might exact tribute from those who possessed nothing of their own in the land but lived from the people’s tithes. All this proves that he not only loved but also understood very well what the worship of divine service required.

**[Col. 0708D] VERSE 25.**—But you. (BEDA, ibid.) The king repeats what he had said above, etc., up to the point that kings and princes often sent letters concerning the welfare of the faithful.

**VERSE 28.**—And I was strengthened. In this way each person becomes capable of gathering others through his teaching; he is strengthened in mind by the grace of God against everything that hinders the work of the saints.

# CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—These, then, are the leaders, etc. (BEDA, on Ezra.) He carefully enumerates the leaders who went up with him from Babylon, etc., up to the point that you will be more glorious in the kingdom of God through the life of those whom you have taught.

**[Col. 0709A] VERSE 15.**—And I gathered them. (BEDA, ibid.) I do not remember having read this place-name elsewhere, etc., up to the point that he provided himself with an adequate number of ministers for the house of God, through whom, when he came to Jerusalem, he could complete what was necessary for the temple’s use.

**VERSE 17.**—And I sent them to Iddo. (ID., ibid.) According to Orosius, the Caspian Sea, etc., up to the point that, with these added, Ezra is found to have had in his army a force of nearly one thousand seven hundred men.

**VERSE 21.**—And I proclaimed a fast there. (BEDA, homily 8.) An example of fasting and prayer is given to us, etc., up to the point that he should thus pray and not doubt that what he asks will turn out favorably.

**VERSE 25.**—And I weighed out for them silver, gold, and the consecrated vessels. (ID., on Ezra, book II.) By the silver, gold, and vessels sent from Babylon to Jerusalem, etc., up to the point that it must be built by their successors to the end.

(ID., ibid.) There is a difference between these vessels which Ezra offers with the priests at Jerusalem and those which Zerubbabel and Jeshua are reported to have offered. The former were transferred from the Lord’s temple to Babylon and then transferred to Jerusalem; the latter were made in Babylonia but sent to Jerusalem out of devotion by the king or princes of the Persians, or even by the people of Israel who lived in those regions. Those vessels therefore signify those who, after receiving knowledge and the sacraments of the faith and beginning works of virtue, are deceived by the devil and carried away into confusion but are recalled to salvation by the grace of Christ. The latter signify those who, born with the sin of the first transgression, are cleansed through the bath of regeneration by the ministry of the priests and are joined to the children of the Church.

**VERSE 28.**—You are holy to the Lord. The teachers of the Church must never forget holiness, because they have been consecrated by the Lord through the Holy Spirit on the day of redemption. They must also train their hearers to receive it, so that those already offered to the Lord through the rudiments of faith may be strengthened still more by the examples and admonitions of those who preceded them in the faith and may be made worthy to enter the heavenly city.

**VERSE 29.**—Watch and guard. The priests must keep watch lest any of the souls entrusted to them—that is, any of the Lord’s vessels—perish, but that they may be brought in their full number to the structures of holy virtue.

**[Col. 0709D] Until you weigh them.** That is, by instructing and teaching those whom heavenly providence has entrusted to you, you should present them as people who are found blameless and fit for the treasury of the heavenly palace—that is, for the seats of eternal peace and light. And this should be done not by the judgment of just anyone, who may be deceived, but by that of the apostles and of those who will judge together with the Lord. These are rightly understood as the leaders of the priests and Levites and the heads of the families of Israel—that is, of men or souls who see God. Concerning them it is said: “You shall appoint them as princes over all the earth” (Ps. 44); and elsewhere: “Noble is her husband in the gates.”

We advanced. (BEDA, ibid.) Everything is full of mysteries, etc., up to the point that, aided by these things, we may more effectively transfer the souls of the faithful to the fellowship of the elect and the citadel of the life of perfection, like holy vessels to the temple of the Lord.

**VERSE 32.**—And we remained. (ID., ibid.) They remain in Jerusalem for three days, etc., up to the point that, as though after the joy of the three-day stay in Jerusalem on account of the gifts and precious vessels they offered, they are honored still more.

**VERSE 34.**—And it was recorded. (ID., ibid.) This happens when teachers carefully examine the life of those subject to them, etc., up to the point that a worthy recompense may be granted in heaven.

**VERSE 35.**—But those who had come. (ID.) Great devotion and reverence are shown when, on reaching the temple, they first of all offer burnt offerings, not only for themselves but also for all Israel—that is, for those who had already returned home and for those who were still in exile.

Mystically, however, those truly and perfectly escaped the captivity of the devil in which they were held through sin who submit themselves with fixed intention to divine service, who, wholly withdrawn from what is below, kindle themselves with the flame of heavenly desire. This is to offer burnt offerings—that is, sacrifices wholly consumed—to the Lord: to think of and do nothing but his will in all things.

They offered burnt offerings to God, etc. Not only for themselves. It is a sign of a perfect mind when someone sacrifices for all Israel—that is, for the general salvation of the faithful—and, mindful of unity and brotherhood, makes supplication to heavenly mercy.

**VERSE 36.**—And they raised up the people. (AUG.) By adorning them with various gifts which the king, his counselors, and his princes had sent, and by freeing his ministers and priests from every distress.

Mystically. The people and the temple of God represent one and the same figure of the Church. Ezra and the children of the transmigration raise it up by removing the sacred vessels from Babylon, when preachers, with the Lord’s help, gather new peoples of believers into it and make it honorable and awe-inspiring to everyone. Likewise, when they advance or raise to the reception of heavenly rewards those whom they have instructed by examples in good conduct or by words, they raise the people into the house of God, because they bring great joy both to the elect remaining in the heavenly homeland and to those still journeying on earth.

(BEDA, on Ezra, book II, tome II.) This transgression is clearly described in the prophet Malachi, etc., up to the point that they refer the matter to the prince—that is, the archbishop—by whose authority the offense may be expiated.

Mystically, however, foreign wives signify heresies and the superstitious philosophical sects which, when carelessly admitted into the Church, contaminate the holy seed of catholic truth and pure conduct with error. They also signify all the sins by which pagans are defiled, when Christians are not ashamed to imitate them. Through such foreign wives they degenerate from the seed of the word of God by which they had been generated, according to the saying: “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word,” etc. (Jas. 1). And they produce, as it were, profane offspring from the daughters of foreigners when, following the allurements of those who have gone astray, they bring their perverse deeds to everyone’s knowledge.

He has not been separated. (BEDA, ibid.) It should be noted that after Israel had been led into captivity, etc., up to the point that the leaders who ought to have corrected the others confess that they themselves were the first to go astray.

# CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 3.**—I tore my cloak. (ID., ibid.) Garments ordinarily signify works, etc., up to the point that he sat mourning, to teach that forgiveness must be obtained through the lamentation of repentance.

**VERSE 4.**—They assembled. Observe how greatly the examples of teachers help. Nothing is written about Ezra’s speaking; only that, upon hearing of the crime, he wept, and drew the multitude of the faithful to himself not by shouting but by weeping.

**[Col. 0711B]** They assembled. A great change of circumstances: through the treachery of the leaders, many who had followed luxury were brought back, while a great leader mourned and indicated what sinners ought to do. All who feared the word of God gathered to him—the word that threatens punishment for transgressors.

With his cloak torn. (BEDA, ibid.) Typologically, because he tore his garment, etc., up to the point that he mercifully deigned to take upon himself even those things that truly suited their frailty.

**VERSE 5.**—I bent my knees, etc. He prepared himself through compunction of heart and bodily devotion so that he might be made worthy to hear heavenly mercy, and he broke into the words of this prayer. He bends his knees, stretches out his hands, and pours forth prayers at the time of the evening sacrifice, knowing that what is done in a spirit of humility and with a contrite heart is more pleasing than what is offered with the flesh and blood of animals.

# CHAPTER X

**VERSE 1.**—While Ezra was thus praying, imploring God, and weeping [lacuna], the people wept. (BEDA, on Ezra, book II.) That is, those who had sinned, doing penance, or those who had remained chaste, grieving over the fall of their brothers, etc., up to the point that now even those who had sinned with their wives and children gathered together to do penance.

Of the sons of Elam. Josephus says that this man was the first of the Jerusalemites who, as befits a leader, immediately assisted Ezra’s purpose with the greatest authority, confessing that the people had sinned with him and urging repentance through the dismissal of the foreign wives and their children.

And now, if there is repentance in Israel. Since, if the people truly repent of this sin, we should first turn to the Lord, promise correction, and ask forgiveness; then, returning to ourselves, we should uproot every root and branch of sin by expelling the wives together with all their offspring. For this is truly to do penance with the whole heart, to turn inwardly to the Lord, and to cut away externally every material for sinning from its very origin.

Rise. He appropriately teaches how one should act in counsel among elders: each person should state, according to his own judgment, what he understands—or thinks he understands—to be best, while leaving the place of decision to the one who presides and being ready to obey everything that he determines should be done according to the will and law of God.

**VERSE 6.**—The sons of Eliasib. He was then the high priest. After Jeshua son of Jehozadak, his son Joiakim held the high priesthood; after him his son Eliasib held it.

He ate no bread. (BEDA, as above.) From this priests have an example, etc., up to: “For if, having escaped the defilements of the world,” etc. (2 Pet. 2).

**VERSE 9.**—It is he. (BEDA, as above.) The Hebrews call this month Casleu, the Romans December, etc., up to the point that by such skill they may either avoid or separate themselves from the adversities that rage outwardly because of sins.

And all the people sat. (ID., ibid.) That is, around the priests’ court, by which the house itself was surrounded on every side. Around it, on all four sides, were very spacious buildings of courts, in which the people could also stand when rain made it necessary and could see what was being done at the doors of the temple or around the temple. For they had inner walls built upon columns near the ground and solid outer walls.

**VERSE 10.**—And Ezra arose. (ID., ibid.) This passage corresponds, etc., up to the point that the deed might rightly be held in memory and handed down to posterity for their knowledge.

**VERSE 16.**—And they sat on the day. (ID., ibid.) Note that the number three is mystical, etc., up to the point that we too ought to imitate this every year during the forty days before Easter. As the Lord’s resurrection approaches, let us cleanse ourselves from every defilement of flesh and spirit, so that we may be able to share in the resurrection (2 Cor. 7).

And they were found. (ID., ibid.) The Hebrews apply this passage, etc., up to the point that it should be observed that Ezra does not write that Jeshua took a foreign wife, but that certain men among his sons and brothers did so, etc.

**VERSE 18.**—And his brothers. (ID., ibid.) His relatives, that is. For his actual brothers in the flesh could not have lived so long and devoted themselves to pleasure, since a hundred years and more had passed from the time when Cyrus began to reign and sent Jeshua and Zerubbabel with the transmigrated people of Judah and Benjamin to Jerusalem to build the house of the Lord.

**VERSE 19.**—And they gave, etc. (ID., ibid.) First they cast away the unlawful wives, etc., up to the point that he may make him worthy of everlasting reward in heaven.

**[Col. 0713]**

# THE BOOK OF NEHEMIAH, ALSO CALLED THE SECOND BOOK OF EZRA (G)*

# CHAPTER I

**[Col. 0713A] VERSE 1.**—The words of Nehemiah son of. (BEDA, on Ezra, book II.) Nehemiah is interpreted as “comforter of the Lord,” etc., up to the point that, as though the walls of Jerusalem had been thrown down by enemies, they restore them.

The words of Nehemiah. (ID., ibid.) Up to this point, the words of Ezra, etc., up to the point that they rejoice to be prepared for everlasting rest—not weakened by temporal flatteries but exercised by adversities.

In the month Casleu. (ID., ibid.) The month Casleu is the one we call December: among the Hebrews it is the ninth month, among us the last. Its name, interpreted as “his hope,” aptly corresponds to the prayers of the man who was intent on raising the ruins of the holy city. For the first foundation of good action is to have hope in the Lord’s help for completing what we desire. In this month the Lord was born, by whose name it was foreshadowed long beforehand that in this month the true Nehemiah, long desired, would come for the building of the Church.

I was in Susa. (ID., ibid.) Susa is the metropolis of the Persians, but so strongly fortified that it appears to be a fortress. Its name is interpreted as “riding” or “returning,” which fittingly applies to the faithful, especially those who care for Jerusalem in captivity—that is, for the salvation of those who, once snatched from the Church through the devil’s treachery, have been restored again through God’s grace by repentance. Such people are in the returning fortress—that is, in the strength of a mind recalled from what is below to desire the heavenly homeland—and in the cavalry of holy hearts, which carry God as their rider.

Those who remained. (ID., ibid.) The literal sense is clear, etc., up to the point that they ought to have kept away the unworthy, lest they perish in the fire of avarice, lust, and the other vices.

**VERSE 4.**—I wept and mourned. If a holy man rightly mourned, fasted, and prayed on hearing that buildings of wood and stone had been destroyed, sitting for a long time in sorrow, how much more must we persist in continual mourning and prayer over the destruction and ruin of souls, so that, through God’s mercy, those who lay in disgrace to religion while the enemy triumphed, filthy and squalid with the prolonged stain of vices, may be raised to their former health.

# CHAPTER II

**[Col. 0713D] VERSE 1.**—And it came to pass. (BEDA, on Ezra.) This is the first month of the year, etc., up to the point that he made known his own inner feeling. He was indeed the chief wine steward and presented the king with his cup; outwardly he performed an office of joy, but inwardly he mourned because he saw the holy city lying in ruins, etc. Hence: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat,” etc. (Ps. 126).

**VERSE 5.**—If it seems good, etc. (ID., ibid.) Just as Christ is signified by Cyrus, the first king of the Persians, etc., up to the point that I have carefully expounded the entire statement of the prophet, as far as I could, in the book of the ages.

**VERSE 10.**—And they heard. Heretics are saddened, etc., up to the point that they recognize that those who have gone astray through sin return through repentance.

**VERSE 15.**—I surveyed the wall of Jerusalem. He travels around, inspecting the various places of the ruined city, and carefully examines how each should be repaired. It is also the task of spiritual teachers to rise frequently at night and, while the others are at rest, examine the state of the Church with diligent inquiry, so that they may investigate watchfully how to correct and raise up those things that have been soiled or cast down by the battles of vices. The wall of Jerusalem lies broken, and the conduct of the faithful is stained by earthly and weak affections. The gates have been consumed by fire when those who ought to open the entrance to life for others, having abandoned the common teacher of truth, grow numb with the rest through sloth and serve temporal concerns.

**[Col. 0714B] VERSE 17.**—Because Jerusalem is desolate. (BEDA, ibid.) These things are plain and agree with the spiritual sense: teachers—in fact, all who burn with zeal for God—are in the greatest distress as long as they see Jerusalem, that is, the vision of peace which God left and entrusted to us, laid waste by the wars of dissension; and the gates of virtue, which according to Isaiah ought to have been occupied by praise, cast down and held in disgrace by the gates of hell, which have prevailed.

# CHAPTER III

**[Col. 0714C] VERSE 1.**—And Eliasib the priest arose. (BEDA, on Ezra, tome II, book III.) That is, the high priest of that time, the son of Joiakim, who, after his father Jeshua son of Jehozadak, held the high priesthood for a considerable time. And rightly the restoration of the city began with the high priest and his brothers, so that those who preceded others in rank might become examples to them in good works. And it is appropriately added to the priests who were building: “And they sanctified it as far as the tower of one hundred cubits, as far as the tower of Hananel.” Priests build with the number one hundred cubits when they kindle in all whom they instruct love and desire for eternal things. For one hundred, which in counting on the fingers passes from the left hand to the right, represents heavenly goods, just as the comparison of earthly things is like the right hand in relation to the left.

And they built. (ID., ibid.) The Old Translation has, etc., up to the point that they may be washed in it.

(ID., ibid.) It appears so according to the literal sense, etc., up to the point that they stretch themselves forward with the sole intention of inward recompense.

The Sheep Gate. This gate, namely, faces Joppa and [Col. 0715A] Diospolis, that is, Lydda, nearer to the sea than any of the roads from Jerusalem. It is now said to be called the Gate of David and to be the first of the gates on the western side of Mount Zion. This opinion seems to be supported by the Books of Chronicles, where it is written concerning Manasseh, king of Judah: “After this he built a wall outside the city of David,” etc. (II Chronicles XII).

(Bede, in the same work.) In the typological sense, just as a flock signifies the faithful of the Lord, etc., up to “that the wall of the city had been doubled in the time of Hezekiah,” the Books of Chronicles show as follows: “He also built diligently the whole wall,” etc. (II Chronicles XXIII).

In the typological sense, this Zephaniah heard the sound of shouting from the Fish Gate and wailing from the Second Gate, because he foresaw that both were to be cast down by enemies. For he saw that the faith [Col. 0715B] and works of teachers, through which the rest ought to be rescued from the waves of corruptible life and brought into the Church, were to be overthrown by the devil’s ambushes and laid low upon the earth—that is, that people were to be deprived of heavenly joys through their desire for earthly pleasure. Appropriately, he heard a sound of shouting and wailing from both gates, the first, namely, and the second, the inner and the outer, because he saw that the works externally and the hearts internally were to be subverted as the devil attacked them. But because the Lord raises up those who are cast down, Nehemiah relates that the Fish Gate was restored after its ruin: for if some preachers should fall through sin, there will not be lacking, until the end of the age, those who succeed them and, with the Lord’s help, open the gates of righteousness to the faithful by living and preaching well.

They covered it. (The same, in the same work.) This verse also concerns the other gates, etc., up to “who by praising bring us more danger than, by being seen by us, they bring salutary assistance.”

VERSE 6.—To the Old Gate. Concerning it John says: “Beloved, I do not write a new commandment to you, but an old one, which you had from the beginning” (I John II). The old commandment is the word that you heard. The Old Gate is built in Jerusalem when the word of faith and love, handed down from the beginning of the Church, is either restored among those who have gone astray or established in those who have recently come to faith.

VERSE 8.—To the wall. That is, to the firmness and defense of perfect love in the hearts of the elect, which its builders reach by building, when, advancing in works of charity, they say: “I have run the way of your commandments,” etc. (Psalm CXVIII)—that is, with that enlargement of an enlightened mind by which they love both friend in God and enemy for God’s sake.

VERSE 13.—And the Valley Gate. (Bede, as above.) The Valley of Jehoshaphat, which is also Gehennon, etc., up to “that is, the humble through the gift of heavenly refreshment.”

And the Valley Gate. (The same, in the same work.) It is fitting that after the Old Gate and the wall of the broader street the Valley Gate is built, because after the beginnings of the catholic faith, which works through love, it is necessary that humility be commended to us as a kind of guardian of the virtues, so that the greater we are, the more we may humble ourselves in all things.

And a thousand. (The same, in the same work.) They relate that the site of the city of Jerusalem, [Col. 0716A] etc., up to “so that they may cast out from themselves all the rubble of harmful action, useless speech, and even superfluous thought.”

VERSE 15.—And Shallum the son built the Fountain Gate, etc. (The same, in the same work.) Writers relate, etc., up to “comparing the steps themselves of the Church with the growth and progress of good works, which are accomplished through humility.”

Of the city of David, etc. Literally, the city of David is called Mount Zion, which lies to the south and rises above the city as its citadel; most of the city lies below the mountain, situated on the level ground of a lower hill. Hence in the Book of Kings: “David took the stronghold of Zion; this is the city of David” (II Kings V). And shortly afterward: “David lived in the stronghold and [Col. 0716B] called it the city of David” (ibid.).

VERSE 16.—Nehemiah the son of Asboth built, etc. (Bede, as above.) After the Fountain Gate and the walls of the Pool of Siloam, etc., up to “and recognize that they will ascend to the heavenly kingdom.”

Opposite the tomb of David, etc. Note that David was buried not in Bethlehem, as some think, but in Jerusalem, for a certain reason of mystery. Just as, being born in Bethlehem and anointed king there, he prefigured that Christ would be born there from his lineage and worshiped by the Magi in the person of a king, so, having died and been buried in Jerusalem, he prefigured that Christ himself would suffer and be buried in that same city.

To the pool, etc. The pool, namely, is divine Scripture, etc., up to “and if the ancient enemy takes away from us [Col. 0716C] the fountain of the word of God, he immediately breaks into the citadel of the mind.”

VERSE 19.—And he built, etc. (The same, in the same work.) Up to this point the first wall of the city is constructed, etc., up to “in which we might offend the eyes of our inward judgment.”

Opposite the ascent, etc. This is Christ, who in his faith and love united the people of the Jews and of the Gentiles; hence he is called the cornerstone. Opposite his ascent the second measure is built, when through the purity of devout thought we strive toward the vision of him, and when, even while held back in this life, we sigh frequently from desire for his vision. There follow many ranks of builders who are said to have built the second measure, because the greatest structure of the Church lies in the defense of inward virtue, when, namely, we guard our heart with every vigilance, for from it life proceeds. To draw each detail into spiritual interpretation would take too long.

VERSE 26.—The Nethinim. The Gibeonites are so called; by faithful devotion they served in the ministry of the house of the Lord according to the arrangement of Joshua son of Nun.

In Ophel. (Bede, in the same work.) It was a tower not far from the Temple, of extraordinary height. Hence it received the name Ophel, that is, “of darkness” or “of cloud,” because it thrust its head into the clouds. Accordingly, where it is written in Micah: “And you, tower of the flock, cloudy” (Micah IV), the tower of Ophel is blessed. The Book of Chronicles shows in what part of the city this tower was situated, saying that Manasseh built a wall outside the city of David, west of [Col. 0717A] Gihon in the valley, from the entrance of the Fish Gate around as far as Ophel (II Chronicles XXXIII). It was therefore appropriate, given the location, that the ministers of the Temple should live in a tower near the Temple.

Mystically, however, the Nethinim dwell in Ophel, that is, in the cloudy tower, when those who have devoted themselves to God in the profession of a more perfect life continually dwell, by action and thought, in the defense and height of the virtues, and their citizenship is in heaven. The admiring crowd says of them: “Who are these who fly like clouds?” (Isaiah LX), etc. Likewise, the Tekoites dwell in Ophel when those distinguished by the habit of religion penetrate the hidden things of Scripture, of which it is written: “Dark water is in the clouds of the air” (Psalm XVII)—that is, mystical knowledge in the prophets—with an enlightened heart, and read [Col. 0717B] and meditate upon them continually.

Opposite. (Bede, in the same work.) The Lord, namely, who daily waters us by the grace of his mercy, lest we slip and fail amid the hardships of the present life, etc., up to “and because after the present gifts of the virtues one ascends to behold the glory of the Lord, it is rightly added: ‘After him the Tekoites built,’ etc.”

VERSE 27.—From the tower. From the great and lofty tower the city’s structure reaches as far as the wall of the Temple, when the righteous, from the height of contemplation—which in this life lifts the mind toward heavenly desires while it disdains temporal things—ascend truly in the future life to behold the glory of the Lord’s incarnation, with the glory of the divine eternity also revealed. And because Tekoah is interpreted as “trumpet” or “horn,” and the Tekoites as “trumpeters,” [Col. 0717C] it is aptly said that the Tekoites built this section. For it belongs to teachers, whose sound goes out into all the earth, to disclose to the faithful in his city—that is, in the Church—the present gifts or future gifts of God.

To the wall of the Temple. The body of Christ, concerning which it is said in John II: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up.” The persecutors destroyed it in death, but lovers never cease to behold it, raised up and exalted to the heavens, in glory.

VERSE 28.—Above, etc. (Bede, in the same work.) Jeremiah indicates that this gate was on the eastern side of the city, etc., up to “when horses are understood in a good sense, just as asses, camels, and mules, they signify peoples of the Gentiles converted to the Lord, or cares for temporal affairs subjected to the Lord of the soul.”

[Col. 0717D] The priests built, etc. The priests of the city of God build the wall to the Water Gate when, after the calling of the Jews, teachers proceed to bring the Gentiles into the Church by sowing the word of God.

(Bede, in the same work.) It would be long to discuss mystically each building or builder, etc., up to “records their names in heaven.”

## CHAPTER IV

VERSE 1.—“. . . Sanballat . . . being greatly stirred, mocked the Jews.” (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, chapter 19, volume II.) Clearly, this is the anger of heretics. These are the words of those who call themselves Samaritans, that is, guardians of the law of God, etc., up to “and may attain the ornaments of the virtues through corrected conduct.”

VERSE 3.—“But Tobiah also,” etc. (The same, in the same work.) The person and words of this Tobiah suit heretics, etc., up to “with which they strive to corrupt the fruitful minds of the faithful.”

VERSE 9.—And we prayed. This is the one refuge against the enemies of the Church: prayer to God, and the diligence of teachers who, meditating day and night on his law, fortify the hearts of the faithful against the snares of the devil and his soldiers by preaching, consoling, and exhorting.

VERSE 10.—The rubble is abundant. That is, it has been heaped up at the site of the wall, etc., up to “and, as the storm of temptation broke upon the house or city, he is shown to have built a ruin.”

VERSE 11.—The enemies said, etc. Such things are usually done in the spiritual building. For the tireless enemy remains with his satellites, namely, unclean spirits and wicked men, who strive to impede and defeat the works of virtue and faith in us when we are heedless, and to kill the minds of the faithful with the sword of evil suggestion. Against these we must take up the armor of God, so that we may be able to resist on the evil day and stand perfect in all things.

VERSE 13.—I stationed them in the place, etc. That is, so that the workers, surrounded by a formation of armed men, might build more freely and securely. The ranks of the faithful are divided: some build by adorning the Church within through good works; others, equipped with the arms of sacred reading, keep watch against attacking heretics. These strengthen their neighbors in the truth of the faith through religious devotion; those wage the necessary battle against the darts of the devil or of vices, and by pastoral vigilance keep away from the Lord’s fold the wolves lying in wait.

VERSE 16.—From that day, half, etc. (Bede, in the same work, chapter 20.) It should be noted that not only did half of the young men do the work, etc., up to “and it is a lesser labor to avoid unknown pleasure of the flesh than to reject pleasure once known.”

VERSE 22.—And let there be shifts for you by night and by day. (The same, in the same work.) Note how great their zeal was in working, etc., up to “by reproving those who oppose, they drive them from the Church.”

## CHAPTER V

VERSE 1.—And there arose a great cry, etc. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, chapter 21.) The people desired to build the wall, etc., up to “and, turning our hands away from our own pleasures, may he direct them toward building the city of Christ.”

(The same, in the same work.) The people’s cry increased for three reasons. Some, compelled by hunger, wanted to sell their children to richer people; others, sparing their children, preferred to sell fields and houses. Some, forbidding the sale of children and fields, persuaded them only to borrow money at interest for the king’s taxes, pledging their fields and vineyards until, when prosperity returned, they could repay the lenders what they had borrowed.

VERSE 7.—And I rebuked the nobles, etc. (Bede, in the same work.) As the excellent commander of the heavenly army and wise architect of the city of God, etc., up to “so that the Father may forgive us our debts.”

VERSE 13.—Moreover I shook out my garment and said: “So may God shake out every,” etc. A terrifying conclusion is imposed upon this sentence. For whoever does not show mercy to the poor, or exacts from those who have nothing as though justly entitled to do so, is shaken out of his house—that is, from the assembly of the Church, in which he thought he would remain forever—and from his labors, namely, from the fruits of good works in which he thought he had labored laudably: he will receive no reward for his labor at all. For labors without piety cannot be fruitful before God.

[Col. 0719B] And the whole assembly said, Amen. It is shown how greatly Nehemiah’s rebuke or imprecation moved the hearts of all: having heard the denunciation, they responded “Amen,” praised God, and did what he had commanded. From this it is clear that they received his words not out of fear but out of love.

VERSE 14.—For twelve years. (Bede, as above.) The Apostle explains this, saying: “The Lord ordained that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel; but I have used none of these things” (I Corinthians IX). For twelve years Nehemiah lived with his brothers in the governorship in such a way that they did not eat the provisions owed to governors. This indicates that evangelical work consists in governing the people: that a ruler should exercise his office notably toward the Church and should not seek earthly advantage from his subjects.

## CHAPTER VI

VERSE 2.—Come, and let us make a covenant, etc. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, chapter 23, volume II.) The enemies of the holy city persuaded Nehemiah to descend into the plain, etc., up to “because the crafty enemy always tries to hinder our hands, let us always take care to strengthen them with divine assistance.”

VERSE 10.—And he entered. Nehemiah, assailed by the enemies’ snares, enters the house of Samaria as though it belonged to a friend and brother, but finds him to be the very plotter and enemy, corrupted, as it were, by the gifts and friendship of outsiders. For the elect always have battles outside and fears within; not only the apostles but also the prophets led lives threatened by dangers from their own people, dangers from the nations, and dangers from false brothers.

VERSE 15.—The month of Eliud. (Bede, as above.) Which is the sixth according to the Hebrews, etc., up to “and thereafter adorn themselves with good works in the love of God and neighbor.”

VERSE 16.—All the nations. (The same, in the same work.) Those who wanted to terrify the builders of the holy city, etc., up to “and, expelled from the Church.”

## CHAPTER VII

VERSE 1.—When the wall had been built, etc. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, chapter 24, volume II.) Mystically: when the wall of the Church has been built through the gathering of new peoples into the faith or the correction of those who had gone astray, the gates of regular discipline must immediately be installed, lest the devil, who goes about like a roaring lion, be able to break into the fold of God.

I appointed gatekeepers. (The same, in the same work.) Gatekeepers who have received, namely, the keys of the kingdom of heaven, so that they may receive the worthy and humble but keep the proud and unworthy from entering the heavenly city, saying: “You have no part or share in this matter. Your heart is not right before God” (Acts VIII).

VERSE 3.—The gates shall not be opened . . . until the heat of the sun, etc. (The same, in the same work), that is, throughout the whole time of night, etc., up to “hence: ‘Its gates shall not be shut by day, and there shall be no night there’” (Revelation XXI).

And I appointed guards. (The same, in the same work.) Guards of souls are not to be appointed from among novices or the common people, but from those who, by God’s grace, have been freed from the struggle against vices and already possess their minds in Jerusalem—that is, in the vision of tranquil peace—and whose citizenship is in heaven. For when some, having completed their course, are taken from this light, others are immediately substituted, and there is never an end of those who keep watch over the peace of the Church because of the terrors of the night, according to this saying: “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you” (Psalm XLIV).

These things typologically suit that time when, after the word of God had been sown far and wide by the apostles, the whole world received the new shoot of faith. The Church had not yet been built, but the peoples were still inexperienced, imbued only by hearing the word and receiving the sacraments. Therefore, after gathering not only the nobles but also the common people, he took care diligently to count their number, so that, once the total of all had been ascertained, he could distinguish who ought to live in Jerusalem and who in other cities.

Each one opposite his house. The guardianship of the holy Church is properly completed in this way: if each person cares for all the faithful in such a manner that he devotes more diligent attention specifically to those over whom, by God’s authority, he has been placed.

VERSE 66.—The whole assembly was like one man. (Josephus.) He also ordered the people who cultivated the fields to offer tithes of their produce at Jerusalem, so that the priests and Levites, having food, would not abandon the perpetual obligations of religion. They willingly followed Nehemiah’s decrees. From that time the city happened to be filled with a multitude of people. After doing many other such good and praiseworthy things with the greatest magnificence, Nehemiah reached old age and died.

## CHAPTER VIII

VERSE 1.—And the seventh month had come. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, chapter 26, volume II.) It was not far off. Since the wall had been completed on the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month, only five days remained before the beginning of the seventh month. From its first day until the twenty-second, it was wholly consecrated by the prescribed ceremonies; after these had been duly celebrated, he returned with the leaders and the people to arrange the inhabitants of the city.

And the whole people gathered like one man at the square which, etc. (Bede, in the same work.) The devotion and harmony of the people should be noted, etc., up to “by whose singing the people would be stirred more ardently during prayers and sacrifices to remember the law.”

Mystically also, after the city has been built, divine reading ought to follow, and the trumpets should sound more frequently, so that the people, initiated into the heavenly sacraments, may also be instructed through the sacred writings, in due course and with greater diligence, how they ought to live.

Before the Water Gate. (The same, in the same work.) I think the Water Gate was in the priests’ court, etc., up to “therefore the people were rightly gathered before the Water Gate, as though they were to be spiritually given drink from the streams of Scripture through their bishop.”

VERSE 4.—Ezra the scribe stood upon a platform. [Col. 0721B] (The same, in the same work.) He seems to remember, etc., up to “so that, timid and ashamed of what he himself had not done, he might prescribe it to others by doing it himself,” etc.

When rulers surpass their subjects in work as much as in honor, the subjects, stirred by their examples, devotedly follow the course of their life; and, piously admonished by them, they delight to pour out tears for their sins or from desire for the heavenly homeland. Hence it is rightly added: “For all the people wept when they heard the words of the law,” etc.

VERSE 10.—Go and eat, etc. (The same, in the same work.) He commands us to strengthen the weaker consciences of our neighbors by the example of pious action and by the sweetness of devout admonition, so that they may be filled, as it were, with fat and richness, and may praise the name [Col. 0721C] of the Lord with others in exultation. Literally also, when on feast days, after prayer, reading, and the study of the psalms have been completed, we refresh our bodies, we must remember the poor and pilgrims.

Do not grieve. Teachers who stir the minds of their hearers to tears through sacred readings, and who also console them while promising the joys that will follow.

VERSE 11.—For the day is holy. That is, while we devote ourselves to hearing and fulfilling the words of the Lord; although on that day we suffer adversity outwardly, we ought to rejoice in hope. Hence: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing” (II Corinthians VI), etc.

VERSE 14.—And they found, etc. (Bede, as above.) These matters are written more fully in Leviticus, etc., up to “we ought to remember that we are inhabitants in the land and pilgrims, like our fathers” (Psalm XXXVIII).

VERSE 15.—Branches of the fairest tree, etc. (The same, in the same work.) This is what the Hebrews call cedar. Whoever can say, “We are the good fragrance of Christ to God in every place” (II Corinthians II), brings with him the foliage of myrtle and its shade.

Branches of the fairest tree and branches of myrtle, etc. The fruit of charity, which is the fairest among all the virtues, is that by which Christ also ascended the wood of the cross for our salvation. When, insofar as we can, we imitate his passion, we are indeed protected by the branches of the fairest tree and of myrtle for the mortification of vices and lusts. For the Magi, offering myrrh to the Lord, taught that those who belong to Christ crucify their flesh with its vices and desires.

[Col. 0722A] Palm branches. (The same, in the same work.) We bring palm branches, which are the adornment of a victorious hand, when we carry a mind victorious over vices and unconquered by all enemies, so that we may stand before the throne in the sight of the Lamb, clothed in white robes, with palms in our hands (Revelation VII).

VERSE 16.—Each one on his roof. (The same, in the same work.) On his roof, etc., up to “and may deserve to abound in the greater fruits of good action.”

VERSE 18.—For seven days. (The same, in the same work.) The Feast of Booths was celebrated for seven days, etc., up to “and, gathered in the sight of God, may rejoice, never again to be separated.”

## CHAPTER IX

VERSE 1.—And on that day, etc. (Bede, as above, [Col. 0722B] chapter 28.) The devotion of the corrected people should be noted, etc., up to “when they cease from other labors and lend their ears more freely to divine readings.”

And Ezra said. Up to the end of his prayer or confession, which was mentioned above—that they were confessing their own sins and the sins of their fathers—it is shown more fully, through Ezra’s prayer, how this took place.

VERSE 38.—Therefore, because of all these things. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, volume II.) He shows with what devotion all their persons made a new assembly after the Feast of Booths, so that, having cleansed themselves with their whole intention from the contagion of crimes, they might join themselves to the divine covenant and confirm the terms of the holy covenant in speech and writing; and thus, separated from the company of the wicked, they might more securely complete the work they had begun earlier, namely, to establish suitable citizens of the city from among the number of the wicked.

## CHAPTER X

VERSE 1.—The signatories, etc. Another translation: Nehemiah, who is said to have been Athersatha—for he had two names—is therefore individually identified as the son of Achelai; this is stated more clearly above: “Now Nehemiah said—and he is Athersatha” (II Esdras VII).

(The same, in the same work.) We too must always celebrate a spiritual Sabbath, etc., up to “on the first day it is necessary to cleanse ourselves from evil, and thereafter to adorn ourselves with good deeds.”

## CHAPTER XI

VERSE 1.—They dwelt, however. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, volume II.) Now the arrangement has been completed, etc., [Col. 0722D] up to “but they receive it as the gift of the hidden Judge and Giver.”

VERSE 3.—And in Jerusalem. (The same, in the same work.) These words show, etc., up to “for it follows: ‘The sons of Judah dwelt in Kiriath-arba’” (II Esdras XI).

(The same, in the same work.) Judah is interpreted as “confessing” or “confession,” etc., up to “when of those who are in the field one will be taken and the other left.”

## CHAPTER XII

VERSE 1.—These are the priests, etc. (Bede, as above.) Here the leaders of the priests, together with their brothers, etc., up to “and therefore could have been born while Nehemiah was still alive.”

[Col. 0723A] (Bede, in the same work.) The succession of the leaders of the priests and Levites has been described, etc., up to “they restore them through friendly foresight and exalt them with the honor due to them.”

(The same, in the same work.) The city had long since been built, etc., up to “then, in reality, among blessed human beings enjoying the divine vision in spiritual bodies amid the angelic ranks.”

VERSE 27.—And with cymbals, etc. (The same, in the same work.) Cymbals, psalteries, and lyres, etc., up to “and kindle the hearts of their neighbors with love for him,” etc.

VERSE 28.—The sons of the singers. (The same, in the same work.) That is, imitators of them, etc., up to “and at the very time of the dedication, that is, of perpetual reward, they are joined together there.”

VERSE 30.—And they purified themselves. (The same, in the same work.) Entirely fitting order, etc., up to “and, with hands and feet bound, be sent into the outer darkness.”

VERSE 31.—The leaders of Judah, etc., that is, of confession or praise, are the more perfect teachers of the Church, who at the dedication of the city ascend upon the wall, because in a time of tribulation they are shown to have surpassed the general conduct of the Church by the height of their life. For it is said of them: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed watchmen” (Isaiah LXII), etc. Rightly, therefore, those who now preside as sentinels over the walls of the Church will then also stand above them in the glory of their reward.

And I appointed two choirs. Either they cleanse the filth of sins from the Church in the present by living more correctly and correcting those who have gone astray; and in the future they expel from the city of the Lord—namely, from entry into the heavenly homeland—those who refused correction, by judicial authority. Or the choirs of those praising go on the right over the wall and ascend to the Dung Gate, when they proclaim worthy of praise those who, by preaching, reproving, and excommunicating, remove all impurity from the Church.

VERSE 34.—And from the sons of the priests, etc. In this life the sons of the priests sing with trumpets at the dedication of the city of God; by preaching, they kindle the hearts of their hearers with remembrance of the heavenly homeland.

VERSE 35.—With the instruments of David’s song. Because they do not rely upon their own understanding or desires, but follow in every respect the life and teaching of the fathers and prophets and devote themselves to the word of preaching.

And Ezra the scribe. Because in everything they do they keep the words of sacred Scripture before their eyes; with these as guides they reach the entrance to eternal life, so that they may be made drunk with the abundance of God’s house and the torrent of his delight, with whom is the fountain of life, etc.

VERSE 36.—And opposite them they went up by the steps. (Bede, in the same work.) When the city was being built, etc., up to “they celebrate the Holy Trinity together with shared exultation.”

Above the house of David. (The same, in the same work.) The sons of the priests ascend, etc., up to “and may deserve to see the rising of the Sun of righteousness without setting.”

VERSE 37.—And above the Tower of the Furnaces. (The same, in the same work.) It would be long to discuss each gate or tower individually, etc., up to “it is always necessary to be fortified with watchful caution and concern.”

[Col. 0724A] VERSE 39.—And the two choirs stood. (The same, in the same work.) Having traversed the walls and gates of the city, etc., up to “in fulfilling whose will I remain with tireless mind.”

VERSE 41.—And they sang loudly. “You have broken my bonds; to you I will sacrifice a sacrifice of praise. I will pay my vows to the Lord in the courts of the house of the Lord, in the sight of all his people, in your midst, Jerusalem” (Psalm CXV). This happens when, with the multitude of all the saints gathered in the heavenly homeland, we offer up those praises for which we now groan and for which, with thanksgiving and daily longing, we thirst.

VERSE 42.—For God had made them rejoice, etc. (Bede, in the same work.) These things concern the dedication of the holy city, etc., up to “and took care to offer the greatest sacrifices of good works.”

But also the women, etc. For at the time of the resurrection, not only do those who built up the Church by preaching or by courageous action receive the fruit of their labor, but also the weaker companions of the same faith rejoice in the reception of the same life. For the Lord has blessed the little ones together with the great (Psalm CXIII).

VERSE 43.—They also appointed, etc. (Bede, in the same work.) While all were rejoicing, etc., up to “and it was dedicated with great praise and joy.”

## CHAPTER XIII

VERSE 1.—On that day the Book was read, etc. (Bede, on Ezra, Book III, volume II.) Because these people were born from incest, etc., up to “but God turned Balaam’s curse into a blessing for his people and protected him from the weapons of his enemies.”

VERSE 3.—And it came to pass, etc. Because we must attend to the hearing of truth, whenever divine reading forbids us because of any single vice, we must immediately also drive from our action and conscience whatever defilement of vice we discover in ourselves.

VERSE 6.—In all these matters. (Bede, in the same work.) This sentence, etc., up to “which Nehemiah, when he returned, immediately eradicated.”

VERSE 8.—And I cast out the vessels of Tobiah’s house. (The same, in the same work.) He was the Ammonite servant mentioned above, an enemy of the people of God, etc., up to “the association of heretics and schismatics with the orthodox and peaceful sons of God.”

And I cast them out. (The same, in the same work.) You too, whatever infidelity and impurity you find among the faithful, etc., up to “for just as Nehemiah represented him in other matters, so also in this.”

(The same, in the same work.) By the law we are commanded to work for six days at the things that are necessary and to rest on the seventh, etc., up to “but should turn their attention entirely away from the things that concern food and clothing and distribute them with suitable moderation.”

VERSE 16.—Bringing fish and all kinds of goods, etc. (The same, in the same work.) A good fish is devout faith; the bad fish [the reading is uncertain] is weak thought, which immerses itself excessively in the cares of this world. The Tyrians—that is, the constrained—seek to sell this to us on the Sabbath, when unclean spirits attempt to bury the repose of our thought beneath the profound cares of the world. But for such commerce Nehemiah rebukes and disciplines the nobles of Judah, while divine inspiration purifies from such thoughts those who strive to serve the profession of piety.

VERSE 19.—And it came to pass. (Bede, in the same work.) Our conscience, etc., up to “therefore it rightly follows.”

VERSE 22.—I also told the Levites to purify themselves, etc. (The same, in the same work.) It is necessary that they be cleansed from the daily exercise of their work, etc., up to “they must first purify their mind and actions from every stain of error.”

VERSE 23.—But also in those days. (The same, in the same work.) In the Church they marry foreign women, etc., up to “but interpreting according to the Gentile understanding.”

[Col. 0725B] VERSE 30.—Therefore I purified them. (The same, in the same work.) The conclusion is clearer throughout and worthy of the building of the holy [Col. 0726A] city and the Temple of the Lord: once the citizens have been cleansed of pollution alien to God, the orders of the priests and Levites are properly preserved in their ministry, so that the teachers of the Church, regularly instituted, may thereafter exhort a people chastened from every sin to remain in goodness and always to grow.

VERSE 31.—And at the offering of wood at appointed times and of firstfruits. Among other things, the people offer wood to maintain the fire of the altar when they perform works of virtue worthy of divine consecration. The wood burns and is consumed on the altar of burnt offerings when, in the hearts of the elect, works of righteousness are perfected by the flame of charity.

Remember me, my God, for good. Rightly, after many labors of devotion, such a founder and dedicator of the city commends himself to the memory of the Creator and giver of all good things.

[Col. 0725]

# THE BOOK OF TOBIT (G)*

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0725B]

VERSE 1.—“Tobias.” (Bede, on Tobit, volume II.) The Book of Tobit is beneficial on the surface of the literal sense. For it abounds in the greatest examples and admonitions for moral living. But as much as fruit surpasses leaves, so much does allegory surpass history. For it contains the greatest mysteries of the Church. Tobias himself signifies the people of Israel, who, while the other nations were devoted to idolatry, served God with right faith [Col. 0725C] and works. Hence: “When they went,” etc. Jeroboam, who fashioned golden calves for the deception of his subjects, expresses the worshipers of idolatry; their accomplices are signified in his subjects.

“Of Naphtali.” (The same, in the same work.) “Breadth,” concerning which it is said: “Your commandment is exceedingly broad” (Psalm CXVIII). Its tribe—that is, the faithful people, its children—and its city signify the Church, concerning which it is said: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden” (Matthew XV).

“Above Naasson.” Naasson means “augury”; his city augurs what is above, that is, contemplates heavenly things.

(Bede, as above.) Tobit’s captivity signifies the captivity of the human race under the king of all wicked things, [Col. 0725D] namely, the devil, who cast us down from our heavenly homeland into the valley of this exile.

VERSE 3.—“So that all things, etc.” (The same, in the same work.) Thus the people of Israel, through the teachers of the divine word, administered alms not only to the inexperienced hearers of their own nation but also to the nations coming to Judaism. Whatever good it possessed naturally, which the enemy who took it captive had not removed, it displayed to its own people as an example of virtue, and it offered to newcomers—that is, to the Gentiles—a portion of salutary knowledge as though it were a tenth of its substance.

VERSE 4.—“Yet there was nothing childish.” He already carried in his heart that apostolic saying: “Do not become children,” etc. (I Corinthians XIV). This, however, was said according to those who walked blamelessly in the commandments of the Lord, according to Tyconius’s rule by which, speaking as though of the same people, we sometimes praise all on account of the good and sometimes condemn all on account of the wicked; this is the second rule.

VERSE 6.—“All the firstfruits” (the same, in the same work). It seems to contradict the fact that the first tithe went toward the use of the Levites, while the second was spent on necessities when the Temple was visited. But the tithes of the third year, which they were then accustomed to give, were granted to the poor. Therefore we say “all that” or “all the second tithes,” because he could not approach the Temple for fear of the king’s guards.

VERSE 9.—“But when he had become a man” (the same, in the same work). Thus the people of Israel, etc., up to “hence: ‘Israel is my firstborn’” (Exodus IV).

VERSE 10.—“Whom he feared from childhood,” etc.—that is, believing and confessing that he would never commit sin, but would be filled with the spirit of the fear of the Lord.

## Verse 13

“Before Salmanasar,” etc. This does not contradict what is said elsewhere about Salmanasar, who is also called Sennacherib: for he had two names; or, more generally, all the kings of the Medes were called by this name, just as the kings of Egypt were called Pharaohs. [Col. 0726D]

## Verse 16

“But when he had come,” etc. (The same author, in the same place.) Thus the people of God, etc., up to the point where they “unveil the hidden things of Scripture.”

## Verse 20

“He provided burial,” etc., of sinners, so that not even their memory might remain among them. In such burial our fathers wished to be honored, in accordance with the burial of Christ. Hence Jacob wished to be buried in Judea, and Joseph gave instructions concerning his bones.

## Verse 21

“Finally, when he had returned,” etc. Sennacherib rightly fled from Judea: for the devil fears true confession, and “does not remain before his face.”

# Chapter II

## Verse 10

“It happened,” etc. (Bede, on Tobit, vol. II.) [Col. 0727A] Let no one be surprised if something good at one time signifies evil figuratively, and something evil signifies good. For if this were not permitted, the name of God would never be written in black ink, but always in shining gold, because God is light. Yet if you write the name of the devil with a white stone, it nevertheless signifies darkness. Thus blinded Tobit signifies the people of Israel: “For blindness has come upon Israel in part” (Romans 11). He was blinded because he was wearied by burying the dead. Whoever persists indefatigably in good works does not admit the light of faith. Thus the person spiritually wearied falls asleep when he neglects to keep watch, stand firm, act courageously, and be strengthened. To him it is said: “Rise, you who sleep, and arise from the dead” (Ephesians 5).

(Bede, in the same place.) Because of their light flight, swallows signify pride and fickleness; their impurity blinds those whom they dominate. The person who sleeps beneath a swallow’s nest submits himself unwarily to fickleness, lust, and pride. This blindness prevailed especially among the people of Israel as the Lord’s coming in the flesh approached, when they were oppressed by the yoke of Roman servitude and violated the commandments of the divine law by their evil way of life. [Col. 0727B]

## Verse 14

“But he remained unmoved,” etc., because judgment begins with the house of God. Hence: “Begin from my sanctuary” (Ezekiel 9). Whoever is not chastised is not a son: “He who spares the rod hates his son” (Proverbs 13). Paul is struck like a child and exalted like a young man.

## Verse 15

“The kings mocked,” etc. (Bede, in the same place.) They were in the people, etc., up to: “Love is patient, love is kind” (1 Corinthians 13).

# Chapter III

[Col. 0727C]

## Verse 7

“As Sarah,” etc. (Bede, on Tobit, vol. II.) She signifies a crowd of notions, etc., up to the point where Daniel prays in the upper room, Elisha has upper rooms, and Christ celebrates the Passover in an upper room.

# Chapter IV

## Verse 3

“Bury my body.” By burying bodies, we entrust them to the earth as a sacred deposit, believing that they will be restored and glorified in the resurrection.

# Chapter V

## Verse 7

“From the sons of Israel.” For he was from the number of the angels, who are the sons of Israel, because they always see [Col. 0727D] God face to face; and they are often sent to guard the sons of Israel, that is, those who see God. Hence: “I established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel” (Deuteronomy 32).

## Verse 10

“Then he entered,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) The angel appeared to Tobit and offered himself as his companion; and the Son of God assumed humanity, lived visibly among human beings, and saved the human race. Tobias brought the angel to his father, etc.; and the Lord, through the miracles he performed in the flesh for the Jewish people, from whom he had taken flesh, showed that he is both son and angel—that is, messenger of the Father’s will. He also proclaimed to them the joy of everlasting salvation, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3). [Col. 0728A] And to those despairing of heavenly light he said: “I am the light of the world; whoever follows me does not walk in darkness” (John 8).

## Verse 15

“And the angel said to him.” (The same author, in the same place.) The angel promises Tobit that he will lead his son to the city of the Medes and bring him back, etc., up to the point where Tobit asks the angel where he is from.

## Verse 18

“I am,” he said, “Azariah, son of the great Hananiah.” (The same author, in the same place.) Azariah means “helper”; Hananiah means “glory of God.” Christ likewise indicates to his faithful that he is the one of whom it is said: “You are my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; do not delay” (Psalm 69). And: “We saw his glory, glory as of the only-begotten from the Father” (John 1).

## Verse 22

“Then, when they had made preparations.” (Bede, cited above.) When the Lord appeared in the flesh, etc., up to the point where salvation thus reached the nations through the apostles. [Col. 0728B]

# Chapter VI

## Verse 1

“He set out,” etc. (Bede, on Ezra, vol. II.) When the Lord came to save the nations, etc., up to the point where they defend the spiritual sheep from thieves, bestial spirits, and heretics.

## Verse 2

“And behold, a fish,” etc. The mystery of the Lord’s Passion is clearly signified, etc., up to the point where “the ruler of this world, when he came, found nothing in him.”

“He went out.” (The same author, in the same place.) Christ accepted the death which he owed nothing, in order to wash his feet—that is, his members—from the contamination of sin and death. The fish rushed forward, wishing to devour him; and when the Lord was suffering on the cross, the devil, through whose agency he had been crucified, came, seeking whether he might find any sin in him. [Col. 0728C]

## Verse 3

“Being terrified by it,” etc. As the moment of death approached, Christ began to be afraid and distressed—not by the devil, but by death, which entered the world through the devil’s envy; he recoiled from it in the natural frailty of the flesh. Hence: “Father, take this cup away from me” (Mark 14).

## Verse 4

“Seize its fin,” etc. (Bede, in the same place.) Christ seized the devil, who had wished to capture him on the cross, and conquered him by dying. He therefore seized the fin so that, by the right hand of his power, he might separate the wicked head from the body—that is, remove the wickedness of the ancient enemy from those whom he had made his body and bring them into his own body, that is, the Church. For the fish has its fin at the boundary between its head and body. Christ is the head of the Church, which is his body, while the devil is the head of the wicked, who are his body.

“When he had done this.” When the Lord revealed the devil’s wickedness, the devil still attempted to stir up persecution against the Lord’s elect. These are his feet, by which he walks on earth, while he reigns everywhere in heaven. [Col. 0728D]

## Verse 5

“Gut this fish.” The Lord gutted the fish when he disclosed the devil’s wickedness more fully to the saints and, as it were, unlocked the secrets of his snares. He kept its heart for himself because he revealed its cunning [Col. 0729A] in the Scriptures. Of it is said: “The serpent was more cunning than all the animals of the earth” (Genesis 3); and elsewhere: “We are not unaware of his schemes” (2 Corinthians 2). He also kept the gall, because he wished the fury of its malice against the human race—how fiercely it rages—to be written down and preserved for the sake of vigilance. He kept the liver because he disclosed its wicked counsels against us through teachers of truth. Physicians say that food is cooked and digested by the heat and hidden power of the liver. When, through careful reflection, we investigate in what order the things we intend to do should be done, we cook them, as it were, like food received into the stomach, by the heat of the liver.

“For these things are necessary.” Knowledge of the devil’s craft and wickedness benefits us as a remedy: the more thoroughly we investigate them, the more thoroughly we avoid them. [Col. 0729B]

## Verse 6

“He roasted its flesh,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) Whatever he took for himself from this fish, etc., up to the point where the foundations of the Church were laid among the nations.

## Verse 12

“And it is necessary.” (The same author, in the same place.) Raguel signifies the people of the nations, etc., up to the point where one is worthy to hear: “I shall no longer call you servants, but my friends” (John 15).

# Chapter VII

## Verse 11

“When Raguel heard this statement, he was terrified,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) When the people of the nations hear the word of faith, etc., up to the point where those who speak foolishly perish foolishly. [Col. 0729C]

# Chapter VIII

## Verse 1

“After they had dined,” etc. (Bede, on Tobit, vol. II.) After Tobias had been brought into the bedroom, he brought forth, etc. God, intending to receive the Church from the nations, commands her at the beginning of her betrothal to renounce the devil and all his pomp, and to confess faith in the Holy Trinity for the remission of sins. This is to burn the innermost parts of the fish with live coals.

(Bede, cited above.) After the renunciation of the devil and the confession of the true faith comes the remission of sins. Through the water of baptism, after expelling the devil, he bound the devil, restraining him by preventing him from harming the faithful.
