Although the devil is sometimes permitted to tempt them for their testing, he is nevertheless forbidden to overcome them. [Col. 0729D]

## Verse 3

“He bound him.” The desert and Egypt signify the hearts of unbelievers, which are deserted by God because they are unworthy of his dwelling and, according to the interpretation of the name Egypt, darkened by the darkness of their unbelief. It is rightly the case that the person deserted by God is filled by a demon. The angel bound the demon who wished to kill Tobit in the desert. Thus, after restraining the devil from the faithful, who are Christ’s members, he permits him to exercise dominion only over unbelievers; yet even among them he keeps him bound, because he is not permitted to harm them as much as he strives to do.

## Verse 11

“And it happened,” etc. (The same author, in the same place.) The crowing of the roosters, etc., up to the point where they truly recognized Christ as the bridegroom of the holy Church after the enemy had been conquered. [Col. 0730A]

## Verse 17

“We bless you, Lord God.” (The same author, in the same place.) Raguel rejoices over Tobit’s life, etc., up to the point where they are filled with the richness of heavenly love.

## Verse 22

“Two also,” etc. (The same author, in the same place.) The Apostle of the nations gives those who had come to the faith, etc., up to the point where they receive banquets from those whose examples nourish them.

“Four rams.” The holy teachers and martyrs preserve the four books of the Gospel in faith and works; they are fortified by prudence, justice, courage, and temperance, and instruct the Church of God in the four regions of the world.

“He had them killed.” Some willingly mortify their bodies so that they may be a living sacrifice; others undergo martyrdom at the hands of unbelievers. By the weapons of righteousness, on the right and on the left—that is, in prosperity and adversity—they conquer the ancient enemy. [Col. 0730B]

## Verse 23

“And Raguel charged Tobit.” (Bede, in the same place.) We charge Christ to remain with us until, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we attain the perfection of rest, in which we may rest both from sins in the body and from evil thoughts in the mind.

# Chapter IX

## Verse 3

“Nevertheless, I beg you.” (Bede, from Isidore.) Send some of the believers who serve you, to whom you may entrust the ministry of preaching, in order to gather the nations that have not yet received the mystery of faith but have nevertheless heard its fame; and let them return, through the obedience of faith, the talent of the word that they learned through report. Every day a new people is gathered into the Church. This may, however, be understood especially of those who received the letter of the law through the seventy translators and therefore accepted the faith more quickly. [Col. 0730C]

# Chapter X

## Verse 8

“But Raguel,” etc. (Bede, cited above.) When the fullness of the nations has entered, no one can prevent the Lord from granting salvation to Israel and regarding its blindness, which has occurred in part. For divine mercy remembered that there is great sorrow and continual pain among believing Jews on behalf of their unbelieving brothers. [Col. 0730D]

## Verse 10

“He handed over,” etc. At the end, the teachers of the Church are sent back to Christ, when the Church herself, full of the riches of the virtues, [is sent] to bring the Jewish people—from whom the Son of God took flesh—to faith and to enrich it with the substance of good works.

# Chapter XI

## Verse 3

“Let us go ahead.” (Bede, in the same place.) After the people of the nations have been enlightened, divine grace goes ahead to enlighten the blindness of the Jews, so that in their books they may recognize Christ as true man and true God. Then at last, as though they had seen the angel and his son whom they had not seen for so long, they will rejoice greatly; and at last, that is, the Jewish people will unite itself with the Church gathered from the nations through communion in the mysteries. [Col. 0731A]

## Verse 9

“By caressing.” (Bede, cited above.) The dog rejoiced when it revisited the dwelling of its masters, which it had not seen for a long time. The teachers rejoice in the outcome of their work when they understand that Judea is to be gathered again by the Lord. They rejoice in the reward of eternal life, proclaim that all hearts will be gladdened by the same reward, and immediately announce the grace of the Holy Spirit that is to come.

## Verse 10

“Rising.” After hearing the word of salvation from the teachers, the Jewish people rise from the long blindness of their unbelief and run toward the Lord in love. Yet they stumble in the steps of their works until, reborn and instructed in Christ, they receive the light of faith and action.

## Verse 13

“Then, taking,” etc. (Bede, in the same place.) The Lord openly reveals to believers how great is the malice of the ancient enemy, who eagerly desired to devour him in the Passion; but by being killed through this very act, he lost his members—that is, those whom he had previously held. [Col. 0731B]

## Verse 14

“The white film.” (Bede, in the same place.) The Jewish people still have a veil before the face of their heart, etc., up to the point where those who, conscious of their frailty and ignorance, say, “Lord God, enlighten my darkness,” are enlightened by the Lord.

## Verse 18

“She entered,” etc. (The same author, in the same place.) This signifies the light of spiritual grace, which is sevenfold. After seven days of illumination, the wife enters, because after Judea has been illuminated through faith and has received the grace of the Holy Spirit, the Church will enter to her, so that there may be one fold and one shepherd, and one house of Christ, established upon one cornerstone.

# Chapter XII

[Col. 0731C]

## Verse 14

“And now,” etc. (Bede, on Tobit.) As the angel is about to return to heaven, he explains more openly what he is, why he came, and where he is going to return; and Christ disclosed his condition more fully to the same people as they advanced, showing that he is in the Father and the Father in the Son. The angel returns to God; Tobit remains with the Father; and Christ is understood by his faithful to be equal to the Father in divinity and consubstantial with human beings in humanity. [Col. 0732A]

# Chapter XIII

## Verse 1

“But Tobit opened his mouth.” (Bede, on Tobit.) He confessed the truth and mercy, etc., up to the point where he proclaimed the joys of the heavenly homeland.

# Chapter XIV

## Verse 1

“And after Tobit had been enlightened,” etc. The number forty signifies labor, fasting, and abstinence. We too must all endure the labors of this life with love of God and neighbor, and thus we shall bear fruit. [Col. 0732B]

## Verse 3

“For he lost the light of his eyes at the age of fifty-six,” etc. He had passed beyond the sacred number fifty but had not reached sixty, which signifies perfection because of the number six, in which all things were made.

## Verse 5

“At the hour of his death he called Tobit to him.” (Bede, on Ezra.) Tobit—that is, the teachers of the Jews—who, as they are about to depart from this world, announce to their relatives that the world is approaching its end and that the blessings of the future life are near.

## Verse 14

“Tobit departed from Nineveh with his wife, his sons, and his grandsons,” etc. (The same author, in the same place.) Christ does this every day, etc., up to the point where, though he lives long, he does not abandon the fickleness of the mind. [Col. 0732C]

## Verse 16

“They buried him.” Tobit’s burial signifies the end of the world, when our Lord enters into rest with his body, which is the Church, while the angels rejoice with the company of human beings and place each one in different dwellings according to the measure of their merits.

[Col. 0731]

# The Book of Judith (G)*

## Jerome’s Prologue to the Book of Judith

(See among the works of Blessed Jerome, vol. VIII.)

## Preface

[Col. 0731D]

(Rabanus, commentary on the Book of Judith, vol. III.) It is asked at what time and under which kings the history of Judith took place, etc., unless perhaps it is said that Cambyses, who is said to have attacked neighboring peoples and conquered Egypt, defeated and subjected to his rule a certain king named Arphaxad who resisted him in Media, when the kingdom of the Assyrians and Persians was one.

# Chapter I

## Verse 1

“Arphaxad.” (Rabanus, cited above.) Mystically, the proud are expressed by Arphaxad. Their attempts and labor, carried on through the vastness of swelling arrogance and self-exaltation, easily fall under the power of Nabuchodonosor, that is, the devil. For he is the king over all the sons [Col. 0732D] of pride: “Which he called.” This is the metropolis of the province of Media, founded by Deioces, king of the Medes, but wonderfully enlarged by Arphaxad. As the prophet Daniel relates, following Josephus, under King Darius a very splendid mausoleum was constructed in that same Median city with remarkable skill. On whatever day it is seen, it appears to have been built on that very day, because of its ever-new beauty and solid material. To this day the kings of the Persians and Medes are buried there, and the person entrusted with this duty is a Jewish priest.

“In glory.” “Some trust in chariots and some in horses,” etc. But God cast Pharaoh’s chariot and his army into the sea. Therefore, “Let the one who boasts, boast in the Lord.”

## Verse 6

“In the great plain.” (Rabanus, cited above.) The names of the places, etc., up to the point where they finally granted victories to the Chaldeans or Assyrians. [Col. 0733A]

“Then he was exalted.” When the devil subjects the multitude of the lost to his will, his heart is lifted up; he attributes this to his own power rather than to divine permission. He burns all the more intensely for the destruction of many of the lost when he sees himself prevailing over certain people through wicked suggestion. Hence what follows:

“And he sent to everyone.” (Rabanus, in the same place.) The devil sends messengers through the various provinces, etc., up to: “They all opposed him with one mind,” etc.

## Verse 12

“Then Nabuchodonosor was angered.” The devil, blinded by his own pride, claims for himself dominion over the whole world, striving to make those who have been torn away from the worship of piety companions of his impiety. Exulting in the power of his kingdom, he says: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will set my throne in the north, and I will be like the Most High.” And in the Gospel: “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me.” [Col. 0733B]

# Chapter II

## Verse 7

“Then Holofernes.” (Rabanus, on the Book of Judith, vol. III.) That Holofernes signifies the leaders of the nations who persecuted the Church, etc., up to the point where they cause everyone to worship the dragon, which gave the beast such power.

## Verse 12

“When he had passed through.” (The same author, in the same place.) Through the various provinces and the names of the places contained in the history, distinctions of persons, ranks, and dignities are signified. From these the devil claims some part for himself. He does not fear the difficulty of battle but strives to bring about a great ruin through his great power. [Col. 0733C]

## Verse 13

“And he plundered everyone.” He took away the benefit of knowledge and the other things by which they ought to have served God, converting them to the use of his own service. He killed those who resisted with the edge of the sword, because he physically kills those whom he cannot bend to consent.

## Verse 17

“He descended into the plains.” Damascus is interpreted as “drinking of blood.” By it the leaders of the nations are expressed—those who thirst for the blood of the faithful—especially at the time of harvest, that is, at the consummation of the age, when the fury of Antichrist rages throughout the breadth of the world.

# Chapter III

## Verse 1

“Then they sent,” etc. The powerful of this world and lovers of pleasure, who strive to reconcile the ruler of the world to themselves so that they may escape the danger of death and the loss of pleasure. Of them it is said: “Whoever wishes to be a friend of this world is made an enemy of God.” In them the anxiety of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it bears no fruit. They are exalted according to the names of these provinces, follow vanity, and enter the land by two roads; they will be joined in hell to the company of those who mourn or pay the penalty for their luxury. There they will pass from the waters of snow into excessive heat, “where their worm will not die and the fire will not be extinguished.” [Col. 0733D]

# Chapter IV

## Verse 13

“Remember.” He strengthens them through the examples of the saints. Hence Job says (chapter 12): “You renew witnesses against me.” And Paul, praising the power of faith in the Letter to the Hebrews, introduced abundant examples of the fathers, who through faith conquered kingdoms and practiced righteousness. [Col. 0734A]

# Chapter V

## Verse 5

“Then Achior the commander,” etc. He is like a leader of heretics, a man wholly devoted to idolatry, who learned from divine works and miracles what he often tells others, although he has not perfectly learned the Catholic faith and has not been reborn through Christ’s baptism. Or Achior represents heretics who, although they do not hold the way of truth in every respect, nevertheless proclaim many true things in their teaching that agree with our faith. They fight against the Catholic Church, but when overcome by reason they do not conceal the truth entirely. For heretics mix good things with evil: if they always said evil things, they could not remain hidden. Just as the person who offers a cup of poison touches the rim of the cup with honey, so that what is sweet may be tasted first and the deadly contents may not be feared. Sometimes, however, after correction they are saved, as Achior, seeing Judith’s victory, joined himself to the people of God and circumcised the flesh of his foreskin. The lepers in the Gospel also express heretics, who, while inserting crooked things into what is right, sprinkle a healthy color with spots. [Col. 0734B]

# Chapter VI

## Verse 10

“Now the children of Israel came down from Bethulia.” The sons—that is, the teachers of the Church—loosen the one bound to the tree when they teach their catechumens to fear neither the fury of persecutors nor death. They loosen the one bound to the tree when they rescue the fearful mind from dread of the cross and prepare it to suffer. This is done more effectively if, following the example of Uzziah and Charmi, who encouraged Achior and poured out devout prayers to the Lord with all the people, the teachers of the Church commend their hearers to the Lord with devout prayers, so that by his gift they may possess what human weakness does not deserve. [Col. 0734C]

## Verse 19

“And he prepared a great feast for him.” After the fast is completed, he prepares it who restores the soul, long weakened and lacking the bread of the Lord’s word, with evangelical teaching and the nourishment of virtues. All the presbyters are invited to this banquet, so that the neophytes may be strengthened by their exhortations and examples to receive or preserve the faith. [Col. 0734D]

# Chapter VII

## Verse 7

“Yet there were springs not far from the walls.” As in the Book of Kings the Philistines removed the blacksmiths so that they could not make either a spear or a sword for the Hebrews, and all Israel went down to the Philistines to sharpen its plowshare, mattock, axe, and hoe, so the devil chiefly strives to remove the streams of doctrine and the weapons of the virtues, and thus to accomplish his wickedness swiftly in the destruction of God’s servants. Hence the leaders of the nations and Julian the Apostate prohibit Christians from studying not only divine philosophy but also human philosophy.

## Verse 12

“Then they gathered around Uzziah.” The carnal are those who say, “Lord, Lord,” while their heart is far from me (Matthew 7; 15). In the Lord’s net there are both good and bad fish, until the shore of the future judgment. They endure the hardships of the present life severely and prefer to enjoy present pleasures rather than have heavenly blessings reserved for them in the future. They afflict their teachers with importunate complaints and force them to approve the luxury of the world. Hence what follows: [Col. 0735A]

## Verse 23

“And these five days,” etc. The five days signify the five bodily senses by which the present life is conducted. The idle teacher asks, as though for a respite of five days, for bodily comfort for his hearers without discernment, as though the magnificence of the supreme Giver were in his own power, when in fact the time and measure of giving depend more on the giver than on the recipient. If the comfort of the present life is denied, they abandon their subjects so that, yielding to persecutions, they may avoid bodily punishment. Our Judith, that is, the Church, rejects and despises this agreement. [Col. 0735B]

# Chapter VIII

## Verse 1

“And it happened when,” etc.; it continues, “the daughter of Merari,” that is, of bitterness. For the Church is brought forth through bitterness and tribulation for the joys of the future life, where she will praise the Lord forever. The fact that she is said to have been born in the fifteenth generation signifies that the Church came forth from the patriarchs and apostles through the heptad of the Law and the ogdoad of the Gospel, and will ascend to heavenly grace. Hence this number of steps is placed in the Psalter as a figure of the future ascent to heaven, by which the holy, as they come, rightly say: “Behold, now bless the Lord.” [Col. 0735C]

## Verse 2

“And her husband was Manasses,” etc. Manasses is interpreted as “forgetful” or “necessity.” Judith, joined to him in marriage, was thus subject either to the decalogue of the Law or to the rites of the nations. But when Christ came and the light of the Gospel shone in the world, all that observance ceased and, like a worthless gathering of the harvest, quickly passed away. Hence the Apostle says: “When faith has come, we are no longer under a pedagogue. For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3). And to the Romans he says: “You have died to the law through the body of Christ Jesus, so that you may belong to another, who has risen from the dead” (Romans 7).

The husband Manasses is Christ, the bridegroom of the Church. Manasses is rightly so called because through the consolation of the future life he makes us forget our former calamity. At the time of the barley harvest—that is, the gathering of the Jewish people—when he sent his apostles to preach and gather sheaves of believers, the heat of persecution came upon his head, that is, upon his divinity. “For God is the head of Christ” (1 Corinthians 11). The Jews were especially scandalized because he said that he was the Son of God. Hence: “You make yourself God” (John 10); and elsewhere: “Because he made himself the Son of God” (John 19).

Jesus suffered among his own people and was buried in a garden. After her bridegroom was taken away, his bride devotes herself to fasting and prayer until the consummation of the age, nor does she deign to be polluted by heretical errors. [Col. 0735D] Her husband left her the riches of spiritual wisdom and virtue and gathered together a household for her, that is, a multitude of nations. [Col. 0736A]

## Verse 7

“Her husband had left her many riches.” The Church, coming to Christ, brought the multiple riches of instruction from the Old Law, philosophy, and moral discipline. Hence Paul boasts that he was educated at the feet of Gamaliel, and Moses is read to have been trained in all the wisdom of the Egyptians.

## Verse 12

“This is not the time for such speech.” When we are afflicted, we must not prescribe either the time or the manner to the Lord; rather, we should leave everything to his judgment. Hence one of the fathers is reported to have said in his prayer: “Son of God, Son of God, have mercy on me as you know and as you will” (Matthew 6). We must seek only the kingdom of God, and everything else will be added. Let the present life be for the faithful a matter of use, and the future life a matter of fruition. Let temporal possessions be for the journey, and let eternal things be desired upon arrival. [Col. 0736B]

## Verse 28

“And they said.” Whatever the Church speaks in the confession of faith and in the teaching of religion is praiseworthy and irreproachable. In prayer she warns each of the faithful that, just as each has recognized the truth of what she teaches, so each should fulfill it in works. Hence it follows:

## Verse 30

“And Judith said to them.” Judith, that is, the Church, entrusts the gate to the presbyters—that is, the Church’s careful guardianship—to ensure that they stand always prepared, with vigilant and diligent care, against the snares of the enemy, and fortified by prayers.

# Chapter IX

[Col. 0736C]

## Verse 1

“When they had departed.” After speaking to the presbyters, Judith enters the oratory, because the care of the saints, after the service of preaching, returns to the secrecy of her heart, so that there she may complete the incense of pure ascent, according to the saying: “When you pray, enter your room.”

## Verse 2

“Lord God.” In her prayer she rightly recalls the deed of Simeon, who, together with his brother Levi, avenged their sister’s violation upon the foreigners. For it was to happen that Holofernes, who wished to fulfill the uncleanness of lust against Judith, would be struck by the sword of vengeance.

## Verse 9

“Look upon the camp.” Just as he compares the lustful with the lustful, so now he compares the proud with the proud—the Assyrians with the Egyptians—because just as divine power is present in the former, so it can be manifested in the latter when they are overthrown: the same Lord, the same power, the same justice. [Col. 0736D]

# Chapter X

## Verse 2

“She removed the sackcloth from herself and took off the garments of her widowhood,” etc. At times the holy Church bears the disposition of penitence for her sins, but nevertheless she brightens her spirit with the hope of forgiveness and future reward.

## Verse 4

“With incomparable beauty.” It is just that the person who burns with love of God should be considered worthy of honor by all. Hence: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in varied adornment” (Psalm 45).

## Verse 5

“And loaves and cheese.” Abra observes all these things in accordance with the arrangement of her mistress. For it is right that one who does not know how to regulate his own life should not suddenly become the ruler of another’s.

“And they said,” etc. They permitted them to remain freely under the rule of secular princes. Although Trajan had at first persecuted the confessors of Christ, after Pliny the Younger’s warning he moderated his edict with milder decrees. Aelius Hadrian, likewise instructed in the Christian religion by Quadratus, a disciple of the apostles, and Aristides of Athens, sent a letter to Minicius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, so that no one might condemn a Christian without an accusation or proof of a crime. [Col. 0737A]

# Chapter XI

[Col. 0737B]

## Verse 4

“And Judith said to him: ‘Take these words,’ etc.” (Augustine, Sermon 229 on the Seasons.) The appearance guards what flatters, etc., up to the point where the sleep he has prepared for you is the sleep in which you will strike him.

## Verse 17

“I have been sent.” The first path of salvation for the nations was to receive the preachers of the Gospel gladly, to offer faith, and through their teaching to come to the knowledge of the truth.

# Chapter XII

## Verse 19

“And he received it.” She is not defiled by the food or superstition of the nations. For the Church, living among the nations, is not polluted by idolatry but makes use of what the devotion of the faithful prepares through obedience. Hence: “My food is to do the will of him who sent me, the Father” (John 4). [Col. 0737C]

# Chapter XIII

## Verse 4

“On the bed.” Of wicked security, by which he confidently believes that he may sin with impunity. Hence: “When the wicked comes into the depths of sins, he despises” (Proverbs 18).

## Verse 11

“The head of Holofernes.” He commands that the memory of the completed battle be carefully remembered. Hence: “Be sober and watchful” (1 Peter 5).

## Verse 13

“To the guards of the walls.” That is, to the teachers, who fortify the Church by word and example and lead her into eternal life. Of them it is said: “Upon your walls, Jerusalem, I have appointed guards” (Isaiah 62). Or the phrase may refer to angelic spirits, who have been sent to guard us and drive out evil spirits.

“Open the gates.” That is, the devotion of the heart. Hence it is said: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Revelation 2). Likewise: “Blessed is the one who speaks his case in the ear of one who listens” (Ecclesiasticus 25). The Lord will give strength to his people, with whom he ascends to the summit of the heavenly kingdom. Hence: “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven” (John 3). [Col. 0737D]

## Verse 16

“But she ascended.” Turning her discourse toward heavenly doctrines and raising her hearers to praise God for his benefits.

## Verse 18

“And he killed.” Of him it is said: “She herself will crush the head,” etc. (Genesis 3). And in the Gospel: “I will give you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10). [Col. 0738A]

## Verse 19

“And behold,” etc. Know how great is the malice and fraud of our enemy, and by what great mercy he has been overcome by us—those whom the Lord guards unharmed from every fraud and contamination of error—so that, having seen these things, you may give thanks to our Creator and Redeemer. Hence: “Be sober and watchful” (1 Peter 5). And: “I fear that, just as the serpent deceived Eve by his cunning, so your minds may be corrupted” (2 Corinthians 11). And again: “Be strengthened in the Lord and in the power of his might, and put on the armor of God” (Ephesians 6).

## Verse 25

“For today your name,” etc. The praise of the Church will not depart from the mouths of those who remember her zeal and works. Through love of God and neighbor, she endures present tribulations securely, full of faith and firm in hope, attentive to the eminence of heavenly rewards, where she will be joined to the blessedness of the angels. [Col. 0738B]

## Verse 29

“When Achior saw.” Achior, the leader of the Ammonites, represents pagans or heretics. When they see that the faith of the Church has overcome the ferocity of her enemies, they are shaken by great fear; humbling their pride, they honor the Church and urge their followers to abandon error and join themselves freely to the faith. Hence Isaiah says: “The bent sons of those who humbled you will come to you, and all who insulted you will worship at the soles of your feet” (Isaiah 60).

# Chapter XIV

[Col. 0738C]

## Verse 13

“Then he entered.” The leaders of the persecutors, seeking aid from their gods against the Church, find them utterly filthy through their own depravity and deprived of every power. Therefore they entrust themselves to flight and abandon the things in which they had placed their temporal confidence. “For there is no wisdom, no understanding, and no counsel against God.” Hence Jeremiah says: “The swift shall not flee, and the strong shall not be saved,” etc. (Jeremiah 46).

# Chapter XV

## Verse 3

“When they saw,” etc. When Gideon was about to fight against the Midianites, he took neither spear nor shield but trumpets and lamps, prefiguring the preachers of the Gospel, whose struggle is not against flesh and blood but against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places, etc. They fight by the voice of preaching and the radiance of miracles.

“Thus all.” From each nation and province, tested persons equipped with strength for the Lord’s warfare come to the preaching of the word of God. Hence Isaiah: “Behold, these will come from afar, and behold, those from the north and from the sea” (Isa. XLIX), etc.

VERSE 13.—“But through the days.” These signify the entire period of the present life, during which the people of God, triumphing spiritually over the enemy, strip him of his possessions. Hence it is said of the Church: “The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he shall have no need of spoils” (Prov. XXXI).

VERSE 14.—“Moreover.” Thus the people of God, departing from Egypt, plundered it, and from its spoils constructed the tabernacle. Thus righteous kings under the Old Testament consecrated to the temple service what they had taken from their enemies.

VERSE 15.—“For the young men.” For then they will neither marry nor be given in marriage, because all will rise into a perfect man, according to the measure of the full age of Christ. Hence, at the Lord’s resurrection, an angel appeared as a young man covered with a white robe.

## CHAPTER XVI

VERSE 12.—“They were terrified.” The reader should consider whether the opinion is true that Cambyses, son of Cyrus, is the one whom most people have called this Nebuchadnezzar, who ruled over the Persians, Medes, and Assyrians.

VERSE 16.—“Adonai, Lord.” One of the ten names among the Hebrews, signifying that the Lord rules over creation. It should also be noted that wherever it is written twice, “Lord,” the first name is the tetragrammaton; it properly belongs to God and is called ineffable. The second is a common name, applicable to human beings. And rightly the Son of God is called “Adonai, Lord,” because he is God and man, Lord and God, ruling over all or feared by all.

VERSE 21.—“Into their flesh.” The flesh that they loved, from which the stench of worms arises. Flesh and blood produce worms, because carnal pleasure, when the salt of continence does not resist it, generates eternal punishment for the lustful. Hence: “Their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI).

VERSE 22.—“And it came to pass.” Having obtained victory over his enemies, each of the elect, cleansed from every stain, hastens to the heavenly city of God, where there is the true vision of peace and where he renders his vows to his Creator.

VERSE 28.—“One hundred and five, etc.” For eternal blessedness, the number one hundred passes from the left to the right.

“His Abram.” He leads and exhorts Abram—carnal conduct, always subject to fear—into the freedom of grace and toward the security of charity, so that he may serve not from fear but from love.

VERSE 29.—“And all the people mourned for her seven days.” Throughout the entire period unfolded in seven days, God’s elect, because of the Church’s pilgrimage in the present world, are afflicted in sorrow and groaning, not through despair but through remembrance of the life to come, according to the saying: “We wept when we remembered Zion” (Ps. CXXXVI).

[Col. 0739]

# THE BOOK OF ESTHER (G)*

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED JEROME ON THE BOOK OF ESTHER

(See among the works of Blessed Jerome, vol. VIII.)

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 0739C]

(RAB., Commentary on the Book of Esther, vol. III.) The book of Esther, which the Hebrews count among the Hagiographa, contains the mysteries of Christ and the Church, etc., through “who reigned after Darius, his paternal uncle, surnamed Nochus, for forty years.”

VERSE 2.—“The city of Susa,” etc. Susa is the metropolis of Persia, which historians say was founded by the brother of Memnon and received its name from the river Susa. There is the royal palace of Cyrus, built of white and variegated stone, with golden columns and ceilings adorned with jewels; it contains an image of heaven marked with shining stars, along with many marvelous things. There Ahasuerus celebrated a great feast, rich in wealth and abundant in delights. For the power of sacred eloquence sometimes narrates past events in such a way as to express what is to come; sometimes it approves the doer while opposing him in his ministry; sometimes it condemns deeds while urging that they be performed mystically.

VERSE 3.—“Therefore, in the third year.” At that time, namely, he revealed the mystery of his incarnation in this age and most abundantly supplied the spiritual banquets of preaching and of his body and blood. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace.

“A great feast for all the princes.”—“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who made a wedding feast for his son” (Matt. XXII). And elsewhere: “A certain man made a great supper and invited many” (Luke XIV). The historical account of this feast displays the pomp of wealth and the king’s luxury, but allegorically signifies the spiritual delights of Christ, which he distributes to each person. For Christ is that richest king who, entreated by the prayers of his wife—that is, the Church—delivers the Jews, that is, his confessors, from the hand of their enemies and justly condemns those enemies. Nor is it necessary that, if some persons’ good qualities signify Christ, their evils should also apply to Christ. Moses signified Christ in many respects, but not in this: that he doubted at the waters of contradiction. Nor did Aaron signify him in the making of the calf, nor Solomon in the filth of lust. Thus Ahasuerus signifies Christ in this judgment as he does in the generous feast; likewise Isaiah signifies Christ in Cyrus, king of the Persians, of whom he later says: “I girded you, though you did not know me” (Isa. XLV), etc. If wicked kings signify the devil in their evil deeds, why should righteous kings not display Christ in their good deeds? Nebuchadnezzar commanded peoples, prostrated at the sound of symphonies and musical instruments, to worship a statue. Likewise the devil, through worldly sweetness, bends the human race away from uprightness of mind toward the pursuit of avarice, which is the service of idols.

VERSE 5.—“The days of the feast.” The great ones, or the first believers, were refreshed first, according to the saying: “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished of the house of Israel” (Matt. XV). This was in the mystery of circumcision, the Lord’s resurrection, the New Testament, and true circumcision. There are also eight beatitudes to which this feast leads; it lasts only for days, whereas the wicked feasted at night.

VERSE 6.—“And they were hanging.” Fine linen signifies the mortification of the flesh; purple, the blood of martyrdom; marble columns, the firmness of teachers. It is therefore rightly said that tents of various colors were hung from linen and purple cords by ivory rings on marble columns, because the beauty of the Church ought to shine forth in teachers through meditation on wisdom and ascent in virtue, through mortification of the flesh and chastity together with the dignity of martyrdom; and it ought to reach the knowledge of others through their word and example, so that those instructed and strengthened by them may deserve to enter the hall of paradise.

“And they were supported by marble columns.” That is, by teachers, of whom it is said: “I have strengthened its columns” (Ps. LXXIV). And elsewhere: “He made its columns of silver, its backrest of gold” (Song III).

“Upon the pavement.” The emerald is so called because of its intense greenness. Parian is the whitest kind of marble. Through the greenness of faith and the whiteness of chastity, the foundation of humility is built. “For blessed are the poor in spirit, because theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). And: “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke X). And elsewhere: “Learn from me, because I am meek” (Matt. XI), etc.

VERSE 7.—“Wine.” According to the saying: “The love of God has been poured into our hearts” (Rom. V), etc. To one is given the word of knowledge, to another of wisdom, to another faith, to another the grace of healings.

“He would not compel them to drink,” etc. No one is compelled to receive a spiritual gift. God desires sons, not slaves; he desires the will, not compulsion, according to the saying: “Let whoever is able to receive it receive it” (Matt. XIX). Likewise: “If you wish to enter into life, keep the commandments” (ibid.). And: “If you wish to be perfect, go and sell all that you have” (ibid.), etc.

VERSE 8.—“Each person according to what he wished,” etc. According to the speed, capacity, and usefulness of each individual. Preaching must be so proportioned that it becomes useful to all and harms no one, passing like a two-edged sword among the vices of everyone. It should cut away pride without increasing timidity; it should impose the concern for work upon the idle and sluggish without increasing the excessive activity of the restless and curious—and so with the rest.

VERSE 9.—“In the palace where King Ahasuerus was,” etc. Jerusalem, where the temple and the Holy of Holies are; or meditation upon Holy Scripture, in which the divinity makes known its power.

VERSE 11.—“To display,” etc. “When the fullness of time came, God sent his Son” (Gal. IV), etc. Then the Son of God, having become incarnate, manifested with more abundant grace the mysteries of the Law by which he had formerly nourished the faithful.

VERSE 12.—“Which refused.” She not only despised the messengers but also the king’s command. Hence, in the Gospel, the elder son, when invited by his father to the feast, refused to enter; and those invited to the supper who were occupied with other matters refused to come. In accordance with the householder’s indignation, they were rejected and others were appointed in their place.

VERSE 16.—“And Mamuchan answered in the hearing of the king and the princes: The queen has wronged not only the king,” etc. Here the last in the order of the seven wise men delivers the judgment, signifying the apostle Paul, who says: “I am the least of the apostles, and am not worthy to be called an apostle” (1 Cor. XV). When the Jews contradicted him and were filled with zeal, he said: “Since you judge yourselves unworthy of eternal life, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts XIII).

## CHAPTER II

VERSE 7.—“Who was.” Esther is said to mean “hidden one,” and Edissa, “one who has obtained mercy.” She is the Church of the Gentiles, nourishing in the hidden place of the heart the chastity of faith and finding mercy and grace before the eyes of the Lord, while the synagogue has been rejected—the synagogue which in Hosea was called “without mercy.” Spiritual Mordecai nourishes her and adopts her as a daughter; he is the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth and is of the stock of Jemini, that is, of the stock of Benjamin.

VERSE 8.—“Esther.” Nebuchadnezzar, spiritually the king of confusion, transferred her from the natural law and the worship of the one God into the confusion of idolatry; but divine piety recalled her to the way of truth through preachers.

VERSE 9.—“And seven young women.” That is, faithful souls regenerated and consecrated by the grace of the Holy Spirit. They follow her footsteps in faith, teaching, and works. Of them it is said: “The young women have loved you exceedingly.”

“Which she did not wish.” Having been cleansed through baptism from the stain of sins and the filth of idolatry, she no longer endured the reproach of her former iniquity.

VERSE 13.—“And when they entered.” Whatever soul strives to hasten to the bridal chamber of Christ receives suitable adornment from its teachers. The more devotedly it prepares itself for knowledge of the faith and the practice of works, the more abundantly it is instructed by its teachers, so that, joining the number of the competent, it may approach the full faith and confession of the Holy Trinity, receive baptism and the anointing of chrism, and be truly joined to the heavenly Bridegroom.

VERSE 14.—“And from there.” Whoever separates himself from the Church through the filth of vices is deservedly thrust into the second chambers, where the king’s concubines remain. For a fall from sound faith deserves a descent in honor, and such a person no longer has power to return to the king unless, visited by heavenly grace, he is restored to his former state of dignity.

VERSE 15.—“When it had passed.” That is, when the five ages of the world had passed, during which the succession of the fathers had advanced, the sixth age was approaching with the coming of the Redeemer. In it the multitude of the Gentiles was to be called through the Gospel.

VERSE 16.—“Tebeeth.” Among the Hebrews, Xudimos among the Greeks, and January among the Latins. In this month the Lord, having become incarnate, was circumcised on the eighth day, worshiped by the magi, and honored with mystical gifts; in it he is also proclaimed to have been baptized by John.

VERSE 19.—“And when the second time.” It is not enough for Christ to join to himself the primitive Church; through preachers he also acquired a great multitude from the Gentiles. Hence: “I have other sheep which are not,” etc. (John X).

VERSE 21.—“The king’s two eunuchs,” etc. The two eunuchs may signify schismatics and heretics. Carrying the poison of deceit and malice in their hearts, they plot against the truth in order to take it away from believers and kill Christ—that is, the faith of Christ—in those believers. But holy teachers expose their wickedness, so that the innocent may be saved and the guilty punished by a just retribution.

VERSE 23.—“It was recorded before the king in the histories and annals,” etc. In the two Testaments, in which it is written what rewards are due to the just and what punishments to the unjust. Hence: “These will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matt. XXV). And in Ezekiel: “The righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him” (Ezek. XVIII).

## CHAPTER III

[Col. 0743C]

VERSE 1.—“Haman the son.” The powerful of this world, abusing the benefits conferred by divine power, disdain to regard as partners in grace those whom they have as partners in nature. They strive to transfer to themselves the honor and reverence owed to God alone. Those who refuse to consent they persecute with hatred and torments; but by God’s just judgment the wicked are caught in their own snares. Hence it is said: “The righteous is delivered from trouble, and the wicked is handed over in his place” (Prov. XI).

Haman—whom Josephus records as being of the stock of Amalek—may represent the people of the Jews. They killed the prophets, the Lord of the prophets, and the apostles; through unbelief and hardness of heart they lost the nobility of their lineage. Through Isaiah they are called “princes of Sodom” and “people of Gomorrah.” Hence Ezekiel: “Your father was an Amorite, and your mother a Hittite.”

VERSE 7.—“The lot was cast.” Those who belong to the Lord’s lot are killed; they are signified by the goat that, according to the Lord’s lot, was killed under the Law.

VERSE 10.—“Therefore he took.” As Haman, sending letters, tries to seal them with the king’s signet so that his desire might be accomplished more easily, so the Jews take as testimony the books of the divine Law, in which is the signet of the supreme King—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—for the advancement of their heresy, rejecting fellowship with the Gentiles and the Gospel of Christ as though it were contrary to the divine commandments.

## CHAPTER IV

[Col. 0744A]

VERSE 2.—“As far as the doors.” Thus the teacher of the Church, through the intercession of the queen—of whom it is said, “The queen stood at your right hand” (Ps. XIV), etc.—who partly journeys as a pilgrim in the world and partly reigns with the Lord, desires to be heard by the King of all ages.

“For not.” No one can enter the heavenly court while subject to the corruption of the present life. Before death, each person must knock at the entrance of the kingdom through chastisement of the body and contrition of heart, so that afterward he may enter the heavenly palace rejoicing.

If anyone asks how the most just King inflicts torments upon the innocent, let him know that this does not proceed from a desire for malice but from the command of the highest counsel. “For wisdom conquers wickedness” (Wis. VII); “it reaches mightily from one end to the other and orders all things sweetly” (ibid., VIII); “Whatever he willed, he did in heaven and in all the depths” (Ps. CXIII). By his just judgment it comes about that the faithful are handed over to the hands of persecutors, either for purification, correction, or the increase of their merits. Thus Job is handed over to Satan; Paul is buffeted by an angel of Satan.

“And again.” Mordecai and Esther, that is, teachers and disciples, pray for one another, just as Paul prays for his disciples and begs that prayers be offered for him; thus in the Acts of the Apostles the Church prayed without ceasing for Peter.

## CHAPTER V

VERSE 2.—“The golden scepter.” The power of governance, or the cross of the Passion, through which he acquired power, of which it is said: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). And elsewhere: “For this reason he exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name” (Phil. II).

VERSE 8.—“If I have found favor in your sight.” The delay in making a request is not counted as sluggishness but as patience. For reward will be given to good and evil in the future, not in the present. “Tomorrow” is used for the future; hence: “Do not be anxious about tomorrow.” And Jacob says in Genesis: “Tomorrow my righteousness will appear to me” (Matt. VI). And of the lamb it is said: “Nothing of it shall remain until morning” (Gen. XXX). When judgment comes, it will be revealed in what kind of garment each person entered the feast.

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 0744D]

VERSE 1.—“The king spent that night sleepless,” etc. Remaining in himself while the course of time and the actions of all things move, he contemplates everything, and no thought is hidden from him, for all things are present to him. Hence the Apostle: “In him there is not ‘was’ and ‘is,’ but there is always ‘is’” (2 Cor. I).

VERSE 2.—“It came to pass.” The deeds of Mordecai are recalled before the king, because the good works of holy teachers will never be given over to oblivion, but “the righteous will be in eternal remembrance.”

VERSE 10.—“Hurry.” The teachers of the Church, illuminated by the worship of every virtue and by the beauty of wisdom, are honored with the diadem of royal dignity as members of the supreme King. They mount the royal horse, that is, the faithful people in whose hearts the King of angels resides. Hence the prophet Habakkuk: “You mounted upon your horses, and your riding is salvation.”

Haman, the particular enemy of the people of God, although unwillingly, offers them this service, just as persecutors of the Church are compelled to bear witness to the Church, being unable to conceal what is manifest.

“And so he took.” This is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High: the one who seemed more glorious appears beneath others as more lowly and inferior, according to the saying: “He has cast down the mighty from their thrones and exalted the humble.” Isaiah likewise says: “Lebanon will be turned into Carmel, and Carmel will be reckoned as a forest.” Thus the pride of the synagogue was brought low, while the humility of the Church was exalted. Thus the persecutors of the faith were reduced to nothing, while the confessors of Christ were exalted throughout the world. The head was turned into the tail and the tail into the head: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke XXIV).

## CHAPTER VII

“On the second day,” etc. But when Esther disclosed her request, the condemned man withdrew to punishment. In the Gospel, both a midday meal and a supper are mentioned. The midday meal signifies the present time of the Church, while the supper signifies the eternal and final banquet. Hence, when the wicked have been separated, the good rejoice forever. Haman, because he did not possess a garment worthy of the feast, deserved to be cast outside.

[Col. 0745C]

VERSE 7.—“He entered the garden.” As the king hastened into the garden—that is, as he invited the elect with himself to the delights of paradise—Haman strove to entreat the queen for his own safety, but he did not have an opportune moment. Remedies for salvation are sought too late when the dangers of death are imminent. Hence Solomon: “Then they will call, and I will not answer them; they will rise early, and they will not find me” (Prov. I).

VERSE 8.—“And immediately.” Haman’s supplication is called oppression, because on the day of judgment the prayer of the wicked is an irritation. Hence: “When he is judged, let him go forth condemned” (Ps. CVIII), etc. Then the oppression with which they oppressed the humble will be reproached to them.

VERSE 9.—“Harbona.” He signifies the teachers of the Law, who foretold the crimes and deceits of the Jews. Hence Moses: “I know that after my death you will act wickedly and turn aside from the way that I showed you” (Deut. XXXI). And in the Gospel: “There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you hope” (John V).

“In Haman’s house.” Haman signifies the wicked raging against Christ and persecuting his Church. Christ had been promised to them in the Law. Therefore the Law, which had been given for the preservation of life, was turned for them into death. Through it they attempted to destroy Christ and kill his confessors; and those who wished through the Law to oppress the innocent received, when the Law itself accused them, the sentence of a just judgment. Those who sinned under the Law will be avenged through the Law.

## CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 0746A]

VERSE 1.—“On that day.” Esther possesses the house of Haman, the enemy of the Jews, when the Church possesses the world formerly possessed by the devil, the enemy of Christians. Hence: “When the strong man, armed, guards his courtyard” (Luke XI), etc. Mordecai enters before the king’s presence when the souls of the saints daily pass from their dwelling in the present life into contemplation of the divine majesty.

“Haman’s house.” The dignity and honor that the Jews possessed through knowledge of the Law and the prophets and through the worship of religion. Hence in Proverbs: “The substance of the sinner is kept for the righteous” (Prov. XIII). And in the Gospel: “The kingdom will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

[Col. 0746B]

VERSE 2.—“And the king took.” When the diligence of the teachers is praised and proclaimed, they receive grace upon grace from the Lord in the sight of the Creator of all. Hence: “He nourished the hearts of the faithful.”

“He gave it to Mordecai.” To the preachers of the Gentiles, so that they might cling to him and minister to the Gentiles.

VERSE 3.—“She fell at his feet,” etc. Because the holy Church, for the deliverance of her children, daily entreats almighty God through faith and the mysteries of the Incarnation, asking that the boldness of her enemies be restrained and the innocence of the faithful be freed.

VERSE 5.—“I beg that.” The evangelical doctrine preached throughout the world in the name of Christ is declared to be confirmed by the seal of the Holy Spirit. Filled with this gift, the preachers remained unconquerable and glorious triumphers over their enemies.

VERSE 9.—“And having summoned the scribes,” etc. The doctrine of the Gospel was so established through the writers of the New Testament, with the Lord’s assistance, that the faith of the Holy Trinity is fully contained in it and the complete perfection of the Decalogue is demonstrated in the two commandments of charity.

“Which is one hundred and twenty.” The whole world is signified by this number. For the number ten, multiplied by twelve, makes one hundred and twenty; when seven is added to it, the fullness of the entire sum is completed. Thus observance of the Decalogue, spread throughout the whole world by apostolic tradition, is poured into the hearts of the faithful—or brought to completion—through the grace of the sevenfold Spirit.

VERSE 11.—“That they should kill,” etc. So that shoots of an evil stock might not sprout again. Likewise, the Lord commanded the seven nations inhabiting the promised land to be killed, and afterward ordered the Amalekites to be completely destroyed, so as to remove every occasion of scandal from them. Hence David says: “In the morning I was killing” (Ps. C), etc.

VERSE 14.—“In Susa,” etc. In the subjugation of the world’s pride. For Susa is interpreted as “riding” or “overturning.” Hence the Savior says: “Take courage; I have conquered the world” (John XVI).

## CHAPTER IX

VERSE 4.—“They had recognized that he had great power.” The praiseworthy activity and power of virtues possessed by teachers confer honor and reverence upon the multitude of the faithful. Hence in the Acts of the Apostles: “Many wonders and signs were being performed” (Acts V); and elsewhere it is read: “Fear came upon every soul” (ibid., II). Likewise: “No one dared to join them, but the people magnified them” (ibid., V).

VERSE 5.—“Therefore the Jews struck.” Not only does the divine judgment of the Holy Spirit judge the other workers of iniquity—those who persist in sins and do not care to receive remission of sins—to be condemned, but it also judges the carnal Jews, transgressors of the Decalogue, who will experience in the cities of hell the guilt of Christ’s cross that they incurred through unbelief.

VERSE 6.—“These are their names.” We do not labor greatly to seek the interpretations of these names, nor do we force them to serve allegory. The type exists in part, not in the whole. For if it exists in the whole, it is not history. The historical interpreter ought to set forth the true sequence of the deed, neither stopping short nor proceeding beyond it; the allegorical interpreter ought to choose distinguished features that accord with the spiritual sense.

VERSE 16.—“To such an extent.” All who receive the Law carnally through the five bodily senses and refuse to understand it spiritually, although it is especially full and perfect through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit, are as though defeated and thrown down over two days.

VERSE 17.—“But the day.” It should be noted that some Jews kill on the thirteenth day and cease on the fourteenth, keeping the solemnity; others kill over two days, that is, on the thirteenth and fourteenth of the same month, and rest solemnly on the fifteenth. For some of the saints, after completing the labors by which they serve God through right belief and right living, already possess in their souls the Sabbath of eternal rest before the time of judgment. Others remain in the flesh until the final day of resurrection; after all enemies have been overcome, they are suddenly changed and receive rest of soul and body. Hence the Apostle: “The dead who are in Christ will rise first. Then we who live, who remain, will rise with them to meet Christ in the air” (1 Thess. IV), etc.

For the fourteenth day, which contains twice seven, signifies the perfect rest of souls; the fifteenth, which embraces seven and eight, signifies the rest of souls and bodies.

VERSE 24.—“And he cast Pur,” etc. The lot cast into an urn signifies the arrangement of any matter in the human mind, though its outcome is governed not by human judgment but by divine decision. Hence Solomon: “Lots are cast into the lap, but they are directed by the Lord” (Prov. XVI).

VERSE 28.—“These are the days.” Because the rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies are rightly and firmly guarded and celebrated by the faithful; or because the keeping of a festival is rightly and firmly observed by the faithful on account of the rest of souls and the resurrection of bodies.

## CHAPTER X

VERSE 1.—“Now King Ahasuerus imposed tribute on all.” Christ, who, cut from the mountain without hands, grew into a great mountain and filled the whole world. Historically, however, he did not make the whole earth tributary, because he did not possess it.

(In ancient copies of the Ordinary Gloss, no exposition of the sacred text is attached from this point to the end of the book. Therefore we omit chapters 11–16.)

[Col. 0747]

# THE BOOK OF JOB (G)*

## TWO PROLOGUES OF BLESSED JEROME ON THE BOOK OF JOB

(See among the works of Blessed Jerome.)

## ARGUMENT

[Col. 0747D]

Job is said to have lived in the land of Hus, on the borders of Idumea and Arabia; formerly his name was Jobab. He took an Arabian woman as his wife and begot a son whom he called Ennon. He himself was a son of Zara, one of the sons of Esau; on his mother’s side he was from Bosra, so that he was the fifth descendant from Abraham. These are the kings who reigned in Edom, in which land he himself also reigned. The first to reign there was Bela, son of Beor; the name of his city was Denaba. After Bela came Jobab, who is called Job. After Job came Husan, who was a leader from the region of the Temanites. After him reigned Adad, son of Badad, who defeated Midian in the field of Moab; the name of his city was Avith.

## INTRODUCTORY MATTERS ON JOB

(From Gregory’s Commentary on Job, passim.)

[Col. 0748D]

Some things here are said historically, allegorically, and morally. Some cannot be taken literally, because they would be erroneous, impossible, or contradictory to one another. Such is the statement: “Under him those who bear up the world are bent” (Job IX), as though giants carried the world; and: “My soul chose hanging” (ibid., VII), as though one so patient wished to end his life by hanging; and: “Let the day perish on which I was born” (ibid., III), etc.

Sometimes one who neglects the literal sense hides from himself the light of truth: while seeking inwardly for something else, he loses what lies outwardly. Thus, when Scripture speaks of works of mercy—“If I denied what the poor desired” (Job XXXI)—he may seek an allegory. For divine speech, just as it wisely exercises the learned in its mysteries, so it refreshes the simple on its surface; it is like a river, both shallow and deep, in which a lamb may walk and an elephant swim.

The Law was given to a man who had gone astray. One who disobeys the Law is confounded by the example of a man who lived lawfully without the Law. Hence Isaiah says: “Be ashamed, Sidon” (Isa. XXIII)—that is, “the stability of those established in the Law”—“the sea says”: the Gentile people, which, while keeping the Law, rebukes those who hear the Law.

Moses is said to have written these things about Job as though about someone who came before him, because in Genesis Jobab is read to have descended from Esau and to have succeeded Balak, son of Beor, in the kingdom. But it is the custom of sacred eloquence, in its earlier parts, briefly to touch upon events that will occur much later, while it hastens toward other matters. Job therefore did not live before the Law but in the time of the Judges, since he is more plausibly believed to have written the account of his victory himself.

Nor is it a problem that Scripture says Job said or did these things, because it is the custom of the saints to speak of themselves as though of others. For it is the Spirit who speaks in them as though about others. Thus Moses’ angel is sometimes called an angel, as one who serves outwardly, and sometimes the Lord, who presides inwardly. Hence David says: “Attend, my people, to my law” (Ps. LXXVII). David was neither the people nor the Law; rather, these words belong to the one who speaks in him.

And he wished prophecy to be given by a Gentile as well as by a Jew, since he had come for both peoples.

Fruitless loquacity, like leaves of words, is cut away from divine things, while the planting of a grove in the temple of God is forbidden. It is unworthy that the words of the heavenly oracle should be confined beneath the rules of Donatus.

Job’s virtue, during his great tranquility, was known to himself and to God; but when stirred by blows, it gives off fragrance for us like spices. Hence the faithful are compared to a grain of mustard seed, which is mild when uncrushed, but when ground becomes hot, revealing what was hidden within it. Hence in the Psalm: “By day the Lord commanded his mercy, and by night he declared it” (Ps. XLI). The gift of mercy, received in the tranquility of day, is said to be manifested in the night of adversity.

He is also scourged so that he might learn to give thanks amid evils, something that was certainly lacking in him. What the enemy requested for evil, God permitted for good. Let no one suppose that any words of Job should be condemned, since God commends him so greatly, and in him, as though in the midst, the devil contends against God.

When he recounts his good deeds, this is not arrogance; through them he strengthens himself so as not to despair, since the many evils and reproaches of his friends were forcing him to despair of life. Job is struck by every kind of temptation: by the loss of possessions, through which he was thought likely to be shaken because he was powerful in the world—but he despises these; by the loss of his children—but he grieves this with equanimity; by the striking of his flesh, which he endures patiently. These were like the external assault of war, like enemies fighting from the front.

Within, however, through his wife as through a fellow citizen, his mind endures the poisons of counsel; yet he also teaches her wisely.

His friends come for consolation but rush forward to rebuke. Among them the youngest, because he is unworthy, rebukes him more sharply, since words sometimes trouble more than wounds. Behold, enemies from the flank. Through wounds his patience is tested; through words his wisdom is exercised. The former he overcame by strength, the latter by reason.

Job’s friends sinned more through ignorance than through malice. Such a great man did not have wicked friends; rather, because they could not discern the cause of his blows, they fell into guilt. One kind of striking falls upon the wicked so that they may be punished; another, so that they may be corrected; another, so that they may not commit future sins; another, so that when salvation comes, the one saved may love the Savior more deeply.

When a good person is struck, merits increase. The friends, not knowing how to distinguish these forms, believed that the one struck had been struck because of guilt. Thus they return more quickly to forgiveness: God humbles them here so that they might receive grace only through the one whom they had despised.

Like all the righteous, Job prefigured Christ not only in words but also in deeds, showing through his passion the Christ who would suffer—that is, the head together with the body, which is the Church.

His wife signifies the carnal, who, the closer they are within the Church through faith, oppress more harshly by their manner of life. Job’s friends signify heretics, who wish to deceive under the appearance of giving advice and who, while speaking as though on behalf of the Lord, oppose the truth.

Job is called “the sorrowing one,” through whom the passion of Christ or the labor of the Church is expressed. Eliphaz means “contempt of the Lord,” that is, heretics who, while holding false opinions about God, contemptuously reject him in their pride.

Baldath means “mere antiquity,” because they speak not with good intention but from a desire for glory—that is, not from the zeal of the new man but from the perversity of the old life.

Sophar means “the scattering of the watchtower,” or “the one who scatters the watchman,” because heretics desire to strike with words the minds that contemplate heavenly things.

By despising God, therefore, they remain in oldness; while remaining there, they harm those who contemplate through their evil speeches. But because they too sometimes return to the Church, this is shown by the reconciliation of the friends, for whom Job prays. The sacrifices of heretics are not acceptable to God unless they are offered by the hands of the Church.

Seven sacrifices are offered for them because, when they receive the sevenfold Spirit, they are cleansed as though by seven offerings. Bulls and rams are offered for them: in the bull, the neck of pride is signified; in the ram, leadership of the flock. For, withdrawing from the Church through pride, they dragged weak flocks after them. This is killed in them when they return to Job, that is, to the Church.

Through Elihu, who speaks with a correct understanding but turns toward words of exaltation, an arrogant yet nevertheless faithful person is represented. He is rebuked, but he is not restored through sacrifice, because he is conquered by the truth of faith, while his swelling pride is displeasing. Hence Elihu is interpreted as “My God” or “Our God.” Although proud, he nevertheless confesses openly through true belief both God in his divinity and the Lord in his incarnation.

After all these calamities, he received double, because the Church also receives a double portion here for its labors: having accepted the Gentiles, at the end it converts the Jews as well, and in the future it will be endowed with a double garment, that is, the blessedness of soul and body. Hence the Prophet says: “In their land they shall possess double” (Isa. LXI). This is said to Job in his affliction; but how long it will last is not stated, because it is known that the Church must be afflicted, but how long this will be is unknown. Hence: “It is not yours to know the times or moments which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts I).

## CHAPTER ONE

### VERSE 1

“There was a man in the land of Hus.” (GREGORY, *Commentary on Job*, vol. I.) Through Job, Christ—that is, the head and the body—is signified. Therefore, after seeing in the head what we are to believe, let us see from the body what we are to retain by contemplation.

GREGORY (ibid.): “Job in the land of Hus,” etc., up to “and the crafty things were gathered together afterward.”

[Col. 0751B] (Id., ibid.) His character is described as suitable before his battle is mentioned, so that he may appear capable of conquering.

“Simple.” It is necessary that the simplicity of the dove be instructed by the serpent’s cunning, and that cunning be tempered by simplicity. Hence the Spirit appeared in a dove and in fire: those filled with him devote themselves to the gentleness of simplicity in such a way that they are inflamed against evil by zeal for righteousness.

“Fearing God.” Solomon says: “Whoever fears God neglects nothing” (Eccl. VII).

(Ibid.) Solomon also says: “Whoever offends in one matter will lose many good things” (Eccl. IX). The animals called legal are those that are clean according to the law: they both chew the cud and divide the hoof. Camels possess one of these characteristics but lack the other, and thus they both conform to the law and diverge from it.

### VERSE 3

(Ibid.) “And a very large household.” An innumerable throng of thoughts which, like maidservants, abandon their work and clamor when their mistress—that is, reason—is absent; but when she returns, they work in silence. If we rule them well, the mind is not overcome by their multitude.

“Among them all,” that is, among the angels who cleave to the rising light, we are great, their companions. All who are in Christ through faith are eastern, concerning whom the Prophet says: “His name is Rising” (Zech. VI). The God-man surpasses them all.

### VERSE 4

“And they held a feast,” etc. (Ibid.) “The sons hold feasts,” etc., up to “because, trembling at everything, he grows sluggish in good works.”

[Col. 0751D] “Throughout their houses, each one,” etc. “Throughout their houses”: Peter throughout Rome, Philip in Samaria, each in his own day, that is, according to the measure of understanding. Paul established one order among the Greeks and Peter another among the Romans, although they did not disagree in faith.

“Three sisters,” that is, faith, hope, and charity. In everything they do, they summon the virtues so that they may rejoice in it. As though from food, they draw strength when they become more confident through good works; as though from drink after food, they become intoxicated when they desire to be infused with the dew of contemplation.

Yet evils also arise from these very goods, such as exaltation; or, when the mind rejoices over them, a certain security is also present, and from this comes sluggishness. Therefore it follows: “And when the days had gone round.” After the feast, to sanctify the sons is to direct the heart’s intention after the experience of the virtues, and to cleanse everything that is done by strict reconsideration, lest one be deceived by the quality of evil, so that evil things are thought good; or by the quantity of good, so that something is judged sufficient when it has not been perfected. But this is discovered better by prayer than by examination. For the mind, raised through compunction, judges everything beneath it more surely.

### VERSE 5

“And when the days had gone round,” etc. The days of the feast go round when the mysteries are carried out through preaching. When all has been completed, Job offers sacrifice for his sons, because Christ prayed to the Father for the apostles returning from their preaching, and, by sending the Holy Spirit, sanctified them, cleansing whatever fault might have been present.

[Col. 0752B] (Ibid.) “He rises at dawn who is of compunction,” etc., up to “which, once completed, require purification.”

(Ibid.) “A holocaust is called something wholly burned,” etc., up to “may cover him before the eyes of God until the end of life.”

### VERSE 6

“Now on a certain day.” (GREGORY, *Moral Commentary on Job*, book II, chapter 2.) At the beginning, the quality and outcome of a matter are expressed. Thus, in this passage, Job’s temptation is said to have begun from a day, because it is spoken of with a view to victory, as also elsewhere.

Sometimes the matter is signified by the quality of the time: thus the angels appear to Abraham at midday, while Judas goes out at night. Sometimes by place: thus Israel, being weak, hears the law not on the mountain but below. Sometimes by the quality of the air: thus it is said, “It was winter,” when he is preaching to those who will not believe, and “it was cold,” when Peter’s denial is imminent. Sometimes by the position of the body: thus Stephen saw Jesus standing.

(Ibid.) “It is not said that something was done before the Lord,” etc., up to “by which King Ahab is deceived according to the demands of his merits.”

“He appeared among them.” (Ibid.) “On the day the Lord saw Satan,” etc., up to “as a blind man does not see the light by which he is illumined.”

“And Satan also among them.” Because he inserts himself among the good thoughts that come from God in order to disturb them; but God reveals him to us when he is hidden. Hence it is said: “From where have you come?” To say this is to disclose his snares to us.

“I have gone around the earth.” He searches carnal hearts in order to insert evil. He does not fly over them but walks through them, because he does not quickly abandon the one he tempts; rather, he lingers so as to imprint the traces of depravity. Against him Job is praised: “Have you considered my servant?” God makes him good and strengthens him, praising him, as it were, in Satan’s hearing. Hence Satan rages against him more fiercely, saying: “Is it for nothing?”—as though to say, “Why do you praise the one whom you protect? He would deserve praise if, disregarding me, he stood by his own strength.” Therefore he maliciously asks: “But stretch out your hand a little.” When good things abound, the mind is raised somewhat, as though the good came from itself; the devil desires this good in an evil way. But God permits a person to be tested beneficially, so that when he is shaken amid those good things, he recognizes his weakness and is established in God. Hence it follows: “Behold, everything that he has is in your hand.”

### VERSE 7

“To whom the Lord said,” etc. (Ibid.) [Col. 0753A] “Not the Lord,” etc., up to “which is to pant with the heats of his malice for the affliction of the good.”

“From where have you come?” (Greek.) He does not ask this of the good, because we ask only about what we do not know; and God’s not knowing is rejection, just as a good man is said not to know how to lie—not because he does not know, but because he rejects it. Therefore, to say “From where have you come?” is to reject his ways as though they were unknown.

“I have gone around the earth.” A circuitous journey signifies the anxiety of labor. He who labored went around the earth; he did not remain peacefully in heaven. He does not fly over it but walks through it, because he fell from the flight of spiritual power, weighed down by the great burden of his own malice. It is also said of his members: “The wicked walk in a circuit” (Ps. XI), that is, they are wearied by labor among external things.

The devil contends not against Job but, in the midst of Job, against God. Hence he did not first ask God for Job; rather, God praised him in Satan’s presence.

### VERSE 9

“Does Job fear God for nothing?” etc. (Ibid.) The devil had perceived that the Redeemer had come, but because of the lowly things he suffered, whatever he had suspected concerning his divinity became doubtful to him through his own pride. He believed not that God had been born, but that a mere man had been protected by God’s grace.

“Have you not hedged him in?” He says that the house was hedged about because, while tempting him, he could not penetrate his conscience; and that his possessions were hedged about because he did not dare to attack God’s elect.

“His possession has increased.” As though he were saying: “Because he has received so many good things on earth, he behaves innocently on their account. But he would not be innocent if he stood firm amid adversity.” Since he cannot test Job by day, he wants to condemn him in the night of adversity. Therefore he asks that Job be tested, knowing that adversity more truly proves everyone—not Job’s strength, but the one who is being tested.

“But stretch out”—he does not attribute to himself the power of striking. His will is always wicked, and this comes from him; the just power comes from God. Hence it is said: “The evil spirit of the Lord was upon Saul”: it is of the Lord by permission, and evil by will.

“Hand.” He complains that the number of the faithful is increasing through the preaching of the apostles. For Satan to say this is to think such things with envy and to grieve, wasting away with sorrow over them.

### VERSE 11

“But stretch out your hand.” (Ibid.) He asks that the external things be struck, because he considers them of little importance unless he injures the soul.

“Into his face.” The face of the Lord is the regard of grace. Therefore he says: “If you take away what he loves, he will not seek your regard—that is, the favor of your grace—but will despise you by cursing.”

### VERSE 12

“Then the Lord said.” (Ibid.) God is not overcome because the devil provokes him by his request. Rather, he grants the enemy, for the enemy’s own pain and deception, what will benefit his servant.

“Behold, everything that he has,” etc. He releases and restrains with a merciful dispensation: he exposes his possessions but protects his body, although he will later hand over the body as well. He does not hand everything over at once, lest things accumulated together destroy what can be endured when divided. Alternatively, the Lord knew Job’s lot and nevertheless divided the battles, so that Job might be more wonderfully victorious when the defeated enemy prepared himself again for new wars.

“Behold, everything … only against him,” etc., that is, “I grant that his goods be tested externally, but I preserve him within for myself.”

“But stretch out.” (Ibid.) He thought that Christ could sin through his sufferings.

“Behold, everything that he has is in your hand.” Satan’s hand is not power but temptation. First, Judea, which had been his possession, was taken from him through unbelief and turned against him; afterward, Christ’s flesh was crucified.

“He went out.” That is, he reached the object of his desire. Or, he goes out when he carries out with evil intent what has been permitted to him for a good purpose.

“Satan went out.” Where did he go out from, if God is everywhere? As long as Satan was restrained by God’s power, he could not carry out what he desired; he stood, as it were, before God’s face. He goes out when he is released to bring his desire into effect.

[Col. 0754B] “And he went out from the presence.” Because, unable to prevail as far as the heart, he wanders outside, excluded from the inner parts. If he disturbs the mind, he is outside, because he does not destroy but instructs.

(Ibid.) The times correspond to the temptations. He chose a suitable time for testing when he found Job’s sons at a feast: the joy of satiety foretells tribulation.

### VERSE 13

“Now on a certain day, while his sons and daughters,” etc. The apostles and all the faithful are meant. The elder son is the Jewish people, generated by the law; the younger is the Gentile people, called at the end.

Thus, in the house of the firstborn, the apostles feast, because they were still feeding on the delights of sacred Scripture within the gathering of the Jewish people alone. To them it was then said: “Do not go on the way of the Gentiles” (Matt. X).

“They were eating and drinking,” etc. To eat is to rejoice in good works; to drink wine is to burn with heavenly desire.

“Of their firstborn brother,” etc. Wisdom is born first in the heart, etc., up to “so that what the preoccupied mind lost, it may recover when afflicted.”

### VERSE 14

“The oxen were plowing,” etc. (Ibid.) The plowing oxen signify the good who work well; the female asses signify those who live simply. They are beside the oxen because they are nourished by their understanding.

The Sabaeans, who take captives, signify demons; the servants signify beginners, not yet possessing manly steadfastness. They strike them with the sword, that is, with despair of eternity.

The messenger who escapes is the prophetic word, which says: “My people have been led captive, because they had no knowledge” (Isa. V). When the evils he foretold occur, he returns to the Lord as though sound: once the weak have been taken captive, he is recognized as having foretold the truth.

### VERSE 15

“And the servants.” He calls servants that careful vigilance by which he provides for these things; this vigilance too is struck in him.

### VERSE 16

“The fire of God fell from heaven.” Heaven signifies the teachers of the law, the priests, from whom the fire of envy falls upon the sheep and servants, that is, the innocent and the weak.

The servant returns unharmed because, when the prophecy proves to have spoken truly, zeal seizes the uneducated people.

(Ibid.) The sheep signify the innocence of thoughts. Fire from heaven—that is, from the aerial powers—means that a flame of envy rushes upon them and often kindles pure thoughts with the heat of lust.
