It is God’s fire, not because he causes it, but because he permits it. And because vigilance is overwhelmed by a sudden assault, the guardians—the servants—are killed. But discernment alone, that is, reason, reports the losses to the mind and summons the Lord, as it were, to lamentation.

### VERSE 17

“The Chaldaeans acted,” etc. The Chaldaeans are interpreted as “the fierce,” etc., up to “these struck the servants with the sword, that is, with sinister persuasion,” etc.

“The camels,” etc. The camel is a clean animal in part, etc., up to “and discernment alone reports to the mind what it should mourn.”

“To tell you,” etc. The evils are announced as numerous and sudden, so that, when wound is inflicted upon wound, he may bear them impatiently. The crafty enemy tests him not so much by the loss of his possessions as by the order in which the news is delivered.

First he announces the lesser evils, then greater ones, and finally the death of the sons, lest the loss of possessions should seem insignificant once he was bereaved and had no heirs for whom he could preserve them. Thus he hears the worse things gradually, so that every wound may find a place in his heart.

### VERSE 18

“Your sons,” etc. (GREGORY.) The sons and daughters, as has been said, are the apostles and the subject peoples who were feeding on Scripture in Judea.

“The wind,” that is, a powerful temptation, bursts forth from the desert—that is, from the hearts of the Jews or from unclean spirits—and shakes the four corners on which the house stands: the priests, scribes, elders of the people, and Pharisees.

The house—that is, Judea—falling in the Lord’s persecution, overwhelms the apostles in despair. The saying is truly about the persecuting people: “My beloved has committed many crimes in my house” (Jer. XI). And about the apostles: “My friends have stood far away” (Ps. XXXVII). Also: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered” (Matt. XXVI), etc.

“In the house of his firstborn brother,” that is, at the feast of the elder brother, Satan overwhelms the sons. Through the negligence of the elders, he seeks an entrance into the death of the younger; and he gains greater strength against others when he sees those who preside over others through vigilance serving pleasure.

They were not, indeed, devoted to their belly; but when, amid feasting, the mind’s good intention burns less fervently, it foresees less.

### VERSE 19

“Suddenly a wind.” (Ibid.) It is said obscurely that he moved the elements against Job whose nod moves them, although the devil, once he has received power from God, is permitted to disturb the elements for the use of his wickedness, just as fire and water serve those condemned in metal.

[Col. 0755D] “From the region of the desert.” The region of the desert, etc., up to “he shows the anger named in the air: the wind rushes upon them.”

### VERSE 20

“Then Job rose and tore his garments.” (Ibid.) When the house collapses, etc., up to “so that the whole heart, burning with the love of God, may consume them through the perfection of devotion.”

“And having shaved his head.” Great steadfastness is thought to be present, etc., up to “and show that he consented to divine power.”

“Falling upon the ground.” (GREGORY.) He fell and worshiped, because the one who humbly sees that he is dust offers true prayer.

Hence he also says: “Naked I came out of my mother’s womb.” The first grace generated him naked in faith; that same grace receives him naked. When, struck by vices, he flees naked to mercy, and, having at some time been exposed through a virtue, he is better clothed by that very humility: attributing to God, not to himself, what he has.

“The Lord gave, and the Lord has also taken away.” This happens for a time so that he may possess the goods more humbly.

### VERSE 21

“Naked I came out.” The earth brought me forth naked when I entered this life; naked the earth will receive me when I leave it.

There is consolation in the condition of things: he has not lost what was his own, but remembers that he received what he must leave behind. He looks ahead to the time when he did not yet possess these things and to what he will be like when he departs. He also consoles himself through God’s justice.

“From my mother’s womb.” The mother of Christ is the Synagogue, which held him within itself, covered by the letter, and did not see him naked in his divinity; but from it he came naked to the Gentiles.

Behold Joseph, whom the Synagogue, believing him to be merely human, tried to embrace adulterously. He left it the covering of the letter and made himself visible to the Gentiles. But he will return naked when, at the end of the world, God makes himself known to the remnant of Israel.

“The Lord gave.” Judea took him away while it believed that he was to come; when he came, it despised him.

“As it pleased the Lord.” When we are troubled, we must return to God’s judgment and offer greater praise, because we recognize more truly that we are being struck.

### VERSE 22

“In all these things Job did not sin.” (Ibid.) A grieving mind must guard itself, etc., up to “his heart did not swell, his mouth did not murmur, and his tongue was not rebellious.”

## CHAPTER TWO

### VERSES 1–2

“Now it came to pass,” etc. “From where have you come?” (GREGORY, *Commentary on Job*, book III.) This is not as before, etc., up to “you who wished to diminish him have served his progress.”

### VERSE 3

“His innocence.” He retains his innocence who, even after falling, awakened by a spark of reason, repents faithfully.

(Ibid.) How was the Father moved against Christ, who is one with him, through Satan? Christ as man would not have suffered unless Adam had sinned. When Satan moved Adam, he moved against Christ God.

It was in vain, because Christ bore punishment without his own fault; but it was not in vain, because he paid what another had seized.

### VERSE 4

“Skin for skin.” Through the miracles, the devil had recognized the Son of God, but because of his lowly condition he thought him a mere man. Judging him, then, by the example of others who, in the place of shepherds, disregard the losses of others, he says that he was not moved when many things were taken away; as though he were testing by the pain of his own flesh one who suffers over things external to himself, as though he grieved for himself and not for others.

When he asks that this be done, he speaks of desires. He brought these things upon him through his limbs, words, and desires, by which he said: “Let us put wood into his bread” (Jer. XI), that is, by fastening a stake of the cross to his body, let us apply it to him.

(Ibid.) “Skin for skin” is given because, often, when a blow comes toward the eye, we place our hand in the way so that we may be wounded in the hand rather than in the more delicate eye. Knowing that this is customarily done, he says: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has.” As though he were saying: “For this reason Job endures so many blows outside himself with equanimity: because he fears being struck himself. Concern for himself makes him feel less for his own possessions.” Therefore he asks to strike Job himself: “Stretch out your hand,” which God rightly permits, so that the defeated one may often fall silent.

### VERSE 5

“Otherwise, stretch out your hand.” Often, after the devil has attacked the mind, he withdraws for a time so that he may break in suddenly upon the unsuspecting. Therefore he asks again for Job, and God grants this by remaining silent.

“And touch his mouth.” By mouth and flesh he understands bodily life; by soul he understands reason, as above.

### VERSE 6

“Behold, he is in your hand.” Satan had power through his agents over Christ’s flesh, but he preserves his soul—not because he does not tempt it, but because he does not overcome it.

Or “soul” signifies those dear to him and chosen by him, whom he loses from his own jurisdiction when he kills him from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head. From the beginning of the world he inflicted harsh things upon his members and, raging, reached even to the head of those members, that is, Christ.

“Behold, he is in your hand.” He permits us to be tempted so that we may recognize ourselves as weak, while nevertheless guarding us.

### VERSE 7

“So Satan went out.” (GREGORY.) Having received permission, etc., up to “by repenting, he looks back, lest exaltation arise.”

### VERSE 8

“Who scraped the discharge with a potsherd.” (Ibid.) A potsherd is made from clay, etc., up to “but worse are those who are led by exaltation, like Job’s wife, who counsels her husband proudly.”

### VERSE 9

“His wife said to him.” (Ibid.) He displays the devil’s first temptation, etc., up to “but they lapse into harshness.”

“Do you still persist in your simplicity?” She reproves his simplicity because he despises earthly things and desires eternal ones, as though saying: “Why do you seek eternal things so simply and groan so grievously over them? Abandon them—despise the eternal—and escape your present evils, even by dying.”

But those who were patterns of righteousness endured such things. Hence he says: “As one of the foolish women,” etc. They endure those who strike them externally, but teach the perverse inwardly. There they are strong; here they are merciful. There they repel adversaries; here they protect their own. It is a great thing to do both in the battle line.

“Do you still persist?” Eve repeats her words, as though saying: “Abandon simplicity,” that is, obedience; despise the prohibition by eating what was forbidden.

“Bless God and die.” That is, by going beyond the commandment, live beyond what you were created for.

Observe the order: after the wounds, the enemy introduced words, because when the force of pain grows heavier, a small persuasion more easily captures someone. For this reason the one who took everything else away preserved the wife.

### VERSE 10

“As one of the foolish women,” etc. (GREGORY.) The fault lies in the mind, not in the sex. He does not say “one of women,” but “of foolish women”: what is morally wrong belongs to the folly that has arisen, not to the condition of nature.

“If we have received good things,” etc. (Ibid.) It is a great consolation amid evils to remember good things, so that there may not be complete despair; likewise, amid joys, foreseeing evil restrains exaltation.

Hence it is said: “On the day of good things, do not be forgetful of evils; and on the day of evils, do not be forgetful of good things.”

“If we have received good things,” that is, if we are striving toward eternal goods, why do we not endure present evils?

“In all these things,” etc. (Ibid.) We sin with our lips in two ways: when we say what is unjust, or when we keep silent about what is just.

But Job neither spoke proudly against the one striking him nor kept silent about what was right against the one offering persuasion. He possessed patience, giving thanks to God; by reproving his wife’s folly, he taught her. Thus the defeated enemy was provoked more fiercely, and because the wife fell silent, he stirred up others to insults.

“In all things.” Thus the saints behave in everything they suffer, externally and internally: they neither go beyond the bounds of justice toward God nor exceed them in the face of the insults of the wicked.

### VERSE 11

“Therefore.” (Ibid.) The friends signify heretics, etc., up to “hypocrites who do not wish to be learned but to appear learned.”

“Hearing.” He does not say “hearing” because they hear these vices, but because the devil, who tempts through these things, understands them.

“Three friends.” This number, morally or mystically, signifies the three troops of the Chaldaeans, that is, the assault made through deed, tongue, and thought; for he attacks all these things.

“They had agreed,” etc. (Ibid.) They agree in falsehood, and while they teach their own doctrines, they seem to offer consolation. Yet those who instruct concerning eternal things truly console in present affliction.

Heretics are called friends not because of their own wickedness but because of our kindness, as in: “Friend, why have you come?” (Matt. XXVI).

“They had agreed.” Certain vices join together against us, such as pride and anger, laxity and fear. Although they are different, they tend toward the same end: the overthrow of the spiritual Job.

### VERSE 12

“When they had lifted their eyes from afar.” Those who are below lift their eyes, etc., up to “as though through the sacrifice of intention we turn enemies into friends.”

“Crying out, they wept.” Because the appearance of the one who had been struck had been changed by the wound, spontaneous grief changed the appearance of the comforters. One who does not share the grief cannot console the grieving person; rather, he clings to him and drags him along.

Therefore, when they saw his body torn, they tore their garments; when they saw him changed, they defiled their heads with dust, so that Job might listen to them more readily when he saw something of his own affliction in them.

Nevertheless, the comforter must take care not to burden the afflicted by grieving excessively or drive the grieving person to despair. Perhaps Job’s friends grieved too much because they did not know the mind of the stricken man, as though he had fallen away at heart.

“They scattered dust.” Dust signifies earthly understanding; the head, the mind; heaven, the commandment of heavenly speech. To cast dust upon the head toward heaven is to corrupt the mind with worldly understanding and to interpret heavenly words in an earthly sense.

Day signifies understanding; night, ignorance; seven, totality. Thus they sit, that is, they pretend to condescend to the weakness of the Church, both in the things where they understand the true light and in those where they possess ignorance; and in this way they prepare the snares of deception.

### VERSE 13

“On the ground.” Because they display the appearance of humility in order to offer proud counsel.

Or the ground signifies Christ’s incarnation, which certain heretics do not deny, although they disagree with us concerning either his divinity or the nature of his incarnation. Since they do not deny it, they sit on the ground with Job, as it were.

“For seven days.” It is unknown whether they remained continuously or persisted in frequent visits for the whole period.

“By day and by night.” Either because, in what they understand truly or in what they understand foolishly, they do not contradict the incarnation.

“No one spoke a word to him.” The enemies are silent when we neglect to generate sons of God through preaching. But if we speak rightly, then they inflict grievous insults and burst forth against us in a voice of pain.

They do indeed speak the seeds of error when they see the hearts of the faithful growing sluggish. But when they see them thinking lofty thoughts, grieving over the world’s misery, and seeking a return to heaven, they carefully restrain their tongue.

“No one spoke.” For there are many, etc., up to “and unless they are cleansed by sacrifice, they must be punished.”

“For they saw the pain.” They then fear speaking perversely when the pain of God’s love shapes the hearts; for then they would not make progress and would also lose those whom they were holding, once those people had been exercised in good things.

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 0759B]

### VERSE 1

“After this,” etc. He makes us attentive, as though to hidden things that had been covered in closed vessels but are disclosed when their mouths are opened, so that we may be refreshed by their inner fragrance.

Up to this point there has been a threefold exposition; from here onward, the interpretation proceeds according to the places required by each passage.

(GREGORY.) “He cursed his day.” This is clearly not according to the surface of the historical sense, because such a thing is both wrong and impossible. The day on which he was born no longer existed, and it is pointless to curse a nonexistent thing, but harmful if it did exist. Nor can a past day now be turned into darkness; nor can the other things that follow apply to it; nor could an aborted child, as he says afterward, enjoy rest. Therefore, nothing here is according to the letter.

[Col. 0759C] “After this,” that is, after all the things mentioned above that he suffered, while even his friends remained silent. Since he gave thanks patiently in everything and taught well, we should not think that, without any instigation, he now burst into cursing out of impatience. Rather, he says this in tranquility, because amid evils he praised God.

“He cursed.” (Ibid.) Cursing is understood in two ways, etc., up to “and he applies a remedy.”

### VERSE 3

“May the day perish on which I was born.” He was not created, etc., up to “but brought in the darkness of sin.”

“May the day perish.” The day signifies worldly prosperity, which ends in night because it leads to tribulation; or the day signifies the pleasure of sin, and the night the blindness of the mind.

A human being is spoken of in three ways: according to nature, according to guilt, and according to weakness. Thus a human being is born in the day and conceived in the night, because he is not carried away into the pleasure of sin unless he is first weakened through the darkness of the mind.

But may the day perish—that is, may the pleasure of sin be destroyed by the strength of justice.

“And the night.” (Gregory, *Commentary on Job*, book IV.) That is, what the blinded mind accomplishes through consent, when it does not carefully discern the blandishments of pleasure, let repentance extinguish, lest the fault that begins by flattering draw him to destruction.

### VERSE 4

“That day,” etc. (Ibid.) That is, let the beginning of pleasure be seen in the end of destruction to which it drags a person, and let it be punished through repentance.

If it has been punished in this way, “let it not be sought.” Let it not be sought in the judgment in order to punish. “And let it not shine.” He illumines with light who reproves; but the one who is not recalled to the judge’s memory is, as it were, covered.

Hence: “Blessed are those whose sins are covered” (Ps. XXXI), so that they may not then be displayed before the eyes of all.

### VERSE 5

“Let it not be illuminated; let darkness obscure it.” That is, let it obscure the day of pleasure, so that it may not be seen by the one who sees everything.

“Darkness.” (GREGORY.) That is, the laments of repentance or the hidden judgments of God, from which we are freed by prevenient grace, though we do not know that we deserve it.

“And the shadow of death.” That is, the death of Christ according to the flesh, etc., up to “in what mercy comes to his aid, let a human being punish himself.” Hence it follows:

“Let gloom seize it.” That is, confusion of mind, concerning which it is said: “There is a confusion that brings glory” (Ecclus. IV).

“And let it be enveloped.” On every side.

“With bitterness.” [Col. 0760B] Of repentance.

But if the day—that is, the pleasure of sin—is punished in this way, what of the night, that is, consent to guilt?

### VERSE 6

“Let a dark whirlwind possess that night.” It is like a tempestuous whirlwind stirred up, etc., up to “for the blindness of damnation in which we were born.”

“Let it not be counted among the days of the year.” The year signifies heavenly grace, etc., up to “but forever excluded from that homeland.” Hence it follows:

### VERSE 7

“Let that night be solitary.” Because it is separated from that company, or because it loses the human being whom it had made its companion. It is handed over alone, with its own body, to Gehenna, while the elect are redeemed by grace.

“Nor worthy of praise.” When a human being had been cast down, he worshiped idols, in which he praised demons as though they were the darkness of night. But once the idols have been rejected, the night is not worthy of praise.

### VERSE 8

“Let them curse it.” (Ibid.) In the old translation, etc., up to “and at the end, once released, he will wage war openly.”

“Leviathan.” That is, “their addition,” meaning the addition of human beings, among whom he does not cease, after suggestion, to add further evils.

Or it signifies reproach, because when he promised Adam that he would add divinity, he took away what Adam had.

Here he is called by the Prophet a twisting serpent, who softly pours snares into the final, seemingly flattering turns of his words. He is also called a bar, because through malice he is hard and strikes toward death. Once roused, he will act openly; for the present, however, he acts secretly.

### VERSE 9

“With darkness”—the darkness of that night.

“Let the stars be darkened.” That is, hypocrites who shine through their works before human eyes. These are dragged by the dragon’s tail, that is, by the final persecution of Antichrist. They are darkened because the enemy’s malice prevails over them so greatly that they are enveloped in manifest evils; inwardly and outwardly they become alike.

“Let it await the light.” This is said according to his members, etc., up to “which it endured while prophesying about Christ, but did not recognize him when he came.”

“Nor the rising of the dawn.” (Ibid.) The rising of the dawn is the new birth of the resurrection, by which the saints will rise with the flesh to see the eternal light.

But however much the elect shine here, they cannot penetrate what the glory of that new birth will be. This night did not close the womb’s doors but opened them, because, when a human being was conceived, it opened the desires of lust toward sin.

[Col. 0761A] Once these doors—that is, the desires of carnal lust—have been opened, we are dragged into countless evils of corruption. Hence we groan under our burden, because justice demands that we unwillingly endure what we willingly did.

### VERSE 10

“Because it did not close the doors of the womb,” etc. This concerns the head itself, etc., up to “just as we say that robbers give life to captives if they do not take it away.”

### VERSE 11

“Why did I not die in the womb?” This should not be understood, etc., up to “lest suggestion should draw him into pleasure.”

“And having come forth from the womb.” (GREGORY.) Because sin, once conceived, comes forth, etc., up to “while they endure the struggle of their own flesh against the spirit.”

### VERSES 13–14

“Now,” etc. (Ibid.) Through “now,” which belongs to the present time and signifies what always stands in the present—that is, eternal rest.

“I would be resting with kings.” That is, with angels, because they rule what has been subjected to them. They are also “counselors,” because by announcing God’s will they offer us counsel.

Or by “kings” he means holy preachers, who rule themselves, and by “counselors of the earth,” because they give good counsel concerning earthly things.

He therefore says that if he had not sinned, he would have ascended there even without redemption—to the place which the apostles and holy preachers reach after redemption with great labor. Unlike the ancients, who were delayed, they enter heaven immediately after death.

“Who build.” Every earthly person is compressed in the heart by the dense turmoil of thoughts and trampled by the crowds of desires as though by throngs. But to build solitudes is to drive the tumult of earthly desires from the heart’s secret place and to pant for the love of inner quiet, so that one may say: “One thing I have asked of the Lord, and this I shall seek,” etc.

### VERSE 15

“With princes who possess gold.” The princes are the rulers of the Church, etc., up to “but whoever foresaw future things already recalls the past.”

### VERSE 16

“Or, like an untimely birth.” (Ibid.) Because what is an aborted child is born before its time and is immediately hidden after being extinguished.

These are the saints with whom he considers that he might have rested: they existed from the beginning of the world before the time of redemption, yet they mortified themselves to the world.

The first period, before the law, which brought forth the fathers who were dead to the world a second time, was like the womb of an abortion. They were as though dead from the womb who feared God naturally without the tablets of the law and, believing in the Redeemer who was to come, put pleasures to death.

“Hidden.” Because, although Moses mentioned only a few of them, etc., up to “whom the spirit of prophecy illumined, like Job himself.”

(Ibid.) He now opens the rest of this light and, in clearer words, demonstrates what is done there each day concerning the way of life of the wicked.

### VERSE 17

“There the wicked are.” That is, in the light of Christ, which the ancients awaited, the Gentiles cease from the multitude of worldly desires and, with tranquil minds, already taste eternal rest.

And this is what follows: “And there they rested.” In the world they are said to be strong in vigor, not weary. But whoever is strengthened in the love of God beneficially fails in his own strength; and the more strongly he seeks eternal things, the more weary he dies to earthly things.

Hence: “My soul longs and faints for the courts of the Lord” (Ps. XXXVIII).

By saying “there” and “light,” he shows the place in which the elect are contained.

### VERSE 18

“Once bound.” The righteous, although at rest from their desires, are nevertheless bound, so long as they remain in the body, by the burden of their corruption. For the body weighs down the soul, and the flesh resists the spirit. There are also bodily bonds—hunger, thirst, and things of this kind—which cannot be loosed here; but from all of them they will be released into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.

Observe the stages: the impious, when converted, cease; those trained in virtue rest in the innermost bosom; released from the bonds of corruption, they attain freedom. But what they do meanwhile is added: “Those who did not hear, [Col. 0762B] etc.”

“The exactor is the devil, who once placed the coin of deception in the human being’s hand and daily demands the debt of death; his voice is temptation. The one who is tempted hears him and resists, but the one who consents heeds him. The same applies to inward peace, because whatever the mind greatly loves it repeats again and again.”

### VERSE 19

“There the small and the great are.” Because here there is a distinction of works, but there there will be distinctions of dignity. Hence: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14).

“And the servant.” Whoever sins is a servant of sin, because here he never becomes free while he fears the Judge; but there he will be free, where there will be no uncertainty about forgiveness. There will indeed be a memory of guilt—not one that defiles the mind, but one that, without harming blessedness, binds it more closely to blessedness and joy—so that, healed, we remember our sufferings without pain; and therefore we give greater thanks to the physician.

[Col. 0762C]

### VERSE 20

“Why was light given to the miserable?” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, Book V.) Having contemplated the rest in which, being free, he despises the prosperity of the world that draws him away from it. “Why was light given to the miserable?” That is, why was prosperity given amid the misery of exile? For although it does not completely crush the righteous person, it nevertheless divides his mind between the love of God and the management of his own affairs. Hence he adds: “And life to those who, etc.” It is bitterness to every righteous person, etc., even to presiding over governance.

### VERSE 21

“Those who await death.” (Ibid.) That is, they desire to put themselves wholly to death with respect to the world, but by the hidden judgment of God death does not come, because they are compelled to occupy positions of honor entrusted to them; they endure this through fear of God. Within them is the desire for devotion, while outwardly they fulfill the ministry of their office, lest they oppose God’s arrangement through pride. Thus they benefit many, and, in proportion as they see themselves imperfect, they rise higher through humility. Because they are held back from their desires, the very delay enlarges their longing for them. Hence he adds, as though they were digging:

“As though digging for a treasure.” For whoever seeks a treasure by digging, etc., finds examples of contemplation from which he may become rich.

### VERSE 22

“For the man whose.” Behold, when it was asked why light was given to the miserable, he shows here that the way is hidden from a man. For even if he is already acting well, he does not know what he will do at the end; or sometimes the things believed to please God displease him.

[Col. 0763A]

### VERSE 23

“God has surrounded him.” (Gregory.) Although he desires heavenly things, he nevertheless does not know what has been arranged inwardly concerning him. He is also surrounded by the darkness of ignorance: he is forgetful of the past, cannot discover the future, barely knows the present, and is unable to penetrate the innermost ordering of God. Whoever fixes his attention upon these darknesses weeps and seeks the heavenly light with all his sight. Hence it sometimes happens that, amid devout weeping, the brightness of inward joy breaks forth. Thus it follows:

### VERSE 24

“Before I eat.” To eat is to be nourished by the light of contemplation. No one possesses this except the one who first, in this exile, groans as though he were in a place where good things are absent, sighs with longing, and gives expression to the force of his tears.

“And as overflowing waters, etc.” Overflowing waters rush along in many surging streams; so those who mourn experience many surges of grief, because they do not know what has been determined concerning them by God; they recall their past, fear the future, and are afraid lest they go astray in their good deeds. When God’s scourges correct them, they suspect that they have offended him. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0763B]

### VERSE 25

“For fear.” They weep because they fear that they have been abandoned; and they fear lest a merciful blow be not discipline but vengeance. Hence: “Who knows the power of your anger?” (Psalm 89). For sometimes what we call anger is grace, and sometimes what we call grace is anger. Therefore it is necessary to fear in all things: in prosperity, lest these things have been given to them for greater blindness rather than for consolation, as usually happens with the good, and lest adversity prove to be the beginning of punishment.

### VERSE 26

“I concealed it.” (Ibid.) Even if, by continually considering, etc., up to the point where Job is presented as an example of what he was when he possessed power.

“Did I not conceal it?” Power must be considered for its usefulness and concealed on account of pride; and the powerful person should know that he has power in order that he may benefit others.

“Did I not keep silent?” Behold what he was in speech.

“Did I not rest?” Behold what he was with regard to unlawful things, etc., up to the point that our perfection is not without fault. Hence he adds:

“And indignation came upon me.” With great artistry, therefore, he was about to speak of blows but first mentioned his right actions, so that in these everyone might consider what punishment awaits the wicked. If he chastises the righteous here in such a way that “the righteous will scarcely be saved,” where will the impious appear?

[Col. 0763C–D]

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSE 2

“If we should begin to speak to you.” (Ibid.) They begin gently but burst forth into harshness. So heretics put forward flattering words so that they may not be guarded against, but then introduce harsh ones.

“But the thought conceived.” (Ibid.) The perfect do not conceive in their hearts the perverse things that they restrain in silence. Others conceive evil things but bind them tightly with the great strength of silence; others both conceive and immediately bring them forth. Frivolous in judgment, rash in speech: Eliphaz belongs to this group, for from his own experience he forms the same judgment about everyone.

“Who will be able to hold it?” As though he wished to restrain himself; by this he hints that he will give offense in speaking.

### VERSE 3

“Behold, you have instructed many.” (Ibid.) The good things are genuine, since even the one who wishes to accuse him admits them. How great must he formerly have been, who, occupied with arranging so many matters of his own, nevertheless freely instructed others, demonstrating what was right in action and word? But because the accuser speaks good things about the same man, he bends them toward accusation, saying:

[Col. 0764A]

### VERSE 5

“But now it has come, etc.”—as though to say: “You have not preserved the right things you used to say.” Observe, however, that there are wicked people who, unable to deny the good deeds of the righteous that are known to them, mention them so as not to appear evil themselves; and, so that they may be believed all the more, they turn those very good deeds into an accumulation of guilt by inserting evil among them. Here Job is reproached as having spoken rightly but not preserved what he said, as though he were shown to be evil by his own testimony. Later he is marked as speaking wrongly, so that he may be silenced. These are the two ways by which the wicked attack the good: they say either that they speak evil things or that they do not keep the good things they say.

“Your strength has failed, etc. Where is your fear?” As though he marveled that the virtues had been lost, arranging them in an appropriate order. Just as, on the road of the world, boldness produces strength and fear produces weakness, so on the way of God boldness produces weakness and fear of God produces strength. For the one who is joined to God is lifted above all things by a certain power. Strength is displayed only in adversity, and therefore patience is added: in strength the one who bears the evils of others without being disturbed makes progress, as it were. From patience perfection is born; hence a person is said to possess his soul in patience—that is, to live rightly in all things and to rule all the movements of his mind through virtue. For the one who conquers himself is strong against everything.

[Col. 0764B]

(Ibid.) Since he has reproved Job by attacking him, he now adds something as though offering encouragement:

[Col. 0764C]

### VERSE 7

“Remember, I beg you.” But he also does this reprehensibly. The innocent and upright are often utterly destroyed here, even though they are preserved for eternal things. But those who serve God not for an eternal reward but for an earthly one fabricate for themselves what they seek; and, presuming to teach, when they proclaim earthly security to everyone, they show through all their efforts what they love.

### VERSE 8

“Rather, I have seen them.” (Ibid.) The one who speaks sows sorrows; the one who prevails by speaking reaps fraud. Or the one who acts perversely sows sorrows, while the one who prospers through them reaps. Such people do not perish, as he says, but live here more successfully than the righteous. For God allows some to prevail here so that the life of the righteous may be purified more thoroughly. He soon punishes others, lest he appear to disregard human affairs and pass over many evils; thus he strengthens the hearts of the innocent who are fainthearted. More truly, however, he would speak of all at the end. In general it could be said that the innocent and upright do not perish, because, even if they are crushed here, they are restored by true salvation in God’s presence. The wicked perish because, even if they grow higher here, they will be struck more severely at the end. But since he says “Remember,” it is clear that past events are being recalled to mind, not future ones announced.

[Col. 0764D]

### VERSE 9

“They perished at God’s breath.” (Ibid.) We blow air when we draw it inward from outside and return it outward from within. God is therefore said to blow in retribution because, from external causes, he conceives the counsel of judgment inwardly, and from his inward counsel issues the sentence outwardly: that is, from our evils, which he sees outwardly, he arranges judgment inwardly, and from the inward conception he produces condemnation outwardly. Or God is said to blow, that is, to be angry, by analogy, because when we become angry we are inflamed by the breath of fury. God therefore blows when, in anger, he considers vengeance; after long patience, the one who is tranquil in himself appears turbulent to the guilty, while they themselves are thrown into turmoil before him by their guilt.

[Col. 0765A]

(Gregory.) After giving a merciful warning, he rebukes openly. “The roaring of the lion”—that is, the severity and terror of Job himself; “the voice of the lioness”—the loquacity of his wife; “the teeth of the lion’s cubs”—the greed of his children—have been destroyed. The rigid man rejoices, as though they had rightly been condemned. He also compares Job to a tiger on account of the spots of pretense. For the hypocrite, who appears upright, has hidden vices that sometimes break forth and alter his color. The spoil is the glory of the righteous, which he seizes for himself. Thus, supposing that holy Job had retained through hypocrisy the good qualities he recognized in him, he says:

[Col. 0765B]

### VERSE 11

“The tiger has perished.” That is, the variety of your pretense has been extinguished, etc., up to the point where such people believe through wisdom that they surpass everyone.

### VERSE 12

“Moreover, a hidden word was spoken to me.” (Ibid.) Heretics pretend that they hear hidden things. They therefore preach secretly, so that their preaching may be regarded as holier and not equal to that of others.

“Secretly, etc.” (Ibid.) They do not enter with others through the door, but seek cracks through which to introduce perverse understanding. Since a thief fears the light, he adds:

[Col. 0765C]

### VERSE 13

“In the horror of a nocturnal vision.” In the terror of a nighttime vision they claim to have perceived veins of a divine whisper, because, in order to boast of lofty things, they say that they could scarcely grasp them. But while they mark such lofty matters, they bear witness against themselves to their wickedness. For in a nocturnal vision things are seen uncertainly.

“When sleep usually seizes.” That is, while everyone below sleeps in torpor, we remain awake to perceive lofty and heavenly things. And when they sometimes see that this is despised, they pretend to fear what they say; hence he adds:

### VERSE 14

“Fear seized me.” So that they may appear marvelous in lofty matters, they pretend to dread the things they invent; yet they are bold enough to proclaim what they assert they could scarcely hear.

“A word was spoken to me.” (Ibid.) The Son of God is called, etc., up to the point where, the more his uprightness has been restrained, it fears him. Hence he adds:

“In the horror of a nocturnal vision, etc.” That is, in the fear of hidden contemplation, in which nothing is seen clearly but rather as though in imagination. Yet no one reaches this unless carnal desires have been restrained. Hence:

“When sleep usually seizes human beings.” The one who gives attention to the cares of the world is awake; the one who flees them sleeps in repose. This is Jacob, who sleeps on his journey and sees angels: that is, in the course of this life he closes his eyes to worldly affairs, which guilt opened to our first parents for the purpose of desiring. No one is led to see inward things unless he is withdrawn from the things that entangle him outwardly. Hence: “Be still and see that I am God” (Psalm 45).

[Col. 0765D–0766A]

But the higher the mind is lifted in contemplation and sees things above itself, the more terribly it trembles within itself. Hence:

“Fear seized me, and trembling, and all my bones.” (Ibid.) That is, stronger deeds, etc., up to the point where he feels the sting of the flesh. He adds:

### VERSE 16

“Someone stood.” (Ibid.) So that they may be judged to know incomprehensible things, etc., up to the point where he arrogated to himself what was a common good.

“The hairs of my flesh bristled.” (Ibid.) The hairs are all the superfluous thoughts of human corruption belonging to the old life. If we exclude them from the mind, we cut the hairs from the flesh, so that we are not wearied by pain. Hence Moses: “Let the Levites shave all the hairs of their flesh” (Leviticus 14).

[Col. 0766B]

We perceive these things more subtly within ourselves when we penetrate lofty matters; hence it is rightly said now:

“When the spirit passed by.” When the mind sees what is true, it torments itself more severely over what is superfluous. Therefore, as the spirit passes by, the hairs are afraid, because superfluous thoughts flee before the force of compunction. For inward vision inflames the soul against itself; and while it cuts away unlawful things with strictness, the mind adheres more broadly to contemplation. It fixes well the spirit that was passing by, yet even the delay of contemplation does not fully disclose the force of devotion. Hence he adds:

“Someone stood whose face I did not recognize.” (Ibid.) He is not called “someone,” etc., up to the point where he sees him through his co-eternal form. He adds:

[Col. 0766C]

“The image before my eyes.” The Son is the image of the Father, and he says: “No one comes to the Father except through me.”

“And I heard a voice like a gentle breeze.” (Ibid.) The voice of the breeze is knowledge, etc., up to the point where he learned from this hearing.

### VERSE 17

“Will a human being be justified in comparison with God?” In contemplation he learns that human righteousness, when compared with divine righteousness, is injustice—just as a lamp shines in darkness but grows dim in the sun. He was able to learn this because whoever sees the light knows what judgment to form about darkness.

“Or will a person be purer than his Maker?” (Ibid.) The one who murmurs against the one who strikes him judges this. But he ought to know that the one who made marvelous things from nothing does not strike impiously, and that the Creator of nature is not an unjust judge of guilt. Although this man reproves Job unjustly, he nevertheless correctly describes the condition of the creature in comparison with the Creator. A man therefore considers himself purer than his Maker if he prepares a complaint against the blow, and he unquestionably places himself before him when he reproves his judgment concerning his own affliction.

[Col. 0766D]

“Behold, those who serve him.” (The same author.) Although an angel remains unchanging in his own state, nevertheless, insofar as he is a creature, he possesses the alternation of mutability and is therefore not entirely stable. For if this nature were not changeable, then, having been created good, none of its members would have fallen. But it had the choice either to fall or to stand, and among those who stood there was merit in fixing the movement of their mutability through the devotion of their will. This mutability is demonstrated by what he adds concerning the apostate:

[Col. 0767A]

“And he found perversity in his angels.” From comparison with them human weakness is inferred.

### VERSE 19

“How much more those who dwell in houses of clay.” (Gregory.) That is, earthly bodies, etc., up to the point where they are seen occupied with worldly cares. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 20

“From morning until evening.” That is, from the beginning of their life until its end they are wounded by the perpetration of iniquity, and, cut down by it, they fall into the depths.

(Ibid.) Alternatively, morning signifies prosperity and evening adversity. Yet they perish through both, because through prosperity they become wanton, while through adversity they rise to madness in their impatience. None of them—that is, of those who “are cut down from morning until evening”—understands what is reserved here for afflicted good people, or what awaits those who consider worldly goods to be good here. But since not all are abandoned in this way, he adds:

[Col. 0767B]

“But those who remain.” That is, those whom the world, judging them unworthy, leaves behind. Like the Egyptian boy—that is, the lover of the world, blackened by sins—the person despised by the world is often left behind, so that he does not run with it but, broken by adversity, grows sluggish. David—that is, Christ—finds him, converts him to his own love, feeds him with the food of the word, and makes him the guide of his journey—that is, his preacher. Under this guide he destroys the revelers—that is, the world’s joy—which had disdained to have him as its companion.

“They will be taken away from them.” Because God has chosen them for himself.

“They will die, but not in wisdom.” After inserting the lot of the righteous, he returns to the destruction of those who lack understanding. The reprobate despise the righteous because, through their death, they seek invisible things, or through death they seek invisible life. But they themselves, fleeing both death and wisdom alike, wholly abandon wisdom, unwilling to die for the truth, yet they do not escape death.

[Col. 0767C]

## CHAPTER V

### VERSE 1

“Call, then.” (Ibid.) Although he has spoken this truthfully against the wicked, he has nevertheless secretly placed Job among their number. Inflated by the pride of wisdom, he adds an open mockery against Job: “Call, then”—that is, if you cry out while afflicted, God does not answer; that is, he does not grant the result you seek, because you despised him in tranquility. And “to some one of the saints”—that is, you do not have the saints as helpers in affliction, because you did not have them as companions in joy.

(Ibid.) After the mockery he adds a judgment, etc., up to the point where this disturbs the wise, while anger, through vice, slaughters the foolish.

“And he kills the little one.” That is, while he envies the one whom he thinks greater, etc., up to the point where, by possessing a share, he diminishes our measure.

[Col. 0767D]

(Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, Book VI, chapter 5.) Because he is firmly established with all his desires in earthly love, Cain was the first to build a city on earth; alienated from heaven, he lives here more prosperously.

### VERSE 3

“And I cursed his beauty.” (The same author.) When the feet of the weak falter at the prosperity they see in the wicked, the strong, seeing what punishment follows upon their glory, immediately reject their prosperity. The weak person changes with the character of events: when he sees prosperity, he praises it; when it changes, he judges it worthless. But the firm person considers the punishment that follows the glory itself and immediately condemns it. Yet because many who prosper in the world draw others along with them, he adds:

[Col. 0768A]

### VERSE 4

“His sons will be far away.” That is, his followers.

“At the gate.” (Ibid.) The gate of the kingdom is the day of judgment, on which the elect enter into glory. Before that day the sons of this world are exalted, but then they will be crushed.

### VERSE 5

“And there will be no one to rescue.” (Ibid.) Because truth rescues there those whom it presses here through discipline.

[Col. 0768B]

“Whose harvest.” Everyone has a gift of understanding by which he understands and speaks what is right. But because he neither loves nor does these things, he fasts from the harvest he possesses. The one who hungers for righteousness, however, refreshes himself by hearing right things from him. Hence: “What they say, do” (Matthew 23).

“And the armed man will seize him.” (Ibid.) The devil is defeated as unarmed when, suggesting open evils, he tries to take away all good things in the same way. But armed, he conquers: he leaves some good things untouched and secretly corrupts others.

“And they will drink.” (The same author.) A foolish person often possesses riches, etc., up to the point where the diligent person is hindered by delay. He answers:

### VERSE 6

“Nothing happens on earth without cause.” For by this one person is punished more justly for negligence, while another is crowned for diligence. But because we are instructed to understand what is right not only by diligence but also by persecutions, he adds: “And it will not come forth from the earth.”

[Col. 0768C]

“And it will not come forth from the earth.” (Ibid.) The earth—that is, the elements of the world—are turned into punishment for those who offend. Hence it is said: “The whole earth will fight on his behalf against the senseless” (Wisdom 5), that is, on behalf of the Lord. Yet pain does not come forth from them, because punishment is not born from the things that strike, but from those who, by sinning, extorted the blows. But in proportion as outward punishment chastises, the mind is lifted toward heavenly things. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 7

“Human beings are born for labor.” It is impossible to be without labor in this exile. Yet insofar as the flesh is afflicted, the mind is lifted to seek lofty things. Or “human being”—that is, the carnal person—experiences the evils of the world because he greedily desires its goods. But the mind that passes beyond these things, lifted like a bird to lofty places on the wings of hope, perceives no evil and may rejoice even in the scourges. Since no one is capable of these things by his own strength, he adds:

[Col. 0768D]

### VERSE 8

“Therefore I would beseech.” That is, I beseech the one through whom I know that these things are granted.

### VERSE 9

“Wonders without number.” The greatness of divine works cannot be examined by their quality or counted by their quantity.

### VERSE 10

“He gives rain.” (Ibid.) These words are mystical, because Job’s friends had been instructed by association with him. “He gives rain to the earth”: when he pours the grace of preaching into the dry hearts of the Gentiles.

“And he waters all things with waters.” When he fills a human being with the Spirit so that he may bear fruit. A human being is called “all things” because he shares something with all things. Or “all things” means the rich and the poor and all human distinctions, because good work is followed by recompense.

[Col. 0769A]

### VERSE 11

“He places the lowly on high.” (Gregory.) So that, now despised, they may judge with the Lord.

“Those who mourn.” The more they are now afflicted by adversities and chastise themselves through lamentation, the more exalted will be their well-being, even in this life. These words can be understood of the elect, in whom the humble transcend all temporal things with an elevated mind and, though afflicted, are raised up in soundness—not in madness, like those who rejoice when they have done evil. Such people rejoice because of the certainty of eternal salvation.

[Col. 0769B]

### VERSE 12

“He frustrates the thoughts.” (The same author.) When the reprobate plan evil, God sometimes removes their strength so that they cannot prevail against the good; thus they are deprived of the accomplishment of their deed, while remaining guilty before God.

### VERSE 13

“He catches the wise.” (Ibid.) Human actions serve God’s purposes fittingly even when they resist them: as in Joseph’s sale, lest he should be worshiped; in Saul’s demand for foreskins, so that David might be destroyed; and in the Lord’s death, lest everyone should believe in him. God grants some things in mercy and permits others in anger. He then turns these things to the use of his counsel, so that what resists his counsel may serve his counsel, and what happens without his will may not be contrary to his will. Hence: “Whatever he has willed, etc.”

[Col. 0769C]

### VERSE 14

“They encounter darkness by day.” In the very presence of truth they are blinded by the error of faithlessness: they see Christ’s miracles yet doubt his divinity.

“As though in the night.” We seek by groping what we do not see with our eyes. The Jews had seen the miracles, yet continued to seek as though groping: “If you are the Christ, tell us openly” (John 10). But Christ could not long be held in their hands.

“They encounter darkness by day.” (Ibid.) When the mind of the envious person is afflicted by another’s good, it is darkened by the sun’s ray.

“And as in the night, so they will grope at midday.” The day of good work shines outwardly before them. They grope as though in the night because, blinded by envy, they strive to find something to criticize. Behold Lot—that is, the righteous person—is shut and protected within the house against wicked adversaries: that is, he returns to his mind and remains inward. The blind Sodomites go around—that is, the envious scrutinize his deeds and words—but they do not find the door, meaning an opening for criticism. Instead they grope along the wall, because the righteous person’s praiseworthy action confronts them everywhere.

[Col. 0769D]

“They will grope.” But the poor in spirit—that is, the person who is not proud in his own estimation—is saved from the sword of the mouth, that is, from wicked persuasion.

### VERSE 15

“Moreover, he will save the needy from the sword of the mouth.” The sword of the mouth is the accusation of the Jews. The hand of the violent is the Gentile people that crucified him; but Christ overcame them by rising again. In this needy person—that is, the humble people of the faithful—the hope of the life to come is made firm.

[Col. 0770A]

The iniquity that now opens its mouth wide in insult against Christ will close it through punishment, or, once converted, will cease from its insults. The same applies generally to the perverse.

“The poor person from the hand of the violent.” That is, from hostile power, so that he is neither drawn away by the flatteries of persuasion nor broken by the pain of punishments. The poor person is not drawn away because his hope, fixed upon eternal things, is strengthened against these attacks. When he arrives at the fruit of this hope, the proud person falls silent and contracts his mouth, because torments bind the tongue that spoke against the righteous by slander. But so that the elect person may escape punishments and reach rewards, he must be purified here by scourges. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 17

“Therefore do not reject the correction of the Lord.” (Ibid.) The person who complains that he suffers unjustly rejects it. Eliphaz therefore supposes that Job is being struck for purification rather than for the testing of his strength. Because Job speaks freely, seeking the causes of his affliction, Eliphaz thinks that he rejects the Lord’s correction. So heretics turn to evil what is rightly done by the Church.

[Col. 0770B]

### VERSE 18

“For he himself wounds.” (The same author.) God wounds those whom he restores to salvation in two ways. Sometimes he strikes the body in order to heal the mind; sometimes, without outward scourges, he strikes the hardness of the mind with the force of his desire and thus heals it—the mind that had been safely lying dead in the world. But while the mind breathes toward God and despises all worldly things, everything immediately becomes a temptation to it and afflicts it. Yet while it is worn down by temporary labor, it is freed from everlasting labor. Therefore he adds:

[Col. 0770C]

### VERSE 19

“In six tribulations.” (Ibid.) The number six, followed by seven, signifies the activity and course of the present life. On the sixth day God completed all things and created the human being; on the seventh he rested, and that day has no evening—that is, no end. Therefore he delivers in the seventh tribulation, so that evil may not reach the seventh. For here, as a father, he instructs by wearing us down, but on the day of judgment he hides us from the scourge.

### VERSE 20

“In famine.” (Ibid.) He enumerates the evils of the present life and God’s aids. The famine of the mind is the silence of God’s word. When that word is withdrawn, the temptation of the flesh grows strong, and this is war. Yet even in famine God rescues the soul from death because he refreshes it with his word.

“And in war.” He makes the person strong against temptations of the flesh. But once such a person has become strong, he sometimes fears slanders. Hence he adds:

[Col. 0770D]

### VERSE 21

“From the scourge of the tongue.” That is, from reproachful insult, on account of which a person mocked by others ceases from doing good. Hence David: “And from an harsh word.” The saint is hidden from this because, while he does not seek praise here, he does not feel insults. But because someone may fear bodily suffering after these things, it follows:

“And you will not fear calamity.” That is, persecution. But because such a person prepares security for himself in the terror of the future judgment, he adds:

### VERSE 22

“In devastation and famine.” Devastation is Gehenna, which is outside, etc., up to the point where, at the moment of death, he does not dread its assault. It follows: “And the beasts of the earth.”

[Col. 0771A]

These beasts run wild at the time of death to seize souls, but the person who did not follow them when they fawned does not fear them when they rage. Security of mind at death is the beginning of recompense. Yet when one lives well, one must beware lest, despising others, one glory in being alone; instead, one should remember the good that is shared with others. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 23

“But with the stones of the regions you will have a covenant.” The regions of the nations are as though divided, differing in the customs and languages of the churches; the stones are the elect, who are placed in the building. Therefore the person who lives rightly joins himself by covenant to the stones, because, in abandoning the world, he binds himself to the saints through imitation. From this the attack grows, but by being worn down through it he is subjected to God with greater humility. Hence he adds: “And with the beasts of the earth.”

[Col. 0771B]

Not pacified but peacemaking, because they do not possess peace but make peace. When a person is attacked more fiercely by the devil, he is driven more strongly toward love, and peace is established more firmly with him. Or the beasts are the movements of the flesh, which, pressed as though in a cage by continence, roar in temptation but do not exceed the bounds of restraint into the frenzy of a bite; in this respect they are peacemaking. Or, because they disturb the person, the place where life is lived without any opposition is loved more intensely; thus they impel him toward love of inward rest.

### VERSE 24

“And you will know that you will have peace.” (Gregory.) This is either the peace begun here, conceived from desire for God, or the complete peace that will come in the future through the vision of God. When the mind is subjected to God, or the flesh to the mind, the righteous person’s tabernacle—that is, the body inhabited by the mind—has peace, because the movements of desire are restrained under righteousness. But bodily chastity is worthless if the mind’s sweetness in love of one’s neighbor is absent.

[Col. 0771C]

“And when you visit your appearance, you will not sin.” (Ibid.) Our appearance is our neighbor, etc., up to the point where he gathers abundant fruits of preaching from the seed of good work. Hence it follows:

### VERSE 25

“You will also know that your seed will be abundant.” The person who lives well receives eloquence in speaking well, and conscience does not hinder the speaker. Hence it is that the Egyptians, having become servants, receive grain for seed, although previously, as free people, they had received it for food: when we are fully subjected to God, we are filled with the word of preaching. Previously, as free people, we were nourished by sacred discourse, yet we remained available for certain things we sought in the world. From preaching follows a great offspring of the faithful. And this is what follows:

“And your offspring will be like the grass of the earth.” That is, innumerable. Or it is compared with grass because, abandoning the world’s dryness and glory, it grows green through inward hope.

[Col. 0771D]

Yet it is not enough for the righteous person to perform great deeds outwardly unless he also enters eternal things through contemplation. Hence it follows:

### VERSE 26

“You will enter the grave in abundance.” (Ibid.) The grave is contemplation, etc., up to the point where they pour what they have received back for the benefit of their neighbors.

“As a heap of grain is brought in.” The time of action comes first, and contemplation last. The perfect person must first exercise the mind in virtues and afterward place it in the granary of rest.

Or the grave is eternal rest, in which one rests more truly in proportion as the life of corruption is more perfectly put to death. The person who enters it in abundance is the one who, after gathering the works of this life, has died completely to this mutability and is hidden in the secret place of the true light, like grain. For the righteous experience blows in another’s time, but in their own time they enter the granary like kernels.

[Col. 0772A]

### VERSE 27

“We have investigated.” By this he indicates that, in speaking above of the grave, the beasts, the stones, the tabernacle, and similar things, he did not speak merely according to their surface meaning but sought their inner significance. “What you have heard, examine carefully in your mind.” These are words of boastfulness. Even if he has taught correctly, it is ignorance to wish to teach someone better than oneself. Thus the words of the friends, although correct, are charged with having been spoken incorrectly.

## CHAPTER VI

### VERSE 2

“Would that they were weighed.” Struck by scourges, he is provoked by words—not so that, lifted up into a stubborn defense, he might fall, but rather: struck, he gave thanks in silence; provoked, he answered rightly: “Would that my sins were weighed.”

[Col. 0772B]

“The scales.” (Ibid.) Christ, in the Father’s hand, holds the balance of mercy and justice. By mercy he loosens sin and shows it to be light; by dying, he shows calamity to be of heavy weight. He grants this further grace: that the calamity itself should become recognizable. For the blind human being rejoiced in exile as though it were his homeland; but God, appearing outwardly, calls the human being back inwardly, so that, seeing what he has lost, he may grieve deeply over what he endures. He says, therefore:

“Would that they were weighed.” That is, the evil of our condition, etc., up to the point where he weighs the judgments of God by which he is afflicted. And this is what follows:

[Col. 0772C]

### VERSE 3

“Therefore my words too are full of pain, because of the arrows of the Lord.” That is, the stroke of God’s correction, which does not leave me unpurified, as it leaves many.

### VERSE 4

“He has drained my spirit.” (Gregory.) That is, he restrains pride, so that he may say: “My spirit has fainted” (Psalm 76). I do not merely groan over what I suffer; I also fear what you threaten. And this is what follows:

“The terrors of the Lord wage war”—lest eternal death follow afterward.

[Col. 0772D]

But because he longs for the coming of the Judge, and indicates with what ardor both the Gentiles and Judea thirst for him, he adds:

### VERSE 5

“Does the wild ass roar”—that is, the ass of the wilderness, etc., up to the point where he was held carnally. He adds:

### VERSE 6

“Or can what is tasteless be eaten?” Salt is the virtue of hidden understanding, etc., up to the point where he received it hungrily through conversion.

(Ibid.) He desires the balance; we already live by faith in him. Nevertheless, we suffer his arrows for purification and fear because of the terror of the future.

[Col. 0773A]

But since we are children, we must not fear him as a lord but love him as a father and pant toward the place where we may be nourished by his food—that is, by his eternity. For this we now roar. Hence:

“Does the wild ass roar?” (Ibid.) The wild ass is the people who, etc., up to the point where they also separate themselves from words of this kind. And this is what follows:

“Or can what is tasteless be eaten?” But now, placed on high and separated from fools, they often seek only what is proper for bearing difficult things, and are not girded for the love of truth.

“Or can anyone taste?” (Gregory.) It is difficult to seek what tortures and drives away life. Yet often, when a person has been raised on high, he bends down to bear the evils of fools in order to draw them along. For as the desire for heavenly things increases, he becomes distressed, and, because of their sweetness, he does not fear the bitter things of the world. Hence, after the impossible taste of death, he adds:

### VERSE 7

“What it previously did not wish to touch”—that is, the evils of the world have now become sweet foods because of love of heaven. And since these things are sweet: “Who will grant that my petition may come?”

[Col. 0773B]

### VERSE 9

“May the one who began it himself crush me.” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, Book VII.) The adversary crushes, and the human being falls away from you. God crushes, and the person broken from vices is made firm in virtue. Therefore the one who desires to draw near to God through scourges says: “May the one who began it himself crush me,” because sometimes God begins the crushing of vices, but at the very beginning of his progress the human being becomes exalted. Then the enemy, driven out, steals in more grievously after taking on other spirits, and crushes his virtues.

“May he release his hand”—that is, may he exercise its effect. When a person inflated by prolonged prosperity does not exercise his love through scourges, he keeps his hand, as it were, bound from striking vices. Hence he says to the sinful people: “Now I will no longer be angry with you, and my jealousy has departed from you.”

[Col. 0773C]

“May he cut me off.” For when pain or temptation does not strike, the exaltation of the mind falls, cut down, so that it may now seek the hand that lifts it.

## Verse 10

“And let this be my consolation, that he afflicting me.” (Ibid.) It is as though he spares some in order to strike them eternally; but let him strike me here without sparing me—that is my consolation. For the saints fear that they may be spared here. That he said this not with a proud but with a humble mind, he shows in what follows.

“Nor will I contradict his words.” God’s words to us are not only what he says but also what he does, as here in Job’s being struck. Job does not contradict them by murmuring, since God calls him holy even while striking him.

## Verse 11

“For what is my strength?” (Ibid.) The strength of the good is one thing, and so on, up to the point at which he refuses to suffer for what he does not love. Therefore he says:

“For what is my strength, or what is my end?” That is, evils, and so on, up to the point at which the weak man has strength. Hence he continues:

## Verse 13

“Behold, there is no help.” To show further how he is deprived of those nearest to him, for the greater merit of his strength, he adds:

“Even those who were close to me.” Although despised outwardly, he presides inwardly on the tribunal of judgment; for he breaks forth into these sentences: “He who removes,” and so on.

## Verse 14

“He who takes away from his friend.” (Ibid.) A friend is any neighbor, and so on, up to those who, by neglecting eternal things within, have long since perished. Of them it is rightly said:

## Verse 17

“And when they have grown hot”—that is, when they have begun to burn through knowledge of their punishment—they will be separated from the pleasure of the flesh, which they held fast through desire. The wicked do not understand eternal things until they are already being punished for earthly things. Then the mind boils, and kindles itself with the fire of delayed repentance; then its hardness is melted by punishment. Hence the prophet says: “Only oppression alone will give understanding to the hearing” (Isaiah 28). This they will suffer then; meanwhile they are entangled in these things.

## Verse 18

“They are entangled.” Everything that is entangled is folded back upon itself. So the wicked, who at some point desire good things as though stretched outward beyond themselves, when tempted, are folded back into their customary evils. Or, “they are entangled”: although at some point they lift their foot after conquering one vice, another that reigns over them entangles them again with the vice they had overcome. Thus one who has already rejected avarice but remains lustful returns to avarice for the sake of the price of his lust.

In this way vices retain their fugitive by mutual assistance and bind him, as it were, after he has escaped from their snares. Hence those who have fallen often return to their pleasures and do not care about the things that endure. Therefore he continues:

“They will walk in emptiness and perish.” For they carry nothing with them from the fruit of their labor. But the righteous does not appear empty in the sight of the Lord, for he carries sheaves of righteousness. He frightens them away from imitating the wicked by speaking of the end: “Consider the paths,” and so on.

## Verse 19

“Consider the paths.” (Ibid.) *Thema* is interpreted as “south wind,” and *Saba* as “net.” The south wind, which loosens the limbs with its warmth, is the laxity of a dissolute way of life; the net is the entanglement of one’s actions. A person is caught in loose actions when he does not wholly renounce the world, when he proceeds not with strict devotion but with relaxed steps—as when, through carnal love of his parents, he is hindered from pursuing the things of God.

“Consider,” he says, because we love doing perverse things but judge them when we see them in others. Therefore, when we return to ourselves, we are ashamed of such conduct.

“Wait a little.” For whatever comes to an end is brief; but whoever considers this long does not care about eternal things. By declaring the brevity of life, the voice of the righteous rises against the wicked:

## Verse 20

“They are confounded.” For the wicked try through hardships to draw the good away from hope. If they succeed, they rejoice; if they do not, they are ashamed that they have acted cruelly in vain. Hence he also says what happens in the retribution:

“They also came.” At the judgment the wicked come before the righteous, because they will see their glory and suffer more grievously when they behold what they have lost. Then shame covers them, when conscience, their witness, burns them.

The same may be understood spiritually. Job’s friends were confounded because, unable to bend him toward despair, they were ashamed. They came when they recognized inwardly the steadfastness of his mind and were embarrassed. He shows that they belonged to the number of those who fear God only when terrified by their own or others’ adversities.

## Verse 21

“Now you have come, and only now, seeing my wound.” (Ibid.) As though he were saying: I feared God even before adversity, whereas you, who do not fear God out of love, are frightened only by the blow.

## Verse 22

“Did I say…” The Church does not need the substance of the heretics—whose figure Job’s friends represent—that is, carnal wisdom. Nor does she agree to hear from them the upright things they sometimes say about conversion against the devil, because through these they draw people into unbelief. The “hand of the enemy” is Satan’s power. The “strong” are the evil spirits.

“Did I say: Bring…” Against the rich of this world, and so on, up to the point at which they despise in themselves what they despise in others.

## Verse 24

“Teach me.” This may be joined to what precedes, or it may be said independently as a rebuke.

## Verse 25

“Why have you criticized?” (Gregory.) The world ought to be pure, and so on, up to the point at which you bring forth reprehensible things for the purpose of rebuke.

(Ibid.) There are two harmful kinds of speech: praising what is perverse and censuring what is right. In the former there is favoritism; in the latter, anger. Job accuses his friends of this. One reaches this vice through idle words, and therefore he continues:

## Verse 26

“And into the wind.” To pour out words into the wind, and so on, up to the point at which the door of the tongue should therefore be closed at one time and opened at another.

## Verse 27

“Upon the orphan.” (Gregory, *Commentary on Job*, Book VIII.) See how clearly he recognizes himself to be of such great weakness, and so on, up to the point at which he endures those whom he does not love or does not endure those whom he loves.

## Verse 28

“See whether I am lying.” (Ibid.) Because, being humble, he does not command what he says on the authority of his position but persuades by reason. Yet because, under the pretext of reason, opponents are driven into unrestrained contention, he adds:

## Verse 29

“Answer, I beg you, without contention.” For heretics do not apply themselves to inquiries in order to attain the truth, but in order to appear victorious.

“And while you speak, and so on.” For whoever speaks submits himself to the judgment of the hearer. Let there be a fair judge between his heart and his tongue, so that nothing rash may proceed from the heart through the tongue, but that he may examine it before he speaks. And because those who judge rightly of their own words first judge rightly of the words of others, he adds:

## Verse 30

“And you will not find it on my tongue.” For folly does not sound in me to you if it does not proceed from your own conscience. Thus the Church first destroys the falsehoods of her enemies and afterward opens the truth; there is no place for truth while falsehoods are held as truths. By the “tongue” is meant open speech; by the “jaws,” hidden discourse, because what the Church preaches outwardly she preserves by her manner of life.

# Chapter VII

## Verse 1

“And as the days of a hireling.” (Gregory.) Just as a man wishes the day to pass quickly so that he may come to the reward of his labor, so does every righteous person. And just as a hireling sweats in another’s work but prepares his own reward, so the righteous sweats amid the world’s evils in order to receive heavenly blessings.

He takes care that no day should pass empty of work and that his reward should not diminish. He suffers hard things so that he may be crowned more greatly, although the reward is already in his heart. Nevertheless, the heat is felt more heavily in the body so that afterward there may be refreshment in rest. And this is:

## Verse 2

“Like a servant.” Every elect person is rightly called a servant so long as he remains under the yoke of this corruption, before he comes into the liberty of glory.

“And like a hireling.” The hireling is wearied by the burden of his labor unless the hope of its end relieves him; but when he sees that end, he considers nothing of what he suffers.

## Verse 3

“Empty months.” Empty of worldly things, because the good do not seek them through their actions; and they endure laborious nights of adversity when they are already in bodily torment. Or, “empty months,” because there is labor now but not yet the reward.

“Laborious nights.” He enumerates these, and so on, up to the point at which he laments all the more that he was long unaware of what he seeks and that he labored in vain.

## Verse 4

“If I sleep.” (Ibid.) According to the historical sense, the mind of the afflicted person is expressed here. Compelled by grief, it wanders through various desires: at night he longs for day, and by day for evening, because grief does not allow what is present to please him. Having already found this condition burdensome, he awaits something else, comforted by desire; but even so the pain does not end. Hence:

“And I am filled with pains.” The cause of the pain is this:

## Verse 5

“It is clothed.” (Ibid.) The same point is treated more subtly in the Church, and so on, up to the point at which they do not possess complete salvation here. Hence he continues:

“And I shall be filled with pains until darkness.” For he finds no security until he has completely left the time of temptation. He then gives the cause of the pain:

“My flesh is clothed.” That is, the carnal life I lead is either polluted by evil action or, being confined within it, darkened by the images remembered from sins, which rise like dust before the eyes.

The Church, however, feels the rottenness of the flesh’s lust in some of her members, while in those devoted to earthly actions she is sprinkled with dust. He speaks of both groups:

“My skin.” The skin signifies those in the Church who devote themselves solely to outward concerns. Despair dries their hearts, and so they contract rather than stretch themselves through perseverance toward eternal life. They cling to present things. This happens because they do not consider how fleeting this life is. But the Church, by contrast, says:

## Verse 6

“My days are swifter.” As a fabric advances through its threads, so life advances through each successive day; but the more it grows, the more it moves toward being cut. The speed of life surpasses even the haste of a fabric, since it is always diminishing. Therefore the elect do not fix their hearts upon it, and he says:

“And they are consumed”—that is, I place no confidence in them. The reprobate do this; I do not.

## Verse 7

“Remember.” (Ibid.) That is, in your goodness, look upon me as I pass swiftly, because consideration of human brevity is a pleasing offering to God.

“For it is wind.” Eternal life is solid; this life is judged neither solid nor enduring.

(Ibid.) And because after life has passed there is no place for obtaining pardon, he adds:

“And it does not return.” That is, after death, when the mind sees its retribution, it is not recalled to perform good works. Hence the rich man, despairing of himself—which aggravates his punishment—asks on behalf of his brothers. Behold, life passes away, but what follows remains. After this, too:

## Verse 8

“Nor will the sight of man see me.” That is, the mercy of the Redeemer, which softens the hardness of sinners, as when he looked upon Peter (Luke 22). But after death it does not free the one whom grace did not reform beforehand. It is not the sight of man, but:

“Your eyes are upon me.” (The source reads “GERG.”) That is, you will see the strict Judge ready to strike; and he who was awaited here for repentance will no longer remain. This applies to the righteous person who fears everything he does and, with mercy removed, foresees that he will perish. He does not remain before those eyes, because a life of punishment is insufficient when justice presses upon him. For even the stars—that is, those who shine with holiness—are not pure before him. The guilt and punishment of the human race are briefly set forth:

## Verse 9

“As a cloud is consumed.” (Ibid.) The cloud is lifted to the heights, and so on, up to the point at which he says, “Go into your house.”

## Verse 10

“Nor will the place know him any longer.” (Ibid.) God is the place of man, and so on, up to the point at which he still feels contradiction arising from the corruption of the flesh.

## Verse 12
