“Am I the sea?” (Ibid.) The prison is the flesh, which hinders, and so on, up to the point at which he now offers counsel against these things.

## Verse 15

“Therefore he chose.” (Ibid.) The soul is the intention of the mind, and so on, up to the words, “If you are going to do this to me, kill me.”

## Verse 16

“Spare me, Lord,” so that you may give eternal things, since by contempt for these present things those things are hoped for more fittingly. By asking that he be spared, he proves that he has not despaired of God. At “he chose hanging”—that is, he despaired—he added on the same subject, “spare me”; at “death to my bones,” that is, “let them live no longer”: this is the third point.

“For my days are nothing.” Whoever considers eternal things, returning to himself, rightly calls these days nothing and fears being strictly judged.

## Verse 17

“What is man?” (Ibid.) God magnifies man with a great spiritual gift and sets his heart upon him, because he judges him more strictly on account of what has been given. But what is man? It is as though he were saying: although man has been magnified beyond himself by your gifts, nevertheless, because he is flesh, he cannot bear judgment without mercy. Hence he continues:

## Verse 18

“You visit him at dawn.” Dawn is when a person comes from the night of vices and ignorance into the light; and immediately he is tested in it. So that he may not boast that he possesses good things from himself, he is permitted to be shaken by temptation, so that God’s greatness and his own weakness may be revealed. Thus Solomon, after receiving wisdom, was tested by prostitutes. Throughout this mortality man suffers such things. Hence: “How long will you not spare me?”

## Verse 19

“Saliva.” (Ibid.) Saliva flows into the mouth from the head, and so on, up to the point at which whoever wishes to merit this confesses the evil he has done: “I have sinned,” and so on.

## Verse 20

“I have sinned; what shall I do to you?” (Ibid.) As though he were saying: I do not find anything to offer you in recompense, because every human virtue is too weak to wash away guilt. Or, “what shall I do to you?” as though he were saying: all good things benefit not you but us.

“O watcher of men.” For he has left us in such a way that we cannot guard ourselves; and if we attempt anything, we are burdened by sins. Hence:

“Why have you set me against you?” When man believed the serpent, and so on, up to the point at which he seeks mercy. Hence he adds:

## Verse 21

“Why do you not take away?” Behold the desire for the Mediator, who takes away the sins of the world. Or, sin will then be completely removed when man is changed into incorruption. He therefore desires either the Redeemer or the resurrection. He joins to this both the punishment he deserved through his origin and the judgment he fears because of his own action.

Behold, it is now said to sinful man: “You are dust, and to dust you shall return.”

“Why have you set me against you?” (Ibid.) Because what is lower, having been made contrary to what is higher—that is, God—has become opposed. Therefore our lower part, namely sensuality, has become contrary to the higher part, namely the spirit, so that they are always at war.

“Until morning”—that is, at the coming of the Judge, to whom all things are open. To seek God is to be strictly judged; before him not even the righteous can stand. Yet this is the consolation of deliverance: the humble person says that he is not sufficient in himself. He therefore laments the death that now exists and fears the judgment that is impending.

# Chapter VIII

## Verse 1

“Then Bildad answered.” (Gregory.) It must first be understood that, just as Eliphaz principally accused the most holy Job of pride, although he briefly touched upon hypocrisy, so this man intends principally to accuse him of hypocrisy. But before doing so, he puts forward something from which it may be discerned how burdensome Job’s words had been to him—words, that is, of edification. As though he could no longer endure someone speaking well, he burst forth indignantly into these words:

## Verse 2

“How long will you speak such things?” As though he were saying: Why do you speak uselessly? “And a manifold spirit…” [lacuna]

“How long will you speak such things?” (Ibid.) For words of edification are burdensome to the wicked, as though he could not bear them; and because he does not wish to be corrected, he accuses what has been said well.

“And a manifold spirit.” (Ibid.) By attributing multiplicity to his speech, he reproves the poverty of his understanding. Note that there are four kinds of speaking. Some are expansive in both mouth and understanding; these are to be praised. Others are constrained in both; these are to be pitied. Others are expansive in understanding but unable to express themselves; these are to be helped. Others are poor in understanding but torrential in speech; these are to be despised. This man turns the last kind into an accusation against Job.

## Verse 3

“Does God…” (Gregory.) Job had neither denied nor ignored these things, and so on, up to the point at which they strike others as though they had justly perished. Hence he continues:

## Verses 4–5

“Even if your sons sinned, and so on. If at dawn…” As though they themselves were in the light while the Church was in the night: they summon her to rise through knowledge of God and to wash away the past through the prayer of repentance—“if pure” in thought, “upright” in action.

## Verse 6

“He will awake.” He sleeps now with respect to the assistance of you who are wandering.

“And he will restore peace.” (Gregory.) That is, he will restore the tranquility of the present life, which they consider to be God’s only reward.

“The dwelling of the righteous.” (Ibid.) They call the intention of the mind “pacified,” because if they draw people over to their own position, they fall silent from contention. They also promise riches of understanding by saying:

## Verse 7

“To such an extent.” But because their words are not readily believed, they twist the judgments of the fathers into support for their error. Hence it is added:

“That former things…” For they promise both the recovery of what has been lost and still greater rewards in the present life.

## Verse 8

“For ask the generations.” They urge that these things not merely be seen but investigated, because they do not want what is plainly evident to everyone to be observed.

## Verse 9

“Of yesterday.” Sometimes they teach morally that the present may be inferred from the past—namely, from the passing of those things, that these present things are nothing. Hence he adds: “of yesterday.” For if the former generation is recalled, it is understood that this life quickly passes like a shadow.

## Verse 10

“They themselves will teach.” They praise the fathers along with us, so that they may attack us all the more.

“From the heart.” (Ibid.) As though he were saying: You have simplicity of spirit in your mouth, not in your heart; they, by contrast, have it in their heart. Often the wicked, without considering themselves, tear the good apart. They either bring forth good things that they have learned not by seeing but by hearing, or impose upon others the evils they themselves commit; thus they excuse themselves by their deeds and judge others by their words.

So Bildad, a pretender to righteousness, says remarkable things against hypocrites and presumes to teach the righteous about matters that would be appropriate to the wicked. He is a fool who pours water into a river while gardens are thirsting.

## Verse 11

“Can the reed live?” (Ibid.) He compares the hypocrite to a rush or sedge, and so on, up to the point at which he exposes himself through the crimes of others.

“Before all the grass.” (Ibid.) The righteous too are grass according to the flesh, since “all flesh is grass” (Isaiah 48). They wither because their works fail together with the life of the flesh. But hypocrites wither first, because as soon as they have obtained the good things for which they pretended, they abandon them. These are “the grass of the roofs, which withered before it was plucked up.”

## Verse 13

“So are the paths of all.” Behold what he compares to the reed or sedge: the hypocrite’s hope is glory and such worldly things, which perish; eternal things endure.

## Verse 14

“His folly will not please him.” (Ibid.) Folly is selling something of great value for a low price—that is, performing laborious good deeds for approval. He is now delighted by this, but it will displease him in punishment. Then he will know that everything that passed away was nothing. Hence:

“And his confidence is like a spider’s web.” A spider’s web is woven with care but scattered by a breath of wind. So whatever the hypocrite produces through toil is carried away by the breeze of approval.

## Verse 15

“He will lean upon his house.” The house of the mind is any reality that the soul inhabits through love. Therefore the hypocrite’s house is approval. Or the house is confidence in holiness, which will stand before men but not before God.

## Verse 16

“He appears moist.” The reed, the hypocrite, appears moist at night—that is, he appears to men to be filled with the grace of holiness—but before the sun on the day of judgment he will wither.

“And at its rising, a shoot.” Every plant is first produced from the earth, and so on, up to the point at which the hypocrite, even when acting rightly, wishes to be seen by many.

## Verse 17

“Upon a heap of stones.” (Ibid.) The roots are thoughts; the stones, because no living thing is added, are good and evil people. The hypocrite, therefore, who dwells among stones multiplies his thoughts in seeking the admiration of men. In everything he does, he seeks praise through hidden intention, while openly he exposes what his enemies may plunder.

Thus Hezekiah, after many benefits had been bestowed upon him, showed all his possessions to the king of Babylon’s messengers. Hence he immediately hears: “All will be carried off to Babylon” (2 Kings 20). In the same way, when praise is sought, virtue and beauty are handed over to the enemy. Hence Bildad says:

“And he will dwell among stones.” For he stands where he solidifies the intention of his mind. Even if he is full of good things, if God absorbs him—that is, takes him away through death—from his place—that is, from the approvals of this life—he will hear: “I do not know you,” as is said to the foolish virgins (Matthew 25). And rightly so, because it is not enough for him unless he has also made others like himself. This is what he says: “This is the joy of his way.”

“For this is the joy,” and so on (Ibid.), so that he may also be punished for their guilt. But:

## Verse 20

“God will not cast away the simple.” The simplicity of such a person is now called folly by the cunning of the double-minded.

“Nor will he stretch out his hand.” (Ibid.) He will not lift them from the depths in which they seek glory. Hypocrites are wicked because they do not even do good things well. Or, because they show themselves outwardly pure and simple to their neighbor while concealing duplicity within, Moses says against them: “You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen” (Deuteronomy 22).

## Verse 21

“Until your mouth is filled.” This does not mean “afterward,” which is certain, but “not before,” which may appear doubtful to human beings. It is as though he were saying: He neither abandons the simple before the judgment nor ceases to strike the wicked.

“May he fill your mouth with laughter”—that is, your mind with the joy of eternal security. Hence:

“And your lips with jubilation.” Jubilation occurs when such great joy is conceived in the heart that speech cannot express it, although the mouth nevertheless gives voice to it.

## Verse 22

“Those who hate.” (Ibid.) The confusion of the righteous’ enemies will clothe them at the judgment, because when they see the Judge, all their evil deeds pass before the eyes of their minds, and the weight of their guilt covers them on every side.

They come to this because here they loved only transitory things. Hence he adds:

“And the tabernacle”—that is, the building of eternal happiness, which they multiply above themselves so that they may defend themselves here from necessities, as from heat and rain. The mind dwells in it, but the good traveler despises it.

# Chapter IX

## Verse 1

“Then Job answered and said.” (Gregory, *Commentary on Job*.) The perverse, who dislike the person speaking, attack everything he says, whether right or wrong. But Job, who does not dislike the person but the fault, saw that Bildad had spoken rightly when he said, “Does God pervert judgment?” He had also uttered truths against hypocrites, and Job approves what he has heard.

Truly I know that a humble person subject to God receives righteousness, but loses it when he composes himself in pride, because whoever compares himself with God, arrogating to himself what belongs to God, deprives himself of the good he received. Indeed, all the merit of our virtue, if it is strictly judged, is vice.

## Verse 3

“If he wishes to contend with him.” (Ibid.) That is, by presuming upon his own merits and arrogating the glory of his virtue not to God but to himself.

“He will not be able to answer him one thing for a thousand.” (Ibid.) That is, he will not be able to defend himself, and so on, up to the point at which the sight of God’s power terrifies the weak person lest he contend.

## Verse 4

“Who has resisted him and had peace?” Who creates so that created things may fit together, and orders them so that they may have peace; whoever attempts to resist his disposition loses peace. Thus the angel lost peace when he was exalted by his own restlessness; and man, who is troubled by the burden of the flesh, lost peace because he did not wish to be subject to his Creator.

## Verse 5

“He who moves the mountains,” and so on. By speaking generally of the confusion of pride, he shows what punishment awaits the exalted at the destruction of Israel. He moved the mountains—the holy preachers—from the Jews to the Gentiles. The Jews did not understand this, and were overturned by it, thinking that the joy was theirs, although they had lost the light. When the mountains were moved, he shakes the earth.

## Verse 6

“He shakes the earth from its place.” For through the Romans he removed the Jews from their borders.

“The pillars.” The priests, rulers, and teachers of the law. They were shaken because they were not permitted to live even for themselves; hence they expelled the apostles, and afterward were abandoned in the darkness of their error.

## Verse 7

“He commands the sun.” (Ibid.) The sun shines by day, and so on, up to the point at which the light is spread among all the nations. Hence:

## Verse 8

“He stretches out the heavens.” (Ibid.) That is, he causes the apostles, driven away from the Jews, to be honored everywhere.

“Alone.” He wonderfully arranged this while the bitterness of the world raged against the deaths of the good.

“He walks upon the waves,” that is, he treads them down while calming them through the wonder of signs. Jeremiah says: “I have set sand as a boundary for the sea” (Jeremiah 5), meaning that, to break the glory of the world, he chose the outcast and the poor. While the sea rages, the Church advances.

## Verse 9

“He makes Arcturus.” (Ibid.) He uses the names of philosophers, and so on, up to the point at which Arcturus turns and rises.

“Orion.” (Ibid.) Those stars rise in the winter season, and so on, up to the point at which he raised them peacefully for the destruction of their enemies.

“The Hyades.” They arise in spring on the forehead of Taurus, and so on, up to the point at which he reaches the inner things of the heavenly homeland. Hence he adds:

“And the inner parts of the south.” The south wind is the fervor of the Holy Spirit, and so on, up to the point at which he grasps more effectively by failing, saying:

## Verse 10

“He who does great things for me.” He fulfills more perfectly whoever confesses that he cannot fulfill; and he speaks more eloquently who falls silent in amazement.

“Great”—in power.

“And incomprehensible”—in reason.

“And marvelous, which cannot be numbered”—in multiplicity.

But why should we marvel at things beyond us when we do not understand even what is done with respect to us? If he should come to me:

## Verse 11

“If he should come to me.” (Ibid.) He comes when he gives gifts, and so on, up to the point at which blind man nevertheless gives an account of his deeds to God.

## Verse 12

“If he should suddenly come among…” (Ibid.) He suddenly interrogates when he brings unexpected things, and so on, up to the point more clearly shown when it is added:

“Who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” We ought to revere God’s deeds, and so on, up to the point at which the proud person kindles an unquenchable fire. Hence he says:

## Verse 13

“God, whose anger no one can resist.” Moses, Phinehas, and the other saints, and so on, up to the point at which, turning back from these matters to himself, he humbles himself and considers himself worthless in the presence of God’s power.

## Verse 14

“How much less, then, shall I…” (Ibid.) That is, if an angel is not sufficient to contemplate him, with what mind do I, burdened by flesh, dispute his judgments? Our words before God are our deeds. Yet because a human being cannot speak with God through these deeds—since before God’s subtle judgment there is no confidence in them—he adds:

## Verse 15

“Even if I had anything, I would entreat him.” After God’s justice, prayer is still needed, so that what is lacking in the person himself may be supplied by the judge’s mercy. Even if justice is complete in the more perfect, it is said to possess “something,” because the human mind scarcely accomplishes what it comprehends, and little is what it comprehends. Prayer, moreover, because it is shaken by many thoughts, fears rejection even when it is heard.

## Verse 16

“When he hears me calling, he will not…” (Ibid.) For, as David says, “they go up to the heavens” and then “descend into the abysses” (Psalm 106), penetrating the heights at one moment and descending through shameful temptations at another; they do not possess certainty that they have been heard. See how subtly he judges himself and lays bare his weakness.

“How much less, then…” He does not trust in righteousness but flees to prayer. Even if he has anything righteous, he is fearful of the prayer itself and says: “When he hears me calling.” He looks around himself in this way because he sees that he cannot endure the force of judgment. Concerning this he says:

## Verse 17

“He will even crush me in a whirlwind.” Whoever despised him when he was awaited in tranquility will be crushed in the whirlwind.

“In a whirlwind.” He fears that, amid the disturbance of the elements, his deeds will be strictly demanded. He sees that some are condemned without deeds on account of original guilt, and he speaks with their voice:

“He will multiply my wounds.” For they themselves have done nothing. Hence it is said: “No one is clean in his sight, not even an infant of one day.”

“Without cause.” This is “without cause” according to human judgment; but before God it is just that a tree should retain in its branches the bitterness it drew from its root.

These things may also be understood spiritually of Job, who both feared and foresaw God’s scourges in the whirlwind and endured what he foresaw. Hence he says: “He will multiply my wounds without cause,” because he was not struck on account of guilt. Above he had said: “That I might afflict him in vain.”

## Verse 18

“He does not permit…” (Gregory.) This is complete proof: outwardly torments tear him apart; inwardly temptations chastise him. Therefore he says that he is filled with bitterness, but the equity and power of the one who strikes him mitigate the force of the pain. And this is:

## Verse 19

“If strength is sought.” As though he were saying: no one dares, because he examines merits—he does not investigate them through another’s testimony, but as a silent observer waits for a long time. No one else can be my witness, because I myself cannot be my own witness.

## Verse 20

“If I justify myself.” (Ibid.) I am not sufficient to testify to my innocence, nor do I know that I possess it.

## Verse 21

“If I am simple.” Whoever knows the good things he does, and so on, up to the point at which he finds this exile of blindness difficult to endure. Hence he continues:

“And my life will become weary to me.” Yet the consolation of this darkness is the righteous power restored to the mind—the power that punishes the wicked and surpasses the righteous.

## Verse 22

“One thing is what I have said.” (Ibid.) Or, “the innocent is consumed,” and so on, up to the point at which he destroys our twofold nature of flesh and soul.

## Verse 23

“If he scourges, let him kill.” (Ibid.) God’s laughter is at affliction, and so on, up to the point at which he reveals that he alone endured the death of the flesh.

## Verse 24

“The earth has been given.” Or, “handed over.” The earth is the flesh; the wicked one is the devil.

“His hand”—the killers of Christ, and so on, up to the point at which Christ came.

## Verse 25

“My days were swifter than a runner.” (Ibid.) It is the task of a runner to announce what is to follow. Thus all the elect who announced Christ before his coming were runners. But because they die before him, they grieve that they pass more quickly than a runner, so that they do not see the one who is uniquely called good in his presence. Concerning them he also adds:

## Verse 26

“Like ships.” Whoever carries fruit enjoys its fragrance, and so on, up to the point at which the discourse turns, through compassion, even toward their hardness:

## Verse 27

“When I say, ‘By no means…’” (Ibid.) Israel, as before, refused to speak when it denied the one whom it had foretold. Its inner face was changed by the filth of unbelief, so that it would not be recognized by God. Therefore it remains to be tormented by eternal pains.

“My days passed more swiftly.” (Ibid.) The first man was created in such a way that his life could be extended through the ages, not unwound. But because he sinned, he suffered the course of decline, which man always endures and nevertheless desires while he longs to live. The human race laments the losses of this decline in its voice.

“They fled,” because man did not wish to stand in the light; by fleeing, he lost sight, so that he could not see the good for which he had been created.

“Like ships carrying fruit.” (Ibid.) The fruits of the earth are carried through the waves, and so on, up to the point at which thought, lest it break out into pride, humbly restrains itself by saying:

“I will by no means speak thus.” But let me, being weak, be restrained from such an inquiry. The face of the mind is changed, because, seeing itself weak, it venerates what it does not understand, although it had sought lofty things. There is pain in this, because the person who is blinded with respect to understanding what concerns him is deeply afflicted. He fears adding his own particular evils to these common evils: “I feared everything,” and so on.

## Verse 28

“I feared all my works.” (Ibid.) They were indeed good, and so on, up to the point at which he seems unable to reach life even through labors. Hence:

## Verse 29

“But if I am wicked even in this way.” He does not repent of having labored, but grieves that amid his labors he is uncertain of the rewards. The righteous person is uncertain in such a way that he has confidence; he has confidence in such a way that he does not become sluggish through security.

“In vain”—I say, because:

## Verse 30

“If I wash myself as with snow-water.” Whoever crushes himself through lamentation, and so on, up to the point at which the person who is moved to compunction in prayer on account of earthly things is earthly water.

“Hands.” (Ibid.) These are works.

“Like the purest.” As though they were not truly pure under this corruption.

## Verse 31

“You will dip me”—that is, you will show that I have been dipped; for the closer we approach him, the more clearly we recognize our uncleanness from his purity.

“Garments.” The garment of the soul is the body, which Solomon commanded to be white at all times; and if it is mixed with blood—that is, with carnal desires—Isaiah says that it must be burned (Isaiah 9).

“They will abhor.” That is, they will make it abominable, as it is said of Judas: “He acquired a field from the reward of iniquity”—that is, he caused it to be possessed. In the abomination of the garment, it is worse that he does not recognize the judgment of his critic.

## Verse 32

“For when he is seen…” Among human beings, we hear accusations, answer them, and are heard. But in God’s judgment, he hears us because he sees everything we do, while we do not hear him, because we do not fully understand what displeases him. He cannot be heard on equal terms.

## Verse 33

“May there be one who can prevail over both”—that is, over God and me:

“To argue.” He argues who, on the authority of reason, and so on, up to the point at which he corrected the hearts of sinners through gentleness rather than terror. Hence he adds:

## Verse 34

“Let him take his rod away from me”—the rod of the law by which he punishes. But Christ removed it and showed the ways of life through gentleness. He willed that God should be feared but loved as a father.

## Verse 35

“I will speak and will not fear him.” (Ibid.) He no longer has fear, but approaches him with the affection due to a father. Behold, the staff—that is, the fear of the law—has been sent but does not raise up the child; rather, Elisha himself, adapting himself to the child and breathing upon him seven times, that is, through the love of the Spirit.

(Gregory.) “To answer” is to make a worthy repayment through deeds. But who, servilely fearing, responds to God’s benefits? Only the one who, through the confidence of love, does not fear rendering him worthy service. The person who would do evil if permitted is not pure. For the one who loves, this life is wearisome; although it was formerly sweet, he now endures it even in mourning.

# Chapter X

## Verse 1

“My soul is weary of my life.” (Ibid.) When this life becomes worthless through love of the heavenly life, the person who previously defended his faults now accuses them. And this is:

“I will dismiss my speech”—the speech I used in my defense—

“Against myself,” because by confessing I accuse myself. This is not like the person who is still ashamed to confess, since he does not abandon evil with such desire; rather, because at times he confesses openly, he does not groan but speaks with mournful joy. Therefore he adds:

“I will speak in bitterness,” so that bitterness may punish what the tongue accuses. Security arises from repentance, and he asks more confidently how he is being treated. And this is:

## Verse 2

“I will say to God: Do not condemn me,” because my punishment extinguishes your punishments.

“Declare to me why you judge me thus,” that is, why you scourge me—whether for security or specifically on account of some fault; for although he is just, he nevertheless has certain evils. Therefore he asks God to make him known to himself, so that he too may punish by weeping what God punishes in him. Thus I seek the reason, for I know that it is not unjust.

“Why do you judge me thus.” He judges in two ways here: either he imposes punishment, etc., up to the point at which by striking he also preserves him in innocence. Therefore he says:

VERSE 3.—“Is it good?” This question requires a negative answer, etc., up to the point that he considers him weak.

“The work of your hands.” As though he were saying: “Why do you wickedly destroy one whom you made freely?”

“Of the wicked,” that is, of the malignant spirits, who, since they cannot return to life, seek companions for death. Their plan was to break Job, upright in prosperity, through adversity; but God does not permit him to be tested beyond his strength.

VERSE 4.—“Have you eyes of flesh?” The eyes of flesh recognize only certain things that occur in time, since they too are closed with time; and human sight follows any work rather than anticipating it.

VERSE 5.—“Days.” The days and years of a human being likewise differ from eternity: for the eternal One has nothing that passes away and nothing that is future, but sees everything as present.

VERSE 6.—“That you should seek out my iniquity.” And so that you may know that I have done nothing wicked, he asks humbly, as it were: “Why do you test by scourges in time the one whom you knew perfectly and before time in your presence?”

VERSE 7.—“Since there is no one” (ibid.). As though he were saying: “What remains for you except to spare one whom no one can resist?” For the one against whose vengeance no one can prevail should all the more easily receive mercy. But in order to appease him, let us offer him his own work, since we cannot offer ours.

VERSE 8.—“Your hands.” As though he were saying: “Consider mercifully, lest what you have made perish.”

“They made.” According to the soul.

“Everything round about.” According to the body, etc., up to the point at which, concerning the other things, he said only, “Let it be.”

“And thus suddenly.” As though he were saying: “Why do you despise with such humiliation one whom you place before so many things with such dignity?” Yet together with this dignity, which exists through the spirit, there is weakness through the flesh, which should move the compassionate Judge. Hence he says:

VERSE 9.—“Remember, I ask,” etc. A fault that is pardonable in man is unforgivable in the angel, who was strong. It is clay when water moistens earth; so a human being is clay when the soul waters the flesh, whose death he openly adds:

“And into dust,” etc. As though he were saying: “See the material and the punishment, and spare the fault.” Since he has described the nature of the created human being, he adds the order of propagation, saying:

VERSE 10.—“Did you not pour me out like milk,” etc. The human being was made like clay, but was propagated as milk is milked from seed and as cheese is curdled in the flesh. He is clothed with flesh and skin and strengthened with bones and sinews. After the creation of the body, which is the lesser thing, the wondrous breathing of animation is added.

“Did you not pour me out like milk,” while the mind is drawn by the Spirit of God and from its old condition as milk is milked, because it is formed in a certain beginning; and as cheese is curdled when, growing rich through thoughts, it is compressed, so that it no longer flows away into desires but is solidified in one love. Against these beginnings, however, the flesh murmurs from its old habit.

VERSE 11.—“With skin and flesh.” That is, the mind is surrounded by the siege of carnal impulses. But the one who loosens them outwardly for battle strengthens it inwardly through the bones of virtues, so that it may be humble and strong. God therefore rightly grants uprightness of conduct, because he spares former sins.

VERSE 12.—“Life and mercy” (ibid.). But he gave these goods in vain unless he himself guards them; hence he adds:

“And your visitation.” The same things concerning the inner person, etc., up to the point at which he considers the gifts of God more subtly.

“Life and mercy” (ibid.). Life is given when evil minds, etc., up to the point at which, after he has generally spoken of the gifts of mercy concerning himself, he adds:

VERSE 13.—“Yet I know that you remember all things.” Since it is said, “Why am I afraid concerning myself, when I know that all nations are to be gathered?”

“Although you conceal these things in your heart” (ibid.). Because you do not yet disclose them in open speech. Those who are certain of pardon are often touched by the memory of their former wickedness and unwillingly afflicted by illicit thought. Hence he adds:

VERSE 14.—“If I have sinned.” For a time God spares, etc., up to the point at which, when struck, they may fix their hope more firmly in God’s help alone.

VERSE 16.—“Because of pride” (GREGORY). When a lioness eagerly seeks food for her cubs, etc., up to the point at which, if we grow sluggish in holy desire, he sets before us the examples of those who keep good watch.

VERSE 17.—“You multiply your wrath against me,” that is, you display it as manifold; for if he scourges the good, what will happen to the wicked? Thus, when manifold wrath is foreseen, a person returns to himself and punishes what is crooked.

VERSE 19.—“I would have been as though I had never existed, from the womb” (ibid.). The same as what was said there: “Like a hidden miscarriage,” etc.; or, those conceived who did not see the light.

VERSE 20.—“Are not my days few?” (ibid.). May the pleasure of the present life not seize me, since it quickly passes away.

“Leave me, then … my sorrow” (ibid.). That is, moderate the scourges, etc., up to the point at which the foresight of hell does this above all. Hence he says:

VERSE 21.—“Before I go.” Hell is called earth because captives are held there.

“Before I go.” Not that the one who mourns goes, but that the one who does not mourn goes—just as if I said to a debtor, “Pay before I bind you.”

“I shall not return” (ibid.). Because mercy does not free the condemned thereafter.

VERSE 22.—“A land of misery and darkness.” For outwardly pain torments those whom blindness of mind darkens inwardly; or, there no one returns again to the light, as one may in this life, where, although there is misery, it is permitted through conversion to return to the light.

“The shadow of death.” Death is separation from God; its shadow is darkness. For penal fire has burning but not light, so that those who sinned in both respects may be punished in both.

“There is no order” (ibid.). Not that God does not order things, up to the point at which the nature of things is not preserved. Hence he adds:

“Everlasting horror.” This fear is of future evil, etc., up to the point that he who saw Lazarus might not see those whom he saw in punishment come to torments.

# CHAPTER XI

VERSE 2.—“Should one who speaks much?” (Gregory, Book X on Job.) He begins with insults, etc., up to those who consider nothing right except what they themselves think.

“Or a talkative man.” A true statement, for it is written: “The practice of justice is silence”; but it was not spoken in the proper place. Whoever cannot endure what is right and neglects correction girds himself for an answer.

VERSE 3.—“Will people keep silent only for you?” etc. (ibid.). Anyone whom conscience gnaws considers every right statement an object of mockery and thinks that general statements are directed at him. Therefore he is inflamed to speak against them, so that at least in this way he may control his shame, as though he were not a criminal if he accused others. Hence, lying, he adds:

VERSE 4.—“For you said: My speech is pure.” Job had not said this; but it is a consolation to a crime if the life of the one who corrects is stained, even falsely.

VERSE 5.—“Would that God might speak with you,” etc. (ibid.). The wicked verbally wish good things in order to appear kind and to show that the things present are evil. Hence this man too says:

“Would that God might speak.” As though he were saying: “You speak only to yourself now, while you think carnally; you are empty of the spirit of truth.” It is as though I pity your ignorance more than your punishment.

(Ibid.) “Lips,” that is, judgments, through which, once opened, etc., up to the point at which he acknowledges God; and if he acknowledges his sins, he patiently endures the scourges. And this is:

VERSE 6.—“And you would understand that he exacts of you less than your iniquity deserves.” He unjustly charges a just man with iniquity, but this insult proceeds from zeal for God and is pardonable. Since he does not know the merits of the just man, he adds mockery out of ignorance:

VERSE 7.—“Perhaps you will comprehend the footsteps of God” (ibid.). The kindness of visitation, etc., up to the point that his essence will be fully seen by no one.

VERSE 8.—“Higher.” Because within the encompassing of his spirit he transcends all things.

“Deeper than hell.” Because by transcending he carries things upward.

VERSE 9.—“Longer than the earth.” Because by the perpetuity of eternity he surpasses the measure of creation.

“Broader than the sea.” Because he possesses the ages in such a way, etc., up to the point at which you do not know how to reproach even yourself in temptations.

VERSE 10.—“If he overturns” (ibid.). He overturns heaven, etc., up to the point at which a person is either exercised by resisting or broken when led astray. Therefore he rightly says:

“Who will contradict him? Or who can say to him, ‘Why do you do this?’” Because no one can resist God’s judgment or penetrate it by questioning. Why does he overturn or confine?

VERSE 11.—“For he himself knows” (ibid.). When the mind is lifted up by pride, etc., up to the point at which vanity drags it along with iniquity, namely, into swelling pride, he adds:

VERSE 12.—“A vain man into pride” (ibid.). Through fault the vain person is made bold, etc., up to the point at which through unrestrained freedom he runs boldly and aimlessly through his desires.

VERSE 13.—“But you have strengthened” (ibid.). To strengthen the heart does not mean here, etc., up to the point at which, as though teaching, he adds: “And you will be steadfast,” etc.

VERSE 14.—“If there are iniquities” (ibid.). Iniquity in the hand, etc., up to the point at which the consciousness of his guilt accuses him.

VERSE 15.—“And you will be steadfast.” For the less he trembles before judgment, the more firmly he stands in good actions.

VERSE 16.—“You will also forget misery” (ibid.). The evils of the present life are felt by the soul with greater harshness insofar as it neglects to weigh the good that follows. But if it fixes the eye of the heart on what endures, it sees that whatever tends toward an end is nothing.

“And like waters.” For passing miseries do not shake one by force, but pour in the touch of sorrow: outwardly there is pain from the blow, while inwardly the person grows cold from temptation. Against this the divine light is kindled more strongly, and therefore it is added:

VERSE 17.—“And as the noonday.” Noonday brightness is the renewal of virtue in temptation.

“And when you have been consumed” (GREGORY). When the just person has begun to fall through outward evils, then his brightness begins. Conversely, for the wicked there is light during the day of this life and darkness at evening.

“And when you have been consumed.” Because, falling outwardly, he is renewed inwardly; and the harsher the things he endures, the more confidently he hopes for rewards. And this is:

VERSE 18.—“And you will have confidence.” Having dug about, you will sleep securely, etc., up to the point at which, hidden from the deeds of the world, he sleeps securely within himself.

VERSE 19.—“You will rest, and there will be no one.” For whoever is fixed on the desire for eternity, while there is nothing in the world that he seeks, has nothing in the world that he fears.

“And they will entreat you.” When the wicked proclaim what is right, they promise others on a grand scale what they themselves desire. But lest what they are become evident through prolonged promising, they quickly return to words of uprightness. Hence it is added:

VERSE 20.—“But the eyes of the wicked.” By the name of eyes, etc., up to the point at which he finds no place where he can hide himself.

“And their hope will be abomination,” etc. (ibid.). For from the very source through which the flesh lives pleasantly for a time, the spirit perishes forever.

# CHAPTER XII

VERSE 1.—“But Job answered” (GREGORY). This is what Zophar truly said, etc., up to the point at which Job adds:

VERSE 2.—“Then you alone are human beings.” Whoever thinks that he surpasses everyone in reason rejoices that he alone is human. “Then you alone are human beings.” For whoever thinks that he alone is wise—what else does he think but that this same wisdom will die with him?

VERSE 3.—“But I also have a heart as you do.” In order to correct their pride, he denies that he is inferior; and, so as not to exceed the limit of his humility, he does not claim superiority. See how discreetly he speaks, indicating what they ought to think about themselves.

“For who does not know these things that you know?” As though he were saying: “Since the things you say are known to everyone, why do you swell with pride over knowledge of what you have said?”

VERSE 4.—“He who is mocked” (ibid.). Human mockery makes that person close to God whom innocence of life keeps alien from human perversities.

VERSE 5.—“A despised lamp” (ibid.). By the name of the rich he signifies the pride of the arrogant. The simplicity of the just person is called both a lamp and despised: a lamp because it shines inwardly; despised because it is considered worthless by carnal minds.

“Prepared for the appointed time.” The appointed time of the despised lamp is the predestined day of the final judgment, when it will be shown with what power each just person who is now despised shines.

VERSE 6.—“The tents of robbers abound” (ibid.). He shows that the riches of the present life are nothing, etc., up to the point at which, nevertheless, they received the goods they possess from God.

“Surely, ask the beasts,” etc. (ibid.). The beasts signify those slower in understanding; the birds of heaven, those wise in lofty things.

VERSE 8.—“The fish” (ibid.). The curious are understood. The meaning is: if you inquire of these, they confess God, the Creator of all things. It may also be understood according to the literal sense.

VERSE 10.—“In whose hand is the soul.” Here the soul of every living creature signifies the life of the body itself.

“The spirit of all flesh” (ibid.). That is, the spiritual effect of intelligence in human beings, which is in God’s power. It can also be understood as signifying through the soul the life of every living beast.

VERSE 11.—“Does not the ear distinguish words?” From these bodily things, etc., up to the point at which what you know tastes deeply and intimately to me through love.

VERSE 13.—“With him is wisdom,” etc. (Gregory on Job, Book XXI). For with God, in the beginning, was God the Word, who is also the power of God and the wisdom of God. He has counsel because he arranges his own affairs; he has understanding because he knows ours.

VERSE 14.—“If he destroys, no one can build.” The Almighty destroys the human race when he abandons it, and builds it when he fills it. Unless this happens, the preacher’s outward exhortation is in vain.

“If he shuts a person in.” Every human being by that very fact, etc., up to the point at which he does not soften the reprobate heart through grace.

VERSE 15.—“If he withholds the waters, everything will dry up.” For if the knowledge of preachers is withdrawn, etc., up to the point at which he referred to the sevenfold grace.

“If he sends them forth, they will overturn.” For if the grace of the Holy Spirit is poured in, etc., up to the point at which the earth is immediately overturned, because the hardness of the sinful mind is changed from the obstinacy of its immobility.

VERSE 16.—“With him is strength.” In the preceding words, when he said, etc., up to the point at which he will judge how the wisdom of the Father is present among the elect in the kingdom.

“He knows both the deceiver and the one deceived” (ibid.). He knows the deceiver, etc., up to the point at which it sometimes becomes the beginning of retribution.

VERSE 17.—“He leads counselors to a foolish end.” By “counselors” he means preachers, who offer their hearers counsel for life. When they preach for the sake of temporal things, they are led to a foolish end, because through labor they strive toward the place from which they ought to flee through uprightness of mind.

“And judges.” Those who preside over the examination of the conduct of others are rightly called judges. But when they do not examine others carefully and do not know how to correct them, they have been led into bewilderment.

VERSE 18.—“He loosens the belt of kings.” In those who seemed to govern their members well, he destroys the belt of chastity on account of the fault of pride. And because pleasure of the flesh is in the loins, he girds their loins with the rope of sin and pleasure.

VERSE 19.—“He leads priests away inglorious” (ibid.). For before the Judge they will not find the glory that they do not now seek through the zeal of preaching in the conduct of their subjects.

“And he overthrows the nobles” (GREGORY). For when he abandons the minds of rulers through just judgment, they neglect heavenly things and fall here into their own pleasures.

VERSE 20.—“Changing the speech of the truthful.” Those who were truthful when preaching heavenly things often fall into love of earthly things when they love temporal matters; thus the speech of the truthful is changed. Or this may be understood of the Jews, who formerly truthfully announced that Christ would come but denied him when he was present.

“And teaching” (ibid.). The teaching of the elders has been taken away, because the Jews did not at all follow by faith what they remembered their fathers had foretold.

VERSE 21.—“He pours contempt upon princes.” The Jews, remaining in the commandments of the Law, seemed to rule through faith; the Gentiles, pressed down in the depths by unbelief, lay hidden. But when Judea denied the mystery of the Lord’s incarnation, the Gentiles believed. Thus:

VERSE 22.—“He reveals deep things from darkness,” when the mystical meanings of allegories are recognized in the hidden words of the prophets.

“And he brings the shadow of death into the light” (ibid.). By “the shadow of death” he means, etc., up to the point at which the death of the flesh is not feared at all.

VERSE 23.—“He multiplies nations” (ibid.). He extends nations both through the fruitfulness of offspring and yet abandons them in their own unbelief; and those whom he had left in the fall of unbelief he eventually brings back to faith. Once these have been restored, what follows takes place: “He changes the heart,” etc.

VERSE 24.—“He changes the heart of princes.” The heart of the princes of the earth has been changed, etc., up to the point at which a way could not be opened against the author of all things.

VERSE 25.—“They will grope as in darkness” (ibid.). For he who gropes as in darkness, etc., up to the words, “Is this not the son of the carpenter?”

# CHAPTER XIII

VERSE 1.—“Behold, all these things” (GREGORY). For he saw all these things in the blessed one, etc., up to the point at which he saw that some things were present in deeds and others in words. He continues:

“My eye has seen all this, and my ear has heard it.” But because words are of no use if they lack understanding, he continues:

“And I have understood each thing.” For when something is shown or heard, if understanding is not granted, it is not prophecy at all. He shows that he is not lifted up by this understanding when he says:

VERSE 2.—“According to true knowledge.” By these words he made known how great his humility was: he denies that he is inferior to those whose lives he had far surpassed by holy living, and he confirms that he knows according to their knowledge. By knowing heavenly things, he surpassed their earthly thoughts through the spirit of prophecy.

VERSE 3.—“Nevertheless I will speak to the Almighty” (ibid.). We speak with the Almighty when we implore his mercy. We dispute with him when, joining ourselves to his justice, we examine our deeds through careful investigation. Or a person disputes with God who, while obeying him here, will afterward judge peoples with him, and who even now does not cease to judge the wicked.

VERSE 4.—“First I will show you,” etc. (ibid.). Thus the Church speaks of heretics: “First I will show you to be fabricators.” Just as a building is made from stones, so a lie is fabricated from words.

VERSE 5.—“Would that you were silent” (ibid.). Seeing that they wish to appear important, etc., up to the point at which they lead weak minds astray.

VERSE 6.—“Hear, then, my correction” (ibid.). He rightly brought correction before judgment, because unless the foolish swelling of pride is first depressed through correction, the judgment of the just is not at all recognized through understanding.

VERSE 9.—“Will he be deceived like a human being by your frauds?” Heretics offer fraud to God when they assert things that do not please the one on whose behalf they speak; and, while striving to defend him, they offend him.

VERSE 10.—“He himself will rebuke you, because…” There are those who perceive God’s truth in their hearts, etc., up to the point at which they recognize God’s righteous judgments more deeply in the secrecy of their thoughts.

VERSE 11.—“Suddenly” (ibid.). In human language, God’s movement is spoken of; it is the very severity of his uprightness, which will trouble through vengeance those reprobates who here refuse to be troubled through repentance.

“And his terror will fall upon you.” For among the reprobate fear does not produce rest, but punishment produces fear. Hence the prophet says: “Only distress will give understanding to hearing” (Isaiah 28), because when they are punished for despising God’s commandments, then they understand what they heard.

VERSE 12.—“Your remembrance.” However much someone may act for the sake of remembrance, etc., up to the point at which proud flesh wastes away in corruption.

VERSE 13.—“Be silent for a little while, so that I may speak.” He indicates that they have spoken according to the sense of the flesh. For this reason he restrains them into silence, so that he may say what the mind has suggested to him. As though he were saying: “I do not speak carnally but spiritually, because through the sense of the spirit I hear what I utter through the ministry of the body.”

VERSE 14.—“Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth?” The teeth here signify the inner senses, etc., up to the point at which I cannot benefit my observers, that is, you.

“With my teeth.” The teeth are the inner senses, which investigate each thing, etc., up to the point at which he may be able to chew spiritual things.

“And I carry my soul in my hands” (ibid.). To carry one’s soul in one’s hands is to display the intention of the heart in action, which is done for the edification of one’s neighbor. The meaning is: “Why do I either judge myself strictly before people or show what I desire in action, if I benefit my neighbors neither by judging evil nor by displaying good?”

VERSE 15.—“Even if he kills me, I will hope in him,” etc. (ibid.). Truly patient is the one who is worn down by adversity and yet is not bent away from the uprightness of hope.

“Nevertheless, my ways.” The Lord the Savior is found in this way: if now, out of fear of the Lord, your sin is reproved by yourselves.

VERSE 16.—“For no hypocrite will come into his sight.” Now he will indeed come before the tribunal of the Judge, etc., up to the point at which he refuses to come into the sight of the Lord.

VERSE 17.—“Hear my speech.” By calling them riddles, he shows that his words are figurative. Hence, in the voice of the faithful people, he adds:

VERSE 18.—“If I am judged, I know that I am just.” This does not depart from his person, etc., up to the point at which he does not fail to recognize that he has been made just by a gift.

VERSE 19.—“Who is he who will be judged with me?” Since he has nothing in his outward actions for which he may be reproached, he freely seeks an accuser. But because even the hearts of the just reproach themselves for foolish thought, it is added:

“Why am I consumed in silence?” As though he were saying: “Just as I lived so that I would fear no external accuser, would that I had lived so that within myself I would not fear an accusing conscience.” The person consumed in silence is the one who finds within himself something by which he is burned.

VERSE 20.—“Only two things do not do to me.” Here he calls the face of God his judgment, in which, when he sees sins, he punishes; no one is hidden from it unless the two things he requests are removed. He continues concerning these:

VERSE 21.—“Remove your hand far from me.” By the hand that he asks to be made distant, etc., up to the point at which he serves through fear.

VERSE 22.—“Call.” (GREGORY.) He seeks Christ’s presence, so that through it he may both hear what he does not know and be heard in the things he knows. Or God calls by choosing, and the human being responds by obeying; the human being speaks by desiring, and God responds by appearing. Yet, while breathing after this, he examines himself more subtly.

“Call me, and I will answer you.” God’s calling is to regard us with love and election. Our answering is to obey his love through good works.

“Or I will speak.” We speak when we ask for his face through desire; he responds to those who speak when he appears to us as we love him.

VERSE 23.—“How many iniquities and sins do I have?” etc. It is the labor of the just to find themselves and, having found themselves, to lead themselves to better things by weeping and correcting themselves. Iniquity appears heavier than sin, and crime heavier than fault.

VERSE 24.—“Why do you hide your face?” (ibid.). The human being possessed contemplation of God in paradise, but through fault fell into darkness. Stirred by punishment, he returns to love and says:

“And do you consider me?” Because if you regarded me as a friend, you would not deprive me of the light of your vision.

VERSE 25.—“Against a leaf,” etc. The human being is called a leaf, etc., up to the point at which you recognize him to be so weak.

VERSE 26.—“You write.” What we speak passes away, but what we write remains. God is said not to speak but to write bitterness when his scourges endure over us for a long time. For he once fixed the sentence of the mortality of the flesh, and this cannot be changed until the end.

“And consume me.” It is clear that the sins of the young and the old are serious, if the just man fears so greatly what he committed in an infirm age.

VERSE 27.—“You have placed my foot in the stocks.” God placed the human being’s foot in the stocks because he bound his perversity by the sentence of his strong severity.

“And you watched all my paths.” A path is narrower than a road. Since roads signify actions, we rightly understand paths to signify the thoughts of actions.

“And you considered the traces of my feet.” He called the intentions of works “traces”; or they are evil deeds which, while we perform them, provide a bad example to our brothers who look on, and, as though with a foot turned out of the way, leave distorted tracks for those who follow.

VERSE 28.—“Who, like decay…” Just as a garment is eaten by the moth arising from it, so a human being has within himself the decay by which he is consumed. Or he is tempted by the corruption of his flesh, just as a garment is consumed by the moth arising from it.

“How many iniquities I have” (ibid.). As though, because of the blindness of exile, a person does not know himself—a blindness that occurs because he has hidden himself from the face of God—which, now admonished by punishment itself, he mourns.

“Against a leaf.” The human being was a tree in creation, but, dried up in temptation, became a leaf; in his fall, he became stubble.

“You wish to consume me,” because he discovers that he sinned in youth, etc., up to the point at which they were as though they had then been undiscerning.

# CHAPTER XIV

VERSE 1.—“A human being born of woman” (GREGORY). By the name “woman,” weakness is signified. The meaning is: “What strength does one possess who is born from weakness, who is confined in relation to life and expanded in relation to misery?”

VERSE 2.—“Who comes forth like a flower.” Because he shines in the flesh.

“He is crushed,” because he is reduced to dust and decay.

“And he flees like a shadow.” He compared the human being not merely to the sun that flees, but to a shadow. For whoever has no warmth of heart in the love of God and yet does not retain the life he loves flees like a shadow.

“And never remains in the same state,” etc. For he is always failing in the very thing through which he thinks he is advancing along the course of life.

VERSE 3.—“And do you deem it worthy concerning such a one?” To open God’s eyes is to exercise judgments and to see whom he should strike.

VERSE 4.—“Who can make,” etc. For the one who alone is clean in himself, etc., up to the point at which he says that Christ alone was not born from unclean seed.

VERSE 5.—“The days of a human being are short,” etc. (ibid.), because with God even things that pass away stand firm; he is said to have the number of months before him. Or, in “days,” the brevity of time is signified; in “months,” the multiplied spans of days are signified. Thus a human being has short days, but because our life is extended afterward, the number of our months is said to exist with God.

“You have appointed his boundaries” (Gregory on Job, Book XII). For nothing that happens to human beings in this world happens without God’s hidden judgment.

VERSE 6.—“Withdraw from him a little.” Withdraw, that is, now remove the scourges of the present life and show the good things of eternal rest.

“Until the desired thing comes,” when he receives eternal rest in recompense for his labor.

VERSE 7.—“A tree has hope,” etc. He presents the human race as despised and indicates how much those things without sensation themselves seem to surpass it. Or according to the mystical sense: the tree is preferred to the human being. Here the carnal human being is understood; the tree signifies the just person, who, when afflicted by suffering in death, is restored through the greenness of eternal life.

“And its branches sprout,” because from the suffering of the just the faithful receive the greenness of spiritual life.

VERSE 8.—“If its root has grown old in the earth” (ibid.). The root of the just person is holy preaching, because from it he arises and in it he subsists. Among earthly hearts it is believed to be exhausted of all strength.

“And its trunk dies in the dust,” because his body is deprived of life among the hands of persecutors.

VERSE 9.—“At the scent of water it will bud,” etc. For through the breath of the Spirit, in the hearts of the elect, it produces a bud of virtue by the example of his work.

“And it will make a crown of foliage,” etc. To make foliage after the trunk has been cut down, etc., up to the point at which it produced foliage, because the apostles, who had withered, flourished again in faith as before.

VERSE 10.—“But when a human being has died” (ibid.). A human being dies through the very loss of righteousness; he is stripped of the garment of innocence granted in paradise and is consumed as the destruction of the flesh follows. “Where, then, is he” who is not in the love of it, where “is true being”?

VERSE 11.—“As when waters depart from the sea.” The sea is the human mind, etc., up to the point at which we are now filled with the sweetness of prosperity.

VERSE 12.—“Until heaven is worn away, he will not awaken.” For unless the end of this world arrives, the human race will not awaken from sleep.

VERSE 13.—“Who will grant me this?” Before the coming of the Mediator, knowing that he would descend into hell, he asks there for the protection of the Creator.

“Appoint for me a time when you will remember me.” He asks for the Redeemer’s coming to those in hell.

VERSE 14.—“Do you think that a dead human being will rise again?” Just men often, etc., up to the point at which he may strengthen him more powerfully afterward.

“All the days.” Therefore, whoever awaits his transformation with such great desire indicates how certain he is of the resurrection.

VERSE 15.—“You will call me, and I will answer you.” We truly answer God when he calls us, when at the command of supreme incorruption we rise incorruptible.

“To the work of your hands you will extend your right hand,” as though he were saying: “For this reason corruptible creation will be able to persist unto incorruption, because it will be raised by the hand of your power.” Or “right hand” signifies the Son, who, having become incarnate, was sent to raise the human being.

VERSE 16.—“You indeed will number my steps,” etc. He numbers the steps and spares sins: he considers our deeds carefully and yet mercifully releases penitents here.

“You have numbered, but spare.” He numbers when he turns us toward mourning each thing we have done; he spares because he does not punish what we have punished. Hence he adds:

VERSE 17.—“You have sealed it as though in a bag,” etc. (ibid.). In secret, etc., up to the point at which he heals because here he completely releases through scourges.

VERSE 18.—“A falling mountain flows away” (ibid.). There are two kinds of temptation, etc., up to the point at which you either permit him to be consumed by a long and slow process, as Solomon was.

“A rock,” that is, the mind of the just person, is carried away.

“From its place,” that is, from righteousness to fault through excessive force.

VERSE 19.—“Stones,” that is, strength; “water,” continual flatteries.

“Earth,” which sanctifies.

VERSE 20.—“You have strengthened him a little,” etc. (ibid.). A human being has been strengthened for a little while because here he received strength for living only briefly. But within this brevity, in which he has been strengthened, he gathers what he may find in perpetuity—either so that he may rejoice forever or so that he may not escape punishments.

“You will change his face and send him away.” The face of a human being, etc., up to the point at which he is compelled to pass over into eternal things against his will.

VERSE 21.—“Whether his sons become noble.” Just as those who are still living do not know where the souls of the dead are, so the dead, in bodily terms, do not know how the life of those placed in the flesh is arranged after them.

VERSE 22.—“Nevertheless, his flesh will grieve while he lives.” Those who live spiritually also suffer the tribulation of the flesh here.

“And his soul will mourn over him.” It is fitting that a human being should always find sorrows within himself, since, having abandoned the Creator, he sought joy within himself.

# CHAPTER XV

VERSE 2.—“Should a wise man answer?” (GREGORY.) Everything perceived in the holy displeases the wicked as though it had been cast into the wind; they consider the words of the good not expressions of reason but goads of fury.

“And fill himself with heat” (ibid.). They also strive to cloak under the defense of the Lord the things they feel they have spoken insultingly. Hence he adds:

VERSE 3.—“Do you rebuke him with words?” (ibid.). They think that no one possesses fear of the Lord except the one whom they have drawn into the folly of their own profession. Hence he adds:

VERSE 4.—“As much as lies in you,” etc., that is, “you have taken away.” As though he were saying: “Relying on your righteousness, you disdain to ask for the grace of your Creator.” When heretics do not find real evils against the good, they invent things for which they may reproach them, so that they themselves may appear just.

VERSE 5.—“For iniquity taught” (GREGORY). Iniquity teaches the mouth when, conceived from an evil life, it produces something worse to be said.

“You imitate the tongue of blasphemers” (ibid.). Heretics, as though venerating God, deny humble things such as the flesh and death, and call the Church, which confesses these things, blasphemous. If anything adverse happens to her, they say that it happens because of this offense. Hence he says:

VERSE 6.—“It will condemn you,” etc. At times they wish to suppress him as though by reasoning. Hence:

VERSE 7.—“Were you the first human being?” They adopt this defense of God for this reason, etc., up to the point at which he says: “Consider that you do not know the counsel.”

VERSE 9.—“What do you know?” (ibid.). These words clearly show the mental pride from which everything that sounds as though it were spoken in defense of the Lord proceeds.

VERSE 10.—“Both the aged and the ancient.” Since heretics cannot establish their own position by reason, they rely on the authority of the ancients to defend themselves before fools; and they say that the teachers of the Church were their masters.

VERSES 11–12.—“Is it a great thing?” It continues: “What does your heart lift you up?” The minds of the just are often suspended in contemplation of higher things, so that outwardly their faces seem to have become astonished. But the wicked think that this force of contemplation arises from hypocrisy; whatever is in themselves, they think is in others.

VERSE 13.—“Why does your spirit swell against God?” The just, afflicted by certain necessities, are often compelled to confess their deeds, as blessed Job had done, and this is considered pride. But in God’s ears things spoken with a humble heart are not proud. Just as it is a serious fault to claim for oneself what one is not, so often there is no fault at all if someone humbly says that he possesses the good that he does possess.

“Such words.” (Ibid.) Concerning your good deeds—but Job did not swell up against God because of these; rather, he humbly stated what he had truly done. Often the righteous and the unrighteous use the same words, and what pleases one offends the other: for example, the Pharisee, who justifies himself in his actions (Luke 18), and Hezekiah, who justifies himself in his thoughts (2 Kings 20).

**VERSE 14.**—“What is man?” By the very fact that he is called “man,” he is shown to be earthly and weak. For he is named from *humus*, “earth.”

[Col. 0797D] “And that he should appear just when born,” etc. How can one appear just who was born from her who became the supplier of injustice? For in paradise the woman first supplied injustice to the man.

**VERSE 15.**—“And the heavens are not clean.” By the name “heavens” he repeats what he signified by the designation “saints”: before God’s strict judgment, not even they can be perfectly clean.

**VERSE 16.**—“How much more abominable.” (Ibid.) Every perverse person is abominable because of the uncleanness of his stain.

“Useless,” with respect to the righteousness of a perfect life. He is said to “drink iniquity,” because what is drunk does not delay in being swallowed. Thus, because guilt is perpetrated by an unjust person without any hesitation, iniquity is drunk as though it were water.

[Col. 0798A] **VERSE 17.**—“I will show you.” Since the one who speaks of what he has heard teaches with less authority than the one who speaks of what he has seen, Eliphaz, in order to claim greater authority for himself, says:

“What I have seen I will recount to you.” It is characteristic of an arrogant person, etc., up to the point where he fortifies them with the authority of the Fathers.

**VERSE 18.**—“The wise confess.” Behold the boldness of heretics, etc., up to the point where he says that the alien one—that is, the devil—has passed into their hearts. Behold the judgments.

**VERSE 20.**—“All his days.” Even the elect sometimes grow proud on certain days, but before they finish life they change their hearts away from arrogance. The impious, however, is proud on all his days and ends his life without withdrawing from arrogance.

[Col. 0798B] “And the number of the years of his tyranny.” Properly speaking, a tyrant, etc., up to the question of whose life is held in uncertainty.

**VERSE 21.**—“The sound of terror is always with him.” (Ibid.) A wicked mind is always in turmoil, whereas a good one is always tranquil: the wicked mind either contrives the evils it will inflict or fears that these same evils will be inflicted upon it by others.

**VERSE 22.**—“He does not believe that he can return from darkness,” because, believing himself to be struck on every side by ambushes, and having despaired of salvation, he continually increases in wickedness.

**VERSE 23.**—“When he has moved,” etc. Here “bread” means the sustenance of the present life, etc., up to the point where greed despises that sustenance.

[Col. 0798C] **VERSE 24.**—“It will terrify,” etc. In everything that the unjust person does, etc., up to the point where he perhaps lacks something that he can bring forward by deceit.

**VERSE 25.**—“He stretched out,” etc. (Ibid.) To stretch out one’s hands against God, etc., up to the point where this is now done by many individually.

**VERSE 26.**—“He ran,” that is, in an evil deed he encountered no obstacle arising from adversity.

“And he armed himself with a fat neck.” A fat neck is prosperous arrogance, supported by abundant possessions as though by much flesh.

**VERSE 27.**—“He covered his face.” Corpulence covers the face because the desired abundance of earthly things weighs down the eyes of the mind.

“And from his sides.” (Ibid.) The rich person’s sides are those who cling to him. Fat hangs from his sides because whoever clings to a powerful and wicked person likewise swells with his power, as though with fat.

**VERSE 28.**—“He dwelt in cities.” Since a city is named from the association of those who dwell together, etc., up to the point where they plainly show that they have fallen from the structure of life.

**VERSE 29.**—“He will not become rich,” because the thought of the proud will not be inhabited by the grace of its Creator.

“Nor will he endure.” (Ibid.) It is as though he were saying: What he appears to possess passes away outwardly, while inwardly he does not possess what could not pass away.

“Nor will he send into the earth,” because his life is snatched away at the movement of a hidden judgment, as by a light breath; or, “he will not send into the earth,” etc., because he never plants the thought of his heart in the desire for eternal life.

[Col. 0799A] **VERSE 30.**—“He will not depart from darkness.” Because he does not seek the light of righteousness, he does not depart from darkness.

“His branches,” etc. For those also who are joined to him burn with earthly desires, so that they bear no fruit of good works, because through wickedness they pant after the pursuit of low things.

“And he will be carried away by the breath,” because he will receive the sentence of punishment by that breath of his mouth which he does not restrain through fear of God.

**VERSE 31.**—“He will not believe.” For almsgiving cannot redeem him, etc., up to the point where it does not redeem the soul that he does not restrain from vices.

**VERSE 32.**—“Before his days.” (GREG.) Because, in his mind, he considers them long, etc., up to the point where death meets the undisciplined.

**VERSE 33.**—“His hand” is dried up from every good work.

“He will be harmed as,” etc. If a flowering vine, etc., up to the point where it makes them strangers to the fruit of holy devotion; hence he adds:

“And like an olive tree casting off its blossom.” When an olive tree is in flower, etc., up to the point where they cannot discern with what intention they act.

Or, “in the first flowering.” One who is weak ought not to govern or undertake lower things, because he grows cold in earthly actions. [Col. 0799C] Or, when he sees that what he does is pleasing, he performs those same good deeds more ardently and burns, as it were, in holy devotion; hence he perishes through the heat.

**VERSE 34.**—“For the assembly of the hypocrite,” etc. Hypocrites gather good works, but their gathering itself is barren, because through what they do they do not desire to receive fruit in eternal recompense.

“And fire will devour their tents,” etc. He calls the bodies in which their souls dwell “tents”: here the desire for praise will consume them, and afterward the fire of Gehenna.

“Tents.” The thought is a tent in which the mind dwells, and the heat of greed lays it waste. Or he calls the heart a tent, which the ardor of praise consumes. Or the body is the soul’s tent, and those who burn in mind here will burn in the flesh amid the fires of Gehenna.

[Col. 0799D] **VERSE 35.**—“He conceived pain.” When he thinks perverse thoughts, he gives birth to iniquity; when he begins to fulfill it, he has conceived it. The hypocrite’s mind is also never free from evil, because it envies what others desire, so that through their contempt he may appear more distinguished; hence he also prepares deceits, so that he alone may receive esteem.

“His womb prepares deceits,” that is, the mind in which thoughts are generated conceives greater malice against its neighbors, the more it seeks to appear alone more innocent than all others. He says this because he thought that Job had been struck down on account of hypocrisy.

# CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 0800A]

**VERSE 2.**—“I have often heard such things.” The elect often hear the evils of others as though they were their own, and crimes are charged against them by those who perpetrate the crimes they charge.

“All of you are burdensome comforters.” The wicked, when they trouble the good, etc., up to the point where the one who ought to lessen the pain instead increases it.

**VERSE 3.**—“Will windy words have an end?” The wicked utter windy words. For although their sayings are sometimes sound in their judgment, they are nevertheless inflated by arrogance.

“Or is something troublesome to you if you speak?” It is as though he were saying: You speak more because you do not hear from me anything troublesome concerning your conduct.

[Col. 0800B] **VERSE 4.**—“I too could speak things like yours.” He explains what he could have done, but, lest he abandon righteousness, he refrains from doing what he could have done.

“And would that your soul were in place of my soul.” By these words he intends to show this, etc., up to the point where he would rebuke their evils with restrained reproach.

**VERSE 6.**—“As though sparing.” Note the word “as though,” because, etc., up to the point where he appears to approve them, and they increase as an example.

**VERSE 8.**—“But now pain has oppressed me,” etc. The Church is pressed by pain, etc., up to the point where it has those within it; hence the voice of the blessed man fittingly adds:

**VERSE 9.**—“My wrinkles,” etc. The wrinkles of the Church are all those who live within it in duplicity: they proclaim faith with their voices but deny it by their works. In a time of peace, because they see that the same faith is honored by the powers of this world, they pretend to be faithful; but when adversity suddenly troubles the Church, they immediately reveal what they are contriving in their faithless minds. The meaning is: they rebuke me by persecuting me, although, placed within my body, they do not correct the wickedness of their duplicity.

“And the false speaker is roused against my face,” etc. Since they do not dare openly to contradict her preaching, the Church suffers false speech, as it were, behind her back. But when the time of wickedness breaks out, the one who now disparages her out of fear comes forward to contradict her openly, because he resists the words of true faith with open speech. Since this happens through the evil spirit, the words turn to describe him.

**VERSE 10.**—“He gathered his fury.” The devil, the prince of false speech, now has fury against the Church, but it is dispersed because he stirs hidden temptations in individuals. When, having received permission, he rages openly against her, he gathers his fury against her, because he concentrates his entire purpose upon afflicting her. He gnashes his teeth against her and looks upon her with terrifying eyes, because through some he carries out cruel acts against her and through others he devises what he will carry out.

**VERSE 11.**—“They opened their mouths against me,” etc. (Ibid.) The wicked open their mouths in reproach when they do not fear preaching error and ridicule the teachings of the true faith.

[Col. 0801A] “They struck my cheek.” The cheek of the Church consists of the holy preachers who turn the lives of carnal people through the word of correction. The wicked especially persecute these men; when they even kill them, they are satisfied by that punishment which especially tortures—or chastises—the mind of the Church.

“My cheek.” Peter is the cheek, who kills and eats. Samson holds the jawbone of an ass and kills his enemies: that is, Christ holds simple heralds in the hand of his power and kills carnal people’s vices. The cheekbone, cast upon the ground, pours out water, because the bodies of preachers given over to death display great miracles.

[Col. 0801B] **VERSE 12.**—“God has shut me in,” etc. The people of the elect are shut in among the wicked when their flesh is temporarily given over to the persecutions of the ancient enemy. They are handed over not to the spirit but to the hands of enemies, because to the extent that the enemies cannot grasp them in mind, they burn more cruelly against their flesh.

**VERSE 13.**—“I, once prosperous.” (GREG.) He signifies the mind of the weak, because, unable to foresee adversity, they find it all the more grievous insofar as they endure it unexpectedly. Or, in certain cases, the Church suffers these things through those who afterward fall away, when people who once possessed the wealth of doctrine suddenly turn to vices.

“He seized my neck.” Here “neck” signifies the uprightness of freedom, which the enemy holds during persecution; he “constricts” it when the weak do not dare freely to preach what they know to be true. Or he calls “his neck” those who, in the Church, under the pretext of defending rectitude, serve the vice of arrogance; the enemy bends this neck through the severity of his persecution.

[Col. 0801C] “And he set me up as a target.” (Ibid.) A target is set up so that it may be struck by the discharge of arrows. Thus the faithful people are set up as a target for their enemy, because he continually attacks them with his blows and afflicts them with his persecutions. Hence the Apostle says: “For you yourselves know that we have been appointed for this” (1 Thess. 3). It is as though he openly said: Why are you surprised at our wounds in this present time? If we seek eternal joys, we have come for this purpose: to be struck.

**VERSE 14.**—“He surrounded me.” The Church is surrounded by spears from her enemy when, in her members, she is attacked on every side by the fiery assailant with the darts of temptation.

“He wounded my loins all around.” When the enemy drags the faithful people into lust, he strikes them in the loins. It is called “wounding all around” because, when we follow what he wickedly suggests to us, we fulfill it by our own will and, as it were, wound ourselves together with him.

“He did not spare, and he poured out my entrails upon the ground.” He calls the entrails of the Church the minds of those who contain her mysteries within themselves. When the ancient enemy drags them toward worldly affairs, he pours her entrails upon the ground.

[Col. 0802A] “He did not spare,” that is, he did not cease.

**VERSE 15.**—“He cut me down.” In her weak members the Church, etc., up to the point where guilt has accumulated upon guilt.
