“He rushed upon me like a giant.” For the evil spirit fights against the soul—that is, against one overcome by a wicked habit—as a giant would, because the more often the soul submits to him, the more intolerable it makes him for itself. But because it often returns to repentance, it follows:

**VERSE 16.**—“I sewed sackcloth upon my skin.” Sackcloth and ashes signify repentance; skin and flesh signify the sin of the flesh. Thus sackcloth is, as it were, sewn upon the skin, and the flesh is covered with ashes, because the guilt of the flesh is covered through repentance, so that it may not appear for punishment in the examination of the strict Judge.

**VERSE 16.**—“My face has swollen.” The faces of the Church are those who, placed in governance, appear first, so that the honor of the faithful people may arise from their appearance. They mourn the faults of the weak; but when they see some returning to forgiveness and others persisting in iniquity, they are astonished at the hidden judgments of God, which they do not understand.

**VERSE 17.**—“And my eyelids.” They are called eyelids because they keep watch to foresee the paths of the peoples. But when even the vigilant overseers do not understand the hidden judgments of God, the eyelids of the holy Church grow dim.

**VERSE 18.**—“I have suffered these things.” From the words concerning the body, etc., up to the question: from whom is the pain endured?

**VERSE 19.**—“Earth, do not cover my blood.” [Col. 0802C] It was said to the sinful man: “You are earth, and you will return to earth.” Yet this earth does not hide the blood of our Redeemer, because every sinner, receiving the price of his redemption, confesses and praises it, and makes it known to his neighbors as far as he is able. The earth also did not cover his blood because the holy Church has proclaimed the mystery of her redemption throughout all the regions of the world.

“Nor let my cry find in you a place to hide.” (Ibid.) The cry of our Redeemer is “the blood of redemption,” which the faithful receive. As the Apostle says, it speaks better than the blood of Abel: the blood of Abel demanded the death of his brother’s murderer, whereas the Lord’s blood obtained life for his persecutors. This cry finds a place to hide in us if the tongue remains silent about what the mind has believed.

[Col. 0802D] **VERSE 20.**—“For behold, in,” etc. The Father is the Son’s witness, as in the Gospel: “The Father who sent me himself has borne witness about me.”

“And my conscience.” Because with one will, etc., up to the point where such a person ought not to fear human criticisms; hence it follows:

**VERSE 21.**—“My friends are full of words.” When friends are full of words—that is, when even those who are joined in faith disparage us—it is necessary that the eye trickle toward God, so that our whole intention may flow away in the compunction of inward love and rise all the more toward the interior, insofar as it is forced to return inward through outward reproaches.

**VERSE 22.**—“And would that,” etc. We are indeed sinners, etc., up to the point where he nevertheless consoles himself with the brevity of his life.

**VERSE 23.**—“For behold, the years pass quickly.” Everything that passes is brief. We walk along the path of death from which we do not return—not because we will not be restored to life by resurrection, but because we do not return again to the labors of this mortal life or to acquiring through labor the rewards that follow.

# CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—“My spirit will be weakened.” (GREG.) The spirit of the elect is weakened by fear of the Judge, and if they discover any carnal thoughts within themselves, they consume them through the heat of repentance. The spirit of the wicked, however, grows dense through the swelling of arrogance.

“And only the grave remains for me.” He considers himself almost dead because he knows that he will certainly die. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0803B] **VERSE 2.**—“I have not sinned.” He did not sin to such an extent that he deserved these scourges, because he was struck not to correct guilt but to increase grace. Or, in the person of the Head, he says this: the one without guilt accepted the punishment of guilt, that is, the bitterness of suffering.

**VERSE 3.**—“Place me beside you.” Through the Ascension. Then, because Judea was stirred against the disciples, he adds: “Let any hand”—because they now labor in vain against the one who sits in heaven.

**VERSE 4.**—“Their heart is far away.” If they had known the guardianship of discipline, they would never have despised the Redeemer’s commands.

“Therefore not,” etc. For those who make no effort to preserve life through discipline always lie below in their desires and do not raise their minds toward the hope of the heavenly homeland.

**VERSE 5.**—“He promises spoil,” etc. He turns his judgment toward the head of evils, namely the devil, whose “companions” are the apostate angels who fell with him. His “sons” are wicked people, who are generated from his evil persuasion for the practice of malice. “Therefore he promises spoil to his companions,” because he promises the souls of the wicked to evil spirits, to be seized at the end.

“The eyes of his sons will fail.” (Ibid.) Because the intentions of human beings, etc., up to the point where they suffer without end what they grieve over.

**VERSE 6.**—“He has set me.” Everyone who is struck by a scourge, etc., up to the point where he wishes for his adversary the punishment he sees has befallen the just man.

**VERSE 7.**—“My eye has grown dim from indignation.” The eye grows dim from indignation when those who possess the light of truth in the Church see the wicked prevail against the innocent, because they are troubled by wonder at the hidden judgment. But when the righteous grow dim with indignation, the weak often fall even into unbelief. Hence it follows:

“And my limbs are as nothing.” By the name “limbs,” the tenderness of the weak is expressed. When they see the wicked flourishing and the righteous being afflicted, they repent of having begun good things and thus quickly turn back to doing evil, as though the good they began had harmed their lives.

[Col. 0804A] **VERSE 8.**—“The righteous will be astonished at this.” This is what he had said: “My eye has grown dim with indignation.”

“And the innocent will rise up against the hypocrite.” The perfect innocent rises against the hypocrite when he despises him together with his flourishing and, by preaching what is right, declares to others that he ought to be despised.

**VERSE 9.**—“And the righteous will hold to his way.” After considering the hypocrite and seeing that, through perverse will, he obtains the things of the world, the righteous is bound more firmly to the love of heavenly things. He knows that eternal rewards will not be lacking for good desires, while temporal goods are not denied even to the wicked and double-hearted.

“And he will add strength to the clean-handed.” Seeing the earthly glory of the wicked, etc., up to the point where such things cannot be common to him and the reprobate.

**VERSE 10.**—“Therefore, all of you.” After presenting the outward advancement of the wicked and the inward advancement of the good, he exhorts the elect to turn back: to abandon evil and come by doing good.

**VERSE 11.**—“And not among you.” Desiring and longing for their conversion, he wishes not to find any wise person among them, as though he were saying: Learn to be fools in your own estimation, so that you may be able truly to be wise in God.

“My days have passed.” “Days” means prosperities. “Thoughts tormenting the heart” means concern for earthly happiness. The more severely these weigh upon the elect, the more carefully they consider that the Judge will exact an account of them; these thoughts are dissipated together with earthly happiness.

[Col. 0804C] **VERSE 12.**—“They have turned night into day.” When thoughts are dissipated, they turn “night into day,” because sometimes the righteous prefer to endure evils arising from adversity rather than to be wearied by concern over earthly prosperity’s management.

“And again, after darkness.” (Ibid.) Light is hoped for after darkness, etc., up to the point where he would already place the souls of the righteous in an everlasting dwelling.

**VERSE 13.**—“If I wait.” The saints of earlier times could endure adversity, etc., up to the point where they prepared rest for themselves in hell.

**VERSE 14.**—“I said to corruption.” He calls the father “corruption,” etc., up to the point where we are wearied in the mind by restless thoughts, as though by worms.

[Col. 0804D] **VERSE 15.**—“Where, then, is my expectation now?” The expectation of the righteous is Christ. They knew that he would come at some time, but they sought that he come sooner; hence the word “now” is added.

“And who will consider my patience?” God considers the patience of the righteous. Yet he is said not to consider it when he appears less quickly than the desire wishes and delays the grace of his dispensation for longer periods.

**VERSE 16.**—“All my things will descend into the deepest hell.” Before the Mediator’s coming, Job was destined to descend into hell, etc., up to the point where he still awaited recompense in the repose of hell alone.

“Do you suppose that at least there will be rest for me?” We must consider which of us can be secure concerning rest, if even the one whose praise for virtue is proclaimed by the very Judge who strikes him trembles concerning it.

# CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 2.**—“How long will you cast out words?” (GREG., *On Job*, Book XIV.) He constructs a case that blessed Job had broken out into pride, since he admits that he is casting out words.

“Understand first.” He indicates with what arrogance he had swollen, since he thought Job was speaking what he did not understand.

**VERSE 3.**—“Why are we considered?” It is characteristic of the human mind to suspect that others are doing to it what it does itself. He thinks that he is despised because he is accustomed to despise the good; and from the suspicion of contempt he leaps to indignation and pours out insults.

**VERSE 4.**—“Why do you destroy your soul?” The reprobate consider zeal for righteousness, or the spiritual grace of holy preaching, to be the madness of rage, by which they think the souls of the faithful are destroyed.

“Will the earth be abandoned because of you?” He speaks of the Church, etc., up to the point where Bildad insults Job over his scourges; hence he adds:

**VERSE 5.**—“Will not the light of the impious be extinguished?” This could rightly be said of the impious, but it ought not to have been said against a holy man. He calls the light the prosperity of the present life. The light of the impious is extinguished because the prosperity of a fleeting life ends together with that life.

“Nor will the flame of his fire shine.” He calls fire the fervor of temporal desires; its flame is outward beauty or power, which proceeds from his inward ardor. But it will not shine, because on the day of departure all outward beauty is taken away.

[Col. 0805C] **VERSE 6.**—“The light will grow dark in his tent.” Sometimes we understand darkness as sadness and light as joy. Thus the light in the impious person’s tent grows dark because the joy that had arisen from temporal things fails in his conscience.

“And the lamp that is over him will be extinguished.” A lamp is a light in a vessel, etc., up to the point where earthly joys possess the minds of the wicked.

**VERSE 7.**—“The steps of his strength will be confined,” etc. The powers of his wickedness, which he now exercises, will later be restrained by punishment.

“And it will cast him down.” The wicked now has the plan of pursuing present things, etc., up to the point expressed when he adds:

**VERSE 8.**—“For he has cast himself into a net.” (Ibid.) Whoever puts his feet into a net cannot remove them whenever he wishes. Thus whoever casts himself into sins does not immediately rise when he wishes.

“And he walks in its meshes.” (Ibid.) Whoever walks in the meshes of a net entangles his steps by walking; and when he strives to free himself in order to walk, he is bound so that he cannot walk.

**VERSE 9.**—“His sole will be held,” etc. For the end will indeed be constrained in sin.

“And it will burn against him.” The more he considers himself bound by evils, the more he despairs of returning; and through that very despair he burns more fiercely with the desires of this world. In his mind thirst burns against him, because the one who has acted perversely is kindled to act still more perversely.

**VERSE 10.**—“It is hidden in the earth.” (Ibid.) A snare is hidden in the earth when guilt is concealed beneath earthly advantages, so that a person sees what he is able to desire, yet by no means sees in what snare of guilt he is placing his foot.

“And his trap.” The enemy observes each person’s character and what vice he is inclined toward, and places before his face the things toward which he recognizes that the mind is more easily bent: luxury before gentle and cheerful characters, anger and pride before harsh minds. There, therefore, he places the trap where he sees the path of the mind to be, because he inserts the danger of deception precisely where he finds a road leading toward the thought to which the person is inclined.

[Col. 0806A] **VERSE 11.**—“They will terrify him on every side.” Often a good person fears being good for this reason: lest he suffer from the wicked what he remembers having done to the good. While he fears suffering what he himself does, terrified and suspicious on every side, he loses his step in good work.

**VERSE 12.**—“Let him be weakened by hunger.” Our flesh is weakness. Strength, however, is the rational soul, which is able by reason to resist in overcoming vices. It is weakened by hunger when it is nourished by no refreshment of inward food.

“And let hunger invade his ribs.” The ribs are the senses of the mind, which, hidden like the entrails, protect the thoughts. Hunger invades the wicked person’s ribs because inward hunger weakens the mind’s senses, so that they cannot in any way govern his thoughts within but wander outward toward the things they seek.

“Let it devour the beauty of his skin and consume his arms.” (The same.) The beauty of the skin is outward temporal glory; the arms signify works. Sin is called death because it kills the soul.

**VERSE 13.**—“The firstborn of death.” Pride, which is the beginning of every sin. Therefore the firstborn of death devours the beauty of his skin and his arms: through pride, it undermines the glory or activity of the wicked. He could have been glorious even in this life if he had not been proud.

**VERSE 14.**—“Let his confidence be torn from his tent.” (The same.) His confidence is torn from his tent when the perverse person, who had prepared many things in this life, is suddenly scattered by death.

“And let the king of destruction trample upon him.” For here he is either oppressed by vices that drag him to destruction, or, at the time of death, is subjected to demonic power.

**VERSE 15.**—“Let them dwell in his tent.” That is, let apostate angels dwell in his mind through the most wicked thoughts—namely, his companions; for he is no longer what he was because he withdrew from the Supreme Being.

“Let sulphur be sprinkled in his tent.” (Ibid.) Sulphur is sprinkled in the tent of the wicked whenever the pleasure of the flesh dominates his mind. Sulphur signifies the stench of the flesh. And because such a person remains in evil, so that he cannot produce the fruit of good, he adds:

**VERSE 16.**—“Let his roots below be dried up.” By “roots” we understand thoughts, etc., up to the point where all his activity is reckoned as nothing by the heavenly judgment.

**VERSE 17.**—“Let his memory perish.” (Ibid.) The wicked person strives to establish his memory on earth when he attempts to extend the glory of his praise. He rejoices that his name is celebrated in the streets when he extends the work of his iniquity far and wide.

(GREG.) The devil is the head of the wicked. In the final times he will enter that vessel of destruction who will be called Antichrist; he will attempt to spread his name far and wide.

**VERSE 18.**—“He will drive him from the light.” He is led from light into darkness when he is condemned from the honor of the present life to eternal punishments. He speaks in this way about each wicked person so that the reference may turn to the head—that is, the devil—who will extend his name in Antichrist, which the wicked now imitate.

“And he will transfer him from the world,” etc. When the heavenly Judge appears, he is transferred from this world to punishments. All these things may also be understood of the head of the wicked, Antichrist.

[Col. 0807B] **VERSE 19.**—“He will have no offspring,” etc. All the wicked, who were born from his persuasion into evil actions, will be struck down together with their head.

Because these things are to be understood of Antichrist, he makes this clear when he says:

**VERSE 20.**—“On his day they will be astonished.” For he will then display such great signs, etc., up to the point where they fear the torments which they overcome.

“And horror will attack the first,” that is, the hearts of the elect will be struck with fear. Hence it is written: “So as to lead astray, if possible, even the elect” (Matthew 24)—not that they will actually fall, but that they will tremble according to the flesh.

**VERSE 21.**—“These, then, are his tents.” He referred this to what he had said, etc., up to the point where they believed that holy Job had been struck down because of iniquity.

# CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 2.**—“How long will you afflict,” etc. (GREG.) The good are worn down by the words of the wicked when those who lie in perverse faith or wicked conduct swell up against them in speech.

**VERSE 3.**—“Behold, you confound me ten times.” (Ibid.) He had heard reproaches from them five times and had answered five times; therefore he declares that he has been confounded ten times. He suffered confusion both because he was gravely reproached and because he spoke words of instruction to those who would not listen: in his own reproaches, because they produced no improvement in them; in their reproaches, because he grieved over the perversity he heard.

[Col. 0807D] “Behold, ten times.” (Ibid.) The Church keeps the Decalogue, and the wicked cause it confusion as often as they resist the divine words in their actions.

“And you are not ashamed to oppress me.” There are some whom a sudden outbreak of malice invites to perpetrate wickedness, yet human shame holds them back.

**VERSE 4.**—“Indeed, even if I have been ignorant.” The knowledge of heretics is not with them but against them, because it inflates them. But the Church’s ignorance—that it cannot penetrate mysteries—is with her, because it is for her benefit when she humbles herself. And because what heretics seek to know is arrogance, so that they may appear learned against the good, he adds: from my being struck down, you ought rather to rise up against yourselves, fearing worse things for yourselves. For the good person first rises up within himself and afterward against others.

[Col. 0808A] **VERSE 5.**—“But you rise up against me.” That is, you leave yourselves to be reproved and rebuke me with strict judgments.

“And you accuse me.” Those who had known him to be just before the scourges now judged him to be unjust on the basis of the very fact that he had been struck down.

**VERSE 6.**—“At least now understand.” The Lord had said concerning him, “You have moved me against him without cause,” and he himself asserts the same concerning himself: that he had been afflicted by the Lord without an equitable judgment. For if his life and his scourges are weighed, he appears to have been afflicted without an equitable judgment. Yet because God increased his merits through the scourges, he did not afflict Job by an unjust judgment.

“Because God has not judged equitably.” It must therefore be maintained both that God acted rightly with Job and that the one who says it was not done equitably is nevertheless not lying. Otherwise the devil would have won in what he had promised concerning the blessed man’s guilt, while God had praised him. This was drawn out not by arrogance but by pain. If a good person, in a humble mind and under the pressure of a circumstance or pain, says good things about himself, he does not sin.

“And he has surrounded me with his scourges.” When such great affliction weighs us down that the mind cannot breathe through the consolation of anything, we are not merely struck by scourges but also surrounded by them, because we are enclosed on every side by the blows of tribulations.

**VERSE 7.**—“Behold, I will cry out while suffering violence.” (Ibid.) God knows what will profit us, etc., up to the point where they cannot discern what ought to be done.

**VERSE 8.**—“He has fenced in my path,” etc. He saw his path enclosed by blows when, desiring to cross over to security, he could not escape the scourges. And, as though in the passageway of his heart, he found the darkness of ignorance because he could not penetrate why he was being scourged.

**VERSE 9.**—“He has stripped me of my glory.” These things plainly apply to Job, etc., up to the point where the army falls more broadly as they collapse.

**VERSE 10.**—“He has destroyed me on every side, and I perish, and as a tree torn up,” etc. A tree is driven by the wind so that it falls; likewise the weak person is drawn toward injustice by threats and abandons the eternal things he had hoped for. And because a person who abandons righteousness out of fear of punishments sometimes nevertheless does not escape the punishments:

**VERSE 11.**—“He has become angry against me.” For one who is struck so that his strength is overcome is not struck by God as a son through discipline, but as an enemy through anger. Hence the prophet says: “I have struck you with the wound of an enemy, with cruel chastisement” (Jeremiah 30).

And because evil spirits often suggest many things to the hearts of the afflicted, and steal whatever good there is, he adds:

**VERSE 12.**—“The robbers came together.” That is, the evil spirits who occupy themselves with investigating human character. They make a path for themselves in the hearts of the afflicted when, amid the adversities endured outwardly, they do not cease to introduce wicked thoughts as well.

“And they besieged the tent in a circle,” etc. They besiege the tent in a circle, etc., up to the point where they wore down his whole body with ulcers.

**VERSE 13.**—“My brothers, far away.” (Ibid.) Here he uses the voice of the Redeemer: the brothers were made far from him, and acquaintances withdrew. They knew him as one who observed the Law and prophesied, but they did not recognize him when he was present. For the Jews, his relatives according to the flesh and his acquaintances through the instruction of the Law, as though they had forgotten the one whom they had prophesied in the words of the Law through faith, denied in words of faithlessness that he had become flesh.

**VERSE 15.**—“The inhabitants of my house.” That is, the priests, whose origin had been assigned to the service of God but who were now held in the condition of a handmaid through their office.

“The souls of the Levites” are devoted to the secrets of the tabernacle, serving more familiarly, as it were, in the inner chamber.

“And I became like a stranger,” etc. For he was not recognized by the synagogue. Hence the prophet also says: “You will be like a settler in the land, and like a traveler turning aside to stay” (Jeremiah 14). Since he was not heard as Lord, he was believed to be not the owner of the field but a “settler”: “He who turned aside like a traveler to stay,” because he took away a few from Judea and, proceeding to the calling of the Gentiles, completed the journey he had begun.

### Verse 16

“‘I called my servant.’” The Jewish people was a servant, obedient through fear. By bestowing gifts upon him, as though sending forth words, He resolved to draw him to Himself; but he did not answer, because he scorned to return worthy deeds for His gifts.

“‘He adorned [him] with his own mouth.’” To him to whom I had entrusted so many commandments through the mouths of the prophets, I pleaded with my own mouth: for, revealed in the flesh, while humbly speaking the commandments of life, He begged the servant, as though he were proud, to come.

### Verse 17

“‘My breath my wife abhorred,’” etc. The Lord’s wife, etc., up to [the point] at which she, devoted to carnal senses, did not recognize the mystery of His incarnation.

“‘And I pleaded with the children of my womb.’” We ought to understand the womb of God as His counsel; in it we were conceived before the ages through predestination, so that, created through the ages, we might be brought forth. He therefore pleaded with the children of His womb, because, having become incarnate, He humbly entreated those whom He had created.

### Verse 18

“‘Fools also despised me,’” etc. Because, while the teachers of the Law despised God, the crowd of the people followed their unbelief. He had come to seek the poor and foolish, having left the wise behind; therefore He says, with an increase of sorrow, “Fools also.” For whose sake, then, I, the Word made flesh, assumed foolishness, they despised me.

“‘And when I had withdrawn from them.’” The Lord seemed to approach the heart of the peoples when He displayed miracles to them; and He seemed to withdraw when He showed no signs. They were unwilling to believe Him when He ceased from miracles.

### Verse 19

“‘They abhorred me,’” etc. The scribes and teachers of the Law, etc., up to the following statement concerning the same order of teachers: “And the one whom I loved most.” The order of teachers, which had previously been especially beloved while serving in preaching, was followed by the crowd not merely into refusing to believe God, but even into persecuting Him. Then what follows took place:

### Verse 20

“‘When my skin and flesh were consumed.’” In the bones there is strength, etc., up to the time of the Passion, when He found the women near Him.

“‘Flesh’” (Gregory). Those who had clung to the bone, while the disciples, though weak, preached the faith of the truth to the peoples. And when the holy women prepared the external bodily supports that were necessary, they remained in the body like skin on the outside.

“‘And they were left.’” The teeth are the apostles; only the lips were left around the teeth, since two men walking after His death knew how to converse about Him, but feared either to preach Him any longer or to bite into the vices of unbelievers. But now he returns to Job’s own words.

“‘Only.’” There is nothing around the teeth of the fortunate except lips; and thus it is clear that this is said mystically.

### Verse 21

“‘Have pity on me.’” It belongs to the godly, when they suffer from adversaries, to be moved not so much to anger as to prayers. He calls himself one touched by the hand of the Lord, just as Satan himself had said: “Stretch out your hand and touch his bone.”

### Verse 22

“‘Why do you persecute me?’” God strikes the vices of others with all the greater justice because He possesses no vice in Himself. The sense is: You afflict me because of my weaknesses as though you yourselves, in God’s manner, possessed nothing weak. “Like God.” They act together with God because they do what almighty God permits to be done; but they do not will the same thing. For while almighty God offers purification out of love, the perversity of the unjust exercises malice by raging.

Or, [the sense is] as though they were not weak, when they ought not to rebuke a person whom God strikes, lest they add pain to pain, but ought rather to console him. When the Lord’s hand ceases, then rebuke may be given to the deserving.

“‘And you are satisfied with my flesh.’” Those whose mind hungers for the punishments of their neighbors seek to be satisfied with another’s flesh. Or, those who feed on slander against another’s life are satisfied with another’s flesh.

“‘Who will grant me,’” etc. He does not wish the harsh things he endures to be concealed through silence, but wishes them to be brought to public knowledge by example, so that others may be strengthened toward patience.

“‘Who will grant me?’” (Ibid.) These things also suit the Church, etc., up to the point where afterward he divides the book itself onto a sheet of lead and into flint.

“‘Who will grant me,’” etc. Through the iron stylus is signified the firm judgment of the Fathers. Through lead, the Jewish people, weighed down by sin. Through flint, the Gentile world is represented. Therefore all that he endured was recognized by the people of Judea and by the Gentile world, instructed by the firm judgment of the Fathers. What is written on lead is erased more quickly. On flint it is difficult to carve, but what is carved remains. Thus Judea quickly received the words of God and quickly abandoned them; the Gentile world received them with difficulty, but, once received, preserved them firmly.

### Verse 25

“‘For I know that my Redeemer,’” etc. He does not say “Creator,” but clearly announces the Redeemer, who, after creating all things, redeemed us from captivity through His Passion. He lives who fell among the hands of the wicked.

“‘And on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and again,’” etc. (Ibid.) Because the resurrection, etc., up to the point where the priest is shown to be flourishing, who intercedes for us.

### Verse 27

“‘Whom I myself shall see,’” etc. (Gregory.) Our flesh after the resurrection will be the same and different: the same by nature, different in glory. It will be spiritual because incorruptible, and tangible because it will not lose the substance of true nature.

“‘I myself, and my eyes shall behold, and not another’s.’” He expressly indicates the truth of the resurrection. It is not that one person dies and another rises—as those say who claim that the future body will be invisible and intangible, as Eutychius said—but the very same person rises.

“‘This hope of mine is stored in my bosom.’” We believe that we possess nothing more certain, etc., up to the point where he immediately adds:

### Verse 28

“‘Why, then, now?’” Because the wicked desire to find an accusation in the speech of the righteous, they seek a root of speech from which they may derive the origin of their speaking and spread out the branches of their loquacity. Yet the holy man mercifully reveals the evils from which they ought to flee.

### Verse 29

“‘Therefore flee.’” (Ibid.) To flee the face of the sword is to appease the sentence of strict punishment before it appears.

“‘And know that there is judgment.’” Everyone who acts perversely, by the very fact that he despises it, does not know that God’s judgment exists.

## Chapter 20

“‘Therefore thoughts.’” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book 15.) It is as though he says: Because I consider the terror of the final judgment, therefore I am confounded in fear by the tumults of my thoughts.

“‘And the mind is carried in different directions.’” This happens when, now with anxious fear, he weighs the evils he neglected to do, now the blameworthy things in which he is involved, now the right things that he sees are still lacking in him. These men, from their association with Job, knew indeed how to live rightly, but, not knowing how to weigh God’s judgments subtly, believed that the righteous could not be struck here. Therefore they suspected this man of being wicked and fell into rebuke, though they descended to it with a certain reverence. Hence he adds:

### Verse 3

“‘The doctrine by which,’” etc. (Ibid.) After these things had been moderately set forth, etc., up to the point where I also find this: “the praise of the wicked,” etc.

### Verse 4

“‘This I know from the beginning.’” For if we lead the eyes of the mind from the very origin of the human race up to the present time, we see how brief everything that could come to an end has been.

### Verse 5

“‘And the joy of the hypocrite.’” The joy of the hypocrite is like a point. For just as a stylus is raised when it is placed upon a point, so the hypocrite loses the praise of the present life as soon as he touches it.

“‘Like a point,’” because joy passes away while punishment remains: it appears for a moment and disappears forever.

### Verse 6

“‘If he should ascend,’” that is, even if he pretends to lead a heavenly life, even if he displays an understanding like that of true preachers, nevertheless he will be destroyed at the end like dung, because his mind will be condemned for the stench of its vices.

### Verse 7

“‘And those who had seen him shall say.’” (Ibid.) Those who saw him exalted will say, once he has been extinguished, “Where is he?” For he appears neither in this world, in which he had been exalted, nor in the rest of eternity, in which he was thought to exist.

### Verse 8

“‘Like a flying dream.’” The life of the hypocrite, etc., up to the point where he saw the favor of human beings while asleep.

### Verse 9

“‘The eye that had seen him.’” The heart of flatterers is the hypocrite’s place; for he rests there where he finds favor. Therefore the eye that had seen him will not see him, because in death he is hidden from those who used to gaze upon him with admiration.

“‘Nor will it look upon him any longer.’” For the tongues of flatterers do not follow him to judgment with their favor.

### Verse 10

“‘His sons shall be crushed,’” etc. For those who are born in hypocrisy through imitation of him, since they do not hold the solidity of truth, fail in the poverty of their heart.

### Verse 11

“‘His bones shall be filled.’” The youth of the hypocrite is the beginning of perversity, etc., up to being emptied of all solidity and perishing.

### Verse 12

“‘For when it has become sweet.’” (Ibid.) In the mouth of the heart, iniquity is sweet; he conceals it beneath the covering of gentle speech. Evil would be in the tongue and not beneath the tongue if the hypocrite, while speaking, openly revealed his malice.

“‘He will spare it, and not.’” He spares the evil he loves when he does not pursue it through repentance; and he does not abandon it, but hides it in his throat, because he preserves it in his thought so that he never brings it forth in speech.

(Bede.) That is, he strokes, cherishes, and nourishes his evil; and, delighting in it, he never repents so as to depart from it.

### Verse 14

“‘His bread in his belly.’” Often the hypocrite strives to be instructed by the bread of sacred eloquence, not in order to live by it, but in order to appear learned. But while he perversely understands the word of doctrine that he wrongly seeks, and falls into heresies, it happens to him that, just as he dies from the gall of asps, so he dies from bread. But because he in no way preserves God’s words in his works, even if he understands them correctly, he loses them in the present life, so that he does not know what he wished to do.

### Verse 15

“‘Riches.’” The riches of sacred Law, which he swallowed by reading, he will vomit out by forgetting; God, in just judgment, tears them from his memory.

“‘The head of the asp.’” (Ibid.) The asp is a small serpent, etc., up to the point where it kills as though from the tongue of a viper.

### Verse 17

“‘May he not see streams.’” (Ibid.) The streams of the river are the gifts of the Holy Spirit, etc., up to the point where it signifies the mystery of Christ’s incarnation.

### Verse 18

“‘He shall pay for all that he has done.’” For in torment he will repay the unlawful desires he preserved here. He will not be consumed in death; rather, he will be compelled to live without end so that he may be tortured without end. Thus the life that was dead here in guilt will live there in punishment. Let him therefore say, “He shall pay for all that he has done,” yet he will not be consumed, because he is tortured and not extinguished: he dies and lives, fails and remains, forever and without end.

### Verse 19

“‘Because he shattered.’” He shatters and strips the house of the poor, because he is not ashamed to despoil through greed the one whom he crushes through power.

### Verse 20

“‘And his belly was not satisfied.’” The belly of the wicked is greed; in it is gathered whatever is swallowed by perverse desire. It is clear that greed is not extinguished by the things desired but increased by them. For, like fire, when it has received wood to consume, it grows; and from the very source by which its flame seems momentarily to be compressed, it is soon seen to spread.

“‘And when he has obtained what he desired.’” It is a greater anger when what is wickedly desired is granted, because sudden vengeance follows from it: he has obtained even that which, with God angry, he desired.

### Verse 21

“‘Nothing remained of his city.’” When the hypocrite is struck, nothing remains of his food, because when he is led to punishments he is separated from everything he had possessed.

“‘Therefore nothing,’” etc. Because, removed from this life, he goes naked to the Judge.

### Verse 22

“‘When he is satisfied, he will be constrained.’” (Gregory.) When he has heaped up many things, he is constrained; for he is anxious about how he may guard what he has acquired.

“‘He will burn, and every pain.’” He fears ambushes from every side, etc., up to the point where he is carried all the more easily to torment. It follows:

### Verse 23

“‘Would that his belly were filled,’” etc.; “may war rain upon him.” For God to rain war, etc., up to the point where he scorned to foresee it.

### Verse 24

“‘He will flee weapons.’” (Ibid.) The greedy person sometimes steals what belongs to others, etc., up to the point where he places himself before the blows of the eternal judgment.

Meanwhile:

### Verse 25

“‘The drawn sword,’” etc. The wicked person, while contriving perverse things in thought, is like a sword in its sheath. It comes out of the sheath when the evil of action is opened through iniquity: drawn out through the seducer, but emerging through his own will.

“‘They will go and come,’” etc. Evil spirits are to good minds, etc., up to the point where exaltation is substituted for self-restraint, etc.

### Verse 26

“‘All darknesses are hidden.’” For the one who does not complete everything at once in action silently holds in his mind all the things that can cause harm.

“‘It will devour him,’” etc. The fire of Gehenna is not kindled by human effort but was created by God from the beginning of the world.

“‘He will be afflicted when abandoned.’” The flesh is the tabernacle of the wicked, because he gladly inhabits it, though his spirit will be tormented with it. The good do not place their joy in the flesh but in heaven. Abandoned by the flesh from which he is taken—the flesh he loved here and did not wish to leave—he will then wish to leave it because of the torments, but he will not be able to.

### Verse 27

“‘They will reveal.’” (Ibid.) Because here he spared neither the good nor the wicked, at the terrible examination the life of the righteous and that of sinners alike will accuse him.

### Verse 28

“‘It shall be opened.’” When every evil that arose in his conscience is displayed at the Judge’s arrival.

“‘He shall be removed into’:” because, at the time of vengeance, he is carried off to punishments and separated from the face of the eternal Judge.

### Verse 29

“‘This is the portion of the wicked man.’” When God’s justice exacts punishment from the reprobate for their perverse acts, it repays them with evils even to the recompense of their words.

## Chapter 21

### Verse 4

“‘Will you perhaps contend against?’” Blessed Job, if he pleased God while displeasing human beings, would have no causes for sadness. But because, through the present scourges, he believed that he had displeased God, he became uncertain about his former life and summoned his spirit to sadness. If, in the absence of scourges, he had disputed with a human being concerning the merits of his life, he ought by no means to have been saddened.

“‘Will you perhaps contend against a human being?’” As though he said: If, while still not a hypocrite, I were dealing with human beings concerning my life, I would not be afraid. If I displeased them, I would not care; but because I am dealing with God, I am rightly saddened. “But attend to me,” as though he said: [I attend to] God, but I do not fear you.

### Verse 5

“‘Attend,’” that is, consider what I have done and marvel at what I suffer.

“‘And place your finger upon your mouth,’” that is, join the virtue of discernment to your speech.

### Verse 6

“‘And I, when I remember.’” (Ibid.) Because he had not forgotten his deeds, etc., up to the point where he adds against their statements:

### Verse 7

“‘Why, then, do the wicked live?’” They are raised up by honors and strengthened by possessions, because divine patience tolerates them.

“‘And, strengthened by riches,’” etc., so that they are permitted to endure in them for a long time. But because there are those for whom possessing these things is punishment, since the heirs to whom they leave them do not possess them, he adds:

### Verse 8

“‘Their offspring endures.’” Heirs are given along with the patrimony as an increase of happiness.

“‘Before them.’” So that no necessity may at least remove from their eyes the things in which their spirit rejoices. But lest their line be extinguished in childlessness, he adds:

“‘A multitude of relatives and grandchildren in their sight.’” Behold, they are said to possess life, honors, riches, children, and grandchildren. But if inward domestic care were burning them, this happiness would not be joyful. Hence he adds:

### Verse 9

“‘Their houses are secure and peaceful, and there is no.’” For what would the happiness described above be if it were not joyful? If things prospered within, then also in the fields.

“‘Their ox conceived.’” For the masters of flocks the first happiness is, etc., up to the point where the fruitfulness of the household is added:

### Verse 11

“‘They go forth like flocks.’” So that, just as greater things have been granted for possession, many offspring may spring up for their keeping.

“‘And their infants leap for joy in play.’” But lest we consider that play worthless, he says:

### Verse 12

“‘They hold the tambourine and the lyre.’” As though, while their masters swell with honors and possessions, their subjects rejoice in playful activities.

### Verse 13

“‘They spend their days in good things.’” For all the length of the present life is recognized as a point when it is terminated by an end. Whatever could pass away was sudden.

“‘And in a moment they descend to the underworld.’” But the end is exceedingly bad. Behold where prosperity was tending: the prosperity of the present life is not a witness to innocence, because those who enjoyed it perish, while those who were scourged are freed—contrary to Job’s friends.

### Verse 14

“‘Who said to God: Depart from us.’” (Gregory.) They say to God, “Depart from us,” who refuse to open access to Him and attack Him by their perverse acts.

“‘We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.’” The way of God is peace, humility, and patience. Those who despise these say, “We do not desire the knowledge of your ways.”

### Verse 15

“‘Who is the Almighty?’” etc. “For the fool said in his heart: There is no God.”

“‘And what does it profit us if we pray?’” The wicked, who seek not God but external gifts, when they see that the same gifts are lacking for those who rage, scorn to serve Him.

### Verse 16

“‘Nevertheless, because they are not.’” The person who despises temporal goods and presses them beneath the rule of his mind holds them in his hand. But whoever loves them excessively subjects himself to them more than he subjects them to himself.

“‘Their counsel is far away.’” The counsel of the wicked is to seek earthly glory and neglect eternal glory. But because they do not prosper continually in this life, it follows:

### Verse 17

“‘How often will the lamp of the wicked be extinguished?’” Often the wicked person considers the life of his children his lamp. But when the son who is loved excessively is taken away, the wicked person’s lamp, which seemed to shine, is extinguished. The same is true of riches and honors.

“And a flood will come upon them.” A flood comes upon the wicked when they suffer waves of grief from some adversity.

“‘And he will divide pains,’” etc. He who reserves eternal pains for the wicked also sometimes pierces his mind here with temporal pain. Because he strikes both here and there, he divides the pains of his fury over the wicked, so that he may be crushed by a twofold destruction.

### Verse 18

“‘They shall be like straw.’” For by the sudden blast of God’s anger they are lifted up and carried off to the fire.

“‘And like chaff which,’” because a whirlwind carries them away to eternal punishments.

### Verse 19

“‘God will store up his iniquity for his sons.’” For whoever imitates his parent’s iniquity is also bound by his parent’s sin.

“And when he repays.” The wicked person does not know the evils he has committed until he begins to be punished.

### Verse 20

“‘His eyes shall see.’” For he had become so hardened in iniquity that he did not fear being struck even in the things he loved, provided only that he might accomplish what he had perversely conceived. Concerning this hardening he adds:

### Verse 21

“‘For what to him?’” Not that in hell he does not think about his relatives, etc., up to the point where, lest anyone presume to investigate, it follows:

### Verse 22

“‘Will anyone teach God knowledge?’” That is, He does nothing unjustly with us, since He has also judged the more subtle angelic nature justly. Therefore nothing remains about which to complain.

### Verse 23

“‘This one dies.’” Here he sets forth those matters in which someone might investigate the secret of the Almighty, asking why He permits these things to be so. The surface meaning of the text is sufficiently clear in itself. But when he says:

### Verse 24

“‘His inward parts are full of fat.’” Fat comes from abundant food, etc., up to the point where the rich man is seen to rejoice vainly and the poor man to be afflicted even more vainly.

### Verse 26

“‘And yet together they shall sleep in the dust.’” What concern is there about a dissimilar life, prosperous or adverse, when the end in the dust is the same? One ought to consider that life in which, with the resurrection, they reach dissimilar ends: the fortunate person passes to punishments, the afflicted person to rest.

“‘And yet together in the dust.’” That is, they will close the eyes of their mind upon earthly desires.

“‘And worms,’” which, arising from flesh—that is, carnal cares—oppress them. This is not true of Job, who neither swelled with pride over what he possessed nor was anxious over what he had lost. But they think this is so; therefore he adds:

### Verse 27

“‘Certainly I know your thoughts.’” For they saw one who had been struck, etc., up to the point where they do not pass perfectly into eternal things. Hence he adds:

### Verse 29

“‘Ask any traveler.’” A traveler is one who considers the present life to be a road for himself and not a homeland. He scorns to fix his heart upon the love of the passing world but seeks eternal things.

### Verse 31

“‘Who will reproach him to his face for his ways?’” When he was speaking about the entire body of the wicked, etc., up to the point where neither Elijah nor Enoch [did so] by their own strength, but by God’s.

### Verse 32

“‘He himself is led to the tombs.’” This applies in life, etc., up to the point where he will be received only in the hearts of the wicked.

“‘And in the heap.’” Because in the assembly of sinners he displays the ambushes of his cunning. Since there are many wicked people, they are rightly called a heap.

### Verse 33

“‘He was sweet.’” Cocytus is called the mourning of the weak, etc., up to the point where they signify that wicked mourning exists there.

“‘And after him every.’” (Ibid.) “A man wise according to human standards” is understood here. He drags every human being after him because he carries all whom he finds carnal beneath the yoke of his dominion. Even now, before he appears, he drags innumerable people after him, though not everyone, since many are drawn back from carnality.

### Verse 34

“‘How, then, do you console,’” etc. If the wicked person is permitted to prosper in this life, as has been shown concerning the Antichrist, then it is necessary that the chosen person be held under the bridle of the scourge.

“‘Since your answer,’” etc. They could not console him, because in their words they contradicted the truth. For when they called him a hypocrite, since they committed a fault by lying, they increased the punishment of the afflicted righteous man; the guilt of another’s deception torments the one who loves the truth.

## Chapter 22

### Verses 1–2

“‘And Eliphaz answered, etc. Can a human being profit God?’” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book 16.) Those who fail against the words of truth repeat even what is known, lest they seem defeated by remaining silent. Therefore Eliphaz, pressed by the words of blessed Job, says things that no one is unaware of. For he says:

“‘Can one be compared with God?’” For in comparison with God’s knowledge, etc., up to the point where he adds as though descending.

### Verse 3

“‘What does it profit?’” In everything that we do well, etc., up to the point where Eliphaz still adds what no one is unaware of.

### Verse 4

“‘Will He rebuke you because He fears you?’” Who, even if foolish, would think that God rebukes us out of fear and brings His judgment against us out of dread?

“‘Will He rebuke you?’” Those who do not know how to measure their words fall into idle speech.

### Verse 5

“‘And not because of your very great wickedness.’” From idle words, etc., up to the point where he continually descends to worse things. For it follows:

### Verse 6

“‘For you took away the pledge.’” These things are clear according to the literal sense, etc., up to the point where those who come to you lose spiritual gifts.

### Verse 9

“‘Widows.’” Heretics call the peoples, etc., up to the point where they say that these things are repaid for sins? And this is: “Therefore you are surrounded by snares.”

### Verse 11

“‘And you thought yourself.’” As though he said, etc., up to the point where it is like wave upon wave.

### Verse 12

“‘Do you not think that God?’” As though [he asked], is it for this reason, etc., up to the point where they consider themselves alone wise by a foolish judgment.

### Verse 15

“‘Will you perhaps follow the path?’” Just as the path of the Redeemer is humility, so the path of the ages is pride. Therefore wicked men tread the path of the ages, who walk in arrogance through the desires of this life.

### Verse 16

“‘Who were taken away before their time, except that all.’” Those who love the present life, etc., up to the point where the sentence is changed, but not the eternal counsel.

“‘And a river overturned their foundation.’” When the wicked do not observe that present things are fleeting, etc., up to the point where the course of mutability destroys the stability of their perverse construction.

### Verse 18

“‘When he had filled.’” The Lord fills the houses of the wicked because He does not deny His gifts even to the ungrateful.

“‘Whose counsel is far away.’” This too [is said by] Job, etc., up to the point where he desires to be unlike the wicked.

### Verse 19

“‘The righteous shall see’” the destruction of the wicked.

“‘And they shall rejoice.’” When they have clung to the strict Judge in perfect security. For now they look upon the reprobate and groan.

### Verse 20

“‘Was not their substance cut off?’” Here the wicked have been raised up, etc., up to the point where they are dragged from the sight of the Judge to Gehenna.

“‘And their remnants the fire devoured.’” For even if they leave the flesh here, they will receive it in the resurrection, so that they may burn in the flesh in which they sinned.

### Verse 21

“‘Submit, therefore.’” It is the fault of pride to teach one who is better, as heretics often do to Catholics.

### Verse 23

“‘If he returns.’” Because you have been destroyed from the building up of justice.

“‘And you will make far away.’” The body is understood as the soul’s tabernacle, and the mind as its thoughts. The sense is: If, after your errors, you return to God, you will be cleansed in thought and in deed.

### Verse 24

“‘He will give instead of earth.’” By earth the weakness of action is signified; by flint, strength; by golden streams, the doctrine of inward brightness. Therefore, for those converted to Him, He gives “flint” instead of earth, the strength of good works, and “golden streams instead of flint.”

“‘Instead of.’” Because, in place of strong action, He multiplies the doctrine of clear preaching.

(Bede.) He says that if, with the Lord propitiated toward him, etc., up to the point where they are silver tested by fire.

### Verse 25

“‘And the Almighty will be against.’” (Ibid.) Often, when we devote ourselves to the sacred writings, we endure the snares of malignant spirits severely. The sense is: When He has driven malignant spirits away from you, the bright talent of divine eloquence will grow in you.

### Verse 26

“‘Then above.’” To abound in delights upon the Almighty is to be satisfied in His love with the banquets of sacred Scripture.

“‘And you will lift up to God.’” To lift one’s face to God is to raise the heart to investigate sublime things.

### Verse 27

“‘And you shall fulfill your vows.’” Whoever has made vows but cannot fulfill them because of weakness is dealt with through the punishment of sin in such a way that the ability to do good is taken away from the one who wills it. But when the guilt that obstructs him is wiped away, it immediately happens that the ability follows the vow.

### Verse 28

“‘You shall decree.’” A thing is decreed and comes to pass when the virtue desired through longing, by the Lord’s gift, also prospers through its effect.

“‘And it shall come.’” Heretics promise the same things to the afflicted if they follow them.

“‘And in the ways.’” For light to shine in the ways of the righteous is to scatter signs of one’s brightness through wondrous works of virtue.

### Verse 29

“‘For he who has been humbled.’” Because whoever humbles himself will be exalted.

“‘And he who.’” As far as can be discerned through the ministry of the bodily members, the first manifestation of pride is usually in the eyes.

### Verse 30

“‘The innocent shall be saved.’” For when grace reaches the point here at which he becomes innocent, when he is led to judgment he is rewarded according to merit.

## Chapter 23

### Verse 1

“‘But Job answered and said: Even now in bitterness.’” (Gregory.) The mind of the righteous is always in bitterness, etc., up to the point where they seek to seduce him with sweet speeches.

### Verse 2

“‘And the hand of my wound.’” The hand of the wound is the strength of the blow. But because, through adversities, the righteous thirst more intensely for the face of their Maker, it follows:

### Verse 3

“‘Who will grant me?’” When the chosen see that things are being done contrary to their desire, they have recourse to the hidden judgments of God, so that they may see in them that what appears to run disorderly outwardly is not arranged disorderly within. And this is what he adds:

“‘I shall find him.’” That is: God now delays so that He may be desired more greatly.

“‘And I shall come even to his throne.’” The throne is the angels, etc., up to the point where they see that God arranges better things. Hence:

“‘I shall set judgment before God.’” To set judgment before God is, etc., up to considering how terrible the Judge who is now hidden and silent will appear afterward.

### Verse 4

“‘I shall fill my mouth.’” Because, while he contemplates the Judge’s examination against himself, he pursues himself bitterly with the reproach of repentance.

### Verse 5

“‘That I may know the words which,’” etc. For when we pursue our faults through repentance, we discover what the Judge could say about them in His examination. The person who neglects his own evils does not know this.

### Verse 6

“‘I do not wish him to contend with great strength.’” For who could be found righteous in the examination if God were to scrutinize human lives according to the majesty of His own strength? However righteous someone may be, if he is judged strictly, he is weighed down by the mass of that greatness. Hence he adds:

“‘Nor by greatness.’” As though he said: If He contended with me according to His strength, He would crush me by His mass. And note that, while he avoids strength, he desires the weakness of the incarnation. Hence he adds:

### Verse 7

“‘Let him set forth equity.’” The Mediator of God and human beings, etc., up to the point where I shall victoriously exclude the judgment of my acquittal.

### Verse 8

“‘If I go to the east.’” (Ibid.) It is as though he says: The incarnate Son, etc., up to the point where the soul does not fully know itself even in all these things. Hence:

### Verse 10

“‘But he knows the way.’” That is, I am unable to see the one who sees me.

“‘And he has tested.’” He does not compare himself to gold in pride, but humbly considers his own condition, which is permitted to every righteous person. And this is: “Test me as gold.” Through the burning of tribulation, vices are removed and merits increased.

### Verse 11

“‘My foot has followed his footsteps.’” Blessed Job, in future action, etc., up to the point where he returns to an example set before him.

### Verse 12

“‘And I hid [them] in my bosom.’” In the bosom of the heart we hide the words of His mouth, because we hear His commandments not as something passing but as something to be fulfilled in action. And if the words emerge in action, they nevertheless remain hidden in the heart. If the mind is not lifted up inwardly, but praise is sought outwardly, then the word of God is not hidden in the bosom.

### Verse 13

“‘For he alone is.’” He is so principally and immutably. For He alone exists through Himself and accomplishes all things; He is to be feared, not the things we suffer. Concerning His immutability he adds:

“‘And no one can turn him away.’” For judgments once fixed can in no way be changed.

“‘And his soul.’” The very power by which He arranges all things is called His soul.

### Verse 14

“‘When he has fulfilled.’” He fulfills His will in me because He afflicts me with many blows. But “many similar things are ready for Him,” because if He intends to strike, there is still room for the wound to grow.

### Verse 15

“‘And therefore from his face.’” He is shaken by fear of righteousness when he sees himself to be unfit to give an account if he is judged strictly.

### Verse 16

“‘God has softened.’” Therefore he attributes the power of His strength not to himself but to the Maker.

“‘He has troubled me.’” The hearts of the righteous are never secure, but are troubled by fear of the Judge. Yet they are consoled by the gifts they have received. Hence: “For I have not perished.” The scourges of the righteous either cleanse former sins or avert future sins; in Job, however, virtue is increased.

### Verse 17

“‘For not.’” The person placed under the scourge perishes from bodily health because of the impending darkness; he is struck for what has passed, so that he may be hidden from future punishments.

## Chapter 24

### Verse 1

“‘But who.’” Although we already know God through faith, we nevertheless do not see how His eternity exists without past or future. Blessed Job, testifying that the days of the Lord cannot be comprehended lest he know more than he ought to know, immediately turns the attention of his mind toward the pride of heretics. They desire to understand lofty things, concerning whom it follows:

### Verse 2

“‘Others move boundary stones.’” Those who are called “others,” etc., up to the point where they nourish them through destructive teachings for slaughter.

### Verse 3

“‘The donkey of orphans.’” By orphans he means the chosen, etc., up to the point where they drive them away from the ministry of good things.

“‘And they took away.’” The Church is called a widow, etc., up to the point where they also drag along their followers. Hence he adds:

### Verse 4

“‘They overturned the poor.’” Sometimes those who seem gentle and humble fall through the examples of others if they do not know how to preserve discernment.

### Verse 5

“‘Others, like wild asses.’” There are heretics who refuse to mix with the peoples but seek a more secluded way of life. By this they infect others all the more with the plague of their persuasion, the more reverent they seem because of the supposed merits of their life. They are compared with wild asses because, released into their own pleasures, they are alienated from the bond of faith and reason.

“‘They go forth.’” They perform not God’s work but their own, since they follow not right doctrines but their own desires.

“‘And keep watch for prey.’” They keep watch for prey who always attempt to seize the words of the righteous for their own meaning, so that by this they may prepare the bread of error for perverse sons.

### Verse 6

“‘A field not his own.’” The Church is signified under the name of a field or vineyard. Perverse preachers reap it and harvest it by oppressing its author in its members. Pursuing the Creator’s grace, when they snatch away from it certain people who seemed upright, what else do they take away than ears of grain or clusters of souls?

### Verse 7

“‘They leave people naked.’” Just as garments protect the body, so good works protect the soul. Therefore heretics, when they destroy the good works of some, take away their garments.

“‘For whom there is no.’” Covering pertains to righteousness, etc., up to the point where they die without the garment of good works.

“‘Whom the rains of the mountains water.’” That is, the streams of preachers satisfy them.

“‘And those who do not have.’” By stones he means strong men, etc., up to the point where they embrace stones?

### Verse 10

“‘Naked and walking without clothing.’” Those who neither do good nor evil, etc., up to the point where we remove the chaff as though from ears of grain, so that we may be refreshed by the marrow of the spirit.

### Verse 11

“‘Who tread the winepresses.’” (Gregory.) Those who persecute the Church, etc., up to the point where they rest in their deeds as at midday.

### Verse 12

“‘From the cities they have made men groan violently.’” Because cities are constituted by peoples living together, etc., up to the point where [he means] those who run along the way of God not sluggishly but manfully.

### Verse 13

“‘And the soul of the wounded cried out.’” The soul of the righteous is wounded when the faith of the weak is disturbed; it cries out when it wastes away at another’s fall.

“Those were rebels against the light.” Those are rebels against the light [Col. 0821D] who, by following their own desires, despise the good they know.

“They did not know his ways.” For those who first become rebels through knowing are afterward blinded, so that they do not know.

“Nor did they return.” The pathway is narrower than the road. Those who disdain doing the more evident things do not attain to understanding the more subtle ones. Yet God waited for them to proceed along his pathways; but would that they had at least wished to return by them, so that the paths of life which they had known through innocence they might at least keep through repentance.

VERSE 14.—“Early in the morning the murderer rises.” For every perverse person, in the prosperity of the present life—which is signified by “morning”—kills by crushing the life of the humble; and, placed in adversity and humiliation—which is signified by “night”—he secretly harms them through wicked counsels, like a thief.

VERSE 15.—“The eye of the adulterer.” This is said of heretics. For just as one who commits adultery illicitly unites to himself the flesh of another man’s wife, so heretics, when they seize a faithful soul into their error, take away what is, as it were, another man’s wife.

“And he will cover his face.” The face of the human heart is the likeness of God. The perverse person covers it so that he cannot be recognized by the strict Judge, when he confounds his life with evil deeds. Hence he will say: “I never knew you.”

VERSE 16.—“He pierces through.” Under the name of houses, etc., up to the point where they scarcely dared to speak perversely.

[Col. 0822B] “As in.” For when they saw the just enjoying prosperity, since they could not speak, they devoted themselves to devising wicked counsels against them.

VERSE 17.—“If suddenly.” For when they see the just rise to the summit of governing power, they are disturbed. These people rejoice in the downfall of the good; but “if dawn should suddenly appear,” that is, if the good should come to rule, “they consider it the shadow of death,” because they fear that the things they have done perversely will be punished. They do not wish to be corrected, but choose to go loosely and to rejoice in their guilt. Hence he says:

“And thus in.” For they rejoice in the night of sin as though the light of righteousness were surrounding them; or, in their present blindness they are so joyful as though they already enjoyed the light of their eternal homeland.

VERSE 18.—“He is light upon the face of the water.” [Col. 0822C] The surface of the water moves here and there, etc., up to the point where the sentence frequently returns to him who is the author of evil.

“Let his portion be cursed.” (The same.) Whoever acts rightly in the present life, etc., up to the point where he is nevertheless held under the guilt of eternal damnation.

“And let him not walk by the way of the vineyards.” He walks by the way of the vineyards who, considering the preacher of the universal Church, deviates neither from the faith nor from the uprightness of good works.

VERSE 19.—“He will pass to excessive heat.” Iniquity is compared with cold, etc., up to the point where he adds that he may believe those who preach what is right.

VERSE 20.—“And his sin down to the underworld.” Sin is led down to the underworld when it is not amended before the end of life. [Col. 0822D]

VERSE 21.—“Its sweetness.” For since it is the nature of worms, etc., up to the point where the decay and stench of rottenness are loved.

“Let it not be remembered.” God looks upon the life of the wicked and forgets it, because what he judges through the strictness of his sentence, as far as the memory of mercy is concerned, he disregards.

VERSE 22.—“For he fed the barren one.” In this passage “barren” signifies the flesh: while it desires only present things, it does not know how to produce good thoughts.

“And the widow.” The soul is called a widow, etc., up to the point where it disdains to serve.

VERSE 23.—“He dragged away the mighty.” He drags away the mighty in the strength of his wickedness, when by the cunning of his error he seizes the powerful of this world.

“And when he stands.” The perverse preacher stands in this world as long as he lives in an earthly body; but he refuses to believe in his own life, because he disdains to learn the truth about God.

“But his eyes.” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book XVII.) The sinner watches his own ways because he strives to think only about and see only those things that may serve his temporal advantage.

VERSE 24.—“They are exalted for a little while.” For those who are separated from eternal stability cannot endure.

“And they will be humbled like all things.” Certainly, like all earthly things. The meaning is: They cannot stand in any way, because even the things on which they lean are themselves fleeing; and while they love temporal things, they pass away with them in the revolving course of time.

“And like the tops of ears of grain,” etc. The tops of ears of grain are awns, etc., up to the point where it is broken by the strength of the final threshing and the grains appear.

VERSE 25.—“But if it is not so,” etc. (The same.) The meaning is: Everything is as I have stated, etc., up to the point where it is nevertheless not fitting that he should be judged by the wicked.

“Who can accuse me of having lied?” As though he were saying: You cannot bring before the Judge the things I say, because, as sinners, you hide his face from yourselves. He places deceitful words before God who examines them in his own presence by the scrutiny of truth; and, considering the inner Judge, he weighs outward things.

CHAPTER XXV

[Col. 0823C]

VERSE 1.—“But Bildad answered,” etc. (The same.) Since Job had said many things, etc., up to the point where he does not know when he will lack that same power by right.

VERSE 2.—“Who makes harmony.” The highest things are arranged into harmony, etc., up to the point where they never wish to obtain what they are unable to possess.

VERSE 3.—“Is there perhaps.” In human knowledge there is no reckoning of the spirits above, because no one knows how great is the multitude of the invisible army there. They are called soldiers because they contend against the powers of the air, not by labor but by command.

“And above.” For the strength of those same soldiers, or of the elect, is strengthened not by their own powers but by the infusion of heavenly grace. If this did not arise in our heart, our mind would certainly remain in darkness. Hence he adds:

VERSE 4.—“Can he perhaps be justified?” Because a human being is born through a woman subject to sin, the guilt and weakness of the first transgression is propagated in the offspring.

VERSE 5.—“Behold, even.” By the moon the Church is signified; by the stars, the souls of individuals who live well and earnestly desire to subdue their faults completely. But as long as they are bound by the corruption of the flesh, they are tied by its bonds: “how much more a human being, who is rottenness!”

VERSE 6.—“And the son,” as though he were saying, etc., up to the point where, just as a human son is born from a human being, so a worm is born from rottenness.

CHAPTER XXVI

[Col. 0824A]

VERSE 1.—“But Job answered.” When the friends’ speeches have ended, Job, now at the climax, rises against them more sharply, as is customary with skilled speakers: to reserve stronger arguments for the conclusion.

(The same.) “Whose helper are you? Is it perhaps the weak man?” To help the weak is an act of charity; to wish to help the powerful is an act of arrogance. The meaning is: While you intend to help the one beneath whose greatness you collapse, the consolation you offer proceeds from ostentation, not from compassion.

VERSE 3.—“To whom did you give.” (The same.) To give counsel to a fool is charity; to give counsel to one who is wise is perversity. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0824B] “And prudence,” etc. Everyone who possesses right prudence does not possess an excess of it, because he does not desire to know more than he ought to know.

“Very much.” Beyond measure, as those who desire to appear more learned than others consequently speak even foolishly. Hence an excess of prudence is added:

VERSE 4.—“Whom do you teach?” We live by the breath without which we do not possess wisdom, but through which we do. Therefore the one who gives life also gives wisdom.

“Breath.” (Augustine.) Just as we cannot exist apart from our nature, etc., up to the point where the created does not create.

“Is it not he who.” (The same.) Because Bildad, seeing Job scourged, etc., up to the point where he expands the matter through propositions, saying:

[Col. 0824C] “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters.” After he had restrained the swelling of wisdom, etc., up to the point where he raises himself on high.

VERSE 5.—“And those who dwell with.” Those who associate with such people groan together with them, because they too are weighed down by sharing their labor; and because the desired heights cannot be administered without sins, the evil that is done is not hidden from divine anger.

VERSE 6.—“Hell is naked.” By the names “hell” and “destruction” he signifies the devil and all his companions in damnation.

VERSE 7.—“He who stretches out.” (The same.) The devil is called by the name “north,” because, in order to constrict the hearts of the nations with the coldness of the body, he said: “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant, on the side of the north.” He is stretched out over the void because he possesses those hearts that are not possessed by the grace of divine love.

“And he suspends the earth.” (The same.) By the name “earth” the Church is signified, etc., up to the words: “All the nations were regarded as nothing and vanity.”

VERSE 8.—“He binds up.” (The same.) He recounts the beginnings of the Church at its birth, saying, etc., up to the point where his hearers would be overwhelmed by his immensity.

VERSE 9.—“He holds back the face.” In the face, knowledge is signified. Therefore the face of his throne is held back, because in this life his kingdom’s glory is not known by us. A cloud is said to be spread over it because that heavenly glory is not seen as it truly is.

[Col. 0825A] “The face of the throne.” His throne is his majesty; or the angels, who cannot now be known fully; or we ourselves, whose face—that is, whose knowledge—is prevented from advancing to higher things. A cloud is over these, in which he reveals hidden judgments. Hence he adds:

VERSE 10.—“He has surrounded the waters with a boundary.” For he regulates the knowledge of the human race, so that, as far as the changes of alternating times pass, they do not attain perfectly to knowledge of the innermost brightness.

VERSE 11.—“The pillars.” (Gregory the Great.) He calls the pillars of heaven the holy angels, or the supreme preachers of the Church.

VERSE 12.—“By his strength.” (The same.) Because, when the Lord was incarnate, hearts that had been divided in the Church believe together in harmony.

“And by his prudence.” The ancient enemy was struck down not by force but by prudence. When he once boldly sought Christ, in whom he had no claim, he justly lost the human being whom he had also justly held. But after the Lord was killed, what glory would follow for the preacher? He continues:

VERSE 13.—“His spirit adorned the heavens.” For unless the preachers had received the promised gifts of the Paraclete, they would not have shone with any adornment of strength.

“And by his hand giving birth.” The ancient enemy, who spoke to humanity through the mouth of a serpent and is called tortuous because he did not stand in the straightness of truth, was cast out of the Church by the Lord’s hand, as by a midwife assisting at birth. In a few statements he has recounted the order of the Lord’s first coming; but concerning the second he adds that it is greatly to be feared.

VERSE 14.—“And behold, these things have been spoken in part concerning his ways.” (The same.) By the name “ways,” etc., up to the point where it flows down to us like a thin drop of heavenly liquid.

“And since we scarcely perceive a small part.” As though he were saying: If we can scarcely endure even the admirable humility of that coming, by what strength shall we endure the terrifying coming of his majesty?

CHAPTER XXVII

VERSE 1.—“Moreover he continued,” etc. (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book XVIII.) The Church suffers bitter things from its enemies in two ways: by words, when its wisdom is exercised; or by swords, when its patience is tested. Now he speaks of the persecution in which it is attacked by false assertions.

VERSE 2.—“As God lives.” There are those who, suffering adversity, do not believe that God exists; others think that God exists but that he scarcely cares for human affairs. This man, placed in the figure of the Church amid affliction, confessed that God exists and said: “As God lives.” But to show that he declared him to care for human affairs, he adds: “Who has taken away my judgment,” etc.

VERSE 4.—“My lips will not speak.” (The same.) What previously concerned iniquity, etc., up to the point of meditating deliberate wickedness.

VERSE 5.—“Far be it from me.” For Solomon says: “He who justifies the wicked and he who condemns the just are both abominable before God.” And this is what he means by: “Far be it from me.” He would depart from innocence if he considered good what belonged to those evils.

[Col. 0826A] VERSE 6.—“My justification.” (The same.) He would abandon the justification he had begun if he turned toward praising sinners. He rightly keeps away from the faults of others who first guards himself from his own—as though he were saying: For this reason I fear sinning concerning them, because my heart does not reproach me.

“For my heart does not reproach me.” As though he were saying, etc., up to the point where he nevertheless firmly resisted the thought.

VERSE 7.—“Let my enemy be like the wicked.” (The same.) “Wicked” means unbelieving, etc., up to the point where he does not agree with me in deed.

VERSE 8.—“For what is the hope of the hypocrite?” A hypocrite, who in Latin is called a *simulator* (“pretender”), is a greedy plunderer who, while acting unjustly and desiring to be honored for holiness, seizes the praise belonging to another’s life.

VERSE 9.—“Will God perhaps hear?” For in judgment he finds no remedy in his cry who now wastes the suitable time for crying out. Concerning his wickedness it is added:

VERSE 10.—“Or will he be able to delight in the Almighty?” Whoever is overcome by love of earthly things cannot delight in God at all.

“And call upon God at every.” The hypocrite invokes God only when the distress of earthly things constrains him.

VERSE 11.—“I will teach you by the hands.” The Son is called the hand of God, etc., up to the point where it is sin for him.

VERSE 14.—“If his children are multiplied.” (The same.) Those who are begotten through the preaching of heretics are struck by the sentence of the coming judgment.

“And his descendants.” The descendants of heretics are, etc., up to the point where he leaves some people stubborn in wickedness. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“Those who remain.” Those left behind from the people of the heretics will be buried in destruction, because, while they do not return to the light of truth, they are weighed down by earthly understanding.

“And his widows will not weep.” By widows he means the peoples left destitute by the death of the heretic. When the preacher of error is carried away to eternal punishments, they often return to the grace of true knowledge.

VERSE 16.—“If he has heaped up.” (The same.) “Silver,” that is, the eloquence of heretics, etc., up to the point where they weave together testimonies of Sacred Scripture.

VERSE 17.—“He will indeed prepare.” For a man full of right faith gathers the testimonies of Scripture that the heretic brings forward and uses them to refute the obstinacy of error, just as David killed Goliath with his own sword.

“And the innocent will divide the silver.” To divide innocent silver, etc., up to the point where they mix falsehoods with truths.
