VERSE 18.—“He built his house like a moth.” (The same.) A moth builds itself a house by corrupting it; so too the heretic creates a place for his false faith only in minds that he corrupts.

“And like a watchman.” The watchman’s shelter, etc., up to the point where the speech is raised when it is added.

VERSE 19.—“The rich man, when he has slept.” The rich man sleeps and opens his eyes, because when he dies in the flesh, his soul is compelled to see what it had disdained to foresee.

[Col. 0827A] VERSE 20.—“It will seize him.” When poverty acts, the rich man is compelled in the underworld to beg for the smallest things; here, when greed acts, he reached the point of denying even the smallest things.

“By night it will oppress him.” He calls the hidden time of sudden departure “night”; by the name “storm” he signifies the whirlwind of judgment.

VERSE 21.—“The wind will carry him away.” The burning wind is called the evil spirit, which drives into the flames of Gehenna the one whom it now inflames with the fire of perverse desire.

“And like a whirlwind it will carry him away.” The place of the perverse is the pleasure of temporal life.

VERSE 22.—“And it will cast upon him.” Whenever God strikes a sinner in order to correct him, he sends the scourge for this purpose: to spare him. But when, by striking, he brings to an end the life of one who persists in sin, he sends the scourge but does not spare him at all.

“From his hand.” Since the hand signifies action, the one struck flees from the hand when, seeing the destruction of the wicked, he abandons the ways of wickedness. Hence it follows:

VERSE 23.—“He will clap his hands over him.” To clap or press the hands means to confirm the works of one’s life in uprightness, by seeing in another’s punishment what one should fear.

CHAPTER XXVIII

VERSE 1.—“It has the beginnings of its veins’ silver.” (Gregory.) After he had described the punishments of the proud and powerful, etc., up to the point where they are not strengthened by the authority of the sacred books.

[Col. 0827C] “And there is a place for gold.” Here he speaks of heretics, etc., up to the point where he first burns here in the workshop of charity.

VERSE 2.—“Iron is taken from the earth.” Heretics are accustomed to boast of justice and to accuse Catholics of having been wicked. Against them it is said through humble confession: “Iron is taken from the earth.” For stronger men are separated from the earthly activity that they previously held and become defenders of the Church.

“And the stone is loosened.” For the hard heart, etc., up to the point where it becomes resonant through preaching.

VERSE 3.—“He set a time for the darkness.” That is, he set a limit by which the wicked may cease to be wicked.

“And for all things.” Because he observes the limit of the elect, etc., up to the point where it blinded itself with the darkness of hardened false faith.

[Col. 0827D] “And the stone of gloom.” The Jewish people, hardened by false faith, etc., up to the point where it expressed his likeness in itself.

VERSE 4.—“The torrent will divide from the people.” (The same.) By the name “torrent,” however, etc., up to the point where the watering of holy preaching can be understood under the name “torrent.”

“Those whom he has forgotten,” that is, the Jews, etc., up to the point where they were unwilling to open a way to the heart through words of life.

VERSE 5.—“The earth from which it arose.” For Judaea first possessed the law that could refresh it, and afterward, having seen the Redeemer’s miracles, the envy that would burn it.

VERSE 6.—“The place of its sapphires is its stones.” (The same.) Sapphires are of an airy color. He says this because holy souls who would lead a heavenly life were never lacking in Judaea.

“And its clods.” By “clods” he means the gatherings of the individual orders, etc., up to the point where he asks why it lost good things and continues:

VERSE 7.—“The bird did not know its path.” Here, under the name of the bird, that one is signified, etc., up to the point where he did not wish to consider.

“Nor did the eye look upon it.” Our Redeemer is compared to a vulture, etc., up to the point where it is added concerning them:

VERSE 8.—“The sons of merchants did not tread it.” Merchants are those who conduct spiritual commerce, etc., up to the point where the sons of merchants are pastors and teachers.

[Col. 0828B] “Nor did the lioness pass through it.” The Church is called a lioness because, through the mouth of holy preaching, it kills those living badly in their vices. Hence it is said to Peter: “Kill and eat.” Thus the Church passed through Judaea, but did not pass completely through it: for it seized a few from it for the faith, yet did not utterly destroy the unbelieving people in its false faith. But when it was rejected by the Jews, what did it do?

VERSE 9.—“He extended his hand to the flint.” For he sent the arm of his preaching against the hardness of the nations.

“He overturned mountains from their roots.” The roots are the innermost thoughts of the proud. The mountains were overturned from their roots because the powers of the world fell from their innermost thoughts in order to worship God.

VERSE 10.—“He cut channels in the rocks,” etc. (The same.) [Col. 0828C] That is, in the hard hearts of the nations he opened rivers of preaching.

“And his eye saw every precious thing.” God saw what was precious when he regarded the human soul, cast away from him, by illuminating it with the light of his grace and wisdom.

VERSE 11.—“He also searches out the depths.” The Lord searches the depths of the rivers, etc., up to the point where the wisdom of God comes to us without any merit of ours.

VERSE 13.—“Nor is it found in the land.” By “land” he means the human soul. This wisdom cannot be found in the land of those who live pleasantly, because whoever is still nourished by the pleasures of this life is separated from understanding eternal wisdom.

VERSE 14.—“The abyss says.” By “abyss” he means the hearts of human beings, etc., up to the point where he calls them foolish before God through wicked works.

“The sea says: It is not in me.” He means the restless minds, etc., up to the point where it would come by itself. It follows:

VERSE 15.—“Refined gold will not be given for it.” By “gold from Ophir” the holy angels are signified, etc., up to the point where it is nevertheless not without the contagion of sin.

“Nor will silver be weighed in exchange for it.” For the life of righteous preachers, or the words of those who write about God, however brightly it may shine with holiness, does not communicate to us the coming of heavenly wisdom through its own presence.

VERSE 16.—“It will not be compared with dyed colors of India.” By India the world is understood here, etc., up to the point where it is a garment without dye.

[Col. 0829A] “Nor with the sardonyx stone.” Sardonyx resembles red earth; sapphire has an airy appearance. Through sardonyx, therefore, human beings or the fathers of the Old Testament are understood, pursuing certain earthly things; through sapphire, the preachers of the New Testament, seeking only heavenly things, or the angels.

VERSE 17.—“Gold or glass will not be equaled to it.” (Gregory.) After it has been said, etc., up to the point where they are creatures.

“Nor will vessels be exchanged for it.” The lofty vessel of gold, etc., up to the point where he believes in the Lord of the prophets.

VERSE 18.—“Nor will they be mentioned in comparison with it.” For what are human beings when compared with God? Nothing.

“But wisdom is drawn forth.” For although it is invisible, etc., up to the words: “And you do not know from where it comes or where it goes.”

VERSE 19.—“Topaz will not be equaled to it.” Because it shines with every color, etc., up to the point that he shows this when he adds:

“Nor the purest dyes.” The purest dyes are those who humbly preserve the grace of virtues that comes upon them. They would not be dyed if they had possessed holiness by nature.

VERSE 20.—“From where, then, does wisdom come?” Because it is born from the invisible Father, etc., up to the words: “And where is the place of understanding?”

VERSE 21.—“It is hidden.” For as long as one lives here, God cannot be seen according to the appearance of his nature; yet he was seen by Moses, Jacob, and others through images.

“It is also hidden from the birds of heaven.” (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book XIX.) Because, established in this corruptible flesh, etc., up to the point where through their words and consolations they breathe again from the weariness of this life.

VERSE 22.—“Destruction and death said,” etc. (The same.) Since to see God is the same as to possess him, the wicked do not see this wisdom because, rejected through pride, they were in no way able to possess it. To have heard its report means to have recognized its power through its effectiveness.

VERSE 23.—“God understands its way.” As though he were saying, etc., up to the point where it was destined to fill the hearts of the elect in every part of the world. It follows:

VERSE 24.—“For he himself looks upon the ends of the world.” For God to look upon something is to restore what was lost to grace.

VERSE 25.—“He who made weight for the winds.” In the speed and height of the winds, etc., up to the point where he tempers glory with mingled weakness.

“And he weighs the waters,” etc. (The same.) By “waters” he means minds filled with the Holy Spirit, etc., up to the point where, struck with fear, he fled from the woman.

VERSE 26.—“When he set a law for the rains.” Rain signifies the words of preachers, etc., up to the point where it preserves in action what it has uttered.

VERSE 27.—“Then he saw it and declared it.” He saw this incarnate Wisdom—that is, he caused it to be seen—and caused it to be declared by preachers, prepared by them, and investigated by hearers. Whoever, by living well, has taken care to have it favorable to him on the day of judgment prepares it for himself.

[Col. 0830A] “He saw it,” etc. He saw it because it is a form, etc., up to the point where a human being would know something about it in himself. Hence it is added:

VERSE 28.—“And he said to the human being,” etc. Because we cannot penetrate the nature of wisdom to know what it is in itself, through God’s condescension we have heard what it is in us. For it is certain that whoever unquestionably fears God possesses this wisdom.

“Behold, the fear of the Lord is itself,” etc. As though he were saying: If you fear God, it is evident that you are full of the wisdom which among human beings is called “the fear of the Lord.” But because the one truly understands the power of divine fear who guards himself from every wicked work, he adds: “And to depart from evil is understanding.”

CHAPTER XXIX

[Col. 0830B]

VERSE 1.—“Moreover Job continued,” etc. (The same.) In this final speech, etc., up to the point where he desires these miserable times of ours with a sigh. Hence he says:

VERSE 2.—“Who will grant me that I might be,” etc. A fixed number of days is called “months,” etc., up to the point where the error that is now hidden will be revealed.

“My former months.” Days, when they are gathered together, are included in months, because the Church, while gathering shining souls, hides them in its innermost places. Or “month” is used for perfection, which will belong to them in rest, just as it now belongs to them in labor; the Church now remembers this perfection.

“According to the days,” etc. For then it will consider itself to be falling among those who fail through persecution, while now it sees itself preserved in these people.

VERSE 3.—“When the lamp shone,” etc. The lamp is called the light of Sacred Scripture. Now, therefore, the lamp shines above the head of the Church, because the sacred words illumine the darkness of our mind.

“And by its light,” etc. (The same.) Although the Church does not penetrate the secrets of another’s thoughts, because in the night it does not know the face of God, as it were, it nevertheless places the steps of good action in the direct light of heavenly speech.

VERSE 4.—“As I was in the days of my youth.” The Church was mature, etc., up to the point where it is unable to bear children through preaching.

[Col. 0830D] “When God was secretly in my tabernacle.” The tabernacle signifies a dwelling, etc., up to the words: “When the Almighty was with me.” It follows:

“And around me,” etc. Children are those who serve the heavenly commandments. They are now around it because they are found among nearly all nations.

VERSE 6.—“When I washed my feet.” The feet of the Church are the ministers of lower works, etc., up to the point where those who minister outward things are its feet.

“And the rock poured out for me,” etc. (The same.) For in it the words of Christ’s inner anointing flow forth. From this rock streams of oil—the books of the evangelists—went out; or he calls the gifts of the Spirit streams of oil.

VERSE 7.—“When I went forth,” etc. Through the gate of the city, etc., up to the point where Job also did this.

[Col. 0831A] “And in the square they prepared,” etc. For in the breadth of the great authority of his teaching he displays freedom. Whoever publicly preaches what he thinks rightly sits, as it were, on a chair in the square, when he fears nothing concerning his preaching and, pressed by no terrors, does not hide himself in silence.

VERSE 8.—“The young men saw me,” etc. He calls them young men because they are not supported by the gravity of old age or made mature by the dignity of their conduct. The meaning is: The immature fear the strength and uprightness of the Church, while the mature glorify them.

VERSE 9.—“The princes ceased speaking.” By princes or leaders he means the authors of heretical wickedness. The meaning is: When I was permitted to preach publicly, everyone who was not subject to the truth was afraid of me. They place a finger upon their mouth when they indicate that they are restrained from making false complaints not by an argument of speech but by the hand of virtue.

VERSE 10.—“The leaders restrained their voice.” Certainly these are the people who try to drag erring peoples after them, etc., up to the point where, by insinuating perverse things, they strengthen them in impiety through nourishment.

VERSE 11.—“The ear that heard.” There he said what he displayed through teaching, etc., up to the point where the one who responds to the example of his life by living well.

VERSE 12.—“Because I had delivered the poor man who cried out.” The Church delivers the poor man who cries out when it releases the sins he has committed for the sinner who begs for forgiveness.

“And the orphan who had no helper.” It delivers the orphan when each person, etc., up to the point where the Church also displays these things both bodily and spiritually.

VERSE 13.—“The blessing of the perishing.” (Gregory.) The blessing of the perishing comes upon her when she forestalls the sinner’s destruction and recalls him from the pit of guilt through holy exhortations.

“And I consoled the widow’s heart.” The widow’s heart receives great consolation when a faithful soul, through the words of the Church, learns something about his coming to whom it is spiritually joined.

VERSE 14.—“I put on righteousness.” He is clothed in righteousness like a garment, etc., up to the point where he is lifted up from the guilt that he has overcome.

“And with my judgment as with a diadem.” The judgment of the just is called a diadem because through it they desire to be rewarded not in earthly and weak things but above.

“I clothed myself with judgment”—which is compared with a crown placed above, because he seeks to be crowned in heaven, not on earth. He reveals his good deeds so that his friends, rather than being rebuked, may be raised up by them, and, remaining silent, may imitate him. The memory of former good deeds is also useful against despair in the face of rebukes.

VERSE 15.—“I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame,” etc. For blessed Job himself had extended a hand to them, etc., up to the point where, if he is wicked to himself, to whom is he good?

VERSE 16.—“I was a father to the poor.” For the poor in spirit are begotten through his preaching.

“And the case that I did not know.” When the Church, through the elect, [Col. 0832A] addresses evils, etc., up to the point where lesser things must nevertheless be abandoned for greater ones.

VERSE 17.—“I crushed the jaws,” etc. The devil is called wicked. By the jaws, his hidden snares are signified; by the teeth, the open perpetration of sins. First, therefore, it is necessary to expose the hidden machinations of his counsels, so that we may afterward be able to recall our hearer’s soul from an open fall.

VERSE 18.—“And I said: In my little nest I will die.” By the name “nest” he expresses, etc., up to the point where he does not, as some do, act more at the beginning and less at the end.

VERSE 19.—“My root,” etc. (The same.) The root of the Church is Christ incarnate, up to the point where the thought of the mind is revealed.

[Col. 0832B] “And the dew will remain,” etc. Supply: “I was saying,” etc., up to the point where we may be worthy to be gathered from lower things.

VERSE 20.—“My glory will always be renewed.” He laments as though his glory had been lost, because he recognizes that those whom he believed to serve the new life are serving ancient desires.

“And my bow.” Scripture is the bow, etc., up to the point that it is so even now.

VERSE 21.—“Those who heard me.” He remembers former times, in which everything said by her was heard with fear by the faithful, and he laments the insolence of her adversaries.

“And they were attentive and silent.” They are silent for the sake of her counsel: they do not dare to oppose her words but believe them.

[Col. 0832C] VERSE 22.—“To add to my words.” Heretics presume to add something to her statements when they attempt, as though correcting them, to amend the uprightness of her teachings.

“And upon them it dripped.” In this dripping of eloquence, the measure of preaching is received according to the capacity of the hearers.

VERSE 23.—“They waited for me like rain.” We receive the words of holy preaching like rain when, with true humility, we acknowledge the dryness of our heart so that we may be watered by the drink of holy preaching.

“And they opened their mouths as for a shower.” Because, when we receive the words of holy preaching at the final part of the world, we open the mouth of our heart as though for the late rain.

VERSE 24.—“If ever I laughed at them, they did not believe it.” [Col. 0832D] (Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book XX.) The Church says this in the voice of the Head, etc., up to the point where excessive severity makes him hateful.

“And the light of my face did not fall.” (The same.) The light of blessed Job’s face, etc., up to the point where the Church does not preach clear mysteries to earthly people.

VERSE 25.—“If I wished to go,” etc. The Lord comes both when he wishes and, when he comes, sits first. For his coming into our heart is gratuitous, and the desire for him in our thought is not equal to our other desires.

“And when I sat, as though,” etc. The letter edifies, etc., up to the point where consolation is a ministry of compassion.

“Consoler of the mourners.” (The same.) Whoever has heard about God’s justice, so that he may fear, should also hear about his mercy, so that he may have confidence, so that fear and hope may exist together. In the ark there are both the tablets and the rod, as well as manna—that is, together with knowledge of Sacred Scripture in the ruler’s breast there are the rod of strictness and the manna of sweetness.

CHAPTER XXX

VERSE 1.—“But now those younger than I.” (Gregory.) Those younger in time ridicule the Church when those who have gone out from her despise the words of her teaching.

“Whose fathers I did not consider worthy,” etc. Therefore the flock of the Church, etc., up to the point where it disdains to count them among true fathers.

VERSE 2.—“With whom the strength of their hands was.” The strength of the hands is greatness, etc., up to the point where they think better of their neighbor than of themselves.

VERSE 3.—“Through want.” For the more they desire knowledge of heavenly things amid immoderate amusements, the more they lose it.

“And barren through hunger.” Because they desire to know so that they may be learned and eloquent, not so that they may be morally ordered. Hence they scarcely grasp outward things, although they think that they have penetrated hidden matters.

“Who gnawed in the wilderness,” etc. Heretics who have withdrawn from the universal Church, etc., up to the point where they lick things away by the flattering speech of their tongue.

“Disfigured by calamity.” They are said to be disfigured by calamity and misery because they are despised both for the ruin of their conduct and for the perversity of their understanding. Calamity is like illness; misery is its neglect, by which it becomes more serious. No one would be disfigured if, in his necessities, he did not add the misery of pleasure.

VERSE 4.—“And they ate herbs,” etc. To eat herbs, etc., up to the point where they do not maintain a right intention in those same works.

(The same.) For what is signified by herbs, etc., up to the point where they serve greed alone, are filled with the root of the juniper, and this is what follows:

“And the root of junipers.” Junipers have something like thorns in place of leaves, etc., up to the point where they usually pursue only outward profits in their words.

VERSE 5.—“Those who, snatching these things from the valleys.” They snatch those things from the valleys, etc., up to the point where they take away the carnal things that press inwardly.

VERSE 6.—“They dwell in the deserts of torrents.” [Col. 0833D] (The same.) Inventors of perverse things, etc., up to the point where the things loved by the wicked are earthly.

“And in the caves of the earth.” (The same.) For heretics, in secret places, etc., up to the point where he descends into evil.

“Or upon gravel.” By gravel we mean very hard stones carried along by river water. Heretics dwell upon gravel because they draw along those human minds that are not made solid by the weight of any stability.

VERSE 7.—“Those who rejoice among such thorns.” By the name “thorns,” etc., up to the point where he adds openly:

“And to be under thorns,” etc. They rejoice in temporal matters, etc., up to the point that they are unwilling to cease from the yoke of worldly servitude, even when they are permitted to do so.

**VERSE 8.**—“Sons of fools and of the ignoble.” The sons of those who were, etc., up to those who have been made exiles from the land of the living.

**VERSE 9.**—“Now I have become their song,” etc. The time of the Church is expressed, when she is publicly mocked by the reprobate.

“And I have become a proverb to them.” He will become a proverb to the wicked, because, when they see good people dying amid torments, they take from them an example for a curse, saying: “May it happen to you as it happened to that slaughtered man.”

**VERSE 10.**—“They abhor me, and flee far from me.” The wicked flee far from the Church, etc., up to the point that he knows how to attribute his evils to the justice of the Judge. It continues:

**VERSE 11.**—“For he has opened his quiver.” [Col. 0834B] By the quiver the hidden judgment of God is signified. Therefore, when the Lord sees sins, etc., up to the point that, in correction, the power of counsel is revealed.

“And he put a bridle in my mouth.” For the holy teachers, when they see that the hearts of those who resist have been divinely abandoned, fall silent, afflicted and groaning, lest they speak to the unworthy, who would thereby become worse. By keeping silent he spares the wicked, while nevertheless, through his patience, he urges them toward life.

**VERSE 12.**—“Calamities at the right hand of the East.” (Ibid.) Our Redeemer is called the East, etc., up to the point that, when the onslaught of the wicked breaks out in persecution, the righteous suffer.

“They have overturned my feet.” By the feet of the Church her lowest members are signified. Since they serve earthly works, they can be deceived all the more quickly the less they understand sublime things.

“And they have overwhelmed my paths as though with waves.” The path of the adversaries is compared with waves, because the life of the wicked, with its insolent restlessness, falls like a storm upon the ship of the heart, so to speak, in order to overwhelm it.

**VERSE 13.**—“They have scattered my roads.” Let blessed Job say this concerning the evil spirits; let the Church say it concerning her persecutors, who scatter her roads when, through sordid persuasion, they disturb the way of truth in the minds of certain weak people.

“They have lain in wait for me and prevailed.” Those lying in wait prevail when they corrupt by pretending good those whom they cannot openly draw toward evil.

“And there was no one who would bring help.” Often the righteous, caught in tribulation, think that the hand of the one bringing aid is slow when the cruelty of their persecutors constrains them for a little longer. The remedies of the rescuer are indeed swift, but they seem slow to the one suffering.

**VERSE 14.**—“As though a wall had been broken.” Our Redeemer is a wall for us, etc., up to the point that this happens because power is given to the enemies by God.

“And when the door had been opened, they rushed upon me.” When the wicked in this life, etc., up to the point that they attempt to destroy the defenses of faith.

“And they have fallen upon my miseries.” The reprobate roll through their own miseries and back into ours when they draw certain people united with us into the evils in which they themselves are entangled. [Col. 0835A]

**VERSE 15.**—“I have been reduced to nothing.” In the estimation of the wicked, etc., up to the point that these things are also to be understood according to the historical sense, which is plain.

“You have taken away my desire like the wind.” The faithful people declare that they suffer because they grieve when those whom they love suffer. The wind therefore takes away desire when any transitory matter destroys the longing for eternity.

“Like a cloud it has passed away.” A cloud rises high, but a breeze drives it along its course. Salvation therefore passed like a cloud, because the glory of the wicked, however high it may be, is not fixed. Once the desires and activities of the weak have been completed, he returns to the voice of the elect.

**VERSE 16.**—“But now in myself.” In ourselves now the soul, etc., up to the point that he immediately returns to those who are falling.

**VERSE 17.**—“At night my mouth is pierced by pains.” He speaks of his own things in such a way that they also suit those who are falling, etc., up to the point that they already possess, as it were, a certain opening of fear.

“And those who consume me.” (GREGORY.) Because the malignant spirits who consume the carnal among the Church do not know how to cease from temptation all the more because they are burdened by no weight of flesh.

**VERSE 18.**—“In the multitude.” What else is Job’s garment, etc., up to the point that they clung to him through the bond of love.

“And as the opening of a tunic.” The opening of a tunic surrounds the neck, etc., up to the point that they attempt to extinguish the voice of preaching. [Col. 0835C]

**VERSE 19.**—“I have been compared to mud.” In the judgment of the reprobate, the Church of the elect is compared with mud, because, trampled underfoot temporarily, she is despised; she is likened to dust and ashes, because they think that she has come only to those evils which they see being displayed bodily in her.

**VERSE 20.**—“I cry out to you.” During the time of her persecution the Church, etc., up to the point that, delayed so that they may make progress, they fear lest they fail.

**VERSE 21.**—“You have changed toward me into cruelty.” Neither cruelty nor mutability exists in God, etc., up to the point: Nothing worthy of him can be said.

“And in the hardness of your hand.” God’s hand is said to be contrary to our will when it pursues by striking whatever displeases him in us.

[Col. 0835D] **VERSE 22.**—“You have lifted me up, and as though…” Because the glory of the present life appears to be seen as though in a high place, etc., up to the point that their elevation immediately collapses.

**VERSE 23.**—“I know that you will hand me over to death.” For no one comes here, etc., up to the point that therefore it is suitably added:

**VERSE 24.**—“Yet not for their destruction.” The Lord extends his hand, etc., up to the point that those who stood outwardly were lying prostrate in the state of their mind.

**VERSE 25.**—“Once I wept.” Compassion is greater than a gift, etc., up to the point that he joins his own weeping to theirs in continual prayer.

(Ibid.) At the time of the Church’s final persecution, he recalls the good things she did during the time of peace. [Col. 0836A] Desiring eternal joys, but oppressed by evils while they are delayed, he adds:

**VERSE 26.**—“I expected good things, and evils came to me.” The faithful people expect good things, but receive evils.

“I waited for light, and darkness burst upon me.” He waits for light and encounters darkness, because he already hopes to share in the joys of the angels as the reward for his merits, yet, delayed here for a longer time, he endures the hands of persecutors, as Tobias did.

**VERSE 27.**—“My inward parts seethed without any rest.” The inward parts of the holy Church seethe, etc., up to the point: “And this is what is meant: ‘Her inward parts seethed.’”

“The days of affliction have overtaken me.” For the Church of the elect knows [Col. 0836B] that she will suffer many evils in the final persecution. But the days of her affliction overtake her because she already bears with great distress the life of the wicked among them even in a time of peace: those who already display in their depraved conduct what is to come.

**VERSE 28.**—“I went about mourning.” The holy man, raised up, etc., up to the point that here he comes to his homeland by a rough road.

“Rising without fury.” Often the tumult of seditious people provokes the minds of their superiors. If the latter are good, they possess a response to the outcry of the insolent, but not fury, because they do not cease to teach those whom they endure with clemency.

**VERSE 29.**—“I was a brother to dragons.” By the name of dragons the malicious are signified, etc., up to the point that the wing of virtue scarcely lifts him from the earth.

**VERSE 30.**—“My skin has become black.” By the name of skin the weak members of the Church are signified, etc., up to the point that those who are in her are tormented by zeal for the faith.

**VERSE 31.**—“My harp has been turned into mourning.” As though he were saying: “In the time of my peace,” etc., up to the point that vices must be extinguished, not the flesh.

## CHAPTER XXXI

**VERSE 1.**—“I made a covenant with my eyes.” (GREGORY, *Moralia on Job*, book XXI.) Now he enumerates his virtues in order, weaving the history of his life in such a way that he inserts something very rare that can be understood allegorically.

“I made a covenant with my eyes.” For, as regards the thoughts of the heart, etc., up to the point: They ought not to look upon what they are not permitted to desire.

**VERSE 2.**—“For what portion would God have in me from above?” As though he were saying: “The Creator of exalted things refuses to possess me as his property if my mind languishes before his sight through weak desires.” For no good pleases God without purity of mind.

**VERSE 3.**—“Is there not destruction for the unrighteous?” Alienation will come upon the reprobate when they see themselves to be accursed from the inheritance of the strict Judge.

**VERSE 4.**—“Does he not himself consider my ways and all …?” By the name of ways, etc., up to the point that things which have become cheap among us through custom remain unexamined.

[Col. 0837A] (GREGORY.) Knowing that he is seen, he takes care; yet, not secure and perfect among the ancient people, he weighs, in the commandments of the future Christ, how much he lacks of perfection. Therefore he says: “If you walk.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Let him weigh me,” as though he were saying: “As far as the standard of human life is concerned, I see no evil in myself; but unless the Mediator appears, who surpasses everyone, I do not recognize how far I am from true simplicity.”

“On a just balance.” By the name of the balance the Mediator of God and human beings is signified, etc., up to the point that he had truly maintained a simple life.

**VERSE 7.**—“If my step has turned aside from the way.” Our step turns aside from the way as often as our thought abandons the path of uprightness through consent to error.

“And if my heart has followed my eyes.” Just as temptation is drawn in through the eyes, so something conceived inwardly sometimes compels the eyes outwardly to serve it. [Col. 0837B]

**VERSE 8.**—“And may my offspring be uprooted.” Whoever does not live according to what he says tears away from the stability of uprightness, by his conduct, those whom he has begotten by his word.

**VERSE 9.**—“If it was deceived.” (Ibid.) By this it is shown that the holy man did not even think of the stain of fornication.

“And if at the door.” By this he plainly shows, etc., up to the point corresponding to what he says: “If the heart was deceived,” and so forth.

**VERSE 11.**—“For this is a crime.” This is the difference between sin and crime, etc., up to the point that it devours even unto destruction.

[Col. 0837C] **VERSE 12.**—“And uprooting all growths.” The growths of the soul are good works, because, if the evil of lust is not resisted, even those things perish which appeared to be good. But how humble he was amid such purity of chastity he reveals when he adds:

**VERSE 13.**—“If I refused to submit.” He who did not refuse to be judged together with his male and female servants, etc., up to the point where he immediately adds: “For what shall I do?”

**VERSE 15.**—“Did he not make me in the womb?” Great is the virtue of humility in powerful men. Having considered the equality of their condition, he now turns to the works of freedom.

**VERSE 16.**—“If I denied what they wanted.” After chastity and humility he adds a discussion of freedom. By this it is shown that he supplied not only the poor in their need but also in their desire.

“And the eyes of the widow.” What she asks with true humility must be given without delay—that is, what is sought not from desire but from necessity—so that the merits of good works may increase not only through the gift but also through the promptness of the gift.

**VERSE 17.**—“If I ate my morsel alone.” I did not give only outwardly, etc., up to the point: Nor does he attribute this compassion to himself but to the grace of God, saying:

**VERSE 19.**—“If I disregarded one passing by.” In not disregarding the poor man he displayed the virtue of humility; in covering him, however, he displayed compassion. He indicates that he had compassion on an unknown neighbor, whom he calls “one passing by,” [Col. 0838A] because, to a compassionate mind, nature is worth more than acquaintance, as in Job.

**VERSE 21.**—“If I raised my hand against the little one.” (Ibid.) As though he were plainly saying, etc., he signifies what was done at the gate.

**VERSE 22.**—“My shoulder.” If the good things I expressed with my mouth, etc., up to the point that, to show that they are joined in him, he enumerates them one by one.

**VERSE 23.**—“For ever, as though swelling …” Waves, when swelling above threaten, etc., up to the point that the saints fear this daily.

“I could not bear its weight,” because one who considers the coming of the final judgment with an attentive mind plainly sees that such terror threatens that he fears not only seeing it then but also anticipating it now. [Col. 0838B]

**VERSE 24.**—“If I thought gold…” (GREGORY, *Moralia on Job*, book XXII.) For he would have despaired of the Creator if he had placed his hope in a creature. Whoever relies on what is falling must necessarily fall with what is falling.

**VERSE 25.**—“If I rejoiced.” Nothing outside God is sufficient for the mind that truly seeks God, etc., up to the point: The understanding either grows sluggish through idleness or vanishes through exaltation; therefore he says:

“If I rejoiced.” But when it rejoices in what it understands, etc., up to the point that, gazing outward from the invisible light, the heart is blinded; and the sense is this:

**VERSE 26.**—“If I saw the sun.” Almost only human beings fail to see their own good things, etc., up to the point that, through contemplation of the mind, the sun from heaven…

[Col. 0838C] “And the moon walking.” He calls the moon fame, which, shining in the night of this life, receives strength from good works. “And my heart did not rejoice in secret.” For there are people who are exalted by their own praises within themselves and rejoice. And this is what follows:

**VERSE 27.**—“And it rejoiced,” etc. And because an unreflective mind, drawn by approval, sometimes praises what it has done, he adds:

“And I kissed”: by the mouth speech is signified. Therefore he kisses his own hand with his mouth who praises what he does.

**VERSE 28.**—“Which is iniquity.” (Ibid.) Whoever attributes to himself what he does is convicted of denying the grace of his author.

“Great.” Every sin that arises from weakness does not lose hope, because it seeks pardon from God. Presumption, however, the farther it is from humility, is the more grievous in despair; and, while it attributes strength to itself, it does not seek it from God.

**VERSE 29.**—“If I rejoiced at…” For, loving even his enemy, he grieved when his adversary fell and thereby himself grew toward the good.

**VERSE 30.**—“For I did not give…” Some people strike those whom they consider adversaries with a curse, because they are altogether unable to overcome them by virtue.

**VERSE 31.**—“If the men did not say…” He endured adversaries dwelling with him, because he did not yield to those acting unjustly through silence, but opposed them through uprightness.

[Col. 0839A] “Who will give us of his flesh?” This is mystically about Christ: either the household Jews desired to be filled with his flesh, wishing to extinguish his body as though by consuming it, or the Gentiles who believe, who are daily refreshed by his body.

**VERSE 32.**—“The stranger did not remain outside.” Since he was about to describe his generosity in the grace of hospitality, he first explained what he had been like within himself, because outward gifts are prepared by the inner purity of the heart.

**VERSE 33.**—“If I hid, like a man…” He sees that it is characteristic of a human being, etc., up to the point that, after an explicit confession of sin, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 34.**—“If I feared the multitude.” To desire nothing worldly is great security, so that one who clings to what is unchanging is not disturbed in mind by all things below being troubled, even though at times he may be disturbed outwardly through the weakness of the flesh.

“And contempt.” The good do not reveal their own matters even when despised, etc., up to the point that they go out as though through the door of the mouth; hence:

“And did not keep silent.” He appropriately puts “I kept silent” first, because one who, unable to endure it, does not know how to remain silent departs from the house of conscience. Mystically this concerns Christ, who did not fear the many who persecuted and despised him; he both kept silent and did not depart to avenge himself by his power.

**VERSE 35.**—“Who will grant me a hearer, so that he may hear my desire?” He seeks the Mediator, knowing that, for human desire to attain the rest of eternal liberation, prayers cannot be heard except through its Advocate. Concerning him it is added:

“And may he write a book.” Hence: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” He who came for our redemption, etc., up to the point: But why, blessed Job, do you desire that a book be written?

**VERSE 36.**—“That I may carry it on my shoulder.” To carry the book on one’s shoulder is to complete Sacred Scripture by putting it into practice. First it is described as being carried on the shoulder, and afterward as being placed around one like a crown, because, if the commandments of sacred discourse are now carried well in action, afterward they present us with the crown of victory in recompense.

**VERSE 37.**—“At each of my steps.” He calls the increases of virtues steps, etc., up to the point that he also demonstrates them through works.

“And I will offer it as to a prince.” What we offer we hold in our hand. Therefore, to offer the book to him coming to judgment is to hold his words of command in action.

**VERSE 38.**—“If [it rises] against me …” For a greater display, etc., up to the point that earth is said to be those unadorned by any works.

“And its furrows…” Furrows are called those who, etc., up to the point that the unformed cry out against him, while the perfected mourn.

**VERSE 39.**—“If I ate its fruits.” The one who rules and the one who is ruled, etc., up to the point that he received the fruits of bodily service from them.

“I afflicted the souls of its farmers.” The ruler of the Church afflicts the souls of the farmers, etc., up to the point that he who does not seek his own glory wishes to be helped by everyone.

**VERSE 40.**—“Instead of wheat.” If, I say, I did this or that, etc., up to the point concerning them: “Its glory is like the flower of hay.”

“Instead of wheat.” For a thorn grows instead of wheat and a briar instead of barley when, in the final recompense—in which the reward of labor is sought—the piercing of pain is found.

## CHAPTER XXXII

**VERSE 1.**—“But the three ceased …” (GREGORY.) At last, [having heard] blessed Job’s full [words], etc., up to the point that, by clinging to antiquity, they harm the ruler’s discernment through their wicked words. [Col. 0840B]

**VERSE 2.**—“And Elihu was angry and indignant.” Elihu means “my God is this,” etc., up to the point that he is separated from their life by the depravity of pride.

“He was angry against Job.” For the seekers of empty glory, etc., up to the point that inwardly they oppress those placed there by the manner of their speech, that is, by the vice of pride.

**VERSE 6.**—“And Elihu the son answered.” (GREGORY, *Moralia on Job*, book XXIII.) Although these things lack the solidity of gravity, etc., he nevertheless employs them vigorously.

(Ibid.) It is no small condemnation to learn from the good, etc., up to the point that they might learn in his ruin what they ought to fear concerning pride.

**VERSE 11.**—“For I waited for your words; I heard your wisdom.” When he says, “I waited,” etc., he declares that he attended to their words, etc., up to the point that in their words they condemn perverse doctrines.

**VERSE 12.**—“But, as I see, there is no one who can refute Job.” Often heretics, because they appear to be something, etc., up to the point that Elihu counters them with the words:

**VERSE 13.**—“Lest perhaps you say…” As though he were saying: “You speak in vain,” etc., up to the point that he preserves eternal rewards for the one who arrives.

**VERSE 14.**—“He did not speak to me.” (Ibid.) Elihu had indeed heard blessed Job publicly, etc., up to the point that they consider themselves wiser than even those who refute them. But because he said:

“And I will not answer according to your words.” He rightly does not answer blessed Job, etc., up to the point that they suppose more about themselves than is necessary, and suppose things worthy of themselves.

**VERSE 15.**—“They were afraid and answered no more.” Elihu is rightly said to have made Job’s friends afraid, because sometimes the defenders of the Church, although they do not maintain the proper order of argument, nevertheless disturb their adversaries by the power of their words, etc. See Gregory, the passage cited above, to the end of the chapter.

## CHAPTER XXXIII

(The exposition of chapters 33 and following, reproduced verbatim from Gregory, is omitted for the sake of brevity. See Gregory, *Moralia on Job*, book XXIII, chapter 7 and following, *Works*, volume II.)

[Col. 0841]

# THE BOOK OF PSALMS (G)*

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED JEROME ON THE BOOK OF PSALMS

(See his *Works*, volume VIII.)

## PREFATORY MATERIALS ON THE PSALTER

[Col. 0841A] (AUGUSTINE.) Among the Hebrews this book is entitled “The Book of Hymns,” for this reason: a hymn is that in which words and praise occur together with song, as is found in the psalms. According to some, it is also entitled “The Book of Soliloquies.” This appears to be because whatever someone investigates within himself and learns from no one except the truth presiding within him is called a soliloquy. For example, just as blessed Augustine investigated with himself the nature of the soul and the nature of God, so the Prophet may be said to have investigated with himself the incarnation of the Son of God and the restoration of the human race.

When King and prophet David was reigning prosperously and wished to magnify the worship of God, as he brought back to Jerusalem the ark returned by the Philistines, which for a long time had wandered in uncertain dwellings, he went before it naked with a harp (2 Samuel VI). He had also chosen four thousand men who would sing psalms not only with the voice but also with musical instruments. Over them he placed four men: Asaph, Jeduthun, Heman, Ethan, or the sons of Korah. These, although degenerate from the crime or sacrilege of their father, whom fire had consumed (Numbers XVI), persevered as most devoted in the worship of God. [Col. 0841B]

(JEROME.) The psalter is a certain musical instrument constructed in the form of the letter Δ; it took its name from that musical instrument through which the present work was performed melodically. Among the Hebrews the psalter is called *nebel*, among the Greeks ψαλτήριον (*psaltērion*), and among the Latins an *organum*. Many say that David did not make all the psalms because some of them are titled in the person of others. But, as blessed Jerome says, they should not be heeded in this matter. For David composed all the psalms, although in doing so he had many assistants, over whom he placed four men: Heman, Ethan, Asaph, and Jeduthun.

This was done by divine counsel, so that the psalms might be titled in the persons of others either because of the interpretation of their names alone, or because of the matter concerned, or because of both. Because of the interpretation of names alone, as in the person of Jeduthun; because of the matter, as in the persons of Haggai and Zechariah; because of both, as in the person of Solomon.

Jeduthun, Asaph, the sons of Korah, and the others of this kind were not the authors of the psalms but the superintendents of the performers who rendered the psalms in three ways: either with the human voice, or with musical instruments, or commonly by both methods. This occurred in two forms: either an instrument followed the voice, or the voice followed the instrument. Hence their names are inserted in the titles, especially for the sake of signifying the matters involved. A psalm is the sound of an instrument; a song is the singing of a human voice in praise of God. “A psalm of a song” means that the voice follows the instrument; “a song of a psalm” means that the instrument follows the voice. [Col. 0841D]

(CASSIODORUS.) It is customary to ask why the psalms, rather than other Scriptures, are read in the Church. The reason is that this custom existed anciently among the Hebrews in the temple of God. Or it is because the psalms contain more mysteries than the other Scriptures and say much briefly, in such a way that the whole Law, the Prophets, and the Gospel are contained in them.

(CASSIODORUS.) Prophecy is divine inspiration or revelation that announces, with unchanging truth, the outcomes of events either through deeds or through words. Hence prophecy is “vision,” and a prophet is “one who sees.” This grace was given in many ways: through human actions, as with Noah’s ark, Abraham’s sacrifice, and the crossing of the Red Sea; through births, as with Esau and Jacob, who signified future things; through angels speaking, as they spoke to Abraham, Lot, and others; through visions, as to Isaiah, Ezekiel, and the others; through dreams, as to Solomon, Joseph, and Daniel; through a cloud and a voice from heaven, as to Moses; and through still other means.

David, however, was completed by none of these but, taught inwardly by heavenly inspiration, was filled with the Spirit speaking in him, as it says in 1 Kings: “The Spirit of the Lord was directed into David” (1 Kings XVI). And the Lord says: “If David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matthew XXII.) The Holy Spirit was given to the prophets in such a way that at times he would depart because of sins and return when appeased. As Peter says: “Prophecy was not at any time brought forth by human will, but holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Peter I).

Those to whom the ability to understand or interpret the Scriptures has been given are not, however, alien to the gift of prophecy.

(JEROME.) There are many kinds of christs. The patriarchs were called christs, as in: “Do not touch my christs” (Psalm CIV). In Proverbs, all who came out of Egypt are called christs. In Exodus, chrism is made, with which priests are anointed. There is another ointment with which kings are anointed, but this occurs in two ways. If it is David and Solomon—that is, “strong of hand” and “peaceful”—the person is anointed with a horn. If it is Jehu and Hazael, it is with a lentil, which is an earthen vessel.

Cyrus also, king of the Persians and Medes, who released Israel, is a christ, according to the words: “Thus says the Lord to my christ, Cyrus” (Isaiah XLV). The context that follows does not permit this to be understood of the Savior, as some think.

There is a prophetic ointment, with which Elijah is commanded to anoint Elisha as prophet (1 Kings XIX). Above all there is a spiritual ointment, called the oil of gladness, with which Christ was anointed above his companions, who possess the chrism of baptism.

If anyone loses this, let him not despair, because Leviticus speaks of separating the chrism. When someone’s leprosy has been cleansed, the priest is to place oil in his left hand, along with the other things mentioned there, and that person is himself to be called the christ of God (Leviticus XIII). This remains: the same person is frequently anointed, so that negligence may not become an occasion of ruin.

It is enough for a leper, after losing the first ointment, to be anointed a second time. But the one who continually makes progress is anointed often: from the oil of the leper he comes to the ointment of the people; from there to the priestly ointment; from that to the chrism of the bishop; from the bishop to the king; from the king to the patriarchs; from the patriarchs to Christ.

(CASSIODORUS.) Just as prophecy occurs in different ways, so it also occurs at different times. One kind concerns the present, as with Elizabeth: “From where is this granted me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?” and so forth (Luke I). Another concerns the past, as with Moses: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis I). Another concerns the future, as in: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” and so forth (Isaiah VII).

There is also prophecy according to God’s foreknowledge, which must be fulfilled in every respect, as in: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” and so forth. Another is according to a threat, as in: “Forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III).

[Col. 0843C] It must therefore be noted that a prophet sometimes speaks indistinctly of future things as though they were present; sometimes of past things; and sometimes properly of future things. This happens because he says everything under the dictation of the Holy Spirit, to whom all things—whether past or future—are known as present.

(REMIGIUS.) This book consists of one hundred and fifty psalms, not without the rationale of a higher mystery. For this number is especially celebrated for its mysteries. It consists of eighty and seventy, whose beginning and significance derive from eight and seven.

The number eight signifies the eighth, the resurrection, because, since there are six ages of the living, the seventh belongs to the dead, and the eighth will belong to those rising again. Through the number seven, the time of this life is signified, which unfolds through the repetition of seven days. The book of psalms has therefore rightly been composed with this number, because it teaches us to work and live in the sevenfold period of this life so that, in the eighth of the resurrection, we may receive the robe of glory.

Or it is because the New Testament is signified by eight. For the fathers of the New Testament serve the octave, observing the eighth day of Christ’s resurrection, that is, the Lord’s Day, and the octaves of the saints, while awaiting the eighth day of the resurrection of the dead.

Through seven, however, the Old Testament is signified, because the fathers of the Old Testament served the week—that is, the number seven—observing the seventh day, the seventh week, the seventh year, and the fiftieth year, which is woven from seven weeks of years, that is, the Jubilee. Hence Solomon says: “Give a portion to seven, and also to eight” (Ecclesiastes XI). This book of psalms was therefore appropriately published with this number, since its parts contain the teaching and commandments of both Testaments. [Col. 0844A]

(AUGUSTINE.) Again, through three groups of fifty, a threefold division of the psalms is made, signifying the three states of the Christian religion. The first is penitence, in which the first group of fifty psalms also ends: “Have mercy on me, O God.” The second is righteousness, in which the second group of fifty also ends: “I will sing mercy and judgment to you.” The third is the state of eternal life, in praise of which the third group of fifty ends: “Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

(ID.) The Book of Psalms is one book, not five, as is read in the Acts of the Apostles: “As it is written in the Book of Psalms” (Acts I). Jerome, nevertheless, says that there are five books, that is, five divisions made by the words “Let it be, let it be.”

The order of the psalms differs from the order of history, because David first sinned with Uriah’s wife and sang of penitence, “Have mercy on me, O God,” before his son persecuted him and he sang, “Lord, how they have multiplied.” But they are believed to have been ordered in this way by the prophet Ezra under divine inspiration.

The subject matter is the whole Christ, bridegroom and bride. The purpose is to conform human beings disfigured in Adam to Christ, the new human being. The method of treatment is sometimes to speak of Christ as the head, sometimes as the body, and sometimes as both.

As the head, he is treated in three ways: sometimes according to his divinity, as in: “With you is the beginning,” and so forth; sometimes according to his humanity, as in: “I slept,” and so forth; and sometimes by transference, when he uses the voice of his members, as in: “Far from my salvation,” and so forth.

The Church, too, is treated in three ways: sometimes according to the perfect, sometimes according to the imperfect, and sometimes according to the wicked. These are in the Church bodily but not mentally; in number but not in merit; in name but not in reality.

# PSALM I

**VERSE 1.**—“Blessed is the man who has not gone away,” etc. (AUGUSTINE, *Expositions on the Psalms*, volume III.) The sequence is this: Adam went away when he withdrew from God; he stood when he delighted in sin; he sat when, established in pride, he could not return except through the one who was free from all these things. Adam went away when he consented to the devil’s persuasion; he stood while he ate the apple; he sat while he excused himself: “The woman whom you gave me deceived me” (Genesis III).

This is like exiles who, while they are still on the road, are more easily called back, but when they stand still are more difficult to recall; and finally, when they have become masters and lords there, they are recalled with the greatest difficulty.

(REMIGIUS.) One sins through thought, through action, and through teaching by words.

(CASSIODORUS.) The impious person is impious toward God, a sinner against himself, and pestilent toward his neighbor.

“In the seat giving an example of sinning.” (CASSIODORUS.) A throne belongs to kings, a tribunal to judges, and a chair properly to teachers.

(Ibid.) It is as though he were saying: “You who fell through the first Adam, conform yourselves to this second, because the blessed man is opposed to the first.” [Col. 0845A]

**VERSE 2.**—“But in the law.” AUGUSTINE. (CASSIODORUS.) Here he is shown to be full of every good thing in himself.

(AUGUSTINE.) It is not perfect praise merely to flee what deserves blame unless what deserves praise follows. In the same order in which they grew in the first man, they are removed by the second.

“In the law.” (Ibid.) The one who is in the law acts according to the law; the one who is under the law is acted upon according to the law. The former is free; the latter is a servant.

(Ibid., AMBROSE.) One thing is the law written for the servant; another is the law perceived in the mind by one who has no need of letters.

“Will.” (CASSIODORUS.) So that it may be neither weariness of labor nor idleness, but he will meditate always. The will of the senses is under the law; the will of reason is in the law; the will of divinity is above the law.

**VERSE 3.**—“And he will be.” (Ibid.) Here he is shown to be useful to us, giving the fruit of life and leaves, and providing shade.

“Blessed is the man. But in the law. And he will be.” A complete definition of the blessed man. All these things do not apply to every blessed man but only to Christ.

“Like a tree.” (Ibid.) According to the likeness of the tree of life that is in paradise, from which the obedient human being would eat.

“Tree.” (Ibid.) In paradise there is the tree of life, a tree leading to life, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

“Of waters.” (AUGUSTINE.) The waters are the Holy Spirit, according to the saying: “Whoever believes in me, rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (John VII); and this is against the heats of vices.

(CASSIODORUS.) Or by water is meant the wisdom of God, by which the inner human being is refreshed, so that there may be a thirst for water.

(AUGUSTINE.) Or the mortal race, as in Job: “Many waters, many peoples,” because they flow into death as waters flow into the sea.

“He will give.” (Ibid.) Giving pertains to rational understanding and to the will of the one offering.

[Col. 0845C] “And the leaf.” (Ibid.) Just as leaves cover fruits, so the words of the Lord guard his promises.

“And all things.” (Ibid.) What is meant by the individual details?

**VERSE 4.**—“Not so the impious.” Here he frightens them concerning the vengeance of the wicked; their fear makes the preceding blessings more desirable.

“From the face of the earth.” (AUGUSTINE.) Of eternal stability, because just as this earth nourishes and contains the human being, so that earth nourishes and contains the inner person.

**VERSE 5.**—“Therefore the impious will not rise.” Because the wind casts them away—that is, because they have been handed over to a depraved mind—they do not rise in the first resurrection, so as to judge themselves in the assembly and prefer God’s will to their own.

Or “in the council,” that is, in the harmonious multitude of the righteous: the impious are idolaters or apostates; sinners are false Christians. Or they do not rise in the future in order to judge, or, having been judged, in the council—that is, in the fellowship of the righteous—they will rest.

“In judgment, etc.” In judgment there will be four orders. Some will judge and will not be judged, such as the most perfect. Others will neither judge nor be judged, such as condemned unbelievers. Others will be judged and saved, such as those who are moderately good. Others will be judged and perish, such as wicked believers.

“In the council.” (AUGUSTINE.) In the eternal good, which it was the saints’ counsel to follow.

Or “in the council,” in the judgment, so that they may judge with them, because judgment occurs when different sins are punished with different penalties; the expression is used by comparison.

“They rise.” What resurrections? Of the soul from sins in the present; of the body from death in the future, when it will become incapable of suffering and immortal.

[Col. 0846A] **VERSE 6.**—“For the Lord knows the way of the righteous,” etc. That is, these people do not rise in the soul, because God does not approve their works, but only those of the righteous.

# PSALM II
“Psalm.” The modulation made by the touch of ten strings is good conduct, carried out through observance of the Ten Commandments. “David.” (CASS.) “Strong of hand,” or “beautiful in appearance”: Christ, who conquered the aerial powers, and upon whom the angels also desire to gaze.

**VERSE 1.**—“Why did the nations rage, etc.” (CASS.) This psalm is second in order but first in its title; hence in the Acts of the Apostles it is called the first. First he rebukes the persecutors, threatens them, and foretells as a prophet, [Col. 0846B] “vain things.” (Ibid.) To keep him in death; or, lest the world should go after him.

**VERSE 2.**—“Kings.” (Ibid.) The first was Herod, who killed the infants; the later one was Herod, who agreed with Pilate in Christ’s death. “Kings and princes.” (Ibid.) According to Ambrose, he could also have spoken of one person in the plural. For in the Acts of the Apostles, Peter’s words reveal that only King Herod and Prince Pilate conspired against Christ.

**VERSE 3.**—“Let us tear apart.” (AMB.) Or, they gathered together, saying: “Let us tear apart their arguments—the arguments of the Lord and Christ, or of Christ and the disciples—by which they wish to bind us to themselves.” (AUG.) Even if it could be expressed otherwise, it applies more plainly to those who do not wish Christ’s yoke to be imposed upon them. “Bonds.” The promises of eternal life [Col. 0846C] and the threats of Gehenna, by which they wish to subjugate us to themselves. “Let us cast them away.” Once their arguments have been destroyed, let us shake his dominion off ourselves. (Ibid.) The yoke, that is, the law; but “he who dwells in the heavens.”

**VERSE 4.**—“He will laugh.” (Ibid.) As when, after guards had been stationed, he rose again. “He will mock,” when they were scattered throughout the world. God’s mockery is the power of foreknowledge that God gives to the saints, so that, seeing Christ’s name destined to be among all the nations, they may understand that those people were contemplating vain things.

**VERSE 5.**—“He will speak to them.” (Ibid.) He explains more clearly when he says, “he will trouble them.” God’s anger is the movement that occurs in the soul which knows God’s law when it sees that law being passed over by evil; through this movement many things are avenged. Or, God’s anger is the darkening of the mind of those who transgress the law [Col. 0846D].

**VERSE 6.**—“But I.” (CASS.) Secondly, he introduces his words concerning his omnipotent kingdom and ineffable generation, where we learn about his divinity and humanity. “King.” (ID.) Thus also the kings of the earth have been established by him. “Preaching upon Zion”; thus also the prophets. “Son”; thus also Israel. “I have begotten you”: this applies to Christ alone.

**VERSE 7.**—“The Lord said.” The person of the one who reigns. “My Son.” (AUG.) Therefore I give you the nations as an inheritance rather than to someone obedient: because he is Son by nature and consubstantial through an ineffable begetting. “Today.” (Ibid.) Although it can be understood of the day on which he was born according to the human being, nevertheless, since “today” signifies presence, it should be understood of the eternal generation of God’s Wisdom [Col. 0847A].

**VERSE 8.**—“Ask.” (AUG.) This pertains to the assumption of humanity, which was undertaken for the salvation of human beings, according to which he intercedes for us. “Inheritance.” (CASS.) *Hereditas* derives from *herus* (“master”), because in it one rules freely with authority.

**VERSE 9.**—“You will rule them.” (AUG.) Some he will rule, while others he will break, according to the saying: “Behold, this one is appointed for the downfall and rising again of many” (Luke 2), so that “the one who is righteous may still be justified, and the one who is filthy may still become filthy” (Rev. 22). “An iron rod.” (CASS.) Christ’s power is the iron rod; the sinner is the potter’s vessel, which is both earthen and easily broken.

**VERSE 10.**—“And now, kings, understand.” Now, [Col. 0847B] that is, through what has been said. (CAS.) Thirdly, having disclosed these things, he admonishes everyone to obey humbly and urges them, for their benefit, not to perish, and for the sake of what is honorable, since blessed are those who trust in him. Here he speaks after Christ, as an Apostle.

(AUG.) Or: with me established as king, do not be saddened, kings of the earth. It is advantageous for you to be subject to him, from whom understanding and instruction come, so that you may not rule rashly but serve the Lord of all and rejoice in blessedness.

**VERSE 12.**—“Lest he become angry.” (Ibid.) The uncertainty is not according to the prophet but according to those who, in uncertainty, contemplate God’s anger. “From the just way,” that is, having been lifted away from Christ, or from good conduct.

[Col. 0847C] **VERSE 13.**—“When he blazes up.” (CASS.) Now he does not burn when he chastises, as a father does; but in the future he will burn, because in the future there will be no patience. “His anger is soon kindled.” Because he does not examine each of these things separately but all of them together.

## PSALM III

**VERSE 1.**—“A psalm.” (AUG.) Concerning Christ’s passion and resurrection: “the Son” is Judas, from whom he fled when Judas departed and withdrew with the others to the mountain; or rather, when the wisdom of God abandoned Judas’s mind, so that he became wholly the devil’s. This abandonment is called “flight” because of its swiftness. Hence: “What you are doing, do quickly” (John 13). Christ offered him peace, as David did to his wicked son; hence it is called the father’s peace. Judas, however, died hanging like Absalom. He sets forth two opposing parts. It is the voice of Christ, as though he were astonished when he came to save: “Lord, why, etc.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Lord, why?” (CASS.) The first psalm among those that briefly speak of the passion and resurrection, directed against those—and especially the pagans—who do not believe that the glory of majesty can descend to lowly things.

**VERSE 3.**—“Many say, etc.” (AUG.) Or, this is said by each person who is attacked by vices and desires.

“They say to the soul: ‘There is no salvation, etc.’” Through the accumulation of vices, despair of healing creeps in, as though the vices were insulting the soul; or even as the devils and their angels do so through suggestions.

[Col. 0848A] **VERSE 4.**—“You are my protector.” (CASS.) In Christ. “The head”: Christ, or the mind that serves God’s law. “You have struck them all.” Properly, in predestination, this is said of the devil and his angels. “Upon the people”: that is, each one of us. (ID.) Or, the Church and its head speak here, established amid the storms of persecution throughout the whole world. Many say, wishing to extinguish the Christian name, “There is no salvation.” Otherwise they would not hope to destroy the Church, which flourishes widely. “Protector.” Because it has been received and exalted in Christ. The head itself is the one who first ascended into heaven.

**VERSE 5.**—“And he heard me from the mountain, etc.” That is, through Christ the Church’s prayer, or righteousness, is heard.

**VERSE 6.**—“I slept,” according to the saying: [Col. 0848B] “Rise from the dead, and Christ will shine upon you” (Eph. 5). There is nothing surprising in the Savior’s saying this, since he accomplished much greater things for the salvation of souls while he was absent from the body, as they are recounted in Saint Peter’s Catholic Epistle: “When he went and preached to the spirits who were in prison, who formerly had been disobedient” (1 Pet. 3).

**VERSE 7.**—“I will not fear thousands,” who try to extinguish Christ’s name. “Arise.” O Christ, the head, in whose resurrection there is salvation.

**VERSE 8.**—“For you have struck, etc.” Now that the Church reigns, the enemies have been struck down through confusion. “The teeth of sinners,” that is, their accursed words; or, they become princes unto destruction. Therefore believe, human beings, [Col. 0848C] that “salvation belongs to the Lord,” and, O Lord, “may your blessing be upon your people. With my voice.” This is rightly said of me, because “with my voice.” The good person who asks for good things cries out with his own voice; with another’s voice, that is, with a voice not in agreement with his life.

“I slept.” The conclusion of the matter, from which he proposes that there is nothing to fear. “I,” with emphasis: as though to say, “They rage, but I would not sleep unless I wished to.” Or, “I slept” by consenting; “I was drowsy” by doing evil; “I arose” by abandoning sins.

“For.” (AUG.) This does not look backward, as though he saves afterward because he struck them; rather, their teeth were broken because he struck them—that is, their accursed words were rendered ineffective. Or, the teeth are those who cut certain people off from the number of the saints and incorporate them into the wicked.

## PSALM IV

[Col. 0848D]

**VERSE 1.**—“To the end.” (AUG.) “End” is used in two ways: when something comes to an end, or when it is perfected. (Ibid.) “Song” indicates joy. Psalms are sung to the psaltery, which the Prophet used in a great mystery. “Psalm”: concerning conduct, for action, so that false gods and the vanities of the world may be abandoned. “Of song”: because mention is made of eternal joy.

**VERSE 2.**—“When I called, etc.” (CASS.) By his own example he rebukes the unbelievers concerning false things. “You enlarged me.” (Ibid.) You led me from the narrowness of sorrow into the breadth of joy. “We rejoice in tribulations, knowing that tribulation, etc.” (Rom. 5.) First he indicated that he had been heard; now, as though having God in his heart, he speaks to him. “Have mercy on me.” He has shown mercy through righteousness and enlargement. Again, have mercy against the miseries of this life. “My prayer”: concerning the things to be requested. And having spoken thus about me: “Children of men, how long with a heavy heart?”

**VERSE 3.**—“You love vanity, etc.” (CASS.) You embrace them by desire; you seek vain idols and lies through labor—things that are not God—or earthly things that do not do what they promise.

**VERSE 4.**—“And know, etc.” Having proposed the new person, he commands the old one to be put off. (AUG.) Note that “and” is placed at the beginnings of passages so that it may join what has been said with the vision that is in the heart; here, for example: “Do not love vain things. And know.” But the *diapsalma* forbids their being joined in this way. According to Jerome, *diapsalma* is always the Hebrew *sela*, that is, always a confirmation of the preceding section. *Sympsalma* means the joining of a psalm. “The Lord will hear”: concerning rest, and so will you; therefore cry out, in this way becoming worthy to be heard.

**VERSE 5.**—“Be angry.” If a movement arises in the soul that is not under its control, reason should not consent to it. (CASS.) The movement of the soul is not under our control, but by God’s grace we can moderate it. Therefore what belongs to habit he permits; what belongs to guilt he forbids.

(HIER.) The Apostle teaches this: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Eph. 4), so that it is wholly or lightly sinful to become angry; righteousness, however, consists in calming anger through swift repentance.

“In your hearts.” (AUG.) Concerning what you handle in your heart, which God knows—that is, concerning consent—and concerning what you turn over in your bedchamber, that is, in the pleasure of the flesh, in which reason lies captive like a wild beast in its lair. “Be pierced,” through repentance; or, the bedchambers are the thoughts of the fierce. (CASS.) Anger is venial when it is not carried into effect.

*Diapsalma.* “Sacrifice.” (CASS.) Once the old person has been put off, we are commanded to offer ourselves as a sacrifice, because we are certain of good things. (AUG.) “A sacrifice of righteousness”: a contrite spirit, so that by punishing itself it may be slain for God; or, righteous works after repentance. The *diapsalma* indicates this: one passes from the old life to the new and thus hopes for good things. But since scarcely anyone loves inward good things, he adds:

**VERSE 6.**—“Many say: ‘Who will show us good things?’” Namely, future things, about which they doubt and despair. In response, he briefly shows what good things are to be sought.

**VERSE 7.**—“The light of your countenance has been marked upon us, etc.” (AUG.) This light is the whole and true good of the human being, by which he is marked, like a denarius by the image of the king. “Light.” (AUG.) Light, that is, a luminous countenance that illuminates us—the image by which you are known. (CASS.) Or, the cross has been impressed upon us as the sign of our king; it is the light of the countenance, because God shines in such people. The image of creation is reason; of re-creation, grace; of likeness, the whole Trinity.

“In the heart.” (AUG.) Joy is to be sought not outside, in vain things, but within, where God dwells.

**VERSE 8.**—“From the fruit.” (CAS.) Because they think that complete goodness consists in these things. He sets these three things, as more suitable to human use, in place of all riches [Col. 0850A].

**VERSE 9.**—“In peace in the same place.” (CASS.) But I will sleep in peace of mind, here having forgotten the world, and I will rest in the future, because already I am in one hope, not in the multiplicity of the world.

“I will sleep and rest in peace.” (AUG.) Away from all the things of the world, when this mortal nature puts on immortality. This will truly happen, because it is already hope; and this is what follows: “For you, Lord”—and certainly what is hoped for will come to pass.

## PSALM V

**VERSE 1.**—“For her who receives the inheritance.” Because honor is given to the one who is affirmed to be destined to possess the inheritance, while her rival is excluded from it. It is the Church [Col. 0850B], which receives the inheritance—that is, eternal life, God himself. She speaks here about the inheritance that she asks for herself and asserts to be hers, saying that her rival is excluded.

(BEDA.) That is, for the Church, which, when Christ rose again, received the gifts of spiritual goods, and which itself is sometimes called the Lord’s inheritance, having been purchased with his precious blood. Hence it is said: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance.” Therefore the whole psalm is spoken by the person of the Catholic Church. In the first section she asks that her prayer be heard, declaring that heretics and schismatics are to be excluded from the Lord’s gifts. In the second section she prays to be directed by understanding the divine Scriptures along the straight path toward that blessed homeland, asserting that the faithless thereby become completely alien. Finally, recalling the rewards of the blessed, she both turns the wicked through the punishment proclaimed and stirs the righteous through the rewards promised, in one proclamation.

**VERSE 2.**—“My words.” (CASS.) Here the prophet intimates that prayer is to be made threefold. There are three principal vices in prosperity and three in adversity, against which we must make a threefold prayer. In prosperity: against the desire of the flesh, against the desire of the eyes, and against the pride of life. In adversity: against fear of death, danger, and loss of advantage.

(Ibid.) The threefold prayer consists in words—that is, the psalmody of the mouth—and in a cry—that is, the affection of the heart; therefore: “You will hear.” Behold, three times concerning the same thing. “With your ears.” God’s ears are his power and mercy: power, by which he can hear; mercy, by which he wills to hear. For unless there were mercy, he would hear no one’s prayers.

**VERSE 3.**—“To the voice.” That prayer has a voice which is worthy to be heard. “King.” (AUG.) Properly, the Son. He is rightly called king first, because through him one goes to the Father; hence he adds, “and my God.” Yet he does not say “give ear” in the plural but “give ear” in the singular, because God is one.

**VERSE 4.**—“For, etc.” (AUG.) Thus far, the prayer that it may be heard, etc., up to “and this morning,” as soon as it abandons the darkness.

**VERSE 5.**—“In the morning I will stand.” (CASS.) Or, in the morning when eternity begins; then I will see fully what iniquity does not please, because then it will not dwell there, “but the wicked will be taken away, so that he may not see the glory of God” (Isa. 26). Then they will not remain, even if they have received his mercy.

**VERSE 6.**—“Nor will the unjust remain.” Those who do evil. For you hate those who practice evil, not those who have practiced it.

**VERSE 7.**—“You will destroy all who speak lies.” (AUG.) Because this is contrary to truth. Truth concerns what is; a lie is neither substance nor nature, but concerns what is not. What turns away from what is toward what is not is rightly destroyed.

(Ibid.) To lie is to speak against what is felt in the mind.

(Ibid.) There are certain lies told for the sake of salvation, etc., up to “I did not think that the madman could repeat it.”

**VERSE 8.**—“But I.” (AUG.) Thirdly, he says that he will be the future house of God and that now he is drawing near in fear before the consummation that drives out fear [Col. 0851B].

“I will enter.” (CASS.) Through this I will enter, because I will worship. (Ibid.) He asks this against the things that his rival brings forward; therefore she herself will perish.

**VERSE 9.**—“Lord, lead me.” (AUG.) Fourthly, as he advances amid obstacles, he prays to be helped inwardly, lest he be turned aside by deceitful tongues.

“In your righteousness.” (CASS.) Because you receive penitents and suppliants.

“In your sight.” (AUG.) Where human beings do not see, and therefore no trust should be placed in one who praises or blames, because he does not see the conscience, in which the way to God is directed. Therefore he adds: “For there is no truth in their mouth.”
