**VERSE 10.**—“For there is not, etc.” Not only is there no truth in their mouth, but there is a tomb, because they bring forth foul things to corrupt others; and if they do not succeed through these, they act deceitfully—that is, they not only plot but accomplish their designs.

**VERSES 11–12.**—“Judge them, God. Let them fall from their plans.” He does not wish this but foretells what will happen. One falls when disappointed in a good hope.

“And let them rejoice.” (CASS.) After the punishments of the wicked, he adds the rewards of the good, so that just as punishment terrifies, rewards may incite.

**VERSE 13.**—“Like a shield.” (CASS.) In one word he indicates God’s freely given benefits. The will that calls is defense against everything, and it is both crown and shield. The crown is fitted to the head; the defense belongs to the heart.

## PSALM VI

[Col. 0851D] **VERSE 1.**—“The eighth” is the Lord’s advent, at which the sinner fears being accused and therefore repents. (AUG.) Some call the eighth the Lord’s advent, etc., up to “therefore the Church, fearing, prays here.”

**VERSE 2.**—“Lord, do not rebuke me in your fury.” (BASIL.) This is a supplicatory confession, which has value before God. First comes the introduction, in which he seeks goodwill through the judge’s power, his own weakness, and the judge’s habitual mercy, because God does not wish to be asked by the dead but by the living.

“Rebuke.” (AUG.) To be rebuked is more severe than to be accused; hence condemnation is feared. To be corrected is milder, that is, to be amended or instructed. Those who are without a foundation are rebuked in judgment. Those are amended, that is, purified, who built wood, hay, and straw upon that foundation [Col. 0852A]. He therefore says here, “Heal me,” so that there may be no need for that there; then he adds, “Have mercy.”

**VERSE 3.**—“Weak.” (AUG.) The soul is weakened by guilt; heal it from this, because the bones—that is, the mind—are troubled at his presence, as is the soul, that is, the sensory faculty. Therefore: “How long will you delay?” As though he were saying, “What remains before you heal me?”

“How long?” (AUG.) He indicates that he has long been struggling with vices. God’s delay is not cruelty, but is intended to show the soul into what evils it has plunged itself. For it does not yet pray so perfectly that it may be told: “While you are still speaking, I will say, ‘Behold, I am here’” (Isa. 65). Thus, from the difficulty of healing, it may take greater care to avoid those evils; and it may be shown what punishment awaits the unconverted, if the converted experience such difficulty. Hence: “If the righteous man is scarcely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?” (1 Pet. 4.)

[Col. 0852B] **VERSE 5.**—“Turn back.” (CASS.) You who had turned away, or turn back from vengeance. “Deliver”: from the death that threatens. Or, deliver the soul bound by sins. “Save me, etc.” by giving virtues.

**VERSE 6.**—“For there is no one.” (CASS.) Therefore I hasten to be released here, because after death and in hell confession is not received.

“In hell.” (AUG.) The rich man confessed when he saw Lazarus, although he saw him from the depths; by comparison with Lazarus he was compelled to confess his own evils, to the point that he even asked that his brothers be warned about them. But after judgment, in the deeper darkness, they will see no light of God to whom they may confess.

Or, he calls sin “death,” in which the person who despises God’s commandments is forgetful of God.

**VERSE 7.**—“I have labored.” (CASS.) He recounts the hardships by which penitents are turned away; he groans while he sees what he has done and what punishment is to come.

“Bed.” The conscience, which is rest for some and torment for others. “Bedstead”: the sensory faculty; I will make fertile what was barren. Or, the bed is bodily pleasure, in which a person is dissolved. The bedstead is a heap of sins, like clothing; when it is dissolved by a rain of tears, a new harvest of virtues grows.

**VERSE 8.**—“From fury.” (AUG.) From anger, whether God’s anger, which occurs in judgment, etc., up to “so that no one may despair because of the gravity of sins.” He adds, “Depart from me, etc.”

(CASS.) This is correction, so that he may separate himself from those in whose company he sinned and devote himself to God’s commandments.

“Enemies.” (AUG.) That is, vices, or evil people, who are truly enemies to those turning toward God. Every good person is separated from them not in place but in spirit. Since such labor of repentance is not fruitless, he signifies that he has been heard and adds: “Depart from me.”

**VERSES 9–10.**—“The Lord.” The Lord is named three times, because he shows that the Trinity has been present to his prayers. He began with tears; having been heard, he rejoices.

“The Lord has heard.” (CAS.) He gives an example that those who pray faithfully are heard.

**VERSE 11.**—“Let them be ashamed and troubled.” (CASS.) As though at the conclusion, now freed from sins and rejoicing, he prays for his enemies, so that they may be converted and, like him, receive forgiveness.

(AUG.) “Let them be ashamed.” This does not happen here—where people instead mock those who abandon everything and cause the weak to be ashamed—but in the judgment.

## PSALM VII

[Col. 0853A] **VERSE 1.**—“To the end, a psalm.” (AUG.) Of Cush, who passed over to Absalom’s side, etc., up to “for the matters on whose behalf it was performed were not to be hidden.”

(AUG.) This psalm can be understood as spoken in the person of Christ. If anything is said humbly, let it be referred to our weakness, which he assumed. First he asks to be delivered from all tribulations.

**VERSE 2.**—“Lord God.” (CASS.) This is the first psalm among those in which, through David’s actions, the future mysteries of the Lord are signified. The mystery of the Incarnation was silence to the Jews. Just as David suffered persecution from his son, so Christ suffered persecution from the people whom he had nourished.

“Deliver.” (AUG.) As though, having overcome every battle with vices, nothing at all remained except the envious devil [Col. 0853B].

**VERSE 3.**—“Let him seize, etc.” “Let him redeem, etc.” (CASS.) These are proper terms: it belongs to the Lord to deliver, to the lion to seize. The order is that he first places the persecutors, and then the lion. Once purified from all spiritual wickedness, he is delivered from the devil.

**VERSES 4–5.**—“Lord, if I have done this.” (Ibid.) Literally, concerning David and Absalom.

“If I have done this,” that is, if this evil has happened to me because of past guilt. Or, if there is now iniquity in my hands—that is, in my deeds.

Or, “if I have repaid those who repaid me with evil, etc.” (which is called equity among human beings), “then deservedly” (even if it does not appear so to human beings) “may I fall empty-handed from my enemies,” deprived of the fruit of gentleness.

[Col. 0853C] (AUG.) “If I have done this,” or, the universal sin that he named without specifying it: pride, which is the root of all evils. Or, the following phrase, “if there is iniquity,” is understood of every sin.

“If I have repaid.” (Ibid.) That is, if I have not imitated you in the just silence—that is, the patience—which you practiced for me.

“May I deservedly fall from my enemies.” (Ibid.) He does not invoke this upon himself by oath; rather, he says what happens to those who avenge themselves. Therefore he prophesies, not swearing by a curse; this is the gravest kind of oath.

He is made empty by vain and proud joy, as though he could not be conquered. Solomon says: “The one who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a city” (Prov. 16).

[Col. 0853D] **VERSE 6.**—“Let him trample, etc.” (Ibid.) The sinner’s soul, of which it is said, “You are earth, and to earth you shall return” (Gen. 3), is the food of the serpent, to whom it was said in the curse, “You shall eat earth”—that is, of the devil, because the soul is earth, that is, earthly.

Therefore he says here: “Let him trample my life upon the earth,” that is, let him incorporate it into himself once it has been reduced to earth, and let it be despised there.

“My glory.” (Ibid.) This ought to be in the conscience, where God sees it, and solid in the Lord, according to the saying: “Let the one who glories, glory in the Lord” (1 Cor. 1).

“Let him bring it down into dust,” that is, into pride and boasting, so that I may wish to glory before human beings.

“Let him bring it down into dust. Dust that the wind drives away.” (Ibid.) The boasting of the proud. Therefore he wishes his glory [Col. 0854A] to be solid within, where God sees. For it is dust if he glories before human beings. Behold how pride must be avoided.

**VERSES 7–8.**—“Arise, Lord.” He asks that the glory of Christ’s resurrection come to his aid.

“In your anger.” For this perfect person does not pray here against human beings but against the devil, so that he may lose his possession—namely, sinners and the ungodly, who are his possession. And because the removal of a human being is punishment for the devil, God’s anger against him is mentioned.

Or, here he prays for Christ’s resurrection, just as in the preceding psalm he prayed for his Incarnation: “O Lord my God, etc.”

“Within the boundaries.” The world or hell are the devil’s boundaries.

“And arise, Lord.” The proud devil is overcome through iniquity. He adds:

Or, “Arise,” that is, make yourself known throughout the whole world by rising again.

“According to the command,” so that you may cause the commandment of humility to be fulfilled. This follows because the Synagogue, from various peoples—or specifically from the Jews—“will surround you,” either by loving or by persecuting you.

“Because of this”: that is, because of the one who loves you. “Return”: that is, make your omnipotence known to them—you who descended so that they might see you.

Or, “because of this”: that is, because of the one who persecutes you, in whom you find no place. “Return on high”: that is, withdraw from those who persecute you.

“Synagogue.” (Ibid.) The gathering of the people, etc., up to “the Lord judges,” having returned from judgment—that is, Christ’s judgment.

“Innocence.” (Ibid.) Because I did not repay those who repaid me.

“Upon me.” (Ibid.) Justice and innocence are upon me, because they are not from me but from God [Col. 0854C].

**VERSE 10.**—“Examining hearts.” (Ibid.) What each person is thinking.

“Kidneys.” What gives each person pleasure, because the end of concern and thought is pleasure, which one strives to reach.

Human beings can see our works in words and deeds; but only God sees with what intention they are done and toward what end they wish to arrive. When he sees that the heart is in heaven and does not take pleasure in the flesh but in the Lord—that is, when thoughts are good—he directs the righteous and not only directs but also helps them.

**VERSE 11.**—“My just help.” (Ibid.) There are two functions of medicine: to heal sickness and to preserve health. With respect to the first he said in another psalm: “I am weak; heal me, Lord.” With respect to the second, the perfect person says here: “My just help is from the Lord.”

Both that medicine and this one bring salvation. The former transfers a person from sickness to health; the latter preserves him in health itself. The former is a remedy for escaping sickness; the latter is a remedy to prevent relapse into sickness. By the former we who are weak are healed; by the latter we who are healthy are guarded.

**VERSE 12.**—“God the judge.” (CASS.) Here he terrifies through fear of the future judgment and promises hope to those who return.

“Does he perhaps become angry?” (AUG.) Another reading is: “Does he bring anger every day?” In Greek, “he brings anger” is more significant, because the anger by which he punishes is not in God himself but in the angels of anger, through whom he punishes. They do not rejoice because of the justice by which they do not delight, but because of their wickedness they take pleasure in human punishment. He does not gather them each day for vengeance but, through patience, invites them to repentance.

**VERSE 13.**—“His sword.” (AUG.) Another reading is: “He has made his sword shine.”

(CASS.) “His sword”: he will exercise manifest vengeance. Nor is this statement inconsistent, because “he bent his bow”: he threatens, lest his patience be thought lax; “he prepared it,” so that he may be thought ready to send the arrow immediately.

“His bow.” (Ibid.) By analogy. Just as one who bends a bow threatens, so through Sacred Scripture he threatens the wicked, lest God’s patience be thought lax; and he “prepared it,” so that he may be thought ready to send the arrow immediately, just as someone prepares a bow in order to shoot an arrow.

“He bent his bow.” (AUG.) By tempering the Old Testament through the New Testament.

“He prepared it,” through explanation.

(Ibid.) Or, “he prepared it”: God prepares and arranges, etc., up to “but for those burning with zeal, the arrows.”

**VERSE 15.**—“Behold.” As though to say: God has prepared these things in the Scriptures.

(Ibid.) From this it seems that there is a cause of condemnation for the human being. But “behold”: it does not come from God but from the human being, because “he opened a pit, etc. He conceived pain.” (Ibid.) That is, through desire for temporal things.

“He gave birth”: he effected and brought forth it. In the iniquity brought forth there is a pit—that is, a precipice for others. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 16.**—“He opened a pit.” Thus he is comparable to one who opens a pit. He opens it by conceiving deceit; he digs it out by giving birth, persisting in the work of deceit; he falls into it by giving birth to deceit—that is, by carrying it out.

**VERSE 17.**—“The pain will return, etc.” The head is the soul; the crown is reason, over which sins dominate and remain. They will descend upon it when they thrust it down into punishments.

**VERSE 18.**—“I will confess to the Lord.” (CASS.) The conclusion, gathering everything into a summary: he declares eagerly that he will confess.

## PSALM VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“To the end, for the winepresses, etc.” “For the winepresses,” that is, for the churches, etc., up to “they flow forth into the soul’s rest.”

[Col. 0855D] **VERSE 2.**—“Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name, etc.” (CASS.) First, God’s praises, his majesty, and his exalted work are described.

“In all.” (Ibid.) Therefore let neither the Jews nor anyone else claim for themselves what belongs to all; this is the intention.

“Above the heavens.” (AUG.) Literally, or the Scriptures, because it surpasses the words of all the Scriptures.

Or, “above the heavens,” continuing with what follows: that is, into the Scriptures, which he bends down to infants because of the enemies of the cross. They are destroyed when they are seen—that is, understood—as the Scriptures are brought down even to infants; and through them, when they are nourished to strength and raised up to the height of understanding.

**VERSE 3.**—“From the mouth of infants.” (Ibid.) Of the foolish, to whom the Apostle gave milk, whom those who praised the Lord prefigured, and to whom the Lord applies this testimony. From these he perfected praise, because if only the perfect were in the Church, the human race would not be instructed. This is as now, when even the very small, who are not yet capable of understanding spiritual realities, are nourished by faith in temporal history.

“Enemies” are all who speak contrary to the dispensation accomplished through the Crucified One.

“Defenders” appear to be heretics defending faith and philosophers defending wisdom, although the former attack true faith and the latter true wisdom.

“Of those who suckle.” (CASS.) Not in age, but as Peter says, “like newborn infants” (1 Pet. 2), who are not yet able to take solid food but can take milk; and you are proclaimed not only by the perfect but also by the foolish.

Or, he calls the infants and those who suckle the apostles, who were simple and uneducated men; hence: “God chose the foolish things of the world to shame the strong” (1 Cor. 1). This is a more perfect praise.

Or, “from the mouth of infants and those who suckle,” that is, from the words of the Hebrew children, you perfected praise, which appeared to be done childishly because of the enemies, so that it might not seem to be human wisdom but divinely given.

“Your enemies”: the pagans.

“An enemy”: the Jew, who is God’s enemy while defending the Father alone, because “the one who does not honor the Son does not honor the Father”; or an enemy in intention.

**VERSE 4.**—“For I will see.” In spirit, in contrast to the Jew.

“Your heavens”: I will see the apostles present in their successors. This applies well to the earliest believers.

“The works of your fingers.” Because they were perfected through the cooperation of the Trinity, which is signified here by three fingers, as there: “Who weighed the mass of the earth with three fingers” (Isa. 40). And through them, “the moon and the stars that you founded.” Not those others.

**VERSE 5.**—“What is the human being?” (Ibid.) Secondly, he says that human nature, once corrupted, was exalted in Christ above all things. Previously he had shown the omnipotence of the Godhead.

By “human being,” he means sinners; by “son of man,” spiritual people.

(Ibid.) “Human being” means anyone insignificant, whom God remembers in mercy. “Son of man” means Christ as human, because through him you visit the human being when the Word became flesh, in which the physician came to the sick.

“Or the son.” (AUG.) The disjunction indicates a distinction between “human being” and “son of man.” Every son of man is a human being, but not every human being is a son of man, as with Adam. Therefore “human being” is everyone who bears the image of the earthly; “son of man” is the one who is heavenly, and rightly the new human being, the son of man, because the new is made from the old through a certain transformation.

(AUG.) Why, having left the higher things, does he speak of these lower ones? But “the sheep,” etc., up to “who cause human hearts to bear fruit by the seed of God’s word.”

**VERSE 8.**—“Moreover, the cattle.” He therefore indicates that the wicked are subject to Christ, which seems a lesser thing. For these are carnal people living in the breadth of the plain—that is, in the expanse of pleasures—not on the mountains of virtues.

“Cattle of the field.” (Ibid.) Those who live in the flesh, where they climb nothing difficult; but the broad way to which they cling is the way that leads to destruction. Hence Abel is also killed in the field.

**VERSE 9.**—“Birds”: the proud, concerning whom it is said: “They have set their mouth in heaven” (Ps. 72). Their head says: “I will ascend into heaven, and I will exalt my throne, and I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14).

“Fish of the sea that travel the paths of the sea”: the curious.

These three—pleasure of the flesh, pride, and curiosity—contain all vices: the desire of the flesh, worldly ambition (that is, pride), and the desire of the eyes, through which curiosity is especially powerful.

## PSALM IX

**VERSE 1.**—“To the end, for the hidden things of the Son.” It is not added whose they are; by excellence, they belong to the only-begotten Son of God.

“Hidden things.” Because some of his works are manifest, etc., up to “and concerning the punishment by which he judges through purifying, converting, and blinding.”

**VERSE 2.**—“I will confess to you, Lord, with my whole heart, etc.” The joyful prophet sings a psalm because the worship of the devil is destroyed by Christ’s coming; and Christ reigns, judges, and helps.

**VERSE 4.**—“When you turn my enemy back, etc., they will perish, etc.” (AUG.) Because when you turned the devil backward, his members are weakened, so that they can do no harm; and they will not exist, or they will be utterly destroyed from opposing you when you say, “Go, accursed ones” (Matt. 25). Or, they will perish when God removes iniquity from them.

**VERSE 5.**—“You have carried out my judgment and my case.” (Ibid.) Because they served me for my benefit, since “you sat down.”

“You judge.” (HIER.) The Father, so that Christ might die for the human race.

(AUG.) Or, Christ will judge at the end, for the Father has given him all judgment.

[Col. 0857C] **VERSE 6.**—“Forever and ever.” (Ibid.) The present age is this age that passes onward; “the age of the age” is the eternal age, of which the former is an image.

Or, this is a specification, so that you would not understand it as referring to the present age.

### PSALM 9

**VERSE 7.**—“The swords.” (CASS.) The power of the devil will be destroyed at the end of the age. “The cities”: his peoples. “With a crash,” that is, with a very great outcry, as happens when prosperous affairs are closed with a grave “end.” But, on the contrary, the Lord remains. “The end.” (AUG.) It is the sword which he will brandish at the second coming, judging openly; and which now acts secretly, until the point at which the enemy’s swords have some power—but then they will fail completely. “Their.” (CASS.) The plural is used although above he said “enemy” in the singular, because there are many demons; yet, since they are alike in wickedness, they are as one. [Col. 0857D] “With a crash.” (AUG.) That is, the noise and tumult of impiety have perished; or, when impiety is overthrown, there is a crash, because no one reaches complete peace unless he has fought against vices amid a great tumult. “His throne.” (CASS.) Judicial power: he who was judged in humility will judge in majesty.

**VERSE 10.**—“And he became.” How great it is that he who is judge should be a refuge for the poor person who desires nothing of the world. “In times of need.” (AUG.) A person is not more opportunely turned away from the world unless labors and sorrows are mingled with these pleasures.

**VERSE 11.**—“Let them hope.” (AUG.) When they cease to hope in worldly things. Those who have turned away from the world and seek where they may fix their hope are received by knowledge of the name. The name is known when he whose name it is is known. His name is “Lord”; the one who willingly serves him knows it. Or, he is the One who is; and therefore no one should hope in transitory things, which possess nothing except “was” and “will be.” For what is future in them, when it comes, immediately becomes past; it is awaited with desire, lost with grief, and not held with certainty. “For you have not abandoned.” The Prophet urges the faithful to praise, looking toward the benefits of the present and future age.

**VERSE 12.**—“Zion.” (Ibid.) Contemplation—*speculatio*—which is now being practiced so that we may reach the vision of peace, that is, from Zion to Jerusalem. Yet every diligent contemplation falls into error unless the Lord dwells in it. [Col. 0858A] “Studies.” (HIER.) That is, his commandments, in which one must labor.

**VERSE 13.**—“For, when seeking.” (Ibid.) But as those who were sent to evangelize might say, “No one believes us, and we are being killed,” he answered: “Not without fruit,” because he is “seeking vengeance for their blood,” in the judgment where glory will belong to the slain and punishment to the slayer. “He has remembered,” etc. (Ibid.) Not after forgetfulness, but after a long time, according to the feeling of the weak, who think that he has forgotten because it does not happen as quickly as they wish. Add to them also: indeed, he has not forgotten, as you suppose. And if I said “remembered,” this is directed against those who, because of the delay, think that he has forgotten.

**VERSE 14.**—“Have mercy.” (CASS.) He says in his own person what each person asks. “See.” (Ibid.) God’s regard is assistance; when it is present, light also drives away darkness. The humility of the one who suffers is measured against the pride of the enemy, because the former are humbled as much as the latter are exalted. [Col. 0858B]

**VERSE 15.**—“You who lift me up from the gates of death,” etc. (AUG.) That is, from all desires by which one goes toward death. Death is already the delight itself in enjoying what is desired; hence the Apostle says: “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead” (1 Tim. 5). “From the gates of the daughter of Zion.” These are all the best pursuits, etc., up to “which eye has not seen, nor ear heard.” (CASS.) Gates correspond to gates, because the former are gates of death, the latter of life. “Zion.” (Ibid.) It generated all the Churches of the world, because Christ was born there, from which faith began. [Col. 0858C]

**VERSE 16.**—“I will rejoice.” (AUG.) Up to this point there has been a cry; from here the Church, which is afflicted, says, “I will rejoice in Jesus.” (CASS.) For she is saved in hope. “In the snare.” (Ibid.) The hidden snare is deceitful thought. The foot is the soul’s love, which, if perverse, is called desire; if upright, charity. By it the soul is moved toward a place in which it rejoices, through love, to have arrived. “In the snare,” therefore, that is, in a deceitful plan: the foot, that is, love, which through fraud has reached empty joy, has been caught, because that pleasure binds them, so that they neither dare to break their love away from it nor turn it toward useful things. For if they try, it is painful to abandon what delights them, and that pain does not allow them to depart. [Col. 0858D]

**VERSE 17.**—“It will be known.” (CASS.) Or concerning the future judgment, etc., up to the point at which some falsely suppose otherwise.

**VERSE 18.**—“Let sinners be turned.” (AUG.) This is the song of the *diapsalma*, as it were the hidden joy of separation. The separation takes place here not in place but in affection, between the good and the wicked. [Col. 0859A] (CASS.) He foretells for sinners, together with the Antichrist, the end of evils—as though this were only for the present; but ultimately they will be turned, so that they may not rejoice in their own things. “Into hell,” so that they may not think themselves destined to be sent elsewhere.

**VERSE 19.**—“Patience.” (AUG.) God will chiefly remember the poor because of their patient endurance.

**VERSE 20.**—“Arise.” (AUG.) He prays for the future judgment. (CASS.) Speaking about the end of the age, the Prophet foresaw the coming of the Antichrist; therefore, as though terrified, he cries out: “Arise.”

**VERSE 21.**—“Let them know.” That is, let them experience through their torments what foolish human beings they have been.

### PSALM 10—ACCORDING TO THE HEBREWS

**VERSE 1.**—“Why?” (AUG.) A *diapsalma*, because it will be permitted to that man—the Antichrist—to do such great things that he will be thought to be God. He then adds, as it were, the voice of those groaning and asking about the delay of judgment. [Col. 0859B]

(CASS., AUG.) “Why?” He treats of the evils of that time, etc., up to “but at the opportune moment,” namely, “while he is exalting himself.”

**VERSE 2.**—“The poor person is set on fire”; they are seized in the schemes by which they plot. (AUG.) In a wonderful providence God brings good out of evils, etc., up to “thus the wicked are condemned and the righteous are saved.”

**VERSE 3.**—“For he is praised.” He is therefore proud, or is captured, because he is praised by his own people through the fulfillment of his sensual desires. [Col. 0859C]

(AUG.) The tongues of flatterers bind souls in sins. For it is pleasing to do things in which the one who reproves is not only not feared but the one who praises is also heard.

**VERSE 4.**—“Of his anger.” (CASS.) Of the Antichrist, because he will do everything turbulently and cruelly; or of God: he will not seek God by repenting; or God will seek him in order to avenge himself here, although he will punish him more severely in the future.

**VERSE 5.**—“Defiled.” (CASS.) The cause of wickedness is that he does not have God before his eyes; therefore his ways, that is, his thoughts and deeds, are filthy.

“In every season.” (AUG.) In his own, that is, during his lifetime, etc., up to “and because he will rule over all his enemies.” [Col. 0859D]

**VERSE 6.**—“He said,” etc. “I will occupy all nations,” but not without evil, that is, sin, which is proper to him. Or: “I will always be without evil”—this is what he promises himself, whose mouth is full of cursing, etc.

“I shall not be moved.” (AUG.) Or, he will think that by evil arts, and in no other way, he will pass from mortal generation into the eternal—something which Simon Magus also supposed.

**VERSE 7.**—“Under his tongue.” (CASS.) That is, his thoughts concern the labor of the saints and bodily pain, as is evident in the martyrs. Or, the labor of the saints and the pain that is in bodily punishments are under his tongue, that is, lighter than his tongue, which inwardly harms; that punishment, namely, is external.

Or “under his tongue,” because words are feared more and will harm more than blows, by which the soul is cast down and will perish. [Col. 0860A]

**VERSE 8.**—“In secret places,” etc. (AUG.) That is, in ambiguous matters, where it is not easily seen what should or should not be asked.

**VERSE 9.**—“His eyes are upon the poor,” etc. (Ibid.) He explains the ambush: his eyes are as though moved by mercy and affection; or, he deceives others in this way, since his eyes look cruelly upon the poor in spirit.

“A lion in his den,” etc. Because there are strength and deceit in him, etc., up to “through heretics and false brothers.”

**VERSE 10.**—“He will bow down.” (CASS.) When he has relaxed his mind into idleness through excessive prosperity, he will fall by sudden destruction, and the Lord will kill him with the breath of his mouth.

“To the end.” They deny that they see God, etc., up to “he stirs up the Lord: Arise, O Lord.” [Col. 0860B]

**VERSE 12.**—“Arise, Lord God, and let your hand be exalted,” lest you forget, etc. (Ibid.) He prays for judgment, so that those things which are so great may soon be brought to an end here; no one wishes the time in which these things occur to be prolonged.

“Arise.” As though unexpectedly, so that they may be crushed while your people, exalted with you, glorify you.

**VERSE 13.**—“For what reason has the wicked provoked God?” (AUG.) Now, understanding and rejoicing in that judgment, he says: “For what reason?” That is, “What does it profit him to do such great evils?”

“For [the wicked] said in his heart [the printed text reads ‘God’],” etc. (Ibid.) This sense requires a pronouncement, etc., up to “so that they may neither labor nor become angry.”

(AUG.) Christ tolerated Judas, sent him to preach, and gave him the Eucharist, in order to show that gifts reach those who receive the faith, whatever kind of person Judas was. [Col. 0860C]

**VERSE 14.**—“For you see that you regard labor and pain.” You have already ordained where you will hand them over into your hand.

“Of the orphan,” etc. (AUG.) The one whose father—the world through which he was begotten carnally—has died, so that he may say: “The world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.”

**VERSE 15.**—“Break the arm.” He terrifies the wicked with punishments and soothes the good.

“It will be sought.” (AUG.) While it is still necessary for our purification, as above: “while the wicked exalts himself,” etc. But because it will not be found—that is, because there is now no place in which his sin can exist—there is no need of a file when the iron is smooth. [Col. 0860D]

**VERSE 16.**—“The Lord will reign forever and throughout the age of the age.” This kingdom will be more welcome because of the evils that converge. It will come once the Antichrist has been destroyed. The nations will perish from this kingdom, but the poor will possess it, because “the desire of the poor,” etc.

**VERSE 17.**—“The preparation of the heart.” (CASS.) Or “desire,” which is what occurs when something is sought more ardently with all the powers of the soul. Or this means that God himself has prepared this in their hearts. Or, that God immediately hears what they wish to ask.

“His ear,” etc. (AUG.) When bodily members that are visible and corporeal in us are named, in God we must understand powers of operation.

“To judge the orphan and the humble,” etc. The second coming will be manifest, etc., up to “the author of evils will be condemned with his people.” [Col. 0861A]

### PSALM 10

**VERSE 1.**—“To the end.” (AUG.) A psalm of David, the prophet who teaches resistance to heretics.

**VERSE 2.**—“In the Lord I trust.” (AUG.) Concerning the heretics who wish to turn Catholics toward their own perversity.

(Ibid.) “In the Lord I trust.” Literally, it can be read concerning the Passion, and Christ speaks according to his humanity—as he commonly does against the terrors of the Jews: “In the Lord I trust.”

“In the Lord I trust,” when sinners wish to shoot at the upright. [Col. 0861B]

“For behold.” (Ibid.) These are the terrors of those who threaten us on account of sinners, so that we may pass over to them as though they were righteous. For they say: “Sinners have bent the bow”—the Scriptures—from which they may shoot poisoned arrows, which they prepare in the secret place of the heart.

**VERSE 3.**—“In darkness.” (CASS.) Either living in a simple understanding, or in their own ambiguous opinions—not that Scripture is capable of this, but because:

**VERSE 4.**—“For what you have perfected.” He turns his speech from them to God, as though saying: “Why do they say, ‘Move away’? Why should one be terrified by sinners who are preparing to shoot at the upright?” Because they have destroyed what you perfected in their assemblies, where they kill with poisons the little ones who ought to be nourished with milk, from whose mouth praise is made perfect. [Col. 0861C]

“But the righteous one, what has he done?” (AUG.) According to both interpretations, etc., up to “it harms his own soul, not the righteous person who trusts in God.”

**VERSE 6.**—“The Lord examines,” etc. “But the righteous one.” He threatens judgment, by fear of which they may abandon falsehoods.

“He examines.” (Ibid.) That is, he tests, because the good are not wearied by obscure matters but are exercised by knowledge. They are not puffed up but strengthened.

“What you have perfected.” That is, you have brought forth perfectly, or by fulfilling what was foretold. “They destroyed,” by interpreting it badly.

(Ibid.) “In darkness.” Or, “the darkened moon.” There are two opinions concerning the moon, etc., up to “who then says that the holy sacraments are given through holy persons.” [Col. 0861D]

**VERSE 7.**—“He will rain upon.” He shows what he returns to the wicked. (AUG.) He rains from the clouds, that is, from false prophets.

Or from the good, from whom snares proceed when Scripture is badly understood—but only for those who are sinners. “Fire.” First they are devastated by the fire of desires; then, because of the stench of evil works, they are cast out from the saints; finally they are plunged into eternal punishments.

**VERSE 8.**—“Righteousnesses.” (Ibid.) It is plural, so that you may understand righteous persons, in whom there are many righteousnesses, although God’s righteousness is one.

“He has seen equity.” Equity is seen in the face, that is, in his knowledge; for the face is his knowledge, that is, the power by which he makes himself known to the worthy. Or, “he has seen,” because he does not give himself to be known by the wicked but by the good—and this is equity.

### PSALM 11

**VERSE 1.**—“For the eighth.” (CASS.) “For the eighth,” because here the Prophet asks that the iniquity of the world be destroyed, so that he may reach the truth of the future promise. [Col. 0862A]

(AUG.) “For the eighth” refers to the day of judgment, as was said in Psalm 6.

**VERSE 2.**—“Save me.” He recalls us from the falsehoods of the world to the words of God, where salvation is found; he asks to be saved from the world’s perversity.

“For the holy one has failed.” (CASS.) He explains the many things he feared, gathering them into one so that their force may be greater.

“Holy.” (Ibid.) God, who is present everywhere, has failed insofar as human beings are concerned—those who do not believe in him.

**VERSE 3.**—“Neighbor.” (AUG.) Every human being is a neighbor, with whom no one should act wickedly. Every human being is a neighbor by the condition of first birth; by kinship of flesh, friends and relatives; by comparison of mercy, anyone who does good. [Col. 0862B]

“Heart,” etc. The repetition signifies a double heart, in which the deceitful person is described; hence: “A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways.” The good have one heart and one soul.

**VERSE 4.**—“May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips,” etc. (CASS.) That is, may those who agree in one perversity perish indiscriminately.

“An arrogant tongue.” (Ibid.) That is, a proud tongue. These are hypocrites, possessing an appearance in speech in order to deceive human beings and not subject to God. (REMIG.) Or philosophers.

**VERSE 5.**—“They said: ‘Our tongue.’” (CASS.) They boast of the power of their lips, as though they had not received it from God. [Col. 0862C]

**VERSE 6.**—“Because of the poverty and groaning of the poor.” AUG., (CASS.) The needy are the Gentiles, who had neither the Law nor the Prophets; the poor are the Jews. “Now”—something that did not occur among the former people. “I will arise”—I will appear in the Son. “I will set”—consolation for the poor. “With confidence”—powerfully, since nothing resists him.

**VERSE 7.**—“The words of the Lord.” (Ibid.) Against the evils of the world, Christ was sent by the Father, whose words are true, whereas those of the impious are false. “Pure.” Against what was said above: “They have spoken vainly.” “Tested.” Against this: “They have spoken deceitful lips with heart and heart.”

“Sevenfold.” (AUG.) Perfectly, etc., up to “and he demonstrates what is perfect.”

**VERSE 8.**—“You, O Lord.” (CASS.) Turning toward the Lord, he shows the usefulness of the divine words. [Col. 0862D]

**VERSE 9.**—“Round about.” A conclusion concerning both parts. (AUG.) “Round about,” that is, in the desire for temporal things, which revolve through seven days and do not arrive at the eighth, that is, eternity. Hence the wise king is a winnower of the wicked and casts upon them the wheel of evils (Prov. 2), that is, the circuit of revolving things.

“You have multiplied the sons of men.” (Ibid.) There is also a multiplication in temporal things that turns one away from the unity of God. But the righteous are multiplied according to height when they go from virtue to virtue.

### PSALM 12

**VERSE 1.**—“To the end.” (CASS.) A psalm concerning the charity of Christ, etc., up to “according to that saying: ‘I desire to depart and to be with Christ’” (Phil. 1). [Col. 0863A]

**VERSE 2.**—“How long?” (CAS.) The great ardor of one who endures, etc., up to “because hope is prolonged.”

“The plans.” (AUG.) Counsel is not necessary, etc., up to “grieving and praying for eternal things.”

**VERSE 3.**—“How long will he be exalted,” etc. (CASS.) He says that, before Christ’s coming, the devil held human beings captive. Or, “over me,” that is, over my cruelty, because he is worshiped throughout the whole world; and because the world thus perishes, he weeps.

**VERSE 4.**—“Look.” (Ibid.) After lamentation comes prayer, so that he may be enlightened and not yield to the enemy’s fraud, who trusts in mercy.

“Look.” (AUG.) Send the one whom you are going to send.

“Hear.” (CASS.) For all those on whose behalf he asks generally.

“Enlighten.” If not bodily, let us see at least with the mind. [Col. 0863B]

“Lest I sleep.” When, once the light of faith has been buried, the eyes are closed by carnal pleasure.

“In death.” That is, in the sin committed against the Holy Spirit, concerning which John says: “There is a sin unto death; I do not say that anyone should pray for it.”

**VERSE 6.**—“They will rejoice.” (AUG.) Not only “enlighten me,” but also “so that the enemy may not rejoice.”

“I have hoped.” (CASS.) Although he hastens, he is nevertheless patient; for even if there is delay, he remains firm in hope, and already rejoices inwardly, seeing the one whom he desires to see in the flesh. Hence he says that good things have been given to him, although earlier he complained.

“He has granted.” Not “he will grant”: the great power of faith already possesses what is future.

“My heart will rejoice.” If he desires him so greatly, if he serves the one who is coming in this way, what must he do once he has received him?

### PSALM 13

**VERSE 1.**—“The fool said.” (CASS.) An accusation of the Jews, describing their wickedness. The first psalm concerning the accusation of the Jews, etc., up to “this man is not God.” [Col. 0863C]

**VERSE 2.**—“The Lord from heaven.” (Ibid.) But from this they are inexcusable, because the Lord looked forth, that is, he stood out from human nature. (AUG.) “From heaven,” that is, he looks forth through holy souls; for nothing is hidden from him in himself. Or, “from heaven,” through holy souls, which are heaven and the seat of God. Or, the Lord the Father is “from heaven,” that is, from the secrecy of the divine mind. (CAS.) Or, from the equality of God the Father.

“If there is one who understands.” Or: “He saw whether there is one who understands,” and found that no one understands, because no one seeks but turns aside; for: “All have turned aside,” etc.

**VERSE 3.**—“A tomb.” (Ibid.) Thus they have become useless to others, because their throat is a tomb, etc. [Col. 0863D]

“Tomb.” These three verses, extending to the second division—“Will they not know?”—are said not to be from the Hebrew, etc., up to “he does not have them.”

“Destruction.” (AUG.) Thus they have become useless to themselves, etc., up to “and unhappiness in the future.”

(CASS.) “The way of the impious,” etc., up to “the fear of God is not before their eyes.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Will they not know?” He threatens judgment to the wicked.

**VERSE 5.**—“They did not call upon the Lord,” etc. (AUG.) For they do not truly call upon him, since they love what displeases God. (CASS.) Their destruction is therefore increased, because it is necessary for them to do evil when, in their pride, they refuse to call upon God. Just as it is prudent to fear at the proper time, so it is cowardice to tremble foolishly, casting aside the fear of God because of people and circumstances. [Col. 0864A]

**VERSE 6.**—“The counsel of the poor.” (CASS.) An invective against the Jews, etc., up to “that is, proceeding from the Jews,” etc.

**VERSE 7.**—“Who will grant salvation from Zion,” etc. (CASS.) Finally, the conversion of the Jews is foretold, which will occur when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. “When he has turned away.” The Apostle also applies this testimony of Isaiah on behalf of the Jews: “He will come from Zion, the one who turns captivity—or impiety—away from Jacob.”

### PSALM 14

**VERSE 1.**—“Lord, who?” (CAS.) This psalm is properly instructional in morals and restrains presumption. It treats of the unity of the present Church and future rest. First the Prophet asks, as a priest standing before the face of the Lord, and requests an answer, wishing to know whom God judges worthy of his Church. [Col. 0864B]

**VERSE 2.**—“The one who.” (Ibid.) The Lord’s answer, etc., up to “so that Christ, the Lamb without the breaking of his limbs, properly entered the temple—not to be purified like the others, but without blemish.”

“He practices righteousness.” As when he drove the sellers and buyers from the temple.

**VERSE 3.**—“The one who speaks.” Here he explains more fully. Truth exists when a matter is as it is said. Christ did this in a particular way.

“In his heart.” He at times kept silent before unworthy people who sought fraudulently.

“He did not act deceitfully.” There is deceit on the tongue when one thing is said while another is in the breast. Or, “he did not act deceitfully,” because he made known to his neighbors—that is, his disciples—everything he had heard from the Father, without any addition or suppression; to the Jews, who were his neighbors according to the flesh. [Col. 0864C]

“He did no evil to his neighbor.” Rather, he prayed for them. He did not accept reproach against his neighbors, as is clear from the fact that he did not tear Judas apart with a biting rebuke.

**VERSE 4.**—“Reduced to nothing,” etc. (AUG.) This is perfection: that the evil one have no power over a person, and that he should be present in God’s sight—that is, should certainly know—that no one is evil except the one who turns from the Creator toward created things.

“The evil one,” that is, the devil, is despised, as when he said: “Get behind me, Satan,” etc.

Conversely, he glorifies those who fear the Lord.

“He swore,” when he promised the apostles with the most certain truth: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends.” [Col. 0864D]

**VERSE 5.**—“The one who swears to his neighbor,” etc. (Ibid.) These three things are not great, etc., up to “since in the preceding conclusion he used the past tense: ‘he has been reduced to nothing.’”

“Money.” Or it is earthly money, which is expressly forbidden to be lent at interest; the Lord handed this money over to Judas to distribute to the poor, not to lend at interest. Or it is spiritual money, which is commanded to be lent at interest, that is, preaching for the instruction of human beings.

“And he does not accept gifts against the innocent.” Christ does indeed receive gifts, as from the Magi and in daily pious offerings; but not against the innocent. Rather, he gave his soul for them.

“The one who does these things will not be moved.” Behold the complete answer to the one asking. He says “does,” so that he may invite us to action, not merely to singing these words. [Col. 0865A]

“The one who does these things will not be moved.” (CASS.) The conclusion: likewise, the one who does these things will rest on the mountain.

### PSALM 15

**VERSE 1.**—“The inscription of the title.” (CASS.) This title is taken from the Gospel, not from the Old Testament. What the title signifies—namely, victory and kingship—belongs to Christ, and this is what is treated here.

**VERSE 2.**—“Preserve,” etc. The second psalm, which briefly touches upon the Passion and resurrection. First, Christ, showing one human nature, asks to be preserved, saying that everything he endured was brought to the glory of his inheritance.

(AUG.) Christ speaks here according to his humanity, by which the royal title was prominent in the Passion: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.”

“Of my goods,” etc. (CASS.) If God does not need the goods of Christ as man but has everything from himself, human arrogance and the heresy of the Pelagians are destroyed—those who think that something can be accomplished by their own good powers. [Col. 0865B]

**VERSE 3.**—“To the saints who are in the land.” (Ibid.) Christ has already explained how he prayed; he now recounts what good things God did for him.

(AUG.) “To the saints,” etc., up to “and power so that I might rise again.”

“He has made wonderful.” (CASS.) As though he were saying: “I have said these things to the Lord.” But the Lord “has made wonderful,” that is, he has made wonderful wills. They are wonderful because, by obeying them, earthly people become heavenly.

**VERSE 4.**—“They have been multiplied.” (Ibid.) By which he made them wonderful, etc., up to “which harmonize in one sound and by which his wills are revealed.” [Col. 0865C]

**VERSE 5.**—“The portion of the inheritance.” (AUG.) Let others choose other things, etc., up to “but those who choose God as their portion.”

(CASS.) Or, “the Lord is the portion,” that is, the share and reward, “of my inheritance,” that is, of the saints. “And the portion of my cup,” that is, the reward of the Passion. The inheritance pertains to the nations, the cup to the Passion, which, when drunk, gives resurrection. But let no one consider himself an heir unless he is illustrious.

**VERSE 6.**—“The cords,” etc. As though by lot, in which there is divine election, so that the lot also fell upon Matthias, and each person receives according to his measure.

“In illustrious places.” That is, among the saints.

**VERSE 7.**—“I will bless the Lord.” (Ibid.) He gives thanks to the Father for understanding, for the Passion—in which, with the Father’s favor, he conquers—for the resurrection, and for confession. These are the means by which the inheritance is restored, so that he may be King of the Jews, as the title says. [Col. 0865D]

“Understanding,” etc. (AUG.) By which this inheritance can be seen and possessed.

“Moreover,” etc. That is, above understanding.

“Until the night,” etc. That is, death. My lower part, the assumption of flesh, instructed me so that it might drive out the darkness of mortality, which that understanding does not possess, since it could neither be troubled nor fail on their account.

“The kidneys.” From them I came forth according to the flesh, namely, from my ancestry; they reproached me with insults, temptation, and the Passion.

**VERSE 8.**—“I kept the Lord before me.” (Ibid.) Draw from this an example by which sins may be avoided. For the one who always beholds God with the sharpness of the mind is not bent toward sins. [Col. 0866A]

### PSALM 16

**VERSE 1.**—“A prayer of David.” (CASS.) The prayer suits the person of the Lord, with the Church joined to him, since she is his body.

“Hear, O Lord.” (Ibid.) This psalm directs attention to the true nature of humanity. Christ’s prayer is an instruction for the faithful. As, by weeping for Lazarus, he taught us to have love of neighbor, and as he fled from persecutors to remove from us the boldness of inconsiderate rashness, so here he first asks that he be repaid according to justice.

“Not with deceitful lips.” As one who is unjustly condemned; or, as one who says “Lord, Lord” but does not perform the works.

(AUG.) Or: “May my judgment not proceed from your face with deceitful lips,” so that, when judging, I may not utter anything other than what I understand. [Col. 0866B]

**VERSE 2.**—“From your face.” (CASS.) That is, according to what you know in me, since I have no sin.

“Judgment.” By which he may be seen to have issued judgment concerning himself.

“From your face,” not from the disposition of the Jews, as was made clear in the resurrection.

Or “judgment” by which he distinguishes all things.

**VERSE 3.**—“You have tested.” (CASS.) From the likeness of a furnace, etc., up to “you know that I am pure.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Difficult ways.” (Ibid.) Namely, the works of human beings—the ways deserved by human works. Or, the ways that human beings ought to imitate, since the path of vices is easy for them and that of virtues difficult.

Or, “it was not found,” so that he does not speak, that is, so that I may not say these things boastfully, or so that I may not sin with my tongue, which is a human work. [Col. 0866C]

(AUG.) Or, “difficult ways” are the ways of the thief, etc., up to “after I have traveled difficult ways and completed my steps.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Perfect.” (CASS.) Until the end; before the end there is only a beginning.

“Steps,” that is, human actions, so that those who wish to imitate them may not be moved away from you, or from their footprints.

**VERSE 6.**—“I cried out.” (Ibid.) Secondly, he prays that his purity may be freed from the ambushes of the Jews. “I also cried out,” as though you were saying: “This belongs only to the righteous person, who prays confidently because he knows that he is heard.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Make wonderful.” (AUG.) Wonderful are the things that are new. These are the things which, in the flesh, he did while the Jews marveled.

**VERSE 8.**—“The apple of the eye.” It is exceedingly small, yet through it the beam of light is directed, by which light and darkness are distinguished. So, through Christ’s humanity, divinity distinguishes between the good and the evil. [Col. 0866D]

**VERSE 10.**—“Fat.” (CASS.) From the likeness of animals, which are swollen with fat: that is, they retained pride; they were not lean, that is, not humble. Or “fat” means that they retained a carnal understanding; or, having been fattened by crimes, they lost true understanding. Hence it remains for them to speak proudly.

“Their mouth has spoken pride.” Not their heart, because the wicked often condemn in their heart what they defend with their mouth.

**VERSE 12.**—“They have received me,” etc. (Ibid.) From where did they obtain this opportunity? I answer: they received it from God, whose arrangement it is; or they received it eagerly from the betrayer or the judge.

“Like a lion prepared,” etc. (AUG., CASS.) The rulers are to be compared with the lion, the devil, by whose authority they act. “The people are a lion’s whelp,” that is, the devil’s son, dwelling and remaining in ambush, because it is customary for the wicked to conceal their desires so that they may fulfill them secretly. [Col. 0867A]

**VERSE 13.**—“Arise, O Lord.” (CASS.) A prayer concerning retribution.

“Go before,” etc. (Ibid.) From the likeness of one running: no one sins first against another rather than against himself.

“Trip him up.” From the likeness of one wrestling: render them ineffective and cast them down.

“Deliver my soul from the wicked.” (AUG.) By raising it from the death inflicted by the wicked.

“The sword.” My soul is the sword which your hand—that is, your power—has taken up, so that through it it may overthrow the kingdoms of iniquity and separate the righteous from the wicked.

“Divide them,” etc. (CASS.) That is, the divided Jews, etc., up to “misery, as though deservedly,” because “from the hidden things.”

“From your hidden things.” That is, from impurities, etc., up to “that is, they will share in evils unto satiety.” [Col. 0867B]

“From the hidden things.” (AUG.) Their visible punishment is not the only one; from the hidden things—that is, sins, which are hidden from the light of your truth—their memory is full, so that they forget God.

### PSALM 17

**VERSE 1.**—“I will love you, O Lord, my strength,” etc. (CASS.) Christ says this, as does the Church—that is, the whole Christ.

(Ibid.) First the Prophet, gathering the whole matter together, gives thanks for deliverance.

**VERSE 3.**—“Refuge.” (Ibid.) When counsel was needed, David fled to him and found refuge.

“Deliverer,” so that, being powerful, he may free a captive from enemies.

“Protector.” (AUG.) Because I did not presume upon myself, as though raising up the horn of pride against you; rather, I found in you the height of salvation, and in order that I might find it, you took me up. [Col. 0867C]

**VERSE 4.**—“Calling upon him, I will praise.” (CASS.) After everything, he does not boast, elated by himself, but attributes everything to God—and therefore he is saved. For whoever acts otherwise perishes when left to himself, even if he seemed to have won.

**VERSE 5.**—“They surrounded me.” (Ibid.) In the person of the righteous before Christ’s coming, etc., up to “who were disturbed by swift iniquities.”

**VERSE 6.**—“The pains of hell.” The Gentiles, who are to be tormented in hell with the pain they deserve.

“The snares of death anticipated me.” What follows is:

**VERSE 8.**—“It was shaken.” Behold how, etc., up to “and this was anticipated by mortality and weakness.” [Col. 0867D]

“From the temple.” (CASS.) Or from heaven, or from Christ’s future body.

“It was shaken.” (AUG.) Once Christ had been glorified, sinners were shaken and trembled in this way.

“The foundations,” etc. (CASS.) The presumptions of the proud, that is, riches and things of that kind on which they relied. For the hope of the world has passed away, and God hates it.

**VERSE 10.**—“The heavens.” (Ibid.) That is, he bent the preachers from contemplation toward ministry and toward bearing hardships.

“He descended,” etc. He himself suffered in them and became known to some.

“Darkness”: the dark ones, who also persecute, are under his power; or those who believe simply are subject to him. [Col. 0868A]

**VERSE 11.**—“And he ascended.” For he makes some full of knowledge, in whom he rises above all, and whose swiftness of understanding he surpasses. But he uses the dark ones secretly; hence: “The rod of my fury is Assyria,” yet he himself did not know, whereas his own people know.

“He flew upon the wings of the wind.” Winds, than which nothing is swifter, cannot surpass his fame; thus, as soon as he was born, he was announced by a star.

**VERSE 12.**—“Darkness.” (AUG.) The obscurities of the sacraments; or, in these darknesses, where we walk by faith and not by sight (Matt. 2).

“Not through the heavens.” (CASS.) He descended and ascended (2 Cor. 5), but through ethereal clouds, as it is in the Hebrew—that is, through the prophets, in whom there is obscure teaching. Yet he also came through clouds that are not ethereal—that is, through the Apostles, who are radiant in knowledge and contemplate him more closely. [Col. 0868B]

**VERSE 13.**—“Hail.” (AUG.) Reproaches that strike hard hearts. But if the fire of charity melts them, in a gentle soul it becomes water that satisfies—or, according to another reading, water that springs up.

“And coals,” because by that fire dark hearts, once kindled, revive.

**VERSE 14.**—“He thundered.” (CASS.) Literally, when thunder was seen, God saying: “I have glorified, and I will glorify again.”

“He gave his voice,” as when he said: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And he sent.” (Ibid.) The Lord thundered, and the Lord sent. For the transition to the Gentiles was not always certain or rationally understood. [Col. 0868C]

**VERSE 16.**—“And the springs appeared.” When Christ came, what the obscurity of the divine word had concealed became clear.

“From rebuke.” Conversion to God, as though with thanksgiving, because through preaching he rebuked sinners and inspired them to fear future wrath.

“He sent.” (Ibid.) Up to this point he has spoken of the Lord’s coming; from here he speaks of Christian times.

“The Father sent Christ.”

“He received me.” The bride, the Church.

“From the waters.” (Ibid.) Of baptism.

Or he sent the Spirit, who is the gift.

“From on high,” because he is equal to the Father and the Son.

“He received,” as though a fugitive.

“He took up,” into the height of virtue and good works.

**VERSE 18.**—“From my enemies.” (AUG.) That is, from vices, which harm more than all enemies.

“And from those who,” etc. That is, from external enemies—human beings and demons—who have been strengthened in a certain respect.

“Behold, they anticipated me,” that is, they prevailed over me.

Through this he delivers all the more, because they have been strengthened. For when the Church is afflicted, she grows more greatly. [Col. 0868D]

**VERSE 20.**—“Into a broad place.” (Ibid.) Through the ferocity of the wicked, the Church grows in number and merit.

“He saved me,” that is, he brought me to the faith.

“Because he desired me.” (AUG.) That is, he chose me freely.

**VERSE 21.**—“And he will repay according to the justice of a good will, and according to the purity of my hands.” (Ibid.) These works follow God’s first gifts, namely faith and charity, which God freely grants without preceding merit.

**VERSE 22.**—“Because I have kept.” (Ibid.) Or it may be joined continuously with the preceding verse, etc., up to “and as I began, I will remain undefiled,” from which it follows that he will repay in the future. [Col. 0869A]

**VERSE 24.**—“With him,” adhering to him; “to him,” adhering to him.

“And I will keep watch,” so that I may not fall again.

“From iniquity,” which is the death of the blessed person.

**VERSE 25.**—“And he will repay.” (CASS.) God repays in two ways: in the present, so that the righteous person may be justified and the one who is in filth may become still filthier. Hence he says here: “With the holy you will be holy,” etc. And in the future he gives reward to the good and punishment to the wicked. Hence there: “For you will save the humble people,” as though saying: “So also here, because in the future you will save the humble people.”

(AUG.) “And he will repay”: now he will repay me not only because of the breadth of faith that works through love, but because of long-suffering.

“In his sight.” This belongs to the righteous: just as they always gaze upon God, so God continually regards them. [Col. 0869B]

**VERSE 26.**—“With the holy.” (CASS.) He had said, “I will be repaid according to justice,” etc., up to “because you, O Lord, will save the humble people.”

“And you will humble the eyes of the proud.”

(AUG.) There is also a hidden depth by which you are understood as “holy with the holy,” because you sanctify.

“For you will enlighten.” What he declared concerning the elect and sanctified, he now prays concerning others.

**VERSE 29.**—“A lamp.” (Ibid.) There were preachers in whom there was light, that is, knowledge of the truth, by which they enlightened others; hence: “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” “Darknesses.” (AUG.) Those who are still in darkness. “My darknesses.” By predestination.

[Col. 0869C] **VERSE 30.**—“In my God.” (CASS.) For my God is the undefiled way by which one travels to heaven. Or, the way by which the holy and immaculate Virgin came into the world. Whatever he said was examined by the Holy Spirit, that is, useful and honorable: a wise man judges whatever he says beforehand within himself. “I will pass over.” (Ibid.) A person cannot demolish the wall completely, but by God’s help he passes through the wall, the obstacle of sins.

**VERSE 31.**—“My God.” (Ibid.) Continuing, it follows: “You will rescue me from the contradictions of the people.” He inserts the rest in order to commend him. “Sayings.” They are tested by the fire of examination. “Of all.” (Ibid.) No one is excluded except the one who does not wish to hope.

**VERSE 32.**—“For who is there?” (Ibid.) “I say God,” because who is another God except the one who is also Lord over created things? And because he was known in Judea, not the gods of the nations: this is directed against the pagans, who invent many gods for themselves.

**VERSE 33.**—“The God who.” (Ibid.) In addition to the common benefits, he commends him through particular ones, because Christ is commended for the third time on account of his virtue and power. “He girded.” (Ibid.) That is, he armed himself completely. Or from the likeness of a runner. Or it indicates dignity and strength, which befit the one who by his power will judge the people, or the world. “Immaculate,” without sin. The stag leaps over thorns and gaping places; so Christ leaps over the thorns and pits of sins. And as the stag climbs high places, so Christ ascends above all creatures.

**VERSE 35.**—“Who teaches”: I make him cautious against impending ambushes. “Hands,” works or desires. “For battle,” [Col. 0870A] against the devil. “So that the bow,” etc., by the likeness of a thing that is not [literally present], that is, invincible strength. “Arms.” Christ’s prophets and apostles, through whom he works; they are a bronze bow because in preaching they do not grow soft but, always strong, shoot forth words of salvation.

**VERSE 36.**—“The protection of salvation.” Not so that I suffer nothing—for suffering nevertheless serves progress. Tribulation is correction, instruction, expansion, and strengthening.

**VERSE 37.**—“You have enlarged.” (AUG.) So that carnal constrictions may not impede me, because you have made charity broad and active with joy, even concerning what is beneath me, namely, mortal things and bodily members.

**VERSE 38.**—“I will pursue.” (CASS.) By reproving and wearing them down through various afflictions.

**VERSE 43.**—“And I will crush.” (AUG.) Behold the same operation of the Father and the Son. Above he says, “You destroyed,” addressing the Father; now he says, “I will crush,” that is, “I will remove the powers,” so that afterward they may yield to every wind of doctrine.

**VERSE 44.**—“You will rescue.” (CASS.) From them there is anger; but “you will rescue me”: the depression of the Jews and the exaltation of the nations.

**VERSE 46.**—“Sons.” The Jews whom I nourished became strangers. “They lied to me,” for my honor. “They grew old and limped from their paths,” following their own traditions rather than God.

**VERSE 47.**—“He lives.” (Ibid.) For the fourth time the Church, rejoicing, praises God’s gifts in summary. Or, “he lives” because he gives life. “Blessed,” because he blesses all things. “And let the God of my salvation be exalted.” (AUG.) I will not think of the God of my salvation in an earthly manner, nor of salvation itself as earthly, [Col. 0870C] but I will hope in him on high.

**VERSE 48.**—“Vengeances.” (CASS.) A pious vengeance, when the rebel is subjected. “From the wrathful.” It is a greater glory to free someone from evils that burn fiercely.

**VERSE 51.**—“Magnifying, salvations.” God who magnifies; “making,” God who makes.

# PSALM XVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“For the end.” (CASS.) A psalm concerning the first advent, through which the tyrant falls and the human being is absolved. Here the prophet looks toward the end, that is, Christ, or toward the final times.

**VERSE 2.**—“The heavens declare.” (Ibid.) First, speaking about the incarnation, he commends the preaching of the new law. (AUG.) “The heavens”: the apostles, concerning the glory of Christ, in which he is equal to the Father. (CASS.) Or “the heavens,” which sent the star. “His glory.” (Ibid.) That God freely forgives sins. “His works.” (AUG.) Those which are according to the human nature, etc., up to “and they themselves became night to those in darkness concerning knowledge of human things.” (CASS.) And this happened so wondrously that it was in all languages, and so extensively that it reached every part of the earth’s circumference.

**VERSE 3.**—“Day unto day.” (CASS.) He acts demonstratively. (AUG.) “Day unto day”: the Spirit brings forth the fullness of wisdom for spiritual people, etc., up to “this teaching is continued through days and nights down to later generations.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Their speech.” (CASS.) Public exhortations. “Their words.” Common narratives. “Of whom there are not.” He would express it more plainly as “in whom their voices are not heard,” or “the voices of all their words are heard”; the relative pronoun produces the same meaning.

(AUG.) The Spirit made the first speak in all languages—the one who was going to gather all nations into one. At that time there was one man for all; so now there is one Christ, head and body.

**VERSE 6.**—“In the sun.” (CASS.) What he praises others for doing, he himself does: he proclaims the incarnation. Or “in the sun,” in the world’s manifestation, or in labor. The sun burns, shines, and changes the seasons. “His tent.” (AUG.) As a military dwelling, that is, the dispensation of his incarnation, in which he came to conquer the world’s errors. Or “tent,” the Church, openly and not secretly, so that it might not remain hidden. “Bridegroom.” (CASS.) Promised so often by the prophets; a great likeness of the mystery. Therefore he was born of a virgin, so that he might join to himself a virgin Church. “From the bridal chamber.” (AUG.) That is, from the virgin womb, where God was joined to human nature as a bridegroom to a bride. Behold humble mercy, but mighty in majesty. “A giant to run.” (CASS.) Undisturbed and irrevocable, surpassing human nature by his power. “From the highest.” Here the Trinity is shown, etc., up to “he indicates the unity of the Trinity.” “And there is no one who can hide himself,” etc. (AUG.) The Word made flesh did not allow anyone to excuse himself on account of the shadow of death, because the heat of the Word penetrated even that. Or, the heat is the Spirit whom he sent after returning; he is the law, testimony, justice, commandment, fear, and judgments, because he accomplishes these things.

**VERSE 8.**—“The law of the Lord.” (CAS.) Second, he praises the commandments of the New and Old Testament. (Ibid.) The law given through Moses, correcting all its words through their arrangement and sending them toward Christ’s grace. “Converting.” (AUG.) With freedom, toward imitating him, not pressing down under the yoke of servitude. “Souls.” Wills, not merely hands, as in the Old Testament. “Testimony.” All the testimonies given to Israel are full of truth and have given wisdom to the humble. “Wisdom,” concerning divine things.

**VERSE 9.**—“The justices of the Lord.” (Ibid.) All things in him are rightly ordered, since he did not teach what he did not do, so that those who imitated him might rejoice in them and freely perform them with charity, not slavishly with fear. (CASS.) “Justices”: the law that justifies; whatever it commands is just.

**VERSE 10.**—“The fear of the Lord.” (Ibid.) The fear of the world is not holy, because it is not beneficial and changes with the times. The fear of the Lord is without all disturbance [Col. 0871D] because it is love mixed with awe: if one fears the judge, one knows him to be merciful. (AUG.) Fear—not the penal fear by which the soul is afraid for earthly things because it loves them, but chaste fear, by which the more one loves, the more one takes care not to offend the bridegroom. Therefore it is not cast out but remains. “Judgments.” God’s judgments do not need the authority of another.

**VERSE 11.**—“Desirable.” (Ibid.) Either, greatly desirable; or, “much gold and precious stone”; or, very precious. “More desirable than gold,” etc., up to “whose will he places before his own, and they are sweeter to him than he himself is to himself.” “Above gold,” that is, everything sought for wealth, power, or pleasure. “Honey.” Honey is God’s food, that is, the one already released from the world; and the honeycomb, that is, the one still wrapped about, which requires the pressure of the hand that squeezes it—God’s hand—so that it may enter into life.

**VERSE 13.**—“Who understands offenses?” (Ibid.) Third, he asks to be cleansed from vices, so that he may be a worthy Psalmist to report these mysteries. Truth is sweet to the mind that sees, and judgments are sweet; but what sweetness is there for one who does not see? Why, then, is it not seen? Because of offenses. And no wonder: “For who understands offenses?” (CASS.) “Offenses”: all of them, for some are known. “Mine” defile me; “others’” afflict me; and now spare me—drive away the tempter. “From hidden things.” He includes all sins under two categories, etc., up to “by which the human being was deceived and, by consenting, made it his own.” (AUG.) There is no greater offense than apostatizing from God, which is the beginning of pride; but pride is the beginning and cause of every sin.

# PSALM XIX

[Col. 0872B]

“For the end.” (CASS.) The prophet sings, in a figure of what is to be accomplished, the things that are to come.

(Ibid.) The prophet, out of excessive charity, wishes prosperity for the Church, which he saw was to come through Christ.

**VERSE 2.**—“May he hear”: what he wishes to happen for it in the time of tribulation. “In the day of tribulation,” when we pray to God with greater longing. “Of the God of Jacob”: so that, as he gave him the grace of blessing, he may give it to you also, and place you before the Jews.

**VERSE 3.**—“May he send”: the Father. “Help,” by sending the Son.

**VERSE 4.**—“Remember.” He speaks as though of a priest about to sacrifice and a king about to fight. “Sacrifice.” (Ibid.) He foresaw the sacrifice of the Church, not of animals, but of Christ’s blood and body.

**VERSE 5.**—“May he grant.” The *diapsalma*, which in the time of glory both wishes and affirms. “All.” (AUG.) Not only the one by which you laid down your soul for the life of many, but also the one by which blindness came upon Israel in part, so that in this way all Israel might be saved.

**VERSE 6.**—“We will rejoice.” (Ibid.) This prayer is offered because “we will rejoice and be magnified”; he shows that he is one of the Church from so long before.

**VERSE 7.**—“In powers.” (AUG.) Our powers are the salvation of his favor, when he also gives help from tribulation, because human salvation is vain and is on the left; hence pride also arises. “The salvation of the right hand.” [Col. 0872D] (Ibid.) That is, spiritual grace, etc., up to “those who preside in earthly dignity.”

# PSALM XX

**VERSE 1.**—“For the end.” The third psalm concerning the two natures in Christ. It describes the heavenly king, so that the world may believe through hearing the one whom the Jew despises when seen. He makes a demonstrative prayer in praise of God.

**VERSE 2.**—“Lord, the king will rejoice in your strength.” (CASS.) He sets forth the whole matter, namely, merit and reward.

**VERSE 4.**—“For you anticipated.” (CASS.) The *diapsalma*; he describes his virtues and glory, etc., up to “as though for the head into a crown.” “A crown.” (Ibid.) Because the circle of the apostles surrounded the teacher, or the whole circle of the world, that is, the universal Church.

**VERSE 6.**—“In your salvation: glory and great beauty,” etc. (CASS.) By the Father’s Word—what glory comes from it? Glory from judgment, because he will judge in his divinity. Beauty in majesty, which will then appear. “Glory and great beauty,” etc. He is glorious, like Peter, whose shadow healed the sick; and beauty is upon him, besides whom there is no other foundation. Therefore upon him, because you will give . . . .

**VERSE 7.**—“In joy with your face.” “For the king hopes in the Lord, and in his mercy,” etc. (Ibid.) That is, because his own people will rejoice in your presence, when you will be all in all.

**VERSE 9.**—“Let your hand be found,” etc. (Ibid.) Concerning the punishments of enemies, just as above concerning Christ’s praises.

**VERSE 11.**—“You will destroy their fruit from the earth, and their seed.” They will have no fruit of blessedness in the land of the living.

**VERSE 13.**—“For you will set.” (CASS.) What was said concerning the future, etc., up to “so that, when they thought they were killing him, salvation might be brought about.”

**VERSE 14.**—“Be exalted.” (Ibid.) The conclusion.

# PSALM XXI

**VERSE 2.**—“God, my God.” (CASS.) A complaint about abandonment is placed first, as well as a prayer, as in all psalms concerning the Passion. (AUG., CASS.) “God, my God”: he repeats it from feeling, or “God” of all through the power of creation, “my” God specifically through worship. (AUG.) When he said this on the cross, he indicated that this psalm had been written about him. “Look upon me.” (CASS.) This is not in the Hebrew but was added by the Seventy translators. “Why have you abandoned me?” (AUG.) This is astonishing, since God was also with him; but he said it for us, who are his body in him. “Far from my salvation,” that is, from the salvation of my old self, because salvation is far from sinners; and these are words not of righteousness but of sins. Or, “the words of my offenses are far from salvation,” since those offenses must be removed.

**VERSE 3.**—“I will cry out.” (AUG.) He speaks concerning us, his body, so that when he says, “Let this cup pass from me,” he may be thought to have feared death; but he said this on behalf of his weak members who fear dying. So also this voice belongs to the members: “I will cry out, and you will not hear.” “By day, and you will not hear; and by night, and not for folly.” (CASS.) Because there were no darknesses in him, yet he was not heard with respect to bodily salvation.

**VERSE 4.**—“You dwell in the holy place.” (AUG.) And so it is astonishing, because you delivered the fathers, whereas I am a worm.

(CASS.) You dwell in the holy place because God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself. “The praise of Israel.” (AUG.) That is, of the one who sees you, not of the one who wished to hide himself from your sight.

**VERSE 5.**—“In you our fathers hoped; they hoped.” (CASS.) Great beauty is shown when “they hoped” is repeated.

[Col. 0874A] **VERSE 7.**—“But I,” etc. (AUG.) Up to this point Christ speaks in the person of the old human being; here he speaks properly in his own person. “But I”: now properly Christ. I was born without seed, so that I might be beyond human beings in the man in whom I was made an object of reproach, so that human pride might at least in this way imitate humility. “A worm and not a man, a reproach.” (CASS.) Thus he was trampled down with such contempt, etc., up to “worm”: born without intercourse, mortal, humble, and lowly, creeping in silence.

**VERSE 9.**—“He hoped in the Lord,” etc. (CASS.) They say: “Hope in the Lord,” etc. This is the irony of the Jews. Behold, it appears as a historical narration, not a prophecy, so that there may be no excuse and no ambiguity.

**VERSE 10.**—“From the breasts.” Not “from the time when I began to be nursed,” [Col. 0874B] etc., up to “but you were my God.” “From the womb.”

**VERSE 11.**—“From the womb.” (AUG.) Not only from the mother’s womb, which is the law of birth for all, but from the darkness of the synagogue, in which he is unbelieving, not yet born into the light of Christ, who trusts in those carnal observances of Sabbath and circumcision.

**VERSE 12.**—“Do not depart from me,” you who have already begun.

“You drew me out”: not a man, so that there might be no doubt about the virgin birth; it was accomplished by God’s power. “My hope from the breasts”: true humanity and great perfection; from the breasts he does what one scarcely mature does.

“Upon you I was cast,” not into human sins. Others are cast into Adam, from whom they are guilty. “From the womb of my mother, my God.” (CASS.) Neither conception was without God, nor was it in sin, as it is for a human being; hence the angel says: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you.”

**VERSE 13.**—“They surrounded.” (Ibid.) The Passion is described, which prayer brings to an end. To convict the Jews, he reports future things as though they were past.

**VERSE 14.**—“They opened.” (Ibid.) Like wild beasts wishing to devour, they opened their mouths—not opened toward wisdom. “Like a lion.” (AUG.) They surrounded him like a seizing lion and opened their mouths like a roaring lion.

**VERSE 15.**—“Like water.” When water is poured out, etc., up to “therefore, after abandoning him, they fled.” (CASS.) “Like water”: the mystery of water is the washing away of sins, etc., up to “and it was made solid.” “Like wax.” He aptly compares the mysteries of the law to wax, etc., up to “because they surrounded me.” “In the midst of my belly.” (AUG.) The belly signifies the weak within the Church, or the Church’s memory.

**VERSE 16.**—“My strength dried up like a potsherd.” (CASS.) Not like grass, but like a potsherd, which becomes firmer through fire. “My tongue.” (AUG.) These people, through whom I was going to speak, kept my commandments within themselves; and through them I was led into kinship with those who were the dust of death.

**VERSE 17.**—“They pierced.” (Ibid.) The Gospel narrative. Although these things are literal, the piercing of the hands suggests that they did not believe his works, and the piercing of the feet that they mangled the apostles. (CASS.) “They pierced.” Plowed earth produces fruit; so Christ, wounded, gave the fruit of life.

[Col. 0875A] **VERSE 18.**—“They counted all my bones.” (CASS.) The punishment of the cross is specifically described.
