Thus they counted the bones, that is, the apostles; they sought to destroy them so that their number would not increase. “They looked upon me.” (Ibid.) With attention and pleasure, although eyes ordinarily turn away from a cruel sight. Behold how obstinate they were: nothing happened by chance, nor were their hearts softened by so many miracles.

**VERSE 19.**—“They divided my garments among themselves,” etc. (AUG.) They were able to divide his mysteries through heresies, but not the tunic from above, that is, given by God; this is charity or unity, which no one can divide. (CASS.) But perhaps it also came to certain people as a gift of God, etc., up to “as an olive branch carried by a dove to the ark.” (AUG.) Or, through one soul, head and body, which rejects divisions.

**VERSE 22.**—“Of unicorns, my humility,” etc. (Ibid.) The Jews, seeking only earthly things; or boasting that they alone worship God; or being uniquely proud, having killed the son after the servants.

**VERSE 24.**—“You who fear the Lord, praise him,” etc. (CASS.) Human fear produces not praise but blame.

**VERSE 25.**—“Let all the seed of Israel fear him, because he did not despise,” etc. He makes clear whom he called the seed of Jacob by adding: “Of the poor.” (AUG.) Not of the one who cries out with words of offenses from a vain life, but of the one who does not swell with the pomp of the world.

**VERSE 26.**—“My praise is with you in the great Church,” etc. (Ibid.) He places praise with God, who teaches that one must not presume upon the human being.

**VERSE 27.**—“Those who seek him will praise the Lord; they will live.” (Ibid.) The poor make God their riches. They are poor for this reason: they praise God in order to seek him, and he himself is the wealth of the poor. “Their hearts will remember throughout the age of the age and will turn to the Lord.” (Ibid.) Because he is food for the heart.

**VERSE 30.**—“They ate and worshiped.” (Ibid.) Let the steward not prevent them from eating, but let him warn the exactor to fear. “In his sight they will fall.” (CASS.) The Church receives both groups, but he himself sees and distinguishes them.

[Col. 0875D] **VERSE 32.**—“It will be announced,” etc. (Ibid.) To the angels who offer human prayers to God—not for their instruction, but for their ministry.

(CASS.) Note that psalms concerning the Passion end in the great hope of Christians, so that it may be known that salvation comes from the Passion.

# PSALM XXII

**VERSE 1.**—“A psalm of David.” (CASS.) The prophet foretold the people’s return from Babylon. “The Lord governs me.” A psalm of mercy, enumerating ten graces, so that all may hope in God’s mercy. (AUG.) The Church speaks concerning Christ.

**VERSE 2.**—“In a place of pasture.” (CASS.) The first grace: a place of pasture, that is, the divine word, which fattens those who meditate. [Col. 0876A] “Beside water.” The second grace: water of refreshment.

**VERSE 3.**—“My soul.” (Ibid.) The third grace, etc., up to “but first he led it out beside the water of refreshment; before that he converted my soul.” “He led.” (Ibid.) The fourth grace: that he led it above the commandments of charity. “Upon paths.” (AUG.) More demanding commandments and more perfect counsels; the few righteous walk as though on paths, since paths are narrower than roads.

**VERSE 4.**—“For even if.” (CASS.) The fifth grace: that he does not fear evils in the shadow of death. “You are with me.” (AUG.) In the heart through faith, so that after the shadow of death I may be with you. “Your rod.” (CASS.) The sixth grace: correction; or the rod is discipline, which converts vices. The staff is governance, which supports the faithful.

[Col. 0876B] **VERSE 5.**—“You have prepared in my sight.” (CASS.) The seventh grace: the Lord’s table, the blessed banquet, the fullness of faith, the heavenly food, concerning which the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” “A table in my sight,” even if not in the sight of the impious. Concerning this it is said: “But these people are at the table of the rich man,” that is, of Christ; know that you too must prepare similar things, that is, suffer as he did. “You have made fat”: the eighth grace, the anointing of the head, namely Christ, which has not withered through any dryness of sin. Hence the other members rejoice, because the ointment descends from the head into Aaron’s beard and to the hem of his garment. “And my cup.” The ninth grace: the cup, Christ’s blood, which intoxicates in such a way that it makes people sober. “My,” because I receive it; or “your,” because you give it. The table and the cup—the flesh and blood—although they are one sacrament, are nevertheless placed here separately under different forms, because both are received separately.

**VERSE 6.**—“And mercy.” (CASS.) The tenth grace: mercy following after the protection that precedes in order to confer grace.

**VERSE 7.**—“And that I may dwell.” (HIER.) This is joined to all the preceding statements. As if he had said: You placed me, led me out, guided me, etc., and you did this so that I might dwell.

# PSALM XXIII

**VERSE 1.**—“A psalm of David.” (AUG.) On the first day of the week the world was created; on that same day humanity was restored through Christ’s resurrection. (CASS.) Therefore he urges the victor to be received with triumph. “The earth belongs to the Lord.” First he says that the whole world belongs to God, etc., up to [Col. 0876D] “but who is on his mountain except the innocent?”

**VERSE 2.**—“And above the rivers.” (AUG.) As rivers flow into the sea, so the greedy flow into the age; and the Church also rises above them, prepared for immortality after conquering desires.

**VERSE 3.**—“Who will ascend?” He determines by what virtues those who are in the Church are endowed.

**VERSE 4.**—“Who will stand?” (HIER.) For many ascend who do not remain. (Ibid.) “Innocent”: toward his neighbor, in hand and heart; and one who is innocent toward himself, etc., up to “they desire presence and knowledge.” “Who has not received.” (AUG., HIER.) That is, one who has not assigned his soul to things that do not endure, but, recognizing it as immortal, will desire eternal things; and therefore he has not sworn deceitfully. “In vanity.” (HIER.) That is, one who has not stained it after baptism with any filth of sins.

**VERSE 7.**—“Lift up.” The *diapsalma*. After the Christian religion has been declared, etc., up to “which were set up by the prince, the devil.” “And be lifted up.” Against the gates of death. “Everlasting gates”: every grace that was given when Christ came.

**VERSE 8.**—“Who is this?” He asks. The prophet does this to convict the Jews’ faithlessness and, by commending him more fully, to invite others.

**VERSE 10.**—“The Lord of virtues” is described as strong, as though by a proper name. “Strong.” (AUG.) Even though you seized him with swords.

“Powerful,” even though you handed him over to Pilate.

[Col. 0877B] “Powerful in battle,” so that you may not think you overcame him in combat. “Virtues.” (HIER., AUG.) The ministering powers that precede Christ in his ascension cry out to the other heavenly powers to open the way for the coming Lord. Astonished by the new mystery of one clothed in flesh, they ask: “Who is this?”

“Lift up.” (CASS.) The repetition, etc., up to “who gives all good things to all,” or [it refers to] the heavenly powers, that is, the angels.

# PSALM XXIV

**VERSE 1.**—“For the end.” (HIER.) Here the scourged penitent is placed before others, so that they may not murmur in adversity. Having experienced mercy in himself, he offers consolation; through justice, he inspires fear.

[Col. 0877C] “To you, Lord, I lifted up.” (AUG.) A psalm against the adversities of the world, etc., up to “who not through all, the less perfect.”

(CASS.) First he asks to be taught the Lord’s ways, because he is raised up toward God.

(Ibid.) For contemplating you; the one who sees divine things easily despises earthly things.

**VERSE 2.**—“I trust.” (Ibid.) Having experienced my weakness in evils, I will not be ashamed before enemies.

“Let my enemies not mock me”: I am certain that one who patiently endures is deceived in nothing.

“Without cause.” (Ibid.) Because all things that are alienated from God are vain and fruitless.

“Show me your ways, Lord.” (CASS.) The ways concern the order of life, etc., up to: “Direct” pertains to life; “teach” to knowledge.

**VERSE 5.**—“Teach.” (AUG.) The truth itself, so that I may understand what I believe, since I have endured; and if this is not enough: “Remember.”

“God my savior.” (CASS.) Two things make people good: that we believe God to be our savior and that we patiently await his retribution.

**VERSE 6.**—“Remember.” (Ibid.) He prays concerning former sins and those committed daily, appealing to the mercy shown in ancient times, and because he fears the true judge.

“Mercies.” Mercy properly consists in the display of good things.

“Which are from the age.” (AUG.) That is, from the beginning of the age; therefore let him not deceive me.

[Col. 0878A] **VERSE 7.**—“Offenses.” (CASS.) They occur whenever the way of equity is abandoned.

“Of youth.” Not with reference to age, but to the rash boldness that occurs when the heat of the spirit exceeds moderation.

“Ignorances.” We do things that we do not know are evil. Or, sins of ignorance in little ones, who are held either by original sin.

(HIER.) “Of youth.” Before I left the house of my wicked father.

“Remember me, you.” (AUG.) It is your work to show mercy and forgive sins.

“According to mercy.” That is, your mercy is abundant. Mercy is shown toward the miserable; goodness toward anyone. God does good both when implored by the miserable and when moved by goodness; no one is good except God.

**VERSE 8.**—“Sweet.” (Ibid.) Because he forgives all the former things, where grace exists without merits.

“Upright.” Because after mercy, etc., up to: “Sweet,” because he gives pleasant things; “upright,” because he corrects.

“For this reason.” (CASS.) Because he is sweet and upright—not out of cruelty but out of kindness.

“On the way.” That is, in faith or in God’s commandments. Or, on the way of this life, where one must live rightly, he will give the law.

**VERSE 9.**—“In judgment.” While punishing, he will direct toward better things. But let those who are corrected be gentle—tamed from wildness so that they may endure. For if they are mild, that is, gentle in spirit, as though possessing this naturally, he will teach them the commandments, on account of whose neglect the scourges came.

**VERSE 10.**—“Mercy and truth.” (AUG.) But what ways will he teach, etc., up to “and afterward he takes care to avoid the judge’s severity.”

“Covenant.” (CASS.) The New Covenant, which is excellently called a Testament, where there is a clear and certain promise of inheritance, and which is also confirmed by death.

“And Testament.” Of the old law, where there were prophets as witnesses to the promises.

**VERSE 11.**—“For the sake of your name, Lord.” (AUG.) That is, your glory, etc., up to “and interpret ‘pure’ as those who assert that they are pure from every sin.”

**VERSE 12.**—“Who is the human being?” (CASS.) Here he deals with eternal things: how they are obtained, laboring and praying that both he himself and all Israel may be freed from these evils.

**VERSE 13.**—“His soul.” (Ibid.) Even if not immediately, etc., up to “whatever others may do,” etc.

“Seed.” (HIER.) It is good, from which fruit is gathered.

“It is a firmament.” (AUG.) Fear appears to belong to the weak, but the Lord is a firmament for those who fear him, and he makes his covenant manifest to them.

“Eyes.” (Solomon.) “The eyes of the wise are in his head,” that is, in his heart.

**VERSE 16.**—“Alone.” (Ibid.) The only child is loved more; the poor person is grieved over more.

**VERSE 17.**—“From necessities.” That is, from adversities, [Col. 0879A] which are necessary for all who wish to live devoutly in Christ.

**VERSE 19.**—“Look upon.” (AUG.) The destruction of so many people cannot exist without grief, and therefore he prays for them.

**VERSE 21.**—“The innocent and upright adhered.” (Ibid.) The wicked were tolerated; they did not adhere.

**VERSE 22.**—“Israel.” (AUG.) The people whom you prepared for the vision of yourself.

# PSALM XXV

**VERSE 1.**—“A psalm.” (CASS.) This psalm advises avoiding the company of the wicked and joining the righteous, because character is formed through association.

“Judge.” (AUG.) Because after mercy, etc., up to “they are carried away by the wind of pride.”

[Col. 0879B] (CASS.) “Judge”: this is not the presumption of the righteous but certainty concerning God’s mercy, which he shows there by hoping in the Lord; then he says, “I will not be weakened.”

“In innocence.” (AUG.) Not the innocence of angels, but the kind found in human beings.

**VERSE 2.**—“Test me.” (CASS.) That is, first examine my strength, etc., up to “I look not to merits but to the mercy that made me such.”

(CASS.) “Test me.” You, however, test me in temptations, so that no offense may remain, etc., up to “so that no one may complain about them.”

“Burn my kidneys.” (Ibid.) With the fire of your word, the heart with the warmth of the Spirit. The heart signifies thoughts; the kidneys, desires.

**VERSE 3.**—“Mercy.” (CASS.) It does not allow one to be tempted beyond one’s strength; or the burning itself is mercy, not harshness.

“I have pleased in truth.” (AUG.) The person to whom his own lie is displeasing, and who pleases himself with truth and in truth.

**VERSE 4.**—“I did not sit.” (CASS.) “I have pleased in truth,” because I did not sit [with them]. “I hated,” which means avoiding evils. “And I will wash,” which means doing what is right.

“Vain.” (CASS.) The vain are those who labor over perishable things; the impious are heretics who pervert the Scriptures. The former seek superfluities; the latter, poison.

**VERSE 5.**—“Of the malicious.” (Ibid.) Those who do evil to their neighbors.

**VERSE 6.**—“I will wash.” (AUG.) By repenting. “And the altar”: I will adorn the mind with virtues, or faith, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church.

[Col. 0879D] “Among the innocent.” (AUG.) Dwelling among them, so that I may hear from them, that is, learn with what voice you are to be praised; or so that I may hear: “Come, blessed of my Father.”

**VERSE 7.**—“The voice of praise”: the Holy Spirit, who teaches one to praise you.

**VERSE 8.**—“Lord.” (CASS.) He asks not to be mixed with the wicked in judgment, because he does not agree with them but with the house of God.

“I loved the beauty.” (CASS.) I will do these things because I have loved making a beautiful house for you and a place where you may dwell gloriously, so that I may receive something of God’s glory and essence.

**VERSE 9.**—“Do not destroy.” (CASS.) Even if you now allow them to be together, do not destroy them together.

[Col. 0880A] (CASS.) Do not destroy me in the future with the impious, with whom I do not share life here.

**VERSE 10.**—“Their right hand.” (AUG.) That is, if they do anything good, etc., up to “may mercy accompany everything,” which you owe because:

**VERSE 12.**—“The foot,” that is, affection, which is accustomed to slip easily, stood immovable against all scandals, reaching beyond them and persisting in the straight path. And because you thus redeem in the churches, I will bless you.

“It stood.” (CASS.) Although shaken on every side or confused by scandals.

# PSALM XXVI

**VERSE 1.**—“For the end.” (AUG., CASS.) First, David is chosen, etc., up to “hence he groans and labors in the mystery, so that he may rejoice in reality.”

[Col. 0880B] “The Lord is my illumination,” etc. (CASS.) He speaks of the first anointing, through which the second is guaranteed.

“The Lord is the protector of my life.” (AUG.) He gives the life of virtues and also protects it; without him all his gifts are lost.

“Whom shall I fear?” (Ibid.) Whom should the flesh fear when it has put on incorruption?

**VERSE 2.**—“The malicious came upon me.” (Ibid.) So that, insulting, they might set themselves above me. God turns this to the better, so that with a slanderous tooth they consume not me but carnal desires. Or, “let them eat,” that is, let the cruelty of the enemies take pleasure in my death; they may consume the flesh, but they cannot consume the soul.

“They were weakened.” (Ibid.) When Christ took flesh, they became unstable, and afterward submitted themselves entirely to the faith.

[Col. 0880C] (CASS.) Or, gradually weakened, they reached the ruin of the soul.

**VERSE 3.**—“Camps.” (CASS.) Efforts, battle, conflict.

“In this I.” (AUG.) I have the hope of victory in the Lord’s eternal reward.

**VERSE 4.**—“One thing I asked.” (AUG.) This one house is eternal, in which one always remains, where the days are eternal. Why there? So that I may contemplate the delight of God, which is the true good.

“All the days of my life.” (AUG.) So that as long as I live, etc., up to “I will make the work manifest.”

“That I may see.” (Ibid.) Another text has: “That I may contemplate the delight of the Lord,” that is, with the aim that at last it may appear, [Col. 0880D] etc., up to “and therefore I do not rashly ask for one thing, even though I am a sinner.”

**VERSE 5.**—“In a hidden place.” (AUG.) As though there were many parts, etc., up to “whom he immediately calls the rock.”

**VERSE 6.**—“I went around.” (AUG.) Because he offered himself to me as a guide, etc., up to “so that I might fulfill all his desires.”

(HIER.) Or, I surveyed all created things, or the examples of the saints.

(AUG.) In my mind I went around all created things, etc., up to “he desires it all the more ardently.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Hear, Lord, my voice,” etc. (CASS.) What labor, what groaning? A prayer before the second anointing, so that it may be possessed—the anointing which he promises himself through the spirit of prophecy.

[Col. 0881A] **VERSE 8.**—“To you he said.” (CASS.) The heart, reason taught by you, speaks with you concerning the one thing, and does not consider anything other than what you teach.

**VERSE 9.**—“Do not turn away.” (AUG.) Another person asks God here for temporal goods and rejoices in what is given; this one asks for nothing but the one thing. Another, possessing such things, fears that God is angry and may take them away; this one does not regard anything as anger except the turning away of God’s face, even if God punishes something in him. Nothing more divine could be said.

“Do not decline.” (AUG.) He does not decline in anger when he turns his face away from sins; or, “do not decline,” so that you do not allow me to slip into anger, that is, into punishment, but so that our weakness may become more cautious.

[Col. 0881B] “My savior,” etc. (AUG.) As if he were saying: You created and recreated me in vain, etc., up to “he was chosen by the Lord through Samuel.”

**VERSE 10.**—“For father,” etc. He made himself little before God and made God his father, because God commands, calls, creates, and governs. He is mother because he cherishes, contains, suckles, and nourishes. But the world is father—or the devil—and Babylon is mother, that is, the society of the impious.

**VERSE 11.**—“Set a law for me,” etc.

**VERSE 12.**—“Of those who trouble.” (CASS.) Such as Saul and his assistants, etc., up to “because they are false.”

**VERSE 13.**—“I believe that I will see.” (AUG.) Amid all dangers, with God directing me, I believe that I will see.

“Good things.” (Ibid.) Good things that are true and eternal. They persuade people toward blessedness on this earth, which belongs to those who die.

**VERSE 14.**—“Wait.” (CASS.) Just as I am certain of that, etc., up to “endure what you suffer.”

# PSALM XXVII

“A psalm for David.” Through David, sometimes the head, that is, Christ, is understood; sometimes the body, that is, the Church; sometimes both together, that is, the whole Christ, as here.

(CASS.) The third psalm that speaks briefly of the Passion and resurrection.

(Ibid.) Here Christ is presented—even though so worthy—not trusting in himself, but asking everything from God; a useful example for the righteous.

**VERSE 1.**—“To you, Lord.” (Ibid.) A prayer uttered at the time of the Passion.

“Do not be silent.” It is shorter in the Hebrew, etc., up to “and resurrection from death.”

“Do not be silent,” etc., “and I shall be made like,” etc. (JEROME.) Because the Word is always united to me, I am not such a man as the others, who are born into the profound misery of the world.

(AUGUSTINE.) Where, as it were, if you are silent, your Word is not recognized.

**VERSE 2.—“Toward the temple.”** (CASSIODORUS.) According to the custom of the Jews, who were commanded, wherever they might be, to pray toward the place where they knew Jerusalem to be—which Jesus also did, fulfilling the Law. Or toward heaven, from which we hope for help.

[Col. 0882A] **VERSE 4.—“Give them.”** (The same.) This is a prophecy, not a wish, according to what they intended, not according to what resulted from it; or he wishes that God’s justice be preserved in this matter.

**VERSE 5.—“For they have not,”** etc. (The same.) Even if their deeds were lacking, this would be sufficient for their condemnation: that they did not understand through the Law and the Prophets what God invisibly accomplishes through me, nor even the visible things.

**“You will destroy.”** (AUGUSTINE.) So that nothing may harm me, neither afterward [harm] your Church or mine.

**“Blessed.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The one heard in the resurrection gives thanks, adding what concerns the salvation of believers.

**“The Lord.”** (The same.) He who is also my helper is the strength of the people who trust in him, and their protector, so that they may not be harmed; and you, O Lord:

**VERSE 9.—“Save.”** Behold how great is the hope of believers when he prays for them: having suffered for them, he is both judge and advocate.

**“And rule,”** etc. (The same.) So that they may not turn aside toward wicked things.

**“Raise up,”** etc.: from earthly things to seek eternal realities, through understanding of the Scriptures and good works throughout this whole age, unto the end.

# PSALM XXVIII

**VERSE 1.—“A psalm of David at the consummation.”** (The same.) After the ark had been brought back by the Philistines, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that they may offer themselves to such a consummator.

**“Bring to the Lord.”** (The same.) First he urges them to offer sacrifices.

[Col. 0882C] **“Sons of rams.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Because opposition is not lacking, etc., until the seventy-two disciples sent to preach are signified.

**“The voice of the Lord.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The preaching of Christ inwardly terrified minds, that is, it gave the spirit of fear to Jews and Gentiles.

(GREGORY.) This one ascends from below, that is, from the spirit of fear to the spirit of wisdom, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that the Lord shakes these people, that is, gives them spiritual understanding.

(JEROME.) As a farmer does to barren land, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that he will give strength and bless it with the same blessing in eternal peace.

**VERSE 3.—“The voice of the Lord is over the waters,”** etc. (CASSIODORUS.) Concerning the establishment of the Church, where he enumerates the powers of the Holy Spirit with great proclamation.

**“Of Lebanon.”** Lebanon is interpreted as “whitening.” The cedars of Lebanon—that is, lofty men exalted in earthly things—God will break and shatter, that is, he will bring them from pride back to himself through his beloved Son. He will shatter them by the spirit of strength, just as a captured unicorn is crushed.

**VERSE 7.—“The desert.”** (CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE.) The Jewish people, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point from which living water flows.

**VERSE 10.—“The Lord.”** He shows what happens to the Church once it has been established.

“For,” he says, “I have given you power to tread upon serpents.” Just as it is unheard-of for stags to strike every kind of wild beast with their horns, so it was unheard-of that the uneducated Apostles should refute all philosophy.

[Col. 0883A] **“The flood.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The waters of baptism, which cleanse the sins of the world.

# PSALM XXIX

**VERSE 1.—“A psalm of song at the dedication.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Above, the subject was the consummation of the tabernacle in time of war; here, however, it is a psalm of joy, because the house is dedicated—that is, confirmed—and will remain in eternal peace, with the body renewed, not only of Christ but also of the whole Church. The whole Christ speaks in this psalm, because some things apply to the Head, some to the body, and some to both.

(The same.) A psalm briefly concerning the passion and resurrection, so that the passion may not terrify those whom the hope of resurrection makes joyful.

**“The house of David.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The whole Christ, the bridegroom, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the future state, when one rests in it.

(CASSIODORUS.) First he speaks of his own dedication and commands the saints who hope for the same thing to sing praises.

**VERSE 3.—“Lord, my God, I cried to you,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Christ, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that this is not yet at the dedication.

**VERSE 4.—“Into the pit.”** (JEROME.) That is, from the pit of hell, where the souls of sinners are, lest I, like them, should fall headlong into death.

**VERSE 5.—“Give thanks,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Because by his goodness and holiness, not by ours, he remembered us.

**VERSE 6.—“For anger.”** (The same.) That is, the vengeance by which he avenged upon us the first sin, which you expiated by death.

**“In the evening.”** (The same.) Because anger, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that this means the time of grace, after the time before the Law and under the Law.

(JEROME.) **“In the evening.”** Because, after the Lord had suffered and been buried, the Apostles and the women remained in weeping and lamentation. “And in the morning, joy,” because when they came to the tomb at dawn, they received from the angels the glory of the resurrection. **“Weeping.”** (CASSIODORUS.) It will remain with those who look toward the evening, when Adam turned aside and left paradise; but there will be joy for those who look toward the morning, when Christ rose.

**VERSE 7.—“But I.”** How he acted before the dedication and merited it. (AUGUSTINE, CASSIODORUS.) “In the evening he makes.” But while abundance was mine in paradise, [Col. 0883D] I said, “I shall not be moved from this good,” believing the devil who said, “You shall not surely die” (Gen. III). But, O Lord, in your favor you established strength for my beauty—that is, I was not good and strong from myself, but from you. To demonstrate this, “You turned your face away”; that is, you drove me outside paradise. Now, placed here, I shall cry to you, etc.

**VERSE 8.—“You turned away.”** (CASSIODORUS.) God turned his face away from Christ by handing him over to suffering and death; thus Christ was troubled: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matt. XVI). **“Troubled.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Recalling that time of trouble and misery, and being placed in it, I hear the voice of the Head who was to die for me, saying, “To you, O Lord, I shall cry.”

[Col. 0884A] **VERSE 10.—“What profit is there in my blood?”** (The same.) He shows the necessity by which he does not allow him to descend into corruption. “While I descend into corruption”: for if I do not rise immediately and the body is corrupted, I shall announce [the message] to no one and win no one. There is a twofold confession, and let us never be without it: when things go badly for us in tribulations, let us confess our sins; when things go well, in exultation over righteousness, let us confess praise to God.

**VERSE 11.—“The Lord has heard.”** (CASSIODORUS.) He treats how he received it, namely, the dedication. He said, “I shall cry; I shall plead,” but the Lord heard me pleading.

**VERSE 12.—“You have torn my sackcloth.”** (The same.) Sackcloth is a rough garment, granted for labor or in time of sorrow, as for the Ninevites; it signifies human flesh, which was torn by dying, and from which the grain of glorious resurrection—or of divinity—came forth. Or it signifies the punishment of sin, which was destroyed in the resurrection, and divinity, previously hidden, was brought forth: just as what an intact sackcloth conceals, when torn open it reveals. (AUGUSTINE.) A sack made from goats or kids signifies mortality, which Christ drew or received from sinners; hence: “When they troubled me, I was clothed in sackcloth” (Ps. XXXIV), so that they might not see what was within.

**VERSE 13.—“I shall not be pierced.”** (The same.) I shall not die forever. “Lord God, I shall confess to you forever.” What is “I shall confess to you forever”? “I shall praise you eternally.”

# PSALM XXX

[Col. 0884C] **VERSE 1.—“A psalm to the end.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Here “ecstasy” is understood as the fear of a troubled people arising from the persecution of all nations and the failure of faith throughout the world.

(CASSIODORUS.) Against fear, hope and prayer are first set forth, etc., until [the explanation reaches]: “They will be two in one flesh” (Gen. II), and therefore also in one voice. (AUGUSTINE.) First the Redeemer speaks; then the redeemed, giving thanks. After that, near the end and at the conclusion, the Prophet’s voice is inserted at length concerning his trouble. Here the humiliation of Christ and of the martyrs is described, and from it exaltation follows.

**VERSE 2.—“In you, O Lord, I have hoped,”** etc. (The same.) There is eternal confusion, from which he asks to be delivered; and there is temporal confusion, lasting for a time, namely, that which is beneficial.

**VERSE 3.—“Hasten.”** (The same.) In accomplishing things, in releasing souls, and in matters of this kind: so that you may deliver me on the third day, do not delay until the general resurrection. In order that this may happen, be such a protector to me as it is fitting for God to be. “Be to me.” He said, “Give righteousness,” etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that he affirms deliverance.

**VERSE 5.—“You will bring out.”** (CASSIODORUS.) From death to heavenly things, so that the plans of the Jews may prove vain. **“From the snare that they hid.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Through two doors the devil tempts, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the words: “You will bring me out of the snare.”

**VERSE 6.—“Into your hands.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Note that here he speaks who uttered the same words in his passion. (AUGUSTINE.) **“Into your hands.”** From these words, which he spoke on the cross, he reminds us that he spoke in this psalm.

**VERSE 8.—“But I, in the Lord,”** etc. (CASSIODORUS.) Concerning joy, because he hopes in the Lord, who hates vain things. “I shall exult and rejoice.” To exult is to rejoice with great liveliness of spirit; to rejoice is to have a moderated affection. **“My humiliation.”** He understands this as infirmity and as the very virtue of humility. **“In necessities.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Necessities are infinite, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that they are fulfilled in the future.

**VERSES 9–10.—“In a spacious place.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The spacious place in which one may freely travel toward the homeland of virtues is charity. But because the flesh is weak and evils press upon us: “Have mercy on me, O Lord.” Fear is now recounted—that is, how many and how great are the things that trouble him, against which the prayer is: “I am troubled.” (AUGUSTINE.) Earlier he said, “You have set me in a spacious place,” etc. But for some the spacious place comes from rejoicing at deliverance; for others, from tribulation and distress. **“Troubled.”** He is angered because of the sins of the chaff, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that the life of the perfect is the progress of others. **“My eye in anger.”** In the anger of persecutors, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that God is sought through all degrees. (CASSIODORUS.) Or the understanding is troubled and the mind confused, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that no presumption of man can exist either in mind or in body. (AUGUSTINE.) Anger arising from vice blinds the eye of the mind; anger arising from zeal troubles it. For this too, when the mind is shaken, scatters contemplation, which exists only in a tranquil mind; yet afterward, from this very disturbance, it makes greater progress toward seeing.

**VERSE 11.—“By poverty.”** (The same.) Or by destitution. I lack bodily health, and the tortures are not spared me. I lack release, and death is withheld from me; and in this my confidence has been weakened.

[Col. 0885C] **VERSE 12.—“Above all my enemies.”** (The same.) They live worse than pagans and Jews, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that acquaintances fear for them, lest all should be such. (CASSIODORUS.) Or “among all my enemies,” regarded with greater reproach than those who deserve it; and among neighbors, relatives, or those who are already about to believe; and among acquaintances and familiars.

**VERSE 13.—“Those who saw me outside.”** (JEROME.) “Outside” means Christ, that is, those who thought him merely a man. **“I have been forgotten as one dead from the heart.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Or I have been removed from their hearts as a dead man whose memory is buried with his body and whose restoration is despaired of. Jesus, as a lost vessel, is thought fit to be cast away.

**VERSE 14.—“The reproach of many.”** (AUGUSTINE.) They are reproached, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that there is no human being. **“In the circuit.”** While they were gathering together in one place. (CASSIODORUS.) Of errors, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that this means the desire for temporal things.

**VERSE 16.—“My lots.”** (The same.) Or the periods of life. (AUGUSTINE.) Because we live or die whenever you will, therefore deliver me. Although the hidden order of election is just and lies with you, nevertheless I, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that without merits he chose those whom he wished.

**VERSE 17.—“Make your light shine.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Make your goodwill toward me manifest, so that just as they despair of me while dying, so they may trust in me when risen. (AUGUSTINE.) **“Make your light shine.”** Let it become apparent who belongs to you, while there is now confusion; hence elsewhere: “Distinguish my cause” (Ps. XLI). Yet lest he appear to justify himself, he adds: “Save me in your mercy,” not in my righteousness.

**VERSE 18.—“I called.”** (The same.) You call upon God when you call him into yourself and invite him into the house of your heart.

**VERSE 19.—“Let them become mute.”** (CASSIODORUS.) They are babblers here because they do not fear judgment; let them be mute in punishments, in hell.

**“Who speak.”** He appropriately sets iniquity against the righteous man.

**“In pride and abuse.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Because the creature rises against the Creator, and because of the perverse use of God’s benefits—he who, among other reasons, came on their account.

**VERSE 20.—“How great.”** (CASSIODORUS.) What good things of God correspond to the evils mentioned above and lighten those very evils. (AUGUSTINE.) Seeing and marveling at these things, the Prophet exclaims, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that it will be revealed in the future.

[Col. 0886B] **VERSE 21.—“From trouble.”** (AUGUSTINE.) So that he may now suffer no human trouble; even those who are presently afflicted, entering in spirit before the face of God, are not troubled. **“You will protect.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Lest the promise of the future alone cause trouble, he adds this: “You will protect,” so that they may not be harmed.

**VERSE 22.—“Blessed.”** (The same.) As though he said, “What more?” He concludes the fullness of the benefit with praise, comparing it with his own weakness. The Prophet or the faithful people speaks. **“He has made wonderful.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Having sent the Spirit, he filled the whole world, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the words: “Your name is oil poured out.” (CASSIODORUS.) Or God the Father made mercy wonderful, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the words: “According to this: He rested in the heart of the earth.”

**VERSE 23.—“I said in my ecstasy.”** (AUGUSTINE.) A figure of our fear, etc., until: “Therefore you heard the voice of my prayer.” (AUGUSTINE.) **“In ecstasy of mind.”** Or, with his mind seized, he saw the height from which he felt himself cast very far away; or he exceeded reason through fear. **“From the face of your eyes.”** If I were in your presence, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that I accused my own heart.

**VERSE 24.—“Love the Lord, all you,”** etc. (CASSIODORUS.) An oratorical or hortatory conclusion, concerning the obtaining of the things mentioned above. (AUGUSTINE.) Having experienced the foregoing, he now exhorts us, as though saying: “I was troubled, I feared, I cried out, and I was not put to shame; so should you be.” His saints are those whose task it is to love God, because they do not love the world or the things that are in the world. The friend of this world is made an enemy of God. Learn, therefore, not to love the world, so that you may learn to love God: turn away, so that you may be converted; empty yourself, so that you may be filled. “The Lord will require,” etc. Even here, if he did this to no one, divine providence would not seem to be watchful, if divine patience were not preserved toward all.

**“For those who act abundantly.”** Those who do not repent quickly.

**“Pride.”** In place of every vice, because it is the root of all.

**VERSE 25.—“Act manfully,”** etc. The force of the whole psalm is that the weakness of the flesh should not fear all the evils of the world.

# PSALM XXXI

**“The understanding of David.”** (AUGUSTINE.) A psalm concerning the grace by which we are Christians, as the Apostle says (Rom. IV). This psalm therefore begins with forgiveness and opposes the vice of people who do not acknowledge or defend their sins and boast of their merits. (CASSIODORUS.) This psalm is therefore set against the vice of people, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point at which it confirms those who stand.

**VERSE 1.—“Blessed are those whose [sins] have been forgiven,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Not those in whom he found no sin, but those whose sins he forgives. **“Iniquities.”** He means the tinder of sin, namely, concupiscence, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that sin may no longer exist. (JEROME.) “Iniquities” refers to the time before faith and baptism; “sin,” to the time after faith and baptism.

**VERSE 2.—“Blessed is the man.”** (JEROME.) The one whom God forgives—for he is not forgiven through himself. He covers the sin so that it may not be revealed in judgment, and thus it will not be counted toward punishment. There is no deceit in one who accuses himself: in his heart he holds what he confesses with his mouth.

“Blessed”—because formerly, when I did not confess to God, I came into sin, although I cried out whenever I did anything good.

**VERSE 3.—“I was silent.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Whoever does not wish to confess sins labors without cause in defending them; and while boasting of merits, he suffers an even greater loss of strength. (CASSIODORUS.) **“Blessed is the one to whom he did not impute.”** To some who have grave sins, God imputes them; to others, by mercy, he does not impute them, even though they have some sins—namely, to those who do not proclaim themselves righteous while they are evil, but, recognizing themselves, make satisfaction. This is what I now profess, but formerly: “Because I was silent,” etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Or “I was silent” means that I was silent with my voice concerning sin while crying out all day: while the punishment of sin or an inner blindness showed me to be a sinner, or while a wicked life cried out, even though I was silent, whenever I did anything good.

**“While I cried out all day,”** etc. Even if someone is not conscious of sin, he is nevertheless not righteous, for who understands his offenses? Hence: “There is a righteous man who perishes in his righteousness.” And the Apostle says: “I am conscious of nothing against myself,” etc.

[Col. 0887C] **VERSE 4.—“A thorn is fixed.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The thorn that raises the whole body upright is pride. (AUGUSTINE.) Likewise, misery, etc., until: “in the hands of a drunkard.”

**VERSE 5.—“My sin.”** *Diapsalma.* Confession, from which comes forgiveness, just as above concerning rectitude and becoming old. **“I made known.”** (CASSIODORUS.) For earlier I said, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that God hears.

**VERSE 6.—“For this every holy person will pray.”** (The same.) *Diapsalma.* Commending repentance, he declares it common to all the saints; various sects reject it, against which he flees to God. (AUGUSTINE.) **“For this.”** Every saint prays from this point, because you have forgiven; otherwise he would not be a saint. **“In time,”** etc. The time is that of grace; the Law, pressing and convicting the guilty, compelled them to cry out, while grace heals. **“Nevertheless, in the flood,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Although the saint prays, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that the saint will pray, saying: “You are my refuge.” **“To him.”** To God; for he changes the person, as he often does. Those who say that fate makes one sin do not draw near to him, nor do those who say that fortune governs all things, nor those who posit a race of darkness rebelling against God.

**VERSE 8.—“I will give you understanding.”** (The same.) *Diapsalma.* The penitent receives this response: “I will give you understanding,” etc. Behold, this is the psalm of understanding, lest the suppliant be thought neglected, with God as witness. **“You, deliver.”** (CASSIODORUS.) He who promised, “I will give you understanding.” Or Christ responds to the penitent: a joyful conclusion—God gives understanding; hence he exhorts others to the same thing.

**VERSE 9.—“Do not become like a horse and a mule,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) Having received understanding, this penitent turns toward the proud who defend their sins: therefore, you whom I invite, etc. The horse is the untamed Gentile; the mule is the Jew, slow to believe. (CASSIODORUS.) The horse is without discrimination regarding its riders; the mule accepts every kind of burden, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that this means boasting of one’s own strength. **“Jaws.”** Or, with the jaws by which they chew—that is, more sparingly—give them food, so that, compelled by necessity, they may return. (AUGUSTINE.) Or “here you will break them,” and in the future there will be many scourges. Or: “Do not become like a horse,” because there are many scourges here and in the future. **“Those who do not draw near to you.”** (CASSIODORUS.) For there are people who, if they sin through the weakness of the flesh, nevertheless do not withdraw from devout prayers.

**VERSE 10.—“Many are the scourges of the sinner,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) After the bridle, scourges are added for taming, lest he belong among those who go unpunished and are now granted unrestricted license to follow their own way. Thus earlier he said that he had been tamed.

# PSALM XXXII

**“To the end.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Here the Prophet enumerates God’s power and deeds, and thus invites praise of God. First he urges the righteous and upright to praise, because we cannot exult in him except by praising him: “Praise,” he says, “befits the upright.”

**VERSE 1.—“Exult,”** etc. (AUGUSTINE.) The crooked person praises God when things go well for him and blasphemes when they go badly; the upright person praises him always, like Job.

**VERSE 2.—“With the lyre.”** (The same.) It sounds from below and is from the earth; with it let us praise—that is, prosperity and adversity, which come to us from him. **“On the psaltery.”** When you attend to the higher things he has given you, namely, heavenly teaching. The flesh is understood through the lyre, and charity through the psaltery; to these the Ten Commandments of the Law pertain: three on the first tablet, concerning God, and seven on the second, concerning one’s neighbor.

[Col. 0888C] **VERSE 3.—“Sing to him,”** etc. As though he said, “What more shall I say? Rejoice especially over the Incarnation.” **“A new song.”** (CASSIODORUS.) For it is not enough unless your righteousness abounds more than that of the scribes and Pharisees (Matt. V).

**“Sing a new song.”** Concerning the Incarnation, over which the world rejoices and concerning which the angels sang.

**VERSE 4.—“For it is upright.”** He has explained the manner of praise; now he explains why God is to be praised. **“And all his works.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Lest anyone think that he came to faith through his merits, since all the works that God loves—that is, rewards—are in faith. (The same.) For he works only in the faithful; hence: “Your faith has saved you” (Matt. X). Or, all his works are upright, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that he remains unrighteous, and is therefore more wicked because he sees that the righteous man favors him.

**“In faith.”** As though he said: if someone is faithful in outward things for the sake of righteousness, he will add inward faith—faith in the one whom, without knowing him, he feared. Hence: “Who will not give him what belongs to him, since he was faithful in what belonged to another?” (AUGUSTINE.) God is faithful, giving a human being what he promised; a human being is faithful, believing the one who promises; and by the promise God has made himself our debtor.

**VERSE 5.—“The earth.”** (The same.) The Church throughout the earth.

**VERSE 6.—“By the word.”** That is, by the wisdom of God the Father. **“The heavens.”** The Apostles were fully instructed by conversing with him bodily as well; afterward all their power was established and strengthened by the Spirit of the Son. Through the heavens he gathers and consolidates them in the unity of faith, hope, and charity. **“A wineskin.”** The Church, in which there is dead flesh. He also places the depths—that is, those sunk in the darkness of vices—among them; these are the treasuries from which he enriches others with wisdom. (AUGUSTINE.) **“The earth.”** The heavens do not need mercy, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that it is accomplished. **“Their power.”** While they were among wolves, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point of permission.

**VERSE 7.—“As in a wineskin.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Literally: just as the sea is enclosed by shores, so in the Church he encloses peoples tossed about by the waves; and in the treasuries of his wisdom he places profound heights, so that he may test who searches the Scriptures with devout zeal.

[Col. 0889B] **VERSE 8.—“Let all the earth fear.”** (The same.) The Church comes from the sea, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that the earth should fear the Lord. Let it fear—or rather, let it be moved by the hand of mercy, unlike one who sleeps. “By him,” because he himself created it; and therefore he governs it beneficially. Something is also moved by the devil, but because it is moved beneficially by God, it is therefore moved by him. **“Let them be moved.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Not by human terrors, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that authority comes only from God.

**VERSE 9.—“He spoke, and they were made.”** He indicates creation together with formation. He commanded restoration.

**VERSE 10.—“He scatters the counsels.”** (CASSIODORUS.) So that counsels against him may not succeed, such as those of the Jews, and counsels against their own people. **“Of the nations.”** When he destroyed idolatry. **“Of the peoples.”** Of the Jews, whose will, although fulfilled, was nevertheless rejected through the resurrection. **“Of the princes.”** Of tyrants [Col. 0889C] or demons.

**VERSE 11.—“But the counsel of the Lord,”** etc. (The same.) The mystery of the Incarnation, in which he counseled for humanity.

**“It remains forever.”** Because it obtains eternal salvation for us.

**“Thoughts.”** Predestination, in which all things have been stored up; and they remain just as they were foreseen.

**VERSE 12.—“Blessed is the nation.”** (CASSIODORUS.) He calls blessed the one who has attained the worship of God. This occurs in Christian times, when the nations have been converted; these are the righteous and upright whom praise befits. (AUGUSTINE.) All blessedness is in the mind, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that the people are blessed because God possesses them.

**VERSE 13.—“From heaven.”** (AUGUSTINE.) From the man Christ. He looked forth at the coming of the Son and saw mercifully—not sins, [Col. 0889D] (CASSIODORUS.) from which he turned his face—but all the sons of men, that is, all who wish to be reborn into a new life. (AUGUSTINE.) How did he choose? etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that he inspired every good will.

**VERSE 15.—“He fashioned.”** (AUGUSTINE.) He formed them by the hand of grace. **“One by one.”** Giving particular things to particular individuals. (JEROME.) Yet from this comes the unity of the body, that is, of the Church. “One by one,” that is, not from Adam, as some say—that soul comes from soul—and he knows them all together, as well as all their acts.

**VERSE 16.—“The king is not saved.”** Thus people become righteous, but even after being made righteous they are not saved by their own power. Not only spiritual things come from God, but external things as well. (JEROME.) No one possesses anything except from him, because no one is powerful as a king or strong, [Col. 0890A] etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that this remains true even if he possesses great abundance of virtue.

**VERSE 17.—“A deceptive horse.”** (AUGUSTINE.) An animal whose speed or strength is trusted; figuratively, this means every worldly greatness from which one takes pride. But the higher you raise yourself upon it, the more grievously you fall. (CASSIODORUS.) Or the horse is the human body, however beautiful and well formed; yet it is deceptive for bodily and spiritual salvation. (AUGUSTINE.) Or the horse is worldly prosperity, which carries people; and while it hastens too much, the horse falls and loses its rider. The horse is human wisdom. The giant is some proud person exalting himself against God.

**VERSE 18.—“Behold, the eyes.”** No one is saved by his own strength, but: “Behold from where salvation comes—the eyes,” etc. The eyes are the regard of the divinity that will protect them. **“Those who fear him.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Fearing the Lord and always hoping are joined together.

**VERSE 19.—“To deliver,”** etc. (The same.) These are the two petitions of the faithful: that he may be rescued from death in judgment, and that here he may be nourished by spiritual things, where there is need of them.

**VERSE 20.—“Our soul waits for the Lord.”** A conclusion indicating what he thinks about the foregoing.

**VERSE 21.—“Because in him.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Because he sent his name through faith to those who were absent.

**“We have hoped.”** We hope that we shall come to God, not through our own merits. (CASSIODORUS.) Lest anyone murmur against patience in him, he adds the gift—namely, that the faithful person rejoices here in the Lord. And we hope in the name of Christ, whom the joyful Prophet patiently awaited as the one who was to come: “We have hoped.” [Col. 0890C] It indicates continuous time, because it is not right to cease; hence the weary soul can always be refreshed.

**“Let your mercy, O Lord, be upon us,”** etc. He desires the Incarnation to be completed, so that he may be made perfect. **“In you.”** He says this so that every superstition and wickedness may be excluded.

# PSALM XXXIII

**VERSE 1.—“A psalm of David.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Christ speaks, and in him the Christian speaks. He teaches humility while commending the body and blood. When Christ changed his face—that is, the sacrifice—in the presence of the Jews, who are the kingdom of his father David, according to the words, “And the Lord God will give him the throne of David,” the Church is the kingdom of the Father.

[Col. 0890D] **VERSE 2.—“I will bless.”** (CASSIODORUS.) The second alphabetic psalm with an imperfect alphabet, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that he is glorified together with him.

**VERSE 3.—“My soul will be praised in the Lord.”** (The same.) For his praise is the preaching of his Lord, so that a good servant may glory in the good reputation of his Lord. **“The meek.”** Not the learned, nor those who fast, since they are proud; but the meek, because they exercise moderation in all things. The meek do not grow proud of their own understanding; they do not bear God’s yoke like the untamed.

**VERSES 4–6.—“Magnify the Lord.”** Spiritual grace does not wish to accomplish alone what benefits many; therefore it calls others: “Magnify,” it says, so that it may draw those whom it has invited. What good came to it from this? “I sought the Lord.” **“From all.”** The magnitude of what he obtained cannot be stated piecemeal, since he sought nothing other than God. **“Draw near.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Now, concerning the new face, he admonishes the saints individually. As though he said: “Magnify”; and, above all, draw near joyfully. Or: “Magnify”—and in what order? Behold: “Draw near through faith.” (AUGUSTINE.) Draw near by adhering through faith and running on the two feet of twofold charity. (CASSIODORUS.) After the preceding praises, he urges them to communion. **“They shall not be ashamed.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Whatever happens here to the righteous person, he is not ashamed, because he is always superior with God; but the proud person is ashamed in adversity, because he has not drawn near to God.

**VERSE 7.—“The poor man.”** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the spiritual person here, because he draws near and is enlightened, and he will not be ashamed. For when he cries out, he is delivered from all the distresses of the world at death, when he is already passing over to God.

[Col. 0891B] **VERSE 8.—“He will send an angel.”** Draw near; and just as this poor man cried out and was heard, so he will send an angel, etc. (AUGUSTINE.) **“He will send an angel.”** Other interpreters translated it thus: “The angel of the Lord encamps around those who fear him.” The angel may be from heaven, or a human being who is a minister of God’s will. Corrupt manuscripts have: “The Lord will send an angel.”

**VERSE 9.—“Taste and see.”** Here he speaks openly of the sacrament that he carried in his hands. Taste the flesh and blood of Christ. “The Lord is sweet.” (The same.) And pleasant, because it is life to the one who receives it, removing all troubles in the future; that is: Hope through this for eternal life. (CASSIODORUS.) And because God is life, the flesh that he united to himself is life-giving.

**VERSE 10.—“All his saints.”** (CASSIODORUS.) No one, however well deserving, will withdraw from this; no one should presume upon security. **“For.”** (AUGUSTINE.) The Lord fed the one who despised him, and he will abandon the one who fears him. He promises not superfluities but necessities. **“There is no want.”** Because even in the present they have as much as nature requires.

**VERSE 11.—“The rich have lacked and have hungered.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Because they do not have faith. They have hungered because they are not satisfied by the Lord’s body. For what do those who do not have God possess? Or, “the rich have lacked” means that they will lack the highest good, although they hunger—that is, desire it. But those who seek it with complete devotion will possess, without diminution, the good that is every good.

[Col. 0891D] **VERSE 12.—“Come, children, hear me.”** *Diapsalma.* Having treated the sacraments of the Church, he admonishes those who are outside and are receiving the first beginnings of faith. Lest the name of fear be dreaded, he adds: “I will teach you, children, the fear of the Lord,” as something useful.

(CASSIODORUS.) He now also admonishes beginners concerning the things from which they must abstain.

**VERSE 13.—“To see good days.”** Because everyone admits that he wishes this.

**VERSE 14.—“Restrain.”** (The same.) Note that he first says that the tongue must be restrained, because when we wish to speak, we first move the lips, which are immediately followed by the movement of the tongue. Restrain yourself, you who desire life. Behold how they should fear.

[Col. 0892A] **VERSE 15.—“Turn away from evil.”** (CASSIODORUS.) This avoids guilt, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that otherwise it will not be attained in the future.

**VERSE 16.—“The eyes of the Lord,”** etc. (The same.) Concerning the rewards of the good and the wicked, lest the righteous person grow weak in dangers through any uncertainty.

**“The eyes of the Lord.”** Do not distrust because of your weakness, because they are eyes.

**“Toward prayers.”** (The same.) The swiftness of being heard, because the one who hears dwells in the prayers themselves.

**VERSE 17.—“The memory.”** (AUGUSTINE.) So that not even mention, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the things they committed.

**VERSE 19.—“The Lord is near.”** He delivered them, for he is inclined to do this because he is near; or there is an allusion to their cry.

**VERSE 20.—“Many are the tribulations of the righteous.”** As also in the New Testament: “He is near, and he will save,” which is necessary because there are many tribulations. (CASSIODORUS.) Many—from the devil, from envious people, and from oneself. **“He will deliver.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Not bodily, but by giving them patience; or he will deliver them spiritually.

**VERSE 21.—“The bones.”** (The same.) The virtues. **“And one,”** etc., so that even patience may not perish.

**VERSE 22.—“Most grievous.”** (The same.) Not merely evil—even if life ends amid riches, perfumes, and human lamentations, it is nevertheless most grievous, because in sins it drags one to hell.

**“Those who hate.”** Whom does he mean? Not all sinners, but those who hate the righteous one who justifies—that is, Christ. Whoever is not reconciled through him perishes; but he will redeem the souls for whom death is most grievous.

# PSALM XXXIV

**VERSE 1.—“Judge, O Lord.”** (CASSIODORUS.) He begins with a prayer for both sides of the conflict, together with a recollection of guilt. He shows that each receives what he deserves, setting forth how much he endured from his adversaries and the punishments returned to them for their iniquity.

**VERSE 2.—“Weapons and shield.”** (JEROME.) With weapons he strikes the enemies; with the shield he protects us. Elsewhere he calls the shield “goodwill.” We are the weapons, because just as we are armed by him, so he is armed with us. (AUGUSTINE.) Or it is the soul of Christ, which defeated the enemies and does nothing unless God fights through it.

**“Take up the weapons.”** Make me possess weapons: teaching and miracles. **“The shield.”** Perseverance.

[Col. 0892D] **“Rise up.”** Make use of what has been received.

**VERSE 3.—“Pour forth.”** Glorify me, who am now in obscurity, so manifestly that you may conclude and convict them, leaving them nothing to protest; and speak to the soul in such a way that all may know that salvation belongs to it, contrary to their claim: “There is no salvation for him in his God” (Ps. III). **“The sword.”** (AUGUSTINE.) The sword is the soul of the righteous. When the righteous abound, the sword is poured forth, as life shines brightly; thus it is concluded that the enemy has nothing evil to say about us. (The same.) This is prophecy, not a wish; or it concerns those who are to be converted.

**VERSE 5.—“Let them become.”** (The same.) A prophecy—or in the manner in which God acts, by just judgment, not with a bitter spirit. **“Like dust before the face of the wind.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Dissolved by God, so that those whom divine grace does not moisten may not cling together even among themselves.

[Col. 0893A] **VERSE 8.—“Let the snare that he does not know come upon him.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Or, in a good sense, the snare of truth, which the sinner does not know. **“And let the capture that he concealed.”** That is, hidden death, namely, Christ’s death. **“Seize them.”** So that they may not be abandoned to their crimes. **“And let him fall into the snare.”** The good thing by which they may be restrained from evil. **“Into it.”** That is, from death itself. **“Into it.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Not into another, but into the very one whom they set. For no evil person exists who does not first harm himself.

**VERSE 9.—“But my soul will exult.”** (The manuscript reads *CAS.*) After setting forth hope for good and joy, he tells how wickedly the wicked act toward the kind. **“In the Lord.”** (AUGUSTINE.) Nothing is sweeter than he, and the one who made all things did not fail. Seek him, therefore, and in him you will have everything.

[Col. 0893B] **VERSE 10.—“All my bones will say.”** Carnal people do not possess the word of praise and confession, because those who are utterly weak before you are silent; but the strong praise and fear you as great. (The same.) **“All my bones.”** All the strength of the mind, because no one else can say this: “O Lord, who is like you?”—as though there were no one, because he alone delivered the poor from the hand. (CASSIODORUS, AUGUSTINE.) The human race is poor because mortal; needy because it seeks bread in the sweat of its brow; poor because, cast down from pure wisdom, it possesses a thin and shadowy understanding.

**VERSE 11.—“Unjust witnesses rise up.”** (CASSIODORUS.) Having spoken of the calamities of humanity, he sets forth his own passion, lest Christ himself appear alien to such things. **“What I did not know.”** (AUGUSTINE.) These are sins, etc., until [the explanation reaches] the point that he did not commit them.

**VERSE 12.—“They repaid.”** (The same.) When I brought fertility, they repaid me with barrenness; I brought life, and they repaid me with death; I brought honors, and they repaid me with insults; I brought medicine, and they repaid me with wounds. **“Barrenness.”** The Lord cursed the fig tree when he sought fruit and found none, but only leaves; so also in the Synagogue there were words without deeds. Hence: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?”

**Verse 13.—** *With sackcloth.* (Augustine.) The flesh is called sackcloth because of its likeness to the flesh of sin. *My prayer.* (Cassiodorus.) As he said, “Your peace will return to you” (Matthew 10), so his prayer, not accepted by the Jews, returned to him. *In my bosom.* (Augustine.) The bosom is the secret place in which we are commanded to pray. The secret place of Christ, however, is his divinity, to which his humanity prays. [Col. 0893D]

**Verse 14.—** *As for a neighbor and as for a brother, etc.* A change of case for a case. As though he said: “I rejoiced over them as over a neighbor and our brother”; that is, I rejoiced in their kinship, though they were persecuting me. Behold, grace in place of hatred, a benefit in place of injury. (Augustine.) *As for a neighbor.* This is fitting for one who draws near to God and rejoices, since he pleases God as a brother and neighbor.

*As one mourning.* (Cassiodorus.) Other interpreters read: “As a mother mourning her son, I bent over them.” *As one mourning.* Although I did all these things, they nevertheless refused to turn; and although they refused to turn, I humbled myself in this way—that is, I grieved—as a father mourning his son.

[Col. 0894A] **Verse 15.—** *And against me, etc.* While I grieve piously, the Jews rejoice impiously.

**Verse 16.—** *They were scattered.* (Cassiodorus.) They were dissolved when they saw the miracles at the Passion, yet they were not pierced with compunction because of their hardness.

Or, they were scattered throughout the whole world; yet they were not pierced with compunction—that is, they did not repent. Or, “scattered” means divided: some say that he is good, others that he is not.

*They tempted me.* (Augustine.) What was done to the Head on the cross is done everywhere to the Body. *They gnashed.* This is the practice of savagery: when reason fails, one gnashes with one’s teeth and silently reveals what one desires. He concludes the prayer with this:

**Verse 17.—** *Lord, when will you look upon this?* (Cassiodorus.) When shall we see vengeance taken on those who insult us? *My only one.* (Cassiodorus.) The soul of Christ is unique, for it alone is free from sin. [Col. 0894B]

**Verse 18.—** *I will confess to you.* (Augustine.) He now anticipates the confession of the whole Church as its fruit; then he prays, recalling guilt, for the confusion of the persecutors and the exultation of the faithful.

**Verse 19.—** *Let them not rejoice exceedingly.* (Augustine.) He repeats what concerns the Passion in order to add what concerns their punishment. *They nod.* (Cassiodorus.) For they mutually warn one another by silent signs in order to deceive and test him.

**Verse 20.—** *Speaking.* (Cassiodorus.) That is, while they were speaking peaceably. *In anger.* That is, destructively. Someone who does not wish to kill may devise a deception; but they devised their plans in this way because they wished to kill.

**Verse 21.—** *And they opened wide.* (Cassiodorus.) First nodding and devising deceptions, they opened their mouths, loudly and openly crying out for his death: “Crucify, crucify!” [Col. 0894C]

**Verse 22.—** *You have seen, Lord.* (Cassiodorus.) This is said when we wish to recall something to memory: “You have seen that they are cruel; do not remain silent, do not delay in pronouncing sentence.”

**Verse 23.—** *Attend.* (Cassiodorus.) By restoring the name that is above every name, so that I, though innocent, may be regarded. *For my cause.* (Ibid.) The punishment is like the crime, but not the cause; for it is not punishment that makes a martyr, but the cause.

**Verse 24.—** *Your own, Lord God.* (Cassiodorus.) Either what exists in itself or what he gave to him. *Let them not rejoice exceedingly.* (Cassiodorus.) Let them lament rather than rejoice that they have accomplished evil.

[Col. 0894D] **Verse 25.—** *We devour.* (Augustine.) Those incorporated into them are devoured.

**Verse 26.—** *Let them be ashamed and stand in awe together.* (Cassiodorus.) Rather, let them be ashamed at the manifestation of the resurrection and stand in awe—that is, fear the punishments. *Let them be ashamed.* One who is ashamed condemns his deeds by his own judgment; yet someone may be ashamed without having reverence. Therefore he adds “reverence,” so that conversion may be signified. Reverence is fear of the Lord together with love. *Let them be clothed with shame and reverence.* With embarrassment, as with the sackcloth of repentance and a mournful garment. Shame is directed against the boldness they displayed in their frenzy; reverence against the shamelessness of their falsehood, so that they may remedy these things by means of those virtues.

**Verse 27.—** *Let them exult and rejoice.* (Cassiodorus.) This is the great hope of the faithful at the end, just as others speak concerning the Passion. *Let them exult and rejoice.* They say, “Well done, to their own soul,” pursuing fleeting joy; but these do not turn their vows toward their own souls. [Col. 0895A] Rather, they turn them toward God and place their joy in his praises, not in themselves. Such joy is perpetual.

**Verse 28.—** *And my tongue shall meditate on your righteousness.* (Augustine.) Let this happen, and let my preachers proclaim with zeal that you are righteous, since you fulfilled your promises and are worthy of universal praise in all things. (Cassiodorus.) *My tongue.* His tongue meditated on righteousness when he preached the New Testament to the peoples.

## Psalm 35

**Verse 1.—** *For the end: a discourse.* (Cassiodorus.) Here he treats of the error of certain people, etc., up to the point that nevertheless threatens everyone.

*There is no fear before his eyes:* because there is deceit—that is, because [Col. 0895B] he obeys the flesh and not God, although reason suggests otherwise; God sees this even if no one else does. Or: what the unjust man himself sees, he knows from God, so that it may be discovered by God himself that his iniquity must be hated by God and by all human beings.

(Augustine.) First he asserts that evils arise from human beings. [Col. 0895A]

**Verse 2.—** *The unjust man said, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) There are two kinds of sinners: those who, through the weakness of the flesh, cannot follow the commands of the law; and blasphemers who sin freely, as though God did not care about it. Hence the words, “He said,” etc. (Augustine.) A description of the unjust man. *There is no fear of God.* (Cassiodorus.) Because the deceitful man did not wish to apply himself to the law, by ignorance of which he might have been excused.

**Verse 3.—** *For he acted deceitfully.* (Augustine.) Many investigate their iniquities, etc., up to the point that they are not excused on grounds of ignorance. [Col. 0895C]

**Verse 4.—** *Words.* (Augustine.) He reveals iniquity, etc., up to the point that he might do good.

**Verse 5.—** *In his bedchamber.* That is, in his heart, in which he takes pleasure in evil deeds. And this is what “he stood by every way” means: with zeal and persistence. He found and knew that they were evil, yet he did not hate them. *He did not wish.* (Augustine.) Not because he was unable; the one who does not wish to do what he can does greater harm to himself. There are certain things that people cannot understand even if they wish to, such as “In the beginning was the Word”; but they can understand what is necessary in order to act rightly. *In his bedchamber.* (Augustine.) That is, in his heart, where the Lord commanded us to pray with the door closed, etc., up to the wisdom of the flesh, which is hostile to God.

**Verse 6.—** *Lord, in heaven.* (Cassiodorus.) Good things come from God [Col. 0895D] through mercy. As though he said: “Evils arise from human beings, but good things arise from mercy. O Lord, among those who are heaven—that is, those who know heavenly mysteries—your mercy is present; and the fact that they are clouds comes from you.” (Augustine.) Or, “in heaven,” that is, in mercy, etc., up to the point that he announces it after sending forth his truth.

*As far as the clouds.* That is, the preachers, through whom God thunders by proclaiming, flashes by miracles, and rains by teachings. They are also mountains, which the sun first clothes with light; afterward, from them, though not from them, that light descends to the lowest valleys. For they are ministers of teaching, but God gives illumination.

**Verse 7.—** *Your judgments.* (Augustine.) In that you show mercy to some and blind others, they are wholly inscrutable; nevertheless, you save both: the former only bodily, the latter both bodily and spiritually. In this there is great mercy. [Col. 0896A]

**Verse 8.—** *Human beings, etc.* He also shows that temporal things come from God.

**Verse 9.—** *They shall be intoxicated.* (Augustine.) The reality cannot be expressed, but this likeness suggests that, when they are filled, they lose awareness of themselves, so that they no longer recognize their fathers, sons, or other friends. Or, they will then be intoxicated in reality, whereas now they hope for it. *From your torrent.* As though he said: “There will be an onrush of grace and mercy to intoxicate them.” (Augustine.) *From your torrent.* Their blessedness will not be transitory but abundant. Or, your will in the human being breaks through every obstacle. Or, Christ’s wisdom is a torrent because it is sudden and swift.

**Verse 10.—** *For with you is the fountain of life.* (Cassiodorus.) With you, Christ, is the fountain—that is, the beginning—of every good thing; and in your light, because through his preaching we see the light of the Father and of the Holy Spirit. Therefore extend it before us, so that we may proceed more safely in this age. [Col. 0896B]

## Psalm 36

(Cassiodorus.) The third psalm of the alphabet: an imperfect alphabet; entirely concerned with the correction of morals.

**Verse 1.—** *A psalm of David.* This psalm is like Christ’s garment, covering his entire body with commandments, protecting it from adversities, and cherishing it as if in the bosom of counsel. It is a potion against those who murmur about the flourishing of the wicked and the labor of the good, as though everything happened by chance, so that, having rejected God, they might cling to the world. The Church therefore warns that no one should imitate those who act maliciously, but should ask from the Lord whatever good he hopes for; for the Lord grants what is beneficial and [Col. 0896C] eternal.

**Verse 2.—** *The herbs of the fields.* (Augustine.) It is now winter, etc., up to the point that what we shall be has not yet appeared.

(Augustine, Cassiodorus.) These are not garden vegetables but field herbs—that is, the most worthless plants, which grow spontaneously through the fields. *Grass:* the noble, who advance easily; *herbs:* the ordinary. Yet the former quickly wither, and the latter fall.

**Verse 8.—** *Cease.* (Augustine.) Sudden anger and long-lasting rage; both must be abandoned, since through them one sins. (Cassiodorus.) This is said to one who is still weak, etc., up to the point that he flourishes for a time by doing evil.

**Verse 10.—** *And yet a little while, etc.* (Augustine.) After this brief life, etc., up to the point that he felt no gnawing worm of conscience. [Col. 0896D]

**Verse 12.—** *He will watch, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) Having said that the good ought not to imitate the wicked, etc., up to the point that he attempts to kill.

**Verse 13.—** *But the Lord, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) Thus we too, seeing that they are destined to perish, may laugh even in the present; this is great consolation.

**Verse 14.—** *The sword, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) If he achieves nothing by flattery or threats, he attacks with punishment. If he still makes no progress, he lies in wait with deceptions, intending evil while speaking well.

**Verse 16.—** *Better is, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) Earlier he spoke of wickedness and endurance; here he speaks of riches and poverty.

**Verse 17.—** *But he strengthens, etc.* (Augustine.) Especially through the example of his cross. Christ’s cross ended in punishment and remains in glory; from places of execution it passes to the foreheads of emperors. [Col. 0897A]

**Verse 18.—** *In the days of famine.* (Cassiodorus.) That is, in this life, etc., up to the point that the more they are elevated, the more quickly they will fail like smoke.

**Verse 21.—** *He will borrow.* (Cassiodorus.) He hears the word of God but does not return it through his works. *And he will not repay.* That is, he does not render through his works what he received by hearing. *He shows mercy and will repay, etc.* Concerning what he receives, etc., up to the point that generosity follows.

**Verse 23.—** *The steps.* (Cassiodorus.) They are crooked in themselves because they were born in sins. *His way.* (Augustine.) The way of the earth is not difficult but is full of robbers; or, God will desire the way of the human being.

**Verse 25.—** *I was young, etc.* (Augustine.) Here he treats [Col. 0897B] of the righteous person never being abandoned, mingling the rewards of the good and the punishments of the wicked with intervening exhortations. (Augustine.) The Church speaks as one person. In its earliest times it was young; at the end of the age it grew old, fruitful in old age because it has been spread among all nations. (Augustine.) *I was young.* A child in Abel; young in the prophets and patriarchs; like an old man in the time of the martyrs; at the end of the world, as though in extreme old age. (Cassiodorus.) Young when I received the beginnings of the law in Adam; I grew old when, at a venerable age, I finally received Christ.

**Verse 26.—** *All day long he shows mercy.* Either he speaks of almsgiving, which begins with mercy and afterward opens the hand; or he speaks of spiritual things.

**Verse 28.—** *He loves judgment and will not abandon [Col. 0897C] his saints.* (Cassiodorus.) Therefore you too should love judgment, so that you may rejoice in your good works.

**Verse 31.—** *They will be tripped up.* (Cassiodorus.) To trip someone up is to set traps of ambush before his feet.

**Verse 33.—** *But the Lord.* (Cassiodorus.) The consolation of the righteous. *In his hands.* (Augustine.) Job’s earth was delivered into the hand of the wicked—that is, the flesh; but God leads out the unconquered soul so that it does not yield.

*When he is judged.* (Cassiodorus.) Either he does not permit the righteous man to be condemned when the wicked man is judged; or he does not permit him to be condemned by that wicked man, namely, to his harm.

**Verse 34.—** *And he will exalt.* (Cassiodorus.) No one can dwell in heaven unless he has first been exalted. *You will see.* (Cassiodorus.) What you now believe. This indicates the joy of the good in two ways: first, because they will then perceive the greatness of their delight; second, because they will see the punishments of the wicked, making their blessedness all the more pleasant since they have been freed from such an evil. [Col. 0897D]

**Verse 35.—** *I saw the wicked man greatly exalted.* (Cassiodorus.) Against this, etc., up to the point that, once he was bound, the opportunity to do harm was taken away from him.

**Verse 36.—** *I passed by.* I passed through the world, striving toward God by a better way of life, and I saw that nothing could endure, since all the things in which human beings glory are nothing. *I sought.* I recalled to memory, because the good then grieve more deeply over the wicked, from whom they have been separated, when they are changed for the better. *His place.* Their world is the place that will also be dissolved. *I passed by.* (Augustine.) He passes by who does not attend to the present but to the last [Col. 0898A] things, etc., up to the point that the one possessing this virtue is placed among the blessed.

**Verse 37.—** *The remnants.* The good things that will remain after this life, or a good memory after death.

**Verse 39.—** *But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord.* All these things belong to the righteous, yet everything is from God; he gathers the whole matter together in summary.

## Psalm 37

**Verse 1.—** *A psalm of David, for remembrance of the Sabbath.* (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) Since we cannot completely escape sin, this psalm introduces the anguish of repentance in many ways, so that we may always keep sin in memory and at least restrain ourselves from it. It seems to set Job himself before beginners as an example, so that they may embrace sufferings, which, though lesser than our deserts, free us from eternal punishment. [Col. 0898B] (Augustine.) The Sabbath is the rest of eternity, which the person conscious of sin fears to lose and desires to possess when gravely afflicted.
