**Verse 2.—** *Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger.* First he seeks mercy by referring generally to punishments. *Rebuke me.* (Cassiodorus.) Let the punishment proceed from mercy for correction, not from anger for vengeance.

**Verse 3.—** *Your arrows.* (Augustine.) The acts of vengeance with which you threatened Adam, saying: “On whatever day you eat, you shall die.” Because he ate, they were fixed in us as well; and not for an hour only—you confirmed them so that they would remain until the end of the age. (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) *For your arrows.* He numbers the things he suffers, etc., up to the point that can be lightly wounded.

**Verse 4.—** *There is no health, etc.* (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) This is [Col. 0898C] because of the constant vengeance inflicted upon Adam. Or, he is terrified by fear of the future anger, so that there is no health in the flesh, like a shamefaced person who is already afflicted by future scourges. Or, “from the face of anger,” because I foresaw the face of anger—that is, what you threaten—in order not to see anger. *There is no peace.* Grave pain reaches the interior from the face of sins, because the holy person is afflicted not only by bodily punishments but by sins, thinking that he deserves worse. *There is no health.* (Cassiodorus.) Here he seeks mercy both from the power of the judge and from his own weakness. *There is no peace in my bones.* He uses “bones” for the flesh. He explains what he had said by adding another phrase: namely, “because of the face of my sins.”

**Verse 5.—** *They have risen above me.* (Augustine.) Or, “they have lifted me up,” that is, because iniquity raised the proud head against God, God weighed it down like a burden and pressed it down [Col. 0898D] so that it could no longer rise.

**Verse 6.—** *They have become foul.* (Cassiodorus.) This is a narrative in which miseries are enumerated. *My scars.* (Augustine.) Or, “my bruises”; another reading has “my sins.” One who has scars that have become foul and stink is not healthy. Turning away from these things, let us worship the Sabbath and groan: “Running with the bridegroom after the fragrance of perfumes.”

**Verse 7.—** *I have become miserable.* (Augustine.) Having said how the iniquities rose above him, he now says how they weighed upon him.

**Verse 8.—** *For my loins.* (Cassiodorus, Augustine.) I do not sin only through my own weakness; the devil too afflicts the body and tires the soul with empty imaginings. Thus again there is no health, just as [Col. 0899A] above through the arrows. (Augustine.) *The loins, or the soul, have been filled, etc.*, up to the point when we shall see the truth as it is.

**Verse 9.—** *I roared because of my groaning.* (Cassiodorus, Augustine.) Groaning belongs to the heart, roaring to the voice. He compares himself with beasts in order to show a stronger groaning. The power of endurance is shown by the fact that it breaks out into groaning, not into words.

**Verse 10.—** *All my desire is before you.* (Cassiodorus.) What deserves to be before you is presented in this way, because he asks on account of sins. (Augustine.) Therefore the groaning is not hidden but heard, because it is offered for the soul’s liberation; God does not concern himself with the others. *My desire.* (Augustine.) It is prayer; and the one who does not cease to love never ceases to pray. Love is a cry. [Col. 0899B]

**Verse 11.—** *My heart is troubled.* (Cassiodorus.) He explains the pains of the soul, because the power of endurance has departed. It is troubled because the mind has yielded to its suffering. *My light:* that is, reason, recently disturbed, which he no longer possesses because of his immense troubles.

**Verse 12.—** *My friends and my neighbors.* (Cassiodorus.) Humanity rejoices in these two consolations, but for him they are an addition to his suffering. (Augustine.) *My friends.* Up to this point he has confessed what he suffers inwardly from himself, etc., up to the point that this too applies to everyone living among human beings.

**Verse 14.—** *Like a deaf man, I did not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth.* (Cassiodorus.) He did not open his mouth against those who counseled iniquity, etc., up to the point that he roared against bodily pains. [Col. 0899C]

**Verse 16.—** *For in you, Lord, I have hoped, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) Because he hoped in the Lord amid so many evils, he asserts that he will be heard when he recalls his amendment. *I have hoped.* Hope is a saving remedy for evils: to hope and not fail. *In you, Lord,* who change sorrowful things into joyful ones.

**Verse 17.—** *For I said: Let my enemies never rejoice over me.* (Augustine.) Again, the Head speaks of its weak feet, although it is in heaven. It does not abandon what it has on earth. *When my feet are shaken.* (Cassiodorus.) If they are sometimes shaken by human weakness, the wicked laugh at what causes the godly sorrow.

**Verse 18.—** *I am ready.* (Cassiodorus.) Knowing that I have sinned. [Col. 0899D] *Sorrow,* because he has sinned; the wicked man defends himself, but the righteous man becomes angry with himself.

**Verse 19.—** *For I will declare my iniquity.* (Cassiodorus.) The two forms of perfect repentance are confession and amendment, through tears, almsgiving, and such things.

**Verse 20.—** *They live.* (Augustine.) They enjoy the world, established in worldly things, and they increase daily.

**Verse 22.—** *Do not abandon me.* (Augustine.) Having been freed from past things and confessing God as the author of salvation with thanksgiving, he joyfully cries out that he may not now be abandoned. (Cassiodorus.) For an offense after forgiveness is more serious. (Augustine.) This is an exultant conclusion, so that there may be certain hope for those who imitate him.

*Do not depart from me.* How, then, does he say above, “Why have you abandoned me?” That is the voice of the old man who was crucified with him; here, however, he speaks in his own person. [Col. 0900A]

## Psalm 38

**Verse 1.—** *For the end.* (Augustine.) Since this concerns eternal blessedness, for which it is joyful to leap across, although it is burdensome to the flesh, he teaches us to pass from the world to God. The one who leaps across the world from a good reputation always incurs the envy and slander of the wicked. Therefore he resolves to remain silent among the wicked, lest he say anything wrong. *Jeduthun.* (Augustine.) “Leaping across them,” that is, those who remain in the world. (Cassiodorus.) At the outset he speaks of restraint of the tongue among blasphemers and slanderers; hence he wishes to know the end, where such things do not exist.

**Verse 2.—** *I said: I will guard my ways, etc.* (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) This psalm urges restraint of the tongue among blasphemers, [Col. 0900B] the wicked, and slanderers, and urges the suppression of quarrels and disputes; such silence is very useful. (Cassiodorus.) *I said:* I deliberated in my heart, where the wise deliberate before they speak. *My ways.* (Jerome.) That is, actions and words, so that I may not sin through foolish or idle speech.

*With my tongue.* (Augustine.) It is not without reason that the tongue is involved in speech, since it slips easily. *I placed a guard on my mouth.* After I passed beyond earthly pleasures, etc., up to the point that he teaches us to beware of imitating this. (Cassiodorus.) *I placed a guard* up to the point that I became silent, etc., up to the one who seeks the cause of contention.

**Verse 3.—** *Because of the good, and my sorrow, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) From proclaiming good things, etc., up to the point that he spoke as one who leaps across. (Augustine.) This means that I unwillingly remained silent before the wicked, etc., up to the point that the actions of one who leaps across are something.

**Verse 4.—** *My heart grew hot within me.* (Augustine.) If the slothful man will be condemned, etc., up to the point that he becomes a greedy steward.

**Verse 5.—** *I spoke.* (Augustine.) Not to an auditor who needed instruction, but to God, who hears me inwardly. *And the number of my days.* (Jerome.) The number of the days that exist now is not real for one who truly leaps across; but to one who clings to them, it appears to be real.

**Verse 6.—** *Behold, you have made them measurable.* (Cassiodorus.) As though, knowing the end and considering the days that exist, he turns his attention to the things he has left behind and compares them with one another. *And his substance, etc.* (Augustine.) The one who sees that this substance is nothing, etc., up to the point that it will be before you. [Col. 0900D]

**Verse 7.—** *Nevertheless.* (Cassiodorus.) Seeing Christ’s coming, he returns to the weakness that he possesses amid his virtues. (Augustine.) The things we have said and believe are great; nevertheless, this is not eternal, but everything is vanity. Desiring the eternal because of its mutability, he reproaches the human life to which he is subject by what he says. Let no one think that the saints are free from temptations. Or, although the days are measurable and although substance is nothing, nevertheless everything is vanity in the rational creature, which according to its varying desires pursues the whole creation. *Nevertheless.* Although I long for eternal things, etc., up to the point whose manner of life is in heaven. *Every human being.* (Augustine.) If evil, he is vain in secular matters; if good, and willing to be with Christ, his life is vanity.

[Col. 0901A] *Nevertheless.* (Augustine.) A diapsalm. He considers how all are under vanity and chance; then he sets against this his expectation of the Lord and asks to be delivered. *He passes by in an image.* (Augustine.) Although he is so devoted to vanity, etc., up to the point that he seeks earthly things amid misery and labor. *He stores up.* (Augustine.) From the other vices the Prophet chose greed in order to show what he means, for greed itself is the root of all evils.

**Verse 8.—** *Expectation.* (Augustine.) Of the first coming or the second, etc., up to the point that it is not in our purses.

**Verse 9.—** *Deliver me from all my iniquities.* (Cassiodorus.) Not merely from some of them, lest he be turned back to those things he has crossed beyond, but from all of them without exception. The human being is imperfect because he has not received what he desires; he is perfect when he knows precisely what is lacking to him.

[Col. 0901B] **Verse 10.—** *I became mute.* (Cassiodorus.) He was treated as an object of reproach, etc., up to the point that it is necessary, because I have failed.

*Remove your scourges from me.* (Augustine.) Since you made me, do not destroy me; only relent, so that I may go forward, not be crushed.

**Verse 11.—** *With rebukes because of iniquity.* These are the rebukes with which you rebuked the human race; yet you rebuked it on account of our deserts, because of our iniquities, and for correction. Otherwise iniquity would remain uncorrected. *You corrected the human being.* (Augustine.) There is an unformed pain that does not amend; there is a formed pain that gives shape through instruction. Such pain is a commandment, that is, it has the function and likeness of a commandment.

**Verse 12.—** *And you made his soul waste away like a spider.* (Augustine.) Dried up from love of virtue and knowledge. [Col. 0901C] As the spider weaves an empty web amid the gathering of temporal things. Or, while it draws iniquity out of itself like a spider, it dies through the expulsion of its entrails. (Cassiodorus.) Or, the spider has a thin body; it does not remain on the ground but is suspended above it, weaving webs by expelling its entrails. So the soul of the converted and afflicted person abandons earthly things and, made thin by the fear of God, completes subtle works. *Nevertheless.* (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) Although he is rebuked and wastes away, he is nevertheless confused by various things through human weakness, unless he contemplates God with a pure mind.

**Verse 14.—** *Hear my prayer.* (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. He asks that aid may be present to him amid the evils of the age and that his sins may be forgiven, so that he may depart with a favorable end. (Cassiodorus.) But since I do not ask these things, etc., up to the point of moving mercy. [Col. 0901D]

*Do not be silent, for I am a sojourner.* (Augustine.) I am already with you, but still a resident alien, because from here I shall pass to eternal things, where I will no longer be a resident alien. *A sojourner with you.* (Cassiodorus.) I have not been received into the city of the devil but into yours; I have been transferred from Babylon to Jerusalem. *Like all my fathers.* Let no one think that anyone is exempt from this condition. *A sojourner.* I abandon my kingdom for yours. *A pilgrim.* I have not yet chosen a dwelling place for myself here.

*Forgive me.* (Cassiodorus.) Here he asks that he may be forgiven, so that he may arrive at judgment with certainty.

## Psalm 39

**Verse 1.—** *For the end: a psalm.* (Cassiodorus.) First he introduces the Church as having awaited the Lord and received him, and as having received from him the New Testament, which many will also follow. Hence he strikes down all superstitions and invites us to the wonders of God.

(Cassiodorus.) Here Christ speaks from his members. [Col. 0902A]

**Verse 2.—** *Waiting, I waited.* (Cassiodorus.) He waits, even though ungrateful; but he waits with expectation. (Augustine.) Authority comes from the ancients, in Abraham and others, etc., up to the point that he is ours through worship, not theirs.

*The Lord.* (Cassiodorus.) Not a human being, who can deceive and be deceived and who needs things together with me. *He inclined.* (Cassiodorus.) He inclined toward me so that he might benefit me; he did not incline me toward himself in order to benefit the wicked also.

**Verse 3.—** *The pit.* (Cassiodorus.) The darkness of iniquities, namely, of unbelief and ignorance, etc., up to the rock opposed to the mud. (Jerome.) In the pit and in the mud are the nations worshiping idols; or, all who love earthly things. [Col. 0902B]

**Verse 4.—** *A song.* (Jerome.) Not a shameful or theatrical song, but one belonging to the New Testament. *They will see.* (Cassiodorus.) The wonders accomplished at the time of the incarnation. (Augustine.) “They will see” refers to what he first said about those who came before; many later peoples will see it.

**Verse 5.—** *The name.* (Cassiodorus.) That is, “Savior.” As though he said: Blessed is the one who does not hope for temporal things from him but for salvation, as his name indicates. In Hebrew, genitives are often doubled in this way; or, blessed is the one whose name is—that is, whose praise is—God, so that he believes salvation comes from him alone, and therefore his hope is in him. *Insanities.* (Cassiodorus.) Idols, which lead one astray from the truth; or insanities in deceptive spectacles. It is plural so that it may be understood of all of them. These things are false, but your works are wondrous: heaven and earth overthrow superstitions.

[Col. 0902C] **Verse 6.—** *Your wonders.* (Augustine.) Peter’s walking upon the waters was a sign, not something belonging to the world—that is, not belonging to the fruits of the world. (Augustine.) True salvation is truthful; false madness is not what it is thought to be. (Jerome.) Earthly things are vain: insanities, anger, and quarrels, etc.

*There is none like you.* (Augustine.) No makers of arts are like you. *I proclaimed.* Here Christ speaks in the Head and in the members. These are the wonders of God, these are the thoughts to which no one is like. (Cassiodorus.) Behold the wonders: the incarnation, the righteousness of preaching, the liberation of human beings from iniquities, the confusion of enemies, and the joy of those who hope. At first, the rough and disordered were prepared so that they might gladly receive Christ’s words. (Augustine.) See the wonders of God. I proclaimed them beforehand through the prophets, and afterward I myself spoke. *They are more numerous than can be counted.* (Jerome, Augustine.) More numerous than the saved [Col. 0902D]; or more numerous than anyone could enumerate; or, while I was speaking, more believed than had believed formerly.

**Verse 7.—** *You did not desire sacrifice and offering.* (Augustine.) When the reality arrived, he did not desire them as words making promises, etc., up to the point that the one who poured them out is deaf and does not hear. *But you perfected ears for me.* That is, you made me understand perfectly what you desired. Or, you prepared a body for me, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews (Hebrews 10): you gave me a body suitable for offering.

**Verse 8.—** *A burnt offering.* You did not even ask for burnt offerings for sin. *For sin.* This stands above “offering,” as with the goat *ἀποπομπαῖος* (*apopompaios*), that is, the scapegoat, which was sent into the desert with the sins of the people; or, “for sin” may consist of two words. [Col. 0903A] *Behold, I come.* (Cassiodorus.) Since sacrifices have ceased, it is clear that Christ is coming.

**Verse 9.—** *In the head of the book it is written concerning me.* Behold, I come at once to do your will, because it is written at the beginning of this book. Or, it was so predetermined with God the Father, who is the head of me, who am the book—that is, the form of righteousness for human beings.

**Verse 10.—** *A great church.* (Augustine.) Throughout the whole world, not small as before; and even if fear arises, it will not prevent him from speaking. *Lord, you know.* (Augustine.) The lips sound to human beings, etc., up to the point that I should not be sluggish in this.

**Verse 11.—** *I did not hide.* (Cassiodorus.) When I was able to benefit others, I did not hide the truth, the promise, or salvation. [Col. 0903B]

**Verse 12.—** *Your mercy.* (Augustine.) Love and fear lead me to you.

**Verse 13.—** *The hairs.* (Augustine.) The hairs are aptly used in comparison with sins. For this reason priests in the Old Testament were shaved, so that they might appear to have put aside the vices of the flesh.

**Verse 14.—** *May it please you.* (Cassiodorus.) “May it please you” signifies the Trinity of persons; “to you,” in the singular, signifies the unity of essence. (Augustine.) He says “may it please you,” not doubting God’s power if the will is present. As though he said: “If you will, you can, Lord.” *Look upon me.* (Cassiodorus.) His regard is our help.

**Verse 16.—** *Those who say to me, “Bravo, bravo.”* (Augustine.) Both the one who speaks good things with an evil intention and the one who deceitfully praises evil are wicked and must be avoided. He spoke of the first: “Those who wish me evil”; of the second: “Those who say to me, ‘Bravo, bravo.’” [Col. 0903C]

**Verse 17.—** *And let them say.* (Cassiodorus.) This is their exultation; for this confession makes Christians rejoice forever.

**Verse 18.—** *But I.* (Cassiodorus.) Christ speaks this from the form of a servant, so that no one might arrogate to himself the glory of the joy mentioned above. *A beggar,* one who is not sufficient for himself. *Do not delay.* (Augustine.) Unless the days had been shortened, etc., up to the point that they now nourish what they have sought.

## Psalm 40

**Verse 1.—** *For the end.* (Jerome.) An understanding for the sons of Korah, so that although poor and suffering, etc., up to the point of the Apostle’s saying, “But for me,” etc. (Augustine.) It is as though this were [Col. 0903D] the voice of one person, of the Head and the Body.

**Verse 2.—** *Blessed.* The one who worships a dead poor man is mocked; but blessed is he. (Augustine.) The Prophet celebrates the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor. (Jerome.) First the Prophet speaks from himself; afterward he introduces Christ. *Who understands.* (Augustine.) Notice the words “who understands,” so that gifts may be given even to those who do not ask. One who gives to a petitioner does well; one who understands the silent person is unquestionably blessed.

**Verse 3.—** *May the Lord preserve him.* (Augustine.) The Prophet rightly wishes for the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor what is a certain promise. *And give him life.* (Augustine.) In the future life, or here through justification.

**Verse 4.—** *May the Lord give help.* (Cassiodorus.) Do not think that the blessed person has rest here: God mitigates his pains, and he prays [Col. 0904A] that human weakness may not be overcome by hardships. It is as though these temporal goods were a bed of rest; but God makes them full of pain so that hope may not be placed in them. *The bed.* (Augustine.) God turns the whole bed—that is, worldly prosperity—into distress. (Cassiodorus.) Here the fearful person himself asks for mercy, because, knowing that he had sinned, he feared with good reason that he would be handed over to these things. But so that the servants of God, afflicted by such things, may not seem abandoned by God, since God himself endured such things, he says: “My enemies said.” Or, the bed of pain. (Augustine.) The flesh in which there is sin, etc., up to the point when Adam was weakened by transgression. *Help.* (Augustine, Jerome.) Help in the weakness of the flesh, which weighs down the soul. *The bed.* (Augustine.) It is some earthly thing which the weak person, etc., up to the point that it serves in place of the house of eternal dwelling. [Col. 0904B]

**Verse 6.—** *My enemies.* (Cassiodorus.) The Lord speaks of his Passion, which belonged to the condition of the needy. (Augustine.) These words concerning my enemies are spoken especially of Christ, but they can also be spoken of his members. Even today tribulation occurs so that the name of Christ may be extinguished; but through his death and that of his followers the Church has grown all the more.

**Verse 7.—** *And if he entered.* (Cassiodorus.) Note that the wicked must be tolerated.

(Cassiodorus.) Not only open enemies, but also those who pretended to be friends.

**Verse 8.—** *He went out.* Away from the bosom of truth: a wicked entrance, a wicked exit. *Together.* (Augustine.) That is, they all whispered against me with one plan. *They whispered.* (Cassiodorus.) They do not dare to disclose their plan because all are partners in the crime, although the authors of crimes are usually few. [Col. 0904C]

**Verse 9.—** *Is it possible?* (Augustine.) Does the one who has the power to lay down his life not also have the power to take it up again?

**Verse 10.—** *I hoped.* (Augustine.) This is said of the members, because the other brothers placed some hope in him, since he appeared to be like the rest. So, too, he says that he is hungry in the poor.

**Verse 11.—** *But you, Lord.* (Augustine.) Concerning the resurrection, which is the glory of the needy, to strengthen the hope of the faithful. *And I will repay them.* (Augustine.) Since they have been scattered throughout the world, this is for admonition, not yet for condemnation.

**Verse 13.—** *But I.* (Augustine.) He affirms what he prayed.

**Verse 14.—** *Blessed.* (Cassiodorus.) A laudatory conclusion after the Passion and resurrection have been expounded. *God of Israel.* [Col. 0904D] (Augustine.) The Jews are our book-carriers, who carry the books for us; we are Israel. Otherwise the pagans would have thought that what is said about Christ and the Church was fabricated, but they are overcome by the testimony of their enemies. *From age to age, etc.* (Cassiodorus.) From the time when all things began to be administered until the future age, in which all things will be eternal.

*So be it.* (Jerome.) The repetition shows that this must be done by everyone. Instead of “so be it,” Hebrew has *amen, amen*, which Aquila translated “truly, truly,” or “faithfully.” Here, according to Jerome, the first book of the Psalter ends.

## Psalm 41

**Verse 1.—** *For the end: an understanding.* (Cassiodorus.) *Korah* is interpreted as “Calvary.” Therefore the sons, [Col. 0905A] etc., up to the point that the insult of the wicked confronts him. (Jerome.) The sons of Korah—that is, the sons of the bald one, etc., up to the word of the boys mocking Elisha.

**Verse 2.—** *As the deer longs, etc.* (Augustine.) This voice is fitting for catechumens and also for all who are still pilgrims.

*The deer.* A deer weighed down by age, with its hair and antlers grown large, draws in a serpent through its nostrils. Burning with the serpent’s poison, it longs most ardently to drink from a spring; after drinking, it casts off its antlers and hair.

**Verse 3.—** *He thirsted.* (Augustine.) He specifies his desire, since one might understand that the deer desires the spring for the sake of drinking or bathing; here it is shown that all desire is directed toward God. *When shall I come?* What is soon for God is slow for human desire. [Col. 0905B] Such a deer, while running, endures those who insult it; hence: “My tears have been my bread.” Even amid prosperity, which he despises, as amid adversity. *Bread.* (Cassiodorus.) Not bitterness or destruction, but bread.

### Psalm 41

**Verse 5 — “I remembered these things.”**  
(AUG.) While they ask, “Where is your God?”, I too have meditated upon all these visible things, and upon my very soul, in order that through those outward things I might find the invisible things of God. Behold the interpretation of the title. “I poured out.” (Ibid.) In order to understand and attain it, I stretched [my soul] out beyond itself. “I poured out.” (CASS.) Or, “I rejoiced.” “My soul melted within me”: not outside itself, but, pierced within itself, it returns to itself. Although I do not visibly see God, I nevertheless consider that through the Church, in which the saints are admirable, I shall arrive at the heavenly Jerusalem, seized by the sweetness of the angelic praise that is received in the mind. “Into the place of the tabernacle.” (AUG.) God’s tabernacle on earth, etc., up to “that is, of those rejoicing in eternal refreshment.” “With the voice of exultation.” (Ibid.) Something sweet to the heart sounds forth from the eternal festival; hence the stag is carried away to the springs of water and is soothed. But because the world resounds around us and the flesh weighs down the soul, comparing this sadness with those pleasant things, he says:

**Verse 6 — “Why are you sad?” etc.**  
(CASS.) He speaks of the disturbances against which reason strengthens the sensitive soul by hope in God. “Why do you trouble me?” (AUG.) If you investigate, there is nothing in the world for which you ought to do this; rather, hope still for the saving remedy, even if not now, fully in the future. “Hope.” (CASS.) Or, he can hope because, while still in the present, “I shall confess,” that is, I shall do penance for my sins, so that I may not oppose you.

**Verse 7 — “To myself.”**  
Turning toward God, he says that his disturbances arise from himself, while their end comes from God; therefore his hope is in him. This is what “to myself,” or “from myself,” means. (CASS.) Behold, the one who above was correcting the soul according to the condition of humanity now returns and says that the soul is troubled by itself; if the vices of the flesh did not exist, it would remain tranquil. Behold from what diversity a human being is composed. As if he said: “Therefore,” that is, because of the soul’s disturbances, “I shall remember.” (AUG.) That is, I hasten to you because you exclude all evils. Behold the remedy by which he may escape disturbances; therefore, indicating what he should remember, he adds: “From the land of the Jordan,” where the Lord consecrated baptism, in which the humbled are washed and become fruitful soil. [Col. 0905C] (CASS.) Remembering these things, he is not troubled by evils. “Therefore I shall remember.” (AUG.) Because my soul is troubled within me, therefore I shall remember, etc. No one runs toward forgiveness unless he displeases himself, unless he confesses himself a sinner; this is signified by Hermon. No one confesses unless he humbles himself; this is signified by the little mountain. “Jordan.” (Ibid.) Descent. Descend, therefore, so that you may be raised up. (CASS.) In the Jordan the Lord consecrated baptism, in which the humbled are washed and become fruitful soil, producing thirtyfold, sixtyfold, and a hundredfold fruit (Matt. 13). “Hermon.” (AUG.) A small mountain near the Jordan, etc., up to “because remembrance of God is found not in the proud but in the humble.”

**Verse 8 — “Deep calls to deep.”**  
(Ibid.) It is fitting that I should remember, etc., up to “and because of all these things I pray in adversity”; and this is: “With me is prayer.” (Ibid.) Or, “deep calls to deep,” that is, the judgment that God brought upon the sinner, etc., up to “because he fears the judgments.” “The cataracts.” Literally, cataracts are the mouths of rivers.

**Verse 9 — “By day.”**  
(Ibid.) That is, in prosperity, etc., up to “from which we may live in adversity.” “With me is prayer.” Prayer is with me in my disturbances, and this is “with me.”

**Verse 10 — “Why have you forgotten?”**  
(CASS.) Why do you now allow me to be harassed by these miseries? He saw the sweetness of his homeland and shuddered at the dangers of the world.

**Verse 11 — “While my bones are crushed.”**  
(AUG.) The bones seem to be broken when the virtue of patience is afflicted, which the wicked ridicule. This is that reproach: “While it is said to me, ‘Where is he?’”—either he does not exist, or he does not care about you.

### Psalm 42

**For the end, a psalm of David.**  
(AUG.) Of the Body of Christ, which here groans among the weeds, that is, among the wicked, sharing many things with them—birth, death, prosperity, and adversity—yet, since it does not share their cause of merit, it cries out: “Judge me,” etc. (Ibid.) This psalm is against afflictions, lest they themselves draw us away from God. (CASS.) He complains of association with the wicked and prays for separation.

**Verse 1 — “Judge me.”**  
(Ibid.) He does not ask that his sins be examined, which would be dangerous, but that his cause be distinguished from that of the ungodly, so that he may be with the elect; therefore he adds: “And distinguish me.” The unholy nation is wicked and deceitful; from them he is separated in judgment, and even now, lest he be corrupted by them.

**Verse 2 — “Why do I go about sorrowful?”**  
(AUG.) He seeks the cause of sadness, which is sin, just as righteousness is the cause of joy. Isaiah speaks because of sin: “I made him sorrowful for a little while”; for thus God punishes.

**Verse 3 — “Send forth your light.”**  
(CASS.) For when it comes, all sadness of confusion will be removed. (AUG.) Because we already possess the pledge of certainty, since those very things—that is, light and truth—have led the present Church away from sins; and she is the tabernacle.

**Verse 4 — “And I shall enter.”**  
As the high priest enters the Holy of Holies. (CASS.) “And I shall enter”: this concerns the final joy, for which the one who above was sad gives praise in tribulation, and therefore strengthens himself.

**Verse 5 — “I shall confess to you with the harp.”**  
(AUG.) Whoever does God’s commandments and does not suffer confesses with the psaltery; whoever both does them and suffers—which arises from the lower nature—confesses with the harp, which resounds from below, just as the psaltery does from above. “With the harp.” (CASS.) Behold, the one who above was sad because of the world’s evils makes joy for himself from understanding the good. “Why do you trouble me?” (Ibid.) He frequently and emphatically persuades us that worldly sadness must be avoided, since it extinguishes patience, charity, and hope and throws the whole of life into confusion. “The salvation of my countenance.” (AUG.) And elsewhere: “Have mercy on me,” etc., up to “almsgiving and prayer, which fly to God on those two wings.”

### Psalm 43

**Verse 1 — “For understanding.”**  
(AUG.) Let them not seek that this be done for themselves in such a way, etc., up to “and let these things not be loved.” (CASS.) He distinguishes God’s benefits: those given to beginners in the world and to the perfected in heaven.

To make it more remarkable that the present should be abandoned, he recalls the past.

**Verse 2 — “God, with our ears.”**  
(AUG., CASS.) First he says, “God,” as a happy person or one gravely afflicted is accustomed to do.

“We have heard.” So that the matter may have greater credibility and not be thought doubtful.

“Our fathers.” Not young men, so that they may appear to be our true ancestors, who would speak with certainty about what they themselves knew.

“The work that you did,” etc. (Ibid.) Although he is always at work, he is said to work when he manifests some sign of newness.

**Verse 4 — “But your right hand.”**  
(AUG.) That is, the good success that you gave them. “And your arm,” etc. (Ibid.) That is, strength; and “illumination,” that is, wise counsel. You did all this from your benevolence.

**Verse 5 — “You are yourself my king and my God.”**  
(AUG.) Times have changed; the author has not changed.

**Verse 7 — “For I shall not hope in my bow.”**  
(CASS.) The lesser human power, since it is of less use in war.

“The sword.” The greater power, which is believed to have greater force in war. (AUG.) Or, “My sword will not save me, but you,” because even in this age you saved us, lest they drag us after them, and you put them to shame; therefore we shall then be praised.

**Verse 8 — “You saved,” etc.**  
(AUG.) Note also that statements made in the past are to be understood as referring to the future.

**Verse 10 — “But now you have rejected us.”**  
(CASS.) A division between sections. He enumerates the evils that the good have suffered here, though they have not forgotten God. (CASS.) He magnifies the evils in order to obtain the judge’s benevolence. “You have confounded us,” while here we are held in reproach by the wicked. (AUG.) These things are truly future, etc., up to “this is fasting not from abstinence but from luxury.”

**Verse 11 — “You turned us away.”**  
(CASS.) On behalf of those who are failing. Or, “to turn away” means to flee from an enemy; hence: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another.”

“They plundered us.” This happens to those who have been put to flight: those unable to resist their enemies fall prey to them.

**Verse 12 — “You gave us like sheep for food.”**  
(CASS.) Those who persevere in the faith. Here are different martyrs, that is, different kinds of martyrdom: some are given as food to wild beasts, others are handed over to the nations in slavery. Hence he says, “like sheep for food,” where the slaughter of some is indicated.

**Verse 13 — “You sold your people without a price.”**  
(AUG.) While they are given over to foreigners and no one acquires them. This happens for testing or correction; either no one is acquired for them, or, if someone is, there are nevertheless few.

**Verse 14 — “A reproach to our neighbors.”**  
(CASS.) A grievous affliction is inflicted by neighbors, since what is imposed by those standing around is not described as something passing. “A derision to those around us.” (CASS.) Derision is confused joy, proclaiming mockery with immoderate hilarity. Contempt is abject worthlessness.

**Verse 15 — “In the likeness of the nations.”**  
(Ibid.) They were placed among the nations in the likeness of Christ when they inflicted comparable punishments upon them.

**Verse 17 — “Of the one who reproaches.”**  
(Ibid.) To reproach is to curse someone to his face; to revile is to disparage someone who is absent and bite him deceitfully.

**Verse 18 — “They came upon us.”**  
(Ibid.) Because they were not in us through guilt.

**Verse 19 — “It did not turn away.”**  
(Ibid.) Thus, it did not turn back, even though at some point he descended in contemplation of the Godhead. “You turned aside.” (AUG.) Our paths were in the pleasures and prosperities of the world; but you took them away from their road and showed the narrow way that leads to life. [Col. 0908C] (HIER.) Or, “you turned aside,” that is, you made our works depend upon your law. Or, “you did not turn aside” (another reading), that is, you did not permit our paths to turn aside and wander. “Our paths,” that is, our works; “from your way,” that is, from your law. Therefore, because you humbled us.

**Verse 20 — “The shadow of death.”**  
(AUG.) Or, this mortality is the shadow of death; true death, however, is condemnation with the devil.

**Verse 21 — “If we have forgotten the name of our God.”**  
(Ibid.) This is the understanding of the sons of Korah: despite all these evils, they do not forget God, knowing that God will investigate these things.

**Verse 22 — “He knows.”**  
(Ibid.) God is said to know both what he knows and what he makes you know. “He knows,” because he will investigate for your sake, so that you may find yourself and give thanks to the one who made you, as happened in Peter, who tested what he was able to do. “For your sake we are put to death.” (CASS.) Not for our crimes, but so that your faith may increase among the nations.

**Verse 23 — “Rise up.”**  
(Ibid.) He prays for help, so that at the time of resurrection he may assist those afflicted here. (AUG.) Until now they have not forgotten; and so that we may persevere: “Rise up,” because “for your sake we are put to death.” (AUG., HIER.) Although they know that Christ does not sleep and that he has risen for himself, they nevertheless pray that he may rise through faith—not for themselves, but for the nations that think he is dead. For if they too believed that he had risen, they would not persecute those who believe in him; they themselves would also believe. (AUG.) Or, “rise up”: strengthen.

“You sleep.” You seem to neglect us. Why this is so, even if we do not know, you know: either because of guilt or for our benefit. If because of guilt, would that it were absent; if for our benefit, would that it were present. You repel some because you withdraw your face, that is, your knowledge, from them; you sleep with respect to some who groan over evils.

**Verse 24 — “Why do you forget?”**  
That is, you do not give the spirit of strength, without which they are helpless. “And affliction.” (CASS.) Because you do not mitigate it, etc., up to “those who easily yield to illicit impulses and cling to earthly things.”

**Verse 26 — “Rise up, Lord.”**  
Here “rise up” is placed without “sleeping,” which pertains to the resurrection, in which lies the hope of all the faithful; in which human captivity is destroyed; through which we have been helped and liberated. “Our belly is on the earth.” (AUG.) Whoever bends his knees to the earth has something by which he may humble himself further; but whoever is humbled still more, so that his belly also clings to the earth, has no further degree of humiliation. He therefore expresses extreme humiliation, so that, since he has reached the lowest point, God’s mercy may now be present. Or, he laments those who are “the belly,” that is, carnal, and who have clung to— that is, consented to—the wicked.

### Psalm 44

**Verse 1 — “For the end,” etc.**  
(AUG.) An epithalamium, that is, a praise of the bridal chamber. A song “for those who are to be changed” and “for the beloved”—that is, for bride and bridegroom—is written for the sons of Korah, so that they may show reverence. For here the one through whom they will be changed is described, since the praise of bridegroom and bride is sung here. (CASS.) The prophet promises that he will pour forth God’s proclamations.

**Verse 2 — “My heart has uttered.”**  
(AUG., HIER.) The prophet speaks inwardly, etc., up to “before what he is going to make exists.” The Father’s counsel, however, is the Word.

“Good.” Through which all good things were made. “I speak.” That is, I bring forth the Word. The same meaning is present here as before; but in the Word itself he says that all God’s works exist. Hence: “What was made in him was life,” so that there is nothing in the work that was not first in the counsel. Of this it is said: “God spoke once.”

“Pen.” He compares the Word not with sound, which passes away, but with writing, which remains. Or, “swiftly,” because there is not one thing after another, but everything together in one eternal Word.

“Swiftly.” The power of prophecy, which does not think under human torment about what it discloses to others from the divine mystery.

**Verse 3 — “You are beautiful in form.”**  
(CASS.) He begins with the bridegroom’s praise, first from his form. “He blessed.” The prophet spoke the preceding words in God’s person, but these in his own; or he spoke everything from himself. Or, he pours forth the Word, being the one who sings a hymn to God.

“I speak of works.” (AUG.) For the praise of the one from whom they come. “Tongue, pen,” because what I say, I also write. Or, “swiftly,” because what I write is soon to come.

(CASS.) “Upon your lips,” because when he spoke, the world received the grace of reconciliation.

**Verse 4 — “Gird yourself.”**  
(Ibid.) Here he praises him for his power; and you, being such a one, gird yourself.

**Verse 5 — “With your beauty and your splendor.”**  
Beauty refers to his humanity, in which he appeared to the world; splendor refers to his divinity, by which he adorns all things.

“Pay attention.” Take pity on the perishing human being and look upon him.

“Prosper.” Liberating human beings.

“Go forth.” From the Virgin’s womb as a bridegroom; or from those who have been conquered to conquer others.

“Reign.” Display your power in the faith of human beings, you who have always reigned. And do this because through yourself and through your followers you teach the truth, by which you destroy our falsehood. And because you are gentle in bearing with the wicked, just as he prayed for his enemies, so also for his own. And because he displayed the righteousness of life. And because he will lead you without stumbling through the course of your whole life, or from people to people.

“Wonderfully.” Because all will wonder, or because he will perform miracles.

**Verse 6 — “Peoples shall fall beneath you.”**  
(AUG.) That is, many of your enemies will submit themselves to you, whether by reason or by will. This is what the title said: “For those who will be changed, from the sons of Korah.” “Into the hearts.” (CASS.) Of your enemies, so that they may become friends, as Saul did.

**Verse 7 — “Your throne.”**  
(Ibid.) Here he praises him from judgment; a throne pertains to judgment. “A rod.” (Ibid.) The rule of divine equity, which is truly straight and never bends: it governs the righteous and strikes the wicked. (AUG.) Let no one presume too much upon mercy or flatter himself, because the rod of uprightness, if it governs some, crushes others: it governs the spiritual and crushes the carnal.

**Verse 8 — “You have loved.”**  
(Ibid.) Or, because you loved righteousness, etc., these rewards were given in return: he made you king, giving you the name that is above every name.

“And you hated.” If a human being hates iniquity within himself, he acts together with God. God hates iniquity; you too must hate it.

“O God.” (AUG.) In Greek it is plainly written twice: one is vocative and the other nominative. This is the anointed one; that is the stone whom Jacob anointed.

**Verse 9 — “Myrrh,” etc.**  
(CASS.) Here the prophet praises the bridegroom on account of his wife and adornment, first on account of adornment. (AUG.) “Myrrh and drop.” Fragrances are properly used for the bridal chamber, etc., up to “that is, redemption through the water of baptism.” “Ivory.” (HIER.) In ivory chastity is signified: what was previously dark becomes bright through saws and files; so the saints, polished through the cutting and abrasion of various punishments, become radiant through the variety of their virtues. “Daughters of kings.” (AUG.) Of earthly kings, not caring about the honor of their fathers, etc., up to “and received them for the raising up of offspring.”

**Verse 10 — “The queen stood,” etc.**  
(CASS.) Here he commends the bridegroom through his wife. “In variety.” (Ibid.) Although there is unity in charity, she is nevertheless adorned with gold—that is, the apostles’ teaching—with scarlet, the martyrs—with gems, the virgins—and with purple, the penitents.

**Verse 11 — “Hear, daughter.”**  
(CASS.) The bride’s praise is more subdued, but fourfold: from her form, her glory, the young women, and her offspring. (AUG.) “Hear, daughter.” The prophet addresses the queen like one of the fathers. The Jews saw and killed; you hear the Gospel, and by believing you will see God—here through an image, in the future face to face. Or, hear the prophecies that foretold the incarnation, and see them fulfilled.

**Verse 12 — “And the king will desire.”**  
(CASS.) Here he praises her for her form.

**Verse 13 — “Tyre.”**  
(CASS.) Through Tyre, which was near Judea, the nations are signified; hence the Canaanite woman is a figure of the Church. (CASS.) “Of Tyre,” that is, of the nations, using the part for the whole. “With gifts.” (AUG.) So that they may offer themselves, etc., namely, the nations that are in the distress of sins.

**Verse 14 — “All her glory.”**  
(CASS.) He now praises the bride from her glory, just as above he praised the bridegroom from his power. “From within.” (AUG.) Or, inwardly. Let almsgiving therefore be done in secret, where God sees. Or, not in a man-made circumcision, as in the old law, but in spiritual things. “With fringes.” (CASS.) The edge of the garment signifies the end of the world or of the human being. “Golden.” Not gilded, as above, but golden, because at the end there is complete perfection, where charity is found in its fullness.

**Verse 15 — “They shall be led to the king.”**  
(Ibid.) Here the bride is praised through her companions, just as above through judgment. “They shall be led,” through timely preaching. “After her.” (Ibid.) First unity is mentioned; afterward the parts are separately enumerated when it says: “Virgins and those near her.”

**Verse 17 — “Instead of your fathers, sons have been born to you.”**  
(Ibid.) Or, instead of the ancient fathers, the worshipers of idols, the apostles were born—leaders of preaching. (AUG.) Or, after the prophets came the apostles, and after the apostles came others.

This psalm is sung for the feast of the Blessed Virgin Mary, because what is said here generally about the Church can be referred particularly to Mary. It is also sung for virgins, because it says: “Virgins shall be led to the king.” And for the apostles, because it says: “Sons have been born to you.” It is likewise sung concerning the Lord’s Nativity, because it treats of the praise of bridegroom and bride and of the marriage of Christ and the Church, whose betrothal took place in the incarnation of the Word.

### Psalm 45

**Verse 1 — “For the end.”**  
(CASS.) A psalm of David, of some faithful person from Judea, so that the testimony may be more certain.

“For hidden things.” For the manifestation of hidden things: that God is human; that the promised salvation belongs to both peoples; that blindness has happened to Israel; that the apostles passed over to the nations; and that there is peace on earth. Hence: “They shall beat their swords into plowshares and their spears into pruning hooks” (Isa. 2).

“Sons of Korah.” (CASS.) Sons of the cross. He speaks of hidden things, that is, of Christ’s coming.

**Verse 2 — “Our God.”**  
(CASS., AUG.) It is shown that all hope must be placed in the Lord’s coming, including in the apostles’ passage to the nations. “They found us exceedingly.” (AUG.) For we were fleeing from them. Or, they found us exposed through Adam. “Exceedingly,” because the one who liberates is all the more powerful.

**Verse 3 — “The earth shall be troubled, and the mountains shall be moved,” etc.**  
(CASS.) Judea, as though dry, without idolatry, surrounded by the bitterness of the nations. Or, “the sea.” (AUG.) The world.

“The heart of the sea.” The savagery of the nations.

**Verse 4 — “They sounded and were troubled,” etc.**  
The nations contradicting, or the apostles preaching.

“And their waters were troubled.” The reference is according to the sense, not according to the wording: that is, the waters of the sea, namely the peoples, or their doctrines, which were made foolish when the Savior’s teaching flashed forth. Hence: “They were swallowed up,” etc. And this is the rod of Moses, which swallowed the rods of the magicians.

**Verse 5 — “The force of the river.”**  
(CASS.) A division between sections. Because the Church is founded upon Christ, to whom nations and kingdoms are subjected. (AUG.) As if he said: “Thus the sea rages; but amid these waves and sounds those who have fled for refuge to that shelter are not afraid.”

**Verse 6 — “He will help her.”**  
(CASS.) Or, “with his face,” that is, by the demonstration of his assistance, when he makes his help known by helping her. “At dawn.” At the very beginning of good work; and this “early,” that is, through the illumination of the Holy Spirit, who is light like the day.

**Verse 7 — “He gave.”**  
As a great reward. “A voice.” Preaching, at which the earthly being trembled. He will tremble from fear of the Judge.

**Verse 8 — “The Lord of hosts.”**  
(Ibid.) He briefly defines what Christ is. “With us.” As if he said: He who sent the angels has now himself come and is with us, because he is our protector with us. Therefore: “Come,” as though I were inviting you, already secure. “Our.” This belongs only to the sons of the cross. “The God of Jacob.” He who gave us as much as he gave Jacob; for he is not God only of Jacob.

**Verse 9 — “Come and see.”**  
(Ibid.) A division between sections. The mighty works of the incarnation. “He placed.” As signs, for calling the people. “Wonders.” Such as the Virgin’s childbirth, the star, and the other events. “Taking away wars.” (AUG.) Because through his coming idolatry and the superstition of the whole world perished; or, at that time the world was pacified because of his presence.

**Verse 11 — “Be still.”**  
(Ibid.) If the weapons have been burned, be still, since you have nothing with which to fight.

### Psalm 46

**Verse 2 — “All nations.”**  
(AUG.) As if he said: “The children insult, saying, ‘Bald one, bald one.’ You are all the nations to which grace has passed: clap your hands,” etc. The nations to which grace has passed, and which he called to faith in the preceding psalm, he now invites to praise.

**Verse 3 — “Most high.”**  
(HIER.) Powerful in whatever he wills. “Terrible.” (REMIG.) Because he will judge in power.

**Verse 4 — “He subjected peoples to us.”**  
(CASS.) This applies to faithful human beings, to whom all outsiders are subject; or, he subjected to us those who were to be joined to us. “Peoples,” that is, the Jews. “To us.” (Ibid.) Namely, to the universal Church. This can be said of all the faithful, to whom outsiders are subject. “Under his feet.” (Ibid.) Understand the feet as the preachers, to whom the peoples are subject. (AUG.) “Under his feet.” The Church has been so exalted that it holds beneath its feet those who do not yet believe.

**Verse 5 — “He chose our inheritance,” etc.**  
Or, in the person of the apostles: he chose to give us his inheritance, consisting of many peoples, so that we might cultivate it, striking their hearts with the sword of preaching and destroying their wickedness. [Col. 0913A] “Inheritance.” (AUG.) The heavenly inheritance is the beauty of the Christian people, in which he will be beautiful, shining like the sun, although now he is despised. “The beauty of Jacob, whom,” etc. That is, those resembling Jacob, or those marked by Jacob, who give earthly things for heavenly things, as Jacob did. This was by God’s grace, because he loved him, rejecting Esau.

**Verse 6 — “He ascended.”**  
(CASS.) The division between sections. The ascension and kingdom of God are described; hence he earnestly urges us to sing psalms. “With jubilation.” (AUG.) The joy of the apostles as they marveled, etc., up to “which can neither be silenced nor expressed.”

**Verse 7 — “Sing psalms.”**  
(CASS.) Praise him by your works. It is greatly salutary that this is repeated so frequently, because God is the one who creates and the king who governs what he has created.

**Verse 8 — “All.”**  
(Ibid.) Not as Jupiter belongs to Crete or Mars to Thrace. “Wisely.” He teaches how one should sing psalms. Formerly they sang without understanding while they worshiped stones. (AUG.) No one acts wisely concerning what he does not understand.

**Verse 9 — “He will reign.”**  
(Ibid.) This prophecy has now been fulfilled: “God sits upon his holy throne.” “Holy throne.” (AUG.) Thrones, Powers, and saints.

**Verse 10 — “The princes of the peoples.”**  
(CASS.) The first members of all the nations came together by believing in Christ, because, after the Jews were expelled, the nations succeed to the place of Abraham’s sons, possessing the promise, since the Jews became proud. (HIER., CASS.) Or, “strong gods,” namely the apostles, whom neither death nor life will separate from the love of Christ. “Raised up,” by miracles and teaching.

### Psalm 47

**Verse 1 — “A psalm or praise of a song for the sons of Korah, a second,” etc.**  
(AUG.) On the first day God made light, etc., up to “of which the sons of Korah sing here.” (CASS.) He speaks of the foundation of the city, which he describes in praise. (AUG.) He commends the city, etc., up to “from eternal stability.”

**Verse 2 — “On his holy mountain,” etc.**  
(Ibid.) This is that mountain, etc., up to “upon which the Church is founded.”

**Verse 3 — “Founded in exultation.”**  
(HIER.) As if he said: She who was formerly subject to curses, etc., up to “he himself is Christ, who spreads joys throughout the whole Church.” “The sides of Mount Zion.” (AUG.) Whoever clings to someone is called his side, etc., up to “likewise, every evil will be spread from the north,” etc.

**Verse 4 — “In her houses.”**  
Or, “in her steps,” that is, according to degrees of merit, because in each one he will give a distinct knowledge of himself. “When he receives her.” To protect her—and what need is there? Because kings are against her. But seeing through faith that this city is so worthy, they were astonished, etc.

**Verse 5 — “The kings.”**  
(AUG., CASS.) The princes of the Jews. “Assembled.” By Herod’s inquiry concerning the place of the birth. “They came together.” Concordantly saying: “In Bethlehem of Judah,” according to the Scriptures.

**Verse 6 — “Seeing.”**  
What they had read in the prophets. “They were astonished.” At such great glory, not lightly or casually. [Col. 0914A] “But they were troubled.” Because of sin. “And they were moved.” Toward faith; and such was their fear that the body trembled.

**Verse 7 — “There were pains like those of a woman in labor.”**  
The pains of repentance, when they saw these things; but:

**Verse 8 — “With a vehement spirit,”**  
That is, of Herod. “You will crush the ships of Tarshish.” Because the ships in Tarsus of Cilicia, which were believed to have carried the Magi back to their homeland, were wrecked by Herod. “Tarshish.” (AUG.) A region of Cilicia named from Tarsus, etc., up to “having passed through everything, he concludes.” Therefore:

**Verse 9 — “As we have heard.”**  
In the city of the Lord of hosts, because there he appoints angelic guardians. “He repeats.” In the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God. That is, the Catholic Church, lest a gathering of heretics usurp this name for itself. But lest it be thought temporal, [Col. 0914B] he adds: “God founded her forever.” Not for an hour, as Moses’ tabernacle formerly was.

**Verse 10 — “We have received your mercy, O God.”**  
(CASS.) Giving thanks for Christ’s coming, he teaches that the degrees of the Church must be distributed, through which the Savior may be recognized. “In the midst of the temple.” Jerusalem. Those who despise the one who appeared in their midst are accused more gravely. This signifies the incarnation of Christ, who, insofar as he is human, was presented in the temple.

**Verse 11 — “Your right hand.”**  
(CASS.) The righteous are placed on this side.

(AUG.) “We have received, O God.” In what order she was founded, or what we have heard and seen. “Your temple.” (Ibid.) That is, the people who do not receive mercy, among whom there are many, so that no grains seem to exist; nevertheless there are some, according to the name. “According to the name.” (CASS.) Which has been spread everywhere, because there is no one—even if he does not know the worship—who does not submit himself to this name. Or, “according to the name”: that is, just as the reverence of your name, etc., up to “your mercy has justified many, and all praise you.”

**Verse 12 — “Let her rejoice.”**  
(AUG.) Although the righteous labor among thorns, etc., up to “their task now is to gather; God’s is to separate.” “Mount Zion, and let them rejoice.” (CASS.) The Church, which is in the contemplation of the people. “Daughters of Judah, because of your judgments, Lord.” Holy women. Through Judah their nation is indicated, which exists because of Christ, who is from Judah; and let these women rejoice, so that the Church may exist in both sexes. (AUG.) The cause of joy is the future judgments, where they know that they will come to blessedness. Those who are within should rejoice; you who are outside, surround her.

**Verse 13 — “Surround her.”**  
By showing honor. “Embrace her.” With charity. “Tell it in her towers.” “Set your hearts upon her.” (CASS.) Preach to others in the concord of the apostles, etc., up to “lest through joy they grow slack and sluggish.”

**Verse 14 — “In her strength.”**  
(AUG.) The strength of the city is charity, which nothing conquers; hence Solomon: “Love is strong as death.” (CASS.) He urges them to set their hearts upon the Church’s strength. “Distribute her houses, so that you may recount them to another generation.” That is, distinct offices, etc., up to “whom the Lord first chose.”

**Verse 15 — “For this is,” etc.**  
This is what must be recounted: a brief statement, but one that embraces everything. “Forever,” against those who made temporal human beings into gods.

### Psalm 48

**For the end, a psalm, etc.**  
(CASS.) The prophet speaks of lovers of the world and of Christ the redeemer—not of those lovers, but of those who despise the world—so that one cast down in the world may not esteem the exalted. (AUG.) Those who worship God, etc., up to “he makes them attentive to new and remarkable things.”

**Verse 2 — “Hear this, all nations.”**  
(CASS.) I exclude no one, etc., up to “when the weeds will be separated from the wheat, and the sheep from the goats.”

**Verse 3 — “All you earthborn.”**  
(AUG.) I withhold speech from no one. Let the heir of the earth hear, because of judgment; the righteous, because of the kingdom.

**Verse 4 — “My mouth shall speak.”**  
(CASS.) He commends what is to be said. Wisdom concerns divine things; prudence concerns instruction in morals. In these two, every divine discourse is indicated.

**Verse 5 — “I shall incline.”**  
(HIER.) I shall humble myself before the truth speaking within, which teaches me to speak in parables so that it may not be open to everyone.

**Verse 6 — “Why should I fear?”**  
(CASS.) He begins to relate what he promised, saying that Christ will not redeem the ungodly. Here the prophet, acting in his own person as the representative of the general cause, asks the reason for the condemnation and fear of the wicked, which is iniquity. (AUG.) “Why should I fear?” As if he said: There is nothing for me to fear, since avoiding iniquity lies within my power. It is for this alone that one will fear on the last day, which will be evil for the condemned, not for the righteous. “Heels.” (Ibid.) He alludes to the words, etc., up to “that is, he will oppress and make fearful.”

**Verse 7 — “Those who trust.”**  
These are the ones who trust, etc., up to “in which they are so foolish.”

**Verse 8 — “A brother cannot redeem.”**  
If a brother—that is, Christ—does not redeem, etc., up to “because such a person does not offer appeasement to God.”

**Verse 9 — “And he will still live.”**  
(Ibid.) After the end of life he will live according to the soul, because the soul will not perish with the body but will be preserved for suffering until, having received the body, he is tormented in both.

**Verse 11 — “He will not see.”**  
(Ibid.) That is, he does not understand, etc., up to “when the wise person passes from life.” Or, “the foolish.” (Ibid.) One who does not pay attention. “The fool.” One who, even if he pays attention, does not guard himself. “Riches.” (CASS.) Because of which they did evil. “Their own,” which are not according to God.

**Verse 12 — “They called their names.”**  
(AUG.) Heirs who become drunk at the tombs of the dead in their memory; yet not even a drop reaches the tongue of the one burning in hell.

**Verse 13 — “And a human being, when,” etc.**  
In this and in other matters alike, a human being does not understand. Or, God is not to be blamed for this: he did not understand his dignity and did not act intelligently, but, having lost reason, was compared with beasts—not in another matter, but in wisdom.

**Verse 14 — “This is their way.”**  
(CASS.) Here he gathers all that has been said into one conclusion. “Way,” that is, life, because it leads to death. “A stumbling-block.” A goad and pain, etc., up to: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me.” “They will be pleased with their mouth.” (AUG.) Although they are such, etc., up to “and they are worse than those who are openly wicked.”

**Verse 15 — “Like sheep.”**  
(CASS.) A division between sections. What distress is to be repaid to the ungodly. They boast, but it is already certain to me that they have been placed in hell. Sheep remain after their wool has been lost; so, in these people, punishment finds something to torment without consuming their substance. “Death.” (AUG.) As Christ is life, so the devil is death; he is their shepherd, as they are sheep whom he leads to the pastures of death. “He will feed upon them.” (CASS.) From the likeness of beasts, etc., up to “he will lead them from punishment to punishment.” “In the morning.” (AUG.) For now it is night, while the merits of the righteous are not apparent and the wicked’s happiness is, as it were, proclaimed. “Their form will grow old in hell.” (AUG.) However much glory they seemed to possess, etc., up to: “They have been expelled from their glory.”

**Verse 17 — “Do not fear.”**  
(CASS.) A division between sections. An admonition not to fear the powerful, who leave everything behind with the light. For why these things are permitted to sinners is a common complaint. “When he becomes rich.” For even the despised possess these things. “Glory.” In worldly honors. “House.” Because not only he himself, but all who belong to him, are included.

**Verse 19 — “He will be blessed.”**  
(Ibid.) He will be blessed not because of a good deed, but because of pleasures, through the favor of those living luxuriously, who wish shepherds well amid their banquets. “He will confess to you when you have done good to him.” (AUG.) Despise the confession produced by prosperity; that confession is of great merit which the force of pain does not remove.

**Verse 20 — “To the generations of his fathers.”**  
(Ibid.) Those who follow the worst fathers will be condemned in their company.

“And a human being.” (CASS.) He repeats the human being’s deformity, so that the wicked may cease from the wicked.

### Psalm 49

**Verse 1 — “A psalm of Asaph.”**  
(HIER.) Asaph means “assembly” in Latin; in Greek, *synagoga* means “assembly.” Here the faithful assembly speaks, awaiting Christ, through which the unbelieving Jews are more thoroughly refuted. (CASS.) Asaph, about to introduce God’s voice concerning the change of sacrifices, first treats of both advents: by the first he invites, by the second he terrifies. “God of gods.” (CASS.) Lest anyone form a mediocre estimation of the incarnation, etc., up to “by designation, like the false gods Jupiter and Venus.” “He spoke and summoned the earth.” (AUG.) Through himself, through heralds. “From the rising of the sun to its setting.” (CASS.) As if he said, etc., up to: “The law will go forth from Zion, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.”

**Verse 2 — “From Zion, the perfection of his beauty,” etc.**  
(AUG.) The beauty of the Gospel began, etc., up to “so that they might be witnesses in Jerusalem and throughout the whole earth.”

### Verses 3–4

“Fire shall blaze before him, and around him.” (The same.) It will go before him; therefore punishment should terrify those whom rewards do not attract, etc., up to: “It will accompany the wicked to hell.” A violent storm. “He will summon heaven above and the earth.” (Cassiodorus.) Not the wind, etc., up to: first he summoned everyone together indiscriminately, [Col. 0917A] then he will summon them in order to distinguish them. “To distinguish his people.” (Augustine.) At first he summoned those mingled together from the rising of the sun to its setting; then, however, in order to distinguish them.

### Verse 5

“Gather his holy ones to him.” (The same.) The Prophet, seeing future events, etc., up to: this is said of the wicked, concerning whom he did not fill his hand. “Those who establish his covenant over sacrifices.” (The same.) The New Testament over the Old, etc., up to: those who value works of charity more highly than the sacrifices of animals.

### Verse 6

“And the heavens shall declare his righteousness,” etc. (The same.) The heavens have already announced this righteousness of God to us, etc., up to: and if they are now mingled together, it is because God is a just judge.

### Verse 7

“Hear, my people,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) The voice of Christ, so that, with the sacrifices of animals abandoned, a sacrifice of praise may be offered. (Augustine.) Or he repeats the same thought under another word: “Hear” [Col. 0917B] as Israel—that is, as one who sees God—and “I will testify”: namely, “I am your God.”

“Your God.” (Augustine.) First he says simply, “I am God.” Afterwards he says, “I am your God.” It is as though he said: Even if I am not your God, I am nevertheless God. I am God by my own goodness, but because of your wickedness I am not your God. “I am.” (Cassiodorus.) Being is proper to the Godhead. “Hear, Israel.” (The same.) It is as though he said: If you are Israel—that is, if you see me—you must not neglect to hear. He is the universal God, but specifically your God.

### Verse 8

“But burnt offerings.” (Augustine.) If the soul is inflamed and draws the limbs into its service, so that they do not serve desire—for this reason it is commanded in Leviticus that they offer the fat together with the kidneys, by which inward charity is signified.

### Verse 9

“I will not take calves from your house,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) Even if you do this: “I will not take calves from your house,” as though I were to accept those signified, not those from your house. “For they are mine,” as though he said: because they are not yours but mine. “For mine are,” etc. (Augustine.) Those things are mine which you do not possess, namely, the untamed: “the beasts of the forests, the cattle, the oxen,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) By these comparisons he represents the Church, etc., up to: he does not want the flesh of bulls in sacrifices, but among the poor.

### Verse 11

“I know all the birds.” (Augustine.) All things are with him through a certain ineffable knowledge of wisdom.

### Verse 12

“If I were hungry, I would not tell you.” (The same.) If you think that I might perhaps become hungry because you give these things, what madness is that?

[Col. 0917D]

### Verse 13

“Shall I eat the flesh of bulls?” These things were formerly sacrificed, not because God took pleasure in them, but so that they would not be offered to demons; they were sacrificed only to God, and in them there was some symbolic meaning.

“Sacrifice to God.” (Cassiodorus.) He does not say “to me,” but speaks of himself as though of another, just as later: “But to the sinner God said,” not “I.”

### Verse 15

“Tribulation.” (Augustine.) Our proper tribulation is for fear of salvation, not of carnal things.

### Verse 16

“But to the sinner.” (The same.) From whom he wishes sacrifice, when the sinner is charged with his own wickedness.

[Col. 0918A]

(Cassiodorus.) He said these things to his own people, etc., up to: for reading is not denied to those who need correction.

### Verse 17

“But you hate discipline.” (The same.) With your mouth you say one thing, but by your conduct you deny discipline: if I correct you, you complain.

“You ran with the thief.” (The same.) In these words he thunders against every vice: the part stands for the whole, or “thief” means one who steals the sound meaning of Scripture. “With adulterers.” Those who establish falsehood by taking away the truth.

### Verse 19

“Your mouth abounded,” etc. (The same.) He accuses conscience and tongue, etc., up to: he does not detract from another by accident, but deliberately.

### Verse 20

“Sitting.” (The same.) What one does while passing by or standing, one does not do with deliberation. “Your brother.” (The same.) Every human being. “And against the son of your mother,” the Church, to which we are joined by charity. “You placed a stumbling-block,” heresies or other things by which an innocent person may be caught.

[Col. 0918B]

“You spoke against.” (Augustine.) When one who seems learned speaks ill, etc., up to: with the nourishment of stronger teaching.

“You became like him.” (Cassiodorus.) By consenting to wicked people.

“I will set before you.” (Augustine.) What you placed behind your back I will place before your face.

### Verse 22

“Let him seize.” (Cassiodorus.) Let God seize him for punishment, and let there be no one to rescue him. When the devil seizes, God rescues; but when God seizes, no one can deliver.

### Verse 23

“A sacrifice of praise.” (Cassiodorus.) Not what criminals sing, but a sacrifice of praise, not of animals. This is the way to God, Jacob’s ladder, by which the angels—that is, the faithful—ascend to praise of the divinity and descend to praise of the humanity. “There is the path by which,” etc. (The same.) In the sacrifice of praise. “The salvation of God.” (Augustine.) Christ, who came with grace; he knows him who attributes something to someone other than the grace of God.

## Psalm 50

### Verse 1

“An end-directed psalm.” (Cassiodorus.) When Nathan rebuked him, the king was not ashamed publicly to confess his sins, etc., up to: which God is able to grant to penitents. David. (Augustine.) He is presented as an example, not of falling, but of rising again if one has fallen, so that one may not despair. (Cassiodorus.) The first part is supplication, etc., up to: the complete remission of sins is granted.

### Verse 3

“Have mercy on me, O God.” (The same.) This is a penitential psalm, etc., up to: because he foresaw that through this psalm many would perish. “According to your great mercy.” One would have to despair of a grave sin unless there were great mercy. How great it is cannot be defined. “Great mercy.” (The same.) Great mercy brought God down from heaven, etc., up to: when God is asked to forgive according to himself? “Of mercies,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) He asks through mercy and compassion. Mercy belongs to the nature; compassion to its effect.

### Verse 4

“Wash me more.” (Cassiodorus.) He adds what kind of erasure he desires: “Cleanse me,” etc. (Jerome.) Wash in such a way that you cleanse, for some things are washed that nevertheless are not pure.

### Verse 5

“For my iniquity,” etc. (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) He asks the mercy of the one who forgives, because he knows that God is just and punishes sins; he adds: Do not punish, because I punish myself. “For my iniquity,” etc. “Against me.” (Augustine.) He had his sin behind his back when, as king, he pronounced judgment against the rich man who had taken the poor man’s sheep, forgetting himself.

### Verse 6

“Against you alone have I sinned.” (Jerome.) For only the one who has nothing in himself deserving reproach punishes justly; among human beings this is Christ alone. “Against you alone.” (Cassiodorus.) Because, as king, he is superior to everyone and therefore must be punished only by God. “Before you.” Because he knows that God is everywhere; hence he reproves himself, since he was not ashamed to sin in God’s presence. “So that you may be justified,” etc. His words do not pass away but are fulfilled. “You may prevail when you are judged.” God is of such great justice, etc., up to: so that he may prevail between himself and the one judged.

“Against you alone.” (Augustine.) To Christ, who had no sin, [Col. 0919B] etc., up to: because he had offended God so gravely. “And prevail.” (Augustine.) Or: You are so just that you prevail over the devil, death, and the Jews when you are judged—and in the judgment by which you were judged.

### Verse 7

“In iniquities.” (Cassiodorus.) The envy of sin is diminished, etc., up to: from one sin he is accused, and he confesses all.

### Verse 8

“For behold,” etc. (Augustine.) He gives mercy in such a way that he preserves truth, so that the sins of the one whom he forgives are not unpunished. He forgives the one who punishes himself. Thus mercy is the fact that the human being is liberated; truth is the fact that sin is punished. “Truth,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) Because in confessing he spoke the truth that God seeks above sacrifices, he begs for help. “Uncertain and hidden things.” (Augustine.) There are also hidden things in such people, etc., up to: hence he ought all the more to have guarded himself from sin. “Hidden things.” (Cassiodorus.) Through the authority of the one who reveals them, confidence in cleansing and whitening.

### Verse 9

“You shall sprinkle me.” (Cassiodorus.) This is the second confidence in God’s mercy, which is very useful, lest despair creep in, since despair is more serious than all sins. “With hyssop.” (The same.) Dipped in the blood of the sacrifice, it was sprinkled over the body of a leper, signifying that the stains of sins are washed away by Christ’s blood. (Augustine.) Hyssop is a humble herb, etc., up to: in those things where there is inflation, just so humility counters pride. “Above snow.” (The same.) Incomparably; hence also on the mountain Christ’s garment shone like snow.

### Verse 10

“To my hearing.” (Augustine.) Note the humility. “You will make me hear,” etc., up to: and because he is now humble, his humbled bones already exult.

### Verse 11

“Turn away.” (Cassiodorus.) Secure through confidence, he asks for the blotting out of all sins and full restoration.

### Verse 12

“Within my inward parts.” (The same.) From which adultery came forth. In both parts, soul and body, he asks for the remedy of healing, because he sinned in both. He desires to be purified in such a way that he appears no longer willing to commit anything of that kind.

### Verse 13

“Do not cast me away from your face.” (Cassiodorus.) Turn your face away from sins, but not me from your face, from which light and health will come.

### Verse 14

“With a principal spirit.” (Augustine.) Here some discern the Trinity in God, who is spirit and not a body: by the right spirit, the Son; by the Holy Spirit, the Spirit under his own name; by the principal spirit, the Father. (Cassiodorus.) The spirit of prophecy, which is more precious to him than everything else: he asks only that its strength not be taken away, saying nothing about the rest.

### Verse 15

“I will teach.” (The same.) What the restored person should repay; first he was weeping, now he becomes a teacher.

### Verse 16

“From bloodguilt.” (The same.) Because there are many carnal sins, etc., up to: which arise from the corruption of flesh and blood. “Your righteousness.” (The same.) He praises righteousness when he ought to give thanks for mercy; but it was also an act of righteousness to receive the one who confessed. These two things are always joined in the Lord’s judgment.

### Verse 17

“Your praise.” (Augustine.) That you created me; [Col. 0920B] that you did not abandon me when I sinned; that you urged me to confess; that you cleansed me.

### Verse 19

“A sacrifice to God.” (Cassiodorus.) What at that time was offered for expiation. “Contrite.” (The same.) A cheerful and wanton spirit binds itself to sin. The promise of this sacrifice follows: “A contrite heart.”

### Verse 20

“Deal kindly.” (The same.) Now rejoicing, he prophesies concerning the building of Jerusalem, where there will be a sacrifice of righteousness. “Walls.” (Augustine.) May the defenses of our immortality be built in faith, hope, and charity.

### Verse 21

“Then you will accept a sacrifice.” (The same.) Now there is a sacrifice for iniquity, etc., up to: then righteousness will be the sacrifice; the offerings of the saints will be lesser offerings, and those of the perfect will be burnt offerings.

[Col. 0920C]

“Then they will place.” (Cassiodorus.) Priests, innocent calves, etc., up to: the faithful who suffer for your name will be pleasing to you. “Altar.” (Augustine.) The heavenly Jerusalem.

## Psalm 51

“An end-directed psalm concerning,” etc. (Jerome, Augustine.) Doeg betrayed David, etc., up to: this is not a prayer for the wicked, but a prophecy of what will happen to them.

### Verse 2

“Doeg.” (Cassiodorus.) David’s adversary signifies Antichrist, who will stir up the whole world; he will come through signs and miracles before the coming of judgment, and, seeking help from Saul—that is, from the devil—he will announce that David, that is, Christ, has come into the house of Ahimelech, that is, to the Church, which is the kingdom [Col. 0920D] of the Father.

“Abimelech.” (Jerome.) He says that in Hebrew it is Achimelech, etc., up to: therefore “Abimelech” means “the kingdom of my father,” and signifies the Jews.

### Verse 3

“Why do you glory in wickedness,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) This is the first attack against Doeg, to strengthen the faithful against Antichrist and his accomplices.

### Verse 4

“He devised.” (The same.) A shallow mind and rash speech do not think before speaking; hence: “In the mouth of fools is their heart.”

“Like a razor,” etc. (The same.) While promising renewal, it cuts; so that deceitful one—namely Antichrist—promises blessedness and kills.

### Verse 5

“You loved wickedness,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) He does not abandon evil who loves it above kindness; and if kindness touches the mind, he recoils.

### Verse 6

“A deceitful tongue.” (The same.) That is, deceitful words, servants of deception, bearing one thing in the heart and bringing forth another from the mouth.

### Verse 7

“Therefore God.” (Cassiodorus.) Concerning the swift end of the wicked. “And your root from the land of the living.” (Augustine.) Our root is charity, etc., up to: for here it is dust that the wind casts from the face of the earth. (The same.) The root of evil is desire, which bears no fruit in the land of the living. Or he speaks of Antichrist, whose root consists of his ministers, who together with him will have no share among the saints.

### Verse 8
