“The righteous will see.” (The same.) His downfall becomes an object of mockery. (The same.) “The righteous will see.” What happens to the wicked, etc., up to: because he will deceive the faithful more than all other evils [Col. 0921B].

### Verse 10

“But I,” etc. (The same.) How the good person should conduct himself against him. (Cassiodorus.) Thus far there has been condemnation of that one; here comes praise of the opposing party: behold, a complete demonstration. “A fruitful olive.” (Augustine.) The people of God are the olive tree, from which the proud branches—that is, the Jews—were broken, and the wild olive from the nations was grafted in. (Cassiodorus.) A fruitful olive, from whose shoot the Lord Christ blossomed forth, anointed with spiritual oil beyond his companions.

“For ever and unto the age of the age.” (Augustine.) What he said “for ever,” he repeats as “unto the age of the age,” so that by repetition he may confirm how firmly he is established in the love of the heavenly kingdom.

[Col. 0921C]

### Verse 11

“You have done it, and I will hope in the name.” (The same.) Namely, the things foretold: that I am like an olive tree and that I have hoped in mercy for ever.

## Psalm 52

### Verse 1

“An end-directed psalm concerning,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) The understanding of the prophet David, etc., up to: here he speaks of the coming of judgment. (Augustine.) Or “concerning mahalath,” etc., up to: consolation at the end of the psalm.

“The fool said.” (The same.) A rebuke of the wicked.

(The same.) “Fool”: everyone who lives wickedly, etc., up to: he says, “There is no God.”

### Verse 3

“God looked down from.” (Cassiodorus.) Or from heaven—that is, through holy souls he admonished, so that he might see, etc. “If there is,” etc. (The same.) Or, if he does not understand, whether at least there is someone seeking to understand God [Col. 0921D].

### Verse 4

“All have turned aside.” (The same.) The order is fitting: first they turn aside; then they become useless; thereafter there is no one who does good.

### Verse 5

“Will they not know?” (The same.) A threat against the wicked concerning the end. (Augustine.) He threatens them, etc., up to: but deservedly this happens to them, because:

### Verse 6

“They did not call upon God.” (The same.) He consoles those who groan, so that they do not imitate the prosperous, because they did not call upon God; hence they will soon perish—this is the consolation of the faithful. “The bones of those who please men.” (Cassiodorus.) The good displease themselves when they chastise the flesh; the wicked please themselves.

“They were confounded.” (The same.) That is, they will be confounded and separated, [Col. 0922A] so that it may be read generally of all the wicked; but Israel will be saved.

### Verse 7

“Who will give from,” etc. (Augustine.) Salvation for the Church in labor.

## Psalm 53

### Verse 2

“The Ziphites.” (Jerome, Augustine.) They are interpreted as “flowering,” etc., up to: he urges us to praise God in adversity.

### Verse 3

“O God, in your name.” (Augustine.) He prays among the Ziphites. (Augustine, Jerome.) Here: “Save me in your name”; afterwards: “I do not fear to be judged in your power.” (Augustine.) “God, in your name”: the words of the Church hidden among the Ziphites, whose good is inward and whose reward is hidden; each asks to be delivered from different things: “I ask in your name.”

### Verse 4

“O God, hear.” (Cassiodorus.) Again he says “God,” the name of power, repeating it so that help may not be delayed. “Give heed.” (Augustine.) The Ziphites hear these things, but do not understand them, since they know only temporal matters.

### Verse 5

“Strangers.” (Augustine.) Ziph was a village belonging to the tribe of Judah; hence the Ziphites.

### Verse 6

“For behold.” (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. What God will do for him and the Ziphites; from this he proceeds to praise. “He helps.” (Augustine.) They themselves do not know this, among whom I lie hidden; but they would see that he helps me if they placed God before their eyes.

### Verse 7

“Turn the evils against my enemies.” (The same.) Or “turn away,” prayed for those who are to be converted; and this is the sacrifice he offers for deliverance. “In truth.” (Augustine.) Or according to another reading: “In power”; destroy those whom you tolerated in your weakness [Col. 0922C]. “I will sacrifice willingly.” (The same.) Because of him himself, not because of something else that I might want from him. Whoever praises because of something else praises out of necessity; if he had that thing, he would not praise. But for me, even the things he has given are pleasing because of the giver.

## Psalm 54

### Verse 1

“An end-directed psalm in songs.” (Augustine.) Understanding. The Church ought to understand with great care, etc., up to: he who fled into solitude because of the troubles caused by his fellow citizens.

### Verse 2

“Give ear, O God, to my prayer.” (Cassiodorus.) The prayer introduced against evils, or against the waves of the world. “Do not despise supplication.” (The same.) For even if God gives temporal things to someone who asks, that person’s prayer is nevertheless not acceptable to him if it lacks the proper end.

[Col. 0922D]

### Verses 3–4

“In exercise,” etc. (Augustine.) Every wicked person lives either so that he may be corrected or so that the good may be exercised through him. “I was troubled by the voice of the enemy.” (Augustine.) In the very struggle, while he wishes both to love his enemies and, as the hostile force increases, begins to hate them, and thus begins to be submerged in the waves. (Jerome.) “I was troubled”: or, “I was troubled by the voice of the enemy,” who said that I was a Samaritan and had a demon.

### Verse 5

“My heart is troubled.” (Cassiodorus.) By the law of the flesh, the mind is troubled within me; it does not go out from me.

### Verse 6

“Fear and trembling.” (The same.) It is characteristic of death that we fear it beforehand, and therefore tremble. “Darkness has covered me.” (Jerome.) The darkness is wicked people who persecute the Church [Col. 0923A] and cover her; whoever hates his brother is in darkness.

### Verse 7

“Who will give me wings like?” (Augustine.) But what does he say in this weakness? “Who will give me wings?” He wishes for a time to be separated from so many stumbling-blocks, lest, while remaining among them in weakness, he increase his sins. “Like a dove,” etc. (The same.) Not like a raven, etc., up to: but it is necessary to remain because of you, and thus merit arises from desire.

(Cassiodorus.) The dove—or a dove sent out, finding mud, returned to the ark—so Christ, finding the hearts of the Jews muddy, flew away to the Gentiles.

### Verse 8

“Behold, I have gone far away.” (Cassiodorus.) He touches upon what Christ avoided: those who persecuted him, so that he might remove the occasion of anger; and he remained in the deserts praying. In this he taught us to pray and rest in the secrecy of conscience when we are oppressed by the wicked. “And I remained in solitude,” among the Gentiles; hence: “Let the desert rejoice and blossom like a lily.” And elsewhere: “Rejoice, barren woman who do not bear” (Isaiah XXXV; the same, XXXIV).

### Verse 9

“I awaited him.” A diapsalm. Now safe in solitude, he hopes for God’s help and invokes punishment upon his fellow citizens. (Cassiodorus.) “I awaited”—if it is read as spoken in Christ’s person—in solitude; not secure in myself, I awaited the protection of the Father, who saved me from faintness of spirit, so that I would not fall or yield to the wicked in the Passion, and from the storm, so that I would not become angry.

### Verse 10

“Bring them down.” (Cassiodorus.) So that their thoughts may not fortify themselves by plotting. “Divide.” (The same.) So that there may not be a proud unity and wickedness may not succeed. “In the city.” This is the city concerning which the Lord says through the prophet: “I am God and not man, and I do not enter a city.” Yet there is another city which God inhabits, of which it is said: “A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden.”

### Verse 11

“And labor is in its midst,” etc. (Augustine.) Now labor is in the midst because of iniquity; rest, however, is in humility.

### Verse 12

“Usury,” etc. (The same.) Because he demands more in the matter of injury. Or, whatever thing he has received, he does not release it so that it may be released to him.

### Verse 13

“For if an enemy.” (Cassiodorus.) A reproach against Judas, when read as spoken in Christ’s person; or, thus far the Church has dealt with open enemies, but now with hidden ones. “I might perhaps have hidden myself from him,” etc. (The same.) Such great patience would give room to his words that he might hide himself and not see the adversary.

### Verse 14

“But you, man.” (Augustine.) Formerly, because at some time you gave good counsel. “United in spirit.” (Cassiodorus.) Because he was a leader among the Apostles, sent ahead to towns and villages. “Known.” Because he foreknew the betrayer, so that Christ speaks specifically against Judas.

(Jerome.) Or thus, generally against any Jewish man, etc., up to: the institutions of the Law or the morsel of bread. “United in spirit.” (Augustine.) You who once gave good advice. “Leader”: I made you leader over my people. “Known”: from the same people.

“My acquaintance.” “Who together.” (The same.) You who were with me in the same Church.

[Col. 0924A]

### Verse 15

“Foods.” (Cassiodorus.) Bodily foods, which could be sweet only to the wicked. A man of iniquity is accustomed to be softened by feasting; hence his guilt is heavier.

### Verse 16

“Let death come.” (The same.) As above he invoked punishment upon the open enemies, so here upon the hidden ones. And lest he be thought to mean only one person, he shares Judas’s punishments with the Jews; that is, he invokes punishment generally upon the Jews together with the others.

(Augustine, Jerome.) “Let death come.” Here he touches on the beginning of the schism, etc., up to: and Christ and the Church speak in the same voice.

(Augustine.) “Let death come”: so that upon those who were the beginning of the schism and separated themselves proudly a new death may come; for the earth opened and swallowed the living. “Let them descend alive into hell.” (The same.) So that the leaders were swallowed up by the earth, etc., up to: thus those who sin knowingly descend [Col. 0924B]. “Alive.” Knowing that they are perishing, yet, while perishing, they are swallowed by the gaping mouth of earthly desire. “In their dwellings.” They are alien, not natural, but received as guests, as something adventitious; or first in the dwellings—that is, in secret—then in the midst—that is, openly.

“But I,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) He affirms what happens to him and to them, proceeding alternately.

### Verse 18

“Evening and morning.” (Jerome.) Because he saved him: evening, when he was arrested; morning, when he was judged; noon, when he was crucified. “I will tell,” the deeds of the past. “I will announce,” the powers and works that he will do; and therefore he will hear, etc.

(Augustine.) “Evening.” I will tell of past things, etc., up to: against those who do not love peace, because I loved peace [Col. 0924C].

(Cassiodorus.) To tell belongs to evening, when he said everything that Judas was arranging. To announce belongs to morning, when he said to Pilate: “For this I was born, that I might bear witness to the truth.”

### Verse 19

“They draw near to me.” In name, not in divinity; in body, not in mind; in number, not in merit. “Because they were with me among many.” (Jerome, Augustine.) Because they were “among many,” with me—that is, in the baptism of the Gospel, in reading, festivals, and such things—but not “among the few,” with me. They were with me in all the sacraments, but not in faith, hope, and charity, without which all the rest are nothing.

(Augustine.) Or “among many,” that is, among the chaff, etc., up to: so they too were with me among many.

### Verse 20

“God will hear,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) At noon, when he gave up the Spirit. Behold how many mysteries are briefly contained here. Or: “You will save me morning, evening, and noon”; hence, being not ungrateful, tell and announce, and he himself will hear, etc. “He will humble them who is before the ages.” (The same.) He will humble them because of their pride, so that they may believe. Or he will humble them in order to take away their place and nation. “For there is no change in them, and they did not fear God; he stretched out his hand in repayment,” etc. (Augustine.) Because the understanding of the faithless is unchangeable.

### Verse 21

“They profaned.” (Cassiodorus.) Because they profaned and were divided: the righteous are armed more strongly, and the weak who place their care in God are delivered.

### Verse 22

“Anger.” (The same.) The vengeance of judgment, etc., up to: he appropriates them to his own people. “Heart.” (Augustine.) The secret will of God, which is contained in the Scriptures. “His words were softened.” (Cassiodorus.) Or this happened to them because they softened their words by flattering; yet those words are darts when they say: “He is guilty of death.” (Augustine.) But if they are still hard for you, a child nourished on the milk of lesser teaching, do not become angry with the breasts of the Church; instead, cast your care upon the Lord, not upon another, for he is the harbor—or the rock of the ship—not a harbor tossed about in the world. “The words themselves,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) Because, although softened, they do not lose their power; rather, evangelists arm themselves with them and strike human hearts with love of peace, freeing the weak from the entangled questions of heretics.

### Verse 23

“Cast your care.” (The same.) The care of the world, etc., up to: just as grief harms the heart of a man. “Fluctuation.” And if here there were words of fluctuation: “I was troubled in exercise,” etc. [Col. 0925B]

### Verse 24

“But you,” etc. (Augustine.) These people will then not be tossed about, etc., up to: Woe to those who sin and do not repent. “Their days,” but I, etc. (The same.) Their days are voluntary, not appointed by God.

## Psalm 55

### Verse 1

“An end-directed psalm,” etc. (Augustine.) The people who are made far from the saints in the inscription of the title; the Jew contradicts this people, as does everyone who does not wish to have Christ as king, and those who afflict the Church. This psalm strengthens the Church against them. “In the inscription of the title, for David, when they seized him.” The inscription of the title, etc., up to: persecutors who trample the Church like grapes. “The foreigners.” The same as the people who have been made far from the saints. “Geth,” that is, “in the winepress.” “David is read,” etc., up to: but when it is pressed, it is not barren.

### Verse 2

“Have mercy on me, O God.” (Cassiodorus.) The Church prays, touching briefly upon the tribulations in which, through hope in God, it declares that it does not fear; that is, at the end of the first part it says that it does not fear. “The attacker oppressed me,” etc. (Augustine.) A human being visibly; the devil invisibly—hence the tribulation is more dangerous.

### Verse 4

“From the height.” (Cassiodorus.) The height of the day is the world, where there is the swelling of pride; to make the tribulation more grievous, he says that he is trampled by the proud. (Augustine.) “From the height.” Another reading, etc., up to: he does not say, “I will not fear,” but “I will hope in you.” “Day.” The day is Christ, whose twelve hours are the twelve Apostles; hence he himself says: “Are there not twelve hours of the day?” The enemies cannot reach the height of this day; hence, in Christ’s Passion, “darkness came to be.”

### Verse 6

“All day,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) He enumerates the evils which, by being endured, bring about the conversion of the enemies; hence, through hope in God, he says that he does not fear, as he had done previously.

### Verse 7

“They will dwell.” (Augustine.) Or, some of those who are far from the saints, etc., up to: for if they speak falsely about you, they do not take heaven away, nor do they harm you.

### Verse 8

“For nothing.” (The same.) Because it causes you no labor, as though it were nothing to you; for even if they are desperate, you nevertheless heal them by your word. Or, “for nothing,” because of none of their merits, but freely through mercy. “In anger you will crush the peoples,” while through God’s scourges they come to their senses, or while they foresee God’s anger. “In anger you will crush the peoples.” Because you terrify them with tribulations, etc., up to: and the anger of destruction, by which the wicked are punished unto annihilation.

### Verse 9

“O God, I have announced my life to you.” Human life is threefold: the life of nature, by which we live and breathe; the life of grace, by which we live in Christ; and the life of sin, which is spent in vices. Two are from God, because they are good—namely, the life of nature and the life of grace; the third is from the human being, because it is evil. We ought to announce all of these to God. (Cassiodorus.) “O God, my life.” “You will crush them,” and I set my life before them for their instruction, a life that was always evil. One announces his life to God who confesses his sin: not teaching God, but condemning himself so that he may be absolved. “You have placed my tears,” etc. (Augustine.) Pious are the tears that pray for enemies, and therefore they are acceptable to God, as he himself promised.

### Verse 10

“On whatever day,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) Whether in childhood, middle age, or at the end of life. Wonderful clemency, which awaits the time of our conversion, whatever it may be, and whenever it is asked, grants forgiveness! “You are my God.” (Augustine.) Although he is God of all, he is specifically mine, because he helps me and because I worship and love him. Others are strangers.

### Verse 11

“In God I will praise the word.” (The same.) “The word,” that is, teaching and speech; whatever I say, I will praise in the Lord—that is, I will attribute it to him. And if anything presses upon me, I have hoped, and therefore I will not fear. (Augustine, Jerome.) Or “in God the Father I will praise the Word,” that is, the Son, because whatever is said about the Father and the Son according to substance is also said about the Holy Spirit. This is said of the Word’s power, by which he is eternal and consubstantial with the Father; afterwards he adds, concerning his humanity: “In the Lord,” that is, in Christ, who is the Word made flesh. “I will praise the speech,” etc., that is, the proclamations by which he gave the world a rule of life and salvation. This speaker proclaims two things: the power of the Word and the humanity of Christ. “In God I will praise.” Or in such a way that the Trinity of nature is expressed personally through the three words he sets down. “In God the Father I will praise the Word,” that is, the Son; “in the Lord,” that is, in the Holy Spirit, I will praise the speech, that is, the Son.

### Verse 12

“In me are.” Within me are the things that never depart from us: vows of praise that will be fulfilled in eternity. (Cassiodorus.) “In me are.” The Church, already freed from the evils of the world in future blessedness—or even here—says that it will sing God’s praise.

### Verse 13

“For you have delivered.” (Cassiodorus.) Or this may be understood of the future in the following way, etc., up to: where he also perfectly pleases God; hence he adds: “That I may please,” etc.

## Psalm 56

### Verse 1

“An end-directed psalm.” (Augustine.) A psalm briefly concerning the resurrection and the Passion. This is what the psalm does: “Do not corrupt David,” whether you are Pilate or whoever you may be, etc., by denying the king, because, covered by flesh, he escaped the Jews’ recognition. (The same.) No title is inscribed for David, etc., up to: where Christ lay hidden, unknown to the Jews.

### Verse 2

“Have mercy on me.” (Cassiodorus.) The Prophet, in the person of the Lord, because the Lord in him, cries out as though amid evils and foretells deliverance. (Cassiodorus.) Christ prays according to his humanity; in the Passion he is so humble that he seems to be crying out as one of the faithful. “And in the shadow.” The voice of the body is joined to the head; speaking in the person both of the members and of himself, he will say how he can be delivered: “He sent the Word.”

### Verse 4

“He sent the Word from heaven.” (Augustine, Jerome.) From his hidden essence, etc., up to: whom they thought they had extinguished. “He sent from heaven.” (Jerome.) A diapsalm. Now he declares what he sent and from what he delivered them, speaking in the person of the members. “He delivered.” (The same.) Because he has already sent the Word, it is certain—as though the one who delivered had already come—that is, he will deliver; and he “gave,” that is, he will give those who trample me over to reproach. “God sent.” (Augustine.) The Word, in whom he acted mercifully and in whom he fulfilled his promises [Col. 0927B]. “Mercy,” because in mercy he died for us. “Truth,” because, as he foretold, he rose again to justify us. “His mercy,” etc. (Jerome, Augustine.) Both are contained in him. For if there had been mercy alone, there would have been license for us to sin; if truth alone, the human being could not have endured it.

### Verse 5

“I slept.” (Augustine.) In deep rest, easily awakened: troubled by the Passion, I slept. David did not sleep in the cave, but Christ in death. (Cassiodorus.) “Troubled,” according to the flesh, by the memory and anguish of the Passion; hence: “My soul is sorrowful,” etc. And: “Jesus began to be sorrowful and afraid.” “The sons of men.” The proper order is: the sons of men prepared snares; but he inserts how they troubled him. “Tongue.” Those voices—“Crucify, crucify,” and the like—also brought about death, like a sharp sword (Matthew XXVI; Mark XIV).

### Verse 6

“Be exalted.” (The same.) From the Prophet’s perspective, having seen the insults and seen that the Jews had been made empty in the resurrection, the man on the cross joyfully cries out: “Be exalted, O God, above the heavens,” so that he may judge the Jews on earth. “Be exalted.” The Lord is above; the Prophet speaks, certainly, but in the Lord’s person, because the Lord speaks in the Prophet. Even when the Prophet speaks in his own person, the Lord speaks through him, dictating to him. (Augustine.) “Be exalted.” The words of Christ. But, O Father, etc., up to: because the whole world is subject to him.

### Verse 7

“They prepared a snare.” After the exaltation has been inserted, he completes the narrative he began. “For my feet.” (Cassiodorus.) The Lord’s feet are the rebukes of the wicked and the promises of the faithful, against which they prepared their plots, as in the case of the adulterous woman. “They bent down,” while, sympathizing with them, he was made barren by them. “Before my face they dug a pit,” etc. When they said to his face: “He is guilty of death.”

### Verse 8

“Prepared.” (The same.) A diapsalm. After the resurrection he promises praises. Or, “prepared” to give thanks, which he shows there: “I will sing.”

### Verse 9

“Rise up, my glory.” (The same.) And therefore, O flesh, which is the cause of my glory, rise up powerfully, as for the working of a miracle; there is rejoicing because he is certain. Hence he repeats the affirmation: “Rise up.” I say, “Rise up,” because I am certain even of the hour, since I will rise at dawn. “Rise up, psaltery and harp.” (Augustine.) One flesh of Christ rose, etc., up to: therefore the psaltery and harp rose and gives thanks to the Lord.

### Verse 11

“To the heavens.” (The same.) To the place above the clouds, where the seats of the angels are, etc., up to: mercy ascended to the heavens.

## Psalm 57

### Verse 1

“An end-directed psalm: do not destroy David in the inscription of the title,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) He warns that no one should oppose Christ’s kingdom. The first part is a reproach against the Jews, so that we may not do similar things.

### Verse 2

“If indeed you speak righteousness.” (Augustine.) It is easy for everyone to speak righteousness, etc., up to: because I am your king, as the title says: “Rightly.” The Jews judged Christ in such a way that they are shown to have spoken about him falsely.

### Verse 3

“Your hands.” The heart follows the hands: [Col. 0928B] whatever you wish and cannot do, God considers done. “They contrive.” Or “they join together,” namely, by attaching one thing to another, etc., up to: hence the Lord drove out with a whip of cords those buying and selling in the Temple.

### Verse 4

“Sinners have been estranged from the womb.” Or, they have been estranged from the womb of the Church, etc., up to: they are shaken out as premature births.

### Verse 5

“Fury is theirs.” (The same.) Scripture does not praise the thing itself; a comparison is drawn from whatever source, as from the unjust judge who scarcely heard the widow who pleaded. “Of a deaf adder that stops its ears.” (Cassiodorus.) They not only fail to act, but do not even wish to hear. (Augustine.) “Earth”: present things, in which the human being delights; “tail”: past things.

### Verse 6

“Of the enchanter’s poison.” (The same.) Or according to another reading: “A medicament prepared by the wise man.” “A medicated medicine,” etc., up to: therefore this is the wise man by whom the medicine is medicated.

### Verse 7

“God will shatter.” (Cassiodorus.) Such is the recompense due them. (Augustine.) The vipers are the Jews when they were attempting things by stealth; the lions, when they cried out for death; their molars were broken when Christ rose. “Teeth”: deceitful words. “In their mouth”: by their own words he will seize them. “The Lord will break the molars of the lions.” “They will come to nothing”: the cries for death. He will break them so that they do not come to fulfillment; this is explained by what follows, “They will come to nothing.”

### Verse 8

“Like water.” (Augustine.) They are also compared with torrents, because, roaring against the rocks of pride, they are sudden and headlong, but quickly pass away. They are compared with so many evils. “He bends his bow”: vengeance, until they are weakened within and without and are removed from God’s sight, sent into Gehenna; here in the present life, from their own land.

### Verse 10

“Before the thorns.” (Augustine.) That is, before they understand their sins. “The thornbush”—that is, sharp condemnation—will consume them at the end, in the fire of their vices; that is, it will devour them. “The thornbush”: a kind of plant that is initially soft but later turns into thorns. So too sins presently delight, but afterward prick. “As living, so…” Because the life of the wicked is not true but false: they seem to live, but do not live. Thus he will consume them in anger, either because God judges tranquilly, or because that anger is nothing in comparison with the future one.

### Verse 11

“The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance.” (Cassiodorus.) The correction of the righteous arises from the punishment of the wicked.

[Col. 0929A]

### Verse 12

“And a man will say.” (Augustine.) As it happens through God’s just judgment, etc., up to: and because fire consumes the wicked, therefore God is judging them on earth.

## Psalm 58

### Verse 1

“To the end: Do not…” (Cassiodorus.) It is useless for anyone to try to destroy what divine authority so often forbids. “Do not destroy.” (Augustine.) When Pilate said, “What I have written, I have written,” etc., up to: and to have a reputation among all the nations. (Cassiodorus.) First he prays to be freed, ascending from the depths to the heights; he also prays for the salvation of the nations. (Augustine.) Here the whole Christ speaks, namely, the head and the body.

### Verse 2

“Deliver me.” (Augustine.) Since the one who is without blemish asks this, he shows what we necessarily ought to ask. “From my enemies.” (Cassiodorus.) There are four kinds of adversaries, etc., up to: concerning these, therefore, he says, “Deliver me,” etc.

### Verse 4

“The mighty.” (Augustine.) There are also those who presume upon their own righteousness, etc., up to: but they prevailed in their vanity, trusting in riches.

### Verse 5

“Iniquity.” (Cassiodorus.) Ill will; “sin,” the deed itself.

### Verse 6

“Rise up.” (Augustine.) Because you appear to sleep. “To meet me”: as though I run toward you by deserving; and you, come to meet me—that is, repay according to merit. “See.” (Augustine.) That is, make it apparent how I run toward you, etc., up to: after you saw me die, you believe that I am equal to the Father.

### Verse 7

“They will return.” (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. The salvation of the nations, for which prayer has been made, is affirmed, and the salvation of the Jews is sought in prayer. “In the evening”—that is, later, after the Ascension and the sending of the Spirit, etc., up to: “I fast twice a week.” “They will go around.” (Augustine.) They will fortify the churches against heretical attacks. “And, behold, they will speak openly.”

### Verse 8

“And the sword”: so that they may slaughter and eat. “For who has heard?” As though no one had heard, so that all would be astonished, etc., up to: you will reduce them to nothing or convert them. “The sword.” (Augustine.) This is the two-edged sword, cutting on both sides in the two Testaments. With it Peter slaughters the reptiles shown to him in the dish, when it was said to him: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat.”

### Verse 9

“You will mock them to nothing.” (Augustine.) Those who say, “Who has heard?” Why? Because he will regard it as nothing to convert all the nations, since all the nations will become Christian; yet you say, “Who has heard?”

[Col. 0929D]

### Verse 10

“I will keep my strength toward you, because you are God, my protector, O God.” (Augustine.) Although I could destroy the Jews who attacked me with force, I nevertheless allow them to live, preserving my strength for you—that is, for your disposition.

### Verse 12

“He has shown.” (Augustine.) That is, he has shown me how great his mercy toward me is by means of those toward whom he does not show it. Hence the Apostle says: “He endured vessels of wrath, fitted for destruction, with much patience, in order to make known the riches of his glory in the vessels of mercy” (Rom. 9). “Do not kill.” This may be understood of the Jews, etc., up to: it is shown what mercy is toward those who have been incorporated. (Cassiodorus.) For one considering what ought to be done with them, if they were not witnesses of the Law and of Christ’s death. “Lest they ever forget.” (Augustine.) Although they have not now forgotten, since they are witnesses of the Law and of Christ’s death. “By your power”: because you are strong, not they. “Bring them down”: there was disgrace there for everyone. Or, bring them down in that in which they are evil, so that the good may rise—as with Paul, since Paul would not have risen unless Saul had first fallen (Acts 9).

### Verses 13–14

“The sin of their mouth.” (Augustine.) Kill not them but their sin, so that they may fear the one whom they wished to destroy, now raised again. (Cassiodorus.) And, having been converted, they may be caught; because their deed, etc., up to: but pardon erased the crime. “In pride.” (Augustine.) Pride is the companion of envy; it cannot happen that a proud person does not envy. Hence the devil also envies humanity. “And from the curse”—or, “from the malediction,” which you thought was a curse, etc., up to: because they were caught in these things. “They will be proclaimed at the consummation.” Or, “consummations will be proclaimed,” that is, it will be preached by the Apostles: where the sin of practice and falsehood abounded, the grace of perfection abounded still more; and this belonged to the medicine of human humility and weakness. “In the anger of consummation.” There is indeed an anger—that is, God’s vengeance—of consummation, because God sometimes takes vengeance in order to bring something to perfection; and there is also an anger of destruction, as when he says: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire.” “And they will know.” Previously the Jews seemed righteous to themselves, but it is shown to them that they are not without Christ, who rules Jacob; and, their pride laid aside, they know that they are equal to the nations, because all have sinned.

[Col. 0930B]

### Verse 15

“They will return in the evening.” (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. The salvation of the Jews is affirmed, and thanks are given after both walls have been gathered together.

### Verse 16

“They will murmur.” (Cassiodorus.) Or, “they will murmur”—that is, they will grieve because they will still be scattered so greatly; or, they will murmur against the sluggish—that is, they will rebuke others who are unwilling to believe.

### Verse 17

“But I…” (Cassiodorus.) The psalm concludes here, when the whole Church, with both walls joined in the cornerstone, already rejoices. “And I will exalt.” When the times have passed and the night of the world has gone by, just as Christ rose in the morning. Hence: “In the evening there will be weeping, and in the morning joy.” The Apostles wept in the evening over the dead man and rejoiced in the morning over the risen one. “Mercy”: because you give everything freely. Although he has said many things, not everything, he comprehends everything in this one word.

## Psalm 59

[Col. 0930D]

### Verse 1

“To the end, for those who will be changed.” (Augustine.) In the historical accounts it is not read, etc., up to: to bring the earthly man to faith, and earthly people to life in heaven.

(Basil and Theodoret.) This describes the history of kings. It foresees the people’s future transgression, their being led away captive, and their restoration after repentance. Therefore he inscribed it: “For those who will be changed.” “For instruction.” (Augustine.) They are changed into instruction, etc., up to: Edom, the earthly one, into heavenly life. “And he struck.” When he struck Edom with the sword of the Spirit, etc., up to: he teaches that blessed is the contrition by which he proves that they must be changed to eternal things.

[Col. 0931A]

### Verse 3

“O God, you have rejected us.” (Cassiodorus.) First the blows inflicted in order to avoid eternal punishments are recounted. “You have rejected us”: in Adam. “And you have destroyed us” from immortality. Because you were angry on account of sins, yet had mercy through the Son, so that you shook us from error. “And you troubled us”—with repentance. Therefore, since you have begun, complete the work; heal us.

### Verse 5

“You have shown.” (Augustine.) For when the human being has been changed for the better, etc., up to: to bear adversities to the end. “Hard things.” (Cassiodorus.) That is, the miseries of time, which are delightful to us through charity and burdensome through the weakness of the flesh. “With wine”—that is, with tribulation, by which the sufferer is cleansed, like a wound with wine; “with wine,” spiritual wine, from which come not vices but compunction.

### Verse 6

“The bow.” (Augustine.) The farther backward it is drawn, the more violently the arrow flies forward. That is, the longer judgment is delayed, the more heavily it will come. “And let them be delivered.” (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. The deliverance for which he prays is both requested and affirmed; for this deliverance the blows are welcomed with gratitude.

### Verse 7

“Your right hand.” (Augustine.) So that we may stand at the right hand, etc., up to: concerning earthly things, only usefully.

### Verse 8

“God has spoken.” (Augustine.) With this confidence I pray, which God promised in Christ, etc., up to: it is the voice of the Church: “I will rejoice.” “Shechem.” It is interpreted as “shoulder,” that is, the burden of Christ, etc., up to: let others bear the yoke of Christ. “The valley of tents”: because of Jacob’s sheep it signifies the Jews, who are also divided, since some believe and others do not—that is, from the Jews I will have not a few.

[Col. 0931C]

### Verse 9

“Manasseh.” (Augustine.) Or, Manasseh is everyone who, having forgotten his former life, etc., up to: “and you will not remember the reproach of your widowhood.” “Ephraim”: fruitfulness. And this is the strength of the head, that is, of Christ; for the grain, when it dies, has within itself the power to produce fruit.

### Verse 10

“Moab is the pot of my hope.” (Augustine.) Daughters who misuse their father, etc., up to: when charity burns against the pot of iniquity. (Cassiodorus.) “Moab is the pot of my hope.” Or, by Moab, etc., up to: from him, therefore, I have hope of life. (Jerome.) “The pot,” whence: “I see a boiling pot,” etc., up to: from that pot of tribulations, therefore, the Church boils over.

### Verse 11

“The fortified city.” (Cassiodorus.) The future Jerusalem. “Into Idumea”—that is, as far as the earthly people, so that, when the number has been completed, they may come together to blessedness.

### Verse 12

“You will not go out.” (Augustine.) But you will work within, and thus you will lead more effectively, because in this way you appear to fight not for temporal life but for the future one.

## Psalm 60

### Verse 3

“I cried when I was distressed.” (Cassiodorus.) In distress, etc., up to: the cry follows, heard in Christ the rock. “You have exalted me.” (Augustine.) From the depths of vices. (Cassiodorus.) “And you guided the exalted one.” (Augustine.) Upon the rock, and therefore I am not conquered. “You have exalted me”: through the example of this one, great hope of being heard is offered to others. “You have led me down.” (Augustine.) Through yourself, the way, to yourself, the truth and the life.

[Col. 0932A]

### Verse 5

“I will dwell.” (Cassiodorus.) He trusts in God’s benefits, so that he may remain safely in God’s tabernacle against the world’s dangers. “For ages.” As long as the ages continue; for although many oppose me: “I will be protected under the shelter.” “I will be protected under the shelter of wings.” These neither weigh us down nor allow any injury to reach us. “For ages”: not one human being forever, but the Church, which dwells on earth until the end of the world and is never uprooted by adversities.

### Verse 6

“For you, my God, have heard my prayer,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. Having now been heard concerning the inheritance possessed or to be possessed, he affirms it and promises praise on its account. “You have given.” I will not say, “You will give”; I am so certain that it is as though I were already in possession of it.

### Verse 7

“Day upon day.” (Augustine.) Whatever you wish to say about eternity, etc., up to: but let the saints reign with him forever. Or, “You will give an inheritance.” (Cassiodorus.) This one, namely, because it is above the days of Christ, etc., up to: because that king remains forever, and so do they. “Mercy and truth.” (Augustine.) It is mercy because he forgives sins and promises life not on the basis of merits but out of goodness. It is truth because he does not deceive but gives what he promised. We ought to follow mercy toward the weak and toward enemies; truth, by not sinning, so that we may be righteous. (Cassiodorus.) “Mercy and truth.” Here is the conclusion of the psalm, etc., up to: who will seek this from him? (Augustine.) Let no one seek to learn these things in books and then live for himself rather than for him.

## Psalm 61

[Col. 0932C]

### Verse 1

“To the end, for Idithun.” (Augustine.) “Leaping over”: seeing so many things occurring, he submits himself to God, who is higher than he is, and from above answers those below by rebuking them. “Leaping over”: he answers the envious, who wish to deceive.

### Verse 2

“Is it not so?” (Augustine.) This means: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me.” “I will not be moved any more”: that is, “Let not the hand of the sinner move me.” He is always subject to God, desiring nothing besides him. “It will indeed be so,” because my salvation is from him; from the Father, the Son is the author of salvation, and he is also God, so that he may not be thought inferior.

### Verse 4

“How long will you attack?” (Augustine.) Or, according to another reading: “How long will you add?” The meaning is the same. The wicked add burdens of sufferings upon a man—that is, upon the Church—so that each believer may fulfill in his body, unto the end, what is lacking of Christ’s sufferings. “All of you.” (Cassiodorus.) Or, according to another reading: “All you,” as though you all kill that man, insofar as he is man; not all one individual, but the Church. Yet because God is the protector, I will not be moved. (Augustine.) “How long?” From the blood of Abel, etc., up to: not, of course, what is established by the Most High Founder. “Upon a man.” (Cassiodorus.) You have been given power over the body, not over the soul. “You attack”: not lightly, but you kill the innocent. You think he is without a defender and easily collapses, like a leaning wall, which would fall even without being pushed. And like a wall of stones without the binding of mortar; and lest you think it firm because of its very newness, he adds “pushed,” or, you ought not to attack, because all of you, even those who consent, are killing yourselves.

[Col. 0933A]

### Verse 5

“The price.” (Cassiodorus.) Christ, so that he might not be worshiped; or, the removal of blessedness. “They plotted.” (Augustine.) Notice the different kinds of enemies, etc., up to: concerning this the prophet says, “Glorious things have been spoken of you, city.” “I ran in thirst.” Although he always drinks them, he is nevertheless always thirsty for more. “With his mouth”: because they cannot act through open evils, they attempt things through flattering words.

### Verse 6

“Nevertheless, to God,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. Again he urges himself—that is, his soul—to submit, and admonishes the others. “My soul is subject.” This petition fixes strength in our mind.

### Verse 8

“In God is my salvation.” (Augustine.) Then he is safe and glorious in him; but now, what? He himself is the God of help.

### Verse 9

“Hope.” (Cassiodorus.) By the faith he has proclaimed, he urges all who labor under superstitions to hope in the Lord. “Pour out.” (Augustine.) Through tears the heart is poured out, etc., up to: hence, “Prick the eye, and it produces a tear; prick the heart, and it produces knowledge” (Eccl. 22). “Hearts,” etc.: perverse thoughts.

### Verse 10

“Nevertheless, the sons of Adam are vain.” (Jerome.) Or join the words in this way: God is our helper; and although he works with us in this manner, nevertheless the sons of Adam are vain and deceitful in the balance, perverting the Scriptures by which they prove falsehoods. (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. He rebukes the wandering and urges them to trust in God, not in fleeting things, which is the psalm’s purpose. “Deceitful in the balances”: those who deceive buyers with unjust weights, or wish to appear righteous while they are deceitful. “In the balances”: in the scale of justice, by which they deceive more easily. “Together”: so that they may be thought equitable.

### Verse 11

“Do not hope in…” (Augustine.) As though he said: Neither hope for nor desire those things which, once gathered, are taken away by others. “Do not”: the thirsty man turns toward them. “Do not.” “Robberies”: the prey you wish to seize is in a trap; you hold it and are held. You hold what belongs to another, and you are held by the devil. O destructive profits! You find money and lose justice. “If riches abound, do not set your heart upon them.” (Cassiodorus.) He does not say, “Do not possess them,” for he does not condemn riches, by which we purchase heaven; rather, he condemns a heart attached to them, which does not spend but stores them away.

### Verse 12

“God has spoken once.” (Augustine.) “Do not set your heart upon them.” Why? Because the power of judging belongs to the Son of God, etc., up to: nor, because of his power, should one despair of mercy. “Power belongs to God”: no one has power except from the just God, even if his justice is hidden from you.

## Psalm 62

### Psalm of David

(Cassiodorus.) He speaks of the Church, which thirsts in the aridity of the world and seeks mercy until it receives eternal things, teaching how to live well in the midst of a crooked generation. (Augustine.) The psalm speaks in the person of the head and the members; his voice is ours, and ours is his.

### Verse 2

“O God, my God, to you from the light,” etc. (Augustine.) The bride desires to see God in the desert, as she is there; she both praises him and wishes to do this more fully. “God.” (Augustine.) In a certain more particular way, my common God. Observe the affection of devout prayer in this repetition. “From the light”—or, “at dawn,” when Christ rose, so that the Church may praise him at the time when, by the example of his resurrection, he stirred her to rise. “I keep watch”: while I sleep, I do not love the things of the world. (Cassiodorus.) I thirst in soul and body. “From the light.” (Augustine.) You would not keep watch unless the light arose to awaken you. “My soul thirsted for you”: here too the flesh thirsts for God when it asks necessary things from him.

### Verse 3

“Desert.” (Augustine.) Where no saint dwells. “Impassable,” because there is no way out from it. “Waterless,” because, while you remain there, there is no water. But here God made Christ the way and sent the water of his Word, filling preachers through the Holy Spirit, “so that in them it might become a spring of water welling up to eternal life” (John 4). “Thus I appeared to you in the holy place, that I might see,” etc. (Augustine.) To the one to whom God does not appear as present in holy desire, etc., up to: just as the sun makes us see by its light, so does God.

### Verse 4

“Above lives.” (Augustine.) Human lives, which are many—such as the life of a soldier, a farmer, and others. What you give to those who have been corrected is better than what the perverse choose. “My lips.” After God’s benefits, he promises praise. “They will praise,” with regard to the neighbor, for whom I am also concerned, since unless your mercy preceded me, I could not praise you; and just as they bless with their lips, so may they bless in life. Or understand it this way: because it is “above lives.”

### Verse 5

“Thus I will bless.” (Augustine.) Just as you have granted me, through mercy, the ability to praise you, so I will bless, attributing to mercy the life in which I praise. “In your name I will lift up my hands.” (Augustine.) A person lifts his hands who, devoted to good works, worships God with outstretched hands in the form of a cross. Hence the Apostle says: “Lifting up pure hands in prayer, without anger or dispute.”

### Verse 6

“With fat.” (Augustine.) In the inward parts. Fat in the flesh signifies wisdom, which is hidden within, and the strength of the spirit.

“I will lift up my hands.” (Augustine.) In Exodus, when Moses lifted his hands to the Lord, etc., up to: he works for earthly things and is defeated by Amalek.

### Verse 7

“If I remembered.” (Cassiodorus.) He explains the good and evil of both sides, etc., up to: except the one who works in Christ.

(Cassiodorus.) “In the mornings,” that is, in the light of Christ. As above, “from the light I keep watch for you,” so that the son of light—that is, of Christ—may keep watch for the author of light, God.

### Verse 8

“Helper,” etc. (Augustine.) In the dangers of Idumea, etc., up to: because your right hand—that is, your propitiation—has received me from dangers.

### Verse 10

“But they sought my soul in vain. The king, however…” He compares the good and evil of the different parties in these two verses.

“Into the lower parts of the earth.” (Cassiodorus.) Because they were not raised to the heavens. Evil thoughts are swallowed up by the earth, because they are born from the earth and sink into the lowest earth, as into mud.

### Verse 11

“They will become portions for foxes,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) The beginning of the world, etc., up to: when they join themselves to deceitful people with perverse intent.

### Verse 12

“In God.” (Cassiodorus.) The Father, whence: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me.” “They swear”: not by him, lest he command an oath, but in him, by promising obedience to him.

## Psalm 63

(Cassiodorus.) This psalm briefly treats, etc., up to: so that in sufferings we may hope in the Lord. (Augustine.) As our head did, so let us pray in our tribulations.

### Verse 2

“Hear, O God, my prayer”: so that you may exalt me and deliver me, since I implore you. “From fear of the enemy.” (Cassiodorus.) But not from fear of death.

### Verse 3

“You protected me.” (Augustine.) This happened in the head, and the members also experience it; by this example the others are strengthened.

### Verse 4

“For they sharpened their tongues like a sword.” Or, those who act maliciously and work iniquity. “The bow”: hidden ambushes, as through a disciple; this is a bitter thing, that the guest should be the betrayer. “Bitter.”

### Verse 6

“They will suddenly shoot arrows.” (Augustine.) Treacherously, as though against someone unaware, as it seems to those who believe they can deceive God. “They will not fear.” (Augustine.) O hardened heart! To kill the man who raised the dead, and then not to fear. “They made firm.” (Cassiodorus.) Through obstinacy, not truth, the statement: “He is guilty of death,” or, “It is expedient that one man should die.” “For themselves.” (Augustine.) Not for the Lord but for themselves, when they say: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.” “So that they might conceal”: it is the way of the wicked that the person who prepares deceit thinks he is deceiving.

### Verse 7

“They searched.” (Cassiodorus.) How they might accuse the righteous man, or how they might destroy him, lest the world follow him. (Augustine.) “They searched”: that is, they formed bitter and hidden plans. But the more sharply they think, the farther they fall from truth and equity and the more deeply they are plunged into darkness, because, not seeing God, they suppose that they are not seen by God. “A man will draw near.” (Cassiodorus.) For the one who searches out iniquities, etc., up to: but it grows great in the human heart. (Augustine.) They searched, but in vain, because the man would willingly approach his Passion. “To the deep heart.” (Augustine.) It was deep to him, because he did this according to a deep counsel.

“The arrows of little ones have been made.” (Cassiodorus.) He mocks the wickedness of the Jews just enumerated: they were more troubled by the announcement of the resurrection, while the righteous rejoiced.

### Verse 9

“They were troubled.” (Cassiodorus.) Those who, seeking the counsel of their salvation, said: “What shall we do, brothers?”

### Verse 10

“And every man feared.” (Augustine.) If a person fears, let him not fear human beings so much that he fails to announce the truth, as did the Apostles, whom the chief priests threatened, ordering them not to preach in Jesus’ name.

“And they understood his works.” (Augustine.) Why did he suffer? Why did he not come down from the cross? Because he had to die and rise again; this was not understood at that time.

### Verse 11

“The righteous man will rejoice in the Lord.” (Cassiodorus.) A conclusion from what was said above, and the promise made to the righteous is displayed. “All.” (Cassiodorus.) Do not think that this is said only of the Apostles.

## Psalm 64

### To the end

(Augustine.) Jeremiah prophesied (25; 29) that the people would return after seventy years. Ezekiel and other prophets were among the captives. When the seventy years were completed, the temple was restored. This is a figure of us, who sigh from Babylon toward Jerusalem—from the world and the body of sin toward heaven.

### Verse 1

“Of Jeremiah.” (Augustine, Jerome.) “Exalted”; and he signifies those who say: “Our citizenship is in heaven.” “Of Haggai”: “festive”; he signifies those who rejoice in hope, who, in the remnants of their thoughts, keep a feast for the Lord. “Ezekiel”: “the Lord strengthened me”; and he signifies those who have been strengthened in the Lord. These prophets foretold the return to Jerusalem.

“From the people of the transmigration.” (Augustine.) That is, those who migrated from heaven to earth, from perfection to misery and confusion. “When he began.” (Augustine.) The person who begins to love begins to depart. Charity makes one a citizen of Jerusalem; desire makes one a citizen of Babylon. Thus, although they are mingled in body, they are separated in desire. (Cassiodorus.) This is consolation in exile, so that no one may despair: it confirms the return, and through whom it will take place, and what riches await those who return. It affirms the return and prays for it.

### Verse 2

“You are worthy.” Not the gods of the nations, and nowhere except in contemplation—that is, in faith—and there the vow will be paid through good works, in the heavenly Jerusalem, just as they paid it to Mars after battles and to the other gods in this manner. “Zion.” The heavenly homeland is Zion; it is the same as Jerusalem.

### Verse 3

“Hear my prayer.” (Cassiodorus.) First he does what he says must be done by others, namely, he says, “Hear.” “All flesh.” (Augustine.) That is, humanity, from every kind: poor and rich, men and women, learned and unlearned, children and old people.

### Verse 4

“The words of the wicked.” (Cassiodorus.) With what hope do you pray this? Because all flesh will come to you—not only the soul, but also the sinful person. It is necessary that you hear. For the words of the wicked are those of the devil and of our first parents, Adam and Eve. “They prevailed.” That is, they cast us into exile. Or, the pagans commended their rites to their children, but you will be propitiated through Christ’s sacrifice. (Augustine.) “The words of the wicked”: we followed the evil rites and practices of our parents, who, just as they excel in age, also excel in authority over children. “You will be propitiated.” (Augustine.) Propitiation takes place through the sacrifice that Christ the priest offered. Therefore the priest and the victim are the same.

### Verse 5

“Blessed is the one whom you have chosen,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) Blessed is every person whom you have chosen from the mass of the lost—“You did not choose me, but I chose you” (John 15)—and whom you have taken into your portion, into eternal rest. (Augustine.) Or understand it this way: “You will be propitiated through the blessed man,” etc., up to: things that cannot be expressed. “In good things.” (Cassiodorus.) Those things that are good: holiness toward oneself and equity toward one’s neighbor. “The temple”: the Church, or the flesh of Christ.

### Verse 6

“Wondrous.” (Augustine.) Not in outward things, such as an earthly house, but in righteousness, which is more beautiful to the inner eye and more lovable. We ought now to hunger for it, so that then we may be satisfied with it. “In equity.” (Cassiodorus.) When he will repay each person what is fitting, to whom he also says: “Hear us, you who are the Savior.” “The hope of all”: he describes God’s praises and virtues. “And in the distant sea.” (Augustine.) It is distant because it is in the sea. The sea is used figuratively for the world, bitter through the falsity of sins and stormy through the tempests of temptations, where the fish devour one another.

### Verse 7

“Preparing the mountains.” (Augustine.) For suitable uses. “By your strength”: because through them he performed miracles. How did he prepare them? “Girded with power”—that is, with divinity—because the humanity of the Word was girded with majesty, so that divinity might give what humanity did not possess. “Girded.” (Augustine.) Christ is enclosed in the midst on every side, because all of us who believe in him possess him in common. But because faith does not come from us but from him, he is said to be girded with his power.

### Verse 8

“You who disturb the depths of the sea.” Behold the one who did this through those prepared, disturbing the depths toward repentance. “The depths of the sea”: not the surface, but hearts sunk more deeply, or the hearts of rulers. These were troubled when they saw both their gods and their hopes coming to nothing. “The sound.” (Augustine.) Resounding through contradiction, tossed about by persecution, etc., up to: when they see these people stronger than their gods.

### Verse 9

“Morning and evening.” (Augustine.) Morning is prosperity, because morning is joyful after the sadness of night. Evening is adversity. In these a person is tested, but he is granted a way out, so that he may not be captured by profits, since God is his wealth, and so that he may not be frightened by adversities, for the sake of whom the Lord suffered. “You will make them glad.” You will make them delightful already in this life. For if the departure itself does not delight a person, he does not labor to depart from it, but is captured by profits because he does not love Christ’s promise; and he is terrified by adversities because he is not delighted by the one who was willing to suffer for him, in order to make a way out for him.

### Verse 10

“You visited the earth and intoxicated it.” You will do this through preachers, for inwardly you teach those to whom they preach.

“A river.” The deep has been filled with waters for receiving them, with the gifts of the Holy Spirit; for you prepared food. “The river of God.” (Cassiodorus.) God’s mercy is compared with a full-flowing river, etc., up to: as it is arranged by him, without whom nothing takes place there.

### Verses 11–12

“Its streams.” The Apostles and others who drank from the river. “Make them drunk,” so that they may suffice for themselves and for others. “Multiply,” so that through succession preaching may not fail. “The crowns of the year”: the whole world, where the Church is. “Its streams.” (Cassiodorus.) “You prepared,” etc. And, O Lord, etc., up to: by which the Word of God grows. “The crowns of the year.” (Cassiodorus.) Because glory is the victory of the one who conquers the devil. “Your goodness,” etc. (Augustine.) Let no one boast of his merits.

“Your fields will be filled.” (Cassiodorus, Augustine.) Human beings, on account of equality—that is, the righteous. “The hills,” because God raises up the humble. “The desert”: all the nations to whom no prophet was sent.

### Verse 13

“The beautiful places of the desert will grow fat.” When the Apostles came to them, through whom they were made beautiful.

[Col. 0938A]

### Verse 14

“The valleys.” (Augustine.) Humble peoples will bear abundant fruit. “They will cry out.” (Augustine.) Not in blasphemy but in a hymn; hence they abound in grain.

This psalm is sung at the funerals of the faithful because it concerns the return from the Babylon of this world to the heavenly homeland. To that homeland the saints, when brought out of the flesh at death, migrate happily, receiving a single robe until, at the resurrection, they are glorified in the robe of double blessedness.

## Psalm 65

### To the end

(Augustine.) The Jews hoped for temporal goods and resurrection from the righteousness of the Law, etc., up to: he would call the nations, through faith, to the same hope of resurrection.

[Col. 0938B]

### Verse 1

“Shout joyfully to God, all the earth,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) First he urges everyone to rejoice in Christ’s resurrection, which gives life to all.

### Verse 3

“Give glory.” (Augustine.) Not as the Jews do, who attribute righteousness to their own merits and begrudge grace to the nations. “How terrible.” (Augustine.) If you rejoice, also fear, lest what has been given to the humble be taken away from the proud, as happened to the Jews. Therefore do not insult the broken branches, but fear, lest he perhaps spare you no more than them. “Your works, O Lord.” (Cassiodorus.) He briefly calls the mysteries of the Incarnation “works”: that God became human, suffered, died, and similar things. “In the multitude of your power.” (Augustine.) Here he hints at the resurrection, to which the nations are admitted after the deceitful Jews have been excluded.

(Bede.) The Lord rose again; many believed in him, etc., up to: they drank through grace. “They will lie.” [Col. 0938C] The works of the earth are those which the enemies falsely accuse; against those who lie, let all the earth worship, etc. (Augustine.) “They will lie.” Enemies are accustomed to lie, etc., up to: let all the earth worship.

### Verse 5

“Come.” (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. He invites those beginning to consider God’s works, so that one faith may join together those who await one reward. In explaining these works, he openly says that the resurrection belongs to the nations, while the Jews are restrained.

### Verse 6

“He turned.” (Cassiodorus.) He adds the works in which he is terrible and what they are: “He turned the sea.” Literally, in the river Jordan; mystically, in the passing world. “In the river.” (Cassiodorus.) Although sins have been forgiven, they still remain in the course of mortality; immortality does not come immediately.

[Col. 0938D]

“In the river.” (Augustine.) The river is the mortality of the world, where some come and others depart. But whoever believes in Christ crosses on foot, humble in himself, not proudly on horseback. “There we will rejoice.” (Augustine.) Or understand it this way: the works are terrible, etc., up to: and Christians rejoice in these things. “In him.” (Augustine.) When he will be all things in all, or in the one who rules, in his power.

### Verse 7

“Let them not be exalted.” (Augustine.) On account of the Law, as though more were owed to them. “For all have sinned,” etc. (Rom. 3).

### Verse 8

“Bless.” (Cassiodorus.) A diapsalm. He urges the nations to bless God, who, although he tests them with tribulations, nevertheless leads them to the kingdom. For these tribulations appear to oppose the promised resurrection. “Make his praise heard.” (Augustine.) Openly, so that whoever loves God may also love his neighbor. “The voice of his praise”: the voice that the Father speaks concerning the Son: “This is my Son.”

### Verse 9

“He who placed the soul.” (Augustine.) Here he enumerates the reasons why he ought to be preached.

### Verse 10

“For you have tested us.” (Augustine.) “You did not give us over to destruction.” “You have tested us”: you did not cast us headlong; you tested us through adversities, through the fire of charity, which does not allow us to feel the torments; or, you examined us through the fire of tribulation, etc.

### Verse 12

“A snare.” (Augustine.) Not one that deceives, but one that tests. “We passed through.” (Cassiodorus, Augustine.) You brought us through all these things, and we did as well, etc., up to: this happens to us in temptations.

### Verse 13

“I will enter.” (Cassiodorus.) Behold the good things set against the preceding evils, so that he may strengthen us. “With burnt offerings.” That is, so that I may offer myself in your sight, etc., up to: but he withdrew what was more precious.

### Verse 14

“They have distinguished.” (Augustine.) The one who says that he is nothing and that God is everything distinguishes himself; he says that he needs God, not that God needs him. “And my mouth spoke.” I made him manifest above all things, showing that he surpasses every other vow in my tribulation, without being overcome by tribulation.

### Verse 15

“Burnt offerings of marrow.” I offer myself with the marrow of inward love. “With the incense of rams.” (Augustine.) Or, with incense, which is prayer, and with rams, because the leaders of the flock pray especially for the flock. “With incense.” (Jerome, Augustine.) With the prayer of the Apostles, because what is done according to their tradition pleases God. Or, with the burning and destruction of bestiality and opposition. “Oxen”: stubbornness. “With goats”: wantonness. These are the vices slaughtered in me.

“I will offer oxen to you.” (Augustine.) If those who thresh are offered, sinners nevertheless do not remain sinners; rather, they are offered after being healed through repentance. And they are not offered by themselves but rather joined to the oxen, because they have made friends for themselves from the mammon of iniquity.

### Verse 16

“Come, hear.” A diapsalm. Having explained everything, he again urges not the unlearned so much as the devoted, so that, following the example of his deliverance, they may trust in the Lord more fully, blessing him for having heard him. “This is what I do; and you nations, come.”

### Verse 17

“To him I cried with my mouth.” (Cassiodorus.) He explains what he did for his soul, adding: “To him,” etc. He did this for my soul: I cried to him, while the nations cried to idols. What I speak outwardly I possess inwardly, and there is no iniquity in me, because in this way the purity of prayer is heard. “I cried and exalted him in my heart.” (Augustine.) That is, I preached him publicly and confessed him in secret. What I have in my mouth, I also have in my heart; nevertheless I will offer burnt offerings of marrow. In these two things the Christian is perfected.

### Verse 18

“Mine.” What is not perverse belongs to him. He puts this forward as a merit, so that they may learn first to labor before seeking the reward.

### Verse 20

“My prayer,” etc. These two things are connected: if prayer is not suspended, mercy is not prolonged.

## Psalm 66
In the end. (CAS.) After the song of the resurrection, the Prophet adds his prayer [Col. 0940A], so that the blessed may be led to the knowledge of God. He prophesies the blessing of all through the coming of Christ. (AUG.) Since in the preceding psalm he had instructed us to bless God—which we cannot do unless he first blesses us—he therefore prays to be blessed, saying: “May God have mercy on us and bless us,” etc.

VERS. 2.—May God have mercy. (Ibid.) The blessing of God comes first; it is like rain watering the soil of our mind. From this we bless him, which is like the fruit, and in both we grow—not he. Let him therefore, desiring the rain of the Lord’s blessing, say: “May God have mercy,” etc.

May God have mercy on us and bless us. (CAS.) But since many desire, etc., up to the point where Christ is known among the nations: [Col. 0940B] “Let the peoples confess,” etc.

May he bless us. (Ibid.) The Creator blesses the creature by multiplying it in number and merit. The creature blesses the Creator by praising him in heart, voice, and deed, and by ascribing to him every good that it possesses.

VERS. 4.—Let the peoples confess to you, O God. (Ibid.) After granting knowledge, he urges confession in view of direction and judgment.

VERS. 5.—Let them rejoice and exult. (AUG.) Since those who have already confessed do not fear the future judgments, for which Christ is advocate rather than judge, let them rejoice.

VERS. 6.—Let the peoples confess to you, O God. (CAS.) The same admonition, directed toward another end, because the earth has yielded its fruit; although the beginning of the meaning is the same, it leads toward different ends.

[Col. 0940C] VERS. 7.—The earth has yielded its fruit. (HIER.) Mary has borne Christ, etc., up to: “But she alone ought not to do this; rather, let him bless us also.”

God, our God. (Ibid.) The three occurrences signify the Trinity; “him” signifies unity.

And let them fear him. (CAS.) Fear is requested amid blessings, so that what has been entrusted may be guarded carefully. The fear of God begins and completes the work; whoever knows how to fear does not cease to love.

PSALM LXVII

VERS. 1.—In the end. (CAS.) A psalm of the prophet David concerning the exultation of Christ and the Church, both in the present and in the future, so that all may sing to God. When Christ arose, like the ark being lifted up, etc., up to the point where Moses is said to have used similar words.

VERS. 2.—Let God arise, and let them be scattered. (Ibid.) [Col. 0940D] He confidently prays for what he knows will happen.

And let those who hate him flee. (HIER.) Alternatively, this may be understood of penitents, etc., up to the point where, when the fire of the Holy Spirit is applied through the tears of repentance, their hardness is dissolved.

Those who hate him. (AUG.) Let the obstinate be removed from the presence of him who is present everywhere. It is a grave curse that they should wish and strive for what can in no way happen.

VERS. 3.—As smoke vanishes. (CAS.) Smoke rises from a flame and disappears; so sinners produce smoky deeds from the flame of wickedness and perish through that very exaltation.

As wax melts. (AUG.) This may be said of penitents; or, at the judgment, the wicked will be removed from the face of God, who will be fire for the punishment of the ungodly and light for the righteous.

[Col. 0941A] VERS. 4.—Let them feast. (CAS., AUG.) Let them feast on the delights that are in God’s presence.

And let them delight. This can delight them: that they rejoice because their joy will not come to an end.

VERS. 5.—Sing to God. (AUG.) He turns to those to whom he has given such great hope and exhorts them.

He who ascended. New life will not receive him unless the old life has died; or, by rising again, he conquered the fall of the body.

Above the setting. (CAS.) The setting of death falls upon the one over whom the sun of righteousness rises. And so that you may not doubt who this is—for “Lord” is his essential name—he is the one whom the Jews killed as though he were an ordinary man.

In his presence. Consideration of the future reward mitigates hardships.

VERS. 6.—Of orphans. (AUG.) Those whose father—the world and the devil—has died, and whose mother is desire.

Of widows. Those whose husband, error, has died. God dwells in them, gathers them, and draws them, because from widows and orphans he makes a temple for himself, in which he dwells.

VERS. 7.—God, who makes them dwell. (HIER.) In Hebrew it reads: “But the Lord makes the monks dwell in a house,” those in whom sin does not dwell together with them.

Of one manner. (AUG.) Of one mind, thinking one thing, etc., up to: not by merits. Hence he adds: “He brings out the prisoners.”

He brings out the prisoners. (CAS.) From hell, with the devil bound.

Those who provoke. Blasphemers against God. Or, those who persecute him, buried in tombs—that is, in foul carnal things—so that they neither wish nor are able to walk.

Those who provoke. (AUG.) By resisting righteousness, although they are altogether dead in dead works. The prisoners, however, wish to walk but cannot; these are released by grace, while the others are raised again.

[Col. 0941C] VERS. 8.—O God, when you went forth. (CAS.) A diapsalm concerning the word of the Gospel, through Christ’s going forth.

O God, when you went forth. Truly you lead them out, because his going forth was prefigured before Israel when he appeared in the pillar of cloud and fire in the desert and satisfied them with manna.

(AUG.) His going forth was when he appeared to human beings through his humanity, or when he led out the prisoners—that is, when he raised them up. He passed through the desert when he came to the nations.

(BASIL.) “When you went forth.” It is as though he said: When you were about to cross that solitude which had not yet received the splendor of light, you indeed shook and moved the earth, but from heaven you caused drops of your grace to fall.

VERS. 9.—The earth was shaken. Because then earthly people were moved when they saw such great miracles.

The heavens dripped. [Col. 0941D] From the face of God: manna descended like a drizzle from the face of God, whose presence was made known through the pillar.

(AUG.) Mount Sinai smoked from the face of God, according to another reading, when Moses received the law there.

VERS. 10.—Rain. This is what the heavens dripped: manna, freely given, which satisfied the will of that nation eager to eat.

You will set apart, O God, a rain for your inheritance. Because he did not give to the other nations what he then gave to the Jews.

It was weakened. For a time, while it did not believe in Christ.

(CAS.) You completed it. God completed his inheritance when he admitted the nations as an addition. He next states how he completed it.

VERS. 11.—Animals. That is, your nations: when they believe, they dwell in the inheritance, that is, in the Church.

He explains what the animals are.

You prepared it. He speaks of the predestined, because they were prepared from the beginning of the world.

(AUG.) Alternatively, “Mount Sinai, from the face of the God of Israel, dripped,” with “dripped” understood, etc., up to the point where grace abounded.

(CAS.) These things are mystical, but according to the figure, etc., up to the point where he therefore refers it to the mystery.

(AUG.) Some books do not have “mountain,” but read: “From the face of God, Sinai, Israel”—that is, the one who gave the law to the people of Israel. For the one who gave the law through Moses, by which he would terrify, also gave blessing through the Apostles, by which he would set free.

In sweetness. (CAS.) Sweetness is that by which something is made good, not through fear of punishment but through delight in righteousness.

VERS. 12.—The Lord will give the word to those who proclaim it with great power.

[Col. 0942B] VERS. 13.—The King of powers. (HIER.) Of the Apostles, or of the beloved.

(CAS.) The Father is the king of the angels, whom he commands; and he himself is beloved.

(AUG.) “The King of the powers of the beloved.” Of the Son—that is, the Father—or, according to the usage of the ancient Scripture, Christ is the king of powers: Christ’s powers, that is, his own, as Moses did what the Lord commanded Moses.

The beloved, the beloved. (CAS.) The repetition of “beloved” is for emphasis. This repetition is not found in all books; but whether it is present or not, the meaning is this: the beloved is appointed not only to other tasks but also to dividing the spoils, and by dividing them he made the Church beautiful.

VERS. 14.—If you sleep. (AUG.) To sleep among the middle lots is to rest in the authority of the two Testaments and to acquiesce peacefully.

The feathers of the dove, silvered. The preachers through whose preaching the glory of the Church is carried into heaven.

Of the dove. (AUG., CAS.) The dove is the Church, etc., up to the point where it is carried into heaven through preaching.

And the hindmost parts. (AUG.) Where the roots of the wings are, etc., up to: charity is the vigor of wisdom.

Among the middle lots. (AUG.) Were it a Latin expression, it would be “among the lots,” etc., up to the point where it is uncertain whether “wings” refers to you.

VERS. 15.—(CAS.) A diapsalm, while he distinguishes the gifts of the ascending Christ, who alone has this power and no other.

(AUG.) While the kings are distinguished by the grace of the Holy Spirit, etc., up to the point where those who believe in him are protected.

VERS. 17.—The mountain of God is a rich mountain. (AUG., CAS.) He next commends the mountain, etc., up to: For this is the mountain that wounds the prince of Tyre in Ezekiel.

It is God’s good pleasure, etc. (AUG.) For the Lord will dwell in it forever—that is, until the limit of his majesty, which is an end without end and the fullness of all things.

For the Lord has dwelt. There is none like this one, because this mountain, namely the Lord, will dwell in those mountains until he leads them to the end—that is, to the contemplation of God in himself.

But the other mountains are chariots by which God is carried throughout the whole world. They are called chariots because they are joined together in unanimity by charity, and God governs them for the service of his will: ten thousand, countless peoples, the multitude of the saints.

In the end. Because he is personally united to the one in whom all the fullness of divinity dwells bodily.

[Col. 0943A] VERS. 18.—Thousands of rejoicing ones. (AUG., CAS.) He signifies a great multitude of saints, etc., up to the point where they therefore rejoice.

Sinai in the holy place. (CAS.) It is the mountain on which the law was given. It is called “commandment,” in which the Lord rests, because his presence is accustomed to be perceived in his holy commandments.

In Sinai. (HIERON.) Or, “in holy Sinai”—that is, the one who once gave the law on Mount Sinai is himself in the holy place, that is, in Christ, who is the Holy of holies.

VERS. 19.—You ascended. (AUG.) He who descended for our instruction.

On high. Above all the heavens.

You took captivity captive. (CAS.) First, those who had been captured in hell. These are spoils, a likeness of triumph.

You received gifts among human beings from the Father—that is, human beings.

Or, “you gave,” according to his divinity, gifts to human beings, which also occurs in triumphs.

You took captivity captive. (AUG.) Hence they are called captives: because they were caught in Peter’s nets and placed under an easy yoke. Hence in this chariot there are thousands rejoicing, not weeping.

You received. Paul, by apostolic authority, etc., up to: “What you did for one of the least of these, you did for me.”

VERS. 20.—Daily. (Ibid.) Because every day he takes captives captive until the end of the age. And because he leads that chariot to the end, he adds “a prosperous journey.”

Journey. The course of life, which is truly prosperous when its guide is the Savior.

VERS. 21.—Our God. (CAS.) A diapsalm. He explains the works that result from the things said above: the crushing of enemies, the conversion of sinners, and martyrdoms of both sexes.

For salvation. (AUG.) He commends grace, because no one is saved except through him. But lest you say, “Why then are they destined to die?” bear it patiently, and do not resent death, since the Lord, who was without sin, also had no other departure than death—yet by his will, so that human beings would not fear death.

The ways out of death. (CAS.) That is, resurrection. Do not complain about death, because Christ came out from it and granted an exit from it.

Lest you think that the evils of the obstinate go unpunished, he adds: “Nevertheless, the heads”—that is, pride, or the leaders of the Jewish faction, sedition, or heresy.

VERS. 22.—The crown of the hair. (Ibid.) The subtleties of empty questions, which seek such hostile calumnies that they seem to examine even the hairs.

VERS. 23.—From Bashan. (AUG.) That is, from confusion, etc., up to those who were most despairing.

VERS. 24.—Your foot. (Ibid.) That is, so that those who were previously enemies may become your foot, preaching even to the shedding of blood, namely, unto death; and the dogs may be those who bark for God and eat from the crumbs, etc.

Your foot. Only those are to be assumed for the office of governance who preach to others what they themselves receive, and who carry out with the hands of good works what they preach or teach with the mouth. Hence in Leviticus: “The mouth of the turtledove is turned back toward the armpits.”

In blood. (BASIL.) Since he showed God, etc., up to: “and when I conquered them, my garments were sprinkled.”
