Of dogs. (AUG.) Gideon was commanded to lead those who, like dogs, lapped water—only three hundred and no more—as a sign of the cross, because of the letter tau, which signifies three hundred.

From him. If you ask where there is such great goodness, that they should be his dogs though they had been his enemies, he says: “From him,” that is, from his grace, not from themselves.

VERS. 25.—They saw your entrances, O God. (Ibid.) Or: “Your footsteps, O God, were seen,” by which you came into the world. This grace was hidden in the Old Testament; now it is revealed when the Son, sent into the nations, is announced.

Who. God. He is in the holy place, in the body, although the faithless do not see him according to the condition in which he suffered. In this respect also, by suffering or believing, the princes went before them, or went before them toward you in praise.

VERS. 26.—Princes. (BASIL., EUTHYM.) He calls the Apostles princes, etc., up to the point where they followed them through preaching.

In the midst. Ministers appointed over new churches that praise God, with the flesh subdued, the leather dried of the moisture of sin, and stretched free from the wrinkle of duplicity.

VERS. 27.—Bless God in the churches. (CAS.) A diapsalm. He prays and affirms that this beginning may be extended and confirmed, and that heretics may be destroyed because of it.

(AUG.) “In the churches.” These are the young women with tambourines, so that no one may think carnally of lascivious dances. For the churches are young women adorned with new grace.

In the churches, not elsewhere and not in other conventicles.

From the springs of Israel. (CAS.) So that you may preach according to their example what is fitting, because they are princes of faith, hope, and charity; and through this, Benjamin—that is, the son of the right hand.

[Col. 0944C] VERS. 28.—There is Benjamin, etc.; the princes, etc. (Ibid.) Through the names of the tribes he indicates Christ and the Apostles.

There, namely, in the temple of Jerusalem or in the Church. The interpretation of the names also suits the Church.

(CAS.) Perhaps the Apostles came from these tribes, etc., up to: confession in faith, strength in hope, breadth in charity.

In the elevation of the mind—or, as the Greek expression properly has it, etc., up to the point where, as a faithful and prudent distributor, he divided.

VERS. 29.—Command, O God, your power. (Ibid.) O God, make the Son known; as though I were announcing what is to happen, bring it to completion.

Or, “your power,” that is, command your strong ones to announce you.

Or, O Father, command your work—your power, the Son, or the Holy Spirit.

(AUG.) For God commends his love toward us because, while we were sinners, Christ died for us. This is rightly and confidently prayed:

Strengthen, O God, what you have accomplished. By beginning it.

VERS. 30.—From your temple in Jerusalem. She is free, our mother, and is the temple from which every perfect gift comes; therefore, from that temple.

The kings of the earth. Or, those specially devoted to you will offer gifts to you, that is, sacrifices of praise.

But because heretics oppose this praise—

VERS. 31.—Rebuke the beasts of the reed. (AUG.) That is, those who are moved by every wind of doctrine.

So that they may exclude those who have been tested. This is what the Apostle says: “Those who have been tested become manifest” (I Cor. XI); or, let those who have been tested exclude them from the cows.

For the stable, strong, and serious have no power to seduce them.

“In a weighty people I shall praise you.” [Col. 0945A]

Scatter them. Rebuke the beasts, and also scatter those who disagree.

The nations that desire wars. Heretics and others who agree with them, whom he calls nations because of the various kinds of sects, lest a sequence of successions there confirm the error.

VERS. 32.—From Egypt, Ethiopia. (AUG.) By the name of Egypt or Ethiopia he signifies the faith of all the nations, using the part for the whole. He therefore prophesies that heralds will come not only from the Jews but from the nations.

(HIER.) Ethiopia, the Gentile world blackened by sins, hastens to give its hands to God. The comparison is drawn from the defeated, who lay down their weapons and give their hands to the victors so that they may not perish.

Its hand will anticipate him. (Ibid.) That is, it will anticipate his vengeance through confession, so that those who remain in sins may not be punished.

VERS. 33.—Kingdoms of the earth, to God. So that “to God” belongs at the beginning of the following verse.

Or, more properly, “to God” belongs at the end of the preceding verse.

Faith is commended—and thus a person is not justified by preceding works—which begins to work through love. Ethiopia will therefore believe in God and thus will anticipate its works—that is, Ethiopia’s own works. In Greek this is not ambiguous: by believing in God, it will anticipate its own works.

Or, “his,” namely Egypt’s, to God—that is, in God.

Kingdoms of the earth, sing to God. (AUG.) Having passed through all the things that we now see fulfilled, he exhorts us to praise Christ and announces his future coming.

Sing psalms. (CASS.) A diapsalm. Sing psalms: he will come who ascended, and there he will bring the saints to completion.

VERS. 34.—He ascends. (Ibid.) According to what he is as human. For according to what he is as God, equal to the Father, he is above the heaven of heaven, above the higher creatures, so that there is nothing above him.

(HIER., CAS.) The East. The Word begotten from the Father. And he ascended from the east by the power of the Word.

Toward the east. He identified the place where he rose and from which he ascended.

(AUG.) Toward the east, the source of our illumination. Or because Jerusalem is in the east.

To his voice. (Ibid.) He who was humble in his passion will give a powerful voice in the universal resurrection.

A powerful voice. (CAS.) The power to raise all the dead.

VERS. 35.—His magnificence and power. (AUG.) Since at that time there will no longer be any mixture of the wicked, his magnificence over the true Israel will then be evident.

In the clouds. Because he will not come alone to judgment but with the elders of the people, who are the clouds. And lest you understand them otherwise, he adds: “Wonderful among the holy ones.”

(EUTHYM.) By “clouds” he understands the Apostles themselves, as those who exist above and rise above earthly affairs, and as though filled with spiritual water, which they drew from the depths of the Holy Spirit, so that they might water the fields and lands of souls—that is, the believers themselves.

VERS. 36.—He himself will give power and strength to his people; blessed be God. (CAS.) He has promised great things, so that no one, because of human weakness, may despair of attaining such rewards.

PSALM LXVIII

VERS. 1.—In the end. (AUG.) Adam was changed from the form of God into something worse, etc., up to the point where he must suffer according to the Greek text.

(CAS.) The fourth psalm that speaks at greater length about the passion and resurrection. It treats the cause of the change, namely, the passion of Christ. Here Christ speaks as both head and body.

Save me. First he prays to be saved, because he suffers many things: in relation to himself freely, but what another stole, he himself repaid.

This is the voice of the despised mustard seed, when it is buried in the garden, which grows into a great plant. It is dark and utterly contemptible. So also Christ, of whom it is said: “We saw him having neither beauty nor attractiveness”; yet he took possession of the face of the earth, becoming a great mountain.

The waters have come up to my soul. (AUG.) That is, the crowds, etc., up to the point beyond which the wicked have nothing they can do to them.

[Col. 0946B] VERS. 3.—In the mire. (AUG.) Man was made from the mire of the earth, etc., up to: that is, the power of the flesh to escape suffering.

Substance. Riches are called substance, etc., up to: that is, I did not find in them what I had made.

I have come. Because willingly.

Into the depth. Into the depth of the maddened people.

VERS. 4.—I have labored. (AUG.) For a long time he cried: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees,” becoming hoarse in relation to them, because he was not understood.

Crying, etc. (CAS.) The one whose wish is not fulfilled labors.

My eyes. Like the eyes of the two who did not recognize him on the road, for whom what was outside became what was within—that is, blindness took place in the heart and in the eyes. For they said: “We were hoping that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke XXIV).

(AUG.) But he restored their hope, etc., up to the point where they would have been lost.

While I hope. (CAS.) The reason follows: I await mercy; I do not plead for power.

VERS. 5.—They have multiplied. (AUG.) What was previously expressed figuratively he now states openly in reality.

Above the hairs. As an expression for an infinite number, or because they are more numerous than those who are ornamental.

I restored what I had not stolen. They wished to seize divinity and lost blessedness. Adam seized it, presuming upon divinity like the devil.

VERS. 6.—O God, you know. (CAS.) Since he paid on behalf of others, he prays that the ancients who await him and the others, namely the moderns, may not be disappointed in him, while he bears so many things with such equanimity.

Foolishness. (AUG.) From the members. Or, “the foolishness of God is wiser than human beings.” You knew why those who seemed wise to themselves mocked what was in me—that such mockery and such death should occur.

(CAS.) Foolishness. Those ignorant of me as God; these are the ones who are changed into the wise and righteous.

VERS. 7.—Let them not be put to shame. (Ibid.) He explains what he has accomplished; here he shows what he had said above concerning the members.

(AUG.) “Let them not be put to shame”—that is, let it not be said to them: “Where is your Christ?” Or, let the Church not be oppressed so that her children may be put to shame.

Those who await you. (CAS.) What the prophets and righteous were unable to see with their eyes.

Lest what the Holy Spirit foretold through them come about otherwise, he adds: “God of powers,” for nothing is impossible for you.

God of Israel. (AUG.) So that those who are able to contemplate his divinity may not be led astray by his carnal weakness.

VERS. 8.—For on your account I endured reproaches. (CAS.) He gathers together many things that he suffered, to arouse hatred against the Jews: reproach, that he cast out demons by Beelzebub, and that he was a drunkard and a glutton (Matt. XI).

It covered me. This usually happens to those who are torn apart while doing good: for a time they become all the sadder the more they recognize that unjust things are being fabricated against them.

VERS. 9.—A stranger. Or, a guest who is received in a house for a time, not as the dearest brother, which I was.

VERS. 10.—Zeal for your house has consumed me. When he drove out those who were selling with a cord.

What follows this zeal, he adds: “And the reproaches of those reproaching you fell upon me.” For the rebuked Jews hurled insults at him like weapons, saying: “Is this not the son of Joseph?” (Luke IV.)

Of those reproaching you. When they said: “Can God prepare a table in the desert?” (Ps. LXXVII); “These are your gods, Israel” (Exod. XXXII). Hence he now says that the same reproaches as those with which they formerly reproached God fell upon him, so that you may see that they did this habitually and impiously, not for the first time.

They fell. (CAS.) Evils fall upon us when we cannot avoid them; therefore “they fell” means that they achieved their effect.

VERS. 11.—And I covered myself with fasting, etc. (AUG.) I chose fasting rather than receiving gall and vinegar—that is, the old and bitter things that do not enter into his body.

(CAS.) And I covered myself. I did not exercise power by taking vengeance. And what became apparent in the spitting occurred as a reproach.

(AUG.) Of those who slander and mock.

VERS. 12.—And I put on. (AUG.) I presented them with flesh against which they could rage, and concealed my divinity.

Sackcloth. (AUG., HIER.) Mortal flesh, so that he might condemn sin with respect to sin.

Sackcloth, mournful flesh, as when he wept over Jerusalem (Luke XIX) and for Lazarus (John XI).

For a parable. (AUG., HIER.) A mocking one, so that in cursing anyone they might say: “May it happen to you as it did to the crucified one.”

Or because I taught them parables; hence: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the Word of God, but to the others in parables.” And then they spoke against me.

VERS. 13.—Those who sat. (CAS.) Those who sit in the gate are those who mingle with human gatherings in persistent curiosity. He therefore says that his passion was the subject of the Jews’ conversation, so that no one who was unfamiliar with such speech would be excluded. Hence Cleopas said: “Are you the only stranger in Jerusalem, and do you not know these things?” (Luke XXIV).

In the gate. Of the city, where judges customarily sit to judge cases—that is, in the public court.

(HIERON.) Like the scribes and Pharisees, who possessed the key of knowledge but neither entered themselves nor allowed others to enter.

And they sang against me. (CAS.) They spoke about me in public gatherings and sang at banquets; my psalm was their mockery.

Those who drank wine. (AUG.) Those who become drunk on temporal pleasure.

Or (CAS.) those who drink spiritual wine sing to God through praiseworthy action.

VERS. 14.—But I. (CAS.) Prayer is set against the evils mentioned above on his own behalf, so that we may learn to oppose prayers rather than quarrels to disputes.

A time of favor. (AUG.) Now is the time of favor and reconciliation through the incarnation, through blood, and through death. Then he explains how this time came about:

In the abundance of mercy.

In truth. He first mentioned mercy and now adds truth, because all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth: mercy in forgiving sins, truth in fulfilling promises.

[Col. 0948B] VERS. 15.—So that I may not be fixed. (AUG.) In mind. Above he said that he was fixed in body; this is said from the weakness of the members.

From the mud. That is, from muddy desires.

From the depths of waters. (CAS.) The Jews are deep in the malignity of their counsel and turbulent in their seditions.

VERS. 16.—The depth. (CAS.) Of sins, which swallows souls. Hence: “When the sinner comes into the depth of sins, he despises” (Prov. XVIII).

These dangers threaten his members.

Nor let it close over me, etc. (AUG.) Even if you have fallen, the pit does not close its mouth over you if you do not close your mouth; but confess and say: “From the depths I have cried to you, O Lord,” and you will escape.

It closes over the one who despises in the depth; from the dead person, as though he did not exist, confession perishes.

[Col. 0948C] VERS. 17.—Hear me, O Lord, etc. (CAS.) Having set forth the dangers of human beings, he prays in their voice: “Hear me, O Lord,” because of your kindly mercy, not because I have deserved it.

Kindly. (AUG.) Mercy is sweet to the afflicted, as bread to the hungry. Tribulation comes; God delays to help, so that he may stir desire and make assistance sweet. When this occurs, there is no longer any reason for delay.

VERS. 18.—From the child, etc. (AUG.) From any holy person, one who is small and not proud; discipline through tribulation removes pride from him.

VERS. 19.—Because of the enemies, etc. (AUG.) So that they may be confounded by my deliverance, etc., up to the point where Nebuchadnezzar himself, having been converted, proclaims God.

Because of the enemies. (ID.) This refers to the open manifestation, so that the flesh may rise and, ascending, send the Spirit. Hence the enemies were converted; it would not benefit them if you freed only the soul.

VERS. 20.—You know my reproach. (ID.) You know why these things happen to me; they do not know. And because they are themselves before your sight, they cannot be confounded or corrected in their ignorance unless you rescue me manifestly.

Therefore he says: Because of the enemies.

(ID.) Reproach or insult, etc., up to the point where he may complete it by assisting.

Humiliation. (ID.) Others read “dishonor,” such as the blows, scourging, and the fact that he was handed over to Pilate as a criminal. He endured these things not for his own guilt but for us, to instruct us in such matters.

VERS. 21.—In your presence. (CAS.) He arouses hatred against them, so that they committed such a great crime in God’s presence.

My heart. Because he endured it willingly, according to the saying: “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you.”

VERS. 21.—And I looked for one who would grieve with me, and there was none; and for one who would comfort me, and I found none. (AUG.) The disciples and the women who wept over him were grieved, but not together with him. For they grieved carnally over mortal life, which was to be changed by death, whereas they ought to have grieved with him over the others who were killing the physician. No one then did this.

VERS. 22.—And they gave gall for my food, and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink. (AUG.) Because I found no one grieving and comforting at the same time, gall was bitter to me on account of sorrow.

Vinegar, etc. That is, something sour, because of their antiquity.

It is read in the Gospel that gall was offered to him, but as a drink, not as food. Mystically, therefore, this means that they cast gall upon the sweet food which he had received with his disciples—the food of the unity of Christ. This is what the contemptuous person still does today, and he sins more gravely who despises the one seated in heaven than the one who crucified him while he walked on earth.

They give a bitter drink to be drunk who, by living badly, cause scandal in the Church, such as heretics.

The Lord tasted it, teaching us also to taste—that is, to suffer such people—but he did not drink, because such people cannot be received into his body. Mystically, therefore, this is foretold, just as it was mystically accomplished in the passion.

[Col. 0949C] (CAS.) And they gave. This is the completion of the passion. When he had said, “I thirst,” they offered gall with vinegar, thereby revealing their exceedingly bitter character.

VERS. 23.—Let their table become. (CAS.) A prophecy against the adversaries.

(AUG.) Let their table become. The table is Scripture. The Jews possessed it while they observed God’s commandment; after they became starved of the law, this table was set before the nations, so that they would grieve more severely.

A snare. So that those who bound others with the letter of the law might fall bound by it themselves.

For retribution. Because it was taken away from them and given to the nations. It was a retribution for their evils: because they were unwilling to feast at it, they were excluded from it.

For a stumbling block. Because, abandoning the author of peace, they stir up quarrels and evil works for themselves.

[Col. 0949D] VERS. 24.—Their eyes. (AUG.) The teachers who go before them.

Let them be darkened. That is, let them lose the light of knowledge.

And their back, etc. That is, the lesser ones. For when those who lead lose the light of knowledge, their followers are inclined to bear the burdens of sins and to desire earthly things.

Or, “their back” means the mind of those same people. Always this is said of those who do not repent.

VERS. 25.—Pour out, etc. (CASS.) So that it may be abundant like the course of a river.

Let it seize. So that escape may not be possible.

VERS. 26.—Let their dwelling become. (AUG.) This is now stated openly, etc., up to the point where they became proud against God.

In their tents. (CAS.) In the temple and the royal palace. He uses “to dwell” for what takes place through the devotion of the mind; “to inhabit houses” for what takes place through bodily dwelling.

VERS. 27.—You struck. (CAS.) Not on account of his own guilt: you struck him through the passion, for the salvation of the nations. They fulfilled this through their cruel desire.

And upon the pain. Because it was for their destruction.

They added. To inflict death.

Or, upon the pain of my wounds—that is, the wounds inflicted on me by the lance and nails—they added the guards of the tomb.

VERS. 28.—Add iniquity upon iniquity, etc. (AUG.) Their iniquity was that they killed a human being; and beyond this God added that they should kill his Son, so that, just as they had killed the servants sent before him, they might kill the heir himself.

[Col. 0950B] VERS. 29.—Let them be blotted out, etc. (ID.) Because they think that they are written, etc., up to the point where they will stand at the right hand.

From the book of the living, etc. (CAS.) The knowledge of God, which predestined those whom he foreknew to life and to conformity with the image of his Son.

It is not to be understood, however, as though God wrote someone in this book and later erased him, but according to the hope of those who think themselves written in it.

VERS. 30.—I am poor, etc. (CAS.) Here he explains the dispensation of the incarnation and the holiness of his purpose, saying: What is the end of the passion?

Grieving. (AUG.) As head, he grieves for all. Hence: “He himself bore our sorrows” (Isa. LIII), something no one else did.

Therefore he says:

VERS. 32.—And it will please. (CAS.) The praise of a pure heart pleases more than the slaughter of cattle.

A young bull. (AUG.) A young bull was offered for sins and signified the newness that was to follow. It has defense in its horns and protection for its feet in its hooves, by which it tramples the roughness of the world, and it grows, because the faithful person increases daily through God’s power.

(AUG.) The bull stirs up the earth with its hooves. Thus the one who does not contradict but nevertheless thinks in an abjectly earthly way must be roused by his hooves. And over this bull my praise will please, together with the angels, where neither an adversary will have to be winnowed nor a sluggish person roused from the earth.

VERS. 33.—Let them see. (CAS.) The offering is already in the mind, not in material things, where the poor is made equal to the rich.

And you poor, nevertheless do this with the vision of God; seek the Lord.

Or, so that you may see, seek God, the food of the mind.

The prisoners. (AUG.) Whoever seeks beyond what is necessary loads himself with fetters; but each day has enough of its own trouble.

The prisoners. (ID.) Those bound by mortality, with which the offended Lord fettered his servants; but he hears those who cry out from there.

VERS. 35.—Heaven, earth, and sea. (CAS.) Literally, the heavenly, earthly, and swimming creatures praise him, while the Creator is praised through them.

The wealth of the poor is to see created things and from them praise the Creator.

Let them praise him, etc. (ID.) What he previously urged collectively, he now urges individually; or, let the heavenly, earthly, and swimming creatures praise him.

And, to conclude everything completely, he adds: “All that is in them.” Thus every creature is invited to praise.

(HIER., CAS.) As though he were saying: “Every knee of the heavenly, earthly, and infernal beings should bow” (Phil. II).

And all creeping things in them. (CAS.) All monstrous forms that cling to earthly sins.

VERS. 36.—For God will save Zion, etc. (AUG.) In the hope of the faithful people, the building of the Church is completed; hence every creature is instructed to praise.

VERS. 37.—And those who love his name, etc. (CAS.) Why speak of each one separately? All who love your name will dwell there.

(AUG.) These are the offspring of servants. For this verse explains the preceding one.

PSALM LXIX

VERS. 1.—For remembrance. (CAS.) Remembrance is understood in two ways, etc., up to the point where they take up the hope of the resurrection.

(AUG.) The voice of those afflicted for Christ, etc., up to the point where they first ask to be helped and for the wicked to be put to shame.

VERS. 2.—O God, come to my assistance. He instructs us to glory in God, not in ourselves.

(CAS.) Here every petition is an affirmation; therefore tribulations are not to be feared.

This verse is said at the beginning before all the hours, because when we customarily pray, the devil especially strives to tempt us, so that dying flies may spoil the sweetness of the ointment.

VERS. 3.—Let them be confounded. (CAS.) To be confounded is to be disturbed because of perversity.

Let them turn back, lest punishment follow their departure from righteousness.

Those who seek, etc. (AUG.) There are different times in the Church. At first there was the assault of persecutors, hence “those who seek”; now the malevolence of those who think wrongly remains, hence “those who desire.” (ID.)

[Col. 0951C] **VERSE 4.**—“Let them be turned back.” (ID.) There are two kinds of persecutors, and so on, up to the point where he emerges whole, who is caught by neither kind.

**VERSE 5.**—“Let all who seek you exult and rejoice in you.” (CAS.) He urges the good to rejoice, whom God helps and delivers in their poverty. “Always.” Because one ought never to cease praising him. “Let God be magnified.” (CAS.) This is said according to our customary manner, when someone grows through praises; for it is not God but we who make progress by praising.

**VERSE 6.**—“But I am poor.” (CAS.) What I urge, I do myself, and so on, up to the point where the rich person is always striving, desiring, and receiving. “Do not delay.” (ID.) What is sought with great desire seems slow. (AUG.) May what you are going to do not seem slow to me; this comes about through patience. To one who lacks patience it seems slow, and he turns away from it—like Lot’s wife, who became a pillar of salt so that she might season you. For she is an example to you, warning you not to look back.

# PSALM LXX

**VERSE 1.**—“For the end.” (AUG.) Concerning the commendation of grace, and so on, up to the point where grace is commended in nearly every syllable.

“Of the sons of Jonadab.” (ID.) To willing sons, and so on, up to those who are evil of themselves.

(CAS.) Or the sense is this: in the title we are warned to possess the devotion of the sons of Jonadab, and so on, up to the point that they, on the other hand, remained in their customary wickedness through obstinacy.

**VERSE 2.**—“In you, Lord, I have hoped.” The general righteous person speaks from the beginning of the world to its end. By placing all his hope in God, he commends his grace, lest we presume falsely upon ourselves.

(CAS.) Or the first captives are those in the world, from which one can escape; the second are those in hell. Or “the first” means those who were taken captive by vices before becoming sons of Christ. This entire psalm commends God’s grace, which is given freely, with the greatest emphasis.

**VERSE 3.**—“Be to me a protecting God and a fortified place,” and so on. He promised two things and gives back two others.

**VERSE 4.**—“Of the sinner.” (AUG.) There are two kinds of sinners: some have received the law, such as Jews and Christians; others have not, such as pagans.

**VERSE 5.**—“From my youth.” (CAS.) That is, from my conversion, or from the time when I began to fight against the devil. [Col. 0952B] (AUG.) “From my youth”: from the time when I began to hope in you, and so on, up to the point where the young man fights but falls unless God is his hope.

**VERSE 7.**—“In you is my song.” (CAS.) It is my delight to be in you. “Always,” so that the benefits may be continuous. “Always.” (AUG.) Both in the present life, and so on, up to the point against which nothing can stand.

**VERSE 8.**—“Let my mouth be filled.” (CAS.) He has mentioned the benefits; now he asks that he may be able to give thanks. For if God does not fill the mouth, desire does not burn. “All day long your greatness.” (AUG.) That is, without interruption, and so on, up to the point where he includes everything under the name of greatness.

**VERSE 9.**—“Do not cast me away.” (CAS.) Concerning the grace to be given in the time of old age and extreme age. “Of old age.” (AUG.) Old age in Christ: when he became a portent, when he was weakened on the cross and mocked. It is called old age because he assumed it from antiquity; hence: “Our old man was crucified together with him” (Rom. VI).

**VERSE 10.**—“For my enemies have said.” (AUG.) This is said of Christ, who became weak in the hands of his enemies and, as though he could do nothing, was seized. But here it is said of his members, because he also possessed such things from our condition.

**VERSE 11.**—“God has forsaken him.” (AUG.) Hence elsewhere: “Why have you forsaken me?” That is, “Why do they think that I have been forsaken,” to their own harm? For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory.

**VERSE 12.**—“Do not be far from me.” (CAS.) They think him far away while he delays; “do not be far,” so that he may expose them to more serious things.

**VERSE 13.**—“Let them be confounded,” and so on. (CAS.) Because God’s decrees are not changed. “Those who detract from my soul.” Another reading: “those who commit my soul.” (AUG.) That is, those who provoke us to resist God, which is to commit war against God, as do those who are displeased that God is present in their adversities—thereby considering him unjust. The soul is also “committed” if one hates those by whom one suffers. “Those who seek.” (ID.) As Job’s wife did, when she said: “Say something against God and die” (Job VII). Tobit’s wife likewise said: “Where are your righteous deeds?” (Tob. IV, 2). She said this in order to make God displeasing to him.

**VERSE 14.**—“And I shall add.” (AUG.) The addition is an addition of praise. After the creation of all things comes praise of the incarnation [Col. 0953A] and resurrection, as the following words teach. “All.” (AUG.) For if he has been praised in all other respects, praise has not yet been added for that by which he raised our flesh to eternal life—this is the added praise for Christ’s resurrection. Or praise would be complete, and nothing would be lacking to praise, if he condemned sinners, since that would be justice; but because he also frees them: “I shall add to all your praise.”

**VERSE 15.**—“My mouth shall proclaim righteousness.” Christ—but lest you understand it otherwise, he adds: “salvation.” Why? Because no one is approved as justified by works of the law. And this is what follows: “For I have not known letters,” that is, the figures of the law, through which I might become powerful. “All day long.” (AUG.) Or in this way, and so on, up to the point where he serves righteousness. “For I have not known letters.” (ID.) I shall proclaim your salvation all day long, and so on, up to the point where [Col. 0953B] “he was found in human form” (Phil. II), and the dead man rises.

**VERSES 17–18.**—“You have taught.” (CAS.) Through books, or by inspiring, up to the present time; through the passage of the ages doctrine has grown. “Wonders.” That the righteous comes from the unrighteous. “Wonders.” (AUG.) What is more wonderful than raising the dead? and so on, up to the point that this is “from youth and now.” “Youth.” (ID.) Some identify four periods of the Church; others distinguish only three, signifying the same thing by “now” and “old age.” Hence the youth of the Church was when the courage of the martyrs fought. (CAS.) The advancing period is “now,” when faith flourishes throughout the churches. (AUG.) “Old age,” that is, a grave age, when the love of many will begin to grow cold as the times of the world diminish. “Extreme old age.” (CAS.) The final period, and so on, [Col. 0953C] up to the point against which the Lord says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age,” and so on (Matt. XXI).—“Until I proclaim your arm.” (CAS.) While through the incarnation he frees captives. “And the justice of judgment,” namely, the justice by which he punishes, through which he condemns sinful humanity by a just judgment.

**VERSES 19–20.**—“Up to the highest places.” And lest you think that only humanity needs grace, and so on, up to the point where he contains in himself what they are.

“Up to the highest places.” Because the human being who is God sits at the right hand of the Father, reigning with him. “The great things that you have done.” Both are wondrous: that humanity, which had been condemned by justice, is redeemed through grace.

“God, who is like you?” You have shown me many and evil tribulations, and, turning back, you have given me life, [Col. 0953D] and from the depths of the earth, and so on. The person to whom grace belongs is the captive; both resurrections, of mind and of body, belong to him. Hence he promises thanksgiving.

**VERSE 22.**—“With the instruments of the psalm.” (CAS.) In the vivification of the spirit, or in the contemplative life.

**VERSE 23.**—“My soul, which you have redeemed.” (AUG.) With those inner lips by which it silently cries out to God.

**VERSE 24.**—“When they have been confounded and put to shame.” Then there is a place for true and secure exaltation, when the wicked are not permitted to rule.

# PSALM LXXI

**VERSE 1.**—“For Solomon,” and so on. (AUG.) The true peacemaker, and so on, up to the point where he is commended here according to [Col. 0954A] both natures. (CAS.) This is the fourth psalm concerning the two natures of Christ. It teaches us to believe that Christ, the true God and true man, is king, and it is a prophecy concerning Christ.

**VERSE 2.**—“God, give your judgment.” (CAS.) Concerning judgment, desiring that it be given to the Son. “Your righteousness,” and so on. (AUG.) Note the repetitions of the same expression, or of the same meaning in other words. The divine utterances commend this greatly, especially in the Psalms and in that form of speech by which the emotions of the soul are to be stirred.

**VERSE 3.**—“The mountains.” (AUG.) The prophets and apostles, who draw near to heaven in height; they announce peace to the faithful people, namely Christ. “And the hills.” Let them receive righteousness, that is, Christ; or, “the mountains” receive peace for the people, and he speaks of the hills as both the earlier and the later preachers. Or “let the mountains receive” means the greater ones.

“Peace.” The word of reconciliation, namely the word of the Gospel, so that they may announce it to the people.

“And the hills.” That is, the lesser ones; “righteousness,” that is, obedience, so that they may obey the teaching of truth.

By saying “your” and “your own,” he shows that all things belonging to the Father belong to the Son, and conversely.

**VERSE 4.**—“He shall judge the poor of the people.” (CAS.) He continues to speak of the same judgment, affirming it. After the expression of desire, by the power of prophecy he states what is to be accomplished at the Lord’s coming. (AUG.) Or according to another reading: “Righteousness shall judge the poor man.” But the manuscripts that have the former wording are more approved. “The poor of the people”: that is, those who are poor within the people, in which good and evil are mingled. “He shall humble the slanderer.” For while he helps by his grace, and so on, up to the one who strives to drag the innocent into guilt. (HIERON., AUG.) Or “he shall humble,” and, once the devil has been conquered, the splendor will remain with the sun—that is, the Son with the Father, sitting at the Father’s right hand forever. This is “before the moon,” from generation to generation.

**VERSE 7.**—“He shall descend like rain,” and so on. (CAS.) Behold what kind of king he is who will judge. (AUG.) He alludes to the deed of Gideon, and so on, up to the point where afterward the Gentiles would be rained upon by the dry fleece of the Jews. (CAS.) Christ will descend, and so on, up to the question: after such clear comparisons, who would doubt the Virgin’s childbirth? “Upon the fleece, and like drops.” (AUG.) The fleece is Judaea, which was to be stripped of the authority of its teaching, like a sheep of its fleece; or because it held back the rain of teaching, which it did not wish to proclaim to the Gentiles.

**VERSE 8.**—“And he shall rule from sea to sea.” (CAS.) He shows the extent of the kingdom. “From the river.” (AUG.) From the Jordan, where the voice said: “This is my beloved Son.” From there, therefore, his teaching began; from there the authority of the teacher spread to the ends of the earth, when the Gospel of the kingdom was preached. (CASS.) From there the rule of baptism flowed throughout the whole world. In a few words he teaches great mysteries.

**VERSE 10.**—“The kings of Tarshish and the islands shall offer gifts.” (CAS.) The enemies are called obstinate, and so on, up to the point where it may also be understood historically of the kings who came to worship Christ.

[Col. 0955A] **VERSE 12.**—“For he shall deliver the poor from the powerful,” and so on. (CASS.) He speaks of his works, and so on, up to the point where it is in participation in righteousness.

**VERSE 14.**—“From usury.” (AUG.) Usuries are sins, and so on, up to the point where he helps by grace to perform righteousness. Or “from usury” refers to the future, that is, eternal punishments; and “from iniquity,” that is, from the sin itself for which punishment was owed. “The name”: Christian. “Before him”: because in his kingdom they will live before him.

**VERSE 15.**—“And he shall live, and gold from Arabia shall be given to him,” and so on. (CAS.) Concerning the honor paid to the king. “Of Arabia.” (AUG.) By Arabia he means the nations; by gold, wisdom, which excels among teachings. “Always concerning him.” (ID.) Whether by multiplying, attaining, or by his instruction, because he himself taught us to pray.

[Col. 0955B] **VERSE 16.**—“Firmament.” (AUG.) It belongs to the prophets, because he fulfilled what they foretold. “On the summits of the mountains.” (ID.) The authors of Scripture are the prophets and apostles; he strengthens them because everything foretold by them was fulfilled in him.

“On the earth.” Because everything was written for those who are on earth. Hence he himself came to earth in order to fulfill it.

“Upon Lebanon.” (AUG.) As Lebanon produces lofty cedars, so Christ raises the saints to heaven. “Like hay.” (CAS.) It is not the age of the old man that is compared with the saints, but their greenness. The good, migrating from this city of the present Church into that blessedness, will flourish. (AUG.) In Genesis, the name “hay” also signifies grain, and so on, up to the point where whatever is considered great in the world will be compared with the hay of the earth.

**VERSE 17.**—“Let his name be blessed,” and so on. (CAS.) He urges everyone to utter praises to him, because all will be blessed in him. “Before the sun.” (ID.) That is, before every creature, lest you think the Son of God temporal. “All nations.” (AUG.) Lest you understand only the twelve tribes, he adds: “all nations.”

**VERSE 18.**—“Blessed is the Lord God of Israel,” and so on. (AUG.) He praises him from his own side. Note the exclamatory blessing, together with admonition and prophecy. “Let it be done, let it be done,” and so on. (CAS.) It is magnificent that he concludes in this way. One who merely wishes says it once; one who desires greatly repeats it. It is as though he said: “What you have commanded, Lord, let it be done, let it be done, until what began from the river reaches the ends of the earth.” (HIER.) It should be known that Psalm Seventy-One [Col. 0955D] is the end of the second book. Hence at its conclusion it has: “Let it be done, let it be done,” for which the Hebrew has: “Amen, amen.”

**VERSE 20.**—“The praises have come to an end.” (ID.) This too must be carefully observed: the words “The hymns of David son of Jesse have come to an end” belong to the conclusion of Psalm Seventy-One. What follows—“A psalm of Asaph”—is the beginning of the next psalm.

A hymn has three elements: the praise of God together with song. Unless it is sung cheerfully, it is not a hymn; and one who does not love does not sing. If there is praise but it is not of God, it is not a hymn; and if it is of God but not accompanied by song, it is not a hymn. Beyond the usual wording he adds “son of Jesse.” David was a man, a certain son of Jesse, who reigned in [Col. 0956A] Israel during the time of the Old Testament, in which the New Testament was present but hidden. So too Christ was present in David and in Abraham, but hidden, as the fruit is in the root but does not appear. Yet a few prophets knew both Christ and the New Testament, namely in hidden form, and foretold that they would be revealed.

At that time, therefore, in place of that kingdom in which the human son of Jesse reigned, a carnal people praised God for such carnal matters. But when that kingdom and the other matters of that kind came to an end, praise came to an end—not the praise of the Son of God, but that of the son of Jesse. When these things, which God withdrew so that the hidden realities concealed within them might be sought, had come to an end, Asaph—that is, the faithful Synagogue, which had worshiped God devoutly, although it sought earthly things from God rather than from demons, as the nations did—speaks.

But when it noticed that blasphemers possessed in abundance the things for which it had served, it began to waver, not knowing what was hidden in these figures, as though there were nothing better for God to give. Then, admonished through the things withdrawn from it to seek what it did not share with the wicked, and chastising itself with astonishment, it says: “How good is God to Israel!” But to whom? “To those who are upright in heart.” First, therefore, describing the wickedness of the evil, it says that it had envied their prosperity; nevertheless, having been corrected by this, it corrects others.

(CAS.) Here it is explained that the praises came to an end because God no longer gives pleasant things, by which children are enticed to serve him. The Synagogue says this, now bearing witness against its former conduct, so that its testimony may be more credible.

# PSALM LXXII

[Col. 0956C] **VERSE 1.**—“How good.” (CAS.) He urges us to praise God not for temporal things but for eternal ones.

**VERSE 2.**—“My feet.” (CAS.) On account of the mind’s judgment, which differed from the truth. “My steps”: precipitate actions. “Almost”: because he quickly returned.

**VERSES 3–4.**—“The peace of sinners.” (AUG.) Temporal, passing, and perishable. “Seeing”: not understanding. For this peace appears but is not understood; it deceives the eyes, since it is passing and perishable. (CAS.) “The peace of sinners,” because there is no turning aside to their death. That is, they do not die quickly but live for a long time; and although punishment sometimes comes, it is not permanent, as the scourging of correction continues. “And firmness in their affliction.” God does not show mercy by solidifying their wounds; or, by comparison, it is incurable, since nothing restrains it.

**VERSE 6.**—“They are covered with their iniquity and impiety.” (CAS.) So that they may not come to their senses. They are not merely clothed, as though their head remained free, but entirely covered.

**VERSE 7.**—“Their iniquity has gone forth as though,” and so on. (AUG.) Some wicked people arise from poverty, that is, necessity; others from abundance. A poor man steals because of want, a rich man because of greed. “They have passed over.” (CAS.) As though departing from straight paths.

**VERSE 8.**—“In the high place.” (AUG.) Openly, in public; or blasphemously against God.

**VERSE 9.**—“Into heaven.” (ID.) As though they were gods; or against God, whom they blaspheme, saying either that God does not know their evils or that he does not punish them. “Their tongue has passed over the earth,” and so on. (ID.) It speaks beyond the measure of human nature, and so on, up to the point where their tongue nevertheless passes beyond human frailty.

**VERSE 10.**—“Therefore he will turn.” (CAS.) As Asaph explains, and so on, up to the point where he will return to it. “Here.” (AUG.) In this condition in which I now am. “Days of fullness will be found in them.” (HIERON.) They are found to be perfect, even if this is not now apparent. (CAS.) Or the days are full when Christ comes. Thus these are among the Jews who knew Christ.

**VERSE 11.**—“And they said.” (AUG.) From where will they turn? and so on, up to the point where this explains why it seemed to them that he did not know. “How does he know?” (ID.) He does not say, “He does not know,” but still hesitates and is near to healing. One who is closer to health is more tormented by so serious an illness, just as the sick are more fevered when health is near.

[Col. 0957B] **VERSE 13.**—“And I said: Therefore I have justified my heart without cause,” and so on. (CAS.) Those who said these things are refuted by what follows; or the words are still spoken by one who doubts. He says that he was deceived by foolish thoughts, so that when he rejects these notions he may care for us better.

**VERSE 14.**—“And my chastisement.” Another reading: “and my judge in the morning.” (CAS.) Behold the remedy already: Christ is the judge who showed the way of truth and, rising in the morning, transferred our hope from the world to the heavens.

**VERSE 15.**—“If I said.” (ID.) Behold, he now restrains himself by the authority of the saints and deliberates in the light of truth already near: “If I said.” “Behold the nation.” (AUG.) He begins to resolve another difficulty. “I rejected”: I judged what is not so. “I thought”: through what was said before I wished to prove that God is not just; but in this way I am only thinking, not acquitting him. “Before me,” that is, as far as present things are concerned; or “greater than I,” surpassing me, unless God reveals it.

Or: “Behold the nation of your sons, which I planned and composed”—understand, “meets and confronts me.” That is, the preaching that I had previously addressed to the Israelites confronts me: that they should worship God, who created all things and restores to everyone according to his works. The teaching to which I belonged and was suited confronts me. But lest I reject the nation of the fathers of old or contradict my former teaching: “I went in,” and so on.

“Your sons.” For Abraham and the others all teach something different, and I must believe them; I am not wiser than everyone. But lest I reject them: “I thought,” or “I undertook to understand.” He is now recalled from his fall, since he does not presume to be knowledgeable against the saints. “To understand” [Col. 0957D] the truth of this matter, which he had not understood before, when he said that God did not care about these things. “I considered in order to know this”: the first stage of knowledge, when one knows that one does not know what one previously seemed to know. He rejects his former understanding while seeking another.

**VERSE 16.**—“Labor is before me.” (AUG.) As though a wall obstructed me, and so on, up to the point where he sees them condemned in the judgment.

**VERSE 17.**—“The sanctuary.” (AUG.) Christ, who, as God, discerns the merits of each person. Or “the sanctuary” means the Holy of Holies, that is, the secret of divine providence.

**VERSE 18.**—“Nevertheless.” (AUG., CASS.) Behold what he learned in the sanctuary: that the wicked are deceived here and afterward, at the end, are abandoned by everyone. He himself was freed from this evil, although he also sought earthly things, but from God. Here he says that the wicked in this world are not free from guilt or punishment; for although they are prosperous, they nevertheless carry guilt and often suffer ruin. “Nevertheless,” that is, “but”; here too you have placed before them this flower and abundance of temporal things on account of deceptions, and so on.

“On account of deceptions.” (AUG.) Or “according to slipperiness.” As though he said: “You have dealt deceitfully with them, giving evil things under the appearance of good.” Or “according to slipperiness,” as temporal things are: those who draw near to them through love fall. For when a deceitful person wishes to bring another down, he places him beside a slippery place.

**VERSE 20.**—“Like a dream.” (ID.) An obvious comparison. With our eyes closed, we see good things that we do not find once our eyes are opened; life is a dream, and in death they awaken, [Col. 0958B] knowing what it is. “In the city.” In the sight of your people, or while your city is being established. (HIER.) Or in the heavenly Jerusalem, their image: the likenesses of the deformities they make for themselves. One is a lion through savagery, another a boar through the filth of lust. (CAS.) Or it refers to the glory of the present age, which is not true but only a likeness of glory. When truth is absent from them, the image will perish; nor will those retain even the likeness who will possess nothing of blessedness. Therefore you will destroy them, because through them—

**VERSE 21.**—“My heart was inflamed.” That is, I was envious of the prosperous. “And my kidneys were changed.” Through them the condition—that is, the steadfastness—of my mind was dissolved, so that I loved prosperity. It is a grave fault to provide others with an occasion for sinning. “I was reduced to nothing.” Clinging to vain things, I became injurious to God. “I did not know.” It is great and profound ignorance not to know that one is sinning. (CAS.) “In your city, their image.” Or this can be understood of heretics, and so on, up to the point where it may also refer to the Church above in heaven. “Because my heart was inflamed.” (AUG.) Behold the conversion of this Asaph, and so on, up to the point where they were changed into spiritual things.

**VERSE 24.**—“With,” and so on. (ID.) Because earlier I was reduced to nothing, that is, I descended to things that are nothing, since I did not know that they were nothing; afterward I became tame like a beast of burden by bearing the load, and I shall always be with you.

“Beast of burden.” (CAS.) With God, those who think against God are counted as cattle. Yet while wandering among them and ignorant of God’s judgments, I was always in some way with you: separated from idols and believing in you. And you held me.

“You held my hand.” (AUG.) Although I was a beast, I did not depart from God. “You held my hand,” that is, the power of the right hand; that is, you covered what was always with you, what was a son. For he gave the power to become children of God to those who believe in his name. “In the left hand”: the beast that loves temporal things. Or, “the right hand.”

(CAS.) Not the left. God holds the right hand when he directs one toward good works and frees one from sinking, as he did Peter. (ID.) Having seen the evil of the wicked and his own good, he reproves himself for having previously sought earthly things from God and invites himself toward the opposite.

(AUG.) He compares the heavenly reward with his earthly pleasure and reproves himself.

“Forever,” and so on. I shall never again be separated from him.

“Those who fornicate away from you,” and so on. Opposed to this fornication is chaste fear, which loves him freely and possesses everything in him.

**VERSE 28.**—“In the gates of the daughter of Zion.” (AUG.) In public, or in the harmony of the apostles, who are the gates of the Church. For preaching that exists outside the unity of the Church is empty. Or the Church is the daughter of Zion, that is, of contemplation, through its virtues.

# PSALM LXXIII

**VERSE 1.**—“An instruction of Asaph.” (AUG.) Of the Synagogue, and so on, up to the point where the hardness of the Jews might either be frightened by calamities or softened by them. (CAS.) He urges us, having left figures behind, to pass over to the truth.

“Why, O God?” (ID.) Describing the irreparable overthrow of Jerusalem, he asks the reason, with astonishment and lamentation; he prays for the rejected people and for vengeance against the destroyers. This is indeed useful to them, and has already occurred. “You have rejected us.” (ID.) As though we were strangers to your protection. “For the end.” Not even the temple is spared. He signifies the destruction and captivity brought about by Titus and Vespasian. He calls them sheep in order to move the mercy of the pious shepherd. “Your own.” We exact vengeance more moderately against those whom we remember once to have been ours.

**VERSE 2.**—“You possessed.” (CASS.) Or “you created,” although he creates and orders everyone, yet he specially created the Jews, to whom he gave the law and the prophets. “You redeemed.” (HIER.) By you as the price—that is, through you as the price. “The mountain.” (AUG.) Eminence. Zion is contemplation, in which—or in which place—you dwelt. Or the expression “in it” is superfluous. (HIER.) The mountain, or the mountain of Zion, or “in it.” Up to this point he has spoken of events of the true Testament; what follows is the promised truth. Through Zion he signifies Jerusalem, in which Christ’s presence dwelt; therefore he implores that he not abandon it to devastation.

“The rod of your inheritance.” (AUG.) The congregation itself is called the rod of inheritance. Wishing to possess it, Moses turned the rod into a serpent; but when he grasped it by the tail, it returned to being a rod. (HIER.) Because death entered the world at the serpent’s persuasion: the rod became a serpent, Christ was in death. Hence the one who looked upon the serpent—that is, believed in Christ dead—was healed from serpents, that is, from eternal death. Moses was terrified and fled; so were the apostles when Christ died. When the tail, that is, the later part, is held, it becomes a rod, because he was first killed and afterward rose. The tail is also the end of the age, in which we return to the hand of God and are made firm; through death, as through a serpent, we have flowed away.

(AUG.) But because these things also concern the Gentiles, he makes clear of whom he speaks: “Mount Zion,” [Col. 0959D] that is, not the Gentiles. Or “this Mount Zion,” which you inhabited in it: “Lift up your hand against their pride,” namely against those by whom Jerusalem was overthrown, that is, the kings of the nations. “For the end,” because they too have now come to know Christ.

**VERSE 3.**—“Lift up.” (CAS.) Your power, so that you may turn their pride into humility, leading them to the end, that is, to Christ. This has also been fulfilled, because Christian religion flourished at Rome. “Lift up,” because what had become exceedingly superstitious has become most holy. “How greatly the enemy has acted wickedly,” and so on. (AUG.) The priests and the ministries of the temple were plundered; the whole people was either killed or taken captive. “The enemy” is the Roman army; he anticipated this by prolepsis.

[Col. 0960A] **VERSE 4.**—“They gloried.” (AUG., CASS.) In their victory. Behold that they did not act from good zeal. They gloried, although crime is normally followed by repentance; they turned it into glory. “Those who hate you”: servants of demons, who are in no way to be tolerated. “In the midst of your solemn assembly.” Not in an out-of-the-way place, but in the middle of the court. Another reading: “They committed sacrilege.” “In the holy place.” (CAS.) In the sanctuary, through contempt for the holy temple, where the divine nature seems to be despised; this provokes indignation against the presumptuous. “Their signs,” and so on. (AUG.) Eagles, and so on, up to the point where he means elevated places.

**VERSE 5.**—“As at the exit.” (CAS.) Or as at an emergence from above; that is, they did not know that this license proceeded from God. “As in a forest,” and so on. (CASS.) Before it was built, he prophesies the overthrow of the temple.

“With axe and adze they polluted the dwelling of your name,” [Col. 0960B] and so on. (AUG.) The axe cuts beams; the adze pursues its work in smaller detail. Through this he says that both great and small things were thrown down, so that the city was utterly devastated: first cut apart, then fire consumed everything.

**VERSE 7.**—“They cast it into the ground,” and so on, up to the point where they threw to the ground the roofs erected for the praise of God. He increases the crime so that it may be punished more severely. (CAS.) Or the whole passage can be read as spoken by the despairing Jews, and so on, up to the point where they do not repent amid these things. (AUG.) They said these things, but “how long will you tolerate the insults of the Jews?” He did not say this because he wished them to perish, but that they might be changed. “Until the end of the world,” namely the evening, when the Jews will be converted.

**VERSE 9.**—“We have not seen our signs.” (AUG., CASS.) [Col. 0960C] As though they said: “These evils have rightly come upon us, because we did not see the signs.” It is as though he said: “We saw them, but did not understand them.” And truly we saw them, because this is the sign: there is no prophet, priest, or anointing. Hence: “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing will cease” (Dan. IX). Nor will any prophet or God through a prophet make himself known to us anymore; that is, he will not announce the coming Christ, because he has already come. “Any more.” (ID.) Or “he will not yet make himself known,” that is, until the Jew recognizes him.

**VERSE 10.**—“How long?” and so on. (CAS.) And as though he had suddenly understood: “How long,” he adds, “will the adversary reproach?” As though he said: “He will reproach for as long as the adversary”—that is, the Jew—“provokes your name.” “Why do you turn away?” (AUG.) After the sign of the rod, the sign of Moses’ hand was added. This is the people of God: sent outside by him, it is unclean, but when recalled it returns to its own color. He therefore says: “How long will you not recall your hand, so that it may recognize the Savior?” “Your hand and your right hand,” that is, the Jews.

**VERSE 12.**—“But God is our king.” (CAS.) Once the signs have been destroyed, he points to the reality itself: namely, that at Christ’s coming salvation was accomplished everywhere. (AUG.) “But God.” Asaph speaks with understanding, and so on, up to the point where, if it did not precede, it should at least follow.

“In the midst of the earth.” (CAS.) Having become man, he is said to be in the midst of Jerusalem.

**VERSE 13.**—“You established.” (AUG.) The parting of the Red Sea established it so that there might be dry land in its midst. He adds its mystery: in the waters of baptism he annihilated the heads of unclean spirits.

**VERSE 14.**—“Food.” (AUG.) Christ is food, and so on, up to the point where they even bite him by reproving and accusing him. (CAS.) Or while he is tempting, he is food, because one makes progress through it. Or it refers to the peoples of the Ethiopians. (HIERON.) To those unwilling to convert, you gave him as food in which they might take delight.

**VERSE 15.**—“Fountains and torrents.” (AUG.) In some people the word comes to be, and so on, up to the point where he indicates the abundance of preaching. (CAS.) Or the whole passage concerns evil people. “Fountains”: those from which evils continually flowed. “Torrents”: those who sin suddenly and rapidly. God breaks and dries these up. “The rivers of Ethan”: the floods and counsels of the devil.

“Yours is the day and yours is the night.” (AUG.) He illuminates the day through unchanging wisdom. The moon consoles the night, that is, the manifestation of the flesh: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I). And again: “Night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. XXVIII). “The dawn and the sun.” (AUG.) Or the moon, that is, the carnal one, which changes like the moon, yet must not be abandoned. Or “the dawn and the sun,” that is, the beginning and progress of wisdom in the foolish and in the perfect.

**VERSE 17.**—“You made all things.” (CAS.) Or from this point everything is historical: “Yours is the day.” “The boundaries of the earth,” and so on. (CAS.) The apostles and prophets, just as boundaries distinguish regions, so they preserve the laws of faith; or everything may be understood historically.

**VERSE 18.**—“Remember.” (CAS.) What is done everywhere now: he prays for the Jews and, by recounting benefits, appeals to the merciful judge. As though he said: “Remember this creature of yours.” “This”—whose creature of yours? “The enemy has reproached the Lord, and the foolish people have provoked your name,” and so on. (AUG.) Asaph, with understanding, grieves over his former blindness and thus prays for the Jews, so that they may confess their errors. He prays for what he knows will happen, for there were vessels of mercy among the Jews.

**VERSE 20.**—“Look upon your covenant.” (ID.) May the remnants be saved, because many who stretch toward the earth have been darkened and filled with earth. (CAS.) “Look upon it”: fulfill what you promised, so that you may establish the New Testament, which concerns eternal things. He recalls the promise because merits fail. Also because they have been filled with iniquities; hence darkness follows, since those filled with iniquities lose the light of wisdom. They are darkened because the houses of the earth are filled with earthly habitation—that is, they are blind through love of earthly things.

**VERSE 21.**—“Let the humble one not turn away, having been put to shame.” (CAS.) “Grateful” is used in place of “hateful,” so that the love of the devout may temper hatred of the obstinate. “Put to shame.” (ID.) It is not the humble person but the proud who is confounded, because he attributes things not to God but to himself.

**VERSE 22.**—“Arise, O God.” (CASS.) Asaph, with understanding, now shakes off the earthly promises of the Old Testament. “Your cause.” For they say: “Where is your God?” He was despised by the Jews while walking on earth and by false Christians while sitting in heaven. Judge, therefore, so that my hope may not be deceived, since I have believed what I did not see.

“Your cause.” [Col. 0962A] After everything, he presents the judge’s case, informing him of the nature of his own litigation. “Your cause” against those who murmur, so that they may proclaim with evident truth what they foolishly denied. “All day long.” (AUG.) He says this so that the very continuity of the matter might stir the patience of the merciful judge.

**VERSE 23.**—“The pride of those who hate you.” (CAS.) At the end he places the detestable evil, which is pride.

# PSALM LXXIV

**VERSE 1.**—“For the end: do not destroy,” and so on. (AUG.) This psalm urges, and so on, up to the point where the Jews may believe and not destroy faith.

**VERSE 2.**—“We shall confess to you, O God.” (AUG.) Therefore, certain of what has been said before, he begins: “We shall confess.” Repetition is affirmation, so that you may not regret having confessed; hence the Lord also repeats: “Amen, amen. Let it be done, let it be done.” The same is shown by Joseph’s interpretation of Pharaoh’s dream, in which he saw seven ears of grain and as many barren ones, and seven fat cows and as many emaciated ones.

(CAS.) Repetition is confirmation signifying truth. One would have been sufficient to signify firmness, but a second was added. Confessing sins even once to an earthly judge brings death, but frequent confession to God brings life. Hence the invocation follows the confession, and afterward the narrative: “We shall recount.” “We shall invoke your name.” (ID.) After confession God may be invoked by a person thus cleansed; and just as confession empties him of evils, invocation fills him with good things.

“We shall recount your wonders,” and so on. (CAS.) The proud person is terrified by judgment, [Col. 0962C] and so on, up to the point where the following is added in his person:

**VERSE 3.**—“When I receive the appointed time.” According to human language, he receives what God himself gives, namely the power to exercise judgment. “Righteous judgments.” Therefore let them first pray to be acquitted in judgment.

**VERSE 4.**—“The earth melted.” (CAS.) He shows that all are without excuse in judgment, because he sent the apostles and prophets beforehand. “The earth and all.” (AUG.) Formerly firm, it dissolves into various desires. Or the earth, previously bound by vices, is melted when the Holy Spirit breathes upon it, so that it may produce shoots of virtues.

**VERSE 5.**—“To act wickedly.” (AUG.) It is evil to sin; worse is to persevere; most destructive is to defend oneself by throwing the blame back upon God. “Do not lift up the horn.” (CAS.) Excuse is the greatest vice. One who attempts to excuse his sins through others raises a horn, whether through the persuasions of demons or through the necessity of the stars.

**VERSE 6.**—“To speak.” This refers to those who say that they sinned not through their own fault but through the necessity of the stars, so that the blame may fall upon God rather than themselves. Or it refers to those who know their sins but promise themselves impunity.

### VERSE 7

“For neither from the east…” (CASSIODORUS.) Why this? Because he is such a Judge that he cannot be avoided: because he is everywhere; for he is God. (AUGUSTINE.) He does not judge from any place separately, since he is everywhere present as God. (CASSIODORUS.) Mystically: “the east” signifies those for whom the Sun of righteousness rises, and so forth, up to the point that God is present and knows all.

### VERSE 9

“For there is a cup…” (AUGUSTINE.) The cup is the Law and all Scripture, and so forth, up to the point that previously he exalts this one as well. (CASSIODORUS.) The cup is the Law; the unmixed wine is the heavenly mystery, and so forth, up to the point that not only the Jews…

### VERSE 10

“But I shall proclaim forever; I shall sing to the God of Jacob.” (CASSIODORUS.) All will drink, but separately: I—that is, Christ, together with his body—shall proclaim forever, for as long as the age endures.

### VERSE 11

“The horns of the righteous”: that is, the gifts of Christ, which are the exaltation of the righteous.

## PSALM 75

### VERSE 1

“A song.” Because it treats of Christ’s blessings—namely, that he is known, that he dwells, that he illumines, and that he saves.

“He breaks the glory of the Jews.”

“To the Assyrians.” (CASSIODORUS.) Against the Jews, who do not proceed rightly but go astray. Or because they exalt themselves: without grace they seek salvation and persecute the Church, just as the Assyrians once persecuted the Jews. Here they are refuted by the removal of the names of their glory, and are proved unable to accomplish anything without grace.

### VERSE 2

“Known in Judaea.” (AUGUSTINE.) The Jew boasts that God is known to the Jew, and this is true—but to the Jew inwardly, not according to the flesh. (AUGUSTINE.) The Prophet says: If you are Jews, then God is known among you; but if he is not, then you are not Jews.

“In Judaea.” (THE SAME.) With the two sons of Joseph received among the remaining eleven sons of Jacob, there are twelve tribes. Exclude the tribe of Levi, which was priestly and lived from the tithes. The land was divided among the twelve tribes. Among them is Judah, from whom the kings came, and from whose kingdom all Jews are named. They confessed Caesar, not Christ, who is from Judah, and so are no longer Jews.

### VERSE 3

“In Salem is his dwelling.” (AUGUSTINE.) Observe the fitting order of the words: Judaea signifies confession; afterward comes Israel, that is, “seeing God”; and thus the place is with God in peace. Hence it follows: “In peace,” and afterward, “in Sion”—that is, in contemplation, when he will see God face to face—“will be his dwelling.”

### VERSE 4

“There he broke the powers.” (CASSIODORUS.) In Judaea, in Israel, in Salem, in Sion, where the God who establishes peace came: all these things—and they are also the names of their glory—flee away.

### VERSE 5

“Shining wonderfully from the everlasting mountains, they were troubled,” and so forth.

*Diapsalma.*

Christ illumines; the Jew sleeps; Christ judges; the other perishes. (AUGUSTINE.) You illumine through the mountains, namely the Prophets and Apostles, who first receive the light. Yet all the foolish in heart were troubled by the illumination. He first indicates why he will be terrible in the future, and so forth.

“They slept.” (CASSIODORUS.) Growing cold toward eternal goods, they yielded to the flesh, not seeing what would benefit them. “Their sleep” differs from the rest of the good, because this sleep is deceptive: in a dream they see themselves possessing treasures, but when they awaken they find nothing. Hence he says: “And all the men of riches found nothing.”

A definition of the greedy.

“They found nothing.” Because they placed nothing in the hands of Christ, who says: “I was hungry,” and so forth. (REMAIGIUS.) For he was hungry in the poor, although he is rich in heaven.

“Men of riches.” Those who place all their hope in the uncertainty of riches. Hence he does not say, “those who possess riches,” for many possess them without loving them.

“In their hands,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) It is as though they were still seeking in their hands, although they already recognize that they had held nothing.

### VERSE 7

“At the rebuke,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) The sound of a rebuke usually awakens, but so great is the weight of the rebuking God that they remain drowsy—that is, they have a hardened heart.

“Those who mounted.” (THE SAME.) Those whose pride increased and who were not humbled by the humble Christ.

“Horses.” (CASSIODORUS.) Every kind of worldly exaltation. Hence it was commanded in the Law to the children of Israel that they should not multiply horses for themselves. Solomon likewise did not have horses from Judaea but bought them from Egypt.

### VERSE 9

“From heaven he was heard.” (AUGUSTINE.) Hence the Apostle says: “At the revelation of our Lord Jesus, he will come from heaven with the angels to execute judgment” (1 Thessalonians 1).

### VERSE 10

“When he arose”—that is, when he appears powerful, though here he was humble. Or, when he arose here from the dead, afterward coming to judgment.

(AUGUSTINE.) When he comes from heaven, his presence will be heard—that is, it will be known to all. The power of the judgment is explained: earthly beings are terrified, and, deprived of their power, become still. “He became still when he arose.”

“The meek of the earth.” (THE SAME.) Those who possess peace of mind and do not resist the yoke of God.

### VERSE 11

“For the thought…” (CASSIODORUS.)

*Diapsalma.*

He now admonishes the devoted to offer their vows. It is as though he said: He rightly saves the meek.

“For the thought”—that is, they will praise you in thought and deed. This means “the remnants of thought,” and so forth.

“The thought of man.” (THE SAME.) The conception of a vow.

“The remnants”: the repayment of the vow, its performance, and what remains after the thought.

“The remnants of thought.” (AUGUSTINE.) “For the first thought,” and so forth, up to the point that it is the celebration of solemn observances.

(CASSIODORUS.) Since the Lord alone is the one to whom a festival is owed, they will repay their vows to God. The first thought condemns evil. The remainder: afterward a person ought always to remember past evils, so that he may mourn. Even though the world celebrates a festival when it feels itself freed from sin, after amendment the Jews are commanded to offer a festive gift to God.

### VERSE 12

“Vow and repay.” (AUGUSTINE.) Some vows are common: those without which there is no salvation. Others are personal, such as vowing chastity and similar things.

(CASSIODORUS.) “Vow.” There are certain things which we are bound to perform even without promising them, such as “You shall not kill,” and similar commandments, and so forth, up to the point concerning those who are around him, so that servants may offer—or may be offered—and so forth.

(AUGUSTINE.) Some are, as it were, intermediate, and so forth, up to the point that the person has the spirit of God, not that of rulers—that is, not a proud spirit.

“Gifts.” (THE SAME.) Those which are offered upon altars.

“To the Terrible One, and to him who takes away.” The good fear him, but the wicked do not fear him.

“The spirit of rulers.” (CASSIODORUS.) He removes pride or fear and makes them kings of themselves—that is, those who govern their bodies.

## PSALM 76

### VERSE 1

“For the end; for Idithun.” (AUGUSTINE.) The congregation speaks as it crosses over, in order to reach the end, which is Christ. It therefore teaches us to trample upon the desires and allurements of the world and to set nothing before ourselves except him from whom all things are.

(CASSIODORUS.) Transcending all things, he seeks and finds God.

### VERSE 2

“With my voice I cried to the Lord.” (AUGUSTINE.) With the intention of devotion I sought nothing else from the Lord, because he is Lord and because he is God.

“My voice to him.” A voice exists for the purpose for which it is uttered. He adds this lest anyone think that he cries to God for any reason other than God himself, above whom there is nothing.

(CASSIODORUS.) He does not say what he asks, because there is no need to tell this to one who knows what is beneficial.

“He attended to me.” (CASSIODORUS.) God’s attending means giving everything that is asked, and more than is asked.

### VERSE 3

“In the day of my tribulation I sought him.” (AUGUSTINE.) How did you seek him? And so forth, up to the point concerning the person who does not practice righteousness before human beings in order to be seen by them.

“He refused to be consoled.” (THE SAME.) He explains the tribulation, and so forth, up to the point concerning the person who either finds scandal in everyone or fears it, and is secure in no one.

### VERSE 4

“And I was exercised.” (AUGUSTINE.) Or, “I chattered,” that is, I rejoiced, speaking like a chatterer who, because of joy, neither wished nor was able to remain silent. Then again, in chattering, the spirit failed—that spirit which had previously wasted away from weariness at evils.

### VERSE 5

“They anticipated the watches.” (CASSIODORUS.)

*Diapsalma.*

Having found God, who alone is good, he deliberates whether he should bring him back.

(AUGUSTINE.) “They anticipated the watches of others.” “My eyes,” like one who rises before the appointed time for business. Or “my eyes” means my affections. “They anticipated” the diligence of others.

Or, by “watches,” he signifies the nightly offices which we perform and customarily call watches in the praises of God. Therefore: “I was troubled.”

(CASSIODORUS.) Because I could not attain what I seek.

“I did not speak.” I did not murmur against God.

Or, “I was troubled” because, while searching the secret places of the soul by night, he sees the human race rushing into sins; and with compassionate grief he is tormented on behalf of others, although he has already passed beyond their vices. He is silent because at night he has no comfort from human conversation, and at that time he thinks more cautiously. Therefore he adds: “I meditated on the days,” and so forth.

“My eyes.” In another version: “My enemies anticipated the watches.”

(AUGUSTINE.) That is, they watched over me, and so forth, up to the point that he nevertheless does not cease, but wishes to cross beyond this also. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 6

“I meditated on the days of old,” and so forth.

Therefore he was troubled: because he meditated on the ancient days of Adam, in which humanity fell. But in opposition to the ancient days he sets eternal years. He was troubled because humanity desires the former and neglects the eternal.

“I kept the ancient days and the eternal years in my mind.” (CASSIODORUS.) What happened to Adam because of disobedience? From that event I learned that this is the defect of humanity. And I kept in mind the eternal years which he would possess by persevering—not foolishly. I also meditated by night, that is, upon this defect, “with my heart,” that is, with reason, wondering whether I might somehow return to the eternal years. The person who is quietly exercised in reason speaks silently with reason.

### VERSE 7

“And I was exercised”—in that very meditation.

“I swept my spirit”: I cleansed my mind.

Others read: “I winnowed my spirit,” handling the matter thus within myself:

### VERSE 8

“Will he cast off forever, the human race?” so that he may be more favorably disposed.

It is as though he said: He who was already pleased by his grace in the Old Testament—will he not add that he should be more favorable in the New Testament through the coming of the Son? This is what the person who meditates upon divine mercy understands.

“I was exercised and I swept.” (AUGUSTINE.) Or, “I chattered,” no longer outwardly, and so forth, up to the point where he discovered that God would not cast off forever.

“So that he may be more favorably disposed”: namely, so that he who was angry when he rejected them and inflicted evils might become gentler by freeing and recalling them.

### VERSE 10

“Or will God forget to show mercy?” (AUGUSTINE.) In another sense: there is no mercy unless God grants it, and he himself will be without it. The stream flows; the spring has dried up.

### VERSE 11

“And I said: Now I have begun.” (CASSIODORUS.) What he discovered through deliberation: namely, that Christ changes and redeems human beings.

“And I said.” To this meditation, and so forth, up to the point that, crossing beyond myself and coming to God, I encounter no danger here.

“I have begun.” (AUGUSTINE.) Something in which I am secure, where enemies do not anticipate me: now the Most High has begun to change me.

“The change of the right hand,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) From anger to mercy; this concerns the transformation of servants into sons.

(THE SAME.) Of this change, and so forth, up to the point that these are the things which delight the holy person.

### VERSE 13

“In your inventions.” (AUGUSTINE.) That is, in the commandments which you have discovered or by which you are found.

(CASSIODORUS.) Or, “in your observances,” that is, in the commandments which must be observed, I shall exercise myself. For it is not enough to read the Scriptures; one must display the fruit of works. Instructed by these things, he breaks forth into praise.

(AUGUSTINE.) “In your inventions,” or “in your affections”—not in mine, nor in earthly things. There is thus an inward affection in the works and meditation of God, when the world is contemplated and the Creator is sought in his creatures. He is found displeasing nowhere, but pleasing everywhere.

### VERSE 14

“God is in the Holy One.” (AUGUSTINE.) Through what has been said I am certain that I shall come, and that he is my guide.

“God is in the Holy One”—that is, in Christ, the way of returning to you.

“And who is a great God like our God?” and so forth.

“Your way.” (THE SAME.) The way of worshiping you and coming to you. Hence he gladly sets God’s power above the images which were falsely worshiped.

### VERSE 15
