“Your wonders.” (AUGUSTINE.) The deaf, blind, weak, dead, and paralyzed were healed. These things happened in bodies. In the soul, some are sober who shortly before were drunkards, unbelievers, and worshipers of images.

“To the peoples your power.” (THE SAME.) To unbelievers, so that they may know Christ only according to the body; to believers, according to reality and divinity. He adds: “What you have accomplished, you redeemed.”

### VERSE 16

“The sons of Joseph.” (AUGUSTINE.) That is, the Gentile people.

Or Joseph signifies Christ: just as Joseph, having been sold into Egypt, reigned there, so Christ reigns among the Gentiles, having first been humbled in the martyrs.

(THE SAME.) Joseph, who reached the Gentiles, is interpreted as “increase,” and signifies the Gentiles, from whom God’s people were increased.

Or Joseph is Christ, sold by the Jews and driven to the Gentiles; his sons are those whom he chose from among the Gentiles.

### VERSE 17

“They saw.” (CASSIODORUS.)

*Diapsalma.*

He explains what Christ accomplishes in the world.

(AUGUSTINE.) It is as though he said: Since you have made your power known, either through him they saw you, O God the Father, or they saw you, O Christ, who are the power and the arm, and so forth.

### VERSE 18

“A multitude.” (CASSIODORUS.) Not a few, but a multitude.

“The sound”: in the groaning over sins and in the giving of thanks. For the diverse vows of the peoples sound like a rough and stormy sea.

“The sound of the waters.” (AUGUSTINE.) Whence are these sounds of the waters and this disturbance of the abysses? Because they have given their voice to the clouds, of which it is said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it.”

### VERSE 19

“The voice of your thunder.” (CASSIODORUS.) The voice of thunder rolls on, so that a wrinkled and winding sound may be perceived.

Allegory: in the wheel of the whole world.

“The wheel.” (JEROME, AUGUSTINE.) This means the circuit of the earth, around which the thunderous clouds passed, resounding with commands and flashing with miracles.

“The earth trembled.” (CASSIODORUS.) The inhabitants of the earth trembled. The earth itself is called “the sea” by analogy, because human life is bitter and subject to storms, where the larger fish devours the smaller.

### VERSE 20

“In the sea.” (AUGUSTINE.) Literally, when Christ walked upon the waters.

Or, in the hearts of human beings whom he subjects to himself.

Or, “the earth” signifies the Jews, and “the sea” the Gentiles.

“And your footsteps will not be known.” This is a silent rebuke of the Jews, as though he said: Although he came openly and displayed himself through miracles, he was not recognized by the unbelieving Jews—those whom he led by the hand of Moses and Aaron, that is, through the working of the miracles which they performed.

“Your footsteps,” and so forth. He touched some people, namely Jews, who say: “The Christ has not yet come”; they do not see him walking upon the sea.

### VERSE 21

“Like sheep.” Because they were not truly sheep but goats.

“By Moses and Aaron.” (CASSIODORUS.) Moses is interpreted as “taken from the river”; Aaron as “mountain of strength.” By these names the virtues they performed are expressed. Among other things, Moses made a way through the sea, signifying that the people would be freed through baptism. Aaron bore the image of the Church, which is compared to a very strong mountain.

## PSALM 77

### VERSE 1

“Understanding.” (AUGUSTINE.) Because these things have been narrated, and so forth, up to the point that those things which appear open are parables and riddles.

“Attend.” (CASSIODORUS.) At first the Lord himself speaks, so that reverence may increase.

“My people”: those who obey me.

“The mouth of God” is Asaph, who later spoke these things: “How many things we have heard from the beginning.”

This refers to the Old Testament; or the faithful Synagogue reproaches the wicked.

### VERSE 2

[Col. 0967D] “In parables.” (AUGUSTINE.) Parables are likenesses of things.

“Propositions.” In Greek, *problemata*—questions containing something to be solved.

### VERSE 3

“How many things.” (CASSIODORUS.) He speaks summarily of what God did for the Jews; yet, although they were ungrateful to him, these things nevertheless benefit their children, so that they do not become like their fathers.

(AUGUSTINE.) At first God spoke in the human being; now the human being himself speaks: “How many things we have heard.” God spoke the preceding statement from himself so that his speech would not be despised.

### VERSE 5

“And he raised up,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) This is the testimony. “Beginning” refers to the earlier statement: “I shall speak propositions from the beginning.” The beginning is the Old Testament; the end is the New. There is fear in the former, which is the beginning; but here there is Christ, the end of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10), who gives the Spirit, from which comes: “Love casts out fear” (1 John 4).

The old Law is called the testimony of this New Testament, because it has testimony from the Law and the Prophets. Hence that which represented so many mystical realities was called the tabernacle of testimony.

It is therefore called “testimony” insofar as the Old Testament proves and bears witness; it is called “law” insofar as it commands.

(CASSIODORUS, REMAIGIUS.) He raised up the testimony as though it had been dead in Adam—that is, the Law—or, when it is written down, it is raised up, having previously been lulled to sleep by ignorance.

“Testimony in Jacob.” Perhaps this refers to Jacob’s wrestling with the angel and his becoming lame when his thigh was touched. This signifies that the Jews stand partly in faith and partly depart from salvation. Thus what happened to Jacob was a testimony of this matter.

“Behold, a parable.”

“To his sons.” These are the same sons as “another generation,” namely, the people of grace.

### VERSE 6

“Another generation.” God’s commandments were transmitted through generations, so that no one might think they were given to one person alone.

### VERSE 7

“That they may place.” This is the benefit of the fathers’ preaching.

“That they may seek.” (AUGUSTINE.) Those who were previously said to have known are now to seek, so that, hoping in God, they may be helped by him to fulfill his commandments.

### VERSE 8

“Perverse.” (CASSIODORUS.) This generation does not receive the truth and is therefore distorted. It became embittered beyond every bitterness, so that its members might arm themselves against the Savior. Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Go and say to the embittering house” (Ezekiel 2).

“He did not direct his heart.” (THE SAME.) A person has a distorted heart when he does not correct what he has understood wrongly and does not carry out what nature teaches.

“His spirit was not faithful with God” (John 1): that is, although reason gave good counsel, he did not consent to it.

“Was not faithful.” (AUGUSTINE.) When the human spirit cooperates with the Spirit of God working within it, what God commands is accomplished. This happens only by believing in him who justifies the ungodly. The perverse and embittered generation does not possess this faith.

(THE SAME.) He says this much more explicitly, and so forth, up to the point that this generation, although it believed God, nevertheless did not believe in God.

### VERSE 9

“Sending the bow.” (AUGUSTINE.) He speaks figuratively, and so forth, up to the comparison of David with his brothers and of the Christian people with the Jewish people.

Or: “The sons of Ephraim.”

(THE SAME.) “Bending and sending the bow”—that is, sending something with a bow.

Or, “bending the bow and sending arrows”—that is, promising to keep the Law, openly saying: “Everything that the Lord has said we will do and we will hear” (Exodus 24).

“They turned back and failed on the day of battle”—that is, of temptation. Hence the Prophet Hosea says: “Ephraim became like a foolish dove without understanding” (Hosea 7), because the promise of obedience is proved not by hearing but by temptation.

“Benefits.” (EUTHYMIUS.) The benefits which he bestowed upon the people of Israel—for example, that he led them through the Red Sea without their becoming wet.

But he calls them “wonders” because he had changed the rivers of the Egyptians into blood. When he says that God showed these things to them, he does not mean that they themselves saw them with their own eyes, but that they received them in this way from their ancestors.

### VERSE 12

“In the presence of their fathers,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) He now begins to recount what he did for them from their departure out of Egypt; yet they did not cease from murmuring and testing him.

(AUGUSTINE.) “In the presence of their fathers.” Who are the fathers? And so forth, up to the point concerning the approach of the wood of the cross, like Moses’ rod.

“In the land of Egypt.” (THE SAME.) To remove every doubt, he names both the province and the place where the deeds occurred.

Thus Christ, placed upon the earth in the presence of the fathers, taught the humble commandment: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (John 7).

### VERSE 14

“In a cloud.” (JEROME AND CASSIODORUS.) They judged that this would happen in the future.

“The day” is Christ, yet he is concealed from the faithless by the cloud of flesh. Just as the cloud was a protection for them against the heat of the sun, so Christ through the incarnation gives us refreshment against the heat of vices.

“All night”: throughout the entire time of life.

“In the illumination of fire.” He guards Christians in this age by the brightness of his name, the fire of the Holy Spirit.

### VERSE 15

“A rock.” (CASSIODORUS.) In the wilderness. At first the water of the sea was like a rock; now the rock is a fountain.

“In the wilderness,” where the gift necessarily seems more gracious.

“He gave them water.” As though they were cattle, not human beings, because they did not give thanks.

### VERSE 16

“Like…” (CASSIODORUS.) The water which proceeds from Christ does not diminish at all, but becomes a fountain of water leaping up into eternal life.

### VERSE 17

“To sin still.” (CASSIODORUS.) They added this: amid so many benefits they still did not believe. To make clear that this was understood as the greatest sin, when the Lord said in the Gospel, “The Spirit will convict the world concerning sin,” he added in explanation: “Concerning sin, indeed, because they do not believe in me” (John 4, 16).

Therefore, just as “sin” there means “not believing,” so here “to sin” means “not believing.”

“Into anger.” (THE SAME.) They did not believe that God could accomplish difficult things for them. This is most serious in God’s sight. In the same way, although washed through baptism, we provoke God to anger.

“In a waterless place.” (AUGUSTINE.) Either literally, in another wilderness, or rather in themselves: although their skins were filled with water from the rock, their minds nevertheless were dry.

### VERSE 19

“A table.” (CASSIODORUS.) Mystically, a refreshment of wisdom, or the body of Christ.

### VERSE 21

“Therefore he heard.” (CASSIODORUS.) Because, while delaying punishment, he first gave them what they were asking, lest he appear unable to do so.

“He delayed.” (AUGUSTINE.) He delayed the punishment, first giving what they requested, although they asked while testing him, lest he appear unable to do it. After he had given it, fire—that is, anger—rose up against Israel. This is what he had said earlier: “Fire was kindled in Jacob.”

### VERSE 23

“And he commanded.” The two matters have been stated briefly: namely, that he heard them and that anger arose. Here he begins to recount them openly. First he explains how he heard them; afterward, in the following section, how he punished them.

“And the doors of heaven.” (CASSIODORUS.) The doors are the preachers, through whom one enters heaven; or they are the Scriptures.

“He opened.” Because he gave his people the Spirit, so that they might understand the Scriptures.

### VERSE 24

“Manna for food.” (AUGUSTINE.) It signifies the bread which descended from heaven, which is the food of angels. In order that a human being might eat it, the Word became flesh (John 1). This bread is rained upon the whole world through the evangelical clouds, and, when the hearts of the preachers are opened as heavenly doors, it is proclaimed to the believing Church, not to the Synagogue that tested God.

(CASSIODORUS.) “Manna”: what is this? This food is sought with wonder, and it is known to be the body of Christ.

“Bread of heaven.” (THE SAME.) It is none other than Christ, from whom heavenly beings—that is, angels—are refreshed through contemplation of him. This bread, namely the Word by which the angels are nourished with great food, made milk through the flesh, is eaten by the human being.

### VERSE 26

“The south wind.” Because quails are found there.

### VERSE 27

“And he rained upon them,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) So too with a small faith, and so forth, up to the point where he says: “If I have told you earthly things and you do not believe me, how will you believe if I tell you heavenly things?” (John 3).

“Like dust.” (CASSIODORUS.) The dust signifies the subtlety of understanding which ascends to heavenly things.

“Sand”: an innumerable abundance of prudence seasoned with the salt of wisdom.

“Winged birds”: heavenly desires by which the soul, nourished, grows fat. We may understand these within the boundaries of the Church. Hence he adds:

### VERSE 28

“And they fell in the midst of their camps.” (AUGUSTINE.) This signifies that the winds come willingly to human beings and bring them words sent from God, so that they may hear them in their own dwellings and around their tents, because “their sound has gone out into all the earth.”

### VERSE 29

“And they ate.” They were convicted, because they had thought this impossible for God.

### VERSE 30

“While their food was still in their mouths,” and “the anger of God,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) This concerns their punishments and their feigned returns, motivated by fear of punishment; nevertheless, God’s judgment was tempered by mercy.

“Their food.” (THE SAME.) Manna and quails.

“He hindered the chosen of Israel.” (AUGUSTINE.) That is, he hindered them from benefiting those whom, with paternal affection, they wished to assist.

Or rather, he shackled them so that the chosen would endure troubles together with them, as an example not only of righteousness but also of patience.

“He hindered.” (THE SAME.) Through their murmuring, as in the case of Moses, who said: “Can we bring water out of the rock for you?” (Numbers 20).

### VERSE 32

“In all these things they still sinned and did not believe in his wonders.” After all these corrections, their sins are more serious, and they continually increase.

### VERSE 33

“And their days failed,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Although, by believing, they could have had days without failure in the truth.

“In vanity are their days and their years.” (CASSIODORUS.) By analogy with one who dies at birth: he was born in vain.

“With haste.” (AUGUSTINE.) Even a life that appears long passes quickly.

### VERSE 34

“They sought him.” (CASSIODORUS AND AUGUSTINE.) Not those who were killed, but those who were left. He speaks in this way because they are one people, as though they were one body.

“At dawn they came to him,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) Diligently, or before daylight. Hence: “It is vain for you to rise before the light.” The pious person prays in the light; the impious person prays before the light.

“They sought.” They returned; they came.

(AUGUSTINE.) All these actions were undertaken to acquire temporal goods and avoid evils. Thus it was not God but those things that they worshiped.

### VERSE 37

“And they were not considered faithful in the covenant,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) Whoever truly believes performs works. Hence faith is so called because what is said is made—because it is done. Therefore he says: “Nor were they faithful in his commandments.”

### VERSE 38

“But he is merciful and will be propitious.” (AUGUSTINE.) Here the wicked promise themselves impunity. Yet mercy is shown even to the wicked, though before judgment, because he makes the sun rise upon the good and the wicked.

Thus he also spared that people, so that he would not utterly uproot them. Instead, they remain in the succession of their descendants, just as Cain received a sign so that no one would kill him.

“Toward their sins,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) The people are one and the same through the succession of their sons. Thus, when it is said that he afterward brought them out of Egypt and led them into the mountain of holiness (Genesis 4), this concerns them only through their succession.

Likewise here, when it says, “He will be propitious toward their sins,” we understand that what the Apostle says was also fulfilled: “The remnant will be saved” (Romans 9)—those who would believe in Christ. This he foresaw here when he adds: “And he did not scatter them.”

“And he abounded in turning away,” and so forth, because “he did not kindle all his anger,” and so forth. That is, he did not punish them as much as they deserved, for he also forgave the crime that they killed the Son.

### VERSE 39

“A spirit departing and not returning,” and so forth. He recalls them by grace because they cannot return by themselves. Hence in Proverbs, concerning the way of iniquity, it is said: “All who walk in it will not return” (Proverbs 2)—that is, not by themselves, but they will be recalled by grace.

This is the wandering sheep which was brought back to the flock upon the shoulders of the compassionate shepherd.

### VERSE 40

“How often?” (CASSIODORUS.) About to speak of the plagues of Egypt, which were inflicted for their sake, and to compare their evils with God’s benefits, he says that they forgot and tested God.

(AUGUSTINE.) Because flesh or spirit is passing away: “How often,” then? As though to say, they embittered him very many times.

### VERSE 41

“And they turned back,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) He repeats their unbelief in order to recall the plagues that God inflicted upon the Egyptians for their sake. From this they ought to have learned not to be ungrateful.

### VERSE 42

“From the hand of tribulation.” (CASSIODORUS.) Tribulation is usually kept in memory, but not by them. Beautifully he sets the hand of God against the hand of tribulation, saying: “His hand, and from the hand of tribulation.” These differ greatly.

(AUGUSTINE AND CASSIODORUS.) Mystical interpretations begin from this point.

### VERSES 44–45

“And he turned,” and so forth. “He sent anger among them,” and so forth.

Here he begins to explain the plagues inflicted in Egypt for the liberation of the Jews. He lists ten plagues, as Exodus also lists ten. Some things are nevertheless placed here which are not in Exodus. We can interpret them only figuratively, since here the things that happened are also called parables, and Scripture often does not follow the historical sequence but adds other matters or changes some things for the sake of their meaning.

Thus water turned into blood signifies thinking about the causes of things in a fleshly manner.

“Dog-fly.” These are doglike habits.

“Frog.” Loquacious vanity.

### VERSES 46–47

“Blight.” Some interpret this as rust. It harms secretly and is compared with a vice that is difficult to perceive, such as placing excessive confidence in oneself. For noxious air secretly produces this effect in fruits; so hidden pride affects behavior when one who is nothing thinks himself to be something.

“Locust.” Malice that wounds with the mouth, namely through false testimony.

“Hail.” This is iniquity that takes away the property of others; hence thefts, robberies, and plunder. Yet the plunderer himself is laid waste even more by his own vice.

“Frost.” The vice by which love of one’s neighbor freezes in the darkness of folly, as if in the cold of night.

### VERSE 48

“Fire.” In Exodus it is understood only together with the hail, in the lightning, so that it might damage the fruit. Yet it is not read there as having burned possessions. Here it signifies the enormity of anger, by which homicide also occurs.

“By the death of their cattle”: damage to chastity is signified. The desire by which offspring is conceived is common to us and to cattle. To keep this desire subdued and ordered is the virtue of chastity.

“The death of the firstborn”: the loss of righteousness, by which each person is joined socially to the human race.

The Egyptians were struck by ten plagues corresponding to the ten commandments written on the tablets. Here too there are ten plagues, although they are not listed in the same order. Three plagues from Exodus are omitted here—gnats, boils, and darkness—and three are added here that are not there: blight, frost, and fire. Such things are frequently varied for the sake of a fitting interpretation.

“Signs.” (CASSIODORUS.) They are like traces impressed upon hard hearts, as by a character.

“Prodigies”: things that signified certain future events.

“Tanis”: a city; it signifies the humble commandment, which is necessary for us here, so that we may be raised up in the future.

“And he gave them to blight.” These things are not read in Exodus, and therefore they should be explained only by mystical interpretation.

“Locust.” (AUGUSTINE.) Those who consume one another signify detractors, who gnaw enviously at the fruits of others.

“Their mulberries in frost.” (AUGUSTINE.) The mulberry is warm by nature; through it charity is understood, and charity is killed by frost.

“To hail.” (THE SAME.) What the hail could not damage—that is, the soft things—Exodus later says were consumed by the locusts.

“He handed over.” (CASSIODORUS.) Through the death of the cattle, the downfall of fools is shown.

(THE SAME.) “To fire.” Fire is desire, which lays waste one’s possession—that is, the condition of the mind.

### VERSE 49

“Anger, indignation,” and so forth. (CASSIODORUS.) The order of punishment is this: first God is angry at sins when there is no repentance. Then, in his indignation, anger, and tribulation, he abandons a person to his own wickedness, so that those who do not obey God may be afflicted by their own adversities. As it is said there: “Therefore God gave them over to a depraved mind” (Romans 1).

Indignation pertains to swollen pride; anger to wicked audacity; tribulation to confused despair. Then, stripped of God’s protection, they are driven by the devil into unlawful assaults.

“By evil angels.” (AUGUSTINE.) These things were done by God’s judgment, and so forth, up to the point that through evil angels God punishes both good and wicked human beings—but the good only with bodily punishments, while the wicked are punished both bodily and spiritually.

### VERSE 50

“His anger.” (AUGUSTINE.) There was a path of God’s anger by which, through hidden justice, he would punish the Egyptians. God made a way for it, bringing them, as it were, from hidden places through evil angels into open crimes, and thus punishing them openly.

### VERSE 51

“The firstborn in Egypt.” (AUGUSTINE.) The firstborn signify the greatest commandments, such as: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart.” When these are not observed, we are deprived of the offspring of reason.

### VERSE 52

“And he took away his people like sheep and led them like a flock in the wilderness.” (AUGUSTINE.) Mystically, this also takes place inwardly in us: instructed and transferred from the power of darkness, we are brought in mind into the kingdom of God, like sheep into spiritual pastures.

(CASSIODORUS.) “And he took away.” He led those whom he had brought out of slavery into the promised land; yet again they offended.

### VERSE 54

“And he led them into the mountain of his holiness.” (AUGUSTINE.) Not the same individuals whom he took away, but the same people in name and nation. Nevertheless, it signifies that many were converted to the Church, which is the reality intended here. She is the mountain which Christ acquired.

“And he cast out the nations before them,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Or, the evil spirits. Christ cast all these out from before the faithful.

“And he divided the land among them by lot.” This signifies that one and the same Spirit accomplishes everything in us, distributing to each person as he wills.

### VERSE 55

“In their tents.” (CASSIODORUS.) In the places where sins had reigned, he caused virtues to reign.

### VERSE 57

“Just as their fathers turned back,” and so forth. (AUGUSTINE.) Throughout, he speaks as though concerning the same people. Yet now he speaks of those who were in the promised land, whose fathers had embittered God in the wilderness.

“A crooked bow,” and so forth. (THE SAME.) The perverse intention of the mind, directed against God, who had said: “You shall have no strange gods” (Exodus 20). The text explains this more fully.

“To provoke to anger,” or “a crooked bow,” which is difficult to bend back, although they easily turned backward.

Or, “a crooked bow” which does not shoot [the transmitted reading is uncertain], but turns its arrows back upon itself—that is, the malice of deceitful people.

### VERSE 58

“To rivalry.” Or, “they rivaled him.” Another reading has: “when they hand over the honor of God to another.”

### VERSE 59

“God heard.” (CASSIODORUS.) This concerns vengeance in the promised land, which was also turned back upon those through whom he punished them.

### VERSE 60

“And he rejected the tabernacle.” (AUGUSTINE.) This occurred in the time of Eli the priest, when they were defeated by the Philistines, the ark of the Lord was captured, and they themselves were devastated by a great slaughter. For it is read in the Book of Kings that thirty thousand infantrymen from the people fell at that time.

“He rejected the tabernacle of Silo.” (BEDE.) It was located at Silo, and so forth, up to the point that, because they did not attend to it and did not make a tabernacle for God, the Lord rightly rejected it.

“He dwelt among human beings.” (AUGUSTINE.) Since there was nothing worthy in which he might dwell, he rejected the tabernacle which he had established not for his own sake but for theirs.

(CASSIODORUS.) In the same way he abandons our bodies, which the Holy Spirit inhabits while they are handled well.

### VERSE 61

“And he handed over.” (CASSIODORUS.) If the good are handed over to captivity together with sinners, this is an exercise, not captivity of the mind. Or they were handed over to the enemy but remained free and joined to God.

“Their strength.” (AUGUSTINE.) In the wicked he diminished freedom of choice and removed their virtues. This does not occur in the good, although they are sometimes bodily taken captive together with the wicked.

### VERSE 65

“And he awoke.” (CASSIODORUS AND AUGUSTINE.) He attributes human behavior to the Lord in order to explain the events.

As though sleeping. This is said from the perspective of the foolish, who think that when he does not come to the aid of those in danger, he is drunk with wine, because he does not come to their aid quickly enough. And in truth, for those who foolishly think this way he sleeps, and he is remote from the negligent and faithless, who rouse him by no voice of praise or deed. But he is roused to vengeance by evil acts, here by the sins of those who placed the ark among idols. As though powerful, because people are then quick to anger and powerful for acts of virtue when they rise from sleep after drunkenness. (AUG.) “And he was roused.” Christ, drunk with the wine of his Passion and sleeping in the tomb, was roused from death, as one powerful in the Resurrection. (ID.) “As though sleeping.” He appeared to sleep when he gave his people into the hands of those whom he hates, at which they say to them: “Where is your God?”

VERSE 66.—And he struck iniquity. (AUG.) By this punishment he will be tormented, etc., up to: for he gave them everlasting disgrace.

VERSE 67.—And he rejected. (CASS.) Concerning King David and the place of the kingdom. (AUG.) He did not say, etc., up to: thus he proceeds from the beginning of the election of the Hebrew people all the way to Christ.

VERSE 69.—As, etc. (AUG.) The unicorns are those whose firm hope is raised toward that one thing of which it is said: “One thing I have asked of the Lord; this I will seek.” A sanctuary. It is a holy people, a royal priesthood.

VERSE 70.—David his servant. (AUG.) He who was from Judah, etc., up to: the teeth of the Church are those through whom it speaks, or through whom, as if by eating, it brings the others into its own body. It is called a flock of shorn sheep because it laid aside the burdens of the world like fleeces and placed at the feet of the Apostles the proceeds from the sale of its possessions; ascending from the laver of baptism, it produces twins, namely, the works of the twofold charity. Hence: “There was not a barren one among them.” From these Christ was transferred, but he feeds among the nations the flocks that are Jacob and Israel.

VERSE 71.—Jacob, Israel his inheritance. (AUG.) He repeats this: unless it is said that, in the present condition, Jacob is a servant; when the inheritance shall see face to face. Hence it also received its name: for Israel is so called from the contemplation of God. He transferred him for this purpose, that he might feed them, and so he did.

VERSE 72.—And he fed them, etc. (AUG.) It may perhaps seem, etc., up to: and this too he taught by what he did.

# PSALM LXXVIII

VERSE 1.—A psalm of Asaph. (CASS.) The second psalm concerning lamentation. He prays Christ to come to the aid of the nation, which is to be severely afflicted because of its hardness. We are warned to rejoice in the goods of our neighbors and to be afflicted by their calamities.

God, the nations have come. (ID.) This is the first complaint, and it enumerates how much Jerusalem suffered in the times of Antiochus, when it was not destroyed; these things signify the persecution of the Church. (AUG.) “They have come.” He does not speak as though to one who is ignorant, etc., up to: but now they have clearly been fulfilled.

Into your inheritance. (ID.) Concerning the people of Israel: God’s inheritance consists of the elect, but not of the blinded. Therefore these words can be understood of the period after Christ’s Ascension. Yet before Christ came, it was also an inheritance, where there were prophets and saints led away in Babylon; or especially under Antiochus. (CASS.) But if anyone, etc., up to: whose circuit extends throughout the whole world, where persecution also takes place.

VERSE 2.—The corpses. (CASS.) Corpses—as though they were raging not only against the living. To bury is an act of piety; to cast away, of cruelty. They poured out. (ID.) He heightens the language in order to move the judge.

VERSE 4.—We have become. (CASS.) Jerusalem’s glory, wondrous throughout the whole world, has been turned into disgrace among its neighbors. This is more grievous than if it had been among those far away, because these are continually present. Or, “neighbors” means affections: those close at hand who are now willing to believe may say this as martyrs.

VERSE 5.—How long, Lord? (CASS.) A prayer on behalf of his own people against enemies and insulting neighbors, as though they were saying: “This is how they rage; but, O Lord, how long?” (AUG.) He asks that God not remain angry forever, that is, that the devastation not continue, but that he moderate correction. By the name of anger, the vengeance of iniquity is understood; by the name of zeal, the demand for chastity, lest the soul commit fornication against God. Note that this happens to people because of sins, even to the just, as the three children and the prophets in captivity testify. Like fire. (ID.) Burn until the gold of virtues has been completely purified and the wood—that is, vices—has been reduced to ashes.

VERSE 7.—They have devoured. (AUG.) By handing them over to the teeth of wild beasts. They have laid waste, by the overthrow of the city, which has been stripped of its citizens; or because they killed those who were substituted in the place of the slain citizens. “Jacob” stands for a man, and “man” for the nation that offended. The patriarch is pleasing, so that his memory may mitigate the people’s sins. Jacob. (AUG.) This is the inheritance mentioned above. The place. (CASS.) The city where the temple was, to which they gathered for the festivals.

[Col. 0975C] VERSE 8.—Of our iniquities. (BEDA.) That is, those which we contracted from our fathers, for which correction is no longer due but condemnation, unless the mercy of your grace is present. For it is written: “The soul that sins shall itself die.” And: “I will visit the sins of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation” (Ezek. XVIII). Of former times. (CASS.) He does not speak only of past sins, since even at that time some Jews were following idols; rather, he means sins like those of the former generations, by which they sinned for countless years. Let them hasten. (ID.) Before the judgment feared by every human being, because unless pardon comes beforehand, the guilty person is not acquitted at the judgment. Exceedingly. So that no one may presume upon his deeds.

VERSE 9.—Help. (CASS.) In the battle for the defense of the laws, because they trust not in their own virtues but in the virtues of God. [Col. 0975D] For the sake of glory. Not because of merit, but so that, having been rescued, we may return honor to your name. For the glory of your name. Let what cannot be obtained through our deeds be attributed to the piety of your holy name, not to us. Help us, O God. By this he is neither ungrateful for grace nor removes free will. For one who is helped also does something by himself. Deliver us. (AUG.) He delivers—that is, he rescues from evils—when he both helps us to practice righteousness and is merciful toward sins, without which no one lives here.

VERSE 10.—Lest perhaps. (AUG.) That familiar taunt of the faithless: “Where is he?” Either he does not exist or he is unable. Such mockery cannot be endured. Let it become known. Either here, among those who are converted, iniquity is destroyed—the very thing it had previously desired—or at the end they perish; here he speaks not by wishing but by prophesying. (AUG.) For the just person does not delight in the punishment of an enemy, since he does not hate him, but in divine justice, because he loves God. The unjust person does the opposite.

VERSE 11.—Of those in fetters. (AUG.) By the corruptibility of the flesh, which weighs down the soul, through which the persecutor sometimes prevails. These fetters are felt only by those who groan under their burden. The Apostle desired to be released from them and to be with Christ. Or the fetters are God’s commandments, by which the saints are bound; when patiently endured, they are turned into ornaments. Hence: “Put your foot into his fetters” (Eccl. VI). (CASS.) “Of those in fetters”: literally, he speaks of those whom the Gentiles bound. They pray with groaning that the Church may not fail in its brothers, and thus punishment consumes them. According to the greatness. (AUG.) For so great a thing has happened among Christians as their enemies would never have believed. Sons, because they have been kindled by example, not terrified. Possess the sons of those put to death. (ID.) The holy martyrs always prayed this: that their blood might not be fruitless for later generations, so that a harvest might grow from the place thought destined to perish. (CASS.) A pious prayer, that he not cast away the sons of those who were punished for him. Possess them, lest they be stained by some error.

VERSE 12.—And repay. (CASS.) Even if he repays them bodily, it is nevertheless salvation for their souls. Sevenfold signifies the perfection of the heavenly gift, when we are filled with the Holy Spirit. In the bosom. In the secret place of souls, where conversion takes place. Disgrace: let them return praise for injuries. It is a glorious vengeance when God is praised by the mouths of his enemies. Or “sevenfold.” Sevenfold repayment signifies the perfection of punishment, just as with good things, when it is said that he will receive sevenfold in this world. This is set for all good things, as though possessing nothing yet possessing everything, because fullness is signified by this number. Or “sevenfold” means indefinitely. Disgrace. (AUG.) “Repay this,” that is, for this disgrace give them over to a debased mind. For when a human being is given over to a debased mind—that is, to an inner judgment—he receives the deserved punishment of future torments.

VERSE 13.—But we. (CASS.) A joyful conclusion, not of victors but of those who endure. And a pleasing conclusion to the lamentation. (AUG.) “But we.” These are the remnant gathered by Mattathias. Or, generally, it is to be understood of every class of the devout and true Christians, so that the Christian people too may be included there. This is the flock for which he prayed that God would not remain angry longer. (ID.) Or, “in the generation,” that is, in the future age, we shall proclaim—not for the instruction of others, but as a duty of honor.

# PSALM LXXIX

VERSE 1.—For those who will be changed. (AUG.) For the better, etc., up to: a testimony of faithlessness. Asaph, the enlightened one, speaks about the coming of Christ and his vine, giving a good testimony concerning the head itself and its body, the king and the people, the shepherd and the flock.

VERSE 2.—You who shepherd, etc. (AUG.) Here the enlightened Asaph speaks about the coming of Christ, who converts the human being and strengthens the vine brought out of Egypt. This is the testimony concerning those who are changed. (CASS.) Above he was fearful, praying because of the sins of the Synagogue; now, with those changed for the better, he confidently gives testimony. This psalm is the testimony of the Synagogue concerning the head itself and its body. (ID.) A prayer for the first coming, through which the human race is restored. (ID.) He brings it to completion and defines it. O God, Son. You who shepherd Israel spiritually, those who see you: attend, that is, pour the light of your mercy upon us, so that we who are dark through ourselves may be made bright by you. Joseph. (ID.) You lead the faithful people into God’s sheepfolds like sheep to pastures, concerning which it is said: “I have other sheep that are not of this fold; these too I must lead, so that there may be one fold and one shepherd” (John X). Distinct words are used for each: Israel is governed, Joseph is led—that is, the devout people. Manifest yourself. (ID.) He asks that the one who was hidden in the secret of majesty may appear before the Jews through the Incarnation, as had been promised, performing in them the virtues signified by these names: Ephraim, Benjamin, and Manasseh. (AUG.) “Manifest yourself before.” Known to angels, make yourself known to human beings.

VERSE 3.—Before Ephraim. (AUG.) That is, before the Jewish people, where these tribes are: before fruitfulness and the son of the right hand, so that we too may be the fullness of knowledge through charity, which is God; and before Manasseh, that is, the forgotten one, so that you may now come to his mind, according to this saying: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord.” (ID.) Stir up. He repeats, etc., up to: crucified in weakness, rise again in power. [Col. 0977C] (CASS.) Stir up the power of miracles, etc., up to: hence: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear,” etc. (I Cor. X).

VERSE 4.—Your face. (AUG.) This face was veiled to Asaph during the time of Christ’s weakness, and then Asaph was sick, unable to look upon the face veiled by the cloud. Concerning this it is said: “God ascended upon a light cloud and entered, or will enter, Egypt,” that is, the flesh free from sin. He illuminated it when he rose and ascended, and thus we are saved.

VERSE 5.—How long will you be angry? (AUG.) Anger passes from the servant, not so that he may no longer chastise, as is clear, but so that he may not condemn. For anger also remains toward those who are converted, but as corrective anger. “He chastises every son whom he receives” (Isa. IX; Heb. XII).

VERSE 6.—You will feed them. (AUG.) Here he explains the sufferings that the saints will endure at the time of the coming. As though he were saying: Although I desire Christ’s coming, nevertheless we shall suffer many things at that time, because he fed them, etc. In measure, etc. (AUG.) According to your strength, so that you may be instructed and not overwhelmed. Hence: “God is faithful, and he will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you can bear,” etc. (I Cor. X). Or according to the measure of their sins.

VERSE 7.—You have made us an object of contradiction. (CASS.) Since the neighbors who are from us are against us. Enemies mock us, but from all these things, so that we may be saved, comes the God of hosts, etc.

VERSE 8.—God of hosts. (AUG.) It is the custom of one who desires something to repeat frequently what he asks for with such great prayers.

VERSES 9–10.—The vine. (CASS.) How the vine was begun and completed. (AUG. and CASS.) “A vine out of Egypt”: as though he were saying, “We shall be saved, but will you destroy the Jews, for whom you did so much?”—not because of a slight fault, but because they did not recognize Christ’s coming. Or, “we shall be saved” because you prefigured it in this way. “A vine out of Egypt.” But why will you destroy it? This concerns the faithless. From Egypt. Just as he led them out of Egypt, so he led the Church out of the darkness of vices: he plants the nations in virtues and leads them through this desert of the world. Its roots: he makes martyrs and other steadfast people firm, and fills the world. (CASS.) “A vine out of Egypt,” through mystical figures, etc., up to: which has thus been spread throughout the world. You led it, while guiding it on a spiritual journey. Its roots are the prophets, Apostles, martyrs, and others, from whom branches extend, occupying and covering the world. Guide of the journey. (AUG.) Or another reading, etc., up to: and it is not another vine, but the same vine. From it come the Apostles and from it the other just, even though some branches were broken off.

VERSES 11–12.—It covered. (CASS.) The height and breadth of the vine are explained here. The vine is heavenly; it overshadows the higher mountains with its life and doctrine and causes them to grow greatly. Vines that climb trees are called vine-arbors; by these the lesser members in the Church are understood. The cedars are not the proud, but those who belong to God: they are the martyrs, who are lofty in the Church. The Church also protects them in her bosom. The shoots are the children of regeneration who flowed from the Jordan River, because the rule of baptism began there. The mountains. (AUG.) The prophets, etc., up to: similarly they cover the cedars of God, that is, the teachers. The cedars of God. (ID.) Because there are cedars destined to be overthrown—namely, the proud, who are the cedars of the world but not of God.

VERSE 13.—Why? He wonders why the Lord’s protection has been withdrawn from such a one. (AUG.) “Why?” Because it was proud against the planter, killed the servants sent to it, and finally the heir’s son. The hedge was destroyed, and the nations found it destroyed and wiped it out. At first Asaph laments this, but not without hope: for he is now speaking about those who direct their hearts.

VERSE 14.—The boar. (AUG. and CASS.) Vespasian, strong and savage, and hostile to the Jews, who count this animal among the unclean. The solitary wild beast. Titus, who consumed the remnants by a terrifying ravaging; he is called “solitary,” that is, proud. Or “boar” and “wild beast” are understood as the same thing, namely, the Roman army. [Col. 0978D] And see with what sins a human being struggles and perishes. Solitary. (AUG.) Every proud person says: “I am, I am, and there is no one else.” The boar. (CASS.) The devil, strong and fierce, from the forest, because his thoughts are wild and wandering. But you, Lord God of hosts. Or connect it this way: The vine has been laid waste in this manner; but, so that the remnant may be saved, O God of hosts, turn back, look upon it serenely at the end of the final age. He prays for this remedy, with things changed for the better.

VERSE 16.—And perfect it, which your right hand planted. (AUG.) Do not establish another, but perfect this one. For in this one is the seed of Abraham; there is the root that bears the wild olive. Perfect it, because blindness has happened in part to Israel, so that the fullness of the nations might enter and thus all Israel might be saved (Rom. XII). Upon the Son. (CASS.) Founded upon you, etc., up to: and concerning the fire of good love it is said: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke XII).

VERSE 18.—Let your hand be upon. (CASS.) A great sacrament and gift for God, because Israel’s salvation could be doubted for so long as Christ had not come. But then the promise was completed, and the Church joined to the Bridegroom does not depart from him thereafter. Therefore he says: “Let your hand be upon”; he prays for the work of the holy Incarnation.

VERSE 19.—We shall not depart. (CASS.) Any longer, when you give life to the Son of Man. This is the benefit that comes from him.

VERSE 20.—Lord God of hosts, turn us, show your face, and we shall be saved. (CASS.) Great is the sweetness of this verse, in which he sets forth the rule of the whole religion. First God converts us; then he shows us before his face, that is, he looks upon us with the light of his mercy; after this, finally, he saves us. The prophet therefore repeats it, because through it each person briefly asks for what is necessary.

# PSALM LXXX

VERSE 1.—For the winepresses. (AUG.) In which there are three things, etc., up to: the psalm of Asaph is sung, that is, for the Lord’s congregation. Asaph, etc. (CASS.) Because according to history he speaks to the Jews, but spiritually to Christians. (AUG.) First he says what must be done by the elect, who are oil, wine, and birds.

VERSE 2.—Rejoice in God. Asaph, having set before himself the image of some solemn celebration, urges the elect to festivity.

VERSE 3.—Take up the psalm. (AUG.) The words of God, so that human actions may come together in one fellowship. For this is the peace of Jerusalem; this is the principle of what is given and received. Hence the Apostle: “If we have sown spiritual things among you, is it a great thing if we reap your material things?” (I Cor. IX).

VERSE 4.—Blow the trumpet. (AUG.) Up to this point, whether according to the division or literally, the passage is to be understood simply of the Jews, or allegorically of Christians. (AUG.) “Blow the trumpet and announce,” etc., up to: hence Isaiah: “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet,” etc. A trumpet at the new moon. (CASS.) The Jews were commanded to blow the trumpet at the beginning of the month, that is, at the beginning of the new moon. This is also called the Feast of Trumpets, which they celebrated in memory of the event when the Lord showed Abraham a ram caught among the thorns and sacrificed it in place of Isaac.

VERSE 5.—For it is a commandment in Israel, and a judgment, etc. (ID.) The trumpet is to be blown because the law was given to the Jews through Moses, and because the one who will judge is to come.

VERSE 6.—In Joseph. (AUG.) The nations are Joseph, etc., up to: where he ought to have his heart.

VERSE 7.—From burdens. (AUG.) From what burdens? “Hands in the basket,” that is, servile labor. Sins are servile works, according to the saying: “Whoever commits sin is a slave of sin” (John VIII). They served in the basket. (ID.) In the uncleannesses of sins, in earthly and muddy works.

[Col. 0980A] VERSE 8.—In tribulation, etc. (CASS.) Thus the prophet says: The Lord turns aside, saying, “In tribulation.” God’s benefits are counted against them, so that the offense may be judged more grievous. I answered you in secret. (AUG.) So that you may believe in your heart unto righteousness. I tested you, so that confession may be made with the mouth unto salvation. Of the storm, etc. Not a storm at sea, but of the heart: there the one who has been heard must be tested, in the water of contradiction. For one who is already walking on God’s path has many kinds of opponents. This is the water of contradiction, which the ancients experienced, but which has now almost dried up. At that time the waters of the peoples were stirred up, and they resisted fiercely. Then, when Samson, the strong man—that is, Christ—went to take a wife from foreigners—that is, the Church from the nations—a roaring lion met him, that is, the people of the nations; but he tore it apart like a young goat. And because this roaring people was nothing but a weakened sinner, once that savagery had been killed in it, it no longer roars in the same way. Indeed, we now find in it laws for the Church, as though a honeycomb were in the lion’s mouth. The water of contradiction. Christ also experienced it in himself, as was said of him at his birth: “This child is destined for the fall and rising of many, and for a sign that will be contradicted” (Luke II), just as the Jews contradicted the inscription on the cross.

VERSE 9.—Hear, my people. (CASS.) A diapsalm. Up to this point he has spoken about the oil of the winepress; now he speaks about the dregs, which is said as a warning. Here the reprobate are rebuked. I will testify against you. The Lord himself makes himself a witness of the truth at the judgment, both here and in the future, so that no one may doubt. Then he adds what he wants them to understand: “Israel, if you will hear me.” By calling him Israel, he signifies one familiar to himself and invites him to obey the commands. Within you, in your heart, where there ought to be truth, not falsehood. “Lest the word of the Father be thought to be recent,” that is, subject to time. A foreign god, foreign in name, not in essence. “Foreign”: it is almost equally wicked to think that God is recent and to serve idols.

VERSE 10.—There shall be no recent god among you, nor any, etc. (AUG.) Some make recent gods for themselves, whether idols or Christ unequal to the Father, and invent other such things in their hearts. Thus temples of idols exist in every earthly thought; the opinion is different, but the vanity is one. Therefore Samson tied together the tails of foxes in order to set the Philistines’ crops on fire. Samson is interpreted as “their sun,” namely, of those for whom he himself shines, not of everyone. Concerning him the wicked will say: “We wandered from the way of truth, and the sun of righteousness did not shine upon us” (Wis. V). And elsewhere: “He is the sun of righteousness, and healing is in his wings” (Mal. IV). The foxes are the crafty, especially heretics, hiding in twisted caverns, deceiving, and stinking with their odor. Although they appear to disagree among themselves, they nevertheless agree in evil—that is, in their hind parts. They are held by a similar vanity, and they set fire to the crops not of our people, for God knows those who are his, but of foreigners, who are vessels of dishonor.

VERSE 11.—I who brought you out. God is indicated by his own deeds.

VERSE 13.—And he let them go. Even though I fulfilled the words of the prophets, they were nevertheless not heard by the dregs; hence the fitting vengeance: because I also let them go, etc.

VERSE 15.—Perhaps for nothing. (CASS.) If we resist God, he does not oppose our enemies, nor place the hand of his protection over them.

VERSE 16.—The enemies of the Lord, etc. (AUG.) This too is the prophet’s statement. They lied to him, by not carrying out their promises. This does not concern the pagans, because they made no promises.

VERSE 17.—He would feed them with the fat of wheat, etc. (AUG.) Literally, or manna, or the body of Christ, or spiritual understanding.

# PSALM LXXXI

VERSE 1.—A psalm of Asaph. (CASS.) A psalm concerning the two natures in Christ, in which Christ—or the prophet speaking—reproaches Asaph himself, that is, the Synagogue, which saw the Lord bodily and nevertheless did not recognize him. First he announces that God has stood and rebukes those who oppose him: the human being stands, God discerns. God stood. The one who fills heaven and earth, who is within all things without being enclosed, outside all things without being excluded, is not one for whom standing is proper. Yet he briefly indicates God as human. He stood. (AUG.) The Son, who was sent to the sheep of the house of Israel; but the spiritual presence of the Godhead, which is everywhere, does not properly belong to the Synagogue alone and is not changed by time. Why did he stand there? “Behold, he judges among the gods,” that is, insofar as he is God—not according to merits, but by grace he distinguishes the vessels, some for honor and others for dishonor. He does this by standing in the midst, hence: “One has stood in your midst whom you do not know.” Hence also here: “They did not know or understand”; but the friend of the bridegroom stands and listens and rejoices with joy. Of the gods. Those whom he calls “sons of the Most High” in the words: “I said, You are gods, and all of you are sons of the Most High.” Hence also: “I nourished and exalted sons, but they themselves despised me.” They are called sons not only by the grace of the New Testament, but also by the grace of the Old, which freed them from Egypt.

VERSE 2.—How long? (AUG.) This is the voice of one who distinguishes. He sent the law and the prophets, and you resisted; but how long? Did I send prophets only until the coming, and did you injure or kill them, or consent to those who did these things? But since it is not fitting even to speak with those who did such things, you who remained silent, and who wished to imitate them—how long will you judge iniquity and assume the faces of sinners? Must the heir also be killed, he who came for you, who for your sake chose to be without a father, like an orphan? He who for your sake hungered and thirsted like one in need, who for your sake became poor although he was rich?

[Col. 0981D] VERSE 3.—Judge the needy and the orphan; justify the poor and the humble. (CASS.) A diapsalm. He warns them to understand that Christ is God, and that although he was needy and poor, they did not do what he says.

VERSE 4.—Rescue the poor. (AUG.) He shows that those too are not free from guilt who allowed Christ to be handed over to the rulers, although they feared them because of the crowd and could have freed them from the deed and themselves from consent. (CASS.) For one who ceases to oppose something when he can does consent.

VERSE 5.—They shall be shaken. (CASS.) From this it is clear what he had spoken about: this sign occurred at the Crucifixion. Or spiritually, earthly people were moved at that time when they saw so great a miracle, like the centurion who said: “Truly this was the Son of God.” (AUG.) “All the foundations shall be shaken.” [Col. 0982A] As though he were saying: Through this blindness of Israel, all the foundations of the earth—that is, the fullness of the nations—will be moved toward faith and will enter. Or, at the death and Passion of the Lord the earth was shaken. Or “foundations” means the happy abundance of earthly possessions, which will be shaken. Or by wondering that a poor man who has died is worshipped. Or by following him while despising earthly things. He adds “all” because there is no one who does not wonder or is not converted. The kingdom of earthly happiness, however, is pride. Against it came Christ in humility, reproaching those whom he wishes to make exalted through humility, with these words: “I said, You are gods”—you who are good; but you who are evil shall die like human beings. Or he says to all: “You are gods,” that is, I promised heavenly things to all; but you, like the first human beings, who sinned by persuasion, and you, the greater ones, like the devil, who sinned through pride.

VERSE 6.—I said. (CASS.) What was proposed to them? But they perished. “I said: They did not know or understand”—nevertheless, I said it. All receive these promises if they keep the commandments, so that they may be sons of God. This concerns the just; “but you” concerns the wicked.

VERSE 7.—Like human beings. (AUG.) As though he were saying: Although, like human beings, you will soon die, you are not corrected by this; instead, like the devil, who does not die in the flesh, you exalt yourselves so that you may fall. For through diabolical pride they envied Christ’s glory, and the humility of the cross became contemptible to them. But so that this vice may be healed, the following is added from the person of the prophet: “Rise, O God,” etc., as one. The crowd that fell is called one because it was alike in pride. “You will fall,” but:

[Col. 0982C] VERSE 8.—Rise, O God. (AUG.) That is, condemn these people, because once they have been rejected, you will inherit. Or judge the world, because it is yours; and this is what “you will inherit” means.

# PSALM LXXXII

VERSE 1.—A song of a psalm. (CASS.) Because divine contemplation must be maintained in practical matters. It deters the wicked from persecuting God’s people, but it urges the good toward patience. A psalm about Christ’s coming to judgment, where the good, who suffer here, will be crowned, while the wicked, who persecute them, will be tormented.

VERSE 2.—O God, who is like you? (CASS.) Having proposed fear of the future judge, he describes the malice of the enemies. (AUG.) “O God, who is like you?” Although he was human, like the others; although judged and counted among the wicked—who is like him when he will judge in glory? Therefore do not remain silent then, you who were silent at first and restrained your power so that you could be seized and killed. “O God, who is like you?” This does not refer to the divinity, to which he thought no human being could be compared. Therefore he does not say: “Who is like you?”—which would certainly refer to the divinity—but says: “Who will be like you?” referring this to the form of a servant, in which at that time he will be unlike other human beings, when he appears as judge in glory. Or this can refer to the divinity, according to the saying: “O God, who is like you?” in the power of the Godhead. For the wicked saw Christ outwardly, while this person sees him inwardly, namely, as the almighty one.

[Col. 0983A] VERSE 3.—For behold, etc. (AUG.) He signifies the final times of the Antichrist, when what is now suppressed by fear will burst forth into an unrestrained voice. Since that voice was irrational, it is called more a sound than speech. Those who hated. (CASS.) They are many, but the Antichrist is one head, who has been exalted so that he may be called God.

VERSE 4.—Against your people. They have lifted up their own head, but they have not cast down your people.

(AUG.) Against your people. He says this mockingly. For they cannot harm God’s people, for whom God stands. Hence the Apostle: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom. VIII).

VERSE 5.—They said, “Come.” (AUG.) Behold the plan by which they devised empty things. This is that sound which is not speech but an empty clamor. Of the nation. (CASS.) In the singular, because all Christians are one nation, born from the one fountain of baptism; or all the good, whom that Antichrist calls one nation. Behold the persecution of the Antichrist, who attempts to remove the Christian name entirely as though it were evil.

VERSE 6.—They have made a covenant. (AUG.) In Scripture, “covenant” does not refer only to what has no force unless the testator has died; every agreement and compact that is valid between the living is also called a covenant, as Laban and Jacob made a covenant. Thus the wicked have made a pact among themselves, as it were, that they would unanimously persecute the good.

VERSE 7.—The tents of the Edomites. He has explained with what zeal they acted wickedly; he then shows who the wicked are, saying: “The tents of the Edomites,” etc. The Edomites and Ishmaelites. (CASS.) By these names he identifies the enemies of Christ, who resemble so many evils in the time of the Antichrist. For as these fought against Israel, so those will then fight against Christians. Moabites. (AUG., HIER.) Hence the Moabites, whom drunken Lot begot from his elder daughter. Hagarenes. From Hagar; they are also interpreted as proselytes.

VERSE 8.—Gebal. (AUG., HIER.) A vain valley. For *Ge* means “valley,” and *Bal*, “vain.” Ammon. Hence the Ammonites, whom drunken Lot begot from his younger daughter.

Amalek. The son of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn, from whom came the Amalekites.

VERSE 9.—Assur. (AUG., HIER.) Literally, Nebuchadnezzar, who was king of the Assyrians. The Edomites. Earthly or bloody. The Ishmaelites. Those who obey themselves rather than God, because they follow their depraved thoughts. Moab, “from the father,” understood in an evil sense. The father was indeed good, but the daughter used him illicitly, just as the law is good if someone uses it lawfully, not incestuously. Hagarenes. Proselytes, that is, newcomers, who are not citizens but enter with a foreign disposition and, when an opportunity to harm is found, reveal themselves. Gebal. A vain valley, that is, deceptively humble. Ammon. A turbulent people, or a people of sorrow. Amalek. A people licking the earth. Foreigners. Although they indicate themselves by a Latin name as foreigners and therefore enemies, in Hebrew they are called *Philisthiim*, that is, “falling through drink,” like those drunk with worldly luxury. Tyre. In Hebrew *ṣor*, “tribulation” or “distress,” according to the saying: “Tribulation and distress upon every soul of the human being who does evil” (Rom. II). Assur. “Depressing” or “exalted.” Lot. “Declining”: the apostate angels, sons of decline, because by declining from the truth they departed into the devil’s service. Hence in the Apocalypse: “The dragon fell and drew with him a third of the stars.” Of these the Apostle says: “Our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers” (Eph. VI).

VERSE 10.—Midian. “Declining from judgment.” Sisera, “exclusion of joy.” Jabin, “wise,” concerning whom it is said: “Where is the wise person? Where is the scribe?” Kishon, where they were defeated; it is interpreted as “hardness.” Endor, where they perished, “fountain of generation.” This is understood as carnal generation, not the water of those regenerated through baptism. Oreb, “dryness.” Zeeb, “wolf.” Zebah, “victim of the wolf,” not of God. Zalmunna, “shadow of agitation.” All these meanings fit the wicked, whom God’s people defeated in the good. “Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent.” (CASS.) This concerns vengeance upon the wicked. Just as all those were defeated figuratively by God’s people, so he prays that these may truly be overcome. As Midian. (AUG.) That is, those who decline from judgment, not thinking that they will be judged; and those who exclude future judgment. All these perished at Kishon and at the fountain of Endor.

VERSE 12.—Set their princes like, etc. This applies to all generally. But specifically, “set their princes”: he asks this concerning the soldiers of the Antichrist, who are not to be converted.

VERSE 13.—Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance. (AUG.) They invade God’s sanctuary as though it were their own.

[Col. 0984C] VERSE 14.—Like a wheel and like stubble before the face of the wind. (CASS.) Through this comparison he foretells their many calamities.

Winds. The lightness of sinners is compared with wind, because it flits here and there.

VERSE 15.—Fire and a burning flame that consumes the mountains. (AUG.) They are appropriately said to exist at the judgment, when both the dense forests of sins and the mountains of pride will be burned.

VERSE 17.—Fill their faces. (CASS.) After prophesying punishments for the obstinate, he prays for those who will believe, who have no praisers of their crimes but accusers; reproach often corrects them. (AUG.) It is better to fall so as to repent than to grow proud under the pretext of religion. Hence the prophet says: “And you, daughter of Zion, shall come as far as Babylon, and there you shall be delivered” (Mic. IV).

Fill their faces. This good and desirable outcome would not be prophesied for them unless there were among them enemies of this kind, to whom it would be granted before the judgment. For even now the same body heals and washes the head, but piecemeal, not universally as at the end; and nevertheless some will be converted from it, for whom he prays here.

## Psalm 82

### Verse 18

“Let them be ashamed and confounded,” etc. (Augustine.) Here he speaks of the wicked who will not be converted: “Let them be ashamed” in the future because of the evils they committed; “and let them be confounded” because of the punishments they will suffer. And this “for ever and ever,” that is, eternally.

“And let them be confounded.” He returns again to those who will be confounded in the present so that they may not be confounded eternally—as if he were saying: Let those others be confounded eternally; but let those who now seek the name of the Lord be salutarily ashamed of their sins, and perish insofar as they are evil. Thus let them come to know; or else, let the wicked then be confounded in soul and body and perish altogether, irreparably. And now let them know what they are unwilling to know at present.

(Cassiodorus.) It should be noted that Asaph was introduced in the eleven preceding psalms so that the hardness of the Jews might be softened by the frequent voice of the Synagogue itself, or so that they might believe in the very name to which they appeared devoted. In those psalms he dealt with the Lord’s incarnation, the faith of the nations, and the judgment—matters by which the transgression of the Jews is reproved. Hence there are appropriately eleven psalms: for the number eleven signifies transgression, since it passes beyond ten but does not reach twelve. Thus there were also eleven curtains of goats’ hair in the Lord’s tabernacle, and there were eleven Apostles after the most unhappy Judas had been rejected at the time of the Passion, when they fell away from the faith. Hence: “You appointed darkness, and it became night” (Psalm 103).

## Psalm 83

### Verse 1

“Unto the end.” (Augustine.) Nothing is said here about visible winepresses; hence it is clear that the reference is spiritual. A grape hanging on the vine and an olive hanging on the tree freely enjoy the air; yet the one is not wine and the other is not oil before pressing. Likewise, those whom God foreknew before the ages to be conformed to the image of his Son enjoy a delightful freedom in the world before they approach the service of God. But when they approach God’s service, it is said to them: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear, and prepare your soul for temptation” (Ecclesiasticus 2).

Behold the winepress: they are crushed and stripped of the coverings of carnal desires; as grape-skins are stripped away, so they are stripped of the old man, and flow into God’s storehouse. Therefore the churches of the present time are called winepresses. But who are “the sons of Core” in these winepresses—that is, the bald ones, namely, Christ’s? For the bald Elisha, mocked by the boys, was a figure of Christ, who was crucified at the place of the Skull. Therefore the Christian is pressed here so that he may seek the rest that is not found here, and God becomes his refuge. For whoever leans upon earthly things leans upon a staff of reed.

“On the winepresses.” (Augustine.) In the winepress the fruit of the grape or olive flows out; so, in afflictions, the merits of the saints become manifest, though they lay hidden in peace.

(Cassiodorus.) The second psalm concerning charity. First, concerning the immeasurable desire for the eternal dwelling.

### Verse 2

“How beloved.” Behold how great the warfare. “For even the sparrow”—how secure it is.

### Verse 4

“For even the sparrow,” etc. (Augustine.) He assigns two things to two things: the heart to the sparrow, the flesh to the turtledove, to which he also gives its young. With the heart we think upon God, as though the sparrow were flying to the house; with the flesh we perform works.

(Cassiodorus.) As the sparrow abandons the forests and rejoices when it finds a house where it does not fear ambushes, so the soul rejoices when it knows that a house has been prepared for it in heaven. The spirit is like a sparrow flying on high and stretching toward God himself.

“A nest,” etc. (Augustine.) A nest is temporary, but a house is eternal. Therefore he calls faith and conformity to the Church’s sacraments a nest; the turtledove seeks this nest in which to place its young. For it does not cast them down anywhere, but performs good works salutarily in the nest of the Church, through which it is saved. In this it differs from others who perform works but not in the nest of faith. Pagans too perform works: they clothe the naked, and so forth; and heretics perform many works. But they do not perform them in the nest of the Church, and therefore they are trampled upon, not preserved.

This flesh is the woman by whom the sparrow is led astray, but it will be saved through the generation of works if it remains in the nest—that is, if it perseveres in the faith. God provides the material from which the nest is made: for he clothed himself in the hay of flesh in order to come to you.

“Your altars, O Lord.” (Cassiodorus.) Where souls feast at the heavenly banquet, where the soul rejoices as though in a house.

(Augustine.) And the flesh places its works there, whence it is said: “Blessed are those,” etc., where he shows to what blessedness the warfare leads.

### Verse 5

“Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they will praise you.” (Augustine.) The good already possess this, namely, that they dwell in your house. What follows—“for ever and ever they will praise you”—is the whole activity of the saints there. There is no necessity there, which is the mother of all human actions, because whom do they serve there, where no one is in need? They both possess and perform what makes them blessed. Everyone is called blessed either through possessing or through doing.

### Verse 6

“Blessed is the man whose help is from you; he has arranged ascents in his heart.” (Cassiodorus.) By what help one comes to the house.

### Verse 7

“In the valley of tears.” (Cassiodorus.) The valley of tears is the humility of the penitent.

(Augustine.) Why is there weeping? Because the law afflicted us, through which we learned that sin resists the spirit, and we groan, wondering how we may come to the place he appointed, certainly through his power and help.

“To the place which he appointed. For he will give blessing.” This cannot be explained as referring to what “the eye has not seen nor ear heard”—that is, the future kingdom—which God arranged and ordered so that one might come to it by stages.

### Verse 9

“O Lord, God of hosts.” (Cassiodorus.) He prays and humbles himself in order to obtain this help.

“God of Jacob.” (Augustine.) You made Israel by appearing to him; so make me Israel also.

### Verse 10

“Look upon the face,” etc. For he himself speaks in us; hence the Apostle says: “Do you seek proof of the Christ who speaks in me?” And he is received in us, as he says: “Whoever receives you receives me.”

“Look upon.” The Father always looks upon Christ.

(Cassiodorus.) But cause him to be regarded by the nations in the reality of his incarnation; or, through the face, we become known to others.

(Augustine.) Therefore “look upon the face,” that is, make Christ known to all, so that we may go from strength to strength.

### Verse 11

“One day.” Immutable, without rising or setting; yesterday does not give way before it, nor does tomorrow press upon it.

“Above thousands”—above the countless present days that have an end.

“Because I have chosen,” even though I could reign, to be cast down in human opinion, “in the house,” in the Church. Behold how sweet it is to be pressed beneath the burden of the winepress.

### Verse 12

“For mercy.” (Cassiodorus.) Therefore I prefer to be in God’s house rather than elsewhere, because in it he gives mercy, by which he justifies, after the truth of the promised reward. But to whom? To those who walk in innocence.

### Verse 13

“O Lord of hosts, blessed is the man who hopes,” etc.—you who do such great things that they cannot be expressed.

## Psalm 84

### Verse 2

“You have blessed, O Lord.” (Augustine.) A psalm concerning the new blessing, etc., up to the turning away of iniquity.

### Verse 3

“You have forgiven.” (The same.) He speaks of future things as though they were past.

### Verse 4

“You have appeased.” (Cassiodorus.) A *diapsalma* concerning the turning away of anger, that is, punishment.

### Verse 5

“Turn us.” He asks for what he knew was still future—as though saying: What I have spoken of as past, I pray may come to pass.

(Augustine.) “Turn us.” Prophetically he spoke of future things as past; here, however, he prays that they may truly be future, saying, “Turn and turn away,” as though saying: I spoke as if these things had already happened. And because I see that they are future, and because they have not yet happened, I pray that they may come to pass.

### Verse 6

“Will you be angry for ever?” He foresees that this punishment will pass away: “For as all die in Adam, so also all will be made alive in Christ.”

“You will be angry.” (Augustine.) The anger of God is every punishment that one suffers. Thus it was said to Adam when he sinned: “Cursed is the earth in your work,” and, “In toil and the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread.” Because of this anger we are mortal and subject to suffering, but we are renewed in Christ.

“From generation.” The first generation was mortal, arising from anger; another will be immortal, arising from mercy. Yet even this mercy is not something we merit by turning to God through ourselves, for he himself turns us. Hence he adds: “God, turning,” as though saying: Just as life-giving comes from you, so also does conversion.

### Verse 7

“God, you will turn.” (Cassiodorus.) Not “extending,” but “God, turning.” First he gives the desire for conversion; afterward he leads to life. Or: “God, you will turn” from anger at the coming of the Son.

“You will give us life.” This is said long before it is possessed. And then: “Your people will rejoice in you,” whereas previously they rejoiced wrongly in themselves.

### Verse 8

“Show us, O Lord.” (Augustine.) The Prophet foretold this by prayer, etc., up to: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

(Cassiodorus.) “Show.” Or he asks that Christ be shown to him only spiritually. He knew that Christ would indeed come, but he asks that we behold him with a pure heart, not with bodily eyes like unbelievers: for the Jews saw him and crucified him.

“And in the future: Give us your salvation,” that is, Christ, to be embraced and possessed, so that he may not be taken away from us. Thus the passage is understood partly of the present and partly of the future.

“Mercy.” (Augustine.) Christ is called mercy because he shows us mercy, teaching that whatever good a human being possesses comes from God, so that the human being does not become proud. Rather, by clinging to and enjoying God, he rejoices in him.

### Verse 9

“I will hear what the Lord God will speak in me.” (Cassiodorus.) Hence he knows through whom it will come to pass and what he himself, on coming, will grant.

“Peace.” (Augustine.) Christ: peace with God and with one’s neighbor, and peace through Christ.

### Verse 10

“Near to those who fear him.” (The same.) Demons were worshiped everywhere, etc., up to immortality in our body, which is now mortal.

### Verse 11

“Mercy,” etc. (The same.) After he said, etc., up to: how truth arose from the earth (Luke 8).

### Verse 12

“Truth has arisen from the earth.” (The same.) Confession arising from the human being, so that he accuses himself, etc., up to: justification was given to the one who confesses.

### Verse 14

“Righteousness before him.” (The same.) The first righteousness of a human being is, etc., up to: “and visiting, he will place his steps on the way.”

“He will walk.” He will increase, or run ahead, preparing a way for him; and the Lord will place his steps on the prepared way.

## Psalm 85

### A Prayer of David

(Augustine.) This psalm is the second of those entitled with the name “prayer.” In it Christ, Son of God and son of man, one God with the Father and one man among human beings, prays in the form of a servant—he who is prayed to by us in the form of God. He prays for us as our priest; he prays in us as our head; he is prayed to by us as our God.

(Cassiodorus.) The prayer of Christ among the faithful, etc., up to: he might restrain the boldness of foolish and ill-considered presumption.

(Augustine.) Christ says these things in us, and we in him.

(Cassiodorus.) He prays while ascending, and therefore concludes: “All the nations worshiping.”

### Verse 2

“For I am holy.” (Augustine.) Christ is properly holy, sanctifying, etc., up to: have mercy on the one who cries out; make joyful the one who has been lifted up.

### Verse 5

“Gentle.” (The same.) Carrying the human being until he perfects him, etc., up to: while he is not yet perfect.

### Verse 6

“Give ear.” (Cassiodorus.) Observe the order of the prayer, etc., up to: hear my supplication.

### Verse 7

“Of tribulation.” (Augustine and Cassiodorus.) When one cries out more earnestly, etc., up to: “for there is none like you among the gods, O Lord.”

### Verse 9

“All whom you have made shall come and worship before you,” etc. (Augustine.) If there were a nation that God had not made, it would not worship. He announces the Church spread everywhere, which has now been fulfilled. And note that, as Scripture says: “In a numerous nation is the glory of a king; in the diminution of a people is the crushing of a prince.” It follows: “And they will glorify your name.”

### Verse 10

“You alone are God.” (The same.) Or: you alone are great in opposition to those who will come, who call themselves great and gods.

### Verse 11

“Lead me, O Lord, in your way.” (Cassiodorus.) He prays for all who are already worshiping and speaks in the members.

“O Lord, lead,” etc. It is one thing to be led to the way and another to be led in the way, so that one does not fall on it. Human beings everywhere need to be helped, whether they are in the way or outside it. The way is Christ, who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life.”

“Let my heart rejoice.” (Augustine.) In worldly fear, the cause comes first, etc., up to: but whoever fears and does not hope is cast down.

### Verse 13

“From the lower hell.” (The same.) By this we understand, etc., up to: these are opinions, not assertions.

### Verse 14
