“O God, the wicked have risen up against me, and the assembly of the powerful,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) Again he prays for himself, mentioning his Passion and his glory; hence those for whom he prayed receive abundant mercy and are rescued from hell.

### Verse 16

“Give your authority.” (Augustine.) As though he were saying: Let the time of patience pass; let the time of judgment come. Hence not only Christ but also the saints will sit as judges, those who are the children of the maidservant, that is, of the Church.

## Psalm 86

### Verse 1

“A psalm.” (Cassiodorus.) Because it treats of the Church according to its active power, where it performs works.

“A song.” So that you may be lifted from the earthly Jerusalem to an understanding of the Jerusalem above—that is, from action to contemplation.

The Prophet proclaims the heavenly Jerusalem to the sons of Core, commending it through its foundations, gates, and renown so that their affection for it may increase.

“Her foundations.” A psalm concerning the heavenly Jerusalem. Filled with the Spirit, the Prophet turns many things over in his mind concerning this city, of which he had not yet spoken, and breaks forth with these words: “Her foundations,” etc. His first praise concerns the foundations; the solidity of the whole city is indicated. “Her” does not refer to anything previously mentioned, but to the Prophet’s meditation in his heart, because he had never been silent about her in his heart, even if he had been silent with his mouth.

### Verse 3

“Things spoken.” (Augustine.) These are the things that the Lord foretold about her through the prophets.

### Verse 4

“I will remember.” (The same.) A *diapsalma*. The Lord speaks concerning the same Jerusalem.

“I will remember Rahab.” He shows what those glorious things are, as though saying: These are the things. In that city, says the Prophet in God’s person, “I will remember Rahab and Babylon,” who do not belong to the Jewish people.

“Glorious things are spoken of you,” where the Jew alone is not present, but all nations.

“Rahab.” Through the window she sent out a scarlet cord; that is, the Church of the nations bears on its forehead the sign of Christ’s blood.

Hence: “Publicans and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of heaven.”

“Rahab”—breadth or force—signifies the nations, which wander broadly and forcefully through vices.

Babylon concerns all the wicked, just as Jerusalem concerns all the saints.

“Behold the foreigners.”

“I will remember.” Why have you said this? Behold the foreigners, that is, the nations: Tyre—whether the narrowness of vices or of repentance.

### Verse 5

“Will Zion say, ‘A man’?” According to another reading: “Mother Zion will say, ‘A man.’”

(Augustine and Cassiodorus.) As though saying: From where will foreigners reach Jerusalem? Hear from where. There is a certain man, that is, Christ, who says: “Mother Zion,” that is, “the Synagogue is my mother according to the flesh.” Through him they come. Who is that man? He is the one who was born in her and founded her; he calls that city “mother.”

(Cassiodorus.) Or he commends spiritual Zion, etc., up to: “whose princes?”

(Augustine.) “These,” according to another reading, “who were made”—namely, princes—“in her”; that is, those who were made princes. Before they were in her, they were not princes, but the rejected things of the world. For God chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong.

### Verse 7

“As of those who rejoice.” (Cassiodorus.) A *diapsalma*. He concludes in a few words, touching upon future blessedness.

(Augustine.) “As of those who rejoice.” He concludes by bringing everything together: “As of those who rejoice.” “As,” because the joy will be of such a kind as we do not know here; and because it could not be expressed, he says, as he is able, “as of those who rejoice.”

## Psalm 87

### Verse 1

“Mahalath.” (Augustine.) A chorus, so that the chorus may answer the singer by singing together, etc., up to: for it is said that there was a certain eastern man.

### Verse 2

“O Lord God.” (Cassiodorus.) He urges us to imitate Christ’s death. First he asks for help, referring to contempt from his enemies; hence, praying to the Father in the form of a servant, he says: “O Lord.”

### Verse 3

“Let my prayer enter into your sight.” (The same.) The power of pure prayer, which enters God as though it were a certain person and carries out its command, whereas flesh cannot reach there.

### Verse 4

“For my soul is filled.” (Augustine.) These are the emotions of human weakness, etc., up to: but indications of human weakness.

### Verse 5

“I am counted.” Because I endured not only grievous things but also insults.

### Verse 6

“Like the wounded who sleep.” (Cassiodorus.) For he too was wounded by a lance and enclosed in a tomb. But this differs by what follows: “whom you no longer remember.”

“In the grave.” That is, asleep in carnal pleasure, from which God does not awaken them.

“And they themselves have been driven away from your hand.” (Augustine.) This does not refer to those who sleep, among whom are the righteous, even though God does not yet remember them so as to raise them. Nevertheless, it was said concerning them: “The souls of the righteous are in the hand of God” (Wisdom 3).

Or they placed me there in the reality of the matter: “in the lower pit,” that is, in the waters of hell, namely, in darkness and the shadow of death.

### Verse 7

“In the lower pit.” (Cassiodorus.) Or in hell, because he was removed in such an abject death, in the darkness of oblivion, that no one would seek him.

“And the shadow of death”—the place of the wicked, where they are punished.

### Verse 8

“Your wrath has been confirmed over me.” (The same.) They thought that he had perished through God’s anger and that God had brought all his indignation upon him when he allowed him to be crucified.

### Verse 9

“You have put far away.” (The same.) What his friends did during the Passion.

“Acquaintances.” Not those whom he knew—for as God he knew everyone then—but those to whom he was known.

### Verse 10

“All day long.” (Augustine.) The extension of the hands signifies the continuation of good works, from which he never ceased. For on the cross that extension was not there for an entire day, nor can the whole be taken for a part when he adds “all.” But because these works did not benefit everyone, he adds [the following].

### Verse 11

“Will you work wonders for the dead?” He calls “dead” those who are dead in heart, for whom Christ’s miracles are indeed performed but do not benefit them. Miracles were performed for the physically dead when certain people were restored to life. And when the Lord entered hell and ascended from there victorious over death, a great miracle was performed for the dead.

“Will you work wonders for the dead?” (Cassiodorus.) He shows those who receive no benefit from his works.

“Or will physicians raise them?” etc. (Augustine.) In Hebrew it does not say “physicians,” etc., up to: “No one can come to me unless the Father draws him.”

### Verse 12

“In the grave.” Hence the Gospel says concerning such people: “You are like whitened tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to human beings, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead”—as though saying: so are you, full of hypocrisy and iniquity.

“Your mercy and your truth.” (Augustine.) Scripture especially loves to join mercy and truth together in the Psalms.

### Verse 13

“In darkness.” Those placed in the grave are the same as the dead, darkness, and the land of forgetfulness.

### Verse 14

“But I cried to you, O Lord.” (Cassiodorus.) What he endures in his members; behold, the chorus answering the leader.

(The same.) “And I too,” as though saying: with them, with whom I am one.

(Augustine.) “And I.” Their works do not benefit these dead, etc., up to: “Why, O Lord, do you reject?”

### Verse 15

“Why?” (Cassiodorus.) Behold how greatly he desires. “Why, O Lord?” He proposes that the reason must be sought. It is that, through the delay of good things and the multiplication of adversities, prayer—having been repulsed—may be inflamed more ardently.

### Verse 16

“When I was exalted.” (The same.) First with a swollen heart; afterward, “humbled,” through confession.

“Confounded”—that is, confused because of sins, condemning them.

### Verse 17

“They have passed over.” (Cassiodorus.) They did not come gently upon me.

(Augustine.) Because this was spoken not concerning the faithful but concerning the unbelieving: “The wrath of God remains upon him” (John 3). For he scourges the children whom he receives; hence: “Those whom I love, I reprove and chastise” (Revelation 3). And elsewhere: “I will strike and heal; I will kill and make alive” (Deuteronomy 32).

(The same.) “They have passed over and confounded me.” We suffer one thing now from condemnation and fear another thing from eternal vengeance.

“Your terrors.” (Cassiodorus.) Those which I suffer, because it has pleased you, not because of my merit.

(Augustine.) The terrors of the future judgment, which all flesh fears.

“They have confounded me.” According to the weakness of the flesh.

(Augustine.) Terrors have at times confounded me. They so disturb the mind of one who considers the evils hanging over him that they seem to flow around him like waters and to surround him simultaneously from every side. Hence friends and acquaintances abandon him through fear; hence the Apostle says: “Everyone abandoned me” (2 Timothy 4).

### Verse 18

“They surrounded me.” (Cassiodorus.) Sins enclose me on every side in an abundant flood.

“All day long.” (Augustine.) Because evils are never absent from the Church until the age is ended. But all these things occur so that the Church’s prayer may anticipate God until that salvation comes where there is no evil.

### Verse 19

“Friend.” (Cassiodorus.) Those who are joined by devout and faithful love.

“Neighbor and acquaintances,” etc.—kinship. Human services are often withheld from the righteous through fear.

## Psalm 88

### Verse 2

“Mercies.” (Cassiodorus.) This psalm says many things about the hope of Christians and the Lord’s magnificence, through which no one who makes a worthy supplication is deceived; the true Israel understands it in this way. First, the Prophet promises that he will sing of mercy and truth.

“For ever.” (Cassiodorus and Remigius.) How does he sing of mercies for ever and give thanks, when he does not remember misery? And how can blessedness be complete if the memory of guilt touches the mind? But often we remember sad things joyfully, and, being healthy, remember pains without pain; thereby we become still more joyful and grateful. So, likewise, the memory of misery takes nothing away from blessedness.

“Truth.” The promise. It does not flow “from the mouth,” but “in the mouth”; it remains there for a long time like something sweet.

### Verse 3

“For you have said.” Here he says: From where does he know, and what are God’s mercies through Christ?

(Augustine.) What mercies, and what truth, shall I sing? Behold.

“For you have said.” As though he were saying: I, a human being, confidently say what you, God, have said, made known through the Spirit.

“Mercy shall be built up.” (Augustine.) He repeats both things that he previously mentioned, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.” Truth is not displayed in the fulfillment of promises unless mercy in the forgiveness of sins precedes it. Finally, truth belongs to the Jews, to whom the promises were made; mercy belongs to the nations, as the Apostle says: “For I say that Jesus Christ was a minister of circumcision in order to fulfill the truth of God; but the nations are to honor God for mercy” (Romans 15).

“In the heavens.” Those who declare the glory of God, through whom mercy is built up.

### Verse 4

“I have sworn to David my servant.” He is confident because God spoke; even more confident because God swore. God’s oath is confirmation of the promise. From both, a person becomes *Ethan*, that is, strong.

### Verse 5

“For ever.” (Cassiodorus.) The building up of mercy is not temporal, as the ruin of iniquity is temporal. Temporal iniquity is destroyed in certain people so that eternal mercy may be built up in them. Hence the Lord says through Jeremiah: “Behold, I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and demolish, to build and to plant.”

“From generation.” (Augustine.) For generation cannot, etc., up to: but he will sit, and then in the saints.

### Verse 6

“The heavens will confess.” (Cassiodorus.) A *diapsalma*. Secondly, he describes the praises and power of God in various ways, as though saying: As you have said, so it will be.

“They will confess”—they will praise.

“The heavens will confess your wonders.” For in every mercy shown to the lost, in the justification of the ungodly, what do we praise except God’s wonders? You praise because the dead have risen; praise still more because the lost have been redeemed. You see a person who yesterday was a pit of drunkenness and today an ornament of sobriety. You see a person who yesterday was filth of lust and today an adornment of self-control; yesterday a blasphemer of God, today a praiser of God. You see a person who yesterday was a slave of creation and today a worshiper of the Creator. These are the wonders that the heavens confess.

“For indeed, your truth.” (Cassiodorus.) Or read it without “for indeed”: wonders—how he acts and governs everything everywhere. Truth is in the Church, where it is believed that the Word was made flesh and that the Trinity is God from the beginning.

### Verse 7

“For who is like the Lord?” (Augustine.) It should be noted that the heavens and clouds are the same, namely, preachers. They are called heavens because of the splendor of truth; clouds, because they are misty on account of the mortality of the flesh and because they pass away. What is hidden in them will later shine clearly in the judgment.

“Among the sons.” Or among those above, or among human beings. Thus he should not be thought to be merely human: he is natural, whereas we are adopted; he is begotten, whereas we are created; he is begotten from eternity, whereas we were made in time; he is unique, whereas we are many.

### Verse 8

“Above all.” (The same.) Above angels or human beings, who are his unequal attendants and draw near to him by his gift.

### Verse 9

“To you.” (The same.) You who made all things, etc., up to: being tempted beyond what a human being can bear.

### Verse 11

“The wounded.” He was humbled by losing those whom he held; he was wounded when the heart in which he was proud was struck.

“The proud one.” (Augustine.) Namely, the dragon, which was made in the sea for him to mock. Through the humble Christ, in whom others are humble, the dragon is humbled. Christ humbled himself in order to humble the proud one. For the proud one held the proud; the devil is wounded when Christ is wounded, though he is not yet entirely dead.

“Enemies.” The aerial powers, or the Jews scattered throughout the world; or, from among human beings, he took some as spoils of the devil and left others, permitting them to follow him.

### Verse 12

“The heavens are yours, and yours is the earth, the world,” etc. (The same.) He triumphed over the devil in heaven because heaven is his; on earth, over Judea, because the earth is his. Why, then, did they grow proud in what belonged to another?

“You founded.” Why, then, do they rise up against him whose is the circuit of the world and all the creatures in it?

### Verse 13

“The north.” The devil.

“You created the sea.” The world. Foolishly, then, they rise up against him by whom they were created.

“Tabor and Hermon in your name.” (Augustine.) They are mountains of Syria; through them the nations are signified, the whole being represented by a part through synecdoche.

“They will rejoice.” Allegorically, when Christ comes. Tabor signifies the Jews, to whom the first light came; Hermon signifies the nations, which had previously been accursed. “They will rejoice in your name,” joined together in the cornerstone where the two walls meet.

(Augustine.) “Tabor”: light coming from the highest light. When it comes, he who held us in his error—that is, the devil—is made accursed (*anathema*). This means: it has been given by you that we may be enlightened and pronounce a curse upon the devil.

### Verse 15

“The preparation of your throne.” (Cassiodorus.) God’s throne is eternal, but it will appear prepared in the judgment, when he is seen judging justly. Or, by distinguishing human beings and holding to what is just, people now prepare themselves as a throne for the Lord.

“Mercy and truth will go before your face.” This is from the likeness of a forerunner who prepares lodging for the Lord.

### Verse 16

“Blessed is the people who know,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) The one who knows is the person who places his joy not in his own power but in the Lord’s, or who understands in his heart what he sings with his mouth. Hence the following reward: “In the light,” that is, in contemplation of the Trinity, they will persevere.

“Jubilation.” Jubilation is a joy that cannot be explained in words, yet cannot be entirely silenced.

“O Lord, they will walk in the light of your face, and in your name they will rejoice.” (Cassiodorus.) He commends the grace from which jubilation arises.

(Augustine.) Or: in your good pleasure, that is, in Christ. Therefore in him, because he assumed our flesh, in whom all hope resides.

### Verse 20

“Then you spoke in a vision.” (Cassiodorus.) A *diapsalma*. Thirdly, the Father’s promises concerning Christ. The preceding praise is not doubtful, since paternal authority confirms it.

(Cassiodorus.)

(Augustine.) “Then”—when you established the covenant, or when you said these things to me. Then you spoke to the saints, the remaining prophets, in a vision. They did not speak in ignorance, as Montanus and certain other heretics claimed.

### Verse 21

“I have anointed him with my holy oil—David my servant.” (Augustine.) Strong in hand, obedient as a servant; therefore I placed my help in him.

### Verse 23

“The enemy shall not prevail against him.” (The same.) The devil. Hence: “The prince of this world is coming, and he has nothing in me” (John 14).

“The son of iniquity shall not add to harm him.” Judas will not add—he will not bring his will to effect.

### Verse 24

“From his face, his enemies.” (Augustine.) When his face looks upon sinners, they are separated from their crimes, which have no place in his presence.

### Verse 25

“And my truth and my mercy are with him, and in my name his horn will be exalted.” (The same.) Mercy and truth are often commended to us, etc., up to: where these things meet one another for him.

### Verse 31

“But if they abandon.” I promise these things not only concerning those who persist but also concerning those who fall.

### Verse 33

“With a rod.” Who, then, is the son? etc., up to: “And with scourges,” etc.

“I will not take away.” (Augustine.) He himself does not remove mercy from the one who is indeed a Christian. But if a person is so wicked that he flees when the father approaches, he alienates himself; it is not the father who casts him away.

### Verse 35

“Nor will I profane.” The promise would be profaned if it were left unfulfilled. Does nothing from that net enter the vessels because of the bad fish? Certainly the good fish will be put there—that is, those whom he predestined.

### Verse 36

“Once I have sworn.” (Cassiodorus.) A human being swears frequently; God swears once, because he does not change.

“In my holy one.” In the human being Christ, in whom what I swore was to be fulfilled; or David, that is, Christ, through holiness.

“Seed”—Christians.

### Verse 38

“Like the sun in his sight.” (Augustine.) According to the soul, etc., up to: in heaven, that is, Christ.

“But you have rejected.” (Cassiodorus.) A *diapsalma*. Fourthly, he sets adversities against the promises mentioned above, lest they be thought to be fulfilled in anyone other than Christ in the future.

“But you have rejected.” As though saying: These good things are for Christians, but not for the Jews, who deprived themselves of the promise. This is the meaning: You rejected your Christ—that is, David, the Anointed—from the kingdom because of the sin he committed against Uriah concerning Bathsheba; and you despised or rejected him because he suffered many unworthy things. You delayed the covenant—the promises made to the Jews—which were extended to the nations.

(Augustine.) “But you.” Or all these things concern Christ and the Church: you rejected your Christ for the gallows and gave him over to contempt. Or you delayed him from glory for a time, or according to his members.

### Verse 40

“The covenant.” The promise appears overturned, and the saints are regarded as profane.

“You destroyed his fences”—the prelates—when they were killed.

“And you made his stronghold a terror.” Those who strengthened others by teaching are now objects of fear while they are afflicted, and some have already been carried away by passersby along the road, which is Christ.

### Verse 44

“You turned away the help of his sword.” That is, preaching. You did not assist him in battle, but gave him over to sufferings.

“You destroyed him from amendment,” etc.—that is, certain people of the world fell away and were brought down to the earth.

“You diminished him,” as it is thought, when they were quickly taken from life.

(Augustine.) Why did God promise those things, etc., up to: so that this promise might be awaited in others.

### Verse 45

“You destroyed him.” All these things came upon the Jews, yet Christ was not taken away from them, nor was the eternal kingdom; rather, it was delayed.

“You struck his throne to the ground.” That is, their kingdom was destroyed throughout the earth, because there is now no ruler from among them.

### Verse 46

“You diminished.” Their kingdom would have endured for a long time if they had remained under God.

“You drenched him with confusion.” Because he bears the disgrace of unbelief.

“You diminished.” (Augustine.) They thought they would reign forever, but you shortened the days of their kingdom so that it would not endure according to their expectation.

### Verse 47

“How long, O Lord?” (Cassiodorus.) A *diapsalma*. Fifthly: behold in whom the promises were fulfilled—in the offspring of David, who lives and rescues his soul, that is, in Christ.

(Augustine.) But how long will you not raise Christ? What substance is there that is anything except through him? “Who is the man who lives and will not see death?” No one.

Here he now asks that help be given to the human being, or specifically to the Jews.

### Verse 48

“Remember what my substance is.” (The same.) David says this with his flesh situated among the Jews, but with his hope in Christ. What is my substance? Even if the Jews fail, my substance does not fail; the root does not perish altogether, from which Mary will come, and from her the seed that was promised.

For from that people came the virgin Mary; from the virgin Mary came Christ’s flesh; and that flesh is not sinful but cleanses sins.

“For [is it] in vain?” All the sons of human beings have gone into vanity, yet you did not establish them in vain. From where, then, do you cleanse them of vanity? Through the seed in which my substance is found. Concerning this he adds: “Who is the man?”

### Verse 49

“Who is the man?” (The same.) This applies to no one except Christ. For even if he finds people rising again and they will no longer see death, they themselves will not rescue their souls from the lower realm; rather, he will do so who is able to lay down his soul and take it up again, and no one will take it from him.

(Cassiodorus.) Or understood in this way: no one will live or rescue his soul. Since this is so, where are the mercies? He now asks that the promises David made be fulfilled.

### Verse 50

“Where are your mercies?” (The same.) A *diapsalma*. Sixthly, the promises are also fulfilled in the members—not temporally but spiritually. He speaks in the person of the Church.

### Verse 51

“Remember, O Lord.” (Augustine.) So that you may repay; he seems to have forgotten while he delays.

“The reproach of your servants.” (Cassiodorus.) Inflicted upon the servants by many nations.

(Augustine.) “Which I bore”—that is, endured.

“In my bosom,” in the secrecy of the mind, because he did not dare to speak openly.

### Verse 53

“Blessed.” (Cassiodorus.) In opposition to the curses of the nations.

(Augustine.) “Blessed.” An exclamation arising from the vision of Christ’s glory.

## Psalm 89

### Verse 1

“A prayer of Moses.” (Augustine.) When the old life and the new, etc., up to: and he sees the wonders of God’s law.

(Cassiodorus and Remigius.) This psalm treats of the failing of the human race, which will be removed through Christ.

“O Lord, our refuge.” (Cassiodorus.) First, he presents the eternal refuge to the human being in time.

### Psalm 89

**Verse 2 — “Before the mountains.”** Lest it seem that he did not exist before he became our refuge, he adds “before.” “Mountains,” “earth.” (AUG.) Behold, every rational creature is distinguished by this difference: by the name “mountains,” the exaltation of the angels; by the name “earth,” the lowliness of human beings. Therefore he has not inappropriately divided the words in this way, saying that the mountains—that is, the angels—were made, and that the earth—that is, human beings—was formed. “They were made” or “it was formed.” “To be formed,” or fashioned, is ordinarily said with reference to bodies; “to be made,” of creation from nothing. “From age to age.” He would more aptly have said … up to … but here “age” is used for eternity. “From age to age.” Behold, that eternity is our refuge … up to “Do not turn away, for a thousand years.” “You are.” He says this most fittingly, because he is immutable. He does not say “you will be” or “you were,” since God’s immutable essence knows neither past nor future. Hence it is said: “I am who I am.” And: “He who is has sent me to you.” And: “But you are the same, and your years will not fail.”

**Verse 3 — “Do not turn away.”** (CASS.) Secondly, he explains the weakness of humanity, for which he asks assistance. “Into lowliness,” that is, earthly desire … up to the one who taught us to seek heavenly things.

**Verse 4 — “Yesterday’s day.”** (AUG.) He does not say, “at least as tomorrow’s day” … up to … in anxiety and trembling, and as though it were nothing.

**Verse 6 — “In the morning like grass.”** (AUG., CASS.) It changes from the condition of night.

“By evening let it fall.” Cut down or broken off at the end. (CASS.) “In the morning like grass.” I said that the years are reckoned … up to … youth, which blooms and passes away.

[Col. 0997A] “By evening.” Old age, when human strength grows cold. Or: “In the morning like grass.” The comparison is apt: just as grass changes from the condition it has during the night into a worse condition when the sun has risen in the morning, so a human being is changed for the worse.

**Verse 7 — “We have failed in your anger, and in your fury we have been troubled.”** (AUG.) We have been made mortal and subject to suffering, yet we fear that this will end in death; hence what follows: “And in your fury we have been troubled.” “The age.” Our corrupt life. Or “the age” means our descendants. “In the illumination of your face.” (CASS.) Those things are covered which receive pardon; those which are punished are illuminated.

**Verse 9 — “For all our days.”** (AUG.) Our knowledge has failed, our understanding having been darkened through sin; or, the time of life has been shortened and has almost vanished, because the days of our life have been reduced to fewness. “Our years are like …” (CASS., AUG.) The misery and brevity of this life are expressed here through the likeness of a spider, which weaves empty webs in order deceitfully to catch flies. Hence, “like a spider,” that is, we were laboring in corruptible things and weaving emptiness. (CASS.) Life was shortened through God’s anger, because people sinned in presuming upon a longer life. “And we ourselves have failed in your anger.” (AUG.) That is, our being has failed through hardships. “They will meditate … years”: they will not accomplish anything, because they pass away without usefulness. Or “they will meditate” is passive, that is, our years will be reckoned as a spider’s web—as empty and useless.

**Verse 10 — “Seventy.”** (ID.) Seventy signifies the desire for earthly things, which are enacted in seven days; eighty, if virtues are pursued, signifies seeking eternity. “Years.” Or “years,” according to another reading.

[Col. 0997C] In this span of time those are said to be long-lived who even up to eighty years seem to retain some strength. “Eighty.” For even before eighty years some are infirm … up to those awaiting the redemption of the body. “Mildness.” If it is God’s, it is clemency; if it is ours, it is taming. For by his clemency he himself is gentle; by taming us he makes us gentle, and thus we are corrected.

**Verse 11 — “Who knows …”** (ID.) Human anger has the power to kill the body and do nothing more. God both punishes here and afterward sends one to Gehenna; and his greater anger is understood by few.

**Verse 12 — “Make your right hand known in this way.”** (CASS.) Thirdly, he prays and affirms deliverance. (AUG.) “Your right hand.” He made Christ known in this way … up to [Col. 0997D] … so that he may place him at his right hand.

“And instruct those learned in heart in wisdom.” Or, “those fettered in heart.” The meaning is the same, because those who are instructed in wisdom put the foot of their mind into God’s fetters, so that they may not stray from his way. God made such people known in the New Testament, so that for the sake of faith they would disdain everything that is considered great in the Old Testament and seek eternal death. Reflecting on this, he says concerning those who suffer many things from the age for the sake of eternal things.

**Verse 13 — “Turn back.”** As though his face had been turned away from those afflicted. “How long?” Elsewhere, “for a little while.” (CASS.) Not completely; this is more beneficial, if some affliction always admonishes us.

**Verse 14 — “In the morning we were filled with your mercy, [Col. 0998A] and we rejoiced.”** (AUG., CASS.) Now is the night, in which we hunger; then we shall be satisfied by your face, whence: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.” And elsewhere: “In the morning I shall stand before you, and I shall see.” But now we have rejoiced because of it, and amid evil days, in which we say: “Look upon your servants.”

**Verse 16 — “Look upon your servants.”** What God does in himself, the Prophet prays that it may be done for his people. He prays, namely, that he spare the Jews who are sinning, if not because of their merits, at least because of the works that he has accomplished in them.

“And direct their children.” As though he were saying: Even if they themselves have been scattered through their iniquities, may their children at the end be corrected in faith, although by themselves they are perverse and incapable of conversion.

**Verse 17 — “May the splendor of the Lord our God be upon us, [Col. 0998B] and work.”** (HIER., CASS.) May the image of God, restoring the mind, be impressed upon it. Or the splendor of God is upon us when we are adorned with the imprint of the cross and carry the banner of triumph upon our forehead. (CASS.) For the image is threefold … up to … “may I remember you, understand you, and love you.”

### Psalm 90

**Verse 1 — “A song of praise.”** Praise can also be human; but this is the praise of a song, because it is divine alone. For this psalm is a hymn against demons. Thus the Prophet says concerning every saint: “He who dwells in the help …”

(CASS.) He shows the temptations of the devil overcome by Christ through humility, and by his own people who remain in God’s help, so that we too may learn through him to overcome temptations. For he is the door through which, if anyone enters, “he will go in and out, and will find pasture.”

(AUG.) Christ is the door. To enter through him is to imitate him—not in divinity, power, and miracles, but in that by which he was made for us, namely humility, to which he calls us, saying: “Learn from me, because I am gentle and humble of heart.” Concerning this psalm the devil tempted Christ. Christ’s temptation, however, is our instruction; by following him, we conquer through him.

“He who dwells.” (CASS.) First he describes one who trusts in God alone, completely surrounded by God’s protection. “He who dwells,” that is, he who always places his entire hope not in himself but in God, will be protected by God in every way. Note the correspondence of the words: just as he always dwells, so also he will always remain. The first affirms that he dwells; the second promises that he will be protected.

“He will remain in the protection of the God of heaven.” That is, so that he may not turn aside to the right or to the left, as was commanded in the Old Testament to the children of Israel: that they should walk on the royal road, turning neither to the right nor to the left. The royal road is the way of Christ our king, who ran the course of the world in such a way that he was neither enticed by prosperity nor broken by adversity.

**Verse 2 — “My God.”** (CASS.) Lest you think that, after receiving him and finding refuge, nothing more should be requested, he adds: “I will hope in him,” so that he may never presume upon himself. If Adam had done this, he would have stood well.

**Verse 3 — “From the snare.”** (ID.) Temptation comes either through deeds, which are here called a snare, or through words, which are here called “a harsh word.” Although it may seem slight, it is nevertheless serious to be tempted through a word. The snare is the cunning of spiritual or bodily enemies; the harsh word is every utterance that moves one away from the divine rules. (AUG.) “From the snare of the hunters”: the demons, who do not set their snares on Christ’s road but around it, to the right or left. Some fall into them through a harsh word—for example, those who refuse to belong to Christ because of people insulting the Christian name, and those who fear human slander and therefore cease from God’s way.

**Verse 4 — “With his shoulders.”** (AUG., CASS.) He promises God’s benefits to the one who hopes. The shoulders are the works of miracles, by which God’s power is displayed as upon shoulders. The feathers are the admonitions of the Prophets, which carry people toward heaven.

[Col. 0999B] “He will overshadow.” So that neither the sun of divinity nor the moon of humanity may burn you. “Protection is in his feathers.” “With his shoulders.” Elsewhere: “Between his shoulders.” (AUG.) That is, he places you before his breast … up to … so that we may hope beneath his wings.

**Verse 5 — “Truth.”** (ID.) It belongs to God, who does not regard persons and does not mix those who hope in themselves with those who hope in God, but distinguishes the humble from the proud. (CASS.) Or “truth” is the incarnation of Christ, whence: “Truth has arisen from the earth” (Psalm 84). It both overshadows with its shoulders and defends with a shield. Just as he has noted kinds of protection, so also he notes kinds of danger, so that deliverance may be more welcome.

“From the fear of the night.” From the likeness of danger, from which fear alone arises. “From the fear of the night.” (AUG.) The one who sins in ignorance … up to … “A thousand will fall at your side.”

**Verse 7 — “They will fall at your side.”** (CASS.) Secondly, he says that the head of the one who trusts in God—that is, Christ, raised up in heaven—can be touched by no one; and that he also protects his offspring on earth. But presumptuous people fall away from him. Behold the certainty of the protection of the one who trusts in God through Christ. “At your side.” God’s side is the crown of the righteous, who will judge with him; hence it is said: “Send from your side,” that is, those who deliberate with you. Christ’s side, therefore, is the Apostles and their imitators, to whom he promised: “You will sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). The twelve thrones signify the perfection of the tribunal, on which all who abandoned everything and followed Christ will sit.

[Col. 0999D] **Verse 8 — “Nevertheless.”** (CASS., AUG.) Although, with your permission, the impious persecute your people, they will not do so with impunity. With your eyes you will consider the evil they desired, not the good that is done through their ignorance; this will be repaid to them. The holy person, who possesses the eyes of faith, sees them now exalted and thundering, and at the end striking like lightning. He said this so that the weak might not be shaken. (CASS.) “Nevertheless, with your eyes.” Even if those who fall try you with harsh things, nevertheless … Or, even if the demon does not approach—which occurs through the wicked—still you will consider not what they do but what they intend.

**Verse 9 — “For you are.”** (AUG.) The one Christ is both head and body. He speaks of him now as head, now as body, without changing the person. Therefore observe carefully where he is speaking of Christ according to the head and where according to the members. “The Most High.” God’s refuge is on high, very much hidden, so that one may flee from the coming wrath. Many make God’s refuge for themselves in this way, fleeing to it from temporal evils. “You have placed the Most High as your refuge,” that is, by rising again and ascending, you have made the refuge high, so that I may now hope to follow where you have gone before.

**Verse 10 —** (ID.) “The tabernacle of God is flesh” … up to … this is rightly understood of Christ.

**Verse 11 — “For he will command his angels.”** The Tempter said this to the Lord when he tempted him, presenting it while doubting his divinity. Christ was tempted for our sake, so that in him we too might learn to conquer the Tempter.

(AUG.) So also he wished to be baptized by a servant, not from personal necessity but for human benefit, so that we would not disdain being baptized by fellow servants.

**Verse 12 — “They will carry you in their hands.”** (ID.) Christ was carried into heaven by the hands of angels … up to … the one who cannot be conquered.

**Verse 13 — “Upon the asp.”** After human weakness, divine power is displayed, which commands such beings. He is speaking of Christ according to the members. “And you will trample.” (AUG.) The Church tramples the serpent because it guards against his cunning. “The lion.” He openly rages against the martyrs.

The dragon lies in wait through heretics, to corrupt the virgin of Christ; hence the Apostle says: “I betrothed you to one man, to present a pure virgin to Christ” (2 Corinthians 11).

**Verse 14 — “Because he hoped in me.”** (AUG.) Thirdly, these are God’s words by which he consoles the Church, promising her protection here and rewards in the future. (CASS.) He commands the angels concerning you, saying: “Because he hoped in me.” The certainty of the promise comes through God’s promise.

**Verse 15 — “He will cry to me.”** (AUG.) One must not fear in tribulation … up to … let us labor all the more at that time to resist.

### Psalm 91

**Verse 1 — “A psalm of a song.”** (AUG.) Because of the weariness of minds … up to … seeking the glory of God, not your own.

**Verse 2 — “It is good to give thanks.”** (CASS.) First, he explains how the undisturbed person keeps the Sabbath of the mind, perceiving that everything is rightly done by God—a truth the fool does not know. (AUG.) Present goods, given to us by God, are consolation; when they are absent, their absence is justice. God both consoles and corrects us; in both, therefore, let us be grateful to him, saying: “It is good to give thanks,” and so forth.

**Verse 4 — “Upon the ten-stringed instrument.”** (ID.) The one who sings praises is the person who does good with gladness. If it is done with sadness, he himself is not acting; he carries the psaltery but does not sing upon it. “Upon the ten-stringed instrument.” If you speak well only, there is a song without a harp; if you act but do not speak, there is a harp without a song. Therefore speak well and do good.

**Verse 5 — “For you have delighted me.”** (ID.) Hence the Apostle says: “We are his workmanship,” and so forth … up to … “How greatly they have been magnified.” “In your creation.” (CASS., HIER.) Both in the beauty of the world’s structure itself and in its obedience, arrangement, causes, effects, and the works of his hands that I use or admire.

[Col. 1001A] **Verse 6 — “How greatly they have been magnified.”** (CASS., HIER.) In substance, form, power, and all the rest. Your thoughts are exceedingly deep, by which you made and govern such things.

**Verse 7 — “The foolish man,” and so forth.** (CASS.) You delighted me in your works, but the foolish man will not know these things; nor will the stupid person understand—who, even if he knows, does not guard himself—the things he has said or will say afterward. The highest kind of knowledge is to know that God accomplishes such great things as human understanding cannot grasp.

The foolish person is one empty of heavenly wisdom and full of human cunning, who does not know God’s works because he thinks everything happens by chance. The stupid person is brutish, one who knows nothing, not even worldly matters.

**Verse 8 — “When the wicked have sprung up.”** (CASS.) He asserts that the wicked will perish … up to … the Jews thought that you would die according to the common lot.

**Verse 9 — “But you, Most High.”** (AUG.) You wait from above, from eternity … up to … not long-suffering, but eternal, as the word indicates.

**Verse 11 — “And he will be exalted.”** (ID.) Even though they themselves will perish … up to … all heresies will perish.

**Verse 12 — “And he looked down.”** (ID.) Therefore even now he has looked down, and he will hear from the truth within. “And from those who rise up.” (CASS.) Or: “those who rise up against me”; he will hear the wicked at the last judgment, when they reproach themselves, saying: “What did pride and riches profit us?” (Wisdom 5.) “My ear.” (AUG.) The ear of the one standing at the right hand will hear in the future: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire.” The righteous will not fear this evil hearing. Behold what is said to these people: “What then of the righteous?” (Matthew 25.)

**Verse 13 — “The righteous will flourish like the palm.”** The wicked are like grass. The righteous is like a palm because of its height, because its root is rough while its crown is beautiful at the top and end, and because it bears fruit slowly. So also labor makes the righteous person rough here, while the beauty of immortality will crown him above; and, as though slowly, after long labors he will receive the reward of his works. “The righteous like a palm.” (CASS.) The third part: he says that the righteous flourish, so that they may rejoice devoutly in this promise. “Like a cedar.” (AUG.) The palm and cedar are trees that do not wither in summer, unlike grass.

**Verse 14 — “In the courts of the house.”** (CASS.) The court is the beginning of the dwelling; the house is the interior. Therefore they will flourish in the courts, that is, at the very beginning of the resurrection, when they hear: “Come, blessed of my Father” (Matthew 25).

**Verse 15 — “They will still multiply.”** (ID.) The Church will begin to be most fruitful when it has been brought to the end of the age; then the number of the blessed will quickly be completed through the sufferings of the elect. Here “old age” is understood differently from above.

**Verse 16 — “They will proclaim.”** (ID.) Here—or, when they receive their reward—they will proclaim that the righteous one fulfills his promises to his own. “And there is no iniquity in him.” (AUG.) He permits those whom he will not adorn there to suffer for his sake. The one who rewards is upright, not unjust so as to defraud them of their reward, but kind so as to increase it.

### Psalm 92

“On the day …” (AUG.) On the day before the Sabbath … up to … which signifies the sixth day.

**Verse 1 — “The Lord has reigned,” and so forth.** (CASS.) Here Christ’s praise is sung … up to … “the praise of the house,” where it says, “Your house.” “Clothed in beauty.” (AUG.) Christ is beautiful in these things … up to … the world that will not be shaken. “He put on beauty.” (CASS.) That is, beauty … up to … from the incarnation, when he taught human beings.

“He girded himself.” He does not say “he girded,” “he tucked up,” or “he equipped himself,” but “he girded himself beforehand.” We are girded when we are about to work, equipped when we are about to fight, tucked up when we are about to go, and girded beforehand when we are about to serve. (AUG.) Girding therefore signifies works … up to … because the one who conquers anger is better than the one who captures a city. “He girded himself beforehand.” (CASS.) Either ascending with the company of angels or through the vigor of working.

“For he established.” (AUG.) He put on beauty and strength in order to establish the earth; hence he adds: “For he established.”

**Verse 2 — “From that time.”** (ID.) Or “from that one”; he designates the time of grace. Perhaps he understands this as beginning from the day before the Sabbath, that is, the sixth period of this world, when the Lord came. But lest you think that he began then, when he came born into the world, he adds: “From eternity you are.”

**Verse 3 — “The rivers have raised their voice.”** (AUG.) Because the disciples, hearing … up to … of the age, which began to rage or persecute. “The rivers have raised their waves,” and so forth. (CASS.) This is lacking in other copies … up to … who does all good things, he adds: “The Lord is wonderful on high.”

**Verse 5 — “Your testimonies.”** (AUG.) Because the rising of the sea is wondrous … up to … and crowns from prophecy. (CASS.) “Your testimonies.” Or in this way … up to … although expressed in brief words, it contains everything.

### Psalm 93

**“A psalm of David.”** (AUG.) For the weak, who also murmur in their hearts … up to … teaching patience throughout. “On the fourth day of the week,” on which day God made the luminaries … up to … hence he urges us to patience.

**Verse 1 — “God, Lord of vengeance.”** Do not hasten to punish another if he has injured you, just as you would not wish to be punished at another’s request when you had injured him. And if he sins against you, do not sin more gravely by blaspheming God, nor desire vengeance; if it comes, perhaps it will find you first.

“He acted freely.” (AUG.) At the time of weakness, when he taught in the temple as one having authority, because neither his truth nor his power can be opposed. And because it was so then, now: “Be exalted,” because … “How long, O sinners?”

**Verse 4 — “They will speak out.”** (CASS.) He explains their sins … up to … he proceeds by exaggeration. “All who work iniquity will speak.” “They will speak out”; according to others, they will have something to answer. (AUG.) That is, they have something that they can answer … up to … the wicked speak, saying that God does not care about these things.

**Verse 6 — “The widow and the stranger.”** (CASS.) God protects these people … up to … without a father, the devil, and without a mother, desire.

**Verse 7 — “Nor will he understand.”** (AUG.) As though he were saying: He will not pay attention to these things; he neglects them and does not attend in order to see. “God does not care what I do.”

**Verse 8 — “Understand.”** (CASS.) The second part, against the blasphemers … up to … he reveals his counsel, unknown to the wicked, to his friends. “Fools.” Those who openly blaspheme, saying that God does not see. Or in this way: “You senseless people,” that is, those who are ignorant, understand—you who, by living well, are already among the people, that is, in the number of the good. “And you fools,” that is, imprudent people: even if you know, acquire wisdom at last.

**Verse 10 — “He who corrects the nations.”** (AUG.) Every day, because of original sin—is he not also going to accuse them for the things mentioned above? Or, “he who instructs.” For the sake of this instruction God sent his Son … up to … hence the Apostle says: “We shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive his due” (Romans 14), and so forth.

**Verse 11 — “The Lord knows.”** (ID.) You, however, do not know God’s thoughts, because they are just. But once they have been made friends, God reveals his counsel to them: why he spares the wicked. “For they are vain.” The thoughts of such people are vain. They themselves cannot know this by their own power, but the Lord knows that they are vain.

**Verse 12 — “Blessed is the man.”** (CASS.) These are the vain ones … up to … all will know God; the heavens will be folded up like a book. “And from your law,” and so forth. (AUG.) Learn patience from the law. Until the pit is dug, it is not yours to know how or why it is being dug for him.

**Verse 13 — “Until,” and so forth.** (AUG.) The prosperity of the wicked is a pit; the labor of the good is the Father’s scourge. Prosperity is a pit because, when God spares someone through impunity, the person becomes proud; and when he thinks himself exalted, he falls. “Let the pit be dug.” Behold God’s counsel: he spares the wicked so that a pit may be dug for them. It is still being dug, yet you already want to bury him; you are rushing too quickly. The pit belongs to the sinner … not to every sinner, but to the proud … up to … give thanks to the one from whom you have received what you possess, and do not despise another.

**Verse 16 — “Who will rise up?”** (CASS.) The third part, in which he says that there is agitation for the righteous, and the waves of the age—that is, evils caused by the wicked—so that, being pierced, they may cry out to God, nothing else may please them, and deliverance may then become more welcome. (AUG.) “Who will rise up?” As though he were saying … up to … but from where shall I conquer? “Unless the Lord.” He will stand with me, and so forth. (CASS.) He is patient in the battle line; but because the one who endures force is the conqueror, the one who strikes loses.

**Verse 17 — “Unless the Lord.”** (CASS.) He could have been deceived by vain persuasions unless the Lord had delivered him.

**Verse 18 — “He was helping me.”** Just as the Lord delivered Peter when he was walking upon the water, so that he would not sink. Peter had said to the Lord: “Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you” (Matthew 26).

(AUG.) So that Christ, by his own power … up to … hence he adds: “Your consolations have gladdened my soul.”

[Col. 1003D] **Verse 19 — “In my heart.”** (ID.) He signifies salutary thoughts, so that, when he considered eternal recompenses, he might despise temporal evils.

**Verse 20 — “Will the seat of iniquity cling to you?”** (ID.) No unrighteous person sits with you. Since they have nothing in common with you, why then are they made? So that you may prick them through these things, and, being pierced, they may cry out to you, and finally they may perish. This is shown in the three verses that follow. “The seat of iniquity.” (CASS.) It is possession of the world with love for it, which does not cling to God, who commands his people to flee such things. “You who fashion.” (AUG.) From this I understand that the unrighteous person does not cling to you … up to … and that pain itself is a command; but another pain is shapeless.

“Pain,” that is, a command arising from pain or labor … up to … and then the wave rises, in which he is stirred up.

**Verse 22 — “And the Lord became my refuge, and my God the help of my hope.”** (ID.) Why? Because if you had not been endangered, you would not have sought refuge. You are pierced by pain so that you may seek a remedy; worldly hope withdraws, and God’s hope comes.

### Psalm 94

“Praise.” (CAS.) Devotion. Song signifies gladness.

**Verse 1 — “Come, let us rejoice.”** (THEOD.) King Josiah was exceedingly devout … up to … but the psalm was composed from the person of Josiah and the priests of God. (CASS.) Concerning the time of grace, when one enters into rest, the Prophet describes God’s praises. First he invites the Jews, whom he foresaw as capable of resisting Christ.

**Verse 2 — “His face,” and so forth.** (AUG., CASS.) The presence of the Judge who is to come, so that there may then be nothing in us requiring examination. “In confession.” (AUG.) Praising him and accusing ourselves … up to … concerning which praise the psalm speaks. “Let us rejoice in psalms.” May we experience in jubilation what we say or do in the psalms.

**Verse 3 — “Above all gods.”** Or rather, he calls human beings gods, over whom he is king, not demons.

**Verse 4 — “For in his hand,” and so forth.** (CASS.) After proclaiming the Lord’s greatness, he comes to his clemency.

**Verse 5 — “The sea.”** (AUG.) The world, whose waves God confines by a boundary, not permitting us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Corinthians 10). These waves also produce growth for us, God bringing this about; nor do the scandals harm you, since they receive their measure from God.

**Verse 6 — “Come, let us worship.”** (CASS.) At first he called the untrained to rejoicing; now, after showing God’s glory, he calls them to repentance, which is more difficult. “Let us weep.” (AUG.) If perhaps you are troubled by sins that have made you far away, weep. A tear extinguishes the flame of sin that burns in the conscience. “Who made us.” Behold great confidence: you can depart from yourself, but you cannot restore yourself; the one who restores you is the one who made you.

**Verse 7 — “And we are the people,” and so forth.** (AUG.) The order of the words has been elegantly changed. He did not say “the sheep of his pasture and the people of his hand,” so that you would understand the same persons to be both sheep and people: sheep of his hand, not sheep whom he sees from afar, because they exist; and sheep whom we did not make, but whom he himself made us by his grace.

**Verse 8 — “Today, if you hear his voice,” and so forth.** (CASS.) We are the people and the sheep. But a condition is set before all these things: if you hear his voice. He adds what this voice is: “Today.” “Do not harden your hearts.” (ID.) Christ himself now warns them not to be hardened, lest what happened to their fathers happen to them.

**Verse 9 — “As in the provocation.”** (ID.) The majesty of Christ speaking … up to … the guilt of the parents is recalled so that vengeance may be feared.

**Verse 10 — “For forty years.”** (AUG.) By forty years he signifies all the ages … up to … as he himself says: “I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

### Psalm 95

[Col. 1005A]

“A psalm of David.” (CASS.) It is read in the Old Testament … up to … this psalm does not concern that active reality.

**Verse 1 — “Sing to the Lord.”** (ID.) In the preceding psalm he warned the Jews that, laying aside their hardness, they should believe in Christ. But because that hardness was to remain, he now warns all nations. The second psalm concerning both advents. First he speaks to those in authority, so that they themselves may sing and announce. “A new song.” (AUG.) Old desire sings … up to … whoever enters will be outside.

**Verse 2 — “To the Lord, and bless him.”** (HIER., CASS.) “To the Lord” is said three times, to distinguish the persons of the Trinity, because Christ’s praise is the honor of the Trinity. There is also a figure called epimone, that is, a frequent repetition of a statement, which intensifies it for praise or blame.

[Col. 1005B] **Verse 3 — “Announce.”** He speaks to those in authority: announce, because in this way the building of the house grows. “From day to day.” (CASS.) The Old and New Testaments are days that shine with the eternal sun. The former foretells; the latter declares what has happened. (HIER.) Thus he announces from day to day … up to … by which the feet of our affections are protected from the thorns of vices.

**Verse 4 — “Great is the Lord.”** (AUG.) He became little because you are little. Understand the great one, and you will be great in him.

**Verse 5 — “He made the heavens.”** (ID.) The Apostles and the angels. Thus, if he made the heavens and the angels, then he also made the Apostles, who command demons.

[Col. 1005C] **Verse 6 — “In his presence.”** For such people—namely, those who confess and are righteous—behold him, and are beheld by him. “Holiness and magnificence.” (AUG.) As though he were saying: Whoever wants to be magnificent and powerful, as the angels are, must first be holy; this comes from the one who sanctifies him. For you cannot be holy by yourself. Through the one who sanctifies him, therefore, a person becomes holy, and thus magnificent.

**Verse 7 — “Bring to the Lord, O families.”** (CASS.) The second part, in which he speaks to those subject to authority … up to … so that no one—native or foreigner—may be excluded. “Glory.” (ID.) Since a person conducts himself well, and God is glorified in him. “Honor.” When gratitude for good things is returned, whence: “No one was found to give glory to God except this foreigner.” “In the courts.” (ID.) The courts are the Prophets or Apostles, through whom one goes to the Lord; from the courts—that is, from the Prophets or Apostles—one comes into the court of the Catholic Church, where majesty is worshiped. (AUG.) Or: “Enter into the court,” that is, into the teaching of the Prophets and Apostles.

**Verse 9 — “Worship the Lord in his court,” and so forth.** That is, in the Catholic Church; or, through the courts, prophecy; through the court, the Gospel. “Let it be moved.” Having admonished everyone, he desires it to be moved. As though he were saying: Enter and worship, you good people. “But the earth,” and so forth: the whole earth. (CASS.) Not merely one part, lest anyone say: “Here is Christ,” or “There is Christ.” He adds: “For he corrected the world,” and so forth.

**Verse 10 — “Say among the nations.”** (ID.) That he has reigned, corrected, and judged. “He has reigned.” Another reading: “He has reigned from the wood” (Matthew 13). (AUG.) From the cross, by which a person crosses the sea and becomes a world that is not moved.

“Peoples in equity,” and so forth. Others add: “And nations in your anger.”

(CASS.) Therefore he will judge the peoples—that is, the good—in equity, but the nations—that is, the wicked—in his anger.

**Verse 12 — “Then they will rejoice.”** (CASS., HIERON.) Then, when he corrects … up to … because he has come—that is, he will come—to judge the earth. “Because he has come.” (AUG.) First he came in the Church, in the clouds—that is, in the Apostles—and filled the whole world. Hence: “From now on you will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds” (Matthew 26). Whoever believes in that coming will rejoice at the final coming.

**Verse 13 — “He will judge the world.”** (CASS.) He includes every human being generally, to be judged according to God’s equity. But he explains how they will be judged by saying, “the peoples in truth,” because at the separation there will be two peoples, to whom he will give the sentence of truth, so that some will go into life and others into punishments. (AUG.) By “the world” he means all the children of Adam … up to … the south.

### Psalm 96

“A psalm for David.” Literally, this touches upon what happened after Absalom’s death. Absalom was David’s wicked son, who, while alive, persecuted his father; after his death the land was restored to David, and he reigned in peace. But this psalm is not concerned with that event, but rather with what it signifies. (AUG.) David signifies Christ, whom the wicked sons—that is, the Jews—crucified and whose kingship they repudiated. But the land was restored to him when Judea, which had crucified him, believed; and the Apostles, who had wavered, were strengthened. Other sheep from the nations were also brought in.

Or the land was restored when his flesh rose again; after the resurrection, all the things sung here took place.

(AUG.) The Prophets, foreseeing these things in the Spirit, rejoiced … up to … for the honey of the divine promise tastes sweet to the palate of faith.

(CASS.) The fourth psalm concerning the first advent, by which the world was freed. First he describes the Lord’s virtues, shows that everything was restored to him, and rebukes idolaters.

**Verse 1 — “The Lord has reigned.”** (CASS.) Seeing that the world’s superstitions abounded before Christ’s resurrection, the Prophet responds: “The Lord has reigned.” (AUG.) Who else, then, should be worshiped? As though he were saying: No one. Hence:

“Let the earth rejoice.” What remains for idols? As though he were saying: Nothing.

“Islands.” The Churches of the whole world. “Many.” Not all, because of the assemblies of heretics.

(CASS.) From this he first describes what the Lord is like at his advent.

**Verse 2 — “Cloud and darkness.”** To the impious, who are blind, he is cloudy and dark, since he shines with no brightness for them; but to the good, there are justice and judgment. Those who have been corrected are his throne. Before his advent fire will go before him, because the impious, inflamed with anger by the preaching of the Prophets, plotted their murder; and they were kindled with indignation all around, because there were many persecutors while the preachers were few.

[Col. 1007A] **Verse 3 — “Fire will go before him,” and so forth.** (AUG.) As though he were saying: Those who have been corrected are God’s throne … up to … if they are evil, for destruction; if good, for restoration.

**Verse 4 — “Lightning flashes appeared.”** (ID.) The clouds took on the lowliness of human form, but wondrous radiance appeared in their words or deeds, and from this the earth was moved.

**Verse 5 — “They melted.”** (ID.) Even if the pagan does not believe at present, he has nevertheless been conquered.

**Verse 7 — “Let them be confounded.”** This has already happened. (AUG.) Idolatry has now ceased. “And let those who worship stones be ashamed,” because the stones are dead.

**Verse 8 — “Worship.”** (ID.) Therefore the worship of angels ceases; but they worship. Evil angels want to be worshiped, whereas good angels worship and do not permit themselves to be worshiped. Or at least, by this example, let idol worship cease.

[Col. 1007B] “She heard and rejoiced.” (CASS.) Secondly, after the restoration of the earth, there is complete rejoicing … up to … so that the brethren rejoiced over Cornelius, whom Peter baptized. “And they rejoiced.” (AUG.) The Apostles who were the brethren in Judea heard that the nations had received the word of God, and they rejoiced and glorified God.

**Verse 9 — “The earth … gods.”** (ID.) Understand by “earth” and “gods” sinners and the righteous. Or he signifies by earthly and heavenly beings that Christ rules over them.

**Verse 10 — “The Lord guards.”** (AUG.) If, once you have begun to hate the wicked person, persecutions follow, do not be afraid, because the Lord guards the souls of his saints. The final kind of persecution consists in taking them away.

### Psalm 97

[Col. 1007C] “A psalm of David.” (CASS.) The third psalm among those that concern both advents. In these there is a cause for hope through the mercy of the first advent, and for fear through the judgment of the second. Although these things are often repeated, they are nevertheless always new because of the varied description of the words and thoughts.

**Verse 1 — “Sing to the Lord.”** (CASS.) First he speaks of the manifestation of the saving right hand.

“He saved.” (AUG.) It is greater that he raised the whole world from eternal death than that he raised the dead. “For himself.” Many are saved bodily, but for themselves, not for him: they receive bodily health and then indulge themselves. But those who are inwardly healed through faith are healed for him, or save themselves.

**Verse 2 — “Salvation … righteousness.”** (AUG.) He who saves and justifies. “He revealed.” The Prophets foretold future things beneath a veil, but the veil was removed when truth arose from the earth.

[Col. 1007D] **Verse 3 — “Mercy and truth.”** (AUG.) Mercy is what he promised; truth follows it because he fulfilled what he promised. But to whom? To Israel—that is, to the one who now sees truth through faith and afterward will see it by sight.

**Verse 4.**—“All.” (The same.) Because Christ was not given only to some.

**Verse 5.**—“Shout for joy.” (Cassiodorus.) Secondly, he says that he must be praised and proclaimed in every way, because the Judge has come.

**Verse 6.**—“With trumpets of beaten metal and the voice of a horn.” (Augustine.) Those made by striking and drawing out bronze, etc., up to the point where the horn clings to the flesh and surpasses it. [Col. 1008A] (Jerome.) “With beaten-metal trumpets,” that is, silver ones, according to Jewish custom. Mystically, they are produced beneath the hammer of the whole earth, that is, beneath the devil. (Augustine.) Tribulation is the striking; progress is the drawing out. Such a trumpet was Job, from whom, as though a trumpet, there sounded forth the words: “The Lord has given, the Lord has taken away.”

**Verse 7.**—“Let the sea be moved.” (The same.) That is, let the sea of the law be sweetened by the wood of the cross placed in it. “And its fullness.” All the mysteries of the law, etc., up to “but the rivers,” etc. “The earth.” (Cassiodorus.) That is, every sinner.

### Psalm 98

[Col. 1008B]

**Verse 1.**—“A psalm of David.” (Augustine.) The prophet describes Christ the king, who gives good things, etc., up to: “but the veil was removed when truth sprang up from the earth and righteousness looked down from heaven” (Psalm 48). “The Lord has reigned.” (Cassiodorus.) Concerning Christ’s power and kingdom, so that he may be worshiped in the human being. He shows Christ reigning and—whoever may resist him—exalted above all; hence he urges submission to him. “Let the peoples be angry.” (Cassiodorus.) This is mockery. It may safely be granted that they be angry, because they will no longer be able to do harm. He says this by permitting, not by commanding. “He sits upon the cherubim.” (The same.) Nothing earthly can prevail against him, even though he himself was on earth, where he endured the anger of the people. “Cherubim.” (Augustine.) It is interpreted as “fullness of knowledge,” which is charity. The fullness of the knowledge of the law, which is the seat of God, will also be in you if you possess charity, against which the angry can do nothing. For what can earth do against heaven?

**Verse 2.**—“The Lord is in Zion.” (The same.) If you do not understand what “above the cherubim” means, observe this: he is great in Zion. Zion is the soul that contemplates God. “Great in Zion.” (Cassiodorus.) He explains who the Lord is: “Born in Zion.” “Great,” lest he be thought of as insignificant because of his suffering. Or, nevertheless, the Lord is great in the Zion of the Jews and above the peoples of the Gentiles.

**Verse 3.**—“Great.” (Augustine.) He was small when they were angry, that is, when he was defamed by a few; but now he has been spread throughout the whole earth. “Terrible.” (The same.) For although he is preached as crucified, he is coming as Judge and will not err in judgment. [Col. 1008D] “And the honor of the king.” (Cassiodorus.) He explains how they ought to confess him. The king’s honor is glorious proclamation; judgment requires discernment. He is not to be worshiped with a shallow inclination, but with firm deliberation, because it comes from him. Hence he adds: “You have prepared uprightness.” Or the king’s honor is the condemnation of the guilty, by which the king’s glory is increased.

**Verse 4.**—“In Jacob.” (Augustine.) Not only in the patriarch, but in the people whom he signifies. “You have done.” These are things which no other could have done.

**Verse 5.**—“Exalt.” (Cassiodorus.) The second section urges worship of him, because he was the God of their fathers. As though he were saying: Since he does these things for us, therefore “Exalt.”

“Footstool.” (Augustine.) Scripture says that the earth is the footstool of his feet, etc., up to the point where it says that the footstool is worshiped in whose honor it stands. “Of his feet.” (Cassiodorus.) The feet signify the unfailing stability of the Godhead. “Holy.” So that you may distinguish the body from the Godhead, although there is one person.

**Verse 6.**—“Moses.” (Cassiodorus.) A priest, because, even if he did not offer sacrifices, he presented the vows of the people and interceded for the people.

**Verse 7.**—“The pillar.” (Cassiodorus.) The strength and beauty of the house. He spoke in this form, which announced the Church or the flesh; but then he spoke in a cloud, whereas now he speaks openly through the Son: “He spoke to them from the cloud.” (The same.) Therefore he spoke to them then in the cloud, who now speaks openly to us in the footstool, that is, in the flesh he assumed. “His testimonies and commandments.” (The same.) A testimony is a signification established through certain signs of a preceding reality; hence it is often said in the law: “This shall be a testimony for you.” Commandments are such as the commandments of the law given through Moses. [Col. 1009B]

**Verse 8.**—“You were propitious toward them.” (Augustine.) This is said only with reference to sins: he is propitious by forgiving, and propitious also by punishing. Behold, although these men were so great, they nevertheless had some sin; hence he adds, “against all their inventions.”

“Punishing.” So that human pride might not steal upon them; hence: “A thorn in my flesh was given to me” (2 Corinthians 12). “Inventions.” Elsewhere, “affections.” (Augustine.) These were known only to God in their hearts. Hence, as a punishment, they had to suffer association with those among whom they lived, because through charity they grieved for their sins as though they were their own. For it was not, as many suppose, Moses’ punishment that he did not enter the land of promise into which even the wretched entered; rather, it was a figure showing that those who were under the law and unwilling to be under grace would not enter into rest.

### Psalm 99

**Verse 1.**—“A psalm of confession.” Confession is twofold: one is confession of praise, the other confession of sins. Confession of praise belongs to the perfect; confession of sins belongs to beginners. Hence in this psalm the prophet urges confession. (Cassiodorus.) This psalm teaches us both to praise God unceasingly and to lament our sins unceasingly, because one must neither despair in evil nor let the spirit be lifted up in good. First, he enjoins upon the perfect the principal kind of confession, namely praise.

“Shout for joy.” (Augustine.) If the voice shouts for joy outwardly, etc., up to the point where it says, “and in what order and how wondrously he made it.” “All the earth.” He urges praise. He does not exhort only one corner of the earth; but just as he knows that blessing has been sown everywhere, so he demands rejoicing from every side. “Serve with gladness.” (Augustine.) This service is not one of bitterness or indignation, but of happiness and freedom. Let charity therefore make you a servant, because truth has made you free. Hence the Lord says: “If you remain in my word, you will truly be my disciples; and you will know the truth, and the truth will set you free” (John 8).

“With gladness.” Because they have been freed—not murmuring as in the wilderness. Hence he adds the reward.

**Verse 2.**—“Enter into his presence.” It is a great thing to rejoice in the presence of so great a one. “Enter.” (Cassiodorus.) Secondly, he addresses those who are about to enter according to the second kind of confession; and there should be no doubt, because he is merciful.

### Psalm 100

**Verse 1.**—“A psalm for David himself.” (Cassiodorus.) This psalm contains the pattern of perfect holiness, just as the number one hundred is perfect.

“For David himself.” So that everything taught here may be applied to the virtues of Christ, and nothing to an earthly king. Here we are taught to desire good and reject evil, which is the perfect conduct of life.

“I shall sing of mercy and judgment.” (Cassiodorus.) Here Christ sings, and we sing in him. He first sets forth mercy and judgment. “I shall sing of mercy and judgment.” These two are joined in mutual association; in them he briefly includes all the works of God. This is also the reason given beforehand for why he behaves as he does, as he later states. (Augustine.) Let no one presume upon mercy for impunity, because judgment exists for him; and let no one who has been changed for the better fear judgment, because mercy precedes it. These are always together in him, but they are distinguished according to their effects through time: mercy is now, judgment in the future.

**Verse 2.**—“I shall sing psalms and understand.” (The same.) He grants this ability to sing psalms so that I may understand with the mind what is not apparent to the eyes, that is, believe that the Lord will come. This one desires him so greatly that he will come in the blameless way. (Cassiodorus.) Because he passed through the world without sin; or, I shall sing psalms and understand while existing in the blameless way, when, etc. Or, I shall sing psalms, I shall work cheerfully, and through this I shall understand. “When will you come to me?” At the second coming, or at each person’s death. Or, “when will you come to me?” in the flesh, at the first coming, because he came in the blameless way. “I shall walk.” (Cassiodorus.) Secondly, he explains what the blameless way is. (Augustine.) “I shall walk.” What is the blameless way? It begins from innocence and is brought to completion in it. There is no need for many words: “Be innocent,” and you have fulfilled righteousness. But a person harms in two ways: if he makes someone miserable, and if he abandons someone miserable. The innocent person harms neither himself nor another. (Cassiodorus.) “I shall walk.” As though he were saying: I did not seek transitory things, but I ran along the way of the world, existing in the midst of your house. Innocence can accomplish this: it can cause one to dwell in the midst of God’s house as an honorable example to others.

**Verse 3.**—“I did not set before myself.” (Cassiodorus.) He explains innocence in its parts. First, because he has nothing in common with the wicked, he says: “I did not set before myself,” up to “my eyes.” After that comes his association with the righteous, and the fact that he drives the devil’s deceptions from his heart, at “in the morning.” (Augustine.) “I did not set before myself.” As though he were saying: I walked in innocence—indeed, the whole Christ says this—because I did not set before myself, that is, I did not love, an unjust thing.

**Verse 4.**—“He did not cling.” (Cassiodorus.) He explains transgressions. “A crooked heart”: the person who transgresses in his heart. “The one who turns aside”: the heretic who dissents from Catholics. “The one who departs from the straight paths”: I did not acknowledge him, because although they are marked with the sacraments together with us, they are nevertheless not true members.

**Verse 5.**—“The proud.” (Augustine.) “And when Jesus was invited to a banquet,” etc., up to: “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness” (Matthew 8).

**Verse 6.**—“My eyes.” Here he treats the other part of innocence, namely, that he shares in the lot of the righteous. As though he were saying: You did not eat with such people; from where, then, did you feed? “Of the earth.” (Augustine.) Those dwelling on earth, where there are so many enticements, and therefore the crown is greater. Or (Cassiodorus), those who are throughout the whole world. “That they may sit with me.” (Augustine.) Let them remain with me in the truth of faith, or share with me in the eternal kingdom, or judge with me.

**Verse 7.**—“He shall not dwell in the midst of my house.” (Cassiodorus.) That is, in the Church. Even if he is tolerated for a time through the grace of correction, he does not prevail by merit and can accomplish nothing; he is not a grain in my people, but chaff. “He shall not dwell”: this applies especially to priests, that they should not live together with the wicked.

**Verse 8.**—“In the morning.” (Cassiodorus.) The third section, in which he shows what the end of the wicked is. Here Christ speaks. “In the morning.” After avoiding the wicked, the righteous person, having returned to himself, adds that in the morning he expelled the suggestions of demons from his heart, that is, at the beginning of temptation, when they begin to appear like the first light of dawn. “I was killing.” By prayer, by which they must be driven out lest they grow. “Sinners.” Demons, who make every fleshly person sin. “From the city of the Lord.” The soul of the righteous, from which the devil is scattered and removed. “All who work iniquity.” That is, the submissions or invasions of the devil.

(Augustine.) He has now enumerated that only the good adhered to him, etc., up to the point where this also applies to the righteous person, who foresees that it will happen and therefore conducts himself accordingly.

### Psalm 101

**Verse 1.**—“The prayer of the poor man.” (Augustine.) According to the form of a servant, etc., up to the point where he is called bridegroom on account of the head and bride on account of the body. Christ, poor in us, with us, and for us, prays here in the person of the penitent, who recognizes his humiliation and the cause of his humiliation, and asks to be freed from sins and restored to his former condition. He therefore urges us to consider our misery and to ask for God’s mercy.

**Verse 2.**—“Lord, hear my prayer.” (Cassiodorus.) The fifth psalm of penitence; the fourth that is called a prayer. The first section is an appeal seeking favor.

“And my cry.” The prayer has grown into a cry. “Let it come”: let not the clouds that belong to the wicked obstruct it. (The same.) An *epimone* through three verses, that is, a frequent repetition of the thought.

**Verse 4.**—“Because they have failed.” (Cassiodorus.) The second section, in which the prayer is tearful and in which the poverty and tribulation are explained. He now reveals why he cries out. “Because they have failed.” “My days have passed away like smoke.” (Augustine.) For when Adam was lifted up in pride, his days failed and the strength of his spirit was contracted. Misery can move a merciful judge. “My bones have dried up like a firebrand.” The strong are those whose frying-pan they are, those who are scandalized, etc., up to the point where a person is already being fried while fearing that he will burn.

**Verse 5.**—“I have been struck like grass, and my heart has dried up.” (The same.) He became mortal. Grass is green, but when struck it quickly feels the injury; so the flesh of human beings, while green under God’s law, withers when cut off from that law.
