**Verse 6.**—“From the voice of my groaning.” (Cassiodorus.) The nature of sinners is shown: when sin is desired, contemplation of God is absent. “My.” (Augustine.) Not those who groan over earthly things and not spiritual ones, etc., up to “to bear the weak.”

**Verse 7.**—“Like a pelican,” etc. (Augustine.) He sets down three birds and three places, etc., up to the point where he says that if he is not among human beings, he is outside, in the heights, saying this to those who sleep in the night.

Or, the sparrow, wise, flees to the heights of virtues, where it is safe from snares. The one who is solitary or single, because charity makes one out of many, is on the roof or building because of the height of faith, so that he does not descend to take anything from the house, that is, from the flesh.

“Dwelling.” (The same.) Or, among ruined walls, commonly called ruins, where the walls stand without a roof and where the night-bird dwells, a bird that loves the night.

**Verse 9.**—“All the day.” (Cassiodorus.) Or, it may all be understood in the person of the righteous. As though he were saying, etc., up to: or, I was refreshed in humiliation, so pleasing was it to me.

**Verse 10.**—“Ashes.” (Augustine.) Penitents are signified by ashes and weeping. Ashes and sackcloth are the weapons of penitents. “Drink.” (Cassiodorus.) Temporal pleasure. Or, I mingled the desire for the homeland, because of the delay, with tears; or, the drink of the Scriptures, which recall ancient things.

**Verse 11.**—“From the face of anger.” (Cassiodorus.) Anger is vengeance; indignation is a movement of the soul by which we are indignant even against sons. Anger is called an impulse toward punishment, things which do not befall God; but this is an anthropopathic expression.

“Of anger.” Hence the Lord also says: “The anger of God remains upon those who do not believe” (John 3). He does not say, “It will come,” but “it remains,” because it is not removed from the condition in which one was born.

[Col. 1012C] **Verse 12.**—“My days have declined like a shadow.” Because I declined from the true day, my declining days are like me.

**Verse 13.**—“But you, etc.” (Cassiodorus.) The third section, in which the certainty of obtaining forgiveness is shown. The fallen man now rises to prophesy; the penitent now lifts his head.

(Augustine.) “A memorial.” The promised memorial is memorable: our restoration comes from you, because you remember us, or because we remember you.

**Verse 14.**—“The time has come.” (Augustine.) Because God wished everything to be done in order, and appointed a time for this, when the opportunity had been fittingly arranged.

**Verse 15.**—“Its stones.” (Augustine.) There are stones in Zion, etc., up to the point where, after the Holy Spirit had been sent, many of those who had crucified the Lord believed.

[Col. 1012D] **Verse 17.**—“In glory.” (Augustine.) He who first appeared in weakness in that Zion; hence: “We saw him without appearance or beauty” (Isaiah 53).

**Verse 18.**—“The prayer.” This takes place in the building of Zion: those who build pray and groan. They are one poor person and many poor persons; hence in the title he is singular, while here he is plural. He is called one because of the truth of the Church’s peace, and many because of its breadth.

**Verse 19.**—“Let these things be written.” (Cassiodorus.) He who above was soiled by penitence, now adorned with the honor of a prophet, commands that what he has said be confirmed by the testimony of Scripture, so that a future generation may learn. “In the generation.” (Augustine.) When these things were written, they did not benefit the generation of the Old Testament in this way; they benefit another, namely, the new generation.

**Verse 20.**—“Because he looked down,” etc. (Augustine.) After the groans of the one who was grieving, words of consolation now follow; the poor man now rejoices. Since he earlier said, “The Lord built Zion,” and likewise, “Let these things be written,” he now explains both, as though this were what he said should be written: “Because he looked down.”

“He looked down.” He speaks of future things as though they were past.

**Verse 21.**—“Of those in fetters.” (Augustine.) The fear of God is fetters, etc., up to the point where those who have been loosed are turned toward glory. (Cassiodorus.) Those in fetters are the saints, etc., up to the point where their speech converges upon the universal Church. “To release the sons.” (Augustine.) We are the sons of those who were put to death; we are released from the knots of sins and the bonds of desires. [Col. 1013B]

**Verse 23.**—“He answered him on the way of his strength.” (Cassiodorus.) The fourth section, in which, after the certainty of forgiveness, he says that he passes from his brevity into eternity. (Augustine.) “He answered.” Because: “I speak in order to proclaim the name of the Lord and his praise in Jerusalem,” etc., up to the point where he does not despise it but produces fruit. “He answered him.” That is, he believed that Christ had risen. But he foresees that some will say: Once there was indeed a Church gathering all into one, but now it is coming to an end.

“I have said: the fewness of my days”—not their eternity, where I shall be, but temporal days, for as long as I shall be in this age. “Declare to me.” On account of those who say that the Church no longer exists. This voice is not idle; this request is not empty. For the way itself, that is, Christ, proclaimed in this manner: “I am with you until the consummation of the age” (Matthew 28). The entire time up to the end is that small number of days, because everything that comes to an end is small, so that from it one may pass into eternity. “Declare also”:

**Verse 24.**—“Do not recall me in the midst of my days.” Let it not happen as the heretics say, etc., up to the point where they are only half-days if the eternal days are not added.

**Verse 25.**—“On the way of strength.” (Augustine.) In the faith by which he believes that Christ rose. Christ was the way of strength after the resurrection, when, no longer weak but strong, he calls the Church into heaven. This is praise of faith—not because it believes that he died, which even a pagan believes, but that he was glorified.

Or, Christian religion is briefly defined when it is called “the way of strength.”

Or, “in the generation of generations.” There is a generation of generations that does not pass away, gathered from all peoples, namely, the saints. In it will be the years of the Lord that do not pass away, that is, the eternity of God, which is God’s very substance and possesses nothing mutable.

**Verse 26.**—“In the beginning, you, Lord.” As though he were saying: Do not recall me, because I am striving toward eternity, which he explains by saying: “In the beginning you, Lord, founded the earth.”

**Verse 27.**—“They will perish.” (Augustine.) The heavens themselves will perish; this is evident concerning those nearest to the earth. Hence Peter also says: “But the earth and the heavens that now exist have been stored up by the same word, reserved for fire” (2 Peter 3). Concerning the higher heavens there is no certainty; but if they remain, they remain not in themselves but in God.

**Verse 28.**—“And like a covering you will change them.” Understand this of the heavens, which cover everything and which will also be changed. “And your years will not fail.” (Augustine.) They will be in the generation of generations. But will we be able to be there? Certainly, because “the sons of your servants will dwell.”

**Verse 29.**—“The sons of your servants.” (Augustine.) As sons entered the land of promise, etc., up to the point where he says, “with all the newness of sons.”

“Sons.” A joyful conclusion: the sons of the prophets and apostles, even more than the prophets and apostles themselves.

“Seed.” Works, from which eternal fruit comes.

“Will be directed.” Because nothing crooked enters.

### Psalm 102

**Verse 2.**—“Bless, O my soul.” (Augustine.) After the prayers of the poor man, come the praises of the rejoicing person. All who are in Christ as one human being awaken and exhort their soul to bless the Lord, wishing to define why he should be blessed, lest anyone be found sluggish in doing so. Cry out with your voice if there is a human being to hear; without your voice if there is no human being to hear, because God hears. (Cassiodorus.) By his benefits he urges us to bless God. (Augustine.) The prophet, speaking in the person of the universal righteous person, according to the soul’s higher power, that is, reason, exhorts the soul to bless, saying: “Do not forget.” Let not the pleasure of sin be before your eyes, but God’s condemnation and remission. Consider all your evils, because as many as they are, so many are God’s good recompenses. “Recompenses,” not “distributions.” A human being gives evil for good, but God recompenses good for evil. He gives when he creates me; he recompenses when he justifies me.

**Verse 3.**—“Who is propitious.” (Augustine.) He does this in the sacrament of baptism. “Who heals all your infirmities.” He does this in the life of the faithful person, while the flesh desires against the spirit, so that we do what we do not wish; the maladies of old age are healed day by day as newness increases, through the faith that works by love.

**Verse 4.**—“Who redeems your life from corruption.” This occurs in the final resurrection of the dead. “Who crowns,” etc. This occurs at the judgment, when the king sits upon the throne to repay each according to his works. Who will boast that he has a glorious heart and is pure from sin? Therefore it was necessary to recall mercy and mercies there, where debts might appear to be repaid in such a way that no place remained for mercy. [Col. 1014D]

**Verse 5.**—“Your youth is renewed like the eagle’s.” (Augustine.) So great a likeness is given, etc., up to those whose old age has closed their mouths, having forgotten to eat our bread.

**Verse 6.**—“Doing.” (Augustine.) The second section, in which he urges blessing through those things that were done for the ancients and are done for their descendants. “Mercies.” Those will obtain them who love their enemies, etc., up to the point where, after mercy, he speaks of judgment, saying, “And judgment.”

[Col. 1015A] **Verse 7.**—“To Moses.” (Augustine.) Through Moses, all the saints, etc., up to the point where he says that through him he gave the law so that transgression might abound.

**Verse 11.**—“For.” (The same.) Heaven is everywhere around the earth; from it even sinners receive light, air, breath, and rain, and from it comes fruit. Without heaven the earth ceases to be; so is God’s protection over those who fear him.

**Verse 12.**—“As far as it is distant,” etc. (The same.) When sin is forgiven, sins set like the sun and grace rises; sins are at their setting. Therefore turn away from the setting of sins and strive toward the rising of grace, and you will rise.

**Verse 14.**—“He remembered,” etc. (The same.) Or, according to another reading: “Remember that we are dust.” As though he were saying: He knew the creature, that is, our weakness. Turning to God, the creature says: “Remember that we are dust,” that is, may your mercy toward us persevere, lest we forget your grace. Or: “Humanity is like grass,” etc. For humanity, like a flower, comes forth, etc., up to “the mercy of the Lord.” “It will blossom fully.” (Cassiodorus.) That is, it will blossom or flourish to the greatest extent; or, “it will fade,” that is, it will cease to flower. Thus the expression may be intensive or privative.

**Verse 16.**—“For the spirit passed through it.” And it will not remain.

**Verse 17.**—“And righteousness.” (Augustine.) Mercy and righteousness constitute recompense. He says, “upon the sons of sons.” Many righteous people have no sons, much less sons of sons; but “sons” are works, and “sons of sons” are the rewards of works.

**Verse 19.**—“The Lord prepared his throne in heaven.” (Cassiodorus.) He proclaims the future judgment, lest sinners grow insolent; as though he were saying: You must remember and act, because the Lord is in heaven.

**Verse 21.**—“Bless the Lord, all his angels, his mighty ones.” (The same.) Thirdly, he urges the heavenly beings and all other creatures to bless. “Bless the Lord,” etc. He speaks by way of congratulation, not command or admonition. “His ministers.” (Augustine.) You bless, etc., up to the point where he says that what one has in one’s mouth should be shown in one’s works.

### Psalm 103

**Verse 1.**—“A psalm of David.” (Cassiodorus.) Again he urges us to bless God, first through heaven and earth and their adornment. (Augustine.) Although everything here can truly be understood religiously according to the letter, etc., up to the point where he says that a spiritual sense must be sought in everything. “Bless the Lord, O my soul,” etc. “You have been magnified.” In knowledge: you are always great by nature, and cannot increase or diminish, because you are perfect. “Confession”: that is, you have creatures everywhere who confess you, and they are beautiful and luminous. Or, beauty is in God’s essence, and light is everywhere. (Cassiodorus.) Or it signifies the incarnation, through which the confession and beauty of the heavenly majesty became known, and human beings confessed him; they are light through knowledge. (Augustine.) “You have clothed yourself with confession,” that is, with the Church, etc., up to the point where he says, “a garment without stain or wrinkle.”

**Verse 2.**—“Stretching out heaven thus.” (Cassiodorus.) What are the things that confess? Heaven, earth, and sea, together with all their adornment; he subsequently discusses each of them. (Augustine.) “Stretching out heaven like.” According to the literal sense, heaven is like a roof, etc., up to the point where, at the end, the book of Scripture will be folded up. [Col. 1016A]

**Verse 3.**—“Who cover.” (The same.) Literally, there are waters, etc., up to the point where he says that its upper parts are the two commandments of charity. Or, “who cover with waters,” that is, in the spiritual sense, you cover the surface of Scripture; or, you fortify them with spiritual gifts, with charity, so that nothing may be able to separate them. “Upon the wings of the winds,” etc. Wind is the movement of air, etc., up to the point where he says that the charity of Christ surpasses the charity of all.

**Verse 4.**—“A burning fire.” (Cassiodorus.) That is, the seraphim, who are the higher order; you make them your ministers. Hence in Isaiah: “One of the seraphim, who belong to the higher order, flew to me.”

**Verse 5.**—“Who founded the earth upon its stability.” (The same.) Therefore the Holy Spirit says difficult things in this psalm according to the literal sense, so that we may seek spiritual meanings.

**Verse 7.**—“At the voice of thunder.” (The same.) The waters will be dried up by terrifying winds; the wicked will fear because of the threat of judgment.

**Verse 8.**—“They ascend.” (Augustine.) The wicked, like mountains, etc., up to the point where he says that the Church may preach freely. (Cassiodorus.) God permits the proud, etc., up to the point where they no longer occupy the world.

**Verse 10.**—“In the valleys.” (Augustine.) From the humble who are subject to grace, and although they are mountains in spiritual height, the springs of the Holy Spirit flow; he rests upon the humble. “In the midst.” (The same.) That is, in the midst, etc., up to the point where he says that such a mountain is not to be heard.

[Col. 1016C] **Verse 11.**—“All will drink.” (The same.) All were in Peter’s dish lowered three times, etc., up to the point where he says that the Church might be gathered. “Wild asses.” (The same.) Great, untamed forest asses, etc., up to the point where he says that perhaps the proud Jews will postpone drinking until the final time.

**Verse 12.**—“Above them the birds of heaven.” (The same.) Not all birds remain, etc., up to the point where he says that others are condemned on the left.

**Verse 13.**—“From the fruit of your works.” (The same.) Therefore let no one boast in his works; but whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord, for by God’s grace the earth is filled. Thus grace is given freely. If it is repaid according to human works, it is called a reward.

**Verse 14.**—“For the service of human beings.” (The same.) Hence, although I was free from all, I made myself the servant of all, etc., up to the point where he says that he gave them an example of receiving necessities from those subject to them. “In oil.” The Spirit is given to each person for manifestation; therefore grace and a certain radiance, etc., up to the point where the face may be made cheerful with oil. “And bread.” Bread and wine are therefore the same. For this bread and wine are righteousness; they are truth; they are Christ. Both this and that gladden and strengthen the heart.

**Verse 16.**—“Which he planted.” (The same.) Why does he abandon the brightness of the world to those planted by him? Because there is the coot, a bird that lives in the waters; these are those who remain in the grace of baptism. Or, the heron, a most rapacious bird; and Christ does not reject such people either.

**Verse 17.**—“There the sparrows.” (Augustine.) Small flying creatures, etc., up to the point where he says that they nest in the cedars of Lebanon. “The houses of the heron.” (Augustine.) He is the leader of those sparrows, or of the cedars; yet this cannot be expressed in Latin, because *cedri* is feminine in gender, whereas this construction is impossible literally. For the house, that is, the nest of the coot, which is a sea bird or marsh bird, how can it be the leader of sparrows? By this he indicates that spiritual meanings must be sought. And if sparrows nest among the wealthy of this age, etc., up to the point where he says that they will not perish, because the rock is their leader. (Cassiodorus.) Or, the coot, a bird that lives in the waters, signifies those who remain in the grace of baptism, whose house is baptism. It is as though he were saying: Who are the sparrows? Those who are baptized. And this is “the house of the coot,” that is, baptism, which is the house of the regenerated and is the leader of those sparrows, that is, of Christians.

(Jerome, Cassiodorus.) “The heron”: a most rapacious bird, etc., up to the point where he says that, having been converted himself, he converted many others to the faith. “For the stags: the rock.” (Augustine.) The stags are the great spiritual people, etc., up to the point where he says: This is the one of which, as was said above, the birds of heaven give voice.

**Verse 19.**—“He made the moon.” (Cassiodorus.) After earthly things he passes to heavenly things, which nevertheless act for the earth, that is, serve it. After so many kinds of Christians, which he signified through animals, and after the order described above, he ascends and adds a discussion of Christ and the Church: namely, how the temporal Church waxes and wanes, as though it were undergoing the settings and risings of the true sun.

**Verse 20.**—“You appointed,” etc. “And night was made among them,” that is, the dark obstinacy of the mind. “And they will pass through.” (Augustine.) Not as above, the converted Gentiles, but the demons, who at the time of the Passion found the hearts of the apostles wavering. But when Christ rose, because they cannot prevail everywhere, they remain in their dens, that is, in the hearts of the obstinate. Thus, when Christ sets in someone, evils flourish; when he rises, they flee. “Setting.” The sun sets in such a way that it rises again. In the same way, when he sleeps—that is, Christ—will he not rise again? He died because he willed to; no one takes his life from him. When he died, darkness came upon the apostles and their hope failed.

**Verse 21.**—“The young lions,” etc. (Augustine.) There are also princes of demons, just as there are contemptible demons symbolized by young lions, which seek to deceive souls in darkness. The greater lion continually prowls about, seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5); they feed on human errors.

**Verse 22.**—“The sun has risen,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) After he said what the setting of the true sun accomplished, he now speaks of its rising.

**Verse 24.**—“Possession.” (Augustine.) Elsewhere, “creation.” (The same.) Through Christ, the Father, etc., up to the point where he says that nevertheless the wood was given by which we may cross over.

**Verse 25.**—“This great sea,” etc. (Cassiodorus.) The second section, in which he says how he leads the Church across the sea of the world to the shore of the homeland. “Creeping things,” etc. (Augustine.) Evil spirits, whose snares creep about.

**Verse 26.**—“This dragon whom you formed.” (The same.) In addition to these animals, etc., up to the point where he became greater in wickedness. “For mockery.” (The same.) It is said in Job 40 that Satan is mocked by the angels of God, who are set over the aerial powers so that they may not harm us.

**Verse 27.**—“Food.” (Augustine.) The dragon’s food is earth, because it was said to him: “You shall eat earth all the days of your life” (Genesis 3). Those who love earthly things are the devil’s food. But the food of the righteous is the word of God, hence: “Humanity does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Deuteronomy 8).

**Verse 28.**—“When you open your hand, all things will be filled with goodness.” (Cassiodorus.) Or, the hand is the power that abundantly fills all things.

**Verse 29.**—“But when you turn away.” (Augustine.) Many who have been filled with goodness have attributed it to themselves. Therefore, wishing to prove to them that they do not possess it from themselves but from God, so that they may have humility together with goodness, God sometimes disturbs them and turns his face away, and they fall into temptation.

**Verse 30.**—“Send forth your spirit.” (Cassiodorus.) Their dust is so called because from themselves they have what they are: dust. But the Spirit of the Lord is the medicine for those who have returned to dust.

**Verse 32.**—“To tremble.” (Augustine.) The trembling of humility is better than the confidence of pride. Hence the Apostle says: “Work out your salvation with trembling” (Philippians 2). “The mountains.” (The same.) Those who were proud, boasting that everything came from themselves. This happened on Mount Sinai.

**Verse 33.**—“I shall sing.” (Cassiodorus.) The third section, in which he promises that he will always sing. As though he were saying: The Lord has done the things described above, and having contemplated them—“in my life.” (Augustine.) In the present and future life; in hope and in vision. Now our life is hope; afterward it will be eternal life. The life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life. “As long as I am.” (The same.) Because I am in him without end, I shall sing as long as I am, lest anyone suppose that there is another activity in that life than singing psalms. For the one who is praised cannot become tedious, nor can praising become tedious; he is always loved and always praised.

**Verse 34.**—“May it be pleasing.” Another reading is: “May my discourse be sweet to him.” (Augustine.) A human being’s discourse with God is confession of sins. Hence Isaiah says: “Take away wickednesses from your souls; learn to do good, judge for the orphan, and come and let us argue, says the Lord” (Isaiah 1). Your discourse, therefore, is the sacrifice of your humility, which is sweet to God.

**Verse 35.**—“Bless the Lord, O my soul.” (The same.) He repeats what he said at the beginning of the psalm, “Bless the Lord, O my soul,” thereby indicating that the end of good things is like the beginning.

### Psalm 104

**Verse 1.**—“Alleluia.” (Cassiodorus.) Here *alleluia* appears for the first time, and no one previously placed it there; no language presumed to change it. *Alleluia*: “Praise.” *Ia* is the name of the invisible God, which belongs to him alone. In the twenty psalms bearing this title, the great deeds of God are recounted, and there is great rejoicing in them. (Cassiodorus.) Here the prophet commends the good among the people of Israel, who together with the other faithful are the true seed of Abraham, the children of the promise.

“Give thanks to the Lord.” (Augustine.) This is the first psalm prefaced by *alleluia*, etc., up to the point where it adds the temporal benefits that God’s mercy gave them.

**Verse 2.**—“All things.” (Cassiodorus.) All things: nothing should be omitted out of shame. Or, all the things they will say are wondrous, for no one can recount them all.

**Verse 3.**—“Be praised in the name,” that is, rejoice, Christians, to be called by Christ.

(Augustine.) “Be praised.” He does not forbid being praised if they are good; if they are not, then let them be praised only in the Lord, who makes them good. “Be praised in the name.” This corresponds to what is said elsewhere: “In the Lord my soul shall be praised.” There he adds: “Let the meek hear and rejoice”; here also, in a certain sense, “let the heart rejoice,” as though he were saying:

**Verse 4.**—“His face,” etc. (The same.) That is, his presence, etc., up to the point where he says that the wicked can fear the presence which the good love. (Jerome.) From the martyr Hippolytus, etc., up to the point where he says that there he will take the Church from among the Gentiles.

**Verse 5.**—“Remember, and so forth.” (Augustine.) “Seek him,” etc., up to the point where he says: If what God is is great to seek, then behold what he has done. “Miracles,” etc. (The same.) He gradually ascends from visible miracles to judgments, then to the eternal covenant, in which there is both commandment and promise.

**Verse 7.**—“Throughout all the earth.” (The same.) Do not think that the sons of Abraham are confined to one nation according to the flesh. For Jacob and Israel are throughout all the earth, to whom he manifests his judgments, but not to another nation.

### VERSE 8

**Forever:** (ID.) That is, eternally; hence later, “an eternal covenant.” If this covenant is understood as the Old Covenant on account of the land of Canaan, which follows, how is it eternal, since that earthly inheritance cannot be eternal? **Covenant:** For that is called a covenant which is promised, and also the teaching in which the promise is declared, and for whose observance it is granted. (ID.) What is promised is what we ought to receive; the commandment is what we ought to do. This is faith: that “the righteous shall live by faith,” and to this faith the inheritance is promised. **Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob:** Behold the three patriarchs of whom He especially says that He is God: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.” Behold a threefold authority.

### VERSE 10

**For an eternal covenant:** (ID.) That is, one which is fulfilled through the very word itself, etc., up to “and the son remains in the house forever.”

### VERSE 11

**The land of Canaan:** (CASS.) That is, what is signified by it: for He also gave this land as a figure of the eternal inheritance (1 John IV). (AUG.) The land of Canaan is appropriately called an eternal inheritance [Col. 1019D], because servants are driven away from it and sons are received.

### VERSE 12

**When they were few in number:** (CASS.) He provided those supports of temporal life for the patriarchs and their children, both according to the flesh and according to faith—not so that they might cling to these things, but so that they might refer them to the eternal good, namely, so that, attracted by these gifts, they might seek God’s ordinances and law.

### VERSE 13

**From kingdom to kingdom:** (AUG.) Not a kingdom that then existed, but the kingdom of Israel that was to come.

### VERSE 15

**Do not touch:** (ID.) Although these words are not found in the historical account, God either spoke them secretly in the hearts of men or through an angel. **Christs:** (ID.) Because they were already Christians, although secretly; hence Abraham “rejoiced that he was to see my day; he saw it and was glad” (John VIII). For no one, whether before or after, was reconciled to God apart from this faith, since there is one mediator, Christ (1 Timothy II).

### VERSE 16

**And He called:** (AUG.) The fourth part begins here, where he starts to narrate, etc., up to “He commanded that what already existed in His disposition should come to be.” Thus, “He called,” and “all the support of bread was broken” (Genesis XXXVII).

### VERSE 17

**A man:** (ID.) Joseph, sold by his brothers, was afterward exalted in Egypt on account of his righteousness. **Joseph:** (ID.) If Joseph was both humbled and exalted, etc., up to “but seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things will be added.”

### VERSE 18

**In fetters:** (ID.) We do not read in Genesis about Joseph’s fetters, but we must believe that what was omitted there is stated by the Spirit in the psalm. [Col. 1020B] (CASS.) Even if he found favor with the keeper of the prison, he was first afflicted with anxiety. It follows: “Iron passed through,” etc. As though, apart from bodily evils, iron—that is, the tribulation of harsh necessity, which was present in his heated and troubled soul—passed through him, etc. Or, according to another reading, “his soul passed through iron,” that is, through the tribulation of harsh necessity. The meaning is the same as above.

### VERSE 23

**In the land of Ham, etc.:** (AUG.) Ham was the father of Canaan, from whom the Egyptians derive their origin.

### VERSE 24

**And He increased His people, etc.:** (ID.) The fifth part. Here he briefly sets forth what happened in Egypt, which he later narrates at greater length. He also says how He established His people over their enemies.

[Col. 1020C] **And He strengthened it [His people]:** Namely, through the signs performed by Moses. Previously the male children of the Israelites were being killed, and the Israelites themselves were being worn down in making bricks. But afterward, by the mighty hand of the Lord and through signs and wonders, they became objects of fear and honor.

### VERSE 25

**He turned:** (ID.) He begins to narrate how this happened. “He turned” does not mean that God is the author of evil, but that He makes good use of evil: when He increased Israel’s prosperity, the Egyptians turned toward envy, because they were already evil. **So that they hated:** Envy is hatred of another’s prosperity.

### VERSE 26

**He sent:** He could have done everything Himself, but He acted thus in order to teach with what moderation He had accomplished these things. **The one whom He chose, him:** (ID.) It would have been sufficient to say “the one whom He chose.” Yet nothing should be sought in the fact that He added “him”; it is simply the customary manner of divine speech for the sake of explanation.

### VERSE 27

**The words of His signs:** (ID.) By which He was proclaimed among them, etc., up to “therefore He performed words—not words of speech, but of signs or wonders—through them.”

### VERSE 28

(ID.) Or: “They embittered His words,” which is clear. Or, “Moses and Aaron did not embitter His words,” because they patiently endured the Egyptians, who were exceedingly harsh, on account of the Lord’s command, until everything that the Lord had ordained had been accomplished among them. **Darkness, etc.:** (CASS.) They suffered these things among the plagues. But here he says that their hearts were darkened, because they despised God’s commands. Blindness was a fitting beginning for the plagues, since without it they would not have fallen into the remaining ones.

### VERSE 29

**He turned their waters:** (AUG.) The second plague, though the first in Exodus; it signified that He would turn the waters of the Red Sea against them for their destruction.

### VERSE 30

**Their land brought forth:** (AUG.) He turned their land into frogs, because there were so many of them that this can appropriately be said by hyperbole.

### VERSE 31

**He spoke, and the dog-fly came, etc.:** (ID.) In His word they existed outside time before they came to be in time through that same Word; or He spoke in a manner of speaking through angels or through Moses, so that it would happen then, when it was to happen.

### VERSE 32

**He gave them rains, etc.:** (AUG.) This is similar to “their land brought forth frogs.”

[Col. 1021B]

### VERSE 34

**The locust and the grasshopper:** (ID.) The locust and the grasshopper constitute one plague, because one is the parent and the other its offspring.

### VERSE 36

**And He struck:** (ID.) Although there were ten plagues, etc., up to “who could not despise the payment for their labors, even though it was temporal.”

### VERSE 37

**And He brought them out, etc.:** This is the sixth part according to Cassiodorus and Augustine. Above he said that the evils inflicted on Israel’s enemies were the justice of God; now he adds the temporal goods that the mercy of God gave them, so that, helped by these, they might seek God’s law. (AUG.) “And He brought them out”: God said to Abraham, etc., up to “then follows the second benefit: ‘And there was not one who was infirm,’ and the rest.”

### VERSE 38

**Because fear of them fell upon them:** [Col. 1021C] Israel feared that the Egyptians’ survivors would consume them.

(AUG.) Here was fulfilled what he said above: “And He strengthened them over their enemy.”

### VERSE 39

**He spread out a cloud for their protection:** According to Augustine, this is the second part, where he adds the temporal goods that the mercy of God gave them, following the evils that the justice of God inflicted on their enemies.

(AUG.) He now begins to recount the benefits bestowed on those traveling through the wilderness.

### VERSE 40

**They asked:** (AUG.) The good asked for the support of the weak. **The quail:** “And He satisfied them with the bread of heaven.” This too is flesh, because here he is not speaking about the bitterness of the wicked but about the faith of the elect. They are to be understood as having asked for what would suppress the murmuring of those who were embittered.

### VERSE 42

**Because He remembered His holy word:** (ID.) Through all these benefits God commends the merit of Abraham’s faith; hence he adds, “because He remembered.”

### VERSE 44

**And He gave them:** (AUG.) Not so that they might worship Him on account of these things, but so that they might refer them to the eternal good, that is, so that they might keep His ordinances. **They possessed, etc.:** Not so that these things should be regarded as the highest good, but so that they might be free to pursue what could enable them to acquire the highest and eternal good—not so that they might drift into luxury or grow sluggish in them.

### VERSE 45

**His ordinances, etc.:** (CASS.) These are found where there is an evident and absolute commandment, such as “You shall love God and your neighbor,” which must be kept. **The law:** Concerning these matters, which are not bodily but spiritual, and therefore must be sought because they are the shadow of things to come. **Law:** For example, the command concerning circumcision and the other matters that must be carefully investigated, because they are spoken mystically.

## PSALM 105

### VERSE 1

**Alleluia. Alleluia:** Some say that one “Alleluia” belongs to the end of the preceding psalm and the other to the following one. Jerome teaches that this rule should be observed, and Cassiodorus also agrees with his assertion. But most assign every “Alleluia” to what follows, sometimes one and sometimes two, just as in the Gospel the Lord sometimes said “Amen” and sometimes “Amen, amen,” for greater certainty concerning the matter. Augustine agrees with them, especially since no Greek manuscripts have “Alleluia” at the end of the psalm.

**Give thanks to the Lord:** (AUG.) This psalm is joined to the preceding one, etc., up to “therefore he urges a twofold confession, of praise and of sins.”

(CASS.) The Hebrew, having abandoned the faithlessness of the fathers and turned toward the mercy of God, urges others to turn toward the same mercy, praying that they may be joined to the people pleasing to God, who was to be gathered at Christ’s coming.

### VERSE 2

**Who shall speak:** (CASS.) The one who asks for mercy is filled with consideration of the divine works and, in wonder, says: “Who shall speak?”

### VERSE 3

**Blessed are those who keep:** (AUG.) Or because what follows says, etc., up to “judgment and righteousness, because blessed are those who…”

### VERSE 5

**That we may see, etc.:** (AUG.) So that we may see You in that goodness which You grant to the elect; that is, by Your grace may we see, lest we remain blind. **That You may be praised:** It is surprising that in most manuscripts, etc., up to “because He is praised only on account of You.”

### VERSE 6

**We have sinned:** The second part, where he enumerates the sins that the fathers committed in Egypt, and yet says that they were delivered by God.

**Iniquity:** (CASS.) He says the same thing for the third time, so that the confession may appear pure; the more vigorously a person condemns himself, the more quickly he is released.

### VERSE 7

**They did not understand:** (AUG.) That is, they did not understand what You wished to give them through those things—not a temporal but an eternal good, which is awaited through patience. Therefore they, being impatient, murmured and wished to be blessed with temporal goods. (CASS.) Two things commend the benefits: understanding and memory. Both are reproved in them. First, understanding, when he says, “They did not understand the wonders.”

**They provoked Him when they went up:** (AUG.) Fearing God and despairing, etc., up to “hence he deserved to obtain, among the others, the privilege or principate of the kingdom.”

### VERSE 9

**As in the wilderness:** (ID.) Because where the depths had been, it became dry land, so that there was a wilderness where there were no waters.

### VERSE 10

**He redeemed them from the hand:** (ID.) At what price? As though he were saying, “At none.” But it happened as a figure of baptism, in which we are redeemed from the hand of the devil by the blood of Christ. Hence he called it the Red Sea, because by its color blood was signified.

### VERSE 12

**And they believed in:** (AUG.) Behold the hard hearts of the Jews, who believe not before the miracles but afterward. It would have been better to believe the One who promised.

### VERSE 13

**They quickly acted, forgetting:** The third part, where he explains the sins they committed after the exodus; yet God’s mercy toward them did not fail, since He was appeased through Moses. Or this may refer to correction through God’s justice, when He took vengeance on some through Moses. (CASS.) “They quickly acted”: They were changed with great speed, etc., up to “for God delayed giving it in order to test them.”

### VERSE 14

**They lusted with lust in the wilderness:** (AUG.) This is a manner of expression like “they praised,” etc. (CASS.) [Col. 1023B] The excessiveness of the desire is shown by the repetition of the word.

### VERSE 15

**Satisfaction:** This is not the satisfaction of which it is said, “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied” (Matthew V).

**Into their souls:** (AUG.) Into their animal life, which is sustained by food. Hence also in the Gospel: “Is not the soul more than food?” Or “into their souls” means that their will, which had asked in despair, was overcome by abundance. **Satisfaction:** Sedition follows; hence he adds:

### VERSE 16

**And they provoked:** (CASS.) Seeking honor through envy, they opposed Moses in the camp and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord. This provocation concerned the priesthood, which Aaron and his sons possessed.

### VERSE 17

**The earth opened:** (ID.) The quality of the punishment shows the praise of God, who avenged His own: those who savored earthly things are swallowed by the earth.

### VERSE 18

**In their assembly:** (ID.) Korah and the two hundred and fifty with him, wishing to have Aaron’s priesthood, took censers to burn incense; therefore they were consumed by divine fire. **Sinners:** (AUG.) He does not say “those who sin,” which can also describe the good, but “sinners,” meaning exceedingly wicked people burdened with heavy loads of sins.

### VERSE 19

**And they made:** (CASS.) Unable to endure Moses’ absence while he remained on the summit of Mount Sinai to receive the law, they made a calf. **Horeb:** It is interpreted as “Calvary,” where the crucifixion took place, etc., up to “the impatience of the frivolous brought this about, just as all evils arise from it.”

### VERSE 20

**In the likeness:** (AUG.) He does not say “into the likeness” but “in the likeness.” This is a manner of expression like the one above, “and they believed in His words.”

### VERSE 21

**They forgot:** (CASS.) There was indeed great forgetfulness in their memory, if they forgot the deliverance.

**The terrible things:** Because He afflicted their adversaries, yet they displayed to these people the One whom they ought to have feared.

### VERSE 23

**If He had not stood in the breach:** (AUG.) He said, “If You do not forgive them, blot me out of Your book.” How powerful is the intercession of the saints! Moses, secure in God’s justice—for that justice could not blot him out—obtained mercy for those who would justly have perished.

**To turn away His wrath:** Concerning the water of contradiction and the sacrifice of the sons, on account of which God was more greatly angered, yet afterward showed mercy. **And for nothing:** The fourth part, where he again enumerates other sins and says that God was appeased through Phinehas.

**They did not believe His word:** (AUG.) They despised what was signified through it, etc., up to “they did not endure His counsel.”

**In His tents:** (CASS.) They murmured, because this happens not to those who labor but to those who are idle; hence the envy of the crime grows greater.

### VERSE 26

**And He raised His hand over them, etc.:** (CASS.) God’s justice is set forth first, so that the mercy that follows may be more greatly glorified. This mercy is shown in what follows, where God is said to have been appeased through the intervention of Phinehas.

### VERSE 28

**And they were initiated into Beelphegor:** (ID.) Or, “they were consecrated,” as though they were worshiping for a time. Their transgression was more grievous, and the wrath more intense: they devoted their sons to demons. (AUG.) “And they were initiated,” before he said, etc., up to “he delivered the one whose destruction was to be greater.”

### VERSE 30

**And Phinehas stood:** (CASS.) With steadfast mind, etc., up to “because whoever acts well also prays.”

### VERSE 31

**And it was reckoned, etc.:** (AUG.) God, who knew with how much love for the people this deed had been performed, reckoned it to His priest as righteousness—not only for as long as that generation lasted, but forever.

### VERSE 32

**And they provoked, etc.:** (CASS.) The fifth part, where he deals with the water of contradiction and the sacrifice of the sons, on account of which God was more greatly angered, yet afterward showed mercy. They provoked Him by their inventions, as was said above; now they provoked Him again.

### VERSE 33

**And he distinguished with his lips, etc.:** (CASS.) This miracle, etc., up to “he did not retain the confidence that he ought to have had.” (AUG.) “And he distinguished”: As though God could not do this, etc., up to “yet he was not alienated from the kingdom of God’s grace.”

### VERSE 35

**The nations:** The seven peoples who possessed the promised land.

### VERSE 36

**And it became a stumbling-block to them:** (CASS.) The promised land, given as a reward, became a ruin to those who transgressed, because through conformity with the nations they became idolaters.

### VERSE 37

**And they sacrificed:** (AUG.) Although the historical account does not narrate this, the prophet here cannot be lying. (CASS.) If it did not happen in the first generation, it happened in the following generation, as David recounts.

### VERSE 38

**And it was slain:** (AUG.) This is a figurative expression, with the container standing for what it contains, namely, human beings. For by sacrificing their children they were killing their own souls, and they were defiled by their deeds.

### VERSE 39

**By their inventions:** (ID.) Not because they were the first to invent them, but because they imitated others. This is clearer in the Greek, both here and above; hence others translate it as “pursuits,” “affections,” or “pleasures.”

### VERSE 40

**He abhorred:** (CASS.) That is, He turned away from them. This turning away is the extreme of all evils; ruin follows from it, and He handed them over.

### VERSE 41

**And He handed them over, etc.:** (ID.) Behold, those who gloried in idols are subjected to the disgrace of servitude, because they serve their enemies; this is difficult. **Those who hated:** It is grievous to serve one who has been offended and cannot be appeased by any service.

### VERSE 43

**He often delivered them, etc.:** (CASS.) There is a twofold mercy. Above He first set forth God’s benefits, yet their iniquity did not cease; He then inflicted vengeance, and again showed mercy to those who were afflicted.

**In their counsel:** (AUG.) Human counsel is evil for the human being who seeks what belongs to himself rather than what belongs to God.

### VERSE 45

**Of the covenant:** (CASS.) The reason is that Israel should not perish on account of its debt: the New Covenant is present here, in which there is the Lord’s coming, promised to Abraham. **He repented:** (AUG.) Because He changed what seemed likely to destroy them. (CASS.) He repents when He sees us repent, and He becomes toward us what we are toward Him. (AUG.) God does nothing as though by a sudden decision, but does what He foreknew from eternity. Yet He is said to change because He appears to follow circumstances, when other causes intervene in the opposite direction. But He foresaw both the causes and what would happen immutably.

### VERSE 46

**Into mercies:** (CASS.) On account of the various gifts: prophets, apostles, martyrs, and confessors came from the Jews, and He gave them as mercies. This happened “in the sight of all,” because He had begun to make them—that is, the nations—wonder at them, though previously the nations had despised them. Or, they were set free in the presence of demons, under whom they had been captives.

### VERSE 47

**Save us:** (CASS.) The sixth part. Now, filled with the abundance of praise of God, he prays for what he foresaw would happen: that the Church would be gathered from all nations [Col. 1025C] and sing eternal praises. (AUG.) “Save us,” as though he were saying, “You have given mercies in the sight of all,” etc., up to what follows: “And gather us from the nations.”

### VERSE 48

**Blessed be the Lord:** (CASS.) This is the praise that he desires the gathered people to sing; the Church now sings it, rejoicing in so great a good. **From age to age, etc.:** That is, from eternity into eternity, because He will be praised without end. This is the third consummation of the body of Christ in immortality, which was prayed for at the beginning of the psalm: “Remember us, Lord, with the favor shown to Your people, that we may see, rejoice, and praise You with Your inheritance.”

## PSALM 106

**Alleluia, alleluia:** (AUG.) This psalm commends the mercy of God, etc., up to the passages that the Apostle set down, although they signify the same things.

### VERSE 1

**Give thanks to the Lord:** (ID.) This psalm teaches what we are in ourselves, etc., up to “first he urges the redeemed to give thanks. Give thanks.”

(CASS., AUG.) It has seven divisions, etc., up to the seventh, where it deals with heretics: “And they became few.”

### VERSE 3

**And by the sea:** (CASS.) Instead of “the south,” he sets “the sea,” understanding the ocean of that region. This can be taken for any part of the world.

### VERSE 4

**They wandered:** (ID.) The second part, where the first temptation occurs, etc., up to “the fourth is confession for being heard, that is, praise.”

[Col. 1026A]

### VERSE 5

**Hungry:** (AUG.) He signifies the curious people of the world, who sought truth through various opinions and did not find it. **Their soul, etc.:** God commends Himself to us, which is beneficial for us. We fail so that we may ask, and we may love the One who comes to our aid.

### VERSE 6

**And He led them:** (AUG.) As though He had rescued them from ignorance, showing them the way, Christ. Behold, He delivered them from error. But how He delivered them from the hunger and thirst with which they were burning, he will say later; for now he places confession first.

### VERSE 8

**Wonders:** (HIER.) As though the mercies were given in a wondrous manner of redemption.

### VERSE 9

**The hungry:** (CASS.) One who desires to know, or one who does not desire to know but is wasting away from extreme hunger, as can happen to someone exhausted by excessive hunger or illness, so that he does not desire to eat but perishes from extreme abstinence.

**Those sitting:** (AUG.) The third part, where the second temptation is set forth, etc., up to “and let us also consider that we can undergo this.”

### VERSE 11

**Because they embittered:** (ID.) This is another attempt, etc., up to “hence He was angry with them.”

**The counsel of the Most High:** So that those who had grown proud might be humbled in distress. This was a salutary counsel, so that the sickness of the world might be cured by the opposite remedy.

### VERSE 12

**And there was no one:** (ID.) When God ceases to give help, you can labor against vices, but you cannot conquer them. When your heart is oppressed by your evil habit, it will be humbled so that you may learn to cry out; hence he adds: “And they cried out.”

[Col. 1026C]

### VERSE 13

**And they cried out:** (CASS.) For the same reason, the same sentence as above.

### VERSE 16

**Bronze gates:** (ID.) The bronze gates are the vicious habits of human beings, which do not allow those enclosed to escape.

**Bars:** Unclean spirits, which secure the gates. He says “bronze” and “iron” to indicate strength, but the power of God breaks them.

### VERSE 18

**Every food:** (AUG.) The fourth part, where the third temptation is set forth, namely, weariness. Those who above languished from hunger are likewise endangered by disgust. Therefore do not think them safe from satiety, since they also die from disgust. This is what “every food,” etc., means.

(AUG.) After one has come from ignorance to truth, from error to the way, from hunger for wisdom to the word of faith, and after overcoming the difficulties of evils so as to live without complaint, weariness remains, so that sometimes one takes no pleasure in reading or praying. He has escaped ignorance and desire, but dies of weariness.

### VERSE 23

**Those who go down to the sea:** The fifth part, etc., up to “if the whole ship is endangered.”

### VERSES 24–25

**They saw the works of the Lord:** (AUG.) Or, “they saw,” etc., up to where he explains their storms, adding, “He spoke, and a storm-wind arose.” **In the deep:** “He spoke, and a storm-wind arose,” etc. (ID.) The deep is the human heart, from which winds burst forth and storms of seditions and dissensions arise.

### VERSE 27

**Like a drunken man:** (ID.) They stagger because their prosperity or adversity is greater than their strength. [Col. 1027A] **And all their wisdom was swallowed up:** They appear to be wisely active when they speak and when they read; but when the storm comes, all human counsels fail, and it is not apparent what should be done. Therefore it remains for them to cry out, so that God may strengthen their hearts and prevent them from being shaken by temptations.

### VERSE 32

**In the assembly:** (AUG.) Behold why he has said all these things, and where all the things foretold are enacted.

### VERSE 33

**He made rivers:** (CASS.) The sixth part extends this far: how He makes even the evils of enemies beneficial. (AUG.) “He made rivers”: Consequently the Church is commended, etc., up to “thus the benefits directed toward the Church of God are plainly displayed.”

### VERSE 34

**Into saltiness:** (CASS.) Where salty moisture dominates, it removes fertility.

[Col. 1027B]

**Because of the wickedness of its inhabitants:** (AUG.) Because of the wickedness of those who inhabited that land—that is, the Lord’s tabernacle—with deceitful minds.

### VERSE 37

**And they sowed:** (CASS.) Those who sow fields and plant vineyards are people who purify their bodies through heavenly instruction, so that they may bear the fruit of good works.

### VERSE 38

**Exceedingly:** (CASS.) This means “very greatly,” or because many are called but few are chosen.

### VERSE 39

**And they became few:** (AUG.) The seventh part, where something is also said about heretics, etc., up to “but they were not among the few elect.”

**Afflicted:** (CASS.) Either those who persist through heretics, or the heretics themselves through the devil’s snares. Pain and tribulation belong to those who abandon the author of salvation.

[Col. 1027C]

### VERSE 40

**Contempt was poured out:** (AUG.) Or, “contempt was poured out,” etc., up to “and what did He also do concerning those who had been led astray? Behold.”

### VERSE 41

**He helped the poor man:** God could have allowed them always to remain within, but we would have gained no benefit from them. Once they were separated and troubled us through their disputations, an eagerness for inquiry and an example of fear arose in us, so that “whoever stands should take heed lest he fall.” And what happens to those who were led astray through the poor man who was helped? “And He set him like sheep.” You thought there was one poor man; but this poor man is a large household, a large Church. Yet it is also one Church, one sheep. These great mysteries had long remained hidden, and were therefore found with sweetness.

### VERSE 42

**The upright shall see and rejoice:** (AUG.) [Col. 1027D] Behold where the Psalmist is heading: namely, to show that the good are exalted through God’s mercy, just as the wicked are crushed through pride.

### VERSE 43

**Who is wise and will keep these things?:** (ID.) This is the conclusion, as though he were saying: Since the Lord helps the poor man, therefore, “Who is wise?” **The mercies:** That He delivers from error, etc., up to “and the wicked shuts his mouth.”

## PSALM 107

### VERSE 1

**A song of the psalm:** (AUG.) It is taken from the concluding parts of two psalms, etc., up to “so that the words of the prophets might be fulfilled.” (CASS.) Here many of the same things as above are found, etc., up to “and they are properly joined, since they in no way conflict.” (ID.) The first section concerns David’s flight, [Col. 1028A] etc., up to “a song refers to divine matters, a psalm to practical works.”

### VERSE 2

**Prepared:** (CASS.) The sixth psalm concerning the two natures in Christ. “My heart is prepared.” First Christ gives thanks because, having accepted suffering, He rose into glory. Second, he shows what salvation has been brought to the whole earth, at “that they may be delivered.”

### VERSE 7

**That they may be delivered:** (ID.) The second part, showing what salvation has been brought to the whole earth over which glory extends. Here too the humility of the humanity and the power of the majesty are displayed.

**Save:** So that they may be delivered in the future; here save them so that they may not fall. Or He asks to be saved in the resurrection, so that the faithful may be delivered, since through such a sign they perceived His divinity. As though He were saying: “So that I may sing and praise, save me in the resurrection by Your right hand”—that is, through the Word, who is the Father’s arm—“so that Your beloved may be delivered.” The order of the words has been reversed. For he says: “Save me and hear me,” and “save me.”

### VERSE 8

**I shall exult:** (AUG.) Or, “I shall be exalted.” Above he says “I shall rejoice,” but here “I shall be exalted,” which fits very well, because joy arises from exaltation. Here Christ speaks in the person of the Church.

### VERSE 9

**And Ephraim:** (ID.) Ephraim is mine—that is, my fruitfulness—which is the acceptance of my head. This fruitfulness comes from the fact that the head accepted me, or that I am the head. (CASS.) Or Ephraim, that is, fruitfulness, is the acceptance of my head, because when my head accepted the crown of thorns, it bore fruit beyond all others: for Christ won the whole world.

### VERSE 11

**Who will lead me into a fortified city?:** (ID.) As a human being, Christ asks in order to answer; He denies that this can be done by a human being. The city is hell, which no one could open. The peoples of Edom are those to whom He became known after the resurrection. These things could be accomplished by divinity alone.

### VERSE 12

**You have rejected us, and You will not go forth:** (ID.) He says “us” in the plural because here Christ suffers with His members, whereas above He says in the singular, “He will lead me.” Seek the explanations of all these matters in the ninth psalm.

## PSALM 108

### VERSE 1

**For the end, a psalm.** (AUG.) A prophecy concerning Christ, etc., as far as “and the things expressly said concerning Judas,” such as: “And let another take his bishopric” [Col. 1028D].

(CASS.) The fifth of those psalms that deal more extensively with the Passion.

### VERSE 2

**O God, praise.** (CASS.) He warns us to avoid Judas's wickedness, etc., as far as “Christ, therefore, praying to the Father according to his humanity, says: ‘Because the mouth of the sinner.’” (ID.) A fitting contrast, because the wicked do not keep silent in their abuse.

### VERSE 3

**Without cause.** (AUG.) Just as equity pleases the devout for its own sake, so iniquity pleases the impious.

### VERSE 4

**In return for … me.** [The supplied lemma is abbreviated: *Pro eo ut me*.] (ID.) Those who disparage Christ in his members do greater harm, because they kill the souls of those who would believe, than those who killed his flesh, which was soon to rise again.

[Col. 1029A]

### VERSE 5

**And they set against.** (AUG.) There are six distinctions, etc., as far as “which is good for evil, which God the judge also does.” (CASS.) Every sin is incurred in three ways, etc., as far as “which Christ did when praying for the Jews.”

### VERSE 6

**Set over.** (AUG.) The second part, where he begins to prophesy what they will receive for their impiety. Above, concerning many, etc., as far as “whose person Judas represented.” **Set a sinner over him.** As concerning Judas, so concerning them.

### VERSE 7

**When he is judged, let him go forth condemned.** Because, persisting in wickedness, they store up wrath for themselves. **Prayer into sin:** because it is not made through the mediator.

### VERSE 8

**Few days.** With reference to the kingdom, which [Col. 1029B] did not stand for long afterward. **His bishopric:** that is, Christ (who was sent to them), whom the people of the Gentiles received.

### VERSE 9

**His children orphans:** having lost the kingdom as their father; or God as their father. **His wife:** that is, the people. **Widows:** having lost the kingdom.

### VERSE 10

**Let him be removed,** as happened in the captivity. **Let them beg,** under the kings of the Gentiles.

### VERSE 11

**All his substance:** that is, his life, punishing each particular of sin; their debts are not forgiven, because they are forgiven in Christ alone. **And strangers:** that is, the devil and his angels. **Let them plunder his labor:** because they do not lay up treasure in heaven.

### VERSE 12

**And let there be none for him,** etc. That is, there is no helper for the person who lacks Christ. **Nor let there be anyone who has mercy.** I do not mean for obtaining temporal things, but eternal things.

[Col. 1029C]

### VERSE 13

**Let his offspring come to everlasting destruction.** For this reason: because they remained in one generation, that is, because they were not born again. **And let the name be blotted out.** That is, the name of the earthly Jerusalem, which is in bondage with her children and which killed the prophets.

### VERSE 15

**And let it perish from the land of the living:** that is, the Church. **Their memory,** because, when they were natural branches, they became … [The supplied sentence ends here without completing the predicate.]

### VERSE 16

**Because he did not remember.** By repenting.

**To show mercy.** Toward the members of Christ.

### VERSE 18

**A curse, and it shall come upon him; and he did not desire blessing.** (AUG.) Sins give pleasure now, but they are called a curse because they prepare torments.

### VERSE 19

**With which he is covered.** He seems to say here, [Col. 1029D] etc., as far as “let him always be ready,” whence he says here, “he is always girded.”

### VERSE 20

**With the Lord.** (ID.) Those especially disparage Christ who say that he is not from the Father, or is less than the Father. **Evils against the soul.** Saying that he could not rise when he wished.

### VERSE 21

**And you, O Lord.** (CASS.) The third part, where he prays, etc., as far as “help me,” according to his humanity. **For your name's sake.** “For no … of works,” etc., as far as “because your mercy is sweet.” [The supplied excerpt is abbreviated.]

### VERSE 22

**Because I am needy and poor.** (ID.) Christ's need and poverty are the weakness in which he was crucified.

[Col. 1030A]

### VERSE 23

**Like a shadow as it declines, I have been taken away.** (CASS.) Just as night comes from the declining shadow, so death comes from mortal flesh.

### VERSE 24

**It was changed.** (AUG.) Therefore Christ's flesh was changed, etc., as far as “because Jesus had not yet been glorified.” **Because of the oil:** that is, spiritual grace, from which he is called Christ.

### VERSE 25

**They shook their heads.** (CASS.) In their fury they threaten by shaking their heads. (AUG.) They shook their heads because they saw him hanging on the cross, but not yet when his flesh was changed.

### VERSE 26

**Help me, O Lord.** (CASS.) He asks as a human being; he grants as God.

### VERSE 27

**This is your hand.** (AUG.) Christ is this hand, and he is the Word with God; and he made it when the Word was made flesh. For it was without [Col. 1030B] time according to divinity, and was made in time according to the flesh.

### VERSE 28

**They will curse, and you will bless.** The curse of the wicked is one thing; God, when he blesses, does what he says. [The supplied Latin lacks punctuation between *malorum*, “of the wicked,” and *Deus*, “God.”]

### VERSE 29

**As with a double cloak,** etc. Others translate, instead of *diploide*, “a double cloak,” that is, let them be put to shame within and without, that is, before God and human beings.

### VERSE 30

**Exceedingly in my mouth.** *Nimis* is ordinarily used for “more than is fitting,” but also for “very much.” **In the midst.** (AUG.) That is, in common, or in the heart.

### VERSE 31

**Because he stood at the right hand of the poor man.** The devil at Judas's right hand, etc., as far as “but that he might save the soul [Col. 1030C] from its persecutors.”

## PSALM 109

### VERSE 1

**A psalm of David:** (CASS.) This is the seventh psalm, etc., up to “whatever is contained in both Testaments.” (CASS.) The prophet urges submission to Christ. First the prophet reports the Father’s words concerning the Son, etc., up to “this refers to His humanity.”

**The Lord said:** (CASS.) He speaks according to our manner, so that the human being may be instructed. **Lord to my Lord:** Distinguish the persons, and understand one nature and one power. **Sit:** After labor, rest and reign with Him, according to His humanity. **At My right hand:** In My more excellent and hidden goods, until You reign openly. And this is what follows: “Until I place Your enemies,” etc. (AUG.) “Sit” means not only sit on high, so that You may rule over exalted things, but also sit in what is hidden, etc., [Col. 1030D] up to “if he does not see what he believes.” **A footstool for Your feet:** This is said by comparison with a footstool, and also denotes complete subjection. Through the feet, eternal stability is signified; this occurs daily among those who are converted.

### VERSE 2

**The rod of Your power:** It begins from Zion, that is, Christ’s kingdom begins from the Jews; hence he adds, “the rod of Your power,” etc. **From Zion:** The prophet is not speaking of that kingdom of Christ, etc., up to “and the remission of sins through all nations, beginning from Jerusalem.”

### VERSE 3

**With You is the beginning:** (CASS.) Second, the Father indicates the nature of the Godhead, etc., up to “when in the resurrection they will be radiant like the angels of God.” (AUG.) [Col. 1031A] He already rules; He is already power. But on the day of special power, etc., up to “in what manner the Father is with Him as beginning.” This will be then, but now—“from the womb,” that is, from the secret and hidden substance of My being, etc., up to “who offers Himself,” from which follows, “He has sworn,” etc. (CASS.) Or, “With You is the beginning” refers to the Father, as though He were saying: “I grant this to You beyond the others, because the Son is so by nature.” (AUG.) Or it may be understood as spoken by the person of the prophet, etc., up to “with the Holy Spirit, who makes the saints radiant.”

### Verse 4

**The Lord has sworn.** (Cassiodorus.) Third, the prophet treats of Christ’s humanity, etc., down to: hence it is clear that the sacrifices pass over according to the order of Aaron. **He will not repent: you are a priest forever.** (Augustine.) No repentance falls upon God: for he knows [Col. 1031B] what he is doing and does not change his purpose. Rather, by the word “repentance,” a change of circumstances—things turning out otherwise than expected—is signified. For when you repent of having done something, you grieve over the deed that you did.

### Verse 5

**Kings.** (Augustine.) Those who wish, or wished, to destroy the name of Christ.

### Verse 6

**He will shatter**, that is, he has made them weak, etc., down to: and now he will judge among the nations, so that he may fill the ruins, not the things that have been raised up.

**He will judge among the nations.** (Cassiodorus.) He breaks kings on account of their pride; he judges peoples on account of their common sins; he does both so that they may be humbled for conversion. Or,

### Verse 7

**From the torrent.** (Cassiodorus.) From transitory and turbulent suffering. **On the way**, by which one goes to another dwelling.

[Col. 1031C] **He will lift up his head.** Hence: “For this reason God exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue should confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father.”

## Psalm 110

**Alleluia.** (Cassiodorus.) The first psalm arranged through all the letters of the alphabet, etc., down to: third, it asserts that the same people have been redeemed, and that the New Testament will endure, in the passage “Redemption.”

### Verse 1

**I will confess.** (Augustine.) This is not a confession of sins, but of praise: the former mourns, the latter rejoices; the former displays a wound to the physician, the latter gives thanks for health.

**In the council.** Not rashly, but rationally—that is, [Col. 1031D] on account of eternal things, as do all the righteous.

(Cassiodorus.) **In the council of the righteous.** Here he does not mean the council among all the righteous where the wicked are mixed in, but they already seem to be singing in the future fellowship, carried away by hope toward heavenly things. **In the council**, that is, when they judge with the Lord. **In the congregation**, when they have been gathered together from everywhere.

### Verse 2

**Great are the works.** This is the subject and cause of confession. The works of the Lord are great: that he makes the impious righteous.

**Sought out.** (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) There is nothing like them, while he permits the devil to rage, etc., down to: not so; for his righteousness endures forever and ever.

**In all his wills.** (Augustine.) Nothing surpasses the will of God. Even if he wills that you not sin, he does not always prevent it. If he wills to spare the penitent, he also wills to punish the impenitent; [Col. 1032A] thus God always fulfills his will in human beings, because there is nothing that a human being does from which God does not bring about what he wills.

### Verse 3

**Confession and majesty are his work.** (Cassiodorus.) As though he were saying: I will confess because the works of the Lord are great. Every work, too, is great if in it one sees the intention and will—which are confession of sins—and the majesty of good works; and also righteousness, that is, the reward that is justly given.

### Verse 4

**He has made a memorial.** (Cassiodorus.) Second, he says that the faithful have been satisfied with an abundant gift, promising the Lord’s coming, so that the inheritance may be eagerly sought.

(Augustine.) **He has made a memorial of his wonders.** Humbling one and exalting another, etc., down to: what will he receive when glorified in the future?

[Col. 1032B]

### Verse 5

**He has given food.** (Cassiodorus.) He makes confession and majesty, etc., down to: so that all things may be fulfilled.

**He will remember, etc.** (Augustine.) He did not give the whole of it, since he gave only a pledge, etc., down to: they enter through the anguish that pierces them because of the Passion.

### Verse 6

**The power of his works.** (Cassiodorus.) The power of his works is that the blind see, etc.

**Which he made known to the Christian people.** His purpose in the miracles was that they should believe.

### Verse 7

**To give them the inheritance of the nations.** (Cassiodorus.) As though he were saying: although he gives them the inheritance, they will nevertheless suffer many things.

**The works of his hands.** (Cassiodorus.) That is, of his power.

**Truth**, when he restores what was promised to the converted; **judgment**, which he threatens against the impious.

(Augustine.) **Truth**, which the holy martyrs hold, for which they are also judged here; and **judgment**, by which in the future they will judge those by whom they are judged here.

(Id.) **The works of his hands are truth and judgment.** Let truth be held by those who are judged, etc., down to: this is the inheritance of the New Testament.

### Verse 8

**All his commandments are faithful.** (Cassiodorus.) Because they preserve those who keep them; they are not lies.

**Confirmed.** They were not sent in vain, like human words. They are deeds, not merely words; they are in truth, because all things are fulfilled.

**In equity.** (Augustine.) Because all things are done with the balance of justice.

### Verses 9–10

**He sent redemption.** (Cassiodorus.) Third, it asserts that they have been redeemed and that the New Testament has been consecrated by eternal grace; or:

**His name: the beginning of wisdom.** (Cassiodorus.) That is, the Son, who in his humanity is holy and in the power of his divinity terrible. Therefore let the Advocate be loved and the Judge feared, so that you may neither be negligent nor despair.

**The fear of the Lord.** (Cassiodorus.) Fear of judgment is the doorway of conversion, if discernment of love is added.

**His praise endures.** The purpose of the psalm, for which “Alleluia” is prescribed, begins with praise and ends with praise. The faithful people, liberated from the devil and giving thanks, have expressed what the devout must do here and carry out in heaven: here, because he liberates; there, because he crowns.

## Psalm 111

**Alleluia of the return.** (Augustine.) Haggai and Zechariah lived long after David, etc., down to: may it be established eternally.

(Cassiodorus.) The completion of this building, etc., down to [Col. 1033A]: like people freed from captivity and cheerful because of the good things they possess.

### Verse 1

**Blessed is the man.** (Cassiodorus.) Here the Psalmist shows what follows liberation, etc., down to: third, he asserts that adversity comes upon the impious.

**Who fears the Lord.** Fear of the world makes people wretched, but fear of God makes them desire those things through which a person is blessed.

**In his commandments.** This is the fear of God: that one should will to do them. He does not say “he will do,” etc., down to: and an earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that is thinking of many things.

### Verse 2

**Mighty.** (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) Behold the rewards of that blessed man.

**His offspring.** That is, the reward of good work. **He will be mighty on earth**, not on this earth, where he is mocked, but in the heavenly one. Or even here, in this present time, in which he is less noticed.

**His offspring**, namely, works of mercy, from which comes the eternal harvest.

**Mighty**, because the kingdom of heaven is purchased even with the smallest thing, as though it were great. **Generation**, not of the flesh but of imitation.

Or, “the works of the upright.” They are upright who do not resist the Father when he corrects them and who believe him when he promises. They do not think their works have perished when they are not rewarded for them in temporal things. For there are some who do such good things while expecting a reward from God here, or wishing to please human beings; but that is not the blessed man. And yet:

### Verse 3

**Glory and riches are in his house.** That is, in the secret place of the heart, where he dwells with the hope of eternal life, where holy riches and eternal glory are stored.

**Righteousness.** This is his glory; these are his riches, although he has them from God.

**It endures forever.** As though he were not blessed only temporarily.

### Verse 4

**Light has risen.** (Cassiodorus.) Second, he treats of the Lord’s coming, etc., down to: so that he may fortify it beforehand in judgment with firm arguments [Col. 1033C] and assertions. Or,

### Verse 5

**He is merciful.** (Cassiodorus.) He who gives to the needy.

**He lends**, who gives a loan expecting to receive the same amount back.

### Verses 7–8

**His heart is ready to hope in the Lord; his heart is strengthened; it endures, etc.** (Augustine.) It is therefore clear that he does not seek his own things here, but the things that are Christ’s. He patiently endures hardships and confidently awaits the promises.

(Cassiodorus.) Or, if someone threatens evil, he does not fear, but remains ready.

### Verse 9

**He has scattered.** He hopes not to fear because he has scattered.

**He has given to the poor.** (Augustine.) Behold, this man was buying what he did not see; but the one who deigns to hunger and thirst in the poor on earth was storing up a treasure in heaven.

**His righteousness endures forever and ever.** (Cassiodorus.) He gave what was his and lived justly and piously; or, whoever gives what is his practices righteousness.

**His horn will be exalted in glory.** Because here he is humble, but there he will have power.

### Verse 10

**The sinner will see.** (Cassiodorus.) Third, he asserts that contrary things will come upon the impious. He encourages the good by the blessings of the blessed, frightens them by the evils of their enemies, and this psalm is an instruction for the faithful.

**He will be angry; he will gnash his teeth and waste away; the desire of sinners will perish**, saying: “What did our pride profit us, and the boasting of riches?” (Wisdom 5)

## Psalm 112

**Alleluia.** (Cassiodorus.) Since the one who takes up the nations on account of the merit of his humility deserves praise, he explains the title of the psalm. For, as we have said, *Alleluia* means “Praise the Lord,” and this is how the psalm begins. [Col. 1034A]

### Verse 1

**Praise.** (Cassiodorus.) First, the Prophet urges the devout to praise continually and proclaim him everywhere. Second, he himself does what he urges others to do, namely, he praises God in the words: “Who is like the Lord?” (1 Cor. 14).

Therefore, in urging praise, he shows who should praise, whom they should praise, for how long, where, and why. He says:

**Children.** Not in understanding, but in malice—especially pride—that is, the humble. Hence: “Do not become children in understanding, but be infants in malice, so that you may be mature in your minds.”

(Augustine, Cassiodorus.) “Praise the Lord, children”: the simple and pure, who ought to praise him.

### Verse 2

**May the name be.** (Cassiodorus.) Behold, he has said who they should praise and whom; then he adds for how long he should be praised: namely, always.

**May the name of the Lord be.** [Col. 1034B] Do not think that I am commanding you to praise only for an hour, etc., down to: through carnal nations, through spiritual heavens.

### Verse 3

**From the rising of the sun.** (Augustine.) Here he says that he ought to be praised everywhere.

### Verse 4

**Above the heavens.** (Augustine.) The apostles, through whom he reigns among the nations; and he is therefore inviting them to praise because he will reign over all.

### Verse 5

**Who is like him?** (Cassiodorus.) Second, he himself does what he urges others to do, so that he may teach others by his deed as well.

**Who?** No one who can exist by his own power.

**In the heights, etc.** Among angels and saints; and although he is exalted, he does not despise the humble.

### Verse 6

**The humble things.** These are those who are made exalted by his gift and in whom he sits.

**He looks upon the humble**, each one.

**On earth**, the saints whom he regards in this way, just as conversely he hates the proud.

[Col. 1034C]

### Verse 7

**Raising up from the earth**, from bodily labor.

**From the dungheap.** He is raised up whose fleshly vices do not dominate him.

### Verse 9

**Who makes her dwell.** (Cassiodorus, Augustine.) He explains where he raises and lifts up, etc., down to: from the mammon of iniquity through works of mercy.

**The barren woman.** (Augustine.) Namely, Sarah, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, which previously was barren; hence she is signified through Sarah.

He makes her, I say, dwell in a house, that is, in the Church of the Jews, among the Jews themselves, so that the two walls may be joined in the cornerstone and there may be one flock.

**Of children.** (Augustine.) These words are spoken in the person of those children, etc., down to: although I know that I am without children and a widow.

## Psalm 113

[Col. 1034D]

**Alleluia.** (Cassiodorus.) Here too “Alleluia” is given on account of another subject, etc., down to: as becomes clear in the exposition of the psalm.

### Verse 1

**When Israel went out.** (Augustine.) Here past events are not being narrated, but future events are being proclaimed, because future things were signified by those deeds.
