For this reason not everything that happened there is said here, but some things are expressed differently, lest the reader think that the past is merely being recalled.

(Cassiodorus.) First, the Prophet says what wonders God gave to the Hebrews figurally and to Christians spiritually. Second, he asks why these things happened there, in the words: “What is the matter with you, sea?” Third, he rejects the empty images of the nations and commends the worship of God, in the passage: “The images of the nations.”

**When Israel went out.** As though he were saying: when Israel, that is, the house of Jacob, went out from Egypt, that is, from a barbarous people.

[Col. 1035A]

**Barbarous.** (Augustine.) A language is barbarous when it does not praise God.

### Verse 2

**It became.** (Cassiodorus.) Just as that people, when it went out of Egypt, etc., down to: they can resist vices, and this too.

### Verse 3

**The sea saw**, that is, the sinners of the world.

**The Jordan**, which carries human beings away through various desires into the great sea—that is, into the bitter wickedness of this world. But these things cease at the Lord’s coming, as though turned backward.

**The sea saw.** (Augustine.) This is said here differently from the way it happened. There it is written that it stood on the side from which the waters flowed downward; nothing is said there about the mountains leaping for joy. Yet both what happened there and what is said here are figures.

[Col. 1035B]

### Verse 4

**Rams.** (Augustine.) Those who, with the horns of both Testaments, etc., down to: raising up every kind of knowledge against Christ.

**Hills.** (Cassiodorus.) From *colere*, “to cultivate”: the middling ones. For these things are not to be understood literally. Hence, through the sea and the Jordan—that is, through ancient events—do not doubt that those things are signified which now take place spiritually.

### Verse 5

**What is the matter with you?** (Cassiodorus.) Second, he asks why these things happened, in order to stir up wonder. And he answers: “At the presence of the Lord.”

### Verse 7

**At the presence.** (Cassiodorus.) One answer is given to both, because there is one author: he caused the ages to be astonished and caused his own things—that is, the mountains and hills—to rejoice. For when Christ appeared, human beings were moved from their superstition to the worship of God.

**At the presence of the God of Jacob.** And as though someone were asking, “Who is the Lord?” [Col. 1035C] he is the God of Jacob, not a recent god—he who makes them wrestle.

### Verse 8

**Who turns the rock.** (Cassiodorus.) The hard hearts of the Jews into the water of baptism.

**The crag.** The Gentiles, so that they too may pour forth flowing springs of preaching.

(Augustine.) That is, he was previously hard when he was unknown, etc., down to: it might overflow upon all believers, saying: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink.”

### Verse 1

**Not to us.** (Cassiodorus.) When he said that God gives good things, etc., down to: truth, when he restores rewards or punishes the impious. Therefore: “Give.”

### Verse 2

**Lest perhaps.** This is often charged by the impious against afflicted good people.

**Mercy.** (Augustine.) That is, restoration.

**Truth**, that is, a fulfilled promise.

[Col. 1035D]

**Where is their God?** (Augustine.) The nations that have visible gods customarily say this, because we worship the invisible God.

### Verse 3

**In heaven.** (Augustine.) That is, in Christ as man, according to the saying: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.” Or:

**In heaven.** (Cassiodorus.) That is, powerful over all creatures.

**He has done everything that he willed.** By this he appears omnipotent.

### Verse 4

**The images of the nations.** (Cassiodorus.) Third, he proves that the images are empty and shows how useful the worship of God is. Here there is a complete demonstration through both blame and praise.

(Augustine.) Having shown the power of the true God through his works, he turns to the visible gods of the nations.

**Silver.** (Augustine.) But because God made this, he says: “The works of human hands.” [Col. 1036A] They worship what they made from it. God created the material, but human folly added the form.

### Verse 5

**They have mouths.** (Augustine.) They are formed by hand, etc., down to: and they served the creature rather than the Creator.

### Verse 7

**They will not cry out.** (Augustine.) After “to speak,” which is proper to human beings, he adds this common feature, etc., down to: an image lacking both life and sense.

### Verse 8

**Like them.** (Augustine.) See the shameful character of the worship, when he says “like them,” because they truly are; or, let them understand themselves to be like them.

### Verse 9

**House of Israel.** (Cassiodorus.) Here he shows the usefulness of the Christian religion.

### Verse 10

**House of Aaron.** (Augustine.) But lest the matter appear greater among the superior groups, while hope belongs to the inferior, he adds: “House of Aaron.” [Col. 1036B]

### Verse 12

**He has remembered.** (Cassiodorus.) So that he might convert them, and through the same one bless those who have been converted.

### Verse 14

**Upon you.** (Augustine.) Because the number of teachers has increased.

**Upon the children.** Because the number of followers has also increased.

Therefore both of you—fathers and children—are blessed by the Lord, who made you heaven in the greater ones and earth in the lesser ones; or, who made every creature.

### Verse 15

**You are blessed by the Lord.** (Cassiodorus.) The one who wished earlier to be blessed now confidently says, “You are blessed.” This belongs to God, so that you may serve him.

Truly, you are blessed by the Lord, because even “the heaven of heavens,” that is, Christ, is for the honor of the Lord; or,

### Verse 16

**The heaven of heavens**, that is, the empyrean, he gave to the Lord Christ according to his humanity. **But the earth**, this lower earth, he gave to the children of human beings, so that they may purify themselves in it, or so that he may give the people to preachers. Hence: “As the Father sent me, I also send you” (John 6).

**The heaven of heavens.** (Augustine.) He says that they are those whose minds, etc., down to: whom the weak are still unable to see without assistance.

### Verse 17

**Nor all those who go down.** (Cassiodorus.) Or, “not all those who go down,” because the saints too have gone down, but not into the lower place.

## Psalm 114

**Alleluia.** This title is often repeated because the praise of God is both the dignity of works and the reward of labors—that is, it is both merit and recompense.

(Augustine.) The Prophet, freed from the pit of sins and established upon the rock, [Col. 1036D] first gives thanks because he has been heard and says that he called upon God against every danger.

This psalm is the consolation of the faithful against the sufferings of the world.

### Verse 1

**I have loved.** (Augustine.) The sheep that had gone astray says this; the son who has returned; the pilgrim of this world.

(Cassiodorus.) **I have loved.** Not on account of temporal goods given to me, like unbelievers, but because, etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; hence: “I will confess to you when you have done good to him” (Ps. 48).

He is loved perfectly when the mind is not moved by adversity but is kindled by hope. He explains this manner afterward: “I have loved.” Not because he made me a king or gave me prosperity, but because he hears prayer in distress.

### Verse 2

**And in my days.** (Augustine.) Namely, in the days of my misery, which I made for myself by sinning—days full of labor and sorrow, that is, of ancient corruption.

**I will call.** This does not occur without faith; hence the Apostle: “How will they call upon him in whom they have not believed?” (Romans 10).

When he says, therefore, “they will call,” he indicates that the lover is not idle.

Or, **in which**, “They surrounded me,” etc. Or, “in the days of salvation,” that is, in the time of fullness; hence: “Behold, now is the acceptable time,” etc. (2 Corinthians 6).

### Verse 3

**The pains.** (Cassiodorus.) Sins, from which come the pain and death of the soul; or eternal pains, which will be in hell.

**The dangers of hell.** (Augustine.) Having been drenched in carnal pleasure, I did not notice the evils surrounding me.

### Verse 4

**Tribulation and sorrow.** (Augustine.) As though he were saying: those things first surrounded me, but afterward I discovered that tribulation and sorrow—that is, outward affliction—are useful.

### Verse 5

**O Lord, deliver me.** (Cassiodorus.) Second, he cries out again, so that, once delivered, he may come to rest.

**The Lord is merciful.** (Augustine.) Because first he inclined his ear to me and called me.

**Righteous.** Because he scourges again.

**He has mercy.** Because he receives me into blessedness.

What he scourges should not be as bitter as what he receives is sweet, because the Lord guards the little ones whom he seeks as great heirs.

### Verse 7

**Return.** (Augustine.) Not because of your merits or strength, but because the Lord has dealt bountifully with you.

### Verse 8

**My eyes from death.** (Augustine.) Death is unbelief; hence: “Let the dead bury their dead”; and again: “The dead will not praise you, O Lord” (Ps. 103).

[Col. 1037C]

### Verse 9

**I will please.** (Augustine.) He said this, etc., down to: and this is in the land of the living, who live eternally.

## Psalm 115

**Alleluia.** This psalm is appropriately given the title “Voice of praise,” because its words are those of the martyrs, who grew strong through confession and obtained God’s rewards.

### Verse 10

**I believed, etc.** (Cassiodorus.) First, God’s benefits are recalled. While they doubt what worthy return they can make, the cup of suffering, which is given by God, comes before them. Second, they call themselves servants and sons of the maidservant, that is, of the Church, in the passage: “O Lord, because I am,” etc.

The true and fitting order is to believe first and afterward to speak, so that one who does not yet believe does not dare to speak, but confession may follow faith.

Yet, lest confession be attributed to human strength, he identifies what is proper to human beings as falsehood—something he would not easily know unless he had been carried upward by an excess of mind toward heavenly things. For it is a great thing if someone recognizes himself as lacking understanding.

And since a human being possesses no good of his own, what can be repaid?

**I believed.** (Augustine.) He does not say, “I believed and therefore spoke,” because he not only believed the other things that faith requires, but also believed together with them that he ought to hope for a reward by speaking and fear punishment by remaining silent. Hence love of speaking is imparted through the reward, while necessity is imposed through the punishment.

For this reason, whoever perfectly believes does not fail to speak what he believes. That servant was lazy or fearful, but faithful: what he received, he invested, and he gained profit from it. Therefore he enters into the joy of his lord, who says: “Well done, good and faithful servant; enter into the joy of your lord” (Matthew 25). [Col. 1038A]

### Verse 11

**In my excess.** Or, “in my ecstasy.”

(Augustine.) Here *ecstasy* is spoken of, etc., down to: which is what every human being is—a liar.

### Verse 12

**What shall I repay the Lord?** (Augustine.) Terrified, this man looks upon his weakness and sees that he must not presume upon himself. From himself a human being is a liar, as Peter also was when he presumed and was found to be a liar. Yet it is the power of God if he does not believe.

Seeing that this had been accomplished in him by God’s grace, he adds: “What has he repaid me?” He does not say, “for all that he has given.”

What good things, then, preceded in a human being, so that all God’s gifts could be called not a payment but a repayment? What preceded them except sins?

God therefore repays human beings [Col. 1038B] with good for evil, having suffered for them, while human beings repay him with evil for good.

### Verse 13

**The cup of salvation.** (Augustine.) Suffering, by comparison with a cup, etc., down to: as is said afterward.

(Cassiodorus.) It is called a cup because it is drunk according to measure. Hence: “God is faithful, who will not permit you to be tempted beyond what you are able” (1 Corinthians 10).

It is called “of salvation” because through it salvation is obtained for eternity.

### Verse 15

**Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.** (Augustine.) The one who suffered first gives others the pattern of imitating his sufferings. Hence: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints.”

He purchased it with the blood that he shed for them, so that they would not hesitate to die for him. Having been purchased by this price, he confesses his condition: “O Lord, because I am,” etc.

[Col. 1038C]

### Verse 16

**O Lord, because I am, etc.** (Cassiodorus.) Second, they call themselves servants and sons of the Church, because there is no place of true sacrifice outside the Catholic Church; no heretic should therefore think that martyrdom is pleasing to God.

**O Lord.** He marvels that he has received such things as the Lord received for the redemption of the world. And to increase his wonder he repeats: “I am your servant.”

**Son of the maidservant.** (Augustine.) The heavenly Jerusalem, free from sins and a maidservant of righteousness.

Those who are outside the Church are not sons of the maidservant, even if they call themselves servants—and martyrs—as the heretics do, because they bear the name of Christ.

**Son of the maidservant**, not a schismatic.

Or, just as the maidservant belongs not to herself but to the Lord, so I too, by my death, will give birth to some children for you, just as I did in my life.

### Verse 17

**You have broken my bonds.** (Cassiodorus.) Through the power [Col. 1038D] of martyrdom the bonds of sins are broken, because everything is washed away by blood.

Some believe this verse to possess such power that a person’s sins are forgiven if it is said in a threefold confession at the end of life.

(Cassiodorus.) **He who is precious.** “O Lord, I will sacrifice to you.” Speaking to God, he affirms what he had said above.

**I will sacrifice.** (Augustine, Cassiodorus.) And because you have broken them, I will sacrifice to you in gratitude, “a sacrifice of praise.” Thus, because—

### Verses 18–19

**I will pay my vows.** Not everywhere, but in the courts—that is, in the Catholic Church, not among heretics.

**The house of the Lord.** He shows what this house is.

**In the sight of all the people.** (Cassiodorus.) He who wished to suffer for all must be praised publicly, so that many may be built up.

**I will pay my vows.** I will give myself, who am the image [Col. 1039A] of God and must be returned to God, etc., down to: and here he names Jerusalem more openly.

(Augustine.) But lest anyone think that “Jerusalem” signifies only the Jews, who boast in that name, let him hear the following psalm: “Praise the Lord, all nations.” These are the courts of the Lord, for that is the people.

## Psalm 116

**Alleluia.** (Cassiodorus.) A brief psalm, the first atom of all—that is, without division. Because of its brevity it does not admit division, but surpasses all others through the concision of its speech. It is like a point among the psalms, from which different forms are produced. This remarkable variation is useful against weariness: sometimes sacred things are expressed briefly, sometimes at length.

### Verse 1

**Praise the Lord, all nations.** (Cassiodorus.) So that none may be omitted from the whole world.

(Augustine.) These are those courts of the house of the Lord, and that is the whole people of whom he spoke in the preceding psalm. I do not say that only the Jews—who try to claim this for themselves—should praise him.

**And praise him together.** (Cassiodorus.) So that the praise of all may be brought together as one, which is the mark of the Catholic Church.

### Verse 2

**It has been confirmed.** (Cassiodorus.) What he promised through the prophets he fulfilled at Christ’s coming; and he made his mercy firm, so that it may never be shaken, because the one who gave it guards it.

**It endures forever.** (Augustine.) Whether in the things he promised to the godly or in the things he threatens against the impious.

## Psalm 117

**Alleluia.** (Cassiodorus.) The fifth psalm concerning the first coming, adorned with many figures. It has verses ending alike, some with the same beginning, some intercalary, and other such ornaments. The faithful people, freed from sin, etc., down to: “Blessed is he who.”

### Verse 2

**Let them say now.** (Cassiodorus.) As I admonish you, so admonish one another; or, “let them say,” that is, “let them confess.”

**For forever.** Behold, four verses ending alike.

### Verse 5

**From tribulation.** (Cassiodorus.) He offers himself as an example in order to invite others to mercy.

### Verse 6

**The Lord is my helper.** (Cassiodorus.) The same beginning occurs in two verses.

### Verse 7

**I will despise.** Elsewhere: “I will see.”

(Cassiodorus.) Here, so that I may become safer and more cautious.

**My enemies.** Those who are to be condemned.

### Verse 8

**It is good.** (Cassiodorus.) Second, he says that one must trust in God alone, through whom he escapes the hostility of the nations and comes to true life.

### Verse 9

**In princes.** (Augustine.) In angels, etc., down to: who makes them good according to their measure.

### Verse 10

**All nations.** (Cassiodorus.) Behold from what he delivers: from hidden or open tribulation, either by not permitting one to fall or by raising one up after a fall.

### Verse 11

**Surrounding me, etc.** (Augustine.) As though he were giving the reason why he is able to overcome so much, he says what he first suffered in his head.

### Verse 12

**They surrounded me, etc.** (Augustine.) What was done by those who did not understand, the Holy Spirit foretells with mystical subtlety. The Jews, without knowing it, did what was good for all of us and made God sweeter to us by his Passion—just as bees, while thinking that they are storing something for themselves, make honey for others.

**And they burned.** Or this is better understood of the Church. After the Lord’s Passion, both the Gentiles and the Jews burned against the Church like fire among [Col. 1040A] the thorns of sinners. For they burned away those things—that is, sins—in the faithful people with the fire of persecution; by wishing to harm them, they advanced them.

**Because he avenged.** When they were converted, their wickedness was extinguished in them and they were joined to the Christian people; or, when at the end they are judged, they will experience the judgment of truth without mercy.

### Verse 13

**Being pushed, etc.** (Cassiodorus.) This occurs when the good are handed over to punishments so that they may fall away from the faith, and the Lord receives them.

(Augustine.) Whoever has the Lord as his strength and praise does not fall any more than the Lord falls. Those fall who wish to be their own strength and praise.

**I was pushed and overturned, etc.** After showing that he delivers by not permitting one to fall, he also shows that he delivers by raising one up from a fall.

### Verse 14

**He has become my salvation.** (Cassiodorus.) He does not become what he was not for himself; but for those who are converted he is salvation, whereas for those who have turned away he was not.

### Verse 17

**I shall not die.** (Cassiodorus.) The Church says this, since the persecutor thinks that he can destroy the Christian name by slaughter and funerals, although he rather increases it.

### Verse 18

**Chastening.** (Cassiodorus.) He indicates why he endured so much: “Chastening.” Whatever they do is the Lord’s chastening. Let them claim nothing for themselves; the one whose vices are being cleansed is not given over to death.

(Augustine.) Often a father corrects his children through wicked servants, preparing punishment for the servants but an inheritance for the children.

What the inheritance is can be learned from this: “Open the gates.” What is inside? “Entering, I will confess.”

### Verse 19

**Open.** (Cassiodorus.) Third, he desires that the gates of Jerusalem be opened to him, where he also speaks of the cornerstone.

**Open**, O prophets, who carry the keys of the kingdom of heaven.

**Gates.** (Cassiodorus, Jerome.) Through these gates, having entered by the doctrine, they truly praise; outside the Catholic Church there is no praise of God.

(Cassiodorus.) All these gates lead to one, which is Christ, through whom the righteous enter heaven. Hence: “I am the door; if anyone enters through me, he will be saved” (John 10). And elsewhere: “No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).

(Augustine.) Behold, he has mentioned both ages. And because this gate, Christ, has appeared, “I will confess to you,” joyfully giving thanks, because you heard me at the coming of the Son; for the earlier righteous were asking for his coming.

**The gates of righteousness.** That is, the gates of death, etc., down to: that is, through it to life.

[Col. 1040D]

### Verse 22

**The builders.** (Augustine.) The Jews alone, worshiping God while the others had been destroyed through idolatry, were building; but they did not complete the work, because they despised Christ.

### Verse 23

**It was done by the Lord.** Or, according to another reading, “It was done for him by the Lord.”

(Cassiodorus.) That is, for the honor of the Father.

### Verse 24

**This is the day.** This is the jubilee year, observed figuratively under the Law. It is called a year of release, or of inauguration, because at that time slaves were set free and possessions were restored to their owners. On this day we too have been redeemed from slavery to sin, and the eternal inheritance has been restored to us.

(Cassiodorus.) **This is the day.** Although he made all days, he singles out this day on which the Lord came. It is fitting to rejoice in it, because the devil lost his claim and humanity came back to life. And because this is so:

[Col. 1041A]

### Verse 25

**O Lord, save, etc.** Behold the desire of a great petition.

**Save**, from the destruction of the world.

**Prosper**, so that these sorrows may be turned into eternal joys.

### Verse 26

**Blessed, etc.** (Cassiodorus.) Fourth, rejoicing over Christ’s coming, he urges that the courts of God be frequented.

(Augustine.) Therefore cursed is the one who comes in his own name, etc., down to: who will be cursed.

(Cassiodorus.) **Blessed.** Praise for the coming; and, O other Christians, we elders, as priests, have blessed you. This is greatly beneficial because we blessed you from the house of the Lord.

**From the house.** (Cassiodorus.) That is, the Catholic Church, etc., down to: because joyful confession follows benefits.

### Verse 27

**Appoint the day.** (Augustine.) Great are those who go beyond, who touch the Word of God, who is with God, with their minds, etc., down to: that is, may he reach eternal joys.

[Col. 1041B]

**A solemn day.** In the Old Law (Deuteronomy 10), Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Booths were the three principal solemnities. At them it was commanded that no one should appear empty before the Lord.

Empty is the one who does not have Christ within himself, for Christ is the foundation that no one can alter. Hence, at those three solemnities, the faithful people offer a coin by hand, signifying the inward offering.

For on a coin there is the name and image of the king. Therefore let each person offer a spiritual coin, so that he may bear in himself the name of the king—that is, Christ, from whom the Christian is named—and may present to God the image, that is, the soul marked by the light of his countenance.

**The horn of the altar.** (Cassiodorus.) Or by the altar is understood the sacrament of the body and blood, etc., down to: he will not have eternal life.

[Col. 1041C]

Or, the altar is understood as the human mind. Hence, in the Law it was commanded (Exodus 27) that an altar be made four-sided and hollow.

It was to be four-sided because the human mind must be fortified by four virtues: prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance. It must likewise be hollow in order to receive the word of God and the fire of love.

For swelling repels what is poured into it. Hence, in Leviticus it was commanded (Leviticus 1) that, when a turtledove or pigeon is offered, the crop and the feathers be cast away.

The crop signifies the inflation of pride; the feathers, empty inquiries into lofty matters. Cast these away, therefore, so that you may be a hollow altar.

### Verse 28

**You are my God.** To put the sense of these words more clearly: let this festive day on earth, on which the lamb was slain, not be sufficient; rather, let it be established in repeated observance until, with minds exalted, one reaches his inward divinity, where we shall sing his praises in this way: “You are my God,” etc.

Thus, just as he began with praise, so he concludes with praise.

### Verse 29

**Confess to the Lord.** From the beginning, when we departed, to the end, when we return, there is nothing more wholesome or delightful than the praise of God.

## Psalm 118

We omit the exposition of this psalm because it is exceedingly long. See the *Enarrationes on the Psalms* of Ambrose, Cassiodorus, and Augustine, from which the Ordinary Gloss in this place has been reproduced word for word.

## Psalm 119

### Verse 1

**A song of ascents.** (Cassiodorus.) The blessedness that the preceding psalm sang in unified variety, etc., down to: by these steps one ascends and descends with the mind’s foot unhindered.

(Augustine.) **A song of ascents.** The name “ascents” is ambiguous among us, etc., down to: and the height of his own divinity.

The first step is to leave behind the evils of the world and renounce all vanity.

(Cassiodorus.) The beginning of progress is to abandon carnal vices and entreat the Lord. Hence, in the Old Law, when a Gentile slave was purchased, his fingernails were pared and his hair was cut (Deuteronomy 12), because one must strip off every kind of vanity before being devoted to God’s service.

From renunciation of the world, through certain steps of merit, one reaches perfect and eternal charity, which is established at the summit.

**To the Lord when I was in tribulation.** (Cassiodorus.) First, as he begins to ascend, he finds many people lying in wait and asks to be delivered from their tongues. Second, he complains about his association with the wicked: “Woe is me.”

### Verse 2

**Lord, deliver, etc.** When a person begins to ascend—that is, when he considers making progress, having despised the world and clinging to God alone—he begins to suffer the tongues of adversaries: those who slander and, what is more serious, who seem to offer counsel while turning him away from salvation.

Whoever does not suffer these attacks has not yet begun to strive for progress. Therefore, as one who is about to ascend, he first prays against them: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips.”

### Verse 3

**What shall be given to you, etc.?** (Cassiodorus.) Like someone thinking intensely, he hesitates and seeks a remedy: “What shall be given to you, or what shall be added to you?”

He uses two words: “given” and “added.” Arrows are given as weapons; coals are added as though for consolation.

### Verse 4

**Arrows.** (Augustine.) The heart is pierced by the words of God, etc., down to: so that the place may be pure for God’s building.

### Psalm 119

**Verse 5—“Alas for me.”** (Cassiodorus.) Secondly, he complains about dwelling among, and being mixed with, the wicked. Having received the arrows and coals, having become wheat, he is not yet in the granary but on the threshing floor, where much chaff is being pressed down. Seeing, therefore, many evils that he had not seen before, he cries out: “Alas for me!” Evils appear to no one unless he has become good. For when the grass grew and produced fruit, the weeds appeared.

**“Prolonged.”** Although the time is short, it seems exceedingly long to desire.

**“Kedar.”** (Id.) The son of Ishmael, from whom the Saracens descended—though they would more properly be called Hagarenes from Hagar. But they claimed their name from Sarah, who was more noble and free; both peoples are read to have lived in tents. Ishmael’s tents are rightly called Kedar: Kedar belongs to Ishmael.

(Augustine.) “Isaac, therefore,” etc., up to the point that, if the wicked cannot now be separated from the good, they must be endured.

## Psalm 120

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second degree is to seek divine protection, against which nothing is shown able to prevail. (Augustine.) When dangers meet someone departing from the world, he ought to request divine help, etc., up to: “Such is the one who raises his eyes to God.” (Cassiodorus.) First he raises his eyes and prays; secondly, he affirms what he prayed, showing the power of the help he obtained.

**“I lifted up my eyes.”** (Id.) He who, as though bent down, cried out now, drawing breath, raises his eyes to the holy intercessors.

**Verse 3—“Nor let him slumber.”** (Augustine.) If faith sleeps in you, Christ sleeps in you.

(Cassiodorus.) This is said according to human custom: when a weary watchman dozes, he suffers theft.

**Verse 4.** (Augustine.) “Behold, he will neither sleep.” “Christ sleeps,” etc., up to the point that, lest you should still think this concerns some human being, he adds: “The Lord keeps watch.”

**“He who keeps Israel.”** (Augustine.) He who cannot see the face, etc., up to the point that Christ does not sleep for him either.

**Verse 5—“The Lord keeps watch.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where he affirms what he had prayed. And as though someone asked, “Who is that guardian?” he adds: “The Lord keeps watch,” etc.

(Augustine.) It is not without reason, etc., up to: namely, the love of God and of one’s neighbor.

**Verse 6—“By day the sun shall not burn you, nor the moon by night,” etc.** (Id.) God is the sun, etc., up to the point that the moon, that is, the Church, will not permit you to be burned in the night of tribulation.

(Hieronymus.) Or, by day are understood prosperous circumstances, etc., up to the point that he thus preserves us now in prosperity and adversity.

**Verse 7—“The Lord guard your going in.”** (Cassiodorus.) He concludes everything, joining good endings to good beginnings.

(Augustine.) “The Lord guard your going in.” He guards those who enter, etc., up to the point that nothing will harm them forever.

## Psalm 121

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The third degree: great joy—to dwell in the Church with a pure mind and to serve God worthily during this pilgrimage. Hence we sigh for the heavenly Jerusalem, to which we are lifted on the two wings of love.

**“I rejoiced in these things,” etc.** First he rejoices that he has been urged to go to Jerusalem, where the saints will judge securely and together with the Lord. Secondly, as one ascending, he desires an abundance of peace: “Pray for the things that are for peace,” etc.

**Verse 4—“The testimony of Israel.”** (Augustine.) That is, in which it is recognized that they truly are Israel. For while the grains are with the chaff, everything is considered chaff; but when they have been separated, then there will be the testimony of Israel.

**Verse 5—“Thrones.”** (Id.) That is, the righteous, in whom God sits, etc., up to the point that all who are to be questioned should beware for themselves.

**Verse 6—“Pray.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where he speaks to the judges, wishing them an abundance of peace, which he proclaimed out of love for the brethren.

**“Those who love you.”** (Augustine.) Whoever loves in another the good that he himself cannot possess is credited as though he possessed it. Hence: If charity has nothing to give, let it give a cup of water; and it is credited to him as much as the many gifts of Zacchaeus are credited to him (Matthew 10). Their means are unequal, but their love is not unequal.

**Verse 7—“Let peace be.”** (Id.) Love is a virtue strong as death, etc., up to the point where he adds: “For the sake of my brethren.”

**“Within your towers.”** (Id.) That is, in your heights. There are few judges, but many will belong to each of them, whom they will receive into eternal dwellings. Then there will be abundance in the towers. God, however, is the whole abundance of both those who receive and those who are received.

**Verse 9—“For the sake of the house of the Lord our God.”** Or read the verse in such a way that it is an exposition of what precedes. It is as though he said: “I spoke peace concerning you for the sake of neighbors and brethren,” namely: “I sought good things for you because of the house of the Lord our God.” The meaning of these words is not changed.

**“For you.”** O heavenly Jerusalem, because you are the house of God; and thus, in loving you, I love God.

## Psalm 122

**A Song of Ascents.** (Cassiodorus.) The fourth degree: amid every kind of distress, one must steadfastly hope in the Lord until, having shown mercy, he hears. The one who previously raised his eyes to the mountains now raises them to God.

**Verse 1—“To you I lifted.”** (Id.) First, the voice of the afflicted looking toward God, not toward other patrons; secondly, he prays for mercy against those who insult him.

(Augustine.) “To you I lifted.” Where could he raise himself except toward the one to whom, ascending, he was making his way? This man does not attend to himself as the proud man does, who pleases himself. For he who displeases himself is pleasing to God; and whoever pleases God displeases himself. “I lifted.” The ascent, therefore, is in the affections, etc., up to the point that he is a pilgrim who longs for his homeland.

**Verse 2—“Behold, as the eyes,” etc.** (Cassiodorus.) A servant raises his eyes to the hands of his lord when he is in need or when he is beaten, because both are in the lord’s power.

**“As the eyes of the maidservant.”** (Augustine.) The servant is the people; the Lord is Christ; the maidservant is the Church; the mistress is the power and wisdom of God. Even if we are already sons and friends by grace, we are nevertheless servants by creation, because every creature serves God.

(Cassiodorus.) He gives the comparison of a male servant and a maidservant, of a lord and a mistress, so that the female and weaker sex may not think itself excluded.

**Verse 3—“Have mercy.”** (Id.) The second part, where he prays for mercy against those who insult him. The servant who is beaten, raising his eyes to God, breaks out into the necessary cry: “Have mercy.”

**“We are filled.”** So that when it is said, “What do you believe, madman? Do you see what you believe? Has anyone returned from the underworld and reported to you what happens there?”—behold, what I love, I see and enjoy.

## Psalm 123

**Verse 1—“Unless it were that.”** (Cassiodorus.) First, the holy martyrs, remembering how much they escaped, attribute it solely to mercy; secondly, they give thanks because they have been delivered.

**Verse 3—“Perhaps they would have swallowed us alive.”** Those are alive who know that an idol is nothing. Those are dead who think it is something. Therefore the dead are swallowed up: those who think that the evil they do ought to be done. But the living are those who indeed know that what they do is evil, yet, overcome by persecution, pass over into the company of the ungodly and prefer the sweetness of this life to God, as happened to certain people who, through fear of death, sacrificed to idols.

(Augustine.) Observe also that Peter, that is, the Church, swallows many, but not the living. To him it is said: “Kill and eat” (Acts 10). For he eats no one—that is, incorporates no one into his members—unless he has been killed, that is, has renounced the devil. He is therefore killed in evil but brought to life in good when he is eaten by Peter. The opposite happens to the one whom the devil swallows.

**Verse 4—“The water.”** (Augustine.) The sinful people—and this is by comparison with the Egyptians. This water flows as a torrent with force, but quickly passes away; hence he adds: “torrent.”

The Latins perhaps render the Greek **ἄρα**, used as an expression of doubt, as best they can. The meaning is clearer if it is said: “Do you suppose that our soul passes through?” That is, the magnitude of the danger scarcely permits this to be believed.

**Verse 5—“The intolerable water.”** (Augustine.) Without substance, as are vices, sins, and the sweetness of this life, etc., up to the point that it would bring the prodigal son, exhausted by prolonged necessity, back to his father.

**Verse 6—“Blessed be the Lord.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where the saints give thanks because they have been delivered and because the snare has been broken.

**Verse 7—“Our soul.”** (Augustine.) Or, just as when someone makes a great noise, etc., up to the point that it is like a snare.

**“Of the hunters.”** (Id.) The hunters are the persecutors; the bait in the trap is the sweetness of this life.

**“The snare is broken.”** (Cassiodorus.) Once the martyrs have been killed, the sweetness of life by which they might again be captured no longer remains; but they themselves were not broken together with it—instead, they were delivered.

**“Broken.”** (Id.) It is as though he said: Because it was made of iron, it was not torn like tow; such was the strength of their suffering and such the power of the one who delivered them.

## Psalm 124

**Verse 1—“A Song.”** (Cassiodorus.) The sixth degree: the confidence of the most faithful Christian is compared with the most solid mountains. He has this confidence in the Lord, so that he does not envy those who prosper in this world.

**“Those who trust.”** (Augustine.) This psalm teaches, etc., up to the point: “Who are these people? What sort of Jerusalem is this?” He describes it briefly.

**Verse 2—“Mountains around it.”** That is, angels, prophets, and apostles are its wall. Hence Isaiah says: “There shall be in it a wall and an outer wall” (Isaiah 26). But lest you remain in the mountains, he adds: “And the Lord is round about.” Therefore let hope not be in the mountains but in the summit of the mountains. Hence Isaiah says: “In the last days there shall be a mountain on the summit” (Isaiah 21), etc.

**“Those who trust.”** (Cassiodorus.) First he asserts, etc., up to the point that they are both many and one.

**“Mount Zion.”** (Hieronymus.) Christ, on whom the Church has been founded. That mountain, literally, will be shaken at the end of the world.

**Verse 3—“The rod of sinners.”** (Augustine.) They sometimes rule for the discipline of the good, but this will not always be so, as the prophet plainly says here. Therefore the righteous do not fail, because they know that a time will come when Christ, appearing in his glory, will gather all nations before him and divide them as a shepherd divides goats from sheep, placing the sheep at his right hand and the goats at his left.

**“The lot.”** (Cassiodorus.) That is, the righteous chosen by lot, or those who are God’s lot and inheritance.

**Verse 4—“Do good, Lord.”** (Id.) The second part, where, after strengthening the people, he prays for what he knows will happen: prosperity for the good and punishment for the wicked.

**Verse 5—“But those who turn aside.”** (Id.) Those perish under an equal judgment who turn aside from the commands of the ruler and those who persist in desiring evil works. They fail when those who compel them fail.

**“Peace upon Israel.”** (Augustine.) The homeland and inheritance are called by one name, which is Christ. For he himself is our peace, who made both one, and he will give us peace upon peace.

## Psalm 125

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The seventh degree, in the figure of the Old Testament, prophesies through the Christ who was to come a return from captivity, as from Babylon. Hence there is now consolation and sowing, so that a greater harvest may be gathered.

(Augustine.) Those redeemed by Christ’s blood and turned back from captivity sing these things while they are pilgrims, groaning on the way. Zion is Jerusalem among the angels, but captive among human beings.

**“When he turned.”** (Cassiodorus.) First the greatness of the deed is shown together with the greatness of joy; secondly, he prays for the conversion from the captivity that is still to come: “Turn, Lord.”

(Augustine.) Or, “when he has turned,” etc., up to: “Turn, Lord, our captivity.”

**“As.”** (Id.) This is not always used merely as a comparison but sometimes according to its proper force, as here. Hence it is also said: “He acted as a righteous man,” which he truly is. So these people become “as those who are consoled,” that is, they rejoiced, receiving consolation in the resurrection of Christ, who went before so that we might follow.

**Verse 2—“Our mouth.”** (Cassiodorus.) The hidden place of the heart, where joys first arise and afterward burst forth through the office of the tongue.

(Augustine.) “Our mouth”—the mouth of the heart. From it proceeds evil or good, which cleanses or defiles us. Hence it is not simply: “What proceeds from the mouth defiles” (Mark 7)—not from the mouth of the flesh but of the heart. You are not unclean merely by naming thefts and other evils; you are unclean when you think them, even if you remain silent.

**“Among the nations.”** (Id.) He does not say “all nations,” because not all believe.

**“He has magnified.”** They see that these people also perform miracles: a firm testimony coming from an adversary.

(Cassiodorus.) And truly he has magnified them, so that you do not doubt the words of the nations.

**Verse 4—“Turn, Lord.”** (Id.) The second part. He prays for the conversion that is to come, in which sowing will take place in hope of joy.

(Id.) At the coming of the Lord, foretold through redemption, they again pray that their sins may be forgiven. They rejoice in the universal remission and pray for pardon for themselves.

**“Turn, Lord, our captivity.”** (Id.) Literally, there was no such captivity in David’s days; but the world was captive under the devil, etc., up to the point that one must not therefore cease, because “the one who sows in tears…”

(Theodoret.) He calls Jerusalem the south, etc., up to the point that they are compelled to make their way like a torrent.

**Verse 5—“In tears.”** (Augustine.) Spiritual sowing is always in tears. Hence: “Blessed are those who mourn.” But those who sow in the flesh sow with joy; afterward comes weeping, because mourning occupies the end of joy.

(Id.) Zacchaeus: “Behold, half,” etc., up to: “Whoever gives a cup of cold water will not lose his reward” (Matthew 10).

**Verse 6—“Going.”** (Cassiodorus.) Through progress in the better life.

**“Carrying.”** Sending ahead, sending their possessions before them into that world.

**“His seed.”** His own, not what was obtained by robbery, but what came from his own labor.

**“Coming.”** To judgment. This is common to all, but only the good come to joy.

**“And they wept.”** (Augustine.) Because they were wretched, etc., up to the point that he desires that many should be sick.

## Psalm 126

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents of Solomon.”** (Cassiodorus.) The eighth degree, etc., up to the point that, in himself as the cornerstone, he built the Church from the two walls of Jews and Gentiles.

(Augustine.) “Of Solomon” is added because Solomon built the temple, as a figure of the peaceful Christ, who built the Church from two walls. Therefore, lest you understand that Solomon, he says: “Unless the Lord builds.”

Hope must be placed in this, but in no human being, because Solomon himself, who built the temple, fell.

(Cassiodorus.) First, he teaches how those who ascend ought to conduct themselves: they must learn that building and guarding come only from God. Exaltation in the future comes only after humiliation. Secondly, he says what the inheritance is and how it is gathered: “Behold, the inheritance.”

**“Unless the Lord.”** (Id.) It is as though he said: Jesus has now come and brought back the captives; Jerusalem, the city, is now being built. But those who ascend must learn that building and guarding come only from God, and that future exaltation comes only after humiliation. Even though they rejoice in the grace of the New Testament, no one should presume upon himself amid so great a gift.

**“The house.”** (Augustine.) Everyone who progresses ascends to this; everyone who fails falls from it. By loving God you ascend; by loving the world you fall. These are songs of lovers, burning with a certain holy desire.

**“They have labored.”** (Id.) All who preach the word of God in the Church labor in this building.

**“The city.”** (Cassiodorus.) He passes from the house to the city, so that presumption may arise neither from individuals nor from a small gathering. Although house and city are different according to the metaphor drawn from different things, there is nevertheless one Church, which both signify.

**Verse 2—“Before dawn.”** (Augustine.) If you rise before the light rises, the light is Christ, after whom one must rise, not before him. This is what the person does who places himself before Christ, wishing to be exalted here where Christ was humble—as did the sons of Zebedee. But resurrection, that is, exaltation, follows sitting, that is, humiliation, just as Christ our light rose exalted after death.

**“You have sat.”** Sitting sometimes signifies the honor of judging, but here it signifies humiliation.

**“You eat the bread of sorrow.”** (Augustine.) He eats the bread of sorrow who groans in this pilgrimage, that is, who refreshes himself in the valley of weeping amid affliction, saying: “My tears have become my bread day and night” (Psalm 41).

**“Sleep.”** (Cassiodorus.) Temporal death, in which there is secure rest.

**Verse 3—“Behold, the inheritance.”** (Id.) Secondly, what the inheritance is and how it is gathered. It is as though he said: The beloved will rise after sleep.

**“The fruit of the womb.”** (Augustine.) The womb of the Church, etc., up to the point that he acquired all through the obedience of his passion. Hence: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Psalm 2).

**Verse 4—“Like arrows.”** (Id.) But from where did so great an inheritance arise? Because the Lord is powerful: when he forcefully sent forth the arrows—the apostles—from the bow of sacred Scripture, they reached the ends of the earth. The children of those sent forth are therefore like those sent forth.

**“The children of those sent forth.”** (Id.) The children of the apostles, to whom it was said: “Shake the dust from your feet” (Matthew 18). But they appear in this way, etc., up to the point that they were sent by the hand of God to the ends of the earth.

## Psalm 127

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The ninth degree is that the peaceful one be feared chastely, since he alone exalts, guards, and builds. First he enumerates the good things of the one who fears; secondly, he wishes good things for the one who fears.

**“Blessed is everyone who fears the Lord.”** It must be known that there are four kinds of fear, etc., up to the point where the prophet says here: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord.”

**Verse 2—“The labors of your hands.”** (Id.) Notice that he began in the plural, saying “Blessed”; but because all are one in Christ, he continues in the singular: “The labors of your hands.”

(Augustine.) He says “labors of fruits” when he ought to say “the fruit of labors.” But because labors themselves are undertaken with joy on account of hope, they themselves bring delight and are now food; their fruit will be more delightful when the saints come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves.

**Verse 3—“Your wife.”** (Cassiodorus.) Although this could be understood literally, etc., up to the point that it pertains to the New Testament.

(Augustine.) Or the wife is understood as the Church, and the speech is directed to Christ when it says “your” and “yours.” Yet the voice or person is not changed because of the unity of head and body. Christ is one man: head and body; and each of the faithful possesses this in the head.

**Verse 4—“She shall be blessed.”** (Cassiodorus.) Where there is blessing, all good things flow together for the joy of sweetness.

**“She shall be blessed.”** (Id.) The second part, where out of piety he asks that those who fear may be blessed. He wishes here the good things of the one who fears, things that are not shared by the wicked.

**Verse 5—“Or, the Lord.”** (Augustine.) Of the Jews: “From Zion,” etc., up to the point that they cannot do so in the same way.

## Psalm 128

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The tenth degree: that the one who fears chastely bear everything for the sake of that which now benefits the Church amid the wicked.

**“They have often attacked me.”** (Augustine.) The wicked, although they hear the word of God, etc., up to the point that they bear so many wicked people.

(Cassiodorus.) First showing what the righteous person has endured, he consoles the weak. Secondly, he deals with the rejection of the persecutors: “The Lord is righteous.”

**“They have often attacked me.”** It is as though he said: O children, do not be amazed at these things, etc., up to the point that the Church grows amid adversities.

**Verse 2—“Indeed, they did not prevail against me.”** (Augustine.) That is, they could not prevail so as to draw me into consent to sin.

**Verse 3—“Upon my back.”** (Cassiodorus.) What the wicked cannot attempt openly against everyone, they secretly try to persuade in individuals, so that those who seemed to come from the front may not be perceived from behind.

**“They prolonged iniquity.”** Elsewhere: “They made their injustice far from me.”

(Augustine.) Although the wicked are with the good in the world, and even in the Church, no one should think that iniquity is close to justice. Although I bear them, their iniquity is far from me. Therefore no one should fear wicked people mixed with him, since they are far away.

**“The Lord is righteous.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where he deals with the rejection of the persecutors.

**Verse 4—“Those who hate Zion.”** (Id.) Not only open persecutors hate her, but also those who enter deceitfully. Whoever refuses to observe the word of God hates the Church.

**“Let them be like the grass of the roofs.”** (Cassiodorus.) The wicked are compared to the grass of roofs, etc., up to the point that there is no fruit for the wicked in either case.

(Gregory.) It is said that rushes dry out before all other grasses, etc., up to the point that they lose the appearance of greenness, etc.

**Verse 6—“Which, before it is plucked up.”** (Augustine.) They have not yet been finished in God’s judgment, and already they have no sap of greenness.

**Verse 8—“And they did not say.”** (Cassiodorus.) It was customary among the Hebrews for a traveler to bless those who were working. Hence this is said in the opposite sense: no blessing is given to those who labor in vain.

**“And they did not say.”** Those whom the angels will not gather, because the apostles did not preach to them. This is what he says:

(Augustine.) “And they did not say,” etc. It was especially customary among the Jews to say to all who were working: “The blessing of the Lord be upon you.” “We have blessed you in the name,” etc.

(Cassiodorus.) They bless the good, not in their own name but in the name of the Lord, from whom all things come, not from them.

## Psalm 129

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Id.) The eleventh degree, etc., up to the point where a joyful conclusion is set down with confidence of forgiveness: “Let Israel hope in the Lord.”

**“From the depths.”** (Augustine.) Whoever feels that he is in the depths, etc., up to the point that Scripture says: “When the sinner has come into the depths of vices, he despises.”

**Verse 3—“Who will endure?”** (Id.) Because almost the whole of human life is surrounded by the barking of sins, and every conscience is accused by its own thoughts. The heart that presumes upon its own righteousness is not pure. Let it therefore presume upon God’s mercy: “For with him there is propitiation.” Hence he adds:

**Verse 4—“For with you there is forgiveness.”** It is as though he said: “With what hope do you cry out?” “Because mercy is in you.” He says this: Or join the words in this way.

(Augustine.) No one can endure, etc., up to the point that there is therefore one hope: “For with you there is propitiation.”

**“Because of your law.”** (Id.) I endured the law of mercy, etc., up to the point that you gave this law in the very necessity itself.

**Verse 6—“The morning watch.”** (Id.) Let the morning watch hope, the one who hopes for nothing else from God than immortality.

**“From the morning watch,”** etc., up to the point that for this reason the head and tail of the victim were offered to the Lord under the Law.

**“Let Israel hope in the Lord.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where there is a joyful conclusion. Secure concerning himself, he proclaims that they should always hope in the Lord. It is as though he said: As the soul has hoped, so let Israel hope.

**Verse 8—“And he himself will redeem Israel from all his iniquities.”** (Id.) Here he has already said what the one whom he called merciful and abundant will do.

## Psalm 130

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The twelfth degree is humility, which he shows himself to possess here inwardly and outwardly. He therefore urges humility.

**“Lord, my heart is not.”** (Id.) First, by presenting himself as humble, he brings punishment upon the non-humble; secondly, by his own example he urges hope.

Showing, therefore, that he is humble inwardly and outwardly, he says:

**“Nor have I walked.”** (Augustine.) I was not proud; I did not desire, as though in miraculous things, etc., up to: “The greater you are, humble yourself in everything.”

**Verse 2—“If I did not think humbly.”** (Id.) Nourished on milk—which is the Word made flesh, so that I might grow toward the bread of angels, toward the Word who was with God—but not…

**“I exalted.”** Like the heretics. If they have begun to grasp anything, however imperfectly, or seem to have grasped it, they grow proud of it. While they are still infants at their mother’s breast and are carried in the hands so that they may grow—those who were carried in the womb so that they might be born—they are separated from the milk before the proper time, and therefore perish.

**“So is the recompense.”** (Id.) He binds himself under a curse, etc., up to the point that God will reveal that he judges otherwise, because he resists the proud and gives grace to the humble.

**“As a weaned child.”** Just as five stages are described, etc., up to the point that God was man but was not changed into a man.

**Verse 3—“Let Israel hope.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where by his own example he concludes while admonishing the others.

## Psalm 131

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Id.) In the thirteenth degree, already humble and gentle, etc., up to the point where Isaiah says: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble and quiet one who trembles at my words?”

**“Remember, Lord, David and all.”** (Id.) First, showing his vow to build the house, he prays that he may fulfill it. Secondly, he shows the house built: “Behold, we heard.” Thirdly, he states the promises of God made to the Zion that has been built: “The Lord has sworn.”

Therefore, wishing to build a house for the Lord, he speaks in the person of the whole Christ, the head: “O Lord,” etc.

**“David.”** (Augustine.) Literally, the gentle one, who did not repay Saul evil for evil.

**“As he swore and vowed a vow.”** That is, so that he may fulfill what he promised. Let no one presume by his own strength to render what he has vowed. The Church vowed in gentleness that she would be the house of God, than which nothing more pleasing can be offered to God. It is a house when it does not seek its own but rejoices in what is common. Evils arise from private possessions; hence he says: “If I enter.” He knew that his own possessions hindered him from becoming a place of God.

**Verse 3—“If I enter the tent of my house until I find a place for the Lord.”** The sentence is suspended, and there is aposiopesis, as though he said: “If I do this or that, let no one ever again believe me.” It is as though David swore to the Lord: “If I enter the tent of my house,” etc.

(Cassiodorus.) Or, from that point, it is spoken in the person of Christ: “If I enter the tent of my house,” namely, of the heavenly dwelling. The tent is the heavenly dwelling. “If I ascend,” etc., to the right hand of the Father, where there is the bed—that is, rest and the end of labors.

**Verse 4—“Sleep.”** The rest of the three-day death. Then he repeats the same thing in other words: “And sleep to my eyelids,” and rest for my temples until the holy Church has been founded through preaching. It is aposiopesis, as though he said: “Let no one believe me any longer.”

**“And to my eyelids.”** (Augustine.) There is one who does not sleep but dozes: now he is withdrawn from earthly things, now he turns back toward them; frequently he inclines his head.

**Verse 5—“And rest.”** From rest for the temples, sleep comes to the eyes, because the temples of those about to sleep begin to grow heavy. Therefore, when some temporal thing begins to give pleasure for sin, the temples grow heavy. But do not surrender yourself to that pleasure, and sleep will not come to your eyes if, as though rubbing your forehead, you drive away sleep by this thought.

**“I shall find.”** (Id.) He says this because he sought for a long time.

**“A place for the Lord.”** He sought it in himself, because God rests upon the humble and quiet person. A person is a place of God if he abandons his own concerns—or at least if he does not love himself but God.

**“The tent.”** (Id.) We still groan. We shall praise in the house, because groaning belongs to pilgrims; praise already belongs to those dwelling in their homeland.

**“Of the God of Jacob.”** He says that he has fulfilled the vow, just as above he said that he had promised.

**Verse 6—“Behold, we heard.”** (Cassiodorus.) The second part, where the house is shown to have been built, where he prays that they may be exalted, and that the Jews may not be wholly alienated.

**“We found it in Ephrata.”** (Augustine.) Or, “we found it,” etc., up to the point where there were thorns of idolatry.

(Cassiodorus.) “Behold, we heard,” namely, that the Lord would be born in Ephrata, Bethlehem, where the Lord was born. It was heard that he was to be born in Bethlehem, but because of the faith of the Gentiles he was discovered in the fields of the forest.

**Verse 7—“We shall enter.”** (Augustine.) We too, by persevering in our warfare, have entered—or shall enter—his tent, the tent of the God of Jacob. Whoever is joined to others through love as to living stones belongs to this house. Therefore the one who loves enters, and the one who enters becomes the house of God.

**“In the place.”** The house of God is where he ought to be worshiped; apart from it, God does not hear unto eternal life. The one who belongs to the house is joined to others by love. Or the place where the feet of the house of the Lord stand is Christ, in whom they persevere.

**Verse 8—“Arise.”** (Id.) It is said by the one who says, “I slept while troubled”: “Arise from death into your rest,” so that you may no longer be troubled, because death will no longer rule.

**Verse 9—“The priests.”** (Id.) He understands the same people as priests and saints, namely, all the faithful. Or, by priests he signifies the leaders of the Church, and by saints the faithful who are subject to them. Thus he distinguishes the ark, whose rising he had prayed for, according to the parts of the Church.

**“The priests.”** Just as in the Old Testament priests wore various ornaments, so evangelical priests are adorned with various virtues. These are the ornaments that God requires. Whatever the legal high priests carried on their garments, evangelical priests ought to have in their hearts.

**Verse 10—“For the sake of David your servant.”** (Cassiodorus.) “Remember.” And rightly do I say “for David’s sake,” because the Lord swore to David.

**“For the sake of.”** Then it is spoken in the person of David himself, asking God the Father.

(Augustine.) Because Christ turned his face away from the Jews toward the Gentiles, the Father is asked, for the sake of the remnant, that they may be saved. This was fulfilled in the apostles and in many others. He says: “For David’s sake,” as though he said: “Remember me also, so that for my sake you may not utterly reject the Jews.”

**Verse 11—“He has sworn.”** (Cassiodorus.) The third part, where he states the promises of God made to Zion once it has been built, that is, to the Church. David speaks either in his own person or in the person of the whole Christ.

**“And he will not frustrate,”** elsewhere “he will not repent.” (Augustine.) God is said to repent, etc., up to the point that you do it because you had gone astray; he does it and delivers.

**“From the fruit of your womb.”** He could have said “from the fruit of your thigh,” etc., up to the point that those whom David ruled temporally, Christ rules spiritually.

**Verse 12—“If they keep.”** (Id.) They appear to acquire merit, etc., up to the point that this is not changed.

**“And their children.”** (Cassiodorus.) If they keep the covenant, they will sit upon your throne, that is, they will share your blessedness. Just as you possess royal power, so will they according to their measure, and this “unto age of age,” that is, forever.

**Verse 14—“This is my rest.”** (Id.) God loves us so much that he says he rests when we rest in him.

**Verse 15—“The widow.”** (Id.) The widow is the soul that understands itself to be abandoned by every help except God alone.

**“With bread.”** God is the bread who made himself milk in the flesh.

**Verse 16—“His priests.”** Or a distinction should be made between priests and saints, as above. It means: “His priests,” that is, the leaders, “I will clothe with salvation,” that is, with Christ, so that they may be honorable in teaching. And “the saints,” that is, the subjects, “will rejoice with rejoicing” because of Christ.

**“They will rejoice with rejoicing.”** (Id.) Because they are clothed with salvation, etc., up to the point that whoever dwells in him is therefore exalted securely.

**Verse 17—“The horn of David; I have prepared a lamp for Christ.”** (Id.) The spiritual height of the Church, etc., up to the point before Christ’s death and resurrection.

**Verse 18—“I will clothe his enemies with shame,” etc.** (Cassiodorus.) The Son will do this, to whom all judgment has been given. But note that the Father, who speaks here, does what the Son does.

## Psalm 132

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Id.) The fourteenth degree: love, which makes the brethren dwell together as one, whence come blessing and life.

**“Behold, how good.”** This psalm is indivisible, etc., up to the point that the righteous man, rejoicing in the cohabitation of the brethren, says: “Behold, how…”

**“Behold, how good.”** (Augustine.) This verse is known throughout the whole world. Like a trumpet of the Holy Spirit, it gathered the divided together and produced very many monasteries.

(Cassiodorus.) “Behold.” It is as though the matter were expressed more by demonstration than by speech.

**“To dwell together as one.”** (Augustine.) This concerns all Christians, but it applies particularly to monasteries. From them, however, blessing descends to the others, including those brethren from Judea of whom it is said: “They had one heart and one soul.”

**Verse 2—“As ointment.”** (Theodoret.) The priestly oil, etc., up to the point that it perfects the fragrance of perfect virtue.

**“The beard.”** (Augustine.) Behold the specification: it refers to the apostles and the other primitive saints, who first contended in faith but could not be overcome, because the head had already gone before them in suffering.

**“Aaron.”** The priest who offered himself, etc., up to the point that they could not be overcome.

**“From there.”**

**“To the hem.”** (Cassiodorus.) Or, by the hem—which is the end of the garment—etc., up to the point that the benefit of harmony reaches the subjects.

**Verse 3—“As dew.”** (Id.) Dew is thin water, from which the earth germinates, and it signifies the grace by which sinners are converted.

**“Hermon.”** (Augustine.) Literally, a mountain beyond the Jordan, etc., up to the point that the others who are of one heart are taken up.

## Psalm 133

**Verse 1—“A Song of Ascents.”** (Cassiodorus.) The fifteenth degree: love of the world. This is the third psalm concerning love. Here he treats of love for God, just as above he treated of love for one’s neighbor. It is not that there is one grace by which God is loved and another by which one’s neighbor is loved. Rather, grace has different acts, and different things are loved.

He therefore urges the love of God. First, he invites them collectively to bless God; secondly, he wishes that the faithful be blessed: “May he bless.”

**“Behold.”** This is the language of one demonstrating. He specifies to whom he makes this demonstration: “you servants of the Lord.”

**“You stand.”** It is characteristic of servants not to sit in the house of their lord. Or the same people are understood: by the house is understood the Church, and by the courts the breadth of love. In love, which extends even to enemies, there is breadth; in hatred, narrowness. It is as though he said: You who stand—that is, persevere—“in the house of the Lord,” that is, in the Churches, and who stand “in the courts of the house of our God,” that is, in the breadth of love, where no one is constricted: bless.

**Verse 2—“Lift up your hands.”** Just as Moses lifted his hands while the people of Israel fought against Amalek, so “lift them up,” I say, “in the holy place,” so that by your intention you may perform eternal good works; otherwise it is of no value.

**“May the Lord bless you.”** The second part, where he wishes the faithful to be blessed. It is as though he said: Bless, and so that you may be able to do this, “May the Lord bless you” with the blessing that comes from Zion. He can do this because he is the one who made heaven and earth.

(Cassiodorus.) “May he bless.” Above he urges many to bless God, but he himself blesses only one, because although there are many, they are nevertheless one, and blessing belongs to unity. Hence one person was healed in the pool—the one who descended first. Be one, therefore, and the blessing will reach you.

## Psalm 134

**Verse 1—“Alleluia.”** (Cassiodorus.) After the degrees that lead to eternity, the Alleluia is composed, so that the Church may delight in the praises of God, for whom such a gift has been prepared.

**“Praise.”** First, by demonstrative exhortation he urges them, etc., up to the point where he adds who ought to praise and why: “Praise, servants…”

### Verse 3

**Praise the Lord, etc.** (AUGUSTINE.) If all things are praised because they are good, etc., up to the point where the whole seed of Israel is understood, the entire Church is contemplated.

**Sing praises to his name**, that is, praise him because he did what the reality signified by his name requires, when he gave himself incarnate to be tasted by human beings.

### Verse 4

**Jacob.** (ID.) The name is interpreted as “wrestler” and signifies those who wrestle against spiritual wickedness.

**Israel as an inheritance.** Literally: the Lord placed the other nations under the guardianship of angels; Jacob he chose for himself, so that he might cultivate, sow, possess, and preserve him as a field.

[Col. 1054B]

### Verse 6

**All whatsoever.** (ID.) As though he were saying: He is great in essence and great in works, etc., up to the point where the spirit of man is unknown; hence it is said, “Behold.”

### Verse 7

**Who brings forth the winds from his treasuries. Who struck the firstborn.** (ID.) Faith is the point from which we begin, by which a living person advances toward what is better. Egypt means affliction. Therefore whoever afflicts the Church and causes scandals, even if he is called a Christian, loses faith.

**From the farthest extremity.** Either from the lowest part of the earth or from the circumference of the earth’s boundaries.

**Lightning and rain.** Lightning produces terror; rain produces joy. Therefore the one who terrifies with lightning restores with rain.

### Verse 8

**Who struck.** (ID.) He did this among human beings because of his cup. If he has told you what you should love, listen also to what you should fear.

**From man to beast.** (CASSIODORUS.) He often repeats this, etc., up to the things that he destroys among both the wise and the ignorant.

### Verse 10

**Mighty kings.** (ID.) The spirits of the world: they are slain when they are unable to accomplish in us what they wish.

### Verse 11

**Sihon king of the Amorites, etc.** This happened under Moses. The Book of Numbers relates that, when they prevented the children of Israel from passing through their territory, they were struck down by him, and the people of Israel took possession of their land.

**Canaan.** (ID.) “Humiliation,” namely the evil that occurs when the holy fall from honor.

### Verse 12

**And he gave their land as an inheritance.** (ID.) That is, he gave the faithful the heavenly blessedness which the demons abandoned through pride. This is the true land of promise, more truly called an inheritance, which is in peace, than that historical land which the children of Israel often lost.

**An inheritance for Israel.** (AUGUSTINE.) The inheritance consists of the nations of Israel, that is, of the faithful people whom they nourish through tribulation by teaching patience, or whom Israel cultivates by conforming them to itself.

### Verse 13

**From generation to generation.** (ID.) One generation is that in which we are reborn through baptism; the other is that in which we shall rise again. God has not forgotten to call us in the former and crown us in the latter.

### Verse 14

**For he will judge.** (CASSIODORUS.) The reason for praise is that the Lord saw the people for whom he had done so much: he sent prophets to them and afterward the Son. But because they were hard-hearted, he will judge them in the future; and in his servants, that is, the faithful, he will take consolation when he restores eternal rewards. Behold, the progression of praise has reached judgment.

(AUGUSTINE.) Or in this way: therefore concerning the present, etc., up to the point where they may see, and those who see may become blind.

### Verse 15

**Images.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the second section. After he has filled himself with the praises of God, he rebukes the worshipers of idols by mocking them, because perfect praise of the truth consists in destroying falsehood. The same things were said above, but when repeated they increase the shame.

### Verse 16

**They have mouths and will not speak.** (AUGUSTINE.) The craftsman was able to make those external objects, but he could not give them a spirit, hearing to their ears, light to their eyes, or a voice to their mouths.

[Col. 1055B]

### Verse 18

**Let those who make them become like them.** (ID.) Those who know these things mock the idols, etc., up to the point where they do not perceive the good fragrance of Christ.

### Verse 19

**House of Israel, bless the Lord.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the third section. After mocking the idols, he urges all orders of people to celebrate the praises of God. It is as though he were saying: “Let the worshipers of idols become like them. But you, who are the house of Israel—”

**House of Aaron, bless the Lord.** (AUGUSTINE.) The superiors are the house of Aaron; the ministers, the house of Levi; and all the people who fear him are the house of Israel. All generally are the house of Israel. Let us all say with one voice: “Blessed.”

### Verse 21

**Blessed is the Lord.** (ID.) Or, according to the interpretation of the names, etc., up to the place where we shall see him in eternal peace.

## Psalm 135

### Verse 1

**Alleluia.** (AUGUSTINE.) This psalm contains the praise of God. Although many things are said here in God’s praise, his mercy is especially commended.

(CASSIODORUS.) The differing beginnings of the verses, etc., up to the point that the divine presence is likewise at hand when the psalm is sung purely.

**Give thanks to the Lord.** (ID.) First he sets forth the magnificence of God and the creation of the whole world. Second, he recounts what he did in Egypt and among the Jewish people as a figure of our own experience, at the words, “Who struck.” Third, he speaks about Christians, at the words, “And he gave their land as an inheritance.”

**Give thanks to the Lord.** (AUGUSTINE.) Let us now praise him, etc., up to the point where eternal blessedness is through mercy.

### Verse 2

**Give thanks to the God of gods.** He calls “gods” those to whom the word of God came, as in another psalm, where he says: “I said, You are gods and sons of the Most High,” etc. They are not called gods for the reason that they are all good. For if they were all good, he would not say in the same psalm: “But he judges among the gods,” that is, he distinguishes among them. Concerning these he also adds: “Give thanks to the Lord of lords.”

[Col. 1055D]

### Verse 3

**Who works wonders.** (ID.) Just as at the end it is placed everywhere, etc., up to the point: therefore give thanks, because his mercy is eternal.

### Verse 4

**Who alone works great wonders.** (ID.) For he performs some things through human beings or angels, but certain great things he does alone; these he goes on to describe first.

### Verse 5

**Who made the heavens.** (ID.) Therefore he made the whole creation by himself, etc., up to the words: ““You made all things in wisdom, O God.””

[Col. 1056A]

Or figuratively: **the heavens** are understanding, that is, the spiritual saints, to whom he has given not merely faith but understanding of divine things. The simple, however, who hold only a firm faith, are called earth, as though beneath the heavens. Because in the baptism they received they stand with firm faith, as it were upon the waters, he established the earth, as it were upon the waters.

### Verse 6

**The earth above the waters.** But how is the heavier earth carried by the lighter waters, etc., up to the point where it is said: “Thus the Lord sat beside the well,” that is, nearby.

### Verse 7

**Who made the great lights.** (ID.) That is, he bestowed gifts of grace upon his faithful.

### Verse 9

**The moon and the stars to rule the night.** (CASSIODORUS.) It can also be said mystically in another way, etc., up to the point where through these the lesser lights may shine.

### Verse 10

**Who struck Egypt.** (ID.) This is the second section, in which he recounts what he did in Egypt and among the Jewish people as a figure of our own experience. He now begins to recount what he did through human beings or angels.

**With their firstborn.** He struck the firstborn of Egypt, etc., up to the point where God excludes him from himself.

### Verse 12

**With a mighty hand.** (ID.) The hand of God is his invincible action, which proceeds from the arm, that is, from every singular power.

### Verse 13

**He divided the Red Sea into divisions.** (ID.) Literally, into twelve divisions according to the number of the tribes, so that each tribe would have its own path for passing through. Figuratively, in this way the world is crossed by various paths toward God. The Red Sea signifies the world.

[Col. 1056C]

### Verse 15

**And he shook off Pharaoh.** (ID.) He shook off the devil together with his ministers like dust, which is shaken off quickly. In this swiftness both God’s power is displayed and those earthly impurities are indicated which we customarily shake off.

**Pharaoh.** (ID.) The devil is appropriately understood through Pharaoh: Pharaoh kills the males and preserves the females; likewise the devil strangles virtues and nourishes lust.

### Verse 21

**And he gave their land as an inheritance.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the third section, where he descends to Christians, explaining the benefits given to them, so that you may know that there is one author of all things.

### Verse 22

**To Israel his servant.** He understands by Israel the servant, Christ, etc., up to the point where he gave no price to the Egyptians.

[Col. 1056D]

### Verse 25

**He gives food.** (THEODORE.) From his singular providence, etc., up to the words he says in the Gospels: “Consider the birds of the air, which neither sow nor gather into barns, and your heavenly Father feeds them.”

**To all flesh.** (AUGUSTINE.) To every class of human beings, both Israel and the nations—not as manna was given only to the Jews.

## Psalm 136

**A psalm of David.** (CASSIODORUS.) The third psalm concerning the lamentation of Jerusalem, etc., up to the point where this one concerns the captivity brought about by Nebuchadnezzar.

(AUGUSTINE.) Two cities are mingled in bodily form, etc., up to the point where those who in mind and desire are citizens of Jerusalem are described.

### Verse 1

**By the rivers.** (CASSIODORUS.) First he speaks of those who would be taken captive long afterward, etc., up to the point where, beginning with longing for his homeland, he says: “By the rivers,” etc.

**When we remembered.** (AUGUSTINE.) In an enemy land the memory of one’s homeland is sweet, etc., up to the point where both things belong to Babylon.

### Verse 2

**Upon the willows.** (ID.) Which are watered by the rivers of Babylon, etc., up to the point where, by delaying, we suspend them.

(CASSIODORUS.) The force of the grief is heightened when the pleasure by which they used to console themselves is suspended.

**For there they questioned us.** (BASIL.) From this they began to gain no small advantage, etc., up to the point where they wanted also to hear our songs.

### Verse 3

**The words of songs.** (AUGUSTINE.) Or “of hymns”: “What benefit is Christ?” or, “What is the other life?” But among those who are full of evils we ought not to strike the instrument so that it sounds; rather, we ought to suspend it.

(ID.) The devil cleverly seeks an opportunity to mock, etc., up to the point where he bound himself by an oath, saying: “If I forget…”

### Verse 4

**How shall we sing?** (ID.) Care must be taken lest someone, fearing to displease such people, seek their friendship and begin to take pleasure in Babylon.

### Verse 5

**My right hand.** (ID.) Whatever you do for eternal things, the right hand performs. If you direct yourself also toward something else, the left hand has intervened; and if you take pleasure in that as though it were the right hand, you lose eternal things.

### Verse 6
