**Let it cleave.** (CASSIODORUS.) Let me become mute in the praises of God—something that is the consolation of weeping and miseries.

**My tongue.** (AUGUSTINE.) The song of Jerusalem is our tongue; the song of the world is a barbarian tongue. A person who has forgotten Jerusalem is mute before God.

[Col. 1057C]

### Verse 7

**Remember.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the second section, in which a turning toward God takes place against the enemies. “Remember,” on the day of separation, so that they may be punished.

**The sons of Edom.** (AUGUSTINE.) The sons of Edom, that is, the Idumeans, hindered those who were rebuilding Jerusalem; or they were joined with Babylon in its destruction. Hence he says: “Daughter of miserable Babylon.”

Morally, Edom is carnality, which leads us into unlawful impulses.

**Edom.** (ID.) Esau signifies all carnal people; Jacob, the spiritual. The elder is the carnal person, the younger the spiritual, because “the natural comes first, then the spiritual.” All carnal people are enemies of the spiritual; hence he says: “Remember; free us from them.”

**Destroy it utterly.** (CASSIODORUS.) From the likeness of a cistern: when the water is drawn out, one reaches its foundation. But what benefit is it to take away the life of such people when eternal life is in the foundation, which is Christ? While the wicked think they are causing harm, they give crowns.

[Col. 1057D]

### Verse 8

**Daughter.** (AUGUSTINE.) Through succession the city of evildoers became the daughter of Babylon, just as Jerusalem, the city of the good, became through succession the daughter of Zion.

(CASSIODORUS.) Morally, the daughter of Babylon is the flesh, which brings confusion, etc., up to the point where they dash them against the rock, Christ, so that, shattered, they may perish.

### Verse 9

**Blessed is the one who will seize.** (AUGUSTINE.) What retribution? Babylon, while its offspring are still small, suffocates those born into the world with the errors of parents and of the age. Likewise, those who are already young, once given knowledge of God, dash Babylon’s little ones to pieces—that is, nascent desires—before they acquire strength, and thus conquer them more easily. But the greater ones too must be slain against the rock.

## Psalm 137

### Verse 1

**A psalm belonging to David.** (CASSIODORUS.) The captive who had wept, as though Jerusalem and the temple had been rebuilt, and as though he were a fellow citizen of that part of Jerusalem which had not been captive, namely the angels, rejoices and first praises the benefits given to him.

Thus, speaking in the person of the Church, which is in the higher realm in hope, awaiting being there in reality, he says: “I will give thanks.”

**I will give thanks to you, Lord.** First he commends the benefits given to him; second, he says how these benefits are extended to everyone, at the words: “Let all kings give thanks to you, Lord,” etc.

**In the sight.** (AUGUSTINE.) In praising, I set the angels before me. I expect to be made equal to them in dignity, both now and afterward. But in praising God they set nothing else before themselves except God himself. Therefore, in the sight of the angels—in that purity with which the angels behold you, so that they rest in you alone—I will sing to you.

[Col. 1058B]

### Verse 2

**Because of mercy.** (ID.) All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth. There are no other ways by which he comes to us, and no others by which we come to him. Let us render these to God: mercy in helping and truth in judging.

**Above all your holy name.** (CASSIODORUS.) Or, “because of your holy name,” when the worship owed to you became known to us.

### Verse 3

**In my soul.** And because a carnal multiplication can take place in the soul, he adds “strength,” as though I ask for nothing else in my soul except strength.

### Verse 4

**Let them give thanks.** (ID.) This is the second section, where he explains how these blessings are to be extended to everyone. As though following my example: “Let them give thanks,” etc.

**All the words of your mouth.** (AUGUSTINE.) These have now been revealed everywhere and sent to all nations, etc., up to the point where, when the fleece had been dried, they heard all the words, etc.

### Verse 5

**Great is the glory.** (AUGUSTINE.) If they are humble, they love and sing this. But if they exalt themselves, let them fear what follows.

**For the Lord is exalted. He regards the humble.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is not the human condition, in which the humble are despised and the proud are regarded; rather, the Lord regards the humble.

**He knows the lofty from afar.** (AUGUSTINE.) The proud person does not do this, etc., up to those who mourn this exile, as is added below.

### Verse 7

**If I walk in the midst of tribulation.** Otherwise he does not give life except in the midst of tribulation. Hence: “Blessed are those who mourn; woe to those who laugh.”

**Against anger.** (ID.) The very fact that they are angry with me is your judgment against them, that is, your punishment. For anger is punishment for them, not merely guilt. Therefore, by permitting this, you extend the hand of vengeance over them all.

**Your right hand.** God has neither a right nor a left hand, but God’s right hand is called eternal blessedness, and his left hand temporal blessedness. Sometimes, therefore, he does not save his saints in the left hand, but he always saves them in the right.

[Col. 1059A]

### Verse 8

**He will repay.** (AUGUSTINE.) What I cannot do, etc., up to the point where, in him, the prince of this world found no sin for which to kill him.

## Psalm 138

### Verse 1

**To the end; a psalm of David.** (CASSIODORUS.) A psalm full of profound mysteries, etc., up to the point where it is veiled in the prophets and revealed in the Gospel.

(AUGUSTINE.) The whole Christ speaks, as one complete man, etc., up to the point where there are “two in one flesh.”

**Lord, you have tested me.** (CASSIODORUS.) First, he speaks of God’s knowledge, etc., up to the fourth point, how the wicked do not harm him, at the words: “If you kill sinners, O God,” etc.

**Lord, you have tested me.** (AUGUSTINE.) Now restored to Jerusalem, etc., up to the point where this is the person of the whole human nature returning.

[Col. 1059B]

### Verse 3

**You understood.** (CASSIODORUS.) Here the foreknowledge of the Godhead is shown, etc., up to the point where the assumed human nature cannot be equal to the divine substance.

**From afar.** (AUGUSTINE.) While I am still in exile, before I come to my homeland, the father comes to meet the returning younger son because he understood his thoughts from afar—because the son had said within himself, exhausted by want: “I will arise and go to my father.”

**My path**, namely the evil path on which I went when I abandoned my father.

**And my cord.** (Alternative reading: “boundary”)—the point as far as I reached. I had gone far, but you were there. He speaks like a fugitive caught with God’s vengeance pursuing him.

### Verse 4

**And all my ways.** Before I went along them, you permitted me to go in hardship, so that I might return if I did not wish to endure hardship; this I confess.

**For there is no deceit in my tongue.** We have now been justified in your grace.

### Verse 5

**My last things**, when I fed pigs; **my former things**, when I asked for my portion of the substance—this according to the parable.

Mystically, **former things** are when we fell through the ancient sin; **last things** are punishment, when we entered this mortality, which is the final state if we wish to return; otherwise what remains is eternal punishment.

**You formed me** for the labors to which we are all born.

**You placed.** (Alternative reading: “You weighed down your hand”)—the avenging hand, weighing down the proud beneficially so that it might raise up the humble, in the burdened hand.

### Verse 6

**Wonderful and incomprehensible to me. Knowledge has been established.** It is not easy for me to contemplate you, whom I proudly abandoned, as things were before, when I was with you, when I said: “Give me my portion of the substance.”

**From myself**, that is, from my sin.

**It has been strengthened.** (Alternative reading: “It has prevailed.”)

**And from myself I shall not be able to reach it.** (AUGUSTINE.) In Exodus we read that the Lord, etc., up to the point where I am not hidden from you, whose boundary you see.

### Verse 7

**Where shall I go from your spirit?** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the second section, where he now considers that he should not flee from him but toward him—from the angry one to the reconciled one. This will happen through him, with whom the world is filled: “The Spirit of the Lord fills all things.”

**Where shall I flee from your face?** He turns here and there as though seeking a place of flight.

### Verse 8

**If I ascend into heaven, you are there, etc.** (AUGUSTINE.) If I exalt myself, I find one who restrains me. If I grow proud of my righteousness, you are there, whose righteousness it truly is.

If I descend, coming through sin, **to hell**, or into the deep, and unwilling to confess, I say: “Who sees me?” You are present to punish. He has found a plan, but in this way I shall be able to flee from the angry one.

### Verse 9

**If I take the wings**, the two wings of charity which I had lost.

**Wings.** (CASSIODORUS.) They are of my power, that is, the efficacy of the Godhead, which raised the body from the tomb. He took them at dawn, before the light, that is, at the time of the resurrection, and dwelt at the farthest limits of the sea, that is, above the vastest extremity of the world.

**And if I dwell at the farthest limits.** (AUGUSTINE.) In my mind, at the end of the world, so that I may not love the world but its end, in which there is rest for me. But he himself also leads there; hence what follows:

### Verse 10

**For there too your hand will lead me.** Considering the length of the journey, he adds:

[Col. 1060B]

### Verse 11

**And I said: Perhaps darkness will trample me, etc.** The iniquity of the world is abundant, by which the wings of charity can grow cold. And because in the night I despaired of crossing the sea, the night became illumination for me.

The woman came—God’s wisdom—which had lost the drachma bearing the image of the king, that is, the human being. She lit from herself a lamp made of clay, that is, flesh, and when the night had been illuminated she found the drachma.

**And I said.** (AUGUSTINE.) I considered the matter.

**Perhaps you.** He calls the lower part of the rational creature “darkness,” which stands in opposition—namely, wicked people or the flesh. Hence he fears. The meaning is: “Darkness,” that is, the lower rational creature holding the left-hand path.

**They trampled me.** (ID.) I was indeed afraid in this way, but the night became illumination in my delights—that is, in those who, previously night, will be illuminated in their delights.

**Because of you.** Sinners.

### Verse 12

**They will not be darkened, etc., and night**, by sinners who dwell in it.

**Like the day**, that is, the saints from the Jews.

**Like its darkness, so also its light**, because to the extent that you acknowledge, to that extent he forgives. But how does this happen to me? Because you possessed my reins.

**Because darkness.** (AUGUSTINE.) Whoever does not confess his sins darkens his own darkness; but if he confesses, God illuminates him.

**Like its darkness.** The night of our human life, that is, its misery, etc., up to the point where the light does not exalt him.

### Verse 13

**For you possessed my reins.** (ID.) How does this distinction arise in you? Because the inner possessor holds not only the heart, that is, the thoughts, but also the reins, that is, the pleasures, so that the light of night may not delight us, but the light of his wisdom.

### Verse 14

**I will give thanks to you.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the third section, where he says how great is the exultation and multiplication of the one flying back to God, when God illuminates him and possesses his reins.

**My soul shall know exceedingly.** (AUGUSTINE.) Now my soul knows very greatly. Previously your knowledge was wonderful to me through myself, and I could not reach it; but now I can, because you have illuminated the night, possessed the reins, and received me from the womb—that is, because your grace came to me and illuminated me.

### Verse 15

**My bone was not hidden from you, which you made in secret.** (ID.) “Bone” derives from *os*, “bone,” not from *os*, “mouth,” etc., up to the words of the Apostle: “As sorrowful, yet always rejoicing.”

(BASIL.) Again he speaks of God’s foreknowledge, either saying that all things are his mysteries, or referring to something else—namely, his workmanship and formation.

**My substance in the lower parts of the earth.** (AUGUSTINE.) In the flesh, and yet the bone does not yield to the evils of this lower realm, etc., up to the point where they should not despair.

### Verse 16

**Your eyes saw my unformed state, and in your book all things, etc.** (ID.) Up to this point he has spoken in the person of the body; here he now speaks in the person of the head.

**Days shall be formed.** (Alternative reading: “They shall wander by day.”) Here “day,” which still remained, was Christ, etc., up to the point where the apostles were made leaders and shepherds of the Church.

As though deservedly I strengthened them, etc., up to the promise made to Abraham: “I will multiply your seed like the stars of heaven and like the sand of the sea.”

[Col. 1061B]

### Verse 18

**I am still with you, etc.** As before the death which the Jews thought they had brought about.

Or, **still**, that is, even in death, which does not appear to belong to the dead.

Or, although the resurrection is a sign of divinity, nevertheless I am still hidden from many: **with you**, that is, as you are.

(AUGUSTINE.) **I am still with you.** Not yet with them through knowledge, because they do not yet recognize him; for they did not recognize Christ immediately after the resurrection.

Or, throughout all this time I am with you in hiddenness at the right hand of the Father, before I am revealed in the glory in which I shall come.

### Verse 19

**If you kill sinners, O God, etc.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the fourth section, concerning how the wicked do not harm him.

(AUGUSTINE.) **If you kill.** He adds what he suffers in the meantime, etc., up to the point where at the judgment he will say openly: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you; depart from me.”

### Verse 21

**Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord?** As though he were saying: “If you kill them, do I not hate those who hate you? I too shall kill them.”

(AUGUSTINE.) It is as though heretics, not understanding, etc., up to the question: “How, then, am I contaminated by their mingling?”

**Test me, Lord.** (ID.) Up to this point he has spoken about heretics and others who follow them, separated from the Church. Now he also speaks about the wicked or hypocrites joined to him, whom the Church endures and mourns.

It is as though heretics separate themselves and others, etc., up to the words: “But you, O God, test me and know.”

## Psalm 139

[Col. 1061D]

### Verse 1

**To the end; a psalm of David.** (ID.) A complaint, groaning, and prayer of the body of Christ placed among the wicked, not yet possessing the good in reality but in hope, where there will be complete exultation. He urges us to pray to God against the evils of the world.

### Verse 2

**Deliver me, Lord, from man.** (CASSIODORUS.) First he sets forth who the enemies are and what evils they stir up, opposing prayers to them. Second, he says what help he has against evil, at the words: “I said to the Lord.” Third, he discloses what the enemies’ evils are, at the words: “The head.”

Thus the Church, laboring among the wicked, cries out.

**From the unjust man.** (AUGUSTINE.) The one who harms is unjust. Therefore, after saying “from the evil man,” he added, as an explanation, “from the unjust man.”

[Col. 1062A]

### Verse 3

**Who have plotted.** (CASSIODORUS.) He explains how the wicked persecute. They attack the good in three ways: with tongue, hand, and heart. He begins with the heart, saying: “Who have plotted,” as though he were saying: “Deliver me from the people of the wicked.”

(AUGUSTINE.) Although they often profess good things with their lips, they nevertheless have plotted iniquity in their hearts.

### Verse 4

**They have sharpened.** He shows how they persecute with the tongue.

**Like a serpent.** (ID.) In a serpent there are cunning and the deceit of harm. Therefore it also crawls, having no feet, so that it will not be heard when it comes. Its movement is smooth but not straight. Thus the wicked crawl toward harming others, concealing poison beneath a gentle movement. Hence he adds: “The poison of asps is beneath their lips.”

[Col. 1062B]

### Verse 5

**Guard me, Lord.** (CASSIODORUS.) He now speaks of the persecution carried out by the hand, that is, through deeds: “Guard me,” because the enemy deceives in many ways that cannot be anticipated.

### Verse 6

**The proud.** (AUGUSTINE.) By this name he briefly described the entire body of the devil. Hence they call themselves righteous and refuse to confess. Every proud person is also envious, like the devil, who envied the human being what he himself had lost.

**And they stretched out cords as a snare, etc.** Hence Isaiah says: “Woe to those who drag sins like a long garment,” because they add sins to sins, etc., up to the point where he is sent into the outer darkness.

### Verse 7

**I said to the Lord.** (ID.) A *diapsalma*. This is the second section, concerning the help available against evils. It is as though he were saying: “The wicked attack in so many ways; what remedy is there amid so many and such great evils?”

**I said to the Lord: You are my God.** Great confidence. Although he is the God of all, he is especially the God of those who enjoy him.

**Hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication.** (ID.) The voice of human beings and their soul, etc., up to the point where they are not the Lord’s people, whom you purchase not with a purse but with your blood.

### Verse 8

**You have overshadowed my head with the strength of my salvation.** (ID.) You who give the powers of my salvation, etc., up to the point however fiercely the enemy may rage.

### Verse 9

**Do not hand me over, Lord, to my desire.** (ID.) The devil proposes profit, etc., up to the point where this happens only according to your desire.

### Verse 10

**The head of the circuit.** (CASSIODORUS.) A *diapsalma*. This is the third section, where he describes what the enemies’ evils are.

(AUGUSTINE.) It is as though he were saying: “Your shadow protects me,” etc., up to the point where they are overcome either by assertion.

**The labor of their lips will cover them.** (CASSIODORUS.) That is, their false and lying assertion will cover them, because they are overcome by their own false assertion.

[Col. 1062D]

### Verse 11

**Coals will fall upon them.** (AUGUSTINE.) Or “coals of fire upon the earth,” etc., up to the words of the Apostle: “To some we are the fragrance of life unto life, to others the fragrance of death unto death” (2 Cor. 2).

### Verse 12

**The talkative man.** (ID.) Whoever wishes to be directed, etc., up to the point where necessity, not will, arises from external things.

**The unjust man**, etc., **in destruction.** This does not happen to the poor man. If he is seized by evils, he is not nevertheless seized for destruction. God scourges every son whom he receives.

And although the good are now afflicted, nevertheless they will confess amid hardships—which is more praiseworthy:

**And they shall dwell**, and therefore nothing in the world is feared.

[Col. 1063A]

### Verse 14

**Nevertheless.** (CASSIODORUS.) The conclusion of the psalm, where he says that if the good are delivered and vengeance is taken upon their enemies, they do not attribute this to themselves but to God. Hence also: “And they shall dwell with him.”

**They shall dwell in your presence.** Because they will see God as he is.

## Psalm 140

### Verse 2

**Let my prayer be directed.** (CASSIODORUS.) Let prayer be incense, etc., up to the point concerning the one who repents at the end.

**The lifting up of my hands, etc.** (AUGUSTINE.) Let everyone understand this from the head, etc., up to the point where he continues from the voice of the body.

[Col. 1063B]

### Verse 3

**Set a guard, Lord.** Observe that he asks for a guard to be placed over both the heart and the mouth. A double defense is necessary, so that neither an evil thought may relish iniquity nor a perverse will burst forth into foolish words.

**A door.** (AUGUSTINE.) From the likeness of one who stands guard at a door so that no one may enter or leave who is not permitted to do so.

### Verse 4

**Do not incline.** (CASSIODORUS.) As though he were saying: “Set a door for this purpose, so that he may not excuse himself.” This is the supreme vice that dominates human beings, and therefore they are slow to repent. Hence it is written in the Book of Kings: “To resist is like the sin of divination, and to refuse to comply is like the crime of idolatry” (1 Kings 15).

**For making excuses for excuses.** (ID.) It is the custom of the shameless that, when caught, they first excuse themselves by means of some falsehood; when convicted of that, they seek other excuses, attributing their vices to circumstances or necessity, lest they ever yield to the truth.

**I will not associate.** (ID.) Or, “I will not be bound together.” Those are said to be bound together when two are tied at the same time, so that one obstructs the other and free escape is impossible.

**I will not be bound together in the likeness of the flesh.**

**With the chosen.** (AUGUSTINE.) The chosen are those who justify themselves, despise others like the Pharisee (Luke 18), and defend their sins by every possible means. This person does not wish to be bound together with such people, that is, associated with them, lest they impede him.

### Verse 5

**The righteous man will correct me.** (CASSIODORUS.) This is the second section, where the faithful person, now corrected by the righteous man, rejects false flatterers and seeks to benefit the wicked by word and conduct; in this he also asks to be guarded.

**But let not the oil of the sinner, etc.** (ID.) Feigned affection, which softens minds away from the rigor of truth toward harmful things.

[Col. 1063D]

### Verse 6

**Judges.** (AUGUSTINE.) Powerful and learned men who judge concerning morals, etc., up to the point where everyone honors him.

### Verse 7

**They will hear.** (ID.) With the ear of obedience, not like Adam, etc., up to those who are near to a curse.

**The fatness of the earth.** (ID.) There are certain contemptible things from which the earth nevertheless receives its richness, etc., up to the point where they are the bones and support of the faithful or of faith.

### Verse 8

**Beside hell.** (AUGUSTINE.) He says “beside hell,” not “in hell,” because although they die by the common lot, they do not descend into hell like the wicked; rather, eternal life is given to them.

**For toward you, Lord.** (CASSIODORUS.) Having acknowledged the frailty of human beings, he flees to divine remedies.

Do not take me away from your good things, but let my hope always be in you, and let my eyes always look toward you. For this person does not ask for anything contrary to what the saints desire: namely, to be snatched away from the world and to be with Christ.

[Col. 1064A]

### Verse 9

**Guard me from the snare.** By “snares” and “scandals” he briefly indicates the evils of the whole world. Snares are the alluring bonds of the desires of the flesh. But when the devil makes no progress through these, he strives through scandals, which he stirs up through restless people.

Or otherwise: by those **who set a snare** he means manifest persecutors; by those **who work iniquity** he means those who consent to them and fall away through fear of persecution.

The meaning is: “Do not take away my soul, but rather guard me from the snare of persecution which they have set for me.”

(AUGUSTINE.) This is what persecutors do: they place the food of this life as though in a mousetrap. If the bird loves this food, it falls into the trap, because through fear of death it succumbs to persecution.

**Guard me from the snare.**

**From the scandals of those who work iniquity.** That is, from the scandal of those who, by consenting to the persecutors, fall and thus work iniquity.

It is as though he were saying: “Guard me from the persecutors who terrify, and from those who have fallen.”

### Verse 10

**They will fall into the net.** The words are appropriate to the comparison, since he does not wish to be bound together with such people.

**They will fall from vice into vice, but—**

**I alone am until I pass over.** “Alone,” that is, because he does not walk with the worst people.

**Alone.** (AUGUSTINE.) The same thing that he says, etc., up to the point where the other ancients did likewise.

[Col. 1064C]

**I shall pass over.** Like a traveler in this world who is captured by no pleasure.

## Psalm 141

### Verse 1

**Understanding of David.** (CASSIODORUS.) This psalm is the fifth of those entitled with the name “prayer.” Nothing different is said here from what has been said in the other psalms, but the same things are repeated.

(AUGUSTINE.) Since such repetition provides for common human weakness, these matters are not repeated uselessly; repeated, they are more firmly committed to memory. Hence it is written in Proverbs: “A desirable treasure rests in the mouth of the wise” (Prov. 12), because the wise person considers what he has heard and ruminates on it by recalling it. But the foolish person swallows it—that is, he does not reflect on it and gives it over to oblivion.

These are the clean animals in the Law, which ruminate; the others are unclean.

David, fleeing Saul, hid in a cave. Yet this psalm does not concern that event, but its signification. David signifies Christ. The cave signifies the flesh, or the world, or the tomb. Thus David, Christ, is with his members in the world; or Christ is in the flesh; or in the tomb.

### Verse 2

**With my voice I cried to the Lord.** First a prayer is set forth against evils; second, he speaks about the end of evils, at the words: “I cried to you, Lord.”

He therefore urges us to pray. Speaking in the person of the whole Christ, as one crying to God from a cave, he says: “I have pleaded.”

(AUGUSTINE.) He explains “I cried” by “I pleaded.” It is as though he were saying: “My cry is a plea, not a murmur and not blasphemy.”

[Col. 1065A]

### Verse 3

**In his sight.** (AUGUSTINE.) The Lord will repay. Pray in secret. Hence in the Gospel: “But when you pray, enter your room, and when you have shut the door, pray to your Father who sees in secret,” etc. (Matt. 6).

### Verse 4

**And you knew.** (ID.) He adds this so that those hearing “my spirit failed” would not think him cast down. It is as though he were saying: “If they think that I have been cast down because my spirit failed, you see me standing, whose Spirit gives me life.”

**Paths.** Of righteousness, which they do not see.

**In the way.** There are many ways because there are many commandments; there is one way because everything is reduced to one thing, namely charity.

[Col. 1065B]

(AUGUSTINE.) **In the way**, according to their desire; **beside the way**, according to the truth. For Christ is the way. He does not allow them to set a snare in the way, so that there may be no path for us to take; nevertheless, he allows them to set one beside the way, so that we may not turn away from the way.

### Verse 5

**I looked to the right hand.** (AUGUSTINE.) The wicked did not see it. Hence: “And there was no one who knew.”

(CASSIODORUS.) When you suffer everything, who knows what you are attending to?

(AUGUSTINE.) Whoever attends to the right hand sees; whoever attends to the left is blinded.

Or, the apostles did not stand at the right hand because they were scattered by carnal fear, but I persevered.

**Flight has perished**, both bodily and mental.

**And there is no one who seeks.** (CASSIODORUS.) Because there is no consolation, and he has been left alone for the Passion.

**Flight has perished.** (AUGUSTINE.) He says that he is enclosed. Flight has perished because he did not flee in spirit, though at times he did so bodily. The enclosed person does not flee bodily because he cannot; the strong person does not flee in mind because he does not wish to.

Flight has perished for the enclosed or the strong—flight, that is, of the kind mentioned in the Gospel: “He sees the wolf coming and flees” (John 10), where the Lord condemns the hireling.

But bodily flight is something else, which the Lord permits when he says: “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matt. 10).

**And there is no one who seeks my soul.** The soul is sought either by persecutors or by those who love it. Thus flight perishes in two ways: both for the captive and for the strong.

### VERSE 6

“I cried out.” (CAS.) The second part, where he treats of the end of evils. “My hope.” Because I choose you from among all things. “Portion.” He humbly and generally says that his portion is in the land of the living, although the whole of it is his. This is clear from what he said to the thief: “Today you will be with me in paradise”; and paradise is the land of the living eternally.

### VERSE 7

“From those who persecute me.” For the devil, through his instruments—that is, through the sons of distrust—persecutes the body, so that the heart’s ruin may take place within.

### VERSE 8

“Bring my soul out of prison,” and so forth. (AUG.) Speaking in the person of the Church, he explains from what it must be delivered: elsewhere, from prison. Because it is distressed in corruption—which is the punishment of the body—after those distresses there will be, throughout its whole life in the house of God, confession, that is, praise of God; for now prison prevents confession. This prison can also be understood as the world, or the cave, where everything is vain; hence he asks that the soul be led out, since it suffers much there, and so forth, up to “but its corruption and its temptation are a prison.”

## PSALM 142

A psalm of David. This psalm is the seventh of the penitential psalms. There are seven of them so that, by the same number by which we sinned, we may wash away our sins. (CAS.) For just as we sin throughout the week of this world, so by this number of psalms a remedy of repentance is set against sins. These psalms have this pattern: they begin with tears and end in joy, so that no one may despair of pardon. (AUG.) As Absalom did to David, so Judas did to Christ; false brethren did so to his body; or the reference is to unlawful impulses and action.

### VERSE 1

“Lord, hear,” and so forth. (CAS.) First he seeks an opening; second, he recounts his evils and what he has done in response, at “because he persecuted”; third, a prayer of supplication is presented, confirmed by reasons, at “hear me speedily”; fourth, a joyful conclusion is given, at “your Spirit.” He urges repentance and prayer, and calls us to pray. In the person of the whole Christ he says: “O Lord,” and so forth.

“In your truth.” (CAS.) This is not contrary to humility, which was asking to be heard; rather, the truth and justice of God prevent him from disputing with the one who prays and from judging the one who condemns himself. Hence it adds: “and do not enter”; he did not ask for the justice of judgment. (AUG., CAS.) “In your truth,” that is, in your justice. Or he calls “justice and truth” that which spares the penitent and absolves those who condemn themselves, taking “truth” and “justice” as referring to the same thing. The sense is: “in your truth and in your justice,” that is, according to the justice and truth by which you pardon the penitent and those who accuse themselves.

### VERSE 2

“And do not enter into judgment.” (AUG.) Those enter into judgment with the Lord who establish their own righteousness; this humble man does not. Hence the prophet says: “Why do you wish to contend with me in judgment? You have all forsaken me, says the Lord.”

“With your servant.” It is unworthy to say “with your servant,” rather than “with your friend.” And if you call him a friend, I call myself a servant: I return as a fugitive, I seek peace; I am not worthy to be called your son.

### VERSE 3

“Because he persecuted.” (CAS.) The second part, containing the account of the evils he suffers and of what the persecutor has done against him.

### VERSE 6

“I remembered.” (AUG.) The members say this, and so forth, up to “but you did not begin to exist.”

“I meditated.” Because all things are indeed good; in this he perceives that whatever good is in him is from God.

“On the works of your hands.” As if he said: I sought the craftsman in his work, and the creator in all created things; your creature has become a spectacle for me.

“I remembered the days.” (CAS.) Recalling that God made heaven and earth and did good to the ancients, he forgets the miseries of the world. From the things God has made, he consoles himself.

### VERSE 7

“Speedily.” (CAS.) The third part, where a prayer of supplication is presented, confirmed by reasons.

“My spirit has failed.” (AUG.) May your Spirit fill me, because mine has failed; now I am poor in spirit. For whoever lives by his own spirit is proud in his spirit and exalts himself against God. Hence elsewhere: “You will take away their spirit, and they will fail” (Psalm 103).

“Into the pit.” He descends into the depths because he also loses confession: he sets before himself license to sin without hope of pardon, with the reins of iniquity let loose. Such a person does not hear God saying: “Turn to me, and I will turn to you” (Zechariah 1).

### VERSE 8

“In the morning.” (CAS.) After the night of sins. (AUG.) It is morning when sins are released.

“Make your way known to me.” God did this, and so forth, up to “we shall reach the pure light, the Word who was in the beginning with God.”

“My soul.” (CAS.) I have brought it as a vessel to the fountain; fill it, therefore.

### VERSE 10

“Your good Spirit.” (CAS.) The fourth part, where there is a joyful conclusion.

“For your name’s sake, O Lord, you will revive me in your equity.” Here the grace of God is commended: he says that he is revived not by merits but by the name that is Jesus. Yet, together with this, the grace of equity shows mercy, because although God does everything freely, it nevertheless belongs to his justice to justify suppliants whom he sees the demons attacking.

## PSALM 143

### VERSE 1

“A psalm of David against Goliath.” (CAS.) David, the whole Christ, and so forth, up to “and thus his head is cut off with his own sword.” David killed Goliath; Christ killed the devil, and so forth, up to “therefore the following psalm is spiritually entitled ‘Praise.’”

“Blessed.” (CAS.) A triumphant psalm, and so forth, up to “praying to be delivered through him,” at “God, my song.”

“Who teaches my hands.” (AUG.) That is, through the Holy Spirit, and so forth, up to what follows.

“My mercy.” (CAS.) Since it would take too long to explain the reasons in detail, he briefly touches on each point, and so forth, up to “because, with contempt and wonder, he adds: ‘Lord, what is man, that …?’” (AUG.) “My mercy.” Because you give me the ability to be merciful, and so forth, up to “therefore forgive, and I forgive; give, and I give.”

### VERSE 3

“Because you regard him.” (AUG.) It is a great thing that God esteems and values a human being so highly that he gave his Son for him; the Son even becomes bread for him, although he is the bread of angels. For God does not esteem a human being in the way a human being does, who buys a horse more dearly than a person.

### VERSE 4

“He has become like vanity; his days are like a shadow.” (ID.) When the human being was created, he was made like truth; by sinning, he became like vanity. All transitory things are vain in comparison with the truth that always remains. (CAS.) That is vain which, falling away from its own substance, fades away, like smoke or a shadow. Thus the human being himself wastes away; hence it adds: “His days,” that is, his conspicuous—or transitory—life, passes away like a shadow.

### VERSE 5

“Lord, bow down.” (AUG.) Humble David, speaking in the person of the Church, full of grace and trusting in God, calls upon God’s help as he fights here. It is as though he said: We are in combat, but do not let us fail.

“Lord, bow down.” (CAS.) “Lord” opens the same matter, and so forth, up to “and the form of God took the form of a servant.”

### VERSE 7

“Send forth your hand.” (CAS.) He directs his words to the Father: “Send forth your hand,” that is, Christ, from on high, where he is with the Father, so that he may put on flesh. (AUG.) Or he is speaking of the second coming in the person of the Church. It is as though he said: Do this now. “Send forth your hand from on high,” that is, Christ from heaven for judgment. For the Lord will come with the voice of an angel and descend from heaven with the trumpet of God. Then, in the person of the Church, he adds: “Deliver me,” namely, by that hand. “And free me,” and so forth, as in the text.

### VERSE 9

“God, I will sing a new song to you.” (CAS.) The second part, where, as though the one whom he was beseeching had come as victor and deliverer, he promises to sing to him in the New Testament and the Old. He also asks to be delivered by him from those who think blessedness consists in earthly things.

“A song.” (AUG.) By another name this signifies the law, which he signified through the five stones.

### VERSE 10

“With the sword.” (AUG.) What he called “waters” above, he calls “the sword” here; hence here also he adds what he said there: “And rescue me from the hand of foreign sons.”

“Of the wicked one.” Concerning this it is said: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Psalm 56). There is also a benevolent sword, of which the Lord says: “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10). This is the two-edged sword (Revelation 19), powerful with its two edges, namely, the Old and New Testaments, by which all putrefaction is cut away from the members of Christ.

### VERSE 12

“Whose sons.” Here he explains who the foreigners are, what their right hand of iniquity is, and how they have spoken vanity. (AUG.) He enumerates their happiness: this is their right hand, this is the vanity they speak when they call these things blessedness. (CASS.) “Whose sons.” Or, mystically, these things can be understood from that point onward, and so forth, up to “but they have sprouted with new errors.”

“Daughters.” (CASS.) Those who do not possess the strength of steadfastness.

“Composed.” They are not beautiful by nature but adorned by human beings. These daughters are the thoughts or preaching of those who do not possess the true Church but only its likeness.

### VERSE 13

“Storehouses.” Hearts made from various things; hence they exhale foulest belchings, which stink.

“From one thing to another.” Unstable, because they have no root in truth.

### VERSE 14

“Their sheep are fruitful.” Literally, because he wishes to show that they cling to perishable things. It is as though he said: Their livestock is fruitful, while they themselves are barren in faith. Hence, mystically, their disciples are these fruitful sheep, because they beget many others in error.

“In their goings-out.” Not in their goings-in, because all the good they appear to possess quickly goes out from them into things destined to perish.

“Oxen.” Not lean from labor but fat from idleness, like those who abound in riches while themselves are starved of truth. Or, mystically, the oxen are teachers who abound in earthly things.

“Walls.” These are made only of stones in gardens or vineyards; and since even these do not collapse for them, they are prosperous.

(CAS.) Neither passage nor tumult interrupts their quiet, and so forth, up to “which leads to death.”

### VERSE 15

“Blessed.” He does not reproach them because they abound in these things, but because they regard them as their right hand, that is, as their blessedness. This is the vanity they have spoken. Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob also abounded in these things. Happiness is the left hand, that is, what is temporal and mortal.

## PSALM 144

### VERSE 1

“A psalm of praise, of David himself.” (CAS.) This psalm briefly contains what is widely spread throughout the divine Scriptures, and so forth, up to “so that no one could err in his praise.”

(AUG.) God fills the saints with the Holy Spirit, and so forth, up to “therefore may his Spirit praise him in his servants, because he causes himself to be praised.”

(CAS.) As there are seven penitential psalms, so there are also seven spirits, according to that mystery in which the Lord commanded Moses to place seven lamps in the tabernacle, shining with perpetual light.

“I will exalt you.” (CAS.) First the prophet promises limitless praise; second, he says that all will complete God’s praise in nine ways, at “generation and generation”; third, he explains the same things more fully, at “merciful.”

“Forever and ever.” (CAS.) Whoever does not begin here will be mute in the future.

### VERSE 2

“Every day,” and so forth. (ID.) Whoever deserves to praise him here every day will praise him with continual exultation in the eternal day.

(AUG.) He rightly says “every day” now, so that when the one day without end comes, he may go from praise to praise, just as from virtue to virtue.

“Forever and unto the age of the age.” (CAS.) Concerning this praise it is said elsewhere: “Throughout the ages of ages they will praise” (Psalm 38), because they will always love the one whom they will always see, and nothing is more delightful than that vision.

### VERSE 3

“Exceedingly.” (CAS.) In one word he gave us something to contemplate that cannot be fully grasped; therefore never cease from praises.

### VERSE 4

“Generation and generation.” (CAS.) Second, he promises in nine ways that all will complete the praise of God.

“Your works.” (AUG.) If we fail in greatness, let us at least praise the one who works because of his works, the creator because of created things, and the creator because of creatures. (CAS.) There are nine works: power, magnificence, holiness, wonders, strength, the greatness of terrible things, remembrance, and justice, which will be explained later. From these, as from places and seeds, all praise is drawn, just as every argument is derived from a limited number of places.

“And your power.” (AUG.) Works do not praise him except to proclaim the power of the one who works. But some eloquent people praise the creature while forgetting the creator. The holy praisers, however, if they love and praise the works, praise the one who made them more greatly; and on account of these things they love him. If some beauty, usefulness, or power is perceived in created things and is praised, it is praised more greatly in the one who made them. If you praise the works, you also praise yourself, who are God’s work. Yet the saying comes to mind: “Let not your own mouth praise you, lest you appear arrogant” (Proverbs 27). But this is not arrogance, because you are praising God in yourself, not yourself.

### VERSE 6

“And the power.” If he did not threaten, there would be no correction; if he did not encourage, there would be no exhortation. He is therefore both lovable and fearsome. Accordingly, those who preach the eternal kingdom will speak of the power of the one who disciplines and punishes; they will not be silent about eternal fire.

### VERSE 7

“They will pour forth the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.” (AUG.) Through his abundant sweetness he himself first remembers us, calling us and anticipating us with his grace; thereafter we remember him.

He says “they will pour forth,” not “they will eat.”

(AUG.) The one who learns eats; the one who teaches pours forth. Yet he pours forth what he eats. This remembrance is exceedingly sweet, and it must be eaten and poured forth. Therefore eat in such a way that you may pour forth.

### VERSE 8

“Merciful and compassionate.” (CAS.) Third, he explains more fully what he proposed briefly in the second part. It is as though he said: They will rightly praise him in these things, because he is compassionate, and so forth. The parts of praise are set out here, as above, but they cannot all be explained individually; for who could fully explain his works or his power?

(AUG.) “Merciful and compassionate.” To those to whom he has granted pardon. “Patient.” Toward those to whom he has not yet granted it, but whom he awaits in order to grant it.

### VERSE 9

(CAS.) “Mercies.” He begins with works, so that he may be called compassionate when he restores those who fall. “Merciful” by nature, even when he creates. “Patient”: this is taken from the second place of praise, namely, from the power that he praises—not because he suspends the earth, restrains the seas, paints the heavens with stars, and so forth, but because he tolerates sinners so that they may be converted.

“And his mercies.” (AUG.) For if you remove your evil works, so that only his works remain in you, his mercy will not abandon you. But if you do not abandon your works, his severity will be directed against your works, when he says: “Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25).

### VERSE 10

“Let all your works confess to you, O Lord.” (AUG.) Let them praise you like things that lack the sense required for praising, yet are the material of praise; for when you investigate them, you discover in them great power that comes from God.

“And your saints.” (CAS.) Everything that exists confesses either by itself or through rational creatures. Or “saints” means angels and human beings. This concerns holiness, for the holiness of God itself requires that the saints confess to him.

### VERSE 11

“The glory of your kingdom.” (ID.) This is therefore taken from wonders. It is as though he said: How wondrous is the one who made heaven and earth and filled them with various good things!

### VERSE 12

“To make known.” (ID.) This is taken from the power of terrible things, and so forth, up to “to which nothing magnificent can be compared.”

### VERSE 13

“Your kingdom,” and so forth. (ID.) He praises him for the permanence and effect of his dominion. This is taken from greatness: if it is great to rule for a time, it is greater to have no end to one’s dominion.

“The Lord is faithful in all things.” (ID.) This is taken from abundant sweetness; hence above: “the memory of the abundance of your sweetness.” He is faithful because his coming has fulfilled the gifts. It also belongs to abundance that he raises those who fall and lifts up those who are crushed. Thus the remembrance of his sweetness is preserved and poured forth in his praises.

### VERSE 14

“Those who fall.” (CAS.) From their evils, for God raises them all. Or from temporal things, as with the saints—for example, Job—who lose something in this world and become cast down: these are those who fall. Yet he confirms them all, because “the just man falls seven times and rises again,” while “the wicked are weakened by evils” (Proverbs 24).

“And lifts up all who are crushed.” (AUG.) Those who belong to him, because he resists the proud.

### VERSE 15

“The eyes of all hope in you, O Lord.” (ID.) He treats justice more fully, so that one who hears of mercy may fear the just one. It belongs to justice to satisfy those who hope, bodily or spiritually. Food is not always to be given, but at the appropriate time; for it is beneficially withheld from many who ask.

“And you give them their food at the proper time.” (ID.) Thus the physician gives the sick person what is appropriate, and so forth, up to “blessing God at all times.”

### VERSE 16

“You open your hand.” (ID.) Even if you do not give at some time, you give at the proper time; you delay, but you do not take away.

### VERSE 17

“Just.” (CAS.) By the very name he reveals justice, so that it may plainly be shown that this praise concerns justice. His ways are his dispositions and wills, all of which are just, even when he scourges.

“On all his ways, and holy in all his works.” It must be understood that “ways” pertain to disposition, while “works” pertain to effect; these are distinguished according to us. But with him, willing is doing, because things have being from his will.

### VERSE 18

“The Lord is near to all who call upon him.” (CAS.) He is propitious, being everywhere; this too concerns justice.

### VERSE 19

“He will do the will of those who fear him.” (ID.) He concludes concerning justice: it is right both to guard those who love him and to destroy sinners.

### VERSE 21

“Praise.” (CAS.) After everything has been explained, a brief conclusion follows, by which he concludes what cannot be explained.

## PSALM 145

### VERSE 1

“Alleluia.” (CAS.) This word is like salutary music, like a heavenly harmony, expressing the praise of God and delighting not only human beings but also angels. It is appropriately prefixed to this psalm, where the just man urges his soul to praise God, because in adversity the soul is sometimes disturbed, whether it wishes to be or not. Hence above: “Why are you sorrowful, my soul, and why do you trouble me?” But in order to remove its disturbance, he suggests joy from hope, if not yet from possession: “Hope in God,” and so forth.

(AUG.) With this hope raised up, the soul praises God here. (CAS.) First he advises himself, as though advising everyone, to praise, so that prayer may not be directed toward vain things; and, as though yielding to this counsel, he asserts that he will praise where he will be able to do so fully. Second, he urges others not to hope in human beings, at “Do not trust.” Third, he teaches that all hope must be placed in the Almighty, at “Blessed,” and so forth.

### VERSE 2

“Praise the Lord, my soul.” But the question is: From whom is this counsel given, and to whom? If the flesh is said to counsel the soul, this does not seem true, since counsel is ordinarily given to an inferior by a better and more worthy being; but the flesh is inferior to the soul. For although the soul is blamed because it is sinful, it is nevertheless said to be better by nature than the body, which is praised in its own kind, because spiritual nature surpasses the body, which it moves, governs, animates, and apprehends; and the soul itself, being infinite, is near to the substance of God. Thus gold, although blamed because it is dirty, surpasses lead, which is praised for its purity; and likewise a bad human being surpasses the best horse.

Therefore the flesh does not give counsel to the soul, even when it is greatly subdued and pacified; nevertheless, it is dead because of sin. Nor does mortal flesh give counsel to the immortal soul, since it is always beneath the soul. Rather, the higher part of the soul, namely the mind, which contemplates divine wisdom, cleaves to it and sighs for it. It sees some parts of itself disturbed by the movements of the world and dragged outward by desire for earthly things; therefore it calls them back inward and upward.

Thus, exhorting itself according to its sensuality, it says: “Praise the Lord, my soul.” What indeed pleases you in this world? Divided among so many loves of worldly things, gather yourself to the creator; here you have peace and security.

Then the soul responds to the mind, as though weighed down here and unable to desist as it ought: “I will praise in life.” Here, in death, I will praise faintly, because the body burdens the soul and the earthly dwelling weighs down the mind that thinks of many things (Wisdom 9); here hope nourishes it, while life is in the future.

“In my life.” (CAS.) When I have clung perfectly to him, separation from whom—as happens now—is death; but hope consoles me, and in hope, as it were living, I praise.

“As long as.” This does not mean that it will ever cease, since it will exist forever; therefore it truly lasts long.

### VERSE 3

“Do not trust,” and so forth. (CAS.) The second part. Having given counsel and affirmed where he will be able to praise fully, he urges those who are, as it were, far away—and who meanwhile are subject to evils that disturb the soul—not to hope in human beings but in God.

(AUG.) Or, as though placed in mind at the end of the world, he teaches that things quickly coming to an end should not be loved as eternal; as though saying, by his own example: “Do not trust,” and so forth.

“In the sons of human beings.” (ID.) In one Son of Man there is salvation, and in him place your hope—not because he is the Son of Man, but because he is the Son of God; not on account of what he received from you, but on account of what he preserved in himself.

### VERSE 4

“His spirit will go forth,” and so forth. (CAS.) First he cleanses hearts by prohibiting harmful things, so that afterward he may direct them toward what is salutary and exhort them to what brings salvation.

### VERSE 5

“Blessed is he whose God is Jacob.” (CAS.) The third part, where he teaches that all hope must be placed in the Almighty, whom he describes by his works, so that the Gentile world, so often convicted, may come to rest.

(AUG.) Once harmful things have been removed, he teaches what belongs to salvation, namely, in whom one ought to hope.

“His helper is his hope.” (CAS.) God was the helper of that Jacob, and so forth, up to “that is, of this true Jacob, as of the former one.”

### VERSE 6

“Who made heaven and earth.” (ID.) Because even the worshipers of demons have hope in their god, he determines in whom hope ought to be placed, namely, in Christ, and he shows this through the end of the psalm by describing him in every respect.

“All that is in them.” So that you do not suppose that someone else is the creator, or that another creator exists even of the smallest things.

### VERSE 7

“Who keeps truth forever.” (CAS.) Christ, who is truth; every human being is a liar.

“He executes judgment.” These two things belong to justice. Christ the judge vindicates those who suffer on account of his name and gives food to those who love him.

“To those who suffer wrong.” (AUG.) Not every distress is an injustice. What you suffer rightly is not an injustice, as with the thief and other criminals. It is one thing to suffer injustice and another to suffer punishment. Punishment is suffered justly; injustice, however, is contrary to justice.

### VERSE 8

“The Lord releases those in chains.” (CAS.) This belongs to abundant sweetness.

“The Lord lifts up those who are crushed.” Those whom the devil has crushed, the Lord lifts up.

“He loves the righteous.” (CAS.) Those whom he places in eternal blessedness.

### VERSE 9

“He will receive the orphan and the widow.” (AUG.) The whole Church of the Gentiles is an outsider in relation to the fathers—not by flesh but by imitation, and therefore a daughter.

All are orphans during their pilgrimage, because their father is absent; and every faithful soul is a widow while her spouse is absent. Hence they desire the father and the spouse all the more, and God protects them, though unseen, because they desire him.

### VERSE 10

“The Lord will reign forever.” (CAS.) This concerns magnificence.

“He will reign in us when our hearts are firm in him,” which is not yet the case.

## PSALM 146

### VERSE 1

“Alleluia.” (AUG.) Here too he speaks of the praise of God, where the prophet urges praise of the one who gathers Israel.

“Praise the Lord.” (CAS.) First he shows whom God gathers and how. Second, after what has been said, he rebukes those who still cling to and doubt, showing from what they can praise God—namely, if they have been humble—at “Sing beforehand.”

“Praise the Lord.” (AUG.) This is said to all nations. And as though we were asking how we should praise, he gives the reason for praise: “because the psalm is good.” (CAS.) In the praise of God, the act itself is the reward that will exist in the future. He is therefore to be praised because he builds up, and because at the end of the age he will gather the scattered of Israel—that is, the faithful—from the whole world into the kingdom. Here the praise concerns wondrous deeds.

(AUG.) This is the entire reward of those who praise, and so forth, up to “now let us exercise ourselves in this praise of good works.”

“May it be pleasing to our God,” and so forth. It is not enough to sing psalms for praise to please God; it is also necessary to please him through purity of life.

### VERSE 2

“The Lord builds Jerusalem.” (AUG.) Or he understood Jerusalem as the universal Church, and so forth, up to “whom the Father sent to redeem our captivity at the price of his blood.”

### VERSE 3

“And he binds up.” From the likeness of a physician, and so forth, up to “and the Lord binds up their bruises.”

(HIER.) Thus that Samaritan who was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho (Luke 10), when he saw the wounded man lying on the road, bound up his wounds. But concerning those who have not broken their hearts, it is said through Isaiah: “There is no balm to apply, nor oil, nor bandages” (Isaiah 1, according to the Septuagint). God’s bandages are the temporal sacraments by which we meanwhile have consolation; they will then be removed when perfect health has come.

### VERSE 4

“He numbers the multitude of the stars and calls them all by name.” (CAS.) He does not give them foreign names, like the astrologers who name Jupiter and Venus. Or, typologically, the reference is to the saints, because he gives each one a proper gift; or all are in his familiarity, after the likeness of the Lord, who knows the names of his servants.

### VERSE 5

“Of his wisdom,” and so forth. (AUG.) Measure itself, and number, and weight, and so forth, up to “see what follows: but he humbles sinners.”

### VERSE 6

“But he humbles sinners.” (AUG.) Those who criticize intelligible things therefore perceive earthly things, thinking corporeally about the incorporeal God. He does this to those who wish to ridicule the law before they know it. Since it is a great thing to advance toward intelligible and spiritual realities, let us be gentle, let us knock, and let us do what follows.

### VERSE 7

“Sing beforehand.” Thus one arrives at understanding; thus the image is restored to God.

“Sing beforehand.” (CAS.) Second, he rebukes and urges forward those who, in view of what has been said, still cling and hesitate, showing that they can understand if they are humble and not proud. It is as though he said: “And in order that you may be able to understand, sing beforehand,” and so forth.

### VERSE 8

“He covers the heavens.” (CAS.) He recalls the works through which power is shown. For this reason he willed certain things in the Scriptures to be obscure: so that the servants of God might have something to pour forth through interpretation over the ears and hearts of people who receive from the clouds of God the richness of spiritual joy.

“For the service of human beings.” For preachers, who serve human beings. Hence the Apostle says: “But we are your servants through Jesus Christ” (2 Corinthians 4). They sow spiritual things and receive hay and grass—that is, temporal things—from the great ones of the world.

### VERSE 9

“And to the young ravens.” (AUG.) For everything given to the Church by the rich is hay.

(ID.) The Jews, who said that they alone were righteous and that all nations were sinners. Truly, our fathers were ravens, but we do not remain so; nevertheless, we are rightly called and are young ravens. The raven does not call, but we, having been sent away, do call.

(CAS.) Young ravens are said to live on dew and the benefit of their age, ignorant of their fathers’ food, namely, the stench of corpses. Thus the innocent children of pagans call upon God.

### VERSE 10

“In the legs of a man.” That is, in the composed bearing of the presumptuous and bold. By “man” he denotes a bold presumptuous person. An uncomposed gait is indicated by “legs”—“in the legs of a man.”

Or, according to another reading, “in the tabernacles of a man,” that is, in the gatherings of heretics, he will take pleasure in them. Notice that he does not say “in the tabernacles of God” but “of a man,” thereby indicating the audacity of heretics.

### VERSE 11

“Upon those who fear,” and so forth. (AUG.) He joined hope to fear, because fear is of no value without hope of pardon. Judas feared but, because he despaired, hanged himself with a noose. Therefore let whoever fears God also hope in him. You will please him if you hope in his mercy and thereafter take care not to sin in such a way that you must ask pardon for past sins.

## PSALM 147

### VERSE 12

“Alleluia.” This psalm produces love for the future Jerusalem. It is attributed to Haggai and Zechariah, who prophesied the restoration of Jerusalem in captivity; as Jeremiah foretold, it was accomplished after seventy years, that is, after the passing of the whole period of time measured by seven days.

“Praise, Jerusalem.” (CASS.) This entire psalm proclaims the power of God. First, it speaks of the good things of the future Jerusalem; second, it speaks of the good things given here to the saints, at “who sends forth.”

(AUG.) The prophet, still established in captivity, and so forth, up to “who have heard him belching in this way.”

### VERSE 13

“He has strengthened the bars of your gates.” (AUG.) Notice that the door is shut once the wise virgins have been admitted and the foolish excluded, so that no one now goes out or enters. Appropriately, after the exhortation to praise, he speaks of closed doors. With the door of Jerusalem closed, it praises securely, because no one goes out whom it would grieve to lose and no one enters whom it would fear; consequently, there are no scandals. Scandals.

### VERSE 14

“With the fat of wheat.” (ID.) With the bread that descended from heaven. In the world it is enclosed in flesh and known only by faith; then it will be seen as it is.

### VERSE 15

“He sends forth his word.” The second part adds what gifts are given here to the elect, through which the truth of the future can be recognized.

“Of the earth.” (AUG.) So that it may be known on earth. For unless he sent the Word to the earth—which weighs us down and hinders our return—we would not be raised up to the fatness of the satisfying grain. On earth, where we labor, weary, languid, sluggish, and cold, namely, in the desert, he does not abandon us; rather, he who sends forth his word gives manna, and so forth.

“He runs swiftly.” (AUG., CASS.) Or, “he reaches into swiftness,” that is, from God, so that the swiftness itself may be present in a form more choice or more clearly expressed than could otherwise be said.

He does not say that the Word is swift or that it is swift by a speed in which it participates more or less; rather, it is swift by that very swiftness than which nothing is swifter. Likewise, something that is swift—such as a horse—is swift in relation to something else and not everywhere. Swiftness itself, however, is everywhere and is not in a part. It belongs to the Word of God not to be in a part but to be everywhere through itself. This is the wisdom that reaches powerfully from end to end, not by local motion but by immobility.

The Spirit of wisdom is also called active, mobile, sure, and undefiled. Swiftness makes it both always present everywhere and never confined anywhere. But who is sufficient to contemplate these things? There is nevertheless hope of grasping the Word, because he predestined us.

### VERSE 16

“He gives snow,” and so forth. (AUG.) “To the earth.” When charity grows cold, and so forth, up to “and while he calls them to repentance, he scatters the cloud like ashes.”

(ID.) “He scatters the cloud like ashes,” and so forth. Ashes belong to repentance, and so forth, up to “and he who predestined also called to repentance.”

Literally: God scatters snow like wool, the cloud like ashes, and makes ice crystals like pieces of white bread. Crystal is a kind of substance resembling glass, but white; it is said to be snow hardened into ice over many years, so that it cannot melt.

“His crystal,” and so forth. That is, the obstinate, who do not easily melt like snow.

### VERSE 17

“He sends it like morsels,” and so forth. Elsewhere: “like pieces of bread,” so that they may feed others and preach the truth which they oppose. All are one bread; individuals are pieces. Hence: “Many are one bread in Christ” (1 Corinthians 10).

Paul was crystal, hard and shining: hard because he persecuted the Church, shining because he was learned in the law. God melted him, and he became bread, teaching the truth. But unless he melts him—

“Who can withstand before the face of his God?” Elsewhere: “Who will stand?” (AUG.) The cold is the one who abandons, does not call, and does not pour in grace; and who else will melt him? No one. Hence the Apostle says: “Who will free me from this body of death?” (Romans 7). It is as though he said: I am growing cold; no one melts me unless the grace of God sends forth his Word.

### VERSE 18

“He will send forth his word, and he will melt it.” (CASS.) When the Word of God comes, neither cold, darkness, nor hardness can cause despair. For they are salutarily melted and pour forth streams of spiritual benefit for others to drink, according to the saying: “All who thirst, come to the waters” (Isaiah 55).

### VERSE 19

“Jacob … Israel.” (AUG.) Or the same thing is signified by “Israel,” and so forth, up to “because he was sent only to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel” (Matthew 15).

“His judgments.” (ID.) Judgment begins from the house of God, and so forth, up to “adding three other psalms of praise, so that the grace of the Trinity may shine forth in this work.”

## PSALM 148

### VERSE 1

“Praise the Lord from the heavens.” (CASS.) By mentioning a few, he urges the whole creation to praise God. Some things possess the spirit of praising God in that affection by which God is pleasing to them. Some lack understanding, but because they are good in their own order and contribute to the beauty of the universe, they do not praise by themselves; rather, God is praised through them by those who attend to them. In this way they praise in a certain sense, because from them praise of God arises in us, and to this praise the prophet urges us here.

### VERSE 5

“For he spoke, and they were made.” (CASS.) This is directed against those who say that the world is coeternal with God. It follows: “He commanded.” By his Word they were created. First he said “made,” and afterward “created.” We too can make, but we cannot create. Therefore he alone creates, which is proper to divinity.

Praise from his works—

### VERSE 6

“He established.” Through power he is omnipotent, and his works are not changed.

“Forever and unto the age of the age.” (CAS.) Even if there is a new heaven, those things established by God are still rightly said to remain, since they are renewed through Christ and remain improved. Here the praise concerns power.

### VERSE 7

“Praise the Lord.” The second part, where, after enumerating the heavenly things, he descends to the earthly. Turning toward them, as though exhorting us to praise God by considering them—for, when considered, they disclose the praise of God—he says: “O you who are from the earth.”

“All abysses.” (AUG.) The depths of the waters, and so forth, up to “thus he urges us, by considering them, to praise.”

### VERSE 8

“Which do his word.” This is because some people thought that God governed the higher things but despised these lower ones, which were governed by chance. Yet God also acts in these things; he is praised in these smallest matters, and the Alleluia is sung.

## Psalm 148

### Verse 13

**Confession.** (Cassiodorus) Above he first spoke about heaven, then about earth; here he speaks about everything together. By “heaven” he understands all things above, and by “earth” all things below.

(Augustine) “His confession is above heaven and earth.” All things confess him, either in themselves or in others; the beauty of all things is the voice of those confessing, in those who attend to them. That is, let those who attend to them praise him, both from earthly and heavenly things, than which nothing is better.

### Verse 14

**He has exalted the horn of his people.** (The same) Behold what Haggai and Zechariah prophesied. At present the horn of his people is humbled in tribulations, but when the Lord comes, it will be exalted.

[Col. 1077C]

## Psalm 149

### Verse 1

**Alleluia.** (Cassiodorus) After all the creatures whom he admonished in the preceding psalm to praise God because they were created by him, here he invites Israel in a particular and more special way to a new song, on account of the newness given to it, which is a more marvelous work of God. This is the sanctification of Israel, through which it has been made new from old.

**Sing to the Lord, etc.** (Cassiodorus) First he admonishes them in many ways to praise the king who is benevolent and beneficent toward them. Second, he treats of the joys of the saints, at “They shall rejoice.” (Augustine) Whoever wishes to sing this song must love eternal things, so as to become new. For the old person sings an old song about earthly things; the new person sings a new song about spiritual things—namely, a song of peace, a song of charity, and a song of joyfulness. Whoever follows the old resentment rather than the new charity does not sing a new song.

**His praise is in the Church.** (Cassiodorus) Here he determines where and by whom this song ought to be sung.

### Verse 2

**In his king.** (The same) That is, in Christ, who is king and priest. (Augustine) As king, he fought for us from the cross, conquering the devil; as priest, he offered himself for us, finding nothing in human beings that he could offer on their behalf.

### Verse 3

**In the choir.** (The same) Because there is no dispersion, but the dearest unity. Then there will be rejoicing with the tambourine and psaltery, not the activity of the instrument itself.

### Verse 4

**For the Lord takes pleasure in his people.** (The same) In the first creation of things we read that everything pleased God, etc., up to “or when he makes him equal to the angels.”

### Verse 5

**The saints shall rejoice.** (The same) The second part, where he treats of the joys and power of the saints.

**Glory.** It is the frequent praise of good deeds, in which the righteous rejoice in their chambers, that is, in their conscience. They rejoice because they have so good a Lord, who gives grace to sinners and eternal life in accordance with their merits. The fool rejoices outside, in the stories of human beings; the mode of rejoicing proper to the saints is that they refer good things to the one who gave them.

### Verse 6

**Exaltations.** (The same) God’s virtue and power are proclaimed in the glory of the saints.

**In their chambers.** The glory of the saints is in their various dwelling places. Concerning these the Lord says: “In my Father’s house there are many dwelling places” (John 14).

**In their throats.** Those who do not cease praising him in heart and tongue, from whom they possess eternal things.

**Swords.** Having received the power of the word of God, they will judge with the Lord, sitting upon twelve thrones. Then vengeance and rebuke will truly be made among the peoples; then the kings of the earth will be bound, so that it will not be permitted them to go out. And nobles will bear iron fetters, heavy to carry and impossible to break. Thus the written judgment will be carried out—that is, judgment approved by the angels. Concerning this the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels?” (1 Corinthians 6). And lest you think that only the apostles will judge, he adds that this glory—namely, the power of judgment—belongs to all his saints, that is, to the perfect, who have left all earthly things for Christ.

(Augustine) “The exaltations of God are in their throat.” For they rejoice in their chambers and in their throats, that is, in heart and tongue, in such a way that they do not attribute to themselves what they are good, but to God, from whom they received what they are and hope for what they are not yet.

### Verse 8

**To bind.** By these bonds of God’s commandments and precepts, the kings of the nations and the nobles of the world are bound by the weak and contemptible things of this world, whom the Lord chose to confound all that is powerful. He filled them with the Holy Spirit and gave them two-edged swords, so that they might turn the hearts of the nobles toward fear of Christ and, despising worldly nobility, choose poverty and nobility in Christ. For he wished the emperor to benefit from the fisherman, not the fisherman from the emperor.

(Augustine) Through these people he binds kings and nobles in iron fetters, so that they may not advance toward unlawful things.

[Col. 1078D]

## Psalm 150

### Verse 1

**Praise the Lord.** (Cassiodorus) This concerns the praise of God in his saints, who, glorified, praise him without end. The city of God—namely, the unity of all the saints—is admonished to sing with mouth and heart. To this summit all psalmody is brought, sung with nuptial sweetness.

**Praise him in the firmament.** (Augustine) There is virtue in the firmament, etc., up to “who, honoring one another, give praise to God.”

(Cassiodorus) To those whom the prophet at the beginning showed the pattern of conduct, now received into that Jerusalem, he says that God, who gave everything, must be praised among them. “In the firmament,” because by his death he conquered the devil and led believers to heaven. “In his virtues” or “powers,” because all things have been subjected beneath his feet.

### Verse 2

**According to the multitude of his greatness.** How can this be, when his greatness has no end? But this is said of spiritual and holy people. Although there is no end to his greatness, God is praised according to it, since he is praised without end.

How he ought to be praised he explains through mystical comparisons to the end of the psalm: let the trumpet sound for the king; let the psaltery sing to God; let the harp, together with the other instruments, sound for the bridegroom. The trumpet is terrifying, or is used in war, or is prepared for the arrival of kings; the psaltery sounds from above, the harp from below. All these things, compared with human actions, are figuratively said there to make the praises of God resound.

### Verse 4

**With strings and organ.** (Cassiodorus) He uses “strings” for every musical instrument that sounds by the tension of strings. An organ is like a tower constructed with various pipes, sounding through the blowing of bellows. And so that you might understand all these things as received from human beings, he comes to the human mouth; and, explaining what it means to praise with strings and organ, he adds:

**Praise him with sounding cymbals, etc.** The well-sounding cymbals are our lips, which, harmonious with the heart, sound well in the praises of God. They resemble cymbals and produce harmony, and therefore rightly belong among musical instruments.

(Cassiodorus) The well-resounding cymbals are very small bowls made from mixed metals, which produce a sharp sound. But because he wishes everything to be understood spiritually, he concludes appropriately:

### Verse 6

Let every spirit—angelic and human—praise the Lord. Not flesh and blood, not the appearance of the world, but that which is more sublime in the nature of things, which understands heavenly things and receives eternal things. This is a brief and perfect teaching: that all things praise God spiritually. In this lies the perfection of all music. There is breath in the trumpet, striking in the harp and cymbals, and a voice in the choir. By these musical instruments is signified a spiritual harmony, perceived not by the ears but by a pure mind.

(Augustine) There are three kinds, etc., up to “the voice of eternal life is: Let every spirit praise the Lord.”

[Col. 1079]

# Book of Proverbs

Which the Hebrews call *Misle*. (G)*

## The Letter and Twofold Prologue of Blessed Jerome concerning the Books of Solomon

(See among his works, volumes I, III, and VIII.)

# Chapter One

[Col. 1079C]

### Verse 1

**The proverbs of Solomon.** It should be noted that the Vulgate edition calls the sayings *parabolae*, which in Hebrew is *misle* and in Greek παροιμίαι (*paroimiai*), that is, “proverbs”; but the terms agree sufficiently. For what are called parables, because they are obscure, are also rightly called proverbs, because they are such sayings as ought often to circulate on the lips of speakers and be retained in memory. Proverbs, too, are often so obscure that they are rightly called parables; hence: “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs” (John 6), etc.

The Book of Proverbs does not contain, as simple-minded people suppose, obvious precepts. Rather, just as gold is sought in the earth, the kernel in a nut, and the hidden fruit beneath the rough shells of chestnuts, so the divine meaning in these sayings must be sought at a deeper level.

The Proverbs of Solomon, translated according to the Hebrew truth by Eusebius at the request of the priest Jerome, for the bishops Chromatius and Heliodorus: Greek *parabolē*, Latin “likenesses.” Solomon gave this title to the work so that we would not understand his words according to the letter. In this he signifies that the Lord would speak parabolically to the crowds, just as, through its name, he signifies the kingdom of Christ and the Church by his peaceful kingdom. Concerning this it is said: “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of his kingdom. He shall sit upon the throne of David and over his kingdom” (Luke 1). Likewise, through the construction and dedication of the temple, he signifies the building of the Church in the time of the resurrection. Christ himself is also the son of David and the spiritual king of Israel, according to the testimony of the crowd that met him with palm branches and praises (Matthew 21).

What benefit these sayings have is shown in the title, where it says: “To know wisdom and discipline”—that is, how one ought rightly to believe and live, and where each person ought to direct the intention of the heart.

### Verse 2

**To understand the words of prudence.** That is, they should not merely embrace the wisdom they have received and devote themselves to the discipline of the virtues, but should also listen carefully to words of prudence by which they may advance, and understand them diligently.

### Verse 5

**A wise person hearing will become wiser.** He fittingly begins with wisdom, because when it was offered him as a choice, he asked for and received wisdom.

**A wise person hearing will become wiser.** He shows that no one is so wise in this life that he cannot become wiser even through the words of lesser people. The queen of Sheba heard Solomon, lesser than the greater, and returned wiser. Moses heard his father-in-law, much inferior to him, and became wiser.
