**And one who understands.** (Rabanus, on Proverbs, volume V) Let no one boast of his own knowledge, etc., up to “to know wisdom and discipline,” etc.

### Verse 7

**The fear of the Lord.** (The same) There are two kinds of fear of the Lord, etc., up to “Both will cease in the future; charity will never fail.”

### Verse 8

**Hear, my son, your father’s discipline.** (The same) Up to this point he has spoken proverbially, etc., up to “for among the Hebrews the spirit that bestows grace is grammatically feminine.”

### Verse 9

**Let grace be added.** To those who observed the law of the Lord, etc., up to “in exchange for the grace of right action.”

**And necklaces for your neck, etc.** The radiance of perfect action, which confirms preaching—proceeding through the neck—with an unfailing bond of virtues.

### Verse 10

**My son.** With the affection of a father he addresses his son, coaxing him not to consent to sinners.

### Verse 11

**Let us lie in wait.** (Rabanus) Either this refers generally to robbers who set ambushes for the innocent, or specifically to those who handed the author of life over to death.

(Strabo) Although this applies generally to all who lie in wait for blood, etc., up to “and by their presumption they destroy themselves instead.”

**The innocent without cause.** He who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.

### Verse 12

**Let us swallow him alive like the underworld.** Let us extinguish the memory of his virtues and teaching, so that it will not even be remembered that he lived among us.

[Col. 1081C]

### Verse 13

**We shall find every precious substance.** Namely, the people whom they saw clinging to Christ, whom they thought they could separate from his love and company if they killed him, and fill their houses with the spoils of such people—that is, their assemblies with their souls.

### Verse 14

**Cast your lot with us.** This is clear in general concerning robbers, because they promise a share of the plunder to the companions whom they recruit. But the persecutors of Christ also joined to themselves anyone they could; those whom they saw following him they expelled from the synagogue, that is, deprived of their fellowship.

### Verse 16

**They run toward evil.** Not only toward what they are going to do, but toward what they will suffer because of what they have done. For the more quickly they hurry to accomplish the crime, the more closely they approach the punishment for the crime.

### Verse 17

**In vain.** (Rabanus) The rest concerns the ambushers of Christ specifically, etc., up to “for among the poor he has no cause.”

### Verse 20

**Wisdom.** Up to this point he has spoken of the persecutions that the Jews inflicted on Christ; from here he speaks through the apostles to those same persecutors after the Passion. Wisdom—that is, Christ—speaks outside, that is, openly in the light, so that, having abandoned childishness, they may be children in malice.

[Col. 1082A]

(Rabanus) The Wisdom of God is indeed Christ, etc., up to “they might say to anyone.”

**Outside.** (The same) Openly, after the resurrection, etc., up to “in the street his voice.”

**She raises her voice in the streets, etc.** What he had previously taught to a few, he repeated publicly; hence: “What I tell you in darkness, say in the light.”

### Verse 21

**At the head of the crowds she cries out, etc.** (The same) Because she also openly brought back to the memory of the rulers, who seemed to have prevailed against him so that he would be crucified, the guilt of the murder they had committed, and called them to the remedy of repentance.

**At the doors of the city gates.** (The same) The city of the Lord, the Church united from both peoples, etc., up to “he was recalling them to his grace,” so that, as Luke says, “a great multitude of priests obeyed the faith” (Acts 6).

### Verse 22

**How long?** You have already seen Christ in the flesh performing miracles, yet you despised him. Now at least love him, raised from the dead, and he will forgive what you have sinned.

**Little ones.** (Rabanus) Those slower in understanding are called little ones, etc., up to “which did the Son himself, coming, bestow on those perfect in understanding?”

### Verse 23

**Turn back.** Wisdom urges them to turn back to God and brings forth the Spirit.

**For correction.** Through the apostles he rebukes the Jews and urges them to turn back even after the Ascension and Resurrection.

### Verse 26

**I also.** (The same) Likewise in the psalm, etc., up to “as though they despised nothing.”

[Col. 1082C]

### Verse 27

**When sudden calamity shall come upon you.** He means the sudden siege of Jerusalem and the conquest of the whole province carried out by the Romans. Concerning this: “When he saw the city, he wept over it” (Luke 19).

**When it comes upon you.** (Rabanus) This entire correction of Wisdom can be understood, etc., up to “for what follows is—”

### Verse 28

**They will rise early and will not find me.** This signifies the time of judgment, when some will rise to life and others to everlasting disgrace.

**They will call.** The Jews are not read to have called upon the Lord during the siege; and if any did call, because they did not truly repent, they were not heard.

### Verse 29

**They hated.** By contrast, the righteous person says: “I have hated the unjust and loved your law.”

[Col. 1082D]

### Verse 31

**Therefore they shall eat.** (The same) Because they were unwilling to enter my ways, etc., up to “and it will be well with you.”

**And they shall be filled with their own counsels.** [Note: [Col. 1081] Of these we give only the beginning and the end up to the end of the book; attribute the passages to Rabanus.] By which they were saying, etc., up to “it can be understood.”

### Verse 32

**The turning away.** Turning away and prosperity destroy, when a mind turned away from fear of its Creator appears to endure nothing adverse from the anger of that same Creator in the things through which it sins. But as Job says: “They spend their days in prosperity, and in a moment they descend to the underworld.”

**Of the little ones.** In understanding; concerning this, above, etc., up to “but because they turn away, they kill themselves.”

### Verse 33

**But whoever hears me shall rest without terror, etc.** This can be understood both in the present life and in the future, etc., up to “shall rest in the resurrection.”

# Chapter Two

### Verse 1

**My son.** Here he notes two things: that wisdom concerns heavenly things, and prudence worldly things.

He hides God’s commandments within himself, etc., up to “as birds carry away seed thrown beside the road.”

### Verse 2

**Let your ear listen to wisdom.** He listens not with the ear, etc., up to “for this is what follows.”

**Incline your heart.** Incline it, humble it, cleanse it, etc., up to “and you have revealed them to the humble.”

**For if you call upon wisdom.** To call upon it, etc., up to “nor should free choice be absent.”

### Verse 4

**And as treasures.** He who digs for treasures, etc., up to “and let him not rest until he finds it.”

### Verse 5

**Then you will understand.** Friendly fear, etc., up to “but you will also find knowledge of his divinity, which makes one blessed forever.”

### Verse 6

**For the Lord gives.** This verse looks back to what he had said above: “For if you call upon wisdom,” etc.

For wisdom, therefore, etc., up to “but is given by the Lord.”

**From his mouth.** Through the eternal birth of the Son, concerning which it is said elsewhere: “I came forth from the mouth of the Most High, the firstborn before every creature” (Isaiah 58). Or, the mouth of the Lord is in the saints, whence: “The mouth of the Lord has spoken.” From his mouth knowledge and prudence are born when the Lord sanctifies the human mouth and makes it his own, so that it may speak knowingly and prudently.

[Col. 1083C]

### Verse 7

**He will guard.** So that he may aid the upright and simple at whatever level of virtue they possess. Job was simple and upright (Job 1): simple through the innocence of gentleness, and upright through the caution of discernment; simple, harming no one and indeed benefiting everyone; upright, corrupted by no one.

### Verse 12

**From the evil way.** To which those who say, “Come with us, let us lie in wait for blood,” call people; the one who is the author of this persuasion speaks perversely.

### Verse 13

**Who abandon the path.** Fittingly, etc., up to “its end is in the outer darkness.”

### Verse 14

**Who rejoice.** Because they walk along dark paths, etc., up to “and would chastise their harmful joy with saving tears.”

### Verse 16

**So that you may be rescued from the woman.** This verse depends upon what precedes, etc., up to “and they themselves are darts.”

### Verse 17

**And she abandons her guide.** This is clear also concerning the heretical mind, etc., up to “whom she had promised to preserve on the day of baptism.”

### Verse 18

**The covenant of her God, etc.** The covenant which she made with her husband at the time of marriage, with the Lord as witness—that is, that they would preserve faithfulness, specifically chastity, toward one another—or the covenant made in baptism.

**For she has inclined.** Every conduct of an adulteress leads to destruction, etc., up to “that is, it tends toward the torments of evil spirits.”

### Verse 19

**They shall not return to her.** To death, that is, not to the woman, etc., up to “let him not attribute it to himself, but to the grace of God.”

[Col. 1084A]

### Verse 21

**For those who.** Here he joins the simple to the upright, etc., up to “they reach the one who reigns with Christ in heaven.”

### Verse 22

**The ungodly.** This is said specifically of them, etc., up to “but whoever hears me shall rest without terror.”

# Chapter Three

**My son, do not.** He teaches that one must persist in works of mercy, etc., up to “he adorns with good deeds the one whom he instructs.”

### Verse 2

**Peace**, that is, a state of blessedness, etc., up to “he might live for a long time in the rest of peace.”

### Verse 3

**Mercy and truth.** Let truth that must be spoken never depart from your mouth, and let mercy to your neighbor never cease from your actions. Thus it comes about that God’s mercy, which wipes away sins, always follows you, and truth, which fulfills his promises, accompanies you.

**Bind them around your throat.** In the throat is the organ of the voice, etc., up to “nor let life contradict the voice.”

### Verse 4

**And you will find grace.** Before the Lord, etc., up to “and provide your neighbors an example of living.”

### Verse 5

**Put your trust in the Lord.** Do not fear on account of your weakness, etc., up to “and he will grant you the ability to fulfill what he has commanded.”

**Do not be wise.** He seems to have said the same thing, etc., up to “but he shows what true human wisdom is in this way.”

### Verse 7

**Fear God and turn away from evil.** Such is the saying in Job, etc., up to “the memory of divine fear restrains him.”

### Verse 8

**For it will be health.** Solid works of virtue in the bones, etc., up to “from which they may receive greater strength.”

### Verse 9

**Honor the Lord from your substance.** So that human beings, who are his handiwork and were made in his image, may be restored.

**And from the firstfruits of all.** Not only from material wealth, etc., up to “he attributes it not to himself but to him.”

### Verse 10

**Your barns shall be filled with abundance.** “Store up treasures for yourselves in heaven.” If the saints have treasures in heaven, etc., up to “it is repaid with heavenly reward.”

**Your winepresses shall overflow.** Because the inward sweetness of eternal things kindles the hearts of all the faithful in praise of their Creator. For here he says: “That you may eat,” etc.

### Verse 11

**Discipline.** There are those who serve the Lord in prosperity, etc., up to “he loses the devotion that he seemed to possess in tranquility.”

### Verse 12

**For whom the Lord loves, he rebukes.** Therefore, so much the less, etc., up to “hence he himself says: ‘Those whom I love, I rebuke and chastise.’”

### Verse 13

**Blessed is the human being, etc.** Because those placed under discipline, etc., up to “and in the future enjoy his vision.”

**And the one who abounds in prudence.** Fittingly, when he said, etc., up to “to open their hearts to receive its breadth.”

### Verse 14

**It is better.** Whoever has acquired the riches of wisdom should not fear correction leading to poverty; for the heavenly gift surpasses all treasures.

**First and purest.** Because the root of wisdom is the fear of the Lord, these are the first and purest fruits, etc., up to “is promised more perfectly by the Lord.”

### Verse 16

**Length of days is in her right hand and in her left.** Through the vision of his divinity, etc., up to “and eternal life in the future.”

### Verse 17

**Her ways.** Actions and teachings, etc., up to “belong to examples of peace and love.”

### Verse 18

**A tree of life.** Just as the tree of life stood in the middle of paradise, etc., up to “will be blessed by his present sight.”

### Verse 19

**The Lord by wisdom.** Typologically, through the Son he placed the Church upon the solidity of faith and established the heavens through prudence, when through him he enlightened the hearts of exalted preachers.

[Col. 1085B]

### Verse 20

**By his wisdom the abysses burst forth.** In the days of Noah, etc., up to “and examine them so that they may show them as an example to lesser people.”

### Verse 21

**My son, do not let them flow away.** Take care lest, wearied by temporal discipline, you lose the grace of wisdom, which is so great.

### Verse 22

**And it will be life to your soul.** Your soul possesses life with God if you keep his decrees, even though the flesh is weighed down by the discipline of correction or even by death.

**And grace to your throat.** The mind therefore has its own throat, etc., up to “blessed is the man who hopes in him.”

### Verse 23

**Then you will walk confidently.** We walk confidently on our way, etc., up to “for this is what follows.”

**And your foot will not stumble.** Because “all things work together for good for those who love God” (Romans 8).

### Verse 24

**If you sleep, you will not fear; you will rest, and it will be sweet.** This is clear according to the literal sense, etc., up to “because he has God everywhere as protector and guardian.”

### Verse 27

**Do not withhold doing good from the one who.** Since above he diligently urged the observance of the Lord’s law and counsel and promised eternal rest to those who observe them, now he repeats in various ways what must be observed. First, returning to what he had interrupted, he teaches that mercy must be shown to one’s neighbor and that one must live justly with him. Then he warns that one must also beware of the enemy. “Do not,” he says, withhold it.

Do not hear the Lord say to you with the Pharisees: “You yourselves did not enter, and you prevented those who were entering” (Luke 11).

[Col. 1085D]

### Verse 28

**Do not say to your friend: Go and return; tomorrow I shall give.** This concerns not only almsgiving but all the commandments of Christ, who says: “You are my friends if you do what I command” (John 15), etc.

### Verse 30

**Do not contend against a human being.** He does not forbid contending against one who does wrong, so that the person may be corrected, because it is not futile to do what a definite necessity compels. Indeed, the one who says, “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him” (Matthew 18), himself wishes you, insofar as you are able, to lead the one who has gone astray back to the way of truth.

### Verse 32

**For everyone who mocks is an abomination to the Lord.** “Everyone who mocks,” he says, because a mocker is one who either scorns fulfilling the words of God that he knows, or corrupts them by understanding and teaching them perversely. A mocker is also one who despises his promises as though they were wicked and scorns the anger of his strict judgment as though it were tolerable. Likewise, one who wickedly insults the simplicity of his neighbors is a mocker. Therefore divine justice rightly abhors every such mocker.

**And his conversation is with the simple.** For the proud, while they mock the simple, judge themselves wiser than those whom they ridicule. But, as James says, their wisdom is “earthly, animal, demonic” (James 3). The Lord’s conversation is with the simple because he enlightens with the secrets of wisdom those whom he sees to possess nothing of earthly arrogance or duplicity. Hence he says: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10).

### Verse 33

**In the house of the ungodly.** As with the purple-clad rich man, who in this life lacked spiritual things and afterward came to such poverty that he did not receive even the drop of water he sought. Hence: “He who blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ,” and at the time of reward they will hear: “Come, blessed ones” (Matthew 25), etc.

But according to the literal sense, it often happens that those who seize what belongs to others are finally consumed by poverty, while those who distribute their own possessions abound even in earthly goods.

### Verse 34

**Mockers.** James and Peter set down these verses according to the ancient translation: “God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (James 4).

# Chapter Four

### Verse 1

**Hear, sons.** Here, intending to exhort them to the pursuit of wisdom, he explains how he himself was taught wisdom by his father.

### Verse 3

**For I too.** Nothing raises minds more toward the hope of acquiring wisdom than remembering that those whom we admire as already shining in wisdom were once little and unlearned.

**The only-begotten in his mother’s presence.** Why does Solomon call himself an only child in his mother’s presence, when Scripture testifies that a uterine brother preceded him, unless it is because that brother, having been born immediately and without a name, died from life as though he had never existed?

[Col. 1086D]

### Verse 4

**Let him receive, etc.** David his father gave Solomon admonitions of this kind; whoever rereads the Books of Chronicles will find them.

### Verse 5

**Acquire.** In everything that you possess, etc., up to “having sold everything, he acquired youth.”

### Verse 9

**She will give to your head.** This is clear concerning Solomon, etc., up to “and in the future a crown of life will also be given.”

### Verse 10

**Hear, my son.** Having explained what he had received from his father, he returns to teaching the hearer the wisdom with which he began.

### Verse 11

**Along the paths of righteousness.** The paths—that is, the actions—of righteousness, etc., up to “they will be directed into the way of peace.”

### Verse 12

**And when you run.** The more fully and eagerly you run to fulfill God’s commandments, the less you will fear the adversities that might impede you. For all who labor in sinful action find an obstacle in the middle of their course, because suddenly, while they are unaware, they are swept away to punishment.

### Verse 17

**They eat the bread of wickedness.** In the practice of crimes, etc., up to “Scripture bears witness.”

### Verse 18

**But the path of the righteous.** The works of the righteous are performed in the light of knowledge and lead to eternal life, which is the perfect day.

### Verse 19

**The way of the ungodly.** He speaks about these, etc., up to “because one who runs will have no obstacle.”

### Verse 20

**My son, listen attentively to my words.** He urges attentive listening to his words and withdrawal from evil thoughts.

### Verse 23

**Guard your heart with all vigilance.** There are those who seem to live rightly in the eyes of human beings, etc., up to “the measure of life is judged.”

### Verse 24

**Remove from yourself.** It must be understood in two ways, so that your mouth may not speak anything perverse: guard your lips so that they do not become accustomed to slander, and flee from others whom you know to be subject to this vice, lest they corrupt you.

### Verse 25

**And your eyelids.** The way of justice, etc., up to “foreseeing through meditation.”

### Verse 26

**Let them be established.** Do not let fickleness of mind move you from your good purpose. Hence the Apostle says: “Be steadfast and immovable, always abounding in the work of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15).

### Verse 27

**Do not turn aside.** The right-hand way is good, etc., up to “the same is to be understood concerning the other virtues and vices.”

**Turn your foot away.** That is, do not deviate from what is straight either here or there, because the virtues require discernment, and every excess in them is a vice.

**If you turn your foot away from evil.** If, with the Lord’s help, you strive to do the good things I have taught, he will be present, favorable to your efforts, so that you may walk rightly now and then be able to reach eternal peace.

# Chapter Five

[Col. 1087D]

**My son, attend.** Up to this point he had admonished the hearer generally; from here, under the figure of a prostitute, he forbids the wickedness of heretics.

**Incline your ear.** He especially urges that the ear be inclined to wisdom and that one flee from the prostitute, the fornicator.

### Verse 2

**Your lips.** The lips, etc., up to “or defiles them by committing shameful acts.”

### Verse 3

**For a honeycomb.** When in the mouth of a heretic, etc., up to “truth is esteemed by fools.”

**The lips of the prostitute.** This is clear concerning the prostitute, because she seeks both sweetness of speech and bodily beauty in order to ensnare the wretched.

**Oil is her throat.** By the oil of the Holy Spirit the Catholic faith is consecrated. He displays his throat more smoothly who places his own opinions before the faith of the fathers.

[Col. 1088A]

### Verse 4

**But her end.** A draught of wormwood becomes bitter within, etc., up to “but the Lord explains why it is called a two-edged sword when he says: ‘Fear him who can destroy both soul and body in Gehenna’” (Luke 12).

### Verse 6

**Wandering, etc.** The steps of heretics are wandering, etc., up to “because one and the same faith is acknowledged by all the faithful throughout the whole world.”

### Verse 8

**Keep far away.** The Apostle says, etc., up to “it benefits weak hearers.”

### Verse 9

**Lest you give, etc.** Do not subject the honor with which you were created in the image of God to the will of unclean spirits, nor spend at the cruel adversary’s pleasure the span of life you have received.

[Col. 1088B]

### Verse 10

**Lest strangers be filled.** Do not assist the works of demons, etc., up to “would that it were hidden.”

**And you groan, etc.** Therefore keep yourself chaste, etc., up to “they may say what follows.”

### Verse 12

**Why did I hate discipline?** This is clear specifically concerning heretics, because they could not be recalled from error by the sayings and examples either of the ancient fathers or of the later ones.

### Verse 14

**In the midst of the assembly.** The same thing is expressed in Greek, etc., up to “he did not fear to lead a life alien to them.”

### Verse 15

**Drink water.** He teaches that one must beware of heretics and attend to the guarding and reading of the Scriptures. “The knowledge,” he says, “that you preach to others, preserve yourself, and pour it out through the watering of your speech.”

[Col. 1088C]

### Verse 16

**Let them flow forth.** Once you have preserved it yourself, then preach it to others, and distribute the divine words among the great multitude of hearers according to each person’s capacity.

### Verse 17

**Let them be yours, etc.** We divide waters in the streets and yet possess them alone, when we pour out preaching widely in public but do not seek human praise through it.

**And let them not be strangers’.** Unclean spirits become partners of a teacher if they corrupt his mind, either through arrogance while he preaches or through any other vice. But he alone possesses the waters when, faithfully joined to the members of the Church, he preserves himself from outsiders.

### Verse 18

**Let your spring be.** Let your teaching, and whatever is born from it, be in the blessing of the Church; and rejoice with her to whom you have been joined from youth, that is, from the time you believed.

[Col. 1088D]

### Verse 19

**A most beloved hind.** Or “most pleasing,” as certain manuscripts have it: the holy Church, etc., up to “we are instructed against the deceits of heretics.”

**In love, etc.** He does not teach that one should devote oneself to conjugal love, but that, while the first wife is alive, one should neither marry another nor ever join oneself to a prostitute.

### Verse 21

**The Lord looks upon.** Adulterers should not imagine themselves hidden by the darkness of night, etc., up to “and night will be illuminated like day.”

### Verse 22

**His iniquities, etc.** The sinner, etc., up to “they act in such a way as to bind themselves more tightly.”

[Col. 1089A]

### Verse 23

**He himself will die.** Because this concerns adulterers, etc., up to “because they detested the discipline of life.”

# Chapter Six

### Verse 1

**My son.** This is clear according to the literal sense, etc., up to “it is first necessary for you yourself to keep what you have said.”

### Verse 3

**Rouse yourself.** Remember not only to remain vigilant by living well yourself, but also, through preaching, to rouse the one over whom you preside from the torpor of sin.

### Verse 4

**Do not give sleep to your eyes, etc.** up to “but because of weariness of mind he does not correct these things with a fitting invective.”

### Verse 5

**Rescue yourself.** As if he were saying: Like a doe from the hand of the one who catches it, etc., up to “and may deserve to enter the pastures of heavenly life.”

[Col. 1089B]

### Verse 6

**Go to the ant.** Here he exhorts the idle person, etc., up to “to bring forth from the storehouse of his former action what he has stored away.”

### Verse 9

**How long, sluggard, will you sleep? When?** How long, sluggard, will you sleep in vices, etc., up to “for this is what follows: and it will come upon you like a traveler.”

### Verse 11

**Poverty and want.** This is clear according to the literal sense, etc., up to “because it is unforeseen and sudden.”

**But if you are diligent.** The fruits of the earth, etc., up to “because he will receive the unfailing reward of his labors.”

### Verse 12

**An apostate person.** He had spoken of heresy and other kinds of vice, etc., up to “which has no root remaining within.”

### Verse 16

**There are six.** Concerning the same matter, he indicates how hateful it is to God to sow discord.

[Col. 1089C]

**His soul detests.** He speaks according to human custom, to signify that he hates such people greatly; hence in Isaiah: “My soul has hated your solemnities” (Isaiah 1).

### Verse 17

**Eyes, etc.** He enumerates six capital crimes, etc., up to “those who have torn apart the harmony of fraternal unity.”

### Verse 20

**Keep, my son.** Now, under the figure of an adulterous woman, he forbids listening to heresy.

### Verse 21

**Bind them upon your heart**, that is, hold God’s commandments firmly fixed in your thoughts.

### Verse 22

**When you walk.** Let meditation on the divine law be so great, etc., up to “let God’s commandments walk with you, so that they may instruct you.”

When you sleep: in death, may they guard your soul [Col. 1089D], lest the enemy seize it. When you awaken in the resurrection, speak with them while awaiting the rewards that had been promised to you, if you had kept them.

**VERSE 25.**—“Let it not desire.” This is plainly about the adulteress; but if heretics seem to live well and conduct themselves appropriately, beware lest you be seduced by their teachings.

**VERSE 28.**—“For the price of a prostitute.” The brief pleasure of fornication, up to the point that it returns more ardently after a little while.

**VERSE 29.**—“Can a man hide fire?” He alone may read the books of heretics who is so firmly grounded in the Catholic faith that neither the sweetness nor the cunning of their words can separate him from it.

**VERSE 30.**—“The fault is not great.” Theft is not in itself [Col. 1090A] …, up to the point that Jerusalem committed more offenses.

**VERSE 34.**—“For the jealousy and anger of a man,” etc. This is also to be understood of the Lord, up to the point that he presumes either to corrupt any faithful soul.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.**—“My son.” This section explains the preceding one more fully in the same sense.

**VERSE 2.**—“And my law.” Keep what I teach so diligently as though you saw nothing right apart from it.

**VERSE 4.**—“Say to wisdom, ‘You are my sister.’” Join the wisdom of ecclesiastical teaching to yourself with sisterly affection, so that it may preserve you from heretical pollution, which is proved foreign to the Church’s true chastity.

[Col. 1090B] **VERSE 6.**—“From the window.” The literal sense is clear, etc., up to the point that he abandoned the narrow way that leads to life.

**VERSE 8.**—“Beside the corner,” because he turns away from uprightness; “and he walks near the way of her house,” because he has departed from the way of truth. Rightly, therefore, he approaches the way of the house of the prostitute, or of the heretic.

**VERSE 9.**—“In the dark, as evening fell.” For such a person, through the blindness of his heart, is already hastening toward the darkness of sin and condemnation.

**VERSE 10.**—“And behold, a woman meets him, dressed in the attire of a prostitute.” All these matters are clear, etc., up to the point that she destroys him by spiritual death.

**VERSE 11.**—“And she was not one who could remain at home.” There is no heresy content with its first disciples—for these are its household [Col. 1090C]—but it is always seeking new people whom it may deceive.

**VERSE 13.**—“And she seized the young man and kissed him,” that is, she tests the unstable person with the flatteries of false words.

“And she flatters him with an impudent face, saying”: The literal sense is clear, etc., up to the point where the Lord also says to the disciples: “But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you,” etc. (John 16).

**VERSE 16.**—“I have woven my bed with cords.” Beds are accustomed, etc., up to the point that the heretical mind boasts that it has woven for itself the meaning of its poisonous teaching, like a prostitute weaving the bed of her crime.

**VERSE 17.**—“I have sprinkled my bed.” Such people promise that they possess the fragrance of heavenly virtues, by which their own hearts and those of their followers are consecrated like beautiful beds woven with cords—as though they were “the good fragrance of Christ before God.”

**VERSE 18.**—“Come, let us be intoxicated with breasts.” Heretics boast that they will satisfy one another with cups of holy teaching and be joined by the grace of the virtues, until eternal light follows their deeds.

**VERSE 20.**—“He took a moneybag with him.” The glory of the resurrection and the splendor of immortality, by which he might gladden and enrich the citizens of that homeland.

**VERSE 26.**—“And the strongest of all were slain by her.” Thus Solomon himself, the wisest of men, etc., up to the point that whoever denies has gone astray.

**VERSE 27.**—“Her house is the way to the underworld, penetrating inward.” [Col. 1091A] But concerning the Church the Lord says: “The gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16).

“The innermost chambers of death.” The darker and narrower torments of Gehenna, into which heretics and fornicators are known to be plunged.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Does not wisdom,” etc. The Lord spoke openly to the world and said nothing in secret. Why, then, do wretched people neglecting his Gospel flock to heresy and lust?

**VERSE 2.**—“On the heights,” etc. He taught both the disciples and the crowds on the mountain, etc., up to the point of those who speak against him in secret.

**VERSE 4.**—“To you, O men.” She cries out to men, that is, to vigorous hearers of the word; for in either sex, women—that is, unstable minds—are unable to receive the words of wisdom.

[Col. 1091B] **VERSE 5.**—“Understand, you simple ones,” etc. This clearly concerns the Lord, etc., up to the point that he seeks those whom he may be able to seduce.

**VERSE 7.**—“My lips.” The two Testaments, etc., up to the point that they are opened throughout the world for proclaiming salvation.

**VERSE 13.**—“Arrogance.” He exposes arrogance and pride in them, etc., up to the point that they alter their words according to the pleasure of their hearers.

**VERSE 14.**—“Counsel is mine.” Human presumption must not exalt itself: the fullness of the virtues belongs solely to God’s wisdom; from it human weakness receives whatever virtue it possesses.

[Col. 1091C] **VERSE 15.**—“By me kings.” He calls the apostles kings, etc., up to the point where he says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15).

**VERSE 17.**—“I love those who love me,” etc. “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father; and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John 14). Those who keep watch for wisdom in the morning are the ones who strive to attain the vision of Christ with the renewed devotion of their minds.

**VERSE 18.**—“With me are riches.” He calls them proud and exalted riches, etc., up to the point that we await his promises, in which righteousness is found.

**VERSE 22.**—“The Lord possessed me.” Up to this point he has spoken parabolically to the Son; but now, because he had mentioned wisdom without saying what she was or how great her dignity, he shows and commends her, as though incidentally, according to both natures, namely the divine and the human. “The Lord says,” etc. The ways of the Lord are his works, etc., up to the point that his flesh exists because of the works, while his divinity existed before the works.

**VERSE 31.**—“Playing in the inhabited world.” When the times and the creatures of the world began, the Son himself, who already was, remained in the Father. This is said so that no one would deny that he existed together with the creatures and times.

**VERSE 34.**—“At the doors.” The Scriptures, or the teachers; they are also the doorposts, without which we cannot enter the life he promises.

## CHAPTER IX

**VERSE 1.**—“Wisdom built.” Since he had spoken sufficiently about the eternity of Christ’s divinity, etc., up to the point that, having separated them from love of the world, he raised them up to bear the structure of the Church.

“Seven pillars.” Namely, the Churches throughout the world, etc., up to the point that they might hold it together as though supporting it.

**VERSE 5.**—“Come, eat my bread.” The divinity and humanity joined in the one person of Christ; or, in the bread, his body, and in the wine, his blood, by which we are nourished on the altar.

**VERSE 6.**—“Abandon.” After offering the banquet, he adds counsels of life, so that those whom he refreshes with the mysteries of his incarnation he may also instruct with the words of his teaching.

**VERSE 7.**—“Whoever instructs,” etc. As though you were asking, etc., up to the point that he believes himself greater.

**VERSE 8.**—“Do not rebuke.” There is no need to fear, etc., up to the point that one must cease because of his love.

[Col. 1092B] **VERSE 12.**—“If you are wise.” I urge you toward wisdom, but what benefits you does not benefit me. For if you are wise, etc.

**VERSE 13.**—“The foolish woman.” Earlier he commended wisdom through divinity and humanity; now, by contrast, he shows her more commendably, where the foolish woman, etc., who is contrary to her, sits, etc. “The woman,” etc. Here the woman is heresy, etc., up to the point that she is lifted up in the arrogance of her mind.

**VERSE 16.**—“Whoever is simple.” Wisdom calls the simple and foolish, etc., up to the point that they turn aside toward her.

**VERSE 17.**—“Stolen waters.” Wisdom openly set a table before everyone, etc., up to the point that she asserts that forbidden and illicit unions are sweeter.

[Col. 1092C] **VERSE 18.**—“And he did not know that she was there.” The adulterous woman does not know, etc., up to the point that the faithful banquet with the inhabitants of the heights of heaven.

## CHAPTER X

“Proverbs of Solomon.” He introduces a new title because a new kind of speech begins: namely, instead of discussing each separate aspect of good and evil at length as before, he describes the deeds of both in alternating verses.

**VERSE 1.**—“A wise son.” Whoever faithfully preserves the mysteries received through faith gladdens God the Father; whoever pollutes them by evil conduct or heresy grieves the mother, the Church.

**VERSE 2.**—“They profit nothing.” And they deliver from temporal death, etc., up to the point that they bestow what was given for life.

[Col. 1092D] **VERSE 3.**—“The Lord will not afflict.” And even if at times, etc., up to the point that he repays it by just vengeance.

**VERSE 4.**—“He who produces poverty.” Whoever lives negligently in this world will lack good things in the future; but those who serve the Lord courageously are rewarded with the riches of eternal blessedness.

**VERSE 5.**—“He who gathers.” Whoever gathers the souls of the faithful for Christ is a wise son. Indeed, “the harvest is plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matthew 9). Whoever grows sluggish in this acceptable time by neglecting to care for his salvation will be confounded on the day of tribulation.

**VERSE 6.**—“But the mouth of the impious.” The mouth that served feasting, drunkenness, and evil conversations will be condemned because of the iniquity it accumulated. Finally, iniquity covered the mouth of the man who, placed in torments, sought relief with the tongue by which he was punished more severely for many crimes.

[Col. 1093A] **VERSE 7.**—“Memory.” In this life the good remember the good, etc., up to the point that their fire will not be extinguished.

**VERSE 8.**—“The fool is chastised by his lips,” either by his own lips, by which he deserved to be condemned, because “death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Isaiah 66); or by the lips of those from whom he received a sentence of condemnation because he could not be corrected. Hence: “Lord, deliver my soul from lying lips” (Psalm 119).

**VERSE 9.**—“Whoever walks.” Whoever knows how to live simply, etc., up to the point that he receives what his deeds deserve, for “nothing is hidden that will not be revealed” (Matthew 10).

**VERSE 13.**—“A rod on his back.” Vengeance in the life to come, etc., up to the point where it rightly follows: “The wise conceal.”

[Col. 1093B] **VERSE 15.**—“The wealth of the rich.” Spiritually: whoever is rich in God through good works trusts in him, like one who lives in an impregnable city that no enemy can overcome. But those who are confined by poverty of virtue lack heavenly riches because, through harmful fear, they dread enduring hardships for the Lord.

**VERSE 18.**—“They conceal knowledge,” etc. Therefore, if you desire to be truthful and wise, conceal hatred neither secretly in your heart nor express it through verbal abuse; instead, let your heart be filled with love and your mouth with truth.

**VERSE 23.**—“The fool works wickedness as though in jest.” Prudence derives its name from foreseeing. Therefore, the person who rejoices in wickedness is a fool. It belongs to the wise person, and to anyone worthy of the name “man,” to foresee that laughter will be mixed with grief and that the joys of sin will be followed by the punishment of retribution.

[Col. 1093C] **VERSE 24.**—“What the impious fears will come upon him.” He speaks of that impious person, etc., up to the point that what they hold in their hearts will arrive.

**VERSE 25.**—“Like a storm.” He speaks of the persecutors of the Church, who seek to overthrow the house of faith. But because it is established on the true foundation, Christ, they themselves immediately perish.

**VERSE 26.**—“Like vinegar to the teeth.” As the perfidy of heretics, etc., up to the point that they also attack with words. Hence: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

[Col. 1093D] **VERSE 28.**—“But hope.” This is not contrary to what was said above, etc., up to the point where he adds this concerning those who sin knowingly.

**VERSE 29.**—“The strength of the simple is his way, and terror.” If the obscure matters of Scripture, etc., up to the point that they disdain to act.

## CHAPTER XI

**VERSE 1.**—“A deceitful balance.” Whether of money or of judgment, etc., up to the point that it corresponds to one’s conduct.

**VERSE 2.**—“Where there is pride.” The proud either behave insultingly through contempt or ignorance of discipline, or inflict insult upon their neighbors; “whoever exalts himself will be humbled.”

**VERSE 7.**—“When the impious man dies.” Origen did not know this, etc., up to the point that what follows perhaps pertains to them.

“The expectation of the anxious.” The concern of the good is to fulfill God’s commands; the concern of wicked sinners who sin knowingly is that they will be carried away to eternal punishment. Therefore, the expectation of the former will be crowned, while that of the latter will be condemned even before judgment, their own conscience condemning them.

**VERSE 9.**—“The hypocrite.” The heretic who pretends to Catholic doctrine deceives his hearer. Those who follow the truth of the Gospel will be freed by Catholic wisdom, lest they be deceived by heretical snares.

**VERSE 12.**—“Whoever despises,” etc. The person who loves us sincerely is not to be despised, even if he acts foolishly; for whoever does this needs wisdom. But the prudent person keeps silent publicly and corrects privately, as is explained more clearly below.

[Col. 1094B] **VERSE 14.**—“Where there is no governor, the people will fall, but there is safety where there is much counsel.” So that you would not think, etc., up to the point that he may be corrected by many.

**VERSE 15.**—“He will suffer.” The literal sense is clear, etc., up to the point that he will make himself deserving of punishment before the eyes of the strict Judge.

“But whoever avoids snares will be secure.” In the future, the person who is now rightly fearful, cares for his sins through repentance, and keeps himself free from the company of the impenitent will be secure.

**VERSE 21.**—“Hand in hand.” Whoever joins hand to hand, etc., up to the point from which the earlier statement follows: “A crooked heart is an abomination to the Lord.”

[Col. 1094C] **VERSE 22.**—“A golden ring in the nostrils,” etc. If you fasten a gold ring in your own nostrils, etc., up to the point that he is devoted to carnal things.

**VERSE 27.**—“He rises early who seeks good,” etc., that is, he rises to life at the time of the resurrection because he now does good in the time of action. But whoever seeks out the evil that he may say or do is held back from higher things by its weight.

**VERSE 28.**—“But the righteous are like,” etc. Those who do good in the present in hope of future rewards receive justly what they hope for. A green leaf on a tree signifies fruits that it has not yet displayed; so the righteous sprout like a green leaf, since, made safe by hope, they do not cease to advance in faith and virtue.

[Col. 1094D] **VERSE 29.**—“Whoever is foolish.” The impious lives for the pious; the former is condemned, while the latter receives the prize for which he contended.

**VERSE 30.**—“Whoever accepts.” Whoever undertakes the care of souls for the Lord, etc., up to the point that he arranges to reign more exaltedly with the Lord.

**VERSE 31.**—“If the righteous.” If martyrs suffer so much unjustly, etc., up to the point that, even if we are not impious, certainly, if we deny that we are sinners, we deceive ourselves and the truth is not in us.

## CHAPTER XII

**VERSE 1.**—“Whoever is good,” etc. The connection of these verses is as follows: the good person does not trust in his own thoughts but seeks the Lord’s grace and through it lives piously. Whoever trusts in his own thoughts cannot be good; for whoever does not care to seek God’s grace persists in evil action.

**VERSE 4.**—“A woman.” Literally, a good and chaste woman, etc., up to the point that the rottenness of an evil doctrine corrupts.

**VERSE 5.**—“Thoughts.” The righteous consider their deeds, etc., up to the point that they have forgotten the fear of the Lord.

**VERSE 7.**—“Overturn the impious.” There is much impiety in the gods of the nations, etc., up to the point that whatever members arrive there from one place or another find the joys they had hoped for.

**VERSE 10.**—“He knows,” that is, he has compassion on the dullness and weakness of those entrusted to him.

“But the inward parts of the impious are cruel”: those who do not sympathize with their subjects, but, as the Lord says, “beat boys and maidservants, saying, ‘My master delays coming.’”

[Col. 1095B] **VERSE 12.**—“Desire.” The impious person desires, etc., up to the point where he speaks conversely about the good.

“But the root of the righteous will flourish.” Faith, hope, and charity, by which they are rooted in Christ, do not deceive them; rather, in the future they will receive more than they hope for.

**VERSE 16.**—“The fool,” etc. Whoever desires to avenge himself in the present is a fool; whoever disregards this for the Lord’s sake is wise.

“But whoever conceals.” He does not wish anger to be hidden so that it may persist, but so that it may be entirely erased. For it is the nature of anger that, once expressed, it grows hotter, while when concealed it weakens.

**VERSE 18.**—“But the tongue of the wise is healing,” etc., because they reach life by fulfilling the good things they promise, and they show others what they should follow.

[Col. 1095C] **VERSE 19.**—“The lip of truth,” etc. Catholic faith will always remain; whoever suddenly introduces new doctrines is a minister of falsehood.

**VERSE 23.**—“A crafty man.” A wise and prudent person sometimes conceals knowledge, either because he is unable to speak to them as spiritual people, but only as carnal people, or because he does not wish to give what is holy to dogs or cast pearls before swine, or to send them.

“The heart of the foolish provokes.” This happens either when they desire to know more than they ought, and, becoming vain in their thoughts, possess and hold folly instead of wisdom; or when, imposing upon others what they cannot grasp, they take away from those who seemed to possess wisdom the light of the sun—that is, wisdom—just as sunlight is taken from weak eyes.

[Col. 1095D] **VERSE 24.**—“The hand of the strong.” The perfect not only overcome the battles of the vices but also preside over their chosen brothers with a greater grace of virtues.

“But what is slack.” Those who are loose in spirit, etc., up to the point that one must not despair of such people, since he adds: “The sorrow of the righteous,” etc.

**VERSE 25.**—“Sorrow in the heart,” etc., because it is necessary first for the sorrow of repentance to humble the sinner beneficially, and afterward for the word of reconciliation given through the priest’s judgment to gladden or refresh him.

“Whoever neglects loss,” etc. If this is understood literally, etc., up to the point that he either hands over his very flesh to death.

[Col. 1096A] **VERSE 27.**—“He will not find,” etc. For money acquired by fraud, etc., up to the point that the splendor of eternal life is purchased by them at a price more precious than gold.

## CHAPTER XIII

**VERSE 1.**—“A wise son.” The difference between the wise and the fool is so great that the former may sometimes advance through instruction until he teaches the one who taught him; the latter, when corrected, refuses to listen.

**VERSE 4.**—“The lazy person wishes and does not wish.” He wishes to reign with the Lord, etc., up to the point where Jesus son of Sirach says: “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways.”

“But the soul of those who perform the commandments will be made fat,” because it will be refreshed with the perfect sweetness of heavenly things. Hence: “As with marrow” (Psalm 26), etc. Alternatively, those who sweat through pious labors for the Lord will be given an unfading crown.

[Col. 1096B] **VERSE 7.**—“There is one who is as though rich,” not truly so, like the man “who was clothed in purple and fine linen” (Luke 16); but because he did not possess God, etc., up to the point where what true poverty does is added.

**VERSE 11.**—“Wealth,” etc. “Those who desire to become rich fall into temptation,” etc., up to the point that he will receive manifold gifts of heavenly blessedness. Concerning him:

**VERSE 12.**—“Hope that is delayed,” etc. For indeed, etc., up to the point that he himself is the tree of life for those who embrace him.

**VERSE 13.**—“Whoever speaks evil.” Alternatively, etc., up to the point where it says: “If a man is overtaken in any transgression,” etc.

[Col. 1096C] **VERSE 14.**—“The law of the wise.” From the moment a person begins to be wise, he uses this law to avoid death and obtain life.

**VERSE 16.**—“With counsel,” especially divine counsel, which is found in the Scriptures. For the person who lives outside this counsel is a fool, even if he appears naturally prudent.

**VERSE 20.**—“Whoever walks with the wise.” Any simple or rustic person who cannot comprehend the secrets of wisdom will nevertheless rightly be counted among the wise if he follows the examples of the wise by his manner of life.

“A friend of fools.” Whoever loves fools—not because they are human beings, but because of their folly, since they are jesters, actors, or similar people—not in order to instruct and correct them but to make them worse by indulging them, will be held liable for the condemnation of fools, even if he appears wise.

[Col. 1096D] **VERSE 22.**—“The good man,” etc. Often good people die without children, etc., up to the point that “the kingdom of God will be given to a nation producing its fruits.”

**VERSE 23.**—“Much food.” Another translator, etc., up to the point that what follows agrees with both interpretations.

**VERSE 24.**—“Whoever spares the rod hates his son,” etc. For a good father carefully instructs his son, and a Catholic teacher his disciple, so that he may not turn aside toward iniquity.

## CHAPTER XIV

**VERSE 1.**—“The wise woman,” etc. She will destroy it by living badly, and sometimes by reigning openly, etc., up to the point where he adds explicitly concerning them:

**VERSE 3.**—“In the mouth of the fool.” Fools afflict the humble whom they despise through empty talk; but the humble fortify themselves through the teaching of the wise, so that they may not be deceived.

**VERSE 4.**—“Where there is no,” etc. These words belong with what precedes, etc., up to the point that he feeds the widow of Zarephath, by whom he himself is also fed.

**VERSE 6.**—“The scoffer seeks wisdom,” etc. Like Caiaphas, etc., up to the point that because they seek perversely, they never find it at all.

**VERSE 7.**—“Go away from,” etc. Therefore the scoffer does not find the wisdom he seeks, etc., up to the point that they strive to devote themselves to her meditation.

[Col. 1097B] **VERSE 10.**—“A stranger.” That is, a reprobate, etc., up to the point where it adds: “The Lord of the impious,” etc.

“The wise person fears and turns aside.” Just as it belongs to the fool to trust in his own confidence, etc., up to the point that he endures punishments courageously after death.

**VERSE 17.**—“The impatient,” etc. The impatient person is certainly blameworthy, etc., up to the point that he is counted among the reprobate.

**VERSE 19.**—“The wicked will lie before the good.” Seeing their torments, etc., up to the point that they may behold their punishments.

**VERSE 24.**—“The foolishness of fools.” It means lack of foresight, as though derived from failure to foresee.

**VERSE 25.**—“A faithful witness delivers souls.” The Catholic preacher is meant, who faithfully proclaims and presents the testimonies of Scripture; the heretic presents falsehoods.

“He presents falsehoods.” Another translation reads: “But the crafty deceiver sets souls on fire with falsehood.”

“Versipellis” [the shape-shifter], that is, the devil, who falsely calls the evils he suggests good; and while promising eternal good, leads people to torments.

**VERSE 26.**—“In the fear of the Lord.” The fear of the Lord provides confidence in strength, etc., up to the point that they hoped in the Lord.

**VERSE 27.**—“The fear of the Lord.” This is their hope, etc., up to the point where it says: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 9).

**VERSE 30.**—“The life of the flesh.” Through the flesh, weakness; through the bones, strength. If innocence of mind is guarded, even what is weak outwardly is eventually strengthened. Hence it adds:

“Rottenness of the bones is envy,” because through the vice of jealousy those things that appear strong in human eyes perish before God’s eyes. For bones to rot through envy means that every strong thing perishes.

## CHAPTER XV

**VERSE 1.**—“A soft answer turns away wrath.” Whoever humbly accepts the words of one rebuking him is already approaching pardon for the guilt he has incurred. Whoever resists the one correcting him provokes the judge’s anger against himself.

**VERSE 2.**—“Pours forth folly.” By perverting Scripture and placing his own opinions above its authority, like the foolish philosophers Porphyry and Julian, who poured forth the streams of their folly against the teachers of the Church.

[Col. 1098A] **VERSE 5.**—“The fool mocks.” Every sinner devoted to earthly actions and foreseeing nothing of the future is a fool; he mocks discipline by disparaging divine correction.

**VERSE 7.**—“The heart of fools is unlike.” Either unlike itself, because of various thoughts, so that it never remains the same; in contrast, it is said of Hannah: “Her face was no longer changed in different directions.”

**VERSE 10.**—“Evil teaching.” “Whoever abolishes one of these least commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven.” Yet for such people, if they are corrected, a return to pardon remains open; but if they do not accept rebukes, they will perish completely.

[Col. 1098B] **VERSE 15.**—“All the days.” The entire time of God’s people, etc., up to the point that they rejoice as though at an unending banquet.

**VERSE 17.**—“It is better to be invited to vegetables.” It is far more beneficial to preserve the innocence of a simple life with charity, etc., up to the words: “Depart from me, you workers of iniquity.”

**VERSE 19.**—“The ways of the lazy,” who are reluctant to practice righteousness, etc., up to the point where he adds, because this does not hinder the good:

“The way of the righteous is without stumbling.” Whatever adversity the righteous encounter in their way of life, they do not stumble, because they leap over adversities through the hope of eternity and the leap of inward contemplation.

**VERSE 23.**—“A man rejoices.” It is human to rejoice at an opinion as though it had been wisely expressed. But the truly wise person carefully considers not only what he says but also the appropriateness of the place, time, and person to whom he speaks.

**VERSE 24.**—“From the final hell,” etc. The first hell is the blindness of the sinful soul, which lacks knowledge of the true light. Concerning it: “They descend alive into hell” (Psalm 54).

**VERSE 25.**—“The widow of the Church,” namely, his bride, for whose life he deigned to die.

**VERSE 26.**—“He will be established”: in judgment, when he will repay all with fitting rewards not only for their deeds but also for their words.

[Col. 1098D] **VERSE 30.**—“The light of the eyes gladdens the soul.” It rightly delights the human mind, etc., up to the point that the work thereby burns more intensely.

“Light of the eyes.” Another translation reads: “The eye that sees good things delights good hearts,” namely, the Lord’s good things in the land of the living. Because the mind contemplates them with its eye, the heart rightly rejoices, although the person may be afflicted outwardly.

## CHAPTER XVI

**VERSE 1.**—“It belongs to a man to prepare his mind.” How, then, does it belong to a man to prepare his mind, but to God to guide his tongue? It signifies the time of persecution, concerning which it is said: “Do not consider how or what you are to speak; for what you are to say will be given in that hour” (Matthew 10).

**VERSE 2.**—“All the ways.” Thus he distinguishes the actions of all, both good and evil, and what they think in secret, with a precise balance. Hence he adds:

**VERSE 3.**—“Reveal your works to the Lord.” We reveal our works when, knowing that nothing is hidden from him, we recall him in everything we do and ask for his help. Then he directs not only our works but also our thoughts.

**VERSE 4.**—“The Lord made everything for himself,” etc. The Lord had no reason for acting except his own will: namely, to display his goodness to a rational creature whom he would make eternally blessed. But the one who voluntarily abandoned the goodness of his created state—that is, the devil, together with his followers—he condemned with just severity.

[Col. 1099B] **VERSE 5.**—“The Lord detests.” Whoever attributes to himself the good he does, even if he appears to perform no evil with his hands, loses the innocence of his heart, in which he has placed himself above the giver of good things. Therefore the Lord detests such a man, whom he sees ungrateful for his benefits.

**VERSE 7.**—“When the ways of the Lord please him.” The holiness of divine worship is so great, etc., up to the point that they were also converted to the truth of the faith.

**VERSE 8.**—“Better is a little with righteousness,” etc. It is better to serve God devoutly in a simple way of life than to abound in many virtues while despising the deeds of one’s neighbors.

**VERSE 10.**—“Divination is on the king’s lips.” What other king does not err in judgment, etc., up to the point that he would fill the mouths of his prophets?

[Col. 1099C] “A weight and a balance.” Just stones are strong, etc., up to the point that he distributes according to the measure of faith and graces.

**VERSE 13.**—“The will of kings,” etc., that is, of the righteous. “Many kings and prophets desired to see what you see, and did not see it.” These people resist vices and are surrounded by the service of the virtues, as by attendants. For the kings of the earth often detest righteous lips, as Herod detested John.

**VERSE 14.**—“Messengers of death.” Angels of Satan, heretics, etc., up to the point where someone happens to offend by speaking foolishly.

“He will appease.” (Jerome, *On the Death of Fabiola*.) David purged homicide and adultery by seven days of fasting.

**VERSE 15.**—“In the brightness of the king’s face is life.” Whoever deserves to see the joyful face of Christ will be granted to live with him eternally. In another sense, all flesh will see the salvation of God; but then the righteous will see him appeased, while the reprobate will see him angry.

“And his kindness is like the late rain.” In Judea, the late rain customarily comes even today after the harvests have ripened, etc., up to the point that the Lord’s heavenly irrigation makes them fruitful.

[Col. 1099D] **VERSE 22.**—“A fountain of life.” The true preacher opens the ways of life to his hearers, etc., up to the point that they despise in foolish hearts the good things they hear.

**VERSE 24.**—“Well-arranged words are a honeycomb,” etc. Many people through eloquence, etc., up to the point that such words proceed from the inward sweetness of the soul.

**VERSE 26.**—“The soul of the laborer labors for itself,” etc. The literal sense is clear, etc., up to the point that he must do the good things he says.

[Col. 1100A] **VERSE 27.**—“The senseless man digs up evil.” This may be understood especially of the heretic, etc., up to the point where James says: “The tongue sets the wheel of our birth on fire, itself set on fire by Gehenna” (James 3).

**VERSE 29.**—“The wicked man entices his friend,” etc. This may be understood of the heretic and of every supporter of evil, since “the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked man is blessed.”

**VERSE 30.**—“Whoever thinks with eyes fixed,” etc. To complete evil is worse than to do it, etc., up to the point that he does not see what recompense will follow his evils.

**VERSE 32.**—“The patient man is better than the strong,” etc. It is a lesser victory to conquer cities, etc., up to the point that he lays it low through the humility of patience.

[Col. 1100B] **VERSE 33.**—“Lots are cast into the lap.” Just as lots are cast into the lap, etc., up to the point that it is as though they came from the lap of divine judgment.

## CHAPTER XVII

**VERSE 1.**—“Better is a morsel.” It is better to do a small good deed with charity, without the knowledge required for preaching—for this is what it means for the morsel to be dry—than to shine more brilliantly with virtues while discord is mixed in.

**VERSE 6.**—“The crown of elders,” etc. The elders, patriarchs, and prophets are celebrated with divine praise by the sons of sons, that is, by the successors of the apostles. The glory of the preachers of the New Testament is that they were found worthy to be sons of the ancient fathers.

[Col. 1100C] **VERSE 8.**—“A most precious gem.” Whoever faithfully awaits future rewards, etc., understanding wisely that “for those who love God all things work together for good” (Romans 8).

**VERSE 12.**—“It is better to meet a she-bear,” etc. It was easier for holy teachers to confront the fury of paganism, etc., up to the point that it is often easier to bring a heretic back to the right faith or a Catholic acting wrongly back to good works.

**VERSE 13.**—“Whoever.” To release water, etc., up to the point where the contrary statement follows: “Whoever imposes silence on a fool calms anger.”

**VERSE 16.**—“What does it profit?” What does it profit the unbelieving Jewish people, etc., up to the point that they neglected to possess the wisdom of pious action?

**VERSE 17.**—“At all times.” Whoever truly loves God preserves his love for him at all times; nor does he abandon in the distress of suffering the one whom he confessed in the tranquility of peace.

**VERSE 18.**—“The foolish man claps his hands.” He is foolish who, when he undertakes to govern his brother’s soul, boasts of his own deeds instead of supplying him, with humble compassion, whatever salutary assistance he can.

“A joyful heart.” Whoever rejoices in the inward consolation of the Holy Spirit, etc., up to the point that he has lost the glory of love.

[Col. 1101A] **VERSE 24.**—“In the face of the prudent.” The wisdom of the Godhead shone in the face of Christ, etc., up to the point that they seek it with complete devotion.

**VERSE 26.**—“It is not good to inflict harm on the righteous.” This may be understood of the Judge and Ruler of the ages himself, who wished to be struck for our salvation, and of all the rulers of the Church, who have either been stripped of their possessions by the impious or consumed by death itself.

## CHAPTER XVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“When the impious man has come into the depths,” etc. Whoever, enveloped in the long darkness of sins, once despairs of the light, loosens the reins of sinning for himself through despair. Yet he cannot in any way escape the reproach of future condemnation, since no memory of divine fear restrained him.

[Col. 1101B] **VERSE 4.**—“Deep water.” The Lord and the apostles openly disclosed to the world the mysteries of both Testaments. Concerning them he adds: “And an overflowing torrent, a fountain of wisdom.” Deep water—that is, the words of the wise—washes and waters minds, lest they remain disfigured by the filth of sins or wither through dryness.

**VERSE 9.**—“Whoever is soft and slack.” Whoever does not strictly carry out the good things he has begun imitates the hand of one who destroys through negligence and laxity.

**VERSE 11.**—“The wealth of the rich is his strong city.” Earthly wealth, etc., up to the point that it keeps all the enemy’s ambushes away as though with an impregnable wall.

[Col. 1101C] **VERSE 13.**—“Whoever answers before he hears.” Whoever wishes to be a teacher before learning does not avoid the guilt of folly. Whoever hastily judges the deeds of his neighbors before fully knowing the case of both parties shows himself worthy of confusion.

**VERSE 14.**—“The spirit of a man sustains his weakness.” The man himself, however, etc., up to the point that he is sustained by strength of mind.

“But a spirit inclined to anger.” An angry person often says things that he later regrets when calm, and frequently does not know what he has said. Nevertheless, his madness is very easily endured and quieted through the moderation of the wise.

“The gift of a man.” The gift of charity, etc., up to the point that he would willingly make him obey himself.

[Col. 1101D] **VERSE 17.**—“The righteous person is first.” Everyone who is truly righteous, etc., up to the point that he rewards his humility with a fitting recompense.

**VERSE 19.**—“A brother who is helped.” When the people of the Jews and of the nations, etc., up to the point that they defend them from the attack of unbelievers.

**VERSE 23.**—“The poor man will speak with entreaties.” The humble in spirit humbly worship the Lord, like the tax collector; the proud boast of their merits, like the Pharisee.

**VERSE 24.**—“A lovable man.” A Gentile who has been converted is loved by the Lord more than an unbelieving Jew who persists in unbelief, from whom he was born according to the flesh. This may also be understood of the apostles, who were born in Judea, because they loved believing Gentiles more than unbelievers of their own nation.

## CHAPTER XIX

**VERSE 1.**—“Better is a poor man.” A simple hearer of the word of God is better if he advances by practicing what he understands in the Scriptures than an educated person who twists his lips toward preaching heresy in matters he has understood cautiously.

**VERSE 2.**—“Where there is no,” etc. Knowledge of heavenly life is necessary for the human soul, etc., up to the point that they fell from a state of blessedness into the punishment of misery and mortality.

### Verse 3.—“Folly,” etc.

When fools abandon the way of truth, etc., up to the point where he reproaches the Lord Himself in his deranged mind, as though He had imposed unbearable burdens [Col. 1102B].

### Verse 4.—“Riches add friends”

The riches of the heavenly kingdom, which holy teachers preach as destined to be bestowed upon the faithful, win many friends both for those same preachers and for God, their giver. But from the prophets, because they promise nothing of certain blessedness, even those whom they have are separated, having turned to the most certain promise of faith in the Lord.

### Verse 5.—“A false witness”

He had reproved the man who followed words alone; now he reproves the man who corrupts the words of the Lord’s authority by interpreting them wrongly. The fact that many things are repeated frequently is a confirmation, as Joseph says, because the word is God’s and will be fulfilled more quickly.

### Verse 10.—“Folly does not befit”

The delights of Scripture do not befit a heretic [Col. 1102C], because he does not know how to use them well; nor is it fitting that one who is still a servant of sin should be preferred to the righteous in the governance of the Church.

### Verse 11.—“The instruction of a man”

Ecclesiastical instruction, etc., up to the point where it rightly adds:

“And his glory is to pass beyond iniquity.” For it belongs to the perfected teacher to endure the wickedness of others patiently, while knowing that he himself is patiently observed by the unrighteous. For personal purity without endurance is not sufficient, nor endurance without purity.

### Verse 13.—“A father’s grief”

God is always impassible in His nature, yet He is said to grieve according to our way of speaking when He sees human beings—whom He created to believe in and praise Him—serving the devil. Hence it is said that He regretted having made man upon the earth, and that He was touched with inward grief of heart: “I will blot out,” He says, “the man whom I created from the face of the earth” (Gen. VI) [Col. 1102D].

“Roofs continually dripping.” Just as dripping roofs certainly receive the rain, etc., up to the point where they return it to their hearers mixed with filth.

### Verse 15.—“Sloth brings on sleep”

A slothful person is one who remains awake through knowing what is right but grows numb by doing nothing. Yet sloth brings on sleep, because vigilance in right thinking is gradually lost when one ceases from action. Rightly, then, it continues:

“And a slack soul shall hunger.” For because it does not direct itself upward by tightening its discipline, it spreads itself downward through desires and, because it is not restrained by the strength of serious study, is wounded by the lowest craving for reputation [Col. 1103A]. Thus, in proportion as it neglects to be bound by discipline, it scatters itself hungrily through desires for pleasure.

### Verse 18.—“Discipline your son”

If you see the person entrusted to you going astray, correct him diligently. But if he refuses correction, deal with him cautiously, so that he may find nothing in your words or deeds by which he could sin further. The following agrees with this:

### Verse 19.—“The impatient man will bear loss, and when he has seized”

For if, because of the harshness of a brother who contradicts you, you fall into the vice of impatience, etc., up to the point where, having violently taken away money, he will unwillingly give his soul in exchange for it.

### Verse 22.—“Better is a poor man”

Than one who, calling himself worthy of the name of man because of the excellence of his virtues, deceives himself unknowingly, having lost through pride the good works he performed [Col. 1103B].

### Verse 24.—“The slothful man hides his hand”

No one is so slothful, etc., up to the point where extending the hand to the mouth means making one’s work agree with one’s speech.

### Verse 28.—“He devours”

As a hungry man eagerly seeks food, so he ardently seeks to perpetrate iniquity.

## Chapter XX

### Verse 2.—“A luxurious thing”

It follows.

### Verse 4.—“In summer”

The kingdom of God is compared with summer, because now the clouds of our sorrow will pass away, and the days of eternal life will shine with the brightness of the sun.

### Verse 7.—“He will leave blessed sons after him”

Not literally, but those who follow his examples. Hence all the elect are sons of Abraham, to whom not present but future blessedness is promised; hence, “The king who sat…”

### Verse 8.—“The king who sits on the throne of judgment”

Although in this life the elect suffer the evils inflicted by the reprobate, etc., up to the point where he receives what is worthy of his deeds.

### Verse 9.—“Who can say”

He does not say, “Who has,” etc., up to the point where they despise their neighbors as though they were worthless. He adds:

“Weight and weight.” A different weight, etc., up to the indications by which we ought to direct our judgment.

### Verse 11.—“He is understood from his pursuits”

For whoever is marked by virtues together with the moderation of self-restraint, etc., up to the parallel statement: “The companion of fools becomes like them.”

### Verse 12.—“The Lord made both”

Let no one fit for preaching despise a simple brother, [Col. 1103D] etc., up to the point where He gives to each according to the measure of his gift.

### Verse 14.—“It is evil”

For one who desires to prepare eternal rewards in heaven, it is evil that he must endure in the present, so that when he departs from the world he may rejoice, clearly seeing that “the sufferings of this present time are not worthy” etc.

### Verse 15.—“There is gold and an abundance”

This is the wise buyer’s boast, etc., up to the point where they are shown to be comparable to precious vessels.

### Verse 17.—“The bread of deceit is sweet to a man,” etc.

In whatever member a person has sinned more greatly, etc., up to the point where he had let those things flow out in excessive words while feasting.

[Col. 1104A] ### Verse 21.—“Inheritance”

Those who desire to multiply themselves in this life through the wickedness of greed, etc., up to the point where it is an abomination before God.

### Verse 23.—“A weight and a weight, a deceitful balance, are an abomination before God,” etc.

He has a double weight and a deceitful balance in his heart, etc., up to the point where he has [concerned] either his soul consecrated to God in baptism.

### Verse 25.—“It is ruin for a man to devour the holy and then retract after making vows”

If it is a sin to harm anyone, etc., up to the point where eternal condemnation awaits those who persecute the saints in order to fulfill their own vows. Therefore it adds:

### Verse 26.—“A wise king scatters the wicked and bends the wheel over them”

It was the custom among the ancients, etc., up to the point where the crown of life promised by God to those who love Him is opposed to that wheel [Col. 1104B].

### Verse 30.—“The livid mark of a wound”

For when we are struck externally, etc., up to the point where, just as the belly digests food, so the mind, by working things over, digests its anxieties.

## Chapter XXI

### Verse 1.—“As are the divisions”

The hearts of all human beings, not only the king’s, are in the hand of the Lord, because all the ends of the earth are in His hand. But he calls every holy person a king, one who knows how to conquer within himself the battles of vices and uproot the shoots of wickedness. For just as the Lord fills the boundaries of the earth and the air with the divisions of the waters, and also covers the regions above the heavens with waters, so He inclines the king’s heart wherever He wills. For just as He distributes the divisions of grace according to His will to angels and human beings, so He makes the hearts of the saints worthy of whatever gifts He wills [Col. 1104C]. Let the Pelagian be silent, because apart from God’s grace there is no place for salvation.

### Verse 8.—“A perverse way”

Justly before the Lord, etc., up to the point where he rightly carries out what he originally received by nature.

### Verse 13.—“He who stops his ear”

Generally, etc., up to the point where he is not worthy even to hear of divine mercy.

### Verse 15.—“Terror to those who practice iniquity”

Because they know that it is forbidden by God. Although they take carnal pleasure in the perpetration of their lust, they are not without inward fear of mind, because they do not doubt that they will suffer forever for the things they did wickedly for a time.

[Col. 1104D] ### Verse 16.—“In the assembly of giants”

Of demons, etc., up to the point where the Judge Himself bears witness: “Depart from me, you accursed, into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. XXV).

### Verse 18.—“The just man is given in exchange”

“Just” and “upright” mean the same thing, etc., up to the point where, although they could have done so much more easily, they did not take care for wisdom.

### Verse 20.—“A desirable treasure”

The reprobate not only fail to attain virtues, etc., up to the point where it is said: “Do not fear those who kill the body,” etc. (Matt. X).

### Verse 22.—“The city of the strong”

That is, the world, etc., up to the point where he reproves ecclesiastical discipline.

[Col. 1105A] ### Verse 28.—“A lying witness”

One who testifies that he serves God, etc., up to the point where, through the justice of the Judge, he receives the palm after victory.

### Verse 29.—“An impious man”

Judas, etc., up to the point where he sinned by denying.

## Chapter XXII

### Verse 1.—“Better is…”

For if someone were to gain the whole world, he would rightly despise it all so that his name might be written in heaven and his memory fixed eternally among the saints and angels.

“A good name.” One praised by the testimony of the faithful, not by that of the ignorant crowd. Hence: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

“Good favor.” Someone is praised by the good for good works; indeed, the Father who is in heaven is glorified for the gifts of merits bestowed upon him [Col. 1105B].

### Verse 2.—“Rich and poor”

Do not honor the rich because of their riches, nor despise the poor because of their poverty, for both are God’s work, made in His image and for His work.

### Verse 3.—“The prudent man saw evil”

Many among the rulers believed, etc., up to the point where they attain it also in ordinary actions.

### Verse 4.—“The end of moderation”

Because, plainly, the perfection of virtues is, etc., up to the point where he might perhaps deserve to be subjected to punishments.

“Wealth and glory.” The end of moderation is the fear of the Lord; glory and life are its end, because the perfection of virtues in this life is that we fear God chastely. The end of virtues in the future is that we receive the riches of the promised inheritance, the glory of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 1105C], and eternal life.

### Verse 6.—“It is a proverb”

“What the fresh jar has once absorbed, it will long retain as its scent.” Greek history relates that Alexander the Great could not rid himself either in character or in gait of the traits of his tutor Leonidas, nor of the vices with which he had been tainted as a child.

### Verse 8.—“He who sows iniquity”

It is clear that the one who teaches iniquity either by word or example will suffer vengeance. But since it follows:

“And the rod of his anger.” He seems to be referring to that iniquity, etc., up to the point where: “All who take the sword will perish by the sword” (Matt. XXVI).

### Verse 13.—“The slothful man says,” concerning good works, etc.

Up to the point where he either, like the other righteous, consumes him with torments.

[Col. 1105D] ### Verse 16.—“He who slanders”

It is established that the rapacious lose both what they take from the poor and what they seemed to possess justly, when in judgment they receive punishment for what they have done.

“My son.” Up to this point the title of the Proverbs of Solomon, which was placed above, etc., has instructed us to apply the heart to understanding what the wise say.

### Verse 24.—“Do not be a friend”

In general, however, etc., up to the point where they begin to imitate them.

“With an angry man, and do not walk with a man.” This applies to anyone, but especially to the Jew who raged with deranged mind against Christ and His disciples. Those who care to be saved are forbidden their friendship, lest through their proximity they too perish, as it was proved could happen in the case of Judas [Col. 1106A].

### Verse 26.—“Do not be among those who strike hands”

Do not associate with such people, etc., up to the point where: “With what were you clothed?”

### Verse 28.—“Do not move”
