Do not move the boundaries of the Catholic faith which the teachers established from the beginning.

### Verse 29.—“Have you seen a man swift in his work?”—“before…”

Whenever you see someone swift in his work, etc., up to the point where he takes care that their error not be adopted.

## Chapter XXIII

### Verse 1.—“When you sit”

It must be read allegorically, etc., up to the point where it rightly adds:

### Verse 3.—“Do not desire”—that is, do not desire [Col. 1106B] to listen to the speeches of the one who deceives his hearers with the sweetness of falsehood.

### Verse 4.—“Set a limit”

Concerning this it was said above: “Do not move the ancient boundaries which the fathers established”—namely, the boundaries of the faith and of the truth handed down by the fathers.

### Verse 6.—“Do not eat”

That is, do not converse about the Scriptures with the heretic who envies human salvation, preferring to deceive rather than to be corrected. For just as a soothsayer and interpreter of dreams judges what he does not know, so the heretic interprets at will what he does not understand in the Scriptures.

“Eat,” etc. He says: Learn without fear what I say and do what I teach, although in what he teaches he himself has no firm faith, knowing that he has fabricated the things he teaches [Col. 1106C].

### Verse 8.—“The food which you have eaten”

The perverse ideas which you learned from heretics must necessarily be abandoned, either to be corrected through repentance or to be punished for them after death. You must also lose the words of confession by which, when they preached to you, you had thought they should be humbly favored.

### Verse 9.—“In the ears”

“Do not give what is holy to dogs, nor cast pearls before swine.” Just as he warned you not to listen to the doctrines of heretics, so now he warns you not, seduced by love of empty glory, to pour out the secrets of truth indiscriminately before unclean people.

### Verse 10.—“Do not touch,” etc.

He calls the Lord the protector of little ones and orphans, etc., up to the point where the one who harms their good conduct by disturbing them does not escape the Lord’s judgment [Col. 1106D].

### Verse 17.—“Let your heart not envy sinners”

If all day long, etc., up to the point where it is said in the Apocalypse: “Be faithful unto death, and I will give you the crown of life” (Apoc. II).

### Verse 20.—“Do not be among the banquets of sinners”

To bring meats for eating means, in conversation marked by detraction, to speak in turn of the vices of one’s neighbors. Their punishment is immediately added: “For they are devoted to drinking,” etc.

“Those who contribute their shares will be consumed.” A “share” is a contribution, etc., up to the point where the languor of his detraction has seized him.

### Verse 29.—“To whom woe? Whose?”

He asks by way of argument, etc., up to the point concerning the Jews: “You are of your father the devil” (John VIII).

[Col. 1107A] “To whom quarrels? To whom pits?” Quarrels, because he does not preserve harmony, etc., up to the point where he very often falls into the pit concerning which it is said: “For a harlot is a deep pit,” etc.

“To whom wounds without cause?” Because many who have drunk too much have received wounds through swelling, which they suffered without any cause requiring a sword.

“To whom redness of the eyes?” Because immoderate drinking of wine brings blindness to both outward and inward sight.

### Verse 30.—“Is it not to those…”

He does not forbid drinking wine when necessity requires it, but he forbids lingering over wine beyond the proper time and usefulness, and competing to empty cups. Hence Isaiah: “Woe to those who are mighty for drinking wine and strong men for mixing drunkenness” (Isa. V).

### Verse 33.—“Your eyes shall see”

It is almost a natural vice, after drinking wine, to desire a woman in one’s heart, with shameful speech accompanying it [Col. 1107B].

### Verse 34.—“And you shall be like one sleeping”

They sleep in the middle of the sea, etc., up to the point where he loses the diligence of careful attention.

### Verse 35.—“They struck me”

It is the voice of one who has been beaten and of one who is sleeping, etc., up to the point where he is perpetually drunk with pleasures.

## Chapter XXIV

### Verse 1.—“Do not envy”

Do not desire to imitate those whom you see entangled in the vices mentioned above; rather, take care to devote yourself to wisdom. Hence it adds: “By wisdom the house shall be built.”

### Verse 4.—“A wise man”

Not every strong man is wise, but the reverse is true. For even if he is weak in body, if wisdom is present he is altogether strong and conquers the contests of the adversary, that is, the devil [Col. 1107C].

### Verse 7.—“High things are beyond a fool”

A fool cannot ascend to wisdom because he lies in the lowest places of vice. Even if at present he thinks that he understands something, at the gate—that is, at the departure from this life—he will discover that he was nothing.

### Verse 8.—“He who devises”

He makes clear whom he calls a fool: not someone slow-witted, but one who sins even by deliberating.

### Verse 10.—“If you despair”

Nothing is more execrable than despair. Whoever possesses it loses constancy both in the ordinary struggles of this life and, worse still, in the contest of faith.

[Col. 1107D] ### Verse 11.—“Rescue them”

Rescue those who are deceived by heretics, etc., up to the point where, if they are about to perish from cold, you restore them with food and clothing.

### Verse 13.—“Eat, my son”

He compares the teaching of wisdom with honey and the honeycomb, etc., up to the point where it is received gradually.

### Verse 15.—“Do not lie in wait”

Do not seek an opportunity, etc., up to the point where it adds:

### Verse 16.—“For the righteous man falls seven times”

The righteous man is said to fall, etc., up to the point where they consent to sin in such a way that they do not repent.

### Verse 17.—“When your enemy falls”

Above he forbade lying in wait for the righteous, etc., up to the point where, when you fall into sin, he may recover and be healed.

[Col. 1108A] ### Verse 21.—“Fear the Lord, my son”

“Lord” and “king” may be understood as the Father and the Son, who are to be honored with the same divine honor: “For whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent Him,” etc. (John III).

“With slanderers.” That is, with those, etc., up to the point where their listening hearers also listen to them.

### Verse 23.—“These things also belong to the wise”

When a reprobate is suddenly snatched from the world by death, etc., up to the point where one may never depart from the way of truth through fear.

### Verse 26.—“He will kiss the lips”

A kiss is a sign of peace and love, etc., up to the point where they have been converted for the better.

### Verse 27.—“Prepare”

Having prepared the field by work, cultivate it diligently, etc., up to the point where the entire structure of virtues within is destroyed as the hunger for goodness grows.

### Verse 30.—“I passed by the field of a slothful man,” etc.

To pass by the field and vineyard of a slothful and foolish person, etc., up to the point where anyone negligent through the devil’s persuasion loses what he possesses.

## Chapter XXV

### Verse 1.—“These also are proverbs”

From this point he begins to speak in a new order, etc., up to the point, namely, of things that appear suited to symbolic figures.

### Verse 2.—“The glory of God”

The glory of the Lord, etc., up to the point where He therefore calls Himself “the Son of Man” more than “the Son of God.”

“To investigate.” The word, etc., up to the point where he immediately heard: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah, because flesh…” [Col. 1108C].

### Verse 3.—“Heaven above and earth below”

Just as the height of heaven and the depth of earth cannot be known by human beings, so the knowledge of the apostles and prophets, who came to know the divine mysteries through revelation by the Spirit, surpasses our frailty.

### Verse 5.—“Take away impiety”

Take away impiety, etc., up to the point where, by becoming rigid through arrogance, they may not incur the hatred of the people.

### Verse 6.—“Do not appear glorious”

Just as he earlier spoke of the one placed in authority, etc., up to the point where: “Humble yourselves under the powerful hand of God, so that He may exalt you at the time of visitation” (I Pet. III).

### Verse 11.—“Golden apples”

The sacred utterances, etc., up to the point where, when the veil of the letter has been removed, he lays them open.

### Verse 12.—“A golden earring shining with pearls”

Rightly the humble hearer, etc., up to the point where he joins to it the more pleasing radiance of a burning jewel [Col. 1108D].

### Verse 13.—“As cold”

It seems inopportune for snow to fall during harvest, etc., up to the point where, acting prudently, he rests.

### Verse 14.—“A glorious man”

This seems to be the same as: “Do not deceive anyone with your lips.” But it is the same thing the Apostle says: “Having the appearance of piety but denying its truth” (II Tim. III).

### Verse 16.—“You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you”

It can also be understood in this way, etc., up to the point where either you come to him so often that he grows tired of you.

### Verse 19.—“A rotten tooth and a lame foot”

Jeremiah, etc., up to the point where he will be exposed naked on the day of judgment.

[Col. 1109A] ### Verse 20.—“Vinegar upon nitre is the one who sings”

“Nitre” takes its name from the province of Nitria, etc., up to the point where it makes water suitable for washing.

### Verse 22.—“For you will heap burning coals”—that is, the ardor of charity

Wisdom would not teach you to do good to an enemy for the sake of evil. Often it happens that an enemy, overcome by repeated benefits, lays aside the rigidity of hatred, and the warmth of charity is placed in his mind.

“The north wind.” If you listen to a slanderer with a cheerful face, you give him fuel for slander. But if you listen with a sad expression, as someone has said, he learns not readily to say what he has learned is not readily heard.

### Verse 24.—“It is better to sit in the corner of the roof than…”

A *doma* is a lofty and secluded place. In the Acts of the Apostles (Acts X), where Peter went up to the upper place to pray, the Greek uses *doma* for “upper place” [Col. 1109B].

### Verse 25.—“Cold water”

Thus cold water, etc., up to the point where they lead them, after the contest is finished, to the palm of reward.

### Verse 26.—“A troubled spring”

It often happens that those who shone with greater knowledge finally fall into the pit of folly, wishing to know more than is permitted to human frailty. Hence it adds:

### Verse 27.—“As one who eats honey”

For the sweetness of honey, etc., up to the point where it follows:

### Verse 28.—“As an open city,” etc.

For if it does not have the wall of silence, etc., up to the point where through many words it fights against itself.

## Chapter XXVI

[Col. 1109C] ### Verse 1.—“As snow in summer”

Snow in summer and rain during harvest, etc., up to the point where the disaster of the Arian storm proved this.

### Verse 2.—“For just as a bird”

He compares words with birds, etc., up to the point concerning which it is said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven” (Matt. XVI).

### Verse 4.—“Do not answer… Answer a fool according to his folly”

These are not contradictory. Both agree according to the time and the difference of persons: the fool despises because he does not receive wisdom, while foolish pride is cast down from its own folly. Hence: “I have become a fool; you compelled me” (II Cor. XII).

### Verse 6.—“Lame in the feet”

A wise person may unknowingly send a fool and nevertheless not lose the glory of his wisdom [Col. 1109D], because he believes the good that he had heard from someone unknown. But one who knowingly sends a heretic to preach is also lame in the feet: “and drinking iniquity,” because he has lost the outward gait of good conduct and intoxicates the inner parts of his understanding by drinking in folly.

### Verse 9.—“As if a thorn should grow”

A thorn grows in the hand of a drunkard, etc., up to the point where he either seeks the disparagement of others.

### Verse 11.—“As a dog”

A dog rejects and casts up the food that had oppressed its breast, etc., up to the point where, after confession, they resume what they desire.

### Verse 12.—“Have you seen a man?”

“Into judgment I have come into this world” (John IX), so that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind (Eccles. X).

[Col. 1110A] ### Verse 13.—“The slothful man says”

Many, when they hear words of exhortation, etc., up to the point where they do not cease lying in their own perversities.

### Verse 16.—“Wiser,” etc.

Seven men speaking sayings, etc., up to the point where they showed that they had perfected many.

### Verse 17.—“As one who seizes”

Do not contend with words; it is useful for nothing except the overthrow of those listening. Whoever is simple-minded and, when two people are quarreling, catches his ear on their biting speech, quickly begins to bark like a dog and generate quarrels; but the wise person entirely avoids this.

## Chapter XXVII

### Verse 1.—“Do not boast”

Do not at any time be confident about the future. For even if today you serve the Lord, you cannot see at all what you may be like in the future or how you will complete the journey [Col. 1110B]. Blessed is the person who is always fearful.

### Verse 3.—“A stone is heavy”

A stone is heavy, etc., up to the point where they likewise examine and chastise the movements of the mind.

“The anger of a fool is heavier than both,” etc. Concerning this, above, etc., up to the point where he loosens the reins to his rage.

### Verse 5.—“Open correction is better”

Hidden love is illicit, etc., up to the point where he secretly loves someone with an eagerness to sin in the same way.

### Verse 7.—“A satisfied soul tramples the honeycomb,” etc.

The soul of the rich, etc., up to the point where it considers it sweet even to suffer death for the Lord.

### Verse 8.—“Like a bird wandering”

Just as a bird abandons its eggs, etc., up to the point where you should not cease from the good you were doing.

[Col. 1110C] ### Verse 10.—“A neighbor is better”

A neighbor is better for you, etc., up to the point concerning one in Jericho, who fell, etc.

### Verse 14.—“He who blesses his neighbor”

That is, one who exalts him through the favor of excessive praise, either by favoring evil deeds or by praising good deeds beyond measure. But such a person is compared with one who curses, because by praising an evil deed he gives confidence, while by praising a good deed he diminishes the simplicity of a pure heart, so that what had begun for the sake of heavenly love is brought to an end for the sake of human favor.

### Verse 17.—“Iron sharpens iron”

Good counsel is the consolation of the wise: while they instruct one another by consoling one another, iron is sharpened by iron.

### Verse 20.—“Hell”

The torments of hell are never filled, etc., up to the point where they would have a nature capable of living without end [Col. 1110D].

### Verse 23.—“Diligently”

This is said to the shepherd of the Church, etc., up to the point where, if you have fed them well in your time.

### Verse 25.—“The meadows are open”

The pastures of the heavenly mysteries are now open, etc., up to the point where they are given for spiritual assistance.

### Verse 26.—“The lambs are for clothing”

You will clothe yourself with the fleeces of lambs when you yourself, as a shepherd, have advanced through the good conduct of obedient disciples. Seeing their praiseworthy deeds, you will become glorious both in the adornment of virtues and in the warmth of love. You buy a field with goats when, by calling sinners to repentance, you acquire for yourself a more exalted place in the land of the living.

[Col. 1111A] ### Verse 27.—“Let the milk of the goats be sufficient for you”

Feed the flock entrusted to you with such diligence, etc., up to the point where the goats will be handed over to the fires as payment for the saints whom they had harmed.

## Chapter XXVIII

### Verse 1.—“The wicked man flees”

One who is not strong, even if no one pursues him, voluntarily abandons the faith, making himself like an unbeliever through robberies, perjuries, and other such things.

“But the righteous man is like a lion.” He does not tremble at the encounter with wild beasts, etc., up to the point where no one loses him unwillingly.

### Verse 5.—“But those who seek”

The elect take notice of everything: the future danger of the universal judgment, the works for which rest is repaid, and those for which eternal punishment is assigned.

[Col. 1111B] ### Verse 10.—“He who deceives the righteous on my way,” etc.

He who deceives lovers of righteousness through heretical teaching, etc., up to the point where they also take an example from his fall.

### Verse 12.—“In exultation,” etc.

Not concerning present things, etc., up to the point where this may be understood of pagans, heretics, and bad Catholics alike.

### Verse 14.—“Blessed is the man,” etc.

The severity of judgment will be borne in proportion to how little it is feared now.

### Verse 22.—“A man who hastens to become rich,” etc.

The one who longs to increase his wealth neglects sin. Like a bird caught while eagerly looking at earthly food, he does not recognize the noose of sin by which he will be strangled. When he desires any of the world’s goods, he does not know what future losses he will suffer.

[Col. 1111C] ### Verse 28.—“When the wicked rise”

He calls the same people righteous because, being righteous, they preserve the order of creation. Hence in Job concerning the repentant person: “He will look upon men and say, ‘I have sinned’” (Job XXXIII). This means: He will look upon those who preserve the nature of human creation and recognize that by sinning they have made themselves like animals.

## Chapter XXIX

### Verse 1.—“A man who, with flattering words,” etc.

One who praises his neighbor with feigned speeches prepares traps for him, so that he may fall more securely into danger through word or deed. But let us see who is caught, to whom it happens, or who causes it. It follows:

### Verse 6.—“A sinful man”

Therefore the snare of sinners is not for the righteous, etc., up to the point where: “He who digs a pit for his neighbor will fall into it” [Col. 1111D].

### Verse 9.—“A wise man”

A faithful and wise teacher, etc., up to the point where he is not heard by a fool.

### Verse 11.—“His whole spirit”

When impatience drives him, his whole spirit bursts forth, etc., up to the point where the wise person gradually weakens and expels it through the maturity of counsel.

### Verse 13.—“The poor man and the creditor meet”

The poor man, etc., up to the point where: “Without me you can do nothing.”

### Verse 18.—“When prophecy”

When the priest’s instruction has ceased, the discipline of the divine law will immediately be dissolved—the discipline by which the people ought to have attained the rewards of blessedness.

[Col. 1112A] ### Verse 20.—“Have you seen a man?”

Folly is indeed a serious vice, but loquacity is no lighter. For it often happens that some uneducated person receives words of correction more quickly than one who boasts more of what he knows—or thinks he knows—than he listens to the admonitions of others.

### Verse 21.—“He who lives delicately from his youth”

Another translation reads beautifully: “He who indulges himself from his youth will be a slave; but at the end he will be saddened.” For the one who refused to do so in tender youth repents of his evils too late.

### Verse 22.—“An angry man”

Anger is the door of all vices. When it is closed, rest is given to the virtues within; when it is open, the mind is armed for every crime.

### Verse 24.—“He who shares with a thief hates his own soul”

Wisdom teaches one to abstain not only from sin but also from consent, lest one hear from the strict Judge: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him,” etc. For not only the thief but also the one who, knowing of the theft, does not report it when the owner asks, is held guilty. And lest he excuse himself through fear of a more powerful person, it adds: “He who fears the Lord,” etc.

## Chapter XXX

### Verse 1.—“The words of the Gatherer”

Up to this point they are the proverbs of Solomon, which the men of King Hezekiah of Judah transferred. From here, again, are the words of Solomon, as is indicated by the very name, which in Greek is *ekklesiastēs* (ἐκκλησιαστής), in Latin “Gatherer”; for *ecclesia* means an assembly.

“The vision which…” The vision which he spoke, because what he saw by contemplating the deeper things with God he disclosed to human beings [Col. 1112C]. Whoever has been strengthened by the Spirit of God says the things that follow with humble heart: “I am the most foolish of men,” etc.

### Verse 2.—“Most foolish”

“The children of this age are more prudent than the children of light in their generation” (Luke XVI). And the Apostle says: “If anyone seems to be wise in this age, let him become a fool so that he may be wise” (I Cor. III).

“I did not learn from man,” but, with God granting it, so that I might know the knowledge of the saints. And the Apostle says: “We are fools for Christ”; again he says: “We speak wisdom among the perfect.” But this wisdom is not that of men, nor of the rulers of this age, who are being destroyed.

### Verse 4.—“Who has ascended into heaven?”

The Son of God ascended after the resurrection, and at the time of our resurrection will descend for judgment [Col. 1112D].

“Who has contained?” Every spirit—of angels, human beings, animals, and storms—is held by God’s power so that it does not fail.

“Who has raised them all?” Even now God raises all things that live and grow throughout the world—human beings, animals, and plants—so that they may subsist by His life. On the day of judgment He will raise the human race from death from the four winds.

“What is his name, and what is the name of his son?” He speaks of the name of God the Father and of the Son. The worldly sciences could not naturally know this mystery, although by the things that have been made they can understand that there is a God who made everything.

[Col. 1113A] “If you know”—you, that is, who boast of your wisdom and call the mysteries of our faith foolishness.

### Verse 5.—“Every word”

The propriety of the Greek name, etc., up to the point where all things are true and fiery.

“He is a shield,” that is, the protector of all who hope in Him. A shield against the ambushes of enemies and against every adversity.

### Verse 7.—“Two things I have asked of you”

The man continues speaking, etc., up to the point where he falls into forgetfulness of eternal things.

### Verse 11.—“A generation that [—] its father”

Above he spoke of purity of life, etc., up to the point where, if he was born, there was a time when he was not a son.

### Verse 14.—“A generation that has swords for teeth”

This is the generation that attempts to implant its faithlessness in others. Just as it kills bodies with swords, so it kills the souls of its hearers with the poison of its speech [Col. 1113B].

### Verse 15.—“The leech has two daughters”

The devil, who burns perpetually with thirst to persuade people to sin. “Two daughters” are those who imitate his ardor: lust and love of money. For the more freely the reins of lust are loosened, the more harmful pleasure becomes; and “the love of money grows as the money itself grows.”

“There are three things that are never satisfied.” Hell never overflows; the harlot has things like it. The body is not satisfied with delights, and the greedy person never says, “It is enough.” Others call the devil hell, because he is not satisfied with human seduction.

### Verse 16.—“The mouth of the womb, and the earth that is not satisfied with water”

As above, fire means the burning of Gehenna, which never ceases [Col. 1113C].

### Verse 17.—“The eye that mocks”

Those who criticize the divine judgments, etc., up to the point where they humbly confess the blackness of sin.

“Sons of the eagle,” because through its grace they have been reborn—the one who flew across to heaven in the flesh. Elsewhere they are called “sons of the bridegroom.”

### Verse 18.—“There are three things too difficult for me”

So it is literally, etc., up to the point where it is difficult to know by how many thoughts a young man is driven when he serves the way of truth.

### Verse 20.—“Such is also the way of an adulterous woman”

The adulterous mind, too, like the things he has mentioned, is always wandering. Whenever it can conceal its sins, it denies that it has done anything evil.

### Verse 24.—“Four”

That is, the righteous appear smaller on earth than the reprobate—that is, more despised—yet they are wiser than the wise of the world because they seek eternal things and desire to suffer for them.

### Verse 25.—“The ants are a weak people”

The people of the Church also, etc., up to the point where they may live forever.

### Verse 26.—“The rabbit—others say the *choerogryllus*,” etc.

Up to the point where some here have “hedgehog” instead of “rabbit.”

**(Jerome.)** The Hebrew has the word *saphan*, which they interpret as “mouse,” “*choerogryllus*,” “hare,” and “hedgehog.”

“Rabbit,” etc. This is the people of the Church, which is weak because it does not seek vengeance for its injuries, and because it has learned to hope for salvation not in its own strength but in God’s help [Col. 1114A]. This is to have a lair in the rock, as it says with the Psalmist: “Be to me a very strong rock, a fortified house, that you may save me, for you are my rock and my fortress.”

### Verse 27.—“A locust is a king”

The locust, etc., up to the point where it nevertheless continues diligently to serve Christ in its appointed places and habitually consume the shoots of carnal pleasures.

### Verse 28.—“The lizard with its hands”

The lizard has no wings, etc., up to the point where the strength of its works raises it to obtain the walls of the eternal kingdom.

### Verse 29.—“There are three that walk”

Let this not disturb us, etc., up to the point where Antichrist prospers for a time in his deceit.

### Verse 31.—“The rooster”

That is, the preachers who announce the true dawn amid the darkness of this age.

[Col. 1114B] “And the ram.” The first order of priests, etc., up to the point where he was raised on high.

### Verse 33.—“But he who presses the breasts firmly,” etc.

Up to the point where what is perceived through excessive examination becomes carnal.

“And he who provokes anger brings forth.” He explains what the preceding proverb means literally, etc., up to the point where he draws blood.

## Chapter XXXI

### Verse 1.—“The words of Lemuel”

Lemuel, “in whom is God,” etc., up to the point where he saw how wisely his mother had instructed him.

**VERSE 3.**—“And your riches.” That is: do not corrupt the hearts of men with earthly delights, etc., up to “through the allurements of the world they deserve to be uprooted from the land of the living” [Col. 1114C].

**VERSE 4.**—“Do not give to kings.” These and the following words are clear in their literal sense, etc., up to “search out carnal things.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Give strong drink to those who are sorrowful.” Wine and strong drink, etc., up to “lest those who are such be swallowed up by excessive grief.”

**VERSE 8.**—“Open your mouth.” On behalf of the poor, etc., up to “but also to extend concern for salvation to all the nations throughout the world.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Open your mouth; judge.” Just as he commanded that the mouth be opened on behalf of the poor and for the rescue of the oppressed, so he advises that those who have gone astray be justly chastised and judged. Moses likewise says: “You shall not pity the poor in judgment” (Exod. XIII). The Prophet says that the Lord does both: “But he shall judge the poor in righteousness, and [Col. 1114D] shall reprove for the wrongs done to the meek of the earth.”

**VERSE 10.**—“A strong woman.” Up to this point are the words of King Lemuel, etc., up to “let virtues and rewards be described.”

“Who will find a strong woman?” The strong woman is the holy Church, etc., up to “he granted her to preach throughout the world,” he added:

**VERSE 11.**—“The heart of her husband trusts in her.” The man is the Redeemer, etc., up to “when through the preachers whom he had deceived he recalls him to the truth.”

“And he shall have no need of spoils.” Because the Church will never cease restoring to Christ’s faith the souls deceived by the devil, until, when the course of the world has ended, the number of the righteous is complete. But because whatever good the holy Church [Col. 1115A] or a faithful soul does, it receives from above, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 12.**—“She will render him good and not evil.” The soul will render good to Christ, etc., up to “let us serve him, who is like him,” etc.

**VERSE 13.**—“She sought.” By what works, etc., up to “the matter of this recompense is explained more clearly below.”

**VERSE 14.**—“She became like a merchant’s ship from afar.” A navigator is called a merchant because he diligently applies himself to acquiring merchandise, etc., up to “of whom it is said: ‘Truly I say to you, they have received their reward.’”

**VERSE 15.**—“At night.” Just as the entire course of the present age, etc., up to “and to practice such things secretly.”

“She arose.” When a faithful person diligently girds himself to care for his neighbors [Col. 1115B]. He does this in two ways: he calls those who are wandering outside to the faith, and he urges those who are in the faith to devote themselves more earnestly to works. Hence it follows:

“And she gave prey to her household.” She gives prey to her household when she reconciles those whom the devil has snatched away to the company of those who have gone before them in the faith. She gives food to her maidservants when she refreshes the humble and those who obey his commands in fear, so that they do not grow weary in their pious labor, by reminding them of their reward.

**VERSE 16.**—“She considered.” Today and until the end of the age the strong woman, etc., up to “what the fullness of blessedness will be in the kingdom of God.”

“From the fruit of her hands.” Because from the fruitful deeds of her faithful, etc., up to “and labors on their behalf as much as she can.”

**VERSE 17.**—“She girded herself.” When she prepares herself for works of virtue, etc., up to “so that you may shine through good works.”

**VERSE 18.**—“She tasted and saw that it was good.” Of that field, namely, etc., up to “thus she also works by night, with her lamp kindled.”

**VERSE 19.**—“She put her hand.” He means strong works, perfected in charity, etc., up to “of whose strength it is said: ‘The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it’” (Matt. XI).

“And her fingers,” he says, “grasped the spindle.” The distaff [Col. 1115D] is in the left hand, the spindle in the right, etc., up to “what the strong woman—that is, the holy Church or the perfect soul—has accomplished with the spindle,” he adds:

**VERSE 20.**—“She opened her hand to the needy, and stretched out her palms.” This concerns almsgiving, etc., up to “when she dispersed preachers far and wide among the nations in need of eternal salvation” [Col. 1116A].

**VERSE 21.**—“She shall not fear.” The cold of snow, etc., up to “because she believed God, who said that the gates of hell would not prevail against her” (Matt. XVI).

“For all her household are clothed in double garments,” etc. With wisdom, namely, for exposing heresies, and with patience for enduring the battles of open enemies, etc., up to “who is rightly bound in the cold because he did not possess the garment of piety.”

**VERSE 22.**—“A variegated garment.” A variegated garment is one that, with its changing weave, is customarily made extremely strong, etc., up to “for the linen garments are the righteous deeds of the saints.”

**VERSE 23.**—“A noble man at the gates.” The man is the Lord [Col. 1116B], who was seen as ignoble, etc., up to “he will appear exalted to all.”

**VERSE 24.**—“She made and sold fine linen.” In the fine linen of the sindon, etc., up to “for the nations have migrated from vices to virtues, from the devil to Christ.”

**VERSE 25.**—“Strength.” Strength for enduring, etc., up to “be strong against detractors.”

**VERSE 26.**—“Her mouth.” She opened her mouth for the sole purpose of speaking, etc., up to “both are suitably followed by this statement:”

“Law of kindness.” So that she does not punish immediately as does the law of Moses, etc., up to “and thus he absolved her: ‘Go, and do not sin again.’”

**VERSE 27.**—“She considered.” Because she carefully investigates all the thoughts of her conscience, etc., up to [Col. 1116C] “and does not cease to practice what she has learned ought to be done.”

“She does not eat the bread of idleness.” Because she puts into practice the sacred utterance that she receives, etc., up to “not only idle, but also talkative and meddlesome.”

**VERSE 28.**—“Her children rose up.” What he knew would happen as a prophet, etc., up to “but at the judgment he will demonstrate how great is the glory of his resurrection.”

**VERSE 29.**—“Many daughters have gathered riches; you have surpassed them all.” The churches of the heretics, etc., up to “who follows the footsteps of her Redeemer with chaste faith and perfect works.”

**VERSE 30.**—“Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain.” [Col. 1116D] The glory of praise is deceitful, etc., up to “for he shows how he praises her: ‘Give her of the fruit.’”

**VERSE 31.**—“Give her of the fruit of her hands.” This is the man of whom it was said above, etc., up to “and with God approving and rewarding, to whom are honor and glory.”

[Col. 1115]

# THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTES

Which the Hebrews call **COHELETH** (G)*

## PROLOGUE OF BLESSED JEROME ON THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTES

(See among Jerome’s Works, volume III.)

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 1115D]

**VERSE 1.**—“The words of Ecclesiastes.” (JEROME, on Ecclesiastes, vol. III.) Solomon was called by three names, etc. [Col. 1116D] up to “and he is an equal teacher, yet does not know that he is a king.”

**(ALBINUS.)** The Hebrews report that this book belongs to Solomon when he was doing penance, because, trusting in wisdom [Col. 1117A] and riches, he offended God through women. For he judged all these things to be vanity and that those who place their hope in them come to misery.

**(JEROME.) Allegorically.** The peaceful and beloved Son of God the Father, etc., up to “hence: ‘Their sound has gone out through all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’” (Ps. XVIII).

**VERSE 2.**—“Vanity of vanities.” (ID.) Instead of “vanity of vanities,” according to certain interpreters we may say, etc., up to “until what is perfect comes.”

Before stating his judgment, he seems to prepare and adorn it when he says: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” Then he begins with the greater matter, namely man, showing that man himself is subject to vanity, that is, to mutability. And this is vanity, etc. “Every living man is vanity”—how much more everything else! Hence: “Creation was subjected to vanity,” not willingly, but because of him who, etc. For whatever cannot remain as it is may be called vanity, because it can change. God alone is always what he is. Whatever changes in some manner vanishes, and is no longer what it was; in comparison with the Creator, every creature may be called vanity and reckoned as almost nothing.

**(JEROME.)** If everything that God made, etc., up to “I am compelled to say not once but twice: ‘Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.’”

**VERSE 3.**—“What more does a man have?” (ID.) After the general judgment, etc., up to “but naked they return to the earth from which they were taken.”

[Col. 1117C]

**VERSE 4.**—“One generation passes.” (ID.) The first generation of the Jews departs, etc., up to “but we praise God not in one age only, but throughout the ages of ages.”

**VERSE 5.**—“The sun rises and sets.” (ID.) The sun itself, etc., up to “it rises for the faithful and sets for the unfaithful.”

**VERSE 6.**—“It travels toward the south.” (ID.) From this we may suppose, etc., up to “and thus returns to the east.”

“The spirit proceeds in its circuit.” (ID.) He calls the sun itself spirit, etc., up to “otherwise it would consume the cold.”

**VERSE 7.**—“All the rivers enter the sea.” Philosophers say that the fresh waters flowing into the sea are either consumed by the burning sun or serve as food for the sea’s saltiness. But our Ecclesiastes, and the Creator of those waters, says that they return through hidden channels of the earth to the sources of springs and continually boil up from the womb of the abyss at their own beginnings. By rivers and the sea we may understand the human race, which returns to the earth from which it was taken, according to the statement: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go” (Gen. III). Nor is the earth filled by the multitude of the dead. Jerome says “torrents,” not “rivers,” because they pass quickly.

**(JEROME.)** All torrents, etc., up to “as in Proverbs: ‘The daughters of the leech.’”

**VERSE 8.**—“All things are difficult.” A human being cannot explain the causes and natures of things, nor can the eye fully see them, nor can the ear, even when instructed by a teacher, attain complete knowledge. For now we see “through a mirror in an enigma” and “in part,” until what is perfect comes (1 Cor. XIII), which cannot exist in this mortal body. This judgment is directed against those who think that they know the Holy Scriptures without labor and study in speaking, and who consider themselves wise when they are foolish.

**VERSE 9.**—“What is that which—?” (JEROME.) He seems to be speaking about these things, etc., up to “so that God might rest from all his works on the seventh day.”

“What is that which—?” He is speaking of the natures created at the beginning of the world and of their succession, how they come and pass away: a human being dies, a human being is born; the nature of the one being born is the same as that of the one who died. So with birds, fish, serpents, and all living creatures; so with herbs, trees, and other natures: nothing new is found that did not exist before, and nothing has passed away that will not occur again later. Hence, “God rested on the seventh day from all his work” (Gen. II): from the creation of new natures, not from governing them, according to the saying: “My Father is working until now, and I am working” (John V). Thus, from the primordial seeds of things, the whole period of the world is completed by its natural course.

**VERSE 10.**—“Nor is it possible,” etc. (JEROME.) Is there a word, etc., up to “and through God’s predestination those things that are future have already been done.”

“For it has already gone before.” Just as oblivion conceals from us the things of the past that occurred long ago, so those who are to be born will not be able to know what is now taking place; for these things will perish in silence and, as though they had never existed, will be hidden away.

“For vanity of vanities and all is vanity,” because [Col. 1118C] all things pass away like flowing water and will not return. The whole world applauds this judgment, and especially the human race.

**VERSE 11.**—“There is no memory of former things.” (JEROME.) The seraphim for this reason, etc., up to “hence later: ‘There is no memory of the wise man with the fool forever.’”

**VERSE 13.**—“And I applied my mind,” etc. Ecclesiastes therefore resolved, etc., up to “which they willingly incurred.”

Up to this point he has spoken generally about the vanities of the world; from here he returns to himself and reveals who he was, how he came to know and teach all things. Hence: “And I applied my mind,” and so forth.

“This occupation.” (JEROME.) The word *anian* is rendered by Aquila, the Septuagint, and Theodotion as *perispasmon*, which in Latin means “distraction,” etc., up to “everything is referred back to the preceding meaning.”

**VERSE 14.**—“I saw,” etc. I considered all worldly things and saw that they were vanity and misery, that is, afflictions of the spirit, by which the mind, wearied by various thoughts, struggles to know what is not granted to human beings.

**(JEROME.)** The word *Routh* is rendered by Aquila and Theodotion, etc., up to “by which the soul is afflicted with various thoughts.”

**VERSE 15.**—“The perverse.” (ID.) What is perverse cannot be made straight, etc., up to “so that it cannot be comprehended.”

**VERSE 17.**—“And errors and folly.” (ID.) The first wisdom is to be free from folly, etc., up to “let what was said above suffice.”

## CHAPTER TWO

**VERSE 1.**—“I said therefore.” (JEROME.) After, amid an abundance of wisdom, etc., up to “then it will not be vanity but truth.”

**VERSE 2.**—“I considered laughter an error.” (ID.) Where we say, etc., up to “they promise themselves happiness and prosperity.”

**VERSE 3.**—“I considered in my heart.” (ID.) Drunkenness, etc., up to “what must be avoided.”

**VERSE 4.**—“I planted vineyards.” In the house of the rich, etc., up to “without which the other trees will dry out.”

**VERSE 6.**—“And I made myself pools,” etc., up to “and awaits the late rain from heaven.”

[Col. 1119B]

**VERSE 7.**—“I acquired servants: those serving through fear and desiring spiritual things, and those who do not fear.”

We call those persons *vernaculi* who are indeed of the Church and precede the aforementioned male and female servants, but nevertheless are not free.

*Vernaculi* are called the children of servants who were born in their master’s house.

“Also herds and great flocks.” These are those who labor in the Church without reason or knowledge of the Scriptures, but have not yet attained humanity, that is, the image of God.

**(JEROME.)** “And indeed the possession of the herd.” Note that, etc., up to “or household servants.”

**VERSE 8.**—“The treasures of kings.” (ID.) The doctrines of philosophers, etc., up to “and rejects the wisdom of the wise.”

“I made myself singers.” A singer, etc., up to “singers, male and female, might delight me.”

“The delights of the sons of men.” Namely, wisdom, which, like paradise, has varied fruits and manifold pleasures. Concerning it the Psalmist says: “Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the requests of your heart” (Ps. XXXVI). And: “You will give them drink from the torrent of your delight” (Ps. XXXV).

**VERSE 9.**—“Who were before me in Jerusalem.” Literally: this is not a great boast. Before Solomon, Saul reigned, in whose time the kingdom began, and David, under whom the kingdom was still quite small.

“She persevered.” Others read “stood,” that is, while he was present in the flesh wisdom remained with him—not advancing moment by moment as it does in us, but standing in fullness.

[Col. 1119D]

**VERSE 10.**—“And everything that—.” But the more eagerly these things increased, the more wisdom was lacking, because desire carried me away in every direction. I thought that this was the fruit of my labors, if I served lust; but at last, returning to myself, I saw that everything was vanity.

**VERSE 11.**—“Under the sun.” (JEROME.) Christ. “He has placed his tabernacle in the sun.” Therefore, whoever has not yet attained the brightness, order, and steadfastness of the sun, in him Christ does not dwell.

**VERSE 13.**—“And I saw that wisdom so greatly—.” As I considered that the wise man is light and the fool darkness—the eyes of the former are in heaven, those of the latter on earth—there suddenly occurred to me the question why they should perish by a common death, be crushed by a common misery, and so forth.

[Col. 1120A]

**VERSE 18.**—“Again I detested.” (JEROME.) Through spiritual labor the saints meditate day and night on the law of the Lord, etc., up to “for wisdom is not the gathering of earthly riches.”

“He who will possess it.” This happened to Solomon himself, who did not have a son like himself, namely Rehoboam. From this we understand that a son, if foolish, is not even worthy of his father’s inheritance.

**VERSE 21.**—“For when another—.” (ID.) Above he spoke about an uncertain heir, etc., up to “according to reason.”

**VERSE 24.**—“Is it not better—?” (ID.) After I had examined everything, etc., up to “how much is sufficient?”

**VERSE 26.**—“To the good man.” (ID.) To the one who corrects his ways, etc., up to “and composed by presumption of spirit.”

## CHAPTER THREE

[Col. 1120B]

**VERSE 1.**—“Everything has its time.” (JEROME.) Above he taught the uncertain and fluctuating condition of human existence, etc., up to “they are contained neither by place nor by time.”

**VERSE 2.**—“A time to plant,” etc. (ID.) No one doubts, etc., up to “because perfect love casts out fear.”

**VERSE 3.**—“A time to destroy,” etc. We cannot build good things unless we have first destroyed evil things, just as God said to Jeremiah that he should first uproot, dig up, and destroy, and afterward build and plant (Jer. I).

**VERSE 4.**—“A time to weep,” etc. We must weep now so that in the future we may dance—that dance which David performed before the ark of the covenant (2 Sam. VI). Though it displeased Saul’s daughter, it pleased God more.

**VERSE 5.**—“A time to scatter stones,” etc. (JEROME.) I wonder, etc., up to “and calls to repentance.”

“A time to embrace.” A time to embrace wisdom and cling more closely to contemplation; and a time to be far from an embrace, namely from wisdom, so that we may serve the concerns of the present age and those things without which we cannot live.

**VERSE 7.**—“A time to be silent and a time—.” (JEROME.) We teach in the churches what we do not know. We do not learn any arts without a teacher; only this art seems so cheap and easy that it needs no instructor. Nothing seems right to us except what we ourselves learn, so that after a long period of silence we become teachers from being disciples.

[Col. 1120D]

“A time to speak.” It is the discipline of Pythagoras to remain silent for five years and afterward to speak once educated.

**VERSE 8.**—“A time of love.” A time to love wives, children, and relatives after God; and a time to hate them in martyrdom. Or: because now we see “through a mirror in an enigma” (1 Cor. XIII), etc., there will be a time to love God’s presence, and a time to hate, when, seeing face to face and progressing toward what is better, we begin to hate and despise what we loved.

“A time of war.” Now, against those who do not repent; a time of peace in the future, when all Israel will be saved. It is a time of war: lest you be secure, take up the armor of God.

[Col. 1121A]

**VERSE 10.**—“I saw the affliction which he gave,” etc. (JEROME.) It is said that for this reason God, etc., up to “caused it to grow, remain, and change until the end of the age.”

**VERSE 12.**—“And I understood.” (JEROME.) For this reason man was placed in the world as a cultivator, etc., up to “hence:”

**VERSE 13.**—“Every man who eats and drinks,” etc. There are many tribulations now for the righteous, but in the future there will be no labor in Jacob.

“I learned,” etc. (ID.) Nothing in the world is new: the course of the sun, the changes of the moon, the dryness or greenness of the earth and trees, were established with the world. God ordered these things according to a fixed reason so that we might understand God’s providence in them and fear before God’s face. The Lord’s countenance is against those who do evil.

[Col. 1121B]

**VERSE 16.**—“I saw under the sun.” (ID.) When I sought judgment and truth in this world, etc., up to “for all things will be sought at their proper time.”

**VERSE 17.**—“I said in my heart.” (ID.) As though he said, etc., up to “and the earth will be filled with sheep and herds.”

**VERSE 21.**—“Who knows?” (ID.) He does not say, etc., up to “and become a certain advocate of what seems doubtful.”

“Downward.” To the underworld. For it can happen that they are quickly changed, and often those who seemed learned are led down to the underworld, while simple peasants are crowned.

**VERSE 22.**—“And I recognized.” Troubled by the preceding error, etc., up to “what will afterward happen in the world.”

## CHAPTER FOUR

**VERSE 1.**—“I turned myself to other things.” David treats this passage more fully in Psalm LXXII, and Jeremiah in his book.

**VERSE 2.**—“And I praised.” (JEROME.) Others understand this passage in this way, etc., up to “and that they are blessed for as long as they enjoy the angelic choir.”

**VERSE 3.**—“And happier.” Because he neither saw nor experienced these evils, and not according to the error of those who suppose that souls exist before human beings come into being. It is therefore better not to exist at all than to live badly. Hence: “It would have been better for that man if he had not been born,” etc. (Matt. XIV).

**VERSE 9.**—“It is better.” (ID.) After anxieties and miseries, etc., up to “we cannot receive the warmth of eternal life.”

**VERSE 13.**—“Better is a child.” (ID.), up to the end of the chapter [Col. 1121D].

## CHAPTER FIVE

**VERSE 1.**—“Do not act rashly before God.” Because he hears and sees everything, and reproves your folly, although he himself is in heaven and you are on earth.

**VERSE 2.**—“Many.” Just as one who thinks about many things frequently dreams of them, so one who argues about God beyond his capacity falls back into folly. Or, because now we see “through a mirror and in an enigma,” as though in a dream, we suppose that we possess what we do not possess, and yet possess nothing.

**VERSE 3.**—“When you have made a vow.” (JEROME.) It is better not to promise, etc., up to “he shall be beaten with many blows.”

[Col. 1122A]

**VERSE 4.**—“And much more.” Like the Jews who said: “Everything that God has commanded us, we will do” (Exod. XXIV, XXXII), and worshiped the calf.

**VERSE 5.**—“Do not let your mouth—.” As though he said: do not claim that you sin because of the weakness of your flesh, as if shifting the blame onto its author.

“Before the angel.” The one who stands beside each person and reports everything to God; do not think that anything is hidden from God.

**VERSE 6.**—“Where there are many—.” As though he said: “Do not let your mouth—,” because this life is like dreams, and many things appear true that are false; so too is your excuse.

**VERSE 7.**—“If you see oppression.” As though he said: do not say before the angel, “There is no providence.” This is directed against those who think that everything is governed by chance and deny God’s providence. If, however, you see the oppression of the needy, [Col. 1122B] etc.

**VERSE 8.**—“Of every land,” etc. God is patient and a giver of recompense, who says: “When I receive the appointed time, I will judge judgments.”

**VERSE 11.**—“Sweet is sleep.” (JEROME.) The rich miser, etc., up to “because they themselves shall see God.”

**VERSE 12.**—“There is also another weakness.” We can understand these things as referring to philosophers, etc., up to “since it is written: ‘I will destroy the wisdom of the wise,’ etc.”

**VERSE 17.**—“Therefore this seemed good to me,” etc. He says that it is better, etc., up to “which God’s grace inspires in those who perform good works.”

## CHAPTER SIX

[Col. 1122C]

**VERSE 1.**—“There is also another evil.” He describes in another way the avaricious rich person who, although he possesses every good thing, nevertheless torments himself through excessive frugality, not knowing for whom he is accumulating them.

**VERSE 2.**—“The man to whom God has given riches.” (JEROME.) This may be understood of the people of Israel, etc., up to “we shall all hasten to judgment.”

**VERSE 3.**—“Burial.” (ID.) So avaricious that he does not even think about burial; or often, having been killed for his riches, he is cast away unburied; or because, despite abounding in every good thing, he leaves no memorial of himself.

**VERSE 7.**—“All labor.” That is: what a person has learned through labor—namely, a rational person—he has in his mouth, because he teaches others.

“His soul will not be filled.” (ID.) Because he always desires to learn what he may teach; and in this he is better than the fool, because with the blessed poor man he moves toward Christ, who is life and who says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

**VERSE 10.**—“What is to be.” (ID.) God already knows the name of all human beings who will be clothed with bodies, so that a person cannot answer against the craftsman, asking why he was made this way or that. For the more we inquire, the more our vanity and superfluous words are revealed. Free will is not removed by God’s foreknowledge; rather, causes precede, explaining why each thing was made.

**VERSE 11.**—“There are words.” As though he said: the Son of God will indeed become man, but do not inquire further [Col. 1123A] what sort, in what manner, or of what kind he will be; instead, believe his generation.

## CHAPTER SEVEN

**VERSE 2.**—“A good name is better.” (JEROME.) The memory of good works, which delights the hearts of those who hear, like nostrils delighting in perfumes. Hence: “The memory of the righteous is in praise, but the name of the wicked will rot.”

“And the day.” That is: it is better to escape through death the torments, tribulations, and labors of a miserable life than to be born for and endure them.

**VERSE 4.**—“Better is anger”—against one’s own sin or another’s, because one corrects, not because one desires vengeance (Prov. XXVII).

**VERSE 6.**—“Better from a wise man.” The wounds of a friend are better than the deceitful kisses of an enemy. [Col. 1123B] The words of a flatterer are more senseless than thorns—that is, they stir up the cares of the world, which lead to the fires of Gehenna. The perfect wise man needs no reproach and is disturbed by no accusation. Therefore this must be understood of the wise man who is advancing, who is sometimes disturbed by the injustice of judgment when God does not immediately punish.

**VERSE 9.**—“Better is the end.” Perfection. “The one who perseveres will be saved.” Completed righteousness is better than righteousness begun, and the epilogue of prayer than its opening: here is the contest, there the victory.

“An arrogant man.” Opposed to this arrogant person is the one who is called poor in spirit in the Gospel (Matt. V).

**VERSE 11.**—“What do you think?” Alternatively: you should live in such a way that the present days are always better for you than those that have passed. There is always time for working, lest, when you begin to decline, it be said: “You were running well; who hindered you from obeying the truth?” (Gal. V).

**VERSE 14.**—“Consider the works of God.” How great and wondrous they are! By gratuitous mercy he chose one person and by just judgment rejected another. Hence: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. I). And: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth.”

**VERSE 15.**—“An evil day.” (JEROME.) The day of judgment, which appears evil to the wicked. Hence: “That day is a day of wrath,” etc. Or: bear good and evil—that is, prosperity and adversity—as they justly befall you, with courage. For all things happen justly, although secretly; and this is what follows: “He does not find,” etc.

**VERSE 18.**—“And do not be.” “The wicked will not halve their days.” As though he said: do not, while unrepentant, provoke God so that he inflicts punishment even on the living, as he did on Dathan [Col. 1123D] and Abiram.

**VERSE 19.**—“He neglects nothing.” He benefits everyone without respect of persons. Or: he provides for them in prosperity and adversity.

**VERSE 20.**—“Ten rulers.” (JEROME.) Angels who preside over our city, that is, the Church, as guardians, that is, as helpers. They are called ten because ten is a perfect number.

**VERSE 22.**—“But also to all.” He teaches the wise person not to pay attention to the tongues of slanderers, lest, while doing the same thing himself, he wish to be forgiven and to condemn others. If he does this, he will always be meddlesome and angry, because he will not be able to restrain even the tongues of servants.

**VERSE 27.**—“Of hunters,” namely demons, who hunt our souls; their women are the nets, and the heretics are the dragnets. [Col. 1124A]

**VERSE 28.**—“Behold, this.” “This I found,” etc., up to “woman is more liable to fall.”

“To find the reason.” Whatever matter or distinction may exist among human beings and their ways: who is perfectly good except Christ alone?

**VERSE 29.**—“A man.” Christ, who is the head of all good things, represented by the thousand, which is a perfect number.

**VERSE 30.**—“Only this.” (JEROME.) Lest he appear to condemn the common nature of all human beings and accuse God, its creator, he added attentively: “Only this,” etc. As though he said: man was indeed made good, but, left to free will, he willingly falls and entangles himself in empty and superfluous cares.

“Who is like the wise man?” etc. (ID.) Above he said that it is scarcely possible to find a good person, although human beings were made good by God. Now, as though giving thanks, he enumerates the good things he gave them: wisdom, reason, and knowledge of hidden things.

## CHAPTER EIGHT

**VERSE 2.**—“I observe the king’s mouth.” (JEROME.) He seems to command this according to the Apostle, etc., up to “his will must be obeyed.”

**VERSE 4.**—“Nor can anyone say to him—,” etc. (ID.) God’s commandments must not be questioned as to why he commanded them, but must be carried out.

**VERSE 8.**—“It is not in human power.” (ID.) As though he said: [Col. 1124C] you ought not to be troubled if you cannot know the future or if you are often oppressed by more powerful wicked people, because everything soon comes to an end and death carries everyone away alike.

**VERSE 10.**—“I saw the wicked buried,” etc. Even in death there is no repentance among those whose accusation is rarer and more difficult; therefore their freedom to sin seems greater.

**VERSE 14.**—“There are righteous people to whom evils happen,” etc. As with the sons of Aaron while they were sacrificing, according to the Hebrew interpretation, and with Manasseh, who after so many evils was brought back from captivity to the kingdom and lived happily.

## CHAPTER NINE

**VERSE 1.**—“There are righteous,” etc. “A dog is better.” (JEROME.) The living dog is the poor righteous person; the dead lion is the powerful wicked person, who takes nothing with him from the world.

**VERSE 5.**—“But the dead.” (ID.) Some assert that even after death people increase, etc., up to “rational creatures and merit reward.”

**VERSE 10.**—“They will be.” That is, they will be useful to you after death.

**VERSE 11.**—“War.” Of victors, or even imitators of war, according to the saying: “Without me you can do nothing.”

“Riches.” Of good works.

**VERSE 12.**—“As fish are caught.” The heretics too have their own dragnet cast out and their snares by which they catch the simple.

**VERSE 15.**—“A poor man.” Christ, of whom the Psalm says: [Col. 1125A] “I am poor and sorrowful” (Ps. LXVIII); and in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. II).

“By his wisdom.” Not by power.

**VERSE 17.**—“The words of the wise.” (JEROME.) Those who do not seek favor and applause but the salvation of their hearers; they do not shout in order to be heard, but desire that their hearers may obey.

“Among fools.” Fools who do not seek to advance but to acquire praise for themselves.

## CHAPTER TEN

**VERSE 4.**—“The place.” Hold fast your station in the faith, lest you be overcome; and do not complete what you have already conceived badly.

“He who digs.” “He opened a pit and dug it out, and he fell into the pit that he made.”

**VERSE 11.**—“If it bites.” (JEROME.) As a serpent that bites secretly injects poison, so does one who slanders. Or the serpent—that is, the devil—bites in silence when a person, having sinned at the devil’s prompting, does not wish to confess.

**VERSE 19.**—“They make bread and wine for laughter, so that those who drink may feast.” They preach more to attract than to advance their hearers.

“Money obeys everything,” etc. And priests were teaching for payment.

**VERSE 20.**—“In your thought,” etc. He simply advises us not to curse our superiors either in anger or frivolity, because what we say is often reported to them even when we do not fear it, even if it was said in the bedroom.

## CHAPTER ELEVEN

[Col. 1125C]

**VERSE 1.**—“Cast your bread.” Suitable for producing fruit.

**VERSE 2.**—“Give portions to seven.” (JEROME.) The Old Testament, whose seventh day, namely the Sabbath, is especially honored; and also to eight, which is the New Testament. For neither is valid without the other.

**VERSE 3.**—“If a tree falls toward the south or toward the north,” (ID.) as though he said: the place that you prepare for yourself here, you will possess in the future.

**VERSE 4.**—“He who observes the wind does not sow.” (ID.) As though he said: give yourself to the Almighty, whether with bodily comfort or with the word of God—lest you perhaps pass by one who is worthy to receive—and do so at all times. “He who observes the wind”: one must sow in the midst of the storm, because we do not know what the Spirit’s will is; and this is the meaning of: “As—,” etc.

[Col. 1125D]

**VERSE 6.**—“In the morning sow your seed,” etc. (ID.) [Col. 1126A] At all times, from morning to evening and conversely; or in youth and old age. For the one who perseveres will be saved.

**VERSE 9.**—“Rejoice therefore, young man,” etc. (ID.) From here to the end of the book, etc., up to “let them know that they will be judged.”

## CHAPTER TWELVE

From here to the end of the chapter the passage is read in three ways: as referring to judgment, old age, and captivity. Some glosses serve two interpretations at times, while at other times they are found according to all the interpretations.

**VERSE 2.**—“Before the sun and the light and the stars and the moon grow dark,” etc. (JEROME.) “The sun will be turned into darkness,” etc., up to “the clouds and rains cease for him.”

[Col. 1126B]

**VERSE 4.**—“And they will close the doors in the street so that they may not see the games of the young; for all such things are burdensome to them.”

“And they will rise.” Because they cannot sleep when the blood cools and the moisture by which sleep is nourished dries up.

**VERSE 5.**—“The caper plant will be scattered.” (JEROME.) The caper is beneficial to the kidneys, etc., up to “but in adversity they cease from doing good.”

**VERSE 6.**—“Before the cord is broken.” He returns to the preceding passage, where he said: “Remember your Creator,” etc.; with a similar ending he concludes the statement.

**VERSE 7.**—“And it returns.” Before you return to Babylon, from which you departed in the loins of Abraham, [Col. 1126C] and begin to be crushed in Mesopotamia, from which you set out.

**VERSE 8.**—“Vanity of vanities.” After describing human frailty and death, he beautifully concludes what he had proposed: “Vanity of vanities.” As though he said: do not indulge in luxury or seek delights, since you know that you pass swiftly to your end and hasten toward judgment.

**VERSE 11.**—“The words of the wise.” (JEROME.) Lest he seem rashly to forge new commandments after the law given through Moses at God’s own warning, he says that these are the words of the wise.

**VERSE 13.**—“The end of the discourse.” Because, like a preacher, he had introduced various opinions of various people, he reconciles them all in this conclusion: “Fear God.” The Hebrews say that this alone is held authoritatively, because here he reveals his intention, although in many passages he appears to encourage pleasures.

[Col. 1125]

# THE SONG OF SONGS (G)*

## PREFACE

[Col. 1125D]

Solomon, son of David, king of Israel, published three books according to the number of his names. The first of these is *misle*, which the Greeks call *parabolai* (παραβολαί), and the Latins *Proverbs*, because in it, under the comparative likeness of figures, he displays forms of speech and images of truth; but he left the truth itself to the understanding of his readers. He called the second book *Qoheleth*, which in Greek is called *Ecclesiastes* (ἐκκλησιαστής), and in Latin *Concionator* (“Preacher”), because its sermons are directed not only spiritually to one person, as in Proverbs, but generally to everyone, teaching that all the things we see in the world are vain and brief, and therefore are by no means to be desired. He entitled the third book *Sir ha-Shirim* [Song of Songs], which is rendered into Latin as *Cantica canticorum* [Song of Songs]. In it, through an epithalamial song, he mystically sings of the union of Christ and the Church. It is called the Song of Songs because it is preferred above all songs, just as in the Law certain things are called “holy,” while greater things are called “the holy of holies.”

In these three books he composed the disciplines of three kinds, by which one reaches knowledge of reality. First he set forth ethics, that is, moral teaching; next physics, which comprehends the qualities of nature; and finally theory, that is, contemplation. In Proverbs, teaching moral matters, he presented a higher understanding through a certain ordinary use of speech, and joined the observance of commandments and instruction in heavenly doctrine in concise words and brief maxims. Proverbs explain one thing through other words: they are understood differently from the way they are spoken, and contain more in the power of their maxims than in the sound of their words. The Greeks call such sayings *parabolai* (παραβολαί), “comparisons.”

Ecclesiastes, examining the natures of things, discovered that everything in the world is vain and perishable; and, having observed the fragility of all things, he admonished the world to renounce them. In the Song of Songs, rising beyond visible things and contemplating what is heavenly or divine, he declares, under the appearance of bridegroom and bride, the unity of Christ and the Church; and, stirring the soul to love heavenly things, he urges it to attain fellowship with God. Yet one must not believe what is reported by our hearers: that among the Hebrews it was their practice not to permit anyone to read this book unless he was already a man of mature knowledge and established faith in learning, lest its teaching should educate slippery minds less than its text should turn them toward bodily desires.

Solomon, that is, “peaceful,” because in his kingdom there was peace by which the future peace of the Church was represented; *Jedidiah*, that is, “beloved,” and he signifies the one of whom it is said: “You are more beautiful in form than the sons of men; therefore God has blessed you forever” (Psalm 44). *Ecclesiastes*, that is, “Preacher,” signifies the one who was to address and gather the Church rationally.

According to the number of his names, he made three books: Proverbs, in which he teaches the little ones—not so much in age as in wisdom—about even-tempered conduct in the world, namely, how they may lawfully use temporal things; Ecclesiastes, in which he instructs people of more advanced age to despise perishable things; and the Song of Songs, this work, in which he teaches the perfected person to love God alone, so that he may rest between the bridegroom’s arms. Hence it is also called the Song of Songs, surpassing all other songs by its dignity. Through the former books, vices are avoided and the enemy is guarded against; through this one, we are enriched with virtues and joined to the Lord.

Philosophers likewise set out their instruction in a similar order. First they teach ethics, then physics, and the person whom they see to have progressed in these they lead on to theory.

The subject is the bridegroom and the bride, that is, the head and the Church. The manner concerns how the members should cling to the head with what desire, strive to please him, and what gifts they receive from him in the present or hope to receive in the future; and with what affection the bridegroom loves the Church, praising, admonishing, and comforting her. The end is the love of God.

I seem to have found four persons in this work: the bridegroom and his companions, the bride, and the young women with her. Some things are spoken by the bridegroom, others by the bride; some by the young women, and some by the bridegroom’s companions. It is fitting that at the beginning there should be a multitude of young women with the bride, and a throng of young men with the bridegroom. Understand the bridegroom as Christ, and the bride as the Church without spot or wrinkle. Understand angels and those who have attained mature manhood as the bridegroom’s friends. The young women are the crowds of beginning brides, who have attained salvation in a certain measure.

From this book the Gentiles claimed an epithalamium for themselves, and a song of this kind was adopted. If you wish to ascend to the Song of Songs, you must leave Egypt, so that after crossing the Red Sea and the enemies’ being submerged, you may first sing the song: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously exalted,” and so forth (Exodus 15). But because you are still far from the Song of Songs, traverse spiritually the land of the desert; then, standing on the bank of the Jordan, sing the second song: “Hear, O heavens, what I speak,” and so forth (Deuteronomy 31). And when you have passed through everything, ascend to higher things, so that, as a beautiful soul with the bridegroom, you may sing this Song of Songs.

It should be noted that the bride always desires to remain with the bridegroom in the house, or in the bedchamber, or in some interior place; this is appropriate for women. He, acting in the manner of men, calls his beloved outward to the vineyards or to works of this kind, because clearly the Church would like, if it could be done in the tranquillity of peace, to raise offspring for the Lord. But in the present he exercises her through frequent persecutions, so that she may reach eternal things purer; lest, if prosperity should come, she might take pleasure in dwelling in or being exiled within the present age and sigh less for the heavenly homeland.

The Synagogue is a congregation, as is also a gathering of stones; the Church is an assembly, namely, of rational beings. Both of these portions of the righteous, in the same faith and love of Christ but at different times—the one awaiting him who was to come, the other receiving him who is present—have become partners. God, the creator of the universe, created all the movements of the soul for good; but through our use it often happens that things good by nature, when we misuse them, lead us into sin. One of the soul’s movements is love. We use it well if we love wisdom and truth, but badly if we love flesh or blood. Therefore, as a spiritual person, hear spiritually the words of love sung in this song, and learn to transfer the movement of your soul and the fire of natural love toward better things.

## CHAPTER ONE

### Verse 1. “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.”

This is the voice of those who preceded the coming of Christ, praying to the Father of the bridegroom, that is, of Christ. In the midst of her prayers she is heard; seeing the bridegroom, she speaks to him: “Let the sweetness of his presence touch me, which I have heard so often promised by the prophets, and, bringing a kiss, let him also receive the touch of my mouth”—that is, let him hear me questioning him about the way of salvation, and, making the two one, let him bring the kiss of peace.

“Kissing” is used for “being reconciled,” after the likeness of those who, because of discord, withdrew from their lords but, returning, kiss one another and are perfectly reconciled. Thus the Synagogue, the human race removed from God through sin, desires to be reconciled through the incarnation of the Son. As many commandments as she recognizes from his preaching, so many kisses of his mouth does she seem to receive.

She speaks in the manner of a lover who, through the fervor of affection, cannot maintain the proper order of speech. For just as two distinct bodies are joined in a kiss, so in the incarnation of the Son the two utterly different substances of divinity and humanity are united in an inseparable conjunction.

“They are better.” She calls the breasts of Christ the bridegroom by a feminine term, so that at the very beginning of the song she may show figuratively that she is speaking. Therefore I desire the kiss, which is also my redemption, because your instructions—which are milk and nourishment for children—are better than other teachings, which do not nurture but kill the simple, just as wine kills little ones. The odor of perfumes commonly signifies the reputation of virtues.

### Verse 2. “Your name is oil poured out.”

For this reason also I desire the kiss, because your name is oil, and so forth. The bridegroom comes from the Father to the bride anointed, so that he may also anoint the bride. From *chrisma* comes *Christ*, that is, “anointed,” from *unction*; this name is poured upon all the faithful through the grace of the Holy Spirit in baptism.

I cannot yet embrace you yourself; meanwhile your name, out of longing for you, will spend the night with me. The name of Jesus came into the world and was immediately preached. “Oil poured out”: the name of Christ is preached throughout the whole earth. Now the name of Moses is heard among the Gentiles, whereas previously it was confined within the narrow limits of Judea.

“Therefore the young women have loved you.” In saying this she looks upon the young women, who were not present while she was speaking earlier, but in the midst of her prayers a chorus of young women enters and is praised in the bride’s words.

All the Churches that make one catholic Church are young women: not old through guilt, but new through grace; not sterile through age, but suited by the age of their mind to spiritual fruitfulness. And because you have removed all the pains of sins through the oil of your grace, therefore the young women have loved you, and so forth.

### Verse 3. “Draw me after you.”

The young women reply: “Draw me after you.” The bride does not follow behind, but enters joined to the bridegroom’s side; the maidservants enter behind her.

“Draw me after you.” Up to this point it is the voice of those awaiting the Savior’s incarnation and commending his gifts; from here follows the voice of those who came to faith after the time of the incarnation. The former asked him to come and offer the kiss; the latter does not similarly demand that he descend any further to her, but rather desires to follow him herself into heaven. Since she sees that this cannot happen by her own power, she implores his guidance, wishing to come to him.

“Into the fragrance of perfumes”: into consideration of his miracles.

“The king brought me into his chambers,” and so forth. Having entered the bridegroom’s inner chamber, the bride returns to the young women and announces to them: “He brought me in.” Or: he brought me into eternal blessedness through hope, expressed in the plural on account of the abundance of every kind of good. It is as though she said: “I have already tasted beforehand the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom; through his revelation I have learned what has been prepared for me in heaven.” Then, turning to the one who reveals this to her, she gives thanks for his benefits.

There are four things in a house: the door, the ascent, the dining room, and the bedchamber. By the door we understand faith; by the ascent, hope; by the dining room, love; and by the bedchamber, blessedness itself.

“We shall exult and rejoice.” As though she were saying: “We do not exalt ourselves over the gifts we have received, but you. We remember throughout with how much mercy you have deigned to soften the austerity of the Law through the grace of evangelical faith. Therefore we shall exult not in ourselves but in you, because all the upright love you and have learned to love you above all things.”

Again, having entered the inner chamber, the bride’s young women, while awaiting her return, sing joyfully in harmony over the bride’s perfection.

“Remembering your breasts.” “The upright love you” refers to the bride’s commendation. “Remembering your breasts,” and so forth: “She who is greater already enjoys the milk of your breasts. We too do not indeed love, but we shall love.”

Then they speak to the bridegroom: “The upright love you.” All who are upright in heart love you above all things; nor are those upright who place anything before your love, since from you alone they possess whatever good they have. “The upright love you.” In vain do those believe that they love the Creator who despise his admonitions. Truly righteous are those who violate God neither in deed, thought, nor word.

### Verse 4. “I am black.”

After the Church has been led into the wine-cellars—that is, through knowledge and hope of future goods—and after she has learned to love him with an upright heart and rejoice in his grace, it remains to show that for love of him and for the acquisition of the goods she has tasted, she undergoes struggle and endures affliction.

“I am black.” As though she were saying: “You promise that you will go with me, but the tribulation that I suffer may frighten you. Yet do not let affliction or disgrace frighten you, because these will confer the beauty of virtues; and after love, endurance remains as love’s test.”

“I am black.” Again the bride answers the young women, and the subject is manifest temptation. “I am black”: I appear worthless in the eyes of my persecutors, but before the God of truth I shine gloriously through my confession.

“Like the tents of Kedar.” Here “like” is used not according to truth but according to the judgment of the foolish, who think her a dwelling of vices or demons; elsewhere “the skins of Solomon” are used according to truth. Kedar was the son of Ishmael, whose hand was against everyone and everyone’s hand against him; he had no place among human beings, but always dwelt in tents because of wickedness and anger. So the righteous, because of their merits, are believed to be expelled and afflicted and are judged as enemies of all; hence it is said: “You will be hated by all people because of my name” (Matthew 10).

“Like the skins of Solomon.” The Church, mortifying carnal desires within herself and adorned with virtues, becomes a dwelling worthy of the true peacemaker. Therefore the flesh of the Lord’s human being is called a curtain: just as a tent is stretched over someone so that he is not burned by the sun, so Christ’s flesh, extended on the cross, became for us a shadowing against vices.

### Verse 5. “The sun has discolored me.”

It is characteristic of the sun both to burn and to illuminate. Thus the true sun outwardly burns his own through persecutions, while illuminating them by giving strength to resist.

“The sons of my mother.” And, as though answering the objection of the weak who were hesitating, she shows where she first endured the fury of the persecutors, which appears more severe because it came from fellow sufferers.
