“The sons”—that is, the apostles—“destroyed our sect.” Paul, the persecutor of the Church, was a son of its mother according to flesh and upbringing; but, doing penance and turning toward the signs of his sister, he preached the faith that he had previously been destroying.

“They set me.” There was one vineyard of Christ in Jerusalem, namely, the primitive Church, established on the day of Pentecost through the coming of the Holy Spirit; at that time the apostles were its guardians. But when persecution arose, they were scattered through the regions of Judea and Samaria, apart from the apostles. Thus it happened that there were many vineyards, that is, in many places. While the Jewish persecutors wished to disturb the Church, they unwillingly scattered the seed of the word more widely; by persecuting one vineyard, they caused many to be established.

Having said that she had been afflicted by the murderous hatred of the Synagogue, she immediately adds how much she had advanced through this affliction, speaking in the person of those entrusted with the work of preaching: “They set me as a keeper of the vineyards.”

(Gregory.) Our vineyards are our actions, which we cultivate through the practice of daily labor. But, placed as keepers in the vineyards, we do not guard our own vineyard, because, while we become entangled in external activities, we neglect the ministry of our own work. While I was guarding many vineyards in order to win others, I suffered losses in some. The bitterness of persecution by the sons of the Synagogue made me fail to guard my own vineyard, because, abandoning evangelical doctrine, they compelled me to the distinctions of legal observances.

### Verse 6. “Tell me,” and so forth.

This is the voice of the beginning Church from the Gentiles addressed to the bride, because many false prophets go out into the world saying: “Behold, here is Christ,” or “There he is.” She asks to be able to discern in whose profession and conduct he may be found.

“Tell me about my shepherd, whom my whole soul loves, and where he has rest and pasture, lest, troubled by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him among the gatherings of companions”—that is, of heretics. Or this is the voice of preachers addressed to the bridegroom, so that they may discern to whom they ought to minister the words of life.

Then she sees the bridegroom, who, once seen, departs. He frequently does this throughout the song: once experienced, the bridegroom is often present and often slips away, until he is truly held.

“At noon,” and so forth: that is, in the splendor of your majesty, which belongs to the perfect, not in the morning or evening. Or “at noon” means in the burning of tribulations, which the devil sends, grieving that the world is being snatched from him.

The quality of things is often indicated by the time. Abraham received the angels at noon. Joseph feasted with his brothers at noon.

“Your companions.” Heretics are called companions because they carry about the mysteries of his name and confession.

### Verse 7. “If you do not know.”

Because the bride, while seeking the help of God’s presence in tribulations, had added, in the person of the weak, “lest I begin to wander,” the bridegroom whom she invoked immediately rebukes that same fear with a kindly correction, according to the saying of the Gospel, “You of little faith” (Matthew 14). It is as though he were saying: “You fear being destroyed by me in tribulation, and you complain that you have been blackened by the heat; but I have determined to make you more beautiful through tribulations. If perhaps you do not know this, and do not remember that no one is crowned unless he has competed lawfully, go out from my company.”

(Gregory, *Moralia*, book 16, chapter 21.) She knows herself when, placed in spirit among sinners, she remembers that she was created according to the image of her author and walks according to the order of the likeness she has received. If she does not know this, she goes out from the secrecy of her heart into external desires; led onto the broad road, she follows the examples of the peoples.

The Lord, rebuking the frightened Church, reminds her of the grace given to her against the enemy’s ambushes.

“Your young goats.” Because they are instructed not according to the rule of my commandments but according to your errors.

“Beside the shepherds’ footsteps you will become last,” not among sheep but among goats. Or “beside” means “so that you may be like the true shepherds,” because hypocrites appear to follow good men.

### Verse 8. “To my cavalry.”

Just as I freed the earlier people from Egyptian slavery, so I will free you from the hands of your persecutors, crushing Pharaoh, if you recognize yourself as my bride; I will free you from the slavery of the devil in the baptismal font reddened by suffering, where the author of sin was submerged.

“To my cavalry.” Since the Lord does not wish the Church to ignore herself but to consider carefully what gifts she has received and what she must suffer, after the threat he consequently soothes her, as though saying: “If you wish to understand how you should know yourself, understand with what I have compared you; then you will recognize yourself as such through the benefits bestowed upon you by me, so that you should not be troubled.”

“To my cavalry.” The horseman is the bridegroom, as the prophet says: “His salvation is his riding” (Habakkuk 3). Therefore, as much as my cavalry differs from Pharaoh’s horses, so much better are you than all the other daughters.

Just as that people was terrified when Pharaoh’s chariots came upon it, but was saved by heavenly protection and brought into the promised land after the enemies had been submerged in the waters, so the wave of death, which will meet all mortals, carries the wicked away to destruction but opens a road to salvation for the devout; and all the other things that were fulfilled there bodily are fulfilled here spiritually.

He kindly rebukes her hesitation and, so that she will not despair, strongly encourages her in faithful love in what follows, where he compares her to Pharaoh’s chariots.

“In Pharaoh’s chariots,” that is, in the time of the chariots. And note the pride: Pharaoh is interpreted as “crushing” or “scattering.” Nor should you begin to wander when you have me as your consoler and leaders on whom you may rely, through whom you may stand firm.

### Verse 9. “Beautiful.”

Since it has been shown how the Lord protects the Church amid adversities, it remains to show how much love for the Lord himself the Church preserves amid adversities. Hence follows: “Your cheeks are beautiful.”

I have adorned you with such a great virtue of salutary modesty that you will not corrupt the chastity of the faith promised to me through any teaching or suggestion of evil teachers, from whom you feared being led into error. The greatest beauty of a woman is said to be in her cheeks.

Allegorically, a sign of modesty is marked in the cheeks, just as in preachers there is the custom of right conduct. Although the Church has been bereaved by the death of her bridegroom, she nevertheless holds his memory so firmly that she can in no way admit the companionship of outsiders; and she groans for her own sins and those of others.

“In your neck,” the teachers; “in your necklaces,” their works, because they practice what they teach in words. He demonstrates the grace by which this sobriety must be guarded by adding: “Your neck is like necklaces.”

Through the neck we convey food into the body to restore it, and we utter words by which we disclose the secrets of the heart to our neighbors. Thus the neck signifies teachers, who instruct by words and pour the food of salvation into the members entrusted to them. They are compared to necklaces: beautiful in conduct, they close the breasts of virgins through words and examples, lest an adulterer insert his hand.

### Verse 10. “We will make you necklaces.”

Another translation reads: “We will make you likenesses of gold, with silver settings, until the king is at his table.”

This means: You will not be able to see gold—that is, my face—in the present life, but through the illumination of the Scriptures you will see a likeness of heavenly radiance, as through a mirror in an enigma, until what is now hidden in the Godhead appears to everyone.

“We will make you necklaces.” The bridegroom beautifully describes her beauty; after this he becomes her bridegroom in repose. Meanwhile, while he sleeps, his companions, that is, the angels, comfort her. We do not possess gold, but we will make for you a likeness of gold until he rises with the marks of silver.

“Necklaces.” All good instructions are like ornaments for the ears. In the necklaces is Holy Scripture, which inwardly shines with the gold of spiritual meanings and outwardly gleams with the silver of heavenly speech. Through the edification of teachers it becomes a safeguard of sobriety, and through meditation on divine Scripture it becomes so as well. They shine inwardly and outwardly with the gold of divine wisdom and the silver of divine speech.

“We will make them”: I and my craftsmen, whom I appointed in great number to distribute the seeds of the word.

### Verse 11. “While the king was at his table.”

Having received such great gifts and promises from her creator, the Church reveals with what devotion of works she received them, saying: “While the king was at his table.” This means: when the Son of God appeared in the flesh, through the mystery of the incarnation the Church grew in the fervor of heavenly virtues.

Or: when the human race was in the humiliation of the cross and was redeemed through the cross, the practice of good works spread the fragrance of sweetness. While Christ the King rests in the blessedness of heavenly secrecy, the virtue of the saints in the Church supplies us with great grace of sweetness; the less they see the one whom they desire, the more ardently they burn through longing.

Or: while he was with the Father, nard—that is, love, by which he first loved us—gave forth its fragrance, because through love he assumed flesh for our sake.

The order of the words is wonderful: “While the king reclined, my nard gave its fragrance,” when, because of the excessive love with which he loved us, the Son became a woman’s child.

Nard is said to drive away swellings, dispel cold, and bring warmth. The Lord’s human being is compared to it: by assuming flesh he humbled himself; by humbling himself he removed every swelling of pride, drove away the cold of unbelief, and brought in the fervor of love. This herb also gives off a greater fragrance the more it is crushed; so does Christ.

### Verse 12. “A bundle.”

The death of my beloved, which he endured for my salvation, will always remain in my memory. Likewise he is compared to a bundle of myrrh, since he endured the injuries of the cross for our sake.

Myrrh is a tree of Arabia, five cubits high, resembling the plant they call acanthus. Its drop is green and bitter, from which it received the name *myrrh*. Its naturally flowing drop is more precious; the drop obtained by wounding the bark is cheaper. It is beneficial for curing illnesses; hence soldiers also gave him myrrh-flavored wine.

“My breasts.” The breasts of chaste women are not broken, but those of prostitutes become wrinkled through loosened skin. Hence Ezekiel says: “Your breasts were broken in Egypt” (Ezekiel 23).

### Verse 13. “My beloved is a cluster of henna.”

The beloved is a cluster of henna when he rose again; he is in the vineyards of Engedi when he distributes spiritual gifts among the faithful. Since the balsam trees that grow in Engedi are cultivated in the manner of vineyards, he calls them vineyards.

Christ the bridegroom, therefore, is in the vineyards of Engedi: coming in the flesh and full of the Holy Spirit, he bestows the gifts of that same Holy Spirit upon believers through the anointing of chrism, in whose preparation oil and balsam are mixed.

Engedi means “the spring of the kid,” on account of the charisms that he bestowed after the resurrection in baptism upon those who share in him.

Engedi also means “the eye of my temptation,” and human life upon earth is temptation. Because the glory of the resurrection immediately followed the Mediator’s death, it is rightly added: the cluster that had been a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of the Passion became a cluster of henna in the sweetness of the resurrection. Myrrh brings sadness, whereas wine brings joy.

### Verse 14. “Behold, you are beautiful.”

Up to this point the Church has testified to what pledges of love she received from the bridegroom; he immediately responds to her in return with a reward: “Behold, you are beautiful,” as though saying: “Through the fact that you love me, you will become beautiful.”

“My friend.” Another translation has: “My close companion.” This means: “In that you are close to me, you are beautiful; and once you have begun to be beautiful, you are beautiful without qualification.”

“Your eyes.” Another praise of the beautiful bride, so that we too may labor to become beautiful. “Your eyes are like those of doves”: you look simply toward God, because you seek nothing other than him.

Whoever looks at a woman in order to desire her (Matthew 5) does not have the eyes of a dove. But whoever has them looks with chaste eyes and understands the Law and the Gospel spiritually. The Holy Spirit appeared in the form of this dove. Therefore spiritual understanding and all spiritual gifts are also designated by the name “dove.”

The dove is without gall, does not injure with its beak, builds its nest in rocky caves, nourishes the young of others, stays near streams, chooses better grains, makes a lament instead of a song, flies in a flock, defends itself with its wings, and recovers its sight. In the same way, the saints, sitting beside the streams of teaching, choose better interpretations; they nourish for God people alienated from Christ; if they find any good interpretations among heretics, they do not corrupt them; they lack irrational anger; in faith they have refuge in the wounds of Christ; and they groan over sins.

### Verse 15. “Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, and comely.”

Hearing that she had merited, through the bridegroom’s love, to be praised by the bridegroom himself, the bride returns his praise in turn—not as though she were granting him through her commendation something he does not possess, but, understanding his beauty, through which she herself was made beautiful, she says: “Behold, you are beautiful,” and so forth.

“Our bed is flowering.” Sometimes the Church rests as though in a bed with the bridegroom, namely, in a time of peace, when she sees God’s beauty more clearly and gives birth to a faithful offspring fragrant with the flower of faith, from water and the Holy Spirit. At other times, when temptation rises with the bridegroom, she stands in the battle line.

Or the bed signifies the little faithful, who are rest for God and for their teachers, at least because they do not wish to commit mortal sin. They flower in the beginnings of good works, thereby giving hope of fruit, that is, of greater works.

Wishing to lead a peaceful life with the bridegroom, she indicates what kind of houses they are in which she wishes to receive him. The peace of the Church flourishes with virtues and multiplies through spiritual offspring.

### Verse 16. “The beams of our houses are of cedar.”

The houses are the various Churches of the Gentiles throughout the world. The beams, which are customarily made for the strengthening of a house, signify preachers, by whose word and example the structure of the Church is held together so that it does not collapse.

The ceilings, which are customarily made for the adornment of a house, signify the simpler servants of Christ, who cling to and are supported by the beams. They adorn the house not through teaching but through virtues.

“Of cypress.” Cypress is so called in Greek because its head rises from roundness into a point. Hence a cone is called *kōnos* (κῶνος), “a high roundness”; from this its fruit is also called a cone. Thus: “cone-bearing cypresses.”

## CHAPTER TWO

### Verse 1. “I am a flower.”

Since in the condition of the present time labor is more fitting than rest, the bridegroom rightly calls the bride, delighted with leisure, to the exercise of labors. It is as though he were saying: “You wish to make your beauty pleasing to me, and you delight in flourishing in hidden virtues during rest; but know that in the present I seek another kind of beauty, because I am the flower of virtues, from which every fruit of the field proceeds. I wish my fragrance to become known to the whole world, and this cannot be fulfilled unless, interrupting the rest in which you delight, you gird yourself for the ministry of preaching.”

“And the lily of the valleys” rather than of the mountains, because I reveal the brightness of my humanity, the splendor of eternal light, or of divinity, more to the humble and to those prepared to suffer.

It is as though he said: “Remember that I, who could be born of a virgin and who am God, appeared humbly in the world; I showed myself to human beings as their companion and came humbly even unto death. Therefore cease seeking the security of rest.” Hence he adds: “Like a lily.” Just as a field is adorned with flowers, so the world is adorned with knowledge and faith in me.

### Verse 2. “Like a lily.”

Having praised himself, he praises the bride in this way: just as a lily cannot be compared with the thorns among which it often grows, so my beloved is a lily above all the daughters.

“Like a lily.” You seek rest and praise of the bed, but know that you will be made whiter by the thorns of tribulations, and that the fruit of preaching is greater than that of rest.

“So is my beloved.”

(Gregory.) In the Church there can be neither the wicked without the good nor the good without the wicked; a good person was not one who could not tolerate the wicked. Her integrity is pierced as by thorns by the doctrines of hostile heresies, so that she may be exercised in vigilance against her enemies, until, rising above them like a lily on the head of her bridegroom, she is adorned by that very whiteness.

### Verse 3. “Like an apple tree,” and so forth.

Having been praised and admonished to suffer by the example of the bridegroom, the bride raises him up with reciprocal praise, declaring that among the works of the good he likewise stands out uniquely as holy, and promising that she will suffer what he suffers, while he presides who is refreshment and restoration.

“Like an apple tree.” Although the fragrance of perfumes smells sweetly, it is not pleasant to eat. But an apple of excellent taste and fragrance is such that it delights the throat with sweetness and soothes the breath with its scent.

“Under his shadow.” Therefore I set my beloved before everyone, because I see that in the protection of his mercy alone, for whose desire I was burning, I have found refreshment from tribulations, and I experience the most delightful fruit of his gifts, by which I trust I shall continually be restored.

She had desired to breathe under the shadow of the author when she complained that she had been darkened by the sun of persecution, when, imploring God’s help, she cried: “Tell me whom my soul loves, where you pasture and where you lie down at noon”; and when, fatigued not only by the weariness of afflictions but also enticed by the memory of his beauty and comeliness, she said: “Our bed is flowering.” She shows herself to have obtained what she desired by saying: “Under his shadow.”

It should be noted that above she praised the cedar beams and cypress ceilings, yet she did not say that their protection was sufficient for her. Rather, she sought only the tree of life, in whose shadow she might rest and by whose fruit she might be restored, because the saints offer help through their examples, teaching, and intercession. Nevertheless, to the Savior alone we may say: “The sons of men will hope in the protection of your wings” (Psalm 35).

“I sat, and his fruit,” and so forth. He does not say, “I sit,” but “I sat.” Such are the advances of the Churches: at the beginning, someone desires to sit in the shadow of virtues, so that the body from which the shadow arises may come to him. Therefore the birth of Jesus also began from a shadow and ends in reality. As it is said: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you” (Luke 1). Thus afterward there is a transition to better things.

“Sweet.” Because in him the soul understands the cause of life, while it also perceives it bodily.

### VERSE 4

**“He brought me in.”** The extent and power of this refreshment, and how sweet it is, are shown when he adds, “He brought me in.” That is: he so gladdened me with hope of future glory that I no longer feel the labors of the world.

**“He brought me in.”** (AMBROSE.) As soon as my throat touched the sweetness of his grace, I feel myself so refreshed in spirit and transferred from love of earthly things to heavenly things, as though I had been brought into a wine cellar and revived by the fragrance and drink of new wine. Typologically, wine signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. The wine cellar is the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is customarily given and received. God gathered this Church from the whole world and fashioned it into a single house for himself, and the Holy Spirit consecrated it with his charismatic gifts. Since this structure stands upon the foundation of the greatest charity, with God himself at work within it, it is rightly added: **“He has ordered charity in me.”**

The charity of many is disordered: they put third or fourth what belongs first. First, God must be loved; second, parents; then children; afterward members of the household, who, if they are good, are to be preferred even to wicked children. In accordance with this order, the Gospel assigns the proper measure to love of each person: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your mind, and your neighbor as yourself” (Mark 12). Enemies are not to be loved with all one’s strength, nor as oneself, but simply: it is enough that we love them and do not hate them.

Alternatively, he himself first loved me, and by loving me gave me the ability to know how to love him. Or, “he ordered” means that, through ordered charity, he joined my individual members—that is, all the elect—to himself; he embraces the more excellent with greater affection. How completely charity absorbs the mind and raises it from love of the weak is shown when it follows:

[Col. 1137B]

### VERSE 5

**“Sustain me.”** Having been strengthened by what has already been said, she burns with such love for God that, through excessive love, bodily weakness threatens her, even because of the sufferings inflicted upon her. Or, “sustain me” means: you others—whether more perfect or beginners—refresh me by doing good, so that I may rest in your good works, since I am not yet able to rest in contemplating the face of God. Therefore, sustain me, so that you may have both present and future support, just as I have support in my weakness.

The more she kindles herself for love of the bridegroom, the more she grows weak from love of temporal things. Hence he adds: **“I am faint.”**

### VERSE 6

**“His left hand is under my head.”** Do not seek rest for your head elsewhere; for if you have his left hand, everything that is mine will be bestowed upon you.

When the hearts of the faithful in this life are strengthened through participation in the sacraments, through the pledge of the Spirit, and through the consolations of Scripture—which God also grants as aid for the journey of exile—then **“his right hand will embrace”** us, when after this life we receive heavenly rewards.

The left hand—that is, the present life and God’s temporal gifts—strengthens the mind through hope and is given beneath the head for consolation. The right hand—that is, eternal life—will embrace us, as though protecting us, when he glorifies us through recompense. It is as if she said: The temporal benefits of God help me here in the place of pilgrimage, so that I may rest somewhat from the desires and disturbances of the world; but the promise of eternal things delights me far more.

### VERSE 7

**“I adjure you.”** The primitive Church, converted from the nations and speaking thus far almost in their person, now suffers bodily weakness through inward love. The bridegroom warns the newly formed Church not to disturb her by sinning. How pleasing to God is the repose of this Church and of every faithful soul is shown by the bridegroom’s reply.

**“By the does.”** That is: if you wish to be like does or stags in the height of virtue, in more precious nourishment, and in knowledge—which is the suitable remedy for your wounds, if you have wounds.

Does and stags are clean animals, hostile to poisons and given to ruminating; they signify the works of spiritual virtues against the snares of the poisonous enemy.

At the time of love, stags leave their native land. One supports another by placing its head upon the haunches of the one ahead, and they proceed in order: the first bears the burden, while the last is merely carried; when the first grows tired, the last takes its place. When dogs pursue them through the thickets, they escape unharmed by placing their antlers upon their backs. When their eyes grow dim, they eat a serpent, drink from a spring, recover their sight, and shed what is superfluous.

In the same way, the saints renounce earthly things for love of God. They support one another’s burdens: those less burdened by sins lift up those who are burdened, by forgiving them and praying for them. When they are pressed by the wicked, they place beneath themselves the strength given to their minds through the Holy Spirit, and so pass unharmed. They eat the devil—that is, they annihilate him within themselves. After drinking from the spring—that is, Christ—they recover their inner sight, and they lay aside their skin—that is, they become free from sins.

**“Do not stir up.”** (GREGORY.) If subjects commit some sin because of which teachers are compelled to rise from their repose, they incur not only the punishment of that sin but are also punished for disturbing the teachers. For whoever presumes to disturb teachers intent upon heavenly things loses even the virtues he thought he possessed.

At the bridegroom’s oath the bride willingly accepts his command. When she hears the qualification added—namely, “until she herself wills it”—she understands that she is secretly being instructed to wish of her own accord to rise. She therefore promises that she will rise and determines that she will do so for such a bridegroom, whenever the appropriate time comes.

After the apostles, placed over the nations in the primitive Church, had brought themselves and others to such perfection that they could devote themselves to contemplation, she again understands that the necessity has been imposed upon her of traveling throughout the whole world and building new Churches.

[Col. 1138D]

### VERSE 8

**“The voice of my beloved.”** This is the voice I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to awaken me. I rejoice to hear his consoling voice, although I do not yet see his face. Nevertheless, with my mind lifted toward heaven, I already taste something of the sweetness of future blessedness, even in the present life.

**“Leaping upon the mountains.”** He leaps upon the mountains and, as it were, places his feet there; by this sign it is recognized that he has been there, because he imitates him through his passion and manner of life.

He made a leap from heaven into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger to the cross, from the cross into the tomb, and from the tomb he returned to heaven. He is the one who was lifted above all mountains and hills—that is, above the heights of the saints, both greater and lesser.

**“Leaping over the hills.”** On the hills the signs of his feet do not appear, but they receive the shadow of him flying overhead. For although they do not imitate him as the greater ones do, they imitate him to some degree and are visited by him.

Mountains and hills are those who, surpassing the general way of life of the Church, like a flowering plain, by the singular purity of their minds, withdraw from what is lowly and contemplate heavenly things more closely. He leaps in them because he illumines the hearts of the exalted by frequent visitation. Yet he does not remain; he leaps and leaps over them, because this sweetness of contemplation is brief and rare on account of the heaviness of the flesh, since an earthly dwelling weighs down the mind occupied with many thoughts.

### VERSE 9

**“Like.”** Because he sees keenly, dwells in the heights of the mountains, and leaps swiftly, he is seen by us more rarely. From his birth onward he is always ascending to the Father’s bosom.

**“Like.”** Although in his divinity he transcends all things in this way, he nevertheless became human and was born for me from the lineage of the Gentiles and the patriarchs. In the assumption of flesh and in his humanity he is compared to a doe; in the variety of his virtues and miracles, to a young stag.

The stag draws the serpent from its cavern with the breath of its nostrils and, having overcome the danger of the poison, delights in its food.

Since these verses have expressed the sublimity of the contemplative life, it remains to display the perfection of the active life, which is shared by the whole Church. Hence what follows:

**“Behold, he stands,”** and so forth.

**“Behind the wall.”** The wall that deceives us and keeps us from his sight is the condition of mortality, which we deserved by sinning. We were so created that, had we not sinned, all the elect would have seen the divine light without weariness. Now only a very few of the more perfect, purified by faith and labor, attain to seeing it.

Yet in this wall God, in his mercy, made windows and lattices through which he enables us to look. Although our minds are weighed down, he has opened to them the grace of knowing him, and through the frequent light of his inspiration he looks upon us.

Because through this outlook of inspiration God chiefly moves us from temporal things to earn heavenly things, it is rightly added:

**“Behold, my beloved speaks to me.”** He who above warned the daughters of Jerusalem to guard my repose now sends me to cultivate the vineyards, showing me the appropriate time.

**“Behind the wall.”** Morally, if you build yourself up, God will come behind your wall and look through the windows—that is, he will look attentively through the five senses. Where the bridegroom does not watch, death climbs up. Hence Jeremiah says: “Behold, death has climbed through our windows” (Jeremiah 9).

**“Through the lattices.”** Everything is full of the devil’s nets, by which you would be caught, except that the bridegroom subjected himself to the nets of the world and, standing above them, cut a path through them, so that you may say: “Our soul has been rescued like a sparrow from the snare of the hunters” (Psalm 123).

**“Through the windows.”** Just as the sun entering through windows illumines a house, so Christ illumined us by the example and admonition of the apostles. As through lattices—that is, through small openings—only a little light enters, so obscure knowledge comes through the prophets.

### VERSE 10

**“Rise, hasten.”** That is: interrupt contemplation and labor for the acquisition of others; or, rise from love of earthly things. Everything has its appointed time. The one who just now adjured the daughters of Jerusalem not to disturb his beloved now invites her to labor.

**“Rise, hasten.”** (GREGORY.) When she is brought out of the body of corruption, the rain has passed for her, because the sluggishness of the present life has departed. She is brought forth to contemplate God in his substance, and no longer does she need drops of words, as though the rain of preaching had to be poured upon her. For what she could hear less clearly she will then see more fully.

Flowers appear upon the earth when the soul begins to taste in advance some beginnings of sweetness from the life of eternal blessedness. As she departs, she already smells the flowers; after she has gone forth, she will possess their fruit more abundantly.

**“The time of pruning has arrived.”** Our pruning takes place when we abandon the fruitless and harmful corruption of the flesh, so that we may reach the fruit of the soul, which is exceedingly abundant for us. In pruning, sterile branches are cut away so that those that are fruitful may bear more abundantly. Therefore rise, because I, suffering for you, have calmed the waves.

**“Come.”** Come also to devote yourself to the salvation of your neighbors through diligent preaching, so that you may deserve to be received at the wedding with a great company. It is as though he said: You think you will come if you devote yourself to contemplation; but you will come more successfully through labor of this kind. You must preach, because now there is knowledge in you, and there is also, among those to whom I send you, the opportunity to receive it.

### VERSE 11

**“The rain has gone away.”** I, rising from the dead, have restored calm after the storm had been subdued. It is now easier to preach, since some have already been converted, than it was before, when no one had yet believed.

### VERSE 12

**“The flowers.”** It is as though he said: You can present as examples to others those who already believe and already do good works; you can set before others those who are already suffering the pruning hook cutting away their vices.

For the sake of your repose, you must not abandon preaching, because Christ, who was in great repose with the Father, interrupted his repose, in a sense, for the sake of preaching.

**“The time of pruning.”** Now that the branches of empty religion have been cut away, human hearts are being prepared for the future fruit of faith. Vices too are being cut away, because the time of the remission of sins has come.

**“The voice of the turtledove has been heard.”** When the Holy Spirit speaks of more hidden mysteries, and of things that many do not understand, he is signified by the name of the turtledove. Thus he appeared to Moses and to one other person. When he speaks of humble things that reach everyone, he is represented by the dove. Therefore, when many stood near the Jordan, he appeared not in the form of a turtledove but of a dove.

The voice of the turtledove is the voice of the apostles, or of any preachers, who by their song announce the departure of winter and the arrival of spring. In place of song they utter a humble groan; they are lovers of chastity; they dwell always on the ridges of mountains or the tops of trees and avoid the company of human beings. Though they live in the body in the world, their manner of life is in heaven, and they remember both their exile and the homeland promised to them.

### VERSE 13

**“The fig tree.”** He calls the first and unripe figs *grossi*, which are not fit to eat and which, even when shaken, fall at a gentle touch. Therefore, when the turtledove sounds—that is, when the apostles preach—the Synagogue brought forth *grossi*: it cast off an immature understanding of legal observance.

Or it may be understood in this way: the Synagogue brought forth the apostles, who would minister sweet food to those who believed. Since, when the Synagogue brought forth the apostles, the faith and salvation of the whole world followed, it is rightly added:

**“The flowering vines.”** Their flowering signifies the beginnings of the many Churches arising from the Church first planted at Jerusalem. From its flower the juice was pressed to make a kind of drink suitable for salvation and pleasure, which gladdens the human heart.

### VERSE 14

**“In the clefts.”** The Church sits and nests in the wounds of Christ when it places the hope of its salvation in the Lord’s passion and thereby trusts that it will be protected from the snares of the hawk—that is, the devil—and gives birth to others in the same place.

**“In the clefts.”** In faith, or in the capacity in which the faithful are placed and kept safe from enemies.

A **wall** is a heap of stones compacted into one structure without mortar. In this way the apostles are united by the same faith and the same sacraments.

**“Show me.”** She did not yet have the confidence to contemplate the glory of God with unveiled face. But because she has now been adorned, it is said: **“Show me your face; let your voice sound in my ears.”**

Her face is shown to the Lord by right action; the sound of her voice is shown by wholesome preaching. Do not be ashamed to preach the cross of Christ, although it appears foolish to unbelievers. The apostles of Christ preached it, and they are the wall and fortification of the Church.

Alternatively, the wall consists of the prophets and patriarchs, in whom the apostles have refuge. Whatever beauty you possess within, whatever you have learned in the secrecy of repose, demonstrate in public action for the benefit of others. For me, who see inward things, I consider your face to have been shown when I observe that you have displayed good action for the benefit of your neighbors.

**“In my ears.”** Not in the ears of another—that is, devote both work and voice to my love, not to anything earthly.

**“For your voice.”** It is not another voice but the one by which, on the day of your betrothal, you promised to serve me.

### VERSE 15

**“Catch them for us.”** It is not enough to present our life to others as an example and to preach well unless we also correct those who go astray and defend the weak from the snares of others. Hence it is rightly said, “Catch them,” not “for you,” but “for us”: in this you serve me, and in this I will reward you.

Foxes hide in dens, and when they appear they never run along straight paths; so it is with heretics.

**“For our vineyard.”** Beautifully, whereas above he used the plural “vineyards,” here he uses the singular “vineyard,” because the many vineyards are one through faith and charity. Therefore those who wish to divide it through heresies must be driven out.

### VERSE 16

**“My beloved is mine.”** To such an address from her beloved, the friend immediately responds with the simplicity of a dove’s heart and promises to obey the duty imposed upon her. It is as though she said: He not only encourages me but also assists me.

**“My beloved is mine.”** He is joined to me in sincere love, and I to him. Or, my beloved gives me such encouragement, and I show him my face and voice. Or, my beloved—mine and no one else’s—will grant grace and return fruit to me; and I, his and no one else’s, will be joined to him in complete obedience and devotion, not among any other crowd of people.

All these senses fit what follows:

**“Who feeds among the lilies.”** He feeds in us because we are his body and members from his member; he himself feeds us, since he is the head. He feeds among the lilies when the faithful, who are his members, are perfected in love of heavenly things by the examples of earlier believers.

**“Lilies.”** Lilies are accustomed to healing burned limbs. In the same way, if the saints see that the hearts of their neighbors are being scorched by the flame of vices, they apply the refreshment of consolation and exhortation.

Since this feeding of the Lord, which takes place through the progress of his saints, reaches to the end of the world, it is rightly added:

**“Until the day breathes.”**

### VERSE 17

**“Return, like.”** Place your footprints in exalted minds, and sometimes, by condescending to those below, appear also to those who are in the valley.

**“Return, like.”** Since you summon me to establish and cultivate Churches, to drive away the cunning of the little foxes, and to show you my face although I still do not see your face clearly and cannot accomplish this by myself, I beg you: illumine more perfectly my heart and the hearts of those to whom I am to preach.

## CHAPTER III

### VERSES 1–2

**“On my bed.”** While the preachers from Judea are praying, behold, the Gentile world, breathed upon by the divine Spirit, comes to the knowledge of its salvation and holds firmly in love what it has found. Hence what follows: **“His voice fully entering.”**

**“On my bed.”** (GREGORY.) Morally, the holy soul makes a bed for itself during the night when, fleeing all the disturbances of the world, it prepares a secret place in which it may rest. On this bed it seeks its beloved, because, while free from anxieties, it rests in the search for how it may reach him.

But while it lives in the world, it cannot completely shake off the darkness of the world. The more heavily it suffers, the more frequently it seeks him, and the more fervently it seeks him so that, once he is found, it may suffer darkness no longer.

But because it does not find him in this world, it is therefore added:

**“I sought him and did not find him.”**

Since it burns with the greatest desire and nothing it possesses is sufficient for it until it finds the beloved, it adds perseverance in the search:

**“I will rise and go around the city.”**

**“On my bed.”** From the time Adam sinned, humanity began to rest in earthly things. Yet, guided by reason and as though in a dream understanding true blessedness, it supposed that blessedness consisted in earthly things.

(HIERONYMUS.) Morally, the soul seeks God on its bed when, in its leisure, it desires to see God and longs to leave the prison of the flesh and go to him, but is not permitted to do so. The bridegroom hides himself so that, when he is not found, he may be sought more ardently.

**“And I did not find him.”** (GREGORY.) Since neither an angel, nor a prophet, nor any teacher showed the Gentiles the light of divine knowledge in their uncertainties, I did not find him. When I discovered that he could not be found on the bed, I resolved in my mind to rise from the bed of carnal pleasures, gird myself for the labor of saving inquiry, and visit publicly and privately, by land and sea, the schools of all whom I heard called wise.

The **streets** are spiritual men who, while proceeding toward heavenly things, keep to the narrow way. The **broad avenues** are worldly people who pursue many pleasures and walk along a broad road.

Thus she goes around them all, because in her mind she observes and imitates all the saints, both those who are and those who have been. Sometimes she also finds among worldly people something useful for the search for the bridegroom.

But after she has displayed the doubled labor of her search, she again adds the difficulty of finding:

**“I sought, and did not find.”**

Yet while she seeks and does not find, she herself is both sought and found. Hence it is said:

**“The watchmen found me.”**

**“I sought.”** After traveling through the world with immense labor and examining the words of the wise, I was unable to learn anything certain about the way of truth.

### VERSE 3

**“They found me.”** While I was searching in this way, the Lord saw the persistence of my search and at last deigned to reveal himself. He gave the seeker the ability to find him, having first inspired her to seek.

**“The one whom she loves?”** (GREGORY.) While they wish to teach, she, aflame with immense love, addresses them first: **“The one whom she loves?”**

The Church questions the watchmen when she receives preaching attentively and bears fruit in the performance of good works.

### VERSE 4

**“When I had passed by.”** (ID.) She passes beyond them because in them she sees the likeness of the one whom she seeks; yet she passes beyond them because she begins to imitate and contemplate God, who is beyond them.

Peter passes beyond the watchmen when he disregards the prophets and says to the Lord of the prophets: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matthew 16).

**“Until I bring him in,”** and so forth. Until the end of the world I will strive to recall the Synagogue, through which I received the hearing of faith, to faith in him and to the mystery of regeneration. At the end, the Church of the Gentiles will recall the Synagogue, which had first called her through the apostles.

### VERSE 5

**“I adjure you.”** Christ, hearing that he is to be brought in through these people, adjures them not to obstruct him.

**“I adjure you.”** This verse is repeated here in the song of love to show that the Lord cares no less for the Church gathered from the Gentiles than for the Church gathered from the Jews, but that he is equally concerned for the peace of both. For this queen from the South is captured by love of the bridegroom no less than the first beloved from the Jews.

**“And by the stags.”** It belongs to the stag, in old age, to eat a serpent and, because of the thirst produced by the poison, to hasten to a spring and grow young again by drinking from it, while its hair and antlers fall away. This applies to every believer through the washing of baptism.

### VERSE 6

**“Who is this?”** He now treats further of the Church converted from the Gentiles: how, after receiving the foundation through the apostles, it multiplied through the progress of times and the advancement of successive stages.

**“Who is this?”** The converted Jews, seeing also the Gentiles converted and received together into love of the bridegroom, ask whether salvation has been promised to the Gentiles. They do not ask out of envy, but as though in wonder and rejoicing with the fellowship of their brothers, since this had been greatly in doubt.

**“Who ascends.”** At the same time she sleeps, when she separates herself from carnal desires, and she approaches the vision of her Creator through good works.

**“Through the desert.”** That is, through the midst of the Gentiles, who were fruitful in no harvest of virtues and whom no prophet or angel had instructed in the worship of God.

Or: **“Through the desert like a column of smoke,”** because, separated from the allurements of the world, she is devoted to heavenly commands.

At the same time smoke partly rises and partly disappears into higher places after it has first arisen. So the Church is continually generated anew in some of her members, while in others, who were born earlier, she is continually gathered toward heavenly things.

Smoke, born from fire and ascending to the heights, gradually withdraws from human sight. So the Church, kindled by the fire of the Holy Spirit alone for love of God, never ceases to ascend until, drawn away from earthly things, she is carried off to the invisible things of heaven.

**“From spices.”** Note that, when he mentions spices, he first places myrrh, then frankincense, and afterward every kind of powdered perfume. For first it is necessary to mortify the desire of the flesh; afterward to offer to God vows of the heart that are pleasing to him; and thus, with humility, to grow in every kind of virtue.

**“Perfumes.”** When ground into powder, they are useful for making a compound. In the same way, virtues bring one to perfection when they do not exalt the mind but are, as it were, reduced to powder through the agent’s low estimation of himself.

The **perfumer** is either a person who devotes himself to virtues or God, who bestows virtues.

### VERSE 7

**“Behold the bed.”** To the first beloved, who expresses wonder, the Gentile Church replies, explaining where she ascends—namely, to the bed—and by what means she ascends—namely, because the middle of the litter has been spread with charity. She proves that she has entered into the same love of the bridegroom as the earlier Church, because she likewise possesses nuptial adornment and has preachers whom God would not have sent to us unless he had chosen them beforehand.

**“Behold the bed.”** The bed of the true peacemaker is eternal blessedness, in which the king rests with the saints. The Church reaches it partly each day through the desert, and at last she will reach it perfectly.

Or, God’s bed is also the peaceful manner of life of the saints in the present. The strongest men surround both beds: preachers defend both present repose and the peace of the Church against attacks, while the more perfect contemplate the inner repose of the heavenly homeland with fixed intention.

**“Israel.”** That is, “the man who sees God.” All who strive toward the joys of the divine vision are rightly called by this name. Among them are the strongest: those who are exalted either by the gift of heavenly contemplation or by undertaking the ministry of preaching.

### VERSE 8

**“All holding swords.”** They continually have the word of God ready, both for cutting away what is superfluous in themselves and in their subjects, and for repelling and trampling down enemies.

**“All holding swords.”** They hold the word of God and know how to use it, conquering vices both in others and in themselves.

**“Most skilled in war.”** Because they have fought against the devil for so many thousands of years in the weakness of the flesh, they have been instructed through constant practice.

**“Because of the terrors.”** They fear that the tempter’s snares may find them unguarded and unarmed and strike them down; and they fear that, once they have been defeated, the bed they were supposed to guard may be defiled—that is, that the Church’s present peace may be violated and future blessedness lost.

### VERSE 9

**“The litter.”** It is not shown merely by the fact that I now rest in the bed of Solomon, hasten toward the future bed, and have the strongest guardians that salvation has been promised to the Gentiles. It is also shown by the fact that he made us into a kind of litter—that is, a vehicle for carrying the ministers of his word from place to place, or a vehicle in which he himself might be carried throughout the world.

Or it may be understood in this way: the peacemaker, toward whose bed I hasten, fortified me in this manner, and he did so through the litter—that is, through the apostles, by whom he is carried, as on a throne, and whom he sent for my salvation, or for ours.

### VERSE 10

**“A golden backrest.”** That is, he makes his observers full of divine wisdom; or he makes a backrest in the litter when he promises the faithful hope of perpetual repose. It is golden because he prepares the repose of his vision, flashing with glory.

**“A purple ascent.”** The ascents are those by which someone can first climb to the virtues and afterward to the holy of holies. They are purple, that is, ready for martyrdom.

Or the virtues themselves are the ascents, and they are true purple, by which faithful souls are adorned.

Or Christ himself is the ascent, through whom one enters both the Church and heaven. He is purple because he washed us in his blood, and no one enters the Church unless imbued with the sacraments of the Lord’s passion.

**“He spread it with charity.”** Or, with the charity by which he suffered for us. “In the middle” means that he prepared the hearts of the Church like a bed, where faithful souls might rest softly, because he filled her interiorly with love of heavenly things. Hence he adds:

**“For the daughters of Jerusalem.”** For souls burning with desire for heavenly things: the more he loved us, the more he kindled us to suffer for him.

**“In the middle.”** (GREGORY.) Behold the consolation. Whoever cannot shed his blood for the Lord should love his neighbor for the sake of the daughters of Jerusalem. They should not be called sons—that is, strong men—but daughters, who through charity are not estranged from the building of God.

### VERSE 11

**“Go forth and see,”** and so forth. After recounting the king’s gifts, he now begins, in beautiful order, to praise his very appearance and adornment and invites us to see him.

We must attend to the order and development of this Church. Established from the first fruits of the Jews, she admonishes that earlier Church, already grown lukewarm after the apostles and possessing rulers, judges, and other ranks, to repay as a mother the successors and fellow citizens of those by whom she was preached.

**“In his diadem.”** As though hidden in his humanity, by which he conquered the devil. The flesh was the cause of this victory: unless God had been veiled by flesh, the devil would not have attacked him.

**“In the diadem,”** that is, in the crown of thorns with which his own Judea crowned him.

**“With which his mother crowned him.”** By what humanity did his mother honor him? By being a virgin, not defiled, like other women, by the stain of original sin. He sends us back to the historical account, as though saying: Believe the birth, passion, and resurrection.

This description is extended in accordance with the multiplicity of the Church.

**“Of his betrothal.”** If “his” refers to the mother, we understand it as the time of the Annunciation; if it refers to the faithful, we understand it as the resurrection, which was the chief joy, because then the human race was set free.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSE 1

**“How beautiful you are.”** When the bride converted from the Gentiles has already attained such perfection that she preaches to the Jews in turn and praises the bridegroom, she also receives from the bridegroom a worthy recompense of praise.

This description is extended in accordance with the multiplicity of the Church.

She is beautiful in action, because she ascends through the desert like a column of smoke; beautiful in preaching, because she draws her neighbors into her fellowship.

**“Your eyes.”** That is, your faculties, through contemplation of spiritual things, are excellent and worthy of reverence.

He intends to praise her by parts. **“Without…”** The glory of an open work is great, but the eternal recompense, which cannot be seen, is incomparably greater.

**“Your hair.”** To make everything easier to understand, let us briefly go through each item. The hair signifies the voluntary poor; the cheeks, the highest prelates; the teeth of the cheeks, other, lower prelates; the lips, preachers.

**“Your hair.”** If the sharpness of spiritual faculties is signified by the eyes, the plurality of thoughts may be signified by the hair, all of which tend toward the one end of heavenly goodness. Hence they are compared with does, which are clean animals and seek the rugged heights of the rocks for pasture.

**“Which have ascended.”** He mentions one characteristic of the doe’s nature, so that the others may be understood from it, and he praises that virtue which he sees his hearers need most.

**“Which have ascended.”** This refers to the one who is a testimony for those who imitate him, as he himself promised: “Whoever confesses me before men…” (Luke 12).

### VERSE 2

**“Your teeth are like flocks of shorn sheep.”** Just as the more fragile peoples of the Church, who provide numerical abundance, are signified by the hair, so the stronger ones, suited to governing the Church and prevailing in firmness, are signified by the teeth.

**“All of them coming up from the washing.”** It belongs to everyone to be purified through baptism; it belongs to the perfect, and especially to those entrusted with care of the sheep, to renounce everything they possess.

**“Bearing twin lambs.”** That is, similar offspring, because they produce others like themselves.

Or, twin offspring means the works of the twofold charity, such as the faithful converted from both peoples.

Or, it means faith and work.

**“And none is barren among them.”** Nor are those counted among the barren who, after being washed, are immediately taken from this life. They possessed offspring of faith, which either they confessed for themselves or others confessed for them. They also possessed the intention of good works, which they would have practiced in fellowship among Christ’s sheep had they been permitted to remain. Hence it is said: “Being perfected in a short time, he fulfilled many years” (Wisdom 4).

### VERSE 3

**“Like a scarlet thread.”** Preachers are called a thread because through their preaching they restrain the wandering thoughts in human hearts, lest those thoughts dissipate and weigh down the eyes of the heart.

**“Scarlet.”** Because they do not cease to preach the price of the Lord’s blood, by which the Church was redeemed; or because holy preaching burns with the ardor of charity.

**“Your lips.”** The teeth grind; the lips open what has been ground.

**“Your speech is sweet.”** When they do what they say, they set their preaching before people like savory food.

**“Like a slice of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks.”** In the pomegranate’s outward scarlet color is the will to martyrdom; in the white seeds, visible when the rind is broken, is the brightness of the virtues, which increases when the flesh is struck. There is also brightness when, after suffering has been completed, they shine with miracles.

In the cheeks there is modesty; in the pomegranate, the passion of Christ. The Church therefore has redness in her cheeks when she confesses the mystery of the Lord’s passion in words, and she displays whiteness when, pressed by hardships, she proves the chastity of her pure heart and reveals through her deeds what grace the saving cross possesses.

**“Without that which is hidden within.”** Although the things that appear outwardly are great, she retains greater things within, which only the divine eyes see.

**“Hidden.”** Everyone in the Church can hear the confession of the life-giving cross and see the Church’s sufferings. Unbelievers as well as believers can even observe the miracles divinely bestowed upon the Church herself. But the soul alone knows how great is the love by which it is held to invisible life and how fiercely it burns with love for God and neighbor.

### Verse 4

**Like the tower of David.** The tower is the unconquerable steadfastness of preachers, which, for defending the structures of the faith and repelling the weapons of enemies, was built with battlements by the strong hand of God and the desired King—that is, with knowledge of the divine Scriptures, when he opens their meaning so that they may understand the Scriptures, and confirm their preaching by the sayings of those who came before them. The battlements also signify the gifts of miracles by which preaching is supported. For when bodily illnesses have been healed, the salvation of the soul is more readily attained.

**Your neck.** We extend the neck when we look farther ahead. Thus preachers are called “the neck” because they survey enemies from afar; and “the tower” because of their strength and because of their lofty contemplation of heavenly joys. Or they are called the neck because they send food down into the body, or because they join the body to the head. Hence the Lord gives the loaves, while the disciples set them before the crowds. [Col. 1147D] Preachers are called eyes for one reason, teeth for another, cheeks for another, and neck for another.

The battlements are the unbreakable judgments found in the divine Scriptures; those who defend themselves from attackers at a distance are safe within them.

**A thousand shields.** The shield is the most steadfast reasoning by which they, relying upon it, go forth willingly against heretics and fortify themselves while striking them.

**All the armor.** That is, every provision, whether of action or of heavenly doctrine, by which the saints not only escape but also overcome the battle-lines of the wicked—while they draw some back from error or vices. All these things depend upon those set over the Church, because from them we receive the example of resistance and of victory.

[Col. 1148A] ### Verse 5

**The two breasts.** The same mysteries of the Church are repeated under many figures; yet the repetitions always contribute something new, and by that very novelty they delight the minds of the hearers more greatly. The two breasts, then, are the preachers from the two peoples, who are called eyes because they advance hidden things.

They are called teeth because they correct the wicked and bring them into the body of the Church; neck because, by preaching eternal joys and the life-giving breath, they provide nourishment and the food of doctrine. They are called breasts because they pour milk into the little ones in Christ, who are “young gazelles”: they discern sharply what must be done and, with the swift course of their activity, fly away from the valley of tears.

They are twins because they preach the same faith and the same sacraments. So that the milk they distribute may not fail in them, they feed upon the flowers of the Scriptures and the examples of the saints, constantly recalling them. [Col. 1148B]

**Two young gazelles.** The two peoples, who through humility understand themselves to be little and sinful, but who, running in charity, pass over all the obstacles of the world and ascend to the heights by leaps of contemplation.

**Which feed.** For they find refreshment in those who flourish in virtues and shine, while they are not yet able to see from near at hand the very God whom they desire.

### Verse 6

**Until that day breathes forth.** After the time for either teaching or learning has passed, when all the darknesses of this world have been brought to completion, all will shine like the sun.

**I will go to the mountain.** And because the Church is such in each of its parts, “I will go” means, “I will add grace,” both to the lower and to the greater.

**I will go.** Because I shall gather new peoples every day. And because the speech is addressed to the Church from the Gentiles, it may not inappropriately be understood as a promise of the future calling of the Synagogue, which will occur at the end of the world—or of the calling of any peoples whatsoever. Therefore, immediately afterward, concerning the most expansive beauty of the one and the same Church, which is to be gathered throughout the whole world from Jews and from whatever peoples, it is added:

### Verse 7

**You are altogether beautiful.** Not only in the more distinguished members whom I have enumerated, but also in those who appear small and fragile.

### Verse 8

**Come from Lebanon.** *(GREGORY.)* Since I am going to you, you ought to come to me—in thought, word, and deed. Or: the first step is in the flesh, through good works; the second is in the liberation from the flesh, to receive blessedness in the soul; the third is when the body has been received, when at the resurrection they receive the twofold robes.

Come by faith; come by works; come by bringing others; or come three times because of faith in the Trinity.

Lebanon, a mountain of Phoenicia, is interpreted in Hebrew as “whitening,” and in Greek as “incense.” Hence above: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense.” When preachers convert such people to salvation, a crown grows from the princes defeated by their struggle.

**Come.** As if he were saying: “Do not be afraid; do not come alone, for I shall add many to you.”

**From the summit of Amana.** Amana is a mountain of Cilicia; Sanir and Hermon are mountains of Judea. Lions dwell in them, by which demons are signified, for they rage against us. Since those whose hearts had been lairs of lions are converted, while the Lord is believed through their confession in turn, they are crowned as if from the lions’ lairs—from which the lion is driven out. [Col. 1149A]

By Amana we understand those whom the devil himself deceives and crushes—and through whom he deceives and crushes others—by the vigilance of great zeal. By Sanir, those toward whom such deception flies through ignorance. By Hermon, those who, as though by nature, are inclined toward wickedness—not that the devil is designated by them. By the lions’ lair, those over whom, and through whom, persecuting savagery rules over others. By the leopards, heretics, whose varied deceits he uses to mislead, and from whose individual leaders God grants his own the crown of victory.

**From the lions’ lairs.** Lions signify pride or violence; leopards, cruelty or the variety of wicked arts. By the name of mountains, the proud hearts of unbelievers are designated.

[Col. 1149B] ### Verse 9

**You have wounded my heart.** Therefore you must come and labor for the acquisition of others, because I love you. Or: therefore I shall give you a crown from those people, because you have prepared within yourself a place of love for me. All your beauty pleases me, but the catholic unity pleases me most, which I see both in those set over the Church and in their subjects.

### Verse 10

**How beautiful, and so forth.** Above, the bride praised the breasts in her beloved; here the beloved commends the breasts. This signifies the unity of Christ and the Church, because they are two, as the Apostle says, “in one flesh.” Therefore each praises the other with similar praise.

It is Christ’s doctrine, because it has been given to the Church and because the Church ministers it. And rightly do I love you, because your doctrine, which is contained in the breasts mentioned above, is beautiful for the consolation of the weak and the support of the little ones.

**The breasts.** The love of God and of neighbor, by which the holy mind nourishes its perceptions while it is joined to God by charity and gives to its neighbors whatever it can.

How greatly the bridegroom loves these breasts he makes clear by repeating his praise, saying: “Your breasts are more beautiful,” and so forth.

**Odor.** That is, the exceedingly sweet reputation of the faith spread throughout the whole world, broader than the law of the fathers, which was confined to Judea alone.

**Beyond all spices.** That is, beyond all the good works performed by the wicked. Although these sometimes please human beings, they never please God, because they do not proceed from charity. Or, beyond the institutions of the Old Testament, which were figures of these things.

### Verse 11

**Dripping honeycomb.** Above, the teachers were signified by the lips; here, the voice of the teachers is signified by the lips themselves. Hence they are aptly compared with honey.

The honeycomb is honey in wax. [Col. 1149D] The honey in the wax is the spiritual meaning of the divine utterances, dripping through the letter, because almost every sentence contains many meanings.

Or otherwise: in the honeycomb the honey is hidden, while the wax is visible. Therefore the lips are called a honeycomb, because while great wisdom is held within the frailty of the flesh, honey is, as it were, hidden in wax.

**Honey and milk beneath your tongue.** *(GREGORY.)* The spiritual sweetness in the words is as great as the bodily sweetness in honey and milk; and it is “beneath the tongue,” that is, not apparent to everyone but only to the good.

Whoever rebukes a sinner harshly and mingles some sweetness with the harshness has honey, not on the tongue but beneath the tongue.

**The odor of your garments.** That is, the reputation of good works with which they are clothed, lest they be found naked, and by which the disgrace of their former sins is covered. It is like incense, because in all his works he prays: when he acts well, he does so with the intention of reaching God. Hence: “Pray without ceasing” (1 Thessalonians 5).

Above, under the name of ointments, the infusion of the Holy Spirit is shown, by which the hearts of the faithful are illumined and prepared for spiritual combat. Under the name of garments, the deeds of the righteous, which are outward, are signified.

Thus, by a beautiful distinction, the works performed by human beings are compared with incense; but the gifts that come from divine generosity exceed the measure of comparison. After the Lord had individually praised each member of the Church, he fittingly commends also the ointments with which the whole Church was anointed. For there are no members, great or small, that have not been consecrated by the infusion of this spiritual anointing.

He also praised the garments, that is, works of righteousness, because here too the whole body is adorned. No one in her deserves life unless clothed in righteous works, whether he himself performed them or, if he was an infant, others performed them for him and in him.

### Verse 12

**A garden.** He had compared her to a woman because of her perfection, her beauty, the arrangement of her individual degrees, and the harmonious composition of her fitting unity. But because it seems too little to a lover to liken the individual parts of the bride to individual precious things, he compares the whole of her at once with many and very great things.

He therefore compares her with a garden because of the abundant fruits of works. In it four things occur. First, there is the fountain of baptism, without which no fruit follows. Then there are the ointments, that is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit, which are the first nourishment, so that the trees may also grow and bear fruit—namely, the intentions formed in the hearts of those who are still inexperienced and tender, when through the Holy Spirit they resolve that they will renounce the world and endure adversities, and similar things.

Afterward there are the trees: those same people, or others, now growing and flowering. Finally there are ripe fruits, by whose perfection of works Christ is already refreshed.

But here he does not arrange them according to the order in which one follows another. Rather, he begins with the more worthy, so that his commendation of this bride may be more attractive to that other bride whom he intends to commend through her.

He sets forth two gardens, in which the two conditions of contemplative and active people are signified. Each is enclosed, because it cannot be gathered up by the adversary or deprived of its fruit. Many live among the faithful in whom the enemy has a place; but these are not to be counted in the fruitful garden. They must be cast out like chaff.

**A sealed fountain.** Because the Church, designated by the name of a fountain, was at first small in Judea and afterward spread throughout the world, what follows is rightly added:

**Your streams.** For that small Church from the Jews, assisted by the fountain, sent forth paradise from itself. The Church is a fountain because it overflows with saving doctrine, by which it waters those nearby. It is sealed because its spiritual meaning is hidden from the unworthy and is not disturbed by any invasion.

### Verse 13

**Your streams.** That is, the fruits of the garden—the works that emerge after the planting and watering of baptism—are pomegranates for me, that is, a mature refreshment, delighting me as much as paradise.

**Cyprus.** That is, upright and growing upward, slender and attenuated in their humanity, with whose works, joined to charity, the prince is anointed.

Cyprus expresses divine grace; nard, the Lord’s passion; saffron, charity.

Cyprus is an aromatic tree in Egypt, with a white and fragrant seed. It is cooked in oil and pressed, and from it royal ointment—called cyprus—is prepared. Thus, in the darknesses of this world, the blessing of divine grace is received in the richness of charity and tested by the flames of temptations. Joined to it is nard, a humble herb—that is, faith in the Lord’s passion and imitation of it.

Cyprus is therefore joined to nard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer with Christ. Again, nard is joined to saffron when in the charity of Christ we willingly accept death.

Nard is fragrant and hot, and signifies charity. Saffron is golden in color and signifies those imbued with divine wisdom.

### Verse 14

**Cane and cinnamon.** Cane, also called cassia, is an aromatic but small tree. It has a strong, purple bark and is useful for curing disorders of the viscera. Because of its shortness, some count it among fragrant herbs. It signifies those who are humble in spirit, who remember the Lord’s passion and are prepared to suffer for the Lord.

Cinnamon is a short but fragrant and sweet tree, ash-colored, and twice as effective as cane for medicinal use. It signifies those who regard themselves as weak, whose humility is sweet and praiseworthy before God.

And rightly is cinnamon, which is ash-colored, placed after the purple cane, because through remembrance of the Lord’s passion contempt for our own virtue arises in us.

Cane and cinnamon grow in the garden together with the trees of Lebanon, because in the Church the humble and patient await the palm of reward together with those who strengthen the Church by preaching or by performing virtues.

**With all the trees.** Just as cane and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the saints, so the trees of Lebanon, which are tall and strong, demonstrate the lofty actions and prayers of the saints.

Myrrh makes the body incorruptible and signifies those who, through bitterness and patience, make their body secure against carnal impulses and every hostile force. Aloe does not have as much power as myrrh, but it nevertheless acts against putrefaction.

**The first.** That is, together with the more excellent charismatic gifts of the virtues.

And beautiful is the joining of herbs and trees with ointments: while we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the Spirit. In the Lord’s enclosed garden these things grow among the others.

### Verse 15

**A fountain of gardens.** From the primitive Church there proceeded into the world a heavenly doctrine that would produce many churches, namely, gardens. Of this fountain it is rightly added:

**A well of living waters.** The same doctrine is both a fountain of gardens, because it produces spiritual fruits in those whom it instructs, and a well, because of the hidden mysteries disclosed through the revelation of the Holy Spirit to the saints alone.

**Of living waters.** Because of the divine utterances that proceed from the invisible treasures of divine grace and lead to eternal life. [Col. 1152A]

**From Lebanon.** That is, from the Church itself, which is white through the purity of faith and lofty through the grace of virtues.

### Verse 16

**Arise.** Since the garden is such, arise—that is, depart or attack.

**Arise.** Once the garden had been planted and watered, it remained that, after everything had been firmly and orderly arranged, access should by no means be denied to its adversaries for testing it. Rather, it was shown that the more it was scourged, the more the inner sweetness of its waves would be revealed.

By the north understand the adversities of the world; by the south, its flatteries, because the Church is tested by a twofold assault.

**Arise** expresses permission, not command.

**Blow through it.** One by harassing it, the other by refreshing it. “Blow through it” means: bring tribulation, or persecute it, so that the Church, struck and tested in both ways, may spread everywhere the wonderful fragrance of its steadfastness and greater virtue, and at the end of the world satisfy those who are there with the indescribable fragrance of its sweetness.

## Chapter 5

### Verse 1

**Let my beloved come.** He who promised to be with me until the consummation of the age: now, when I need greater grace, let him visit me with greater grace.

**Let my beloved come.** The Church, hearing that it must be tested by temptations, does not resist the beloved’s providence. Rather, lest she be overcome, she seeks the help of the one who does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Corinthians 10).

Or this may be understood as spoken by the perfect:

**Let my beloved come.** As if she were saying: “Just as we always love him and take care to serve him, so may he not allow us to be shaken by temptations to the point of collapse, but now repay us for our devout dedication.”

**Come into the garden.** The bridegroom, responding to the Church’s desire, testifies that he has already done what was being requested. Hence outsiders too may be greatly kindled to love him.

Come by correcting those who err, lifting up the weak, strengthening those who do good, and placing the mature with me in rest.

**I have gathered.** With a certain sickle of death I have cut them away from this life and brought them into the storehouses of blessedness.

**I have eaten the honeycomb.** By the honeycomb are meant those who seek the sweetness of spiritual understanding in the Scriptures and make it clear to others. By honey, those who willingly taste the banquets of the divine word set before them and desire to feed upon them without satiety. By wine, the strong preachers of heavenly things. By milk, hearers who are still weak. Although they differ in various modes of study, they are nevertheless united by one hope of heavenly reward, and the heavenly judge approves them.

**Eat, friends.** He is delighted not only by the pious acts of the elect; he also urges the faithful to rejoice together at such a banquet, so that they may show one another a greater care of mutual love and strive to imitate attentively in their lesser state what they have seen in the greater.

**Drink deeply, beloved.** *(GREGORY.)* After drinking the joy, recall the very virtues of the good, dispel the mind’s sluggishness, and, kindled toward the love of eternal things, do not feel temporal punishments—like a drunken person who forgets all temporal matters.

He has eaten but is not satisfied: this is the one who has learned the banquets of the Scriptures and knows the examples of the righteous, yet has not reformed his life. He has drunk but is not intoxicated: this is the one who joyfully hears the commandments of life but remains sluggish in fulfilling them.

### Verse 2

**I sleep.** The Church of the Gentiles, commended in many ways, is instructed not to abandon preaching through complacency and devote herself solely to contemplation, but to undertake the strengthening of others.

Here he treats of that succession of the Church which exists in the present age—from the time when the fullness of the Gentiles had entered until the end of the world, when the Jews will enter. Here she does not seem to be sent to unbelievers of every kind, but rather to exhort those in the Church who are lukewarm. Thus the Church herself says:

**I sleep. Open to me, my sister, and so forth.** Arise from the leisure and repose of contemplation, and open your hearts, so that, when the obstacles of vices have been removed, they may clearly admit the light of truth. [Col. 1153B]

**From my blood, my sister; through my coming, my neighbor; from my spirit, my dove; through my speech, which you learned more fully in repose, my perfect one.**

**My head.** That is, my faith and my love. In their hearts, blinded by love of earthly things, the love of me has grown cold and has almost entirely failed.

**My locks.** That is, the love of neighbor, which is like my hair attached to the head. They are full of the drops of night: that is, they suffer the severe cold of the persecution of the dark ones—those who are unbelieving toward me and persecute their neighbors. To correct these people, you ought to insert and interpose the sweetness of contemplation.

### Verse 3

**I have stripped myself.** The Church, not disobedient to the duty imposed upon her but fearful in undertaking responsibility for the brethren lest she fall into sins, without which this life cannot be lived, replies:
