**I have stripped myself.** How can it happen that, leaving the summit of contemplation, I should again be stained by the filth of the world? For once the care of temporal necessities has been undertaken, even an outstanding teacher scarcely avoids sin.

*(GREGORY.)* Whoever girds himself for the care of governing souls must also watch over providing them with the necessities of temporal support, for those to whom he preaches eternal things.

### Verse 4

**My beloved.** Since the Church fears falling, because the Lord wishes our love for him to be recognized through the greatest love of our neighbors, it is fittingly added:

**My beloved.** As if she were saying: “I certainly fear the world’s way of life, but I understand that charity covers a multitude of sins; and I trust in the help of my beloved, by whom their hearts have already been pierced.” [Col. 1153D]

**His hand.** Producing compunction; or, he brought back to our memory the work that he performed in us, because, needing nothing, he chose to leave the Father’s bosom and live among us on earth for our sake.

He sends his hand when, by his power, he strikes the mind through subtle understanding.

**And his belly.** By the belly may be understood the softness and frailty of those who undertake the office of preaching, because they recognize themselves as less capable and are afraid.

**The belly.** That is, the soft and fluid part among us. Or, by the name of the belly the heart is signified, in which thoughts are digested just as food is digested in the belly.

The heart trembles if it refuses to do for its neighbors what God did for his enemies. And the belly quakes because the weakness that rejoices in heavenly understanding is disturbed in its exultation and fears losing what it does not know how to retain.

### Verse 5

**I arose to open.** I arose from sleep to labor, because whoever intends to preach the truth must first rise to do what he preaches, lest, while preaching to others, he himself become disqualified. The words that follow suit him:

**My hands dripped, and so forth.**

**My fingers are full of myrrh.** The fingers signify discernment, so that one’s works may be displayed solely with an eye to heavenly reward, not for human advantage. For just as the fingers are distinct in the hand, so discernment must be applied in works; otherwise they are of no avail.

### Verse 6

**The bolt of the door.** The cause of sin—that is, unbelief, or any other cause. For just as the bolt is to the door, so the cause holds sin fast; when it is removed, sin is removed, and when sin is taken away, the way is open to Christ.

He had said that the beloved, having put his hand through the opening, touched her and shook her with trembling. Set intensely aflame by his touch, she now desires not to be touched by his hand through the narrowness of the opening, but, with the door of her heart opened, to enjoy his most blessed embrace—that is, to be filled more fully with the sweetness of divine illumination which she had felt briefly.

But because no elect person is granted in this life the perfect vision of eternal things, which is reserved for the life to come, it is rightly added:

**But he had turned aside. My soul, and so forth.**

Behold now the third stage. The first Church was converted from the Jews; through it, and after it, came this Gentile Church of which we have so far spoken. This Gentile Church, as we said, established the third Church, which is now described and which will last, through the succession of those set over it and of its subjects, until the final entry of the remnant of Israel.

He did indeed pass by, but he spoke to me, leaving me his commandments so that I might await him patiently. And after he had spoken, my soul melted.

**I sought him and did not find him; I called, and so forth.** This is the voice of the same Church, which opened according to those whom she opened; she had previously been the belly or the voice of those people.

### Verse 7

**They took away my mantle.** *(GREGORY.)* Preachers take away the mantle when they remove from the soul whatever remnant of worldly pomp there may be, or uncover whatever sin has been present through ignorance.

### Verse 8

**I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find him, and so forth.** Young women who have already advanced to some knowledge devoutly come to the servants of God, whom they believe to live an angelic life on earth, and beseech them to commend them to the Lord at the time of their prayer.

Or, “daughters of Jerusalem” means the heavenly spirits who already reign with God. Alternatively, by the daughters of Jerusalem we may also understand those who are lower in the Church, whom their superiors likewise urge to seek together with them. For what is sought by many is sometimes found more quickly, and so the care of loving charity may be shown everywhere.

### Verse 9

**What is your beloved like?** Recalling the depths of her conscience, the bride is terrified and, accusing her own sluggishness, hastens toward labor in humility, saying:

“I beg you: since you have adjured us by the fervor of the divine charity that you possess, make me burn as well, and confirm me in his love by a saving exhortation.”

As she sings fitting praises of his virtues and power in appropriate commendation, she is again asked in whose minds his traces usually appear.

### Verse 10

**My beloved is white and ruddy.** A fitting response from the bride to those who were seeking.

**My beloved.** First he came into the world pure and holy; afterward, reddened by his passion, he departed from the world.

By “white,” understand the love of divinity; by “ruddy,” the flesh that suffered, so that he may signify God and man, and be elect in both.

**Chosen from thousands.** Because the one Mediator is accepted from the whole number of angels and human beings. Hence it is said: “This is my beloved Son,” and so forth (Matthew 3). For no other was found, either in heaven or on earth, who could take the book (Revelation 5).

### Verse 11

**His head is the finest gold.** Another translation has: “His locks are fir trees.” Fir is called ἐλάτη (*elate*) in Greek. Hence *elate* here appears to be not Latin but Greek.

Or the head means divinity, because “the head of Christ is God” (1 Corinthians 11:3).

**His locks.** That is, his holy and upright thoughts, yet thoughts despised by fools.

**Black like a raven.** Despised by the world, like that noisy and wicked bird. Or “like a raven,” because they entrust the mysteries of the Church to no one until they see that person likened to themselves or to their mother; or because, although they are beautiful, they understand that by nature they were once black.

### Verse 12

**His eyes are like doves.** *(GREGORY.)* Doves customarily sit beside streams of water so that they may see in the water the shadow of flying birds and thus avoid their claws. So the saints discern the deceits of demons in the Scriptures; from the deception they observe, they recognize and flee the enemy as though from a shadow.

These waters are called very full because, whatever counsel is sought in Scripture, it is found there completely.

The streams may be understood as the instruction of the old law, and the full waters as evangelical perfection, because preachers bring forth both new and old things.

**His eyes.** That is, the gifts of the Holy Spirit which he himself gives. They do not allow his lovers to wallow in mud like pigs, but make them clear and transparent in the likeness of waters, possessing nothing dark.

Hence they are compared with streams and pure waters, not with turbid pools, because they see God and are filled with the light of divine gifts.

Since these gifts are given by grace alone, it is added:

**Washed with milk.** Just as a mother supplies milk to her children solely through natural love, so God gives the gifts of the charisms to his children solely by grace.

**Sitting beside very full waters.** For the more clearly they see from God, the more they strive to know higher things.

### Verse 13

**His cheeks.** That is, the modesty and piety of the Savior, which shone uniquely in him.

**Like beds of flowers.** Just as beds are arranged by people awaiting the sweetness of fragrance and the grace of appearance, so the Mediator, appearing in the flesh, delighted those present and attracted those absent through the modesty and sweetness of his teaching.

**Planted by perfumers.** That is, by the apostles and prophets, who with harmonious voice described in the sacred pages not only his words but also his conduct. In the mystery of his future incarnation, he wept over Lazarus out of modesty; he was silent like a lamb, and so forth.

**His lips are lilies dripping with myrrh.** The words of his teaching are lilies that promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom, burdensome to those who suffer. They are first myrrh because they preach contempt for pleasures.

### Verse 14

**His hands.** That is, Christ’s works. Whatever he taught by word, he fulfilled in action, so that, while people marveled at his teaching, he might confirm it by his works.

**Fashioned on a lathe.** Because he readily does whatever he wills, just as lathe-work is readier than other crafts; and because he holds within himself the whole rule of righteousness. Hence it is said: “It is fitting for me to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3).

**Golden, filled with hyacinths.** The virtues he practiced as a human being he perfected through the grace of divinity, and these virtues arouse us to hope and to love of heavenly things. For hyacinth is sky-colored.

**His belly is ivory.** That is, the frailty of his humanity. It is ivory because of the beauty of chastity, since it was free from every sin.

**Variegated.** That is, neither wholly ivory nor wholly sapphire. Sapphire signifies the sublimity of heavenly things. It is therefore variegated because partly human frailty is understood through hunger, temptation, weariness, and death, while partly divine exaltation is understood through miracles, resurrection, and ascension. Sapphire has the appearance of a serene sky.

### Verse 15

**His legs are pillars.** That is, the paths of his passion and incarnation. They are called pillars because of their uprightness and firmness, since whatever was done through him had been ordained by God before the ages.

**Founded upon bases.** That is, upon the prophets, because he appeared as he had been foretold by them, who read within the divine ordering. Or the bases themselves are God’s arrangement, which ordained everything.

**His appearance is like Lebanon.** What I praise in detail through the individual members of the Redeemer, I shall comprehend briefly as a whole. As Lebanon is distinguished by height and breadth, so the Lord surpasses all who have arisen from the earth.

And as that mountain is rich in noble trees, so he raises up and preserves all the saints rooted in him. And as the cedar surpasses all the beauty of the forests in beauty, strength, height, and fragrance, so the beloved is “beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Psalm 44), because he did not receive by measure, and from his fullness we have all received (John 1).

### Verse 16

**His throat is most sweet, and so forth.** That is, the inward savor and sweetness of Christ’s words, which few taste; but those who taste them hunger for more.

Alternatively: just as life-giving breath proceeds through the throat to the lips so that one may speak, so the words he spoke proceeded through the Lord’s lips. In the throat, however, the hidden disposition of his goodness may be understood, by which it came about that he spoke outwardly to us.

**Altogether.** That is, God and man.

**Desirable.** Not only according to his divinity, but also according to his humanity, from the very beginning of his conception until the triumph of his passion, resurrection, and ascension.

**Such is my beloved.** As if he were saying: “If you love him and wish to be loved by him, you must understand him as such and cling to him with such affection.”

**Daughters of Jerusalem.** For the beauty of the poem, the persons speaking vary; but the same Church of Christ is indicated both by the name “bride” and by the name “daughters.” When she sighs for the heavenly homeland, she is called a daughter; when she cares to hear or speak of nothing except God, she is called a bride.

### Verse 17

**Where has your beloved gone?** Having heard the beloved’s qualities, about which the daughters of Jerusalem had asked, they add another question. For once so many praises have been enumerated, who could hear them without longing for him?

This must be sought within the unity of the holy Church: in whose heart, above all, and in what manner of life the Lord is accustomed to be found.

**Where has he gone?** Not by abandoning those in whom he was, but by joining others to them and inviting still others after them. Thus he is said to go away and withdraw in the manner of a candle which, once lit, lights many others all around it while suffering no loss itself.

**Where has your beloved gone?** *(GREGORY.)* We must know that God, who is everywhere, is in a place but is not local. “Local” is said of what is bounded according to the parts of a place—above and below, before and behind, right and left. Since angels and human souls cannot be bounded by place, still less can that incomprehensible substance be so bounded.

Moreover, the knowledge of God that can be had in the present life is only according to his works; for, while in the flesh, we can attentively consider the wondrous character of God’s works, which is higher.

**Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful among women?** Although God is present to all things in the common manner—by presence, power, and substance—he is said to be present in a familiar manner, that is, through grace, to those for whom his works appear more wondrous. Although they do not possess full knowledge of God, they nevertheless consider the wonder of God’s works more keenly.

## Chapter 6

### Verse 1

**My beloved.** He descended, watering with the fountain of baptism; coming from on high, he visited those placed in humility. So that we might ascend upward, the Lord descended to the mountain, while Moses ascended the mountain.

When he had said that he descended into the garden, he adds how that garden is constituted and with what fruit it is fertile, when he says, “to the bed of spices.”

The garden is the Church; the garden is any faithful soul. The bed is the faithful mind, which, taught by the discipline of right faith, is arranged, as it were, with equal sides on either hand, and, as though frequently turned over by a diligent cultivator, is cleansed of superfluous weeds.

He declares that he delights in the pious desires and fruitful works of the saints and gathers the perfect into eternal joys through the virtues of chastity.

He gathers lilies when he leads those who attain the whiteness of perfect merits out of the condition in which they previously were and brings them to the heavenly kingdoms.

### Verse 2

**I am my beloved’s.** He adds this verse to intensify the stimulus of the immense charity that burns within.

As if she were saying: “He descended into me; in me you can have the form of the one whom you seek.”

**I am my nephew’s, and my nephew is mine, who feeds among the lilies.**
[Col. 1158A] **VERSE 3.—“You are beautiful, my friend.”** Until now it has been the voice of the Church praising and seeking her Lord. Since he is not far from those who love him, what the one sought answers now follows: he declares that he was present while they spoke and heard what they were saying, and he repays their devotion with fitting praise.

**“Terrible as an army arranged for battle.”** Because, joined together by the unity of charity, she leaves no opening through the evil of discord for her enemies—that is, heretics or unclean spirits. The Roman armies were terrible because they oppressed the whole world, but they were not gracious, since they did not possess true peace. In the Church neither terror removes sweetness nor sweetness terror. She lives a heavenly life on earth and strives to draw the barbarous minds of different nations [Col. 1158B] to her own way of life. Yet because she has not yet been deemed worthy to behold the face of her beloved, which she seeks above all, she next hears:

**VERSE 4.—“Turn your eyes away from me.”** As if he said: “I have given you dove-like eyes, by which you might discern the paths of righteousness; yet during the time of your pilgrimage do not seek to know me perfectly. For ‘man shall not see me and live’ (Exod. 33). Do not seek on the way the reward reserved for you in your homeland.”

**“For they themselves have made me fly away.”** Do not cease desiring to know me, but do not presume upon the ability to know me. Hence it is said: “Of his greatness there is no end” (Ps. 144).

**“They have made me fly away.”** (RAB.) The more intensely you seek to know me, the more intensely you understand that I am incomprehensible; and it is not your fault if you do not know me, [Col. 1158C] but the weakness of human nature.

**“Your hair is like a flock of goats,”** etc. These verses were set forth and explained above. Yet let us not be reluctant to explain again what the author was not reluctant to repeat in writing, so that something new may be added. Lest the Church take heavily the fact that she is suspended from knowledge of her beloved, a description follows in which she is likened to that primitive Church of Jerusalem, of which there is no doubt that it was beloved of God.

**“All with twin offspring, and none among them is barren.”** With offspring like one another, because they produce others such as themselves. Or, twin offspring means the twofold work of charity; or the faithful converted from both peoples; or faith and works.

**VERSE 6.—“As the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks,”** etc. (GREG.) Although many perform wondrous deeds, prophesy future things, completely renounce the world, and burn with heavenly desires, they are compared to the sacred Church as the rind of a pomegranate. Yet all these things are nothing in comparison with the reality of which it is written: “What eye has not seen nor ear heard,” etc. (Isa. 64). Therefore he suitably adds: **“Apart from your hidden things,”** as if he said: “Great indeed are the things in you that are not hidden, but the things that are hidden are utterly ineffable.”

**VERSE 7.—“There are sixty queens and eighty concubines,”** etc. Queens and concubines alike approach the king’s throne and alike bear children, but not all possess the diadem of the kingdom. Queens are those who serve doctrine with regard to the heavenly kingdom; concubines are those who proclaim Christ out of love for temporal things.

Therefore there are sixty, because they possess perfection of works through the sole love of God’s commandments. This may be understood through the multiplication of twelve by five, or because they regulate the five bodily senses according to the rule of apostolic teaching. But when eighty is taken in an evil sense, it signifies the cares and entanglements of temporal things: for the course of the world revolves through four seasons, and the world itself is divided into four regions—east, west, north, and south—or is composed of four elements.

**VERSE 8.—“One is my dove, my perfect one.”** Although the persons are many and diverse, the faith in them is one, the baptism one, God one, and the work one. There is not one Church before the Law, another under the Law, and another under grace; rather, she is established in one peace and one fear.

Our mother is regenerating grace, which chose the simple and preserves and strengthens the elect. Or our mother is the heavenly Jerusalem, since every good gift descends from above (Jas. 1). That heavenly Jerusalem approves from human conduct only what desires to serve God in the unity of her faith and love.

**“The maidens saw her.”** This is great praise of Catholic unity: both the mother, grace that gave birth to her, chooses her forever, and the daughters whom she herself has begotten and nourished through the Spirit immediately saw her—that is, they learned her chastity of life.

**“They proclaimed her blessed.”** Either those who are truly participants in the kingdom, or even those who cling to her in name only and, although their hope is in earthly things, acknowledge that she is worthy of praise.

**VERSE 9.—“Who is this?”** The Church of the Gentiles, so firmly established and everywhere spread and extended through her multiplicity, advancing through her stages and successions to the final times—when the Synagogue, in those last times, now beholds her, the holy Church, having acted and acting so well, so widely spread, following one faith without schism and so many most wise teachers, and beholding moreover the miracles of the living and the dead and many other proofs of the Christian faith—now joined, repentant, and contrite, says in wonder: **“Who is this?”**

**“Rising like the dawn.”** The Church becomes dawn when she wholly casts off the darkness of mortality and ignorance. At the judgment she will still be dawn, but in the kingdom she will be day, where she will possess the full vision of the true sun.

**“Beautiful as the moon.”** In the night of the present life, where the condition of temporal things changes, she is compared to the moon: now bright to the world, now despised; now full of the whiteness of virtues, now dishonored by the vices of the wicked. In the future blessedness, where her condition will be unchanging, the righteous will shine like the sun.

**“Terrible as an army arranged for battle.”** Such people have leaders arranged for them who invalidate our faith with plausible arguments and strike us with terror. The more perfectly she orders virtues within herself, the more terrible the Church—or any faithful soul—is to the powers of the air.

**VERSE 10.—“I went down into the garden of nuts,”** etc. While Judea marvels at the struggles of the Church and inquires about them, the bridegroom himself bears witness to the Church. Or these may be understood as the words of the Church, which assents to the Synagogue praising her and immediately explains to her the reason for her military equipment, answering through the voice of her teachers, that is, the leaders of her spiritual warfare.

**VERSE 11.—“I did not know, my soul.”** While the bridegroom—or the Church herself—proclaims her evangelical labors to the Synagogue, which marvels at them, the latter, struck by salutary repentance, confesses that she wandered for a long time because of profane blindness.

**“It troubled me.”** Because of the evangelical preaching of the Church, which runs swiftly through the four parts of the world and rests upon the four wheels of faith. Hence it was written by four persons; yet those four horses, moved by the same spirit, draw one chariot to war.

**VERSE 12.—“Return.”** When the Synagogue confesses her slowness, the Church answers by consoling and exhorting her. She says “return” four times because the Jews, now scattered everywhere throughout the four parts of the world, are to be converted at the end.

Or: return in body, return in mind from error, so that you may turn away from evil. Again, return in body, return in mind, so that you may do good and not wish to remain troubled. It is not enough to return by intention unless the return is shown to the Church.

**“That we may look upon you.”** So that we may recognize the appearance of chastity and, as Christ’s love joins us to one another, so that both of us may build one house of faith upon him, the cornerstone.

## CHAPTER VII

**VERSE 1.—“What will you see in the Shulammite?”** While the Church admonishes the Synagogue, the Redeemer himself, assenting to her exhortations, promises that he will bring them to fulfillment. For Elijah and Enoch would not labor for the conversion of those people unless they possessed certainty of their conversion through the divine Scriptures and apostolic testimonies.

**“What will you see?”** As if he said: “You grieve over the unbelief of the Synagogue; but know that she will soon be converted, so that unbelief will no longer appear in her, but rather the works of spiritual struggles and virtues.”

**“How beautiful are the steps.”** In the preceding descriptions there is a descent from the higher members to the lower, and only the higher members are commended. Here the lower members too are commended, and the ascent proceeds from the lower to the higher, so that it may be shown that this Church, summoned at the end from those formerly rejected, will nevertheless have members not inferior to the higher ones. Her steps are mentioned because she will not remain idle but will advance to battle; her first beauty will be shown through combat.

**“How beautiful they are.”** First he praises in her steadfastness in works and the mortification of pleasures: **“How beautiful they are.”** In saying this, he turns to praise of the Church herself, joined together through sweetness, so that the Jews may be converted more easily and the Church may labor more earnestly for their conversion.

**“The joints of the thighs.”** Properly, after shod feet, the joints of the thighs are praised, because through the ministry of preachers the unanimous union of believing peoples is brought to perfection.

**“Necklaces.”** They are most pure, since these no longer disagree with those, but agree in all things and shine through the testimony of their works.

**“Which have been fashioned.”** This union has been arranged by the art of an inscrutable plan. For who knows why God blinded the Jews until that time?

**“Which have been fashioned by the hand.”** That is, established by the ineffable generosity of the Creator.

**“Your navel.”** Even those among the tender ones who beget children, although they cling lawfully to the world, nevertheless proclaim the good.

**VERSE 2.—“The navel.”** That is, the weakness of our mortality becomes a mixing bowl when, having experienced our weakness within ourselves, we labor so that others may recognize it through us, or when at times we give alms.

**“Turned,”** that is, round and perfect. For whoever, for this reason, gives drink to the thirsty or offers the cup of the divine word to the wandering, expecting earthly wisdom from God the rewarder, does not have a cup made on a lathe. The work of mercy that he performed was not done for the purpose of raising his weakness toward God, but he seeks an earthly reward.

**“Your belly.”** Our belly is a heap of wheat when, mindful of our weakness, we prepare for ourselves in the present life the fruits of good works by which we may continually be refreshed.

**“Your belly.”** Although this is a lower rank, its wheat-like nourishment will nevertheless be pleasing to God, because there are many in the lower place and few in the higher. Yet we do not mean “in the lower place” as “in sin.”

**“A heap.”** At the bottom it grows broader and at the top narrower. So too in our actions: the higher their merit, the fewer workers they find. There are more workers in the lower things. Many give alms from their possessions; few abandon their possessions.

The alms that we distribute to the poor may be understood as the heap of wheat. It is fitting that, after the cup, the bride’s members are compared to a heap of wheat, so that giving both drink and bread to the poor may be signified. This may equally be understood of bodily and spiritual nourishment. In the open teachings there is the cup; in the mysteries there is the bread.

**“Fenced about with lilies.”** When we perform all the good things we do with a view to seeing eternal brightness, we thereby block on every side the entrance to our heart against the enemy lying in wait.

**VERSE 3.—“Your two breasts.”** The teachers of the inexperienced do not proclaim their own teachings, but take from the words of both Testaments what was issued by one author, so that the one shepherd may fill one sheepfold from two flocks. They are compared to does because the animal is clean, distinguished by its sight and speed, and cloven-hoofed, which pertains to the discernment of good and evil; and it chews the cud, which signifies what must be done after discernment. They are twins because of their single concord.

**VERSE 4.—“Your neck.”** That is, those through whom the voice comes forth and food is conveyed into the body. They are towers because by the example of their lives they both fortify and adorn others. In ivory whiteness is signified.

**“Your eyes.”** They look into hidden things so that they may be able to speak openly. They continually pour forth the streams of doctrine to their hearers, like the pools of Heshbon, always abundant in water and supplying water copiously to the people at the entrance of the city.

They are rightly said to be waters at the city gate, because no one can enter the Church unless first sprinkled with the water of doctrine and baptism. Hence at the entrance of Solomon’s temple there was a bronze sea, where the priests washed their hands and feet before entering.

**“Pools.”** They contain many waters of wisdom and doctrine, for those who will be in the belt of mourning while Antichrist persecutes them. These pools are in that full entrance of both multitudes, which will be the daughter of the multitude.

**“Your nose.”** These are the most cautious discerners of good and evil, just as smell or stench is distinguished through the nostrils. No hypocrisy deceives them, and they hold the most eminent place.

**“Like the tower of Lebanon.”** A tower is placed on a mountain for watchfulness, so that approaching enemies may be seen from far away. Likewise, the preacher’s life must always remain firmly elevated, so that it may foresee from afar the attacks of the wicked and detect a fault before it arrives.

**“Facing Damascus.”** Damascus, the metropolis of Syria, brought many evils upon Israel and even led it into captivity. By it the entire multitude of demons, or of wicked people, is signified.

**VERSE 5.—“Your head.”** Your mind, because it governs the whole body of thoughts, is high like a mountain through its manner of life; and it is such a mountain as possesses knowledge of circumcision—not the removal of flesh, but of the heart’s superfluities.

Sea snails, circumcised with iron, emit tears of a purple color, from which, when collected, purple dye is prepared. The channels that receive the king’s purple are the inner hearts of the faithful. The wool that is dipped so as to become the king’s garment is humility in suffering. It is joined to the channels when, with steadfast heart, the virtue of humility and continual remembrance of the Lord’s blood are stirred to endurance.

They always hold in memory the purple of the true King—that is, his passion—and are prepared to imitate him, so that they may rise again with Christ.

**VERSE 7.—“Your stature.”** Because the Church tastes in advance the joys of the future life amid the struggle of the present life, it is added: **“She is compared to a palm tree.”** This is the uprightness of good action, which disdains to bend toward earthly things, raises its whole self toward heavenly things, and, placed in combat, reaches toward the prize for which, when the contest is finished, it will be crowned with the palm of victory.

Below it is rough, but above it is beautiful and bears fruit. So too the Church endures harsh labors on earth but hopes to receive her reward in heaven. The palm preserves its leaves; so the Church, while the condition of the world changes, retains the same mysteries of faith.

**“Your breasts.”** That is, the teachers, who temper their doctrine according to the capacity of their hearers, intoxicate each person with the abundance of the house of God (Ps. 35), and gladden their hearts.

**VERSE 8.—“I said, ‘I will climb.’”** As if he said: “That you have such teachers, preaching with such discernment, is not your merit but my gift, because I climbed the palm tree”—that is, I gave the Church an increase of virtues—“until she comes to perfection, and I will seize her fruits.” That is, I will so strengthen and multiply the virtues in them that they cannot fall in any way until they reach maturity.

Through this, your breasts will be like a cluster of henna (cyprus), because those who know little, if they proclaim it kindly, will sometimes be intoxicated with a more excellent wisdom.

**“I said.”** As if to say: “One must persist in the conversion of the Jews, because such a beautiful union is to follow, and because I suffered chiefly for them, since I had foreseen that they would be saved.”

**“Its fruits.”** The fruit of the Cross may be said to be the resurrection, the ascension, the coming of the Holy Spirit, and the salvation of the world. Through these things the teachers have been intoxicated and strengthened.

**“And the fragrance of the mouth.”** The fragrance is compared to apples, the throat to wine, because an apple receives praise from its freshness, while wine receives praise from its age. As wine surpasses an apple, so the present address of the Church surpasses the reputation that the speech of her hearers can spread about her.

The fragrance in the throat is the voice of present doctrine. In the fragrance, the reputation of one absent is signified. Therefore the former is compared to wine because of the fragrance of virtues, while the latter is compared to apples because of the sweetness of an absent reputation.

**VERSE 9.—“Worthy of my beloved.”** The word that the beloved placed in my mouth is of such sublimity that it ought not to have been proclaimed to the world by anyone other than the bridegroom himself, because no other was found who could open the book. Others received it from him. Christ, as it were, drank, because, with divinity teaching him, he quickly advanced to perfection of knowledge and willingly endured the passion; his members did not do so in the same way.

While the bridegroom praises the bride’s throat, she understands that the word through which salvation is given to the world is signified in the throat. Desiring to dispense the word out of great love, she snatches words from the bridegroom’s mouth. He compared her to the finest wine, and she added: **“Worthy of my beloved.”**

**“For chewing.”** It is not so readily taken for drinking as what he first offered to others in prayer; rather, it is to be meditated upon with labor and diligence.

**VERSE 10.—“I belong to my beloved.”** I refer the whole work of my service and devotion to him. In the present life he helps me, lest I fail through labor; and at the end he will receive me with himself into joys.

I was first an exile from God, but I was converted from every error to God, so as to become a citizen and member of his household. He too, previously angry with the human race, was converted toward me, having put on the nature of my mortality.

**VERSE 11.—“Come, my beloved.”** You who placed in heaven the humanity assumed for my sake, visit me through the presence of divine grace, so that I may be able to sow the seed of your word in the field of the world and establish the villages of our dwelling in one faith.

**“Come.”** The Church, seeing that she is not sufficient by herself either to perform good works or to go forth, nor to persist in goodness or discern how far her hearers have advanced, implores help.

In the field, Christians are signified; in the villages, pagans; in the vineyards, Churches; in the flowers, faith; in the fruits, virtues; and in the pomegranates, martyrdom. In each of these the bride seeks the presence of her beloved.

**VERSE 12.—“Let us rise early.”** Because the night of unbelief has passed and the light of faith appears, proceeding from Christ’s morning resurrection, let us labor from the morning of the resurrection—he by inspiring, and I by preaching.

**“Let us see.”** So that I, who am the teacher of the little ones, may discern those who have been acquired, how they are doing and how far they are progressing, and may understand how they are to be nourished.

One must not look merely to see whether the vineyards are flowering, but whether the flowers are growing strong enough to produce fruit. For it is not remarkable if someone begins good things; it is very remarkable if, with right intention, he perseveres in a good work.

**“There I will give you my breasts.”** That is, when we have come into your service to see the vineyards and whether the pomegranates are flowering, I will present the deeds and words of my preachers in the likeness of a diligent nurse.

**VERSE 13.—“The mandrakes.”** She rightly calls upon the bridegroom for help in preaching where the preachers burn with outstanding virtues.

**“The gates.”** The apostles and their successors.

**“The mandrakes.”** That is, their virtues, which are suitable as medicines: they bring rest against the anxieties of the world; they drive away nausea toward the word of God; they cause vices to be cut away from people without pain; and they bring forth apples—that is, Churches—sweetly fragrant in confessors and resembling pomegranates in martyrs.

**“They have given their fragrance.”** For through the examples of their elders, their juniors are strengthened.

**“I have kept them for you.”** Or, “I have kept them,” that is, I have understood that all the commandments and testimonies, or promises, of both Testaments were given by you. Or, “I have understood all the apples”—that is, the righteous of both Testaments—to have been justified through you alone, who were made incarnate.

## CHAPTER VIII

**VERSE 1.—“Who will give me?”** Judea is introduced as already inspired and instructed, investigating God with the greatest desire.

**“Outside.”** The beloved was within, when “in the beginning was the Word”; outside, when “the Word became flesh” (John 1).

**“May I kiss you,”** etc. That is, “May I see you face to face and speak mouth to mouth.”

**VERSE 2.—“There you will teach me.”** You will increase grace in me, and I, ungrateful neither for it nor for you, will increase my service.

**VERSE 3.—“The left hand.”** That is, the mystery of the Incarnation and the gifts he gives in the present life will be beneath my head, because, supported by them in the present against worldly disturbances, I rest and, in a certain sense, sleep with him.

And his right hand—that is, future goods, namely, the full vision of him—will embrace me. That is, it will surround me on every side, so that no storm of misery can intervene.

**VERSE 4.—“I adjure you.”** The bridegroom hears that final Church wishing to sleep in the present and eventually to rest. Seeing that many are begotten by the Church who disturb others, he admonishes them to desist from disturbances.

**“Until she herself wishes it.”** That is, until, when the duties of divine service have been completed, she consents—admonished by the needs of human weakness—to return to the common care.

**VERSE 5.—“Who is this?”** As Judea burns with such love for the recognized bridegroom, the Gentile, admiring and rejoicing, says: **“Who is this?”**

**“Under the tree.”** He who is our peace and who made both one answers those admiring from among the Gentiles. He reminds them to remember the grace by which she herself was rescued and to rejoice together in the salvation of others.

**“I awakened you.”** This was the effect of great kindness, because under that tree your mother was inwardly blinded, after she had said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27).

**VERSE 6.—“Set me as a seal.”** We set Christ as a seal upon the heart when we learn what he said as though they were truly the words of divine wisdom.

We customarily carry some sign tied to a finger or arm, so that we may be reminded of the thing whose memory we wish to keep most frequently. We set him as a sign upon the arm when we strive to hear and follow what he did as though they were true examples of virtue.

**“For love is strong as death.”** After the corruption of the mother, he suitably adds a discussion of love, so that it may be shown that the Church was not given on the basis of merits.

**“As death.”** Just as death separates the soul from the body, so the love of God separates us from the love of temporal things.

**“Hard as hell,”** etc. Because it could not be recalled from care for our salvation by any temptation of its enemies, just as hell is not softened by any torments of the wretched nor changed from the severity of its judgment. The harsher the comparison, the more sharply the Lord’s zeal for us is commended.

**“Its lamps.”** That is, the hearts of the faithful, in which love is contained as in a vessel. They are fire because they burn inwardly with love of God and neighbor. They are also flame because outwardly they shine through works of righteousness. These lamps are not extinguished at the bridegroom’s coming.

**VERSE 7.—“Many waters,”** etc. The house founded above upon the rock of charity cannot fall when the rivers rush against it.

**“Rivers.”** These are temptations, which test the hearts of the faithful either visibly or invisibly.

**“If a man gives.”** Since, where love of eternal things abounds, possession of passing things immediately becomes worthless, it is rightly added: **“If a man gives.”** The apostles and other saints, having abandoned everything, seemed to themselves to have lost nothing, provided that they could possess the true goods. Hence Paul says: “I consider all things loss as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3).

**VERSE 8.—“Our sister,”** etc. O you, my ministers and fellow soldiers, this Church is new and tender in retaining a new love.

**“Our little sister.”** Before she grows through increases of virtue, the Church cannot provide the breasts of preaching to weak hearers. She is called grown when, joined to the word of God and filled with the Holy Spirit, she is made fruitful through the ministry of preaching in the conception of children, whom she brings to birth by exhorting and bears by converting.

**“What shall we do for our sister?”** As if he said openly: “The Church of the Gentiles is small in number and is not yet sufficient to undertake the ministry of the word. What, then, seems to you, O Synagogue, should be done for her, our sister, at the time when I begin to address her through my apostles and the successors of my apostles? Shall we entrust to her, as still a little one, the small secrets of heavenly mysteries, or shall we make her greater through growth, so that, progressing well, she may be capable of more perfect virtues?”

When she remains silent and listens more attentively to what he himself wishes, he immediately reveals what ought to be done, adding:

**VERSE 9.—“If she is a wall,”** etc. If someone is found who can defend others from the attacks of the wandering, resisting the weapons of wickedness bravely, whether fortified by natural ability or instructed in philosophical learning, let us educate him through the divine Scriptures.

**“If she is a door.”** If someone is not sufficiently instructed to repel the sophistries of heretics, but nevertheless, through the simplicity of faith, is able to open the right way by preaching to those who wish to enter the courts of the heavenly homeland and by instructing the little ones, let us set before him the unfading examples of men of former times, by which he may fulfill his office more effectively.

**VERSE 10.—“I am a wall.”** He now speaks generally about the whole Church begun upon the foundation of the apostles, because from that time there have been breasts in the Church, continuing to the final times.

**“I am a wall.”** When the Church hears these counsels, or promises, of her Redeemer, one person no longer waits for another, but each answers for himself with a devoted voice.

**“From the time when.”** I could not have had all these things from myself, but from the time when he bestowed upon me the gift of his peace through the word of his reconciliation.

**“As one finding peace.”** I rightly say “finding peace,” because in that peace which I have described, the vineyard was established by Christ the peacemaker. It was formerly foretold by the Law and the Prophets.

That peace contains not merely one nation of the Jews, but many peoples gathered from the whole world—not through any merits of human beings, but through the sole peace that he came to make between God and humanity. Since the Lord cares for this vineyard, and since it is beneficial for people to become participants in it, it is rightly added:

**VERSE 11.—“He entrusted it to keepers.”** The voice of that peacemaker himself follows, showing how great a concern he has for this vineyard, what he preserves forever for those who leave their own things, and what singular reward he arranges for its teachers.

**VERSE 12.—“A thousand for you, O peacemaker.”** Whatever it possesses is a perfect price. Through “a thousand,” perfection is understood; through silver, everything worldly is understood—something that may at times be small, yet great in devotion.

**“A thousand,”** etc. The same perfection signified by a thousand is also signified by a hundred, because both numbers are perfect; and it has the same value as two hundred, just as if he had said “two thousand.”

**“A thousand,”** etc. “Silver” and “peacemaker” have the same meaning, because money expended for God reconciles peace between God and humanity.

**VERSE 13.—“You who dwell in gardens.”** The Church, or any faithful soul, dwells in gardens, already filled with the greenery of hope and good works. The hope of this world is indeed dry, because everything loved here withers rapidly.

Therefore, whoever dwells in gardens ought to make the bridegroom hear her voice—that is, she ought to bring forth good preaching to the extent that the one whom she desires takes delight in it. For her friends listen: all the elect who desire to hear the words of life, so that they may revive for the heavenly homeland.

**“You who dwell.”** Since a reward according to merits and a double recompense for teachers are reserved with me for each person, while the time for earning merits is present and the wedding day is delayed, let each person persist, according to his ability, in cultivating this vineyard.

**“Friends.”** That is, the angels whom I have given you as helpers, and the spirits of the righteous who are already with God and pray for their brothers.

**“Make me hear.”** I require of you that you dwell there, departing amid no tumult; afterward I also require that you make me hear your voice.

[Col. 1167A] **VERSE 14.—“Flee, my beloved.”** The Church assents and answers: “Remain absent as long as you wish; delay your presence. In patient hope I will endure or do whatever you command.”

**“Flee, my beloved.”** She does not speak as one wishing this—for who should want the one he loves to flee? Rather, mindful of her condition, she consents to his will.

**“Flee, my beloved.”** As if she said: “You who, having taken flesh, have become comprehensible, exceed the understanding of our senses through your divinity, and remain incomprehensible to us in yourself.”

The Church cries this to the Lord in the prophetic spirit after describing the Lord’s death, resurrection, and ascension. We are said to flee when what we wish to remember does not come before us, or when we do not retain in memory what we wish to retain.

**“Be like.”** Flee in such a way that you appear frequently through the grace of compunction in the hearts of the faithful. They are mountains of spices because, despising every desire, cleansing away vices, and being held by love of heavenly things, they give off the fragrance of virtues and are the good fragrance of Christ.

[Col. 1167]

# THE BOOK OF WISDOM (G)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1167B]

The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews. Hence its style also smells more strongly of Greek eloquence. The Jews assert that it belongs to Philo. It is therefore called “of Wisdom” because in it the coming of Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father, and his passion are clearly expressed.

## CHAPTER I

**VERSE 1.—“Love righteousness,”** etc. (RAB. in the Book of Wisdom, vol. III.) Jerome asserts that this book was not written by Solomon, etc., up to: **“Love righteousness,”** etc.

**“The earth.”** That is, restrain the flesh with discernment, lest it grow proud against the spirit. As if he said: “Seek first the kingdom of God” (Matt. 6), etc.

**“In simplicity.”** That is, subject yourselves to his will and keep his commandments. As if he said: “You who do not understand, do not criticize, because the secrets of God cannot be grasped by human reason, since ‘his judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable’” (Rom. 11).

**VERSE 4.—“For wisdom will not enter into a malevolent soul,”** etc. That is, into the animal human being, according to the saying: “The animal person does not perceive” (1 Cor. 2), etc. Therefore he did not say “spirit,” that is, the spiritual soul.

(RAB.) Philosophers, heretics, and false Christians flatter themselves in vain. Only those pure in heart can receive the wisdom of God.

**VERSE 6.—“Kind.”** He attacks those who say that good and evil thoughts are sent by God, whereas God wishes all people to be saved and to come to knowledge of the truth.

For he tempts no one in order to deceive him, but in order to test him. Hence: “God tested Abraham” (Gen. 22); and: “Test me and try me” (Ps. 25), etc. But each person is tempted by his own desire, and by God’s just judgment the one who refuses to obey the Spirit of truth is permitted to fall.

**VERSE 7.—“And that which contains all things.”** That is, the Spirit who governs and rules all things.

Or, “who reaches from end to end” and possesses knowledge of speech—that is, grants human beings understanding of the Scriptures.

Or, “that which contains all things,” namely, the human being, who has a fitting relationship with every creature. “It possesses knowledge of speech,” that is, of various languages, through the Holy Spirit, who gave the apostles the ability to speak in different languages the mighty works of God.

Or, “that which contains all things,” namely, the Holy Spirit, who fills all things with his essence, possesses knowledge of speech—that is, of the Word of God—and has the same knowledge as the Word.

Or, “that which contains all things,” namely, the Church, in which “to one is given the word of knowledge,” etc.

(RAB.) He is the one who in the beginning was borne over the waters and by his majesty fills and contains every creature.

**VERSE 8.—“Therefore.”** (RAB.) Just as the elect receive the gift of knowledge and piety through the Spirit, so the reprobate, puffed up by their pride, shamelessly proclaim their error. They cannot conceal the Spirit of God, nor do they escape just punishment. For just as the eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous and his ears attentive to their prayers, so the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.

**VERSE 11.—“Therefore keep watch.”** (RAB.) Murmurings and detractions are destructive. Hence: “Whisperers and detractors are hateful to God” (Rom. 1); and: “He who disparages another binds himself for the future” (Prov. 13).

**“A mouth that lies.”** (ID.) There is a lie that is a lighter fault, etc., up to: and it rewards the good itself.

**VERSE 12.—“Do not be jealous.”** (ID.) He enumerated the things harmful to a human being, etc., up to: but rather proceeds from vice.

**VERSE 16.—“And covenants.”** “We have made a covenant with death, and with hell we have made an agreement.”

## CHAPTER II

**VERSE 1.—“For they said.”** (RAB.) The voice of the lost, etc., up to: “and we shall be reduced to nothing.”

**VERSE 2.—“For we are smoke.”** Truly we shall be nothing, because we are smoke and breath in our nostrils—that is, in our body. Our body is compared to smoke and breath, which arise and fail together.

**“And a word is a spark.”** That is, the soul is comparable to a spark, which immediately becomes nothing. “A word,” I say—that is, the soul.

**“To stir our heart.”** That is, it gives life to the body. That this is how it should be explained he proves by adding: **“For the extinguished ash, and afterward the spirit, will be dispersed.”**

**VERSE 10.—“Let us oppress.”** (RAB.) These things generally pertain to them, etc., up to: nor do they obey their own head, but blaspheme and accuse.

**VERSE 17.—“Let us see.”** (RAB.) Similar things are said in the Gospel, where the chief priests and Pharisees took counsel about how to hand Jesus over to death; and when he was hanging on the cross they mocked him, saying: “He saved others, but he cannot save himself,” [Col. 1169A] etc. “If he is the King of Israel, let him now come down from the cross” (Matt. 27), etc.

**VERSE 20.—“A most shameful death.”** The cross, namely, which until Christ’s passion was the punishment of criminals but is now the trophy of victory.

**VERSE 23.—“For God.”** That is, God is not the author of evils. He created the human being for immortality, but the one who consented to the devil’s suggestion was subjected to the sentence of death.

## CHAPTER III
Verses 1.—“But the souls of the righteous.” (RAB.) In the preceding chapter the sentence against the wicked was expressed, etc., up to the point where it says: “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Ps. 115).

[Col. 1169B] Verse 7.—“Sparks.” A spark does two things: namely, it quickly sets a reed-bed ablaze and takes vengeance.

Verse 8.—“And the Lord shall reign.” With him his members also shall reign. Hence in Daniel: “The kingdom and power and greatness of the kingdom which is above heaven shall be given to the people of the saints of the Most High” (Dan. 7).

Verse 11.—“Wisdom.” (RAB.) Heretics can be indicated in this statement, etc., up to the point where it shows that the activity of the reprobate is worthy of eternal condemnation.

Verse 13.—“For she is blessed.” (ID.) The order of virgins may be understood in the barren woman and the eunuch, etc., up to the point where it says that this is in the will of the mind, not in bodily weakness.

Verse 18.—“On the day of recognition.” That is, of judgment, when the chosen, recognized by their judge, shall be invited to possess the kingdom; but the wicked shall be consoled by no hope of restoration, and shall be driven from the presence of the supreme King to be tormented forever.

CHAPTER IV

Verse 1.—“O how beautiful,” etc. (RAB.) Having reproved heretics and schismatics, he praises Catholics, etc., up to the point where he says: “With glory,” etc.

Verse 2.—“A prize surpassing.” The prize given for a passing contest, which is greater than those contests and persecutions.

Verse 3.—“The many-branched growths of the impious.” He speaks alternately of Catholics and heretics, so as to display the praiseworthy wisdom of the former and the blameworthy cunning of the latter. “Plantations.” Since μόσχος in Greek means “calf” in Latin, some did not understand μοσκεύματα to mean “plantations” and interpreted it as “calf-shoots.” This error so occupied many manuscripts that it is scarcely possible to find the passage written otherwise.

Verse 7.—“The righteous,” etc. (RAB.) Having spoken of the destruction of the wicked, etc., up to the point where it says that they pass from life to eternal death.

Verse 10.—“Pleasing to God.” (RAB.) God does not therefore remove him, etc., up to the point where Peter says: “God knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment” (1 Pet. 1).

Verse 12.—“Fascination.” (ID.) This statement marks out, etc., up to the point where God separated them from the company of the wicked, “to hide them in the hiding-place of his face from the disturbance of men” (Ps. 30).

[Col. 1170A] Verse 19.—“He will shatter them, swollen with pride, without a sound,” because they will be without excuse: “For although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became futile in their reasoning” (Rom. 1).

CHAPTER V

Verses 1–7.—“Then,” etc. “We have grown weary,” etc. (RAB.) The philosophers have grown weary, etc., up to the point where, grieving, they say: “What did pride profit us?”

Verses 9–12.—“Like a shadow.” (RAB.) By “shadow,” forgetfulness of mind, etc., up to the point where these things precede the setting of corruptible life. (ID.) By “bird,” excellence, etc., up to the point where, groaning, they shall be relieved by no voice of consolation.

Verse 14.—“These things they said in hell, these men who…” [Col. 1170B] He introduces four further kinds of examples, by which he demonstrates the foolish hope of the wicked: they think that the present life is measured out only for these things, or that they will escape unpunished.

Verse 15.—“It is down, which is borne away by the wind.” Arising from the withered blossom of grasses, it expresses the frailty of the flesh, which will quickly be carried away by the wind of illness or bodily affliction, because “all flesh is grass.” “And like thin foam.” Foam produced from the waters floats upon the water. Here it is the desire for human favor and popular boasting, which is dissolved or scattered by the storm of temptation or by the examination of judgment—that is, it is shown to have been vain.

Verse 16.—“But the righteous shall live forever.” (RAB.) After the punishments of sinners, etc., up to the point where they shall enjoy God, in whom they placed all their hope.

[Col. 1170C] Verse 18.—“He will take up armor.” (RAB.) The Creator of all, etc., up to the point where they are unable to resist.

Verse 22.—“And to a fixed place.” Wherever it is necessary; for that which has been ordered by divine wisdom cannot be confused.

Verse 23.—“And the rivers”—that is, the disturbances of persecutions. For often the scourge of correction breaks the hearts of the wicked, which preaching does not soften.

CHAPTER VI

“Better is wisdom,” etc. (RAB.) He admonishes the rulers of the Church, etc., up to the point where he will judge not only works but also knowledge and intentions.

Verse 7.—“For mercy is granted to the lowly.” Namely, to those who sinned through ignorance, weakness, or necessity and erased their sins through humble repentance. “But the mighty shall be mightily tested,” namely, those who, by despising God’s commandments, committed serious sins and did not repent. For just as they were more powerful in ungodliness, so they will endure stronger torments in Gehenna. (ANAST.) For what reason, etc., up to the point where “from the one to whom much has been given, much also will be required.”

Verse 8.—“For he will not withdraw his person.” Hence: “God is not a respecter of persons; he judges each one according to his ways” (Acts 10).

Verse 10.—“To you, therefore, O kings,” etc. Having completed his discourse to the powerful and rebuked their harshness with harsh words, he turns to exhort the rulers of the Church and extols wisdom with wondrous praises.

Verse 12.—“Love,” etc., “and you shall possess discipline.” Whoever loves wisdom preserves discipline in his conduct. For he does not love wisdom who does not preserve discipline. Hence: “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John 14).

Verse 14.—“She anticipates those who desire her.” Offering herself freely. For he himself is “the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14): through him one travels, toward him one strives, and to him one arrives.

Verse 15.—“She sits beside him,” etc. Always ready, namely, to help. Hence: “Behold, I stand at the door and knock; if anyone opens to me, I will enter in to him and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3). In the present life one must devote oneself to wisdom and live according to the rule of her discipline.

[Col. 1171B] Verse 22.—“If therefore you delight,” etc. (RAB.) He admonishes kings, etc., up to the point where he shall obtain the crown of the heavenly kingdom.

Verse 25.—“Nor with wasting envy.” Envy does not share in wisdom, because through the envy of the devil death entered the world, and through wisdom the human race is delivered from it.

Verse 27.—“Therefore receive,” etc. (RAB.) Wisdom will show, etc., up to the point where they are said to be more perfect, healing, and life-giving.

CHAPTER VII

Verse 5.—“For no one among kings.” (RAB.) He shows that every human being, etc., up to the point where, just as God is perfect, so Jesus Christ is perfect man.

Verse 9.—“Nor did I compare,” etc. Hence: “Having found one precious pearl, he sells everything and buys it.” For whoever truly finds heavenly wisdom—that is, the word of God—despises all the profits of the present life, philosophy, and eloquence, and strives to devote himself to divine contemplation.

Verse 11.—“They came,” etc. (RAB.) Solomon, having experienced this, etc., up to the point where the sun is so called because it alone shines among the stars by day.

Verse 15.—“She herself is the guide of wisdom.” (RAB.) God the Father of the incarnate Son, to whom he gave all power in heaven and on earth.

Verse 17.—“For he himself,” etc. Scripture says of Solomon: “God gave,” etc., up to the point where “he himself enlightens every person coming into this world; whoever follows him does not walk in darkness” (John 1).

Verses 22–24.—“For in her there is a holy spirit of understanding,” etc. (RAB.) As Isaiah shows, all the gifts of the Holy Spirit exist in the humanity of the Savior. In him are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, and the fullness of divinity, to whom the Spirit is not given by measure. (ID.) The Spirit who fills all things is called both mobile and stable. For a human being ranges everywhere, comes everywhere to meet another, and is suddenly found where he is not expected. Therefore the almighty Spirit is called both stable and mobile, to signify that he is present everywhere. (ID.) Hence: “He is the brightness of his glory and the likeness of his substance” (Heb. 1), governing all things by his word, etc., up to the point where, in time, “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”

CHAPTER VIII

[Col. 1172A]

Verse 1.—“She reaches from end to end.” That is, from the beginning of the world to the coming of Christ, she firmly asserts wondrous works and sincere testimonies throughout the Old Testament; and from the incarnation of the Word to the end of the world she explains the sweetness of the Gospel. Thus she reaches powerfully from end to end, because she acts perfectly everywhere; for “end” signifies perfection.

Verse 3.—“She glorifies his companionship,” that is, she displays his nobility—namely, that of the Father, who is coeternal and co-omnipotent with him. Alternatively, the passage may be read partly of his temporal birth and partly of his eternal birth. “She possesses God’s companionship,” that is, humanity, in which God dwells, who is the Father’s wisdom. Or, “she glorifies his nobility,” that is, the nobility of God the Father: he is of the same essence as the Father, begotten from him eternally and born in time from his mother.

[Col. 1172B] Verse 4.—“For she is the teacher of discipline.” “From his fullness we have all received”; through him grace and truth came to be—that is, were revealed. “No one has ever seen God, but the Son, who is in the bosom of the Father, has himself declared him” (John 1).

Verse 7.—“And the labors of this.” For there is nothing idle in his works. He does whatever is true, whatever is honorable, whatever is just, and entrusts to his own the things that must be done. “For temperance and wisdom.” (RAB.) Whoever is temperate, etc., up to the point where he gave it to his servant Jacob.

Verse 11.—“Wonderful.” The Virgin’s childbirth was wondrous to all, because he became for the rising and downfall of many; he stands as a sign for the peoples, before whom kings will close their mouths, and whom the nations will entreat.

Verse 16.—“Entering into a house.” (RAB.) After preaching and laboring in works, through which the saints provide consolation to their hearers, they return to themselves and devote themselves to divine contemplation, where they find rest in heavenly sweetness. (ID., from Gregory.) Bodily delights, etc., up to the point where David says: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Ps. 33), etc. (ORIG.) Whoever opens the mute mouth, etc., up to the point where justice is understood to be the distributor and judge of merits.

Verse 19.—“But I was a child,” etc. (RAB.) In his youth Solomon had asked God for wisdom, so that he might judge the people rightly [Col. 1172D] and distinguish between good and evil. Thus he became the wisest of men, and he appears to have received a good soul, since he had a wise and understanding heart. But how does what is said of him agree with this?

Verse 20.—“I came into an undefiled body,” etc., when he loved a foreign woman and built idols? It therefore seems rather to fit the people of the saints, who were regenerated in baptism, instructed in the faith of the Savior, received the childhood of their good nature and simple innocence, and strove through every pursuit to reach the summit of virtue. Hence what follows: “And when I was more good,” etc. “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” Those who imitate him have become his members.

CHAPTER IX

[Col. 1173A]

Verse 7.—“But you chose,” etc. (RAB.) David, because he was a man, etc., up to the point where he is “the power and wisdom of God, and the image of the invisible God.”

Verse 13.—“For what human being?” He marvels at the excellence of God. It is as though he said: “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11). And: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. 40).

Verse 17.—“But the understanding.” No one knows what takes place in a human being’s heart except the human spirit, and no one knows what belongs to God except the Spirit of God. But “the Spirit searches all things, even the deep things of God,” who enlightens the hearts of the saints.

CHAPTER X

[Col. 1173B] Verse 1.—“This protected the one who was first.” (RAB.) The first human being, created through God’s goodness, placed in paradise, and set over all living creatures, was cast down through the transgression of the command into the miseries of this age; and through God’s wisdom, that is, Christ, he was restored. This is a great sign of divine compassion.

Verse 3.—“The unjust man in his anger.” Such was Cain, who unjustly killed his brother; the punishment for whose crime was discharged in the flood, and Cain’s generation was destroyed. But God’s wisdom preserved Noah, from the stock of Seth, with his sons in the ark for the restoration of the world.

Verse 5.—“And this also, in the agreement of pride,” etc. (RAB.) The devil, through pride, etc., up to the point where Christ’s humility united.

Verse 6.—“This rescued the righteous,” etc. Hence Peter says: “He condemned the cities of Sodom and Gomorrah to destruction by reducing them to ashes, making them an example of those who would act ungodly; and he rescued righteous Lot, oppressed by the outrage and luxurious conduct of the lawless” (2 Pet. 2), etc. Lot’s wife, looking back, was changed into a pillar of salt, lest we who have been called to life through God’s grace should look back to the old human being and remain midway. Changed into a pillar of salt, she salts others; hence: “Remember Lot’s wife” (Luke 17), so that we may not neglect things foolishly but guard against them prudently.

Verse 8.—“For wisdom,” etc. “But this,” etc. Jacob, fleeing from his brother Esau, came to his uncle Laban. On the journey, in a dream, he saw a ladder set up, with the angels of God ascending and descending, and the Lord himself leaning upon the ladder and saying to him: “I am the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac; the land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your offspring” (Gen. 28). When he came to Mesopotamia, he took Leah and Rachel, for whom he tended Laban’s sheep for a long time. Laban tried deceitfully to deprive him of his wages. But through God’s wisdom Laban was deprived, while Jacob grew rich and returned with many possessions. Mystically, these things pertain to the martyrs, whom Christ’s mercy delivered from their persecutors, strengthening them by the grace of the Holy Spirit and the hope of future reward; and finally, after their enemies had been conquered, led them to the kingdom of heaven, to the praise and glory of his name.

Verse 13.—“This rescued the righteous man who had been sold,” etc. (RAB.) Mystically, the Wisdom of God rescued the martyrs from persecutions and exalted them in the heavenly kingdom. Hence they shall come with Christ as judges of their enemies.

Verse 15.—“This preserved the righteous people.” (RAB.) Mystically, God delivers his chosen from their persecutors, etc., up to the point where he brings them to the rewards of the kingdom, where they continually sing praises to their deliverer.

Verse 21.—“For wisdom,” etc. Without the wisdom of God, the human mind cannot worthily think anything, nor can the mouth utter anything. Therefore wisdom and eloquence must be sought from him.

CHAPTER XI

Verse 1.—“She guided the works,” etc. (RAB.) The Christian people follows prophecy through the desert of this world, so that it may reach the homeland of the heavenly kingdom. Hence Peter says: “We possess the prophetic word, to which you do well to attend as to a lamp shining in a dark place” (2 Pet. 1), etc.

Verse 4.—“From the exceedingly high rock,” etc. The rock was Christ, who, struck by the rod of the cross held in the hands—that is, in the writings of the prophets—poured forth living water.

Verse 5.—“For by the things through which they suffered punishments,” etc. (RAB.) Having recalled these benefits, etc., up to the point where, whether they suffer or not, it is glory for them.

Verse 10.—“For when they were tested.” (RAB.) God rebuked the sinful Israelites with deserved blows and consoled them when they repented; but he destroyed the Egyptians and Canaanites as unworthy of mercy. “Torments,” etc. [Col. 1174C] “From Pharaoh,” wherever they might be. Or, it was not only those whom the Israelites killed in each city in their recent slaughter who were punished; all the Canaanites who heard of the victory of God’s people were punished as well. Hence Rahab says: “Your terror has fallen upon us” (Josh. 2), etc. Mystically, the Jews, who despised the incarnation of the Son of God and his preaching, wander throughout the world and are afflicted by various disasters as fugitives. The Gentiles, however, converted to the faith and accepting the Father’s correction, do not depart from God’s mercy, so that those who had been at the head may be at the tail, and conversely.

Verse 13.—“A double punishment,” etc. The memory of past evils is not diminished, and the storm of present evils is increased. Hence they have no hope of remedy, because, while pretending repentance, they do not devote themselves to amendment. Hence: “When he killed them, they sought him, and they loved him” (Ps. 77), etc.

Verse 15.—“Not similarly with the righteous,” etc. Because they do not sin in the same way. “For the righteous falls seven times and rises again”; but “when the wicked has come into the depths of evils, he despises.”

Verse 16.—“Which certain wanderers,” etc. (RAB.) It was fitting, etc., up to the point where their entire intention is to persecute and torment the human race in every way.

Verse 21.—“But you have ordered all things by measure,” etc. (RAB.) Because all things are according to truth, etc., up to the point where the hidden things of darkness will be brought to light and the counsels of hearts revealed.

[Col. 1175A] Verse 23.—“A moment on the balance,” etc. Isaiah says something similar: “Behold, the nations are like a drop from a bucket, and are counted as a speck on the balance” (Isa. 40). He wishes it to be understood that the mind, reason, and understanding of the Lord, through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made, is the one of whom it is said: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were established” (Ps. 32), etc. All the nations that did not know their Creator are, in comparison with God, like a drop from a bucket and like a moment on the balance that is easily tilted, and like the drop of the dawn dew (Wis. 11), which is dried at the first sight of the sun. Or, just as a drop from a bucket is disregarded or neglected when it flows from the person carrying it, so the multitude of the nations, compared with heavenly splendor, heavenly mysteries, and the multitude of angels, is counted as nothing.

[Col. 1175B] Verse 25.—“For you love all things,” etc. A good craftsman loves and governs his work; and if a human being sometimes sins, he endures him with great patience and converts him to better things through repentance. Hence: “He makes his sun rise on the good and the evil, and sends rain on the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5). But the unrepentant are condemned by just judgment: “For the Lord is just, and he has loved justice” (Ps. 10).

CHAPTER XII

“O how good and gracious,” etc. Through those whom you fill, or through others whom you choose. Hence: “He will convict the world concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment” (John 16).

Verse 3.—“For those ancient inhabitants.” (RAB.) Historically he speaks, etc., up to the point where, with the Holy Spirit assisting their virtues, they will produce useful fruits.

Verse 12.—“For who will say,” etc. (RAB.) He shows by clear reasoning that one must not contradict the Creator if he orders his creature according to his own will, because all things are established in his will and no one can resist him. “The Lord is just in all his ways” (Ps. 144). Hence it follows: “Since you are just” (Rom. 9), etc.

Verse 16.—“For your power,” etc. Because God’s judgment, whether in the correction of the chosen or in the condemnation of the wicked, is the perfection of supreme equity. Therefore, through his goodness, he delays and suspends judgment for a long time, so that he may have more people to whom he can grant his benefit. When the creature rises against the Creator, it is punished by a just vengeance, so that it may recognize itself as inferior.

[Col. 1175D] These words can be referred to Christ’s passion: the Father handed him over to death for us and made him who knew no sin to be sin for us. If he had not accepted an undeserved death, he would not have freed us from the death we deserved. Therefore the just Father, punishing the just one, disposes all things justly.

Almighty God judges all things with the greatest tranquility. Nevertheless, human emotions and bodily members are attributed to him by a figurative manner of speaking, so that the divine words may be adapted to our capacity. For Scripture speaks of the Lord’s eyes, ears, hands, mouth, feet, anger, wrath, and similar things, although simple nature never receives variation, nor true unity division. Yet one and the same being performs manifold and diverse works. Hence: “You will change them, and they will be changed; but you are the same, and your years” (Ps. 101), etc. And elsewhere: “I am God, and I do not change” (Mal. 3). And elsewhere: “With him there is no alteration” (Jas. 1), etc.

“But you have instructed your people”: through God’s wondrous works the faithful are instructed not to become entangled with the wicked, but to strive to keep themselves undefiled by confessing and hoping in the Lord, and not to neglect the time of repentance.

Verse 15.—“Since, therefore,” etc. Hence: “Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord” (Ps. 31). There is a great difference between the judgment of the chosen and that of the reprobate. The Lord rebukes the former so that he may correct them; the latter pay the penalties of pride and faithlessness, so that they may recognize that they cannot resist the ruler of all. Blessed is the judge who always regards the compassion and goodness of his judge. “Judgment without mercy awaits the one who has shown no mercy” (Jas. 2).

Verse 23.—“Senseless,” etc. Those who did not wish to recognize and honor the Creator were justly handed over to a reprobate mind and did things that are improper, dishonoring their bodies in themselves: “For they exchanged the truth of God for a lie and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator” (Rom. 1).

Verse 26.—“But those who were not corrected by mockeries,” etc. That is, those who, though scourged by God, were not corrected experienced deserved condemnation. God rebukes in order to correct. But whoever, ungrateful and impatient, murmurs is led from temporal torment to eternal torment.

Verse 27.—“For in these,” etc. (RAB.) While the Gentiles were serving idols, etc., up to the point where he inflicts eternal punishment on the uncorrected.

CHAPTER XIII

Verse 1.—“Knowledge.” Namely, fear and reverence. Hence: “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding.” For the one who departs from the worship of idols departs from evil; the one who fears God keeps his commandments, because “the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ps. 110).

From these works of man they were able to recognize the good craftsman, who alone truly is, because he is immutable and always the same, always abiding in himself, and governs all things. Utterly vain, therefore, is the vanity of human beings who venerate creatures instead of the Creator.

“Nor by works.” Some worshiped fire, which they called Vulcan; others the ether or air, which they called Jupiter and Juno; others excessive water, that is, Neptune; others the circuit of the stars, distributing the positions and courses of the heavenly bodies into various animal figures; others the sun, which they called Phoebus; others the moon, that is, Diana. (RAB.) They sin in two ways, etc., up to the point where human desire is condemned.

Verse 6.—“Yet,” etc. Hence Paul says: “For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and wickedness of those who suppress the truth of God in wickedness, because what is known of God is manifest among them” (Rom. 1), etc. Knowledge of God is perceived from the structure of the world. For, so that the invisible God might be known through invisible things, a work was made by him that would reveal its craftsman, so that God might be understood as the maker of all, since no others can make what he has made. But although they knew him, they did not glorify him as God, but became futile in their thoughts (RAB.).

Verse 10.—“Wretched,” etc. Those who honor gods so as to feast their eyes on gold, the gleam of polished marble or ivory, or garments distinguished by gems and colors; and the more ornate the temples and the more beautiful the images, the more majesty they are said to possess—or are thought to possess. Therefore, what human desire admires is regarded, or believed to be, religion.

Verse 11.—“Or if some craftsman.” (RAB.) Wisdom mocks these people, etc., up to the point where: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3).

CHAPTER XIV

[Col. 1177B] Verse 1.—“Again, another preparing to sail,” etc. These things too are spoken against idolatry.
