For it is the greatest madness that a human being, created in the image of God and possessing from him a rational mind by which he devised how to cross the waves and constructed a ship according to his skill in craftsmanship, should not honor the one who gave him this knowledge, but should invoke an idol that he formed by similar skill and with greater vanity. Since the maker is greater than what is made, to worship one’s own work is madness. The course of navigation must be sought from God, from whom comes the preparation of the ship. Heretics, however, who fabricate empty images of errors, perish amid the waves of the world because they have abandoned the ship of the Church [Col. 1177C] and God its pilot.

Verse 3.—“For you have given.” By God’s power he led the Israelites across the Red Sea on dry ground and divided the waters of the Jordan, so as to inspire terror in the nations destined for destruction. Likewise, amid the waves and persecutions of the world, he prepares for the faithful a path of faith and steadfastness, so that they may cross unharmed. Human assistance is unnecessary where God displays the wondrous effects of his power.

Verse 5.—“But so that they might not be,” etc. The Creator gave his creature knowledge by which it might provide for itself in the present and serve his will. Hence he commanded Noah to make an ark, in which he and his descendants would be saved and the other living creatures preserved for the restoration of the world, while the human race was destroyed by the flood because of its iniquity. Hence Peter: “In it a few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water; and baptism, corresponding to this, now saves you also” (1 Pet. 3), etc.

The ark, constructed from smoothed wood, signifies the Church, which is made from the gathering of the faithful through the craftsmanship of preachers. “A few, that is, eight souls, were saved through water” while the world was perishing, because the number of the chosen is small in comparison with the reprobate. For “few are those who find the way of life.”

The water of the flood killed those outside, because the very waters that lifted the ark to heaven submerge the heretic, even though he possesses the sacrament of baptism, and plunge him into hell. The number eight also signifies the Church, which receives the washing of baptism in the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection: “As Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life,” cleansed by the water of regeneration.

Hence Jeremiah: “Every human being has become foolish through his knowledge; every craftsman has been put to shame by his carved image, because his cast image is a lie, and there is no spirit in them. For their works are vain and worthy of laughter, and at the time of visitation they will perish” (Jer. 10).

Verse 8.—“And the one who made it.” The image and worship of false gods. For the devil will be punished because he usurps divine honor, and the human being because he honors a creature instead of the Creator. Wood, moreover, often signifies a human being. Blessed, therefore, is the person who speaks and does the truth. But the heretic, who worships his own fabrications, is accursed and given over to destruction, as is his work—that is, his doctrine.

[Col. 1178B] Verse 11.—“Therefore.” Idols, or their inhabitants—that is, demons—must not be forgiven, because they draw human beings, made in the image of God, away from him and overthrow them in the trap of error. Heretics also, who lead human beings astray, will not escape strict judgment.

Verse 12.—“The beginning.” For this is the worst kind of fornication: the soul departs from God and fornicates with idols, or abandons the truth of divine teaching and follows the falsehood of heretical depravity or opinion. Hence Paul calls greed “the service of idols.” It is therefore clear that every evil desire is called fornication: when the soul abandons the higher law for the pleasure of lower things, it is corrupted by being prostrated or prostituted, as though by the shameful payment of its natural desires.

[Col. 1178C] Verse 13.—“For not,” etc. “May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and every tongue that speaks lies” (Ps. 11). Hence Jeremiah: “The gods who did not make heaven and earth shall perish from the earth” (Jer. 10), etc. (LACTANTIUS, book 1.) Because of human folly, etc., up to the point where they bestowed divine honors upon parents and commanded that such honors be bestowed.

Verse 21.—“An incommunicable name.” They attributed the incommunicable name of God Almighty—who alone is incomprehensible—to insensible and fragile matter or to an image.

Verse 23.—“Or indeed their own children.” Thus in the rites of Saturn, to whom, because of his hatred of Jupiter, they sacrificed their little children without regard for natural affection; and the priests themselves sacrificed to Bellona with their own blood. Hence Quintilian: “If this,” he says, “is commanded by an angry god, he is angry; and if he is angry, he does not accept your sacrifices.”

“Or secret sacrifices.” Such as those performed in the rites of Egyptian Isis and Eleusinian Ceres. For just as Osiris is sought there amid the mother’s lamentation, so here Proserpina was carried off into the incestuous marriage of her uncle Pluto. Because Ceres is said to have sought her in Sicily with torches lit from Etna, her rites were therefore celebrated by the tossing about of burning torches. Similarly, they raged in the rites of Liber Pater and of the Great Mother, where they play in imitation of the gods, who, satiated at the festival, spent the entire night in debauchery. For they thought that they pleased their gods through lust and impurity.

[Col. 1179A] Verse 25.—“All things mingled together.” Everything was confused; there was no reason and no true religion. The more wicked someone was, the more he thought that he pleased his god.

Verse 27.—“For the worship of the unspeakable,” etc. There is no greater madness than to abandon the living God and serve the dead. When the mind turns away from its Creator, it becomes entangled in every crime. For “the beginning of every sin is pride” (Ecclus. 10). “The end”: completion and fullness. For those who worship an idol instead of God regard everything as sin in themselves.

Verse 28.—“Or while they rejoice.” For when they swear, they profane God’s name, who says: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain,” and “You shall not swear by the names of foreign gods” (Exod. 20). But while they think that they are mocking God, they hurl themselves into eternal death.

Heretics, however, who worship the images of their errors, become the cause of their own destruction. Their doctrine is false, their life unjust, their joy insane, and their death wicked; because, when they swear unjustly by an idol and do not hope in their God, they will therefore receive the vengeance due for their deeds. Hence it follows: “For power does not belong to those who swear.”

CHAPTER XV

Verse 1.—“But you,” etc. (RAB.) Condemned by just judgment, they recognize too late, in their repentance, what they previously refused to believe. Hence: “The Lord is known by executing judgment; the sinner is caught in the work of his hands” (Ps. 9). Hence John: “Everyone who has this hope in him purifies himself, just as he is pure; and everyone who abides in him does not sin” (1 John 3).

Verse 3.—“For to know you,” etc. This is the possession of incorruption and, in the future, of contemplation. Hence: “This is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God” (John 17), etc.

Verse 4.—“For not into error.” He speaks in the person of the faithful, who, fortified by God’s grace, did not mingle with the iniquity or idolatry of the Gentiles, because this labor is without the fruit of righteousness and deserves eternal death.

Verse 6.—“Lovers of evil,” etc. “May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them” (Ps. 134). The inventors of false doctrines and their worshipers likewise deserve death. “For God will destroy the person who does this”—that is, both the teacher and his disciple.

Earlier he rejected wooden, stone, and bronze idols; now he also condemns those made of clay. Their retribution is just: since they were made from the earth, and refused to follow the better part of themselves—that is, the soul, created in the image of God—to acknowledge the living God, they imitated the earthly body, their inferior part, and worshiped a clayen god. Thus, without the fruit of good works, they became senseless and useless like the earth from which they were taken.

Mystically, heretics and schismatics, who suppress the truth of God in wickedness and worship falsehood instead of truth in the images of their doctrines, though they conceal them under eloquence or pretended virtue, nevertheless fabricate things fragile and clayen.

[Col. 1180A] Verse 10.—“Their heart is ashes, and their thought is foul, and their life is dirtier than mire,” because they do not know their maker and become futile in their thoughts. They despise the understanding of the holy fathers and invent new errors, like empty games, for the sake of human favor and earthly profit—wandering themselves and leading others into error—so that they may be without excuse when God judges the secrets of hearts and repays each person according to his works.

Verse 13.—“For this man knows,” etc. Heretics have no excuse, because they sin knowingly by refusing to imitate sound faith and right doctrine, following an earthly and fragile understanding rather than a spiritual one.

Verse 17.—“Better is.” A human being is better than idols according to the order of creation, because he lives and understands, whereas they never do. But because he follows the vanity of error rather than knowledge of the truth, although he is held in honor he does not understand, and is compared with foolish beasts (Ps. 48).

Verse 18.—“Senseless.” As though he said: they had no discernment. In truth, living things are better than dead things, sensible things than insensible, rational things than irrational. But it was fitting that those who did not know the Creator should not know distinctions among creatures. Whoever neglects to possess God’s praise and blessing within himself shows, in his discernment of animals, that he himself errs.

CHAPTER XVI

[Col. 1180C] Verse 2.—“In place of these,” etc. (RAB.) The people of Israel desired meat in the desert, etc., up to the point where they were therefore justly handed over to be tormented.

Verse 6.—“But not forever.” (RAB.) For the bronze serpent was not, etc., up to the point where, having died according to his humanity, he is like bronze according to his divinity.

Verse 9.—“For those,” etc. The chosen are tested through affliction and admonished to avoid sins and do good. The reprobate are scattered because they are not corrected. Therefore small animals kill the idolaters. But serpents cannot destroy the Israelites, worshipers of God, because “the Lord knows how to rescue the godly from temptation, but to reserve the unjust for punishment on the day of judgment.”

### VERSE 12

“But your word, Lord”—that is, the Son, through whom all things exist, whose power is everywhere, who did everything whatsoever he willed. He cares for bodies; he saves souls from spiritual beasts.

### VERSE 14

“But man kills.” (CHRYS.) Man does so through wickedness, etc., up to “he is free from every crime.”

### VERSE 16

“For although they denied knowing [him], etc.” (RAB.) The Egyptians were afflicted with various plagues, etc., up to “because all things assent to the Creator’s will.”

### VERSE 18

“For at one time.” (RAB.) As it is read in Genesis: “The Lord rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and Gomorrah in order to destroy the ungodly”; and in Exodus, hail together with fire. In the Book of Numbers: “He sent fiery serpents against those who murmured,” so that the ungodly might recognize that every creature is prepared to avenge an injury done to its Creator.

### VERSE 20

“For these things, etc.” (RAB.) In the desert manna was given to the children of Israel, etc., up to “Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy will surround the one who hopes in the Lord” (Psalm 31).

### VERSE 24

“For creation, etc.” (RAB.) Let sinners be confounded here: while the other creatures serve their Maker, they themselves resist him. Therefore they are scourged by the concord of all creatures; and if they do not repent, they will be tormented forever. But true goods are prepared for the good.

### VERSE 25

“Therefore, etc.” (RAB.) God rained manna from heaven, etc., up to “like a transgressor of the law, he will perish forever.”

[Col. 1181B]

### VERSE 28

“So that it might be known to all, etc.” (RAB.) Historically, this food nourished them, etc., up to “but at the rising of the sun—that is, of Christ—let us say: ‘The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’”

## CHAPTER XVII

### VERSE 1

“For great indeed.” (RAB.) Mystically: all the persecutors of Christ’s Church suffer the darkness of their crimes and can never be secure. They are tormented by “the rulers of the darkness of this age” until the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth. Hence: “Everyone who does evil hates the light” (John 3), etc. Here Paul says: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Ephesians 5), etc.

### VERSE 4

“For neither.” Darkness is always accompanied by terror; and the less a person discerns what is around him, the more he fears, dreading adversity from every side. Thus the Egyptians endured the greatest darkness for three days, which neither the sun nor the stars could illuminate, and wherever they lay they were terrified by excessive fear. As for the statement that “gloomy faces” terrified them, it could have happened that demons presented them with various apparitions in order to increase their punishments and frighten them. The persecutors of faith and truth are likewise surrounded by the darkness of sins, because they do not know the sun of righteousness, nor do preachers illumine them with the radiance of doctrine. A descending sound—that is, a heavenly threat—also disturbs them; and gloomy faces—that is, demons—sometimes terrify them as torturers. Yet they do not usefully perform repentance; rather, in despair, they store up wrath for themselves on the day of judgment.

### VERSE 6

“Full of fear.” Because they were afraid of punishments from every side. For the more grievous the pains, the greater the terrors feared.

“And magical art, etc.” (RAB.) When the magicians were in Egypt, etc., up to “and patiently endure the ancient serpent, savage with his angels, as an enemy.”

### VERSE 9

“And the air, etc.” (RAB.) He indicates the excessiveness of the fear that they suffer when conscience rebukes them for the punishments threatening them. Since wickedness is always fearful, it gives evidence of its own terror; condemned to punishment, it has been sentenced.

### VERSE 11

“Betrayal, etc.” Fear, namely, exposes the weakness of the proud person who raises himself up through the vain hope of assistance, imagining that he can accomplish what he cannot—or may perhaps be able to accomplish it. While his strength is lesser, he considers the power of the circumstances he suffers externally to be greater. This frequently happens among the persecutors of the faithful: when they believe themselves powerful while torturing the saints, they are overcome by their power and saddened by distress of mind; they recognize that they cannot accomplish what they desired, and that God’s strength is greater, since he conquers in this way through his soldiers.

### VERSE 13

“But those others, etc.” (RAB.) The Egyptians, namely, surrounded by the horror of darkness, etc., up to “they feared it as something dangerous.”

### VERSE 19

“For the whole world.” As if he were saying: The ungodly were in darkness, but wherever the children of Israel lived, there was light.

[Col. 1182B]

### VERSE 20

“An image of darkness.” Spiritual darkness is more grievous than bodily darkness, because it leads human beings to the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth; the Egyptian darkness prefigures this. For just as bodies there are useless for every good work, so here souls together with bodies are condemned to an eternal prison, where there is neither reason, nor place, nor time for working.

## CHAPTER XVIII

### VERSE 1

“But your holy ones.” (RAB.) The Israelites in Egypt, etc., up to “he protects them in prosperity and adversity.”

### VERSE 4

“Indeed worthy, etc.” (RAB.) The Egyptians deservedly suffered the punishment of darkness, etc., up to “the meaning of this mystery was foreshadowed in the ancient fathers and completed at Christ’s coming.”

### VERSE 9

“For they secretly offered sacrifice.” (RAB.) The people of Israel celebrated Passover in Egypt at the Lord’s command, etc., up to “but in the secrecy of their hearts they always sacrifice to the Lord.” Hence: “A sacrifice to God is a contrite spirit” (Psalm 50). And elsewhere: “My vows are upon me, O God” (Psalm 55), etc.

(ID.) He recalls that God struck the firstborn of Egypt. At that point the Egyptians did not pretend as before, but openly compelled the people of God to leave, saying: “We shall all die” (Exodus 11).

### VERSE 15

“Your almighty word.” The Son, of whom it is said: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), etc. He is called the arm and right hand because of the effective power of divine might. At that time, through the ministry of an angel, he carried out his judgments against the firstborn of the Egyptians; afterward he sanctified the firstborn of the Hebrews for himself. Now also, through the water of baptism, he saves the multitude of believers and destroys the multitude of spiritual enemies.

### VERSE 19

“Visions.” (RAB.) This is an expression of divine goodness, which chastises sinners so that they may abstain and repent. But if they abuse God’s patience, they will be punished eternally without excuse.

### VERSE 20

“But then it touched even the righteous.” (RAB.) He recalls, etc., up to “through whom we may escape destruction.”

### VERSE 24

“For in the robe reaching to the feet.” (RAB.) The Hebrews attribute linen to the earth, etc., up to “in the priestly figure he foresaw Christ who was to come; but because he saw him clothed in flesh, he believed him to be not God but merely a human being. Hence: ‘If they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory’” (1 Corinthians 2).

## CHAPTER XIX

“But for the ungodly, etc.” Against the enemies of God’s people, vengeance came upon them to the point of destruction, because they corrected neither their life nor their conduct. For they feigned repentance with deceptive arguments and therefore did not deserve pardon. Thus Pharaoh, although afflicted by the plagues and promising that he would release God’s people, after a brief respite returned to his habitual cruelty until he was drowned by the waves in the Red Sea. For if the persecutors of the Christian name persist in their wickedness, they will learn through punishment how powerful God’s justice is.

### VERSE 8

“Seeing your wonders.” Thus we ought to give joyful thanks to our liberator, saying: “Bless the Lord, O my soul” (Psalm 103). Hence the Apostle: “Pray without ceasing; give thanks in all things” (1 Thessalonians 5).

### VERSE 10

“The earth brought forth.” Notice that for God’s enemies the earth produced flies and the river frogs; but for God’s worshipers the earth gave fruit and the sea provided food of flesh. For it is fitting that divine providence should provide nourishment for the faithful through its works, while through the creature subject to it it should inflict upon its enemies a fitting punishment.

“For they were justly suffering.” (RAB.) Those who did not recognize the way of truth, etc., up to “and did not find the door, which is Christ.”

### VERSE 17

“The elements within themselves.” Just as different sounds in an instrument agree in the harmony of melody through measured arrangement, so the differing elements, while preserving the law of nature, are bent to the Creator’s will. For he did not create a creature opposed to himself, but one wholly consonant with his will. Hence one may conclude, etc.

(RAB.) Human beings and beasts, etc., up to “so that it might be evident that the elements of the world served not only their own created order, but also the will of the Creator.”

### VERSE 20

“For in all things you have magnified.” The merciful and compassionate Lord is always present to his faithful, whom he continually protects and governs; at times he purifies them through martyrdom. Hence: “The furnace tests the potter’s vessels, and temptation through tribulation tests righteous people” (Ecclesiasticus 27). For “many are the tribulations of the righteous, and the Lord delivered them from them all.”

[Col. 1183]

# THE BOOK OF ECCLESIASTICUS (G)*

## CHAPTER I

[Col. 1183C]

### VERSE 1

“All wisdom, etc.” (RAB., on Ecclesiasticus, vol. 3.) He begins with the eternal wisdom of God, which is Christ, who is always with the Father before the ages, according to the saying: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God” (John 1). “It is from the Lord God.” For Christ is the fountain of life and the true light; he is born from the Father, and all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made (ibid.). Whoever lacks this wisdom walks in darkness and does not know where he is going. For “the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God,” and “the prudence of the flesh is death” (Wisdom 11).

### VERSE 2

“The sand of the sea and the drops of rain.” (RAB., in the same place.) He compares bodily things with spiritual things, so that what is altogether impossible may be inferred from things exceedingly difficult. If no one can count these things, which were established with definite number, measure, and weight, how much less can anyone investigate God’s wisdom, which is without beginning or end, ineffable and immeasurable?

### VERSE 4

“She was created before all things.” Created according to his humanity in the plan of God the Father, he was predestined to become incarnate for the salvation of the human race. It should be noted, however, that because of the unity of the person Christ is sometimes said to have been begotten and sometimes created.

### VERSE 5

“The fountain of wisdom.” The origin of all wisdom proceeds from the Word of God, who is God from God and remains eternally with the Father in heaven. But having entered the world through the dispensation of his humanity, he gave commandments of salvation. Hence: “You have the words of eternal life” (John 6).

### VERSE 6

“The root of wisdom.” He shows that no one can penetrate the depth of God or comprehend the greatness of his goodness and mercy. Therefore, for the liberation and illumination of the human race, he deigned to become human. Hence: “Who will declare his generation?” (Isaiah 53).

### VERSE 9

“He himself created her.” He arranged the coming of the Only-Begotten—through the Word coeternal with himself and with the Holy Spirit—namely, how he would come for the salvation of the world through birth from the Virgin, restore creation, and recall humanity to the knowledge and love of himself, giving it the gift of the Holy Spirit, so that by this gift it might be released forever.

### VERSE 11

“The fear of the Lord is glory, etc.” “Blessed is the man who fears the Lord; he greatly delights in his commandments. Glory and riches are in his house” (Psalm 3), etc.

“The fear of the Lord.” There are two kinds of fear. Concerning one it is said: “There is no fear in love” (John 4), etc. Those who possess this fear cease to sin because of their dread of Gehenna and correct their lives. It introduces love, but it is also cast out. For one who fears in this way does not yet love or desire good things, but avoids evil; nevertheless, he corrects himself and begins to desire good things.

Concerning the other it is written: “The holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psalm 19). Each person fears losing the good things and the presence of God, which he desires to enjoy eternally. Concerning this it is said:

### VERSE 12

“The fear of the Lord will delight the heart.” This grants inward sweetness and, in the future, eternal life.

### VERSE 14

“Love.” (RAB.) The true love of God is wisdom, etc., up to “itself will be the reward in the future.” Hence: “You will fill me with joy in your presence; delights are in your right hand” (Psalm 15), etc.

### VERSE 17

“The fear of the Lord.” Without the fear of God and observance of his commandments, there is no religion. Hence: “If anyone thinks he is religious but does not bridle his tongue and deceives his heart, his religion is worthless” (James 1).

### VERSE 19

“For one who fears the Lord.” Namely, the one who through the fear of God preserves the rule of righteousness in faith, doctrine, and conduct.

### VERSE 23

“And he saw.” (RAB.) All things are in his sight; he preserves for each person a fitting recompense.

### VERSE 25

“Branches.” Through divine wisdom a person possesses knowledge of avoiding evil and understanding for doing good. It works both in the hearer at the end. Hence: “Whoever listens to me will not be put to shame, and those who work in me will not sin. Those who make me clear will possess eternal life” (Ecclesiasticus 24). “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Psalm 110).

### VERSE 26

“In the treasuries.” Both matters are explained in meditation on the law: namely, how evils are to be avoided, how spiritual wisdom is to be learned, and how good works are to be practiced, in which true religion consists.

“Understanding of wisdom.” It prohibits sins and carnal desires. Hence: “A pestilent person does not love one who corrects him, nor does he go to the wise” (Proverbs 15).

### VERSE 27

“Fear, etc.” Because through repentance it cleanses from past sins or restrains from sins yet to be committed. For whoever does not correct himself through the fear of God falls into the abyss of sin.

### VERSE 30

“Good sense.” Hence in Proverbs: “The lips of the wise preserve them” (Proverbs 14). And elsewhere: “The prudent act with counsel, but the fool displays his foolishness” (ibid. 31). It is therefore characteristic of a wise person to restrain his words and to conduct everything modestly.

“They will explain understanding.” Equably—not returning evil for evil, but good for good.

### VERSE 33

“My son, if you desire wisdom.” Wisdom itself shows how you may attain wisdom, because no one reaches the summit of wisdom without preserving righteousness. Hence James: “Who is wise and disciplined among you? Let him show his good conduct in the gentleness of wisdom” (James 3).

### VERSE 34

“For wisdom and discipline.” (RAB.) As has often been said, “The fear of the Lord is the discipline and guardianship of wisdom” (Proverbs 13). Right faith and moderation of conduct belong with it, because without faith it is impossible to please God, and the life of the good is always tranquil. Hence in Matthew: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11).

For whoever truly fears God cannot be without faith and good works, which fill a person with virtues and make him acceptable to God. Hence: “God has given a good person, in his sight, wisdom, knowledge, and joy. But to the sinner he has given affliction and excessive care” (Ecclesiastes 2).

### VERSE 36

“Double-hearted.” A double-minded man is unstable in all his ways—namely, one who wishes to rejoice with the world and reign with Christ.

### VERSE 37

“Hypocrite.” Carrying one thing in his heart and displaying another in his conduct. Hence: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing” (Matthew 7).

### VERSE 38

“Pay attention to them, etc.” It is clear that whoever follows heretics acquires condemnation for his soul, because at the judgment the hidden things of hearts will be revealed, and each person will be repaid according to his works. For “God will destroy all who speak lies” (Psalm 61), and he “abhors the bloody and deceitful man.” Hence: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy.” And elsewhere: “The lord of that servant will come and cut him in two, and appoint his portion with the hypocrites; there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth” (Matthew 24).

## CHAPTER II

### VERSE 1

“My son, when you approach, etc.” He has shown what must be avoided; now he shows what must be done, saying: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and fear.” Whoever wishes to abstain from the enticements of the world and live devoutly in Christ suffers persecution. When he prepares himself for divine service, he arouses the devil’s warfare against himself; and while he subdues certain vices, he struggles against others. By divine providence this happens so that he may both conquer and be conquered, lest he become proud. But because humility and patience are necessary for him, it follows: “Humble your heart and endure,” etc.

### VERSE 4

“Have patience.” As if he were saying: “By your patience you will possess your souls” (Luke 21), because patience is the root and guardian of all virtues.

It must be understood, however, that patience is exercised in three ways. We are scourged by God, but we must beware lest we murmur. We suffer persecutions, losses, and insults from our neighbor, and we must beware lest we repay evil with evil. We are tempted by the adversary, but we must take care not to be bent toward the pleasure of sin or consent to it, or seek present things because of these trials; instead, we must await future things.

### VERSE 6

“Believe in God, and he will restore you.” (RAB.) A person who is afflicted ought to believe, direct the steps of his works into God’s sight, and hope in him. Hence: “Commit your way to the Lord, and hope in him, and he will act” (Psalm 36). Jeremiah likewise says: “Blessed is the one who trusts in the Lord, and the Lord will be his confidence” (Jeremiah 17), etc.

### VERSE 7

“You who fear the Lord, etc.” “The Lord is pleased with those who fear him and with those who hope in his mercy” (Psalm 146). For whoever truly fears patiently awaits his compassion. But “those who forsake God will be confounded and written in the earth” (Jeremiah 17).

### VERSE 8

“You who fear the Lord, believe in him.” He urges those who fear the Lord to believe in him, so that they may attain a sure reward. Hence: “The righteous person lives by faith” (Romans 1). Hence also: “Take heart, my son; your sins are forgiven you” (Matthew 9). And elsewhere: “Your faith has saved you” (ibid. 10).

### VERSE 9

“You who fear the Lord, hope in him.” He commends three things to those who fear God: believing, hoping, and loving. For God is truly worshiped through faith, hope, and love, and through them one reaches contemplation, which is eternal blessedness.

### VERSE 11

“Look, etc.” (RAB.) Here too he says three things, etc., up to “because a contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Psalm 50), etc. And: “God is near to all who call upon him in truth” (Psalm 144).

### VERSE 14

“Woe to the double-hearted, etc.” He warned that no one should approach God with a double heart; now he says: “Woe to the double-hearted and sinful lips.” For whoever thinks and speaks perversely and persists in perverse works will perish eternally unless he repents.

He is like one entering the land by two roads: one who does evil and hopes for good; or one who pursues the works of the flesh while believing that he is perfecting the sanctification of the spirit through fear; or one who performs outwardly what belongs to God while inwardly seeking what belongs to the world. Such people are unstable in all their ways, because they are easily terrified by adversity and ensnared by prosperity.

### VERSE 15

“Those whose hearts are undone, etc.” (RAB.) He continues to teach avoidance of error, etc., up to “upon those who do not accept the truth but believe in iniquity come wrath and indignation,” etc.

### VERSE 17

“To inspect, etc.” Although God inspects everything at all times, he is said to inspect something when he is recognized as testing or rejecting it.

### VERSE 18

“Those who fear the Lord will not be unbelieving, etc.” He alternates between speaking of the love and affection of God, because “the holy fear of the Lord endures forever and ever” (Psalm 19), and “everyone who loves is born of God and knows God” (1 John 4).

Whoever fears and loves God and believes the Scriptures keeps God’s commandments through his actions and continually seeks, through meditation, what is pleasing to him. He will therefore be filled with wisdom and the love of God. For “the end of the commandment is love,” and whoever loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law.

### VERSE 20

“Those who fear the Lord will prepare, etc.” Blessed is the soul that daily cleanses its heart so that it may receive God as its inhabitant. Whoever possesses him lacks no good thing, because he has within himself the author of all good things.

Since the keeping of the commandments and the patience of good works are necessary for this—and through them one reaches knowledge of the truth—it follows: “Those who fear the Lord keep his commandments,” etc.

The righteous person is first of all his own accuser. For just as reward remains for humility, punishment remains for pride. Hence John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves” (2 John 1). Whoever is truly wise is a true worshiper of righteousness, because wisdom dictates the rule of righteousness.

## CHAPTER III

### VERSE 2

“The judgment of the father.” Of God, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth derives, because all things are from him. He loves the things he made and wishes them to remain in the state in which they were made. Whoever hears his judgment and does his commandments will be saved. His commandment is also that reverence be shown to an earthly father and mother. Hence: “Honor your father” (Deuteronomy 5), etc. Therefore it follows: “Whoever honors his father.” Since God established honor for him, he must not be dishonored by his children, because God will inquire by his judgment how his commandment is observed.

### VERSE 4

“Whoever loves.” Namely, whoever keeps the commandments, abstains from sins, and nevertheless does not cease praying for those who offend, because he knows that the merciful judge hears prayers at all times.

### VERSE 6

“In children.” (RAB.) In offspring or in disciples, etc., up to “to honor parents is the first commandment with a promise.”

[Col. 1188B]

### VERSE 9

“In deed and speech,” not, of course, in the womb. From this it is shown that a spiritual father is especially worthy of honor. Hence Paul: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4). And elsewhere: “Let the presbyters who preside well be considered worthy of double honor, especially those who labor in preaching and teaching” (1 Timothy 5).

### VERSE 11

“A father’s blessing, etc.” (RAB.) The patriarchs blessed their sons, etc., up to “they savagely tore the mockers apart.”

### VERSE 15

“Almsgiving.” Namely, that which blots out sin. A sacrifice offered for sin is itself called sin. But whoever shows mercy to parents or to other poor people will receive the reward of righteousness, having been absolved from sins. “Blessed are the merciful” (Matthew 5), etc. And elsewhere: “Whoever has mercy on the poor lends to the Lord” (Proverbs 19).

Hence Daniel says to Nebuchadnezzar: “May my counsel please you, O king: redeem your sins by almsgiving and your iniquities by mercy toward the poor” (Daniel 4), “if perhaps God may forgive your offenses.” Hence the Lord says: “Give alms, and behold, everything is clean for you” (Luke 11).

### VERSE 19

“My son, in gentleness.” Gentleness and humility produce grace; pride and fury produce ruin. Hence: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11), etc. And elsewhere: “Whoever exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 14), etc.

### VERSE 21

“The greater you are, etc.” (RAB.) Above he taught gentleness, etc., up to “it is enough for a person to think piously and fulfill in deed what God has commanded.”

[Col. 1188D]

### VERSE 24

“Among superfluous matters, etc.” (RAB.) That is, do not investigate needlessly, etc., up to “while disputing, they fall into errors and depart from the truth.”

### VERSE 27

“A hard heart.” Because “according to your hardness you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of judgment” (Romans 2).

### VERSE 28

“A heart entering.” A heart that neither cares nor strives to avoid what leads to destruction, such as heresies and profane novelties. Hence it follows: “A heart entering upon two paths will have no success,” etc.

## CHAPTER IV

### VERSE 1

“My son, the alms of the poor, etc.” (RAB.) How valuable almsgiving is, etc., up to “the one who reproves him in words or deeds from the heart.”

[Col. 1189A]

### VERSE 3

“The heart of the poor, etc.” Almsgiving should not be delayed when the ability to give is present. Hence: “Do not say to your friend, ‘Go and come back; tomorrow I will give,’ when you can give immediately” (Proverbs 3). And elsewhere: “Whoever despises his neighbor sins; whoever has mercy on the poor will be blessed” (ibid. 14).

Almsgiving should be performed not out of compulsion, for “God loves a cheerful giver” (1 Corinthians 9). And elsewhere: “The poor widow put in more than all the others into the treasury,” because God does not weigh the amount of the gift but the devotion of the heart.

### VERSE 5

“Do not turn away from the poor, etc.” The poor person should not be provoked through anger but appeased with gentle speech, for “the anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James 1). And: “Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself cry out and not be heard by the Lord” (Proverbs 21).

Whoever can give ought to do so, because “a hidden gift extinguishes anger,” and “a gift in the bosom” extinguishes the greatest indignation. But whoever cannot give should offer a kind word, which is better than a valuable gift.

“Whoever has the world’s goods and sees his brother in need but closes his compassion toward him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John 3.) For faith, if it does not have works, is dead. Let us therefore not love in word and speech, but in deed and truth.

### VERSE 7

“To the assembly of the poor.” Gentleness and humility are commended in these words, because gentleness despises no one, while humility subjects itself to all. It is fitting for a Christian to be approachable and mild toward equals and inferiors, and humble toward elders. Hence: “Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up” (Psalm 130).

### VERSE 9

“Deliver, etc.” (RAB.) Just as he said that generosity toward the poor is almsgiving, so he shows that the liberation of one unjustly oppressed is mercy. Hence: “Rescue those who are being led to death.”

### VERSE 10

“In judging.” (RAB.) No form of almsgiving, etc., up to “and likewise the widow’s consolation from her husband.”

### VERSE 13

“And those who keep watch, etc.” “Blessed is the person who listens to me, watching daily at my doors and keeping watch at the posts of my gates” (Proverbs 8). By the doors, however, you can understand the Scriptures and their teachers.

### VERSE 15

“Those who serve, etc.” Whoever loves the one who begot him will love the one who was born from God; and the one whom the Father loves, the Son loves. Hence: “Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him.”

But because the proof of love is the presentation of works, it follows: “Whoever listens to her will judge nations.” Hence: “When the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you too will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19).

### VERSE 19

“Fear and dread, etc.” Indwelling wisdom directs works and, through various temptations, prepares a person by training and testing for the joys of future life. This is confirmed by the following sentence: “Fear and dread and testing, etc.” For “tribulation produces patience, patience produces testing, and testing produces hope; and hope does not disappoint, because the love of God has been poured out in the saints through the Holy Spirit.”

[Col. 1190A]

### VERSE 23

“My son, preserve time, etc.” Above he commended the gift of wisdom; now he shows its effect. Whoever keeps the commandments of wisdom is cautious amid changes of time and does not abandon the way of righteousness in a time of persecution and distress.

Therefore wisdom exhorts her children to preserve time, because there is a time for every matter under heaven: there is a time for war and a time for peace.

### VERSE 28

“Do not hide your wisdom, etc.” (RAB.) Wisdom should not be hidden from those who wish to hear. For whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples, but blessing will be upon the head of those who sell it. Hence: “Trade until I come” (Luke 19).

[Col. 1190B]

### VERSE 30

“Do not contradict.” One must obey those who are greater, provided they agree with truth and righteousness; otherwise, for the sake of right faith and true religion, in which the salvation of the soul consists, one must contend. Hence: “If your eye causes you to stumble, tear it out and throw it away from you” (Matthew 5). And: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself” (Luke 9), etc.

### VERSE 34

“Do not be quick with your tongue.” (RAB.) “Death and life, etc.,” up to “it is written: ‘The kingdom of God is not in speech but in power’” (1 Corinthians 4).

### VERSE 35

“Do not be like a lion.” In the Church there are heretics like lions. Through the fickleness of their tongue they lead the hearts of the innocent astray, and through the arrogance of their conduct they disturb the gentleness of the simple.

## CHAPTER V

[Col. 1190C]

### VERSE 11

“Do not toss yourself about, etc.” (RAB.) He rebukes fickleness, etc., up to “the duplicity of their doctrine, in which they produce now truth and now falsehood, shows them to be sinners.”

### VERSE 13

“Be gentle.” It is good to listen gently and receive the word of truth, and to speak modestly and prudently. Hence: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1). And shortly afterward: “In gentleness receive the implanted word, which is able to save your souls” (ibid.). It is also said in Proverbs: “Have you seen a person who is quick to speak? There is more hope for a fool than for him” (Proverbs 29).

## CHAPTER VI

[Col. 1190D]

### VERSE 1

“Do not become, etc.” (RAB.) He shows the force of true love, etc., up to “his strength will be shattered.”

### VERSE 4

“Wicked.” The fruit of good works follows good intention, but nothing prosperous follows a malicious mind. For if love is absent, you labor in vain for virtue. Hence: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (James 2). And: “From the one who does not have, even what he has will be taken away” (Luke 19).

### VERSE 6

“Many are peaceful, etc.” Peace must be maintained with everyone insofar as our weakness permits, but one should not take counsel with many, because it is written: “Merciful people are called, but who will find a faithful man?” (Proverbs 20).

[Col. 1191A]

### VERSE 7

“If you possess a friend, etc.” (RAB.) By describing false friends in their various forms, he finally reaches the true friend, because many profess to be friends in prosperity but appear as enemies in adversity. Hence: “If he humbles himself before you,” etc.

### VERSE 13

“Pay attention.” (RAB.) That is, exercise discernment, etc., up to: “I urge you, brothers, to watch out for those who cause dissensions and offenses” (Romans 16).

### VERSE 14

“A strong friend.” A friend is one who shares your love. Attach your soul to him so that the two may become one; entrust yourself to him as to yourself, fear nothing from him, and ask nothing dishonorable. Friendship is not a tax imposed for revenue, but something full of honor. Hence: “You are my friends if you do what I command you” (John 15), etc.

The Lord gave us a model of friendship to follow: we should do our friend’s will, disclose our secrets to him, and he his to us. Hence: “I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything I heard from my Father” (ibid.).

### VERSE 16

“A faithful friend.” Namely, one who is faithful according to God. Such a friend, when one discusses with him what is necessary for the remedy of eternal life and immortality, is indispensable. Hence Cicero says that friendship can exist only among the good; friendship ought to be free and inclined toward every happiness.

### VERSE 17

“Whoever fears the Lord.” (RAB.) The full and perfect grace of friendship, etc., up to “so that you may believe that you will depart from this world daily.”

### VERSE 27

“With your whole soul.” (RAB.) One must approach wisdom with the heart, not with the body, etc., up to “the apprehension of truth.” Hence: “This is eternal life: that they know you, the only true God” (John 17), etc.

### VERSE 33

“My son, if you pay attention.” Wisdom urges us to meditate continually on the divine law. First it urges us to learn; afterward, to apply our soul to this; finally, to incline it; and then to devote diligence to listening. In this way wisdom promises to make a person wise.

For whoever desires knowledge of true wisdom, which is Christ, must first humbly submit himself to catholic teachers and all the affections of his soul to their discipline. Then, turning the intention of his heart away from every evil desire, he must diligently devote himself to hearing the word of God. He must take care not to apply himself to meditation on the law for the reward of earthly things or human praise, but for love of goodness itself, so that he may receive the fruit of true wisdom.

[Col. 1191D]

### VERSE 35

“In the multitude.” As if he were saying: Do not be wise in your own eyes. Do not trust your own understanding. The arrogance of pride has especially overthrown heretics.

### VERSE 38

“Keep the thought in the commandments.” (RAB.) It is deservedly given to him, etc., up to “and continually meditates on the law and fulfills it in practice.”

## CHAPTER VII

“You will not reap them sevenfold.” (RAB.) Perfect vengeance, etc., up to “He takes seven other spirits more wicked than himself” (Luke 11).

[Col. 1192A]

### VERSE 4

“Nor from a king the seat of honor.” One who has neglected the judgment of true devotion cannot carry out the work of righteous governance. Hence: “The kings of the nations lord it over them, but you must not be so; rather, let the greater among you become like the lesser” (Luke 22).

### VERSE 5

“Because he is the knower.” No presumption is more destructive than pride in one’s own righteousness or knowledge. Hence: “There is no one on earth who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7). And elsewhere: “Have you seen someone who seems wise in his own eyes? There is more hope for a fool than for him” (Proverbs 26).

### VERSE 6

“Do not seek to become a judge unless you are able.” Each person ought to weigh his own virtues and, according to the measure of his strength, undertake responsibility for others, lest, while delighting in a position of glory, he become the author of ruin for his subjects; and lest one who is burdened by the weight of his own faults wish to become judge of the faults of others.

### VERSE 7

“Do not sin against the multitude.” Whoever possesses reason and prevails through the power of free will should not sin because of the insolence of his subjects, but should steadfastly resist another’s wickedness. Nor should he think that he sins with impunity if he assents to the will of the majority. Hence: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to the one who does them” (Romans 1), etc.

**Verse 13. — Do not love falsehood.** Every lie is evil, and to cause scandal to one’s neighbors is destructive. How much more, then, to plot fraud against a friend and bring an accusation against him, since “the lying witness will perish”; hence in Proverbs: “As a guilty man who shoots arrows toward death, so is one who deceitfully harms a friend” [Col. 1192C] (Prov. XX).

**Verse 15. — Do not be wordy.** As though he were saying: Do not teach your own opinion; listen to the wisdom of your elders. For it is safer to listen than to speak; hence: “Let every person be quick to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (Jas. I).

**Do not hate toilsome work.** Knowledge was given to sinful humanity so that by the labor of its hands it might seek its livelihood; hence: “By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread” (Gen. III), etc.

**Verse 19. — For the vengeance of the flesh, etc.** For the flesh of sinners, which is corrupted by lust, will be tormented by the fire and worms of hell, where “the worm does not die and the fire is not extinguished.” In the worm, the corruption of Gehenna is signified; in the fire, its burning heat. Or the worm is late repentance for crimes [Col. 1192D], which in the midst of torments never ceases to gnaw the conscience of sinners: thus the fire is punishment raging outwardly, while the worm is inward pain accusing them.

**Verse 20. — Do not betray a friend for money.** (RAB.) “Many have perished through avarice,” etc., up to: “He who hates gifts will live” (Prov. I).

**Verse 21. — For the grace of modesty.** “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the human heart what God has prepared for those who love him.” By this woman wisdom may be understood, which elsewhere is called a precious pearl; when the spiritual merchant finds it, he sells everything and buys it. Hence: “Live life with the woman whom you have loved”—as though he were saying: Follow wisdom [Col. 1193A] and knowledge of the Scriptures, and join it to yourself as a wife.

**Verse 22. — Do not harm a servant.** It is clearly shown how servants are to be cared for: with the affection of children, that is, according to the law of nature; and they are to be disciplined because of the instability of their minds. Hence it says below: “Food and a rod and a burden for the donkey; bread and discipline and work for the servant.”

**Verse 23. — Nor should you abandon the needy man.** One oppressed by the violence of servitude. For whether servants or free persons, “we are all one in Christ” (1 Cor. XII).

**Verse 26. — Daughters, etc.** Just as he teaches that good servants are to be treated with the affection of children, so maidservants are to be treated as daughters, but with discipline. Hence: “Nurse your son, and he will make you afraid; play with him, and he will grieve you. Do not smile at him, lest you suffer, and in the end [Col. 1193B] your teeth be set on edge” (Ecclus. XXX).

**Verse 28. — A woman.** He commends conjugal chastity, removing every detestable union. Mystically, however, he admonishes us firmly to hold the Catholic faith in the true religion, which we first received after baptism, and to reject the faithlessness of heretics.

**Verse 32. — Love, etc.** (RAB.) “The fear and love of God,” etc., up to: “because love covers a multitude of sins.”

**Verse 35. — The gift of arms.** Earlier he promised the cleansing of sins for offerings presented to God’s ministers; now, for almsgiving, he promises forgiveness and the grace of blessing, because just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins.

[Col. 1193C] **Verse 37. — And when he is dead.** Burial of the dead belongs to almsgiving; therefore consolation of the living belongs to it even more. Hence Paul teaches us to rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep. The proof of love is the performance of a deed; hence: “Whoever has the substance of this world, and sees his brother in need, and closes his heart against him—how does the love of God remain in him?” (1 John III).

## Chapter VIII

**Verse 1. — Do not quarrel with a powerful man.** (RAB.) With a proud man. Hence: “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. XXVI), because “there are always quarrels among the proud”; but the servant of the Lord must not quarrel.

[Col. 1193D] **Verse 2. — With a wealthy man.** One who pants under the heat of avarice. From it arise envy, disputes, and things of this kind, for “the root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. VI).

**Verse 13. — Do not kindle coals.** (Same author.) Hence the Apostle: “If anyone is overtaken in any offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI).

**Verse 15. — Do not lend at interest.** (RAB.) Hence: “Drink water from your own cistern, and have the streams of your own well for yourself alone.”

**Verse 17. — Do not judge against a judge.** As though he were saying: Be subject to superiors and judges who judge according to God.

## Chapter IX

[Col. 1194A]

**Do not be jealous of a woman, etc.** (RAB.) He teaches chastity, etc., up to: “he does not consent to heretical perversity.”

**Verse 3. — A woman who has many lovers.** The synagogue of the heretics, which flits about through various errors.

**Verse 4. — Do not be continually with a dancing girl.** The crowd of heretics, which leaps about through various errors, so that when it sees someone attracted by its eloquence it may draw him to itself like a prostitute. Hence: “She ensnared him with many words and drew him on with the blandishments of her lips” (Prov. VII), etc.

**Verse 5. — Do not look at a virgin.** Turn your eyes away, lest they see vanity; do not take pleasure in seeing what it is not permitted to desire. Mystically, however, we must not love the beauty of heretical eloquence or attend to its feigned [Col. 1194B] virtues.

**Verse 7. — In the streets of the city, etc.** The same point under another figure. For the streets of the city are the gatherings of heretics, who separate themselves from the city of which it is said: “Glorious things are spoken of you, city of God” (Ps. LXXXVI).

**Verse 14. — Do not abandon a friend.** Confidence is greater in what is known than in what is unknown. Nor should we turn away from the teaching of the holy Fathers and listen to novel teachers.

**Verse 15. — New wine, etc.** A new teacher ought to strive first to grasp sound doctrine and practice firmly, and afterward to be of benefit to himself and to others.

**Verse 25. — A talkative person.** A heretic, who is always contentious and therefore hateful to God and to human beings.

## Chapter X

[Col. 1194C]

**Verse 1. — A wise judge, etc.** (RAB.) “The government has been placed upon his shoulder.” Hence: “Woe to the land whose king is a child” (Isa. IX)—that is, the devil, who always loves novelties—and whose princes eat in the early morning, that is, before the day of death, saying: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die” (Isa. XXII).

**Verse 5. — Upon the face of the scribe.** (Same author.) “My tongue is the pen of a swift-writing scribe,” because in his place he sends him to preach.

**Verse 8. — A kingdom from one nation.** (RAB.) Nearly all interpreters understand this, etc., up to: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. XXI).

[Col. 1194D] **Verse 9. — To the avaricious man.** After the change of the kingdom, he speaks about avarice, on account of which the power of rule is especially neglected: “For the root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. VI). Pride accompanies avarice; hence: “Command the rich not to be high-minded” (ibid.).

**Verse 12. — And he is king today.** Power and riches cannot prolong life. A limit has been established that cannot be passed. The pleasure of the flesh will be changed into corruption and stench, and finally into worms. Mystically, however, a person who lives in sins and does not repent will die an eternal death; nor will he escape the ancient serpent, the devil, and his beasts, that is, the demons.

**Verse 14. — The beginning of pride.** For there is no greater apostasy than for a creature [Col. 1195A] to depart from the Creator, and this is rightly attributed to pride. Pride consists in a creature’s wishing to be equal to the Creator. This was the beginning of destruction both for the devil and for humanity; hence: “For the beginning of every sin is pride.” Although elsewhere it is said: “The root of all evils is greed” (1 Tim. VI). There is no greed without pride, for no one is proud without being greedy, and vice versa. From pride arise heresies, schisms, slanders, envy, wordiness, boasting, disputes, and things of this kind, which proceed from greed. Greed makes people gluttonous, intemperate, drunkards, fornicators, and so forth; and such people cannot exist without pride. Let us therefore beware of greed and pride—not two evils, but one from which all evils draw their beginning.

[Col. 1195B] **Verse 19. — Lands.** (RAB.) When Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans, etc., up to: “their posterity was destroyed, and the glory of the martyrs was exalted.” Hence: “The Lord guards all who love him, but he will destroy all sinners” (Ps. CXLIV).

**Verse 22. — It was not created.** (Same author.) Vices were not created, etc., up to: “anger arises, which steadfastness in virtue overcomes.”

**Verse 23. — The seed of human beings will be honored.** Holy teachers are held in honor among the good, especially among those who fear the Lord. Hence: “Let the presbyters who rule well be considered worthy of double honor” (1 Tim. V), etc.

**Verse 25. — The glory of the rich, etc.** Truly, glory consists in fearing God. Whoever fears him preserves justice in everything. Hence: “Do not hold the faith of Jesus [Col. 1195C] Christ with partiality” (Jas. II).

**Verse 27. — Great is the judge.** Although earthly power may be great, it cannot surpass one who fears the Lord. For those who fear God lack nothing; “the rich have become poor and hungry” (Ps. XXXIII), etc.

**Verse 28. — A sensible servant.** Literally, this often happens: a person ignoble by birth is preferred to nobles because of knowledge and faith. Hence: “A wise servant will rule over foolish sons” (Prov. XVII). Mystically, however, the ecclesiastical servant who devoutly preserves the Christian religion is placed above the synagogue. Hence: “The elder shall serve the younger.” And: “I loved Jacob, but I hated Esau” (Gen. XXV).

**Verse 30. — Better is.** As though he were saying: It is better for you always to strive to labor in good works, so that the reward of righteousness may be given to you [Col. 1195D], than to consume your days in vanity and lack that bread which came down from heaven. Whoever establishes his glory in the fear of God and the observance of religion should say: “Let the one who boasts boast in the Lord” (2 Cor. X).

## Chapter XI

**Verses 1–2. — The wisdom of the humbled will exalt his head.** It continues: “Do not praise a man,” etc. As though he were saying: Do not estimate the quality of the mind according to the appearance of the body. Hence: “Do not look at his face or the height of his stature, because I have rejected him; nor do I judge according to human appearance” (1 Sam. XVI). For a human being sees what is outward, but the Lord looks upon the heart. One must not be proud of worldly honors [Col. 1196A], because “the world and its desire are passing away.”

**Verse 5. — Many tyrants.** (RAB.) It happens by divine dispensation, etc., up to: “he inherited the blessing of the patriarchs.”

**Verse 8. — Before you hear.** Whoever answers before hearing—that is, whoever desires to be a teacher before learning—or judges the causes of others before understanding them—demonstrates that he is a fool.

**Verse 10. — My son, do not busy yourself with many things, etc.** As though he were saying: Do not be inquisitive about superfluous matters, and do not consent to the perversity of sinners. For not only those who do evil but also those who consent to those who do it are worthy of death.

“My son, do not busy yourself with many things, etc.” There are many activities of heretics who do not preserve the unity of faith or the path of truth [Col. 1196B], and who spend their labor composing books. They are rich in rhetorical and dialectical skill, yet they are not free from guilt, because their meditation is deceitful. Hence Ecclesiasticus: “My son, do not make many books, for there is no end to them.” All the books of divine Scripture, because they agree with one another, are one book. Hence: “In the beginning of the book it is written of me” (Ps. XXXVI), etc.

“My son, do not busy yourself with many things”—with earthly profits or any kind of business—for when one is occupied with many matters, one’s judgment is less capable in each individual matter. Once the care of governing has been undertaken, a person is found unequal to individual tasks while being divided among many; nor does he consider his own losses while handling those of others.

**Verse 11. — There is a laboring man.** He signifies Christian works, in which the poor in spirit abound in every [Col. 1196C] good, while those who labor to acquire riches are needy. Hence: “The rich have become poor and hungry,” etc.

**Verse 18. — There is one who becomes wealthy, etc.** (RAB.) “He stores up and does not know,” etc., up to: “but they leave them to others who distinguish truth from falsehood.”

**Verse 30. — Before death, etc.** (Same author.) It is foolish to praise, etc., up to: “who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.”

**Verse 32. — For just as the more cunning animals belch forth, etc.** (RAB.) He gives the likeness of the more cunning animals, etc., up to: “they plunge into the cage of error and the snare of deception.”

## Chapter XII

**Verse 3. — For it is not, etc.** It is a very grave sin to refuse to repent and not to redeem sins through almsgiving [Col. 1196D], but to add sins to sins. Hence: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke its punishment” (Amos I). This refers to the doubtful and deceitful teaching which they expend in explaining divine Scripture.

**Verse 5. — Give to the good, etc.** A similar statement is found in Tobit: “Set your bread and wine upon the burial of a righteous person, and do not eat or drink from it with sinners” (Tob. IV). That is, because they are sinners, do not share with them—just as those who nourish actors do so while Christ’s poor are hungry. Whoever gives to a needy sinner, not because he is a sinner but because he is a human being, nourishes not a sinner but a righteous person, because he does not love the guilt but the nature. If he means a sinful and impious heretic [Col. 1197A] while they remain in error, one must not share with them. Hence: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. VII).

**Verse 8. — A friend will not be recognized in good fortune.** A friend and an enemy are more easily tested in adversity, because there are many friends of the table who do not remain in the day of need. Therefore he was a true friend who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak?” (2 Cor. XI).

**Verse 10. — Do not trust an enemy.** Historically, he speaks about false friends, whom we must avoid. Mystically, however, he indicates heretics, who are not truly friends; their teaching is full of the rust of error and wickedness, and their speech spreads like cancer, even though they pretend to be faithful and Catholic. Therefore let us not comply with them, nor grant them power, which the right hand signifies [Col. 1197B], lest they cast us out of our place—that is, from the state of right faith. For they strive maliciously to overturn our chair, that is, our doctrine.

**Who will heal him?** A heretic who performs the office of teacher and calls himself a physician of souls. “For if the salt has lost its savor, it is good for nothing thereafter except to be thrown out” (Matt. V).

**Verse 15. — On his lips.** By these sayings he marks those who speak in their hearts and lie in wait to kill the innocent. When they have deceived someone, they shake their heads, clap their hands, and rejoice when they have done evil.

## Chapter XIII

[Col. 1197C] **Verse 1. — Whoever touches pitch will be defiled.** (RAB.) By a comparison he shows, etc., up to: “lest they wish to imitate the evils they frequently observe.”

**Verse 2. — He will take a burden upon himself.** (Same author.) These words instruct us morally to pursue humble things and flee proud ones: “For God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble” (Jas. IV). Mystically, however, he teaches, etc., up to: “because they will show themselves worthy of eternal shame when they are tormented forever.”

**Verse 11. — Do not be, etc.** He does not reject the virtue of humility; rather, he teaches us to maintain firm authority against those who attack the truth, and to resist them courageously.

[Col. 1197D] **Verse 12. — An advocate.** One must act modestly with the powerful of this age, who frequently mock the simplicity of the innocent. Nevertheless, we must give them their due honor, but not against God or his commandments [Col. 1197D]. Hence: “Honor everyone, love the brotherhood, fear God, honor the king” (1 Pet. II).

**Verse 16. — Beware of yourself and pay attention.** As though he were saying: Nothing is safe among lovers of the world, who follow changeable things and change along with them. Hence: “A fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. XXVII). Heretics and false Christians may also be understood here; we must not believe them, because they are inconstant in all their ways.

**Verse 18. — Throughout all life.** (RAB.) After rejecting the others, etc., up to: “because the Lord is near to all who call upon him in truth.”

**Verse 19. — Every animal.** He looks back to what came before [Col. 1198A], so that you may avoid the company of the rich and powerful and join yourself to the one who is your companion in devotion and religion. For this is firm friendship: likeness in virtues joins people together.

**If it will share.** The rapacity of a wolf does not agree with the innocence of a lamb, nor the frenzy of the miser with the modesty of the simple person. There is no fellowship between purity and impurity: “For as a dog returns to its vomit, so one who repeats his folly” (Prov. VI). Therefore there is no equality between the proud rich man and the humility of Christ’s poor man.

**Verse 25. — The rich man is moved.** He develops what he says in rebuke of the rich and the poor: many are those who exalt the deeds and words of the rich; few understand the teaching and virtue of the humble. Arrogant people find [Col. 1198B] preachers, while the humble find despisers. Hence: “Riches add many friends, but the poor are separated even from those whom they had” (Prov. XIX).

**Verse 31. — It changes the human heart.** In the judgment of the face, the change of the mind is detected. Hence: “A joyful heart brightens the face, but in sorrow of spirit the spirit is cast down.”

**Verse 32. — The mark of a good heart.** Because there are many who are hypocritical and counterfeit, it is difficult to find someone in whom heart and face—that is, thought, conduct, and teaching—agree in goodness. When you find such a person, give glory to God, because this is his gift.

## Chapter XIV

**Verse 1. — Blessed is the man, etc.** (RAB.) “By sinning.” Hence [Col. 1198C] James says: “Whoever does not offend in word is perfect” (Jas. III)—that is, in the word whose offense human frailty can avoid.

**Verse 3. — For a covetous and grasping man.** He describes the plague of avarice, which tortures the miser by preventing him from attaining the fruit of his labor: “He who stores up and does not know for whom he will gather these things” (Ps. XXXVIII).

**Verse 5. — The one who is evil to himself.** Literally, these words describe the mind of the miser and the envious person, who do not rejoice in their own goods. Allegorically, however, they signify philosophers and heretics who, without the faith of Christ, gather riches of false doctrine, which profit them nothing but instead bring them eternal punishment.

**Verse 7. — And if he does well.** (Same author.) He had said that nothing was more [Col. 1198D] wicked, etc., up to: “but now he repeats the same point.”

**Verse 9. — An insatiable eye.** Because it consumes life without the fruit of good works and delivers the barren soul to be tormented by the fires of Gehenna.

**Verse 10. — An evil eye toward evil things.** The eye of heretics is always directed toward evil; it does not deserve the heavenly bread—that is, the understanding of divine wisdom—and languishes in want at the table of Scripture.

**Verse 11. — My son, if you have something.** He urges us, having despised the luxury of the world, to offer God the offerings of good works, because the span of life in which we can work is short. After death, which hastens on, there is no time for working but only for receiving the reward. Hence: “Work while it is day; for night is coming, when no one can work.”

[Col. 1199A] **Verse 18. — All flesh.** Just as grass grows on the earth or a leaf on a tree, is born, grows, becomes green, dries up, and falls, so our flesh is born from the lineage of our parents, grows through infancy and childhood, blossoms in adolescence, ripens in youth, dries up in old age, and falls in death.

**Verse 22. — Blessed is the man, etc.** “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord. Blessed are those who search his testimonies” (Ps. CXVIII).

**Verse 25. — He will establish a hut.** That is, performing the office of a teacher, he will join works of justice to sound doctrine, so that he may instruct his hearers by word and example.

## Chapter XV

**Verse 3. — The water of wisdom.** (RAB.) The grace of the Holy Spirit. Hence: “Whoever drinks the water that I shall give you will become in him a spring of water [Col. 1199B] welling up to eternal life” (John XIV)—that is, he will not yield to persecution or heretical perversity.

**Verse 5. — And in the midst of the Church.** He signifies the apostles and preachers of the Gospel, whom the wisdom of God—that is, Christ—placed over the Church.

**Verse 7. — Foolish people, etc.** Pagans, idolaters, and Jews, who crucify the Son of God, following the shadow of the Law and rejecting the truth of the Gospel; or heretics, who pervert the Scriptures.

**Verse 8. — And truthful men.** “Everyone who is of the truth hears my voice.”

**Verse 9. — In the mouth of a sinner.** Of heretics, who despise the teaching of the Fathers and deceive the simple. God does not begrudge his gift of generosity to anyone [Col. 1199C], for he desires all people to be saved.

**Verse 12. — Do not say.** (Same author.) Our evils must not be attributed to God, who has no need of them: “God is not a tempter of evils” (Jas. I).

**Verse 14. — He established the human being in his image and likeness, and gave him free will.**

**Verse 16. — If you wish.** That is, if you wish to fulfill the works and commandments of God, you will have consolation; if not, you will have the burning of Gehenna.

**Verse 19. — For there is much wisdom.** (Same author.) No one can comprehend the foreknowledge of God, etc., up to: “let a person do nothing except what is worthy of the divine sight.”

**Verse 21. — He commanded no one.** God is not the author of sinning, nor does he grant a period in which a person [Col. 1199D] may sin with impunity. He always commands good things and forbids evil ones. Only what is good pleases him; faithlessness and uselessness displease him, because “the Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness” (Ps. X).

## Chapter XVI

**Verse 5. — The homeland will be inhabited by one sensible person.** (RAB.) One who remains in the path of righteousness according to the sound rule of Scripture in faith and works.

**It will be deserted by three impious people.** That is, those who in thought, speech, and deed separate themselves from the fellowship of the good.

**Verse 6. — The eye has seen many such things.** The more ardently a person learns the law of God, the more he is illumined by the light of knowledge [Col. 1200A]. Hence: “Whoever has my commandments and keeps them is the one who loves me. Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him” (John XIV).

**Verse 8. — They did not pray for their sins.** (RAB.) The ancient giants, ensnared by earthly desires and weighed down by the burden of sins; or heretics, who trust in their own power and glory in the riches of dialectic and rhetoric.

**Verse 12. — For mercy and anger are with him.** (RAB.) Divine judgment preserves equality, etc., up to: “Whoever pursues righteousness and mercy will find life, righteousness, and glory” (Prov. XXI).

**Verse 16. — Do not say: I shall be hidden from God.** He rebukes those who think that God does not care about mortal affairs. Hence Eliphaz: “What does God know? Does he judge through the [Col. 1200B] darkness? Clouds are his hiding place, and he does not consider our affairs” (Job XXII). From this Paul says: “The word of God is living and effective, and sharper than every two-edged sword, reaching to the division of soul and spirit, of joints and marrow, and discerning the thoughts and intentions of the heart” (Heb. IV).

**Verse 18. — Behold heaven and the heaven of heavens.** As though he were saying: If he dispenses and comprehends greater things according to his will, lesser things cannot be hidden from him, at whose command all things fear and tremble; and no one can resist his will.

**Verse 22. — And the works of righteousness.** No one can declare the height of his righteousness or endure the strictness of his justice. “By some people; and the inquiry of human beings,” etc. This refers to idolaters, heretics, or false Catholics. Hence: “It is not the hearers of the law who are justified [Col. 1200C], but the doers” (Rom. II).

**Verse 25. — And I shall speak in equity.** (RAB.) One who desires with attentive heart, etc., up to: “but clearly manifests the condition of the holy Church.”

**Verse 26. — He distinguished their portions.** He separated the origins of the individual nations among the different regions of the world, so that each nation, named after its ancestor, might possess its own dwelling places. Mystically, however, divine wisdom, establishing the Church, spread it throughout all the regions of the world and placed it among the various nations, so that in different places it might claim different names for itself. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “Write to the angel of the church of Smyrna” (Rev. II), and of Pergamum and Thyatira and the others.

**Verse 29. — Do not be incredulous toward his word.** Earlier he said [Col. 1200D] how, from the beginning, God ordered his works in knowledge and judgment. Now, inserting a sentence, he urges the hearer not to be turned from the state of uprightness by disbelief in his word; then he returns to the narrative, showing how God’s mercy restored the human race: “After this God looked upon the earth,” etc.

**Verse 31. — He declared the secrets of thought.** Hence: “You have understood my thoughts from afar” (Ps. CXXXVIII). And: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings” (Ps. XCIII).

## Chapter XVII

**Verse 1. — God created.** (RAB.) So that the human being might live and understand, etc., up to: “so that a person might possess love and be good and just,” etc.

[Col. 1201A] **Verse 2. — And he clothed him according to himself, etc.** Hence: “Put on the new person, who was created according to God in the righteousness and holiness of truth” (Eph. IX).

**Verse 3. — And he gave him power.** In this also the human being was made in the image of God: by reason he surpasses irrational creatures, rules and exercises dominion over them, and recognizes the Creator of all things. But because he did not understand his own honor, “he was compared with foolish beasts” (Ps. XLVIII).

**Verse 5. — He created from him.** Just as Eve was formed from the side of the sleeping Adam, so from the side of Christ dying on the cross came blood and water, from which the Church is formed.

**Verse 9. — And the law of life.** The natural law, which he gave to every human being so that each might submit to his Creator and preserve within himself the honor of good [Col. 1201B] works. Or the law of the letter, which he wished to be written for the correction of morals and the restoration of the natural law. For both the natural and the written law teach us to love God with all our heart, all our soul, and all our strength, and to keep his commandments in love of God and neighbor.

**Verse 13. — Before him.** (RAB.) Hence: “The Lord knows the way of the righteous, but the path of the impious will perish” (Ps. I).

**Verse 14. — A ruler.** The angels to whom God entrusted the guardianship of the individual nations. Hence: “He established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Deut. XXXII). Or the teachers whom he sent to preach.

**Verse 21. — Turn back.** Having shown the condition of the human being—namely, how he was created in the image of God and placed above [Col. 1201C] the other creatures—he urges him, after the fall into sin, to return to his Maker, abandoning the error by which he deceived himself. He should beseech God concerning his offenses and flee with his whole mind to divine mercy, rejecting idolatry and the deceitfulness of the devil’s service. Let him also learn the rule of God’s commandments, so that he may remain in the portion of holiness to which he was chosen and persevere in the praises of the Most High.

**Verse 27. — You will give thanks while living.** (RAB.) In the present life, since afterward there is no time for working but only for receiving the reward. Hence: “Run while you have the light, lest the darkness overtake you” (John XII).

**Verse 30. — What is brighter than the sun?** (Same author.) He shows that the structure of the world is transitory and that even bodily light does not remain perpetually the same [Col. 1201D]—how much less the vain thought of human frailty.

## Chapter XVIII

**Verse 1. — He who lives forever.** (RAB.) The substance of created things was made at once, etc., up to: “to know or declare the greatness of his power.” Hence: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son and the one to whom the Son wishes to reveal him” (Matt. XI).

**Verse 5. — Nothing must be diminished.** (Same author.) Nothing is to be taken away from the holy Scriptures, and nothing added. Hence: “If anyone adds to these things, God will add to him the plagues written in this book” (Rev. XXII), etc.

**Verse 8. — A hundred years.** (Same author.) He compares the small number of our days with a drop of the sea and a grain of [Col. 1202A] sand, because in comparison with eternal happiness our life is exceedingly brief and our misery exceedingly great. Hence: “A human being born of woman lives for a short time and is filled with many miseries” (Job XIV).

**Verse 12. — The compassion of a human being.** Few are those who show compassion to their neighbor, while God’s mercy overflows throughout the whole world, for he makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil.
