**Verse 14. — Receiving instruction.** He urges those who receive the teaching of the Gospel to show mercy to their neighbors and to hasten to forestall the day of judgment by works of mercy. Hence: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. V).

**Verse 15. — An evil word.** A gracious tongue makes a person [Col. 1202B] pleasing. Hence: “Whoever controls his speech is learned and prudent” (Prov. XVII).

**Verse 16. — Does it not ward off the heat?** Dew protects the crops from the heat of the sun, and a person who speaks a good word protects another from the wickedness of anger. Hence: “A harsh word stirs up quarrels, but a gentle one calms those that have arisen” (Prov. XV).

**Verse 18. — A fool will rebuke sharply.** (RAB.) In the mouth of a fool there are quarrels, etc., up to: “they defile others with a lying word.”

**Verse 19. — Prepare justice.** So that you may see what in yourself pleases or displeases God and correct your offenses.

**Verse 20. — Before judgment.** (RAB.) These words warn us always to be prepared and not to flatter ourselves with foolish security, but to labor in God’s service until the end of life.

[Col. 1202C] **Verse 23. — Before prayer.** When you stand to pray, forgive whatever you may have against anyone.

**Verse 24. — Remember.** Hence: “The Lord is righteous and has loved righteousness; his face has seen equity” (Ps. X).

**Verse 25. — Of poverty.** The poverty that will follow this life, so that you may make friends who will receive you into eternal dwellings.

**Verse 26. — All these things.** Spring, summer, autumn, winter, day, and night never all rest; nevertheless, compared with eternity, they all pass quickly, and all things are closed before the eyes of the Lord by a fixed end. He himself, however, always remains the same, and his years will not fail.

**Verse 27. — A wise person.** Blessed is the person who is always fearful, so that he may beware of his sins and fulfill the commandments [Col. 1202D] of the Lord: “For the beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord. Good understanding belongs to all who practice it” (Ps. CX).

**Verse 28. — To the one who finds it.** That is, when he has found it and received its recognition, it will itself provide a confession of right preaching and zeal for good works.

**Verse 29. — Sensible people.** As though they were shrewd, they recognize wisdom, and as sensible people they demonstrate prudence in their words and deeds.

**Verse 33. — Do not be mediocre.** He urges us toward works of mercy. For if we are lazy, not only will temporal comforts be lacking to us, but also future goods for our souls, when temporal almsgiving will be rewarded with an eternal recompense.

## Chapter XIX

[Col. 1203A]

**Verse 1. — A drunken laborer.** (RAB.) He refers back to what came before, where he said: “Do not take pleasure in crowds,” in which, that is, the vice of drunkenness is thought to be insignificant, although it is the loss of good things and the multiplication of crimes.

**Moderate things.** An idle word, laughter, feasting, drinking, and things of this kind.

**Verse 2. — And women.** (RAB.) Fornication, by which, having abandoned the truth of the faith, people join themselves to demons.

**Verse 3. — He joins himself to fornicators.** He shows them to be blameworthy, because, having abandoned true wisdom, they have become fools and join themselves to fornicators.

**Whoever believes, etc.** He describes fickleness of spirit, which is weak and changeable. Hence: “A fool changes like the moon.”

“Whoever believes.” The Apostle speaks about love: “It believes all [Col. 1203B] things, hopes all things, endures all things” (1 Cor. XII). But there he is describing the perfection of good will, which is always ready for every good work. Here, however, he describes fickleness of spirit, which lacks a stable condition.

**Verse 7. — Do not repeat a harsh and wicked word.** (RAB.) That is, after weeping, etc., up to: “do not repeat it in an evil deed.”

**Verse 8. — To friend and enemy.** He urges us to exercise caution and discernment, lest we disclose our secrets to friend and enemy—that is, to Catholic and heretic—for an enemy, even when he flatters, attempts to deceive.

**Verse 10. — You have heard, etc.** A foolish word does not disturb a fool and a wise person equally. A fool disturbs his own understanding, so that he expresses a groan of grief through a wicked deed; but whatever may [Col. 1203C] happen does not disturb the wise person’s steadfastness. Nevertheless, the one who trusts in the firmness of his heart must beware lest he retain the memory of a harsh word.

**Verse 15. — Rebuke a friend.** We ought to rebuke friends who are sinning with complete patience, because they sometimes sin through ignorance, sometimes through negligence, sometimes through disobedience and contempt. Perhaps, when rebuked with discernment, they may repent and in the future show diligence and caution. Hence: “Restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness” (Gal. VI).

**Verse 16. — There is one who slips with his tongue.** There is a great difference between one who sins through simplicity or ignorance and one who sins through malice. It can happen that someone offends in speech without thinking that what he says is [Col. 1203D] evil; but the one who is full of deceit and wickedness sins more gravely.

**Verse 20. — Wisdom is diminished.** The understanding of mysteries is diminished, but not the observance of God’s commandments. Hence it follows:

**Verse 21. — Better is, etc.** That is, the person who fulfills what he knows through fear of God. Hence: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it will be beaten with few blows” (Luke XII), for little mercy is granted to the one who knows.

**Verse 22. — There is a certain skill, etc.** He begins to distinguish between saints and hypocrites. (RAB.) Thus heretics and hypocrites display the appearance of virtues but do not possess their truth; and whenever they find an opportunity for sinning, they reveal what they had in their hearts.

[Col. 1204A] **Verse 26. — From appearance.** (Same author.) The disposition of the mind is known from outward indications. Hence: “There is no good tree that produces bad fruit” (Luke VI), etc. And: “The mouth speaks from the abundance of the heart” (Matt. XII).

## Chapter XX

**Verse 1. — How good it is.** (RAB.) He prohibited anger in judgment, etc., up to: “and every doctrine is discerned through patience.”

**Verse 2.—“Desire.”** He proves by an example that it is good not to become angry: for just as the desire of a eunuch defiles a virgin but does not beget offspring, so the violence of the wicked simulates judgment but does not preserve the measure of equity.

**Verses 5–6.—“There is one who is silent.”** Here the modest person is praised [Col. 1204B] and the rash person blamed. “There is one who is silent,” and so forth. He explains what kind of silence he praises. Some are silent because they do not know how to speak; others because they know that there is a time for keeping silent and a time for speaking.

**Verse 7.—“A wise man,”** and so forth. The prudent moderate their speech and observe the proper time; but the fool pours out his entire spirit.

**Verse 12.—“There is one who has much,”** and so forth. (RAB.) Namely, the person who through a confession of humility is released from all guilt. “And restoring,” and so forth: when he substitutes a multiplied number of virtues for vices, so that “where sin abounded, grace might abound still more” (Romans 5).

**Verse 14.—“For the eyes,”** and so forth. That is, the intention, stained by various wickednesses and always ready to do harm. For the number seven signifies totality.

[Col. 1204C]

**Verse 16.—“Today he lends at interest,”** and so forth. He displays the instability of heretics, because they violently extort the meaning of their error from their hearers, and therefore are hateful to God and to human beings. Or, the person who seeks repayment in the present for his almsgiving makes himself hateful; hence: “Call the poor and the weak, the blind and the lame, and you will be blessed, because they have nothing with which to repay you. You will be repaid at the resurrection of the righteous” (Luke 14).

**Verse 17.—“The fool will have no friend,”** and so forth. Because he seeks the reward of his labor in this life; or, it refers to the heretic who desires human glory.

**Verse 18.—“How often and how many,”** and so forth. The assembly of heretics is detestable because they interpret the Scripture of God with a perverse meaning and wickedly proclaim their own exposition.

[Col. 1204D]

**Verse 20.—“The fall of a false tongue,”** and so forth. Just as someone falls uselessly on the level surface of a pavement where there are no obstacles, so the understanding of heretics, blinded by its own wickedness, finds a fall on the open path of truth.

**Verse 21.—“A graceless man,”** and so forth. Without the grace of the Holy Spirit; or, “bitter,” because he introduces a bitter and harmful meaning to his hearers.

**Verse 22.—“The parable of a fool will be rejected,”** and so forth. (RAB.) The Jews, who still suppose … up to the heretics who strive by sophistical arguments to overthrow the truth of the Gospel.

[Col. 1205A]

**Verse 23.—“There is one who is restrained.”** Having reproved the falsehood of heretics, he censures the intention of their perverse will. For there are those who, when they cannot sin in action, refuse to rest in their will.

**Verse 24.—“There is one who will destroy his own soul.”** Because, fearing the power of this world, he does not dare to confess the truth of the Gospel; hence: “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him the Son of Man will be ashamed” (Luke 9).

**Verse 25.—“There is one who, because of shame,”** and so forth. There are people who promise many things and deliver few, and make those to whom they promise by lying into their enemies.

**Verse 27.—“A thief is preferable.”** He does not excuse the thief, but by comparison aggravates the persistence of lying. Mystically, however, the thieves are the Jews, to whom it is said: “You who preach against stealing, do you steal?” (Romans 2). Heretics, however, are liars who are worse, because after receiving the grace of baptism they returned to their vomit and insulted the Spirit of grace.

[Col. 1205B]

**Verse 29.—“Wise in words,”** and so forth. Because he demonstrates wisdom of mind in his good speech; hence: “The good man brings forth good things from the good treasure of his heart” (Matthew 12).

**Verse 32.—“Hidden wisdom.”** There is no usefulness in a treasure that is hidden and unknown, nor in wisdom hidden without discernment.

## Chapter XXI

**Verse 1.—“My son, you have sinned,”** and so forth. (RAB.) He gives counsel for when we sin: “For there is no one who does good and does not sin” (Ecclesiastes 7), so that we may not sin again but may repent of past sins, begging that they be forgiven us.

[Col. 1205C]

**Verse 2.—“Serpents.”** (ID.) The devils, who always cultivate the shadows of sin and reign in the children of darkness.

**Verse 3.—“The teeth of lions,”** and so forth. “Our adversary the devil, like a roaring lion, goes about seeking someone to devour” (1 Peter 5).

**Verse 5.—“Reproach and insults,”** and so forth. (ID.) “By harmony the smallest things increase,” and so forth, up to because he abhors the truth of faith and the unity of peace.

**Verse 6.—“The supplication of the poor,”** and so forth. Because God will judge the ungodly who afflict the saints.

**Verse 7.—“Correction.”** That is, judgment upon his sin, because he hardened his mind so that he would not obey the truth.

[Col. 1205D]

**Verse 8.—“Known from afar.”** Heretical presumption is revealed in a rash tongue that speaks wickedness against God.

**Verse 9.—“He who builds a house,”** and so forth. He signifies the heretic who gathers testimonies of Scripture, alienating them from their proper meaning, to confirm his own error. But by the vengeance of just retribution the hardness of his wicked deed will be destroyed. Or, tropologically: it signifies the greedy robber who increases his wealth from the possessions of others and, empty of every good, will be punished for his wickedness on the day of judgment.

**Verse 11.—“The way of sinners.”** The destruction of the wicked is therefore swift, because their way—that is, their life—is full of sorrows and of the harsh works of sinners.

**Verse 14.—“He will not be instructed,”** and so forth. (RAB.) By these sayings he confounds … up to and he himself entangled himself in endless questions.

[Col. 1206A]

**Verse 18.—“It displeases him,”** and so forth. Hence: “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke 16).

**Verse 22.—“Fetters on their feet,”** and so forth. (ID.) Because the ruin of wickedness opposes the steps with which they walk, condemning and reproving their actions.

**Verse 23.—“A fool in laughter,”** and so forth. The assembly of heretics seeks the favor of its hearers through plausible performance and instruction by rhetorical art. The holy teachers, however, likewise mingle pleasantness of speech with their preaching, but in such a way that they do not depart from the path of truth.

**Verse 25.—“The fool’s foot,”** and so forth. Because heretics strive to imitate the sect of their founders, which lies hidden in the dwelling of their writings.

[Col. 1206B]

**Verse 26.—“A fool from the window.”** (ID.) He points out the cunning of heretics and the simplicity of Catholics.

**Verse 30.—“While he curses.”** Not because he curses the devil, but because, knowing whom to be accursed, he does not cease to imitate him. Since he prefers to imitate the devil rather than Christ, he is rightly condemned.

## Chapter XXII

**Verse 1.—“On a stone,”** and so forth. (RAB.) When the foulness of sinners is reproached by the hard judgments of Scripture … up to being reproached by preachers.

**Verse 6.—“Music.”** He denotes those who seek the applause and favor of the people in the Church, rather than arousing compunction through tears.

[Col. 1206C]

**Verse 7.—“He who teaches a fool.”** A vessel fashioned with much labor does not escape its own fragility. Likewise, although the fool is carefully instructed, he is scarcely brought to perfection.

**Verse 10.—“Above a dead man.”** (ID.) One death is the death of the body, and so forth, up to for the death of the body is the end of worldly labor.

**Verse 14.—“With a fool.”** (ID.) He teaches that conversation with fools should not be prolonged, and so forth, up to: “For whoever says to him, ‘Hail,’ shares in his evil works” (2 John 1).

**Verse 17.—“Heavier than lead.”** Hence Solomon says: “A stone is heavy, and sand is burdensome, but the anger of a fool is heavier than both” (Proverbs 27). The heretic sins more grievously than the Catholic, because of the multitude of his many evils; or the philosopher who relies on human wisdom; or the pagan who has not attained faith and sins in ignorance. Hence: “The servant who knew his master’s will and did not do it will be beaten with many blows” (Luke 12). “But the one who did not know will receive few.”

[Col. 1206D]

**Verse 19.—“A wooden bond.”** The wood signifies the righteous, who bear fruit in their season, whose leaves do not fall, and all that they do prospers. The foundation of the building signifies the apostles or prophets, whose preaching supports the Church. Therefore a wooden bond fastened to the foundation of a building is not dissolved, because the faith in Christ’s passion, joined in human hearts to the teaching of the apostles, makes the building of the Church indissoluble.

**Verse 21.—“Like straw,”** and so forth. Hence: “The one who hears my words and does not do them is like a foolish man who builds his house upon sand.”

[Col. 1207A]

**Verse 23.—“Like the heart.”** (RAB.) Just as a clear wall, and so forth, up to so the heart of the fool despises remembrance of crimes and does not fear eternal punishments.

**Verse 25.—“Throwing a stone.”** He shows what preserves a good friend, or rather what alienates him. “Throwing a stone”: just as the blow of a stone brings down the flight of birds, so the force of friendship is dissolved by a word of insult.

**Verse 26.—“Do not despair.”** Concerning his friendship, because once he recognizes the benefit of correction, he returns to the right of his former friendship.

**Verse 27.—“The friend will flee.”** He will not return, not even after reconciliation; hence: “Never trust a friend after reconciliation.”

**Verse 29.—“In a time of tribulation.”** A friend is tested more fully in adversity. For many are friends of the table, but do not remain on the day of need.

[Col. 1207B]

**Verse 30.—“Before fire,”** and so forth. Just as smoke precedes the burning of a fire, so harsh words precede murder; hence: “A harsh word stirs up quarrels” (Proverbs 15). And elsewhere: “Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgment” (Matthew 5).

**Verse 31.—“To greet a friend.”** There are many good things in true friendship: a true friend rejoices in your good fortune and grieves over your misfortunes.

**Verse 32.—“Everyone who hears.”** That is, whoever understands how many good things there are in true friendship will beware of harming a friend by insult or reproach.

## Chapter XXIII

**Verse 1.—“Lord, Father.”** (RAB.) As though he said: “By your gift may I be defended from the abyss of vices.”

[Col. 1207C]

**Verse 2.—“Who will place upon me?”** In his thought he desires the lashes of discipline and in his heart the teaching of wisdom, lest perhaps through ignorance he fail to recognize the dangers of sins and his crimes multiply, for which he may fall into the hands of his adversaries.

**Verse 8.—“In vanity.”** (ID.) Because he places it before the love of God and the desire for eternal blessedness.

**Verses 9–10.—“For swearing,”** and so forth. He forbids an oath, lest it become perjury; hence: “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth” (James 5).

**Verse 13.—“In two ways.”** (ID.) Because through pretense he conceals the truth and sends others into error through falsehood.

[Col. 1207D]

**Verse 15.—“There is another kind of speech.”** Blasphemy, which is worse than the things mentioned above; hence it must not be found among the inheritance of Jacob—that is, among the people of the Church, who overthrow vices and serve God in virtues.

**Verse 17.—“Undisciplined.”** As though he said: “Do not abandon discipline, and do not utter your words with an undisciplined mouth.”

**Verse 22.—“A crafty soul.”** (ID.) Heretics and schismatics have a burning soul, and so forth, up to but they abandoned their former husband and fornicated with idols.

**Verse 26.—“Darkness surrounds them.”** (ID.) Whoever loses the virtue of chastity, and so forth, up to since the face of the Lord is against those who do evil.

[Col. 1208A]

**Verse 28.—“The eyes of the Lord.”** Because for him nothing is past and nothing is future; everything is present.

**Verse 30.—“This one in the streets.”** The lustful adulterer mentioned above, who, like a horse and a mule, runs about in wantonness along the broad and spacious road that leads to death.

**Verse 32.—“So also the woman.”** Adultery is condemned equally in man and woman, and the offspring of such a union is abominable to God. Mystically, however, it signifies the synagogue of heretics, or the soul deceived by heretical perversity, which is abominable to God because it abandons the former husband who joined himself to it in baptism and adorned it with the ornament of virtues.

**Verse 34.—“This in the Church.”** Because her perversity is exposed in the assembly of the faithful through the skill of teachers.

[Col. 1208B]

**Verse 35.—“And the branches.”** Because her sect does not possess the foundation of truth, it cannot produce the fruit of good works.

**Verse 38.—“Length,”** and so forth. Because those who follow God will remain forever in eternal blessedness.

## Chapter XXIV

**Verses 2–3.—“And in the midst of the people,”** and so forth. (RAB.) Because by displaying miracles he urged the people to the praise of God. “Of his virtue,” and so forth: of angels and of religious persons.

**Verse 5.—“I came forth from the mouth.”** Because he is the consubstantial, coeternal Word; because he is not a creature. Yet he is called “the firstborn of every creature,” not in time but in honor (Exodus 4).

[Col. 1208C]

**Verse 6.—“I made in the heavens.”** (RAB.) In the heavens light arises; the flesh is covered by a cloud. For just as by its brightness it surpasses the darkness of the cloud, so spiritual creation surpasses bodily dignity.

**Verse 7.—“My throne.”** (ID.) The human body, not weighed down by any burden of sin but exalted by the power of God, in which the power of divinity exercised its judgments.

**Verse 12.—“He created me,”** and so forth. According to his humanity, conceived in singular purity from the Holy Spirit and brought forth from the Virgin.

**Verse 13.—“In Jacob.”** In the incarnation of the Savior, it was granted especially to the Jews, and he came especially to the Jews. Hence the Jews are represented by Jacob, while the Gentiles are represented by Israel.

[Col. 1208D]

**Verse 14.—“From the beginning.”** The mystery of the incarnation, foreknown and predestined before the ages, remains forever and ever. And he arranged the dwellings of the Church—that is, the order of true religion.

**Verse 15.—“And so in Zion.”** (RAB.) Zion is the Church, which is also Jerusalem, built up from the first righteous person to the last, and in which wisdom bears fruit daily.

**Verse 17.—“In Lebanon.”** (RAB.) Lebanon is a mountain of Phoenicia, and so forth, up to expressing the steadfastness and activity of those who adorn the Church with higher virtues.

[Col. 1209A]

**Verse 18.—“Like a palm tree.”** A tree long-lasting in its leaves and bearing sweet fruits. It is called *palma* because it is the ornament of a victorious hand, or because its branch spreads out in the form of a human palm. The Greeks call it **φοινίκον** (*phoinikon*), because the phoenix bird lives for a very long time. The Church is compared to it because, scorning to bend toward earthly things, she raises herself toward heavenly things, so that when the contest is finished she may receive the heavenly palm and, like enduring leaves, preserve the words of right confession forever.

**Verse 19.—“Like an olive tree.”** In Greek, **ἐλαῖον** (*elaion*) means the fruit, while **ἐλαία** (*elaia*) is the tree, and its sap is oil. It is a notable tree of peace. Through it the Church is signified: she illumines the fields of the whole world with her beauty and sanctifies them by a special grace through the anointing of chrism.

“Like a plane tree.” The plane tree is named from its height, or because it is spreading and broad; for the Greeks call something broad **πλατός** (*platos*). He therefore expressed both the name and the form of the tree, saying: “Like a plane tree I have spread out in the streets.” It is very tender, with soft leaves, and resembles vines; it signifies Christ, who through his members is spread throughout the world, gentle and meek.

[Col. 1209B]

**Verse 20.—“Like cinnamon.”** Cinnamon and balsam are aromatic trees. Cinnamon is so called because its bark is round and slender like a reed. It grows in India and Ethiopia, as a short shrub only two cubits high, blackish or ash-colored, with extremely slender branches. For what is thick is despised, while what is more slender is more valuable. When it is broken, it emits a visible vapor in the form of mist or dust.

**Verse 21.—“Balsam.”** (RAB.) Pliny calls it *aspaltum*; it is born in the same course of the heavens, and so forth, up to those who, mindful of the Lord’s passion, are prepared to suffer for the Lord.

“Like myrrh.” Myrrh is a tree in Arabia, five cubits high and resembling a thorn, which the Greeks call **ἄκανθον** (*akanthon*). Its sap is green and bitter, from which it also received its name. All these features correspond to the mortification of the flesh, which is experienced as bitter for a time but is willingly accepted in hope of the homeland that is ever green. It is compared to a thorn because it afflicts the body in order to save the mind. The drop that flows spontaneously is more precious; that extracted by wounding the bark is cheaper, because it is a greater virtue to mortify a healthy body, to which an abundance of possessions is attractive, than one that is sick or oppressed by poverty.

“Like storax.” (ID.) Storax, galbanum, and so forth, up to storax is so called because it is the flowing and congealed drop of a tree; for the Greeks call a drop **στακτήμ** (*staktēm*).

[Col. 1209D]

“And galbanum.” Galbanum (ID.), and so forth, up to resembling ammoniacum and scarcely woody.

“Onyx.” Onyx is what is called *onycha* in Exodus. In Greek, **ὄνυξ** (*onyx*), in Latin *ungula*, because it resembles a human fingernail.

“A drop.” (ID.) The drop that is also called ammoniacum, and so forth, up to the more closely virtue is joined to virtue, the purer the incense that is offered.

“Frankincense.” Frankincense, as they say, is a tree (ID.), and so forth, up to when the trees are cut, the tear flows, because the contrite hearts of the humble pour forth pure prayer to God. In Hebrew, *libanon* signifies “whiteness”; in Greek, **θοῦς** (*thous*). Hence in the Song of Songs, where we read “to the hill of frankincense” (Song of Songs 4), some manuscripts have “to the hill of Lebanon.”

“Balsam unmixed.” (ID.) The balsam tree is in Judea, and so forth, up to and poured forth the mysteries of salvation. Hence: “And my fragrance is like unmixed balsam.”

[Col. 1210A]

**Verse 22.—“Terebinth,”** and so forth. (ID.) It is a tree, and so forth, up to and they are without blemish before the throne of God.

**Verse 29.—“Those who eat me,”** and so forth. (ID.) We eat wisdom, and so forth, up to: “Taste and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33), and so forth.

**Verse 34.—“David appointed.”** (ID.) The four rivers of paradise, and so forth, up to he sends discipline like light, because his commandments grant eternal life. Hence: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you” (Matthew 27).

[Col. 1210B]

**Verse 35.—“Like the Pishon.”** (ID.) Pishon, which is also the Ganges, and so forth, up to and is said to overflow like the Nile across the lands of the East.

“Like the Tigris,” and so forth. (ID.) The Tigris is a river of Mesopotamia, and so forth, up to because, like a tiger, it moves swiftly.

**Verse 36.—“Like the Euphrates.”** (ID.) The Euphrates is a river of Mesopotamia, and so forth, up to the land enclosed by these rivers is called Mesopotamia.

“Like the Jordan.” The Jordan is a river of Judea, named from two springs, namely Jor and Dan, which unite to form it. It rises beneath Mount Lebanon, divides Judea and Arabia, and near Jericho flows into the Dead Sea.

**Verse 37.—“Like the Gihon.”** Here Gihon encircles Ethiopia; it is so called because it irrigates the land of Egypt. For *ge* means “earth” in Greek. Among the Egyptians it is called the Nile because of the silt it carries, which produces fertility; hence it is also called the Nile.

[Col. 1210C]

**Verse 38.—“He will not investigate.”** (RAB.) Christ is the author of wisdom, and so forth, up to: “No one knows the Son except the Father, nor does anyone know the Father except the Son” (Matthew 11), and so forth.

**Verse 39.—“For from the sea.”** The sea signifies that the depth of wisdom is immeasurable and incomprehensible, since no one can penetrate it except the one God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—who truly knows himself and his counsel, and grants his creature knowledge only to the extent that it is beneficial.

**Verse 41.—“Like a channel.”** (ID.) Because he is God from God, light from light. Tropologically, the Father is called the source of divinity, because the Son is begotten from the Father and the Holy Spirit proceeds from him; the Spirit is signified by water. Hence: “Rivers of living water will flow from his belly” (Job 7). “The water of saving wisdom gave him drink” (Sirach 15).

[Col. 1210D]

“I am like the river Dorix.” Wisdom is compared to a very swift river, and so forth, up to hence the third language of the Greeks is called Doric.

**Verse 46.—“Still further instruction.”** (RAB.) He signifies that the writer of this work considers the book mystical and useful for reading. Historically it teaches morality, and allegorically the mystery of faith.

**Verse 47.—“See,”** and so forth. The ecclesiastical teacher benefits not only himself but also others by writing and teaching. Hence: “Those who are learned will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like stars forever and ever” (Daniel 12).

[Col. 1211A]

## Chapter XXV

**Verse 2.—“Man and woman.”** (RAB.) Hence Paul says: “Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ also loved the Church” (Ephesians 5). We may understand the spirit in the man and the soul in the woman; if they agree in the fear and love of God, whatever they ask will be done for them. Hence: “If two of you agree, it will be done for them” (Matthew 18).

**Verse 3.—“Three kinds.”** (ID.) These things can be transferred to the devil, and so forth, up to because he refused to submit to his Creator.

**Verse 5.—“What is learned in youth.”** Whoever does not learn wisdom in youth does not possess its fruit in old age. Hence: “The slack hand produces poverty, but the hand of the diligent prepares riches” (Proverbs 10). “But whoever meditates on the law of the Lord will yield his fruit in due season” (Psalm 1).

[Col. 1211B]

**Verse 6.—“How beautiful.”** (ID.) A gray head is fitting, and so forth, up to they must not be ignorant of knowledge of the law and of wisdom.

**Verse 9.—“Nine things beyond suspicion,”** and so forth. “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10). There are therefore nine things beyond suspicion—that is, free from every suspicion of falsehood—which right faith produces in a person.

**Verse 13.—“Wisdom.”** This is to avoid evil. Hence: “Behold, the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and to depart from evil is understanding” (Job 28). This is why one thing is added to the kinds of virtues.

[Col. 1211C]

**Verse 16.—“The fear of God.”** (RAB.) Because just as the number nine is incomplete, and so forth, up to but so that the presence of God, which you embrace and desire to enjoy forever, may not abandon you.

**Verse 17.—“Every wound.”** There is no greater grace than true joy of mind, nor a greater wound than the sadness of a deceitful heart in idolatry or heresy, because every evil is contained in its wickedness.

**Verse 18.—“And every wound.”** The one who understands the injury caused by his perversity sees the wound of the heart; but the one who does not correct it through repentance does not see it.

**Verse 22.—“There is no head,”** and so forth. (RAB.) The wickedness of heretics, when compared, and so forth, up to therefore their dwelling is harmful to everyone.

[Col. 1211D]

**Verse 26.—“Every wickedness is brief.”** Every wickedness is small in comparison with idolatry and heretical perversity, because such people sin not through the weakness of the flesh but through the pride of the mind.

**Verse 30.—“If a woman has the primacy.”** Historically he shows how harmful the primacy of a woman is, and so forth, up to she will be contrary to her husband—that is, to the Catholic teacher—by thinking perversely and teaching what is wrong.

## Chapter XXVI

**Verse 1.—“A good woman.”** (RAB.) Just as earlier he condemned the wicked woman, and so forth, up to and in the future she will rejoice in receiving rewards.

[Col. 1212A]

**Verse 4.—“But of the rich.”** Whether rich or poor, whoever approaches the grace of Christ with a devoted mind will enjoy the vision of God forever, because God is not a respecter of persons.

**Verse 5.—“Three.”** By these comparisons he calls those who have separated themselves from the unity of true religion: Jews, pagans, heretics, and false Christians.

**Verse 6.—“The denunciation of a city.”** The foolishness of fools. For just as brute animals do not know how to distinguish between friend and enemy, or between good and evil, so the foolish do not recognize the difference between Catholic and heretical doctrine but obey true and false teachers equally. Against such people it is said elsewhere: “Immediately she follows him like an ox to the slaughter, and like a lamb playing about, and he does not know that he is being led to the slaughter” (Proverbs 7). But the cunning of heretics deceives the unwary not openly but deceitfully.

[Col. 1212B]

**Verse 11.—“A drunken woman.”** He describes the dress and behavior of a prostitute, who displays lust through the movement of her body and the movement of her eyes. Mystically, however, he signifies the heretic who, in the pride of his understanding and eloquence of words, boasts of his fornication, so that he may more easily attract lovers of novelties, itching in their ears, who turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to fables.

**Verse 12.—“The fornication of a woman.”** (RAB.) Through these three things he displays the curiosity of the human mind, and so forth, up to through the pride of life, when it added, “You will be like gods” (Genesis 3).

**Verse 16.—“He will make her bones fat.”** That is, with charity. Hence: “The one who keeps my commandments is the one who loves me, and he will be loved by my Father, and I will love him” (John 14).

[Col. 1212C]

**Verse 18.—“A woman,”** and so forth. Because the wisdom of God waters the souls of the elect and grants them guardianship of the mouth and effectiveness in action. It does not permit them to turn away from it, because everyone born of God does not sin—that is, by violating faith or charity—because he has within him the seed of God, namely the word by which he was reborn.

**Verse 23.—“Golden pillars.”** Teachers shining with wisdom are placed upon silver bases when they are marked out in Holy Scripture by their preaching.

**Verse 25.—“In two.”** (RAB.) Wisdom points this out, and so forth, up to or follows the byways of error after abandoning the path of truth.

[Col. 1212D]

**Verse 28.—“It is difficult to strip away.”** (RAB.) The worst action, not an honorable occupation, is condemned. That merchant is abominable who, through immoderate ambition, burdens his merchandise more with perjury than with its price.

## Chapter XXVII

**Verse 1.—“Because of poverty,”** and so forth. (RAB.) “As in the middle,” and so forth. Here by comparison, and so forth, up to and eternal punishment remains in the future.

**Verse 5.—“As in the shaking of a sieve.”** (ID.) Just as a sieve, and so forth, up to: “Satan demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat.”

**Verse 7.—“As cultivation from a tree.”** (ID.) Every tree, and so forth, up to therefore the cultivation of a tree reveals its quality in its fruit.

[Col. 1213A]

**Verse 8.—“Before the speech.”** Because speech indicates thought. It is as though he said: Let no one praise someone whom he has not recognized through clear signs as worthy of praise. Speech can also be understood as a good work, so that we praise no one before testing his good works. Hence: “Do not praise anyone before death.”

**Verse 13.—“In the midst.”** (RAB.) He teaches moderation and caution in speaking, and so forth, up to: “Whoever does and teaches, he will be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 5).

**Verse 15.—“Speech,”** and so forth. Because their action is contrary to good things, and their speech is inclined toward saying evil and burdensome to hear.

**Verse 17.—“Whoever exposes.”** He shows in what friendship is most seriously wounded: namely, by the evil of betrayal, which destroys trust, does not preserve the equity of friendship, and therefore dissipates charity.

[Col. 1213B]

**Verse 22.—“Like a gazelle.”** The *caprea* is a wild goat, so called as if from “seizing heights.” Gazelles are also called ibexes or *avices*, because, like birds, they occupy high and lofty places and dwell in elevated regions, so that from their heights they are scarcely visible to human eyes. Whenever they sense the approach of wild beasts or human beings, they hurl themselves from the high peaks and catch themselves unharmed on the branches of trees with their horns.

**Verse 24.—“But to expose,”** and so forth. (RAB.) He shows the instability of the betrayer’s character, and so forth, up to: “An apostate man, a worthless person, walks with a perverse mouth, winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot,” and so forth (Proverbs 6).

**Verse 30.—“For the one who makes the most wicked plan.”** Because he does not foresee that his day will come. The heretic or schismatic thinks that his sect is better than Catholic truth; hence he mocks himself.

## Chapter XXVIII

**Verse 8.—“Remember.”** (RAB.) Whoever fears God restrains anger and rage and does not forget the covenant of God, who says: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke 9).

**Verse 13.—“Strife.”** An indiscriminate action; hence: “Do not be overly righteous, and do not be wiser than necessary, lest you become bewildered.” Excessive discipline therefore arouses the heat of fury, and forward speech brings about the shedding of blood.

**Verse 19.—“A third tongue.”** Heretical doctrine, which agrees with neither the Old nor the New Testament, disturbs the hearts of its hearers, and, going from nation to nation, provokes sedition.

[Col. 1213D]

**Verse 21.—“But the wound.”** The destruction of the soul, which heretics bring about, is worse than any bodily torture.

**“Blessed is the one who is covered.”** Blessed is the person who does not consent to heretics and whose heart their eloquence does not overthrow; for just as he is separate from their wickedness, so he is separated from their punishment.

**Verse 28.—“Hedge the ears.”** After uprooting the evil of the tongue, he turns to the instruction of the hearer.

## Chapter XXIX

**Verse 5.—“Until they receive.”** (RAB.) The fear of God cures this kind of disease better. Whoever fears God as always present intends to defraud no one.

[Col. 1214A]

**Verse 10.—“To many,”** and so forth. (ID.) He points to those who do not wish to harm anyone but, through fear of losing perishable things, are unwilling to benefit anyone. Against such people it is said: “Do not store up treasures for yourselves on earth” (Matthew 6).

**Verse 12.—“For the commandment’s sake.”** Mercy must be shown to all who are in need, and charity toward one’s neighbor must not be lost through greed.

**Verse 13.—“And do not hide it.”** For whoever sees his brother in need and closes his compassion against him—how does the charity of God remain in him?

**Verses 16–18.—“Upon the shield of the powerful,”** and so forth. Almsgiving is more effective against the darts of the enemy than earthly weapons, because the latter produces a doubtful victory, while the former produces a most certain one, so that death may be swallowed up in victory.

[Col. 1214B]

**Verse 23.—“Whoever has lost,”** and so forth. That is, whoever does not preserve the unity of faith and the purity of the law but becomes entangled in various errors.

**Verse 20.—“The favor of a surety,”** and so forth. Namely, the teacher who promises eternal life on the basis of faith and good works. This saying censures Pelagius, who places free will before grace, although the elect are freed by grace alone.

**Verse 27.—“Recover your neighbor.”** He advises you to offer your neighbor comfort according to your ability, and thus to provide for yourself, lest you fall into a snare.

[Col. 1214C]

**Verse 28.—“The beginning of life,”** and so forth. (RAB.) He teaches fragility, hospitality, and decency, and so forth, up to and after the sin the Lord made tunics of skins for the first parents.

**Verse 29.—“The food of the poor is better,”** and so forth. Literally: it is better to eat a meager meal beneath a poor shelter in security than to seek splendid banquets with weariness in uncertain places.

(ID.) Allegorically: “The food is better,” and so forth, up to where there is labor and excessive anxiety.

**Verse 30.—“The little.”** (ID.) Let what you have be sufficient for you, and so forth, up to a good name is better than many delights.

**Verse 33.—“Pass on.”** As though he said: Whoever delights in another’s hospitality, return to your own home and feed yourself and others by your labor. Do not seek excessive nourishment for yourself from another’s house. The hospitality of your neighbors is sufficient for you.

[Col. 1214D]

**Verse 35.—“Reproach.”** (RAB.) Mystically, the ecclesiastical man is warned, and so forth, up to in the future judgment he will endure eternal reproach of confusion.

## Chapter XXX

**Verse 1.—“Whoever loves his son.”** (RAB.) He admonishes both carnal and spiritual fathers to educate their sons diligently so that they may live honorably and not run about wantonly through the doctrines of others.

**Verse 8.—“An untamed horse.”** An untamed horse goes over a precipice; an undisciplined son rushes into sin. He therefore teaches spiritual fathers to educate and correct their sons, lest they loosen the reins upon them without measure, lest they fall into the shamefulness of vices and the fathers themselves endure everlasting disgrace.

[Col. 1215A]

**Verse 14.—“Better is the poor.”** Sleep is sweet to the laborer, whether he eats much or little. For the satiety of the rich does not allow him to sleep.

**Verse 15.—“The health of the soul.”** The true health of the soul is righteousness, with which gold and silver cannot be compared, because riches will not profit on the day of vengeance. Righteousness, however, will deliver the soul from death.

**Verse 18.—“Hidden good things.”** (RAB.) He speaks against those who hide the talent of the word, whose knowledge is useless without virtues, like food for the dead and a treasure.

**Verse 21.—“Like a eunuch.”** A eunuch is not suited to the embrace of a virgin; so the worship of an idol is incongruous and useless for those who worship it.

[Col. 1215B]

**Verse 23.—“Joy of heart.”** Because no virtue endures without it. “The greatest of these is charity” (1 Corinthians 13).

**Verse 26.—“They shorten their days,”** and so forth. “Men of blood will not live out half their days” (Psalm 54). (ID.) That is, they cannot possess forever the prosperity they promise themselves.

## Chapter XXXI

**Verse 1.—“A stumbling block.”** (RAB.) Just as Adam stumbled through the forbidden tree, and so forth, up to which shines with the splendor of eloquence and seduces the curious.

**Verse 12.—“Above the table.”** (ID.) Literally, continence, and so forth, up to but let us follow the way of the holy teachers.

[Col. 01215C]

**Verse 13.—“Do not say,”** and so forth. (ID.) As though he said: Do nothing presumptuously, nor put your hand to writing before you have learned.

**Verse 19.—“Use,”** and so forth. As though he said: Love sobriety, act temperately, and do not go beyond measure, lest you fall into the scandal of disgrace. It is therefore fitting for a Christian above all to love humility, to be cautious in reading Scripture, to hold the right faith, to observe moderation in knowledge, and to follow the rule of charity, so that he may be approved before God and human beings.

**Verse 22.—“How sufficient.”** A meager diet is useful both to soul and body, while excess has the opposite effect.

[Col. 1215D]

“A little wine.” Spiritual wine, too, when taken moderately, is useful both to body and soul. Taken immoderately, however, it causes madness and separates one from God, producing anxious care, great disturbance, and perpetual torment.

**Verse 24.—“A sleep of health.”** Sleep is more refined on a small amount of food. Mystically, the person who is sober with regard to spiritual wine rests in contemplation of the truth until the morning of the resurrection.

**Verse 25.—“And vomit,”** and so forth. Physicians say that vomiting cleanses the stomach and reduces bile. Mystically, however, whoever transgresses the measure and is weighed down by carnal sins should vomit out his foulness through confession of sin and return to health through the chastisement of the body.

[Col. 1216A]

**Verse 27.—“In all works.”** He urges us not to waste time but to do good works, so that by keeping God’s commandments we may find rest for our souls.

### Chapter XXVIII

**Verse 28.—“Splendid.”** Literally, he invites to almsgiving: “For whoever sows with blessings will also reap from blessings” (II Cor. IX). Mystically, whoever faithfully dispenses the bread of the word and does not conceal the testimony of the truth will be blessed both in the present and in the future.

**Verse 30.—“For many,” etc.** (RAB.) That is, drunkenness has overthrown many: it diminishes understanding, arouses anger, inflames lust, and reveals the secrets of the mind.

**Verse 31.—“Fire.”** That is, just as fire softens the hardness of iron and makes it glow, so wine inflames the hearts of the proud and drives them to crime.

**Verse 32.—“An equitable life.”** Wine drunk soberly does not take away a life of equity [Col. 1216B], but brings sobriety and the other ornaments of the virtues. “Wine.” It is evident that provocation, anger, and many collapses arise from drunkenness, and that bitterness of soul and the wounds of crimes are multiplied.

### Chapter XXXII

**Verse 1.—“Ruler.”** (RAB.) Whoever presides by dignity ought not to be proud: “Let the one who is greatest among you become as the lesser,” etc. (Matt. X).

**Verse 7.—“A little carbuncle.”** (RAB.) It holds the first place among fiery gems, etc., up to the point where he reverently honors the mysteries of the Lord’s Passion with an appropriate sacrament.

**Verse 14.—“Before the hail.”** (ID.) The flash of lightning will precede the weight of the hail; so the radiance of grace [Col. 1216C] will precede shame.

**Verse 15.—“For one rising at the hour.”** (ID.) He admonishes us not to be sad, etc., up to the one who made us through grace and filled us with every good work.

**Verse 22.—“A man of counsel.”** The more prudent someone is, the more he makes use of the counsel of those nearby, so that he may increase his understanding.

**Verse 24.—“My son, do nothing without counsel.”** These words can be understood of the Catholic and the heretic. The Catholic, fearing God, does everything according to the counsel of teachers and the testimony of the Scriptures. The heretic, however, trusting in his own wisdom, persists in his own inventions; but when his folly has become apparent, he will be refuted by divine judgments through holy preachers.

### Chapter XXXIII

[Col. 1216D]

**Verse 5.—“The inward parts of a fool.”** (RAB.) Just as a wheel and an axle of a cart, etc., up to: “The heart of fools will be unlike” (Prov. XV).

**Verse 6.—“A horse,” etc.** (ID.) Just as there is no reason in a beast of burden, etc., up to the point where he equally opens his secrets to both through the duties of the mouth.

**Verse 7.—“Why the days?”** (ID.) Because above he condemned the fool, etc., up to the point where they may serve as signs and seasons, days and years.

**Verse 8.—“When the sun has been made.”** (ID.) God commanded in the Law, etc., up to the point where he especially approves what is done with order and reason.

**Verse 10.—“From these he exalted.”** (ID.) That is, by his own judgment he distinguished those whom he rewarded for their good deeds and to whom he repaid a fitting recompense for their evil deeds. “And all human beings.” After the arrangement of the stars, etc., up to the point where he condemned the wicked with eternal cursing.

**Verse 13.—“Like clay,” etc.** (RAB.) The Creator has in his hand the mass of the human race, etc., up to the point of determining whom he should harden according to justice.

**Verse 15.—“Against evil.”** The investigator of God’s works finds in them a certain opposition, but one wondrously ordered by God. God is therefore not the creator of evil, since he made all things very good; nor did he make death, nor does he rejoice in the destruction of the dead, but he is the wondrous governor of the whole universe. Thus natures are good and come from God; vices, however, do not come from God.

[Col. 1217B]

**Verse 18.—“Look.”** He admonishes everyone collectively not to neglect the account of his own jurisdiction, because otherwise he cannot have peace and quiet. For whoever loses the authority of his office brings himself into contempt and distress; but whoever wisely guards his position directs himself and his people toward progress in virtue.

**Verse 19.—“Listen.”** Literally, he teaches fathers to govern their sons and raise them with discipline until they reach mature age, so that they may be worthy heirs of their fathers. Spiritually, he instructs the rulers of the Church to retain their dignity to the end and leave their disciples, well nourished, as heirs of their labor. Rulers ought to hold externally what they undertake for the benefit of others.

**Verse 25.—“Food and the rod,” etc.** (RAB.) It is necessary that wicked servants, etc., up to the point that they have, namely, food and clothing, but not the leisure to wander about.

**Verse 31.—“If he is faithful to you,” etc.** (ID.) He handed down the law concerning good servants, etc., up to the point that it is not the person who should be persecuted, but the vices.

### Chapter XXXIV

**Verse 2.—“Like one who grasps.”** (RAB.) He signifies deceptive dreams, etc., up to the point where they may know what they receive from a good spirit and what they suffer from deception.

**Verse 8.—“Without falsehood.”** Having rejected dreams, he exhorts us to believe the teaching of wisdom, which, planted in the mouth of a faithful man, brings the word to completion without falsehood.

[Col. 1217D]

**Verse 9.—“He will explain understanding.”** By instructing others: hence, “Blessed be God, who consoles us in all our tribulation, so that we may be able to console those who are in every distress” (II Cor. XII).

**Verses 10–11.—“But whoever is involved in many things,” etc.** He is changeable in mind and unstable in action. Or, whoever, having lost the unity of faith, follows the various sects of heretics serves many forms of impiety.

**Verse 12.—“Many words.”** (RAB.) He signifies Scripture. Whoever attentively meditates on Scripture and humbly entreats the Lord attains knowledge both of things and of words.

**Verse 23.—“The gifts of the wicked.”** A sacrifice is utterly detestable when it is compared with the grief of a bereaved father. Some weigh how much they give, but not how much they steal. “They gather wages and put them into a pierced sack.” In a pierced sack, one sees when money is put in, but not when it is lost. Therefore those who look at how much they give but not how much they steal put their wages into a pierced sack, because they heap them up while looking toward the hope of their confidence, but lose them because they do not look at themselves.

[Col. 1218A]

**Verse 26.—“Whoever takes away.”** (RAB.) The poor man acquires bread in the sweat of his face. Whoever violently takes it from him is like one who kills his neighbor.

**Verse 28.—“One man building.”** This is what he said above: a sacrifice made from plunder is not acceptable. Whoever offers from plunder seems to himself to be preparing a building of virtues, but he does not consider the crime of greed and plunder.

[Col. 1218B]

**Verse 30.—“Whoever is baptized.”** (ID.) “Wash yourselves,” etc., up to the point where they again commit deeds deserving of mourning.

### Chapter XXXV

**Verse 1.—“Whoever preserves.”** (RAB.) He prays well, etc., up to the point that by doing good he preserves justice.

**Verse 3.—“Of propitiations.”** There is this difference between making propitiation and sacrificing: whoever makes a sacrifice sacrifices; whoever makes a sacrifice and obtains what he requested through the sacrifice makes propitiation.

**Verse 4.—“He will repay,” etc.** Both are pleasing to God: what is offered on the altar in commemoration of Jesus Christ, and what is given to one’s neighbor through charity.

**Verse 10.—“With a good disposition.”** (ID.) Whatever is not given with a good disposition earns no grace with God. For a human being looks at the face, but God looks at the heart. “And do not diminish,” etc. Mystically: the first fruits of crops, etc., up to the point at which both the beginning and the perfection of good work are given by him.

[Col. 1218C]

**Verse 13.—“Sevenfold.”** That is, a perfect recompense. For the number seven, etc., up to the point where it also provides the exercise of the four principal virtues.

**Verse 14.—“Do not offer gifts,” etc.** With God, the quantity of the gift does not matter, nor is the person of the powerful considered, but rather the love and humility of the heart. Therefore a sacrifice must not be offered from iniquity, but from honest labor.

**Verse 21.—“And until he draws near,” etc.** He looks back to the preceding words, affirming that the Lord mercifully hears the prayer of the humble, who do not cease until they receive consolation.

[Col. 1218D]

### Chapter XXXVI

**Verse 1.—“Have mercy on us.”** (RAB.) On behalf of the faithful, he directs a prayer to God that he defend them and bring down their enemies, so that, having been duly corrected, they may again acknowledge God and abandon idols.

**Verse 7.—“Glorify the hand,” etc.** (ID.) He desires that the divine majesty, through the hand and right arm—that is, through Christ, through whom the ancient miracles were performed—renew these things in the time of grace, so that the God of the old and the new Law may be understood to be one and the same.

[Col. 1219A]

**Verse 15.—“Raise up the adversary,” etc.** (RAB.) He signifies through the coming of Christ, etc., up to the point concerning the condition of the Church and the salvation of the faithful.

**Verse 16.—“Zion,” etc.** The knowledge of Scripture, in which the ineffable power of God is proclaimed.

**Verse 17.—“And raise up,” etc.** All the prophets bear witness to the incarnation of Christ, by which God, having become human, would espouse the Church to himself.

**Verse 19.—“According to the blessing,” etc.** (ID.) That is, the order and rite of the priesthood, etc., up to the point where what Aaron represented in temporal sacrifices he fulfills in the spiritual sacrifices of the Gospel.

**Verse 20.—“Every food.”** (ID.) After he had foretold the calling of the nations, etc., up to the point where we distinguish true teaching from false.

[Col. 1219B]

**Verse 24.—“The appearance of a woman.”** The grace of Christ, which through preaching heals souls and moderates the desire of the flesh. It abounds in the Church, whose desire is above every human desire, because in it are the beauty of virtues and the loveliness of teaching. “Above every.” No human desire can be compared with this desire, because “Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain; the woman who fears God is the one who will be praised” (Prov. XXXI).

**Verse 25.—“There is no man.”** Christ, who surpasses human nature. Hence, “You are beautiful beyond the sons of men” (Ps. XLIV). For he committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth.

**Verse 26.—“Help.”** The help of the Church is according to Christ’s dispensation. Hence, “My just help is from the Lord” (Ps. VII), etc. He himself is its pillar of infinity and the rest from labor.

**Verse 28.—“Who has no nest.”** That is, the Church, where the souls of the elect nourish children of good works. Hence, “The sparrow has found a house for itself, and the turtledove a nest where it may place its young” (Ps. LXXXIII).

### Chapter XXXVII

**Verse 1.—“Every friend.”** (RAB.) Above he more carefully described the true and false friend, saying: “And he will not remain in the day of tribulation.”

**Verse 2.—“But a companion.”** A true friend loves with his whole heart and does good by his actions. Hence, “Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth” (I John III).

**Verse 3.—“O presumption.”** He condemns hypocrisy, when an evil person pretends to be good by covering over dry wickedness—in which, evidently, there is no richness of charity or mercy.

[Col. 1219D]

**Verse 5.—“For the sake of the belly.”** For gluttony, not for friendship. Heretics can be understood as false friends: they do everything correctly in appearance, as though they were advisers of souls, when they are actually traitors. Hence, “Beware of false prophets” (Matt. VII), etc. “With a father-in-law.” A father-in-law, who is related through the female side, displays a womanly and changeable disposition; so too does jealousy, which is especially characteristic of souls.

**Verse 8.—“Every counselor.”** He continues to teach that every precaution must be taken in accepting friends and counselors. For many pretend to be friends and counselors [Col. 1220A] while laying snares. Hence Jeremiah: “Let each one guard himself from his neighbor” (Jer. IX).

**Verse 14.—“Do not attend.”** (RAB.) He enumerated various kinds of counselors, in which he indicated many persons who deviate from the truth. Hence he commanded that one should not seek counsel with such people, whose counsel is dangerous. The counselor’s prudence, faith, intention, and religion must therefore be examined beforehand.

**Verse 18.—“The soul of a holy man.”** Having shown the diversity of counselors, he adds how much the knowledge of the saints, infused by the Holy Spirit, surpasses human wisdom.

**Verse 22.—“A skilled man.”** Since he had spoken about the tongue, he continues with good and bad teachers.

**Verse 28.—“The life of a man.”** (ID.) The present life of human beings is not uncertain before him [Col. 1220B]. Hence, “The days of a human being are short; the number of my months is with you” (Job XIV).

**Verse 32.—“Do not be greedy.”** According to the literal sense, he praises frugality and condemns overindulgence, which brings the one who devours to illness. Mystically, however, he admonishes us to be temperate in temporal matters. Hence, “You have found honey; eat what is sufficient for you” (Prov. XXV), etc. And elsewhere: “Do not be wiser than is necessary” (Rom. XII).

### Chapter XXXVIII

**Verse 1.—“Honor the physician.”** (RAB.) He wants us to be discerning, etc., up to the point that both are to be honored, but spiritual physicians are to be preferred.

**Verse 5.—“Is it not from wood?”** He touches upon the ancient narrative [Col. 1220C], because in the desert of Shur the children of Israel found bitter water, but God showed Moses a piece of wood which, when thrown into the water, sweetened it. Historically, this demonstrates that the medicine of wood sweetens waters. Mystically, however, the bitter water signifies the Law; when the confession of the cross and its sacrament are joined to it, it becomes drinkable.

**Verse 7.—“By these he heals.”** (ID.) Against different illnesses, physicians apply different remedies—foods and drinks, plasters, and ointments—so that the medicines may suit the diseases. Spiritual physicians act similarly.

**Verse 10.—“Turn away.”** This is like: “Turn away from evil and do good.” “And from every,” etc.—not merely so that you may be sound in body, but so that you may be innocent in your hands and pure in heart.

[Col. 1220D]

**Verse 11.—“Give sweetness.”** The sacrifice of bread and wine offered in memory of the Lord’s Passion especially heals the wounds of souls, and is greatly necessary not only for the living but also for the dead.

**Verse 15.—“He will fall into the hands of a physician.”** (ID.) Of illness and distress, etc., up to the point where they earnestly beseech the Lord to direct their work and grant relief to the sick.

**Verse 16.—“My son,” etc.** Since he has discussed illnesses and the treatments of physicians, he adds the funeral rites of the dead.

**Verse 21.—“Remember the last things.”** (ID.) An admonition of good fathers, so that sons may prepare for themselves provisions for the journey consisting of good works.

[Col. 1221A]

**Verse 22.—“For there is no conversion.”** As if he were saying: Therefore be cautious in everything, lest at the death of a neighbor you grieve more than is fitting.

**Verse 24.—“In repose.”** As if to say: Preserve continually the memory of the one who is dying; trust and take courage in hope, lest he fail at the final moment.

**Verse 26.—“Whoever holds the plow.”** He signifies the holy preachers, who at all times, by teaching and exhorting, instruct their hearers so that they may draw forth the virtue of the inner person and reform the human soul according to the image of God. Hence, “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (I Cor. III). And elsewhere: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. IV). As many kinds of virtues as there are, so many operations and teachings do they impress upon the minds of the elect through instruction.

[Col. 1221B]

**Verse 28.—“So does every craftsman,” etc.** The order of preachers, who carry out their ministry through diverse offices, adapting their teaching to their hearers. They form the fragile and infirm through word and example, so that they may make vessels for honor.

**“He will give his heart.”** When, through the traces of good works, he displays to those subject to him the unchanging way of life amid the instability of the present life.

**Verse 33.—“On his arm.”** (RAB.) Because through many examples, etc., up to the point where, in the furnace of the heart, he solidifies the activity of the disciples with the fire of charity.

### Chapter XXXIX

**Verse 15.—“If he has remained.”** (RAB.) The members of Christ have everything from him, who is the power and wisdom of the Father.

[Col. 1221C]

**Verse 17.—“Obey me.”** (ID.) Understand my teaching, you minds of the elect generated through baptism, and produce the fruit of martyrdom throughout the course of mortal life.

**Verse 20.—“And with harps.”** (ID.) Hence: “Give thanks to the Lord with the harp” (Ps. XXXII). The harp is a hollow cavity of wood at the bottom of its body, etc., up to the point where they come to us from above according to the form of the psaltery.

**Verse 22.—“At his word.”** (ID.) When he gathered the waters, etc., up to the point where either the water of persecution is restrained by God’s dispensation.

**Verse 24.—“The works of all flesh.”** The presence of God precedes all things, and whatever happens temporally is present to him without time [Col. 1221D]. Nothing, therefore, is new or changeable in his sight (Acts I).

**Verse 26.—“It is not for us to say,” etc.** He forbids us to be curious and investigate what it is not fitting for us to know. For everything will be revealed in its own time, when the Lord illuminates the hidden things of darkness and reveals the purposes of hearts.

**Verse 27.—“Blessing,” etc.** Just as, after the waters of the Flood had poured forth, they receded so that the dry land might appear and produce vegetation, so after the destruction of the wicked, the elect are given the opportunity to bear fruit.

**Verse 31.—“The beginning of necessity.”** Before the Flood, human beings were nourished by the natural food of the earth; meat had not yet been granted.

[Col. 1222A]

**Verse 35.—“Fire, hail.”** (RAB.) Before sin, everything obeyed the human being; after sin, however, the world struggles against him. Hence famine and death, and a thousand dangers of death; wild beasts also rage against him, as does the sword of heavenly vengeance.

**Verse 37.—“In the commandments.”** Because, according to the heavenly sentence, at the appropriate time a fitting vengeance will lay waste the sinners.

**Verse 38.—“Therefore from the beginning I was confirmed.”** He looks back to the preceding words, where he said: “It is not for us to say,” etc. For he sees the incomprehensible judgments of God and his unsearchable ways, and does not dare rashly to speak or write anything about them. Rather, discussing these matters with moderation, he leaves manifest not the cause but the manner of the divine plan.

**Verse 40.—“It is not for us to say.”** He gives useful advice [Col. 1222B], that we should not carelessly examine God’s works, but praise and bless the Creator in everything.

**Verse 41.—“And now in all its own time.”** As if he were saying: Do not say that former times were better than the present. Virtues make days good; vices make them bad.

### Chapter XL

**Verse 2.—“Thoughts.”** (RAB.) He enumerates the evils that a human being suffers for sins.

**Verse 6.—“A little while.”** Because the dead and insensible flesh seems to rest for a time, but the soul already feels pain and, after the resurrection, will live with its body in eternal punishments.

**Verse 7.—“He was troubled.”** (ID.) Therefore the wicked will be tortured in punishment, etc., up to the point concerning the noble and the ignoble [Col. 1222C].

**Verse 10.—“And because of them the cataclysm came to be.”** A manifold punishment was assigned to sinful humanity, so that, corrected, it might repent and thereafter beware. But because humanity neglects this and grows worse amid punishments, God brings a flood upon the world to destroy the human being whom he created. Compared with the punishment to come, however, nothing is what a human being suffers in the present.

**Verse 11.—“And all the waters.”** (ID.) The works of sinners do not acquire the fruit of a heavenly reward, but the destruction of punishments.

**Verse 13.—“The substance of the unrighteous.”** They begin to sprout, but waver in temptation and suddenly wither at the first heat of persecution.

**Verse 15.—“The descendants of the wicked are not many.”** Often we see the offspring of the wicked quickly fail, especially when the children imitate the wickedness of their fathers.

[Col. 1222D]

**Verse 18.—“The life of one who is self-sufficient.”** Sleep is sweet to the laborer, whether he eats little or much. “You will find a treasure.” For the one who believes and does Christ’s commandments truly proves himself to be a Christian.

**Verse 20.—“Wine and music gladden the heart.”** These things naturally soothe and cheer the soul, but love of wisdom and a tongue teaching sweetly strengthen the understanding much more.

**Verse 22.—“The eye will desire grace and beauty.”** That is, the adornment of the temple and the variety of worship that the former people possessed under the Law; the preaching of the Gospel, sown throughout the world, surpasses it in the freshness of good works.

[Col. 1223A]

**Verse 26.—“Resources and virtues.”** (RAB.) Riches given in the Lord, etc., up to the point concerning these and all the resources of the world.

**Verse 30.—“A man who looks around.”** For it is foolish to be idle and seek payment from another’s labor. Each person will receive according to his works.

**Verse 32.—“Poverty will be trampled in the mouth of the imprudent,” etc.** Whoever prefers to lie sluggishly idle and not benefit his neighbors by teaching will eventually burn with the pains of hell and tardy repentance.

### Chapter XLI

**Verse 1.—“O death,” etc.** (RAB.) For the one who loves the prosperity and riches of the world, bodily death is bitter, because he neglects the joys of the life to come.

[Col. 1223B]

**Verse 5.—“This judgment.”** (ID.) It is common to all flesh, and no one can escape it, even if he lives a hundred or a thousand years or longer. Hence: “What human being is there who will live and not see death?” (Ps. LXXXVIII).

**Verse 8.—“Children of abominations.”** The children of sinners are abominable—namely, those who have imitated their wicked fathers.

**Verse 10.—“From a wicked father.”** Whoever raises his children badly or destroys them by his example is guilty of their destruction. Or, whoever produces evil works from a perverse will will be condemned for them.

**Verse 13.—“Into destruction.”** He responds to the preceding discussion, in which he spoke about temporal death. Just as a human being, created from the earth, returns to the earth because of original sin, although he will rise in incorruption, so the wicked, cursed for their sins, will go with body and soul into eternal destruction.

[Col. 1223C]

**Verse 15.—“Take care of a good name,” etc.** So that you may live well and religiously. A good name is acquired in this way.

**Verse 18.—“Better is the person who hides his folly,” etc.** “Whoever hides grain will be cursed among the peoples, but blessing will be upon the head of those who sell.”

**Verse 19.—“Nevertheless, return to the things that proceed.”** Since he had stated that a good name and a good and useful life are beneficial, and had reproved those who conceal knowledge, he urges them to return to the study of teaching, because it is not good to be irreverent and disobedient toward one’s teacher.

[Col. 1223D]

**Verse 20.—“It is not good to observe every irreverence.”** According to the literal sense, he instructs us to avoid vices and devote ourselves to virtues, and not, after rejecting better things, choose worse ones, which are followed by eternal confusion.

**Verse 26.—“Do not turn your face away from your neighbor,” etc.** (RAB.) When the angels gather every scandal from the Church, etc., up to the point where he mingled himself with the fornications of heretics.

**Verse 27.—“Do not look upon the wife of another man,” etc.** Carnal desire ought to be subject to the spirit; we must not investigate it or subject ourselves to its suggestions.

### Chapter XLII

[Col. 1224A]

**Verse 1.—“Do not double your speech,” etc.** (RAB.) He forbids speaking both good and evil at the same time from the hidden place of the heart. Hence: “Does a fountain pour forth sweet and bitter water from the same opening?”

**Verse 4.—“Concerning equality of the balance,” etc.** (ID.) Equity must be followed everywhere, etc., up to the point where we also govern those subject to us with disciplined discretion.

**“Concerning equality of the balance.”** These words show how displeasing hypocrisy and deceit are to the Lord: “A deceitful balance is an abomination before God.” Whoever weighs the case of a poor person differently from that of a powerful person; or considers his own errors lighter than those of others; or lays unbearable burdens on people’s shoulders; or does good publicly and evil secretly—is abominable to the Lord [Col. 1224B].

**Verse 5.—“And to the worst servant.”** He signifies that a servant who is not corrected by words must be restrained by blows. The servant of vices, too, must be corrected by severe discipline.

**Verse 7.—“Where there are many hands,” etc.** He admonishes us to distribute carefully where different wills are eager for spiritual profit. Some seek the word in order to test; others with a desire to learn, but not everything suits everyone.

**Verse 8.—“Concerning discipline.”** Whoever rebukes each person with appropriate discipline shows himself to be an educated and approved teacher in the sight of the saints. Nor should youthful age be despised in a teacher whom life and discernment commend.

[Col. 1224C]

**Verse 9.—“A daughter of a father.”** (RAB.) Mystically, “a daughter of a father,” etc., up to the point where she may transgress the law of God, rendered sterile in every good work.

**“A daughter of a father.”** Literally, he teaches parents to care for their offspring and raise them with discipline, and not to loosen the reins to wantonness and pleasure.

**Verse 11.—“Over a wanton daughter,” etc.** She requires careful guardianship. For if she is left to her own will, she shames her teacher and causes him to blush before the assembled people. Hence, “He serves you dangerously whose face you frequently look upon.” For immodest eyes do not know how to contemplate the beauty of the soul, but only that of bodies.

**Verse 14.—“For a man’s iniquity is better,” etc.** (ID.) A woman signifies either the sex, etc., up to the point where she performs things deserving of confusion.

[Col. 1224D]

**Verse 15.—“Therefore I will remember the works,” etc.** (ID.) Up to this point he has discussed various matters, etc., and afterward he describes the brave deeds of the fathers.

**Verse 19.—“For the Lord knew,” etc.** All the ages of the world are present to him, before whom nothing is past and nothing future. He alone reveals mysteries; he knows the hearts of individuals and observes all thoughts and words.

**Verse 21.—“The great things of wisdom.”** When he revealed to the prophets and apostles the mystery of his counsel, hidden from ages and generations, to the faithful. For he is before all and after all; nothing is added to him, and nothing is diminished.

[Col. 1225A]

**Verse 23.—“And like a spark.”** We contemplate it as a spark in the work of God, because we scarcely perceive a small portion of knowledge from it.

**Verse 25.—“All things are twofold,” etc.** (RAB.) God ordered everything in such a way that things which appear contrary to one another harmonize, such as the elements or the four seasons.

### Chapter XLIII

**Verse 1.—“Of height,” etc.** (ID.) The beauty of the firmament, etc., up to the point where no one with bodily eyes can endure the splendor of divinity.

**Verse 3.—“Guarding the furnace.”** Because he tortures the proud with eternal flame for their evil thoughts, words, and deeds.

**Verse 5.—“And in his words,” etc.** (ID.) [Col. 1225B] Through mystical words he plays with the understanding of the proud. “He hastened,” etc. When the way of salvation and the entrance to the heavenly kingdom were prepared in the preaching of the Gospel.

**Verse 6.—“And the moon,” etc.** (ID.) After he had discussed the sun, etc., up to the point where it is more correctly assigned to April, because in that month it either begins, ends, or is wholly contained.

**Verse 7.—“The luminary that diminishes,” etc.** The moon does not have its own native splendor, but receives it from the sun. So too the Church receives hers from Christ. She seems to diminish in persecution, but shines forth in part; for she grows wondrously toward consummation.

**Verse 9.—“A vessel of camps,” etc.** Because in it resides the multitude of the faithful, which throughout the whole world shines gloriously in the firmament of truth and divine preaching.

[Col. 1225C]

**Verse 10.—“The appearance of heaven,” etc.** The adornment of the Church and the fullness of the saints, whom the exalted God appointed to illuminate the world through the preaching of the Gospel. Remaining in holy words and in the teaching of the true faith, they await God’s judgment.

**Verse 11.—“In words.”** Because in their patience they possess their souls, with their loins girded and lamps held in their hands, awaiting their Lord, when he returns from the wedding.

**Verse 12.—“See the bow,” etc.** The writing of the Old or New Testament. Here it is shown as a gentle yoke to the faithful, but as terrifying weapons to the disobedient.

**Verse 13.—“He encircled heaven,” etc.** When, through the power and wisdom of God—that is, Christ—the Old and New Testaments were established.

[Col. 1225D]

**Verse 16.—“And the stones of hail were shattered.”** The teachers who irrigate the soil of the human heart, bear upon themselves the storm of rebuke, and pour it out at the proper time shatter the stones of hail. That is, by rebuking, they stone the hardness of the perverse heart; the final phrase, *lapident vitale gramen*, is textually uncertain, literally “that they may stone the life-giving grass.”

**Verse 17.—“The South Wind will blow.”** (RAB.) The South Wind, that is, the Auster, etc., up to the point where it signifies the powerful persecutors of the Christian name and sometimes their conversion to repentance.

**Verse 18.—“Storm.”** Through evil spirits, God inflicts various temptations so that they may cause the fervor of faith and love to grow cold.

**Verse 21.—“Frost like salt,” etc.** That is, sterility. Wherever salt is scattered, sterility follows; the devil, through the cold of unbelief, makes earthly hearts sterile for good works.

[Col. 1226A]

**Verse 24.—“Medicine,” etc.** All eloquence fails in comparison with it, and is insufficient to recount its power.

**Verse 26.—“Those who sail the sea,” etc.** Literally, there are many dangers of the sea, and there the wondrous works of God appear in various beasts, as writers on natural things have reported. In the sea of this world, too, there are many demonic monsters and many of their snares.

**Verse 34.—“Do not labor,” etc.** (RAB.) To comprehend what is incomprehensible. Hence, do not seek riches that you cannot attain.

### Chapter XLIV

[Col. 1226B]

**Verse 1.—“Let us praise famous men,” etc.** In discussing morality and touching upon allegory and anagogy in many places, he brought forth the mysteries of the divine sacrament; then he begins to recount the holy fathers. “Our ancestors.” The patriarchs, who enjoyed divine speech and vision; and the prophets, who, filled with the Holy Spirit, foretold many mysteries of Christ and the Church.

**Verse 12.—“He stood firm in the covenants,” etc.** (RAB.) These things concern the patriarchs according to the historical sense, etc., up to the point when the seed of good works will be repaid with a heavenly reward.

**Verse 16.—“Enoch pleased God.”** Not from Adam, etc., up to the point where he gives human beings the counsel to repent.

**Verse 17.—“Noah was found,” etc.** When he was preserved while the world perished in the Flood [Col. 1226C], so that he might preach repentance to the nations and demonstrate by his example that those who devotedly serve God are freed from eternal destruction. God established a covenant with him not to destroy all flesh again with the waters of the Flood (Gen. XVII). He signifies the rulers who guide the ark—that is, the Church—amid the waves of the world and preach the baptism of repentance, appeasing God on behalf of the human race through prayers and sacrifices.

**Verse 21.—“In his flesh he causes the covenant to stand,” etc.** (RAB.) So that our renewed nature through the baptism of Christ might be signified, after the stripping off of the old person.

**Verse 22.—“Therefore by oath,” etc.** Abraham has a twofold promise. In the sand of the sea are represented the sterile Jews; in the likeness of the stars, the faithful Christians, who will flash with the light of the resurrection like the stars of heaven.

[Col. 1226D]

**Verse 26.—“And he gave him an inheritance,” etc.** The gentile people, who came later to the grace of faith and the regeneration of baptism, and to whom the fullness of the paternal blessing came.

### Chapter XLV

**Verse 6.—“Commandments.”** On Mount Sinai he gave him the Law and commandments of life, speaking with him in the cloud.

**Verse 9.—“And he girded him,” etc.** He describes the rite of the ancient priesthood and the adornment of the high priest, all of which were figures of the New Testament and of the true priest, Jesus Christ. “And he clothed him.” The high priest’s garments are works of virtue: wisdom and teaching.
