**VERSE 1.—Jacob.** Note the precision of the words. Jacob, who is still wrestling, has compassion; Israel, who received his name after the victory, chooses.

### Chapter XIV

**Verse 4.**—“How,” etc. He wonders how the devastator of the lands, etc., up to: “But at the end the hostile death will be destroyed.”

**The exactor.**—(Jerome.) He who exacts from his debtors down to the last farthing, who say: “Forgive us our debts” (Matt. 6). Debtors will be handed over to him; to him Paul handed over Corinth when it was committing fornication.

**Verse 5.**—**The staff.** He calls Nebuchadnezzar—or the devil—the staff, because just as the impious are scourged by God through him, so through this one they are punished in hell, or daily tempted and enticed into sin through his plots and ambushes.

**Verse 8.**—**The fir trees also.** The rulers of various nations afflicted by him; or their sons, whose fathers he killed.

**Since you have fallen asleep.** Since, when the strong one was conquered and his vessels plundered, his satellites also fell. Hence: “Go into the eternal fire which has been prepared for the devil and his angels” (Matt. 25). Note that the death of death is called sleep.

**Which might cut it down.** Hence the Psalm: “His shadow covered the mountains, and his branches the cedars of God” (Ps. 79). At times the Lord hands these sinners over to punishment to be crushed; hence it is said: “The Lord will crush the cedars of Lebanon” (Ps. 28).

**Verse 9.**—**Hell.** Its inhabitants or rulers: “The underworld beneath you.” Hell is beneath the earth; there the rich man was seen by Lazarus. From there the Lord brought out his captives and sent the devil away bound.

**All the kings.** Even if these things did not happen, they could have happened. It is a consolation to the wicked to have their enemies as companions in punishment.

**Verse 10.**—**You have been wounded.** You who seemed immortal and divine. Because of the weakness of our understanding, we thought that we could not resist God’s power, and that you alone remained in your height.

**Verse 11.**—**Beneath.** (The same.) “Rottenness, moth, and a covering of worms,” etc., up to the one who said to Christ: “I will give you all these things, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matt. 4).

**Verse 12.**—**You who used to rise in the morning.** (Jerome.) These are the false apostles, etc., up to “and on the sides of the north,” in the cold places.

**Verse 13.**—**I will ascend into heaven.** (The same.) He was in the firmament and desired to ascend into heaven, where the Lord’s throne is. All this must be referred to heretics, who, although they are below with their prince, boast that they are exalted.

[Col. 1254A] **On the sides of the north.** Hence: “From the north evils flare up, and Jeremiah’s pot is set ablaze.” Concerning this: “I will say to the north, ‘Give’”—that is, “Return the captives.”

**Of the clouds.** That is, of the prophets, concerning whom it is said: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it” (Ps. 35). And: “Your truth reaches to the clouds.” Judas was a cloud with the other apostles, but through his own fault he accepted the devil as his rider.

**Verse 15.**—**Nevertheless you will be dragged down to hell.** You who were able to ascend through virtues will fall through vices. The saints have the wings of a dove and of an eagle, so that they may fly and rest; the impious, like lead, are plunged into mighty waters and descend into the depths like a stone (Zech. 5). Iniquity sits upon a talent of lead.

[Col. 1254B] **You will be dragged down.** Christ descended unwillingly; he descended voluntarily.

**The depth.** To the lowest and worst punishments. For the higher the level, the heavier the fall.

**The pit.** That is, hell, etc., up to: “but they are rejected by the Lord because of lukewarmness and a pretence of faith.”

**Verse 16.**—**Is this a man?** (The same.) Not God; hence: “An enemy has sown weeds over it” (Matt. 13).

**Verse 17.**—**Cities.** (The same.) Churches, so that he might make them synagogues of the devil and defile the purity of faith with heretical depravity.

**Not his prisoners.** Those whom the apostles, imitators of their master, set free, etc., up to: “but he shut him up in darkness, so that he did not even reveal him to his son Evil-merodach.”

**Verse 18.**—**All the kings.** (The same.) The kings of the nations, etc., up to: “nor does he rest from tortures even in death.”

**Verse 19.**—**But you.** He appears to agree with the story, etc., up to: “your father will revive.”

**Like a corpse.** (The same.) “They have rotted through the multitude of their sins, and my scars have become foul” (Ps. 37). Virtue is of sweet fragrance.

**Verse 20.**—**Association.** Namely, in burial. One punishment belongs to the author, another to the one compelled by authority: “This is the sword by which many were wounded and killed.”

**For you destroyed the land.** As though he said: Through your pride the Chaldean kingdom was destroyed, although it would still have remained had your pride not existed.

[Col. 1254D] **The people.** The people whom God had entrusted to you to correct and govern.

**You killed.** You did not reserve the living for God, but prepared companions for your punishment.

**It will not be called.** Therefore it will not be called forever, etc., up to: “the whole offspring has been destroyed because of the father’s pride and impiety.”

**Verse 21.**—**Iniquity.** (The same.) The Septuagint: “Because of the iniquity of your father.” Some, not understanding this, want the dragon who rules in the sea, whom the Hebrews call Leviathan, to be the father of the devil, according to: “Because he is a liar and his father is so” (John 8); by misunderstanding this, they corrupt it.

**Verse 23.**—**And I will make it.** There is nothing in it except royal game enclosed within brick walls repaired after many years.

[Col. 1255A] **As a possession of the hedgehog.** The world too is now possessed by the hedgehog and marshes—that is, by unclean spirits; but at the end of the world the Lord will sweep it, that is, cleanse it, with purifying fire.

**Verse 24.**—**The Lord swore.** Up to this point he has spoken of Babylon and its kings, etc., up to: “and this in the land of Judah and in its mountains, just as the Lord had foretold.”

**Verse 25.**—**On the mountains.** Note the propriety of the wording, etc., up to: “but also those who have advanced in virtues.”

**Verse 26.**—**This plan.** That is, “Let his yoke be removed,” etc., up to: “generally pertains to the whole world.”

[Col. 1255B] **Verse 28.**—**In the year in which he died.** From the beginning of the book up to this point Isaiah prophesied under Uzziah, Jotham, and Ahaz; what follows was foretold and partly fulfilled under Hezekiah.

**Ahaz.** While he was alive and reigning among sinners, neither a burden against foreigners nor the word of God, according to the Septuagint, could be delivered to the prophet.

**Verse 29.**—**Do not rejoice.** When a king dies, enemies rejoice as though they will gain something from the changed circumstances. Thus the Philistines, whom Ahaz had afflicted, rejoiced at his death and insulted the Jews, because, having lost a mature king, they were subject to his son; while he reigned, they thought they could invade their borders.

**The rod of the smiter.** (Jerome.) When God’s yoke has been cast off, etc., up to: “and from them flying serpents, or those that devour birds.”

**Verse 31.**—**Howl.** (The same.) As though he said: Philistines, mourn your misery, which has come through Sennacherib.

**Howl, gate; cry out, city.** The Philistines, falling through drunkenness, etc., up to: “the soul filled with evil thoughts.”

**For smoke comes from the north.** When the arrows of the devil blaze—he is harmful to the eyes and opposed to the light. Jeremiah’s pot is kindled from the north.

**There is no one who escapes his army.** No one except Jerusalem, etc., up to: “and Jerusalem alone is to be delivered.”

**Verse 32.**—**To the messengers of the nation.** To the angels who preside over cities and nations, each wondering why Zion alone avoided or escaped the bitterness of the smoke.

[Col. 1255D] **He founded Zion.** Upon the foundation of prudence, justice, fortitude, and temperance, which are Christ.

### Chapter XV

**Verse 1.**—**The burden of Moab.** This is Isaiah’s vision concerning the burden—that is, the destruction—of Moab. Moab was the son of Lot, whose offspring and province were called Moab. Ar is in that province and is now the metropolitan city Ariopolis.

**The burden of Moab.** (Jerome.) There is a carnal and a spiritual circumcision, etc., up to: “Lot too, when Sodom was passing away, came into Segor, and the sun rose.”

[Col. 1256A] **Ar**, that is, “adversary,” etc., up to: “afterward they were devastated by the Chaldeans.”

**Verse 2.**—**The house has gone up.** To the heights on which it had been arrogant, not to sacrifice but to mourn where it had sinned.

**Dibon.** (The same.) “Their flowing.” Falsehood passes and flows, never remaining in the same condition; but the word of the Lord is compact and stable. Hence manna appears like ice: it does not flow but remains fixed.

**Upon Nabo.** (The same.) Since the whole meaning of this prophecy is one, etc., up to: “when their soul has howled for itself.”

**Verse 3.**—**Every howl.** Another reading has: “Everyone howls”—namely, Moab—and thus descends into weeping. As though he said: It went up to the heights to weep before idols. But when it found no help there, it descended to weeping on the ground or in its house.

[Col. 1256B] **Verse 4.**—**Hesebon will cry out.** From the beginning of the kingdom, which is in Hesebon, to the city of Jasa, where it ends, there is crying everywhere and mourning everywhere.

**The armed men of Moab will howl.** Separated from their wives, they are strong warriors. Hence it is said that Abraham chose the armed servants of his household—that is, those without wives.

**Verse 5.**—**My heart is for Moab.** So that I may call them to repentance, etc., up to: “which is interpreted ‘lion of God.’”

**To Segor.** (The same.) Segor is one of the five cities of the Sodomites, etc., up to: “if he had not sinned after his deliverance.”

[Col. 1256C] **Verse 6.**—**Nemrim.** Nemrim is a town beside the sea, etc., up to: “and therefore the grass will wither.”

**Verse 7.**—**And their visitation.** Visitation in evil: “I will visit their iniquities with a rod” (Ps. 88); visitation in good: “The dawn from on high has visited us” (Luke 1).

**To the torrent of the willows.** Up to this point he speaks of the captivity of the Moabites by the Assyrians; now he speaks of that by the Chaldeans.

**Verse 8.**—**Its howling.** As though he said: Moab will howl for this reason: where previously there were luxury and delight because of irrigated places and pleasant springs, there are now streams of blood.

**Verse 9.**—**The water of Dibon.** Dibon means “silence”; Dibon is weeping, and yet it is one city.

### Chapter XVI

[Col. 1256D]

**Verse 1.**—**Send the lamb.** (Jerome.) For this reason the prophets are scarcely understood, etc., up to: “who rules throughout the whole world.”

**The rock of the desert.** (The same.) Namely, Ruth, because according to the Lord’s command, etc., up to: “for just as Christ came for both peoples, so he wished to be born from both.”

**To the mountain of the daughter of Zion.** Jerusalem, or rather the Church, which is in contemplation, like the daughter of a watchtower. In Jerusalem especially he preached, performed miracles, suffered, died, rose again, and redeemed the human race.

**Verse 2.**—**So they will be.** Thus they will pass into captivity across the Arnon, which is the boundary of the Moabites and Amorites.

(Jerome.) Arnon, which is interpreted “illumination,” signifies those who, abandoning errors, rise toward knowledge of the truth.

**Verse 3.**—**Take counsel.** Do nothing without counsel, and do not be carried about by every wind of doctrine; follow the angel of great counsel.

**Force counsel.** Namely, by forming a Church from the wandering and erring.

**Make it like night.** Namely, the tabernacle in which you thought you would rest, etc., up to: “so that it may receive and hide with itself God’s fleeing people.”

**Verse 4.**—**My fugitives.** Those who fled from me, who went out from the Church, who followed their own judgment and not the teaching of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 1257B] **For the dust has ended.** He suddenly turns to the killing of Sennacherib, who was dust and wretched, because his glory was like dust blown by the wind from the face of the earth; he departed miserably from this life, killed by his sons in the temple of his god.

**Verse 5.**—**And he will prepare.** The Jews explain this concerning Hezekiah, who reigned in peace after Sennacherib’s death. But it is better referred to Christ, with some things referring to the first advent and some to the second.

**Verse 6.**—**He will sit upon it.** Resting and judging upon the hearts of the good.

**We have heard of Moab’s pride.** In the manner of Scripture, because he had announced good things, lest he make them negligent, he frightens them with a threat.

**And indignation.** (The same.) Against God he set his mouth in heaven, disparaging the prophets. He adds the Gospel saying: “All who came before me were thieves and robbers.” He calls Moses and David murderers, and Joshua bloodthirsty.

**Verse 7.**—**He will howl.** All the different groups of heretics and philosophers will roar against one another in torments.

**Upon the walls.** Not built with squared stone, as God’s temple is, in which the stones were polished so that neither hammer nor axe was heard.

**Verse 8.**—**The suburbs of Hesebon.** All their thoughts—which Hesebon signifies—do not belong to the city of God, concerning which it is said: “The river’s stream gladdens the city of God” (Ps. 45); rather, they are suburbs, so that they may be thought to belong to the Lord’s city.

**Sabama.** “Raising up height,” etc., up to: “therefore the apostles and apostolic men of the Lord of the nations cut off the shoots of the vineyard of Sabama.”

**They have wandered.** Surveying the whole land of Moab.

**In the desert.** So that at last they would have no one whom they might kill.

**Branches.** He continues the metaphor of the vineyard.

**They crossed the sea.** (The same.) So that, freed from the depths of temptations, they might see the Lord’s wonders.

**Verse 9.**—**The vineyard.** The vineyard of Moab, because of the proximity of the place, is like Sodom.

**Sabama.** The one who exalts himself against God’s judgment.

[Col. 1258A] **Verse 10.**—**From Carmel.** Carmel is a mountain between Phoenicia and Palestine, rising above Ptolemais, on which Elijah prayed. It is often used for any fertility; hence here too: “Joy and exultation will be removed from Carmel” (1 Kings 18)—that is, the fertility in which the Moabites rejoiced.

**He will exult.** Because heretics boast that they possess knowledge of spiritual circumcision.

**The voice.** So that the dragon’s poisons may not be expressed from there and those who drink may be killed.

**Verse 11.**—**My belly.** The prophet, who, composed like a cithara by musical art and conceiving the fear of God, gives birth to many children, so that every string may return its own sound.

**And my inward parts.** Just as a cithara does not emit a composed sound, etc., up to: “and James, who is lacking one, lacks them all.”

[Col. 1258B] **Verse 12.**—**His holy place.** To the holy place, namely the Church, which he will try to make his own but will not prevail. We do not immediately grasp virtue perfectly.

**He will not prevail.** They will find no help in those in whom they had hoped, and so it became clear that he worshiped in vain.

**Verse 13.**—**This word.** In the prologue, etc., up to: “For what had begun for you has here been completed.”

**Verse 14.**—**Within three years.** As though he said: Just as few grapes remain, etc., up to: “but after abandoning error and turning back, he is left for only three years, small, insignificant, and inglorious.”

**Mercenaries.** (The same.) False doctrine does everything for the sake of profit, etc., up to: “it is a lighter sin to sin openly than to pretend holiness.”

### Chapter XVII

**Verse 1.**—**The burden of Damascus.** Behold Damascus. (The same.) Damascus is the metropolis of Syria, etc., up to: “but because they did not repent, they were taken captive.”

**Verse 2.**—**Aroer for flocks.** The tamarisk, which is a fruitless tree growing in deserts and rocky places, as though he said: All the Syrians will be fruitless and desolate. Others say that hatred is stirred up by this tree through magical arts.

**Verse 3.**—**And the kingdom.** So that sin may not reign in it, which previously loved blood.

**The remnant of Syria.** Ironically, as an insult, etc., up to: “therefore both were taken captive in disgrace.”

**Verse 4.**—**And it will be on that day.** (The same.) When Syria has been devastated by the Assyrians, etc., up to: “others were transferred to Cyrene, which is the region beyond Egypt.”

**It will wither.** (The same.) They will have neither prophets, signs, powers, kingdom, nor priesthood; rather, the whole body of the nation will wither.

**Verse 5.**—**In the harvest.** It is said concerning the nations: “The harvest is indeed plentiful, but the laborers are few” (Matt. 9). Those poor men gather the remnants of the harvest that were saved through the apostles, and very few ears. They gather them not on the mountains but in the valley of Raphaim—that is, in humility and the truth of the letter. Raphaim means “giants.”

**Verse 6.**—**Like a gleaning.** (The same.) When the Jewish people had been struck down, the olive tree—which under Moses had had six hundred thousand armed men, and under David, when Joab counted them, an innumerable people—offered scarcely a few fruits to the Savior.

**Of two or three.** Paul and Barnabas; and the three Peter, James, and John, who saw the Lord transfigured on the mountain and saw the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter raised.

**Or four.** (Jerome.) These are the remaining nine, among whom Matthias, Judas the betrayer’s replacement, obtained a place. Because of the diversity of their gifts, unknown to us, they are divided into four or five, displaying in themselves the number of the Gospels and the books of the Law, as preachers of both Testaments.

**Verse 7.**—**On that day he will bow down.** As though he said: The Lord, hungry, will scarcely have a few, etc., up to: “as it is read in Chronicles, and they cast away the idols.”

**Verse 9.**—**On that day they will be.** When the Assyrians rush in and devastate not only Damascus but also the land of the ten tribes.

**Ploughs.** (The same.) Of the Amorites. This is against the ten tribes, as though he said: Just as the Amorites fled when the sons of Israel came, leaving their ploughs, so now the ten tribes will flee when the Assyrians come.

**Verse 10.**—**A faithful planting.** A planting is faithful when someone plants, cultivates, and gathers the fruit. It is an unfaithful planting and an alien shoot when someone else gathers it: “Every planting that my Father did not plant will be uprooted” (Matt. 15).

**An alien shoot.** Not receiving the Father, because you do not receive the Son; for whoever believes in the Father believes in the Son. An alien shoot means blasphemies against Christ.

**Verse 11.**—**In the morning your seed.** (The same.) When the shoot has appeared, etc., up to: “all the saints will be saved with the branches of the wild olive around the root.”

**Verse 12.**—**Woe to the multitude.** Sennacherib and his army, etc., up to: “desiring to oppress and occupy everything.”

**Verse 13.**—**He will be carried away.** He was carried away from Jerusalem when he fled with a few men to Nineveh. He was carried away from the world when he was soon killed by his sons, as is evident.

**Verse 14.**—**This is the portion of those who devastated.** The prophet speaks in the person of Israel, as though he said: God is accustomed to bless our enemies in this way.

### Chapter XVIII

**Verse 1.**—**Woe to the land.** (The same.) Since he had spoken of the other persecutors of the Church, etc., up to: “as though by wandering he had made useless things.”

**Woe to the land of the cymbal of wings.** He turns again to Egypt and calls it, etc., up to: “they have taken away from them the fear of the Lord.”

**Verse 2.**—**In vessels of papyrus**—that is, in ships made of papyrus, etc., up to: “it passes through and slips away.”

**Verse 3.**—**A nation waiting and trampled down.** For all heretics promise themselves great things, etc., up to: “that is, they hear their doctrine.”

[Col. 1260A] **Verse 4.**—**A cloud of dew.** It is welcome to weary harvesters, to whom it provides refreshment and, by moistening it, makes dry straw able to be cut. Thus my word against Egypt will be welcome to all who believe in me, and to the Assyrians, to whom victory over them has been given by me.

**Verse 5.**—**The branches.** (The same.) Useless branches. Hence: “I am the true vine, and my Father is the farmer: he will remove every branch in me that does not bear fruit, and every one that bears fruit he will cleanse.”

**Verse 6.**—**And all the beasts of the earth.** Hyperbolically. For not all the beasts of the earth will winter upon it. Rather, he signifies both an immense slaughter and a very great multitude of beasts that will come upon it, for which the corpses will provide sufficient food in summer and winter.

[Col. 1260B] **Verse 7.**—**At that time.** The prophet returns to the people of Israel and promises them good things, saying: “At that time”—as though he said: Once Egypt has been devastated, Judah will no longer hope in its shadow but will offer a gift to the Lord of faith and good works. This was fulfilled in the seventieth year after the captivity, under Zerubbabel and the other leaders.

### Chapter XIX

**Verse 1.**—**The burden of Egypt**, etc. (The same.) It must be understood that many things said here refer historically to Egypt; but here and elsewhere in Scripture many things are set forth that cannot stand according to the historical account, so that the necessity of the matter compels us to seek a higher understanding.

**Behold, the Lord will ascend**, etc. (The same.) Egypt means darkness or mourning, etc., up to: “and the hearts of Egypt’s wise men melted with fear.”

**The images of Egypt.** Idolatry, feeling itself broken, so that even the magicians taught by demons—or, according to Balaam’s prophecy, understanding that the Son of God had been born, the one who had destroyed magical art—came to Bethlehem and worshiped the Child.

**Verse 2.**—**And I will make them clash.** Hence in the Gospel: “I have not come to bring peace upon the earth but a sword; for I have come to separate a man from his father,” etc. (Matt. 10).

**Verse 3.**—**And it will be broken**, etc. (The same.) Egypt’s will will be divided against itself, so that they will no longer think great thoughts as before; separated by the spiritual sword, they will recognize that their counsel has been brought to ruin.

[Col. 1260D] **Verse 4.**—**Cruel masters.** Egypt was handed over to many masters: first to the Assyrians, then to Nebuchadnezzar, third to Alexander, and finally to the Romans, after Antony and Cleopatra had been defeated by Augustus. The Chaldeans were more cruel; the Romans more powerful.

**Verse 5.**—**And it will dry up.** It often happens that, when captivity comes with God’s anger, pestilence follows his indignation and the elements rage against sinners. Therefore, when captivity came through the Chaldeans or Romans, perhaps the Nile and the springs also dried up. Hyperbolically, because of the excessive tribulation, the rivers can be said to have failed, the springs to have dried, and the streams likewise.

**Verse 11.**—**Fools.** When Babylonian or Roman captivity arrived, all the plans of the magicians failed.

**The princes of Tanis.** (Jerome.) “Of a humble command.” For all heretics teach a humility opposed to exaltation; they drag people down to hell, and the princes are of humble command and cast down.

**The son of the wise.** Each of them said this to Pharaoh, etc., up to: “and they boast that Isis, Osiris, and Typhon were great gods and the founders of their nation.”

**Of the ancient kings.** As though he said: I possess knowledge of Scripture together with secular wisdom.

**Verse 14.**—**Drunk and vomiting.** (The same.) Through the fury of dragons, so that at last, after vomiting, they may understand their drunkenness. For as long as they are drunk, they will have neither beginning nor end.

[Col. 1261B] **Verse 15.**—**The one who restrains.** (Haymo, on Isaiah.) Instead of what Jerome ought to have translated, etc., up to: “others do not know what to do because of their wantonness.”

**Verse 16.**—**Women.** Those whom Egypt loves, whom Pharaoh alone wants to live after the men have been killed. The devil kills virtues and preserves vices.

**The land of Judah to Egypt.** The knowledge of Scripture—the Law and the Prophets—and the Gospels will be for Egypt a cause of celebration when it recognizes itself, or a cause of fear when it understands that it possessed falsehoods.

**For fear.** Others read “for celebration,” etc., up to: “by promising them help.”

**Verse 18.**—**Five cities.** Some understand the five books of Moses, etc., up to: “because they are changed from vices to virtues.”

[Col. 1261C] **The language of Canaan.** It is asked why it is not the Hebrew language, etc., up to: “and those who delight in unclean touch.”

**Verse 19.**—**On that day.** (The same.) Not understanding this, the priest Onias, etc., up to: “and that they have retained their own language down to the present day.”

**And the inscription.** The Lord’s inscription is the evangelical and apostolic teaching, which extends to the ends of the earth; hence: “Their sound has gone out through all the earth” (Ps. 18). Or, according to the boundary of faith, the inscription is good work, which ought to extend as far as faith extends; or it is imitation of Christ’s passion.

**Verse 20.**—**For they will cry out.** When evangelical teaching has grown and persecution has descended, then those who have believed will cry out to God the Father.

[Col. 1261D] **Verse 23.**—**On that day.** Before the Lord’s coming, the individual nations, etc., up to: “who run from kingdom to kingdom.”

**And the Egyptians will serve.** Not because they would afterward have been subjected, etc., up to: “of the same condition as they.”

**On that day there will be.** (The same.) He will not be oppressed alternately by the Assyrians and Egyptians as an intermediary, but will be third with them in serving the Romans.

**Verse 25.**—**Blessed.** These regions had abounded above all other monarchies, and therefore deserved to be blessed.

### Chapter XX

**Verse 1.**—**In the year.** (The same.) These are Assyrian names, etc., up to: “he conquers those who serve birth and lust.”

**In the year.** Azotus was the most powerful of the five cities of the Philistines, etc., up to: “through whom the Lord spoke.”

**When he had sent him.** Beautifully, the king of the Assyrians is called Sargon—that is, “prince of gardens”—who resembles Ahab, who wanted to turn Naboth’s vineyard into a garden. Understanding this tropologically, Naboth preferred to die rather than do it, so that his ancestral inheritance and ancient possession would not be changed into the delights of an impious king.

**Verse 2.**—**Go and loosen.** The prophet is commanded to set aside his sackcloth and sandals, etc., up to: “for nothing is hidden that will not be revealed.”

**And he did so.** An extraordinary obedience: the very noble man wore only haircloth, as the Hebrews relate. King Manasseh took his daughter in marriage, yet he was not ashamed to walk naked, judging nothing more honorable than obedience to the Lord.

**Verse 3.**—**Barefoot.** (The same.) It must be noted that before Azotus is captured, etc., up to: “toward which he hastens, whether to stand or to walk.”

**Verse 4.**—**For disgrace.** Since they could not eat the Lord’s Passover, which is eaten with the loins girded, a staff held in the hand, and shod feet, lest, while passing through the wilderness of this world, one be bitten by serpents.

**Verse 6.**—**Was this it?** The providence of God is to be admired, etc., up to: “at the end it will perish completely, when Christ’s kingdom has shone forth.”

### Chapter XXI

[Col. 1262C]

**Verse 1.**—**The burden of the desert of the sea.** Babylon, called “sea” because of the multitude of its people.

**From the desert he came.** In the desert the Lord was tempted, and in it the Israelites were struck by serpents.

**Verse 2.**—**The treacherous one.** A general judgment: it is as though the fault of individuals causes them to be overwhelmed in the storm.

**Go up, Elam.** The Septuagint: “Elamites and ambassadors of the Persians.” Elamites means “despisers.” “Go up,” as though he said: O Persians and Medes, do not fear; mount your horses and besiege Babylon. “Go up”: trusting in God’s strength, he speaks boldly against the adversaries.

**All his groaning.** With which he made you and other nations groan; or so that no one would now groan under Babylon’s power; or because she was afflicted by such evils that she did not dare to groan against you.

**Verse 5.**—**Set the table.** As though he said: O Persians and Medes, take food, etc., up to: “in which you may restrain the fiery darts of the devil.”

**Look out**, etc. See what will rush in after the table; or, “Look out, O Belshazzar, for what he has written on the wall: ‘Mane, Tethel, Phares.’”

**Verse 6.**—**A watchman.** Prophets are called watchmen.

**Verse 7.**—**A rider.** Cyrus, the ruler, commanded the Medes and Persians, etc., up to: “namely, the letter and the spirit refer to the two Testaments.”

[Col. 1263A] **Verse 8.**—**A lion.** The same lion signifies courage of spirit, while the watchman signifies the privilege of contemplation.

**Upon the Lord’s watchtower.** That is, placed in contemplation by day, prepared by day and night to hear and speak what he commands.

**Standing all night.** So that I may guard myself from every sin and be worthy to hear the word of the Lord.

**Verse 9.**—**Behold, this man is coming.** What follows signifies that he saw him coming—namely, the Savior seated upon a two-animal chariot, joining two animals, an ass and a camel, to one cart.

**It has fallen, it has fallen.** When Cyrus and Darius devastated Babylon, the idols too were broken, the temple of Bel overturned and burned with fire.

**Verse 10.**—**My threshing.** As though he said: O people who are to be stored in my granaries, whom I have threshed through various hardships in order to separate the chaff and bring pure wheat into the granaries—what I heard from the Lord, from the God of Israel, etc.

**Verse 11.**—**The burden of Duma.** The Septuagint: “of Idumaea,” etc., up to: “the burden of Duma cries out to me.”

**It cries out to me.** (Jerome.) God, namely my guardian, etc., up to: “then he speaks to the nations: ‘If you seek me, seek me more diligently’” (John 9).

**Verse 12.**—**Morning has come**, etc. As though he said: I will give my people the light of joy, etc., up to: “through action, and then I will hear you.”

**Verse 13.**—**The burden in Arabia.** The Arabs are the Saracens, etc., up to: “then God addresses the fleeing Jews in this way.”

[Col. 1263C] **In the forest at evening.** O Jews who will flee the Babylonian siege into the forest—that is, you will sleep in the woods of the Saracens—fleeing the Chaldeans along the paths of Dodanim, which is interpreted as “toward relatives or kinsmen,” that is, on the road leading to your Saracen relatives.

**Evening.** (The same.) It is the beginning of night. Whoever begins to sin is in the evening; whoever reaches the summit is in the middle of the night. At midnight the firstborn of Egypt were killed. Peter denied, and repented when daylight was already near.

**On the paths.** (The same.) Because evening is the beginning of evils, etc., up to: “when he rebelled against his father.”

**Verse 14.**—**Bring water to meet the thirsty.** This can be said against those who have surrendered themselves to idleness and sloth and are content with their own salvation, neither extending a hand to penitents and converts.

[Col. 1263D] **Bring water to the thirsty.** Bring water to weary brothers, exhausted by the heat of the sun and thirst, lest they perish in the wilderness.

**Verse 16.**—**Still within one year**, etc. As though he said: Because you showed them no mercy, you will soon endure the misery of captivity. One year after the Jewish captivity and the destruction of Jerusalem, these people too were devastated.

**As in a mercenary’s year.** (The same.) That is: Just as a mercenary completes his year, etc., up to: “and have eaten the heavenly bread.”

### Chapter XXII

**Verse 1.**—**The burden of the valley.** Jerusalem, once mistress of the nations, etc., up to: “who have fallen from the lofty understanding of Scripture to low things.”

[Col. 1264A] **The valley of vision.** The Septuagint: “Zion,” that is, “watchtower,” namely the Church.

**What is happening to you also?** As though he said: When philosophy and secular wisdom, discussing lofty matters, despise the simplicity of the Church, why do you too pursue exalted things?

**Verse 2.**—**Full.** The doctrine of heretics is full of verbosity and shouting.

**Your slain.** (Jerome.) The valley—namely Zion—passed over to the heretics of its own will. Compared with those defeated after battle, those who surrender themselves voluntarily are wounded more miserably. Thus in martyrdom, the one who denies after punishments is punished less severely than the one who denies Christ without necessity.

**Verse 3.**—**All your princes**, etc. As is read in Jeremiah, Zedekiah escaped by night through a breach in the wall, etc., up to: “and they were led away to Babylon.”

**They fled.** They were united in flight; their prince is the fleeing dragon, the twisting serpent.

**Verse 5.**—**And of weeping.** (The same.) The Septuagint: “of error.” This does not mean that weeping and error come from the Lord, but that the opportunity for error arises from the Scriptures he gave them to read; and they can say: “Why have you made us wander from your way?” (Isa. 63).

**Verse 6.**—**Elam.** A city in the Persian province, in which the best archers lived: Elam took up the quiver. Elam, “their ascent”—that is, the pride of heretics—took up the quiver to shoot at the upright in heart in darkness.

**The wall.** He stripped the Church’s defenses of their shield—that is, of their opposition.

[Col. 1264C] **Verse 8.**—**The covering.** The temple, which had previously been covered and closed to gentiles and the unclean.

**The armory.** Near the temple was a house David built for storing weapons; many trees surrounded it, hence it is called the house of the forest. It too was not made of stone but of wood; for, as they say, moisture from mortar and stones causes iron to rust.

**Verse 9.**—**And you gathered.** The promised land, although extremely fertile, etc., up to: “the lower part, which could be captured by enemies, and the upper part, which could not.”

**Verse 11.**—**And the pool.** (The same.) Not a well containing living and eternal water, but cracked cisterns that cannot hold water.

**Between the two walls.** Namely, the New and the Old Testament. They made for themselves new waters, which they think are more inward and contain greater mysteries than the Old Testament.

**Verse 12.**—**And the Lord God of hosts will call.** Every day the Lord calls heretics to repentance, etc., up to: “but despising and despairing, they said: ‘Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die’” (Jer. 34).

**Verse 14.**—**You will die.** (The same.) Through vices, or when you descend with them to hell, etc., up to: “the things said here do not concern the captivity that occurred in Hezekiah’s time.”

**Verse 15.**—**Shebna.** (Jerome.) Turn now, etc., up to: “therefore the Lord threatens him with these evils.”

[Col. 1265A] **Verse 16.**—**What are you doing here?** As though he said: Why do you want to build a house for yourself? etc., up to: “which should be called a tomb and a memorial.”

**Verse 18.**—**He will crown you with a crown.** You who once had the priestly crown and sanctification on the golden plate, on which God’s name was written, will be crowned with tribulation and distress.

**With tribulation.** Instead of the golden plate on which the Lord’s name was written, which the priest wore on his forehead once a year.

**Like a ball.** Just as a sphere cannot remain in a sloping and spacious place, so your people will be scattered to the ends of the earth.

**Verse 20.**—**My servant Eliakim.** Through proud Shebna, etc., up to: “the son of Hilkiah, that is, of the Father of the Lord.”

**Verse 22.**—**The key.** By the key that he carries upon his shoulder we can understand the royal scepter and sign of victory—that is, the cross, which Christ himself carried upon his own shoulder.

**The house of David.** He calls the Lord’s house the house of David, in which there was a golden key.

**And he will open.** Hence: “He who opens and no one shuts, who shuts and no one opens.” What he opened in the Passion cannot be shut; what he closed in the ceremonies no one will open.

**Verse 24.**—**And I will hang upon him.** Hence in the Gospel: “All the people hung upon him.” Today too they hang upon his word of wisdom.

**Verse 25.**—**The peg will be removed.** What is said, etc., up to: “the Jews will be converted to the faith.”

### Chapter XXIII

**Verse 1.**—**The burden of Tyre.** Tyre, the most distinguished city of the Canaanites, etc., up to: “Isaiah foretells this misery: ‘The burden of Tyre,’ etc.”

**Howl.** In Greek it is clearer: “Howl, ships of Carthage”—namely, you who were accustomed to come to Tyre for trade. Carthage was a colony of the Tyrians, built and cultivated by them.

Ships of the sea. In Hebrew, *Tharsis*, that is, “exploration of joy” or “contemplation,” because the contemplation of joy and gladness will be turned into tears.

**VERSE 3.**—Commerce. (JEROME.) Merchants, etc., up to “and they pass from one vice to another.”

The seed of the Nile, the harvest of the river, its produce, etc. It is constructed in this way: [Col. 1265D] the seed of the Nile River was its harvest and produce, namely, Tyre’s. The land of Canaan, in which Tyre is situated, is infertile; Egypt, which the Nile waters, is fertile in produce, and Tyre exchanged goods with the Egyptians for it.

**VERSE 4.**—Sea. That is, the world, in which small creatures exist together with great ones; the dragon—whom the Lord formed to mock it—seeing them captured by Christ’s hunters, although they had been captured by demons, says to the opposing power of the hunters, signified by Sidon: “Be ashamed, Sidon.”

I have not travailed. As though she were saying: It did no good to travail, give birth, and nourish young men, because Tyre was captured without defense.

**VERSE 5.**—When this is heard in Egypt, etc. [Col. 1266A] This is understood both of all vices and of heresies, because when one is captured, another becomes afraid, and in the downfall of one, another realizes that it too will be captured.

**VERSE 6.**—Cross over, howl, you who dwell there. As was said above, when they could not resist Nebuchadnezzar, those who could hastened to board ships; others remained in the city.

**VERSE 7.**—Is this not your city, which gloried from former days in antiquity, etc.? As though he were saying: I command this for the following reason: your city, Tyre, having abandoned its former error, will pass over to the truth.

**VERSE 8.**—Its merchants’ princes, the illustrious of the earth, etc. (SAME AUTHOR.) Among other merchants, or even among kingdoms.

**VERSE 9.**—To bring it to disgrace, etc. The Lord is not the author of disgrace, but he reveals what is disgraceful, according to the saying: “He will defile him with defilement”—not that the priest is the author of the defilement, but that he shows the person whom many had thought clean to be defiled.

**VERSE 10.**—River. That of the Babylonians: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept, when we remembered Zion” (Psalm 136).

Your girdle is no more. The strength to resist; for we tighten the loins with a girdle, and are said to possess strength in the loins.

**VERSE 11.**—He disturbed kingdoms. Namely, those of the Egyptians and Moabites, and of the other surrounding peoples. For when Tyre was captured and overthrown, the other kingdoms were thrown into confusion by fear. The kingdom of Egypt also was given to Nebuchadnezzar in place of Tyre, which had been overthrown.

[Col. 1266C] **VERSE 12.**—Daughter of Sidon. (SAME AUTHOR.) Tyre and Sidon are in the land of Canaan; hence: “The Canaanite woman came out from the regions of Tyre and Sidon to meet the Savior” (Matthew 15).

Cross over. We often see certain people pass from their intended occupation to another: they change their activity from military service to commerce, from lawsuits to weapons, in order to change their misfortune. But by God’s providence everything turns out contrariwise, so that, compelled by miseries, they may trust not in themselves but in the Lord their Creator.

**VERSE 13.**—Such a people has not existed. Up to the death of Nebuchadnezzar, the Chaldeans and Assyrians were the strongest of all; afterward the Greek and Roman peoples were stronger.

They dug through. When Nebuchadnezzar invaded Tyre by ship, he overthrew not only the wall but also the houses; and what had been the commerce of cities became, for seventy years, the drying of nets.

**VERSE 14.**—Ships of the sea, etc. In Hebrew, *Tharsis*, etc., up to “an ecclesiastical man destroys and subjects it to himself.”

**VERSE 15.**—For seventy years. (JEROME.) Tyre, once distressed, etc., up to “who, then, would not have hope of salvation if he should sing well, if he should properly arrange the strings, that is, the virtues?”

(SAME AUTHOR.) The number seven and the number seventy, whether completed in individual days or in seven decades, signifies perfect repentance, so that, when the time of repentance has been completed, Tyre may justly be restored to its former condition.

[Col. 1267A] The song of the prostitute. A woman abandoned by her lovers usually composes songs for her consolation and recalls the past; so too did Tyre after her restoration.

**VERSE 16.**—Take a lyre for yourself. What follows concerning this burden refers to Tyre’s restoration.

Sing well, often, etc. He admonishes her always to sing the song of her miseries, lest she suffer the same things again. For they say that this is the nature of music: if it finds someone joyful, it makes him more joyful; if it finds someone sad, it makes him sadder.

**VERSE 18.**—And her commerce and her wages will be. As Jerome says in Jeremiah, etc., up to “they offered their wages to the Lord.”

## CHAPTER 24

**VERSE 1.**—Behold, the Lord will strip, etc. (JEROME.) After the specific correction of the individual nations, etc., up to the point where he passes from the Egyptians and many others to the general burden of the final judgment.

**VERSE 2.**—It will be. (SAME AUTHOR.) All will alike either be rewarded for good deeds or condemned for evil deeds. There will be no distinction between noble and ignoble, priest and layman, slave and master, etc. For all will stand on equal terms before the tribunal of Christ, and there will be no partiality with God.

So the priest. A good people will receive the crown of life together with a good priest; the wicked will likewise endure the torments of Gehenna, without respect of persons.

Earth. (SAME AUTHOR.) Earthly works will be reduced to nothing, so that, once the image of the earthly man has been abolished, the image of the heavenly man may remain. For flesh and blood will not possess the kingdom of God, because this mortal nature will put on immortality.

**VERSE 6.**—The curse will devour the earth. Just as at the beginning God blessed every creature, so at the end he curses those who are earthly—not strangers, but inhabitants of the earth—and those who sin in it, having forgotten their condition and raging against one another. Only a few will remain who possess the image of the heavenly man.

**VERSE 7.**—The vintage mourns; the vine has languished. (SAME AUTHOR.) At the consummation of the world, the memory of former pleasures will be a source of torments. Hence the rich man dressed in purple, who had received good things during his life, raising his eyes from hell, sees Lazarus at rest (Luke 19); hence: “Woe to you who are filled, for you will hunger” (Luke 6).

All who rejoice have groaned, etc. We bring forward this testimony [Col. 1267D] against those who at banquets indulge not only their stomachs in gluttony and drunkenness, but also their ears in sensuality, so that through all the senses the strength of the soul may grow weak.

**VERSE 10.**—The city of vanity has been crushed. The world, in which everything is vain: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

**VERSE 11.**—There will be a cry over wine. By wine we understand error, for drunkards wander astray. By the streets—which in Greek are called so from their breadth—we understand the spacious and broad way that leads to death. Therefore, over those who have gone astray on the broad and spacious way of this age there will be a cry of grief on the day of judgment.

**VERSE 13.**—In the midst of the earth. Jerusalem, which, as they say, is the navel of the earth. Many believe that because the Lord will judge upon Mount Zion, from which he ascended, he will sit in the air and come upon a cloud.

As with a few olives, etc. When only a few have been left, after persecution has devoured the earth, etc., up to the point where, after the grapes have also been gathered, scarcely a few remain on the empty vines.

**VERSE 14.**—And they will praise: when the Lord has been glorified. (SAME AUTHOR.) Those who are able to remain and escape the pressure of Antichrist, or the heat of the impending Gehenna, will praise.

They will neigh. In the likeness of horses, leaping with the greatness of their joy.

**VERSE 16.**—From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the righteous. In Hebrew, “the wings of the earth.” The wings, or ends, of the earth are the prophets and apostles, who fly from earthly things to heavenly ones and set the manner of life within certain limits of the commandments. Therefore the saints say: [Col. 1268B] Just as we heard from the prophets and apostles, so now we see it fulfilled.

My secret is for me. (SAME AUTHOR.) He can neither fully recount the rewards of the good nor the punishments of the wicked, which he foresees through the Spirit; and therefore he grieves, saying: “Woe is me.”

**VERSE 17.**—Terror and the pit. These words can refer both to the times of the martyrs, etc., up to the point where “so it will also happen in the time of Antichrist.”

**VERSE 18.**—The windows have been opened, etc. So that God may see the iniquities of Antichrist and judge them. For when he does not punish sins, he pretends not to see them.

The foundations of the earth. The rulers of the age; earthly works.

**VERSE 19.**—It will be utterly shattered. Not that the earth will be reduced to dust or nothingness, but that all earthly things will pass away. And just as a drunkard does not know what he is doing, so all who are engaged upon the earth will be drunk and stupefied by the magnitude of evils, and will be astonished at everything.

**VERSE 20.**—A tent for one night. (SAME AUTHOR.) Just as a tent is moved by a traveler so that no trace remains, so the form of this world will pass away (1 Corinthians 7), and the earth will be deserted, so that no human habitation will remain in it.

**VERSE 21.**—And it will happen, etc. As though he were saying: The windows of heaven have been opened, so that, while the Lord observes earthly sins, every form of earthly works may pass away and collapse and not rise again in its former shape. Therefore on that day the Lord will visit the host of heaven, so that he may judge not only earthly things but also heavenly things.

Upon the host. (SAME AUTHOR.) “My sword has been drunk in heaven. The stars are not clean in his sight. And in his angels he found perversity” (Isaiah 34; Job 15, 4).

[Col. 1268D] The kings of the earth. (JEROME.) “The rulers of the darkness of this age, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6); hence in Daniel: “The prince of the kingdom of Persia came to meet me, and the prince of the kingdom of the Medes” (Daniel 10).

**VERSE 22.**—And they will be gathered. (SAME AUTHOR.) Origen says that, after this sentence—“Go, accursed ones, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25)—after many days, that is, after a thousand years, they will be visited and liberated. But the Church does not accept this. For it is said: “The wicked will go into eternal punishment, but the righteous into eternal life” (Matthew 13). What is eternal is without any end; and just as joy is eternal, so also is punishment.

One bundle in the pit. Hence: “Bind them in bundles for burning.”

[Col. 1269A] And after many. It should be noted that he does not add “by the Lord” or “by the angels,” etc., up to the point that it is left to the Lord’s decision.

**VERSE 23.**—And it will be ashamed. Hence the creature groans and travails, etc., up to “such as Abraham was when he died in a good old age.”

## CHAPTER 25

**VERSE 1.**—Amen. (JEROME.) The Hebrew word that the Lord often uses in the Gospel: “Amen, amen,” that is, “Truly, truly, I say to you.”

**VERSE 2.**—The city. Overthrown by Nebuchadnezzar, it was restored by Nehemiah and by Jesus the high priest. Overthrown by the Romans, it was restored by Aelius Hadrian, but not in the same place or to its former condition.

And forever. (SAME AUTHOR.) So that the fable of the thousand-year kingdom and of golden and jeweled Jerusalem may finally come to rest.

**VERSE 10.**—And Moab will be threshed, etc. (SAME AUTHOR.) Although he was speaking generally about the consummation of the world, etc., up to the point where “we rightly understand Moab as the devil, who is always an adversary of the children of God.”

Straw in a cart. Straw is threshed with iron-toothed carts, so that animals may more easily eat and ruminate it.

## CHAPTER 26

**VERSE 1.**—On that day, etc. (SAME AUTHOR.) This can refer to the present Church and to the day of judgment. Now the Church sings a new song: Christ’s birth, passion, resurrection, and ascension. For it is old for the ancient man to descend to the underworld; it is new to ascend to heaven.

The city of strength. The voice of the righteous, both now and in the future.

**VERSE 2.**—Open the gates. This song suddenly changes speakers.

Gates. Of righteousness; hence: “Open to me the gates of righteousness.” The gates of life and righteousness, etc., up to “and through many gates to him who says: No one comes to the Father except through me” (John 14).

**VERSE 3.**—Peace. (SAME AUTHOR.) Repetition is a confirmation. This peace belongs to the one of whom it is said: “Man, man, of the children of Israel” (Ezekiel 14); and elsewhere: “The man, the man whose wife has defiled the marriage bed” (Numbers 5), so that the double man and the double husband may obtain double peace.

**VERSE 6.**—The foot will trample it, etc. Because “everyone who exalts himself will be humbled” (Luke 1). We can also refer this to opposing powers.

[Col. 1269D] The needy. (JEROME.) The apostles, whom the Jews expelled from their borders, who, by imitating the Lord’s poverty, attained the privilege of his power.

**VERSE 9.**—My soul has desired, etc. Not the flesh; hence: “My soul has thirsted for God, the living fountain” (Psalm 41). “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians 5).

**VERSE 10.**—Let us have mercy. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Lord says to the prophet: Should we have mercy on the wicked, so that he may learn—namely, my clemency—while he himself is saved? As though to say: This is better.

And the righteous will not learn, etc. As though he were saying: How will he be able to know your righteousness if he has experienced your clemency?

And he will not see. The Lord says to the prophet, as though it were better for him to see and be ashamed of his evils. “And he will not see,” as though he were saying: For punishment it is enough that he will not see me reigning in heaven with my saints. The Septuagint has: “The wicked will be taken away, so that he will not see the glory of God.”

**VERSE 11.**—Let those who are jealous be confounded. The Septuagint has: “Jealousy will seize the untaught people.”

**VERSE 12.**—Lord, you will grant. (SAME AUTHOR.) It should be noted that after he has repaid our works to us, he will also give peace, and that they ask for peace because he has worked in them. They say that they have endured torments so that afterward they might obtain mercy.

**VERSE 13.**—Lord, others have possessed us. (SAME AUTHOR.) The demons whom we worshiped in idols. The Septuagint has: “Lord, apart from you we know no other,” not absolutely “another,” but “apart from you”; for the Father is in the Son, and the Son in the Father.

[Col. 1270B] We will remember only you. (SAME AUTHOR.) We ask nothing else except that, after our errors, we may be deemed worthy to remember your name.

You have destroyed every. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Septuagint has the masculine form, etc., up to the point where “memory” has been interpreted as masculine, contrary to the saying: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked.”

**VERSE 15.**—Surely? He did not repent, and this is the meaning of “Surely?” As though he were saying: Security gives birth to negligence, and negligence to contempt.

**VERSE 18.**—And we have given birth. Others punctuate it this way: “And we have given birth to spirit; we have not produced salvation on the earth.”

Spirit: salvation, etc. So that we may believe with our whole mind and, since we did not perceive benefits through it, learn through torments.

**VERSE 21.**—The earth will reveal. (SAME AUTHOR.) At that time earthly things will not be able to conceal those whom they killed, because then everything will be open; or the earth that received and covered the martyrs’ blood will then be revealed when they rise again.

## CHAPTER 27

**VERSE 1.**—On that day, etc. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Hebrews relate that the devil, etc., up to the point where “the sword may be brought against him.”

The bar. (JEROME.) The Septuagint has: “The fugitive.” For then he will flee, etc., while he is called a serpent because he subtly pours in his ambushes.

Sea monster. The Hebrews have *Tanniu*; hence the Hebrews imagined that Leviathan dwells beneath the earth and in the air, but *Tanniu* in the sea.

**VERSE 2.**—The vineyard of pure wine will sing. To it Jeremiah gives a cup of the purest wine. *Merum* is Greek; in Latin, “pure.”

[Col. 1270D] **VERSE 5.**—Or rather? The voice of the Father deliberating, etc., up to “who have not been saved by the authority of the law.”

**VERSE 6.**—Israel, that is, the converted Jewish people, seeing the world flourish through the teaching of its children.

**VERSE 9.**—Therefore. As though he were saying: For this reason iniquity will be forgiven the house of Jacob; and the rest, because of the merits of the apostles, who throughout the world smashed the altars of idols.

**VERSE 11.**—They will be crushed. (SAME AUTHOR.) Just as Deborah went to war and judged the people to the disgrace of the Jews, and, when the captivity of the Chaldeans was imminent, Huldah prophesied while the men remained silent, so, when the captivity under the Romans was imminent, women came forward and taught them.

[Col. 1271A] Women. The various synagogues; or literally women, who strike their arms with bared and bleeding breasts.

Teaching her. (JEROME.) It is a great misfortune and reproach for the people to learn the songs of lamentation from women.

**VERSE 12.**—From the channel. The Septuagint has: “From the Euphrates,” etc., up to the point where “because it has turbid waters, and they do not flow continuously.”

## CHAPTER 28

**VERSE 1.**—Woe to the crown of pride. (SAME AUTHOR.) Up to the consummation of the world, etc., up to the point where “it had no fruit of repentance for salvation.”

Of the very fertile valley. Gethsemane, because of the fertility of its crops; by way of it they ascended into the city, and while staying in the city some pitched tents there for recreation.

[Col. 1271B] **VERSE 5.**—On that day. (SAME AUTHOR.) According to the prophecy, when the Lord, etc., up to the point where “the scribes and Pharisees were drunk with wine and strong drink.”

**VERSE 6.**—Strength for those returning. (SAME AUTHOR.) The wars of Hezekiah are not recorded, but the Lord fought the battle for him, killing one hundred and eighty-five thousand Assyrians, whose spoils the Jews collected; and they returned joyfully to the gates of Jerusalem.

**VERSE 8.**—For all. Since they do not digest the food of the Scriptures or make it life-giving to the body, they instead expel it immature and foul, so that the Lord finds no place in them.

**VERSE 9.**—Weaned from milk, removed from the breast. Not others, because they cannot bear it. These are those who can already use solid food; to others the Apostle says: “I gave you milk to drink, not food” (1 Corinthians 3).

**VERSE 10.**—For “command, command again; command, command again; wait, wait again; wait, wait again; a little here, a little here.” (SAME AUTHOR.) As though he were saying: You cannot be taught, because, mocking the prophets—through whom the Lord foretells the evils that will come upon you so that you may repent and be delivered—you respond: “Command, command again; command, command again,” as though saying: Prophet, command whatever you wish; threaten whatever you wish; nevertheless, the things you threaten will not happen.

**VERSE 11.**—For with the speech. As though he were saying: You say these things to your own harm, because from now on the Lord will not announce evils to you but will immediately inflict them. And this is the meaning: “With the speech of the lip and with another tongue he will speak to this people,” etc.

[Col. 1271D] **VERSE 16.**—A stone. The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.

**VERSE 19.**—Only distress will give understanding to the hearing.

**VERSE 21.**—For just as. When David, with the Lord’s help, came upon the Philistines gathered for battle, he divided the living from the dead and scattered the “perverse places” [reading uncertain]; hence that place received the name Baal-perazim.

An alien work. (SAME AUTHOR.) God’s proper work is to have mercy, spare, and forgive. It is not his own but an alien work to become angry and punish.

(GREGORY.) He will come into the world to do his own work, namely, to redeem the human race; but his work is alien to him, for it is not fitting for the Godhead to be spat upon, scourged, and crucified.

**VERSE 24.**—Does the whole. (JEROME.) The pious and merciful God plows the human race so that it may bear the fruit of good work: like a farmer, he plows with the plowshare of preaching; he breaks up the soil with the blows of tribulation; now through pestilence, now through captivity, he corrects it. And this is the meaning: “Does the whole day,” etc.

[Col. 1272A] **VERSE 25.**—Black cumin and cumin. Black cumin and cumin, which are threshed with a rod, etc., up to “possessing the key of knowledge.”

**VERSE 29.**—And this too has come forth from the Lord God.

## CHAPTER 29

**VERSE 1.**—Woe to Ariel. (SAME AUTHOR.) He addresses Jerusalem with compassion: “If you too had known” (Luke 19). Ariel means “lion of God”; for Jerusalem, the lion of God, was once most powerful and strong.

He conquered it. (SAME AUTHOR.) Although it was extremely powerful, it was captured when the blind and the lame resisted and Joab first climbed the heights of the fortress.

A year has been added. When they were carried into captivity by Nebuchadnezzar, they had neither temple nor sacrifice, and this continued for many years; hence “year has been added to year.”

**VERSE 3.**—Like a sphere around you. Retaining the likeness of the ancient temple, but not its magnificence.

**VERSE 4.**—Of the Pythoness, etc. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Pythoness who was at Endor raised Samuel—or rather a demon—through necromancy, and foretold such things concerning that people. *Mania* means madness or insanity; hence *Manichaeans*, *manthoi*, divination.

**VERSE 6.**—In thunder. The Romans seemed to rush in with thunder, the earth to quake at their arrival, and with the flame of fire, because they set the city and the temple ablaze.

**VERSE 9.**—Be astonished and wonder. (JEROME.) After the overthrow of Jerusalem and the temple, that is, Ariel, the prophecy is directed against the scribes and Pharisees.

**VERSE 11.**—For it has been sealed. These things were fulfilled when they lost both their dignity and priesthood, and the city and temple were destroyed by the Roman leaders.

**VERSE 13.**—Because this people draws near. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Lord uses this in the Gospel of Matthew, etc., up to the point where “they used the very words.”

With their lips. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Septuagint has: “With his lips he honors me, but his heart is far from me; in vain do they worship me, teaching the commandments and doctrines of men.”

[Col. 1272D] **VERSE 14.**—For it will perish. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Apostle cites testimony from this passage: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and I will reject the understanding of the prudent.” In other words, the same meaning: God performed a truly great miracle among the people, so that at the same time the city burned, the temple collapsed, and all the learning of the teachers perished.

**VERSE 15.**—You hide yourselves from the Lord. (SAME AUTHOR.) As though God did not see. Adam and Eve hid themselves in this error; Cain too said: “I shall be hidden from your face.”

**VERSE 16.**—It is perverse, etc. (SAME AUTHOR.) As though the Creator were ignorant of the creature; hence the Apostle: “O man, who are you to answer back to God? Does the work say to its maker, ‘Why did you make me?’” (Romans 9).

[Col. 1273A] **VERSE 17.**—In a little while and briefly. (JEROME.) The “little while” and “briefly” extend from the time when this was foretold until the Lord’s ascension; for all periods, compared with eternity, are brief and momentary.

Lebanon into Carmel. Lebanon is a mountain in Phoenicia, etc., up to the point where “if he were with an adulterous man.”

**VERSE 21.**—And they have turned aside from the just in vain. The demons attempted, etc., up to the point where “the scribes and Pharisees turned aside from the just in vain, saying: ‘We have no king but Caesar’” (John 19).

**VERSE 22.**—He redeemed Abraham. From the fire of the Chaldeans, etc., up to the point where “their tongue is called *ur*, for fire.”

## CHAPTER 30

**VERSE 1.**—Woe to the apostate sons, says the Lord. [Col. 1273B] (SAME AUTHOR.) After the prophecy against Ariel and the rest, etc., up to the point where “they fled into Egypt”; and this is the meaning of “woe to the apostate sons.”

**VERSE 2.**—Who walk. As Jerome says: Jeremiah went with them, etc., up to “so that you might dwell in your own land.”

For they were in Tahpanhes. As though he were saying: Did you withdraw from me for this reason, so that you might flee as far as Tahpanhes and Anes? Tahpanhes is the city in which the magicians performed signs against Moses; Anes lies on the borders of Egypt. Perhaps, disturbed by fear, they did not dare remain in Tahpanhes and fled as far as Anes.

**VERSE 6.**—The burden of the beasts. (SAME AUTHOR.) After the ten burdens of the various nations, he places an eleventh burden upon the remaining two tribes, which remained after Zedekiah and the other leaders had been led to Babylon.

In the land. (SAME AUTHOR.) The wilderness through which Johanan son of Kareah and the other commanders led the remnant into Egypt, contrary to the Lord’s command; or Egypt itself, in which they endured many tribulations and hardships.

**VERSE 8.**—Now therefore. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Lord speaks to Jeremiah—or, according to the Hebrews, to Isaiah—etc., up to the point where “because I treated them well, taught them well, and they rejected me.”

**VERSE 12.**—Because you rejected the word. (SAME AUTHOR.) Heretics also, and every doctrine contrary to the truth, etc., up to “and at least to offer the thirsty muddy and scant water.”

**VERSE 13.**—Like a breach falling. As though to say: Just as a breach in a very high wall, whose ruin has extended over a long time, is difficult to restore and return to its former beauty, so sudden destruction will come upon you.

**VERSE 19.**—Weeping, he will by no means weep. (SAME AUTHOR.) The Jews refer this to the time when, under Zerubbabel, etc., up to “namely, in the watchtower and vision of peace, that is, the Church.”

**VERSE 21.**—Behind you. In the first condition, as though Adam had heard the Lord speaking to him face to face, etc., up to “and this is the meaning: Your ears will hear the word of the one admonishing you from behind.”

Nor to the right. On either side, whatever exceeds the proper measure is blameworthy. One must not turn to the right, etc., but walk along the public road, that is, the royal road, which does not mislead.

**VERSE 22.**—And you will defile the plates. (SAME AUTHOR.) The idols [Col. 1274A] which the craftsman’s tongue has fashioned in the likeness of truth: you will crush, scatter, and judge them unclean in the splendor of eloquence, signified by silver, and in the reasoning of wisdom, signified by gold.

**VERSE 23.**—And rain will be given. (SAME AUTHOR.) It is written in the Book of Kings, etc., up to “for unless they cast away vices, virtues do not enter.”

He will be fed. Some argue that these things were fulfilled hyperbolically in the time of Cyrus, who released the people from captivity, in Judea.

**VERSE 24.**—Mixed mash. Isaac sowed barley, etc., up to “and gradually advance through straw and barley and pass over to wheat.”

**VERSE 25.**—And there will be. On the day of judgment there will be streams upon the mountains [Col. 1274B] and hills, etc., up to “for whoever drinks from its waters will never thirst.”

The slaughter of many. (SAME AUTHOR.) For many are called, etc., up to “whose tongues were confused in Babylon and upon whom the tower at Siloam fell.”

**VERSE 26.**—And the light will be. When they receive the reward of their labor, because creation will be liberated from slavery to corruption. It is not surprising if the moon receives the sun’s brilliance, since “the righteous will shine like the sun” (Matthew 13).

**VERSE 27.**—Behold, the name of the Lord. The Son is in the name of the Father, for the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one name. Hence: “Baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit”—not “in the names,” but “in the name,” which is God.

**VERSE 28.**—His spirit like an overflowing torrent. [Col. 1274C] (JEROME.) Just as an overflowing torrent, when it reaches the neck, suffocates a living creature, so the spirit of God’s wrath will suffocate the wicked in the judgment. This signifies that the end of all things has come: just as a torrent suffocates the one whose neck it reaches, so God’s judgment will allow no one to pass unpunished.

What was in the jaws. So that they might be carried about according to the devil’s will, the Lord will destroy these things on the day of judgment; or in the preaching of the apostles, when the Gentiles come to the faith and abandon their idols.

**VERSE 29.**—There will be a song for you. After the punishment of the wicked, he discusses the glory of the saints. Just as the children of Israel, having crossed the Red Sea and seen Pharaoh and the Egyptians submerged, said joyfully: “Let us sing to the Lord, for he has triumphed gloriously,” etc., so on the day of judgment, when the world has been crossed over and the devil and his members condemned, the saints will rejoice with gladness in the praises of God; the same will occur in the conversion of the Gentiles.

Like one who proceeds. The children of Israel were commanded to offer a tenth of their goods to the Lord, glorifying the Giver of good things; so the saints at the judgment will offer their sheaves while rejoicing and praising God, and the converted Gentiles will do likewise.

**VERSE 33.**—Of sulfur. In hell there is intolerable stench and unquenchable fire.

## CHAPTER 31

**VERSE 1.**—Woe to those who go down to Egypt. (SAME AUTHOR.) He has spoken of the glory of the good and the punishment of the reprobate; now he returns to the remnant that remained [Col. 1275A] in the land of Judah after Zedekiah and the others had been led to Babylon. But first he warned them not to go to Egypt; now, because they have gone, he threatens evil.

They did not trust in the Holy One of Israel. They did not seek him with their heart, but with words; for they said to Jeremiah: “Pray to the Lord for us, what should we do?” Yet they refused to obey. To this is comparable: “They did not call upon God.” This was said of wicked priests.

**VERSE 2.**—But he himself is wise. Hence Jeremiah: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man,” etc., up to the point where “the place where the Lord was crucified is specifically called Sodom and Egypt” (Revelation 11).

**VERSE 4.**—For thus he says. (JEROME.) This concerns those who, having been carried into captivity with Zedekiah, returned after seventy years through the Lord’s mercy, while the Israelites and Egyptians in whose assistance they had trusted were slain in Egypt.

**VERSE 5.**—So the Lord will protect. Thus the Lord acted against the Samaritans, who attempted to obstruct the building of the temple. In the time of the Maccabees also, he struck down many by means of a few.

**VERSE 6.**—Return. In prophecy he does not preserve the order of time or history, etc., up to the point where “so they might return with the full devotion of their mind.”

**VERSE 9.**—There is fire in Zion. Zion is the Church, in which there is fire and a furnace that devours sinners, namely, consuming wood, hay, and straw.

## CHAPTER 32

**VERSE 1.**—Behold, a king will reign in righteousness. (JEROME.) Having finished the prophecy concerning those who went down to Egypt, he begins [Col. 1275C] to speak about the coming of Christ and his apostles.

**VERSE 2.**—And a man will be like. (SAME AUTHOR.) As though he were saying: He will be safe amid tribulations, like one who, fleeing wind and storm, hides safely in a secure place; like one who finds the purest springs in the desert; like one who avoids the sun’s heat beneath an overhanging rock.

**VERSE 9.**—Women. (SAME AUTHOR.) He addresses the matrons who will be taken captive by the Romans, so that they may repent; or by “women” he indicates the synagogues or the cities of Judea. Wealthy women, rise: after the calling of the Gentiles, whom Christ ruled in righteousness, the speech is directed to the wealthy women.

**VERSE 10.**—After days and a year. Hence: “Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6); and elsewhere: “The year acceptable to the Lord” (Isaiah 61).

[Col. 1275D] After days. That is, after Christ’s preaching. For those who were unrepentant, even if they were not immediately taken captive, were nevertheless immediately thrown into confusion because they refused to receive the Lord’s preaching.

**VERSE 12.**—Beat your breasts. “Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves and over your children.”

**VERSE 14.**—Of wild asses. (SAME AUTHOR.) Of every kind of wild animal and bird that dwelled there for a long time.

**VERSE 15.**—Until it is poured out. The Holy Spirit, when Elijah and Enoch preach, will descend upon us, as at Pentecost upon the apostles. The prophet joins himself to them in compassion.

[Col. 1276A] Desert. The wilderness of the Gentiles will be turned into Israel’s riches, and Israel will be reckoned among the Gentiles.

**VERSE 17.**—And the work of righteousness. So that we may pray in silence, not in the streets, neither shouting nor using many words.

**VERSE 18.**—In tents. (SAME AUTHOR.) Now he dwells confidently in the dwellings of heaven; hence: “In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14); or in the churches that trust confidently in the Lord.

**VERSE 19.**—Hail. As though he were saying: When the Christian people have sat in the beauty of peace, then the wrath of God will rage against the forest.

**VERSE 20.**—Blessed are you who sow. (SAME AUTHOR.) In his exposition of Ecclesiastes: That teacher is considered worthy of blessedness who sows upon the watered breast of his hearers, [Col. 1276B] gathered from both the Jewish and Gentile peoples.

## CHAPTER 33

**VERSE 1.**—Woe to you who plunder. (SAME AUTHOR.) Against Sennacherib; these words can also refer to any plunderer and to the devil himself.

**VERSE 2.**—Lord, have mercy on us. (SAME AUTHOR.) In the person of the people besieged by Sennacherib, or rather in the person of the apostles and all the faithful.

In the morning. Those who remained from Sennacherib’s army; they saw their comrades dead and were turned to flight.

**VERSE 3.**—Angels. Namely Michael, who is the prince of the Jews, or Gabriel, the strength and commander of battles.

**VERSE 4.**—The locust larva. The locust larva is born from the locust, etc., up to the point where “even dead ones produce locust larvae.”

[Col. 1276C] **VERSE 6.**—Your. O Hezekiah; or, according to others, “his own,” namely the people who were delivered.

His. (JEROME.) Namely, of salvation; for without fear neither wisdom nor knowledge is of any use. Hence: “You will have many good things if you fear God” (Tobit 4); and: “The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom” (Psalm 110).

**VERSE 8.**—The covenant. Which the Lord made with Abraham, namely: “I will multiply your seed like the stars,” etc. (Genesis 22); and elsewhere: “You will dwell in this place from now and forever” (Zechariah 11).

**VERSE 9.**—Lebanon. The temple; Bashan, the region of Og, which Moses gave beyond the Jordan to two and a half tribes; this too was exceedingly fertile. Carmel, the most fertile mountain of the Promised Land. Through these images, therefore, we must understand that the Jews lost all fertility.

[Col. 1276D] **VERSE 14.**—Who will be able? He recounts God’s mighty deeds and calls God fire.

**VERSE 17.**—The land. Of the living. “Blessed are the meek, for they will possess the land”; or, placed in heaven, they look down upon earthly things.

**VERSE 20.**—The tent which. (SAME AUTHOR.) The tent that the Jews had in the wilderness, etc., up to the point where “the Church, however, has been founded immovably upon a firm rock.”

**VERSE 22.**—For the Lord. (SAME AUTHOR.) He will judge the world in righteousness.

**VERSE 23.**—Your ropes have been loosened, etc. He returns to earthly Jerusalem and speaks of it under the figure of a ship. What was said above concerned the city of our solemnity, which the Lord surrounds with his rivers.

## CHAPTER 34

**VERSE 4.**—All the host of heaven. (JEROME.) The sun, moon, and stars will seem to be darkened as the true light, which is Christ, shines forth. The evil spirits also, having lost their power, will be shut up in hell.

And they will be rolled up like a scroll. Not, of course, the inner part, etc., up to the point where “nothing will afterward be written upon them.”

**VERSE 6.**—In Bozrah. (SAME AUTHOR.) In the city of the world fortified against God. For *Bozrah* means “fortified,” or “from God”; the world is established by the Lord’s will. Hence: “He founded it upon the seas,” and: “I strengthened its pillars.” The teachers of the Hebrews wish Bozrah and Edom to be understood as Rome, and all the things contained in the following chapter to be said about it.

[Col. 1277B] **VERSE 8.**—For the day of the Lord’s vengeance is the year of recompense. After the general vengeance upon the world, he returns to Jerusalem, to which he was first speaking, and describes its destruction in plain speech—the destruction carried out by the Romans.

**VERSE 11.**—The ibis. A water bird hostile to serpents. Josephus says that Moses brought these birds into the war against the Ethiopians, because serpents abound in the land through which he was going to pass.

12. **Its nobles.** For the apostles had already passed over to the Gentiles; other believers, warned by the Holy Spirit as the captivity approached, crossed the Jordan into the kingdom of Agrippa, who was at peace with the Romans.

## CHAPTER XXXV

**Verse 1.—“It will rejoice.”** After setting forth the captivity of the Jews, he discusses the conversion of the Gentiles.

**Verse 2.—“Sharon.”** The people of the Jews; hence: “Sharon will be like a wilderness” (Isa. XXXII).

**Verse 7.—“The greenery of the reed.”** The fulfillment of Scripture, which is through the reed; and the assistance of intention, which is through the rush—for the reed and the rush grow and become green beside the waters.

## CHAPTER XXXVI

**Verse 1.—“And it came to pass.”** (Jerome.) The Books of Kings and Chronicles agree, and so on, up to “he besieged Jerusalem.”

**Verse 3.—“Shebna.”** (Same.) Shebna the scribe—another man, not the proud one—who, as the Hebrews relate, terrified by Rabshakeh’s threats, surrendered the lower part of the city, while the citadel and temple remained.

**Verse 4.—“Thus says.”** Perhaps as he had heard from his father: “Thus says the Lord.” And, so that his words might have greater weight, he marks his arrogance: “Thus says the great king,” as though possessing an opposing power.

**Verse 6.—“Behold, you trust.”** (Same.) He is plainly lying. Nowhere, in fact, is Hezekiah said to have placed his hope in Egypt.

**Verse 8.—“Nor will you be able.”** Not because of weakness, but because of the Lord’s commandments, who through Moses gave instructions concerning the king of Israel, saying: “You shall not multiply horses, chariots, or many wives for yourself.”

**Verse 16.—“Make a blessing with me,” and so on.** Praise me; bless me. Or, as another edition has it: “Do what is useful for you, so that you may receive me and peace may remain with you.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII

**Verse 1.—“And it came to pass, when King Hezekiah heard it, that he tore his garments.”** (Same.) They tear their garments because they had heard Rabshakeh blaspheming. The king tore his, believing that this had come about because of his own sins and those of the people.

**Verse 2.—“Isaiah the son of Amoz.”** In the Book of Kings it says that he sent to Isaiah the prophet. But here, because Isaiah composed the history concerning himself, he calls himself not a prophet but the son of a prophet.
