**Verse 4.—“For the remnant.”** For the ten tribes had already been led away, and the cities of Judah and Benjamin had been devastated; even the lower part of the city had been handed over to the enemy by the wicked and proud high priest Shebna. “Lift up your eyes,” and so on.

**Verse 7.—“Behold, I will give him a spirit,” and so on.** It is as though he said: “I will not recount everything that I shall do to the Assyrian, lest I seem to boast of my power; but this one thing: Behold, I will give.”

**Verse 8.—“And he found.”** Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, fought against the Egyptians, and so on, up to the Chaldean writers of history.

**Verse 15.—“He prayed.”** (Jerome.) Now he was more confident of deliverance. Earlier he had indeed gone up, but he is not said to have prayed, because he feared that these things would happen on account of his sins.

**Verse 18.—“For truly, Lord.”** Many histories confirm that the kings of Persia came into Greece, overturned its temples, and plundered them.

**Verse 21.—“And he sent.”** The history of the Book of Kings and Chronicles is interwoven with prophecy, because there is prophecy concerning the city’s deliverance, the destruction of the Assyrian, the sun’s return, and the additional years of Hezekiah.

**Verse 22.—“The daughter of Jerusalem.”** She who earlier had not answered is now certain of vengeance and secure concerning punishment.

**Verse 25.—“And I dried up.”** The army was so large that it dried up the streams, and therefore caused the wells to fail for lack of water.

**Verse 29.—“Pride.”** (Same.) “I will endure no more, so that you may know that you were able to do these things not by your own strength but by my will. For the impious and fruitless nations deserved to be cut down by you, as by an axe.”

**Verse 30.—“But for you.”** (Same.) Through messengers the Prophet has been speaking all these things to Hezekiah: what Sennacherib had said and what the Lord had answered him. Now he turns his words to Hezekiah himself, so that he may not doubt that what he foretold will come to pass. For this especially was belief placed in the prophets: they testified not only to things far in the future but also to those soon to be fulfilled.

**“And in the year.”** That is, as the harvest was approaching, the Assyrians attacked and devastated the crops, vineyards, and olive groves. Because of the excessive siege, they used for food during the first and second years whatever they found among the grain. Since they could not sow during the year of the siege, they consumed whatever they found among the fruits and produce.

**Verse 33.—“Therefore.”** (Same.) He returns to his subject and, after giving hope concerning future events, removes the present fear. For there would not be as much joy over the future things he promised as there was concern over the things immediately impending.

**Verse 35.—“For my sake.”** This signifies that they were preserved not through their own merit but through God’s mercy—and indeed also through the memory of their father David. In this they are admonished concerning their own negligence and his faith and righteousness, which God loves so greatly that, because of the merits of the saints, he protects their descendants.

**Verse 37.—“And he returned.”** He was spared so that he might learn God’s power, silence blasphemous mouths, and proclaim the majesty of the one whom he had previously despised.

**Verse 38.—“His sons.”** (Same.) The Jews relate that they envied Esar-haddon, and so on, up to the account that he was preserved to be killed by his sons in the temple of his god.

**“Ararat.”** (Jerome.) A level region of Armenia through which the Araxes flows, of unbelievable fertility, at the foot of Mount Taurus, which extends as far as that place. Noah’s ark, however, was not carried generally to the mountains of Armenia called Ararat, but to the highest mountains of Taurus, which overlook the plains of Ararat.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII

**Verse 1.—“In those days he fell ill.”** (Jerome.) Because he did not offer God worthy thanks for the victory but became vain in pride, as the Book of Kings and Chronicles makes clear. Hence: “Whom God loves, he disciplines,” lest, after unbelievable triumphs, he be lifted up in pride.

**“You will die.”** Compare: “Nineveh will be overthrown,” and many things foretold under threat that were not fulfilled—not because God changed his decision, but because he provokes us to know him. For the Lord is patient concerning wickedness.

**Verse 2.—“Toward the wall.”** (Same.) Of the temple, that is, beside the palace which Solomon built.

**Verse 3.—“I beseech you, Lord.”** As he is about to go to the Lord, he recounts his deeds. Blessed is the conscience that, in times of evil, can remember good deeds.

**“I beseech you, Lord.”** Hearing that he would die, he does not ask for many years, but leaves it to God’s judgment to decide what he wishes to grant. He knew that Solomon had pleased God because Solomon had not asked for longer years of life.

**“And what is good.”** He destroyed the idols of his father; he opened the doors of the Lord’s house, which his father had closed; he broke into pieces the bronze serpent that the Jews worshiped at Gibeon and scattered it to the wind.

**“And he wept.”** He wept because he was dying without children, and so on, up to the statement that we read of many being raised after death.

**Verse 4.—“And the word of the Lord came.”** Here the history is related in an inverted order; it is presented more sequentially in the Book of Kings.

**Verse 5.—“Behold, I will add to your days.”** According to what was seen, and so on, up to the account of the additional years of Hezekiah.

**Verse 7.—“And this shall be a sign for you from the Lord, that the Lord will do this word which he has spoken.”** (Same.) It concerns both the present and the future: just as the sun returns to the beginning of its course, so Hezekiah’s life returns to the years that had passed. May the spans of life also be extended for us, who live in the seventh and eighth ages, after Christ’s resurrection.

**Verse 10.—“I said.”** (Same.) When God had given Hezekiah victory without labor, and so on, up to the statement that sinners die in the middle of their days.

**“In the middle of my days.”** Hence: “Wicked and deceitful men will not halve their days,” because they neither complete works of virtue nor correct their sins through repentance.

**“At the gates of hell I sought.”** Where the dwelling of every living person was established before Christ’s coming.

**Verse 11.—“Of rest.”** Some manuscripts read: “My generation has ceased,” which Jerome also once translated, deceived by the ambiguity of the word, and later corrected.

**Verse 15.—“He will answer me.”** (Same.) “I will correct what I have done wrong; be my guarantor and protector. For it depends not on the one who wills or the one who runs, but on God who shows mercy” (Rom. IX).

**“When he himself.”** These things are justly due to me, as though he were saying: “Nothing remains except to endure patiently and to entreat the strong one himself, who has done what he wished.”

**“I will reflect.”** What has passed does not help the one who is enduring; hence foolish is Epicurus’s opinion, who claims that recollection of past goods mitigates present evils.

**“In the bitterness of my soul.”** It is as though he were saying: “These things too are in bitterness,” because present tribulation feels none of the good of the past, and human happiness is always sprinkled with some contrary element.

**Verse 18.—“For hell will not give thanks.”** Those condemned without end neither repent in hell nor return praises to God.

**Verse 19.—“The living, the living,” and so on.** Not hell or death.

**“The father to the children.”** Hence: “Ask your father, and he will announce it,” and so on.

**Verse 21.—“Upon his wound.”** The Hebrews say that *Sehin* means an ulcer, not a wound, and so on, up to “when God had done this.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX

**Verse 1.—“At that time.”** (Jerome.) It was stated above that Esar-haddon succeeded Sennacherib, and so on, up to the statement that, having lost his manly strength, he is reduced to feminine softness.

**Verse 2.—“And in all his power.”** (Same.) In the treasures of the Lord’s house, in which he chiefly offended. For this was not within his authority. Yet he had already taken the gold plates from those temple doors.

**“In his treasures.”** He is silent about the Lord’s treasures, fearing to be reproved for having shown them whatever he possessed in his power—that is, the temple furnishings. Hence:

**Verse 7.—“And they shall be eunuchs.”** (Same.) The Hebrews relate that this was fulfilled in Daniel and his companions. After Jehoiakim, son of Josiah, was captured, they were captured with their people, led to Babylon, and made eunuchs, or emasculated. It should not, however, be thought that they were eunuchs in body but rather in mind, like those who castrated themselves for the sake of the kingdom of heaven (Matt. XIX).

**Verse 8.—“Let there be only peace.”** He ought to have confessed his sin with David and removed God’s anger from his descendants, or to have shared Moses’ compassion when he said: “Forgive them this offense, or erase me from the book that you have written” (Exod. XXXII). Because he did not do this, he therefore receives no answer; instead, turning to the people, he says: “Be comforted,” and so on.

## CHAPTER XL

**Verse 1.—“Be comforted.”** It is as though he said: “Because your king does not sympathize with you, take comfort in Christ.” This can be referred to the Gentiles, concerning whom the Lord says through Zechariah: “I will gather the people of the east, and they shall be my people, and I shall be their God” (Zech. VIII).

**“Speak to the heart.”** (Jerome.) He speaks to the heart who comforts the sorrowful, as it is said concerning Shechem: “Shechem spoke to her heart and comforted her” (Gen. XXIV).

**“Jerusalem.”** Jerusalem: afflicted in body and soul by the Chaldeans and Romans; the Church: afflicted in body by persecutors and distressed in spirit.

**“Her wickedness.”** “Wickedness” means affliction, as in: “If there is evil in a city that the Lord has not done” (Amos III).

**“She has been forgiven.”** The cause of consolation is the forgiveness of sins, and so on, up to the statement that they were cleansed and released through punishments.

**Verse 3.—“The voice of one crying.”** (Same.) Remembering this voice, the Jews sent to John to ask him: “Who are you?”

**Verse 4.—“Every valley shall be exalted.”** Whoever exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself, and so on. To this day the teachers of the Gentile Churches cry this in the wilderness.

**Verse 5.—“And all flesh shall see.”** He suddenly passes from the first coming to the second when he says: “And all flesh shall see.”

**“The mouth of the Lord.”** The prophets who proclaimed the future Christ, namely, the salvation of our God.

**Verse 6.—“What shall I cry?”** (Same.) He does not ask without reason. For when he offered himself willingly, saying: “Behold, here I am; send me,” he announced hard things to his people, and now he fears the same things.

**“All flesh.”** Whoever bears the image of the earthly, and so on, up to the statement that in the succession of ages a human being loses his beauty and falls into death.

**Verse 8.—“But the word of the Lord.”** The Word is Christ with his body, which is the Church.

**Verse 9.—“Zion.”** (Same.) By Zion and Jerusalem he understands the apostles and other teachers. He admonishes them to proclaim what they have received from the Lord and, ascending the heights of virtue, to teach by word and example.

**Verse 11.—“His flock,” and so on.** Now through contemplation, but in the future through direct vision; now by teaching, afterward by saving or satisfying.

**“Those giving birth.”** Teachers who daily give birth to children for God.

**Verse 12.—“Who has measured?”** (Same.) So that there may be no doubt concerning the calling of the Gentiles, the greatness of the one who calls is described.

**“By the hollow of the hand.”** A fist is formed by closing the fingers; a palm is the hand extended from the thumb to the little finger. Thus, through the palm and the fist, we are to understand the extended heavens and the globe of the earth.

**Verse 13.—“The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to announce good news to the meek. And the Spirit of the Lord will rest upon him.”**

**Verse 15.—“Like a little speck of dust.”** (Same.) The Hebrews think that this word signifies extremely fine dust, and so on, up to the poverty of both the Greek and Latin languages.

**Verse 16.—“Lebanon would not suffice.”** Lebanon is a very great mountain, rich in pastures and trees. But even if all its trees were cut down to be burned, and all its animals sacrificed as a burnt offering, they would still not suffice to fulfill or appease the power of the divine majesty.

**Verse 19.—“To whom.”** He rebukes the foolishness of the Gentiles so that they may withdraw from idolatry.

**Verse 20.—“Perhaps a piece of wood.”** (Same.) In Hebrew, *mesuchan*, because it is a kind of incorruptible wood from which idols are chiefly made. He says this so that, once idols have been rejected, the teaching of the Gospel may be received and the glory of the Lord revealed, so that all flesh may see the salvation of God.

**Verse 21.—“From the beginning.”** From the Law of Moses, or from the beginning of the world, in the creatures themselves, all of which proclaim their maker in their own way.

**Verse 22.—“Above the circle.”** From this some argue that the earth is like a point and a globe.

**“Like grasshoppers.”** Either in comparison with him, or considering the earth’s size.

**“A tabernacle.”** From this as well they argue that the heavens are spherical in likeness, and that one hemisphere of them hangs over the earth.

**Verse 23.—“Who brings secret investigators to nothing.”** God made the wisdom of this world foolish; and this is what is meant: “Who brings secret investigators to nothing, as though they did not exist” (I Cor. I).

**Verse 25.—“To whom have you likened me, equated me, says the Holy One?”** It is as though he said: “Why do you compare God to an image, rather than understand the creator God from the greatness of his creatures? If you do not believe the words, believe your own eyes, and from the servitude of all the elements consider the Lord’s omnipotence.”

**Verse 26.—“In number.”** (Same.) Those things were numbered that Abraham could not number; and they serve according to an assigned function, so that the sun completes the course of heaven in one year, and the other bodies do so in their own manner.

**“Their host,” and so on.** That is, the angels. Hence: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (Dan. VII). Therefore the Lord is also called *Sabaoth*, that is, of the host, armies, or powers.

**Verse 27.—“Why do you say,” and so on.** (Same.) When the prophet said these things, and so on, up to “we are without a judge and are afflicted unjustly.”

**“My way.”** Good works. He does not concern himself with earthly things or consider what each person does. Hence one is oppressed unjustly, like cattle and fish, without a ruler.

**Verse 28.—“He created.”** He knows all things, contains all things, and administers all things by his majesty.

**“Of his wisdom.”** (Same.) Another passage of the Apostle seems to have been taken from this place: “His judgments are incomprehensible and his ways unsearchable.” It is as though he said: “God alone is eternal and impassible; all other things fail.”

**Verse 30.—“Boys will fail.”** Those who rejoice in bodily health and think that childhood and adolescence will last forever.

**Verse 31.—“They will change.”** So that they may be strong in God, they will become weak to the world, and after the death of the flesh they will become immortal.

**“Like eagles.”** According to the natural philosophers, just as an eagle is renewed by striking its beak against a flint, when its excessive age has made it hooked, so those who mortify the old age of sin through the rock that is Christ, having died to the world, are renewed for God. Hence: “Your youth will be renewed like the eagle’s” (Ps. CII).

## CHAPTER XLI

**Verse 1.—“Let the islands be silent.”** (Jerome.) Because the Gentiles are in the sea, namely, those who are battered by the salty and bitter waves of the age. [The final printed “I” is uncertain.]

**Verse 2.—“Who raised up from the east?”** (Same.) Some of the Hebrews refer this to Cyrus, king of the Persians, and so on, up to the one who knew these things from the beginning.

**Verse 3.—“A path with his feet.”** He will not feel the labor or weariness of his life: “He rejoiced like a giant to run his course.”

**Verse 5.—“The islands saw.”** (Same.) That is, the surrounding nations, and so on, up to “and strengthened him with the nails of the commandments, so that he might remain in the fear of the Lord.”

**Verse 8.—“And you, Israel, my servant.”** (Same.) The Lord addresses the apostles affectionately, and so on, up to “afterward we are joined to God in friendship.”

**Verse 9.—“And from distant places.”** The Jews, already scattered as far as the ends of the earth, and from there many were called toward the end.

**Verse 14.—“Worm of Jacob.”** (Same.) The apostles are called worms, as imitators of the one who says: “I am a worm and not a man” (Ps. XXI). And just as a worm penetrates the earth, so their preaching penetrates the hearts of their hearers.

**“You who are dead from Israel.”** Like the one who says: “I die daily for your glory, brothers” (I Cor. XV); and elsewhere: “I live, yet no longer I; rather, Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

**Verse 15.—“I have made you like a threshing-sledge.”** The ecclesiastical man has the beaks of preaching, and so on, up to “so that those badly gathered may be properly divided.”

**Verse 19.—“I will give cedars in the wilderness.”** (Same.) The varieties of trees signify the diversity of spiritual grace, so that not even one string of the Lord’s lyre, nor any virtue of the Church’s graces, may seem to be lacking. Their sublimity, hastening toward heavenly things, is illuminated by the olive tree, the fuel of light and the rest of one who labors or is weary.

**“The thorn, the myrtle, and the olive tree.”** The Septuagint has *setim*, which is a tree resembling a white thorn, and so on, up to the statement that it therefore signifies the comforters of the holy Church.

**Verse 22.—“Announce.”** (Same.) This signifies that idols have neither the ability to hear nor to answer, and so on, up to the evident conclusion that, after Christ’s coming, idols lost their voice.

**Verse 23.—“If you can.”** Neither can demons, who attend upon idols, do anything except by God’s permission. For they could neither destroy the pigs nor the livestock of holy Job without God’s permission. Paul also handed certain people over to Satan.

**Verse 25.—“I have raised up.”** (Same.) He is still speaking against idols and their worshipers, and so on, up to “so that they may believe in him who came from the rising of the sun.”

**Verse 26.—“Who announced from the beginning?”** It is as though he said: “There was no one among the Gentiles who announced the coming of the Son. But if there is one who announced it, we shall say that he is righteous.” At the Son’s coming, the demons who had announced future things through idols fell silent.

**“Hearing your words.”** Because the brutish hearts of the Gentiles understood their error and abandoned false prophecies.

**Verse 27.—“The first shall say to Zion.”** They signify the Church. “Behold, your children have stood forth,” namely, those whom I gave you through faith—namely, the apostles, through whose preaching children have been born to you.

**Verse 29.—“Behold, all are unjust.”** Whatever we have said about idols or the Gentiles, let us refer it to the founders of heresies and to perverse doctrines. While Christ announces peace to the Church and displays the truth, they pursue errors and are compared with wind and storm.

## CHAPTER XLII

**Verse 1.—“Behold my servant.”** (Jerome.) It should be noted that the apostles are called Jacob, Israel, and the offspring of Abraham. Later, as servants and human beings, they are told: “Do not fear, worm of Jacob,” and so on. Christ, however, is called a servant, not the offspring of Jacob or Israel.

**“I have given my Spirit.”** At the conception; hence: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you,” and so on (Phil. II). It also became evident at his baptism, when the Spirit rested upon him in the form of a dove (Luke I).

**Verse 3.—“A smoking flax.”** The priesthood, already almost extinguished; the priestly garment, however, is made of linen.

**“He will bring forth judgment.”** He will judge, not fearing the scribes and Pharisees.

**Verse 4.—“He will not be sad.”** (Same.) Matthew did not include this, or the words may have been removed through a copyist’s error between “judgment” and “judgment.” The meaning is that he will preserve an even expression at all times. Philosophers falsely boast this of Socrates: namely, that he was neither sadder nor happier than usual.

**“Judgment in the earth.”** Hence: “For judgment I came into this world, so that those who do not see may see,” and so on (John IX).

**Verse 6.—“Righteousness.”** It was right that the one despised by the Jews should pass through the apostles to the Gentiles.

**Verse 7.—“Bound.”** With the cords of sins. In the Gospel, the Lord set free the one whom Satan had bound.

**Verse 8.—“To another.”** The Son and the Holy Spirit are not other than the Father in divinity; therefore they have the same glory and praise.

**Verse 9.—“I will do for you.”** So that you may know that I am the Lord and that there is no other besides me; and, seeing the earlier things fulfilled, you may believe the future things I promise.

**Verse 10.—“New.”** In the newness of the Spirit, not in the oldness of the letter; and not only in the Old Testament but also in the New.

**“You who go down to the sea.”** (Same.) Formerly fishermen of fish, afterward of human beings; hence, literally, they crossed many seas.

**Verse 11.—“Kedar.”** The son of Ishmael; the Saracens descend from him, though *Hagarenes* would be more accurate. By calling themselves Saracens, they veiled the disgrace of the slave woman. For Ishmael was the son of the slave woman Hagar, and the Saracens descend from her. He fathered twelve leaders, and the province itself is also called by his name.

**“From the summit of the mountains.”** (Jerome.) “Climb upon a high mountain.” “From the summit of the mountain”: from the height of virtue and contemplation, so that by their example they may also teach what they preach.

**Verse 13.—“He will cry out.”** Hence: “They provoked me with what was not God” (Deut. XXXII); “and I will provoke them with a foolish nation.”

**Verse 14.—“Like a woman in labor.”** I will bring to light the conception of my counsel as a woman brings forth an infant; thus I will disclose the hidden pain.

**Verse 16.—“On the paths.”** (Same.) In the knowledge of the prophets, who are paths to Christ when they proclaim his birth, resurrection, and ascension.

**Verse 17.—“Let them be confounded.”** When the fullness of the Gentiles has entered. Then Israel too, having been converted, will repent of its error, having previously served idols.

**Verse 22.—“A snare for the young.”** He returns to the Lord’s preaching, rebuking the scribes and Pharisees. They were snares for the simple, preventing them from turning to the Lord.

**Verse 23.—“Who is there?”** The prophet urges them so that at least some may listen, understand the cause of their captivity, and take care.

**Verse 25.—“Upon him.”** So that what he had previously kept silent about he would now not keep silent, but would chastise it not with words but with torments.

**“And he did not know.”** As the histories relate, neither did the Gentiles understand that this was being done as vengeance for the Son, nor did the Jews, blinded by their wickedness, understand it.

## CHAPTER XLIII

**Verse 1.—“And now these things.”** Above he spoke of the captivity of the Jews who refused to believe; now he addresses the primitive Church, which is from the Jews, so that they may understand the Creator of their soul and body.

**“Creating you, Jacob.”** Jacob means “supplanter”; Israel, “a man seeing God.” These are the apostles and apostolic men, who both supplanted vices and deserved to see God.

**Verse 2.—“Through the waters,” and so on.** (Same.) According to the Hebrews: “Through the waters of Egypt,” and so on, up to the statement that the apostles also passed through these kingdoms while preaching, with the Lord everywhere accompanying them.

**Verse 3.—“I gave a ransom.”** So that by preaching to the Egyptians, Ethiopians—who are nearly the last—and Sabaeans, you might acquire mercy and a crown for yourself. Sheba is a city situated at the borders of Ethiopia: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and to the ends of the world,” and so on.

**Verse 5.—“From the east.”** Many will come from east and west and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob—that is, from every part of the world.

**Verse 8.—“Bring out.”** The voice of the Father to the Son concerning the Jews who are blind in mind. Notice that the calling of the Jews occurred first, and afterward that of the Gentiles.

**Verse 9.—“All nations.”** The prophet addresses the Gentiles, rebuking them for idolatry and marveling that no one among the Gentiles could have foreknown this; only the people of God could, who had received God’s law and possessed the prophets.

**Verse 10.—“It was not formed.”** Some manuscripts read “fashioned,” but this does not fit as well. It can nevertheless be explained as follows: “Before me no idol was formed,” because I made a righteous human being from whom an idol was unjustly formed.

**Verse 12.—“I announced and saved.”** Through the prophets: the Son’s birth, the calling of the Gentiles, and the expulsion of demons.

**Verse 14.—“Thus says the Lord, your Savior,” and so on.** These are the things that follow: the Father speaks to the apostles. “For your sake,” namely, because you are my witnesses and preach the Gospel. To them he said: “Do not fear.”

**“The Chaldeans in ships.”** Historically, the Chaldeans abound in rivers and are skilled in ships, and boast of this.

**Verse 15.—“I am the Lord, your Holy One.”** Formerly he spoke to the children of Israel; now to you apostles, with the demons expelled from the world and all rulers defeated.

**Verse 19.—“I am doing new things.”** Many things that restore souls, not bodies. Formerly I brought forth from the rock one fountain only, to restore bodies.

**Verse 20.—“Dragons and ostriches.”** The wicked and venomous, who dwelt in the wilderness of the Gentiles and were bestial through the blood of idolatry and the savagery of their conduct.

The ostrich has the appearance of wings but cannot fly. So the hypocrite has the appearance of holiness but not its substance.

**Verse 22.—“You did not call upon me.”** (Jerome.) He speaks to the Jews, who before the Lord’s coming worshiped idols; or to those who refused to believe after his coming.

**“Nor did you labor.”** I did not make you labor after the Son’s coming so that you might offer costly things, because: “A sacrifice to God is a troubled spirit,” and so on (Ps. L). Or: “You did not labor for me alone,” since you offered to idols.

**Verse 23.—“In incense.”** By “incense” and “reed,” which is the twig of an aromatic tree, understand all spices.

**Verse 25.—“I am he.”** (Same.) It is as though he said: “You made me labor under the burden of your sin. Therefore I no longer call you my servant or my child, but simply address you as Jacob and Israel, so that I may expose and convict sinners.”

**Verse 26.—“Remind me.”** Remind me of the good things I did for you. What more ought I to have done for you that I did not do? Or: If you have anything righteous, I will gladly receive it.

**Verse 27.—“Your father.”** Abraham, who, when the Lord promised the land of promise, replied: “How shall I know that I shall possess it?” Or Abraham himself, who is said to have sinned in regard to the promise of the son by doubting; or the people in the wilderness, murmuring against God—as though he were saying: “He will recognize that he was begotten from sinners.”

**“Interpreters.”** It is as though he said: “Among the parties,” namely, those bringing peace.

## CHAPTER XLIV

**Verse 1.—“And now hear, Jacob.”** He addresses the first believers from the Jews, while the others were hardened, with a certain privilege of name and dignity of honor—namely, the company of the apostles. “Hear, Jacob, my servant.” First comes servitude, second election.

**Verse 2.—“Your helper from the womb.”** Either because you seized your brother’s heel, or because at the beginning of the Church you escaped the hands of persecutors.

**“And you most upright one, whom I chose.”** Israel, according to the Hebrew truth, means “upright” or “most upright.” The earlier designation, “a man seeing God,” is derived not from the meaning of the name but from the sound of the word.

**Verse 3.—“I will pour out my Spirit.”** Namely, in baptism through the laying on of hands.

**Verse 4.—“Like willows beside flowing waters.”** The willow is an unfruitful tree, and so on, up to the statement that it quickly believed the apostles as they preached.

**Verse 5.—“This one will say.”** He describes the diversity of believers.

**“And he will be likened to Israel.”** So that they may receive the law, the prophets, and the graces of the Holy Spirit that were promised to Israel.

**Verse 6.—“I am the first and I am the last.”** After the calling of the Gentiles, who rejected idols and believed, he speaks against those who refused to convert.

**“Besides me there is no God.”** He does not say that he alone exists, but that apart from his power and wisdom there is no external god, condemning the belief in many gods and their images.

**Verse 12.—“He will hunger and grow faint.”** (Jerome.) From hunger and thirst the craftsman, and so on, up to “whose god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame.”

**Verse 23.—“Sing for joy, ends of the earth.”** (Same.) Angels preside, as it were, over the inhabitants of the earth; or the apostles, or the prophets, above whom others are also established. Hence it is said to the Ephesians: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets,” and so on.

**Verse 24.—“Thus says the Lord, your Redeemer,” and so on.** (Same.) Above he spoke of the overthrow of idols and the redemption of repentant Israel; now he speaks of the greatness of his power, so that no one may doubt the salvation he promises.

**Verse 26.—“Who says.”** He speaks of the restoration accomplished by Zerubbabel and the other leaders, with Cyrus’s permission, although the captivity still had to be fulfilled.

**Verse 27.—“Your rivers.”** Under Darius and his grandson Cyrus. On the night when Belshazzar was killed by them, the Euphrates, which flowed through the middle of the city, was divided into channels by their army, so that they could enter the city through its riverbed.

## CHAPTER XLV

**Verse 1.—“Thus says the Lord to his Christ.”** Among the Romans a diadem, among the Jews anointing, makes kings and priests; from this they are also called *christs*. Cyrus is a christ, not by anointing but by dignity.

**“And the backs of kings.”** (Same.) What city did not lie open to him? What king did not turn his back? What walls, previously impregnable, were not overthrown by his siege? You will find these events more fully completed in the history of Xenophon.

**Verse 3.—“Hidden treasures.”** The treasures of all the cities, so that, invited by benefits after rejecting idols, you might recognize the one God who foretold your name before you existed.

**Verse 4.—“And I called you.”** (Same.) Just as I called Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and so on, up to “but Christ the Son was anointed with the oil of gladness above his companions.”

**Verse 5.—“Besides me.”** Because the Son and the Holy Spirit are in the Father; for apart from my Word, reason, power, and wisdom—which are in me—there is no other God.

**Verse 6.—“So that they may know.”** Ezra says that Cyrus wrote to all the nations that there is no God except the God of Israel. Alternatively, God’s mercy and power became more evident to everyone through the liberation of the captives. Josephus, however, says in the *Book of Antiquities* that the people were released because Cyrus read in the Book of Isaiah what the Lord had said about him through the prophet beforehand.

**Verse 7.—“Darkness.”** Night or captivity. As one who has taken pity on penitents, I bring them back from captivity; in anger, I take sinners captive.

**“Evil.”** (Same.) War, namely affliction, according to the saying: “Sufficient for the day is its evil.” Let those who think that God is the creator of evils therefore be confounded. Here “evil” does not mean what is opposed to good, but is used for affliction and war.

**Verse 8.—“Drop down, heavens.”** (Same.) He appropriately joins this to the coming of Christ, signified through Cyrus, because Christ will free the human race from the captivity of the devil. Or these words may be attached to what precedes, so that, when Cyrus releases the captivity, heaven and earth may rejoice by metonymy.

**“And the clouds.”** The prophets irrigate our hearts with saving rain and announce Christ’s birth, resurrection, and ascension. Hence: “I will command my clouds not to rain upon it,” and elsewhere: “Your truth reaches to the clouds.”

**“I created him who”—** namely, was a worm and is read to have sprung from the earth according to his humanity.

**Verse 9.—“Woe to him who contradicts.”** It is as though he said: “Believe what I proclaim—namely, that Christ will come—for ‘woe to him who contradicts his maker’” (Ps. XXXV). Or this refers to Cyrus, to whom I shall subject all kingdoms through the liberation of my people.

**Verse 10.—“Woman, what are you giving birth to?”** A man is powerful over a woman, and a woman is powerful over a man.

**Verse 11.—“His maker.”** The Son, according to his humanity, in the virgin’s womb; hence: “The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you,” and so on.

**Verse 12.—“And all his host.”** On this occasion some think that the stars are rational beings. For they say that he would not command things without understanding, since such things could not understand commands.

**Verse 13.—“I have raised him up.”** (Same.) It is as though he said: “Since I did the things mentioned above, what is surprising if I also send the Son into the world to redeem the human race and raise him from the dead?”

**“I will direct his ways.”** He who committed no sin, and no deceit was found in his mouth (I Pet. II).

**“He himself will build.”** (Same.) Concerning him it was said: “You did not know me.” Nor did he himself build the city or temple, but he permitted it to be built; nor was it completed in his time, but in the time of Ahasuerus.

**Verse 14.—“The labor of Egypt.”** The worship of idols. For Egypt labored greatly in carrying out sacrifices to idols. But when the apostles preached, the Egyptians were converted, and above all kingdoms the religious communities of monks flourish there, so that where sin abounded, grace might also abound (Rom. V).

**Verse 19.—“Not in secret,” and so on.** (Same.) Formerly, on Mount Sinai, he said to one people alone: “You shall have no foreign gods” (Exod. XX). But through the apostles he preached the Gospel to all nations. Hence: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. XVIII).

**“I did not say.”** (Jerome.) First I came to the Jews, and I admonished them, as they abandoned the shadow of the law, to follow the truth.

**“Announcing what is right.”** So that creation may worship the Creator and, abandoning figures, follow the truth of the Gospel.

**Verse 20.—“They did not know.”** Some who remained in error refused to know, weighed down by the burden of images and hoping in things in which there is no salvation.

**Verse 21.—“Take counsel together.”** So that, going throughout the world, you may all announce the same thing. From this they composed together the Creed concerning the Trinity and unity, the communion of the Church, and the general resurrection.

**“I foretold it.”** That the Gentiles would be saved, but that an idol is nothing—whether when I spoke to Abraham or when I gave the law.

**VERSE 23.**—“He will go forth”: visibly into the world in the flesh.

“The word of righteousness”: the Son, until he has fulfilled obedience, etc., up to the point where the Jews, demonstrating their arrogance of mind, do not do this at all.

**VERSE 25.**—“In the Lord he will say”: all the nations, even the barbarian peoples, confessing him not in synagogues but in churches.

## CHAPTER XLVI

**VERSE 1.**—“Bel is broken.” (JEROME.) After the calling of the nations, the destruction of idols is added.

“Nebo.” Nebo means “gold,” etc., up to the point where the prophecy of demons and the divination of magicians came to nothing.

“By beasts and cattle.” (ID.) For they worshiped beasts and cattle, and their region gave many towns names derived from the beasts and cattle they worshiped—for example, Leonata from *leo* (“lion”), and other names of this kind.

**VERSE 2.**—“And their soul.” This does not mean that images possess a soul, etc., up to the point where he subjected them to the devil and demons.

**VERSE 3.**—“House of Jacob.” He does not say “Jacob, my servants, my chosen ones,” with an added expression of honor, but simply “Jacob”; and he addresses them as carnal people who have departed from his commandments.

[Col. 1289D] “You who are carried.” You who are borne like a fetus conceived through the desert all the way to the promised land. For a long time he patiently awaited them, both in the promised land and, after the Passion, for forty-two years.

**VERSE 5.**—“To whom have you likened me?” He attacks especially those who, in the time of Ahaz and Ezekiel, worshiped idols in the corners of the streets, in gardens, in sacred groves, and upon houses.

**VERSE 8.**—“Remember this.” Because I gave you birth and carried you up to old age, abandon the idols you made and return to the worship of the one God.

“To the heart.” To the understanding. You lived almost like beasts, venerating images, so that, like madmen, you stumbled against wood and stones.

[Col. 1290A] **VERSE 10.**—“Announcing.” Through the prophets, so that, when I have fulfilled what was foretold through divination—that is, through a prophet announcing future events—I may prove my divinity.

“The last.” “We are those upon whom the ends of the ages have come” (1 Cor. 10). And elsewhere: “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent his Son” (Gal. 4). And John says: “Little children, it is the last hour” (1 John 2).

“Counsel”: the plan to redeem the world through the Son. It is as though he said: “Now I declare my established plan, so that, when you see its fulfillment, you may know that there is no God except the one who knew future events and commanded them to occur.”

**VERSE 11.**—“Calling a bird from the east.” (ID.) According to the Hebrews, Cyrus, king of the Persians, etc., up to the point where the Magi, coming from the east, worshiped him.

**VERSE 12.**—“Hard of heart.” You who always resist the truth—first the prophets, and finally the Son.

## CHAPTER XLVII

**VERSE 1.**—“Come down, sit,” etc. (JEROME.) For we are all God’s creatures; nor, according to the heretics, is Babylon’s nature condemnable. Rather, the reference is to the luxury and adornment of the most powerful city, which, now old and near its decline, boasts of being a young woman and a girl.

**VERSE 2.**—“Provide flour,” or “offer intercourse,” to the Medes and Persians, who are most ardent in this matter. According to this interpretation, the Hebrews say that the Philistines forced Samson, after gouging out his eyes, to grind—that is, to have intercourse with their women—so that they might receive from him men of great and invincible stature.

**VERSE 3.**—“And he will not resist,” as Moses did not resist God when he wished to destroy the children of Israel. He signifies, however, the angel placed over Babylon, who, together with the others, says: “We treated Babylon, but it was not healed.”

**VERSE 5.**—“Sit.” The speech is addressed to Babylon, and he addresses her as a former queen who has now become a slave. Sit, humbled and vile. Be silent, like a grieving woman contemplating your misery.

**VERSE 6.**—“I was angry.” He gives the reason why he afflicted the Chaldeans in this way, so that it would not seem that he had acted without cause, since he does nothing without cause; and so that the Chaldeans might know that they had not overcome God’s people by their own strength.

**VERSE 9.**—“Suddenly.” When Cyrus and Darius burst in unexpectedly. For she did not fear that she could be overcome by the Medes and Persians, who, in comparison with her, possessed no strength and were themselves subject to her.

**VERSE 11.**—“You will not know its rising.” Calamity will come unexpectedly, foretold neither by magicians nor by diviners; for they did not fear a despised and subjugated people.

**VERSE 13.**—“Astrologers of heaven.” Astrologers, who suppose that everything is governed by the stars. It is as though he said: “Did they not foresee everything for you?” These people are commonly called *mathematici*, because they think that worldly affairs are governed by the course of the stars. Hence: “Magi came from the east, saying, ‘We have seen his star in the east’” (Matt. 2). Or they were stirred by Balaam’s prophecy, who said: “A star shall rise from Jacob” (Num. 24).

**VERSE 14.**—“They became like stubble,” etc. The Septuagint reads: “Having coals of fire, you will sit upon them; these will be your help.” It is as though he said: “The Gazarenes and the magicians lead you into pride through error.” By “fire,” however, he means Babylon’s burning; through punishments he calls it to repentance.

## CHAPTER XLVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Hear these things.” (JEROME.) It is customary that, when the subject is carnal Israel, Jacob or Israel is mentioned simply and without any addition to the name, as in this passage, where he addresses those who are called Jacob or Israel in name only.

“And from the waters of Judah.” He mentions Judah because, after the ten tribes had been taken captive, Judah, Benjamin, and the Levites remained in the promised land and had a king from Judah.

**VERSE 2.**—“For you are from the holy city.” (ID.) It is as though he said: “You boast that you are inhabitants of Jerusalem and that you possess the privilege of the Lord of hosts, while you vainly assume the names Jacob, Israel, and holy city of the almighty God.”

**VERSE 3.**—“The former things from that time.” I foretold that the Babylonians would be defeated, and suddenly I will do what I threatened, so that, when what was foretold comes to pass, you may know that it happened neither by chance nor at the command of your gods.

“The former miracles”: namely, those I performed among them from the time they came out of Egypt, and when captivity by Nebuchadnezzar was impending. Now, however, before they are taken captive, he foretells their liberation and the devastation of the Chaldeans. Thus I suddenly performed what I foretold was to come.

**VERSE 4.**—“An iron sinew.” Hence Stephen says: “Stiff-necked and uncircumcised in heart” (Acts 7).

“Your brow is bronze.” Hence Ezekiel says: “For the whole house of Israel is hardened in forehead” (Ezek. 3), etc. And Jeremiah says: “You have acquired the forehead of a prostitute; you refused to be ashamed” (Jer. 3).

**VERSE 6.**—“And they were preserved.” It is as though he said: “I was about to announce many things, but because you do not remember what I say, I withhold what I was about to say.”

**VERSE 9.**—“For my name’s sake.” Namely, so that it might not be violated: “I will put far away”—that is, I kept my anger from destroying you because you worshiped the calf; “and for my praise”—that is, so that you might praise me—“I will restrain you by my law.”

**VERSE 10.**—“In the furnace of poverty.” (ID.) Purifying you through poverty by giving your riches to your enemies; or in Egypt, where it is shown that most people are tested through wealth and poverty.

**VERSE 12.**—“Hear me, Jacob.” (JEROME.) He still addresses the same people, etc., up to the point where he calls them “the called.”

[Col. 1291D] **VERSE 14.**—“Gather together, all of you.” Why, then, does earth and ashes, ignorant of its own fragility, boast?

“He announced these things.” Either that Cyrus would destroy Babylon, or that my Son would be born of a virgin.

“The Lord loved him.” These words properly concern Christ. Nevertheless, they can also be referred to Cyrus and Darius, up to the passage: “His way was made straight.”

“His own”: because he will capture it. Or, the Son, in redeeming the world, will capture the one who also expelled the Chaldeans—that is, the demons. Hence: “The ruler of this world will be cast out.”

**VERSE 15.**—“I called him.” Cyrus, or the Son, through Gabriel, who said: “And you shall call his name Jesus.”

**VERSE 16.**—“He sent me.” (ID.) He briefly, fully, and openly distinguishes the whole Trinity.

[Col. 1292A] **VERSE 17.**—“I am the Lord.” I who promise Israel future things. He gives the reason why he afflicted them previously.

**VERSE 21.**—“They did not thirst.” (ID.) Literally, concerning those coming out of Egypt, etc., up to the point where they were satisfied with the water of wisdom.

“He split the rock.” The rock was Christ. The divine word is split into parts, so that we may receive in portions what we cannot receive in its entirety.

“And the waters flowed.” One of the soldiers opened his side with a lance, and immediately there came forth the blood of our redemption and the water of baptism, dedicating baptism and martyrdom to us.

## CHAPTER XLIX

**VERSE 1.**—“Listen, islands.” (JEROME.) After the calling of the remnant of Israel and the objection of the unbelieving—concerning whom the Lord says, “There is no peace for the wicked”—he addresses, under the name of “islands,” the churches from the nations, speaking in the person of the Son.

**VERSE 2.**—“A sharp sword.” “I have not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matt. 10), separating the wicked from the good.

**VERSE 3.**—“I will be glorified.” Not as in the case of other servants: “Father, I have glorified your name” (John 17). And elsewhere: “Awake, my glory” (Ps. 56), etc.

**VERSE 4.**—“And I said.” (ID.) It is as though he said: “How have I glorified you, when I was unable to bring a large part of the Jews back to you?” Here human free will is shown: it belongs to God to call, and to us to believe, although he himself assists us, so that the righteous may receive the reward of their will.

“Therefore judgment,” etc. (ID.) The Father will judge whether I did for them everything I ought to have done: “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me.” And elsewhere: “I glorified you on earth” (John 17).

“My work.” Others read: “My labor and my pain,” because he wept over the city and said in the Psalm: “What profit is there in my blood?” (Ps. 29). According to the Hebrew text, while hanging on the cross he was far from my salvation—the words of my lamentation.

**VERSE 5.**—“Glorified.” It is as though he said: “I lost the Jews, but I was glorified among the nations.” Hence: “All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (Matt. 28).

**VERSE 7.**—“Abhorred.” Christ and his Nazarenes, whom the Jews curse daily in the synagogues, because on their account they lost their kingdom, place, and nation.

“Kings.” The prophet speaks to the Son. “Kings will see you coming to judgment”—namely, the apostles and others who will judge with the Lord.

**VERSE 8.**—“At an acceptable time.” The time of the Passion and Resurrection, in which it pleased God to redeem the human race.

**VERSE 16.**—“Behold, on my hands,” etc. (ID.) From this we learn that Jerusalem is not to be sought in the region of Palestine, which is the worst part of the entire province, roughened by rocky mountains and suffering from a scarcity of springs.

**VERSE 17.**—“Builders.” The apostles and others. You were destroyed through the guilt of the Jews—that is, the scribes and Pharisees—but through the preaching of certain Jews—that is, the apostles—you were gathered from both Jews and nations.

**VERSE 18.**—“All these have gathered together.” Jews from every nation, etc., up to the point where they are gathered daily into the faith of the Church.

[Col. 1293A] “As an ornament.” Through the various graces of the Holy Spirit, by which the bride’s adornment is embellished. Concerning her it is said: “The queen stood at your right hand in a garment of gold, clothed in varied attire” (Ps. 44).

**VERSE 21.**—“I was barren.” For after Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who was also Ezra, they had no prophets to nourish them in the law, until John the Baptist.

**VERSE 23.**—“Queens.” The same meaning, but expressed more affectionately. Hence: “The queen stood,” etc. She daily nourishes Christ’s little ones and leads them to mature age.

“They will worship.” They will venerate, according to the statement: “They will worship the footstool of his feet” (Ps. 98), in which the foot indicates majesty.

“The dust of your feet.” (JEROME.) They will cleanse every earthly thing by word and example, according to what was said: “Whatever you loose on earth will be loosed” (Matt. 16), etc. Hence: “Shake the dust from your feet” (Matt. 10).

**VERSE 25.**—“For thus says the Lord.” (ID.) He answers the question, because he says that these things are fulfilled at his coming.

**VERSE 26.**—“With their own flesh.” Not by another’s death, but by their own, etc., up to the point where death is exposed to the bites of savage beasts.

“Strong one of Jacob.” He who gave Jacob strength to wrestle, etc., up to the point where, as it were, through prayer you will prevail against Esau, whom you fear.

## CHAPTER L

**VERSE 1.**—“Thus says the Lord: Who is he?” (JEROME.) After the calling of the nations and the capture of the strong one, whose spoils were divided among the apostles, he speaks to the Jewish people concerning Zion, of which he earlier said: “The Lord has abandoned me,” etc.

“I sold.” “I am carnal, sold under sin” (Rom. 7). “Everyone who commits sin is a slave of sin” (John 8). Hence: “Let sin therefore not reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6).

**VERSE 2.**—“Because I came.” (ID.) This means: “So that you may know that I did not reject your mother, but that she departed of her own will. After many benefits I assumed flesh, and now I have spoken not through prophets but in person.”

“There was no man.” Herod, on account of his wickedness, etc., up to the point where all are considered together: “The vision of the four-footed creatures in the desert” (Isa. 30).

“I called.” It is as though he said: “Rational beings, incline your ear to the words of my mouth” (Ps. 77). “Let the one who thirsts come and drink” (John 7), and similar passages.

“Is it possible?” (ID.) He attacks those who thought, etc., up to the point where he would furnish me with more than twelve legions of angels (Matt. 26).

**VERSE 3.**—“I will clothe the heavens with darkness.” Philosophers say that clouds rise no more than ten stades above the earth and conceal the sun’s brilliance; thus, when the light of heaven is shut out, the lower air is darkened. “I will clothe”: namely, the saints, so that sinners may recognize themselves.

“And I will put sackcloth on it.” So that they may repent in fear and sackcloth.

[Col. 1294A] **VERSE 4.**—“The Lord has given,” etc. (ID.) Although these words can be referred to Isaiah, they properly refer to Christ. It is as though he said: “I who once performed such deeds can now perform similar ones; my power has not diminished.”

**VERSE 9.**—“Like a garment.” (ID.) A garment is consumed by age and moth. The Jews too were called to repentance for forty-two years after the Passion; finally, because they neglected it, they were crushed when the Romans arrived and devoured by the moth of an evil conscience.

**VERSE 10.**—“Who among you?” The one who fears is not perfect, etc., up to the point where he preserves the souls of the saints whole, chaste, and pure.

“Who walked in darkness.” The Gentile people were in darkness, etc., up to the point where I call them to repentance; for I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn and live (Ezek. 18).

**VERSE 11.**—“Behold, all of you.” It is as though he said: “Exhortation is useless, and after such crimes there is no hope of salvation: ‘All have turned aside; together they have become worthless’” (Ps. 13).

“Lighting a fire.” They lit the fire of the city by which it was burned by the Romans, etc., up to the point where, in this way, different kinds of sinful matter kindle sinners to a greater or lesser degree.

“You will sleep in pains.” Because they refused to receive the Son of God either through benefits or through punishments. Hence: “Go, you cursed, into the eternal fire” (Matt. 25).

## CHAPTER LI

**VERSE 1.**—“Hear me, you who follow what.” (JEROME.) Pay attention to the rock, Christ. Concerning it: “The rock was Christ,” from whom you were hewn (1 Cor. 10); Christians are named from Christ.

“And to the hollow of the pit.” Because of the piercing of Christ’s side, etc., up to the point where we are born through the washing of baptism.

**VERSE 3.**—“Joy and gladness.” Note that in Zion, which is compared with God’s paradise, there ought to be so much joy, gladness, thanksgiving, and the voice of praise that what they will do in heaven with the angels they may continually contemplate on earth.

**VERSE 5.**—“My righteous one.” The one who justifies everyone; or, elegantly, “righteousness,” so that not one nation but the entire world may be saved.

**VERSE 6.**—“The heavens like smoke.” (ID.) It is written concerning the saints, etc., up to the point where some understand “perish” and “grow old” as referring to abolition and death.

[Col. 1240D] **VERSE 9.**—“Awake.” The voice of the prophet and of the faithful people imploring the coming of Christ, in whom help had been promised.

**VERSE 12.**—“Who are you that you should fear a man?” etc., up to the point where they may be ashamed and repent.

**VERSE 17.**—“Rise up, rise up.” (ID.) He exhorts to repentance those who denied him during the Passion, or who persisted in unbelief, crying: “Crucify, crucify” (John 19), etc.

“The cup of wrath.” (ID.) Physicians customarily administer a very bitter antidote, etc., up to the point where it is not evident that this refers to the final captivity.

**VERSE 22.**—“Behold.” (JEROME.) He foretold the captivity to come; now he exhorts them to repentance so that they may escape it.

**VERSE 23.**—“I will put it.” According to the literal sense, they humbled, etc., up to the point where they will be completely humbled in judgment.

## CHAPTER LII

**VERSE 1.**—“Awake, awake.” The prophet exhorts those who, after the Ascension, believed when the apostles preached.

“For he will not add.” This concerns the heavenly Jerusalem, into which no unclean person enters.

**VERSE 2.**—“Shake yourself.” A soul polluted by filth loses its former brightness, etc., up to the point where it is not redeemed with perishable silver and gold but with the blood of an immaculate lamb.

**VERSE 3.**—“Freely.” You gained no advantage and escaped no disadvantage when you handed over the Son of God.

**VERSE 4.**—“Into Egypt.” (JEROME.) He rebukes the Jews and foretells what is to come, etc., up to the point where he oppresses him even in his own land and brings accusations against him.

**VERSE 5.**—“What have I here?” (ID.) “I find nothing here among them,” he says, etc., up to the point where they crucified their Redeemer.

**VERSE 7.**—“How beautiful.” (ID.) Concerning the one who earlier said: “I myself who spoke—behold, I am here,” the prophet testifies that he himself preached the Gospel above the mountains.

“Of the one announcing”: Christ, through himself and through the apostles, to whom he said: “Peace I leave you; my peace I give you” (John 14). Upon whom the Lord, seated, preached; they too are the feet of Christ, carrying his preaching.

**VERSE 8.**—“The voice of the watchmen.” (ID.) Of the apostles and others who are always on the watchtower, so that they may foresee everything and advance those entrusted to them.

[Col. 1295C] **VERSE 9.**—“Rejoice.” He consoles the primitive Church, etc., up to the point where it was restored and multiplied through the multitude of the nations.

**VERSE 10.**—“The nations will hope in my arm” (Ps. 97). And elsewhere: “Your arm with power” (Ps. 88).

**VERSE 11.**—“Depart.” (ID.) The Jews refer this to themselves, etc., up to the point where they were admonished by the Holy Spirit.

“Go out,” preaching the Gospel throughout the whole world: “Go, teach all nations” (Matt. 18).

“The vessels of the Lord.” (ID.) The temple of the Lord is holy, and that temple is what you are—golden and silver vessels. Hence Paul is called a chosen vessel. Or “the vessels of the Lord” means the armor of God: the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God.

[Col. 1295D] **VERSE 13.**—“Behold, he will understand.” So that there may be no doubt about who said, “The one who spoke—behold, I am here”; and the Father plainly teaches what the arm of the Lord is.

**VERSE 14.**—“As they were astonished.” The historical sequence is not preserved. Earlier the prophet was speaking in the person of the Father about the Son’s Ascension, and suddenly he returns to the Passion.

## CHAPTER LIII

[Col. 1296D] **VERSE 1.**—“Who has believed?” (JEROME.) The prophet, speaking in the person of the prophets, complains that few of the Jews believe what they hear from them concerning the Son’s coming.

“And the arm of the Lord.” (ID.) The Father announced to the world that his Son would come, and, before the scandal of the cross, he foretold the glory of the risen one: “He will be lifted up and exalted,” etc. The chorus of the prophets therefore responds that it has fulfilled its duty and announced the arm of the Lord.

**VERSE 2.**—“A shoot.” Symmachus has “branch,” signifying the man who proceeded from the virgin’s womb.

“To the thirsty ground.” Aquila has “impassable,” where the privilege of virginity is demonstrated, because he was created without seed from earth previously impassable.

**VERSE 5.**—“By his bruise.” (ID.) It is clear that, just as his body was lacerated and scourged, so his soul truly suffered for us, lest Christ be believed to be partly truth and partly falsehood.

**VERSE 7.**—“He did not open,” etc. Before Pilate or Herod. For he answered briefly, so that the salvation of the human race would not be delayed.

“And like a lamb.” (ID.) In whose figure the people of Israel ate the lamb in Egypt (Exod. 12). This is the lamb who takes away the sins of the world (John 1), who was slain from the foundation of the world (Rev. 13), who nourishes us with his flesh and blood and clothes us with the fleece of his protection.

**VERSE 8.**—“From judgment.” The judge of all found no truth in the judgment, but was condemned though guiltless. Hence the prophet marvels that the God of all surrendered himself to suffering.

**VERSE 9.**—“He will give the wicked.” (ID.) That is, the nations, who were without piety, to God the Father, because by dying and being buried he acquired them; and the rich—that is, the Jews, who boasted in the riches of the law and the prophets.

“Rich.” The scribes and Pharisees, who boasted in the riches of the teaching of the law.

**VERSE 10.**—“Long-lived seed.” The word of the Gospel, which will not grow old like the Old Testament. Hence: “The one who sowed went out to sow his seed” (Luke 8).

**VERSE 11.**—“He will be satisfied.” With the faith of the nations. Thus, when he was hungry and thirsty beside Jacob’s well, he did not wish to use the food that had been bought, because he was already satisfied by the faith of the Samaritan woman and of those who came out to him from the city.

**VERSE 12.**—“And with criminals.” So that he might redeem criminals from sin, he became all things to all: “He himself bore our sins in his body” (1 Pet. 2). His imitator Paul says: “I have become all things to all, that I might save all” (1 Cor. 9).

“He prayed.” “Father, forgive them.” According to the Gospel of the Nazarenes, at this utterance many thousands of Jews standing around the cross believed.

## CHAPTER LIV

[Col. 1296D] **VERSE 1.**—“Sing praise, barren woman.” (JEROME.) Thus far he has spoken about the birth, Passion, and Resurrection, etc., up to the point where she was gathered from both Jews and Gentiles.

“Sing praise, barren woman.” The apostle, according to the Septuagint, says: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear; break forth and cry aloud, you who do not travail, because the children of the desolate woman are many” (Gal. 4), etc. “But we, brothers, are children of the promise according to Isaac.”

**VERSE 3.**—“For to the right hand”: to all the places of the world. Or, neither lifted up by prosperity nor broken by adversity. Or, to the good things of the future and of the present.

**VERSE 4.**—“Do not fear.” (ID.) When the tower of Babel was being built, etc., up to the incomplete source fragment: “who [funiculu-, ‘cord’; uncertain].”

**VERSE 6.**—“For as a woman.” (ID.) Those who follow the allegorical interpretation, even in very difficult passages, etc., up to the point where he extends a robe and a kiss.

**VERSE 9.**—“As in the days of Noah,” etc. He gives the examples of the ancients so that the assembly of the saints may believe that the Lord’s mercy is everlasting, and that they were abandoned only for a moment, so that they might become God’s friends through an eternal covenant.

**VERSE 14.**—“Withdraw far away.” (JEROME.) He has consoled the Church from the nations, promising them spiritual gifts; now he teaches what she should do so that she need not fear adversaries.

**VERSE 15.**—“Behold, a sojourner.” The Jews twist this to refer to themselves, as though they were to become future proselytes from the nations in the time of their Christ.

**VERSE 16.**—“Behold, I.” This does not mean that I am the cause of their destruction, but that the adversary who fights is the cause of destruction for the defeated and the cause of reward for the victorious.

[Col. 1297B] **VERSE 17.**—“This is the inheritance.” So that the righteous person, when afflicted, may not fail, he adds the rewards.

## CHAPTER LV

**VERSE 1.**—“All you who thirst, come.” (JEROME.) Because he had said that the earthen vessel against the Church must be shattered and every tongue armed against the knowledge of God must be overcome, he invites believers to the river of God, which is filled with waters.

“Eat.” By hearing, speaking, reading, meditating, acting, and retaining it in the heart. Divine Scripture is both drink when it is open and food when it is hidden. It is also both water and the bread that came down from heaven.

“Why do you weigh out silver?” You assess the sacred words but do not receive nourishment. By preserving only the outward form of the letter, you lose the richness of inward nourishment that comes from spiritual understanding.

**VERSE 4.**—“Behold, a witness.” He invited the Jews to believe, but because he knew that the Gentiles would believe though they did not, he says that he sent his Son to announce his commands to the peoples.

**VERSE 5.**—“The Lord your God.” (ID.) When the Father is mentioned, he is called the Father of Christ according to divinity, the Father of glory; according to humanity, the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.

**VERSE 6.**—“Seek the Lord.” These words apply either specifically to the Jews or to the nations, and generally to every person. The prophet says to the Jews: “Seek the Lord,” as though he said: “The nations receive the mercies of David, while you disdain them. Repent, therefore, and be converted while you have the opportunity.”

[Col. 1297D] “While he is near.” (ID.) Do not let him depart because of your vices—he who draws near to those who draw near to him and joyfully meets the returning son.

**VERSE 8.**—“For,” so that you do not think what I promise difficult: consider how great the difference is between my plans and yours; the difference in will is as great as the difference in nature.

**VERSE 10.**—“And how.” (ID.) By another comparison he shows that he is abundant in forgiveness.

“To the one eating bread.” Hence Solomon says: “Cast your bread upon the waters, for after many days you will find it” (Eccles. 11). That is: Pour out the bread of your teaching and spiritual grace upon everyone, because at the end you will receive rewards.

[Col. 1298A] **VERSE 11.**—“It will not return.” But after it has fulfilled my will on earth, it will return and sit at my right hand, according to the statement: “Sit at my right hand,” etc.

**VERSE 12.**—“Mountains”: namely, the souls of the saints, who are called mountains and hills according to the variety of their virtues.

**VERSE 13.**—“Instead of the thornbush.” The thornbush is full of sharp points and pricks. The fir is tall and lofty, suitable for building houses and rich in pitch.

“And the Lord will be.” Others read: “And the Lord will be a name and an everlasting sign that will not fail.”

## CHAPTER LVI

**VERSE 1.**—“Thus says the Lord: Keep judgment.” (JEROME.) Once the prophecy concerning the nations has ended—those who, at Christ’s coming, are changed from thornbushes and nettles into fir trees and myrtles—he addresses the hearers of that time, so that they may prepare themselves for the coming of the Savior, who is mercy and righteousness.

“Keep judgment.” (ID.) Do not show partiality in judgment. For the Lord’s judgment belongs to him who judges those who judge rightly.

**VERSE 2.**—“Keeping the Sabbath.” (ID.) Let it not be, that is, one of the six days in which the world was made. The apostles did not belong to those days, to whom it is said: “If you were of the world, the world would love what was its own,” etc. “But I chose you from the world; therefore the world hates you” (John 15).

**VERSE 3.**—“And let him not say.” (ID.) This is directed against the Jews, who claimed Christ’s coming exclusively for themselves and compelled others to despair. But “there is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Rom. 10).

“Eunuch.” (ID.) One who, for the sake of the kingdom of heaven, mortifies his members on earth, etc., up to the point where the reference is to the offspring of spiritual works, not to children.

**VERSE 4.**—“For thus says the Lord.” (ID.) He put forward two groups, namely proselytes and eunuchs, etc., up to the point where they should not think themselves subject to the curse of the law.

**VERSE 6.**—“And the sons of the sojourner.” After eunuchs he turns to sojourners and promises rewards.

“Among servants.” Such as Paul, who says of himself: “Paul, a servant of Christ Jesus,” and Moses, the servant of God.

**VERSE 7.**—“Their burnt offerings.” “Mortify your members that are upon the earth” (Col. 3). And: “Present your bodies as a living sacrifice to God.” A burnt offering is offered wholly to God and consumed by fire. Part of a victim is given to the priests. The one who leaves the world and devotes himself continually to prayer offers a burnt offering to God. The one who serves God and rightly orders the things of the world offers a victim.

“Upon my altar.” Faith, upon which all things are offered, without which it is impossible to please God. Hence: “The righteous person will live by his faith.”

**VERSE 9.**—“All the beasts.” The voice of the prophet, who summons the Romans to destroy Jerusalem, to whom almost the entire world was subject. Or, by “beasts” he means demons, to whom the Jews were handed over to be devoured.

**VERSE 10.**—“Blind.” Those who do not possess Christ, the true light, or faith and the other virtues.

“Dogs.” (ID.) Just as dogs guard the flock, so leaders ought to guard the people. “Most shameless dogs”: that is, just as dogs without discernment often attack even the good, so the Jews shamelessly cried, “Crucify, crucify him” (Luke 23), and were not satisfied with insulting the Lord.

**VERSE 12.**—“Come, let us take.” Thus those who ought to have corrected them were perverting them. And because all had sinned, they were handed over to the Romans.

## CHAPTER LVII

**VERSE 1.**—“The righteous person perishes.” (JEROME.) The Jews refer this to Isaiah, who was cut in two with a wooden saw by the most wicked king Manasseh, and to other prophets whom he himself killed, men of mercy. But more truly this is said of the one who is supremely righteous.

“And no one is there.” Because of the blind watchmen and mute dogs.

“Who considers.” Because, being blind and mute and ignorant of wisdom, they do not consider the things that belong to God.

[Col. 1299B] **VERSE 2.**—“Let peace come; let him who walked in … rest in his bed.” (ID.) The prophet prays that Christ may come, rise from the dead, and rest in his bed in glory—that is, in the majesty of the Father—or in the Church, in which he walked in uprightness.

**VERSE 6.**—“Drink offering.” Wine, oil, and liquids of this kind; a sacrifice of bread, a victim, and things of this kind.

**VERSE 7.**—“Upon a high mountain.” Heretics also, etc., up to the point where they may be trampled by men.

**VERSE 8.**—“And behind the door.” It is as though he said: “You worshiped idols not only on the mountains; you also placed them behind the door, so that when you entered you would see them and worship continually.”

“Because you uncovered yourself beside me.” A metaphor for an adulteress, as above with the prostitute, etc., up to the point where she is exposed to everyone entering.

[Col. 1299C] **VERSE 9.**—“You sent messengers.” So that they might bring distant idols, as though those nearby were not enough. By this he signifies the gods of Babylon and Egypt.

**VERSE 10.**—“You have grown weary in the multitude of your way.” Whoever walks on the royal road does not grow weary. There is one way of truth, which says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). There are many ways of worldly people. Hence: “My ways are not like your ways” (Isa. 40).

**VERSE 13.**—“But the one who places his trust in me.” (ID.) Those who did not worship idols, or who repented after being led into captivity and returned under Zerubbabel and other leaders, worshiped their God in his own place, according to the Hebrew text.

“He will possess your holy mountain”: namely, the law of the Old and New Testaments, for both were given on a mountain. He also invites them to the height of rewards, or to Christ.

**VERSE 14.**—“And I will say”—namely, Christ to the apostles: “I have made a way by preaching well; provide them a path by giving an example through good works; remove obstacles by washing away sins through baptism and removing the worship of idols through preaching.”

**VERSE 15.**—“For thus says.” Having finished his rebuke against Jerusalem, he comes to those who trust in the Lord, for whose return he had commanded that a road be prepared. Hence he begins with praises of God and then shows what he promised to the returning people.

**VERSE 16.**—“For I will not contend forever.” (ID.) I will not preserve my anger forever, nor bring charges against my creature, but I will strike in the present so that I may heal in the future.

“Because the spirit.” Peace, joy, and the life of all, etc., up to the point where the reference is specifically to the Jews.

**VERSE 17.**—“I hid from you,” namely, my help, so that you might desire it more, saying: “Show us your face, and we shall be saved” (Ps. 79).

“He went away.” (ID.) Understanding this, someone said: “All day long I went about mourning” (Ps. 37).

**VERSE 19.**—“I created.” It is as though he said: “I fulfilled in deed the liberation from captivity that I promised through Jeremiah after seventy years.”

“I created the fruit of the lips: peace.”

**VERSE 20.**—“But the wicked.” Above he spoke about those who repented in captivity and were therefore liberated, and about those who believed after the Ascension. Here he speaks specifically about those who remained in their unbelief.

## CHAPTER LVIII

**VERSE 1.**—“Cry aloud.” (JEROME.) The Lord speaks to the prophets or apostles, after the preceding chapter has ended with peace being announced to the righteous and no rest to the wicked.

“Like a trumpet.” (ID.) Where he addresses the apostles, etc., up to the point where sinful Israel, dead through sin, may hear its crimes.

“To my people.” It is as though he said: “Let them see what sort of Father they have lost—the one who still calls sinners his people.”

**VERSE 2.**—“As though.” This means: “Why should I not hear them as I hear those who practice righteousness in the Church, living justly and piously and confessing Christ as true God and true man?”

“They ask.” (ID.) Another rashness of the Jews: as though they were confident in a good conscience, they demand a just judgment, according to the statement: “Judge me, Lord, for I have walked in my innocence.”

**VERSE 3.**—“Why have we fasted?” They have forgotten the ancient story: the Lord did not look upon Cain’s offerings because he did not rightly share with his brother, toward whom he begrudged love before God.

“Behold, on the day.” A fast acceptable to God consists not only in abstaining from food but from every unlawful thing.

“You exact.” Whoever exacts from one who has nothing does violence to God.

**VERSE 4.**—“Do not fast as you have done up to this day.” So that he will not appear to reject fasting, he teaches how one ought to fast.

**VERSE 5.**—“Can such a fast be?”

**VERSE 6.**—“Bonds.” (ID.) We understand these as sins, etc., up to the point where he says: “Do not despise the members of your own household, of your own seed.”

**VERSE 7.**—“Break your bread for the hungry.” (ID.) We break bread for the hungry, etc., up to the point where he speaks of the soul’s satiety.

“And your flesh.” (ID.) In every kind of need, recognize your neighbor as like yourself, considering that you are mortal and subject to suffering.

**VERSE 8.**—“Your light.” Just as the morning light dissolves darkness, so the light of truth drives away errors.

[Col. 1301A] “Righteousness.” Christ, who justifies everyone, will go before you into glory.

“And the glory of the Lord will gather you,” that is, will receive you to himself—he who said: “Where I am, there my servant will be also” (John 12).

**VERSE 9.**—“To extend the finger.” To point out and slander one’s neighbors. That is: not only must you refrain from thinking and doing these things, but you must not slander.

**VERSE 11.**—“A watered garden”: the paradise of delight that the Lord God planted at the beginning, namely the Church. The fountain in the midst is Christ, whose waters of spiritual teaching do not fail and irrigate the Church. This is what follows: “You will be like a watered garden,” O faithful one, or O Church.

“Like a fountain.” You will be made like Christ, your head.

[Col. 1301B] **VERSE 12.**—“They shall be built.” (Jerome.) The Jews refer this to the restoration that took place under Zerubbabel and Jesus the high priest, or to that which they foolishly imagine will occur at the end. It is better to refer these words to the Church.

“Foundations.” (The same.) The apostles, prophets, and their like. Hence: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Psalm 86). The foundation, however, in the singular is Christ; hence: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus” (1 Corinthians 3).

“Of iniquities,” or alternatively, “into rest,” that is, the paths of error into rest or true peace.

**VERSE 14.**—“Of the earth.” Of the living, which is above, not below; hence Lot is told: “Save yourself on the mountain.”

[Col. 1301C] “As an inheritance.” A heavenly inheritance, which I gave to Jacob, whose son you are through faith and action, trampling down vices and sins. For whoever imitates someone is called that person’s son.

## CHAPTER 59

**VERSE 2.**—“But your iniquities.” He shows why they were not heard and why they were led into captivity.

**VERSE 3.**—“His hands.” (Jerome.) He explains the iniquities in detail, and so forth, up to their finally crying out against the Son of God: “His blood be upon us and upon our children.”

**VERSE 4.**—“They have conceived.” (The same.) Those who await Antichrist. For the one whom they seek with great labor they will receive in iniquity.

**VERSE 5.**—“Eggs.” (The same.) From an egg comes offspring; from the heart, a plan, from which action proceeds. Thus they broke the eggs when they displayed their evil hearts and poisonous plans in words, saying: “He is deserving of death” (Matthew 26).

“Of asps.” When the asp hears the enchanter’s first utterance, it thrusts one ear into the earth and blocks the other with its tail so that it cannot be enchanted. In the same way the Jews, clinging to earthly things and fearing lest they should lose their place and nation, rejected Christ’s preaching; they were poisoned children of poisonous parents.

“It will burst forth into a basilisk.” From the eggs of asps comes the basilisk, also called the regulus; among the Jews, Antichrist. For from them he will be born, killing many by his breath—that is, by his poisonous speech—as they fly toward their heavenly homeland. For the basilisk kills flying birds by its breath.

**VERSE 9.**—“Therefore.” (The same.) After the accusation, the prophet, speaking in the person of the repentant people, answers what the penitents ought to say.

**VERSE 11.**—“We shall all growl like bears.” The Jews’ meditation and teaching in Sacred Scripture are compared to the growling of a bear and the moaning of a dove, as useless and vain as that growling and moaning. Against those subject to them they rage like bears; against their superiors or equals they moan like doves.

**VERSE 15.**—“Truth in.” (The same.) Christ, who is the way, and so forth, up to the point where Christ’s person is shown: having abandoned him, they followed falsehood.

**VERSE 16.**—“And he saw.” (The same.) Having shown that they repented, he shows that their repentance did not please the Lord, because many repented without a pure heart.

“For there was no man.” In their minds they were all effeminate, as in the statement: “I called, and there was no one who would hear.”

“And he saved for himself.” The Father, namely, through the Son, the nations. “And his righteousness,” or mercy according to the Septuagint, will strengthen the one who wishes to convert—not by merit, but by mercy and righteousness. For it is just that the Creator should spare the repentant creature, which could not be saved by its own merits.

**VERSE 19.**—“And they shall fear who.” Having foretold God’s vengeance upon the Jews through the Romans, he describes the faith of the nations coming from the four regions of the world after hearing the apostles’ preaching.
