“Like a river.” Because he filled the world very quickly through his preaching and faith.

“Whom the Spirit of the Lord.” (The same.) The Holy Spirit, namely, for the redemption of the human race. Hence: “Who was conceived of the Holy Spirit.” And: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him” (Isaiah 11), and so forth.

**VERSE 21.**—“This covenant,” namely, that I should redeem them by the blood of the Son, and that they should observe my commandments, hold fast to me in a proper manner; and this is: “My Spirit, which is in you.”

## CHAPTER 60

**VERSE 1.**—“Arise, be enlightened.” (Jerome.) The Jews refer these words to the time of their Christ, and so forth, up to the point where they might receive the Son of God either for their sake or instead of them.

“Arise.” In the churches, which you killed in the synagogues; arise among the nations, where you fell among the Jews. Arise through confession and through the virtues by which you fell through commerce and through vices; and when you have risen, be enlightened, that is, receive the faith of Christ.

“Light.” Promised to you long beforehand, coming for your redemption; it enlightens every person coming into this world—namely, the one who says: “I am the light of the world” (John 1, 8). You will be enlightened by him if you receive the faith of Christ.

“The glory of the Lord.” For enlightening. The Son, namely; just as the rising sun illuminates the world. As a figure of this, the glory of the Lord was shown to Moses and Solomon, the one when building the tabernacle and the other when building the temple. The resurrection of the dead, the cleansing of the leper, and similar acts were also the glory of the Lord.

**VERSE 2.**—“The earth.” (The same.) The Jews, who love earthly things, to whom it is said: “You shall eat the good things of the earth,” which they understand carnally.

**VERSE 3.**—“Your rising.” (The same.) Since you were born from water and the Holy Spirit, we all walk in the brightness of the rising of the primitive Church, because we have the same faith and are reborn through the same baptism.

**VERSE 4.**—“Lift up your eyes around you.” Comparable is the saying: “Lift up your eyes and see the regions, because they are already white for the harvest” (John 4).

“Your sons.” (Jerome.) Those whom you begot in faith. Hence Paul says: “Through the Gospel I begot you” (1 Corinthians 4). The first believers from the Jews, when the Holy Spirit was given, were in Jerusalem “devout men from every nation under heaven” (Acts 2), or the nations from every part of the world.

“They shall come from afar.” Because through idolatry they were far from God; hence: “You who were far off have been brought near” (Ephesians 2).

[Col. 1303B] “From the side.” (The same.) Some manuscripts have …, up to the point where Jerome’s interpretation does not incline in this direction.

**VERSE 6.**—“Of camels.” The camel is a humped animal that bears burdens. These are the rich, carrying the hump of riches and sins as a burden.

“Dromedaries.” A dromedary, or dromas—for both terms are used—is an animal smaller than a camel but faster. By it are represented the nations running swiftly to the faith.

“Madian and Ephah.” Regions beyond Arabia, abundant in camels and dromedaries, and so forth, up to the point where they offered to the Lord what is represented by frankincense.

**VERSE 7.**—“All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered.” (The same.) The simple, who formerly were darkness and mourning, and so forth, up to the place where the Saracens, descended from his lineage, lived.

[Col. 1303C] “Rams.” Preachers, leaders of the flock, sons of the prophets, who taught that the things the prophets foretold concerning Christ had been fulfilled.

“Nebaioth,” the son of Ishmael; its interpretation is “prophecy.”

“They shall minister to you.” Holy bishops and presbyters, ministers of the Church, administering the body and blood of Christ to the faithful.

**VERSE 8.**—“Who are these?” The prophet marvels at the nations running so quickly to the faith; or this refers to the primitive Church.

“To the windows.” The saints stand at their windows, guarding the five bodily senses, lest death enter souls through them as through windows.

**VERSE 9.**—“Their silver.” That is: “With the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Romans 10).

[Col. 1303D] **VERSE 10.**—“The sons of foreigners.” The leaders of the nations who built churches throughout the world, such as Constantine, who built twelve churches in Rome in honor of the twelve apostles, and many others who constructed numerous churches and supplied what was necessary.

**VERSE 13.**—“The glory of Lebanon.” Lebanon is a mountain adjoining the Promised Land, and so forth, up to the kings and princes who came to the Church.

“Fir trees.” (The same.) The proud—that is, the rich and philosophers. Pride follows riches and knowledge. Cyprian and Hilary, trees lofty in the world, built the Church of God. The diversity of the trees signifies the various orders in the Church. From all these the Church was constructed, distinguished by marvelous beauty.

[Col. 1304A] “The place of my feet.” The Church, in which the apostles, and so forth, up to those who sustain the Church through institutions, miracles, and examples.

**VERSE 14.**—“The city of the Lord.” A city is so called from communion, and so forth, up to the one who would carefully go about and provide assistance.

**VERSE 15.**—“Hated.” By the Jews, because it preached the faith of Christ and destroyed the observances of the law; by the nations, because it brought the one God and asserted that idols were nothing.

“There was no one who passed through you.” Who would pass through you and bless you, and so forth, up to the point where pride is sometimes evil and sometimes good.

**VERSE 17.**—“Bronze instead of wood.” (The same.) Through wood and stone, and so forth, up to others strong in faith, such as Cyprian, and others who are martyrs, like iron.

[Col. 1304B] “Your visitation.” (The same.) Christ, or peaceful apostles and just leaders, so that they may teach and judge correctly.

**VERSE 19.**—“It shall not be.” This concerns the day of judgment. By this chapter we are compelled to refer everything that has been said or is to be said to the final time, because the service of heaven and earth, of the sun and moon, will cease for us, and the Lord himself will be our light forever.

**VERSE 21.**—“The shoot.” (The same.) The angels and all the elect, who fulfill by their works the faith they possess. They are the shoot of the Lord’s planting and the work of his hands, because they were created by him and planted in the Church through faith to glorify their Creator.

**VERSE 22.**—“In its time”: the coming of Christ; or at the appropriate or appointed time. “When the Son of Man sends the angels, and they gather from his kingdom all scandals.”

## CHAPTER 61

**VERSE 1.**—“The Spirit of the Lord.” (Jerome.) Christ according to his humanity, who had said above: “I, the Lord, will gather them in time,” and so forth.

“Because he has anointed me”: with the oil of gladness, the abundance of grace. (The same.) This anointing was completed at baptism, because the Spirit of the Lord descended upon him in the form of a dove and remained in him.

“To announce.” The Septuagint: “To evangelize the poor.”

“Opening,” namely, release; for Symmachus translated it more explicitly in this way.

**VERSE 2.**—“The day of vengeance.” (The same.) Of condemnation, which comes through the Romans, according to the saying: “The day will come,” and: “When you see Jerusalem surrounded by an army,” and so forth.

**VERSE 3.**—“A crown.” When they see that very many of the Jews have believed and have received, in place of mourning garments, an exceedingly pure robe.

“For ashes.” In place of mourning and grief over their fruits; when they see the nations streaming to the faith, they will have the oil of gladness instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of grief.

**VERSE 5.**—“Vinedressers.” (The same.) Evil cultivators of the vineyard, the scribes and Pharisees, of whom it is said: “He will put those evil men to an evil end, and will lease his vineyard to other farmers.”

**VERSE 6.**—“But you.” This concerns preachers from the nations, and so forth, up to those who were priests in the house of the Lord.

**VERSE 7.**—“Their portion.” The Lord’s. Hence the Psalmist says: “The Lord is the portion of my inheritance,” and so forth. No one truly says this who seeks another portion.

**VERSE 8.**—“For I am the Lord.” As though he said: This will be done by the Lord, who loves the justice of the poor and true judgment more than the gifts of the rich, which often come from robbery; nor do those gifts please him any more than a prostitute’s wage or the price of flesh offered in sacrifice, or the sacrifice of a son to the Lord.

“In truth.” So that they may eat the lamb in truth, perform circumcision of the heart, and carry out in truth everything that was given in figure.

“An everlasting covenant.” The eternal Gospel, unlike the Old Testament, which the Gospel succeeds.

**VERSE 9.**—“Their seed.” The faithful, to whom the apostles entrusted the seed of the word that they had received from the Lord.

**VERSE 10.**—“Rejoicing, I shall rejoice in the Lord,” not in the world.

“In garments of salvation”: in virtues, in Christ himself, and so forth, up to the point that the Church is nevertheless one in the head and in the members.

“And as a bride.” He gives examples from another comparison: the first refers to the bridegroom, the following one to the bride.

**VERSE 11.**—“And praise”: its own, and so forth, up to the point where it will render to the Lord the fruit of praise and good works.

## CHAPTER 62

**VERSE 1.**—“For the sake of Zion.” (Jerome.) The prophet, speaking in his own person, is exceedingly joyful because of all that the incarnate Son bestows upon the world. This is the meaning of: “For the sake of Zion I will not be silent,” even though he forbids me to speak and threatens me with death.

“Let a lamp be kindled.” *Lampas* is Greek; *flamma* is Latin. Hence: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” The apostles, set aflame by this, spoke in various languages.

**VERSE 2.**—“A new name.” (The same.) It is customary among the Hebrews to impose new names upon new things, and so forth, up to the similar case of Simon, who afterward became Peter.

**VERSE 3.**—“A crown of glory.” The faithful come from all parts of the world as though forming a crown.

**VERSE 4.**—“You shall not be called.” He addresses the Church composed of both peoples, as though saying: You will not be content with this designation.

[Col. 1305D] **VERSE 5.**—“And he will rejoice,” and so forth. “Therefore a man shall leave father and mother” (Genesis 2; Matthew 19). “This is a great mystery in Christ and in the Church” (Ephesians 5).

**VERSE 6.**—“Upon your walls.” (The same.) The apostles and preachers who fortify the Church; their guardians are the angels. Hence: “Are they not all ministering spirits sent for the sake of those who are to inherit salvation?” (Hebrews 1). Or the walls of the churches are the disciples of the apostles, whose guardians are the apostles themselves.

**VERSE 7.**—“Until he establishes Jerusalem.” This means either that Jerusalem, spread far and wide, should be praised everywhere, or that everywhere it should always praise its Creator.

**VERSE 8.**—“He swore by the Son,” namely, who is the power of God [Col. 1306A] and the wisdom of God. “In his right hand”: in the Son. Hence: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Psalm 103). He is also the arm and strength of the Father; hence: “All things were made through him” (John 1).

“If I give your wheat.” I often gave the Jews’ wheat and wine to their enemies, as is read in the Book of Judges (Judges 6): at harvest time the Midianites would invade and gather their crops. When they were led into captivity, Samaritans were substituted in their place to consume their harvests. But in this passage he understands the food of the Church: virtues and good works, the body and blood of Christ—that is, the praises and works that, when you offered them to idols, demons consumed. After the Son’s coming, however, the Lord took delight in them. The wheat and wine, therefore, the food of the Jews, signified the body and blood of Christ. Hence: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John 6). This is not received today by heretics, pagans, Jews, or enemies of the Church.

**VERSE 10.**—“Through the gates.” The ministers of the Church, who bring others in; or the virtues that lead into heaven, as though from virtue to virtue. “Make the way level”: by removing stumbling blocks and forgiving sins in baptism. “Choose,” or, according to the Septuagint, “cast out,” which means: remove the hardness of unbelief from human hearts; or cast out the reprobate and hard-hearted from the fellowship of the faithful.

**VERSE 11.**—“Say to the daughter of Zion.” Namely, to the primitive Church, which first arose from the Jews. Hence: “The sons of my mother fought against me” (Song of Songs 1). Or according to the saying: “But as many as received him” (John 1), and so forth.

“And they will call him, saying: ‘You are a holy people; you are those redeemed by the Lord God.’” For some manuscripts have this reading.

## CHAPTER 63

**VERSE 1.**—“Who is this?” Some angels, not fully understanding the mystery of the incarnation and passion, see the Lord ascending into heaven with a multitude of angels and holy men, by his own power and without the aid of angels. They marvel at the mystery of the incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension, and at how he opens the kingdom of heaven to himself and to others. Hence they say to the angels accompanying the Lord: “Who is this?” David likewise says: “Who is this King of glory?” (Psalm 23). Augustine, however, appears to say in his exposition of Genesis that all the angels, from the moment of their creation, immediately knew, in contemplating their Creator, whatever he was going to do. Jerome, on the other hand, clearly declares that certain angels did not fully understand until the mystery of the incarnation had been completed.

“From Edom.” Edom (according to Jerome) is derived from the eating of the red lentil, and so forth, up to the victorious one returning from the plundered underworld with his faithful.

“Beautiful in his robe.” “Beautiful” means warm. Hence *formosus*, as though “warm,” because the face becomes red and rosy in color, and thus beautiful.

**VERSE 2.**—“Why then?” (The same.) As though the angels were saying: We have learned, and so forth, up to the point that mercy suits you more than cruelty.

**VERSE 3.**—“Alone.” Samson alone, with his hair cut, is presented against the Philistines; neither an angel, nor an archangel, nor any heavenly spirit is present. In the end, no one of the human race, whether Jew or Gentile, is his helper. He alone fights; he alone conquers.

“I am sprinkled.” (Jerome.) My blood is sprinkled because of their rancor, and so forth, up to the point where the victor’s blood is often sprinkled upon his garments.

**VERSE 5.**—“And there was no one,” and so forth. Hence: “All my friends have abandoned me, and my acquaintances have withdrawn from me like strangers” (Job 19).

“And he saved.” Jerome, writing to Augustine and Alypius, says: To avoid the impiety of Sabellius, we distinguish the three persons explicitly according to their individual properties, not saying that the Father is himself the Son, or that the Son is himself the Father, or that the Holy Spirit is himself either of them, but that the person of the Father is distinct from the person of the Son and the person of the Holy Spirit. For we confess not merely the names, [Col. 1307B] but the properties of the names.

**VERSE 7.**—“Mercies.” (Jerome.) The prophet speaks in the person of the Jewish people, repenting and recognizing the Lord’s mercy.

**VERSE 9.**—“He was not afflicted.” (The same.) The voice that says, and so forth, up to: “There is no helper except Michael, your prince, who stands for the sons of my people” (Daniel 10).

“And the angel.” (The same.) The Septuagint has: “Not a messenger, nor the angel himself, but the Lord saved them.”

**VERSE 10.**—“The Spirit of his Holy One.” That is, of Moses. Hence: “They provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord” (Psalm 105). Or “his Holy One,” Christ, in whom they were unwilling to believe. For the Son of God who redeemed us also freed them from Egypt and the Red Sea.

“The Holy Spirit,” or “his Holy One.” Some manuscripts [Col. 1307C] have “the Holy Spirit,” namely, the one whom he grieves—the one who grieves the spiritual person. Hence: “Whoever touches you is like one who touches the pupil of my eye” (Zechariah 2). Or this refers to the angel sent for their protection, whom they often offended by doing evil.

**VERSE 11.**—“Moses.” Because there is no one else who prays for them.

“Where is he?” The prophet, seeing the rejection, misery, and affliction of his people already impending because of their denial of the Son of God, cries out in compassion, saying: “Where is he?” As though he were saying: Where is the mercy of the Almighty? “Where is he who placed”—namely, in Moses—for when Moses prayed, the Lord took some of his spirit and gave it to the seventy men.

**VERSE 12.**—“Who divided the waters before them.” Or it is said that when Moses struck the sea and divided it into twelve paths, while the others hesitated, the tribe of Judah entered; for this reason it obtained royal dignity.

**VERSE 14.**—“The Spirit of the Lord.” An angel, namely; hence: “My angel will go before you” (Exodus 14). “Spirit” is the name of a nature; “angel” is the name of an office.

**VERSE 15.**—“Look down from heaven and see.” The Lord is wholly and always everywhere; hence: “I fill heaven and earth” (Jeremiah 23). Nevertheless, he is said to have a seat in heaven, according to: “Heaven is my throne” (Isaiah 66), because his will is especially done in the heavenly angels and righteous human beings, whose manner of life is in heaven.

“Where is your jealousy?” and so forth. As though he said: Because we sinned and you began to hate us, your jealousy withdrew; when it withdrew, strength also departed, and the affection of paternal compassion was overcome.

[Col. 1308A] **VERSE 16.**—“Abraham did not know.” (Jerome.) As though he said: Because we offended you, and so forth, up to the point that he should not forget his sons, lest through them the name of God be blasphemed among the nations.

**VERSE 17.**—“Why do you make us wander?” When Paul writes to the Corinthians, addressing the people of a single city because of the variety of its inhabitants—both saints and sinners—he sometimes praises and sometimes reproves them. So too this chapter, woven from the prayer of a people beseeching God, sometimes praises the Lord and sometimes accuses him, according to Tichonius’s second rule, which concerns the body of the Lord.

**VERSE 19.**—“As at the beginning.” (Jerome.) Before you called us, and so forth, up to the point where they will not be called the people of God—Christians, namely, by Christ.

## CHAPTER 64

[Col. 1308B] **VERSE 1.**—“Would that you would tear open.” (Jerome.) In his own person, and so forth, up to the similar statement of David: “He bowed the heavens and came down” (Psalm 17).

**VERSE 2.**—“The waters would burn.” (Symmachus.) May the waters of the sea burn with fire. This means that the peoples of the world would be inflamed with the fire of charity. Hence: “I have come to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I desire except that it burn?” (Luke 12). Thus your name, which is Christ Jesus, would become known to your enemies, namely, the Jews.

**VERSE 3.**—“We shall not endure.” We Jews will not endure it, but will blaspheme, saying: “By Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out demons” (Matthew 12). The prophet says this in the person of unbelievers.

“You descended.” As though, with his prayers heard, he said: “You descended,” and so forth.

“Mountains.” Their power having been taken away: “Now the ruler of this world will be cast out” (John 12). And it is said to the Jews: “The kingdom of God will be taken away from you” (Matthew 21), namely, Sacred Scripture, all glory, and all dignity.

**VERSE 4.**—“From of old.” From this passage Paul takes testimony when writing to the Corinthians, expressing not word for word but the sense.

“Eye.” Because he is neither body nor color. The Apostle says that it has not ascended into the human heart, because he is greater, and the heart ought to be directed toward him. For he prepared himself: knowledge of himself, knowledge of the Holy Trinity. Hence: “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). No one can see him; hence: “No one has ever seen God” (John 1).

**VERSE 5.**—“Behold, you,” and so forth. In the person of the unbelieving people, [Col. 1308D] who, wishing to pass over to the truth of the Gospel, preferred repentance on their lips, although they did not possess it in their hearts.

**VERSE 6.**—“Like a menstruating woman,” and so forth. *Mene* is Hebrew for “moon” in Latin; hence menstruating women, who customarily undergo a flow of blood each month. At such times men ought to abstain from them. For then children are conceived who are condemned in their limbs—blind, lame, leprous, and the like—so that, because the parents were not ashamed to unite in the bedchamber, their sins may be exposed to all and openly reproved in their children.

“Wind.” A disturbance of the air, as in: “He commanded the winds and the sea” (Matthew 8). Or the Holy Spirit: “The coming of a mighty Spirit” (Acts 1). Here “wind” is used figuratively for the Holy Spirit. Or the temptation of demons and evil people, as in: “The rivers came and the winds blew” (Matthew 7); and this is like wind.

**VERSE 8.**—“And now, Lord.” As though he said: If we consider our merits, we must despair; but if we consider your mercy—you who chastise every son whom you receive—we dare to pour out prayers, for you are our Father. “The work of your hands.” As though he said: Look upon your work, not upon our merits. The correct confession of the mystery of the Trinity is ignorance of knowledge.

**VERSE 9.**—“Do not be angry, Lord.” This means: We do not avoid anger, nor do we seek any further patience by which we store up anger for ourselves on the day of vengeance; but we ask that you not be angry with us excessively—that is, that at the time of vengeance you not remember our iniquity.

**VERSE 10.**—“Zion is desolate.” Zion and Jerusalem signify the same thing here: the temple and the city, which once were the watchtower of virtues and the vision of peace. But after the Jewish people denied their king and added: “We have no king but Caesar” (John 19), Jerusalem was deserted by God. Hence: “Your house will be left to you desolate” (Luke 13), and: “Arise, let us go from here” (John 14). In the temple, voices were also heard, as ecclesiastical history relates: “Let us depart from these dwellings.”

**VERSE 11.**—“The house.” Allegorically, the house of God is the Church, and each faithful soul, which is sometimes corrupted by the fires of lust and avarice.

## CHAPTER 65

[Col. 1309C] **VERSE 1.**—“They sought,” and so forth. (Jerome.) The Son responds to this, and so forth, up to: “And the sons of foreigners have lied to me” (Psalm 17).

**VERSE 2.**—“I spread out my hands.” (The same.) Praying for them on the cross, and so forth, up to the point that they nevertheless always remained unbelieving.

**VERSE 3.**—“A people provoking me to anger.” (The same.) Allegorically, every heretic provokes God to anger, and so forth, up to the point where they construct it four-square and strengthen the cut side of the dust with lines.

**VERSE 4.**—“In shrines.” Shrines are so called from *delere*, “to destroy,” because people thought that the soul was cleansed there. Or because pools were nearby, where the priest and the victim were washed.

Allegorically. (Jerome.) Heretics in the memorials of their teachers, and so forth, up to the point that anyone unlike them is detested as lost.

**VERSE 5.**—“In my fury.” We must understand “fury,” “forgetfulness,” “anger,” and “repentance” in God in the same way as the hands, feet, eyes, ears, and other limbs that he is said to possess. This does not mean that he is subject to the disturbances which he extinguishes in us; rather, through our words we understand God’s disposition toward us.

**VERSE 6.**—“I will not be silent.” The one who said above: “I was silent, I kept still, I was patient,” now says: “I will not be silent,” that is, I will no longer spare them or endure their iniquities.

**VERSE 7.**—“The iniquities of the fathers,” and so forth. That is, you will be punished not only for your own sins but also for the iniquities of the fathers whom you imitated. Otherwise, the son does not bear the iniquity of the father.

“Who sacrificed upon the mountains.” When they worshiped golden calves at Bethel and Dan. The heretic likewise, despising the simplicity of the Church, sacrifices upon the mountains and reproaches God by despising his commandments.

**VERSE 8.**—“How?” (Jerome.) As though he said: Because of the evil I will not destroy the good. But how? and so forth. For he had said that Israel would perish.

**VERSE 9.**—“From Jacob a seed.” The seed of Jacob and Judah—the apostles—possessing mountains, namely, other believers who excel in virtues. Hence: “Unless the Lord of hosts had left us a seed, we would have become like Sodom” (Romans 9).

“My holy mountains.” The Septuagint has: “My mountain,” namely Christ, who is the mountain of mountains. For the mountains are the apostles, who, coming from the Jews, possessed Christ, upon whom they were founded.

“And they shall inherit.” [Col. 1310B] (Jerome.) Hence: “The seed of Abraham, his servants; the sons of Jacob, his chosen ones.” Whoever are still seed, and so forth, up to: “You did not receive the spirit of slavery again in fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption as sons of God” (Romans 9).

**VERSE 10.**—“The plains.” (The same.) Others have “forests.” Hence: “The Lord will reveal the dense places of the forests” (Psalm 18), so that robbers may cease to lurk there and beasts and poisonous animals may pass into the Church of God.

“Into sheepfolds.” Another translation has “Sharon,” a region between Joppa, Lydda, and Jamnia, fertile and rich in pasture but infested with robbers. Hence its interpretation is “a valley pouring out blood.”

“And the valley of Achor.” There Achor, the son of Carmi, perished with his entire household after stealing from the spoils of Jericho. Because he troubled the people and perished there, the place is called the valley of Achor, that is, of trouble or tumult. By it the Gentile world is signified, as also by Sharon, which is interpreted as “a valley pouring out blood”: filled with the shedding of blood, it remained amid the tumult and confusion of vices. But the valley of Achor was changed into sheepfolds or sheep pens, and into a resting place for cattle—that is, into churches and the repose of preachers and other faithful people, represented by cattle and flocks of sheep.

“Cattle.” Preachers, who arm and defend the Church. For cattle are so called from “arming.”

**VERSE 11.**—“But you who have forsaken,” and so forth. Allegorically, all who abandon the Church and forget God’s holy mountain, surrendering themselves to spirits of error or to the unclean teachings of demons, prepare a table for Fortune. Believing that nothing pertains to God, but that everything is governed either by the course of the stars or by the changes of fortune, they will be handed over to eternal punishments, so that none of them can escape.

“A table for Fortune.” (Jerome.) For the Egyptian goddess, for whom at the end of the year they prepared a table filled with every kind of food and cups mixed with mead, either because she had provided a fortunate year or because she was expected to provide one in the future.

**VERSE 12.**—“I called.” Through the prophets, saying: “Turn to me, and you shall be saved” (Isaiah 45). And through myself: “Repent” (Matthew 3). And elsewhere: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened” (Matthew 11).

**VERSE 13.**—“Behold, my servants.” (Jerome.) As though he said: Not only will you fall by the sword, and so forth, up to: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears.”

**VERSE 15.**—“And you shall leave your name.” So that some, affirming this, may say: If I do otherwise, may what happened to the Jews, who were killed by the sword of the Romans, happen to me. Or in this way: I swear by the God in whom the Jews once believed. Or because God was their oath, as Christians now swear when compelled by necessity: “The Lord lives,” namely.

“And he will kill you.” So that you may no longer have him who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 14). Nor will you be called “circumcision,” but “mutilation.”

**VERSE 16.**—“Because of oblivion.” (Jerome.) So that they may not remember idols, and so forth, up to the possibility that even in the future the memory of their former way of life will be completely erased.

[Col. 1311B] **VERSE 18.**—“For behold.” From angels and human beings, namely, one Church; and they will exult and rejoice, so that I, who created them, may exult and rejoice in them.

“Exultation.” Of the whole earth, so that what was formerly the joy of the Only-begotten may become new gladness for all nations.

“Joy.” This may be understood either after the resurrection or after baptism, in the first resurrection. This refers to the general resurrection, when all will rise in the perfect age. And this is the meaning of: “There shall not be,” and so forth.

**VERSE 20.**—“A child of a hundred years,” and so forth. Namely, one who, although he lived a long time, lived childishly, serving vices. Gregory explains this as follows: “A child of a hundred years,” and “a sinner of a hundred years.” The child’s life is prolonged so that he may be corrected from childish deeds; but if he is not restrained from committing sin even by the length of time, that very longevity of life, which he received through God’s mercy, increases for him the accumulation of his curse.

**VERSE 21.**—“Houses.” (Jerome.) Virtues, for which they will rest in heavenly places, and so forth, up to: Many saints build houses but do not dwell in them.

**VERSE 22.**—“For according to.” (The same.) Just as Christ, and so forth, up to: “It is a tree of life to those who grasp it,” namely, wisdom, which is Christ.

**VERSE 23.**—“The seed of the blessed.” The apostles and other teachers, in preaching or in other works, like the Jews, because they will receive an eternal reward, since they will come with rejoicing, carrying their sheaves (Psalm 125).

“Grandchildren.” Those whom their sons begot in faith, [Col. 1311D] such as Mark, the disciple of Peter, and Luke, the son of Paul.

**VERSE 24.**—“Before they call.” In disturbance and anguish of mind, but in joy and gladness. Hence: “For what is our hope or joy or crown of glory? Is it not you?” (2 Thessalonians 2), and so forth.

**VERSE 25.**—“The wolf.” The wolf is Saul, that is, the persecutor, of whom it is said: “Benjamin is a ravenous wolf” (Genesis 49).

“The lamb.” Those who follow the Lamb in white garments wherever he goes. Concerning them Peter is told: “Feed my lambs” (John 21).

“And the lion and the ox shall eat.” A man eloquent and powerful in the world, rejecting philosophical eloquence, will eat straw—that is, the usefulness and surface of history—with the oxen, namely, the preachers of the Church. Lions eat this until, through many labors, they reach the depth of the mystery, as Augustine, Cyprian, and others did.

“They shall not kill.” Having laid aside their fierceness, either in the present or in the future. And this is the meaning of: “On every mountain,” and so forth.

The Jews understand this carnally, saying that in the time of their Christ there will be such peace and security for them that wolves and lambs, lions and oxen, serpents and human beings will dwell together and eat together without harming one another—those who live in the temple and on the holy mountain. From this it follows that everyone else will be killed. But this is shown to be false by these words: “Thus says the Lord: Heaven is my throne, and the earth is the footstool of my feet,” and so forth. Nevertheless, the Jews understand this carnally.

## CHAPTER 66

[Col. 1312B] **VERSE 1.**—“Heaven.” All the saints whose manner of life is in heaven. Hence: “The soul of the righteous is the seat of God.”

“Heaven is my throne.” As though he said: Do not think that these things are to be fulfilled literally.

“What is this?” As though he said: Do you think that I am confined to a place and dwell only in the temple? But what is this house? and so forth.

**VERSE 2.**—“To whom,” and so forth. Once the earthly altar and temple built by human hands have been removed, the sacrifices of the Jews will rightly be removed as well, lest they say: We are not so foolish as to think that God can be confined to this place; rather, in a separate place we sacrifice victims for the glorification of God, as the law commands.

**VERSE 3.**—“The one who sacrifices an ox.” (Jerome.) As though he said: Your sacrifice does not please me after the sacrifice of the true offering, in whose shadow I granted those sacrifices to you and forbade you to sacrifice to idols.

“A dog.” Concerning this Moses says: “You shall not bring into the house of your God the payment of a prostitute or the price of a dog” (Deuteronomy 23). Dog and prostitute are properly joined, because they are similarly lustful.

“They chose in their ways.” Not according to my will, from the time when the true Lamb was sacrificed. Hence: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5).

**VERSE 4.**—“And the things they feared.” The Romans. Hence: “The Romans will come and take away our place and nation” (John 11). Or famine, pestilence, and captivity.

### Verse 5

**“Those who hate you.”** Because you are not of the world, because you believe in me, because you bear my name—for Christians are named from Christ. Hence: “For the Jews had already agreed that if anyone confessed Christ, he should be expelled from the synagogue” [Col. 1312D] (John 9). **“May he be glorified.”** (Jerome.) That is: “May he appear glorious,” etc., up to “with great power and majesty and might,” or even in the present time.

### Verse 6

**“The voice of the people from the city.”** When the Roman army arrived, according to Josephus, the Jews were divided into three factions contending for supremacy. Some set up one leader for themselves, others another. One faction of the people and the priests held the Temple; the citadel and royal palace were held by a faction of the people and the leaders; the remaining part of the city was held by the third faction, consisting chiefly of the common people. Thus they fought outside against the enemies and inside against their fellow citizens.

When the Romans therefore broke into the city, the voice of the people lamenting from the city was heard—the voice of the priests and of those who were with them in the Temple. The voice of the Lord was also heard in the Romans rejoicing, who had come at God’s command; through the Romans, he was rendering recompense to his enemies, namely the Jews. [Col. 1313A]

### Verse 7

**“Before she was in labor.”** (Jerome.) Not gradually, nor after a long time, etc., up to: “And David,” he says, “the Hope of all the ends of the earth and of the distant sea” (Psalm 74).

**“A male child.”** A strong people, concerning whom Stephen and Paul speak—the latter saying: “Who will separate us from the love of Christ?” (Romans 8).

### Verse 8

**“In one day.”** The Apostle begot his children all together as though on one day, because they were in Christ, who is light and day, and in the unity of faith.

### Verse 9

**“Shall I.”** As though he were saying: “I, who created all human beings [Col. 1313B] out of nothing, shall create for myself from all the nations one Church, which is built of living stones.”

### Verse 10

**“Rejoice,” etc.** (Jerome.) O angels, O apostles, who are sorrowful over the destruction of the unbelieving Jews: rejoice, having been consoled by the faith and salvation of the nations from whom the Church is built.

### Verse 11

**“That you may suck.”** The faith of the simple, and, delighted by it, their good works. The faith of believers is milk and food for preachers. Hence Christ also says: “I have food to eat of which you do not know” (John 4).

**“And be filled.”** A woman who has given birth to a male child does not lack an abundance of milk for raising the nation and the little ones who were born together, so that she might provide them with the two breasts of the Old and New Testaments. It should be noted that the little ones need the milk of consolation, as though they were still living in the flesh. But those who, after the milk of consolation [Col. 1313C], have advanced to solid food will abound in the delights of truth and in the glory of complete knowledge.

**“That you may milk.”** The holy Church, one in all things, has milk in some—that is, simple faith and works. In others it overflows with complete glory: namely, an abundance of spiritual gifts, knowledge of divinity, and knowledge of Christ’s humanity. Holy preachers therefore delight in all things, as though drawing from some one thing and from others another.

**“From the breast.”** From the apostles and preachers, toward the gifts of the Holy Spirit, or toward the teaching of the Old and New Testaments. For what they preach, they demonstrate by their works, so that they may thus provide guidance to their hearers.

### Verse 12

**“They shall fondle you.”** (Jerome.) Supporting you and giving you milk, like the one who says: “I beseech you, [Col. 1313D] brothers, by the mercy of God, to present your hearts” (Romans 12), etc. And: “I beseech you as sojourners” (1 Peter 2), etc.

### Verse 13

**“As.”** Almighty God, as merciful and compassionate, compares himself now to an eagle, now to a hen, now to a gently murmuring sea, so that he may at least attract you by caresses.

Just as an eagle prepares its nest in inaccessible crags, so that access to it may be open to no one, and, according to the natural philosophers, places in its midst an amethyst stone—which repels every poison—along with certain other secrets of nature, in order to keep away serpents, so he himself places a stone in our hearts, that is, his faith—namely, himself, who is the stone cut without hands from the mountain—by which all the poisons of the devil are driven away.

[Col. 1314A] For the eagle loves its young more than all beasts, cattle, livestock, and birds, as those who have written about the natures of living creatures say.

### Verse 14

**“You shall see.”** O apostles, you shall see a multitude of the living coming to the faith. Your heart shall rejoice over their salvation, and your bones—that is, your virtues—shall sprout in the hearts of others, producing the fruit of good will and good works. For just as the body is supported by bones, so the soul is sustained by virtues.

**“And your bones.”** On the day of judgment your bodies shall revive in immortality, so that just as in the present life you served God in body and soul, so in body and soul you may receive rewards.

**“He shall be known.”** In the judgment, that is, the Son shall be known to the good as gracious and gentle, and to the impious as avenger and strong—the Son who is the hand of the Father, through whom he accomplishes all things.

[Col. 1314B] ### Verse 16

**“In fire.”** This fire will be eternal for the wicked whom it will envelop and bring to eternal punishment; by it whatever in the good requires purification will be purified.

**“His chariots.”** Chariots, because then he will triumph and defeat all his adversaries—not because he requires the service of angels.

**“The Lord in fire.”** In judgment. Or, his discernment and justice are displayed when he separates the good from the evil by just judgment, not by power.

**“With the sword.”** (Jerome.) The sentence of judgment. Hence Amos: “By the sword of God all sinners shall perish,” etc. (Amos 9). For when he gives each person what he deserves, all will recognize him as a just judge and will praise his judgment.

### Verse 17

**“Those who sanctified themselves.”** (The same author.) In their own opinion, at springs and in baptisms, etc., up to: “Yet [Col. 1314C] this is said to their shame, because they are not even ashamed to do it.”

**“Those who sanctified themselves.”** According to the tropological sense, we can say that all who are lovers of pleasure rather than of God are said to be sanctified in gardens and on thresholds, according to the Septuagint, because they are unable to enter into the mysteries of truth and to eat the food of piety. For they are not holy in body and spirit, nor do they eat the flesh of Christ so as to possess eternal life. “For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5), and he is eaten not outside, but in one house and within it.

**“In gardens.”** Not in the sacrifice of the red heifer, which was prescribed in the Law.

### Verse 18

**“But I.”** As though he were saying: “Therefore I come to judgment with all nations and languages, so that I may judge together all their works and thoughts [Col. 1314D], and give them everything they deserve.”

**“Languages.”** (Jerome.) Which, according to the apostles, are not only those of human beings, etc., up to: “According to this passage: ‘My sword is drunk in heaven, and it has descended even to the earth’” (Isaiah 34).

### Verse 19

**“And I shall set a sign among them.”** The sign of the cross, of Christianity, and of salvation. Those marked with it are not killed in Ezekiel; by it the doorposts in Egypt were marked and the Israelites were saved. Ahaz refused to ask for this sign, which Isaiah then introduces: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive,” etc.

**“And I shall send some of them.”** This may seem contradictory, since judgment was mentioned first, yet the passage returns to the first coming, when the apostles are sent to the nations and hear: “Go, teach all nations” (Matthew 28). But the day of judgment [Col. 1315A] is foretold so that, terrified by fear of future punishment, people may receive the coming of the Savior and the preaching of the apostles who are to be sent beforehand.

**“To the sea.”** That is, to the world, whose parts he next names: Africa, etc.—the southern region, namely the area in which Africa lies.

### Verse 20

**“On horses.”** (Jerome.) Those who are brought are people who believe swiftly and run quickly to the faith.

**“On chariots and litters.”** Philosophers, namely those shining with learning and moral uprightness. Hence they came more quickly to the teaching of the four Evangelists, and, lifted up by the four principal virtues, attained heavenly things in mind.

**“On mules.”** On which David and Solomon are read to have sat. Those who are sterile with respect to the filth of the world serve the Lord, who is signified by them, as though they were tame.

**“On wagons.”** The Septuagint has “covered vehicles”; others have it simply. These are those to whom it is said: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6).

[Col. 1315B] **“How.”** As though he were saying: “With what great joy the apostles bring your brothers, whose offerings are faith, hope, charity, pure prayer, good works, and so forth—pure vessels, hearts and undefiled bodies.”

**“Let them bring.”** This is what they did three times a year according to the Law: at Passover, at Pentecost, and at the Feast of Tabernacles. Hence: “You shall not appear before me empty-handed” (Exodus 23).

**“The house of the Lord.”** The holy temple of God is what you are (1 Corinthians 3). And elsewhere: “You are the temple of God, and the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (2 Corinthians 6).

### Verse 22

**“For as the heavens.”** As though he were saying: “Just as these things, renewed, will remain immovable forever, so your seed, O apostles, renewed and freed from all corruption [Col. 1315C] of the flesh, will reign with me forever.”

**“For as,” etc.** (Jerome.) These words up to the end of the book pertain to the day of judgment.

[Col. 1316A] ### Verse 23

**“From month to month.”** *Mēnē* (Greek), in Latin *luna* (“moon”), whence *neomenia*, as though meaning “new moon.” From *mēnē* comes *mensis* (“month”), among those who determine and begin the opening of the calendar not according to the course of the sun and the differing lengths of the months, but according to the moon’s circuit, as the Hebrews do.

By “month,” therefore, the moon is understood; and by the moon—which now waxes and, as the natural philosophers say, receives from the sun the light that it does not possess—the Church is understood. Concerning her it is said: “He shall remain with the sun and before the moon” (Psalm 71). And elsewhere: “Fair as the moon, chosen as the sun” (Song of Songs 6). This is what is meant by “from month to month.”

### Verse 24

**“And they shall go out.”** As though to see—not in terms of place, but by understanding or manifest vision—so that they may be inflamed all the more toward the praise of God.

**“And they shall see.”** [Col. 1316B] (Jerome.) It is no wonder if the saints, already immortal, see the reprobate, since the prophets, while still mortal, were deemed worthy to see all these things.

**“Corpses.”** Because they will fall into eternal damnation; in this sense demons too may be called corpses, just as human beings are also called such. Hence: “An enemy has done this” (Matthew 13).

**“Their worm.”** Either a material worm or that of conscience. Hence: “As the moth eats clothing, and the worm gnaws wood, and fire devours timber, so grief and sorrow torment a man’s heart” (Proverbs 25).

**“To satiety.”** That is, because the good will see them separated from themselves by God’s just judgment, deprived of the power with which they raged against the good, and suffering such vengeance from God that they will desire no greater. Those who now say: “How long, Lord, will you not avenge our blood [Col. 1316C]?” (Revelation 6) will be satisfied. They will also be filled with their own blessedness, giving thanks when they see the ineffable punishment of the wicked.
